papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow-based generative models support high-quality image, audio, and video synthesis. Sampling can require dozens to hundreds of denoiser evaluations, with each pass becoming more expensive as resolution, video length, or model size increases. This cost affects latency and energy use in interactive and edge applications. We examine four approaches to accelerating inference: distillation, consistency training, sampling methods, and denoiser design. We express training objectives, transition maps, and numerical updates in a common notation to compare changes to the learning target, the sampling trajectory, and the work performed within each denoiser pass. Published image and video benchmarks illustrate the quality--cost trade-offs of one- and few-step generation, the interaction between solvers and timestep schedules, the effect of feature caching, and the difference between first-frame latency and sustained streaming throughput. We close with open problems in visual-native architectures and post-compression distillation, solver-aware few-step training, and semantic trajectory alignment with factorized distribution matching.
bullets: Diffusion sampling can require dozens to hundreds of denoiser evaluations, creating latency and energy costs that grow with resolution, video length, and model size.
The survey compares distillation, consistency training, sampling methods, and denoiser design using a common framework for learning targets, sampling trajectories, and per-step computation.
Published image and video benchmarks examine one- and few-step quality–cost trade-offs, solver and timestep-schedule interactions, feature caching, and streaming performance.
Open questions include visual-native architectures, post-compression distillation, solver-aware few-step training, and semantic trajectory alignment.

papers.abstract: Mamba is a neural network architecture that reduces computational complexity, and has been shown to be effective for 3D medical image segmentation. However, existing models still remain computationally expensive. We propose compressing Mamba by distillation while achieving competitive performance. Specifically, we demonstrate compression of a 139M-parameter SegMamba-V2 teacher into a lightweight TinyUNet3D student with about 0.96M parameters, achieving about 145$\times$ compression with a performance drop of just over one Dice point. We further investigate the utility of knowledge distillation in a range of data-labeling scenarios under identical experimental settings, and show that its advantage is most prominent when labeled data is scarce. To demonstrate the generalizability of our approach, experiments are conducted on three datasets: BraTS 2023, MSD Spleen and MSD Hippocampus. The code for TinyUNet3D is publicly available at: https://github.com/2802990u/tinyunet3d-dist-kd.
bullets: Compresses a 139M-parameter SegMamba-V2 teacher into a roughly 0.96M-parameter TinyUNet3D student.
Achieves about 145× parameter compression with a performance decrease of just over one Dice point.
Evaluates knowledge distillation across different labeling scenarios, finding its advantage is strongest with limited labeled data.
Demonstrates the approach on BraTS 2023, MSD Spleen, and MSD Hippocampus.
TinyUNet3D code is publicly available.

papers.abstract: Mamba has the capability to capture global context in linear time for 3D medical image segmentation. However, existing methods employ Mamba with full-width directional scans at every resolution, keeping the model large (64-138M parameters and high FLOPs). We propose Grouped Multi-Directional (GMD) Mamba, a lightweight network based on the GMD scan that divides input channels $C$ into groups $G$ and flattens each group in different directions in one pass. This gives multi-directional context at $O(C^2/G)$ instead of $O(K \cdot C^2)$, where $K$ is the number of scan directions. Additionally, we employ Mamba only at the deepest encoder stages, resulting in 19.2M parameters. On BraTS2023, it achieves the best average Dice of 92.0% and the lowest HD95 of 2.7 at $\sim$1/7 the parameters of SegMamba-V2. For model validation, we also ran experiments on the MSD Spleen dataset, achieving competitive performance. The implementation details and code are publicly available at https://github.com/2802990u/GMD-Mamba.
bullets: Existing 3D Mamba segmenters use full-width scans at every resolution, leading to large models and high computational cost.
GMD scanning splits channels into groups and processes them in different directions in one pass, reducing scan complexity to O(C²/G).
Mamba is restricted to the deepest encoder stages, producing a 19.2M-parameter network.
On BraTS2023, GMD-Mamba reports 92.0% average Dice and 2.7 HD95, using about one-seventh the parameters of SegMamba-V2.
It also achieves competitive results on the MSD Spleen dataset; broader scope is limited to the reported datasets.

papers.abstract: DeepSearch LLM agents repeatedly search and carry retrieved sources into subsequent reasoning steps. This expanding context increases token consumption and latency, although many results do not contribute to later reasoning. We propose Query-Relevant Attention Entropy (QRAE), an online context compression method that uses sparse evidence-assessment heads to decide which intact retrieved chunks should persist across reasoning steps. It scores bounded candidate batches through paired prefills: a query-free control suppresses shared attention responses, while normalized entropy measures the breadth of the positive response within each chunk. High-scoring chunks enter a persistent evidence whitelist and are included in the reasoning context. Uncertain chunks remain outside the reasoning context but are retained in a candidate cache, where they can be retrieved for later reevaluation. QRAE requires neither an additional generative compression pass nor modification of the attention operator. Across multiple DeepSearch benchmarks and reasoning models, QRAE improves task success by an average of 2.35 percentage points and reduces end-to-end latency and reported token usage by an average of 30% and 45%, respectively. These benefits generalize to a model with nearly 100B parameters.
bullets: Targets context growth in iterative DeepSearch agents, where many retrieved sources are not useful for later reasoning.
Uses sparse evidence-assessment heads and paired prefills to score candidate chunks via normalized attention-response entropy.
Persists high-scoring chunks in an evidence whitelist; uncertain chunks remain in a cache for possible later reevaluation.
Across multiple benchmarks and reasoning models, it improves task success by 2.35 percentage points on average, while reducing latency by 30% and reported token usage by 45%.
The approach generalizes to a model with nearly 100B parameters and requires no extra generative compression pass or attention-operator changes.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at https://github.com/hustvl/MoLT
authors: Lianghui Zhu, Shijie Wang, Xinggang Wang, Jinze Bai, Bo Wang, Xiang Bai
bullets: Introduces Mixture-of-Loops Attention, which uses keys and values as reusable memory across depths and loops.
MoLT-KV removes same-position cross-loop dependence and supports single-traversal decoding beyond the training loop horizon through loop forcing.
U-MoLT separates memory construction from prediction readout, skipping unnecessary decoder traversals without changing predictions.
Across multiple model scales and settings, U-MoLT improves token efficiency, perplexity, and task accuracy while matching non-looped inference latency in one evaluation.

papers.abstract: While video diffusion models have grown faster and increasingly streamable, the video VAE remains a primary latency bottleneck across interactive generation and editing pipelines. Existing VAEs and their acceleration methods rely mainly on heavy convolutions or full frame attention, and most focus only on decoding, leaving encoding costly for streaming conditional generation and editing. This raises a natural question: Do video VAE encoding and decoding actually require such global spatiotemporal modeling? By analyzing the effective receptive fields of pretrained video VAEs, we find that both encoding and decoding a patch rely almost entirely on its spatial and temporal neighbors. To exploit this strong locality, we introduce LiveVAE, a streaming encoder and decoder built on causal window attention, which cuts per frame compute while keeping the temporal KV cache bounded for streaming. Decoupled encoder/decoder distillation followed by joint finetuning preserves the pretrained latent space, making LiveVAE a drop-in replacement for the original VAE. On MiniMax-H3, LiveVAE achieves 5.2-6.2x faster encoding and 3.0-3.3x faster decoding than the official VAE with higher PSNR. Paired with our dedicated inference infrastructure, LiveVAE pushes the speedup to 13.4x with almost no quality loss. Code and models will be released.
authors: Jiachen An, Sijie Zhao, Le Li, Hongyu Liu, Zhiyuan Li, Tianyu Yang, Xiaoyu Kong, Xunliang Cai, Yong Zhang, Chi-Man Pun, Xiaoming Wei, Xiaodong Cun
bullets: Existing video VAEs are latency bottlenecks, especially for encoding, due to heavy convolutions or global spatiotemporal attention.
Effective receptive-field analysis shows that VAE patches depend mainly on nearby spatial and temporal neighbors.
Causal window attention reduces per-frame computation and keeps the temporal KV cache bounded for streaming.
Decoupled encoder/decoder distillation and joint finetuning enable drop-in replacement with the original VAE.
On MiniMax-H3, LiveVAE delivers 5.2–6.2× faster encoding and 3.0–3.3× faster decoding with higher PSNR; infrastructure raises speedup to 13.4× with nearly no quality loss.

papers.abstract: Processing long videos with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is prohibitively expensive, making informative frame selection essential for accurate video understanding. The default uniform sampling often misses task-relevant keyframes, while recent training-free selectors instead pick frames by how well each one matches the question under an image-text alignment (ITA) score. However, we show that ITA signals correspond poorly with the MLLM's true needs: their rankings correlate weakly with downstream accuracy and are even negatively correlated on over 40% of questions, whereas the MLLM's internal yes/no judgment yields a much stronger signal. We present ProbFaS, a training- and label-free probabilistic pipeline that fuses both signals for key frame selection. ProbFaS treats dense ITA scores as cheap, biased measurements and sparse MLLM judgments as accurate, costly ones, unifying them via co-kriging, a multi-fidelity Gaussian process, to calibrate relevance across all frames. A temporal determinantal point process then selects frames capturing relevance peaks while preserving temporal coverage. Across Video-MME, MLVU and LongVideoBench, ProbFaS is the most accurate among fourteen state-of-the-art training-free selectors and uniform sampling in 13 of 15 settings (8-128 frames), outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 3.1 percentage points. On MLVU and LongVideoBench, 32 ProbFaS frames match or surpass the top baseline at 128 frames and uniform sampling with up to 768 frames.
authors: Tianru Zhang, Mayank Nautiyal, Hugo Eidmann, Prashant Singh, Ekta Vats
bullets: Uniform sampling can miss keyframes, while image-text alignment rankings often poorly reflect the MLLM’s actual needs.
The training- and label-free method fuses dense ITA scores with sparse, more accurate MLLM yes/no judgments using co-kriging.
A temporal determinantal point process selects relevance peaks while maintaining temporal coverage.
Across Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, ProbFaS leads training-free selectors and uniform sampling in 13 of 15 settings.
Using 32 frames, it matches or surpasses top-baseline performance obtained with 128 frames on MLVU and LongVideoBench.

papers.abstract: Vision transformers are strong but costly image encoders for video object segmentation. Training-free token merging cuts compute uniformly across the frame, including on tracked objects. We give a frozen DINOv3 ViT inside a trained Cutie head a training-free focus map: full resolution where the segmenter expects its objects and coarser merging elsewhere. Protecting only the previous frame's mask works on short clips but fails on long videos, where fast motion pushes targets outside the margin and into background merging, locking in loss. Our policy instead takes the union of velocity-shifted and block-matched masks, runs a camera-compensated surprise check, delegates uncertain regions to the compared merger, and falls back to it when all objects are lost. On long videos (LVOS V2 valid, pre-specified protocol, three ViT-S seeds), it beats ALGM 0.98 by +2.76 J&F (95% object CI [+1.22,+4.44]; video-cluster [+0.99,+4.52]) at 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs (0.385 vs. 0.459), sitting 1.0 J&F point below the dense-encoder baseline; at ViT-B the gain over ALGM 0.95 is +3.89 [+2.03,+5.87]. On DAVIS 2017 val it stays within -0.19 J&F of the dense encoder at ViT-S (-0.12 at ViT-B). Controls qualify the result: protecting only the previous mask under ALGM matches or exceeds accuracy at higher FLOPs (0.486), so expectation and surprise mainly reduce counted encoder compute. Practically, lower counted encoder compute did not reduce startup-inclusive mean Cutie step time on a 12-video LVOS sample (3%-8% lower in steady state; an equally engineered ALGM is faster at ViT-S and ViT-B). Section 5.2 separately examines a Cutie permanent-memory schedule and its latency and memory trade-offs. Code: https://github.com/boletoms/focused-cv
bullets: Addresses object loss in long videos when uniform token merging accidentally coarsens fast-moving targets.
Uses velocity-shifted and block-matched mask unions, camera-compensated surprise checks, uncertainty delegation, and an all-objects-lost fallback.
On LVOS V2, improves J&F over ALGM by 2.76 points at ViT-S and 3.89 points at ViT-B, with 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs at ViT-S.
Remains close to dense-encoder accuracy on DAVIS 2017 validation, within 0.19 J&F points at ViT-S.
Reduced counted encoder FLOPs did not translate into lower startup-inclusive mean Cutie step time; latency depends on implementation and regime.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free focus-map token merging for efficient long-video object segmentation.
papers.title: Focus Only on What's Important: Training-Free Focus Maps for Frozen Vision Transformers in Long-Video Object Segmentation
papers.tldr: A training-free focus-map policy for frozen ViTs preserves high-resolution processing around likely objects, improving long-video segmentation accuracy while reducing counted encoder FLOPs, though not necessarily end-to-end latency.

papers.abstract: Underexposure weakens object details, and overexposure obscures boundaries. Spike cameras encode light into high-frequency binary streams. Long-window spike counts give stable appearance cues, while short observations reveal changes in firing rates from sparse measurements. We propose SPIRE, a sensor-grounded semantic-spiking framework for illumination-robust object detection from a single spike stream. SPIRE builds an appearance view from the full packet through detection-oriented illumination adaptation and constructs a sequence of cumulative views from progressively longer prefixes. Each prefix supplies a rate map, an edge map, and a rate difference that tracks changes as spikes accumulate. At selected scales, ANN features and spike-derived initialization jointly set the initial membrane potentials and firing thresholds, allowing semantic cues to shape the responses during temporal encoding. Local spike-count contrasts supervise both branches during training. The residual between measured and ANN-predicted contrasts combines with the spiking features to produce a bounded correction to the fused feature pyramid. On simulated VOC and COCO, SPIRE-D outperforms the strongest baseline by 4.00-5.50 AP50 points across the four under- and overexposure settings. On real PKU-Vidar-DVS recordings, it achieves 67.07 AP50 and 40.10 AP75. SPIRE-D also uses 50.4% fewer MACs than SPFD.

bullets: Addresses object-detail loss under underexposure and boundary loss under overexposure.

Applies contrast supervision and a residual correction to refine the fused feature pyramid.
Outperforms the strongest baseline by 4.00–5.50 AP50 points in simulated settings, reaches 67.07 AP50 and 40.10 AP75 on real recordings, and uses 50.4% fewer MACs than SPFD.

papers.abstract: Existing Knowledge Distillation (KD) methods for semantic segmentation often guide the student to mimic the teacher's structured information generated from an individual image. However, they ignore the global semantic relations across various images that are valuable for KD. This paper proposes Cross-Image Relational KD V2 (CIRKDV2), which focuses on transferring structured pixel-to-pixel, pixel-to-region, and channel-to-channel relations modeled from global images in the dataset. A large teacher network often constructs a well-structured feature space in terms of global contextual dependencies. CIRKDV2 makes the student mimic the better structured semantic relations of the teacher, thus improving the feature representational capability. Beyond relational distillation, we further propose contextual feature distillation by using context aggregation to augment student pixel embeddings to match the semantic level with the teacher. This avoids the semantic gap problem between the teacher and student occurred in traditional feature distillation studies. Experimental results on Cityscapes, ADE20K, Pascal VOC, and COCO-Stuff-164K demonstrate that CIRKDV2 outperforms the state-of-the-art semantic segmentation distillation methods by large margins across various network architectures. Our code and pre-trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/winycg/CIRKD.
authors: Chuanguang Yang, Yu Wang, Chengqing Yu, Xinqiang Yu, Weilun Feng, Yuqi Li, Zhulin An, Libo Huang, Boyu Diao, Fei Wang, Fuzhen Zhuang, Yongjun Xu, Yingli Tian, Tingwen Huang, Yongduan Song

Transfers teacher-modeled pixel-to-pixel, pixel-to-region, and channel-to-channel relations across the dataset.

Experiments on Cityscapes, ADE20K, Pascal VOC, and COCO-Stuff-164K show large-margin improvements over state-of-the-art distillation methods across architectures.

papers.abstract: To avoid the quadratic cost of dense attention over long contexts, models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 have turned natively sparse, and speculative decoding, which matters most where decoding is slowest, increasingly runs on them. Their drafters, however, still keep a context cache of their own, over the whole prompt or a sliding window. Beyond memory, such a cache costs prefill time, prefix-cache hits and decode concurrency. Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway. Both of the drafter's choices are therefore already made, and paid for, by the target: its cache and its selection. We measure how far one selection carries: made a step early, it still covers close to nine tenths of what each later token selects on DS-V4.1-Flash. We present DFly2, a block-parallel drafter that shares the target's sparsity. Each draft layer reads the KV its paired target layer cached (KV sharing), at the positions that layer's indexer selected, a fixed number anywhere in the context (Index sharing). DFly2 thus runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. On DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Hy4~flash, whose sparse attention and architecture differ, it accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe, over general, long-context and agentic benchmarks. Its margin over the stronger baseline widens from 3.9%-10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic ones. At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, its throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K sets.
authors: Hong Liu, Rui Cen, Junhan Shi, Lin Niu, Runzhi Fan, Zhaojing Zhou, Haodi Lei, Jiebin Zhang, Saiyong Yang, Junqiang Zheng, Zhenghai Xue, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu

papers.abstract: Compression based on singular value decomposition (SVD) often requires subsequent fine-tuning or weight correction to mitigate performance degradation. Budget-specific optimization must be repeated for different compression ratios. We introduce LLift, which prepares a pretrained model for SVD compression across ratios without further fine-tuning. LLift fine-tunes a low-rank approximation at a single ratio using the original model as a teacher. We merge the learned updates into the original weights while preserving the complementary components excluded from the training forward pass. We apply SVD to the prepared model's target matrices and reuse the decompositions at different truncation ranks. On LLaMA-7B, we demonstrate accuracy gains across three compression ratios using a single prepared model. The gains extend across model families, model sizes, and SVD compression operators. We analyze gradients and an early training update to provide local evidence that updates learned at one ratio can benefit compression at other ratios. These results show that LLift can improve compression across deployment budgets without fine-tuning each compressed model separately.
authors: Chenyue Fang, Danila Mishin, Babak Falsafi
bullets: SVD compression can degrade performance and typically requires ratio-specific fine-tuning or weight correction.
LLift trains a low-rank approximation at one ratio using the original model as a teacher.
The learned updates are merged into the original weights while preserving components omitted during the training forward pass.
The prepared model’s SVD decompositions can be reused at different truncation ranks.
Experiments report accuracy gains across three ratios, model families, model sizes, and SVD operators; the method’s scope is evaluated through local gradient and early-update analyses.

papers.abstract: Recent work on Weight-Space Programming uses LLMs to edit neural weights with forward passes only, conflating LLM scripting with the underlying algebra of forward-only editing. We show that for core structured editing regimes, an LLM optimizer is unnecessary, and introduce Forward Weight-Space Programming (FWSP): a deterministic pipeline combining probing, localization, stratified operators (O1-O4), automatic blind routing (83.3% vs. 33.3% for a 27B LLM with the same tool library), and paired verification with zero additional per-token computation. For reasoning LLMs, we propose Protected FisherGate, a closed-form covariance-whitened readout edit orthogonal to normal-reasoning states: on DeepSeek-R1-0528-8B, a single frozen math-calibrated patch achieves 84.2% HumanEval pass@1 (1K budget; 75.4 +/- 9.4% across 3/5 Stage-4-passing subsets), beating 512-token-reserved budget forcing by +14.6 pp (-23.4% tokens) while transferring across HF-to-vLLM backends on full GSM8K and MATH-500. Across five modalities and thirteen models (50K to 27B dense and FP8 MoE), we further prove and verify two operator boundaries, subspace entanglement and frozen representation span, where FWSP-localized LoRA bridges forward-only and gradient adaptation.
bullets: LLM optimizers are unnecessary for core weight-space programming regimes.
FWSP combines probing, localization, stratified operators, blind routing, and paired verification without extra per-token computation.
Protected FisherGate enables a closed-form, reasoning-state-orthogonal readout edit for math-calibrated reasoning models.
On DeepSeek-R1-0528-8B, one frozen patch reaches 84.2% HumanEval pass@1 and improves over 512-token budget forcing by 14.6 percentage points with fewer tokens.
Across five modalities and thirteen models, FWSP identifies subspace entanglement and frozen representation span as operator boundaries; localized LoRA can bridge these limits.

papers.abstract: Dense global attention is crucial for capturing cross-view geometry in visual geometry foundation models, yet its quadratic complexity limits efficient inference on long image sequences. Existing sparse attention methods primarily select entries of the global attention matrix based on attention probabilities and construct masks independently across layers, overlooking value redundancy and cross-layer information reuse. By analyzing attention distributions and clustering value representations across layers, we reveal two forms of \emph{cross-layer consistency}, characterized by highly similar attention probability distributions and localized changes in value redundancy structures. Building on these observations, we propose \textbf{DuCo}, a training-free sparse attention framework that exploits historical attention information and value redundancy for efficient geometric inference. Specifically, DuCo leverages historical attention information to estimate current-layer dense attention probabilities and introduces value clustering to exploit redundancy, with clusters efficiently refined through local updates across layers. Both factors are integrated through probability-weighted value distortion to jointly optimize four cluster representation states under an attention budget for sparse mask construction. Experiments across three visual geometry foundation models and five benchmarks demonstrate favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-offs.
authors: Liangyu Xiang, Junyu Gao, Xiaofeng Wang, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Dense global attention captures cross-view geometry but has quadratic cost on long image sequences.
DuCo estimates current attention from historical layers and reuses clustered value representations with efficient local updates.
Probability-weighted value distortion jointly optimizes cluster states under an attention budget to construct sparse masks.
Experiments on three visual geometry foundation models and five benchmarks show favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DuCo. The resulting probabilities and clusters are jointly used to optimize cluster representation states based on probability-weighted value distortion, constructing sparse attention masks. Updated attention information and value clusters are propagated to subsequent layers as historical priors.

papers.tldr: DuCo is a training-free sparse attention framework that uses cross-layer attention consistency and value redundancy to make long-sequence geometric inference more efficient.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in video understanding, yet existing video question answering (VQA) benchmarks mainly evaluate models in offline settings. Real-world streaming scenarios instead require models to answer context-dependent queries by retrieving and reasoning over evidence distributed across the video history. We introduce StreamRecall, a benchmark for context-aware Multi evidence reasoning in streaming video QA. StreamRecall requires models to retrieve, associate, and reason over temporally scattered evidence to answer queries at the appropriate moment. It contains 4,983 questions over 462 videos, with context-aligned query times and fine-grained temporal evidence annotations. We further propose the Evidence Utilization Cascade to diagnose model reasoning through evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation. To enable efficient long-term streaming reasoning, we present EviStream, a training-free causal visual memory mechanism that preserves reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed KV budget. Experiments reveal substantial gaps between current VLMs and realistic streaming requirements, establishing StreamRecall as a foundation for developing evidence-aware streaming video intelligence.
authors: Cui Yakun, Tiantian Geng, Huixiang Kong, Xingqun Qi, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Targets the gap between offline video QA evaluation and real-time, context-dependent streaming scenarios.
Introduces 4,983 questions across 462 videos with context-aligned query times and fine-grained temporal evidence annotations.
Uses the Evidence Utilization Cascade to diagnose evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation.
Presents EviStream, a causal visual memory mechanism that preserves reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed KV budget.
Experiments show current VLMs remain substantially short of realistic streaming video reasoning requirements.

papers.abstract: Due to context-length constraints, most MLLMs cannot process full-length videos and therefore rely on sampling a subset of frames as input. However, existing sampling methods, ranging from uniform sampling to relevance-based selection, are often driven by a single sampling principle and thus struggle to accommodate the heterogeneous evidential requirements of different queries: some demand a holistic understanding of how the video unfolds over time, while others hinge on fine-grained events within a short temporal window. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling (HAS)}, a two-stage frame sampling framework. In the first stage, \emph{Backbone Frame Construction}, we apply a Determinantal Point Process (DPP) to sample frames that are both query-relevant and non-redundant. These selected frames capture key moments across the video and form the backbone of the sampling set, providing a foundation for subsequent enrichment. In the second stage, \emph{Adaptive Contextual Enrichment}, we analyze the temporal distribution of the backbone frames to infer the query's requirements and adaptively allocate the remaining frame budget between Local and Global Context. The Local Context enriches the backbone with fine-grained temporal dynamics and short-range causal relations, whereas the Global Context connects temporally isolated evidence and provides a holistic view of the entire video to support global understanding. Through such a hierarchical two-stage process, HAS effectively addresses diverse query requirements. Incorporated into three leading MLLMs, it demonstrates consistently superior performance across the Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU benchmarks.
authors: Yuyao Sun, Daiqi Shi, Shuang Li, Liao Zhang, Yang Cai, Deqing Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of sampling frames for queries requiring either holistic video understanding or fine-grained local evidence.
Uses a Determinantal Point Process to select relevant, non-redundant backbone frames spanning key moments.
Infers query needs from the backbone’s temporal distribution and allocates remaining budget to local or global context.
Local enrichment captures short-range dynamics and causal relations, while global enrichment connects isolated evidence across the video.
Shows consistently superior performance when integrated with three leading MLLMs on Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU.

papers.abstract: Classifying a whole-slide image requires encoding thousands of high-resolution tiles with a pathology foundation model, which accounts for most of the inference cost. Existing efficient methods reduce this cost by selecting fewer tiles, but typically train a new model around their selection strategy. A largely unexplored alternative is to keep an existing full-bag model frozen and run it on selected tiles at the same encoder cost. We introduce this comparison, alongside random tile sampling at matched cost. To select tiles, we fit a lightweight selector with 3.3K parameters to the attention of a frozen model, without additional slide labels. The selector ranks regions from a slide thumbnail, encodes the top K regions at 5x magnification, and selects b for processing at 20x. We evaluate seven frozen MIL aggregators on six tasks and compare them with nine efficient methods trained on the same features and splits. At a budget of (K,b)=(1000,10), encoding costs about 6.6% of the full bag and is 10-14x faster, excluding tiling. The AUROC drop is no more than 0.005 in 33 of 36 aggregator-task pairs. At (500,10), the cost falls to about 4% and inference is 13-22x faster, but AUROC drops by up to 0.035 on CAMELYON17, where small metastases are easily missed. Selection improves over random sampling by about 0.10 AUROC on tasks with focal lesions, while random sampling performs well on diffuse tasks. In our comparisons, the frozen model at (500,10) is ahead of nine efficient methods in 55 of 60 paired comparisons. Giving an existing WSI model fewer tiles is thus a baseline that a new efficient model should be compared with at matched encoder cost.
bullets: Motivation: Whole-slide classification is dominated by encoding thousands of high-resolution tiles.
Method: A 3.3K-parameter selector ranks regions from a slide thumbnail using a frozen model’s attention, then encodes only the top regions at higher magnification.
Evaluation: Seven frozen MIL aggregators were tested on six tasks against random sampling and nine efficient methods at matched feature and split settings.
Results: Encoding 10 selected tiles from 1,000 candidates costs about 6.6% of a full bag and is 10–14× faster, with AUROC loss ≤0.005 in 33/36 aggregator-task pairs.
Scope: More aggressive selection can miss small focal lesions; at 500 candidates, AUROC dropped by up to 0.035 on CAMELYON17, while random sampling worked well for diffuse tasks.

papers.abstract: Video large language models incur substantial inference costs from long visual token sequences. Existing video token compression methods mitigate these costs by exploiting spatial redundancy within frames and temporal redundancy across frames. However, many approaches impose predefined processing orders or fixed allocation ratios for spatial and temporal compression, limiting their ability to adapt to the varying balance of spatiotemporal redundancy across videos. To address this limitation, we propose PURA, a training-free method that prunes visual tokens through unified spatiotemporal redundancy assessment. For each token, PURA constructs spatial and temporal reference candidates and selects the reference with the lowest representation error across the two dimensions. The representation error is combined with token importance to determine each token's removal cost. To avoid the time overhead of removing the lowest-cost token one by one, we introduce Coordinated Pruning, which iteratively groups mutually compatible low-cost removals into batches for simultaneous execution and updates the pruning state after each batch until the target budget is reached. Extensive experiments on three video large language models and five video understanding benchmarks demonstrate that PURA achieves a favorable trade-off between task performance and inference efficiency.
authors: Yuyao Sun, Hongli Yuan, Shuang Li, Tao Deng, Deqing Wang
bullets: Addresses the high cost of long visual token sequences in video large language models.
Builds spatial and temporal reference candidates for each token and selects the one with lower representation error.
Combines representation error with token importance to estimate each token’s removal cost.
Uses Coordinated Pruning to batch compatible low-cost removals instead of pruning tokens individually.
Experiments across three video large language models and five video understanding benchmarks show a favorable performance–efficiency trade-off.

papers.abstract: Recurrent-depth language models generate each token by iterating a shared block of layers until its hidden state converges. Inference methods for these models decide when to stop the iteration, yet every token still starts from random noise and pays the full cost of converging. We show that where the iteration starts is a second, independent lever. A token's fixed point is predictable from the state at which the previous token stopped, after a learned change of coordinates, and we introduce FlyingStart, a linear warm start that is fitted in closed form on the frozen model and costs under 5% of one loop. The iteration and its stopping rule are unchanged, so the exit criterion certifies the same distance to the fixed point from any start: a better start removes loops at unchanged accuracy. On Huginn-0125, FlyingStart matches the accuracy of the strongest training-free baseline with 14--19% fewer decoding layers, raises batched throughput by 16--18% in two serving engines, and adds a further 10--14% on top of self-speculative decoding. A contraction analysis predicts the number of loops saved on all four models we study, including one where the prediction was recorded before any evaluation, and token by token on Huginn, and it identifies when a warm start pays off: the saving grows with the number of loops a model needs to converge.
authors: Runguo Li, Dezhen Lu, Zixiang Ni
bullets: Targets recurrent-depth language models where each token repeatedly applies shared layers until convergence.
Uses a learned linear change-of-coordinates warm start fitted in closed form on the frozen model, costing under 5% of one loop.
On Huginn-0125, matches the strongest training-free baseline with 14–19% fewer decoding layers.
Improves batched throughput by 16–18% in two serving engines and adds 10–14% gains alongside self-speculative decoding.
A contraction analysis predicts loop savings and indicates warm starts help most when convergence normally requires more loops.

papers.abstract: Recent feed-forward approaches mark a paradigm shift in novel view synthesis by eliminating the reliance on per-scene optimization, directly inferring 3D representations from input views. However, their reliance on global scene-token context incurs substantial memory and latency overhead, constraining their ability to handle increasingly dense source-view contexts. Compressing source representations offers an intuitive way to limit this token budget. Prior general-purpose compression methods are not tailored for novel view synthesis, as their fixed, target-agnostic nature fails to adapt evidence allocation to individual target views. To overcome this, we introduce TACC, a target-aware compression module tailored for feed-forward latent NVS. Specifically, TACC organizes each source view into a progressive carrier hierarchy. Driven by source-target geometric relevance, it adaptively retrieves tokens to dynamically allocate exact computational quotas. This selective retrieval directly yields a compact, target-conditioned representation. Extensive experiments on the RE10K demonstrate that under dense input settings, TACC achieves $9.23\times$ and $64\times$ higher Effective FPS than Full Context on LagerNVS and LVSM, respectively. Effective FPS excludes one-time source encoding and Carrier construction.

papers.abstract: Nested multi-precision quantization derives multiple precisions from a single checkpoint by reading only the leading bits of each weight, which makes it attractive for on-device deployment under varying memory and energy budgets. However, existing methods offer only integer bits, leaving large accuracy gaps between adjacent precisions and severe degradation at 2 bits. To address this, we propose Any-Rate, which serves 2-8 bits from one checkpoint, in half-bit steps over 2-4 bits. Any-Rate restricts some bit-planes to extended Hamming codewords in 8-weight blocks (0.5 bits per weight), shares one LUT per row across precisions, and encodes all precisions jointly with a separate target for each, reducing the loss from sharing bit-planes. Across four LLMs, Any-Rate achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, keeping 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits. It decodes about as fast as existing kernels, and an LPDDR energy model estimates up to 27% less energy at equal accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/Any-Rate.
authors: Hoonki Lee, Haechan Shin, Hyuntaek Jung, Yeonu Choi, Sangyeob Kim
bullets: Addresses accuracy gaps between integer precisions and severe degradation at 2-bit quantization.
Uses coded bit-planes with extended Hamming codewords in 8-weight blocks, shared row-level lookup tables, and joint multi-precision encoding.
Supports 2–4-bit half-step precisions while deriving all rates from a single checkpoint.
Across four LLMs, retains 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits.
Decoding speed is comparable to existing kernels; an LPDDR energy model estimates up to 27% lower energy at equal accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces half-bit multi-precision LLM quantization that reduces memory footprint; directly relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Any-Rate: Half-Bit Multi-Precision LLM Quantization with Coded Bit-Planes
papers.tldr: Any-Rate enables one LLM checkpoint to support 2–8-bit inference, including half-bit steps from 2–4 bits, with improved low-bit accuracy and potentially lower energy use.

papers.abstract: Biological intelligence thrives on minimal power despite its noisy, imperfect components, with neurons that communicate through voltage spikes. Brain-inspired computing seeks to bring such efficiency to real devices, which requires training methods tailored to them. The standard way to train spiking neural networks, backpropagation through time, computes weight updates through every step of a simulated device, so faithful or long simulations can make training costly and unstable. Here we show that spiking networks can learn reliably and efficiently by decoupling the clock of learning from that of computing. Our method, ChronoProp, calculates weight updates from each neuron's spike counts in fixed time bins using its measured input-output function. Compared with backpropagation through time, ChronoProp reaches similar accuracy in image classification, with about 3 times less training time and 20 times less memory at the finest timestep tested, and up to 10 times fewer spikes. On spoken-word benchmarks, ChronoProp is far more accurate in recurrent networks at fine timesteps, and with simple, hardware-compatible techniques it approaches the best published models. These networks also tolerate simulated hardware defects and limitations better than those trained with backpropagation through time. Therefore, ChronoProp enables stable and efficient training in simulations close to the continuous time of analog hardware.
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and instability of backpropagation through time for long or faithful spiking-neural simulations.
Computes updates from neuron spike counts in fixed time bins and measured input–output functions.
Matches image-classification accuracy with about 3× less training time and 20× less memory, while using up to 10× fewer spikes.
Performs especially well on spoken-word benchmarks, including improved recurrent-network accuracy at fine timesteps.
Improves tolerance to simulated hardware defects and limitations, supporting near-continuous-time analog hardware simulations.
papers.selection_reason: Decouples learning and computing clocks in spiking networks, reducing training time, memory, and spikes; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: Decoupling the clocks of learning and computing in spiking neural networks
papers.tldr: ChronoProp decouples learning from simulation time in spiking neural networks, achieving comparable or better accuracy with substantially lower training cost and greater hardware robustness than backpropagation through time.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) outperform single-agent systems, but inter-agent communication incurs substantial token overhead. While assigning a large LLM to every agent is common, it results in inefficient resource utilization, leaving the system far from the Pareto frontier. The cost of answering a query is set jointly by how many agents are recruited, the role and LLM assigned to each, and communication topology among them. Most existing routers treat cost only implicitly rather than as an explicit optimization constraint. A fixed accuracy-cost preference also cannot express how much a caller is willing to pay for a particular query. We introduce MeterRouter, a budget-aware dynamic router that incrementally synthesizes a collaboration graph by selecting each agent's role, LLM, incoming connections, and termination conditioned on the query and a per-query monetary budget. We initialize the router by imitating successful execution graphs, then jointly refine its decisions with a variant of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) whose reward favors correct answers and penalizes spending and budget overruns. Across five benchmarks and a three-tier LLM pool, MeterRouter is (1) accurate, achieving performance comparable to the strongest MAS; (2) economical, reaching that accuracy at 82% lower cost than the strongest MAS router and extending the accuracy-cost frontier beyond the ceiling of single-agent systems; and (3) controllable, adapting its spending to the specified budget while rarely exceeding it.
authors: Yue Xu, Leikun Yin, Ruiming Min, Yufeng Lai, Justin Andrew Johnson, Sitao Luan, Xiaotong Shen
bullets: Targets inefficient LLM assignment and communication overhead in multi-agent systems.
Selects agent roles, LLMs, incoming connections, and termination decisions conditioned on the query and monetary budget.
Initializes from successful execution graphs and refines routing with a GRPO variant rewarding correctness while penalizing cost and budget overruns.
Evaluated on five benchmarks with a three-tier LLM pool, it matches the strongest MAS while using 82% lower cost.
Adapts spending to specified budgets, rarely exceeds them, and extends the accuracy–cost frontier beyond single-agent systems.

papers.title: MeterRouter: Budget-Aware Dynamic Routing for Multi-Agent Systems

papers.abstract: Random projection is a basic compression primitive for Euclidean representation learning, with the Johnson--Lindenstrauss lemma giving a target dimension $k=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ independent of the ambient dimension. As hyperbolic representations gain increasing attention in modern Transformers, vision-language models, and large language models, the same need for oblivious dimensionality reduction arises, but no analogous primitive yet exists for hyperbolic representations. We study this gap. Two natural attempts fail in dual ways: a tangent-space scheme gives a clean local guarantee but is chart-bound and pays a curvature penalty, while a fully hyperbolic projection in the hyperboloid model is geometrically native but mixes radial and angular error before feeding them into the conditioning of $\operatorname{arcosh}$. We propose radial-angular random projection (RAP), which preserves the radial coordinate exactly and applies a Euclidean random projection only to the angular direction, lifting the result back to the target hyperboloid. RAP is hyperbolic-to-hyperbolic by construction, costs one Gaussian matrix-vector product, and reduces hyperbolic compression to a normalized angular JL question on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. We prove a finite-set RAP guarantee with explicit $\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_x)\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_y)$ conditioning, complemented by a local tangent-space JL theorem and an arcosh-conditioning lemma for the fully hyperbolic comparator. Across an origin-centered broad-radius point cloud, a balanced tree, a clustered Gaussian, and the WordNet noun hierarchy, RAP attains the lowest mean relative distortion in every $(n,k)$ cell, reducing distortion over the strongest hyperbolic baseline by approximately $48\%$--$49\%$ on broad-radius data. RAP also scales to million-point datasets and improves retrieval on vision--language representations over hyperbolic projection baselines.
authors: Jiahong Liu, Wenhao Yu, Yifan Li, Yanyu Chen, Rex Ying, Menglin Yang, Irwin King
bullets: Addresses the lack of a Johnson–Lindenstrauss-style dimensionality reduction primitive for hyperbolic representations.
Preserves each point’s radial coordinate while applying a Euclidean random projection to its angular direction.
Provides finite-set guarantees with explicit curvature- and radius-dependent conditioning, plus analyses of tangent-space and fully hyperbolic alternatives.
Achieves the lowest mean relative distortion across all tested settings and reduces distortion by approximately 48%–49% over the strongest baseline on broad-radius data.
Scales to million-point datasets and improves retrieval for vision–language representations over hyperbolic projection baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Unified schematic of the three hyperbolic random projection paradigms studied in this paper. Panel (a) shows the tangent-space baseline: points are sent to a Euclidean tangent chart by loga, sketched by a Gaussian JL matrix, and mapped back by an exponential map. Panel (b) shows the fully hyperbolic baseline: spatial coordinates are projected in the hyperboloid model and the time coordinate is recomputed, which keeps the output on the hyperboloid but couples radial and angular perturbations. Panel (c) shows RAP, our proposed radial-angular projection: the radius rx is preserved exactly while only the angular direction ux is projected and renormalized. This separation keeps hierarchy-carrying radial depth unchanged and confines compression error to angular information.

papers.selection_reason: Random projection for hyperbolic representations, transferable to efficient AI.
papers.title: RAP: Radial-Angular Random Projection for Hyperbolic Representations
papers.tldr: RAP is a hyperbolic-to-hyperbolic random projection that preserves radial distance exactly and compresses only angular information, achieving strong theoretical guarantees and lower distortion than prior hyperbolic projections.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models excel at image and video generation, but iterative denoising incurs substantial inference latency. Recent token-adaptive acceleration methods select Taylor prediction orders for the full-model residual using shallow-layer proxy scores. However, candidate orders are evaluated on these proxy features but used to predict the full-model residual, creating a proxy--target mismatch: the proxy-preferred order may not minimize residual prediction error. To address this mismatch, we propose \textbf{TORE} (\textbf{T}aylor \textbf{O}rder selection via \textbf{R}esidual \textbf{E}rror estimation), which selects token-wise Taylor orders based on estimated prediction errors for the full-model residual. Yet direct error evaluation requires future ground-truth residuals, which are unavailable during order selection. TORE therefore estimates prediction error by analyzing how errors arise in Taylor extrapolation. Specifically, it decomposes prediction error into truncation error and finite-difference derivative error, then estimates both contributions from cached residuals to preselect token-wise orders for upcoming skip steps. Extensive experiments show that TORE achieves $4.31\times$ speedup on FLUX.1-dev and $4.18\times$ on Wan2.1 while maintaining high generation quality and fidelity.
authors: Lei Tang, Baoquan Zhang, Yakun Zhang, Yunming Ye
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between shallow proxy scores and full-model residual prediction accuracy in token-adaptive acceleration.
Decomposes Taylor prediction error into truncation and finite-difference derivative errors.
Uses cached residuals to estimate these errors without unavailable future ground-truth residuals.
Preselects token-wise Taylor orders for upcoming denoising skip steps.
Reports 4.31× speedup on FLUX.1-dev and 4.18× on Wan2.1 while maintaining high generation quality and fidelity.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of TORE. Full-steps preselect Taylor orders for each token at each of the next N − 1 skip steps. Skip steps use the stored orders for residual forecasting, without further error estimation or order selection.

papers.abstract: Infrared and visible images offer complementary cues for all-weather object detection, yet real-world sensor dropouts can leave one stream unavailable and degrade paired-input detectors. Meanwhile, existing modality-adaptive methods apply heavy cross-modal attention uniformly across scales, incurring prohibitive token overhead on high-resolution maps. We propose Admoab-DETR, a unified real-time detector supporting infrared-only, visible-only, and paired inputs with a single set of weights. Specifically, \emph{Resolution-Tiered Fusion} (RTF) allocates fusion capacity by spatial token density and feature granularity: a lightweight Spatial Modality Gate governs fine local fusion at the highest-resolution scale with zero-cost single-view pass-through, while channel-compressed deformable Admoab necks capture cross-modal correspondence at coarser semantic scales. Furthermore, \emph{Mode-Matched Feature Distillation} (MMFD) aligns multi-scale encoder features with an availability-synchronized full-fusion teacher, avoiding ill-posed cross-modal hallucination while cutting parameters by 18.1\% and paired latency by 39.6\% at zero inference overhead. We also construct Admoab, a strictly registered 20,000-pair infrared--visible benchmark across diverse scenes. Experiments show Admoab-DETR achieves state-of-the-art accuracy--efficiency trade-offs across missing-modality and paired benchmarks. Our code will be available at https://github.com/liwenchao0615/Admoab-DETR.
authors: Wenchao Li, Haoran Jia, Shuyuan Wen, Keyan Chen
bullets: Addresses performance degradation when one sensing modality is unavailable in real-world all-weather detection.
Uses Resolution-Tiered Fusion: lightweight fine-scale spatial gating and channel-compressed deformable fusion at coarser semantic scales.
Applies Mode-Matched Feature Distillation with an availability-synchronized full-fusion teacher to avoid ill-posed cross-modal hallucination.
Reduces parameters by 18.1% and paired-input latency by 39.6% without inference overhead.
Introduces the registered 20,000-pair Admoab infrared-visible benchmark and reports state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across paired and missing-modality settings.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, \emph{model-driven} context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: \textbf{GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget} on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~$\rightarrow$~56\%), and \textbf{Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens}. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that \textbf{inference engines can make model-driven edits cheaper}: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, \textbf{we cut prefill compute by up to 15\% per request with no measurable change in accuracy}. Together, these results point to a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that support KV cache editing.
authors: Alessio Devoto, Avinash Vem, Tara Safavi, Sanjay Kariyappa, Yu-Hsuan Tseng, Paul Furgale, Ricardo Silveira Cabral
bullets: Replaces harness-triggered summarization with a context API that lets models decide when and what to compact.
Evaluated on document research and machine learning engineering across 8K–512K-token budgets.
Effective API use improves performance at tight budgets: GPT 6.1’s OfficeQA Pro v2 score rose from 21% to 56% at 32K tokens, while Kimi used up to 41% fewer input tokens.
Models vary widely in compaction frequency, aggressiveness, and timing; prompt changes also affect when compaction begins.
KV-cache reuse after context edits reduced prefill compute by up to 15% per request without measurable accuracy changes.

papers.abstract: Recent 3D generative models can produce high-quality meshes with complex structures and fine geometric details, with broad applications in games, film, and digital design. However, high-quality generation typically relies on long multi-step sampling processes that repeatedly evaluate large networks, leading to long inference times. At the same time, reference-driven tasks such as game-asset reconstruction and product digitization demand close correspondence to the input image: generated geometry must faithfully reconstruct the specific reference object. Acceleration must therefore reduce sampling computation while preserving the model's ability to reconstruct that object. To enable fast and faithful 3D generation, we introduce Spe3DUp, a coarse-to-fine framework based on Faithful Trajectory Distillation (FTD). FTD directly supervises few-step students with the teacher's input-conditioned denoising trajectories to preserve its generation behavior. We apply FTD separately to coarse geometry generation and geometric refinement, compressing both sampling processes while maintaining correspondence to the reference input. We further accelerate the complete mesh-generation pipeline with efficient geometry decoding and parallel remeshing. Experiments show that Spe3DUp maintains geometric quality and input correspondence close to those of the teacher, accelerates the coarse and refinement DiTs by 10.0x and 19.9x, respectively, and achieves a 7.7x end-to-end speedup over the original teacher pipeline.
authors: Liangchao Xu, Jiaye Fu, Youtian Lin, Feihu Zhang, Yao Yao
bullets: Targets the slow, multi-step sampling required by high-quality 3D generation.
Introduces Faithful Trajectory Distillation (FTD), which trains few-step students using input-conditioned teacher denoising trajectories.
Applies FTD separately to coarse geometry generation and geometric refinement in a coarse-to-fine framework.
Further accelerates mesh decoding and remeshing through efficient decoding and parallel processing.
Reports 10.0× and 19.9× speedups for coarse and refinement DiTs, and 7.7× end-to-end acceleration while maintaining quality and input correspondence.

papers.abstract: Executing monolithic neural weights, frontier foundation models, or entire multi-agent workflows uniformly on every input incurs substantial computational, latency, and monetary overhead. Conditional computation mitigates this cost by deciding dynamically which internal experts, model endpoints, or specialized agents to invoke per request. Yet token-level gating in sparse neural architectures, query-level model cascades, and task-level multi-agent coordination have largely progressed in disconnected research silos, obscuring recurring system failures and transferable fixes. In this systematic review, we synthesize 2,289 studies published between 2017 and September 2026 (selected from 13,884 unique records) across 20 methodological families under a unified two-step inspect-then-allocate framework. Discrete hard selection accounts for 70%, 83%, and 91% of token-, query-, and task-scale literature respectively, and computational overhead appears as a top operational bottleneck across every layer. Engineering safeguards remain sharply asymmetric: intra-layer gating prioritizes load balancing while rarely incorporating uncertainty estimation, whereas model selection and agent orchestration rely on confidence thresholds and budget rules while confronting miscalibration and cascading errors. At the same time, publication volume is accelerating fastest in agentic task delegation, where routing mechanisms are least often isolated experimentally and methodological bias risk is highest.
authors: Dat Tat Mai, Hung Tran Quy, Thai Viet Pham, James Jin Kang
bullets: Reviews 2,289 studies from 2017–September 2026 across 20 methodological families using an inspect-then-allocate framework.
Hard selection dominates token-, query-, and task-level research, while computational overhead is a bottleneck at every layer.
Intra-layer gating emphasizes load balancing but seldom uses uncertainty estimation.
Model cascades and agent workflows use confidence thresholds and budgets, but face miscalibration and cascading errors.
Agentic task delegation is growing fastest, yet routing is least often isolated experimentally and carries the highest methodological-bias risk.

papers.abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) modules and EAGLE-style drafters support efficient speculative decoding by reusing target-model hidden states. Their autoregressive use, however, introduces a training-inference mismatch: training supplies sequences of hidden states from the backbone or a single MTP step, whereas inference attends to a target-model prefix followed by a growing tail of recurrently generated MTP states. EAGLE-3's training-time test (TTT) explicitly simulates this behavior during training, at the cost of additional memory and specialized attention masks. We introduce two training-only methods for improving autoregressive drafting. Hidden State Mixing (HSM) samples among backbone and MTP hidden states aligned to the same prediction target, exposing the drafter to mixtures of states from different MTP steps without explicitly simulating inference. Hidden State Gradient Detach (HSGD) is a regularization method that stochastically blocks gradients through hidden state and embedding pathways while preserving the forward computation. Neither method adds inference cost. In joint pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning, HSGD yields the highest acceptance rates at early draft positions, while HSM performs best later in the draft. These acceptance rate trends favor HSM for long-draft-length serving and HSGD for short-draft-length serving. Furthermore, across four Nemotron models and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, HSM-based MTP boosting with a frozen backbone improves mean acceptance length by up to 52.2% over the co-trained MTP. For EAGLE-3 drafters, HSM offers competitive acceptance with TTT, with 48% lower peak reserved training memory in a four-step Qwen3-8B comparison. HSM implementations are publicly available in Megatron-LM and NVIDIA Model Optimizer.
authors: Yaniv Galron, Rabeeh Karimi Mahabadi, Maor Ashkenazi, Roger Waleffe, Talor Abramovich, Tiyasa Mitra, Yoav Miron, Dor Tsur, Sanjeev Satheesh, Jimmy Zhang, Jiaji Huang, Yonatan Geifman, Mostofa Patwary, Mohammad Shoeybi, Bita Rouhani, Ran Zilberstein

HSGD achieves the strongest early-position acceptance, while HSM performs best at later draft positions.
HSM improves mean acceptance length by up to 52.2% over co-trained MTP and uses 48% less peak reserved training memory than TTT in a Qwen3-8B comparison.

papers.abstract: We present SPARC, a geometry-guided attention pruning framework that turns the native self-attention of pretrained video diffusion transformers into a unified mechanism for camera control and persistent scene memory. Our key insight is that attention connectivity can simultaneously serve as geometric conditioning for camera control and spatial addressing for historical memory retrieval. Motivated by the asymmetric contextual requirements of reconstructing observed content and synthesizing novel regions, SPARC restricts observed tokens to geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context, while preserving dense attention for unobserved regions. Correspondence-aware attention biasing and order-invariant historical positioning further enable stable retrieval across long temporal gaps. Without introducing additional learnable control or memory modules, SPARC achieves precise camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation while substantially reducing attention computation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of aggressive attention pruning in improving camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity, with an inference speedup of over 50x when combined with four-step distillation. Project page is available at https://zju3dv.github.io/SPARC.
authors: Zesong Yang, Weikai Chen, Liyuan Cui, Yuan Li, Jiaxin Huang, Lutao Jiang, Runze Zhang, Yingda Yin, Xiaoyang Huang, Kai Yan, Keyang Luo, Xin Wang, Hujun Bao, Zhaopeng Cui
bullets: Addresses camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation in long-horizon camera-controlled video generation.
Uses geometric correspondences to guide attention and retrieve relevant historical scene content.
Restricts observed regions to matching historical tokens plus local context, while retaining dense attention for novel regions.
Adds correspondence-aware attention biases and order-invariant historical positioning for stable retrieval across long temporal gaps.
Reports improved camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity while substantially reducing attention computation.

figures.caption: Figure 3. System Overview. For each target chunk, SPARC establishes token-level correspondences with historical observations through local geometric projection, and then prunes the backbone’s native self-attention to focus on geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context for previously observed regions, while newly revealed regions retain dense attention for flexible content synthesis. Historical RoPE re-indexing is employed to eliminate artificial temporal ordering biases among retrieved historical observations. The generated observations are subsequently appended to the history bank for continuous rollout.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on DL3DV-Eval. Given the same input image and camera trajectory, we show frames generated with different methods along the roaming time. Explicit-3D baselines drift from the target trajectory or accumulate geometric distortions, and implicit baselines fail to follow the prescribed camera path, whereas SPARC preserves scene appearance and accurate camera control throughout the rollout. See Supp. for additional scenes and video comparisons.

Figure 6. Qualitative comparison of revisitation on WorldScore-Static. Each scene follows a closed-loop camera trajectory (top view), and frames are sampled along the roaming time. Baselines either distort the scene or fail to recover the originally observed content upon revisiting, whereas our SPARC faithfully restores the scene at both revisits. See Supp. for additional scenes and video comparisons.

Figure 9. Additional long-horizon generation results. Without any degradation-aware augmentation, SPARC generates high-fidelity, minute-long videos with precise camera adherence and persistent scene consistency.

Figure 7. Ablation on attention pruning and historical RoPE indexing. Progressively incorporating geometric correspondence, local window attention, and correspondence bias improves camera adherence and reconstruction fidelity. The bottom rows visualize the pixel-wise difference |∆| between outputs generated using the original and shuffled history orders: sequential history RoPE yields discrepancies that grow along the trajectory, whereas our shared indexing remains invariant.

Figure 2. Redundancy of dense full self-attention. Most target regions have been observed in historical frames and require only sparse geometric correspondences for faithful reconstruction, while newly revealed regions benefit from broader contextual interactions.
Figure 8. Attention weight visualization. Given target queries, dense attention with the camera adapter exhibits attention peaks that deviate from geometrically corresponding historical regions.
Figure 5. Camera alignment. SPARC achieves the best camera alignment on DL3DV-Evaluation.

Figure 10. Training-free dynamic scene generation. We segment the foreground object and shift its correspondence locations along a prescribed motion trajectory, allowing SPARC to synthesize natural object motion consistent with the specified trajectory.

Table 4. Computational efficiency. By combining attention pruning with 4-step distillation, SPARC achieves a 50× inference speedup over the original dense backbone.

papers.abstract: Standard Transformers allocate independent dense weight matrices to every feed-forward network (FFN) layer, coupling parameters linearly with depth (O(L)) and discarding prior compute when scaling capacity. Conversely, weight-tied Looped Transformers decouple depth from parameters (O(1)) but enforce time-homogeneous updates. We formulate the L-layer FFN stack as a 3D Tensor Cuboid and introduce QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT, unifying: (1) 4D Quaternion Hamilton GEMMs in bfloat16 (4x FFN compression), (2) 64x64 Block-Diagonal Tucker SwiGLU Cores for depth-specific rotations over a shared basis, (3) Braided ZigZag Diamond Routing (L0 -> L2 -> L1 -> L3) for zero-FLOP top-down refinement, and (4) Exact 2D Zero-Loss Continual Scaling in both width and depth. We also introduce Annealed Gated Bounce-Back Scaffolding (GatedBounce), which self-distills to 0.0% inference overhead. Across algorithmic tasks (8-bit Parity, 56-seed routing ablations, Mod-53 Grokking) and language modeling (TinyStories, FineWeb-Edu), our model outperforms standard Transformers at 2x-7.6x compression. On A100, QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT-12 (39.0M backbone) beats StandardGPT-12 (85.0M backbone) at 5/5 controlled checkpoints. Continually scaling one lineage across 6.00B tokens via zero-loss width growth (rank 6144 -> 8192), two bit-exact depth expansions (L = 12 -> 16 -> 20, 70.9M backbone, max_diff = 0.000000), and WSD cooldown reaches 3.3582 FineWeb-Edu loss (28.74 PPL) and 44.75% full-split zero-shot accuracy across 16,955 questions (ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, BoolQ), matching GPT-3 Small (125M, 300B tokens) at 50x fewer tokens.
bullets: Targets the linear parameter growth of independently parameterized Transformer layers and the time-homogeneity of weight-tied models.
Represents the FFN stack as a tensor and combines quaternion GEMMs, Tucker-factorized SwiGLU cores, ZigZag routing, and GatedBounce scaffolding.
Claims 2×–7.6× compression while outperforming standard Transformers across algorithmic tasks and language modeling benchmarks.
A 39.0M-parameter model outperformed an 85.0M-parameter StandardGPT-12 at all five reported controlled checkpoints.
Supports bit-exact continual scaling from 12 to 20 layers and width growth without loss changes, reaching 3.3582 FineWeb-Edu loss and 44.75% zero-shot accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Transformer parameter compression and scaling, relevant to Efficient AI.
papers.title: Quaternion-Tucker ZigZag Networks: Halving Transformer Backbone Parameters and Enabling Exact 2D Zero-Loss Continual Scaling
papers.tldr: QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT compresses Transformer FFN backbones while enabling exact, zero-loss expansion in width and depth, achieving strong algorithmic and language-modeling results.

papers.abstract: Departing from the paradigm of diffusion and autoregressive models, Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) enables high-quality image generation through iterative refinements. However, this repeated processing over the entire visual representations results in substantial computation overhead. Furthermore, the binary representations and global refinement mechanism in GRN disable the direct application of acceleration strategies developed for other generative models. To accelerate GRN model, we first observe several key properties by analyzing the entire generative process. That includes the stage characteristic, dual branch similarity and more importantly, the $\textbf{refinement redundancy}$. Motivated by the observations, we present $\textbf{FasterGRN}$, a training-free acceleration method for the Generative Refinement Network. $\textbf{FasterGRN}$ first divides the GRN into the semantic establishment stage and detail refinement stage according to its semantic establishment. For alleviating the refinement redundancy mainly resulting from the detail refinement stage, we propose Adaptive Retention Expansion ($\textbf{ARE}$) and Selective Token Freezing ($\textbf{STF}$) to shrink refinement steps and reduce token computations, respectively. In the experiments on GenEval and DPG-Bench benchmarks, our method $\textbf{FasterGRN}$ achieves a $2.03\times$ sampling speedup while largely preserving image generation performance. Our evaluation on COCO datasets additionally demonstrates that $\textbf{FasterGRN}$ even outperforms the original GRN in image fidelity.
authors: Ziqian Zhang, Pengcheng Wang, Yulong Chen, Yaxing Wang, Senmao Li, Kai Wang
bullets: GRNs incur high computation because they repeatedly refine entire visual representations.
The method identifies semantic establishment and detail refinement stages, with redundancy concentrated in detail refinement.
Adaptive Retention Expansion reduces refinement steps, while Selective Token Freezing reduces token computations.
FasterGRN is training-free and achieves a 2.03× sampling speedup on GenEval and DPG-Bench while largely preserving performance.
On COCO, it also surpasses the original GRN in image fidelity.

papers.abstract: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) for register-transfer level (RTL) design are usually improved by fine-tuning on curated Verilog corpora, which needs large sets of verified designs and GPU training. We present Kolpona, an agentic framework that improves such models without gradient training. Its first component is neuron programming, a new form of weight-space programming (WSP) that writes single neurons in closed form into the weights to remove failure habits found on practice tasks, and keeps each edit only when testbench results on fresh tasks favour it. At inference time, tool-using agents propose designs, and a label-free selection stage delivers one design per task from the specification, the candidates and their simulations alone. On Qwen3.5-4B, edits to 16 neurons raise the VerilogEval v2 pass@1 of the model alone from 31.7% to 55.4%, and the full framework reaches 77.6%. On Qwen3.8-27B, Kolpona lifts pass@1 from 73.1% to 94.9% on VerilogEval v2 and from 66.0% to 92.0% on RTLLM v2.1 on a single 32 GB GPU, above every published system in our comparison. The RTL edits also carry over to Python and raise the pass@1 of the 4B model alone from 84.8% to 91.5% on HumanEval+ and from 67.7% to 77.5% on MBPP+.
authors: Musa Tur Farazi, Md Nasir Uddin, Soumik Bhattacharjee, Tishna Sabrina, Chowdhury Mohammad Rakin Haider
bullets: Addresses the need for verified Verilog data and GPU-intensive fine-tuning.
Programs individual neurons in closed form to remove failure patterns, retaining edits validated on fresh testbench tasks.
Uses tool-using agents to generate candidates and a label-free selector to choose designs from specifications and simulations.
On reported benchmarks, the framework raises pass@1 to 77.6% for Qwen3.5-4B and 94.9%/92.0% for Qwen3.8-27B on VerilogEval v2/RTLLM v2.1.
Neuron edits also improve Python code-generation performance on HumanEval+ and MBPP+ for the 4B model.
