papers.tldr: Kolpona improves open-weight LLMs for RTL generation without gradient training by programming neurons and using simulation-guided agents to select designs.

papers.abstract: Can a classifier computed in closed form on a frozen encoder match gradient fine-tuning? We present closed-form weight-space programming (WSP): a large language model (LLM), used as a design assistant, writes programs that read a frozen masked language model through cloze-style prompt templates at several layers, fit closed-form heads (shrinkage discriminant analysis, kernel ridge regression and the encoder's label-word prior) on labelled data, and select among a pool of candidate heads by cross-fitting. No gradient is computed and no encoder weight changes. We instantiate the framework on RoBERTa-large. On 11 development datasets with 512 to 8,192 training labels, WSP is ahead of full fine-tuning (FT) and LoRA at every label budget (by 0.3 to 0.6 points on average; the registered non-inferiority tests pass) and within 0.5 points of prompt-based fine-tuning (PFT); these datasets also shaped the recipe. With fewer labels its lead over FT and LoRA grows: 1.2 to 3.5 points with 64 and 128 labels, and 3.8 to 5.3 points in the few-shot setting of 16 labels per class, where WSP is again within half a point of PFT on the development datasets. On six held-out datasets, WSP stays ahead of LoRA and within half a point of FT on average, although with six datasets no registered test passes, and PFT is ahead, by 1.30 points with 8,192 labels. WSP never collapses and is deterministic, but it needs one encoder pass per template (17 here). We report all eight recipe versions, every decision that saw test results, and 27 ideas that did not help.
authors: Md Nasir Uddin, Musa Tur Farazi, Soumik Bhattacharjee, Tishna Sabrina, Chowdhury Mohammad Rakin Haider
bullets: WSP uses an LLM-written program to combine cloze-template representations from multiple encoder layers with closed-form classifier heads.
It selects among shrinkage discriminant analysis, kernel ridge regression, and label-word-prior heads using cross-fitting.
On development datasets, WSP outperformed full fine-tuning and LoRA across label budgets and remained within 0.5 points of prompt-based fine-tuning.
Its advantage over full fine-tuning and LoRA increased as labels became scarce, including the 16-labels-per-class setting.
On held-out datasets, WSP remained ahead of LoRA and near full fine-tuning, but prompt-based fine-tuning performed better; WSP requires one encoder pass per template.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Closed-form weight-space programming. At design time an LLM editor writes the program: the cloze templates a text is wrapped in, the views read from the frozen encoder, the closed-form heads (shrinkage LDA, kernel ridge, the MLM label-word prior) and the rule that selects among them. The plain input and Tv view templates are read as V = (1 + Tv) × 2 × L views (2 poolings at each of L layers); Tp ≥ Tv templates give label-word scores at <mask>, so one prediction reads the encoder 1 + Tp times. In our RoBERTa-large instantiation, Tv = 8, Tp = 16, L = 12, V = 216 and H = 113. The classifier’s weights are computed from labelled data, not trained, and no encoder weight changes.

Table 2: Test accuracy (%) on each development dataset. Bold: the best of the four methods at that label budget; Underlined: the second best (none when two tie for the best); many gaps are a few hundredths of a point, so the ranks are descriptive, and the registered tests (Table 3) are the evidence. Means over 3 data subsets (WSP; one run where the whole pool is used) or 3 seeds (baselines); standard deviations and the 2,048-label results are in Appendix C.

Table 4: Low-label extension: test accuracy (%) on each development dataset with 64 and 128 labelled training examples. Every method selects on the same 1,024-example dev set (BBC News: 245), more labelled data than the training set itself. Bold: the best of the four in the row and budget; underlined: the second best (none when two tie for the best); the ranks are descriptive, and the registered tests (Table 5) are the evidence. WSP is v8 unchanged, except for a fix for classes absent from a cross-fitting part, which changes TREC-6 only. Standard deviations, the probes per dataset and the fix: Appendix F.

Table 1: Average test accuracy (%) over datasets. Every method is trained or fitted on the same labelled examples and selects on the same 1,024-example dev set. Bold: the best of WSP, FT, LoRA and PFT in the row; Underlined: the second best (none when two tie for the best); many gaps are a few hundredths of a point, so the ranks are descriptive, and the registered tests (Table 3) are the evidence. Zero-shot: the calibrated label-word scores of the frozen MLM head; it fits no head, but its calibration uses the training subset and, for the datasets revised by the editor rounds, its prompts were chosen on dev, so it varies slightly with the budget. LP and LP-prompt are linear probes on the last layer of the same frozen encoder (LP-prompt: PFT’s template). LP-ml and LP-prompt-ml read many views, as WSP does: the top 12 layers of the plain input with both poolings (24 views), and the <mask> state of the 16 templates of WSP’s prior in the top 12 layers (192 views), each view reduced to principal components (6,144 features). WSP: mean over 3 data subsets (one run where the whole pool is used); FT, LoRA, PFT: mean over 3 seeds on the same subsets (collapsed seeds left out). WSP − PFT: the mean of the per-dataset differences, from unrounded accuracies. Development rows: these datasets shaped the recipe; held-out rows: programs fixed before any run on them. BBC News has no 2,048-label row (its pool is smaller).

Table 16: The registered non-inferiority tests in full, with the complementary statistics added in the revision. k: datasets; Mean diff.: mean over datasets of WSP minus the baseline (points); SD: sample standard deviation of the per-dataset differences; 90% interval: two-sided t-interval. Lower bound: 5th percentile of 10,000 bootstrap resamples of datasets. Non-inferior: one-sided paired t-test of H0: mean difference ≤ −0.5 with p < 0.05, and the lower bound above −0.5 (the registered test). Inferior: the complementary one-sided test of H0: mean difference ≥ −0.5. papers.title: Fine-Tuning Without Gradients? Closed-Form, LLM-Written Classifiers on a Frozen Encoder
papers.tldr: Closed-form classifiers built on a frozen encoder can rival or outperform gradient-based fine-tuning, especially in low-label settings, without updating encoder weights.

papers.abstract: Low-bit storage of optimizer states can substantially reduce the memory footprint of large-scale training. In practice, however, these states are not quantized once: at every training step, they are dequantized, updated, requantized, and written back. This iterative quantization pipeline can destabilize training. We identify a failure mode behind this instability: for states updated via exponential moving averages (EMAs), quantization errors are recursively fed into subsequent updates. As a result, biased errors accumulate over time while high-variance errors are amplified, particularly when the EMA decay factor is close to 1. To address this error accumulation, we propose BReD (Block Replay Dithering), a method that reduces rounding bias and controls rounding variance during quantization. BReD adapts classical subtractive dithering to optimizer-state quantization by combining deterministic seed replay with block-wise shared dither values, avoiding auxiliary random-tensor storage and per-element dither values generation. Across the default pretraining settings (five optimizers at 120M; AdamW and Muon at 1.1B and 3.4B model) and supervised fine-tuning (AdamW and Muon at 7B model), 4-bit BReD closely matches training with full-precision optimizer states, with PPL shifts $\leq0.5$ in pretraining and $\leq0.2$ in fine-tuning and average downstream performance changes within 0.7 points. Moreover, 3-bit BReD preserves stable convergence in the evaluated settings, offering a more aggressive alternative. Our implementation of BReD is available at: https://github.com/ZhanHeshen/BReD
authors: Heshen Zhan, Youhan Huang, Yunke Peng, Yao Wang, Linghui Kong, Ziwei Zhu, Qingyu Han, Yaoyuan Wang, Congliang Chen, Ruoyu Sun
bullets: Problem: Repeated quantization errors in EMA optimizer states accumulate recursively, destabilizing training, especially with decay factors near 1.
Method: Combines deterministic seed replay with block-wise shared subtractive dithering to control rounding bias and variance without storing auxiliary random tensors.
Contribution: Adapts subtractive dithering to optimizer-state quantization under an efficient, storage-conscious design.
Results: Across the evaluated pretraining and fine-tuning settings, 4-bit BReD closely tracks full-precision optimizer-state training; 3-bit BReD also maintains stable convergence.
Scope: Reported results cover the tested optimizers, model sizes, and training settings; broader generalization is not established by the abstract.

papers.title: BReD: Block Replay Dithering for Stable Low-Bit EMA Optimizer States
papers.tldr: BReD stabilizes iterative low-bit EMA optimizer-state quantization by reducing accumulated rounding bias and variance, enabling effective 4-bit—and promising 3-bit—training.

papers.abstract: Looped multi-view reconstruction refines scene features by repeatedly applying a shared transformer block. Making these updates cheaper requires knowing how an approximation at one step affects the rest of the refinement. We study this with paired interventions in D\'ej\`a View and stacked reconstruction transformers, separating the error an approximation injects, how that error propagates, and how it affects the output. In D\'ej\`a View, approximation errors are attenuated more strongly than matched random perturbations under a scale-adjusted state-error measure, and a local Jacobian decomposition separates the contribution of channel gating from the response to spatial error structure. Spatial approximations made early benefit from subsequent refinement, whereas cross-step reuse depends on which quantity is cached and how reuse steps are spaced. At equal final norm, approximation errors change the predicted rotations 1.55 times as much as random errors. These findings guide our proposed method, which reduces spatial resolution and pools keys and values early in refinement, then interleaves attention-output reuse with full attention, and is adapted through lightweight self-distillation. Across five reconstruction benchmarks, the balanced configuration runs $1.63\times$ faster than the official 16-step D\'ej\`a View model with a 1.86-point reduction in average pose AUC@$3^\circ$. At matched latency, it exceeds the interpolated curve of a trained baseline using full refinement blocks by 4.73 points in AUC@$3^\circ$ and improves the corresponding geometry metrics.
authors: Siyuan Zhang, Yuhan Chen, Yangyang Ning, Nan Wang, Jun Yan
bullets: Studies how approximation errors are injected, propagated, and translated into reconstruction outputs in Déjà View and stacked reconstruction transformers.
Finds that early spatial approximations are mitigated by later refinement, while cross-step reuse depends on the cached quantity and reuse spacing.
Shows approximation errors affect predicted rotations 1.55× more than matched random errors at equal final norm.
Proposes early spatial reduction and key/value pooling, interleaved attention-output reuse, and lightweight self-distillation.

Across five benchmarks, the balanced model is 1.63× faster with a 1.86-point average pose AUC@3° reduction; at matched latency, it improves AUC@3° by 4.73 points over an interpolated full-refinement baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and accelerates looped multi-view reconstruction via spatial token reduction, key/value pooling, and attention-output reuse.
papers.title: Where to Approximate: Understanding and Accelerating Looped Multi-View Reconstruction
papers.tldr: The paper analyzes where approximation errors matter in looped multi-view reconstruction and uses the findings to design a faster model with modest pose-accuracy loss and better accuracy at matched latency.

papers.abstract: Looped language models can adapt computation for predicting a token without a proportional rescaling in unique model parameters by adjusting the number of loops. This property has been used for self-speculative decoding, taking shallow loops as fast drafters and deep loops as verifiers, which is effective since drafting still uses full parameters. In this paper, we show that shallow loops can be also predictive of several future tokens and leverage this to drastically accelerate the inference of looped language models. To that end, we present Floodgates, a simple self-speculative decoding method that appends a block of mask tokens as a suffix and learns via low-rank adaptation to draft these tokens in parallel. Across seven models, five benchmarks, a range of batch sizes, and both greedy and sampled decoding, Floodgates is the fastest lossless decoding method in most cases, attaining up to 7.5x acceleration. Through analysis, we show that this speedup is enabled by all-depth training of looped models, with the shallow drafter's ability to leverage full-depth computation by conditioning on deep prefix cache evaluated during verification.
authors: Ayhan Suleymanzade, Sean McLeish, Sehoon Kim, Jinwoo Kim, Antoine Bosselut
bullets: Looped models vary computation through the number of recurrent loops without proportionally increasing unique parameters.
The method appends mask-token suffixes and uses low-rank adaptation to draft several tokens simultaneously.
It exploits deep prefix-cache information during verification, allowing shallow drafts to benefit from full-depth computation.
Across seven models and five benchmarks, Floodgates is usually the fastest lossless method across batch sizes and decoding modes.
The approach is specific to looped models trained at all depths.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are widely used for image segmentation. However, existing methods either use a decoder or use patch-based approach which trades boundary precision against the number of decisions as coarse grid cells mix foreground and background pixels, while finer grids require many more predictions, and autoregressive mask generation adds sequential decoding overhead. We propose SPiXSeg, which shifts the output from per-patch to per-superpixel label assignment, using superpixel tokens formed by aggregating patch-level visual features. An off-the-shelf model partitions each image into task-agnostic superpixels, so the partition is computed once and reused across tasks. A Spix-to-Mask (S2M) module scores each superpixel token in a single MLLM forward pass by directly comparing the MLLM's hidden representations, without autoregressive generation or a separate scoring network, and the selected superpixels are mapped directly to pixels without refinement. Without any trainable decoder head or post-hoc refinement, SPiXSeg achieves an average cIoU of 80.5 with LLaVA-1.5-7B and 81.9 with InternVL2.5-8B on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg and, when trained only on COCO-Stuff, extends to open-vocabulary semantic segmentation with mIoU of 29.0, 59.5 and 95.4 on ADE20K, PASCAL Context and PASCAL VOC, outperforming several SoTA MLLM baselines. Our results suggest that a fixed, query-agnostic superpixel partition is enough for accurate language-guided segmentation.

bullets: Addresses the trade-off between coarse patch boundaries, costly fine-grained predictions, and sequential mask decoding.

Achieves 80.5/81.9 average cIoU with LLaVA-1.5-7B/InternVL2.5-8B on RefCOCO variants and supports open-vocabulary semantic segmentation when trained only on COCO-Stuff.
The approach omits a trainable decoder head and post-hoc refinement; its scope depends on the quality of the fixed superpixel partition.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress in visual reasoning, but extended generation over large visual contexts remains computationally expensive. During autoregressive decoding, visual attention is recomputed for every generated token, even when consecutive tokens rely on similar visual evidence. We introduce VAPOR (Visual Attention Persistence with On-demand Refresh), a training-free framework that reduces this redundancy by reusing visual attention outputs across decoding steps and refreshing them when needed. VAPOR caches the visual attention output while continuing to update textual attention at every step, helping reduce visual grounding drift during extended reasoning. To decide when to reuse cached outputs, VAPOR estimates visual attention mass using a low-rank approximation. It also uses prefill-based attention consistency and cache age to make independent Persist and Refresh decisions for each attention head. VAPOR retains the full visual key-value (KV) cache, so all visual tokens remain available when new evidence is needed. Experiments on eight image and four video reasoning benchmarks across two MLLM families show that VAPOR improves accuracy over dense attention on nearly all benchmarks while achieving 1.11-1.21x decoding speedups. Compared with the strongest state-of-the-art acceleration baseline in each setting, VAPOR further improves accuracy by 0.35-2.15 percentage points while achieving comparable or lower decoding latency. Our code is available at https://github.com/Su-my/VAPOR.
authors: Mingyu Su, Wei Wu, Erle Zhu, Chengxing Xie, Deyao Hong, Hongning Wang
bullets: Targets the high cost of recomputing visual attention for every generated token in long visual-context reasoning.

Retains the full visual KV cache so all visual tokens remain accessible when new evidence is needed.
Across image and video benchmarks, improves accuracy over dense attention while delivering 1.11–1.21× decoding speedups.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and LLM based agents have expanded the capabilities of AI glasses, enabling egocentric visual question answering, memory retrieval, and proactive assistance. These applications involve diverse inputs, including speech, images, and video, and range from simple device control to complex visual reasoning, posing challenges for efficient computation and communication. While video centric capabilities have received considerable attention, simple text based and device executable tasks remain underexplored despite their prevalence in daily interactions. Efficiently supporting diverse workloads within a unified assistant remains an open challenge. We propose JOVE ICE, an intent guided cloud, edge, and device collaborative framework that routes requests among AI glasses, a paired smartphone, and cloud servers according to user intent. JOVE ICE integrates hierarchical intent classification with dynamic subagent orchestration to select efficient execution paths and flexibly incorporate new applications through specialized subagents. Analysis of real world AI glasses requests reveals that simple device control tasks account for over 30% of interactions, which JOVE ICE handles directly on device to avoid unnecessary cloud computation and costs. Evaluations on three public benchmarks demonstrate that JOVE ICE reduces time to first token by approximately 13% and token usage by over 11% compared with conventional device and cloud architectures, while maintaining task quality. These results demonstrate the potential of intent guided collaboration to improve the efficiency and scalability of AI glasses.

papers.abstract: When a large language model (LLM) evicts prompt keys and values at the end of prefill, it must decide what to keep before it sees the queries from subsequent decoding steps. Generating a draft continuation can approximate those queries at the cost of extra autoregressive steps. Can we use the embedding of the first output token, already available from the final prefill logits, to construct low-cost pseudo queries that approximate future decoding queries? We start with FTQ-8, which places eight copies of the first token ID at consecutive future positions and reads their attention to the prompt in one causal forward pass. Each copy sees a different prefix, but a generic opening such as the offers a poor literal guess for seven successive tokens. Faster and Better Query (FBQ) preserves the first embedding and learns an additive offset at each of the seven remaining positions. We train these offsets to predict the average prompt attention of a full-cache continuation. On LongBench, FBQ performs comparably to eight-step Lookahead Q-Cache at the same cache budget, using a single forward pass to compute all probe queries.

bullets: Addresses cache-eviction decisions made before future decoding queries are available.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based 3D reconstruction models such as VGGT and $\pi^3$ predict cameras, depth and point maps directly from many input views. Causal attention models such as StreamVGGT extend them to online video but cache all past tokens, so their total compute grows quadratically with the stream length. Recurrent models such as CUT3R and TTT3R keep a fixed-size state at constant cost, but they progressively forget early geometry. We present LinearVGGT, a hybrid model distilled from StreamVGGT, which uses Mamba2 layers for efficient sequence modeling in three of every four global layers. The remaining layers use register-guided sparse attention to retrieve a few relevant past frames, compensating for the limited exact long-range recall of Mamba2. Our distillation needs only 9\% of the GPU hours and 31\% of the training frames that StreamVGGT uses to learn from VGGT. LinearVGGT keeps an almost constant latency of 27 ms per frame over 1,024 frames and is on average $12 \times$ faster than StreamVGGT. It outperforms its teacher and is competitive with the state-of-the-art streaming model LingBot-Map, while running $2.5\times$ faster and using $2.7\times$ less memory.

papers.abstract: Multi-scale architectures are widely adopted in all-in-one image restoration (AIO-IR) to capture larger-scale context at low-resolution stages and refine details at high-resolution (HR) stages. However, processing spatially large feature maps at HR stages incurs substantial computational costs and memory traffic, making efficient HR processing challenging. To address this challenge, we propose High-resolution Global-Local Restoration (HiGLR), an efficient multi-scale AIO-IR network grounded in an analysis of spatial redundancy in self-attention and convolutional feed-forward networks (ConvFFNs). Specifically, this analysis identifies three key redundancies: per-query readout at the finest-scale stage, key routing across neighboring queries at intermediate stages, and spatial mixing in the expanded feature spaces of ConvFFNs. Accordingly, HiGLR replaces costly self-attention at the finest-scale stage with a learned input-independent kernel. At intermediate stages, we propose a Block-Routed Hybrid Attention, which combines coarse-scale dense attention with fine-scale block-sparse attention over value residuals relative to coarse summaries, and shares routing indices across neighboring queries. We further introduce a Dual-Space FFN that performs spatial mixing in a compact space and pointwise nonlinear transformation in an expanded space, enabling efficient kernel fusion. Combining these designs, HiGLR achieves state-of-the-art performance while delivering up to a $4.24\times$ inference speedup over existing methods.
authors: Dongheon Lee, DongJae Lee, Sewhan Chun, Chanseul Cho, Youngwook Kim, Youngmin Ro, Yonghyun Jeong
bullets: High-resolution stages are costly because large feature maps create substantial computation and memory traffic.

HiGLR replaces finest-scale self-attention with a learned input-independent kernel.

papers.title: What Is Redundant at High Resolution? Efficient Attention and Feed-Forward Design for All-in-One Image Restoration

papers.abstract: Standard attention's key-value cache grows linearly with context length. Bounding it raises the question of what a sequence model should retain for long-context reasoning. We argue this choice should be learned, and introduce State Space Attention (SSA), which learns to keep a bounded set of past representations and reads them with standard attention. A learned scorer rescores every chunk against newly arriving context and the rest of memory. A fixed-context Transformer is then the special case that always keeps the most recent tokens. We train the scorer and reader jointly, either moving gradually from a differentiable soft weighting of memories to hard retention, or with hard retention from the start. To produce signal for the scorer, we generate supervised samples during training, a technique we call recovery. We compare SSA with recurrent models, bounded-memory attention methods, and full-attention Transformers across retrieval, variable tracking, multi-hop reasoning, and language modeling. On our retrieval and reasoning benchmarks, SSA matches or comes within a few points of full attention on most tasks, far outperforms a Transformer with the same readable budget on every long-context retrieval task we evaluate, and matches or outperforms one with about 4 times that budget, while using constant inference memory. The largest remaining gap to full attention at small language model scale is on RULER. SSA makes a fixed number of tokens useful over a longer context, and since it reads memory with standard attention, we propose that it can be stacked with KV cache eviction methods. We also pretrain and post-train 400M-parameter models and measure how SSA's training and inference costs scale with context length and model size. Together, these experiments examine the capabilities and limitations of learned memory retention for long-context sequence modeling.
bullets: Addresses the linear growth of standard attention’s key-value cache by learning context-dependent memory retention.
Uses a learned scorer to rescore memory chunks as new context arrives, while a standard attention reader accesses retained representations.
Trains retention jointly with reading using either gradual soft-to-hard selection or hard retention from the outset, aided by generated recovery supervision.

Across retrieval, variable tracking, reasoning, and language modeling, SSA substantially outperforms equal-budget bounded attention and can match or exceed attention with roughly four times its readable budget on retrieval tasks.
Its main remaining gap to full attention at small model scale is on RULER; the approach is evaluated across different training and inference context/model scales.

papers.abstract: Modern large language model (LLM) inference increasingly adopts disaggregated architectures that separate Prefill (P) and Decode (D) phases. Meanwhile, Expert Parallelism (EP) has been widely adopted in large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model serving. However, load imbalance still slows down MoE inference because each layer must wait for the busiest EP rank. The main source of latency differs between prefill and decode. Prefill is compute-bound, and its MoE layers' latency is determined by the maximum token count of the busiest rank. At the same time, under moderate batch sizes, Decode is memory-bound, so the latency is dominated by the maximum active-expert count across ranks. To solve both problems under a unified framework, we present RankCast, a system that reduces rank-level maximum token counts during prefill and active-expert counts during decode. For every token, RankCast preserves the predicted Top-p experts and chooses the remaining k-p from its Top-L candidates (L > k). In prefill, RankCast yields a price per rank that steers flexible assignments to less loaded ranks. In decode, RankCast closes experts on the busiest ranks while preserving the constraints for each token. Both paths are implemented and tested in the state-of-the-art inference frameworks SGLang and DeepEP. We overlap RankCast's kernels with model execution and reuse the existing DeepEP communication channel for metadata transmission. On Qwen3-235B-A22B with EP=8 and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with EP=16, RankCast removes over 75% of the busiest rank's excess prefill load, improves prefill input throughput by up to 19%, and reduces decode time per output token by up to 10%. The quality cost is below one percentage point.
authors: Kaidi Fu, Xu-Hao Lu, Pingwei Sun, Jianchao Tan, Yuchen Xie, Xunliang Cai
bullets: Addresses EP load imbalance, where each MoE layer waits for the busiest rank.
Uses Top-p expert assignments unchanged and selects the remaining experts from Top-L candidates to steer load.
In prefill, it reduces maximum token counts per rank; in decode, it limits maximum active-expert counts.
Integrated with SGLang and DeepEP, with overlapped kernels and reused communication channels.

On two large Qwen models, it removes over 75% of excess prefill load, improves prefill throughput by up to 19%, reduces decode time per token by up to 10%, and incurs under one percentage point of quality loss.

papers.abstract: Detailed knowledge of a user's persona is valuable for personalizing generative AI models and agents, yet such details are difficult to obtain and change over time. We address the task of inferring persona attributes from a single day of mobile activity logs. No suitable publicly available benchmark exists for this task, so we introduce a synthetic benchmark of 1,600 persona-log pairs. We target on-device inference so that raw logs never leave the phone, which makes memory rather than speed the limiting constraint: a day of activity yields roughly 30K tokens, whose key-value cache alone exceeds the INT4 weights of a 4B-parameter model. We therefore propose a log filtering method that retains only behaviorally distinct entries. Filtering reduces the memory footprint by up to 39% across nine models from four families and more than halves prefill time, while maintaining or improving prediction quality. For Qwen3-4B it removes 2.5GB, bringing the model from well beyond a realistic per-process budget to a manageable one. Within our benchmark, these results indicate that preserving diverse behavioral events matters more for persona prediction than retaining every semantically similar log entry.

papers.abstract: Attention over long sequences is a major computational bottleneck in video generation, which can be alleviated through sparsity and low-bit quantization. We propose JetDiffusion, a video generation system built on trainable Video Sparse Quantized Attention (VSQA), with custom inference kernels that combine native NVFP4 computation and kernel fusion. At 90% sparsity, VSQA accelerates attention by 8-29x compared with FlashAttention on different hardwares. To further accelerate video generation, we combine VSQA with NVFP4 linear quantization and step distillation. Although each technique can individually preserve generation quality, jointly adapting to all three remains challenging, particularly under aggressive NVFP4 quantization. Through empirical studies, we develop an effective staged training recipe that enables stable adaptation to quantization, sparsity, and few-step denoising. On Wan2.1-14B, the resulting model achieves 273x end-to-end video generation speedup on the RTX 5090 while maintaining comparable video quality.
authors: Yulun Wu, Zihan Min, Minshen Zhang, Kaiqin Kong, Ji Xie, Will Lin, Junda Chen, Wenxuan Tan, Aryan Kumar, Loay Rashid, Qingyu Yin, Hao Zhang
bullets: Targets attention’s long-sequence computational bottleneck in video generation.
Introduces trainable Video Sparse Quantized Attention with fused native NVFP4 inference kernels.
At 90% sparsity, attention is accelerated 8–29× over FlashAttention across hardware.
Uses staged training to jointly adapt sparsity, quantization, and few-step denoising.
Reports 273× end-to-end speedup on Wan2.1-14B using an RTX 5090 with comparable video quality.

papers.abstract: Abstract interpretation can certify properties of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), but precise analyses remain expensive. General implementations repeat work when analyzing the same architecture under different inputs and properties. Interleaving this work with numerical operations limits GPU utilization and restricts how much of the analysis a tensor compiler can process together. We present Scepter, a framework for specializing DNN abstract interpreters through structural semantics. The semantics determine the structure of intermediate abstract values while deferring their numerical evaluation. Structural computations from successive operations can therefore be performed together before certification, generating an executable tensor program. With the abstract interpreter and DNN architecture fixed, the program can be reused with different weights and input regions. We prove that it computes the same bounds as the general interpreter in exact arithmetic. The generated program also exposes operations and their dependencies for tensor compilation and memory planning. We implement Scepter for the tensor programs that Neuton generates from ConstraintFlow specifications. We evaluate Scepter on eight abstract interpreters and 44 DNNs against six baseline systems on GPUs and CPUs. Scepter handles networks with up to 153x as many neurons as the largest completed by the corresponding baselines. It completes DeepPoly on ResNet50 and VGG-16, whereas none of the evaluated DeepPoly baselines completes either network. On configurations completed by both systems, GPU geometric-mean speedups over Neuton range from 11.9x to 44.4x across eight analyses, with a 2.60x geometric-mean reduction in peak memory. In an input-splitting case study, Scepter proves 68 properties for which the baselines time out. Code: https://github.com/uiuc-focal-lab/constraintflow.git
authors: Avaljot Singh, Dushyant Bharadwaj, Yasmin Chandini Sarita, Heng Zhong, Charith Mendis, Gagandeep Singh
bullets: Abstract interpretation can certify DNN properties, but repeated numerical work and limited GPU/compiler utilization make precise analyses expensive.
Scepter separates structural computations from numerical evaluation and fuses successive operations into executable tensor programs.
Programs can be reused across different weights and input regions while preserving the general interpreter’s exact-arithmetic bounds.
Evaluated across eight interpreters and 44 DNNs, Scepter scaled to networks with up to 153× more neurons than corresponding baselines and achieved GPU speedups of 11.9×–44.4×.
The approach completed DeepPoly analyses for ResNet50 and VGG-16, and proved 68 input-splitting properties where baselines timed out.

papers.abstract: Linear attention compresses historical context into a fixed-size recurrent state, reducing the computational and memory costs of long-sequence modeling. From the perspective of test-time regression (TTR), the state matrix can be viewed as an online-learned regression model, where keys and values serve as inputs and targets respectively, and queries are used to read from the model. From this perspective, the effectiveness of state learning depends not only on the update rule but also on how the key-value learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. While existing work has largely focused on how the state is updated and organized, we investigate how the learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. To this end, we propose Sliding-Window Gated DeltaNet (SWGDN), which replaces short convolutions in Delta-Rule linear attention with sliding-window attention to perform content-dependent local aggregation of projected queries, keys, and values. Our experiments show that SWGDN makes the key-value pairs used in consecutive updates more similar in both GDN2 and KDA. In SWGDN, carrying information from the same token across updates can help the recurrent state reinforce a previously learned association. The local mixing strategy can be incorporated into any Delta-Rule-based linear attention architecture without changing its state update equations or chunkwise parallel algorithms. We apply this strategy to two Delta-Rule variants, GDN2 and KDA, and experimental results demonstrate that SWGDN outperforms the original Delta-Rule baseline across multiple benchmarks.
bullets: Linear attention treats its recurrent state as an online-learned key-value regression model, making update-pair construction important.
SWGDN replaces short convolutions with content-dependent sliding-window aggregation of queries, keys, and values.
The method produces more similar key-value pairs across consecutive updates, helping the state reinforce learned associations.
It applies to both GDN2 and KDA while preserving their state-update equations and chunkwise parallel algorithms.
Experiments report improvements over the original Delta-Rule baseline across multiple benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Sliding-Window Gated DeltaNet (SWGDN). papers.abstract: Full fine-tuning of large pretrained models is expensive, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is the standard alternative. Most PEFT methods use low-rank updates, whose rank lies far below that of full fine-tuning and is the same for every input. Input-adaptive variants vary the capacity per input but remain within the low-rank bottleneck, and whether a task benefits from input conditioning is not known before training. This paper introduces Kronecker input-gated rank adaptation (KiRA). Instead of the conventional low-rank product, the update $\Delta W$ is the Kronecker product of a frozen random $p\times p$ matrix $A$ and a trainable factor $M(x)$, which overcomes the rank ceiling: because rank is multiplicative under this product, $A$ multiplies the rank of $M(x)$ by $p$ without adding trainable parameters. The factor $M(x)$ is further decomposed as $B_1\,\mathrm{diag}(g(x))\,B_2$, where the input gate $g(x)$, computed once per sample by a network shared across all adapted layers, adjusts the rank of the update to each input in steps of $p$. Where input conditioning is unnecessary, the gate is folded into $B_1$ at deployment. Because the gate changes the rank only in discrete steps, the benefit of input conditioning can be predicted before training from a few hundred labeled inputs. Across six medical imaging and language benchmarks, KiRA attains the highest mean score against five published baselines with 8.7--9.7 times fewer trainable parameters than low-rank adaptation, and the pre-training criterion agrees with the measured benefit of input conditioning on all six tasks.
authors: Akil Ahmad Taki, Shaikh Anowarul Fattah
bullets: Addresses the low-rank capacity ceiling and fixed-rank limitation of conventional PEFT methods.
Represents updates as a Kronecker product with a frozen random matrix, multiplying the trainable factor’s rank without extra trainable parameters.
Uses a shared per-sample gate to adjust update rank in discrete steps; the gate can be folded away when input conditioning is unnecessary.
Across six medical imaging and language benchmarks, KiRA achieved the highest mean score among five published baselines while using 8.7–9.7× fewer trainable parameters than low-rank adaptation.
A pre-training criterion correctly predicted the benefit of input conditioning on all six tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning via Kronecker input-gated rank adaptation reduces trainable parameters and memory, fitting the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: KiRA: Kronecker Input-Gated Rank Adaptation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Pretrained Models
papers.tldr: KiRA enables input-adaptive, high-rank parameter-efficient fine-tuning by combining Kronecker products with shared input gates, achieving strong benchmark performance with far fewer trainable parameters.

papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) deliver the strongest response quality but carry per-token prices often more than an order of magnitude above those of smaller, task-adequate models. Smart model routing addresses this mismatch by assigning each query to the cheapest model expected to answer it adequately, rather than sending every request to the most capable, most expensive endpoint. This paper develops a formal cost-quality optimization framework for routing -- including a derived optimal threshold-policy structure, a calibration-versus-discrimination distinction, a cascade breakeven condition, and a sensitivity analysis over price ratio and traffic skew -- situates that framework against the principal routing architectures and the signals used to estimate query difficulty, and works through a numerical example showing how a calibrated router can reduce blended inference cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to an always-frontier deployment under specific, stated pricing and traffic assumptions, reporting both the gross reduction from routing policy alone and the net figure with the router's own overhead priced in. We situate this figure against the range reported by published routing systems (roughly 2x to frontier-level accuracy at one-fifth the cost), and close with the practical risks -- under- and over-routing, aggregate quality constraints masking segment-level harm, calibration without discrimination, calibration drift, prompt injection into routing signals, and operational failures such as tier outages and multi-provider price variation -- that determine whether the savings materialize in production. The analysis is primarily analytical, complemented by a GSM8K evaluation of the cascade framework (Section 5), validated (Section 5.2); extending the evaluation across tasks and model families is future work.
bullets: Frames routing as a cost–quality optimization problem and derives an optimal threshold-policy structure.
Distinguishes router calibration from discrimination and analyzes cascade breakeven points, price ratios, and traffic skew.
A numerical example reports roughly 10× lower blended cost than always using a frontier model under stated pricing and traffic assumptions, including router overhead.
The cascade framework is evaluated on GSM8K; broader evaluation across tasks and model families remains future work.
Production savings can be undermined by misrouting, calibration drift, segment-level quality harm, prompt injection, outages, and changing provider prices.

papers.selection_reason: Model routing reduces LLM inference cost, a computation/cost-efficiency method, though it does not map to a specific efficiency subtopic.
papers.title: Smart Model Routing for Order-of-Magnitude LLM Cost Reduction
papers.tldr: Smart routing can cut LLM inference costs by roughly an order of magnitude by sending each query to the cheapest model likely to answer adequately, subject to quality and operational risks.

papers.abstract: Low-bit post-training quantization reduces language-model memory but can sharply degrade downstream task accuracy. Calibration usually relies on generic text, but when task-informed data recover accuracy and which quantizers benefit remain poorly understood. We introduce FragCal-DC, which supplements generic text with training documents from task families with low retention of full-precision accuracy in a two-bit scan. We use a two- to four-bit sweep to locate functional regimes and four-seed calibration comparisons to evaluate six data-dependent methods across six dense models (1.7B-8B) and ten tasks. At their lowest tested functional bit widths, iterative SignRound V2 and OmniQuant improve at two bits, whereas single-pass GPTQ and AWQ show small mean responses at three bits. At two bits, SignRound V2 gains 1.83 percentage points in mean ten-task accuracy over generic-text calibration across six models. At 70 billion parameters, GPTQ and SignRound V2 both improve at two bits, with functional generic-calibration baselines. For two-bit SignRound V2, task-level controls show that recovery concentrates on families included in calibration, while incorrect answer designations retain about 90% of the mean accuracy gain. Changes in reconstruction error do not consistently track accuracy gains. These findings support task-informed calibration as a design principle for preserving downstream accuracy in low-bit quantization.
bullets: Generic-text calibration often loses downstream accuracy at very low bit widths.
FragCal-DC adds training documents from task families that retain little full-precision accuracy under two-bit quantization.
Across six dense models and ten tasks, SignRound V2 improved mean accuracy by 1.83 percentage points at two bits over generic-text calibration.
Benefits depend on the quantizer and bit width: iterative methods improved at two bits, while GPTQ and AWQ showed small mean responses at three bits.
Accuracy recovery concentrated on task families represented in calibration, and reconstruction error did not consistently predict gains.

papers.abstract: Reproducible evaluation, verifiable inference and on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) need an LLM engine to give a request the same output bits whichever requests share its batch. Batch-invariant kernels exist, but engines still select each kernel and its parameters from the batch. Two kernels that compute the same sum can round it differently. The engines' deterministic modes remove the choice by keeping one conservative kernel per operator and pay for it in latency. Many fast kernels are batch-invariant by themselves, so it is enough to fix the few batch-dependent values that kernel selection reads. Detent expresses kernel selection as a program that the engine executes. It finds the fewest values in this program that must be fixed and tunes them for the workload before deployment. On multi-GPU deployments of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-30B-A3B in vLLM and SGLang, Detent is batch-invariant. Tuned per load, it serves at 1.04-1.17x the latency per output token of Stock (each engine with its standard settings), against 1.67-10.3x for the deterministic modes. In SGLang it matches the GSM8K accuracy of SGLang's deterministic mode. Detent covers multiple deployment combinations, including multiple engines, GPU generations, tensor-parallel degrees, and dense and MoE models. Seeded RL rollouts of models up to Llama-3.1-70B replay bit for bit under other batches and cache splits. A trainer on Detent's kernels and values matches every rollout logprob bit for bit at 1.03x Stock's rollout time per token. BF16 GRPO then stays stable where Stock's run collapses.
bullets: Batch-dependent kernel selection can change floating-point results, undermining reproducible evaluation, verifiable inference, and on-policy RL.
Detent represents kernel selection as an executable program, identifies the minimal values requiring fixation, and tunes them per workload before deployment.
Across Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-30B-A3B deployments in vLLM and SGLang, it achieves 1.04–1.17× Stock latency per output token versus 1.67–10.3× for deterministic modes.
It reproduces seeded RL rollouts bit for bit across batches and cache splits; training logprob computation runs at 1.03× Stock rollout time per token.
BF16 GRPO remains stable with Detent where Stock collapses, while SGLang matches its deterministic-mode GSM8K accuracy.

papers.abstract: Under matched conditions, classifier-head fine-tuning (\textsc{cls}) paradigm consistently outperforms the LLM-as-Judge sequence-to-sequence (\textsc{s2s}) on binary hallucination detection. We trace this gap to the representations induced by the two objectives. Static analysis shows that \textsc{cls} learns a task-specific discriminative direction, pushing hidden states into a clear two-cluster geometry with stronger class separation and linearly decodable label information. By contrast, \textsc{s2s} relies on the pretrained language-modeling head to make decisions. This minimizes the pressure to reorganize representations, leaving the hidden states much closer to the pretrained backbone. Our analysis also reveals that the \textsc{cls} signal saturates before the final layer, after which upper layers form a plateau of statistically interchangeable and largely redundant representations. However, endpoint redundancy alone does not show whether these layers are dispensable during training. Further training-dynamics analysis reveals 1) a lower pretrained substrate, 2) a narrow upper-middle \textbf{InfoWindow} where task information emerges, and 3) a later-synchronizing upper plateau that mirrors this signal. This mechanism motivates us to remove layers above the InfoWindow. Truncating 31\% of the network leaves accuracy unchanged within seed noise on Qwen3-4B and 8B and cuts latency by $1.4\times$. The same depth fraction, fixed before any analysis of the target models, transfers to Llama-3.2-3B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, and the layer structure behind it reappears there and on QNLI and SST-2. We hope this helps guide efficient task-specific LLM design.
bullets: Classifier fine-tuning forms clearly separated hidden-state clusters with more linearly decodable labels, while sequence-to-sequence fine-tuning leaves representations closer to the pretrained model.
Task information emerges in a narrow upper-middle-layer InfoWindow, followed by a redundant upper plateau that synchronizes with and mirrors the signal.
Removing layers above the InfoWindow cuts 31% of the network while preserving accuracy within seed variation on Qwen3-4B and 8B.
The same fixed depth fraction transfers to Llama-3.2-3B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, with similar layer structure also observed on QNLI and SST-2.
The analysis is based on matched comparisons and training dynamics; the reported efficiency scope covers the evaluated models and tasks.

papers.title: How Fine-Tuning Objectives Shape Layer-Wise Information in LLM Hallucination Detection

papers.abstract: High-resolution Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) preserve critical, fine-grained visual details by encoding a global thumbnail alongside multiple local crops. However, the resulting thousands of vision tokens introduce severe computational bottlenecks during Large Language Model (LLM) inference. Existing token pruning methods rely primarily on query-agnostic visual saliency, while current query-aware approaches either operate at a coarse crop-level resolution or compute token relevance too late, after vision tokens have already entered the heavy LLM layers. To address this, we propose a training-free, hierarchical token pruning framework that utilizes query guidance prior to executing any LLM blocks. Our top-down hierarchy first operates at the instance-level, dynamically scaling the vision token retention ratio of each sample based on its visual complexity. Next, at the crop-level, we distribute this sample budget across local crops using sentence-level cross-modal similarity. Finally, at the token-level, we exploit projected vision tokens alongside textual query token embeddings in the shared space to measure fine-grained alignment, applying a text-debiasing normalization to produce high-fidelity query scores. These query-guided budgets and scores are fused with local and global visual saliency metrics to select the most critical vision tokens. Extensive experiments on LLaVA-NeXT-7B demonstrate that our plug-and-play framework retains 98.0% and 94.8% of unpruned performance at 25% and 10% vision token retention, respectively. Notably, at 25% retention, our method delivers a 2.0x inference throughput speedup and even surpasses the unpruned baseline on POPE by 0.7 points.
bullets: Addresses the computational bottleneck caused by thousands of vision tokens from global thumbnails and local crops.
Dynamically allocates retention budgets across samples, crops, and tokens using visual complexity and query-aware cross-modal alignment.
Combines query-guided scores with local and global visual saliency to select critical tokens before any LLM blocks execute.
On LLaVA-NeXT-7B, retains 98.0% and 94.8% of unpruned performance at 25% and 10% token retention, respectively.
At 25% retention, achieves a 2.0× inference throughput speedup and exceeds the unpruned baseline on POPE by 0.7 points.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of our training-free token pruning framework for high-resolution LVLMs. An input image is processed into a full-image view and multiple sub-images, which are passed through a Visual Encoder and Projector to produce visual tokens (V ). A text query is tokenized into embeddings (E). The pruning process consists of three main stages: (1) Adaptive Budget Allocation: A two-level budget is computed. At the Sample-level, a token retention ratio (Rj) is dynamically set for each image based on its visual token diversity (Hj). At the Crop-level, this budget is distributed among the sub-images based on the query-crop relevance. (2) Query Score Algorithm: A fine-grained relevance score is computed between the query embeddings (E) and the visual tokens (V ). Raw cross-modal similarities are standardized using a text-debiasing z-score to produce a robust query score (qsi) for each token. (3) Fuse & Select: The final token selection score is calculated by fusing the Query Score with two visual saliency cues: a local score from the sub-image’s own [CLS] attention (ai) and a global score derived from the full-image view (gi). The top-bi tokens are selected and fed to LLM for inference.

Fig. 2: Adaptive per-sample budget allocation on POPE examples. Our query-aware framework dynamically scales token retention according to scene complexity. The visually redundant snow scene (left) retains only 516 of 2,880 visual tokens, whereas the cluttered baseball scene (right) dynamically allocates 860 tokens to preserve fine-grained details needed for accurate question answering.

Fig. 1: Pruning masks on a POPE sample at a 25% retention ratio. GlobalCom2 uses an image-only mask that is unchanged by the query; for the chair question shown here, it removes most chair evidence before the LLM and answers incorrectly. Our query-aware mask retains the relevant chair tokens and answers correctly.

papers.title: Hierarchical and Query-Aware Visual Token Pruning for High-Resolution LVLMs
papers.tldr: A training-free hierarchical method prunes high-resolution LVLM vision tokens using query relevance and visual saliency before LLM inference, substantially reducing computation while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by employing a lightweight draft model to propose draft tokens and allowing the target model to verify the new tokens in parallel to improve inference-time compute utilization. The speedup relies on the acceptance probability of draft tokens in target verification, which is directly related to the gap $\|p-q\|_1$ between the target distribution $p$ and the draft distribution $q$. In this paper, we study draft calibration of speculative decoding to improve the speedup of speculative decoding, where we employ post-hoc methods to calibrate the draft distribution to mitigate the distribution gap. We observe that though current community open-source draft models may learn the top candidate token correctly, they are generally underconfident compared to the target model, suggesting a consistent distribution mismatch. To mitigate the effect of this mismatch on the acceptance rate of the draft models, we try various post-hoc calibration methods, including standard temperature scaling and token-wise calibration. Our results suggest that a standard temperature scaling applied to the draft distribution improves the acceptance length by up to approximately 10\% with almost no additional cost across different tasks. Throughput analysis further verifies that this improvement in serving efficiency. Analysis of more general calibration methods reveals further potential room for improvement.
authors: Yuxing Liu, Wei Zuo, Walid Krichene, Tong Zhang, Li Zhang
bullets: Speculative decoding speed depends on how closely the draft distribution matches the target distribution.
Open-source draft models often identify the top token correctly but are systematically underconfident.
The paper evaluates post-hoc calibration methods, including standard temperature scaling and token-wise calibration.
Standard temperature scaling improves acceptance length by up to approximately 10% across tasks with almost no added cost.
Broader calibration methods may provide further improvements, though their potential is not fully realized here.

papers.title: Draft Calibration for Speculative Decoding: Accelerating LLM Serving by Matching Draft and Target Distributions

papers.abstract: We present RenGen, a latent diffusion model that generates simple scenes from a few tokens and busy scenes from many, saving time and compute on simple scenes without losing realism. Most latent generators represent every image as a fixed grid of patch tokens, so a simple image costs as much to generate as a complex one. Prior methods that vary the token count through content-adaptive tokenization lose image quality as the count shrinks. RenGen instead trades scene complexity, rather than image quality, for fewer tokens. It does so by generating in the latent space of a pretrained region encoder, where each token represents one region of the image, and a decoder renders these region tokens back into pixels. Unlike patch tokens, region tokens cover areas of varying shape and position, so each token must capture both what its region contains and where it lies on the image canvas. We encode this spatial extent by adding positional embeddings to the encoder features before pooling, and we generate it by anchoring each token to a single randomly sampled point, from which the generator infers the region's shape, size, and content. At sampling time, the number of anchor points sets the trade-off between scene complexity and compute. On ImageNet $256{\times}256$, RenGen reaches a gFID of 1.34 with 88 tokens per image on average, the best among methods that vary their token count. It approaches the quality of RAEv2, a state-of-the-art patch-based model, at $2.5{\times}$ lower latency, advancing the Pareto frontier of generation quality versus compute. RenGen's gFID stays flat across scene complexity while latency varies by $2.4{\times}$ between simplest and busiest scenes, and its autoencoder reconstructs nearly as well as RAEv2 (rFID 0.32 vs. 0.30) with $2.9{\times}$ fewer tokens.
authors: Savya Khosla, Jay Mahajan, Akin Tuna Sakalli, Derek Hoiem, David Forsyth, Alex Schwing
bullets: Fixed-grid latent diffusion models spend similar compute on simple and busy images; prior adaptive tokenization can degrade quality.
RenGen represents images with variable-sized, spatially grounded region tokens from a pretrained region encoder.
The number of randomly sampled anchor points controls token count, scene complexity, and sampling latency.
On ImageNet 256×256, it achieves gFID 1.34 with 88 tokens on average and approaches RAEv2 quality at 2.5× lower latency.
Latency varies 2.4× by scene complexity, while gFID remains flat; reconstruction quality is close to RAEv2 with 2.9× fewer tokens.

figures.caption: Figure 2. RenGen overview. (a) The region encoder partitions an image into N regions with Felzenszwalb–Huttenlocher (FH) segmentation and pools frozen DINOv3 patch features within each region into region tokens, which the decoder renders back into an image. (b) For generation, P random anchor points fix the region positions. A DiT denoises one region token per anchor point, using the anchor coordinates as 2D RoPE positions, and the shared decoder renders the generated tokens into an image.

Figure 6. RenGen sets a new quality–compute trade-off. Left: gFID versus total TFLOPs per image on ImageNet 256×256. RenGen lies below the Pareto frontier of prior methods (dashed). Right: The source of this gain. At matched model size, RenGen generates 2.9× fewer tokens than RAEv2, which translates directly into 2.6× fewer TFLOPs and 2.5× less wall-clock time per image.

Figure 7. RenGen reconstructs fine detail as faithfully as RAEv2 with far fewer tokens. Each tile shows its token count; RenGen’s follows image complexity, from 31 tokens for the hairpin on a plain background to 103 for the crowded scene.

Figure 1. RenGen’s generation cost follows image content. Top: Wall-clock time and TFLOPs per image for end-to-end generation at different token counts for RenGen. Green values give the speedup over RAEv2, which always uses a fixed grid of 256 patch tokens (dashed line). Bottom: 256×256 samples from a single RenGen model. Each row uses the same class label, and each column uses the token count of the point above it, so fewer tokens yield simpler scenes at lower cost.

Figure 3. Image complexity varies, but patch tokenizers spend the same budget on every image. Top: ImageNet images of increasing complexity, overlaid with the 16×16 patch grid of patchbased latent diffusion models and with their region partitions. The simplest of the four scenes has only 22 regions, while the busiest has 130. Bottom: Regions per image across ImageNet validation set. The mean of 88 is 2.9× fewer than the 256 tokens of a patch grid (dashed line).

Figure 5. RenGen adapts its compute to scene complexity without losing quality. gFID stays flat across four complexity buckets, so in low-resource settings RenGen can generate simple, realistic scenes 2.4× faster and with 2.5× less compute than complex ones. Samples of the same class (bottom; anchor points in white) grow busier as the token budget increases.

Figure 4. Constructing DiT targets. During training, we place P anchor points on the image canvas, partition the canvas into their Voronoi cells, compute each cell’s coverage mask on the patch grid, and encode the image with the region encoder to obtain one target region token per anchor.

Table 3. RenGen achieves the best rFID and gFID among methods that vary their token count. It also reconstructs and generates nearly as well as RAEv2 with 2.6× fewer TFLOPs and 2.5× less wall-clock time (Fig. 6). The checkmark columns indicate whether a method’s token count varies with image content (content adaptive), whether a user can choose the token budget of a single model at inference (controllable complexity), and whether its latents come from a frozen pretrained representation encoder (frozen enc.). §Included as the closest prior generator that adapts its compute to image content; it operates in pixel space, so reconstruction metrics do not apply.

Table 4. RenGen scales to higher resolutions more efficiently than RAEv2. At 512×512, RenGen reconstructs slightly better than RAEv2 while using about a third of the tokens and DiT compute. Because its token count depends on image content rather than resolution, RenGen can also encode the full 512×512 image into the same 88 tokens, improving reconstruction further at no extra cost. A single RenGen model handles both 256×256 and 512×512 inputs here.

Table 2. Randomly fixing region positions with anchor points enables strong generation at low cost. Without any spatial prior, the DiT trains poorly. Conditioning on real layouts separately leads to memorization and requires real images at sampling time, while generating layouts roughly doubles sampling time and still degrades quality. Random anchor points avoid both and outperform held-out real layouts with a single DiT. At sampling, the DiT receives only the points; the training regions determine how the targets are partitioned around them. Sampling time is measured per image at batch size 64 on one NVIDIA GH200.

Table 1. Adding positional embeddings to patch features before pooling them into region tokens gives the best reconstruction and generation. REN tokens reconstruct poorly because their regions overlap and their features encode little position. Fine-tuning REN makes the number of tokens grow during training (∗mean token count at the start→end of training). Pooling patch features within fixed FH regions keeps the token count stable, but the tokens still encode little position. Adding an explicit mask code to each token improves reconstruction but hurts generation, because the DiT must generate these codes precisely.

papers.selection_reason: Content-adaptive token count in latent diffusion reduces compute for simple scenes; relevant to token-level efficiency.
papers.title: RenGen: Generating Images with as Many Tokens as the Scene Needs
papers.tldr: RenGen adaptively uses more tokens for complex scenes and fewer for simple ones, reducing generation cost while preserving image quality.

papers.abstract: Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. Code: https://github.com/castorini/delegent
bullets: Targets the high cost of frontier agents repeatedly processing context and handling every subtask.
Keeps the frontier model in charge while SLM subagents investigate code, run tests, or search corpora.
Unlike cascades and routers, it delegates subtasks rather than selecting one model for the entire task; no model training is required.
A 27B FP8 SLM reduces frontier cost by 67% for long-horizon coding and 59% for agentic search without performance loss.
A laptop-sized 2B SLM achieves a 66% coding-cost reduction; savings increase with delegated legwork.

papers.selection_reason: Reduces frontier-model cost by delegating subtasks to small models; efficiency-focused agent harness.
papers.title: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance
papers.tldr: Delegent cuts frontier-model costs by delegating focused, easy subtasks to local small language models while preserving task performance.

papers.abstract: Groupwise quantization is used in LLM quantization to improve accuracy at low bit widths, but grouping weights keeps standard integer MMA from spanning the full dot product for efficient GPU inference. We develop a new quantization method, Shifter Quantization (SQ), that reconstructs native-width integer operands by appending and shifting shared bits. To further extend the efficiency, we develop a special variant of SQ, Shifter Integer (SHI), to use INT4 kernels. We show that SQ and SHI formats perform better than standard groupwise quantization in quality, as measured by projection error and KL divergence, and in inference speed, as measured during decoding and prefill. For low precision like 2-bit quantization, SQ2 and SHI2 achieve 2.71-3.77x the 4,096-token prefill throughput of llama.cpp on a Q2_K checkpoint and reduce WikiText-2 KL by 6.6-7.8%. For mid precision like 4-bit quantization, SQ4 achieves 1.43-2.47x the prefill throughput of NInfer's groupwise-integer baselines across the tested models and prompt lengths, with 24-40% lower KL than the NInfer baselines. For high precision like 8-bit quantization, SQ8 achieves 27.4% higher batch-one prefill throughput and 72.7% lower KL than vLLM's online FP8.
bullets: Addresses the loss of efficient full-dot-product integer MMA caused by groupwise quantization.
Reconstructs native-width integer operands by appending and shifting shared bits; SHI adapts the approach to INT4 kernels.
SQ and SHI improve projection error and KL divergence while increasing decoding and prefill speed over standard baselines.
Reported gains span 2–8-bit settings, including higher prefill throughput and lower KL divergence than the compared systems.
Scope is evaluated across tested models, prompt lengths, and precision levels; the abstract does not establish broader generalization beyond these settings.

papers.title: Shifter Quantization: Compact Representations for Native Integer Computation
papers.tldr: Shifter Quantization enables compact low-bit LLM representations while preserving full-width integer computation for faster GPU inference.

papers.abstract: Model-generated labels offer a scalable route to training lightweight vision models, but what makes a model a good teacher, and can we tell before training a student? We study this in gaze target estimation, where interactive robots need models that are both accurate and efficient. In a controlled comparison of eleven supervision conditions, we vary only the source of gaze-point labels, keeping the student, training protocol and 361k training samples fixed, across three video datasets, two student sizes and three seeds; every student is evaluated against human annotation. Three findings emerge. First, imperfect model-generated labels can replace human annotation: Gaze-LLE, never trained on the target datasets' gaze annotation, trains students that match annotation-trained ones on ViT-Tiny and are significantly more accurate on ViT-Small (average distance error 0.187 vs 0.196), and the ViT-Tiny student runs 32$\times$ faster than its teacher on a laptop CPU. Second, apparent competence can conceal unreliable supervision: given another person's face centre in the prompt, InternVL3 and Qwen3-VL return it on 93.4% and 81.1% of test samples, and a copy-the-coordinate baseline matches InternVL3's labels and students. Without that coordinate, both models fall far behind the specialist. Third, good teachers can be identified before training: validation label error ranks student test error (Spearman's $\rho = 0.91$), and ten annotated clips single out the two specialist teachers in 95% of draws. These findings give practical principles for assessing supervision, exposing shortcuts and selecting teachers for lightweight models.
bullets: Imperfect model-generated gaze labels can replace human annotations: Gaze-LLE matches annotation-trained students on ViT-Tiny and improves accuracy on ViT-Small.
The ViT-Tiny student runs 32× faster than its Gaze-LLE teacher on a laptop CPU.
Vision-language models may appear competent because they copy face-center coordinates; removing this shortcut causes their performance to fall substantially.
Teacher quality can be screened before student training: validation label error strongly predicts student test error (Spearman’s ρ = 0.91).
Just ten annotated clips identify the two specialist teachers in 95% of sampling trials.

papers.selection_reason: Gaze target estimation for interactive robots and lightweight student training; relevant to embodied perception and efficient models.
papers.title: Training Lightweight Gaze Models without Target Gaze Annotation: What Makes a Good Teacher?
papers.tldr: A systematic study shows that specialist gaze models can provide effective, scalable supervision for lightweight students, while simple validation checks expose unreliable teachers and shortcuts before training.

papers.abstract: Visual token compaction reduces inference cost by passing only selected image patches or video tokens to later layers. In sequence models with local convolutions, each removal changes which tokens are neighbors. Learning which tokens to keep therefore requires a training signal that accounts for the new neighborhoods. We introduce ProbConv, which computes the exact expected convolution before activation at a kept position under independent keep decisions. The operator is differentiable in the keep probabilities. With binary decisions, ProbConv and step gating reproduce the compacted Mamba block. Across image, vision--language and video backbones, ProbConv is strongest under strong compaction: its advantage over matched training controls grows as more tokens are removed. In Cobra, it also outperforms adaptations of published vision--language pruning methods at matched inference budgets. ProbConv also improves over matched zero-mask training in video frame selection and speech frame dropping. Our code is available at: https://github.com/gmum/probconv
authors: Piotr Kubaty (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland, Doctoral School of Exact and Natural Sciences, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland), Mikhail Saladkou (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland), Jacek Tabor (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland, Centre for Credible Artificial Intelligence, Warsaw University of Technology, Poland), {\L}ukasz Struski (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland)
bullets: Token removal alters neighboring relationships in local-convolution sequence models, making standard training signals inaccurate.
ProbConv computes the exact expected pre-activation convolution at each kept position under independent token-keep probabilities.
The operator is differentiable, and binary decisions with step gating recover the compacted Mamba block.
It performs best under aggressive compaction and outperforms matched controls and several pruning adaptations across image, vision-language, video, and speech settings.
The abstract does not specify quantitative gains or discuss limitations beyond its evaluated application scope.

papers.selection_reason: Differentiable probabilistic token compaction for state space models; directly relevant to token pruning and efficient inference.
papers.title: Train What You Run: Probabilistic Convolutions for Learning Token Compaction in State Space Models
papers.tldr: ProbConv trains token-selection policies by modeling how removing tokens changes local convolution neighborhoods, improving strongly compacted state-space models across vision, multimodal, video, and speech tasks.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) generation using a lightweight draft. Existing methods evaluate complete recipes under different training configurations, leaving component effects, interactions, and composition benefits unclear. Therefore, we present LEGOSpec, a composable framework for speculative draft design and training. LEGOSpec decomposes draft models into Context, Backbone, Proposal, and Objective components that share a unified training infrastructure. Using LEGOSpec, we systematically vary components and evaluate selected combinations under matched training conditions to isolate their effects and interactions. These experiments reveal three findings: (1) Different workloads favor different backbones, depending on context length and memory budget, with within-block dependency modeling particularly important for long contexts. (2) Proposal design must balance acceptance and latency. (3) The training objective should match token distributions locally and optimize acceptance length across the block. These findings guide workload-aware configurations and DFlux, a balanced general-purpose draft combining a convolution-equipped SWA--GQA hybrid backbone, Residual Corrector, and hierarchical supervision. Across Qwen and Gemma models, DFlux improves acceptance length over the strongest baseline by up to 13.7% on regular benchmarks and 34.7% on long-context workloads. To support efficient training, LEGOSpec integrates metadata-aware scheduling and asynchronous execution, increasing training throughput by up to 79% and accelerating offline supervision preparation by up to $3.11\times$ over SpecForge.
authors: Hanzhen Wang, Jiaming Xu, Guohao Dai
bullets: Separates draft models into Context, Backbone, Proposal, and Objective components under matched training conditions.
Finds that backbone choice depends on context length and memory budget, while proposal design must balance acceptance with latency.
Shows that objectives should model local token distributions and optimize acceptance length across decoding blocks.
Introduces DFlux, combining a convolution-equipped SWA–GQA hybrid backbone, Residual Corrector, and hierarchical supervision.
DFlux improves acceptance length by up to 13.7% on regular benchmarks and 34.7% on long-context workloads; LEGOSpec also raises training throughput by up to 79%.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are built through large-scale pretraining, often followed by post-training, and are then adapted to specific tasks and behaviors. But, does the adaptation add truly new capabilities, or the base model already holds it? We decompose the update induced by different adaptations into a component shared across all inputs and a residual that varies with the input. We find that the shared component suffices for most of the adaptation gain and can be learned directly: a shift adapter that learns a constant vector per layer, identical for every input, reproduces the behavior of LoRA and full fine-tuning. We call this the potentiality principle of foundation models: the base model already contains the capacity needed for task-specific expertise. To adapt to a new task, the model just needs to be actualized, i.e., pushed in a certain direction via a constant, input-independent shift. We show the implications of this principle on parameter-efficient adaptation, steering, and convergence across models, and how it explains the neural thickets phenomenon.
authors: Fabian Gr\"oger, Shuo Wen, Maria Brbi\'c
bullets: Adaptation updates are decomposed into an input-shared component and an input-dependent residual.
A shift adapter using one constant vector per layer reproduces the behavior of LoRA and full fine-tuning for most adaptation gains.
The work proposes the “potentiality principle”: pretraining provides the needed capacity, while adaptation selects or activates it.
The principle has implications for parameter-efficient adaptation, model steering, convergence, and neural thickets.
The abstract does not specify quantitative results or the scope of evaluated models and tasks.
