papers.selection_reason: Shows constant shift adapters reproduce LoRA/fine-tuning; relevant to foundation-model adaptation and parameter-efficient methods.
papers.title: On Potentiality and Actuality Of Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Foundation models often already contain task-specific capabilities, and adaptation mainly actualizes them through a simple input-independent shift.

papers.abstract: Attention costs $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ in the number of tokens. Vector-quantized attention reduces this to $\mathcal{O}(NM)$ by clustering the $N$ keys, attending to the $M$ codewords instead, and its adaptive form, AVQ-attention, concentrates codebook resolution where a query's attention mass actually falls. We present AVQ-Attention-2, a better design that merges it with exact local attention and attends to the mean of each cluster's keys rather than to a codeword. We show three improvements: consistently better quality at comparable cost; training that now also costs $\mathcal{O}(NM)$ rather than $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$; and an approximation accurate enough that the layer can be dropped into a pretrained transformer without fine-tuning. Across a variety of sequence lengths the result is competitive not merely with other approximate attention but with exact dense attention, running faster than FlashAttention at little to no loss in quality.
authors: Winfried van den Dool, Patrick Forr\'e, Amir Habibian, Yuki M. Asano, Max Welling
bullets: Reduces attention complexity from quadratic to O(NM) by clustering keys and attending to cluster representatives.
Uses adaptive quantization to allocate codebook resolution where each query’s attention mass is concentrated.
Adds exact local attention and represents clusters by the mean of their keys rather than codewords.
Achieves better quality at comparable cost and is accurate enough to replace attention in pretrained transformers without fine-tuning.
Across sequence lengths, competes with exact dense attention and runs faster than FlashAttention with little to no quality loss.

papers.title: AVQ-Attention-2: Adaptive Vector-Quantized Attention with Exact Local Blocks and Linear-Cost Training
papers.tldr: AVQ-Attention-2 combines adaptive vector-quantized attention with exact local attention to achieve linear-cost training and inference while retaining quality competitive with dense attention.

papers.abstract: Linear attention models exhibit a disproportionate deficit relative to softmax attention in associative recall (AR) in language modeling. We investigate this gap through natural language evaluations, synthetic recall tasks, and targeted training interventions. Using a synthetic setting, we quantify the role of state-size in how many items can be recalled from memory and find a similar empirical scaling across the tested linear-attention architectures. Testing this relationship reveals that even a single layer at scale can learn to retrieve thousands of associations across long distances. Yet, standard language model training does not reliably teach a linear model to copy from context, whereas a comparable softmax model learns to do so. Considering this, we strengthen recall supervision during training through in-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting. Both methods improve recall-intensive benchmark performance and narrow the long-distance AR gap to the softmax baseline without changing the architecture, token budget, or number of optimization steps, at a slight cost to general language modeling. These targeted changes to training can thus elicit substantial but underutilized retrieval capacity in linear-attention models. These findings suggest that, although linear-attention architectures have substantial capacity for recall, their inductive biases and the demands of language model training make it difficult to develop this capability without dedicated incentives.
bullets: The study examines why linear attention underperforms softmax attention on associative recall in language modeling.
Synthetic experiments find that recall capacity scales with state size similarly across tested linear-attention architectures.
Even a single sufficiently scaled layer can retrieve thousands of long-distance associations.
In-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting improve recall benchmarks and narrow the gap to softmax attention.
These gains come without architectural or compute-budget changes, but with a slight cost to general language modeling.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates linear attention recall capacity and training interventions, directly relevant to efficient attention and language modeling.
papers.title: Eliciting the Recall Capacity of Linear Attention
papers.tldr: Linear-attention models can recall far more associations than standard training elicits, and targeted recall-focused supervision substantially improves their long-distance retrieval.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving engines offload the key/value (KV) cache from GPU memory to host DRAM and SSD so multi-turn and agent requests can reuse prompt prefixes. Capacity then limits service at two levels: external tiers govern prefix reuse before eviction, while the GPU KV pool bounds concurrent long requests, and lossy compression alters KV values and outputs. LoomKV brings lossless KV compression to both external tiers (tier mode) and the GPU pool (pool mode) on an unmodified engine. Using a calibrated per-head two-level 3-bit code over BF16 high bytes (sign and upper seven exponent bits), LoomKV stores BF16 KV at 0.71 of its raw size across nine models and FP8 KV at 0.85-0.87. In tier mode, TileStream writes exact-length records with length readback off the load path, leaving tier storage, eviction, and prefetch unchanged, and decompresses fetched records straight into scattered GPU pages. In pool mode, FragPack packs variable-length records into smaller shared-budget GPU pages read in place by a fused decode-attention kernel faster than FlashAttention-3 on BF16. Built with LMCache and vLLM, LoomKV makes compressed tiers act as 1.4x larger raw tiers on AgentX: across LMCache's LRU cliff, tier mode delivers 2.7-3.6x raw's goodput and 1.9-3.1x lower mean time-to-first-token (TTFT), shifts the cliff identically under other simulated replacement policies, and cuts repeated-prompt TTFT up to 1.7x via SSD-to-DRAM promotion. When tiers hold the working set, pool mode fits 1.31-1.34x as many GPU tokens, admitting 12 long requests with roughly raw's queue and goodput at 8. On an AI IDE trace where both tiers and the GPU pool are constrained, tier and pool modes raise goodput by 1.24x and 1.59x. Where raw capacity suffices, compression costs at most 2.2% throughput; tier mode is bit-exact with raw tiers, and pool mode matches FlashAttention-3's numerical accuracy.
authors: Wentao Zhu, Ziao Sheng, Peng Deng, Huiqi Hu, Xuan Zhou, Xing Wei, Zhuang Wang
bullets: Compresses BF16 KV caches to 0.71× and FP8 caches to 0.85–0.87× of raw size using a calibrated per-head 3-bit code.
Supports external-tier compression with unchanged storage, eviction, and prefetch behavior, plus GPU-pool compression with in-place decode-attention.
On AgentX, tier mode delivers 2.7–3.6× raw goodput across the cache-capacity cliff and reduces mean TTFT by 1.9–3.1×.
Pool mode fits 1.31–1.34× more GPU tokens; under joint tier and pool constraints, goodput increases by 1.24×–1.59×.
Compression is lossless/bit-exact for tier mode, matches FlashAttention-3 accuracy in pool mode, and costs at most 2.2% throughput when capacity is sufficient.

papers.title: LoomKV: Lossless KV Cache Compression from GPU Memory to SSD for LLM Serving

papers.abstract: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.
authors: Ayush Barik, Fan Lai, Francis Y. Yan
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of selecting and compressing video evidence without modeling the value of additional tokens.
Formulates video retrieval-augmented generation as token allocation over frames and subtitles under a shared budget.
Uses an iterative water-filling algorithm with a provable convergence guarantee to optimize allocation.
Reuses tokens and VLM attention across multi-turn conversations without extra processing cost.
Improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points at comparable compute, and by up to 1.5 points with 1.7–17.3× fewer TFLOPs in multi-turn understanding.

papers.abstract: A developer checking an assistant's report may need only an alarm that a claim is unsupported. A generative verifier, however, can continue decoding to quote and classify the errors. We study how much of that output is needed to recover its decision. In a frozen 2B span verifier, the choice between an empty error list and its first object precedes all localization. Native8 stops generation at this branch. The preceding seven syntax tokens are fixed, so Prefill1 supplies them as input and generates only the unrestricted branch token, using the same native instruction. On 2,015 code-agent TEST responses, Prefill1 reduces eager resident service by 84.84% relative to full generation, with released-reference F1 of 83.43 versus 83.41. It saves 31.98% over Native8 even though their logical token totals are identical. Under default compiled execution, the extra saving is 6.74-26.73% on the complete workload, with small decision changes. Controlled evidence interventions and first-location decoding establish what these shorter readouts retain and what requires further generation.
bullets: The study targets efficient verification when users need only an unsupported-claim alarm, not full error localization.
In a frozen 2B span verifier, the empty-list versus first-error-object decision occurs before detailed span generation.
Prefill1 supplies seven fixed syntax tokens and generates only the unrestricted branch token using the original instruction.
Across 2,015 code-agent responses, Prefill1 cuts eager resident service by 84.84% while maintaining nearly identical released-reference F1 (83.43 vs. 83.41).

papers.title: Reading Decisions Before Spans: Efficient Generative Verification

papers.abstract: Self-attention's quadratic complexity constitutes a core bottleneck for Vision Transformers (ViTs). Existing efficiency-oriented optimizations, including softmax-based and linear attention (LA) variants, generally compromise model representational capacity, leading to inevitable performance degradation. We propose a novel linear attention which alleviates this efficiency-capability dilemma. For the first time, we embed an Adaptive Channel Compression and Activation Purification (ACCAP) mechanism into the QKV projection of linear attention, which enables the model to retain high-dimensional feature information while performing computations with reduced channels. We further fuse a focused kernel function and a self-gating module into ACCAP to construct a lightweight linear attention module (ACCAP-LA). Our theoretical analysis shows that, compared to standard linear attention, ACCAP-LA reduces the attention module's parameter count by 79.17% and FLOPs by 77.5%. Extensive experiments demonstrate ACCAP-LA's effectiveness: when applied to ViT, it achieves 79.4% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with only 5.8M parameters, and more notably, it boasts strong cross-architecture compatibility, boosting EfficientViT-b1 and PVT-T by 3.3% and 3.4% respectively.
authors: Senqi Guan, Xianchao Zhang, Moyan Tian, Linlin Zong, Wenxin Liang, Xinyue Liu
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–capability trade-off caused by quadratic self-attention and capacity loss in efficient attention variants.
Embeds Adaptive Channel Compression and Activation Purification into QKV projections, with a focused kernel and self-gating module.
Reduces linear-attention parameter count by 79.17% and FLOPs by 77.5% relative to standard linear attention.
Achieves 79.4% ImageNet-1K Top-1 accuracy with 5.8M parameters in ViT.
Improves EfficientViT-b1 and PVT-T accuracy by 3.3% and 3.4%, respectively, indicating cross-architecture compatibility.

papers.tldr: ACCAP-LA makes linear attention substantially more efficient while preserving or improving ViT representation capability through adaptive channel compression and activation purification.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in low-precision representation have introduced several microscaling numerical formats for LLM quantization. By sharing a scale factor across groups of 16 or 32 elements, these formats enable aggressive low-precision quantization with minimal accuracy degradation, particularly when combined with modern PTQ algorithms. Their accuracy depends on how the numerical format interacts with rotation, PTQ, and scale selection. We study the composability of PTQ configurations across six LLMs and three microscaling formats: MXFP6, MXFP4, and NVFP4, systematically varying Hadamard rotation granularity, PTQ algorithm, and scale-selection strategy. Our central finding is that effective quantization recipes are format dependent: both MXFP4 and NVFP4 support accurate 4-bit inference, but techniques that benefit one do not necessarily transfer to the other. MXFP4 benefits substantially from rotation and error-correcting PTQ, whereas NVFP4 gains less from rotation, consistent with its finer-grained scales capturing more within-block variation. Building on these findings, we introduce Midmax, a calibration-free scale-selection strategy that mitigates clipping error in power-of-two block scales and improves accuracy across a majority of the evaluated MXFP4 configurations. We show that pairing MXFP6 activations with MXFP4 weights recovers most of the accuracy lost at 4-bit and, on Llama-3.1-8B, matches or exceeds our in-house BF16 baseline. An additional study finds that augmenting MXFP4 with a per-tensor macroscale, a mechanism intrinsic to NVFP4, does not improve average accuracy, suggesting that global rescaling alone does not address the limitations of E8M0 block scales for MXFP4 quantization. Together, these results provide practical guidance for combining numerical formats, rotation, PTQ, and scale selection for accurate low-precision LLM inference.
authors: Natalia Frumkin, Alireza Khodamoradi, Kristof Denolf, Eric Dellinger, Stuart Biles
bullets: The study evaluates MXFP6, MXFP4, and NVFP4 across six LLMs while varying rotation granularity, PTQ algorithm, and scale selection.
MXFP4 benefits substantially from Hadamard rotation and error-correcting PTQ, while NVFP4 benefits less from rotation due to finer-grained scaling.
Midmax, a calibration-free scale-selection method, reduces clipping from power-of-two block scales and improves most tested MXFP4 configurations.
Using MXFP6 activations with MXFP4 weights recovers most 4-bit accuracy loss and matches or exceeds an in-house BF16 baseline on Llama-3.1-8B.
Adding a per-tensor macroscale does not improve average MXFP4 accuracy, indicating global rescaling does not resolve block-scale limitations.

Among the best-performing MXFP4 PTQ configurations, macroscaling does not improve average accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Systematically studies quantization techniques (MXFP4) for LLM inference, providing practical guidance on combining numerical formats and scale selection for memory efficiency.
papers.title: MXFP4 for LLM Inference: Complementary Post-Training Quantization Techniques and Their Interactions
papers.tldr: Accurate MXFP4 LLM inference depends on format-specific combinations of rotation, PTQ, and scale selection rather than directly transferable quantization recipes.

papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models make different trade-offs between prediction accuracy and latency. We study whether a compact ensemble can deliver higher accuracy in less time. Across 816 TabArena splits, our blend of four-estimator Kumo and one LimiX pipeline reaches 2063.8 Elo, 45.4 points above the top published entry in the same fit. Its normalized fit + predict time is 15% lower than Kumo-16's and 98% lower than full LimiX's. We find that greater prediction diversity between the two models helps explain the reduction in error.
bullets: Targets the accuracy–latency trade-off of tabular foundation models.
Blends four-estimator Kumo with one LimiX pipeline.
Achieves 2063.8 Elo, 45.4 points above the top published entry in the same fit.
Uses 15% less normalized fit-plus-predict time than Kumo-16 and 98% less than full LimiX.
Greater prediction diversity between the models appears to explain the error reduction.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The labels 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 give the number of Kumo estimators blended with one LimiX pipeline. Diamonds mark the original Kumo and LimiX models.
Figure 2. Top five published references in our TabArena pool. The scores are from the Elo fit with the four-estimator blend.

Table 1. Accuracy and stage-normalized time on TabArena. Dataset medians in normalized seconds per 1,000 rows. Blends, ablations, and Kumo-16 use GH200 timing. Full LimiX, TabPFN-3.5 variants, and TabICLv2 use published TabArena timings. The TabPFN-4 preview reports Elo from a separate fit and predict time on RTX PRO 6000.

Table 2. Head-to-head results for Kumo-4 + one LimiX pipeline. Each dataset counts once, using its mean error across splits. Error change is the geometric mean of per-dataset error ratios, minus one, as a percentage.

Table 3. Squared-loss gain from adding a 50/50 partner to Kumo-4. Changes are relative to Kumo-4’s dataset loss S(p) and averaged across datasets. A negative penalty means the partner has lower standalone loss.

papers.selection_reason: Improves accuracy-latency trade-off via compact complementary tabular ensembles, relevant to efficient AI broadly.
papers.title: Tabra Blends: Improving the Accuracy--Latency Trade-off with Complementary Tabular Models
papers.tldr: A compact blend of Kumo and LimiX improves both tabular prediction accuracy and latency across 816 TabArena splits.

papers.abstract: Grammar-constrained decoding enables large language models to generate outputs that satisfy formal constraints, but in code and domain-specific language generation, the relevant constraints are not always fully available before decoding and may emerge progressively from new declarations, inferred type information, or runtime analysis feedback. Existing structured-decoding engines efficiently handle fixed, predeclared, or previously seen constraint structures; however, when a first-seen grammar update changes the parser state induced by an already committed prefix, the straightforward solution reconstructs the constraint state under the updated grammar, repeating parsing work already performed over the prefix. We introduce GramDelta, an incremental framework for constrained decoding with append-only runtime grammar updates. GramDelta maintains parse state over the committed prefix and propagates only changes induced by newly added grammar rules through historical dependencies, avoiding prefix replay. It then maps the updated parse state to exact next-token masks via compilation-free factorized projection over shared historical charts, avoiding per-update mask-cache recompilation. GramDelta therefore preserves the result of full reconstruction while making update cost sensitive to the actual impact of a grammar change. Experiments across four model configurations show that GramDelta adds negligible overhead without updates; under sustained runtime grammar evolution, it reduces median first-seen grammar-update latency by 10.7--11.5x and reduces the additional TPOT overhead over unconstrained decoding by 53.1--81.9% relative to the strongest reconstruction baseline. These results enable efficient constrained decoding when constraints progressively emerge and evolve with the generated prefix.
authors: Hantao Hua, Jiming Su, Yonggang Che, Feng Zhu
bullets: Targets append-only grammar updates caused by new declarations, inferred types, or runtime feedback.
Propagates only grammar-induced changes through historical parse dependencies instead of replaying the prefix.
Projects updated parse states into exact next-token masks without recompiling per-update mask caches.
Across four model configurations, it achieves 10.7–11.5× lower median first-seen update latency under sustained grammar evolution.
It also reduces added TPOT overhead versus unconstrained decoding by 53.1–81.9% relative to reconstruction-based decoding.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of GRAMDELTA. The top panel shows a committed code prefix, the current grammar, a late grammar update, and the resulting change in the valid next-token set. The middle panel depicts the reference reconstruction path, which replays the committed prefix under the updated grammar. The bottom panel shows the incremental GRAMDELTA pipeline: historical dependency lookup finds the earliest affected waiting positions, incremental Earley closure propagates only newly enabled states while reusing historical completions, and factorized token projection computes the exact updated next-token mask. The completed augmented item @START→ Start • indicates that the statement is fully accepted after consuming the closing parenthesis.

Table 4: Complete four-model GPU results on declaration-driven code synthesis (CodeEvo, 8K prefix, K = 32) with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals and p95 update latency.
Table 3: Complete four-model GPU results on BFCL (8K prefix, K ∈ {16, 32}) with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals and p95 update latency.

papers.selection_reason: Incremental constrained decoding reduces latency under grammar evolution, an efficiency contribution to LLM inference.
papers.title: From Grammar Deltas to Token Masks: Incremental Constrained Decoding under Runtime Grammar Evolution
papers.tldr: GramDelta efficiently updates grammar-constrained decoding when new rules emerge at runtime, avoiding repeated parsing of the committed prefix.

papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) keep the feed-forward network (FFN) intermediate width identical across every layer, a convention inherited from the original Transformer. Yet mechanistic work suggests layers at different depths do qualitatively different work, raising a natural question: are their capacity demands also non-uniform, and if so, can a fixed parameter budget be allocated more wisely than uniformly? To probe this, we apply principal component analysis (PCA) to the input of each FFN down-projection and measure, for every layer, its intrinsic dimensionality as the smallest number of principal components needed to reconstruct the activation up to a fixed cosine similarity. Scanning 58 open-weight LLMs spanning 14 families and 70M to 72B parameters, we find a recurring middle-heavy profile in which middle layers carry higher intrinsic dimensionality than edge layers; the profile is robust to the calibration corpus, even across English and Chinese, and is largely preserved through post-training fine-tuning. As a direct test that this signal is structurally meaningful, we use it to guide width pruning in a knowledge-distilled student under a matched parameter budget: the PCA-guided allocation outperforms the uniform-width convention by +2.3 points on Qwen3-8B and +2.5 on Qwen2.5-3B, while lower-dispersion teachers show smaller gaps (+0.9 on Gemma-3-4B, +0.5 on LLaMA-3-8B), and a budget-matched inverted control does worst on all four teachers. Across these four teachers, the size of the gap tracks how unevenly the teacher's intrinsic dimensionality is distributed across layers (a single-number summary we call $\sigma_{99}$), and the advantage persists through downstream supervised fine-tuning. Code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/lidf.
bullets: Across 58 open-weight LLMs from 14 families, FFN intrinsic dimensionality consistently follows a middle-heavy layer profile.
The profile is robust across calibration corpora and languages and remains largely preserved after post-training fine-tuning.
PCA-guided width pruning improves distilled students over uniform widths on four teachers, with gains depending on how unevenly dimensionality is distributed.
An inverted allocation performs worst, supporting the structural relevance of the measured dimensionality signal.
The advantage also persists after downstream supervised fine-tuning.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Per-layer dθ,l/Dl profiles for 51 of the 58 models in the scan, grouped by family. Profiles of all 58 models are in the supplementary material. Horizontal axis is normalized layer index; vertical axis is dθ,l/Dl at θ = 0.99. The middle-heavy profile recurs across architecture, training corpus, and scale. How strongly middle-heavy it is varies by family (Qwen2.5/Qwen3 most pronounced, LLaMA-3.x, Mistral, and Yi-1.5 [Young et al., 2024] flatter); checkpoints that are visibly not middle-heavy are concentrated in the ≤ 1.7B-parameter regime and the low-σ99 families flagged in the body.

Figure 2: σ99 by model family. Each column is one family, ordered by median σ99; markers are individual models of 2B parameters or more, labeled by size. Among the plotted models, σ99 shows a substantial association with model family. Within most families, σ99 also tends to rise with scale, although Qwen2.5 drops at 72B, the largest scanned model.

Figure 3: σ99 trajectories across six families. The horizontal axis is the Chinchilla-optimal compute multiplier: training tokens divided by 20× the model’s parameter count, where 20 tokens-perparameter is the compute-optimal ratio identified by Hoffmann et al. [2022]. Values < 1 indicate under-trained models relative to compute-optimal; values > 1 indicate over-trained. Vertical dotted line marks the compute-optimal point. (a) 7B-class (and OLMo-2-13B) trajectories. OLMo-2 and BLOOM show growth followed by sustained decline, and MAP-Neo-7B declines during its decay phase; Pythia-6.9b (terminating at 2.2× Chinchilla) and Amber show no decline. (b) All 21 trajectories.

Figure 1: Calibration robustness on Qwen3-8B. Per-layer cosine similarity between hl and its rank-d PCA reconstruction at width fractions d/Dl ∈ {10%, 20%, . . . , 90%}, measured on six 100Ktoken calibration corpora: five English (SlimPajama, MMLU, ARC-C, HellaSwag, WikiText) and Chinese SkyPile. Red dashed line marks the θ = 0.99 threshold. All six panels show the same dip at middle layers when d/Dl is small, indicating that more principal directions are required to faithfully reconstruct middle-layer activations. PCA (blue, solid) follows dθ,l at θ = 0.99; UNIFORM (orange, dashed) is B/L; INVERTED (red, dotted) is the mirror of PCA around UNIFORM, clipped at Dl. Within each panel the three curves are budget-matched (§4.1). Visual dispersion across the curves scales with σ99: large in Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen3-8B (σ99 ≈ 0.19), smaller in Gemma-3-4B (σ99 = 0.124) and LLaMA-3-8B (σ99 = 0.105).

Figure 6: Per-layer widths of the cosine (PCA) and explained-variance (PCA-EV) readouts on Qwen2.5-3B and Gemma-3-4B. Both panels show the trained allocations, budget-matched on each teacher. Open red circles mark the layers whose covariance is dominated by a single direction (top-1 eigenvalue share above 0.9): layer 2 of Qwen2.5-3B and layers 10 and 11 of Gemma-3-4B. Per-layer correlation of the two width vectors: r = 0.975 (Qwen2.5-3B) and 0.31 (Gemma-3-4B).

papers.selection_reason: Layer-wise intrinsic dimensionality analysis guides width pruning in LLMs, relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Measuring Layer-wise Intrinsic Dimensionality of FFNs in LLMs via PCA
papers.tldr: PCA reveals that LLM FFN capacity needs are typically highest in middle layers, enabling better width allocation than uniform designs under matched parameter budgets.

papers.abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent lies at the core of modern machine learning. However its classical analysis typically restricts the stepsize to be below a curvature-dependent stability threshold. Recent developments in deterministic optimization have challenged this paradigm, showing that suitably chosen large stepsizes can not only preserve convergence, but also accelerate Gradient Descent (GD). Whether this phenomenon persists in the presence of stochastic gradient noise has remained an open question (Wu et al., 2024). In this work, we answer this question affirmatively for the cross-entropy loss with linear predictors and two-layer neural networks, establishing an accelerated $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$ convergence rate. At the core of our analysis is a fine-grained characterization of the stochastic large-stepsize dynamics. This sharper control of the trajectory further yields tight convergence guarantees within the stable regime, improving existing bounds even in the deterministic setting. Taken together, our results show that the acceleration mechanism induced by large stepsizes survives stochasticity and extends beyond linear models. Numerical experiments demonstrate the benefits of large learning rates in practice.
authors: Konstantinos Emmanouilidis, Ziqing Xu, Salma Tarmoun, Lachlan MacDonald, Rene Vidal
bullets: Challenges the classical view that SGD stepsizes must remain below a curvature-dependent stability threshold.
Analyzes the dynamics of SGD with large stepsizes under stochastic gradient noise.
Proves accelerated O(T⁻²) convergence for linear predictors and two-layer neural networks.
Also improves convergence guarantees in the stable stepsize regime, including for deterministic optimization.
Numerical experiments show practical benefits from using large learning rates.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Training dynamics and final-loss scaling for the linear model (top) and two-layer model on frozen ConvNeXt features (bottom). Left panels show mean training loss at T = 6400, with the first 50 iterations enlarged in the insets. Right panels show mean final loss versus T under η = cT . Dashed lines indicate the T−2 reference rate which is derived in Corollary 4.2 and Corollary 5.4. Averages are over independent minibatch-sampling streams with the data and features held fixed.

Figure 2: Proof dependencies for the linear and two-layer neural-network analyses. Arrows indicate how the preparatory estimates lead to entrance, permanent stability, last-iterate convergence, and large-stepsize acceleration.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a general analysis of SGD with large learning rates, establishing accelerated convergence rates for LLMs and neural networks, which is highly relevant to optimization and training efficiency.
papers.title: SGD with Large Learning Rates: General Analysis & Improved Rates
papers.tldr: Large learning rates can accelerate stochastic gradient descent, achieving an O(T⁻²) convergence rate for cross-entropy with linear and two-layer neural-network predictors.

papers.abstract: Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipelines reconstruct a scene from images in a single forward pass, representing it as real-time-renderable 3D Gaussians. However, the resulting representations contain far more Gaussians than are needed to render the scene faithfully, especially when there are many input views. This drastically increases memory and storage requirements. Existing pruning methods either require costly re-optimization, which defeats the purpose of a single forward pass, or rely on simple strategies that do not exploit all the available information. We present AnyPrune, a transformer-based, optimization-free pruning module designed to work on top of any feedforward 3DGS pipeline. To remove unnecessary Gaussians, AnyPrune learns and exploits pipeline-specific redundancy patterns through a short single-GPU training on the frozen target feedforward pipeline. AnyPrune achieves better rendering quality than existing optimization-free pruning methods in most settings and generalizes to unseen datasets, as shown through extensive experiments across multiple feedforward pipelines, datasets, and input view counts. It prunes a 1.6M-Gaussian field in about $5\,\mathrm{s}$ on a consumer GPU, faster than every method that merges Gaussians or re-optimizes the field. It can also be combined with the pruning built into feedforward pipelines, pruning further at moderate ratios while preserving or improving rendering quality. Finally, it can even suggest a scene-specific pruning ratio that retains most of the quality.
authors: Nicola Leonetti, Federico Stella, Aoxiang Fan, Saqib Javed, Pascal Fua, Luigi Di Stefano
bullets: Addresses excessive Gaussian counts that increase memory and storage, particularly with many input views.
Uses a transformer-based pruning module trained briefly on a frozen target pipeline to learn pipeline-specific redundancy.
Works across multiple feedforward pipelines, datasets, and input-view counts, including unseen datasets.
Prunes a 1.6M-Gaussian field in about 5 seconds on a consumer GPU.
Can complement built-in pruning and suggest a scene-specific pruning ratio that preserves most quality.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of AnyPrune. A frozen feedforward 3DGS pipeline predicts the Gaussians G from the input views. G is rendered from the input poses and the render error Ev is used to compute a per-Gaussian feature vector fi which is encoded by an MLP and processed by the transformer together with the other features. As in SplatFormer, every head reads the per-Gaussian features computed by the backbone and, via a residual connection, the attributes of the input Gaussians. The residual heads predict adjustments to refine G into G′; the mask head predicts a log-space adjustment hi to be added to the Speedy-Splat sensitivity score Si to obtain each Gaussian’s keep logit zi (Eq. (3)). zi is used at training time to compute a factor mi = σ(zi/τ) by which to multiply the refined opacities of the Gaussians before rendering them. The masked field is rendered from the input and held-out views and supervised with Eq. (4), whose photometric term is denoted Lphoto. A sparsity term in the loss pushes the network to prune the redundant Gaussians. papers.abstract: A small ground robot can carry one camera and a few watts of compute, but the depth foundation models that could turn that camera into a range sensor are vision transformers sized for GPUs. We bring one to a Raspberry Pi 5 with the Hailo-8L, an accelerator that runs every layer in integer arithmetic, attention included. Quantised for it, Depth Anything V2 loses large parts of the scene, and we measure why: at 449 tokens, 91% of softmax weights fall below one int8 step while carrying 17-33% of the attention mass. Our answer is to distil, not quantise. An attention-free ResNet-34 U-Net student of Depth Anything V2-Large (24.5M parameters) runs at 27.1 FPS on the chip, its int8 output matches its float twin (Pearson 0.99993), and on held-out scenes of its simulated yard it is the most accurate depth network on the chip (AbsRel 0.269 against 0.354-0.530). On 1,000 stereo-verified points of a real outdoor drive it is not resolvably different from the vendor's Depth Anything V2-Small build, while running faster (27.1 vs 21.6 FPS). Ranging obstacles by where they meet the floor needs only the camera height, so mapping, hybrid-A* planning and SLAM run on the Pi's own CPU. In real-time hardware-in-the-loop tests in a Gaussian-splat reconstruction of a real yard, the stack reaches the goal without contact in 7.9$\pm$1.1 of 10 scenes, against 9.2$\pm$0.4 with exact obstacles, and in 7.7$\pm$0.7 on its own pose with simulated wheel odometry (ten seeds each; 8.2$\pm$0.4 with the real Pi and Hailo-8L in the loop, five seeds). The source code, pre-trained models and data are available at https://github.com/itaim18/DANIEL.
bullets: Quantising the transformer-based Depth Anything V2 directly causes severe information loss because many attention weights fall below int8 precision.
The proposed ResNet-34 U-Net student, distilled from Depth Anything V2-Large, runs at 27.1 FPS using 24.5M parameters.
Its int8 predictions closely match its float version (Pearson 0.99993) and achieve the best held-out simulated-yard accuracy among tested onboard models (AbsRel 0.269).
On 1,000 stereo-verified real-drive points, it performs comparably to the vendor’s Depth Anything V2-Small while running faster (27.1 vs. 21.6 FPS).
Integrated with mapping, planning, and SLAM, the system reaches goals without contact in most hardware-in-the-loop yard trials, though less often than with exact obstacle maps.

papers.selection_reason: Attention-free depth distillation enabling onboard robot navigation on low-power hardware; efficiency contribution.
papers.title: Seeing to Drive on a Single Board: Attention-Free Depth for Onboard Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: An attention-free, distilled depth model enables real-time monocular obstacle ranging and navigation on a Raspberry Pi 5 with Hailo-8L hardware.

papers.abstract: Block floating-point (BFP) quantization is widely adopted for efficient low-bit large language model (LLM) inference, where the choice of block scales plays a critical role in quantization accuracy. HiFloat4 (HiF4) employs a hierarchical scale encoding scheme consisting of a global E6M2 scale and two levels of binary scale extensions. However, its conventional rounding rule and fixed scale extension thresholds may not fully capture the statistical characteristics of the quantized tensors in practice, leading to suboptimal scale representations. In this work, we propose HiCal, an offline calibration approach that improves HiF4 quantization accuracy by refining the encoding decisions across all three scale levels. Specifically, we introduce a calibrated rounding bias for the Level-1 E6M2 scale and optimize the scale-extension thresholds at Levels 2 and 3 based on the empirical distributions of local group magnitudes. The resulting calibration parameters are determined offline and remain fixed during inference, while the hierarchical encoding continues to adapt to individual blocks through their local values. This design eliminates the need for per-block multi-candidate scale search while preserving the original deterministic HiF4 encoding procedure. Experiments across five synthetic and real activation distributions show that the proposed method reduces quantization MSE by 9.91%-23.50% relative to the original HiF4 scheme, including a 13.00% reduction on real Qwen3-8B activations. End-to-end evaluations across six benchmarks further show average-score improvements of 0.91 and 1.25 percentage points on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, respectively, without per-block multi-candidate search during inference.
authors: Zhiyuan Zhang, Yanzhao Li, Hui Dong, Sifan Cheng, Mingen Zheng, Hui Wang
bullets: Addresses suboptimal HiF4 scale representations caused by conventional rounding and fixed extension thresholds.
Calibrates the Level-1 E6M2 rounding bias and optimizes Level-2/3 scale-extension thresholds using empirical magnitude distributions.
Calibration parameters are fixed offline, while block-level hierarchical encoding remains deterministic and adaptive.
Reduces quantization MSE by 9.91%–23.50% across five activation distributions, including 13.00% on real Qwen3-8B activations.
Improves average end-to-end benchmark scores by 0.91 and 1.25 percentage points for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, respectively.

The three components highlighted in red—the E6M2 rounding rule and the Level-2 and Level-3 magnitude thresholds—are the parameters calibrated in this work; all other operations follow the original HiF4 procedure.

papers.selection_reason: Offline calibration for low-bit LLM quantization reduces inference memory requirements, fitting efficient inference.
papers.title: HiCal: Offline Calibration for Hierarchical Scale Encoding in Accurate HiF4 Quantization
papers.tldr: HiCal improves HiF4 low-bit LLM quantization through offline calibration of hierarchical scale encoding, reducing error and improving benchmark scores without added per-block search at inference.

papers.abstract: We present VenusOCR2.0, a compact 1B-parameter vision-language recognizer designed for both high-accuracy and high-throughput document parsing across text, tables, and formulas. To continuously improve recognition quality without self-training collapse, we build a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) data engine where the model acts strictly as a weakness probe, while external multi-expert medoid consensus, VLM visual verification, and factorized synthesis supply reliable supervision across pretraining, curated SFT, and RLVR. VenusOCR2.0 couples a dynamic-resolution SigLIP2 encoder and 2x2 spatial token merging with a Qwen3-0.6B decoder, adopting compact atomic OTSL tokens to shorten table sequences and reduce structural errors. To further eliminate the autoregressive decoding bottleneck, we introduce PTPv2, a lightweight ($\sim$67M) decoupled parallel draft module that combines frozen multi-layer verifier conditioning, a standalone learned mask, and block-causal all-position next-token prediction. On OmniDocBenchv1.6, VenusOCR2.0 achieves an overall score of 96.45 and a state-of-the-art 98.57 formula CDM, substantially outperforming massive general-purpose VLMs such as Gemini-3-Pro (92.91) and Qwen3-VL-235B (89.78). Deployed in vLLM on a single H20 GPU, PTPv2 delivers a 2.96x single-request speedup and up to 2.36x higher batched throughput while guaranteeing lossless, token-for-token equivalence with standard autoregressive decoding.
authors: Lei Li, Zheng Wei, Yi Yuan, Qingbin Liu, Jiang Bian, Zang Li
bullets: Targets unified parsing of text, tables, and formulas with high accuracy and throughput.
Uses bounded recursive self-improvement with external expert consensus, visual verification, and factorized synthesis to create reliable supervision.
Combines a dynamic-resolution SigLIP2 encoder, spatial token merging, Qwen3-0.6B decoder, and compact OTSL table tokens.
Introduces PTPv2, a ~67M-parameter parallel draft module that preserves token-for-token equivalence with autoregressive decoding.
On OmniDocBenchv1.6, reports 96.45 overall and 98.57 formula CDM; PTPv2 provides up to 2.96× single-request speedup and 2.36× batched throughput on one H20 GPU.

papers.title: VenusOCR2.0: Towards Efficient and Effective Document Parsing

papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have emerged as a serious competitor to gradient-boosted trees, predicting on a new table in a single forward pass by in-context learning. However, their attention is quadratic in the number of samples and features, which caps pretraining at small synthetic tables and forces inference on large ones to rely on chunking or subsampling. Row-compression models reduce the feature-wise cost, but only by discarding the cell-level representation, and remain quadratic in the number of samples. We introduce InducedTFM, which replaces both attention stages of a bidimensional TFM with the induced attention of the Set Transformer, preserving cell-level representations while making its cost linear in both samples and features. Under a training budget matched to a full-attention TabICLv2 reimplementation, InducedTFM matches its accuracy on TabArena and on a benchmark of larger datasets, and clearly outperforms a kernel linear-attention baseline of the same asymptotic cost. It overtakes TabICLv2 in inference time on narrow tables, reaching a 30x speed-up at 640K rows, although row compression remains preferable on wide tables.
authors: Salome Gobbi, Nicolas Atienza, Nicola Cancedda, Michael Arbel
bullets: Addresses the quadratic attention cost that limits TFM pretraining and inference on large tables.
Replaces both attention stages in a bidimensional TFM with Set Transformer-style induced attention.
Preserves cell-level representations while achieving linear cost in the number of samples and features.
Matches a full-attention TabICLv2 reimplementation on TabArena and larger-dataset benchmarks, and outperforms a same-cost kernel linear-attention baseline.
Provides up to a 30× inference speed-up at 640K rows on narrow tables; row compression remains preferable for wide tables.

papers.selection_reason: Induced attention makes tabular foundation models sub-quadratic, directly fitting efficient-attention research.
papers.title: InducedTFMs: A Family of Sub-Quadratic Tabular Foundation Models Using Induced Attention
papers.tldr: InducedTFM uses induced attention to make tabular foundation models linear in both rows and features while preserving cell-level representations, matching full attention accuracy and greatly accelerating inference on narrow, large tables.

papers.abstract: Models read a book, an hour of video, or an image in one forward pass. As the context grows, this pass slows down, loses accuracy, and stops at the context window. Sparse attention is efficient, but keeps the other two limitations. Grid probing, a recent training-free method, recovers the accuracy and extends the reach by asking a frozen model the same question about short local and strided spans of the input, but every question repeats the whole computation, since each span is encoded again. Our insight is that grid probing is emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside the model through prompts, since each probe only restricts which part of the input the question can see. We introduce Factorized Context Attention (FCA), a training-free block-sparse attention that runs the same pattern natively, as the attention of the model itself. FCA encodes the input once into a KV cache, reads all spans as masked sequences in one batched forward, and uses a stair position schedule to keep every span inside the trained position range. Across long video understanding, long-context text inference and image grounding, FCA matches the accuracy and the reach of grid probing at a fraction of its cost. It gains about 10 points over the single pass on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels, finds needles in videos of over a thousand frames and in texts four times the length of the window, and answers a later question about the same input in as little as a tenth of the time of grid probing. Native attention thus keeps what emulated attention gains without its cost, all with existing frozen language and vision-language models.
authors: Mohamed Eltahir, Manar Eyad, Yara Alzahrani, Fatimah Albesher, Duaa M. Tahir, Tanveer Hussain, Naeemullah Khan
bullets: Addresses the slowdown, accuracy loss, and context-window limits of one-pass long-context inference.
Uses training-free block-sparse attention to read local and strided spans from a single KV cache in one batched forward pass.
Employs a stair position schedule to keep spans within the model’s trained position range.
Matches grid probing’s accuracy and reach across long video, long-text inference, and image grounding while using a fraction of its cost.
Reports up to roughly 10-point gains over single-pass inference, finds information beyond the context window, and can be as fast as one-tenth of grid probing.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free block-sparse attention for native grid probing over long contexts; fits efficient attention and long-context models.
papers.title: Factorized Context Attention: From Emulated to Native Grid Probing
papers.tldr: Factorized Context Attention natively reproduces grid probing’s long-context benefits with much lower inference cost in frozen language and vision-language models.

papers.abstract: Accelerating instruction-based image editing when one instruction requests several edits is challenging. Many training-free accelerators for flow-matching image editors skip tokens whose prediction has stopped changing, but decide this with a single threshold for the whole image. With several edits, such a threshold, tuned for speed, freezes small and slowly settling edits first, and requested edits disappear. We propose TIDE (Training-free Instruction-aware Drift-based Editing), which gives every instruction part its own compute budget. First, TIDE finds the region of each part in the editor's own attention by unbalanced optimal transport, without masks or external models. Second, it freezes a token once its drift is small relative to its own part and moves it along the straight path to its endpoint estimate. Third, a sparse engine computes only the remaining tokens. We prove that part-agnostic rules cannot guarantee per-part error budgets, characterize the optimal per-part threshold policy up to one tie class per part, and derive when our rule attains it. On FLUX.2 Klein, one global threshold breaks at least one edit's budget in 89% of MICE-Bench images, and TIDE drops up to 77% fewer edits at matched or higher speed (48% on MICE-Bench), a gap human raters confirm. On the many-step Klein Base, TIDE is the fastest compared method on six benchmarks (4.81-4.89x) and needs 5.3x fewer TFLOPs than vanilla, the largest saving we measure. With the same settings, it is also the fastest compared method on Qwen-Image-Edit-2511, a second model family (3.46-3.52x), and drops the fewest edits on all six benchmarks. Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Jyotirmoy Nath, Neeraj Kumar, Brejesh Lall
bullets: Global freezing thresholds can prematurely remove small or slowly converging edits in multi-edit instructions.
TIDE localizes each instruction part using the editor’s attention and unbalanced optimal transport, without masks or external models.
It freezes tokens based on part-relative prediction drift, estimates their endpoints, and sparsely computes only active tokens.
On FLUX.2 Klein, TIDE reduces dropped edits by up to 77% at matched or higher speed and achieves up to 4.89× acceleration with 5.3× fewer TFLOPs.
It also performs fastest on Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 across the reported benchmarks, though results are limited to the evaluated models and benchmarks.

papers.title: Every Edit Its Own Budget: Per-Instruction Token Freezing for Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-Edit Image Editing
papers.tldr: TIDE accelerates multi-edit image generation without retraining by assigning each instruction part its own token-freezing budget, preserving edits while reducing computation.

papers.abstract: Conventional neural networks store synaptic parameters as explicit tensors whose persistent Flash footprint scales linearly (O(W)) with parameter count, constraining resource-limited edge microcontrollers. We formulate and systematically evaluate Fractal Neural Synthesis (FNS), a procedural weight derivation architecture that replaces hidden-layer matrices with a constant 24-byte coordinate seed Theta = (c_x, c_y, ell) in F_64^3 anchored near the complex quadratic bifurcation boundary dM of f_c(z) = z^2 + c. We introduce a large-bailout (R = 256) smooth escape kernel, four zero-overhead geometric sampling apertures--Cartesian Grid, coprime 3x3 Rule-of-Thirds (Z/9Z), phi-Vogel spiral, and multi-scale Harmonic Tripod--and prove conditional Kolmogorov (K_Kolm <= 192 + c_0 bits) and Shannon entropy bounds. Across magnifications zeta in [10^0, 10^8], C^1 Fourier and lattice-noise bases collapse to post-standardization rank ~2.25 and SHA-256 PRNG exhibits avalanche discontinuity (rho ~ 0.019, 50.6% micro-step retention), whereas dM uniquely sustains both rank (~10.0) and local continuity (rho in [0.81, 0.97], 89.2% retention). Under leak-free 10-fold CV across four zero-scaler-byte non-linear benchmarks, FNS with an INT8 readout surpasses 0-hidden Linear-INT8 by +3.6 to +10.8 pp while delivering 10.7x-129x total Flash reduction (725x-2,773x hidden reduction) relative to converged Float32 MLPs (90.30% Ionosphere in 285 B; 97.22% Optical Digits in 2,598 B; 97.90% PenDigits in 2,598 B; 87.00% Satimage in 1,570 B).
authors: Volkan Dagli, Zerrin Dagli, Daghan Dagli
bullets: Addresses the O(W) Flash cost of explicitly stored neural-network parameters on resource-limited microcontrollers.
Derives hidden-layer weights procedurally from a constant-size seed near the complex quadratic bifurcation boundary, using smooth escape dynamics and geometric sampling schemes.
The bifurcation-boundary representation preserves local continuity and effective rank across magnifications, unlike Fourier/lattice-noise bases and SHA-256 PRNGs evaluated in the abstract.
With an INT8 readout, FNS outperforms a zero-hidden Linear-INT8 baseline by 3.6–10.8 percentage points across four benchmarks while reducing Flash substantially versus Float32 MLPs.
Reported accuracies range from 87.00% to 97.90%, with total Flash reductions of 10.7×–129× relative to converged Float32 MLPs.

papers.selection_reason: Procedural constant-storage weight derivation directly targets memory-efficient neural deployment on edge devices.
papers.title: Fractal Neural Synthesis: Constant-Storage Procedural Weight Derivation via Complex Quadratic Boundary Dynamics
papers.tldr: Fractal Neural Synthesis generates neural weights from a 24-byte complex-dynamics seed, achieving strong benchmark accuracy with dramatically lower Flash storage on edge devices.

papers.abstract: Neural architecture search and LLM-driven evolution often reduce evaluation to a scalar fitness score, discarding failures that could explain why designs succeed or fail. We present a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves, the loop identifies two principles for 3D medical image segmentation. First, reallocating computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin-anatomy boundaries while reducing cost. Second, support-confined region contrast addresses errors between nested anatomical compartments, with anatomy-dependent triggers selecting when the rule applies. These principles produce LeanNeXt (0.78 MACs and 0.92 training-step time relative to nnU-Net; +1.63 Dice points on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation) and trigger-routed LeanNeXt+. The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop shows how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.
authors: Songtao Jiang, Yuan Wang, Fucheng Niu, Hualiang Wang, Jian Wu, Zuozhu Liu
bullets: Scalar fitness-only search discards diagnostic failure information; the proposed loop analyzes structured errors and tests falsifiable architectural hypotheses.
Under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, agents use counterfactual controls to convert validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules.

The loop finds that shifting computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin boundaries while reducing cost, while support-confined region contrast helps separate nested compartments.
LeanNeXt reaches 0.78× nnU-Net MACs and 0.92× training-step time, with a +1.63 Dice-point gain on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation.
Trigger-routed LeanNeXt+ improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and surpasses the larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30× its parameter count.

papers.title: Can AI Design a Better nnU-Net? A Hypothesis-Driven Architecture Discovery Loop from Failures to Design Rules
papers.tldr: A failure-analysis loop for LLM agents discovers reusable nnU-Net architecture rules that improve 3D medical image segmentation across diverse CT/MRI settings.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers (DiTs) achieve high-fidelity generation, but inference is expensive because every denoising step evaluates a large transformer over all spatiotemporal tokens of the video. Temporal caching accelerates them by reusing intermediate features across denoising steps. However, retaining dense feature tensors introduces a persistent storage cost that grows with video length, resolution, and cache coverage, reaching 109-346 GiB per video for the predictive caches we evaluate. Such states exceed the memory of a single GPU, so native caches must either be offloaded to the CPU, which slows generation, or be sharded across several GPUs, e.g., with sequence parallelism, so that the cache rather than the compute sets the number of GPUs. We instead shrink the cached state itself, exploiting its redundancy: a few channel patterns shared across tokens capture much of the energy of each cached feature. Based on this observation, we propose LRQ-Cache, a training-free method that combines low-rank approximation and quantization for feature-cache compression. LRQ-Cache represents each cached feature with a small set of factors, quantizes them before storage, and reconstructs the feature at reuse time, leaving cache mechanisms unchanged. Across three caching mechanisms on HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, LRQ-Cache reduces the persistent state of predictive caches by 42-71x, to 2.3-4.9 GiB per video. VBench stays within 0.25 pp of the native cache for TeaCache, and the larger drops of the Wan2.1 predictive caches, up to 3.5 pp, shrink at higher ranks. As a result, predictive caches that exceed the memory of a single 80 GB H100 GPU fit on it with LRQ-Cache, making generation 2.7-5.9x faster than with CPU-offloaded native caches.
authors: Ruizhe Yao, Zhen Huang, Songpan Gao, Danyi Liu, Zijian Cao, Weijie Zheng, Haohuan Fu
bullets: Video diffusion caches can require 109–346 GiB per video, forcing CPU offloading or multi-GPU sharding.
The training-free method stores low-rank factors of cached features in quantized form and reconstructs them when reused.
Across three caching mechanisms on HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, cache size drops 42–71× to 2.3–4.9 GiB per video.
Quality remains within 0.25 percentage points for TeaCache; Wan2.1 predictive-cache drops reach up to 3.5 points but improve with higher ranks.
Previously oversized predictive caches fit on a single 80 GB H100 and run 2.7–5.9× faster than CPU-offloaded native caches.

papers.selection_reason: Low-rank and quantization compression of video diffusion feature caches directly targets memory efficiency during inference, fitting the KV-cache/memory-efficiency subtopic.
papers.title: LRQ-Cache: Compressing Feature Caches in Video Diffusion via Low-Rank Approximation and Quantization
papers.tldr: LRQ-Cache compresses video diffusion feature caches with low-rank approximation and quantization, greatly reducing memory use while largely preserving generation quality and improving speed.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models often retain only a limited set of past token positions for an attention query. A common strategy scores positions individually and keeps the highest-ranked K. Yet attention weights are renormalized over the chosen set: two individually important positions need not form the best pair. We ask whether independent ranking suffices even when each importance score measures the exact downstream change in next-token predictions caused by deleting that position alone. It does not. A four-position construction makes the ranked pair incur 133.2 times the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence of the optimal pair, and a parametric family proves that this multiplicative gap is unbounded. An exact exchange identity and preference reversals for every K >= 2 explain the interaction. In exhaustive frozen-model audits of SmolLM2, Gemma, and Qwen, exact-singleton Top-4 leaves at least 10% relative improvement within a fully enumerated 24-position candidate pool in 55/60, 49/60, and 60/60 cases, respectively. SwapCert, a same-budget one-swap audit, detects 157/164 such cases and returns directly checkable improving supports. A KL-margin certificate relates support fidelity to next-token stability; larger-budget, multi-layer cached-decoding experiments measure predictive fidelity at K = 128 and 256. These results establish joint support quality as an essential object of analysis for sparse attention and motivate downstream-aware support selection under inference constraints.
bullets: Individually important positions may form a poor set after attention renormalization; optimal selection must account for interactions.
A four-position example yields a 133.2× KL-divergence gap, while a parametric family shows the gap can be unbounded.

papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have demonstrated significant accuracy across various machine learning tasks. However, these networks suffer from a huge number of parameters and computations, which leads to time-consuming processes. Consequently, parameter pruning approaches have been proposed to compress DNNs and efficiently implement them. The main challenge in pruning is selecting the appropriate parameters for pruning without significantly damaging the accuracy. In this paper, we propose SPRUNN, an algorithmic pruning approach based on the structural proximity criterion for filter pruning in convolutional layers of deep neural networks. Structural Proximity (SP) calculates filter similarity by considering all filters and comparing each one with the others, effectively identifying less important filters for pruning in the convolutional layers. Furthermore, we integrate this approach with fine-grained pruning in Fully Connected(FC)layerstocompresstheDNNsthatinclude both convolutional and FC layers.Toenhancetheaccuracyoftheprunedmodel,weproposealearning rate refinement strategy during the retraining phase. Experimental results demonstrate that SPRUNN achieves significant compression with high accuracy across diverse architectures and datasets.

bullets: Targets the computational and parameter overhead of deep neural networks.

Combines filter pruning in convolutional layers with fine-grained pruning in fully connected layers.
Applies learning-rate refinement during retraining to improve the accuracy of pruned models.
Reports significant compression with high accuracy across diverse architectures and datasets.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) decoding emits one token per forward pass, reloading the full model each time, so LLM inference on edge devices is memory-bound while the compute units sit idle. Speculative decoding puts that idle compute to work by verifying several drafted tokens in a single pass. State-of-the-art parallel drafters such as DFlash and DSpark propose an entire block of draft tokens in one forward pass, which makes drafting compute-efficient. However, they are deployed with draft chains whose length is capped by the block size they are trained for, leaving most of the computational budget for verification unused. To tackle this problem, we propose Pando, which builds dynamic draft trees on top of a parallel drafter and thereby removes this cap. Pando employs noise-coupled pruning, which draws the target model's sampling noise before drafting and ranks candidate branches under that noise, so the tree retains the branches the target will actually sample. Noise coupling is lossless and requires no retraining or additional model pass, yet increases acceptance length by up to $8.4\%$ on Qwen3-8B. To optimize and evaluate Pando configurations across hardware, we normalize an operator-level roofline to AR decoding, reducing every platform to its ridge point. On a representative edge device, a 16-node Pando tree attains $5.3\times$ speedup and $4.2\times$ energy reduction over AR decoding: $25\%$ faster than DSpark's released chain, and $27\%$ faster and $72\%$ more energy-efficient than an EAGLE-3 tree. The best configurations remain memory-bound on every edge device we model, so added compute capacity does not reduce their latency.
authors: Joren Dumoulin, Hyoukjun Kwon, Subhankar Pal, Steven Li, Vignesh Vivekraja, Marian Verhelst

Increases acceptance length by up to 8.4% on Qwen3-8B; a 16-node tree reaches 5.3× speedup and 4.2× lower energy on a representative edge device.

papers.abstract: Purpose: To develop, evaluate, and publicly release FlashSegmentator, an open-source inference pipeline that increases the throughput of TotalSegmentator without retraining or loss of segmentation accuracy. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study used public datasets: 73 CT examinations from the TotalSegmentator test split (median age, 65 years; 37 male, 35 female, one unknown), 30 abdominal CT examinations from the Beyond the Cranial Vault (BTCV) dataset, 512 training-split CT examinations for concurrent-process analysis, and 55 MRI examinations. FlashSegmentator adds static-shape compilation, pipelining, batched sliding-window inference, and GPU postprocessing. Throughput was compared with the reference implementation (including its lower-resolution modes) and FastSegmentator on GH200, A100, and T4 GPUs. Dice agreement was tested with two one-sided tests (margin, +/-0.01). Results: FlashSegmentator processed 3782, 1810, and 270 examinations per hour on the GH200, A100, and T4 (57.7, 33.9, and 6.4 times the reference implementation and 3.20, 2.50, and 1.22 times compiled FastSegmentator). Dice scores were equivalent for all 117 structures on every GPU (mean difference <= 1.2 x 10^-5; P < .001) and at the examination level on BTCV. In contrast, the lower-resolution modes of the reference implementation processed 181 and 213 examinations per hour on the A100 but reduced mean Dice by 0.116 and 0.241. On MRI, throughput increased 94-fold with all 50 structures equivalent. Estimated A100 cloud cost per 10,000 examinations decreased from 997 to 29 US dollars. Conclusion: FlashSegmentator increased the throughput of TotalSegmentator on data center and entry-level GPUs without loss of segmentation accuracy compared with the reference implementation.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses large vision-language models (LVLMs) by calibrating quantization parameters on a small dataset without retraining. However, despite increasingly sophisticated calibration strategies, prior methods suffer substantial performance degradation under low-bit weight--activation quantization. To understand this degradation, we locate where quantization error is concentrated and examine the corresponding weight and activation distributions. We observe that a few outliers dominate the ranges shared by per-channel (PC) weights and per-token (PT) activations, leaving insufficient resolution for most values and mapping many of them to zero. These findings motivate a shift in focus from calibration refinement to the underlying quantization representation. We therefore present Rotate-and-Refine Quantization (RRQ) as a simple, effective baseline for LVLM PTQ, combining local Hadamard transforms with group quantization and efficient group-aware execution. Across 8 multimodal tasks and diverse quantization settings, RRQ substantially outperforms baselines while reducing inference time and memory usage. At W4A4, it retains over 96\% of full-precision performance on 8B models and over 99\% on a 32B model, compared with less than 8\% for these baselines. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/kmc3661/RRQ
authors: Minchan Kang, Kyeonghye Park, Seoyoung Cho, Junhee Lee, Daeshik Kim, Yucheol Cho

Across 8 multimodal tasks, RRQ improves performance over prior baselines while reducing inference time and memory use.

papers.abstract: We propose LoopDVR, a framework for converting pretrained Transformer-based dense visual recognition models into parameter-efficient looped networks. Rather than reducing the network width or depth directly, LoopDVR reuses Transformer blocks across layers in both the ViT backbone and Transformer decoder, reducing the number of parameters while retaining the original computational structure. However, naively sharing parameters can disrupt the distinct transformations learned at different depths. To address this challenge, we identify suitable sharing groups based on inter-layer representation dissimilarity and keep the final backbone block independent for multi-scale feature construction. We then initialize each shared backbone block with the pretrained weights of its group's terminal layer to better preserve the learned representations. An independent Loop Adapter at each layer further helps retain depth-specific transformations within shared blocks. Subsequently, we distill visual representations into the looped backbone and integrate it with a looped decoder for task-specific training. Experiments demonstrate that LoopDVR achieves the best accuracy--parameter trade-offs across dense recognition tasks. Compared with the reference models, it reduces parameters by approximately 28% while maintaining competitive accuracy. Notably, LoopDet-S achieves 50.9 box AP with only 7.0M parameters, highlighting its effectiveness in compact models.

papers.abstract: Linear attention replaces softmax attention with a linear formulation, enabling linear-time computation with a fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value cache. These computational and memory advantages have attracted growing interest in linear attention for long-context language modeling. However, compressing past information into a fixed-size state causes memory collisions that hinder long-context understanding. Although DeltaNet mitigates memory collisions through delta-rule updates and Gated DeltaNet extends this approach with gating, these mechanisms may also discard information relevant to future predictions. To address this limitation, we introduce Integral DeltaNet, which maintains two complementary recurrent states: a fast-updating delta state that captures current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of the delta state. At readout, the model adaptively combines these states to access information across different timescales. We further derive a chunkwise parallel formulation that enables hardware-efficient training. We evaluate Integral DeltaNet using 340M and 1.3B parameter models trained from scratch on 15B and 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, respectively. Comparisons with strong recurrent baselines show improved overall performance in language modeling, commonsense reasoning, real-world and synthetic retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation. We also compare training throughput and activation memory, as well as decoding latency and memory.
authors: Junsoo Oh, Jihun Yun, Junhyuck Kim, Hanbaek Lyu
bullets: Linear attention avoids growing key-value caches but can lose information through fixed-size memory collisions.
The method uses a delta state for current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of past delta states.
An adaptive readout combines both states to retrieve information across multiple timescales.
A chunkwise parallel formulation supports hardware-efficient training.
Experiments report improved performance across language modeling, reasoning, retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation, alongside evaluations of efficiency and memory use.

papers.abstract: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) achieves linear computational complexity through recurrent state updates, but sequential dependencies between chunks limit parallelism, particularly for long-context workloads with small batch sizes or limited head-level parallelism per GPU. We present FlashQLA, a context-parallel execution framework for GDN that exposes additional sequence-level parallelism while reducing boundary-state preprocessing overhead. FlashQLA reduces boundary-state preprocessing overhead through decay-aware preparation and extends sequence parallelism across GPUs with Dual CP, which shares summary computation across parallelism levels. Workload-adaptive Auto CP and CP-aware kernel co-design further improve execution efficiency. FlashQLA achieves $1.7\times$-$3.1\times$ forward speedup and up to $4.4\times$ backward speedup over Flash Linear Attention (FLA) on a single GPU. On eight GPUs with context lengths up to 1M tokens, Dual CP achieves up to $4.8\times$ forward speedup and $4.4\times$ speedup for combined forward and backward execution over FLA KCP.

bullets: Addresses limited parallelism from GDN’s sequential chunk dependencies, especially for long contexts and small batch sizes.

Adds workload-adaptive Auto CP and context-parallel-aware kernel co-design for improved efficiency.
Reports 1.7×–3.1× forward and up to 4.4× backward speedup over FLA on one GPU.
Across eight GPUs and up to 1M-token contexts, Dual CP reaches up to 4.8× forward speedup and 4.4× combined forward/backward speedup over FLA KCP.

papers.abstract: Self-attention over tens of thousands of tokens dominates the generation time of video diffusion transformers, because its cost grows quadratically with sequence length. The FP4 matrix products of modern GPUs can speed up attention, but the 4-bit rounding of the queries Q and the keys K introduces large errors. We show that the exponential in softmax amplifies the error of their product QK, which therefore dominates the attention error. We propose DeCo-Attention, a co-design of algorithm and system for low-precision attention. DeCo-Attention is training-free and compensates the rounding error of Q and K along a few principal directions found by a per-head eigendecomposition. The lightweight compensation terms are appended to Q and K as extra channels, so the FP4 matrix product corrects its own rounding error while it computes the attention scores. Once the products run in FP4, the softmax bounds the kernel, and we optimize the softmax so that the gain of FP4 computation translates into realized speedup. With QK in FP4, we implement DeCo-Attention with the rest of attention in FP8 on GB300 and VR200 and in FP4 on RTX PRO 6000. On Wan2.2, these kernels run 2.13x, 2.49x, and 2.82x faster than BF16 attention, and the whole generation runs 1.55x, 1.68x, and 1.80x faster. On four video generation models, the FP8 configuration achieves LPIPS comparable to prior 8-bit QK methods, and the fully FP4 configuration lower LPIPS than prior fully 4-bit kernels.
authors: Yuhang He, Harrison Zhang, Fanrong Li, Chang Liu, RuQing G. Xu, Perkz Zheng, Zhenhua Wang, Rajeev Rao, Mengdi Wang, Sharan Chetlur, Jun Yang
bullets: Targets the quadratic cost of attention over tens of thousands of video tokens.
Uses per-head eigendecomposition to identify principal error directions in quantized queries and keys.
Appends compensation channels to Q and K, allowing the FP4 matrix product to correct its own rounding error.
Combines FP4 QK with optimized softmax and lower-precision attention components for practical speedups.
Reports 2.13–2.82× faster attention and 1.55–1.80× faster generation on Wan2.2, with competitive or improved LPIPS versus prior low-precision methods.

An eigendecomposition (EVD) of the Gram matrices of 1/256 of the tokens gives the 32 principal directions 𝐵. The projections of the residuals and of the quantized operands onto 𝐵 are appended as NVFP4 compensation channels, so 𝑄′ and 𝐾 ′ have 192 channels. papers.selection_reason: Proposes DeCo-Attention, a training-free method to compensate for low-precision (FP4) errors in video diffusion transformers. This directly addresses efficient attention mechanisms in video generation models.
papers.title: DeCo-Attention: Decompose to Compensate for Low-Precision Attention
papers.tldr: DeCo-Attention makes long-context video diffusion attention faster in FP4 by correcting QK rounding errors with lightweight, training-free compensation.

papers.abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) requires choosing both a batch size and a parallel configuration. Existing systems make these decisions in isolation, tuning parallelism for throughput and batch size for convergence, but neither objective alone determines training efficiency. We present LIBRA, a lightweight runtime framework that co-tunes batch size and parallel configuration to minimize end-to-end time. LIBRA treats throughput and convergence as two noisy objectives and searches their joint space using parallel noisy expected hypervolume improvement (qNEHVI). To make this runtime search efficient, we propose hierarchical pruning, which removes infeasible and low-throughput parallel configurations through system-level performance estimation and then narrows batch-size candidates through critical-batch-size-aware convergence monitoring. We further design acquisition-guided parallel evaluation (AGPE), which evaluates surviving candidates concurrently across GPU groups in order of their acquisition values. On clusters of up to 256 GPUs, LIBRA reduces time-to-convergence by 31.1% on average over state-of-the-art methods, while runtime tuning accounts for only 0.3-3.5% of overall time.
authors: Shengkai Lyu, Hairui Zhao, Daran Sun, Yida Gu, Xingchen Liu, YueYuan Zhou, Zheng Wei, Guangming Tan, Dingwen Tao
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of tuning parallelism for throughput and batch size for convergence separately.
Uses parallel noisy expected hypervolume improvement (qNEHVI) to search the joint configuration space.
Applies hierarchical pruning to discard infeasible or low-throughput parallel setups and refine batch-size candidates using convergence monitoring.
Uses acquisition-guided parallel evaluation to test promising configurations concurrently across GPU groups.
On clusters of up to 256 GPUs, reduces time-to-convergence by 31.1% on average, with tuning overhead of 0.3–3.5% of total time.
