papers.abstract: Recently, physics-inspired neural networks have gained widespread attention due to their interpretability. The closed-form, frequency-time decoupled solution of the wave equation offers linear complexity and allows different frequency components to evolve independently, making it a potential alternative solution for efficient image super-resolution. Therefore, a physics-inspired wave evolution attention framework is proposed, namely WaveSR. The WaveSR framework involves two key modules, i.e., wave evolution attention (WEA) and Frequency-Adaptive Feed-Forward Network (FA-FFN). The WEA module achieves feature interactions through the analytical solution of the 2D wave equation in the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) domain, enabling independent evolution of different frequency components with learnable wave speed \(c\) and damping coefficient \(\alpha\). The FA-FFN module realizes adaptive frequency feature selection through learnable spectral modulation, effectively enhancing feature representation capability. Subsequently, we employ a two-stage training strategy with a hybrid objective that combines a spatial-domain pixel loss and a frequency-domain loss to improve reconstruction quality. Our method provides a preliminary exploration of physics-inspired neural networks for efficient image super-resolution.
authors: Xiaoyan Lei, Biao Luo, Wenlong Zhang, Tingwen Huang, Chunhua Yang, Weihua Gui

Frequency-Adaptive Feed-Forward Network selects and enhances frequency features through learnable spectral modulation.
A two-stage training strategy combines spatial pixel loss with frequency-domain loss to improve reconstruction quality.
The work is presented as a preliminary exploration of physics-inspired neural networks for efficient super-resolution.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of shared weights along the depth of the network. Recent looped diffusion transformers are trained from scratch, which repeats the full pretraining cost although strong pretrained non-looped diffusion transformers exist. We propose Distill to Loop (Dooop), which distills a pretrained non-looped diffusion transformer into a looped student whose blocks are initialized from the teacher's. We cast distillation as a fixed-point iteration toward the teacher, in which the output after every loop is trained toward the teacher, and each loop is one step of an ordinary differential equation in depth. As a result, one model runs any number of loops at test time without retraining, and the higher-order ODE solvers of diffusion model sampling can be applied along the depth dimension for better results. Meanwhile, because a looped model produces an output after every loop, we also construct loop guidance between the outputs of different loop counts, which improves the generated samples at little extra compute. On SD3-medium, a looped student with about 37% of the teacher's parameters matches the teacher on average over GenEval, ImageReward, PickScore and HPSv2.1 with two to four loops, and with two loops it uses about 58% of the teacher's compute. And on a four-step SD3-medium, loop guidance raises the average of the four metrics from 88.2 to 99.2.
bullets: Addresses the cost of training looped diffusion transformers from scratch by distilling an existing non-looped teacher.
Shares one block across depth and trains each loop output toward the teacher using a fixed-point, ODE-inspired distillation process.
Supports variable loop counts at inference without retraining and applies higher-order ODE solvers along the depth dimension.
Introduces loop guidance using outputs from different loop counts to improve samples with little extra computation.

On SD3-medium, a student with about 37% of the teacher’s parameters matches average evaluation quality with two to four loops; two loops use about 58% of teacher compute, while loop guidance improves the reported four-step score average from 88.2 to 99.2.

papers.abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) accelerates autoregressive decoding through block-wise prediction, but remains vulnerable to error accumulation across sequentially generated blocks. To investigate this limitation, we analyze the distinction between block-wise and sequence-level cumulative information loss (CIL). Specifically, when the model generates using its own previous outputs without access to reference answers, the input-conditional gap equals the cross-block dependence of the reference targets. To improve prediction when these generated prefixes are imperfect, we propose Dual-MTP, which supervises shared prediction heads under full and randomly masked contexts. Together, complete-prefix supervision and context perturbations provide complementary training signals while retaining the MTP architecture. To characterize this training objective, we use the normalized dual loss to bound the divergence between the model's predictive distributions under full and masked contexts. Experiments across five backbones and six tasks spanning mathematical reasoning and GLUE understanding show that Dual-MTP achieves the highest average task score on four of five backbones, with gains of up to 2.46 points over MTP. On mathematical reasoning tasks, Dual-MTP also achieves 1.4 to 1.9 times the decoding throughput of the NTP reference. Together, these results show that dual-context supervision can improve prediction accuracy while retaining efficient multi-token decoding.
authors: Tangyu Jiang, Zhanke Zhou, Haodi Wang, Yiu-ming Cheung, Xiaohua Jia, Bo Han
bullets: MTP suffers from cumulative information loss when generated prefixes contain errors and differ from reference contexts.
The paper distinguishes block-wise from sequence-level loss and links the input-conditional gap to cross-block dependence in reference targets.
Dual-MTP applies shared prediction heads with full-prefix and randomly masked-context supervision.
A normalized dual loss bounds divergence between predictions under full and masked contexts.
Across five backbones and six tasks, Dual-MTP improves average scores on four backbones, with gains up to 2.46 points; reasoning-task throughput is 1.4–1.9× NTP.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models must process continuous streams of visual observations, and the resulting computational cost limits real-time robotic control. Token pruning reduces this cost, but a fixed semantic scale of perceptual representation can overlook information needed at different stages of manipulation. We show that perceptual semantics can guide effective token selection without relying on internal attention when the selection scale adapts to the scene's evolving semantic structure. Based on this observation, we introduce TauPrune-VLA, a training-free method that controls the scale of the retained perceptual representation through a single perception temperature $\tau$. To adapt this scale as manipulation proceeds, TauPrune-VLA updates $\tau$ online using trends in perceptual semantics, with robot-state changes and action magnitude regulating the adjustment strength. While these semantics evolve over the course of manipulation, they remain relatively stable between consecutive frames. This continuity allows retention indices computed from the current observation to be applied at the next policy invocation, enabling token selection to run asynchronously with inference and reducing pruning overhead. Evaluated across diverse VLA models and simulation benchmarks, TauPrune-VLA achieves up to a $1.86\times$ inference speedup while maintaining near-baseline task success rates. We further validate its effectiveness on two real-world robotic platforms.
authors: Yifeng Lin, Liuxiang Qiu, Yunfeng Chen, Tiesong Zhao
bullets: Fixed-scale token pruning can miss information needed at different manipulation stages and adds computational overhead.
The training-free method uses a single perception temperature, τ, to control the scale of retained visual representations.
τ is updated online from semantic trends, with robot-state changes and action magnitude regulating adaptation strength.
Stable semantics across consecutive frames enable asynchronous reuse of token-retention indices during inference.
Evaluations across VLA models, simulation benchmarks, and two real robots show effective speedups with near-baseline success rates.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models enable action- and camera-controlled exploration, yet struggle to maintain consistent spatial geometry and appearance when revisiting previously explored locations. Historical KV caches help auto-regressive video diffusion models maintain long-term consistency, but their retrieval and attention computation introduce substantial latency as history grows. We propose DraftKV, a training-free framework that retrieves historical KV caches based on geometric grounding and query-conditioned relevance, while combining CPU offloading with tile-wise streaming attention to reduce GPU memory usage and inference latency. Theoretically, we show that draft relevance reproduces the mean branch of full-resolution block relevance exactly, so its deviation is confined to the $\beta$-weighted max branch, and we bound retrieval utility loss in terms of the measured Top-K selection overlap. We further show that draft relevance cannot distinguish blocks with similar pooled descriptors regardless of camera pose, motivating geometric grounding before refinement. Then, we introduce streaming CG-Attention, which overlaps CPU-to-GPU KV transfers with attention computation through tile-wise streaming, hiding transfer latency while maintaining bounded GPU memory usage. Experiments across diverse model families show that DraftKV achieves superior generation quality and consistency while achieving $3.27\times$ end-to-end speedup and 42.2% peak GPU memory reduction over other CPU-offloaded KV cache retrieval methods. Notably, DraftKV enables high-quality interactive world generation with historical KV retrieval on a single H100 GPU using SolarWM-33B.
authors: Xiaoling Zhou, Haopeng Li, Yufa Zhou, Rui Ding, Yu Li, Jun Lin, Enze Xie, Chunhua Shen, Xuan Shen
bullets: Addresses spatial and visual inconsistency when revisiting locations, while reducing the latency and memory cost of growing KV histories.
Uses geometric grounding and query-conditioned draft relevance to retrieve the most useful historical KV cache blocks.
Introduces tile-wise streaming attention with CPU offloading to overlap KV transfers and computation under bounded GPU memory.
Reports 3.27× end-to-end speedup and 42.2% lower peak GPU memory than other CPU-offloaded retrieval methods.
Supports high-quality historical-KV world generation on a single H100 GPU with SolarWM-33B.

papers.abstract: For latency-constrained candidate ranking, we propose a similarity-identity decoupling framework that separates target-history compatibility from target-only information. We study two orders for computing pooled similarity, similarity-then-pool and pool-then-similarity, and identify linearity of the similarity operator in its history argument, for each fixed target, as sufficient for their equivalence, justifying the cheaper pool-then-similarity form. We instantiate the framework as multi-head efficient lightweight operator for decoupling identity and similarity (MELODI), whose similarity branch combines target-conditioned multi-head history pooling with a single residual-free cross layer that is linear in its pooled-history input and whose identity branch is problem-dependent. On public benchmark datasets, MELODI matches or surpasses the evaluated target-aware and target-agnostic baselines. On two large-scale industrial datasets, its area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), normalised discounted cumulative gain (NDCG), and recall values are equal to or higher than those of the evaluated target-aware baselines. Processor measurements show lower latency than the evaluated candidate-conditioned baselines at large candidate counts, further reduced by request-local history reuse.
authors: Quoc Phong Nguyen, Vuong Le, Volodymyr Vaskovych, Julien Monteil
bullets: Separates target-history compatibility from target-only information for latency-constrained ranking.
Shows that pool-then-similarity is equivalent to similarity-then-pool when the similarity operator is linear in the history input.
Uses target-conditioned multi-head history pooling and a residual-free cross layer for its similarity branch, with a problem-dependent identity branch.
Matches or surpasses evaluated baselines on public benchmarks and achieves equal or higher reported AUPRC, NDCG, and recall than target-aware baselines on two industrial datasets.
Has lower measured latency than evaluated candidate-conditioned baselines at large candidate counts; request-local history reuse reduces latency further.

papers.title: MELODI: Similarity-Identity Decoupling for Lightweight Ranking
papers.tldr: MELODI decouples target-history similarity from target identity to enable lightweight, low-latency candidate ranking without sacrificing evaluated ranking quality.

papers.abstract: Comparing language-model checkpoints requires estimating performance differences, yet evaluation pipelines can pay to score responses whose contributions cancel from those differences. We introduce Contrast-Aware Feedback Acquisition (CAFA), a sampler-agnostic method that identifies which scores a requested linear report needs before acquiring feedback. CAFA groups identical scoring inputs and aggregates their report coefficients, removing queries beyond ordinary caching while preserving the fully scored result. For a fixed response bank and an otherwise unrestricted scalar scorer, we characterize necessary and sufficient query sets for exact recovery of sample means, either alone or jointly with ordinary sample covariances. On controlled updates, CAFA removes 55.8% and 90.1% of the scoring inputs remaining after caching for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, respectively, averaged over four generation repetitions. Across three online group relative policy optimization (GRPO) trajectories, Independent Star sampling with CAFA achieves 46.1-51.3% lower recorded generation-plus-feedback cost than independent autoregressive sampling with caching at a common empirical precision threshold (RMS MCSE $\leq 0.04$). This is a post hoc comparison of completed runs on a fixed budget grid. All 504 evaluated report cells reproduce the fully scored means and covariances to numerical precision. We provide a modular implementation supporting existing response banks, versioned caches and external scorers.
authors: Hui Zhang, Haoda Yue, Bicheng Deng, Yuanchao Zhu, Jun He, Rui Qian
bullets: Targets redundant scoring when contributions cancel in checkpoint-difference reports.
Groups identical scoring inputs and aggregates report coefficients before requesting feedback.
Characterizes necessary and sufficient query sets for exact sample means and joint covariances under an unrestricted scalar scorer.
Removed 55.8%–90.1% of post-caching scoring inputs in controlled updates and reduced recorded generation-plus-feedback cost by 46.1%–51.3% in three GRPO trajectories.
Reproduced all 504 evaluated report cells to numerical precision; comparisons were post hoc on completed runs and a fixed budget grid.

papers.selection_reason: Reduces scoring/feedback cost in LLM evaluation pipelines, fitting the broad Efficient AI interest.
papers.title: Scoring What Matters: Exact Feedback Reduction for Language Model Comparison
papers.tldr: CAFA exactly reduces language-model comparison feedback by acquiring only scores that affect the requested reports, substantially lowering evaluation cost after caching.

papers.abstract: Block-causal video diffusion generates long videos block by block, conditioned on a persistent key-value (KV) cache. After each block is denoised, an extra noise-free ($t=0$) forward pass writes its clean KV into the cache; once distillation and speculative early exit make denoising cheap, this clean KV update dominates the runtime. Reusing stale KV shortens the update, but stale memory corrupts the conditioning of later blocks and inflates their denoising steps, so the saved compute reappears downstream. We present SAMR (Step-Aware Memory Reconstruction), a training-free method for frozen causal video DiTs that refreshes only part of the cache and reconstructs the rest without DiT forwards. Our key observation is that, once rotary position phases are removed, motion-aligned historical KV and the in-flight KV a token holds at its exit step are complementary estimates of its clean KV. SAMR debiases in-flight KV with offline-calibrated per-head affine maps in Pre-RoPE space, fuses the two estimates, and reserves true $t=0$ refreshes for tokens flagged by an attention-readout error proxy, all executed by tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels. On 48-second LongLive-1.3B videos, SAMR reduces DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7% relative to dense KV updates, lowers downstream denoising steps, and improves final-quarter PSNR over token reuse by 1.61 dB (1.14 dB on held-out VidProM-16). The reconstruction also transfers to frozen Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B: zero-shot, it reduces reuse-induced step inflation ($2.47 \to 2.30$ steps/token) and improves late PSNR by $+0.33$ dB, and a one-time training-free calibration recovers the diagnostic score that zero-shot transfer lowers ($89.62 \to 91.10$).
authors: Jian Yang, Zhizhuo Kou, Qiyuan Zhu, Han Chen, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Persistent clean-KV updates can dominate runtime once denoising is accelerated, while stale-cache reuse increases later denoising work.
SAMR combines motion-aligned historical KV with in-flight KV, using calibrated affine correction and selective true $t=0$ refreshes.
Tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels implement the reconstruction efficiently without retraining the frozen video DiT.
On LongLive-1.3B, it cuts DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7%, while improving final-quarter PSNR over token reuse.
It transfers to Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B, reducing reuse-induced step inflation and improving late-stage PSNR, with calibration further recovering diagnostic quality.

papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks for multimodal audio-visual classification reach high accuracy by adopting deep-learning machinery: multi-stage convolutional or transformer encoders trained end-to-end with surrogate-gradient backpropagation through time. These prior works typically rely on full-precision (32-bit) parameters and do not treat hardware efficiency as a primary design objective. In this paper, we propose NeuTNN-AV, a much simpler hardware-amenable multimodal substrate built on the recently proposed NeuroAI Temporal Neural Network (NeuTNN) and demonstrate that it can match or outperform state-of-the-art SNN baselines with a fraction of their synapse counts. NeuTNN neurons carry multiple active dendritic segments. Each input line spikes at most once (temporal coding) and every weight is learned via a local reward-modulated spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) rule. All weights are 4-bit integers and inference uses only comparisons and additions. On CREMA-D, it reaches 78.6% with 2.34M synapses establishing a new state-of-the-art SNN accuracy, against 77.14% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). On UrbanSound8K-AV, NeuTNN reaches 98.82% with 1.38M synapses, against 96.85% for SMMT (9.99M parameters) and 98.96% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). Weight memory is 23-106x smaller than the spiking baselines, and the measured synaptic energy per inference is two to three orders of magnitude lower. Furthermore, the proposed NeuTNN learns CREMA-D in a single pass with 73.8% accuracy and demonstrates rapid online continual learning by adapting to unseen actors from a few dozen clips.
authors: Shanmuga Venkatachalam, Quinn Jacobson, John Paul Shen
bullets: Uses temporal coding with at most one spike per input line and multi-segment dendritic neurons.
Learns all 4-bit integer weights through local reward-modulated STDP, avoiding backpropagation through time; inference uses comparisons and additions.
Achieves 78.6% on CREMA-D with 2.34M synapses and 98.82% on UrbanSound8K-AV with 1.38M synapses.
Reports 23–106× lower weight memory and two- to three-orders-of-magnitude lower measured synaptic energy than spiking baselines.
Supports single-pass learning on CREMA-D and rapid continual adaptation to unseen actors from a few dozen clips.

papers.abstract: Converting pretrained softmax Transformers to efficient attention often causes substantial performance degradation, while recovery typically requires costly fine-tuning. We propose ET (Efficient Transfer), a framework for high-fidelity attention conversion with minimal optimization cost. ET combines exact local and shared-key softmax attention with a mean-anchored, scan-free global linear correction and adaptive gating, achieving linear complexity in sequence length. To preserve pretrained knowledge, ET freezes pretrained weights and calibrates only newly introduced parameters through alternating least squares on a small set of unlabeled samples, without gradient updates. On ImageNet-1K, ET achieves 79.64% and 81.55% top-1 accuracy on DeiT-S and DeiT-B, respectively, within 0.25 percentage points of their softmax teachers. At $768\times768$, ET outperforms T$^5$ by 3.59 percentage points at comparable inference FLOPs, without gradient-based fine-tuning. On DiT-XL/2, ET achieves an FID-50K of 2.59 with only 250 LoRA updates. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, ET matches the teacher's GenEval score at 1K resolution with just 0.73 A100 GPU-hours of gradient-free conversion and a 1.39$\times$ inference speedup.
authors: Guangfu Guo, Xiaoqian Lu, Linsey Pang, Weiran Yao, Haolin Chen, Long Cheng, Kunpeng Liu
bullets: Addresses the performance loss and costly fine-tuning typically associated with efficient-attention conversion.
Combines exact local/shared-key softmax attention with a mean-anchored, scan-free global linear correction and adaptive gating.
Freezes pretrained weights and uses alternating least squares on a small unlabeled sample set to calibrate added parameters.
On ImageNet-1K, remains within 0.25 percentage points of DeiT-S and DeiT-B softmax teachers; also improves over T$^5$ at comparable FLOPs.
Demonstrates gradient-free conversion for diffusion models, matching Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium's GenEval score with faster inference.

papers.abstract: Expert pruning reduces the memory footprint of mixture-of-experts language models, but retaining model quality depends on which experts are removed. Frequency- and magnitude-based scores measure the expert in isolation and overlook how normalization consumes its contribution: subtracting one expert changes both the direction of the residual stream and the scale applied to what remains. We propose FN-Prune, a training-free criterion that compares the next RMSNorm outputs before and after subtracting each router-weighted expert contribution, holding original routes and weights fixed. Squared differences are averaged over all calibration tokens in one pass; low-scoring experts are physically deleted at uniform per-layer ratios, and inference reroutes among survivors. At 50% expert removal, FN-Prune achieves lower WikiText-2 perplexity than the best published methods on Qwen3, ERNIE, and OLMoE, including a 32% reduction on OLMoE. At the same budget, GSM8K accuracy improves over the best published methods by 7.5 and 7.0 percentage points on Qwen3 and ERNIE, respectively, while multiple-choice gains remain task-dependent.
bullets: Targets MoE expert pruning while preserving model quality and reducing memory.
Scores each expert by the change in the next RMSNorm output when its routed contribution is removed.
Uses one-pass calibration with original routes and weights fixed, then uniformly deletes low-scoring experts per layer.
At 50% pruning, reports lower WikiText-2 perplexity on Qwen3, ERNIE, and OLMoE, including a 32% reduction on OLMoE.
GSM8K accuracy improves over prior methods on Qwen3 and ERNIE; multiple-choice results are task-dependent.

papers.abstract: Sustained Large Language Model (LLM) inference generates significant heat that exacerbates silicon aging and reduces GPU reliability. Because GPU temperature fluctuates continuously with workload intensity and ambient conditions, keeping it in a safe range requires real-time frequency scaling, which inevitably comes at the cost of either throughput or accuracy. To address this tightly coupled challenge, we propose GreenDynaMix, the first runtime system to jointly integrate a DVFS-based thermal manager with a dynamic precision-tuning throughput compensator. A sensitivity-aware allocator leverages intrinsic importance signals from the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router to assign higher precision to critical experts, preserving accuracy. Experiments on server, desktop, and embedded platforms demonstrate that GreenDynaMix reduces the temperature-induced aging rate of GPUs during LLM inference by 25-33%. Without offline profiling or model retraining, it recovers throughput at a perplexity cost of 0.9-1.6% with 8-bit/4-bit mixed precision, rising to 9.4% where memory forces 4-bit/2-bit.
authors: Han-Yi Lin, Kieran Griperay, Qiang Zhou, Xiangyu Zhou, Nate Bonacci, Zinachidi Achikeh, Li He, Shaofei Qi, Hongqiang Wang, Jeff Zhang, Tianlong Chen, Pi-Cheng Hsiu, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Targets thermal stress from sustained LLM inference, which can accelerate GPU aging and reduce reliability.
Combines DVFS-based thermal management with runtime dynamic precision tuning as a throughput compensator.
Uses MoE router importance signals to assign higher precision to more critical experts.
Across server, desktop, and embedded platforms, reduces temperature-induced GPU aging rates by 25–33%.
Requires no offline profiling or retraining; incurs 0.9–1.6% perplexity cost with 8/4-bit precision and 9.4% when memory constraints require 4/2-bit precision.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by letting a cheap drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Parallel block drafters such as DFlash and P-EAGLE propose a whole block in one forward pass, but they lose the dependence between tokens in the block; DSpark restores part of it with a lightweight correction head that runs sequentially. Measuring DSpark, we find that this head overrides the base prediction on most slots, so the expensive base readout through the target's full lm_head mostly provides a seed. We therefore propose Wavefront, which follows a simple principle: shrink the base and strengthen the correction head. Wavefront replaces the full lm_head with a learned low-rank base, conditions the correction head on the whole drafted prefix within the same block, and resolves it with a few parallel Jacobi passes. A fixed pass budget makes the draft step free of data-dependent control flow, so we capture it as a single CUDA graph in vLLM with fused kernels. On Qwen3-8B, Wavefront improves throughput over xPress, DSpark and DFlash by 2.6%, 10.7% and 23.6% on average across math, code, chat and agentic benchmarks, and by 9.6%, 14.3% and 28.9% on SPEED-Bench long-context prompts. On Qwen3.8-27B it leads DFlash2, DSpark and xPress by 7.6%, 10.6% and 5.0%, and by 7.4%, 5.8% and 6.0% on the same long-context prompts. The gains persist as serving load grows to concurrency 32.
bullets: Targets the limited within-block token dependence of parallel drafters such as DFlash and P-EAGLE.
Uses a learned low-rank base, a correction head conditioned on the full drafted prefix, and fixed-budget parallel refinement.
Implements the draft step as a single CUDA graph with fused kernels in vLLM, avoiding data-dependent control flow.
Reports throughput gains over prior drafters across math, code, chat, agentic, and long-context benchmarks on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.8-27B.
Gains remain as serving load increases to concurrency 32.

figures.caption: Figure 4. WAVEFRONT on a parallel block drafter (e.g., DFlash or P-EAGLE). (a) One draft step: the backbone and the low-rank base run once, giving the base logits Uk and the seed x(0); the chain-aware head then refines the block for P passes, each pass reading the previous block x(t). (b) One pass of the chain-aware head for slot k: the code of the predecessor token is concatenated with the normalized feature zk, mixed across earlier slots by causal attention, and projected to a correction of the base logits. Teal: weights learned by WAVEFRONT.

papers.abstract: Object detectors often transfer poorly to specialized domains, where box annotations are scarce and deployment requires compact, real-time models. Large vision foundation models can provide offline supervision, but their zero-shot predictions may be poorly aligned with the target domain. We present an adapt-label-distill pipeline that uses limited target annotations to specialize a foundation teacher and transfer its supervision to compact detectors. We adapt SAM3 on the labeled subset, generate pseudo-labels for the remaining unlabeled images, and train YOLOv11 students with confidence-guided supervision. Teacher confidence weights pseudo-label losses, while zero-gating retains uncertain hypotheses during assignment without applying their associated training losses. Experiments across six target domains and three student capacities show substantial gains in several domains, while revealing limited or negative transfer in others. Teacher comparisons under a common hard-label training recipe support the choice of SAM3, and comparisons with an EfficientTeacher adaptation provide additional evidence against an online SSOD baseline. With YOLOv11m, our pipeline improves over STAC-style self-training by up to 15.3 AP and reaches 51.6 AP on Garbage, compared with 54.1 under full supervision. On NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the deployed student achieves 188 FPS versus 2.9 FPS for SAM3, benefiting from foundation-model supervision without incurring the teacher's deployment cost. Code is available at https://github.com/zk2172-columbia/ProjectAdaptLabelDistill_ObjectDetection.
authors: Zhengye Yang, Anthony Wang, Yuyang Li, Mehmet Kerem Turkcan, Beizhan Yan, Zoran Kostic
bullets: Addresses poor cross-domain transfer, scarce box annotations, and the deployment cost of large vision foundation models.
Adapts SAM3 with limited labeled target data, generates pseudo-labels for unlabeled images, and trains YOLOv11 students with confidence-guided supervision.
Confidence weights pseudo-label losses, while zero-gating retains uncertain hypotheses without using their losses for training.
Across six domains and three student capacities, results show substantial gains in some domains but limited or negative transfer in others.
YOLOv11m improves over STAC-style self-training by up to 15.3 AP, reaches 51.6 AP on Garbage, and runs at 188 FPS on Jetson AGX Orin versus 2.9 FPS for SAM3.

The compact student is trained on Dl with groundtruth annotations and on Du with pseudo-labels, where each pseudo-label contributes to the loss in proportion to the teacher’s confidence in it and uncertain pseudo-labels contribute nothing. papers.abstract: Early exit neural networks reduce average inference cost by terminating once sufficient confidence is reached. On FPGAs, conventional confidence-based exits add arithmetic control paths poorly matched to LUT fabrics, consuming resources that could otherwise support the main datapath. We present ExitLUT, which replaces softmax-style exit decisions with learned Boolean functions mapped directly into FPGA LUTs. In our CNN evaluation, fpgaConvNet is the static spatial-dataflow baseline, while ATHEENA is its softmax-based early exit extension. ExitLUT reduces ATHEENA's exit-decision LUT usage by 2.58$\times$ over the softmax path and eliminates decision-path DSP usage, while preserving accuracy and exit behavior. Rerunning design-space exploration reinvests these savings into the datapath, improving throughput by up to 4.08$\times$ over fpgaConvNet and 1.82$\times$ over ATHEENA. For LUT-based NNs, embedded ExitLUT exits achieve 1.41-1.89$\times$ average time-to-decision speedup over static NeuraLUT-Assemble designs with under 1% LUT overhead.
authors: Oliver Cassidy, Marta Andronic, George A. Constantinides
bullets: Targets FPGA neural-network inference, where conventional confidence-based exits consume resources poorly matched to LUT fabrics.
Learns Boolean exit functions that map directly to FPGA LUTs, eliminating DSP usage on the exit decision path.
Reduces exit-decision LUT usage by 2.58× versus the softmax path.
Reinvesting saved resources improves throughput by up to 4.08× over fpgaConvNet and 1.82× over ATHEENA.
For LUT-based NNs, achieves 1.41–1.89× average time-to-decision speedup with under 1% LUT overhead.

papers.abstract: Recurrent-depth models are trained with truncated backpropagation, yet it remains unclear why this works. We show that input injection, commonly used in recurrent-depth models, is exactly Halpern iteration, and that a slowly vanishing stepsize provably converges with a backpropagation window polylogarithmic in the depth. The guarantees require a Lipschitz operator, which for SwiGLU leads to a weight constraint in both row and spectral norm, while only a row norm constraint for gates. Based on these constraints, we develop an optimizer tailored to each parameter group, Sparrow, which provides a drop-in replacement of Muon/MuonH with no overhead, that speeds up training even beyond recurrent models.
bullets: Input injection is identified as Halpern iteration, clarifying why truncated backpropagation can work.
With a slowly vanishing stepsize, convergence is provable using a backpropagation window that grows polylogarithmically with depth.
The theory requires Lipschitz operators; for SwiGLU, this implies specific row, spectral, and gate-norm constraints.
Sparrow applies tailored optimization to different parameter groups and is a no-overhead drop-in replacement for Muon/MuonH.
The abstract reports faster training, including beyond recurrent models, but gives no quantitative results or experimental details.

papers.abstract: ELECTRA-style replaced-token detection (RTD) is a sample-efficient objective for pre-training text encoders, and RTD-trained models such as DeBERTaV3 are strong on classification benchmarks. The same models, however, are known to be poor backbones for embedding tasks such as retrieval and semantic similarity: the binary "original vs. replaced" signal does not ask the final layer to retain the token identity and contextual content that dense representations rely on. We introduce ModernELECTRA, a pre-training recipe that keeps RTD as the main objective and adds a lightweight auxiliary task, boundary-window reconstruction. For every token, we sample a window of 3-12 tokens that strictly contains it and reconstruct the token's original identity only from the discriminator's hidden states at the two window boundaries. The task costs one small FFN at training time and is discarded afterwards, yet it forces every final-layer state to carry information about its neighbourhood. Combined with a frozen, separately pre-trained generator, a temperature curriculum for hard negatives and a 512-to-8192 length curriculum, we train two compact encoders: EdgeCoder-31M, an 8-layer English model, and EdgeCoder-Multilingual-61M, a 16-layer model covering 46 languages, each on about 1T tokens. They reach 86.0 and 85.1 on GLUE. The English model outperforms Ettin-Enc-32m (83.5) and MiniLM-L12 (84.6) on GLUE while matching them on MTEB English v2 (51.1), and the multilingual model outperforms the 2.3x larger mmBERT-small on GLUE and Multilingual MiniLM and mDistilBERT on XTREME over the languages it covers. We also describe FlashDeBERTa, our open-source fused implementation of DeBERTa's disentangled attention that stores no $n \times n$ score matrix: at 4096 tokens it is 10x faster and uses 93% less memory than the reference implementation, and it loads existing DeBERTa checkpoints unchanged.
authors: Mykhailo Shtopko, Ihor Stepanov, Dmytro Vodianytskyi, Oleksandr Lukashov
bullets: RTD is efficient for classification but often yields weak dense embeddings because it does not preserve token identity and contextual content.
The auxiliary task reconstructs each token from hidden states at the boundaries of a surrounding 3–12-token window, using a small training-only FFN.
Two compact models trained on about 1T tokens achieve GLUE scores of 86.0 (31M English) and 85.1 (61M multilingual, 46 languages).

The English model matches comparable models on MTEB English v2 while outperforming them on GLUE; the multilingual model improves over larger or established multilingual baselines on reported benchmarks.
FlashDeBERTa provides a memory-efficient fused DeBERTa attention implementation, but its reported speed and memory gains are specific to the reference comparison.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers advance implicit chain-of-thought reasoning through recurrent latent refinement. However, existing looped reasoners typically employ fixed-depth recurrence, updating all latent positions at every iteration and incurring redundancy when further refinement is unnecessary. We introduce \textsc{SwiftLoop}, an inference-time framework for selective recurrent refinement through position-wise freezing, enabling adaptive computation allocation across both recurrent depth and active width. SwiftLoop learns lightweight freezing policies through hindsight-guided supervision derived from two complementary criteria: K/V reusability at the internal representation level and functional impact at the output level. At inference time, these policies guide adaptive freezing based on observed hidden states. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SwiftLoop achieves favorable accuracy--computation trade-offs over fixed-loop inference and adaptive baselines, with measured inference acceleration. Beyond implicit reasoning, we further demonstrate its applicability to recurrent prompt prefilling in general looped models.
authors: Tianyi Zhao, Ke Wan, Chen Chen
bullets: Addresses redundant computation from fixed-depth recurrence that updates all latent positions at every iteration.
Uses position-wise freezing to adapt computation across both recurrent depth and active width.
Learns lightweight freezing policies from hindsight signals measuring internal K/V reusability and output-level functional impact.
Experiments show favorable accuracy–computation trade-offs and inference acceleration versus fixed-loop and adaptive baselines.
Also applies to recurrent prompt prefilling beyond implicit reasoning.

papers.abstract: Incompressible diffeomorphic registration requires continuous spatial mappings that preserve local tissue volume (det(D\Phi) = 1) without topological folding (det(D\Phi) > 0). Standard velocity-field methods (SVF, LDDMM) approximate incompressibility via numerical ODE integration or soft penalties, exhibiting numerical volume drift (~10^-4 to 10^-1), iterative grid inversions, and linear backpropagation memory O(L * N_vox). We formulate an exact structure-preserving framework for 3D registration based on cascaded coordinate shears. By decomposing the divergence-free Lie algebra sdiff(\Omega) into six coordinate-shear generators whose convective non-linearities vanish identically, each elementary stage integrates analytically to a closed-form triangular shear with det(DS_k) = 1 and exact machine-precision inverse requiring zero iterations and zero spatial interpolations. Multi-stage compositions generate the connected volume-preserving group SDiff_0(\Omega). We establish: (i) an unconditional global diffeomorphism proof closing the Hadamard-Caccioppoli injectivity gap; (ii) a Dirichlet boundary confinement lemma; (iii) an anisotropic Riemannian similarity invariance; (iv) a Sobolev H^2 spectral budget preventing chaotic mixing; and (v) an exact reversible backpropagation engine eliminating O(L) trajectory storage (0.00 MB intermediate activations). We prove second-order O(h^2) sub-voxel convergence across 16^3 to 64^3 lattices and second-order trajectory accuracy for palindromic Strang splitting (468.1x error reduction vs. Lie-Trotter; drift |det(D\Phi)-1| <= 2.22e-16). Execution is 2.1x-4.0x faster than SVF with 78.4% GPU memory reduction. On cardiac cine-MRI (ACDC, N=100) and brain MRI (OASIS-1, N=414), our model achieves competitive Dice (0.884 and 0.841) while strictly maintaining 0.0000% folding and zero volume drift.
bullets: Addresses numerical volume drift, folding risk, iterative inversion, and trajectory-memory costs in incompressible diffeomorphic registration.
Uses six divergence-free coordinate-shear generators composed into analytically invertible triangular transformations with unit Jacobian.
Provides theoretical guarantees including global diffeomorphism, boundary confinement, similarity invariance, and limits on chaotic mixing.
Palindromic Strang splitting achieves second-order trajectory accuracy; the abstract reports zero folding and machine-precision volume preservation.
On ACDC and OASIS-1, it reports competitive Dice scores of 0.884 and 0.841, with faster execution and reduced GPU memory versus SVF.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as persistent services that must reason over large volumes of external knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds model responses in relevant documents, but the retrieved content must still be encoded and stored in the key-value (KV) cache. As this content accumulates, the cache grows linearly, increasing memory consumption and inference cost. Existing memory-compression methods address this problem either by retaining a subset of cached states or by learning context compressors that map documents to compact latent representations. Despite these advances, consolidating information under tight memory budgets while preserving its usefulness for future queries remains challenging. We investigate how the model's native KV states can be selectively consolidated into a fixed-size working memory without access to future queries. To this end, we introduce SD-Cache (State-guided and Dynamically updated Cache), a query-agnostic KV-memory consolidation framework that operates alongside a frozen generator LLM. SD-Cache learns to consolidate layer-wise KV states into fixed-size memory through selective anchor-based pooling and state-guided refinement, processing new contexts in a single forward pass without context-specific optimisation. Experiments on retrieval-augmented question answering and synthetic long-context benchmarks show that SD-Cache maintains competitive downstream performance under constrained memory budgets.
authors: Yuanhong Chen, Yiping Ji, Cameron Gordon, Emily Hackett-Jones, Hemanth Saratchandran, Anton van den Hengel
bullets: Addresses the rising memory and inference costs of accumulating retrieved content in RAG KV caches.
Learns to selectively consolidate layer-wise native KV states without access to future queries.
Uses anchor-based pooling and state-guided refinement alongside a frozen generator LLM.
Processes new contexts in a single forward pass without context-specific optimization.
Maintains competitive performance on retrieval-augmented QA and synthetic long-context benchmarks under constrained memory.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a lightweight draft model to propose tokens for verification by a target model. Draft training commonly optimizes token-level distribution alignment, but this does not directly optimize the length of the accepted prefix: once a draft token is rejected, all subsequent draft tokens are discarded. We propose FreDraft, an on-policy training method that directly maximizes the expected accepted length of drafts sampled from the current draft model. This objective accounts for first-rejection truncation and induces prefix-aware credit assignment, weighting each token by its contribution to the acceptance of the current and subsequent tokens. To optimize the objective efficiently, we analytically marginalize token-level acceptance rate, using the target model's vocabulary distribution to reduce gradient variance. We further redistribute part of this distribution-level gradient into an explicit penalty for sampled tokens whose probabilities are overestimated by the draft model, while preserving the expected gradient. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and target models show that FreDraft improves accepted length and decoding speedup over strong baselines, achieving faster on-policy training convergence.
authors: Ziying Zhang, Yaqing Wang, Yong Liu, Quanming Yao
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between token-level distribution alignment and the actual objective of retaining long accepted draft prefixes.
Uses on-policy training with prefix-aware credit assignment that accounts for first-rejection truncation.
Analytically marginalizes token-level acceptance rates with the target model’s vocabulary distribution to reduce gradient variance.
Redistributes part of the gradient into a penalty for overestimated sampled-token probabilities without changing the expected gradient.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks and target models report higher accepted lengths, greater decoding speedups, and faster training convergence than strong baselines.

papers.abstract: Estimating the quality of generative AI workflows is challenging because these workflows comprise multiple stages, and errors can propagate across them, making end-to-end performance depend not only on the accuracy of individual models but also on how their outputs affect downstream stages. Each stage can use one of many candidate models. Estimating end-to-end workflow quality by deploying and evaluating every resulting model configuration is therefore prohibitively expensive. As a result, existing approaches face a tradeoff between estimation cost and accuracy: inexpensive methods often produce unreliable quality estimates, while accurate methods require deploying and evaluating many workflow configurations. In this paper, we introduce DAGGER, a framework for estimating the quality of generative AI workflows without exhaustive deployment and profiling. DAGGER represents a workflow as a graph, in which nodes correspond to stages and edges capture how outputs from one stage affect subsequent stages. It then decomposes workflow quality into per-node accuracy terms and per-edge dependency terms. Using a novel analytical formulation and SVD-based matrix completion, DAGGER estimates workflow quality from sparse observations without executing every candidate workflow. We evaluate DAGGER on three generative AI workflows across three datasets. DAGGER estimates workflow quality with a median error of 6.8 percentage points while reducing profiling cost by 10.2$\times$ relative to BenchPress, a state-of-the-art baseline, and selects workflow configurations competitive with state-of-the-art frameworks such as LLMSelector.
bullets: Models workflows as graphs of stages and dependencies, capturing how upstream outputs affect downstream quality.
Decomposes end-to-end quality into per-stage accuracy and cross-stage dependency terms.
Uses an analytical formulation with SVD-based matrix completion to infer untested workflow configurations.
Across three workflows and datasets, achieves a median estimation error of 6.8 percentage points and reduces profiling cost 10.2× versus BenchPress.
Selects configurations competitive with frameworks such as LLMSelector.

papers.abstract: Post-training compression of vision models is commonly screened using output-level proxies such as normalized RMSE (NRMSE), cosine similarity, and flow angular error. We evaluated post-training quantization of Cellpose-SAM, a promptless Segment-Anything model for cellular instance segmentation, on a stratified 245-field panel spanning BBBC038, BBBC039, and NIST iPSC images across density regimes. These proxies failed to reliably predict downstream mask retention under activation quantization. Angular error saturated at 90{\deg} from A8 through A2, while cosine and NRMSE preserved rank-order information without providing an interpretable acceptance threshold. At W8A8-cal-QDQ, cosine similarity was 0.944 despite 89/245 empty masks; moreover, performance varied sharply by modality, with BBBC039 yielding 0/47 empty masks versus 63/99 for NIST iPSC fields at the same proxy footprint. Across five modality-density strata, cosine similarity and empty-mask rate showed weak rank agreement (\r{ho}=~0.3), with the highest-cosine stratum producing the second-worst downstream outcome. Below A8, all modalities collapsed to 245/245 empty fields. By contrast, ternary weight quantization produced a 12.08x storage reduction and was correctly identified as catastrophic by the proxies. These results show that FP32-referenced output proxies are insufficient as standalone acceptance criteria for promptless dense-prediction models; compression should instead be validated against downstream retention stratified by deployment-relevant imaging conditions.
bullets: Evaluated post-training quantization of Cellpose-SAM across 245 fields from three imaging sources and varied density regimes.
NRMSE and cosine similarity retained ranking information but lacked reliable acceptance thresholds; angular error saturated at 90° from A8 to A2.
At W8A8-cal-QDQ, cosine similarity was 0.944 despite 89/245 empty masks, with substantially different failure rates across modalities.
All modalities produced empty masks below A8, while ternary weight quantization caused catastrophic failure that the proxies did detect.
Compression should be assessed using downstream mask retention stratified by deployment-relevant imaging conditions, not proxies alone.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) are a predominant architecture for computer vision, with token reduction emerging as a popular paradigm to improve their efficiency. Prior work compares reduction algorithms, but not how models respond to them, nor how their response changes with model depth. We propose Monte Carlo Token Pruning (MCTP), which estimates each token's impact on the prediction when tokens are explicitly removed during the forward pass. Applying MCTP to recent pretrained models, we observe that most, such as DINOv3, maintain a similar ranking of token importance at every depth (high Coherent Aggregation), while SigLIP 2 does not. This coherence requires predictions to survive pruning, which depends on keeping high-norm "sink" tokens: prefix tokens are kept by design, while prefix-free SigLIP 2 forms them on patch tokens, which pruning may remove. We show that in removing DINOv3's prefix tokens, its predictions and coherence collapse, while protecting only 5 tokens for SigLIP 2 cuts the token impact outside the object's bounding box by up to 62%. Beyond this, MCTP offers a post-hoc method to evaluate how a pretrained ViT responds to pruning, and suggests that token reduction methods should keep "sinks".
bullets: Introduces Monte Carlo Token Pruning (MCTP), which measures token importance by explicitly removing tokens during inference.
Most tested pretrained models, including DINOv3, preserve similar token-importance rankings across depth; SigLIP 2 does not.
DINOv3’s prefix tokens act as protected sink tokens, while prefix-free SigLIP 2 forms sinks on patch tokens that pruning can remove.
Removing DINOv3 prefix tokens collapses prediction quality and coherence; protecting five SigLIP 2 tokens reduces out-of-object token impact by up to 62%.
MCTP provides a post-hoc way to assess pruning responses and motivates protecting sink tokens during token reduction.

papers.abstract: Agent workflows issue dependent model calls that share long context prefixes, so serving them efficiently depends on reusing the key-value (KV) cache of those prefixes. On accelerators that compile model graphs ahead of time, however, the device KV budget is fixed, and prefixes evicted under load must be recomputed. Restoring them from host memory avoids this recomputation, but the transfer occupies the same engine thread as prefill and decode, so its benefit is not guaranteed. In this paper, we study when restoring beats recomputing on a commercial static-graph neural processing unit (NPU) stack (Rebellions ATOM+, vllm-rbln 0.10.2) that serves a Qwen3-8B planner on two cards and a Qwen3-0.6B executor on one. We first show that repeated prefill dominates planner work when default serving collapses: 89.5% of the executed planner prompt tokens had been materialized before. We then build a synchronous host-DRAM tier on the runtime's public KV copy calls, together with a scheduler-aware event model whose predictions are frozen before each test cohort. Experimental results show that the host tier raises workflow service-level objective (SLO) attainment from 22.8% to 100% and from 9.4% to 99.8% in the two tested overload conditions, and endpoint confirmation on two new seeds supports conservative load gains of 11.8% (chain) and 18.2% (fork), while mixed and bursty workloads remain seed-sensitive. The frozen model predicts median and 99th-percentile (P99) latency within its 15% tolerance in all 24 common-load conditions, including the 16-18% P99 increase that the tier causes for fork workflows, but it misorders three policy contrasts and overestimates the benefit of a cheaper store path (11% predicted against 3.1% measured). The trade-off therefore depends on runtime scheduling and transfer cost as well as cache capacity.
bullets: Repeated planner prefill accounted for 89.5% of executed planner prompt tokens in default overload conditions, motivating KV reuse.
The authors add host-DRAM KV restoration through public runtime copy calls and a scheduler-aware event model.
SLO attainment rose from 22.8% to 100% and from 9.4% to 99.8% in two tested overload conditions.
Endpoint tests indicated conservative load gains of 11.8% for chain workflows and 18.2% for fork workflows; mixed and bursty workloads were seed-sensitive.
The model stayed within 15% of median and P99 latency in 24 common-load conditions, but misordered some policy comparisons and overestimated a cheaper transfer path’s benefit.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the serving path (top) and the prospective evaluation (bottom), with a chain workflow as the dependency example. On the planner, restore, prefill, store, and decode share one engine thread: the full host prefix is restored when the usable host prefix is longer than the local one (Hh > Hl), and missing host entries are stored after prefill. Boxes show the order of operations, not their durations. The event model makes predictions from the frozen trace and does not control serving.

Figure 4: Frozen common-load forecasts against measurements for 24 conditions (top) and predicted against observed host-tier effects at fixed F6 admission (bottom). Every P50 and P99 forecast falls within the frozen 15% tolerance (shaded band, not an uncertainty interval), while crosses mark the three host-tier effects whose sign was mispredicted. In the top panels, dark and pale fills are seeds 702 and 703.

Each point summarizes a 60 s arrival cohort; the horizontal axis is arrival time, not completion time. SLO attainment counts all workflows including errors, and latency quantiles use successful workflows only. With the host tier, both B0 and F6 keep SLO attainment near 100% and latency flat, whereas without it SLO attainment falls to zero and latency rises to hundreds of seconds. Error counts are in Table 2.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward geometry models such as VGGT recover camera parameters, depth maps, and point maps from one to hundreds of views in a single forward pass, making them powerful backbones for multi-view 3D perception. However, VGGT's global attention is quadratic in the number of frames and dominates end-to-end runtime on long sequences, which has motivated a range of training-free efficiency methods such as token merging. These methods, however, come with a drop in accuracy that makes them hard to use in place of VGGT. We propose GPA-VGGT, a training-free acceleration method that replaces global attention in early blocks with frame attention augmented by a shared cross-frame K/V set. In the remaining blocks, we merge only keys and values while preserving all queries, restore the attention mass of the tokens each merged key represents, and randomly project the matching metric to 128 dimensions to reduce matching cost. Across diverse multi-view geometry tasks, GPA-VGGT provides training-free acceleration at speedups comparable to prior work while preserving the information required for precise geometric estimation, retaining over 99% of VGGT's pose accuracy under AUC@3.
bullets: Targets VGGT’s quadratic global-attention runtime on long multi-view sequences.
Uses frame attention with shared cross-frame keys/values in early blocks.
Later merges only keys and values, preserves all queries, and restores represented-token attention mass.
Randomly projects the matching metric to 128 dimensions to reduce matching overhead.
Achieves speedups comparable to prior training-free methods across multi-view geometry tasks while preserving precise estimation.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of GPA-VGGT. Early blocks 0–8 replace global attention with frame attention augmented by a shared cross-frame K/V set containing special tokens and content-adaptive pooled image-token summaries. Later blocks 9–23 preserve all queries and merge only K/V tokens, using a weaker merge ratio in the core blocks 13–16. (a) Pooled summaries are constructed by assigning patch tokens to stride-8 seeds according to cosine similarity and averaging the K/V tokens within each content-adaptive cluster; the summary size determines the + log s correction. (b) K/V matching is computed after a 128-dimensional Gaussian projection, while all queries are retained for global attention.

Figure 5. Qualitative reconstruction under estimated camera poses. Each column shows the point cloud produced by the corresponding method, and red boxes indicate the enlarged regions below. GPA-VGGT most closely matches the geometry reconstructed by vanilla VGGT.

Figure 2. Two sources of accuracy degradation in existing token-merging methods. Top: Query merging collapses the block-12 outputs of 83 tokens into 12 shared outputs, whereas retaining all queries while merging only K/V preserves the output diversity of the unmerged model. Bottom: Omitting the + log s correction disproportionately allocates attention to the first frame. Restoring the correction recovers an attention distribution close to that of the unmerged model.

Figure 1. Accuracy and runtime scaling with the number of input frames. Although existing acceleration methods substantially reduce end-to-end runtime, they incur pronounced camera-pose degradation under the strict AUC@3 metric. GPA-VGGT achieves comparable runtime while maintaining camera-pose accuracy close to that of vanilla VGGT.

Figure 3. Effect of cross-frame context in the early blocks. Top: Replacing global attention with frame attention substantially displaces the block-8 output field from the full-global-attention reference, whereas the shared cross-frame K/V set largely preserves it. Bottom: Pairwise alignment of per-frame drift directions. Cross-frame special tokens partially align the drift, and image-token summaries further reduce its variation, preserving a coherent geometric reference across views.

papers.abstract: Contrastive objectives power state-of-the-art multimodal models, but their training remains slow, relying on long stochastic optimization. We propose a Unified Framework for Efficient Contrastive Alignment via Kernels (UniCon), which spans linear and nonlinear encoders as well as one-to-one and many-to-many alignments. At its core, UniCon introduces the contrastive similarity weight matrix $S(\gamma)$, which enables closed-form global solutions that provably replace minibatch back-propagation with exact updates. Through the lens of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS), UniCon provides a kernelized perspective that unifies contrastive alignment and reveals its connection to spectral methods. To validate the theory, we conduct experiments on synthetic, unimodal, multimodal, and zero-shot tasks, demonstrating that UniCon achieves substantial efficiency gains while preserving generality and strong empirical performance.
authors: Hangke Sui, Yuqing Wang, Minh N Do
bullets: Targets the training inefficiency of contrastive objectives in multimodal and related models.
Supports linear and nonlinear encoders, plus one-to-one and many-to-many alignment settings.
Introduces a contrastive similarity weight matrix, S(γ), for closed-form global solutions.
Uses a reproducing kernel Hilbert space view to connect contrastive alignment with spectral methods.
Experiments across synthetic, unimodal, multimodal, and zero-shot tasks show efficiency gains with strong empirical performance.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Unified Framework for Efficient Contrastive Alignment via Kernels (UniCon). Starting from paired inputs, UniCon builds a contrastive similarity weight matrix S(γ) using hyper-spherical similarities, then computes either (i) a closed-form spectral update in the linear case (orange) or (ii) a kernelized solution in the nonlinear case (blue).

Figure 4: Visualizations of unimodal alignment on CIFAR-10. (a) Self-supervised contrastive learning clusters semantically similar images and uniformly distributes clusters on the hypersphere. (b–c) Unimodal confusion matrices for UniCon and SGD-CLIP, showing predicted vs. true class accuracy. The near-identity structure and visual similarity of both matrices indicate that UniCon and SGD-CLIP achieve comparable discriminative performance in unimodal contrastive alignment.

Figure 2: Visualization of cross-modal alignment using t-SNE embeddings of the shared representation space. Modality 1 (cross) and modality 2 (circle) are projected from different spaces into a shared representation space Rr. Colors indicate ground-truth clusters, and lines connect matched image–text pairs. Both SGD-CLIP (left) and UniCon (right) successfully align paired samples while preserving cluster structure. The visual similarity between the two plots is expected: UniCon achieves a comparable aligned representation to SGD-CLIP with substantially less training time.
Figure 3: Evolution of the contrastive similarity weight matrix S(γ) in the nonlinear latent-factor model across training.

papers.abstract: Text-to-audio (T2A) diffusion models generate high-quality audio but require tens of neural function evaluations (NFEs), resulting in substantial inference latency. Existing acceleration methods primarily optimize each generation trajectory independently, even when reusable acoustic structure exists in prior examples. We introduce SoundWeaver, the first training-free framework for compositional cross example acoustic reuse. Rather than generating from pure noise, SoundWeaver constructs a prompt-conditioned acoustic prior from segments distributed across cached audios and warm-starts diffusion from an intermediate noise level. We introduce an Acoustic Composition Graph (ACG), which uses neural codec representations and segment-level identification to identify candidate cross-cache transitions and structured path search to jointly optimize prompt relevance and acoustic continuity. We further establish a warm-start error bound showing how prior quality and diffusion SNR jointly govern the admissible skip depth, motivating an adaptive contextual-bandit Skip Gater that selects the warm-start level for each request. Across T2A diffusion backbones, SoundWeaver achieves 1.48-3.74x generation speedup with only a 1K-clip cache while improving generation quality.
authors: Ayush Barik, Sofia Stoica, Nikhil Sarda, Arnav Kethana, Abhinav Khanduja, Muchen Xu, Fan Lai
bullets: Addresses high T2A diffusion latency caused by the need for many neural function evaluations.
Builds prompt-conditioned acoustic priors from segments in cached audios instead of starting from pure noise.
Uses an Acoustic Composition Graph to select cross-cache segments and optimize prompt relevance and acoustic continuity.
An adaptive contextual-bandit Skip Gater chooses the warm-start noise level using prior quality and diffusion SNR.
Across T2A backbones, delivers 1.48–3.74× speedup with only a 1K-clip cache and improved generation quality.

papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.
authors: Seongchan Kim, Soowon Son, Sangoh Kim, Hyunah Ko, Eunbeen Hong, Hyunkoo Lee, Sanghyun Lee, WonJun Moon, Kihong Kim, Dongyeon Son, Woongchan Nam, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Reasoning and trajectory objectives prioritize different VLM structures, so pruning based on either alone can damage performance.
Action-expert MLP channels have more stable importance across denoising steps than query heads, with a small subset carrying most importance.
MoOP combines both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select expert MLP channels.
At 24.0% parameter reduction, it retains 94.0% of dense-model LingoQA performance and matches or slightly exceeds strong driving baselines.
At 39.4% reduction, it achieves 1.37× faster inference and 36.6% lower peak memory without post-pruning fine-tuning, while preserving competitive driving performance.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Mixture-of-Objective Pruning (MoOP). (a) Pruning the VLM with reasoning-driven (CE) importance alone preserves the CoC but degrades the predicted trajectory. (b) Pruning with action-driven (FM) importance alone corrupts the reasoning that conditions the action expert. (c) MoOP combines both objectives to select VLM units and uses FM importance to prune the action expert, preserving both reasoning and driving.
Figure 2: Alpamayo architecture. The VLM encodes frames, prompt and ego history, generates the CoC, and its KV cache conditions the action expert, which denoises noise ϵ into a trajectory.

papers.abstract: Modern visual generative models operate on tokens, and every visual asset they receive, whether an identity, a scribble, a depth map, or a motion video, is tokenized and appended to the input token sequence. Consequently, conditioning quickly dominates the computation cost. Yet most of these tokens carry redundant spatiotemporal information. Our key insight is that identifying what is genuinely new is exactly the problem that classical video codecs have long solved. Thus, we first introduce a codec-based token pruning method that discards redundant tokens. Then, we propose an on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) strategy to train a DiT adapter capable of learning the codec pruning pattern well without quality degradation. Together, they form On-Policy Codec Distillation (CodecOPSD). We scale CodecOPSD to 16 condition modalities on our own video diffusion model, where it prunes 66% of the condition tokens on average with almost no quality drop. Therefore, denoising becomes 2x faster, and the cache memory shrinks by up to 73% in KV cache mode. CodecOPSD also extends to other state-of-the-art pretrained image and video generative models, where its benefit grows further with more conditions, longer frames, and higher resolution.
authors: Boyang Wang, Kevin Blackburn-Matzen, Oindrila Saha, Matheus Gadelha, Zezhou Cheng
bullets: Condition tokens from modalities such as identity, scribbles, depth, and motion videos create substantial computation and memory costs.
A codec-based pruning method removes redundant spatiotemporal conditioning tokens.
On-policy self-distillation trains a DiT adapter to reproduce the codec’s pruning pattern without degrading quality.
Scaled to 16 conditioning modalities, it prunes 66% of condition tokens on average, makes denoising 2× faster, and reduces KV-cache memory by up to 73%.
Benefits extend to pretrained image and video generators and increase with more conditions, longer videos, and higher resolution.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Pipeline of CodecOPSD. Left: Codec pruning runs in parallel with the VAE encoder and drops condition tokens at a dynamic rate per condition, and the kept tokens concatenate with the noisy latent as the DiT input. It optionally drops the vision tokens of a VLM, which enter the DiT by cross-attention or joint attention depending on the model. Right: On-Policy Codec Distillation provides the tokens removed by codec pruning to the frozen teacher as privileged information and compares the student’s prediction with the teacher’s.

Figure 6. Scaling tokens on MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA and MiniMax-H3-Image. Top: MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA with more reference videos, higher resolution, and more frames; the speedup keeps growing without a clear quality drop relative to the dense teacher. For both speedup and quality, MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA runs the 8-step FastH3-Omni of FastVideo [79]. Bottom: MiniMax-H3-Image with more reference images and higher resolution, which has the same trend. At 20482 pixels, with every module (DiT, VLM, and VAE) loaded on the GPU and no offloading, ours still fits 16 images, while the dense model runs out of memory from 12 images on. Quality averages the five scores of Tab. 4 and the three judge scores of Tab. 5, relative to the dense model.

Figure 5. Per-condition drop rates. We drop the tokens of a single condition at different rates in the order of Eq. 3 and measure quality relative to the teacher in each target metric, for (a) dense conditions and (b) sparse conditions. The grey band is the teacher’s seed noise (±2σ). The green region marks the free drop, where quality stays within this band, and the orange region marks the lossy drop. (c) provides the free drop value of each condition.

Figure 4. Denoising time and memory change. Test cases run at 512×896 with 121 frames, 8 sampling steps [76], and one H200. Ours is faster both without the KV cache (left) and with the KV cache (right top). The KV cache requires extra memory cost, and ours needs much less of it (right bottom).

Figure 2. From codec signals to kept tokens. (a) An I-frame predicts each block from its coded neighbours. (b) A P-frame finds the best match of each block in a previous frame and stores its motion vector. (c) The residual is the difference between the block and its best match. (d) Each token receives a motion score and a residual score from the blocks it covers, and threshold-based or priority-based pruning then selects the kept tokens.

papers.abstract: Preference tuning of text-to-image diffusion models spends most of its compute generating candidate images, yet training prompts are typically sampled uniformly at random, wasting compute generating images that provide too little signal for model alignment. To best utilize the available compute, we study prompt selection, where at each iteration we identify the most useful prompts for preference tuning. We separate prompt selection into a utility score, an estimator of that utility score, and batch selection. Within this framework, we propose Selection by PRedicting Objective-grounded UTility (SPROUT). The utility score is predicted on every prompt in the pool, including unseen prompts, by a text-only model, refit after every iteration on all utilities observed so far. A randomized acceptance rule then turns these predictions into a batch, so no images are generated beyond those used for training. For direct group preference optimization (DGPO), the objective-grounded utility is the norm of the gradient that the objective produces from a prompt's group of images. Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion 1.5 with DGPO on GenEval, SPROUT matches the final score of uniform sampling in about 44% of the iterations and improves the area under the learning curve with respect to both uniform sampling and CGPO, a recent variance-based prompt sampler. The efficiency gains hold under four held-out reward models never used in training, and the ranking of methods carries over to DPG-Bench and T2I-CompBench++. Our code is available at https://github.com/ADDAPT-ML/SPROUT.
authors: Kangping Hu, Akshay Mehra, Stephen Mussmann
bullets: Uniformly sampled prompts can waste compute on examples with little training value.
SPROUT uses a text-only model to predict each prompt’s objective-grounded utility, refitting after every iteration.
For DGPO, utility is defined as the norm of the objective gradient from a prompt’s image group.
A randomized acceptance rule forms training batches without generating images beyond those used for training.
On Stable Diffusion 1.5, SPROUT reaches uniform sampling’s final GenEval score in about 44% of the iterations and improves learning-curve area across multiple reward models and benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SPROUT at iteration t, with stages 1 and 2 as in Algorithm 2. (1) Generalizable utility model: a text-only utility model ft is fit on the train set of prompt–utility pairs from earlier iterations (circled prompts) and predicts the utility ŷt(p) of every prompt in D, including prompts never generated from; its predictions are scaled into acceptance probabilities at(p). (2) Diversitypreserving batch selection: the pool D is visited in a random order and each prompt is accepted with probability at(p) until B prompts pt,1, . . . , pt,B are accepted; the inset contrasts this with top-B selection (Appendix F). (3) Focused data generation: πt−1 generates G images for each accepted prompt only, the reward model scores them, and preference tuning updates the model to πt; each accepted prompt pt,i is then labeled with its utility yt,i, computed from its rewards or from the update (dashed arrows), and (pt,i, yt,i) joins the train set of the next iteration.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based view synthesis models render each target viewpoint from the source images, without an explicit 3D representation, which lets them reproduce fine detail and view-dependent effects. However, their decoder attends to every source token for every frame, so rendering slows with each source image. Rasterization avoids this by culling primitives that the viewpoint does not see, but source tokens cannot be culled this way, as they have no explicit position or extent. Our key insight is that source tokens are nonetheless spatial anchors: each encodes a local region of the scene, so the decoder's attention for any viewpoint concentrates on a few of them. A lightweight router predicts these tokens from the source tokens and the viewpoint, and the decoder attends only to a fixed budget of top-ranked tokens, so its cost no longer depends on the number of source tokens. We supervise the router with the decoder's attention, using non-maximum suppression to demote redundant tokens. With 24 source images and two views' worth of tokens, our model renders 6.4 times faster than LagerNVS, at a PSNR only 0.68 dB lower. One ranking serves every budget, so the budget can change at render time.
bullets: Source tokens act as local spatial anchors, enabling viewpoint-dependent token culling without explicit 3D geometry.
A lightweight router ranks tokens using source features and the target viewpoint; the decoder attends only to a fixed top-token budget.
Router training uses decoder attention supervision and non-maximum suppression to reduce redundant selections.
With 24 source images, rendering is 6.4× faster than LagerNVS while achieving PSNR only 0.68 dB lower.
A single token ranking supports changing the compute budget at render time.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview. The source tokens and the keys of the router are computed once per scene and cached, so the scene branch can afford to be heavy. For every target viewpoint, the lightweight target branch (an MLP) maps the viewpoint to a query, the score head scores all N keys, and the decoder attends only to the B ≪ N top-scoring tokens. The images show a synthetic scene with 8× 8 tokens per view.

Figure 8. Switching source views along a 300-frame trajectory, with four source views captured at the vertical lines. The whole view (orange) is the source view from which our router selects the most tokens, and tags mark the views it uses at t−1 and t; blue lanes show the share of our router’s tokens from each view, and the views show its tokens at frame t. At the marked switch, the boxed content turns translucent with the whole view, while our router keeps 95% of its tokens. Figures S3 and S4 show further switches, also with two views’ worth of tokens.

Figure 3. The decoder attends to few, local source tokens. Attention in the decoder block that supervises our router (Sec. 3.2). (b) The 1024 target tokens and the 1369 tokens of each source view are in raster order and max-pooled for display; darker is more attention, and the ticks mark the patches of (a).

Figure 6. Speed and quality. Frames per second against PSNR on the 140 test scenes of DL3DV [41], with 4 to 24 source views (numbers next to the points) spaced evenly over the first 300 frames of each scene and the same 228 target viewpoints per scene at every number of views. B is the number of source tokens, 1369 per view, that our decoder attends to per frame; teal shows increasing B at 24 views, up to all 32,856 tokens. Speed is measured at 256×256 on an RTX PRO 5000 and excludes the work done once per scene, such as encoding the source views (Sec. L).

Figure 7. Selection strategies. PSNR with one view’s worth of source tokens (B = 1369) on the 140 test scenes of DL3DV [41], with 4 to 24 source views spaced evenly over the first 300 frames and the same 228 target viewpoints per scene.
