papers.abstract: Live free-viewpoint video streaming of humans enables immersive telepresence and interactive XR applications. However, this requires reconstructing each frame in real time, transmitting the data within strict bandwidth budgets, and decoding it on lightweight client GPUs. Existing approaches, whether relying on per-frame optimization or feed-forward inference, generate massive 3D Gaussian payloads that exceed practical streaming limits, while aggressive compression severely degrades rendering quality. In this work, we present HoloSplat, a real-time streaming framework for human-centric volumetric video. HoloSplat splits a feed-forward reconstructor before its Gaussian head, introducing a multi-rate streaming codec driven by server-side token compression and client-side token restoration. On the server side, we apply opacity-guided token pruning, PCA-based dimensionality reduction, and lossless geometry coding for token anchors. On the client side, a feature reconstruction hypernetwork is fused into the Gaussian head to recover compression-induced quality loss. Furthermore, we introduce Neural Session Calibration (NSC), which rapidly fine-tunes the Gaussian head online using incoming camera views during a warm-up phase. This resolves quality degradation from novel camera parameters and varying capture conditions with zero per-frame overhead. In our evaluations, HoloSplat averages 32.2 FPS on four RTX 5090 GPUs at 50 Mbit/s. It decodes each frame into 3D Gaussians in 22.1 ms on an RTX 3050 Ti laptop GPU, transmitting 22.8$\times$ less data than uncompressed float32 Gaussians, while calibrated decoding improves PSNR by 1.050 dB.
authors: Chaofan Li, Qihan Ding, Shihan Wang, Zhehao Shen, Boyu Shen, Quanyu Chen, Haoyu Wu, Lan Xu, Xin Lou
bullets: Targets the challenge of streaming feed-forward 3D Gaussian human reconstructions under strict bandwidth and lightweight-client constraints.
Splits the reconstructor before its Gaussian head and uses multi-rate token streaming with server-side compression and client-side restoration.
Combines opacity-guided pruning, PCA reduction, lossless anchor geometry coding, and a feature-reconstruction hypernetwork.
Neural Session Calibration fine-tunes the Gaussian head during warm-up to handle novel cameras and changing capture conditions without per-frame overhead.
Achieves 32.2 FPS at 50 Mbit/s, 22.1 ms decoding on an RTX 3050 Ti, 22.8× less data than float32 Gaussians, and a 1.050 dB PSNR gain after calibration.

papers.abstract: Parallel speculative decoders propose an entire token block at once, yet one early inconsistency can cause the target to reject its remaining suffix. We introduce Corrective Prefix Attention (CPA), which combines prefix-aware selection with autoregressive supervision to improve these parallel drafts. CPA lets each candidate attend to earlier choices within the block. Fixed candidate shortlists allow all pairwise interactions to be computed before selection, reducing the sequential walk to table lookups, accumulation and lightweight scoring rather than repeated neural evaluations. An auxiliary autoregressive loss trains the shared backbone on clean prefixes without adding an inference pass. Across eight math, code and dialogue benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B targets on Ascend NPUs, CPA commits 13--15\% more tokens per verification round than DSpark and 25--26\% more than DFlash. Its mean speedups reach $3.35\times$ and $3.37\times$ under greedy decoding and $2.86\times$ under sampling for both targets. Ablations support both components, while capacity sweeps demonstrate that greater acceptance alone does not guarantee faster decoding. These results motivate correcting parallel proposals with causal information while keeping sequential computation inexpensive.
authors: Mohammad Mahdi Moradi, Ali Pourranjbar, Zongzuo Wang, Mingming Zhu, Ben Feng, Boxing Chen
bullets: Addresses early draft errors that cause target models to reject later tokens in a proposed block.
Lets candidates attend to earlier block choices using precomputed shortlist interactions and lightweight scoring.
Adds autoregressive supervision during training without requiring an extra inference pass.
Across eight math, code, and dialogue benchmarks, it commits 13–15% more tokens per round than DSpark and 25–26% more than DFlash.
Reports mean speedups up to 3.37×, with gains under both greedy decoding and sampling; acceptance rate alone does not ensure faster decoding.

papers.abstract: Updating an LLM adapter should not require replaying the full interaction history of every active session. Yet reusing key-value (KV) cache entries computed under an earlier version mixes model versions, while full-history re-prefill becomes increasingly costly as histories and session fleets grow. We introduce LiveLora, a model-runtime co-design for exact final-block KV cache migration. Frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections preserve each token's base projections and low-rank coordinates across adapter versions. The runtime reconstructs candidate K/V, reevaluates the latest token through the final block, and commits the adapter, cache, and next-token logits together. We prove continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under the stated model assumptions. On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, median paired publication speedups over full-history re-prefill average $68.98\times$ across five runs for 32 active sessions with 8K tokens each. Serving benchmarks show approximately 4.8% decoding overhead relative to native cached decoding. Compared with retained-boundary replay, compact retention gives a $3.42\times$ reduction in additional session storage at 8K, with similar measured publication-plus-decoding cost. LiveLora allows persistent LLM agents to adopt new adapter versions without replaying their full interaction histories.
authors: Tianyi Huang, Samuel Xu, Ivy Gu, Nathan Huang, Siqi Zhang
bullets: Addresses costly full-history re-prefill and the incompatibility of reusing KV caches across adapter versions.
Uses frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections to preserve base projections and low-rank coordinates.
Migrates the final-block cache by reconstructing K/V, reevaluating the latest token, and atomically committing the adapter, cache, and logits.
Proves continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under its model assumptions.
Reports 68.98× median paired publication speedup at 32 sessions with 8K-token histories, about 4.8% decoding overhead, and 3.42× lower additional storage than retained-boundary replay at 8K.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $\pi_{0.5}$ re-encode the camera images and the instruction with a 2B-parameter backbone at every control step, and the feed-forward layers of this prefix account for most of its compute. A natural way to save this compute is to send most tokens through a low-rank MLP and compute exactly only the tokens whose approximation error is large. We find that this intuition is wrong. Even a verifier that knows every token's exact error picks the wrong tokens, producing 1.3--1.7$\times$ larger action deviation than a simple test of whether a token's input is novel, that is, whether it falls outside the subspace seen during calibration. Large errors concentrate in tokens the policy relies on little, such as the third-person camera, while the novelty test favors the wrist camera, a view the action depends on heavily. We call this the error--reliance gap. Building on it, we propose NoveltyGate, a training-free method that routes each prefix token, once per layer and before any multiplication, to either a low-rank or the original MLP. Deciding once per layer instead of once per matrix product avoids moving wide intermediate tensors and keeps every shape static, so the whole prefix runs as a single CUDA graph. On LIBERO, NoveltyGate accelerates the $\pi_{0.5}$ prefix by up to 1.61$\times$, stays 2.7--2.9$\times$ closer to the original policy than channel pruning and low-rank compression at equal compute, and preserves closed-loop task success.
bullets: Token approximation error is a poor routing signal: it can be 1.3–1.7× worse for action deviation than input novelty.
Novelty is measured by whether a token falls outside the calibration subspace, favoring action-relevant views such as the wrist camera.
The training-free method routes each token once per layer to either a low-rank or original MLP, enabling static-shape CUDA-graph execution.
On LIBERO, it accelerates the π₀.₅ prefix by up to 1.61× and remains 2.7–2.9× closer to the original policy than competing compression methods at equal compute.
Closed-loop task success is preserved.

papers.title: NoveltyGate: Novelty, Not Error, Decides Which VLA Prefix Tokens to Compute Exactly
papers.tldr: NoveltyGate speeds up VLA prefix computation by routing novel tokens through the exact MLP, outperforming error-based token selection while preserving task success.

papers.abstract: LLM quantization reduces storage but often degrades predictive fidelity at low bit rates. We propose a training-free, CDF-free, Gaussian-CLT-motivated progressive residual-sign quantization framework that uses randomized orthogonal mixing to promote Gaussian-like residual distributions and improve sign based reconstruction of Transformer weights. Each stage independently normalizes residuals and analytically calibrates reconstruction, progressively recovering quantization errors. The framework enables flexible storage-fidelity trade-offs without learned codebooks, empirical CDFs, or trellis optimization. We evaluate GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B across attention and MLP projections. At five residual stages, joint quantization preserves near-baseline predictive fidelity, achieving perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73, compared with full-precision values of 29.89 and 11.07, respectively. Ablations further demonstrate that orthogonal mixing substantially improves reconstruction over identity-based sign coding, while activation-aware scaling improves output fidelity and reduced-precision statistics lower storage overhead with negligible perplexity degradation. Comparisons with conventional quantizers establish the method's progressive fidelity recovery and characterize its storage-quality and runtime trade-offs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of orthogonally mixed residual-sign coding for flexible, training-free Transformer weight compression.
authors: Anindya Roy Chowdhury, Atanu Barai, Nandakishore Santhi
bullets: Targets predictive-fidelity loss in low-bit LLM weight quantization.
Randomized orthogonal mixing makes residuals more Gaussian-like, improving sign-based reconstruction.
Progressive residual stages independently normalize and analytically calibrate reconstruction without codebooks, CDFs, or trellis optimization.
On GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B, five stages achieve perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73 versus full-precision 29.89 and 11.07.
Ablations show benefits from orthogonal mixing and activation-aware scaling, with reduced-precision statistics lowering storage overhead at negligible perplexity cost.

papers.tldr: A training-free residual-sign quantization method uses orthogonal mixing to compress Transformer weights while progressively recovering accuracy at low bit rates.

papers.abstract: AI agents are given GPUs to do AI research on their own. Do they use those GPUs well? A busy GPU does not tell us, because it can be busy with work the answer did not need. This matters, because the tokens the agent spends cost almost nothing next to the GPUs its experiments run on, so using those GPUs better has a huge impact. So we built ComputeWise, an open benchmark of research tasks on which this waste can be measured and reduced. For it we developed our own simulated GPU, which replays recorded runs to the agent's code. With no real GPU needed, we ran hundreds of experiments, far more than would be reasonable on real GPUs. With no help, the agents put only 52% of their GPU time into work the answer needed. Another 22% went to work it did not need, and 26% sat idle. Asking the agent to finish the work faster, telling it to keep every GPU busy, or giving it a job scheduler does not fix this. So we built an open-source harness, part prompting and part deterministic code. Across five models, it removed over 80% of the extra time to the answer.
authors: Egor Pakhomov, Nina Pakhomova, Anurag Koul, Shafiq Joty, Erik Nijkamp
bullets: Introduces an open benchmark for measuring GPU inefficiency in autonomous AI research tasks.
Uses a simulated GPU that replays recorded runs, enabling large-scale experiments without real GPUs.
Without assistance, agents spend 22% of GPU time on unnecessary work and leave 26% idle.
Simple interventions—speed prompts, GPU-utilization prompts, and job scheduling—do not resolve the waste.
An open-source combination of prompting and deterministic code reduces over 80% of extra time across five models.

papers.abstract: The search for computationally efficient alternatives to the Transformer has yielded numerous architectures in recent years; however, most exhibit severe weaknesses in associative recall-such as key-value (KV) retrieval-and length extrapolation, where even standard Transformers struggle. This paper introduces LimeTree, a linear-complexity architecture in both memory and compute for sequence modeling. By integrating synthetic KV retrieval tasks directly into standard language modeling training, LimeTree achieves strong perplexity alongside reliable recall. Two variants were evaluated on WikiText-103 and PG-19 under strict compute constraints. On WikiText-103, LimeTree reaches a token-level perplexity of 19 in just 6 hours on four Quadro RTX 8000 GPUs, while maintaining 100\% KV retrieval accuracy even when extrapolating from a training context length of 512 to an evaluation length of 16,384. On PG-19, the model achieves a token-level perplexity of 13 in 35 hours on a single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with minimal hyperparameter tuning. These results position LimeTree as a competitive linear-complexity alternative to Transformers, combining superior perplexity and training throughput with robust in-context retrieval and length extrapolation.
bullets: Targets Transformer inefficiencies, especially associative recall and context-length extrapolation.
Uses a tree-graph architecture and incorporates synthetic key-value retrieval tasks into language-model training.
Evaluated on WikiText-103 and PG-19 under strict compute constraints.
On WikiText-103, achieves perplexity 19 and 100% KV retrieval accuracy when extrapolating from context length 512 to 16,384.
Reports perplexity 13 on PG-19 with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) scale model capacity by increasing both parameter count and computation. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants expand parameter capacity while keeping per-token computation roughly fixed, but still require substantial parameter storage. In this paper, we propose Dynamic Looped MoE DiT (DyLoMo-DiT), which reuses parameters rather than adding them: a weight-shared loop repeatedly applies the middle layers, while sparse experts allocate parameter capacity across tokens. This design deepens the network without adding parameters, freeing the parameter budget for other uses, such as more experts or more distinct layers. It also allocates compute dynamically, varying the number of passes across noise levels. Experiments show that DyLoMo-DiT makes more effective use of parameter and compute budgets, with further gains from assigning more passes to low-noise steps. On ImageNet $256\times256$, DyLoMo-DiT reduces FID by 11-24% relative to DiT and 36-56% relative to DiT-MoE at matched parameter and compute budgets. For text-to-image generation, a scaled DyLoMo-DiT achieves a higher GenEval score than FLUX.1 (0.714 vs. 0.673), with less than one tenth of its active parameters (1.05B vs. 12B).
authors: Lernie Li, Yuanliu Liu, Pengfei Xiong, Wei Zhang
bullets: Addresses the parameter-storage and compute costs of scaling Diffusion Transformers with Mixture-of-Experts.
Uses a weight-shared loop over middle layers, allowing greater depth without adding parameters while retaining sparse experts.
Dynamically varies the number of loop passes by noise level, with more passes assigned to low-noise steps.
At matched parameter and compute budgets, reduces ImageNet 256×256 FID by 11–24% versus DiT and 36–56% versus DiT-MoE.
A scaled model achieves 0.714 GenEval on text-to-image generation versus FLUX.1’s 0.673, using under one-tenth the active parameters.

papers.abstract: Few-step samplers make large text-to-image flow models fast, but from the same noise they no longer generate the image of the standard 50-step sampler. Subjects, attributes and layout change, not just fine detail. We trace this loss of seed fidelity to the start of sampling. The coarse part of the initial noise decides coarse structure first, while the noise level is still above 0.9. Few-step samplers cross this range in their first steps, which account for 25-52% of their distance to the 50-step reference. Because this decision is coarse, a half-resolution run from the same coarse noise can make nearly the same decision at a third of the cost. We therefore propose Decide-then-Render (DtR), a training-free sampler that decides the composition in a few low-resolution steps, rebuilds the full-resolution state with the seed's own noise and renders the details. On 4 large models, DtR runs 11-25$\times$ faster than the reference sampler. At each speed-up, it is closer to the reference and rated higher by ImageReward than every compared sampler, including few-step schedules calibrated per budget and published multi-resolution samplers. On FLUX.1-dev, it remains the most faithful sampler down to about $8\times$, ahead of caching accelerators. A user study on this model found DtR's samples closer to the reference in 86% of pairwise trials. DtR transfers to a held-out model and to video, and distilled models can serve as its renderers. Project link: https://duanhuiran.github.io/DtR
authors: Huiran Duan, Weilun Feng, Yuqi Li, Yingli Tian
bullets: Few-step samplers lose seed fidelity because the initial, high-noise steps determine coarse structure, including subjects, attributes, and layout.
DtR performs these early decisions in a half-resolution run, reconstructs the full-resolution state using the original seed noise, and completes sampling without training.
Across four large models, it is 11–25× faster than the reference sampler while achieving higher reference fidelity and ImageReward than compared samplers at matched speeds.
On FLUX.1-dev, DtR remained the most faithful method to roughly 8× speed-up; a user study preferred it over alternatives in 86% of pairwise trials.
The approach transfers to a held-out model and video, and distilled models can be used for its rendering stage.

papers.abstract: Repeating rows then selecting originals retains layout-dependent drift despite equal encoding counts. We measure when existing checks fail to establish preservation contracts in fixed quantized KV-cache implementations. In four-bit HQQ axis zero at sixteen cycles, median paired relative-L2 increases over same-shape re-encoding are 7.22 percentage points for Qwen3-1.7B and 11.59 for SmolLM3-3B. Matched encoded states cover sixteen shared questions per model at one and sixteen cycles. Axis one matches the shape-preserving control; lazy reorders preserve the initial state. On one known input, fixed update counts retain the difference; preserving group members removes it. Our prefix-view extension passes current-prefix checks yet changes history and next logits in six model/codec settings at residual capacities four and 128. Public lookup reaches this boundary, including one of four precommitted project-new GPU inputs; fixed query swaps isolate a conditional old-history effect. Checkpoint/dense rollback is exact. An explicit delayed lookup client admits a supported 129-token path excluded by native AR on one known context. Failed task-harm expansion precludes population failure-rate or general answer-degradation claims. Native MLX-LM fixtures expose stale caller caches; synchronization restores the tested in-place contract with native computations preserved. In rejection tests, stale callers change logits but not greedy tokens.
bullets: Layout-dependent drift appears after repeated four-bit HQQ axis-zero updates, while axis-one and lazy-reorder controls match shape-preserving behavior.

A delayed-lookup client supports a 129-token path excluded by native autoregressive handling on one known context.

papers.abstract: Self-speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive image generation by leveraging the same model for parallel drafting and sequential verification, without requiring an additional draft model. While existing methods primarily focus on improving drafting and verification strategies, recent advances in random-order autoregressive modeling introduce an additional degree of freedom: the generation order. In this work, we theoretically analyze how generation order affects self-speculative decoding efficiency, identifying two key factors: draft-target mismatch, which determines token rejection probabilities, and early-rejection cost, which reflects the higher cost of rejecting tokens earlier in a speculative round. Motivated by these insights, we propose Speculation-Aware Ordering (SAO), a training-free framework for offline optimization of generation orders. Instead of evaluating candidate orders through costly speculative decoding, SAO uses simple pairwise conditional-TV statistics to formulate a rejection-cost-aware objective and efficiently construct speculation-friendly generation orders offline. Extensive experiments across different backbones and speculative widths demonstrate that SAO improves decoding efficiency, with the additional benefit of improved generation quality. Furthermore, SAO provides complementary efficiency gains when combined with existing self-speculative decoding methods. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to identify generation order as a new optimization dimension for efficient self-speculative decoding in autoregressive image generation.
authors: Yihan Chen, Jintao Zhang, Jun Zhu
bullets: Generation order affects efficiency through draft–target mismatch and the cost of rejecting tokens early in a speculative round.
Speculation-Aware Ordering (SAO) is a training-free, offline method that uses pairwise conditional-TV statistics instead of costly speculative-decoding evaluations.
SAO constructs rejection-cost-aware, speculation-friendly generation orders across different backbones and speculative widths.
Experiments show improved decoding efficiency and generation quality, with additional gains when combined with existing self-speculative methods.
The approach is designed for random-order autoregressive image generation and focuses on offline order optimization.

papers.abstract: Long-term time series forecasting supports decisions in energy, transportation, weather and finance, where forecasts are produced continuously and often on constrained hardware. Recent work has moved in two directions. One scales Transformers and pre-trained foundation models to millions or hundreds of millions of parameters. The other shows that models with only hundreds to tens of thousands of parameters remain competitive on the standard benchmarks. Existing surveys organize forecasting models by backbone and treat efficiency as a side topic, so the reasons these small models work, and the way their sizes are reported, remain unexamined. This survey focuses on lightweight long-term forecasting. It provides a taxonomy of about thirty-five models in six families, with a common notation and an architecture diagram for each core model. It offers a structured-linear view in which the smallest models are linear maps restricted by frequency truncation or period folding, and it tests each restriction in closed form on eight benchmarks. It complements the literature review with an audit of sixteen official code repositories, which reproduces published parameter counts and reveals reporting gaps of up to 289 times. Finally, it gives practical guidance on model selection and reporting, and summarizes open problems.
authors: Issam Ait Yahia, Abdelkader El Mahdaouy, Ismail Berrada
bullets: Reviews about 35 lightweight long-term forecasting models across six families using a shared taxonomy and notation.
Frames the smallest models as structured linear maps based on frequency truncation or period folding.
Tests these structural restrictions in closed form across eight standard benchmarks.
Audits 16 official code repositories, reproducing parameter counts and finding reporting gaps of up to 289×.
Provides model-selection and reporting guidance while identifying open problems.

papers.selection_reason: Survey and audit of lightweight forecasting models directly addresses parameter efficiency in AI systems.
papers.title: How Many Parameters Does Forecasting Need? A Survey and Code-Level Audit of Lightweight Long-Term Time Series Forecasting

papers.abstract: We propose loom attention, which allows a Transformer to dynamically rewire its circuits at every token by interweaving a head's vertical attention over the outputs of earlier heads (to obtain its query, key and value) with its horizontal attention over tokens. We instantiate vertical attention efficiently with normalized and gated linear attention over a per-token matrix memory, which stores the compressed head outputs and serves as a second residual stream. This yields LoomFormer, a dual-stream architecture that splits control and content between the vector and matrix streams. Across model sizes and training token budgets in language modeling and downstream tasks, LoomFormer matches Transformers trained with over 3x compute and recent residual-stream baselines (HC/mHC, MUDDFormer, AttnRes) trained with ~1.7-2.8x. For example, trained on the same 300B tokens with only 2% extra FLOPs, LoomPythia-2.8B achieves ~1.6x the average downstream gain of mHC-Pythia-2.8B over Pythia-2.8B, and matches (0-shot) or surpasses (5-shot) Pythia-12B. Code is available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/LoomFormer
authors: Da Xiao, Qingye Meng, Shengping Li, Xingyuan Yuan
bullets: Motivation: Standard Transformer circuits have relatively fixed information pathways across heads and layers.
Method: Loom attention interleaves vertical attention over earlier head outputs with horizontal token attention, using normalized, gated linear attention over per-token matrix memories.
Architecture: LoomFormer uses dual residual streams, separating control in vector states from content in matrix states.
Results: Across language modeling and downstream tasks, it matches models trained with over 3× compute and recent residual-stream baselines trained with roughly 1.7–2.8× compute.
Scope: Demonstrated across multiple model sizes and training-token budgets; code is publicly available. ],

papers.selection_reason: Introduces loom attention, a dual-stream transformer with linear attention, improving efficiency and performance in language modeling.
papers.title: Rewirable Circuits in Transformers with Loom Attention
papers.tldr: LoomFormer lets Transformers dynamically rewire information flow between attention heads at each token, improving parameter- and compute efficiency.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are served with accelerated decoders that cache context and commit, in one step, every masked position whose confidence clears a threshold. Yet post-training quantization of dLLMs has so far been calibrated and evaluated under fixed-step samplers without caching. We study W4A4 quantization under the deployed decoder and find that the decoder determines both where quantization harms accuracy and what it costs. Irreversible errors enter chiefly through forced commitments, made when no position clears the threshold: they are a minority of commitments but carry most quantization-induced flips. Quantization also levies a parallelism tax, extra forward passes per response: by compressing top logit gaps, it pushes positions below the threshold while leaving predictions largely intact. We propose DECAL, which reweights layer-wise calibration by a commitment-risk prior measured on the deployed decoder, and an argmax-preserving commit temperature that recovers the tax. On LLaDA and Dream, DECAL attains the best average accuracy among W4A4 methods, with lower run-to-run variance than the closest existing calibration method.
authors: Huan Xu, Maosen Zhao, Pengtao Chen, Tao Chen
bullets: Deployed parallel decoders, rather than fixed-step samplers, determine where quantization hurts dLLM accuracy and efficiency.
Most quantization-induced prediction flips arise from forced commitments when no position reaches the confidence threshold.
Quantization compresses top-logit gaps, causing extra forward passes even when predictions remain mostly unchanged—a parallelism tax.
DECAL reweights layer calibration using deployed-decoder commitment risk and applies an argmax-preserving commit temperature.
On LLaDA and Dream, DECAL achieves the best average W4A4 accuracy among evaluated methods with lower run-to-run variance than the closest baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of DECAL and the commit temperature. Top left: a W4A4 student is calibrated layer by layer against the full-precision teacher with a hidden-state MSE weighted by w[p], and decodes with the commit temperature Tmatch. Bottom: how w[p] is obtained. Under the deployed parallel decoder, positions committed above τ are safe (low flip risk π), whereas forced commitments at small logit margins may flip (high π); positions committed early are read by more later passes (high reach a); w[p] follows from r[p] = E[π · a]. Top right: dividing the logits by Tmatch restores the top-logit gaps that W4A4 compresses, and with them the full-precision commit rate.

papers.selection_reason: Quantization of diffusion LLMs under parallel decoding; memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Quantizing Diffusion LLMs under Parallel Decoding: Commitment Risk and the Parallelism Tax
papers.tldr: DECAL improves W4A4 quantization for diffusion LLMs by targeting commitment-risk errors and reducing quantization-induced decoding slowdowns.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can process hour-long videos, but the large number of input frames incurs substantial inference overhead. Existing approaches to efficient long-video understanding largely overlook video decoding, which can take longer than LLM prefill. We propose RAPID (Reference- and Access-Point-Informed Decoding), a codec-aware framework that exploits information embedded in compressed bitstreams to reduce both frame decoding and selection costs. RAPID consists of two components. RAPID-Dec exploits reference-frame information and random access points to skip unnecessary frames and decode the retained frames in parallel while preserving exact reconstruction of the target frames. It achieves up to a 3.7x decoding speedup over the fastest baseline on H.264/AVC videos. RAPID-Sel uses keyframes as coarse representatives of video segments, avoiding the dense candidate decoding and scoring required by existing frame selection methods. It achieves comparable accuracy with up to a 3.0x preprocessing speedup. Together, RAPID achieves a 4.9x time to first token (TTFT) speedup on hour-long videos over a state-of-the-art frame selection method using the fastest baseline decoder.
bullets: Targets the substantial video-decoding and frame-selection overhead in hour-long VLM inputs.
RAPID-Dec uses reference-frame dependencies and random access points to skip unnecessary frames and decode retained frames in parallel with exact reconstruction.
RAPID-Sel uses keyframes as coarse segment representatives, avoiding dense candidate decoding and scoring.
Reports up to 3.7× decoding speedup and up to 3.0× preprocessing speedup, while maintaining comparable selection accuracy.
Scope: results are reported for H.264/AVC videos and hour-long video workloads.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of RAPID. RAPID-Dec (right) decodes target frames chosen by any sampling strategy, including RAPID-Sel (left). It skips groups without target frames, frames after the last target frame of each group, and non-reference frames other than target frames, while preserving exact reconstruction of the targets. The retained groups are then distributed across threads for parallel decoding. RAPIDSel decodes and scores only the keyframes against the query and selects target frames by combining uniform frames with relevant frames allocated to groups by relevance.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces the cost of long-context decoding, but token selection introduces additional scoring and ranking overhead. Moreover, uniform page scoring overlooks differences in relevance between near and far context. We propose Near-Far Attention (NFA), which adapts retrieval to regional attention patterns while keeping candidate scoring lightweight. During prefill, the Lightweight Gate Estimator identifies regions that can be skipped during decoding, adding less than 1% to dense-prefill time. For the remaining regions, the Calibration-Free Subspace Extractor supplies compact features shared by page-level and token-level scoring without offline calibration. The Distance-Aware Two-Level Selector then scores near and far pages differently and jointly ranks candidate tokens under a shared budget. Evaluations across model families, parameter scales, and GQA/MLA architectures show aggregate task quality comparable to full attention. On Qwen3-8B at 512K context length, NFA achieves up to $5.49\times$ operator speedup and $2.97\times$ whole-model decoding speedup over FlashInfer, including selection overhead.

Uses a Lightweight Gate Estimator during prefill to skip low-value regions with under 1% added dense-prefill time.
Extracts compact, calibration-free features for both page- and token-level scoring.
A distance-aware two-level selector ranks near and far pages and candidate tokens under a shared budget.
On Qwen3-8B at 512K context, achieves up to 5.49× operator and 2.97× whole-model decoding speedup over FlashInfer, including selection overhead.

papers.title: Near-Far Attention: Region-Aware Sparse Retrieval for Long-Context LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: Near-Far Attention accelerates long-context LLM decoding by sparsely retrieving tokens with region-aware scoring while preserving task quality comparable to full attention.

papers.abstract: Kimi K3 combines a latent routed mixture of experts with full-width shared experts. A complete feed-forward evaluation must score and select experts, project tokens into the latent space, exchange tokens across expert-parallel ranks, compute the routed and shared branches, and normalize and project the routed sum before joining the branches. We present GC-MoE K3, a datacenter Blackwell implementation that schedules this entire evaluation as a CUDA Graph across two Green Contexts. Five base roles split input projection, routing, dispatch, expert computation, and finalization. Dispatch can fill the routed input ring while the compute partition evaluates shared experts. Finalize waits for the expert owners needed by each token and overlaps routed reduction and RMSNorm with loading the output projection weights. Conditional roles reuse the communication partition for routed computation and reduce split-$K$ projection partials. On GB200 at EP8, EP16, and EP32, the operator is faster at all 24 measured configurations than the paired SGLang-style reference (mean speedup $1.1324\times$). A comparison with historical vLLM-style measurements gives $1.3651\times$ across the same 24 shapes. Both latency comparisons time single-layer graph replay on synthetic K3-shaped inputs with a residual prefix. The separate paired numerical suite passes all 142 cases and 2,936 rank checks.
authors: Yong Li, Haoyu Wang, Kan Liu, Tao Lan
bullets: Implements the full K3 feed-forward path, including expert selection, latent projection, token exchange, routed/shared branches, normalization, and output projection.
Uses five CUDA Graph roles for input projection, routing, dispatch, expert computation, and finalization, with overlap between communication, shared-expert work, reduction, and weight loading.
Supports conditional role reuse for routed computation and split-K projection partial reductions.
On GB200 across EP8, EP16, and EP32, it is faster in all 24 measured configurations, with a mean 1.1324× speedup over the paired SGLang-style reference.
The numerical suite passes 142 cases and 2,936 rank checks; latency results use single-layer graph replay on synthetic K3-shaped inputs with a residual prefix.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents repeatedly feed an ever-growing interaction trajectory to a specialized agent model. Prefix caching reuses computation over repeated history, but cannot prevent context growth or remove information irrelevant to the current decision. This is especially costly when the specialized agent lacks the cached-input discounts available to general-purpose models, making trajectory compression a natural alternative. However, existing compression methods on selective context risk losing global information, recursively rewriting summary leads to semantic drift, while repeatedly recompressing the full history shifts the growing cost to the compressor. Therefore, we introduce DMC-5 (Dual-Model Collaboration with CaChe-aware Context Compression), an asymmetric framework that assigns full-history integration to a general compression model and action generation to a specialized agent model. DMC-5 maintains the raw trajectory as an Append-only Canonical View, preserving global access while allowing the compressor to reuse a stable historical prefix instead of recursively rewriting or recomputing prior context. The agent operates only on a compact Decision View with recent raw interactions, reducing repeated input while retaining the information needed for the next action. DMC-5 further incorporates YAMATO (integritY-Aware Memory Abstractions for Tool Operations) to preserve execution-critical information during lossy compression. Experiments on AppWorld, OfficeBench, and 8-objective QA show that DMC-5 reduces agent model input by 38.5-57.0% and end-to-end cost by 14.5-28.0% with 78.0-85.0% compressor cache-hit rates, while improving task performance by 1.0-5.8% over the uncompressed baseline.
authors: Haochen Li, Xiaobing Tu, Yinggui Wang, Jinkui Ren, Xiantao Zhang
bullets: Addresses growing trajectory context, irrelevant history, semantic drift, and repeated recompression costs.
Uses an Append-only Canonical View for stable full-history access and a compact Decision View for action generation.
Combines dual-model collaboration with YAMATO to preserve execution-critical tool information during lossy compression.
On AppWorld, OfficeBench, and 8-objective QA, reduces agent input by 38.5–57.0% and end-to-end cost by 14.5–28.0%.
Reports 78.0–85.0% compressor cache-hit rates and 1.0–5.8% higher task performance than the uncompressed baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a dual-model framework for cache-aware context compression in long-horizon agents, directly relevant to efficient context management.
papers.title: DMC-5: Dual-Model Collaboration with Cache-aware Context Compression for Long-horizon Agents
papers.tldr: DMC-5 compresses long-horizon agent histories using cache-aware collaboration between a general compressor and a specialized action model, reducing input and cost while improving task performance.

papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast zero-shot with accuracy exceeding that of task-specific models, and the smaller ones fit on edge devices. Operational deployments must refresh their forecast as new observations arrive, and privacy and latency requirements often force this refresh onto resource-constrained edge devices. To serve as a forecasting system there, a TSFM must refresh quickly, keep latency and peak memory bounded as the stream grows, and retain its accuracy as the observed history accumulates. Refreshing incrementally without altering the forecast requires temporal causality: non-causal models recompute at every update, causal attention admits a KV cache that grows linearly, and causal recurrent models update a fixed-size state in constant time and memory. We make these states persist across refreshes for every causal architecture and verify equivalence to full recomputation. We evaluate nine TSFM configurations on univariate forecasting against all three requirements, measuring accuracy as a function of context length, single-refresh latency, and latency and memory on streams of up to one million time steps on a server-grade GPU and three edge devices. No model gains on average accuracy beyond its trained context and most lose it well before the full history is reached, while KV caches leave latency and memory growing linearly with the retained history. TiRex-2 is the only one of the nine configurations meeting all three requirements: it refreshes in 14 ms on the GPU and 120 ms on a Raspberry Pi 5, keeps latency, energy and peak memory constant over a million steps, and retains its accuracy on the untruncated history.
authors: Marco Pichler, Patrick Podest, G\"unter Klambauer, Sepp Hochreiter
bullets: Edge forecasting requires fast refreshes, bounded latency and memory, and stable accuracy as observations accumulate.
Causal recurrent models support fixed-size state updates, unlike non-causal models and KV-cache approaches whose costs grow with history.
The authors persist recurrent states across refreshes and verify equivalence with full recomputation.
Nine TSFM configurations are evaluated on univariate forecasting across a GPU and three edge devices.
Most models lose accuracy beyond their trained context; only TiRex-2 meets all requirements, including constant resource use over one million steps.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates causal attention and recurrent models for streaming time-series forecasting on edge devices, focusing on KV cache growth and bounded memory/latency.
papers.title: Time Series Foundation Models on the Edge
papers.tldr: The study evaluates time-series foundation models for streaming forecasts on edge devices and finds that only TiRex-2 satisfies accuracy, latency, and bounded-memory requirements over million-step histories.

papers.abstract: Dense feed-forward networks are unaffected by how their neurons are grouped: every neuron is evaluated. Sparse execution makes this grouping consequential, because each input can access only a few experts. An arbitrary partition can therefore retain pretrained weights while separating computations that an input needs together. We argue that upcycling should organize neurons according to their responses to similar inputs. To establish this correspondence, we introduce a context-guided upcycling approach REACT, Response-based Expert Assembly from Contextual Trajectories, that uses frozen denoising trajectories to connect input contexts with pretrained neuron responses. We first identify contexts after timestep-wise centering to account for distribution shifts across noise levels, then use their associated responses to allocate intact neurons to routed experts. The same contexts initialize the corresponding router entries, aligning expert contents with their intended inputs, while global activation statistics select an always-active shared expert. Layer-wise reconstruction and end-to-end adaptation refine this initialization for sparse execution. On ImageNet-1K, our approach achieves better generation quality while activating only 37.5% of the original FFN parameters and reducing total per-token activated parameters by 27.6%.
authors: Hesen Yang, Yuxue Liu, Yanzhe Chen, Weibo Zhao, Junwei Su, Dan Hu, Shenggan Cheng, Xuanlei Zhao, Wenchao Zhou, Junhua Wang, Lansong Diao, Yang You
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between arbitrary neuron partitioning and the input-dependent computation required by sparse execution.
Uses frozen denoising trajectories to identify timestep-normalized contexts and associate them with pretrained neuron responses.
Allocates intact neurons to routed experts, initializes router entries from the same contexts, and adds a globally active shared expert.
Refines the initialization through layer-wise reconstruction and end-to-end adaptation.
On ImageNet-1K, achieves better generation quality while activating 37.5% of original FFN parameters and reducing total per-token activation by 27.6%.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes REACT for sparse execution in feed-forward networks using 'contextual trajectories' to route experts. The concept of using trajectories for routing and efficiency is transferable to World Models (Latent Action Models) and Embodied AI (memory/trajectories).
papers.title: REACT: Response-based Expert Assembly from Contextual Trajectories
papers.tldr: REACT upcycles dense feed-forward networks into sparse routed experts by grouping neurons according to their responses to similar input contexts.

papers.abstract: By accumulating spikes over multiple timesteps, rate coding approximates the real-valued activations of an ANN, a principle that underpins numerous ANN-to-SNN conversion methods. However, the converted SNNs typically incur loss in accuracy compared to the original ANN. Existing methods either increase a number of timesteps or introduce more complex neuronal dynamics to reduce this accuracy gap. Yet, both approaches ultimately lead to the same outcome: redundancy either in information or in computation, thereby suffering from efficiency degradation. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{PRIME} (\underline{P}otential-\underline{R}esidual \underline{I}ntegration for \underline{M}ulti-threshold \underline{E}ncoding), a multi-threshold concurrent spiking neuron framework redesigned from a hardware data representation perspective:a) We introduce the Residual Membrane Potential Amplification (RMPA) mechanism, which replaces rate coding with Integration Coding by actively amplifying the residual membrane potential. RMPA enables the binary representation of spikes to carry substantially more information, achieving near-lossless conversion with as few as two timesteps.b) Complementarily, we implement concurrent spike firing in multi-threshold neurons, where spikes are decoded directly from the binary representation of floating-point data, eliminating membrane potential--threshold comparisons and replacing multiplications with lightweight bit-shift and accumulation operations that align with hardware computation primitives. At $T=2$ and $D=3$, we achieve competitive performance across both vision and language benchmarks with only 40.6\% of the FP32 bit-transmission cost and 13.4\% of the FP32 multiplication energy consumption. The PRIME framework establishes a new design principle for efficient ANN-to-SNN conversion, bridging the gap between algorithmic efficiency and hardware constraints.
authors: Shaohong Gu, Jiyuan Zhang, Yimeng Shan, Chenxiao Dou, Wei Hua, Malu Zhang, Honglin Cao, Choonghyun Lee, Jingwei Chen
bullets: ANN-to-SNN conversion often loses accuracy or requires redundant timesteps and complex neuron dynamics.
PRIME uses Residual Membrane Potential Amplification to replace rate coding with higher-information Integration Coding.
Multi-threshold neurons decode concurrent spikes from floating-point bit representations, avoiding membrane-potential comparisons.
At T=2 and D=3, the method achieves competitive results across vision and language benchmarks.
The reported cost is 40.6% of FP32 bit transmission and 13.4% of FP32 multiplication energy.

papers.abstract: Looped language models reuse one block of weights T times per token, trading parameters for test-time depth, but autoregressive decoding then pays T sequential passes per token. Self-speculative decoders recover 2-10x for a single request, yet their gains fade as requests share a GPU, and current practice is to speculate less as load grows. We show that what fails under load is the layout of speculative work, not speculation. In concurrent decoding the unit of cost is the row, one request advancing on one loop, which reads that loop's key-value (KV) cache once; additional positions inside a row are nearly free. Pipelined schedules such as the wavefront place every speculative position on a different loop, hence in a row of its own, so each token is still read T times. We present PackLoop, built on one principle: speculate only inside rows that are read anyway. Deep loops accumulate positions and advance them as a block in one row, context-copy proposals join the row that the first loop already reads, and a closed-form admission rule, the economic order quantity of inventory theory, sets how long to accumulate from a cost model calibrated once per engine. PackLoop is exact: in FP32 its output is token-for-token identical to autoregressive decoding, also under sampling and early exit. Across 164 load points spanning three GPUs, four Ouro models, six benchmarks, and contexts up to 32K tokens, one PackLoop configuration is faster than the best existing schedule, chosen per point, at 161 points (median 1.25x, up to 1.76x) and never significantly slower. Its lead grows with concurrency and context length, the regime in which existing self-speculation gains least.
bullets: Looped language models require multiple sequential passes per token, and existing self-speculation loses efficiency as concurrency increases.
The key bottleneck is speculative-work layout: separate rows repeatedly reread the same loop-specific KV caches.
PackLoop packs deep-loop and context-copy proposals into already-used rows, with an economic-order-quantity rule controlling accumulation.
It is token-for-token exact in FP32, including sampling and early exit.
Across 164 load points, it beat the best existing schedule at 161 points, with a median 1.25× and maximum 1.76× speedup, without significant slowdowns.

papers.selection_reason: Row-packed self-speculative decoding for looped LLMs under concurrency; strong efficient-inference contribution via KV-cache scheduling.
papers.title: PackLoop: Row-Packed Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models under Concurrency
papers.tldr: PackLoop preserves exact self-speculative decoding while improving throughput under concurrent GPU workloads by packing speculative positions into rows that are already being read.

papers.abstract: World action models guide robots by predicting the effects of actions or generating commands from observations. A model may compare hundreds of candidate futures before acting, repeatedly reading weights that must fit in device memory. Post-training quantization reduces the number of bits used to store pretrained weights, but a smaller model is not necessarily a deployable one: temporary tensors can exceed graphics processing unit (GPU) memory limits, while even small prediction errors can change the selected action. This creates two coupled challenges: identifying bit assignments that preserve task performance and determining which of them meet real execution constraints, without exhausting costly task trials. We present PTQ4WAM, a framework for choosing layer-wise bit assignments and execution routes under memory, latency and task-evaluation budgets. Calibration measurements guide candidate proposals, optionally with a language model agent. We profile full-model routes on the GPU before spending task trials on feasible assignments. Fusing group rescaling and reading visual history in place can make an otherwise infeasible assignment deployable. Across 15 workloads from four model families, the median task score is 99.2% of the corresponding 32-bit floating-point (FP32) score. On fixed GPU replays, the median speedup over FP32 is 2.36 times and the median reduction in peak allocated memory is 71.5%. The code will be released soon.
authors: Tianqi Li, Xin He, Xue Geng, Le Zhang, Ming-Ming Cheng, Yun Liu
bullets: Addresses the gap between smaller quantized models and actual deployability, where temporary tensors, latency, and action-sensitive errors matter.
Chooses layer-wise bit assignments and GPU execution routes under memory, latency, and task-evaluation budgets.
Uses calibration-guided candidate proposals, optional language-model assistance, and full-model GPU profiling before costly task trials.
Across 15 workloads and four model families, achieved a median 99.2% of FP32 task score, 2.36× speedup, and 71.5% lower peak allocated memory.
Scope: results focus on fixed GPU replays; code release is forthcoming.

papers.abstract: Treating independent layers as the minimal pruning unit allows layer pruning to efficiently eliminate many redundant parameters and achieve high compression rates. Layer pruning has become a promising and prevalent structured pruning technique for large language models (LLMs). However, multi-layer removal can lead to significant performance degradation for LLMs. Although some works have explored various compensation methods for pruned layers, they are inefficient and costly. Observing that the expression of a large proportion of information is concentrated on a small number of pivotal channels, we propose a novel post-pruning compensation method for layer pruning, called pivotal channel compensation (PCC). PCC can achieve significant performance improvement by compensating for a small number of channels through learnable linear transformations at the pruning interface. Besides, we propose a new evaluation metric, called channel-wise average performance improvement (CAPI), which can measure the efficiency of channel-wise compensation. Our experimental results across various LLMs demonstrate that PCC can achieve significant and consistent improvements and high CAPI on language modeling and zero-shot question answering for the state-of-the-art cross-layer and consecutive-layer pruning methods. Compared with existing compensation methods, PCC can achieve competitive results with fewer additional parameters and less training cost.
authors: Xiangqian Wang, Yucheng Zhang, Zhaohong Jia, Kun Jing, Chunchun Li
bullets: Layer pruning offers high compression but removing multiple layers can substantially degrade LLM performance.
PCC applies learnable linear transformations at pruning interfaces to compensate for information concentrated in pivotal channels.
The proposed CAPI metric measures the efficiency of channel-wise compensation.
Experiments across various LLMs show consistent gains in language modeling and zero-shot question answering for cross-layer and consecutive-layer pruning.
Compared with existing compensation methods, PCC achieves competitive performance with fewer added parameters and less training cost.

papers.abstract: Deploying large vision-language-action (VLA) models on resource-constrained robots demands extreme compression, yet existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods frequently collapse at ultra-low bit-widths ($\le$ 2 bits). We trace this failure to two mismatches in standard pipelines. First, calibrating on static offline demonstrations induces distribution shift: minor quantization perturbations drive the policy into unseen states where uncalibrated errors compound. Second, minimizing the layer-wise weight reconstruction error is a flawed proxy, as action generation depends only on the representations consumed by the action head. We present LoopQ, an on-policy ultra-low-bit quantization framework. LoopQ closes the loop by calibrating on states from the quantized policy's own rollouts. It then adds readout-aligned fine-tuning, which freezes the trellis codes and optimizes only lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors to align the backbone readout with the full-precision teacher. With all linear layers at 2 bits, LoopQ achieves a 60.4% success rate on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T N1.7, close to the 61.8% of full precision. Even at 1 bit per weight, $\pi_{0.5}$ still completes 80.0% of LIBERO tasks. With 8-bit activations, the 2-bit $\pi_{0.5}$ runs on integer kernels on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, with 4.1$\times$ smaller weights and 44% less memory. On a real AgileX Piper arm, it stays within one success of full precision on each of three tasks. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/LoopQ
authors: Yanlong Chen, Thongthornpatch Chamadol, Yichen Guo, Yunfei Gao, Mohan Liu, Addison Lin Wang, Yawei Li
bullets: Standard PTQ fails at ≤2 bits because static calibration misses quantization-induced state drift and layer-wise reconstruction does not reflect action-generation needs.
LoopQ uses on-policy rollouts from the quantized policy for drift-aware calibration.
Readout-aligned fine-tuning updates lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors while keeping trellis codes fixed.
At 2-bit weights, LoopQ reaches 60.4% on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T N1.7 versus 61.8% full precision; 1-bit π₀.₅ completes 80.0% of LIBERO tasks.
The 2-bit π₀.₅ model uses integer kernels on Jetson AGX Thor, reducing weight storage by 4.1× and memory by 44%, and remains close to full precision on three real-arm tasks.

papers.title: Quantizing in the Loop: Drift-Aware Ultra-Low-Bit Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: LoopQ enables ultra-low-bit VLA models to retain near-full-precision robot performance by calibrating on their own rollouts and aligning quantized representations with action readouts.

papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents enable automated interactions with mobile, web, and desktop interfaces. However, their large memory footprint and repeated model calls hinder deployment on resource-constrained devices, motivating post-training quantization (PTQ) without full retraining. Quantization can degrade GUI response accuracy and distort the instruction-vision affinities and local spatial relations needed for GUI target selection. Small coordinate errors can cause missed clicks, while early action errors can alter subsequent interface states and disrupt task execution. Local reconstruction error alone does not directly assess whether these responses and relations are preserved. We propose GUI-Q, a PTQ framework that targets response and relation preservation with 4-bit weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16). Task-Sensitive Granularity Allocation (TSGA) allocates finer groups under a scale-byte budget by combining response sensitivity with the measured reduction in activation-weighted distortion. Relation-Preserving Symmetry Selection (RPSS) then selects symmetric or asymmetric grids to preserve instruction-vision affinities and local spatial relations in GUIs. Across three GUI-capable models, GUI-Q improves mean grounding TargetHit by 8.04 to 12.55 points over the strongest evaluated 4-bit configurations, while reducing static peak graphics processing unit (GPU) memory by 49.9% to 56.2% relative to bfloat16 (BF16). Fixed-output replay with packed 4-bit execution provides 1.7 to 2.8 times model-call speedups. The code will be released.
authors: Tianqi Li, Yang Wang, Xin He, Le Zhang, Yun Liu
bullets: Addresses GUI-agent deployment constraints from large memory use and repeated model calls.
Uses Task-Sensitive Granularity Allocation to assign finer quantization groups where response-sensitive distortion is reduced most.
Uses Relation-Preserving Symmetry Selection to retain instruction–vision affinities and local spatial relations.
Across three GUI-capable models, improves grounding TargetHit by 8.04–12.55 points over evaluated 4-bit baselines.
Reduces peak GPU memory by 49.9%–56.2% versus BF16 and achieves 1.7–2.8× model-call speedups with packed 4-bit execution.

papers.abstract: Model routing assigns each query to a suitable foundation model, but tasks and available models keep changing, and existing routers are either untrained for the pool at hand or fit once and forget earlier tasks when updated. We present AdaptRouter, an adaptive router trained by policy learning: a compact multimodal decision model reads each question with cards describing the current experts and learns from native task feedback, without routing labels, to select one frozen expert. Open-weight and API experts share the router, its inputs, and the quality-cost trade-off but use different losses: cheap open-weight experts are explored with RL, whereas paid API experts are queried once and their cached feedback is reused as soft labels. New tasks are learned without replay, new experts enter as cards, and an open-weight quality-first advantage provably keeps cost from overriding quality. Across four task stages, AdaptRouter loses at most 0.4 points on earlier tasks, whereas feedback-trained routers lose up to 7.0, and as its pool grows from three to ten experts, its accuracy rises from 67.2% to 72.1%. On five API models, it exceeds GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra (low) by over 22 points at under a third of their cost.
authors: Jingpu Yang, Fengxian Ji, Tianhao Li, Juanfan Wu, Yufeng Wang, Shuxin Zheng, Xiaoqing Zhang
bullets: Addresses routers that cannot adapt to new tasks or forget earlier ones when updated.

Adds new tasks without replay and incorporates new experts by adding their cards.

Across four task stages, earlier-task performance drops by at most 0.4 points; accuracy increases from 67.2% to 72.1% as the pool grows from 3 to 10 experts, while outperforming two cited API models by over 22 points at less than one-third their cost.

papers.abstract: LLM agents now propose research ideas and run the experiments that test them, but they train every run to its end, whereas a researcher reads a run's configuration and the beginning of its curve and stops the runs that show no promise. Reading a run this way takes more than describing or implementing a training method: it takes knowing what a design choice does to a run. We build Tea Leaves to measure this knowledge on 682 real training runs across pretraining, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning (RL): a forecaster sees the first 20% of a run with its configuration, description, and code, and predicts the rest. Across 11 LLMs and a range of forecasting baselines, the strongest LLMs match or exceed the best curve fitter on smooth loss curves (skill 0.66 against 0.62) and lead on noisy RL reward curves (0.43 against 0.13). What bounds every forecaster is what the log carries: on sparsely logged community runs all methods lose most of their skill, and none reliably flags a failing run in advance. Beyond the curve, information helps and effort does not: related runs in the prompt cut the error on loss curves by 39%, and knowledge of training dynamics lets the strongest LLMs order all 36 pairs of runs that differ by a described code change, which the early curves do not separate, whereas tools add little. This knowledge can be learned from logged runs: a small open model trained on public runs matches the best LLM on loss curves. Applied to the progress curves of research agents, the same reading ranks tasks by their remaining headroom, although for a single agent run it does not improve on the last value. We release the benchmark, the trained readers, and their training data to test and train LLMs' understanding of training and to help research agents decide which runs deserve their compute.
authors: Xinran Zhao, Xiang Li, Tong Chen, Jinchuan Tian, Zichun Yu, Tongshuang Wu
bullets: Benchmarks 11 LLMs and forecasting baselines on 682 pretraining, fine-tuning, and RL runs.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and trained forecasters for predicting LLM training runs; transferable to compute-efficient run selection and research-agent compute allocation.
papers.title: Reading the Tea Leaves, Again: Can Large Language Models Predict Language Model Training Runs?
papers.tldr: Tea Leaves evaluates whether LLMs can forecast the outcomes of training runs from their early curves and configurations, finding strong performance on smooth losses but major limits with noisy or sparsely logged runs.

papers.abstract: Rendering long text as images lets a vision-language model (VLM) read a document with fewer input tokens, and evaluations often count mainly these prefill tokens. We show that for reasoning models this accounting is incomplete. Across five models and two long-context benchmarks, reading the rendered document makes the model think longer: decode length grows by 1.5-3.5x on the four general-purpose VLMs tested, and under typical output pricing this decode tax makes image input more expensive than text for two of the five models on QuALITY. Unrecoverable information loss is not sufficient to explain the tax at moderate compression: Qwen's OCR of the same images recovers 98.7% of words, and feeding Kimi-K3 its own transcription as text restores text-mode reasoning length and accuracy. Whether compression pays off reduces to an exchange rate, (1-1/c)/(r-1), that must exceed the workload's price-weighted ratio of output to input tokens; this accounting decomposition shows why Kimi-K3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash can benefit and Qwen and GLM cannot. None of the training-free signals we test predicts the tax before generation. As a practical heuristic, an image-first policy that sends only inputs with a per-input compression ratio of at least 1.6 to images and falls back to text once image-mode reasoning costs as much as the input's prefill saving cuts the bill by 6-14% on Kimi-K3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at an accuracy cost of 0.3-1.2 points; on QuALITY, asking for a reasoning budget on both paths is a stronger lever.
bullets: Across five models and two long-context benchmarks, rendered documents increased decode length by 1.5–3.5× for four general-purpose VLMs.
The added reasoning cost is not explained solely by OCR loss: Qwen recovered 98.7% of words, while Kimi-K3’s text transcription restored text-mode reasoning length and accuracy.
Compression is worthwhile when its input-token savings outweigh the price-weighted output-token increase, favoring Kimi-K3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash but not Qwen and GLM.
An image-first policy using a 1.6× compression threshold reduced bills by 6–14% on two models, with a 0.3–1.2 point accuracy cost.
Training-free signals tested did not predict the decode tax before generation; matched reasoning budgets were a stronger lever on QuALITY.

papers.selection_reason: Decode-aware cost analysis of optical context compression in reasoning VLMs; relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: When Does Optical Context Compression Pay Off? A Decode-Aware Cost Analysis of Reasoning VLMs
papers.tldr: Optical context compression can reduce input tokens but often increases reasoning output enough to erase its cost advantage, so it pays off only under favorable model- and workload-specific conditions.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting renders photorealistic views in real time. However, a single scene often needs millions of Gaussians, so these models are costly to store and render. Pruning reduces this cost by keeping a subset of the Gaussians. A common score is the leave-one-out importance, which is the loss increase when a Gaussian alone is removed. At high pruning ratios, many Gaussians are removed together, so Gaussians that are redundant alone but essential together are lost. We present LMnOP (Leave-Many-Out Pruning), which estimates the importance of each Gaussian under the removal of the other Gaussians. This leave-many-out importance is the average loss increase when a Gaussian is removed while the others are also removed at random. We compute the exact mean and variance of each pixel's color under random removal in closed form, and approximate the importance from them without sampling removal patterns. We refine each Gaussian's probability of remaining with its importance and prune once at the end. Without fine-tuning, LMnOP achieves the best results in 16 of 18 metrics on three datasets at 90% and 99% removal. It improves SSIM and LPIPS over GaussianPOP in all 13 scenes.
authors: Sunjae Jeong, Jaeseung Kim, Hyoseok Hwang
bullets: Targets the storage and rendering cost of scenes containing millions of 3D Gaussians.
Addresses the limitation of leave-one-out scores, which can miss Gaussians that are redundant individually but important together.
Computes exact per-pixel color mean and variance under random Gaussian removal in closed form, avoiding sampled removal patterns.
Updates each Gaussian’s retention probability from its estimated leave-many-out importance and prunes only once.
Without fine-tuning, achieves the best result on 16 of 18 metrics across three datasets at 90% and 99% removal; improves SSIM and LPIPS over GaussianPOP in all 13 scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LMnOP. Every Gaussian starts with the keep probability K/N , and the histograms show the keep probabilities after r updates. µ-σ rendering gives the mean and variance of each pixel’s color under the current keep probabilities, and we compute the LMO importance of every Gaussian from them. We then move each keep probability halfway toward bi and compute the importance again. Here bi is 1 for the K Gaussians with the highest importance and 0 for the others. After R importance computations, we keep these K Gaussians and prune the rest in one final step.

Figure 3. Quality of pruned models on the 3DGS training curve. Bicycle, without fine-tuning. Top: the original model and LMnOP at 90% removal, with the PSNR / LPIPS of the view. The zoomed region in the red box shows slight white artifacts in the pruned model. Bottom: test PSNR and LPIPS of 3DGS during training. Each marker places a pruned model where 3DGS reaches the same value. The markers indicate quality, not training time.

papers.title: LMnOP: Pruning 3D Gaussian Splatting via Leave-Many-Out Importance

papers.abstract: As robotic arms undertake diverse manipulation tasks, a deployment may need to serve many task-specific vision-language-action (VLA) policies concurrently. Dedicating a GPU to each robot is costly, motivating shared-GPU inference. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) allows compatible policies to share a frozen backbone with lightweight policy-specific adapters, reducing model-weight memory and enabling cross-policy batching. However, robot inference must keep pace with physical execution. With action chunking, robots continue executing buffered actions while awaiting new predictions, and the remaining buffered time provides each robot's execution slack for serving its next request. Once this slack is exhausted, the robot stalls until new actions arrive, interrupting task progress. Observing earlier preserves more slack but can lead to disruptive replanning and lower task success, whereas delaying dispatch to form larger batches can improve GPU efficiency but consumes slack and risks stalls. To balance these competing demands, we present MotionServe, a shared-GPU serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with server-side batch formation. MotionExec selects observation triggers based on motion structure in predicted action chunks, allowing inference to overlap with remaining buffered execution. SlackBatch combines the resulting per-robot execution budgets with estimated outstanding GPU work to determine when to wait, which requests to batch, and when to dispatch them. We evaluate X-VLA on LIBERO and SimplerEnv's WidowX tasks and OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO, with up to 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU. At 96 robots, MotionServe reduces mean stall per episode by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively, over each model's lowest-stall baseline. Backbone sharing also reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.
authors: Zikang Wen, Yuning Zhang, Dong Yuan
bullets: Shared-GPU inference reduces the cost of deploying many task-specific VLA policies, especially with LoRA adapters sharing a frozen backbone.
MotionExec triggers observations using motion structure in predicted action chunks to overlap inference with buffered execution.
SlackBatch uses per-robot slack and estimated GPU workload to decide when to wait, batch requests, or dispatch them.
With up to 96 simulated robots, it reduces mean episode stall by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points across evaluated settings.
Backbone sharing reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.
