papers.abstract: An artificial neuron computes and learns, but it does not live: the units of a network are fixed when it is designed, and every one of them is kept and paid for whether it is used or not. We give each neuron a second pathway. Beside its Task Path, the usual computation and gradient learning, a dual-pathway neuron has a Growth Path: a nutrient flows from the outputs back through the network, every layer receives the same fixed budget, and each unit is fed in proportion to how much the units above it use it. A well-fed unit divides and a starving unit dies. This allocation is not a separate analysis or pruning step: it runs throughout training and reads only activations and weights. The task is still learned from labels with the ordinary loss, and the training procedure gains no phase, no schedule and no target size. Because the budget is conserved, the competition is zero-sum and a single number sets the size of the network. Switched on in a pretrained network that is deployed on a narrower domain, the Growth Path shrinks the network while it keeps learning. With Adam the network ends 1.0 to 1.2 points more accurate on the domain than the same network trained ordinarily, at 24% to 60% of its compute, and at 12% of the compute it is still ahead; a random choice of the same number of units gives no gain. Letting starving pretrained units sleep instead of die keeps 1.2 to 4.6 points more of the rarely used content. Over 800 changing tasks a network with the Growth Path holds its accuracy while ordinary networks decline. With plain SGD the gains are smaller: at deployment the method trades compute against rarely used content, and on one of the two continual-learning streams it only ties networks of equal size. The experiments are small (three-layer perceptrons on MNIST-like data); what they show is that a conserved, loss-free second pathway can decide by itself which units a network needs.
bullets: Adds a second, label-free pathway alongside ordinary task learning: nutrient flows backward from outputs and is allocated according to unit use.
Well-fed units divide while starving units die or sleep; a fixed budget controls network size without a separate pruning phase, schedule, or target size.
On narrower deployment domains with Adam, networks retained higher accuracy while using 24–60% of the compute, with gains still reported at 12%.
Sleeping rather than deleting unused pretrained units preserved more rarely used knowledge; across 800 changing tasks, accuracy remained stable while ordinary networks declined.
Results were smaller with SGD and are limited to small three-layer perceptrons on MNIST-like data.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Switched on at deployment, the Growth Path shrinks the network while it keeps learning. Top: the deployment stream. Bottom: mean number of live units per hidden layer, accuracy on the common content (windows of 100 tasks) and on the rare content (windows of 250 tasks), means of five seeds. The size settles within about 200 tasks at a level set by the budget B. With Adam the smaller network is more accurate than the ordinary network on both kinds of content, and a random choice of the same number of units is not. With SGD it matches the ordinary network on the common content and falls behind on the rare content.

Figure 1: The Growth Path is a second pathway in every neuron. (a) An ordinary unit has a Task Path only: signals go up and gradients come back. A dual-pathway neuron also receives a nutrient from the units above it. (b) The nutrient enters at the outputs and is passed down; every layer receives the same budget B, split among its units in proportion to their use by the layer above. A well-fed unit divides, a starved unit dies, the others survive. The allocation is repeated every 100 updates while the network trains, and it never reads the loss. (c) Switched on in a pretrained network that is deployed on a narrower domain, the Growth Path shrinks the network while it keeps learning. Each point is one budget (B = 25 to 100). At 12% of the compute the network is still more accurate on the domain than the ordinary network at full size. (d) Trained from scratch on 800 tasks that keep rewiring the input, a network with the Growth Path holds its accuracy, while ordinary networks of the same size and of the starting width decline. Panels (c) and (d) are for Adam (means of five seeds); the results with SGD, which are less favourable at deployment, are in Sections 4 and 5.

Figure 3: The budget trades compute against accuracy along a smooth curve. Difference to the ordinary network against compute, for budgets B = 25, 35, 50, 65, 80 and 100 (left to right on each curve); bars are 95% intervals of the paired differences. Dotted lines mark the rules of Table 1. With Adam the Growth Path is above the ordinary network on the common content at every budget, down to 12% of the compute, and dormancy keeps the rare content as well. With SGD the common content holds down to about 30% of the compute and the rare content is lost progressively. Open squares: ordinary networks of the sizes reached at B = 50 and B = 100, trained from scratch on the whole stream.

Figure 4: The rule removes what the domain no longer needs, without ever seeing a label. Share of the pretrained units removed in the first 100 tasks after switch-on (B = 100), by the content a unit mattered for when the Growth Path was switched on (the content whose loss rises most when the unit is silenced; “none”: silencing it changes nothing). Bars are means of five seeds with 95% intervals. A random choice of the same number of units makes no such difference.

Figure 6: On a stream that keeps rewiring its input, a network with the Growth Path keeps learning. Left and middle: online accuracy over 800 pixel-permutation tasks (blocks of 20 tasks, five seeds; λ = 0). The ordinary network of the same size is the stronger of our two size-matched baselines (peak size). With Adam the Growth Path is ahead throughout; with SGD it starts behind the larger ordinary network, draws level after about 200 tasks and is ahead from then on. Right: accuracy against cost after 200 tasks (Adam); each orange point is the setting selected for one inheritance ratio λ (the point marked “low cost” is a second setting with λ = 0.25), and the blue line is the ordinary network at widths 50 to 400.

Figure 5: Dormant units wake when the content they serve returns. (a) Wakes per task on rare-content tasks and on common-content tasks (means of five seeds, 95% intervals). (b) The pretrained units at the end of the stream, by the content they mattered for at switch-on (Adam, B = 100).

Table 1: Deployment: differences to the ordinary network (seeds 15–19, paired by seed, 95% intervals). Compute is the counted cost as a percentage of the ordinary network. The first row of each block gives the accuracy of the ordinary network in percent. Rules, fixed in advance (Section 3): (a) common content not more than 0.5 points worse; (b) compute at most 75%; (c) late rare content not more than 1.0 point worse. Each is judged on the end of the interval, so a positive mean with a wide interval can fail rule (c). The Growth Path without dormancy is judged on (a) and (b); rule (c) was added for dormancy and is shown for all rows. Appendix C lists all six budgets.

papers.selection_reason: Dual-pathway neuron allocation adapts network size during training/deployment; relevant to continual learning and compute-efficient adaptation.
papers.title: The Growth Path Is the Missing Half of Neural Networks
papers.tldr: A conserved Growth Path lets neural networks adapt their size during training by rewarding useful units and removing or sleeping unused ones, improving efficiency and adaptation in small-scale experiments.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how the world responds to actions and offer a promising path toward general embodied intelligence, but they are large and run the network many times per plan, so they are hard to deploy on robots. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) compute with sparse binary spikes and use additions instead of multiplications, which saves power. However, existing WAMs use dense videos as the world state, so a spiking version would spend most of its computation on the background. We therefore introduce SpikingWAM, the first spiking WAM, which uses a sparse task skeleton as the world state. Inspired by biological motor control, which attends only to the key positions of a task, the Task Skeleton State (TSS) keeps the keypoints of the arm and the task objects, and a small spiking front end estimates the object keypoints from images. Body Frame Spike Coding (BFSC) and Grid Coincidence Attention (GCA) keep millimetre precision, and the Persistent Single Step Readout (PSR) runs the network once per plan. On the simulated benchmarks LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, SpikingWAM achieves competitive success rates with far less energy than ANN methods and surpasses all compared methods on LIBERO-Plus. Real robot experiments further confirm its effectiveness. These results show that a task skeleton lets spiking networks implement WAMs at very low energy, offering a new solution for low power embodied intelligence. Project page: https://wxqnl.github.io/spikingwam/
authors: Mingquan Liu, Peng Zhou, Shanming Yao, Shuai Wang, Simo Wu, Malu Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high computational and energy costs of large world-action models that repeatedly process dense video observations.
Represents the world with a sparse Task Skeleton State containing arm and object keypoints, estimated from images by a spiking front end.
Introduces Body Frame Spike Coding, Grid Coincidence Attention, and Persistent Single Step Readout for precise, efficient planning.
Achieves competitive simulated-task success with substantially lower energy than ANN methods, surpasses compared methods on LIBERO-Plus, and works in real-robot experiments.

The two experts compute self-attention together in every layer, and GCA adds a relative geometry term to it. (iii) At inference the future skeleton is removed. papers.title: Spiking World-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: SpikingWAM enables low-energy robotic manipulation by modeling task-relevant keypoints with a spiking world-action model instead of dense video states.

papers.abstract: A 4-bit KV cache reads about half the bytes of FP8, but Hopper GPUs have no FP4 hardware and little instruction-issue capacity per byte of memory bandwidth, so 4-bit values must be decoded in software. On H200, vLLM's NVFP4 KV path (FlashInfer's decode) reaches 10-20% of memory bandwidth and is up to 1.7x slower than FP8. NVBit instruction counts show two causes: the kernels behind vLLM's 4-bit paths (FlashInfer NVFP4, Triton UltraQuant) execute 2-6x Hopper's issue budget per byte and serialize loading, decoding and matrix multiplies. Our Hopper-native decode kernel overlaps a TMA producer warp with two compute warpgroups, lays the cache out at write time so decoded values feed the tensor cores from registers, and swaps the matrix operands so small query groups need no padding. On H200 it reaches 67-75% of peak bandwidth at batch 32-128 and at all 11 shapes is 1.12-1.49x faster than the faster of XQA and FlashAttention-4's proposed native FP8. Inside vLLM, with an accuracy recipe (K mean removal and rotation, 4 BF16 sink tokens, BF16 layer 0), it decodes 1.12-1.64x faster per step on Llama-3.1-8B than vLLM's FlashInfer FP8 path at batch 8 and above (1.04-1.24x over FlashAttention-4's FP8), is level at batch 1, and holds 1.63x as many tokens. On one H200 under a reasoning-like request stream, the highest rate at which 99% of requests meet the latency targets is 1.23-1.32x FP8's on Llama-3.1-8B and 1.67-2.20x on Qwen2.5-72B, as the cache becomes the limit; prefill-heavy streams are worse (7% slower prefill). On five 7B-32B models, repeated runs show no significant accuracy difference from BF16 KV. In Qwen2-family models, whose reasoning variants collapse under FP8 KV, layer 0's key mean is almost entirely the key-projection bias identified by prior work, seen through RoPE and computable from the weights alone; keeping that layer in BF16 restores FP8 KV and, with K mean removal, 4-bit KV.
bullets: Existing Hopper 4-bit KV kernels underuse memory bandwidth because decoding and matrix operations are serialized and exceed instruction capacity per byte.
The proposed kernel overlaps TMA loading with computation, stores the cache for register-fed tensor-core inputs, and avoids padding for small query groups.
It reaches 67–75% of peak H200 bandwidth and is 1.12–1.49× faster across 11 tested shapes than the faster of XQA and FlashAttention-4’s proposed native FP8 path.
In vLLM, it is 1.12–1.64× faster per decode step than FlashInfer FP8 at batch sizes ≥8 and supports 1.63× as many tokens; prefill-heavy workloads lose 7% speed.
K mean removal, rotation, BF16 sink tokens, and retaining layer 0 in BF16 preserve accuracy across tested models, including Qwen variants that degrade with FP8 KV.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a fast 4-bit KV-cache decoding kernel with memory-efficiency and inference-speed improvements, directly fitting the KV-cache and memory-efficiency subtopic.
papers.title: Fast 4-bit KV-Cache Decoding on Hopper GPUs: Why Existing Kernels Are Slow and How to Fix Them
papers.tldr: A Hopper-optimized 4-bit KV-cache decoder fixes software-decoding bottlenecks, achieving near-bandwidth performance and higher throughput than FP8 while preserving accuracy with targeted safeguards.

papers.abstract: Reliable 3D object detection for autonomous trucks requires both the semantic detail provided by cameras and the geometric and motion cues measured by 4D radar. Existing radar-camera detectors commonly construct global radar bird's-eye-view (BEV) representations, whose computational and memory costs grow with the perception range. Sparse query-based detectors offer greater efficiency, but global feature construction can obscure point-level radar geometry and motion information. We present QSRadar, a query-conditioned sparse radar fusion framework for efficient long-range 3D detection. Built on a Sparse4Dv3-style visual-temporal detector, QSRadar retrieves a compact set of raw radar points around each evolving object hypothesis. The selected points are represented in an anchor-aligned coordinate frame, augmented with motion residuals, radar cross section, and sweep timing, and aggregated by a query-conditioned set encoder. Radar neighborhoods are retrieved again after each anchor refinement, coupling evidence selection with object estimation. Under the official MAN TruckScenes validation protocol, QSRadar achieves 38.09 mAP and 52.20 NDS, compared with 37.08 mAP and 50.78 NDS for our reproduced Sparse4D-Radar global Radar-BEV baseline. In matched tests on an RTX 4090 D, QSRadar reduces latency by 45%, peak memory usage by 49%, and GFLOPs by 43%.
authors: Chenhao Yan, Hongyu Liu, Xiang Cai, Yifei Sun, Zhe Zhang
bullets: Avoids costly global radar BEV construction by retrieving sparse radar neighborhoods around each object hypothesis.
Encodes radar points in anchor-aligned coordinates with motion residuals, radar cross section, and sweep timing.
Re-retrieves radar evidence after each anchor refinement, linking point selection to object estimation.
On MAN TruckScenes validation, achieves 38.09 mAP and 52.20 NDS versus 37.08 mAP and 50.78 NDS for the reproduced global Radar-BEV baseline.
On an RTX 4090 D, reduces latency by 45%, peak memory by 49%, and GFLOPs by 43% in matched tests.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of QSRadar. Blue and orange dashed boxes denote the Sparse4D visual–temporal path and the local radar path, respectively; the gray dashed box outlines one decoder layer. Current anchors guide visual sampling and local radar retrieval, while query features modulate radar point encoding. Visual and radar features are concatenated and fused to update queries and anchors. Updated anchors trigger new radar retrieval at the next layer, forming an iterative loop. Six decoder layers produce box, class, and velocity predictions.

Fig. 4. Qualitative detection results in long-range and crowded scenes. Shared camera views are shown at the top, followed by BEV results from Sparse4D, Sparse4D-Radar, and QSRadar. Green dashed boxes denote ground truth, solid colored boxes denote predictions, and BEV radar points are colored by speed magnitude. Cyan rectangles and dashed lines indicate the regions enlarged on the right. All methods use identical display ranges and a confidence threshold of 0.3.

Fig. 3. Query-conditioned local radar branch. (a) Planar distance to the anchor center determines top-16 candidates, followed by radius filtering. (b) A 13-dimensional geometric and motion descriptor is constructed in the anchor frame and encoded by a shared point MLP. (c) Query-conditioned channel gating, masked max/mean pooling, and the valid-point ratio produce a local radar feature; empty neighborhoods use a learned embedding. Points and feature tiles are schematic illustrations.

Fig. 1. mAP–FPS comparison on the MAN TruckScenes validation set. Results at 256×864 for RCTrans, CRT-Fusion, BEVFusion, and Horizon3D are compiled from the public Horizon3D report [18]; QSRadar’s FPS at this resolution is measured on an RTX 4090 D. Hardware and timing scopes differ across methods, so this plot provides efficiency context rather than a strictly controlled speed ranking.

papers.selection_reason: Sparse query-conditioned radar-camera fusion for efficient long-range 3D detection; fits 3D perception and efficiency-oriented methods.
papers.title: QSRadar: Query-Conditioned Sparse Radar-Camera Fusion for Efficient 3D Object Detection
papers.tldr: QSRadar efficiently fuses camera and raw 4D-radar evidence through evolving object queries, improving long-range 3D detection while reducing computation and memory.

papers.abstract: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.
authors: Ce Zhang, Jianshu Zhang, Jinxi He, Xiyuan Yang, Pan Wang, Han Liu, Katia Sycara, Yaqi Xie
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining useful evidence in a single pass under bounded frame storage and unknown future questions.
Groups recurring failures by cause and searches papers, model cards, and code for adaptable methods or pretrained perception models.
Can jointly add perceptual capabilities and revise how their evidence is stored and retrieved.
Selects accuracy-improving revisions on validation streams, then optimizes for faster revisions within a quality tolerance.
Across three benchmarks, it achieves the best accuracy within frozen-backbone comparisons; on OVO-Bench, it reaches 75.1% accuracy with 0.30-second average response time using Qwen3-VL-8B.

figures.caption: Figure 1. From manual design to open-world harness evolution. (a) Researchers design and revise the memory and retrieval pipelines of streaming systems [8, 54, 57, 63]. (b) Video recursive self-improvement (RSI) methods [22, 24, 26] automate harness revision from execution feedback within a preconfigured set of models and tools. (c) MORSE makes online research part of this loop. An LLM-based Editor investigates observed failures through papers, model cards, and code, then adapts existing methods and requests missing perception tools. Host-reviewed tool acquisition lets the harness and its available capabilities evolve together around a frozen answering VLM.

Figure 4. Inference efficiency on OVO-Bench. Measured mean answer latency and streaming write cost, using Qwen3-VL-8B for all methods. Each bar separates VLM calls from calls to other models. The direct VLM uses at most 128 frames at 1 fps without memory; H0, HS7, and HS11 are the seed, the harness after the accuracy rounds, and the final harness.

Figure 2. The MORSE optimization loop. Left: the harness Hk writes observations to memory through WH and retrieves evidence through RH for the frozen VLM F . Middle: the LLM-based Editor diagnoses errors and costly operations from training traces, researches solutions, proposes executable revisions, and validates them on private streams. Right: papers, model cards, and code inform program edits and tool requests; approved tools become callable after host integration. Below: accuracy rounds improve answer quality; efficiency rounds reduce latency with bounded quality loss relative to both the parent and the stage-entry harness.

Figure 5. Memory of the final harness at question time on three OVO-Bench test questions (tasks EPM, ASI, and FPD). Questions and options are reproduced verbatim. Each panel gives the question, its options (green: correct; red: the seed’s choice), and both answers with the probability P (gold) of the correct option. The timeline shows what the write path stored from the start of the video to the question (black marker). Notes: captions every 16 s, chapter notes over four captions, and a step log of who does what (purple outline: steps cited in the answer prompt). Index: ViCLIP vectors of 16-s segments and 4-frame windows, darker when closer to the question and options. Frames: the 64-frame store (tall ticks: segment key frames; pale ticks: frames since forgotten). Tools: OWLv2 detections, dark if the noun is named in the question or options. Read: the frames sent to the VLM, retrieved key frames in purple and the 4 most recent frames in gray. Thumbnails show six of them with the selector that chose each: similarity to the question (CLIP, ViCLIP index), temporal coverage (recency, gap fill, caption gap), or the last strong scene change (visual change). The seed sends only the captions and the 4 most recent frames.

papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces MORSE, a framework for optimizing the memory harness of a frozen video-language model (Qwen3-VL-8B). It addresses the problem of selecting evidence to retain in a streaming video system, which aligns with both Multimodal Foundation Models (VLMs) and Efficient AI (token eviction/pruning). The use of open-world auto-research to adapt the system is a novel approach to memory optimization.
papers.title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research
papers.tldr: MORSE improves streaming video memory by using recurring failures to search for and integrate external research, achieving strong accuracy and efficient querying with frozen video-language backbones.

papers.abstract: Runtime model selection trades detection quality against energy and latency. However, comparing a selector only with a more costly static detector conflates detector choice with the benefit of adaptation. We present a framework for analysis and physical measurement that combines a pairwise reward criterion, matched static controls, paired blocks, a fixed load-prevalence factorial design, and reporting of actions outside training support. On one Raspberry Pi 4B with four frozen TON-IoT detectors, tabular Q-learning and a deep Q-network (DQN) both select LightLR throughout. A retrospective audit using validation data only rules out preference reversals for MedRF versus LightLR and HeavyMLP versus LightLR. However, TinyDT has a higher reward than LightLR in seven of the 2,500 windows, so the audit does not establish global LightLR optimality. We also evaluate a causal DeadlineGuard rule under a fixed factorial design with three arrival rates (50, 100, and 4,000 rows/s) and three attack prevalences (0.10, 0.50, and 0.90). Compared with Static-MedRF, DeadlineGuard saves 43.7 J per 500-s run (2.98%; 95% paired CI 41.4--46.0 J) and eliminates all 512 deadline misses among 5,000 windows, at a cost of 1.373 percentage points in F1. Outside training support, Tabular-Q's deterministic tie-breaking rule selects TinyDT, resulting in a false-positive rate of 67.76%. These single-board results motivate joint audits of reward attainability, realized actions, attribution against matched static controls, service feasibility, and default actions outside training support.
authors: Nuonan Ouyang, Bonan Zhang, Adrian Shatte, Zhigang Lu, Chao Chen, Wei Xiang
bullets: The study argues that comparing adaptive selectors only with costly static detectors can exaggerate adaptation benefits.
It combines pairwise rewards, matched static controls, paired blocks, fixed load–prevalence experiments, and audits of actions outside training support.
Tabular Q-learning and DQN selected LightLR in all observed windows; validation audits did not prove LightLR globally optimal because TinyDT performed better in 7 of 2,500 windows.
DeadlineGuard saved 43.7 J per 500-second run and eliminated 512 deadline misses, while reducing F1 by 1.373 percentage points versus Static-MedRF.
Outside training support, Tabular-Q selected TinyDT by deterministic tie-breaking, producing a 67.76% false-positive rate.

DeadlineGuard is the only method with load-conditioned switching, and it records zero deadline misses; Tabular-Q’s TinyDT default under new load states appears in (a) and (e).

papers.selection_reason: Runtime model selection for energy/latency tradeoffs is relevant to efficient AI deployment.
papers.title: When Learned IDS Model Selection Collapses to a Static Choice: A Measurement Study at the Edge
papers.tldr: On a Raspberry Pi 4B, learned model selection collapsed to always choosing LightLR, while a causal deadline-aware rule reduced energy and deadline misses at a modest F1 cost but exposed serious out-of-support behavior.

papers.abstract: Parallel-trainable recurrences such as Mamba, linear attention, and DeltaNet offer constant-cost streaming inference, but they suffer from two limitations: 1) they struggle to track discrete state, and 2) they read every parameter at every step, tying model capacity directly to CPU latency. We introduce Yggdrasil, a recurrent architecture that decouples capacity from per-step compute by looking up each layer's transition in a large, tree-routed bank of recurrent experts. Each router addresses its bank using the current token and the state of the layer below. We prove that this cross-layer context is necessary---a single token-indexed layer of non-expanding transitions with finitely many reachable states cannot perform conditional resets---while avoiding feedback from the layer's own past preserves parallel-scan training. Because each step traverses one tree path and reads a single expert per layer, active weights stay within a few hundred kilobytes in CPU L2 cache while the full bank resides in RAM. Among the parallel-trainable models we evaluate, Yggdrasil is the only one to solve all five state-tracking tasks. At matched active parameter counts, it achieves the lowest test bits on enwik8 (1.540 bpb) and the human genome hg38 (1.567 bpb), while stepping $3.0\times$ and $3.3\times$ faster on a single CPU core ($6.7\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ and $5.8\,\mu\mathrm{s}$) than the fastest streaming baseline, and delivering the highest GPU throughput of all models at batch 1024. On the Genomic Benchmarks, it is the strongest causal model at matched active parameters (86.0% mean accuracy).
bullets: Addresses state-tracking weaknesses and per-step latency that limit parallel-trainable recurrent models.
Routes each layer’s transition through a tree using the current token and the lower layer’s state, activating one expert per layer.
Cross-layer routing enables conditional resets while preserving parallel-scan training by avoiding feedback from a layer’s own past.
Active weights fit in a few hundred kilobytes of CPU L2 cache, while the larger expert bank remains in RAM.
It solves all five evaluated state-tracking tasks and reports strong language, genomic, CPU-speed, GPU-throughput, and genomic-classification results.

papers.abstract: Explicit reasoning enables autonomous vehicles (AVs) to interpret complex traffic interactions and support trajectory planning, but introduces additional computational demands. Determining when explicit reasoning can improve planning accuracy remains a key challenge, as its benefits vary across driving scenarios. To address this challenge, this study proposes Scene-Adaptive Gating of Explicit Reasoning for Driving (SAGE-Drive), a benefit-aware adaptive reasoning framework for autonomous driving planning. First, paired planning outcomes with and without explicit reasoning are analyzed to measure the reasoning benefit, i.e., the reduction in planning error achieved by explicit reasoning, which serves as the supervision label. SAGE-Drive then learns to predict these benefits using geometric features of the initial trajectory planned without reasoning and multimodal scene information, and invokes explicit reasoning only for the scenarios with the highest predicted benefits under a predefined reasoning budget. Experiments on 1,497 paired driving scenarios reveal that explicit reasoning improves planning accuracy in 53.5% of cases while degrading it in 46.5%, yielding a near-zero average benefit. On the test set, with a 20% reasoning budget, SAGE-Drive achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 1.5191 m, compared with 1.5252 m for random selection. At a 35% budget, it achieves an ADE of 1.5148 m, close to the 1.5141 m obtained when reasoning is applied to every scenario. These findings establish the predicted reasoning benefit as an effective criterion for reasoning selection, allowing explicit reasoning to be invoked where it improves planning accuracy at a fraction of its computational cost.
authors: Donglei Rong, Wenbin Yao, Congcong Bai, Xi Gao, Qiaoqiao Ren, Sheng Jin, Cheng Xu
bullets: Explicit reasoning is not uniformly helpful: it improves planning in 53.5% of scenarios and degrades it in 46.5%, producing near-zero average benefit.
The framework defines reasoning benefit as the reduction in planning error from using explicit reasoning versus not using it.
A predictor uses initial trajectory geometry and multimodal scene information to estimate this benefit.
Explicit reasoning is allocated to the highest-benefit scenarios under a predefined reasoning budget.
With 20% and 35% reasoning budgets, SAGE-Drive approaches the accuracy of reasoning on every scenario while outperforming random selection at 20%.

papers.abstract: Runtime guardrails protect mobile GUI agents by assessing each proposed action before execution, but existing guardrails rely on cloud hosted large multimodal models, exposing every screen to a remote server, including private information such as payments, messages, and medical records. We propose MobileGrail, an on-device deployable model that addresses both. It maintains a recurrent task state that retains only the evidence subsequent safety decisions depend on, so that authorization and execution progress persist beyond the short context. To intervene early while keeping the safety boundary precise, it learns two labels, unsafe and block: unsafe marks the action that commits a violation, whereas block may be issued at any step of an intervention window, which spans from the first action that the user's authorization no longer explains to the committing action itself. To support training, we build an environment of 32 applications whose backends verify the effect of every action, supplying verified labels for supervision and rewards for reinforcement learning to calibrate intervention timing. We also build MobileVeto, an offline benchmark of unsafe trajectories largely on held-out applications, each paired with a benign counterpart. On MobileVeto, MobileGrail built on Qwen3.5-2B intercepts 76.2% of violations, up from 64.5% for its prompted backbone, while reducing premature intervention from 58.6% to 5.2%, outperforming the cloud-based OS-Sentinel on both. We further conduct online evaluation on GhostEIBench, where MobileGrail guarding a Qwen3.8-27B agent reduces fully successful attacks from 13 to 3 of 110 tasks while raising task completion from 48 to 58. Quantized to 4 bits, MobileGrail runs on a Snapdragon 8 Elite at a median latency of 4.7 s, comparable to the 5.1s of cloud-hosted Gemini 3.8 Flash.
authors: Zhiyu Zhang, Yuankai Li, Muhao Chen
bullets: Maintains recurrent task state so safety decisions retain relevant authorization and execution progress beyond short context windows.
Separates “unsafe” committing actions from “block” decisions allowed throughout an intervention window, enabling earlier but more precise intervention.
Trains with verified action-effect labels and reinforcement learning rewards in a 32-app environment, and evaluates on the offline MobileVeto benchmark plus online GhostEIBench.
On MobileVeto, its Qwen3.5-2B version intercepts 76.2% of violations and cuts premature intervention to 5.2%, compared with 64.5% and 58.6% for the prompted backbone.
Runs quantized on a Snapdragon 8 Elite at 4.7 s median latency; online evaluation reduces fully successful attacks from 13 to 3 of 110 tasks while improving completion from 48 to 58.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers achieve remarkable recognition performance but incur substantial computational cost during inference, limiting their use in latency- and compute-constrained deployment scenarios. Early-exit inference offers a promising solution by allowing easy samples to terminate at intermediate layers. However, existing approaches typically couple early classification with the shared backbone, requiring intermediate representations to support both early classification and subsequent feature refinement. Under joint training, the corresponding optimization objectives jointly update shared backbone parameters, which can lead to conflicting gradient directions. Motivated by this observation, we introduce DeclareViT, a framework that decouples early classification from feature refinement. Each exit uses a dedicated query to read intermediate features through one-way cross-attention without modifying the backbone token stream. The query branches are optimized for early classification while the backbone and final classifier remain frozen. Across ViT, DeiT, and Swin on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, and Food-101, DeclareViT consistently establishes a state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off: It achieves 1.58 times to 2.57 times multiply-accumulate (MAC)-based speed-up with only a 0.39-1.91 percentage-point accuracy drop. Wall-clock measurements on CPU and GPU further demonstrate practical inference acceleration. Code is available at https://github.com/TUDa-HWAI/DeclareViT.
authors: Xinrui Gong, Yao Rong, Chuangtao Chen, Daniel Ochs, Ulf Schlichtmann, Bing Li, Kristian Kersting, Grace Li Zhang
bullets: Early-exit ViTs can reduce inference cost, but shared optimization may create conflicting gradients between early classification and later feature refinement.
Each exit uses a dedicated query with one-way cross-attention to read intermediate features without altering the backbone token stream.
Only the query branches are optimized for early classification, while the backbone and final classifier remain frozen.
Across ViT, DeiT, and Swin on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, and Food-101, it delivers 1.58×–2.57× MAC-based speed-ups with 0.39–1.91 percentage-point accuracy drops.
CPU and GPU measurements also show practical wall-clock inference acceleration.

papers.abstract: Top-k sparse attention relies on an indexer, a lightweight per-layer module that ranks cached tokens so attention covers only the k highest-scoring ones. Indexers are usually distilled from dense attention at the full serving length, so every training step pays for long-context dense attention. We show that when an indexer is distilled on short sequences, its failure to generalise to longer contexts is driven mainly by rotary positional encoding (RoPE), not by degraded content matching. We propose position-skipped distillation: the indexer and the frozen teacher see short sequences whose position IDs contain a randomly placed gap, so neither ever processes more than the short training length. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, an indexer distilled on 8K tokens this way matches a 32K-distilled indexer to within about 0.5 perplexity up to 32K, and on DeepSeek-V2-Lite matches a 64K-distilled indexer at 64K with roughly 6x less training compute per token. On Llama-3.1-8B it trails the stronger 32K run by 0.6 perplexity, and at 64K simple position compression is often as good, so the main gain is training cost rather than quality. We also quantise indexer keys to 3-4 bits without retraining and score them with a fused integer kernel: at 4 bits, perplexity changes by at most 0.05 and the scan is 1.6-2.2x faster than half precision. In a current serving engine, the indexer speeds up decoding only for long contexts with multiple concurrent streams.
authors: Fu Dai, Haodi Quan, Kamal Taha
bullets: Short-sequence failures are mainly attributed to rotary positional encoding rather than content matching.
Random gaps in position IDs let the indexer and frozen teacher learn long-range positions without processing long sequences.
An 8K-distilled indexer nearly matches 32K- and, on one model, 64K-distilled quality; the reported training-cost reduction is about 6× per token.
3–4-bit key quantization requires no retraining; 4-bit keys change perplexity by at most 0.05 and yield 1.6–2.2× faster scans.
Benefits vary by model and serving setting: position compression can be competitive, and decoding speedups appear mainly for long contexts with multiple streams.

papers.selection_reason: Improves sparse-attention indexer distillation for long-context serving with position-skipped training and quantization, relevant to efficient long-context LLMs.
papers.title: Position-Skipped Distillation of Sparse-Attention Indexers: Train Short, Serve Long
papers.tldr: Position-skipped distillation trains sparse-attention indexers on short sequences that generalize to long contexts, substantially reducing training cost while preserving quality in several models.

papers.abstract: Teams enable serving features such as prefix caching, chunked prefill and speculative decoding after checking that benchmark accuracy is unchanged, because the engine documents them as exact. Accuracy is an aggregate, so a feature can hold it while flipping which requests are answered correctly. We serve one 4B instruction model in vLLM under nine single feature configurations and five replicas of a reference configuration, grade 3,380 requests from five benchmarks in every run, and compare each candidate with a restart floor (fresh process) and a scheduling floor (same requests in a different order). With default kernels every configuration keeps accuracy within one point, and the seven exact features flip the graded outcome of 1.47% (95% CI 1.13 to 1.85) to 1.78% (1.39 to 2.20) of requests, none above the scheduling floor of 1.72%, while the FP8 KV cache flips 3.36% (2.80 to 3.96), as many as FP8 weights. With batch invariant kernels all seven exact features, speculative decoding included, reproduce the reference text on every request, while the FP8 KV cache still flips 3.91% (3.28 to 4.53) of graded outcomes. A gate that compares against a single replica pair rejected an unchanged configuration, so we recommend certifying a serving change under batch invariant kernels, where the floor is zero, or against a scheduling floor measured from at least three replicas.
bullets: Aggregate accuracy can remain stable while individual graded answers change.
Across nine feature configurations, seven exact features flipped 1.47%–1.78% of requests, no higher than the 1.72% scheduling floor.
FP8 KV caching flipped 3.36% of graded outcomes, comparable to FP8 weights, and 3.91% with batch-invariant kernels.
Batch-invariant kernels made all seven exact features, including speculative decoding, reproduce reference text on every request.
Certification should use batch-invariant kernels or a scheduling floor measured from at least three replicas; single-replica comparisons can reject unchanged configurations.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLM serving efficiency shortcuts including FP8 KV cache compression and prefix caching, directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency research.
papers.title: Exact on Paper: Which LLM Serving Shortcuts Flip Graded Answers, Measured Against the Noise of Reordering the Same Requests
papers.tldr: Most exact serving features cause answer flips no more often than request-reordering noise, but FP8 KV caching produces substantially more changes unless batch-invariant kernels are used.

papers.abstract: High-resolution images contain rich visual details that require fine geometric structures for faithful 3D reconstruction. However, generating extremely detailed 3D geometry from images requires substantial computational resources and training data, making high-resolution geometry generation challenging for existing state-of-the-art models. In this paper, we present SuperFine3D, an efficient framework for generating extremely detailed 3D geometry through global-local recursive refinement. SuperFine3D learns a shared refinement operator from paired coarse-to-fine representations and recursively reuses it to progressively synthesize finer geometry beyond the training resolutions, without requiring additional paired supervision at target resolutions. To make recursive refinement computationally efficient, we introduce spatial-cell attention, which restricts high-resolution interactions to local spatial neighborhoods while maintaining bounded communication across neighboring cells. We further propose spatially anchored cross-scale guidance, which leverages globally contextualized coarse geometry to guide local detail synthesis and preserve structural consistency. In addition, geometry-aware training objectives encourage the refinement process to preserve stable geometric structures while introducing fine-grained surface details. Experiments demonstrate that SuperFine3D generates geometry at a $4096^3$ decoder-grid resolution, corresponding to a sparse $256^3$ latent lattice, using a shared refinement operator trained only on $512^3$--$1024^3$ representations. Compared with a full-attention recursive baseline, SuperFine3D achieves a $9.4\times$ speedup in end-to-end inference and reduces peak GPU memory usage by $23.0\%$, while improving cross-scale structural consistency and producing cleaner surfaces with finer geometric details.
authors: Lihan Li, Junwei Zhou, Yu-wing Tai
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and data demands of high-resolution 3D geometry generation.
Learns a shared coarse-to-fine refinement operator and reuses it recursively beyond the training resolutions.
Uses spatial-cell attention for efficient local interactions and spatially anchored cross-scale guidance for global structural consistency.
Trained on 512³–1024³ representations, it generates geometry at 4096³ decoder-grid resolution with a sparse 256³ latent lattice.
Compared with full-attention recursive refinement, it achieves 9.4× faster inference, 23.0% lower peak GPU memory, and cleaner, finer surfaces.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SuperFine3D. A pretrained generator produces a coarse 5123 shape, from which the input camera is estimated. At every level, detail normals estimated from the input image are injected into the current mesh; the corrected mesh is encoded at twice the resolution, partially noised, and refined by the shared refinement network conditioned on the preceding latent and the image (bottom).

papers.abstract: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.
authors: Shuaiwei Huang, Weihua Du, Allen Wu, Ivan Fox, Manupa Karunaratne, Yiming Yang, Sean Welleck
bullets: Introduces a benchmark pipeline and hardware-feedback environments for agent-based kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures.
Builds 99 kernels from real-world repositories, including inference workloads from model executions, spanning Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2.
On established extensions, agents outperform auto-vectorized compilers by 2.4–19.8× and can exceed general-purpose ncnn kernels, but trail hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels.
Agent-written kernels improve LLM prefill speed by 1.3–1.6× over llama.cpp’s fast path in two end-to-end inference workloads.
Agents do not yet reliably handle new extensions with unfamiliar programming models, particularly SME2 matrix tiles.

papers.selection_reason: Kernel optimization and agent-written kernels for LLM inference latency reduction fit Efficient AI.
papers.title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware

papers.abstract: Mid-generation abstention aims to stop an unpromising response before spending its remaining computation budget. Intermediate transformer states may help predict eventual correctness, but whether scalar summaries of their vocabulary predictions add useful evidence is less clear. We compare Tuned Lens entropy and divergence features with final-state and raw intermediate-state probes under matched, causal evaluation. Across eight instruction-tuned models on MATH-500, raw intermediate states improve ranking, whereas scalar-only probes usually trail the final-state baseline. Scalar hybrids have positive exceptions, but their advantage over position-matched permutation controls is small. Cross-fitted residual comparisons further show that gains over a final-state probe need not require aligned scalar features. Actual stopping runs on two model sizes and two benchmarks reveal a separate accuracy--computation trade-off, with token savings overstating wall-time savings for scalar policies. The evidence supports a restricted empirical conclusion about these scalar features, not a general negative claim about intermediate representations.
bullets: Evaluates entropy and divergence features from Tuned Lens summaries against final-state and raw intermediate-state probes.
Across eight instruction-tuned models on MATH-500, raw intermediate states improve ranking, but scalar-only probes usually underperform the final-state baseline.
Some scalar hybrids help, yet their gains over position-matched permutation controls are small and need not depend on aligned scalar features.
Stopping experiments show a separate accuracy–computation trade-off, with scalar policies saving fewer wall-clock resources than token counts suggest.
Conclusion is limited to these scalar features rather than intermediate representations in general.

papers.selection_reason: Mid-generation abstention to save computation; fits efficient AI, with limited positive evidence.
papers.title: Scalar Tuned Lens Summaries Offer Limited Incremental Value for Mid-Generation Abstention
papers.tldr: Scalar Tuned Lens summaries provide little consistent extra value for predicting when to stop generation early, while raw intermediate states are more useful.

papers.abstract: Deploying a conversational model and a specialist together could avoid maintaining a separate specialist service. We present LM2, which embeds a trained story generator into a larger conversational model. The larger model handles the conversation and invokes the generator for story requests. We constrain the generator arithmetic during training so its calculations can be compiled directly into added model layers. We compare this approach with QwenPU, which executes the stories260K language model on an embedded processor. LM2 requires one host token per generated character, compared with approximately 25,000 for QwenPU. However, its story generator predicts held out text less well, i.e. 1.145 bits per character versus 0.894 for stories260K, where lower is better. The Qwen3.5, 0.8B implementation occupies 18.1 GB and generates the same characters as a standalone integer implementation of the inner model in the tested runs. These results illustrate a tradeoff between host-token cost and text-prediction performance.
bullets: Embeds a trained story generator into a conversational model so one system can handle dialogue and story requests.
Constrains generator arithmetic during training to compile its computations into added model layers.
Uses one host token per generated character, versus approximately 25,000 with the QwenPU approach.
Achieves 1.145 bits per character on held-out text versus 0.894 for stories260K, where lower is better.
The tested Qwen3.5 0.8B implementation occupies 18.1 GB and matches the standalone integer implementation’s generated characters.

papers.selection_reason: Compiles a language model into another's weights, reducing deployment overhead.
papers.title: LM2 Compiling a Language Model into Another Model Weights

papers.abstract: Representation alignment markedly accelerates diffusion training, but one-step generators raise a question that diffusion does not: \emph{which training path should receive the loss?} A one-step generator sees two kinds of inputs. Corrupted real images come with their clean counterpart, which provides an instance-paired target. Samples generated from pure noise have no corresponding real image, yet this is where the final model operates. We study this question on Priming, which trains one-step generators from scratch by reconstructing corrupted images and then matching feature distributions with optimal transport. Aligning the generative path, the natural choice, collapses recall ($0.45\!\to\!0.15$--$0.25$) in all 17 configurations we test, including five target constructions and loss weights down to $0.05$. Aligning the paired reconstruction path with a frozen DINOv2 encoder instead helps in every setting we test. A short analysis explains this asymmetry: when the target carries no instance information about the input, the optimal aligned feature is constant within each class, so the loss pulls samples toward class prototypes. A control confirms this: aligning the paired path to a random same-class image instead of the input's own image removes most of the gain. Inside the generator, paired-path alignment creates an interface block through which post-training routes noise, and the image semantics carried through it predict sample quality across 16 models. The resulting recipe, \method, accelerates \emph{both} training stages on ImageNet $256\!\times\!256$: it matches the 160-epoch baseline with $2\times$ fewer priming epochs, surpasses its final quality with $4\times$ fewer post-training updates, and lowers FID to 1.30 (B) and 1.155 (L) at the standard budget. A joint single-stage variant trains native one-step generators and reaches FID 1.22 with 115M parameters.
authors: Mingxiao Li, Xuantuo Huang, Encheng Su, Aoran Wang, Han Zhang, Jinouwen Zhang, Shixiang Tang
bullets: Generative-path alignment consistently harms recall, collapsing it from 0.45 to 0.15–0.25 across 17 configurations.
Paired-path alignment with a frozen DINOv2 encoder improves performance in every tested setting.
Unpaired targets lack instance information and pull samples toward class prototypes; a same-class-image control confirms the importance of exact pairing.
The proposed recipe matches the baseline with 2× fewer priming epochs and exceeds its final quality with 4× fewer post-training updates.
At the standard budget, it achieves FID 1.30 (B) and 1.155 (L); a joint variant reaches FID 1.22 with 115M parameters.

(a) On the paired path, the generator reconstructs a corrupted real image xs, and an intermediate feature hℓ is aligned, through a light projector Pψ , with frozen DINOv2 features of the same clean image x0. (b) On the generative path, the same weights map noise to samples that are matched to real images by OT in frozen ConvNeXt/MAE feature spaces. A sample has no corresponding real image, so every alignment target we construct lacks instance correspondence and collapses coverage (Sec. 4.2). (c) RePrime aligns only during priming; RePrime-J trains both paths jointly.

papers.selection_reason: One-step generator training and distillation reduce inference and training cost, with representation-alignment ideas transferable to efficient generative models.
papers.title: Align the Pair, Not the Sample: Representation Alignment for Faster and Better One-Step Generato
papers.tldr: Aligning one-step generators on paired corrupted–clean images, rather than unpaired generated samples, improves training speed and final image quality.

papers.abstract: Quantization is the standard way to shrink large language models, and it is usually judged by perplexity and task accuracy. We ask a different question: after quantization, which words can the model still say at all? A token is silenced when no hidden state can make it the top choice of the output layer, so a greedy decoder can never produce it. We give a simple, scalable way to estimate how many tokens a quantized output head silences, combining three checks: a direction that lets a token win (so it is safe), an upper bound on how close a token's row is to being trapped inside the others, and an exact match that proves a token can never win. Each count is therefore a certified range: exact matches give its lower end and flagged tokens can only raise its upper end. In nearly all settings we report down to 3 bits the two ends coincide, so the counts are exact. Across three open models we find that quantization silences tokens: on large-vocabulary models it already appears at 8-bit precision, up to a few hundred previously reachable tokens on a 1B-parameter model, and grows as precision drops, while a small-vocabulary model resists until 3 bits. The loss is far from uniform across languages: on a multilingual vocabulary the silenced tokens are overwhelmingly non-Latin (Korean, Chinese, Thai, Arabic and Hebrew), even though Latin tokens dominate the vocabulary. Silencing is thus a measurable, language-sensitive side effect that standard averages miss, and it should be reported alongside them.
bullets: Defines a token as silenced when no hidden state can make it the output-layer winner.
Introduces scalable certified lower and upper bounds using winning directions, geometric trapping bounds, and exact impossibility checks.
The bounds coincide in nearly all tested settings down to 3-bit precision, yielding exact counts.
Silencing appears at 8 bits in large-vocabulary models, reaches a few hundred tokens in one 1B model, and increases at lower precision; small vocabularies resist until 3 bits.
On multilingual vocabularies, silenced tokens are overwhelmingly Korean, Chinese, Thai, Arabic, and Hebrew rather than Latin.

papers.selection_reason: Studies quantization's effect on token availability, a side effect of model compression.
papers.title: Estimating Silenced Tokens in Quantized LLMs
papers.tldr: Quantization can make some vocabulary tokens impossible for a greedy decoder to generate, disproportionately silencing non-Latin tokens as precision decreases.

papers.abstract: Agent frameworks typically orchestrate language models through prompt-and-response interfaces. We propose a harness design that exposes intermediate model states and layer-level execution controls to the agent runtime. By connecting state collection, policy fitting, and execution, the design enables policies to allocate computation within and across models based on intermediate states. We demonstrate the approach with a prototype that learns stitching bridges and state-conditioned execution policies from paired model states, then applies them during inference to select among continue, exit, and stitch. For dispatcher supervision, we select the least-computation action whose full-vocabulary next-token prediction matches the source model's full-depth prediction, using continue when neither early action matches. We train these components on a frozen proxy corpus of 5,000 typed-decision items authored using source texts sampled from WildChat conversations, then evaluate the prototype on JevBench measuring task accuracy, agreement with full-model predictions, and end-to-end latency including runtime overhead. Preliminary results show an approximately 15% reduction in mean latency while maintaining task accuracy comparable to full-model inference.
authors: Ran Guan, Yiqi Lin, Xiangxi Tian, Yige Luo, Mi Zhou
bullets: Addresses the limits of prompt-and-response-only agent frameworks by exposing intermediate model states and layer-level controls.
Learns state-conditioned execution policies and stitching bridges from paired states across models.
Selects the least-computation action—exit, stitch, or continue—based on agreement with the source model’s full-depth prediction.
Evaluated on JevBench for task accuracy, prediction agreement, and end-to-end latency including runtime overhead.
Preliminary results report about 15% lower mean latency with task accuracy comparable to full-model inference.

papers.tldr: A layer-aware agent harness adaptively exits, continues, or stitches language-model execution to reduce inference latency while preserving task accuracy.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning is an effective way to accelerate multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing methods degrade substantially under aggressive pruning, especially on visual grounding (VG). We analyze the sources of this degradation from the perspective of the output shift that pruning causes in decoder layers, and decompose this shift in closed form into two terms, an image summary error and an attention allocation error. The summary error stems from the loss of visual information, and the allocation error from the drop in the share of attention assigned to visual tokens. To reduce both errors, we propose CAR (Coverage selection and Attention Reallocation), a token pruning framework that restores attention share while maintaining information. Specifically, to minimize the summary error, whose upper bound tightens as the retained tokens better cover all visual tokens, our coverage selection retains tokens that are both salient and non-redundant, with saliency from encoder heads chosen by a label-free probe. To minimize the allocation error, our attention reallocation reassigns the attention of the discarded tokens to the retained ones through a closed-form logit bias. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B with $90\%$ of the visual tokens pruned, CAR retains $93.0\%$ of the unpruned accuracy on visual question answering (VQA) and $77.9\%$ on VG, against $26.5\%$ for the best existing method on VG; the logit bias alone raises the VG accuracy of existing methods by up to $24$ points. Experiments on multiple MLLMs across VQA, VG and video understanding show that CAR generalizes well and consistently outperforms existing methods.
authors: Xixi Jiang, Pingcheng Dong, Chen Yang, Xin Yang, Kwang-Ting Cheng
bullets: Visual token pruning accelerates MLLMs but can sharply hurt performance, especially visual grounding, due to decoder output shift.
The shift is decomposed into image summary error from lost information and attention allocation error from reduced visual-token attention.
Coverage selection keeps salient, non-redundant tokens using a label-free encoder-head probe.
Attention reallocation transfers discarded-token attention to retained tokens via a closed-form logit bias.
With 90% pruning on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, CAR retains 93.0% of unpruned VQA accuracy and 77.9% of visual-grounding accuracy; results generalize across MLLMs and tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses visual token pruning in MLLMs with a novel coverage-selection and attention-reallocation framework.
papers.title: CAR: Reducing Decoder Output Shift in Visual Token Pruning via Coverage Selection and Attention Reallocation
papers.tldr: CAR makes aggressive visual token pruning more reliable by preserving broad visual coverage and reallocating attention from discarded tokens to retained ones.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have revolutionized generative tasks but incur high inference latency due to iterative denoising. Cache-based strategies accelerate inference by reusing intermediate features, yet they largely rely on static, sample-agnostic schedules. Our empirical analysis reveals two factors that these schedules overlook. (i) denoising dynamics and computational requirements vary across prompts, motivating adaptive computation allocation. (ii) sensitivity to caching errors varies across timesteps, so static schedules may reuse features at error-sensitive steps or waste computation at less sensitive ones. We therefore propose OnCache, a dynamic caching framework that makes prompt-adaptive decisions online about how much computation to allocate and when to refresh cached features. A policy is trained offline on paired compute and cache continuations from identical denoising states, using differences in terminal fidelity and the number of function evaluations (NFE) to account for the downstream consequences of each decision. To further improve the generation quality, a neural corrector compensates for caching-induced errors and mitigates their accumulation throughout the denoising trajectory. Both components are lightweight and introduce negligible additional inference latency. On FLUX.1-dev, OnCache achieves a nearly $3\times$ generation speedup at $1024^2$ resolution, with LPIPS of $0.156$ and SSIM of $0.860$. We further extend OnCache to video generation on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, achieving state-of-the-art efficiency--quality trade-offs across both modalities.
authors: Zhikang Xie, Xichen Ye, Yifan Wu, Yuxuan Liu, Qianlong Wang, Haoshen Yu, Peizhu Gong, Weizhong Zhang, Cheng Jin
bullets: Static caching schedules overlook prompt-dependent denoising costs and timestep-varying sensitivity to caching errors.
OnCache uses an offline-trained policy to allocate computation and refresh cached features online during denoising.
A lightweight neural corrector reduces caching errors and their accumulation with negligible added inference latency.
On FLUX.1-dev at 1024², it achieves nearly 3× speedup with LPIPS 0.156 and SSIM 0.860.
The framework also extends to video generation on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, yielding state-of-the-art efficiency–quality trade-offs across image and video modalities.

papers.abstract: Adaptive visual token routers aim to save computation while preserving the image detail needed to answer each question. A higher average score could reflect better choices for individual images or more frequent use of high resolution on tasks that need it. We distinguish the two by keeping action counts fixed within each task and comparing the router's assignments with random pairings of the same actions and images. On equally weighted ChartQA and TextVQA, both Qwen2.5-VL-3B and -7B gain from matching but lose more from their action frequencies relative to a task table, with a 1.71-point gain and a 3.95-point loss on 7B. Exchanging the continuous resolutions chosen by the external selector CARES also lowers quality on 7B. When requests arrive with task labels, the table outscores the discrete router by 1.92 points and saves 31.76 ms per complete 7B request on average.
bullets: The study separates routing quality into action allocation and image–action matching while holding per-task action counts fixed.
On equally weighted ChartQA and TextVQA, both Qwen2.5-VL-3B and -7B benefit from matching, but deviate more from task-optimal action frequencies.
For Qwen2.5-VL-7B, matching adds 1.71 points, while its action-frequency choices cost 3.95 points relative to a task table.
Randomly exchanging CARES-selected continuous resolutions also reduces 7B quality, supporting the value of image–resolution matching.
With task labels, a task table beats the discrete router by 1.92 points and saves 31.76 ms per complete 7B request on average.

papers.selection_reason: Studies adaptive visual token routing to save computation, directly relevant to token-level efficiency in multimodal models.
papers.title: Separating Action Allocation from Image Matching in Visual Token Routing
papers.tldr: Visual token routers benefit from both choosing the right action frequencies and matching actions to images, with action allocation often having the larger impact.

papers.abstract: Sequential recommender systems aim to predict a user's next interaction by modeling temporal dependencies in historical behavior sequences. To capture such dependencies, recent approaches increasingly rely on attention-based architectures, particularly transformers. While effective at modeling long-range sequential patterns, these models apply a fixed computation depth to all interaction items, treating them as equally complex. However, user behavior is inherently heterogeneous, with many interactions following simple repetitive patterns, whereas others require modeling higher-order dependencies. This mismatch leads to inefficient utilization of model capacity and unnecessary computational overhead, particularly in deep transformer-based architectures. To address this issue, we propose MoR4Rec, a sequential recommendation framework based on a Mixture-of-Recursion paradigm, which enables item-wise adaptive computation through a shared transformer backbone. A learned routing mechanism dynamically assigns each item to an appropriate recursion depth, allocating deeper computation to complex interactions while processing simpler patterns more efficiently. To improve computational efficiency, we develop a cascade-based strategy with key-value sharing across recursion steps. We further introduce a gated attention mechanism that adaptively regulates contextual information during recursive sequence modeling. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that MoR4Rec consistently outperforms strong transformer-based baselines, achieving average gains of 2.28% in Recall@5, 2.50% in NDCG@5, and 2.0% in MRR@5 over the strongest baseline. The improvements remain consistent across top-10 and top-20 recommendation cutoffs, while comparisons with vanilla transformers demonstrate the computational efficiency of adaptive recursive processing.
authors: Tiwari Ankit Satyaprakash, Adamya Shyam, Vikas Kumar, Bharti Rana, Venkateswara Rao Kagita
bullets: Targets inefficient fixed-depth computation in transformer-based sequential recommenders.
Uses a shared transformer backbone with learned routing to assign item-wise recursion depths.
Employs cascade-based key-value sharing for efficiency and gated attention for adaptive context regulation.
Outperforms strong transformer baselines across three benchmarks, with average gains of 2.28% Recall@5, 2.50% NDCG@5, and 2.0% MRR@5.
Gains remain consistent at top-10 and top-20 cutoffs; efficiency is demonstrated against vanilla transformers.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) extract structured data from documents by generating the requested JSON one token at a time, so their sequential steps grow with the length of the answer. Yet in key information extraction (KIE) the schema already fixes the answer's structure: keys, nesting and lists are known before decoding, and only the values are unknown. We exploit this with a non-autoregressive extractor that writes the structure from the schema, sizes every list with a count pass, and predicts all values in parallel, in a fixed number of passes that does not grow with the document. Each value is decoded with connectionist temporal classification (CTC) in its own block of slots, so its length never has to be predicted, and a value that is still open after its block gets a larger token budget. Zero-shot on VAREX, CORD and FUNSD, our 4B extractor is 3.5$\times$ faster than the diffusion-VLM competition on average (up to 5.6$\times$) and more accurate, with 4--6 forward passes per document where block diffusion needs 12--74. The same extractor also drafts for speculative decoding with its own autoregressive base: it runs 8.3$\times$ faster than autoregressive decoding (up to 10.4$\times$) within 0.4 points of its accuracy, and 3.3$\times$ faster than speculative diffusion decoding while 13.0 points more accurate. We release the model and code.
authors: Shaked Perek, Avihu Dekel, Ben Wiesel, Sivan Harary, Eli Schwartz
bullets: Problem: Autoregressive VLMs decode JSON sequentially even though KIE schemas already specify the output structure, causing latency to grow with answer length.
Method: Fill the schema directly, use a count pass to size lists, and decode each value in parallel with CTC slot blocks and adaptive token budgets.
Results: Zero-shot on VAREX, CORD, and FUNSD, the 4B model is 3.5× faster than diffusion-VLM competitors on average and uses 4–6 forward passes per document.
It also serves as a speculative-decoding draft model, running 8.3× faster than autoregressive decoding with accuracy within 0.4 points.
The model and code are released.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Decoding trace on a VAREX test form, coloured by the forward that wrote each token. The first bidirectional pass commits most of every value (blue) and the later confidence passes fill what it was unsure of (orange). The extended budget (green) writes the end of the longest value, the physician’s details, and all eleven values are exact. In the speculative mode the verifier accepts all eleven unchanged.

Figure 2. Schema-parallel CTC decoding. (a) A count pass reads the image and the schema and sizes every list. (b) The schema is written out as a skeleton in which every value gets a block of n [M] slots. (c) A bidirectional forward predicts all slots of all values at once; this is repeated for T passes, each but the last revealing the slots predicted with probability above τ and re-predicting the rest (blanks are never revealed; the last pass takes the argmax of every slot), with the image–prompt key/values computed once. (d) CTC collapse first merges repeats, then drops blanks (∅); a value still open after its block gets n more slots (budget +n).

Figure 4. Sequential cost vs. document size. Forward passes (left, log scale) and latency (right) per document against the number of keys in its schema, pooled over VAREX, CORD and FUNSD (1,924 documents; median and interquartile range per bin). Our forward count stays at 4–6 for every document, while block diffusion’s grows with the size of the JSON it generates. Masked diffusion on our own skeleton (value-decoder ablation, 8 steps) is also flat but needs more forwards than CTC and is slower.

papers.abstract: The domain of genomic language models (gLMs) has advanced rapidly, with models pretrained on diverse multi-species genomic corpora demonstrating their remarkable capabilities. While the effect of simple nucleotide-level tokenization on long-context modeling is well established, overlapping k-mer tokenization remains underexplored in causal pretraining, despite its rich neighborhood information. Here, we thoroughly revisit overlapping tokenization and introduce HGDNA, a hybrid linear-attention gLM with causal language modeling (CLM) pretraining and a shared token-prediction interface for downstream adaptation, using a species-classification auxiliary task and shared class tokens. HGDNA delivers competitive performance across sequence classification and frozen-embedding evaluations, supporting both short-range and long-range tasks with 30M parameters and 19B pretraining tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/Sophie10001b/HGDNA
authors: Xudong Wang, Siwei Cheng, Haozhe Hu
bullets: Addresses the limited study of overlapping k-mers for causal genomic pretraining, motivated by their richer neighborhood information.
Uses a hybrid linear-attention architecture pretrained with causal language modeling and a shared token-prediction interface for downstream adaptation.
Adds a species-classification auxiliary task with shared class tokens.
Achieves competitive results on sequence-classification and frozen-embedding evaluations spanning short- and long-range tasks.
The abstract reports a 30M-parameter model trained on 19B genomic tokens; broader generalization beyond the evaluated tasks is not specified.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning can reduce the inference cost of vision language models, but its effectiveness depends on preserving complementary visual information under a limited token budget. A central challenge is to quantify the additional information a candidate token contributes beyond the retained set, a contribution that conventional scores based on attention or similarity struggle to capture directly. In this work, we revisit visual token pruning from the perspective of information gain and use mutual information to characterize the incremental value of candidate tokens. We further establish theoretically that frame potential serves as an effective surrogate for mutual information. Building on this observation, we propose FP-Prune, a training-free visual token pruning method that iteratively removes tokens with low information gain to preserve as much complementary visual information as possible. Experiments on three widely used VLMs and eight datasets demonstrate that FP-Prune outperforms baseline methods in both accuracy and inference efficiency. Further analysis shows that the surrogate objective closely aligns with model performance. Our work provides theoretical grounding and an effective method for visual token pruning.
authors: Haozhe Zhao, Junxiang Zhang, Junxin Wang, Yuan Ge, Xiangchen Song, Dingyang Zhang, JingBo Zhu, Tong Xiao
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of measuring a candidate token’s additional information beyond retained tokens.
Uses mutual information to characterize incremental token value and theoretically links it to frame potential.
Introduces a training-free, iterative pruning method that removes tokens with low information gain.
Experiments across three VLMs and eight datasets show improved accuracy and inference efficiency over baselines.
Analysis finds strong alignment between the surrogate objective and model performance.

papers.abstract: Long-sequence inference in large language models is constrained by the high cost of prefilling, where dense attention scales quadratically with context length. Exploiting similarity across attention heads offers a way to reduce redundant computation. Prior approaches in this direction have relied on localized query observations to determine head-level computation reuse or budget allocation. However, inter-head similarity does not imply uniform query requirements, leaving adaptation to varying budget needs and selection preferences across query regions a key challenge. We introduce QASparse, a Query-Adaptive Sparse attention mechanism with hardware-efficient execution. QASparse preserves the efficiency of shared cross-head importance estimation while adapting computational budgets and token selections to query requirements, and it executes these dynamic sparse decisions through dedicated kernels. Its query adaptivity stems from two complementary innovations: Local Budget Regression models local variations in computational demand along query positions to estimate budgets for different query regions and attention heads; Boundary Voting lets queries within each head vote over candidates near the selection cutoff using actual query/key scores, refining the retained set while preserving the initial selection size. To reduce the execution overhead of dynamic budgets, we further design length-specialized selection kernels that efficiently support query-adaptive sparse patterns across context lengths. Together, these designs efficiently combine shared estimation with local decisions while adapting both how much attention is computed and which interactions are retained. Experimental results demonstrate improved benchmark scores and faster prefill attention computation compared with existing sparse attention baselines.
authors: Zhiyuan Chen, Zihao Yang, Quanjiang Li, Haijiang Li, Jiancheng Pan, Qichao Zhao, Zihan Dong, Qiushi Shi, Jinshi Liu
bullets: Targets the quadratic cost of dense attention during long-sequence prefill and the limitations of uniform head-level sparsity.
Uses shared cross-head importance estimation, then applies query-specific decisions for computational budgets and token selection.
Local Budget Regression estimates attention budgets across query regions and heads.
Boundary Voting refines tokens near the selection cutoff using actual query–key scores without changing the initial selection size.
Length-specialized kernels reduce the overhead of executing dynamic sparse patterns; experiments report better benchmark scores and faster prefill attention than prior sparse-attention baselines.
