papers.abstract: Large language model agents accomplish complex tasks by coordinating multiple reasoning steps and tool operations, which form dependencies among their operations. Existing orchestration methods primarily consider hard dependencies that determine when an operation can legally begin, but overlook soft dependencies, i.e., information that is not required for execution but may improve an already executable operation. We identify soft-dependency scheduling as an important problem in agent execution. To this end, we introduce Neural Agent Compiler (NAC), a learned scheduler that predicts the task-quality and resource consequences of three execution modes and selects the highest-utility legal mode at a scheduling boundary. NAC represents the executable continuation, pending information event, and resource state in a shared memory, and uses a utility function to adapt the consequence predictions to different resource preferences. Across AppWorld, WebShop, and $\tau^2$-bench, NAC achieves 276/417 AppWorld task completions, a 74.69 WebShop Task Score, and 59/100 $\tau^2$-bench successes. Additional studies show that the learned scheduler reduces execution work, establishing soft-dependency scheduling as a promising solution for orchestrating tool-using agents.
authors: Bo Yan, Peng Wang, Zihan Chen, Ziwen Kan, Zhen Tan, Huiyuan Chen, Bo Sun, Shuai Shao, Tianlong Chen, Song Wang
bullets: Addresses soft dependencies: information that is not required to start an operation but may improve its outcome.
Predicts task-quality and resource consequences for three legal execution modes, then selects the highest-utility mode.
Represents executable continuations, pending information events, and resource state in shared memory.
Reports 276/417 AppWorld completions, a 74.69 WebShop Task Score, and 59/100 τ²-bench successes.
Additional studies find reduced execution work, though the abstract does not specify the study setup or limitations.

papers.abstract: With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results into a persistent, provenance-preserving knowledge base with three planes: source evidence, reusable synthesis, and agent memory. Decision-aware retrieval assembles compact evidence packs, role-specific agents reason over them and invoke a simulator (Vidur or GAUSS) whenever quantitative support is needed, and every finding is written back as a scoped evidence record, so knowledge guides experiments and experiments refine knowledge. In configuration search over four serving scenarios, NoeVera comes within 5% of the optimum in a median of 6-7 simulator calls, versus 9 for Bayesian optimization and 15 for a knowledge-free agent with the same tools; on A100 GPUs, its representative configurations deliver ~1.30x vLLM-default throughput and meet every scenario's latency objective. When reused, provenance-preserving evidence records over-generalize on only 8% of applicability traps, versus 28% for a general-purpose agent memory. On the held-out 48-task split of a 72-task benchmark, NoeVera scores 29% higher than an equally equipped agent and 36% higher than its single-call retrieval counterpart (0.80 vs. 0.62 and 0.59), and even when baselines receive NoeVera's own prompts, a statistically significant part of its evidence-evolution advantage remains.

papers.abstract: Standard dense visual prediction architectures scale representation capacity by stacking deep feedforward decoders (6-16 transformer layers with 50M-200M parameters). This explicit layer stacking brings substantial activation memory overhead during backpropagation, requires high off-chip memory bandwidth for non-tied weights, and uses static computational allocation that cannot adapt to spatial image complexity. We propose loopxDINO, which replaces physical decoder depth with iterative latent reasoning. It has two decoupled components: (1) a frozen DINOv2-Base backbone extracting spatial features in one forward pass and caching static Key-Value representations in GPU memory; (2) a compact weight-tied Looped Cross-Attention Decoder (7.96M core, 14.85M total trainable parameters) that recurrently updates queries across T iterations. Recurrence is stabilized by step-conditioned adaLN, LayerNorm-based hyper-ellipsoid manifold regularization, and learnable residual contraction damping. Intermediate mask predictions are fed back as spatial attention biases to guide queries toward ambiguous contours with no extra parameters. On Pascal VOC 2012 semantic segmentation with a single RTX 5060 Ti 16GB GPU, loopxDINO (T=2) achieves 85.66% mIoU and 65.01% Boundary IoU. It outperforms 6-layer DINO-Trans6L (54.06M params) by +1.09% mIoU and +7.41% Boundary IoU with 72.5% fewer parameters. Compared to 4-layer DINO-FCN4L probe (2.43M params, 83.82% mIoU), loopxDINO improves boundary delineation by +6.43% bIoU and occlusion resilience by +6.76% mIoU (60% patch masking). With Adaptive Computation Time (ACT), it reaches 87.3 FPS and retains 29.64% mIoU under 60% occlusion (+5.83% over DINO-Trans6L). Source code, pre-trained weights and evaluation suites are open-sourced under Apache 2.0 at https://github.com/loopxDINO/loopxDINO
authors: Xiangjing An, Zhibin Jiao, Aiting Chen
bullets: Addresses activation-memory, bandwidth, and fixed-compute costs of stacked transformer decoders.
Uses frozen DINOv2-Base features with cached key-value representations and a weight-tied Looped Cross-Attention Decoder.
Stabilizes iterative reasoning with step-conditioned adaLN, manifold regularization, residual damping, and feedback from intermediate masks.
On Pascal VOC 2012, T=2 achieves 85.66% mIoU and 65.01% Boundary IoU, outperforming a 6-layer baseline with 72.5% fewer parameters.
ACT enables adaptive computation, reaching 87.3 FPS and retaining 29.64% mIoU under 60% patch masking.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Architectural overview of loopxDINO. (a) Immutable Perception Base: An input image X ∈ R3×H×W is processed in a single forward pass by a frozen foundation backbone (∇θ = 0), producing spatial features and a persistent Key-Value cache (Kv,Vv) ∈ RHpWp×D. (b) Looped Latent Reasoning Engine: A compact, weight-tied Looped Cross-Attention Decoder (≈ 7.96M core parameters) iteratively refines learned queries Qt across t = 1 . . . T . Recurrent updates are modulated by step-conditioned Adaptive Layer Normalization (adaLN), regularized by LayerNorm hyper-ellipsoid projection, and guided by spatial attention biases derived from intermediate mask predictions. (c) Readout & Dynamic ACT: Multi-scale representations from layers 4, 8, and 12 are fused to generate dense masks Mt, while a halting controller predicts termination probabilities ht for adaptive computational allocation.

Figure 2: Compute-Optimal Pareto Frontier on Pascal VOC 2012. (a) Latency-Accuracy Pareto Frontier: Trade-off between inference latency (RTX 5060 Ti) and validation mIoU. loopxDINO (T = 1, 2) and Dynamic ACT define an optimal Pareto frontier, outperforming the 6-layer physically stacked baseline (DINO-Trans6L, 54.06M) and substantially exceeding the boundary precision of the convolutional probe anchor (DINO-FCN4L, 2.43M). (b) Parameter Efficiency Scaling: Achieving +1.09% higher mIoU and +7.41% higher Boundary IoU with 72.5% fewer trainable decoder parameters than DINO-Trans6L.

Figure 3: Dynamical Stability and Recurrent Contraction Analysis. (a) Latent Norm Boundedness on Hyper-Ellipsoid Manifold: Norm evolution ∥Qt∥2 over 32 recurrence steps. Naive additive embeddings diverge past 140, whereas loopxDINO (adaLN + LayerNorm) stabilizes on the invariant manifold ∥q∥2 ≈√ D = 27.71. (b) Exponential Velocity Decay & Fixed Point: The step displacement ∥Qt −Qt−1∥2 exhibits geometric decay alongside the analytical Lipschitz contraction bound (ρ = 0.74 < 1.0).

Figure 5: Dynamic Halting and Occlusion Robustness. (a) Adaptive Pondering vs. Occlusion Depth: Under increasing patch masking (0% to 60%), the differentiable ACT controller autonomously shifts halting probability mass toward higher reasoning iterations (mean steps shift from µ = 2.9 to µ = 7.4). (b) Occlusion Retention: Evaluated across clean and randomly occluded inputs on Pascal VOC 2012. Both DINO-FCN4L and DINO-Trans6L degrade under heavy masking, whereas loopxDINO (T = 4) achieves 29.64% mIoU (+5.83% over DINO-Trans6L, +6.76% over DINO-FCN4L).

Figure 4: Boundary Refinement and Attention Sharpening Dynamics. (a) Edge Boundary IoU vs. Recurrent Loops: Boundary IoU across trimap bands (1px, 3px, and overall) on Pascal VOC 2012. Fine boundary precision peaks at T = 2 (65.01% bIoU), outperforming the 6-layer baseline by +7.41%. (b) Attention Sharpening & Spatial Focusing: Cross-attention entropy drops steadily as queries transition from diffuse scene exploration to concentrated boundary saliency.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) tokenize images using fixed spatial grids, so visual token count grows with pixel area rather than scene content. We propose to group neighboring patches based on their visual appearance, allowing tokens to represent coherent image regions rather than fixed spatial windows. We introduce RVLM, a VLM trained to use regions rather than patches as its visual units. Analyzing region construction for general-purpose VLMs, we find that regions must cover the full image, stay spatially connected during end-to-end training, and preserve fine structure such as small text, while semantic grouping adds little. RVLM therefore partitions images using training-free Felzenszwalb-Huttenlocher segmentation, assigns each ViT patch to a region, and pools patches within each region into a variable-length sequence of visual tokens. The patch-to-region assignment is retained to support spatially precise prediction through coarse-to-fine decoding. Across tasks spanning VQA, pointing, counting, segmentation, and depth estimation, RVLM matches or improves example-weighted task performance while using 21.5% fewer visual tokens than an identically trained patch baseline. The advantage grows with image resolution, reaching a 5.3-point gain while using 51.8% fewer visual tokens at the highest-resolution setting. The gains are largest on spatially demanding tasks, where prior token-reduction methods degrade most sharply. RVLM adds no model parameters and improves inference throughput by up to 35.9%. On unseen pathology and satellite images and on video benchmarks without any video training, RVLM performs on par with the patch baseline while using 2-3$\times$ fewer visual tokens. These results establish regions as a scalable alternative to patch-based visual representations while preserving the spatial precision required for grounded prediction.
authors: Savya Khosla, Chris Dongjoo Kim, Alex Schwing, Derek Hoiem, Christopher Clark, Sangho Lee
bullets: Uses training-free Felzenszwalb–Huttenlocher segmentation to group patches into variable-length, spatially connected regions.
Preserves full-image coverage and fine structure, including small text; semantic grouping is not essential.
Retains patch-to-region mappings for coarse-to-fine spatial prediction.
Matches or improves performance across VQA, pointing, counting, segmentation, and depth estimation while using 21.5% fewer tokens overall.
At higher resolutions, gains reach 5.3 points with 51.8% fewer tokens; inference throughput improves by up to 35.9%, with strong transfer to pathology, satellite, and video benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of RVLM. We generate content-adaptive regions using FelzenszwalbHuttenlocher segmentation and assign each ViT patch to a region. This is a CPU-side preprocessing that runs in parallel to the model execution. Patch features within each region are aggregated through attention pooling to produce a sequence of region tokens for the LLM. The retained patch-to-region correspondence enables coarse-to-fine spatial grounding, where the LLM selects a region, then a patch within it, and finally a precise point within the patch.

Figure 4: Comparing region generation methods. SAM leaves image regions uncovered (white boxes), while learned feature-based methods (DiVT, T-REN) produce disconnected regions during VLM training. SLIC often fails to isolate text, whereas FH preserves fine text structures with connected regions and complete image coverage.
Figure 1: Region tokens scale better with image resolution while improving inference efficiency. See Section 4.2 for details.

Figure 3: Post-hoc token compression methods degrade sharply on tasks requiring spatial precision. RVLM outperforms token pruning (FastV), token merging (ToMe), and hybrid (VisionZip) methods on pointing, segmentation, counting, and depth estimation, while all methods perform comparably on Image QA. Horizontal line denotes the PVLM baseline.

Figure 5: Failure cases of T-REN-based RVLM. During VLM training, region tokens become spatially disconnected, making it difficult to associate text and visual elements with their correct locations. The model recognizes individual labels but misattributes them to neighboring rows, columns, or objects, producing incorrect descriptions of the image structure. For instance, in the first example, it incorrectly describes some initiatives as “on the table” for Obama, even though the image lists none. PVLM and FH-based RVLM do not show these failures.

Latencies are reported as mean ± standard deviation. While PVLM is slightly faster at low crop counts, RVLM achieves increasing latency and memory savings as image resolution grows.

Table 7: Our main evaluation suite. Metrics match those reported in the main native-resolution comparison. papers.title: RVLM: Fewer Tokens, Better Resolution Scaling, Fine-Grained Spatial Grounding

papers.abstract: A diffusion language sampler makes two choices for every position in its denoising window: where the next token comes from, and when the position is committed to the KV cache. Using the entropy-bound sampler in DiffusionGemma, we study two extremes of the second choice. Committing each token as soon as it is accepted removes the chance to revise it, which hurts when the entropy bound is relaxed to trade accuracy for speed. When accepted tokens are frozen, macro accuracy falls from 73% to 20% as the bound is relaxed, while the unfrozen sampler stays near 70%. Committing a whole block at once wastes computation, since tokens converge in a largely left-to-right order and more than half of the window holds already-final tokens by twenty denoising steps. These findings motivate the Rolling Entropy Sampler (RES), which commits a contiguous accepted prefix once it reaches a minimum length and keeps positions farther ahead open to revision. Unlike earlier rolling samplers, RES runs on uniform diffusion, where accepted tokens can still change, and it needs no training. Across seven benchmarks, RES increases tokens per forward pass from 19.3 to 25.5, while macro accuracy goes from 80.7% to 78.8%, and it extends the speed-quality Pareto frontier beyond what tuning the entropy bound alone reaches.
authors: Patrick Pynadath, Nicolas Perez-Nieves, Bobak Shahriari, Jean Tarbouriech, Ruqi Zhang, Ivan Lobov
bullets: Immediate commitment harms quality when the entropy bound is relaxed, whereas leaving tokens revisable maintains accuracy.
Committing entire blocks wastes computation because tokens typically converge in a left-to-right order.
RES commits a contiguous accepted prefix after it reaches a minimum length and keeps later positions open for revision.
Across seven benchmarks, RES raises tokens per forward pass from 19.3 to 25.5, with macro accuracy decreasing from 80.7% to 78.8%.
RES requires no training and extends the speed–quality Pareto frontier beyond entropy-bound tuning alone.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | Columns in the top and middle rows show LiveCodeBench, GPQA Diamond, and Natural2Code. Top row: Spearman 𝜌 and Kendall 𝜏 between the acceptance order of the DiffusionGemma EB sampler and the AR generation order; across all tasks the sampler is strongly biased towards left-to-right order. Middle row: Percentage of wasted denoising slots averaged across canvases for LCB v6, GPQA Diamond and Natural2Code. For a given sampling step, a slot is wasted if it belongs to a contiguous prefix that has already converged to its final token. By denoising step 20, the mean fraction of wasted canvas slots exceeds 50% on all three tasks. Bottom row: Accepted tokens are revised more often at higher entropy bounds (in both argmax and sampled-token stability), independent of renoising.

Figure 4 | Three passes of the rolling sampler. Every pass spends a fixed budget of ten positions (dashed frame), split between an encoded prefix of the tokens committed on the previous pass and the remaining denoising window; the mask panel on the right is exactly that block of ten. Left: positions keep their column, so each slot can be read down its column. Out-of-order acceptances wait for a contiguous prefix (w at 𝑡) and unaccepted slots stay mutable (column ten: r→ o). The prefix completing at 𝑡+1 is four slots long, so four slots must be encoded at 𝑡+2: the block advances by however many positions graduated into the KV cache, and the split is 0+10, then 2+8, then 4+6. Right: rows are queries, columns are keys; a coloured cell means the query attends to the key. The encoded prefix is causal, so its KV-cache entries depend only on committed tokens and are never revised, while denoising positions are bidirectional among themselves and attend fully to the prefix. Committing more positions per pass therefore moves the KV cache forward faster, but leaves fewer positions to denoise on the next pass. Every query additionally attends to the whole KV cache (white cells), which the panels omit for space.

Figure 1 | (a) The unified stopping criterion matches the original at a slight speedup. (b) Simulation of per-position commitment in DiffusionGemma: freezing each token upon acceptance removes the chance for later revision. Frozen variants degrade much faster than unfrozen variants as the entropy bound is relaxed, showing the cost of losing this sampler flexibility.

Figure 2 | Where the denoising slots go. Both samplers denoise a width-8 window per pass in the same order, and the colours are those of Figure 4: teal = still denoising, amber = accepted on this pass, white = already encoded and in the KV cache, gray = not yet admitted. Brick marks a slot spent re-denoising a position that was already accepted but is still waiting for its prefix, that is, wasted work. (a) The block sampler appends only once the block is fully resolved, so converged positions idle and each block re-pays warm-up. (b) The rolling sampler appends the accepted prefix immediately and admits fresh positions in its place, wasting far fewer slots.

Figure 7 | Frontiers obtained by varying both the minimum shift ℓmin in 𝐹𝑐𝑜𝑚𝑚𝑖𝑡 (“S” in the legend) and the entropy bound in 𝐹𝑟𝑜𝑢𝑡𝑒 for RES. Small shifts extend the frontier to higher throughput than Unified EB reaches.

Figure 6 | Pareto frontiers of RES with minimum shift ℓmin = 32 and Unified EB under varied entropy bounds for LCB v6 and Natural2Code averaged over 5 seeds, and GPQA Diamond averaged over 20 seeds due to its higher evaluation variance.

Figure 5 |Macro Average Pass@𝑘 vs. Sample Count 𝑘. While Unified EB achieves higher Pass@1, RES (ℓmin = 32) exhibits stronger multi-sample scaling, overtaking Unified EB at 𝑘 ≥ 6 and maintaining its advantage through 𝑘 = 20. Table 2 reports a 32.5% increase in tokens per forward pass.

(6)), 𝐴𝜏 the confidence set, ℓ(𝐴) the longest accepted prefix, 𝐴<𝑡 the positions accepted at earlier steps. Shaded cells highlight the commitment rules introduced here; RES with minimum shift ℓmin = 𝑤 recovers Unified EB when the remaining sampler settings, including the temperature schedule, are matched. Freezing is encoded by a rule that forces future stay probabilities to one, whereas 𝑐𝑖 denotes cache commitment. Frozen EB simulates per-position commitment by preventing later revision; RES waits for a contiguous accepted prefix and leaves accepted positions farther ahead revisable.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) generators produce detailed images but remain slow at inference. Speculative decoding can reduce this cost, yet its behavior across the rendering requirements of T2I prompts remains insufficiently understood. We introduce T2ISpec, a benchmark of 1,400 prompts balanced across seven rendering topics and two difficulty levels. It evaluates autoregressive and diffusion/flow accelerators by latency, work performed by the target model, and image quality. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) aggregate results hide large differences between topics, (2) alignment and preference scores can disagree with prompt constraint satisfaction, and (3) large reductions in target work can yield limited latency gains. Motivated by these findings, we propose TopicRoute, a plugin that combines prompt routing with speculative and cache controls without retraining the generator. Across six model--method pairs, it achieves a geometric mean speedup of 1.0308x over the native methods, and the speedup carries over to external prompts with the same settings, while quality gains and losses vary across configurations.
authors: Yifan Zhang, Shatong Zhu, Hui Shen, Yunta Hsieh, Jianing Ma, Muxin Fu, Xin Wang, Ping Zhang, Qian Chen, Chaofan Tao
bullets: Benchmarks 1,400 prompts spanning seven rendering topics and two difficulty levels.
Evaluates autoregressive and diffusion/flow accelerators using latency, target-model work, and image quality.
Finds that aggregate scores can hide topic differences, preference metrics may miss prompt-constraint satisfaction, and reduced target work does not always improve latency.
TopicRoute combines prompt routing with speculative and cache controls across six model–method pairs.
Reports a 1.0308× geometric-mean speedup over native methods, with configuration-dependent quality changes and transfer to external prompts.

papers.abstract: The decay exponent $\alpha$ in KV-cache eviction is an intrinsic property of the model: calibrated once on a single corpus, it transfers directly across domains. Attention-based accumulation (H2O) and recency-based sliding windows (StreamingLLM) are two dominant eviction frameworks, often treated as unrelated, but we show that they are the two endpoints of a single power-law family: by scoring each token as $s_i = A_i \cdot (t-i)^{-\alpha}$, where $A_i$ is cumulative attention and $\alpha$ controls the age penalty, H2O and StreamingLLM correspond to $\alpha=0$ and $\alpha\to\infty$, respectively (with StreamingLLM additionally hard-coding an attention-sink patch). The no-hair mechanism of \citet{xiang2026nohair} bounds the admissible range of $\alpha$, and the measured exponents agree: calibrating once on WikiText yields $[0.556, 0.822]$ for a representative model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps. \textsc{NoHairCache} achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM ($p < 0.05$ on all three datasets, with $0.06$--$0.10$ PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget $512$). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining $98.2\%$ of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at $25\%$ retention versus $91.1\%$ for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.
bullets: Frames H2O and StreamingLLM as endpoints of a shared score: cumulative attention weighted by token age via exponent α.
Calibrating α on WikiText produces model-consistent ranges that also align with perplexity-based optimal regions across five models.
Achieves the lowest perplexity on WikiText, PG19, and arXiv without per-dataset tuning, outperforming H2O and StreamingLLM.
Matches or exceeds StreamingLLM on all evaluated QA task–budget cells; QA results are treated as corroborating because per-cell tests are not significant.
The approach is scoped to calibrated model-specific exponent ranges and is accompanied by a calibration script and drop-in scorer.

papers.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) has been widely adopted in autoregressive (AR) models for high-quality image generation. Despite its strong empirical performance, its mechanism in AR models remains unclear. This paper demystifies the mechanism of CFG through both empirical and theoretical studies. By examining the top-ranked semantics of different components in CFG, we show that texture information is primarily encoded in the difference between the conditional and unconditional logits, whereas both logits share previous-token repetition as their leading semantics. This strong repetition semantics obscures the desired texture information, causing greedy decoding from the conditional logits alone to produce nearly pure-color images. Through a training-dynamics analysis of shallow transformers, we prove that this shared repetition semantics does not arise from limitations or failures of pretraining, but instead originates from the texture sparsity of images. We further show that CFG improves generation quality by rectifying this repetition bias during inference. Motivated by the shared semantics between conditional and unconditional logits, we propose Attention Weight Reuse (AttnReuse), which reuses intermediate attention computations from the conditional-logit forward pass to accelerate the unconditional-logit computation. AttnReuse reduces about $25\%$ of attention computation with little performance degradation across different models.
authors: Zhiling Zhou, Jiachun Pan, Fengzhuo Zhang, Dirk Bergemann, Zhuoran Yang
bullets: CFG’s conditional and unconditional logits both strongly encode previous-token repetition; their difference primarily captures texture information.
Greedy decoding from conditional logits alone can yield nearly pure-color images because repetition semantics obscure texture.
Theoretical and empirical analyses attribute this shared repetition bias to image texture sparsity, not pretraining failure.
CFG improves quality by rectifying the repetition bias during inference.
Attention Weight Reuse cuts about 25% of attention computation with little performance degradation across models.

figures.caption: Figure 7: Overview of the proof. (1) Training WV makes text and background tokens favor background repetition, while feature tokens favor feature repetition. (2) Training WQK makes the conditional branch attend to text when predicting the first feature token. Inside the block, both branches attend to earlier feature tokens. (3) CFG uses the logit difference to generate the first feature token. Repetition then completes the feature block; without CFG, generation repeats the background.

Figure 8: Illustration of the proposed AttnReuse method. In selected layers, we reuse conditional attention weights by masking out text-token entries and renormalizing over image tokens. We then apply these weights to the conditional value vectors to approximate the unconditional attention output.

papers.abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has achieved state-of-the-art performance across diverse tasks, but its high computational cost remains a major barrier. We introduce PruneNAS, a novel framework that integrates structured pruning into NAS to efficiently explore high-performing architectures while leveraging pretrained models. Unlike conventional NAS methods that train each candidate from scratch, PruneNAS generates a candidate pool by pruning pretrained networks at multiple granularity levels and formulates the selection as a global optimization problem using training-free importance metrics. This approach enables rapid evaluation of candidate architectures under strict resource constraints, dramatically reducing search time from hundreds of GPU hours to mere minutes. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that PruneNAS discovers compact, high-accuracy architectures that nearly halve the computational cost (MACs) of prior methods on ResNet-50, while also showing strong generalization on object detection tasks with YOLO. Our method bridges structured pruning and NAS, offering a practical solution for resource-constrained model deployment.
authors: Sudhakar Sah, Nikhil Chhabra, Honnesh Rohmetra, Andy Li
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of conventional NAS under strict deployment constraints.
Builds candidate architectures by pruning pretrained models at multiple granularity levels.
Uses training-free importance metrics and global optimization to select architectures without training each candidate from scratch.
Reduces search time from hundreds of GPU hours to minutes, according to the abstract.
Finds compact architectures with nearly half the MACs of prior methods on ResNet-50 and generalizes to YOLO object detection.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) involves detecting the underlying emotion behind each utterance within a conversation, which is essential for emotionally aware human-computer interaction. While omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) demonstrate strong capability for MER by jointly processing modalities including text, audio, and vision, different modality combinations yield different prediction outcomes across utterances: acoustic and visual inputs can help recover annotated labels missed by text-only inference, but can also turn correct predictions into errors. Processing all modalities for every utterance is also computationally expensive. To this end, we introduce EmoRouter, a training-free, model-agnostic framework for adaptive modality cascading that selects an exit tier for each utterance along a predefined modality order. The routing is guided by prediction-uncertainty estimates derived from Conformal Prediction. EmoRouter routes each utterance through a sequence of increasing-cost modality levels and exits at the first level when the model is confident in the emotion. To determine when to exit, we propose Conformal Set Contraction, a structural calibration criterion that calibrates the per-tier CP error budgets used for these exit decisions. Comprehensive evaluations on 4 MER benchmarks and 3 Omni-LLMs reveal that EmoRouter matches or outperforms the full modalities while reducing inference latency by 67.9--94.5%. Furthermore, EmoRouter demonstrates high transferability across different models, validating its robustness. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyi-lab/EmoRouter.
authors: Fangxu Yu, Lingzhi Yuan, Dehai Min, Tao Feng, Ge Liu, Furong Huang, Tianyi Zhou
bullets: Addresses the variable usefulness and high cost of processing text, audio, and vision for every utterance in multimodal emotion recognition.
Uses a training-free, model-agnostic cascading router that evaluates increasingly expensive modality combinations and exits when sufficiently confident.
Introduces Conformal Set Contraction to calibrate per-tier error budgets for reliable exit decisions.
Evaluated on 4 MER benchmarks and 3 Omni-LLMs, matching or outperforming full-modality inference while reducing latency by 67.9–94.5%.
Transfers effectively across models, supporting the framework’s robustness.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of EmoRouter. Given an utterance with text, audio, and visual modalities, EmoRouter cascades the Omni-LLM through three modality tiers of increasing cost: Tier 1 (T), Tier 2 (T+A), and Tier 3 (T+A+V). At each non-terminal tier, a conformal prediction set is constructed using the CSC-selected error rate α˚ ℓ . If the set contains at most one label, the cascade exits and returns the top-1 prediction; otherwise, it escalates to the next tier. The per-tier error budgets are obtained by maximizing Conformal Set Contraction (CSC) on the calibration set.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based sequence models have achieved strong performance in language and time-series modeling, but self-attention remains computationally and memory intensive for deployment on resource-constrained edge accelerators. We propose STEdgeFormer, a lightweight, hardware-aware sequence architecture designed for efficient execution on embedded neural accelerators. STEdgeFormer combines polynomial mixture layers and DyT normalization with an accelerator-aware causal memory block, replacing pairwise self-attention with compact causal aggregation. On TinyStories, the fully NPU-supported STEdgeFormer (MW) achieves a perplexity of 7.39 with 4.12M parameters and 6.51 MB RAM, with an end-to-end latency of 40 ms. In comparison, the standard 4.12M-parameter configuration achieves a lower perplexity of 6.79 but requires CPU fallback for unsupported operators, resulting in 1450 ms latency. Vanilla Transformer, on the other hand, achieves a perplexity score of 5.71 using a 4.40M-parameter model, but it cannot be deployed on the hardware. On downstream tasks, STEdgeFormer achieves 94% accuracy on ECG5000 and 93% accuracy on Speech Commands with 1.39M parameters. These results demonstrate that hardware-aware architectural choices and operator compatibility can have a substantial impact on practical inference latency, beyond model size and task accuracy alone. Rather than targeting state-of-the-art accuracy on individual benchmarks, STEdgeFormer is designed to provide a deployable sequence modeling architecture under the memory, computational, and operator constraints of embedded neural accelerators.
bullets: Targets the high compute, memory, and operator-compatibility costs of self-attention on resource-constrained edge accelerators.
Combines polynomial mixture layers, DyT normalization, and an accelerator-aware causal memory block.
A fully NPU-supported 4.12M-parameter model reaches 7.39 perplexity with 6.51 MB RAM and 40 ms latency on TinyStories.
The standard configuration has better perplexity (6.79) but requires CPU fallback, increasing latency to 1450 ms; vanilla Transformer is not deployable on the target hardware.
Achieves 94% accuracy on ECG5000 and 93% on Speech Commands with 1.39M parameters.

papers.abstract: World models hold great promise for autonomous driving planning, yet their ability to imagine the future often comes at a formidable computational cost. Efficiency efforts, such as knowledge distillation and domain-specific pre-training, often shift this burden to costly teachers or training pipelines, leaving lightweight world modeling an open challenge. We introduce FastWorld, a natively lightweight world-model framework for efficient autonomous driving planning. FastWorld reduces computation through compact scene representations, short-horizon action-conditioned prediction, and selective candidate verification and score refinement. These designs support efficient future-informed planning without teacher distillation or additional domain-specific pre-training. On NAVSIMv1, FastWorld achieves 92.2 PDMS at 132 FPS on a single 4090 GPU. It also achieves 89.4 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2 and an average L2 of 0.40 over 3 seconds at 17 FPS on nuScenes. Code and models can be found at https://github.com/MoyangSensei/FastWorld.
authors: Feiyang Jia, Lin Liu, Zhicheng Bao, Caiyan Jia, Ziying Song, Shengkai Zhang, Lina Han, Yan Zhao, Xiaoshuai Hao
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of imagining future driving scenarios for planning.
Uses compact scene representations, short-horizon action-conditioned prediction, and selective candidate verification with score refinement.
Avoids costly teacher distillation and additional domain-specific pre-training.
Achieves 92.2 PDMS at 132 FPS on NAVSIMv1, 89.4 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2, and 0.40 average 3-second L2 at 17 FPS on nuScenes.
Scope is demonstrated on NAVSIM and nuScenes benchmarks; the abstract does not report broader deployment limitations.

papers.abstract: We present OSplit, an exact analytical method that enables efficient partitioning of a GPU L1 domain into prefill and decode workers, including sharding for classical and advanced GPUs. OSplit takes into consideration model parameters, enabling any inference model to be partitioned into prefill and decode workers with a goal of producing the maximum throughput possible. OSplit is based on a capacity model that takes as inputs the model, the loading scheme (batch size, max sequence length), and models an inference serving framework (vLLM) and computes the efficiency of each GPU. For this, we model H100 and GB300 GPUs, and model a scale-up domain, along with FlashAttention-based kernels. OSplit first computes an optimal collective generation policy, which gives inputs to the capacity model that enables optimal split of prefill and decode GPUs. We evaluate our scheme over H100 (NVL8) and GB300 (NVL72) using vLLM inference serving and show throughput, predicted and measured latency, showing near-perfect theoretical-to-measured values over leading LLMs (Llama and Qwen)
authors: Akshat Pandey, Dominic Cheng, Sidharth Sharma, Ashwin Gumaste
bullets: Models GPU capacity using the inference model, batch size, sequence length, loading scheme, vLLM, and FlashAttention-based kernels.
Supports sharding and partitioning across classical and advanced GPU configurations, including H100 NVL8 and GB300 NVL72.
Computes an optimal collective generation policy before selecting the prefill/decode GPU split.
Evaluation on Llama and Qwen shows near-perfect agreement between predicted and measured latency and throughput.
Scope is evaluated on modeled H100 and GB300 scale-up domains with vLLM serving.

papers.abstract: Neural networks are typically trained separately for individual datasets or tasks, resulting in many task-specific models. This redundancy increases memory footprint, deployment costs, and energy consumption limiting their scalability. We propose UNIFY, a unified learning framework that enables a single model to jointly learn and perform inference across multiple datasets via Batch Normalization Switching (BNS). Instead of maintaining separate models for each dataset, UNIFY shares the parameter-intensive backbone while maintaining dataset-specific BN statistics and parameters, along with dataset-specific classification heads. We validate our framework using five datasets (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet) across six Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) of different sizes (SqueezeNet 1.1, WideResNet-40-2, WideResNet-16-8, ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50). Notably, a single UNIFIED ResNet-34 trained on these datasets achieves accuracies of 99.53%, 94.84%, 96.12%, 80.32%, and 67.67%, respectively, outperforming the average performance of the corresponding independently trained task-specific models while reducing the memory footprint by approximately 4.94x, from 428.30 MB (five separate models) to 86.71 MB (one unified model). UNIFY aims not only to consolidate (K) models into a single model but also to enhance model-effectiveness by leveraging complementary knowledge across datasets. It paves the way for scalable, efficient, and unified learning capable of handling diverse image classification tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/saktx/UNIFY.
authors: Shaharyar Ahmed Khan Tareen, Xiaojing Yuan
bullets: Addresses the memory, deployment, and energy costs of maintaining separate models for different datasets or tasks.
Uses Batch Normalization Switching with shared backbone parameters, dataset-specific BN statistics/parameters, and dataset-specific classification heads.
Evaluated across five datasets and six CNN architectures.
A unified ResNet-34 achieved the reported accuracies while reducing memory from 428.30 MB to 86.71 MB—about 4.94× lower than five separate models.
The framework is scoped to jointly learning and inferring across diverse image-classification datasets.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: An example UNIFIED architecture for 3 datasets, having 4 feature-extraction layers, 2 switchable BN layers, and an output layer. Each switchable BN layer maintains 3 sets of BN parameters (and statistics), while the output layer contains 3 classification heads, corresponding to the 3 participating datasets. To preserve dataset-specific parameters, the corresponding BN layers and classification head are switched while routing the data from different datasets. The shared feature-extraction layers can be linear, convolutional, or residual connections, depending on the architecture used (UNIFY is architecture-flexible framework that can be adopted in various CNN architectures). Batch Normalization Switching (BNS) and dedicated classification heads preserve dataset-specific representations while enabling joint optimization through a shared backbone.

Fig. 1: (a) A UNIFIED model jointly trained across multiple datasets enables effective inference on all datasets through Batch Normalization Switching (BNS) and dataset-specific classification heads. (b) A UNIFIED model trained on K datasets, reduces the memory footprint to approximately 1/K of that required by K independently trained models, while preserving strong performance. (c) A UNIFIED ResNet-34, jointly trained on 5 datasets, achieves overall superior performance compared with independently trained ResNet-34 models on these datasets.

The differences in the statistical distributions across the 5 BN sets highlight the importance of BNS in accommodating dataset-specific feature characteristics. These results suggest that sharing a single BN configuration is ineffective and sub-optimal for accommodating distinct data characteristics of the 5 datasets, resulting in degraded performance, as also supported by the results in Table IV.

papers.abstract: Image enhancement spans degradations with distinct spectral characteristics. Standard convolutions use fixed kernels, whereas dynamic convolutions gain adaptability at additional inference cost. We propose Dynamic Spectrum Re-parameterized Convolution (DSRC), a plug-and-play module that learns task-adaptive spectral responses during training while retaining standard convolution at inference. DSRC decomposes convolution kernels into frequency bands, applies learnable high/low-pass modulation, and incorporates lightweight residual branches. Owing to the linearity of these operations, all training-time components are analytically fused into a single kernel for inference. Experiments on low-light enhancement, underwater enhancement, and image super-resolution show consistent PSNR gains and generally improved or preserved SSIM and LPIPS across twelve backbone-task configurations, with unchanged deployed parameter counts and theoretical FLOPs, and no additional inference operators.
authors: Zhiyan Zhou, Hailong Yan, Hanlin Liu, Yongrui Zhang, Xiangtao Zhang, Le Zhang
bullets: Targets the mismatch between fixed convolution kernels and degradations with different spectral characteristics.
Decomposes kernels into frequency bands and learns high-/low-pass modulation with lightweight residual branches.
Uses analytical re-parameterization to fuse all training-time components into one standard convolution.
Across 12 backbone–task configurations for low-light, underwater enhancement, and super-resolution, it reports consistent PSNR gains and generally improved or preserved SSIM and LPIPS.
Deployed parameter counts and theoretical FLOPs remain unchanged, with no extra inference operators.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Large Vision-Language Models solve multimodal reasoning tasks by retaining hundreds or thousands of visual tokens, allowing every generated token to attend to the visual tokens at any time during the generation process. However, whether continuous access to these visual tokens is necessary remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate how visual token influence evolves along two dimensions: generation time and transformer depth. Using long-form visual reasoning benchmarks and multiple model scales, we first analyze the attention dynamics across generation time and transformer depth. We identify a temporal and depth-wise structure in the use of visual information. Visual attention peaks during the initial generation steps and then rapidly declines as attention shifts toward previously generated reasoning tokens. Across depth, visual influence is concentrated in intermediate layers and becomes very weak in the final layers. We further verify these observations with causal intervention that removes all visual tokens across generation time and model depth. These interventions confirm that visual-token dependence in multimodal reasoning is neither temporally persistent nor uniformly distributed across transformer depth. Thus, retaining the complete visual context at every layer and decoding step may be unnecessary. Our experiments demonstrate that we can remove up to 59\% of tokens from the full input prompt across generation time and 11\% across all transformer layers, while incurring only a very small performance drop. On video benchmarks, up to 65\% of the input prompt tokens can be removed during generation without affecting performance.
bullets: Visual-token influence declines rapidly after the initial generation steps as models rely more on previously generated reasoning tokens.
Across transformer depth, visual influence is concentrated in intermediate layers and is weak in final layers.
Attention analyses and causal interventions show that visual dependence is neither temporally persistent nor uniform across depth.
The approach removes up to 59% of input-prompt tokens during generation and 11% across all layers with only a very small performance drop.
On video benchmarks, up to 65% of prompt tokens can be removed without affecting performance.

papers.abstract: Industrial anomaly inspection requires not only accurate anomaly discrimination but also trustworthy explanations for operators, while satisfying the strict latency constraints of online inspection. Existing methods, however, typically apply a fixed computational path to all samples, making it difficult to strike a good balance among detection accuracy, inference efficiency, and interpretability. To address this issue, we propose UACR, an uncertainty-aware collaborative routing framework for explainable industrial anomaly inspection. UACR aims to deliver reliable anomaly decisions together with operator-facing explanations under the online inspection budget, while adaptively allocating computation so that ambiguous cases receive deeper scrutiny. The framework consists of two stages. Stage I, Offline Training and Routing Hyperparameter Search, learns the anomaly inspection modules and calibrates the uncertainty estimator that drives routing. Stage II, Uncertainty-Aware Adaptive Routing, collaboratively dispatches each input across inspection paths according to its estimated uncertainty. Experimental results on multiple public datasets show that UACR achieves over 5.16% improvement in accuracy compared to the baseline method, while reducing latency by over 31.5%. It also enhances the interpretability of industrial detection by over 15%.
authors: Yiwei Li, Qiyang Chen, Zheming Yang
bullets: Targets the trade-off among anomaly detection accuracy, online inference efficiency, and trustworthy operator-facing explanations.
Uses uncertainty estimation to allocate deeper computation to ambiguous samples while avoiding unnecessary processing for easier cases.
Operates in two stages: offline module training and routing calibration, followed by uncertainty-aware adaptive routing at inference.
Experiments on multiple public datasets report over 5.16% higher accuracy, over 31.5% lower latency, and over 15% improved interpretability than a baseline.

papers.abstract: Decoding with large language models at small batch sizes is limited by memory bandwidth, so the bits stored per weight largely set its cost. Group-wise integer quantization stores every weight of a group at the same precision, although the input channels of a group differ in sensitivity. We present BITSHARE, a codebook-free weight format that keeps the integer grid and the dequantizer of group-wise quantization but varies precision within each group. Sensitivity-aware binning places the channels of each group into three bins at fixed positions, and static bit sharing with optimal bit-value allocation lets the less sensitive weights share their lower bits, each stored once per group or once per pair of weights. A sharing-aware version of GPTQ chooses every stored value, with no fine-tuning and no codebook. BITSHARE has two modes. BITSHARE-U gives every group the same layout, so its decoder routes bits by fixed wiring, while BITSHARE-N chooses a layout per group within the same bit budget. With calibration on the Pile and at the same storage, both modes have lower perplexity than GPTQ at 3 and 2 bits on WikiText-2 and C4. At 2 bits across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, BITSHARE-N lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by up to 70% against SliM-LLM and up to 35% against GPTAQ. At the 2-bit perplexity of SliM-LLM, BITSHARE-U stores 13.6-19.4% fewer bits per weight, cutting DRAM weight traffic by the same fraction. A verified hardware decoder implementation synthesized in SkyWater 130 nm reconstructs BITSHARE weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.
authors: Qiuyu Ren, Sudipta Paria, Aritra Dasgupta, Swarup Bhunia
bullets: Targets memory-bandwidth bottlenecks in small-batch LLM decoding, where bits per weight determine weight traffic.
Bins channels by sensitivity and applies variable precision within each quantization group, without codebooks or fine-tuning.
BITSHARE-U uses a fixed layout for simple decoding; BITSHARE-N selects layouts per group under the same bit budget.
At 2–3 bits, both modes achieve lower WikiText-2 and C4 perplexity than GPTQ at matched storage; BITSHARE-N also outperforms reported SliM-LLM and GPTAQ baselines.
A verified SkyWater 130 nm decoder reconstructs weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.

papers.abstract: Memory-efficient Muon methods aim to reduce storage overhead while preserving strong performance, yet existing approaches compromise either convergence guarantees or practical efficiency. In this paper, we focus on subspace optimization for Muon, where the choice of subspace determines the gradient information retained for updating. To preserve dominant information while providing the coverage needed for stochastic convergence guarantees, we construct a principal-random subspace that combines leading singular directions of the stochastic gradient with random directions sampled from their orthogonal complement. Under a fixed rank budget, there is a trade-off between principal exploitation and complementary coverage, making rank allocation important for practical optimization. Our key observation is that the preferred balance shifts from principal-heavy early in training to random-heavy later. Motivated by this shift, we propose \dram, a memory-efficient Muon optimizer that reallocates principal and random ranks across stages while maintaining momentum and performing matrix-sign normalization entirely in the subspace. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees for general rank-allocation schedules with nondecreasing coverage factors, obtaining rates of $O(T^{-1/4})$ in the stochastic setting and $O(T^{-1/2})$ in the deterministic setting, with fixed allocation as a special case. Using a simple linear reallocation schedule, \dram achieves the best low-memory performance across three pre-training scales and nine fine-tuning settings.
authors: Haomin Bai, Dingzhi Yu, Xuling Zhao, Sifan Yang, Yibo Wang, Lijun Zhang
bullets: Targets the trade-off between preserving dominant gradient information and maintaining stochastic convergence coverage under a fixed rank budget.
Builds a principal-random subspace from leading stochastic-gradient singular directions plus random orthogonal-complement directions.
Reallocates principal and random ranks from principal-heavy early training to random-heavy later training, while keeping momentum and matrix-sign normalization in the subspace.
Proves convergence rates of O(T^-1/4) for stochastic optimization and O(T^-1/2) for deterministic optimization under general allocation schedules.
A simple linear schedule achieves the best low-memory performance across three pre-training scales and nine fine-tuning settings reported in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the memory demands of the key-value (KV) cache, whose size scales linearly with context length. Dynamic sparse attention reduces this bottleneck by fetching and attending only to a critical subset of tokens. The dominant primitive in dynamic sparse attention research and deployment is fixed-budget top-$k$ selection, which is favored because its deterministic block count aligns with the static memory allocation that systems like vLLM rely on. Top-$k$ uses a fixed budget regardless of how attention mass is distributed across heads, layers, and decode steps, leading to either wasted bandwidth on heads with peaky attention or dropped context on heads with diffuse attention. Top-$p$ (nucleus) selection adapts naturally to this variation but has seen limited adoption in production serving systems due to two system-level challenges: variable block counts that break deterministic block allocation and computationally expensive selection kernels that exceed the cost of attention itself. We present DisSparse, a serving system that integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM end-to-end. DisSparse decouples block selection from the scheduler's critical path, hides selection latency behind layer computation via a two-stream pipeline, and introduces a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel. We further observe intra-block sparsity, the inflation of selection budgets caused by mixing high- and low-importance tokens within fixed-size KV cache blocks, and address it with a token relocation kernel guided by accumulated prefill attention scores. Across long- and medium-context benchmarks on multiple models, DisSparse achieves 1.17x to 1.80x speedup in sparsity analysis (block selection) over state-of-the-art top-$p$ methods with negligible accuracy loss and supports up to 8x larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.
authors: Nurlan Nazaraliyev, Elaheh Sadredini, Nael Abu-Ghazaleh
bullets: Top-$p$ selection adapts computation to attention distributions, avoiding top-$k$’s fixed-budget waste or context loss.
Integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM with scheduler-decoupled block selection and a two-stream pipeline that overlaps selection with layer computation.
Uses a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel to reduce selection cost.
Relocates tokens based on prefill attention scores to reduce intra-block sparsity and inflated selection budgets.
Reports 1.17×–1.80× faster sparsity analysis, negligible accuracy loss, and up to 8× larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.

papers.abstract: Coupling a property-graph database to an external language-model server imposes a three-part socket tax: serialization overhead dwarfing microsecond graph reads, repeated prefill of verbose schemas, and blind decoding divorced from the live catalog and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) engine. We present Shoonya, from-scratch commercially clean (0.0% non-commercial or share-alike data) tri-modal (Python, Rust, OpenCypher) small language models (16.8M to 1.07B parameters) co-designed with shoonya-infer, a zero-dependency pure-Rust runtime embedded inside the samyama-graph-enterprise address space. Direct GraphStore references unlock three database-native primitives: (1) an epoch-invalidated SchemaPrefixCache over a copy-on-write PagedKvArena accelerating warm CPU time-to-first-token by 4.91x--13.68x with O(1) DDL invalidation; (2) a 36 us columnar catalog and source-span logit mask enforcing valid ontology identifiers and verbatim spans; and (3) a sub-65 us read-only MVCC gate serving Tier-0 queries inside 389.8 MiB INT8 RSS (59.8--67.9 tok/s) with 0.0% hallucination leak. Rank-factorized tied embeddings (-74.5% vocabulary weights), atomic indentation tokens (0/421 indentation errors), 4:1 grouped-query attention with 2:1 cross-layer KV sharing (-93.75% INT8 KV memory), Warmup-Stable-Decay training, KnOTS SVD merging, Step-GRPO, and Rust Jacobi SVD governance keep 100% of layers heavy-tailed ($\alpha \in [1.88, 2.20]$). Finally, we synthesize nine lessons across v0.1--v1.0, resolving a Reverse-Token-Density Distillation Trap via teacher scaling and zero-VRAM Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation (AdvKD), recovering +13.61 MBPP points (33.07%) while reaching 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool planning.
bullets: Targets serialization cost, repeated schema prefill, and decoding that is unaware of live catalogs and MVCC.
Uses an in-process Rust runtime with Python, Rust, and OpenCypher models ranging from 16.8M to 1.07B parameters.
Introduces epoch-invalidated schema KV caching, catalog/source-span logit masking, and an MVCC gate for read-only queries.
Reports 4.91–13.68× faster warm CPU time-to-first-token, 0.0% hallucination leak, and 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool-planning tasks.
Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation recovers 13.61 MBPP points while operating without VRAM for the distillation verifier.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization provides a computationally efficient approach to fine-tuning large language models (LLMs), but conventional methods typically rely on isotropic perturbations that ignore the anisotropic structure of neural-network parameter spaces. We introduce Preconditioned Activation-Metric Subspace (PAMS), a ZO optimization framework that uses forward-pass activation statistics to construct structured, layer-wise perturbation geometries without computing gradients or forming dense curvature matrices. PAMS tracks a low-rank approximation of the dominant activation subspace and its associated spectrum online, and uses the spectrum to softly reweight perturbation variance while preserving exploration in directions outside the retained subspace. A trace normalization separates the perturbation geometry from its overall scale, enabling consistent perturbation magnitudes across layers. We show theoretically that the resulting perturbation covariance induces right-side preconditioning of the gradient of the corresponding Gaussian-smoothed objective. We further characterize the estimator's smoothing bias and second moment and derive a nonconvex convergence guarantee that captures the effects of the perturbation geometry and smoothing radius. The proposed low-rank tracking procedure requires $\mathcal{O}(n_l r)$ persistent memory for a layer with input dimension nl and retained rank r, avoiding the $\mathcal{O}(n_l^2)$ memory required by a dense activation covariance. Experiments on transformer-based language-model fine-tuning tasks across GLUE and SuperGLUE demonstrate that PAMS improves the effectiveness and stability of zeroth-order optimization while retaining its gradient-free and objective-evaluation-based advantages.
authors: Pradeep Kumar Ragu Chanthar, Saksham Sahai Srivastava, Jaewoo Lee
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of isotropic perturbations, which ignore anisotropic parameter structure.
Uses forward-pass activation statistics to track dominant layer-wise subspaces and softly reweight perturbation variance.
Applies trace normalization to maintain consistent perturbation scales across layers while preserving exploration outside the tracked subspace.
Provides theoretical analyses of preconditioning, smoothing bias, estimator variance, and nonconvex convergence.
Experiments on GLUE and SuperGLUE transformer fine-tuning tasks report improved zeroth-order effectiveness and stability while retaining gradient-free optimization.

papers.tldr: PAMS improves zeroth-order LLM fine-tuning by using activation-informed, low-rank perturbation geometries instead of isotropic noise, without gradients or dense curvature matrices.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion streams a video chunk by chunk, but large AR models are too slow for real-time use. We ask where in an AR rollout a large model is actually needed. Pairing Krea-Realtime-14B with Self-Forcing-1.3B, which share their latent space and denoising schedule, we find that the order of the two models matters: when the 14B model generates only the first chunk and the 1.3B model continues, the rollout keeps 95\% of the 14B model's semantic advantage, whereas the reverse allocation keeps 16\% at about ten times the cost. The large model decides what the video shows; the small model only has to carry it forward. We turn this into BigSmall, a training-free planner--renderer sampler. The 14B model plans the opening chunk and sketches the chunks in which content changes, which preserves motion, and the 1.3B model renders the rest; a faster variant, BigSmall, plans only the opening chunk. A cross-model KV cache that is approximate, windowed and lazy lets the planner leave and re-enter the rollout at low cost. On VBench, BigSmall is $3.02\times$ faster than the 14B model at an unchanged semantic score and motion, and $1.55\times$ faster than SDVG, which lets the small model draft first; BigSmall reaches $3.77\times$ at the same semantic score, trading away 10\% of the motion. On minute-long videos (LoCoT2V-Bench), where the 14B model degrades when it reads its own long history, BigSmall is $3.14\times$ faster than the 14B model and scores higher ($+1.78$).`
bullets: Large-model computation is most valuable at the rollout’s beginning and when video content changes; reversing the model order largely loses the semantic benefit.
BigSmall is a training-free planner–renderer sampler: the 14B model plans the opening and selected transition chunks, while the 1.3B model renders the rest.
An approximate, windowed, lazy cross-model KV cache enables the large planner to leave and re-enter generation efficiently.
On VBench, BigSmall is 3.02× faster than the 14B model with unchanged semantic score and motion; a faster variant reaches 3.77× speedup with a 10% motion trade-off.
On minute-long videos, BigSmall is 3.14× faster and scores 1.78 points higher than the 14B model.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of BIGSMALL on a real rollout (“a teddy bear and a frisbee”). Top: a zero-cost change score decides, chunk by chunk, whether the 14B planner is called. The planner generates the plan chunk c0 with all four denoising steps and only the first step t1 of each sketch chunk; the 1.3B renderer takes all other steps (squares: denoising steps t1–t4; orange: 14B, blue: 1.3B). Bottom: each model reads its own KV cache; dashed arrows write a finished chunk into a cache, solid arrows read from it. The renderer’s cache is exact: every chunk is written. The planner’s cache is windowed: a planner call reads only the sink c0 and the previous chunk. It is lazy: that previous chunk is written only when the planner needs it (c1 when c2 is sketched, c4 when c5 is sketched), and other chunks are never written. It is approximate: a chunk is re-encoded sparsely, only its moving tokens, while the others copy K/V from the previous frame with re-rotated RoPE; it is re-encoded densely if the chunk before it was never written, as for c4. Right: inside sketch chunk c5, the planner’s first step from noise already fixes the layout (x̂(1) 0 ); it is re-noised to σ2, keeping 6% of the signal, and the renderer completes the chunk from its own cache.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison with large–small cooperation and acceleration baselines (VBench, seed 0, same noise for all methods; frames at t = 0, 2.5 and 5 s). BIGSMALL produces videos of the same quality as SDVG, Speculative Forcing and SRDiffusion (two 14B steps per chunk) while running at 10.0 instead of 4.6–6.5 FPS. Prompts drawn at random from the evaluation set and selected for diverse content and motion.

Figure 1. Semantic score versus throughput on VBench (946 prompts, 5 seeds). BIGSMALL is 3.02× faster than KreaRealtime-14B at the same semantic score, and BIGSMALL-Fast, which calls the 14B model only for the first chunk, is 3.77× faster, also at the same semantic score. Fewer 14B steps lose semantics quickly; single-model accelerators and large–small cooperation stay at or below 6.5 FPS. ∆Semantic: paired difference to the 14B model; FPS: DiT throughput for 81-frame videos on one GPU (Tab. 1).

Figure 6. The 14B model fades over a minute. Mean frame saturation over time on LoCoT2V-Bench. The 1.3B model and BIGSMALL do not fade; Forcing-KV, the 14B model attending to a few recent frames, fades much less than the 14B model.

Figure 2. Who begins decides. Noise fixed; only the model allocation changes. Each row is an allocation (peach: 14B, blue: 1.3B). (a) Within one chunk, over denoising steps t1–t4: LPIPS to the 14B video (24 prompts). (b) Along the video, over chunks c0–c6 (a split c0: 14B on its first one or three steps): semantic gap recovered on VBench; cost = share of the 14B model’s additional computation.

Figure 5. (a) Motion on the VBench dynamic-degree prompts (mean RAFT peak flow, relative to the 14B model). BIGSMALLFast keeps the semantics but loses motion; the sketches of BIGSMALL restore it. (b) Gain of BIGSMALL over the 14B model on LoCoT2V-Bench by thirds of the video length: the longer the video, the larger the gain.

Table 1. Standard VBench (946 extended prompts, five seeds). Time: DiT time per video. ∆Sem: paired semantic difference to the 14B model (95% CI) on the videos both methods share (same prompt and seed), so it can differ slightly from the difference of the Semantic columns, which use all videos. †Plan chunk only: 14B on chunk 0, 1.3B on all others.
Table 3. Other renderers (VBench, Krea-14B planner, thresholds not re-calibrated). Gap: semantic gap to the 14B model closed relative to the renderer alone.

Table 2. Minute-long generation on LoCoT2V-Bench. Avg: official mean of the five dimensions; ∆Avg: paired difference to the 14B model (95% CI). Speed-up from DiT time; SDVG spends another 49 s per video decoding and scoring drafts.
Table 4. Ablations (VBench, seed 0, 944 videos). ∗The 869 prompts of Tab. 3. §A 14B step 1 on every chunk.

papers.selection_reason: Semantic-aware computation allocation between large and small autoregressive video models with a cross-model KV cache; relevant to video generation and inference efficiency.
papers.title: Plan Big, Paint Small: Semantic-Aware Computation Allocation for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.tldr: BigSmall accelerates autoregressive video generation by using a large model to plan key content and a small model to render the remaining chunks, preserving semantics and motion at substantially lower cost.

papers.abstract: Under structured outputs (JSON schemas, regexes, tool calls), speculative drafters do not see the grammar constraint and repeatedly propose invalid keys, delimiters, and indentation, while the grammar engine already knows which tokens must come next. We present Grammar-as-a-Draft (GaaD), which treats the grammar as a second drafter. Before each verify step, the scheduler merges the drafter's proposal with grammar-forced tokens into one draft row: matching tokens stay as GRAMMAR, the proposal is cut where it leaves the forced path, and forced tokens fill the rest of a row wider than the drafter's proposal. The verify step accepts GRAMMAR drafts without computing their logits, composing with any drafter with no new kernels or compilation on the critical path. Because grammars fix text rather than tokens, committing canonical forced tokens changes the output distribution relative to grammar-masked target decoding. We implement GaaD in vllm-torchtpu and an independent Rust serving runtime, evaluating on TPU v7x with MTP, DFlash, and n-gram drafters on a JSON character-profile benchmark. GaaD raises average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43 (MTP, Qwen3.5-0.8B), 1.99 to 5.31 (MTP, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), 1.57 to 4.13 (DFlash, Qwen3-4B), and 1.30 to 3.64 (n-gram, Qwen3-4B), decoding 2.66-2.81x faster at batch size 1 and 1.14-1.70x at batch size 64. In Rust, MTP+GaaD is 2.23x faster on Qwen3.5-0.8B, 2.02x on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8, and 1.22x at 128 concurrent requests. Under mixed traffic (25-50% structured), GaaD finishes the workload 1.03-1.23x sooner (structured requests 2.2-3.2x sooner) while plain-text TPOT rises 7-42%. We also show grammar-masked greedy decoding can pick non-canonical tokenizations, so GaaD can yield different valid outputs that an fp32 reference finds equally likely.
bullets: Targets wasted speculative proposals for invalid JSON keys, delimiters, indentation, and other grammar-disallowed tokens.
Merges drafter proposals with grammar-forced tokens; forced-token drafts are verified without computing target logits and require no new critical-path kernels or compilation.
Works with MTP, DFlash, and n-gram drafters across TPU and Rust serving implementations.
Raises average acceptance length roughly 2.5–2.7× and delivers up to 2.81× speedup at batch size 1 and 1.70× at batch size 64 in the reported benchmark.

Canonical forced-token choices can change outputs relative to grammar-masked decoding, producing different but valid and equally likely results; mixed traffic also incurs a plain-text latency increase.

figures.caption: Figure 3: GaaD in the engine. The scheduler plans each row from the grammar state and the drafter’s proposal before the step is dispatched; the worker runs the verify step on token buckets compiled at start-up and accepts G slots.

Figure 2: Combining the grammar’s draft with a model drafter’s (Qwen tokenization). An illustration: the drafter proposes five tokens into a row of K=7, whereas the evaluated configurations use K=8 with KM =3 for MTP and KM =7 for DFlash and n-gram. Model tokens at free positions are kept as M, those that agree with a forced token as G; the model draft stops where the two disagree, and forced tokens continue from there.
Figure 4: Speedup of GaaD (K=8) over the best configuration of the drafter alone at each point, in vllm-torchtpu.

Figure 1: Forced tokens as a separate prefill need a new shape per jump length and compete with drafts for the same positions. GaaD writes them into the draft row, which the verify step already handles.

Best vs. best: over the drafter alone with K = KM and the faster scheduling at each point. Same K=8: over MTP alone with K=8 (asynchronous). K=KM : GaaD with K = KM over the best-vs.-best reference. B=4 was measured for two of the four configurations.

Table 2: The three factors of the best-vs.-best speedup of Table 1: the reference’s output tokens over GaaD’s (tokens), GaaD’s τ over the reference’s (τ), and the reference’s wall time per request step over GaaD’s (per step). Their product is the speedup. Reference: the scheduling of the faster drafter-alone configuration.

Table 5: Mixed traffic in vllm-torchtpu (Qwen3.5-0.8B, MTP, 256 requests, a share of them under the regular expression and the rest unconstrained). Speedup: MTP alone’s wall time (K=3, asynchronous) over GaaD’s (K=8, KM =3), with asynchronous scheduling off for the whole engine (engine sync, the configuration of Table 1) or synchronous only for batches with a GaaD request (per batch). Plain TPOT : time per output token of the unconstrained requests, which emit the same tokens in every arm. Structured request: mean time of a structured request, its TPOT times its mean output length. GaaD columns are per batch.
Table 4: Outputs identical, token for token, to the drafter alone with the same scheduling, and output tokens of each (64 requests).
Table 3: Rust runtime: speedup of MTP + GaaD over MTP alone (MTP alone’s wall time over MTP + GaaD’s, for the same 128 requests) at each concurrency.

Table 6: Host time GaaD spends planning rows per engine step (MTP + GaaD on Qwen3.5-0.8B, K=8, KM =3, 256 requests, single-process engine), and its share of the engine step’s wall time, which includes prefill and the single-process engine’s synchronous overhead.

papers.selection_reason: Grammar-as-a-Draft improves speculative decoding throughput for structured outputs, directly reducing inference latency.
papers.title: Grammar-as-a-Draft: More Tokens per Speculative Decoding Step on Grammar-Constrained Structured Outputs
papers.tldr: Grammar-as-a-Draft accelerates grammar-constrained structured decoding by combining speculative drafts with grammar-forced tokens, substantially increasing accepted tokens per step and reducing latency.

papers.abstract: Can changing which matrices receive 2, 4, or 8 bits improve a small language model without increasing its parameter storage? I compare two parent-selection rules in the same genetic algorithm: a binary-tournament variant and an Alternis-inspired rule. A separate baseline samples repaired random allocations without crossover or mutation. All three use the same MLX affine quantizer, byte ceiling, initialization and candidate allowance within each study. An exploratory study on Qwen3.5-2B evaluates 90 allocations per run. The main study on Qwen3-1.7B evaluates 500 distinct allocations per run over 10 paired seeds. Against uniform four-bit, tournament reduces held-out next-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) by 0.0616 on AG News and 0.0152 on IMDb on average, improving all 10 seeds on each corpus at identical parameter storage. Alternis improves five seeds and ties five on AG News; on IMDb its mean gain is near zero. Random returns uniform four-bit in every seed. The tournament representative answers 156 of 400 ARC-Challenge questions correctly versus 163 for uniform; no accuracy gain is demonstrated on this subset. The result favors this tournament variant for text prediction under the tested protocol, not for compression ratio or task accuracy.
bullets: The study asks whether assigning 2, 4, and 8 bits to different matrices can improve small language models without increasing parameter storage.
It compares binary-tournament and Alternis-inspired selection within the same genetic algorithm against repaired random allocation, using a shared MLX affine quantizer and byte ceiling.
On Qwen3-1.7B, tournament selection reduced mean NLL by 0.0616 on AG News and 0.0152 on IMDb across 10 paired seeds, improving every seed.
Alternis helped on AG News but showed near-zero mean gain on IMDb; random allocation matched uniform 4-bit in every seed.
The tournament representative scored lower than uniform 4-bit on the tested ARC-Challenge subset, so benefits are limited to the evaluated text-prediction setting.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Experimental pipeline. Read left to right. The two genetic arms change the parent selector; random uses fresh repaired proposals without crossover or mutation. The model, quantizer, byte ceiling, data and evaluation protocol are shared.

Figure 3. Corrected fresh held-out NLL reduction at equal parameter bytes. Positive values favor the searched allocation; zero is a tie. Bars are means across 10 paired seeds and whiskers are paired 95% t intervals. Panel x-axis scales differ; compare the labeled NLL units, not bar lengths across panels.
Figure 4. V3 search dynamics across 30 generations. Lower best-search NLL is better. Higher mean pairwise Hamming distance means that more matrix bit assignments differ within the population.

Figure 2. V2 Qwen3.5-2B storage and metrics. Lower held-out NLL is better; higher ARC-Easy accuracy is better. U3/U4/U6/U8 are uniform bit-widths, FP is higher precision, Sens. is sensitivity allocation, and Alt.+GPTQ is the combined allocation-plus-GPTQ control.
Table 6. Closest automated-allocation studies. Protocols, models, and quantizers differ; the table maps methodological roles rather than claiming leaderboard comparability.
Table 3. Frozen protocols. V2 and V3 differ in model, data, population, allowance, sequence length, and task; their numeric outcomes must not be pooled or treated as a causal depth ablation.

papers.selection_reason: Mixed-precision quantization of language models directly targets memory and compute efficiency, fitting the Efficient AI parent topic.
papers.title: Selection Policies for Equal-Byte Mixed-Precision Quantization of Small Language Models
papers.tldr: A genetic algorithm using binary-tournament parent selection improves held-out language-model NLL over uniform 4-bit quantization at the same storage, but does not improve ARC-Challenge accuracy.

papers.abstract: Scientific information extraction (IE) is a fundamental component of AI for Science, transforming experimental knowledge embedded in scientific literature into structured and traceable data for evidence synthesis, scientific database construction, and data-driven discovery. However, critical experimental details are often distributed across text, tables, figures, captions, and surrounding discussion, making them difficult to recover using conventional text-only extraction. Existing LLM-based and multimodal RAG pipelines typically rely on full-document context or coarse page-level retrieval, introducing substantial irrelevant evidence and high textual and visual token costs. We propose GERF, a Graph-based Evidence Retrieval Framework for token-efficient, schema-guided multimodal scientific IE. GERF represents each article as a heterogeneous evidence graph that connects schema fields, text chunks, figures, and figure-derived content through semantic and structural relations. Using schema fields as retrieval anchors, GERF combines direct semantic retrieval, Random Walk with Restart, and null-aware evidence expansion to construct compact, field-specific multimodal evidence packages. Visual interpretation is applied only to graph-selected figures, avoiding indiscriminate processing of the entire document. We evaluate GERF from two complementary perspectives: evidence retrieval quality and pipeline-level input-token consumption. On the expert-annotated SOFC-Exp corpus, GERF retrieves gold-supported evidence for 94.55% of the evaluated field instances, providing broad field-level evidence coverage for downstream extraction. In the token comparison, GERF reduces average input-token usage by 73.40% relative to full-context processing and uses fewer tokens than the evaluated page-level pipelines.
authors: Yiyu Qian (Cornell University), Xing Wu (Shanghai University)
bullets: Targets experimental details distributed across text, tables, figures, captions, and discussion—beyond the reach of text-only extraction.
Builds a heterogeneous graph linking schema fields, text chunks, figures, and figure-derived content.
Combines semantic retrieval, Random Walk with Restart, and null-aware evidence expansion to assemble multimodal evidence packages.
Applies visual interpretation only to graph-selected figures rather than the entire document.
On the SOFC-Exp corpus, retrieves gold-supported evidence for 94.55% of evaluated field instances and reduces average input tokens by 73.40% versus full-context processing.
