Table 2: Retrieval-quality ablation on SOFC-Exp.
Table 3: Average input-token composition per paper on SOFC-Exp.

papers.selection_reason: Token-efficient multimodal evidence retrieval that reduces input-token consumption, directly relevant to efficient AI and token-selection methods.
papers.title: GERF: A Token-Efficient Multimodal Retrieval Framework for Schema-Guided Scientific Information Extraction
papers.tldr: GERF uses a schema-guided evidence graph to retrieve compact, field-specific text and visual evidence for scientific information extraction while substantially reducing input-token use.

papers.abstract: Standard autoregressive large language models attend to the growing history of generated tokens, making the key-value (KV) cache a central memory and throughput bottleneck in long-chain reasoning and multi-branch sampling. Yet an important class of reasoning problems is naturally first-order Markovian: the next step depends on a sufficient representation of the current state, rather than on the raw sequence of all earlier steps. We develop a unified design paradigm for Markovian-reasoning specialized large language models. At the cache level, the Markovian state interface transforms history-dependent KV storage into constant-size state transfer with respect to the number of reasoning steps. At the learning level, we reformulate long-chain prediction as independently trainable one-step transition objectives, with explicit state bottlenecks, distillation, invariance, and drift-consistency losses. At the architectural level, we introduce a dual-loop Transformer: an outer loop advances the reasoning state, while an inner recurrent-depth loop allocates adaptive computation to each transition through shared weights and explicit memory tokens or recurrent matrix states. We connect this architecture to a three-region cache, step-relative positions, truncated backpropagation, branch-aware checkpoints, and a transition-centric evaluation protocol. The organizing principle is simple: the optimal reasoning system need not remember everything; it must carry forward exactly what the future needs. This principle opens a path toward specialized reasoning engines whose memory footprint is decoupled from reasoning-chain length.
authors: Haibin Tong, Liangliang Xin, Yamei Zhu, Jiang Yu
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and throughput bottlenecks in long-chain reasoning and multi-branch sampling.
Uses explicit state bottlenecks and independently trainable one-step transition objectives with distillation, invariance, and drift-consistency losses.
Introduces a dual-loop Transformer: an outer loop advances states, while an inner recurrent loop adaptively computes each transition with shared weights.
Integrates three-region caching, step-relative positions, truncated backpropagation, branch-aware checkpoints, and transition-centric evaluation.
Scope is reasoning tasks where the next step depends on a sufficient Markovian state rather than the full history.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Dual-loop Transformer architecture with transition-centric pretraining. The outer loop advances the reduced state (qt,Mt) across reasoning steps and releases step-local KV, while the inner loop repeatedly applies a shared Transformer core for Rt computation iterations. The transition training objectives shape the same shared core to support state evolution and compact cross-step memory.

Figure 1: Structural KV-cache compression for a Markovian reasoning chain. Conventional autoregressive attention retains the entire sequence of previous reasoning steps. In contrast, a Markovian state-rolling interface retains the fixed context Q, the latest sufficient state zt, and the bounded current-step KV workspace, which is released after each transition. With a fixed-size sufficient-state interface and bounded step length, cross-step memory does not grow with the number of completed steps k.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes specialized LLMs for Markovian reasoning using a dual-loop transformer and structural cache compression to decouple memory footprint from reasoning length.
papers.title: Specialized Large Language Models for Markovian Reasoning: Structural Cache Compression, Transition Pretraining, and Dual-Loop Transformers
papers.tldr: A specialized LLM design treats Markovian reasoning as state transitions, reducing KV-cache growth from sequence-dependent storage to constant-size state transfer.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied AI, yet their high inference latency and memory footprint remain major barriers to edge deployment. Existing training-free acceleration techniques, such as visual token pruning and action caching, typically rely on static resource allocation. This mismatch with dynamic robotic interactions not only degrades control performance but also causes severe hardware inefficiencies, including fragmented KV-cache layouts and wasted compute on non-critical regions. To address this, we propose FlowPAC, a locality-aware framework that leverages task-aware optical flow as a shared physical signal to jointly optimize visual and action computation. Specifically, we introduce Direction-Aware Trajectory Propagation (DATP) and Locality-Aware Contiguous Token Selection (LACT) to jointly handle visual token dynamics and enforce spatial locality, reducing memory fragmentation and enabling efficient KV-cache compression. This is complemented by Flow-Conditioned Action-Block Refresh (FCAR) for adaptive action computation based on motion dynamics. Extensive closed-loop evaluations on LIBERO demonstrate that FlowPAC achieves a 2.13$\times$ end-to-end speedup over the dense baseline while essentially maintaining the success rate with 30% visual-token retention. These results validate that aligning computation allocation with both physical dynamics and hardware constraints is essential for efficient VLA deployment on edge systems.
authors: Jintao Cheng, Yipu Zhang, Haozhe Wang, Lin Jiang, Jiang Xu, Wei Zhang
bullets: Targets high latency and memory use that hinder VLA deployment on edge devices.
Combines trajectory-aware token propagation, contiguous spatial token selection, and flow-conditioned action-block refresh.
Aligns computation with both scene motion and hardware locality to reduce wasted compute and KV-cache fragmentation.
Closed-loop LIBERO evaluations report a 2.13× end-to-end speedup over dense inference with 30% visual-token retention and essentially unchanged success rate.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Profiling and overview of FlowPAC. (a) Dense π0.5 profiling exposes two resource imbalances: action denoising dominates runtime (77.6%), while visual tokens dominate the prefix KV state (79.3%). The rightmost profiling panel shows optical-flow magnitude between consecutive observations, normalized within one representative rollout to visualize relative changes across task phases. (b) FlowPAC uses instruction-conditioned optical flow as a shared signal to coordinate where visual tokens are preserved (DATP, LACT) and when action-expert computation is refreshed (FCAR).

Fig. 2. Direction-aware trajectory propagation. DATP advects instructionconditioned semantic relevance along signed optical flow over multiple future horizons and merges them into a future-critical interaction corridor.

Fig. 4. Flow-conditioned action-block refresh. Dual-view task-aware motion is calibrated by the causal episode history and converted into a refresh budget. Refresh steps compute and store attention/FFN residuals, whereas stable steps reuse them while preserving all action-state updates.
Fig. 5. Qualitative comparison of visual token masks.
Fig. 6. Same-budget packing-gather memory accesses and prefixmaterialization latency of Global Top-K and LACT.

papers.selection_reason: Efficient VLA inference via flow-guided visual token pruning and action caching with KV-cache compression, directly relevant to embodied AI and efficient AI.
papers.title: FlowPAC: Flow-Guided Visual Pruning and Action Caching for Efficient VLA Inference
papers.tldr: FlowPAC uses task-aware optical flow to dynamically prune visual tokens and cache actions, achieving faster VLA inference while preserving control performance.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent videos as thousands of visual tokens, creating a large key-value cache whose memory grows with video length. At the same time, small VLMs that fit on limited hardware understand video far worse than large models. Existing compression methods shorten visual tokens into a brief prompt to save memory, yet the small model still processes them through fixed weights and cannot close this capability gap. To address both challenges, we introduce Video-as-Weights (VaW), which compiles a video once without seeing any question into the parametric and token memory of a frozen interpreter VLM. Specifically, a compiler VLM watches the video, and a single weight decoder jointly generates the interpreter's LoRA weights and optional prefix tokens from every compiler layer, enabling both same-model compilation and strong-to-weak transfer across model sizes and depths. Across six video QA benchmarks, a 0.8B interpreter beats full in-context reading by 1.7 points when compiled by itself and by 4.3 points with a 9B compiler, reducing context from up to 8,192 visual tokens to 64 prefix tokens while using 5.5x less memory than the video's key-value cache. Generated weights add 3.9 points over token compression alone, and all-layer decoding outperforms layer-wise generation by 2.9 points. Mechanistic analysis shows that with prefix tokens, the weights mainly alter attention queries and MLP down projections to guide retrieval and store a baseline summary, whereas without tokens, they shift to attention output projections to write video content directly into the residual stream.
authors: Wentao Zhang, Ian Miao, Chen Qu, Bill Bi, Donna Schut, Yuntian Deng, Yale Song
bullets: Addresses video VLMs’ growing key-value memory and the capability gap of small models.
A compiler VLM processes the video once and a decoder generates interpreter LoRA weights plus optional prefix tokens, without seeing questions.
Across six video QA benchmarks, a 0.8B interpreter improved over full in-context reading by 1.7 points alone and 4.3 points with a 9B compiler.
Compression reduces up to 8,192 visual tokens to 64 prefix tokens and uses 5.5× less memory than the video’s key-value cache.
Generated weights add 3.9 points over token compression alone; their roles differ depending on whether prefix tokens are used.

figures.caption: Figure 2. VaW architecture. (a) Video compiler: a frozen vision encoder and LoRA-adapted LLM read the video with K readout tokens, outputting readout states H across all L layers. (b) Weight decoder: N blocks refine learned LoRA and optional prefix queries by cross-attending to H . (c) LoRA & prefix heads: decoder states map to rank-r updates ∆W = BA and optional prefix tokens. (d) Interpreter: the frozen model applies ∆W across layers and reads any prefix tokens before the query. Panels (a)–(c) never see the query, so compilation runs once per video; flame marks trained parts and snowflake marks frozen parts.

Figure 4. Scaling VaW (average accuracy over the six benchmarks). (a) Compilers of different sizes writing for the same 0.8B interpreter, against that interpreter reading the full video in context. (b) Interpreters of different sizes, with VaW reading 64 tokens and in-context reading up to 8,192. Labels give the gap. (c) Storage of a compiled video as the LoRA rank r varies (top axis), with P = 64 prefix tokens unless noted. Gray marks read the video in context and keep its KV cache (112.4 MB, Section E), and the shaded region beats in-context reading with less memory.

papers.abstract: Query-based 4D reconstruction models such as D4RT encode a video once into a global scene representation and obtain outputs by decoding independent point queries. However, inference is often influenced by dense outputs and long videos. Although D4RT separates encoding from decoding, a dense output still requires one decoder query for every pixel of every frame, and a long video is still encoded as many overlapping segments. In this work, we analyze the inference cost of D4RT and show that a large part of it is redundant. In particular, we find that the later decoder blocks attend to a small set of tokens shared by all queries. Based on these findings, we propose FastD4RT, a training-free framework that accelerates D4RT. By exploiting the smoothness of the outputs over time and across pixels, FastD4RT encodes and decodes only at sparse anchors and recovers the remaining outputs via interpolation. It decodes the remaining queries against a shared token set selected once per segment. We further characterize the errors introduced by both components. Experimental results show that FastD4RT accelerates D4RT by about 5 times on average across all its tasks with competitive accuracy, and further improves accuracy on long videos. Our code is available at https://github.com/Lycheemeng/fastd4rt.
authors: Meng Bi, Yili Jin, Kaiyuan Hu, Xize Duan, Jiaxin Huang, Hong Huang, Xue Liu
bullets: Targets redundant computation from dense pixel-frame queries and overlapping long-video segments in D4RT.
Uses sparse spatial-temporal anchors and interpolation to recover remaining outputs.
Decodes queries against a shared token set selected once per video segment.
Analyzes the errors introduced by sparse interpolation and shared-token decoding.
Reports competitive accuracy across D4RT tasks and improved accuracy on long videos.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of FastD4RT. Given a video, FastD4RT encodes only sparse anchor frames, so that a long video is split into fewer segments. For each segment, a small set of calibration queries selects a shared token set once. Each task then issues queries only at sparse anchors, which attend to all tokens in the early decoder blocks and only to the shared tokens in the later blocks. Finally, the remaining outputs are recovered by interpolation, and adjacent segments are aligned.

papers.abstract: Repeatedly accessing the full key--value (KV) cache is a major bottleneck in long-context language model decoding. We find that small query-specific subsets can accurately approximate full attention, yet their union covers nearly the entire cache, motivating query-adaptive access for the KV cache. A natural approach is to split the KV cache into clusters, using compact representatives for clusters that incur negligible error while expanding the rest to their original KV entries. We derive a selection criterion from an upper bound on attention-output error, which reveals two complementary factors governing the error: importance measures the impact of a cluster, while distortion measures how faithfully the cluster can be represented. Based on this criterion, we propose RefineKV, a decoding-time query-adaptive KV compression method. Experiments on two models and three benchmarks demonstrate that RefineKV retains near-full-attention quality while achieving up to 7.6x speedup in the attention phase and 1.66x faster decoding, establishing a new quality-latency Pareto frontier.
authors: Kewei Lian, Jiayi Zhai, Anji Liu
bullets: Full KV-cache access is a major long-context decoding bottleneck, and query-specific relevant subsets can be much smaller than the full cache.
The method clusters KV entries and represents low-error clusters with compact summaries while expanding higher-error clusters to their original entries.
An attention-output error bound guides selection using two factors: cluster importance and representation distortion.
Across two models and three benchmarks, RefineKV achieves up to 7.6× attention-phase speedup and 1.66× faster decoding while retaining near-full-attention quality.
The approach targets decoding-time KV compression and its reported evaluation covers the stated models and benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Quality-latency trade-off of REFINEKV and existing KV-cache compression baselines. Experiments are evaluated across two models (Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2.5) on three longcontext benchmarks (LongBench, RULER, and HELMET), with results averaged across all tasks. We present a conservative threshold τ = 0.01, which matches full attention performance across all settings while achieving up to 1.56× decode speedup as measured by Time Per Output Token (TPOT). Our method extends the quality–latency Pareto frontier.

Figure 3: REFINEKV Pipeline. Prefill phase: The KV cache is partitioned into contiguous clusters, and a representative key-value pair together with auxiliary metadata is computed for each cluster. Decode phase: Each query qt uses the cached summaries to calculate risk score RC . Clusters with RC > τ are expanded, while clusters with RC ≤ τ retain only their representatives. The resulting mixed KV sequence is used to compute the output ot. The color depth of each block indicates attention score.

Figure 2: Left: Cluster selection is jointly determined by importance and distortion. Each point represents a cluster positioned by its global importance p̂C and local distortion δboundC . Background color encodes the risk score RC , with the dashed line denoting the decision boundary at RC = τ . The tilted boundary captures their trade-off: important clusters tolerate only small local distortion, whereas low-importance clusters can tolerate larger distortion. Point colors indicate the error incurred on approximating cluster. Three cases show the within-cluster attention-score patterns. Right: Risk score RC strongly correlated with approximation error. These figures illustrate the correlation between Risk Score and cluster approximation error ∥oC − ôC∥2, where oC and ôC denote original output and approximate output for cluster C.

Figure 1: Left: Each query needs only a small KV subset, but together these subsets cover nearly the entire cache. For each query, we select the highest-weight KV entries needed to retain p% of its total attention weight. The figure compares sizes of these per-query subsets and their union across queries, alongside the resulting attention output error. At roughly 10% output error, each query needs only a small subset of the cache, yet their union covers most KV entries. Right: Queryadaptive methods surpass query-independent methods. Oracle query-adaptive top-k attention achieves a markedly better perplexity–access trade-off than representative eviction baselines. Our method recovers a substantial portion of this advantage without oracle access.

papers.abstract: Interactive long-video generation lets users build a story through successive prompts and reuse earlier characters and settings under new instructions. Existing memory methods retain past content, yet they often fail at precise selective recall, returning the wrong appearance of a person, mixing different people, or keeping an unrequested background. Based on our analysis of memory form and retrieval, we introduce an object-aware key--value (KV) memory framework for a frozen autoregressive diffusion generator. It keeps the original KV of tracked object regions, selects background KV outside them by attention-scores, and links each memory with a readable record of its source scene and observed appearance. An LLM selects the requested records, and a memory integrator supplies their KV for generation under the current prompt. We also introduce a six-scene evaluation that tests selective attribute modification, time-specific appearance recall, and multi-object composition, in which each person's requested past appearance changes across requests. Experiments show that our framework more reliably preserves each person's identity while reproducing their requested past appearance than existing memory methods, under both explicit scene references and natural-language cues.
authors: Hyunwook Kang, Junoh Park, Hyunggyu Lim, Taesup Kim
bullets: Targets failures in existing memory methods, including wrong appearances, identity mixing, and unrequested background retention.
Stores tracked-object KV features, selectively retains background KV using attention scores, and attaches readable scene/appearance records.
Uses an LLM to select requested memories, then integrates their KV into a frozen autoregressive diffusion generator.
Introduces a six-scene evaluation covering selective attribute edits, time-specific appearance recall, and multi-object composition.
More reliably preserves identities and requested past appearances under explicit references and natural-language cues than existing memory methods.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon image animation must keep the scene fixed while natural material (e.g., water, smoke, or fire) continues to move. Autoregressive video generators read recent frames for temporal continuity, but this history also carries accumulated appearance errors, and sparsifying it disrupts motion. We introduce SceneTether, a training-free attention-read policy that keeps where attention reads recent memory but changes what appearance that memory returns. SceneTether keeps every key of the newest latent, blends its low-activity values toward co-located source-image values, and leaves high-activity values untouched so motion can evolve; an activity map estimated from the first generated latents and then frozen decides where to blend. It adds no denoising evaluations and leaves the cache-update rule unchanged. On a Causal Forcing++ generator, SceneTether raises source-support PSNR by 5.15 dB over its framewise Echo host across two seeds with 1.5x its late activity, and by 7.31 dB over spatial Echo-Forcing on a preselected four-minute subset. At equal recent-memory coverage, value anchoring alone adds 8.14 dB. A post-hoc pixel composite with the same map matches static fidelity but retains nearly twice the moving-region color drift, and viewers in a small blinded study preferred SceneTether for its natural scene and motion preservation. Project page: https://minar09.github.io/scenetether/
authors: Matiur Rahman Minar, Seunghun Oh, Ganghyeon Jeong, Unsang Park
bullets: Targets accumulated appearance drift in static scene regions without disrupting evolving materials such as water, smoke, or fire.
Uses a training-free attention-read policy: retains the newest latent’s keys, blends low-activity values with co-located source-image values, and leaves active values unchanged.
Freezes an activity map estimated from early generated latents; adds no denoising evaluations and does not alter cache updates.
Improves source-support PSNR over framewise and spatial Echo baselines, with additional gains from value anchoring alone.
A small blinded study favored SceneTether for preserving natural scene appearance and motion; evaluation covers two seeds and a preselected four-minute subset.

papers.abstract: 3D vision-language models (3D VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning. However, their reliance on multi-view inputs produces long visual token sequences, imposing substantial computational overhead during inference. Existing pruning methods often rely on token salience or feature diversity as proxies for representativeness, without explicitly modeling the representation gap between the original token set and the retained subset, thereby leading to suboptimal representation of the original scene. In this paper, we propose ReMiC, a training-free, representation-driven token pruning framework based on minimax hierarchical clustering. ReMiC treats retained tokens as prototypes for the original observations, formulating pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget. Local prototype initialization allocates tokens according to regional representation needs, while global prototype refinement updates the selected prototypes using cross-region information to further reduce the maximum representation error. Extensive experiments conducted on three representative 3D VLMs across five 3D scene understanding benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of our method. Notably, by retaining only 10% of visual tokens, ReMiC preserves 93.2% of the performance of Video-3D LLM and achieves a $2.04\times$ faster inference speed.
authors: Bangfeng Yan, Chaoning Zhang, Yuanhao Liu, Pengcheng Zheng, Mengyuan Li, Wei Dong, Sheng Zheng, Yang Yang
bullets: Targets the long visual token sequences created by multi-view 3D inputs.
Formulates pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget.
Uses local prototype initialization followed by global cross-region refinement via minimax hierarchical clustering.
Evaluated across three 3D VLMs and five 3D scene-understanding benchmarks.
With 10% of visual tokens retained, preserves 93.2% of Video-3D LLM performance and delivers 2.04× faster inference.

In Stage 2, global prototype refinement reassigns all original tokens to their nearest prototypes across regions and reselects a prototype for each cluster.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers (vDiTs) have become the main backbone for video generation. The quadratic cost of self-attention limits their efficiency at high resolutions and long durations. Existing sparse attention methods often rely on preserving high attention weights. However, these criteria do not fully capture the fidelity of the final value-weighted output, whose error depends jointly on changes to the attention numerator and the softmax denominator. We propose NOVA, a coarse-to-fine sparse attention framework that first approximates the full normalized output using size-weighted key/value centroids. Building on this estimate, we construct a residual proxy that accounts for coupled numerator-denominator errors by centering value contributions around the estimated output. This proxy guides the selection of query-key blocks for refinement under a predefined block budget for each query cluster. Selected blocks are evaluated through exact token-level computation, while the remaining blocks contribute through their centroids under a shared softmax normalization. On five vDiTs, NOVA achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among sparse attention methods, improving PSNR by up to 1.55\,dB over the strongest baseline, while delivering up to 1.82$\times$ end-to-end speedup on an H100 GPU.
authors: Wenxuan Miao, Haosong Liu, Aiyue Chen, Yiwu Yao, Zihan Liu, Anbang Wu, Yiming Gan, Jingwen Leng, Minyi Guo, Yu Feng

Refines selected query-key blocks exactly while approximating the rest with centroids under shared normalization.
Across five vDiTs, reports the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among compared sparse-attention methods, with up to 1.55 dB PSNR improvement.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is commonly optimized with multiple reconstruction losses, which naturally forms a multi-objective optimization problem. This issue becomes more pronounced when perceptual losses are introduced to improve visual quality, as different objectives may impose competing update directions on Gaussian primitives and make it difficult to simultaneously improve fidelity, perceptual quality, and representation efficiency. Based on this view, we reformulate 3DGS training as a multi-objective optimization problem and derive selective conflict-aware position updates that reduce interference between competing objectives while preserving the contribution of each loss. We further observe that gradient conflicts persist throughout training and are most severe in Gaussian position parameters, indicating that objective conflict is closely tied to geometry optimization. We therefore treat position-gradient conflict as a geometry-aware signal to guide densification and pruning. Experiments show that our method achieves better rendering performance while improving representation compactness and rendering efficiency over existing 3DGS variants.
authors: Chenhao Zhang, Fengze Zhang, Fengqing Zhu
bullets: Reframes 3D Gaussian Splatting training with multiple reconstruction and perceptual losses as a multi-objective optimization problem.
Applies selective conflict-aware position updates to reduce interference while retaining each loss’s contribution.
Finds that conflicts persist during training and are strongest in Gaussian position parameters.
Uses position-gradient conflict to guide Gaussian densification and pruning.
Reports better rendering performance, greater representation compactness, and improved rendering efficiency over existing 3DGS variants.

papers.abstract: Thinking at length before answering is expected to strengthen the visual reasoning of vision-language models (VLMs), yet hybrid VLMs often get lost in thought: their thoughts loop or exhaust the budget without an answer, so thinking can score below answering directly. Existing early-exit methods watch a thought for the moment its answer is ready and force the answer out of it, but in a hybrid VLM that moment often never comes. We find that the remedy is not to stop a failing thought earlier, but to stop taking its answer: once a thought is given up, the model's own direct answers decide. Based on this, we propose **YOTO (You Only Think Once)**, a method that answers first and thinks at most once. YOTO draws direct answers until a probe-weighted vote settles; only an unsettled problem receives a single thought, which a failure head on the hidden state monitors and stops as soon as it predicts failure, handing the problem back to direct answers. At a matched 20k-token budget, YOTO is up to 5.9 points more accurate than the strongest early-exit baseline, using one failure-head threshold across model sizes. Keeping the released weights frozen, it adds only two linear probes. On the full MathVision benchmark, YOTO improves Qwen3.5-2B from 40.1% to 57.3% and Qwen3.5-4B from 68.3% to 73.7%, above the 72.8% that Qwen3.5-9B, a model more than twice its size, reaches with thinking. Its gains carry over to five further benchmarks and a second model family. These results suggest that hybrid VLMs reason better by answering first and thinking once than by thinking longer.
authors: Tianyi Tan, Wentao Wang, Xiaohan Li, Zining Ren, Siyuan Li, Xutao Mao, Rui Qian, Luoxi Zhang, Shiwen Ni
bullets: Hybrid VLMs can loop or exhaust their thinking budget, making extended reasoning worse than direct answering.

A failure head monitors the thought and returns to direct answers when failure is predicted.
With frozen model weights and two linear probes, YOTO gains up to 5.9 accuracy points over the strongest early-exit baseline at a matched 20k-token budget.
On MathVision, it raises Qwen3.5-2B from 40.1% to 57.3% and Qwen3.5-4B from 68.3% to 73.7%, with gains transferring across additional benchmarks and a second model family.

papers.abstract: Convolutional networks for optical flow typically adopt progressively deeper pyramidal encoders under the assumption that larger receptive fields improve motion estimation. For particle image velocimetry (PIV), however, tracer-particle displacement between frames is bounded by the acquisition geometry, allowing network depth to be derived from the physically admissible displacement rather than inherited from general-purpose architectures. Using a layer-by-layer analysis of spatial-support growth, we derive its explicit upper bound and show that deeper architectures substantially exceed the support required for PIV, compromising training stability, spatial resolution under particle loss, and inference efficiency. Based on this analysis, we develop LIMA3, a lightweight pyramidal displacement estimator with 589,000 trainable parameters. Across synthetic and experimental benchmarks, LIMA3 matches the accuracy of established learned and classical methods with at least an order of magnitude less memory and substantially higher throughput, while retaining the physically expected coarsening of spatial resolution as tracer information is lost. Its linear memory scaling enables megapixel processing within embedded memory budgets, such that LIMA3 can reach over 900 image pairs per second at $640\times480$~pixel on an RTX 5090 and 99 image pairs per second on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. The spatial-support analysis provides a transferable design principle for compact optical-flow architectures and bounded-window attention, offering an alternative to compressing oversized general-purpose networks and enabling efficient operation alongside image acquisition.
authors: Claudio Mucignat, Kamila Zdybal, Ivan Lunati
bullets: PIV displacement limits allow the required spatial support—and thus network depth—to be derived from acquisition geometry.
The analysis shows conventional deeper pyramidal networks exceed PIV’s needs, potentially harming stability, resolution under particle loss, and efficiency.
LIMA3 is a 589,000-parameter lightweight pyramidal displacement estimator designed around these physical constraints.
It matches established learned and classical methods across synthetic and experimental benchmarks while using at least an order of magnitude less memory and achieving high throughput.
The design supports megapixel processing on embedded hardware and offers a transferable principle for compact optical-flow and bounded-window-attention architectures.

papers.title: Shallow may be better: Physics-Constrained Lightweight Networks for High-Throughput Particle Image Velocimetry

papers.abstract: We study the compression of the 48 feed-forward network (FFN) matrices of the Vision Transformer ViT-L/16 to 2--8 bits with four schemes: a per-token grid, a fixed Gaussian Lloyd--Max table, a table fitted to the matrix, and a random-sign Hadamard rotation followed by the fixed table. We evaluate on 50,000 images. At 4 bits the top-1 accuracy of the four schemes lies within 0.8 points of the float32 model, while the agreement with its predictions ranges from 98.4\% to 94.4\%. We use the angular error between the compressed and the float32 residual stream, followed through the blocks, as a portable measure that ranks the schemes as the final classification does and shows where the ranking is built: with rotation the angle grows close to the square root of the number of blocks, the signature of independently accumulating errors, while the other schemes are amplified in the later blocks. The same measure shows that a scheme that is better on one block in isolation can be worse in the whole network. To address this inconsistency we introduce an angular measure of the spectrum of the output of a block, which in isolation orders the schemes as the whole network does where they diverge most. We support these observations with real samples and with statistically generated ones. The scope is one model, the FFN weights only, and float evaluation of compressed weights; no speed-up is claimed. The error measures and the sample generation, however, can be applied to other models and precisions.
bullets: Studies compressing all 48 ViT-L/16 FFN matrices to 2–8 bits using four quantization schemes.
At 4 bits, all schemes remain within 0.8 top-1 accuracy points of the float32 model, with 94.4–98.4% prediction agreement.
Angular error in the residual stream ranks schemes similarly to final classification and reveals where errors accumulate across blocks.
Rotation produces near-independent error growth, while other schemes experience stronger amplification in later blocks.
An angular measure of block-output spectra resolves cases where isolated block performance conflicts with whole-network behavior.

papers.selection_reason: Presents FFN weight compression for ViT, reducing memory footprint, fitting the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: Following the Error Through a Compressed Network:An Angular Measure for FFN Weight Compression in ViT-L/16
papers.tldr: An angular error measure tracks how FFN weight-quantization errors accumulate through ViT-L/16 and generally predicts final classification behavior without claiming inference speedups.

papers.abstract: Deploying large language models on commodity CPUs is often constrained not only by computational throughput but also by the resident memory required to execute quantized models within fixed system budgets. We present MemVanta, an experimental C++20 inference runtime for quantized GGUF language models that treats memory residency as a first-class systems objective. MemVanta combines memory-mapped model access, bounded tensor caching, quantized execution paths, paged key-value state, and explicit memory-pressure validation. We evaluate MemVanta against a pinned llama.cpp baseline using the same OpenLLaMA 7B v2 Q4_0 GGUF under CPU-only execution. Across five measured runs following warm-up, MemVanta records a peak resident set size of 3,983,412 KiB compared with 7,586,960 KiB for llama.cpp, corresponding to a 47.50 percent reduction in peak RSS. This memory reduction involves a substantial throughput trade-off: MemVanta achieves 3.15 +/- 0.04 tokens/s for prompt processing and 1.52 +/- 0.02 tokens/s for token generation, compared with 45.82 +/- 0.96 and 7.76 +/- 0.09 tokens/s, respectively, for llama.cpp. In a separate Linux cgroup-v2 experiment with swap disabled, MemVanta completes execution at a tested 3584 MiB memory ceiling, while llama.cpp is OOM-killed at that ceiling and first succeeds at the tested 3840 MiB level. These results position MemVanta as a memory-efficiency research prototype rather than a throughput competitor. We analyze the architectural mechanisms underlying this trade-off and discuss reproducibility, correctness, limitations, and opportunities for memory-constrained CPU and edge inference.
authors: Saurav Singla, Aarav Singla, Advik Gupta, Parnika Gupta
bullets: Targets memory-constrained deployment of large language models on commodity CPUs.
Uses memory mapping, bounded tensor caching, quantized execution, paged key-value state, and memory-pressure validation.
In the reported OpenLLaMA 7B Q4_0 comparison, peak RSS is reduced by 47.50% versus llama.cpp.
Runs under a tested 3584 MiB memory ceiling where llama.cpp is OOM-killed, but is much slower for prompt processing and generation.
Presented as a memory-efficiency research prototype, not a throughput competitor.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures activate only a subset of experts for each token, allowing large language models (LLMs) to scale parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation per token. However, intermediate data movement and uneven expert loads limit the efficiency of MoE inference on TPUs. To address these bottlenecks, we introduce Fuse-All MoE, a TPU kernel design that jointly optimizes expert computation, output communication, and load balancing. The kernel fuses token collection, expert projections, gated activation, and output writes, retaining expert computation intermediates on chip. Fixed token-slot destinations allow scheduling and expert placement to change while preserving routing semantics. In prefill-decode (PD) disaggregated serving, Fuse-All MoE balances EP16 prefill workloads through scheduling and expert redistribution, while symmetric EP8TP2 shares active expert computation between the two TensorCore devices within each chip during decode. Our experiments show that Fuse-All MoE reduces kernel runtime for a measured skewed EP16 prefill workload from 2.3x to 1.09x the same fixed reference time for a balanced workload. Across 32-512 decode tokens, symmetric EP8TP2 reduces kernel latency by up to 21.3% relative to fused EP16. With accompanying serving stack optimizations, the integrated system improves serving throughput by up to 34.5% over the Megablox EP16 baseline.
bullets: Targets TPU MoE bottlenecks from intermediate data movement and uneven expert loads.
Fuses token collection, expert projections, gated activation, and output writes while retaining intermediates on chip.
Uses fixed token-slot destinations to permit flexible scheduling and expert placement without changing routing semantics.
Balances prefill through scheduling and expert redistribution, and shares decode computation across TensorCore devices.
Reduces skewed prefill kernel runtime from 2.3× to 1.09× of a balanced reference, cuts decode latency by up to 21.3%, and improves serving throughput by up to 34.5% over the Megablox EP16 baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a fused MoE inference kernel with load balancing, directly improving efficiency of LLM inference.
papers.title: Fuse-All MoE Inference Kernel with Load Balancing on TPUs

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate responses longer than necessary, increasing inference latency and computational cost. While prompting can encourage conciseness, controlling output length without compromising response completeness remains challenging. Aggressive early stopping can reduce generation costs but risks terminating responses prematurely. We introduce MinimalLM, a training-free framework for reliable verbosity control that combines uncertainty-aware, length-dependent stop-token adjustment with structural completeness guardrails. MinimalLM separates the decision of when to stop from whether stopping is structurally appropriate, coordinating response-level instructions, decoding-time intervention, and completion checks without modifying model parameters or requiring auxiliary models. We evaluate MinimalLM across three open-source LLMs and 330 questions, producing 5,940 responses across baseline and ablation configurations. MinimalLM reduces generated tokens by 47.6%, accelerates individual responses by 19-68%, and eliminates structurally truncated outputs in the primary evaluation. Despite substantial token savings, it achieves an average quality score of 8.04/10, compared with 8.42/10 for unmodified models and 6.46/10 for length-matched truncation. Evaluations across diverse subject domains (such as healthcare, programming, law, and science) demonstrate robust efficiency gains, while ablations establish the complementary roles of decoding control and completeness constraints. Our findings highlight that efficient generation requires more than producing fewer tokens: it requires controlling when generation ends while preserving response integrity. MinimalLM offers a lightweight, training-free approach toward this goal.
bullets: Targets overly long LLM responses and the risks of premature early stopping.
Combines uncertainty-aware, length-dependent stop-token adjustment with structural completeness guardrails.
Coordinates prompting, decoding-time intervention, and completion checks without parameter updates or auxiliary models.
Across three open-source LLMs and 330 questions, reduces generated tokens by 47.6% and response time by 19–68%.
Achieves 8.04/10 average quality and eliminates structurally truncated outputs in the primary evaluation, though slightly below unmodified models at 8.42/10.

papers.abstract: Local learning algorithms can reshape resource requirements of artificial intelligence. The memory bottleneck of standard end-to-end backpropagation lies in the need to store all network activations until the loss gradient has been propagated back through. Local learning avoids this, but typically at a cost in accuracy. We study how to achieve accurate and memory efficient local learning in transformers. For each transformer block, we train a local proxy network to predict the global network output via distillation. Gradients can be independently propagated through this local proxy while estimating well the backpropagation gradients. In theory, this approach is exact for deep linear networks; in non-linear residual models, the gradient error can be bounded when using the appropriate residual proxy. We verify this numerically and demonstrate that optimizing the distillation loss improves gradient estimation. Evaluating the performance of proxy propagation on CIFAR-100 in vision transformers, we find that it achieves a better accuracy/memory trade-off compared to other local algorithms. Finally, we show that the method is further relevant for fine-tuning large language models on a small memory budget. Our method trains faster and achieves higher performance than memory-efficient zeroth-order learning algorithms with comparable memory cost.
bullets: Addresses the activation-memory bottleneck of standard backpropagation and the accuracy loss of typical local-learning methods.
Trains a local proxy for each transformer block to distill the global network output and estimate backpropagation gradients independently.
Provides exactness guarantees for deep linear networks and bounded gradient error for suitable nonlinear residual proxies.
Experiments show improved gradient estimation, a better accuracy–memory trade-off on CIFAR-100 vision transformers, and stronger, faster fine-tuning than comparable zeroth-order methods.
The approach is demonstrated for vision transformers and memory-constrained large-language-model fine-tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes local proxy distillation for memory-efficient transformer training, directly reducing the training memory footprint.
papers.title: Local proxies for memory-efficient training
papers.tldr: Local proxy networks enable accurate, memory-efficient local training of transformers without storing all activations for end-to-end backpropagation.

papers.abstract: Reducing memory use in large language model (LLM) training is an ongoing challenge. Activation checkpointing saves memory by recomputation, while lossy compression changes the stored activations. The reemergence of sparse $\relu$ and $\relu^2$ activations creates a third opportunity: losslessly compressing the activation cache itself. We present BitSparse, a GPU-resident lossless compression format for sparse activations. Compression and reconstruction run in custom Triton kernels fused into an autograd function, shrinking the activation cache while recovering it exactly for the backward pass. Bfloat16 (BF16) and FP8 activations are supported. Optional sign-bit packing further increases compression up to close to the theoretical limit. We analyze its compression ratio and compare it to the theoretical optimum. BitSparse lowers per-token VRAM by 31\% and 30\% Modded-NanoGPT and Nemotron-H respectively, with overheads of no more than 1\% at practical sequence lengths. Additionally, a new preallocated buffer system avoids host synchronization during training when variable size tensors are allocated.
bullets: Targets activation-cache memory, complementing checkpointing and lossy compression.
Uses custom Triton kernels fused with autograd for GPU-resident compression and exact reconstruction.
Supports BF16 and FP8 activations, with optional sign-bit packing for higher compression.
Reduces per-token VRAM by 31% in Modded-NanoGPT and 30% in Nemotron-H, with up to 1% overhead at practical sequence lengths.
Introduces preallocated buffers to avoid host synchronization for variable-size tensors.

papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) reduce or eliminate the need for large labelled datasets by enforcing governing equations during training. Physics-informed Deep Operator Networks (PI-DeepONets) extend this approach to learning solution operators, enabling rapid prediction across families of problems. Despite these advantages, we show that their application to higher-dimensional problems remains limited by the computational cost of training. To address this issue, we propose a modified PI-DeepONet architecture that reduces this cost by removing redundancy in how the Branch network processes input functions across collocation points. The proposed formulation is mathematically equivalent to the original architecture but reduces input tensor sizes and the number of Branch network evaluations. We analyse the computational complexity of both architectures and derive theoretical scaling laws for training time with respect to the number of collocation points and input functions. The proposed architecture is evaluated on 1D, 2D, and 3D linear advection problems. In all cases, it achieves comparable predictive accuracy to the original PI-DeepONet while consistently reducing training time. In 2D experiments, a maximum speed-up of $3.75\times$ is observed, with empirical training-time scaling agreeing with the predicted linear dependence on collocation points and input functions. Furthermore, training a 3D model on an NVIDIA A100 GPU is only feasible using the proposed architecture, as the original formulation exceeds memory limits. These results demonstrate that careful consideration of how PI-DeepONets are implemented can yield substantial gains, enhancing the practical performance of PI-DeepONets and enabling their application to otherwise intractable physics-informed learning problems.
bullets: Reduces redundancy by processing each input function once across collocation points rather than repeatedly in the Branch network.
Mathematically equivalent reformulation lowers input tensor sizes and the number of Branch-network evaluations.
Validated on 1D, 2D, and 3D linear advection problems with comparable predictive accuracy and consistently shorter training times.
Achieves up to 3.75× speed-up in 2D; a 3D model fits on an NVIDIA A100 only with the proposed architecture.
Empirical training-time scaling matches the predicted linear dependence on collocation points and input functions.

papers.abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.
authors: Chang Nie, Chaoyou Fu, Songlin Liu, Yiqing Hu, Caifeng Shan
bullets: Addresses the linear GPU-memory growth and quadratic computation of Transformer KV caches, while preserving more detail than fixed-size state compression.
Uses a memory encoder-decoder to store selected final-layer hidden states and dynamically reconstruct attention KV caches.
Applies sparse attention that retrieves relevant memories once per input and shares the sparse indices across layers.
Reports substantial efficiency gains, including 1313× lower memory-state cache, 6.9× lower prefill latency, and 3.5× higher throughput at 1M context in one adaptation setting.
Generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks with competitive performance against specialized models.

papers.abstract: Machine learning has largely kept separate the choice of architecture and the process of training. A classic Transformer, for instance, trains a fixed set of attention and MLP sublayers at every layer, in the same order, and optimizes the weights within. This uniformity is a convention rather than a principled design choice, and it is likely suboptimal: the best architecture for a given task may be smaller, more efficient, and far from uniform. We believe that, ideally, training itself should shape the model's topology. To this end, we introduce Model Carving, which learns both a Transformer's weights and its architecture in a single run. By applying learnable, scalar gates to each sublayer, we allow the training loss to remove the model's own components during training -- freeing a smaller heterogeneous network inside. We evaluate Model Carving by pre-training standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers from 140M to 1.3B. At equal training compute, carved models reach a lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute. Furthermore, carved models also outperform size-matched models produced by pruning or distillation, suggesting that the best way to obtain small models for edge devices is to carve them during training, not to compress a large one afterwards. This advantage both grows with scale and carries over to downstream tasks such as few-shot evaluation and generation. Because the removed sublayers no longer run, carved models also cost up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decode up to 1.6 times faster without cost in quality. Our results show that architecture, like weights, should be learned and not fixed in advance, and that inside every large transformer is a smaller, faster, stronger one waiting to be carved out.
bullets: Fixed, uniform Transformer architectures may be inefficient for individual tasks.
Learnable scalar gates remove attention or MLP sublayers during training, creating a heterogeneous subnetwork in one run.
Evaluated on standard and looped Transformers ranging from 140M to 2.7B parameters.
Carved models achieve lower validation loss at equal compute and outperform size-matched pruning or distillation models.
Removing sublayers reduces inference cost by up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and up to 1.6× faster decoding, with quality preserved.

papers.abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when candidate configurations require repeated training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. The method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is then used for HPO with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, Heterogeneous Recombination and Cataclysmic Mutation (CHC), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Experiments on seven tabular, two text, and two image benchmark datasets show that RPC substantially reduces HPO time while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO across decision tree, text classification, and image classification tasks. Across datasets and optimizers, HPO-stage speedups range from approximately 1.14x to 8.80x, while the one-time coreset construction cost is accounted for separately through end-to-end runtime and break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations excluded from coreset construction, RPC achieves higher ranking correlation than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets (dataset-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.014). These results show that ranking preservation extends beyond the configurations used during selection. The one-time construction cost can be amortized when the coreset is reused across HPO runs.
bullets: Targets the high cost of repeatedly training candidate configurations on large datasets.
Selects a compact coreset by maximizing Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based rankings while penalizing subset size.
Evaluates the coreset with GA, CHC, and PSO across tabular, text, and image benchmarks.
Reports HPO-stage speedups of approximately 1.14×–8.80×, with comparable test accuracy to full-dataset HPO.
Outperforms same-size random sampling in ranking correlation on held-out configurations for 8 of 11 datasets; construction cost can be amortized through reuse.

papers.selection_reason: Ranking-preserving coreset selection reduces HPO computation by shrinking training data, fitting the broad efficient-AI computation-reduction interest.
papers.title: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization
papers.tldr: A ranking-preserving coreset accelerates evolutionary hyperparameter optimization by using a small data subset that retains full-data configuration rankings while maintaining comparable test accuracy.

papers.abstract: Long-context models use sparse or structured attention to avoid quadratic cost, yet retrieving a small set of relevant facts embedded among hundreds of thousands of distractors degrades as normalization mass disperses with length. Hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) replaces the dense $L \times L$ matrix with a linear-size graph over local windows and $K$ shared hubs balanced by Sinkhorn scaling. Building on block-wise tail refinement and fixed-support transport topology (arXiv:2605.08123, arXiv:2609.07954), we introduce Topology Hub Optimal Transport (THOT): (1) bounded-support capacity gating via simplex sparsemax ($O(L\log L)$) or sorting-free token-local thresholded ReLU ($O(L)$), driving excess distractor mass to zero; (2) a three-sweep $1+2$ annealed row-closed Sinkhorn schedule that damps bipartite residuals; (3) an exact rank-$(D+2R+1)$ One-Reference-Tile adjoint in batched split-factor Triton kernels (BF16 Tensor Cores, FP32 potentials); and (4) a chunked exclusive-prefix causal variant with verified zero future leakage. On NVIDIA L4, sparsemax THOT trained at $L=128$ reaches 97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at $L=262{,}144$ under pure task loss ($\alpha=0$) and 98.83% at $\alpha=0.05$ (matched by $O(L)$ thresholded ReLU at $\alpha=0.05$, vs. 80.60% at $\alpha=0$), while softmax-gated hub OT drops to 3.52%. In bidirectional operator microbenchmarks, our kernel runs forward+VJP in 100.1 ms at $H=8, D=64, L=262\mathrm{K}$ (2.2x faster with 4.0x smaller compiler temporaries than latent softmax) and 1.34 ms vs. 4.37 ms for cuDNN FlashAttention at $L=4{,}096$; multi-layer LM runs use the unfused path. Zero-shot WikiText-103 multi-needle retrieval hits 100.00% (128/128 queries at $L=65\mathrm{K}$) vs. 0.78% for short-trained RoPE FlashAttention, and compact 4-layer WikiText-4K runs show modest causal and masked LM gains.
bullets: Addresses long-context retrieval degradation caused by attention normalization mass spreading across distractors.
Builds a linear-size local-window-plus-hub transport graph with sparsemax or thresholded-ReLU gating to eliminate excess distractor mass.
Adds annealed Sinkhorn updates, an exact low-rank adjoint, fused Triton kernels, and a causal chunked variant with zero future leakage.
At 262K tokens, sparsemax THOT achieves 97.40% or 98.83% fixed-binding recall depending on loss regularization, while softmax-gated hub OT reaches 3.52%.
Reports 100% multi-needle retrieval on 65K-token WikiText-103 queries and faster operator benchmarks than the compared baselines; broader multi-layer LM runs use an unfused path.

(b) On compact 4-layer Causal Next-Token LM (512 steps) and Deep 4-Layer MLM (640 steps) over WikiText-103 4K documents, THOT achieves the lowest held-out NLL, with modest margins (0.015–0.016 nats) over the strongest nearby structured baselines.

papers.title: Topology Hub Optimal Transport: Eliminating Long Context Dilution at Flash Speed
papers.tldr: THOT uses sparse capacity-gated hub optimal transport and optimized kernels to preserve relevant facts in extremely long contexts while reducing attention overhead.

papers.abstract: Streaming visual geometry transformers retain historical key-value (KV) states as cross-view geometric memory, but growing caches constrain long-sequence inference. We systematically characterize KV quantization in streaming geometry and uncover two linked challenges: Nonuniform Geometric Sensitivity and Cache-Geometry Mismatch. Quantization sensitivity varies across precision choices and cache locations, while perturbed retrieval changes geometry-head inputs and propagates through subsequent predictions and KV writes. Guided by these findings, we propose QuantStream3D, to our knowledge the first dedicated KV quantization framework for streaming visual geometry transformers. Geometry-Guided Mixed-Precision KV Quantization protects sensitive cross-view evidence, while Geometry-Aligned Quantization-Aware Distillation jointly adapts transformer blocks and geometry heads on student-generated quantized history. Across five benchmarks and two backbones, QuantStream3D achieves near-lossless geometric accuracy in most settings with predominantly 2-bit KV caches, and many configurations surpass unquantized inference. Compared with LLM-oriented KV quantizers, it reduces TUM absolute trajectory error and NeuralRGBD completeness error by up to 57.4% and 69.7%, respectively. Integration with existing native cache-pruning methods further pushes compression while improving reconstruction quality on NeuralRGBD. Our optimized StreamVGGT backend achieves $5.05\times$ physical KV compression and 23.1% lower latency at batch size one. Under a fixed memory budget on the same GPU, it supports $5.4\times$ the maximum batch size and up to $1.67\times$ the peak throughput of unquantized inference. Code and pretrained checkpoints will be made publicly available.
authors: Zunhai Su, Keyu Fan, Ruishan Guo, Zhongzhu Zhou, Jingzehua Xu, Bohan Sun, Hansen Feng, Ruihan Hu, Yik-Chung Wu, Ngai Wong
bullets: Streaming geometry transformers face growing KV caches and sensitivity to quantization across cache locations, causing cache–geometry mismatch.
Geometry-Guided Mixed-Precision KV Quantization preserves sensitive cross-view evidence.
Geometry-Aligned Quantization-Aware Distillation adapts transformer blocks and geometry heads using quantized history.
Across five benchmarks and two backbones, it achieves near-lossless geometric accuracy in most settings and can outperform unquantized inference.
The optimized backend reaches 5.05× physical KV compression, 23.1% lower latency, and up to 5.4× larger batch size under the same memory budget.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by preparing candidate continuations before the target model generates them. Its efficiency depends on how well limited drafting computation anticipates the path the target will actually follow. Anticipating this path involves two sources of uncertainty: the target model's predictions and the randomness of sampling. Yet the former requires a target-model forward pass, while the latter can be fixed before drafting. Building on this observation, we introduce DICE (Draw-Informed Candidate Selection), which pre-samples and synchronizes verification randomness across drafting and verification. By combining these known draws with predictions from an existing drafter, DICE allocates computation toward continuations more likely to be used in the current sampling run. This principle guides node selection throughout draft-tree construction and extends to asynchronous prefetching, where DICE predicts which next-round drafts to prepare. Without additional drafter training or changes to the target sampling distribution, DICE achieves state-of-the-art decoding throughput across diverse settings, with speedups of up to 24.6pp over strong baselines.
bullets: Speculative decoding faces uncertainty from both target-model predictions and sampling randomness.
Sampling randomness can be fixed before drafting, enabling more informed candidate selection.
DICE synchronizes verification draws with drafting and guides draft-tree node selection and asynchronous prefetching.
It requires no additional drafter training or changes to the target sampling distribution.
The method reports throughput gains of up to 24.6 percentage points over strong baselines across diverse settings.

papers.abstract: Anchor tokens let a vision transformer exchange global information through a few summaries, but nothing forces different anchors to summarise different things. On one shared backbone we show that a Perceiver-style pathway and an AnchorFormer pathway collapse to a single summary, the latter despite its mass normalisation (pooling-map similarity 0.99), while other soft pathways, including Representative Attention, stay partly redundant (0.59-0.79). These results concern the routing modules inside our block, not the full published models. An exclusive partition of the patch grid cannot collapse by construction, and matched component by component it is 2.4-3.6 points more accurate than Representative Attention on CIFAR-100. We then propose focus anchors, which place most anchors at the peaks of a learned importance map while all anchors keep one exclusive Voronoi partition. Focus anchors beat a fixed partition on a cluttered canvas (+1.5 points, 95% CI [0.5, 2.6]) but not on full-HD traffic-sign recognition. There, both variants match dense attention with local windows at about a fifth of its FLOPs, and the fixed partition also trains 1.5x faster per step than dense attention with FlashAttention, though both use more memory; a ViT on a downsampled input loses half its mean average precision. Hard exclusive assignment is the only region assignment we tested that is both stable and most accurate: softmax and Sinkhorn relaxations diverge, and Gumbel-softmax trains but is less accurate. We also report the limits: a ResNet-18 is more accurate on every task we trained it on in this from-scratch regime, and anchors train faster than FlashAttention only from about 1536x1536 pixels and never use less memory.
bullets: Soft anchor-routing pathways can produce highly redundant summaries, whereas exclusive patch partitions prevent collapse by construction.
The proposed focus anchors concentrate anchors near learned importance peaks while preserving exclusive Voronoi regions.
On CIFAR-100, exclusive routing is 2.4–3.6 points more accurate than Representative Attention; focus anchors add 1.5 points on a cluttered canvas.
For full-HD traffic-sign recognition, both anchor variants match dense local-window attention at about one-fifth the FLOPs; fixed partitions train 1.5× faster per step.
Hard exclusive assignment was the most stable and accurate tested option, but anchors use more memory and do not outperform the trained ResNet-18 in this regime.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained recognition benefits from high resolution, but not every image region needs it. We study a foveated Vision Transformer (FoVT) that uses last-block class attention from a 224-pixel glance to select regions for refinement. Fine patches from the 448-pixel image replace the selected coarse cells, and the same backbone classifies the mixed-resolution input. We evaluate FoVT on five benchmarks with two seeds and 26 configurations per dataset. Attention beats random selection on all five benchmarks, by up to 2.45 percentage points overall and 4.18 points on the smallest objects. At equal transformer cost, Holm-corrected tests detect no FoVT deficit relative to a port of the official CF-ViT, but no dataset shows a corrected FoVT advantage in both seeds. FoVT requires no feature reuse, distillation loss, or selection schedule. Reusing coarse features shows no significant benefit and costs 1 to 3 points when the reuse module is trained at the head learning rate. Skipping refinement for the most confident 19 to 24 percent of images leaves accuracy unchanged to two decimal places. At the transformer cost of uniform 336-pixel inference, gated FoVT improves accuracy on four benchmarks, with the largest gains on NABirds and FGVC-Aircraft and no significant gain on Stanford Dogs. Foveation primarily saves computation: relative to a uniform 448-pixel model trained with the same auxiliary glance loss, ungated FoVT uses 44 percent fewer transformer operations, with no significant accuracy difference on four benchmarks and a 0.53-point deficit on FGVC-Aircraft. Wall-clock savings are smaller than the reduction in transformer operations.
bullets: A 224-pixel glance uses last-block class attention to select regions for 448-pixel refinement within the same backbone.
Attention-based selection consistently beats random selection, by up to 2.45 percentage points overall and 4.18 points for the smallest objects.
At equal transformer cost, FoVT shows no corrected accuracy deficit versus ported CF-ViT, but also no consistent corrected advantage.
Gating refinement for the most confident 19–24% of images preserves accuracy; at uniform 336-pixel cost, gated FoVT improves four of five benchmarks.
Ungated FoVT reduces transformer operations by 44% versus uniform 448-pixel inference, but wall-clock savings are smaller and FGVC-Aircraft shows a 0.53-point deficit.

papers.abstract: Many high-accuracy referring expression comprehension (REC) methods produce image-dependent multimodal representations. These representations must be recomputed for every video frame, even when the referring expression remains unchanged. Fast open-vocabulary detectors such as YOLO-World instead pre-encode text once and reuse it throughout the stream. However, encoding each referring expression as a single embedding prevents explicit token-level correspondence. We propose Ref-YOLO-World, which separates text-side computation that depends only on the referring expression from image processing and reuses its outputs across frames. Two lightweight modules inject cached per-token text features into YOLO-World's detection path. Ref-YOLO-World achieves 81.29% Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg val, the highest among REC models with a decoupled text branch, and consistently outperforms a fine-tuned YOLO-World. Precomputation reduces per-image inference time by 18.5%, yielding 47.0 FPS. A Core ML version runs at 15.73 FPS on an iPhone 15 Pro, demonstrating efficient on-device REC. Code is available at https://github.com/sakusaku3939/Ref-YOLO-World.
authors: Yuki Aoki, Hiroo Bekku, Tadashi Okoshi, Jin Nakazawa
bullets: Separates text-side computation from image processing while preserving token-level text–image correspondence.

papers.abstract: Layer skipping can reduce large language model inference costs, but a request budget does not specify how to allocate layer execution across generated tokens. We introduce \method{}, which allows tokens to execute different numbers of layers while matching each request's mean executed depth to a continuous budget. At each routed layer, a router reads the current token state and its request's budget and decides whether to execute the Transformer block. Tokens that skip the block pass through a lightweight residual adapter and write no key/value (K/V) entry at that layer. A single checkpoint serves requests with different budgets in the same batch. Across three LLaMA backbones, six quality metrics, and 13 budgets, AVERT is best or tied for best in 206 of 234 comparisons. Across single- and mixed-budget batches, the mean absolute per-request budget error is at most 1.15 percentage points. When grouping requests by budget leaves batches underfilled, mixing budgets reduces decode time per output token (TPOT) by 4.3--21.2%.
authors: Pengjie Zheng, Mengwei Xie, Huan Yang, Si Wu, Pengfei Hu, Feng Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of allocating a request-level layer-execution budget across generated tokens.

papers.abstract: Image-guided multimodal machine translation (MMT) leverages visual context to resolve translation-relevant uncertainty. However, prevailing systems either process images unconditionally or apply gating only after visual encoding, leaving redundant visual computation unavoidable. To mitigate this computational overhead, routing decisions must rely on a pre-visual source signal. Crucially, surface-level ambiguity does not equate to visual dependence, as intra-sentence textual context often suffices for disambiguation. We therefore formulate visual invocation as source-text sufficiency prediction: determining exclusively from the source text whether translation-relevant uncertainty remains unresolved. To support this formulation, we construct a visual-dependency dataset with three fine-grained labels (no_ambiguity, text_resolved, and vision_needed) and verify discriminative visual evidence for vision_needed instances. We further propose PreVIR, a lightweight, backend-agnostic text-only router that selects between text-only and multimodal branches before computing visual features. Experiments on English-to-Chinese MMT demonstrate that PreVIR achieves a favorable COMET-budget trade-off relative to strong routing baselines. At its default operating point, it substantially reduces visual calls while maintaining translation quality comparable to always-on multimodal inference. Label-wise and case analyses show that this trade-off stems from distinguishing genuine visual dependency from contextually resolved ambiguity.
authors: Xinyu Wang, Yingfeng Luo, Yuxin Gao, Anxiang Ma, Jingbo Zhu, Tong Xiao
bullets: Frames visual invocation as predicting whether source text leaves translation-relevant uncertainty unresolved.
Introduces a three-label visual-dependency dataset: no_ambiguity, text_resolved, and vision_needed.
Proposes PreVIR, a lightweight, backend-agnostic router that selects text-only or multimodal translation before visual encoding.
English-to-Chinese experiments show a favorable COMET–compute trade-off, with substantially fewer visual calls and comparable quality to always-on multimodal inference.
Analysis indicates the router separates genuine visual dependence from ambiguity resolved by sentence context.

papers.title: When Are Images Needed in Multimodal Machine Translation? Text-Only Routing for On-Demand Visual Context
papers.tldr: PreVIR uses source text alone to decide when visual input is truly needed, reducing image processing while preserving multimodal translation quality.

papers.abstract: Data selection has emerged as an effective approach to reducing the model training costs. However, most existing methods often rely heavily on sample hardness, which may overlook differences in sample learning dynamics and lead to suboptimal sample selection. In this paper, we propose LeDAS, an end-to-end Learning Dynamics-Aware Selection framework for dynamic data selection, which jointly characterizes sample importance through hardness, learning progress, and deterioration, enabling adaptive sample prioritization throughout training with marginal additional computational overhead. Specifically, we track per-sample loss dynamics using exponential moving averages (EMA) to obtain three complementary signals that capture current learning difficulty, ongoing learning improvements, and potential degradation. To accommodate evolving training dynamics, we introduce Adaptive Metric Fusion, a contextual bandit-based mechanism that dynamically adjusts the relative importance of these signals based on training feedback. Furthermore, a bounded staleness compensation mechanism accounts for historical selection patterns by increasing the selection priority of samples that have not been selected for extended periods. Extensive experiments across diverse vision and language tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of LeDAS. Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, LeDAS consistently achieves superior performance, matching or surpassing full-dataset training at a 50\% selection ratio on ImageNet-1K and in LLM supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, its modular and task-agnostic design enables the integration of complementary selection signals, demonstrating strong robustness to noisy and corrupted datasets.
authors: Hai Gan, Suorong Yang, Guang Li, Baile Xu, Furao Shen
bullets: Addresses the limitations of hardness-only data selection, which can overlook how samples evolve during training.
Tracks per-sample loss with exponential moving averages to estimate difficulty, improvement, and degradation.
Uses contextual-bandit Adaptive Metric Fusion to adjust signal importance based on training feedback.
Adds bounded staleness compensation to prioritize samples that have been selected less recently.
Across vision and language tasks, LeDAS matches or surpasses full-dataset training at a 50% selection ratio and remains robust to noisy or corrupted data.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the proposed LeDAS framework. At each training epoch, LeDAS characterizes sample-level learning dynamics using three metrics: hardness, progress, and deterioration. It then adaptively fuses these signals via a contextual bandit guided by target model features. Staleness Compensation further adjusts sample selection priorities based on historical selection patterns. The selected subset is finally used to update the target model, thereby establishing a closed-loop data selection framework.

papers.tldr: LeDAS improves dynamic data selection by combining sample hardness, learning progress, deterioration, and selection history to prioritize training examples adaptively.

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan by rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences through a transformer predictor, so a single decision can take tens of seconds. Existing accelerations prune spatial tokens as in vision-language models, yet a sampling-based planner uses predicted costs only to rank candidates, so a rollout can be compressed freely as long as the ranking survives. We propose SOAR, a training-free method that adapts rollout compression to each planning decision. At every decision, SOAR probes a few candidates under several token budgets and keeps the smallest budget that preserves their ranking, so it compresses as far as the current decision allows, without task labels. A closed-loop study of more than 80,000 episodes fixes the rest of the rollout: the first step, which alone reads a real observation, stays exact, and the context frame is cached rather than recomputed. On seven navigation and manipulation tasks with frozen checkpoints, SOAR matches dense-level planning success at 2.3x speedup and retains 98% at 2.5x. Our code is available at https://github.com/starrywiki/SOAR.
authors: Anqi Li, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Targets the high cost of rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences for each decision.
Probes a few candidates at multiple token budgets and selects the smallest budget that maintains their ranking.
Requires no training or task labels; the first observation-processing step remains exact and context frames are cached.
Across seven navigation and manipulation tasks, matches dense planning success at 2.3× speedup and retains 98% at 2.5×.
Evaluated in a closed-loop study spanning more than 80,000 episodes with frozen checkpoints.
