papers.abstract: Whole-body segmentation tools such as TotalSegmentator and MOOSE split more than 100 classes across five or six networks. The reason is memory. Standard 3D inference, as implemented in nnU-Net and MONAI, holds a logit for every class and voxel, on the working grid and again on the scanner's grid. For a median whole-body CT at 125 classes, that is 76 GB. We show that this memory wall lies in what inference materializes, not in the task, and remove it without approximation. Every step after the network is local along one axis, so its outputs can be streamed through a ring one patch thick. The classification head commutes with blending and resampling, so the ring carries the network's features instead of the class logits. Memory thus no longer grows with classes times volume, and the label map on the scanner's grid stays exact. This holds for any model with a pointwise affine head, without retraining. Many-class models, previously impractical, become deployable. One model trained on all classes matches or slightly exceeds the toolkits' five or six specialists in segmentation quality and runs 5.8-15x faster end to end, with 3.2-7.6x less RAM and under 8 GB of VRAM. We provide the method as a drop-in for nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator and MOOSE. The code is part of nnU-Net (https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nnUNet), and unified models for both toolkits will be released.
authors: Fabian Isensee, Jakob Wasserthal, Lalith Kumar Shiyam Sundar, Maximilian Rokuss, Moritz Langenberg, Constantin Ulrich Harsy, Stefan Michael Happold, Klaus H. Maier-Hein
bullets: Standard inference materializes per-class logits on multiple grids, causing extreme memory use for whole-body CT segmentation.
The method streams intermediate features through a one-patch ring instead of storing class logits, while preserving exact outputs.
It applies to models with a pointwise affine classification head and requires no retraining.
A single all-class model matches or slightly exceeds specialist-toolkit quality, runs 5.8–15× faster, and uses 3.2–7.6× less RAM with under 8 GB VRAM.
The approach is provided as a drop-in for nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator, and MOOSE.

papers.selection_reason: Streaming inference method that removes the memory wall for many-class 3D segmentation, directly relevant to memory-efficient AI.
papers.title: Segment Everything, Materialize Nothing: Exact Streaming Inference for Many-Class 3D Segmentation
papers.tldr: An exact streaming inference method removes the class-dependent memory bottleneck in many-class 3D segmentation, enabling one unified model to run substantially faster with much lower memory.

papers.abstract: Online batch selection lowers the cost of fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) by replacing each candidate batch with a smaller informative subset. Existing selectors typically depend on a held-out validation or proxy set, or else rely on Euclidean facility-location objectives over unpreconditioned gradients whose diameter-shifted similarities are distorted by heavy-tailed gradient norms and cross-layer anisotropy. We introduce PRISM (Preconditioned Ray-Isotropic Submodular Matching), a validation-free online batch selector that aligns candidate gradients in a factored second-moment metric and casts subset construction as conic facility location over positive ray projections. Computing the required pairwise geometry through factored preconditioned ghost inner products avoids materializing per-example parameter gradients, while the conic objective remains normalized, nonnegative, and monotone submodular---guaranteeing a $(1-1/e)$ greedy approximation whose additive error scales with total batch gradient energy rather than the worst-case outlier diameter. Assigning each candidate to its best-aligned selected ray induces closed-form radial projection weights that automatically shrink orthogonal or noisy examples toward zero. We derive a nonconvex convergence bound showing that optimization error is governed directly by the conic representation cost. Across four LLM fine-tuning configurations spanning 1.5B to 8B parameters, PRISM outperforms full-batch training, Euclidean facility location, and zeroth-order selectors, and rivals or surpasses validation-guided baselines without held-out data.
authors: Lin Tang, Wei Zhang, Jing Li, Hongyu Chen, Ming Zhao, Yuxuan Wang
bullets: Targets costly online batch selection without requiring a held-out validation or proxy set.
Uses factored second-moment preconditioning and positive-ray geometry to correct heavy-tailed norms and cross-layer anisotropy.
Computes pairwise similarity with preconditioned ghost inner products, avoiding per-example parameter-gradient materialization.
Provides a monotone submodular objective with a $(1-1/e)$ greedy approximation and error tied to total gradient energy rather than worst-case outliers.
Across four 1.5B–8B LLM fine-tuning configurations, outperforms full-batch, Euclidean, and zeroth-order selectors and matches or exceeds validation-guided methods without held-out data.

papers.title: PRISM: Validation-Free Online Batch Selection for LLM Fine-Tuning via Preconditioned Conic Ghost Matching
papers.tldr: PRISM is a validation-free LLM fine-tuning batch selector that uses preconditioned conic gradient matching to choose informative subsets while reducing sensitivity to noisy and anisotropic gradients.

papers.abstract: Serving engines treat the ways of running a greedy language model as interchangeable: cached or not, padded or not, alone or batched, one token or several verified at once (speculative decoding). In finite precision they round differently. We measure how often the greedy text of Qwen3-0.6B (bfloat16, 128 new tokens, GSM8K and ARC prompts) differs from a reference that decodes one token per pass. Verifying 4 guessed tokens per pass changes 60% of 150 prompts and padding changes 68%; every first divergence has a top-1 minus top-2 logit gap of 0.375 or less. A split of the noise shows that cache entries written by multi-token passes are about as noisy as the multi-token pass itself. A margin gate (fall back to one token when the gap is below a bound calibrated on separate GSM8K prompts) whose fallback reads that cache does not help: 58 of 100 prompts differ, against 61 of 100 for plain verification. Rebuilding the cache with one-token passes leaves 0 of 100 different but costs 7.2 model passes per token, against 1.0 for the reference. Fixed-width decoding makes drafted and plain decoding identical (0 of 100 prompts differ) at 0.75 passes per token. On shifted MMLU and HellaSwag prompts the rebuild gate leaves 0 of 60 different, plain verification 48 of 60. On 138 further and shifted prompts the bound was exceeded at 0.6% of positions and missed 0 of 309 flips. One GPU, one drafter, small models.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Navin Kumar R
bullets: Multi-token verification changed outputs on 60% of prompts, while padding changed 68%; divergences occurred only when the top-1/top-2 logit margin was at most 0.375.
Cache entries written during multi-token passes were a comparable source of noise to the passes themselves.
A margin-based fallback that reused the noisy cache barely helped: 58/100 prompts differed versus 61/100 with plain verification.
Rebuilding the cache with one-token passes eliminated observed differences, but increased cost to 7.2 model passes per token versus 1.0 for the reference.
Fixed-width decoding matched plain decoding on all tested prompts at 0.75 passes per token; scope was limited to one GPU, one drafter, and small models.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes rounding noise and cache effects in speculative decoding for LLM inference, directly contributing to efficient inference and cache management.
papers.title: Vega-Fafnir: Is Greedy Decoding the Same Decoding? Where Rounding Noise in Speculative Verification Comes From and What Removing It Costs
papers.tldr: Finite-precision rounding makes supposedly equivalent greedy and speculative decoding produce different text, but fixed-width decoding removes the mismatch more efficiently than rebuilding the cache.

papers.abstract: Visually rich documents (VRDs) convey knowledge through textual, visual, and layout information that text-centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Text-RAG) struggles to fully exploit. Recent Vision-RAG approaches enable retrieval and generation directly from document images, retaining this multimodal information. However, earlier Vision-RAG methods commonly adopt coarse retrieval representations and full-page visual contexts, which can obscure local evidence and introduce substantial redundancy and computational overhead. To address these challenges, we propose MV-VisRAG, a region-level Vision-RAG framework that uses semantically complete regions for both document representation and visual augmentation. Specifically, MV-VisRAG first constructs these regions through a ContentAdaptive Regionalization module. It then encodes them into local region vectors and a page-level global vector using a VLM-based retriever trained through multimodal reconstruction pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning. With this compact multi-vector representation, MV-VisRAG performs late-interaction retrieval and estimates region contributions from the resulting matching scores. These contributions guide the selection of relevant regions, which are then rearranged into a compact visual context for generation. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate retrieval and generation gains over corresponding baselines, while region-level augmentation substantially reduces visual tokens and computational cost. Our code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xandery-geek/MV-VisRAG.
authors: Xu Yuan, Liangbo Ning, Yujuan Ding, Qing Li, Wenqi Fan
bullets: Targets the loss of local multimodal evidence and high overhead in text-centric and earlier Vision-RAG systems.
Builds semantically complete regions with Content-Adaptive Regionalization.
Represents each page with local region vectors plus a global vector, trained using multimodal reconstruction pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning.
Uses late-interaction matching to estimate region relevance, then rearranges selected regions into a compact visual context.
Across five benchmarks, it improves retrieval and generation over corresponding baselines while reducing visual tokens and computation.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive inference in large transformer models is limited by token-level sequential execution, resulting in high latency and low GPU utilization. Speculative decoding (SD) mitigates this bottleneck by introducing a draft-and-verifier model. However, the drafting stage remains sequential, leaving the verifier idle and underutilizing compute. To address this, we propose a plug-and-play drafting adaptive drafting method that parallelizes inference across transformer layers during draft generation. Starting from a shared hidden state, our approach evaluates multiple layers in parallel and verifies consistency by measuring divergence in hidden-state space. Layer-wise draft states are accepted when deviations are small; otherwise, a correction step is applied. By exploiting redundancy across transformer layers, our method accelerates draft generation and improves hardware utilization without modifying architectures or requiring retraining. Experimental results on NLP tasks show that our method speeds up the drafting stage by up to $1.65\times$ with minimal degradation in accuracy, while maintaining the same performance as SD.
authors: Divya Jyoti Bajpai, Arun Verma, Manjesh Kumar Hanawal
bullets: Addresses sequential draft generation, which leaves the verifier idle and underutilizes GPUs.
Evaluates multiple transformer layers in parallel from a shared hidden state.
Accepts layer-wise drafts based on hidden-state divergence and corrects inconsistent states.
Requires no architecture changes or retraining and maintains the performance of speculative decoding.
Evaluated on NLP tasks, with up to 1.65× faster drafting and minimal accuracy degradation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Vanilla versus Adaptive Layer-parallel Drafting (ALD). Vanilla drafting executes layers sequentially, leaving parallel compute underutilized. ALD evaluates future layer transformations concurrently using proxy hidden states and adaptively controls their advancement through a similarity check, reducing drafting latency while preserving draft quality.

Figure 3: Effect of the similarity threshold τ on drafting speedup and draft-model quality, measured using BLEU-4 and ROUGE-L. Lower τ permits more aggressive layer-parallel proxy execution and increases speedup, while higher τ produces more conservative execution and better preserves draft quality. The default setting τ = 0.95 provides a favorable operating point between these objectives.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) often generate future visual states alongside robot actions, introducing substantial computational overhead during inference. During closed-loop execution, consecutive inference cycles often predict similar action sequences, leading to redundant computation. However, reducing this redundancy requires distinguishing consistent actions from changes that demand fresh computation. To address these challenges, we propose ReActWAM, a training-free framework that combines action-intent-guided prefix skipping with inner-chunk prediction reuse. A coarse-to-fine assessment evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action prediction conflicts. For eligible chunks, we draw on first-step differences to adapt the cached latent and network features to the current condition, providing an estimate at a later denoising step that bypasses the redundant prefix. Subsequent inference refines this estimate while reusing stable denoising predictions within the chunk. Experiments across LingBot-VA, FastWAM and the Cosmos family on LIBERO-Long and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate $1.41\times$--$5.44\times$ GPU inference speedup, with minimal degradation in task success rates. Real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot further achieve $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining success rate.
authors: Zhaochen Guo, Yunke Wang, Siyu Xu, Zijian Wang, Chenghao Xia, Chengbin Du, Shinan Liu, Chang Xu
bullets: Addresses redundant computation in closed-loop WAM inference caused by similar consecutive action-sequence predictions.
Uses training-free action-intent-guided prefix skipping and inner-chunk prediction reuse.
Evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action conflicts to determine when cached computation is safe.
Reports 1.41×–5.44× GPU inference speedups with minimal task-success degradation across several WAMs and benchmarks.
Achieves 1.46× end-to-end speedup on a Franka Research 3 robot while maintaining success rate.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought prompting significantly improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) but incurs high inference costs due to lengthy autoregressive decoding. While previous efficiency approaches reduce costs by discarding tokens or utilizing continuous latent representations, these lossy methods fundamentally sacrifice interpretability and auditability. In this work, we introduce a novel compression framework for intermediate reasoning. We apply Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) to reasoning corpora to learn a compressed vocabulary of Private Use Area (PUA) tokens, each representing frequent semantic spans. After expanding the LLM's vocabulary, we fine-tune the model via strictly 1:1, our method is lossless. We evaluate our approach on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, and Qwen2.5-32B across four diverse benchmarks. Our method reduces total generated tokens by 14.7% on average with reasoning trace lengths dropping by up to 27.1%, while incurring a negligible average accuracy cost of 1.6 percentage points. Crucially, this approach is orthogonal to existing lossy methods, allowing practitioners to stack lossless and irreversible compression techniques. We demonstrate that a compressed intermediate language provides a highly efficient computational resource that accelerates inference while fully preserving the transparency of LLM reasoning.
authors: Rabimba Karanjai, Suryabhan Singh Hada, Hemanth Hegadehalli Madhavarao, Qun Gu, Libin N. George, Wenhuan Sun, Neha Monga, Richard Williamson, Prakhar Mehrotra
bullets: Addresses the inference cost of lengthy chain-of-thought without sacrificing transparency through lossy token dropping or latent representations.
Learns semantic-span tokens with BPE in the Private Use Area and fine-tunes expanded-vocabulary LLMs using strict 1:1 supervision.
Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, and Qwen2.5-32B across four benchmarks.
Cuts total generated tokens by 14.7% on average and reasoning-trace length by up to 27.1%, with a 1.6-point average accuracy cost.
The lossless approach can be combined with existing irreversible compression methods.

papers.title: Reasoning in Fewer Tokens: Concept-Normalized Multilingual Scratchpads and Reversible Model-Adaptive Reasoning Codes
papers.tldr: A lossless compressed reasoning language reduces LLM reasoning-token usage while preserving interpretable, auditable traces.

papers.abstract: Understanding how spiking neural networks (SNNs) efficiently process data streams is key to (i) studying how biological brains conserve energy for lifelong predictions and (ii) enabling efficient continuous AI inference. In this work, we propose a theory on how an SNN incrementally tracks its corresponding firing-rate network, a continuous-valued neural network (ANN). We prove that the output of a discrete SNN continuously tracks the instantaneous ANN output implicitly determined by the SNN input. Based on this principle, we develop LIF-Stream, a conversion framework for efficient SNN inference over unbounded data streams. It enables the converted SNN to reuse its prior activation state and compute only the activation updates between frames, thereby reducing the average number of time steps needed per frame. Specifically, LIF-Stream controls the SNN to continuously track the reference ANN output, which gives a high-accuracy prediction for every frame. Evaluation on three large-scale streaming inference benchmarks with distinct modalities shows that LIF-Stream achieves the best efficiency-accuracy trade-off compared to high-accuracy SNN techniques.
bullets: The work addresses energy-efficient, lifelong prediction over continuous data streams.
It proves that a discrete SNN can continuously track the instantaneous output of its corresponding firing-rate ANN.
LIF-Stream converts ANNs into SNNs that reuse prior activation states and compute only frame-to-frame updates.
The method reduces the average number of time steps per frame while maintaining high-accuracy predictions.
Across three large-scale streaming benchmarks and distinct modalities, it achieves the best reported efficiency–accuracy trade-off among high-accuracy SNN methods.

(Right) Empirical validation on MOT17 video sequences (Milan et al., 2016) evaluated as a streaming pedestrian detection task. LIF-Stream efficiently tracks the continuous ANN output by updating only inter-frame delta, whereas standard reset-based IF and LIF-SNNs suffer from re-convergence latency overhead for every frame.

Figure 4: Finer temporal resolution benefits ours (post-hoc analysis).

papers.title: Spiking Neural Networks Incrementally Track Firing-Rate Networks
papers.tldr: LIF-Stream lets spiking neural networks continuously track ANN outputs while reusing activation states, enabling efficient high-accuracy inference on unbounded data streams.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-based sparse attention, exemplified by DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), reduces attention computation by selecting a small subset of key-value entries. However, selecting these entries can still require searching the entire visible history. For long sequences, retrieval becomes a major bottleneck, limiting the efficiency gains from sparse attention. To address this problem, we propose LongCat Recall Sparse Attention (LRSA), which combines fine-grained representatives with paged retrieval in an incrementally maintained index. LRSA partitions the sequence into time buckets that can be indexed independently as new keys arrive, without regrouping existing history. Within each bucket, it organizes indexing keys into capacity-balanced directional groups and packs a fixed number of complete groups into each page, retaining a separate center for every group. These centers provide fine-grained representatives for page selection, after which refinement scores members of the selected pages together with sink, sliding-window, and visible unindexed candidates to select the final Top-$K$ logical positions. To execute this retrieval process efficiently, we store members in reordered pages, fuse construction stages according to group size, and share storage for overlapping fixed candidates across queries during chunked prefill. These choices support regular member access while reducing kernel launches during construction and repeated candidate transfers. Moreover, we integrate LRSA into SGLang to maintain the index during inference, overlapping asynchronous index construction for new buckets with subsequent computation and reusing compatible bucket indices and member pages after a prefix match in the original key-value pool. With a 1024K-token context, LRSA accelerates key selection by 4.70$\times$ over DSA and combined selection and attention by 35.60$\times$ over full attention.
authors: Hao Zhang, Bin Xiao, Kefeng Zhang
bullets: Problem: Sparse attention can reduce computation, but searching the entire visible history makes key retrieval a bottleneck for very long contexts.

Method: Partition history into independently indexed time buckets, organize keys into balanced directional groups, and use group centers for coarse page selection before refining candidates to select Top-K positions.
Implementation: Reordered pages, fused index-construction stages, shared fixed-candidate storage, and asynchronous index maintenance improve retrieval and inference efficiency.
Result: At 1024K-token context, LRSA accelerates key selection 4.70× over DSA and combined selection plus attention 35.60× over full attention.
Scope: The reported gains target long-context inference with incrementally arriving keys and prefix reuse.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of LRSA. (a) Each completed bucket is independently partitioned into capacity-balanced directional groups, which are packed into member pages. With the default capacities, the expanded page contains eight groups of eight keys, with one center per group. (b) Queries score group centers and select the Top-Kpage pages using the maximum group score within each page. Retrieved members are combined with sink, sliding-window, and visible unindexed candidates, deduplicated, and scored to select the final Top-K positions for attention. The position map supports deduplication and recovery of original logical positions. Reordered page and slot addresses are depicted as one-dimensional indices for simplicity.

In all panels, solid lines with circles indicate directional grouping, and dashed lines with squares indicate temporal grouping.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) models rely on large pretrained encoders, yet typically process every modality to its full depth, regardless of its computational cost or predictive contribution. This raises a fundamental question: how should limited computation be allocated across modalities to preserve predictive performance? We reveal a substantial mismatch between the computational cost of modality encoders and the predictive benefit of processing them more deeply, suggesting that different modalities require different encoding depths. However, enabling heterogeneous depths introduces a key challenge: representations extracted at different depths must still be effectively fused. To address this, we propose $\textbf{DepthMSA}$, a budget-aware framework that supports flexible modality depths within a single MSA model. Specifically, we introduce combinatorial anytime training, which supervises the fusion head across all cross-modal depth combinations using a single full-depth encoder pass. At inference, a training-free, cost-aware allocator selects the configuration with the lowest validation-calibrated error under a sample-specific FLOPs budget. On CMU-MOSEI, DepthMSA maintains accuracy within one percentage point of the full-depth model while reducing measured FLOPs by 45\%, or by 82\% with a separately trained skip-enabled variant. When a CLIP visual encoder dominates computation, the allocation shifts toward reducing visual depth, achieving 56\% fewer FLOPs at unchanged accuracy. Compared with ADMN, an adaptive layer-allocation method that trains a controller for each budget, the skip-enabled variant reaches its accuracy with 3.2$\times$ fewer FLOPs and lower latency, without any per-budget training. Our project is available at https://pwang322.github.io/DepthMSA/.
authors: Pan Wang, Jie Peng, Zhimin Li, Jingxian Chen, Hui Ji, Huanrui Yang, Pengfei Zhou, Tianlong Chen, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between modality encoder cost and the predictive value of deeper processing.
Uses combinatorial anytime training to supervise fusion across all cross-modal depth combinations in one full-depth pass.
A training-free, validation-calibrated allocator selects the lowest-error depth configuration within each sample’s FLOPs budget.
On CMU-MOSEI, it stays within one percentage point of full-depth accuracy while reducing measured FLOPs by 45%, or 82% with skip-enabled training.
When vision dominates computation, it reduces visual depth for 56% fewer FLOPs at unchanged accuracy; scope is demonstrated on CMU-MOSEI.

(b) Combinatorial anytime training supervises all cross-modal depth configurations using a single full-depth encoder pass. papers.title: DepthMSA: Combinatorial Training and Budget-Aware Depth Allocation for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis

papers.abstract: Reward models and LLM judges are routinely quantized to 4 bits so that scoring many candidates stays affordable, and the usual check is that benchmark accuracy barely moves. That check is close to blind. Across eight reward models from two families (0.6B-8B), three generative judges and four 4-bit quantizers, quantization rewrites 1.1-12.3% of pairwise preference decisions on RewardBench while aggregate accuracy moves by as little as 0.03 points (p = 1.00), because the errors it fixes and introduces cancel. Flips concentrate where the full-precision margin is small relative to the quantization noise scale sigma: a Gaussian approximation Phi(-|m|/sigma) describes the aggregate rate, over-predicting it in all 30 scalar settings and failing for generative judges, and occupancy of the resulting vulnerability window falls from 25% to 7% with model size, which is what makes small judges fragile. The churn stays within noise under benign best-of-16 and becomes clear under adversarial pressure for some quantizers (146:54 harmful:helpful flips on one family, reversing sign on another). Downstream it changes what ships: across six (model, quantizer) pairs from two families, 14.6-65.7% of problems get a different best-of-64 selection while only 2.6-9.6% get a different final answer, with selections changing 5-8x more often than answers in every pair, and the pair the benchmark calls identical (0.03 points, p = 1.00) still changes 34.5% of them. Benchmark churn ranks that downstream change (rho = 0.89); benchmark accuracy does not order it reliably. Held-out audits then locate the useful diagnostic in the margin rather than the Gaussian: every margin-based predictor orders flips identically (AUC 0.927), and on the level a directly measured churn rate wins in-distribution. As a routing signal it is matched by plain top-k. The contribution is the characterization, not the model.
authors: Omkar Shewale, Deepak Kumar, Divakar Kumar Yadav
bullets: Across eight reward models, three generative judges, and four quantizers, quantization changed 1.1–12.3% of RewardBench pairwise preferences while aggregate accuracy sometimes shifted by only 0.03 points.
Decision flips concentrate in a vulnerability window where full-precision margins are small relative to quantization noise; this window shrinks from 25% to 7% as model size increases.
Under adversarial pressure, some quantizers produced strongly harmful flip patterns, while benign best-of-16 evaluation often kept churn within noise.
Downstream, 14.6–65.7% of best-of-64 selections changed, versus 2.6–9.6% of final answers; benchmark churn tracked this change better than benchmark accuracy.
Margin-based predictors identified flips well (AUC 0.927), but directly measured churn was most useful in-distribution and was matched by plain top-k routing.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Relative noise and exposure both fall with size. (a) The scale-free noise ratio σ/std(mBF16) within each family; raw σ is confounded by architecture-specific logit scale. (b) Window occupancy P (z < 2) falls steeply with size. Small models are relatively noisier and more exposed; the two are the same fact in different units.

Figure 5: (a) Adversarial fooling rate by model and quantizer, both families (dotted line separates them); ∗ marks p < 0.05 for INT4-RTN. (b) Best-of-N regret against the BF16 selector on the 1,000-problem pool, with problem-level bootstrap intervals. Point estimates increase with N in both families, but only N = 4 and N = 16 for Skywork-0.6B exclude zero.

Figure 2: (a) Flip rate versus normalized margin z = |mBF16|/σ for all six Skywork models under NF4. After rescaling by each model’s own σ, the curves lie close to the additive-noise prediction Φ(−z) (dashed). This is one family under one quantizer, not a claim of exact collapse. (b) Predicted versus observed aggregate flip rate for all 30 model× quantizer settings. Every point lies below the diagonal: the Gaussian expectation over-predicts, so the envelope is conservative for these scalar models.

Figure 1: (a) Decision flip rate falls with reward model size (bootstrap 95% CIs); monotone for NF4, FP4 and INT4-RTN, with one GPTQ exception at Llama-3.2-1B. (b) The accuracy delta that a practitioner would actually look at shows no such structure and is near zero in several of the highest-churn settings.

Figure 4: Accuracy–cost frontier for selective escalation, Skywork pair, N = 32, 1,000 problems, cost in proposer forward passes at the measured ratio R = 5.03. The GRM pair is omitted: its measured R is 1.00, so its cost axis is degenerate. Error bars are problem-level bootstrap intervals.

Table 3: Decomposition of quantization damage. Raw σ is in score units and differs by architecture (Llama-3.2 heads emit smaller margins), so compare it within a family; occupancy P (z < 2) is scale-free and is what predicts the flip rate. Nearly all flips fall inside the window, and the model’s prediction exceeds the observation in every row. The comparison set pools RewardBench with every correct-vs-trap comparison from the adversarial pools for NF4, INT4-RTN and GPTQ (n = 6,765), so those rates are diluted by the wider-margin trap comparisons and sit below the RewardBenchonly rates of Table 1. FP4 and all Qwen3-4B rows have no trap runs and use RewardBench only (n = 2,985), which is why their rates coincide with Table 1.

Table 5: Held-out audit and cross-distribution transfer. Mean absolute error in predicting churn on data not used to fit the predictor; n counts (setting × seed) rows, and the last two columns count the rows in which the σ model’s absolute error is the smaller one. A paired bootstrap on the transfer rows (2,000 resamples of source and target problems, refitting σ and the logistic on each draw) puts the σ-over-rate difference entirely below zero in 16/19 settings for RewardBench → traps (mean −2.80 pp) and 13/19 for the reverse (−2.25 pp); against the logistic the same test gives 3/19 and 2/19 wins against 8/19 and 0/19 losses. Per-setting values for every row are released in paper/audit per setting.csv.

Table 9: The downstream result replicates across families and quantizers. Six (model, quantizer) pairs, each against its own BF16 reference, identical pools, draws and tie rule. Selections change far more often than answers in every pair, by 5.3–7.7× at N = 64, and only 4 of the 24 accuracy intervals (6 pairs × 4 values of N ) exclude zero. ∆acc. is BF16 minus quantized, so positive favours BF16.

Table 1: Decision churn is invisible to accuracy. 4-bit quantization changes a large fraction of RewardBench decisions while aggregate accuracy moves little. The Llama-3.2-1B/NF4 row is the extreme case: 3.99% of decisions flip and accuracy moves 0.03 points, with harmful and helpful flips almost perfectly balanced. Harm:help is (BF16 right, quantized wrong):(the reverse); p is an exact two-sided McNemar test. n = 2,985 pairs.

Among comparisons with z < 2: the share originally correct, the harmful:helpful counts, the per-comparison flip rate of originally-correct and originally-incorrect decisions, and the one-parameter model’s over-prediction factor on the harmful side. Incorrect decisions flip more often per comparison; the count asymmetry is base rates.

Table 20: Adversarial best-of-4 fooling rates (n = 1,260 problems; each has one verified correct and three verified-wrong but persuasive candidates). “Fooled” means the model ranked a verifiably wrong solution first. Pooled rows aggregate each family; † marks tests that are significant at raw p < 0.05 but do not survive Benjamini–Hochberg correction at q < 0.05 across all 66 tests in the paper (also used in Table 1).

A negative value lowers positive margins but, as Table 16 shows, is mostly scale contraction rather than an additive tilt; it should not be read as bias against the correct answer. INT4-RTN is negative in all seven models; NF4’s shift is smaller and changes sign by model.
Table 4: Selective escalation, N = 32, 1,000 problems. “Gap”: fraction of the gap recovered; “Save”: compute reduction at measured R = 5.03. GRM’s measured R is 1.00 (“–”).

Table 19: Every headline claim, the population it is measured on, where the evidence appears, and how uncertainty is quantified.

The two 7B judges move in opposite directions under the same quantizer. Qwen2.5-3B was excluded: its BF16 trap error is too high for a fooling-rate comparison to be meaningful. papers.selection_reason: Characterizes decision instability caused by 4-bit quantization of reward models, relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: The Vulnerability Window: Decision Instability in Quantized Reward Models
papers.tldr: 4-bit quantization can substantially alter reward-model and LLM-judge decisions despite nearly unchanged benchmark accuracy, especially for small-margin cases and downstream candidate selection.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains a student to match a teacher's output distribution. However, full-vocabulary KD requires costly output-head backpropagation. To reduce this cost, we introduce Distillation with Errors (DWE). Our key insight is that minibatch training already approximates the training gradient, so per-position backpropagation does not need to be exact. DWE therefore exploits the zero-sum structure of logit gradients to construct sparse paired gradient estimates whose expectation matches the full-vocabulary gradient. It then uses geometry-aware pairing and stratified sampling to further reduce estimation variance. We prove that the estimator is unbiased and evaluate DWE's gradient estimation accuracy and training efficiency. At the same sampling budget, DWE reduces hidden-state and output-weight gradient MSE by 63.5% and 57.9%, respectively, compared with importance sampling. In off-policy KD, it achieves up to a $1.95\times$ output-head speedup and reduces training time by 10.4-15.7% relative to full-vocabulary KD. In on-policy distillation (OPD), it achieves up to a $2.20\times$ output-head speedup. DWE maintains competitive downstream performance in both settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/dwe-lab/DWE.
bullets: Targets the high cost of backpropagating through the full vocabulary during knowledge distillation.
Builds sparse paired gradient estimates using the zero-sum structure of logit gradients, with geometry-aware pairing and stratified sampling.
Proves the resulting gradient estimator is unbiased.
Reduces gradient-estimation MSE versus importance sampling and speeds up the output head in off-policy and on-policy distillation while maintaining competitive downstream performance.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of DWE. The positive and negative parts of the logit gradient are normalized into two sampling distributions (a). Both distributions are reordered using the fixed geometric order τ (b), then sampled at shared, stratified quantiles to obtain K coordinate pairs (c). Averaging the corresponding paired estimates gives a sparse gradient estimate that preserves the full gradient in expectation. This estimate enables backpropagation through only the selected output rows, at most 2K per token (d). The illustration uses K = 2.

Figure 2: Output-head time across model scales. (a) We compare mean total output-head time for Full and DWE at 8K token positions across the three model configurations. Stacked segments show forward and backward time; DWE forward includes estimator preparation. (b) Each cell reports DWE’s total output-head speedup over Full for the corresponding model configuration and number of token positions.

Figure 5: Training dynamics. Full and DWE across three training seeds. Columns correspond to seeds 42, 43, and 44. The top row shows response-token throughput; the bottom row shows full-vocabulary reverse KL. Curves summarize consecutive blocks of five updates. Each method is evaluated on its own responses.

Figure 3: Gradient estimation error and output-head time. Top: relative MSE with 95% Monte Carlo confidence intervals. Bottom: DWE runtime on 1K positions, with Full as reference. Both methods use 2K draws per token.
Figure 4: Output-head time. Runtimes are normalized to Full. Labels above the bars give total speedups, and times below give Full’s absolute runtime.

Table 4: KD training configuration. Shared settings across student sizes.
Table 7: OPD evaluation benchmarks. Question counts refer to the evaluated sets.

Table 11: Reasoning performance across 13 benchmarks. Scores (%) are means with standard deviations over repeated evaluations. Superscripts give evaluation counts. Best scores among Full, IS, and DWE are bolded. Average is the unweighted mean across all 13 benchmarks.
Table 10: OPD training runtime. We report mean seconds per update across seeds (top) and by stage (bottom). Stage timings average three updates after two warmups.

papers.selection_reason: Sparse unbiased gradient estimation reduces training compute for knowledge distillation, an efficiency contribution.
papers.title: Distillation with Errors: Sparse Unbiased Backpropagation for Knowledge Distillation
papers.tldr: DWE makes knowledge distillation cheaper by using sparse, unbiased estimates of full-vocabulary gradients with variance-reducing sampling.

papers.abstract: The Query-derived Erase Direction (QED) augments a rank-one linear attention update with a key-orthogonal query component. Under scalar decay, this correction leaves the eigenvalues of each homogeneous state transition unchanged, while the propagation of an initial perturbation depends on the ordered product of these transitions. We construct a periodic token sequence with fixed key and query projections for which every one-step spectral radius is below one but the spectral radius of the period product exceeds one. The same construction yields a sufficient condition for mean-square growth under independent uniform token sampling. For rank-one erasure with channel-wise decay, we derive a necessary and sufficient spectral-norm test for one-step nonexpansiveness that can be evaluated in $O(d)$ time. The test agrees with direct singular value decomposition on all 1,800 operators evaluated. In a counterfactual replay of a selected head of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, the terminal gain on a 4,096-token repeated-text sequence increased from 0.99938 to 1.3977 with the feature and checkpoint gate trajectories held fixed.
bullets: Shows a periodic sequence where every transition has spectral radius below one, yet the period product is expansive.
Extends the construction to sufficient conditions for mean-square growth under independent uniform token sampling.
Derives a necessary-and-sufficient spectral-norm criterion for channel-wise-decay rank-one erasure, computable in O(d) time.
The criterion matched direct SVD on all 1,800 tested operators.
In a Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base replay, terminal gain rose from 0.99938 to 1.3977 under repeated text with feature and gate trajectories fixed.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of rank-one linear attention dynamics, relevant to linear-attention efficiency research.
papers.title: Recurrent Amplification and Exact Nonexpansiveness Criteria for Query-Driven Erasure
papers.tldr: QED can cause recurrent amplification despite contractive individual steps, while rank-one erasure admits an exact fast test for one-step nonexpansiveness.

papers.abstract: Low-bit activation quantization of large language models remains challenging, as a small number of dominant directions dictate the quantization range. State-of-the-art methods isolate these directions in a high-precision subspace through transformations calibrated offline and folded into the weights, which fixes the subspace for all prompts, leaving each prompt's few unique directions unprotected, and rules it out wherever no weight can absorb the transformation. We present PLoQ, a prompt-adaptive low-rank decomposition that extracts the dominant activation components before quantization, quantizes them separately, and restores them within the layer's GEMM, without modifying the weights. The low-rank component's basis is estimated from each prompt during prefill and reused throughout decoding. At the same bit width as state-of-the-art mixed-precision quantization (4-bit weights, activations and K/V cache with an eighth of the channels at 8 bits, about 4.2 bits per activation on average), PLoQ outperforms it on all six Llama and Qwen models from 1B to 70B parameters, at up to 8k tokens (16k on two of them), recovering up to 46% of the perplexity that the state of the art still loses to 4-bit activations. On Llama-3.1-8B at 8k tokens it adds only 4% to prefill and 8% to decoding.
authors: Faraz Tahmasebi, Michael Pellauer, Hyoukjun Kwon, Sitao Huang
bullets: Addresses prompt-specific dominant activation directions that fixed, offline-calibrated subspaces may miss.
Extracts dominant components during prefill, quantizes them separately, and restores them within the layer’s GEMM.
Reuses each prompt’s low-rank basis throughout decoding, avoiding weight modifications.
At comparable mixed-precision bit width, outperforms the referenced state of the art across six Llama and Qwen models from 1B to 70B parameters.
Recovers up to 46% of perplexity lost by 4-bit activations, with 4% prefill and 8% decoding overhead on Llama-3.1-8B at 8k tokens.

figures.caption: Figure 2. PLoQ at one layer input, on an activation example (6 tokens, 12 channels; color: magnitude). Steps 1–3 and the INT8 GEMM are the offline mixed-precision method: a calibrated basis U , folded into the weights, gathers the directions that are large in every prompt into a block kept at 8 bits. PLoQ (dashed box) handles the remaining 4-bit part Xc, whose dominant direction depends on the prompt. Once per prompt, during prefill, it estimates that direction V from a sample of the prompt’s tokens (4). Each token’s component along it, C = XcV ⊤, is subtracted (5, 6); the remainder R has a smaller range and is quantized to 4 bits with clipping, and C to 4 bits on its own scale (7). C is restored through k extra rows VW⊤ c of the 4-bit GEMM (8). V and VW⊤ c are kept for decoding.

Figure 4. Activation magnitudes |X| over tokens and channels (max-pooled to a 128× 128 grid) for one WikiText-2 prompt on Llama3.2-1B, layer 15. From left to right: the original input; after QuaRot’s Hadamard rotation, all at 4 bits; what a calibrated 8-bit block leaves at 4 bits; and what PLoQ leaves at 4 bits after subtracting the prompt’s own 32 leading directions. The last two share one scale. Each title gives the mean per-token range, which sets the token’s 4-bit step. PLoQ narrows the calibrated block’s range by 12% at the attention input and by 47% at the down-projection input, where a few tokens carry very large values; averaged over all 16 layers, by 10% and 27%.

Figure 1. Four ways to treat the dominant activation directions, Llama-3.1-8B, W4A4KV4, 8k tokens. QuaRot (Ashkboos et al., 2024b): a rotation, all activations at 4 bits. ResQ (Saxena et al., 2025): a calibrated eighth of the directions at 8 bits and the rest at 4. Per-prompt: each prompt’s own leading eighth at 8 bits instead, mapped into the 8-bit channels by a per-prompt block reflection. (b) Prefill time relative to ResQ on an RTX 4090, batch 1. Per-prompt is unfused: ResQ’s time plus its measured extra work; dotted: lower bound, at the GPU’s peak fp16 rate.

papers.selection_reason: Prompt-adaptive low-bit quantization of LLM activations and KV cache for memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: PLoQ: A Prompt-Specific Low-Rank Basis for 4-bit Quantization of LLM Activations
papers.tldr: PLoQ improves 4-bit LLM activation quantization by adapting a low-rank protection subspace to each prompt without changing model weights.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent each image with hundreds of visual tokens, which can make inference costly even when a prompt depends on only part of the image. Dynamic Token Merging (DTM), introduced in MrT5 for byte-level text encoders, learns which tokens to remove: a lightweight delete gate scores contextualized hidden states, acts as a differentiable attention bias during training, and physically removes tokens at inference. We argue that DTM is a general token deletion framework rather than a byte-level technique, and extend it to the vision modality and to decoder-only models. Applying DTM to T5Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 yields V-MrT5Gemma2, which deletes visual tokens inside a bidirectional multimodal encoder, and V-MrGemma3, which compacts the prompt and its key-value caches during decoder-only prefill. Across ten benchmarks, DTM's advantage over attention-based and random deletion grows with the deletion rate and is largest on document, chart, and scene-text reading. At 80% visual token deletion (approximately 60% fewer FLOPs), DTM raises accuracy over FastV from 51.8 to 63.0 on ChartQA and from 63.3 to 67.8 on TextVQA with V-MrT5Gemma2, as well as from 62.2 to 68.8 and from 71.2 to 75.1 with V-MrGemma3, retaining 90-96% of unpruned performance on both tasks with significant efficiency gains. These results support DTM as a general framework for efficient transformers.
authors: Chris Gu, Marco Andono Sie, Nathan Zhou, Christopher Potts, Julie Kallini
bullets: VLMs often process hundreds of visual tokens, creating unnecessary inference cost when only part of an image matters.
DTM uses a lightweight delete gate to score contextualized tokens, trains deletion differentiably, and physically removes tokens during inference.
The framework is extended to bidirectional multimodal encoders and decoder-only models, producing V-MrT5Gemma2 and V-MrGemma3.
With 80% visual-token deletion—about 60% fewer FLOPs—DTM outperforms FastV on ChartQA and TextVQA while retaining 90–96% of unpruned performance.
Benefits increase at higher deletion rates and are strongest for document, chart, and scene-text reading tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Dynamic Token Merging (DTM) in encoder–decoder and decoder-only VLMs. (a) V-MrT5Gemma2 deletes selected visual tokens before encoder layer k, retaining all text tokens. The shortened encoder output feeds the decoder’s merged self- and cross-attention. (b) V-MrGemma3’s prefill uses bidirectional attention within images and causal attention for text, caching the full prompt before the gate and the compacted prompt after it; decoding reuses these caches and appends generated K/V without further deletion. Both diagrams show hard deletion at inference. The gate and deletion rule are the same in both architectures; only where the gate takes effect differs.

Figure 2: One 60%-trained T5Gemma 2 1B–1B checkpoint (V-MrT5Gemma2) across inference budgets, deletion after layer 5. Each curve holds one task- and method-specific checkpoint fixed and evaluates it at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate, 60%, is highlighted. DTM’s advantage widens as the inference budget tightens beyond the training target.

Figure 6: T5Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 language-backbone architectures. Visual tokens enter after SigLIP encoding, pooling, and image projection. (a) T5Gemma 2 uses a bidirectional encoder and a decoder with merged self- and cross-attention. Each decoder block projects the final normalized encoder states H into its own keys and values. (b) Gemma 3 uses a decoder-only backbone. Here Le and Ld denote encoder and decoder depths: both are 26 for T5Gemma 2 1B–1B and 18 for 270M–270M; Gemma 3 4B has L = 34 decoder blocks.

Figure 7: Matched-rate evaluation on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B (V-MrT5Gemma2), deletion after layer 5. Each point uses a model trained and evaluated at the deletion rate δ on the horizontal axis. DTM leads on all ten benchmarks at 60% and 80% deletion; at 20–40%, the methods are close.

Figure 8: Matched-rate evaluation on Gemma 3 4B (V-MrGemma3), deletion after five decoder layers during prompt prefill. Each point uses a model trained and evaluated at the deletion rate δ on the horizontal axis. DTM leads on nine benchmarks at 80% and six at 60%; at 20–40%, the methods are close.

Figure 4: Spatial evidence retention at matched 80% visual token deletion after layer 5. Bars show the mean percentage of evidence patches retained on the same eligible questions for each model–dataset pair; dashed lines mark the expected retention of random deletion. T5 1B, T5 270M, and G3 4B denote T5Gemma 2 1B–1B, T5Gemma 2 270M–270M, and Gemma 3 4B. DTM retains the most evidence in 22 of 24 comparisons.

Figure 3: One 60%-trained Gemma 3 4B checkpoint (V-MrGemma3) decoder-only across inference budgets, deletion after five decoder layers during prefill. Each curve holds one checkpoint fixed across deletion rates from 10% to 90%, with 60% highlighted. V-MrGemma3 shows the same widening advantage at 80–90% deletion.

Figure 5: Soft and hard visual token deletion in DTM. Vision and text tokens, denoted as svi and sti , are processed normally from layers 1 through k − 1. The hidden states before layer k are entered into the deletion gate, producing a score for each token. During hard deletion, hidden states with gate scores less than τ are pruned; the gate scores are applied as biases to only the remaining pre-softmax attention scores. Soft deletion adds gate scores to key columns; hard deletion removes sv1 and sv3 and retains the text tokens.

Figure 22: Deletion-depth sensitivity across budgets for Gemma 3 4B on DocVQA. Panels show individual methods; line colors indicate matched deletion rates (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%); shading marks L5. The attention-based selectors improve with later deletion on this backbone, while DTM stays nearly constant and is highest at 40–80%.

Figure 23: Deletion-depth sensitivity across budgets for T5Gemma 2 270M–270M on DocVQA. Panels show individual methods; line colors indicate matched deletion rates (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%); shading marks L5. The smallest backbone benefits most from later deletion, especially at 80%.

Figure 21: Deletion-depth sensitivity across budgets for T5Gemma 2 1B–1B on DocVQA. Panels show individual methods; line colors indicate matched training and evaluation deletion rates (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%). The horizontal axis gives the number of layers before deletion; shading marks L5. DTM is nearly flat across depth, whereas FastV and φ-R peak at L5 and fall at L6 at every rate.

Figure 16: Checkpoint reuse across deletion budgets at L5. Rows specify training targets; grouped columns specify inference deletion. Gray diagonal cells show matched scores, with the strongest method in bold and underlined. Off-diagonal cells show St(e) − Se(e); negative values favor training at the evaluation rate. All cells average the same ten benchmarks equally. Red shading deepens with the size of the penalty. A 60%-trained DTM checkpoint used at 80% costs at most 0.6 points on average, and on Gemma 3 even a 20%-trained DTM checkpoint loses less at 80% than any baseline.

Figure 9: Matched-rate evaluation on T5Gemma 2 270M–270M, deletion after layer 5. Each point uses a model trained and evaluated at the deletion rate δ on the horizontal axis. The advantage emerges at higher deletion rates on the smallest backbone: DTM leads on 1, 3, 7, and 8 benchmarks at 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80%.

Figure 27: Randomly sampled ChartQA questions at matched 80% deletion on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B (1 of 2). Each row shows the input with its question and gold answer, then the 52 of 256 visual tokens kept by each method in full contrast (outlined), with deleted patches washed out. Below each panel: the prediction and its relaxed-accuracy score. Blue: DTM; gold: FastV; magenta: φ-R; green: Random. DTM concentrates its budget on labels, tick values, and bar ends.

Figure 29: Randomly sampled TextVQA questions at matched 80% deletion on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B (1 of 2). Each row shows the input with its question and gold answer, then the 52 of 256 visual tokens kept by each method in full contrast (outlined), with deleted patches washed out; below each panel, the prediction (long answers truncated) and its VQA-accuracy score. Blue: DTM; gold: FastV; magenta: φ-R; green: Random. All three informed selectors keep much of the scene text; they differ in which words remain.

Figure 26 shows one way the attention-based selectors spend budget that DTM does not. On Gemma 3, FastV and φ-R keep the four corner patches of the image at median rates of 0.50 and 0.42, above the uniform rate of 0.20 on nine of ten benchmarks, whereas DTM keeps them at 0.02–0.12 on every model and benchmark. The two attention-based selectors also agree with each other far more than either agrees with DTM (median Cohen’s κ of 0.59, against 0.29 and 0.30), while DTM’s keep-sets agree across the three separately trained backbones (median κ 0.63, against 0.34 for FastV and 0.29 for φ-R). Gates trained on different models thus converge on similar selections.

Figure 20: Sensitivity to deletion depth on DocVQA. Models are separately trained and evaluated at 40% (dotted) or 80% (solid) deletion with the gate after each layer. The horizontal axis gives the number of layers before deletion; shading marks L5, the setting used in our main experiments. On T5Gemma 2 1B–1B, the attention-based selectors drop when they read the first global-attention layer (L6), whereas DTM does not.

Table 2: Matched-rate evaluation at 40% and 80% visual token deletion for T5Gemma 2 (1B– 1B) and Gemma 3 (4B), deletion after layer 5. Each score comes from a model trained and evaluated at the given deletion rate δ; Base is the unpruned model fine-tuned in the same way. Bold marks the best method per column within each model; each task uses its own metric (Section 5). The gray row gives the percentage of language-model FLOPs saved, which is the same for every method. Figures 2 and 3 include 60%, and Figures 7–9 (appendix) show 20–80%. DTM’s lead grows with the deletion rate on both architectures and is largest on DocVQA, ChartQA, and TextVQA.

Figure 10: Fixed checkpoints on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B trained at 20% (a) and 40% (b) deletion. Each curve evaluates one checkpoint at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate is highlighted. Blue diamonds: DTM; gold triangles: FastV; magenta crosses: φ-R; green circles: Random; dotted line: unpruned Base, fine-tuned the same way. Trained at 40%, DTM leads on nine benchmarks at 80% inference deletion; checkpoints trained at only 20% transfer less well, and DTM leads on half.

Figure 11: Fixed checkpoints on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B trained at 60% (a) and 80% (b) deletion. Each curve evaluates one checkpoint at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate is highlighted. Blue diamonds: DTM; gold triangles: FastV; magenta crosses: φ-R; green circles: Random; dotted line: unpruned Base, fine-tuned the same way. Trained at 60% or 80%, DTM leads on all ten benchmarks at 80% and 90% inference deletion.

Figure 12: Fixed checkpoints on Gemma 3 4B trained at 20% (a) and 40% (b) deletion, deletion during prefill. Each curve evaluates one checkpoint at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate is highlighted. Blue diamonds: DTM; gold triangles: FastV; magenta crosses: φ-R; green circles: Random; dotted line: unpruned Base, fine-tuned the same way. Even DTM checkpoints trained at 20% or 40% lead on all ten benchmarks at 80% and 90% inference deletion.

Figure 13: Fixed checkpoints on Gemma 3 4B trained at 60% (a) and 80% (b) deletion, deletion during prefill. Each curve evaluates one checkpoint at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate is highlighted. Blue diamonds: DTM; gold triangles: FastV; magenta crosses: φ-R; green circles: Random; dotted line: unpruned Base, fine-tuned the same way. Trained at 60%, DTM leads on all ten benchmarks at 80% and 90% inference deletion; trained at 80%, on nine.

Figure 14: Fixed checkpoints on T5Gemma 2 270M–270M trained at 20% (a) and 40% (b) deletion. Each curve evaluates one checkpoint at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate is highlighted. Blue diamonds: DTM; gold triangles: FastV; magenta crosses: φ-R; green circles: Random; dotted line: unpruned Base, fine-tuned the same way. The smallest backbone transfers less well from low training targets: DTM leads on five or six benchmarks at 80% and 90% inference deletion.

Figure 15: Fixed checkpoints on T5Gemma 2 270M–270M trained at 60% (a) and 80% (b) deletion. Each curve evaluates one checkpoint at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate is highlighted. Blue diamonds: DTM; gold triangles: FastV; magenta crosses: φ-R; green circles: Random; dotted line: unpruned Base, fine-tuned the same way. Trained at 60%, DTM leads on all ten benchmarks at 80% inference deletion (eight at 90%); trained at 80%, on eight and six.

Figure 19: Query aggregation for FastV and φ-R on T5Gemma 2 270M–270M, matched deletion after layer 5. Variants and line styles as in Figure 17. On the smallest backbone, text queries help φ-R on DocVQA and TextVQA but not FastV; neither reaches DTM at 60–80% deletion on these tasks.

Figure 18: Query aggregation for FastV and φ-R on Gemma 3 4B, matched deletion after five decoder layers during prefill. Variants and line styles as in Figure 17. FastV again prefers all-query scoring (35 of 36 settings against text last), whereas φ-R gains from text queries on DocVQA and InfoVQA at 80%.

Figure 17: Query aggregation for FastV and φ-R on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B, matched deletion after layer 5. Each selector ranks visual tokens by attention averaged over all valid queries (all mean, used in the main results), over text queries only (text mean), or from the final text query (text last); each variant is separately fine-tuned. Dashed: DTM; dotted: unpruned Base. Allquery scoring is the strongest FastV variant almost everywhere, by up to 17 points on DocVQA.

Figure 16 separates the loss associated with a tighter budget from the additional cost of checkpoint reuse. For DTM, moving from matched 60% to matched 80% deletion lowers the mean score by 3.3, 3.5, and 3.6 points for T5Gemma 2 1B–1B, Gemma 3 4B, and T5Gemma 2 270M–270M, respectively. Reusing the 60%-trained checkpoint at 80% incurs only a further 0.6, 0.2, and 0.2 points. Matched training is not uniformly best: at 60% inference deletion, Gemma 3’s 40%-trained DTM checkpoints average 0.7 points above their 60%-trained counterparts. These means summarize heterogeneous task metrics and are descriptive comparisons of the selected checkpoints.

Figure 28: Randomly sampled ChartQA questions at matched 80% deletion on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B (2 of 2). Presented as in Figure 27: kept tokens in full contrast, predictions and relaxedaccuracy scores below each panel; blue DTM, gold FastV, magenta φ-R, green Random.
Figure 30: Randomly sampled TextVQA questions at matched 80% deletion on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B (2 of 2). Presented as in Figure 29; blue DTM, gold FastV, magenta φ-R, green Random.

Table 10: Normalized area over inference deletion rates 10–90%. All checkpoints are trained at 60% deletion and evaluated at nine deletion rates; the area is the trapezoidal integral divided by the 0.8-wide interval, so values remain on each task’s 0–100 metric scale. The final row weights tasks equally. Bold marks the strongest method within each model. DTM has the highest area on 10 of 10 T5Gemma 2 1B–1B benchmarks, 9 of 10 Gemma 3 4B benchmarks and 8 of 10 T5Gemma 2 270M–270M benchmarks, and the highest equal-weight mean on all three backbones.

Table 1: Three instances of the DTM framework. All share the delete gate, soft-to-hard deletion, and controlled deletion objective (Section 3.2). MrT5 (Kallini et al., 2025) uses PI control with full fine-tuning; our instances use PID control with LoRA. Only the tokens eligible for deletion and where the shortened sequence takes effect differ across instances.

Table 8: Evaluation populations and training steps (T5Gemma 2 1B–1B). Every method and deletion rate is evaluated on the same examples. VQAv2 and GQA use fixed, uniformly random subsets of their validation splits (25,600 of 214,354 and 12,800 of 132,062 questions); every other benchmark uses its full split. POPE evaluates the VQAv2-trained checkpoints. Budgets differ across tasks, so we compare methods within each task rather than at equal training compute. The last column gives the source of the evidence regions in Figures 4 and 24, which are computed on the evaluated examples that have at least one evidence region (“With evidence”); OCR-word regions are the words that spell a gold answer.

Table 4: PI versus PID deletion-rate control on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B at all four training targets. Each DTM arm is retrained with the derivative term disabled (kd = 0), changing nothing else (L5, c = −22, τ = −7). Scores are best in-training validation scores at the trained deletion rate; tracking error |et| and overshoot above the target are in percentage points of training-time deletion. The derivative term tightens tracking at every target (lower mean |et| in 19 of 20 pairs, one tie) but improves accuracy only at the 80% target, where PID wins on all five tasks by 0.81 points on average.

Table 13: What each method keeps on ChartQA and OCR-text benchmarks at matched 80% deletion. Recall is the percentage of patches in each category that a method keeps; uniform selection keeps 20.3%. ChartQA categories come from the dataset’s element annotations (text labels include titles, axis, and legend text; bar and line marks are plotted elements). “Blank” is the share of the kept budget spent on blank patches, which make up 47% of ChartQA patches. OCR text covers every word detected in the image. On charts, DTM keeps more text labels and marks than both attentionbased selectors on every backbone; on documents, the attention-based selectors cover more text.

Table 6: Natural thresholding versus a fixed per-example budget within the same checkpoint (T5Gemma 2 1B–1B, L5). Each row uses the main-experiment DTM checkpoint for that task and training target. Natural deletion removes every visual token with gj ≤ τ , so the per-example rate varies (mean and 5th–95th percentiles shown); forced deletion removes the same mean fraction from every example. The two passes’ FLOPs differ by at most 0.61%. Metrics follow the main results, except that RefCOCO+ uses mean IoU. Natural thresholding scores higher in 16 of 18 pairs, including all nine at the 60% target, by 0.29 points on average.

Table 12: Largest tested deletion rate retaining at least 90% of Base. All checkpoints are trained at 60% deletion and evaluated at 10–90% deletion in 10-point increments; Base is the separately fine-tuned unpruned model. None indicates that no tested rate meets this threshold. DTM reaches the largest budget (ties included) on 9 of 10, 9 of 10, 10 of 10 benchmarks for T5Gemma 2 1B–1B, Gemma 3 4B and T5Gemma 2 270M–270M, respectively, but no DTM checkpoint preserves 90% of Base on InfoVQA.

Table 7: Configurations of the three model backbones. T5Gemma 2 dimensions and head counts apply to both language stacks. Language parameter counts include the shared text embeddings once; totals additionally include the vision encoder and image projector. All three backbones receive the same 256 visual tokens per image, so a deletion rate removes the same number of visual tokens in each.
Table 9: Shared adaptation and gate recipe. Apart from batch size, every listed setting is identical across the three backbones and all plotted arms.

Table 3: Calibrated initial deletion rate versus the default constant gate intercept on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B. Step-0 deletion is the validation deletion rate measured before the first optimizer step; best scores are best in-training validation scores at the trained rate (L5, c = −22). The default intercept starts training at 84–99.6% deletion regardless of the target, whereas calibration starts within 1.5 points of the target in all 16 configurations. Calibration improves the best score by 0.45 and 0.75 points on average at 60% and 80% targets but has no consistent effect at 20% and 40% (−0.13 and −0.05).

Table 5: Attention-score regularization for the delete gate. The first column is the DTM score without regularization (best checkpoint), and the next two are changes relative to it. “Cap 20 without gate” is the cap’s effect on a fine-tuned model with no deletion. The soft−hard gap is the score difference between soft and hard deletion without regularization. Arms within a row share a training recipe. Neither defense improves accuracy on average, so we use neither.

Table 14: Per-dataset input and output lengths and FLOPs savings for T5Gemma 2 1B–1B at L5. FLOPs are calculated consistent with the description in Appendix G. Input text counts are unpadded, nonvisual encoder-input tokens, including prompt and special markers but excluding the generated answer. Output text counts include generated stop tokens and are pooled across the nine deletion rates. The additional selection FLOPs of DTM, FastV, and φ-R are negligible (Appendices G.4.2 and G.4.3). SD is the population standard deviation across evaluated examples. Each saving is computed from summed theoretical forward costs at the recorded input and generatedoutput lengths; the vision encoder and image projector are excluded. The final row weights tasks equally. Savings are nearly constant across benchmarks except RefCOCO+, whose longer prompts and outputs are never deleted.

Table 15: Per-dataset input and output lengths and FLOPs savings for Gemma 3 4B at L5. FLOPs savings are presented in the same way as Table 14. Gemma 3 saves slightly more than T5Gemma 2 1B–1B at every deletion rate.

Table 16: Per-dataset input and output lengths and FLOPs savings for T5Gemma 2 270M– 270M at L5. FLOPs savings are presented in the same way as Table 14. T5Gemma 2 270M–270M saves the least of the three backbones at every rate.

Table 11: Mean normalized AUC over 10–90% inference deletion, by training target. Each mean weights the ten benchmarks equally on their 0–100 score scales. Bold marks the strongest training target for each method within each backbone. The final row counts tasks where the 60%- trained method exceeds all three other methods in AUC. DTM’s mean area peaks at 60% training on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B, 40% on Gemma 3 4B and 60% on T5Gemma 2 270M–270M, and DTM has the highest mean area at every training target on all three backbones.

Table 17: Per-layer FLOPs savings on DocVQA. Each row shows the FLOPs saved (%) when the gate follows the indicated layer, evaluated across visual deletion rates. FLOPs are calculated in the same way as Table 14.

papers.selection_reason: Dynamic token merging for vision-language models directly targets token-level efficiency.
papers.title: Dynamic Token Merging for Efficient Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Dynamic Token Merging removes unimportant visual tokens in vision-language models, substantially reducing computation while preserving strong performance, especially for document and text-heavy image understanding.

papers.abstract: Quantization is a critical piece of the deployment pipeline in the era of large generative models. Low-bit quantization, particularly 2-bits or sub-2-bits, is a notoriously difficult problem, particularly when using a channelwise quantization scheme which has been shown as a leading candidate for hardware-efficiency. The key challenges with low-bit quantization range from limited quantization levels to saddle points or flat regions in the loss surface. In this paper, we look at the problem of flat quantization loss surfaces through a lens of dynamically changing bitwidth. Unlike existing techniques which either change the bit-precision abruptly or keep it fixed, we propose to gradually alter the bitwidth as the model trains. To this end, we propose RelaxQAT, a continuous relaxation of the QAT process. We also provide simple theoretical and empirical insights behind why RelaxQAT helps the QAT performance. Our extensive experiments demonstrate up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision and up to 7.7% better average accuracy on natural language tasks, compared to the leading QAT methods.
authors: Kartikeya Bhardwaj, Mohammed Almousa, Chaitanya Mullapudi, Ananth Balasubramanian, Nithin Ramesan, Tuc Nguyen, Harris Teague
bullets: Targets flat quantization loss surfaces and optimization difficulties in 2-bit and sub-2-bit channelwise quantization.
Introduces a continuous relaxation of the quantization-aware training process with dynamically changing bitwidth.
Provides theoretical and empirical insights into why gradual bitwidth changes can improve QAT.
Reports up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision tasks and 7.7% on natural language tasks versus leading QAT methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1. (a) An example of our proposed RelaxQAT bitwidth schedule which gradually and smoothly reduces the bitwidth. The gradient of the schedule 0 whenever it is approaches 2-bits; this helps to ease into the 2-bit precision instead of an abrupt change. (b) Prior progressive quantization methods reduce the bitwidth suddenly during training like UPQ, or (c) keep it the same throughout.

Figure 7. (a) ParetoQ SEQ simulation for a 1-d optimization problem. QAT gets stuck near the minimum point around step 2000 and stays there until the end of training (10000 steps). (b) RelaxQAT (with just a half cycle bit schedule) converges within the first 2000 steps.

Figure 6. (a-d) Clip-then-Round operation in the existing SEQ (Eq. (2)) creates integers at the extremes (see vertical red dotted lines) since the round operation follows the clip. As the bitwidth reduces, the extreme integers are suddenly lost (e.g., from {−15, 15} to {−13, 13} and so on). This means that a training assumes that the previous range of integers (say {−15, 15}) was available until k = 2b−1 reduces sufficiently; once k is sufficiently small, the round abruptly moves on to the new range of integers (i.e., {−13, 13}). The sudden change in integer ranges can cause loss spikes (similar to UPQ (Lee et al., 2025)) and unstable training behavior. (e-h) RelaxSEQ employs the Round-then-Clip operation (Eq. (3)) which keeps the extremes in floating point as the k reduces. The range of the distribution changes slowly and the extremes stay floating point until the end of the schedule. This causes the loss to change smoothly as the bitwidth shrinks.

Figure 3. (a) A simple 1-d function to minimize. (b) The 1-d function above results in a highly complex 2-d, 2-bit quantization loss surface (generated using LSQ) where the width of the hyperplanes (defined as the flat regions between integer changes) increases with larger scales. Red line shows the QAT trajectory.
Figure 4. RelaxQAT converges significantly faster than ParetoQ.

Figure 2. ParetoQ SEQ with a bitwidth schedule loses extreme integers as k = 2bt−1 decreases with a shrinking bitwidth. RelaxSEQ shows a smooth change in extreme values which results in a smoothly changing loss.

Figure 5. Existing SEQ (Clip-then-Round) with a bitwidth schedule shows an unstable training behavior with sudden loss spikes as predicted by Fig. 2. The new RelaxSEQ with Round-the-Clip has a smooth transition in loss with changing bitwidth. Although, the final loss after the end of schedule was similar for both Clip-thenRound vs. Round-then-Clip, we found that RelaxSEQ resulted in better benchmark scores (see Table 10).

papers.selection_reason: Continuous relaxation of quantization-aware training reduces model memory footprint, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: A Continuous Relaxation of Quantization-Aware Training
papers.tldr: RelaxQAT improves difficult low-bit quantization-aware training by gradually changing bitwidth during training instead of fixing or abruptly switching it.

papers.abstract: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.
authors: Colin Hong, Bryan Shan, Wei Siong Pang, Chengzhi Lu, Xu Guo, Nitin Shivaraman, Tao Luo, Esha Choukse, Kisson Lin, Dmitrii Ustiugov
bullets: Agent execution histories grow over time, driving shared GPU KV-cache demand and limiting throughput.
Tool-operation provenance identifies earlier outputs and turns superseded by later operations; 64% of final-history tokens are removal candidates.
Contexture separates the complete harness history from the model’s execution context and evicts context based on supersession, cache residency, and GPU pressure.
Across two models, harnesses, and benchmarks, it improves SLO-constrained throughput by 20–73% versus the strongest baseline and reduces GPU energy per session by up to 11%.
Live-agent accuracy improves by 1.4 percentage points on average versus unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points.

papers.selection_reason: A runtime context eviction framework for high-throughput LLM agent serving that uses tool-execution information to manage KV cache and improve memory efficiency.
papers.title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
papers.tldr: Contexture improves high-throughput LLM-agent serving by evicting superseded conversation context at runtime while coordinating with shared KV-cache state.

papers.abstract: Sub-4-bit quantization allows mobile devices to run larger LLMs, but its memory savings do not always translate into faster decoding on mobile NPUs. Their matrix units support only a few native integer datatypes, and converting unsupported weight formats on the vector unit can erase the gains from fewer bits. Mixed precision faces an additional constraint: each matrix-unit tile uses one datatype. MixFold executes 3-bit and perfectly symmetric 2-bit weights using native integer operations without expanding the weights to wider datatypes during decoding. MixFold then assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with the matrix-unit tiles, enabling finer-than-layer assignment without disrupting matrix-unit execution. We compare MixFold with llama.cpp Hexagon backend on the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU of a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. Across the Qwen3 model family, MixFold achieves comparable or higher accuracy than llama.cpp's sub-4-bit formats at matched bits per weight, while decoding 1.16-1.41 times faster and generating 1.5-4.3 times more tokens per joule.
authors: Vinnam Kim, Seong Hoon Seo, Junhan Kim, Jaeseong You, An Chen
bullets: Addresses the gap between sub-4-bit memory savings and decoding speed on mobile NPUs, where unsupported formats may require costly conversion.
Executes 3-bit and symmetric 2-bit weights directly with native integer operations, avoiding wider weight expansion during decoding.
Assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with matrix-unit tiles, enabling finer-grained mixed precision without disrupting execution.
On a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 Hexagon NPU across Qwen3 models, it matches or exceeds llama.cpp sub-4-bit accuracy at equal bits per weight.
Reports 1.16–1.41× faster decoding and 1.5–4.3× higher tokens per joule than the llama.cpp Hexagon backend.
