papers.selection_reason: Sub-4-bit mixed-precision quantization and output-channel grouping for memory-efficient LLM inference on mobile NPUs.
papers.title: MixFold: Sub-4-Bit Mixed-Precision LLM Inference via Output-Channel Grouping on Mobile NPUs
papers.tldr: MixFold enables efficient sub-4-bit LLM inference on mobile NPUs by combining native 2-/3-bit execution with tile-aligned output-channel mixed precision.

papers.abstract: Local LLM assistants decode for one user at a time, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and leaves compute idle. Streaming safety checks today trade accuracy against cost. A dedicated guard model is accurate but nearly doubles the latency per token, while a hidden-state probe is cheap but less accurate. We present ToRA, an adapter that runs a second model as an extra row in the generator's decode step, sharing its weights and KV cache. Dual-row kernels read each weight once for both rows. On Qwen3-0.6B, ToRA matches or beats a dedicated streaming guard, with higher F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks. It detects 11.8 points more unsafe responses than the probe at a similar cost, under 4% added latency per token.
authors: Soheil Zibakhsh, Pedram Aghazadeh, Farinaz Koushanfar
bullets: Local LLM decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound, leaving compute capacity unused for safety checks.
ToRA runs a guard model as an extra decode row, sharing generator weights and KV cache through dual-row kernels.
On Qwen3-0.6B, it matches or outperforms a dedicated streaming guard, achieving higher F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks.
It detects 11.8 percentage points more unsafe responses than a cheap hidden-state probe at similar cost.
Scope: results are reported for Qwen3-0.6B and 17 benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (LLMs) represent each video with thousands of visual tokens, and training-free accelerators that prune or merge these tokens lose accuracy on long videos. Analyzing frame similarity and the vision tokenizers of 16 open models, we trace this loss to a step before token selection. Under a token budget, the frames of a long video are sampled farther apart than the roughly 2 s over which frames remain similar. The two-frame 3D patches of models such as Qwen-VL then blend two unrelated scenes into each visual token, a double exposure that arises before any pruning or merging. Fixed-size tokenizers such as InternVL's avoid this blend but respond differently to the same reduction. We propose ESSENCE, a training-free method that tokenizes moments, segments within which frames remain similar, rather than frames. Before encoding, a closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and the tokenizer class to set the number of token grids and the dimension to reduce; visual tokens are then released from later LLM layers. Against five recent accelerators on Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5, ESSENCE achieves higher accuracy in 58 of 60 comparisons at matched mean time to first token (TTFT). With 80% of the tokens, it matches the average accuracy of the full Qwen models at $1.6\times$ faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it exceeds the full model by up to 3.4 points. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhkandsrz/ESSENCE.
authors: Zirui Zhao, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong
bullets: Long-video token pruning and merging can lose accuracy because sparse frames may span unrelated scenes, causing 3D patch tokenizers to blend them before token selection.
The method analyzes frame similarity and tokenizer behavior across 16 open models to guide budget allocation.
A closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and tokenizer class to choose token grids and the reduction dimension before encoding.
Across five accelerators and three video LLMs, ESSENCE is more accurate in 58 of 60 matched-TTFT comparisons.
Using 80% of tokens, it matches full Qwen-model accuracy with 1.6× faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it improves accuracy by up to 3.4 points.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a training-free method to accelerate video LLMs by tokenizing 'moments' (segments of frame similarity) rather than individual frames, addressing tokenization inefficiencies.
papers.title: Tokenize Moments, Not Frames: Tokenizer-Aware Budget Allocation for Training-Free Video LLM Acceleration
papers.tldr: ESSENCE accelerates video LLMs without training by allocating tokens to temporally coherent moments instead of uniformly sampled frames.

papers.abstract: Production retrieval systems are tied to the embedding model that indexed their corpus. Moving queries to a different encoder normally requires re-embedding the whole corpus, and at cold start there are no query logs while every document embedded by the new encoder incurs an API or compute cost. We present ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt), a system for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval. ERA spends a small anchor budget on maximally informative documents, selected from the existing target index via Cosine Farthest Point Sampling, trains a lightweight adapter with a Manifold Alignment Loss that couples directional alignment with orthogonal regularization to prevent representation collapse, and pairs the adapter with a deterministic router that escalates the rare, hard queries that define perceived retrieval quality. Across five BEIR datasets, ERA matches or outperforms point-wise L2 and embedding-conversion baselines, with relative gains of up to 35% nDCG@10 on Arguana, and on clustered corpora its anchor selection also improves prior methods under a fixed anchor budget. With 1.2 ms of adapter and router overhead on top of a ~20 ms local encoder, ERA at a 20% nominal escalation budget reduces end-to-end query latency from roughly 160 ms to 38-86 ms while concentrating escalations on the queries where the projection fails most.
authors: Venkata Chivukula, Zifeng Wang, Jinsung Yoon
bullets: Addresses the costly need to re-embed an entire corpus when changing embedding models, without query logs.
Selects informative anchors using Cosine Farthest Point Sampling from the existing target index.
Trains a lightweight adapter with Manifold Alignment Loss and orthogonal regularization to align representations without collapse.
Uses a deterministic router to escalate rare, difficult queries that most affect retrieval quality.
Across five BEIR datasets, achieves up to 35% relative nDCG@10 improvement on Arguana and reduces latency from roughly 160 ms to 38–86 ms at a 20% nominal escalation budget.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Overview of the ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt) architecture for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval.
Figure 2 | Effect of Cosine FPS anchor count 𝑁 on retrieval fidelity. Performance generally improves with more anchors, with diminishing returns on most datasets.

Table 4 | Escalation rate by query disagreement gap (target nDCG minus projected nDCG) at a 20% budget across all five BEIR datasets. Agnostic is a single uniformly random escalation draw at the same routed count as ERA. Because hard-query buckets are small (e.g., 𝑛=8 on SciFact), a random policy’s capture of them varies widely from draw to draw, whereas ERA’s escalation is deterministic (see text for exact miss probabilities). Here ERA escalates the 20% of test queries with the lowest router scores (text-embedding-004 → gemini-embedding-001, Foundation phase).

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. We present BudgetPV, an agentic budget-aware predict-and-verify system that allocates computation across unresolved subgoals and heterogeneous LLM solvers. BudgetPV uses a cross-solver predictor to guide solver selection for each subgoal and revises the allocation as verification feedback becomes available. The allocation problem changes as proving progresses. Early decisions mainly determine which solver should handle an untried subgoal, while later decisions determine which previously attempted subgoals should receive additional computation. We train the predictor with two objectives for these two stages. Class-weighted cross-entropy improves assignment to less frequent stronger solvers during the initial stage, while plain cross-entropy provides better calibrated probabilities for later allocation among previously attempted subgoals. We evaluate BudgetPV on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench using three progressively expanded solver settings: a strong but expensive solver alone, adding a medium-cost solver with intermediate solving capability, and further adding a cheap solver with lower solving capability. BudgetPV requires less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation to solve the same number of subgoals across the evaluated settings. The experiments further show the computation savings obtained as medium- and lower-cost solvers are added.
authors: Wei Jiang, Ziran Liu, Wei Wang
bullets: Targets the trade-off between expensive, capable solvers and cheaper, weaker solvers in multi-subgoal theorem proving.
Uses a cross-solver predictor to select solvers and revise computation allocation as proof attempts and verification feedback accumulate.
Trains with class-weighted cross-entropy for early solver assignment and plain cross-entropy for calibrated later-stage allocation.
Evaluated on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench across progressively broader solver configurations.
Uses less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation for solving the same number of subgoals; savings increase as cheaper solvers are added.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The overall framework of BudgetPV. A theorem p is decomposed into a proof sketch, and standard proof-assistant procedures first process all subgoals. At each decision step, BudgetPV predicts the success probability of each available LLM solver for each unresolved subgoal and selects a subgoal–solver action based on predicted success, computation cost, and the remaining allowed proof attempts. The selected subgoal is processed using the corresponding solver and verified by the proof assistant. The outcome is used to update the predictions for the next allocation decision.

papers.abstract: An embodied agent cannot afford a large vision-language model (VLM) at every step of a long video, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only uncertain decisions to a large one. Each escalation, however, forces the large model to re-encode a history the small model has already perceived, and this dominates its cost. We present Baton, which hands the large model the small model's visual memory, its key-value (KV) cache over the history. Baton rests on one finding: the large model needs a usable memory, not a faithful copy of its own. A map trained to reproduce the large model's cache matches it most closely, yet brings no gain over the small model alone. Baton instead distills a per-layer linear map, without labels, from the large model's own answers, with the large model encoding only the current frame. Interventions on the map trace the gain to one direction, carried by the middle third of the large model's layers. On RoboMME, Baton beats the small model alone, a pruned or shortened re-watch, and a text memory; as the escalation channel of a cascade it matches re-watching to within about one point at 28-47% less compute, and 8x less per escalation at 64 frames. Its gain grows with the large model, from 8B to 32B, tracks the large model's headroom across eight model pairs from four families, and transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA.
authors: Qiang Zhou, Jianing Deng, Siyan Dong, Jingxian Chen, Han-Yi Lin, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Targets the high cost of re-encoding long video histories when escalating from a continuously running small VLM to a large VLM.
Distills a label-free, per-layer linear map from the large model’s answers, using only the current frame to transform the small model’s KV cache.
The useful transfer is concentrated in one direction across the middle third of the large model’s layers; faithfully reproducing the large model’s cache does not improve performance.
On RoboMME, Baton outperforms the small model alone, pruned or shortened re-watching, and text memory, while matching re-watching with 28–47% less compute.
The approach transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA and scales with the large model’s capability across eight model pairs from four families.

(b) The translation maps are eleven times closer to the large model’s cache than BATON and gain nothing; BATON carries the gain in each of four runs (dots; bars: mean, 95% interval).

(b) Reader compute per escalation on 16-frame histories. (c) At a 25% escalation budget the memory cascade is within 0.7 points of re-watching for both readers.

papers.abstract: Iterative architectures such as looped language models improve parameter efficiency and reasoning capacity of transformers, yet their sequential backbone iterations introduce substantial computational latency. Conversely, parallelizable learnable special tokens (such as the register tokens in Vision Transformer) enable efficient single-pass inference, but often suffer from the absence of sequential refinement and exhibit redundant representations across tokens. To address these challenges, we introduce Depth-Linked Residual Tokens (DepThink), an efficient framework designed for multimodal retrieval and generation. Operating within a single pre-filling forward pass, DepThink appends a sequence of K learnable residual tokens whose hidden states are coupled through a lightweight, learnable residual recurrence. This mechanism enables each residual token to progressively capture complementary information missed by preceding tokens. Theoretically, we prove that DepThink provides strictly expanded geometric directional reachability over standard learnable tokens and guarantees a provable one-step descent advantage. We evaluate DepThink across multimodal retrieval and generation tasks. DepThink consistently outperforms learnable-token baselines and matches or exceeds looped architectures across dense (2B, 8B) and sparse mixture-of-experts (30B-A3B) backbones under both LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning, while accelerating training by up to 11.9 and inference by 4.3 over looped architectures.
authors: Jiangfan Zhang, Wentao Bao, Xian Wu, Xiangjun Fan, Jianpeng Cheng, Jun Xiao
bullets: Targets the latency of iterative transformer architectures and the redundancy and limited refinement of standard learnable tokens.
Appends K learnable residual tokens whose hidden states are progressively coupled through a residual recurrence in one pre-filling pass.
Provides theoretical guarantees of expanded geometric directional reachability and a one-step descent advantage over standard tokens.
Consistently outperforms learnable-token baselines and matches or exceeds looped architectures across dense and sparse MoE backbones.
Reports up to 11.9× faster training and 4.3× faster inference than looped architectures.

papers.abstract: Recent gated linear attention models use state-independent gates, computed from token representations without directly reading the recurrent memory. This design supports efficient chunkwise computation: sequences are divided into chunks of consecutive tokens, with parallel computation within each chunk. However, the same token representation produces the same gate, even when the layer stores different information. We introduce State-Dependent Gating (SDG), which computes element-wise gates from the change in memory over a chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary. This provides state feedback for forgetting while preserving parallel computation within each chunk. We develop fused kernels for Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, Gated DeltaNet-2, and Mamba-3. Our theoretical analysis quantifies the potential reconstruction benefits of state-dependent, element-wise gating under a signal--noise model. We also show that boundary decay is an element-wise ridge proximal step when the gate is held fixed. Empirical evaluation of 1.3B linear attention and hybrid models trained on 100B tokens shows improvements across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, synthetic and real-world retrieval, and long-context understanding. These results demonstrate that SDG is an effective approach to enhancing existing linear attention models.
authors: Renjia Deng, Yuxi Liu, Yutong He, Xue Wang, Kun Yuan
bullets: Existing gated linear attention uses state-independent gates, which ignore the information currently stored in recurrent memory.
SDG computes element-wise gates from the memory change over each chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary.
The approach preserves parallel within-chunk computation and is implemented with fused kernels for several linear-attention architectures.
Theory connects SDG to improved signal reconstruction and interprets fixed-gate boundary decay as an element-wise ridge proximal step.
Experiments on 1.3B models trained on 100B tokens report improvements across language modeling, reasoning, retrieval, and long-context understanding.

papers.abstract: We study causal error-feedback coefficients as design variables for model quantization. Modeling instantaneous quantization errors as independent, zero-mean variables with a common fixed variance, we formulated a metric-dependent trace problem for designing feedback coefficients. The formulation resembles fixed-order GPTQ/LDLQ feedback and supports Jacobian-aware designs that account for downstream error propagation. For a positive-definite metric $\boldsymbol{H}$, we prove that the joint rotation-feedback trace minimum is $n\det(\boldsymbol{H})^{1/n}$ and present an attaining pair using the geometric mean decomposition. Experiments on synthetic networks, trained MLPs, and language models show benefits from downstream-sensitive feedback, but also reveal that trace optimality need not improve finite-level performance. Small QAT experiments further illustrate direct loss-driven feedback tuning with fixed or trainable network weights.
bullets: Models quantization errors as independent, zero-mean variables with fixed variance and optimizes metric-dependent feedback coefficients.
Develops Jacobian-aware designs that account for how errors propagate through downstream layers.
Proves that the joint rotation-feedback trace minimum for positive-definite H is n det(H)^(1/n), with an attaining construction via geometric mean decomposition.
Experiments across synthetic networks, MLPs, and language models find benefits from downstream-sensitive feedback, but trace optimality does not consistently improve finite-level performance.
Small QAT studies demonstrate direct loss-driven feedback tuning with fixed or trainable weights.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on diverse vision-language tasks, but their computational demands limit deployment under constrained budgets, particularly on edge devices. Many works focus on Knowledge Distillation (KD) and try to transfer knowledge from powerful teacher models to students. In addition to reducing model size, visual token compression provides a complementary route to efficiency, but introduces mismatched visual token counts that complicate direct token-wise knowledge transfer. To mitigate this, we propose DVTR-KD, a knowledge distillation framework based on \textbf{D}ense \textbf{V}isual \textbf{T}oken \textbf{R}econstruction, which reconstructs the teacher's dense visual tokens from the student's compressed tokens. We reconstruct visual states after the final LLM layer and at the input to an intermediate layer identified as important for visual-information readout. At the intermediate layer, reconstruction is supervised through the teacher's response predictions rather than by direct token-wise KL or MSE matching. An auxiliary attention-readout loss complements this response-level supervision by aligning how the student and the original teacher integrate contextual information when predicting responses. Evaluations on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DVTR-KD improves the performance of token-compressed students while retaining the inference efficiency afforded by visual token compression.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of knowledge transfer when visual token compression creates mismatched teacher and student token counts.
Reconstructs teacher visual states after the final LLM layer and before an important intermediate layer.
Uses response-level supervision at the intermediate layer instead of direct token-wise KL or MSE matching.
Adds an attention-readout loss to align contextual information integration during response prediction.
Evaluations across diverse benchmarks show improved performance for token-compressed students while retaining inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models typically use a fixed denoising schedule across workloads. We show that the cheapest schedule that preserves quality depends on the task, model, and sampler. We propose Task-Calibrated Denoising Allocation (TCDA), a deployment rule with an explicit error guarantee. Given candidate samplers, paired calibration data, a utility tolerance, and guardrails against degeneration, TCDA uses simultaneous one-sided bootstrap bounds to certify which candidates meet both the utility and guardrail criteria. It deploys the cheapest certified candidate or falls back to the full schedule. The probability of deploying an infeasible schedule is asymptotically at most alpha. Candidates include early prefix decoding, state-reusing continuation, reduced time grids, and confidence-threshold decoding. Across seven datasets and two model families, TCDA certifies reductions in denoiser evaluations by factors of 3.4 on XSum and 2.0 on WMT14 for ELF-B; 8.0 on WMT14 and 4.1 on GSM8K for LLaDA-8B; and 1.33 on OpenWebText for both ELF-M and ELF-L. A validation protocol fixed before generation confirmed every selection on fresh seeds. Across 500 calibration splits, false certification remained below 2% in every setting at a nominal level of 5%. Certified schedules vary across tasks and model scales. Trajectory measurements suggest that when decoded tokens commit is more informative for schedule selection than the remaining latent discretization error. We also find that the ELF reference sampler draws its time grid at random, so reproducible schedule comparisons for unconditional generation require fixing the grid.
authors: Rabimba Karanjai, Linsey Pang, Hemanth Hegadehalli Madhavarao, Richard Williamson, Uma Kona, Prakhar Mehrotra

papers.abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) encode each frame into hundreds of visual tokens, making video inference expensive. Existing methods reduce this cost through similarity-based merging or attention-based selection but face two challenges: Hierarchy-blind Pruning, which overlooks regional compressibility and can discard critical evidence, and Attention Drift, where positional effects and attention sinks shift text-to-vision attention away from task relevance. We propose FoveaTree, a two-stage, training-free visual-token pruning framework. First, Merge-Gain Density Estimation measures the feature distortion caused by regional merging and constructs a quadtree-derived density map to guide token dropping, merging, and retention. Second, Attention Tree Pruning uses the surviving units and inherited tree topology to refine text-to-vision attention in intermediate LLM layers, preserving relevant regional evidence while removing low-relevance content. We evaluate FoveaTree on InternVL3.5-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B across five video question-answering benchmarks and one captioning benchmark at 50%, 30%, and 10% visual-token retention. FoveaTree consistently achieves overall state-of-the-art performance across the evaluated settings, offering a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
bullets: Targets hierarchy-blind pruning and attention drift in Video LLMs.
Estimates regional merge distortion to build a quadtree-based density map for token dropping, merging, and retention.
Refines intermediate-layer text-to-vision attention using surviving tokens and inherited tree structure.
Evaluated on InternVL3.5-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B across five video QA and one captioning benchmark at 50%, 30%, and 10% retention.
Reports consistent overall state-of-the-art performance across evaluated settings, with a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

papers.abstract: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU--GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20--59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40--3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.
authors: Jinbin Luo, Xiaozhe Yao, Shang Yang, Zhijian Liu, Song Han, Qinghao Hu
bullets: Targets heterogeneous cache demands in hybrid models under long contexts and concurrent requests.
Uses a transparent cache pool to redistribute GPU pages without changing cache layouts or backend interfaces.
Streams global-attention prefixes layer by layer during bounded-state computation while keeping generated KV resident.
A scheduler selects resident versus streamed execution and adjusts capacity based on request size and queue state.
Across seven configurations on GB300 and GH200, it achieves up to 2.04× more agent turns, 20–59% lower P50 per-token latency, and 1.40–3.05× better agent P50 TTFT than SGLang with HiCache.

papers.abstract: Decision models enable fast, confidence-aware decisions by scoring candidate answers in a single forward pass, without generating text or intermediate reasoning. Yet reasoning can substantially improve decision quality, raising the question of whether its benefits can be retained without the cost of generating it. We investigate this question with \textbf{GLiDE}, a family of decision models spanning 0.4B to 27B parameters. Building on Qwen hybrid language models, GLiDE enables bidirectional interactions between the context, question, and candidate answers by removing causal masking from full-attention layers. To transfer reasoning capabilities into single-pass inference, we combine soft-target distillation from multiple teachers, including a reasoning model, with progressive post-training on diverse decision tasks. We further explore parameter-free recurrent depth to increase inference-time computation without generating tokens. Across five model sizes, GLiDE lies on the performance--parameter Pareto frontier of the Hugging Face \DI{}, with each model outperforming evaluated alternatives of equal or smaller size. \dmtwo{} (27B) achieves a hidden-set score of 71.52, with an expected calibration error of 2.0\% and a median latency of 92.9\,ms on a single GPU. Further checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth yield GLiDE~27B, which reaches 73.37 with an expected calibration error of 2.1\%.
authors: Sahibzada Allahyar, Julia White, Dhruv Atreja, George Hurn-Maloney, Urchade Zaratiana
bullets: Targets confidence-aware candidate selection while avoiding the latency and token generation costs of explicit reasoning.
Uses bidirectional full-attention interactions among context, questions, and candidate answers in Qwen-based hybrid models.
Combines soft-target distillation from multiple teachers—including a reasoning model—with progressive post-training across diverse decision tasks.
Provides models from 0.4B to 27B parameters that the abstract reports as lying on the Hugging Face decision-model performance–parameter Pareto frontier.

The 27B variant reaches a hidden-set score of 73.37 with 2.1% expected calibration error after checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth; scope is evaluated on five model sizes and the stated benchmark.

A dedicated 255-way readout scores the final hidden state, and a softmax over the offered options produces a normalized probability distribution. Decisions are computed in a single forward pass, without generating tokens or intermediate reasoning. Appendix C details the output semantics and deployment policies.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward models have been very successful in 3D reconstruction with ad hoc attention designs that relate all view patches densely. However, the cost of this dense global attention grows quadratically with the number of views, preventing the model from applying to larger-scale reconstruction settings. In this paper, we argue that most dense attention computations are unnecessary from a classical structure-from-motion perspective: 3D structures stem from geometrically matching regions in 2D. We bring this principle to learning-based feed-forward reconstruction with our Sparse Geometric Attention Reconstruction (SGAR) method. In SGAR, each patch token attends to only a small set of patch tokens from other views, chosen by a lightweight learned key selection module trained to predict cross-view 3D proximity of tokens. Thus, dense global attention is replaced by much more efficient geometric-similarity-guided sparse attention. SGAR is a general method that can be applied to different feed-forward models by fine-tuning. In our experiments, we show that SGAR is the fastest among both state-of-the-art dense and sparse methods and the most accurate sparse one. It runs up to 12-times faster than dense attention at 1,000 views with stable pose accuracy where existing sparse methods fail, and shows the best performance in reconstructing more complete geometries on the same time budget.
authors: Aoxiang Fan, Maria Pilligua, Corentin Dumery, Oliver Heinimann, Pascal Fua
bullets: Dense global attention scales quadratically with the number of views, limiting large-scale reconstruction.
A lightweight key-selection module predicts cross-view 3D proximity and selects only relevant patch tokens.
The approach can be integrated into different feed-forward reconstruction models through fine-tuning.
Experiments report the fastest runtime among compared dense and sparse methods, with the strongest accuracy among sparse methods.
At 1,000 views, SGAR runs up to 12× faster than dense attention while maintaining stable pose accuracy and producing more complete geometry under equal time budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative comparison. Point clouds predicted by FastVGGT, ZipMap and SGAR (DejaView), with the ground truth, on one scene of each of 7-Scenes (chess/seq-03), ETH3D (courtyard, laser scan), LaMAR (HGE) and Mip-NeRF 360 (bonsai, SfM points). Left: four of the input views. Below each reconstruction: the AUC@30 of its cameras. SGAR (DejaView) keeps the structure of the scene where the other efficient models fragment it, most visibly on the long LaMAR trajectory.

Figure 3. Overview of SGAR. We replace the global dense attention of DejaView [8] with our sparse geometric attention as an example. The images are encoded by DINOv2 and augmented with camera and register tokens. A single shared block, unrolled over its L steps, runs frame attention, key selection and sparse attention. In sparse attention, each patch attends to the special tokens of all views, the patches of the reference view, a summary of each cluster, and all the patches of the nearest clusters, so that its cost grows near-linearly with the number of views. Key Selection projects the patch tokens by Wadj into a geometric embedding and clusters the embeddings by spherical k-means into √ N clusters, re-clustered at every step. Each cluster probes its m = 4 nearest clusters, itself first. With the patches sorted by cluster, the selected keys form a block-sparse mask over tiles of 128 tokens. A contrastive loss pulls together the embeddings of patches that observe the same surface in the ground-truth geometry and pushes the others apart.

papers.abstract: We present a new adaptive stepsize rule that biases gradient descent toward flatter minima in both theory and practice, and establish the first uniform-in-time guarantees for both sharpness and loss reduction for a broad class of locally quadratic objectives. Our critically damped Polyak (CDP) stepsizes multiply the classical Polyak rule by $4$ and a mild damping factor. The factor $4$ is critical in that it produces equioscillations around the manifold of minimizers $\mathcal{M}$ to leading order. Damping provably drives convergence to $\mathcal{M}$. CDP thus operates at the edge of stability by adapting its stepsizes to local curvature. Once the loss is small, its projected iterates follow gradient descent on $\log{\lambda_1(\nabla^2 \mathcal{L})}$ along $\mathcal{M}$ to leading order, paralleling the flatness bias of normalized gradient descent (Arora et al., 2022). Unlike normalized gradient descent, CDP step lengths shrink with the distance to $\mathcal{M}$, enabling convergence to an interpolating solution that locally minimizes sharpness at finite learning rate. We establish our theory for a broad class of non-negative losses with locally quadratic Morse-Bott structure near $\mathcal{M}$, capturing regular interpolation regimes in smooth overparameterized neural networks. Empirically, CDP stepsizes produce a flattening effect similar to that of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM, Foret et al., 2021), reducing sharpness even in settings beyond our theory, including nonlinear teacher-student networks and fine-tuning of pre-trained LLMs.
authors: Francesco Caporali, Jason M. Altschuler, Boris Hanin
bullets: Introduces CDP, which scales the classical Polyak stepsize by a critical factor of 4 and a damping term.
Proves uniform-in-time guarantees for loss reduction and sharpness on locally quadratic, Morse-Bott objectives.
Shows damping drives iterates toward the minimizer manifold, while near interpolation they follow sharpness-reducing dynamics along it.
Unlike normalized gradient descent, CDP step lengths vanish near the minimizer manifold, enabling finite-learning-rate convergence.
Experiments observe SAM-like flattening in nonlinear teacher-student networks and pretrained-LLM fine-tuning.

Figure 5. CDP trajectories with κ = 0.1 for 2000 steps on eq. (5), from two different initializations. Left: trajectories over loss contours, with the minimizer manifold M shown dashed. Right: sharpness λ1 along M, parametrized by θ = (θ(1), sin(θ(1))). Depending on initialization, CDP approaches either a global or a strict local minimum of sharpness.

Figure 7. Test loss (left) and top eigenvalue of the test-loss Hessian (right) for smooth tanh student-teacher networks, with varying CDP switching thresholds τ and damping parameters κ. Earlier switching with weaker damping slows loss decreases, but accelerates sharpness decrease.

Figure 9. Schematic CDP dynamics near M. Left: θk = pk + nk oscillates across the manifold, with decreasing normal distance and tangential drift toward lower sharpness. Right: the initial alignment condition selects cones about ±v1(p0).

Figure 14. Trajectories of the curvature λ1(pk) together with the quadratic Morse-Bott surface and the interpolation manifold M = {L = 0}. The CDP trajectories first approach the manifold and then drift along it toward flatter interpolating points, with κ = 0 showing the expected period-2 normal oscillations and κ = 0.12 smoothing it out.

Figure 18. Analogous to Fig. 8, with training sequence length 128 and test evaluation without a sliding window (10 seeds). The optimizer settings and the 500-step CDP phase followed by 2500 Adam steps are unchanged. Left: test perplexity, with a zoom on the final 500 steps. Right: the top Hessian eigenvalue. The lower sharpness persists after the switch to Adam.

Figure 11. CDP dynamics for L(p, n) = 1 2 (1 + p4)n2 over 106 steps, starting from (0.5, 0.1) with κ = 1. Left, loss. Right, sharpness gap λ1(pk) − λ1(p⋆) = p4k. The constant c is chosen to match the final sharpness gap. The loss decays as k−1, while the sharpness gap decays only as (log k)−2.

Figure 19. Qwen2.5-0.5B fine-tuned on WikiText-2. Left: test perplexity. Right: mean of the top Hessian eigenvalues on 16 fixed test sequences, each estimated with 20 Lanczos iterations in fp32. CDP followed by Adam reaches nearly the same final perplexity as Adam alone, with about 7 times smaller final sharpness.

Figure 12. Sharpness dynamics over 1000 CDP steps with κ = 0 starting from (p0, n1,0, n2,0) = (−0.12, 0, 0.03), without noise (left) and with independent centered Gaussian noise of standard deviation 10−3 in n1 and n2 (right). After the eigenvalue crossing, the noiseless trajectory remains on the same branch and sharpness increases, whereas noise allows switching and keeps sharpness near its minimum.
Figure 15. Analog of Fig. 6 for a residual ReLU student-teacher network with 4 hidden layers, N teacher

Figure 17. Test loss and test sharpness for the batch-size experiment. After a GD warmup, the CDP phase decreases λtest 1 (θk) while keeping the test loss small, with similar behavior for batch sizes 256, 512, and 1024.

Figure 13. Trajectories of the tangential and normal coordinates pk and nk. CDP with κ = 0 reaches the flat region quickly but keeps a visible period-2 oscillation in nk, while a mild damping κ = 0.12 contracts the oscillation and retains the same tangential drift. By contrast, GD with η = 0.08 reaches interpolation with much less tangential motion and therefore remains near a sharper point.

Figure 1. CDP dynamics near the manifold of loss minima M. Here θ0 is the initial iterate, p0 its nearest point on M, and n0 = θ0 − p0 the normal displacement. Oscillations bias the iterates toward flatter minima, but this drift slows as the loss decreases. Our stepsizes exploit this tension, damping the oscillations gradually to reduce the loss while sustaining motion along M.
Figure 10. Proof structure of Appendix A. In addition, Lemma A.5 transfers estimates between damping rules.

papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.
authors: Chenyang Jin, Susanne F. Yelin, Andi Gu
bullets: Addresses the speed–accuracy trade-off in decoding rapid syndrome measurements for superconducting quantum processors.
Uses hardware-efficient operations and training in integer arithmetic to run efficiently on FPGAs.
Decodes distance-19 surface-code syndrome rounds in under a microsecond on one FPGA.
Reports a 240× lower logical error rate than existing real-time hardware decoders for the surface code and 16× higher accuracy than Relay for a bivariate-bicycle code.
Can scale across multiple FPGAs or into custom silicon to improve speed, accuracy, or code size.

figures.caption: FIG. 4. Color-code. (a) d = 9 color code: each tile holds an X and a Z check, and dots mark the data qubits. Each convolution computes a tile (dark) from itself and its six neighbors (light). (b) Logical error rate against the time per round, with Rapids compact and fast as in Fig. 1. Chromobius, AQ2-RT, and AQ2 show values from Ref. [15]. (c) Latency against code distance, with AQ2-RT as in Fig. 1(e). (d) Logical error rate against the floating-point operations (FLOPs) per round at d = 9 for models with different channel widths C and model densities (see Methods).

FIG. 1. Rapids on the surface code. (a) Implementation of one neural network block in hardware. (b) Decoder floorplan for Rapids at d = 19 on an AMD VP1802 FPGA. (c,d) Surface-code memory experiments under SI1000 noise at p = 0.15%. AQ2-RT [15], Willow RT [8], and union-find [10, 11] are prior real-time decoders. Rapids compact and fast are two FPGA implementations of the same trained decoder: compact uses a single FPGA, and fast variants use more hardware (up to two FPGAs) to decode faster; the open diamond is an estimate of speed on an ASIC (Methods). (c) Logical error rate against throughput, with the dotted line indicating the 1 MHz throughput required for superconducting processors. (d) Error suppression factor Λ (lines are dotted where a decoder does not reach 1 MHz throughput). (e) Latency against code distance, extrapolated to d = 27 (faded). The dark dashed line is an estimate of the lowest latency achievable upon scaling to arbitrarily many FPGAs (Extended Data Fig. 4). We show the median and 99th percentile latency of AQ2-RT [15]. (f) Breakdown of the d = 19 latency. Doubling the hardware halves the buffer latency, but adds a small chip-to-chip communication delay.

FIG. 3. Gross code. (a) The J144,12,12K code on a torus. Squares are checks and dots are data qubits. Colors mark the six memory banks; the six checks of a data qubit q lie in different banks, so a convolution reads all six in one clock cycle. (b) Logical error rate per logical qubit per round at p = 0.1% as a function of the hardware space-time cost of the decoder. The dashed line shows offline (i.e., not real-time) joint-basis floating-point Relay decoding [13]. X/Z-Relay-BP-1 is the real-time int4 variant of Relay proposed in Ref. [39]. We show the median, 99%, and 99.9% cost of Relay, whose runtime depends on the syndrome. (c) The most accurate decoder (which used C = 128 channels) laid out on two VP1802s at 0.33 µs per round, joined by a stream of activations over transceiver links (Methods).

FIG. 2. Rapids as a parallel-window decoder, co-designed with the FPGA. (a) One CNN block, with numerical precision of the weights w and activations. (b) With L = 2 CNN blocks, the pooled vector zt depends on a bounded window of input rounds. This vector zt can be understood as a representation of the commitment for round t, with buffers of size L on either side. (c) This leads to a streaming design on an FPGA: each layer computes the features of one new round from the rounds it stores in block RAM (hatched), so the layers work on different rounds at once. (d) Monarch linear layers [29] and hardware-efficient nonlinearities sparsify each multilayer perceptron, halving its LUTs. (e) Sparse depthwise convolutions further reduce hardware requirements. (f) Fixed weights compiled into shift-and-add logic require 5 times fewer LUTs than general multipliers.

FIG. 5. Splitting the decoder across FPGAs and across modules. Left: a modular hyperbolic surface code [27], drawn schematically as a {4,5} tiling of the Poincaré disk. Each face is one planar module, with its own decoder (white squares); a link joins the decoders of two modules that share a seam. Right: two adjacent modules, A and B (outlined). The readout of each module enters its own decoder, whose L blocks are cut at block boundaries over K FPGAs. The site stream, C INT8 channels per site, leaves each FPGA once and enters the next. A quantum coupler joins the qubits of A and B, and a classical link joins FPGA i of A to FPGA i of B, carrying the sites at the seam that the convolutions on these FPGAs need.

papers.selection_reason: Hardware co-designed streaming neural decoder with low-latency integer arithmetic, transferable to efficient AI inference.
papers.title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
papers.tldr: Rapids is an FPGA-co-designed neural decoder that enables fast, low-latency, and highly accurate real-time quantum error correction.

papers.abstract: Frontier text-to-image (T2I) foundation models predominantly rely on multi-billion parameter Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) pretrained across massive compute clusters, creating an accessibility barrier for academic laboratories. When training DiTs from scratch on single consumer GPUs (e.g., an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 24\,GB VRAM), practitioners encounter three primary bottlenecks: quadratic attention sequence costs, Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation graph breaks induced by variable aspect-ratio bucketing, and an autoencoder throughput wall where frozen Variational Autoencoder (VAE) operations dominate step latency. In this work, we introduce \textbf{Asuka-FM}, an end-to-end system and architectural framework demonstrating that competitive dual-stream DiTs ($\sim$206M parameters) can be pretrained from scratch on a single consumer GPU in $\sim$160 GPU hours for under \$55. Asuka-FM integrates four core designs: (i) an AdaLN-free dual-stream DiT backbone reducing parameter count; (ii) structured sequence sparsification via Sparse-Dense Residual Fusion (SPRINT) to cut attention FLOPs by over 50\%; (iii) continuous aspect-normalized Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) coupled with shifted square crop training, guaranteeing static tensor shapes while unlocking zero-shot virtual camera control; and (iv) a pixel adaptation phase utilizing a lightweight (10M parameter) Patch Detailer Head operating under velocity regression ($v$-prediction). Evaluated on open-domain benchmarks without benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Asuka-FM achieves GenEval 0.588 / DPG 78.96 scores at 256px and GenEval 0.609 / DPG 78.51 scores at 512px, setting a new Pareto-optimal efficiency standard for democratic foundation modeling.
authors: V\'ictor Rodrigo Gonz\'alez, Pablo M. Olmos, Ignacio Peis, Alejandro Lancho
bullets: Targets quadratic attention, variable-resolution compilation breaks, and VAE throughput bottlenecks in single-GPU DiT pretraining.
Uses an AdaLN-free dual-stream backbone, SPRINT sequence sparsification, continuous aspect-normalized RoPE, and shifted square crops.
Adds a lightweight Patch Detailer Head for pixel adaptation with velocity regression.
Pretrains an approximately 206M-parameter model in about 160 GPU hours for under $55 on consumer hardware.
Reports GenEval scores of 0.588 at 256px and 0.609 at 512px, with DPG scores of 78.96 and 78.51, respectively, without benchmark-specific fine-tuning.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Asuka-FM system-architectural co-design pipeline. Top Row (Stage 1): Raw images Iorig undergo shifted square cropping to enforce static tensor dimensions (X × X) and eliminate JIT recompilations, while continuous aspect-normalized RoPE prevents phase collapse. Precomputed FLUX.2 VAE latents zt receive prepended in-context temporal conditioning (ztime) alongside text representations from a 2-layer adapter without per-block AdaLN parameters. Bottom Row (Stage 2): The 13-layer dual-stream DiT executes SPRINT sequence sparsification: shallow blocks (fθ) supply high-frequency dense skips ft, deep middle blocks (gθ) process macro-semantics over a 75%-sparse grid, and dense decoder blocks (hθ) fuse representations to predict flow trajectories. Finally, the lightweight 10.09M Patch Detailer Head (PDH) transfers representations directly to RGB pixels under native v-prediction.

Figure 2: High-fidelity zero-shot visual synthesis from scratch on a single consumer GPU. Curated opendomain samples synthesized by Asuka-FM (206M backbone) following two-stage pretraining (2562 → 5122) on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU in 149.0 hours ($49.17).

Top Row: (A) Adjacent patch phase step ∆θk across channels k ∈ [0, 7]: uncalibrated normalized coordinates collapse phase shifts to < 7.16◦ (K → 1.0), while calibrated frequencies (ω ∈ [π/4, 2π]) restore angular separation (22.5◦–45◦). Pretraining advances through two latent resolution tiers (2562 → 5122) coupling 75% SPRINT sequence sparsification with fulltoken dense refinement and Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD). Stage 3 transitions the converged 512px foundation prior to pixel space using a 10M convolutional Patch Detailer Head (PDH) trained under native v-prediction across synthetic and real datasets, permanently removing the VAE decode barrier during few-step inference.

Figure 14: Failure mode comparison under continuous RoPE zoom on a complex organic composition. (a) At canonical scale (z = 1.0×), the 206M dual-stream backbone synthesizes a coherent scene with sharp lighting, structured perspective, and clean floral silhouettes. (b) Applying continuous RoPE focal zoom (z > 1.0×) compresses the evaluation grid, inducing: (i) painterly high-frequency texture smearing on the stone pathway, (ii) semantic attribute bleeding (pink pigment leaking into ground cobblestones), and (iii) spatial non-rigidity and warping along linear wooden bench slats.
Figure 8: Quantitative convergence on the toy-diffusion benchmark. Evaluation of SPRINT token drop schedules (r = 0.75 → 0.00) on FID.

Figure 9: Qualitative and quantitative comparison of x0-prediction vs. native v-prediction in 5122 Latent-to-Pixel adaptation under identical random seeds. Native v-prediction eliminates dynamic clipping artifacts and color blowout.

At z = 1.25×, transformer attention capacity concentrates on local topological features, resolving fine rose petal contours and porcelain teacup glazes while strictly maintaining global structural alignment.

papers.abstract: Long-term agents accumulate large external memory stores as interactions unfold, increasing the costs of storage, retrieval, and response generation. Efficiency is constrained by two coupled factors: a growing record count increases retrieval overhead, while longer retrieved contexts increase prefill computation and decoding-time attention costs. Existing methods prune or consolidate records, but pruning can discard useful evidence, whereas consolidation may produce fewer yet longer retrieval units. We introduce MemFolder, a structure-guided memory folding framework that sequentially reduces record count and context length. The framework comprises two core components that share memory groups, using cross-record structure to guide both evidence consolidation and compact representation. RecordFolder grounds entity mentions, progressively selects representative yet complementary anchors, and combines semantic and entity affinity with temporal chaining to consolidate compatible records into fewer retrieval units. ContextFolder encodes the original records within these groups into compact text and uses verification feedback to revise encodings when key facts cannot be recovered. Experiments on the three text-based memory benchmarks LoCoMo, PersonaMem, and LongMemEval and the two multimodal benchmarks M3-Bench-web and M3-Bench-robot demonstrate the strong performance of our methods. Notably, on Mem0, RecordFolder retains 99.0% of the original average performance across the three text-based benchmarks with 50% fewer records, exceeding the strongest baseline by 1.9 percentage points in performance retention. Combined with ContextFolder, existing record compression methods further shorten their output records while retaining most of their performance.

papers.abstract: Deep-research agents repeatedly decide what to search, read, and verify, often using large cloud-hosted language models for action proposal. However, privacy and local control motivate running agents on users' devices, where limited memory and compute favor smaller models and complicate on-device training. Yet inference-time guidance faces three obstacles: exploring alternatives through real execution adds tool calls, prompted self-evaluation is bounded by the agent's judgment, and model-specific guidance risks repeated adaptation costs. We introduce Seer, an inference-time framework providing local guidance that separates the agent's action proposal from learned consequence prediction and value estimation. From a shared corpus of real research trajectories, we train two models: a tool-response simulator on observed call--response pairs and a value estimator on histories labeled with discounted terminal correctness. The simulator and estimator are trained offline and reused across agents without further training. Moreover, Seer executes only the selected action and adds only real tool responses to the committed history, avoiding tool calls on discarded candidates at additional inference cost. Across multiple deep-research benchmarks, Seer substantially improves agent performance for different language models. For instance, GAIA accuracy rises from 13.6% to 41.7% for Qwen3.5-4B and from 22.3% to 50.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Furthermore, our analyses suggest that broader candidate coverage can compensate for imperfect simulation, while prediction and scoring errors limit the benefits of wider imagined search. These findings highlight the potential of reusable models for prediction and evaluation to strengthen small research agents through extra local computation without the real execution of the discarded candidates.

papers.abstract: Flow matching is a versatile framework for generative modeling that transports a source distribution to a target data distribution. A key advantage is its flexibility in the choice of source distribution, such as heavy-tailed and multimodal sources. Yet finite-step sampling guarantees for non-Gaussian sources remain limited. We establish a nonasymptotic convergence theory for Euler discretization of flow matching with linear interpolation. Suppose the source distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ has an everywhere positive, continuously differentiable density, finite total variance $\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}$, and an $L$-Lipschitz score. Using the population velocity field and a suitable time grid, this sampler achieves total variation error at most $\varepsilon$ in $\widetilde{O}(Ld\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}/\varepsilon)$ iterations, provided the target distribution satisfies a mild second-moment condition. These assumptions cover, among many examples, source distributions such as multivariate Student's $t$ distributions with more than two degrees of freedom and finite Gaussian mixtures with shared covariance, while accommodating target distributions with neither a smooth density nor bounded support.
authors: Yuchen Zhou, Lili Zheng, Yuxin Chen, Gen Li
bullets: Addresses limited sampling theory for heavy-tailed and multimodal flow-matching sources.
Analyzes Euler discretization with linear interpolation using the population velocity field and a suitable time grid.
Under positive differentiable source densities, finite total variance, Lipschitz scores, and a mild target second-moment condition, achieves error ε in ~O(Ld·TotVar_base/ε) iterations.
Covers multivariate Student’s t sources with more than two degrees of freedom and finite Gaussian mixtures with shared covariance.
Allows target distributions without smooth densities or bounded support.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical foundation for efficient sampling in flow matching with non-Gaussian sources, establishing non-asymptotic convergence guarantees that improve sampling efficiency.
papers.title: Flow Matching from Non-Gaussian Sources: A Theory of Efficient Sampling
papers.tldr: Provides finite-step total-variation convergence guarantees for Euler flow-matching samplers initialized from broad non-Gaussian source distributions.

papers.abstract: Attention in large language models (LLMs) scores every query against every key with a full dot product. We investigate whether this dot product must be computed completely for attention to be effective. We propose Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA), which keeps the query and key projections intact but only computes a partial dot product, following a static, parameter-free rule set by the token positions: attention becomes sparse in the hidden (feature) dimension, an axis much less explored than token sparsity, rather than over tokens as in almost all sparse attention methods. Based on the structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE), we decompose keys and queries into parts which can be omitted when computing attention. By training LLMs from scratch with HiSA, we find that this partial dot product does not hurt but improves performance compared with the complete product while computing only about a third of the query-key products. During inference HiSA improves decoding speed and shrinks memory footprint. We also extend HiSA to FlashAttention-3 kernels for training and inference. Finally, we motivate our approach by showing that dense attention learns to suppress the attention score parts that HiSA drops. Code is available at https://github.com/ambroise-b/hisa.
authors: Ambroise Borbely, Mathieu Salzmann, Olivier Verscheure
bullets: Targets the full query-key dot product in LLM attention rather than sparsifying across tokens.
Uses a static, parameter-free rule based on token positions and RoPE structure to omit selected query/key components.
Preserves full query and key projections while computing only a partial attention score.
Training from scratch shows no performance loss and reported improvements over complete dot products.
Extends to FlashAttention-3 and reduces decoding time and memory usage; dense attention also learns to suppress the omitted components.

papers.abstract: Large multimodal models can support long-horizon robot manipulation, but frequent model calls incur substantial latency and token costs. The central challenge is determining when agent assistance or intervention is needed and whether errors require correcting robot execution, subtask planning, or both. To address this problem, we propose RoC (Reasoning on Call), an efficient framework that coordinates a low-level policy and a high-level reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor combines temporal visual observations with ordered interaction memory to jointly estimate progress within the active subtask and predict its successor. These predictions guide event-triggered agent review for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. Verified outcomes govern memory updates and subtask transitions, allowing routine execution to remain with the policy while reasoning focuses on decisions requiring additional assessment. On RMBench, RoC improves task success rate by 24.0 percentage points and reduces token consumption by 65.3% compared with the strongest agent-based baseline. It also outperforms the strongest policy-based baseline by 15.1 percentage points in task success rate. Real-world experiments further validate its effectiveness across three long-horizon manipulation tasks. Overall, RoC supports efficient agent intervention and coordinated recovery across execution and planning for long-horizon robot manipulation.
authors: Zilang Cen, Chao Tang, Fangcheng Liu, Weishi Mi, Wei Hao, JiaYu Xu, Dehao Huang, Yehui Tang, Xiaohui Cui, Tingguang Li, Xiaoyuan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the latency and token costs of frequent multimodal-model calls during long-horizon manipulation.
Coordinates a low-level policy with a high-level reasoning agent using an online monitor of visual progress and interaction history.
Triggers agent review to repair execution, revise subtasks, or coordinate both, while verified outcomes update memory and transitions.
On RMBench, improves task success by 24.0 percentage points over the strongest agent-based baseline while reducing token use by 65.3%.
Improves task success by 15.1 percentage points over the strongest policy-based baseline and is validated on three real-world tasks.

During review, the agent can authorize continued execution or intervene through execution repair, plan revision, or both. (b) The agent approves the initial subtask and is called selectively thereafter. Monitor queries continue during policy holds, so routine execution can proceed between agent calls.

papers.abstract: A one-pass decision encoder reads a text, a question and several named options, and returns a probability for each option in a single forward pass. We ask how far Laya, a 421M-parameter encoder of this kind, can be compressed before its decisions change. We count decisions that differ from Laya's own full-precision (fp32) answer, and track calibration (how well confidence matches accuracy, measured by expected calibration error, ECE), on 1,221 synthetic items with the training schemas, 273 with an unseen schema, and 800 out-of-family questions from ARC, MMLU and HellaSwag. Layer pruning of a related model family is known; we add flips, calibration, held-out data and retraining. bf16 changes 0.2% of in-family decisions but 2.2% out of family; 6-bit grouped rounding 1.3% and 5.9%; deleting 6 layers 0.9% and 9.1%, while ECE rises from 5.9% to 39.2%. One fitted temperature, needing no labels, restores it to 3.6%. One scale per tensor fails below six bits, and CPU dynamic int8 changes 30% of decisions, nearly all through one layer. Total variation tracks flips for rounding but not for deletion, and an early exit saves layers over a static cut only if its confidence gate is first recalibrated. Distilling a 16-layer student cuts its in-family flips from 44% to 9% (45% out of family). At equal stored size, rounding flips fewer decisions than deletion. Data are synthetic and LLM-labelled, for one architecture.
bullets: Evaluates decision flips and expected calibration error (ECE) after precision reduction, layer deletion, early exit, and distillation.
bf16 changes 0.2% of in-family versus 2.2% of out-of-family decisions; 6-bit grouped rounding changes 1.3% versus 5.9%.
Deleting six layers causes 0.9% in-family and 9.1% out-of-family flips, with ECE rising from 5.9% to 39.2%; label-free temperature fitting reduces ECE to 3.6%.
Per-tensor scaling fails below six bits, while CPU dynamic int8 changes 30% of decisions, mostly through one layer.
A 16-layer distilled student reduces in-family flips from 44% to 9%, but still has 45% out-of-family flips; results are limited to one architecture and synthetic, LLM-labelled data.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies model compression (quantization, pruning, distillation) and its effect on decision flips and calibration, fitting the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: Sirius-Tiamat: How Small Can a One-Pass Decision Encoder Get Before Its Decisions Change?
papers.tldr: For the 421M-parameter Sirius-Tiamat decision encoder, modest compression preserves in-family decisions better than out-of-family behavior, while layer deletion severely harms calibration unless recalibrated.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers reuse key--value (KV) caches across denoising steps, which quickly becomes a bottleneck for long video generation. We find that quantizing temporally distant cache vectors leads to a large range and high quantization error, but that nearby video tokens in the KV-cache share a persistent pattern per channel. These patterns also vary across videos, motivating rotations that are adapted to each video's unique cache. We propose Temporal Rotation Quantization (TRQ), a method that rotates frames in the cache that are adjacent in time before quantization. For each block of temporally adjacent cache vectors, TRQ fits an orthogonal transform that maps the block's per-channel means to a vector that is close to a constant across channels. To keep the quantization format lightweight, we parameterize this rotation as a tree of $2 \times 2$ planar rotations, each stored with only two bits, followed by a fixed Hadamard transform shared across all blocks. The rotations are fit without gradients or changes to model weights, and we prove that a simple greedy fit is globally optimal for our 'mean-flattening' objective. The transforms are fit online for each new video, and we release fused Triton kernels to make this process efficient at inference. At 2-bit precision and matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over the state-of-the-art method QVG from 90.38 to 92.02 on LongCat-Video-13B and from 86.33 to 87.61 on HY-WorldPlay-8B, as well as improving other metrics.
authors: Ryan Lucas, Petros Prastakos, Rahul Mazumder
bullets: Temporal KV-cache reuse creates memory bottlenecks, while distant-token quantization suffers from large ranges and errors.
TRQ rotates temporally adjacent cache vectors to flatten per-channel means before quantization.
It uses gradient-free, online-fitted trees of 2-bit planar rotations followed by a shared Hadamard transform.
A greedy fitting procedure is proven globally optimal for the mean-flattening objective, with efficient fused Triton inference kernels.
At matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over QVG on LongCat-Video-13B and HY-WorldPlay-8B, while also improving other metrics.

We observe that (i) Within a video, nearby frames share persistent spatial patterns and (ii) the final two panels show that these patterns differ across videos, even at the same frame index and channel. Together, these observations motivate fitting rotations online to each video’s cache and sharing them within local temporal blocks. For other channels, see Section 7 of the appendix.

papers.title: Online Temporal Rotations for 2 Bit KV-Cache Quantization in Video Diffusion Transformers

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agentic tasks require a model to call tools over many steps at contexts of 100K tokens or more, yet many low-bit quantization methods are calibrated on short web text and judged on perplexity. This mismatch is costly: existing quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B at or below 3 bits per weight match BF16 on shorter tasks like AIME, yet in published results solve at most 72% as many tasks as BF16 on DeepSWE, a long-horizon agentic benchmark. We propose NariQ, a trellis-coded post-training quantization method that calibrates on tokens generated by the BF16 model in agent sessions. On Qwen3.8-27B, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight stays level with BF16 on two long-horizon agentic benchmarks, DeepSWE and Terminal Bench, as well as on AIME and RealWorldQA. Our checkpoint at 2.0 bits per weight trails this performance. To our knowledge, these are the first quantizations at or below 3 bits per weight shown to match their full-precision version on long-horizon agentic tasks. We release the files as Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF (https://huggingface.co/nari-labs/Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF), with inference available through our llama.cpp fork at https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp.
bullets: Targets the mismatch between short-text quantization calibration and 100K+-token, tool-using agent sessions.
Uses trellis-coded post-training quantization calibrated on tokens generated by the BF16 model during agent sessions.
At 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight, matches BF16 on DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, AIME, and RealWorldQA.
The 2.0-bit checkpoint performs worse than the higher-bit versions.
Releases Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF and a supporting llama.cpp fork for inference.

papers.abstract: Differentiable programming enables online calibration of numerical models by minimizing errors accumulated along simulated trajectories. This includes estimating physical parameters and training neural sub-models in hybrid configurations. Gradients are typically computed using adjoint methods, or backpropagation through time (BPTT), whose computational and memory costs grow with the length of the training window. This limits the duration and resolution of hybrid-model training, a major bottleneck for realistic geophysical applications. Approaches like truncated BPTT reduces memory use by discarding sensitivities across truncation boundaries, introducing gradient bias and neglecting long-range dependencies. We propose a class of gradient approximation methods that preserve the adjoint recurrence over the full trajectory while approximating only the pullback operators within it. Exact pullbacks are computed by automatic differentiation at sparse anchor states only. Between anchors, sensitivities propagate either through the identity (Zero-order) or through a reused, frozen pullback (Pullback Reuse). This approximation makes the parameter pullback constant within each chunk, allowing the gradient sum to factorize so that a single evaluation per chunk replaces one per time step. We evaluate both on three systems of increasing complexity, an incomplete Lorenz-63 model, a large-eddy closure for two-dimensional quasi-geostrophic turbulence, and bias correction in a multilayer quasi-geostrophic ocean model. Peak memory falls by up to an order of magnitude and runtime up to fourfold, with Pullback Reuse staying closest to the exact gradient direction. In all three cases, approximate gradients support hybrid-model training at comparable accuracy, showing that effective online learning does not require exact gradients.
authors: Emilio Gonz\'alez-Zamora, Pierre Tandeo, Laurent Debreu, Said Ouala
bullets: Full-trajectory adjoint methods are costly because memory and computation grow with training-window length, limiting realistic geophysical applications.
The proposed approach keeps the adjoint recurrence but approximates pullback operators between sparse anchor states.
Two variants propagate sensitivities through the identity or reuse a frozen pullback within each chunk, enabling one pullback evaluation per chunk instead of per time step.
Across three geophysical systems, peak memory decreases by up to an order of magnitude and runtime by up to fourfold.
Pullback Reuse most closely matches the exact gradient direction, and both methods support comparable hybrid-model training accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Memory- and compute-efficient approximate adjoint gradients for online hybrid-model learning, fitting efficient AI and online adaptation.
papers.title: Approximate Adjoint Models for Memory and Compute-Efficient Online Learning of Hybrid Models
papers.tldr: Approximate adjoint methods reduce the memory and runtime costs of online learning for hybrid models while preserving training accuracy.

papers.abstract: Post-training low-rank compression of neural networks must not only approximate the original weights but also preserve the model's input-output behavior. Recent output-aware methods measure the compression error beyond the compressed layer, at the model output, weighting logit changes by the observed next token or by the model's predicted probabilities. We propose Complete-SVD, a method for large language models that minimizes the $L_2$ distance between the logits of the original and compressed models, weighting all logit changes equally. Linearizing the network around the original weights, together with a Kronecker-factored approximation, reduces this objective to a weighted SVD with a closed-form solution. Its output-side factor is intractable to compute; we estimate it without bias from random probes, at a cost of $K$ backward passes per sequence, independent of vocabulary size and sequence length. At matched settings with uniform ranks and WikiText-2 calibration, Complete-SVD achieves the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity in every setting, and at ratio 0.7 under LEMS rank allocation. Replacing the $L_2$ distance by the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL-SVD), with the same estimation framework, lowers calibration perplexity in most settings and raises downstream accuracy, but raises cross-corpus perplexity. Complete-SVD also improves IFEval instruction-following accuracy over the strongest prior output-aware methods throughout.
authors: Alper Kalle, Theo Rudkiewicz, Mohamed-Oumar Ouerfelli, Mohamed Tamaazousti
bullets: Targets post-training low-rank compression that preserves input-output behavior, not just layer weights.
Linearizes the network and uses a Kronecker-factored approximation to reduce compression to a closed-form weighted SVD.
Estimates the otherwise intractable output-side factor unbiasedly with random probes, requiring K backward passes per sequence.
On WikiText-2 calibration, it reports the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity across matched uniform-rank settings and at ratio 0.7 with LEMS allocation.
KL-SVD usually improves calibration perplexity and downstream accuracy but increases cross-corpus perplexity; Complete-SVD improves IFEval accuracy over prior output-aware methods.
papers.selection_reason: Output-aware low-rank SVD compression for LLMs; reduces model memory while preserving logit behavior.
papers.title: Complete-SVD: A Functional Norm Approach to Low-Rank LLM Compression
papers.tldr: Complete-SVD compresses LLMs by minimizing equal-weighted changes to the model’s output logits, achieving strong perplexity and instruction-following performance in the reported settings.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models combine self-attention with recurrent layers whose in-place state updates restrict prefix reuse to exact saved positions. Saving states on a coarse grid wastes reusable prefixes, whereas existing fine-grained exact caches must cut the prefill forward pass at each mid-prompt checkpoint, adding scheduler steps that outweigh the reuse gains under load. We observe that across multi-turn chat, agent loops, document question answering, and tree search, prefix reuse almost always ends at structural boundaries predictable in advance, such as turn ends and known branch points. We present FrontierReplay, a prefix caching system that materializes exact checkpoints at these boundaries without cutting the prefill. While the forward pass runs uncut, FrontierReplay logs a short window of recurrent-layer inputs and invokes a cross-layer, state-only replay kernel to build the target state 6-37x cheaper per token than full recomputation without host synchronization. A frontier-aware retention policy prioritizes active anchors and proven branches while lending dead checkpoint slots to the attention KV cache. Across diverse hybrid architectures, model scales, and workloads, FrontierReplay delivers clear gains over existing exact caches, lowering median time to first token (TTFT) by 16-89% (up to 8.9x), raising 80% service-level objective (SLO) capacity by up to 1.73x, and improving goodput by up to 4.26x (3.67x at larger scales). Compared with approximate replay methods, FrontierReplay delivers up to 1.54x higher goodput while preserving exact task accuracy, avoiding the up to 17% accuracy drop suffered by approximation on long contexts.
bullets: Targets hybrid models whose recurrent states can only be reused from exact saved positions.
Predicts checkpoint frontiers such as chat turn ends and search branch points, avoiding mid-prompt prefill cuts.
Logs recurrent-layer inputs and uses a cross-layer, state-only replay kernel to construct checkpoints 6–37× cheaper per token than full recomputation.
A frontier-aware policy prioritizes active and proven branches while reallocating unused checkpoint capacity to attention KV caching.
Across architectures and workloads, it reduces median TTFT by 16–89%, increases SLO capacity by up to 1.73×, and improves goodput by up to 4.26× while preserving exact accuracy.

papers.abstract: End-to-end approaches to Optical Music Recognition (OMR) have recently shown promising results, but their performance often degrades on unseen data. A common solution is to pretrain and fine-tune models with annotated samples from the target domain, improving adaptation to new distributions. However, this process typically requires extensive manual annotation to yield competitive models, making it costly and time-consuming. In this work, we explore Active Learning to reduce this burden by selecting informative samples for labeling in low-resource scenarios, where the amount of manual annotation that can be performed is limited. We evaluate both uncertainty- and diversity-based sampling strategies on staff-level and full-page corpora. Results show that confidence-based sampling performs comparably to oracle selection (based on true error), and that each scenario benefits from a tailored strategy.
authors: Eric Ayllon, Francisco J. Castellanos, Antonio Rios-Vila
bullets: OMR models often degrade on unseen data and require costly target-domain annotation for adaptation.
The study evaluates uncertainty- and diversity-based sample selection in low-resource labeling scenarios.
Experiments cover both staff-level and full-page corpora.
Confidence-based sampling performs comparably to oracle selection based on true error.
The best sampling strategy depends on the evaluation scenario.
