papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly need to process long documents and codebases, making long-context attention a major prefill bottleneck. Block sparse attention reduces computation by skipping unimportant blocks of the attention matrix, but scoring blocks accurately can itself be expensive. We propose Delta-Based Tile Scoring (DTS), a training-free, content-adaptive tile scoring method for sparse block attention. DTS selects query and key anchors according to local vector changes, using fewer representatives in redundant regions while retaining more detail in heterogeneous regions. To accelerate anchor selection, parallel delta packing partitions the query and key sequences into tile-aligned chunks and performs bounded local scans over these chunks concurrently. The selected tiles are then computed using the original query, key, and value vectors. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DTS keeps average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, with RULER evaluated up to 128K tokens. At 128K tokens, DTS reduces measured scoring-pipeline latency by 38% compared with XAttention. On four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it achieves a 3.3$\times$ prefill speedup over a PyTorch full-attention baseline using FlashAttention-2 at 512K tokens.
authors: Emre U\u{g}ur, Jiawen Qi, Qinyu Chen
bullets: Addresses the prefill bottleneck of long-context attention, where accurately scoring skippable blocks can be costly.
Uses training-free, content-adaptive delta scoring with fewer anchors in redundant regions and more in heterogeneous ones.
Accelerates scoring through parallel, tile-aligned local scans, then computes selected tiles with the original vectors.
Maintains average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, including RULER up to 128K tokens.
Reports 38% lower scoring-pipeline latency than XAttention at 128K tokens and 3.3× prefill speedup over a FlashAttention-2 PyTorch baseline at 512K tokens on four H100 GPUs.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised foundation models are often said to need fewer labels than supervised training. We test this on a forestry task: classifying 20 tree species classes in 0.2 m aerial images from the TreeSatAI dataset. We compare a frozen DINOv3 model pretrained on 493 million satellite images, with only a linear classifier trained on top, against an ImageNet ResNet-50 that is fine-tuned end to end. On the official split, fine-tuning wins clearly (macro F1 0.764 vs. 0.685). However, 28.8% of the official test patches overlap a training or validation patch, and copying the label of the nearest such patch is correct for 83.6% of them. We therefore build a spatial split that holds out whole 2 km squares with a 200 m buffer. On this split the comparison becomes inconclusive (0.648 vs. 0.640, paired 95% CI of the difference [-0.054, 0.016]), and the learning curves of the two models overlap at every label budget from 343 to 33,126 training patches. On the five rarest classes, the frozen model achieves a higher mean F1 (0.566 vs. 0.445), although the confidence interval for this difference includes zero ([-0.05, 0.23]). Diagnostics show that the frozen features mainly miss differences between closely related species, such as the two native oaks. Choosing the input size and layer on validation data (224 px, block 16) raises the frozen model to 0.662 on the spatial split. A comparison that looks decisive on the official split is thus inconclusive under geographically separated evaluation. We release the spatial split and our code.
bullets: Studies 20-class tree-species mapping in 0.2 m aerial imagery from TreeSatAI.
Compares a frozen DINOv3 encoder with a linear classifier against end-to-end fine-tuned ImageNet ResNet-50s.
On the official split, fine-tuning scores higher, but substantial patch overlap may inflate performance.
On a spatial split with held-out 2 km squares and buffers, performance is statistically inconclusive and learning curves overlap across label budgets.
Frozen features perform better on the rarest classes but mainly confuse closely related species; validation-based input/layer selection improves them.

papers.selection_reason: Empirically compares frozen foundation model features against fine-tuned CNNs for tree species mapping, highlighting the efficiency and data leakage issues in current evaluation splits.
papers.title: Does It Depend on the Split? Frozen Satellite Features vs. Fine-Tuned CNNs for Tree Species Mapping
papers.tldr: Fine-tuned CNNs outperform frozen satellite features on the official split, but geographically separated evaluation makes the difference inconclusive and favors frozen features for rare species.

papers.abstract: Table question answering with large language models remains difficult to scale: tables range from compact to million-token sizes, while questions require precise grounding of columns, values, and computations. Existing methods often specialize in a fixed inference strategy, which is brittle across different table scales and model capabilities. Full-table reading is efficient for compact inputs but suffers from irrelevant context. Table reduction helps long inputs but depends on reliable evidence localization, while execution is required when tables exceed the model context window and remains sensitive to schema and value grounding errors. We propose TableRoute, a capability-aware routing framework with evidence-conditioned inference for scalable TableQA. TableRoute first generates validated question--table evidence and identifies the required operations, then routes each instance among these three strategies according to serialized table length and calibrated estimates of how reliably the base model handles these operations. The validated evidence supports the selected route by grounding columns, values, and conditions. Across WikiTQ, WTQ-L, BirdQA, and TableBench, TableRoute consistently improves accuracy through complementary routing and evidence conditioning across table scales, while reducing online token cost. Code will be made available upon publication.
authors: Yuxiang Wang, Junhao Gan, Jianzhong Qi
bullets: Addresses the challenge of answering questions over tables ranging from compact to million-token inputs.
Generates validated question–table evidence and identifies required operations before inference.
Selects among full-table reading, table reduction, and execution based on table length and calibrated model capabilities.
Reports consistent accuracy improvements across WikiTQ, WTQ-L, BirdQA, and TableBench while reducing online token cost.

papers.abstract: Preference training is the standard recipe for reducing object hallucination in vision-language models, and each new method reports a lower CHAIR score. We ask what that reduction consists of. Every trained system is compared with its base model's caption truncated to the same object recall, which removes the part of the gain that comes from saying less; the remainder is compared with what a deliberately weak, frozen, eleven-feature post-hoc probe fitted on 500 annotated images can reproduce. All criteria were specified in the analysis code and frozen before the outputs they judge existed. For eight public methods on LLaVA-1.5-7B, the probe reproduces at least two thirds of what training removes beyond saying less for 7 of 8 methods on COCO, 8 of 8 on AMBER and 6 of 8 on Object HalBench, with RLAIF-V the consistent exception; a later public method released for both LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL (SENTINEL) meets the same bar on both. On our own DPO checkpoints the accounting holds on Qwen2.5-VL but fails on InternVL2.5 on COCO (2 of 4 training designs). At matched recall, the base model plus the probe beats truncation for 8 of 9 LLaVA-1.5 systems on COCO and 9 of 9 on AMBER, on the two newer backbones, and when realized as actual sentence deletion. The same measure prices training signals: DPO on the model's own samples labelled by the probe or by an object-level CLIP score recovers 0.70 and 0.87 of the beyond-brevity gain of ground-truth-labelled DPO on Qwen2.5-VL (the probe 0.73 on InternVL2.5), both beat length-matched random labels, and CLIP labels buy more than probe labels on COCO. Human judgements show that the sentences the probe deletes are wrong more often than those truncation would delete; a human check of the CHAIR evaluator's precision falls below our pre-set bar, which we report as a limitation.
bullets: The study separates CHAIR improvements into reduced verbosity versus genuine hallucination reduction by matching object recall with truncated base-model captions.
A frozen, 11-feature probe trained on 500 annotated images reproduces at least two thirds of beyond-brevity gains for most evaluated methods, with RLAIF-V as the main exception.
At matched recall, the base model plus probe generally outperforms truncation across LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL2.5, COCO, and AMBER evaluations.
Probe- or CLIP-based preference labels recover substantial portions of ground-truth-labelled DPO gains, while outperforming random labels; CLIP labels perform better on COCO.
Human checks support the probe’s deletions, but also identify insufficient precision in the CHAIR evaluator as a limitation.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates 'cheap pruning' techniques in vision-language models (VLMs) to reduce object hallucinations, directly addressing efficiency (token pruning) and VLM robustness.
papers.title: What Does Anti-Hallucination Training Buy? Saying Less, Cheap Pruning, and the Rest
papers.tldr: Much of anti-hallucination training’s apparent benefit comes from shorter captions and can be replicated by a cheap post-hoc probe, though some methods and backbones retain gains beyond brevity.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has emerged as a critical technique for accelerating Large Language Model (LLM) inference by decoupling generation into a drafting phase and a parallel verification phase. A crucial challenge is therefore designing a drafter that is both lightweight and accurate enough to approximate the predictions of the target model. We present a highly optimized Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) architecture that extends existing backbone LLMs to efficiently produce high-quality drafts. Built around a single shared drafting head, our approach features three core architectural optimizations: target activation injection to anchor semantic planning, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention to bypass prefill compute and reduce memory overhead, and an efficient clustered vocabulary projection to reduce the cost of full-vocabulary decoding. Testing these improvements with the Gemma 4 model family, our G-MTP shows out-of-the-box speedups for both large server-side setups (up to 3.1$\times$) and smaller models targeting memory-constrained on-device environments (up to 2.3$\times$ on H100 and up to 2.2$\times$ on a smartphone GPU). In addition, we present parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes for G-MTP that keep the drafter aligned with the backbone LLM under domain shift, requiring up to 1.83$\times$ fewer target forward passes than tuning only the backbone.
authors: Filippo Galgani, Ziwei Ji, Omri Homburger, Ganesh Jawahar, Michelle Ramanovich, Ivan Korotkov, Luciano Martins, Utku Evci, Edouard Yvinec, Pooja Consul, Vivek Kumar, Tal Schuster
bullets: Addresses the need for lightweight, accurate draft generation in speculative decoding.
Uses a shared drafting head with target activation injection, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention, and clustered vocabulary projection.
Evaluated with the Gemma 4 family, achieving reported speedups of up to 3.1× on server-side setups and 2.2× on a smartphone GPU.
Introduces parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes that require up to 1.83× fewer target-model forward passes than tuning only the backbone.
Scope: results are reported for Gemma 4 models and the specified hardware environments.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Architecture of the optimized Multi-Token Prediction (G-MTP) module. The input to the drafter is constructed by concatenating the token embedding (𝑒(𝑥)) with the backbone hidden state (ℎ(𝐿)), both of dimension 𝑑target, and reducing to the drafter dimension 𝑑draft. The draft tokens are then propagated through the MTP layers, utilizing cross-attention against the backbone’s frozen KV Cache to bypass prefill computations before recursively triggering the next forward step. For subsequent drafting steps, the drafter’s output state is up-projected (𝑊up), concatenated with the embedding of the sampled draft token, and down-projected (𝑊down) to form the next input (Equation 3).

Figure 2 | The autoregressive G-MTP drafter (blue blocks) is initialized with activations from the main model (gray blocks) and cross-attends to its KV cache. Across successive drafting steps, the positional encoding (𝑝1) remains constant, as the drafter repeatedly queries a static, pre-computed KV snapshot.

Figure 3 | Empirical scaling of theoretical Block Efficiency (BE) and speculative wall-clock throughput across varying lookahead horizons (𝛾). While longer draft sequences monotonically increase token acceptance, throughput degrades for some models (e.g., 26B MoE) as drafting and verification costs exceed generation gains.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models offer an architectural route to low-budget generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, which can reduce the number of sequential decoding steps relative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. However, realizing this advantage at low budgets is challenging, as generation quality often declines when the number of denoising and refinement steps is reduced. Editable diffusion models address this quality loss through post-draft refinement, but useful intermediate results may still be lost before final submission. We introduce CaRR (Commitment-aware Refinement and Recovery), a training-free framework which improves submission quality from a fixed editable checkpoint through updated-context refill and trajectory-based recovery within its existing forward schedule. Token Commitment Remasking (TCR) remasks selected native pure replacements and refills them on the next scheduled edit forward using the updated context. Submission Commitment Recovery (SCR) uses the resulting refinement trajectory to recover supported candidates when the final response does not satisfy task-specific output requirements. Both modules operate within the native mask/edit schedule without additional backbone forwards. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning show consistent gains in average accuracy over native ME-DLM across four inference budgets, with the largest gains under tight budgets. At one-eighth of the full scheduled forward budget, CaRR improves the six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 pp, including gains of 11.37 and 10.05 on MBPP and MBPP+.
authors: Hao Wu, Sipeng Chen, Jingwen Fu, Yuwang Wang
bullets: Diffusion language models can decode multiple tokens in parallel, but quality often drops when denoising steps are reduced.
CaRR is a training-free framework for improving outputs from a fixed editable checkpoint within the existing edit schedule.
Token Commitment Remasking refills selected replacements using updated context, while Submission Commitment Recovery rescues supported candidates that fail output requirements.
Experiments in code generation and mathematical reasoning show consistent accuracy gains across four inference budgets, especially under tight budgets.
At one-eighth of the full budget, CaRR raises six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 percentage points, including 11.37 on MBPP and 10.05 on MBPP+.

papers.abstract: In recent years, GPUs have incorporated increasingly specialized support for low-precision computation, from Hopper's FP8 to Blackwell's FP4 Tensor Cores. Precision formats have evolved alongside this hardware, from MXFP4 and NVFP4 on Blackwell to E2M1 FP4 with direct UE5M3 block scaling on Vera Rubin, which we term as $\boldsymbol{VRFP4}$. These advances help serve larger language models at lower cost, but four-bit activation quantization can substantially degrade model quality. We introduce VR-SparseQuant, which uses Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 sparsity to recover accuracy while retaining native FP4 execution. By allowing two sparse streams to overlap, we use the same FP4 value budget as dense quantization to refine activations with larger errors. Offline scale-ratio calibration avoids runtime search, while a shared-weight GEMM accumulates both streams efficiently. On Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, VR-SparseQuant reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from $\boldsymbol{6.85}$ to $\boldsymbol{5.57}$ versus dense RTN W4A4. Including activation preparation, our native Rubin kernels for VRFP4 achieve up to $\boldsymbol{3.1\times}$ GEMM and $\boldsymbol{2.7\times}$ MoE speedup over BF16. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of adaptive activation quantization using Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 structured sparse FP4 instructions.
authors: Samir Khaki, Wei-Chen Wang, Song Han, Ryan Hanrui Wang
bullets: Addresses quality degradation from four-bit activation quantization for large-language-model inference.
Uses overlapping sparse streams to refine high-error activations without increasing the FP4 value budget.
Applies offline scale-ratio calibration and shared-weight GEMM accumulation to avoid runtime search and improve efficiency.
On Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, lowers WikiText-2 perplexity from 6.85 to 5.57 versus dense RTN W4A4.
Native VRFP4 kernels achieve up to 3.1× GEMM and 2.7× MoE speedups over BF16, including activation preparation.

papers.abstract: We enable accurate low-bit recovery from small synthetic pools by improving both image synthesis and student preparation. A grid with lower local response error can incur greater error in the student's block context. Functional Grid Calibration (FGC) selects activation scales and integer offsets against full-precision responses constructed from the student's current block input. With weights fixed during calibration, FGC evaluates candidates only at their consuming operators, bringing block context to calibration at nearly local-scoring cost. For DeiT and ViT, progressive inversion updates the same images through increasingly deep teacher prefixes. With 1,000 images, the complete pipeline exceeds MimiQ's reported accuracy in all 18 W4A4/W5A5 settings across nine backbones. With 256 images, DeiT-S and ViT-S reach 68.20% and 66.90% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at W4A4 in 26-27 minutes on one RTX 5090. The pipeline outperforms strengthened 1K-image MimiQ by 13.03 and 24.36 percentage points at lower preparation cost and the same recovery-update count. The same low-budget checkpoints retain their advantage on ImageNetV2.
authors: Haowen Hua, Sen Lin, Yaokun Huang, Zeyi Shao, Hao Zhang, Wei Sui, John See, Zeyd Boukhers, Cong Yang

With 1,000 images, the pipeline surpasses reported MimiQ accuracy across all 18 settings and nine backbones.
With 256 images, it achieves 68.20% top-1 on DeiT-S and 66.90% on ViT-S at W4A4; gains also persist on ImageNetV2.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers generate high-quality images and videos, but every sampling step requires a full network evaluation. Training-free caching reduces this cost by reusing or forecasting network outputs across steps, but common approaches use per-model calibrated skip criteria or maintain per-layer prediction histories. We present D3-Cache, which applies Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) to Diffusion sampling: it fits DMD to a short history of exact velocities and forecasts only the velocity that the scheduler consumes. A horizon-aware gate decides when to skip: whenever the network is evaluated, its output is compared with the forecast for that step, and the larger the error, the sooner the network is evaluated again, up to a cap on consecutive skipped steps. D3-Cache requires no training or per-model offline calibration curve and adds negligible memory. It shares one history length and risk tolerance across the four evaluated models. On four state-of-the-art image and video models, D3-Cache achieves speedups of 2.6-3.8x with high fidelity to the base model output.
authors: Yanbo Li, An Xiang, Xiaoxin Hu, Feng Wang, Cheng-zhong Xu, Kejiang Ye, Xitong Gao
bullets: Targets the cost of full network evaluation at every diffusion sampling step.
Fits Dynamic Mode Decomposition to a short history of exact velocities and forecasts the next scheduler-consumed velocity.
Uses a horizon-aware error gate to determine when to reevaluate the network, with a cap on consecutive skips.
Requires no training or per-model offline calibration and adds negligible memory.
Across four image and video models, reports 2.6–3.8× speedups with high fidelity to base outputs.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of D3-Cache. (a) After warmup, each sampling step either runs a full evaluation or reuses a DMD forecast of the velocity. The estimated risk grows with the horizon since the last full evaluation; exceeding τ or reaching the skip cap S triggers a refresh. (b) At a refresh, the exact velocity first scores the forecast made from the preceding history 1⃝, which updates the risk slope for later steps, and is then pushed into the history used for the next DMD fit 2⃝. For subsequent steps, the gate selects the forecast when Rk(t) ≤ τ and s < S; the DiT blocks and output head are then skipped entirely. Otherwise they are evaluated and the exact velocity is selected.

papers.abstract: Efficient chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) requires reducing both intermediate reasoning steps and their execution cost. Latent CoT methods compress textual rationales into continuous thoughts, yet their full-precision (FP) models retain substantial storage and computation costs. Lowering numerical precision could reduce these remaining costs, yet direct quantization severely degrades reasoning accuracy, particularly with 4-bit weights and activations. Operator and perturbation analyses reveal key sensitivity and direction-dependent predictive effects of continuous-thought errors, motivating preservation of information retrieval and subsequent reasoning beyond reconstruction accuracy. We therefore introduce QL-VLM, a dynamics-aware Quantization framework for efficient Latent reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). First, Dynamics-Guided Quantization (DGQ) uses nonuniform codebooks that preserve rotary-key structure, mitigating quantization-induced distortion in vision-language information retrieval. Second, Dynamics-Preserving Distillation (DPD) aligns continuous thoughts, latent-query readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher, maintaining predictive consistency through subsequent low-precision reasoning. On ScienceQA-IMG with Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM achieves 90.43% accuracy and improves baseline by 40.33%, with 16.64x fewer bit-operations and 6.40x lower measured latency than explicit CoT.
authors: Yanjing Li, Sheng Xu, Baochang Zhang, Xianbin Cao, Yawei Li
bullets: Targets the storage and computation costs of full-precision latent reasoning in VLMs.
Dynamics-Guided Quantization preserves rotary-key structure to reduce distortions in vision-language information retrieval.
Dynamics-Preserving Distillation aligns latent thoughts, readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher.
On ScienceQA-IMG using Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM reaches 90.43% accuracy.
Reports 16.64× fewer bit-operations and 6.40× lower measured latency than explicit chain-of-thought.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference. In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.
authors: Zhihao Liu, Zixiong Guo, Shuo Shao, Yu He, Wenli Wang, Meihui Chen, Di Wang, Yuke Hu
bullets: Addresses privacy risks in remote LLM inference, where sensitive user queries are exposed to the service provider.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference method that reuses shared-prefix KV caches to improve efficiency while maintaining privacy.
papers.title: Ask in the Crowd: Differentially Private LLM Inference via Dummy-Augmented Shuffling
papers.tldr: DP-SPD protects LLM queries by mixing them with client-generated dummy queries, shuffling them, and reusing shared-prefix KV caches to preserve utility and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Machine translation with large language models requires both high translation quality and low generation latency. Accelerating translation while preserving quality is therefore essential for practical deployment. Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate tokens at arbitrary target positions through iterative denoising, offering a new paradigm for parallel translation beyond sequential autoregressive decoding. However, existing methods still incur redundant computation: fixed target generation lengths waste computation on unused positions, while confidence-only commitment delays medium-confidence tokens whose predictions have largely stabilized. To address these issues, we propose TRAC, a training-free adaptive decoding method for diffusion machine translation. TRAC adapts the target generation length using source length and translation direction, with a conservative fallback to the maximum length for empty or unusually short outputs. It preserves high-confidence commitment while identifying temporally stable medium-confidence tokens for early commitment using cross-step top-1 persistence and approximate Jensen-Shannon divergence over Top-$K$ distributions. On bidirectional Chinese-English translation across FLORES-200, WMT23, and NTREX-128, TRAC reduces model forward calls by 24.9% to 36.8% and achieves sentence-level generation speedups of 1.91 to 2.19 times over Fast-dLLM, with only a 0.02-point decrease in macro-average COMET. These results demonstrate that adaptive generation lengths and stability-aware token commitment improve the efficiency of diffusion machine translation.
authors: Tianyuan Li, Xihan Yang, Chenglong Wang, Yuzhang Wu, Jingbo Zhu, Tong Xiao
bullets: Targets redundant computation from fixed output lengths and delayed commitment of medium-confidence tokens.
Uses source-length- and direction-aware target length estimation with a fallback for empty or unusually short outputs.
Commits tokens based on high confidence plus temporal stability measured by cross-step top-1 persistence and approximate Jensen–Shannon divergence over Top-K distributions.
Training-free evaluation on bidirectional Chinese–English translation reports 24.9%–36.8% fewer forward calls and 1.91×–2.19× sentence-level speedups over Fast-dLLM.
Macro-average COMET decreases by only 0.02 points; scope is limited to the reported translation directions and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Splice-Core is a temporal-unary/binary (tub) hybrid general matrix multiplication (GEMM) unit that minimizes low-order accumulation latency, while retaining value-dependent execution for high-order activation bits. We present two novel processing element (PE) variants: (i) Splice-BP utilizing bit planes, and (ii) Splice-LUT, which selects a shared weight multiple in a single cycle. Compared to a binary systolic array, Splice-BP/Splice-LUT achieve 77.4%/76.4% geometric-mean tile energy reductions, respectively, across 26 INT4 convolutional neural network (CNN) and large language model (LLM) workloads in 45nm. Splice-LUT further increases geometric-mean tile throughput by 44.4% and reduces geometric-mean energy-delay product (EDP) by 6.13x across the 26 configurations. Across the evaluated W8A8 convolution and expert-projection workloads, Splice-BP and Splice-LUT reduce tile energy by 77.3-88.1%. Post-place-and-route INT4 yields 14%/9% smaller area for Splice-BP/Splice-LUT, compared to the systolic array.
authors: Prabhu Vellaisamy, Hsien-Fu Hung, Andrew Kim, Shawn Blanton, John Paul Shen

Splice-LUT improves geometric-mean tile throughput by 44.4% and reduces energy-delay product by 6.13× across the evaluated configurations.
For W8A8 convolution and expert-projection workloads, both variants reduce tile energy by 77.3–88.1%.
Post-place-and-route INT4 implementations reduce area by 14% (Splice-BP) and 9% (Splice-LUT).

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how a scene will evolve and condition their actions on this predicted future. Deploying them on a robot's onboard computer calls for 4-bit weights, activations and key-value caches (W4A4KV4). Existing 4-bit quantizers for WAMs preserve the generated action, and estimate sensitivity one denoising step at a time. However, they fail to preserve the fidelity of the predicted future: once the action pathway is protected, the remaining action error enters mostly through a degraded future that none of them deliberately protects. We propose LAQ, a latent-aware quantization framework that preserves the predicted future where it is written, stored and read. Specifically, we introduce a reader metric, which measures future error by its effect on the action, and a read count, which weights each rounding error by the number of denoising steps that read it. Together they give the allocation of precision over activations and caches a closed-form solution. We further develop gaze-guided refinement, which gives the tokens the action attends to a second 4-bit pass in the denoising loop and in the cache. All weights stay at 4 bits, with no high-precision branch and no per-task recalibration. On the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, LAQ reaches 76.4% and 83.3% average success on Fast-WAM and Cosmos-Policy, within 1.2 percentage points of the 16-bit models and all above the baselines with 16-bit KV caches. It compresses the model by 3.8x, reduces the peak GPU memory of the whole policy by 2.3x, and runs 1.66x faster than the 16-bit model. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, it reaches 47.0% average success over three tasks, against 52.0% for the 16-bit model and 30.0% higher than QuaRot.
authors: Yichen Guo, Yanlong Chen, Xinyue Zhang, Mohan Liu, Song Zhang, Yawei Li
bullets: Targets W4A4KV4 deployment of world action models on onboard robot computers.
Uses a reader metric to measure future errors by their impact on actions, and read counts to allocate activation/cache precision across denoising steps.
Adds gaze-guided refinement, giving action-relevant tokens a second 4-bit quantization pass in the denoising loop and cache.
On LIBERO-Plus, achieves 76.4% and 83.3% success—within 1.2 points of 16-bit models—while compressing 3.8×, reducing peak memory 2.3×, and running 1.66× faster.
On a real AgileX PiPER arm, reaches 47.0% success versus 52.0% for 16-bit and 30.0% higher than QuaRot.

At every control step, gaze-guided refinement (d) gives the tokens selected under the current gaze a second 4-bit code in the linear layers and in the cache, and the attention of the action tokens gives the gaze for the next step.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using $7.4\times$ less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.
authors: Anh Dao, Xinxin Liu, Hang Yu, Jeffrey A Chan Santiago, Yuzhang Shang
bullets: WAMs are costly because they combine video generation with action prediction using large transformers.
A shared six-block core is recurrently applied to execute 30 layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert; video and action experts use different depths.
Elastic self-distillation trains one checkpoint to support varied action-depth and sampling-step budgets.
The 0.58B-parameter model reports 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, with 7.4× lower peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched measurements.
On real hardware, it achieved 71.3% success over 80 trials; performance degrades when action depth is aggressively reduced without budget-aware training.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. (a) Each expert stores a prelude, a shared core, and a coda, and loops the core Kv times in the video expert and Ka times in the action expert (shown for Kv=4, Ka=2). The video expert encodes the current frame once per query and caches its keys and values. At every sampling step, the action expert reads them in a joint attention; late alignment lets action loop r attend to video loop σ(r), so even a single action loop sees the deepest visual features. Both experts also cross-attend to frozen text embeddings of the instruction, and future frames are predicted only during training. (b) One student learns every setting (Ka, N) in S. The target of each macro step is the frozen teacher’s fine Euler map started from the student’s own state (Llocal), and the final chunk is matched to the teacher’s chunk from the same noise (Lend).

papers.selection_reason: Compact world action model for robotic manipulation with elastic inference; fits embodied AI, world models, and efficiency.
papers.title: LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models for Elastic Inference
papers.tldr: LoopedWAM makes world action models more memory- and latency-efficient by reusing transformer blocks and adapting inference depth without substantially sacrificing robotic task success.

papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models are advancing embodied navigation, but frequent inference incurs substantial computational cost. We present Cognitive-Horizon Action Chunking (CHAC), a training-free framework for memory-guided adaptive reasoning with a frozen navigation policy. Retained visual context, completion cues, and controller feedback determine the cognitive horizon, or how many cached waypoints the robot executes before refreshing its prediction. At the policy's stop request, local visitation history guides a bounded correction with at most one extra movement and no additional model calls. CHAC reduces vision-language model calls by 33.4% on HM3D-OVON and 64.7% on R2R-CE, with success-rate decreases of 0.63 and 10.82 percentage points, respectively. Success rate and success weighted by path length improve per model call on both benchmarks. Across four physical navigation tasks with 40 runs per method, CHAC achieves 18 successes versus 14 for native execution, reducing model calls by 54.9% and GPU inference time by 49.7%.

Cuts model calls by 33.4% on HM3D-OVON and 64.7% on R2R-CE, with corresponding success-rate decreases of 0.63 and 10.82 percentage points.
In physical tasks, achieves 18 versus 14 successes, while reducing model calls by 54.9% and GPU inference time by 49.7%.

papers.abstract: Extending multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from images to videos faces substantial memory and latency challenges due to the massive number of visual tokens. These challenges have driven the development of numerous visual token compression methods and more efficient LLM architectures. However, existing compression methods are often evaluated with different training setups, tasks, and models, making fair comparison difficult. Meanwhile, the growing use of hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures raises questions about whether compression strategies transfer across backbones. We present VidToC, a controlled evaluation framework for representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time encoding strategies, covering training-free and fine-tuned settings on three complementary video understanding tasks. Our results reveal task-dependent compression behavior and characterize the effects of compression placement, time encoding, and backbone choice. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing and selecting video token compression strategies across tasks and training settings.
authors: Zihan Xiao (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China), Boshen Xu (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China), Pei Fu (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Jianzhong Ju (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Zhenbo Luo (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Jian Luan (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Qin Jin (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China)
bullets: Video MLLMs face major memory and latency costs from large numbers of visual tokens.
Existing compression methods are difficult to compare fairly because evaluations use different setups, tasks, and models.
VidToC provides a controlled framework spanning representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time-encoding strategies.
Experiments across three video-understanding tasks show that compression behavior depends on the task, compression placement, time encoding, and backbone.
The study offers empirical guidance for selecting compression strategies, including across hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures.

papers.abstract: Video Large Language Models process large numbers of visual tokens, making token pruning important for efficient inference. Training-free pruning methods differ in whether and how they use the user query, and the value of query conditioning remains unclear. We present a controlled study of training-free, pre-LLM video token selection. Using a shared Qwen-3-VL backbone, token budgets, and decoding settings, we compare 21 pruning principles spanning query-agnostic, shallow query-conditioned, structured query-conditioned, and holistic strategies. To instantiate the last two categories, we introduce Structured Query Pruning, which decomposes the question into semantic anchors, and a Pareto variant, which combines anchor relevance with query-agnostic visual diversity. Across Video-MME, MVBench, and LongVideoBench, relevance computed from the raw question embedding is unreliable (8--16 points below the best methods), whereas anchors derived from query decomposition avoid this failure. However, query access is not inherently advantageous: strong query-agnostic coverage methods remain competitive or superior in the full-field comparison. Relative to a redundancy-only baseline, structured selection helps most on evidence-specific and long-context tasks at tight budgets; on broad tasks, the holistic selector improves over either relevance or redundancy alone. Further, pruning reduces cost and memory. These results support a practical design rule: preserve visual coverage by default, and add structured relevance when the task and token budget demand selective evidence retrieval.
authors: Divya Kothandaraman, Timo Kumkel, Jaclyn Pytlarz
bullets: Compares 21 training-free video token pruning strategies under shared backbone, token budgets, and decoding settings.
Raw question-embedding relevance is unreliable, performing 8–16 points below the best methods across evaluated benchmarks.
Structured query decomposition avoids this failure by selecting tokens linked to semantic anchors.
Query access is not always beneficial: strong coverage-based, query-agnostic methods can match or outperform query-conditioned approaches.
Structured selection helps evidence-specific and long-context tasks at tight budgets; holistic selection helps broad tasks, while pruning reduces cost and memory.

Tokens are ranked and the top-k are retained for LLM generation. The hybrid Pareto strategy jointly optimizes semantic relevance and visual diversity.

papers.abstract: Visual token compression often treats salience or similarity as a proxy for transcription importance. Complete document OCR breaks this assumption: small symbols and repeated entries can be indispensable to the transcript despite being visually inconspicuous. We present Select and Compensate, a two-stage framework built on a simple idea: choosing where to retain a token need not determine all the evidence it carries. Selection combines adaptive encoding resolution with global importance and local contrast to choose which tokens to retain as anchors. Compensation enriches these anchors with nearby discarded content and its relative position, without adding tokens. The OCR backbone remains frozen, and native coordinates and structural tokens are preserved. We evaluate complete page transcription across five backbones on OmniDocBench and document reconstruction on MPDocBench. With half the original visual tokens, our input-adapted configuration reaches 95.42 OmniDocBench Overall on Ovis versus 96.09 for the uncompressed model, and paired evaluations show gains over simply reducing the input resolution on both benchmarks. With the original input grid, our method stays within 0.17 points of the uncompressed model at 75% retention and exceeds a learned global selector by 4.70 points at 25%. On a fixed 200-page Ovis workload at the same 50% visual-token budget, only 3 of its outputs hit the length limit, versus 30-34 for the evaluated RTPrune, DivPrune, and HiPrune adaptations, and it finishes the batch 35-40% sooner. Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Yixuan Huang, ShengFan Zhang, Jiawei Chen
bullets: Targets a key OCR limitation: visually subtle symbols and repeated entries may be essential despite low salience.
Selects anchor tokens using adaptive resolution, global importance, and local contrast.
Compensates retained anchors with nearby discarded content and relative positions without adding tokens; the OCR backbone remains frozen.
At 50% of the original tokens, Ovis reaches 95.42 OmniDocBench Overall versus 96.09 uncompressed, and paired evaluations outperform simple input-resolution reduction.
At 25% retention, it exceeds a learned global selector by 4.70 points; at a 50% budget, it also reduces length-limit hits and finishes a fixed workload 35–40% sooner.

papers.title: Carry the Fine Print: Budget-Aware Visual Token Compression for Document OCR

papers.abstract: Deploying fruit instance segmentation in real agricultural settings requires generalizing across unseen species, orchards, and imaging conditions under strict onboard compute and annotation budgets. We introduce SegAnyFruit (SAF), a data construction and progressive training framework that distills foundation-model priors into lightweight, prompt-free segmenters. SAF combines generic mask pre-training, broad mid-training on automatically annotated web imagery from our curated WebFruits dataset, and human-verified agricultural refinement post-training on PaperFruits, together spanning 733K images and 9.66M whole-fruit masks across 165 fruit types. Across seven benchmarks, zero-shot SAF-RF-DETR-XL reaches 69.06 average mask AP50:95 (+4.76 over SAM 3) while remaining deployable on edge devices. SAF initialization also boosts few-shot to full-shot adaptation across five agricultural domains while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Finally, we systematically analyze training stages, data scale, model capacity, and generative augmentation, and validate our pipeline's transferability to underwater, cell, and human segmentation. We will release our datasets, code, and SAF models.

Across seven benchmarks, zero-shot SAF-RF-DETR-XL achieves 69.06 average mask AP50:95 and is deployable on edge devices.
SAF improves few-shot and full-shot adaptation across five agricultural domains, reduces catastrophic forgetting, and transfers to underwater, cell, and human segmentation.

papers.abstract: Physical AI requires models that understand spatial relationships and dynamic environments and translate observations into actions under limited onboard compute. We present TuringPAI, a family of models for on-device Physical AI comprising TuringPAI-VL for shared vision-language understanding, TuringPAI-Drive for autonomous driving, and TuringPAI-Embodied for robotic manipulation. TuringPAI-VL is a 0.65B model built on HybridViT-MLQ, which combines convolutional local aggregation with Transformer-based global modeling. Multi-scale Latent Queries integrate spatial features and observation history within the same visual Transformer, providing a compact, structured interface to the language model. Training combines general vision-language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal supervision. TuringPAI-VL supports general multimodal understanding and improves quantitative geometric perception over Qwen2-VL-2B, while providing a shared initialization for the two downstream VLA models. For autonomous driving, TuringPAI-Drive maintains all evaluated ADE/FDE metrics within 1.2\% of a full-token HybridViT baseline using the MLQ interface and achieves comparable aggregate scores in an in-house simulation evaluation. Using XPeng Native Runtime (XNRT) on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC, TuringPAI-Drive generates trajectories at 12\,Hz in on-vehicle operation. For robotic manipulation, TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8\% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites. These results demonstrate a shared vision-language foundation for driving and robotic manipulation under practical on-device constraints.
authors: Qiman Wu, Hanlin Chen, Yuhua Wei, Mingyuan Wang, Shaman Tang, Minghao Li, Rui Xin, Xingye Liu, Zhichao Yang, Yiqi Yu, Hongyan Pei, Xiaowen Tian, YingYing Liu, Shiwen Liu, Jiahui Hu, Yizhao Wang, Yuheng Zhang, Anhua Liu, Yue He, Shuang Su, Da Zhu, Hua Zhou, Pengfei Diao, Haojie Yang, Weichao Huang, Hang Zhang, Honggou Yang, Xianming Liu

Provides a shared initialization for TuringPAI-Drive and TuringPAI-Embodied, supporting driving and manipulation applications.
TuringPAI-Drive stays within 1.2% of a full-token baseline on evaluated ADE/FDE metrics and runs at 12 Hz on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC.

papers.abstract: Analyses of error feedback bound the memory buffer through a compressor contraction constant -- $r/p$ for the best rank-$r$ approximation of a $p$-dimensional spectrum -- which survives into the rate. We show it need not appear at all. When the compressed momentum is re-injected into the pre-compression accumulator, the previous compressed momentum $\beta_1 M_{t-1}$ is an admissible competitor in the projection, and the buffer obeys $\|E_t\|_F \le (1-\beta_1)\|G_t\|_F + \gamma\|E_{t-1}\|_F$, free of the dimensions $m,n$ and of the rank $r$. The argument uses only that the compressor is a metric projection onto a closed cone, so it covers top-$k$ selection as well as truncated SVD, holds for every selection from the projection set with no condition on singular-value crossings, and in its trajectory-tracking form assumes nothing about the gradients. In the two-stage template of the standard analyses it replaces a Stage-2 constant of order $p^2/r^2$ by one of order $1$, against $\Theta(p/r)$ for the sharpest contraction-based bounds. Transferring the full rate costs a leakage term, which we bound by the step-weighted gradient mass $\sum_{u\le t}\eta_u\|G_u\|_F$ and show tight up to a factor $\sqrt{2}$; the price is an additive $O(\log^2 T)$ floor, not a slower rate. On BERT fine-tuning at rank ratio $32/768$ the feedback decay costs under $0.008$ validation $F_1$.
bullets: The buffer bound depends on gradient norms and decay, not matrix dimensions or approximation rank.
The proof applies to metric projections onto closed cones, covering top-$k$ selection and truncated SVD without singular-value separation assumptions.
In standard two-stage analyses, a dimension-dependent factor of order $p^2/r^2$ improves to order $1$.
Rate transfer incurs a leakage term controlled by the step-weighted gradient mass, producing an additive $O(log^2 T)$ floor rather than a slower rate.
On BERT fine-tuning at rank ratio $32/768$, feedback decay reduces validation $F_1$ by under $0.008.

papers.abstract: Tree-structured speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models (VLMs) by verifying multiple candidate continuations in parallel. However, long visual contexts increase the cost of speculative computation, making candidate coverage and redundant expansion important considerations beyond tree topology adaptation. We propose Raptor, a training-free framework that uses rejection feedback to jointly regulate candidate coverage and drafting effort. Our key insight is that acceptance length alone cannot distinguish insufficient candidate coverage from excessive deep expansion, and these conditions require different allocation decisions. Raptor therefore extracts complementary rejection-aware signals to characterize speculative progress, frontier coverage, and redundant expansion. These signals jointly guide bounded, momentum-smoothed updates of tree depth, branching width, and drafting budget, together with execution control that limits unnecessary drafting and progressively restores expansion when appropriate. Extensive experiments with two VLMs across seven multimodal benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Raptor, achieving up to 2.39x average speedup over autoregressive decoding.
authors: Qishu Hu, Haozhao Wang, Zicong Hong, Yufeng Zhan, Yuanqing Xia
bullets: Addresses the high speculative-computation cost of long visual contexts, including insufficient candidate coverage and redundant expansion.
Uses rejection-aware signals for speculative progress, frontier coverage, and redundant expansion rather than relying only on acceptance length.
Adaptively updates tree depth, branching width, and drafting budget with bounded, momentum-smoothed control.
Experiments across two VLMs and seven multimodal benchmarks report up to 2.39× average speedup over autoregressive decoding.

papers.abstract: KV cache compression is critical for large reasoning models, where most of the cost comes from long generated reasoning traces rather than the input prompt. These traces often contain redundant and low-utility tokens due to looping, self-verification, and corrections. However, such tokens may still receive high attention scores, making it difficult to remove them without harming the reasoning process. We propose RoCoKV, a KV cache compression method designed for large reasoning models. RoCoKV introduces two key components. First, uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning adjusts the compression strength based on the model's confidence, allocating more memory during uncertain phases and applying stronger pruning when the model is confident. Second, redundancy-aware token selection reduces the impact of tokens that are highly similar to recent reasoning content, encouraging the model to retain more informative and diverse tokens. Beyond the algorithm, we co-design RoCoKV with the serving stack: we develop fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels and integrate them into vLLM as a drop-in plugin that preserves its paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture, turning algorithmic savings into real end-to-end speedups. Extensive experiments across three reasoning benchmarks and two reasoning models demonstrate that RoCoKV consistently improves reasoning accuracy under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art KV cache compression methods. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM, RoCoKV achieves a 1.27X speedup and 38% higher throughput on AIME25, the most challenging evaluated reasoning benchmark, and a 1.43X speedup and 45% higher throughput on the long synthetic benchmark, compared with Full-KV.
authors: Payman Behnam, Elaheh Sobhani, Saad Amin, Yahya Hassan, Daniyal Khan, Biswadeep Chakraborty, Tanish Patwa, Souvik Kundu, Alexey Tumanov
bullets: Targets redundant, low-utility tokens in long reasoning traces, which can nevertheless receive high attention scores.
Uses uncertainty-guided pruning: retains more cache during uncertain phases and prunes more aggressively when confidence is high.
Uses redundancy-aware selection to favor informative and diverse tokens over content similar to recent reasoning.
Co-designs the method with vLLM through fused CUDA decode kernels while preserving paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture.
Across three benchmarks and two reasoning models, improves accuracy under constrained cache budgets; for one 8B model, reports up to 1.43× speedup and 45% higher throughput versus Full-KV.

papers.abstract: We study the problem of computational efficiency for linear bandits in high-dimensional settings with a finite arm set. In linear bandits, the increase in the dimension $d$ of the feature vectors leads to growing computational costs of $O(d^2)$ at each round of update. Traditional low-rank approximation methods such as SOFUL reduce computation via fixed-size matrix sketching, yet run the risk of incurring vacuous linear regret when the spectral tail of the data is heavy and the approximation rank is inadequately selected. To guarantee regret convergence and effectively reduce computational costs, we introduce a clustering mechanism and propose the Coordinate Basis Linear Bandit (CBL) algorithm. Our method preserves the full covariance information in each cluster by maintaining an exact orthonormal basis of the cluster's column space together with a low-dimensional coordinate representation, which guarantees robust sublinear regret without spectral-tail vulnerabilities. It performs cluster switching by assigning a sentinel for each cluster, and reduces per-round update computation to $O(\bar r^2)$ in the cluster's effective dimension $\bar r=\min(r,l)$, where $r$ is the intrinsic rank of the data and $l<d$ is a tunable rank bound.
authors: Hantao Yang, Hong Xie, Defu Lian
bullets: Targets the $O(d^2)$ per-round update cost of high-dimensional linear bandits.
Avoids the vacuous linear regret risk of fixed-rank sketching under heavy spectral tails.
Maintains an exact orthonormal basis and low-dimensional coordinates for each cluster.
Uses cluster sentinels for switching and reduces updates to $O(\bar r^2)$, where $\bar r=\min(r,l)$.
The abstract states sublinear regret and computational savings, but gives no numerical experimental results.

papers.title: Coordinate Basis Linear Bandits with Sublinear Regret over Low-Rank Clusters
papers.tldr: CBL accelerates finite-arm linear bandits by clustering arms and preserving exact low-dimensional covariance structure, achieving robust sublinear regret without spectral-tail failures.

papers.abstract: Medical vision--language models (VLMs) often need to identify small, subtle lesions within high-resolution images containing extensive normal anatomy and redundant visual information. Visual-token compression improves efficiency, but preserving salient regions alone can discard the context needed for diagnostic interpretation. This context can extend across images: in bilateral mammography, the opposite breast provides a patient-specific anatomical reference. Yet retaining such evidence does not ensure that the model uses it effectively. We propose Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (BESR), which connects evidence preservation with comparative assessment through a bilateral-guided token selector and a bilateral reward. Under a shared token budget, the selector jointly prioritizes lesion appearance and its local and bilateral context, while the reward encourages assessments that benefit from the preserved comparison. Experiments on a bilateral dataset constructed from CBIS-DDSM and on VinDr-Mammo demonstrate improved evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained visual-token budgets. Inference benchmarking further shows reduced prefill latency.
authors: Zhengbo Zhou, Dooman Arefan, Shandong Wu
bullets: Addresses the risk that visual-token compression removes contextual information needed to interpret subtle mammographic lesions.
Uses a bilateral-guided token selector to prioritize lesions and their local and contralateral-breast context within a shared token budget.
Applies a bilateral reward to encourage diagnostic reasoning that benefits from preserved cross-image evidence.
Experiments on datasets built from CBIS-DDSM and VinDr-Mammo report better evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained token budgets.
Inference benchmarking shows reduced prefill latency.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) unify world modeling and action generation for robotic control by integrating flow-matching velocities, yet suffer from high multi-step denoising latency. Recent studies have explored speculative inference to accelerate WAMs by drafting and verifying denoising steps in parallel. However, existing methods either require training task-specific draft models or overlook critical WAM denoising dynamics when reusing past velocities as drafts. We revisit the denoising dynamics of WAMs and identify a dual nonuniformity that breaks standard velocity-reuse assumptions: velocity smoothness is nonuniform as adjacent velocity residuals differ sharply at early and final steps, so reuse there yields large residuals, which nonuniform integration time steps further translate into local state errors that accumulate into the final action distribution. Accordingly, we formalize this by theoretically deriving a trajectory error tolerance bound that characterizes how velocity residuals and integration time steps affect the final action distribution. Based on this, we propose WAMotor, the first speculative inference method tailored to the dual nonuniformity in WAMs. It selects reliable anchor velocities by deferring speculation and employs time-step-aware verification that scales acceptance thresholds by integration time step size. WAMotor offers plug-and-play benefits, enabling seamless integration with prior WAMs. Extensive evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show that WAMotor achieves 2.86$\times$--4.28$\times$ end-to-end speedups while maintaining task success rates. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Overdue-Lin/WAMotor
authors: Zexun Lin, Yuan Feng, Xike Xie
bullets: WAMs incur high latency from multi-step denoising during robotic control.
The method addresses dual nonuniformity: velocity residuals vary sharply across denoising stages, and integration step sizes unevenly amplify state errors.
It derives a trajectory error tolerance bound linking velocity residuals and integration steps to final action-distribution error.
WAMotor selects reliable anchor velocities, delays speculation when needed, and uses integration-step-aware verification thresholds.
Evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show 2.86×–4.28× speedups with maintained success rates.

papers.abstract: System 1 decision models (represented by Jev) provide fast, low-cost action selection, but existing agent integrations do not reliably translate these local advantages into task completion. At certain points during execution, an agent may repeatedly select the same actions without making progress toward its goal. LLM-based policies offer strong reasoning capabilities that support planning within an agent, but invoking them at every step incurs substantial overhead. The effective coordination should therefore preserve Jev's fast local action selection while introducing LLM reasoning when execution stalls. We observe that recurring state-action pairs can signal stalled execution. We therefore propose LoopRoute, a simple but effective action router that uses this signal to allocate control within an agent. The decision model acts by default. When a loop is detected, the LLM provides brief, feedback-driven assistance and then returns control to the decision model. Later loops can request further assistance. The rule requires neither additional training nor model-specific confidence calibration. Across three benchmarks and seven LLMs, LoopRoute improves task success over standalone Jev with only limited use of the LLM policy. The mean gains are 21.0%, 60.1%, and 30.1% on ALFWorld, MapReader, and TextWorld cooking, respectively. Compared with full LLM control, LoopRoute also substantially reduces the mean cumulative API time and API-call cost per task. The same rule also improves the success rates of six frozen decision models.
authors: Zeming Yu, Huamin Ma, Yingyu Chen, Yuan Sun, Peng Hu, Yang Qin

Requires no additional training or model-specific confidence calibration.
Across three benchmarks and seven LLMs, improves success over standalone Jev by 21.0%, 60.1%, and 30.1%, while reducing API time and cost versus full LLM control.
Also improves success rates for six frozen decision models.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers generate high-quality images, but iterative sampling remains computationally expensive. Feature caching reduces the number of full network evaluations, yet its approximation error can become more severe under short sampling schedules, where fewer full-compute steps and a coarser sampling grid can make history-based extrapolation less reliable. In this paper, we propose CalibCache, a lightweight offline calibration method that corrects systematic discrepancies between cached and full-compute feature dynamics. Specifically, CalibCache calibrates feature acceleration, defined as the second-order finite difference across sampling steps. Using only a single pair of full-compute and naive-cache trajectories at each setting, CalibCache fits scalar acceleration maps offline by centered least squares. These maps are then applied during sampling without additional full-network evaluations or online optimization. Across FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image on DrawBench and DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256, CalibCache consistently improves fidelity or generation quality over TaylorSeer under 20-step sampling at cache intervals $N=3,4,5$. At $N=5$, it reduces FLUX.1-dev LPIPS from $0.563$ to $0.429$ while achieving a $2.86\times$ denoising speedup over full-compute sampling, and lowers DiT-XL/2 FID from $16.39$ to $10.37$ relative to TaylorSeer.
authors: Mingyu Liang, Dingkun Xu, Jingwei Xu
bullets: Targets growing cache approximation errors caused by few sampling steps and coarse sampling grids.
Calibrates feature acceleration—the second-order finite difference across sampling steps—using one full-compute/naive-cache trajectory pair per setting.
Fits scalar acceleration maps offline with centered least squares and applies them during sampling without online optimization.
Improves fidelity or generation quality over TaylorSeer across FLUX.1-dev, Qwen-Image, and DiT-XL/2 at 20 steps and cache intervals of 3–5.
At cache interval 5, reports FLUX.1-dev LPIPS of 0.429 with a 2.86× denoising speedup, and DiT-XL/2 FID of 10.37 versus TaylorSeer’s 16.39.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as text classifiers, but their labels are only useful when we know to what extent we can trust them. We compare black-box methods (verbalised confidence and sampling) with white-box methods that read token probabilities (P(True), and multiple logit-scoring methods using constrained generation). We evaluate eleven open-weight LLMs (1B-32B parameters) on five classification datasets with 3 to 151 labels, measuring classification performance (accuracy, F1-macro), discrimination (AUROC), and calibration (ECE and Brier score). The choice of confidence method rarely impacts accuracy significantly, but logit-based scoring methods lead to much better discrimination (AUROC 0.74-0.77) than black-box methods (AUROC 0.57-0.66). Replacing labels with single-token identifiers preserves discrimination but costs 3-6 accuracy points on average. We also introduce decision-only scoring, which only scores positions where labels diverge in the prefix tree (trie). It reduces decode steps by 88-96% on the three largest label sets and performs comparably to full-label scoring. The best open-weight model-method configurations (Gemma 4 31B and Qwen 3.5 9B) are competitive with the commercial Jev 1.13.0 classifier.
bullets: Evaluates black-box confidence methods against token-probability and constrained-generation scoring across 11 open-weight LLMs and five classification datasets.
Confidence method choice has little effect on accuracy, but logit-based methods achieve much stronger discrimination (AUROC 0.74–0.77 vs. 0.57–0.66).
Replacing natural labels with single-token identifiers preserves discrimination but lowers accuracy by 3–6 points on average.
Decision-only scoring reduces decoding steps by 88–96% for the largest label sets while performing comparably to full-label scoring.
Top open-weight configurations are competitive with the commercial Jev 1.13.0 classifier.

papers.abstract: Modern recommendation systems face substantial memory pressure, largely from the sparse embedding layer that maps high-cardinality categorical features into dense vectors. In-training embedding pruning (ITEP) removes less important embedding rows during training, yielding end-to-end memory savings but sometimes degrading accuracy because per-table pruning ratios are set by size-based heuristics. We use feature importance (FI) to guide these ratios (FI-ITEP), assigning higher pruning to tables tied to less important features. Across three large-scale recommendation models, FI-ITEP achieves 20--40% total memory reduction while matching or improving accuracy relative to percentile-based ITEP. Because the feature-importance signal requires minimal resources to compute, these memory savings translate into concrete systems benefits: the same models train on fewer GPU trainers (e.g., 112 to 80) with higher per-GPU throughput, saving 1,000+ GPU-hours per model launch. We reproduce these trends on the open-source DLRM (Criteo 1TB) and quantify the end-to-end training-time and GPU-cost tradeoff---including the burden of computing FI---offering practical guidance for embedding pruning in real-world systems.
authors: Anish Khazane, Alex Saad-Falcon, Guanchu Wu, Marcio Porto, Jasper Shan, Fei Yu, Eugene Shulga, Intaik Park, Yongzhe Zhang, Xiaoyu Deng, Sheng Luo, Xiaoya Wang
bullets: Targets memory pressure from large sparse embedding tables in recommendation systems.
Assigns higher pruning rates to embedding tables associated with less important features, replacing size-based heuristics.
Validated across three large-scale models and reproduced on DLRM with the Criteo 1TB dataset.
Enables training with fewer GPU trainers, higher per-GPU throughput, and over 1,000 fewer GPU-hours per model launch.
Evaluates the end-to-end tradeoff, including the cost of computing feature importance.

papers.abstract: Can a distilled image generator save time by reusing features between its few remaining denoising steps? We study a fixed branch cache that replaces selected attention and MLP evaluations while preserving the student's noise schedule. One full trajectory and one raw-cache trajectory from the same initial noise supply a scalar correction for each branch type and reuse position. At $1024^2$, one internal reuse reduces four-step Qwen-Image-Lightning denoising time from 1.279 to 0.977 seconds. Three reuses yield $1.51\times$ speedup on eight-step Lightning and $1.53\times$ on eight-step Hyper-FLUX. We evaluate image quality on all 200 DrawBench prompts. With the reuse positions held fixed, correction improves mean same-seed image fidelity over raw reuse by 0.66 and 0.87 dB on the two Lightning students. On Hyper-FLUX the PSNR difference is 0.01 dB, while LPIPS improves from 0.1625 to 0.1546. These results measure the effect of branch caching and correction while retaining each student's original sampling grid.
bullets: Reuses selected attention and MLP features across denoising steps without changing the student’s noise schedule.
A scalar correction is computed per branch type and reuse position from full and raw-cache trajectories with the same initial noise.
One reuse cuts four-step Qwen-Image-Lightning denoising from 1.279 to 0.977 seconds; three reuses provide 1.51× and 1.53× speedups on eight-step Lightning and Hyper-FLUX.
Across 200 DrawBench prompts, correction improves Lightning same-seed fidelity by 0.66 and 0.87 dB over raw reuse; Hyper-FLUX shows similar PSNR and better LPIPS.
Results are scoped to fixed reuse positions and preserve each model’s original sampling grid.

papers.abstract: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory bottlenecks in long-context LLM inference.
Propagates token importance across attention-induced transition graphs beyond recency or immediate attention.
Evaluated on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning across multiple LLM families.
Maintains competitive task performance under moderate to aggressive compression, including up to 90%, with low end-to-end overhead.
Scope: performance is demonstrated across the reported tasks and model families, with a favorable accuracy–memory trade-off rather than universal superiority.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free KV cache eviction method based on global importance estimation, directly targeting memory-efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
papers.tldr: PRKV uses Personalized PageRank to estimate globally important tokens for training-free KV-cache eviction, enabling substantial memory savings while preserving long-context performance.

papers.abstract: Computational complexity theory offers a principled framework for characterizing the efficiency of computational problems, and Large Language Models (LLMs) can similarly be viewed as computational systems executing a structured process of input, inference-time compute, and output. In this context, the number of generated tokens emerges as a natural and directly observable proxy for inference-time compute. However, we show that the tempting analogy between LLM token length and classical time complexity does not hold. We disprove the hypothesis that inference-time token usage aligns monotonically with classical time complexity, demonstrating a fundamental divergence grounded in how LLMs actually allocate computation during inference. To this end, we introduce LLM Complexity, a new metric designed to quantify problem complexity from the perspective of LLMs by characterizing the area bounded above by the accuracy-token curve. We find that diverse LLMs induce highly consistent task rankings under LLM Complexity, indicating that the metric captures stable notions of difficulty across models. We leverage this property to construct an easy-to-hard curriculum for supervised fine-tuning, which improves accuracy while reducing token consumption. Finally, we demonstrate that LLM Complexity generalizes to real-world tasks, producing more stable cross-model correlations than human-annotated difficulty labels.
authors: Yu-Hung Wu, Shao-Xiang Yuan, Chan-Hung Yu, Zih-Ching Chen, Kuan-Hao Huang, Shao-Hua Sun
bullets: Generated-token count is an observable proxy for inference compute, but it does not monotonically align with classical computational complexity.
LLM Complexity is defined by the area bounded above by the accuracy–token curve.
Different LLMs produce highly consistent task-difficulty rankings under this metric.
An easy-to-hard curriculum based on LLM Complexity improves accuracy while reducing token consumption.
The metric extends to real-world tasks and yields more stable cross-model correlations than human difficulty labels.

(b) For four sum closest, accuracy at a 10K-token budget does not decrease monotonically with problem size. Together, these results highlight a mismatch between algorithmic complexity and LLM inference behavior.

SFT yields higher accuracy on seen instances than unseen instances for seen algorithms, confirming effective adaptation, while curriculum SFT improves held-out performance and transfers better to unseen algorithms.

papers.selection_reason: Characterizes LLM inference complexity via token usage and builds an efficiency-improving curriculum; fits LLM and efficient-AI topics.
papers.title: LLM Complexity: Towards a Computational Complexity View of Large Language Model Inference
papers.tldr: LLM Complexity measures task difficulty from the accuracy–token tradeoff, revealing that token usage does not directly follow classical time complexity and enabling more efficient fine-tuning curricula.

papers.abstract: A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track, a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend's current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track. It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate's refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait.
authors: Benjamin Novotny, Doug Szeto, Chang Wang, Shicheng Chen, George Zhihua Yuan, Bob Kamma, Michael Ge, John Xin Zhou, Andrea Olgiati
bullets: Addresses stale fixed dispatch rates caused by changing fleet capacity and unpredictable output lengths.
Uses fail-fast capacity checks, durable priority queues, and a stateful controller that probes upward and backs off based only on refusals.
Production A/B testing served a classifier with 43% fewer H100s, though lower-priority work waited longer during backfill peaks.
In replay, it achieved within 1% of tuned fixed-rate goodput with about one-quarter the refusal share.
Deployed at Meta for post and live-video understanding, processing over 300 million requests and hundreds of terabytes of media daily.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The traffic shaper implements CAP-AND-TRACK. (a) One enqueue interface feeds online and batch queues. TRACK runs in the online workers and dispatches each queue through the gateway at its learned rate. A refusal from any of the four kinds of CAP (model-server cap, provider admission, per-caller quota, or engine queue-depth aware router) returns as HTTP 429. Other failures stay outside the feedback loop. (b) Each worker paces each queue at the rate the leader pushes. A 429 returns the request to the front of its ready queue with media staged. Up to 3N media items are in flight, but only N download and N upload at once. The rest wait between the two stages to keep each worker container’s network bandwidth saturated.

Figure 2. Controlled replay at about twice a replica’s capacity, median of three runs per arm. Without the cap, goodput (successes per minute) falls to zero and stays there once requests queued inside the model server outlive the timeout. With the cap, goodput holds steady.

Goodput per host (top) and refusal share (bottom) are in 15-second bins. Dashed lines mark measured full and cut capacity. During the cut TRACK’s refusals fell as it descended toward the new ceiling. The 100 and 120% rates drew 49% and 58% refusals over the cut. TRACK regained full capacity within about 5 minutes of the restore. Every arm tested at both caps had cap-64 goodput within about 0.8% of its cap-40 goodput in every phase (Table C1). Median of three runs per arm; bands span the runs.

The queue is in hours of median completions. Each morning the pool lost capacity and the queue held the excess. Each afternoon TRACK followed the pool’s 429s back up and drained the queue.
