papers.title: Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity
papers.tldr: Cap-and-Track adaptively dispatches LLM inference requests to shifting capacity using refusal signals, reducing required GPUs while maintaining near-fixed-rate goodput.

papers.abstract: Hybrid attention models combine full and linear attention to achieve a better quality--efficiency trade-off. Converting pretrained Transformers into such models requires identifying which layers should retain full attention under a prescribed budget. We identify two off-policy mismatches in FlashMorph's layer selection: (i) continuous branch interpolation and teacher-forced hidden states differ from discrete hybrid computation; and (ii) frozen model weights fail to account for parameter adaptation during subsequent recovery. We introduce FlashMorph2, an on-policy layer-selection method that (I) evaluates sampled discrete hybrid architectures end to end using their own hidden states, and (II) jointly optimizes layer-selection scores and model weights under the recovery objective to reflect post-adaptation performance. Experiments across Qwen3 model scales and linear-attention variants show that FlashMorph2 consistently outperforms existing layer-selection methods, improving average scores over FlashMorph by $+2.42$ points on RULER, $+1.08$ on LongBench, and $+0.76$ on recall-intensive tasks, while completing layer selection in only $0.72$--$3.57$ GPU hours across 0.6B--8B models, demonstrating high efficiency and scalability.
authors: Disen Lan, Xuanda Wang, Jianbin Zheng, Huafeng Kuang, Wei Tang, Yu Cheng
bullets: Hybrid attention models need to choose which layers retain full attention under a compute budget.
FlashMorph2 evaluates discrete hybrid architectures end to end using their own hidden states, avoiding off-policy selection errors.
It jointly optimizes layer-selection scores and model weights to reflect performance after recovery.
Across Qwen3 scales and linear-attention variants, it improves over FlashMorph by 2.42 RULER points, 1.08 LongBench points, and 0.76 points on recall-intensive tasks.
Layer selection takes 0.72–3.57 GPU hours for 0.6B–8B models, indicating efficient scaling.

papers.abstract: Looped language models deepen reasoning at a compact parameter count by iterating a shared layer stack T times per token, turning recurrence depth directly into sequential decoding latency. Conventional early-exit decoding halts after initial passes without cache completion, truncating cached key-value states of past tokens to shallow depth. We study the opposite strategy, late entry, where new tokens skip initial passes and enter directly into the final K T alongside subsequent steps at zero extra serial calls. Projecting these finished T-pass wake states inside the existing output GEMM (Wake verification, governed by logit-margin tolerance tau in [0, inf]) unifies greedy-exact T-pass decoding (tau = 0, matching K = T block decoding within bf16 reduction order), margin-gated verification (tau > 0), and non-rollback lossy late entry (tau = inf) inside a single static CUDA graph. On Ouro-2.6B (T = 4), K = 2 Wake reaches 5.2x greedy-exact speedup at tau = 0 (+26% over K = 4 block decoding on GSM8K) and 6.8x at tau = inf (+16.9 points over trained early exit at matched speed). Scaling test-time recurrence across T in {8, 16, 32, 64} on Huginn-3.5B cuts K = T/4 rollbacks 21.5x with depth, driving greedy-exact (tau = 0) speedups to 6.1x (T = 32) and 8.4x (T = 64, +153% over K = 64 block) and tau = inf speedups to 10.6 to 12.5x.
authors: Ziqi Jin, Jiaxi Li, Weiwen Xu, Aixin Sun
bullets: Problem: Standard early exit leaves past-token key-value caches incomplete, while full recurrence increases sequential decoding latency.
Method: New tokens enter directly into the final K recurrent steps; Wake verification checks projected states using a logit-margin tolerance τ within a static CUDA graph.
Modes: τ=0 provides greedy-exact decoding, τ>0 enables margin-gated verification, and τ=∞ gives non-rollback lossy late entry.
Results: On Ouro-2.6B, K=2 achieved 5.2× exact and 6.8× lossy speedups; scaling recurrence on Huginn-3.5B reached up to 8.4× exact and 12.5× lossy speedups.

papers.selection_reason: Decoding strategy for looped LLMs that reduces latency and cache-related overhead; relevant to efficient inference and LLM architecture.
papers.title: Late Entry in Looped Language Models
papers.tldr: Late entry accelerates looped language-model decoding by letting new tokens skip early recurrent passes while preserving configurable exactness or accepting controlled approximation.

papers.abstract: GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. Under expert parallelism, MoE experts are spread across GPUs, and because the router sends uneven numbers of tokens to each GPU, lightly loaded GPUs wait for the most loaded one. Even after applying load balancing solutions, such bubbles still take 8--13% of prefill time. We present BubbleTea, the first colocation system that leverages expert-parallel bubbles for fine-tuning. Unlike existing colocation systems, which make one scheduling decision for all GPUs per forward pass, BubbleTea predicts each GPU's bubble at every layer from the router's token assignment, and fills it with short chunks of fine-tuning work that reuse the weights already loaded for serving. We also introduce compiler passes that automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM as-is, without porting each model architecture to a separate training engine. Our evaluation on three MoE models, served on four A100 GPUs, shows that fine-tuning throughput with BubbleTea is 1.9--6.2$\times$ faster than with LLMStation, a state-of-the-art colocation system. BubbleTea keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads, compared to 44 for LLMStation. On bursty production traces, BubbleTea trains 3.3$\times$ faster than LLMStation and 14$\times$ faster than a stock trainer colocated under CUDA MPS, with p90 inference latency staying within 7% of serving alone.
authors: Oana Balmau, Saurav Banka, Jiaxuan Chen, Anne-Marie Kermarrec, Ramya Narasimha Prabhu, Rafael Pires, Mathis Randl, Martijn de Vos
bullets: MoE expert parallelism creates 8–13% prefill-time bubbles because GPUs receive uneven token loads.
BubbleTea predicts each GPU’s bubble at every layer and schedules short fine-tuning chunks during that idle time.
Compiler passes automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM without requiring model-specific training-engine ports.
Across three MoE models on four A100 GPUs, BubbleTea achieves 1.9–6.2× higher fine-tuning throughput than LLMStation.
It keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads and performs strongly on bursty production traces.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the problem of idle compute in MoE inference (expert-parallel bubbles) and proposes a system to utilize these idle periods for fine-tuning, directly contributing to inference efficiency and resource utilization.
papers.title: Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: BubbleTea improves colocated fine-tuning by filling per-GPU idle gaps created by expert parallelism while preserving inference latency.

papers.abstract: Self-attention over long token sequences dominates the inference cost of video diffusion transformers. Clustering-based sparse attention clusters both queries and keys and lets all queries in a cluster share one selection of key clusters. We show that this sharing limits accuracy: with key clusters and density fixed, attention grows more accurate as the query clusters are refined, and is most accurate when each query selects on its own, which needs no query clustering at all. We therefore propose Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention (PQRS), a training-free method that clusters only keys, lets each query select its own key clusters, and compensates for the unselected ones with their centroids. Per-query selections leave no query tile with a shared key list, so PQRS traverses key clusters instead of queries, buckets queries with identical selections into dense tasks, and merges their partial results in one pass under a fixed softmax offset carried from the previous denoising step. On four text-to-video and image-to-video models from the Wan and HunyuanVideo families, PQRS is the fastest of all the sparse attention methods we evaluate and the closest to the dense output, reaching $28.9$ dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and $35.4$ dB on HunyuanVideo at $1.66$--$2.10\times$ end-to-end speedup.
authors: Zhen Huang, Shuwei Li, Ruizhe Yao, Xinrui Chen, Danyi Liu, Haoyuan Liang, Zhiyu Ye, Qiuyan Sun, Bingwei Chen, Yiyuan Li, Xu Zhou, Haohuan Fu
bullets: Clustering queries and keys together limits sparse-attention accuracy because queries in a cluster share key selections.
PQRS clusters only keys, performs per-query key-cluster selection, and approximates unselected keys with cluster centroids.
It efficiently executes per-query routing by grouping queries with identical selections and merging results with a carried softmax offset.
Evaluated on four Wan and HunyuanVideo text-to-video and image-to-video models, it achieves 1.66–2.10× end-to-end speedup.
It reports 28.9 dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and 35.4 dB on HunyuanVideo, while remaining closest to dense attention among evaluated sparse methods.

papers.title: Every Query Routes Itself: Accelerating Video Diffusion Transformers with Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about long interleaved inputs, such as documents of many pages and collections of hundreds of images, but they are slow to start: on inputs of about 100K tokens, the prefill takes most of the wait for the first output token. A common approach prunes the input by scoring its tokens with the target model itself or with a small model of the same family that first writes an answer. However, this scoring takes much of the time that pruning saves. We find that the evidence for a question lies in a few whole units (images or paragraphs), and that a small hybrid model finds them with one attention head of an early layer, even at half image resolution. Based on these findings, we propose SkimPrefill, which lets the small hybrid model read the whole input first, up to that early layer, with images at half resolution. Most layers of the small hybrid model (Qwen3.5-0.8B) run in linear time, so this pass is short. SkimPrefill then ranks every unit with that head and gives the target the top units as an ordinary shorter prompt. One untrained selector serves targets of different model families. Extensive experiments on MMLongBench at 128K tokens, with 19 datasets of five task types, show the effectiveness of SkimPrefill. With 10% of the input tokens kept, SkimPrefill speeds up the prefill of Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3-VL-32B by 3.7 times, 11.6 time and 8.2 times while maintaining their average accuracy.
authors: Xiaolin Lin, Kai-Chiang Wu, Bing Li, Grace Li Zhang
bullets: Targets the high first-token latency caused by prefill on roughly 100K-token interleaved image-text inputs.
Uses an early attention head in a small hybrid model, with images at half resolution, to rank whole input units.
Keeps the top 10% of tokens/units and feeds them to the target VLM as a shorter ordinary prompt.
A single untrained selector transfers across different target model families.
On MMLongBench at 128K tokens, it maintains average accuracy while reporting 3.7×, 11.6×, and 8.2× prefill speedups for three target models.

papers.title: Let a Small Model Read First: Faster Prefill for Long Interleaved Image-Text Inputs
papers.tldr: SkimPrefill accelerates long-context VLMs by using a small model to identify relevant images and paragraphs before the target model processes a shortened prompt.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents accumulate extensive interaction histories when solving complex, long-horizon tasks, making efficient memory management critical to their performance and scalability. While existing memory management methods primarily focus on what to retain or retrieve, they often overlook how much perceptual detail should be allocated to individual past interactions. We posit that effective agent memory depends not only on the information preserved, but also on the granularity at which each past interaction is perceived. Motivated by this insight, we propose Resolution as Attention (RAA), a memory perception mechanism that uses visual resolution as a means of attention allocation across interaction histories. RAA renders past interactions as images and dynamically adjusts their resolution at every step according to their relevance to the agent's upcoming decision, preserving fine-grained information for critical interactions while reducing visual-token consumption for less relevant ones. To adaptively determine the perceptual fidelity of each interaction, we train a lightweight relevance estimator with teacher-model guidance and further optimize it to preserve the agent's decision consistency at a reduced visual-token cost. Experiments across multiple tasks and backbones show that RAA reduces token consumption by over 50% without compromising task performance. Moreover, RAA can be integrated as a plug-in perception layer with existing memory management methods, yielding further token savings and revealing adaptive perception as a complementary dimension of agent memory.
authors: Siqi Xiang, Zhipeng Xu, Shengrui Liu, Zulong Chen, Chunyan Miao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Targets inefficient perception of long interaction histories in LLM-based agents.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a memory perception mechanism that dynamically adjusts the resolution of past interactions to reduce token consumption, directly addressing token efficiency and agent memory.
papers.title: Resolution as Attention for Efficient Agent Memory Perception
papers.tldr: Resolution as Attention dynamically adjusts the visual detail of past interactions, cutting memory token use by over 50% while maintaining task performance.

papers.abstract: We convert a trained attention network as a whole, attention included, into a hard-logic predicate circuit that runs in its place. Every unit of the circuit is a 0/1 predicate on tokens, and every map between predicates is a minimised truth table. Short tables, such as the product of a query code and a key code, are minimised exactly, and wide feature-to-feature transitions become implication rules by noise-tolerant minimisation. Blocks are replaced one at a time from the output down, in the manner of the Ship of Theseus, and after each replacement the remaining soft part re-adapts to the frozen circuit. Attention selection takes two forms, a row-wise comparison of integer scores (order selection) and a learned rule (rule selection). Both are fitted on the ordinary training set alone, and only on the examples that the teacher classifies correctly, so that the circuit imitates the teacher where the teacher is right. On TweetEval-emotion, the complete circuit of DistilGPT2 reaches a test gold accuracy of 66.5 $\pm$ 1.3% with order selection and 57.4 $\pm$ 2.5% with rule selection over three seeds, against 74.7% for the teacher and 64.0% for a bag of word pieces fitted on the same tweets, and that of BERT-base reaches 70.0 $\pm$ 0.5% with order selection and 63.7 $\pm$ 1.2% with rule selection against 77.8%. The circuit needs no multiplier and no weight traffic, and its exported hardware description reproduces it bit for bit. By a synthesis-based estimate it classifies one tweet in about 1-2 $\mu$s (DistilGPT2) and 3-5 $\mu$s (BERT) on an FPGA card and in 5-9 $\mu$s on a palm-sized board whose module draws 7.5-15 W, two to three orders of magnitude faster than the network on a GPU at batch 1 (measured, 0.9-2.6 ms for DistilGPT2 including an optimised CUDA-graph baseline), at a cost of 8.5 (DistilGPT2) and 8.6 (BERT) points of gold accuracy for the synthesised seed-0 circuits.
authors: Yuchen Li, Zongqi Fan, Xintong Li, Nguyen H. Tran, Ken-Tye Yong
bullets: Extracts 0/1 token predicates and minimised truth-table or implication-rule mappings from the entire trained network, including attention.
Uses iterative Ship-of-Theseus block replacement, allowing the remaining soft network to adapt after each circuit component is frozen.
Fits attention selection using either integer-score ordering or learned rules, trained only on teacher-correct examples.
On TweetEval-emotion, circuits achieve 57.4–70.0% test accuracy versus 74.7–77.8% for the teacher, depending on model and selection method.

The synthesized hardware uses no multipliers or weight traffic and is estimated to run 2–3 orders of magnitude faster than batch-1 GPU inference, with an 8.5–8.6 point accuracy loss for seed-0 circuits.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The method. (a) Blocks are hardened from the top down (reverse Ship of Theseus), and after each stage the soft blocks below re-adapt to the frozen circuit, so that every stage is a complete classifier. papers.selection_reason: Converts attention networks into hard-logic circuits achieving orders-of-magnitude speedup, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: How to Turn an Attention Neural Network into an Interpretable Hard-Logic Predicate Circuit: Truth-Table Predicate Extraction and State-Machine Merging under Ship-of-Theseus Replacement
papers.tldr: The work replaces attention networks with interpretable hard-logic predicate circuits, achieving much faster low-power inference while sacrificing some accuracy.

papers.abstract: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. We report these results openly, along with two cheap usage patterns that block switching enables: undoing a failed attempt and running subagents without a new context.
bullets: Splits history into blocks and uses a fast yes/no selector to reveal relevant blocks while masking others in one key-value cache.
On a synthetic lookup task with Qwen3-1.7B, selective context improved accuracy from 93/120 to 119/120; masking was comparable to deletion.
Context selection is the main weakness: a supervised linear probe reached 110/120, while keyword search achieved perfect task performance.
The probe did not transfer to a second task, limiting evidence for general-purpose selection.
Block switching also supports undoing failed attempts and running subagents without creating a new context.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for efficient context handling in LLMs by selectively showing relevant blocks and masking irrelevant ones, directly contributing to token pruning and eviction strategies.
papers.title: MoE-Context: Show the Model Only What It Needs
papers.tldr: MoE-Context lets language models selectively expose only the context blocks needed for each step while preserving the rest as recoverable notes.

papers.abstract: Active visual reasoning enables multimodal models to answer challenging visual questions by gathering fine-grained evidence through iterative image inspection and tool use. However, accumulating crops and reasoning tokens expands the key-value (KV) cache, making compression important for reducing memory and inference costs. Existing KV compression methods typically select historical tokens based on attention, recency, or redundancy. These criteria do not explicitly distinguish locally replaced evidence from complementary information needed for future exploration: each crop refreshes a local region, while earlier views may still support subsequent decisions. Discarding such evidence can impair accuracy or require additional search, while scoring and cache reorganization can offset the computational savings from compression. We introduce CanopyKV, a training-free KV compression framework that uses parent-child crop relationships to retain complementary evidence, keeps retained history stable, and protects the state needed for ongoing reasoning. Tool metadata provides retention signals without additional attention scoring, while compact KV storage reduces subsequent attention costs. Across VisualProbe, V*, HR-Bench, and MME-Lite, CanopyKV achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and end-to-end efficiency among the evaluated KV compression methods. On MME-Lite, it retains approximately one-quarter of Dense's total KV while improving accuracy by 10.5 percentage points and accelerating complete reasoning by $1.64\times$.
authors: Lei Yang, Dayan Wu, Yiliang Zhu, Xinze Liu, Hengjie Zhu, Zihao Zhang, Ding Wang, Peng Fu, Zheng Lin
bullets: Active visual reasoning accumulates crop and reasoning tokens, causing KV-cache growth and higher memory and inference costs.
Existing compression criteria may discard earlier views that remain useful for future exploration, especially when crops replace only local evidence.
CanopyKV uses parent–child crop relationships and tool metadata to retain complementary history, stabilize retained tokens, and protect ongoing reasoning state.
It avoids additional attention-based scoring and reduces subsequent attention costs through compact KV storage.

Across four evaluated benchmarks, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and end-to-end efficiency among the compared KV-compression methods; on MME-Lite, it retains about one-quarter of Dense’s KV, improves accuracy by 10.5 percentage points, and speeds reasoning by 1.64×.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free KV cache compression for active visual reasoning in multimodal LLMs; directly fits memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: CanopyKV: Remember beyond the Crop for Fast Active Visual Reasoning
papers.tldr: CanopyKV is a training-free KV-cache compression method that preserves complementary visual evidence from prior crops, improving active visual reasoning efficiency and accuracy.

papers.abstract: Reliable tissue detection is essential for whole-slide image analysis, yet high average segmentation accuracy can conceal failures involving pale tissue, small fragments, and heterogeneous staining. Pathology foundation models offer transferable representations, but exhaustive inference is computationally demanding and may introduce false-positive tissue predictions. We propose SCOUT (Selective Correction of Uncertain Tissue), a risk-guided cascade that selectively refines an initial thumbnail-based tissue mask. A lightweight audit network estimates the spatial distribution of segmentation errors and prioritizes candidate regions for processing by a frozen pathology foundation model. An asymmetric consensus rule integrates the resulting predictions with the initial mask to recover missed tissue while limiting false positives. A calibrated slide-level review score additionally controls the marginal rate of unflagged case-group failures under the calibration assumptions. Evaluation on a public multi-source, multi-stain benchmark shows that SCOUT reduces the proportion of case groups requiring mask correction from 38.1% for the best released detector to 18.6%, with particularly pronounced improvements in immunohistochemistry. Source-held-out experiments demonstrate better generalization than a segmentation network trained on the same annotations, while selective inference achieves an observed failure rate no higher than processing all candidate regions. Downstream, lymph-node classification with SCOUT masks is non-inferior to that obtained with two of the three released detectors evaluated. A variant built on an openly licensed foundation model is publicly released as an installable Python package with trained weights. These results support risk-guided foundation-model inference as an effective approach to tissue detection across heterogeneous histopathology data.
bullets: Targets failures hidden by average accuracy, including pale tissue, small fragments, and heterogeneous staining.
Uses a lightweight audit network to identify likely mask errors and prioritize regions for foundation-model refinement.
Combines initial and refined masks with an asymmetric consensus rule to recover missed tissue while limiting false positives.
On a multi-source, multi-stain benchmark, reduced case groups needing correction from 38.1% to 18.6%, with strong gains in immunohistochemistry.
Source-held-out results showed better generalization than a similarly annotated segmentation network; an openly licensed implementation was released.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents have become one of the most popular applications of large language models. Yet, agentic AI comes at the cost of a tremendous amount of GPU compute resources, which limits its profitability and its viability at scale. In this paper, we investigate whether smaller, cheaper models can cut this cost without sacrificing accuracy. We evaluate 36 popular large and small open-weight models released since 2024 on a software engineering benchmark, and find that recent small models are closing the accuracy gap compared to their large counterparts. We investigate the structure of this gap and find that the gap is highly concentrated around hard tasks that small language models fail to solve while achieving remarkably good accuracy for easy and medium complexity tasks. Following this observation, we show that by utilizing a hybrid inference strategy that tries a small model first and escalates to a large one only when needed, we can achieve up to 33% reduction in total GPU-hour costs and 16.4% on all tasks from SWE-bench Verified, without sacrificing accuracy. Strikingly, this simple cascade nearly matches an oracle-style task router, highlighting a practical path for deploying cost-aware coding agents in production without complex learned task routers and with minimal engineering complexity.
authors: Boxi Zhou, German Sviridov, Dmitrii Ustiugov, Haris Javaid
bullets: Recent small open-weight models perform well on easy and medium software-engineering tasks, with most of the accuracy gap concentrated on hard tasks.
The study evaluates 36 large and small models released since 2024 on SWE-bench Verified.
A hybrid strategy starts with a small model and escalates to a large model when needed.
The cascade reduces GPU-hour costs by up to 33% overall and 16.4% across all tasks without sacrificing accuracy.
It nearly matches an oracle-style task router while requiring minimal engineering complexity.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers achieve large effective depth with compact models by repeatedly applying a weight-shared block across R recurrent steps, each maintaining a loop-specific key-value (KV) cache. To accelerate sequential loop execution, recent wave-style self-speculative methods like WaveFront Decoding (WFD) and LoopSpec pipeline draft and target tokens across loops in a single step. However, they face two critical limitations. First, they draft only at fixed loops and ignore intermediate prediction changes, wasting computation on stale trajectories. Second, batching tokens from different loops loads up to Rx the KV cache per step, severely amplifying memory traffic in long-context scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose LoopCache, an efficient self-speculative decoding framework for long-context Looped Transformers. Based on the correlation between prediction switches and output confidence, LoopCache introduces confidence-guided dynamic draft updating to refine drafts in flight across all intermediate loops. Furthermore, LoopCache employs a cyclic loop KV cache strategy that rotates through loop-specific KV caches, restricting per-step KV traffic to a single loop while batching tokens at the nearest matching cycle for lossless verification. By also selectively retaining independent KV caches for a few loop-sensitive shallow layers, LoopCache improves acceptance rates with negligible overhead. Experiments show that LoopCache achieves average 10.25x and 14.56x speedup over WFD and LoopSpec.
authors: Zizhuo Fu, Haochen Huang, Shengxuan Qiu, Linye Wei, Ziyu Tang, Runsheng Wang, Meng Li
bullets: Existing wave-style methods waste computation by drafting at fixed loops and following stale predictions.
They can also amplify memory traffic by loading KV caches from multiple loops per decoding step.
LoopCache uses confidence-guided draft updates across intermediate loops to improve speculative trajectories.
A cyclic loop KV-cache strategy limits each step to one loop’s KV traffic while enabling lossless verification; selective shallow-layer caches further improve acceptance.
It reports average speedups of 10.25× over WFD and 14.56× over LoopSpec.

papers.abstract: Vision foundation models produce semantically strong features on a coarse patch grid, and dense prediction needs them at pixel resolution. Existing learned upsamplers close that gap by regressing the high-resolution feature map from the low-resolution one, typically through cross-attention driven by the input image. We observe that most of what they regress needs no learning: plain bilinear interpolation already reproduces the smooth regions of the target, and recent benchmarks even report bilinear and bicubic on par with several learned upsamplers. The rest is mostly edges and fine details, which suggests that these learned upsamplers spend much of their capacity re-computing the smooth content that classical interpolation provides. We therefore introduce AnchorUp, which stops predicting the high-resolution feature map and predicts only its correction from the interpolation. It keeps a parameter-free classical upsampler as an anchor, obtains a second prediction from a small guidance network, and blends the two through a single learnable scalar gate. Because the anchor supplies the smooth content, the guidance network only has to correct what remains. An analysis of the learned correction confirms that it concentrates on edges and fine details, and so the network can be small: AnchorUp uses 167,425 parameters, a quarter of the budget of the strongest baseline, NAF, and runs at 64% of its latency. Trained once on DINOv3 with only the first of NAF's two training stages, and evaluated on that backbone plus six held-out ones, it is already on par with NAF trained through both stages on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes. Our method surpasses it on DAVIS-2017 video object segmentation; the gain holds on every backbone and is larger in contour accuracy F. Code is available at https://github.com/KotaroHorikawa/AnchorUp.
authors: Kotaro Horikawa, Keisuke Toida, Junya Komori, Kazuhiro Hotta
bullets: Motivation: Bilinear or bicubic interpolation already captures smooth feature content, leaving learned upsamplers to mainly recover edges and fine details.
Method: Interpolate the coarse features, predict a residual correction with a small guidance network, and blend them using one learnable scalar gate.
Contribution: A parameter-efficient upsampler with 167,425 parameters and 64% of NAF’s latency.
Results: Trained only on DINOv3 with one training stage, AnchorUp matches two-stage NAF on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes across six held-out backbones.
On DAVIS-2017, it surpasses NAF on every backbone, with larger gains in contour accuracy F.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) reason about long videos over hundreds to thousands of tokens. Every decoding step re-reads the key-value (KV) cache of the entire video. Must the model keep looking while it reasons? In LookAway, the model first writes timestamped notes on what the question needs and then puts the video away. Once the notes close, the inference engine hides the video's KV cache for the rest of the response. Across both hybrid and pure-attention VLMs, dependence on the video is concentrated early in the response. On Qwen3.6-27B, writing notes preserves accuracy better than free reasoning at the same withdrawal step. Replacing them with another video's notes harms accuracy, whereas keeping the video visible alongside the model's own notes adds no significant benefit. Without additional training, LookAway nearly matches full-video thinking accuracy at 0.12-0.13 times its modeled decode cost. To shorten this initial look, we fine-tune the model on its own correct LookAway responses. Reinforcement learning then rewards correct answers while penalizing KV reads. The trained model puts the video away after a median of 66-68 tokens. Across three held-out benchmarks, it writes more tokens than an identically trained full-video model yet reads only 27-35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy.
authors: Pengyu Li, Zhitao Gao, Lingling Zhang, Heng Wang, Chengqian Ma, WenHao Wang, Wenxuan Huang, Chen Zheng, Jun Liu
bullets: Long-video dependence is concentrated early in the response, so continued video access is often unnecessary.
The method first creates question-focused, timestamped notes before withdrawing the video from inference.
On Qwen3.6-27B, notes preserve accuracy better than unrestricted reasoning at the same withdrawal point; substituted notes hurt, while retaining the video adds no significant benefit.
Without extra training, LookAway nearly matches full-video accuracy at 0.12–0.13× the modeled decode cost.
With fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, the model withdraws after a median of 66–68 tokens and reads 27–35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy across three held-out benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Long video sequences make attention a substantial cost in video diffusion models. Block sparse attention (BSA) reduces this cost by computing selected blocks exactly while compressing the remaining blocks. However, fixed token grouping can place tokens with dissimilar attention preferences in the same group, while uniform key averaging can underestimate the attention mass of compressed blocks. We introduce Spark-Attn, a training-free BSA method comprising Spark-Reblock and Spark-Reweight. Spark-Reblock recursively groups tokens by attention preference while preserving regular block shapes for efficient GPU execution. Spark-Reweight uses the global mean query as an anchor to construct attention-weighted key-value representations and logit biases for the compressed blocks, calibrating their attention mass. We instantiate Spark-Attn in MiniMax-H3 as Spark-H3. At 10% exact-block density, Spark-H3 delivers a 2.49$\times$ DiT speedup and reaches 24.81 dB PSNR against the corresponding dense outputs on MiniMax-H3 (20 denoising steps, 345 frames, 1344$\times$768). Increasing the density to 20% further improves PSNR to 26.76 dB while still achieving a 2.26$\times$ DiT speedup. These results demonstrate that Spark-H3 achieves a state-of-the-art quality-efficiency trade-off for training-free BSA on video diffusion models.
authors: Zecheng Tang, Jiaye Fu, Youtian Lin, Xinyao Rao, Liuxuan Sun, Jian Zhang, Yao Yao, Wei Li
bullets: Targets the high attention cost of long video sequences in diffusion models.
Spark-Reblock recursively groups tokens with similar attention preferences while retaining GPU-friendly regular blocks.
Spark-Reweight uses a global-mean-query anchor to build weighted key-value summaries and calibrate compressed-block attention mass.
At 10% exact-block density, it achieves a 2.49× DiT speedup and 24.81 dB PSNR versus dense outputs.
At 20% density, PSNR rises to 26.76 dB with a 2.26× speedup; the method is training-free and instantiated in MiniMax-H3.

Both branches share one softmax normalization, with compressed entries for selected blocks masked to avoid double counting. papers.abstract: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.
authors: Xiaoyang Xing, Wenyu Dai, Xiaoliang Gong, Asoke K Nandi, Anthony Cohn
bullets: Targets the scalability costs of multi-agent red teaming, including redundant communication, inefficient routing, and weak feedback attribution.
Represents agent roles, dependencies, and input bindings as versioned executable graphs with records of information flow.
An LLM controller uses workflow records, target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain, refine, restructure, or freeze workflows.
Evaluated on HarmBench with multiple execution backbones and target models, including ablations, transfer, and evaluator checks.
Across six configurations, L2C raises ASR by 1.4–4.5 percentage points over EvoSynth while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6–37.3%.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large vision-language models (LVLMs) have significantly improved video understanding capabilities, yet processing long videos remains challenging due to the substantial computational cost of extensive visual inputs. Frame selection offers an efficient alternative, but many existing region-based methods rely on fixed or predefined temporal partitions, which may result in suboptimal temporal regions, compromising subsequent budget allocation and frame selection. In this work, we propose Adaptive Partitioning-Based Frame Selection (APS), a training-free framework that adapts temporal partitions to local variations in query-frame relevance. Specifically, APS formulates temporal partitioning as a complexity-regularized fitting problem, jointly optimizing partition boundaries and local models through dynamic programming. The resulting adaptive temporal partitions guide frame budget allocation based on query relevance and temporal extent, enabling informative frame selection under limited visual budgets. Extensive experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate that APS consistently improves performance across diverse LVLM backbones, achieving the highest average gains over uniform sampling among competing methods. Further analyses validate the effectiveness of adaptive partitioning and demonstrate its generalizability across model scales, similarity encoders, and advanced LVLMs.
authors: Junxiang Wen, Yinxi Zhao, Jiawei Chen, Jingying Hu, Lijun Wang, Zhen Qin, Shuiguang Deng
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of processing long videos with LVLMs.
Uses a training-free, complexity-regularized fitting objective with dynamic programming to jointly optimize temporal boundaries and local relevance models.
Allocates frame budgets according to local query relevance and temporal extent.
Improves performance over uniform sampling across Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench and diverse LVLM backbones.
Generalizes across model scales, similarity encoders, and advanced LVLMs.

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) services charge for repeated context, yet billing weights need not reflect its contribution to answer quality. We present a three-layer framework separating content relevance, observable proxies and auditable positional weights. Context-ablation experiments show that relevance dominates position and that distance-decay families do not outperform a relevance-only baseline. A measured serving stack shows that cache hits reduce repeated-prefix compute cost by over two orders of magnitude at 65,536 tokens, while cold resends constrain sustainable discounts. Cross-provider measurements separate cache value from tokenisation and list-price differences. Calibrated simulations reduce the 99th percentile of session charges by 31-42%, although revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs achieve similar reductions and median charges increase. The framework provides a bounded per-token accounting rule and measured deployment constraints, rather than a validated utility estimator.
authors: Yi Lu, Qianshi Lin, Yumeng Yang, Hongxia Wang
bullets: Separates content relevance, observable proxies, and auditable positional weights for context billing.
Context ablations find relevance dominates position; distance-decay weighting does not beat a relevance-only baseline.
Serving measurements show cache hits cut repeated-prefix compute costs by over 100× at 65,536 tokens, while cold resends limit discounts.
Calibrated simulations reduce 99th-percentile session charges by 31–42%, but revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs produce similar reductions and increase median charges.
The work offers bounded per-token accounting and deployment constraints, not a validated utility estimator.

papers.abstract: We present a pilot study characterising the effect of post-training quantisation on multilingual machine translation quality and inference cost for three African languages - Hausa, Swahili, and Yoruba - across three model families: a small general-purpose LLM (Qwen2.5-1.5B), a larger multilingual instruction-tuned LLM (Aya-23-8B), and a dedicated multilingual MT model (NLLB-200-distilled-1.3B). Evaluating on the FLORES-200 devtest set (1,012 sentences per direction) under FP16, bitsandbytes INT8, and NF4 INT4 precisions on consumer-grade NVIDIA T4 GPUs, we find: (i) the specialised MT model outperforms both LLMs by 32.7-43.3 chrF on the Hausa and Swahili directions, and by 12.9-24.7 chrF on Yoruba, despite being roughly a sixth the size of the 8B instruction-tuned LLM; (ii) post-training quantisation preserves aggregate translation quality within approximately 1 chrF across all model families and language directions, with a single worst case of 2.19 chrF; (iii) on consumer GPUs, INT8 and INT4 quantisation provide substantial memory savings (49-61% at INT4) but do not reduce inference latency relative to FP16 - in fact, latency increases by 1.3x to 5.3x; (iv) a clear performance gradient tracking training-resource availability is visible across languages (Swahili > Hausa > Yoruba). These findings motivate a research agenda focused on hardware-aware compression and error-type analysis beyond aggregate metrics for low-resource deployment.
bullets: The study evaluates Hausa, Swahili, and Yoruba translation across three model families and FP16, INT8, and INT4 precision settings.
The specialised NLLB-200 model substantially outperforms both tested LLMs, despite being much smaller than the 8B instruction-tuned model.
Quantisation changes aggregate quality by about 1 chrF or less in nearly all settings, with a worst case of 2.19 chrF.
INT4 cuts memory use by 49–61%, but INT8 and INT4 are slower than FP16, with latency increasing 1.3×–5.3×.
Performance follows apparent training-resource availability: Swahili performs best, followed by Hausa and Yoruba.

papers.abstract: Existing latent reasoners typically run for a preset latent horizon during inference. Intuitively, a longer horizon should provide more opportunity for reasoning. However, in this work, we find that extending latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to the full preset horizon may in fact degrade reasoning performance. We observe that latent CoT evolves through distinct functional stages, with earlier computation forming frontier reasoning states, while later computation mainly reorganizes existing candidates and can weaken gold candidate support. These findings motivate a rethink of fixed-horizon latent inference. To address this, we characterize the reasoning benefits of latent CoT by realized and remaining constructive progress. Empirically, we find that higher realized constructive progress corresponds to higher current reasoning accuracy, while more remaining progress corresponds to larger future gains from continued latent CoT. To this end, we introduce a lightweight method that estimates the remaining reasoning progress and adaptively adjusts the latent horizon during inference. Across representative latent CoT reasoners and multiple arithmetic benchmarks, our method improves reasoning accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points while reducing latent computation by up to 29.0%, without retraining the LLM.
authors: Tianxiang Chen, Jingyuan Zhou, Weiming Yang, Kaidi Yang
bullets: Fixed latent horizons can hurt performance because later reasoning may reorganize candidates and weaken support for the correct answer.
Latent CoT progresses through stages: early steps form frontier reasoning states, while later steps may provide diminishing or negative benefits.
The work characterizes progress using realized constructive progress and remaining constructive progress.
A lightweight estimator adaptively adjusts the inference horizon without retraining the language model.
Across multiple arithmetic benchmarks, it improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points and reduces latent computation by up to 29.0%.

papers.abstract: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel ``box'' quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors across diverse compression rates. Considering partial system observability and distinct node objectives, we formulate two interdependent optimization problems: (i)~mobile devices (MDs) maximize inference accuracy under quality-of-service (QoS) and queue-stability constraints by jointly adapting dynamic split deep neural network (DNN) branches and cell association; and (ii)~each edge server (ES) allocates bandwidth, graphics processing unit (GPU) frequency, and modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to maximize the max--min inference accuracy among associated MDs under cell capacity limits. We solve these problems using a multi-agent distributed optimization framework, where MDs act as causal contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) agents under backlog-aware Lyapunov control, while each ES executes resource allocation via block coordinate descent (BCD). Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, OMNIS+ reduces the QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while achieving a better accuracy--violation trade-off.
authors: Langtian Qin, Avishkar Dnyaneshwar Kawadgave, Ian Andrew Harshbarger, Le\"ila Nasraoui, Carla Fabiana Chiasserini, Marco Levorato
bullets: Targets the limitations of static RAN slicing for dynamic semantic representations in split neural networks.
Uses dynamic neural compression with adaptive “box” quantization to balance communication payload, computation, and robustness to transmission errors.
Formulates device-side accuracy optimization and edge-server max–min accuracy resource allocation under QoS, queue-stability, and capacity constraints.
Applies causal contextual multi-armed bandits with Lyapunov control at devices and block coordinate descent at edge servers.
Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, reduces QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while improving the accuracy–violation trade-off.

papers.abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are expected to achieve semantic reasoning, intelligent decision-making, and long-horizon navigation under strict onboard constraints. While recent foundation-model-driven approaches have shown promising progress toward this goal, existing methods remain limited by challenges in 3D data availability, trajectory feasibility, long-horizon reasoning, and computational efficiency in complex environments. To bridge these gaps, we propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical vision-language-navigation (VLN) framework for aerial robots. VLN-AR decouples multimodal reasoning and low-level control, enabling structured prediction of 3D pose commands and navigation intentions that are translated into dynamically feasible actions. To mitigate data scarcity and domain gaps, we introduce a fully automated 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based pipeline to generate scalable photorealistic UAV navigation data. A progressive three-stage training strategy further enhances grounding, scene reasoning, and complex navigation. In addition, a lightweight cognitive agent improves long-horizon reasoning via memory-aware task decomposition. Finally, we design onboard optimization techniques, including token sparsification and model lightweighting, achieving 7.1x-9.4x speedup while maintaining high navigation performance on resource-limited UAV platforms. Experiments show great improvements over existing methods in both simulation and real-world UAV navigation. Project website: https://wyz000.github.io/VLN-AR/
authors: Yuze Wu, Mo Zhu, Xingxing Li, Yuheng Du, Zhaoqi Wang, Yuxin Fan, Wenjun Li, Kenghou Hoi, Zhichao Han, Xin Zhou, Fei Gao
bullets: Separates multimodal reasoning from low-level control by predicting 3D poses and navigation intentions that are converted into dynamically feasible actions.
Uses an automated 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline to generate scalable, photorealistic UAV navigation data and address data scarcity and domain gaps.
Employs progressive three-stage training for improved grounding, scene reasoning, and complex navigation.
Adds a memory-aware cognitive agent for long-horizon task decomposition and onboard optimizations such as token sparsification and model lightweighting.
Reports 7.1×–9.4× speedups while maintaining high navigation performance, with improvements demonstrated in simulation and real-world UAV experiments.

papers.abstract: Vision-language agents that browse websites, operate phones and act in homes reason before every action, so every step waits for a large model, a latency and cost that stand in the way of deployment. Step-level speculation lets a small model draft each step and calls the large model only on rejected drafts, but its outcome rests on the judge, and a judge that reads only a step's text cannot tell whether the step fits the screen it acts on. We find that a few samples of a small model can contain a correct step about as often as the large model gets the step right, and not always on the same steps: checked against the screen, small drafts can be not only cheaper but better. We present Vanguard, a training-free judge that leaves the draft and target models unchanged: a general decision model, with the screenshot in view, gives each candidate step a probability of being right in one forward pass; the best candidate is kept if it clears a threshold, and otherwise the large model writes the step. On web, mobile and embodied agents, a 2B draft judged by Vanguard is at least as accurate as its 8B target and significantly more accurate on Mind2Web and EB-ALFRED, while the target writes only a minority of the steps; it completes far more closed-loop episodes, and with a 27B target from another family it is both faster and more accurate. Vanguard is the most accurate judge we compare on the agent tasks; it relies on the screenshot on web and mobile tasks, its calibrated threshold transfers to unseen websites, and across model families its gain over the target grows with the draft's pass@4 relative to the target's accuracy. Vanguard composes with token-level speculative decoding and matches trained process reward models on mathematics, turning speculation from a way to save the large model's work into one that can improve on it.
authors: Hanqi Mao, Jiajun Fan, Ruihan Guo, Shuaike Shen, Ziwen Wang, Hui Ren, Xianrui Zhong, Ge Liu
bullets: Addresses the latency and cost of requiring a large model before every vision-language agent action.

The large model generates only a minority of steps, enabling more completed closed-loop episodes and faster, more accurate operation with a 27B target.
The calibrated threshold transfers to unseen websites, and Vanguard also composes with token-level speculative decoding and matches trained process reward models on mathematics.

papers.abstract: Long video understanding remains a daunting challenge for existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs), mainly due to the large number of visual tokens accumulated in long videos. Currently, frame selection and token selection are two main paradigms for addressing this issue, both aiming to select relevant visual information to form a compact input for MLLMs. A natural approach combines these two paradigms by selecting frames before pruning tokens, but noisy frame-level relevance estimates can cause irreversible evidence loss. In this paper, we study this problem from the perspective of assessing the spatiotemporal distribution of query-specific evidence and propose a novel and training-free approach termed NULLTOK. For every patch across all frames, we construct an empirical-null distribution from 64 group-matched irrelevant control queries, capturing the scores expected in the absence of target-specific evidence. Target affinities are calibrated against these same-position references into right-tail Monte Carlo p-values, which are discrete super-uniform under a conditional exchangeability assumption. Calibrated screening and a high-recall semantic guard produce candidate tokens for deterministic visual deduplication and joint spatiotemporal budget allocation. To validate NullTok, we apply it to two representative MLLMs and conduct extensive experiments on a set of video benchmarks. The experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness under a bounded visual token budget. For example, it achieves 65.81% and 68.85% on Video-MME using frozen LLaVA-Video-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B backbones, respectively, at a cap of 64 full-frame equivalents (FFE), without subtitles or audio. These results outperform all evaluated baselines on Video-MME under the same budget for both backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/potato-kitty/NullTok.
authors: Zhang Ziyue, Juwei Jian, Baiyang Song, Yunshan Zhong, Jun Peng, Yiyi Zhou, Rongrong Ji
bullets: Addresses evidence loss caused by selecting frames before pruning tokens in long videos.
Builds position-matched empirical-null distributions from irrelevant control queries and converts affinities into Monte Carlo p-values.
Combines calibrated screening with a high-recall semantic guard, deduplication, and joint spatiotemporal budget allocation.
Evaluated with frozen LLaVA-Video-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B on video benchmarks without subtitles or audio.
On Video-MME at 64 full-frame equivalents, achieves 65.81% and 68.85%, outperforming evaluated baselines for the respective backbones.

papers.abstract: Modern GPU workloads increasingly rely on device-initiated communication to let GPU kernels communicate directly without synchronizing with the host at kernel boundaries. Existing libraries commonly favor placing transport control on GPU threads, an approach known as GPUDirect Async (GDA), and treat reverse offload to host proxy threads as a slower fallback. We argue that reverse offload can outperform GDA and should be a first-class communication path. We further propose exposing reverse offload as a programming interface that lets users define workload-specific communication operations. We present KIWI, a programmable reverse-offload framework that achieves sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of operations per second. We address practical challenges of scaling reverse offload, including contention on shared queues, polling overhead, and load imbalance across proxies. KIWI-P2P, a SHMEM-like library built on KIWI, outperforms state-of-the-art GDA implementations in both latency and bandwidth. More importantly, KIWI-EP redesigns low-latency mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine kernels around workload-defined operations, lowering expert-parallel communication latency by up to 2.3x over the best existing backend on AMD GPUs and time per output token in vLLM by up to 29%. The source code of KIWI is available at https://github.com/AMDResearch/kiwi.
authors: Jiakun Yan, Shiksha Patel, David Sidler, Gengyu Rao, Brandon Potter, Bradford Beckmann
bullets: Motivation: GPU-initiated communication is increasingly important, but reverse offload to host proxy threads is typically treated as a slower fallback to GPUDirect Async.
Method: KIWI provides a programmable GPU-to-CPU invocation layer and addresses shared-queue contention, polling overhead, and proxy load imbalance.
Contribution: KIWI-P2P offers SHMEM-like communication, while KIWI-EP redesigns mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine operations around workload-specific primitives.
Results: KIWI achieves sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of operations per second.
Scope: Reported gains include up to 2.3× lower expert-parallel communication latency on AMD GPUs and up to 29% lower vLLM time per output token.

papers.title: A Fast, Programmable GPU-to-CPU Invocation Layer for GPU-Initiated Communication
papers.tldr: KIWI makes GPU-to-CPU reverse offload a fast, programmable first-class communication path, outperforming GPU-controlled alternatives for several communication and mixture-of-experts workloads.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. From batch 32 to the largest batch each GPU fits, narrowing reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.
authors: Alagappan Valliappan, Ankit More, Dheevatsa Mudigere, Jatin Mitra
bullets: Targets draft models that inherit the large model’s hidden width, creating unnecessary compute and memory cost.
Applies width reduction to DFlash and EAGLE-3, evaluated with Qwen3-8B and GPT-OSS-20B.
For DFlash, the output adapter folds into the target’s vocabulary projection, preserving logits up to floating-point rounding.
End-to-end decoding accelerates by 1.06–1.12× on B200 and 1.13–1.44× on DGX Spark at batch size 1.
Speedups persist at larger batches, reaching up to 1.21× without narrow drafts becoming slower than full-width ones.

papers.selection_reason: Narrows draft hidden width in speculative decoding to speed up LLM inference, a direct efficiency contribution for AI systems.
papers.title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: Narrowing speculative-decoding draft models to half or quarter hidden width can speed up generation while largely preserving token acceptance.

papers.abstract: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation models write a graphic as code with one forward pass per token, so drawing is slow. Speculative decoding speeds them up losslessly, and block drafters guess many tokens per pass. On SVG, many of their rounds accept the whole draft and end only at the verification window. We find that their misses are rare and clumped, and that they stay accurate far deeper into a block than on natural language. A run-length identity and three propositions show that a longer window pays once the candidates are wide, up to the drafter's horizon. We propose Sightline, which pairs a window as long as the drafter's horizon with a draft tree wide enough to fill it. Experiments cover text-to-SVG and image-to-SVG with three models on six benchmarks from MMSVG, MMSVG-2M and SArena. In every setting, Sightline is the fastest of the compared lossless decoders. On SArena, it stays the fastest when every decoder shares one loop control. It also leads in almost every setting of six models from four other families, which write SVG code, compressed SVG tokens or Lottie JSON. Analyses trace the lead to rounds that shorter windows cut off, both in loop-free content and in loops. Speculative decoding also saves time for choosing samples by rendering, which beats choosing by likelihood. These results suggest that speculative decoding on vector graphics should verify as far as the drafter sees. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/Sightline.
authors: Yanchao Li, Ben Gao, Jiaqing Xie, Yusu Zhang, Beilun Wang, Yanbo Wang, Xiaohua Xu, Nanqing Dong, Tianfan Fu, Zhongyu Huang
bullets: SVG generation is slow because models require one forward pass per output token.
The authors find SVG speculative-decoding errors are rare and clustered, with accuracy remaining high deeper into drafts than in natural language.
Sightline uses a verification window as long as the drafter’s horizon and a draft tree wide enough to fill it.
Across text-to-SVG, image-to-SVG, compressed SVG, and Lottie JSON tasks, it is the fastest compared decoder in nearly all reported settings.
Longer windows recover rounds that shorter windows truncate; speculative decoding also speeds rendering-based sample selection.

papers.abstract: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks DAS-restricted training with a line search matches full-space training even where the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned, showing empirically that convergence does not require all Hessian eigendirections but only a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset. We extend the analysis to Gauss-Newton within the DAS and discuss what this structure implies for future subspace-aware optimizers.
bullets: Hessian eigenvalue magnitude alone does not reliably identify the directions used by optimization.
The dominant aligned subspace (DAS) selects Hessian eigendirections by their alignment with the gradient.
PINNs provide a challenging testbed because parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic operators create anisotropic, ill-conditioned losses.
Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers problems, DAS-restricted line-search training matches full-space training.
The analysis also examines Gauss–Newton structure within DAS and motivates subspace-aware optimizers.

Figure 1: The edge of stability, as a river (an illustration of the idea). The loss is a descending river: the many flat directions run downstream (gentle slope — the channel darkens as the loss falls), the sharp direction λmax is across the channel, and the banks steepen as training progresses (denser hachures). A small learning rate settles to the centre and glides. A large one glides too, until the banks are steep enough that ηλ ≈ 2: from there every step overshoots the centre and lands on the opposite bank, so the trajectory stops sinking and rides the fringe — slaloming bank-to-bank along the dashed rails at the largest swing the walls can hold, while still drifting downstream. papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) think for thousands of tokens before they answer, and retention policies keep the KV cache affordable by pruning it as the reasoning grows. We find that this pruning sacrifices the image in multi-turn conversations: the image and the reasoning share one budget, so the growing reasoning crowds the visual entries out. A chart question that loses 8 points to the full cache when asked first loses 24 points when asked after a round of reasoning. Protecting a small visual reserve from eviction recovers most of this loss, while adding the same slots to the shared budget recovers considerably less. The image therefore lacks protection, not capacity. Based on this finding, we propose ShelfKV, a training-free method that works on top of existing retention policies. It keeps every visual entry in CPU memory and, at each decoding step, swaps the visual entries that the current query scores highest into the attention slots of the text entries it scores lowest. The image is never evicted, yet it occupies attention slots only while it is read. We evaluate ShelfKV on four benchmarks, three of them conversational, with two retention policies and two reasoning VLMs. In conversations, it improves the strongest existing policy, DBTrimKV, by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory, and still leads by 8.7 points when DBTrimKV uses twice the memory. It also consistently outperforms a fixed visual reserve of matched GPU memory in these settings, without hurting accuracy on standalone questions. These results show that the image should be protected from the reasoning but read only on demand.
authors: Ziyi Wang, Xiyue Zhang, Bing Hu, Guangmin Song, Chenyi Zhang, Li Wang
bullets: Problem: KV-cache pruning lets growing reasoning tokens evict image tokens, causing larger accuracy losses in later conversational turns.
Method: Keep all visual entries in CPU memory and dynamically swap query-relevant visual entries into slots occupied by low-scoring text entries.
Training-free and compatible with existing retention policies, including DBTrimKV.
Across four benchmarks, two retention policies, and two reasoning VLMs, ShelfKV improves DBTrimKV by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory and 8.7 points when DBTrimKV has twice the memory.
It outperforms a fixed visual reserve in conversational settings without reducing standalone-question accuracy.

papers.abstract: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.
authors: Rui Li, Liyang He, Zheng Zhang, Zhenya Huang, Qi Liu
bullets: Targets the high cost and latency of invoking a large System-2 model at every agent step.
Mines decision points from human-authored procedural skills rather than requiring workflow-specific hooks.
Trains a calibrated 4B pointer model on execution-grounded states, with System-2 fallback for low-confidence decisions.
Across three unseen benchmarks and multiple System-2 families, reduces episode cost by 75–91% and model-call time by 63–92%.
Supports zero-shot transfer of confidence thresholds while maintaining performance.

papers.abstract: Federated low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables clients with different resource budgets to collaboratively fine-tune foundation models. To distribute an aggregated update within each client's rank budget, existing methods commonly retain its leading singular directions. However, directions that best reconstruct the update matrix need not best preserve its responses on a particular client's inputs: a lower-energy direction may matter more to that recipient. We formalize this mismatch and show that matrix-optimal truncation can incur arbitrarily larger response error than another readout of the same rank. Motivated by this result, we propose Receiver-Aware Subspace Adaptation (RASA), a plug-in framework for receiver-aware knowledge transfer. RASA uses compact diagonal input second moments to perform uncentered PCA of receiver-weighted update responses. The resulting readout is globally optimal for the rank-constrained receiver objective and preserves at least as much response energy as spectral truncation under the diagonal metric. RASA also introduces spectral-reference aggregation, which removes the personalized initialization offset while retaining the locally learned increment. Experiments on DomainNet-100, NICO++, GLUE, and SuperNI demonstrate RASA's effectiveness across methods under resource, task, and data heterogeneity. In particular, RASA improves DomainNet-100 accuracy by 3.23 percentage points with FlexLoRA and achieves gains of up to 8.33 ROUGE-L points on seen SuperNI tasks and 4.37 on unseen tasks with modest overhead.
authors: Jinqian Chen, Jihua Zhu, Chang Liu
bullets: Problem: Leading-singular-value truncation can poorly preserve a client’s task-relevant responses, even at the same rank.
Method: RASA performs receiver-aware subspace adaptation using diagonal input second moments and uncentered PCA of weighted update responses.
Guarantee: Its rank-constrained readout is globally optimal for the receiver objective and preserves at least as much response energy as spectral truncation under the diagonal metric.
Additional technique: Spectral-reference aggregation removes personalized initialization offsets while retaining locally learned increments.

Results: Across DomainNet-100, NICO++, GLUE, and SuperNI, RASA improves accuracy by 3.23 points with FlexLoRA and gains up to 8.33 ROUGE-L on seen and 4.37 on unseen SuperNI tasks, with modest overhead.

papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise event-driven and energy-efficient vision, yet existing spiking vision transformers (S-ViTs) largely confine spiking tokens to fixed and uniform firing schemes along the temporal, spatial and channel dimensions, whereas suppressing the computational redundancy thus incurred calls for adaptive firing mechanisms that operate jointly across all three axes at test time. To this end, we propose the Adaptive Efficient Integrate-and-Fire (AdaE-IF) model, which consults the attention score of each spiking token and routes salient regions to fine-grained firing patterns while assigning energy-frugal coarse patterns to the remaining regions. Building on AdaE-IF, we further introduce Spiking Gated Self-Attention (S-GSA) and Spiking Local-Gated Unit (S-LGU), which enforce selective spike emission at token and channel granularity. We integrate the aforementioned mechanisms and modules into AdaS-ViT, a test-time adaptive-routing architecture trained with a progressive spatio-temporal curriculum that stabilizes the co-adaptation of firing precision and routing masks. Extensive experiments across benchmarks spanning diverse data scales and modalities demonstrate that AdaS-ViT consistently achieves highly competitive performance. Notably, on ImageNet-1k it consumes only 1.02 to 2.45 millijoules per image and attains an accuracy-per-energy ratio of 32$\times$ to 72$\times$, operating in an economical inference regime and thereby pushing the energy-efficiency boundary further.
authors: Zecheng Hao, Zihan Huang, Shenghao Xie, Jiyuan Zhang, Zhaofei Yu, Tiejun Huang
bullets: Addresses redundant computation from fixed, uniform firing patterns in spiking vision transformers.
Uses attention-guided AdaE-IF routing to assign fine-grained firing to salient regions and coarse firing elsewhere.
Adds S-GSA and S-LGU for selective spike emission at token and channel granularity.
Trains routing and firing precision with a progressive spatio-temporal curriculum.
On ImageNet-1k, reports 1.02–2.45 mJ per image and a 32×–72× accuracy-per-energy ratio.

For each block, Bar hues identify the module family, the total height of a bar denotes the theoretical SOPs Upper-bound while its dark lower segment denotes the actually incurred SOPs, the curve on the right axis reports the average firing rate.

papers.selection_reason: Test-time adaptive token routing in spiking vision transformers to suppress computational redundancy, fitting efficient AI and test-time adaptation.

papers.tldr: AdaS-ViT adaptively routes spiking tokens across temporal, spatial, and channel dimensions to maintain competitive vision performance with very low inference energy.

papers.abstract: The rapid growth of deep learning has driven the deployment of computer vision directly on resource-constrained edge devices. However, the extreme heterogeneity of edge hardware architectures poses major challenges in selecting and designing suitable vision models. This survey bridges the gap between edge hardware constraints, model architectures, and deployment software toolchains. We establish a comprehensive taxonomy classifying edge hardware into three distinct tiers: mid-range devices (GPUs and dedicated NPUs or TPUs), dedicated embedded MPU or SoC processors, and microcontrollers (MCUs). We aggregate and analyze multi-source benchmark results for image classification and object detection across the computing spectrum, spanning from tens of watts down to milliwatt-scale bare-metal MCUs. Based on these empirical findings, we propose a two-tiered hardware-to-model mapping framework that provides concrete model selection matrices across performance priorities (Speed, Balanced, Accuracy) and actionable architectural design principles (peak SRAM budgeting, resolution-first scaling, and algorithm-compiler co-design). Finally, we highlight critical deployment challenges including toolchain fragmentation, operator incompatibility, and Vision Transformer feasibility, and outline promising future research directions in on-device adaptation and sustainable Edge AI.
authors: Le Duc An, Le Duc Thanh, Vo Hoai Viet
bullets: Classifies edge hardware into mid-range GPU/NPU/TPU devices, embedded MPU/SoC processors, and microcontrollers.
Analyzes multi-source image-classification and object-detection benchmarks across power levels from tens of watts to milliwatt-scale MCUs.
Introduces a two-tier hardware-to-model mapping framework with Speed, Balanced, and Accuracy selection matrices.
Proposes design principles including peak-SRAM budgeting, resolution-first scaling, and algorithm–compiler co-design.
Identifies toolchain fragmentation, operator incompatibility, and Vision Transformer feasibility as key challenges.
