papers.abstract: The rise of the agentic web has been accompanied by growing demand for on-device Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that perform diverse cross-modal web tasks with enhanced privacy and reduced latency. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely adopted in modern VLMs for compute-efficient scalability, yet their multi-expert architecture poses deployment challenges due to substantial memory demands. Mixed-precision quantization is an effective compression technique that reduces bit-widths while adapting to the heterogeneous hardware budgets of edge devices, particularly well-suited for MoE due to its inherent structural sparsity, which causes imbalanced importance among experts. While prior work has applied quantization for efficient MoE inference at the edge, we point out that in MoE-based VLMs, the modality-specific characteristics of visual and text tokens further impact expert quantization. To address this issue, we present MoMoVL, a modality-aware adaptive compression framework for MoE-based VLMs that brings vision-language inference within reach of on-device resource budgets. Motivated by our empirical findings on modality-induced disparities across experts, MoMoVL jointly exploits the per-expert activation profile and per-modality quantization sensitivity to guide bit-width assignment. Experimental results show that MoMoVL improves the accuracy-compression trade-off relative to state-of-the-art mixed-precision baselines and reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% with a modest drop in accuracy over its uniform-precision baseline. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/sco-edge/MoMoVL.
bullets: Targets the memory and deployment challenges of sparsely activated MoE VLMs on edge devices.
Accounts for differences between visual and text tokens when quantizing experts.
Jointly uses per-expert activation profiles and per-modality quantization sensitivity to guide mixed-precision assignment.
Improves the accuracy–compression trade-off over existing mixed-precision baselines.
Reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% with a modest accuracy drop versus uniform precision.],

papers.abstract: Wearable EEG inference is constrained not only by model size, but also by the channel-dependent sensing front end that must process high-dimensional inputs before compact downstream computation. We present EEG2MCU, a sensing-to-execution co-design framework that treats electrode count as a hardware design variable through task-aware montage selection. EEG2MCU retains a compact time-frequency representation and generates only the INT8 regions required by each first-layer tile, avoiding full input materialization. Halo reuse and access-aware placement across Flash, SRAM, and tightly coupled memory further reduce redundant generation and data movement. On a Cortex-M7 MCU, EEG2MCU reduces peak SRAM by 11.38x relative to the baseline, including a 1.71x reduction from the 62-to-19 electrode montage, while reducing latency by 2.57x and energy by 2.48x. It retains 94-96% of full-montage accuracy, demonstrating practical high-dimensional EEG inference under tight embedded-resource constraints.
authors: Shoma Yukawa, Meghna Roychowdhury, Arnab Sanyal, Chengwei Zhou, Shreyas Sen, Gourav Datta
bullets: Treats electrode count as a hardware variable using task-aware montage selection.
Generates only INT8 input regions needed by each first-layer tile, avoiding full input materialization.
Uses halo reuse and memory-aware placement across Flash, SRAM, and tightly coupled memory to reduce data movement.
On a Cortex-M7, achieves 11.38× lower peak SRAM, 2.57× lower latency, and 2.48× lower energy than baseline.
Retains 94–96% of full-montage accuracy using 19 rather than 62 electrodes.

papers.abstract: VGGT reconstructs cameras and geometry from unposed images in one pass, but its global attention grows quadratically with the number of views. Training-free accelerators thin this attention and work well on redundant video, but lose pose accuracy when views share little geometry. This paper traces these losses to two kinds of cross-view information that a uniform sparse approximation can fail to preserve together: diffuse layers aggregate distributed context, whereas matching layers depend on query-specific interactions that carry little attention mass. A per-layer statistic measures the log-mass missed by a mean token. Its row-free proxy is the logit variance, and it selects the estimator for each layer. Diffuse layers use shared, importance-sampled hub keys, with log-weights that make the softmax numerator and denominator unbiased. Matching layers stay exact: every aggressive thinning tested cost accuracy. At equal cost, the selected layers outperform the four shifted windows tested. On 13 unseen low-redundancy scenes with 32 views, LMSA stays within 1.4 AUC@5 of dense attention, compared with 10.3 for AVGGT and 4.5 for SAF3R; its difference from contemporaneous GPA-VGGT is not significant, and only its gains over AVGGT pass both scene-level tests. With 100 views, it stays within 1.9 AUC@5 while its aggregator runs $2.0\times$ faster. Used post hoc to choose the layers GPA-VGGT protects, the statistic improves it by 1.2 AUC@5 for 5% more FLOPs. Applied untuned to $\pi^3$, it beats AVGGT but remains further from dense accuracy.
authors: Sammam Mahdi, Fariha Binta Salim, K. M. Jubair Sami, Rakin Bin Rabbani
bullets: Uniform attention thinning can lose pose accuracy when views share little geometry.
A logit-variance statistic selects between shared importance-sampled hubs for diffuse layers and exact attention for matching layers.
On 13 unseen 32-view scenes, LMSA stayed within 1.4 AUC@5 of dense attention, versus 10.3 for AVGGT and 4.5 for SAF3R.
With 100 views, it remained within 1.9 AUC@5 of dense attention while running 2.0× faster in aggregation.
The statistic also improved GPA-VGGT by 1.2 AUC@5 at 5% more FLOPs, but untuned transfer to π³ remained farther from dense accuracy.

papers.abstract: Time-series sensing increasingly relies on neural networks, yet deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers remains challenging. Aggressive model compression can reduce accuracy, while restricting weights to multiplication-free representations introduces further losses. We present BeFit, an end-to-end framework that shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations. BeFit (i) finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional neural networks (BeCNNs) through hardware-aware neural architecture search and trains them via knowledge distillation; (ii) projects their weights to multiplication-free codes, freezes the codes, and recovers the resulting accuracy loss through the learnable activations; and (iii) generates model-specific kernels that exploit the projected weights for multiplication-free convolutions. On human activity recognition, BeCNNs are 2.75 percentage points (pp) more accurate on average than ReLU CNNs of identical architecture. On a TI CC3220SF (Cortex-M4), weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 pp, compared with 2.4 pp for ReLU CNNs. Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference model running on TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN, the unprojected BeCNN achieves 1.0 pp higher accuracy, 2.2x lower latency, and 6.4x lower flash, while the projected model remains within 1.0 pp of the reference accuracy and runs 5.9x faster. In emulation on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier, the instruction-count reduction relative to the DS-CNN increases from 5.2x on the Cortex-M4 to 147x. BeFit also extends to transformers and MLPs, and across all tasks the final models stay within 1.56 pp of their float32 teachers on average.
authors: Malak Gamal El-Din, Yasser Shoukry, Salma Elmalaki
bullets: Addresses accuracy and efficiency losses when compressing models or removing weight multiplications on microcontrollers.
Uses hardware-aware architecture search and knowledge distillation to find compact Bernstein-activation CNNs.
Projects weights into multiplication-free codes, then recovers accuracy with learnable activations and generates specialized kernels.
On human activity recognition, BeCNNs improve accuracy by 2.75 percentage points over same-architecture ReLU CNNs; projected models lose only 0.8 points while achieving 2.2× speedup on a Cortex-M4.

Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference, the unprojected model provides higher accuracy, 2.2× lower latency, and 6.4× lower flash; projected models remain within 1 point of reference accuracy and run 5.9× faster.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model generation by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target-model pass. However, better draft predictions and longer accepted continuations do not necessarily produce faster generation. To examine this gap, we present FACT (Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training), an experimental framework for studying how drafter training, candidate allocation, and execution conditions jointly affect acceptance and latency. Using a lightweight feature-prediction drafter with a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target under greedy decoding, we first examine how training translates into accepted tokens. Backpropagating through predicted-feature rollouts with greater weight on early steps improves acceptance by 15-24% over uniformly weighted detached training, yet average rollout proxy cross-entropy does not reliably rank drafters by acceptance. Beyond prediction quality, the placement of draft candidates also matters: with a fixed 256-node budget and matched per-depth widths, replacing static allocation with confidence-guided allocation increases speedup over autoregressive decoding from $1.46\times$ to $2.02\times$ on HumanEval and from $1.31\times$ to $1.75\times$ on MT-Bench. This allocation benefit extends to an independently trained drafter, but stronger training does not consistently amplify it, showing that the two improvements do not necessarily reinforce each other. Even these speed gains depend on execution conditions: changing only host-thread settings can nearly eliminate speedup without changing acceptance. Together, these findings show why training and allocation must be evaluated jointly using both acceptance and end-to-end latency under controlled execution conditions.
authors: Hadi Fares, Mayssa Hajj Hassan, Ali Salman, Ammar Mohanna
bullets: Early-step-weighted cross-step training improves acceptance by 15–24% over uniformly weighted detached training, while proxy cross-entropy does not reliably predict acceptance.
Under a fixed 256-node budget, confidence-guided candidate allocation raises speedup from 1.46× to 2.02× on HumanEval and from 1.31× to 1.75× on MT-Bench.
Allocation gains also transfer to an independently trained drafter, but stronger training does not consistently amplify them.
Host-thread settings can nearly remove speedups without changing acceptance, highlighting the need for controlled end-to-end latency evaluation.
The study uses a lightweight feature-prediction drafter, a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target, and greedy decoding.

papers.abstract: Compact convolutional backbones such as EfficientNet achieve strong parameter efficiency through local depthwise separable convolutions, yet two structural questions remain central to hybrid design: where does global self-attention improve recognition over pure convolution, and can repeated blocks share weights without losing representational capacity? We investigate both questions on ImageNet-1k (50,000-image validation) using controlled EfficientNet-B0 experiments. First, we show that wrapping a classification backbone in multi-scale feature pyramids (BiFPN) fails to outperform a plain MBConv trunk (69.99% - 71.81% vs. 72.86% plain B0) until paired with stage attention (73.15%). In contrast, keeping the MBConv trunk intact and inserting lightweight zero-gated residual self-attention adapters at stages P3 (28x28 windowed), P4 (14x14 global), and P5 (7x7 global) reaches 74.02% standalone and outperforms a bit-for-bit matched plain-B0 control by +0.954 percentage points (73.88% vs. 72.92%) across an 88-epoch stateless replay schedule, with learned attention amplitude rising monotonically with semantic depth (27.2% at P3 -> 45.4% at P4 -> 66.3% at P5). Second, we evaluate recurrent weight sharing across repeated MBConv blocks with pass-specific BatchNorm statistics (+1,536 parameters per pass). While post-hoc kernel averaging degrades accuracy to 17.03% and single-template stage tying (-27.6% parameters) plateaus at 66.10%, alternating two shared block templates ([B1, A, B, A]) in Stage 6 cuts total model parameters by 10.9% (582K weights) and recovers by +10.82 points in a single epoch to 70.92% (-1.84 points vs. unshared control).
bullets: BiFPN alone does not beat a plain MBConv trunk, but adding stage attention raises accuracy to 73.15%.
Zero-gated residual attention adapters at P3–P5 achieve 74.02% standalone and a +0.954-point gain over a matched plain-B0 control.
Attention strength increases with semantic depth, from P3 through P5.
Naive kernel averaging and single-template tying substantially hurt accuracy.
Alternating two shared block templates reduces parameters by 10.9% and reaches 70.92% after one epoch, 1.84 points below the unshared control.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Architectural efficiency through targeted global context and alternating weight sharing. (A) Each residual adapter ys = xs + αs · Projs(MHSAs(LN(xs))) initializes at αs = 0 so early convolutional feature learning is undisturbed. By epoch 80, learned branch update-to-input RMS rises monotonically with semantic depth (27.2% at P3 windowed MHSA → 45.4% at P4 global MHSA → 66.3% at P5 global MHSA). Under bit-for-bit identical stateless data replay across 88 epochs, Sparse Attention outperforms Plain-B0 by +0.954 percentage points (73.88% vs. 72.92%; standalone recovery reaches 74.02%). (B) In Stage 6 (the largest parameter stage in EfficientNet-B0), post-hoc kernel averaging degrades zero-shot accuracy to 17.03% and tying all repeated blocks in Stages 4–6 to a single template ([B1, A,A,A]) plateaus at 66.10% (−6.66 pp vs. control), whereas alternating two shared templates ([B1, A,B,A]) with pass-specific BatchNorm statistics reduces total model parameters by 10.9% (582K weights) and recovers to 70.92% in a single continuation epoch.

Figure 2: Full-validation accuracy and resource trajectories across B0–B2 baselines, BiFPN hybrids, and Sparse Stage Attention. While BiFPN-only variants plateau below the plain B0 baseline (69.99%–71.81%), Sparse Stage Attention (P3/P4/P5) achieves the strongest B0-scale trajectory (74.02% standalone; 73.88% vs. 72.92% in the matched pair).

Figure 3: Bit-for-bit matched 88-epoch comparison of Sparse Stage Attention (P3/P4/P5) vs. Plain-B0. Both arms consume identical stateless training streams. Sparse Attention maintains a consistent ∼ 1.0-point lead throughout convergence, finishing at 73.88% vs. 72.92% (+0.954 pp).

papers.abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.
bullets: Quantization degradation is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers across ResNet and EfficientNet backbones.
A structured recovery analysis tests selective INT4/INT8 precision and floating-point scales.
Retaining less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of accuracy lost under aggressive sub-4-bit compression.
On ARM and x86 CPUs, software bit-unpacking causes reported execution slowdowns of 1.48×–21.5× depending on batch size.
The study highlights a trade-off between reduced model storage and practical edge throughput.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Mechanisms of sub-4-bit quantization failure and the 5-step mixed-precision recovery waterfall on EfficientNet-B0. (A) Uniform 3-bit quantization fails due to three compounding effects: (1) each 3×3 depthwise spatial filter has only 9 weights per channel (unlike dense layers that average hundreds of inputs), so 7 signed levels ({−3..+3}) erase edge orientation in low-channel early stages; (2) a single outlier weight stretches the symmetric max-abs step size ∆ = max |w|/3, collapsing the inner 95% of weights into the zero bin (q = 0); and (3) coarse weight rounding shifts output channel means and variances, causing frozen FP32 BatchNorm statistics to mis-center activations and saturate ReLU6. (B) Protecting 0.34% of early weights (14 KB) at W8 rescues +42.92 pp when the rest of the model is W4 (65.95%). For a 3.55–3.56-bit mixed W8/W4/W3 model, combining per-channel MSE clipping (+9.00 pp), 1,000-image BatchNorm recalibration (+3.94 pp), 82-layer dynamic-programming bit allocation (+3.85 pp to 67.94% PTQ), and 1 epoch of QAT with post-QAT BN recalibration recovers top-1 accuracy from 0.30% to 68.98% across all 50,000 validation images.

Figure 3: The 82-layer mixed-precision allocation blueprint for EfficientNet-B0 (DP0.5, 3.56 mean bits, 2.35 MB). Top row: Architectural precision tiers showing Tier 0 (0.34% of weights, 13, 952 parameters in the stem and Stage 1–2 depthwise/pointwise layers protected at W8, which alone restores +42.92 pp on W4 while FP16 adds only +0.03 pp), Tier 1 (∼ 55.8% of weights in mid/deep 3× 3 and 5× 5 depthwise filters, Squeeze-and-Excitation bottlenecks, and the 1280× 1000 classifier head assigned to W4), and Tier 2 (∼ 43.9% of weights in wide Stage 5–7 1× 1 pointwise projections where high channel fan-in tolerates W3). Bottom row: The three post-selection calibration stages: per-output-channel MSE clipping (α∗ = argminα∈[0.5,1.0] ∥w−Qα(w)∥22), 1,000-image BatchNorm moment recalibration, and 82-layer dynamic-programming allocation followed by 1 epoch of QAT and post-QAT BN recalibration (68.98% top-1).

Figure 2: Uniform 4-bit (INT4) weight quantization on mature B0 and B1 checkpoints. Converged checkpoints suffer severe post-training accuracy drops (−49.82 pp on B0 and −24.39 pp on B1) across all 50,000 validation images, contrasting sharply with early-epoch pilots.

Figure 5: Measured LiteRT artifact size, full-validation accuracy, and CPU latency on mature EfficientNet-B0. Full-integer INT8 dominates FP32 on both size and speed with negligible accuracy loss (−0.058 pp). Mixed 4-bit (WI4) reduces storage further (−82.4%) but loses 9.60 points and increases median latency by 47.9% due to missing native sub-byte depthwise kernels.

Figure 4: The deployment gap between storage compression and execution speed on EfficientNetB0. Converting from 32-bit floats (20.43 MB, 9.81 ms) to full-integer INT8 (6.00 MB, 6.65 ms) simultaneously reduces file size by 70.7% and median CPU latency by 32.2% with negligible accuracy loss (−0.06 pp) because all 82 convolutional and dense layers execute on native 8-bit integer SIMD instructions. Below 8 bits, standard CPU runtimes lack native sub-byte depthwise kernels: LiteRT’s mixed 4-bit path (WI4, 66 INT4 + 16 FP32 depthwise operators) and custom packed 3-bit (INT3) bitstreams reduce storage to 3.59 MB (−82.4%) and 2.47 MB (−88.4%), but runtime bit-unpacking into floating-point buffers slows inference to 15.43 ms (+47.9%) and 376.8 ms (21.5× slower than FP32; 0.30% uniform INT3 accuracy in the packed CPU benchmark vs. *68.98% for the 3.56-bit DP0.5 + QAT recovery model).

Table 1: Localized vs. whole-model quantization sensitivity on mature EfficientNet-B0 (50,000- image validation). Protecting 0.34% of weights (13, 952 parameters in early stem and Stage 1–2 depthwise/pointwise layers) at W8 restores +42.92 percentage points when the remaining 99.66% of weights are quantized to W4.

Table 2: Full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k results for the 16-arm Precision × Clipping × BatchNorm factorial study and 1-epoch DP QAT continuation. MSE clipping and 1,000-image BN recalibration exhibit a strong −5.07 pp interaction that lifts the 3.55-bit tiered map by +12.94 pp overall (51.15% → 64.09%). Dynamic programming (DP0.5, 3.56 bits) adds +3.85 pp in PTQ (67.94%) and reaches 68.98% after 1-epoch QAT + BN recalibration.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes low-bit quantization collapse and mixed-precision recovery for efficient vision deployment, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
papers.tldr: Sub-4-bit quantization collapses Vision CNN accuracy mainly in late pointwise and depthwise layers, while sparse 8-bit recovery can restore much of the loss but may incur substantial CPU unpacking overhead.

papers.abstract: Selecting less computation in a neural operator need not reduce inference time. We study this gap using conformal calibration to choose Fourier modes or channel width per input subject to a fixed error budget. A triangle-inequality envelope bounds all candidates simultaneously; a direct-score rule handles non-monotone candidate errors and, with an input-independent score, calibrates a static baseline under the same marginal guarantee. Under frozen-model and exchangeability assumptions, both rules bound the probability of issuing a prediction outside the budget and abstain when calibration is infeasible. On Burgers and Darcy flow across three training seeds, mode selection reduces active spectral support without a measurable latency reduction, because full-grid transforms and channel mixing dominate the cost. Narrowing channels does reduce Darcy forward cost, but reference-based selection must first compute the dense prediction. An input-only binary width selector avoids that pass and runs at 0.52-0.95 times dense latency; yet static widths calibrated under the same rule are often as fast or faster, and on a separately generated 1,000-example test set they generally achieve higher coverage, while the selector falls below its 90% target in more than half of the settings. Adaptive computation in neural operators should therefore be judged by achieved coverage and complete runtime against a matched static comparator.
authors: Abdul Qadir Ibrahim, Martin Burger, Abel Maviano Jonathan
bullets: Calibrated rules bound the probability of exceeding the error budget under frozen-model and exchangeability assumptions, abstaining when calibration is infeasible.
Mode selection reduces active Fourier support but not measurable latency because full-grid transforms and channel mixing dominate runtime.
Channel narrowing reduces Darcy forward cost, but reference-based selection requires the dense prediction first.
An input-only width selector runs at 0.52–0.95× dense latency, yet often misses its 90% coverage target and is generally slower or less covered than matched static widths.
Adaptive methods should be evaluated by coverage and complete runtime against calibrated static baselines.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.
authors: Xingyang Li, Tianlang Zhao, Song Han, Ligeng Zhu
bullets: Addresses the time-consuming, model-specific redesign of post-training quantization recipes.
The agent iteratively builds and evaluates candidate recipes using output KL divergence on hidden reasoning traces, with long-generation checks for failures.
A compatible library of public PTQ methods speeds recipe construction across model architectures.
Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe at W4A16, W4A8, and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search.
For GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of FP8 accuracy; checkpoints run on existing serving kernels without inference overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 4. System architecture of QDA. QDA has three components: the composable library (§ 5.1), the isolated evaluator (§ 5.2) and the harness (§ 5.3), which runs the agent in a sandbox and schedules its GPU jobs. From the sandbox, the agent can reach the rest of the system only through four commands: (1) qda builds a recipe in the library and returns its checkpoint, (2) kl sends a checkpoint to the evaluator and returns its KL, (3) qsched submits other jobs, such as long-generation checks, to the scheduler, and (4) handin submits the final checkpoints, which are evaluated on the test benchmarks after the search.

Figure 6. Final recipes of the 12 searches. Each row is one final checkpoint, read left to right. “Self-generated” calibration mixes reasoning traces that the BF16 model wrote with public text, scale KD distills the BF16 model into the quantized one by tuning the scales (and, where marked, the norms), and ×n marks n rounds of it.

papers.abstract: Language models can gain capacity at little computational cost from n-gram embedding tables: large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens, which are looked up and added to the model's input or to its intermediate layers. Recent designs commonly use a separate n-gram embedding table for each layer, which makes the tables costly in memory and prevents layers from sharing what they learn. Sharing a single table, however, gives every layer the same embedding and leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and it performs poorly in practice. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way. Each layer maps the refined embedding through its own projection layer, after rescaling its components by factors computed from its current hidden state. Chorus matches the quality of existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables: with 1.2B table parameters it predicts text better than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram do with 9.6B. It outperforms Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram in every setting where we compared them, across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters. We also show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.
bullets: Separate per-layer n-gram tables are memory-intensive, while naïve sharing limits layer-specific preferences.
Chorus lets each layer adapt shared embeddings using a layer-specific projection and hidden-state-conditioned rescaling.
With 1.2B table parameters, Chorus outperforms FactorEngram and DeepSeek’s Engram using 9.6B parameters.
It outperforms Engram, TN-gram, and FactorEngram across the compared table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters.
Combined with Ember, Chorus reduces table-optimizer memory by 99.2% versus AdamW without degrading training performance.

papers.abstract: Quantization is an effective technique to reduce memory storage, computation complexity and power for Transformers, and the binarization of the weights is important for meeting these requirements. Approximate memory can further reduce the power for memory, but it also introduces errors. Current research for binary Transformers focuses on task performance, but the model dependable operation against errors on the memory has not been well studied. In this paper, we first evaluate the dependability of binary Transformers with the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) as a case study. A large accuracy loss occurs only at high Bit Error Rates (e.g. BER = 5% or 10%). Then we propose a novel Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) scheme to protect the binary weights at very low overhead. This scheme exploits the invariance of Transformers to permutations in the rows and columns to group the critical weights and perform selective protection on those weights. Simulation results show that PIES can recover most of the performance loss caused by bit errors at BERs as high as 10%, at an overhead significantly lower than traditional error correction schemes. These results confirm the feasibility of running binary Transformers using approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low power edge devices. The code for PIES is released on github (https://github.com/YangZhutian/binary-transformer-prefix-repair).
authors: Zhen Gao, Xiao Yin, Kexin Liang, Pedro Reviriego, Shanshan Liu, Fabrizio Lombardi
bullets: Binary Transformers are evaluated for dependability under approximate-memory errors using BERT as a case study.
Significant accuracy degradation occurs primarily at high bit-error rates, such as 5%–10%.
PIES exploits row and column permutation invariance to group and selectively protect critical weights.
Simulations show PIES recovers most performance loss at bit-error rates up to 10%.
The approach targets low-power edge devices using aggressive memory voltage scaling, with lower overhead than traditional error correction.

papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) inference differs substantially from conventional LLM serving, featuring long input sequences, wide beam search, and only a few fixed output tokens. Existing LLM serving engines such as vLLM process beams as batched independent sequences, causing redundant KV cache accesses over the shared prompt prefix. Furthermore, vLLM executes each beam search generation step as a separate engine invocation, incurring host-side beam processing overhead between decoding steps and substantial runtime KV block management in PagedAttention. Using Tree Attention, we concatenate beams along the sequence dimension to eliminate redundant KV accesses, and further optimize execution through pre-generated partial-attention masks, static KV cache allocation, loop-unrolled generation dispatch, TorchAir graph compilation, automatic operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding. Without the use of custom kernels, our approach reduces end-to-end latency by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs, and achieves generation latency comparable to a SOTA solution using custom kernels, showing that the generation pipeline should be optimized holistically before resorting to custom kernel development.
authors: Shing Wai Pun, Kai Wu, Pengfei Xia, Hui Zang, Wei Guo, Yong Liu
bullets: Targets GR inference with long prompts, wide beam search, and short fixed outputs.
Uses Tree Attention to share prompt-prefix computation and avoid redundant KV-cache accesses across beams.
Reduces overhead with pre-generated masks, static KV allocation, loop-unrolled dispatch, graph compilation, operator fusion, and constrained decoding.
Achieves latency comparable to a state-of-the-art custom-kernel solution.
Shows that end-to-end pipeline optimization can precede custom-kernel development.

papers.abstract: Comparing AI models across resource budgets yields quality-resource frontiers relating error to latency, parameter count, training compute, and energy. Offset power laws summarize such frontiers, but their fitted parameters reveal neither the price-independent geometry nor the manner in which trade-offs extend across several resource channels. This paper addresses both gaps by developing a differential theory in which this structure is made explicit. Each frontier admits a price-independent plane-curve representation relating the effective number of active resource channels, $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = s^2/\kappa$ (squared slope over curvature), to the remaining log-error depth, $\Delta S = \ln(\varepsilon/\varepsilon_{\infty})$. This representation separates intrinsic shape from the scale and origin of the resource axis. Complete monotonicity and divisibility yield differential inequalities and frontier bounds. When each of $N$ resources contributes one active channel, the theory gives the parameter-free operating rule $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1$ in delivered units and derives minimax resource prices $\lambda^{\star}_i = \alpha_i/(N+1)$ with an exact worst-case regret of $\ln(N+1)$ nats. The results make it possible to interpret measured frontiers and compare resource costs without hand-chosen exchange rates. The theory is evaluated on 117 published frontiers and implemented in the open-source package nn-rank, which derives prices from measured quality and cost, ranks candidates, and reports supported choices and minimax regret: https://github.com/ABrain-One/nn-rank
bullets: Represents each quality-resource frontier using effective active channels, $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=s^2/\kappa$, versus remaining log-error depth.
Separates intrinsic frontier shape from the scale and origin of each resource axis, with bounds from complete monotonicity and divisibility.
For $N$ active resources, recommends operating where $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=1$ in delivered units.
Derives minimax prices $\lambda_i^\star=\alpha_i/(N+1)$ and worst-case regret $\ln(N+1)$ nats.
Evaluates the theory on 117 published frontiers and provides the open-source nn-rank package for pricing and ranking candidates.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The paper in one picture, and where each part is proved. The object is a Laplace transform of a task’s difficulty law evaluated at what the resource buys; the theory is the plane curve it traces; the two structural hypotheses are two differential inequalities on that curve, and the two walls that bound every frontier are those inequalities integrated from the floor. Everything in the dashed box is a consequence of the figure above it.

Figure 8: The rules actually in use, scored against the derived price on the same frontiers. (a) Regret of each selection rule, one point per frontier, bars at the median; the dashed line is the 0.05-nat band inside which the recommendation does not change. The canonical rule lies inside the band on almost every frontier, while the comparison quantifies the cost of alternative choices. (b) The bits gained against the extra resource spent past the canonical point: the median frontier buys 0.99 bits at 44× the cost, which is the price of not knowing where to operate. (c) The floor read from three models against the floor from a full fit. Detail in the Appendix, § “The empirical study”.

Figure 2: The theory as one curve. (a) The primitive is Neff against the depth still available, with Neff(0) = 0 at the floor. The axiom bounds its growth by ˙Neff ≤ Neff +1 and the hypothesis by ˙Neff ≤ 1; integrated from the same initial condition those two inequalities are the two charts, so the tangency at the origin is a property of one initial-value problem. The shaded wedge is the whole divisibility question, and the dotted rays represent the admissible constant-slope chart family. (b) The working statistic c3 ≥ 0 is ˙Neff ≤ 2: it cannot see the band between the two slopes, which D̂1 ≥ 0 closes at no extra measurement cost. (c) In the gaugefree coordinates of Proposition 6 the single-channel regret is − ln sinφ identically, the rule is the right angle, and the axiom states that φ is 1-Lipschitz with respect to arc length—whence L ≥ π over the complete sweep. (d) What the stronger rung is worth on clean charts at matched level; on this corpus both statistics stay at their nominal level.

Figure 3: The theory is one plane curve. (a) Channels remaining against depth remaining. The axiom confines every completely monotone frontier below e∆S −1 and the hypothesis below that curve’s own tangent at the origin, ∆S; the two bounding solutions are charts, the two-atom chart and the cure chart, and each is the unique frontier saturating its wall (Proposition 1(iii)). Every constant-σ chart is a ray whose slope is |σ| and whose intercept is the floor, so the admissible charts form a pencil (Corollary 4). The operating point is the height Neff = 1/t; where it meets a wall is the recommended depth, one bit on the axiom’s extremal against one nat on the hypothesis’s. (b) The gap between the walls closes quadratically at the origin, and the origin is the floor: a second-order test is powerless at the deep end by theorem, not by accident of this corpus. (c) The admissible arc is a functional of the same curve, so the walls bound it from below; with the covering law the right-hand axis reads the number of operating points a benchmark needs, and the hypothesis bound passes the axiom’s limiting value π at λ = π2/4. (d) The archive’s 117 frontiers, read with three accuracies per point and no bandwidth. The curve is noise-dominated: the median straightness is R2 = 0.22 and against a design-matched null no statistic read from it has power (Section 10).

Figure 4: (a) The regret law (30): the fraction of a complete frontier within ϱ nats of the canonical point, with the 0.900√ ϱ form, and (inset) the 35 panel cells’ observed inband fractions against the prediction conditional on each cell’s own arc. (b) The mean regret (32) of an operating point placed uniformly in arc length: exactly one bit for a single reducible channel, rising to γ+ ln 2 and never beyond. This is the cost of not knowing where to operate, and it is bounded. (c) The microfoundation comparison: measured pairwise co-failure rates for the three mechanisms on the per-item panel of the technical report in the archive, § “What the item level says”.

Figure 6: The floor is not a parameter. (a) A two-atom fit to a frontier whose floor is exactly zero returns a floor that is a large fraction of the best observed error, monotone in the shape index, and the curve sweeps the whole of (0, 1) as the index does; the archive’s own median fitted share, 0.96 of the best observed error, is what a floorless frontier with β = 0.10 produces. (b) The shape index from three independent routes—a direct floorless fit, the bandwidth-free three-point chord arc, and the collapse coordinate ζ—on the frontiers where each is defined. (c) The arc predicted from β against the measured chord arc; the increasing-hazard frontiers, which have no arc at all, are the three distribution-shift evaluations. Statements, proofs and scripts in the Appendix, § “Proofs: The floor”.

Figure 7: (a) Held-out error against the number of models used to fit, on 117 frontiers carrying the archive’s eight corpus labels. The three-parameter law plateaus well above the measurement noise (shaded); the whole completely monotone class, fitted nonparametrically, plateaus with it; the one shape parameter β of the stretched-exponential form removes most of the gap. (b) Agreement on the 2 025 pooled interior leave-one-out predictions. (c) The fitted β, with one point per frontier and a bar at the corpus median: corpus-specific and, on these windows, weakly identified. Details are provided in the Appendix, § “The empirical study”.

Figure 5: (a) The complete sweep of a single-channel frontier is the same arc of Fisher–Rao length π, from the pure power law at φ = π to the floor at φ = 0; a frontier with a floor reaches only 2 arccos √ ε∞ of it at or below chance level. The shaded segment is the 0.05-nat band, the open circles are the five checkpoints of Theorem 15, and the inner curves are the 12 of the 18 archived ImageNet single-resource windows that have a measurable chord arc, median 0.39π, drawn on the same absolute scale and centered on the right angle so that their lengths can be compared—the chord returns a length and not a position, and the positions the jet does return sit deep, at a median Neff = 0.465 and hence φ = 1.20 < π/2. (b) Regret from the reference is minus the log sine of arc position, (29); the shaded cells are the five checkpoints’ covering neighborhoods. (c) Checkpoints the arc needs against Pareto points measured, one point per frontier; crosses are the six frontiers whose log-convexity defect is non-positive, on which the chord returns no arc and the law fails.

Table 3: Held-out prediction, scored per frontier. Interior is leave-one-out on each interior measurement; forward trains on the least expensive two-thirds and predicts the most expensive third; backward trains on the most expensive two-thirds and predicts the least expensive third. The error is | ln εpred − ln εobs|, summarized per frontier and then across frontiers, with intervals bootstrapped over the 117 frontiers—never over the 2 025 dependent prediction events. The lower panel is the paired comparison on the same frontiers. The law is better than the floorless power law on a majority of frontiers in all three regimes; it loses the interior to a model-free interpolator and wins the backward extrapolation against every baseline. Script 169, from script 68’s per-frontier output.

Table 5: Where each reported number comes from. The archive’s scripts are numbered and run in order; each writes a CSV under results/, so every figure below can be checked without typesetting a table. Three of the 163 scripts reach the network and none is needed to reproduce a number in this paper.

Table 1: What refutes the divisibility hypothesis, what it costs, and where it can be read. “Order” is the lowest derivative of S the test involves. In the derivatives of S alone the axiom and the hypothesis coincide at every order ≤ 2, so without a floor the discriminating content begins at order three; the order-2 rows buy their discrimination with a floor instead, which is the second of the two currencies named below.

Table 4: Selection rules on the 26 attainable single-resource frontiers of the archive, scored against the derived price. Regret is in nats; the tolerance is 0.05 nats inside which the recommendation does not change. Each rule is implemented directly on a discrete measured frontier. This explains why the knee row is not zero even though the knee and the canonical point coincide on the chart. The ratio of accuracy to log10 cost is the “efficiency score” of Prucs et al. (2025), whose limitations are discussed by Dehghani et al. (2022); the knee is Das (1999); Satopää et al. (2011); the budget is the rule of Sun et al. (2026) at the geometric midpoint of each frontier’s own range. The fixed-exponent row is the soft objective of Tan et al. (2019), ACC · (LAT/T )w, whose target enters only through the constant T−w

Table 2: The admissible-ceiling test of Corollary 3, read against a null in which each frontier is the three-parameter form (4) fitted to it, drawn on its own nodes at its own residual scale. “False” is the per-frontier rate at which the procedure declares a violation when none exists, and power is measured against the deformed wall Neff = θ(e∆S − 1) at θ = 2, a floor at twice its admissible value. The incumbent statistic minimizes ε/(1 + Neff) over every triple and is not calibrated under the null at any precision reported here. The two pre-registered readings are at their nominal level and have no power on these windows, which is what Corollary 3(iii) predicts. Precision is not the binding constraint: the incumbent’s false-violation rate is 1.000 at every precision down to 2 milli-nats, a factor 25 below the archive’s own residual scale, and the two pre-registered readings never leave [0.01, 0.10] in power. The constraint is depth, not noise—see the text.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a differential theory for quality-resource trade-offs in AI model selection, providing a framework for optimizing resource usage.
papers.title: A Differential Theory of Quality-Resource Trade-offs for AI Model Selection: The Multiresource Frontier and Its Minimax Price
papers.tldr: A differential framework turns multi-resource AI quality frontiers into price-independent geometry and derives minimax resource prices and regret for model selection.

papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer theoretical energy-efficiency advantages over conventional deep networks, but realizing these advantages on vision tasks requires sparse spike representations that naive rate-coding methods fail to provide. We combine biologically motivated spike-encoding schemes with two training improvements: Rouser adaptive-threshold surrogate gradients and Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) second-order optimization. The spike encoding schemes experimented with are rate coding, latency coding, DVS-style delta modulation, and Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) filtering. Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST demonstrate that biologically inspired encoders yield the largest accuracy gains in capacity-constrained regimes and serve as an effective parameter-efficiency lever. DoG and delta modulation encoders produce significantly sparser spike trains than rate coding. K-FAC yields modest but consistent accuracy improvements over Adam-trained baselines, and Rouser's learnable per-neuron thresholds improve Fashion-MNIST accuracy from 87.37% to 88.13% by enabling homeostatic firing-rate regulation. Biologically grounded pre-processing methods can help close the accuracy gap between SNNs and non-spiking baselines without increasing model size.
authors: Ayaan Qayyum, Bruce Yi Bu, Zicong Li, Jingfeng Zhou
bullets: Naive rate coding can produce inefficiently dense spike representations for vision tasks.
DoG and DVS-style delta modulation generate substantially sparser spike trains than rate coding.
Biologically inspired encoders provide the largest accuracy gains when model capacity is constrained.
K-FAC gives modest, consistent improvements over Adam, while Rouser thresholds improve Fashion-MNIST accuracy from 87.37% to 88.13%.
Results are demonstrated on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST; broader generalization and hardware-level energy gains are not established here.

papers.title: Biologically-Inspired Spike Encoding and Optimization for Spiking Neural Networks
papers.tldr: Biologically inspired spike encoders, combined with adaptive thresholds and K-FAC optimization, improve SNN accuracy and sparsity without increasing model size.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly targets small language models, and executing these workloads efficiently across multiple accelerators requires effective coordination. On TPUs, Pathways-based RL uses a single controller to coordinate computation across hosts. This execution model is effective for large models, but its coordination computational costs are harder to amortize when small models repeatedly invoke short computations. To characterize these computational costs, we sweep dense models from 0.6B to 405B parameters on TPU v7x under a decode-heavy workload and measure how host and network computational overhead vary with model size. At 0.6B, host orchestration occupies 36% of step time and network communication 2%, whereas for large models, estimated network computational costs dominate the non-compute time. Motivated by these findings, we present Local Coordination JAX (LoCoJAX), which implements local rollout and reward processing on each TPU host with synchronous global training. In controlled comparisons against a tuned and optimized Pathways baseline on Qwen3-0.6B across three workloads and 8-64 TPU v7x chips, its colocated mode (LoCoJAX-CO) is 1.3-3.6x faster per step; on GSM8K, it completes a step faster on 8 chips than Pathways does on 64. Finally, a Ray-managed disaggregated mode (LoCoJAX-DA) overlaps rollout and training on separate hosts, and placement experiments establish when this overlap compensates for dividing devices and transferring weights: only when rollout dominates the step and receives most of the hosts. On NuminaMath-CoT at 256 chips, giving rollout 75% of hosts cuts step time by about 15% compared with LoCoJAX-CO.
bullets: Pathways’ centralized coordination is costly for short, repeated computations with small models: at 0.6B parameters, host orchestration accounts for 36% of step time.
LoCoJAX-CO colocates rollout and reward processing on each TPU host and achieves 1.3–3.6× faster steps than an optimized Pathways baseline across tested workloads and TPU scales.
On GSM8K, LoCoJAX-CO completes a step faster using 8 TPU chips than Pathways does using 64.
LoCoJAX-DA uses separate rollout and training hosts to overlap execution; this helps only when rollout dominates and receives most of the devices.
On NuminaMath-CoT with 256 chips, allocating 75% of hosts to rollout reduces step time by about 15% versus LoCoJAX-CO.

papers.selection_reason: Efficient coordination for RL training on TPUs, reduces step time.
papers.title: Local Coordination for Efficient Small-Model RL on TPUs
papers.tldr: LoCoJAX reduces coordination overhead for small-model RL on TPUs by moving rollout and reward processing locally while keeping training synchronized globally.

papers.abstract: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.
authors: Rui Ning, Om Chabra, Hari Balakrishnan
bullets: Targets prompt responses for video-based agents operating over bounded histories.
Caches each frame’s recurrent-state transformation and composes transformations associatively as the window advances.
Uses a specialized data structure and GPU kernels to limit caching and composition overhead.
Across five hybrid VLMs and four benchmarks, it achieved the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 tests.
Reduced p95 time-to-first-token by 6.6× on average versus the faster of two vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Architecture of the hybrid VLM. Multiple input frames are converted into visual tokens by a vision encoder and passed alongside text tokens into a unified backbone. This backbone interleaves recurrent layers, which update a fixed-size state for each token, with attention layers, which retain per-token key–value entries.

Figure 8. Mean GDN state error. Relative Frobenius error averaged over each model’s GDN layers, comparing Spool with Spool without reconstruction against the vLLM reference. The evaluation uses all 9,000 Beyond3D questions.

Figure 1. Spool maintains a sliding video window without replaying retained frames. (a) Shifting the window retains four of five frames. (b) Prefix-cache invalidation forces the retained context to be rebuilt. (c) Spool composes cached recurrent transformations and reclaims key–value slots by moving surviving tail entries into holes left by eviction.

Figure 4. Efficient recurrent-state reconstruction with cached transformations. Spool caches each block’s affine state transformation and then replays them without the effect of a given block. A segment tree composes consecutive transformations, enabling reconstruction of the active window in O(logW ) operations. In this example, frames 5–8 occupy cyclic slots 1–3 and 0, with frame 8 wrapping around to slot 0. Spool first applies F5, then the combined transformation F6,7, and finally F8 to the prefix state Sp. This recovers the window state using only three cached transformations, without reprocessing video tokens or updating the tree during reconstruction.

Figure 5. KV tail filling and RoPE rebasing. Top: surviving tokens 11 and 12 fill holes in slots 1 and 2, releasing the final page; P denotes the fixed prefix. Bottom: filling changes storage slots while preserving position coordinates. A separate rebase shifts all cached positions by a common offset (−100 here) and rotates cached keys consistently.
Figure 3. Cost of window rebuilding. Here we plot time for a frame to be processed by Qwen3.5-9B on 1 A100. Every time the window must be rebuilt from scratch, a 29.2x latency cost must be paid.
Figure 6. Component ablation: latency per ingested frame (ms, ↓) as caching components are added, from a naive cache to the segment tree cache and KV filling.

Figure 7. Effect of state reconstruction on output fidelity. (a) Output KL divergence from vLLM-Omni remains near 0.04 through 1024 expired frames with reconstruction, but accumulates without it. (b) Accuracy gain (points) from reconstruction on PhoStream’s backward questions, which target earlier video content, grouped by expired frames relative to window size. Both variants perform identically before expiration; reconstruction gains 2.4 points after half a window expires and 3.8–4.7 points beyond two windows.

Figure 9. Per-layer GDN state error for Qwen3.5-9B. Relative Frobenius error against the vLLM reference for all 24 GDN layers, averaged over questions within each expired-frame bin. The evaluation uses all 9,000 Beyond3D questions and a 64-frame retained window.

Figure 10. Empirical CDFs of online TTFT. Rows correspond to Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Nemotron-VL Nano-12B, and Qwen3.5-27B. Columns correspond to PhoStream, StreamingBench, FastBench, and BEYOND3D.

Table 1. Online p95 TTFT (s, ↓). Spool can maintain real-time performance as live video streams in, achieving the lowest tail latency in all 20 model–benchmark tests: a geometric-mean speedup of 6.6× over the faster baseline and 33.8× over vLLM-Omni. Gains are largest on smaller models (0.34 s vs. 12.22 s on PhoStream with Qwen3.5-9B, 35.7×) and remain clear at the largest scale (0.33 s vs. 1.99 s on StreamingBench with Qwen3.5-122B-A10B). (Parentheses are speedup over the faster baseline.)

Table 3. Offline accuracy (%, ↑). Spool’s windowed state maintenance preserves the backbone’s answer quality: without timing pressure, it stays within −1.6 to +1.8 points of the more accurate baseline in each of the 24 tests and has the highest mean accuracy, 54.4% vs. 54.1% for vLLM-Incremental and 53.7% for vLLM-Omni. Combined with the large online gains (Table 2), this shows that Spool’s online advantage comes from answering on time, not from changing what the model sees. (Parentheses are percentage points change over the more accurate baseline.)

Table 4. Peak GPU memory (GiB, ↓). Each of Spool’s components has a modest memory cost: the segment tree trades 2.3– 4.4 GiB for 4.7–14.8% lower per-frame latency (Figure 6), and KV filling recovers 0.38–1.77 GiB of it while lowering latency further. Overall, the full system uses 9.2% more memory on average than the naive cache.

Table 2. Online accuracy (%, ↑). By answering on time, Spool drops fewer questions under live load and answers more correctly than both baselines where they fall behind. On BEYOND3D, it improves over the more accurate baseline by 3.6–18.4 points (mean 9.5), such as 30.32% vs. 11.94% with Nemotron-VL Nano-12B. On the other benchmarks, it stays within −2.5 to +3.6 points. Averaged over all tests, Spool reaches 52.8%, compared with 50.3% for vLLM-Incremental and 45.4% for vLLM-Omni. Questions dropped while the server is busy count as incorrect. (Parentheses are percentage points change over the more accurate baseline.)

Table 5. Online p50 TTFT (s, ↓). Spool’s latency advantage is concentrated in the tail: vLLM-Incremental answers typical questions quickly but stalls on a minority, which dominates its p95 (Table 1). Spool still has the lowest or tied-lowest p50 in 18 of 20 tests (1.9× geometric mean over the faster baseline, 32.2× over vLLM-Omni), with the largest gap on FastBench with Nemotron-VL Nano-12B (0.14 s vs. 2.66 s). vLLM-Incremental is marginally faster on StreamingBench with Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, by 0.01– 0.02 s. Parentheses: speedup over the faster baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Low-latency streaming inference for hybrid VLMs via state transformation caching.
papers.title: Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Spool enables exact, low-latency sliding-window inference for hybrid vision-language models by efficiently removing expired video frames without replaying the full window.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models are orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8x slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8x B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.
authors: Gene Chou, Guandao Yang, Fujun Luan, Lars Mescheder, Wei Dong, Stephan Richter, Vladlen Koltun
bullets: Existing autoregressive video diffusion models are too slow for fluid interactive experiences.
Profiling shows VAE decoding and KV-cache updates contribute over half of end-to-end inference latency.
FastFrames replaces these components with lightweight alternatives in a family of fast models.
The 1.3B model achieves 36 ms per frame on a single B200 GPU while matching a much slower state-of-the-art model’s quality.
The 14B model achieves 45 ms per frame on an 8×B200 node with significantly better visual quality and realism, enabling real-time camera- and physics-conditioned generation.

Figure 5 Interactive generation and latency results. Left: example of interaction with LingBot’s official implementation vs. with FastFrames optimizations. Given a single keypress, FastFrames is 16× faster to respond. Right: generation latency of officially released implementations and our optimized implementations. We measure steady-state latency on NVIDIA B200 GPUs at 832×480 resolution with a full KV cache and include distributed optimizations such as Ulysses where officially supported. Times include diffusion sampling (four steps for LingBot and three for RealWonder), action conditioning, KV-cache updates, and pixel decoding. Our optimizations provide speedups of 3× to 22×. A single linear projection (middle) cannot render sharp outputs, but is sufficient for recognizing the scene and suggests that pixel rendering does not require an expensive decoder.

Figure 4 Qualitative comparisons. We compare FastFrames-S with Causal Forcing++ at 1.3B parameters and FastFrames-L with Krea-Realtime at 14B. Each example shows frames at 0 and 5 seconds. FastFrames-S achieves comparable visual sharpness to Causal Forcing++, such as the details in the sculpture (first example) and leaves (second example), while being nearly 8× faster. FastFrames-L achieves comparable visual realism to Krea-Realtime, including composition of “paper origami dragon” (third), and legible text of “stay curious” (fourth) while being 10× faster. papers.selection_reason: Fast autoregressive video diffusion with latency optimizations.

papers.tldr: FastFrames accelerates autoregressive video diffusion to interactive latency by redesigning costly inference components while preserving or improving visual quality.

papers.abstract: Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processing (DSP) conventions. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B with 66 checked examples covering 11 signal-processing MATLAB subtasks, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized LoRA (QLoRA) on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of a laptop, and deploy the 8-bit integer (int8) models with the adapters through OpenVINO. On held-out variants scored by deterministic checkers, the pass rate rises from 18/66 to 37/66 (LoRA) and 37/66 (QLoRA) for E2B and from 32/66 to 47/66 for E4B (QLoRA). Reading all 159 failing programs shows that the adapters remove most errors of convention, such as the sign of a lag, units and array shapes, but few errors in building signals and noise. Applied at run time, the adapter costs 17-19% of the generation speed.
bullets: Targets systematic DSP convention errors in small, offline-capable language models.
Fine-tunes E2B and E4B on 66 checked examples spanning 11 MATLAB signal-processing subtasks.
Uses LoRA or QLoRA on a laptop iGPU and deploys int8 models with adapters through OpenVINO.
Held-out pass rates improve from 18/66 to 37/66 for E2B and 32/66 to 47/66 for E4B with QLoRA.
Adapters fix many convention errors but few signal- and noise-construction errors; runtime generation slows by 17–19%.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates QLoRA and int8 deployment on a laptop iGPU, fitting the efficient-AI focus on reduced memory and compute for model adaptation.
papers.title: Fine-Tuning Gemma 4 Edge Models for MATLAB Signal-Processing Code with SFT and QLoRA on a Laptop iGPU
papers.tldr: SFT with LoRA/QLoRA substantially improves Gemma 4 edge models’ MATLAB DSP code correctness on a laptop iGPU, especially for convention-related errors, while preserving near-real-time deployment with modest speed overhead.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual question answering on lightweight user devices requires balancing speed, memory usage, privacy, and communication. One approach is to run audio-visual encoders on a server and a lightweight language decoder on the user device, keeping questions local while offloading media encoding. However, transferring and processing the full multimodal representation remains costly. We propose a training-free, query-agnostic token pruning framework that constructs a compact, reusable memory before transmission. We define video spatio-temporal blocks and aligned audio windows as players and estimate their importance through Monte Carlo Shapley valuation. We use an embedding coverage objective that combines query-independent utility with cross-modal redundancy calibration and rewards unimodal diversity through marginal coverage gains. We retain the original token embeddings of high-scoring players under a limited token budget and transfer the resulting memory once for reuse across subsequent local questions. Experiments on Video-MME, Daily-Omni, and Video-Holmes using video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) and video-SALMONN 2 Pro (4B) show that our method achieves the best or tied-best QA accuracy among the compared compression methods across all evaluated settings. On Daily-Omni with video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) at 80\% pruning, our method improves accuracy by 12.86--14.62 percentage points over these methods while achieving the lowest device-side LLM prefill and decoding latency, with up to $1.92\times$ decoding speedup at comparable embedding memory usage.
authors: Qitong Wang, Jihui Jin, Divya Kothandaraman, Vishnu Raj, Christopher Rasmussen
bullets: Targets the cost of transferring and processing full multimodal representations on lightweight devices.
Estimates the importance of spatio-temporal video blocks and aligned audio windows using Monte Carlo Shapley valuation.
Uses query-agnostic embedding coverage to balance utility, cross-modal redundancy, and unimodal diversity under a token budget.
Retains original embeddings for reuse across multiple local questions, avoiding repeated media transmission.
Across three benchmarks and two models, it matches or exceeds competing compression methods; in one setting, it improves accuracy by 12.86–14.62 points and reaches up to 1.92× decoding speedup.

figures.caption: Figure 1. A server processes video and audio into a compact memory and transfers it once to a personal device. The device reuses this memory to answer multiple questions locally, keeping user queries on the device. To construct the compact memory, we propose a novel token selection method. Fig. 2 provides an overview of our framework and the proposed method.

Figure 2. (a) The server encodes audio-visual content, constructs token groups as players, and performs query-agnostic selection to build a compact multimodal memory. The memory is transferred once to a lightweight device and reused to answer subsequent questions locally. Selection considers unimodal utility, intra-modal diversity, and cross-modal redundancy. papers.abstract: In the global attention layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The Gemma 4 report states that this design reduces the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, but the open serving engines that we checked still store a full key and a full value: 1,024 values per KV head and token. We store one 640-value row instead, exact in real arithmetic, and an unchanged paged attention kernel reads it through two overlapping strided views as its key cache and its value cache. In a vLLM prototype with the 16-bit 31B model, the outputs are bit-identical to an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache, 2 of 432 final answers differ from the stock engine (within its run-to-run noise), and the steady decode KV memory per request falls by a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 at 32K to 64K tokens. On a prefill/decode pair of two A100 GPUs with NIXL transfer and CPU offload, a decode engine with a full 15 GiB pool ran 1.38 times the stock decode tokens per step for 16K-token prompts (repeated to 0.06%) and 1.24 times for 8K-token prompts; a model of the vLLM block pool predicted both ratios to within 1% (the engine was 0.7% to 0.9% higher) and matched the change between them. The eager decode throughput rose by 1.30 and 1.11 times, and on this path the compact engine gave the same output tokens as the emulation for 8 prompts at batch 1. The run-time prototype makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch, and the method does not yet stack with an 8-bit KV cache at the default scale.
bullets: Gemma 4’s key is a scaled value, allowing one 640-value row to replace separate 1,024-value key and value rows.
The implementation uses two overlapping strided cache views, leaving the paged attention kernel unchanged.
In a vLLM prototype, outputs were bit-identical to arithmetic emulation; 2 of 432 final answers differed from the stock engine, within run-to-run noise.
With a 15 GiB decode pool, throughput increased by 1.38× for 16K-token prompts and 1.24× for 8K prompts; the block-pool model predicted both within 1%.
The approach adds 4–9% eager-step latency at equal batch and does not yet combine with default-scale 8-bit KV caching.

papers.title: Storing the Gemma 4 K=V Cache Once: Exact Global-KV Memory Savings in a Paged Serving Engine with Unchanged Attention Kernels

papers.abstract: Logic networks built from Boolean gates or lookup tables (LUTs) promise efficient hardware inference, but training them at depth and learning their connectivity remain difficult. We do not train logic as logic. Instead, ResoLUT distills a trained residual network (ResNet) layer by layer into LUT trees, preserving its multi-bit residual stream and BatchNorm while extracting connectivity from the teacher rather than learning it. To our knowledge, ResoLUT is the first convolutional logic network in computer vision to retain a ResNet-style multi-bit residual stream. Hard LUT decisions are used throughout training and inference, avoiding a discretization gap in the logic. ResoLUT-20 reaches 95.66% on CIFAR-10 with twice the trees, and ResoLUT-56 reaches 78.87% on CIFAR-100 and 53.69% on ImageNet at 64px, the best results of logic and lookup-table networks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, showing that LUT networks can scale in depth. We explore and quantify the role of the residuals and the tree budget and shape. The most optimized model, a ResoLUT-8 with one eighth of the trees and further optimizations, fits on an FPGA and reaches 90.04% at 189k images per second, the highest throughput among the compared models above 85% on CIFAR-10.
authors: Katarzyna Fojcik, Aidas Mikalauskas, Matthias Kampa, Renaldas Zioma, Jogundas Armaitis
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of training deep logic networks and learning their connectivity.
Distills a trained ResNet layer by layer into LUT trees, preserving multi-bit residual streams and BatchNorm.
Uses hard LUT decisions during both training and inference, avoiding a discretization gap.
Reports strong results across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and 64px ImageNet, demonstrating improved depth scalability for LUT networks.
An optimized FPGA model achieves 90.04% on CIFAR-10 at 189k images/s; results depend on tree budget and shape.

papers.abstract: Kernelized attention methods, which aim to replace the $O(N^2)$ complexity of softmax attention with $O(N)$ alternatives, have been the focus of intense research in the last five years. Despite growing interest, systematic evaluations and fair comparisons across approaches and scales are still missing. We analyze kernelized attention in two halves and highlight prominent limitations on each. On efficiency, FlashAttention achieves lower memory consumption and faster wall-clock time than SOTA kernelized methods during training and in vision transformers across most sequence lengths (with inference-time memory in causal language models the only clear exception), contradicting the core assumption for pure kernelized attention used as a drop-in replacement for softmax. We also discover that reported efficiency gains often fail to reproduce against modern baselines. On quality, current kernelized methods leave gaps of 2-10 points relative to softmax under a unified distillation protocol, and model scala alone does not close these gaps. We show this gap is not intrinsic to kernelization: LARA++, a principled extension of LARA that approximates softmax via importance sampling with adaptive proposal distributions, recovers up to 99% of softmax accuracy. We establish that the gap is closable; however, the computational overhead remains substantial, leaving the efficiency wall intact. Code is available at https://github.com/firatoncel/KernelRealityCheckNeurIPS2026
authors: F{\i}rat \"Oncel, Cem Subakan, Mirco Ravanelli, \c{C}a\u{g}atay Y{\i}ld{\i}z
bullets: Existing efficiency claims for kernelized attention often fail to reproduce against modern baselines.
FlashAttention generally uses less memory and runs faster during training and in vision transformers; causal-language-model inference is the main exception.
Under a unified distillation protocol, current kernelized methods lag softmax by 2–10 points, and scaling alone does not eliminate the gap.
LARA++, using importance sampling with adaptive proposal distributions, recovers up to 99% of softmax accuracy.
The remaining computational overhead means improved quality does not resolve kernelized attention’s efficiency disadvantage.

papers.abstract: When a twelve-lead electrocardiogram is written as text for a large language model, the number of tokens has to be balanced against the information lost through compression. This paper presents a deterministic encoding that writes eight independent leads as amplitude letters and exact time gaps and recovers the remaining four limb leads algebraically. The key points are selected with a cardiac-cycle-dependent tolerance, the amplitudes are parameterized by a 26-letter logarithmic codebook learned from a training set, and a 10-step tolerance schedule keeps all records within a fixed token budget. The encoding was applied to 21,388 records from the public PTB-XL database and evaluated using an exact decode-and-re-encode round trip, waveform reconstruction error, and a paired comparison of convolutional classifiers trained with 5 different seeds on signals from the original and decoded databases. All records were contained in 4,080 tokens (average: 2,866 tokens, 64.3% fewer than a per-sample transcription), and all stored lead strings were exactly reproduced. The average correlation between the decoded and reference signals was 0.982. The macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.9167 for the reference signals and 0.9157 for the decoded signals (paired difference -0.0010; 95% patient-level bootstrap interval, -0.0028 to 0.0007), within the pre-specified non-inferiority margin of -0.010; this is not a confirmatory result, because the test fold had been used during encoder development. The diagnostic content of a compact text can therefore be preserved, while the language model's ability to read the text is yet another matter.
bullets: Encodes eight independent ECG leads with amplitude letters and exact time gaps; derives the remaining four algebraically.
Uses cardiac-cycle-dependent key-point selection, a learned 26-letter logarithmic codebook, and a 10-step tolerance schedule under a fixed token budget.
Applied to 21,388 PTB-XL records, all fit within 4,080 tokens and stored lead strings were exactly recoverable.
Decoded signals correlated 0.982 with references; classifier macro-AUROC was 0.9157 versus 0.9167 for original signals, meeting the stated non-inferiority margin.
The result is not confirmatory because the test fold informed encoder development, and LLM ability to interpret the encoding remains untested.
