papers.abstract: Aggregating observations into a limited number of latent tokens and learning physical interactions in the latent space has emerged as an effective approach for Transformer-based neural operators to solve Partial Differential Equation (PDE) problems involving large-scale observations. However, existing methods typically compress observations using a single aggregation pattern, making physical information not retained by that pattern invisible to the latent space and thereby constraining physical interactions within it. To address this limitation, we propose PArallel Latent Space Neural Operator (PANO), a novel neural operator for solving PDEs that formulates physical interactions among observations as an additive combination of interaction results from parallel latent spaces with shared parameters. Specifically, PANO transforms observations into multiple distinct compressed representations through independent mappings, learns physical interactions in parallel based on these representations, and finally fuses the decoded results to predict the target physical field. Within PANO, we further propose Coupled Assignment Projection (CAP) to construct bidirectionally consistent encoding and decoding mappings, and Pairwise Latent Space Attention Layer (PaLA) to jointly update latent representations of each latent space through adaptive cross-space interactions. Extensive experiments on nine benchmarks spanning diverse physical systems, geometries, and observation scales demonstrate that PANO achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, PANO reduces equivalent plastic strain prediction errors on Unilateral Stamping by 28.3% (or more) and lift-coefficient prediction errors on AirCraft by 21.4% (or more) compared with existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/ZijiangY1116/PANO.
authors: Zijiang Yang, Xiaomeng Wu, Chen Kuang, Dongmei Fu
bullets: Single-pattern latent compression can hide physical information and limit learned interactions.
PANO independently maps observations into multiple latent representations, models interactions in parallel with shared parameters, and fuses decoded outputs.
Coupled Assignment Projection (CAP) builds bidirectionally consistent encoding and decoding mappings.
Pairwise Latent Space Attention (PaLA) enables adaptive cross-space interaction when updating latent representations.
Across nine benchmarks, PANO achieves state-of-the-art performance, including at least 28.3% lower error on Unilateral Stamping and 21.4% lower error on AirCraft than existing methods.

papers.abstract: Looped diffusion Transformers reuse shared blocks to deepen computation and match larger models with fewer parameters, reducing storage and deployment burdens. Yet repeated attention and MLP computations remain costly. Pruning reduces storage and computation by removing redundant parameters or units. Training-free methods struggle to resolve recurrent contributions, while training-based methods lack explicit constraints on position-specific errors affecting later inputs and final outputs. We propose LoopPrune, a pruning and recovery framework addressing these requirements. Recurrent importance estimation combines shared-removal effects and position variation to select a shared structure; shared reconstruction pools recurrent input statistics to compensate weights. Loop-position recovery compares complete denoising predictions at identical student states and matches text guidance, updating all student parameters against a fixed dense teacher. Extensive experiments across four open-source models, six benchmarks, and three pruning paradigms demonstrate effectiveness. At 30% structured parameter pruning, Looped-DiT B/16 retains 93.14% of dense six-benchmark average accuracy, exceeding the best baseline by 9.49%. Across PyTorch, vLLM-Omni, and SGLang Diffusion, pruned SDXSv3 reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 34.36-44.64% and accelerates denoising 1.46-1.74x over dense models.
authors: Weizhong Huang, Huaijia Kou, Yan Zhang, Fei Chao, Xiawu Zheng, Liujuan Cao
bullets: Targets the compute and memory costs of repeatedly executing shared attention and MLP blocks in looped diffusion Transformers.
Estimates importance using both shared-structure removal effects and variation across recurrent positions.
Reconstructs shared weights from pooled recurrent input statistics, then recovers performance by matching dense-teacher denoising predictions and text guidance.
Across four models, six benchmarks, and three pruning paradigms, 30% structured pruning retains 93.14% of dense Looped-DiT B/16 accuracy and improves over the best baseline by 9.49%.
For pruned SDXSv3, peak GPU memory drops 34.36–44.64% and denoising accelerates 1.46–1.74× across three inference frameworks.

papers.abstract: Looped vision-language models (VLMs) deepen computation by reusing shared layers, approaching larger models' capabilities with fewer parameters and easing the storage and deployment burden of stacking independent layers. However, repeatedly processing long visual sequences still incurs substantial compute and GPU memory costs. Visual token compression reduces these costs by shortening sequences. Existing methods mainly select original tokens directly or combine selection with aggregation. In looped models, the former may overlook changing token importance across calls and discard information needed later; the latter lack joint consideration of output changes across calls, limiting information preservation. We propose LoopZip, a training-free visual token compression algorithm addressing both issues. Visual aggregation builds a compact candidate pool before the looped backbone, and cross-invocation selection averages instruction attention from the first two existing calls of the same shared attention layer to retain tokens needed by both states. Weight-tied value correction then jointly fits shared visual-value adjustments to both pre-selection layer outputs, reducing output deviations across states. To validate LoopZip's effectiveness, we conduct extensive experiments covering two open-source looped VLMs, eleven benchmarks, and three pruning ratios. On LoopVL-1B, LoopZip retains 97.16% of the original model's performance at 50% pruning ratio and exceeds the strongest baseline by 5.36% at 87.5% pruning ratio. Across Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, and SGLang, LoopVL-1B with LoopZip reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 58.36%-58.98% and achieves 2.01-2.47x end-to-end speedups over the original model.
authors: Weizhong Huang, Zhicheng Liu, Yan Zhang, Fei Chao, Xiawu Zheng, Liujuan Cao
bullets: Targets the high compute and GPU-memory cost of repeatedly processing long visual-token sequences in looped VLMs.
Builds a compact candidate pool through visual aggregation before the looped backbone.
Selects tokens using averaged instruction attention from the first two calls of shared layers, capturing changing token importance across states.
Applies weight-tied value correction to reduce output deviations after pruning.

Across two looped VLMs and eleven benchmarks, it retains 97.16% performance at 50% pruning and delivers up to 58.98% lower peak GPU memory and 2.47× speedup; scope is limited to the evaluated models, benchmarks, and pruning ratios.
papers.selection_reason: Visual token compression for looped vision-language models; combines token pruning with cross-invocation selection and reduces memory/compute in VLMs.
papers.title: LoopZip: Visual Token Compression for Efficient Looped Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: LoopZip is a training-free visual-token compression method for looped VLMs that preserves performance while substantially reducing memory use and inference time.

papers.abstract: Ultra-low-bit quantization of large language models is a challenging task because aggressive compression severely distorts model parameters and disproportionately harms a small number of highly sensitive channels. We present a vector quantization method tailored for this regime. Our approach begins with random preconditioning, which regularizes the weight space and makes it more amenable to quantization. We then represent weights in polar coordinates and decouple the quantization of directions and magnitudes. To quantize directions, we leverage the structure induced by random preconditioning and design a structured codebook based on the $E_8$ lattice, yielding a compact yet expressive representation. To further reduce degradation, we detect extremely important channels using a proxy Hessian and preserve them with an additional cost of only 0.16 bits. Together, these components provide an effective quantization pipeline for LLMs in the extremely low-bit regime. Empirical results demonstrate improved accuracy, highlighting the benefit of combining geometric structure, lattice-based codebooks, and selective channel preservation.
authors: Daniil Li, Mars Davletshin, Vadim Klyzhenko, Artem Danilishin, Valery Sandul, Daniil Ryazanov, Ekaterina Muravleva
bullets: Addresses severe distortion from aggressive quantization, especially in highly sensitive channels.
Uses random preconditioning to regularize weights before quantization.
Separately quantizes weight directions and magnitudes in polar coordinates.
Employs an E8-lattice codebook for compact directional representation.
Preserves highly important channels identified by a proxy Hessian at an additional 0.16 bits, with empirical accuracy improvements.

papers.abstract: Reference-to-video diffusion transformers pack the variational autoencoder (VAE) latents of all references and the generated tokens into one full-attention sequence, in which reference tokens make up about half. Because attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, these tokens take up an even larger share of the attention computation, yet most of them are static, smooth or irrelevant to the output. To accelerate reference-conditioned generation, we propose pruning and caching of reference tokens for video generation (PCRG), a training-free, plug-and-play method that uses two signals the model already computes to assign each reference token to one of three tiers, namely pruned, cached or kept. The first is a low-level redundancy r from VAE latents, since a token whose latent barely changes over time or across its neighbors adds little new content. The second is a high-level importance g from the vision-language-model (VLM) conditioner, where the attention that the prompt and any first or last frames pay to a token tells whether the output needs to read it. Tokens that are not redundant are kept, and redundant tokens are cached if important and pruned otherwise. Pruned tokens leave the sequence before the first step with all rotary position embedding positions unchanged. Cached tokens have their keys and values computed once and reused, and kept tokens are processed as usual. On MiniMax-H3, already distilled to 8 timesteps and quantized to int8, PCRG is 1.57x faster end to end on our V2V-Bench and 1.49x faster on the public VACE-Benchmark, while the quality of VBench drops by only 0.24% and 0.17%, respectively. PCRG shortens the sequence rather than changing how attention is computed or which steps are run, so it also stacks on step caching and sparse attention. On V2V-Bench it reaches 1.86x with TeaCache, 1.82x with Spark at nearly unchanged fidelity and 2.15x with Veda.
authors: Siyuan Wang, Haoran Li, Yi Yue, Tak L. Fung, Quan Chen
bullets: Targets the quadratic attention cost caused by reference tokens, which comprise roughly half of the sequence.
Ranks tokens using latent redundancy and VLM-derived importance, assigning them to prune, cache, or keep tiers.
Pruned tokens are removed before generation while preserving rotary positions; cached tokens reuse their keys and values.
Achieves 1.57× and 1.49× end-to-end speedups on two benchmarks with only 0.24% and 0.17% VBench quality drops.
Combines with existing acceleration methods, reaching up to 2.15× speedup in the reported experiments.

papers.abstract: Spiking transformers combine attention-based representation learning with sparse spike communication, yet their weights and membrane variables still incur substantial storage and computation overhead. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers a practical way to reduce these overheads, but preserving neuronal firing under weight and membrane quantization remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Decision-Aligned Post-Training Quantization (DAQ), a method that calibrates the quantizers to align neuronal firing decisions with those of a floating-point reference. We analyze how errors from these quantizers affect firing at decision boundaries and how they propagate over time steps in recurrent neurons. Based on this analysis, we formulate an objective that encourages quantized membrane variables to remain within the reference firing regions along the quantized model's own state trajectory. Experiments across multiple spiking transformer architectures on image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking demonstrate the effectiveness of DAQ with 4-bit weights and membrane variables. On FE108, DAQ achieves 58.8\% AUC and 90.9\% PR with SDTrack, while reducing energy by 66.2\%.
authors: Jialin Chen, Xiaochen Zhao, Aili Wang
bullets: Addresses storage and computation overhead from weights and membrane variables in spiking transformers.
Calibrates quantizers to align quantized neuronal firing decisions with a floating-point reference.
Models firing-boundary errors and their propagation across recurrent time steps.
Uses an objective that keeps quantized membrane states within reference firing regions along the quantized trajectory.
Across classification, segmentation, and event-based tracking, 4-bit quantization is demonstrated; on FE108 with SDTrack, it reports 58.8% AUC, 90.9% PR, and 66.2% lower energy.

papers.abstract: Visual place recognition (VPR) faces critical challenges in handling extreme environmental variations while meeting the computational constraints of practical applications. Current methods predominantly address these challenges by either scaling up model capacity or employing computationally intensive reranking stages, creating a significant efficiency bottleneck. To overcome this limitation, we propose EfficientVPR, a lightweight one-stage framework that achieves speed-accuracy trade-offs through two key innovations: i) a scene-aware visual prompt tuning method which adapts pretrained features with less parameters while dynamically adjusting to sample-specific characteristics, and ii) an instance-dependent key local feature enhancement module that further reinforces discriminative regions. Comprehensive evaluations on Pitts250k, MSLS, Eynsham, AmsterTime and SVOX demonstrate that our method establishes a new SOTA for DINOv2-small models by outperforming all same-scale competitors, and delivers a $73\times$ speedup with 60\% lower-dimensional features while maintaining competitive (within 2.5% average R@1 gap) against the SOTA DINOv2-large-based two-stage method. Our code will be available at https://github.com/WiniTang/EfficientVPR.
authors: Wenjing Tang, Chuanguang Yang, Zhulin An, Libo Huang, Yongjun Xu
bullets: Targets the accuracy–efficiency bottleneck of VPR methods that rely on larger models or costly reranking.
Uses scene-aware visual prompt tuning to adapt pretrained features with fewer parameters and sample-specific adjustments.
Enhances discriminative regions with an instance-dependent key local feature module.
Evaluated on Pitts250k, MSLS, Eynsham, AmsterTime, and SVOX; achieves state-of-the-art results among DINOv2-small models.
Compared with a DINOv2-large two-stage method, provides a 73× speedup and 60% lower-dimensional features while staying within a 2.5% average R@1 gap.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The overall architecture of our one-stage method. To maintain strong discriminative power while ensuring lightweight efficiency, we employ DINOv2-small as the backbone with SceneVPT for fine-tuning, preserving generalizable features while adapting to instance-specific characteristics. During feature enhancement, EfficientVPR uses MsIA and OLE to extract multi-scale global features and orientation-aware local features respectively, while SGFS performs instance-specific local feature enhancement of key regions based on sample-dependent semantic cues obtained from backbone.

In the first and third row, our method successfully retrieves the correct image containing the main building with non-overlapping area, while all other methods fail. The second and fourth row shows their retrieval results (green boxes: correct matches; red boxes: errors). In both cases, while the sky and clouds occupy most of the area, they lack distinctiveness. The core discriminative features lie in the smaller objects, such as street lamps, signs, and building details. Fine-tuned by SceneVPT, the backbone effectively learns to focus on image-specific discriminative regions, such as the signs and street lamps in the first query and the architectural details in the second, while suppressing interference from irrelevant areas like the clouds. In contrast, with other approaches the backbone is prone to either missing the core discriminative features or paying excessive attention to non-essential parts of the image.

Current one-stage methods tend to be misled by these irrelevant features, producing false matches to incorrect locations with visually similar nonoverlapping elements (red border in the third picture). By enhancing the discriminative representation of task-relevant and samplespecific key local regions and structural information, our method effectively mitigates this issue.

papers.selection_reason: Lightweight visual place recognition with prompt tuning and feature enhancement; directly targets efficiency.
papers.title: EfficientVPR: Toward Efficient Visual Place Recognition via Scene-Aware Prompt Tuning and Adaptive Feature Enhancement
papers.tldr: EfficientVPR is a lightweight one-stage VPR framework that improves efficiency under environmental variation through scene-aware prompt tuning and adaptive local-feature enhancement.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art world models have been used to produce sequences of gameplay that accord with provided user-input actions. However, high quality, consistent gameplay generation often comes at the cost of inference speed, making real-time interactive play and ideation challenging. The substantial quantities of data used to train state-of-the-art models have also made custom training of these models appear impractical, limiting many of their potential uses in creative fields. In this work we demonstrate a major step towards efficient world models: achieving both fast high-quality inference, and improved data efficiency. This is done by replacing the next-token prediction paradigm with a two-stage discrete diffusion-based approach, introducing a lightweight refinement transformer which carries out iterative masked predictions. Building on an autoregressive world model capable of generating highly consistent and complex sequences over minutes (Kanervisto et al., 2025), we achieve substantial model speed-up (79x) with a modest quality trade-off. Additionally, we demonstrate that this model can be trained to reproduce high-quality, consistent gameplay using a dataset containing approximately one day (28 hours) of gameplay data. Our results demonstrate progress towards removing barriers to the use of world models in settings where real-time inference and data efficiency are essential.
authors: Raluca Stevenson, David Bignell, Jennifer C. White, Tabish Rashid, Emanuele Aiello, Mariya Hendriksen, Junha Hyung, Sadegh Aliakbarian, Abdelhak Lemkhenter, Marko Tot, Katja Hofmann, Sarah Parisot
bullets: Targets the slow inference and heavy data requirements that limit interactive and creative uses of world models.
Replaces next-token prediction with two-stage discrete diffusion and iterative masked prediction via a lightweight refinement transformer.
Builds on an autoregressive model designed for consistent, complex gameplay over minutes.
Demonstrates high-quality, consistent gameplay training using approximately one day of gameplay data.
Scope: the speed–quality trade-off and data-efficiency claims are demonstrated for gameplay generation.

papers.title: Towards Data-Efficient, Real-Time World Models
papers.tldr: A two-stage discrete diffusion world model enables 79× faster gameplay generation with modest quality loss and effective training from just 28 hours of data.

papers.abstract: JEPA-style latent world models let embodied agents plan toward new goals with model predictive control, but they are still too slow for real-life embodied control: sampling-based MPC repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, and even on high-end GPUs one planning step can take tens of seconds. We observe substantial latent locality in this repeated-inference workload: the predictor maps close actions to close latents, and inside a quantized predictor this closeness takes a form that hardware can exploit, differential bit-level sparsity. Unlike an input stream, whose temporal similarity is given, a planner itself decides which candidates it evaluates together, so the planner can choose its own references and, with reference forest sampling, manufacture more sparsity: it couples the sampled action sequences of each group to a shared root, with competitive planning quality. We build the accelerator on the insights of the rich line of bit-level sparsity accelerators and design it and the planner tightly coupled as a single co-design: the planner increases sparsity and exposes structure for hardware scheduling, and the bit-exact hardware effectively uses the sparsity that the planner creates. On three JEPA world models, our co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and uses 38-52% less energy, and it is 1.22-1.58x faster than prior bit-sparse design and uses 16-36% less energy, with the same area. To our knowledge, our planner is the first planner that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity across its candidates and exposes its structure for hardware scheduling, and our co-design is the first algorithm-hardware co-design for JEPA-style world-model planning.
authors: Wenbo Zhu, Paul Yi-Chia Chen, Yuanhan Li, Zishen Wan, Christopher Torng
bullets: JEPA world-model planning is slow because sampling-based MPC repeatedly runs predictor inference at large scale.
The method groups action sequences around shared reference roots, manufacturing latent similarity and hardware-exploitable differential sparsity.
A tightly coupled accelerator uses this sparsity and planner-exposed structure for efficient scheduling.
Across three JEPA world models, it achieves 1.28–1.80× speedup and 38–52% lower energy than a dense accelerator.
Compared with prior bit-sparse hardware at the same area, it achieves 1.22–1.58× speedup and 16–36% lower energy.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses efficient planning with JEPA-style latent world models by introducing differential bit-level sparsity. This combines World Models (Latent Action Models) with Efficient AI (Token Pruning) through a planner-hardware co-design.
papers.title: Manufacturing Differential Sparsity: Planner-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient World Model Planning
papers.tldr: A planner–hardware co-design accelerates JEPA-style world-model MPC by deliberately creating differential bit-level sparsity among candidate action sequences.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning speeds up large vision-language models (VLMs) by keeping only a part of their visual tokens. Most existing methods improve the ranking of the tokens and then answer every question once with the same budget. With strong rankings, pruning hurts only a few questions, and signals computed on the kept tokens see little of what it removed. We find that, on most of these questions, a small VLM given the full image disagrees with the pruned answer, since it still sees the missing evidence. We propose PRUDENT, which first answers with about half the budget and spends the saved tokens on re-answering the disagreeing questions at twice the budget. We show when such re-answering pays and why the small VLM should read the full image. On 18 benchmarks, PRUDENT outperforms eight existing pruning methods at the same average budget of visual tokens. Its lead widens as the budget tightens, and holds across five InternVL sizes. PRUDENT also has the highest average in two more model families. The disagreement of the small VLM flags most pruning failures of all eight methods, and re-answering on it also improves the two strongest with their own rankings. Other checkers give similar gains, and the extra tokens go where the first pass hurts the answer. These results suggest that identifying which pruned answers are trustworthy provides an additional lever for visual token pruning beyond the ranking of tokens. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/PRUDENT.
authors: Yanchao Li, Jiaqing Xie, Ben Gao, Yusu Zhang, Beilun Wang, Yanbo Wang, Xiaohua Xu, Zhongyu Huang, Tianfan Fu, Nanqing Dong
bullets: Existing pruning methods typically use one fixed token budget for every question, even though pruning harms only some answers.
PRUDENT first answers with roughly half the token budget, then reallocates saved tokens to questions where a small full-image VLM disagrees with the pruned answer.
Across 18 benchmarks, it outperforms eight pruning methods at the same average visual-token budget, with larger gains under tighter budgets.
The disagreement signal identifies most pruning failures and also improves strong existing pruning methods and multiple VLM families.
The approach focuses extra computation on uncertain answers rather than improving token ranking alone.

papers.title: Disagree to Prune: Reallocating Visual Tokens Where a Small VLM Dissents

papers.abstract: Occlusions and limited sensor range make ego-only 3D perception insufficient for safe driving. Collaborative perception addresses this by enabling connected vehicles to share complementary observations, yet it remains constrained by tight vehicular communication budgets. While spatial selection is more flexible than fixed-rate feature compression, existing selectors remain largely sender-driven and waste scarce bandwidth on ego-visible targets. Furthermore, applying convolutions after masking spreads isolated tokens into their neighborhoods, silently violating low-bandwidth constraints. To address this, we propose Spatial Elastic Consensus (SEC), a bandwidth-adaptive framework centered on bilateral demand-supply consensus. Instead of unilateral token selection, the ego vehicle formulates a content-aware demand prior while each collaborator evaluates its local supply. This single-round consensus allocates the token budget to critical ego-missed evidence rather than ego-visible redundancy, without transmitting dense maps. To guarantee exact budget compliance, an anti-dilation refine-before-mask pipeline refines features prior to discrete token selection, preventing receptive-field leakage. A lightweight deformable sampler then aggregates these sparse messages with learned local offsets, compensating for the spatial context lost to token selection and mitigating inter-agent pose drift. Evaluated at a stringent 64KiB budget, SEC consistently achieves the best AP@0.7 on the simulated OPV2V and V2XSet datasets and the real-world DAIR-V2X dataset. These results demonstrate that combining bilateral consensus with budget-exact transmission is key to efficient low-bandwidth collaborative perception.
bullets: Addresses occlusions and limited sensor range that make ego-only perception unsafe.
Uses bilateral demand–supply consensus: the ego proposes content-aware needs, while collaborators assess available evidence.
Refines features before discrete masking to prevent convolutional receptive-field leakage and guarantee budget-exact transmission.
Applies lightweight deformable sampling to recover local context and reduce effects of token sparsity and pose drift.
At 64KiB, achieves the best AP@0.7 across simulated OPV2V/V2XSet and real-world DAIR-V2X evaluations.

papers.abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.
authors: Siqi Lai, Haitao Li, Hao Liu
bullets: Addresses the latency and computational cost of repeatedly invoking LLM-based System-2 reasoning.
Builds a modular harness containing procedures, state memory, and world models for richer decision context.
Uses utility-driven retrieval and environmental feedback to select and recursively revise harness modules.
Experiments on three datasets show improved decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings while preserving low-latency execution.
As the harness improves, fewer System-2 interventions are needed, amortizing reasoning costs over time.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur control stalls when inference blocks the next action chunk. Asynchronous early inference can hide latency, but its results may be inconsistent with the arriving actual inputs. Unconditional reuse risks acting on mismatched inputs, whereas full recomputation discards useful precomputation. We propose SR-VLA, combining predicted-input lookahead with selective KV cache repair. During current chunk execution, a lightweight action-conditioned predictor generates next-boundary visual observations and proprioceptive state. These predictions, together with the task instruction, drive the frozen VLA to precompute a speculative KV cache and action chunk. After real inputs are available to VLA, predicted--real differences and task conditions determine whether to accept the action chunk or trigger selective KV repair. On LIBERO, SR-VLA achieves $2.67\times$ and $1.27\times$ query speedups over the respective synchronous $\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenVLA-OFT baselines, while maintaining competitive average task success rates. Under target-motion perturbation, success remains baseline-comparable, with $1.52\times$--$1.93\times$ query speedup.
authors: Tao Zhang, Yi Zhong, Jinhao Ruan, Yipeng Gao, Linfeng Zhong, Youming Yang, Yuan Wang
bullets: Addresses inference-induced stalls caused by blocking action-chunk generation.
Uses an action-conditioned predictor to forecast next-boundary visual observations and proprioceptive state.
Precomputes a speculative KV cache and action chunk with a frozen VLA, then accepts or repairs them based on predicted–real differences and task conditions.
On LIBERO, reports 2.67× and 1.27× query speedups over synchronous π0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT baselines while maintaining competitive success rates.
Under target-motion perturbations, retains baseline-comparable success with 1.52×–1.93× query speedup.

papers.tldr: SR-VLA reduces VLA control stalls by speculatively precomputing actions from predicted inputs and selectively repairing the KV cache when reality differs.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of quantized large language models is dominated by QLoRA, which combines 4-bit weight quantization with FP16 low-rank adapters. We ask whether the FP16 adapter precision is necessary. Replacing it with a single binary bit per adapter parameter, combined with a learned per-layer scale $s$ and a Scaled Straight-Through Estimator, reduces adapter storage by 13-16x. We introduce two variants -- NormScale, which binarizes under a norm-preserving scale with a clipped STE, and LearnThresh, which makes the binarization threshold learnable -- unified under a framework we call BQ-LoRA. Our main theoretical contribution is a tight characterization of the BQ-LoRA hypothesis class: it has bounded entrywise norm, a typical-set spectral norm bound that is $\Theta(r)$ times sharper than the worst case, a full-rank, near-isotropic update, and consequently a Rademacher complexity that yields an explicit $\tilde{O}(s_{\max}\alpha\sqrt{d_{out}/(rn)})$ generalization bound. FP16 LoRA has no comparable a priori norm or isotropy control. On Qwen2.5 (1.5B-72B), BQ-LoRA exceeds QLoRA's benchmark averages at every scale by 0.8-3.5 points; on LLaMA-2 (7B/70B) it remains competitive at the same storage reduction but does not uniformly lead the strongest FP16-adapter baselines (LoftQ at 7B, QLoRA at 70B). On Qwen2.5-7B the binary adapter preserves the 4-bit base WikiText-2 PPL within 0.06 (9.86 vs. 9.80) while QLoRA worsens it by 0.59. The reduction applies to inference-time adapter storage and serving; training memory matches QLoRA and step time rises by under 4%. We translate the storage saving into a deployment study, BQ-SGMV, by extending Punica's SGMV kernel with a binary inner-product primitive: the same A100-80GB holds 15.6x more adapters in HBM, and our research prototype eliminates cache misses under a skewed synthetic workload.
bullets: Targets the storage and serving overhead of FP16 adapters in QLoRA-style fine-tuning.
Introduces NormScale and LearnThresh, using learned layer scales and straight-through estimation for binary adapters.
Theory shows bounded norms, near-isotropic full-rank updates, and an explicit generalization bound unavailable for standard FP16 LoRA.
On Qwen2.5, BQ-LoRA improves benchmark averages over QLoRA by 0.8–3.5 points across model scales; results on LLaMA-2 are competitive but not uniformly best.
BQ-SGMV enables up to 15.6× more adapters in A100 HBM; training memory matches QLoRA and step time increases by under 4%.

papers.abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) predicts catalog entries as short semantic identifiers (SIDs). Trie-constrained beam search keeps these identifiers valid, but wide beams expose two serving costs: vocabulary-wide score tensors that are mostly discarded, and repeated attention over the same prompt. We present Trie-Head, a model-native output interface that stores the identifier trie as validated GPU tensors. Compared with a Python custom logit processor (CLP), it reduces CPU--GPU coordination and memory traffic by avoiding Python constraint callbacks and vocabulary-wide candidate buffers. It scores compact codebook candidates and streams the full-vocabulary normalizer, preserving the original model's valid-token scores in real arithmetic without retraining. Shared-context attention complements this output path by reusing prompt key/value blocks across beams while preserving their private decode tails. We implement both mechanisms in SGLang and evaluate candidate sourcing for LinkedIn Hiring Assistant and qualification retrieval for the Qualification Retrieval Platform. The combined system improves closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57x over the CLP baseline and up to 2.63x over BF16 FlashRec at a common beam width of 200 on the Qualification Retrieval Platform workload.
authors: Vedant Jhaveri, Arashpreet Singh Mor, Satyam Kumar, Alex Tsun, Qing Lan, Shaunak Mishra, Sriram Vasudevan
bullets: Targets two serving bottlenecks: discarded vocabulary-wide scores and repeated prompt attention across beams.
Trie-Head stores the identifier trie in validated GPU tensors, reducing Python callbacks, CPU–GPU coordination, and memory traffic.
Scores compact codebook candidates while streaming the full-vocabulary normalizer to preserve the model’s valid-token scores.
Shared-context attention reuses prompt key/value blocks while keeping beam-specific decode tails.
Implemented in SGLang; the combined system achieves up to 5.57× throughput over CLP and 2.63× over BF16 FlashRec at beam width 200 on one workload.

papers.tldr: Trie-Head and shared-context attention make wide-beam generative retrieval substantially more efficient without retraining or changing valid-token scores.

papers.abstract: Video understanding with multiple multimodal language models requires a communication interface that can transfer complementary visual observations. Text-based communication is interpretable, but introduces an intermediate generation stage and can omit information relevant to subsequent reasoning. We study Cross-Modal StateKV Injection, a provider--carrier framework that communicates through key--value (KV) states at visual-token positions. Provider models observe complementary video frames; their visual KV states are aligned and projected into the carrier representation space and integrated through gated residual updates. Injection preserves the carrier KV-cache sequence length, while retaining the additional computation required by the providers and the communication module. The reported experiments on MLVU and Video-MME compare carrier-only inference, text-based communication, and StateKV with two provider architectures. Results show modest, task-dependent accuracy gains and lower reported latency than the evaluated text-communication baseline, with some categories remaining unchanged or decreasing. Increasing provider-side frame coverage offers additional gains on selected tasks without extending the carrier cache. These findings motivate further study of visual KV communication under explicitly controlled observation and computation budgets.
bullets: Addresses information loss and extra generation cost in text-based communication between multimodal language models.
Provider models observe complementary video frames and transfer projected, aligned visual KV states to a carrier model via gated residual updates.
The injection preserves the carrier KV-cache sequence length, while adding provider and communication-module computation.
Experiments on MLVU and Video-MME report modest, task-dependent accuracy gains and lower latency than the evaluated text-based baseline.
More provider-side frame coverage helps selected tasks, but some categories are unchanged or worse; computation budgets remain an open consideration.

papers.selection_reason: Cross-modal KV-state communication between MLLMs for video understanding while preserving carrier cache length, touching both video understanding and KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: Cross-Modal StateKV Injection for Communication in Multi-LLM Systems across Temporal Segments
papers.tldr: Cross-Modal StateKV Injection enables multimodal LLMs to communicate complementary video information through aligned visual KV states, yielding modest task-dependent gains and lower latency than text communication.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference, but its optimal configuration depends jointly on workload characteristics, GPU hardware, and available memory. For example, on the RTX~5090, the state-of-the-art speculative drafter DFlash achieves $3.50\times$ the throughput of autoregressive (AR) decoding at low concurrency, but only $0.76\times$ at high concurrency with short outputs. We present SpecSearch, a hardware-aware search engine that jointly optimizes decoding strategy, draft length, and precision across workload--GPU pairs. Its analytical cost model captures memory and compute constraints to identify feasible configurations and narrow the search space for throughput optimization. Guided by this model, calibration measurements are collected from multiple GPUs. Using the measurements, a Jev-based predictor learns to select high-throughput decoding configurations on held-out GPUs without requiring deployment-GPU calibration. The predictor is parameter-efficiently trained on calibration data, while adapting a frozen Qwen3-4B using LoRA adapters and a linear correction layer. Across NVIDIA RTX~5090, H100, L40 and AMD MI300X GPUs, SpecSearch with full calibration achieves an average of $2.01\times$ the throughput of AR and $1.36\times$ the throughput of SD, both served by vLLM. The proposed Jev-based predictor closely matches this search performance with $1.30\times$ throughput improvement over SD with vLLM, while eliminating the need for held-out GPU calibration. Additionally, it retains $97.36\%$ of the throughput achieved by SpecSearch that utilizes full calibration.
authors: Selin Yildirim, Ali Zeyrek, Deming Chen
bullets: Speculative decoding performance varies substantially with GPU, concurrency, output length, draft length, and precision.
An analytical cost model captures memory and compute constraints to identify feasible configurations and reduce the search space.
Calibration measurements guide a Jev-based predictor that selects high-throughput configurations on held-out GPUs.
Across four NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, full calibration achieved 2.01× AR throughput and 1.36× standard SD throughput; the predictor achieved 1.30× over SD.
The predictor retained 97.36% of full-calibration SpecSearch throughput while avoiding deployment-GPU calibration.

papers.selection_reason: Hardware-aware search for speculative decoding directly targets inference efficiency and throughput.
papers.title: SpecSearch: Towards Hardware-Aware Efficient Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: SpecSearch selects hardware- and workload-specific speculative decoding settings to improve LLM inference throughput without requiring calibration on the deployment GPU.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention has been increasingly adopted by production LLMs for long-context inference, yet serving systems must still retain the full KV history, making GPU HBM capacity a key limit on serving concurrency. Existing systems offload the KV cache to host memory, but suffer from the limited bandwidth of PCIe and the limited capacity of host memory. Emerging scale-up memory pools (e.g., X-Mem) relieve both limits and open new opportunities for sparse-attention offloading. In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis and reveal that, even with scale-up memory pools, decode throughput remains bounded by HBM capacity, as hot KV buffers and the fully resident indexer key (K-index) cache occupy substantial HBM. Moreover, the two caches exhibit distinct access patterns. Based on these insights, we present XM-Sparse, the first sparse-attention offloading system over scale-up memory expansion. The core idea of XM-Sparse is to offload both caches aggressively while matching each with an I/O mechanism tailored to its access pattern. Specifically, for dynamically selected KV entries, XM-Sparse fuses TMA-based retrieval with attention in a tile-level pipeline to hide on-demand retrieval latency. For predictable K-index accesses, it prefetches pages via SM-efficient GPU-initiated DMA and coordinates prefetching with latency-critical operations to avoid interfering with decoding. We have implemented XM-Sparse atop SGLang, and our experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool show that XM-Sparse delivers up to 4.98$\times$ and 4.52$\times$ higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, respectively, and up to 1.34$\times$ over a naive integration on the same platform, across 16K-1M contexts.
authors: Yijun Sun, Xudong Liao, Zhuobin Huang, Kai Chen, Nikita Lazarev, Zhizhen Zhong
bullets: Problem: GPU HBM capacity limits serving concurrency because hot KV buffers and fully resident K-index caches consume substantial memory, even with scale-up memory pools.
Method: Dynamically selected KV entries use TMA-based retrieval fused with attention in a tile-level pipeline, while predictable K-index pages use GPU-initiated DMA prefetching.
Contribution: A sparse-attention offloading system implemented atop SGLang for scale-up memory expansion.

Results: On emulated scale-up memory, it achieves up to 4.98× and 4.52× higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, and up to 1.34× over naive same-platform integration across 16K–1M contexts.
Scope: Evaluated on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool.

papers.title: XM-Sparse: High-Throughput Sparse-Attention LLM Serving over Scale-up Memory Pools

papers.abstract: Coding agents repeatedly send their conversation history to a language model. Adding useful code may reduce search, while removing old tool outputs may shorten later prompts. But do these changes reduce the cost of solving a task? We study this as a measurement problem in more than 20,000 runs of open models on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench and Loc-Bench. We account separately for uncached input, cached input and output tokens. Three findings emerge. First, in our main evidence-package experiments, retrieved code reduces read and search commands by 18--34%, but increases cost by 33--42% when cached input costs one tenth of uncached input, without a measurable improvement in resolution. Second, removing old observations can either save money or increase cost: the same approach saves 19--36% without a cache discount but increases cost by 38--116% with a tenth-price cache. Third, shorter prompts do not guarantee cheaper runs because agents may respond by taking more steps. We also find that concurrent experiments can share cached prefixes and distort cost comparisons. These results show why context-management methods should be evaluated using both token prices and the agent's subsequent behavior.
authors: Zerui Yang, Miaomiao Dong, Quan Xue, Chaorui Zhang, Xuanyu Zheng, Xiyuan Wang, Haolin Ruan, Xueyan Niu, Guangcheng Song, Weixi Zhang, Wei Han, Bo Bai
bullets: Evaluated context addition and removal across more than 20,000 runs on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench, and Loc-Bench.
Retrieved code reduced read/search commands by 18–34% but increased cost by 33–42% with heavily discounted cached input, without measurable resolution gains.
Removing old observations saved 19–36% without cache discounts but increased cost by 38–116% when cached input cost one tenth as much.
Shorter prompts may trigger more agent steps, offsetting token savings.
Concurrent experiments can share cached prefixes, distorting cost comparisons; evaluation should account for token prices and subsequent behavior.

papers.selection_reason: Context-management cost under prefix caching directly relates to cache and memory efficiency for LLM agents.
papers.title: Context Has a Price: Adding and Removing Context for LLM Coding Agents under Prefix Caching
papers.tldr: Context management can change an LLM coding agent’s behavior enough that shorter prompts or added code do not necessarily reduce total cost under prefix caching.

papers.abstract: Attribution-guided pruning scores components by their causal contribution and protects the important ones, and it is increasingly applied to compress reasoning language models without destroying their chain of thought. Its reliability rests on an unexamined assumption: that reasoning importance can be faithfully measured. Across four small reasoning models, we show this measurement is fragile in three ways, each of which changes pruning decisions. First, scoring final-answer tokens, the natural choice, saturates in every chain-of-thought model we test (answer-token negative log-likelihood, NLL, of $10^{-4}$--$10^{-3}$) because the model states its answer inside its own reasoning; guiding head pruning with this target costs 27.6 and 32.2 accuracy points relative to scoring reasoning tokens on the two models we power with five seeds, while perplexity barely moves and even reverses sign at 7B. Second, causal importance is not localizable to single units: single-neuron effects sit at the measurement floor, their cross-split ranking is noise, and they cancel: a group's ablation effect disagrees in sign with the summed effects of its members in 90\% of groups. Reproducible importance emerges only at groups of $\sim 100$ neurons. Third, contrastively isolated ``reasoning-specific'' importance is not separable from generic importance, and protecting it is worse than protecting raw importance. We additionally pre-registered the hypothesis that distillation-induced concentration of importance predicts the pruning cost; it is not supported, and since our grid confounds concentration with scale, we report it as unresolved rather than reversed. The result is a short set of measurement rules: score reasoning tokens, attribute at coarse granularity, and evaluate with accuracy rather than perplexity.
bullets: Scoring final-answer tokens saturates because answers are already stated in the chain of thought, causing major accuracy losses versus scoring reasoning tokens.
Causal importance is not reliably localized to individual neurons; stable attribution emerges only for groups of roughly 100 neurons.
Reasoning-specific importance cannot be cleanly separated from generic importance and performs worse when used for protection.
Perplexity can mask pruning damage, so accuracy is the preferred evaluation metric.
The study recommends scoring reasoning tokens, attributing importance at coarse granularity, and evaluating with accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Pruning reasoning language models and importance attribution directly fits efficient AI model compression.
papers.title: The Fragility of Reasoning-Importance Attribution for Pruning Language Models
papers.tldr: Attribution-guided pruning for reasoning language models is highly sensitive to how importance is measured, making naive pruning decisions unreliable.

papers.abstract: Scaling has driven the success of large language models (LLM), with sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures enabling greater parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation. At large scales, MoE models rely on expert parallelism to distribute experts across devices. Each MoE layer requires two synchronous collective communication steps during inference: dispatching hidden states to the activated experts and combining the resulting expert outputs. As compute throughput has outpaced interconnect bandwidth, these synchronous collectives have become a major bottleneck to MoE scaling and efficiency. We address this challenge with EchoMoE, a lightweight architecture modification that retrofits existing MoE models, requiring approximately 8,500x fewer training tokens than full pretraining. Motivated by the observation that transformer blocks update the residual stream incrementally, we use a hidden state from an earlier layer as a reference and communicate only the compressed difference between it and the current state, rather than communicating each hidden state in full. EchoMoE periodically refreshes these reference states and transmits only the compressed differences synchronously, reducing the traffic on latency-critical paths without significant computational overhead. EchoMoE reduces inter-node communication volume by 58% and improves throughput by 22.6%, while preserving average performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks. EchoMoE further improves inference throughput by up to 2.38x over bandwidth-constrained Ethernet, paving the way for wide-area distributed inference. EchoMoE also tolerates quantization of the communicated representations without measurable quality loss. We release an efficient implementation for applying EchoMoE to pretrained MoE models, together with an inference integration for vLLM.
authors: Fengyuan Liu, Jay Gala, Siva Reddy, Dzmitry Bahdanau
bullets: MoE expert parallelism is bottlenecked by synchronous inter-device communication, especially as compute outpaces network bandwidth.
EchoMoE uses an earlier-layer hidden state as a reference and transmits only compressed differences, with periodic reference refreshes.
The method can retrofit pretrained MoE models with roughly 8,500× fewer training tokens than full pretraining and little computational overhead.
It reduces inter-node communication by 58% and improves throughput by 22.6%, while keeping average benchmark performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks.
The approach supports quantized communication without measurable quality loss and provides integrations for pretrained models and vLLM.

papers.selection_reason: Activation compression for efficient MoE inference reduces communication and improves throughput, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Communicate the Change: Efficient Expert Parallelism via Activation Compression
papers.tldr: EchoMoE accelerates distributed MoE inference by communicating compressed changes to hidden states instead of full activations.

papers.abstract: Block-wise diffusion language models (DLMs) refine multiple tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. Their long-context inference, however, remains bottlenecked by memory-bound attention: every denoising step repeatedly reads a growing historical key--value (KV) cache. Directly applying sparse attention does not fully solve this problem, because different queries can select different pages, inflating the block's collective read set, while repeated support construction adds overhead and permanent eviction can discard information needed later. We present RISA, a recoverable sparse-attention method with shared read plans for block-wise DLMs. RISA exploits the fact that historical KV remains fixed within a block while queries evolve across denoising steps. Newly generated history is organized into exact priority and recovery tiers; seed queries then build a protected, bounded read plan whose indices are reused across the block while attention is recomputed with fresh queries and current-block KV. This separates history preservation from repeated reading and amortizes sparse-support construction without changing the backbone or decoder. On DreamReasoner-8B, RISA retains comparable task performance. At 32K, the default configuration speeds up attention by $2.67\times$ and fixed-trajectory requests by $1.36\times$ over dense, and attention speedup reaches $5.53\times$ at 128K. Across eight settings on three models, RISA decodes faster than the tested MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA budgets at matched KL.
authors: Xinrui Zhong, Fanjiang Ye, Yuke Wang
bullets: Targets memory-bound attention caused by repeatedly reading growing historical KV caches.
Builds shared read plans from seed queries using exact priority and recovery tiers, while recomputing attention with fresh queries and current-block KV.
Protects potentially useful history from permanent eviction and amortizes sparse-support construction without modifying the backbone or decoder.
On DreamReasoner-8B, it preserves comparable task performance and reports up to 5.53× attention speedup at 128K context.
Across eight settings and three models, it decodes faster than tested MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA budgets at matched KL.

papers.abstract: Deformation-based 4D Gaussian splatting (4DGS) enables dynamic scene rendering. However, evaluating deformation networks for all Gaussians at every frame is compute-intensive on edge devices. We find that Gaussian trajectories are often locally predictable, yet prediction reliability varies across Gaussians and time. Thus, we propose CueSplat, a post-training framework that exploits local temporal regularity while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen and retaining its Gaussian set. Specifically, CueSplat predicts Gaussian attributes from recent history and uses a lightweight learned router to select exact deformation updates within a scene-specific budget calibrated offline. Selection accounts for prediction reliability and rendering contribution. Selected indices are reused across nearby frames to reduce routing overhead, while selected Gaussians still receive exact updates each frame. To control accumulated prediction error, we use drift signals to schedule three consecutive full-deformation frames that rebuild the prediction history. Evaluated across four mainstream 4DGS algorithms, CueSplat achieves up to $6.74\times$ and $8.15\times$ speedups on Jetson AGX Orin and Orin NX, respectively, with a negligible quality drop (at most $0.16$ dB in dataset-average PSNR).
authors: Qingyuan Tang (Shanghai Jiaotong University), He Zhu (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Shixuan Sun (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Anbang Wu (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Jingwen Leng (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Minyi Guo (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Yu Feng (Shanghai Jiaotong University)
bullets: Addresses the high cost of evaluating deformation networks for every Gaussian at every frame in 4DGS.
Uses a frozen pretrained backbone, local temporal prediction, and a lightweight router to select exact updates within an offline-calibrated scene budget.
Selection considers prediction reliability and rendering contribution; selected Gaussians are reused across nearby frames to reduce routing overhead.
Drift-triggered full-deformation frames periodically rebuild prediction history and limit accumulated error.
Across four 4DGS algorithms, achieves up to 6.74× speedup on Jetson AGX Orin and 8.15× on Orin NX, with at most a 0.16 dB average PSNR drop.

The merged state is rendered and stored in history. (3) Adaptive refresh uses drift signals to schedule three consecutive full-deformation frames that rebuild history, with partial precomputation after target timestamps are fixed.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving relies predominantly on cloud GPUs, yet autoregressive decoding is memory-bound and often leaves their arithmetic units underutilized. Edge FPGAs offer attractive decoding efficiency, but are ill suited to sustaining a high-concurrency serving workload alone. This paper presents HyCoInfer, a heterogeneous cloud-edge serving system that assigns prefill to cloud GPUs and distributes decoding across cloud GPUs and edge FPGAs. The design addresses three barriers to practical offloading: capacity balancing across heterogeneous accelerators, the large KV cache crossing a constrained wide-area link, and the latency added by heterogeneous execution. HyCoInfer incorporates FPGA decode capacity into GPU prefill/decode role partitioning and places requests according to queue load, prompt length, and network state. It further combines layer-wise pipelined transfer, decoder-side precomputation, and bandwidth-adaptive KV cache compression based on residual vector quantization. We implement HyCoInfer using two NVIDIA V100 GPUs and an AMD Xilinx Alveo U280 and evaluate it over 100-1000 Mbps links. At 500 Mbps, HyCoInfer delivers up to 4.11 times the request goodput of cloud-only vLLM and reduces mean end-to-end latency by up to 61.1%. Across different network conditions and workloads, the system improves overall serving capacity, with the largest gains on communication-intensive tasks, and reduces per-request energy.
authors: Zewen Huang, Xiangwen Zhuge, Yingkun Hu, Zheng Yang, Qiang Ma
bullets: Targets underutilized cloud-GPU decoding and the limited concurrency of edge FPGAs.
Assigns prefill to cloud GPUs and distributes decoding based on accelerator capacity, queue load, prompt length, and network state.
Reduces offloading overhead using pipelined layer transfer, decoder-side precomputation, and bandwidth-adaptive KV-cache compression.
On a V100–Alveo U280 prototype, achieves up to 4.11× request goodput and 61.1% lower mean latency than cloud-only vLLM at 500 Mbps.
Benefits are strongest for communication-intensive workloads and include lower per-request energy, with performance dependent on network conditions.

papers.abstract: When applied to two-dimensional features such as images, Mamba-based methods either flatten the feature map into 1D sequences and fuse multiple scans, which breaks spatial adjacency and multiplies computation, or recurse directly on the 2D grid but rescale the recurrence with a fixed input-independent factor and aggregate only the predecessors on a single anti-diagonal, leaving the discrete step unconstrained by 2D stability theory. We propose \textbf{FM-Mamba}, a native 2D selective state space model built on the general Fornasini--Marchesini (FM) model. Its coupled recurrence evolves along both spatial axes; cross-axis coupling induces a discrete diagonal-predecessor term $\tilde A_0$, and two independent input-dependent step sizes $\Delta_1(i,j)$, $\Delta_2(i,j)$ govern propagation along the two axes, so that the coefficients adapt per position and per direction. A normalized ratio $r_k=a_{0,k}/(a_{1,k}a_{2,k})$ yields a closed-form piecewise bound on the two step sizes; when a configuration falls outside the stable interval the steps are projected onto this bound, and the criterion is re-verified per position after training, which suppresses systematic local amplification without global damping. The recurrence is executed by a dual-diagonal wavefront scan: each update gathers information from two anti-diagonals, and the input enters the current state through a single projection, so that neither training nor inference flattens the feature map. Code is available at https://github.com/BitSsm/FM-Mamba-Runtime
authors: Shengyuan Hu, Yiyong Sun, Weihang Shan, Yongzhe Chang
bullets: Addresses inefficiency and spatial-adjacency loss from flattening 2D features, as well as stability limitations in prior recursive 2D Mamba methods.
Uses the Fornasini–Marchesini model with coupled recurrences along both spatial axes and a diagonal-predecessor interaction.
Employs two input-dependent step sizes per position and direction, constrained by a closed-form stability bound and projected when unstable.
Implements a dual-diagonal wavefront scan without flattening during training or inference.
Scope: the abstract describes the architecture and stability mechanism but does not report experimental results.

papers.abstract: The effectiveness of a video diffusion model's inference budget depends on where computation is spent along the denoising trajectory. Across eight equal-budget inference configurations, VBench total scores span 4.80 points, highlighting the importance of explicit allocation design. Our key insight is that guidance evaluations are not equally valuable across diffusion time: retaining the sampling updates while selectively reusing guidance can preserve generation quality with fewer denoiser evaluations. We introduce BATMoS (Budget Aware Temporal Mixture of Strategies), which routes between fresh classifier-free guidance and cached guidance using a single pretrained denoiser. A magnitude-based temporal rule assigns guidance reuse to low-magnitude blocks and reserves fresh guidance for the remaining blocks, with a single integer controlling the computation budget. The resulting schedule requires no additional router training or per-budget threshold search. Evaluated on CogVideoX-2B with 4,720 videos per configuration across all sixteen official VBench dimensions, BATMoS achieves the highest total score among the eight allocation policies and comes within 0.10 points of full classifier-free guidance using 20\% fewer branch evaluations. BATMoS also composes with feature reuse, reducing computation from 80 to 62 effective branch evaluations with a 0.11-point decrease in total score. These findings make temporal guidance allocation a practical mechanism for extracting more generation quality from a fixed inference budget.
authors: Zhixu Du, Kuo Yang, Jingwei Sun, Hai "Helen" Li, Yiran Chen
bullets: Inference quality varies substantially with how a fixed computation budget is allocated along the denoising trajectory.
BATMoS routes between fresh classifier-free guidance and cached guidance using a single pretrained denoiser.
A magnitude-based temporal rule reuses guidance in low-magnitude blocks and reserves fresh evaluations elsewhere, controlled by one integer budget parameter.
On CogVideoX-2B across all 16 VBench dimensions, it achieves the best score among eight allocation policies and comes within 0.10 points of full guidance with 20% fewer branch evaluations.
Combined with feature reuse, it reduces effective branch evaluations from 80 to 62 with a 0.11-point score decrease.

papers.abstract: We propose Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format for tensors written once and read many times. Formats that round each value on its own, such as INT4 and FP4, waste a large part of their bits against the information-theoretic ideal. Trellis codes recover this loss by encoding values jointly, but prior decoders either need a large lookup table for their best quality or compute values with a hash that restricts what they can decode. CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and adds the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table. Because that sum is not uniformly distributed, the rarely used ends of a small table can hold values far out in the tails. One decoder serves every bit width from 1 to 6, reproduces the standard integer and floating-point formats exactly, and comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits. It matches a random-permutation trellis code whose table is thousands of times larger, and exceeds every QTIP codebook. In LLM weight quantization without fine-tuning, CPTC has the lowest KL divergence to the unquantized model at every tested bit width on Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP's codebooks (by up to 27%). The decoder has been built into the AWS Trainium 4 AI accelerator, where it runs at the throughput of the native FP4 and FP8 formats for a negligible fraction of the systolic array's area. Fused encoding kernels quantize an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU and, in cycle-level simulation, on one Trainium 4 chip.
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of independently rounded INT4/FP4 values and the large tables or restricted decoders of prior trellis codes.
Decodes 1–6-bit formats by multiplying a state by two coefficients, using product top bits to index a compact 64-byte table.
Comes within 0.07 bits of the information-theoretic ideal at 4 bits and matches a random-permutation trellis code with a table thousands of times larger.
Achieves the lowest reported KL divergence across tested bit widths for Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP codebooks, by up to 27%.
Runs at native FP4/FP8 throughput on AWS Trainium 4 with negligible systolic-array area; scope is tensor quantization without fine-tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a low-bit quantization method for LLM weights, reducing memory requirements and improving efficiency.
papers.title: Computed Permutation Trellis Coding: Near-Optimal Quantization from Two Multiplications and a 64-Byte Table
papers.tldr: CPTC delivers near-optimal low-bit tensor quantization using two multiplications and a 64-byte lookup table, with efficient decoding and strong LLM weight-quantization results.

papers.abstract: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.
bullets: Addresses information loss and extra derivation between stored conversations and assistant queries.
Restores cached sessions and appends the question, while retaining raw text as the authoritative fallback.
Defines budget-based retention, append-only reads, bounded aggregation, and a cost model for storage and querying.
Estimates substantially higher cache storage than text, with costs varying by model architecture and retention scenario.
Introduces logical QA evaluation via session prefill plus a separate real-cache replay test for numerical equivalence and runtime cost.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Published system-level comparisons under two different benchmarks and source evaluation protocols: (a) LongMemEval’s 97-question subset with 3–6-session histories [1, Fig. 4a]; (b) LoCoMo J scores from Mem0’s vendor-authored evaluation [2]. Full-history reading scores highest among the selected systems shown in each panel, not across all evidence. Zep’s separate vendor-reported LongMemEval-S comparison favours its retrieval system over a full-context baseline averaging about 115K tokens and is not plotted here (§3.2, §8.1). These comparisons do not isolate a memory mechanism, and scores depend on evaluation labels and judges (§9.1). L1–L4 are our descriptive memory modes; KV-LTM has no measured accuracy bar (§8). Costs are modelled separately (§7).

Figure 2: KV-LTM write flow (once per session): canonical per-session prefill creates the stored state at session end; session text, metadata with integrity digests, and native reader state are retained under the §4.8 storage and latency policy, which may evict or invalidate state — the text is always kept. Boxes denote logical steps or stored objects, not software components.

MLA values assume compressed-latent storage. Kimi-Linear shows only its MLA-layer component (bMLA = 8,064 B/token); its per-session recurrent state is symbolic and not drawn. The plotted per-token spread is ∼40× (the hybrid’s bMLA part at the low end); among the non-hybrid configs the spread is ≈10.5× (31,104 → 327,680).

Figure 3: KV-LTM read flow (per question): each retained session’s text is verified against its stored digest first — a known-good copy is recovered and re-verified on failure, and an unrecoverable session counts as unavailable (out of coverage), never as evidence. Valid state is read from a request-local working copy; when policy allows, invalid or evicted state is rebuilt from the verified text (§4.3), otherwise the session is counted as not cached and delegated to the §4.8 text fallback, outside the depicted cache-read path. Per-session outputs supply bounded evidence to the aggregator (§4.6); optional hybrid, verifier/reranker and joint-evidence lanes (§4.5, §4.7) complement the reference read. Boxes denote logical steps or stored objects, not software components.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes persistent per-session KV caches as long-term memory for LLM assistants, directly addressing LLM memory and KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants
papers.tldr: KV-LTM proposes storing each conversation session’s raw text and model KV cache to preserve long-term memory while accelerating future question answering without recomputation.

papers.abstract: Low-bit LLM quantization is useful only if a model preserves service-relevant accuracy, executes through supported GPU kernels, and meets measured memory and latency limits. We study Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 with vLLM, including INT2/INT3, GPTQ, NVFP4, and mixed-precision configurations. We verify native packed execution and precision on all 144 fused linear modules and evaluate Korean, English, numerical, and reasoning quality under preregistered gates. Packed INT2 and INT3 execute, but all seven tested INT2 grids degenerate on generation. Isolated module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive; Korean and reasoning sensitivity rankings disagree, and a promising INT4/INT8 development candidate fails independent final evaluation. A configuration with 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head passes all gates on the untouched FINAL-81 set (5,168 items): 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory (limit 5.98), Korean teacher-correct retention 0.904 (gate 0.90), and TPOT ratio 0.939 relative to BF16. It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by +1.4 percentage points (Bonferroni-adjusted interval [+0.2, +2.6]), compared with +3.4 points on the selection set. This comparison changes both activation precision and INT8 protection; exploratory analyses suggest that the activation change contributes substantially, but the isolated allocation effect is not established. Final checkpoints were not retained, and bitwise rebuild reproducibility remains unverified.
bullets: Packed INT2/INT3 kernels execute natively, but all tested INT2 configurations degenerate during generation.
Module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive, with Korean and reasoning tasks showing different sensitivity patterns.
The final recipe uses 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head.
On the untouched FINAL-81 set, it uses 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory, retains 0.904 Korean teacher-correct accuracy, and reaches a 0.939 TPOT ratio versus BF16.
It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by 1.4 percentage points, though the roles of activation precision and INT8 allocation are not isolated.

papers.selection_reason: Mixed-precision quantization for efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: Beyond Bitwidth: Deployment-Constrained Mixed-Precision Quantization for Multilingual LLM Inference on NVIDIA Blackwell
papers.tldr: A deployment-constrained mixed-precision recipe for Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 passes memory, Korean-quality, and latency gates, outperforming NVFP4 W4A4 while revealing major risks in ultra-low-bit quantization and candidate selection.

papers.abstract: A reasoning model that has reached a correct answer can lose it by continuing to think. Deciding whether to stop means comparing two probabilities at the same point of a chain: that the answer the model would give if stopped now is correct (its commitment), and that the answer it will finish with is correct (its verdict). We show that the verdict alone, which is what final-correctness probes estimate, cannot make this comparison. As a forecast of a fixed outcome it has no predictable drift, whether continuing helps or hurts. The commitment-verdict gap equals the expected remaining change in answer quality and the accuracy gained by stopping. A second identity splits any accuracy-versus-budget curve into answer change within chains and change in which chains are still running. We measure both on MATH-500. At all 379 points where DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B holds a correct answer, selected without regard to how its chain ends, continuing loses 3.6 points on average (95% CI [2.2, 5.2]), and the loss concentrates in a few problems. In six reasoning models from three families, on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench and with budgets up to 16,384 tokens, declining accuracy curves come from which chains remain, while the chains still reasoning keep or improve their answers. An oracle stopping rule gains at most +1.8 and +2.5 points at 1.5B and 7B. The framework says what to measure before building a stopping rule.
authors: Jianghong Zhou, Hao Rong, Chen Lin
bullets: The commitment–verdict gap measures expected remaining change in answer quality and the benefit of stopping immediately.
Accuracy-versus-budget declines are driven mainly by which chains continue running, not by answers deteriorating within those chains.
On MATH-500, continuing from an already-correct commitment lost 3.6 percentage points on average for one evaluated model, with losses concentrated in a few problems.
Across six models on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench, chains still reasoning generally maintained or improved their answers despite declining aggregate accuracy curves.
An oracle stopping rule provided limited gains: up to 1.8 points for the 1.5B model and 2.5 points for the 7B model.
