papers.selection_reason: Framework for stopping rules and harmful overthinking in reasoning models; informs efficient inference.
papers.title: Conserved Verdicts, Drifting Commitments: Identifying Harmful Overthinking
papers.tldr: Final correctness alone cannot detect harmful overthinking; comparing a model’s current commitment with its eventual verdict reveals when continuing reasoning reduces accuracy.

papers.abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.
authors: Jameson Sandler, Shane Bergsma, Mostafa Elhoushi, Bin Claire Zhang, Gavia Gray, Joel Hestness, Nolan Dey, Ferdinando Fioretto
bullets: Existing feature encoders can distort target features, forget rejected proposals, and overlook important target hidden states.
DNeo introduces Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA) with working memory for previously rejected proposals.
It further uses 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target-layer selection.
The resulting system reports 1.3× faster generation than DFlash-2 with unchanged drafter footprint and generation quality.

figures.caption: Figure 3: DNeo architecture. Target model (left) produces residual streams for the clean-prefix, and rejected positions. Streams are aggregated into prefix hidden states and rejection states (A). The most useful states are kept with the DNeo feature selector (B) (Section 4.5), then passed to the MoFA gate (C) (Section 4.1) to obtain the encoded prefix, and rejection memory (D) (Section 4.3). Parallel draft blocks perform cross-attention to the target features (E), utilize 2-tap convolutions (F), and finally apply the fused DNeo head (G) (Section 4.2) to produce the new draft.
Figure 2: Draft quality comparison. Tokens per forward (τ) over the test-set (Section 5.1), using official SGLang inference implementations. DNeo dominates existing methods in draft quality.

papers.selection_reason: Speculative decoding with parallel draft models reduces LLM inference latency; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding
papers.tldr: DNeo improves speculative-diffusion decoding by giving parallel draft models richer, memory-aware target-feature encoding, achieving 1.3× faster generation than DFlash-2 without reducing quality.

papers.abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.
authors: Xin Guo, Qiang Zhang, Xiang Zhou, Arushi Rai, Siyu Lin, Yifan Wu, Xiang Shen, Lei Huang, Qunshu Zhang, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang
bullets: Repeated profile-text prefills dominate ranking inference because profiles appear after varying prompt prefixes, preventing effective prefix caching.
Lightweight LoRA writers, trained by self-distillation, generate reusable profile KV caches during profile updates.
A KV scheduler overlaps host-to-GPU cache transfers with computation for the next batch.
On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, ranking quality shows no statistically significant difference from full prefill across memory updates.
Under saturated load, throughput improves 4.0–4.5× for scoring and 1.4–1.9× for profile updates.

papers.title: KVUse: Reusable-KV User Memory for Efficient LLM Recommenders
papers.tldr: KVUse accelerates LLM recommendation serving by storing user profiles as reusable KV caches instead of repeatedly prefilling their text.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention models read a few blocks of keys for every query at a fixed budget and can lose much of their long-context retrieval accuracy at that budget. We ask where this loss is made. Using exact attention mass selection at the shipped budget as an oracle, we show that the selector under-ranks the needle rather than running out of budget. We find attention heads that miss the needle by running a calibration probe that teacher-forces the answer and reads two quantities in every head. The first is the needle attention that the selector forfeits, and the second is the share of the answer's log-probability that fixing the head's selection restores, integrated along the path from the shipped selector to full attention. Four checkpoints of the InfLLM-V2 family and NOSA-8B lose multi-key retrieval in the same three blind heads, which attend to the needle while a mean-pooled key summary dilutes its single decisive token. Full attention in those heads or a 4-bit scorer that keeps the shipped budget recovers most of the loss without training. On MiniCPM4.1-8B at 64K, either fix lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 54.1 to 97.5%, level with full attention in every head. In production serving engines, full attention in those heads keeps 84 to 89% of the time to first token (TTFT) that sparse attention saves at 32K to 128K context length. Beyond the InfLLM-V2 selector lineage, one unified rule flags attention heads above a threshold swept on each checkpoint until they close most of the gap to full attention on calibration prompts. A similar small set of blind attention heads carry the loss for the SeerAttention-R gates, NSA, and DashAttention, whereas many such heads exist in MoBA. On Qwen3-8B with the SeerAttention-R gates, full attention in 18 of 288 key-value heads lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 29.8 to 97.7%.
bullets: Exact-attention analysis shows the main issue is selector mis-ranking of relevant blocks, not exhausting the fixed budget.
A teacher-forced calibration probe identifies heads that attend to the needle but lose it when mean-pooled key summaries dilute its decisive token.
For InfLLM-V2 and NOSA-8B, the same three blind heads explain much of the multi-key retrieval loss; similar patterns appear in several other sparse-attention methods.
Repairing flagged heads with full attention or a 4-bit scorer preserves the shipped budget and recovers most of the loss without training.
Reported gains include MiniCPM4.1-8B improving from 54.1% to 97.5% at 64K, while selective full attention retains 84–89% of sparse attention’s TTFT savings; MoBA shows many more blind heads.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Method overview. (a) InfLLM-V2 scores each block from mean-pooled keys, gathers the top-k blocks and attends to them in every head. (b) A needle probe, run once per checkpoint, compares the shipped selection with exact attention mass at the same budget, which explains the failure, and keeps the heads with the largest gain of fixing their selection. (c) In the flagged heads, full attention reads every block, and every other head keeps the shipped selector. A 4-bit scorer that keeps the shipped budget can replace full attention in those heads.

Figure 1: Where the selector forfeits the needle. Per key-value head, the needle recall that the shipped selector loses against exact mass, times the attention the head puts on the needle block, on calibration prompts at 32K, or 16K for Dash-8B and NSA-8B. The first group holds the five checkpoints of the MiniCPM4-8B lineage, with the InfLLM-V2 selector or the NOSA variant of it, head 0 above head 1. Dash-8B and NSA-8B share the backbone under other selectors, and the last band is Qwen3-8B under the SeerAttention-R gate, heads 0 to 7 from the top. Outlined heads are the heads that each model’s fixes use, the three blind heads in the lineage and the heads of the threshold rule on the other selectors. Scores at or below 10−4 share the lightest color.

Figure 7: Latency against the dense model on one H100. (a) TTFT of InfLLM-V2-8B at batch size one in CPM.cu, the inference engine that OpenBMB ships for these checkpoints. (b) Attention time of one decode step of 64 sequences over all 32 layers in the release’s kernels. The label above each bar of a fix is the share of the sparse model’s saving that it keeps.

Figure 2: Inside a blind head. One calibration prompt of InfLLM-V2-8B at 32K, ten teacherforced answer tokens. Top, the blind head L9.h0. Bottom, L26.h0, whose selector finds the needle. (a) Attention mass of the key blocks around the needle, averaged over the query heads of the group. Outlined blocks are read by the shipped selector and dotted blocks by exact mass selection. (b) At one answer token, the pooled score of every free block against its attention mass, the needle block in red, with the shipped cutoff dashed and the exact mass cutoff dotted. The blind head attends to the needle, but the pooled score leaves the needle block below the shipped cutoff, while exact mass keeps it.

Figure 5: The loss by needle depth. MK3 accuracy in five bands of the needle’s position in the prompt, at prompt lengths from 16K to 128K, for the shipped selector, full attention in the blind heads and full attention. The native range ends at 32K for InfLLM-V2-8B and at 64K for MiniCPM4.1-8B. About 40 prompts per cell, from the 200 prompts of the first seed at each length.

Figure 3: Pooling erases the needle’s lead on every probed token of the calibration prompts, InfLLM-V2-8B at 32K, in the query head of each group with the most needle mass. The horizontal axis is the needle block’s lead over the block at the selection cutoff under exact mass. The vertical axis is its lead under the pooled score. Both axes are in nats, the units of the natural logarithm (Cover & Thomas, 2006), so that each sign reproduces whether that selection keeps the needle. Where the selector finds the needle, the two leads move together. In the blind heads, the pooled lead stays near zero whatever the exact lead, and a quarter to more than half of the tokens fall in the shaded window of Proposition 1, kept by exact mass and lost by pooling.

Figure 6: How many heads carry the loss. The share of the gap between the shipped selector and full attention in every head that full attention in the top heads by fix gain closes on calibration prompts, at each step of the threshold sweep. The dashed line is the share ρ = 0.9, and the marked point is the count the rule keeps.

Figure 8: The deficit grows with the length (MK3 at the shipped budget, 200 prompts per point, 100 at 96K and 128K). The 16K, 24K and 48K points are draws of the same generator seed as the first seed at 32K and 64K, and the flagged heads are those calibrated at 32K. The shaded ranges lie beyond each model’s native range.

Table 3: What each fix gains and costs on InfLLM-V2-8B at 32K. MK3 and common word extraction (CWE) as mean over five seeds. PopQA, Natural Questions (NQ) and HotpotQA are HELMET’s retrieval-augmented question answering at its default size, 600 examples each from 100 questions for PopQA and NQ and from 200 for HotpotQA, every arm on H100. Bytes are read per cached token and decode step beyond the blocks every sparse method reads, as in Table 5, at 32K for the larger budget, whose extra blocks are a fixed count per step. The two rows marked 16 CWE heads run the scorer in the 16 heads calibrated on common word extraction’s own prompts.

Table 5: Against published selectors on the two checkpoints that Fu et al. (2026) evaluate, MK3 and the mean of RULER’s 12 tasks at the shipped budget. Quest scores a block by the bound from the per-channel extremes of its keys, Double Sparsity and Loki by the group’s attention on 16 label channels and on 32 principal directions chosen from each prompt’s own keys, all three in every head at the decode and question tokens, and SnapKV (Li et al., 2024) selects at decode the blocks that the last 32 prompt tokens attend to most. “Loki, flagged heads” acts at every token of the flagged heads at the scorer’s bytes. Bytes per cached token is what a method reads per cached token and decode step beyond the blocks every sparse method reads, and the whole cache for Dense.

Table 2: Multi-key retrieval (MK3) on the five seeds held out from every design choice, mean over five seeds. The first seed guided the design choices. “Full Attention, Flagged Heads” gives the flagged heads full attention at every token. “Decode”, “+ Question” and “Every Token” are the 4-bit scorer in the flagged heads at the decode tokens, also at the question tokens and at every token.

Table 7: OpenAI MRCR on the SeerAttention-R gates, by its official metric on all 593 prompts of its bins from 8K to 32K. The flagged heads are those of Table 6, chosen on synthetic multi-key prompts. “Random” is the mean over three random sets of as many heads, none of them flagged.

Table 1: Where the multi-key loss is made. Each row applies Equation 3 at the tokens and heads its label names and keeps the shipped selector elsewhere. Dense rows read every block without a selector. The mean over the five seeds held out from every design choice, 200 prompts each. In all tables, bold is the best number and underlined the second best, full attention excluded.

Table 4: Choosing a fix for an unknown workload on InfLLM-V2-8B at 32K. The fixes of Table 3 on 17 task types of the first seed, the 12 RULER tasks, HELMET’s PopQA, Natural Questions, HotpotQA and JSON key-value retrieval, and LongFuncEval. “Worst Change” is the largest loss against the shipped selector on any one task, with that task, and “Mean Change” averages the 17 tasks. “Beats Shipped” is the share of 10,000 random mixtures of the tasks in which the fix scores above the shipped selector, with weights drawn uniformly over the tasks and, after the slash, over the three benchmarks and then their tasks.

Table 6: The rule on other selector designs. The flagged heads are those above the threshold that closes ρ = 0.9 of the gap on calibration prompts, key-value heads for the block selectors and query heads for MoBA. “Full Attention” and “4-bit Scorer” are the two fixes in the flagged heads. The scorer acts at each release’s budget, at the decode tokens on Dash-8B and at every token on MoBA. “Echo” and “Random” give full attention to as many heads by RazorAttention’s echo score and at random. ‡NSA-8B ships no dense path, so its dense column selects every block.

Table 10: What the calibration source and the score decide on InfLLM-V2-8B. The heads that the forfeited attention flags from each source and the three best heads by each score, with MK3 at 32K for the scorer at every token of those heads. When no head is flagged, the scorer is the shipped selector.

Table 9: Three versions of the fix gain. The count the rule keeps, the first step of the √ 2 sweep that closes 90 percent of the gap on calibration prompts, for the first-order, complete and integrated versions of the fix gain, the last of them Equation 5.
Table 11: A scan without the probe. The gain in MK3 at 32K when one key-value head of InfLLMV2-8B gets full attention and the other 63 keep the shipped selector.

Table 16: The calibration per checkpoint on one H100, over its 200 calibration prompts. The sweep step is the median over the steps that were run. “Gap Recovered” is the share of the logprobability gap between the shipped selector and full attention that the integrated gains of all units sum to.
Table 15: Share and step. The count the integrated rule keeps at each share with the step √ 2 and at each step with the share 0.9. MoBA’s sweep is not monotone in the count.

Table 19: Real data. LongFuncEval (Kate et al., 2025), LongCodeU (Li et al., 2025), RepoQA (Liu et al., 2024a), OpenAI MRCR (OpenAI, 2025) and OOLONG (Bertsch et al., 2025), each with its own data, prompts and metric. The scorer acts at every token of the three flagged heads.

Table 8: Selector settings of the lineage. The four checkpoints share the MiniCPM4-8B backbone, 32 layers of 32 query heads and 2 key-value heads of dimension 128. The selector scores keys mean-pooled over windows of 32 at a stride of 16, maps the window scores onto blocks of 64 tokens and always reads the initial block, a local window and the query’s own block. Tokens below the last column’s position attend densely.

Table 12: The rule on the lineage. The heads that the integrated fix gain ranks first on sixty calibration prompts, the count at the first step of its sweep that closes 90 percent of the gap on the 200 calibration prompts and the share of the gap closed there.

Table 13: Proposition 1 on the probed tokens of InfLLM-V2-8B at 32K. “Sparse Recall” is the share of probed tokens on which the shipped selector keeps the needle block. In each head’s query head with the most needle mass, “Needle Key” is the median margin of the needle key over the other keys of its block and “Rest of Block” the median of those other keys over the head’s median window, in nats, and “Exact Keeps” and “Pooled Loses” are the shares of tokens on which exact block mass keeps the needle block and the pooled score loses it. The last two columns give how often the three query heads with the most needle mass rank the needle block among their own top free blocks.

Table 14: Precision against resolution on InfLLM-V2-8B at 32K. Left, Proposition 2 against the probe on the five heads of Table 13. Predicted noise is √ D of the optimal uniform quantizer of a unit Gaussian, measured noise is the standard deviation of the logit error over that of the exact logits, and recall is the needle recall of the per-head criterion on the quantized keys minus that of exact mass. Right, keys averaged over windows of w tokens. MK3 is the criterion at the decode tokens of the flagged heads on each kind of key.

Table 20: Latency beside Figure 7, InfLLM-V2-8B on one H100. Left, the time per output token at batch size one in CPM.cu, to which the scorer is not ported. Right, the attention time of one prefill over all 32 layers in the release’s kernels, with the scorer at every prompt token.
Table 17: Where fixing the selector stops. MK3 on the first seed. Exact mass selects at every token and keeps the shipped budget. Where it falls short of full attention, the budget binds.
Table 18: Aggregation tasks on MiniCPM4.1-8B at 64K. RULER’s variable tracking and common word extraction on the first seed. Each fix acts in the three flagged heads or in their layers.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and repairs block selection in sparse attention for long-context LLMs; directly relevant to efficient attention and long-context models.
papers.title: Lost in a Few Heads: Diagnosing and Repairing Block Selection in Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: A small number of blind attention heads cause most sparse-attention retrieval failures, and selectively repairing them largely restores full-attention accuracy at much of sparse serving’s speed benefit.

papers.abstract: We present WM-Quant, to our knowledge, the first post-training quantization (PTQ) framework designed specifically for JEPA-style world models. Although world models typically feature relatively few parameters, action planning algorithms often require thousands of inferences, which can quickly become computationally expensive. PTQ is a natural way to reduce this cost. However, we show that in world models using autoregressive model predictive control (MPC) rollouts, quantization error can compound with each predictor step, resulting in action rankings from the quantized model becoming near-random. WM-Quant addresses this with three components that build on existing PTQ methods: early-encoder precision, control-path preservation, and rollout-aware scaling. Early-encoder precision protects accurate latent state and goal information to mitigate long-term error propagation. Control-path preservation allows the world model predictor to distinguish between fine-grained actions, significantly improving action rankings and execution. Rollout-aware scaling jointly calibrates encoder and per-step predictor activation ranges with respect to an entire rollout rather than a single prediction, reducing the cumulative rollout error. Across multiple world models, environments, and PTQ methods, WM-Quant substantially improves planning success at low bit-widths, approaching full-precision performance at W4A4.
authors: William Hammer, Andrew Heuer, Nikhil Krishna, Matthew Grenier, Ramtin Zand
bullets: Quantization errors can compound across autoregressive rollouts, making action rankings nearly random.
The framework combines early-encoder precision, control-path preservation, and rollout-aware scaling.
Calibration accounts for entire rollouts and jointly handles encoder and per-step predictor activations.
Across multiple models, environments, and PTQ methods, WM-Quant substantially improves low-bit planning success.
At W4A4, performance approaches that of full-precision models.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our proposed world model quantization framework. We preserve action information to improve candidate action ranking and the first three encoder blocks to limit early encoder error in the predictor. We also calibrate per-iteration scales with respect to an entire rollout, rather than a single prediction. These additions work together to limit error propagation and increase the rate at which models reach the goal state.

Figure 5. Activation distributions and clipping ranges across rollout steps (LeWM, PushT, W4A4) entering one quantized MLP predictor layer. Bars show the clipping range used by the activation quantizer: min/max calibration for the base method, and the range learned by rollout-aware scaling for WM-Quant.

Figure 3. Latent error over a planning rollout on LeWM PushT (W4A4), relative to the full-precision model. Step 0 is the encoded initial state; steps 1–5 are successive predictor outputs. Lines show the median over start states and shaded regions the interquartile range. The rate of error propagation with WM-Quant is substantially slower than without it.

Figure 4. Agreement between the quantized and full-precision rankings of 64 CEM candidate action sequences on LeWM PushT (W3A3), median over 16 start states; bars show the interquartile range. Dashed line: chance level; dotted line: identical to FP. Top-8 overlap is displayed.
Figure 1. Planning latency vs. planning success on LeWM (W4A4), averaged over 3 seeds. WM-Quant approaches floating point results on both TwoRoom and PushT datasets with little impact on latency.
Table 3. Planning success (%) on DINO-WM Wall at each MPC iteration. ∆ is +WM-Quant minus the base method.

papers.selection_reason: Post-training quantization for JEPA-style world models with rollout-aware calibration; relevant to efficient AI and interactive world models.
papers.title: WM-Quant: Rollout-Aware Post-Training Quantization for JEPA-Style World Models
papers.tldr: WM-Quant enables low-bit post-training quantization of JEPA-style world models while preserving action rankings and planning performance across long MPC rollouts.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) decode by iteratively denoising a full canvas of tokens, so every forward pass runs a per-token sampling and stopping pipeline over the entire canvas-by-vocabulary logits tensor. We profile single-user decoding of a 26B-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts model on a bandwidth-bound edge accelerator (NVIDIA GB10) and report a result that is easy to miss: after weight quantisation, this logits pipeline, not the expert GEMMs, is the single largest consumer of decode time. Unlike autoregressive decoding, where sampling touches one position's logits per committed token, diffusion decoding processes S times as many logit entries per output token, where S is the number of denoising steps. We show this pipeline is largely redundant or fusable and remove it in two lossless tiers: a bit-exact tier whose output is byte-identical to the reference decoder, and an accuracy-parity tier using a fused single-pass entropy kernel and Gumbel-max sampling. Combined with a W4A16 expert kernel, the full stack reaches 2.4-2.7 times end-to-end speedup over bf16 at unchanged benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH, on a single 273 GB/s device. We confirm the finding on a second, independently built diffusion MoE (LLaDA2.0-mini: pipeline 28.8% of decode, fused W4A16 3.3 times at accuracy parity) and show it disappears on a dense diffusion model (3.6%). The cost is specific to MoE diffusion, where quantisation makes the backbone cheap. Code and quantised weights are released.
bullets: Profiling a 26B MoE diffusion model on an NVIDIA GB10 shows full-canvas logits processing dominates decode time after weight quantisation.
The pipeline processes logits across all tokens at every denoising step, creating substantially more sampling work than autoregressive decoding.
Two lossless optimization tiers remove redundant or fusable work: a bit-exact decoder and an accuracy-parity fused entropy kernel with Gumbel-max sampling.
Combined with a W4A16 expert kernel, the stack achieves 2.4–2.7× end-to-end speedup over bf16 with unchanged benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH.
The bottleneck is specific to MoE diffusion: it is also observed in LLaDA2.0-mini but largely disappears for dense diffusion models.

figures.caption: Table 1: Decode-time breakdown of the W4A16 model (GB10, canvas 256): share of wall-clock time per bucket, mean ± std over n=20 queries per benchmark, and mean ms per forward over all 40. Buckets are disjoint. The logits/sampling pipeline (with host glue) is the largest bucket on every query.

Table 4: Logits-pipeline share of per-forward decode across three masked-diffusion LMs (GB10). It is first-order on MoE models, negligible on the dense one. Below: porting the fused W4A16 MoE kernel to LLaDA2.0-mini gives 3.3–3.4× over its bfloat16 reference at accuracy parity (n=50; ∆ within run-to-run sampling noise).

Table 3: Attribution of pipeline optimisations, GSM8K n=20, same load. Accuracy is stable (19– 20/20) throughout. The bit-exact tier’s outputs are byte-identical to the quantised reference (texts and step counts match 20/20 on GSM8K and HumanEval).

Table 2: End-to-end decode throughput on GB10, single user, reference model.generate; each cell is tok/s (speedup over the bfloat16 baseline). Quantising the experts alone gives ∼ 1.6– 1.7×; the two logits-pipeline tiers of Section 3 contribute the rest, reaching 2.4–2.7×. Accuracy is preserved at every step: on a same-session n=100 comparison, bfloat16 scores 96/89/88 and turbo scores 97/88/87 (GSM8K / HumanEval / MATH, exact-match or pass@1); the bit-exact tier is token-identical to the W4A16 decoder, and W4A16 quantisation is accuracy-neutral versus bfloat16 (96→96, 87→87 on GSM8K / MATH).

papers.selection_reason: Profiling and optimizing diffusion MoE decoding; clear efficiency contribution, though no specific subtopic matches.
papers.title: The Hidden Cost of MoE Diffusion Decoding: Profiling and Fixing the Sampler
papers.tldr: In MoE diffusion decoding, the logits sampling pipeline—not expert computation—becomes the main bottleneck after quantisation, and fused lossless optimizations substantially accelerate decoding.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models(VLMs) while preserving the target model's outputs, but its speedup diminishes under high concurrency serving as the system becomes more compute bounded as the batch size increases. This problem is pronounced for multimodal speculative decoding as the long range of the image tokens in the prompt can significantly increase the computational cost during draft token prediction. The block-diffusion drafters (e.g. DFlash, DSpark) can effectively speed up the draft model efficiency by predicting multiple draft tokens in one forward pass, but their speedup for VLMs under high concurrency is still modest (<9%). In order to understand this gap, we examine the information flow between different modalities from target model to draft model and identify the sparsity pattern of visual attention between the target and draft models: only small set of key-value heads in the draft model need direct visual feature attention in the context and only visual features from top level layers in the target model need to be attended in the context. We therefore propose VisHead-Spec, which selects a small, fixed set of key-value (KV) heads to attend to all image features from top level layers in the target model and restricts the remaining heads to text features. On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, VisHead-Spec-8 lets 8 of the drafter's 40 KV heads read the image while keeping accepted length within 0.3% of the block-diffusion draft model baseline (i.e. DSpark). At batch size 64, its throughput gain over autoregressive decoding increases to 16.0%, compared with 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, its speedup remains comparable to DSpark.
authors: Xin Guo, Arushi Rai, Xiang Zhou, Qiang Zhang, Siyu Lin, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang
bullets: High-concurrency VLM serving becomes compute-bound, while long image-token contexts make draft prediction expensive.
The method identifies sparse cross-modal information flow: only a few draft KV heads need visual features, primarily from the target model’s top layers.
VisHead-Spec-8 routes image features to 8 of 40 KV heads and restricts the rest to text features.
On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, accepted length stays within 0.3% of the DSpark baseline.
At batch size 64, throughput gain reaches 16.0% versus 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, performance remains comparable.

papers.selection_reason: Head-routed visual attention for efficient multimodal speculative decoding.
papers.title: VisHead-Spec: Head-Routed Visual Attention for Multimodal Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: VisHead-Spec accelerates multimodal speculative decoding under high concurrency by routing visual attention through only a small subset of draft-model KV heads.

papers.abstract: Multimodal models increasingly reason by synthesizing pixels, sketching maze paths within interleaved chains of thought or rolling out video solutions frame by frame. Each visual thought runs the full diffusion schedule inherited from photorealistic synthesis, so iterative denoising dominates inference cost. We study how to allocate test-time compute along two axes: when to render visual thoughts rather than thinking in text or answering directly, and how many denoising steps each thought requires. Controlled interventions that vary only how the thought is rendered uncover three regimes. Causal thoughts carry the plan and become legible early: an 8-step sketch nearly matches a 50-step render in accuracy, commits to the same plan as often as two independent full renders agree, and in video models mostly fails by stalling short of the goal, so the rollout abstains. Decorative thoughts can be omitted without loss, whereas harmful thoughts lower accuracy. Because the regime depends on both model and task, always drawing is suboptimal. Across 14 model-benchmark pairs of three interleaved reasoners, answering directly, without any thinking, wins 9 pairs, and choosing among direct, text-only, and visual tiers from ten labeled examples per pair raises mean accuracy from 60.7% (always drawing) to 65.1%. Where drawing pays, we propose sketch-and-vote, which samples 8-step sketches (a step count chosen without labels) from independent noises until one answer reaches three votes. With this one setting, sketch-and-vote beats full rendering with fewer denoising steps on an image reasoner and two video reasoners, by 8.6 points on VSP spatial planning and by 9.6 and 22.1 points on mazes.
authors: Sheng Lu, Guangpin Tao, Tong Lu, Ying Tai
bullets: Full diffusion denoising makes visual thoughts expensive, but causal plans often become clear after only 8 steps.
Visual thoughts vary by role: causal sketches help, decorative thoughts can be omitted, and harmful thoughts may reduce accuracy.
Across 14 model–benchmark pairs, direct answering was best in 9; selecting among direct, text-only, and visual modes improved mean accuracy from 60.7% to 65.1%.
The proposed sketch-and-vote method samples 8-step sketches until one answer gets three votes, outperforming full rendering on selected image and video reasoning tasks.

papers.abstract: The rise of mobile devices equipped with numerous sensors, such as LiDAR and cameras, has driven the adoption of multi-modal deep intelligence for distributed sensing tasks, such as smart cabins and driving assistance. However, the arrival time of mobile sensory data vary due to modality size and network dynamics, which can lead to delays (if waiting for slow data) or accuracy decline (if inference proceeds without waiting). Moreover, the diversity and dynamic nature of mobile systems exacerbate this challenge. In response, we present a shift to \textit{opportunistic} inference for asynchronous distributed multi-modal data, enabling inference as soon as partial data arrives. While existing methods focus on optimizing modality consistency and complementarity, known as modal affinity, they lack a \textit{computational} approach to control this affinity in open-world mobile environments. % \sysname pioneers the formulation of structured cross-modality affinity in mobile contexts using a hierarchical analysis-based normalized matrix. This approach accommodates the diversity and dynamics of modalities, generalizing across different types and numbers of inputs. Employing an multi-modal lightweight Swin Transformer (MMLST), \sysname facilitates real-time and flexible data imputation, adapting to various modalities and downstream tasks without retraining. Experiments show that \sysname significantly reduces inference latency by up to 80.4\% and enhances accuracy by up to 62.1\%, while achieving nearly a 50\% reduction in energy consumption, outperforming status quo approaches. Also, this method can enhance LLM performance to preprocess asynchronous data.
authors: Sicong Liu, Fengmin Wu, Yuan Gao, Bin Guo, Zimu Zhou, Hongkai Wen, Zhiwen Yu
bullets: Mobile sensors and network variability cause delays when systems wait for all modalities, or accuracy loss when they do not.
A hierarchical normalized matrix models cross-modality affinity across changing input types and quantities.
A lightweight Swin Transformer performs flexible real-time data imputation without retraining for different modalities and tasks.
The approach reduces inference latency by up to 80.4%, improves accuracy by up to 62.1%, and nearly halves energy consumption.
It can also improve LLM processing of asynchronous data.

papers.abstract: Despite recent advances, vision-language models (VLMs) still struggle with fine-grained visual understanding, often failing to effectively utilize critical evidence already encoded in their visual representations. Existing approaches address this limitation through repeated visual processing or explicit reasoning, introducing substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we propose ReAccess, a lightweight framework that preserves and reuses question-relevant visual evidence through compact associative memory. Constructed during a single visual prefill, the memory supports progressive evidence retrieval that steers both attention queries and hidden representations, enabling effective visual grounding without repeated image encoding or explicit reasoning traces. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both general visual understanding and fine-grained perception, while achieving substantially faster inference than existing reasoning-intensive approaches, demonstrating a promising path to efficient multimodal reasoning.
bullets: Addresses VLMs’ difficulty in exploiting critical evidence already present in visual representations.
Builds a compact associative memory during a single visual prefill, avoiding repeated image encoding.
Progressively retrieves evidence to guide attention queries and hidden representations without explicit reasoning traces.
Experiments report consistent gains in general visual understanding and fine-grained perception.
Achieves faster inference than reasoning-intensive approaches, though specific benchmarks and quantitative results are not given.

papers.abstract: Training with MXFP4, a 4-bit microscaling format, is non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different results across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors. These differences complicate debugging and training audits and can cause training and inference engines to disagree. We present CertiSum to make MXFP4 training bitwise invariant across runs, parallelism layouts, and GPU vendors. Its key insight is that native FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is often already exact for every summation order. CertiSum collects statistics during quantization to certify native matrix multiplication results, recomputes uncertified outputs exactly, and uses exact kernels directly where certification rarely succeeds. CertiSum keeps quantization blocks unchanged across layouts and merges partial sums without rounding, including in attention and weight-gradient computation. In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, CertiSum preserves training states bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across changes in data, tensor, and context parallelism on MI350X. Across three 8B--14B models on FineWeb-Edu using MI350X, it adds 11.8--60.5% to training-step latency relative to its non-exact MXFP4 counterpart at the larger evaluated input shapes, with speedups of up to $1.24\times$ over BF16 and $1.70\times$ over deterministic BF16.
authors: Steve Rhyner, Yubo Gao, Stefan de Lasa, Sankeerth Durvasula, Nandita Vijaykumar
bullets: Addresses MXFP4 nondeterminism, which complicates debugging, audits, and consistency between training and inference.
Collects quantization statistics to certify exact native matrix-multiplication results and applies exact kernels to uncertified or difficult cases.
Preserves quantization blocks and merges partial sums without rounding across matrix multiplication, attention, and weight-gradient computations.
In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, training states matched bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across multiple parallelism layouts.
Adds 11.8–60.5% training-step latency over non-exact MXFP4, while achieving up to 1.24× speedup over BF16 and 1.70× over deterministic BF16.

papers.abstract: Weight Factorization (WF) methods aim to reduce a model's latency, memory, or both. These typically decompose a pretrained model into two or more factors that approximate the original model weights with fewer parameters and floating point operations (FLOPs). However, translating fewer FLOPs into reduced latency is challenging for WF methods in practice due to overhead introduced by replacing a single large weight matrix with multiple smaller ones. To address this, we propose Balanced Twin Weight Factorization (BTWF), which uses the unique structure of factorized models to simultaneously lower latency and increase learning capacity. Specifically, BTWF operates in the shared basis WF setting, where two or more layers are decomposed into a shared basis matrix and a layer-specific mixing matrix. If these shared layers have the same input (i.e., are twins), then we need only perform this shared forward pass once, reducing inference time. However, twin layers are often of varying sizes, and methods from prior work tend to favor the larger layer. In contrast, our approach boosts performance by combining Factor Component Balancing (FCB), which ensures every shared member is well represented in the selected factors, with Block Contribution Balancing (BCB), which considers downstream model effects. Further, we also show that an overparameterized BTWF, where some layer's factors result in higher FLOPs than the original during training, can boost task performance without additional resources at test time. Experiments on six models over nine benchmarks show BTWF obtains a 2-6% gain over the state-of-the-art without expensive finetuning (1-3.5% gain with it) at comparable computational costs.
authors: Bryan A. Plummer, Shan Lu, Keval Doshi, Noranart Vesdapunt, Wei Wang, Jim Thomas, Kah Kuen Fu
bullets: Addresses the gap between reduced FLOPs and real-world latency caused by replacing one large matrix with multiple smaller matrices.
Exploits twin layers with the same input to compute their shared forward pass only once.
Combines Factor Component Balancing and Block Contribution Balancing to represent layers more evenly and account for downstream effects.
Uses overparameterized factors during training to improve task performance without increasing test-time resources.
Across six models and nine benchmarks, achieves 2–6% gains without expensive finetuning and 1–3.5% gains with it at comparable computational cost.

papers.abstract: Streaming video generation must sustain quality beyond the training horizon while handling self-generated history and growing cache costs. To address these challenges, we present MovieRoll, a base-to-distilled framework that connects streaming fine-tuning, long-rollout distillation, and long-horizon inference. We first establish a robust multi-step base through Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF), which jointly denoises chunks at progressive noise levels with bidirectional attention within each window and causal access to preceding history. To retain historical context efficiently, hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) exploits layer-wise attention patterns, retaining full history in shallow layers and sink--recent history in deeper layers. This reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality. Building on this base, cumulative long tuning with distribution matching distillation (CuLT-DMD) holds parameters fixed throughout each long self-rollout and averages local gradients before updating. Each update therefore combines supervision across temporal positions while retaining only one local computation graph, enabling efficient long-rollout training of a few-step generator. To extend generation beyond the training horizon, KV recomputation bounds context for both models, while guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) reduces guidance toward the clean endpoint to stabilize MovieRoll-Base. Complementing these modeling advances, FBCA attention and PS-VAE decoding support efficient training and streaming output. On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30s after training on videos of up to 15s, and MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among the compared methods across single- and multi-event evaluations up to 60s, combining sustained naturalness with active motion.
authors: Yunyang Ge, Weijie Kong, Ryan Xu, Yue Wu, Qi Tian, Jiangfeng Xiong, Bin Lin, Mingzhe Zheng, Shenghai Yuan, Zheyuan Liu, Jianwei Zhang, Li Yuan
bullets: Targets quality degradation beyond the training horizon, self-generated history, and increasing KV-cache costs.
WinTF builds a multi-step base using window-wise denoising with local bidirectional attention and causal access to prior history.
HieraKV reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality by adapting retained history across layers.
CuLT-DMD enables efficient long-rollout distillation by aggregating gradients across temporal positions while keeping one local computation graph.
On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30 seconds, while MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among compared methods through 60 seconds.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of MovieRoll. Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF) trains MovieRoll-Base through parallel window supervision conditioned on clean history and event prompts. After ODE initialization, Cumulative Long Tuning with Distribution Matching Distillation (CuLT-DMD) trains a few-step generator by averaging local gradients across long self-rollouts. Both models jointly denoise a rolling window, use hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) to retain history across layers, and rebuild the cache at a history threshold or prompt switch. Classifier-free guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) gradually reduces guidance during base-model denoising.

Figure 3 WinTF learns rolling generation through parallel supervision of windows with progressive noise levels. Phase offsets expose the model to both short prefill windows and full decoding windows. Within each window, later chunks receive higher noise levels. The attention mask combines bidirectional interactions within a noisy window with access to clean preceding history, while isolating noisy windows from one another. This allows multiple windows to be trained in parallel, each conditioned on its own event prompt and preceding clean history.

Figure 5 CuLT-DMD combines supervision across a long rollout in each generator update. The top panel shows local distillation supervision from teacher and critic predictions. LongLive-style training updates the generator from individual windows while carrying detached history forward. CuLT-DMD instead keeps parameters fixed throughout the rollout and averages the local gradients before updating. This incorporates supervision from multiple temporal positions while retaining one local computation graph at a time.

Figure 6 AnnealCFG reduces the late-denoising extrapolation produced by constant guidance throughout 30s generation. Across prefill and early, middle, and late decoding, the left plots show the additional latent-update magnitude induced by guidance. The right plots show its share in the final 20% of denoising steps. Annealing lowers both the late-step peaks and their contribution to the total update. Results aggregate 32 paired prompts, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals shown by bands and whiskers.

Figure 7 KV recomputation refreshes historical context for generation beyond the training horizon. Fullhistory caching expands the context as video length grows, while sliding-window caching retains dependencies on evicted chunks. At the history threshold, recomputation selects sink, intermediate, and recent chunks and causally re-encodes them into a fresh cache. This bounds the retained context and removes cached dependencies on discarded chunks before generation continues.

Figure 8 Flash Block-wise Causal Attention (FBCA) implements block-causal attention with efficient FlashAttention kernels. Each query block gathers its visible prefix, historical states, and current states into an independent attention sequence. KV unfolding and grouping organize these sequences within a per-call packing budget, and variable-length FlashAttention processes them before restoring the original block order. This preserves the required attention pattern while controlling the size of each packed buffer.

Figure 1 MovieRoll generates a minute-long video with continuous subject identity across six events. The sequence shows the same woman performing successive actions in one studio setting, with a new prompt every 10s. Each frame represents one event, and the text below summarizes its prompt.

Figure 4 Layer-dependent attention patterns motivate hierarchical history retention. In the WinTF-trained model, shallow layers distribute attention broadly across historical chunks, while deeper layers place relatively more attention on the sink and most recent chunks. The heatmap and lower entropy and coverage plots show this shift with depth. HieraKV follows these patterns by retaining full historical context in shallow layers and restricting deeper layers to the sink and most recent chunks.

Figure 9 The Parallel Streaming Variational Autoencoder (PS-VAE) supports continuous video decoding through temporal caching and spatial parallelism. The upper panel shows how cached decoder states carry temporal context across arriving latent chunks, allowing each chunk to be decoded as it becomes available. The lower panel distributes high-resolution decoding across GPUs through row partitioning and boundary exchange. Together, these designs support streaming output and reduce per-GPU decoding cost.

Figure 10 Qualitative comparison of 10s single-event video generation. Under the same prompt of a mermaid combing her hair on a seaside rock, MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled retain recognizable subjects and consistent surroundings as poses and waves change. Rows compare methods evaluated under the same prompt, and columns show successive temporal intervals within each 241-frame video.

Figure 11 Qualitative comparison of 30s single-event video generation. MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled preserve the facial features, clothing, and surroundings of a man eating at a bar as the action continues. Rows compare methods under the same prompt, and columns follow the 721-frame sequence, showing how subject and background consistency evolve during generation.

Figure 17 Memory and latency comparison across full-history and sink--recent attention allocations. The left plot shows slower cache-memory growth when fewer layers retain full history. At 18 cached chunks, the default HieraKV allocation of 6 global and 48 local layers reduces memory from 48.7 to 10.8 GiB and peak denoising-step latency from 33.8 to 15.8s relative to all-global attention. Measurements use MovieRoll-Base with CFG on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. Each timed denoising step includes both conditional and unconditional DiT evaluations. Timing excludes KV recomputation and VAE encoding/decoding.

Figure 16 Ablation of long-horizon extrapolation strategies. All three strategies use the same Stage 1 MovieRollBase checkpoint to extend generation from 10s training clips to 30s videos. Full-history and sliding-window caching produce increasingly washed-out backgrounds, whereas KV recomputation preserves clearer subject and street details through the end of the sequence.

Figure 12 Qualitative comparison of 60s single-event video generation. MovieRoll-Distilled preserves the diver and underwater environment with relatively stable colors as generation continues. Rows compare methods under the same diver-and-wreck prompt, and columns follow successive 10s intervals of the 1441-frame videos.

Figure 26 Examples of multi-event video generation with sequential prompts. The upper examples show threeevent, 30s videos from MovieRoll-Base, and the lower examples show six-event, 60s videos from MovieRoll-Distilled. Prompts change every 10s, with one frame representing each event. Both models retain recurring characters and settings as new interactions develop, such as a cat reacting to a robotic vacuum and a keeper responding to a seagull.

Figure 13 Qualitative comparison of 30s multi-event video generation. The sequence progresses from sketching a flower to observing a frog and raising a camera, with a prompt change every 10s. MovieRoll-Distilled depicts these action changes while retaining the botanist and rainforest setting. Each row shows one method, and each pair of columns corresponds to one event.

Figure 14 Qualitative comparison of 60s multi-event video generation. The sequence develops from paddling to successive interactions with an otter, including surfacing beside the kayak, handling a rock, and approaching the hull. MovieRoll-Distilled depicts this event progression while maintaining a consistent lake setting. Rows compare methods under the same six sequential prompts, and each column represents one 10s event.

Figure 27 Potential extensions of rolling-window video pretraining. (a) Smaller chunks allow finer noise progression and temporal advances at a fixed frame budget, while loss weighting or regularization could balance learning across noise levels. (b) Total-duration conditioning could guide overall pacing, while duration triggers locate active windows and shot transitions. Together with multi-shot training, these conditions could support coordinated shot sequences under one prompt.

Figure 24 Examples of 60s single-event videos generated by MovieRoll-Distilled. This first set of six examples includes miniature ships, an origami dragon, and underwater performances. MovieRoll-Distilled preserves subject appearance as waves, steam, and gestures evolve. Each two-row group follows one 1441-frame video from left to right and then top to bottom, with frame indices overlaid and its prompt below.

Figure 18 Ablation of HieraKV attention allocations. The comparison varies the allocation of 54 transformer blocks between full-history and sink–recent attention. With the default HieraKV allocation of 6 global and 48 local blocks, the rider and horse remain recognizable throughout the sequence. All-global attention progressively crops the subje ts, while all-local attention shifts toward a close rear view.

Figure 22 User preference comparison for multi-event video generation. MovieRoll-Distilled wins a majority of judgments against every evaluated baseline, with win rates from 62.3% to 81.9%. Each bar reports win, tie, and loss rates from the MovieRoll-Distilled perspective under the same prompt sequences, pooling judgments across 30s three-event and 60s six-event videos with ties included in the denominator.

Table 8 Shared architecture and history-cache configuration of the MovieRoll models. Both variants use an 8.3-billion-parameter backbone with text conditioning, a causal video VAE, and a five-chunk active window. The first six transformer blocks retain full history, while the remaining 48 retain the sink and most recent chunks, preserving broad historical context through a small subset of layers.

Table 2 Comparison of video decoding speed, memory use, and reconstruction quality. Single-GPU PSVAE outperforms the tested tiling methods in runtime and reconstruction PSNR. Spatial parallelism further reduces decoding time and per-GPU memory. With eight GPUs, PS-VAE achieves a 3.97× decoding speedup over its singleGPU version while preserving high numerical agreement. Measurements decode 1441 frames at 480× 864 on NVIDIA H20 GPUs in FP16.

Table 9 Inference settings of MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled. Distillation reduces sampling from 50 steps to 5 while preserving the shared rolling-generation pipeline. MovieRoll-Base uses guidance annealed from 4 to 1, whereas MovieRoll-Distilled operates without CFG. Both use the same chunk and window sizes and rebuild their KV caches at the same history threshold. Denoising passes are counted per output chunk, with the conditional and unconditional CFG branches contributing separately to the reported count.

Table 1 Efficiency comparison of block-causal attention implementations. The comparison evaluates fullhistory attention with three or five windows on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. FBCA achieves the lowest forward and backward runtimes across fixed and varying input shapes, with preparation taking less than 0.1s when shapes vary. In multiple-shape tests, it also reduces peak memory relative to FlexAttention, supporting efficient training across inputs with different spatial resolutions.

Table 10 Training stages and hyperparameters of MovieRoll. The two base-model stages introduce single-event and multi-event streaming generation. ODE initialization then transfers the base model to a few-step student, and CuLT-DMD trains it on self-generated rollouts. The columns summarize the data and optimization settings supporting this progression. The two distillation phases are denoted by P1 and P2, while G and F identify the generator and fake-score critic in the optimization settings for each phase.

Table 6 Single-GPU inference efficiency for 60s video generation. The table compares denoising and endto-end costs across methods at the listed resolutions for 1441-frame videos on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. Switching from FlashAttention-3 to SageAttention increases MovieRoll-Distilled end-to-end throughput from 1.52 to 2.04 FPS. Single-GPU throughput remains below the 24 FPS playback rate required for real-time generation.

Table 5 Quantitative ablations of training and inference designs. WinTF outperforms chunk-wise formulations, while the selected HieraKV allocation, KV recomputation, long-rollout CuLT-DMD, and AnnealCFG schedule achieve the highest total scores within their respective comparisons. Shaded rows identify these choices. Autoregressive formulations are evaluated at 241 and 721 frames, and the remaining comparisons use 721 frames. Higher ratings indicate better quality and less drift.

Table 14 Comparison ofGPT-5.2 andGemini-2.5-Proas video evaluators. Both evaluate the same 30s single-event videos and rank MovieRoll-Distilled first and MovieRoll-Base second. Method rankings agree closely, with Spearman correlation ρ = 0.930. We use Gemini-2.5-Pro because it provides greater score separation between methods, as shown by the statistical measures in the lower section.

Table 11 Rollout settings for the two CuLT-DMD training phases. Phase 1 uses single-event, 241-frame rollouts lasting 10s. Phase 2 extends training to two-event, 721-frame rollouts lasting 30s. Both phases average local gradients across each rollout, allowing one update to incorporate supervision from multiple temporal positions. Bounded score clips keep distillation supervision local as the generated sequence grows.

Table 15 Distribution of user-study judgments across baselines and video durations. The study collects 2616 preference judgments across single-event and multi-event comparisons. Each cell counts individual judgments for MovieRoll-Distilled versus the listed baseline at a given duration. Judgments are pooled across durations to calculate win, tie, and loss rates for each baseline, separately for single-event and multi-event generation. Each judgment contributes one vote, including ties.

Table 13 Conversion of HeliosBench quality and drift metrics to a common rating scale. The listed intervals map raw metric values to ratings from 1 to 10 for weighted aggregation. Higher quality scores and lower drift scores receive higher ratings, so higher converted ratings consistently indicate better performance.

Table 7 Inference scaling across GPU counts and attention backends. Increasing the GPU count improves MovieRoll-Distilled throughput with both backends, and SageAttention is faster at every tested count. On eight NVIDIA H20 GPUs, the best setting generates a 60s video in 152.2s, reaching 9.47 FPS. Real-time generation at 24 FPS remains a limitation even with eight GPUs. Videos contain 1441 frames at 480× 864.

Table 12 HeliosBench metrics, evaluators, and aggregation weights. Five full-video metrics cover aesthetics, dynamics, motion smoothness, semantic alignment, and naturalness. Four drift metrics measure changes between the beginning and end of a video. The aggregation weights give greater emphasis to semantic alignment and naturalness while retaining contributions from all four metrics of temporal drift.

papers.selection_reason: Streaming video generation with KV-cache compression and distillation.
papers.title: MovieRoll: A Systematic Framework for Rolling Out Long-Form Videos
papers.tldr: MovieRoll is a framework for generating long-form videos by combining streaming fine-tuning, compressed context caching, long-rollout distillation, and stabilized long-horizon inference.

papers.abstract: Text-based model collaboration requires a large model to generate intermediate responses before a smaller model can use its guidance, adding large-model decoding cost to inference. We introduce POND (Prefill-Only, No-Decode), a method that uses a frozen large sender for prefill and a small receiver for all autoregressive decoding. A trainable bridge maps the sender's hidden states to additional attention keys and values, allowing the receiver to use these representations throughout generation. POND also supports periodic review, in which the sender processes the receiver's partial response and updates its guidance through additional prefill passes while preserving the receiver's existing KV cache. Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, POND improves receiver performance with senders from different model families. In particular, GLM-5.3 provides gains comparable to those of Qwen3.8-Max when paired with a Qwen receiver, supporting the effectiveness of representation transfer between independently trained model families. POND further demonstrates its ability to generalize across domains. When trained on math and coding tasks, it transfers directly to general knowledge tasks without additional domain-specific training. These results demonstrate that large frontier model prefill representations can improve small-model generation without requiring large-model autoregressive decoding.
authors: Qichao Wang, Tingyu Qu, Pengcheng Wu, Yiran Zhong, Feida Zhu, Zhiqi Shen, Peilin Zhao, Steven Hoi
bullets: Addresses the inference overhead of generating textual guidance with a large model before small-model generation.
Uses a trainable bridge to convert frozen sender hidden states into attention keys and values for the receiver.
Supports periodic review, where the sender updates guidance from the receiver’s partial output while preserving the receiver’s KV cache.
Improves reasoning and coding performance across independently trained model families, with gains comparable to a stronger sender pairing.
Transfers from math and coding training to general-knowledge tasks without domain-specific retraining.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of POND. A frozen sender prefills the input, and a trainable bridge compresses its last layer hidden states into a shared latent message, which layer-specific adapters project into KV entries for the receiver. The receiver, fine-tuned jointly with the bridge, generates the full response. At review boundaries, the sender prefills the newly generated segment and the resulting entries are appended to the latent memory, leaving the receiver’s KV cache untouched.

Figure 2: Accuracy gains and sender compute savings. Left: Math and code scores for the receiver (Qwen3.5-4B), the receiver with POND, and the sender (GLM-5.3); labels give the gain in points. Center: Estimated sender FLOPs for GLM-5.3 (40B active) with 1k input and 10k output tokens. Prefill-only guidance reduces sender compute from 880 to 80 TFLOPs. Right: Fraction of sender compute saved, T/(L + T ), as a function of output length T with L = 1k. Estimates use 2Pactive FLOPs per token and exclude attention, routing, communication, and bridge or receiver inference. The panels are not a matched end-to-end comparison of accuracy and cost.

Table 1: Math and code results. Senders are frozen and prefill-only. POND uses one latent transfer; +Review adds periodic prefill updates. Acc.: accuracy/pass@1 (%, higher is better); Token: total decoded receiver tokens, including both thinking and final-response tokens (thousands per 100 runs, lower is better); Speed: end-to-end latency (s/run, lower is better). Bold marks the better of POND and +Review for each metric, including ties. Improve compares the bold value with the receiver alone: accuracy gain in percentage points, or relative reduction in tokens/latency; an upward latency arrow indicates an increase. Avg averages the five tasks.

Table 2: Knowledge benchmark results. Configurations, metrics, and metric-wise bolding follow Table 1. Improve reports accuracy gains (percentage points) or relative token/latency reductions (%) against the receiver; upward latency arrows denote increases. Avg averages all four tasks. Differences and reductions are computed before rounding.
Table 3: Training and review controls. Suite-average accuracy. Receiver-only training uses math/code data; POND uses Qwen3.8-Max as the sender.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes POND, a 'prefill-only, no-decode' method using a latent bridge to transfer representations from large to small models, improving efficiency and model collaboration.
papers.title: Latent Bridge: Asking for Help Without Words
papers.tldr: POND lets a small model benefit from a large model’s hidden representations without paying the cost of large-model autoregressive decoding.

papers.abstract: Large language models read Thai through subword tokens, without a word segmenter. Yet Thai treebanks, speech metrics and morphological resources are built on words, often at several granularities, and word boundaries resolve ambiguities that subword tokens leave open. LATTE (Lattice ATTentive Encoding) reads a text at several granularities at once, through a lattice of dictionary words, but it is a large GPU model. We distil it into LATTE-WordSeg-Lite, a CPU segmenter of 1.17M parameters that keeps the lattice as features. It outputs compounds, words and morphemes in one pass, and learns only from annotated data and text whose licences allow commercial use. To compare it with other tools, published Thai scores do not suffice, as they come from different files, splits and scorers. We therefore rebuild seven test sets from pinned sources and score twelve systems under one protocol. With the unit that fits each test set, LATTE-WordSeg-Lite scores above DeepCut on five sets, four of them from corpora that its teachers learnt from. Called line by line on one CPU thread, it runs 23 times as fast as DeepCut. We release the model, the benchmark scripts and all predictions.
authors: Thodsaporn Chay-intr, Kobkrit Viriyayudhakorn, Thanaruk Theeramunkong
bullets: Addresses Thai’s need for word- and morpheme-level boundaries beyond subword tokenization.
Distils the lattice-based LATTE approach into a 1.17M-parameter CPU model.
Produces compound, word, and morpheme segmentations in one pass.
Rebuilds seven test sets and evaluates 12 systems under a common scoring protocol.
Outscores DeepCut on five test sets and releases the model, scripts, and predictions.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a distilled, CPU-efficient Thai word segmentation model (LATTE-WordSeg-Lite) to support LLM tokenization, addressing efficiency and LLM infrastructure.
papers.title: LATTE-WordSeg-Lite: Multi-Granularity Thai Word Segmentation on a CPU, with a Reproducible Benchmark
papers.tldr: LATTE-WordSeg-Lite is a compact CPU Thai segmenter that predicts compounds, words, and morphemes using lattice features, with a reproducible benchmark showing strong accuracy and 23× faster inference than DeepCut.

papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly support longer contexts and serve more concurrent requests, increasing both sequence lengths and batch sizes. Both trends increase KV-cache size and memory traffic during inference. KV-cache quantization reduces these costs, with recent approaches using codebook-based vector quantization to achieve extremely low bit widths. However, hardware constraints limit codebook size, and most methods reconstruct the cache in higher-precision floating-point formats for attention, limiting the computational benefits of quantization. To address these limitations, we introduce MiSTiQ, a drop-in replacement for codebook-based vector quantizers that combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats for low-precision computation. We combine trellis quantization with beam search to encode the KV cache over large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks. To support MX computation, we derive MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX element format. These functions use the scale-conditioned marginal distribution of block-normalized Gaussian inputs. On Llama3 and Qwen3, MiSTiQ achieves lower WikiText perplexity and higher GSM8K accuracy than the evaluated baselines across several block-scale formats at approximately 1.25 effective bits per element. With NVFP4, it also achieves the highest LongBench average on both models.
authors: Ofir Gordon, Lior Dikstein, Paul Balanca, Idan Achituve, Douglas Orr, Hai Victor Habi
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and bandwidth growth from longer contexts and larger batches.
Combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats as a drop-in codebook-quantization replacement.
Uses beam search for large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks.
Introduces MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX format.
Reports lower WikiText perplexity, higher GSM8K accuracy, and the best NVFP4 LongBench average on Llama3 and Qwen3 among evaluated baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Novel KV-cache quantization combining trellis coding with microscaling formats for extreme compression in LLM inference.
papers.title: MiSTiQ: MicroScaling Trellis Quantization for Extreme KV Cache Compression
papers.tldr: MiSTiQ compresses LLM KV caches to about 1.25 bits per element while enabling low-precision computation and improving quality over evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient long video generation, but inference still incurs substantial computational costs from repeated denoising and KV cache operations. Existing acceleration methods reduce parts of this overhead, while historical KV reading and cache construction remain costly across video chunks. To address these challenges, we propose ScoutCache, a training-free framework that jointly optimizes denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction. We observe that shallow feature changes provide useful information for estimating clean latent updates, while historical KV dependence varies across Transformer layers and attention heads but remains relatively stable across video chunks. Based on these observations, we develop Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. We further introduce Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical reading budgets based on attention output perturbations, and Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to reduce cache construction costs by selecting informative spatial tokens while maintaining spatial coverage. Extensive experiments on Self-Forcing and LongLive using VBench and MovieGen demonstrate that ScoutCache achieves up to 2.28$\times$ and 1.86$\times$ speedups, respectively, while consistently improving generation quality without modifying pretrained model parameters.
authors: Hao Tan, Jinghui Qin, Xuming Hu
bullets: Targets the remaining inference bottlenecks in long-video generation: repeated denoising and KV-cache operations across video chunks.
Uses Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations.
Applies Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical KV-reading budgets across layers and attention heads.
Uses Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to select informative spatial tokens while preserving coverage.
Achieves up to 2.28× speedup on Self-Forcing and 1.86× on LongLive, with consistently improved quality and no pretrained-parameter changes.

(c) CCSC reduces cache construction costs through content and coverage guided spatial token selection.

(c-e) Effects of shallow feature projection dimension rs, staleness threshold A, and regularization scale λ/m on generation quality and speedup using Self-Forcing.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, but attention-based scores do not directly measure a token's effect on the predicted action. We define action sensitivity as the magnitude of the first-order action change when a token is replaced by its camera's mean token and estimate it for all tokens with a single backward pass. Computing it online is costly: scoring on the full (unpruned) graph needs an extra forward pass at every control step. Scoring on the pruned forward pass is cheaper but causes scoring-graph lock-in: removed tokens lose their direct paths through later layers and tend to receive lower scores, making those locations less likely to return. On replayed observations, even with a random conditioning mask, pruned-graph scoring re-selects 59% of the mask's tokens, versus 6% expected by chance; attention histories show a similar bias. POKE (Probe Offline, Keep Efficiently) computes full-graph action sensitivities offline and distills them into a student with under 0.3M parameters. At inference, the student scores the current observation without backpropagation or previous masks, and score-guided diversity selection retains the tokens. Keeping 32 of 512 visual tokens on LIBERO, POKE achieves 95.2% success on OpenVLA-OFT and 90.8% on $\pi_{0.5}$ at $1.85\times$ and $1.26\times$ speedups, outperforming attention-, diversity-, and distillation-based pruners, with larger margins on LIBERO-Plus.
authors: Jaehyuk Lee, Yeajin Lee, Suhyun Bae, Donghun Lee
bullets: Attention scores poorly reflect how visual tokens affect predicted actions, while online action-sensitivity scoring is computationally expensive and biased by prior pruning.
POKE computes full-graph action sensitivities offline and distills them into a student with fewer than 0.3M parameters.
At inference, the student scores observations without backpropagation or previous masks, and diversity selection retains informative tokens.
Keeping 32 of 512 tokens achieves 95.2% success on OpenVLA-OFT and 90.8% on π0.5, with 1.85× and 1.26× speedups on LIBERO.
The method reports larger gains on LIBERO-Plus than competing attention-, diversity-, and distillation-based pruners.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in image and video generation have enabled high-fidelity synthesis at higher resolutions and longer durations, making the quadratic cost of dense self-attention a major bottleneck as visual token sequences grow. Sparse attention seeks to preserve generation quality at lower computational cost by retaining informative query-key interactions and omitting less consequential ones, with end-to-end gains depending on the cost of constructing sparse support and the efficiency with which the system maps the resulting workload to hardware. We survey sparse attention for visual generation through a 4+1+3 analytical framework that links algorithmic design to system implementation. The framework examines how static and dynamic methods use source information and the evidence derived from it to decide which interactions to retain and at what granularity, while accounting for the roles of reuse in reducing repeated computation and correction in compensating for omitted contributions. We relate these algorithmic choices to their implementation on hardware through the framework's three system dimensions of data organization, execution, and dataflow. We summarize common evaluation metrics and discuss open challenges and research directions, providing researchers and practitioners with a reference for the joint design of sparse attention algorithms and systems.
authors: Majun Zhang, Yuan Guo, Decheng Wu, Jiayang Xu, Changhao Pan, Fan Zhuo, Xiaoda Yang, Chenyuhao Wen, Zhou Zhao
bullets: Dense self-attention becomes a major bottleneck as image and video token sequences grow.
The proposed 4+1+3 framework analyzes static and dynamic sparsity, selection granularity, reuse, and correction for omitted interactions.
It links algorithmic choices to three system dimensions: data organization, execution, and dataflow.
The survey reviews evaluation metrics, implementation considerations, open challenges, and future research directions.

papers.abstract: We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and beyond. The models lead or are competitive with strong open models of their size on agentic and coding benchmarks. On the modeling side, to strengthen reasoning, we introduce Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA), applying MoE to attention value projections, and softplus attention gating, a more flexible, theoretically motivated gate. Our 36B-A4B model uses both and nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data, with one-seventh the active parameters. We also introduce Uno, lossless diffusion adapters that speed up decoding by up to 2.2x without a separate draft model. Our release follows the LLM360 definition of open source for transparency and reproducibility: the full development history, including intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, pre-training data, training logs, and all training, evaluation, and infrastructure code, notably our production-scale xLLM framework for dense and MoE training and the RL360 reinforcement-learning stack. Beyond the data itself, we release and document in detail every pipeline that built it, the part of model development that open releases most rarely disclose. These pipelines produced roughly 10T synthetic pre-training tokens, showing that synthetic data can be a major ingredient of pre-training at scale. Four of the models share one 22T-token pre-training corpus and recipe, revealing consistent scaling behavior and enabling controlled studies of scale and sparsity. All artifacts are available at https://ifm.ai/k2/
