Rewriting derives the reference patches from the diff without a model and uses the model only for the task specification, the predicted environment, and the test commands. Environment synthesis is an agent loop that produces a container image. The two checks below it are distinct: acceptance is mechanical, whereas the trajectory judge runs a solver against an already-accepted environment and decides whether it is worth training on. Solid arrows carry artifacts and dashed arrows carry feedback: acceptance failures return to the responsible sub-agent, and judged misalignment returns to the rewrite stage. Filter thresholds, the eight scoring dimensions of the filtering judge, the checklist items, and the selection rule are given in the text.

Figure 33: How one PR chain becomes a single long episode. Each PR is attempted in its own fresh agent session against the same working tree, so state reaches the next turn two ways: through the filesystem, which accumulates, and through a compacted handoff, which does not. Per-turn context therefore stays roughly constant however long the episode runs, while cumulative token usage climbs until it crosses the budget, at which point the run stops and the partial episode is kept. The whole episode runs inside a sandbox in which the network tools are gated: dependency installs resolve against a local package mirror and git operations against a local repository mirror, so a build can still fetch what it needs while the obvious routes to the upstream change are closed. The gating is at the tool layer rather than the network layer, so the public internet remains reachable by an agent that writes its own client; we did not observe this in the trajectories we inspected. The number of turns an episode reaches is set by the budget rather than by the number of PRs the chain offers.

papers.abstract: In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users' requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. For the serial workflow, the problem is similarly decoupled into service time allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems; the optimal service time allocation is obtained via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, while the latter two sub-problems are addressed by extending the proposed algorithms to the serial scenario. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.
authors: Yuanyan Song, Kezhi Wang, Xinmian Xu, Yongmin Li
bullets: A supervisor agent decomposes user requests and dispatches subtasks to worker agents through parallel or serial workflows.
A two-level retry mechanism is used to improve execution reliability.
Energy minimization jointly optimizes agent selection and resource allocation while satisfying latency and QoS requirements.
An alternating-optimization scheme uses SCA, Lagrangian relaxation, Gale-Shapley or LLM-based selection, and KKT-based service-time allocation.
Simulations report lower energy consumption than benchmarks, while Qwen/Llama experiments show higher task execution success rates.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent self-improvement enables agents to improve through interaction and feedback. However, sequential dependencies across agents and refinement rounds can propagate errors, increase computational costs, and limit parallelism. Moreover, refining individual features or agents in isolation can overlook their dependencies and restrict collective coordination. To address these challenges, we propose ConvRSI, a framework for parallelizing multi-agent self-improvement through convolution. ConvRSI couples intra-agent convolution, which jointly refines related agent features, with inter-agent graph convolution, which aggregates messages according to the collaboration topology. Both stages operate in latent space, enabling parallel updates without repeatedly decoding and re-encoding intermediate messages. Experiments on MATH-500 show that ConvRSI achieves 5.04% performance improvement while reducing 17.27% inference cost, and 45.11% latency compared with RecursiveMAS. It also supports diverse collaboration patterns by representing their topologies as adjacency matrices. These results demonstrate the potential of convolutional co-evolution for efficient multi-agent self-improvement. Our code and datasets are provided in https://github.com/LYA2333/ConvRSI.
authors: Zheng Wang, Yuang Liu, Sachith Abeywickrama, Yangkai Ding, Tao Yu, Xinyu Zhang, Hongbo Wang, Qi Ye, Xuefeng Jin, Zhangchun Zhao
bullets: Addresses error propagation, high computation, and limited parallelism in sequential multi-agent refinement.
Uses latent-space intra-agent convolution to jointly refine related features.
Uses inter-agent graph convolution to exchange information according to collaboration topology.
Reports 5.04% higher performance, 17.27% lower inference cost, and 45.11% lower latency than RecursiveMAS on MATH-500.
Supports diverse collaboration patterns through adjacency-matrix representations.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts Multimodal Large Language Models (MoE-MLLMs) offer scalable inference through sparse expert activation, yet substantial computational redundancy remains among the activated experts. Existing expert skipping methods typically calibrate thresholds based on target skipping ratios or final-output divergence, overlooking the accumulation of skipping-induced error across layers and the varying semantic importance of individual tokens. To address that, we propose ProSE, a training-free, semantic-guided expert skipping framework that probes layer-wise reconstruction error to promote representation consistency compared with default activation. Specifically, we construct query-aware semantic masks to identify salient visual tokens and progressively calibrate modality-specific skipping thresholds for each MoE layer. By minimizing masked reconstruction error under a given budget, ProSE maintains semantic consistency after skipping and allows adaptive expert allocation under limited activation budgets. Extensive experiments on 9 benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements on average over existing expert skipping methods, particularly under aggressive skipping settings. ProSE maintains over 96\% performance on KimiVL-A3B-Inst with 83\% expert skipping and accelerates prefilling by $1.7\times$.
authors: Jiameng Li, Minye Wu, Matthew B. Blaschko
bullets: Targets computational redundancy among activated experts in MoE multimodal large language models.
Uses query-aware semantic masks to identify salient visual tokens and modality-specific thresholds for each layer.
Calibrates skipping by minimizing masked reconstruction error relative to default expert activation.
Improves over existing expert-skipping methods across 9 benchmarks, especially under aggressive skipping.
On KimiVL-A3B-Inst, retains over 96% performance with 83% expert skipping and achieves 1.7× faster prefilling.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have achieved strong performance in generation based video editing, but suffer from high inference latency due to the long token sequences formed by conditioning inputs and generated videos. Although training-free sparse attention reduces this cost, existing methods typically apply a fixed retention ratio or a single threshold shared across all tokens. In this work, we view video editing as conditional generation and identify a key insight: attention demand varies significantly both across different key sources (e.g., source videos, reference images, audio, text, and generated videos) and across queries within each source. Motivated by this, we propose QASK-Edit (Query-Adaptive Sparsity over Key Sources for Video Editing), a training-free sparse attention framework that allocates computation independently for each query and key source. Specifically, for each query, QASK-Edit considers both the attention mass and approximation risk of each block. It then evaluates candidate routing thresholds against each key source's risk budget, choosing exact computation or approximations to dynamically adjust sparsity for each query. Extensive experiments on three video editing models demonstrate that QASK-Edit achieves up to $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup over dense attention pipeline while preserving both editing quality and unedited region fidelity. Furthermore, QASK-Edit generalizes directly to Reference-to-Video generation, delivering up to $1.36\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality.
authors: Hengrui Liu, Wenbo Xu, Ziqi Sheng, Wei lu
bullets: Addresses high inference latency caused by long conditioning and video token sequences.
Training-free routing adapts computation across sources such as videos, images, audio, text, and generated content.
Balances attention mass and approximation risk to select source-specific thresholds per query.
Achieves up to 1.46× end-to-end speedup in video editing while preserving editing quality and unedited regions.
Also applies to Reference-to-Video generation, achieving up to 1.36× speedup without degrading quality.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of QASK-Edit. The process begins with the generation of summaries for blocks, sub-blocks, and second-level sub-blocks. For each query tile, we independently select a routing threshold for each key source within the risk budget, based on the residual risk introduced by approximate calculations. This routing threshold then determines whether to perform exact or approximate calculations. Finally, we aggregate the contributions of all key sources into a single softmax and output the final result.

papers.title: QASK-Edit: Adaptive Sparse Attention Across Queries and Key Sources for Efficient Video Editing

papers.abstract: Generating consistent multi-view RGB images and normal maps from a single input image provides complementary appearance and geometric cues for 3D reconstruction. However, maintaining cross-view consistency requires information exchange across viewpoints, and dense cross-view attention becomes computationally expensive as the number of views and spatial resolution increase. In this paper, we propose Global-Local Proxy Attention (GLPA) to reduce cross-view communication costs while preserving fine-grained within-view processing. Specifically, GLPA retains full-resolution interactions within each view and uses compact global proxies for cross-view communication. To further leverage the exchanged information, GLPA incorporates iterative proxy refinement, which rebuilds the proxies from updated features and reuses the same attention parameters for subsequent interactions within a single denoising step. We evaluate GLPA on two structurally different diffusion backbones, FLUX and Stable Diffusion. Experiments on FLUX show that GLPA achieves a $2.65\times$ speedup in attention computation per denoising step over dense attention, while improving reconstruction IoU from 0.6849 to 0.7019 and reducing NVS LPIPS from 0.086 to 0.076. Results on Stable Diffusion further demonstrate the effectiveness of GLPA, with a $1.80\times$ attention speedup and improvements across all five quality metrics.
authors: Wei Tan, Kunming Luo, Hongyu Yan, Yu Zhang, Zihao Zhang, Xiatian Zhu, Lei Xie
bullets: Targets the computational cost of cross-view attention, which grows with the number of views and spatial resolution.
Maintains full-resolution attention within each view and uses compact proxies for communication across views.
Iteratively rebuilds and refines proxies, reusing attention parameters during each denoising step.
Across FLUX and Stable Diffusion backbones, GLPA improves efficiency and multi-view reconstruction quality.
On FLUX, it provides a 2.65× attention-computation speedup, higher reconstruction IoU, and lower NVS LPIPS; Stable Diffusion shows a 1.80× speedup and improvements on all five reported metrics.

papers.title: Efficient Multi-View Generation with Iterative Global-Local Proxy Attention
papers.tldr: GLPA accelerates consistent multi-view image and normal-map generation by replacing costly dense cross-view attention with refined global proxies while preserving detailed within-view processing.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision along student-generated trajectories, yet the learning benefits of longer trajectories may not scale proportionally with their computational cost. We investigate how supervision utility evolves with trajectory length. Controlled experiments reveal diminishing returns from additional supervised tokens, while showing that later positions remain learnable and exhibit substantial cross-position supervision transfer. Gradient analysis further identifies shared update components across response positions and diverse position-specific residuals whose cross-rollout consistency decreases at greater depths. Motivated by these findings, we propose Stochastic Horizons On-Policy Distillation (SH-OPD), which reduces redundant supervision by randomly varying rollout horizons while preserving access to deeper response states. SH-OPD samples a shared horizon for each training batch, enabling efficient parallel generation without per-sequence horizon scheduling overhead. We characterize the resulting reweighting bias and derive a compute-reweighting trade-off under standard optimization assumptions. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that SH-OPD achieves slightly higher mathematical reasoning accuracy at approximately 45% of the per-update cost of standard OPD, while maintaining competitive code generation performance at around 60% of the baseline cost. These results highlight the benefits of efficient supervision allocation across response depths.
authors: Xinhao Yao, Zhenxing Dou, Yong Liu
bullets: Standard OPD shows diminishing returns from supervising more tokens, although later response positions remain learnable and receive cross-position supervision transfer.
Gradient analysis finds shared update components across positions alongside depth-dependent, less consistent residuals.
SH-OPD samples one shared rollout horizon per batch, avoiding per-sequence scheduling overhead while retaining access to deeper states.
The method achieves slightly higher mathematical reasoning accuracy at about 45% of standard OPD’s per-update cost and competitive code generation at about 60%.
The study focuses on compute–reweighting trade-offs introduced by stochastic horizon sampling.

papers.title: Rethinking Supervision Scaling in On-Policy Distillation: From Dense Supervision to Stochastic Horizons

papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) simplifies reinforcement learning from human feedback, but still relies on traditional backpropagation and its associated activation-memory cost. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimisation avoids backpropagation, yet isotropic perturbations can produce noisy updates for preference objectives defined by differences between chosen and rejected responses. We introduce Contrastive Activation-guided Zeroth-Order Direct Preference Optimisation (CA-ZODPO), which constructs a low-rank search subspace from the activation discrepancy between the chosen and rejected responses in each preference pair. Perturbations are restricted to this subspace, while momentum is maintained in low-rank coordinates to preserve the memory advantages of ZO training. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with Anthropic HH-RLHF, CA-ZODPO outperforms common ZO baselines and remains competitive with first-order DPO in pairwise preference evaluation. It also reduces peak GPU memory by about 59\% at a sequence length of 2048 while retaining the sequence-length scaling behaviour of zeroth-order training.
bullets: Addresses DPO’s activation-memory cost and the noise of isotropic zeroth-order perturbations.
Builds a low-rank search subspace from activation differences between chosen and rejected responses.
Maintains momentum in low-rank coordinates to preserve zeroth-order memory efficiency.
On Qwen2.5-1.5B with Anthropic HH-RLHF, it outperforms common zeroth-order baselines and remains competitive with first-order DPO.
Reduces peak GPU memory by about 59% at sequence length 2048 while retaining zeroth-order sequence-length scaling.

papers.title: Contrastive Activation-Guided Zeroth-Order Preference Optimisation for Memory-Efficient LLM Alignment
papers.tldr: CA-ZODPO makes zeroth-order LLM preference optimisation more targeted and memory-efficient by restricting updates to activation-derived contrastive subspaces.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs) activate only a few experts per token while generally keeping all the experts in GPU memory for high efficiency. Expert pruning reduces this GPU memory footprint cost, yet discards the contribution of pruned experts. Existing remedies either rely on static substitutes, merge experts at the cost of altering their functions, or require costly recovery training. In this paper, we find that the functionalities of pruned experts can be efficiently reconstructed from the activated remaining experts. We propose GEAR (Gated Expert Activation Reuse), which reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation. In addition, we propose GEAR$^2$ to further recover what reuse cannot express with an ultra-lightweight residual. On five MoE LLMs from 16B to 106B parameters with 25% and 50% of experts pruned, GEAR improves over its training-free counterparts in nearly every setting (up to 4 pp.) in terms of accuracy, and GEAR$^2$ outperforms baseline approaches (up to 2.75 pp.) in every setting on nine zero-shot benchmarks, with larger advantages (up to 2.72 pp. higher) under more aggressive pruning (up to 50%).
authors: Linliang Chen, Yan Zhong, Wang Kang, Sai Li, Ji Wu, Ji Liu
bullets: Expert pruning reduces GPU memory but can lose the functions of removed experts.
GEAR gates and reuses scaled outputs from reliable activated experts to reconstruct pruned-expert behavior.
GEAR² adds an ultra-lightweight missing-mass residual for functionality that reuse cannot capture.
Across five 16B–106B MoE LLMs and 25%–50% pruning, it improves over baselines on nine zero-shot benchmarks, with gains up to 2.75 percentage points.
The approach is evaluated specifically in training-free, aggressively pruned MoE settings.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding reduces generation cost, but it stores two KV caches: one for the target model and one for the draft model. We reduce this extra memory by quantizing the draft cache. The target cache and verifier remain in BF16, so that compression cannot change the target model's final correction rule. We first study how to divide precision between keys and values. A naive per-token quantizer makes keys appear much more sensitive: splitting a 12-bit budget, K8V4 beats K4V8 in acceptance by 10.87pp. However, with grouped per-channel keys, the gap becomes -0.25pp. A controlled Qwen test confirms that changing only the key quantizer can erase or reverse the preferred bit split. Hence, following KIVI, we propose K4V4 quantization with per-channel keys and per-token values. Across six model pairs, our method reduces draft cache memory by 66.20%, and combined memory across both caches by 23.95%. Mean acceptance drops from 57.93% to 57.14%, only 1.36% relative. Overall, quantized draft caches can make speculative decoding more memory efficient; as a predictive principle for efficient AI design, key and value precision must be co-designed with the quantizer layout.
bullets: Speculative decoding normally stores target and draft KV caches, creating substantial extra memory use.
The target cache and verifier remain in BF16, preserving the target model’s correction rule.
The proposed K4V4 scheme uses per-channel keys and per-token values, co-designing precision with quantizer layout.
Across six model pairs, draft-cache memory falls 66.20% and total cache memory 23.95%.
Mean acceptance decreases only slightly, from 57.93% to 57.14% (1.36% relative).

papers.abstract: Activation sparsity accelerates LLM decoding by skipping unnecessary weight reads and computation. However, SiLU-based LLMs exhibit little natural sparsity, and imposing high sparsity can substantially degrade accuracy. We propose RoShift, a training-free method that transforms activations into sparsity-friendly representations. RoShift introduces lazy shift, which recenters SiLU activation distributions around zero and defers correction to the end of the FFN to obtain additional sparsity. It also reduces sparsification-induced output error through rotation that jointly accounts for activation and weight information. By fusing the corrections required for shifting and rotation, RoShift translates these gains into decoding speedup. At 50% and 60% sparsity, RoShift improves average accuracy over TEAL by 1.60 and 3.29 percentage points, respectively, across five models. It achieves up to $1.72\times$ decoding speedup over the dense model on an RTX 5090 at 50% sparsity and yields a better accuracy-speedup Pareto frontier than TEAL. Code is available at https://github.com/hulahula3247/RoShift
authors: Geunsoo Song, Jiwon Seo, Hoeseok Yang, Youngmin Yi
bullets: Addresses the low natural activation sparsity of SiLU-based LLMs and accuracy loss from aggressive sparsification.
Uses lazy shift to recenter activations around zero while deferring correction to the FFN output.
Applies weight-aware rotation to reduce sparsification-induced output error.
Fuses shift and rotation corrections to enable decoding speedups.
Across five models, it improves accuracy over TEAL by 1.60 and 3.29 percentage points at 50% and 60% sparsity, respectively, and reaches up to 1.72× speedup on an RTX 5090 at 50% sparsity.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of RoShift, which introduces lazy shift and weight-aware rotation, tightly integrating both with efficient correction fusion for activation sparsification.

papers.abstract: Trajectory rendering, which renders novel views of a reconstructed 3D scene along a camera path, is a core operation in digital twins and autonomous inspection. Structured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders a single view in real time by decoding sparse anchors into Gaussians on demand, but it renders a trajectory view by view: every view projects all anchors to select them, re-decodes anchors already requested by neighboring views, and runs all steps on the GPU while the CPU idles. We treat this as a spatial data management problem, where anchors are spatial objects, views are range queries, and decoded Gaussians are shared derived data, and propose GDM-GS, which removes redundancy at three levels. Within a view, an anchor index and an occluder index answer each view as a holed-frustum range query, so out-of-view and provably hidden anchors are never decoded. Across views, shared materialization decodes each requested anchor once per group of consecutive views while preserving each view's selection. Across processors, a hybrid pipeline balances selections between the CPU and the GPU before grouped decoding under bounded memory. Experiments on large-scale public scenes show that GDM-GS substantially reduces trajectory rendering latency while preserving image quality.
authors: Haolun Ma, Ziyi Liu, Zizhuo Xu, Chuhan Hu, Lei Li
bullets: Frames trajectory rendering as spatial data management: anchors are spatial objects, views are range queries, and decoded Gaussians are shared data.
Uses anchor and occluder indexes to query holed frustums, avoiding decoding anchors that are out of view or provably occluded.
Shares decoded Gaussians across consecutive views, decoding each requested anchor once per view group while preserving per-view selection.
Employs a hybrid CPU–GPU pipeline to balance selection and grouped decoding under bounded memory.
Experiments on large-scale public scenes report substantially lower trajectory-rendering latency with preserved image quality.

papers.abstract: Latent KV cache compression reduces memory footprint by mapping historical keys and values into compact representations. However, generic compressed key states require reconstruction to native dimension before applying RoPE and computing attention scores, adding sequence-scaling overhead to the decode path. We characterize when a latent KV representation can serve directly as the execution state of pretrained RoPE. For RoPE-based transformers, exact static linear execution of the rotary key path requires the latent-to-native map to preserve the pretrained RoPE action through an intertwining relation, restricting exact mixing to coordinates that share the same RoPE frequency. Guided by this characterization, we build GaugeRoPE, a training-free executable latent KV representation. It combines a RoPE-compatible carrier that preserves the rotary action with an approximate position-independent residual key--value (RKV) correction for complementary key and value information, both evaluated without per-token dense historical K/V reconstruction. On Mistral-7B, GaugeRoPE achieves $5.85\times$ KV compression while maintaining quality close to the full-cache baseline. Additional MHA results validate the construction beyond GQA. GaugeRoPE achieves up to $2.48\times$ the decode throughput of the vanilla uncompressed baseline through direct latent execution.
authors: Yuanhang Gao, Xiangrui Yang, Lingyuan Meng, Yuanfeng Chen, Dongsheng Li
bullets: Generic latent KV compression requires costly reconstruction before RoPE and attention during decoding.
Exact execution requires the latent map to preserve RoPE rotations, allowing mixing only among coordinates with shared frequencies.
GaugeRoPE combines a RoPE-compatible carrier with an approximate position-independent residual key–value correction.
The training-free method achieves 5.85× KV compression on Mistral-7B with quality close to the full-cache baseline.
Direct latent execution provides up to 2.48× the decode throughput of the uncompressed baseline; results also extend to MHA.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning improves the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by removing redundant visual tokens, yet the reliability of existing selection signals has not been systematically examined. We analyze token selection under semantics-preserving perturbations and across representative pruning criteria, revealing two limitations. First, attention-based importance shifts non-uniformly under perturbations, so magnitude alone cannot distinguish stable evidence from unstable saliency (local instability). Second, attention- and diversity-based methods select substantially different subsets despite comparable performance, showing that useful evidence is not confined to a unique subset (global inconsistency). These findings motivate reliable token-set construction. We instantiate this perspective in CoRePruner, a training-free framework combining instruction-aware diversity with reliability-aware attention. Across image benchmarks, multiple MLLM architectures, and token budgets, CoRePruner improves performance, especially under aggressive pruning, and remains competitive on video benchmarks. Our results establish reliability as a central consideration in visual token selection.
authors: Chaehee Song, Seokil Ham, KiHyun Seol, Jihyun Lee, Yubin Choi, Changick Kim
bullets: Attention importance can change unevenly under semantics-preserving perturbations, exposing local instability.
Different pruning criteria often select substantially different token subsets despite similar performance, revealing global inconsistency.
CoRePruner is a training-free method using instruction-aware diversity and reliability-aware attention.
It improves performance across image benchmarks, MLLM architectures, and token budgets, particularly under aggressive pruning, while remaining competitive for video.
The study argues that reliability should be a central criterion for visual token selection.

papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models (MFMs) support generalizable inference in distributed mobile sensing applications by integrating heterogeneous data streams. However, existing MFM inference pipelines typically require complete and synchronized multimodal inputs, whereas mobile sensing streams arrive asynchronously due to network variability and heterogeneous data volumes across modalities. Waiting for all modalities increases end-to-end latency, while inference with incomplete inputs can reduce accuracy. We argue that multimodal inference should depend on the utility of available information rather than modality completeness. Based on this principle, we propose AdaModalX, a progressive multimodal inference framework that decouples inference execution from modality synchronization through runtime utility-aware orchestration. At each device, importance-aware data uploading uses a lightweight probe distilled from the edge-side MFM to allow reliable samples to exit locally while uncertain samples continue uploading. At the edge, on-demand MFM activation constructs candidates from fully received samples and, when needed, imputed features derived from partially received delayed inputs. A lightweight contribution assessor built on frozen MFM encoders estimates candidate utility and activates the MFM once the candidate meets its corresponding utility threshold. Experiments on four mobile sensing applications show that AdaModalX improves the accuracy-latency trade-off, achieving up to 26.97% accuracy improvement and up to 64.75% end-to-end latency reduction.
authors: Xiangrui Xu, Sicong Liu, Zhiwen Yu, Zimu Zhou, Bin Guo
bullets: Addresses the latency and accuracy challenges caused by asynchronous, heterogeneous mobile sensing streams.
Uses utility-aware data orchestration: local probes retain reliable samples while uncertain ones continue uploading.
At the edge, constructs inference candidates from complete inputs or imputed features from delayed partial inputs.
A contribution assessor using frozen MFM encoders triggers full MFM inference when candidate utility reaches a threshold.
Across four mobile sensing applications, reports up to 26.97% higher accuracy and 64.75% lower end-to-end latency.

papers.abstract: Mamba-3, the latest Mamba state-space model (SSM), enables efficient long-context modeling, matching Mamba-2 perplexity with half the state size and increasing decoding arithmetic intensity. However, its multi-input multi-output (MIMO) computation, exponential-trapezoidal discretization, and rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) introduce dense, element-wise, and sequential operations. Despite kernel fusion, conventional GPUs execute these operations inefficiently. Our characterization of Mamba-3 hybrid models reveals numerous kernel launches, substantial data movement, and increased register pressure that reduces warp occupancy and memory-latency hiding. We propose RescuCore, a specialized GPU execution unit for Mamba-3 inference that retains other hybrid model layers on existing GPU resources. Integrated alongside CUDA Cores and Tensor Cores within each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) sub-partition, RescuCore shares the register file, shared memory, and warp schedulers. Dense projections remain on conventional GPU resources, while RescuCore pipelines discretization, normalization, RoPE, MIMO computation, recurrent state updates, and output gating to reduce kernel fragmentation and intermediate data movement. We select BF16 after evaluating multiple numerical formats, preserving model accuracy with an estimated area overhead of 5.9% of an A100 die for state size 32 and MIMO rank 4. We evaluate RescuCore using cycle-accurate Accel-Sim simulation, RTL synthesis, and synthesis-informed AccelWattch power modeling. Compared with conventional GPU execution, RescuCore achieves 1.4-9.4x speedup and 1.4-5.0x energy reduction during prefill, and 1.3-2.8x speedup and 1.2-2.6x energy reduction during autoregressive decoding. These results demonstrate the potential of GPU-integrated specialized execution for SSM-based hybrid models.
authors: Shiva Raja, William Desueza, Ajay Joshi
bullets: Mamba-3’s MIMO computation, discretization, RoPE, and recurrent updates cause kernel fragmentation, data movement, and register pressure on conventional GPUs.
RescuCore integrates alongside CUDA and Tensor Cores, while leaving dense projections on existing GPU resources.
It pipelines discretization, normalization, RoPE, MIMO, state updates, and output gating to reduce intermediate data movement.
Using BF16, the design estimates 5.9% A100 die-area overhead for state size 32 and MIMO rank 4.
Simulation and synthesis-based evaluation reports 1.4–9.4× prefill speedup and 1.3–2.8× decoding speedup, with corresponding energy reductions.

papers.selection_reason: Specialized GPU core for Mamba-3 inference reduces data movement and kernel fragmentation, directly addressing memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Integrated GPU Core for Mamba-3
papers.tldr: RescuCore is a specialized GPU execution unit that accelerates Mamba-3 inference by fusing and pipelining its sequential and element-wise operations.

papers.abstract: When high-quality data runs out, a common practice is to train on it for several epochs, but each repeat is worth less than the last. Latent feedback, which feeds each token's top-layer state into the next token's input, is another way to spend that compute, yet it has not been tested against a vanilla Transformer that spends the same compute on more epochs. We run this test across a ladder of model sizes, unique data and epochs, tuning both models at every size and amount of unique data. Latent feedback makes every FLOP and every token count for more except when unique data is scarce relative to model size, a regime that today's models are far from. We find that latent feedback serves as an amplifier: with unique data fixed, it reaches a Transformer's loss with less compute; with epochs fixed, it reaches that loss with less unique data. Furthermore, both savings grow with unique data per parameter and with repetition, and downstream tasks agree. To go beyond our grid, we fit one scaling law to both models, in which latent feedback enters as a Transformer with more parameters; it predicts that both savings keep growing with unique data and repetition. Fitted on models from 60M to 271M parameters, the law predicts the losses at a held-out 778M size to within 0.3% and the gap between the two models to within 0.05%. At most, latent feedback saves 48% of the compute and 47% of the unique data. When data, not compute, is the limit, latent feedback is the better use of a FLOP for a model of a given size.
authors: Benhao Huang, Chaitanya Dwivedi, Xuezhe Ma, Alexander Moreno, Hector Liu
bullets: Feeds each token’s top-layer state into the next token’s input and is compared with a vanilla Transformer at matched compute.
Across model sizes and data regimes, it generally improves the value of both FLOPs and unique tokens, except when data is very scarce relative to model size.
With fixed unique data, it reaches a target loss using less compute; with fixed epochs, it reaches the target using less unique data.
A shared scaling law models latent feedback as equivalent to using a larger Transformer and generalizes accurately to a held-out model size.
Reported maximum savings are 48% compute and 47% unique data; downstream tasks show the same trend.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that latent feedback (feeding top-layer states to the next token) acts as a compute and data amplifier, effectively reducing the need for multiple training epochs.
papers.title: Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier
papers.tldr: Latent feedback makes language-model training more compute- and data-efficient than spending equivalent compute on repeated epochs, especially when unique data is plentiful.

papers.abstract: Coherent optical neural networks based on interferometric architectures offer a promising route toward high-throughput, energy-efficient computation by exploiting the multiple degrees of freedom of light, including spatial, temporal, and spectral modes. However, practical implementations are constrained by the number of tunable parameters due to fabrication complexity, device footprint, and control overhead. In such parameter-constrained settings, achieving high expressive power remains a central challenge. We identify two key architectural requirements for maintaining high expressive power under these constraints: (i) statistical uniformity in the implemented transformations and (ii) strong mixing capability per parameter, which enables rapid and unbiased redistribution of information across modes. To realize these requirements, we develop a logarithmic-depth butterfly-topology architecture whose fundamental building block is a single phase-shifter--beam-splitter pair, in contrast to conventional rectangular mesh architectures based on Mach-Zehnder interferometers. Computational evaluations show that, particularly at restricted parameter counts, the proposed architecture achieves lower matrix-reconstruction errors and higher classification accuracies than conventional meshes in both feedforward and recurrent networks. We further quantify these design principles using graph-theoretic measures, expected squared moduli of transformation-matrix entries, and matrix-reconstruction error. The resulting framework provides a quantitative and physically interpretable basis for parameter-efficient optical neural networks.
authors: Kazuo Aoyama, Hiroshi Sawada, Shota Kita, Akihiko Shinya, Masaya Notomi
bullets: Parameter limits from fabrication, footprint, and control overhead constrain optical neural-network expressivity.
The design targets statistically uniform transformations and strong information mixing per parameter.
Compared with Mach–Zehnder-based rectangular meshes, the butterfly topology uses simpler building blocks and logarithmic depth.
Computational evaluations report lower matrix-reconstruction error and higher classification accuracy, especially at restricted parameter counts.
Graph-theoretic and matrix-based measures provide a physically interpretable framework for evaluating parameter-efficient designs.

papers.selection_reason: Develops architectural principles for parameter-efficient unitary transformations in coherent optical neural networks, focusing on statistical uniformity and mixing capability.
papers.title: Architectural Principles for Parameter-Efficient Unitary Transformations in Coherent Optical Neural Networks
papers.tldr: A logarithmic-depth butterfly architecture using phase-shifter–beam-splitter pairs improves expressive, parameter-efficient unitary transformations in coherent optical neural networks.

papers.abstract: GPTQ is the de facto standard solver for layer-wise post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models, yet the solver itself has received less attention than weight preprocessing and cross-layer objectives. We target a bottleneck of GPTQ: its greedy procedure optimizes continuous group scales separately from the assignment of discrete integers. Evaluating each integer candidate with its closed-form optimal scale has been used for per-channel quantization; JointQ extends it to group-wise quantization, where a row's scales are coupled through the Hessian, and applies it to refine the GPTQ solution. Each local-search move changes one integer and recomputes its group's optimal scale in closed form, accounting for the other groups through the full Hessian; all scales are periodically re-solved jointly. The search starts from a row-wise selection among scale-refitted candidates including the GPTQ solution, so unregularized JointQ never has a larger layer-wise calibration error than GPTQ. JointQ preserves the GPTQ output format and is thus a drop-in replacement. Across four models and four settings, JointQ improves six-task average zero-shot accuracy over vanilla GPTQ in 14 of 16 comparisons and perplexity in 12 of 16. The mean accuracy gain increases from 0.0044 in W4G128 to 0.1559 in W3 per-channel, and JointQ also improves average accuracy over GPTQ with MSE-based scale search and activation ordering in all eight per-channel comparisons, though rarely in G128. An ablation shows that JointQ's diagonal Tikhonov regularization mitigates severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation, so the largest gains are not due to the local search alone. Overall, JointQ's primary empirical benefit is downstream accuracy preservation in challenging low-bit and large-group regimes. Code is available in the OneComp library at https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/OneCompression.
bullets: Targets GPTQ’s greedy separation of discrete integer selection from continuous scale optimization.
Uses Hessian-aware local search: each integer update recomputes its group’s closed-form optimal scale, followed by periodic joint scale refinement.
Starts from scale-refitted GPTQ candidates, so unregularized JointQ does not increase layer-wise calibration error relative to GPTQ.
Across four models and four settings, it improves average zero-shot accuracy in 14/16 comparisons and perplexity in 12/16.
Diagonal Tikhonov regularization helps prevent severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation; JointQ remains a drop-in GPTQ replacement.

papers.title: JointQ: Joint Scale-and-Integer Quantization for Large Language Models

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers rely on 3D full attention over tens of thousands of spatiotemporal tokens, and its quadratic cost dominates inference latency. Sparse attention reduces this cost, but existing methods face a dilemma: static methods apply predefined masks and cannot capture input-dependent attention, whereas dynamic methods reconstruct the sparse mask repeatedly, paying online to rediscover positional structure that is largely stable across inputs. To this end, we propose PoCoAttn, a training-free sparse attention framework that separates input-stable from input-dependent attention and resolves the former offline and the latter online. PoCoAttn features: (1) A relative-offset analysis of 3D query-key pairs, which shows that video attention decomposes into an input-stable positional prior that carries most of the attention mass and a small content-dependent residual. (2) A position-content collaborative sparse attention mechanism, which retrieves positional keys from offline-calibrated tables, selects content keys online with a head-adaptive ratio between the two sources, and compensates for the discarded keys to approximate full attention. (3) A step-adaptive budget allocation algorithm, which models how early-step sparse attention errors are amplified along the denoising trajectory and derives the optimal sparsity budget per step. Extensive experiments across four video diffusion models and three tasks show that PoCoAttn consistently achieves a better speed-fidelity Pareto frontier than state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, improving PSNR by 1.9 to 5.0 dB over baselines and delivering up to 4.1$\times$ attention and 2.0$\times$ denoising speedups over dense FlashAttention-3 attention.
authors: Jianwen Wu, Meiling Wang, Junkang Zhou, Yipeng Shen, Haoran You
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of 3D full attention over large spatiotemporal token sequences.
Separates mostly input-stable positional attention from a smaller input-dependent content residual.
Retrieves positional keys from offline-calibrated tables, selects content keys online, and compensates for discarded keys.
Allocates sparsity budgets across denoising steps based on error amplification, with head-adaptive position/content ratios.
Across four video diffusion models and three tasks, reports 1.9–5.0 dB PSNR gains over baselines and up to 4.1× attention and 2.0× denoising speedups versus dense FlashAttention-3.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PoCoAttn. (a) PoCoAttn decomposes attention into an input-stable positional part and an input-dependent content part. (b) At inference, each query tile looks up its positional key tiles in the positional table, selects content keys by pooled-query scores, and merges the discarded keys into virtual keys by weighted pooling; the per-head position–content ratio is solved offline. (c) The positional table is compiled offline from the per-head positional prior Ph(∆), obtained by averaging calibration attention over each relative offset ∆. (d) The step-wise budget ρs is solved offline by minimizing the local error et(ρt) weighted by its amplification A(t).

papers.title: PoCoAttn: Position-Content Collaborative Sparse Attention for Fast and High-Fidelity Video Generation
papers.tldr: PoCoAttn accelerates video diffusion transformers with training-free sparse attention by combining offline positional patterns, online content selection, and step-adaptive sparsity budgets.

papers.abstract: Multi-round diffusion image editing can reduce computation by reusing intermediate activations, but retaining these activations across editing rounds introduces substantial memory and bandwidth overheads. Compression can reduce these overheads, but efficient cache construction is challenging: compressing only after editing requires buffering over 100 GB of activations per request. Moreover, the compressed cache must support selective reuse, as future masked edits require only a subset of the cached activations. It also exposes a scheduling challenge, as cached edits are faster than initial generations, causing naive policies to severely delay either initial generations or editing requests. In this paper, we aim to address both challenges through compression-informed serving. We develop TileCache, a serving system for multi-round diffusion editing. It compresses reusable activations and incorporates a scheduler that balances both edits and initial generation requests. Compared with the state-of-the-art image editing baseline, TileCache sustains over 2x the request arrival rate at 90% SLO attainment. It completes edits 2.4-4.5x and initial generations 1.3-2.2x faster than the baseline, while preserving image quality.
authors: Yuyang Tian, Desen Sun, Shuncheng Jie, Lishan Yang, Sihang Liu
bullets: Problem: Uncompressed activation caches impose high memory and bandwidth costs, while post-edit compression may require buffering over 100 GB per request.
Method: Compresses reusable activations during serving and supports selective reuse for masked edits.
Method: Uses a scheduler designed to balance faster cached edits with initial generation requests.
Result: Sustains over 2× the baseline request arrival rate at 90% SLO attainment.
Result: Speeds up edits by 2.4–4.5× and initial generations by 1.3–2.2× while preserving image quality.

papers.abstract: Modern multi-camera 3D detectors increasingly rely on large Vision Transformer (ViT) image encoders, making repeated full-depth encoding a dominant inference cost even though adjacent driving frames are highly redundant. We present EvoMem3D, an adaptive-depth temporal framework that caches the most recent full-depth detector-interface appearance representation as a read-only anchor and combines it with policy-selected partial features from the current frame. A lightweight pre-encoding controller chooses among semantic encoder exits before image processing, allocating shallow computation to stable frames and deeper computation when the visual state changes. To reuse appearance without carrying stale geometry, we decouple temporal appearance from geometric alignment: current-frame calibration defines the decoder geometry at every timestamp, while a motion-conditioned positional adapter accounts for anchor-to-current ego motion. On nuScenes, EvoMem3D achieves 61.50 NDS and 52.76 mAP while reducing end-to-end latency from 364.4 to 168.7 ms (x2.16) relative to standard dense DETR3D. With StreamPETR, it reaches 61.36 NDS and 52.55 mAP at a x1.92 speedup. Controlled studies isolate the effects of current evidence, temporal reuse, memory correction, and adaptive routing, while our audit confirms that the policy learns to distinguish semantic driving regimes.
authors: Moshe Kimhi, Idan Kligvasser, Yotam Intrator, Regev Cohen, Ehud Rivlin
bullets: Caches a full-depth appearance representation as a read-only temporal anchor and combines it with selected partial features from the current frame.
A lightweight controller selects encoder exits before processing, using shallow computation for stable scenes and deeper computation when visual conditions change.
Separates temporal appearance reuse from geometric alignment: current calibration defines geometry, while a motion-conditioned adapter handles ego motion.
On nuScenes, achieves 61.50 NDS and 52.76 mAP with 2.16× lower latency than dense DETR3D; StreamPETR sees a 1.92× speedup with similar accuracy.
Scope: the method targets temporally redundant driving sequences and relies on policy-based recognition of semantic driving regimes.

papers.abstract: The CAPSARII project advances a cyber-secure, ultra-low-power wearable platform and Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT) framework to support real-time monitoring of military personnel and data-driven decision support. The architecture integrates smart-textile sensing, a body/squad area mesh, edge-deployed AI on secure RISC-V microcontrollers, and cloud/federated analytics for cross-mission learning and comparative studies. Two representative use cases--pilot fatigue and warfighters operating in harsh environments--guide requirements, validation, and interface design (including HUD and haptic feedback). As an initial step toward embedded models, we benchmark stress classification on a public wearable dataset: tree-ensemble baselines achieve state-of-the-art performance for accuracy and F1 (e.g., XGBoost: $\mathrm{Accuracy}=0.901\!\pm\!0.023$, $\mathrm{F1}=0.920\!\pm\!0.019$), while a feature-based Transformer attains the highest AUC ($0.963\!\pm\!0.025$), informing feature-engineering and compression choices for edge deployment. Building on these results, CAPSARII employs HW/SW co-design, model compression (pruning, quantization, distillation), and precision tuning to meet stringent energy and memory budgets; it further investigates Processing-in-Memory accelerators for future efficiency gains. A structured gap analysis highlights the remaining challenges: establishing validation standards for physiological signal quality and textile durability; achieving low-latency, scalable BAN/SAN communications under mobility and interference; and deploying hybrid lightweight/post-quantum cryptography with robust device identity and side-channel resilience on constrained endpoints. By consolidating these elements into a coherent, secure IoBT stack, CAPSARII delineates a practical roadmap from laboratory baselines to mission-ready soldier monitoring in both training and operational scenarios.
authors: Luciano Bozzi, Christian Celidonio, Umberto Nuzzi, Massimo Biagini, Stefano Cherubin, Asbj{\o}rn Djupdal, Tor Andre Haugdahl, Andrea Aliverti, Alessandra Angelucci, Giovanni Agosta, Gerardo Pelosi, Paolo Belluco, Samuele Polistina, Gaia Strada, Luigi Sossi Ortega, Alexandra-Ioana Albu, Riccardo Volpi, Luigi Malag\`o, Michael Schneider, Xabier Eguiluz, Haritz Saiz, Mar\'ia Viqueria
bullets: Targets fatigue, stress, and harsh-environment monitoring for pilots and warfighters, with HUD and haptic feedback interfaces.
Integrates body/squad-area mesh networking, secure RISC-V edge devices, and cloud/federated analytics for cross-mission learning.
On a public wearable dataset, XGBoost achieved 0.901 accuracy and 0.920 F1, while a feature-based Transformer achieved the highest AUC at 0.963.
Plans HW/SW co-design, pruning, quantization, distillation, precision tuning, and possible Processing-in-Memory acceleration for constrained deployment.
Key gaps include physiological-signal and textile validation, reliable low-latency communications under mobility and interference, and lightweight post-quantum security with robust device identity.

papers.abstract: Neural networks are typically programmed through optimization, rather than by explicitly specifying their computations. Recent work on weight-space programming suggests that large language models (LLMs) can instead reason about and manipulate neural-network weights directly. In this work, we show that LLMs can directly program statistical computations in tabular foundation models (TFMs), whose parameters enable inference across different datasets. We investigate three complementary settings using GPT-6 Astra, without gradient-based optimization. First, Astra directly programs nanoTabPFN from zero-initialized weights, achieving a mean ROC AUC of 0.849 across 20 TabArena datasets, compared to 0.876 for a pretrained baseline. Second, Astra diagnoses and repairs a signed-product regression failure in pretrained TabPFN-3.5, restoring near-perfect predictions on held-out synthetic datasets while preserving performance on TabArena-Lite, with only a 0.08% average relative increase in error. Third, it writes KV-cache-editing programs that steer TabPFN-3.5's predictions on unseen synthetic datasets, demonstrating transformations such as reversing linear trends and converting sine waves into approximate square waves, without modifying model weights. Together, our findings suggest that LLM-driven programming could complement gradient-based optimization across TFMs' development and usage, while offering a new way to investigate and intervene in their internal computations.
authors: Shi Bin Hoo, Magnus Buehler, Omar Swelam, Frank Hutter, Lennart Purucker
bullets: GPT-6 Astra programs nanoTabPFN from zero-initialized weights, achieving mean ROC AUC 0.849 across 20 TabArena datasets versus 0.876 for a pretrained baseline.
It diagnoses and repairs a signed-product regression failure in pretrained TabPFN-3.5, restoring near-perfect predictions on held-out synthetic data while largely preserving benchmark performance.
It writes KV-cache-editing programs that steer predictions on unseen synthetic datasets, including reversing linear trends and approximating square waves from sine waves.
The results suggest LLM-driven programming can complement optimization and provide tools for probing and intervening in TFM computations.

papers.abstract: Determining whether an embedding is sufficiently similar to any vector in a vector store without performing a nearest-neighbor search can substantially improve query throughput in vector-store systems. We study Semantic Approximate Membership Queries (SAMQs), which allow queries to be rejected when no indexed vector meets the requested similarity threshold, while guaranteeing no false negatives. We introduce CapCover Filter, a geometric data structure that summarizes a set of embeddings using spherical caps. Its representation is independent of the query threshold, allowing a single filter to support arbitrary thresholds without reconstruction. We evaluate alternative construction and quantization methods, compare CapCover Filter with competing filters, and measure its impact on query throughput. Across five real-world datasets, at a cosine similarity threshold of 0.95, CapCover Filter eliminates approximately 20--100\% of index accesses while using only 2\% of the raw (FP32) embedding memory. When placed before a FAISS flat index, it improves query throughput by up to 382\% and by approximately 116\% on average across the five datasets, while returning the same range-search result. We also evaluate lower similarity thresholds. Our results show that CapCover Filter can substantially improve vector-store throughput when similarity thresholds are tight, retrieval is expensive, and indexed embeddings are highly clustered. We release an optimized implementation of CapCover Filter and its evaluation framework.
authors: Dvir David Biton, Shay Hahiashvili, Nadav Keren, Gil Einziger, Roy Friedman
bullets: Targets Semantic Approximate Membership Queries: safely rejects queries when no indexed vector can meet a similarity threshold, with no false negatives.
Summarizes embeddings using spherical caps; one representation supports arbitrary thresholds without reconstruction.
Uses about 2% of raw FP32 embedding memory and eliminates approximately 20–100% of index accesses at cosine similarity 0.95 across five real-world datasets.
Placed before a FAISS flat index, improves throughput by up to 382% and about 116% on average while preserving range-search results.
Benefits are strongest for tight thresholds, expensive retrieval, and highly clustered embeddings; lower thresholds are also evaluated.

papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in on-device LLM deployment, large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models remain impractical on resource-constrained devices, as sparse expert activation still requires all expert weights to be memory-resident. To address this, we identify three key observations for on-device MoE inference: (a) cache hit rates are fundamentally bounded even under Belady's optimal policy; (b) these bounds are insufficient for low-latency on-device inference; and (c) prior cache-aware routing based on binary cache presence can induce routing instability. Based on these insights, we propose CECAR (Cache & Expert Co-Aware Routing), a MoE inference system that jointly considers expert routing and cache management. Unlike prior cache-aware routing methods, CECAR uses an ML-based cache policy to predict the expected reuse distance of each expert and prioritizes routing and execution toward experts with smaller predicted reuse distances. On the Qwen3-30B-A3B model, CECAR achieves 12.5 tokens/s on a consumer-grade GPU with only 16 GB of VRAM, where non-resident experts are fetched from SSD, delivering a 4.5x speedup over conventional MoE inference and exceeding the decode speed of baselines that keep the entire model fully resident in DRAM. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/CECAR.
authors: Byeongju Kim, Hoonki Lee, Byungjun Kim, Inyul Ra, Yongjin Kim, Yongseong Lee, Sangyeob Kim
bullets: On-device MoE inference is constrained because all expert weights cannot fit in memory, requiring SSD transfers for non-resident experts.
Cache hit rates are fundamentally limited, and binary cache-aware routing can cause unstable expert selection.
CECAR predicts each expert’s expected reuse distance with an ML-based cache policy and favors experts likely to be reused soon.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it reaches 12.5 tokens/s on a consumer GPU with 16 GB VRAM and outperforms fully DRAM-resident baselines in decode speed.

papers.abstract: Reasoning LLMs generate long outputs whose key--value (KV) caches occupy GPU memory for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request can repeatedly lose and recover its state while producing little new output. We call this behavior KV thrashing. In certain cases, existing systems leave more than a fifth of requests stalled for over a minute. Because preemption cannot be avoided without delaying admission, we ask how to make it productive. We present Stint, a serving system that preserves a preempted request's work, bounds how long it waits, and gives it fresh output after it returns. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in a contiguity-first CPU pool with an exact-extent allocator, and moves them with fused K/V gather/scatter kernels and double buffering. Age-based readmission brings stalled requests back, and protection gives them a turn of fresh decoding before another preemption. Remaining-length estimates from decoding hidden states guide victim selection. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds under Stint and p99 time per output token falls by 50.7\% relative to recomputation in the same engine. The replay as a whole finishes 10.7\% sooner (12.0\% higher throughput), because the requests that baselines starve no longer finish last.
authors: Ziji Shi, Xinyi Wan, Chaoyi Ruan, Guangxing Huang, Min Lin, Jialin Li
bullets: Long-output reasoning requests can suffer KV thrashing, repeatedly losing and recovering state while producing little output.
Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in CPU memory and transfers them efficiently using fused gather/scatter kernels with double buffering.
Age-based readmission and protected decoding turns prevent repeatedly stalled requests; hidden-state length estimates guide preemption victims.
On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request waited over 50 seconds, while p99 time per output token decreased 50.7% versus recomputation.
The full replay finished 10.7% sooner, with 12.0% higher throughput.

papers.title: Making Preemption Productive in Long-Output LLM Serving
papers.tldr: Stint makes LLM request preemption productive by preserving KV-cache work and ensuring stalled requests resume with bounded waits and fresh decoding.

papers.abstract: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR leaderboards. Serving it efficiently takes more than fast operators: continuous batching changes the amount and mix of work at every iteration, and the best fusion granularity changes with it. We present a serving engine that, for every pass, chooses between persistent megakernels and chains of fused kernels at crossovers measured offline. On an H100 SXM GPU, throughput of our accuracy-preserving serving peaks at 4,345x real time, 1.39x the peak of tuned vLLM, and is up to 4.39x faster at low concurrency; on B200 it peaks at 6,367x, 1.64x vLLM at the highest concurrency we measured. Word error rate (WER) is 1.91 to 1.93% against 1.88 to 1.93% for vLLM. Within a 400 ms budget for p95 end-to-end completion time, it serves 8x as many concurrent requests. Choosing per pass beats either level alone: 23% higher throughput than always using megakernels at 128 concurrent requests, and 9% higher than always using fused kernels at 8. Opt-in switches, including greedy MoE layer skipping, add 13 to 16% throughput on B200 for offline jobs that can accept higher WER.
authors: Aditya Chatterjee, Sanjay Singh Chauhan, Mayank Jain, Arushi Dhingra, Sahin Chowdhury, Rahul Mittal
bullets: Addresses changing workloads under continuous batching, where the best kernel-fusion granularity varies by iteration.
Chooses between persistent megakernels and fused-kernel chains using offline-measured performance crossovers.
Peaks at 4,345× real time on H100 SXM and 6,367× on B200, outperforming tuned vLLM at measured peak concurrency.
Maintains comparable WER to vLLM and serves 8× more concurrent requests within a 400 ms p95 completion-time budget.
Optional accuracy–throughput trade-offs, including greedy MoE layer skipping, add 13–16% throughput on B200 for offline jobs.

papers.abstract: We present a Scalable Windowed Axial-attention Neural Receiver (SWAN-Rx) for multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) systems. The receiver improves reception accuracy and reduces forward-pass computation while supporting frozen-weight reuse across bandwidth allocations and channel conditions. It combines a common resource-element representation of received observations and pilot context with alternating time-axis and local frequency-axis attention. Shared parameters and relative positional information permit soft detection across allocation lengths without inference-time parameter updates. At fixed subcarrier spacing, model configuration, and symbol count, bounded frequency neighborhoods give linear growth of forward-pass computation with bandwidth. Evaluations compatible with the 5G New Radio physical layer reuse weights trained on four physical resource blocks (PRBs) at up to 273 PRBs and on unseen channels. At the training bandwidth, SWAN-Rx achieves lower pre- and post-decoding bit error rates than the implemented three-step neural receiver (NRX) and DeepRx-MIMO baselines, with 16.9% and 39.7% fewer parameters and 56.3% and 35.7% fewer forward-pass operations, respectively. The same weights achieve lower pre-decoding error rates than these baselines throughout the evaluated bandwidth-extrapolation and 16-PRB channel-transfer tests, with an estimated 0.4-0.9 dB signal-to-noise ratio reduction relative to NRX at a pre-decoding error rate of $10^{-2}$ in the 16-PRB tests.
bullets: Targets efficient neural reception for MIMO-OFDM across varying bandwidth allocations and channel conditions.
Combines shared resource-element and pilot representations with alternating time-axis and local frequency-axis attention.
Uses shared parameters and relative positional information for soft detection without inference-time updates.
Bounded frequency neighborhoods make forward-pass computation grow linearly with bandwidth under fixed configuration and symbol count.

In 5G NR-compatible evaluations, it outperformed the implemented NRX and DeepRx-MIMO baselines at training bandwidth and retained lower pre-decoding error across bandwidth extrapolation and 16-PRB channel-transfer tests.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) encode a high-resolution image into thousands of visual tokens, which dominate the cost of the prefill stage. Visual token reduction removes most of these tokens, but two problems remain at extreme budgets. The vision encoder still processes every patch of the image, and the few surviving tokens often miss the small regions that hold the answer. In this paper, we propose Glance-ETD, a two-stage token reduction framework guided by a lightweight question-conditioned scorer. In the first stage, a glance encoder views the image at low resolution and re-encodes only the question-relevant regions at native resolution. In the second stage, Evidence-Tempered Diversity (ETD) selects the final tokens by combining diversity with the evidence predicted by the scorer, so that the kept tokens cover the scene and retain the answer. A single-rollout self-distillation recipe trains the MLLM with the glance encoder. With only 5% of the visual tokens, Glance-ETD retains 91.6% of the full-token performance of Qwen3.5-4B across fourteen benchmarks and outperforms the strongest prior method, LT-OPD, by 17.3 points and the same training recipe with DivPrune by 6.0. It also speeds up the time to first token on 4K images by 3.1x and generalizes to three other MLLMs and to high-resolution document benchmarks, with the largest gains on text-rich tasks.
authors: Yuxuan Wang, Guangxiang Zhao, Yuxuan Tian, Yahui Han, Xinyu Tan, Feiyu Wang, Zongwei Lv, Xiangzheng Zhang, Lin Sun, Tong Yang
bullets: Addresses the cost of processing thousands of image tokens and the risk of missing small, answer-relevant regions.
Uses a two-stage, question-conditioned process: low-resolution region glancing followed by native-resolution re-encoding of relevant areas.
Selects final tokens with Evidence-Tempered Diversity, balancing scene coverage with predicted answer evidence.
At 5% of visual tokens, retains 91.6% of Qwen3.5-4B’s full-token performance across 14 benchmarks and improves over prior baselines.
Provides 3.1× faster time to first token on 4K images, with especially strong gains on text-rich tasks and transfer to other MLLMs.

(b) Inference: Stage 1 (Sec. 3.2) encodes the image at a quarter of the patches, the scorer fϕ picks the 25% of the coarse cells with the highest question relevance, and only these are re-encoded at native resolution, giving a grid X with all N native positions. papers.title: Glance, then Select: Evidence-Tempered Visual Token Selection for Extremely Compressed Multimodal LLMs

papers.abstract: Rendered images are cheap to label, but a microcontroller classifier must survive 8-bit integer (INT8) quantisation and compute correctly on the chip. Five models, from MobileNetV2 at 224 px to a 61K-parameter convolutional neural network (CNN), were fine-tuned on a six-class scene dataset with and without a synthetic stage, against thresholds fixed in advance, and deployed on an ESP32-S3 and an RP2040. With full real data the stage gave no detectable gain. For the main deployable model the INT8 difference was +0.312 percentage points (pp), its interval below the +1.6 pp gain recomputed from the source study; quantisation did not detectably change it, nor did model size. With 10% of the real data the stage paid off for the CNN, by +3.438 pp on one seed and +2.715 pp over three; its cause is open. On the ESP32-S3 the main model took 152.7 ms and 16.3 mJ above idle per inference, and adding the stage changed neither beyond preset bounds. The model's INT8 outputs matched TensorFlow Lite's reference kernels exactly, but only after a memory overrun in a vendor kernel was patched. On the RP2040 the same model took 1.80 s and 27.3 mJ above idle, about twelve times slower, and the largest 96 px model exceeded the board's flash-capacity limit. Neither the RP2040 nor the host interpreter used for scoring reproduced the reference arithmetic. A synthetic stage is worth adding only when real data are scarce, and on-device INT8 outputs should be checked against reference kernels, not inferred from host scores.
bullets: Five models were evaluated on a six-class scene dataset with and without synthetic pre-training, then deployed on an ESP32-S3 and RP2040.
With full real data, synthetic pre-training produced no detectable accuracy gain; with 10% of real data, the CNN improved by 2.715 pp across three seeds.
On the ESP32-S3, the main model required 152.7 ms and 16.3 mJ per inference, with no detectable deployment-cost change from pre-training.
The same model took 1.80 s and 27.3 mJ on the RP2040; its largest 96 px variant exceeded the board’s flash capacity.
INT8 outputs matched reference kernels only after patching a vendor-kernel memory overrun, so host scores alone were insufficient for validation.

papers.title: Does synthetic pre-training pay off on a microcontroller? Accuracy, latency and energy across two MCUs
papers.tldr: Synthetic pre-training helps when real data are scarce, but offers no clear benefit with full data and does not materially change INT8 accuracy, latency, or energy on the tested MCUs.

papers.abstract: Open large language models (LLMs) and speech models ship vocabularies of up to 262k tokens, and every user downloads the tables those tokens index (the input embedding, an untied output head and, in recent on-device models, per-layer embeddings), whatever languages they need. We call the bytes in rows a deployment never uses the vocabulary tax and measure it, without downloading weights, for 1,244 generative and speech-recognition models on the Hugging Face Hub. For a Thai and English deployment it is a median 4.4% of model bytes below 0.5B parameters and 2.1% above 8B, and 1.93 GB in Gemma 4 E2B: it falls hardest on the small models that edge devices run. Keeping only the rows of the deployment's writing systems is exact. Keeping the tokens seen in the user's own text removes much more, a median 29.0% below 0.5B, but the usual way of doing it breaks BPE tokenizers: it drops the intermediate tokens that merges build on, so new text is split differently 1.9 times as often as the standard check reports. We repair this with merge closure, at a cost of 5.9% more rows, and add a trim certificate: a Good-Turing estimate, from the trimming text alone, of how much new text the trimmed tokenizer will split differently (correlation 0.996 over 300 settings in 22 languages) and of how much more text a target needs. Without test data our method never exceeds a 2% target, while prior keep rules checked on test data exceed it in 9-13 of 44 settings. On six models of 270M to 3B parameters in 11 languages, trimmed models keep their predictions: where the certificate passes, a median 89.7% of rows is removed and bits per character rise by at most 2.0%. The census, the trimming and the certificate are released as an open Python package, and the per-model tax for 41 languages as an open dataset.
bullets: Large vocabularies impose a measurable deployment memory tax, especially on small edge models; for Thai–English deployments, the median tax is 4.4% below 0.5B parameters.
Retaining tokens from a deployment’s writing systems is exact, while retaining tokens observed in user text removes substantially more vocabulary rows.
Naive text-based trimming breaks BPE tokenization by removing intermediate merge tokens; merge closure repairs this with only 5.9% more rows.
A Good-Turing trim certificate estimates tokenizer shift and required text from trimming data alone, closely matching observed behavior across languages and settings.
Across six models and 11 languages, certified trims removed a median 89.7% of rows, with bits-per-character increasing by at most 2.0% while predictions were preserved.

papers.title: The Vocabulary Tax: Safely Trimming Unused Tokens from LLMs for On-Device Use
papers.tldr: A tokenizer-aware trimming method can safely remove most unused vocabulary rows from LLMs for on-device deployment while preserving model behavior and certifying text-splitting risk without test data.

papers.abstract: Panoramic multi-object tracking (MOT) requires reliable identity association across a 360{\deg} field of view, yet bandwidth-constrained operation forces a trade-off between low-resolution (LR) identity ambiguity and costly high-resolution (HR) transmission. We propose HIVE-ECIA, an identity-aware framework that selectively retrieves historical HR evidence to recover fragmented identities without modifying detection boxes or the underlying tracker. An ECIA Base-Guided query policy determines when additional HR evidence is warranted; HIVE ranks historical LR observations to select an informative retrieval timestamp; and ECIA Full integrates the retrieved HR crop through learned gated fusion and conservative identity safeguards. We further introduce DualPano-MOT, a real-world dual-fisheye panoramic evaluation dataset featuring controlled pedestrian interactions, panorama-seam challenges, and occlusions, with model-assisted, manually verified tracking annotations. On held-out QuadTrack sequences and zero-shot DualPano-MOT, HIVE-ECIA improves identity association across four MOT trackers without tracker-specific retraining. Across these trackers, identity switches decrease by up to 21.8% and 23.4%, while the largest IDF1 gains reach 3.81 and 6.74 percentage points, respectively. Under an offline JPEG-based acquisition model, our framework reduces encoded data volume by 89.2% and 79.3% relative to continuous Full-HR acquisition.
authors: Hai Nguyen, Tarik Taleb, Qize Guo
bullets: Targets identity ambiguity caused by low-resolution transmission and fragmented tracks in 360° panoramic video.
Uses ECIA to decide when extra high-resolution evidence is needed, HIVE to select a useful historical timestamp, and gated fusion with identity safeguards to integrate the retrieved crop.
Works with four MOT trackers without tracker-specific retraining or changes to detection boxes or the underlying tracker.
On held-out QuadTrack and zero-shot DualPano-MOT sequences, it reduces identity switches by up to 21.8% and 23.4%, with IDF1 gains up to 3.81 and 6.74 percentage points.
Reduces encoded data volume by 89.2% and 79.3% versus continuous Full-HR acquisition under the stated offline JPEG-based acquisition model.

papers.abstract: Looped language models such as Ouro and Raven apply one weight-shared block several times per token, so autoregressive decoding (AR) runs every loop of every token in sequence. Pipelined self-speculative decoders overlap these loops by drafting tokens from shallow readouts and verifying them at full depth. Yet every loop of a looped LM ends in a readout of the next token, and draft tokens pass through every depth anyway, so each depth can check them without an extra pass. We introduce LoopSkim, in which the depth of the pipeline is the verifier. Draft tokens copied from the context, as in prompt lookup decoding, enter after the first loops, any later readout that contradicts one replaces it at that depth, and only full-depth readouts commit tokens. LoopSkim fixes the random draws of every position in advance, so each check compares two tokens and decoding stays lossless in exact arithmetic under sampling for any number of checks and draft chains. Without training, its speedup over AR averages 1.73x that of LoopSpec across greedy decoding and sampling, and its checks between the first loops and full depth speed it up on every model. An optional draft head adds a second chain and raises this average to 1.99x.
bullets: Targets looped LMs whose shared block runs multiple times per token, making autoregressive decoding expensive.
Pipelines prompt-lookup draft tokens into later loops, allowing each depth to check and potentially replace them.
Only full-depth readouts commit tokens, preserving exact-arithmetic sampling behavior with fixed random draws.
Without training, it averages 1.73× the speedup of LoopSpec across greedy decoding and sampling; an optional draft head raises this to 1.99×.
The method is lossless under exact arithmetic and applies across any number of checks and draft chains.
