papers.selection_reason: Lossless speculative decoding method that reduces inference latency for looped language models; relevant to efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: LoopSkim: Lossless Multi-Depth Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models
papers.tldr: LoopSkim accelerates lossless speculative decoding in looped language models by using intermediate depths as token verifiers without extra passes.

papers.abstract: Reflective skill optimizers improve multi-turn LLM agents by revising instructions from failed and successful rollouts, yet accumulating edge-case rules bloats prompts, inflates token use, and pushes agents into long, error-prone loops. We introduce EfficientSkill, a two-step framework that first discovers a reliable skill without token penalties, and then warm-starts accuracy-guarded pruning from that skill to compress instructions, bound agent turns, and offload reusable code into workspace utilities with zero implementation prompt cost. Across four frontier, mid-tier, and open-weight models on MATH-500, ALFWorld, and SpreadsheetBench, EfficientSkill cuts output tokens over unconstrained EvoSkill on 11 of 12 configurations (by up to 80%) while raising mean accuracy on every benchmark, including +14.3 and +17.5 percentage-point gains on SpreadsheetBench with Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.1 Fast by replacing stalled loops with compact workflows. By shrinking both generated tokens and replayed history, EfficientSkill lowers total token usage and serving cost across every evaluated configuration, with or without full-prefix KV caching.
authors: Deep Shah, Sanket Badhe, Nehal Kathrotia, Priyanka Tiwari
bullets: Targets prompt bloat, excessive token consumption, and error-prone loops in reflective multi-turn agents.
Uses a two-stage process: penalty-free skill discovery followed by accuracy-guarded pruning and code offloading to workspace utilities.
Evaluated across four models on MATH-500, ALFWorld, and SpreadsheetBench.
Reduced output tokens in 11 of 12 configurations, by up to 80% versus unconstrained EvoSkill, while improving mean accuracy on every benchmark.
Lowered total token usage and serving cost across all configurations, with or without full-prefix KV caching.

papers.tldr: EfficientSkill learns reliable agent instructions first, then prunes and refactors them to reduce token use and looping while preserving or improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Transformer language models are commonly scaled by making their blocks wider or stacking them deeper. In this work, we explore a complementary path: branching, the parallel composition of full Transformer blocks. We introduce the Multi-Branch Transformer (MBT), which processes the input through shared initial layers, executes independently parameterized branches of sequential blocks in parallel, and fuses their outputs before shared final layers. At comparable training compute, we study three MBT variants: Wide-Shallow preserves block width, Narrow-Deep preserves sequential depth, and Balanced interpolates between them. In controlled pretraining experiments at four mixture-of-experts scales (0.8B to 2.1B total parameters), 2-branch Wide-Shallow MBTs consistently outperform sequential Transformers under matched parameter and training-compute budgets. Balanced MBTs improve further and retain comparable quality as the number of branches increases. To improve inference efficiency at long contexts, we introduce Joint-KV, which constructs a shared KV cache from branch representations at each depth. Our final recipe combines Balanced MBTs with Joint-KV, supported by an inference engine that exploits branch grouping and shared-cache reuse. Fitted scaling curves indicate that standard Transformers require up to 1.26x as much training body compute to match our final models' validation loss. These models reduce full-model KV-cache storage by up to 34% and deliver up to 51.4% higher decoding throughput on a single H200 GPU. Ablation studies show that branching yields gains beyond changes in width and depth, enables an effective KV-sharing strategy (Joint-KV), remains robust across fusion functions, and performs best in the middle layers. These findings show that branching offers a practical path for scaling language models toward both better modeling quality and faster inference.
authors: Gaotang Li, Lingjie Chen, Chunyuan Deng, Zhiwei Xu, Hongzheng Chen, Christopher De Sa, Jingrui He, Yingheng Wang, Hanghang Tong
bullets: Uses shared initial and final layers around independently parameterized parallel branches, with Wide-Shallow, Narrow-Deep, and Balanced variants.
Balanced branching improves validation quality and remains effective as the number of branches grows.
Joint-KV shares key-value caches across branches to reduce long-context inference memory and improve decoding throughput.
Across controlled pretraining scales, branching provides gains beyond width and depth changes and works across fusion functions.
The approach is most effective in middle layers and is evaluated within the reported pretraining and single-GPU inference settings.

papers.abstract: Recent efforts to improve the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have explored visual token pruning, quantization, and feature compression. However, the properties that determine whether transformed visual tokens remain usable by a frozen decoder are not well characterized. We introduce \textbf{TIVS (Token Identity Versus Statistics)}, a training-free intervention framework that separately studies sequence permutation, token retention, numerical precision, and statistical replacement under controlled conditions. On 192 POPE questions, three token permutations change TinyLLaVA accuracy by only $-0.17$ percentage points on average, while changing 4.69\% of individual predictions. Diagonal and rank-64 Gaussian replacements decrease accuracy by 25.0 and 28.1 points on the same subset. Further experiments with exact moment constraints, quantization error, token retention, and additional visual tasks reveal how strongly the effects depend on the original feature values and the evaluation setting. These findings provide an empirical basis for assessing visual token transformations in frozen MLLMs and designing more reliable multimodal interfaces.
authors: Yikang Qiao, Jianye Zeng, Duan Huang, Ziying Song
bullets: Introduces a training-free framework separating permutation, retention, precision, and statistical replacement effects.
On 192 POPE questions, three token permutations changed TinyLLaVA accuracy by only −0.17 points on average, despite altering 4.69% of predictions.
Diagonal and rank-64 Gaussian replacements reduced accuracy by 25.0 and 28.1 points, respectively.
Additional experiments show that transformation effects depend on original feature values and evaluation setting.
Provides empirical guidance for evaluating visual-token transformations and designing multimodal interfaces.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. During autoregressive decoding, however, generating each token requires several sequential passes through these layers, leading to high decoding latency. Pipelined self-speculative methods use shallow-loop predictions to process tokens at different loops in the same batch, but each token must reach the drafting depth before the next can enter the pipeline. We introduce LoopFill, a training-free speculative decoding algorithm for looped LLM that combines multi-token suffix drafts with shallow-loop predictions in a single draft tree. Both drafters contribute to one tree, so a suffix lookup can immediately extend a shallow prediction and several future tokens can enter the pipeline together. The shared block computes the highest-scoring draft candidates at different loop depths in one batch, and full-depth verification preserves the model's autoregressive output distribution. Across seven benchmarks, LoopFill's average speedup over greedy autoregressive decoding is $5.85\times$ on Ouro-2.6B and $5.13\times$ on Huginn-3.5B. The speedups exceed those of LoopAhead, the strongest baseline, by \(40\%\) on Ouro-2.6B and \(25\%\) on Huginn-3.5B.
authors: Siqi Zhu, Suozhi Huang, Yi Zhao, Jiaxuan You
bullets: Targets the latency caused by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers for each generated token.
Uses a training-free pipeline where suffix lookups can extend shallow predictions and admit multiple future tokens together.
Batches high-scoring draft candidates from different loop depths, then verifies them at full depth while preserving the model’s autoregressive distribution.
Across seven benchmarks, achieves average speedups of 5.85× on Ouro-2.6B and 5.13× on Huginn-3.5B over greedy decoding.
Outperforms LoopAhead in speedup by 40% on Ouro-2.6B and 25% on Huginn-3.5B.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding lets a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large language model verifies in a single forward pass. When the verifier keeps a KV cache, verification is cheap and drafting must be nearly free. Session-local drafters, which predict from the prompt and the text generated so far, meet that bar without training. We compare a recency-weighted, backing-off, confidence-gated session memory against prompt lookup decoding in its reference form, which copies from the earliest earlier match, and in a variant that copies from the most recent one, with paired per-prompt bootstrap intervals throughout. On general, medical, and legal text with a Mistral-7B verifier, recency accounts for the speed: most-recent lookup gains up to 0.09 in speedup over earliest-match lookup on 500-token generations, and session memory's weighting and backoff add nothing measurable on top, at 30 to 40 times the drafting cost. Energy tells a different story. On medical and legal text, unselective drafters are 14% faster than plain decoding yet use as much energy per token, while drafters that abstain on weak evidence save 3 to 4 joules per 100 tokens; a three-token minimum match length on prompt lookup matches the confidence-gated session memory. Outputs are token-identical to greedy decoding in 94% of generations, with every divergence at a numerical near-tie. Under a repetition penalty, long-generation speedups shrink from 1.4-1.7x to 1.1-1.2x, but recency still helps and the length floor is the only drafter that saves energy in both domains.
bullets: Session-local drafters require no training and make drafting nearly free while a verifier reuses its KV cache.
Most-recent prompt lookup improves speedup by up to 0.09 over earliest-match lookup; session-memory weighting and backoff add no measurable benefit.
On medical and legal text, selective abstention saves 3–4 J per 100 tokens, whereas unselective drafting is faster but uses similar energy to plain decoding.
Drafted outputs match greedy decoding in 94% of generations; divergences occur only at numerical near-ties.
Repetition penalties reduce long-generation speedups to 1.1–1.2×, though recency remains beneficial and a minimum match-length floor consistently saves energy.

papers.title: Text Speeding Itself Up: Recency and Restraint in Session-Local Drafting
papers.tldr: Recency-based session-local drafting delivers most of the speed benefit in speculative decoding, while confidence-based abstention is key to reducing energy use.

papers.abstract: Depth recurrence increases effective model depth by repeatedly applying a fixed computation block. However, sharing attention parameters does not share the key-value (KV) states generated at different recurrence iterations, which causes memory growth with recurrence depth during autoregressive decoding. We study how to reduce this memory cost through architectural and cache-sharing approaches within a common depth-recurrent framework. We first study a looped hybrid that repeats a stack of Transformer layers, with recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks replacing most attention layers and periodic Transformer attention anchors retained. We then restrict recurrence to a dedicated recurrent workspace in a Parcae-style architecture and test its stabilising adapter as a wrapper for the looped hybrid. Finally, we train a looped Transformer with recurrent KV replay, where only selected recurrence iterations write KV states that later iterations reuse. This trains the model to operate with the same shared KV topology used during inference. We find that looped hybrids require sufficiently frequent attention anchors, with performance depending strongly on the recurrent mixer. For cross-iteration KV sharing, recurrent KV replay allows multiple recurrence iterations to reuse the same KV states while retaining performance close to the full looped Transformer with separate KV caches for each iteration.
authors: Lucia Licakova, Niklas Schmidinger, Lukas Hauzenberger, Sebastian B\"ock, Sepp Hochreiter
bullets: Depth recurrence increases effective depth but normally grows autoregressive KV memory with each iteration.
The authors evaluate looped Transformer hybrids using recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks plus periodic attention anchors.
A Parcae-style recurrent workspace and stabilising adapter are tested to constrain recurrence and improve stability.
Recurrent KV replay trains later iterations to reuse KV states written by selected earlier iterations.
Hybrid quality depends on sufficiently frequent attention anchors and the choice of recurrent mixer; KV replay retains near-baseline performance while reducing cache sharing overhead.

papers.abstract: With the rapid growth of space activities, near-Earth space is becoming increasingly congested, leading to a higher risk of spacecraft collisions and space debris generation. Recent close-proximity encounters and collision incidents necessitate efficient and cost-effective onboard systems for space object detection (SOD) and collision avoidance. While deep learning (DL) enabled Edge AI using low-cost vision sensors on single or multiple satellites has shown promises for SOD, significant challenges remain, including limited datasets, small SOD, and the lack of comprehensive performance assessments. This paper presents a collaborative Edge AI framework for multiview SOD and systematically benchmarks DL models and fusion strategies. Results show that higher image resolution significantly improves small SOD. For multiple views, image-level fusion reduces the combined communication and inference latency by 30.13% and 32.80% on average compared with feature-level and attention-based fusion across the evaluated inter-satellite link (ISL) bandwidth. For larger view sets, feature-level and attention-based fusion achieve better detection accuracy at the cost of analysis in the sensing-communication pipeline, revealing that multiview collaboration introduces minimal latency overhead under ISL constraints when reception capacity is not exceeded. Our work provides valuable design insights for future collaborative satellite network design, supporting the emerging space situational awareness and space traffic management requirements.
bullets: Motivated by increasing orbital congestion and the need for efficient onboard space-object detection and collision avoidance.
Introduces a collaborative multiview Edge AI framework and benchmarks deep-learning models and fusion strategies.
Higher image resolution substantially improves detection of small objects.
Image-level fusion reduces combined communication and inference latency by 30.13% and 32.80% on average versus feature-level and attention-based fusion, respectively.

Feature-level and attention-based fusion can improve accuracy with larger view sets but add sensing–communication pipeline cost; conclusions are scoped to evaluated ISL bandwidths and reception capacity.

papers.abstract: Empirical evidence suggests that large neural networks rarely make effective use of all available parameters, with learned solutions exhibiting pronounced sparsity. Despite this ubiquity, existing generalization theory only partially explains how such sparsity influences statistical performance. In this paper, we derive non-asymptotic generalization gap bounds for deep neural networks whose layer-wise weight matrices are restricted by $\ell_p$ quasi-norm ($0<p\leq 1$) constraints. Our analysis gives rise to a novel result that interpolates between classical norm-based generalization guarantees and parameter-counting bounds. Remarkably, in the extreme sparsity limit as the quasi-norm order $p$ approaches zero, our analysis reveals a transition to a square-root dependence on the number of \emph{active} (non-zero) parameters, resulting in bounds that are strictly tighter than existing parameter-counting approaches. Experiments demonstrate that our bounds exhibit a milder dependence on initial architectural choice at the over-parametrization regime, effectively capturing the generalization benefit of the sparsity arising from training on natural data.
bullets: Addresses limited theoretical understanding of how sparse connectivity affects generalization.
Analyzes deep networks whose layer-wise weight matrices satisfy ℓp quasi-norm constraints for 0<p≤1.
Provides bounds interpolating between classical norm-based guarantees and parameter-counting bounds.
As p approaches zero, the bounds depend on the square root of the number of nonzero parameters and are tighter than existing parameter-counting results.
Experiments show milder dependence on initial architecture in over-parameterized settings, reflecting sparsity learned from natural data.

papers.abstract: Federated fine-tuning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to collaboratively adapt to distributed private data. However, long-context fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices faces substantial challenges arising from excessive activation memory, heterogeneous token-importance patterns across clients, and communication overhead. To address these challenges, we propose SMELL, a Sparsity-aware and Memory-Efficient federated fine-tuning framework for Long-context LLMs. SMELL integrates three complementary mechanisms: Local Sparse-Forward Adaptation (LSFA), Consensus-Anchored Sparsity Coordination (CASC), and Communication-Efficient Progressive Update Recovery (CPUR). These mechanisms jointly enable memory-efficient local adaptation, heterogeneity-aware sparsity coordination, and lightweight model-update transmission. Experiments on OPT-350M and LLaMA2-7B demonstrate that SMELL reduces peak memory consumption by up to 88.35% compared with conventional fine-tuning and 13.25% compared with forward-only LoRA fine-tuning at a 16K context length. Furthermore, SMELL improves fine-tuning performance under certain non-IID settings and supports compact update transmission with progressive reconstruction, demonstrating its potential for resource-efficient federated long-context LLM adaptation.

bullets: Addresses excessive activation memory, client-specific token-importance patterns, and communication overhead in federated long-context fine-tuning.
Combines Local Sparse-Forward Adaptation, Consensus-Anchored Sparsity Coordination, and Communication-Efficient Progressive Update Recovery.
Reduces peak memory by up to 88.35% versus conventional fine-tuning and 13.25% versus forward-only LoRA at 16K context length.
Evaluated on OPT-350M and LLaMA2-7B, with improved performance under certain non-IID settings and compact progressive update transmission.
Scope: results focus on the reported models, 16K context length, and selected non-IID federated settings.

papers.abstract: Staged LLM agents make market and social simulators realistic, but one 102-day run of a 200-agent, ten-index market simulator issues 203,100 language-model calls and returns one realization. Conventional low-compute distillation drops their free-form intermediate state. We present staged semantic distillation, a low-compute method that preserves non-structured semantics in a non-LLM student trained from one recorded trace. A frozen encoder maps each teacher output to a 1024-d vector; the student sees typed stage-tagged vectors with stage-specific visibility, is jointly supervised, and trains with scheduled self-history. One TwinMarket trace yields a 13.2M-parameter deterministic student that trains in 1,658 seconds on one 8-GB GPU and runs with zero teacher or decoder calls and no text generation (0.14 ms per decision). Its analysis stays close to the teacher (cosine 0.943), and swapping semantic inputs between agents moves 64.7% of decisions against 12.8% for a matched donor, so the channel is preserved and live. We use the surrogate to study what the transfer carries. It reaches 0.8347 balanced accuracy on the teacher-forced replay and 0.7783 [0.766,0.791] on the deployment decoder; the five-seed gain over a no-semantic retrain is +2.2 [1.21,3.14]. Against the teacher's own re-sampling level, round-one R is 97.1% [95.8,98.4] and 92.3% [89.0,95.4]; R is a diagnostic, not an accuracy. A five-seed content-by-schedule study isolates the gain: scheduled self-history carries it (+2.2 [1.21,3.14]); shuffled and constant content controls reproduce it, while content matters teacher-forced. The design rule: invest in the deployment schedule, let content earn its place at the teacher-forced operating point. A 20-seed, 200,000-decision sweep takes 12 minutes with zero LLM calls, versus three hours for the teacher. The paper is a method-and-case-study contribution on one simulator and trace.
authors: Zhiyang Niu, Huayuan Shen, Chuanjie Li, Mengmeng Zhao, Jiajia Zhang
bullets: A frozen encoder converts teacher outputs into semantic vectors, while a stage-aware student uses scheduled self-history and joint supervision.
The 13.2M-parameter student trains in 1,658 seconds on one 8-GB GPU and makes decisions in 0.14 ms with no teacher, decoder, or text-generation calls.
Semantic behavior remains closely aligned with the teacher (cosine 0.943), and swapping semantic inputs changes 64.7% of decisions versus 12.8% for a matched donor.
The surrogate achieves 0.7783 deployment-decoder balanced accuracy and enables large sweeps 15× faster than the teacher, with zero LLM calls.
The gain is attributed primarily to the deployment schedule; content contributes at the teacher-forced operating point.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) enable on-device image generation and editing but incur high attention costs at high resolutions. Existing sparse attention reduces computation, yet dynamic sparsity introduces preprocessing and irregular data accesses that poorly fit mobile NPUs. We present DiT.XPU, a sparse DiT inference framework for heterogeneous mobile SoCs. DiT.XPU combines tile-aligned sparse attention with anchor-based error compensation by exploiting slowly varying dense-sparse output residuals across denoising steps. Heterogeneous XPU collaboration overlaps NPU dense attention with GPU sparse calibration, while mask-guided dataflow reduces data transfers and layout conversion by overlapping data movement with computation. Across five DiT models on two Snapdragon smartphones, DiT.XPU achieves up to 1.56x end-to-end denoising speedup over the Hexagon-NPU backend and 11.5x attention-kernel speedup over the fastest alternative, while preserving generation quality close to dense attention. Code is available at https://github.com/IF-LAB-PKU/dit.xpu.
authors: Jiayu Chen, Jinye Hu, Maoliang Li, Anqian Cen, Hailong Zou, Zihao Zheng, Xinming Wei, Guojie Luo, Jie Zhang, Xuanzhe Liu, Xiang Chen
bullets: Targets the high attention cost of high-resolution on-device DiT image generation and editing.

Coordinates dense attention on the NPU with sparse calibration on the GPU, while overlapping data movement and computation.
Evaluated on five DiT models across two Snapdragon smartphones, achieving up to 1.56× end-to-end denoising speedup over a Hexagon-NPU backend.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving is turning to vision-language-action models (VLAs). They answer and plan by decoding, one step at a time. Each step is another forward pass, so a plan can take over a second of GPU time. Embodied AI often pairs such a slow, reasoning System 2 with a fast System 1 that acts. Human drivers plan at a glance, with System 1. Faster designs usually put System 1 outside the vision-language model (VLM), in a planner without its abilities. Yet before a VLM writes its first token, it has already read the scene into one hidden state. We show that, once trained, this hidden state is enough to drive and to answer questions about what the model sees. SuperGlance reads it to turn a decoder-only VLM into an encoder-style driving policy. Its linear head scores a fixed set of 5,273 candidate trajectories. With the set fixed, rewards are computed offline, so supervised targets can be reward-weighted and reinforcement learning maximizes the exact expected reward. Before and during policy training, multiple-choice training keeps the VLM's visual abilities in one pass, so the policy still answers questions about driving scenes. Training questions are built against shortcuts. Each must be answered right in two option orders. Against drift, a KL term keeps each stage near its starting model. One pass offers VLAs a more plausible path to System 1. SuperGlance answers visual multiple-choice questions as well as its base VLM does by decoding. It plans in 84 ms of GPU time, six times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0, and at least as well on NAVSIM, PAI-AV and WOD-E2E. In AlpaSim closed loop, km per at-fault incident holds for both planners up to a 300-ms delay and drops beyond. With GPU time charged as delay, SuperGlance's lead over Qwen-Drive-1.0 grows from 2.8 to 3.9 times. Delayed by 1.2 s, our model falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 at its own 518 ms.
authors: Jieyuan Pei, Xin Yan, Mingwei Xu, Haiyi Zhang, Siyu Zou, Zhangyi Hu, Zhuoxuan Li, Yuguang Yang, Rongjunchen Zhang, Cheng Chi, Hui Xiong, Yan Wang
bullets: Uses the VLM’s pre-decoding hidden state to drive and answer scene questions without autoregressive generation.
A linear head scores 5,273 fixed candidate trajectories, enabling offline reward weighting and exact expected-reward reinforcement learning.
Maintains visual capabilities with multiple-choice training and limits drift with KL regularization.
Plans in 84 ms—six times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0—while matching or exceeding it on reported driving benchmarks.
Performance remains comparable under delays up to 300 ms but degrades beyond that; at 1.2 s, it falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 at its native latency.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable embodied artificial intelligence (AI) by translating visual observations and language instructions into robotic actions. Emerging use cases in physical AI are expected to drive the need for efficient inference and communication, as the computational demands of the VLA models pose challenges for real-time control with limited onboard resources. Test-time scaling through latent reasoning allows these models to refine hidden representations without generating explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, but introduces a trade-off between task success, inference latency, and energy consumption. In this paper, we address the efficient collaborative inference under a realistic communication scenario. We propose a wireless edge-assisted framework for adaptive latent reasoning (WEALR) that augments onboard computation with edge computing. A decision-making agent jointly selects the execution location and latent-reasoning convergence threshold. We formulate this joint adaptation as a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). A Lagrangian-constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) approach, namely trust region policy optimization Lagrangian (TRPO-Lag), learns to balance task performance and resource consumption under varying wireless conditions and task requirements. We evaluate the framework using LIBERO manipulation tasks, profiled VLA inference costs, and ray-traced wireless channels. Experimental results demonstrate that TRPO-Lag achieves up to 23% higher feasibility-weighted task success rate compared to benchmark CDRL methods.
bullets: Targets efficient real-time VLA inference for physically embodied AI with limited onboard resources.
Jointly adapts where inference runs and when latent reasoning should stop based on wireless conditions and task needs.
Models the decision process as a constrained Markov decision process and solves it with TRPO-Lag.
Evaluated on LIBERO manipulation tasks using profiled VLA costs and ray-traced wireless channels.
Achieves up to 23% higher feasibility-weighted task success than benchmark constrained deep-RL methods.

Fig. 3: Training Performance and Normalized Constraint Costs

Fig. 6: TRPO-Lag action distribution by task suite the offline characteristics in Fig. 2. TRPO-Lag predominantly selects τ = 10−3 for Goal and Object, preserving high task success while requiring fewer recurrent iterations than stricter thresholds. For LIBERO-10, which comprises longer-horizon tasks, it selects τ = 5 × 10−4 in approximately 82% of requests, consistent with the substantial success degradation observed at larger thresholds. Location selection complements these decisions: Spatial and LIBERO-10 are offloaded in 63.0% and 67.9% of requests, whereas Goal and Object are primarily executed locally. These results indicate that TRPOLag also learns suite-dependent operating points that preserve task success while reducing inference latency and managing shared edge resources.

papers.abstract: The Apple Neural Engine (ANE) is in over a billion devices, but is characterized indirectly via CoreML. Using a CoreML-free fused-graph dispatch path, we measure the ANE, along with the Apple GPU and CPU on the same device, with per-engine energy accounting. The consumer-available roofline does not predict the ANE in practice. A critical correction is that the ANE sees two effective memory bandwidths: a slow activation path and a fast weight-stream path. Two roofline ridges follow, and the weight-stream ridge is below that of the GPU. The ANE single-operand compute peak decreases instead of plateauing. Its weight stream is byte-bound in fp16 but limited by the dequantizer's element rate in int8. As a result, int8 compression saves energy at unchanged throughput and an int4 lookup-table stream raises throughput and efficiency at a cost of 2.55 points of ImageNet top-1. The corrected roofline identifies the lower-energy ANE paths and bounds it from below. A constructed device map reproduces across four unique ANE generations. Results show that operators should be placed by arithmetic intensity and fused for optimal performance.
bullets: The standard consumer roofline fails to predict ANE performance in practice.
The ANE has separate slow activation and fast weight-stream bandwidths, producing two roofline ridges; its weight-stream ridge is below the GPU’s.
Compute performance declines rather than plateaus at higher single-operand workloads.
FP16 weight streaming is byte-bound, while int8 is limited by dequantizer element rate; int4 improves throughput and efficiency but costs 2.55 ImageNet top-1 points.
The model reproduces behavior across four ANE generations and identifies lower-energy execution paths.

papers.abstract: Industrial recommendation faces a resolution--complexity dilemma: dense interactions make detailed modeling of long behavior histories expensive, while compact history summaries restrict the evidence available to prediction. A unified backbone must preserve rich behavioral details within strict serving budgets. We introduce \textbf{TokenFormer V2}, a unified architecture that explicitly decouples \emph{representation resolution} from \emph{interaction density}. Its group-wise token layout jointly encodes behavior segments with non-sequential context, expands interaction ranges via hierarchical group merging, and coordinates distributed groups through \emph{NS Fusion} and \emph{Global Sync} modules. Through this \emph{local--global decomposition} paradigm, computation is concentrated on structured interactions while preserving fine-grained evidence, ensuring that every encoded event remains directly accessible to the \emph{Full-Resolution Readout} module. On the Tencent Advertising Algorithm Competition 2026 (TAAC 2026) benchmark, TokenFormer V2 achieves top-ranking accuracy among unified recommendation baselines while using \textbf{5.1$\times$ fewer FLOPs} than leading baselines, sustaining its advantage across long histories and imbalanced behavior domains. Furthermore, in billion-parameter evaluations on WeChat Channels advertising, it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art industrial baselines, yielding up to a \textbf{+0.07 pp} overall AUC gain. In live online A/B testing against the production model, TokenFormer V2 delivers a statistically significant \textbf{2.33\% increase in GMV}. These results establish TokenFormer V2 as a battle-tested blueprint for scalable, full-resolution behavior modeling in industrial recommendation.
authors: Kaihui Wu, Guoming Li, Liang Guo, Yifeng Zhou, Yuehong Hu, Junwei Pan, Zhixiang Feng, Chengguo Yin, Wenqi Fan, Haijie Gu, Jie Jiang
bullets: Addresses the resolution–complexity trade-off between detailed long-history modeling and strict serving budgets.
Uses group-wise tokens, hierarchical merging, NS Fusion, Global Sync, and Full-Resolution Readout to combine local detail with global context.
Ranks highly on the TAAC 2026 benchmark using 5.1× fewer FLOPs than leading baselines, with strong performance on long histories and imbalanced domains.
Outperforms industrial baselines in billion-parameter WeChat Channels evaluations by up to +0.07 percentage points in AUC.
In online A/B testing against the production model, increases GMV by 2.33%.

papers.abstract: Decision models such as Jev return probabilities over caller-defined options and are increasingly used for classification. Large label spaces challenge both accuracy and scalability: larger menus can impair decisions, increase input costs, and exceed option limits. Hierarchical classification reduces menu size but introduces serial calls and error propagation. We propose AdaMenu, which builds a compact candidate menu from retrieved labeled examples and makes a single decision-model request. Its candidate labels adapt to the query, and its default setting also adjusts menu size using aggregated retrieval scores. We evaluate AdaMenu with open and closed decision models on four label sets containing up to 1,016 labels. It outperforms TypeSafe's beam-search baseline on all 16 model and label-set pairs where both methods run, improving accuracy by 16.6-34.3 percentage points. Relative to the full menu on the three smaller label sets, accuracy differences range from -0.5 to +7.2 percentage points, while input token usage falls by factors of 3.2-22.9. AdaMenu also runs when option limits exclude the full menu, including settings where the hierarchical baseline is unavailable.
authors: Jiangze Yan, Yi Shen, Jieyun Huang, Wenjing Zhang, Zhaoxiang Liu, Ning Wang, Kai Wang, Shiguo Lian
bullets: Large label spaces can reduce accuracy, increase input costs, and exceed decision-model option limits.
AdaMenu builds a compact, query-specific menu from retrieved labeled examples and can adapt its size using retrieval scores.
It avoids the serial calls and error propagation of hierarchical classification by using a single decision-model request.
Across four label sets with up to 1,016 labels, AdaMenu outperformed TypeSafe’s beam-search baseline in every comparable setting.
Compared with full menus on smaller label sets, it reduced input tokens by 3.2–22.9× while changing accuracy by −0.5 to +7.2 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Does input-conditioned parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) improve because it uses the current input, or because it adds a useful learned correction? We investigate this distinction with PREFACE, a bounded channel controller for PEFT-adapted projections that requires no test-time gradients. The controller reads observed context; in multiple-choice likelihood scoring, its state is independent of the candidate continuation. Our central study freezes IA3, tuned LoRA, and DoRA adapters and matches controller architecture, initialization, batches, and updates across current-prefix and learned-global controls. Across ARC-Challenge and SciQ, current-prefix control improves all six mean accuracies over frozen adapters, but none of its paired contrasts with learned-global control excludes zero. Replacing its corrections with their training-prefix mean changes accuracy by at most 0.34 percentage points; input-varying corrections contribute only 1.8-2.8% of correction RMS. On ARC test, frozen-adapter current/global controls score 25.68%/25.77%, distinct from the earlier jointly trained 23.1% to 26.4% gain over IA3. We derive and evaluate static compilation of fixed corrections, separating deployment simplification from statistical equivalence. Broader GPT-2, Pythia, and Qwen experiments show family-, task-, and scoring-dependent gains, with modest recent-model effects. The study provides an intervention-based evaluation of conditional PEFT: improvements over a static adapter do not by themselves demonstrate a benefit from input matching.
bullets: Introduces a bounded, gradient-free controller for PEFT-adapted projections whose state depends on observed context but not candidate continuations.
Controls for architecture, initialization, batches, and updates when comparing current-prefix controls with learned-global controls for IA3, LoRA, and DoRA.
Current-prefix control improves accuracy over frozen adapters, but paired comparisons with learned-global control do not reliably show an input-conditioning benefit.
Replacing input-varying corrections with training-prefix means changes accuracy by at most 0.34 percentage points; variation contributes only 1.8–2.8% of correction RMS.
Results vary by model family, task, and scoring method; static compilation is evaluated as a deployment simplification, not assumed to be statistically equivalent.

papers.abstract: Sequence models represent past context at different resolutions, using token-level keys and values, fixed-size recurrent states, or hierarchies of compressed summaries. Full attention supports strong associative recall but requires quadratic work during training and prefill and a linearly growing key-value cache during inference. Linear attention and state-space models reduce these costs through fixed-size recurrent memory, but this compression can limit recall. Log-linear attention offers a middle ground by maintaining logarithmically many state matrices. However, its hierarchy favors finer resolution near the current query while compressing earlier context into coarser summaries. To complement this allocation of resolution, we introduce bilateral log-linear attention, which pairs the existing hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence origin. By combining their reads, the two branches provide finer access to both early and recent context while remaining causal. We derive recurrent and chunkwise parallel formulations for the added branch, preserving log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding work per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage at fixed feature dimensions and chunk size. In multi-query associative recall, this design raises mean overall test accuracy from 76.37% to 96.12% over forward log-linear attention across multiple training seeds. For pretrained language models under approximate parameter matching, it raises the mean score on six selected RULER needle-in-a-haystack tasks from 26.97% to 50.03% at a context length of 6144 tokens. In the same setting, bilateral attention also outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.
bullets: Full attention recalls well but has quadratic training/prefill cost and a linearly growing inference cache.
The method complements the existing recent-context hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence start, enabling finer access to both early and recent tokens while remaining causal.
Recurrent and chunkwise-parallel formulations retain log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage.
Mean associative-recall accuracy improves from 76.37% to 96.12%; selected RULER retrieval scores improve from 26.97% to 50.03% at 6,144-token context.
It outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.

papers.abstract: Edge-cloud speculative decoding moves autoregressive drafting to an edge device while a larger cloud model verifies draft tokens in parallel, so that edge drafting and cloud verification overlap under a synchronous draft-verify schedule. Beyond low-latency local networks, however, the next verification request of that schedule can be sent only after the previous reply arrives, so every round still waits out a full round trip, and throughput falls as the network RTT grows. To recover this loss, we present SpecRelay, an edge-cloud LLM inference system that addresses this cost at two levels: it amortizes round trips when cloud verification is necessary and avoids them when local reasoning suffices. For cloud-bound queries, an asynchronous verification pipeline keeps fixed-budget draft trees in flight while earlier replies are still outstanding, and the cloud rejects stale requests before the target-model forward pass (the asynchronous schedule). At the query level, an RTT-conditioned router (the Latency-Aware Router) estimates quality and completion latency for three on-device modes (direct generation, Chain-of-Draft, and full reasoning) and cloud speculative decoding, selecting among them under a configurable accuracy-latency objective without adding latency during inference, since the router runs concurrently with the draft-model prefill. The asynchronous schedule alone improves decoding throughput by up to 50% over a reproduced synchronous baseline across multiple benchmarks. At matched target-model accuracy and 250 ms of added round-trip latency, the full system with the router delivers 1.95x and 1.55x the throughput of the same baseline on SPROUT and OlympiadBench, respectively, while sending only 47% and 39% of the queries to the cloud.
authors: Jai Jain, Chihyo Ahn, Yong Liu, Charles Chen, Duc N. M Hoang, Ajay Kumar Jaiswal, Fatih Ilhan, Han-Byul Kim, Lauren Hannah, Richa Dixit, Minsik Cho, Yingyan Celine Lin, Hyesoon Kim

Method: An RTT-aware router selects among direct generation, Chain-of-Draft, full local reasoning, and cloud speculative decoding.
Results: Asynchronous verification improves throughput by up to 50% over a reproduced synchronous baseline.
Results: With 250 ms added RTT, the full system achieves 1.95× and 1.55× baseline throughput on SPROUT and OlympiadBench while sending 47% and 39% of queries to the cloud.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models add parameters without proportionally increasing per-token compute. However, training cost also depends on bytes moved, memory held, and kernels launched, and many of those costs follow total parameter size rather than active compute. On infrastructure built for dense models, this mismatch is costly: in early baselines, throughput fell as stored expert parameter size grew, even though the useful work per token stayed nearly fixed. To close this gap, we present a redesigned training stack in Olmo-core, built for efficient, scalable MoE training. We replace the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) of earlier Olmo-core versions with an architecture built on Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), and add Expert Parallelism (EP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), a distributed optimizer, and activation recompute. We propose NVSHMEM-based rowwise EP, which writes each token directly into its expert's buffer, avoiding dispatch and combine permutation overhead. We make EP fully synchronization-free by keeping routing metadata on the GPU and using device-scheduled grouped GEMMs. Closely integrated MXFP8 cuts compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, and topology-agnostic checkpoints let the parallel layout change between runs. On NVL8 B300 nodes, the stack supports training configurations from 12.9 billion to 1.2 trillion total parameters on up to 512 GPUs, reaching 858 useful-model TFLOP/s/GPU at 1.2 trillion with MXFP8 and per-layer recompute; an experimental capacity test with the optional DeepEP v2 backend reaches 2.38 trillion. We also explain each design choice and share findings for other training systems; for example, we identify a failure pattern we call Token Gerrymandering, in which the MoE router can learn to hack the load-balancing loss, and find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides.
authors: Tianhua Tao, Akshita Bhagia, Dirk Groeneveld, Pete Walsh, Tyler Romero, Yashas Samaga, Jacob Morrison, Iz Beltagy, Taira Anderson, Noah A. Smith, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
bullets: MoE training costs can grow with total stored parameters because of memory, communication, and kernel-launch overhead, even when active compute remains similar.
The stack replaces FSDP with DDP and adds expert, pipeline, and optimizer parallelism plus activation recomputation.
NVSHMEM-based rowwise expert parallelism and GPU-managed routing avoid dispatch/combine permutations and synchronization overhead.
Integrated MXFP8 reduces compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, while topology-agnostic checkpoints allow parallel layouts to change between runs.
On NVL8 B300 nodes, it scales from 12.9B to 1.2T parameters across up to 512 GPUs; the authors also report Token Gerrymandering and cases where communication overlap hurts kernel speed.

Figure 74 Captured timelines show the two submission regimes. Both Nsight Systems profiles run the same eight-layer development model (128 routed experts, top-8, one shared expert, EP8, BF16, two sequences per rank microbatch) on eight B300 GPUs; only the expert-parallel path differs. This capture predates and differs from the reduced profiling workload of Table 46. In the synchronized trace (a), the per-block host wait appears as cudaEventSynchronize in the CUDA API lane, the CPU and GPU ranges of each forward block stay in lock step, and the GPU kernel rows show recurring gaps. In the rowwise trace (b), no host wait interrupts submission: the CPU finishes submitting the microbatch while the GPU is still executing earlier work, and the GPU-side forward blocks run back to back. Figure 6 A four-GPU DDP example with no model-parallel sharding. With DP = 4, every GPU holds a static replica of the same attention layers and complete routed-expert pool, experts 0–15, while processing different input data. Figure 36 A host loop executes exact-size expert GEMMs. It avoids padded arithmetic, but GPU-produced row counts must become host-visible before the runtime can submit the per-expert operations. The separate streams in this conceptual drawing are not required by the method; the legacy Olmo fallback submits its GEMMs on the current stream.

Figure 65 Under a pipeline schedule, static per-layer replay needs one saved-context slot per in-flight microbatch. (a) Without a pipeline the backward of each microbatch consumes the layer’s saved context before the next forward overwrites it, so one graph per layer serves every microbatch. (b) With three microbatches in flight, a shared slot is overwritten by F1 and F2 before B0 reads it; three slots, each with its own graph and static buffers, are recycled as each microbatch’s backward for the layer completes. Conceptual illustration after the design described for Megatron-Core (Yan et al., 2026); no measured quantities.

The experiment isolates one BF16 square expert projection on one B300 with Nlocal = 16 and d = h = 4096. Preliminary single-node measurements use eight B300 GPUs, an eight-layer BF16 MoE model, top-4 random routing, no PP, and approximately 3.2B active parameters. Figure 54 Conversion and layout costs in MXFP8 execution. MXFP8 is faster only when its GEMM savings exceed these costs. This is a schematic cost model, not measured timing. The displayed O(MK + KN) conversion term assumes both operands are quantized on the critical path. In Olmo training, the K × N weight conversion is normally paid during cache refresh and reused across microbatches, leaving activation conversion as the principal per-invocation cost. For small GEMMs, that remaining overhead can still turn the expected speedup into a slowdown.

Figure 9 The distributed optimizer and EP reduce different parts of DDP’s persistent parameter-sized training state. Under the illustrated BF16-execution, FP32-gradient, and two-moment FP32 optimizer policy, naive DDP uses 18 bytes per parameter. Sharding the FP32 main weights and optimizer states evenly over D replica ranks reduces this to 6+12/D bytes while compute weights and gradient buffers remain replicated. Sharding routed-expert compute weights and gradients over the expert-parallel model-sharding degree ME (EP-MP; defined in Section 5) further reduces their per-rank memory contribution to 6/ME + 12/D bytes when D = MEDE . Dense and shared parameters follow their separate replica groups. This accounting excludes execution working memory, including activations, routing and communication buffers, kernel workspaces, execution caches, and allocator fragmentation, as well as uneven shards and small auxiliary tensors that are not sharded.

Figure 62 Block recompute removes nearly two thirds of activation memory at a one-fifth throughput cost in this matched configuration. Bars show the arithmetic mean of three fresh-process repetitions; dots show the individual ten-step windows, and the sample standard deviations are smaller than the dot markers. Normal training in this campaign sustains 54.68K tokens/s/GPU at 103.03 GiB peak active memory; recomputing every transformer block sustains 43.22K tokens/s/GPU at 76.90 GiB, 20.95% lower throughput for 26.13 GiB (25.36%) less peak memory. The lower segment of each memory bar, labeled “persistent”, is the memory resident between steps (parameters, gradient buffers, optimizer states, and persistent buffers), 62.21 GiB in both modes; the reduction therefore falls entirely on the transient activation part, which shrinks from 40.82 to 14.69 GiB. Measurements use four NVIDIA B300 GPUs and the fixed model, batch, routing, and timing protocol described in the text.

Figure 7 Weight materialization and gradient synchronization run on different clocks. Under the illustrated FSDP schedule, unsharded weights are materialized around layer use in each microbatch. DDP instead uses static replicas of its local weights throughout the accumulation window and synchronizes accumulated gradients at the optimizer-step boundary. When EP is enabled, token dispatch and combine still recur in every routed layer and microbatch. The phase widths were manually reconstructed from one representative profile and preserve its approximate timing proportions; the diagram is not an aggregate benchmark.

Figure 16 Rowwise EP targets remote expert rows without block packing. In the same illustrative two-rank, top-2 example as Figure 15, GPU-resident route indices drive a rowwise dispatch kernel that places accepted rows directly into fixed-capacity rank- and expert-major storage. Grouped GEMM consumes that layout without a second permutation. Rowwise combine returns expert outputs directly to their source-token positions for weighted merging, without materializing a peer-packed return buffer. The “AllToAll” labels inside the drawing denote the logical rank exchange; the implementation uses indexed one-sided row movement rather than an NCCL all-to-all collective. As in Figure 15, token E’s route to expert 1 does not fit in rank 0’s 12-row capacity, so it is dropped and combine treats it as zero. The drawing explains data layout and movement, not measured performance.

Figure 42 The load-balancing loss falls while load imbalance rises. Orange is the original λLBL = 0.05 trajectory; blue reloads the step-17,000 checkpoint with λLBL = 0.005. Unscaled LBL is the sum over the 47 MoE blocks; imbalance is the worst max/mean expert count over blocks and ranks. Smoothed traces only; Figure 45 adds the raw measurements and the cross-entropy panel, and Section 10.8.1 gives the protocol.

Figure 11 A four-GPU example with DP = 4, EP-MP = 2, and 16 total experts. Starting from the fully replicated layout in Figure 6, the same four DP ranks form EP-MP groups of size 2 and EP-DP groups of size 2. Each EP-MP group keeps attention replicated and shards experts 0–7 and 8–15 across its two ranks. Dispatch moves selected token rows to the appropriate expert rank, and combine returns their contributions. Ranks holding corresponding shards in the two EP-MP groups are EP-DP replicas and reduce gradients together.

Figure 70 Olmo’s merge rule preserves dense-like scale at random initialization. The four conventions are those of Table 37. (a) The Olmo output RMS is 1.016× the matched dense reference, corresponding to a 1.032× variance ratio. (b) Its fixed-router input-gradient RMS is also 1.016× dense; differentiating through the router raises the ratio to 1.054×. (d) Olmo’s output also stays closest in direction to the dense output. Forward measurements use the full-size initialization configuration; backward measurements use the dimensionally scaled surrogate described in the text.

Figure 60 Layer recompute trades additional forward work for lower activation memory. In this illustrative schedule, F0 and F1 are checkpointed, whereas F2 and F3 retain their backward-needed activations. Checkpointing discards F0/F1’s internal activations but retains their boundary inputs; the two forwards are therefore recomputed immediately before B1 and B0. The 5 GB increments and smooth memory curve illustrate the accounting and are not measurements from a training run.

Figure 43 Soft router mass and requested routes can diverge sharply. Orange denotes expert 1 (A), and teal denotes expert 2 (B). Each outlined tile is one token in a two-expert, top-1 router. Its ten interior dots discretize the normalized scores used to form P ; the tile border marks the sole selected route, which is also executed in this capacityfree construction. Panels (a) and (b) hold P = (3/5, 2/5) fixed. Panel (a) is hard-balanced, with f = (1/2, 1/2) and unscaled LBL equal to one. Panel (b) concentrates expert 1’s soft mass into two decisive wins while expert 2 wins four tokens 0.6–0.4, giving f = (1/3, 2/3), Ireqmax = 4/3, and LBL = 14/15. Panel (c) draws all ten tokens in an extreme limit: one (1, 0) expert-1 win and nine (1/2− ϵ, 1/2 + ϵ) expert-2 wins yield f = (0.1, 0.9), P → (0.55, 0.45), Ireqmax = 1.8, and LBL → 0.92. Panel (c)’s five-orange/five-teal dot patterns show the ϵ → 0+ limiting soft mass; their teal borders mark the strict expert-2 wins for every ϵ > 0. Dots belonging to the losing expert are soft scores, not selected routes. Exact zeros, ones, and ϵ → 0+ are boundary idealizations approachable with finite logits; the panels are feasible score tables, not a training trajectory, and the displayed values are counterexamples rather than minima.

Figure 15 Block all-to-all EP exposes the complete packing path. In this illustrative two-rank, top-2 example, local dispatch replicates token rows and packs routes by destination rank. The first all-to-all exchanges peer-contiguous blocks, and a global permutation converts the received rank-major layout into local-expert order for grouped GEMM. Combine reverses the global layout conversion and all-to-all, restores token order, fills a capacity-dropped route with zero, and merges route contributions using the router weights. The drawing explains data layout and movement, not measured performance.

Figure 30 Submission headroom is the queued, not-yet-executed device work. Both curves are computed exactly from the drawn boxes: headroom jumps up by a kernel’s device duration when the CPU completes that kernel’s submission and drains at unit rate while the GPU executes, so the GPU is idle exactly where the curve sits at zero. (a) Cheap submissions of large kernels (k1–k3) build the lead; a host-heavy stretch of small kernels (k4–k7) spends it faster than it is replaced, and after the lead reaches zero the GPU waits for k7’s submission. (b) Within one microbatch, each Python-driven forward submission costs the CPU more time than its kernel costs the GPU, so the lead carried in from the previous backward drains layer by layer and grazes zero just as the last forward submission arrives. The autograd-driven backward inverts the imbalance, and while the GPU executes it, the CPU is already submitting the next microbatch’s forward: the rebuilt surplus is the lead that forward will spend. Each CPU box’s width is the full host cost of its submission, including Python and dispatcher time. Conceptual illustration with no measured quantities.

Figure 14 Routing overhead grows from dense execution to local MoE and conventional all-to-all EP. A dense MLP has no routing path. MoE without EP adds one local permutation into expert order and one unpermutation back to token order. Conventional all-to-all EP expands dispatch into permute–all-to-all–permute and combine into unpermute–all-to-all–unpermute. Rowwise EP instead attempts to move selected rows directly between token-source and expert ranks. The drawing is not performance evidence.

Figure 21 A shared symmetric buffer saves memory but can overwrite saved payloads. With a private symmetric buffer per block, each saved payload survives untouched until its block’s backward, but resident symmetric memory grows with the number of local blocks; one shared buffer keeps the footprint constant, but forward visits blocks in order 1, 2, 3 while backward returns in order 3, 2, 1, so block 1’s backward reads a payload that later blocks have overwritten. Scratch buffers, which no later operation reads, safely take the shared path; payloads saved for backward keep per-block slots whose reuse is controlled by the lease system of Figure 22, and activation recomputation turns a saved payload back into scratch, restoring the shared option. Conceptual illustration with no measured quantities.

Figure 31 A per-block synchronization point stops the CPU from running ahead. In the dense timeline (top), the CPU submits blocks well in advance of their GPU start times, so several blocks of device work stay queued and the GPU always finds its next operation waiting. In the routed timeline (bottom), every block contains a synchronization point: the CPU begins a sync wait, blocks until the GPU reaches the matching point, and only then submits the remainder of the block. Submission headroom cannot accumulate beyond one block, so the two processors advance in lock step and any GPU stall is exposed. The timeline is conceptual and does not encode measured duration. Section 8.4 examines the synchronizing operations themselves.

Figure 35 Padded BMM regularizes the ragged row dimension. Every expert is padded to capacity C, enabling one regular batched operation. Empty rows nevertheless consume matrix-multiply work, and their outputs are discarded. Expert weight shapes are fixed; only routed row counts differ.

Figure 28 The same ranks participate in several logical topologies. This illustrative eight-rank example uses PP = 2, DP = 4, EP-MP = 2, and EP-DP = 2. Each PP stage stores one layer range; EP-MP pairs form a complete expert set; EP-DP pairs connect replicas of an expert shard; and PP groups join matching data-parallel coordinates across stages. Context parallelism is omitted. The diagram establishes group membership, not the hardware path or a measured production placement.

Figure 40 GroupedGEMM throughput generally falls as expert loads concentrate. The experiment isolates one BF16 square expert projection on one B300 with Nlocal = 16, M = 65,536 routed rows, and d = h = 4096. We draw symmetric-Dirichlet proposals, convert them to exact eight-row-aligned counts with at least one tile per expert, and select ten distinct histograms from each of ten equal-width IH ranges. Every dot therefore has the same total rows, operands, dimensions, and useful FLOPs. Each dot averages four fixed expert-index permutations in each of three fresh processes. Each of those 12 conditions averages 20 queued CUDA-event samples after 10 warm-ups; execution order is randomized and balanced controls bracket every ten cases. The magenta curve connects the median of each ten-histogram range. The correlation and bootstrap interval are computed over the 100 histogram means. This kernel-only test excludes dispatch, communication, and cross-rank waiting.

Figure 66 Square-root learning-rate scaling leaves visible curvature changes at large batch-size transitions. Training cross-entropy loss is shown against cumulative tokens for a 3.21B@23.10B MoE trained for approximately 2.07 trillion tokens. The light trace is the raw loss and the dark trace is a time-weighted exponential moving average (TWEMA). Dotted lines mark each global-batch increase, labeled with the new batch in Mi tokens (written as M in the figure); the batch progresses through 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 15, and 24 Mi tokens, and the later transitions occur at approximately 409B, 777B, and 1.375T cumulative tokens. Appendix B.8 records the run’s recipe and reproduction artifacts.

Figure 32 A faster GPU can move the critical microbatch size to the right. The solid red curve represents CPU submission time, while the blue, purple, and green curves represent H100, B200, and B300 execution time. Below a crossover, the device can consume work faster than the host supplies it; faster execution with an unchanged host path therefore requires a larger microbatch to restore submission headroom. Additional GPU memory can extend the feasible microbatch range, while reducing submission overhead (dashed red; CUDA Graph replay is one way to reduce this overhead) can move the crossover to the left. The curves, intersections, and memory limits are qualitative annotations rather than measurements; no numerical critical size is implied.

Figure 25 Interleaved-1F1B and 1F1B-V schedules with PP = 4 and eight microbatches. A label such as 4B2 denotes backward for virtual stage 4 and microbatch 2; the lighter forward/backward shades identify stages 4–7, the second virtual stage stored by each rank. Gray cells are empty schedule slots. The bubble percentages are empty-slot fractions in the symbolic schedule, not measured GPU idle time.

Figure 55 One FP32mainweight becomes two orientedMXFP8 caches. After every optimizer update, the FP32 main weight is quantized into the forward cache and, through an explicit transpose, the dgrad cache, each consumed as the RHS of its scaled grouped GEMM and reused across microbatches until the next update. The figure treats W as the right-hand operand (xW ), so its W and W .T labels are W⊤ and W in the notation of the text. The gather that assembles the sharded main weight stages through a transient BF16 copy freed immediately after quantization; under the FP8-only expert-parameter mode evaluated here, forward and backward hold no weight other than the two caches. The loop closes through the weight-gradient path: the BF16 Wgrad output accumulates into the FP32 gradient buffer and is reduced across ranks before the optimizer update writes the FP32 main weight and triggers the next refresh; the dgrad output flows to the previous layer. Notation: Q quantizes to MXFP8 and T transposes; (fp8, R) is qdata with rowwise scales; (fp8,R+B) keeps rowwise plus blocked (swizzled) scales; mx8mx8bf16 names the two MXFP8 inputs and BF16 output of the grouped GEMM. Conceptual illustration with no measured quantities.

Figure 57 Routed-expert MXFP8 forward and backward. Forward quantizes routed rows for dispatch, applies MXFP8 grouped GEMMs for the up/gate and down projections, and quantizes the combine payload. Backward reverses the communication path, uses MXFP8 weight caches for dgrad, and uses the current BF16 grouped-GEMM path for Wgrad before accumulation into FP32 gradient buffers that are then reduced with the other ranks’ contributions (dashed arrows). The drawing also identifies saved, discarded, recomputed, quantized, and dequantized values across the custom-autograd boundary. Notation: (fp8, R) is qdata with rowwise scales; (fp8,R+B) keeps rowwise plus blocked (swizzled) scales; Q, DQ, and T are quantize, dequantize, and transpose; Q+S is a fused quantize-plus-swizzle; mx8mx8bf16 and bf16bf16bf16 name each grouped GEMM’s two input dtypes and output dtype. Weight labels treat W as the right-hand operand (xW ), so W and W .T correspond to W⊤ and W in the notation of the text.

Figure 39 Splitting one projection into four or eight expert GEMMs. The four-expert path executes four [T, 8192] @ [8192, 20480] GEMMs; the eight-expert path executes eight [T, 8192] @ [8192, 10240] GEMMs. Both are exact partitions of the same [T, 8192] @ [8192, 81920] dense projection and therefore match its useful FLOPs, weights, and outputs. Grouped inputs repeat the dense input four or eight times. Curves show means across eight paired trials, one on each of eight B300 GPUs, and light bands show the full eight-GPU ranges; each GPU measures the dense control with both grouped partitions, and its two dense measurements are averaged before the dense curve is summarized. The horizontal axis is logarithmic through T = 4096 and linear thereafter; the dashed divider marks the scale change, and no values are omitted. The final two points, T = 32,768 and 65,536, are oversized diagnostics rather than representative training shapes. Only the projection is timed; Appendix A.11 records the complete timing protocol and representative ratios.

Figure 73 The very-large-Me grouped GEMM slowdown follows SM clock, not per-clock efficiency. Lines show medians and bands show the full range across eight trials. Both paths execute the same useful FLOPs, although the dense control reuses one weight matrix while grouped GEMM reads 16 expert matrices. The software power-cap limiter was active in 99.3% of telemetry samples; no thermal, hardware-brake, or reliability limiter was observed.

Figure 72 The same Imax can describe different grouped GEMM workloads. Left: sorted expert loads for a representative 64K-row case. Right: rank-local grouped GEMM throughput normalized to the balanced assignment in the same process. Large markers report arithmetic means, while small translucent points show five independent runs on the same B300. In each run, let a be the base expert index. The matched single spike overloads expert a, while the three-hot assignment overloads experts (a, a+ 5, a+ 10) mod 16; the five values of a are 0, 3, 6, 9, and 12. Every run averages 20 queued CUDA-event samples after 10 warm-ups. The benchmark isolates one BF16 d = h = 4096 projection and excludes dispatch, communication, and cross-rank waiting.

Figure 20 Crossing the regular–symmetric boundary: staging copies versus direct access. The remote endpoint of a one-sided transfer must live in the symmetric heap, which is allocated separately from regular PyTorch tensors; inter-node GPU-initiated transfers require the local endpoint to be symmetric as well. (a) A generic integration pays one copy on each side of the boundary. (b) The Olmo-core rowwise path removes these copies where kernels can target symmetric memory directly: the expert grouped GEMM reads the dispatch buffer in place, the down projection writes its output directly into the symmetric combine buffer, and MXFP8 dispatch fuses quantization into the PUT kernel. Conceptual illustration with no measured quantities.

Figure 23 Communication–compute overlap lengthens this measured forward path. This two-node DeepEP v2, EP-MP = 16, 128-expert, top-8 BF16 benchmark uses 16,384 tokens per rank, d = h = 8,192, and a 32-SM communication budget. Both panels align time to the first dispatch. papers.selection_reason: Efficient and scalable MoE training stack for large language models; directly relevant to LLM architecture/training and AI efficiency.
papers.title: Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training
papers.tldr: A redesigned Olmo-core stack makes large-scale MoE training more efficient and scalable by combining specialized parallelism, communication-free routing, MXFP8, and flexible checkpointing.

papers.abstract: Generating a token with a language model requires a fixed amount of arithmetic, whose energy sets a floor beneath any hardware. For Qwen3-1.7B at a 16K-token context, gate-level measurements at 5 nm place this floor at 0.89 mJ per token, yet an NVIDIA B300 spends 391-1,120x that. The excess is the price of generality, software layers, programmable hardware and moving weights and key-value (KV) caches from external memory, and it widens with each process generation. We present a co-design approach that brings token generation close to this floor and then lowers the floor itself, optimizing silicon and model together in a gate-level search loop. Fixing one model architecture in the datapath, with weights still loadable, and holding weights and every conversation's KV cache on-die, a pre-silicon 5 nm design brings an unchanged Qwen3-1.7B token to 3.4x its floor. Co-designing the model with the circuits at fixed quality lowers the floor to 0.29 mJ and the token to 0.52 mJ, 1.8x the new floor and less than the baseline model's arithmetic alone, while on-die capacity grows from one user to twelve. Against a measured B300 serving the same twelve users, the design decodes each user's tokens 110x faster at 690x lower energy. To show that one fixed architecture can serve, as a co-processor, the latency-critical workloads around a frontier model, we introduce Polyglot-DC (1.7B and 4B, each with its own design), specialized for each job by distillation and task-specific training into its own weights. As a drafter it speeds single-user speculative decoding of large open models by up to 6.6x at the maximum reasoning effort. Its guard returns multilingual verdicts in a millisecond or less, within a point of the strongest open guard. Its agent and financial-reasoning models lead comparable open models on established benchmarks, with a reasoning turn falling from seconds to tens of milliseconds.
bullets: Targets the large energy gap between unavoidable token-generation arithmetic and general-purpose GPUs, where memory movement and programmability dominate.
Keeps model weights and all users’ KV caches on-chip, with a datapath specialized to one loadable model architecture.
A pre-silicon design reaches 0.52 mJ per token—1.8× its co-designed arithmetic floor—and supports up to twelve users on-chip.
Compared with a measured NVIDIA B300 serving twelve users, it reports 110× higher per-user decoding speed and 690× lower energy.
Polyglot-DC extends the fixed architecture to distilled drafting, multilingual guarding, agent, and financial-reasoning models, with reported latency and benchmark gains.

Figure 15 | Speculative decoding across two machines, in the draft-then-verify flow of Xia et al. (2024), the steps numbered in the order of one round. Each machine reads the prompt for itself and keeps its own cache, so no cache ever crosses the link between them. The Exstill card drafts six tokens one after another at about 50 µs each, every token conditioned on the ones before it, and the six token identifiers cross to the target, gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3-Next, Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4-Pro or Muse Spark Open, on whatever system serves it. papers.selection_reason: Chip co-design for near-floor LLM token generation with on-die KV cache; directly relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: Exstill: The Most Efficient Single-Chip Processor for the Next Token
papers.tldr: Exstill co-designs a fixed-function 5 nm chip and language models to approach the arithmetic energy floor, achieving dramatically faster and more energy-efficient token generation while supporting multiple specialized workloads.

papers.abstract: Iterative machine-learning algorithms repeatedly access large real-valued matrices through matrix-vector products, and their performance is limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic throughput. Lossless compression schemes that support computation directly over the compressed data reduce both the data moved and the memory footprint of these workloads. The mm-RePair framework [11] follows this approach by applying the RePair grammar compressor to the Compressed Sparse Row/Value (CSRV) representation of a matrix and performing matrix-vector multiplications directly on the compressed data. Its effectiveness, however, degrades on matrices that are dense or contain many distinct values. In this paper we present a hybrid strategy for the mm-RePair framework that combines grammar and entropy compression. The CSRV sequence is partitioned into a grammar-compressible component, formed by the entries that mm-RePair can compress effectively, and an entropy-compressible component holding the remaining entries, which is encoded with the ans-fold coder [24]. Compression improves further by sorting and delta encoding the entries of each row in the CSRV representation, and by remapping the alphabet to a contiguous range. Experiments on real-valued machine-learning matrices, including word embeddings and transformer hidden states, show that our hybrid strategy is more compact than the original \mmRepair on every input and reduces the peak memory of multiplication, with the largest gains on dense matrices with many distinct values, at competitive multiplication times. It also outperforms the column-reordering variant of \mmRepair on most of the matrices, and combining the two is even more compact on the sparse ones, at the cost of a much longer compression time. Finally, our strategy scales with the number of threads as well as the original \mmRepair does.
authors: Felipe A. Louza, Giovanni Manzini, Guilherme P. Telles
bullets: Targets memory-bandwidth bottlenecks in repeated matrix-vector products by reducing stored and transferred data.
Partitions CSRV matrix data between RePair grammar compression and ans-fold entropy coding.
Further improves compression through row sorting, delta encoding, and contiguous alphabet remapping.
Experiments on word embeddings and transformer hidden states show greater compactness and lower peak multiplication memory than mm-RePair, with competitive multiplication times.
Combining the method with column reordering improves compactness on sparse matrices but substantially increases compression time; thread scaling remains comparable to mm-RePair.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of the partitioning scheme. The integer sequence Sint is partitioned into two components: SA is compressed with RePair as in mm-RePair, and SB is encoded with ans-fold, while V is stored unchanged.

Figure 5: Compression pipeline of hybrid mm-RePair. The matrix is converted into its CSRV representation (V, S) (step 1), and S is encoded as the integer sequence Sint (step 2). When criterion (1) holds, the identifiers of Sint are replaced by their ranks and the reverse mapping wcode is produced (step 3). The remapping is computed once on the whole sequence, so a single wcode serves both components, and it does not affect the partition, which depends only on digram frequencies. The sequence is partitioned into SA and SB (step 4), and SA is compressed with RePair into RA and CA (step 5). The rows of CA and of SB are sorted and delta encoded (ole) and entropy coded with ans-fold, as is wcode, while RA is stored as a packed array (step 6). The five blocks on the right form the compressed representation (RA, CA, SB, V ), plus wcode.

Figure 3: Compression pipeline of mm-RePair in its re-ans variant. The matrix is converted into its CSRV representation (V, S) (step 1), the sequence S is encoded as the integer sequence Sint (step 2), Sint is compressed with RePair, modified so that no rule contains the delimiter 0, into the rule set R and the final sequence C (step 3), and R is stored as a packed array while C is entropy coded with ans-fold (step 4). The compressed representation is the triple (R, C, V ), with V stored uncompressed.

Figure 6: The compression pipeline of hybrid mm-RePair on the matrix of Figure 1. To keep the example small, an incident digram occurring twice is enough here to keep an entry in SA. The CSRV sequence is encoded as Sint (steps 1–2). Criterion (1) holds, since |Sint| = 36, |Σ| = 12 and b = 4 give 36 · 28 > 32 · 12, producing wcode (step 3). The remapped sequence is partitioned into SA and SB (step 4), SA is compressed with RePair (step 5), and the rows of SB are sorted and delta encoded (step 6).

Figure 7: Relative improvement in compression ratio of re-pc, re-hybd and re-hybd-pc over reans, computed as (co − cr)/co, where co and cr are the compression ratios of re-ans and of the compared method.

Figure 2: The mm-RePair representation of the matrix of Figure 1. The top part shows the integer sequence Sint with m = 6, obtained by encoding $ as 0 and each pair ⟨ℓ, j⟩ as ℓm+ j+1, and the numbers above the cells are positions. The bottom part shows the rule set R and the final sequence C produced by RePair. Since no rule may contain 0, every delimiter remains in C, which also contains terminals, such as 10 in the first row and 1 in the second.

Figure 1: A matrix M (left) and its CSRV representation (V, S) (right). The array V holds the distinct nonzero values of M , and S is a single sequence of t+n symbols, obtained by scanning M row by row: each nonzero M [i, j] becomes the pair ⟨ℓ, j⟩ with V [ℓ] = M [i, j], and the delimiter $ closes each row. In S the pair ⟨2, 5⟩ of the second row denotes the value V [2] = 6.0 in column 5, while the same value in column 4 of the first row is the different pair ⟨2, 4⟩, since a pair identifies a value in a given column.
