papers.selection_reason: Proposes hybrid compression strategies for matrix-vector multiplication to reduce memory footprint in iterative ML algorithms.
papers.title: Hybrid Compression for Memory-Efficient Matrix-Vector Multiplication
papers.tldr: A hybrid grammar–entropy compression scheme makes compressed matrix-vector multiplication more memory-efficient, especially for dense matrices with many distinct values.

papers.abstract: Blackwell tensor cores support native inference with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4), but NVFP4 leaves a perplexity (PPL) gap to BF16. Choosing a format for each 16-element block can improve accuracy, but current matrix multiply instructions cannot execute choices this fine. Applying these rules at hardware-compatible tiles loses most of their benefit. We introduce FlipQuant, which selects E2M1 or E0M3 for each MMA weight tile. It keeps both quantized weight candidates fixed and learns a binary format map from end-to-end gradients of a bucketed KL loss to a BF16 teacher, re-evaluating them after each update. Native kernels execute 16 x 64 tiles on SM120 and 256 x 64 tiles on SM100 with median GEMM overheads of 1.9% and 1.7%, respectively. Across six language models and two corpora, FlipQuant at 16 x 64 closes 42.5% of NVFP4's PPL gap to BF16 on average, compared with 13.3% for FourOverSix. Code is available at https://github.com/brian030128/flipquant.
authors: Jian-Jia Chen, Brian J. Chan, Wen-Hung Lee, Yi-Ting Li, Po-Shen Chen, Kuan-Te Kuo, Hsien-Cheng Huang, Cody Hao Yu, Chi-Chih Chang, Mohamed S. Abdelfattah, Kai-Chiang Wu
bullets: Targets the accuracy gap of native 4-bit W4A4 NVFP4 inference versus BF16.
Learns a binary format map for each MMA weight tile using gradients from a bucketed KL loss to a BF16 teacher.
Keeps both quantized candidates fixed while re-evaluating tile-format choices after each update.
Uses native 16×64 tiles on SM120 and 256×64 tiles on SM100, with median GEMM overheads of 1.9% and 1.7%.
Across six language models and two corpora, closes 42.5% of the NVFP4–BF16 PPL gap on average, versus 13.3% for FourOverSix.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a hardware-native quantization method for efficient LLM inference, relevant to memory efficiency.
papers.title: Gradient-Guided Hardware-Native MIXFP4
papers.tldr: FlipQuant learns hardware-compatible per-tile choices between E2M1 and E0M3 formats, substantially reducing NVFP4’s perplexity gap to BF16 with minimal GEMM overhead.

papers.abstract: Occupancy estimation for automated vehicles is a crucial task that builds a 3D map using vehicle sensors. This map allows the vehicle to identify drivable areas and various obstacle classes. The task involves complex subtasks such as depth estimation, object classification, and segmentation to align semantic information with the 3D grid. Moreover, producing these estimations from multiple sensors demands significant computational power and memory, as high-dimensional data fusion requires complex feature extraction and processing. Consequently, most existing methods rely on large and computationally intensive architectures that are not suitable for real-time or real-world applications. We present a real-time, lightweight architecture that leverages camera and radar sensors through a residual multi-stage head. Unlike prior methods that rely on heavy camera-only blocks, our architecture employs camera-radar fusion and lightweight components. Additionally, we introduce a task-specific data augmentation strategy that enhances data diversity and improves generalisation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance, attaining 45.7 mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) on Occ3D and 41.9 Ray-level Intersection over Union (RayIoU) (41.9) on OpenOcc datasets, running at 17.2 frames per second (FPS) and using only 5.3 GB of memory, compared with 4.1 FPS and 7.7 GB for STCOcc.
authors: Ruan Bispo, Tim Brophy, Reenu Mohandas, Anthony Scanlan, Ciaran Eising
bullets: Targets the high cost and complexity of multi-sensor 3D occupancy estimation for automated vehicles.
Uses a residual multi-stage head with lightweight camera–radar fusion instead of heavy camera-only blocks.
Introduces task-specific data augmentation to improve data diversity and generalisation.
Reports 45.7 mIoU on Occ3D and 41.9 RayIoU on OpenOcc.
Runs at 17.2 FPS with 5.3 GB memory, compared with 4.1 FPS and 7.7 GB for STCOcc.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed dual-supervised Occupancy Head. The BEV features are expanded and enriched via Z-embedding, which are processed by a ResNet3D backbone and an FPN3D neck. An auxiliary head and a final 3D U-Net decoder perform hierarchical decoding with independent supervision. The final occupancy prediction is obtained by residual fusion of both predictions.

Fig. 1. Our proposed architecture using camera and radar data. Firstly, the camera and radar features are extracted using the respective feature extractors. Secondly, we lift and fuse these features into a BEV using a BEV Transformation and fusion module. Finally, the proposed occupancy head (highlighted in blue) processes the BEV features to produce the 3D occupancy estimation.

Despite slightly lower RayIoU, LiNO produces visually denser and more consistent voxel predictions than the baseline, which may result from GT sparsity and the sensitivity of the RayIoU to mislabels (red boxes).

Each class is evaluated under three distance tolerances: RayIoU@1, RayIoU@2, and RayIoU@4 (1 m, 2 m, and 4 m). Black numbers above each marker denote the mean RayIoU per class across the three thresholds. As the distance tolerance increases, the metric becomes more permissive, leading to higher RayIoU values as larger spatial errors are still counted as correct matches.

papers.selection_reason: Real-time lightweight camera-radar 3D occupancy estimation is relevant to 3D perception and efficient inference.
papers.title: LiNO: Lightweight Network for Occupancy Estimation
papers.tldr: LiNO is a lightweight camera–radar occupancy-estimation network designed for real-time 3D mapping with lower computational and memory demands.

papers.abstract: A vision transformer read at a higher resolution than it was trained at spreads each attention row over many more patches, yet every row must still hand out exactly one unit of weight. A law of softmax attention predicts that a growing crowd of bounded scores dilutes the attention on any patch or register whose score stays fixed. The same law gives a remedy that needs no training: multiply every score, the sink's included, by the ratio of the logarithms of the test and training token counts. Given sufficient margins at the training resolution, this keeps the attention on a match when one is present, and on a sink such as a register when none is, though trained models need not meet those margins. We test these predictions in public vision transformers and in controlled models read far above their training token count. Attention spreads as predicted. Registers lose their share, though production models compensate in part, and the rescaling holds the share of DINOv2's registers nearly level. Applied at test time without training, the rescaling recovers part of the lost accuracy in nearly every model, with absolute or rotary positions and with registers, and on images with native detail. The calibrated multiplier rises with the logarithmic ratio on average and varies across models. Its rise is steeper than the square-root rule used in image generators; in controlled models the log ratio is also more accurate, while in the public models the two rules' accuracy difference remains unresolved. The rescaling does not restore the attention a model learned, and why it helps, beyond countering the dilution, remains open.
bullets: Problem: Increasing resolution creates more tokens while each attention row still sums to one, reducing attention to fixed-score patches or register tokens.
Method: Apply a training-free multiplier to all attention scores, including sink/register scores, based on the logarithmic ratio of test and training token counts.
Finding: Attention dilution and register-share loss appear as predicted; the rescaling keeps DINOv2 register attention nearly stable.
Result: Test-time rescaling recovers part of the lost accuracy across nearly every tested model, including models with absolute or rotary positional encodings and native-detail images.
Scope: The method does not fully restore learned attention, and the mechanism beyond counteracting dilution remains unresolved; its advantage over square-root scaling varies by model.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes attention dilution in Vision Transformers at high resolution and proposes a training-free rescaling method to recover accuracy.
papers.title: Spread Too Thin: How Higher Resolution Dilutes a Vision Transformer's Attention, and a Training-Free Rescaling
papers.tldr: Higher-resolution inputs dilute vision-transformer attention across more patches, but scaling attention scores by the log ratio of test-to-training token counts can recover some lost accuracy without retraining.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on long contexts, making Key-Value (KV) caches dominate memory usage and inference latency. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods effectively compress KV caches to sub-4-bit levels but often overlook inefficiencies in memory alignment and decoding speed. This work introduces MeltKV, a memory-latency co-optimized KV cache quantization framework for long-context LLM serving. MeltKV employs a memory-aligned variable-bit index packing scheme that adaptively assigns bit-widths to grouped key channels and compactly stores indices within standard data-types, eliminating redundant bits. Additionally, head-wise codebook sharing reduces the total codebook size while maintaining accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that MeltKV effectively compresses KV representations to sub-4-bit levels down to 1 bit and, at comparable perplexity, achieves 48.1% lower memory usage and 52.9% lower latency than state-of-the-art VQ methods.
authors: Jiyun Han, Seongjoon Cho, Seungkyu Choi
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and inference-latency bottlenecks in long-context LLM serving.
Adaptively assigns bit-widths to grouped key channels and packs indices into standard data types to remove redundant bits.
Shares codebooks across attention heads to reduce codebook storage while preserving accuracy.
Reaches sub-4-bit compression, down to 1 bit, with comparable perplexity.
Reports 48.1% lower memory usage and 52.9% lower latency than prior VQ methods at comparable perplexity.

papers.selection_reason: KV cache compression via variable-bit vector quantization for long-context LLM serving, directly fitting KV cache efficiency and long-context topics.
papers.title: MeltKV: Memory-Aligned KV Cache Compression via Variable-Bit Packed Vector Quantization for Long-Context LLMs

papers.abstract: 4-bit weight-activation quantization (W4A4) is an important approach for efficient large language model (LLM) inference. Recent hierarchical formats such as HiFloat4 (HIF4) improve the representational range of 4-bit quantization through multi-level scaling. However, the same local mantissa representation in HIF4 may not be equally suitable for weights and activations, which exhibit distinct distribution characteristics. To address this limitation, we propose HiMX, a mixed-mantissa framework built upon the hierarchical scaling structure of HIF4. Our key observation is that the two HIF4-compatible mantissa representations, S1P2 and E2M1, exhibit complementary quantization behavior: the denser S1P2 format provides higher resolution for concentrated weight distributions, while the wider-spaced E2M1 format provides complementary quantization characteristics for activation tensors. HiMX enables operand-tailored mantissa representations while converting heterogeneous mantissas into fixed-point integer operands with operand-specific widths, allowing different operand formats to share a unified integer multiply-accumulate (MAC) array. Block-level analysis on Qwen3-8B shows that HIF4-S1P2 is better suited for weights while HIF4 E2M1 is better suited for activations, and their mixed-format combination achieves lower output MSE than homogeneous configurations. Across multiple benchmarks, HiMX reduces the average end-to-end accuracy loss from 2.38 to 1.77 points on Qwen3-8B and from 2.23 to 1.85 points on Qwen3-30B-A3B, demonstrating the potential benefit of heterogeneous mantissa representations for W4A4 LLM inference.
authors: Zhiyuan Zhang, Yanzhao Li, Hui Dong, Sifan Cheng, Jingwei Zhang
bullets: W4A4 quantization is efficient but weights and activations have different distribution characteristics.
HiMX combines HIF4-S1P2 for weights, which offers denser resolution, with HIF4-E2M1 for activations, which provides wider spacing.
Operand-specific widths convert the heterogeneous mantissas into integer operands compatible with one unified MAC array.
On Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, the mixed format reduces average end-to-end accuracy loss compared with homogeneous HIF4 configurations.
The approach is evaluated for W4A4 LLM inference; the abstract does not establish broader hardware or model generality.

papers.tldr: HiMX improves 4-bit LLM inference by tailoring HIF4 mantissa formats separately to weights and activations while using a shared integer MAC array.

papers.abstract: Compressing large language models lowers serving cost, but a single automatic metric may miss quality loss. For the WMT26 Model Compression constrained track, we compress google/gemma-3-12b-it (24.4 GB in bf16) for three translation directions on one H100. Paired bootstrap analysis exposes metric disagreement on 4-bit quantization; guided by WMT24 human meta-evaluation, we use MetricX24-XXL as primary and CometKiwi-XXL as a cross-check. Removing the unused vision stack and non-task vocabulary and using int8 weights or fp8 activations causes no resolved loss, whereas int4 leaves a small residual. QLoRA healing overfits its calibration domain. A Cometoid best-of-4 reranker at $T=0.3$ improves both the 8-bit and 4-bit systems under WMT25 test set. On post-submission WMT26, both remain competitive with bf16 under reference-free metrics; the small difference between the reranked variants is treated as noise.
bullets: Metric disagreement can obscure quality loss, so MetricX24-XXL is paired with CometKiwi-XXL for evaluation.
Removing unused vision components and non-task vocabulary, plus int8 weights or fp8 activations, causes no resolved loss; int4 leaves a small residual.
QLoRA healing overfits its calibration domain rather than reliably recovering quality.
A Cometoid best-of-4 reranker at T=0.3 improves both 8-bit and 4-bit systems.
On post-submission WMT26 evaluation, both compressed systems remain competitive with bf16; differences between reranked variants are treated as noise.

papers.abstract: Wafer-scale accelerators offer massive compute capacity through hundreds of thousands of processing elements (PEs) interconnected across a single wafer, but realizing this potential requires efficient application mapping. Their scale makes programming these systems and mapping applications onto them challenging. Existing approaches rely on template-based mappings to maintain productivity, but these templates restrict the mapping design space. In particular, they impose fixed geometric layouts over the PE grid, often leaving compute and memory resources underutilized. In this work, we present WaferTetris, a system that removes these geometric restrictions through freeform mapping. Its Tetris-like strategy flexibly packs computation across the wafer, improving PE utilization and usable memory capacity while preserving PE-task code. We develop a recurrence-based throughput model that captures branch-and-join dependencies to guide spatial parallelism, and an architecture model with per-color gates that enable existing FPGA place-and-route algorithms to enforce WSE routing constraints. We evaluate WaferTetris on Cerebras WSE-3 using LLM decoding and scientific stencil benchmarks. For LLM decoding, it achieves up to $4.42\times$ the system throughput of a template-based automatic mapping baseline on the same fabric size. Compared with the manually optimized WaferLLM, WaferTetris supports $1.8\times$ the context length for LLaMA3.1-8B (80k versus 44k), while delivering equal or higher per-user throughput at matched context lengths, up to $1.10\times$.
bullets: Template-based mappings constrain PE layouts and can underutilize compute and memory resources.
WaferTetris uses a Tetris-like strategy to pack computation freely while preserving existing PE-task code.
A recurrence-based throughput model captures branch-and-join dependencies to guide spatial parallelism.
Per-color gates adapt FPGA place-and-route algorithms to satisfy wafer-scale routing constraints.
On Cerebras WSE-3, it achieves up to 4.42× the throughput of an automatic template-based baseline and supports 80k versus 44k context length for LLaMA3.1-8B compared with WaferLLM.

papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint of large language models, but preserving accuracy with efficient training remains challenging. Scalar quantization encodes weights independently, while explicit-codebook vector quantization introduces costly search during training. We propose E8-QAT, a 2-bit quantization-aware training framework that uses the $E_8$ lattice as an implicit eight-dimensional codebook. It jointly quantizes weight groups through arithmetic projection without storing or searching an explicit codebook during the training forward pass. A 2-bit core encoding and sparse extension preserve the selected lattice points exactly, adding less than 0.1\% to core index storage. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, E8-QAT matches the performance of the full-precision model in terms of the average score across the four tasks. E8-QAT improves over the state-of-the-art baseline by 2.03\% on IFEval and by 1.51\% on LiveCodeBench, under the same data, schedule, and bit width. The 2-bit representation reduces peak memory by 80\% and supports a $4\times$ larger batch. At each representation's largest feasible batch, E8-QAT reaches $1.97\times$ the decoding throughput of BF16.
bullets: Uses arithmetic projection to jointly quantize weight groups without storing or searching an explicit codebook during training.
Employs a 2-bit core encoding with a sparse extension that adds less than 0.1% to core index storage.

Outperforms the stated baseline on IFEval and LiveCodeBench under matched training conditions.
Reduces peak memory by 80%, enables a 4× larger batch, and achieves 1.97× BF16 decoding throughput at maximum feasible batch size.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) enables efficient deployment, yet transformer architectures remain challenging to quantize due to nonlinear layers. While existing methods attribute accuracy loss to insufficient numerical precision, often necessitating floating-point fallbacks, we demonstrate that degradation is actually driven by specific structural error sources. We find that learned scale parameters in normalization layers and compounded approximations in GELU are the primary error contributors, whereas SoftMax remains inherently robust to aggressive quantization. To address these bottlenecks, we introduce TR-PTQ, a unified integer-only formulation using shared Taylor Region (TR) exponential and logarithm primitives. This approach allows computationally expensive operations, including division and square roots, to be performed entirely in the log-domain via standard integer arithmetic. Combined with a calibration-free, outlier-aware optimization for LayerNorm parameters, our method eliminates the need for floating-point hardware units for nonlinearities, achieving less than 1.5\% absolute accuracy degradation across vision and language benchmarks.
bullets: Identifies LayerNorm scale parameters and compounded GELU approximations as the main sources of quantization error, while SoftMax is robust.
Uses shared Taylor Region exponential and logarithm primitives for a unified integer-only formulation.
Performs division and square roots in the log domain using standard integer arithmetic.
Adds calibration-free, outlier-aware optimization for LayerNorm parameters.
Reports less than 1.5% absolute accuracy degradation across vision and language benchmarks, without floating-point hardware for nonlinearities.

papers.abstract: Batch size scheduling (BSS) plays a critical role in large-scale deep learning training, influencing both optimization dynamics and computational efficiency. Yet, its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that the functional scaling law (FSL) framework introduced in Li et al. (2025a) provides a principled lens for analyzing BSS. Specifically, we characterize the optimal BSS under a fixed data budget and show that its structure depends sharply on task difficulty. For easy tasks, optimal schedules keep increasing batch size throughout. In contrast, for hard tasks, the optimal schedule maintains small batch sizes for most of training and switches to large batches only in a late stage. To explain the emergence of late switching, we uncover a dynamical mechanism -- the fast catch-up effect -- which also manifests in large language model (LLM) pretraining. After switching from small to large batches, the loss rapidly aligns with the constant large-batch trajectory. Using FSL, we show that this effect stems from rapid forgetting of accumulated gradient noise, with the catch-up speed determined by task difficulty. Crucially, this effect implies that large batches can be safely deferred to late training without sacrificing performance, while substantially reducing data consumption. Finally, extensive LLM pretraining experiments -- covering both Dense and MoE architectures with up to 1.1B parameters and 1T tokens -- validate our theoretical predictions. Across all settings, late-switch schedules consistently outperform constant-batch and early-switch baselines.
authors: Jinbo Wang, Binghui Li, Zhanpeng Zhou, Mingze Wang, Yuxuan Sun, Jiaqi Zhang, Xunliang Cai, Lei Wu
bullets: Optimal batch-size schedules depend sharply on task difficulty: easy tasks favor steadily increasing batches, while hard tasks favor late switching.
The proposed “fast catch-up” effect explains why a late switch works: loss quickly aligns with the trajectory of constant large-batch training.
This catch-up arises because accumulated gradient noise is rapidly forgotten, with the speed determined by task difficulty.
Experiments on Dense and MoE LLMs up to 1.1B parameters and 1T tokens support the theory; late-switch schedules outperform constant-batch and early-switch baselines.

papers.abstract: Transformers consist of diverse building blocks, such as embedding layers, normalization layers, self-attention mechanisms, and point-wise feedforward networks. Thus, understanding the differences and interactions among these blocks is important. In this paper, we uncover a clear Sharpness Disparity across these blocks, which emerges early in training and intriguingly persists throughout the training process. Motivated by this finding, we propose Blockwise Learning Rate (LR), a strategy that tailors the LR to each block's sharpness, accelerating large language model (LLM) pre-training. By integrating Blockwise LR into AdamW, we consistently achieve lower terminal loss and nearly $2\times$ speedup compared to vanilla AdamW. We demonstrate this acceleration across GPT-2 and LLaMA, with model sizes ranging from 0.12B to 2B and datasets of OpenWebText, MiniPile, and C4. Finally, we incorporate Blockwise LR into Adam-mini (Zhang et al., 2024), a recently proposed memory-efficient variant of Adam, achieving a combined $2\times$ speedup and $2\times$ memory saving. These results underscore the potential of exploiting the sharpness disparity to improve LLM training.
authors: Jinbo Wang, Mingze Wang, Zhanpeng Zhou, Junchi Yan, Weinan E, Lei Wu
bullets: Identifies a sharpness disparity among embeddings, normalization, attention, and feedforward blocks that appears early and persists during training.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in speech neuroprostheses have enabled new communication avenues for people who have lost the ability to speak due to neurological illness or injury. These systems can decode neural activity during attempted speech into text by relying on language priors to achieve high decoding accuracy. This performance currently comes at the cost of using a compute-intensive language modeling stack, presenting a major bottleneck for real-world use. Further, current language models incur highly variable and disruptive inference latencies, limiting communication throughput and preventing users from reliably participating in natural conversation. We introduce FETTUCCINE, an end-to-end brain-to-text framework that leverages the speed and portability of automatic speech recognition (ASR) models to address the aforementioned practical challenges, while achieving usable (<10%) word error rates (WER), efficient adaptation to neural non-stationarities, and reliable performance on mobile devices. When evaluated using publicly available data from an intracortical speech neuroprosthesis user, FETTUCCINE outperforms previous end-to-end methods, achieving as low as 4.39% WER. Most notably, our models successfully run on a commercially-available mobile device with throughput reaching up to 370x real-time, providing the first demonstration of brain-to-text decoding on a mobile device. We also show that our models can be successfully finetuned to extend usable performance to future days. Beyond performance, our approach enables localization of the neural features most relevant for decoding via gradient-based saliency maps, which we show align with well-established physiological priors across different ASR model families. Taken together, our results show that FETTUCCINE overcomes core infrastructural and computational barriers, yielding a new class of portable brain-to-text communication.

bullets: Addresses compute-heavy language modeling and unpredictable latency in speech neuroprostheses.
Uses an end-to-end framework based on portable automatic speech recognition models.
Achieves as low as 4.39% word error rate on public intracortical neuroprosthesis data.
Runs on a commercial mobile device and can be fine-tuned across future recording days.
Provides gradient-based saliency maps that identify neural features consistent with physiological priors.

papers.abstract: Screen history can serve as searchable visual memory for people and agents, but unlike an offline corpus, it must be encoded and indexed as each screenshot arrives. OCR-based indexing is fast but loses visual information; visual encoding takes over two seconds. Yet screens change incrementally: most pixels repeat within and across screenshots. This raises a question: do visual encoders need to recompute their representations from scratch for every new screenshot? We present StreamEmbed, a system for incremental visual embedding that exploits this redundancy. Guided solely by pixel differences, it combines spatial token pruning, which skips blocks that repeat a neighbor, with temporal KV reuse, which reuses cached keys and values for blocks unchanged across screenshots. A small learned adapter compensates for pruning and reuse to preserve fidelity to full-screenshot embeddings. On ScreenMemEval, our benchmark of 10,426 questions over 184 hours of screen histories from two humans and a computer-use agent, StreamEmbed sets a new accuracy-latency Pareto frontier on an M2 Pro GPU: it encodes up to 3.7x faster than full-screenshot encoding without sacrificing accuracy and improves accuracy over OCR-based indexing by up to 6.3 Recall@10 points at matched latency. A memory-efficient vector index stores a simulated year of screenshots in 0.13 GB of RAM. Together, these results make real-time indexing of screen history in its native visual form practical, laying a foundation for fully local visual assistants.
authors: Dayoon Ko, Yichuan Wang, Soyeong Jeong, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Gunhee Kim, Sewon Min
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between fast but information-limited OCR indexing and slow full visual encoding for continuously arriving screenshots.
Uses pixel differences to prune redundant spatial tokens and reuse cached temporal key-value representations for unchanged regions.
A learned adapter preserves similarity to full-screenshot embeddings despite pruning and reuse.
On ScreenMemEval, it achieves up to 3.7× faster encoding without accuracy loss and up to 6.3 Recall@10 points over OCR at matched latency.
A memory-efficient index stores a simulated year of screenshots using 0.13 GB of RAM, supporting local visual screen-history assistants.

papers.abstract: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens. Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted. We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load. We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.
bullets: Targets agent sessions where context edits invalidate cached KV and delay decoding.
Uses invalidated KV to generate speculative drafts, then verifies them against the correct post-prefill KV before committing tokens.
Schedules speculation during underutilized decode capacity and preempts low-value speculation.
On a two-GPU testbed across three model families, achieved 1.05–1.19× all-request speedups over vLLM at moderate load.
Cluster-level simulations using real-world traces indicate the gains can extend to larger-scale deployments.

papers.selection_reason: LLM serving optimization that reuses invalidated KV cache for speculative decoding; fits KV-cache and inference-efficiency interests.
papers.title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
papers.tldr: Callo reduces cache-miss latency in disaggregated LLM serving by speculatively decoding with invalidated KV states and verifying drafts after exact prefill.

papers.abstract: Linear-attention language models replace a growing key-value cache with a recurrent state of fixed size. On an edge FPGA, this state can exceed the on-chip memory and must be paged to external memory. This paper asks whether such paging dominates the cost of decoding (generating tokens). We built a hardware tile that computes one complete layer of a custom 369-million-parameter hybrid Gated DeltaNet model on an Agilex 5 FPGA and pages its recurrent state. The model state needs 6.2 MiB, whereas the device has 0.87 MiB of block memory. Paging adds 26.0 MB of memory traffic per decoded token, at most 11.2 percent of the calculated total. On the board at 75 MHz, with synthetic weights, one token takes 11.15 ms in this layer. The matrix-vector products with the weights take about 62 percent of this time and the state phase, including the paging, 13 percent. The tile is one node of a multicast mesh of tri-mode processing elements. We measure the error of the fixed-point arithmetic against floating point and check that the hardware agrees bit for bit with a fixed-point reference. In simulation, the state logic agrees with the reference on all 18 recurrent layers. On the board, six builds pass all 30 runs of 64 tokens and two runs of 1,024 tokens. For this model and memory interface, the delivery of the weights limits the decoding performance, and the recurrent state does not. State paging is therefore practical for such a model on an edge FPGA.
bullets: The 6.2 MiB recurrent state exceeds the FPGA’s 0.87 MiB on-chip memory, requiring external-memory paging.
Paging adds 26.0 MB of traffic per token, but accounts for at most 11.2% of calculated total cost; the state phase takes 13% of measured layer time.
The tile computes a complete layer of a 369-million-parameter hybrid Gated DeltaNet model at 75 MHz, with one token taking 11.15 ms using synthetic weights.
Fixed-point hardware matches a fixed-point reference bit for bit; state logic also agrees across all 18 recurrent layers in simulation and all reported board tests.
The conclusion is scoped to this model and memory interface: weight delivery remains the decoding bottleneck.

papers.title: The State Is Not the Bottleneck: A Paged-State Gated-DeltaNet Tile on a Tri-Mode Multicast Mesh, Bit-Exact from RTL to Silicon

papers.abstract: Interactive LLM services must meet latency service-level objectives (SLOs) for the time to first token (TTFT) and the time between tokens (TBT), as streaming and soft real-time applications require predictable token delivery. We identify decode jitters in both aggregated and disaggregated serving. A jitter delays every request in the batch, and long responses span hundreds of steps, so even rare overruns cause many SLO violations. In aggregated serving, SLO-aware schedulers set each step's prefill budget until its predicted latency just meets the TBT target, leaving no room for mispredictions or host stalls. Disaggregation meets average TBT targets at a cost in capacity, yet the steps that admit new requests still run late. We present \sysname, a scheduler that calibrates how much prefill work each decode step carries using the measured tail of its own iteration latency. The SLO determines how rare a late step must be, and \sysname leaves enough headroom in each iteration to prevent overruns and meet the target decode latency. This headroom slows prefill, so \sysname serves the shortest waiting prompt first. When TTFT deadlines grow with prompt length, the long prompts it delays have the most time to spare. Under disaggregation, it spaces admissions so that no request waits on more slow admission steps than its P99 target allows. On three attention families and varying workloads, \sysname sustains 2.4--2.9$\times$ the SLO goodput of the strongest baseline on Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and at least 4.4$\times$ on DeepSeek-V2-Lite. With prefill and decode disaggregated on eight GPUs, \sysname meets the SLO for more than twice as many requests as state-of-the-art baselines.
authors: Ishaan Datta, Alind Khare, Koushik Kumar Dey, Ratnesh Jamidar, Anand Kumar Singh
bullets: Decode jitters can delay every request in a batch, causing repeated SLO violations across long responses.
VelServe uses measured tail iteration latency to reserve headroom for each decode step, with the SLO setting the acceptable rarity of late steps.
It serves the shortest waiting prompt first to offset the prefill slowdown caused by added headroom.
For disaggregated serving, it spaces admissions so requests encounter no more slow admission steps than their P99 target permits.

Across tested attention families and workloads, it achieves 2.4–2.9× baseline SLO goodput on Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and at least 4.4× on DeepSeek-V2-Lite; on eight GPUs, it meets SLOs for more than twice as many requests as state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.abstract: Efficient sequential recommendation has emerged as a promising paradigm for providing real-time personalized service. To deploy models under resource-constrained environment, model compression becomes a necessity, yet existing methods typically apply uniform compression ratios, overlooking the heterogeneity in user intent complexity. This "one-size-fits-all" approach leads to a fundamental Capacity-Complexity Mismatch, where computational resources are either wasted on simple instances or insufficient for complex ones. To address this, we propose RACE (Ranking-uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation), a framework that dynamically adapts both model structures and input sequences with uncertainty-aware compression ratios. To ensure capacity-adaptive inference, RACE captures the model's intrinsic uncertainty of its predictions and transforms it into a proactive resource allocator. Specifically, we derive a list-wise ranking-uncertainty metric from the distributional stability of top-$K$ predictions, which serves as a measurable proxy for instance complexity. A lightweight predictor is then trained via self-supervision to anticipate this uncertainty from early-layer features. Guided by this signal, RACE performs instance-specific slimming in two dimensions: a hypernetwork-style channel sensitivity extractor identifies parameter redundancy, while importance-aware progressive sequence filtering mitigates data redundancy. Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate that RACE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on accuracy, efficiency, and adaptability.
authors: Tianqi Liu, Kaipu Sun, Kairui Fu, Wenkai Wang, Sihao Liu, Hui Zang, Ran Chen, Tao Wang, Shengyu Zhang
bullets: Addresses capacity–complexity mismatch caused by uniform compression for users with different intent complexity.
Estimates instance complexity using top-K list-wise ranking uncertainty and predicts it from early-layer features with a lightweight self-supervised model.
Performs adaptive compression through channel slimming and importance-aware progressive sequence filtering.
Experiments on four datasets report gains over state-of-the-art baselines in accuracy, efficiency, and adaptability.

(b) Interest-Compatible Subnets Identification: Using the predicted ratio, a lightweight hypernetwork-style sensitivity extractor generates channel-wise masks to customize each feed-forward layer. (c) Progressive Sequence Filtering: Using the predicted ratio, RACE calculates relative importance scores to retain semantically relevant items while suppressing noise block by block.

(c) Our proposed RACE framework introduces a Ranking-Uncertainty Driven mechanism to dynamically adapt model size to instance complexity. papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation usually trains a compact student from scratch, which needs a large amount of data even though the teacher's weights already encode most of what the student has to learn. In this work, we explore building the student directly from the teacher's weights. We propose Concertina, which folds every group of N adjacent teacher layers into one shared block that is executed N times. Each loop step carries a low-rank correction initialized from the layer it replaces, and a per-token gate mixes these corrections, to let every token recover the behavior of the original layers from a single shared block. We further design a distillation data recipe that balances general, mathematical, academic and targeted multiple-choice data, to recover all capabilities of the teacher together rather than one at the expense of another. On Qwen3-4B, a 2.27B Concertina model distilled on 22B tokens retains about 90% of the teacher on commonsense and mathematical reasoning and 84% on average across eight benchmarks. It outperforms same-size dense and layer-sharing baselines, as well as Qwen3-1.7B, which is trained on over a thousand times more data. These results suggest that a compact model need not be retrained at scale, since folding the teacher into itself and distilling it on the right data recovers most of its capabilities. Code is available at https://github.com/myboker/concertina.
authors: Ziyang Zhang, Yubin Jing, Yuyao Li, Haofan Wang, Yichen Gong

Folds every N adjacent teacher layers into one shared block, using low-rank corrections and per-token gates to recover layer-specific behavior.
Uses a balanced distillation recipe spanning general, mathematical, academic, and targeted multiple-choice data.
On Qwen3-4B, a 2.27B Concertina model retains about 90% of teacher performance on commonsense and mathematical reasoning and 84% on average across eight benchmarks.
Outperforms same-size dense and layer-sharing baselines and Qwen3-1.7B trained on substantially more data.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward multi-view transformers such as VGGT recover the cameras and geometry of a video in one pass, but the cost of their cross-frame attention grows quadratically with the frame count, and their accuracy drops on long videos. Most remedies approximate attention over all frames within a budget or select a few keys by their content. We hypothesize that the keys of a long video can be chosen without looking at its content, and our experiments on VGGT and $\pi^3$ support it: a few dozen evenly spread frames can serve as the keys of every frame. We present EcoVGGT, a training-free inference framework whose keys form a Pinned Key Set of 31 such frames. A pin pass stores their tokens in a Scene Cache, and the other frames read it in independent batches that reproduce joint inference with these keys exactly, at a constant cost per frame. An Online Stream updates the pinned frames during recording. Six middle global blocks align the frames and form a reusable VGGT module: the Alignment Score reads their attention to flag failures, and Alignment Refocusing reduces them by fine-tuning only these blocks (3.6 GPU hours). EcoVGGT ($\pi^3$) matches the success rate of $\pi^3$ on 1,000-frame ScanNet videos at 13.8 times its speed. With refocusing, EcoVGGT (VGGT) raises the success rate of VGGT from 70% to 82% at 8.5 times its speed on 500 frames. EcoVGGT reconstructs 4,000 frames on one GPU, and EcoVGGT ($\pi^3$) streams 1,000 frames at 18.6 frames per second with the lowest online absolute trajectory error.
authors: Hongsen Cao, Shanxin Yuan, Mona Jaber, Ahmed Sayed

Supports online streaming by updating pinned frames during recording.
An Alignment Score detects failures, while Alignment Refocusing fine-tunes six global blocks to improve robustness.
On long ScanNet videos, it matches or improves baseline success rates while achieving substantially higher speed and scaling to thousands of frames on one GPU.

papers.title: EcoVGGT: Pinned-Key Inference for Efficient and Streamable Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction from Long Videos

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) achieve strong performance on image recognition tasks, yet their quadratic self-attention complexity over input tokens creates prohibitive computational costs for practical deployment. Token reduction methods offer a practical solution by progressively reducing the token sequence during the forward pass. We propose Saliency-Weighted Asymmetric Merging (SWAM), a training-based token merging framework that extends the Bipartite Soft Matching (BSM) with two saliency-aware mechanisms. We introduce a two-step matching formulation in which cosine similarity decides candidate pairs, while a multiplicative maximum saliency penalty regulates their selection for merging. We then further use asymmetric exponential saliency-weighted aggregation, which allows more salient tokens to contribute more strongly to the merged representation. A lightweight MLP-based saliency prediction module (75k parameters per stage, 1% of backbone parameters) supervised via attention rollout is trained end-to-end jointly with a DeiT-Small backbone using a composite cross-entropy, knowledge-distillation, and saliency-alignment objective. On CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet-100, under a conservative schedule that reduces tokens from 196 to 100 patch tokens, with the CLS token retained throughout, 27.5% FLOPs reduction and 1.35 times speedup, SWAM matches or exceeds baseline across the reported results. Under an aggressive schedule (196 to 70 tokens with the CLS token kept throughout, 33.8% FLOPs reduction, and 1.46 times speedup), accuracy gains are achieved on ImageNet-100 (+0.23%) with minimal losses on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet.
authors: Utkarsh Kumar Singh, Manish Das, Shiv Ram Dubey, Satish Kumar Singh
bullets: Addresses the quadratic self-attention cost of ViTs through progressive token reduction.
Extends Bipartite Soft Matching with saliency-guided pair selection and asymmetric saliency-weighted aggregation.
Uses a lightweight MLP saliency predictor trained jointly with a DeiT-Small backbone and supervised through attention rollout.
With conservative merging, reduces FLOPs by 27.5% and achieves 1.35× speedup while matching or exceeding baselines across reported datasets.
With aggressive merging, reaches 33.8% FLOPs reduction and 1.46× speedup, including a 0.23% ImageNet-100 accuracy gain, with minimal losses elsewhere.

papers.abstract: Deep learning-based hyperspectral unmixing (HSU) has followed a trajectory of increasing architectural complexity, from simple autoencoders to transformers and, most recently, Mamba-based models, each claiming to advance the state of the art. Contrary to this trend, we propose a lightweight CNN-based autoencoder, coined "Not New Autoencoder Unmixing" (nnAEU). It is derived from the backbone of UNMamba (2025) through a pruning study that removes the Mamba component entirely. nnAEU uses less than 10 times fewer parameters than UNMamba, and far fewer than other transformer- and GAN-based methods, while outperforming them in accuracy. We provide a complete, minimal, reproducible code, available at https://gitlab.telecom-paris.fr/ring/nnAEU.git.

papers.abstract: Attention is essential for modeling spatio-temporal dependencies in video diffusion transformers, but its quadratic cost makes it a major inference bottleneck. Its high sparsity offers an opportunity to accelerate generation by focusing computation on important interactions. However, accuracy and execution favor different granularities: each query attends to its own key tokens, whereas GPU kernels work on tiles. We present Token2Tile, a training-free sparse attention operator that combines per-query scoring and a per-query residual with tile execution. An online low-rank space, computed directly from queries and keys to preserve attention logits, makes clustering, scoring, and residual approximation efficient. Token2Tile unites query-specific selections to allocate exact work across query clusters, then packs the selected keys into GPU tiles. On MiniMax-H3 and Wan2.1-14B, Token2Tile delivers 1.48-1.54x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention-3 with VBench scores within 0.5 points of dense. At comparable speeds on H3, it improves PSNR over SOL and SubBlock by 5.5-6.8 dB; on Wan, it exceeds SOL by 4.6-4.8 dB while running faster.
authors: Xuecheng Wu, Aichen Feng, Jinyan Chen, Qingjie Zhao, Julien Lai
bullets: Targets the quadratic inference cost of spatio-temporal attention in video diffusion transformers.
Uses per-query scoring and residual approximation in an online low-rank space derived from queries and keys.

Achieves 1.48–1.54× end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention-3, with VBench within 0.5 points of dense.
Outperforms SOL and SubBlock in PSNR at comparable or higher speeds on the evaluated models.

papers.abstract: Synchronous, colocated RL post-training of large language models (LLMs) today suffers from severe under-utilization due to long-tail rollouts. Inference engines fall idle waiting for long-tail rollouts or decode at low, inefficient batch sizes. To address this, we present TIDE, an RL training system that preserves on-policy training semantics while recovering resource utilization. TIDE does so by two complementary techniques: (1) dynamically repurposing rollout GPUs for training while long-tail rollouts complete and (2) dynamically migrating rollouts between inference engines to boost decoding throughput. TIDE automatically determines the right time to repurpose rollout resources through an adaptive migration policy, obtaining performance improvements that generalize across multiple applications and hardware configurations without requiring bespoke configuration. In our evaluation, TIDE provides end-to-end speedups of up to 1.36x over colocated systems, outperforming all evaluated on-policy baselines and achieving up to 97% of optimal throughput.
authors: Mathew Jacob, Morgan Borjigin-Wang, Kan Zhu, Po Hao Chen, Yi Pan, Andy Ruan, Nayani Modugula, Ethan Lavi, Luis Ceze, Malte Schwarzkopf, Akshay Narayan, Deepti Raghavan, Stephanie Wang
bullets: Addresses under-utilization caused by long-tail rollouts in synchronous, colocated RL training.
Repurposes rollout GPUs for training while delayed rollouts finish.
Migrates rollouts across inference engines to increase decoding throughput.
Uses an adaptive migration policy that generalizes across applications and hardware without bespoke configuration.
Achieves up to 1.36× end-to-end speedup and up to 97% of optimal throughput in evaluation.

papers.abstract: Generative recommendation benefits from long interaction histories, but the cost of processing them directly grows with history length. We propose RecMem, a recurrent memory compression framework guided by three desiderata: space invariance, semantic fidelity, and lifelong evolvability. RecMem compresses historical segments into a fixed set of memory slots using a bifurcated encoder-decoder with shared lower layers and slot-wise forget-gated updates. Recommendation supervision trains the memory to preserve predictive information, while stream-consistency training aligns predictions from sequential and packed processing. By construction, the memory state and decoder context are independent of history length; under contraction and approximate semigroup consistency, we further derive a horizon-independent bound on the state discrepancy between these two processing orders. On MerRec, RecMem uses 16 memory slots and a 216-token decoder context, compared with 1,200 tokens for HSTU-1200, while retaining 87.9% of HSTU-1200's Recall@10 and 97.0% of its Recall@200. It outperforms PHSTU and the evaluated recent-only and retrieval baselines, and analyses of distant history show that archived interactions contribute predictive signal.
authors: Haoyi Hu, Gaoyang Guo, Yunjia Xi, Wen Chen, Weiwen Liu, Jian Wu, Yuning Jiang, Weinan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the growing cost of directly processing long interaction histories in generative recommendation.
Uses bifurcated encoder-decoder compression with slot-wise forget-gated recurrent updates.
Trains memory with recommendation supervision and stream-consistency objectives for sequential-versus-packed processing.
Provides a horizon-independent discrepancy bound under contraction and approximate semigroup consistency.
On MerRec, 16 memory slots plus a 216-token context retain 87.9% of HSTU-1200’s Recall@10 and 97.0% of its Recall@200; archived distant history remains predictive.

papers.abstract: Growing visual data overwhelms storage on resource-constrained edge devices, making compression essential. Traditional codecs offer inadequate rate-distortion performance, motivating the exploration of diffusion codecs. Diffusion codecs face two limitations: (1) At the algorithm level, diffusion decoders preserve perceptual quality under extreme compression, but require substantial computation. (2) At the architecture level, in NPU-centered devices, neural codecs occupy the NPU, interfering with other AI applications. Meanwhile, the complex codec pipeline incurs long I/O paths, leading to additional overhead and energy cost. To address these issues, we propose DiffusionSSD, a cross-level near-data processing framework for extreme visual data compression on edge devices, using an algorithm-architecture co-design method. Specifically, (1) at algorithm level, we present Dual-stage Diffusion, a lightweight solution tailored for diffusion codecs that employs patchification and single-step diffusion, reducing computation cost while preserving perceptual quality; (2) at architecture level, we introduce a Cross-level Near Data Processing architecture that integrates the proposed computational universal flash storage (cUFS) and LPDDR-PIM, enabling codecs to be entirely offloaded to data side while reducing visual-data movement and avoiding SoC redesign; (3) at system level, combining both the algorithm and the underlying architecture, we propose a Patch-Workload co-aware scheduling scheme to enable more efficient system-level execution. Experiments show that Dual-stage Diffusion maintains comparable perceptual quality while reducing computation cost by up to 92.7%. Compared with NPU+DRAM and near-data-processing design such as SmartSSD, cUFS+PIM improves coding throughput by 2.32 times and 2.91 times on average, respectively.
authors: Kuai Yu, Wen Li, Shengwen Liang, Jie Zhang, Ying Wang, Huawei Li, Xin Yao, Renhai Chen, Gong Zhang

Uses patchification and single-step diffusion to preserve perceptual quality while reducing computation cost by up to 92.7%.
Offloads codec processing to cUFS and LPDDR-PIM, reducing visual-data movement and avoiding SoC redesign.
Introduces patch-workload co-aware scheduling for more efficient system-level execution.
Improves coding throughput by 2.32× over NPU+DRAM and 2.91× over SmartSSD on average.

papers.abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. We present Superfluid, an open-source LLM server built for local inference at both scales. On one device, Superfluid drives llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT in isolated worker processes through one scheduler that moves interactive requests ahead of agent work, computes a prompt shared by many requests once, and writes every token to a durable log before it reaches the client. Across devices, one Superfluid server turns a fleet of machines into a single API endpoint. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. For Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro, a chat sent while eight agents are working receives its first token in 1.5 s, against 291-612 s on llama-server, Ollama, and mlx_lm.server. On six machines from three chip vendors serving 64 simulated users for one hour, Superfluid answers all 5,041 requests while machines join one at a time and one is killed and rejoins; throughput grows from 112 to 534 tok/s and the median first-token time falls from 99 to 12 s. On twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustains 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without a failure. Superfluid is available under the Apache-2.0 licence at https://github.com/basecompute/superfluid.
authors: Prabod Rathnayaka, Isura Manchanayake, Srikandabala Kogul, Steve Siu, Fabian Waschkowski, Lukas Wesemann
bullets: Addresses local serving for multiple interactive users and agents, plus fleets of heterogeneous devices that would otherwise sit idle.
Uses isolated llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT workers with one scheduler, shared prompt computation, and durable token logging.
Distributes model replicas according to measured machine speed, allowing devices to join or fail without losing requests.
In reported tests, it reduced interactive latency under agent load, scaled throughput as machines joined, and completed workloads during machine failure and rejoining.
Released under the Apache-2.0 licence.

papers.abstract: Multi-view 3D transformers such as VGGT reconstruct a scene from a set of unposed images in a single forward pass, predicting camera poses, depth and 3D points, but the cost of their global attention grows quadratically with the num- ber of images. Accelerators borrowed from large language models assume that each token attends to only a few oth- ers; on these models they lose accuracy or gain little speed. We study the global attention of three multi-view transform- ers on seven datasets and find that every layer plays one of three roles: it averages over the whole scene, matches points across many images, or anchors on the first image, whose coordinates the outputs use. Building on this anal- ysis, we propose Regime-AWare ATTention Approximation (RAWATTA), a training-free method that runs attention in 8- bit precision and keeps 16-bit precision only in the layers where a worst-case calibration check requires it. Its fast set- ting, RAWATTA-Fast, also approximates attention in a few averaging and anchoring layers, while matching layers and the first image keep all their keys. On a 12 GB GPU at 50 im- ages, RAWATTA runs VGGT faster than the released code, mostly through our CUDA engine, and loses at most about one point of pose accuracy (AUC@3) on any dataset; RAWATTA-Fast is slightly faster and less accurate. Both fit 200 images, where the released code runs out of memory at 100.
authors: Muhammed Izzet Sezer, Sevval Belkis Dikkaya
bullets: Global attention in multi-view 3D transformers is costly because its complexity grows quadratically with the number of images.
The study identifies three layer roles: scene-wide averaging, cross-image point matching, and anchoring to the first image.
RAWATTA uses 8-bit attention by default and retains 16-bit precision when a worst-case calibration check requires it.
RAWATTA-Fast additionally approximates attention in selected averaging and anchoring layers while preserving full keys for matching layers and the first image.
On VGGT, RAWATTA is faster than the released implementation, loses at most about one AUC@3 pose-accuracy point, and supports 200 images on a 12 GB GPU where the baseline runs out of memory at 100.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free attention approximation for multi-view 3D transformers, improving efficiency while preserving accuracy, relevant to efficient AI and 3D foundation models.
papers.title: Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-View 3D Transformers via Regime-Aware Attention Approximation
papers.tldr: RAWATTA accelerates multi-view 3D transformers without retraining by adapting attention precision and approximation to each layer’s functional regime.

papers.abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.

papers.abstract: A developer running a code assistant on a laptop downloads one model file, and local inference moves the energy of every request onto that machine. A common rule says a larger model at lower precision tends to beat a smaller one at higher precision. We ran 24 GGUF files of Qwen2.5-Coder at four sizes on a fanless MacBook Air M2 and priced each in energy per solved task on 542 EvalPlus tasks. The result is a selection guide indexed by Ollama's listed file size, with an evidence label on each pick. At 1 and 2 GB it picks the q4_K_M files of the 1.5B and 3B models, both on the correctness and energy frontier under every accounting. At 3 GB as listed, the larger-model rule picks 7B-q2_K, the only measured 7B file that fits, and there it does not pay. That file brings no significant gain in solves over the 2 GB pick, 3B-q4_K_M, and the 90% CI limits any 3B-q4_K_M deficit to 2.4 points. Yet 7B-q2_K needs 2.03 times the energy per solved task on CPU, GPU and memory rails, or 1.66 to 1.81 times on whole-system power. On HumanEval+, five alternating session pairs give a ratio of 1.925 against 1.956 in the main grid. At 8 GB, 7B-q6_K buys a significant gain over the 2 GB pick at a higher energy price. From 1.5B up, q4_K_M trails the highest precision measured at its size by less than 3 points (90% CI). We release per-task results, power logs and the analysis script.
bullets: Evaluates 24 GGUF files across four Qwen2.5-Coder sizes on a fanless MacBook Air M2 using 542 EvalPlus tasks.
At 1–2 GB, the 1.5B-q4_K_M and 3B-q4_K_M files lie on the correctness and energy frontiers under all accounting methods.
At 3 GB, 7B-q2_K does not significantly improve solves over 3B-q4_K_M, while using substantially more energy per solved task.
At 8 GB, 7B-q6_K provides a significant accuracy gain over the 2 GB choice, but at a higher energy cost.
For models 1.5B and larger, q4_K_M is within 3 percentage points of the highest measured precision at the same size; results and power logs are released.

papers.title: Choosing Quantized Code LLMs by File Size and Energy per Solved Task

papers.abstract: Machine learning in physical hardware promises to reduce training cost by colocating computation, memory and adaptation within device physics. Contrastive local learning networks (CLLNs) offer a compelling route: an electrical circuit relaxes to equilibrium in free and weakly clamped states, and each adaptive element updates from local voltage contrasts rather than backpropagated error signals. Yet whether nonlinear transistor implementations can scale beyond proof-of-concept circuits, and what design principles control that scaling, have remained unknown. Here we show that nonlinear analog circuits trained by contrastive local rules can learn larger machine-learning tasks and remain robust under hardware nonidealities. Using device-level circuit simulations, we systematically explore initialization, operating regime, loss-dependent clamping and training parameters, and scale CLLNs beyond ten thousand adaptive edges. The same local rule trains classifiers that reach the accuracy regime of conventional digital methods on Ionosphere and handwritten-digit benchmarks, and a network that autoregressively generates language over a 122-token vocabulary. These results establish the feasibility of local learning in large nonlinear analog circuits.
authors: Pragyan Pandey, Peter Wu, Deema Alyahya, Eric Y. Ma
bullets: Addresses whether transistor-based contrastive local learning networks can scale beyond small proof-of-concept circuits.
Uses device-level circuit simulations to study initialization, operating regime, clamping, and training parameters.
Shows robustness to hardware nonidealities and scaling beyond 10,000 adaptive edges.
Achieves the accuracy regime of conventional digital methods on Ionosphere and handwritten-digit classification benchmarks.
Demonstrates autoregressive language generation with a 122-token vocabulary.

papers.selection_reason: Contrastive local learning in large analog circuits targets reduced training cost and energy via in-hardware computation, relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Contrastive local learning in large nonlinear analog circuits
papers.tldr: Contrastive local learning can train large nonlinear analog circuits, scaling beyond 10,000 adaptive edges while supporting classification and language generation.

papers.abstract: Quantization lets language models run on edge devices, but it sharply increases the number of tensor kernels a library must maintain: every weight format must be paired with every activation format on every instruction set and GPU, with an encoder and a decoder that agree on the stored bytes. In GGML, the tensor library used by llama.cpp, these kernels are written by hand, and only 8 of the 54 weight-activation pairs it runs on our Arm CPU have a tiled matrix-multiplication kernel. We extend Halide's separation of algorithm and schedule to the representation of values. Each approximation is a codec, an encoder paired with a decoder, composed from reusable units: quantizers, integer representations, bit packers and layouts. A new directive, approximate_by, applies a codec to one stage of a program and returns the encoder and decoder as ordinary stages that Halide can schedule, so both decoders fuse into the register tiles of a matrix product. Optional contracts, such as a round-trip law, are checked by property tests; the law exposed an inconsistent block sum in GGML's q8_1. One algorithm and one schedule library generate 347 kernels for 31 of GGML's and KleidiAI's formats on Arm CPUs and Apple GPUs, covering 38 weight-activation pairs for which GGML has no kernel, in 3.7x less code than GGML and KleidiAI. On an Apple M3 Max, our kernels reach at least 95% of the speed of GGML's format-specific kernels in 91.0% of the cases that have one, with a median speedup of 1.13x, and are faster still where GGML falls back to blocked dot products. Counting Apple's BLAS library, which is usually faster for larger f32 products, we still reach that threshold in 86.9% of CPU cases. A port to x86 with Intel's AMX adds 793 lines of code and matches GGML in 83.5% of its cases.
bullets: Quantization creates a combinatorial kernel-maintenance problem across weight formats, activation formats, and hardware targets.
The approach represents approximations as composable encoder–decoder codecs and exposes them to Halide scheduling via `approximate_by`, enabling decoder fusion into matrix-multiplication tiles.
Property-tested contracts can detect format inconsistencies, including an issue in GGML’s `q8_1` block sum.
The system generates 347 kernels for 31 formats, covering 38 Arm CPU and Apple GPU pairs lacking GGML kernels, using 3.7× less code than GGML and KleidiAI.
Performance reaches at least 95% of format-specific GGML kernels in 91.0% of applicable Apple M3 Max cases; an x86/AMX port matches GGML in 83.5% of cases.

papers.selection_reason: Codec-based quantization framework for tensor programs reduces memory and compute for on-device LLM inference, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: User-Schedulable Approximations for Quantized Tensor Programs
papers.tldr: A Halide-based codec abstraction generates many efficient quantized tensor kernels from one algorithm and schedule library, reducing hand-written code while retaining near-GGML performance.

papers.abstract: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.
authors: Yavuz Yetim, Bor-Yiing Su, Zhe Wang, Arthur Liu, Pranav Sharma, Ying Wang, Randy Shuai, Luke Pfister, Ruichao Xiao, Bill Zhao, Zihao Liu, Liyuan Li, Jiangyuan Li, Gaoxiang Liu, Nathan Yan, Geonhwa Jeong, Jatin Chhugani, Elias Ellison, Uladzimir Pashkevich
bullets: R&R models need very high throughput but tolerate almost no quantization-induced quality loss: NE must stay within 0.01% of baseline.
The study evaluates MXFP8 and 6-bit MXFP6 on AMD MI350X, including native MXFP6 GEMMs that quantize weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements.
Selective MXFP6 achieves end-to-end throughput gains of 1.5–5.3% on Model A and 7.6–14.3% on Model B relative to FP8 configurations.
Across supported linear layers, MXFP8 GEMMs are 1.33–1.55× faster than FP16, while MXFP6 reaches 1.73–1.99× and up to 2.90× on individual layers.
MXFP8 provides accuracy nearly equivalent to row-wise FP8, allowing the faster format to be selected by GEMM shape.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces microscaling formats for quantized inference, reducing memory and compute.
papers.title: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
papers.tldr: Microscaling MXFP8 and MXFP6 enables substantial inference acceleration for production recommendation and ranking models while maintaining the strict required quality margin.

papers.abstract: Existing adaptive-reasoning methods shorten the explicit reasoning a model writes, or skip it by switching modes; either way the answer is still written out token by token. \emph{Rather than deciding how much to think}, we explore a different paradigm, \emph{zero-or-$T$ thinking}: a single model either answers from the implicit thinking inside one forward pass, generating no token, or performs full autoregressive reasoning at a cost of $T$ tokens when that is worth paying. We realise it in a \emph{hybrid decision model} (HDM), where one frozen backbone serves both modes and a lightweight \emph{self-routing block} chooses between them. The block estimates the \emph{value of thinking}, the utility the slow mode is expected to add over the fast one, from what that implicit thinking has already produced, and the slow mode runs only where that value exceeds a price $λ$ set per request. Where no per-decision label exists, as in episodic agentic tasks, we introduce \emph{Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation} (CDPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that trains the block from episode-level returns. We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond, JevBench, BANKING77 and MiniWoB. Specifically, on JevBench HDM-4B scores $0.857$ against Jev's $0.851$ ($+0.7\%$) at a median $0.179$\,s against $0.652$ ($-72.5\%$). On the agentic venue MiniWoB HDM-27B cuts token cost by $80.1\%$.
bullets: Introduces zero-or-T thinking: each request either uses one-pass implicit reasoning or pays for full token-by-token reasoning.
A lightweight self-routing block estimates the value of additional thinking and compares it with a request-specific price λ.
For episodic agentic tasks without per-decision labels, CDPO trains routing decisions from episode-level returns.
On JevBench, HDM-4B slightly outperforms Jev while reducing median latency by 72.5%.
On MiniWoB, HDM-27B reduces token cost by 80.1%.

papers.selection_reason: Adaptive reasoning to reduce token cost, fits efficient AI.
papers.title: The Value of Thinking: Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models
papers.tldr: A hybrid model learns whether the expected benefit of full autoregressive reasoning justifies its cost, enabling faster decisions while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: As GPU accelerators grow larger to meet rising compute demands, they exhibit increasingly pronounced non-uniform memory access (NUMA) characteristics that challenge existing LLM frameworks. Chiplet-based architectures provide a practical path to larger GPUs while mitigating manufacturing yield constraints. Modern GPUs such as AMD Instinct MI300X employs such a multi-die design, and further offer GPU partitioning capabilities, partitioning a single physical GPU into multiple logical devices with NUMA-aware memory domains, promising faster kernel launches, and reduced memory access latencies with improved locality. However, current parallelization strategies, designed for homogeneous GPU topologies, when applied under partitioning, extend its unidimensional sharding causing significant performance degradation. Three bottlenecks emerge: (1) memory redundancy; (2) arithmetic intensity collapse; (3) communication overhead from flat collectives. We present Starscream, a rethinking of LLM sharding for the chiplet era. Rather than stretching inter-GPU sharding thinner, Starscream adds intra-GPU sharding along an orthogonal dimension, grounded in three foundational principles: kernel shape preservation, memory redundancy elimination, and communication overhead minimization. These principles form the basis for extending any sharding strategy into the partitioning regime. We demonstrate their effectiveness using tensor parallelism as a case study. On AMD MI300X and MI355X, exploiting partitioning capabilities yields up to 4x speedup for attention and 1.43x for fused GEMMs compared to chiplet-oblivious baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of chiplet-aware designs. Starscream's principles generalize across sharding strategies and future architectures.
bullets: Targets performance losses caused by applying homogeneous-GPU sharding to NUMA-aware GPU partitions.
Addresses memory redundancy, reduced arithmetic intensity, and communication overhead from flat collectives.
Uses orthogonal intra-GPU sharding based on kernel shape preservation, redundancy elimination, and communication minimization.
Demonstrated with tensor parallelism on AMD MI300X and MI355X, achieving up to 4× attention and 1.43× fused-GEMM speedups.
The principles are intended to generalize to other sharding strategies and future chiplet-based architectures.
