papers.abstract: Model merging aims to build a multi-task model cheaply by combining the weights of individual task-specific models. To perform well across multiple tasks, most existing merging methods use an additional dataset to find the coefficients for the best linear combination of task-specific weight updates. However, we identify an implicit regularization in this standard practice: searching over coefficients restricts the candidate models to a subspace spanned by task-specific weight updates. In this work, we investigate whether this regularization is actually useful. Surprisingly, empirical results show that optimizing merged-model weights without this regularization significantly boosts the performance of common merging methods across multiple architectures, domains, and even in an extremely data-limited scenario where only one instance is available per class. Moreover, directly optimizing the pretrained model weights even outperforms some existing merging methods. Analysis shows that better multi-task weights exist outside the subspace and can be found using multiple methods. We study different strategies for using the additional dataset, discussing their practical use and implications for model merging. Overall, this work calls for revisiting the existing model-merging pipeline, motivating a broader exploration of the weight space and a reconsideration of the implicit regularization induced by task arithmetic.
bullets: Existing merging methods often tune coefficients over task-specific weight updates using an additional dataset, implicitly restricting solutions to their spanned subspace.
The study finds that removing this restriction improves common merging methods across architectures and domains, including an extremely data-limited setting.
Direct optimization of pretrained weights can outperform some existing merging approaches.
Analysis indicates that better multi-task weights exist outside the task-update subspace and can be reached through multiple strategies.
The work reassesses how additional data should be used and encourages broader exploration of the weight space.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A new perspective on the model-merging pipeline. The existing model-merging pipeline builds the merged model θmerge by adding a linear combination of task-specific weight updates τi to the pretrained model θ0. Standard practice uses an additional dataset, which we term auxiliary data, to optimize the coefficients λ for multi-task performance. This coefficient optimization regularizes model updates to the subspace spanned by τi. We challenge this pipeline by using the same auxiliary data to optimize the merged-model weights, allowing optimization beyond this subspace. Experimental results show that exploring the broader weight space generally leads to significant performance improvements across merging methods (TA, TIES, DARE, and TSV-M).

Figure 2: Average test accuracy under different uses of auxiliary data. Across vision tasks (top) and language tasks (bottom) with different models, Gradient Descent (GD) from the merged models consistently outperforms both coefficient search and the empirical best performance of its search space (Subspace best) for every merging method (TA, TIES, DARE, and TSV-M).

Figure 7: Positive correlation between Init accuracy of merged models and their afterGD accuracy. Existing model merging methods provide strong initializations for gradient descent, and stronger methods have better afterGD performance.

Figure 6: Computational usage of different ways to use the auxiliary data. Gradient descent on weights (Weight GD) uses slightly more memory than coefficient search. While doing gradient descent requires more compute effort (time/FLOPs), it trades compute for better performance.

Figure 3: Average test accuracy under different sizes and uses of auxiliary data for TA. We downsample the auxiliary data and compare different uses of auxiliary data for TA. We run three random seeds for downsampling, and report error bars as the shaded regions. Gradient Descent (GD) consistently outperforms the other two approaches that optimize weights within the subspace.

Figure 10: Gradient Descent (GD) Initialization results across vision and language models. For vision, we measure average test accuracy, and report the average accuracy of three random initialization points. Init accuracy is the naive coefficient’s performance.

Figure 5: S-RandOpt sampled weights’ test performance. We sample 64 random weights in language models using S-RandOpt, and compare their test performance with the best point on the task-vector subspace (subspace best). A high proportion of sampled weights from outside the subspace outperforms the best weight on the subspace (Subspace best).

Figure 4: Gradient descent trajectories in the 2-task setting (ViT-B-32, EuroSAT and GTSRB). Each panel shows one run initialized on the task-vector subspace (blue plane). The axes e1, e2, and e3 are the directions of τ1, τ⊥2 , and each run’s update’s orthogonal component to the subspace ∆⊥. In all runs, gradient descent leaves the subspace as the score (accuracy) increases.

Figure 8: Auxiliary data scaling for TA in 2- task setting. The number of classes (53) is smaller than in the 9-task setting (856). Gradient descent’s performance is worse than coefficient search when data is extremely limited, but still outperforms it when more data are provided. Adding regularization for GD mitigates the issue. The results indicate that generalization is a key factor when using auxiliary data.

Figure 9: Average test accuracy under different sizes and uses of auxiliary data for TIES. We downsample the auxiliary data and compare three different uses of auxiliary data for TIES. We run three random seeds for downsampling, and report error bars as shaded regions. The findings are consistent with the TA’s result in Figure 3.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates model merging and implicit regularization, offering insights into efficient multi-task learning and weight space optimization (Adaptation).
papers.title: A Broader Look at Model Merging: Rethinking Implicit Regularization Induced by Task Arithmetic
papers.tldr: Optimizing merged model weights beyond the task-update subspace can substantially improve multi-task model merging, challenging the assumed benefit of task-arithmetic regularization.

papers.abstract: Adversarial training is one of the most reliable defenses against adversarial attacks, but its high computational cost must generally be paid anew for each task. Robust foundation models offer a promising alternative: adversarially pretrain a model once and then transfer its robustness to downstream tasks through lightweight adaptation. However, a fundamental question remains open: can robustness acquired during pretraining transfer to unseen tasks without further adversarial training? In this study, we answer this question affirmatively. A single model adversarially pretrained at scale can achieve optimal robustness on new tasks without additional task-specific training. Specifically, we show that, for a family of Gaussian-mixture classification tasks, a sufficiently deep linear transformer adversarially trained across tasks can asymptotically attain the robust Bayes error on previously unseen tasks through in-context learning from clean demonstrations. By contrast, a standardly trained model cannot. We further analyze convergence under gradient flow, an accuracy--robustness trade-off, and demonstration complexity.
bullets: Studies whether robustness learned during pretraining transfers to new tasks.
Shows this transfer for Gaussian-mixture classification with sufficiently deep linear transformers.
Adversarially trained models asymptotically achieve robust Bayes error on unseen tasks via clean demonstrations.
Standardly trained models do not achieve the same robust performance.
Also analyzes gradient-flow convergence, the accuracy–robustness trade-off, and demonstration complexity.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that adversarially trained linear transformers achieve optimal robustness via in-context learning, connecting Efficient Attention and Test-Time Learning.
papers.title: Adversarially Trained Linear Transformers Are Optimal Robust In-Context Learners for Gaussian Mixtures
papers.tldr: Adversarially pretrained deep linear transformers can transfer optimal robustness to unseen Gaussian-mixture classification tasks through clean in-context demonstrations, without task-specific adversarial training.

papers.abstract: Accurate bioactivity prediction is a central challenge in early-stage drug discovery, as individual assays often contain too few measurements to train reliable models independently. Meta-learning offers a principled approach to this few-shot setting, but assay heterogeneity may limit its effectiveness. Here, we test this hypothesis and show that meta-learning performance degrades as meta-training tasks become more heterogeneous. To address this, we introduce MetaHeta, a meta-learning framework that accounts for assay heterogeneity by conditioning predictions on auxiliary data from related assays, with relatedness defined flexibly from available assay information. The architecture of MetaHeta combines linear attention over large auxiliary datasets with exact attention over scarce task-specific context, enabling efficient scaling to the former without compromising exact attention over the latter. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach on assays from ChEMBL and BindingDB, improving few-shot bioactivity prediction and downstream compound prioritization in retrospective Bayesian optimization.
bullets: Few-shot assay datasets often lack enough measurements for reliable independent models.
Meta-learning performance declines when meta-training assays are highly heterogeneous.
MetaHeta conditions predictions on auxiliary data from flexibly defined related assays.
It combines linear attention for large auxiliary datasets with exact attention for scarce task-specific context.
Experiments on ChEMBL and BindingDB show improved prediction and retrospective Bayesian-optimization compound prioritization.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture overview of MetaHeta. A shared input MLP embeds context, target, and concatenated auxiliary observations, augmented with task-of-origin indicators, with target activities masked to 0. Encoder layers use exact self-attention for the context and FAVOR+ for auxiliary data, followed by context-to-auxiliary and target-to-context cross-attention. When Daux = ∅, the auxiliary branch is skipped. Finally, an output MLP parameterizes a mean-field Gaussian predictive distribution. Formal definitions of the attention operators are given in Appendix F.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces MetaHeta, a meta-learning framework combining linear attention (Efficient AI) with meta-learning (Adaptation) to handle assay heterogeneity in few-shot prediction.
papers.title: Few-Shot Bioactivity Prediction with Meta-Learning under Assay Heterogeneity
papers.tldr: MetaHeta improves few-shot bioactivity prediction by adapting meta-learning to heterogeneous assays through related-assay information and efficient attention.

papers.abstract: LLM workloads sometimes ask many independent questions about the same long document, as in document QA, data labeling and LLM-based evaluation. Prefix caching removes the redundant prefill shared by these queries, but each decode step still reads the document's key-value (KV) cache once per question, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and scales with the number of questions. We present Parallel Prompting, which decodes P questions as P independent streams of a single request all at once, fixing this issue. In our method, every step reads the shared document once for all P streams, and a stream-id attention mask, evaluated inside the attention kernel, keeps each answer conditioned only on the document and its own question. We implement Parallel Prompting in SGLang by adding about 80 lines to three existing files and a small engine package; the mask needs no dense tensor, and every decode step has a fixed shape that is captured as a CUDA graph. With CodeLlama-7B, 8k-16k-token documents and 64-256 questions per document, Parallel Prompting is 3.7x faster than stock SGLang with its FlashInfer backend on an A100 and 5.9-6.0x faster on an RTX A6000, on two SGLang releases, including the most recent release. Timed on identical inputs, it is faster than stock SGLang in all 144 runs (2 GPUs x 2 releases x 6 workloads x 6 input sets). Code: https://github.com/jlab-nlp/parallel-prompting
bullets: Targets document QA, labeling, and evaluation workloads with many independent questions sharing one context.
Uses independent parallel decode streams plus a stream-ID attention mask so each answer attends only to the document and its own question.
Implemented in SGLang with lightweight code changes, dense-mask-free attention, and fixed-shape CUDA graphs.
For CodeLlama-7B workloads, it achieved 3.7× speedup on an A100 and 5.9–6.0× on an RTX A6000 versus stock SGLang.
Evaluation covered 144 identical-input runs across two GPUs, two SGLang releases, six workloads, and six input sets; it was faster in every run.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Three ways to answer several questions about one document, shown at one decode step (dark: the token generated in this step). A serving engine such as SGLang or vLLM runs a batch of requests, and every decode step adds one token to each request. Batched requests with prefix caching store the document’s KV once but use one request per question, so every step reads the document once per question. Batch prompting (Cheng et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024) puts all questions and answers in one sequence: it reads the document once, but the answers are generated one after another, and later answers attend to earlier ones. Parallel Prompting decodes the questions as streams of one request: every step adds one token per stream and reads the document once for all of them, and a stream mask (Figure 2) keeps the answers independent. The batch still has room for other requests, for example for other documents (Figure 6).
Figure 5: Wall time versus streams per request P on the calibration seed, normalized to the best P (16k-token documents). The curve is U-shaped, with its minimum at P = 16–64 on every setting.

Figure 4: Left: speedup over the faster stock configuration as document length and questions per document grow (128 output tokens). Right: speedup as answers get longer (8k-token document, 128 questions).
Figure 3: Speedup of Parallel Prompting over stock SGLang on 8k/16k-token documents with 64–256 questions. Error bars are 95% bootstrap CIs over 36 paired runs per setting. PP wins all 144 runs.

Figure 6: Speedup of PP over the faster stock configuration as more documents share a batch (4k-token documents, 64 questions each, 128 output tokens). Sixteen documents do not fit in the A6000’s KV pool.

Figure 2: The in-kernel mask in one decode step: a request with a 3-token document, P = 3 streams and 1-token questions, at decode step 2 (aki is stream i’s k-th answer token). Each KV slot carries its stream id slot sid (−1 for the document), and the streams share positions. The new token a21 of stream 1 attends only to the document and to stream 1’s slots. Stage 1 of the kernel reads the cached slots through kv indices; stage 2 reads the step’s new tokens.

papers.selection_reason: Parallel decoding with shared context reduces memory bandwidth and inference cost, fitting KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: Read Once, Answer Many: Parallel Prompting for Shared-Context LLM Inference
papers.tldr: Parallel Prompting accelerates multi-question LLM inference over the same long document by decoding all questions together while reading the shared KV cache only once per step.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation. In our production setting, hundreds of VLA-powered robots are already operating in real-world environments, creating an immediate need for efficient fleet serving. We present XInfer, a production-deployed VLA serving system designed to reduce the inference infrastructure cost of large-scale robotic deployments. XInfer jointly coordinates heterogeneous VLA computation with the evolving response requirements of robotic execution. By exploiting computational parallelism while managing interference, XInfer improves GPU efficiency while protecting time-critical robotic feedback. We evaluate XInfer across three VLA models using production-derived workloads, achieving 1.26-3.75 times the effective robot capacity (ERC) of state-of-the-art systems under physical-execution constraints. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/X-Square-Robot/xinfer.
bullets: Addresses the infrastructure cost and serving challenges of hundreds of real-world VLA-powered robots.
Coordinates heterogeneous VLA computation with changing robotic execution requirements.
Uses computational parallelism while managing interference to protect latency-sensitive feedback.
Evaluated on three VLA models with production-derived workloads under physical-execution constraints.
Achieves 1.26–3.75× the effective robot capacity of state-of-the-art systems; implementation is publicly available.

papers.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache of autoregressive transformers grows linearly with context length and dominates memory at long context. Most training-free remedies evict low-importance tokens, an irreversible choice along the sequence axis. We instead keep every token and store it more cheaply along the "feature" axis. We therefore propose AttSVD, a new "interpretable" low-rank compression whose basis is derived from each prompt's own attention geometry: an online, per-prompt truncated SVD that keeps only the directions attention actually reads, cutting persistent per-head KV memory in proportion to the retained rank. We propose two decode-time caching strategies, accumulating and streaming, for short and long generation regimes. Furthermore, we propose two refinements that make compression adaptive. A per-matrix energy rule sizes the logit space and the attention mass independently. An attention-aware basis truncates only in the spaces attention actually reads, preserving both the attention logits and the attention output. The same factors also provide free, per-head interpretability insights into the effective rank and the geometry attention consumes. Across multiple models, on both an agentic benchmark and the full LongBench suite AttSVD stays on par with the dense cache while using up to 50% of the KV-cache memory.
bullets: Addresses the linear KV-cache memory growth of long-context autoregressive transformers without evicting tokens.
Derives an online, per-prompt SVD basis from attention geometry and retains only attention-relevant feature directions.
Introduces accumulating and streaming decode-time caching strategies for short- and long-generation settings.
Uses independent energy-based rank selection and attention-aware truncation to preserve attention logits and outputs.
Matches dense-cache performance across multiple models, an agentic benchmark, and LongBench, with up to 50% KV-memory reduction.

papers.abstract: Acoustic Anomaly Detection (AAD) serves as a non-contact approach for machine condition monitoring, yet much of the existing research is evaluated offline and rarely addresses embedded hardware constraints or microphone variations under operational drift. This paper presents a comparative evaluation of on-edge continual AAD across two embedded platforms the ESP32-S3 (with an external I2S digital microphone) and the Arduino Nicla Vision (with an onboard Pulse Density Modulation (PDM) microphone) using a shared detection model. The model utilizes a lightweight ShallowNet encoder and contrastive prototype learning to map spectrograms into a 32-dimensional embedding space. Both boards run an identical TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers (TFLM) encoder, performing on-device prototype learning updated via an exponential moving average. A cloud pipeline orchestrated through Firebase and MQTT enables remote data collection and retraining. Evaluated via a controlled speaker-replay protocol using standardized Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events (DCASE) Challenge Task 2 machine sounds, the ESP32-S3 achieved 82.35% to 95.00% accuracy across five machine types, while the Nicla Vision achieved 79.41% to 95.00%. The two platforms demonstrated comparable performance, confirming that the lightweight prototypical architecture transfers reliably across distinct hardware and sensor tiers.
bullets: Addresses the gap between offline AAD research and deployment under embedded constraints and operational drift.
Uses a shared ShallowNet encoder with contrastive prototype learning in a 32-dimensional embedding space.
Both devices perform TensorFlow Lite Micro inference and on-device prototype updates via exponential moving averages.
Evaluated with controlled speaker replay on DCASE Task 2 machine sounds; accuracy ranged from 82.35%–95.00% on ESP32-S3 and 79.41%–95.00% on Nicla Vision.
Results support cross-platform transferability, though evaluation used a controlled replay protocol and the reported machine-sound benchmark.

papers.abstract: Mixed-precision post-training quantization needs a per-module sensitivity signal; for a text embedder the obvious one -- the retrieval quality a module costs when quantized -- needs relevance labels that deployments rarely have. We measure a label-free substitute: quantization-induced representation drift, obtained by quantizing one module, re-encoding the corpus, and recording how far the output embeddings moved from their full-precision positions. What is specific is the observable: the deployed output representation a dense retriever ranks with. Across five development embedders, configuration-level drift orders sampled mixed-precision plans against held-out retrieval quality at a macro Spearman of 0.911, the sensitivity transports across calibration corpora and retrieval domains in the usable regime, module drifts compose rank-consistently but not numerically, and relevance-derived sensitivity adds no consistent value. The method is one additive allocation under a hard packed-byte budget, with no labels and no search. On three embedders held untouched until method, baselines and hypotheses were frozen and sealed, the pre-registered directional hypothesis against the prior LieQ criterion holds (3/3 at the main budget, no collapse) and drift scores above a two-sided LieQ steelman in 2/3; but at the main budget drift is numerically lower than same-budget uniform precision on all three (-0.99, -0.85, -1.01 points), having reduced module and whole-model drift as designed. Output drift is thus a robust coarse sensitivity signal, not a universally optimal allocation objective: it avoids the catastrophic failures of the transferred signed-geometry adaptation and can remain usable at stressed budgets where uniform collapses, but fine-grained redistribution around a strong uniform operating point remains unresolved.
bullets: Addresses the need for module sensitivity signals without relevance labels in deployment settings.
Quantizes modules individually, re-encodes a corpus, and measures movement of output embeddings from full-precision representations.
Across five development embedders, drift ranked mixed-precision plans against retrieval quality with macro Spearman 0.911 and transferred across calibration corpora and domains in usable regimes.
A no-search additive allocation under a hard packed-byte budget beat a strengthened LieQ criterion on 2/3 untouched embedders, while the preregistered directional hypothesis held on all 3.
At the main budget, drift underperformed same-budget uniform precision on all three held-out embedders; fine-grained redistribution near strong uniform settings remains unresolved.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Full-precision retention of the drift allocation against the actual packed budget. Retention is quantized NDCG@10 divided by full-precision NDCG@10 on the same corpus. The same normalized budget lands in very different regimes on different architectures.

The cloud in (a) sits systematically below y = x — the compressive bias quantified in Table 9 — and (b) shows how far the disagreement reaches: a tenth of configurations are off by more than a third. Panel (a) read alone invites “near-additive”; (b) is why the text below claims ordering rather than magnitude. Module drifts and configuration drifts are measured on the same corpus, so the spread here is composition error and not cross-corpus transfer.

The top-decile column has n ≈ 16 per model and is shown for shape only.

Each curve reports the best held-out NDCG@10 reached after evaluating k configurations, selecting by label-free whole-model drift alone; NDCG is never consulted during selection. “no signal” picks uniformly at random from the same candidates. “additive” is the drift allocation, which costs 36 single-module encodings rather than k configuration evaluations. Curves are single trajectories; seed variance is not measured (§8).

Table 3: Development comparison (the five models the method was designed against; the three untouched confirmation models are reported separately in §4.3, and no aggregate win count against LieQ is given over these five). Held-out NDCG@10 at B3, all arms under the same packed-byte budget. §marks a cliff-crossing cell, where one allocation falls below the usability threshold, so the difference is not a quality margin. LieQ-signed is the literal port of the prior directional criterion; LieQ-abs replaces its score with |∆r| and is a two-sided steelman fixed in advance of computing it, after a systematic sign reversal was observed on the development models. ≡Umarks a LieQ-abs allocation that is byte-identical to uniform precision — in those cells the unsigned criterion does not discriminate between modules, and the drift margin should be read as a margin over uniform rather than over LieQ. ‡InfoQ-X was rejected by a pre-specified estimator-stability gate before any retrieval score was computed — an empty cell here is a resolved negative result, not a missing measurement. LieQ-adapt uses LieQ’s own diagnostic [33] — the training-induced concentration of a projection’s output spectrum, measured against an untrained weight matrix of matched statistics — as the sensitivity score, with the quantizer, bit set, group size, packing overhead, budget, allocator and calibration inputs held identical to ours. It is an adaptation rather than a reproduction: LieQ allocates per layer, we allocate over twelve units. Fifteen arms are run, and the one reported here is fixed a priori as closest to the method as described, not chosen on the held-out score; the arm and the selection rule are given in Table 4, and the post-hoc best of the fifteen is reported separately as a LieQ-family upper bound in Table 17. InfoQ-X is reported only if it satisfies the estimator-stability criterion fixed in advance (Appendix B); InfoQ-X did not satisfy the pre-specified estimator-stability gate, so no retrieval score is reported for it; see Appendix B. Our own static-geometry operationalization is not a published system and is reported in Appendix I (Table 18) rather than here.

Table 4: Which LieQ-adapt arm is reported and how reproducible its score is. The reported arm is fixed in advance, not selected on the held-out score. Fifteen arms are run — three sensitivity variants crossed with five allocation rules, the latter being LieQ’s own top-m four-/two-bit split at a matched packed budget plus two bit-penalty forms crossed with two scopes — and the arm in Table 3 is the one chosen a priori as closest to the method as described: an isotropic untrained reference, LieQ’s own per-head split, LieQ’s criterion applied to the layer bands with the vocabulary bands held at uniform (LieQ is layer-wise and has no vocabulary-band notion), and the 4−b bit penalty that matches uniform-quantization error scaling. Choosing instead the best of the fifteen by held-out NDCG would be a LieQ-family post-hoc upper bound, not a baseline; that quantity is reported separately in Appendix I (Table 17) together with the arm that uses LieQ’s own two-level allocation rule, and our method is given no comparable advantage. Arm names are abbreviated: the prefix is the sensitivity variant (init = isotropic untrained reference, wd = every projection split at a fixed width d, colmatch = a reference matched to the trained weight’s column statistics), top-m is LieQ’s own allocation rule, and 2−b/4−b with all/lay name the bit-penalty form and whether embedding bands participate. These are display abbreviations for one ledger key and not separate recipes: the reported arm is written init/L2_mse/layers in the ledger and renders here as init/4−b/lay, where L2_mse is the 4−b penalty — the error of a uniform quantizer scales as 4−b, so the two names denote the same quantity. Seed ρ is the rank correlation of the module scores across draws of the untrained reference matrix, which is the only stochastic element of the diagnostic. Agreement ρ is the rank correlation between the two sensitivity criteria over the twelve allocation units; since the allocator, bit set, group size, packing overhead, budget and calibration inputs are identical between the arms, it isolates the disagreement between criteria from everything else.

Table 8: Four-probe domain stability. Module sensitivity is measured independently on SciFact, FiQA, ArguAna and NFCorpus; every resulting plan is evaluated on SciDocs, which appears in no probe. ρ is the median pairwise Spearman of the 12× 3 module-by-bit sensitivities over the six probe pairs. Identical is the fraction of probe pairs selecting a byte-identical bit plan at that budget, and Max ∆NDCG the largest held-out disagreement any pair produces. †marks cells the budget collapses (best probe retains under half of full-precision). Those cells are reported separately rather than dismissed: all of their resulting systems lie in the collapsed regime, so a plan disagreement there is not comparable to one between usable systems, but it is not evidence that the signal is stable either — the Qwen3-0.6B cell shows the signal-to-decision chain becoming more consequential past the cliff. The macro row is computed over the non-collapsed cells and the all-cell macro is given in the text.

Table 18: Our own static-geometry operationalization at B3, retained for reference now that a prior geometry-based baseline (LieQ-adapt, Table 3) is available. Layer importance is read from full-precision activation spectra with no quantization intervention and routed through the same allocator. It is not a reproduction of any published system. “Pre-specified” is a single variant fixed in advance and is the honest baseline; “post-hoc bound” is the best of the listed variants selected on the held-out set, which makes it an upper bound for the family rather than a competitor — our method is not given the same advantage. Unlike LieQ, these proxies read the spectrum in absolute terms, with no untrained reference, so they do not measure training-induced concentration.

The stratum is the pre-registered pairwise classification by each arm’s own retention against the 0.5×full-precision usability threshold: graded (drift and LieQ-signed both usable), cliff (one usable), dead (neither).

Table 22: Compression frontier, with the realized packed bits per weight for each budget name (§3, §4.2). The realized cost of a given budget name differs across models, which is why the names must not be read as bit widths. A cell is marked collapse when the drift allocation retains under half of full-precision quality, and saturated when uniform quantization already retains over 95%, leaving little for any allocator to win.

The gap between the pre-specified column and the post-hoc column measures how much of that family’s headroom is invisible without looking at the test metric.

D̂held-out is the sum of single-module held-out drifts under the plan (the allocator itself minimised the calibration-corpus analogue), D the measured whole-model balanced drift. The inversion rate is Pr[(D̂A − D̂B)(DA −DB) < 0] over configuration pairs, restricted to three regions: the whole pool, the top quartile by true held-out NDCG, and the budget-preserving neighbourhood of the additive plan — the region a local search actually explores. papers.abstract: Network pruning can reduce parameter redundancy in robotic policies. However, generic pruning criteria are tailored for image recognition tasks and commonly designed to preserve weight magnitude, local reconstruction, or language-model likelihood rather than closed-loop action behavior. Directly applying these pruning algorithms to robotic tasks yields unsatisfactory performance. In this paper, we propose Loss-Conditioned Activation-Moment (LCAM) pruning, a training-free method for unstructured pruning of pre-trained robotic manipulation policies. Specifically, we first rank connections using row-normalized weight contribution, activation moments measured on calibration demonstrations, and the sensitivity of output directions to the action-prediction loss. We further design a self-recursive coarse-to-fine procedure: importance is recalibrated after each nested coarse pruning stage, while held-out offline action distortion guides fine-grained budget allocation after a sparsity knee. Our algorithm is free from costly recovery training and simulator rollouts after pruning. Experiments on three LIBERO suites with competitive robotic policies, together with evaluations on OpenVLA, show that LCAM attains competitive performance across a broad range of pruning ratios. Notably, on LIBERO-Object with OpenVLA, our LCAM achieves 84.0% success at 50% unstructured pruning, retaining over 90% of the dense policy's success rate. Promising results on real-world robotic ping pong further demonstrate the effectiveness of our pruning algorithm.
bullets: Generic pruning methods often degrade closed-loop robotic behavior because they are not designed around action performance.
LCAM ranks connections using normalized weight contribution, calibration-demo activation moments, and action-loss sensitivity.
A self-recursive coarse-to-fine procedure recalibrates importance and allocates pruning budgets using offline action distortion.
Across three LIBERO suites, OpenVLA, and real-world ping pong, LCAM performs competitively across pruning ratios.
On LIBERO-Object with OpenVLA, it achieves 84.0% success at 50% unstructured pruning—over 90% of the dense policy’s success rate.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Framework overview of LCAM with self-recursive coarse-to-fine pruning. Left: a first calibration pass estimates the layer-wise gradient scale, while a second pass combines row-normalized weight contribution with loss-conditioned activation moments to score individual connections. Right: connection importance is recalibrated as nested masks become sparser. Offline action distortion D(M), evaluated on the held-out set Dval, identifies a sparsity knee; afterward, equal-size candidate masks that prune an additional 1% of eligible weights are compared across feasible functional groups, and the candidate with the smallest distortion increase per newly pruned connection is accepted. LCAM constructs these masks without retraining or simulator rollouts.

Fig. 1. Comparison between generic pruning and our LCAM. Generic pruning may preserve its pruning objective without directly ensuring task-relevant action behavior. LCAM evaluates each connection using its row-normalized weight contribution and action-conditioned activation evidence from a small offline calibration set, and recursively recalibrates connection importance as sparsity increases to construct nested pruning masks.

papers.abstract: Looped models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for reasoning, with successes on simple reasoning puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. However, these models can be unstable, slow to train, and use many parameters and FLOPs to solve simple puzzles. Descent on an energy not only mitigates these issues but also offers advantages: built-in early stopping, compute that adapts to problem difficulty, fast training without differentiating through a solver, and interpretable weights that learn the constraints of the puzzle. Here we demonstrate this with a learned version of Hopfield & Tank's energy from the 80s, which we term CRAM, solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one GPU, at least 1,000x faster than looped models on these tasks. CRAM also matches baseline looped models at their highest accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme using at least 282x fewer inference FLOPs. Our work suggests two things. First, that energies are an extremely promising direction for training reasoning from data. Second, a caution against using trivially solvable benchmarks like Sudoku and Maze to test the scalability of looped reasoning techniques.
authors: Benjamin Hoover, Hugh Blayney, James C. R. Whittington
bullets: Looped reasoning models can be unstable, slow, and computationally heavy even on simple puzzles.
CRAM learns constraints through descent on a Hopfield–Tank-inspired energy without differentiating through a solver.
It achieves 99.996% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme and 100% on Maze-Unique.
Training takes 42 ms and 132 ms on one GPU, respectively, reported as at least 1,000× faster than looped models.
CRAM matches looped-model Sudoku accuracy with at least 282× fewer inference FLOPs; the authors caution that these benchmarks may be too easy for evaluating scalability.

figures.caption: Figure 2: (a) CRAM matches each looped model’s highest accuracy using at least 282× fewer inference FLOPs. Each point is one method showing what fraction of a 10,000 Sudoku-Extreme test puzzle was solved within a given inference budget, reported as the mean accuracy over three training runs with error bars spanning the lowest to the highest run. The arrow joins the most accurate point of EBR, the cheapest looped model, to the cheapest CRAM point that solves at least as many puzzles. The upper panel zooms into the top 2% shaded are of the lower panel. CRAM, TRMP and EBR points include early stopping, and FLOPs include the full reasoning search including every search chain (see App. C.2 for details). (b) CRAM learns weights that describe the reasoning task. Maze-Unique learns 3×3 shared weights, shown in units of the mean coupling to the four side neighbours, that describe a dead-end pruning algorithm for solving Maze-Unique, by exclusively observing valid maze solutions. On Sudoku-Extreme, CRAM learns correct sudoku costs despite receiving no positional constraint graph. Trained weights for sudoku and maze correspond to the CRAM model reported in Table 2.

Figure 1: CRAM learns an energy from solved puzzles in seconds, and the energy tells the search when to stop. Training (left) pulls down the energy of each solution and pushes up the energy of negative samples, without differentiating through a reasoning trajectory (shown is a pseudolikelihood objective, Eq. (5)). On one H200, training takes 42 ms on Sudoku-Extreme and 132 ms on MazeUnique, at least 1,000× faster than the looped models of Table 2. Reasoning (right) clamps the clues of a new puzzle, starts several chains from random fills of the other cells (light-blue guesses; one board per chain), and minimizes the energy one cell at a time, using at least 282× fewer inference FLOPs (Fig. 2) than looped models at matched accuracy. The chains are independent, and the descent can be noisy, which lets a chain escape spurious local minima. The search stops when any chain’s energy falls below a stopping threshold fitted from the training solutions.

Figure 3: (a) CRAM’s compute grows gently with puzzle difficulty. The 10,000 Sudoku-Extreme test puzzles of Fig. 2 are binned by difficulty rating provided by the dataset, where each tick gives the lowest rating of its bin (0, 1, 2–3, 4–7, 8–15, 16–31, 32–63, and 64+). FRM uses static compute for every puzzle, whereas both CRAM and EBR implement early stopping. EBR’s early stop barely lowers its compute on easy puzzles: its median stays between 3.3 and 4.2× 1011 FLOPs in every bin, near its minimum cost. Top: median FLOPs per puzzle, with bands spanning the 10th to 90th percentiles. Bottom: test accuracy, median over three training runs, with bands spanning the runs. (b) CRAM is data efficient, learning Sudoku using an order of magnitude fewer examples. Shown is model accuracy on the same 10,000 test puzzles vs. the number of unique training puzzles seen in the data (each data point is augmented with the same 99 augmentations). Points connect the median value across 6 training runs.

Figure 4: Local methods that avoid sampling the energy train significantly faster. We train CRAM with five objectives, the four named below and one-step BPTT [62], and plot the mean solve rate on 512 Sudoku-Extreme development puzzles over 20 training runs against training time. Bands span the 25th to 75th percentile of the runs. The mean reaches 99% (circles) after 48 ms with pseudolikelihood [8] and 0.21 s with minimum probability flow [56], against 4.4 s with one-step BPTT and 33 s with contrastive divergence [31]. Full BPTT [63] ends at a mean of 27% after 245 s, still rising at the end of its schedule; with 3,840,000 updates (about 5 h) it solves 48.8% of test puzzles. Training times include fitting the stopping threshold from the training solutions (24–75 ms) and exclude each run’s one-time start-up (0.08–0.30 s), as do the T99 times of Table 7, which compares twelve methods on Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique; App. D gives details of each objective.

Figure 6: CRAM+z solves a Maze-Hard test maze in two relaxations: the hidden layer settles to a distance-like field, and the answers prune the tree of pointers down to the path. Left: the hidden layer on test maze 0 (seed-0 model), settled first by Eq. (13): log z⋆i (white: not connected to G; dark gray: walls) and each cell’s pointer, a line toward its largest weight in Eq. (14); the pointers form a tree rooted at G. Top right: rounded answers of the answer flow, run second with the hidden layer fixed, from the all-on board: leaves switch off first; at the stop the board equals the labeled path. Bottom right: the answer energy (Eq. (1), entropy included) decreases at every step of that flow; the lighter line continues the flow for 48 steps after the stop, to its fixed point.

Figure 5: Hand-set weights on CRAM energy. Each title gives the number of distinct nonzero values. (a) Sudoku: board cell j shows the 9× 9 cost block Kij between the digits of the chosen cell i (rows) and of cell j (columns), on the color scale of the learned costs in Fig. 2b. It is the identity on the 20 cells that share a row, column or box with i. (b) Maze-Unique: change in energy when an open cell turns on; the center is the change with no neighbor on, and each other entry is the change that a neighbor on at that offset adds. (c) N-Queens (8× 8): cost of a queen at each cell together with a queen at the dark cell, 1 when they attack each other. (d) Graph coloring: cost of the colors of the two vertices of an edge; pairs without an edge cost 0.

Table 3: CRAM matches larger baselines on N-Queens and graph coloring. Both N-Queens on 8×8 and 10×10 boards and graph coloring of graphs with 8 and 10 vertices are evaluated on GRAM’s test sets. All numbers report mean ±stdev over three training seeds; the best learned value of each row is in bold. Acc.: test inputs whose kept answer is correct (%); N=1 keeps one sample, and N=20 keeps the majority vote of 20 samples for GRAM and the lowest-energy sample of 20 for EBR and CRAM; TRM and HRM are deterministic, so their two values are equal. Cov@20: share of each input’s solutions found by 20 samples (%). Conflict: conflicting edges of the kept answer, summed over the test graphs. Params: as in Table 2; each task trains its own model. Fit time: training seed 0 on one H200; one run for each baseline, and for CRAM the median of seven runs that follow a first run in the same process (App. C.5).

Table 2: CRAM trains faster and is more accurate and efficient than every looped baseline. The table reports accuracies and FLOPs at each model’s listed inference setting. Note that we also report a hand-set CRAM energy (gray). Solved: mean ±stdev test accuracy (%) over 3 training seeds. Params: nonzero, contributing params of the evaluated model. FLOPs/puzl: avg inference FLOPs per puzzle, including all search chains and failed searches (App. C.2). Fit time: wall clock of training seed 0 on one H200 (App. C.2); one run in a fresh process for each baseline, including initialization and compilation, and for CRAM the median of seven complete runs that follow a first run in the same process. More details in App. C.1.

Table 4: CRAM never halts at an incorrect board. Each looped model runs one rollout in its halting mode, capped at its trained depth; EBR’s first sample stops at a gradient norm below 0.2 or after 64 segments, as in its code. Halted: puzzles on which the rule stopped before the cap. Wrong halts: halted puzzles whose board is incorrect (% of halted). Full test sets (412,786 puzzles and 1,000 mazes), pooled over three training runs.

Table 7: Nine of the twelve training methods reach at least 99% test accuracy on both tasks, and a local objective is the first to reach 99% on the development probe of each task. T99: training time until the mean development solve rate of three runs first reaches 99% (dash: never). FLOPs99: training arithmetic to that point. Solved: exact test solve rate (%), mean ± SD over three runs. Classes, protocol and notes in App. D; bold: best value of each column. Every method runs in one shared training harness that is slower than the recipes of Table 2, so compare these times with each other, not with Table 2: a full pseudolikelihood fit on Sudoku-Extreme takes about 70 ms here, against 42 ms there.

Table 5: Every CRAM fit is a few dozen to a few thousand SGD updates of pseudolikelihood, and every search is a single-cell local search. All fits start at zero and use SGD with momentum 0.5 and a cosine schedule; the L1 term is a soft-threshold after each step. Values in parentheses are for the larger N-Queens board or graph. h̄: mean positive learned cost; u: the N-Queens temperature unit (App. C.5); τ : highest energy of a training solution.

Table 1: Supplied priors by task. M×C is the shape of the answer grid (num cells×num values). NParams is the total number of parameters available to train. NChains is the number of independent search chains per input: for N-Queens and graph coloring it is N , which varies in Table 3 (N=1 or N=20). Init is the value xi at the start of a search chain; U(C) draws it uniformly from the C values.

papers.selection_reason: Energy-based reasoning with adaptive compute and major FLOP reductions; directly relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000x Faster than Looped Models
papers.tldr: CRAM, a learned classical energy model, solves Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique dramatically faster than looped reasoning models while using far fewer inference FLOPs.

papers.abstract: On-device inference requires kernels that make effective use of local accelerators. Efficient training and evaluation of models that generate Apple Metal kernels benefit from native macOS tools and concurrent agent sessions. These sessions alternate between model requests, development commands, and GPU execution, leaving GPU capacity idle for much of a rollout. We present Metal Sandbox, infrastructure that combines restricted per-instance file access, native command execution, and command-level scheduling across interconnected Macs. Each agent retains its workspace and private development environment. Parallel commands can run concurrently, while serial commands share one execution slot per node; eligible waiting commands can migrate to available Macs and return results to the original agent. Integration with Harbor supports task execution, automatic verification, and rollout collection through a common workflow. Controlled experiments on four Mac mini M4 nodes achieve $1.68\times$--$2.05\times$ gains in command throughput under concentrated demand. Sixteen static agent traces give an estimated $2.14\times$ sustained-throughput gain for four sessions per node versus one, assuming continuously replenished sessions and unchanged mean durations. Replaying these measured traces under dynamic scheduling reduces mean tool waiting by 18.8% and batch elapsed time by 22.3%, assuming unchanged phase durations. Metal Sandbox and its Harbor integration are open-source on GitHub.
authors: Haozhe Wang, Lina Chen, Fanqi Wan, Qi Han, Yinmin Zhang, Zheng Ge, Daxin Jiang, Junchi Yan
bullets: Addresses GPU underutilization caused by alternating model requests, development commands, and execution during agent rollouts.
Provides per-instance file isolation, native macOS command execution, and scheduling that runs parallel commands concurrently while serial commands share node capacity.
Waiting commands can migrate to available Macs and return results to their originating agents; Harbor integrates execution, verification, and rollout collection.
On four Mac mini M4 nodes, concentrated-demand command throughput increased 1.68×–2.05×.
Trace replay showed 18.8% lower mean tool waiting and 22.3% shorter batch elapsed time under dynamic scheduling, with stated assumptions.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks for image processing are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained edge devices such as drones, medical systems, and smartphones, where limited computational resources and memory bandwidth pose significant challenges for efficient inference. Pruning during training often produces highly sparse convolutional kernels, offering the potential to significantly reduce computation and memory requirements. However, exploiting this sparsity efficiently at runtime remains challenging due to irregular memory access patterns and workload imbalance across processing elements. In this work, we investigate the standard convolution with sparse weights and analyze its performance characteristics through roofline analysis, showing that a 3 x 3 sparse convolution achieves an arithmetic intensity of approximately 10 FLOP/byte compared to roughly 96 FLOP/byte for its dense counterpart. We propose techniques for an efficient sparse convolution at high sparsities. Preliminary results demonstrate that our approach achieves upto 1.65x speedup as compared to dense convolution on NVIDIA A100 and upto 1.52x on NVIDIA Jetson Nano (Tegra X1) , motivating further exploration of direct convolution as a practical path to efficient sparse inference on modern accelerators/edge devices.
authors: Keshvi Tuteja, Yu-Hsiang Tsai, Gregor Olenik, Markus G\"otz, Achim Streit, Hartwig Anzt, Charlotte Debus
bullets: Sparse weights can reduce computation and memory needs for edge-device inference, but irregular access and workload imbalance hinder runtime efficiency.
Roofline analysis estimates arithmetic intensity of about 10 FLOP/byte for 3×3 sparse convolution versus roughly 96 FLOP/byte for dense convolution.
The proposed techniques target efficient sparse convolution at high sparsity levels.
Preliminary results show speedups on both a data-center GPU and an edge accelerator.
The study motivates direct convolution as a practical route to sparse inference, while presenting the results as preliminary.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Roofline model for sparse convolution on NVIDIA A100 and Jetson Nano (NVIDIA Tegra X1)

Figure 1: Sparse convolution with sparse weights. Here, the input image has 3 input channels (IC), output image has 2 output channels (OC). OC denotes the number of output channels, with each output channel generated using a distinct set of convolutional kernels spanning all input channels. The convolution filter has a 3x3 weight matrix for each OC and IC.

Figure 3: Mapping of an output tile to a warp. In this example, one warp computes four output columns across two output rows. The warp is partitioned into four groups of eight threads, with each group assigned to one output column. For the first column, threads 0–7 initially compute output channels (OCs) 0–7, before proceeding to OCs 8–15, 16–23, and 24–31 in subsequent steps. Similarly, threads 8–15, 16–23, and 24–31 process the second, third, and fourth output columns, respectively. The same mapping is repeated for every output row assigned to the warp. The number inside each thread box indicates the OC computed by that thread at the corresponding execution step.

Since sparse convolution is primarily memory bound, reducing memory traffic and improving load efficiency are critical for achieving high performance.

papers.title: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Sparse Convolution

papers.abstract: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as a leading paradigm for distilling diffusion models into few-step students, where an auxiliary fake score model tracks the student's distribution and the discrepancy between the teacher and fake predictions drives the student toward the teacher. In multi-step distillation, although only the student's final output is delivered, existing methods train the fake model on intermediate states or across all denoising steps. Consequently, the student's update signal becomes entangled with intermediate distributions, which can distort the matching direction and remain nonzero even after the student's final outputs already match the teacher distribution. To resolve this mismatch, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains a single shared fake model exclusively on the student's final outputs and uses it to correct every denoising step. Our theoretical analysis proves that this endpoint reference guarantees that the distribution matching term vanishes if and only if the student's final output distribution matches the teacher's, regardless of intermediate distributions. Beyond the fake reference, we further strengthen teacher supervision through a precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step guided predictions with short multi-step trajectories on the final noise interval, paired with a calibrated query density for intermediate steps. Experiments on SD3-Medium, FLUX.2-klein (4B and 9B), and Qwen-Image-2.1 demonstrate that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching methods for 4-step generation.
authors: Tong Zhao, Xianfang Zeng, Yucheng Han, Ruoyu Wang, Mingkun Lei, Gang Yu, Chi Zhang
bullets: Existing DMD methods train fake score models on intermediate states, which can misalign updates with the final output distribution.
eDMD trains one shared fake model exclusively on student endpoints while applying its correction at every denoising step.
Theoretical analysis shows the matching loss vanishes exactly when the student’s final distribution matches the teacher’s, independent of intermediate states.
A precise teacher uses short multi-step trajectories on the final noise interval, with calibrated sampling for intermediate queries.
Experiments on SD3-Medium, FLUX.2-klein, and Qwen-Image-2.1 show consistent improvements over prior distribution-matching methods for 4-step generation.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of eDMD on a 2D tree-structured toy distribution (gray). Left: a 4-step student denoises from noise (σ = 1) to its final output (σ = 0, “delivered”); each update noises one step’s prediction to a level τ (green bar: its range) and compares the teacher and the fake model at the resulting query y. Right: compared with DMD2 and TDM, eDMD trains the fake model on final outputs only (top), draws the queries of intermediate steps from a calibrated density (middle; ticks: the level each step denoises to), and answers low-noise queries with a multi-step teacher instead of a single prediction (bottom; percentages: answers on the tree).

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Endpoint Distribution Matching (eDMD) for few-step diffusion distillation, improving generation speed and quality by decoupling the student's update signal from intermediate distributions.
papers.title: eDMD: Endpoint Distribution Matching for Few-Step Diffusion Distillation
papers.tldr: eDMD distills diffusion models into 4-step generators by matching only final student outputs to the teacher distribution, improving generation quality across several models.

papers.abstract: Smaller language models (SLMs) make it feasible to deploy clinical natural language processing where large proprietary models are too costly, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning allows them to be specialised on commodity hardware. One obstacle persists after training: on medical tasks these models answer at far greater length than the clinical question requires. In clinical decision support and point-of-care use, where time is short, such verbosity is hard to act on even when the underlying reasoning is sound. Existing length-control methods depend on preference optimisation, reward models, or proprietary teachers that undercut the accessibility making SLMs attractive. We introduce Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation (PECA), which adds a single differentiable conciseness term to the QLoRA supervised fine-tuning objective. Because the token count is discrete and non-differentiable, PECA instead raises the end-of-sequence probability once generation exceeds a token budget, a smooth signal optimised during ordinary training, with no preference data, no auxiliary model, and a single commodity GPU. On a 1.7-billion-parameter model fine-tuned on the medical-o1-reasoning-SFT corpus, PECA reduces mean response length by 72.8% while improving multiple-choice diagnostic accuracy from 40.8% to 44.0%. A sweep over the conciseness strength traces an interpretable accuracy-to-length frontier for balancing brevity and diagnostic completeness.
authors: Tanzeel Abbas, Ahmad Kamran Malik, Nafees Qamar, Sana Liaqat
bullets: Addresses excessive verbosity in smaller models used for clinical decision support and point-of-care applications.
Adds a differentiable conciseness term that increases end-of-sequence probability after a specified token budget.
Requires no preference data, reward model, proprietary teacher, or auxiliary model, and is designed for commodity hardware.
On a 1.7B-parameter model, mean response length fell by 72.8% while multiple-choice diagnostic accuracy rose from 40.8% to 44.0%.
Varying conciseness strength produces an interpretable accuracy–length trade-off for balancing brevity and completeness.

papers.abstract: Distributed fiber-optic sensing (DFOS) technologies such as Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) generate continuous, high-resolution spatio-temporal data at rates exceeding hundreds of megabytes per second, creating severe challenges for real-time storage and transmission. While neural compression methods can achieve strong rate-distortion performance on sensing data, prior approaches either require per-segment retraining incompatible with streaming, or have only been validated offline. None have been demonstrated end-to-end on a continuously streaming DAS acquisition system at scale. We present STeP-C (Spatio-Temporal Predictive Compression), a neural compression framework that decouples spatial encoding, temporal prediction, and entropy-optimized residual coding, trained end-to-end with a rate-distortion objective motivated by conditional entropy reduction. Critically, we identify entropy coding as the dominant bottleneck for streaming deployment. We address it through GPU-side symbol computation, cached probability tables, and parallel GIL-free arithmetic coding, together with FP16 inference and batched entropy coding, enabling a full real-time pipeline built around a GPU ring buffer. We validate this pipeline on a live DAS testbed, achieving a 98.85% file size reduction at 31.04 dB full-band PSNR and an average throughput of 535 MB/s, exceeding the 324 MB/s requirement for 1 kHz, 81 km DAS streams. We further show that STeP-C substantially outperforms conventional codecs at practical streaming bitrates, can be applied to unseen channel ranges within the same acquisition system without retraining, and largely maintains downstream detector consistency, with 96.62% high-confidence class agreement and 100% Jaccard similarity on detected event types.
authors: Tingfeng Li, Ming-Fang Huang, Shaobo Han, Yue Tian
bullets: Addresses the storage and transmission burden of continuous, high-resolution distributed acoustic sensing streams.
Decouples spatial encoding, temporal prediction, and entropy-optimized residual coding in an end-to-end rate-distortion framework.
Accelerates streaming deployment with GPU-side symbol computation, cached probability tables, parallel arithmetic coding, FP16 inference, batching, and a GPU ring buffer.
Validated on a live DAS testbed at 535 MB/s and 31.04 dB full-band PSNR, exceeding the stated 324 MB/s requirement.
Preserves downstream detection consistency and generalizes to unseen channel ranges within the same system without retraining.

papers.abstract: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a $4$ GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an $8$ GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, $\texttt{llama.cpp}$'s K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At $1\%$ and $3.5\%$ perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are $5.7-31.4\%$ smaller than the best $\texttt{llama.cpp}$ format. A bit-exact $0.21$ mm$^2$ ASIC decoder unit ($1$ GHz, $7$ nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to $36\%$ and $38\%$ ($54\%$ and $44\%$ with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ needs $58-64\%$ less time and $53-57\%$ less energy per token than CPU $\texttt{llama.cpp}$, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6$\times$ faster at $3.89$ bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).
authors: Arnab Sanyal, Gourav Datta, Sandeep P. Chinchali
bullets: Targets memory capacity and bandwidth limits on resource-constrained edge devices.
Tunes GPTQ code distributions, then applies lossless Huffman coding in interleaved lanes.
Uses a small DRAM-to-L2 decoder, preserving existing deployed weight formats and GPU execution.
Across tested models, achieves 5.7–31.4% smaller weights within stated perplexity budgets.
Reports up to 36% lower latency and 38% lower energy per token on Orin, with larger gains under prompt-lookup speculation; also improves Nano performance and energy use.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. LazyWeights overview: entropy-aware quantization and a permatrix Huffman bundle in the cloud; on the device, a decode unit between the memory controller and L2 restores fixed-width codes. Without the unit, the GPU kernels decode in software inside GEMV (32 lanes) as the reference. Bottom: bits per weight.

Fig. 3. (a) Bundle layout: a 64×256 tile of 4-bit codes is 32 lanes of two rows; each lane is one Huffman stream of 32-bit words (code boundaries illustrative); the lanes’ words are interleaved, so one aligned read fetches the next word of every lane, and per-tile lane offsets let any tile start independently; two 4-bit codes form one 8-bit pair symbol. (b) Decode unit between the memory controller and L2 (as in Fig. 1): T engines of 32 lanes sharing an 8-word read port through a masked round-robin arbiter; a lane compares an 11-bit peek against per-length limits (no 2048-entry table), adds the length’s offset to index the symbol table, and shifts its buffer by the length.

Fig. 4. Rate–quality frontiers. Dots: coded models, including llama.cpp’s imatrix codes behind our Huffman stage; lines: lowest ∆PPL reachable at or below a rate; shading: where coding wins; rings: released operating points; dashed: the 1% and 3.5% budgets and fp16. Axis linear below 1%.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a weight compression and decode-on-demand approach that reduces memory footprint for LLM inference, fitting memory efficiency.
papers.title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
papers.tldr: LazyWeights compresses quantized LLM weights and decodes them on demand to reduce edge-device memory traffic, latency, and energy without changing GPU kernels.

papers.abstract: Change detection in remote sensing conventionally relies on spatially aligned bi-temporal imagery, which may be unavailable or unreliable in practical scenarios. Recent single-temporal approaches address this limitation by learning structural evidence, such as building regions, from a labeled source dataset and transferring it to unseen target imagery using only the current image. However, adaptation to the source dataset can over-specialize pretrained features and reduce their cross-dataset generalization, a risk that this paper argues is higher when the feature adaptation is parameterized independently of the states used for prediction. To address this issue, the current study introduces SALT, a State-Aligned Low-Rank Transfer framework. SALT keeps a DINOv3 backbone frozen and learns negative and positive structural states that both score each patch and, through State-Aligned Low-Rank Adaptation (SALA), span the rank-2 subspace in which patch features are corrected. Directional State Alignment supervises these corrections to raise the evidence of positive patches and lower that of negative ones, while Geometry Preservation limits changes to the pairwise relations among pretrained patch features. Experiments on LEVIR-CD and the WHU aerial building dataset show that, at the pixel level and in both transfer directions, SALT outperforms four baselines reproduced under a common source-only protocol, improving over the strongest reproduced baselines by 9.45 and 5.79 points in pixel-level AP and by 27.69 and 14.25 points in IoU (LEVIR-CD to WHU and WHU to LEVIR-CD, respectively), with only 0.068M trainable parameters and 40.2 ms per image. In order to facilitate reproducibility and further research, the source code of SALT is available at https://github.com/gthpapadopoulos/SALT
authors: Aggelos Psiris, Georgios Angelidis, Giorgos Sfikas, Maria Vakalopoulou, Thomas Lagkas, Panagiotis Sarigiannidis, Georgios Th. Papadopoulos
bullets: Addresses single-temporal cross-dataset structural localization when aligned bi-temporal imagery is unavailable or unreliable.
Freezes a DINOv3 backbone and learns positive/negative structural states that score patches and define a rank-2 correction subspace.
Uses directional state alignment to separate positive and negative evidence, with geometry preservation limiting distortion of pretrained patch relationships.
On LEVIR-CD and WHU, outperforms four reproduced source-only baselines in both transfer directions at pixel-level AP and IoU.
Uses 0.068M trainable parameters and 40.2 ms per image; code is publicly available.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SALT. A frozen DINOv3 extracts patch features from a single image. SALA uses the learned negative and positive structural states to define a rank-2 adaptation space, within which each patch feature is corrected. The adapted features are then scored to produce a dense structural response map. The four training objectives (top) supervise structural predictions, guide feature corrections, preserve feature relationships, and separate the learned states. Green arrows indicate training on the source dataset, while red arrows indicate inference on the unseen target dataset. Only the structural states and the lightweight coefficient predictor are trained.

Figure 3. Indicative cross-dataset localization results. Rows are labeled by the target dataset (WHU rows from LEVIR-CD→WHU, LEVIR rows from WHU→LEVIR-CD, with LEVIR denoting LEVIR-CD). For each method, the heatmap shows the dense response map and the binary mask uses the threshold selected on the source validation split.

Figure 1. Localization performance versus adaptation size. Pixel-level AP versus trainable parameters (logarithmic scale). Colors identify the methods; circles and triangles denote LEVIRCD→WHU and WHU→LEVIR-CD, respectively. Thin vertical lines connect each method’s two transfer results, and error bars show standard deviations over three seeds. SALT achieves the highest pixel AP in both directions with 69× to 465× fewer trainable parameters than the reproduced baselines.

Table 1. Cross-dataset localization performance (%, mean±standard deviation over three seeds). All methods are reproduced under the common source-only protocol, and F1 and IoU use the threshold selected on the source validation split. Best results are in bold and secondbest are underlined.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces State-Aligned Low-Rank Adaptation (SALA) for adapting a frozen DINOv3 backbone, focusing on parameter efficiency (0.068M params) and state alignment for cross-dataset localization.
papers.title: SALT: State-Aligned Low-Rank Transfer for Single-Temporal Cross-Dataset Structural Localization in Remote Sensing
papers.tldr: SALT transfers structural localization across remote-sensing datasets using state-aligned low-rank feature adaptation while preserving pretrained feature geometry.

papers.abstract: Second-order optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP's dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP's dense second moment, and we measure only a 15-20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP's optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP's gains need not require SOAP's cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam
authors: Jaemyung Yu, Byeongho Heo, Sangdoo Yun, Dongyoon Han
bullets: Targets the high memory and eigendecomposition costs that limit practical use of SOAP.
Uses input-only preconditioning, removing the output-side Kronecker factor and one eigendecomposition.
Replaces SOAP’s dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator using row-by-column statistics.
Matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss, uses half of SOAP’s optimizer state, and runs at Muon-class wall-clock time.
Demonstrated across 124M–760M-parameter LLM pretraining and a three-fold learning-rate range.

figures.caption: Figure 1: FOAM is a Pareto-efficient second-order optimizer. GPT-2 large (760M), 29.55K steps, each optimizer at its tuned learning rate. Curves are 3-seed means smoothed over 1K steps, and grey boxes mark the regions magnified in the insets. (a) Per-step. Validation loss against training step. In the last 4K steps (inset) SOAP ends slightly below FOAM (2.791 vs. 2.796, within about one seed std), both below Muon, while AdamW stays above the inset range. (b) Wall-clock. Same runs vs. wall time, normalized so AdamW finishes at 1.0× (Muon, FOAM, and SOAP finish at 1.15×, 1.17×, and 2.31×). Within AdamW’s own budget, FOAM is already 0.04 nats below AdamW’s final loss (inset), and it reaches SOAP’s quality band at 51% of SOAP’s wall-clock time. (c) Time to AdamW’s final loss (2.847; Table 2). FOAM gets there as fast as AdamW itself (10.53 vs. 10.55 h) and slightly ahead of Muon, while bilateral SOAP needs 2.15× as long.

Figure 3: Hyperparameter robustness around each optimizer’s best cell on GPT-2 small. For AdamW, SOAP, and FOAM we sweep 5 LR points (factor 101/8), 5 WD points (factor 101/4) at the best LR, and 3 values each of β1 and β2 at the best LR/WD. All other HPs are held fixed. Panel (c) breaks the y-axis at the top: AdamW’s point at β1 = 0.99 is 3.86, far above the other values.

Figure 4: Layer-wise Gauss-Newton alignment. For each of 72 matrix parameters, we estimate HGN = J⊤ ℓ GyJℓ via 10 to 30 Hutchinson probes with the closed-form softmax-CE output Hessian, and compute the Frobenius cosine cos(P,HGN) in sqrt-power form for six implicit preconditioners. Curves are means over the 72 matrices along one SOAP run on GPT-2 small.

Figure 5: Validity of the factored second moment. On the dense run of each regime, we form the rank-1 approximation Vfac=(V 1)(1⊤V )/(1⊤V 1) from the row and column sums of the second-moment estimate V , and report (a) the rank-1 share σ1(V )/ ∑ iσi(V ) and (b) the Frobenius cosine between Vfac and V , averaged across all matrix parameters.

Table 2: Pre-training results. For each method and scale at the best LR/WD (details in Appendix A) of its own search, we report validation loss (val, mean ± std over 11 seeds and 3 at large), matrix-group optimizer state in GiB (state), per-step wall time in ms on one 8×H100 node (iter), and the wall-clock tA (minutes at small, hours otherwise) to reach AdamW’s per-size final loss, i.e., the steps to reach it times iter.

Table 3: FOAM-construction ablation on GPT-2 small (124M). Starting from SOAP, input R and output L mark which Kronecker factor (with its rotation) is kept, and factored v replaces the dense second moment by r, c. Each variant uses its own best LR/WD cell; mean ± std over 3 seeds of the ablation runs’ final evaluation. state is the matrix-parameter optimizer state (GiB) and wall is the total training wall-clock on a single 8×H100 node.
Table 1: Per-parameter complexity. State, per-step compute, and amortized eigendecomposition cost for W ∈ Rm×n with output-side L ∈ Rm×m and input-side R ∈ Rn×n. FOAM keeps Muon’s per-step cost.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a memory- and compute-efficient second-order optimizer for LLM pretraining, matching SOAP quality at near-AdamW cost.
papers.title: Factored One-sided Adam-Moment for Practical and Scalable SOAP
papers.tldr: FOAM preserves SOAP-like optimization benefits while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory and computational overhead, approaching AdamW/Muon practicality for LLM pretraining.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates text generation with large language models by letting a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large verifier checks in a single forward pass. We introduce Olifant, a draft model built on a memory-based classifier. It predicts the next token from a four-token window in under 0.3 ms on CPU, requiring no GPU, no backpropagation, and no accelerator memory. We measure throughput and energy under two verifier regimes on consumer hardware. Without a KV cache, drafting is nearly free: a domain-matched Olifant model reaches 38.1% acceptance on EU legal text, delivering 2.43x throughput and 2.51x lower energy per token than the neural verifier model alone. With a KV-cached verifier, itself a ~10x energy saver, drafting costs matter: a TinyLlama draft model halves throughput and triples energy despite high acceptance, whereas Olifant still yields 1.25x throughput and the lowest energy in the study (93 J per 100 tokens, 14x below the uncached baseline). We further show that KV caching decouples time from energy: verification of longer drafts raises power draw, shifting the energy-optimal draft length below the speed-optimal one. Speculative decoding is not dead in the age of fast verifiers, provided drafting is nearly free.
bullets: Uses a four-token context to predict the next token in under 0.3 ms on CPU, without GPU, backpropagation, or accelerator memory.
On EU legal text without KV caching, it achieves 38.1% acceptance, 2.43× throughput, and 2.51× lower energy per token.
With a KV-cached verifier, Olifant still improves throughput by 1.25× and reaches the study’s lowest energy use: 93 J per 100 tokens.
KV caching separates speed from energy efficiency, making the energy-optimal draft length shorter than the speed-optimal length.
Speculative decoding remains beneficial when the draft model’s computational and energy costs are nearly negligible.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Speedup over plain decoding vs. draft length k on legal text, under the two verifier regimes (shared y-axis). Without a KV cache (left), draft tokens are nearly free and speedup grows with k; with a KV cache (right), each draft position has real verification cost and every curve slopes downward: profit requires high acceptance (domain-matched olifant-eurlex), and the expensive neural draft falls far below break-even (dashed line). k ≥ 12 uncached points are from a preliminary +D sweep, speedups computed against the same plain baseline.

Figure 2: Energy efficiency ladder on legal text (tokens generated per Joule, best k per strategy). KV caching is the largest single lever; domain-matched memory-based drafting adds to it, while the neural draft costs energy in the cached regime.

Table 6: Complete acceptance rates (%) and mean accepted lengths (MAL, tokens per verification step) for all draft models, tasks, and draft lengths k, uncached verifier regime (100 prompts per task).

Plain rows are repeat measurements (k unused). Bold: best per task.
