papers.selection_reason: Memory-based speculative decoding directly targets efficient LLM inference, reducing latency and energy.
papers.title: Towards Green Text Generation: Memory-Based Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: Olifant is a nearly cost-free, memory-based draft model that can make speculative decoding faster and more energy-efficient, even with KV-cached verifiers.

papers.abstract: Image-to-3D generative models now produce asset-quality textured meshes, but at minutes per asset they remain slow to iterate with and costly to deploy. Prior work has mostly accelerated the sampling of the networks, and where it also optimizes the mesh processing, it trains its own generators. We instead start from a publicly released pipeline and ask how much of its end-to-end time can be saved. Profiling the public Pixal3D pipeline shows that its latency is dominated by what happens after the networks: the four rectified flows take 14% of the wall-clock time and mesh post-processing takes 85%, most of it in CPU-based UV unwrapping. We therefore first rebuild the mesh post-processing on the GPU and take it off the critical path, then cut the per-evaluation overhead of the flows and distill them from 76 to 8 network evaluations. The resulting pipeline, Sprint3D, reduces the median time per asset from 133 s to 4.05 s on one H200 GPU at the same export settings (33$\times$). At the same time, on 2,653 held-out Toys4K objects it improves every input-view normal metric of the Pixal3D protocol, with a slightly lower mean silhouette IoU, lower point-cloud alignment scores and less fine texture detail. The rebuilt post-processing alone also speeds up TRELLIS.2, which uses the same export code, by 6.7$\times$ without a detectable change in the evaluated metrics.
authors: Sho Kuno, Ruihan Yu, Yonghao Yu, Guixu Lin, Lian Fu, Muyao Niu, Yu-Ju Tsai, Zheng-Hui Huang, Yi-Chuan Huang, Siqi Yang, Fengbo Lan, Erwin Wu, Kaipeng Zhang, Zhixiang Wang
bullets: The Pixal3D pipeline spends most of its runtime after neural inference, especially on CPU-based UV unwrapping.
Sprint3D moves mesh post-processing to the GPU and removes it from the critical path.
It reduces rectified-flow evaluations from 76 to 8 and cuts per-evaluation overhead.
On one H200 GPU, median generation time drops 33× under the same export settings.
Quality improves on input-view normal metrics, but silhouette IoU, point-cloud alignment, and fine texture detail decline; the post-processing optimization also speeds TRELLIS.2 by 6.7×.

papers.abstract: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned. Furthermore, these methods have been successfully applied to training and evaluation workflows for the Ling-3.x model series, accelerating the model-development cycle.
authors: Wei Feng, Meiling Chen, Boxiao Chen, Lu Liu, Bin Zi, Libin Ye, Xingyu Lu, Lei Xu, Jun Zhou
bullets: Targets agent workloads that alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction.
Uses workload-based GPU-memory allocation, reference concurrency, and trajectory-aware routing to improve parallelism and cache reuse.
Introduces CAAS to prioritize progressing long chains when environment capacity is constrained.
Controlled replay enables ablation of the proposed optimizations.
Live evaluations report 10.4%–65.0% makespan reductions across four benchmarks, with aligned evaluation scores.

papers.abstract: The task of dataset distillation concerns the learning of a small set of synthetic samples that can serve as an effective replacement for a large real dataset when used for downstream tasks. While many solutions have been proposed since the problem's inception, most of them primarily seek to optimize the distilled data with respect to a classifier. In this work, we propose a new distillation method that learns a set of samples such that they directly approximate the per-class data distribution. Specifically, we "drift" our distilled data in the latent space of a feature extractor such that they move both toward the real data and away from each other without using a classification objective. We find that our drifted data cover the real distribution significantly better than existing methods while still serving as powerful training samples for classification. Furthermore, we showcase our method's use as a visualization tool for better interpreting models and extend it beyond images to other modalities. Our work advances the frontier of dataset distillation, offering a novel synthesis method and proposing distribution-based metrics as a complementary evaluation. More broadly, our findings help address the growing need to understand both data and models by uncovering more about how they interact.
authors: George Cazenavette, Angelina Quan, Giannis Daras, Antonio Torralba, Vincent Sitzmann
bullets: Targets distribution coverage rather than directly optimizing a classifier.
Moves distilled samples toward real data and away from one another in a feature extractor’s latent space.
Reports significantly better coverage of the real distribution than existing methods while remaining effective for classification.
Uses the distilled samples for model visualization and extends the approach beyond images.
Introduces distribution-based metrics as a complementary way to evaluate dataset distillation.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Comparing Noise-Initialized Distillation Methods. Even when using ResNet-18 as the distillation backbone, our method yields higher-quality and more diverse samples. When using a stronger backbone (DINOv3 [53]), the visual quality and diversity of our method increase further.

Figure 5: Distilled images elucidate model representations. Each of the models shown here induces a different style of distilled images to best cover its own distribution. CLIP [45] is a notable outlier, possibly due to its strong text-entanglement and the contrastive loss not used in more recent vision-text models, such as SigLIP2 [60].

Figure 3: We represent distilled data as a Laplacian pyramid of cascading resolutions. To reconstruct a synthetic sample, each level (top) is bicubically interpolated to the full resolution (middle) before being added together (bottom). This acts as a hyperparameter-free implicit regularizer on the distilled data, preventing overfitting to adversarial patterns often seen in model inversion tasks.

Figure 2: Augmentations of Distilled Images Cover the Real Distribution. At each distillation step, we take multiple augmentations of each synthetic sample (left). The synthetic data, together with their augmentations, approximately cover the distribution of real data (right). In this plot, the stars represent the distilled images, the triangles 10 augmentations of each distilled image, and the circles real data. Drifting multiple augmentations of each synthetic sample at each step leads to high intra-image diversity, allowing some distilled images (such as the orange star) to cover many parts of the real distribution at the same time.

Figure 7: Distilling Canvases. We can distill a collection of images into a single large canvas via drifting by using a large number of random crops at each step. The above 2048× 2048 pixel images were synthesized by drifting SigLIP2 [60] features to match the distribution of Claude Monet’s (left) and Qi Baishi’s (right) paintings.

Figure A.1: Effects of augmentations. Here, we visualize the effect the number of augmentations per step has on the distilled data. As we increase the number of augmentations, the images appear to (qualitatively) become richer in semantic information. Images shown here were initialized with noise and distilled with DINOv3 to match ImageNet-1k’s “orange” class. For quantitative results, please see Table A.1.

All 10 distilled images of the ImageNet-1k “golden retriever” class when the drifting loss is applied to the CLS token only, the CLS token plus the mean patch token, or the CLS token plus every patch token (default). For quantitative results, see Table A.4.
Figure 6: Four frames of a basketball dribbling video from HMDB51 [32] distilled via drifting with VideoMAE-v2 [63] into a 3D Laplacian pyramid.

Table 2: Feature-Space Metrics. Coverage (left), k-NN accuracy (middle), and linear probe accuracy (right) of distilled ImageNet-1k data in the SigLIP2 [60] and MoCo-v3 [7] latent spaces (see Appendix D). Parenthesized entries are self-evaluations and are not ranked. Methods marked with a dagger† distill using an ensemble of encoders. Our method outperforms all baselines in every feature-space setting except for RDED [56] on IPC 10 k-NN in both latent spaces. The performance gap is especially large on the coverage metric.

Table 1: From-Scratch Training. This table shows ImageNet-1k [12] classification performance when training a ResNet-18 [26] from scratch. We include results using one-hot hard labels (left), one-time soft labels (middle), and full knowledge distillation (right). Methods marked with a dagger† distill using an ensemble of encoders. Across all three training paradigms, our distilled data lead to the best downstream performance.

Table B.2: Comparison with Diffusion-Based Methods. Our method matches the performance of the best diffusion-based methods in the soft-label setting while falling slightly behind on hard-label and knowledge distillation. Despite not leveraging a pre-trained generative model, our distilled data remain competitive.

Table B.3: Feature-Space Comparison with Diffusion-Based Methods. Unlike in the from-scratch regime, our method (DINOv3 [53] variant) consistently outperforms the diffusion-based methods across all feature-space metrics. Table 3: Our drifting method generalizes to both audio and video, outperforming the coreset baseline.

Table B.1: From-scratch training across distillation backbones. Most backbones yield distilled data that can effectively train a model from scratch, with MoCo-v3 [7] and DINOv3 [53] eking out a slight edge over the others.

Coverage of our noise-initialized ImageNet-1k distilled sets (IPC 10), distilled with the backbone in each row and evaluated in the feature space of the backbone in each column. papers.abstract: Medical image classification in resource-constrained settings must contend with limited annotations and computational capacity. We evaluate four ZACH-ViT variants with linear, Euclidean prototype, Poincare and spherical heads alongside two compact multiple-instance-learning baselines. All models are trained from scratch with fewer than 260,000 parameters across seven MedMNIST+ datasets and three external benchmarks (PCam, ISIC2017 and Shenzhen tuberculosis radiographs). The low-data protocol uses 50 training images per class and five seeds, with validation-selected checkpoints at 23 and 47 epochs; a full-data reference uses one seed. Compact-TransMIL achieves the highest ten-dataset mean test Macro-F1 at 23 epochs (53.34%) and with full data (73.93%). At 47 epochs, ZACH-Linear narrowly leads (57.76% versus 57.54% for Compact-TransMIL). Extending training improves Macro-F1 in 239 of 300 paired comparisons. On ISIC2017, hZACH-Spherical has the highest 47-epoch low-data Macro-F1 (44.09% with SD 4.09%), whereas ZACH-EuclideanProto leads with full data (51.27%). We additionally conduct 40 CPU-only training runs on ISIC2017 and Shenzhen using four CPU threads; model-only single-image inference requires approximately 4-9 ms, while image decoding and preprocessing substantially increase end-to-end latency. The results demonstrate the feasibility of CPU-only training on the tested platform and the task- and regime-dependence of compact medical imaging under strict resource constraints.

papers.abstract: Photonic neural network accelerators have emerged as a promising solution for reducing the power consumption of deep neural network (DNN) inference by executing matrix multiplication on analog photonic hardware. However, their inference accuracy is limited by low-bit quantization required for photonic processing and by analog photonic noise. This paper proposes an approach for improving inference accuracy by exploiting the high similarity among activation vectors in DNNs. Specifically, our approach constructs a representative vector for each group of similar activation vectors, computes its inner product digitally with high precision, and offloads the residual inner products to the photonic accelerator. Since the activation vectors within each group are highly similar, the residual vectors have much smaller norms, thereby reducing the effects of quantization errors and analog photonic noise. Furthermore, our approach preserves the photonic inner-product computation pipeline, allowing seamless integration into existing and future photonic accelerators without hardware modification. Experimental results on six representative DNN models demonstrate that the proposed approach can improve inference accuracy across diverse network architectures and application domains.
authors: Yasuhiro Fujiwara, Tatsuhiro Nakamori, Hideyuki Kawashima
bullets: Addresses accuracy loss from low-bit quantization and analog photonic noise.
Groups similar activation vectors and constructs a representative vector for each group.
Computes representative-vector inner products digitally at high precision, while photonics processes residual inner products.
Smaller residual norms reduce sensitivity to quantization and photonic noise.
Evaluated across six representative DNN models, improving inference accuracy across varied architectures and domains.

papers.abstract: Predicting every observation in a high-rate stream requires a model to finish before the next arrival. A large model may offer better predictions but miss that deadline. We propose RESYNC: the large model runs asynchronously, while a fast path updates its latest exact but stale latent state using the observations received since that state was computed and applies its unchanged prediction head. The updater learns from the frozen model's representations without task labels. Across one real and two synthetic streams and five architecture families, RESYNC beats the best compact or distilled alternative with a paired 95% interval above zero in all twelve dataset--architecture pairs with a material teacher advantage at anchor ages of 4--12 observations, and in eleven pairs at older tested ages up to 32. The share of the teacher's gain preserved remains complete on the real stream but is lower and generally declines with anchor age on the synthetic streams. In live replay with 1 ms arrivals, the synchronous large models cannot deliver any predictions on time while RESYNC serves at least 99.4% of arrivals within the interval, with 0.35--0.62 ms median latency on one CPU thread: around the same speed as or faster than the compact model, and 7.9--17.7$\times$ faster than synchronous large-model inference. RESYNC targets settings with background compute available but a strict per-observation response deadline.
authors: Eljas Linna, Hao Dong, Juho Kanniainen
bullets: Targets high-rate streams where large models miss per-observation deadlines.
Runs the large model asynchronously, then updates its latest latent representation using new observations without task labels.
Across five architecture families and three streams, it outperforms compact or distilled alternatives in most tested teacher-advantage settings.
In 1 ms-arrival replay, it serves at least 99.4% of arrivals on time with 0.35–0.62 ms median latency on one CPU thread.
Performance retention is complete on the real stream but lower and generally declines with anchor age on synthetic streams.

papers.abstract: We present UniSpark-9B, a unified multimodal model that investigates hybrid attention for visual understanding and generation. Built on a Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts backbone with approximately 9B parameters in each branch, UniSpark combines full attention for explicit token interactions with GatedDeltaNet linear attention for compact context propagation. Autoregressive text prediction and visual flow matching jointly support visual question answering, text-to-image generation, instruction-guided editing, and interleaved text-image prediction. In interleaved generation, noisy visual targets are isolated from subsequent predictions, while clean visual representations provide context for later outputs. A blockwise protocol enforces this distinction through attention masks in full-attention layers and recurrent-state retention rules in linear-attention layers. The selected training sources contain 159.7M generation samples, 213.4M understanding samples, and 624.8K interleaved sequences. A four-stage curriculum jointly trains multimodal understanding and visual generation, refining answer accuracy and instruction following while extending image synthesis to 2K. UniSpark scores 2470.3 on MME-S and 0.83 on GenEval. Qualitative examples further illustrate its capabilities in interleaved image generation, video synthesis, and video editing. Together, these results demonstrate that hybrid attention provides an effective backbone for unified multimodal understanding and generation.
authors: Jiancheng Pan, Yuzheng Liu, Hengyuan Cao, Qiyuan Zhang, Yangyan Li, Biao Gong, Zheng Zhang, Ka Long Cheng, Xinyang Wang, Yujun Shen
bullets: Combines full attention for explicit token interactions with GatedDeltaNet linear attention for compact context propagation.
Uses autoregressive text prediction and visual flow matching across visual question answering, text-to-image generation, editing, and interleaved generation.
Applies blockwise attention masks and recurrent-state rules to separate noisy visual targets from later predictions.
Trained with a four-stage curriculum spanning multimodal understanding, generation, and interleaved sequences, with image synthesis extended to 2K.
Reports 2470.3 on MME-S and 0.83 on GenEval; qualitative examples include video synthesis and editing.

papers.abstract: While quantization compresses LLMs and accelerates inference, outlier activations impede efficient low-bit representation. In particular, massive outliers cause substantial performance degradation. Although rotation-based methods that rely on randomized Hadamard transforms for online inference aim to mitigate this, they can produce fragmented distributions with empty bins when a massive outlier dominates a token's activation. This fragmentation severely undermines uniform quantization performance. Moreover, massive outliers concentrate in the down-projection input, where the preceding nonlinearity requires the rotation to be applied at inference time. This constraint prevents training-based approaches such as SpinQuant from learning the online rotation at this position, as a learned dense matrix cannot use the Fast Walsh-Hadamard Transform and would require a full matrix multiplication during inference. To address this, we propose SignRot (Sign-adjusted Rotation), which identifies massive outlier channels and constructs a sign adjustment vector that unifies the signs of the corresponding Hadamard row, collapsing the bimodal distribution into a unimodal profile amenable to quantization. Since the aligned outlier shifts the activation mean away from zero, we pair SignRot with asymmetric activation quantization, whose zero-point absorbs this shift. As a lightweight, drop-in improvement compatible with any Hadamard-based quantization method, SignRot requires only a single calibration forward pass and adds only element-wise sign flips at inference, without an additional matrix multiplication. Applying SignRot to QuaRot achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 5.88 and an average zero-shot reasoning accuracy of 72.73, surpassing SpinQuant on the LLaMA3-70B model. Code is available at https://github.com/HYU-ARK-Lab/SignRot.
authors: Jaehun Gim, Jaewoo Kim, Gyuwan Kim, Seo Yeon Park
bullets: Massive activation outliers fragment distributions and degrade uniform low-bit quantization, especially at down-projection inputs.
SignRot detects outlier channels and applies a sign vector that aligns Hadamard-row signs, converting a bimodal distribution into a quantization-friendly unimodal one.
It combines the rotation with asymmetric activation quantization so the zero-point absorbs the resulting mean shift.
The method requires one calibration forward pass and only element-wise sign flips at inference, making it compatible with Hadamard-based quantizers without extra matrix multiplication.
When applied to QuaRot on LLaMA3-70B, SignRot reports 5.88 WikiText2 perplexity and 72.73 average zero-shot reasoning accuracy, surpassing SpinQuant.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents make decisions by combining information from heterogeneous memory modules, including declarative memory for explicit knowledge, procedural memory for learned routines, and working memory for current observations. During interaction, the memory contents required for decision making change with the agent's state, goal, and task progress, while many contents remain shared across consecutive decisions. However, existing memory modules are typically accessed through separate interfaces, so each updated memory context is often processed as a new input to the foundation model. This prevents selective key-value (KV) cache reuse for unchanged memory contents and forces full KV cache recomputation even when much of the memory context remains valid. We introduce HeMeR, an inference framework that performs KV reconciliation between dynamically updated memory contexts and reusable KV states. HeMeR tracks declarative, procedural, and working memory contents across action decisions, preserves KV states for unchanged contents, and reconciles only the KV states affected by memory-content updates. This enables efficient and stable inference as memory contents evolve during interaction. We evaluate HeMeR on ALFWorld, Habitat, and real-world robotic deployments requiring coordinated use of heterogeneous memory contents. In the real-world setting, HeMeR achieves 83.20% task success and reduces per-step inference time from 2.94 to 1.87 seconds compared with MemRL, while preserving compatible KV states as task progress updates the memory context.
authors: Saehun Chun, Wonje Choi, Jinwoo Jang, Taeyoon Kwack, Honguk Woo
bullets: Addresses the costly full KV-cache recomputation caused by separately accessed declarative, procedural, and working memory.
Tracks memory contents across action decisions and preserves KV states for unchanged information.

In the real-world setting, achieves 83.20% task success and reduces per-step inference time from 2.94 to 1.87 seconds versus MemRL.

papers.abstract: Local language models often exist at several precisions, and quantization is known to change individual answers. This study asks whether the disagreement between two precisions of the same weights, an 8-bit copy that answers and a lower-precision copy that reads the same prompt, works as a per-question error score for abstention, escalation and re-asking. The cost is one extra forward pass over fewer bytes, with no sampling and no training. We simulate round-to-nearest quantization with per-group scales (3 to 6 bits, groups of 32 to 256) on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B and score 8,398 multiple-choice questions from ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag subsets. Error detection is measured by AUROC, risk-coverage curves and ECE on a held-out half, with paired bootstrap intervals over questions. For Qwen3-0.6B, the entropy of the 8-bit answer reaches AUROC 0.682; the best disagreement score, selected on a development half, reaches 0.684 (+0.001 [-0.009, +0.011]), and combining it with the confidence features adds +0.009 [+0.002, +0.015], mostly on ARC. On Qwen3-1.7B the selected score is -0.001 [-0.009, +0.006] from entropy and the combination +0.003 [-0.001, +0.006] on the test half. Gaussian weight noise at matched error energy is about as informative as rounding (0.6B only), so we find no evidence that the signal is specific to quantization, and shuffling the features within task and entropy cells removes the gain. One extra 8-bit pass that shifts the option order does better (+0.049 [+0.031, +0.067] over entropy) at about a third more weight traffic; routing to a larger model on free entropy beats both extra-pass scores at equal total traffic. After logistic recalibration the 0.6B confidences are calibrated within a few points of ECE. A deployment recipe and the cases where the method does not help are given.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Allan Kevin T
bullets: The study tests whether comparing an 8-bit model with lower-precision copies can identify questions the model is likely to answer incorrectly.
Quantization disagreement requires one extra forward pass and no sampling or training; it is evaluated across 8,398 multiple-choice questions and two small Qwen3 models.
For Qwen3-0.6B, the best disagreement score is essentially tied with entropy (AUROC 0.684 vs. 0.682), while combining both yields a modest gain, mainly on ARC.
For Qwen3-1.7B, disagreement adds negligible value; matched Gaussian noise is similarly informative, suggesting the signal is not specific to quantization.
Shifting option order in an extra pass works better, and routing to a larger model is stronger at equal traffic; calibrated 0.6B confidences are close to reliable.

papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), yet accurate FP4 quantization remains challenging. Practical formats such as MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4 pair a 4-bit floating-point payload with block-wise or hierarchical scale codes, making accuracy highly sensitive to how each local distribution is scaled. Default maximum-absolute-value scaling preserves dynamic range, but can spend scarce FP4 levels on rarely occupied outlier regions and leave dense tensor values poorly resolved. Existing scale-search methods minimize local element-wise reconstruction error, optimizing tensor fidelity rather than layer-output fidelity. We propose SoScale, a second-order weight scale-code search method for hierarchical FP4 quantization. SoScale searches hardware-valid scale codes under a Hessian-aware layer reconstruction objective and couples this search with GPTQ-style error recovery, selecting scales by their impact on layer outputs. Across Qwen3 models, SoScale consistently reduces downstream quantization degradation under MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4.
authors: Pengxiang Zhao, Xing Li, Hui-Ling Zhen, Weizhe Lin, Xianzhi Yu, Zhenhua Dong
bullets: FP4 quantization is sensitive to block-wise and hierarchical scale selection, especially when outliers consume limited quantization levels.
Existing scale-search methods optimize element-wise reconstruction and may not preserve layer outputs effectively.
SoScale searches hardware-valid scale codes using a Hessian-aware layer reconstruction objective.
It combines scale search with GPTQ-style error recovery for improved quantization accuracy.
Across Qwen3 models, it reduces downstream degradation for MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Workflow of SoScale for one linear layer. Calibration builds the empirical Hessian and damped inverse-Hessian factor. In 2.1, SoScale searches legal FP4 scale codes with a Hessian-aware layer loss, whereas scale-only baselines such as ScaleSearch and Four Over Six use local MSE-style objectives without Hessian information; in 2.2, it propagates the selected block’s error to future blocks. Inference uses only stored FP4 payloads, legal scale codes, and lightweight per-token activation scales.

(b) The searched scale reduces element-wise reconstruction error for most elements. (c) Local element-wise scale search does not consistently reduce perplexity, whereas SoScale does.

papers.abstract: Multimodal dataset distillation (MDD) aims to reduce the cost of vision-language pre-training by synthesizing compact image-text datasets. Although recent feature-matching methods have improved distillation efficiency, synthetic data may become specialized to the model representations encountered during optimization, limiting generalization to unseen model states. We propose Model Distribution-Aware Multimodal Dataset Distillation (MDA-DD), which leverages supervision from a dynamic staggered queue of models at different training stages. We further introduce asymmetric dual projection for complementary alignment in visual and linguistic spaces and an uncentered second-order moment objective that retains mean-related cross-modal information. Experiments on Flickr30K and MS-COCO demonstrate consistent retrieval improvements over existing methods across synthetic-data budgets. With only 100 synthetic pairs, MDA-DD improves IR@1 and TR@1 on Flickr30K by 12.9 and 18.2 percentage points, respectively, over the strongest baseline at the same budget, outperforming all compared methods using 500 pairs on both datasets across all six retrieval metrics.
authors: Jiajun Shen, Yonglin Wu, Ruonan Yu, Xinchao Wang
bullets: Addresses over-specialization of synthetic data to the model representations used during optimization.
Uses a dynamic staggered queue of models at different training stages for broader supervision.
Introduces asymmetric dual projection for complementary visual–linguistic alignment.
Uses an uncentered second-order moment objective to preserve mean-related cross-modal information.
On Flickr30K, 100 synthetic pairs improve IR@1 and TR@1 by 12.9 and 18.2 percentage points over the strongest same-budget baseline; results are consistent across Flickr30K and MS-COCO.

papers.abstract: Optional reasoning, retrieval, web search, and tool use can improve large language model responses but incur unnecessary computation when activated indiscriminately. This study investigates whether prompt optimization can compensate for limited router capacity and whether classification gains translate into downstream efficiency. The proposed framework uses prompt-driven small language models to make four independent capability decisions, allowing multiple capabilities to be selected per query. Qwen2.5 routers ranging from 1.5B to 14B parameters are compared across five prompting strategies, followed by an evaluation of capability-specific optimized configurations using a fixed GPT-OSS-120B downstream model on 127 questions. Under minimal prompting, increasing router capacity does not consistently improve classification performance. Prompt optimization narrows the capacity gap for reasoning and calculator routing, whereas RAG and web search retain larger benefits from higher capacity. Similar classification F1 scores do not necessarily imply equivalent downstream behavior: false-positive activations increase unnecessary computation, while missed capabilities can reduce answer quality. The 14B router achieves a mean BERTScore F1 of 0.8408, compared with 0.8418 when all capabilities are enabled, while reducing average downstream token consumption by 68.7\% (8,837 to 2,764 tokens) and median downstream latency by 80.5\% (9.79 to 1.91 seconds). These savings exclude router overhead, which is measured separately in a different inference environment and increases with router capacity. The findings demonstrate that the relationship between router capacity, prompt design, and downstream efficiency is capability-dependent. Consequently, router selection must consider error profiles and routing overhead alongside classification performance.
bullets: The study routes queries independently to reasoning, retrieval, web search, and calculator capabilities, allowing multiple selections per query.
Larger routers do not consistently improve classification under minimal prompting; prompt optimization reduces capacity gaps mainly for reasoning and calculator routing.
RAG and web-search routing benefit more from higher model capacity, showing capability-dependent scaling effects.
A 14B router nearly matches always-on quality (BERTScore F1 0.8408 vs. 0.8418) while reducing downstream token use by 68.7% and median latency by 80.5%.
Classification scores alone are insufficient: false positives waste computation, missed capabilities can hurt quality, and router overhead increases with capacity.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward increasingly long inputs, soft context compression offers a promising approach to efficient inference by converting long inputs into compact memory slots. Under limited memory budgets, effective context compression remains challenging because task-relevant evidence varies substantially across queries, ranging from localized evidence to multiple distant spans or information dispersed throughout the full document. Instead of compressing everything indiscriminately, we propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query. CoMem develops Contrastive Compressor Learning to achieve query-sensitive yet context-preserving memory representations. To inject a strong prior over query-dependent evidence distributions, we devise a same-context hard negative mining strategy by pairing a single document with multiple queries, requiring the compressor to selectively retain information according to each query's distinct evidence needs. To address the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, we further enable bidirectional attention among memory slots. Experiments demonstrate that CoMem consistently outperforms existing context compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.
authors: Sikui Zhang, Haowei Liu, Ziyun Gan, Chunfeng Yuan, Guangze Gao, Nian Liu, Boyu Cai, Bo Li, Xiaolei Lv, Jun Gao, Bing Li, Weiming Hu
bullets: Addresses context compression when relevant evidence may be local, scattered, or distributed across a document.
Uses query-guided memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query.
Applies contrastive compressor learning with same-document, multi-query hard negatives to distinguish differing evidence needs.
Enables bidirectional attention among memory slots to improve information flow despite causal masking.
Outperforms existing compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Multimodal diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text through iterative masked denoising with bidirectional attention, offering a compelling alternative to autoregressive vision-language modeling. However, each denoising step requires a full forward pass over long multimodal sequences in which visual tokens dominate the sequence length, and a fixed step budget further compounds this quadratic per-step cost. Existing inference acceleration approaches for multimodal dLLMs characterize attention redundancy implicitly, motivating designs from isolated attention visualizations rather than from measurement. We close this gap with DRAMA, a training-free acceleration framework grounded in a systematic dissection of attention redundancy in multimodal dLLMs. By probing attention tensors along spatial and temporal axes, we reveal two persistent redundancy structures: (i) attention mass consistently concentrates on a sparse subset of visual tokens, and (ii) attention distributions rapidly stabilize across denoising steps after an initial formation phase. These findings motivate two complementary mechanisms: Spatial-Redundancy-Aware Visual Token Pruning (SVTP) and Sufficiency-Guided Adaptive Stopping (SGAS). Together, DRAMA achieves an average 18.67 times inference speedup across six vision-language benchmarks without training, architectural modification, or attention caching, while maintaining competitive accuracy. Our results establish a strong, measurement-grounded acceleration baseline for multimodal dLLM inference.
authors: Yi-Hsin Hung, Fangfu Liu, Shao-Yuan Lo, Chu-Song Chen
bullets: Identifies two redundancy patterns: attention concentrates on a sparse subset of visual tokens and stabilizes across denoising steps.
Introduces SVTP for spatially aware visual-token pruning.
Introduces SGAS for sufficiency-guided adaptive stopping of denoising.
Training-free and requires no architectural changes or attention caching.
Reports an average 18.67× inference speedup across six vision-language benchmarks while maintaining competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Transferring LLMs into System One decision models typically replaces the language modeling head with a decision head while retaining the full backbone, making every decision pay for all layers. Yet it remains unclear how much depth such decisions require. We find that decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers, with early layers building essential features and the final six layers removable without loss, while independently trained smaller models largely mimic the full model rather than developing specialized decision capabilities. These findings suggest that efficiency requires not simply smaller backbones, but shared computation across different depths. Building on this, we propose \method{}, which jointly trains a full model with prefix sub-models that share its final layers and decision head through self-distillation. A lightweight gate reads the hidden state at each exit to determine whether additional computation is needed, allowing one model to operate at multiple layers. Across seven decision benchmarks, our approach matches or outperforms independently trained models at every depth, while achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs through adaptive computation.
bullets: Decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers; the final six layers can be removed without accuracy loss.
Independently trained smaller models mostly mimic the full model instead of learning specialized decision representations.
The proposed method jointly trains a full model and prefix sub-models that share later layers and a decision head via self-distillation.
A lightweight gate chooses whether each input needs additional layers, enabling multi-depth inference in one model.
Across seven decision benchmarks, the method matches or outperforms independent models at every depth with improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of NESTONE. (a) Nested training with self-distillation. Prefix exits share the full model’s weights and final block. The model runs layer by layer, with a lightweight gate evaluating the hidden state at each intermediate exit. If ge ≥ τ , it runs the final block and returns a decision; otherwise, it continues from the saved states without recomputation.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models through forward-only evaluations, but high-dimensional random perturbations can limit optimization efficiency. Sparse perturbations reduce the search dimension, making the selection of informative coordinates critical. We propose Wanda-Importance Sparsity-MeZO (WIS-MeZO), which uses Wanda weight--activation saliency to construct task-conditioned sparse perturbation masks while keeping the pretrained model dense. We analyze support quality through gradient energy capture and relate it to gradient estimation and convergence. Across 16 benchmarks with LLaMA and Qwen models ranging from 3B to 32B parameters, WIS-MeZO achieves higher aggregate scores than MeZO and reaches comparable validation losses in fewer optimization steps. Comparisons with random and magnitude-based sparse perturbations further highlight the importance of informative support selection.
authors: Ziqing Wen, Xiaohui Song, Jiahuan Wang, Ping Luo, Junlin Zeng, Dongsheng Li, Tao Sun
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of high-dimensional random perturbations in memory-efficient ZO fine-tuning.
Constructs task-conditioned sparse masks from Wanda weight–activation saliency while keeping the pretrained model dense.
Analyzes support quality through gradient-energy capture and its relationship to gradient estimation and convergence.
Across 16 benchmarks on LLaMA and Qwen models from 3B–32B parameters, it achieves higher aggregate scores than MeZO and comparable validation losses in fewer steps.
Results against random and magnitude-based sparsity emphasize the value of informative support selection.

papers.abstract: Expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts decoding is latency bound: each layer serializes a token exchange, a grouped GEMM over routed experts, and a combine, while only a few tokens per rank are in flight. Prior GC-MoE fused these phases into one persistent, Green-Context-partitioned CUDA Graph on Hopper (SM90) and datacenter Blackwell (SM100). This paper rebuilds the operator for SM120 (compute capability 12.0, e.g. RTX PRO 5000) over PCIe. SM120 exposes block-scaled tensor cores only through warp-level mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf8f6f4: no tensor memory, no two-CTA MMA, no cluster multicast. We rebuild the kernel around a swap-AB warp-level block-scaled MMA with FP4 weights in the register A operand and FP8 activations in B, plus SM120-specific mechanisms: scale-byte selection through MMA immediates, a compact-weights path, an adaptive token-tile geometry, an expert-granular streaming dispatch with a batched bulk-pull engine and a 64-bit deduplicating pull cache, full-width BF16 returns drained by resident relay copiers over a position-major arena, and shared experts folded into the compute role. On 8xRTX PRO 5000 over PCIe the operator is 1.522x and 1.387x faster than the FlashInfer CuTe DSL W4A8 MegaMoE and the Cake MegaMoE across 18 decode points (18/18 wins each), and 1.388x faster than Cake with shared experts fused; all 94 numerical cases and 752 per-rank checks pass, at cross-operator cosine similarity of at least 0.9999997.
authors: Yong Li, Haoyu Wang, Kan Liu, Tao Lan
bullets: Targets latency from serialized token exchange, expert GEMM, and combine phases in low-concurrency decoding.
Uses warp-level FP8×FP4 block-scaled MMA with register-resident FP4 weights and SM120-specific scale selection.
Overlaps expert-granular dispatch, computation, and returns using adaptive tiling, batched pulls, a deduplicating cache, and resident relay copiers.
On 8× RTX PRO 5000 GPUs, it wins all 18 tested decode points against two baselines and also outperforms shared-expert-fused Cake.
All reported numerical cases and per-rank checks pass, with cross-operator cosine similarity of at least 0.9999997.

papers.abstract: Latent 3D representations have significantly expanded the capabilities of modern shape modeling, enabling compact encoding of 3D scenes and supporting powerful 3D generative models. Despite this progress, current representations struggle to capture the fine details of complex objects, fundamentally limited by the capacity of their latents. However, scaling latent capacity at training time is computationally expensive and often infeasible under memory limits, and naively increasing the number of latents at inference fails to make effective use of the added capacity. In this paper, we address both challenges with \textit{split-and-scale}, a method that effectively expands latent capacity at inference while keeping training cost tractable. Our key observation is that by representing 3D scenes as continuous functions of 3D coordinates, a single pretrained tokenizer can be applied at inference to arbitrarily small sub-regions of a scene, allocating the same latent capacity to a smaller spatial extent and thus capturing far higher detail. We validate this insight by conducting extensive ablations to study the trade-offs between compute, memory, latent capacity, and reconstruction quality, demonstrating our inference-time scaling method achieves quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory limits. We further demonstrate that split-and-scale supports high-quality generative modeling, training an autoregressive 3D generator that performs competitively with state-of-the-art baselines.
authors: Dorian Chan, Muhammed Kocabas, Xiaoming Zhao, Oncel Tuzel, Jen-Hao Rick Chang
bullets: Addresses limited latent capacity for modeling fine details in complex 3D objects.
Uses continuous coordinate-based scene representations to tokenize arbitrarily small sub-regions at inference.
Explores trade-offs among compute, memory, latent capacity, and reconstruction quality through ablations.
Achieves quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory limits.
Also supports high-quality generative modeling with an autoregressive 3D generator.

Note that training LiTo-32768 requires larger memory than all other methods, and its training takes 2.7× more time. All models are trained to the same number of iterations. papers.abstract: Transformers typically cache an independent key-value (KV) representation for each token at every layer. Recent work reveals that a token's KV representations across neighboring layers are correlated and contain shared information. We hypothesize that this correlation implies incremental inter-layer changes, which can be effectively captured by low-dimensional deltas. Motivated by this, we propose KVPath, a new KV representation paradigm that connects KV representations across the network depth into a path. The path establishes a full-dimensional base KV at the first layer, while subsequent layers generate low-dimensional delta KVs to update the preceding KV, thereby constructing their own KV states. By caching the base KV once alongside these compact delta KVs, KVPath preserves distinct layer-specific representations without storing full KV states at every layer. We develop two variants of KVPath: KVPath-Residual, which updates vector values via residual addition, and KVPath-Rolling, which progressively updates feature dimensions in a rolling manner. Under matched parameter counts, KVPath reduces KV-cache storage by up to 68\% for Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and 55\% for Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), while maintaining or even improving model performance.
authors: Xuan Luo, Zhiyuan Wang, Hanzhong Cao, Xifeng Yan
bullets: Motivation: KV representations for the same token across neighboring layers share information and exhibit correlated changes.
Method: Store a full-dimensional base KV at the first layer, then generate compact delta KVs for subsequent layers.
Variants: KVPath-Residual uses residual additions; KVPath-Rolling updates feature dimensions progressively.
Result: Under matched parameter counts, KVPath reduces KV-cache storage by up to 68% for GQA and 55% for MLA while maintaining or improving performance.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Two KVPath constructions across depth, shown from bottom to top. (a) KVPath-Residual adds an expanded low-dimensional update to the preceding full state. (b) KVPath-Rolling replaces the oldest slot with a new low-dimensional state.

papers.title: KVPath: Connecting Key-Value Representations Across Transformer Layers
papers.tldr: KVPath reduces Transformer KV-cache storage by representing later-layer KVs as low-dimensional updates to a shared base KV while preserving layer-specific states.

papers.abstract: A mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model uses only a few experts per token, so a server can keep most expert weights in CPU memory and copy an expert to the GPU when the router requests it. Recent methods train the router to keep the same experts for several tokens, and treat fewer routing switches as a proxy for fewer copies. We measure the trade-off directly, in a harness that performs and times real CPU-to-GPU copies for OLMoE-1B-7B. On an L40S GPU, every tested policy that holds an expert set fixed and decodes faster than the least-recently-used (LRU) cache increases next-token loss by at least 0.067 nats. A change that leaves every routing decision intact does better: when the cache must evict an expert, evict the one whose next use lies farthest in the future. This rule copies 2.1x fewer experts than LRU at no loss in quality and is within 3.5% of the fewest copies possible. It needs future requests; the next sixteen tokens of demand recover 96% of its reduction, whereas a rule based on counts of past requests recovers 27%.
authors: Pierre-Luc Bacon, Diego Calanzone, Jean-Maxime Larouche
bullets: MoE offloading keeps most expert weights in CPU memory and transfers requested experts to the GPU.
Reducing routing switches is not a reliable proxy for reducing real transfer cost: faster fixed-set policies increased next-token loss by at least 0.067 nats.
When eviction is necessary, evicting the expert needed farthest in the future outperforms LRU.
The approach achieves 2.1× fewer copies than LRU, with no quality loss, and comes within 3.5% of the minimum possible copies.
Future demand from the next 16 tokens recovers 96% of the reduction; past-request counts recover only 27%.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks for electromagnetic signal processing are typically developed as single-task experts with fixed inputs and objectives, limiting cross-task transferability. Electromagnetic foundation models offer broader task coverage but incur substantial pretraining and inference costs. To balance accuracy and efficiency, we adopt model routing to dynamically dispatch unknown signals to matched experts within a heterogeneous pool. We construct HeteroSignal-7, a multi-task routing benchmark with 140,000 samples from seven datasets covering six task types, paired with seven classification and waveform-recovery experts and a unified evaluation protocol. We then propose GLCR, a two-stage routing method combining global dispatch with local discrimination of similar tasks. First, a lightweight one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN) with an additive-margin head predicts one of seven routing classes. Second, a gradient-boosted-tree specialist uses four physical statistics to re-evaluate samples whose top two candidates match a confusion pair automatically identified from validation errors. The pipeline is trained across the full signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) range and requires neither SNR labels nor noise estimation at inference time. GLCR outperforms all 19 baselines, achieving 96.16% routing accuracy and a 76.30% system score, exceeding the respective second-best baselines by 1.16% and 1.14%. It achieves the lowest routing latency among the compared methods at 1.43 ms per sample and reduces expected overall system FLOPs by 5.9 times compared with executing all experts. This work provides a public evaluation platform and an efficient, reproducible baseline for heterogeneous expert routing in electromagnetic signal processing.
authors: Fang Lu, Yao Lu, Zhuangzhi Chen, Sicheng Zhang, Shanqing Yu, Yun Lin, Qi Xuan, Guan Gui
bullets: Addresses limited cross-task transfer in single-task signal-processing models and the cost of electromagnetic foundation models.
Introduces HeteroSignal-7, a benchmark with 140,000 samples spanning seven datasets and six task types, plus seven heterogeneous experts.
Uses a two-stage router: a lightweight 1D CNN for global classification, followed by a gradient-boosted-tree specialist for automatically identified confusing task pairs.
Trains across all SNRs without requiring SNR labels or noise estimation during inference.
Reports 96.16% routing accuracy, a 76.30% system score, 1.43 ms routing latency per sample, and 5.9× lower expected system FLOPs than running all experts.

papers.tldr: GLCR efficiently routes unknown electromagnetic signals to specialized experts using global CNN dispatch and local physical-statistic discrimination, achieving high accuracy with low latency and computation.

papers.abstract: In September 2026, TypeSafe announced Jev as the first model in its System One category: unstructured state goes in, and typed, calibrated decisions that software can use directly come out. Jev's architecture and training data are unpublished, but many open typed-decision models have followed, including Nimble, the Decision 1.0--3.0 family and Clef. They answer structured questions about a piece of text, such as a yes/no check, a choice among labelled options or a graded score, by reading the text with a language model and scoring the options with a small readout. Each pairs a different readout with a different backbone, training mix and recipe, so it is unclear which design choices matter. We re-implement five readouts and train all of them under one protocol: the same backbone, the same 15 public English training sources, the same recipe with a per-head learning-rate sweep, and the same seed. Our experiments demonstrate that: The complexity of the head does not affect accuracy: on Qwen3-0.6B every readout reaches 81.3--82.0\% in-domain accuracy, and a 0.5M-parameter cosine head, which scores each option by its cosine similarity to the question, matches the 27M-parameter joint schema head adapted from Clef in-domain at half its inference time. Reading all of a text's questions from one prompt also matches one prompt per question in accuracy, with 1.6 times faster inference and 2.1--2.5 times faster training on one H100. The backbone's size matters more than either choice: moving from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-4B adds 4 points in-domain and 11 points on held-out sources, while the base, instruct and thinking checkpoints of the same model tie. We recommend spending effort on the backbone and keeping the head minimal.
bullets: Five readouts were reimplemented and trained under a shared protocol using the same backbone, data sources, recipe, and seed.
On Qwen3-0.6B, all heads achieved 81.3–82.0% in-domain accuracy; a 0.5M-parameter cosine head matched a 27M-parameter joint schema head.
Processing all questions from one prompt preserved accuracy while making inference 1.6× faster and training 2.1–2.5× faster on one H100.
Scaling the backbone from Qwen3-0.6B to 4B improved accuracy by 4 points in-domain and 11 points on held-out sources.
Base, instruct, and thinking checkpoints of the same model performed similarly; the study recommends minimal heads and stronger backbones.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The LM letter readout of Nimble and the learned letter readout of Decision 3.0. Each question gets its own chat prompt, with its options labelled by single-token answer codes, ending right after the assistant’s empty thinking block. Option k scores the dot product between the hidden state at the last token and code k’s row. With Nimble’s frozen LM-head rows, this is exactly the language model’s next-token logit for the code, restricted to the question’s codes; Decision 3.0 learns the rows instead, starting from the same values. Nimble’s prompt also lists the other fields in its schema and names the requested one. In our implementation, a row’s questions share the joint prompt, and each field ends with ANSWER:, read at its colon.

Figure 3: Clef’s joint schema head. From the normalised hidden states it builds a token memory M and pooled question, option, lexical and last-token vectors. Each option gathers evidence from the memory; each question becomes a field vector, and four decoder layers refine the fields jointly. An option’s logit adds a lexical prior to a gated joint score that compares its question’s field with the option (ôp = LN(op)). The width is W=512, with 8 attention heads and sℓ, sf , γ learned scalars, giving 27.3M parameters at H=1024.

Figure 2: The bilinear-MLP head of Decision 1.0/2.0. Each question gets its own plain-text prompt: the state, the question type, the question, one block per option, and an instruction ending in Decision:. The head reads one hidden state per option (the endpoint ei, the closing > of its block) and one per question (the query rj , the final colon), layer-normalises each, and adds a scaled dot product to a small MLP correction; d=256, giving 1.05M parameters at H=1024. No term compares two options, so options interact only through the causal backbone. In our implementation, a row’s questions share the joint prompt: the endpoint is the last token of each option’s JSON and the query is the field’s END FIELD line.

Figure 5: The cosine head. One forward pass encodes the state and every question. For each question, the head pools the question span and each of its option spans, projects both into a shared W -dimensional space, and scores each option by its scaled cosine with its own question. Options are never compared with another question, and the head has no per-type parameters.

papers.selection_reason: Controlled study showing minimal decision readouts match much larger heads at lower inference cost, informing efficient LLM-based decision model design.
papers.title: Small Heads, Strong Decisions: A Controlled Study of Typed-Decision Models
papers.tldr: For typed-decision models, backbone scale matters far more than readout complexity, while a tiny cosine head performs as well as a much larger head at lower cost.

papers.abstract: Deploying real-time object detection on power-constrained edge platforms is challenging as processing full-resolution frames is often computationally redundant. Inspired by biological foveation which assigns variable resolution based on visual saliency, we propose a novel software-hardware co-design framework called FoveaDet. On the software side, FoveaDet dynamically identifies salient regions to predict fixation points, followed by aggressive patch pruning in Vision Transformers (ViT) to discard irrelevant background data. To mitigate slowdowns from sequential patch generation, we implement optimized interpolation and patch selection algorithms. Evaluated on standard GPUs, this foveated approach reduces floating-point operations by 65.4% to 92.2% and accelerates inference by 4.76x, while suffering a negligible mAP drop compared to dense baselines. To eliminate hardware bottlenecks, we complement the algorithm with a custom RISC-V core featuring specialized instructions to accelerate the foveated processing pipeline. FoveaDet provides a scalable, efficient architecture capable of unlocking advanced vision processing on severely constrained mobile platforms.
authors: Deepak Mewada, Apporva Saraf, Ashwin Lele
bullets: Targets the redundant computation and hardware bottlenecks of full-resolution object detection on power-constrained platforms.
Dynamically predicts salient fixation points and prunes irrelevant background patches in Vision Transformers.
Uses optimized interpolation and patch-selection algorithms to reduce sequential patch-generation overhead.
On standard GPUs, reduces floating-point operations by 65.4%–92.2% and achieves 4.76× faster inference with negligible mAP loss.
Adds a custom RISC-V core with specialized instructions for the foveated processing pipeline.

papers.title: FoveaDet: Software-Hardware Co-Design of Foveated CNN-Transformer for Object Detection

papers.abstract: Long-context multimodal intelligence requires revisiting earlier images as conversations and documents accumulate, yet retaining an image does not guarantee reliable access to its details. By varying context length, redistributing a fixed text passage around the image, and changing positions without adding text, we identify the positional relation between images and questions as a direct influence on visual access. To address this gap, we propose Visual Position Re-Anchoring (VPR), a training-free method that shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing. It operates directly on the existing KV cache, preserving standard attention computation without extracting attention maps or adding model forward passes. We develop static and continuous compensation schedules, using the static schedule by default. Across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks, static VPR improves 97 of 100 model--task scores. Further analysis shows greater attention to regions containing answer evidence across six checkpoints, with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies. These findings demonstrate an efficient way to sustain visual access through positional adjustment within the cache.
authors: Juntao Xu, Qichai Zhao, Rui Sun, Zhouyang Jiang, Shiwei Wu, Zhi Li, Kaisheng Ma, Yu Liu
bullets: Image–question positional relationships can impair visual access even when the image remains in context.
VPR shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing.
The training-free method works directly on the KV cache without attention-map extraction or extra forward passes.
Static VPR improved 97 of 100 model–task scores across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks.
It increased attention to answer-relevant image regions with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies.

papers.selection_reason: Improves long-context multimodal LLM visual access by re-anchoring visual-key rotary phases in the KV cache, fitting long-context and cache-efficiency topics.
papers.title: Keep Images in Sight: Visual Position Re-Anchoring for Long-Context MLLMs
papers.tldr: Visual Position Re-Anchoring improves long-context MLLMs’ access to earlier images by adjusting cached visual positions before answering questions.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models, but answer accuracy only partly reflects its effect. Pruning can change the probabilities of alternative response tokens even when greedy answers remain correct and unchanged. We compare full and pruned response distributions under shared reference prefixes. Average predictive drift grows with compression on fixed correctly answered samples. Separate analyses associate larger drift with more confidence-decision disagreements and sampling failures. We propose DiFiT (Distribution-Fidelity-guided Token pruning) to learn discrete selection from reference answers and full-token response distributions. Dual-View Distillation matches probabilities across the vocabulary, while answer supervision supports task quality. A learned scorer and differentiable Top-$K$ learn which visual evidence to retain. A multi-budget mask objective supports different retention ratios through one shared ranking over a frozen model. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, DiFiT reduces sampling-induced negative flips by 30.3% relative to FastV at 10% retention on four-task greedy-correct controls. It preserves 98.74% of baseline performance on MME at 30% retention.
authors: Jingyuan Zhang, Nihao Niu, Xinyang Lv, Beibei Han, Xiaoyun Wang, Yanning Hou, Ke Xu
bullets: Visual token pruning can alter alternative-token probabilities even when greedy answers stay unchanged.
DiFiT learns which visual tokens to retain using full-model response distributions and reference-answer supervision.
Dual-View Distillation aligns vocabulary-level probabilities, while differentiable Top-K selection supports discrete pruning.
A shared ranking supports multiple retention budgets with one frozen model.
On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, it reduces sampling-induced negative flips by 30.3% versus FastV at 10% retention and preserves 98.74% of baseline MME performance at 30% retention.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks typically realize dense computation by propagating information through all intermediate channels, while many approximation methods rank and retain individual computational components. We ask whether dense neural computation can instead be represented exactly as an expectation over a combinatorial state space, and approximated by evaluating only its most probable configurations. We introduce a novel probabilistic state-space framework for Transformer MLPs. The framework partitions the intermediate dimension into channel groups, defines an input-dependent distribution over binary inclusion states, and uses importance-corrected masked outputs such that the full expectation exactly recovers the dense MLP output. The key algorithmic novelty is NORDER-II, which enumerates complete joint states in decreasing probability without constructing or sorting the exponentially large state space. Truncating this ordering yields an anytime approximation governed by cumulative probability mass and a state budget. On Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-2-2B, NORDER-II at a state budget of B=2048 achieves 92.4% and 93.8% MLP-output approximation accuracy, compared with 76.9% and 79.8% for Channel Top-k. When the first, middle, and last MLP layers are approximated jointly, WikiText-2 perplexity remains within 0.06% and 0.54% of dense inference. Relative to expected-count Grouped Top-k, NORDER-II yields 82.6% to 126.4% relative accuracy gains with only 0.18% to 0.19% additional local analytic FLOPs. These results establish the significance of joint-state structure beyond atomic salience and point to a new paradigm for neural computation: dense layers can be viewed as structured probabilistic inference over combinatorial computational states. This framework opens a path toward adaptive, probability-mass-controlled computation in pretrained neural networks.
authors: Victor O. K. Li, Yang Han, Jacqueline C. K. Lam
bullets: Partitions MLP channels into groups and defines input-dependent binary inclusion states with importance-corrected outputs.
NORDER-II enumerates complete joint states in decreasing probability without materializing the exponential state space.
At budget B=2048, it achieves 92.4% and 93.8% MLP-output accuracy on Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-2-2B, outperforming Channel Top-k.
Joint approximation of selected MLP layers keeps WikiText-2 perplexity within 0.06% and 0.54% of dense inference.
Results support probability-mass-controlled, adaptive computation based on joint-state structure rather than individual channel salience.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces NORDER-II to approximate dense MLP computation via probabilistic state enumeration, offering a new efficiency mechanism for LLMs.
papers.title: Probabilistic State Space Enumeration in Neural Network Computation
papers.tldr: NORDER-II represents dense Transformer MLPs exactly as expectations over probabilistic joint channel states and efficiently approximates them by enumerating the most likely states.

papers.abstract: Reference capacitively coupled plasma (CCP) simulations provide spatially resolved plasma fields but are costly to generate across operating conditions. We compare the data efficiency of five surrogate architectures--Coordinate MLP, PCA-Net, U-Net, Fourier neural operator (FNO), and Transolver--for predicting RF-cycle-averaged electron density, ion density, electric potential, and electron temperature in 1D planar and 2D axisymmetric GEC CCP benchmarks. We assess the number of reference simulations needed to achieve 1% and 2% mean relative L2 error for parameter-interior and parameter-boundary test cases, and examine architecture-specific mechanisms. FNO achieves the lowest or joint-lowest reference-case requirement in seven of eight comparisons. In 1D, FNO reaches 1% interior error with 50 training cases, compared with 100 for Transolver and 200 for U-Net. In 2D, FNO and U-Net each reach 1% interior error with 100 cases; FNO and Transolver each reach 2% parameter-boundary error with 200 cases, compared with 400 for U-Net. At the stricter 1% 2D parameter-boundary target, Transolver requires 400 cases versus 800 for FNO. Additional analyses investigate FNO spectral modes and padding, U-Net skip connections, Transolver adaptive slicing, and PCA-Net projection versus prediction error. The results support FNO as a data-efficient baseline for the tested CCP settings, while showing that the preferred architecture depends on the accuracy target and operating-parameter region.

papers.abstract: Parallel test-time scaling (TTS) has been shown to enhance reasoning in large language models by generating and aggregating multiple independent reasoning paths. Internal confidence scores can further improve this process by identifying paths of varying quality. However, existing methods remain computationally inefficient, as low-quality paths are fully expanded before being evaluated. In this work, we aim to improve the use of internal confidence signals for better model performance and computational efficiency. We begin by offering a new perspective on the role of confidence in aggregation, showing that it is most impactful for questions near the decision boundary. Notably, when amplified by multi-sample aggregation, even small confidence signals derived from short prefixes can meaningfully influence outcomes in these boundary cases. Building on this insight, we introduce Prefix-Guided Sampling (PreG), a method that reallocates computation by first generating short prefixes, ranking them using internal confidence scores, and then completing only the most promising candidates. This strategy reduces token usage while maintaining gains in path quality. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that, under a fixed compute budget, PreG strengthens the effective signal by widening the decision boundary margin. Empirically, our method consistently outperforms standard parallel TTS approaches across benchmarks, while significantly improving token efficiency and reducing overall computation.
authors: Jie Ren, Jonathan Rosenfeld, Neil Thompson
bullets: Parallel test-time scaling wastes compute by fully expanding low-quality reasoning paths before evaluation.
Confidence signals matter most on questions near the decision boundary, where short prefixes can already guide aggregation.
PreG generates short prefixes, ranks them by internal confidence, and completes only the strongest candidates.
Theoretical analysis shows PreG can widen the effective decision-boundary margin under a fixed compute budget.
Experiments report consistent gains over standard parallel TTS with improved token efficiency and lower computation.

papers.abstract: Deployment of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for Edge-AI is constrained by memory and bandwidth limitations. A standard 7B parameter model consumes 14 GB Video Random Access Memory (VRAM) in half-precision (FP16), precluding co-location of vector indices and Key-Value (KV) caches. This paper presents an engineering integration and empirical evaluation of a multimodal RAG framework optimized for consumer-grade Turing hardware (e.g., NVIDIA Tesla T4). Our system-level analysis identifies a critical trade-off: while generative pre-trained transformer quantization (GPTQ) offers superior throughput (51.6 tok/s), it exhibits significant context instability at 2048+ tokens on Turing architectures. Conversely, NormalFloat 4-bit (NF4) maintains robust long-context performance with viable latency (81 ms/tok). By coupling NF4 with a decoupled Florence-2 vision integration, we achieve visual reasoning with only 430 MB VRAM overhead. Furthermore, empirical observations of prompt-induced search space pruning show that structured prompting reduces latency by 47% without altering computational intensity (1.88 GFLOPs/token). The integrated architecture maintains an 8.37 GB footprint, establishing a viable RAG pipeline for 12-16 GB GPUs. Finally, structured few-shot prompting effectively compensates for quantization-induced reasoning loss, restoring mathematical accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0% across 200 trials.
authors: Zahraa Selim, Menna Hamed, Wesam Ahmed, Sohyla Said, Sara Basheer, Rami Zewail
bullets: Addresses VRAM and bandwidth constraints that prevent co-locating models, vector indices, and KV caches on edge GPUs.
Finds GPTQ offers higher throughput but becomes unstable for contexts of 2048+ tokens, while NF4 provides more reliable long-context behavior.
Integrates Florence-2 vision processing with only 430 MB of additional VRAM.
Structured prompting reduces latency by 47% and improves quantization-affected mathematical accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0% across 200 trials.
The complete architecture uses 8.37 GB of memory, targeting 12–16 GB GPUs, with evaluation focused on Turing hardware such as the Tesla T4.

papers.abstract: Forward-KL language-model distillation normally computes dense teacher and student scores over the full vocabulary at every supervised position, making training and stored teacher targets expensive. We instead distill from the teacher's highest-probability vocabulary fraction, renormalizing the retained mass as we sweep support from 100% to 0.01%. Our main study distills Qwen3 4B -> 1.7B. We confirm the broader support-reduction finding on larger Qwen3 8B -> 4B and Nemotron Nano 12B -> 9B pairs and under answer-only supervision. We evaluate generation primarily on MMLU-Pro and secondarily on GPQA-Diamond. Across the Qwen3 settings, retaining 0.01% of the vocabulary causes no observed MMLU-Pro degradation relative to full-vocabulary distillation, although disagreement with the complete teacher distribution increases. Nemotron Nano matches full-vocabulary MMLU-Pro at 0.1%, but smaller fractions fail to emit the closing reasoning tag, showing that the reliable cutoff depends on the model family. At 0.01% support, caching the retained next-token scores from the teacher forward pass cuts training step time by 38%, while restricting student output computation to those tokens cuts peak memory by 24%; neither causes observed MMLU-Pro degradation.
bullets: Full-vocabulary forward-KL distillation is expensive because it uses dense teacher and student scores at every supervised position.
The method retains and renormalizes only the teacher’s highest-probability tokens, sweeping support from 100% down to 0.01%.
Across Qwen3 model pairs, 0.01% support caused no observed MMLU-Pro degradation; results were also confirmed on larger pairs and answer-only supervision.
For Nemotron Nano, 0.1% matched full-vocabulary MMLU-Pro, while smaller supports disrupted closing reasoning-tag generation.
At 0.01% support, cached teacher scores reduced training step time by 38% and restricted student computation reduced peak memory by 24%, without observed MMLU-Pro degradation.

papers.abstract: Many advances in ML systems came from breaking an assumption that earlier methods took for granted: speculative decoding dropped the assumption that a model needs one forward pass per token. Yet algorithms rarely state their assumptions, so experts and discovery harnesses search over programs, where one edit changes several design choices and gains are difficult to attribute. Searching over the assumptions themselves remains largely unexplored. Writing algorithms as proofs makes their assumptions explicit and turns algorithm design into a search over a small, structured space that an LLM can explore and a proof checker can audit. We formalize 89 algorithms from KV-cache eviction, weight pruning and speculative decoding as proof graphs with explicit assumptions, checked in Lean. Our harness, AutoAssumption, relaxes one assumption of a published method, re-derives and re-proves it, and generates its code. In KV-cache eviction and weight pruning, this search improved on every published algorithm we ran and produced state-of-the-art algorithms. The eviction algorithm has the highest RULER-4K score of the published methods we ran, and the pruning algorithm the lowest perplexity of thirteen on four LLaMA models. At equal budget, the harness scores within a point of OpenEvolve, an open-source implementation of AlphaEvolve, with a lower standard deviation across repeats. Future work will formalize more fields and combine them through the principal assumptions they share.
authors: Igor Sadalski, Minghao Guo, Benjamin Jones, Wojciech Matusik
bullets: Recasts algorithms as proof graphs whose assumptions are explicit and auditable.
Uses an LLM to relax one assumption, re-derive and re-prove the algorithm in Lean, then generate code.
Formalizes 89 algorithms spanning KV-cache eviction, weight pruning, and speculative decoding.
Improved on every evaluated published algorithm in KV-cache eviction and weight pruning.
Matched OpenEvolve within a point at equal budget, with lower repeat-to-repeat variability.

papers.selection_reason: Directly proposes algorithms for KV-cache eviction and weight pruning via assumption search, fitting efficient-AI methods for token/memory reduction.
papers.title: AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
papers.tldr: AutoAssumption searches over explicit algorithmic assumptions, using checked proofs to discover new ML-systems algorithms and achieve state-of-the-art results in KV-cache eviction and weight pruning.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20$\mu$s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering. We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. Across seven dense models spanning 16-800 GB, SlipStream with a 40 MB staging buffer achieves 92.4% of the performance of an ideal HBF with HBM-like latency. H3 achieves only 43.1%, even with a 320 MB buffer. The buffer sizing of SlipStream is independent of HBF latency and workload. SlipStream with 16 MB buffer, 20x smaller than that of H3, performs within 4% of SlipStream-40MB. SlipStream also supports Mixture-of-Experts models and reaches 91.2% of ideal performance (40 MB buffer).

bullets: HBF offers much higher capacity than HBM but its roughly 20× higher read latency can severely slow on-demand LLM inference.
