papers.selection_reason: Block-sparse Gauss-Newton optimization with sparse automatic differentiation reduces compute and memory for large neural network training, transferable to efficient AI.
papers.title: Block-Sparse Gauss-Newton Optimization of Finite Basis Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Sparse Automatic Differentiation Approach
papers.tldr: A block-sparse Gauss–Newton method makes large FBPINN training more scalable by exploiting sparsity from overlapping domain decomposition.

papers.abstract: Expert parallelism (EP) shards the experts of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer across GPUs, so every MoE layer requires two all-to-all communications, namely dispatch and combine. Compared with training, inference processes relatively few tokens per GPU at a time, and at small batch sizes fixed costs that do not grow with the number of tokens, rather than data movement, dominate the latency. We present NVLinkOneSided, a one-sided EP all-to-all for GPUs within a single NVLink domain. Each source rank pushes its tokens, without first exchanging metadata, into rank-major buffers on the target GPUs, and the grouped GEMMs read them in place instead of from a per-expert copy. We provide two protocols for the synchronization that the communication requires, namely Fence and Sentinel, for high-throughput and low-latency scenarios respectively. On Blackwell GPUs, NVLinkOneSided completes dispatch and combine 1.2-3.0$\times$ faster than DeepEP, with the largest speedups at small batch sizes. The resulting MoE layer is up to 2.4$\times$ faster than DeepEP with DeepGEMM. It even outperforms the fused DeepGEMM MegaMoE at up to 128 tokens per GPU, making it still competitive for decoding. We expose NVLinkOneSided through a modular interface, so that it is agnostic to the activation quantization format, decoupled from the MoE compute backend and easy to integrate into inference frameworks.
authors: Bo Li, Chulian Zhang, Or Biri, Anthony Chang, Anton Korzh, Noam Duvdevani, XingFei Xi, Daniel Stokes, Zhenhuan Chen, Ludwig Schneider, Artem Y. Polyakov, Julien Demouth, Chandler Zhou
bullets: Targets fixed communication overheads that dominate MoE inference latency at low tokens per GPU.
Sources push tokens directly into rank-major buffers on target GPUs, which grouped GEMMs read in place.
Provides Fence and Sentinel synchronization protocols for high-throughput and low-latency use cases.
On Blackwell GPUs, dispatch and combine are 1.2–3.0× faster than DeepEP, while the MoE layer is up to 2.4× faster with DeepGEMM.
A modular interface supports different quantization formats, compute backends, and inference frameworks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Data path for the routing of Figure 1, with the FENCE synchronization protocol. Dispatch: each source rank stores its tokens into its own region of the dispatch workspaces of the target ranks and records the target rank and slot of each selection; T1 selects E0 and E1, both on R0, so it takes one slot there and its second selection records no slot (−1). MoE compute turns the tokens from each source rank into partial results at the same slots of the combine workspace. Combine: each source rank loads the partial results from the target ranks and slots recorded in dispatch and adds them. White slots are empty.

Figure 3. The MoE layer on R0, detailing Figure 2; MoE compute comprises indexing, FC1, FC2 and finalize, and slots are numbered 0–7 across the two regions. The indexing kernel turns the expert ids of the received slots into per-expert lists of slot indices (empty slots 3, 6 and 7 carry invalid ids); FC1 gathers tokens through these lists and multiplies them by the expert weights, FC2 multiplies the FC1 output by its own weights, and finalize adds the outputs of each token into its slot of the combine workspace.
Figure 5. NVLinkOneSided completes dispatch and combine faster than DeepEP at every batch. Round trip on eight B300 GPUs; bottom: speedup over DeepEP.

Figure 4. The dispatch workspace of R1 at the end of dispatch. (a) FENCE gathers the tokens of each source rank into a prefix of its region, so each source rank sends its slot count C; the slots past the count get invalid expert ids (−1). (b) SENTINEL pushes token i of each source rank into slot i of its region, so every slot signals its own arrival; a slot without a token keeps the sentinel payload (hatched) and gets invalid expert ids. Bottom: the critical path of dispatch until MoE compute starts; SENTINEL shortens it, which pays off at small batches.

papers.selection_reason: Optimizes MoE inference all-to-all communication over NVLink, reducing latency for expert-parallel LLM serving.
papers.title: One-Sided Expert-Parallel All-to-All for Mixture-of-Experts Inference over NVLink
papers.tldr: NVLinkOneSided accelerates small-batch MoE inference by using one-sided, metadata-free token exchange over NVLink.

papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) grounding maps a screenshot and a natural-language instruction to the screen location where an agent should act. Zoomed views can reveal small targets but may lose the context needed to identify them. We introduce GroundCascade, a training-free controller that uses agreement between a grounder's full-screen and zoomed predictions to decide when to consult a complementary model. It selects between zoomed predictions while preserving corroborated full-screen locations. An optional Finalizer predicts from an unmarked joint crop when disagreement remains (Full); omitting it yields the two-stage Selective variant. GroundCascade reaches 85.33% on ScreenSpot-Pro with Indeed-UI-32B/8B/32B and 88.43% on the visible-target OSWorld-G-Refined subset with Qwen3.6-27B/3.8-27B/3.8-27B, gains of 2.66 and 2.35 percentage points over the stronger standalone two-pass grounder. On UI-Vision, GroundCascade reaches 72.20% category-balanced accuracy, with Selective slightly higher at 72.28%. Across these three evaluations, GroundCascade in Full mode uses 2.42-2.73 calls per request, 31-39% fewer than unconditionally acquiring both models' two-pass predictions. At matched second-model call budgets, selective acquisition gains 1.52-2.56 points over standalone Two-pass, compared with 0.22-0.69 points from stratified random acquisition. GroundCascade leads the official ScreenSpot-Pro leaderboard and exceeds reported GUI-specialist comparisons on OSWorld-G-Refined and UI-Vision, subject to differences in external evaluation protocols.
bullets: GUI grounding must balance zoomed detail against full-screen context, which can cause incorrect target selection.
The training-free controller compares full-screen and zoomed predictions, preserving corroborated locations and consulting a complementary model selectively.
An optional Finalizer resolves remaining disagreements from an unmarked joint crop; the Selective variant omits it.
It achieves 85.33% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 88.43% on visible-target OSWorld-G-Refined, and 72.20–72.28% on UI-Vision.
Full mode uses 31–39% fewer model calls than unconditional two-model, two-pass acquisition; results depend on external evaluation protocols.

papers.selection_reason: GUI grounding as vision-language spatial localization; selective second-opinion controller reduces inference calls and is transferable to efficient multimodal systems.
papers.title: GroundCascade: Selective Second Opinions for GUI Grounding
papers.tldr: GroundCascade selectively seeks a second GUI-grounding opinion when full-screen and zoomed predictions disagree, improving accuracy while reducing model calls.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated strong generalization in robotic manipulation, yet processing dense visual tokens often incurs high inference latency. Visual token pruning offers a practical way to reduce this cost, but identifying a compact set of tokens that preserves reliable action generation remains challenging. Existing methods largely rely on static or immediate heuristic cues to estimate token importance. We introduce APS-VLA, a framework that learns visual token selection from robot demonstrations while keeping the pretrained VLA backbone frozen. A lightweight Decision Influence Estimator scores tokens conditioned on current visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioception. Its training combines two complementary signals: action supervision matches both the full-input policy predictions and demonstrated actions, while an auxiliary visual transition objective uses demonstrated actions to predict subsequent visual features from the selected representation. At deployment, the estimator performs a single hard selection and packing step before the policy's native action-generation procedure; the auxiliary predictor is removed. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and with $\pi_{0.5}$ and XR-1 on RoboCasa365 demonstrate inference acceleration with modest changes in task success. Across five real-world tasks on two dual-arm platforms, APS-VLA reduces mean policy inference latency from 137.25 to 93.25 ms, achieving a $1.47\times$ speedup with an average success rate of 61%, compared with 60% for the unpruned baseline. Together, these results support APS-VLA as a modular, plug-in framework for efficient robotic control across VLA architectures, preserving the underlying policy parameters and native action-generation procedure.
authors: Xiaoyang Xing, Chun-Mei Feng, Anthony Cohn, Xiaoliang Gong, Asoke Nandi
bullets: Addresses high inference latency caused by dense visual-token processing in robotic manipulation.
Uses a lightweight Decision Influence Estimator conditioned on visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioception.
Trains token selection with action supervision plus an auxiliary objective predicting future visual features from demonstrated actions.
Performs one hard token-selection and packing step at deployment, then uses the VLA policy’s native action generation.

papers.abstract: Block drafters such as DFlash draft a block of future tokens in one forward pass, and draft trees such as DDTree verify the prefixes ranked highest by the product of the drafter's per-position distributions. Under tree verification, the expected number of accepted tokens is the probability mass the tree covers. We show that a product misallocates it: when the continuation can follow several futures, it splices them into chimeras, prefixes stitched together from different futures that the target never produces, and gives them as much budget as the futures themselves. Barring ties, no product-ranked tree can hold two futures that disagree in $m$ positions without $2^{m-1}-1$ chimeras, however well the drafter is trained, and in practice chimeras make up 27-33% of a 64-node tree. We propose Multi-Future Drafting (MFD), which restores the coupling with a latent variable instead of the chain rule: $K$ learned mode embeddings at the drafter's input draft $K$ coherent blocks in the same pass, and a mixture DDTree lets the verifier pick the future the target takes, losslessly and with $K+1$ extra vectors. On four Qwen targets from 4B to 27B parameters, at batch size 1, MFD reaches up to 7.8$\times$ speedup, 5-8% faster than the best single-mode tree trained identically and, on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, 9-16% faster than the released DARTree trained on the same prompts.
authors: Haoyu Huang, Jialiang Kang, Linlin Yang, Xiao Yang, Baochang Zhang
bullets: Product-ranked draft trees can waste 27–33% of a 64-node tree on chimeric prefixes that combine incompatible futures.
MFD uses K learned mode embeddings to draft K coherent future blocks in one forward pass.
A mixture DDTree lets verification select the future matching the target, with only K+1 extra vectors.
Across four Qwen targets from 4B to 27B parameters, MFD is 5–8% faster than an identically trained single-mode tree.
It is 9–16% faster than released DARTree on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B under the reported setup.

papers.selection_reason: Speculative decoding with mixture block drafters reduces LLM inference latency, a clear efficiency contribution.
papers.title: Multi-Future Drafting: Mixture Block Drafters for Tree-Verified Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: Multi-Future Drafting improves tree-verified speculative decoding by drafting multiple coherent futures instead of probability-product chimeras, achieving up to 7.8× speedup on Qwen targets.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning agents are often deployed with policies that cannot be retrained or modified. In digital environments whose states can be copied and resumed, an operator has another option: sample several continuations from the current state, evaluate them, and continue from the endpoint of the selected branch. We call this procedure branch-and-commit. We study when it improves return, what produces the improvement, and where its computational budget should be spent. Across four environments, two frozen policies, five continuation verifiers, and a model-free selection rule, we find that the benefit of branching depends on dispersion: the difference between the best candidate return and the mean candidate return. Branching provides no benefit in low-dispersion settings, while increasing return by 12.8% in our main Craftax-Medium setting. Most of this gain comes not from selecting better actions, but from selecting among different stochastic realizations of the same action. Several competent verifiers achieve similar episode returns, suggesting that verifier quality is not the main constraint at our operating budget. Instead, computation is better allocated to states where useful dispersion is likely. On held-out seeds, gating branching using predicted dispersion retains 69% of the improvement from uniform branching while using 48% as many branching calls. These results characterize when branch-and-commit is useful and clarify what its gains represent.
authors: Sahar Admoni, Assaf Hallak, Yftah Ziser, Ofra Amir
bullets: Evaluates branching across four environments, two frozen policies, five continuation verifiers, and a model-free selection rule.
Branching provides little benefit in low-dispersion states but raises return by 12.8% in the main Craftax-Medium setting.
Most gains come from choosing among stochastic outcomes of the same action, not from selecting better actions.
Verifier quality is not the primary bottleneck at the tested compute budget; allocating computation to promising states matters more.
Predicted-dispersion gating retains 69% of uniform branching’s improvement with 48% as many branching calls on held-out seeds.

papers.abstract: Spike cameras encode dynamic scenes into high-temporal-resolution binary spike streams for efficient high-speed vision. Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) can process such signals with sparse and accumulate-only computation, existing SNN-based reconstruction methods are typically shallow and still lag behind ANN-based models in reconstruction fidelity. This paper proposes MADSNet, a Multi-scale Axial-attentive Dense Spiking Network for spike camera image reconstruction. MADSNet adopts a hierarchical spiking encoder--decoder, where a multi-scale spike stem extracts early features, axial spike attention captures long-range dependencies, a dense spiking bottleneck enhances feature reuse, and a spike-to-continuous decoder reconstructs continuous intensity images from spike-domain representations. Experiments on gray-scale and color spike reconstruction show that MADSNet outperforms SSIR by 4.3 dB PSNR and Spk2ImgNet by 1.94 dB on SREDS. Compared with Spk2ImgNet, it achieves about 15$\times$ lower latency and uses only about 1/40 of the estimated energy, demonstrating that carefully designed SNN architectures can improve reconstruction quality while preserving computational efficiency.
authors: Sirui Li, Rui Zhao, Siqi Cai, Haizhou Li, Tiejun Huang, Yajing Zheng
bullets: Targets the limited reconstruction fidelity and shallow designs of existing SNN-based methods.
Uses a multi-scale spike stem, axial spike attention, dense spiking bottleneck, and spike-to-continuous decoder.
Evaluated on grayscale and color spike reconstruction using SREDS.
Outperforms SSIR by 4.3 dB PSNR and Spk2ImgNet by 1.94 dB on SREDS.
Compared with Spk2ImgNet, reports about 15× lower latency and 1/40 the estimated energy.

papers.abstract: Federated fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces communication and computational overhead by training and exchanging compact trainable LoRA factors. Clients may use different LoRA ranks to meet adapter communication budgets and accommodate different local adaptation needs. The server must process these differences during aggregation and construct adapters at each client's rank for local training. We distinguish pre-aggregation alignment, which handles factor dimensions and scaling conventions before aggregation and rank-specific LoRA adapter extraction, which constructs client-sized pairs from the aggregated global model. Two common approaches to rank-specific extraction are direct rank truncation and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of the dense update. Direct prefix truncation keeps the leading columns of one aggregated factor and the corresponding rows of the other. It is cheap but can increase reconstruction error. The dense SVD approach first forms the product of aggregated LoRA factors. It then decomposes this matrix and retains the leading singular components to construct adapters at the target rank. This gives the optimal rank-constrained approximation in Frobenius norm but incurs significant computational overhead. To address this trade-off, we propose RBLA+ as an extension of RBLA. It uses established compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to minimize Frobenius error for the extracted LoRA update without forming the dense update. It also accounts for client and server scaling conventions during upload and broadcast. Across vision and language tasks, RBLA+ improves accuracy over RBLA in multiple heterogeneous settings. In CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters, RBLA+ has lower extraction time than the dense partial-SVD baseline. RBLA+ preserves each client's prescribed adapter size and per-round communication payload.
authors: Shuaijun Chen, Omid Tavallaie, Xin Chen, Wentao Gao, Nguyen Tran, Albert Y. Zomaya
bullets: Addresses federated fine-tuning where clients use different LoRA ranks and scaling conventions.
Uses compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to minimize Frobenius reconstruction error without forming the dense update.
Improves accuracy over RBLA across vision and language tasks in multiple heterogeneous settings.
Runs faster than dense partial-SVD extraction in CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters.
Preserves each client’s prescribed adapter size and per-round communication payload.

papers.abstract: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces the computational cost of attention through token-level selection. However, its indexer still scores the entire causal prefix for each query, making indexing a dominant source of latency in long-context inference. Notably, the indexer alone can account for more than 50% of total prefill GPU time at long context lengths. To address this bottleneck, we propose ADIndex, an Adaptive and Distillation-driven Indexing method for token-level sparse attention. ADIndex integrates three key components: (i) a layer-wise calibration strategy that adaptively accommodates cross-query retrieval overlap, motivated by our observation of pronounced inter-layer heterogeneity; (ii) a group-level distillation scheme that leverages this heterogeneity to efficiently train adaptive layer-wise group indexers, capturing salient retrieval signals from individual queries; and (iii) a low-latency inference strategy that reduces repeated full-prefix scans through token bank sharing within query groups while retaining query-specific refinement. Experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 demonstrate that ADIndex preserves near-lossless task performance on LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER while delivering substantial efficiency gains over standard DSA, including prefill and decoding kernel speedups of up to 6.22x and 3.40x, respectively, at a context length of 256K across the layer-wise reuse configurations, as well as an end-to-end serving speedup of 1.54x at a context length of 128K.
authors: Jin-Fei Qi, Yiduo Li, Jiang-Xin Shi, Kan Liu, Tao Lan, Hanlin Tang, Yu-Feng Li
bullets: Targets the indexer bottleneck, which can exceed half of prefill GPU time at long context lengths.
Uses layer-wise calibration to handle heterogeneous cross-query retrieval overlap across layers.
Trains adaptive layer-wise group indexers through group-level distillation while retaining query-specific refinement.
Reduces repeated full-prefix scans via token-bank sharing within query groups.
On DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1, reports up to 6.22× prefill, 3.40× decoding-kernel, and 1.54× end-to-end serving speedups while maintaining near-lossless LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER performance.

papers.abstract: Context compression is now routine for language models with long inputs, but a compressed context is useful only if it keeps the evidence for the answer. Existing checks compare the reader model's answer or its most likely words, and thus miss a frequent failure, silent evidence loss: key evidence is removed while the answer stays the same, leaving the answer unsupported and risky for other models that reuse the context. To address this challenge, we propose SELD (Silent Evidence Loss Detector), which needs no training and no labels. Its principle is that when evidence is lost, a reader model's preferences among the answers it leaves unsaid shift even if its answer does not, so comparing these preferences before and after compression reveals losses that answer checks cannot see. We also build SEL-Pairs, a benchmark of length-matched evidence and control deletions from three question-answering datasets. Quantitative and qualitative experiments with five reader models on it show that SELD consistently outperforms strong and recent baselines across compressors, compression rates and models, identifying the evidence-removing edit in 83% of matched pairs with unchanged answers, against 70% for the strongest baseline. These results show that evidence loss in compressed contexts can be detected even when the answer is unchanged.
bullets: Silent evidence loss can make compressed contexts unsafe for reuse because answers may remain correct but unsupported.
SELD compares shifts in a reader model’s preferences among unchosen answers before and after compression, requiring no training or labels.
The authors introduce SEL-Pairs, a benchmark of matched evidence-removal and control deletions from three QA datasets.
Across five reader models, compressors, and compression rates, SELD identified the evidence-removing edit in 83% of unchanged-answer pairs, versus 70% for the strongest baseline.
The method targets evidence loss beyond answer-preservation checks; its evaluation scope is the benchmark’s datasets, models, and compression settings.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Test 1: single-sentence deletion on 2,414 new questions. (a) How often each check scores the keysentence deletion above its equal-length control, among pairs whose answer did not change (50% is chance; LUMINA-ECU is post hoc). (b) The two main tests (pooled over reader models) and eight per-reader tests. (c) Post-hoc checks: SELD minus JS divergence by answer group and SELD minus six text-only scores among unchanged answers. Intervals are Bonferroni-corrected within each family (Section A).

Figure 1: Silent evidence loss and how SELD detects it (illustrative; bars: gray for the original context, blue for the compressed one). (1) Compression removes the only sentence that states the answer. (2) With the full guide, both reader models answer the right. After compression, reader model A still answers the right from its default, so an answer check passes; reader model B, reading the same compressed context downstream, falls back on a different default and answers the left. The loss was silent for A, so nothing stopped the context from reaching B. (3) Checks that look at the top answer (answer agreement, JS divergence, answer-likelihood drop) see almost no change; in our tests they change less than when an equally long, harmless sentence is deleted. SELD compares the reader model’s preferences among all the answers it leaves unsaid, which shift when the evidence is gone. A real case with measured scores is given in Section I.

Figure 2: SEL-Pairs and SELD (schematic). (1) For each input, an evidence edit (red) removes evidence and a control edit (gray, dashed) removes other text of exactly the same token length: single-sentence deletion from the original context on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA (denoted S and C in the text); swaps inside LLMLingua-2 outputs at 25, 50 and 75% and inside Provence outputs (B and C, with the output as input A; LLMLingua-2 swaps are refilled to equal length); and MuSiQue’s official unanswerable context against a control that keeps the key paragraphs (U and T ). (2) SELD (step 1) reads the reader model’s scores for every possible next word under O and X , so that the answers left unsaid count; (2) centers them and ignores their scale, so that a mere change in confidence does not count; and (3) measures the angle between the two patterns. A check passes a pair when it scores the evidence edit above its equal-length control.

papers.abstract: User-facing LLM agents must identify which behavioral policies apply at each turn, but evaluating every policy with an LLM is costly. We introduce Signals and Queries (S&Q), a lightweight first-stage relevance filter developed for Parlant 4.0 that removes at least 30% of candidate policies before downstream evaluation while preserving high recall. For each policy, an LLM generates activating examples and hard negatives offline. An independent logistic classifier trained on their embeddings then predicts relevance using embeddings and vector dot products, with no per-turn LLM calls. This shifts expensive relevance evaluation to a smaller candidate set, while allowing each policy's classifier to be updated independently. Evaluated against 9,144 LLM-judge relevance labels covering 254 $τ^2$-bench conversation prefixes and 36 airline policies, S&Q achieves higher precision than top-K and cosine-threshold retrieval at every evaluated recall level, with consistent results across two embedding providers. These findings support inexpensive, per-policy classification as a practical first stage for reducing downstream evaluation workload in customer-facing agents.
bullets: Addresses the cost of evaluating every behavioral policy with an LLM at each conversation turn.
Generates policy-specific activating examples and hard negatives offline, then trains an independent logistic classifier on their embeddings.
Uses embedding dot products for fast first-stage relevance filtering before downstream evaluation.
Outperformed top-K and cosine-threshold retrieval in precision across all tested recall levels, with consistent results across two embedding providers.
Evaluated on 9,144 relevance labels from 254 conversation prefixes and 36 airline policies; scope is customer-facing agent policy selection.

figures.caption: Figure 7: Absorbing the same exemplar upgrade. Every method is fitted first on generated exemplars and then on exemplars mined from held-in conversations, and evaluated on the identical held-out scenarios and artifacts; the slope is therefore what each method converts an exemplar improvement into. Colour marks the method family and line style the encoder. Trained discriminants (blue, green) absorb the upgrade; similarity over signals (orange) has no place to put a negative and saturates.
Figure 4: Recall-first operating points (Gemini): best precision subject to macro recall ≥90%; top-K methods shown at their maximum-recall setting K=15, which still fails the recall target.
Figure 5: S&Q per-policy recall (left) and precision (right) under the two embedding providers, at each provider’s recall-first operating point (16 highest-base-rate policies; black line: mean).

Figure 2: Where points land on one artifact’s logistic classifier (Cancel flight). Signals and anti-signals separate cleanly; real conversation queries labeled relevant by the LLM judge (stars) score above the irrelevant ones (crosses) but below the signals. This signal→query domain shift motivates the recall-first margin θ < 0.

Figure 1: One live conversation turn (query, star) projected into two artifacts’ classifier spaces (x-axis: the artifact’s own discriminant w·q + b; y-axis: first residual PC of its exemplars). In the Cancel flight space the query lands among the signals (relevant); in the Traveling with Pets space the same query lands among the anti-signals (not relevant).

Figure 3: Macro recall–precision Pareto frontiers vs. the LLM judge. S&Q (blue) dominates all four baselines at every recall level, under both embedders (solid: Gemini; dashed: OpenAI). Fixed-K retrieval cannot exceed ∼66% recall because the number of simultaneously relevant policies varies per turn.

Figure 8: Decomposing S&Q’s gain. Replacing generated positives alone is worth almost nothing; essentially the whole improvement arrives with the mined hard negatives, the channel that similarity retrieval cannot express.

Figure 6: Per-turn relevance-discovery cost (log scale): the per-policy LLM judge vs. S&Q. All of S&Q’s LLM usage is a one-time offline generation step; its per-turn cost is one embedding call and 37µs of CPU.

Table 3: Ablations: each block varies one component from the full method (bold = default; others held at pooling both, anti-signals, centered, logistic regression, m=10). AUPRC is the area under the macro recall–precision curve; P@R90 is macro precision at 90% recall; both are averaged over the 31 occurring policies. G = Gemini, O = OpenAI.

Table 2: Recall-first operating points (best macro precision s.t. macro recall ≥90%). Top-K methods never reach 90% recall; shown at K=15. ∗This operating point is not fixed: §5 shows S&Q improves it substantially from exemplars mined from deployment traffic.

Table 7: The same exemplar upgrade, absorbed differently. Each method is fitted first on generated exemplars and then on exemplars mined from one half of the scenarios, and evaluated on the held-out other half (§5), with artifacts and pooling fixed. The change, not the level, is the quantity of interest: it is what a method converts an exemplar improvement into.

Table 4: Multi-topic stress test: recall (%) on the recent topic’s (B’s) policies at the end of a stitched A-then-B conversation, at a matched false-positive rate. Max-over-turns recovers the recent topic that the blended cumulative embedding dilutes; the method’s both pooling tracks max-overturns. G = Gemini, O = OpenAI.

Table 1: Capabilities of S&Q relative to the two inferencefree embedding-retrieval families it competes with (the baselines of §3). ✓: supported; ×: not supported; (✓): partial. Each property is defined and motivated in the text; the signal-scored baseline variants (B2, B4) do not change any entry.
Table 6: Measured per-turn cost of relevance discovery over N=36 policies. The LLM-judge row uses the production ranker prompt on a median-length conversation prefix.

Table 5: Fine-tuning the encoder (SetFit) versus S&Q’s frozen encoder, at the recall-first operating point. On the same local base model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, 384-dim), finetuning does not beat a logistic head on frozen features, and both match the far larger frozen API embedders. Same benchmark, exemplars, and pooling throughout.

papers.selection_reason: Lightweight first-stage policy relevance filter reduces per-turn LLM evaluation cost in agents.
papers.title: Signals and Queries: Token-Efficient Agentic Context Discovery
papers.tldr: Signals and Queries is a lightweight per-policy embedding classifier that filters out at least 30% of candidate policies without per-turn LLM calls while maintaining high recall.

papers.abstract: Deploying large language models in regulated industries requires more than picking the fastest inference engine: it requires evidence that a configuration meets contractual and legal obligations before it serves a single customer request. We describe Runway, an internal validation harness built at MasterControl that builds a governed decision pipeline around NVIDIA AIPerf. The key insight is separating concerns: AIPerf provides the trusted measurement, while Runway provides the experiment design that comes before it and the compliance, cost, and audit decisions that come after. We describe the architecture and the storage model that makes caching and audit one mechanism. We report three findings from Runway sweeps: TensorRT-LLM and vLLM rankings invert with concurrency; a newer, pricier GPU instance can be the cheaper one per request; and speculative decoding behaves differently across engines under load, so engine configuration can outweigh engine choice.
bullets: Targets the evidence and governance requirements of deploying LLMs in regulated industries.
Separates trusted performance measurement by NVIDIA AIPerf from experiment design and post-measurement decisions.
Uses a shared storage model to support both caching and auditability.
Finds that engine rankings change with concurrency, newer GPUs may lower cost per request, and speculative decoding varies by engine under load.
Shows that configuration choices can matter more than the engine choice itself.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Runway system overview. Each phase is a separate layer; AIPerf is the only component that touches the engine under test. A cache hit skips measurement entirely.
Figure 2: Argo Workflows execution. The engine and AIPerf share the pod, so load is generated over localhost.
Figure 4: Per-cell cache decision. --only-cache turns any miss into an error, which lets a report be regenerated on a machine with no GPU.
Figure 3: Artifact store layout. The path encodes what was measured; the fingerprint file records how. Synthetic sweeps use synthetic as the dataset segment.
Table 3: Throughput with MTP relative to the same engine without it.
Table 2: g7e.2xlarge relative to g6e.xlarge, median over 16 token shapes. Cost per request is the price ratio divided by the throughput ratio.
Table 1: Engine comparison across concurrency levels. Throughput advantage is the winner’s mean throughput ratio over the 12 token shapes; latency winner counts wins out of 12 shapes.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of LLM inference engine configurations, cost, and speculative decoding under load, relevant to efficient deployment.
papers.title: Inference Validation for Regulated AI: A Governed Decision Pipeline for LLM Serving
papers.tldr: Runway adds governed experiment design and compliance, cost, and audit decisions around AIPerf to validate LLM-serving configurations before regulated deployment.

papers.abstract: Sliced inference such as SAHI is the standard remedy for small objects in high-resolution imagery, but its gains are usually measured against low-resolution baselines. We revisit sliced inference with scale as the explicit variable and ask when tiling actually pays off. We compare nine dense detectors, eight YOLO models of four generations and FCOS, on VisDrone and DOTA, under pre-specified hypotheses, calibration-only tuning and a single evaluation on held-out test data. Two findings emerge. First, much of the benefit attributed to slicing is a resolution effect: on VisDrone, a single pass trained at a higher resolution outperforms tiling with box fusion (merging decoded boxes) for every detector that could be trained at that resolution, and at equal compute a higher resolution helps more than a larger model. Second, tiles carry complementary information that box fusion wastes. We introduce SCAHI (Slicing with Coverage-Aware Hyper Inference), which accumulates the dense outputs of all passes with weights that give every image position the same total coverage, and reads objects off a peak grid fine enough to keep crowded neighbours apart. On identical passes, SCAHI outperforms box fusion for every YOLO detector on both datasets and matches it for FCOS. On DOTA, whose images far exceed the resolution a single pass can be trained at, tiles with SCAHI beat the best single pass for every detector, by 4.3 to 5.6 mAP50 at 2048 px, and replacing only SAHI's merge step by SCAHI adds 2.3 to 4.0 mAP50. An ablation attributes the gain to the border weighting and the resolution of the peak grid. Source code is available at https://github.com/beckerio/scahi.
bullets: The study evaluates nine dense detectors, including eight YOLO models and FCOS, on VisDrone and DOTA with controlled tuning and held-out testing.

On VisDrone, training a single detector at higher resolution outperforms tiled inference with box fusion whenever that resolution is feasible; higher resolution also beats a larger model at equal compute.
SCAHI combines dense outputs from tiles using coverage-aware weighting and a fine peak grid, avoiding information loss from decoded-box fusion.
With identical tiles, SCAHI outperforms box fusion for every YOLO detector on both datasets and matches it for FCOS.
On DOTA, where full-image resolution is infeasible, SCAHI improves over the best single pass and replacing SAHI's merge step yields substantial gains.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview. One detector processes a whole-image pass at its training size and overlapping tiles. The baseline merges decoded boxes across passes (orange). SCAHI accumulates the dense outputs of all passes in a global volume over position and object size, weights them so that every position receives the same total weight, and extracts one peak per object. For YOLOv10 and YOLO26, SCAHI uses the one-to-many head.

Figure 5. Pre-specified questions across detectors (VisDrone model extension). Differences with paired bootstrap 95 % confidence intervals on val (filled) and test-dev (hollow); dashed line: threshold ε = 0.30AP. Q2 is shown for passes at 1280 and 2048 px; the last panel compares the two heads under SCAHI for YOLOv10m and YOLO26. The pooled row covers the five detectors of the original extension; YOLO26s/m, added by addendum, are shown below it. YOLOv12m could only be tested at 1280 px, as it could not be trained at 2048 px. YOLOv10s, the detector of the main study, is reported in Sec. 10.

Figure 2. Why dense fusion removes tile-border fragments. (a) Box fusion sees two decoded boxes for one object that straddles a tile seam: the fragment predicted by tile A overlaps the full box from tile B too little to be suppressed. (b) Dense fusion weights every prediction by a raised-cosine taper bt over the overlap; the tapers of overlapping tiles sum to one (Eq. 2), so a prediction near a tile border carries little weight and the cluster around the object yields one detection. The fusion must also keep adjacent objects apart: its peak search has to be fine relative to object size (Sec. 5.2). Schematic, not to scale.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces SCAHI, a method for efficient small object detection using dense fusion and coverage-aware inference, which is relevant for perception in embodied systems.
papers.title: When Does Sliced Inference Pay Off? Resolution, Tiling and Dense Fusion for Small Object Detection
papers.tldr: Slicing helps mainly when full-image resolution is insufficient, and SCAHI improves tile fusion by preserving dense, complementary predictions.

papers.abstract: Serving systems choose a weight format for each model and deployment. A low-cost screen predicts the resulting KL divergence from the unquantized model's Fisher information using $\tfrac12Δ^\top FΔ$, the expansion underlying Hessian-aware and second-order post-training quantizers. We assess the reliability of this screen in GPU batches with channel-wise int8, per-tensor fp8 and group-wise int4 on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. Relative predictions hold across a 16-fold range of perturbation scales, int4 group sizes and rounding modes, while absolute predictions are heavy-tailed. A trimmed average brings 10 of 12 cells on Qwen3-4B and OLMo-2 within 15% of measured KL. The MoE model exhibits nonquadratic response at small perturbations, with int8 KL scaling as $α^{0.63}$. Computing per-sequence gradients in bf16 can cause fourfold prediction errors. We trace these errors to arithmetic in the lower half of the backward pass and eliminate them by using fp32 there. Batch-invariant kernels run at 0.55 times the throughput, while changes in reduction order introduce a floor of 0.17-0.22 nats per sequence. We build a screener with one streamed fp32 Fisher pass, trimmed tensor-block predictions with a band, a flag for aligned tensors and per-layer format allocation. On the unseen Mistral-7B-v0.3 family, all six predictions fall within the band, all three KL budgets are met, and vLLM throughput is predicted within 0.4%.
bullets: The study evaluates the approximation ½ΔᵀFΔ for channel-wise int8, per-tensor fp8, and group-wise int4 quantization across five language models and varied perturbation settings.
Relative predictions remain consistent across scales, group sizes, and rounding modes, while absolute errors are heavy-tailed; trimmed averaging improves calibration in most tested cells.
The MoE model shows nonquadratic behavior at small perturbations, with int8 KL scaling as α^0.63 rather than quadratically.
bf16 per-sequence gradients can produce fourfold prediction errors; fp32 computation in the lower backward pass removes these errors, at 0.55× throughput for batch-invariant kernels.
A proposed screener accurately predicts all six held-out Mistral-7B-v0.3 cases, meets three KL budgets, and predicts vLLM throughput within 0.4%.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Per-sequence ratio of the bf16 to the fp32 quadratic form (int8), sorted. Dotted: the post-hoc threshold 10.
Figure 2: R by sample set and gradient precision (int8). On set C the bf16 estimate is off by 3–4× until the blown-up sequences are removed.

Figure 3: Measured over predicted KL (5%-trimmed) for the 17 archived dense cells at α = 1 that set the band (blue) and the six pre-registered test cells on Mistral-7B-v0.3 (orange), under the tensor-block form (filled) and the element-diagonal form (open). Shaded: the frozen band [0.75,1.50]. i4 rest: Qwen3-32B int4 without its one coherent tensor; Bk: budgets.

Band [0.75,1.50].

papers.selection_reason: Quantization mismatch prediction and efficient LLM serving directly target inference efficiency.
papers.title: How Far Does Second-Order Linear Response Predict Quantization Mismatch? Pre-Registered Measurements on Five Language Models
papers.tldr: Second-order Fisher-based estimates can screen quantization mismatch reliably, but require robust aggregation and fp32 backward computation to handle heavy tails, nonquadratic behavior, and numerical error.

papers.abstract: Alternating minimization is a standard tool for optimization problems with two coupled variable blocks. Its cost is dominated by the inner subproblem solvers, which rarely have a closed-form solution. In this paper, we propose to learn an inexact alternating scheme in which neural networks approximate the subproblem solution at each iteration. For convex problems with quadratic couplings between the variable blocks that satisfy a quadratic growth condition, we derive a worst-case bound on the optimality gap that exposes the per-iteration error that each network is trained to minimize in a greedy fashion. Combining the bound with a PAC-Bayes argument, we obtain a fixed-horizon, high-probability bound on the expected optimality gap over the distribution of problem instances. We apply the learned scheme to robust matrix completion and low-dose CT reconstruction with dictionary regularization where we achieve a 5x-13x speedup over the inexact first-order baseline at matched accuracy. A brief end-to-end fine-tuning stage extends this up to 30x and outperforms other learned schemes. The code is available at https://github.com/paulhausner/learned-alternating-minimization.
bullets: Targets the high cost of solving coupled alternating-minimization subproblems exactly or iteratively.
Uses learned networks to approximate each subproblem solution and trains them greedily according to a derived per-iteration error bound.
For convex problems with quadratic coupling and quadratic growth, combines worst-case analysis with PAC-Bayes to bound expected optimality gaps with high probability.
In robust matrix completion and low-dose CT reconstruction, achieves 5×–13× speedups at matched accuracy versus an inexact first-order baseline.
Brief end-to-end fine-tuning increases the speedup to 30× and outperforms other learned schemes.

papers.tldr: Neural networks learn approximate alternating-minimization updates for convex problems, with theoretical guarantees and substantial speedups in two reconstruction tasks.

papers.abstract: Foundation models can supply predictions for a downstream task that draw on knowledge from extensive pretraining, but they differ in task-specific accuracy and query cost. We develop a framework that improves prediction for the task under a budget on the average query cost per input, using training data to learn which models to query and how to combine their outputs with features available without querying. The first method queries the same models for every input; the second lets them vary across inputs and uses Q-learning to decide which model to query next and when to stop. For the first method, we show that several individually inaccurate outputs can jointly outperform the best single one. It attains the minimax rate when the regression function depends on the outputs only through models within the budget. Otherwise, any method within the budget can be forced to a slower rate, which the first method attains. For the second method, we show when varying the queried models across inputs strictly improves on querying the same models for every input, and bound its prediction risk and average cost in finite samples. In simulations and a multimodal laptop price application, both methods outperform existing methods.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between foundation-model accuracy and per-input query cost.
Introduces a fixed-query method that combines outputs with non-query features, and an adaptive method using Q-learning to select models and stop querying.
Shows that multiple individually inaccurate models can jointly outperform the best single model.
Provides minimax-rate guarantees for fixed querying and finite-sample risk/cost bounds for adaptive querying.
Simulations and a multimodal laptop-price application show both methods outperform existing approaches.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoders raise throughput by banking more target tokens per forward pass, and Medusa, EAGLE-3, DFlash and DSpark all do it the same way: more candidates that survive verification. All of them draft in the target's own vocabulary, so one node of the candidate tree is one target token, and the tokenizer makes that unit look like a constant. It is not. BPE's pretokenizer splits on whitespace before merges are learned, so no multi-word string can ever become a single token: in Qwen3-4B, "United States of America" is four tokens and no adjacent pair of them exists as one entry, so a phrase is out of reach of any method drafting in the target's vocabulary. We change the unit. A small MLP head reads the frozen target's hidden state and predicts a one- to three-word phrase as one entry in a separate draft vocabulary; greedy longest-match expansion maps it back into the target's own tokens, and N candidates are verified in one forward pass behind a prefix-tree mask, so the change is orthogonal to tree depth and width. The target and its tokenizer stay frozen and a candidate is accepted only while it matches the target's own argmax, so the served output is identical to greedy decoding up to floating-point tie-breaking. On one A5000 at batch 1, against HuggingFace generate(), a 21.94M head (0.545% of Qwen3-4B) reaches 2.391x on GSM8K, 2.444x on MATH-500 and 1.544x on MT-Bench. Because the head's output layer is one row of 257 parameters per entry, the draft vocabulary size is the parameter budget: an 8,000-entry head is 3.434M parameters, 0.0854% of the target and 64x smaller than EAGLE-3's drafter, and keeps 92.3% of the larger head's GSM8K tokens per pass. With EAGLE-3 run on same prompts and baseline, our 21.94M head is ahead of tree-16 on both maths sets and behind tree-60 on every set.
bullets: Addresses the limitation that target-vocabulary drafting cannot represent multi-word phrases as single candidate units.
A small MLP predicts one- to three-word entries from a separate draft vocabulary, expands them into target tokens, and verifies candidates in one prefix-tree-masked pass.
Accepted tokens exactly match the target model’s greedy output, aside from floating-point tie-breaking.
On an A5000 at batch 1, it achieves 2.391× on GSM8K, 2.444× on MATH-500, and 1.544× on MT-Bench versus HuggingFace generate().
An 8,000-entry head uses 3.434M parameters and retains 92.3% of the larger head’s GSM8K tokens per pass; performance is ahead of EAGLE-3 tree-16 but behind tree-60.

papers.tldr: Phrase-level speculative decoding accelerates greedy generation by drafting multi-word phrases with a small head while keeping the target model and tokenizer frozen.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts language models are cheap to run per token but expensive to hold in GPU memory, which drives the cost of serving them in production. One-shot expert compression shrinks them after a single calibration pass. Its two current state-of-the-art methods are REAP for expert pruning, which deletes the least salient experts, and REAM for expert merging, which merges them into the most salient ones. Both have been evaluated only on academic benchmarks. We compare the two on five multilingual production tasks of a web-hosting company, from classification to the generation of marketing HTML email templates, with two 30B-parameter models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and the hybrid Mamba-attention Nemotron-3.5-Lightning) at 25% and 50% of experts removed and the same calibration data. Pruning wins: on the same rows, REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2. At 25%, REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality and REAM 62.5%, although on benchmarks the two are within a point for the same model. The damage concentrates in the output contract rather than the content: 89.8-95.2% of each significant loss on email templates comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts and runaway generation, and most failed non-English domain descriptions copy the prompt's English opening phrase. Cross-perplexity and logit divergence, two diagnostics from the REAP paper, also track production quality, as does the rate of repetition loops; n-gram diversity does not. We close with practical guidance for compressing MoE models for production.
bullets: The study compares REAP expert pruning with REAM expert merging across five web-hosting production tasks and two 30B-parameter MoE models.
At 25% expert removal, REAP preserves 93.6% of Qwen3-30B’s generative quality, versus 62.5% for REAM.
Across 20 matched comparisons, REAP performs significantly better in 16, while REAM does so in 2.
Most quality loss in email generation comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts, and runaway generation—not loss of content.
Cross-perplexity, logit divergence, and repetition-loop rates track production quality; n-gram diversity does not.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates expert compression methods for MoE LLMs, directly relevant to LLM efficiency and memory optimization.
papers.title: Prune, Don't Merge: Expert Compression of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on Multilingual Production Tasks
papers.tldr: On multilingual production tasks, one-shot expert pruning substantially outperforms expert merging for compressing MoE LLMs, mainly by preserving required output formats and behavior.

papers.abstract: External tool calls are a major running cost of an LLM agent, while its training objectives align almost exclusively with task completion. In a step-level diagnosis of Qwen3.5 trajectories at two model sizes on GAIA, a long-horizon tool-use benchmark, we find that most contain removable calls, at a similar rate at both sizes. Some methods add an efficiency reward to the objective to reduce the call count, but introduce problems of their own: the anchor they price calls against is computed from the policy's own rollouts (e.g., the group's shortest correct rollout) and so moves with the policy; training can drift toward a collapsed policy that issues no tool call at all, a degeneracy seen in published reports and in our 27B baseline; and a training run delivers a single operating point, so the user cannot trade efficiency against capability. We present CARE-PO (Controllable Anchored Relative Efficiency Policy Optimization) to mitigate these problems. The efficiency reward prices calls against a reference budget anchored to the task's own difficulty and fixed before training. Injecting a successful trajectory from the training data into each online GRPO rollout group and charging for evidence a trajectory never gathers ease the drift toward a collapsed call count. Shaping the cost curve by an effort tag in the prompt yields an efficiency and a capability operating point from a single training run. On GAIA, five of the six operating points across three model sizes improve on their base model in success rate and call count at once. On four held-out multi-hop benchmarks the result is size-dependent: at 27B and 4B success rate is held or raised at a lower call count, while at 9B both operating points trade success rate for fewer calls. The call count remains well above zero throughout training at all three sizes.
bullets: Tool-call costs are substantial, and many GAIA trajectories contain removable calls across model sizes.
Existing efficiency rewards can drift toward policies that make no tool calls and typically provide only one efficiency–capability setting.
CARE-PO anchors call costs to fixed task difficulty, injects successful trajectories, and penalizes missing evidence to prevent call-collapse.
Prompt effort tags produce multiple efficiency/capability operating points from one training run.
On GAIA, 5 of 6 operating points improve success rate and reduce calls; held-out results vary by model size, with 9B showing a capability–efficiency trade-off.

papers.selection_reason: RL method for controllable tool-call efficiency in LLM agents, reducing inference cost while preserving task capability.
papers.title: CARE-PO: Controllable Tool-Call Efficiency for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: CARE-PO trains LLM agents to reduce unnecessary tool calls while preserving task performance and enabling user-controlled efficiency–capability trade-offs.

papers.abstract: AI agent harnesses play the critical role of providing LLMs with an interface to a computing environment. Recent studies show that AI agents' task-execution accuracy depends mostly on the LLM used, while harness-side variances such as system prompts or tools have minimal impact. Rather, such harness-side variances show a larger impact on the cost of agent executions, achieving cost reductions up to 2.6 times on the same model and task. To further explore these harness-side cost optimization opportunities, we analyze the cost accumulation patterns across various agent traces and identify system opportunities to reduce token use and LLM calls without modifying the model or affecting task accuracy. Based on this analysis, we design Agency, a harness interposition platform that provides a unified abstraction and allows easy and portable implementation of harness-side system optimizations on existing off-the-shelf harnesses such as Claude Code or OpenAI Codex. Using Agency, we implement proof-of-concept optimization techniques based on our analysis and achieve cost reductions up to 35% across various real-world benchmarks on existing harnesses without compromising accuracy.
bullets: Agent harness choices have limited effect on accuracy but can substantially affect execution cost.
The study analyzes agent traces to identify opportunities to reduce token consumption and LLM calls.
Agency provides a portable interposition layer for implementing optimizations across existing harnesses.
Proof-of-concept optimizations reduce costs by up to 35% on real-world benchmarks without compromising accuracy.

papers.abstract: Wearable Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) enable pervasive Human Activity Recognition (HAR), but traditional Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) suffer from an "arithmetic-latency deadlock" due to dense floating-point MAC operations. While Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer ultra-low power, existing ones face spatial blind spots, rigid neurons, and gradient degradation. To address these, we propose TSFFormer, a purely spiking Fourier Transformer for Green HAR. It introduces two key innovations: (1) a MultiHeadFourier attention that performs frequency-domain global mixing, reducing complexity from \(O(V^2)\) to \(O(V\log V)\), eliminating spatial blind spots, and saving \(\sim\)50% GPU memory; and (2) a dual-compartment Temporal Spiking LIF (TSLIFNode) that utilizes dynamic thresholds to adapt to non-stationary rhythms and mitigate gradient degradation. Extensive experiments on 8 public IMU benchmarks demonstrate that TSFFormer surpasses state-of-the-art SNNs and even the classic DeepConvLSTM, achieving a \(\sim\)3\(\times\) faster training speed with an energy footprint of 0.1 pJ. Ablation studies confirm the synergistic effect of our modules, providing a highly accurate, ultra-low-power event-driven paradigm for wearable sensing.
bullets: Uses frequency-domain global mixing to reduce attention complexity from O(V²) to O(V log V) and address spatial blind spots.
Introduces a dual-compartment temporal spiking LIF neuron with dynamic thresholds for non-stationary motion rhythms and improved gradient behavior.
Evaluated on 8 public IMU benchmarks, it outperforms state-of-the-art SNNs and DeepConvLSTM.
The abstract reports approximately 3× faster training, about 50% lower GPU memory use, and a 0.1 pJ energy footprint.
Ablation studies support the complementary effects of the proposed Fourier attention and temporal neuron modules.

papers.abstract: A model that takes over another model's conversation must normally re-read the whole history; a text hand-off shortens the re-read only by dropping content. KV-cache translation instead maps the source's cache into the target's own format, so the target continues from the full context without re-reading it. It works for grouped-query attention (GQA), but open-weights frontier models now cache compressed latents (MLA), sparse-attention indexer keys and fixed-size linear-attention states. We replicate KV-Lingo on a GQA pair and then give, for each of these objects, where to capture and inject it and a mechanism that reaches native quality. We study two hybrid pairs at 16-48B scale in both directions, Kimi-VL-A3B - Kimi-Linear-48B (MLA - MLA + Kimi Delta Attention) and Qwen3.5-27B - Qwen3.8-27B (Gated DeltaNet hybrids), plus a sparse-attention target (Qwen3.8-27B - Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). MLA latents translate with token-wise linear maps; recurrent states are copied with a closed-form correction or synthesised by replaying the target's own recurrence. Exact long-range recall needs token identity: decoding token ids from the source's layer-0 MLA latent raises needle recall from 0.09 to 0.99 at 2-32K and to 0.83-1.00 at 64K, eight times the longest training prompt. The hybrid full-MLA direction is within the paired confidence interval of native quality on every task metric, and same-shape GDN hybrids reach the native level in both directions (apart from 6% refusals inherited from the source), with time to first token 18.7 and 46.8 times shorter than a re-read at 64K tokens. Segment-wise multi-turn transfer stays at the re-prefill level; naive re-translation collapses. On the sparse-attention target, predicted indexer keys recall the needle as well as the target's own keys (one seed). We state as a hypothesis how the recipes transfer to 300B+ hybrid flagships.
bullets: Extends KV-Lingo beyond GQA to MLA latents, recurrent linear-attention states, and sparse-attention indexer keys.
Uses token-wise linear maps for MLA, corrected or replayed recurrences for linear-attention states, and predicted keys for sparse attention.
Across several 16–48B hybrid model pairs, transfers generally reach native or re-prefill quality in both directions.
Decoding token identities from MLA latents restores long-range needle recall, reaching 0.99 at 2–32K tokens and 0.83–1.00 at 64K.
At 64K context, transfer reduces time to first token by 18.7–46.8× versus re-reading; naive repeated translation fails.

papers.selection_reason: KV-cache translation between hybrid-attention LLMs directly targets KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Translating KV Caches Between Hybrid-Attention Language Models: MLA Latents, Linear-Attention States and Sparse-Attention Indexers

papers.abstract: Training Gaussian processes (GPs) at large scale is computationally challenging because evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. We develop a scalable low-rank GP training approach that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction. The resulting objective and its analytic gradients can be evaluated using low-rank factors, diagonal quantities, and small dense matrices, without forming the full kernel matrix or its derivatives. The complete training procedure is implemented in single precision and evaluated on nine large-scale regression datasets. Across these problems, the method reaches the reference predictive accuracy while substantially reducing training time, although the required approximation rank varies across datasets. We also study the numerical behavior of the full-kernel predictive solve and show that single precision can become limiting for ill-conditioned problems. Finally, we investigate further reducing selected matrix operations to fp16 or TF32. These lower-precision variants provide only modest additional speedups and can become unreliable when the reduced system is poorly conditioned.
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of dense kernel matrices in large-scale GP training.
Combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction.
Computes the objective and analytic gradients using low-rank factors, diagonal terms, and small dense matrices.
On nine large-scale regression datasets, it substantially reduces training time while reaching reference predictive accuracy; the needed rank varies.
FP16/TF32 offer modest extra speedups but may be unreliable for poorly conditioned reduced systems; single precision can also limit predictive solves.

papers.abstract: Generating text-bearing images requires coherent scenes and accurate characters. Large text-to-image models improve both capabilities through repeated denoising, at substantial sampling cost. Few-step distillation reduces this cost but requires the student to organize scenes and refine glyphs within a short trajectory. We present a four-step distillation framework combining local response regularization with teacher-guided text training. Built on distribution matching, the framework distills the GLM-Image DiT while retaining its autoregressive visual prior, glyph encoder, and VAE. A path-length penalty promotes consistent local responses of the conditional denoising field. Progressive training combines synthetic strings with teacher-generated imagery to preserve character accuracy and scene-integrated typography. The student achieves GenEval Overall 0.84 and CVTG-2K word accuracy 0.5045, compared with 0.81 and 0.1690 for four-step TDM. A coefficient study favors $10^{-5}$, and Qwen-Image experiments show additional gains from response regularization and text supervision. Single-image inference takes 1.742 s, compared with 5.818 s for the teacher, yielding a $3.34\times$ speedup at the same 40 GB GPU memory requirement.
bullets: Addresses the high sampling cost of large text-to-image models and the difficulty of refining typography in few-step generation.
Combines distribution matching, local response regularization, and teacher-guided text training.
Retains the GLM-Image DiT’s autoregressive visual prior, glyph encoder, and VAE.
Reports GenEval Overall 0.84 and CVTG-2K word accuracy 0.5045, outperforming four-step TDM results in the abstract.
Reduces single-image inference time to 1.742 s versus 5.818 s for the teacher, a reported 3.34× speedup at the same 40 GB memory requirement.

papers.title: Four-Step Text-Bearing Image Generation via Distillation with Local Response Regularization and Teacher-Guided Training

papers.abstract: In this work, we study whether frontier agents can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from $6.82\times$ with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to $19.86\times$. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, our Infrathon framework provides resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/InfrathonX/Infrathon
bullets: Introduces a benchmark covering diverse, multi-level, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks.
Evaluates six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours.
Further improvements occurred in 135 of 150 runs during the second half of evaluation, showing shorter tests may miss progress.
Agents discovered solutions surpassing human-designed baselines; Claude Opus 5.5 improved mean KV-cache compression from 6.82× to 19.86× on one task.
Trajectory analysis highlights task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained optimization.

papers.abstract: Sequence-to-function models such as AlphaGenome and Borzoi read up to a megabase of DNA and score a genetic variant by comparing their predictions for the reference and alternate sequences. Insertions and deletions (indels) are costly to score, because an indel usually shifts the unchanged DNA after it onto a different pooling grid, which prevents direct reuse of the reference's encoder activations. The AlphaGenome Atlas scored more than 100 million indels with three full model passes each, although the DNA after an indel matches the reference shifted by the indel's length. We present ShiftCache, an exact reuse system that encodes each shifted reference once and shares it among all variants scored in the same window with the same shift. ShiftCache copies every encoder output a variant can reuse and recomputes the rest in batched tiles. On held-out AlphaGenome windows shared by many indels, in strict fp32 on one A6000, ShiftCache is 3.5 to 6.5$\times$ faster than deduplicated dense execution and 1.6 to 2.7$\times$ faster than our adaptation of layer-by-layer reuse to indels. It is 3.5 to 4.1$\times$ faster than dense reimplementations of two published analyses with Borzoi and AlphaGenome, and 2.6$\times$ faster than dense execution with Enformer. Scoring each variant in its own centered 131 kb window makes ShiftCache only 1.36$\times$ faster than deduplicated dense execution, and highly diverse insertion lengths or many dispersed edits can make it slower than layer-by-layer reuse or dense execution. For encoders that meet our conditions, ShiftCache computes the same predictions as dense execution in exact arithmetic. On an A6000, every checked output of the default AlphaGenome and Borzoi runs matches dense execution within an absolute and relative tolerance of $10^{-5}$. With larger tile batches, with Enformer or on an H100, a small fraction of values exceeds this tolerance.
bullets: Indels disrupt pooling-grid alignment, making conventional reuse of reference encodings difficult and costly.
ShiftCache encodes each shifted reference once, shares it across variants with the same shift, and recomputes only non-reusable outputs in batched tiles.
On shared AlphaGenome windows, it is 3.5–6.5× faster than deduplicated dense execution and 1.6–2.7× faster than layer-by-layer reuse.
It also outperforms dense Borzoi, AlphaGenome, and Enformer analyses by 3.5–4.1×, 3.5–4.1×, and 2.6×, respectively.
Speedups are smaller for independently centered windows or diverse/dispersed edits; outputs generally match dense execution within 1e-5 tolerance, with occasional deviations under other settings.

papers.abstract: Quantization reduces LLM deployment costs, but effective strategies must balance model quality and storage. LLM-driven search can automate strategy design through repeated proposal and evaluation. This process must identify useful strategies within a limited evaluation budget. The key challenge is that \textit{actual quantization is expensive, while inexpensive proxies may not reflect quantized-model performance.} To address this challenge, we present AutoQS, an \textbf{Auto}mated \textbf{Q}uantization \textbf{S}trategy Design with LLMs. AutoQS keeps weight precision fixed and searches group-size allocations across layers and operators under deployment constraints. Evaluation history guides coordinated LLM proposals, while deterministic validation ensures compatible allocations. An inexpensive quality proxy evaluates candidates, and an candidate repository retains alternative allocations to inform subsequent proposals. Periodic actual quantization complements these proxy evaluations with measured quality and checkpoint storage, providing feedback for further search within the evaluation budget. Experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show that AutoQS improves seven-task average accuracy over uniform-group GPTQ and AWQ by 0.70 and 1.12 percentage points, respectively, at four-bit weight precision.
bullets: Addresses the costly, potentially unreliable evaluation of quantization strategies.
Searches layer- and operator-specific group-size allocations while keeping weight precision fixed.
Uses evaluation history, deterministic validation, and a repository of alternative candidates to guide proposals.
Combines inexpensive proxy scoring with periodic actual quantization and checkpoint storage.
On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, improves seven-task average accuracy by 0.70 points over uniform-group GPTQ and 1.12 points over AWQ.

Every K = 5 search iterations, the procedure selects the latest eligible candidate in the current five-iteration window for fresh GPTQ quantization. This target selection is independent of the proxy-score ordering. The resulting checkpoint is evaluated for task accuracy and storage, providing measured outcomes for subsequent policy selection.

papers.abstract: Feature subsampling is used to accelerate gradient-boosted trees, yet standard approaches fix the feature count in advance and largely ignore the split-gain evidence accumulated during training. We introduce CRAFT-GBM (Confidence-Ranked Adaptive Feature Tracking), a native LightGBM extension that uses this evidence to adapt which---and, by default, how many---features are searched each boosting round. CRAFT-GBM transforms root-split gains into bounded observations and constructs joint time-uniform bounds valid under adaptive, non-stationary training histories. In its default endogenous mode, after initialization, CRAFT-GBM retains exactly the features that cannot yet be ruled out as best, letting the selected feature-set size $K_t$ emerge from training history rather than a pre-specified fraction. With probability at least $1-δ$, every feature with the largest expected gain is retained jointly across all rounds after initialization. When a feature fraction $f$ is specified instead, CRAFT-GBM ranks features by their interval point estimates and provides an approximate top-$K$ guarantee for feature budget $K_f$. We implement CRAFT-GBM within LightGBM while preserving its native feature-bundling representation, and evaluate it across 14 public and synthetic dataset families and four noise-augmented settings. In the fully endogenous setting, CRAFT-GBM reduces per-fit training time by 39.74\% with 1.04\% lower test loss in the geometric mean across all 18 RQ1 experiments. Under pre-specified feature fraction $f$, Exogenous CRAFT-GBM also yields aggregate training-time reductions up to 13.52 percentage points larger than random feature subsampling, with no increase in aggregate test loss relative to full-feature LightGBM. Accumulated training evidence can thus support adaptive feature search with statistical guarantees while retaining the practical advantages of native gradient boosting.
bullets: Addresses fixed feature-count subsampling that overlooks split-gain evidence accumulated during training.
Uses time-uniform confidence bounds on root-split gains to track features that may still be best under adaptive, non-stationary histories.
Its default endogenous mode determines the number of searched features from training history; a specified-fraction mode supports approximate top-K selection.
Implemented as a native LightGBM extension while preserving feature bundling.

Across 18 experiments, endogenous CRAFT-GBM reduced geometric-mean training time by 39.74% with 1.04% lower test loss; the fraction-controlled mode improved time savings over random subsampling without increasing aggregate test loss versus full-feature LightGBM.

figures.caption: Figure 2: At f = 0.10, Exogenous CRAFT-GBM substantially reduces training time with essentially unchanged aggregate test loss. Shaded bands show pointwise 95% dataset-resampling intervals, reflecting sensitivity to the composition of the 14 dataset families. At f = 0.10, Exogenous CRAFT-GBM reduces aggregate training time by 62.74% with essentially unchanged test loss (−0.04%). Random subsampling by LightGBM-Fixed saves 49.22% time but raises loss by 4.60%. Thus CRAFT-GBM delivers 13.52 percentage points more time reduction without the aggregate loss increase seen with LightGBM-Fixed. Greedy mean-gain ranking (Mean ablation) and exposure balancing of features (Exposure ablation) save the same training time (63.83% and 64.71%), but incur greater test loss especially at smaller feature fractions (12.69% and 5.71% more test loss at f = 0.10). This contrast is consistent with the expected benefit of combining gain evidence with uncertainty in CRAFT-GBM, especially when the feature budget Kf is restrictive.

Figure 1: Endogenous CRAFT-GBM reduces training time in 15 of the 16 displayed experiments. Endogenous CRAFT-GBM reduces aggregate training time by 40.36% and test loss by 1.10%. LightGBM-Fixed saves 30.65% of training time and has the same aggregate loss change, so endogenous CRAFT-GBM delivers a further 9.70 percentage points of time reduction. Endogenous CRAFT-GBM improves both outcomes in 11/16 experiments, compared with 8/16 for random LightGBM-Fixed. Across almost all datasets, XGBoost and CatBoost are slower and incur higher test loss in some datasets.

papers.abstract: Wearables, mobile devices, and IoT platforms generate multimodal time-series data continuously and at scale, making efficient storage and transfer a primary concern. The same recordings are reused after collection by many downstream models, often at different temporal resolutions, so a compressed representation should be small, useful across resolutions, and produced at a bit rate known in advance. Prior work meets parts of this: symbolic and error-bounded compressors reconstruct accurately but fix resolution at compression time, learned codecs target one signal domain, and discrete tokenizers reconstruct without accounting for rate. We introduce CHORD, a coarse-to-fine compressor for heterogeneous multimodal time series. A residual cascade orders each payload from broad to fine temporal scales and synthesizes corrections through learned shapelet-inspired atoms. A shared pathway supplies a reusable synthesis basis across modalities, while private pathways retain capacity for sensor-specific morphology. Finite scalar quantization fixes the bit width of every modality and scale, so payload size is known before encoding, and scale dropout trains each coarse-to-fine prefix to be a valid reconstruction operating point. Across seven wearable-sensing and forecasting benchmarks, CHORD stays within 0.62 points of uncompressed classification accuracy on average at the 8x target, the smallest gap of any compressed method, with all resolutions decoded from one payload.
bullets: Targets efficient storage and transfer for wearable, mobile, and IoT time-series data reused by downstream models.
Uses a coarse-to-fine residual cascade with learned shapelet-inspired atoms to encode broad-to-fine temporal information.
Combines shared synthesis pathways across modalities with private pathways for sensor-specific patterns.
Finite scalar quantization fixes bit width and payload size, while scale dropout makes each prefix a valid reconstruction point.
Across seven benchmarks, it stayed within 0.62 accuracy points of uncompressed classification at 8× compression, with all resolutions decoded from one payload.
