papers.abstract: Retinal disease monitoring with optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) relies on segmentation of vessels and the foveal avascular zone (FAZ). Promptable models such as SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) allow click-based refinement, but without adaptation SEEM segments thin vessels poorly and needs many clicks. Fully fine-tuning its 342 million parameters on a few hundred images is costly and risks overfitting, and parameter-efficient methods such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) usually adapt only the encoder. Yet SEEM reads every candidate mask from one feature map at quarter resolution, too coarse for vessels one to three pixels wide. This study introduces the Read-out Basis Adapter (RBA), whose read-out branch generates 32 image-specific basis maps at half resolution. Each candidate accesses them through its own vector and a zero-initialised projection, so the model starts exactly as SEEM. The encoder branch, a standard rank-1 LoRA, supplies the information needed to tell arteries from veins. RBA adds 0.47 million trainable parameters. Under simulated error-driven clicks, with the ground truth used only to place them, RBA outperforms LoRA, Conv-LoRA andAdaptFormer on OCTA-500 3mmlarge vessels. Averaged over three seeds, it reaches an intersection over union (IoU) of 85.16% and a Dice score of 91.93%, 2.90 and 1.72 percentage points above Conv-LoRA. On the 6 mm subset, one run gives margins of 4.35 and 2.76 points. The gain extends to arteries, veins and ROSE-O but not to the FAZ. In SEEM, adaptation capacity pays more at the mask read-out than in the encoder.
bullets: SEEM’s quarter-resolution mask feature map is too coarse for 1–3-pixel vessels and requires many corrective clicks without adaptation.
RBA generates 32 image-specific basis maps at half resolution, with candidate-specific access through a zero-initialized projection so it initially matches SEEM.
A rank-1 LoRA encoder branch helps distinguish arteries from veins; the full adapter adds 0.47 million trainable parameters.
With simulated error-driven clicks, RBA achieves 85.16% IoU and 91.93% Dice on OCTA-500 3 mm large vessels, outperforming Conv-LoRA by 2.90 and 1.72 points.
Improvements extend to arteries, veins, and ROSE-O, but not the FAZ; results suggest adaptation is more valuable in mask read-out than in the encoder.

papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) produce explicit chains of thought to improve transparency, but they frequently overthink, generating long yet inefficient reasoning chains that inflate computational costs and risk introducing errors. While numerous reinforcement learning methods struggle to penalize verbosity to achieve conciseness, they typically apply the penalty uniformly across lengthy sequences, which leads to credit confounding, that is, the failure to distinguish essential reasoning steps from superfluous ones. In this paper, we study a measurable proxy for this confounding: high-entropy tokens that often coincide with surface transition points where reasoning re-enters verification. Based on this insight, we propose Adaptive Entropy-Sparing (AES), which selectively spares high-entropy tokens that occur before an efficient in-group reference, while penalizing overlength high-entropy suffix tokens associated with superfluous branching. Our AES thereby navigates the suppression-exploration trade-off, reducing overthinking while preserving average reasoning accuracy. We also present an entropy-length model that motivates why local uncertainty can serve as a proxy for future reasoning cost. Across eight reasoning benchmarks, AES reduces reasoning length by up to 52.9% while increasing mean accuracy by up to 3.8% over the base models, consistently outperforming existing efficiency-oriented methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/MobiusDai/AES.
bullets: Addresses overthinking in large reasoning models, where uniformly penalizing long outputs can suppress essential reasoning steps.
Uses high-entropy tokens as a proxy for reasoning transitions and future computational cost.
Spares high-entropy tokens before efficient in-group references, while penalizing high-entropy suffixes linked to unnecessary branching.
Across eight reasoning benchmarks, reduces reasoning length by up to 52.9% and increases mean accuracy by up to 3.8% over base models.
Scope: targets verbosity and efficiency in explicit reasoning chains; the abstract does not specify broader generalization beyond the evaluated benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation~(DMD) enables strong few-step diffusion generation by matching the student distribution to a pretrained teacher. Existing improvements to DMD often augment its supervision or modify its optimization machinery. We ask a complementary question: \emph{can DMD diagnose its own updates using signals already produced during training?} DMD inherently computes the discrepancy between a pretrained teacher and a fake model tracking the student distribution, but conventionally uses it primarily to determine the distribution matching direction. We find that the magnitude of this teacher--fake disagreement provides additional diagnostic information. Across extensive experiments, large disagreement in the high-noise regime consistently coincides with substantially higher-energy DMD updates. This reveals a dual role of disagreement: it determines not only \emph{where} the student should move, but also provides an intrinsic signal of \emph{how aggressively} the update should be applied. Based on this observation, we introduce Disagreement-Aware Distribution Matching Distillation (DA-DMD), which activates only in the high-noise regime and continuously modulates the update strength according to teacher--fake disagreement. DA-DMD reuses quantities already available during DMD training and requires no additional model, evaluator, or inference-time modification. We show that it exactly recovers vanilla DMD outside the selected region, reduces update energy only through selected samples, and exhibits redescending influence under extreme disagreement. Across multiple diffusion backbones, DA-DMD consistently improves few-step generation at the same inference cost. On SD3.5-L, DA-DMD improves HPSv2 from $28.23$ to $30.93$, while achieving a $64.4\%$ average win rate over DMD2.
bullets: DMD disagreement indicates both the direction and appropriate aggressiveness of student updates.
Large high-noise disagreement is associated with substantially higher-energy DMD updates.
DA-DMD continuously modulates update strength using signals already available during DMD training.
It leaves vanilla DMD unchanged outside the selected high-noise region and requires no extra model or inference-time changes.
Across multiple backbones, it improves generation at the same inference cost; on SD3.5-L, HPSv2 rises from 28.23 to 30.93.],

papers.abstract: Sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM query a learned world model thousands of times per control step, so low-bit world models are an obvious way to make model-based control cheaper on a robot. With round-to-nearest activation quantization and no calibration, we find that planning can collapse, by up to 100 points of success, while the world model's latent one-step prediction error stays no larger than that of a stochastic rounding scheme that plans well. At the same bit width, what decides the outcome is not the size of the rounding error but whether it persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Round-to-nearest leaves an error that persists, and an iterating planner drifts toward the candidates that this error favors; in TD-MPC2, holding the same dither fixed within a step or an episode brings the drift back. Dither shared by all candidates and redrawn at every iteration removes most of the damage at the same bit width and without training: at least half of it in all 19 affected Meta-World cells (task $\times$ bit width) of TD-MPC2 (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2. Captured as CUDA graphs on an Ampere GPU, a W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model runs its planning rollouts 1.9-3.3$\times$ and the whole planning step 1.3-1.5$\times$ faster than FP32, though not faster than BF16 with pre-converted weights; shared dither adds at most 2.3% latency. In TD-MPC2, block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage and MXFP4 part of it, which ties the failure to coarse grids with a shared scale. Hypotheses, thresholds and analysis code were fixed before the data that test them, and the hypotheses that failed are reported.
bullets: Round-to-nearest activation quantization can severely degrade planning despite one-step prediction error comparable to stochastic rounding.
The key issue is error persistence and sharing across planner candidates, not simply rounding-error magnitude.
Redrawing common dither each planner iteration removes most of the degradation without retraining across tested TD-MPC2 and DINO-WM settings.
An W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model speeds planning rollouts by 1.9–3.3× and full planning steps by 1.3–1.5× versus FP32; dither adds at most 2.3% latency.
Block-scaled NVFP4 largely avoids the problem, while fixed dither within a step or episode restores planner drift.

papers.abstract: LLM inference has two phases with different bottlenecks: LLM prefill runs once per request and is compute-intensive. Decoding repeats for every output token and is limited by memory bandwidth. To address the challenges associated with this issue, different solutions have been proposed. All of these solutions use the same model for both prefill and decode phases. We propose BridgeKV, which uses a larger model for prefill and a smaller model of the same family for decoding. A lightweight KV-stitching module translates the larger model's prompt cache into the smaller model's cache layout. It handles differences in cache shape and representation through learned local layer mixing and separate nonlinear maps for keys and values. With both models frozen, we train the module to align their caches and make the smaller model follow the larger model's next-token predictions. A second training stage adds low-rank adapters when further task adaptation is needed. Across six model pairs and five datasets, BridgeKV outperforms fine-tuned small-model baselines with matched trainable parameter budgets in all 30 settings. It closes up to 80% of the quality gap to using the larger model for both phases. On one A40 GPU, Llama-3.1-Instruct-8B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B achieves 3.0X faster requests than the larger model alone, with latency close to the smaller model alone. BridgeKV can improve the hardware and system solutions that separate prefill and decode phases across GPUs. A separate serving simulation models request arrivals, queues, and cache transfer. For Llama-3.1-Instruct-70B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B, it predicts up to 33.86X faster requests and 27.5X lower energy use than using the larger model for both prefill and decode phases.
bullets: Targets the compute-heavy prefill phase and memory-bandwidth-limited decoding phase with different model sizes.
Uses a lightweight KV-stitching module with local layer mixing and separate nonlinear key/value mappings to reconcile cache differences.
Trains the translation module with both models frozen; optional low-rank adapters support further task adaptation.
Across six model pairs and five datasets, it outperformed matched-budget fine-tuned small-model baselines in all 30 settings and closed up to 80% of the quality gap to the large model.
Reported serving gains include 3.0× faster requests for an 8B-to-1B pair and simulated gains up to 33.86× faster with 27.5% lower energy for a 70B-to-1B pair.

papers.selection_reason: KV cache translation for heterogeneous prefill/decode; directly targets memory efficiency in LLM inference.
papers.title: BridgeKV: Large-Model Prefill and Small-Model Decoding for LLM Inference via KV Cache Translation
papers.tldr: BridgeKV accelerates LLM serving by using a large model for prompt prefill and a small same-family model for decoding, translating the large model’s KV cache between them.

papers.abstract: Energy claims for efficient neural networks are often inferred from operation counts. We report direct GPU energy measurements on two workloads that batch very differently, recurrent policies in GPU-vectorised multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) and mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, and ask one question of both: can the rows of a batch be made to share computation, across the batch and over time, at a measured saving? On recurrent policies the answer so far is no. Shared activity patterns exist but rarely last one step, masking a frozen policy fails, and trained-in masks succeed only because a fixed mask is equivalent to a narrow GRU, at 11x the energy of a small dense policy in our implementation. Test-time steering adds nothing beyond re-picking on either workload. On MoE models the answer is yes, and granularity decides how much: on Qwen3-30B-A3B, batch-aware routing reads 25-31% fewer expert weights within KL 0.05, with benchmark changes within noise at 500 items, and uses 12-18% less energy per token on a fused forward. We also introduce persistence-aware OEA, a one-parameter rule that keeps the batch-aware cut with about 40% fewer new experts per step than native routing at batch 32-64, though its energy has not yet been measured. These are pilot measurements on one GPU type, and we state their limits.
bullets: The study tests whether batch rows can share computation across examples and over time, using direct GPU energy measurements rather than operation counts.
For recurrent MARL policies, shared patterns are too short-lived; masking and test-time steering do not provide useful savings, while trained-in masks reduce the model to a narrow GRU.
For Qwen3-30B-A3B, batch-aware MoE routing reads 25–31% fewer expert weights within KL 0.05 and reduces fused-forward energy per token by 12–18%.
Persistence-aware OEA achieves about 40% fewer new experts per step than native routing at batch sizes 32–64, but its energy impact remains unmeasured.
Results are pilot measurements on one GPU type and are limited to the studied workloads and implementation.

papers.abstract: Ray Tracing enables rendering capabilities that are difficult to achieve with rasterization-based approaches such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). However, the training cost of Gaussian-based ray tracing (GRT) is much higher than that of 3DGS. In this paper, we study how ray tracing using Gaussians executes on GPUs and show that a considerable fraction of the training cost arises from how the computation is organized. We develop FastGRT, which decouples ray traversal from blending and reuses work done in the forward pass for the backward pass. FastGRT further incorporates optimizations such as fast gradient accumulation and a hybrid BVH update strategy to tackle other major bottlenecks in the training pipeline. We implement FastGRT in Vulkan. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first Vulkan-based GRT implementation that supports both training and rendering. Compared to 3DGRT, FastGRT improves training time by 1.9$\times$ to 4.97$\times$, while preserving the original rendering formulation. Our code is open source.
bullets: 3D Gaussian ray tracing offers capabilities beyond rasterization-based 3D Gaussian Splatting but has substantially higher training costs.
FastGRT decouples ray traversal from blending and reuses forward-pass computations during backpropagation.
It adds fast gradient accumulation and a hybrid BVH update strategy to address other training bottlenecks.
Implemented in Vulkan, FastGRT supports both training and rendering while preserving the original rendering formulation.
The reported training speedup over 3DGRT is 1.9× to 4.97×; the code is open source.

papers.abstract: As long-video understanding gains increasing attention, augmented reality (AR) devices are emerging as a compelling deployment platform. However, egocentric videos exhibit significant temporal redundancy, imposing substantial memory and computational burdens on resource-constrained AR hardware. To address this challenge, we introduce UTOPI, a plug-and-play pre-compression module designed specifically for egocentric long videos on AR platforms. First, we leverage user motion signals to estimate inter-frame overlap and propose a viewpoint-shift-invariant pruning algorithm. Second, we exploit eye-tracking sensors to identify user fixations, enabling the separation of attended foreground content from background and its preferential retention via a fine-tuned neural network-based adjustment mechanism. Across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, UTOPI achieves up to 95% compression while preserving performance. Code and project page are available at https://sai-lab-nyu.github.io/utopi/.
bullets: Addresses the memory and computation costs of temporally redundant egocentric videos on resource-constrained AR hardware.
Uses user motion to estimate inter-frame overlap and perform viewpoint-shift-invariant token pruning.
Uses eye tracking to distinguish attended foreground content from background and preferentially retain it.
Works as a plug-and-play pre-compression module across multiple benchmarks and model backbones.
Achieves up to 95% compression while preserving performance, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly run on workstations with a few consumer GPUs, where large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models keep part of their experts in host memory. With existing CPU-GPU engines, these agents get fast prefill or fast decode, not both: llama.cpp's expert cache skips forward passes of more than 32 tokens to keep the experts of decode cached, so an agent waits 2.1-2.8 s after each tool output, whereas its default layer placement shortens this wait but is 1.5-1.6$\times$ slower in decode. Our key insight is that a short prefill touches too many distinct experts to upload, yet sends 84% of its expert activations (routes) to a stable set of experts that fits in GPU memory. We present Ostinato, a CPU-GPU MoE inference engine that computes these experts on the GPUs in every forward pass without changing what the model computes. Short prefills split their routes, leaving fewer than one of a token's six routed experts per layer to the CPU; long prefills upload each distinct cold expert once; and each decode step runs as one fixed-shape CUDA graph per GPU. On real coding and customer-service agent sessions with DeepSeek-V4-Flash on four RTX 4090D GPUs, Ostinato is the fastest engine in both phases and finishes every session sooner than all six baselines. Against llama.cpp and KTransformers, it cuts the median wait after a tool output by 22-55% and finishes sessions 1.4-2.5$\times$ sooner.
bullets: Existing CPU-GPU MoE engines trade off fast prefill against fast decode, causing multi-second waits after tool outputs.
Ostinato routes stable, frequently used experts to GPUs while sending only a small remainder to the CPU; long prefills upload each cold expert once.
Each decode step uses a fixed-shape CUDA graph per GPU without changing the model’s computation.
On coding and customer-service sessions, Ostinato was fastest in both phases and completed sessions 1.4–2.5× sooner than llama.cpp and KTransformers.
It reduced median post-tool-output waits by 22–55% against those baselines on four RTX 4090D GPUs.

papers.title: Ostinato: Fast CPU-GPU MoE Inference for Local Agents via Resident Experts in Every Forward Pass
papers.tldr: Ostinato accelerates local MoE agents by keeping frequently routed experts on GPUs during every forward pass, improving both prefill and decode performance.

papers.abstract: Agentic autoregressive video generation combines semantic planning, sequential generation, and visual verification for controllable synthesis. Growing visual histories enlarge the key-value (KV) cache, increasing memory use and attention costs across candidate rollouts. Existing compression methods primarily optimize individual generators without the planner's semantic constraints, risking low priority for states supporting requested attributes or actions. We introduce SemanticKV, a training-free method for semantically aligned KV cache compression. To our knowledge, SemanticKV is the first KV cache compression method for agentic autoregressive video generation that explicitly uses planner-extracted semantic constraints to guide retention. Text cross-attention identifies constraint-related video positions, whose self-attention queries are collected into separate groups. Attention weights are averaged within each group and maximized across groups, giving each cached entry a high score when strongly used by any represented constraint. A single top-k selection retains high-scoring entries under the memory budget, leaving their keys, values, and positions unchanged. For fixed query groups and equal entry costs, this selection minimizes an additive upper bound on worst-group discarded attention. The method operates independently within each candidate without retraining or additional video generations. We evaluate four AR video backbones on three benchmarks for 5-, 30-, and 60-second generation. On Causal Forcing at a compression ratio of 0.7, SemanticKV obtains a VBench Total Score of 84.10, compared with 84.05 for the strongest compressed baseline and 83.99 for Full KV. It achieves a 1.22x speedup over Full KV and reduces KV-cache memory from 6.04 GB to 1.81 GB, a 3.35x reduction.
bullets: Addresses growing KV-cache memory and attention costs from long visual histories and candidate rollouts.
Uses planner-extracted constraints and text cross-attention to group relevant queries, then selects a single top-k set of high-value cache entries.
Training-free, operates independently per candidate, and preserves retained keys, values, and positions without extra video generation.
Across four backbones and three benchmarks, it supports 5-, 30-, and 60-second generation; on Causal Forcing, it reports a 1.22× speedup and 3.35× lower KV-cache memory.
At 0.7 compression on Causal Forcing, it reports a VBench score of 84.10 versus 84.05 for the strongest compressed baseline and 83.99 for Full KV.

papers.selection_reason: Semantic KV cache compression for agentic autoregressive video generation; directly targets KV-cache memory and video generation efficiency.
papers.title: Semantically Aligned KV Cache Compression for Efficient Agentic Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.tldr: SemanticKV compresses KV caches for agentic autoregressive video generation by preserving entries most relevant to planner-specified semantic constraints, reducing memory and improving speed with minimal reported quality change.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training-inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained. Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student-teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair. OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget. Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision. In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods. Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address. To put these findings into practice, we introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget without requiring a full training run for each candidate. Model-specific FP8 recipes preserve training quality while providing capacity for at least $1.93\times$ as many KV-cache tokens as BF16. Combining FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches the same training quality $1.62\times$ sooner than synchronous BF16 training. Code is available at https://github.com/benyucong/train-inference-mismatch-opd
bullets: Quantization, weight staleness, and injected noise introduce mismatch, but OPD quality degrades meaningfully only beyond an empirical mismatch budget.
Mismatch tolerance and quantization sensitivity vary across models and layers, with some layers especially vulnerable to reduced precision.
OPD stays stable under rollout settings that destabilize reinforcement-learning methods.
Weight noise can alter generated prefixes, causing errors that per-token corrections cannot fix.

A lightweight admission check screens rollout configurations; model-specific FP8 recipes support at least 1.93× more KV-cache tokens, while FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches equivalent quality 1.62× sooner than synchronous BF16.

papers.title: How Much Training-Inference Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate?

papers.abstract: Block-diffusion drafters propose a whole block of tokens in one forward pass, and draft trees built from their position-wise marginals increase the expected accepted length of speculative decoding. Every tree node occupies a query row in target verification, so under concurrent serving low-yield branches compete with other requests for verification capacity. Existing tree methods select verified nodes by draft probability under a fixed or cost-selected per-request budget, and thus always retain a prefix of the drafter's ranking. We present D3Tree, which learns which nodes of a block-diffusion draft tree are worth verifying. A tree-size head with 2H+2 parameters predicts each candidate's conditional survival from the draft state, the candidate embedding, and its draft log-probability. Thresholding the product of these scores along parent chains yields an ancestor-closed subtree whose size adapts to each request and decoding round. The head is trained on a frozen drafter with conditional labels on the full candidate tree; an optional joint mode also steers the drafter toward the retained reference path. At serving time, D3Tree verifies whole trees under light load and, under heavy load, allocates one batch-wide node budget by predicted survival, sized to the target's matrix-multiplication tiles. Retained trees share one ancestor-masked target pass, while construction, pruning, and scheduling run on the GPU and overlap with the host. Across six vision-language verifiers and 17 text and multimodal benchmarks, D3Tree is fastest in 70 of 72 load settings, with 3.2-4.0x speedup over autoregressive decoding for one request and 1.3-1.8x at 64 concurrent requests, where fixed-budget trees fall below autoregressive speed. Under a time-varying arrival trace, it has the lowest mean end-to-end latency in every arrival phase.
bullets: Fixed probability-ranked trees waste verification capacity on low-yield branches when requests compete for resources.
D3Tree predicts each candidate’s conditional survival and retains an ancestor-closed subtree with request- and round-adaptive size.
It supports whole-tree verification under light load and batch-wide, tile-aligned node budgeting under heavy load.
Across six vision-language verifiers and 17 benchmarks, it is fastest in 70 of 72 load settings.
Reported speedups are 3.2–4.0× for one request and 1.3–1.8× at 64 concurrent requests; it also achieves the lowest latency across all phases of a time-varying arrival trace.

papers.title: D3Tree: Learning to Prune Block-Diffusion Draft Trees for Efficient Verification

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformer (DiT) models, while having become a powerful backbone for generative synthesis, suffer from high inference cost on generating high-resolution images. Diffusion caching has emerged as a promising acceleration technique to reduce inference cost. However, existing caching strategies fail to accurately identify the varying importance of different computational modules and rarely coordinate cache reusing across the timestep and layer granularities, making it difficult to control error accumulation. To address these limitations, we propose multi-granularity caching (MG-Cache) for DiTs, a novel and fully training-free approach to exploit computational redundancy both on timesteps and Transformer layers. Our core innovation contains a two-stage caching strategy: an offline timestep profiling analysis that identifies redundant timesteps for cache reuse, followed by an adaptive layer-wise caching strategy that combines input stability with importance of each Transformer layer to selectively cache stable Attention and MLP submodules. Extensive experiments on mainstream open-source DiT models validate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving significant acceleration while maintaining high fidelity to the uncached output, with up to a 4.18x acceleration on HunyuanVideo.
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of DiT-based high-resolution image generation.
Coordinates cache reuse across both diffusion timesteps and Transformer layers to limit error accumulation.
Uses offline timestep profiling to identify redundant timesteps for reuse.
Adaptively caches stable Attention and MLP submodules based on input stability and layer importance.
Reports up to 4.18× acceleration on HunyuanVideo while maintaining high output fidelity.

Stage 1 performs a static offline analysis to identify and preserve critical timesteps based on a timestep feature table [M̂t ] constructed from a small batch of calibration dataset. Stage 2 introduces a dynamic layer-wise caching mechanism that computes layer importance scores and input stability to adaptively determine whether to reuse cached features.

papers.abstract: Offloading model state to host memory and streaming layer weights let a single multi-GPU node train large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. GPU memory then becomes a performance budget, shared by resident expert state, retained activations, and execution worksets. The best allocation depends on the expert execution path, batch size, and sequence length. We present OOM (Offload-Optimized MoE), a full-parameter MoE training system that co-designs expert execution and memory allocation. For expert-parallel execution, OOM updates resident experts on their owning GPUs and jointly plans state residency and MoE activation retention according to pipeline dependencies. For local execution, OOM bounds GPU worksets through dependency-aware partitioning; in hybrid models, it also retains attention results on the host to avoid costly recomputation and selectively regenerates layer boundaries through cheaper layers to make room. Calibrated cost models guide joint configuration within GPU and host budgets to minimize step time; OOM selects among the configured paths through short executions. On four H100s, OOM trains with 1M-token contexts, whereas FSDP2, ZeRO-Offload, and MegaTrain exhaust GPU memory at 512K. It also trains a 122B-parameter MoE model, on which all three exhaust host memory. On four 24 GB RTX 4090s, it trains 512K-token contexts and 1,024 1K-token sequences per step without gradient accumulation. Across matched-global-batch comparisons, OOM delivers 1.58x and 4.08x geometric-mean (up to 2.14x and 7.77x) throughput over CPU-offloaded FSDP2 on the two platforms while using the least host memory among the evaluated systems -- as little as 1/3.0 of FSDP2's.
bullets: Targets GPU-memory bottlenecks caused by resident experts, retained activations, and execution worksets during host-offloaded MoE training.
Jointly plans expert residency, activation retention, workset partitioning, recomputation, and host retention across expert-parallel, local, and hybrid execution paths.
Uses calibrated cost models and short trial executions to select configurations that minimize training step time within GPU and host-memory budgets.
On four H100s, supports 1M-token contexts and a 122B-parameter MoE model; on four RTX 4090s, supports 512K-token contexts and 1,024 sequences per step without gradient accumulation.
Achieves 1.58× and 4.08× geometric-mean throughput over CPU-offloaded FSDP2 on the two platforms, while using as little as one-third of its host memory.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, yet their computational and memory demands pose significant challenges for deployment on mobile devices. Data-free quantization (DFQ) enables the compression of ViTs without access to their original training data. Existing DFQ methods often synthesize calibration samples by maximizing the entropy of patch similarity. However, similarity entropy describes the dispersion of similarity values without ensuring that the generated samples cover diverse feature directions, potentially limiting their effectiveness for quantization calibration. To address this limitation, we propose RankQ-ViT, a rank-guided DFQ framework for ViTs. We first observe that patch similarity matrices derived from Gaussian noise tend to have lower ranks than those derived from real images. Motivated by this observation, we introduce a block-aware self-contrastive objective that promotes feature diversity during synthetic data generation without explicitly computing matrix rank at each optimization step. We then select calibration samples based on their rank and semantic consistency and use them for block-wise reconstruction of the quantized model. Experiments on ImageNet, COCO, ModelNet40, and ShapeNet demonstrate the effectiveness of RankQ-ViT across multiple architectures and tasks, particularly under low-bit quantization. The code is available at https://github.com/Runqing-forMost/rankq-vit.git
bullets: Addresses the limited feature-direction diversity of calibration samples generated by similarity-entropy-based DFQ methods.
Uses a block-aware self-contrastive objective to promote feature diversity without explicitly computing matrix rank during optimization.
Selects synthetic calibration samples using rank and semantic consistency, then applies them to block-wise quantized-model reconstruction.
Evaluations on ImageNet, COCO, ModelNet40, and ShapeNet show effectiveness across architectures and tasks, particularly at low bit widths.
Scope: performance depends on synthetic calibration data and is evaluated across the listed vision tasks and architectures.

papers.abstract: Long-context applications, long-lived agents, and multi-agent systems require large language models (LLMs) to process and retain extensive information. In these settings, the KV cache can exceed GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, necessitating offloading to host memory, where CPU-to-GPU transfers can dominate inference latency. While KV cache compression can reduce data movement, query-agnostic compression that guarantees accurate attention for arbitrary queries is extremely challenging, if not impossible. We introduce VerKV, a hybrid approach that provides $(ε, δ)$ guarantees for approximating attention on any given query. VerKV maintains a compact set of query-agnostic pivotal tokens on the GPU, together with a token-level sketch of the full KV cache, while retaining the complete cache in CPU memory. We introduce a novel stochastic sampling procedure, PoissonComp, to select the pivotal tokens. At inference time, our proposed KVFetch algorithm uses the pivotal tokens and the sketch to estimate the relative error of the resulting attention computation. If the estimate satisfies a user-specified $(ε, δ)$ tolerance, inference proceeds without accessing host memory. Otherwise, VerKV performs query-aware retrieval to fetch additional tokens from the CPU, refining the attention computation to meet the required tolerance. Thus, VerKV enables attention with bounded approximation error while minimizing CPU-to-GPU transfers. We show that PoissonComp outperforms state-of-the-art approaches to KV cache compression. Combined with KVFetch, it achieves near-dense performance (90-100% of dense quality at 32K context length, averaged over RULER and LOFT), using Qwen3-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Ministral-3-8B, while reducing the GPU memory footprint by 8-32x and keeping CPU-to-GPU memory fetches within 2-23% of the cache per generated token, depending on the model.
bullets: Targets long-context inference where the KV cache exceeds GPU HBM and host-memory transfers dominate latency.
Keeps query-agnostic pivotal tokens and a token-level sketch on the GPU, while storing the full cache in CPU memory.
Uses PoissonComp for pivotal-token sampling and KVFetch to verify attention error against a user-specified $(ε, δ)$ tolerance.
Fetches additional CPU-resident tokens only when the tolerance cannot be met locally.
Reports 90–100% of dense quality at 32K context, with 8–32× lower GPU memory use and 2–23% cache fetched per generated token across the evaluated models and benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of VERKV. The GPU holds query-agnostic pivotal tokens (deterministic and stochastic) and a sparse attention indexer (sketch), while the full KV cache resides in CPU memory. An error-estimation module uses the pivotal tokens and sketch to decide whether the approximation already meets a user tolerance (ϵ, δ); if not, a query-aware fetch recovers additional tokens from the host so that the final attention is guaranteed to have error (ϵ, δ).

Figure 3. Quality vs. compression rate. Average quality of different compression setups across the RULER and LOFT benchmarks at context lengths of 32K and 128K for three models. We observe that (1) POISSONCOMP(C=KVzip) consistently outperforms KVzip, and (2) VERKV(C=KVzip, A=2-bit sketch) = POISSONCOMP(C=KVzip) + KVFETCH improves upon POISSONCOMP under all settings. (3) Relative to dense attention, quality is better preserved at shorter context lengths for a given compression rate, for the Qwen family compared to Ministral, and on RULER compared to LOFT. In particular, VERKV recovers near-dense quality on RULER-32K across all three models. Our algorithm currently uses a naive 2-bit sketch to bootstrap its estimates; improving sketch accuracy is a promising direction for further quality gains as can be seen with VERKV(C=KVzip, A=perfect sketch) which matches Dense in nearly every setting. Host traffic for these runs is reported per generated token in Table 1 and per forward pass in Table 2.

Figure 7. Decode throughput, time per output token and time to first token vs. batch size in vLLM (Qwen3-4B, RULER-32K and RULER-128K, 16×, δ = 0.05). At 32K, VERKV stays ahead of Dense (offload) at every batch size, and its throughput grows from 13.8 to 20.6 tokens/s at ε0 = 0.05 and from 26.8 to 42.4 tokens/s at ε0 = 0.5, while Dense (offload) is bound by PCIe and stays near 9 tokens/s. The gain from batching is small because the decide kernel saturates shared memory and runs the requests of a batch one after another. At 128K, VERKV at ε0 = 0.05 approaches Dense (offload) as the batch grows, whereas ε0 = 0.5 keeps a 4–5× advantage. Fast KVzip is fastest throughout but loses most of its quality (Table 1).

Figure 6. Quality vs. speed in vLLM. VERKV(C=Fast KVzip, A=2-bit sketch) on Qwen3-4B, RULER-32K at 16×, sweeping ε0 at δ = 0.1 against dense attention with the cache offloaded to host memory. At the default ε0 = 0.05, VERKV decodes 1.6× faster and cuts end-to-end latency by 5 s at near-dense quality; larger ε0 trades a few points of quality for up to 3× throughput, with gains flattening once fetching becomes negligible.

Figure 2. Binary shrinkage. In practice we apply a simpler bound, with λi ∈ {1, ri}. The figure shows the MSE of the denominator estimate for one query row (Qwen3-4B, RULER-32K, 16×) as more tokens of L are switched from λi = 1 to λi = ri, relative to the unbiased estimator. Shrinking a few tokens cuts the MSE nearly in half, while shrinking all of them makes it worse (1.62×); the deployed sketch finds a slightly earlier, shallower minimum than exact weights. See Appendix A.2.

Figure 5. Error adherence of VERKV(C=KVzip) on Qwen3-4B, RULER-32K, 16×, δ = 0.1 (about one million attention decisions per setting). With a perfect sketch, under 1% of decisions exceed ε0, far below δ at every tolerance. The naive 2-bit sketch stays within δ only at ε0 = 0.3, but remains far below the failure rate without fetching. Sketch error, not the certificate, is what limits adherence.

Figure 4. Effect of the tolerance ε0 and failure probability δ. VERKV(C=KVzip, A=2-bit sketch) on Qwen3-4B, RULER-32K, 16×: KV read from host per decode step (a) and score change relative to Dense (b). ε0 controls traffic, which falls about 43× from ε0 = 0.01 to 0.3, while δ changes it by less than 2×. Quality stays within one point of Dense up to ε0 = 0.05, the default (circled), and degrades slightly beyond it.

Figure 8. GPU kernel time per decode step, split by phase (Qwen34B, RULER-32K, 16×, batch size 1, δ = 0.05). Dense (offload) spends almost all of its step fetching the cache over PCIe. VERKV spends most of its step in the decide kernel that computes the certificate and the fetch set, and only 1–37 ms fetching; at the default ε0 = 0.05, fetching takes 8 ms against 107 ms for Dense (offload). Faster decide kernels are therefore the main lever for further speedups.

Figure 9. Host-to-GPU PCIe utilization during decode (Qwen34B, RULER-32K, 16×, batch size 1, δ = 0.05; measured link bandwidth 55.5 GB/s). Dense (offload) saturates the link at 92%, while VERKV uses 2–16% of it (4.4% at the default ε0 = 0.05), leaving bandwidth for other requests or larger contexts.

Table 2. Fetch statistics of VERKV(C=KVzip, 16×, RULER-32K, δ = 0.1). Decisions that fetch: share of decisions (one query head in one layer at one forward pass) that fetch at least one token. KV-head steps that fetch: the same per KV head, after merging the query heads that share it. Tokens per fetch: tokens fetched by a fetching decision, as % of the context. KV read: fetched keys and values plus shortlist keys over all forward passes, as % of the full cache. At the default ε0 = 0.05, three quarters of decisions fetch, yet each fetches only 4–6% of the context and the overall read is 10.8% of the cache. [Top] Detailed statistics for Qwen3-4B [Bottom] 2-bit sketch fetches across models.

Table 1. Quality, GPU-resident memory and host traffic of dense attention, KVzip, Fast KVzip and VERKV on three models. Quality is the mean fraction of dense performance across 18 tasks spanning RULER (multi-key and multi-value needle retrieval, common-word extraction, question answering) and LOFT (NQ, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, QAMPARI, QUEST) at 32K and 128K context (C = Fast KVzip, A = 2-bit sketch, ε0 = 0.05, δ = 0.1). VERKV delivers a score comparable to dense attention, while keeping a low GPU-resident memory and simultaneously fetching a fraction of the full cache per generated token.

papers.selection_reason: KV cache compression with bounded-error attention and reduced CPU-to-GPU transfer for LLM inference.
papers.title: Verify Before You Fetch: Reliable KV Cache Compression for LLM Inference
papers.tldr: VerKV provides error-bounded KV-cache compression that avoids unnecessary CPU-to-GPU transfers while preserving near-dense LLM attention quality.

papers.abstract: High-resolution weather prediction is important for resolving local atmospheric patterns missed by coarse global forecasts. Large pretrained weather backbones have improved global forecasting, but adapting them to produce future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states remains challenging and costly. We formulate this setting as Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD), a task that jointly refines spatial and temporal resolution while predicting future high-resolution trajectories. To this end, we propose a framework that decomposes prediction into spatial and temporal stages using a shared pretrained backbone, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads. For backbone adaptation, we introduce PROLA (PRincipal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), which allocates a fixed low-rank budget between pretrained weights' principal directions and their orthogonal complement. PROLA further rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient signals, improving adaptation without increasing trainable rank. Experiments in the PSWD setting show that PROLA outperforms representative low-rank adaptation baselines. Further experiments across diverse datasets and tasks support the broader applicability of PROLA, showing that its benefits extend beyond the primary weather downscaling setting.
bullets: Addresses predictive spatiotemporal weather downscaling: forecasting future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states.
Uses a shared pretrained backbone with separate spatial and temporal stages, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads.
Introduces PROLA, which splits a fixed low-rank budget between principal weight directions and their orthogonal complement.
Rescales rank-1 optimizer updates according to gradient signals without increasing trainable rank.
Experiments report improvements over representative low-rank adaptation baselines, with benefits also observed across diverse datasets and tasks.

papers.abstract: We evaluate AI agents in an online setting where tasks arrive sequentially and, before running each task, we construct an upper predictive bound on its \emph{time-to-success}---the number of interactions until the task is completed successfully. Under a limited budget, some runs are stopped early, so their time-to-success is unobserved (right-censored), and the correctness of the bound may be unknown. We introduce \emph{\textbf{PR}edictive Bounds for \textbf{O}nline \textbf{B}udget \textbf{E}fficiency} (\texttt{PROBE}), a method for constructing calibrated upper predictive bounds while adaptively allocating a limited budget across agent tasks to reduce the anticipated coverage deficit. Our method calibrates the bounds online using inverse-probability-weighted feedback together with a correction designed to minimize coverage deficit while remaining unbiased. We prove that \texttt{PROBE} provides a coverage guarantee for any finite time horizon while satisfying the budget constraint. Experiments on software engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and instruction following show that \texttt{PROBE} attains a coverage rate closer to the target level with tighter predictive bounds than a calibrated baseline.
bullets: Addresses online agent evaluation when tasks arrive sequentially and early stopping leaves completion times unobserved.
Constructs upper predictive bounds for the number of interactions needed to complete each task successfully.
Uses inverse-probability-weighted feedback and an unbiased correction to reduce anticipated coverage deficit.
Provides finite-horizon coverage guarantees while respecting the budget constraint.
Experiments across software engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and instruction following show coverage closer to target with tighter bounds than a calibrated baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of PROBE framework. For each arriving task (1), the system predicts the required time-to-success or token count (2). After environmental interaction where the agent executes the provided task (3), a budget is allocated for additional execution for agent evaluation (4). The result evaluation step (5) determines whether the task finished on time, leading to either a censored outcome with history-based correction (5a) or an observed outcome with direct trajectory evaluation (5b). Both outcomes are integrated via a coverage-aware update (6) (Theorem 3) consisting of (6a) online calibration to adjust predictive upper bounds (τt+1) and (6b) a budget strategy to optimize future budget allocation (πt+1).

papers.abstract: Activation sparsity can reduce FFN weight traffic during single-user LLM decoding, but active channels must be identified early enough to avoid fetching unused weights. In pretrained SwiGLU models, training-free routing with the native gate performs substantially worse than routing with the up activation at high sparsity. We show that this ordering reverses after sparsity-aware training. Based on this insight, we introduce SGA-Sparse, which converts pretrained SwiGLU LLMs into fixed-budget activation-sparse models by training the existing gate projection directly as a top-k router. SGA-Sparse updates all model parameters end-to-end while preserving the original SwiGLU activation and introducing no auxiliary router parameters. After approximately 30B training tokens, LLaMA models from 1B to 8B achieve uniform per-token 75-85% FFN channel sparsity while remaining within 0.2-2.7 pp of their original dense checkpoints in average zero-shot accuracy. Because post-training quantization degrades sparsity-trained checkpoints, we further study two complementary quantization-aware training (QAT) recipes: continued-QAT largely recovers performance at 4-bit weight quantization, while joint-QAT performs better for the more aggressive sub-4-bit target. To compare activation sparsity with dense low-bit quantization, we translate the sparsity-induced reduction in weight traffic into an equivalent bit-width. Under this unified weight-traffic metric, our 2.5- and 1.5-bit-equivalent models establish a new accuracy-traffic Pareto frontier: the 2.5-bit-equivalent models match dense 3-bit QAT accuracy, while the 1.5-bit-equivalent models approach dense 2-bit models and outperform dense ternary models by 1.3 pp on average. These results establish native-gate training as a practical approach for combining high FFN sparsity with low-bit weights.
bullets: Problem: Native-gate routing performs poorly at high sparsity in pretrained SwiGLU models, and inactive FFN weights must be avoided early to reduce decoding traffic.
Method: End-to-end sparsity-aware training turns the existing gate projection into a fixed-budget top-k router without adding auxiliary router parameters or changing the SwiGLU activation.
Result: After approximately 30B tokens, 1B–8B LLaMA models retain average zero-shot accuracy within 0.2–2.7 percentage points of dense checkpoints at 75–85% sparsity.
Quantization: Continued-QAT helps recover accuracy at 4-bit weights, while joint-QAT is more effective below 4 bits.
Contribution: Under a unified weight-traffic metric, the approach reaches 2.5- and 1.5-bit-equivalent trade-offs, matching dense 3-bit QAT and approaching dense 2-bit performance.

papers.selection_reason: Improves LLM inference efficiency via native-gate activation sparsity and low-bit quantization.
papers.title: SGA-Sparse: Training Native SwiGLU Gates for Activation-Sparse and Low-Bit LLMs
papers.tldr: SGA-Sparse trains SwiGLU’s native gate into a top-k router, enabling 75–85% FFN activation sparsity with near-original accuracy and strong low-bit weight-traffic efficiency.

papers.abstract: We study prompted chain-of-thought (CoT) with self-consistency (SC), i.e. sampling N traces and plurality-voting, on small language models, a regime where per-query compute budgets are tight yet SC is commonly applied with a fixed sample budget inherited from large-model practice, regardless of instance difficulty. Across two model families (Qwen-2.5-0.5B, Gemma-3-1B) at FP16 and MLX-Q4 (4-bit quantisation in Apple's MLX framework), on GSM8K and MATH-500, we run 8 per-task and 4 task-pooled experiments at n=200-400 with 1,000x paired-bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs). Our first result is an upper bound: an oracle gate deciding per prompt whether to invoke SC reaches 109-174% of always-SC's accuracy at 23-30% of its compute in all 12/12 cases, so at N=5 always-SC is dominated everywhere on our grid. That margin is exactly the rate at which SC flips correct greedy answers to wrong, here 3-10.5% of prompts, which on Qwen-Q4 x MATH-500 exceeds the wrong-to-right rate and leaves always-SC 3 pt worse than always-greedy. Our second result is a deployable approximation: a gate over greedy-pass signals skips 45-99% of SC calls, with bootstrap CI half-widths under 5 pt, removing 36-79% of always-SC compute. Accuracy retention at those operating points has point estimates of 98.1-98.8%, which we report as point estimates because their CIs are wide (lower bounds 76-86%) over an SC accuracy of only 15-36%. The evidence covers N=5 on two <=1B families and two math benchmarks, which is the scope we claim. Code is available at https://github.com/heywanrong/SiftSC.
bullets: Across Qwen-2.5-0.5B and Gemma-3-1B on GSM8K and MATH-500, always using self-consistency with N=5 was dominated by an oracle that selectively invoked it.
Self-consistency flipped correct greedy answers to wrong on 3–10.5% of prompts; on Qwen-Q4/MATH-500, it made accuracy 3 points worse than greedy decoding.
A deployable gate using greedy-pass signals skipped 45–99% of self-consistency calls and reduced compute by 36–79% versus always using it.
Gated accuracy point estimates retained 98.1–98.8% of always-self-consistency accuracy, though confidence intervals were wide.
Results are scoped to N=5, two sub-billion-parameter model families, two math benchmarks, and FP16/MLX-Q4 inference.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient image-to-video transfer adapts frozen image foundation models to video via lightweight trainable adapters. Existing methods insert the same adapter at every transformer layer, implicitly assuming all layers require equal temporal modeling. A layer-wise sensitivity analysis across four video-native model families and two pretraining paradigms reveals that this assumption is wrong: temporal sensitivity increases with depth, and the pretraining paradigm determines its growth profile. Vision-only models exhibit a gradual rise, while vision-language models show early suppression followed by late recovery. This finding motivates STRAP, a training-free adapter placement rule that derives a spatial-to-temporal transition boundary from a paradigm-matched video model. Spatial adapters are assigned before this boundary and temporal adapters after it, without modifying the adapter architecture itself. On four fine-grained action recognition benchmarks, STRAP improves accuracy by up to 11.8% over uniform placement, reduces trainable parameters by 29 to 48%, and lowers inference time by up to 10%. On standard benchmarks, it matches accuracy with fewer parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/th-nesh/STRAP.
bullets: Temporal sensitivity generally increases with transformer depth, but its pattern depends on the model’s pretraining paradigm.
Vision-only models show a gradual sensitivity increase; vision-language models show early suppression followed by late recovery.
STRAP is a training-free placement rule that derives a spatial-to-temporal transition boundary from a paradigm-matched video model.
Across four fine-grained action-recognition benchmarks, it improves accuracy by up to 11.8%, reduces trainable parameters by 29–48%, and lowers inference time by up to 10%.
On standard benchmarks, STRAP matches accuracy with fewer parameters.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes Graphene, a lightweight image super-resolution architecture with two complementary feature refinement mechanisms: Ising-model-inspired local feature refinement using an Ising Refinement Block (IRB) and stage-history-based feature refinement using a History Attention (HistAttn) module. The IRB reuses attention output features and pre-softmax attention logits to construct signed pairwise token couplings within each local window, applies unrolled mean-field updates, and refines features through a gated residual correction. These signed couplings allow alignment and opposition between latent spins to modulate local feature refinement. HistAttn attends over the current stage output and earlier representations at the same token position and adaptively blends the current stage output with a history-weighted feature aggregate without adding spatial pairwise attention. On Urban100 at $\times4$, Graphene and Graphene-light improve over IET and IET-light by 0.24 dB and 0.38 dB, respectively, with 34.3%/13.7% fewer parameters, 44.8%/44.4% fewer FLOPs, 83.9%/95.9% lower latency, and 63.7%/92.0% lower peak memory. Real-world SR comparisons further show that Graphene recovers fine details and preserves textures across diverse degradations. Code and reference checkpoints are available at https://github.com/skethz/Graphene
bullets: Targets efficient image super-resolution while preserving fine textures and details.
Uses an Ising Refinement Block with signed local token couplings and unrolled mean-field updates for gated feature refinement.
Uses History Attention to blend current features with earlier stage representations without spatial pairwise attention.
On Urban100 at ×4, it improves over IET/IET-light by 0.24/0.38 dB while substantially reducing parameters, FLOPs, latency, and peak memory.
Real-world comparisons indicate improved detail recovery and texture preservation across diverse degradations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of Graphene. Top: Given an LR input, Graphene applies shallow feature extraction with a convolutional stem, deep feature extraction through six Graphene stages, each containing six Graphene Blocks (GBLKs), followed by a trunk convolution, and HR reconstruction with a PixelShuffle head (Shi et al., 2016) and a long residual connection. Bottom-left: Each GBLK applies LayerNorm, PSA (Zhou et al., 2023), an Ising Refinement Block (IRB), and a residual LayerNorm–ConvFFN branch. The IRB takes the PSA output features y and pre-softmax logits L as inputs: each token feature yi is projected to a scalar field hi and an initial magnetization m(0) i , while the logits L are mapped to a signed, symmetric window-level coupling matrix J with a zero diagonal. Thus, the resulting couplings define a window-local, undirected spin interaction graph. The IRB then performs Kmf mean-field updates to obtain magnetizations m, which gate a lightweight residual MLP correction. The final magnetizations modulate token-wise residual corrections through their gates. Bottom-right: HistAttn connects successive Graphene stages by matching a learnable stagehistory probe ηs with LayerNorm-normalized stored features, producing dynamic history selection weights w(s) r over the stage history {z(0), . . . , z(s)}, where r indexes the stored feature. The selected history is then fused with the current stage output z(s) using a learnable history fusion strength λs: ẑ(s) = z(s) + λs( ∑s r=0 w (s) r z(r) − z(s)). This update refines the current stage output by adaptively blending it with a history-weighted feature aggregate.

papers.title: Graphene: A Lightweight Transformer with Ising Mean-Field Refinement for Image Super-Resolution
papers.tldr: Graphene is a lightweight image super-resolution Transformer that combines Ising-inspired local refinement with history-aware feature aggregation for improved efficiency and detail recovery.

papers.abstract: Multi-stage large language model (LLM) cascades balance accuracy and inference cost, but reliable deployment also requires controlling error risk and identifying its sources across stages. We propose Compositional Conformal Risk Control (CompCRC), a risk-control framework for pre-specified multi-stage LLM cascades. We decompose the risk of accepting incorrect answers into additive stage-wise contributions over the full query population, linking local risk budgets to a system-level guarantee. CompCRC constructs and freezes candidate budget allocations and acceptance thresholds, selects one candidate on independent data, and certifies its stage-wise risk contributions on separate held-out data. Under conditional exchangeability, we establish a finite-sample guarantee: the marginal expected accepted-error risk of the complete deployment procedure does not exceed the global risk budget. At the reported comparison budget of $α=0.45$, all three stages of CompCRC pass their local checks on MMLU, GSM8K, and HellaSwag. Compared with Global-CRC, which passes system-level risk certification at the same budget, CompCRC reduces observed accepted-error risk by 1.33--2.00 percentage points, improves final accuracy by 0.67--2.00 percentage points, and reduces weighted inference cost by 30.37\% on HellaSwag. The selected cost-based budget allocation also improves accuracy per unit cost by 10.6\%--46.7\% over uniform allocation. Further experiments show that stage-wise statistics identify stages that fail local certification checks, providing diagnostic information alongside system-level risk control.
bullets: Decomposes accepted-error risk into additive contributions from individual cascade stages.
Pre-specifies budget allocations and thresholds, selects among candidates on independent data, and certifies the choice on held-out data.
Under conditional exchangeability, guarantees that the complete deployment procedure stays within a global marginal expected accepted-error budget.
At α=0.45, all stages pass local checks on MMLU, GSM8K, and HellaSwag; compared with Global-CRC, it lowers observed risk and improves accuracy.
Stage-wise diagnostics reveal which stages fail local certification, while cost-based allocation improves accuracy per unit cost over uniform allocation.

papers.abstract: In edge intelligence systems, computation offloading and dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) are widely used to improve energy efficiency. However, as applications like deep neural network (DNN) inference evolve in complexity, their demands for memory resources have progressively increased, establishing memory as a critical bottleneck that impacts both latency and energy consumption. In this paper, we propose a joint optimization scheme integrating memory, computing and offloading for energy-efficient DNN inference. We formulate the energy minimization problem under deadline constraints as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem, where the main challenge arises from the coupling between offloading and resource optimization. To address this issue, we decompose the original problem into two subproblems under a fixed offloading policy. The local subproblem is transformed into an equivalent geometric programming (GP) problem to derive the optimal memory frequency and computing frequency, while the edge subproblem is solved via convex optimization. An efficient coordinate descent (CD) algorithm is further developed to jointly optimize all variables. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm achieves near-optimal performance with the gap from the optimal policy being at most 9.3%, and reduces the energy consumption of devices by up to 16.1% compared with benchmarks without memory frequency optimization.
bullets: Memory frequency is treated as a critical resource alongside computation and offloading.
The energy-minimization problem is formulated as a mixed-integer nonlinear program.
The approach decomposes the problem into local geometric programming and edge convex optimization subproblems.
A coordinate descent algorithm jointly optimizes offloading, memory frequency, and computing frequency.
Simulations show at most a 9.3% gap from the optimum and up to 16.1% device-energy reduction versus benchmarks without memory-frequency optimization.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms. In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.
bullets: Targets the high latency of autoregressive action generation on resource-constrained robots.
Uses a lightweight retrieval-augmented draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without an additional neural draft model.
Reduces verification overhead through kinematics-guided action acceptance and KV-cache-sharing attention.
Introduces the Zora core to accelerate irregular memory access during retrieval.
On four VLA models using LIBERO, it retains comparable accuracy and achieves up to 3.4× software-only and 7.6× hardware-supported speedup over GPUs.

figures.caption: Fig. 12. Overview of the ZORA core architecture. The core accelerates HNSW-based DG retrieval through a four-stage pipeline: fetch, compute, accumulation, and update. The PE array exploits node-level parallelism and embedding-level parallelism to compute partial similarity scores between the query embedding and neighbor embeddings. Partial similarity scores are accumulated and then consumed by either the reduction unit for greedy search in upper HNSW layers or the comparison units for top-k selection in the bottom layer. Lastly, the neighbor index fetch unit updates the search frontier for unvisited nodes.

papers.title: Efficient VLA Inference via Retrieval-Based Speculation and Hardware Acceleration

papers.abstract: Adaptive tokenization aims to reduce the compute spent on uninformative image regions while preserving accuracy. Existing work relies on (i) fixed or frozen scoring rules, which cannot be trained toward the task loss, or (ii) discrete masks trained with straight-through estimators, which yield noisy gradients, while fully differentiable alternatives instead leave the pre-trained regular grid. We revisit adaptive tokenization from a regular-grid perspective and ask: can a two-scale quadtree be learned end-to-end without deleting a single token during training? We show that one coarse token and its four fine children can be made the two endpoints of a single continuous interpolation. We introduce Differentiable Virtual-Slot Partitioning (\dvsp{}), which keeps four \emph{virtual slots} per $2{\times}2$ region and blends their token features and attention mass with a single weight $α$, exactly reproducing the discrete grid at $α\in \{0,1\}$. On COCO detection with EVA-02-B, \dvsp{} retains $97.9\%$ of dense Box AP while removing $64.2\%$ of visual tokens, giving a $1.61\times$ end-to-end speedup, and it outperforms entropy-based APT, DART, and uniform lower-resolution dense adaptation at matched budgets; these gains depend on the conserved attention mass, whose removal costs $1.59$ Box AP. On a frozen Segmenter it also improves Cityscapes mIoU, and on frozen DeiT backbones it exceeds entropy selection at identical per-image token counts.
bullets: Addresses fixed scoring rules, noisy straight-through masks, and differentiable methods that abandon the pre-trained regular grid.
Uses four virtual slots per 2×2 region and a single interpolation weight to blend coarse and fine token features and attention mass.
On COCO detection with EVA-02-B, removes 64.2% of visual tokens while retaining 97.9% of dense Box AP and achieving a 1.61× end-to-end speedup.
Outperforms entropy-based APT, DART, and uniform lower-resolution adaptation at matched token budgets.
Improves Cityscapes mIoU on a frozen Segmenter and exceeds entropy selection on frozen DeiT backbones; conserving attention mass is important.

papers.abstract: Implementing intelligent learning systems on low- power edge devices is challenging due to the high compu- tational complexity, training latency, and energy demands of traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), biologically plausible and spike-driven, come as an alternative. However, SNN training commonly relies on backpropagation through time (BPTT), which is computationally expensive, inherently global, and unsuitable for battery-driven devices. This work proposes a novel local learning framework for multi-layered SNNs inspired by Neural Activity Synchronization (NAS). Each layer updates its own weights using locally com- puted gradients. No gradient backpropagation is needed. This significantly reduces computational complexity, training latency, and energy consumption. The proposed SNN model is trained and evaluated on the MNIST dataset, achieving a classification accuracy of 97.78%. The model is also analyzed with Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise, demonstrating robust performance across different noise levels.
bullets: Targets the computational cost, latency, and energy demands of training SNNs on low-power edge devices.
Uses Neural Activity Synchronization to update each layer’s weights with locally computed gradients.
Eliminates global gradient backpropagation through time (BPTT).
Achieves 97.78% classification accuracy on MNIST.
Maintains robust performance under Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise at different noise levels.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Implementation of the Local Neuronal Synchronous Model. The figure illustrates the formation of the basis matrix using periodic function in the proposed architecture. A distinct spatial frequency fc is assigned to each class c, thus they become class-specific periodic basis vectors. For a layer containing D neurons and C classes, the basis matrix B ∈ RC×D is formed by stacking these basis vectors. The spike count vector SC(ℓ) of the layer, with dimension 1 ×D, is projected onto the transposed basis matrix B⊤ ∈ RD×C to compute the logits, resulting in a logit vector of dimension 1× C.

Fig. 1: Neural Activity Synchronization based Spiking Neural Network architecture. This figure illustrates the processing of image data at a single time-step after Poisson rate encoding. The data is encoded for T time steps. Here, I represents the input vector dimension, Dn denotes the number of neurons in the n-th hidden layer, and C represents the number of classes. The Red Tick mark indicates the firing of a neuron at that instant.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models often continue generating after producing an answer, yet stopping prematurely may interrupt useful verification or revision. In this work, we investigate whether targeted interventions in a model's internal computation can provide a reliable signal for when to stop reasoning. We introduce Prune-to-Probe, an inference-time controller that uses causal activation interventions to probe the stability of a model's current answer. Specifically, we identify late-MLP coordinates that contribute to post-answer continuation while excluding those important for answer completion. Once an answer is stated, Prune-to-Probe temporarily suppresses the selected coordinates and measures the resulting stopping response relative to matched random interventions. Crucially, these interventions serve only as probes: the model either returns its existing answer or resumes generation from an untouched cache. On MATH, Prune-to-Probe reduces reasoning-token forwards by 2.60%, preserving all naturally correct trajectories while repairing six errors. On MMLU-Pro, it achieves 1.145% pooled savings with no observed harm. Further analysis shows that the intervention captures decision stability rather than correctness (AUROC 0.502). These results demonstrate the potential of causal activation probes for efficient inference-time control without permanent model modification.
bullets: Targets late-MLP coordinates linked to post-answer continuation but not answer completion.
After an answer is stated, temporarily suppresses these coordinates and compares the stopping response with matched random interventions.
Uses interventions only as probes: the model either keeps its answer or resumes from an untouched cache.
Reduces reasoning-token forwards by 2.60% on MATH while preserving naturally correct trajectories and repairing six errors; saves 1.145% on MMLU-Pro with no observed harm.
The probe reflects decision stability rather than correctness, with AUROC 0.502, limiting its use as an accuracy signal.

papers.abstract: Extended reasoning can help language models solve complex problems, but long responses often contain both useful computations and redundant checks. Conventional length penalties encourage shorter responses without distinguishing the functions of intermediate steps. We propose Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping (PCRS), a framework that combines phase identification with training-time reward allocation. We investigate two classification routes: PCRS-H with a hidden-state classifier and PCRS-T with a frozen text classifier. Our main text classifier implementation assigns overlapping reasoning, execution, and revision labels to native chunks, then uses these labels and exact repetition to adjust existing token penalties. We compare the completed configurations on six mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks and examine four reward-weight settings with the text classifier. Compared with a baseline using token-level length penalties, the default text classifier configuration reduces mean response length by 3.13%; sampled Pass@1 is approximately 62.07% for both methods, while oracle Pass@16 rises from 86.08% to 87.67%. These results show how phase-informed penalty allocation can reduce output volume and improve multi-attempt coverage without inference-time classification.
bullets: Targets redundant checks in extended reasoning that conventional length penalties treat the same as useful computation.
Uses phase identification to label chunks as reasoning, execution, or revision, then adjusts existing token penalties during training.
Evaluates hidden-state and frozen text-classifier variants across six mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks.
The default text-classifier setup reduces mean response length by 3.13%; sampled Pass@1 remains about 62.07%, while oracle Pass@16 increases from 86.08% to 87.67%.
The approach performs phase classification during training rather than at inference time.

papers.title: Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping for Token-Efficient LLM Reasoning

papers.abstract: Embodied intelligence systems rely on fast and reliable inference to enable real-time perception, reasoning, and control. Recent advances in large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) models, including Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, have significantly enhanced the capabilities of embodied agents in complex environments. However, deploying these models remains challenging due to the limited computational resources and energy budgets of robotic platforms. A fundamental question is where inference should be executed. Collaborative inference, which partitions models across end devices, edge servers, and the cloud, has emerged as a promising solution. Yet determining the optimal partitioning point remains an open problem, as it depends on wireless network conditions, model structure, and privacy requirements. This article reviews the state of the art in collaborative inference for embodied intelligence and proposes an edge-centric framework in which the edge coordinates model partitioning and execution. Through both simulation and real-world experiments over WiFi and 5G networks, we demonstrate that the optimal partitioning strategy varies with network conditions and model structure. We further identify latency-minimizing partition points for ResNet-101, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and OpenVLA-7B in collaborative inference between NVIDIA Jetson Nano or AGX Xavier devices and an AGX Thor edge server under varying wireless conditions. Finally, we discuss the future directions for collaborative inference in 6G-empowered embodied intelligence systems.
bullets: Reviews collaborative inference for embodied intelligence using large AI models such as LLMs and VLA models.
Addresses robots’ limited computation and energy by coordinating model partitioning at the edge.
Shows through WiFi and 5G simulations and real-world experiments that optimal partition points depend on wireless conditions and model structure.
Identifies latency-minimizing partition points for ResNet-101, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and OpenVLA-7B across NVIDIA Jetson devices and an AGX Thor edge server.
Discusses future directions for 6G-enabled collaborative inference.

The architecture supports both two-way splitting (device–edge) and three-way splitting (device–edge–device), with the prediction head retained on the device in the latter.
