papers.abstract: Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a core component of recommendation and advertising systems. Large language models (LLMs) offer rich semantic priors that improve prediction quality, particularly in cold-start and long-tail settings. Injecting a full-scale LLM into a CTR pipeline is, however, prohibitively expensive at inference time: existing LLM-enhanced CTR methods avoid this cost by caching LLM outputs offline rather than serving the LLM online. We propose a resource-efficient pipeline, SlimFM, that makes online LLM-based semantic modeling practical: (1) dependency-aware structured pruning compresses LLaMA3-8B by 44% to a 4.5B-parameter backbone; (2) LoRA-based field-aware fine-tuning trains the pruned model to produce discriminative field-level semantic embeddings from lightweight textual prompts; (3) a semantic-guided fusion module injects these embeddings into the feature interactions of a conventional CTR model. Across four datasets and six CTR backbones, SlimFM retains over 99% of uncompressed-model accuracy while reducing inference latency by up to 3.4x relative to existing LLM-enhanced baselines.
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of serving full-scale LLMs in CTR systems, especially for semantic modeling.
Prunes LLaMA3-8B into a 4.5B-parameter backbone, reducing its size by 44%.
Uses LoRA-based, field-aware fine-tuning to generate discriminative semantic embeddings from lightweight prompts.
Fuses these embeddings with conventional CTR feature interactions through a semantic-guided module.
Across four datasets and six CTR backbones, retains over 99% of uncompressed-model accuracy and achieves up to 3.4× lower latency than existing LLM-enhanced baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The SlimFM framework. The upper branch fine-tunes a pruned LLaMA with feature-field prompts to extract field embeddings, which are projected into pairwise field interactions. The lower branch generates feature embeddings from the CTR model and computes feature interactions. The two streams are fused via element-wise multiplication and aggregated for prediction, with a KLdivergence loss aligning the embedding distributions during training.

Table 3: Performance comparisons of SlimFM with existing LLM-enhanced CTR methods across six backbone models and four datasets. SlimFM uses a pruned LLaMA3 (4.5B parameters). LL denotes Logloss and RelImp denotes Relative Improvement. Bold values indicate the best result within each backbone group.

papers.title: Slim Foundation Models for Latency-Critical Recommendation Serving

papers.abstract: Small hand-tracking networks are deployed as 4- and 8-bit codes, and they should keep adapting to a user's camera after deployment, on the device and within roughly the memory of the model itself. Quantization-aware training cannot do this cheaply, because it keeps a 32-bit master copy of every weight together with its optimizer state, about 96 bits per weight. Training the codes directly with stochastic rounding needs no copy but injects rounding noise at every step, and the methods that remove this noise keep a residual buffer for every weight. We introduce sensitivity-gated accumulator caching (SGAC), which keeps residual state for only a small and changing set of weight groups. A set-associative cache of 8-bit accumulators collects the sub-step updates of the groups with the largest Fisher-weighted squared code step and writes them into the codes as whole steps; an evicted line is flushed by stochastic rounding, and a group without a line does not move until it is admitted. We prove that the write-back is unbiased and show, under a local quadratic model, that rounding a sub-step update costs loss of the same order as the update's own gain, so that rounding pays only where the expected gradient is large relative to the curvature. On a 383k-parameter hand-keypoint network, SGAC trains with 8.1 bits of state per weight. Scored on the 4/8-bit network that the device runs after adaptation, it has the highest mean accuracy of nine deployed low-bit networks on two simulated cameras. On twelve ImageNet-C corruptions it has the highest average of corrupted and clean accuracy of seven deployed methods, ahead of the PEQA-style, ECO-style and direct low-bit baselines with confidence intervals that exclude zero, and it matches an 8-bit accumulator kept for every weight with 56% of that state.
bullets: Targets post-deployment learning within roughly the model’s memory budget, avoiding full-precision master weights and per-weight residuals.

Theoretical analysis shows unbiased write-back and that sub-step rounding costs are controlled by update gain relative to local curvature.
On a 383k-parameter hand-keypoint network, it uses 8.1 state bits per weight and achieves the highest mean accuracy among nine deployed low-bit networks on two simulated cameras.
Across twelve ImageNet-C corruptions, it has the highest combined corrupted/clean accuracy among seven methods and matches a full 8-bit accumulator with 56% of its state.

papers.abstract: Collective Communication Libraries (CCL) are critical for large-scale distributed AI/ML training, yet their configurations are determined by static heuristics that do not account for real-time network conditions. Our empirical study shows that these heuristics perform near-optimally in contention-free environments, but degrade substantially under background traffic. To address this, we present a cooperative multi-agent run-time optimizer for accelerator collective communication. Our approach employs a two-agent architecture: (i) detector- a Long Short Term Memory(LSTM) recurring neural network fed classifier head with a sequential probability ratio test that distinguishes sustained contention from transient spikes; and (ii) selector- a configuration selector built on a Dueling Double DQN (D3QN) with Conservative Q-Learning that adapts configuration parameters in response. We implemented this dynamic tuner over NCCL, a widely used CCL developed by NVIDIA. When evaluated on Chameleon Cloud's isolated bare-metal cluster, this dynamic tuning approach reduces AllReduce latency by 36% over NCCL and 32% over a fully converged AutoCCL. We further evaluated it across six real AI workloads spanning convolutional networks, transformers, and recommendation architectures. Our multi-agent tuner approach delivers up to 65% speedups on Delta cluster with NVIDIA A100 GPUs and Slingshot-11 fabric internode connectivity.
bullets: Static collective-communication heuristics work well without contention but degrade under background traffic.
A detector uses an LSTM classifier with a sequential probability ratio test to distinguish sustained contention from transient spikes.
A selector uses Dueling Double DQN with Conservative Q-Learning to adapt communication configurations.
Implemented over NCCL, the method reduces AllReduce latency by 36% over NCCL and 32% over fully converged AutoCCL on an isolated Chameleon Cloud cluster.
Across six AI workloads, it achieves up to 65% speedup on a Delta cluster with NVIDIA A100 GPUs and Slingshot-11 networking.

papers.abstract: We propose a new mathematical formalism in which all kinds of tensors and of operations on those tensors are represented as simple function compositions. Tensors are functions from indices to values. An element-wise operation (e.g. an activation function) is a composition with a function applied to values; re-indexing (e.g. reshape, transposition) is a composition with a function applied to indices; and a reduction is a composition with both an index function, mapping each index to several indices, and a reduction operation (e.g. product, sum, max). Combined with tensor stacking, these compositions can represent most interesting kinds of tensors (e.g. dense, jagged, all kinds of sparsity patterns, matrix factorizations), as well as lazy versions of almost every operation available in modern tensor computation frameworks, including einsums between tensors of any kind. Identities between compositions can then be used to rewrite such expressions into equivalent ones, without evaluating them. For instance, the product of two sparse matrices can be rewritten so that only products between non-zero values are computed, turning a sparse problem into a dense one. Using this algebra as the intermediate representation of a tensor computation engine would shift the focus from defining operations on tensors (e.g. einsum between sparse tensors) to defining an algebra on index functions. This should reduce the codebase complexity from $\mathcal{O}(mn^2)$, with $m$ the number of binary operations between tensors and $n$ the number of tensor types, to $\mathcal{O}(m + k^2)$, with $k$ the number of types of index functions. A draft implementation of a tensor computation framework based on this algebra is publicly available.
bullets: Represents tensors as functions from indices to values and operations as compositions over values, indices, and reductions.
With stacking, the formalism covers dense, jagged, sparse, and factorized tensors, plus many framework operations such as einsum.
Algebraic identities rewrite computations without evaluation; sparse matrix multiplication can thus avoid products involving zero values.
Using index functions as the abstraction could reduce tensor-framework operation complexity from O(mn²) to O(m + k²).
A draft implementation is publicly available; the abstract does not report benchmark results or limitations beyond its stated scope.

papers.abstract: In a multi-turn conversation, the choice of language model at one turn can affect which model should answer the next. The selected model's reply shapes the context for the next query, and its cached prompt prefix can reduce the cost of using that model again. We introduce MultiTurnRoute, a platform for building and evaluating multi-turn LLM routers. A shared interface gives built-in and user-defined routers the current query, dialogue history, and an estimate of each model's reusable prefix length. Our routing algorithm, Chain-of-Route (CoR), uses a learned gate over recent and recurrent dialogue history to predict response quality and estimates cost from each model's reusable prefix. MultiTurnRoute Arena ranks routers on recorded conversations and compares session quality and cost in interactive runs where a simulated user responds to each reply. On a benchmark drawn from WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M with per-turn quality annotations for five LLMs, CoR reduces the normalized cost required to match the strongest model's quality by up to 20.3% relative to the strongest routing baseline, while matching or improving peak response quality.
bullets: Multi-turn routing must account for how each model’s response changes future context and reuse opportunities.
The platform exposes the current query, dialogue history, and estimated reusable prefix length to built-in or custom routers.
Chain-of-Route uses a learned gate over recent and recurrent history to predict quality and estimate model-use cost.
Its Arena evaluates routers on recorded conversations and interactive sessions with simulated users.
On WildChat- and LMSYS-Chat-1M-derived benchmarks covering five LLMs, CoR reduced normalized cost by up to 20.3% versus the strongest baseline while matching or improving peak quality.

papers.title: MultiTurnRoute: A Platform for Building and Evaluating Multi-Turn LLM Routers

papers.abstract: Iterative neural policies usually spend the same computation on every decision, although the benefit of additional processing varies across states. We introduce Adaptive Internal Computation (AIC), an iterative policy that learns when to stop refining its latent representation and act. In AIC, we train action selection and stopping jointly, an expected-depth penalty values computation and intermediate value predictions provide auxiliary supervision. We show that when only some states benefit from further refinement, an ideal state-dependent allocator outperforms every state-independent stopping schedule at the same expected depth. With at most eight refinement steps per decision, AIC executes 3.3 steps on average across twelve benchmark tasks and lowers per-decision latency by 31--44% relative to a fixed eight-step policy on four control and robotics tasks. Its mean reward exceeds the best fixed-depth policy on seven tasks and trails it on four. Ablating adaptive stopping and value supervision separately shows that stopping accounts for most of the reward gain on PickCube and AntMaze, where it also executes more refinement steps and that supervision accounts for most of it on RareEvent.
bullets: The work addresses the inefficiency of using the same number of iterative computations for every decision.
AIC jointly learns action selection and when to stop refining, using an expected-depth penalty and intermediate value predictions.
With up to eight refinement steps, it averages 3.3 steps across twelve benchmark tasks.
On four control and robotics tasks, AIC reduces per-decision latency by 31–44% versus a fixed eight-step policy.
AIC beats the best fixed-depth policy on seven tasks and trails it on four; stopping and value supervision contribute differently across tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Adaptive Internal Computation for RL to reduce latency, fitting Robot Learning and KV Cache/Memory Efficiency.
papers.title: Learning When to Think: Adaptive Internal Computation for Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Adaptive Internal Computation lets reinforcement-learning policies spend more reasoning on difficult states and less on easy ones, reducing latency while often preserving or improving reward.

papers.abstract: Video fusion aims to integrate complementary cues from heterogeneous sources, producing visually informative videos with coherent spatio-temporal structures. Jointly learning cross-modal complementarity and temporal dependencies typically relies on large-scale, high-quality video datasets, whose storage and repeated use during optimization incur substantial costs, making data-efficient learning highly desirable. To address this challenge, we rethink video fusion from the perspective of dataset condensation and propose STAR-VF, the first framework that condenses spatio-temporal representations for data-efficient video fusion. STAR-VF condenses the original training set into a compact set of learnable spatio-temporal representations, which are decoded into synthetic video clips and optimized using feature-level supervision provided by a frozen proxy model. The resulting condensed data preserves fusion-relevant spatial and temporal cues without requiring ground-truth fused videos as supervision. To adapt fusion learning to condensed representations, we equip the final fusion model with flow-free inter-frame temporal modeling and query-driven intra-frame aggregation, enabling direct temporal interaction and adaptive selection of fusion-relevant information in representation space. Extensive experiments on infrared-visible, multi-exposure, multi-focus, and medical video fusion benchmarks demonstrate that STAR-VF, trained with only approximately 1/16 of the original temporal training set, achieves fusion quality comparable to methods trained on the full data. Further analyses validate the contributions of learned condensation and flow-free temporal modeling, and demonstrate the robustness of the condensed supervision across different proxy encoders and downstream fusion models. Project page: https://zju-xyc.github.io/STAR-VF-Project-Page/.
bullets: Targets the storage and optimization costs of large video-fusion training datasets.
Learns compact spatio-temporal representations, decodes them into synthetic clips, and optimizes them with feature-level supervision from a frozen proxy model.
Uses flow-free inter-frame temporal modeling and query-driven intra-frame aggregation for fusion directly in representation space.
Supports infrared-visible, multi-exposure, multi-focus, and medical video fusion without requiring ground-truth fused videos.
Using approximately 1/16 of the original temporal training data, it achieves fusion quality comparable to full-data training; robustness is shown across proxy encoders and downstream fusion models.

In Stage II, the learned condensed set is decoded into synthetic temporal samples to train the final fusion model 𝐹𝜃 with flow-free temporal alignment and query-driven intra-frame aggregation. During inference, only the trained fusion model is used, without the condensed set or proxy model.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization estimates descent directions from function values alone, which removes the activation storage required by backpropagation and makes it attractive for memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). Existing low-rank ZO methods either parameterize the additive update through Euclidean factors with a non-unique representation, or restrict each finite-difference direction to be low-rank. In this work, we propose to constrain each additive update block to a fixed-rank matrix manifold while keeping the pretrained weights frozen, so the learned update remains rank-constrained throughout fine-tuning. On this geometry, we build a Riemannian ZO gradient estimator that projects a random matrix onto the tangent space, normalizes it to correct the scale mismatch induced by projection, and further propose Zeroth-order Riemannian Gradient Descent (ZO-RGD) and its smoothed variant, ZO-RGD-S. We show that the ambient finite difference matches its retracted counterpart, the normalized estimator recovers the Riemannian gradient in expectation, and ZO-RGD converges under trajectory-regularity conditions. Experiments on LLM fine-tuning tasks show that the proposed algorithms are competitive with strong forward-only baselines across model families and tasks, with gains in several settings.
bullets: Targets activation-memory costs of backpropagation using zeroth-order optimization.
Keeps pretrained weights frozen while constraining additive updates to fixed-rank matrix manifolds.
Introduces a tangent-space-projected, scale-normalized Riemannian zeroth-order gradient estimator.
Proposes ZO-RGD and smoothed ZO-RGD-S, with convergence results under trajectory-regularity conditions.
Performs competitively with strong forward-only baselines across model families and tasks, improving results in some settings.

papers.abstract: Dense prediction and generative modeling remain challenging in resource-constrained environments, particularly because repeated downsampling can lead to the loss of spatial details and less accurate object boundaries. Although attention mechanisms have been widely adopted to address semantic ambiguity, preserving high-frequency information while maintaining computational efficiency remains an important challenge. To address this issue, we propose Frequency-Guided Depthwise Separable Attention for Efficient Dense Prediction (FG-DSA), a framework that integrates frequency-domain information into lightweight vision architectures for dense visual understanding and generation. Specifically, FG-DSA uses a 2D Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)-based high-pass filtering module to guide spatial attention, aiming to retain fine-grained features and improve object-boundary representation. Experimental results show that FG-DSA can improve boundary-related performance in semantic segmentation under the evaluated setting. Beyond discriminative tasks, we also examine its application in a generative U-Net for single-step image restoration. The results suggest that incorporating FG-DSA can enhance reconstruction quality and help preserve high-frequency details.
bullets: Targets spatial-detail and boundary loss caused by repeated downsampling in resource-constrained vision systems.
Combines 2D FFT-based high-pass filtering with spatial attention and depthwise-separable design.
Improves boundary-related semantic-segmentation performance in the evaluated setting.
Also enhances reconstruction quality and high-frequency detail preservation in single-step image restoration.
Scope is limited to the tasks and evaluation settings described in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM. Code is available at https://github.com/huawei-csl/MACaQ .
bullets: Targets low-precision weights and activations to reduce neural-network inference memory and compute costs.
Uses per-channel scaling and online block-Hadamard activation transforms, with inverse transforms absorbed into weights.
Introduces Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent method that adjusts individual FP4 codes beyond round-to-nearest quantization.
Adds 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM and matches competing methods’ best Llama-3-8B perplexity using 11× less quantization time.
Its layer-local design supports streaming quantization, diffusion models, and a 122B-parameter model using 32.5 GB GPU RAM in 64 minutes.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention accelerates long-context decoding by reading a subset of the KV cache, but existing methods are open-loop: the kernel commits to its selection with no signal indicating whether enough attention mass was preserved and no recovery path when it was not. The needed signal already exists inside the kernel. The fraction of softmax mass on the selected tokens, which we call coverage, satisfies an exact algebraic equality with per-step output error and serves a dual role as the acceptance criterion and the interpolation weight for recovery. Coverage-Verified Sparse Attention (CVSA) turns coverage into a training-free, closed-loop verify-then-correct decode loop that accepts high-coverage drafts and recovers only the heads that fall short, with no sampling, no draft model, and no speculative-decoding infrastructure. Quality varies by only $0.14$ points across the threshold sweep; budget and scheduling ablations characterize the deployed operating point. On LongBench at 7B and 70B, CVSA comes within $1.13$ points of dense attention, statistically matching it at 70B, and it loses $0.8$ points on RULER; measured median decode-step speedup reaches $6.21\times$ at 128K context.
bullets: Addresses the open-loop risk that sparse attention may omit too much attention mass without detecting or correcting the error.
Uses coverage—the softmax mass on selected tokens—as both an exact error-related signal and the acceptance/recovery control.
Implements a training-free verify-then-correct loop without sampling, draft models, or speculative-decoding infrastructure.
Quality changes by only 0.14 points across the threshold sweep; operating points are examined through budget and scheduling ablations.
On LongBench, it comes within 1.13 points of dense attention at 7B and statistically matches it at 70B; median speedup reaches 6.21× at 128K context.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have established themselves as the preeminent paradigm for high-fidelity generative modeling across various modalities, yet their practical deployment is hindered by the severe computational overhead of iterative sampling. While recent feature-caching methods mitigate this latency through feature reuse or forecasting based on integer-order operators, they remain limited in adapting to the non-stationary and highly curved dynamics of DiT latent trajectories. In this work, we reveal that DiT feature evolution exhibits anomalous diffusion characteristics and a certain degree of spatiotemporal heterogeneity, rendering static, integer-order forecasting operators inadequate and prone to error accumulation. To address this, we propose Fractional Anomalous Dynamics Extrapolation (FADE), a unified framework for training-free diffusion transformers acceleration. FADE models DiT feature evolution via anomalous diffusion and employs a Mittag--Leffler fractional operator to better adapt to high-curvature and non-linear latent trajectories of DiTs. Leveraging the empirical observation that these complex dynamics maintain cross-sample stability, we further construct a Look-Up Table with multiple dimensions through offline profiling. This enables negligible LUT-retrieval overhead, spatiotemporally adaptive parameter retrieval during online inference. Extensive evaluations across diverse architectures and modalities demonstrate that FADE achieves state-of-the-art acceleration, preserving exceptional generation fidelity under aggressive skip intervals with negligible latency overhead. Our project page is available at https://youngkinlon.github.io/fade-project-page/.
bullets: DiT sampling is computationally expensive, and existing integer-order feature forecasting struggles with non-stationary, highly curved latent trajectories.
FADE models feature evolution as anomalous diffusion using a Mittag–Leffler fractional operator.
An offline-profiled multidimensional lookup table enables spatiotemporally adaptive parameter retrieval with negligible online overhead.
Evaluations across diverse architectures and modalities report state-of-the-art acceleration and strong fidelity under aggressive skip intervals.
Scope: the method is training-free and relies on cross-sample stability of complex DiT dynamics.

papers.abstract: 1-bit key-value (KV) cache compression can combine quantizer calibration with selective high-precision storage to reduce reconstruction error. We propose Calibration and Fisher-guided Anchors for KV cache compression (CALFA-KV). Offline, we jointly fit a key center, radial normalization parameters, and K/V vector codebooks to match the frozen model's projected attention output. We also estimate channel-wise Fisher-type sensitivities from squared gradients of a reference next-token cross-entropy loss. Online, we use these sensitivities to weight the squared reconstruction errors of each KV state. Here, a KV state is one token's key-value pair within one layer and KV head. We retain the highest-scoring states at high precision under a per-layer, per-KV-head budget. Under exact restoration, we bound the excess risk of score-based anchor selection relative to the optimum at the same anchor budget, where risk is the conditional mean square of the first-order loss change. With a budget of 56 additional FP16 anchors per layer and KV head, CALFA-KV (d8b8) outperforms all evaluated nominal 1-bit baselines on the mean score across seven benchmarks for each of the three models. At the same anchor budget, CALFA-KV (d8b10) uses a nominal index rate of 1.25 bits per channel and narrows the gap to BF16 to 0.90--2.01 points on the same metric.
bullets: Offline, it fits key normalization and K/V codebooks to preserve the frozen model’s projected attention output.
It estimates channel sensitivity from squared gradients of a reference next-token loss, then scores KV states by sensitivity-weighted reconstruction error.
Online, it stores the highest-scoring token key-value states at FP16 under per-layer, per-KV-head budgets.
With 56 extra FP16 anchors per layer and KV head, d8b8 outperforms evaluated nominal 1-bit baselines across seven benchmarks and three models.
The d8b10 variant narrows the gap to BF16 to 0.90–2.01 points at a nominal 1.25 bits per channel; the theory bounds selection risk under exact restoration.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. CALFA-KV for 1-bit KV cache compression. (a) Offline joint calibration proposes updates with fixed codeword assignments and tests them using deployment-precision replay after re-encoding. Channel sensitivities are estimated separately from reference-loss gradients. (b) During inference, sensitivityweighted reconstruction errors rank historical KV states for FP16 retention, with up to N anchors per layer and KV head. Attention combines decoded history, restored anchors, and unquantized recent and live K/V. The nominal 1-bit rate refers to codeword indices.

papers.abstract: Local AI promises capable personal assistants that run on users' own devices, keeping data and computation under their control. Open-weight models that fit on local devices can now handle practical tasks such as coding. Yet current inference engines fall short. Popular engines such as vLLM and SGLang target datacenter GPUs with dedicated host memory, while local engines underuse the memory hierarchy of unified-memory devices. We present Hibana, an inference engine for unified-memory devices that co-optimizes model representation, memory management, and decoding strategy. Model surgery, the process of editing a trained model's architecture to suit its hardware, changes how the model computes, shrinking its memory footprint and data movement. Unified-memory management preserves each agent's state across turns, so long-running agents can resume instantly instead of recomputing their state. Adaptive speculation generates several tokens per step. Hibana codesigns these features around the shared memory capacity and limited bandwidth of unified-memory systems-on-chip to support local multi-agent workloads. On a single DGX Spark serving Qwen and Nemotron models of up to 125B parameters, Hibana completes up to 3.4$\times$ more agentic tasks per hour and delivers up to 3.9$\times$ higher decoding throughput than other established frameworks such as vLLM, NVIDIA Flare, llama.cpp, and TensorFold. Code is available at https://github.com/sharar-project/hibana.
bullets: Targets unified-memory systems-on-chip, which existing datacenter and local inference engines do not fully exploit.
Uses model surgery to reduce model memory footprint and data movement.
Preserves agent state across turns, enabling instant resumption without recomputation.
Applies adaptive speculation to generate multiple tokens per decoding step.
On a DGX Spark with models up to 125B parameters, achieves up to 3.4× more agentic tasks per hour and 3.9× higher decoding throughput than established frameworks.

papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts interleave model reasoning with tool calls in persistent workspaces. Scaling these rollouts incurs substantial memory costs for concurrent environments, while slow tool calls delay entire rollout batches. We present BunshinRL, an agentic RL rollout system that exploits shared environment state and recurring tool calls through three techniques: memory sharing across environments, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution. These techniques build on BunshinFork, a novel live whole-workspace forking mechanism for containers. BunshinFork reconstructs process trees, shares memory copy-on-write, and preserves file, communication, and GUI state, enabling cached-state reuse and rollback after incorrect speculation. We implement BunshinRL and BunshinFork through Linux kernel module and CRIU modifications. BunshinRL reduces peak memory by up to 43%, total memory consumption by up to 51%, and end-to-end rollout latency by 23%.
bullets: Targets memory overhead from concurrent environments and delays from slow tool calls.
Combines shared environment state, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution.
Introduces BunshinFork, which supports live whole-workspace forks with copy-on-write memory, preserved state, and rollback.
Implemented via Linux kernel-module and CRIU modifications.
Reports up to 43% lower peak memory, 51% lower total memory, and 23% lower end-to-end rollout latency.

figures.caption: Figure 4. BunshinFork architecture. A brief freeze captures a consistent workspace state. The live fork path reconstructs isolated clones that share unchanged pages copy-on-write and allocate private pages on writes. Retained snapshot holders support asynchronous serialization, allowing the source to resume without waiting for disk writes.

Figure 3. Illustration of BunshinRL. Right shows two samples in a simplified rollout step; left shows the on-disk and in-memory workspace snapshot stores for tool call prefix. Reasoning steps’ generated tool call signatures are matched with the tool prefix tree. All initial matched tool calls are skipped until the first miss in tool signature (Tool 3 for R1 and Tool 4 for R2), at which point the corresponding snapshots are used to reconstruct the workspaces. As C3 is not cached in memory, Tool 3 is replayed for R2 and its delta write is added to the C0+C1+C2 snapshot. The samples execute actual Tool 3 for R1 and actual Tool 4 for R2, creating new delta CoW pages. After these calls finish, speculation starts from the resulting workspaces: Tool 4 for R1 and Tools 5 and 6 for R2. The Spec Tool Selector selects tool calls that are likely to happen from previous tool call history. When a reasoning step finishes, its output tool signature is compared with the speculative tool signature. For failed speculation, the system rolls back to the workspace snapshot before speculation.

Figure 5. Linux Process Fork vs. BunshinFork Process-Tree Fork. Left: native fork() duplicates one process as a child of the source process. Right: BunshinFork creates a sibling container and reconstructs the whole process tree inside an independent namespace.

papers.title: BunshinRL: Whole-Workspace Forking for Agentic Reinforcement Learning Rollouts
papers.tldr: BunshinRL accelerates agentic RL rollouts by forking and reusing live container workspaces, reducing memory use and rollout latency.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos, but attention over long spatiotemporal sequences makes inference computationally expensive. Sparse attention reduces this cost by computing only a subset of query-key interactions exactly, and recent training-free methods further approximate the remaining interactions. These methods, however, degrade quickly at high sparsity, which limits the achievable speedup. We present ESTRA (Extreme Sparsity Through Refined Attention), a training-free acceleration method that preserves generation quality even at extreme sparsity. ESTRA concentrates exact attention computation on a small set of important key-value tokens and approximates the remaining contributions with cluster representatives. To identify these tokens efficiently, it groups similar queries and uses their representatives to score individual keys. A variance-based correction further refines the attention weights of the cluster representatives, improving the accuracy of the approximation. Experiments on Wan2.1-14B and HunyuanVideo-13B show that ESTRA establishes a new quality-efficiency frontier for training-free sparse attention, achieving $3.26\times$ and $4.71\times$ end-to-end speedups at 5% attention density while surpassing Sol-Attn and SVG-EAR in fidelity to dense generation and on most VBench dimensions. Even at 1% density, ESTRA remains more faithful to dense generation than Sol-Attn at 12.5%, while reaching up to $5.39\times$ speedup.
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of attention over long spatiotemporal video sequences.
Selects a small set of important key-value tokens using clustered query representatives.
Approximates remaining attention with cluster representatives and applies variance-based weight correction.
At 5% attention density, achieves 3.26× and 4.71× end-to-end speedups on Wan2.1-14B and HunyuanVideo-13B.
At 1% density, remains more faithful to dense generation than Sol-Attn at 12.5% density, with up to 5.39× speedup.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a training-free method for extreme attention sparsity in video diffusion transformers, relevant to video diffusion and efficient attention.
papers.title: ESTRA: Enabling Extreme Attention Sparsity for Training-Free Video Diffusion Acceleration
papers.tldr: ESTRA accelerates video diffusion transformers with training-free sparse attention, retaining high fidelity at extreme sparsity and delivering up to 5.39× speedup.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding efficiency depends on the number of consecutively accepted draft tokens, yet token-level training objectives do not directly optimize this quantity. We introduce D-REAL (Drafter Reinforcement of Expected Acceptance Length), a post-training method that directly optimizes expected acceptance length for a fixed decoding context. D-REAL weights position-wise draft-target distributional overlap by prefix survival probabilities along a draft-sampled prefix, faithfully capturing the sequential dependence of verification on earlier proposals. By accounting for the parameter dependence of the proposal distribution, we derive an unbiased gradient estimator for this single-round objective under stochastic verification. We evaluate D-REAL on DSpark and DFlash2 with Qwen3-8B as the target model across ten benchmarks. Starting from baselines whose mean acceptance length has plateaued, one epoch of D-REAL post-training consistently improves the benchmark-averaged mean acceptance length by up to 0.23 tokens across both architectures under greedy (T = 0.0) and stochastic (T = 1.0) sampling, translating into up to a 9.4% end-to-end serving throughput improvement.
bullets: Targets the sequential objective that determines how many draft tokens are accepted, rather than optimizing tokens independently.
Weights position-wise draft–target overlap by prefix survival probabilities to account for earlier proposal acceptance.
Derives an unbiased gradient estimator that includes the proposal distribution’s parameter dependence under stochastic verification.
Evaluated on DSpark and DFlash2 with Qwen3-8B across ten benchmarks and under greedy and stochastic sampling.
Improves benchmark-averaged mean acceptance length by up to 0.23 tokens and end-to-end throughput by up to 9.4%.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of draft-training objectives. Unlike (a) standard token-level losses and (b) D-PACE, which weight token likelihoods along fixed offline reference prefixes, (c) D-REAL directly optimizes expected acceptance length along online draft-sampled trajectories by combining exact local distributional overlap (left inset) with differentiable prefix survival factors (right inset) via stop-gradient proposal denominators.

Figure 2. Per-task cumulative acceptance rate Pr(N ≥ t) across speculative positions t ∈ {1, . . . , 7} for DFlash2 under (a) greedy (T = 0.0) and (b) stochastic (T = 1.0) decoding. Across both regimes and all ten benchmarks, D-REAL consistently slows down prefix survival decay compared to the baseline, yielding compounding gains with draft depth. Table 2. End-to-end serving performance of DFlash2 and DSpark on GSM8K in SGLang, measured on an 8-GPU Hopper node (concurrency = 32). D-REAL translates higher acceptance lengths into substantial throughput gains and latency reductions without modifying the inference architecture.

While D-PACE drops below the baseline at T = 1.0, D-REAL achieves consistent, substantial gains across the entire draft depth.

papers.selection_reason: Optimizes speculative decoding acceptance length for improved serving throughput; fits efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: D-REAL: Acceptance-Length Optimization with Unbiased Gradients for Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: D-REAL directly optimizes speculative decoding’s expected acceptance length with an unbiased gradient estimator, improving acceptance and serving throughput after one post-training epoch.

papers.abstract: Semantic response caching reuses a cached response for a semantically similar query to improve LLM inference efficiency. However, query similarity alone can lead to unsafe reuse when safety conditions change. Existing approaches improve cache safety through stricter similarity checks, context-aware validation, or response verification, yet they may still miss safety conflicts between the cached response and the new request or introduce unnecessary verification overhead. We argue that safe and efficient semantic caching requires a reuse policy that makes the cached response's safety conditions explicit and uses them to guide the reuse decision with a balance between safety and utility. In this paper, we propose SafeCache, a safety-aware framework that separates candidate retrieval from safety approval and formulates semantic response reuse as a safety-conditioned routing problem. SafeCache matches each cached-response condition against the new request and aggregates the per-condition mismatches into an overall risk score. A separate contradiction guard prevents explicit conflicts from being diluted by strong matches. It further estimates matching uncertainty and calibrates the routing policy under a required unsafe-reuse target and a verifier-call budget to choose among direct reuse, selective verification, or regeneration. Experiments show that SafeCache achieves the better safety-utility trade-off among the evaluated baselines, enabling safer response reuse at comparable cache utility.
bullets: Addresses unsafe cache reuse when a new request’s safety requirements differ from those of a cached response.
Separates semantic candidate retrieval from safety approval rather than relying on query similarity alone.
Aggregates condition mismatches into a risk score and uses a contradiction guard to catch explicit conflicts.
Calibrates routing under an unsafe-reuse target and verifier-call budget to balance safety and cache utility.
Experiments report a better safety–utility trade-off than evaluated baselines at comparable cache utility.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SafeCache. From left to right, SafeCache first extracts the reuse requirements of the cached response and the safety facts of the new request. It then matches the two condition sets to compute the condition mismatch and matching uncertainty, while rule- and context-level guards preserve explicit conflicts. Finally, risk calibration produces the routing risk and uncertainty, which are combined with query similarity and the conflict indicator to choose direct reuse, verification, or regeneration. A verified response is reused if accepted and regenerated otherwise.

papers.title: Beyond Query Similarity: Safety-Conditioned Cache Routing for LLM Response Reuse
papers.tldr: SafeCache makes LLM response caching safety-aware by routing reuse, verification, or regeneration based on explicit safety-condition matching and calibrated risk.

papers.abstract: Accurate indoor localization on resource-constrained edge devices remains challenging due to the tension between modeling fidelity and computational efficiency. Wi-Fi Channel State Information (CSI) enables low-cost deployment using existing Wi-Fi infrastructure but is heavily distorted by multipath propagation. Transformer-based solutions mitigate these effects but their quadratic complexity limits real-time edge deployment. Ultra-Wideband (UWB) provides geometrically precise ranging yet requires dedicated infrastructure. We present MambaLoc, a cross-modal distillation framework that improves the accuracy-efficiency balance in CSI-based localization. MambaLoc uses a linear-time Selective State Space Model (Mamba) as a lightweight CSI student, guided during training by a UWB-Transformer teacher. A Feature Alignment Module bridges the representational gap between heterogeneous RF modalities, allowing the CSI model to inherit UWB-derived geometric structure without UWB hardware at inference. A probabilistic Gaussian Mixture regression head models multi-modal spatial ambiguity from multipath effects, avoiding the physically implausible averaging of deterministic regression. Evaluations on a real-world dataset show MambaLoc achieves a median localization error of 0.230 m, reducing error by 22.2% over a standalone Mamba baseline, while requiring 65.1% fewer FLOPs and 58% lower inference latency than Transformer-based approaches.
bullets: Targets real-time indoor localization on resource-constrained edge devices using existing Wi-Fi infrastructure.
Uses a linear-time Mamba CSI student trained with a UWB-Transformer teacher, plus feature alignment across RF modalities.
Employs a Gaussian Mixture regression head to represent multi-modal position uncertainty caused by multipath effects.
On a real-world dataset, reaches 0.230 m median error and improves over a standalone Mamba baseline while reducing computation and latency versus Transformer approaches.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. MambaLoc system architecture. The UWB Transformer teacher guides the CSI Mamba student via the Feature Alignment Module during training; at inference, only the Mamba student runs on CSI data.
Fig. 2. Mamba Block Architecture. Processes CSI features using a 1D convolution and a Selective SSM for efficient, linear-time sequence modeling.
Fig. 3. Feature Alignment Module architecture. Projects teacher (UWB) and student (CSI) features into a shared 144-dimensional space using MSE, Cosine Similarity, and Cross-Attention losses.

Fig. 6. (a,b) The CSI student favors a “shallow-wide” design to capture high-dimensional CSI features without overfitting noise. (c,d) The UWB teacher exhibits a complexity “sweet spot” (3 layers, 80 dim); exceeding this widens the capacity gap, hindering effective distillation.
Fig. 5. Impact of Distillation Strategies. Progressive improvements in localization accuracy (lower MAE is better) as distillation components are introduced.
Fig. 8. (a) Localization error is minimized at 8 attention heads. (b) A minimum at T=15 balances distribution sharpness with entropy.
Fig. 7. A dimension of 144 balances capacity with regularization; lower values cause bottlenecks (< 120) and higher values permit overfitting (> 150).
Fig. 4. Comparison with State-of-the-Art. MambaLoc achieves the lowest Median AE (0.230m), outperforming CNN and Transformer-based baselines.

papers.abstract: A generative recommender names each candidate with a short token sequence, a Semantic ID, and recommends by generating those tokens. Some generative recommenders, including the Uber Eats search engine we are building, write a whole results page, stores with their menu items, in one decoding pass. Every Semantic ID on such a page must name a real store or item that is eligible for the search, such as a store that delivers to the user's location, and that is not already on the page. Each item must also belong to the store above it. A trie over the catalog keeps identifiers real, but eligibility and repetition change with every request and token, and the grammar-constrained decoder we tried could not enforce these changing rules exactly and quickly. We call this constraint LEGIT, for live eligibility gating over identifier tries. Numbering trie leaves depth first turns each rule into a range lookup over one store trie and one item trie, and every generated page passes an independent catalog check. On one NVIDIA B200 GPU with one or two requests per decode step, a direct implementation that walks the trie on the GPU makes each token about 5 times as slow as unconstrained decoding. Across 36 implementations, hardware counters and ablations are consistent with kernel launches and CPU-GPU waits as the source of this slowdown. Our fastest implementation walks the trie on the CPU while the GPU runs the model, needs no custom kernel, and cuts time per output token by 65.9 percent against the direct GPU implementation, to about 1.7 times the unconstrained cost. This implementation is also the fastest on a page layout that puts each item before its store.
bullets: Targets whole-page generation where every store and item must be catalog-valid, eligible for the request, non-repeated, and correctly nested.
Uses depth-first trie leaf numbering to reduce changing constraints to range lookups over store and item tries.
Validates every generated page independently against the catalog.
A direct GPU trie-walking implementation costs about 5× unconstrained decoding per token; profiling attributes the slowdown mainly to kernel launches and CPU–GPU synchronization.

A CPU trie-walking implementation overlapping GPU model execution reduces this to about 1.7× unconstrained cost, a 65.9% improvement over the direct GPU version, and also handles item-before-store layouts fastest.

figures.caption: Figure 1. From a ranking pipeline to one decode. (a) The pipeline ranks candidates, then applies the rules. (b) One decode writes the page and checks the same rules at every token.

Figure 2. Where the constraint sits in the page decoder. One decode step. Everything that decides what goes into the mask is the constraint. The trie walk can execute on either side of the boundary between the CPU and the GPU. The three inputs at the bottom carry their sizes in our benchmark and how often each changes. In the full CPU stack (Section 5.5), the constraint box sends a short list of legal tokens, and the GPU applies it to the logits.
Figure 4. One decode step, four ways to build the mask. Schematic, with three groups of two prefix tokens each. Each panel title names the implementation and how it launches (Appendix K).

Figure 3. The structures, on a five-leaf trie. Panel A numbers the leaves depth first, so the leaves under any node form one range, which the node stores as node_lo and node_hi. Panel B shows how we store the trie: per-node arrays hold each node’s leaf range and offsets, and per-edge arrays hold each edge’s token and child node. Node v’s children are edges offsets[v] to offsets[v + 1] - 1, one slice. Panel C runs the legal-child test at the root for a request whose eligible leaves are 1, 2 and 4, on a page that has already used 1 and 2. The test refuses prefix a: the request can reach it, but every eligible leaf under it is already blocked.

Figure 5. The legal set is assembled per request and then narrowed per token. The map cell selects the eligible store set through the map-cell-to-store index. The blocked set then removes what the page has already used. An ahead-of-time compile would need to fix both of these, but only the first one is fixed when the request arrives.

Figure 7. How the request’s filters reach the legal child test. Each filter is a sorted array of leaf ids. For an outer slot the eligible array comes from the map-cell-to-store index and the blocked array from the stores already on the page, each widened to its chain; for an inner slot the eligible array is the chosen store’s menu and the blocked array the items already in its carousel. The test is the one of Figure 3.

Figure 8. Padded or ragged child expansion. Both layouts store the same compressed sparse row arrays; they differ in how a group’s child lists are expanded when its mask is built. (A) Padded gives every row the width of the widest node, a fixed 8,192 slots on the real tries, so the shape is known in advance and the GPU needs no read-back. (B) Ragged lists only the real children, but its length must be read on the CPU before the list can be allocated, which on the GPU is a read-back once per group per step. (C) Each layout suits one placement, which is the interaction of Table 3.

Figure 10. Two things the decoder does not recompute every token. (A) The blocked set changes only when a slot closes, so the memo keeps it per row and adds each new slot, instead of expanding every filled slot to its chain and sorting on every step. (B) Each row keeps its position in the trie, so a step advances one edge; the ablation replays the whole page prefix every step, and its cost grows with page length (Table 16).

Figure 9. Inner subtrie compaction. When a store’s carousel opens, the decoder builds a trie over only that store’s menu and renumbers its leaves from zero, then walks the small trie for the rest of the carousel. Every leaf of the small trie is on the menu, so counting eligible leaves in a node’s range becomes a subtraction instead of two binary searches per child edge. Outer subtrie compaction does the same over the stores of the request’s map cell; it had no significant effect on the GPU, and on the CPU it never ran in the same round as its base, so we cannot separate it from the base. With it, the CPU trie is 16.7 percent faster than the control at light load and 55.1 percent faster when saturated (Table 4).

Figure 11. The full CPU stack: three changes on top of the CPU recipe. Schematic. (A) The overlap walks every group before the first copy, so the walks run under the forward pass and the step no longer waits for them. (B) The tensor trie re-walks the current identifier’s few prefix tokens from the trie root on every query; the page prefix is incremental in both, so this is not the ablation of Figure 10(B). The numpy trie runs the same steps from a cached state, slicing the child edges instead of expanding them, as numpy calls at about 1 microsecond each instead of about 10 by our estimate of dispatch overhead, and returns a short list of allowed ids instead of a vocabulary wide mask. Filled boxes mark the steps that differ. (C) The batched write sends every group’s rows in one pinned copy and a fixed set of kernels per step. None changes which tokens are allowed; together they take the CPU recipe’s 20.1 percent at light load to 65.9 percent (Tables 4, 9 and 17).

Figure 6. Where the three axes act on a decode step. Placement and layout change how the child list is read. Launch structure changes how many times the mask work is handed to the GPU. Each acts on one or both of the two stages that run once per group (the brackets mark which), which is why none of them changes the arithmetic.

The per-token penalty grows, but the rate at which it grows falls by a factor of 3.4, so the per-token penalty grows more slowly than page length. papers.selection_reason: Constrained decoding method reducing per-token latency for generative recommenders via trie-based eligibility gating.
papers.title: LEGIT: Live Eligibility Gating over Identifier Tries for Constrained Decoding of Heterogeneous Pages
papers.tldr: LEGIT enforces dynamic eligibility, uniqueness, and store–item constraints during generative recommendation decoding with low overhead.

papers.abstract: Feature caching accelerates Diffusion Transformers by reusing intermediate computations across denoising timesteps, yet existing methods share a fundamental blind spot: they treat the standard reference denoising trajectory as the optimisation target, approximating its per-step states and thus inheriting its output as an implicit quality ceiling. We argue that this target is arbitrary -- what truly matters is the ideal result, not the intermediate path taken to reach it. We propose IdealCache, a training-free framework that abandons step-wise imitation of the reference trajectory. Instead, it anchors caching on a per-input ensemble of ideal trajectories constructed from candidate target results, aggregates their geometry into a single graph, and discovers optimal non-uniform schedules via a constrained shortest path on this graph. By decoupling from the reference process, IdealCache breaks the performance bottleneck of trajectory-approximation; our schedules can attain near-lossless fidelity in generation and even surpass on task-specific metrics (e.g., maintaining higher semantic consistency in image editing). Without retraining, IdealCache achieves 6.35x speedup on Qwen-Image, 5.84x on Qwen-Image-Edit, and 4.32x on HunyuanVideo, with competitive or superior quality across tasks.
bullets: Existing cache schedulers optimize approximation of the reference denoising trajectory, imposing an implicit quality ceiling.
IdealCache constructs per-input ensembles of ideal trajectories from candidate target results and aggregates their geometry into a graph.
A constrained shortest-path search identifies input-specific, non-uniform caching schedules.
The training-free method reports speedups of 6.35× on Qwen-Image, 5.84× on Qwen-Image-Edit, and 4.32× on HunyuanVideo.
It maintains competitive or superior generation quality, including higher semantic consistency for image editing.

papers.abstract: Reproducibility is important for LoRA-adapted language models used in repeated evaluation, auditing, and decision-making. However, Split-K kernels used to introduce parallelism in low-rank LoRA multiplications can have the unintended consequence of numerical nondeterminism when partial results are combined using floating-point atomic additions. We investigate this non-determinism in vLLM across GSM8K mathematical reasoning, MBPP code generation, and Jev-style structured toxicity decisions on Civil Comments and introduce a deterministic Triton Split-K implementation. Under identical-input replay, Atomic Split-K=8 produces different FP32 shrink outputs in 97.61% of comparisons, while our Deterministic Split-K=8 shows no observed variation. Repeated atomic inference changes generated outputs in 17.30% of GSM8K and 14.96% of MBPP comparisons, sometimes altering task correctness. Structured-decision probabilities vary in 81.47% of atomic comparisons, with decision flips. Controlled tracing demonstrates how shrink-output differences propagate into the KV cache and how accumulated cache differences can change token decisions and final answers. Our deterministic Triton Split-K=8 implementation preserves parallelism, achieving 16.8-21.1% latency-based speedup over unsplit reduction with only 1.02-2.62% additional latency relative to Atomic Split-K=8.
bullets: Floating-point atomic additions in vLLM’s Split-K LoRA kernels cause nondeterministic outputs under identical-input replay.
Nondeterminism propagates through the KV cache, changing generated answers, task correctness, and structured toxicity decisions.
Atomic Split-K=8 varied FP32 outputs in 97.61% of comparisons, while deterministic Split-K=8 showed no observed variation.
The deterministic implementation achieved a 16.8–21.1% speedup over unsplit reduction with only 1.02–2.62% higher latency than Atomic Split-K=8.
Evaluation covered GSM8K, MBPP, and Civil Comments-based structured toxicity decisions.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate sessions of up to millions of tokens, far more key-value (KV) cache than one GPU holds, so serving systems keep a small budget of tokens and evict the rest. Eviction methods differ in which tokens they keep but share one goal: that the tokens a later step needs are still cached. We show this is not enough. In 100K-token coding sessions on Qwen3-8B with a 2,048-token budget, a planner-guided policy that keeps over 99% of the needed tokens resident still fails late steps increasingly often: its accuracy falls from 93% to 64% as the gap between a definition and its use grows from 2K to 90K tokens, at residency 0.996. The needed tokens are resident but unretrievable: what grows is their rotary-position distance to the query. We present PACE (Planner-Aware Context Engine), a KV-cache engine that couples plan-aware retention, in which the agent's planner tells the cache which context future steps will read, with bounded positions, which renumber kept tokens so their rotary distance to the query stays below 8K at any session length. In a pre-registered evaluation on fresh tasks, PACE passes 97% of hidden unit tests at 100K tokens, against 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV under the same budget, and needs both components: either alone reaches 63% (the combination beats each, p < 10^-4). The result holds with length: in 1M- and 2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with definitions written 0.9M and 1.8M tokens before use, PACE passes 99% and 100% of checks and recalls every session fact, while bounded positions without foresight falls from 33% to 13%; PACE holds under 0.7 GB of KV state where the full cache would need 147-295 GB. Renumbering is exact, costs no measurable perplexity, and adds 9% wall time. On Mistral-7B, whose coding ability caps it at 40% even with nothing evicted, PACE stays at that ceiling while retention alone falls below it.
bullets: Long sessions can exceed one GPU’s KV-cache capacity, requiring aggressive token eviction.
Even when over 99% of later-needed tokens remain cached, accuracy drops as their rotary-position distance from the query grows.
PACE uses the agent’s plan to retain future-relevant context and bounds rotary distances by renumbering retained tokens.
On 100K-token Qwen3-8B coding tasks with a 2,048-token budget, PACE passes 97% of hidden-unit tests versus 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV.
The method scales to 1M–2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with 9% added wall time and no measurable perplexity cost.

papers.abstract: Context selection can reduce input length during long-input inference but can remove evidence required to answer a query. We introduce CoRA-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating evidence preservation under shared token budgets. We compare head and tail truncation, BM25, dense retrieval, dense retrieval with reranking, LLMLingua-2, and Provence across BABILong, LOONG Financial Spotlight, a custom NoLiMa diagnostic, and LongMemEval. Evidence-preservation results reveal task-dependent tradeoffs: BM25 achieves 0.921 supporting-fact recall on BABILong at 128K, dense retrieval and dense reranking each achieve 0.908 needle recall on NoLiMa at 64K, and dense retrieval achieves 0.993 answer-bearing-turn recall on LongMemEval at 64K. Evidence, token retention, and complementary reader evaluations use the same selected contexts. Reader evaluations use dataset-native answer metrics and three runs on the same questions, with paired bootstrap confidence intervals. At a 32K budget, BM25 achieves 46.20% BABILong answer accuracy and dense retrieval achieves 71.13% LongMemEval accuracy. The results show that method rankings vary across evidence types and between evidence recall and downstream accuracy.
bullets: Compares truncation, BM25, dense retrieval, reranking, LLMLingua-2, and Provence across four long-context benchmarks.
Evaluates evidence recall, token retention, and downstream reader accuracy using the same selected contexts.
Reports strong but task-specific recall: BM25 reaches 0.921 supporting-fact recall on BABILong, while dense retrieval reaches 0.993 answer-bearing-turn recall on LongMemEval.
At 32K tokens, BM25 obtains 46.20% BABILong answer accuracy and dense retrieval obtains 71.13% LongMemEval accuracy.
Finds that evidence-recall rankings do not consistently predict downstream answer accuracy.

papers.abstract: Modern Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference is constrained by GPU memory. This constraint is mitigated by expert offloading, which stores part of the model's weight in host memory and executes on demand. Though MoE architecture has computation sparsity, more GPUs are needed for serving increasingly larger frontier models. However, existing expert offloading systems overlook this need and fail to scale performance with additional GPUs. We present AdaOffload, a general and efficient multi-GPU hybrid expert execution framework that effectively handles heterogeneous hardware and workloads. We co-design GPU-CPU parallelism and GPU-CPU co-execution for decode and prefill with online workload observation that adapts to different hardware, workload, and batch size heterogeneity. We evaluated AdaOffload on five different platforms with varying GPU capability (L4, Pro6000, B200), number of GPUs, CPU capability, and NUMA topology on three different frontier open-weight models (284B to 753B). AdaOffload achieves $1.9\times$ to $15.5\times$ throughput speedups across different models over state-of-the-art systems.
bullets: Targets GPU-memory limits and poor scalability of existing expert-offloading systems as models and GPU counts grow.
Uses a multi-GPU hybrid execution framework that adapts online to hardware, workload, and batch-size heterogeneity.
Co-designs GPU–CPU parallelism and co-execution for both decode and prefill phases.
Evaluated across five hardware platforms and three frontier open-weight models ranging from 284B to 753B parameters.
Reports 1.9×–15.5× throughput speedups over state-of-the-art systems across evaluated settings.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support Web-based services that must balance response quality and inference cost across heterogeneous requests. Conventional routing selects one model per prompt, while fixed ensembles cannot adapt their composition and cost to individual requests. We introduce PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router, and PISA-E, its extension to ensemble routing. At the core of both methods, PISA combines soft cluster memberships with model-specific predictors to estimate individual model capabilities. Building on these estimates, PISA-E jointly selects ensemble composition and cardinality under an explicit cost--quality preference that can be adjusted at inference time without retraining. A tractable ensemble-success surrogate and efficient candidate selection enable this extension without ensemble-specific training. Across four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, PISA achieves the highest macro-average cost--performance hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings. Meanwhile, PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches when prioritizing response quality, surpassing the strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points under ID and OOD conditions, respectively. At selected lower-cost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest ensemble competitors' macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of prompt-adaptive capability estimation for both single-model routing and selective ensembling.
bullets: Addresses the limits of one-model-per-prompt routing and fixed ensembles for heterogeneous requests.
PISA estimates each model’s prompt-specific capability using soft cluster memberships and model-specific predictors.
PISA-E selects ensemble composition and size according to an inference-time adjustable cost–quality preference.
Across four routing benchmarks, PISA leads single-model routers in cost–performance hypervolume under both ID and OOD conditions.
PISA-E leads evaluated ensemble methods on task performance and achieves lower-cost operating points with reduced average inference cost.

In the illustrated five-model example, the candidates are 𝐸1, 𝐸3, and 𝐸5. The selected ensemble is queried in parallel, and self-weighted BERTScore selects the final response using the estimated model capabilities.

papers.abstract: Existing LLM post-training quantization techniques determine precision before inference begins, yet the precision a model requires varies dynamically across prompts, layers, and inference phases. We present AutoEMatic, a full-stack co-design that adapts the precision of weights, activations, and the KV cache at runtime. A lightweight policy selects each layer's precision at every prefill and decode step from two runtime signals: the entropy of the next-token distribution and the magnitude of each layer's update to its hidden states. This runtime adaptation is made practical by AutoFP, a multi-scale floating-point format that derives 2-, 4-, and 6-bit precisions from a single NVFP4 base format. We realize AutoEMatic on two targets: GPU kernels that execute AutoFP on NVFP4 Tensor Cores, and an accelerator whose vector MAC datapath executes all AutoFP formats natively. Across reasoning and agentic benchmarks, AutoEMatic improves accuracy by up to 21.7% over NVFP4 and matches group-scaled FP6 accuracy on most benchmarks, using 4.9 bits per weight versus 4.5 for NVFP4. On GB300 GPUs, AutoEMatic retains approximately 90-98% of NVFP4 decode throughput across the evaluated configurations. Furthermore, the AutoEMatic accelerator reduces latency by 1.6-2.3x and energy by 7-23% compared to an accelerator with NVFP4-only datapath at iso-accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed-precision post-training quantization, whose optimal precision varies by prompt, layer, and inference phase.
Uses next-token entropy and per-layer hidden-state update magnitude to select weight, activation, and KV-cache precision at each prefill and decode step.
Introduces AutoFP, a multi-scale floating-point format supporting 2-, 4-, and 6-bit precision from a shared NVFP4 base format.
Improves accuracy by up to 21.7% over NVFP4 and matches group-scaled FP6 accuracy on most evaluated benchmarks, at 4.9 bits per weight.
Maintains roughly 90–98% of NVFP4 decode throughput on GB300 GPUs; a dedicated accelerator achieves 1.6–2.3× lower latency and 7–23% lower energy at iso-accuracy.

papers.abstract: A language model that never had to forget would keep every document it has read and every turn it has spoken, and answer from any of it. This paper shows that two stock models can do that on unmodified weights by manipulating their geometry. Rotary attention turns each pair of key dimensions, a plane, at its own rate. The slow planes turn once in thousands of tokens and carry the address a query matches when it reads a far key; the fast planes turn once in a few tokens, and the order of the tokens inside a span is already written into its keys and values by the time the span leaves the near window. At distance the position blurs, and what attention reads is a bag rather than a sequence. A far span is read by its words: under competition it is read only if it is visible at the query of the question's own handle word, and a read through a description rather than a word fails at distance in every model measured, a 70B included. These facts allow a trick. What sits in the far part of attention does not have to be the history as it was; it can be installed ahead of the prediction. The design keeps a near window of 8K tokens at their true positions and changes what lies beyond it with the prompt: every far key and value goes to the host exact, a word index finds the units the request's rare words name, a far window of slots inside the trained range holds them while the request is encoded, and a rare word the model generates fetches its units mid-generation with one exact re-encode. Implemented in llama.cpp on Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, the design reads planted single needles at 99 to 100 of 100 and three-key discrimination at 88 to 100 of 100 from 32K to one million tokens, scores 70.8 on RULER against 69.9 for dense attention on Llama-3.1-8B at 128K and 67.8 against 75.5 on Mistral-7B at 32K, and at 128K prefills at 1.85 times and decodes at 1.65 to 1.68 times stock speed.
bullets: Rotary attention preserves address-like information in slow dimensions but loses order for distant spans, making far-context retrieval largely word-based.
The method keeps the nearest 8K tokens at true positions and remaps distant keys and values into trained-range slots selected using rare query words.
During generation, rare generated words can trigger an exact re-encoding to retrieve additional relevant units.
On Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, it retrieved planted needles with 99–100/100 accuracy and achieved 88–100/100 on three-key discrimination from 32K to 1M tokens.
At 128K, it reported 1.85× faster prefilling and 1.65–1.68× faster decoding than stock speed, with task scores varying by model and benchmark.

Figure 1: The life of a far unit, numbered in the order it happens. (a) Store: prefill runs the near window over the document; the keys and values of every token that leaves the window go to the host exact, as written at the token’s true position, and a whole word above 15 nats of surprisal enters the word index with its sentence unit (1). The document is unbounded and the host store grows with it. (b) Retrieve: before the request is encoded, its rare words and the seed look up the index (2); the postings name the units, and the store supplies their keys and values. (c) Insert: a unit is placed at a slot s in the far window, just beyond the near window and inside the trained range, its keys re-rotated from p to s plane by plane (3); the slow planes address it at s, and the order inside it is as written. The request is then encoded over the far window. A rare word the model generates looks up the index the same way (4); the cache is then rewound to the start of the request, and the request and the generated tail are encoded again, exactly, with the fetched units present. The GPU cache holds about 25K cells per layer at any document length.

papers.selection_reason: Modifies attention geometry (rotary attention) to enable stock models to handle unbounded context (up to 1M tokens) with improved speed, contributing to efficient attention mechanisms.
papers.title: Retrofitting Unbounded Context onto Stock Language Models
papers.tldr: A prompt-driven KV-cache remapping strategy gives unmodified language models practical million-token context by preserving an 8K near window and selectively staging relevant far-away text.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) combines student-generated rollouts with dense token-level supervision from a teacher, but providing such supervision for every rollout requires substantial teacher computation. We introduce Success-Referenced On-Policy Distillation (SR-OPD), which reduces this cost by selecting which prompts and rollouts receive teacher supervision. When the student produces both successful and failed rollouts for the same prompt, a successful rollout can serve as a natural reference for selecting failed rollouts. SR-OPD therefore focuses on such prompts and prioritizes failed rollouts whose hidden-state trajectories show sustained divergence from a successful reference, while accounting for estimated teacher-input cost. Across three teacher-student pairs and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, SR-OPD uses only 3.46-5.02% of the teacher-input tokens required by Vanilla OPD in the one-pass setting while maintaining comparable reasoning performance. Under a controlled setting matched to 5% of Vanilla OPD's teacher-input budget, further experiments support both key design choices: focusing supervision on prompts with both successful and failed rollouts, and using successful rollouts to guide failure selection. These results indicate that a student's own successful behavior can serve as a useful reference for allocating teacher supervision under a fixed teacher-input budget.
bullets: Addresses the high teacher-computation cost of supervising every on-policy rollout.
Selects prompts containing both successful and failed student rollouts.
Prioritizes failed rollouts whose hidden-state trajectories persistently diverge from a successful reference, while considering teacher-input cost.
Evaluated across three teacher–student pairs and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
At a matched 5% teacher-input budget, experiments support both success-referenced failure selection and prompt filtering.

papers.selection_reason: Reduces teacher computation in on-policy distillation via selective supervision, an efficiency-oriented method.
papers.title: Spend Teacher Tokens Where They Matter: Success-Referenced On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: SR-OPD cuts teacher supervision to roughly 3.46–5.02% of Vanilla OPD’s token cost while maintaining comparable mathematical reasoning performance by using successful student rollouts to target informative failures.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) improve task performance by generating longer intermediate reasoning traces, but this substantially increases inference costs and makes low-precision quantization increasingly important. However, aggressively quantized models often perform poorly on reasoning tasks. We observe larger activation fluctuations during the first decoding steps of reasoning. Calibration that omits these early states may miss their activation fluctuations. To address these reasoning-specific quantization challenges, we propose \textbf{CodeQuant2}, a clustering-based LUT quantization framework for low-precision large reasoning models. CodeQuant2 mitigates activation outliers with rotation and scaling, uses clustering to represent non-uniform weight distributions, and adapts codebook sizes to the quantization difficulty of each layer. Guided by our observation of reasoning-time activation behavior, CodeQuant2 further improves calibration sample selection to better match actual decoding statistics. Combined with our customized LUT CUDA kernel, CodeQuant2 delivers substantial accuracy improvements on reasoning benchmarks while achieving up to $2.85\times$ speedup over BF16.
authors: Xingyu Liu, Xiangyang Yin, Tianhua Xia, Haiyu Wang, Sai Qian Zhang
bullets: Targets the accuracy degradation and high inference cost caused by aggressive quantization of reasoning models.
Mitigates activation outliers through rotation and scaling, and represents non-uniform weights with clustering-based lookup-table quantization.
Adapts codebook sizes to the quantization difficulty of individual layers.
Selects calibration samples to better capture activation behavior during the early steps of reasoning.
Reports substantial accuracy gains on reasoning benchmarks and up to 2.85× speedup over BF16.
