papers.selection_reason: Low-precision quantization of large reasoning models directly reduces inference memory and compute, fitting the Efficient AI scope.
papers.title: CodeQuant2: Enhanced Outlier Mitigation and Adaptive Clustering for Low-Precision LRMs
papers.tldr: CodeQuant2 improves low-precision quantization for large reasoning models by modeling early decoding activations and adapting weight codebooks, while accelerating inference by up to 2.85× over BF16.

papers.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.

Stays within 0.5 accuracy points of BF16 KV with NVFP4 and within 1 point with MXFP4 across dense and MoE models.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel, lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) designed for edge device deployment. The CNN is developed to recognize and classify threats or targets of interest. The model is equipped with a real-time hotspot detection algorithm, which enables it to process information quickly and accurately, resulting in improved inference time of up to 20 fps and a detection range of more than 400 meters with typical thermal situational awareness sensors. The proposed CNN has been rigorously tested and validated to demonstrate its high accuracy, sensitivity, and low false positive rate, providing a reliable solution for edge devices to detect potential targets. Additionally, the lightweight design of the CNN allows for easy deployment, making it an ideal solution for extending the security bubble for edge devices. The proposed model can be used for a variety of applications, including surveillance, security, and object recognition.
authors: Hughes Perreault, Ola Ahmad, Daniel Czuboka
bullets: Proposes a lightweight CNN for recognizing and classifying targets or threats on edge devices.

papers.abstract: Large-language-model decode attention streams the key-value (KV) cache for every generated token. Packing that cache into 2-bit or 4-bit quantized integers reduces memory traffic but does not automatically translate into latency saving. Existing 2-bit fused kernels reach under 31%/15% of peak HBM throughput on H100/B200. Converting each value and applying its scale and offset before feeding Tensor Cores is a major bottleneck because instruction-issue throughput is scarce on modern GPUs. Instead of applying scale and offset to each KV value, FOSCAR uses affine folding to apply them to the other operand or the output of decode-attention matrix products, depending on the quantization scheme (token-wise or channel-wise). This reduces scale-and-offset operations by up to two orders of magnitude while preserving the dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic. FOSCAR also uses bit manipulation to feed KV operands to Tensor Cores efficiently, requiring only 1 and 0.19 ALU instructions per INT2 element on H100 and B200, respectively. Finally, FOSCAR builds warp-specialized GPU pipelines for Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) using wgmma and tcgen05. On H100, FOSCAR INT2 and INT4 kernels achieve geo-mean speedups of $3.36\times$ and $2.83\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, and $2.03\times$ and $1.71\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8. On B200, the corresponding INT2 and INT4 speedups are $2.67\times$ and $2.30\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, $1.48\times$ and $1.28\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8, and $1.16\times$ and $1.00\times$ over TensorRT-LLM NVFP4. We integrate FOSCAR into SGLang to benchmark serving efficiency. On long-context serving workloads, FOSCAR increases peak aggregate throughput by up to 170% and 341% over 2-bit and 16-bit baselines, respectively. We open-source FOSCAR as a kernel library at https://github.com/FutureMLS-Lab/FOSCAR.
authors: Donglin Zhuang, Pragaash Ponnusamy, Xiaoxia Wu, Shuaiwen Leon Song, Zhongzhu Zhou
bullets: Targets decode attention, where quantized KV caches reduce memory traffic but can remain latency-bound by dequantization overhead.
Uses affine folding tailored to token-wise or channel-wise quantization, preserving the exact dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic.
Employs bit manipulation and warp-specialized Hopper/Blackwell GPU pipelines to efficiently feed quantized operands to Tensor Cores.
Reports substantial kernel speedups on H100 and B200 against BF16, FP8, and, in some cases, NVFP4 baselines.
Integrated into SGLang, it improves peak aggregate throughput on long-context serving workloads by up to 170% versus 2-bit and 341% versus 16-bit baselines.

papers.abstract: Modern LLM serving systems use prefix caching to accelerate multi-turn conversational workloads. They cache the key-value states of previous conversation prefixes and reuse them when subsequent requests share the same prefix, to avoid redundant prefill computation and reduce serving latency. However, achieving a high cache hit rate remains challenging because cache reuse depends on whether a conversation continues and how soon the next turn arrives. Our analysis of real workloads shows that user intent is a useful signal for this behavior, as different intents exhibit different continuation probabilities and inter-turn delays. Based on this key insight, we propose Intent-Aware Caching (IAC), an online eviction policy that classifies requests by intent, learns lightweight reuse statistics from recent serving logs and leverages these statistics to guide an oracle-inspired eviction strategy. Extensive evaluation on real workloads (WildChat and ShareChat) shows that IAC reaches a 34.6% cache hit rate. This substantially outperforms both the previous learning-based approach (18.8%) and traditional methods such as least recently used (LRU, 12.2%), while reducing average serving latency by up to 46.1%.
authors: Kazi Hasan Ibn Arif, JinYi Yoon, Dimitrios S. Nikolopoulos, Hans Vandierendonck, Deepu John, Bo Ji
bullets: Prefix caching accelerates multi-turn LLM serving by reusing key-value states, but reuse is difficult to predict.
User intent correlates with conversation continuation probability and inter-turn delay.
IAC classifies requests, learns lightweight reuse statistics from recent logs, and applies an oracle-inspired online eviction policy.
On WildChat and ShareChat, IAC achieves a 34.6% cache hit rate versus 18.8% for a prior learning-based method and 12.2% for LRU.
IAC reduces average serving latency by up to 46.1%.

papers.abstract: RidgeFill shortens prefill by not computing most of a model's upper layers for the prompt. The lower layers run exactly up to a split; from the split layer's state a per-layer map predicts every later layer's input, and each late layer writes its cache from that prediction. The design follows YOCO and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, where the projection is trained into the model. RidgeFill retrofits it onto models that were never trained for it: the map is a ridge regression fitted once in closed form from one pass over calibration text, the layer's own projections run unchanged, and a chosen set of rows, the last few thousand tokens, and every decoding step run the full model. Nothing is trained and no token is dropped. Most of the work was in measurement, finding a repeatable methodology. Loss averaged over all tokens hides RidgeFill's error. Needle retrieval in the filled region, loss on tokens that depend on distant context, and splice tests that swap filled keys or values for exact ones show which component carries it: the keys on Llama-3.1-8B, half of it in their scale, and the values and the recurrent state on Qwen3.5-9B. On Qwen3.8-27B in a llama.cpp fork on an A100, time to first token is 1.25 to 1.31x faster at 16K to 120K tokens with the maps in VRAM; RULER changes by -1.2 and -1.4 points and LongBench v2 by -1.4; the 95 % intervals include zero but do not rule out losses of a few points. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in vLLM it is 1.50 to 1.60x faster than exact at 9K to 32K tokens, with RULER's needle tasks at 99.8 against 100.0 and perplexity on novel tokens 2.65 % higher [-0.02 %, +4.93 %]. On three 8 to 9B reference models, at the same split and tail as the identity fill, the fitted map retrieves 49.1 and 49.6 more filled-region RULER points on the two dense models (at that split Llama's loss is worse), and its long-document loss is +/-0.03 nats of the released SwiftKV checkpoint's.
bullets: Runs lower layers normally, predicts later-layer inputs, and fills their caches while preserving selected rows, recent tokens, and all decoding steps exactly.
Fits each prediction map once in closed form from calibration text, making the approach training-free and applicable to models not designed for cache filling.
Evaluation finds that keys dominate error on Llama-3.1-8B, while values and recurrent state matter more on Qwen3.5-9B.
On evaluated systems, prefill speed improves 1.25–1.31× at 16K–120K tokens and 1.50–1.60× at 9K–32K tokens.
Quality changes are generally small but uncertain: reported benchmark shifts include roughly 1–1.4 point decreases, while some needle tasks remain near exact performance.

Row positions are illustrative.

Figure 4. Why the correction matters only on layers that remember. A prompt row’s weight in a Gated DeltaNet layer’s final state is the product of the gates after it; tan is the filled prefix and blue the exact tail. (a) With gates of 0.90, the filled rows’ share of the final state is about 0.005. (b) With gates of 0.995 it is 0.65. Illustrative: 200 rows, the last 50 exact. The share shown is the share of the state the tail ends with, not ρ at the end of the prefix (§2.3).

Figure 5. The two-sweep prefill on Qwen3.8-27B, split at layer 16. (1) The first sweep runs layers 0 to 15 for every row and writes the prefix rows’ late attention caches from the maps; the tail and the late Gated DeltaNet layers are not yet computed. (2) The probe: the last 256 rows run the exact late layers over the filled cache, with the Gated DeltaNet layers starting from an empty state, and every prefix row is ranked by the attention it receives from them. (3) The second sweep runs the late layers for the chosen rows and the tail, and carries the Gated DeltaNet state once over every prefix row; the other rows keep their filled attention caches.

Figure 1. Speculative decoding and RidgeFill each spend the resource their phase has spare. Decoding is bandwidth-bound, so a draft head spends the spare compute guessing tokens and the full model verifies every guess. Prefill reuses each weight read across hundreds of prompt rows, so it is limited by arithmetic. RidgeFill spends the spare bandwidth on extra reads, the fill maps from VRAM or host memory, and in return skips most of the late layers’ arithmetic. A filled cache has no affordable verifier, so the rows most likely to matter are kept exact instead (§2.4).

Figure 6. How the probe’s budget is set. The base rules, the rarer half of the protected-class matches, every digit token, and the top 20 % of the prefix by lower-layer question attention, are used only to count E, the number of exact prefix rows. The probe fills E with the rows that receive the most late-layer attention from the last 256 rows; lexical-net rows are reserved inside E, at most 5 % of the prefix. Special tokens are added on top, and the 4,096-token tail is outside the count. On the 27B timing prompts E came to 28 to 31 % of the prefix.

papers.abstract: Attention is a major scalability bottleneck in large language models (LLMs), with its computational cost and key-value (KV) memory traffic becoming increasingly prohibitive as context length grows. Sparse attention addresses this bottleneck by restricting each query to a subset of the context, but its effectiveness hinges on identifying relevant regions both cheaply and reliably. Existing training-free methods primarily rely on runtime relevance estimates, with selection dimensionality and granularity typically governed by fixed heuristics rather than the intrinsic interaction structure of pretrained attention heads. We take a different perspective: the query-key operator of each pretrained head defines a characteristic response structure that determines the resolution needed for sparse selection, both across feature directions and across context tokens. Building on this insight, we propose Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention (HASA), a training-free sparse attention framework that jointly adapts selection resolution along these two dimensions. Along the feature dimension, the singular spectrum of each head's query-key operator determines an effective rank, yielding a compact, head-specific response space. Along the sequence dimension, neighboring regions are progressively merged according to the directional coherence of their token responses in this same space, while heterogeneous regions remain separate. Exact attention is then computed using the original full-dimensional KV states of the selected regions. HASA captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass and, compared with UNIQUE, a strong recent sparse-attention baseline, improves accuracy by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points on RULER and LongBench-Pro, respectively, and accelerates self-attention by up to 1.32x, while achieving up to 14.07x speedup over dense attention.
authors: Wajih Hassan Raza, Ahsan Bilal, Yidan Shen, Renjie Hu, Xin Fu, Yu Wen
bullets: Targets the computational and KV-memory bottleneck of attention as context length grows.
Uses each head’s query-key operator to determine an effective feature rank and compact response space.
Merges neighboring token regions when their responses are directionally coherent, while preserving heterogeneous regions separately.
Computes exact attention with original full-dimensional KV states for selected regions.
Captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass, improves reported RULER and LongBench-Pro accuracy over UNIQUE by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points, and reaches up to 14.07× speedup over dense attention.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model training is increasingly constrained by memory capacity. Activation Checkpointing reduces activation memory by avoiding storing selected activations during the forward pass and rematerializing them during backpropagation, thereby trading memory savings for additional computation. Although this technique is essential for scaling model training, rematerialization can be prohibitively expensive, particularly for Transformer linear layers. Approximate computation could reduce this overhead, but conventional approaches either introduce errors that accumulate over the backward pass or fail to exploit information available from the initial forward pass. We introduce a novel approximate rematerialization method that can yield unbiased gradient estimates: using information collected during the initial forward pass, the method selectively recomputes only the most important layer components, either through greedy selection or randomized sketching. Ablation studies show that the resulting gradients closely match the exact gradients. When applied to feed-forward layers, attention layers, or both, our method can recompute only two-thirds of the layer components in a Llama-488M model, while increasing perplexity by just 1.7%, 1.2%, and 2.5%, respectively.
bullets: Targets the memory–computation tradeoff in large language model training.
Uses information from the original forward pass to guide approximate rematerialization.
Selects components via greedy selection or randomized sketching.
Ablations find gradients closely match exact gradients.
In a Llama-488M model, recomputing two-thirds of feed-forward, attention, or both layer components raises perplexity by 1.7%, 1.2%, or 2.5%, respectively.

papers.abstract: Private, personalised language models must run on local consumer devices, where large, frontier models cannot fit, and retaining long contexts is non-trivial. Sequential memory---the key-value (KV) cache---grows linearly with context length, quickly dwarfing the model itself: for Qwen3-1.7B-Base, 200,000 retained entries require 21 GiB, 6.6 times more than the model weights. Yet the KV-cache compression methods we measured fail beyond moderate compression ratios. We introduce Transformer-FSQ, addressing extreme KV-cache compression by replacing standard key and value projections with a finite scalar quantisation bottleneck. Our cache stores a packed vector of discrete integer codes per token, with no per-token quantisation metadata. Converting a pretrained transformer trains only these projections on 0.25 tokens per original parameter. We evaluate Transformer-FSQ against five baseline families on models from 0.6B to 8B parameters. On long-context retrieval (RULER), from 12$\times$ to 97.5$\times$ Transformer-FSQ is the most accurate method we evaluate, across scales. A fused Triton kernel decodes directly from the integer codes; with baselines given their authors' kernels where available, it decodes at $1.01\times$ (95% interval $0.98$--$1.05$) the throughput of native SDPA attention on the uncompressed Qwen3-8B-Base at $32\times$ and $1.54\times$ at $97.5\times$. Extreme KV-cache compression is therefore a practical way to extend how much context a fixed device can hold.
authors: Andras Szecsenyi, Thomas L. Lee, Vaisakh Shaj, Elliot J. Crowley, Amos Storkey
bullets: Targets the memory bottleneck of long-context inference on local consumer devices, where KV caches can exceed model weights.
Replaces standard key/value projections with a finite scalar quantisation bottleneck and stores packed, metadata-free integer codes.
Adapts pretrained transformers by retraining only the key/value projections using 0.25 tokens per original parameter.
Across 0.6B–8B models, it is the most accurate evaluated method on RULER at 12×–97.5× compression.
A fused Triton decoder reaches near-native SDPA throughput at 32× compression and 1.54× native throughput at 97.5× on Qwen3-8B-Base.

papers.abstract: AI weather prediction models are released with 32-bit (fp32) weights and run in fp32 by default, although current GPUs compute much faster in 16-bit formats. We run five publicly available models -- Aurora, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, SFNO and FastNet -- on a single 16 GB GPU from 52 initial dates in 2024, in fp32 and with their networks in half precision (fp16), and verify the forecasts against ERA5. The physical state must stay in fp32: converting the whole model rounds it in physical units, which in fp16 overflows and in bf16 discards meaningful information. With the state, its normalisation and denormalisation in fp32, running the network in fp16 changes the global RMSE by at most 1.4%, and by about 0.5% or less for four of the five models, equivalent to less than one hour of lead time up to day 8 and at most two hours at day 10. The differences show no systematic pattern by region, scale or for tropical and extratropical storms, apart from a small tropical penalty in FourCastNet, and fp16 leaves the CRPS, spread and calibration of Aurora's ensemble almost unchanged. No value overflowed fp16's numeric range (+/-65,504); the largest stay 38 to 544 times below it. A 10-day forecast in fp16 is 1.3-3.5 times faster than in fp32 and uses 1.4-3.7 times less energy. Sensitivity experiments show that rules of thumb from other applications of reduced precision carry over only partly: the first and last layers dominate for some models but not for others, and no type of layer is sensitive on its own. For running AI weather models on a single GPU, fp16 with the state in fp32 is practically lossless at a fraction of the cost. bf16, often preferred for its wider range, is as fast but less accurate than fp16 for every model, and simple 8-bit quantisation costs far more skill.

fp16 inference is 1.3–3.5× faster and uses 1.4–3.7× less energy on a single 16 GB GPU.
bf16 is less accurate than fp16 in these tests, while simple 8-bit quantization causes substantially greater skill loss.

papers.selection_reason: Half-precision inference of AI weather models reduces compute and energy cost, fitting efficient AI, while the models themselves are environment-dynamics predictors.
papers.title: Half-precision inference of AI weather prediction models: negligible loss of skill at a fraction of the cost
papers.tldr: Running AI weather models with fp16 networks while keeping physical states in fp32 preserves forecast skill almost entirely while substantially reducing inference cost.

papers.abstract: Non-contact fruit sizing from RGB-D imagery reaches sub-centimetre accuracy on workstation hardware, but in-field grading requires the same pipeline to run on a low-power single-board computer, and the cost of that transition is rarely reported. We deploy a curvature-aware cucumber length-measurement pipeline (YOLO26n detection, prompt-based segmentation and a medial arc spline estimator) on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and a Raspberry Pi 4, and characterize both against an RTX 3050 Ti workstation by replaying 50 identical greenhouse captures of 7 specimens, with specimen-level cluster-bootstrap statistics. Accuracy is preserved: mean absolute error (MAE) is 0.58 cm (95% CI 0.46-0.69) on both the workstation and the Jetson at matched precision, with a paired difference of zero. TensorRT FP16 compilation cuts Jetson detection latency 2.57x, giving two operating points on one board: 72 ms per fruit at 0.84 cm, or 2.74 s at 0.64 cm. Four ablations map the design space. For prompted segmentation backends, measurement accuracy is fixed by the backend and reproduces across platforms to within 0.01 cm, while its cost is fixed by the platform and varies 214x, so the two choices are separable. Whole-graph INT8 quantization of the NMS-free detection head fails structurally, returning no detections, because one output tensor carries both pixel coordinates and confidences; we show that no calibration strategy can avoid this. Excluding the head restores function at 1.37x. Energy per fruit is 42.2 J on the Jetson, and its 7 W mode consumes 73% more than its 15 W mode. The Raspberry Pi with MobileSAM costs 2.5x more per fruit than the Jetson with SAM despite drawing 47% less power, and it runs without thermal throttling under sustained load. The results define an accuracy-throughput-energy envelope with three non-dominated configurations and give rules for selecting among them.
authors: Manveen Kaur, Rajmeet Singh, Saeed Mozaffari, Majid Ahmadi, Shahpour Alirezaee
bullets: The pipeline combines YOLO26n detection, prompted segmentation, and medial arc spline estimation, evaluated on identical greenhouse captures across a workstation, Jetson Orin Nano, and Raspberry Pi 4.
Jetson accuracy matches the workstation at 0.58 cm MAE; TensorRT FP16 enables either 72 ms-per-fruit processing at 0.84 cm MAE or 2.74 s at 0.64 cm MAE.

Segmentation accuracy is largely backend-dependent, while segmentation cost is platform-dependent; whole-graph INT8 quantization fails for the coupled detection output, but excluding that head restores operation at 1.37× speedup.
Jetson energy use is 42.2 J per fruit; its 7 W mode consumes more energy per fruit than its 15 W mode, while the Raspberry Pi runs without thermal throttling but costs more energy per fruit.
The study identifies three non-dominated accuracy–throughput–energy configurations and provides selection rules for edge deployment.

papers.selection_reason: Characterizes the accuracy, throughput, and energy of an RGB-D cucumber sizing pipeline deployed on edge devices, relevant to efficient AI and 3D vision applications.
papers.title: CucumberVision at the Edge: Accuracy, Throughput, and Energy of RGB-D Cucumber Sizing on Jetson Orin Nano and Raspberry Pi 4
papers.tldr: A curvature-aware RGB-D cucumber-sizing pipeline preserves sub-centimetre accuracy on the Jetson Orin Nano while revealing clear accuracy, throughput, and energy trade-offs across edge hardware and configurations.

papers.abstract: We present MINE (Memory-efficient INference Engine), a lossless entropy coding approach that accelerates single-stream inference of Large Language Models (LLMs), where existing lossless compression methods yield speedups only for specific data types such as \texttt{BF16} and under additional assumptions. Single-stream decoding is strongly memory-bound, since every weight must be streamed from memory once per generated token and requests cannot be batched in local or low-latency deployments. At the core of MINE is dtANS-LLM, a GPU entropy coding scheme adapted from the prior dtANS to the needs of LLM inference. It exploits the non-uniform distribution of weights, which persists even after quantization, and exposes hyper-parameters that trade compression ratio against decoding cost. We auto-tune these parameters for each tensor and GPU to obtain the Pareto front between model size and decoding latency. MINE integrates into vLLM as a plugin and selects the best kernel configuration for a given memory budget. On Llama~3.1~8B~Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint, MINE achieves speedups of 2.52$\times$ and 1.48$\times$ over the fastest baseline on an RTX~4060~Ti and an RTX~5090, at effective bitrates of 2.24 and 3.43~bits per weight. MINE is available as open source.
bullets: Targets single-stream inference, where weights must be streamed from memory for each generated token and batching is unavailable.
Introduces dtANS-LLM, which exploits non-uniform weight distributions that remain after quantization.
Auto-tunes tensor- and GPU-specific parameters to balance compression ratio and decoding latency under a memory budget.
Integrates with vLLM and reports speedups on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint on two GPUs.
Scope: results focus on single-stream inference and the evaluated Llama checkpoint/GPU configurations.

papers.selection_reason: Entropy-coded memory-efficient LLM inference directly reduces model memory requirements and speeds up deployment.
papers.title: MINE: Entropy-coded Memory-efficient Inference for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: MINE accelerates memory-bound single-stream LLM inference through GPU entropy coding that compresses and decodes weights losslessly.

papers.abstract: Multimodal model training breaks the loose coupling between data loading and model execution assumed by conventional training pipelines. Large per-sample variation in decoding cost, token/latent count, and tensor size causes both CPU preprocessing time and GPU compute time to vary substantially across data-parallel ranks (training processes). In synchronous training, these two sources of heterogeneity interact tightly: GPU execution determines how long the input pipeline has to prepare the next batch, while delayed preprocessing in any rank in turn stalls all GPUs at synchronization. As a result, optimizing CPU throughput or GPU load balance in isolation cannot eliminate pipeline bubbles. We present DataHelix, a metadata-first CPU-GPU co-scheduling data plane for multimodal training. DataHelix jointly reasons about preprocessing demand and GPU execution progress, treating each GPU compute window as the readiness budget for the next batch and coordinating preprocessing across ranks to minimize deadline misses rather than CPU makespan. To avoid expensive data movement, placement is decided while samples remain lightweight descriptors, before decoding and collation amplify them into large tensors. Descriptor-level token-latent-aware batching performs coarse pre-balancing, while cost-gated collective rebalancing corrects residual skew only when its expected benefit exceeds transfer cost. Across 11 video and multimodal workloads on 8 Ascend 910B accelerators, DataHelix reduces mean deadline-miss rate by 67.8% and mean p95 input-wait latency by 87.0%, while achieving 2.72x geometric-mean throughput over rank-local DataLoaders and 1.82x over a Ray actor pool under the same CPU budget.
authors: Yuanhe Li, Jiazhen Wu, Dian Ding, Guangtao Xue, Yiming Zhang
bullets: Addresses variable decoding, token/latent counts, and tensor sizes that cause rank imbalance and synchronization stalls.
Uses GPU compute windows as readiness budgets, optimizing deadline misses rather than CPU preprocessing makespan.
Performs descriptor-level token/latent-aware batching before expensive decoding and tensor expansion.
Applies collective rebalancing only when its expected benefit outweighs data-transfer cost.
Across 11 workloads on 8 Ascend 910B accelerators, reduces mean deadline misses by 67.8%, cuts p95 input-wait latency by 87.0%, and improves throughput over two baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses computational efficiency in multimodal model training through CPU-GPU co-scheduling to handle heterogeneity in data loading and execution, fitting the Efficient AI category.
papers.title: DataHelix: A CPU-GPU Co-Scheduling Data Plane for Multimodal Model Training
papers.tldr: DataHelix co-schedules CPU preprocessing with GPU execution to reduce pipeline stalls in heterogeneous multimodal training.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable parallel token generation through iterative denoising, yet their inference remains costly due to repeated attention over a growing historical prefix and repeated processing of the entire current generation block. Historical attention becomes increasingly expensive as generation progresses, while all current-block positions are propagated through the Transformer at every denoising step even though only a small fraction are typically resolved at that step. In this paper, we introduce Duet, a training-free dual-sparse inference framework that addresses these challenges through prefix Key-Value (KV) sparsity and early query sparsity, respectively. Specifically, Duet exploits the concentration and cross-step stability of historical attention within each generation block to construct a compact historical KV subset that is reused across denoising steps. For query sparsity, Duet predicts update positions from shallow representations and propagates only the corresponding queries through the suffix Transformer layers, avoiding deep computation at positions unlikely to be updated in the current step. Experiments show that Duet maintains competitive accuracy while achieving 1.34$\times$/2.83$\times$ end-to-end/per-step speedups on LLaDA2.1-mini and 2.41$\times$/4.72$\times$ on SDAR-8B-Chat-b32 at a 32K context length.
authors: Siyuan Yan, Shen Gu, Xiaoxing Ma, Chun Cao, Jingwei Xu
bullets: Targets two inference costs: growing historical-prefix attention and repeated processing of mostly unchanged generation positions.
Uses prefix KV sparsity by selecting a compact, cross-step-stable subset of historical keys and values.
Uses early query sparsity to predict which positions will update, then runs only their queries through deeper Transformer layers.
Training-free and evaluated at 32K context length.
Reports end-to-end/per-step speedups of 1.34×/2.83× on LLaDA2.1-mini and 2.41×/4.72× on SDAR-8B-Chat-b32.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Duet. (A) Block-level prefix selection: After the first dense step, Duet selects a compact historical prefix subset for each sparse suffix layer and reuses the resulting KV cache within the generation block. (B) Step-wise query selection: in subsequent denoising steps, Duet identifies active query rows at an early selection layer and propagates only these rows through the remaining Transformer layers, reducing redundant computation in both attention and FFN/MoE. Active and bypassed states are then recombined for the next denoising step.

Figure 4: Inference speedup across context lengths. End-to-end and stable-step speedups over dense inference on LLaDA2.1-mini and SDAR-8B at 8K, 16K, and 32K context lengths. Stable-step latency averages all denoising steps except the first step, highlighting the execution efficiency of sparse decoding. Duet achieves increasingly larger speedups as the context grows and consistently provides the strongest stable-step acceleration among the compared methods.

Figure 3: LongBench quality–throughput trade-off. Five-task Macro-F1 relative to each model’s dense score (100%) versus 32K end-to-end throughput. Absolute Macro-F1 scores are reported in Table 1; task-wise results appear in Appendix Table 4.

Our method is designed around the two orthogonal computation dimensions, selectively reducing both the query rows propagated through deep layers and the historical prefix KV states they attend to.

Figure 5: Two sparsity opportunities in BDLM inference. (a) A compact prefix subset selected at the beginning of a generation block continues to cover most of the prefix-attention mass throughout denoising. (b) Intermediate representations can identify, with high recall, the positions selected by the final-layer decoding policy. Results are shown on LLaDA2.1-mini as a representative example.

For LoSA, parentheses give the measured average number of attended prefix KV tokens per task; the Macro-F1 column gives the mean of these five KV counts. Higher F1 is better.

papers.selection_reason: Directly targets efficient inference for diffusion language models via prefix KV sparsity and query sparsity.
papers.title: DUET: Dual-Sparse Inference for Block Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Duet accelerates block diffusion language model inference by sparsifying both historical attention and current-step query computation while maintaining competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Low-precision matrix throughput on modern GPUs is growing far faster than vector-arithmetic throughput. Attention therefore cannot realize the available GEMM performance because softmax has become the pipeline bottleneck. We introduce Fused-Softmax Attention, a training-free algorithm that reformulates and approximates softmax to fold its dominant operations into the attention GEMMs, moving work from vector units to matrix cores. Implemented for the AMD CDNA 4 architecture, our MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4 kernels reach approximately 3.0, 4.0 and 4.6 PFLOP/s on an AMD Instinct MI355X GPU, yielding speedups of $2.1\times$, $2.8\times$ and $3.2\times$ over the BF16 attention. Importantly, the additional error introduced by Fused-Softmax remains below the error floor set by quantizing the GEMM operands. On Wan2.2-T2V-A14B, a hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule delivers up to $2.05\times$ end-to-end speedup while preserving the visual quality of the outputs. The kernels ship in AMD's open-source AITER library, and they powered AMD's MLPerf Inference v6.1 Wan2.2 submission, which ran $1.7\times$ faster than AMD's previous-round result on the same hardware. Our results show that redesigning softmax to utilize the matrix pipeline enables attention to capitalize on continued growth in low-precision matrix throughput.
authors: Tianxing Wu, Juuso Korhonen, Jesus Carabano Bravo
bullets: Addresses softmax as the bottleneck preventing attention from exploiting rapidly increasing low-precision matrix throughput.
Introduces a training-free approximation that folds dominant softmax operations into attention GEMMs.
On AMD CDNA 4, MXFP8/6/4 kernels achieve about 3.0/4.0/4.6 PFLOP/s and 2.1×/2.8×/3.2× speedups over BF16 attention.
A hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule provides up to 2.05× end-to-end speedup on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B without degrading visual quality.
Implemented in AMD’s open-source AITER library and used in an MLPerf Inference v6.1 submission.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a training-free algorithm that folds softmax operations into attention GEMMs to exploit low-precision matrix throughput, a direct efficiency contribution to attention computation.
papers.title: Fused-Softmax for efficient quantized attention
papers.tldr: Fused-Softmax reformulates softmax to use GPU matrix cores, substantially accelerating quantized attention while keeping its added error within the GEMM quantization error floor.

papers.abstract: Although time-series foundation models (TSFMs) achieve strong zero-shot transferability across high-information-density physical systems, applying overparameterized TSFMs to quantitative finance is fundamentally constrained by low signal-to-noise ratios, non-stationarity, and prohibitive autoregressive decoding latency. To reconcile representation learning with institutional operational constraints, this study presents TailDART, a dense 2.68 million-parameter foundation model engineered for financial time-series forecasting. By integrating grouped-query attention into a lightweight backbone, the architecture drastically reduces Key-Value cache memory bandwidth overhead, achieving major inference acceleration (up to 48.1%) over prevailing state-of-the-art TSFMs to enable low-latency, high-throughput streaming execution. Furthermore, multi-asset benchmarks across varying temporal resolutions show that a compact model can remain competitive for market forecasting: TailDART matches the predictive fidelity of substantially larger baselines while demonstrating superior error resilience in high-volatility regimes.
authors: Chiang Qin Zhi, Ranjan Satapathy, Erik Cambria, Joyjit Chattoraj
bullets: Targets finance-specific challenges including low signal-to-noise ratios, non-stationarity, and costly autoregressive decoding.
Uses a lightweight 2.68M-parameter backbone with grouped-query attention to reduce Key-Value cache memory-bandwidth overhead.
Reports inference acceleration of up to 48.1% compared with existing state-of-the-art time-series foundation models.
Across multi-asset, multi-resolution benchmarks, matches larger baselines’ predictive fidelity and is more resilient during high-volatility periods.

papers.selection_reason: Lightweight financial time-series foundation model with grouped-query attention reduces KV cache memory and inference latency, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: TailDART: Compute-Efficient Foundation Models for Financial Time-Series Forecasting
papers.tldr: TailDART is a compact financial time-series foundation model designed to deliver competitive forecasting with substantially lower inference latency.

papers.abstract: Reasoning traces improve vision-language models on complex multimodal tasks, but forcing every input to follow a long reasoning process leads to overthinking and unnecessary inference cost. We study adaptive fast/slow thinking for VLMs, where one model answers directly for simple inputs and reasons step by step when needed. Fast answers and slow traces often come from distinct behavior policies, making a single-reference offline objective misweight one mode. We propose DUAL-REFERENCE BOLT (DR-BOLT), which distinguishes the desired fast/slow mixture reference from the sampling distribution and corrects their mismatch in reward-weighted training. Fast/slow partition competition explains routing in the optimal target; an efficient source-wise correction approximates the exact objective when response formats are well separated. Matched Qwen3-VL comparisons use identical candidate banks to isolate the objective from slow-teacher quality. DR-BOLT improves score-length trade-offs over the evaluated offline and online baselines on ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, with a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and a 2.90-fold end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO. These results support adaptive reasoning in the studied two-reference setting, while broader robustness remains open. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongbinLin3589/DR-BOLT.
authors: Hongbin Lin, Sizhe Zou, Juangui Xu, Xinyue Xu, Zhuoli Ouyang, Stanislav Kolchin, Chengwei Qin, Zhongxiang Dai, Yao Shu
bullets: Addresses overthinking and unnecessary inference cost from forcing long reasoning on every input.
Uses dual references to model the desired fast/slow mixture separately from the sampling distribution.
Explains routing through competition between fast and slow response partitions, with an efficient source-wise correction when formats are separated.
On ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, improves score–length trade-offs over evaluated offline and online baselines.
Reports a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and 2.90× end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO; broader robustness remains open.

papers.abstract: Hand-object interactions (HOIs) can be captured by smartglasses to learn how people manipulate objects in daily life. Automatic logging of these interactions from an egocentric perspective provides time-stamped evidence of daily actions for applications like memory assistance. However, continuous RGB capture and wireless transmission exceed the energy and bandwidth budgets of smartglasses. We present EventHOI, an event-driven sensing and compression system that couples selective RGB capture with HOI-aware encoding to enable egocentric logging over Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) while preserving downstream HOI logging performance. Our key insight is to use low-power event sensing both to determine when RGB capture is needed and to identify where visual detail must be preserved. A lightweight IMU-based egomotion cancellation pipeline suppresses egomotion-induced events so that residual HOI motion can guide RGB triggering and spatial compression. We build a smartglasses prototype and conduct an end-to-end evaluation of EventHOI on a 50-hour egocentric benchmark with 97 subjects and a 20-hour real-world dataset we collect from 10 participants, together covering a broad range of daily-life scenarios and environments. Compared to RGB-only baselines, EventHOI reduces always-on backend power consumption by 5.8-10.4x and uplink bandwidth by 2.9x, with minimal HOI recognition accuracy loss. The resulting RGB uplink of less than 130 kbps fits within commodity BLE bandwidth budgets, making stable BLE video streaming feasible for egocentric HOI logging. Demo video and project website: https://eventhoi.github.io

Evaluated on a 50-hour benchmark with 97 subjects and a 20-hour real-world dataset from 10 participants.
Achieves 5.8–10.4× lower backend power and 2.9× lower uplink bandwidth than RGB-only baselines, with minimal HOI accuracy loss and under 130 kbps RGB uplink.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed many areas of artificial intelligence (AI), but their substantial resource requirements limit their deployment on mobile and edge devices. Although LLMs have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various applications, the next challenge is deploying these models on resource-limited edge devices. Recent innovations in software optimizations and specialized hardware have made it feasible to deploy LLMs on edge devices. Edge deployment offers benefits including local data processing, cost savings, reduced latency, and personalized responses. This paper reviews the latest techniques that make the deployment of LLMs on edge devices feasible.

bullets: LLMs’ substantial resource requirements hinder deployment on mobile and edge hardware.

Local inference can improve privacy through on-device processing, reduce costs and latency, and support personalization.
The paper focuses on practical techniques for deploying LLMs under edge-device resource constraints.

papers.abstract: Routers typically choose a model per query by trading predicted correctness against cost. Most price each model at a fixed cost, as if every query used the same number of output tokens, but the output length of reasoning models varies by an order of magnitude across queries. When is per-query cost worth predicting? What factors drive cost? How cheaply can predictions be made? We predict both the success probability and the output length of candidate models from the prefill activations of a single small frozen LLM, the scout. With reasoning candidates, perfect per-query cost knowledge would save 29-61% of spending on eight of nine datasets, and much less with non-reasoning candidates on the same problems. On those eight datasets, our predicted costs save 9-33% at matched accuracy relative to median-length pricing, up to 69% of what perfect knowledge would save. They are significantly cheaper than each estimator we reimplemented or adapted from published work, including ZeroRouter and a MixLLM-style predictor, on a majority of datasets. Output length depends mostly on the problem. On most math and code datasets, harder problems are longer, so predicted success alone prices cost nearly as well. On knowledge and mixed-format datasets they are not, and predicted success falls well behind a probe trained on length. The probe keeps most of its saving with 20 labelled problems and transfers without labels to four of seven new benchmarks. On a mixture of all nine benchmarks, it saves 22% beyond pricing each benchmark at its own median length. Savings stop growing at about a 2B scout, so above 4B a larger scout costs more than it adds.
bullets: Per-query cost prediction matters most for reasoning models, whose output lengths vary widely across queries.
The method uses prefill activations from one small frozen LLM (“scout”) to predict candidate-model success and output length.
Predicted costs save 9–33% at matched accuracy on eight of nine datasets, capturing up to 69% of the savings available with perfect cost knowledge.
Problem difficulty often predicts length on math and code tasks, while explicit length probes help more on knowledge and mixed-format tasks.
A probe retains most savings with only 20 labelled problems and transfers to four of seven new benchmarks; savings plateau around a 2B scout.

papers.title: Scout Before You Route: Predicting Task Success and Token Count from a Small LLM Prefill
papers.tldr: A small frozen LLM can cheaply predict both task success and reasoning-output length, enabling routers to reduce model costs substantially compared with fixed median-length pricing.

papers.abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top-r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r x r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%.
authors: Liqun Ma, Shengkun Tang, Liangyu Wang, Lin Zhao, Wei Luo, Xinjun Niu, Spandan Tiwari, Ashish Sirasao, Kun Zhang, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Addresses the memory cost of AdamW’s two dense FP32 optimizer states in quantization-aware training.
Uses Adam updates in a low-rank principal subspace plus a normalized sign update from the residual momentum.
Evaluated across two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, including weights quantized to 2 bits.
Reduces optimizer-state memory by 71–74% relative to AdamW and keeps throughput loss below 2%.
Performance remains close to AdamW in most tested settings.

papers.abstract: As long-horizon agents increasingly rely on multi-step tool interactions to accomplish complex tasks, their execution trajectories continuously accumulate structured outputs and intermediate artifacts, leading to growing context overhead. Existing compression methods primarily rely on text importance or fixed truncation rules, often overlooking cross-step dependencies within workflows and potentially discarding critical information required for subsequent task execution. To address this challenge, we propose WAAC, a workflow-aware framework for agent trajectory compression. WAAC structurally models successful historical trajectories to extract reusable workflow compression experience and incorporates online backward dependency analysis to dynamically identify information retention requirements. By combining current dependency constraints with historical experience, WAAC selects appropriate compression strategies for different types of historical information. Experiments on PinchBench and Odysseys demonstrate that WAAC achieves an overall score of 87.6 and a perfect completion rate of 19.0%, respectively, while reducing execution costs by 19.7% and 29.1% compared with the strongest baseline methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of workflow-aware trajectory compression in improving task performance and cost efficiency for long-horizon agents. Code and resources are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/waac-6527/.
authors: Qijia Zhuang, Rui Liu, Yuxiang Ren
bullets: Long-horizon tool use creates growing context overhead from structured outputs and intermediate artifacts.
Existing text-importance and truncation methods may discard information needed by later workflow steps.
WAAC models successful trajectories to learn reusable compression experience and performs online backward dependency analysis.
It combines historical experience with current dependency constraints to choose compression strategies for different information types.
On PinchBench and Odysseys, WAAC reports an overall score of 87.6, a 19.0% perfect completion rate, and execution-cost reductions of 19.7% and 29.1% versus the strongest baselines.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models perform versatile manipulation tasks from language instructions, but their inference cost limits how fast a robot can respond in closed-loop control. Visual token pruning reduces this cost; however, prior methods estimate token redundancy from encoded visual embeddings or attention, only after the visual encoder has processed the entire observation. We propose \ours, a training-free token pruning method that moves the pruning decision ahead of the vision encoder by grounding it in a geometric prior derived from the robot's own action. The action chunk predicted at the previous control step is already available before the current observation is encoded, and it specifies the end-effector and camera motion between consecutive observations. The same action affects the two standard camera views asymmetrically: in the fixed third-person view, \ours retains patches along the projected end-effector trajectory together with semantic anchors, while in the wrist view, it prunes patches that remain unchanged after compensating for the action-induced camera motion. Extensive experiments on two simulation environments (LIBERO and VLABench) and four real-robot tasks demonstrate that \ours achieves up to 1.61 $\times$ speedup and 59.5\% FLOPs reduction with negligible degradation in success rates.
authors: Sungwon Moon, Minji Kim, Hyemin Boo, Daeun Song, Jiyoung Lee
bullets: Targets slow closed-loop robot response caused by expensive visual processing.
Training-free pruning uses the predicted prior action as a geometric prior before the vision encoder runs.
In the fixed third-person view, it keeps patches along the projected end-effector path and semantic anchors.
In the wrist view, it removes patches that remain unchanged after compensating for action-induced camera motion.
Evaluated in LIBERO, VLABench, and four real-robot tasks, achieving up to 1.61× speedup and 59.5% FLOPs reduction with negligible success-rate degradation.

papers.selection_reason: Action-grounded visual token pruning for efficient VLA inference, combining embodied action priors with token efficiency.
papers.title: ActPrune: Action-Grounded Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: ActPrune uses the robot’s previous action to prune visual tokens before encoding, reducing VLA inference cost with minimal impact on task success.

papers.abstract: Most LLM architectures have fixed compute demands determined at training time. We propose a novel architecture that combines the Mixture-of-Experts architecture with shallow experts and a novel dynamic-depth system to make the extent of a forward pass dynamically adjustable. Our approach lets the model automatically determine the compute needed for a given task, paired with a system to scale it down after training without retraining when the execution environment demands faster or cheaper inference. To achieve this, we introduce an iterative computation mechanism, sequence-level depth-based routing steered by a halting mechanism within the experts, a depth encoding that lets the model track its progress in the chain, and a regularization mechanism that incentivizes the model to use allocated compute efficiently. We present initial benchmarks and discuss future research directions.
bullets: Targets the fixed compute demands of conventional LLM architectures.
Uses shallow experts with iterative computation and sequence-level depth routing.
Employs learned halting within experts to determine how much computation each task needs.
Adds depth encoding and compute-efficiency regularization to support dynamic execution.
Reports initial benchmarks, while leaving broader evaluation and future research open.

papers.title: AlterNet: Adaptive-Depth Mixture-of-Experts with Learned Halting for Elastic Inference
papers.tldr: AlterNet enables adaptive, post-training-adjustable inference by combining mixture-of-experts with learned dynamic depth and halting.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has become a standard way to accelerate LLM inference: a lightweight drafter proposes tokens that the target verifies in one parallel pass. Existing drafters face trade-offs that limits their speedups: autoregressive drafters generate tokens one at a time, so drafting cost grows with draft length, while diffusion drafters generate tokens in parallel but predict each position independently, ignoring inter-token dependencies. We introduce ChainFlow, a new speculative decoding paradigm and the first flow-matching drafter conditioned on the target's hidden states. ChainFlow treats drafting as a short transport over hidden states, needing one or two flow steps instead of the many denoising steps of generation from noise. A variational autoencoder compresses these states so drafting cost barely grows with target size, lightweight feedback heads restore inter-token dependencies, and tree drafting raises acceptance. On Qwen3.5 models, at matched drafter size and training data, ChainFlow outperforms EAGLE-3 and DFlash in vLLM by 39% and 11%, respectively. These gains further widen as drafters are adapted to new languages sequentially. Our ablations cover drafter design and concurrent serving, and we open-source our code and drafter models.
authors: Selim Aktas, Yusuf Erdem Erdem, Ahmed Zeer, Himmet Toprak Kesgin, Muzaffer Kaan Yuce, Mehmet Fatih Amasyali
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between slow autoregressive drafters and parallel drafters that ignore inter-token dependencies.
Conditions drafting on the target model’s hidden states and uses a variational autoencoder to compress them.
Uses lightweight feedback heads to restore token dependencies and tree drafting to improve acceptance.
On Qwen3.5 models, it outperforms EAGLE-3 and DFlash in vLLM by 39% and 11%, respectively, under matched drafter size and training data.
The abstract reports further widening gains during sequential adaptation to new languages; code and drafter models are released.

papers.selection_reason: Flow-matching drafter for speculative decoding to accelerate LLM inference.
papers.title: ChainFlow: Few-Step Latent Flow Matching for Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: ChainFlow accelerates speculative decoding with a compact flow-matching drafter that generates dependent token sequences in one or two hidden-state transport steps.

papers.abstract: Medical vision--language models can interpret volumetric images, but processing full volumes is costly because hundreds of slices produce long, redundant visual-token sequences. Existing compression methods often couple content selection with budget determination. We observe that neighboring slices share visual features and that attention concentration varies across visual encoders. We propose VoluCompose, a training-free, model-agnostic framework that separates what visual content to retain from how many tokens to allocate. Its hyperbolic token composition module groups contiguous slices into ordered support units and uses the Lorentz distance to account for feature magnitude and direction during token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement. Its capacity control module uses visual-encoder attention entropy to allocate more tokens when attention is more dispersed. We evaluate VoluCompose on two tasks across three datasets and four backbones. Across nine calibrated settings, VoluCompose attains the highest mean quality--retention hypervolume among the compared methods. It achieves a mean relative quality of 121.68\% against the uncompressed references while retaining 22.78% of visual tokens on average. Compression remains robust even at a 10% token budget. Across settings, the lowest ROUGE-L ratio to the uncompressed reference is 96.4\% for VoluCompose. The corresponding minima for the compression baselines range from 15.0% to 70.5%. Code is available at https://github.com/yezanting/VoluCompose.
authors: Zanting Ye, Yunrui Lin, Shengyuan Liu, Jing Hao, Chen Hu, Yefeng Zheng, Lijun Lu
bullets: Addresses the high cost and redundancy of processing hundreds of volume slices in medical vision–language models.
Separates visual-content selection from token-budget allocation instead of coupling them.
Groups contiguous slices into ordered units and uses Lorentz distance for token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement.
Uses visual-encoder attention entropy to assign more tokens where attention is more dispersed.
Across nine settings, retains 22.78% of tokens on average while achieving 121.68% mean relative quality and robust performance at a 10% budget.

The attention-calibrated capacity control module determines the total budget 𝐵 from a prescribed retention fraction or normalized attention entropy. The compact token sequence is supplied to the language decoder for downstream tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes VoluCompose, a training-free framework for compressing volumetric medical images by separating content selection from token allocation, improving efficiency for vision-language models.
papers.title: VoluCompose: Constructing Compact Volumetric Visual Representations for Medical Image Understanding
papers.tldr: VoluCompose is a training-free, model-agnostic method that compresses volumetric medical images into compact visual-token sequences while preserving understanding quality.

papers.abstract: Camera-based driving models build a dense bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid and spend the same computation on every cell of it, although the vehicle crosses only a few of those cells within the planning horizon. We present BEVCast, a two-stage BEV whose resolution adapts to the predicted driving path. A coarse pass encodes the whole scene on a grid of 4.096 m cells. A heat head trained on the recorded path assigns a heat to every coarse cell and the cells with the highest heat are refined into 1.024 m cells under a fixed budget. The remaining cells keep their coarse resolution, so the trajectory head reads a mixed-resolution BEV that still covers the entire scene and needs neither an HD map nor a navigation command. Against a full grid of 1.024 m cells with the same architecture and training recipe, BEVCast at a 10% refinement budget encodes 28% of the BEV queries and needs 66% of the BEV encoder time at batch size 1. On nuScenes its mean displacement error is 1.078 m against 1.149 m and its drivable area violation rate is 1.46% against 2.29%. On NAVSIM navtest its mean displacement error is 0.577 m against 0.598 m and its extended predictive driver model score is 82.51 against 81.28. Next to published planners BEVCast reaches a comparable error on both benchmarks without a navigation command. The resolution of a driving BEV can therefore follow the task instead of the grid.
authors: Qiren Wang, Mingyu Guo, Zixuan Wang, Weisong Shi
bullets: Dense BEV grids waste computation on regions the vehicle will not traverse.
A coarse scene encoding predicts path-related heat, then selectively refines high-heat cells under a fixed budget.
The mixed-resolution BEV covers the full scene and requires neither an HD map nor a navigation command.
With 10% refinement, it uses 28% of BEV queries and 66% of encoder time versus a full fine grid, while achieving lower reported errors on nuScenes and NAVSIM navtest.
The approach is evaluated on two benchmarks and is intended for path-focused, efficient end-to-end driving.

Both encoders read the shared image features and the ego motion embedding and the coarse memory of the previous keyframe. The full grid baseline encodes 10,000 cells of 1.024 m in one pass with the same encoder architecture.

The bottom row shows the heat in pale blue on the coarse grid over the whole 102.4 m range with the 62 refined cells outlined in orange and subdivided into 1.024 m cells and the annotated agents in grey.

papers.selection_reason: Path-adaptive BEV refinement for end-to-end autonomous driving; fits learned navigation policies and token/cell selection for efficiency.
papers.title: BEVCast: Path-Adaptive BEV for Efficient End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: BEVCast reduces BEV computation by refining only cells near the predicted driving path while maintaining or improving planning performance.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are the dominant architecture for video generation, but their quadratic attention complexity results in substantial computational cost and latency. Permuted block-sparse attention (PBSA) offers a promising approach to reducing this cost by selectively computing blocks of a semantically permuted attention matrix. However, existing approaches typically select only the top few key blocks for each query block, following a top-$p$ paradigm. We find that top-$p$ selection can be highly sample inefficient in high-entropy attention regimes, which are common in video generation. In these regimes, we show that sampling can provide substantially better approximations under the same computational budget. More generally, we cast block selection as importance sampling, where the top-scoring keys form an exact set that is computed in full and the remaining keys are represented by a sample drawn in proportion to their estimated attention and reweighted by inverse sampling probability. Building on this formulation, we present InstaGen, which can be parameterized by any PBSA method: it replaces the method's block selection with an exact set plus a weighted sample. Each query cluster draws one sample shared by all its queries, so the sampled keys form blocks amenable to efficient GPU execution. In this paper, we take the SVG family of PBSA methods and show that, on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen parameterized by SVG2 improves PSNR over SVG2 by 3.4 dB and 2 dB, respectively, at matched attention density, and by 1.6 dB and 2.2 dB at matched wall-clock time. On Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen also beats SVG-EAR by 1.1 dB PSNR at nearly the same density while running faster (1.65x against 1.48x over dense).
authors: Kislay Aditya Oj, Kumar Krishna Agrawal, Sri Surya Varma Datla, Aditya Desai
bullets: Top-p block selection can be sample-inefficient when video attention has high entropy.
It treats block selection as importance sampling: exact computation for top-scoring keys and inverse-probability-weighted samples for the rest.
Each query cluster shares a sampled set, preserving block structure for efficient GPU execution.
With SVG2, InstaGen improves PSNR at matched attention density and wall-clock time on Wan2.1-T2V models.
It also outperforms SVG-EAR on Wan2.1-T2V-14B while running faster at nearly the same density.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of InstaGen. (a) Queries and keys are clustered into groups. (b) Centroid scores give each key group a probability π of being used by each query group. (c) The top key group is always kept; the remaining keys are sampled in proportion to π and weighted by 1/π. (d) Queries in a group share the same keys, so attention runs over dense blocks in one kernel.

The hollow diamond is SVG2 without its one-layer warmup; the InstaGen runs have none. The prompt used is svg2 ex1, Appendix A.1.

SVG2 in its paper configuration (p=0.9) reaches 25.03 dB at 44.1%; InstaGen (importance sampling) reaches the same PSNR at 34.0% with the same 30% warm-up, and at 20.0% with no warm-up. Right: PSNR against attention density, the share of attention computed over the whole generation. papers.selection_reason: Improves diffusion-based video generation with sparse/block attention and importance sampling, fitting video diffusion and efficient attention.
papers.title: InstaGen: Group-Shared Importance Sampling for Fast Video Generation
papers.tldr: InstaGen accelerates video diffusion by replacing inefficient top-block selection with group-shared importance sampling, improving reconstruction quality at comparable compute.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are attractive rerankers for recommendation. Running an expensive model on every request is costly, and for users with sparse interaction histories it often lowers quality. We present CascadeRec, a two-tier LLM reranking cascade deployed in production at a large financial planning and analysis (FP&A) SaaS provider. It serves content recommendations to enterprise tenants on AWS EKS and GKE. A lightweight Tier-1 model reranks every request. A router escalates only the requests where extra inference-time compute is likely to help, and sends them to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure (self-consistency sampling, multi-path reasoning, or a larger model). The system has run in a production A/B experiment for over a month. Compared with uniform use of the expensive tier, CascadeRec has reduced inference cost by about 10%, with minimal latency impact and no quality regression observed to date. Tenant data cannot be released, so we also evaluate the pipeline on public benchmarks (MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Electronics). Segment-level analysis with paired-bootstrap confidence intervals shows that uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and its only statistically significant gain appears on the segment with the longest histories. Escalating cold users can make the loss larger instead of repairing it. Which segments benefit from escalation depends on the domain, and this motivates the segment-gated rollout we use in production. We describe the deployment architecture, the measured benefits, and lessons learned, including inter-tenant load imbalance as a driver for cascading and the handling of LLM output-parsing failures at the serving layer.
authors: Kai Zhao, Guilin Zhang, Xiang Cheng, Xiquan Cui, Henry Heng, Xu Chu, Alet Blanken
bullets: Uniform expensive LLM reranking can hurt sparse-history users, lowering NDCG@10 by up to 30% on public benchmarks.
A lightweight Tier-1 reranks every request, while a router sends potentially beneficial cases to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure.
The production system runs across multi-tenant AWS EKS and GKE deployments with minimal latency impact reported.
Escalation benefits vary by user segment and domain; cold-user escalation can worsen performance, motivating segment-gated rollout.
The deployment addresses practical serving issues including inter-tenant load imbalance and LLM output-parsing failures.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CascadeRec architecture. Tier-1 reranks every request and emits a confidence signal. The router accepts the Tier-1 ranking or escalates the request to Tier-2.
Figure 2: Production request path. The router escalates a minority of requests to the Tier-2 pool. Any LLM failure falls back to the best earlier ranking (dashed red). Orange boxes are LLM inference.
Figure 3: Cost and quality on MovieLens-1M: aggregate NDCG@10 against average tokens per user, with values from Table 2. The dashed line marks B0.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a cascade architecture for LLM reranking that reduces inference cost by routing requests based on user history, demonstrating a practical efficiency strategy.
papers.title: CascadeRec: Deployed Adaptive LLM Compute Allocation for Multi-Tenant Content Recommendation
papers.tldr: CascadeRec reduces costly LLM reranking by selectively escalating requests to a stronger tier, cutting production inference cost by about 10% without observed quality loss.

papers.abstract: To train a sparse autoencoder (SAE), you need a massive cache of model activations. We look into the effects that compression has on an SAE in two ways: we keep the original fp32-trained SAE and pass the compressed cache into the same SAE to see how many feature activations stay the same (the frozen-SAE test), and we retrain an SAE on the compressed cache and see how many of the original features still exist (the retraining test). We found that in the retraining test, there is no clear scale for retained features. On a GPT-2 cache, rounding everything to fp16 keeps 60.6% of features, but changing one value in a million by the smallest step fp32 allows (a change eight orders of magnitude smaller) keeps only 70.5%. Meanwhile, changing the random seed keeps 23.0%. For the frozen-SAE test, the frozen SAE's correlation with the original increases in order of how precise the codecs are, but plain $L_2$ distance gives nearly the same ordering. We also see the same frozen reading correspond to different percentages retained at different sites. This leaves the question of the right measurement. We build one by calibrating: retraining on identical bytes sets the ceiling, and a reseed sets the floor. We then measure the effect of each compressed codec against its own site's floor. With TopK SAEs on GPT-2 small and Pythia-1.4B at research-scale budgets, na\"ive per-token int4 loses more features than a reseed everywhere we tested, as do PCA and random projection on GPT-2. Standardizing each channel before quantizing brings int4 back above the floor in terms of retained features, at the same raw file size. At our smallest budget, a bf16 forward pass, which some pipelines use to save memory, loses slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage. Calibrating a site costs four training runs and two evaluation passes.
bullets: The study tests compression by evaluating both a frozen SAE on compressed activations and an SAE retrained on them.
Feature retention after retraining has no clear universal scale: compression effects can be smaller or larger than changing the random seed.
Frozen-SAE correlation broadly follows codec precision, but simple L2 distance gives nearly the same ranking and does not transfer consistently across sites.
The authors calibrate each site using identical-byte retraining as a ceiling and reseeding as a floor, requiring four training runs and two evaluation passes.

At research-scale budgets, naive per-token int4, PCA, and random projection can underperform reseeding; channel standardization improves int4, while bf16 can lose slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage.

Blue: calibrated isotropic noise, fp32 on both sides; orange: real codecs; star and diamond: one ulp on one scalar and on a millionth of them; the shaded band marks fp32’s own precision, below which no dense fp32 noise can go.
