papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses memory-efficiency in AI by studying activation-cache compression for SAE training, fitting the efficient-AI and memory-efficiency subtopic.
papers.title: How Small Can We Go? Calibrating Activation-Cache Compression for SAE Training
papers.tldr: A calibrated evaluation framework shows that activation-cache compression can severely alter SAE features, while channel-standardized int4 preserves more features than naive int4 at the same storage cost.

papers.abstract: Wafer-scale accelerators promise ultra-low-latency AI inference, but current system stacks still carry an unsustainably high cost premium. The reason is that many current and emerging inference techniques, such as batching and MoE, introduce runtime dynamism that existing wafer-scale systems cannot support efficiently. As a result, they must choose between two unsatisfactory options: accept suboptimal latency, or preserve low latency by restricting dynamic techniques, thereby limiting the models they can support and reducing aggregate throughput. This tradeoff significantly increases the cost of low-latency serving. We present MeshRT, the first wafer-scale system to achieve both ultra-low latency and high throughput for LLM inference. MeshRT achieves this via a novel system architecture, which we call compile-time governance of runtime dynamism. This architecture features new system abstractions and mechanisms that enable MeshRT to compile dynamic events arising from LLM inference directly into per-core schedules, enabling asynchronous and decentralized execution with low runtime overhead. Implemented on a commodity wafer-scale accelerator, MeshRT preserves ultra-low latency while improving throughput by up to 56$\times$ over the state-of-the-art system for wafer-scale accelerators. Against measured single-instance SGLang results on H200, MeshRT achieves 4.5-7.0$\times$ lower latency. Under ideal linear scaling of those GPU measurements to an approximately power-matched H200 cluster, MeshRT achieves 1.7-13.0$\times$ higher decode system throughput in the low-latency regime.
authors: Congjie He, Le Xu, Zhan Lu, Yeqi Huang, Haocheng Xiao, Cheng Deng, Lingxiao Ma, Ziming Miao, Fan Yang, Luo Mai
bullets: Addresses the tension between low latency and dynamic techniques such as batching and mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference.
Introduces “compile-time governance of runtime dynamism,” compiling inference events into per-core schedules.
Enables asynchronous, decentralized execution with low runtime overhead on a commodity wafer-scale accelerator.
Reports up to 56× higher throughput than the prior state of the art for wafer-scale accelerators.
Achieves 4.5–7.0× lower latency than measured single-instance SGLang on H200; GPU-cluster throughput comparisons use ideal linear scaling assumptions.

figures.caption: Figure 4.MeshRT system overview. Given a computation graph and mapping choices, MeshRT synthesizes dynamismaware per-core event tables (§4.2), partitions them into segments that fit hardware resource limits (§4.3), and deploys the result onto the wafer-scale accelerator.

Figure 9. System throughput vs. single-user throughput on WSE-3 at 4K context for prefill (top) and decode (bottom). Comparing each system’s peak over the evaluated micro-batches, MeshRT improves system throughput by 4.0–6.6× during prefill and by up to 55.8× during decode. Decode points do not apply workload-level padding correction.

Figure 8. MeshRT system boundary. The host compiles and installs per-core schedules once (top left). During serving (bottom left), it asynchronously pushes prefill contexts and decode KV caches. All per-step execution, continuous batching, and dynamism resolution proceed on chip without host involvement (right).
Figure 2. Padding compute ratios across different models increase with serving batch size.

Figure 1. Wafer-scale accelerators as a distinct runtime setting. Host-mediated control incurs expensive round trips. Cores form a neighbor-only mesh of𝑀 × 𝑁 cores, so chipwide synchronization takes 𝑂 (𝑀+𝑁 ) hops and grows with physical distance. Each core exposes only bounded local resources, including local SRAM, finite routing-table state, and simple local branching rather than a general scheduler. These properties limit design choices.

Figure 6. Synthesized per-core sub-schedules for continuous batching. The last-layer core prepends batch-state metainfo to outgoing data; the first-layer core parses it and updates its local request table to select active slots.

Figure 7. Synthesized per-core sub-schedules for MoE routing. The top-𝑘 core prepends expert-distribution metainfo to token data; downstream relay cores parse it to reconfigure routing, and expert cores parse it to select which tokens to compute.

Figure 5. Per-core schedule synthesis for an AllReduce kernel mapped to one row of cores. The kernel function and mapping determine role-specific event-action tables: edge cores receive a partial sum, accumulate locally, forward it, and later receive the broadcast result; mid cores relay and accumulate; and the root reduces and broadcasts.

Figure 3. MeshRT design intuition: compile-time governance of runtime dynamism. Instead of deferring dynamic decisions to host control, MeshRT compiles them directly into per-core schedules as control events that execute alongside data events entirely on chip. Each core then runs its own schedule asynchronously, coordinating only through data arrival.

Figure 10. Decode TPOT (lower is better). (a) At 4K context and micro-batch size 1, under matched configurations, MeshRT adds only 40 𝜇s (9.5%) on Qwen3.5-9B and 25 𝜇s (7.6%) on GPT-OSS-20B relative to WaferLLM. (b) At batch size 1, GPT-OSS-20B long-context decode, showing E2E TPOT and the time spent in full-attention layers as the context grows to 128K.

Table 4. Policy-level decomposition of serving performance. In the table headers, mbs denotes micro-batch size. Each non-total column reports the multiplier over the preceding configuration after adding the named policy; the total is their product using unrounded values. Policy factors are derived from device-measured component cycles. Decode additionally uses the measured ShareGPT padding ratios for continuous batching. The prefill block reports the three MoE models: its first factor compares pipelined MeshRT at micro-bs=1 with the static bs=1 baseline, and the second factor moves MeshRT from micro-bs=1 to micro-bs=4. The total therefore differs from Figure 9, which compares each system’s peak over all evaluated micro-batches.

Table 3. Matched-configuration per-step throughput and peak system throughput relative to static WaferLLM. Singleuser throughput uses micro-bs=1 for MeshRT and bs=1 for WaferLLM; runtime governance latency overhead for the matched-configuration 9B and 20B comparisons is reported separately in Figure 10. System throughput is each system’s peak over the evaluatedmicro-batches and includes the effect of enabled policies. The 35B and 120B results follow the projection methodology in §6.1. No workload-level padding correction is applied.

papers.selection_reason: Wafer-scale runtime that reduces LLM inference latency and improves throughput, fitting the efficiency-oriented scope of Efficient AI.
papers.title: MeshRT: Compile-Time Governed Wafer-Scale Runtime for Low-Latency High-Throughput Inference
papers.tldr: MeshRT uses compile-time scheduling of runtime dynamism to deliver both ultra-low-latency and high-throughput LLM inference on wafer-scale accelerators.

papers.abstract: Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. To address this challenge, we propose Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine that decouples the logical tree structure of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. By expressing branch topologies directly in GPU-resident metadata, Flide accommodates diverse request mixtures with a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs while enabling expanding agent histories to resume from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. Extensive evaluations on public hybrid and decision models demonstrate that Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance. By unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in agent systems.
bullets: Targets prefix recomputation and probability distortion in existing generation-oriented inference engines.
Uses ForkAttention with GPU-resident indices to represent logical request trees across standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers.
Ensures each query branch matches an isolated forward pass in exact arithmetic.
Supports diverse request mixtures through compact pre-recorded execution graphs and checkpoint-based resumption of expanding agent histories.
Evaluations on public hybrid and decision models report up to 9.5× faster queries than vLLM and SGLang, with outputs closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance.

papers.selection_reason: Presents an exact inference engine that reduces latency for decision-model agent workloads, fitting the efficient-AI scope through inference-time execution optimization.
papers.title: Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking
papers.tldr: Flide accelerates decision-model inference by exactly executing branched requests in a shared, flattened token stream without changing their outputs.

papers.abstract: Local online training on resource-constrained platforms requires low computational and training-state overhead. We study the numerical stability and computational efficiency of half-precision proximal policy optimization (PPO) on commodity GPUs. Directly converting PPO training to FP16 is unreliable because numerical errors feed back through policy updates and subsequent data collection, while PPO repeatedly compares a current policy with a fixed behavior policy. We propose PPO-FP16 with three structure-aware modules. Global scalar protection stabilizes statistics shared across a minibatch or parameter update. Policy-change residual protection extracts and preserves small differences between the current and behavior policies. Efficient persistent-update protection stabilizes optimizer state and parameter writeback while reducing state storage. These changes preserve the PPO objective, hyperparameters, and training budget. Across six continuous-control tasks and five seeds, PPO-FP16 achieves the lowest mean return-AUC rank (1.90) among the four methods and ranks first in 17 of 30 environment-seed comparisons. Eight of nine performance configurations yield PPO update speedups ranging from 1.16 to 2.03 times. Relative to Full FP32 Adam, optimizer-state memory is reduced by 71.7 to 74.9 percent, and peak allocated GPU memory is reduced by up to 44.5 percent. The results show that protecting a small set of structurally important quantities can deliver stable, efficient FP16 PPO without retuning.
bullets: Direct FP16 PPO is unstable because numerical errors influence later policy updates and data collection.
Three protections target shared scalars, small current-versus-behavior policy differences, and persistent optimizer/parameter updates.
Across six continuous-control tasks and five seeds, PPO-FP16 had the best mean return-AUC rank and ranked first in 17 of 30 environment-seed comparisons.
Update speed improved by 1.16–2.03× in eight of nine configurations, while optimizer-state and peak GPU memory were substantially reduced.
The approach is evaluated for stable local training on commodity GPUs and does not require retuning PPO hyperparameters.

figures.caption: Figure 1: PPO-FP16 training pipeline and its three structure-aware protection modules. Module A protects global statistics and gradient scale, Module B protects small policy changes in the residual domain, and Module C stabilizes optimizer state.
Figure 2: Module ablations on HalfCheetah-v5 over three seeds. Bars showmean ± standard deviation; Crash denotes instability.
Figure 3: Long-horizon evaluation over six tasks and five seeds; shading shows 95% confidence intervals.
Table 1: PPO update time and speedup over five processes.
Table 2: Mixed-precision performance at batch size 2,048. Time is in ms; memory is in MiB.
Table 3: Return AUC over five seeds (mean ± standard deviation). Bold marks the best mean per environment.

papers.selection_reason: Half-precision PPO with memory and compute reduction fits efficient AI, though no specific subtopic.
papers.title: Structure-Aware Numerical Stabilization for Half-Precision Proximal Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: PPO-FP16 enables stable, faster, and more memory-efficient half-precision PPO by protecting structurally important numerical quantities without changing PPO settings.

papers.abstract: Real-time video generation, interactive world models, and on-device image synthesis are almost a reality. Diffusion Transformers (DiT) achieve excellent sample quality, shifting the bottleneck to the throughput of the models themselves. Natural images are inherently sparse, as large portions of an image are often background, contribute little to the scene content, and are easy to denoise. DiTs fail to exploit this sparsity, as they process image tokens statically and uniformly. We propose MoDDiT, a simple architecture modification that learns to route tokens through both MLP and self-attention operations. By routing tokens through both blocks independently, MoDDiT allows for dynamic compute allocation in MLPs that varies across tokens, images, and denoising timesteps. Using MoDDiT to train image generation models from scratch significantly reduces computational costs of training and inference, processing as few as 12.5% of the tokens. By increasing sparsity and model depth, MoDDiT reduces costs and improves generation performance over unrouted baselines. The learned allocation is interpretable, revealing how computation varies with visual content and noise level. We also use MoDDiT to train video generation models, where allocation correlates with motion, and to distill a dense bidirectional video model into a sparse autoregressive student.
bullets: Targets DiTs’ inefficient uniform processing of mostly sparse visual content.
Routes tokens independently through MLP and self-attention operations, adapting compute by token, image, and denoising timestep.
Processes as few as 12.5% of tokens, substantially reducing training and inference costs.
Higher sparsity and model depth improve generation performance over unrouted baselines.
Token allocation is interpretable, correlating with visual content, noise level, and video motion.

papers.selection_reason: Token routing in diffusion transformers reduces compute for image/video generation, fitting efficient token pruning and video diffusion.
papers.title: MoDDiT: Simple Token Routing in Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: MoDDiT dynamically routes image and video tokens through DiT MLP and attention blocks, reducing computation while maintaining or improving generation quality.

papers.abstract: Activation memory, not compute, limits CNN inference on constrained hardware such as microcontrollers. Direct in-place convolution removes the dual-buffer cost, but the memory-optimal formulation of Gural and Murmann assumes valid padding, unit stride, unit dilation, and odd square kernels, and needs a non-sequential traversal costing $2\times$ inference time in transposes. We identify two regimes in which their published closed form does not hold: (1) an under-allocation of exactly $(k-1)C_{in} \bmod (C_{out}-C_{in})$ scalars, active on every convolutional layer of their own deployed network and manifesting as a silent corruption of still-live input; (2) an unbounded overestimate, up to $2{,}432\times$, once the critical leg leaves the output grid. We correct both and generalize to arbitrary stride, dilation, padding, and rectangular kernels. We then propose Right In-Place (RiP) convolution, a bit-identical operation in which every layer reads its input right-aligned in a shared workspace and writes its output left-aligned from index zero. The debt is piecewise affine in the output pixel index, so evaluating its breakpoints in $O(1)$ yields the minimum safe gap without enumerating the output grid, with row-major access preserved. Across $10{,}000$ random layers RiP produced no corruption, and across 84 convolutional layers from 25 architectures it matches the herringbone workspace exactly on 58 and within 5% on 81, using 24.8% less memory than dual buffering on average. Written into TinyEngine's kernels and deployed to a Raspberry Pi Pico 1 and Pico 2, it cuts peak activation memory across eleven MCUNet models by 12.5 to 33.3% at unchanged cycle counts and bit-identical outputs, raising the number of models that fit the Pico 1's 256 KB SRAM from six to nine.
bullets: Addresses activation-memory limits caused by dual-buffer CNN inference on microcontrollers.
Corrects flaws in prior memory-optimal formulations and generalizes them to arbitrary stride, dilation, padding, and rectangular kernels.
Uses right-aligned inputs, left-aligned outputs, and O(1) breakpoint analysis to find the minimum safe workspace gap while preserving row-major access.
Matches the exact herringbone workspace on 58 of 84 layers and comes within 5% on 81; it uses 24.8% less memory than dual buffering on average.
On Raspberry Pi Pico devices, it reduces peak activation memory by 12.5–33.3% with unchanged cycles and bit-identical outputs, increasing fitting models from 6 to 9 on the Pico 1.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Workspace layout on a Pico 1 for MCUNet-in3 under naive dual buffering, TinyEngine’s scheduler, and RiP. All three are placed by the same MILP memory allocator (Sec. 4.3). On the first two it reaches the same peak as TinyEngine’s first-fit memory allocator [19], so the allocator alone does not account for the saving; under in-place convolution first-fit fragments the arena and does not allow the full utilization of the extra memory, so the MILP is what lets RiP’s gap be reclaimed rather than stranded.
Figure 2. Convolution traversal order.
Figure 3. Herringbone traversal order on uneven output grids.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on memory-efficient CNN inference (RiP convolution) to reduce activation memory on constrained hardware, directly addressing a key challenge in Efficient AI.
papers.title: Right In-Place (RiP) Convolution: A Simple, General, and Near-Optimal Strategy for Memory-Efficient CNN Inference
papers.tldr: RiP convolution enables safe, near-minimal in-place CNN inference for constrained devices while preserving speed and bit-identical outputs.

papers.abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.
bullets: Targets the high latency and cost of maintaining diverse populations in iterative LLM-based program evolution.
Uses hundreds of low-cost agents organized into swarms, with each swarm exploring a different perspective.
Promotes diversity through hidden-state distance filtering and combines ideas by aggregating agents’ KV caches for a summarizer.
Across 21 mathematical discovery and scientific computing problems, it reaches benchmark best scores in a median of 3–8 minutes versus 60 minutes for other frameworks.
Qwen3 8B sometimes improves solutions initially found by AlphaEvolve using frontier LLMs.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Minutes that SwarmEvolve needs to reach the best score that OpenEvolve (left), ShinkaEvolve (middle), and CodeEvolve (right) reach in 60 minutes. All frameworks use Qwen3 8B and run for three seeds. Hollow circles mark problems where SwarmEvolve does not reach the target within 60 minutes. On most problems, SwarmEvolve reaches in a few minutes what the baselines reach in one hour.

Figure 2: Workflow of SwarmEvolve. In each round, SwarmEvolve launches 10 swarms of 45 latent agents. Each swarm draws parent programs from the archive and gets a focus prompt to refine, hybridize, explore, or start fresh. In each swarm, the agents take 40 latent reasoning steps, a novelty filter removes the 15 most similar agents (hollow circles), and the summarizer reads the KV caches of the rest to write one new program. The new programs are evaluated and added to the archive. A parameter tuning agent tunes the hyperparameters of the best program.

Figure 5: Mean hidden states of the latent agents for a circle packing problem with Qwen3 8B, projected onto their first two principal components: the 450 latent agents of all 10 swarms with the swarm centers (left), and the 45 latent agents of one exploration-focused swarm, each reading different parent programs (right). The swarms occupy distinct regions, and the novelty filter keeps latent agents from every cluster.

Figure 3: Latent reasoning and communication in a swarm. Each latent agent reasons recursively in the embedding space without decoding to text. Its latent reasoning steps are stored as KV cache. The summarizer then reads the concatenated KV caches from all agents and writes a new program in text.

Table 1: Best score within 60 minutes, averaged over three seeds (scores defined in Section 4 and Appendix D). For each model, bold marks the best score and underline marks the second best. SwarmEvolve (ours) has the highest average score with every model.

papers.selection_reason: Latent-space agent communication via shared KV caches is a technically meaningful efficiency contribution for LLM-based search.
papers.title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
papers.tldr: SwarmEvolve accelerates LLM-guided evolutionary program search by using large latent-space agent swarms that share KV caches instead of repeatedly generating long text.

papers.abstract: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.
bullets: Targets the high cost of autoregressively generating coordinates for visual plans such as points, boxes, and trajectories.
Uses a lightweight drafter to predict each primitive in one forward pass, adapting to its type, dimensionality, and length.
Trains on annotated primitives and accepts structurally valid predictions without requiring exact autoregressive token matching.
Reduces prediction errors across evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks and reports approximately 25× faster 3D point-motion generation.
A world action model using VFlash plans reaches 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces suites, versus 62.6% for the baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Visual planning for robotics via faster primitive decoding; directly relevant to embodied navigation and efficiency.
papers.title: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
papers.tldr: VFlash speeds up visual planning by jointly decoding structured primitives while maintaining or improving spatial accuracy.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable end-to-end robot control, but inference is increasingly expensive. Each decision processes hundreds of visual tokens, often across multiple cameras, leading to substantial computation while allowing irrelevant background content to distract action prediction under distribution shift. We argue that these issues stem from two complementary forms of redundancy: many visual tokens are spatially irrelevant, while attention over the remaining tokens is often misallocated. Based on this observation, we propose T3R, a Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement framework. In the first stage, segmentation-guided token pruning removes irrelevant visual patches to reduce computation and eliminate distracting context. In the second stage, saliency-guided attention biasing reallocates attention toward action-critical visual regions and language instructions within the retained tokens. Together, pruning produces a cleaner candidate set, while attention biasing further emphasizes the most decision-relevant evidence, yielding a better accuracy-efficiency frontier than either stage alone. On LIBERO-Spatial, T3R removes 85% of scene-camera visual tokens while essentially matching the unpruned success rate, and improves success by up to 7 percentage points under out-of-distribution object-placement perturbations. The timing comparison attributes 7.8 ms per inference call to pruning and attention-bias application. As input resolution increases, LLM-forward profiling shows up to a 3.3x speedup over the unpruned baseline. Evaluations across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones show the strongest accuracy-efficiency benefits in multi-camera settings. These results demonstrate that training-free token refinement is a practical approach to efficient and robust VLA inference.
bullets: Targets high VLA inference cost and distraction from redundant visual tokens, especially across multiple cameras and under distribution shift.
Uses segmentation-guided pruning to remove irrelevant patches, followed by saliency-guided attention biasing over retained visual tokens and language instructions.
On LIBERO-Spatial, removes 85% of scene-camera tokens while essentially matching unpruned success and improves OOD success by up to 7 percentage points.
Adds 7.8 ms per inference call for refinement and achieves up to 3.3× LLM-forward speedup at higher input resolutions.
Across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones, benefits are strongest in multi-camera settings.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Two-stage T3R pipeline. Stage 1 (pruning): POS-weighted SigLIP text–patch similarity localizes the target; the topscoring patch positions (with SigLIP/DINOv2 features) prompt EfficientTAM to produce an object mask, which is converted to a patch-level pruning decision while preserving original RoPE positions, so only the “interested tokens” enter the LLM. Stage 2 (biasing): Integrated Gradients over the instruction identifies salient words; an additive attention bias (𝛽=2.0) is injected into the middle decoder layers for action-token queries, steering attention toward salient text tokens and retained visual patches before the action chunk is decoded.

Figure 4: OOD robustness under object-placement perturbation (21 noise levels, 10 episodes/task). T3R (Full Pipeline) tracks the unpruned baseline for small shifts and pulls ahead beyond ∼2 cm, leading by up to 7 pp at 4 cm, while TeamVLA degrades fastest. The crossover is consistent with pruning reducing misleading background context.

Figure 3: Most visual tokens are near-inert. (a) Across all 32 decoder layers, 93.9% of visual tokens receive <0.2% of the action queries’ attention each. (b) Per-patch action-query attention concentrates on a few task-relevant patches (here the gripper and target bowls), while the background receives negligible weight.

Figure 2: Qualitative pruning on a sparse LIBERO-Spatial scene (“pick up the bowl between the plate and the ramekin”). Top: input, POS-weighted SigLIP similarity, and the EfficientTAMmask with its point prompts. Middle: T3R keeps only 13/256 patches (95% pruned), tightly localized on the target. Bottom: TeamVLA’s similarity+expansion+merge retains 226/256 (12% pruned), leaving most of the background in the sequence through the early decoder layers.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free token pruning and attention biasing for efficient, robust VLA robot inference; directly fits VLA and token pruning topics.
papers.title: T3R: Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement Towards Efficient and Robust VLA Models
papers.tldr: T3R enables faster and more robust VLA inference by pruning irrelevant visual tokens and biasing attention toward action-critical regions without training.

papers.abstract: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.
bullets: GDN-2’s erasure updates are less sensitive than value writes, motivating lower-rank, sensitivity-allocated gating.
Muir fuses gates into a low-rank projection and re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout to reduce interference from high-norm, slow-decaying rows.
A numerically stable parallel update enables efficient training with the large chunks needed for wide matrix units.
Across 166M–1.34B parameters, Muir reduces perplexity versus GDN-2 and Transformer, improves commonsense accuracy and extractive recall, and matches GDN-2 throughput.
At 1.34B, it supports long-context extrapolation to 10M tokens and near-perfect passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Muir outperforms GDN-2 and Transformer on language modeling and long-context throughput while improving recall over GDN-2. (a) Sensitivity-allocated low-rank gates with FFN expansion drive the bulk of the validation NLL gain over GDN-2, while dynamic matched-filter readout drives the gain on extractive recall. (b) Across 166M–1.34B parameters, Muir lowers validation NLL by 18.0–20.4 millinats over GDN-2 and 25.0–36.2 millinats over Transformer. (c) On 8 TPU7x chips (0.5M tokens/step) at 1.34B with our chunkwise kernel, Muir matches GDN-2 throughput despite an additional readout gate and a 30.4% wider FFN, and trains 1.64× and 2.74× faster than Transformer at 16K and 32K, respectively.

Figure 6 |Muir improves synthetic single-needle, multi-hop, multi-needle, and real-world retrieval over GDN-2. (a) Averaged across the three single-needle tasks, all Muir variants mitigate the 4K degradation of GDN-2 and extrapolate to 8K, where unextended RoPE Transformer degrades beyond its 4K training window. (b) On 5-hop variable-binding chains, static 𝛾 fails to match the varying hop lags, whereas dynamic 𝛾𝑡 leads all models at every context length. (c, d) When retrieving four values bound to a single key or four distinct keys queried jointly, dynamic 𝛾𝑡 matches or outperforms both GDN-2 and Transformer across 1K–4K. (e) Averaged across the RULER tasks (a–d) by needle depth and context length, Muir achieves the largest gains over GDN-2 on early needles (0–40% depth) at 4K–8K. (f) On real-world document extraction at 2K, Muir improves over GDN-2 on all six tasks, with dynamic 𝛾𝑡 driving 69% of the gain.

Figure 4 | Boundary-pivoted chunkwise kernel eliminates 3D decay tensors, division overflow, and VPU bottlenecks. (a) Memory hierarchy of a TPU7x chip. (b) On the 256× 256 MXU, an unfused 256 × 128 right-hand side 𝑉 achieves only 50% utilization due to zero-padded lanes, whereas the fused solve [︀ 𝑈 𝑌 ]︀ = 𝑇−1 [︀𝑉 ?̂?⊙𝜋 ]︀ achieves 100% utilization. (c) At chunk size 𝐶 = 256, leaf size 8, and 𝑑𝑘 = 𝑑𝑣 = 128, replacing naive 𝐶 × 𝐶 × 𝑑𝑘 3D VPU decay and sequential VPU triangular solves with boundary-pivoted MXU matrix multiplications, recursive block inversion, and a custom backward pass cuts forward-and-backward VPU compute by 24× and total kernel FLOPs by 12%, routing 98% of chunkwise arithmetic onto the MXU. (d) Boundary-pivoted chunkwise execution combines pre-permutation VREG fusion for 𝑞𝑡 and 𝑣𝑡, MXU cumulative log-decay, numerically stable VPU decay splitting, recursive block inversion of 𝑇 on the MXU, and a packed MXU scan carrying 𝑆0 → 𝑆𝐶 in VMEM (saving 𝑆0 only for backward).

Figure 3 | Muir co-designs asymmetric low-rank gate parameterization and matched-filter query readout with MXU tile alignment and iso-parameter FFN reallocation. (a) Standard residual block with a Muir token mixer. (b) Within the Muir block, 𝑥𝑡 feeds linear-Conv-SiLU pathways for (𝑞𝑡,𝑘𝑡,𝑣𝑡) alongside a single fused low-rank gate projection that produces all five gates (log𝛼𝑡, 𝑏𝑡, 𝑔𝑡,𝑤𝑡,𝛾𝑡). (c) Asymmetric gate ranks (𝑟𝑓 , 𝑟𝑏, 𝑟𝑔, 𝑟𝑤, 𝑟𝑞) = (64, 64, 128, 128, 128) sum to 𝑅tot = 512 = 2 × 256, which fills two 256-column MXU tiles in the fused down-projection and aligns (𝑓, 𝑏) and (𝑔, 𝑤, 𝑞) on 128-lane VMEM tile boundaries for batched up-projections. (d) At 𝑑 = 2,048, replacing the dense (𝑏, 𝑤) gate matrices in GDN-2 cuts gate-projection parameters by 4.5×; this either reduces per-layer parameters and FLOPs by 14.6% at fixed FFN width, or frees +7.3M parameters per layer to widen the FFN under an iso-parameter budget.

Figure 2 |Matched-filter readout and low-rank erase gates improve synthetic associative retrieval and lower optimal erase strength. (a) Full whitening worsens retrieval error relative to unit gain (GDN-2), whereas half-power scaling and the Corollary 3.8 filter reduce error and shift 𝜇* from 0.60 to 0.50, with the Corollary 3.8 filter matching the static oracle. (b) On a 50/50 mixture of lags ℓ ∈ {2, 80} at 𝜇 = 0.60, the lag-matched oracle outperforms the static oracle across all horizons, while the Proposition 3.6 filter matches the lag-matched oracle at ℓ = 80 and beats the static oracle on long and mixed horizons. (c) Low-rank erase gates 𝑟𝑏 outperform dense gates at every bottleneck rank on long-lag recall, whereas low-rank write gates 𝑟𝑤 degrade below dense at 𝑟𝑤 ≤ 8 and recover once 𝑟𝑤 ≥ 16.

Figure 13 | Muir preserves early variable bindings and routes readout to the target hop at each answer step. (a) On 4-value MV-NIAH, Transformer drops on the final write 𝑉4 and unit-readout recurrences degrade after 𝑉1, whereas Muir remains accurate across 𝑉1–𝑉4. (b) On 5-hop RULER VT, Transformer recalls only the root assignment 𝐻1, whereas Muir maintains accuracy across all five hops 𝐻1–𝐻5. (c) Within-model root-needle (𝐻1) retention in 𝑆𝑡 from write milestone 𝑠1 (100%) to query milestone 𝑡q across 16 held-out prompts (interquartile bands across prompts). (d) Within-model retention of written needles 𝐻1–𝐻5 from each write (100%) across sequence milestones 𝑠1–𝑠5 to 𝑡q. (e) Share of readout weight 𝑞𝑡𝑆𝑡 (over the haystack) on each needle 𝐻1–𝐻5 across the four answer-generation steps 𝐴1–𝐴4 that chain 𝐻1 → · · · → 𝐻5.

Figure 10 | Trained models exhibit the predicted write-erase sensitivity asymmetry under both SVD rank truncation and causal gate freezing. (a) Truncating each rank-128 gate projection of the uniform-rank Muir checkpoint via SVD (one gate at a time across all layers) shows that the decay (𝑓) and erase (𝑏) gates saturate by rank 64, whereas the output (𝑔), write (𝑤), and readout gain (𝑞) gates require rank 128. (b) Replacing the dynamic write gate with its token-averaged channel mean (𝑤𝑡 ← ?̄?) across all layers degrades validation NLL 14.5× more than freezing the erase gate (𝑏𝑡 ← ?̄?) in both GDN-2 and Muir.

Figure 5 |Muir consistently lowers validation NLL relative to GDN-2 and Transformer throughout 100B-token pretraining. Held-out FineWeb-Edu validation token NLL difference relative to GDN-2 across 166M–1.34B parameters as a function of training tokens. All three Muir variants improve over GDN-2 within the first 10B tokens and reach a 12–20 mnat reduction by 100B tokens, while static and dynamic matched-filter readout provide additional reductions over Muir (no 𝛾).

Figure 7 | Muir extrapolates to 128K-token documents and 10M-token streams with the lowest perplexity at a constant 25 MB state. (a, c) Zero-shot from 4K pretraining, Dynamic YaRN Transformer diverges past 8K and unchunked evaluation exceeds HBM at ≥128K, while Muir (static 𝛾) drifts upward past 32K; dynamic 𝛾𝑡 avoids this static-gain drift and outperforms GDN-2 across 128K documents and 10M-token streams (2,560× training length). (b, d) After a 64K cooldown (0.3% of pretraining), Transformer improves through 64K before unchunked evaluation exceeds HBM at ≥ 128K, static-𝛾 drift vanishes, and all Muir variants improve monotonically below GDN-2 through 10M tokens (160× beyond cooldown).

Figure 8 | Static matched-filter readout extends passkey retrieval to 1M tokens both zero-shot and after a 64K cooldown. S-NIAH-1 accuracy across 10 needle-depth bins and context lengths 1K–1M (256× pretraining length) at 1.34B scale under (top) zero-shot evaluation from 4K pretraining and (bottom) pure-text continual cooldown at 64K. Cooldown extends Dynamic YaRN Transformer from 8K to 32K before early-depth accuracy drops at 64K and unchunked prefill exceeds HBM at ≥128K, whereas recurrent horizons change little under pure-text cooldown: GDN-2 collapses past 4K–8K, Muir (no 𝛾) fades past 32K, Muir (dynamic 𝛾𝑡, splitting (𝑟𝑤, 𝑟𝑞) = (128, 128) for multi-lag recall) holds through 32K before tapering at ≥64K, and Muir (static 𝛾, keeping 𝑟𝑤 = 256 for single-lag lookup) maintains near-perfect recall to 1M tokens in both regimes.

Figure 9 | Boundary-pivoted chunkwise execution eliminates decay overflow and maintains wellconditioned forward and backward passes. (a) Against an exact float64 sequential reference, naive unpivoted float32 decay factorization overflows and produces NaN on 25% of heads, whereas the boundarypivoted bfloat16 and float32 kernels match the reference to machine precision on both chunk outputs and final state. (b) Across synthetic stress regimes spanning 𝜅2(𝑇 ) ∈ [1, 104], the bfloat16 block-Neumann inverse stays near its precision floor throughout the well-conditioned regime (𝜅2(𝑇 ) < 40, shaded), which contains the sampled 100B-token checkpoints of GDN-2 and Muir (markers show medians). (c) Single-layer backward gradients (𝑇 =128, 𝐶=64, 𝑑𝑘=16) match the float64 reference across all six inputs without log-decay drift.

Figure 11 | Stationary state row energies obey the closed-form law and are balanced by fractional power-law readout gains. (a) Across state channels, the analytical fixed point 𝑚* 𝑗 (5) closely tracks measured stationary row energy 𝑚𝑗 = E[‖𝑆𝑡,𝑗,:‖22] in both GDN-2 and Muir. (b) Across all heads, weighting state rows by the learned readout gain compresses the within-head p90/p10 energy spread by 35% relative to GDN-2. (c) Within each head, learned static gains |𝛾𝑗 | follow a fractional power law 𝛾𝑗 ∝ 𝜌−𝑝 𝑗 (𝑝 = 0.35) of stationary row RMS 𝜌𝑗 , intermediate between unit readout (𝑝 = 0) and full whitening (𝑝 = 1).

Figure 12 | Readout-exponent sweeps and erase-logit shifts confirm the optimality of fractional power-law readout and the early-vs.-late erasure trade-off. (a) Replacing the learned static gain in each head with an RMS-matched power law 𝛾𝑗(𝑝) ∝ 𝜌−𝑝 𝑗 yields a U-shaped loss curve minimized near the learned exponent (𝑝 ≈ 0.35), outperforming both unit readout (𝑝 = 0) and full whitening (𝑝 = 1). (b) Shifting the pre-activation erase logit (𝑧𝑏 𝑡 ← 𝑧𝑏 𝑡 +𝛿𝑏) shows that weaker erasure degrades predictions across all positions, whereas stronger erasure leaves early tokens [0, 16) nearly unchanged while degrading late tokens [256, 4K).

papers.title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
papers.tldr: Muir improves gated linear attention by allocating gate capacity according to update sensitivity and using matched-filter state readout, achieving better language modeling, recall, and long-context performance at similar or lower training cost.

papers.abstract: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified-memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory. These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.
bullets: Targets the accuracy–memory/bandwidth tradeoff in 2–4-bit weights and 2–3-bit KV-cache quantization.
Co-designs precision representation, selection, and delivery, overlapping transfers with computation and reusing fetched precision across decoding steps.
On 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, lowers WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while retaining 95.4% of quantized-base throughput on an RTX 5090.
With 2-bit weights and KV cache, improves Qwen3-8B AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use.
At 128K context, 3-bit weights plus 2-bit KV matches the reported perplexity and speed of 4-bit AWQ plus 8-bit KV while using approximately half the GPU memory.

papers.selection_reason: Low-bit LLM inference with selective precision streaming and KV-cache quantization; directly relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
papers.tldr: StrataFlux recovers much of the accuracy lost by ultra-low-bit LLM quantization by streaming selective higher-precision data from host memory and storage without sacrificing most inference speed or GPU-memory savings.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models offer parallel text generation, but independently sampling multiple tokens can disrupt their dependencies and change the output distribution. Exact continuous-time sampling avoids this approximation, yet typically requires one sequential model evaluation per token. We introduce SpecCTMC, a training-free speculative sampler that reduces this sequential bottleneck without a separate draft model. SpecCTMC proposes successive token updates using previously computed model predictions, evaluates their intermediate states in parallel, and applies an exact acceptance-and-correction procedure. We prove that SpecCTMC preserves the joint distribution of event times, generation order, and token values of the underlying continuous-time Markov chain. It therefore introduces neither time-discretization error nor additional factorization error from parallel decoding. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B across five benchmarks demonstrate 1.73-4.38x fewer sequential model evaluations than direct continuous-time sampling, while preserving the reference sampling distribution. Our code is available at: https://github.com/kasakh/specctmc
bullets: Addresses the sequential evaluation bottleneck in exact continuous-time sampling, where independent parallel token sampling can disrupt dependencies.
Uses previously computed model predictions to propose successive updates, evaluates intermediate states in parallel, and applies exact acceptance-and-correction.
Requires no separate draft model and no training.
Theoretical analysis shows preservation of event times, generation order, and token values, avoiding discretization and added factorization errors.
Experiments on two diffusion language models and five benchmarks reduce sequential model evaluations by 1.73–4.38× while preserving the reference sampling distribution.

papers.selection_reason: Speculative exact sampling for diffusion language models; reduces sequential evaluations while preserving the sampling distribution.
papers.title: SpecCTMC: Exact Speculative Simulation of Diffusion Language Model Continuous-Time Markov Chains
papers.tldr: SpecCTMC accelerates exact continuous-time sampling for diffusion language models by speculatively parallelizing token updates without changing the target distribution.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models can write many tokens per step, but must choose which tokens are safe to commit together. Mean-field decoding penalizes pairs of positions whose predictions look alike. We replace this proxy with the coupling itself: how much committing one token changes the model's confidence at another. Cheap probes inside the main forward pass measure it, with no training or extra model, and it plugs into the same mean-field rule. On three models and four benchmarks, our method needs far fewer steps than mean-field decoding and is faster in most settings, also with a key-value cache, at an average accuracy cost of 1.1 points. Shuffling the couplings or replacing them with a uniform bonus loses this gain.
bullets: Targets inefficient parallel decoding, where tokens must be selected jointly without harmful interactions.
Measures how committing one token changes another token’s confidence, replacing mean-field similarity penalties.
Uses cheap probes within the existing forward pass, requiring no training or additional model.
Works with the same mean-field decoding rule and key-value caching across three models and four benchmarks.
Achieves far fewer decoding steps and faster decoding in most settings, with a 1.1-point average accuracy cost; shuffled or uniform couplings remove the benefit.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of measured coupling. Top: mean-field decoding penalizes two positions whose predicted distributions overlap (left). Each probe row reveals one candidate and recomputes only the masked positions, reading the main keys and values of the same layer everywhere else. The resulting margins give the coupling ∆ij = ci − c (j) i , which enters the mean-field update, and positions with qi ≥ τ are committed for the next step.

papers.selection_reason: Parallel decoding for diffusion language models, relevant to LLM and efficiency.
papers.title: Measured Coupling for Parallel Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Measured coupling enables diffusion language models to commit safely in parallel, reducing decoding steps and usually improving speed with only a small accuracy tradeoff.

papers.abstract: LLM pruning must preserve quality while meeting hardware- and workload-specific constraints on latency, throughput, and memory. Existing pruning workflows often target parameter counts, requiring practitioners to manually select model sizes that meet latency, throughput, and GPU memory limits. However, parameter count alone does not predict these metrics, which depend on the model architecture, workload, hardware, and serving engine. We introduce AutoCompress, a hardware-guided compression framework that directly incorporates such constraints into differentiable architecture search. AutoCompress jointly optimizes global and per-layer structure to produce heterogeneous architectures, guided by serving-engine cost models validated against end-to-end latency, throughput, and memory measurements. We evaluate AutoCompress on long-context local coding, batched datacenter serving, and latency-sensitive in-game interaction. Compared to the state-of-the-art Minitron pruning framework, AutoCompress improves average accuracy across eight benchmarks by 6.57, 2.35, and 0.57 percentage points on RTX 5070, RTX 5080, and H100, respectively. AutoCompress also compresses Nemotron 3.5 Super from 120B to 74B parameters for single-B200 BF16 serving at 128K context, retaining 95% of its mean benchmark score.
bullets: Parameter count alone poorly predicts deployment performance across architectures, workloads, hardware, and serving engines.
The framework uses differentiable architecture search with serving-engine cost models validated against end-to-end measurements.
It jointly optimizes global and per-layer structure, producing heterogeneous compressed architectures.
Evaluated across long-context coding, batched datacenter serving, and latency-sensitive interaction workloads.

Compared with Minitron, it improves average accuracy across eight benchmarks and compresses Nemotron 3.5 Super from 120B to 74B parameters while retaining 95% of its mean benchmark score for a specified deployment setting.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | AutoCompress overview. Given a base model and deployment constraints, AutoCompress automatically selects, prunes, and distills an architecture for on-device gaming, local coding, or datacenter serving. papers.abstract: Self-attention carries a quadratic cost in token count, which limits how far Vision Transformers can scale with input resolution. We introduce SSoG, a separable sum-of-Gaussians spatial operator that replaces dense self-attention with a learned mixture of axis-factorized Gaussian kernels, reducing the per-layer cost from $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ to subquadratic in $N$. Unlike dot-product self-attention, whose Lipschitz constant is unbounded outside a compact input domain, SSoG with fixed kernels is globally Lipschitz continuous, which, via the Picard--Lindelöf theorem, guarantees that the continuous-depth variant has a unique solution on the whole integration interval, a global guarantee that dense-attention counterparts lack in general. On CIFAR-100 at $224\times224$, in a matched discrete-Transformer setting and in the continuous setting, SSoG improves Top-1 accuracy by 2.2--4.1 points across three model widths while using 8.8--16.6\% fewer parameters, with depth and training recipe held fixed. In a looped-Transformer setting, SSoG improves Top-1 accuracy by 5.4--8.1 points. We further probe inference-time scaling by evaluating on inputs up to $1024\times1024$ at matched batch size: in the continuous-depth (Neural ODE) architecture, SSoG reaches up to 154\% higher throughput and over 60\% lower peak memory than dense attention, with the gap widening as resolution grows, consistent with the difference in asymptotic cost. In the discrete and looped settings, SSoG also achieves over 30\% higher throughput than dense attention at this resolution. Together, these results establish SSoG as a practical, parameter-efficient, and theoretically grounded alternative to dense attention across discrete, weight-shared, and continuous-depth Transformer variants.
bullets: Addresses the quadratic token-cost bottleneck of dense self-attention at high image resolutions.
Uses a learned mixture of axis-factorized Gaussian kernels, reducing per-layer complexity to subquadratic in the token count.
With fixed kernels, SSoG is globally Lipschitz, supporting unique whole-interval solutions for its continuous-depth Neural ODE formulation.
On CIFAR-100, it improves Top-1 accuracy across discrete, continuous, and looped Transformer settings while using fewer parameters.
At up to 1024×1024 resolution, it delivers substantially higher throughput and lower peak memory than dense attention, especially in the continuous-depth model.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with impressive perception and understanding capabilities will enable a range of downstream applications. However, their substantial computational and memory requirements hinder the real-world implementation, particularly for resource-constrained edge devices. Quantization has emerged as an effective solution for deploying large models. While post-training quantization (PTQ) successfully retains the performance at moderate bit-width (e.g., W8A8), it suffers from severe performance degradation under low-bit quantization (e.g., W4A8), especially for small-scale models that are more suitable for edge deployment. In this paper, we propose ProQuant, a novel weight-activation quantization-aware training (QAT) framework tailored for low-bit MLLMs. First, to align the limited finetuning dataset distribution with the pretrained dataset distribution, we propose a self-relabeling (SRL) scheme to resample the responses of the open-source multimodal dataset. Second, we are the first to take a decoupled view of multi-modal (MM) understanding and language modeling abilities. We propose a progressive block activation (PBA) mechanism to prioritize the MM understanding recovery. We also introduce a vision-sensitive factor $\vecτ$ that effectively identifies the MM-critical layers. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks, covering models with 2B-8B parameters, show that ProQuant significantly outperforms existing methods. For example, our W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct improves average accuracy by impressively 6.6% and achieves performance comparable to full precision counterparts with only approximately 1% performance drop. Code is available at https://github.com/yufeixue-ai/ProQuant/.
bullets: Targets severe accuracy degradation from low-bit quantization in resource-constrained edge MLLMs, especially small models.
Uses self-relabeling to better align limited fine-tuning data with the pretrained data distribution.
Introduces progressive block activation to recover multimodal understanding before language-modeling capabilities.
Employs a vision-sensitive factor to identify layers critical to multimodal understanding.
Across 2B–8B models and multiple benchmarks, W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct gains 6.6% average accuracy and remains about 1% below full precision.

papers.abstract: World-action models adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on vision-language backbones, tying policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. While recent world-action models mostly scale the video backbone and its data, we argue that the choice of latent space is just as critical, and that the policy should be trained natively in that space. We introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder; it predicts future features with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art average RoboTwin 2.0 success under both clean-only and full training, and state-of-the-art LIBERO-Plus success with corrected instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competitors; with full training, its success scales with model size up to 2.1B. Its S and B policies run two to five times faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM while outperforming both on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, and La-JEPA outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, its average success is comparable to $π_{0.5}$. A design study shows that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction improves the policy even when skipped at inference. Tailoring the policy's design, including its latent space, to control can thus matter more than the knowledge transferred from a pretrained generative backbone, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.
bullets: Motivation: Existing world-action and vision-language-action policies inherit costly architectures designed for video or language generation rather than control.
Method: Train a policy transformer from scratch in pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 feature space; use action-conditioned future-feature prediction during training, but generate only actions at inference.
Results: La-JEPA attains state-of-the-art average performance among policies without embodied pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0 and corrected-instruction LIBERO-Plus benchmarks.
Efficiency: Its S and B variants run 2–5× faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM while outperforming them on the reported benchmarks.
Design insight: JEPA features outperform video-VAE latents, and training-time future prediction helps even when omitted during inference; real-robot performance is comparable to π0.5 on four tasks.

papers.abstract: Dense optical flow allows small drones to avoid obstacles. However, few dense optical flow networks are designed for microcontrollers (MCUs) with neural accelerators, whose on-chip SRAM limits the input resolution. We present PACE-NAS, a macro-to-micro neural architecture search framework that decouples memory from latency: a macro design fixes the backbone and its peak SRAM, and a micro design searches operators and depths to trade accuracy against compiler-estimated latency. We apply it to EdgeFlowNet on a Grove Vision AI V2 board (Ethos-U55), where profiling locates the peak SRAM at the full-resolution output head. Replacing transposed convolutions with bilinear upsampling and convolutions lowers the peak SRAM by 18%, and two lightweight context modules lower the endpoint error (EPE) without raising the peak. All searched subnets share this peak, so the search needs no memory constraint. We name the Pareto-optimal models MCUFlowNet; the fastest variant, MCUFlowNet-S, runs 1.76x faster than a retrained EdgeFlowNet at a 1.6% higher EPE and, in simulated forest flights at 2 m/s, reaches the goal without collision in 51.5% of trials, against 41.8%. PACE-NAS also applies to semantic segmentation, where a searched PIDNet-S variant runs 1.17x faster at similar accuracy. Code is available at https://gitlab.kuleuven.be/emedia-research-lab/esat-stadius/mcuflownet/mcuflownet.
bullets: Targets dense optical flow on MCUs, where limited on-chip SRAM restricts input resolution.
PACE-NAS separates macro design for peak SRAM from micro search over operators and depths for accuracy–latency trade-offs.
Replacing transposed convolutions and adding lightweight context modules reduces memory use and endpoint error without increasing peak SRAM.
MCUFlowNet-S runs 1.76× faster than retrained EdgeFlowNet with 1.6% higher EPE, and avoids collisions more often in simulated forest flights.
The framework also speeds up a PIDNet-S semantic-segmentation variant by 1.17× at similar accuracy.

papers.abstract: Production deployments often use different models to balance cost and quality through cascading, routing, and switching models during long conversations. Context accumulates across turns. Each switch requires the target to repeat prefill over this context. Existing methods transfer full-attention (FA) K/V caches across models. Hybrid linear-attention models also retain recurrent states (REC) and convolution histories (Conv). The interaction between Conv and REC complicates cross-model state transfer. Conv perturbations can change keys and values in recurrent layers and alter REC updates. Conv histories are overwritten, but changes in REC can still affect later outputs. More accurate REC reconstruction need not improve continuation. Building on this, we propose Hybrid State Transfer (HST) for all three state types. It uses structured REC maps and preserves history order during Conv alignment. We calibrate the adapters using the frozen target's outputs during continuation. FA cache map updates are merged offline. Across five benchmarks, Qwen3.5 4B$\rightarrow$27B and 9B$\rightarrow$27B achieve mean task retentions of 89.88% and 94.11%, respectively. With source caches already available, separate timing on synthetic 16K inputs yields handoff body speedups of $21.66\times$ and $21.91\times$.
bullets: Model switching in long conversations normally repeats context prefill, while hybrid models additionally maintain recurrent and convolution histories.
HST transfers all three state types using structured recurrent-state maps and order-preserving convolution-history alignment.
Adapters are calibrated against the frozen target model’s continuation outputs; full-attention cache updates are merged offline.
Across five benchmarks, reported task retention is 89.88% for 4B→27B and 94.11% for 9B→27B transfers.
On synthetic 16K inputs with source caches available, handoff body speedups are 21.66× and 21.91×.

papers.selection_reason: Cross-model state handoff for hybrid linear-attention LLMs; directly targets KV cache and recurrent-state transfer efficiency.
papers.title: Beyond K/V Caches: Cross-Model State Handoff in Hybrid Linear-Attention LLMs
papers.tldr: Hybrid State Transfer enables efficient cross-model handoff by transferring full-attention, recurrent, and convolutional states, preserving up to 94.11% task performance with over 21× handoff speedups in tested settings.

papers.abstract: Tensor network kernel machines (TNKMs) combine nonlinear features with low-rank tensor representations to model complex relationships efficiently. However, selecting an appropriate tensor rank remains challenging, as conventional rank-search methods require training multiple candidate models, increasing computational costs. In this work, we focus on a canonical polyadic (CP) tensor network parameterization and propose GB-CPKM, a gradient boosting framework that builds a higher-capacity predictor by sequentially adding fixed-rank learners. This approach provides a new perspective on rank selection by incrementally increasing model capacity, with ensemble size selected based on validation performance rather than through explicit rank search. Experiments on real-world regression benchmarks show that GB-CPKM trains up to 6x faster and uses up to 2x less peak memory than a conventional rank-selection method based on cross-validation, while achieving comparable predictive performance. These results highlight the potential of gradient boosting to improve the computational efficiency and scalability of tensor-network learning.
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of selecting tensor ranks in tensor network kernel machines.
Uses a canonical polyadic (CP) parameterization with gradient boosting to incrementally increase model capacity.
Selects ensemble size through validation performance instead of training many candidate ranks.
On real-world regression benchmarks, trains up to 6× faster and uses up to 2× less peak memory than cross-validation-based rank selection.
Achieves comparable predictive performance, with scope demonstrated on regression tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Ablation study of base-learner rank in GB-CPKM on four real-world datasets, with each column corresponding to a dataset. The top row shows cumulative training time (in seconds), while the bottom row reports validation MSE on a logarithmic scale. Across the evaluated datasets, higher-rank base learners achieve better predictive performance while also reducing cumulative training time. However, rank selection should also account for memory requirements, which may constrain the use of higher-rank models in practice.

Figure 1: Comparison of the training procedures for CP tensor network kernel machines (CPKMs) using gradient boosting (GB) and rank selection via validation (CV). (a) GB-CPKM incrementally builds an ensemble by training fixed-rank R̂ base learners and concatenating their factor matrices along the rank dimension to represent the combined model. The ensemble size M is selected based on validation performance. (b) In contrast, CV-CPKM independently trains candidate models with different CP ranks and selects the rank that achieves the lowest validation error. In the diagrams, each base learner model is represented by D factor matrices of size I ˆ R̂, where I is the number of rows and R̂ is the CP rank. Different colors distinguish the trainable factor matrices. Factors in gray are fixed and are not updated.

Figure 3: Comparison of GB-CPKM (red) and CV-CPKM (blue) on four real-world datasets, with each column corresponding to a dataset. From top to bottom, the rows show cumulative training time (in seconds), test MSE, and peak memory consumption (in MiB), plotted against the number of considered candidate CP ranks. Solid lines indicate the mean across 10 runs, and shaded regions represent ˘ 1 standard deviation. GB-CPKM consistently requires less training time and peak memory than CV-CPKM, while achieving comparable predictive performance. The test MSE of GB-CPKM is similar to that of CV-CPKM, with overlapping variability bands in some cases, and approaches comparable values across the evaluated datasets. These results highlight the potential of GB-CPKM to reduce computational costs without substantially compromising predictive accuracy.

Table 1: Performance comparison of GB-CPKM and CV-CPKM across regression benchmarks. We report test mean squared error (MSE), training time (seconds), and peak memory consumption (MiB). Each experiment is repeated over 10 runs, with results reported as mean ˘ 1 standard deviation. N denotes the number of samples, and D denotes the input dimensionality. Overall, GB-CPKM trains up to 6ˆ faster and uses up to 2ˆ less peak memory, on average, than CV-CPKM, while achieving comparable test MSE. The hybrid variant, GB-CPKM(H), further improves predictive performance on most datasets by performing an additional full ALS sweep on the combined model.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a gradient boosting framework to improve the computational efficiency (training speed and memory) of tensor network kernel machines, fitting the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: Gradient Boosting for Efficient Rank Discovery in Tensor Network Kernel Machines
papers.tldr: GB-CPKM avoids expensive explicit tensor-rank searches by sequentially boosting fixed-rank tensor network kernel learners.

papers.abstract: Efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices requires balancing performance with compute and memory constraints. Post-training compression is an effective approach to managing this trade-off, while requiring much less computation than in-training counterparts. We propose DictLLM, a dictionary-based compression scheme in which weight matrices within grouped layers are decomposed into a shared dictionary and layer-specific sparse coefficients, directly obtained from a pre-trained model without further training. Specifically, we cast DictLLM as a four-step post-training optimization. First, we obtain shared dictionaries via singular value decomposition (SVD) of input-scaled weight matrices, amortizing rank across grouped layers; second, we sparsify the layer-specific coefficients to the target compression ratio using a dictionary-aware Hessian; and third, we refine the dictionaries given the resulting sparse coefficients. Finally, we aggressively quantize both components using factor-specific Hessian information: input covariance for the dictionaries and the dictionary-aware Hessian for the coefficients. The resulting representation reduces memory footprint by storing a single shared dictionary per layer group, along with sparse layer-specific coefficients. On language modeling and zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, DictLLM consistently outperforms existing post-training low-rank compression methods and pushes the Pareto frontier between model size and performance. DictLLM compresses the original LLaMA-7B model by 5.1x with only a 2.9-point increase in WikiText-2 perplexity, achieving a 3.6x higher compression ratio than the state-of-the-art low-rank method.
bullets: Targets mobile deployment under compute and memory constraints without additional training.
Decomposes grouped-layer weights into shared SVD-derived dictionaries and sparse, layer-specific coefficients.
Uses Hessian-aware sparsification, dictionary refinement, and factor-specific quantization.
On language modeling and zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, it outperforms existing post-training low-rank methods.
Compresses LLaMA-7B by 5.1× with a 2.9-point WikiText-2 perplexity increase; the abstract reports a 3.6× higher compression ratio than the prior low-rank state of the art.

figures.caption: Figure 1: DictLLM: Dictionary-based compression method. DictLLM resolves the weight memory bottleneck by compressing transformer weights into a shareable dictionary. It compounds four compression steps. ➊ The first step factorizes input-scaled weight matrices of grouped layers into a shared dictionary and layer-specific coefficients. ➋ We then prune the layer-specific coefficients using a dictionary-aware Hessian. ➌ We refit the shared dictionary to the resulting sparse coefficients. ➍ We quantize both the dictionary and the coefficients into NVFP4 using input statistics for the dictionary and dictionary-aware Hessians for the coefficients. The resulting compressed representation enables efficient projections by transferring a small set of shared dictionaries.

Figure 3: Motivation for staged dictionary refinement. We compare (a) activation reconstruction error and (b) runtime of our factorize– prune–update pipeline against k-SVD on a single LLaMA-7B query projection.

Figure 4: Perplexity-model size trade-off. WikiText-2 perplexity of compressed LLaMA-7B across factorization ratios and coefficient sparsities. DictLLM factorizes weights at rate ρfac and then prunes layer-specific coefficients with 20%– 50% sparsity. We also report their NVFP4 versions.

Figure 2: Dictionary-based forward operation. Each weight matrix Wℓ is replaced by the product of a shared dictionary D̃g and a layer-specific sparse coefficient matrix C̃ℓ. The forward pass computes Yℓ = XℓD̃gC̃ℓ.
Figure 5: Ablation of dictionary update. WikiText-2 perplexity of LLaMA7B across different sparsity levels, with and without dictionary update.
Figure 6: Effect of calibration size. WikiText-2 perplexity of LLaMA-7B as a function of calibration set size.

Table 3: Choice of pruning method. We prune the coefficients of LLaMA-7B based on magnitude, full Hessian inversion, and Hessian with lazy updates. We measure the perplexity on WikiText2 with 50% sparsity on a 20% factorized model.

Table 1: Benchmark on language modeling and reasoning tasks. We benchmark DictLLM against low-rank compression baselines on language modeling and commonsense reasoning tasks for LLaMA-7B at different compression ratios. We additionally report the FP4-quantized DictLLMFP4 models at the bottom of the table. We measure perplexity on WikiText-2, Penn TreeBank (PTB), and C4, and zero-shot accuracy on OpenBookQA (OB), WinoGrande (WG), HellaSwag (HS), PIQA (PQ), MathQA (MQ), ARC-Easy (AE), and ARC-Challenge (AC).
Table A11: Comparison with low rank methods including SVD-LLM V2. We measure WikiText-2 perplexity at 20% compression.

Perplexity is measured on WikiText-2 using LLaMA-7B, and compression gain denotes the reduction in model size. The FP16/FP16 baseline corresponds to the factorized model with a 30% factorization reduction and 50% coefficient sparsity before quantization.
