Table 5: Generalization across model families. Perplexity (↓) of three different LLMs, e.g., LLaMA 2-7B, OPT-6.7B, and Mistral-7B, under 1.25× compression on WikiText-2.

Table A13: Effect of compounding pruning and quantization on Basis Sharing. ‘BS’ denotes Basis Sharing [9]. Magnitude pruning acts on the coefficient matrix. We measure language and reasoning performance on LLaMA-7B. All results are reproduced by us.
Table A12: Effect of compounding quantization on Basis Sharing. ‘BS’ denotes Basis Sharing [9]. We measure language and reasoning performances on LLaMA-7B. All results are reproduced by us.
Table A14: End-to-end decoding on LLaMA-7B. DictLLM uses MACKO for sparse coefficients. The measurement excludes the prompt prefill stage.
Table 6: Effect of LoRA fine-tuning. WikiText-2 perplexity (↓) of LLaMA-7B with post-compression LoRA fine-tuning across compression gains.

papers.selection_reason: Post-training LLM compression via dictionary kernels reduces model memory footprint; fits memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: DictLLM: Post-training Compression of Large Language Model with Dictionary Kernels
papers.tldr: DictLLM compresses LLMs after training by sharing dictionary kernels across layer groups and sparsifying and quantizing layer-specific coefficients, achieving strong size–performance trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D models use Transformers to predict camera poses, depth, and structure in one pass, avoiding iterative multi-view optimization. Long sequences and deep attention incur high compute and memory costs, motivating Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) for deployment. Existing PTQ methods mainly suppress channel-wise outliers by smoothing or orthogonal rotation. Geometry Transformers introduce a different challenge: heterogeneous token types share one activation quantization grid. A few special tokens may exert high leverage over global outputs and be updated by only a subset of blocks. Token-blind transforms, which apply the same transformation to every token, reduce overall quantization error but cannot remove differentiated degradation across token types. We propose QMapAnything, a structure-aware PTQ framework. We cast floating-point-preserving rotation and smoothing as a token-blind reparameterization group, and prove that they yield common-mode gains while leaving relative token SNR unchanged. We introduce a statistic $Γ$ that combines a special token's quantization disadvantage and output leverage to predict whether differentiated bias correction is needed beyond rotation. Experiments on geometric benchmarks show that W4A8 closely matches full-precision performance. Under W8A8, peak memory falls by $2.2$--$3.1\times$ versus FP32, with up to $3.1\times$ speedup on real hardware. These results provide a principled and efficient approach to deploying feed-forward 3D reconstruction models in resource-constrained edges.
bullets: Feed-forward geometry Transformers face high compute and memory costs, while heterogeneous tokens share a single activation quantization grid.
Token-blind reparameterizations reduce overall quantization error but cannot change relative signal-to-noise differences between token types.
The proposed statistic Γ combines special-token quantization disadvantage with output leverage to predict the need for differentiated bias correction.
Experiments report near-full-precision performance with W4A8; W8A8 reduces peak memory by 2.2–3.1× and achieves up to 3.1× hardware speedup.
The approach targets deployment of feed-forward 3D reconstruction models on resource-constrained edge devices.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of QMapAnything on a quantized Transformer block. attn.qkv, mlp.w12 and mlp.w3 apply a rotation matrix transform R to their input, the matching inverse folded offline into the weights. attn.proj needs no input-side transform, since its rotation is absorbed entirely into Wproj. R is the group element addressing S3. The standard token-uniform correction removes a shared systematic offset and can be folded into a layer bias. The group-external term bs targets the S1–S2 interaction by correcting only the special-token row.
Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on three scenes. MapAnything is the FP32 reconstruction. RTN, QuaRot, and QMapAnything are W4A4.

Figure 3: Structural properties of MapAnything that guide the PTQ recipe. (a): block-wise relative scale error. Global blocks (red) are more sensitive than frame blocks, consistent with S4. (b): histogram of flattened activation magnitudes |x| in attn.qkv. A few maxima set the per-tensor scale (S3). (c): patch vs. scale activation ranges. The type-level gap supports the shared-grid mismatch in S1. S2 follows from the multiplicative role of the scale token.

Table 1: Camera pose estimation, averaged over ETH3D, SN++v2 and TAV2.
Table 3: Component ablation under W4A4. R: rotation, β: token-uniform bias correction, bs: row-selective correction.

papers.selection_reason: PTQ for 3D geometry transformers; efficiency and 3D relevance.
papers.title: Rotation Is Token-Blind: A Structural Criterion for Post-Training Quantization of Feed-Forward Geometry Transformers
papers.tldr: QMapAnything provides a structure-aware PTQ approach for feed-forward 3D Transformers by identifying when token-specific correction is needed beyond token-blind rotation and smoothing.

papers.abstract: Quantization and pruning reduce the cost of deploying language models, but their effects are usually reported as benchmark scores. Such scores record only the loss that remains at the output. Inside the model, compression damages some components more than others, and the rest of the network can partly compensate. The observed loss therefore reflects both the damage and this compensation, which benchmark scores cannot separate. How the two combine, and whether their balance changes with model size, remains unclear. We study this compensation for in-context retrieval, a capability carried by a small, identifiable set of attention heads. To separate the two, the expected loss from ablating these heads is decomposed exactly into the part restored by the rest of the network, attributed to the components responsible, and the part that reaches the output. This decomposition is then compared across model sizes. For damage of comparable size, smaller models restore most of the loss, whereas larger models retain most of it, because the compensating responses offset less of it as models grow. Compressing the heads produces the same pattern. Compression that is nearly harmless in small models can therefore be costly in large ones.
bullets: Benchmark loss alone conflates internal damage with the network’s ability to compensate for it.
The study examines in-context retrieval, supported by a small, identifiable set of attention heads.
It exactly decomposes ablation-induced loss into damage, compensation from other components, and output-level loss.
For comparable damage, smaller models restore most of the loss, while larger models retain most of it.
The same scaling pattern appears under head compression, making compression relatively benign in small models but costly in large ones.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Repair decomposition under retrieval-head ablation in Pythia-410M and Pythia-12B (top row), and OPT-125M and OPT-6.7B (bottom row). Their difference is total repair, decomposed into copy-suppression release, the backup response, and final normalization. Values are percentages of each model’s clean logit difference. Figure 22: Revision from the intermediate peak to the final value of the mean layer-renormalized answer–distractor trajectory in four Pythia models. papers.selection_reason: Analyzes how quantization/pruning damage scales with model size, relevant to efficient LLM deployment.
papers.title: When Bigger Becomes Brittle: Why Compression Hurts More as Language Models Scale
papers.tldr: Compression can become disproportionately harmful as language models grow because larger models compensate less for damage to critical attention heads.

papers.abstract: Head pose estimation is important for human computer interaction and driver monitoring, but many image based methods remain too costly for resource constrained deployment. We propose STAG-Net, a structure-aware attention over landmark groups for lightweight head Pose estimation that estimates head pose from facial landmarks using movement aware selection, spatial clustering, compact DeepSet encoders, self attention, and a global geometry descriptor. We develop variants using FaceMesh and Face Alignment Network landmarks and evaluate them under cross dataset and subject independent protocols on 300W-LP, AFLW2000, and BIWI. STAG-Net achieves the lowest mean absolute error among all compared landmark based methods in every evaluated setting. On BIWI frames with valid detections, the FAN variant also records the lowest overall error among all compared methods, reaching $3.51^\circ$ under cross dataset evaluation and $2.39^\circ$ under subject independent evaluation. The regressors use only 0.012 to 0.043 million parameters and 24.1 to 83.6 thousand FLOPs, about three orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs than FSA-Net. Despite including landmark extraction and regression, the FaceMesh pipeline reaches 322.9 frames per second on a Tesla T4 GPU, nearly twice the 164.5 frames per second of the fastest measured image based baseline, and 111.0 frames per second on CPU. After normalization by dataset size, STAG-Net processes training samples seven to eight times faster than FSA-Net and more than one hundred times faster than HopeNet and TokenHPE, while complete training finishes within 28 minutes. These results show that STAG-Net combines leading landmark based accuracy with substantially lower training and inference cost.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) lets robots search for run-time object queries, but fixed-rate inference spends embedded compute on low-value frames during idle motion, map revisits, or stable viewpoints. This paper presents an energy-aware OVD scheduler for low-power mobile robots. The scheduler uses odometry, map change, and detector confidence to switch among low-, mid-, and high-power YOLO-World-S modes on a Jetson Orin Nano. We evaluate the energy-quality trade-off on an AgileX LIMO using 40 real navigation trials: two target objects, five placements per target-policy pair, and four perception policies. Across bottle and cup trials, the scheduler records 8/10 mission success compared with 7/10 for each fixed-rate baseline, while reducing mean Jetson input power (a Jetson-side power-draw metric) by 5.2% relative to an 8 Hz high-rate baseline and lowering achieved OVD call rate by 34.0%. It does not minimize mission-window Jetson input energy because longer missions can erase instantaneous power savings. A separate 60 s stationary microbenchmark isolates the perception workload: the scheduler lowers mean power from 8.045 W to 7.301 W and energy from 484.7 J to 438.1 J relative to the 8 Hz baseline. These results support robot-state-aware OVD scheduling as a promising power-management mechanism with competitive task reliability, while showing that mission-window Jetson input energy must be read together with task progress and runtime.
bullets: Targets wasted compute during idle motion, map revisits, and stable viewpoints in low-power robotic autonomy.
Uses odometry, map change, and detector confidence to switch among low-, mid-, and high-power YOLO-World-S modes.
In 40 real AgileX LIMO navigation trials, it achieved 8/10 mission success versus 7/10 for each fixed-rate baseline.
Reduced mean Jetson input power by 5.2% and OVD call rate by 34.0% versus an 8 Hz baseline.
A stationary 60-second benchmark showed lower mean power and energy, but mission-window energy was not always reduced because longer missions can offset instantaneous savings.

papers.abstract: Expert pruning compresses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models by removing the experts that a calibration set marks as unimportant. Studies of high-resource languages largely find that English calibration transfers well to other languages. We test this for Lithuanian: we pruned four MoE models with REAP, removing 25% or 50% of the experts with English, Lithuanian or mixed calibration, and evaluated both languages on reading comprehension, translation and language modelling. English calibration does not transfer to Lithuanian: at 25% pruning, English comprehension fell by a median of 1.7 points but Lithuanian by 21.4. The transfer is asymmetric. Lithuanian calibration removed most of the Lithuanian loss and never significantly hurt English comprehension, which was on average 2.5 points better than under English calibration; only English language modeling got slightly worse. Routing suggests why: in the last layers, Lithuanian sends 55-72% of its expert selections to just eight experts, against 19-39% for English, and English calibration removes some of these experts. Compressed models should be calibrated, and evaluated, in every language they must serve.
bullets: The study tests REAP pruning on four MoE models at 25% and 50% expert removal using English, Lithuanian, or mixed calibration.
At 25% pruning, English comprehension dropped by a median of 1.7 points, versus 21.4 points for Lithuanian under English calibration.
Lithuanian calibration recovered most Lithuanian performance loss and did not significantly harm English comprehension; English language modeling worsened slightly.
Routing analysis indicates Lithuanian concentrates selections on eight experts in later layers, some of which English calibration removes.
Calibration and evaluation should include every language the compressed model is intended to serve.

papers.abstract: LiDAR is a critical sensor for autonomous driving and robotics, yet it remains vulnerable to adverse conditions such as fog, rain, transparent objects, and low-reflectance surfaces. Full-waveform LiDAR (FWL) addresses these limitations by capturing the complete return waveform as a histogram, preserving rich reflection characteristics including multi-path echoes and weak signals. While recent Transformer-based approaches have demonstrated promise on FWL data, two fundamental bottlenecks remain: high computational cost from redundant tokens in low-intensity background regions, and limited generalization due to scarce annotated training data. We address both bottlenecks by exploiting the physical structure inherent to FWL data. First, we propose FWL-ToPM, a token pruning and merging mechanism that leverages intensity distributions to selectively reduce tokens while retaining critical waveform content. Second, we introduce FWLAug, a data augmentation framework designed as a regularization method that preserves waveform structure, retaining the Time-of-Flight waveform of each ray and the frustum geometry, to improve generalization to unseen scenes. Evaluated on the Ghost-FWL benchmark, FWL-ToPM achieves over 8 times speedup at real-time throughput alongside a nearly 9-point F1 gain over the prior state of the art, establishing the first real-time FWL Transformer that simultaneously improves accuracy. FWLAug further improves performance on both the standard benchmark and an out-of-distribution test set of unseen scenes. Together, these methods push FWL-based perception toward practical deployment. The code and the OOD dataset are publicly available and can be accessed via the project page: https://keio-csg.github.io/FWL-ToPM
bullets: Addresses Transformer inefficiency from redundant low-intensity background tokens and limited labeled data in full-waveform LiDAR.
FWL-ToPM prunes and merges tokens using intensity distributions while preserving important waveform content.
FWLAug augments data while retaining each ray’s Time-of-Flight waveform and frustum geometry.
On Ghost-FWL, FWL-ToPM delivers over 8× speedup and nearly 9-point higher F1 than the prior state of the art.
FWLAug improves performance on both the standard benchmark and an out-of-distribution set of unseen scenes; code and the OOD dataset are public.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed framework. (Top) During training, FWLAug augments FWL samples while preserving ToF waveform structure and frustum geometry. High-intensity patches are selected by pruning, spatially reordered along a space-filling curve, and processed by the FWL-ToPM Encoder, which merges redundant tokens before self-attention and unmerges afterward across L Transformer blocks. (Bottom Left) Pruning removes low-intensity background tokens, and merging aggregates the remainder, concentrating computation on object-relevant waveform content. (Bottom Right) Proportion of pixel classes across intensity bins in FWL data. Most regions in FWL data correspond to noisy background, and our pruning strategy removes these dominant low-intensity regions.

Figure 3: (Left) F1-mean vs. FPS trade-off for all compared methods. (Right) Comparison of F1-mean and FPS without additional training. For pruning and merging, ρlow and ρm are varied from 0 to 0.9, respectively. For pruning+merging, ρlow is fixed to 0.7 while ρm is varied. All models are trained without FWLAug.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of classification results with existing FWL-based recognition methods.

Figure 2: Illustration of FWLAug. FWLShiftMix (top): an object in Sample 1 is shifted away from the LiDAR, creating a blank region Ωblank. A glass-containing region Ωsrc is then selected from Sample 2 and pasted into the blank, producing an augmented scene in which the waveform structure of each ray is preserved. FWLCutMix (bottom): a crop region Ωsrc containing minority class (glass) is selected from a source frame and pasted into a destination frame at a random location. Both methods prioritize glass-containing regions to mitigate class imbalance.

Figure 1: Our OOD Test Set. Based on the dense 3D maps as shown in Scene, we annotated FWL data with 4 labels: Ghost (red), Object (green), Glass (blue), Noise. Blue crosses indicate the LiDAR positions during data acquisition. The RGB images show the scenery of the capture locations.

Figure 4: Visualization of token merging on two real Ghost-FWL scenes. Color indicates patch intensity (red: high, white: low). After pruning low-intensity background tokens, the remaining high-intensity tokens are merged by aggregating similar-feature source tokens into destination tokens, reducing the total token count while preserving object-relevant content. The zoomed-in regions show that merged tokens retain the spatial structure of reflected objects across diverse scenes.

Figure 2: Waveforms along single rays in Ghost-FWL Scene 001 (left) and Scene 007 (right). Markers indicate annotated Object (green), Glass (blue), and Ghost (red) bins, labels indicate the Top-3 highest-intensity peaks of each ray, and the dashed line indicates the intensity threshold below which patches are pruned at ρlow = 0.7. The photographs show the corresponding scenes, with the red marker indicating the observed ray. Top-3 peak extraction discards the Object and the Glass return, whereas our intensity-based pruning retains both because they lie above the pruning threshold.

Table 1: Statistical significance of the main comparison with FWL-based methods. F1-mean is reported as mean ± standard deviation over 3 independent runs with different random seeds. All methods are trained without FWLAug.

Table 2: Comparison of space-filling curves used to serialize tokens for merging. F1 scores on the Ghost-FWL test set are reported. We set ρlow = 0.7 (pruning + merging only), ρm = 0.9, and ρd = 0.1. All models are trained without FWLAug.

papers.abstract: KV cache eviction must decide which entries carry information that the rest of the cache can no longer supply. A natural way to estimate this is a learnable gate: give each cached entry a gate on its attention weight and train the gate on the model's own objective. The gate belongs inside the normalizing softmax, where suppressing one entry hands its mass to the others rather than discarding it. That same normalizer absorbs any per-query constant, so a constant gate cancels and reproduces the frozen model exactly. Trained on the language-modeling loss the gate stays near a constant score while its loss falls throughout: optimization succeeds, but a frozen backbone was fit for dense attention, so its loss prefers the no-op, and a near-constant score ranks nothing. The no-op is not a floor the gate improves from but what its objective asks for. A second obstacle survives once the gate moves, since the same gradient charges the gate for errors the frozen model already makes, which no reweighting of positions separates out. Much of the machinery in learnable eviction, from sparsity penalties to relaxations of the discrete decision, works around the first obstacle rather than removing it; both are removed by putting dense attention beyond the gate's reach and making the dense model's predictions its target. Under these two conditions capacity is never the missing ingredient: neither a larger scorer, nor explicit access to the past, nor a trainable backbone helps. The same holds for what eviction unavoidably discards, which is recovered by parameter-free centroids read inside the same softmax far better than by any memory read outside it, since the mass they must return is a share of that normalizer and available nowhere else. At 75\% KV cache compression, this gate reaches 90.14 on RULER at 8K and 46.03 on LongBench with Qwen3-8B, 3.72 and 1.36 points below full-cache inference.
bullets: A gate inside the attention softmax reallocates suppressed entries’ probability mass instead of discarding it; constant gates exactly reproduce dense attention.
Language-modeling loss on a frozen dense model favors this no-op, leaving gate scores nearly constant and unable to rank entries.
Even after gates move, gradients conflate eviction decisions with errors already present in the frozen model.
The proposed setup gives the gate a target beyond dense attention and uses parameter-free centroids inside the softmax to recover discarded information.
At 75% KV-cache compression, it scores 90.14 on RULER at 8K and 46.03 on LongBench with Qwen3-8B, within 3.72 and 1.36 points of full-cache inference.

All keep the gate in the computation graph, but they have different effects on attention mass. A value gate suppresses a contribution without renormalizing the other weights, whereas a per-key logit bias log 𝑔𝑗 redistributes mass and recovers attention over the retained set in the binary limit.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) applied to 3D medical scans face a structural memory wall. A single CT or MRI volume produces tens of thousands of vision tokens, and the resulting key-value (KV) cache scales linearly with both batch and context. Existing KV compression methods operate on the cache's feature or token statistics, or apply 1D and 2D transforms, leaving the three-axis spatial structure in the cache unexploited. We propose TACT-KV (Tri-Axis Cosine Transform), a calibration-free KV compression method that exploits strong spatial correlations in visual KV states along all three anatomical axes of 3D scans. This correlation concentrates the KV cache energy under a frequency-domain transform. TACT-KV applies a separable 3D discrete cosine transform to the KV cache, allocates a per-layer bit budget across frequency bins via reverse water-filling (more bits to high-energy components), and quantizes each bin with a fixed scalar codebook. We derive a close-form relation: the distortion reduction from adaptive bit allocation is dominated by the spectral concentration of the transformed cache. Across six medical VLMs and two 3D CT benchmarks, TACT-KV achieves the lowest 1-bit prediction-flip rate on eleven of twelve model and dataset pairs in our main comparison. The same advantage reproduces on four general-purpose VLMs evaluated on video tasks, indicating that the benefit of exploiting three-axis structure generalizes beyond medical imaging. At equal high-bandwidth memory (HBM), TACT-KV scales the decoding batch size on a single GPU by up to $8\times$.
bullets: Addresses the memory bottleneck caused by tens of thousands of vision tokens in 3D CT/MRI volumes.
Applies a separable 3D discrete cosine transform, reverse-water-filling bit allocation, and fixed scalar quantization without calibration.
Exploits spatial frequency concentration to preserve high-energy KV components more effectively.
Achieves the lowest 1-bit prediction-flip rate in 11 of 12 medical VLM–benchmark comparisons.
The three-axis approach also generalizes to video VLMs; results are reported across four general-purpose VLMs.

papers.abstract: Serving large language models (LLMs) under tight memory and latency service-level objectives (SLOs), including on edge devices, requires jointly selecting the model size, batch size, quantization algorithm, and mixed-precision quantization recipes. Exhaustive search over this combinatorially large space is infeasible. Unlike data-center serving, which often prioritizes throughput or generation speed, resource-constrained deployments typically set memory and latency budgets as constraints and then seek the configuration with the highest generation quality among feasible ones. To this end, we propose ACSeL, a framework that identifies configurations predicted to satisfy deployment constraints while achieving high predicted generation quality. To enable efficient quality estimation, we use Relative Model Quality Degradation (RMQD), a proxy based on the divergence between the candidate and reference models' next-token distributions over a small calibration corpus. Across the evaluated model sizes and precisions, RMQD is inexpensive to evaluate and strongly correlated with downstream benchmark performance. ACSeL combines (i) a lightweight quality surrogate that predicts RMQD directly from a configuration; (ii) Few-shot Median Calibration (FMC), which calibrates operator-profile-based latency estimates using a small number of end-to-end profiles; and (iii) a structured search algorithm BandPareto for exploring layerwise mixed-precision configurations. Experiments on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 workstation and an NVIDIA Jetson Thor edge platform show that FMC substantially improves deployment feasibility, while BandPareto + FMC achieves the highest feasibility and the lowest RMQD gaps to the best measured configurations in the evaluation set.
bullets: Targets joint selection of model size, batch size, quantization algorithm, and layerwise mixed-precision recipes without exhaustive search.
Uses RMQD, based on next-token distribution divergence, as an inexpensive proxy for downstream generation quality.
Combines a quality surrogate, Few-shot Median Calibration for more accurate latency estimates, and BandPareto for structured configuration search.
Experiments on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 and Jetson Thor show improved feasibility and small RMQD gaps to the best measured configurations.
Scope is evaluated across the model sizes and precisions included in the study, with quality estimated using a small calibration corpus.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed under structured generation, where grammar constraints enforce output format at inference time. Whereas existing compression methods target unconstrained generation, we first identify a fundamental mismatch: under structured generation, grammar constraints reduce the model's output distribution to valid tokens, and the logits matter most at the small set of positions that decide the agent's action. Motivated by this finding, we propose SKIM (Selective Knowledge-Informed Masking), the first pruning and distillation framework for LLM agents under structured generation, with both stages guided by token role. SKIM partitions token positions into context, decision, and format categories, and this partition drives two complementary axes: (1) category-aware pruning saliency scores that preserve parameters most relevant for decision positions; and (2) an on-policy distillation objective that aligns student and teacher on valid tokens, paired with category-aware feature matching. We evaluate SKIM on tool-calling benchmarks and within multi-step agent loops, across multiple model scales and sparsity levels. SKIM consistently improves accuracy over baselines, with its superiority becoming most striking in high-sparsity regimes where conventional methods struggle, demonstrating the potential of category-aware compression for deployment-time grammar-constrained agents.
bullets: Targets a gap in existing compression methods, which are designed for unconstrained generation rather than structured agent outputs.
Partitions tokens into context, decision, and format categories to guide pruning and distillation.
Uses category-aware saliency to preserve decision-relevant parameters and on-policy distillation over valid tokens.
Evaluated on tool-calling benchmarks and multi-step agent loops across model scales and sparsity levels.
Consistently improves accuracy over baselines, especially under high sparsity; scope is grammar-constrained LLM agents.

papers.abstract: Linear attention reduces the quadratic sequence-length complexity of softmax attention by maintaining fixed-size recurrent states. However, these states scale quadratically with the representation dimension and require repeated data transfers during decoding, creating a substantial GPU memory bottleneck. Recent studies have revealed significant low-rank redundancy in recurrent states, suggesting opportunities for more efficient representations. We introduce SPARE (State Projection for Accelerated Recurrent Execution), a training-free method that exploits this redundancy through fixed low-dimensional subspaces, heterogeneous rank allocation, and lightweight write compensation. By performing recurrent reads and updates directly on compact states, SPARE reduces memory traffic without online decomposition or dense-state reconstruction. SPARE achieves 2.55x full-model decoding speedup, 7.49x lower recurrent-kernel DRAM traffic, and 3.31x lower peak GPU memory, while preserving better associative-retrieval accuracy than structured pruning at matched memory budgets.
bullets: Addresses quadratic-in-representation-dimension recurrent states and repeated GPU data transfers in linear attention.
Uses fixed low-dimensional subspaces, heterogeneous rank allocation, and lightweight write compensation.
Performs recurrent reads and updates directly on compact states without online decomposition or dense-state reconstruction.
Reports 2.55× faster full-model decoding, 7.49× lower recurrent-kernel DRAM traffic, and 3.31× lower peak GPU memory.
Preserves better associative-retrieval accuracy than structured pruning at matched memory budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Ablation studies of the key design choices in SPARE. All panels report associative retrieval accuracy on 512 four-choice prompts, with 256 prompts each at retrieval depths of 64 and 128. (a) Heterogeneous rank allocation. We compare SPARE with Uniform SPARE at matched recurrent-state budgets of 6, 9, and 12 MiB. Both methods use the same Key-PCA basis construction and write-compensation mechanism, differing only in how ranks are distributed across layers and heads. Heterogeneous allocation consistently achieves higher retrieval accuracy. (b) Subspace construction. We compare Key-based, State-based, and Value-based PCA projections under a fixed 12 MiB state budget, matched calibration data, and identical per-head rank allocations. Key and State PCA use right-side projections, whereas Value PCA uses a left-side projection. Key-side write compensation is disabled for this comparison and is not applicable to the Value-side formulation. Key PCA achieves the highest retrieval accuracy among the evaluated subspaces. (c) Write compensation. We compare SPARE-H32 and SPARE-H64 with and without projected-Key write compensation, holding their respective rank allocations and projection bases fixed. Enabling compensation improves retrieval accuracy at both compression budgets. All state budgets refer to persistent recurrent-state storage per request rather than peak GPU memory.

Figure 3: Decoding efficiency and memory savings of SPARE. We evaluate SPARE-H32 and SPARE-H64 against the Dense Gated DeltaNet baseline across batch sizes of 32, 128, and 512. (a) Full-model decoding speedup relative to Dense. (b) Reduction in recurrent-kernel DRAM traffic, measured using hardware counters and normalized by the corresponding Dense kernels. (c) Reduction in peak GPU memory, computed as the ratio of Dense to SPARE peak memory usage during full-model inference. Experiments are conducted on NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs using stateful CUDA Graph decoding. The results demonstrate that compact recurrent states reduce memory traffic and GPU memory requirements while accelerating full-model decoding.

Figure 2: Quality–memory trade-off of recurrent-state compression. We compare SPARE with DRRQR structured pruning across different compression budgets. (a) Next-token NLL on WikiText-103 (lower is better). (b) Associative retrieval accuracy over 512 four-choice prompts (higher is better). (c) Mean accuracy across three selected downstream tasks: SQuAD Completion, TriviaQA, and DROP (higher is better). Peak GPU memory is measured during full-model inference with batch size 512, a prefill length of 128 tokens, and 64 decoding steps. Across these evaluations, SPARE provides a favorable quality–memory trade-off, particularly under aggressive compression.

State denotes persistent recurrent-state storage per request, excluding model weights and other runtime memory. Bold values indicate the better result within each matched-budget comparison.

papers.title: SPARE: Fast Linear Attention Decoding with Compact Recurrent States
papers.tldr: SPARE accelerates linear-attention decoding by storing recurrent states in compact low-dimensional subspaces, reducing memory traffic and GPU memory use without retraining.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk and have made efficient video generation practical. However, further accelerating these models toward real-time generation remains challenging, as few-step distillation leaves little cross-step redundancy for existing training-free caching methods to exploit. We revisit this regime and identify two token-level redundancy patterns: cross-frame redundancy from static content shared across adjacent frames, and cross-step redundancy from tokens that converge early during denoising. Crucially, we find that early clean estimates along the model's own denoising trajectory provide an effective online signal for locating both patterns, requiring no retraining, auxiliary predictor, or reference video. Based on these findings, we propose PreSTP (Predictive Spatio-Temporal Token Pruning), a training-free framework that constructs a unified token-wise redundancy mask from cross-frame similarity and cross-step convergence. Tokens marked as redundant skip subsequent computation under a consistent last-computed-value restoration rule, and a content-adaptive mask reuse strategy further reduces dense probing cost. On 5-second generation, PreSTP achieves 1.52x-3.20x speedups and a better efficiency-fidelity trade-off than coarse-grained caching baselines such as TeaCache and FlowCache. On 30-second generation, it reaches up to 1.96x speedup while improving VBench-Long and suppressing long-horizon drift. Notably, it continues to reduce inference cost even in the extreme one-step regime, where cross-step redundancy vanishes entirely and coarse step-wise caching is no longer applicable.
bullets: Targets limited cross-step redundancy in few-step autoregressive video generation.
Uses early clean denoising estimates to detect cross-frame similarity and cross-step convergence online.
Applies a unified token mask, last-computed-value restoration, and adaptive mask reuse without retraining or auxiliary predictors.
Reports 1.52×–3.20× speedups for 5-second videos and up to 1.96× for 30-second videos, with improved long-horizon fidelity.
Remains effective in the one-step regime, where cross-step redundancy and step-wise caching are unavailable.

papers.abstract: In large language model (LLM) serving systems, the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and concurrency, so long-context inference easily hits the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity wall and results in low concurrency. Offloading the KV cache to host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) frees HBM space and raises concurrency, but the additional cache management and host-to-device (H2D) load overhead inflates inference latency, higher concurrency fails to translate into effective throughput. We present FlashOffloading, a host-DRAM-centric inference architecture that fully offloads the KV cache in both the prefill and decode phases. FlashOffloading builds rolling HBM cache for prefill, a hot cache for decode, a reverse sparse index with zero extra miss-lookup overhead, and a compute--load overlapped kernel, optimizing KV offloading latency across the entire pipeline and delivering throughput gains under a time-per-output-token (TPOT) service-level objective (SLO). In experiments deploying GLM-5.2 with multi-token prediction (MTP3) speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill--decode (PD)-disaggregated platform, FlashOffloading improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38\(\times\) and decode throughput by up to 1.91\(\times\) under a 30 ms TPOT constraint. FlashOffloading is integrated into an open-source serving framework: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/tree/releases/v0.30.0.
bullets: Long-context inference can exhaust HBM because KV-cache usage grows with sequence length and concurrency, limiting concurrency.
The architecture fully offloads KV caches for both prefill and decode while optimizing cache access across the serving pipeline.
Key techniques include rolling HBM and hot decode caches, a reverse sparse index, and compute–load overlap.
On GLM-5.2 with MTP3 speculative decoding, it improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38× and decode throughput by up to 1.91× under a 30 ms TPOT SLO.
The system is integrated into the open-source vLLM-Ascend serving framework.

papers.abstract: Attention is a core building block of frontier models and often dominates compute-bound prefill at long context. FP8 matrix instructions offer twice the peak throughput of BF16, but they accelerate only matrix multiplication, and the softmax between the two matrix multiplications of attention runs on vector units that FP8 does not accelerate. On the AMD Instinct MI355X, the vendor's AITER kernels reach 39% of peak FP8 matrix throughput at 32K tokens, compared with 49% in BF16. Attention is also more numerically sensitive to quantization than feed-forward layers, and unlike NVIDIA's Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, the MI355X does not track the completion of matrix instructions in hardware, so overlapping the softmax with the matrix multiplications depends on instruction order. We present ZYFA, prefill kernels for the MI355X built on three techniques: (1) computing each FP8 probability directly from its score with a multiply-add and an integer conversion instead of an exponential; (2) a ping-pong schedule in which one group of threads computes its softmax while another executes its matrix multiplications; and (3) scaling each block of probabilities up by a power of two before rounding, and normalizing by the sum of the rounded probabilities. On attention inputs captured from three models and timed at sustained clock speeds, ZYFA achieves 1.16-1.76x the throughput of AITER. On the Gaussian inputs of kernel benchmarks at 32K tokens, it achieves 1.26-1.37x at head dimension 128 and 1.99x for DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention. The sustained clock of the MI355X depends on operand values, so throughput on random inputs does not reliably predict throughput on real model activations. At head dimension 128, ZYFA's numerical error is within a few percent of that of Composable Kernel and Triton and 62-78% lower than that of AITER's. The source code is available at https://github.com/Zyphra/zyfa.
bullets: Targets long-context attention, where softmax limits the benefits of FP8 matrix throughput on MI355X.
Uses direct FP8 probability computation, ping-pong overlap of softmax and matrix multiplication, and power-of-two probability scaling before rounding.
Achieves 1.16–1.76× AITER throughput on inputs from three models at sustained clock speeds.
On 32K-token Gaussian benchmarks, reaches 1.26–1.37× speedup at head dimension 128 and 1.99× for DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention.
At head dimension 128, numerical error is within a few percent of Composable Kernel and Triton, and 62–78% lower than AITER’s.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Thread traces showing that AITER’s FP8 kernel leaves the matrix pipe idle while its waves compute exponentials and wait at barriers, and that ZYFA’s FP8 kernel keeps the matrix pipe busy most of the time. A thread trace records every instruction that a wave issues, cycle by cycle, here with the thread-trace mode of AMD’s rocprofv3 profiler. Each panel shows the two waves that share one SIMD over 2500 cycles in the middle of the loop over key blocks, where every block repeats the same work, in the FP8 kernels at dqk=128 (S=8K tokens, H=32 heads, multi-head attention). Each wave row shows the class of each instruction that the wave issues, and the matrix-pipe row below it shows when that wave’s MFMAs run. A vector instruction runs on the vector pipe during its bar in the wave row, so the wave rows already show when the vector pipe works. An MFMA keeps running on the matrix pipe for 32 to 64 cycles after its short bar in the wave row, while the wave issues other instructions, so the matrix-pipe rows show that work separately.

Fig. 16: Output error of one attention call for every layer of each model, as relative RMS error against attention computed in fp64 on the same inputs (lower is more accurate). The inputs are the q, k, and v that each model produces on the first 4095 tokens of WikiText-2 (S=4K). The FP8 row uses a logarithmic axis.

Fig. 5: Scaling each block of probabilities before rounding keeps them in the range where FP8 is accurate, and dividing by the sum of the same rounded values keeps the attention weights summing to one. The schematic shows the probabilities p of one query row by 64-key block. (1) AITER’s FP8 kernel rounds p to e4m3 relative to the row maximum. Blocks more than 6 binades (factors of two) below the maximum become subnormal, with fewer significant bits, and values more than 10 binades below underflow to zero in the numerator. The row sum adds the unrounded p in FP32. (2) ZYFA multiplies each block by 2o so that its largest probability gets the same e4m3 value as p=1, and the scaled matrix instruction (MFMA) that computes PV divides the factor out at no cost. The numerator and the row sum use the same rounded values p̂. The P error is the relative error that rounding p adds to the attention output on Mistral-7B (Figure 20).

Fig. 1: Throughput of ZYFA and AITER’s default kernels on the queries, keys, and values captured from one layer per model at sequence length 16K, timed at sustained clocks (the steady clock after warmup launches). L20 is layer 20. The label above each pair is AITER’s time divided by ZYFA’s time. Mistral-7B and Qwen3-8B have head dimension 128, where the FP8 kernel uses lean P, which writes each FP8 probability with one multiply-add instead of an exponential. DeepSeekV2-Lite has the MLA shape, where the FP8 kernel uses exact P, which evaluates the exponential (Section IV-B), and AITER uses Composable Kernel (CK) in FP8 and its OPUS kernel, written with AITER’s C++ template library, in BF16. Table X gives the clock of these runs.

Fig. 8: Throughput of ZYFA and AITER against sequence length on Gaussian inputs (random q, k, and v with standard deviation 0.1). Times are kernel-only, the device time of the kernel alone without the time that the host takes to launch it. AITER is AITER’s default kernel for each configuration, which at dqk=192 is its OPUS kernel in BF16 and Composable Kernel in FP8. The BF16 panels also show AITER’s Triton kernel and, at dqk=192, AITER’s assembly kernel.

Fig. 21: Error that each stage of one FP8 attention call adds to the attention output, as relative RMS error against fp64 attention, on all three models, without and with a Hadamard rotation of Q and K. The stages are quantizing Q, K, and V (input), quantizing the probabilities (P ), and the rest of the kernel’s arithmetic (Section V-E). The dashed line is the total error of ZYFA’s BF16 kernel. At dqk=192 AITER runs Composable Kernel (CK), whose P arithmetic is not emulated, so only its input term and total are shown.

Fig. 17: Kernel time against output error for each kernel on captured layers at S=4K, the q, k, and v that each model produces on WikiText-2. Output error is the relative RMS error against attention computed in fp64 on the same inputs. Filled markers are FP8 kernels, and open markers are BF16 kernels. Each marker is one kernel on one layer, and markers toward the lower left are faster and more accurate. At the head dimensions of DeepSeek-V2-Lite, AITER’s FP8 kernel is Composable Kernel, so their FP8 markers coincide.

Fig. 28: The speedup of ZYFA over AITER barely changes between layers. Each line is the time of one attention call of ZYFA or of AITER’s default kernel in every layer, measured inside a full forward pass of each model at sequence length S=16K on two PG-19 documents. The label in each panel gives AITER’s time divided by ZYFA’s time, as the median and the range over layers, so a value above 1 means that ZYFA takes less time. In the shaded first layers of Qwen3-8B the running row maximum keeps growing, so ZYFA rescales its output accumulator far more often than in the other layers.

Fig. 18: KL divergence of each next-token distribution from that of the same model with attention computed in fp64, when every attention call uses the kernel under test, averaged over the tokens of eight WikiText-2 sequences of 4K tokens (lower is closer to fp64). Each marker is the mean over the sequences, and its bar spans the lowest to the highest sequence. The dashed line is attention computed in fp32. Filled markers are FP8 kernels, and open markers are BF16 kernels. Triton has no FP8 kernel at the head dimensions of DeepSeek-V2-Lite.

Fig. 15: Output error of one attention call on synthetic inputs at S=8K tokens, as each kernel’s relative RMS error against attention computed in fp64 on the same inputs, divided by AITER’s error (below 1 is more accurate than AITER). Gaussian draws q, k, and v from N (0, 0.12), as in the timing runs. Every other input starts from standard normal q, k, and v. Logit SD 1, 4, and 16 scale q and k by 1, 2, and 4, which gives logits with these standard deviations in nats. Stepped Max raises the logits of each successive block of 64 keys by a fixed step, so the row maximum keeps growing. 4-Key Sink scales the first four keys by 8. Rising Logits adds a linear ramp along the keys to every row, and Alternating Rows adds it to every other row. Sink + Flat Tail puts the first key 12 nats above a nearly uniform rest. Full Range draws magnitudes log-uniformly between 2−6 and 28 with random signs, which spans the e4m3 range after scaling.

Fig. 9: Roofline for FP8 multi-head attention at dqk=dv=128, kernel-only on Gaussian inputs. At a given arithmetic intensity, the FLOPs per byte moved from memory, a kernel cannot exceed the sloped memory roof or the flat arithmetic roofs. The roofs are the empirical HBM bandwidth, the datasheet FP8 peak, and the empirical peak of the 32×32×64 FP8 matrix instruction (MFMA) that the kernels use. The 16×16 shape, which has the higher throughput, reaches 4.60 PFLOP/s (Table V). Each vector roof is the throughput at which all vector instructions of a kernel, packed FP32 included, fill the vector pipe, the unit that runs elementwise arithmetic such as the softmax. The roof of exact P, which evaluates the exponential, comes from a thread trace of an earlier build of the assembly kernel. With FLOPs = BHS2(dqk + dv) the arithmetic intensity is 0.4S FLOP/byte, so every length from 2K up is compute-bound.

Fig. 12: Cycles per launch against the shader clock (SCLK) for ZYFA’s and AITER’s FP8 kernels on Mistral-7B layer 20 at S=16K, at sustained clocks. Kernel time is cycles divided by clock, so a kernel can take less time by needing fewer cycles or by running at a higher clock. Cycles are kernel time multiplied by the SCLK of the slowest chiplet. Filled markers are captured activations, the q, k, and v of the real model, and open markers are Gaussian inputs of the same shape. Points on a dashed line take the same time as the captured-activation point of that kernel.

Fig. 24: Rotating Q and K with a Hadamard matrix before FP8 quantization buys more accuracy per unit of time than running heads or layers in BF16. Each line starts from all-FP8 attention with one input transform (large dot) and moves a growing share of heads or layers to BF16. Time is attention time inside the model relative to all-FP8 ZYFA, including one fused quantization pass. The KL divergence measures how far the next-token distributions move from those of the BF16 model, on 48 PG-19 documents per model. On Mistral-7B and Qwen3-8B, only all-BF16 attention reaches the gray BF16 noise band, where a policy (a choice of the heads or layers that run in BF16) is as close to the BF16 model as a second, equally correct BF16 kernel would be.

Fig. 3: The chiplet map helps most at short sequences. The figure gives the throughput of ZYFA with the chiplet map divided by that of the same kernel without it. The map sends consecutive tile pairs of one head to the same chiplet (XCD), so that they share its L2 cache. Multi-head attention, batch size B=1, kernel-only timing on Gaussian inputs as in Table VIII.

Fig. 4: Lean P, which computes each FP8 probability with one multiply-add instead of an exponential, stays within 7.5% of the true probability, against 5.9% for rounding the exact value. The figure gives the relative error of the e4m3 probability with exact P and lean P over one binade (one factor of two) of p, plotted against x = log2 p. Exact P rounds 2x to the nearest e4m3 value. Lean P rounds y from Equation 2 (with shift σ=6 and bias β=0.35) to the nearest integer and uses it as the e4m3 bit pattern, and the dashed line is the error of y before rounding. Over the normal e4m3 range the error depends on the fractional part of x alone, so one binade shows all of it.

Fig. 10: Speed of ZYFA’s FP8 kernels relative to AITER’s default kernel as design decisions are added from left to right, kernel-only on Gaussian inputs, multi-head at B=1. Error bars span the repetitions. At dqk=192 the baseline is Composable Kernel (CK), AITER’s default FP8 kernel for that shape. Step “+Lean P” computes each FP8 probability with a multiply-add instead of an exponential, and step “+Row Sum on MFMA” sums each row of probabilities on the matrix unit. Both steps also turn on per-block scaling, and step “+Assembly Schedule” replaces the HIP kernel with the hand-scheduled assembly kernel. The rightmost point of each line is the final kernel, measured in the same jobs as Table VIII. Section VI-A defines every step, and Figure 11 shows the BF16 kernels.

Fig. 11: Speed of ZYFA’s BF16 kernels relative to AITER’s default kernel as design decisions are added from left to right, kernel-only on Gaussian inputs, multi-head at B=1. At dqk=192 the baseline is AITER’s OPUS kernel, a HIP kernel built with AITER’s C++ template library. Section VI-A defines every step.

Fig. 27: Once its error bound has a cost, an in-kernel two-stage scheme is less accurate (it has a higher KL divergence from the BF16 model) than a static policy that takes the same time. The two-stage scheme runs attention in FP8 with an error bound per block and recomputes the flagged blocks in BF16, at a modeled time of 1 + c+ r w, where c is the cost of the bound, w the share of recomputed blocks, and r the ratio of BF16 to FP8 time. Static policies keep fixed heads or layers in BF16, and their time and KL divergence are measured. The data predate lean P.

Fig. 26: On the NLL, most FP8 policies also differ from the BF16 model, and on Qwen3-8B rotation raises the NLL although it lowers the KL divergence. Each point is the change in negative log-likelihood per token against the BF16 model, with its 95% interval over PG-19 books, for the mixed-precision policies of Figure 24 (choices of the heads or layers that run in BF16), against attention time relative to all-FP8 ZYFA. A lower NLL does not mean that a policy is closer to BF16, as AITER’s FP8 kernel on Qwen3-8B shows.

Fig. 23: Share of the FP8 error energy of the attention outputs that falls in the worst x% of layers, heads, and 128-row blocks, ranked by their own FP8 error, for the median document. The dotted curve is the share if the error were spread evenly, x% of the error energy in x% of the units. The horizontal axis is linear below 1% and logarithmic above.

Fig. 22: Scores that measure the local FP8 error (the error of each unit’s own attention output), such as the error on calibration documents and the quantization error bound, find almost as much of it as ranking by the true error (gray band). ge2 (the gradient-weighted error of a head) and layer KL (how much FP8 attention in one layer alone changes the model output) find little of it, because they rank units by their effect on the model output, which works better end to end (Table XIV). Each line gives the share of the true FP8 error energy in the heads (top) or 128-row blocks (bottom) that a score ranks highest. Static scores are computed in advance on calibration documents and dynamic scores at inference time, and the dotted line ranks the heads or row blocks in random order.

Fig. 19: KL divergence per token from the model with ZYFA’s BF16 attention, KL(BF16 ∥ variant), when every attention call of the model uses one FP8 kernel variant, at 8K, 16K, and 32K tokens on 42 PG-19 documents per model. Lower means closer to the BF16 model. The first two rows are references, attention in fp64 and AITER’s BF16 kernel, which show how far two correct kernels differ through rounding alone, and the gray band covers their range.

Fig. 20: Quantizing the inputs Q, K, and V to FP8 adds most of the error of ZYFA’s FP8 attention, and rounding the probabilities p adds much less. The top row shows the stages of one FP8 attention call. Each bar below is the error that a stage adds on Mistral-7B (12 PG-19 documents, log scale), as the RMS of the change that the stage makes to the attention output O, divided by the RMS of fp64 attention on the BF16 inputs, in percent, pooled over all layers, heads, and rows. A relative RMS error of r% is a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of −20 log10(r/100) dB, and the stages of ZYFA add in quadrature to its total error. Bars show ZYFA with lean P, ZYFA with a Hadamard rotation of Q and K, and AITER’s FP8 kernel. The dashed line is the error of rounding the exact output O to BF16. The error of the running maximum and of the FP32 sums is counted in the last stage.

Fig. 25: Occupancy of the compute units (CUs) of the GPU over time for one attention layer (schematic). (1) With all heads in FP8, one kernel launch runs whole rounds of query-tile pairs, the units of work of the kernel, on every CU. (2) With some heads in BF16, the layer needs two launches. The FP8 launch ends with a partial round, in which only some CUs still have work, and the BF16 launch has too few pairs to occupy all CUs. On Mistral-7B with 5% of heads in BF16, attention takes 1.204 times the all-FP8 time, against 1.049 times by its share of the work. Both times exclude the gather and scatter copies of Table XVIII.

TABLE I: Properties of one MI355X from [Advanced Micro Devices, 2025b,a]. The peaks assume the maximum clock. VGPRs are the vector registers of a wave, XCDs are the eight chiplets, and LDS is the shared memory of a compute unit (CU). Our system caps the board power at the TBP.

TABLE III: In FP8 the softmax needs about as many vectorpipe cycles as the matrix products need matrix-pipe cycles, so the two must overlap almost perfectly to keep the matrix pipe busy, while in BF16 the matrix products take more than twice as long as the softmax. The table gives pipe cycles for one wave (a group of 64 threads) that computes 32 queries against one 128-key block at dqk=dv=128, and each of its 64 lanes holds 64 of the 4096 scores. Matrix cycles, on the pipe that runs matrix (MFMA) instructions, follow from the matrix rate per cycle, and vector cycles, on the pipe that runs elementwise instructions, follow from the measured costs in Section III-A. Exact P, the standard method, evaluates the exponential and converts the result to e4m3 or BF16, and the packed BF16 conversion occupies the vector pipe for 4 cycles instead of 8. Lean P, ZYFA’s method, writes the e4m3 bit pattern of each probability with one multiply-add and one integer conversion (Section IV-B1). Rescaling the output adds vector work when the row maximum grows.

TABLE X: ZYFA and AITER on one layer per model at S=16K (Mistral-7B layer 20, Qwen3-8B layer 18, DeepSeekV2-Lite layer 13). The captured columns use the q, k, and v that the model produces on WikiText-2 text, and the Gaussian columns use random inputs of the same shape. Each run launches one kernel back to back for seconds and is timed only after the GPU clock has settled (sustained clocks). The time ratio is AITER’s time divided by ZYFA’s time, so values above 1 mean that ZYFA takes less time. SCLK is the shader clock of the slowest of the eight chiplets, which sets the kernel time.

TABLE XIII: Effect of rotating Q and K with a Hadamard matrix (rotation) and of subtracting the mean key of each head (K smoothing) before FP8 quantization, for all-FP8 ZYFA attention. The error of one call is the relative RMS error of the attention output O against fp64 attention, from quantizing the inputs alone (input) and in total. KL is the per-token KL divergence from the model with BF16 attention, and dNLL the change in negative log-likelihood per token, both on the 48 PG-19 evaluation documents. Times are relative to all-FP8 attention without transforms. The fused column includes one quantization pass that also applies the transforms. The separate column runs the transforms as PyTorch operations and includes no quantization. The last column is the time of the separate transforms per forward pass at 16K.

TABLE XIV: How well each score chooses the units (heads, 128-row blocks, or layers) that run in BF16. Each value is the KL divergence from the BF16 model that remains when the top 5, 10, or 20% of units by the score run in BF16, divided by the KL divergence of all-FP8 attention (lower is better), on 12 evaluation documents per model with the exact-P build of ZYFA’s FP8 kernel. The local-error oracle ranks units by the true FP8 error of their own attention output. ge2 ranks heads by their gradient-weighted error g2e2, and layer KL ranks layers by how much FP8 attention in that layer alone changes the output of the model. Both use calibration documents (Section VI-C), and the scores below the rule are computed at inference time. A row block has 128 query rows, and its BF16 share of the causal work differs slightly from the nominal share. On the 48 documents of Figure 24 with lean P, ge2 and layer KL give values within 0.02 of these.
TABLE II: Terms used throughout the paper.

TABLE V: Under sustained load the MFMA loops run below the 2.4GHz clock that the datasheet peaks assume, so each reaches less than its datasheet throughput. The BF16 rows use v_mfma_f32_32x32x16_bf16 and v_mfma_f32_16x16x32_bf16, the FP8 rows v_mfma_f32_32x32x64_f8f6f4 and v_mfma_f32_16x16x128_f8f6f4 with e4m3 operands, and the FP4 row v_mfma_f32_16x16x128_f8f6f4 with FP4 operands, all in their unscaled forms. The datasheet peaks assume 2.4GHz.

BHSD and BSHD give the order of the batch, head, sequence, and head-dimension axes in memory, M and N are the numbers of queries and keys, and LSE is the log-sum-exp of each row of scores.

TABLE IV: Both kernels keep the vector pipe about as busy as the matrix pipe, and neither overlaps the two fully. The table gives pipe cycles per SIMD at S=32K for FP8 multi-head attention at dqk=128, for two units of work of one wave on 32 queries and 64 keys each, which together equal the work of one wave on one 128-key block in Table III. AITER is AITER’s FP8 assembly kernel. Base is an earlier HIP version of ZYFA’s FP8 kernel with a Schraudolph exponential (an exponential that writes the bits of an FP32 number directly from the score) and an FP32 row sum, and its instruction mix comes from S=8K traces. The matrix row includes the cycles in which packed FP32 instructions block the matrix pipe, given in parentheses. The serialized row is the sum of matrix and vector cycles, which the work would take if the two never overlapped, and the achieved row gives the cycles that each kernel actually takes. SCLK is the shader clock.

TABLE XI: Output error of one attention call, measured against attention computed in fp64 on the same quantized inputs, so it counts only the error that each kernel adds. Values are means over all layers of each model on WikiText-2 at S=4K. The AITER column gives the relative RMS error of AITER’s default FP8 kernel, which is Composable Kernel (CK) at dqk=192. The other FP8 columns give each kernel’s error divided by AITER’s, so values below 1 mean a smaller error. AITER’s Triton kernel does not support FP8 when dqk ̸=dv. The BF16 column gives ZYFA’s BF16 error divided by the error of AITER’s BF16 kernel.

TABLE VII: FP8 matrix (MFMA) instructions of each FP8 kernel, read from the disassembled kernel binaries. The count is the number of times each instruction appears in the kernel binary, and the rate is in FLOP per clock per SIMD unit, measured with two waves (groups of 64 threads) per SIMD on all 256 compute units (CUs). ZYFA’s PV instruction applies the per-block scale of Section IV-B2, a power of two for each block of 64 probabilities. Composable Kernel (CK) is AITER’s FP8 kernel at dqk=192.

TABLE VIII: Throughput of ZYFA divided by that of AITER’s default kernel at batch size B=1, so values above 1 mean that ZYFA takes less time. Inputs are Gaussian (random q, k, and v with standard deviation 0.1), and times are kernel-only (the device time of the kernel alone), averaged over repetitions. Rows give the precision and the query-key head dimension dqk. At dqk=192 the FP8 baseline is Composable Kernel (CK). The last column is the spread of ZYFA’s multi-head throughput over repetitions at 32K. Figure 8 gives all sequence lengths, and Table IX gives B=4.

TABLE IX: Throughput of ZYFA divided by that of AITER’s default kernel at batch sizes B=1 and B=4, for multi-head attention on Gaussian inputs, kernel-only. Values above 1 mean that ZYFA takes less time.

papers.abstract: Tensor and sequence parallelism (TP+SP) and expert parallelism (EP) put collectives on the critical path of transformer layers. State-of-the-art fused kernels mitigate this with fixed roles or schedules, but this rigidity leaves large idle windows. Predicting a communication-computation split does not remove them either; a predetermined split cannot follow data readiness. We present KOSMOS, a library for self-scheduling persistent kernels whose workgroups use queues ordered by consumer demand to switch between communication and computation roles as data become ready, with no scheduler, per-call cost model, or tuned split. KOSMOS fuses every TP+SP collective of a transformer layer with its GEMM, and runs an entire expert layer, from router to fold, in one launch per direction. Evaluated on AMD Instinct MI350X and AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, KOSMOS speeds up TP+SP end-to-end training in Megatron-LM by 1.10-1.28x in BF16 and 1.10-1.25x in MXFP8. KOSMOS accelerates end-to-end training of DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3-235B proxies by 1.29-1.83x over DeepEP.
bullets: Targets idle windows caused by rigid communication-computation schedules in tensor, sequence, and expert parallelism.
Workgroups switch between communication and computation as data become ready, without a scheduler, cost model, or tuned split.
Fuses TP+SP collectives with GEMMs and executes an entire expert layer in one launch per direction.
On AMD MI350X/MI355X, achieves 1.10–1.28× BF16 and 1.10–1.25× MXFP8 TP+SP training speedups.
Improves DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3-235B proxy training by 1.29–1.83× over DeepEP.

papers.title: KOSMOS: Self-scheduling Persistent Kernels for Communication-Compute Overlap

papers.abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language model responses by spending additional computation at inference time, and the right amount of compute depends on the prompt. Adaptive TTC methods allocate compute based on signals of response quality such as observed rewards, often by stopping once the signal exceeds a fixed threshold, and generally measure cost by the number of generations or tokens. But in online serving, latency is also a cost: it grows with server load, so a method using a fixed threshold spends too little compute when generation is fast and too much when it is slow. For Best-of-$N$ sampling, a widely used TTC method, we propose a two-stage adaptive algorithm that draws an initial batch, then uses the observed rewards and the batch's latency to decide whether to draw a second batch and at what size by comparing expected improvement against predicted cost: it draws one when the first batch's best reward is below a threshold that decreases with the first batch's latency, without explicitly measuring server load. We map each reward to its value under the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the prompt's reward distribution, so the same tradeoff parameters can be reused across tasks; a regression fitted offline on other prompts predicts a distribution for the CDF value of the first batch's best reward, giving the expected improvement in closed form. We evaluate the method by simulation on a preference-based alignment benchmark, measuring generations-equivalent cost: generations plus latency, converted to generations. The method reaches Best-of-$N$'s reward at lower generations-equivalent cost, and conditioning on the measured first-batch latency saves at least as much of that cost as fixed-threshold (latency-unaware) baselines, and more when latency is highly variable, when it grows with batch size, and when the second batch's latency is highly predictable from the first's.
bullets: Targets adaptive test-time compute where latency, not just generation count, is a significant serving cost.
Uses a two-stage strategy: sample an initial batch, then decide whether and how large a second batch should be.
Triggers additional sampling when the first batch’s best reward is below a latency-dependent threshold.
Normalizes rewards via the prompt reward CDF and uses offline regression to estimate expected improvement in closed form.
Simulation results show lower generations-equivalent cost than Best-of-N, with larger savings under variable latency and predictable batch delays.

papers.tldr: A latency-aware adaptive Best-of-N method adjusts second-stage sampling to balance response quality against inference latency, reducing cost especially under variable or predictable server delays.

papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has increased the volume of data generated at the network edge, where many devices operate under severe memory, processing, and energy constraints. In this context, Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) enables machine learning (ML) tasks to be executed on microcontrollers, smart sensors, and other resource-constrained platforms. However, the literature remains heterogeneous regarding the algorithms evaluated, energy-measurement methods, reported metrics, influencing factors, and optimization strategies. This study presents a systematic mapping of energy-aware TinyML research. It identifies the main models and learning approaches, classifies energy-evaluation methodologies and metrics, examines the technical factors affecting energy consumption, and organizes the reported optimization techniques into a structured taxonomy. The findings highlight the frequent use of convolutional and lightweight architectures, direct measurements and analytical estimations, and factors related to model architecture, hardware, communication, numerical precision, and input characteristics. The optimization strategies were grouped into model compression, hardware-aware design, system and communication optimization, and data and processing optimization. The results also reveal limited standardization in experimental platforms, measurement procedures, and reporting practices, limiting reproducibility and direct comparison across studies. This mapping provides an updated overview of the field and guidance for developing and evaluating more energy-efficient TinyML solutions.
bullets: Reviews energy-aware TinyML research for highly resource-constrained edge and embedded devices.
Classifies models, learning approaches, energy-measurement methods, metrics, and energy-influencing factors.
Identifies common use of convolutional and lightweight architectures, alongside direct measurement and analytical estimation.
Groups optimization techniques into model compression, hardware-aware, system/communication, and data/processing strategies.
Highlights inconsistent platforms, procedures, and reporting practices across studies.

papers.abstract: Parallel block drafting accelerates speculative decoding by predicting multiple future positions in a single backbone pass, but on-device deployment constrains both drafter capacity and context storage. Under tight memory budgets, drafters must model long-range dependencies and fine-grained draft-position interactions without the growing KV-cache overhead of full-context attention. We propose HyFlash, a compact parallel drafter that introduces a prefix-memory prior to separate long-range context modeling from fine-grained draft-position interactions with limited capacity. Local attention captures recent context and draft-position interactions, while recurrent memory compresses historical target features into fixed-size states. This inductive bias enables effective local and long-range modeling with bounded draft-side memory. Experiments show that HyFlash achieves higher acceptance than full-context attention with substantially less KV storage and with larger gains for shallow drafters and long contexts.
bullets: Targets on-device speculative decoding under limited drafter capacity and context-storage budgets.
Uses local attention for recent context and draft-position interactions, plus recurrent memory for compressed long-range target features.
Maintains bounded draft-side memory through a fixed-size prefix-memory state instead of growing full-context KV storage.
Experiments report higher acceptance than full-context attention, with larger gains for shallow drafters and long contexts.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes HyFlash, a speculative decoding method that uses a prefix-memory prior to reduce KV cache storage and memory requirements for on-device LLM inference, improving speed without sacrificing quality.
papers.title: HyFlash: A Prefix-Memory Prior for On-Device Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: HyFlash is a compact speculative-decoding drafter that improves draft acceptance while sharply reducing draft-side KV-memory needs on devices.

papers.abstract: Sparsity and quantization reduce the cost of attention by skipping interactions and lowering the precision of those retained. However, useful interactions differ in their precision requirements: some tolerate low-precision scores while remaining sensitive to removal. We therefore introduce TriAttention, which assigns query-key (QK) tiles to skipping, 4-bit, or 8-bit computation, using 4-bit to retain quantization-tolerant interactions at lower cost. To represent compactly, we encode each head's computation regions with two diagonal-distance boundaries, keeping policy storage independent of context length. Offline calibration then evaluates candidate boundary pairs using normalized projected-output errors and complete-tile execution costs. Using these measurements, a model-wide allocator selects each head's boundaries to minimize calibration error under a shared computation budget. During prefill, the selected boundaries generate precision-grouped traversals for a fused kernel that skips omitted tiles and combines contributions from both QK precisions into one normalized attention output. The quantized keys and values prepared during prefill are then reused in a compressed key-value (KV) cache for decoding, reducing repeated reads of prompt data. Experiments show that TriAttention achieves end-to-end generation speedups of up to 7.88x over the Torch attention and 2.65x over the BF16 baseline. Meanwhile, TriAttention maintains quality comparable to the original models on general-purpose and long-context tasks. These results show how a compact retention-and-precision policy translates local sensitivities into attention computation and repeated KV-cache access. The implementation is https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TriAttention.
bullets: Targets the differing precision and retention sensitivities of query-key interactions in long-context attention.
Uses two diagonal-distance boundaries per head to compactly define skipped, 4-bit, and 8-bit computation regions.
Calibrates boundary choices with projected-output error and tile execution cost, then allocates policies across heads under a shared budget.
Employs a fused prefill kernel and reuses quantized keys and values in a compressed KV cache during decoding.
Reports up to 7.88× speedup over Torch attention and 2.65× over BF16, with quality comparable to the original models on general-purpose and long-context tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TriAttention, a unified sparse mixed-precision attention mechanism for long-context LLM inference. It optimizes computation by assigning different precision levels (4-bit vs 8-bit) to different tiles based on sensitivity.
papers.title: TriAttention: Unified Sparse Mixed-Precision Attention for Long-Context LLM Inference
papers.tldr: TriAttention accelerates long-context LLM inference by jointly skipping attention tiles and assigning retained tiles 4-bit or 8-bit precision while preserving model quality.

papers.abstract: AI agents may consume massive tokens across a wide range of tasks, but how many of those tokens are really necessary? Although prior work has shown that agents can incur unexpectedly high token costs, we still lack a systematic way to identify and measure token waste. In this work, we introduce a unified framework for measuring token waste across heterogeneous agent systems. Our framework records and normalizes complete agent trajectories, identifies removable spans using an LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaJ), and maps the identified text spans back to the original trajectory for token-level measurement. We validate the identified waste through direct interventions by removing marked spans, resuming agent execution, and measuring changes in task outcomes and subsequent actions. In online pruning experiments, we remove 41-46% of the model's reasoning while largely preserving task performance across two distinct agent benchmarks. Using this framework, we analyze agents across multiple settings. Our analysis shows that token waste has a system-level structure that aggregate token usage alone cannot reveal. First, waste varies more across tasks and agent settings than across models. Second, reasoning and visible execution can exhibit different waste patterns. Third, different harnesses can introduce distinct sources of inefficiency even under the same model and task. Overall, our framework transforms token waste into an actionable optimization signal, enabling researchers and practitioners to train more efficient models, design better reasoning strategies, and optimize agent harnesses toward reducing unnecessary computation rather than merely reducing token usage.
bullets: Token waste is measured by normalizing full agent trajectories, identifying removable spans with an LLM judge, and mapping them to token-level costs.
The framework validates waste through interventions that remove marked spans and observe task outcomes and subsequent actions.
Online pruning removes 41–46% of model reasoning while largely preserving performance across two agent benchmarks.
Waste varies more by task and agent setting than by model, with distinct patterns in reasoning, execution, and harnesses.
The framework turns token waste into an actionable signal for improving models, reasoning strategies, and agent harnesses.

papers.abstract: Neural networks admit many parameterizations of the same or nearly the same function, but deployment typically stores whichever parameter vector training happens to produce. We show that this representational freedom can itself be used for compression. Rather than redesigning the codec, we search over exact function-preserving transformations and controlled functional perturbations, using the unchanged physical compressor itself to select cheaper representations. Exact gauge families provide a zero-distortion reference under the strict audit; allowing small functional changes exposes much larger rate-distortion gains. Across SmolLM2 and Qwen3, our method reduces Zstandard-compressed checkpoint size by up to 23.4\%, with similar relative reductions under gzip, Brotli, and ZipNN, establishing trained-network representational freedom as a practical storage resource.
bullets: Neural networks can represent the same function with different parameter vectors, creating untapped storage flexibility.
The method searches exact gauges and controlled functional perturbations, then uses the existing compressor to select cheaper representations.
Exact transformations provide zero-distortion compression under strict functional auditing.
Small functional changes yield larger rate-distortion gains across SmolLM2 and Qwen3.
Checkpoint sizes decrease by up to 23.4% with Zstandard, with similar relative reductions for gzip, Brotli, and ZipNN.
