papers.abstract: At context lengths of about 1M tokens, dense attention is costly in prefill and decoding, and training typically relies on long documents, which become scarcer as the target length increases. Most sparse attention methods score all preceding blocks or tokens, so their selection cost per query is $O(L)$ at context length $L$; hierarchical selection reduces it to $O(\log L)$, but prior trainable hierarchical methods report accuracy only within their training length. We propose RecSA (Recursive Sparse Attention), which builds a tree over the KV cache in which each node summarizes its subtree with one key and one mean-pooled value. The keys come from one pooler per layer, shared by all levels and distilled from dense attention. Each level above the tokens selects at most $k$ candidates, so each query has $O(\log L)$ selection cost and reads $O(\log L)$ entries; the summaries of unselected candidates share one softmax with the exact tokens. Each entry's RoPE position is its index among the candidates of its level, so at any length every relative distance stays within the range seen during training. Initialized from Qwen3-4B and trained on 0.62B tokens at the original model's 32K training length, RecSA outperforms all baselines on RULER at every length from 131K to 2M; at 1M, it scores 60.5, compared with 40.0 for the best baseline, Dense + DCA. With our optimized kernels, RecSA is faster than dense attention in end-to-end prefill and decoding from 64K to 2M; at 524K on one H200 GPU, it accelerates prefill by 3.2x and decoding by 3.8x.
bullets: Builds a hierarchical KV-cache tree whose nodes summarize subtrees with pooled keys and values.
Selects at most k candidates per level, reducing per-query selection and reads to O(log L).
Uses shared, dense-attention-distilled poolers and level-relative RoPE positions to support length extrapolation.
Outperforms reported baselines from 131K to 2M tokens; at 1M, scores 60.5 versus 40.0 for Dense + DCA on RULER.
With optimized kernels, achieves 3.2× prefill and 3.8× decoding speedups at 524K on one H200 GPU.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces large language model (LLM) deployment costs, but preserving quality requires accounting for uneven weight sensitivity. Uniform PTQ uses one weight bit-width, importance-aware PTQ adjusts scales or reconstructs weights within that width, and column-wise mixed precision retains selected columns at higher precision. However, sensitivity varies within columns, so whole-column retention also protects less sensitive weights, while runtime outlier detection adds decoding overhead. We therefore introduce TileQuant, a training-free framework that assigns precision to hardware-aligned 2D weight tiles. Offline calibration provides input-activation-aware scoring from forward statistics for lower calibration cost and gradient-informed scoring from loss sensitivity for stronger quality preservation. Within each projection's retention budget, the highest-scoring tiles remain at 16-bit and the rest use 8-bit. The resulting map guides reconstruction into compact weight buffers, which the kernel reuses for native integer and 16-bit computation with local accumulation to reduce memory traffic. Experiments show that TileQuant reaches 2.66x the original model's generation throughput. Across language modeling, reasoning, long-context retrieval, and question answering, it preserves quality and surpasses quantized and original models on multiple tasks. These results support selecting precision units that capture local sensitivity while enabling efficient hardware execution. The implementation is: https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TileQuant
bullets: Addresses uneven within-column weight sensitivity and the decoding overhead of runtime outlier detection.
Uses training-free, offline calibration with activation-aware or gradient-informed tile scoring.
Retains top-scoring tiles at 16-bit within a budget and quantizes the rest to 8-bit.
Employs compact weight buffers and local accumulation for efficient mixed-precision execution.
Reports 2.66× original-model generation throughput while preserving or improving quality across several task types.

figures.caption: Figure 2: TileQuant framework for calibration-driven mixed-precision linear layers. The input-activation-aware route (top left) combines forward activation statistics with weight magnitudes, while the gradient-informed route (bottom left) accumulates weight-gradient importance over calibration batches. Per-layer top-k selection converts either tile-score map into a 16-bit/8-bit decision map. Retained tile IDs and grid metadata guide load-time reconstruction (right). The reconstructed layer supplies the selected weights to two arithmetic paths, whose tile products are combined through output-local 32-bit floating-point accumulation.

papers.abstract: Attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD) separates attention from the experts of a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model and has been reported to raise decode throughput over colocated serving. Whether this advantage holds on rack-scale NVLink systems such as GB200 NVL72 remains unclear: prior results were obtained on other hardware, against narrower colocated baselines, or with analytical models, whereas production engines serve large MoE models on these systems with wide expert parallelism (wide EP). We build and tune FastAFD, an AFD engine for GB200 NVL72 that overlaps the MoE of one microbatch with the attention of the other, and compare it against the best vLLM wide EP setting. Experiments show that AFD has a throughput advantage of up to 1.17x over wide EP on Qwen3 and 1.16x on Qwen3.5, and matches it on MiniMax-M2.5. We derive an analytical model that predicts AFD throughput within 3% using only profiles of colocated vLLM, telling whether switching to AFD would pay off before deploying it. The model yields a concise insight: AFD's speedup factors into a batch gain (larger batches, since attention GPUs hold no expert weights), an overlap gain (shorter steps, since the MoE runs on the expert GPUs behind attention), and a disaggregation cost (the GPUs given to experts). AFD has the advantage when the two gains outweigh the cost. This view explains which models benefit from AFD, and shows that speculative decoding helps light-expert models most, where the enlarged overlap gain outweighs the larger disaggregation cost and adds a further 8% to AFD's advantage over wide EP. Looking ahead, serving the experts on accelerators that keep their weights in on-chip SRAM, such as the Groq LPX accelerators paired with Vera Rubin NVL72, would remove most of the disaggregation cost, raising the ideal speedup to 2.48x with speculative decoding. FastAFD is open source at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/FastAFD.
bullets: Evaluated on GB200 NVL72 against the best vLLM wide-EP configuration for Qwen3, Qwen3.5, and MiniMax-M2.5.
Achieves up to 1.17× throughput on Qwen3, 1.16× on Qwen3.5, and matches wide EP on MiniMax-M2.5.
An analytical model predicts AFD throughput within 3% using only colocated-vLLM profiles.
Speculative decoding benefits light-expert models most, adding up to 8% to AFD’s advantage in the reported setting.
The projected 2.48× speedup with SRAM-based expert accelerators is an ideal forward-looking estimate, not a demonstrated result.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly recognized for their remarkable capabilities; federated learning (FL) offers a promising framework for collaboratively fine-tuning LLMs on edge devices while achieving data privacy. However, edge devices are inherently heterogeneous: clients may exhibit diverse data distributions and resource constraints, including limited memory and computation budgets. Recent federated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches address these challenges by using sparse expert activation or partial expert loading. However, existing partial-expert methods rely on heuristic full-pool observations or prioritize system-wide load balance, without guarantees for recovering client-specific relevant experts from partial observations. We propose $S^3$-MoE, a server-side sparse expert assignment framework that estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations and refines assignments through an exploit--explore mechanism. We also establish relevance-estimation error and exact Top-$K$ recovery guarantees. Experiments using a CNN-based MoE on CIFAR-100 show that $S^3$-MoE recovers task-dependent client--expert preferences and reduces conflicts caused by correlated expert selection across clients. Compared with Full-20 FedAvg, which gives each client access to all 20 experts for local Top-5 routing, $S^3$-MoE achieves 1.31 percentage points higher mean final accuracy while loading only $5$ experts per client.
bullets: Addresses heterogeneous client data and resource constraints in federated Mixture-of-Experts training.
Estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations and refines assignments via exploit–explore selection.
Provides relevance-estimation error bounds and exact Top-K recovery guarantees.
On a CNN-based CIFAR-100 MoE, loading 5 experts per client improves mean final accuracy by 1.31 percentage points over Full-20 FedAvg with 20 available experts.
Reduces conflicts from correlated expert selection across clients.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers, and feature dimensions, or lower numerical precision. We identify a complementary axis: within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys. We exploit this with value cache amortisation, which fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving $4\times$ near-lossless value compression. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning for substantially reduced prefill overhead, or fitted from scratch in settings that allow a one-off cost, such as multi-query inference. We pair value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression to produce LowRAM, an asymmetric compression pipeline that stays close to lossless across three model families. By reconstructing only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, LowRAM can keep decoding overhead minimal and achieve up to $5\times$ higher peak decode throughput at $4\times$ compression. LowRAM further composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching $26.9\times$ compression at $94.5\%$ of baseline performance on long contexts. These results show that treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive, and composable KV cache compression.
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory growth, which limits context length, batch size, and decoding throughput.
Amortises values using lightweight per-head predictors, storing residuals only for poorly reconstructed tokens; this provides 4× near-lossless value compression.
Combines value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression in an asymmetric pipeline.
Reconstructs only selected KV pairs during decoding, achieving up to 5× higher peak decode throughput at 4× compression.
Composes with quantisation and eviction to reach 26.9× compression at 94.5% of baseline performance on long contexts.

papers.abstract: LLM agents use context compaction to manage growing interaction histories, but summarizing long histories with large models can introduce substantial delays. Compaction therefore requires balancing information retention against latency. We observe that structured summary slots can retain information when generated independently. Based on this observation, we present SpecCompact, a framework that accelerates compaction through slot-parallel semantic speculation. SpecCompact fine-tunes a small drafter and generates slots in parallel. The target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, while subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix. System optimizations further reduce repeated context processing and model calls. Across AppWorld and $\tau^3$ benchmarks with two target models, SpecCompact achieves $2.04$--$5.63\times$ compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization. Separate downstream evaluations reveal model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs. A user study within Hermes further shows an $8.68\times$ median compaction speedup.
authors: Yulu An, Yifei Feng, Xiangyang Yin
bullets: Addresses the latency of summarizing growing agent histories while preserving important information.

papers.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) have recently achieved superhuman performance on several long-horizon benchmarks. However, their computational cost limits their use in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains such as video games. A key bottleneck is representing each screenshot as thousands of visual tokens, which accumulate into long contexts as agents reason over extended interaction histories. We observe that most of these visual tokens are either semantically irrelevant to the agent's next action or temporally redundant across screenshots. Building on this observation, we introduce Visual Token Routing (VTR), a joint training framework for learning sparse visual representations that preserve the information needed for action prediction. In VTR, we train the vision-language model together with a lightweight spatio-temporal router that examines each image region in the current and previous screenshots and decides whether its visual token enters the language model. We optimize the router using an adaptive loss to keep the number of visual tokens as small as possible while minimizing performance degradation. With just 2,000 training steps, VTR matches the performance of the full-resolution model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video game action prediction, while using 2.5-5.8x fewer visual tokens. These savings reduce inference cost by up to 3.3x and speed up prefill by up to 2.9x. VTR also outperforms lowering the image resolution and other baselines for dropping tokens, by up to 12.8 points on OSWorld. Overall, VTR enables computer-use agents to process only the visual tokens they need, allowing them to be used in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains at a fraction of the computational cost. Code and models are available at https://pranjal2041.github.io/vtr
bullets: Targets the computational bottleneck caused by thousands of visual tokens accumulating across long interaction histories.
Jointly trains a vision-language model with a lightweight spatio-temporal router that selects action-relevant, nonredundant image-region tokens.
Uses an adaptive loss to minimize token count while limiting performance degradation.
Matches the full-resolution model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video-game action prediction using 2.5–5.8× fewer visual tokens.
Reduces inference cost by up to 3.3× and prefilling time by up to 2.9×; outperforms resolution reduction and other token-dropping baselines on OSWorld.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Visual Token Routing (VTR). Spatio-temporal router: A lightweight router reads each image region across the current and previous screenshots and decides whether its visual token enters the language model. Zoomed-in region: While the agent types a file name into a save dialog in front of a playing video, the router keeps only the tokens of the typed file name. It drops the regions that did not change, and also drops the circled part of the video, which changed but is not relevant to the task.

Figure 5: VTR makes inference cheaper and faster. Score on OSWorld (left), average score on CUA-World (middle), and click accuracy in video games (right), against inference cost relative to the dense model at full resolution (top) and prefill time per step (bottom). The dashed line marks the dense model at full resolution.

Figure 4: VTR matches full-resolution performance with far fewer visual tokens. Score on OSWorld (left), average score on CUA-World (middle), and click accuracy in video games (right), against visual tokens per image. The dashed line marks the dense model at full resolution.

Figure 6: VTR adapts how many visual tokens it keeps to each domain and game. Percentage of visual tokens kept by each method on desktop tasks and on video games grouped by how much of the screen changes between consecutive frames.

Figure 7: VTR keeps only the regions that the agent needs. The previous observation (top) and the current observation with the regions that VTR drops dimmed (bottom), in three video games and a desktop application.

Figure 8: Further examples of the regions that VTR keeps. For each example, the previous observation (left) and the current observation with the regions that VTR drops dimmed (right), in video games and desktop applications.

Figure 3: Training in VTR. Joint training: We train πθ and the router together with the crossentropy (CE) loss on the kept tokens, and also train the router to keep fewer tokens with L = Ltok + λLdeg. The full and blind models see all tokens and only the anchors, and are used only during training. Measuring degradation: We compare the losses of the three models to measure how much the full history helps (in) and how much dropping tokens hurts (dn). Adaptive weight λ: We increase λ when the share of this help that πθ loses, r̄, exceeds the small tolerance r⋆, so that the router keeps more tokens, and decrease it otherwise.
Figure 2: Where the router acts. The first observation of each block is an anchor and is kept in full, while the router keeps only some regions, shown shaded, of the other observations in the block.

papers.tldr: Visual Token Routing sparsifies screenshot representations for computer-use agents, preserving action performance while substantially reducing visual-token and inference costs.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by re-executing shared layers, but three limitations hinder their adoption: memory grows with the loop count, compute can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. We propose LooM (Loop-invariant Memory), which addresses each in turn. In a causal encoder-decoder (CED), LooM loops only the decoder layers after the first, which read a global memory written once per token, and each of them publishes the key-value (KV) entry for a token only on its first visit, so the cache does not grow with the loop count. These layers loop independently, providing every budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token, and one model trained on randomly sampled budgets covers all of them without a router. With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size. Our analysis further shows that the training budget distribution decides what extra depth buys. These results suggest that a CED is a natural place to loop: memory is written once, and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment.
authors: Lele Yang, Muxi Diao, Zhonghao Yan, Jiankang Chen, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Wentao Zhang, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma, Weiran Xu
bullets: Targets looped Transformer limitations: loop-dependent memory growth, coarse compute control, and fixed post-training loop counts.
Loops decoder layers after the first, using global memory written once per token and publishing each token’s KV entry only on its first visit.
Independent layer loops provide budgets from 3 to 21 layer executions per token; one model supports all budgets without a router.
With sufficient looping, LooM improves language modeling, zero-shot accuracy, and long-context perplexity over a same-data single-pass baseline while keeping cache size unchanged.
Training-budget distributions determine what additional depth provides; the approach supports deployment-time depth selection.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Loop-invariant memory in LooM. (a) Decoder layer 1 (D1) writes global memory once per token, before any repetition; each of D2–D6 then runs dℓ ∈ {0, . . . , 4} times (D3 and D5 at least once). Squares are decoder calls on Random-Depth’s locked paths at three budgets. Every visit re-reads global memory (left), but only a layer’s first visit publishes the token’s local KV entry (right); publishing arrows are drawn for the 21-call path only. (b) D2, standing for any of D2–D6: a later token reads one local entry per earlier token however often the layer ran, so the cache (after a 128-token prompt) is the same on every path. papers.title: LooM: Loop-Invariant Memory for Causal Encoder-Decoder Language Models
papers.tldr: LooM enables flexible, memory-efficient looping in causal encoder-decoder language models, allowing deployment-time depth adjustment without increasing cache size.

papers.abstract: Small language models offer a compact basis for shell simulation without executing submitted commands, but full-output decoding requires them to predict recurring utility structure alongside content that varies across executions. We introduce template gap reconstruction (TGR), which supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels to be interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps. A template selector chooses which template to be reconstructed, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding. We construct a template bank from 18.7 million outputs collected across heterogeneous execution environments and train a template selector and five reconstruction models initialized from various small language model checkpoints on a target environment excluded from bank construction. Evaluation demonstrates that TGR improves output edit similarity (O-ES) over full-output decoding (FOD) when the optimal template covers more than 25\% of the template, while performing similarly for lower-coverage outputs. Additionally, TGR outperforms FOD for shorter gap sequences, with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812, respectively, while maintaining similar performance for longer sequences. TGR reduces the number of tokens generated by 26.3--38.3\% across used tokenizer families. These results support using a reusable output structure as a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to response quality.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of predicting recurring shell-output structure alongside execution-specific content without running commands.
Provides reusable output templates with sentinels; the model autoregressively generates only the missing gaps.
A template selector chooses a reconstruction template, while an empty template preserves full-output decoding.
Improves output edit similarity when templates cover more than 25% of the output and performs similarly at lower coverage.
Outperforms full-output decoding on shorter gap sequences, with O-ES of 0.964 versus 0.812, while maintaining similar performance on longer sequences.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera observations and language instructions to robot actions. However, their large backbones and repeated action generation can make inference take longer than the robot's real-time requirements for its next action. To reduce the load of VLA computations, researchers have proposed multiple optimization approaches, including quantization and pruning. These optimizations can be combined with other general optimizations such as better kernel compilation or using CUDA graphs instead of the eager mode. However, most of these optimization results are usually reported on a single GPU type, typically for a few VLA models, with no analysis of what the real bottlenecks are for a model on a particular hardware or how these optimizations would generalize beyond the reported results. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive measurement study of seven families of inference optimization methods, from CUDA graphs and compilation to token pruning and quantization, on seven state-of-the-art VLAs evaluated on four GPU families ranging from a datacenter H100 to an embedded Jetson Thor. We analyse how CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth, and kernel efficiency jointly shape optimization gains, and how applying one method changes the benefit of another. From this analysis, we derive VLA-Triage, guidelines for stacking optimizations under latency budgets. The guidelines identify which stages can provide the required savings and which combinations need testing in the deployed execution mode.
authors: Muhammad Danish Waseem, Ahmed Ali-Eldin Hassan
bullets: Evaluates seven inference-optimization families across seven VLAs and four GPU families, from H100 to Jetson Thor.
Analyzes the roles of CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth, and kernel efficiency in determining optimization gains.
Shows that optimization benefits and interactions depend on the model, hardware, and deployed execution mode.
Introduces VLA-Triage, guidelines for selecting and stacking optimizations under latency budgets.

papers.title: Where Is VLA Inference Time Spent? Bottlenecks and Optimization Interactions Across GPUs
papers.tldr: A cross-GPU study identifies where VLA inference time is spent and provides guidelines for combining optimizations to meet robot latency requirements.

papers.abstract: Efficient video human pose estimation must balance localisation accuracy, motion quality, and energy cost. We present SpikePose, a lightweight video pose estimator that pairs a frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder with motion-aligned heatmap memory (MAM). The encoder supplies per-frame spatial evidence, while MAM estimates joint displacement, aligns historical heatmaps, and adaptively fuses them with current predictions. By confining temporal reasoning to a compact, lightweight module outside the spiking backbone, SpikePose helps bridge the gap between spiking and classical Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) on large-scale, non-event-driven video tasks. We evaluate spatial accuracy, motion errors, and estimated arithmetic energy on MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset. Against the architecture-matched ANN with MAM, SpikePose cuts estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% at a cost of just 1.12 points in head-bone-normalised PCK at 0.5 threshold (PCK_HB(0.5)). Within SpikePose, adding MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46% while slightly improving localisation, at a cost of only 0.003M parameters and 0.0023 analytical GFLOPs per frame. Code will be released on GitHub upon acceptance.
authors: Yunhao Huang, Kaushik Bhargav Sivangi, Tianyi Yu, Fani Deligianni
bullets: Targets the trade-off among pose localisation, temporal motion quality, and energy use in non-event-driven video.
Uses a frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder for spatial evidence and MAM to estimate joint motion, align past heatmaps, and fuse them adaptively with current predictions.
Evaluated on MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset using localisation, motion-error, and estimated arithmetic-energy metrics.
Compared with an architecture-matched ANN using MAM, it reduces estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% with a 1.12-point PCK_HB(0.5) decrease.
Adding MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46%, respectively, with minimal computational and parameter overhead.

papers.title: SpikePose: Lightweight Video Human Pose Estimation

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting enables efficient generalizable novel view synthesis, but existing pixel-aligned methods often generate highly redundant Gaussian primitives, causing the final representation size and rendering cost to grow rapidly with image resolution and the number of input views. We propose BudgetSplat, a budget-controllable feed-forward framework that adapts the final Gaussian representation to a user-specified preservation ratio. Rather than treating compaction as simple importance ranking, we formulate it as a joint problem of importance estimation, spatial coverage, and cross-view redundancy. A single trained model supports varying numbers of context views and multiple test-time budgets without per-budget retraining or per-scene compression. To realize this formulation, Intra-Cross Mask Supervision provides structure-, coverage-, and redundancy-aware guidance for learning Gaussian importance, while budget-conditioned feature modulation adapts Gaussian opacity and attributes to the requested preservation ratio. Coverage-Aware Budget Selection further combines patch-wise pre-selection, view-wise opacity ranking, and 3D redundancy suppression to construct compact yet spatially distributed Gaussian representations. Experiments on indoor reconstruction and cross-dataset generalization demonstrate consistent quality--size trade-offs across different input view counts and preservation ratios, substantially reducing final representation storage and rendering cost while preserving rendering quality.
authors: Yuxi Hu, Jun Zhang, Wei Mao, Yuchen Rao, Friedrich Fraundorfer
bullets: Addresses redundant Gaussian primitives that make representation size and rendering cost grow with image resolution and input views.
Jointly models Gaussian importance, spatial coverage, and cross-view redundancy rather than relying on simple importance ranking.
Uses Intra-Cross Mask Supervision and budget-conditioned feature modulation to adapt Gaussian attributes to different preservation ratios.
Coverage-Aware Budget Selection combines patch pre-selection, view-wise opacity ranking, and 3D redundancy suppression.
Experiments show consistent quality–size trade-offs across varying input views and budgets, without per-budget retraining or per-scene compression.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of BudgetSplat. (A) Given 𝑁 posed context images, a pixel-aligned reconstruction backbone estimates dense geometry and base Gaussian features. (B) During training, Intra-Cross Mask Supervision constructs pseudo importance targets that preserve high-frequency structures, maintain sparse coverage in low-frequency regions, and down-weight redundant cross-view observations. (C) Budget-Conditioned Feature Modulation injects the user-specified preservation ratio 𝜌 into the base Gaussian features before parameter prediction, allowing the predicted opacity and Gaussian attributes to adapt to the requested budget. (D) Coverage-Aware Budget Selection combines patch-wise pre-selection, view-wise global opacity ranking, and 3D redundancy suppression to retain a compact and spatially distributed Gaussian representation. A single trained model supports arbitrary test-time preservation ratios 𝜌 ∈ (0, 1] without retraining.
Figure 2: Qualitative results on ScanNet [6] with 10 context views. Ours is rendered using only 25% of the Gaussian budget.

papers.title: BudgetSplat: Budget-Controllable Generalizable Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: BudgetSplat generates compact, quality-preserving Gaussian Splatting representations whose size and rendering cost can be controlled at test time by a user-specified budget.

papers.abstract: Simultaneous Speech Translation (SimulST) requires balancing translation quality and latency. While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in offline translation, current LLM-based SimulST systems predominantly rely on prefix-incremental generation. This paradigm suffers from redundant Key-Value cache recomputation and necessitates external Voice Activity Detection to process unbounded streams. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose an end-to-end interleaved read-write framework built upon an omni-modal LLM. By interleaving speech chunks and text tokens, our architecture achieves full KV cache reuse, natively supporting segmentation-free, infinite-length inference. Furthermore, to learn optimal streaming policies without rigid offline alignments, we introduce a novel Actor-Critic self-enhancement pipeline. An RNN-T Actor dynamically samples read-write trajectories, while an LLM-based Critic evaluates these paths via intrinsic semantic and latency rewards, distilling the optimal policy back to the Actor. Extensive experiments on sentence-level (FLEURS, CoVoST2) and document-level (MuST-C, ACL 60/60) benchmarks demonstrate that our model establishes new state-of-the-art quality-latency Pareto frontiers, substantially outperforming existing cascaded and static-alignment baselines.
authors: Chenyang Le, Pei Zhang, Yuxiang Chen, Bing Han, Derek F. Wong, Baosong Yang, Yanmin Qian
bullets: Targets the quality–latency trade-off in LLM-based SimulST and avoids redundant KV-cache recomputation.
Uses an end-to-end interleaved read-write architecture with an omni-modal LLM, supporting full KV-cache reuse and unbounded streaming.
Introduces an Actor-Critic pipeline: an RNN-T Actor samples read-write trajectories, while an LLM Critic scores semantic and latency rewards.
Evaluations on sentence- and document-level benchmarks show improved quality–latency Pareto frontiers over cascaded and static-alignment baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Ablation on training strategies. “Direct SFT” uses RNN-T aligned data directly (similar to InfiniSST). “Stage 1 & 2” represents pipeline training without the final joint optimization. “CRESiST” indicates our full joint training framework, which yields the most significant latency reduction, particularly on resource-rich directions (e.g., zh↔ en).

Figure 3: Sentence-level quality-latency trade-off curves on the CoVoST2 and FLEURS datasets. The proposed framework consistently establishes a superior Pareto frontier compared to Seamless Streaming and AlignATT across all sub-tasks.

Figure 7: Translation timing visualization for a sample from the FLEURS EN-ZH test set. The timeline illustrates the latency advantage of our model, which performs fine-grained, word-level adaptive translation, in contrast to the coarse-grained, clause-level buffering strategy employed by the Seed LiveInterpret 2.0 API.
Figure 2: Structural details of the RNN-T aligner and the Refiner layer.

Figure 1: Training and inference diagram of CRESiST. In the interleaved sequence, red and green target tokens mark whether the Router score at that position passes the decision threshold, i.e., whether the LLM body loss Lbody is computed there (tokens judged to be emitted too early are masked out). The Refiner loss Lrefiner is computed at every text position, and the two losses are summed; the same ground-truth token is thus the target of two prediction heads over one sequence, not duplicated in it.

Figure 5: Impact of the latency penalty weight on the quality-latency trade-off. Larger weights aggressively compress latency at the expense of quality, while excessively small weights lead to prolonged delays at specific thresholds.

Figure 6: Comparison of emission probabilities and decoding paths. The proposed RNN-T with axial attention (a) successfully maintains an incremental, monotonic alignment for simultaneous translation. In contrast, the conventional RNN-T (b) fails to emit tokens timely during the speech stream, causing its decoding path to delay and degenerate into an offline translation behavior at the end of the utterance.

papers.selection_reason: Interleaved read-write architecture achieving full KV cache reuse for infinite-length streaming inference is a technically meaningful efficiency contribution.
papers.title: CRESiST: Self-Enhancing Explorative Policy Learning for Simultaneous Speech Translation
papers.tldr: CRESiST enables segmentation-free, low-latency simultaneous speech translation by combining interleaved speech-text processing with self-enhancing policy learning.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon language-model agents accumulate increasingly large interaction histories, making context compaction essential for efficient execution. Existing learned compaction methods often rely on downstream task outcomes or solver behavior, coupling training to specific tasks or agents. We introduce SumOne, a standalone summarizer trained to preserve information in agent histories through masked reconstruction. Given a summary of the expired history, a frozen reconstructor recovers randomly masked portions of the original trajectory; reconstruction quality, combined with a length penalty, provides a task-agnostic reward for optimizing the summarizer with GRPO. This yields self-supervision directly from raw trajectories, without reference summaries or downstream task execution. At inference time, only the lightweight summarizer is retained, enabling plug-and-play context compression for otherwise unchanged agents. We conduct a systematic evaluation of SumOne in long-horizon search and software-engineering tasks. SumOne reduces estimated inference cost by approximately 78\% on DeepSearchQA and 75\% on SWE-bench Verified relative to operating with full context, with absolute decreases of 0.04. The same checkpoint also transfers across downstream models and agent harnesses without additional fine-tuning.
authors: Jizhe Zhang, Ang Li, Chenheng Zhang, Yisen Wang
bullets: Addresses context growth in long-horizon language-model agents without tying summarizer training to specific tasks, agents, or outcomes.
Trains a standalone summarizer using masked reconstruction by a frozen reconstructor, with reconstruction quality and summary length providing the optimization signal.
Requires only the lightweight summarizer at inference, leaving the underlying agent unchanged.
Reduces estimated inference cost by about 78% on DeepSearchQA and 75% on SWE-bench Verified, with reported absolute decreases of 0.04.
A single checkpoint transfers across downstream models and agent harnesses without additional fine-tuning.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SUMONE. The summarizer compresses the expired history into a short summary. papers.selection_reason: Task-agnostic summarizer for compacting agent interaction histories, relevant to LLM agent memory and inference-cost reduction.
papers.title: SUMONE: A Simple and Efficient Summarizer for Plug-and-Play Agent Memory
papers.tldr: SumOne is a task-agnostic, plug-and-play agent-memory summarizer that compresses long histories while retaining information needed for reconstruction and downstream execution.

papers.abstract: Target-conditioned diffusion drafters predict candidate tokens in parallel, yet each new block must wait for updated target-model hidden states. This forces drafting and verification to run sequentially, limiting speedup even though each block is generated in one pass. We introduce D3D, a standalone diffusion drafter that removes this inter-round dependency. D3D combines blockwise denoising with auxiliary autoregressive supervision to achieve long accepted prefixes without target hidden states. This independence lets D3D draft successor blocks during verification in one packed pass, enabling asynchronous speculative decoding. We progressively prune layers according to their effect on acceptance length to reduce the cost of packed drafting. Removing five of 36 layers retains over 99\% of mean acceptance length across three benchmarks with Qwen3-8B as the target. Across seven benchmarks, D3D averages 5.00$\times$ and 5.71$\times$ decoding speedup with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B targets, compared with 4.03$\times$ and 3.67$\times$ for DFlash. On GSM8K with Qwen3-32B, speedup reaches 7.48$\times$. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/fudan-generative-vision/D3D.
authors: Baoyou Chen, Ruiqiao Mei, Guancong Lin, Tao Song, Weihao Yuan, Qun Liu, Siyu Zhu
bullets: Addresses the sequential dependency caused by target-conditioned diffusion drafters needing updated target hidden states.
Combines blockwise denoising with auxiliary autoregressive supervision to produce long accepted prefixes without target hidden states.
Packs successor-block drafting with verification for asynchronous decoding, and prunes layers based on acceptance-length impact to reduce cost.
Removing 5 of 36 layers retains over 99% of mean acceptance length across three benchmarks.
Across seven benchmarks, D3D achieves average speedups of 5.00× with Qwen3-8B and 5.71× with Qwen3-32B, reaching 7.48× on GSM8K with Qwen3-32B.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of D3D. (a) Drafter training. Target-generated responses supervise blockwise denoising and auxiliary autoregressive prediction. Packed attention shares causal prefix computation while isolating diffusion blocks and allowing bidirectional attention within each block. (b) Progressive layer pruning. Each iteration removes the layer causing the smallest decrease in validation acceptance length, followed by recovery and reevaluation of layer importance. Recovery uses distillation from a fixed unpruned drafter whose output distribution is adjusted toward the supervised token. (c) Asynchronous inference. During target verification, one packed drafter pass prepares successor blocks for alternative rejection outcomes and full acceptance. A branch matching the verified prefix is reused; otherwise, the drafter generates a new block synchronously.

Figure 2: Ablations of D3D-8B depth and initialization with Qwen3-8B as the target and B = 16. Left: decoding speedup and acceptance length τ , averaged over MATH-500, HumanEval, and MT-Bench. Right: GSM8K τ during training from pretrained or random initialization.

Figure 3: Decoding speedup and cache hit rate versus asynchronous draft budget on AIME25, using the 31-layer D3D-8B drafter with Qwen3-8B and B = 16. Left: varying position coverage C at F = 2. Right: varying token fan-out F at C = 12.
Figure 4: GSM8K acceptance length τ during D3D-1.7B training with different auxiliary autoregressive loss weights λ. The target is Qwen3-8B and the block size is B = 16.

Figure 5: Selective prefilling and sequential speculative decoding with D3D. The same standalone drafter scores prompt chunks for target prefilling and generates candidate blocks for verification. Retained chunks preserve their original order, and the drafter and target maintain separate KV caches.

Table 7: LongBench results with an 8B D3D drafter and Qwen3-32B target model.

papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based speculative decoding for faster LLM inference, contributing to efficient language-model decoding.
papers.title: D3D: Decoupled Diffusion Drafting for Asynchronous Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: D3D enables asynchronous speculative decoding by using a standalone diffusion drafter that drafts future token blocks while the target model verifies current ones.

papers.abstract: Non-prefix KV-cache reuse encodes retrieved chunks independently and concatenates their caches. To find where a small repair budget should be spent, we vary the chunks around the answer-bearing one (the target) across three 7B-8B models and four datasets of dialogue memory, open-domain QA and API documentation. Reuse loses 19-100% of the context-dependent questions that full prefill answers, and it loses more when the other chunks are of the same kind as the target. Because the recoverable damage is spread over these other chunks, restoring a few of them recovers little, and the budget is better spent on the target. This works through contextual compatibility: recomputing the target against the reused cache beats inserting its full-prefill KV in all seven settings tested, although the recomputed KV stays far from the full-prefill KV. Question attention over reused caches, however, selects the target in at most 18.8% of development questions. A retriever finds it more often, and recomputing its top chunk after moving it next to the question significantly beats InfoFlow-style reordering at the same 5% budget in six of nine open-domain QA and API-documentation settings. On dialogue memory, though, recomputing chunks never significantly beats the token-level selector chosen for each setting.
authors: Yuxing Peng, Zhiqing Tang, Weijia Jia
bullets: Reuse loses 19–100% of context-dependent questions answered by full prefill, with greater losses when distractors resemble the target chunk.
Damage is distributed across other chunks, so repairing a few distractors recovers little; repairing the target is more effective.
Recomputing the target against the reused cache outperforms inserting its full-prefill KV in all seven tested settings, despite remaining different from full-prefill KV.
Question attention identifies the target in at most 18.8% of development questions; retrieval finds it more often.

At the same 5% budget, retrieving, moving, and recomputing the top chunk beats InfoFlow-style reordering in six of nine QA/API-documentation settings, but not dialogue memory versus its token-level selector.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Reuse cuts each chunk off from the chunks before it, and similar chunks then mislead the model. (a) Full prefill encodes each chunk after the earlier ones, whereas non-prefix reuse encodes each chunk alone and joins the caches, so only the question and the answer attend across chunks. (b) An NQ-Open question answered by Qwen3-8B with 30 passages (actual outputs and passages, both shortened). (c) Where a small repair budget goes. The inset shows that, when the target is unknown, the retriever’s top chunk is moved last (Sections 3–5).

In the bottom row, open markers show two cases: intervals that include zero, and the similarity terms on Gorilla, which cannot be positive because retention under RAND is zero. The vertical line marks k = 16, where the predictions differ most and are tested (Table 7).

SurroKV full: a 1,024-token surrogate followed by recomputing 10% of the tokens ranked by question attention. papers.selection_reason: KV-cache reuse and repair-budget allocation directly fits KV-cache and memory-efficiency interest.
papers.title: Where Should a KV-Cache Repair Budget Go? Distractor Structure and Contextual Compatibility in Non-Prefix Reuse
papers.tldr: For non-prefix KV-cache reuse, a small repair budget is usually best spent recomputing the answer-bearing chunk—ideally after retrieving and placing it near the question—though this advantage depends on the task.

papers.abstract: Context compression reduces inference cost by encoding inputs into compact representations while preserving semantic content. An open question is whether semantic preservation alone is sufficient to maintain downstream behaviours such as refusal alignment. We investigate this question and find that encoder-based compression systematically weakens refusal behaviour in instruction-tuned language models, despite high reconstruction fidelity. This effect persists across model families and compression architectures. Mechanistic analysis shows that compression attenuates activation along the decoder's learned refusal direction. We further explore Memory Steering, a lightweight inference-time intervention that restores refusal rates to near-baseline levels without retraining and operates entirely in compressed representation space. These results demonstrate that semantic preservation does not guarantee behavioural preservation under compression, highlighting the need to explicitly preserve alignment-relevant features in compression-aware systems.
bullets: Encoder-based compression systematically reduces refusal behavior despite high reconstruction fidelity.
The degradation persists across model families and compression architectures.
Mechanistic analysis links weaker refusals to attenuation of the decoder’s learned refusal direction.
Memory Steering restores refusal rates to near-baseline levels without retraining.
Semantic preservation alone is insufficient for preserving alignment-relevant behavior.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video models rely on historical key-value (KV) caches to preserve scene consistency over extended rollouts, making KV storage and repeated attention over history a growing memory and computational bottleneck. Aggressive compression can degrade generation quality, while reconstructing full-dimensional KV leaves attention computation largely unchanged. We introduce NanoKV, a frozen-backbone framework for generation-aware high-ratio KV compression. NanoKV exploits redundancy across tokens and attention heads by storing shared content in cluster centers and encoding joint head-channel residuals into low-bit coefficients. Crucially, NanoKV uses different fitting objectives for Keys and Values according to their distinct roles in attention: Key decoders are optimized to preserve downstream block outputs, whereas Value encoders and decoders are fitted for faithful reconstruction through the deployed quantization path. Building on the same compressed representation, the optional NanoKV-Fast variant reuses the stored coefficients for mixed-dimensional attention, reducing computation without modifying the video backbone. Across three autoregressive video backbones, NanoKV consistently improves the quality-storage trade-off. On HY-WorldPlay, NanoKV achieves $26.09\times$ effective KV compression, nearly twice that of KVTC, while improving PSNR by 1.0 dB. NanoKV-Fast retains $20.53\times$ effective compression and achieves an approximately $1.15\times$ end-to-end speedup over KVTC.
authors: Jiacheng Lu, Haoyi Zhu, Sipei Yi, Enze Xie, Cheng Zhuo, Yu Li
bullets: Addresses KV-cache memory and historical-attention costs in long video generation.
Uses cluster centers and low-bit joint head-channel residual coefficients to exploit token and head redundancy.

Across three video backbones, it improves the quality–storage trade-off; on HY-WorldPlay, it reaches 26.09× effective compression and improves PSNR by 1.0 dB over KVTC.
NanoKV-Fast enables mixed-dimensional attention, retaining 20.53× compression and delivering an approximately 1.15× end-to-end speedup over KVTC.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models send each token through a few of many expert subnetworks. Serving methods make these models faster by running even fewer experts per token, and they are validated on accuracy benchmarks. We show that these methods can weaken the model's refusal of harmful requests, and we introduce SafeStart, which largely restores refusal while keeping most of the speedup. In vLLM on one RTX A6000, keeping about two thirds of the selected experts speeds up offline decoding by 15 to 28% at batch size 8. We find that, at this setting, under a jailbreak that tells the model not to refuse, the share of harmful requests that the model answers rises by 18.4 percentage points on Qwen1.5-MoE, 9.5 on OLMoE, and 6.6 on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, the three of nine models where it rises significantly, while MMLU accuracy drops by less than two points. We discover that most of this increase arises while the model processes the prompt and generates its first few tokens. SafeStart therefore runs all experts for the prompt and the first eight generated tokens, and the reduced set of experts afterwards, through a fused kernel in vLLM. With experts removed, SafeStart keeps at least 85% of the offline decode speedup at batch sizes 8 and 32 and brings the change under this jailbreak to between -2.1 and +1.3 points for three expert-reduction methods on these three models. On 889 held-out requests, in an analysis fixed before generation, truncation raises harmful compliance by 5.8 to 21.4 points, and SafeStart leaves a rise of 0.6 to 2.6 points, non-inferior to the original model on two of the three models. Our results show that faster MoE serving need not cost safety: a serving system can keep most of the gain from running fewer experts by running all of them at the start of each response, and it should test refusal, not only accuracy, before it enables such a method.
authors: Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo, Saeid Shokoufa, Seyedarmin Azizi, Arya Fayyazi, Souvik Kundu, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram

papers.abstract: The full-attention layers of large language models (LLMs) make every generated token more expensive than the previous one, slowing models down on long-context tasks. Hybrid models reduce this cost by replacing most full-attention layers with linear-attention layers, but the first still dominate decoding at long contexts. We accelerate these remaining layers without any training or weight changes using combined sparse attention: each layer attends to a sliding window of recent tokens, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of most relevant tokens in the context. The window size and budget are found on a per-layer basis using a multi-objective search algorithm. Across six hybrid models from three families, from 4B to 397B parameters, the selected configurations preserve their baseline model's accuracy on 21 long-context datasets. Decoding 64k/256k tokens becomes up to 1.26x/2.22x faster on Qwen3.5-4B, 1.20x/2.23x on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 1.16x/2.06x on Ornith-1.0-397B.
authors: Jo\~ao Eduardo Batista, Emil Vatai, Mohamed Wahib
bullets: Targets full-attention layers that remain costly at long contexts in hybrid models.
Combines a recent-token sliding window, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of salient context tokens.
Uses per-layer multi-objective search to select the window size and token budget without changing weights.
Across six models and 21 long-context datasets, configurations preserve baseline accuracy.
Provides up to 2.22× faster decoding at 256k tokens, depending on the model.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have recently been extended to handle multiple input images, but this extension dramatically increases the visual token budget, making visual-token pruning not merely an efficiency option but a practical necessity. Existing visual-token pruning methods, primarily designed for the single-image setting, rely on attention-derived saliency signals to estimate per-token importance. However, this attention-centric design transfers poorly to the multi-image regime: it causes substantial performance degradation on multi-image benchmarks, suffers from strong positional bias, and loses discriminative attention signals as the number of input images increases. To test whether attention-selected tokens are truly important for multi-image reasoning, we conduct two complementary causal probes Leave-One-In and Leave-One-Deletion, which measure token importance by restoring individual tokens to a zeroed visual sequence or removing them from the full sequence. Attention-based pruners provide only marginal gains over random selection, showing that attention is a weak proxy for visual-token importance in multi-image reasoning. Motivated by this gap, we propose Relation and Information Aware Pruning (RI-Prune), a training-free, attention-free pre-decoder selector for multi-image visual token pruning. RI-Prune scores each visual token using a z-normalized combination of three signals computed from projector outputs: query relevance, cross-image correspondence with compact per-image prototypes, and intra image representativeness. By integrating these signals, RI-Prune performs balanced per-image Top-K selection to preserve information across input images. Across multiple multi-image benchmarks and three LVLM backbones, RI-Prune achieves a stronger trade-off between token reduction and task performance than prior pruning methods, particularly under aggressive token budgets.
authors: Dongjin Lee, Eunju Lee, Jinhee Jang, Yoonji Lee, Youngbin Kim
bullets: Multi-image inputs greatly increase visual-token budgets, making pruning necessary for practical LVLM inference.
Attention-based pruning transfers poorly to multi-image reasoning due to positional bias and weakening attention signals as image count grows.
Causal Leave-One-In and Leave-One-Deletion probes show attention-selected tokens are only marginally better than random selections.
RI-Prune is a training-free, attention-free pre-decoder selector using three z-normalized projector-output signals.
Balanced per-image Top-K selection preserves information across images and yields a better token-reduction/task-performance trade-off, especially at aggressive budgets.

papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces a novel, training-free visual token pruning method specifically designed for multi-image LVLMs. It addresses the limitations of attention-based pruning in multi-image settings by incorporating cross-image correspondence and intra-image representativeness, directly contributing to efficiency in multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: RI-Prune: Relation and Information Aware Visual Token Pruning for Multi-Image Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: RI-Prune improves multi-image LVLM efficiency by selecting visual tokens using relevance, cross-image relations, and within-image representativeness instead of attention alone.

papers.abstract: High-content multi-channel imaging, from Cell Painting assays to remote sensing, is central to modern scientific pipelines. Because these channels are highly heterogeneous and experimental configurations frequently evolve, a practical vision backbone must be fundamentally channel-agnostic. Current channel-adaptive vision transformers rely on global self-attention with learnable channel embeddings, which can be computed only for previously known channels. Attempts to overcome this limitation of new channels either discard the embeddings, losing channel identity, or process each channel independently, thereby eliminating critical cross-channel interactions. To address this, we introduce ChanSFormer, an efficient Vision Transformer that replaces rigid embeddings with disentangled spatial-channel attention and individual channel CLS tokens. This architecture natively preserves both distinct channel identities and cross-channel information flow. Furthermore, the individual channel class token design unlocks more informative feature representations for self-supervised learning and enables representation-based channel sampling while remaining channel-agnostic. We evaluate ChanSFormer on two biology multi-channel datasets, CHAMMI, JUMP-CP and a satellite dataset, So2Sat. Experimental results show that ChanSFormer outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 3.93%-4.27% on JUMP-CP in classification accuracy. It also demonstrates exceptional cross-dataset transferability under a self-supervised setting, outperforming previous methods by up to 2.72% in accuracy in the same classification tasks. Furthermore, the disentangled attention reduces the quadratic complexity of channel-by-spatial sequence length of the global attention baseline, thus improving throughput by 55%-313%. Code is available at https://github.com/cvlab-stonybrook/ChanSFormer.
authors: Jingwei Zhang, Srinivasan Sivanandan, Dimitris Samaras
bullets: Addresses the limitation of channel-adaptive transformers that depend on predefined channel embeddings and handle new channels poorly.
Uses disentangled spatial-channel attention with individual channel CLS tokens to retain channel identities and enable cross-channel information flow.
Supports more informative self-supervised representations and representation-based channel sampling.
Evaluated on CHAMMI, JUMP-CP, and So2Sat; on JUMP-CP, it improves classification accuracy by 3.93–4.27% over state-of-the-art methods and improves cross-dataset transfer by up to 2.72%.
Reduces attention complexity and improves throughput by 55–313% compared with global attention baselines.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to scale capacity efficiently, but expert parameters dominate memory even though only a few experts are activated per token: they account for over 90% of model size in modern MoE-MLLMs (e.g., 54 GB out of about 58 GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B). Expert pruning has emerged as an effective compression strategy, but existing methods aggregate importance uniformly across tokens, ignoring that the same expert may serve different roles for vision versus language processing. To address this, we propose MAEP (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning), a training-free framework that decomposes expert importance by modality in a single forward pass. MAEP introduces (1) Delta-H Output ($\Delta H$), a redistribution-aware metric measuring the MoE output change when an expert is removed, and (2) low-attention vision tokens as a vision-side pruning signal that is dataset-stable: its expert-importance ranking remains stable across different datasets. Text-side importance serves as a preservation signal while vision-side importance serves as a pruning signal, and experts are ranked globally across layers. Experiments on three MoE-based MLLMs across multimodal and text benchmarks show that MAEP outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on the majority of multimodal benchmarks while remaining competitive on text-only tasks, reducing the BF16 expert weight footprint by about 27 GB (about 47% of total memory) so that the full weight footprint of an approximately 58 GB model fits within a single 40 GB GPU. Code is available at https://github.com/nota-github/MAEP.
bullets: Targets MoE expert parameters, which dominate the memory footprint of multimodal large language models.
Separates expert importance for vision and language in a single forward pass using redistribution-aware output change and low-attention vision tokens.
Uses text-side importance for preservation, vision-side importance for pruning, and globally ranks experts across layers.
Across three MoE-MLLMs, outperforms modality-agnostic pruning on most multimodal benchmarks and remains competitive on text-only tasks.
Reduces the BF16 expert footprint by about 27 GB, enabling an approximately 58 GB model to fit on one 40 GB GPU.

papers.selection_reason: Modality-aware expert pruning for MoE-based multimodal LLMs, reducing memory footprint and fitting both efficient AI and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Modality-Aware Expert Pruning for MoE-Based Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: MAEP is a training-free, modality-aware expert-pruning method that substantially reduces MoE-MLLM memory while preserving multimodal and text performance.

papers.abstract: Diffusion drafters accelerate speculative decoding by denoising multiple draft tokens in parallel. Their training uses anchor sampling to construct compact draft queries and performs cross-attention with a block-sparse mask over a much longer context. We empirically show that acceptance length remains stable as context scales with a fixed query budget, while increasing the query budget yields diminishing quality gains, jointly establishing a practical regime with queries far shorter than the context. No existing context parallelism (CP) method jointly exploits this query--context asymmetry and meets the nonlinear, sample-dependent load-balancing requirement created by anchor sampling. We present Split-KV, an exact CP method that keeps key/value shards local and limits per-layer attention communication to query-sized tensors, making this communication independent of context length. Its global query view further enables a cost-aware longest-processing-time-first (LPT) strategy that balances context key/value chunks by their realized attention cost. At a CP size of 64, Split-KV retains 85--91\% weak-scaling efficiency and achieves up to $3.67\times$ speedup over the fastest available CP baseline. LPT achieves $<$1\% imbalance and plans three orders of magnitude faster than the best load-balancing baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/zxgx/verl.
authors: Geng Zhang, Fangzhao Zhang, Cong Xie, Tiantian Fan, Yang You
bullets: Diffusion drafters use compact draft queries to attend over much longer, block-sparse contexts.
Split-KV keeps key/value shards local and communicates only query-sized tensors, making attention communication independent of context length.
A global query view enables longest-processing-time-first scheduling to balance sample-dependent attention costs.
At context-parallel size 64, Split-KV achieves 85–91% weak-scaling efficiency and up to 3.67× speedup over the fastest baseline.
LPT reduces load imbalance to below 1% and plans three orders of magnitude faster than the best compared balancer.

papers.tldr: Split-KV efficiently parallelizes diffusion-drafter training by exploiting short queries, local key/value shards, and cost-aware load balancing.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention accelerates few-step video diffusion transformers by computing a few key blocks exactly and compensating for the rest. However, existing sparse attention still faces key challenges, including identification overhead from finding critical blocks at every denoising step, suboptimal budget allocation that sets sparsity budgets uniformly or by local metrics, and cross-step error accumulation as reused masks or clusters go stale. Observing that the errors left on skipped blocks cancel each other once every key is compensated, we propose DecoupAttn, a new paradigm of decoupled sparse attention: semantic clusters compensate every key, and exact attention corrects their error on a few blocks fixed once offline by position. To support this paradigm, we introduce Distortion Budget, a rate-distortion objective for budget allocation that places exact computation across timesteps, layers, and heads where it removes the most distortion that compensation leaves in the final latent. Built on this budget, we further propose Reassign Cache, in which each step reassigns the drifting keys to cached centroids and refreshes compensation while the budgeted blocks stay fixed. Moreover, DecoupAttn is training-free: a few calibration clips compile one plan offline, and inference runs standard block-sparse kernels with one fused compensation kernel. Our code will be released after submission.
authors: Yanjin Li, Bingbing Qiu, Qiang Huang, Rui Qian, Yanfeng Li, Jian Wang, Xiaoying Tang, Mingda Zhang
bullets: Targets identification overhead, poor uniform/local budget allocation, and stale masks or clusters in sparse video diffusion attention.
Uses semantic clusters to compensate skipped keys and exact attention on a small set of offline-fixed blocks to correct residual error.
Introduces Distortion Budget to allocate exact computation across timesteps, layers, and heads based on its effect on final-latent distortion.
Uses Reassign Cache to update drifting key-to-centroid assignments and refresh compensation at each denoising step.
Compiles the plan from a few calibration clips and performs inference with block-sparse kernels plus one fused compensation kernel; no training is required.

papers.selection_reason: Decoupled sparse attention with distortion-budget allocation for training-free acceleration of video diffusion, directly relevant to efficient attention and video diffusion.
papers.title: DecoupAttn: Decoupled Sparse Attention for Training-Free Acceleration of Video Diffusion
papers.tldr: DecoupAttn accelerates video diffusion without retraining by combining fixed exact-attention blocks, semantic compensation, and distortion-aware sparse-budget allocation.

papers.abstract: As sequence lengths continue to grow, distributed attention based on sequence parallel (e.g., Ring-Attention) has become a mainstream solution for large language models (LLMs). Nevertheless, inherent communication dependencies limit computation-communication overlap, reducing GPU utilization. Moreover, in cross-hardware (NUMA or node) architectures, due to imbalanced communication bandwidth, frequent communication synchronization will limit overall performance. Based on these insights, we propose CHARM+, Cross-Hardware Attention with Re-Merge Multistream Mechanism. We reorganize sequential communications into several levels and achieve intra-level parallelism and computation overlap. Furthermore, we decouple cross-hardware communication from intra-hardware communication, eliminating synchronization overhead caused by bandwidth imbalance. Forward and backward algorithms were evaluated on multiple hardware architectures and consistently outperformed state-of-the-art methods. Compared to Ring-Attention, our forward and backward algorithms achieve average speedups of 1.3x and 1.7x on a dual-NUMA PCIe architecture, and 2.8x and 2.9x on a dual-node NVLink architecture, respectively.
authors: Xinhang Zhang, Boning Zhang, Chengchun Liu, Chunpu Li, Lei Sun, Weifeng Zhang, Limin Xiao
bullets: Targets poor GPU utilization from communication dependencies in sequence-parallel attention, especially under cross-hardware bandwidth imbalance.
Uses hierarchical sequential communication to enable intra-level parallelism and overlap communication with computation.
Decouples cross-hardware and intra-hardware communication to remove synchronization overhead caused by unequal bandwidth.
Evaluated forward and backward attention across multiple hardware architectures, outperforming prior methods.
Against Ring-Attention, reports 1.3×/1.7× average forward/backward speedups on dual-NUMA PCIe and 2.8×/2.9× on dual-node NVLink.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overall Framework of CHARM+. (a) - (d) illustrate the complete process of the algorithm using an 8-GPU system with a dual-NUMA configuration. (b) shows the parallel communication and computation of q and kv. In this step, GPU 3 communicates q with GPU 0 and kv with GPU 1. After completing the computation of Q0,4, GPU3 communicates back to GPU 0 and receives the output. (c) performs the last step of RM+, where GPU 3 only communicates kv with GPU 2. papers.tldr: CHARM+ accelerates distributed attention across heterogeneous hardware by restructuring communication for greater overlap and less synchronization.

papers.abstract: KV cache eviction is not merely a token-ranking problem: the workspace retained for generating eviction queries also determines the quality of those queries. Consequently, an early workspace error can distort later query observations and reinforce an incorrect final eviction decision, particularly when evidence is dispersed across a long context. We present EchoKV, which discovers and addresses this failure mode with iterative correction. It initializes a feedback-compatible bootstrap workspace using proposals at future decode positions, then uses early decode-generated queries to recover the workspace before the remaining lookahead steps. It uses the same number of workspace forward passes as LAQ while adding a tensor re-scoring operation for workspace repair. On LongBench (16 tasks, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), EchoKV shows notable improvements over LAQ on several tasks requiring dispersed evidence, including multi-hop cross-document QA and long single-document comprehension. Across budgets and backbones, EchoKV selectively improves evidence-intensive tasks while maintaining comparable performance on the remaining LongBench subsets. These results identify query--workspace coupling as a practical failure mode of query-driven KV eviction.
bullets: Problem: Early workspace errors can corrupt later queries and reinforce incorrect eviction decisions.
Method: Bootstrap a feedback-compatible workspace, use early decode queries to recover it, then continue lookahead-based eviction.
Efficiency: Matches LAQ’s number of workspace forward passes and adds tensor re-scoring for workspace repair.
Results: Improves several LongBench evidence-intensive tasks, including multi-hop cross-document QA and long-document comprehension, across budgets and two model backbones.
Scope: Gains are selective, while performance remains comparable on other LongBench subsets.

papers.abstract: Recycling a target model's own predictions offers a training-free source of proposals for speculative decoding. In vision-language models, however, existing recycling indexes predictions by the last token alone, conflating predictions computed under different images and prefixes; we find that such reuse fails most often at image-sensitive decoding states. Longer keys reduce this aliasing but match fewer states. We introduce \method, which stores target predictions under one-, two-, and three-token keys: contextual memories live only for the current request and are thus implicitly conditioned on its image, while token-level memory persists across requests to retain coverage. At each lookup, entropy-confidence weighting fuses the retrieved predictions according to their key specificity and concentration. Best-first search composes the fused transitions into a candidate tree, supplemented by suffix-matched continuations, and one target pass verifies the tree under greedy decoding. Without training or an auxiliary draft model, \method\ achieves mean speedups over autoregressive decoding of $1.66\speed$ and $1.56\speed$ across seven single-turn benchmarks on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.6-7B, exceeding the strongest training-free baseline, Token Recycling ($1.51\speed$ and $1.37\speed$). Our implementation is available in https://github.com/Senmo996/RECAP-official-code.
authors: Hengjie Zhu, Dayan Wu, Xinze Liu, Peng Fu, Zheng Lin, Weiping Wang
bullets: Addresses prediction reuse errors caused by indexing only the last token, especially at image-sensitive states.
Combines request-local one-, two-, and three-token memories with persistent token-level memory to balance specificity and coverage.
Uses entropy-confidence weighting, best-first candidate-tree construction, suffix continuations, and one target pass for greedy verification.
Reports mean speedups of 1.66× on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and 1.56× on LLaVA-1.6-7B across seven single-turn benchmarks.
Outperforms the cited Token Recycling baseline, which achieves 1.51× and 1.37× respectively; results are scoped to the evaluated models and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLM) have been the key focus of recent machine learning breakthroughs. As the model size grows exponentially, the computation needed for training is astronomical. A GPU can do a huge amount of arithmetic. However, the data its compute units need is not always available when they are ready. This data may still be in slow memory or on another GPU. While the chip waits, expensive compute sits idle, and at scale even a small drop in utilization translates into substantial cost. In this paper, we treat this waiting time as the primary bottleneck. We focus on hardware features designed for explicit data movement. These features load data from off-chip memory onto the chip, rearrange it into the layout the computation requires as it is loaded, and transfer it between GPUs. By orchestrating them, we keep a steady pipeline of data flowing to the compute units so that they remain busy. We present kernel and framework implementations that address this bottleneck using three key data-movement instructions and hardware features. The Tensor Data Mover (TDM) moves tensor data from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) into on-chip memory. Transpose-load instructions transpose tensor data into the layout that LLM computations require as it is loaded on-chip. Finally, System DMA (SDMA) and Remote DMA (RDMA) move data between GPUs over the scale-up and scale-out networks, respectively. Our results show that TDM and transpose-load provide on average 1.88x and 1.19x speedup at the kernel level, respectively. The SDMA and RDMA lead to on average 1.16x and 1.33x speedup for computation overlapped with communication. This is the first AMD LLM training system to utilize all the GPU data pipelining features. Our implementation has been integrated into open source framework and library for AMD GPUs. https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Primus-Turbo https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Primus
authors: Gengyu Rao, Ghadeer Ahmed H Alabandi, Su Ann Chong, Thomas Huber, Kailash Gogineni, Subhajit Dutta Chowdhury, Saleel Kudchadker, Suchita Pati, Zirui Zhang, Zhen Huang, Yanyuan Qin, Xiaoming Peng, Lihuan Zhang, Botao Hu, Wei Huang, Yang Bo, Wen Xie, Xiangyu Zhao, Ruibin Zhang, Xiaobo Chen, Vidushi Goyal, Anshu Raina, Claire Songhyun Lee, Jiakun Yan, Yao Fu, Nusrat Islam, Ravi Dwivedula, Jie Zhang, Maria Garzaran, Zhenyu Gu, Emad Barsoum
bullets: Targets idle compute caused by data arriving late from off-chip memory or other GPUs.
Uses Tensor Data Mover (TDM), transpose-load, System DMA (SDMA), and Remote DMA (RDMA) to pipeline data movement.
Reports average kernel speedups of 1.88× with TDM and 1.19× with transpose-load.
Reports average speedups of 1.16× with SDMA and 1.33× with RDMA when computation overlaps communication.
Integrated into the open-source Primus-Turbo and Primus frameworks for AMD GPUs.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) are bottlenecked by the length of their input token sequence. Standard patchification fixes this length with a single patch size applied across the image, regardless of regional content. Prior work on adaptive patch sizing reduces token count by assigning coarser patches to visually simple regions, but relies on noisy pixel-level heuristics such as local entropy to make patchification decisions. We argue that this compute allocation should be grounded in the model's interpretation of task relevant information, not in raw pixel statistics. We introduce Split Policy Learned Image Tokenization which learns to allocate token resolution based on what the model finds meaningful, producing shorter token sequences that are better matched to task-relevant content. SPLIT matches the accuracy of full-resolution ViT classification baselines while using 30% fewer tokens. The same gains hold on dense prediction: SPLIT achieves competitive accuracy on COCO and ADE20K, demonstrating that semantically aligned patchification generalises well beyond classification.
authors: Aditya Gupta, Jean Sebastien Dandurand, Kai Qiu, Rohan Choudhury, Laszlo A. Jeni
bullets: Standard fixed-size patchification ignores regional complexity and creates unnecessarily long sequences.
SPLIT replaces pixel-level heuristics with a learned hierarchical patch-splitting policy guided by the model’s interpretation.
It matches full-resolution ViT classification accuracy while using 30% fewer tokens.
The approach also delivers competitive dense-prediction accuracy on COCO and ADE20K.
The abstract focuses on image classification and dense prediction; broader scope is not established.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SPLIT. An input image is first divided into coarse patches. The example uses two splitting stages, yielding a mixed-resolution token sequence. For each parent-child group, a lightweight cross-attention module pools the four child embeddings with the parent embedding as the query. The pooled summary is concatenated with the parent embedding and passed to a two-layer MLP to predict the split probability pi.
