papers.abstract: Many temporal approaches for video recognition rely on explicit cross-channel aggregation projections, which have quadratic complexity in the number of channels, introducing significant computational overhead. In addition, the spatio-temporal representation used for video recognition is biased either toward local order interactions (for CNNs) or toward global order interactions (for transformers). Starting from the multi-order spatial representation of MogaNet, our method introduces two complementary contributions to tackle these problems. First, for the temporal modelling, we introduce parallel multi-order processing with depthwise-only convolutions and implicit gating-based aggregation, which is linear in the number of channels, inducing a considerable computational reduction. Second, we propose a dual interaction between spatial and temporal dimensions, which allows a better spatio-temporal representation without increasing the computational cost. By combining these two contributions, our proposed VideoMogaNet achieves performance on par with or better than state-of-the-art action recognition approaches across multiple video benchmarks (UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics-400, Diving48), while considerably reducing the cost of the temporal branch.
authors: Kevin D. Nguetche, Lilian Hollard, Eric Granger, Marco Pedersoli
bullets: Targets the quadratic channel cost of explicit cross-channel aggregation in temporal video models.
Uses parallel multi-order depthwise-only convolutions with implicit gating-based aggregation for linear channel complexity.
Introduces dual interaction between spatial and temporal dimensions to improve representation without added computational cost.
Matches or exceeds state-of-the-art action-recognition performance across UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics-400, and Diving48.
Scope: focuses on reducing temporal modeling overhead while balancing local and global order interactions.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) speeds up large language model (LLM) serving, but its gain depends on the workload's \emph{shape}, such as batch size and context length, and on its \emph{content}. A model-based drafter proposes a short block on any content, while a model-free drafter such as n-gram lookup proposes long copies at almost no cost when the output repeats its input, as in code editing. Adaptive verification spends a batch-wide verification budget on the draft tokens most likely to be accepted, but it supports only one model-based drafter. Model-free drafters provide no per-token confidence, so they cannot take part in budget allocation, and deployments must either fix one drafter or split their GPUs between drafters. We present \sys, a framework that runs a model-based and a model-free drafter on every step and gives each request the better of their chains, within adaptive verification and entirely on the GPU, which keeps asynchronous scheduling intact. The key idea is a price per verified draft token: the goodput that slot would earn elsewhere in the batch. Once the model-free drafter's tokens carry calibrated acceptance estimates, fit once on general text, this price puts both drafters' chains on one scale. Instantiated with \dspark and an n-gram drafter in vLLM, \sys achieves 1.10--1.62\x the output throughput of \dspark on code editing at batch size~4 and 1.04--1.27\x at batch size~128, while staying at 0.97--1.01\x of it on chat at temperature~0. A single deployment can therefore serve both workloads.
bullets: Addresses workload- and content-dependent speculative decoding gains, especially repeated-input workloads such as code editing.
Runs both drafters on every step and selects the better proposal chain within a shared adaptive verification budget.
Uses calibrated acceptance estimates and a per-token opportunity-cost price to compare model-free and model-based drafts.
Implemented in vLLM, it reaches 1.10–1.62× throughput on code editing at batch size 4 and 1.04–1.27× at batch size 128 versus the model-based drafter.
Maintains 0.97–1.01× throughput on temperature-0 chat, enabling a single deployment for both workloads.

papers.selection_reason: Speculative decoding framework improving LLM serving efficiency; fits Efficient AI.
papers.title: Hybrid Spark: Adaptive Speculative Decoding That Lets the Content Choose the Drafter
papers.tldr: Hybrid Spark adaptively chooses between model-based and model-free speculative drafters per request, improving code-editing throughput while preserving near-baseline chat performance in one deployment.

papers.abstract: Whole-page ranking jointly optimizes advertisements and organic content to balance business outcomes and user engagement under complex layout and business constraints. Existing non-autoregressive (NAR) approaches enable efficient page generation but typically score candidate items independently of previously selected items, limiting their ability to capture order-dependent interactions. Autoregressive (AR) methods address this limitation through sequential conditioning, but incur substantial inference overhead that challenges large-scale deployment. Bridging this quality-efficiency gap remains a challenge in industrial whole-page ranking. We propose Multi-Item Scoring (MIS), a prefix-aware NAR-style framework that incorporates sequential context into efficient multi-item scoring. MIS integrates global candidate interactions, localized prefix conditioning, and position-aware scoring within a shared representation architecture. By computing reusable representations once per request and performing lightweight prefix-conditioned scoring during constrained beam search, MIS captures important sequential dependencies without repeated full-model inference. Experiments on KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS demonstrate that MIS approaches the generation quality of an autoregressive CGA baseline while achieving 4.07x and 3.54x faster CPU decoding, respectively. In a randomized evaluation on a large-scale social-video platform, MIS improves the realization metric by 0.104% and watch time by 0.058%, while reducing ranking-service CPU consumption by 9.73%. These results demonstrate that prefix-aware multi-item scoring can narrow the quality gap between NAR and AR generation while retaining the efficiency required for industrial scalability.
authors: Qi Xu, Zhigang Hua, Zijie Lei, Yan Xie, Jizhe Zhang, Lynn Lu, Delun Du, Sha Hua, Ren Mao, Ke Pan, Haomin Yu, Sandeep Pandey, Luke Simon
bullets: Whole-page ranking must jointly arrange ads and organic content while satisfying business and layout constraints.
Existing NAR methods are efficient but miss order-dependent item interactions; AR methods capture them but require costly sequential inference.
MIS combines global candidate interactions, localized prefix conditioning, and position-aware scoring in a shared representation architecture.
It reuses per-request representations and applies lightweight prefix-conditioned scoring during constrained beam search.
On two benchmarks, MIS achieved 4.07× and 3.54× faster CPU decoding; a large-scale randomized evaluation also reported gains in realization and watch time with lower CPU usage.

papers.abstract: The RTX 2080 Ti (TU102) ships full second-generation Tensor Cores in hardware, yet the vendor throttles FP16 matrix multiplication at the driver level, leaving usable tensor throughput well below the hardware peak. turing-unlock lifts this restriction with a kernel module that, before the nvidia driver binds the device, writes the FP16 speed selectors (SS0=0x88888888, SS1=0x8) and releases the ACR mutex; published measurements report cuBLAS FP16 matmul throughput rising from 55.7 to 91.4 TFLOPS (about 1.6x). On the same 22G 2080 Ti and under the same from-scratch pre-training protocol as the companion memory ledger (five tiers of Chinese encoder-decoder models, 2,451 steps per tier, 16,384 tokens per step, seed 42), we obtain a before/after throughput account: the small tier (75.7M parameters, 512-wide, 8+8 layers, activation checkpointing on) improves in steady-state throughput from 6,480 to 7,246 tok/s (+11.8%) with wall time cut from 1.77h to 1.61h (9.0% saved); the tiny tier goes from 15,150 to 15,866 tok/s (+4.7%) with wall time savings of 3.8%; the three smaller tiers (pico-micro) gain at most +0.3%; per-tier peak memory stays bit-identical, and final quality metrics are bit-identical or consistent within 10^-3. We conclude that the unlock gain is a function of matrix size, rising monotonically with tier -- imperceptible for pico-micro, visible from tiny upward, and cashed out as a double-digit percentage at small -- and that it is a pure throughput gain that leaves training dynamics untouched.
bullets: The driver limits FP16 matrix-multiplication throughput despite the GPU’s Tensor Core hardware capabilities.
A kernel-module unlock raises published cuBLAS FP16 throughput from 55.7 to 91.4 TFLOPS.
On a fixed from-scratch pre-training setup, gains are negligible for pico-micro, 4.7% for tiny, and 11.8% for small.
The small model’s wall time falls from 1.77 to 1.61 hours; peak memory remains bit-identical.
Training quality metrics remain bit-identical or within 10^-3, indicating unchanged training dynamics.

papers.title: Unlocking Turing Tensor Cores: A Measured Throughput Account of From-Scratch Pre-training on a Single 22G RTX 2080 Ti
papers.tldr: Unlocking the RTX 2080 Ti’s restricted FP16 Tensor Core throughput yields tier-dependent training speedups, reaching 11.8% for the small model without changing memory use or final quality.

papers.abstract: Tiered inference distributes large language model computation across a hierarchy of devices, from on-device and edge hardware to the datacenter, and is increasingly offered as the route to cheaper, lower-latency, and more private serving. Most such systems orchestrate frozen model checkpoints, and most decide what to resolve locally and what to escalate using a confidence signal produced by a forward-deployed model. We give a closed-form condition for when no threshold on that signal makes a tiered cascade worthwhile relative to sending every query to the backstop. Modeling the routing decision as a binary test and separating local from escalation cost through an architecture cost ratio $\kappa$, we derive a feasibility condition bracketed by a signal-free floor, below which a cascade is feasible at any signal quality, and a perfect-signal ceiling, above which none is. Read along the $\kappa$ axis the condition inverts: where local compute is billed, cost binds, matching a recent empirical finding; where it is sunk, on decentralized hardware, feasibility becomes unconditional and signal quality instead sets what the cascade achieves. We turn the condition into three design requirements that existing trained-in primitives satisfy only in isolation, and we propose, as future work, a co-designed architecture and a protocol to test it. The condition and the inversion hold independently of that architecture; they are the paper's contribution.
bullets: Models tiered inference as a binary routing test between local execution and escalation.
Derives signal-quality bounds: below a floor, cascades are feasible regardless of signal quality; above a ceiling, they are infeasible even with a perfect signal.
Shows that the role of local compute cost reverses with the architecture cost ratio: billed local compute can make cost binding, while sunk local compute makes feasibility unconditional.
Translates the condition into three design requirements and notes that existing trained-in components satisfy them only separately.
Proposes a co-designed architecture and evaluation protocol as future work; the feasibility condition itself is architecture-independent.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The tier model and the seam. Forward tiers (local, edge, regional) resolve queries that a routing decision at the seam accepts; the datacenter backstop receives escalations. The architecture cost ratio κ (Section 2.4) is small where forward-tier compute is sunk and appreciable where it is billed.

Figure 2: The feasibility region of Proposition 1 in the cost-ratio / signal-quality plane. Below κ⋆ floor a cascade is feasible at any signal quality; above κ⋆ ceil it is infeasible at every signal quality; between them feasibility is contingent on the signal. Decentralization moves a deployment leftward, where feasibility is unconditional below κ⋆ floor and signal quality sets the operating point a feasible cascade achieves. Illustrative parameters q = 0.6, u = 0.05, δ = 0.02.

The primitives originate in three separate literatures, adaptive-depth inference, split computing, and mixture-of-experts systems, developed for unrelated ends.

papers.selection_reason: Closed-form feasibility condition for confidence-gated tiered LLM inference is directly relevant to efficient AI and low-cost LLM serving.
papers.title: A Feasibility Condition for Confidence-Gated Tiered LLM Inference
papers.tldr: A closed-form cost condition determines when confidence-gated tiered LLM inference can outperform always using a backstop model, depending on routing-signal quality and the local-to-escalation cost ratio.

papers.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems powered by large language models (LLMs) execute as autonomous multi-step pipelines that dynamically invoke tools, integrate observations into memory, and iterate until a task is resolved or a resource budget is exhausted. Unlike classical workflows with fixed graphs, the aggregate compute, bandwidth, and end-to-end latency demands of such pipelines are unknown at dispatch time: they emerge at runtime from intermediate observations and stochastic token sampling, yielding heavy-tailed, multi-modal random variables. This unpredictability forces infrastructure orchestrators into a dilemma: under-provisioning risks mid-execution throttling and deadline violations, while over-provisioning wastes scarce edge or cloud capacity. Existing schedulers require a fully known pipeline graph, while edge resource-management methods rely on parametric or stationary demand models, and neither fits the unknown, non-stationary profiles of agentic pipelines. We formalize this setting as the uncertainty-aware agentic orchestration problem, where the goal is to reserve, at dispatch time, compute and bandwidth allocations that cover actual pipeline demands, and to verify that the pipeline can meet its deadline, each with a prescribed probability. We then propose Conformal Reservation for Orchestration (CRO), an online algorithm that translates a sliding window of past execution traces into dispatch-time resource allocations with finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees via conformal prediction. Simulations over heterogeneous task mixes with multi-modal and heavy-tailed profiles show that CRO is the only evaluated method that simultaneously satisfies target probabilistic coverage across all risk levels while, among coverage-feasible methods, attaining the lowest over-reservation, roughly halving the resource waste of the Chebyshev-bound baseline.
bullets: Agentic pipelines have runtime-dependent, stochastic, heavy-tailed compute, bandwidth, and latency demands.
The orchestration goal is to reserve resources at dispatch while meeting demand and deadlines with prescribed probabilities.
CRO converts a sliding window of past traces into dispatch-time allocations with finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees.
Simulations on heterogeneous, multi-modal, heavy-tailed workloads show CRO meets target coverage across risk levels and roughly halves over-reservation versus a Chebyshev baseline.
The evaluation is simulation-based and focuses on the tested workload mixes and risk settings.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. System model overview. The agentic system A (LLM backbone, memory, tool set) executes a ReAct loop that produces a runtime pipeline G = (v1, . . . , vN ) whose depth N and tool sequence are unknown at dispatch. Each step incurs compute and network demands that aggregate into total consumption C, B, and latency L. Four structural sources (path, depth, per-step demand, duration) make these quantities stochastic, motivating the uncertainty-aware orchestration problem (3).

Fig. 2. Simulation results (n=100 unless noted, ϵ=0.10, 400 trials). (a) Compute coverage Pr(C ≤ ρc) vs. target 1−δ; (b) bandwidth coverage Pr(B ≤ ρb) vs. target; (c) normalized compute over-reservation vs. target coverage; (d) compute coverage vs. calibration window size at δ=0.10. CRO tracks the ideal diagonal in (a)–(b) and meets the 0.90 target in (d) for all n ≥ 10; EmpQ, Gaussian, and Parametric under-reserve; Chebyshev over-covers at nearly 2× the waste of CRO in (c).

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Resource Orchestration for Agentic AI Systems

papers.abstract: Visual autoregressive generation spans two dominant paradigms: next-scale prediction for images and video, and next-frame prediction for video. Both decode block-by-block rather than token-by-token, yielding KV caches whose statistics diverge from those of language models. At scale, KV memory exceeds the weights and limits large-scale deployment caused by a large amount of visual tokens. Our analysis of these caches reveals three findings. First, a small set of massive-value channels carries the functional load: ablating these outlier channels collapses generation, whereas ablating a matched set of inlier channels leaves quality intact. Second, the outliers organize along two axes, feature and block, with magnitudes persistent within each cell and shifting across cells. Third, this structure arises from two independent mechanisms: projection bias and RoPE-induced scattering. Guided by these findings, we propose VAR-Q, a tuning-free KV-cache quantization framework that groups along the same two axes. The generation loop provides block boundaries for free, removing the need for outlier detection or calibration. Paired with bit-packing kernels for runtime memory reduction, VAR-Q delivers low-bit quantization across nine models spanning both paradigms, cutting KV memory by up to 78.5% with negligible quality degradation and enabling 6x larger inference batches.
authors: Boxun Xu, Jiaji Lu, Yuxuan Yin, Zihu Wang, Ziyue Liu, Yu Wang, Zirui Liu, Peng Li
bullets: Visual autoregressive models decode in blocks, creating KV-cache statistics that differ from language models and can make KV memory exceed model weights.
A small set of persistent outlier channels is functionally critical, with outliers structured across feature and block axes.
VAR-Q groups cache values along these two axes and uses naturally available block boundaries, avoiding outlier detection and calibration.
Bit-packing kernels reduce KV memory by up to 78.5% across nine models and enable inference batches up to 6× larger.
The approach targets next-scale and next-frame image/video generation; the abstract does not report broader settings beyond these paradigms.

papers.abstract: Under expert parallelism, mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers pay all-to-all token dispatch, grouped GEMMs, and a combine step in every layer. In decode each rank holds only 1-256 tokens: dispatch latency and weight traffic dominate while tensor-core utilization is inherently low. In fused operators such as DeepGEMM's Mega MoE, dispatch and computation overlap only by sharing every SM: dispatch warps compete with TMA/MMA and epilogue warps for registers, shared memory, and issue slots; every phase shares one CTA resource budget, synchronization spans the whole SM array, and every replay ends with a workspace-clean pass and a cross-rank barrier. We present GC-MoE, an open-source FP8/FP4 MoE inference operator for NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs that uses CUDA Green Contexts to split the device into a small communication partition and a large compute partition. Each role gets its own kernel, resource budget, and synchronization domain, so dispatch and GEMM tune independently. A three-node CUDA Graph (four on Hopper with fused shared experts) launches the dispatch and grouped-GEMM kernels as concurrent roots; a token-ring handshake starts computation on the first filled ring blocks, and double-buffered receive counters remove the trailing cross-rank barrier between replays. The compute partition runs operand-swapped tcgen05 block-scaled MMA on Blackwell and register-A WGMMA with in-register FP4 decoding on Hopper, with fused SwiGLU, requantization, and optional shared experts. On 8 H20 GPUs GC-MoE accelerates DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode by 1.188x on average on both the routed and shared-expert suites (peaks 1.296x and 1.353x); on 8 B300 GPUs it accelerates GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash by 1.106x (1.123x with fused shared experts, peak 1.209x), beating Mega MoE at all 54 measured points at matched accuracy. GC-MoE reserves only 20 of 148 SMs on B300 for dispatch.
authors: Yong Li, Kan Liu, Tao Lan
bullets: Targets decode-time MoE bottlenecks where all-to-all dispatch and weight traffic dominate and tensor-core utilization is low.
Uses CUDA Green Contexts to assign dispatch and grouped GEMM separate SM partitions, resource budgets, kernels, and synchronization domains.
Overlaps work through CUDA Graph roots, token-ring handshaking, and double-buffered receive counters that eliminate trailing cross-rank barriers.
Supports FP8/FP4 inference on Hopper and Blackwell, with fused SwiGLU, requantization, and optional shared experts.
Reports 1.188× average speedup on 8 H20s and 1.106× on 8 B300s, outperforming Mega MoE at all 54 matched-accuracy test points.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of one GC-MoE layer replay. The child CUDA Graph holds three nodes: role1 (dispatch) and role2 (grouped GEMM) have no dependency edge and are concurrent roots, whereas role3 (finalize/combine) depends on both (solid arrows). Dashed arrows map each role to the green context that launches it—role1 to the 20-SM communication context, role2 and role3 to the 128-SM compute context—each with its own balanced workqueue so that the driver co-schedules them on disjoint SM sets. All cross-rank state lives in one symmetric-memory workspace whose boxes name the buffers exchanged over NVLink (double arrows): activations and scales, routing metadata, the role1→role2 token ring, the role2→role3 combine buffer, and the counters and parity signals. Every synchronization object is device-persistent and replay-aware, so a replay needs no host-side reset.

Figure 1: Execution timelines. (a) On B300 the baseline is DeepGEMM’s Mega MoE, one persistent fused kernel on all 148 SMs: after routing counts and a tag-1 cross-rank barrier, the dispatch warps stream tokens, scales, and routing metadata into a per-block token ring while the GEMM consumes each ring block as soon as it is full. The phases overlap, but on the same SMs, with the dispatch warps and their staging buffers carved out of every SM’s register file and shared memory; the tail is max(Tcombine, tclean + ttag2)—the workspace clean overlaps the combine, but the tag-2 barrier is still a cross-rank round trip on every replay. (b) GC-MoE runs role1 (dispatch) on the 20-SM communication context and role2 (grouped GEMM) plus role3 (combine) on the 128-SM compute context. Role2 starts when the first ring block is filled (dashed trigger), and parity-double-buffered receive counters remove the tag-2 barrier, so the next replay can start as soon as role3 completes (green band). Each role is an ordinary kernel with its own register, shared-memory, and synchronization budget, so the dispatch and GEMM paths can be optimized independently. Bars are illustrative; measured end-to-end speedups span 1.03–1.30× across the routed-expert sweeps and 1.01–1.35× including shared experts (Section 6.2). Partitions are the B300 values.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon video generation is increasingly moving toward autoregressive rollout, where each newly generated segment becomes part of the evidence used for future prediction. Recent causal decoders, long-context training, and KV-cache mechanisms have extended feasible duration, but most inference pipelines still decide the visible past implicitly through recent windows, compressed caches, or external memory. This raises a direct question: \textbf{can the choice of which past frames or segments to show to the decoder be treated as an explicit test-time decision?} We answer this question with \textsc{ReCR}, a training-free method that formulates autoregressive video decoding as representation-guided context rewriting. At each step, \textsc{ReCR} builds a selected visible context from the generated history by using internal decoder representations to favor context units that match the global rollout state, avoid redundancy with the recent continuation, preserve temporal boundary coverage, and widen the range of spatial layouts in view. The selected units are then mapped onto a compact causal axis before decoding the next block. Across long-horizon text-to-video benchmarks, \textsc{ReCR} consistently improves multiple autoregressive backbones under matched visible-token budgets. Empirical analyses such as representation-space diagnostics and transition-count prompt switching further show that improving what remains visible is an effective path toward more stable long-video decoding.
authors: Lixuan He, Jihyeon Je, Yang You, Leonidas Guibas
bullets: Frames or segments shown to the decoder are treated as an explicit test-time selection decision.
The training-free method uses internal representations to select globally relevant, nonredundant context.
It preserves temporal boundary coverage and increases the diversity of visible spatial layouts.
Selected context units are placed on a compact causal axis before generating the next video block.
Across long-horizon text-to-video benchmarks, ReCR improves multiple autoregressive backbones under matched visible-token budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the ReCR framework. Instead of exposing the full generated history or a fixed recent window, ReCR scores context units with unit-level representations and selects a compact visible context. The selection objective favors high representation utility, preserves boundary coverage over early and recent context, and discourages redundant selected units. At most one spatial-range exchange, not drawn here, then refines the selection (Sec. 3.2). The selected context is then temporally reindexed onto a compact causal axis before being passed to the causal video decoder.

Figure 1: Qualitative overview of ReCR across backbones. ReCR is applied as a training-free context rewriting module on top of different autoregressive video backbones. On 60-second rollouts, ReCR reduces common long-horizon failures such as scene drift, visual artifacts, and oversaturation. On 300-second ultra-long rollouts, ReCR further extends backbones with stable visual continuity.

Figure 3: ReCR further strengthens training-free decoding methods. Qualitative comparisons on two 60-second prompts. For both methods, ReCR improves temporal consistency and visual fidelity over time: it reduces drift and artifacts in Deep Forcing, and further improves the stability and text-alignment ability of Infinity-RoPE. These results show that ReCR is a complementary context-rewriting module that can be added on top of strong training-free methods.
Figure 5: Qualitative transition examples. ReCR improves cross-segment consistency of persistent visual anchors and requested local actions under the same directive-switch schedules.

Figure 4: Dynamic allocation of ReCR’s selected visible context. (a) Selection frequency over rollout time and context-unit index. (b) Composition of Ct and normalized DINO feature velocity over rollout. (c) Representation-utility space induced by gt and ℓt, with selected units highlighted.

Figure 6: Transition-count prompt-switch scaling. (a) Overall text alignment (TA) to the active directive versus transition count K. (b) Early post-switch alignment, summarized by AUC over 0–8 seconds, versus K. (c) Absolute DINO tail shown as a radial dot plot: each spoke corresponds to a transition count, and distance from the center represents the metric value; closer to the center is better. All panels share the same method colors and markers. Higher is better in (a,b), and lower is better in (c).
Figure 7: ReCR’s results on more backbone and more frame.
Figure 8: Mechanistic robustness analysis. We compare four context construction rules under controlled perturbations: contiguous recent context, Full Context, random intermediate context, and ReCR.

papers.abstract: Model merging combines multiple fine-tuned models without additional training, and arithmetic methods have emerged as a simple yet effective way to merge models without data. However, existing arithmetic methods treat task vectors in parameter space and apply a single element-wise rule to directions that can differ in mergeability. In a shared directional basis, we find a consistent two-regime structure: a low-dispersion common bulk shared across tasks and a high-dispersion task-dominated tail that carries disproportionate energy. These findings motivate Common--Unique Subspace Decomposition (CUSD), a data-free pre-merging method that separates task vectors into common and unique directional components, merges the common components with a downstream arithmetic operator, and retains unique residuals separately. Experiments across $11$ base models, four model families, and four arithmetic-based merging operators show that CUSD improves 42 of 44 model--operator combinations and achieves up to 22.5% improvement over the corresponding baselines. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/stwang666/CUSD
authors: Shiting Wang, Yingjie Zou, Ke Li
bullets: Existing arithmetic merging methods apply one element-wise rule to task vectors despite differences in directional mergeability.
Task vectors exhibit a common, low-dispersion bulk and a high-dispersion, task-dominated tail with disproportionate energy.
CUSD decomposes task vectors into common and unique components, merges the common part, and preserves unique residuals separately.
Across 11 base models, four model families, and four operators, CUSD improves 42 of 44 model–operator combinations, with up to 22.5% improvement over baselines.
The method is data-free and requires no additional training; scope is limited to the evaluated model families and arithmetic operators.

papers.abstract: We introduce Dory1.0-4B, a 4-billion-parameter looped (latent-recurrent) language model with elastic depth: a single checkpoint serves different inference compute budgets. Dory1.0-4B is built on a normalized Transformer (nGPT) backbone with interleaved sliding-window and full-attention layers, organized into an input block, a shared recurrent block, and an output block. At inference, the recurrent block can be applied a variable number of times. We pre-trained Dory1.0-4B on 6 trillion tokens. The first 4.5 trillion tokens were trained in NVFP4, and additional pre-training then extended the context length to 256K tokens. Next, we post-trained the model using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), with a difficulty-aware loop curriculum that routes harder prompts to deeper loops. Increasing the loop count improves accuracy, with the largest gains on coding, agentic, and long-context benchmarks. With two or more loops, Dory1.0-4B outperforms larger models such as Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 12B, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B on average across 12 benchmarks. Looping also makes Dory1.0-4B more token-efficient on agentic benchmarks: with four loops, it generates 1.3-2.5x fewer tokens than with one loop, as the extra computation is spent in latent space rather than on longer outputs. To reduce memory during looping, Dory1.0-4B caches keys and values only from the last loop, keeping its KV-cache footprint equal to that of a non-looped model at any loop count while retaining most of the accuracy gains. We open-source the BF16, MXFP8, NVFP4, and GGUF quantized checkpoints.
bullets: Uses a normalized Transformer with interleaved sliding-window and full-attention layers, divided into input, recurrent, and output blocks.
Variable loop counts provide elastic inference compute, with harder prompts routed to deeper loops during post-training.
More loops yield the largest accuracy gains on coding, agentic, and long-context benchmarks.
With at least two loops, it outperforms several larger models across 12 benchmarks, according to the abstract.
Caching only the final loop’s keys and values keeps KV-cache memory comparable to a non-looped model; quantized checkpoints are released.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | Overview of the post-training pipeline for Dory1.0-4B. The base context window is 262,144 tokens (256K). SFT trains on packed sequences of 262,144 tokens, and samples loop counts for each microbatch randomly, while RLVR routes harder prompts to deeper loops with higher probability.

Figure 2 | Dory1.0-4B’s looped nGPT architecture. A 16-layer input block produces a fixed representation 𝑢. A 40-layer recurrent block refines the state over 𝑘 passes (up to four), sharing all of its weights and learned scales across each loop. Each loop adds 𝑢 to the current state, initialized as 𝑠0 = 𝑢, and applies L2 normalization before and after the recurrent block. A 16-layer output block processes the final state before the LM head. Within each block, an eight-layer pattern contains three SWA–SwiGLU pairs followed by one full-attention–SwiGLU pair, giving a 3:1 ratio of sliding-window attention (SWA) to full attention. SWA uses a window of 𝑊 =1024 tokens with RoPE base 𝜃S = 104; full attention uses 𝜃F = 107. RoPE acts on all Q/K dimensions. Each sublayer updates the residual stream by blending its normalized output with the normalized residual using learned per-channel weights, then normalizing the result.
Figure 5 | Loop-curriculum ablation with an early SFT checkpoint.

papers.title: Dory1.0-4B: A Looped Normalized-GPT
papers.tldr: Dory1.0-4B is a 4B-parameter recurrent language model that improves accuracy and token efficiency by flexibly repeating shared latent layers at inference.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose $\textbf{LoopVQ}$, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to $4.3\times$ and $6.1\times$ on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.
bullets: Looped transformers reduce parameter memory, but their KV caches grow with the number of loop steps and become the main bottleneck.
LoopVQ jointly vector-quantizes channels across multiple loop steps and fine-tunes codebooks to match full-precision outputs.
At 0.5 bits per element, it outperforms existing KV-cache quantization methods across general, long-chain-of-thought, and long-context retrieval tasks.
Combined with TaSQ, it retains much of BF16 accuracy at 0.25 bits per element.
In SGLang, it nearly halves decode latency at 32K context and increases peak throughput by up to 4.3× and 6.1× on the evaluated Ouro models.

papers.abstract: The growing energy requirements of large language model inference highlight the need for datacenters to support safe grid operation by providing power demand flexibility, while maintaining service for interactive workloads. This work investigates query routing as a mechanism to enable such capability by dynamically allocating queries across different language model instances without deferring requests. We develop a general analytical framework that connects query arrival rates and sequence length distributions to token iteration time, request residence time, serving capacity, and power consumption of model instances. Leveraging this framework, we characterize the feasible query routing allocations and the corresponding power demand flexibilities, enabling the selection of routing strategies to achieve desired power consumption behavior. We validate our framework across four GPU platforms on language models ranging from 1B to 70B parameters, obtaining 2.8% mean absolute percentage error in estimating achievable power flexibility. We evaluate our approach on a real trace-driven simulation of a 10,000 H100 GPUs datacenter, exhibiting flexibility up to 16% of total power consumption, with 90% of the desired power reduction achieved within approximately 10 seconds. These results establish query routing as an effective mechanism for datacenter power demand flexibility and demonstrate the broader applicability of our proposed framework to datacenter level planning and orchestration.
authors: Shivam Patel, Bingqing Chen, Jared Fernandez, Guannan Qu, Gauri Joshi
bullets: Addresses the need for LLM datacenters to provide power flexibility while preserving interactive service.
Develops an analytical framework linking query arrivals and sequence lengths to serving performance and instance power consumption.
Uses the framework to identify feasible routing allocations for achieving target power-consumption behavior.
Validation across four GPU platforms and 1B–70B models estimates power flexibility with 2.8% mean absolute percentage error.
A trace-driven 10,000-H100 simulation achieves up to 16% power flexibility, with 90% of the target reduction reached in about 10 seconds.

papers.abstract: LLM inference decode executes fine-grained collectives whose latency directly limits per-user interactivity, yet scale-up fabrics are still built from electronic packet switches designed for training. We observe that, for a given model deployment and parallelization, the communication structure of decode is fixed, and propose workload-static optical circuit switching (OCS): circuits are configured once per deployment, co-designed with model parallelism and with topology-aware collective schedules that turn spare accelerator ports into fewer communication phases or higher bandwidth. We evaluate this design with GXNET, a graph-based workload emulator coupled to analytical and flit-level network models grounded in hardware measurements. In a 576-accelerator scale-up domain serving 5T-parameter MoE models with up to 5M tokens of context, all-OCS fabrics improve interactivity by up to 65% and energy efficiency by up to 119% over 4:1 oversubscribed packet-switched fabrics.
authors: Maximilian Th\"urmer, Nicolas Scotto di Perto, Eloise Stein, Natanijel Vasic, Mikaeil Bagherli, Zhenguo Wu, Benjamin Klenk, Holger Fr\"oning, Johannes Feldmann
bullets: LLM decode relies on fine-grained collectives whose latency constrains per-user responsiveness.
For a fixed deployment and parallelization, decode communication is sufficiently predictable to configure optical circuits once.
The approach co-designs OCS connectivity with model parallelism and topology-aware collective schedules.
GXNET combines graph-based emulation with analytical and flit-level network models grounded in hardware measurements.
In a 576-accelerator domain serving large MoE models, all-OCS fabrics improve interactivity by up to 65% and energy efficiency by up to 119% versus 4:1 oversubscribed packet-switched fabrics.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) for vision-language-action (VLA) models promises smaller and faster VLA deployments. However, when analyzing existing VLA quantization works, we realised that it is hard to reason about the performance of the suggested quantization method compared to existing, similar, or in many cases, simpler PTQ methods. We present LoopQ, a closed-loop benchmark that compares multiple quantization policies on the same checkpoint, layers and engine, varying only the method and the kernels. We evaluate RTN, AWQ, GPTQ, ActQuant and QuantVLA on four VLAs with more than 180,000 episodes of LIBERO and LIBERO-plus, compare against QVLA's reported results on the same layers, and benchmark whether the four public VLA-quantization releases can be reproduced. We benchmark the methods on an NVIDIA H100, an L4, and a Jetson AGX Thor. Our results show that while quantization reliably saves memory, 2-3x for real low-bit models, VLA-specific PTQ methods underperform compared to simpler generic baselines. At 4 bits, RTN, AWQ and GPTQ match or exceed ActQuant and QuantVLA, plain RTN matches the calibrated methods, and plain AWQ matches the success QVLA reports for itself. Standard LIBERO hides the losses that do exist: configurations with no significant LIBERO loss lose 1.5-4.3 points under paired LIBERO-plus perturbations. Speed is a weaker story. At batch 1 on the H100, no quantized pi0.5 or OpenVLA-OFT configuration is faster than its 16-bit model (1.06-1.58x slower on library kernels); only the L4 with int8 kernels gains (4-14%), the Thor is slower on every 4-bit configuration, and the engine alone changes latency by 2.1x. Profiling explains why: pi0.5's quantized backbone is compute-bound, while its memory-bound action expert, 63% of GPU time and 13% of the parameters, stays in 16 bits.
authors: Syed Umer Bukhari, Magnus Almgren, Ahmed Ali-Eldin
bullets: Evaluates RTN, AWQ, GPTQ, ActQuant, and QuantVLA under controlled conditions: same checkpoints, layers, engines, and varying only methods and kernels.
Covers four VLAs, over 180,000 LIBERO/LIBERO-plus episodes, and NVIDIA H100, L4, and Jetson AGX Thor hardware.
At 4 bits, RTN, AWQ, and GPTQ match or exceed ActQuant and QuantVLA; standard LIBERO can hide 1.5–4.3-point losses revealed by LIBERO-plus perturbations.
Quantization consistently reduces memory, but speedups are hardware- and kernel-dependent; some configurations are slower than 16-bit models.
Profiling attributes limited speed gains partly to a 16-bit, memory-bound action expert that accounts for most runtime in pi0.5.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training increasingly targets low-bit deployment, with NVFP4 weight-and activation quantization (W4A4) becoming the state-of-the-practice format. However, integrating NVFP4 into RL degrades rollout quality and amplifies cross-engine training-inference mismatch (TIM), destabilizing training. We show that these failures are concentrated rather than uniform - severely mismatched tail tokens concentrate in a few outlier sequences, while policy weights remain largely intact and quantization error concentrates in a few high-variance activation channels. Guided by this, we present FourSight, an algorithm-system co-design with two targeted solutions: TIM-aware sequence filtering that excludes drifted trajectories from policy updates, and sparse precision compensation that keeps only top-variance channels in BF16 while retaining native NVFP4 elsewhere. We further design a fused SpliceGEMM kernel with specialized prefill and decode datapaths to minimize overhead. FourSight sustains near-BF16 accuracy and strong FP4 deployment quality across models and engines, while improving step-to-accuracy by 1.76-2.60x and staying within 2.3% of FP4 step time up to 120B-scale models.
authors: Yining Wei, Tianyuan Wu, Gu Gong, Yuechen Tao, Yinghao Yu, Xiaowen Chu, Wei Wang
bullets: NVFP4 W4A4 can degrade rollout quality and amplify training–inference mismatch, destabilizing RL post-training.
The method targets concentrated errors with TIM-aware filtering of drifted trajectories and sparse BF16 compensation for outlier activation channels.
A fused SpliceGEMM kernel reduces the runtime cost of these protections across prefill and decode.
It maintains near-BF16 accuracy and strong FP4 deployment quality, improving step-to-accuracy by 1.76–2.60× while remaining within 2.3% of FP4 step time up to 120B-scale models.

papers.abstract: Anomaly detection at the edge requires the deployment of models that achieve competitive performance, while minimizing computational cost and memory footprint. In this article, we investigate the suitability of the Mahalanobis Distance of Reservoir States (MDRS), an unsupervised time-series anomaly detection method, for resource-constrained devices and propose two optimizations to reduce its computational requirements. Specifically, we replace random reservoir connectivity (MDRS-Rand) with a circular shift (MDRS-Circ) and show that the anomaly score for an entire time series can be computed from the final reservoir state alone. Furthermore, we show that exploiting the reservoir's temporal memory enables more efficient input preprocessing, further reducing computational cost. We evaluate the MDRS variants on the MLPerf Tiny anomaly detection benchmark against the reference autoencoder and other anomaly detection methods, and deploy their inference kernels on a NUCLEO-F401RE microcontroller to assess latency, estimate energy consumption, and measure memory footprint. Among the evaluated methods, only MDRS and the autoencoder meet the benchmark's performance target, with MDRS requiring fewer operations and smaller models. With optimized preprocessing, MDRS achieves an ROC AUC of 0.869, a model size of 24 KB, an estimated energy consumption of 24 uJ per inference, and a latency of 0.32 ms, corresponding to a 75.9x speedup over the autoencoder with standard preprocessing.

Uses the reservoir’s temporal memory to reduce input-preprocessing costs.

Optimized MDRS achieved 0.869 ROC AUC, 24 KB model size, 24 µJ estimated energy per inference, and 0.32 ms latency; standard-preprocessing inference was 75.9× faster than the autoencoder.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models achieve strong performance on challenging tasks, but their long chain-of-thought often incurs substantial inference costs by continuing to deliberate after sufficient information has been obtained. Existing reasoning compression methods primarily operate on reasoning trajectories, paying less attention to the local decision of whether further reasoning is necessary given the current state. We propose LoCo, a local preference learning method for reasoning compression. LoCo detects candidate overthinking states from the model's own traces, freezes the corresponding reasoning prefixes, regenerates shorter verified continuations from the same states, and trains on the resulting state-conditioned preference pairs with DPO. This formulation teaches the model when to continue reasoning and when to conclude, rather than simply encouraging shorter trajectories overall. We construct training data entirely from self-generated mathematical traces and evaluate LoCo on five mathematical and three code generation benchmarks. LoCo reduces completion length by 41.7\%--45.4\% on mathematics and 23.4\%--36.3\% on code, while maintaining or improving accuracy and achieving the best AUC across all code benchmarks. LoCo consistently improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off on mathematics and transfers effectively to code generation despite math-only training, demonstrating the cross-domain generality of local preference learning for reasoning compression. The code and model will be publicly released at https://github.com/MuyaoYuan/LoCo.
authors: Muyao Yuan, Liyan Xu, Weizhan Zhang, Muyan Jiao, Jiangnan Li, Jinchao Zhang, Jie Zhou
bullets: Targets unnecessary deliberation after the model has enough information to solve a task.
Detects overthinking states from self-generated traces, freezes prefixes, and creates shorter verified continuations.
Uses state-conditioned preference pairs trained with direct preference optimization (DPO).
Trained only on mathematical traces, it reduces completion length by 41.7%–45.4% on math and 23.4%–36.3% on code.
Improves the accuracy–efficiency trade-off and transfers to code generation, with best AUC across all code benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference, the process by which a pre-trained model receives an input prompt and generates output tokens sequentially, has become increasingly important with the widespread deployment of LLM-based applications. As inference workloads continue to scale, GPU memory has emerged as a critical bottleneck: the long input prompts and generation sequences common in agentic and reasoning workloads lead to substantial key-value (KV) cache usage. In this paper, we study the resulting online scheduling problem from a queueing perspective. Requests arrive stochastically with heterogeneous prompt and output lengths, undergo prefill and autoregressive decode, and compete for a finite KV-cache capacity. Unlike classical queueing models, the duration of a processing step depends on both prefill computation and KV-cache I/O, so service capacity is jointly determined by computation, memory access, and memory occupancy. We develop a fluid model that reduces the system to a multiclass single-server queue with effective service rates capturing computation, memory access, and memory capacity. This fluid analysis yields a $c\mu$ priority rule, where the effective service rate $\mu$ is jointly determined by computational speed, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity. We prove that this rule minimizes cumulative holding cost in the fluid model and, for a finite workload, also minimizes completion time and maximizes full-run output-token throughput. We then construct a feasible scheduling policy for the original finite system and prove that its scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy. Finally, experiments on a real LLM serving engine using an NVIDIA H800 show that practical implementations of the proposed priority rule substantially reduce average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies.
authors: Zhenghao Li, Shengbo Wang, Nian Si
bullets: Models LLM inference as an online multiclass queue with heterogeneous prompts, outputs, computation, KV-cache access, and memory occupancy.
Derives effective service rates that jointly account for compute speed, memory bandwidth, and KV-cache capacity.
Proves the $c\mu$ rule minimizes cumulative holding cost in the fluid model, while also minimizing finite-workload completion time and maximizing full-run output-token throughput.
Constructs a feasible policy for the finite system and proves convergence of its scaled dynamics to the optimal fluid policy.
Experiments on an NVIDIA H800 show lower average latency while maintaining high throughput compared with existing scheduling policies.

papers.abstract: Expert offloading enables large mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models to run locally, but conventional batching stalls the GPU while missing experts are fetched. A popular remedy, known as prefetching, is to predict what experts will be needed soon and fetch them using idle link bandwidth. Imprecise prediction, however, wastes bandwidth and GPU memory on fetching unnecessary experts. Our key finding is that prefetching can be harmful when there is an expert cache in GPU memory. This is because as the cache includes more necessary experts, expert prediction becomes less precise. Our key insight is that proper request scheduling beats prefetching. Building on this insight, we present Bevy, an MoE inference system based on runahead inference for concurrent requests. A request whose experts are available can run ahead to later layers while other requests wait for fetches, revealing the experts it needs next. Bevy can then fetch the missing experts so identified while computing ready requests, overlapping computation and fetching without predicting expert selections. Running requests separately, however, repeats reads of shared weights in GPU memory and increases compute time. To limit this cost, Bevy's self-balancing scheduler batches ready requests at each layer and prioritizes lagging requests, adapting their grouping as expert availability changes. Across two local platforms, Bevy delivers up to 3.46$\times$ the decode throughput of llama.cpp and up to 1.55$\times$ that of the fastest prefetching baseline.
authors: Hongseung Yu, In Gim, Kyunghan Lee, Lin Zhong
bullets: Expert offloading can stall GPU execution when required experts must be fetched.
Prefetching may waste bandwidth and GPU memory because larger expert caches reduce prediction precision.
Bevy uses runahead inference: requests with available experts advance to reveal future needs while others wait.
A self-balancing scheduler batches ready requests and prioritizes lagging requests to reduce repeated weight reads and computation.
Across two local platforms, Bevy achieves up to 3.46× the decode throughput of llama.cpp and 1.55× that of the fastest prefetching baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Bevy, a system for accelerating MoE inference by interleaving concurrent requests and using a self-balancing scheduler. This addresses inference efficiency and optimization, fitting the Efficient AI subtopic.
papers.title: Accelerating Offloading-Based MoE Inference by Interleaving Concurrent Requests
papers.tldr: Bevy accelerates local MoE inference by scheduling concurrent requests to overlap expert fetching with computation, avoiding inaccurate prefetch predictions.

papers.abstract: Split Inference (SI) addresses the hardware resource limitations of Internet of Things (IoT) devices by distributing tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) model segments across multiple IoT devices. However, a device failure can interrupt the inference pipeline. This paper proposes a replica-aware recovery approach that deploys replicas of TinyML model segments originally hosted on failed devices onto surviving devices. We formulate the joint selection of replica hosts and communication protocols as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem that minimizes post-reconfiguration inference latency, accounting for computation and transmission latencies, under flash memory and runtime memory constraints. Simulations using MobileNetV2 on heterogeneous IoT networks compare the proposed approach with four baselines. We implement the model in a network of 15 IoT devices with a maximum link-rate reduction of 75%, and show that MILP approach achieves an average modeled end-to-end inference latency that is 6.8% lower than that of Computation Greedy and 18.3% lower than that of Random. Index Terms TinyML, split inference, Internet of Things, fault tolerance, replica placement.

Simulations with MobileNetV2 on heterogeneous IoT networks report lower modeled latency than Computation Greedy and Random baselines.

papers.abstract: Attention is known to be sparse in vision transformers. In particular, we analyze the unequal relevance of attention-matrix columns to the final computation and show that this phenomenon becomes increasingly pronounced with network depth. This can be interpreted as saying that tokens have an absolute importance for the attention process, independently of queries. Inspired by this, we propose a reformulation of the attention formula that makes this phenomenon explicit by adding an input-dependent bias to the query-key dot product. We show that this new term gives each token a scalar value indicating its anticipated influence on other tokens during the attention process, and can thus serve as a proxy for pruning attention maps. Across multiple transformer model sizes, this allows us to substantially reduce the computational cost of attention, in terms of both FLOPs and inference latency, while retaining most of the original classification accuracy. We publicly released the code and models at https://github.com/EIDOSLAB/AttentionWithBias.
authors: Charles Herr, Gabriele Spadaro, Enzo Tartaglione
bullets: Attention-matrix columns contribute unequally to the final computation, with this imbalance increasing at greater network depth.
The method adds an input-dependent bias to query–key dot products to estimate each token’s anticipated influence on others.
These scalar token scores act as a proxy for pruning attention maps.
Across multiple transformer sizes, pruning substantially reduces attention FLOPs and inference latency while retaining most classification accuracy.
Code and models are publicly released.

papers.abstract: Per-step selective back-propagation forwards every example of a mini-batch but back-propagates only some of them. Most rules rank examples by loss or gradient magnitude, but such scalar scores ignore cancellation between per-example gradients: the gradient removed by a set can be much smaller than its individual magnitudes suggest. We introduce CAPSkip (Cancellation-Aware Prefix Skipping). Among the examples the model already classifies correctly, CAPSkip skips the longest prefix, in increasing order of last-layer gradient norm, whose vector sum stays within a relative budget $b$ of the batch's last-layer gradient. In exact arithmetic this bounds the change of the raw final-layer gradient, using rank-one contributions already available from the forward pass; the bound does not extend to deeper layers, optimizer updates, or the training trajectory. Because the cumulative distortion is not monotone in the prefix length, CAPSkip scans all prefixes; a factorised Gram matrix makes the scan cheap and keeps it on the device. With activation reuse and selected-row backward, CAPSkip fine-tunes DeiT-S on CIFAR-100 for 103 epochs in 0.576x the time of 103-epoch dense training, and is +0.25 pp [+0.08, +0.42] above an approximately time-matched 59-epoch dense run (n=3).
bullets: Targets the failure of loss- or gradient-magnitude ranking to account for cancellation among per-example gradients.
Skips the longest prefix ordered by increasing last-layer gradient norm whose summed gradient remains within relative budget b of the full batch gradient.
Scans all prefixes because cumulative distortion is non-monotonic; a factorized Gram matrix enables an efficient on-device scan.
The bound applies only to the raw final-layer gradient, not deeper layers, optimizer updates, or the overall training trajectory.
On DeiT-S fine-tuning on CIFAR-100, it used 0.576× the time of dense 103-epoch training and was 0.25 percentage points above a time-matched 59-epoch dense run.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) often process hundreds or thousands of visual tokens, resulting in substantial computational and memory overhead during inference. Existing training-free pruning methods typically estimate token importance using language-model attention, visual attention, or feature similarity. However, these methods treat visual tokens with uniform criteria and overlook that tokens may serve different roles during visual encoding. In this work, we investigate the evolution of visual token roles in LVLMs and observe that tokens progressively transition from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives as encoding proceeds. Based on this observation, we propose BtsPruner, a training-free role-aware visual token pruning framework that preserves complementary token roles under a fixed budget. Specifically, BtsPruner first identifies the token-role transition point based on the evolution of attention concentration. It then discovers globally referenced representatives from later encoding stages and recursively retrieves local detail tokens from earlier stages to recover complementary fine-grained evidence. Extensive experiments across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen-VL, InternVL, and CogVLM demonstrate that BtsPruner achieves superior performance retention under aggressive token reduction. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, BtsPruner preserves 91.6% of the dense model's performance using only 32 of 576 visual tokens (5.6%). In the high-resolution LLaVA-NeXT-7B setting, it achieves up to a 5.95x CUDA-latency speedup.
authors: Zihao Qi, Zhibo Zhang, Miaoxin Zhang, Jincheng Cai, Zengqiang Yan
bullets: LVLM inference is costly because it processes hundreds or thousands of visual tokens.
The method observes that tokens evolve from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives during encoding.
It identifies this role-transition point, selects global representatives from later stages, and recursively retrieves complementary local tokens from earlier stages.
Across multiple LVLMs, it retains strong performance under substantial token reduction.
On LLaVA-1.5-7B, it retains 91.6% of dense-model performance with 32/576 tokens; on LLaVA-NeXT-7B, it provides up to 5.95× CUDA-latency speedup.

papers.abstract: We present a spatial-memory system that enables optical see-through AR glasses to recall earlier physical encounters. The dual-camera prototype combines hierarchical visual acquisition with source-linked storage and staged retrieval. Quality screen-ing, global and regional appearance novelty, and temporal support select monochrome observations for detailed RGB cap-ture. Semantic observations retain links to their source images, allowing retrieval to answer indexed historical questions direct-ly or inspect visual details omitted from scene descriptions. The architecture separates capture acceptance, interpretation out-come, and support for a particular question. This distinction motivates two core control mechanisms: bounded reassessment of familiar views when earlier processing leaves an evidence gap, and retention guided by source dependencies. In a 131.35 s egocentric replay, the implemented acquisition policy selected six RGB views from 648 monitoring observations, while feature extraction ran on 97.7% of observations. These results demon-strate selective RGB acquisition and identify frequent local inference as a remaining cost. Exposure duration and cross-view timing further constrain the evidence preserved from se-lected encounters. The system provides a practical acquisition-to-recall architecture for persistent AR assistance, with explicit boundaries between captured evidence, indexed interpretations, and supported historical claims.

Uses hierarchical acquisition: quality, novelty, and temporal cues select monochrome observations for detailed RGB capture.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation (MDE) has advanced rapidly with the emergence of foundation models such as Depth Anything. Their transformer-based architectures provide strong generalization across diverse scenes and domains, but also incur high computational and memory cost, making efficient deployment challenging. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) provides an efficient and practical solution for model compression, yet low-bit PTQ remains challenging for MDE models. When applying PTQ to Depth Anything, we identify two key challenges: (i) independently minimizing the quantization error of the query and key projections fails to preserve the attention maps induced by their interaction, and (ii) quantization errors accumulate across layers, resulting in intermediate feature distribution shifts. To address these issues, we propose SPA-Q, a Structure-Preserving Adaptive PTQ framework for MDE, consisting of two main components. First, Attention-Preserving Calibration (APC) determines query and key quantization parameters by matching the full-precision attention distribution. Second, Channel-Wise Distribution Alignment (CWDA) learns channel-wise affine transformations to mitigate quantization-induced distribution shifts, and the learned parameters are absorbed into the weights after training. Experimental results show that SPA-Q consistently outperforms existing PTQ methods under 4-bit quantization, achieving an average 25.9% reduction in AbsRel and a 17.3% improvement in $\delta_1$ across NYUv2 and KITTI datasets.
authors: Jaemin Choi, Jincheol Yang, Nahyun Lim, Yun-Seong Jeong, Matti Zinke, Hyunwoo Yu, Suk-Ju Kang
bullets: Low-bit PTQ for Depth Anything is difficult because query–key interactions and layerwise feature shifts amplify quantization errors.
Attention-Preserving Calibration matches quantized attention distributions to their full-precision counterparts.
Channel-Wise Distribution Alignment uses learnable affine transformations to correct channel-level shifts, then folds them into the weights.
Across NYUv2 and KITTI, SPA-Q reduces AbsRel by 25.9% on average and improves δ1 by 17.3% under 4-bit quantization.

After optimization, the learned affine parameters are fused into the weights, introducing no additional inference overhead.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Cone Alignment Index (CAI), a scale-invariant sparsity measure associated with a Lorentz-cone geometry. We provide a probabilistic analysis of the distribution of the CAI score, including a general theorem and explicit corollaries for Gaussian and uniform distributions. As a consequence, we show that, in the high-sparsity regime, the probability that the samples lie within the convex cone tends to one. Building upon this formulation, we derive two complementary projections: the \emph{Parametric Linear Conic Projection} (PLCP), an efficient closed-form approximation, and the \emph{Parametric Euclidean Conic Projection} (PECP), the exact Euclidean projection onto the cone boundary. Our analysis establishes several fundamental theoretical properties. We prove that PLCP and PECP are collinear, differ only by a positive radial scaling factor, and induce exactly the same sparsity threshold, thereby preserving an identical active support. Furthermore, we derive a support-identification theorem showing that, for any prescribed sparsity level $l<n$, the number of coefficients discarded at each iteration is theoretically controlled. Building on this theoretical foundation, we develop a bilevel PLCP framework for structured matrix sparsification. The proposed method naturally generates hardware-friendly structured sparsity patterns, including row-wise, column-wise, and diagonal masks, making it particularly well suited for accelerating Transformer attention mechanisms.
authors: Michel Barlaud, Clement Genninasca, Maxime Zanella, Benoit Macq, Benoit Legat

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has attracted significant attention in the parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) landscape. However, its design suffers from two fundamental limitations. First, its invariance manifold induces flat directions in the loss landscape, creating an optimization bottleneck for adaptive optimizers. Second, its effective rank scales only linearly with the parameter budget. In this paper, we propose Scalable Morpho Adaptation (SaMA), a PEFT method grounded in a principled generalization of the Kronecker product. By relaxing the shared-block constraint in the perfect-shuffle factorization, SaMA spans from low to full rank and achieves a practical rank that scales quadratically with the parameter budget, up to full-rank. Furthermore, we show that its invariance manifold collapses to a diagonal group, making it structurally more optimizer-friendly. Empirically, SaMA consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks while being more parameter-efficient.
bullets: Addresses LoRA’s flat optimization directions and linear effective-rank scaling.
Relaxes the shared-block constraint in perfect-shuffle factorization to span low- through full-rank adaptations.
Its effective rank can scale quadratically with the parameter budget, up to full rank.
Collapses the invariance manifold to a diagonal group, potentially easing optimization.
Consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks with greater parameter efficiency.

papers.abstract: A team serving a 9B-20B open-weight language model on vLLM or SGLang must choose a quantization recipe, and needs two numbers: the speedup over BF16 and the accuracy given up. We assemble every public measurement of these numbers that we could verify and find that the record supplies them only in pieces. Only two checkpoints, both INT4 builds of Gemma 3 12B, have both a vLLM timing and an accuracy score, and that score covers a single MMLU subject, one that the AWQ build was calibrated on. The batch-1 timings predate current engine releases, AMD and Intel Gaudi have no timing in this band at all, and FP4 has none against BF16. The timings that do exist follow one rule. Decoding a small batch is limited by memory bandwidth, so 4-bit weights roughly double speed (2.12x for Qwen2.5-14B on an A100), but the gain vanishes once a large batch makes the GPU compute-bound (1.02x for Gemma 3 12B at batch size 256), where FP8 is the recipe that can still help. Many published accuracy deltas, including every HumanEval delta, lie within benchmark sampling noise. We close with a seven-item reporting checklist for future measurements.
authors: Smit Kadvani, Kriti Faujdar, Spurthi Tallam
bullets: The literature lacks complete, directly comparable measurements of speedup over BF16 and accuracy loss for 9B–20B open LLMs.
Only two checkpoints—both INT4 Gemma 3 12B builds—combine vLLM timing with an accuracy score, and that accuracy evidence is narrowly scoped.
Small-batch decoding is memory-bandwidth-limited, producing roughly 2× speedup in one reported case; large batches can reduce the gain to about 1×.
FP8 may remain beneficial when large batches make the GPU compute-bound.
Many reported accuracy differences, including all HumanEval deltas, fall within benchmark sampling noise; the paper proposes a seven-item reporting checklist.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient linearization turns a pretrained autoregressive Transformer into an efficient model by hybridizing sliding-window attention (SWA) with a constant-size recurrent memory. But does every layer's recurrent state contribute to long-context retrieval? Investigating an SWA and Test-Time Training (TTT) hybrid, we find that retrieval is sparse across depth, concentrated in a few anchor layers, and that the remaining states hold similar information expressed through layer-specific transformations. We exploit both observations in Anchor: TTT memory placed only at the anchor layers, and a cross-layer recurrent state written once and read by many layers, each through its own learned read map that realizes a layer-specific stretch and rotation, along with demonstrated generalization to other hybrid attentions. On Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, Anchor delivers 2.3-3.1x higher recall and 6.7-8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs with a 10x smaller recurrent state, retains 91-95% of the teacher's MMLU accuracy, and cuts end-to-end latency by up to 4.3x relative to softmax attention.
authors: Vimal William, Yuanzhe Li, Danella Zhao, Huanrui Yang
bullets: Long-context retrieval is concentrated in a small number of layers, while other recurrent states encode similar information via layer-specific transformations.
Anchor places recurrent TTT memory only at these anchor layers and uses a cross-layer state read by many layers.
Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, it achieves 2.3–3.1× higher recall and 6.7–8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs.
It uses a 10× smaller recurrent state, retains 91–95% of teacher MMLU accuracy, and reduces latency by up to 4.3× versus softmax attention.
The approach also generalizes to other hybrid-attention designs.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Anchor architecture and recurrent-state coverage. Left: Anchor-F maintains a private recurrent state in every layer, while Anchor keeps one shared state per anchor group and removes the interior states entirely, reducing recurrent state by 16× (201.0 → 12.6MB at 32k context). Each reader accesses the shared state through its own learned read map χ(·). Right: coverage over query (rows) and key (columns) positions. Green marks the local sliding window, red the span served by the recurrent state. Anchor-F requires one such state per layer; Anchor serves layers l1, . . . , L from a single shared state.

Debiased CKA against mean cosine similarity for every pair of layers, on the recurrent-state readouts of our TTT hybrid (Anchor-F), LoLCATs, and Liger on Mistral-7B over identical PG-19 and WikiText inputs. In all three models, layers share information while their cosine similarity remains small, indicating that this information is encoded in different bases.

Figure 7. Hybrid architecture of ANCHOR and full self-attention. ANCHOR and full self-attention layers are interleaved at a 3:1 ratio, so that softmax attention accounts for 25% of all layers. Within each group, the three ANCHOR layers retain their own sliding-window attention for local context but share a single recurrent state for long-range context: the leading layer writes the state, and each layer reads it through its own learned read map χℓ(·). The subsequent full self-attention layer attends over the entire sequence, providing exact retrieval at regular depth intervals, while the recurrent state per group remains constant in sequence length.

papers.title: Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training
papers.tldr: Anchor improves long-context retrieval and efficiency by storing TTT memory only in a few anchor layers and sharing it across layers through learned read transformations.

papers.abstract: We introduce a training-free sparse attention method that builds a prompt-specific key index to accelerate both prefill and decoding. The method clusters the keys into large semantic blocks that group tokens from noncontiguous positions. Each query position selects blocks by scoring their centroids and attends to the original keys and values within them. Queries that select the same block are processed together, so prefill stays fast even though each query chooses its own blocks. Large blocks make centroid scoring and this grouped processing cheap, so each query can attend to more tokens in the same time. Larger blocks with a larger token budget can thus be both faster and more accurate on long-context tasks than smaller blocks with a smaller budget. We evaluate two hybrid LLMs, Qwen3.5-4B and 35B-A3B, on one NVIDIA H200. Including the cost of building and using the index, whole-model wall-clock speedups over dense attention are 2.3-2.4x for prefill and 1.7-2.0x for decoding at 512K tokens, and 2.9-3.0x for prefill at 1M. The 35B-A3B model stays close to dense attention on five RULER tasks through 1M, on LongBench-v2 overall, and on MRCR through 256K. The 4B model loses accuracy mainly on multi-key retrieval, yet outperforms dense Qwen3.5-2B, whose latency is similar at 512K, on all three benchmarks.
authors: Sosuke Kobayashi, Shoichiro Yamaguchi, Seiya Tokui
bullets: Builds a prompt-specific index by clustering noncontiguous keys into large semantic blocks.
Each query scores block centroids, then attends to the original keys and values within selected blocks.
Groups queries selecting the same blocks to keep prefill efficient despite query-specific routing.
On one H200, whole-model speedups reach 2.3–2.4× for 512K prefill, 1.7–2.0× for 512K decoding, and 2.9–3.0× for 1M prefill.
The 35B-A3B model remains close to dense attention on several long-context evaluations; the 4B model mainly degrades on multi-key retrieval.

papers.abstract: As deep learning (DL) models become increasingly complex and hardware architectures grow more heterogeneous, DL compilers play a critical role in optimizing computational efficiency and enabling scalable deployment. This paper presents a systematic analysis of DL compilers, covering their architectural evolution, compilation workflows, optimization techniques, and emerging research directions. We organize DL compiler architectures into frontend, middle-end, and backend stages, emphasizing the role of the middle-end in connecting high-level model representations with hardware-specific optimizations. We further examine representative DL compilers and recent optimization techniques across different compilation stages. Beyond architectural and technical analysis, we conduct an empirical evaluation of compiler behaviors to investigate the effectiveness of graph optimization, compilation overhead, and dynamic-shape handling. Experiments using PyTorch/TorchInductor on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 demonstrate that compiler benefits depend strongly on workload characteristics, with speedups of up to 8.21\times for fusion-friendly computation graphs, while other workloads exhibit limited improvements. Our results further reveal that compilation overhead can require thousands of executions to amortize, and dynamic-shape compilation reduces cumulative shape-transition costs by approximately 70\% at the expense of modest steady-state performance degradation. By combining systematic architectural analysis with quantitative experimental evidence, this work provides insights into the design, optimization, and practical deployment of modern DL compilers.
authors: Jinghao Wen, Ruixuan Wang, Xun Jiao
bullets: Organizes DL compilers into frontend, middle-end, and backend stages, highlighting the middle-end’s role in linking model representations to hardware optimization.
Reviews representative compilers and optimization techniques across compilation stages.
Evaluates graph optimization, compilation overhead, and dynamic-shape handling using PyTorch/TorchInductor on an NVIDIA RTX A6000.
Fusion-friendly graphs achieve speedups of up to 8.21×, while other workloads see limited gains.
Compilation overhead may require thousands of executions to amortize; dynamic-shape compilation cuts cumulative shape-transition costs by about 70% with modest steady-state degradation.
