papers.abstract: Self-attention has become the standard for modern sequence modeling, enabling Transformers to model long-range dependencies across a wide range of modalities. Despite these advances, its quadratic cost with respect to sequence length remains a significant computational bottleneck. Recent work addresses this limitation by introducing linear variants of self-attention, namely with kernel approximations of the softmax operator. However, their first-order aggregation restricts expressivity and struggles to capture higher-order structure. We propose Linear Stochastic Attention (LiSA), a linear attention plug-in module that enables higher-order token interactions via a stochastic diffusion process based on truncated random walks. LiSA incorporates adaptive locality, favoring semantically similar neighbors to preserve fine-grained structures, while maintaining stable and efficient training. We conduct extensive experiments on classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection tasks and show improved results over state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Sahar Dastani, Fereshteh Shakeri, Samuel Barbeau, Kunal Mahatha, Ismail Ben Ayed, Herve Lombaert, Christian Desrosiers
bullets: Addresses the quadratic sequence-length cost of standard self-attention and the limited expressivity of first-order linear attention.
Uses truncated random walks to enable higher-order token interactions within a linear-attention framework.
Employs adaptive locality to emphasize semantically similar neighbors and preserve fine-grained visual structure.
Evaluated on classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection, with improved results over state-of-the-art methods.
The abstract does not specify numerical gains or experimental datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LiSA. We patchify the input image into tokens and treat them as nodes in a graph G = (V,E), where edge weights define a row-stochastic transition matrix S. Aggregating the truncated terms on S yields a global attention map that captures transitive (higher-order) dependencies. In parallel, we compute content-based similarity within each token’s local neighborhood to form a local attention map. The layer output is a convex combination of the two, blending sharp local context with long-range structure.

papers.abstract: Wearable sports sensors can recognize actions on the device itself, where lower-precision numbers reduce model storage and memory traffic. Two 4-bit block-scaled formats, MXFP4 from the Open Compute Project, introduced in 2023, and NVFP4 from NVIDIA, introduced in 2025, are drawing interest. Published evaluations cover general deep-learning benchmarks and large language models; to our knowledge, nobody has yet measured what they cost a small wearable-sensor model. We train a 159,492-parameter 1D CNN to recognize four basketball actions from wrist-accelerometer data in Hang-Time HAR and test it on players it has never seen, using five-fold cross-validation grouped by player. Every comparison between number formats is made fold by fold. In full precision the model reaches 69.26\% macro-F1. Measured TFLite FP16 and INT8 models lose at most 0.16 percentage points. In simulation, 4-bit weights cost 1.45 points with MXFP4 and 0.72 points with NVFP4. When activations are quantized to 4 bits as well, MXFP4 loses 5.14 points and NVFP4 only 0.75, and NVFP4 comes out ahead in all five held-out-player folds. The ranking survives two alternative simulator settings, with NVFP4 leading by 3.49 to 4.40 points. A $2 \times 3$ ablation with 4-bit weights and activations (two block sizes and three scale rules) points to scale selection as the main source of MXFP4's loss. The reference MXFP4 conversion we simulate rounds the scale down, which can pick scales that are too small, so many blocks clip their largest values. Rounding the scale up recovers 3.18 points with 32-value blocks and 3.63 points with 16-value blocks, and switching to an 8-bit floating-point scale, as NVFP4 does, adds another 0.84 and 1.20 points. Block size matters less. Under this round-down rule, 16-value blocks score 0.44 points below 32-value blocks in all five folds; under the other two rules there is no consistent effect.
bullets: The study evaluates 4-bit MXFP4 and NVFP4 on a 159,492-parameter 1D CNN using wrist-accelerometer data from previously unseen players.
Full precision achieves 69.26% macro-F1; FP16 and INT8 lose at most 0.16 percentage points.
With 4-bit weights and activations, MXFP4 loses 5.14 points, while NVFP4 loses only 0.75 points and leads in every held-out-player fold.
Scale selection is the main source of MXFP4's degradation: rounding scales down causes clipping, while rounding up substantially recovers accuracy.
Results are specific to this small four-action wearable-sensor model and simulation settings; block size has a smaller, inconsistent effect.

papers.title: What Does 4-Bit Microscaling Cost a Wearable Activity Recognizer?
papers.tldr: For a small wearable basketball-action recognizer, NVFP4 preserves accuracy far better than MXFP4 when both weights and activations use 4-bit microscaling, largely because of better scale selection.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers apply a shared block several times per token to improve accuracy without adding parameters. For models such as Ouro that keep a separate key-value (KV) cache per loop, cache memory limits the batch size that amortizes repeated weight reads. Uniform-bit quantization and fixed rules per loop do not allocate precision according to each layer's sensitivity in each loop. Measurements on Ouro show that quantization sensitivity varies across (loop, layer) cells, and the sum of individual cell damages approximates the overall output damage. Sharing damage also varies by cell, with later loops generally tolerating sharing better. Skipping low-attention values to save reads produces errors that compound across loops. LoopKV uses a one-time offline profile to choose 4-bit storage, 2-bit storage or reuse of the final loop's KV for each cell. The planner minimizes reads under budgets for predicted damage and storage. During decoding, each loop reads the high 2 bits of each 4-bit value and fetches the low bits only where its own attention weights require 4-bit precision. A single fused kernel in vLLM executes the plan. Serving Ouro-1.4B on one RTX PRO 6000, the memory-optimized LoopKV-M plan stores 35% less KV than uniform 4-bit quantization (KIVI-4) on the same fused kernel and CUDA graph. It sustains 1.7-2.2x KIVI-4's goodput under a latency service-level objective with a 16K-token maximum length. None of its averages on six public benchmarks falls significantly below BF16's.
authors: Tianle Zhou, Yang Zhang, Tianyu Wu, Zhuohan Wang, William Nixon, Juncheng Yang
bullets: Looped transformers keep separate KV caches per loop, creating substantial memory pressure during serving.
An offline profile estimates quantization and sharing sensitivity for each (loop, layer) cell.
A planner selects 4-bit, 2-bit, or final-loop KV reuse under damage and storage budgets.
Runtime decoding fetches low bits only when attention requires 4-bit precision, using a fused vLLM kernel.
On Ouro-1.4B, LoopKV-M stores 35% less KV than uniform 4-bit KIVI-4 and achieves 1.7–2.2× higher goodput under the stated latency objective, without significant benchmark degradation versus BF16.

(a) Goodput relative to BF16 on one RTX PRO 6000 for the memory-optimized plan (LoopKV-M), which minimizes reads under a tight storage budget, the read-optimized plan (LoopKV-R), which minimizes reads with no storage budget, and comparable methods. Goodput is the highest request rate at which 95% of requests meet the SLO2. In the figure, LoopKV-M sustains 8.0× BF16’s goodput and 2.0× that of KIVI-4 (§5.4). (b) Over all the public suites we tested (Table 1), neither LoopKV-M nor LoopKV-R is significantly less accurate than BF16, whereas naive INT2 on loops 1–3 in the KIVI style and naive last-loop KV reuse lose accuracy significantly on several suites. Other comparable methods: KIVI-4 + V adds our V precision to KIVI-style INT4 on every loop, on the same fused kernel and graph. BF16, FP8 and FP8 + loop-3 sharing use vLLM’s own kernels, and KIVI-4 is uniform INT4 without V precision.

papers.selection_reason: KV cache compression for looped transformers; directly targets memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: LoopKV: Loop-Aware KV Cache Compression for Serving Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: LoopKV compresses loop-specific KV caches by assigning per-cell precision or reuse, reducing memory while preserving model quality and improving serving goodput.

papers.abstract: As large language models are fine-tuned for increasingly specialized tasks, their performance depends more on which training examples are selected than on how many. Given a large heterogeneous training pool and a small target set specifying the desired capability, targeted data selection aims to find a compact subset that maximizes downstream performance. Existing methods score each candidate independently against the target and select the top-ranked examples, yet this point-wise strategy ignores inter-example interactions: at tight budgets the selected subset is dominated by near-redundant points that waste capacity on overlapping information. We propose Query-based Submodular functions with Gradient-guided Synthesis (QSGS), which formulates targeted selection as a submodular graph cut over a gradient similarity graph. A modular relevance term pulls selected examples toward the target task, while a pairwise dispersion penalty suppresses intra-subset redundancy. The resulting objective balances target relevance and intra-subset redundancy using the same formulation across different selection budgets. Empirically, the benefit of diversity-aware selection becomes increasingly pronounced as the data budget decreases. To further close coverage gaps that no selection from existing data can bridge, we introduce a gradient-guided synthesis step that identifies under-covered target directions via residual subspace analysis and generates synthetic examples to fill them. Experiments on MMLU, BBH, and TydiQA across Llama-2, Llama-3, and Mistral, show that QSGS at a 0.5% budget matches or exceeds full-data performance on Mistral-7B, outperforms the strongest baseline across all benchmarks, and yields increasing gains as the budget shrinks.
authors: Zhenghao Zhao, Yasutomo Kawanishi, Huihuo Zheng, Michael E. Papka, Yan Yan
bullets: Targets task-relevant examples while reducing redundancy through a submodular graph-cut objective over gradient similarities.
Uses a modular relevance term and pairwise dispersion penalty under one formulation across selection budgets.
Adds gradient-guided synthesis to fill target directions not covered by the available data.
Diversity-aware selection becomes more beneficial as the data budget shrinks.
Across MMLU, BBH, and TydiQA, QSGS matches or exceeds full-data performance for Mistral-7B at 0.5% budget and outperforms the strongest baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed QSGS framework. Given a candidate pool D and a target validation set V , QSGS constructs a high-quality coreset through three stages. (1) Gradient feature computation. A warmup model is trained on a small random subset of the training data and used to compute per-sample gradient features for all examples in D and V . (2) Query-based graph cut selection. For each candidate x, we compute the similarity w(x,x′) to already-selected samples, and the influence score I(x,v) measuring its relevance to the validation set. The submodular graph cut objective maximizes I(x,v) while penalizing w(x,x′), jointly promoting candidate–target relevance and minimizing intra-subset redundancy to yield a diverse yet task-aligned coreset. (3) Gradientguided synthesis. To fill coverage gaps, we compute the gradient residual to find uncovered directions, then use the warmup model to generate synthetic candidates and select to the coreset.

Figure 1: Losses dataset compression with QSGS framework. On all three benchmarks, our method achieves full set performance with using only 0.5% of the data. The data keep ratio of ours is 90% less than the SOTA method (Xia et al., 2024).
Figure 5: Analysis on Llama-2-7B / MMLU at the 0.5% budget. (a) Computational cost breakdown of each pipeline stage. (b) Representative synthetic examples generated for under-covered subtasks.

papers.abstract: In mixed-vendor accelerator fleets, many training jobs can run on several hardware types, and the best choice depends on each job's throughput on each type. Routing a job needs a throughput estimate for every candidate type before the job runs. We present LEAP, a machine learning performance prediction service that predicts each training job's throughput on every candidate hardware type at submission time and ranks the candidates by predicted throughput per unit cost. It routes tens of thousands of training job attempts a day across hundreds of different model types and more than 20 hardware types in a production fleet. LEAP predicts throughput from submission-time training configuration, including each job's prior throughput. LEAP reaches an accuracy of 77% over 30 nightly retrains, higher than the lookup table it replaced and at least as high as every alternative model we tested, including fine-tuned language models. Over six months, the share of eligible training GPU-hours that received a ranking by LEAP grew from 58% to 95%, and we estimate that it saves about 3% of training computational cost. In this paper, we identify the drivers that actually move accuracy and those that do not. We offer these as lessons for teams building performance predictors at fleet scale.
authors: Hossein Askari, Wei Sun, Chenguang Zhu, Bin Zan, Sreen Tallam, Keyu Man
bullets: Addresses hardware-selection decisions in mixed-vendor fleets where job throughput varies by accelerator type.
Uses submission-time training configuration, including a job’s prior throughput, to predict performance on each candidate type.
Ranks hardware by predicted throughput per unit cost and routes tens of thousands of daily job attempts across 20+ hardware types.
Achieves 77% accuracy over 30 nightly retrains and replaces a lookup table while matching or exceeding tested alternatives.
Coverage rose from 58% to 95% of eligible training GPU-hours, with an estimated 3% reduction in computational cost.

figures.caption: Figure 2 LEAP architecture. Serving: (1) jobs are submitted to the job launcher, which (2) calls the inference API with the job and its candidate hardware types. (3) Inference builds the job’s features with the same code as training, taking its prior throughput from the history snapshot, scores every candidate with the bin classifier and that bin’s gradient-boosted model, and ranks candidates by predicted throughput per unit cost. (4) The preference list goes to the cluster scheduler, which (5) places the job on the fleet. Training: (6) each completed job attempt records its measured throughput in the job history; (7) a nightly trigger retrains the 13-bin cascade on the last 30 days and evaluates it on the next, unseen day; (8) the run publishes a versioned model and history snapshot to blob storage; and (9) inference loads the latest version through a stable pointer.

Figure 3 LEAP end to end. (1) A fungible job arrives with several candidate hardware types. (2) LEAP builds features from the job’s configuration, its prior throughput, and each type’s specifications; bars give each feature group’s share of importance. (3) A 13-bin cascade of gradient-boosted models, retrained nightly, predicts the job’s throughput on every candidate. (4) The ranking stage orders the candidates for the cluster scheduler. The job’s measured throughput becomes training data for the next night’s models.

Figure 6 The prediction model. For each candidate hardware type, the job’s feature row x goes to the bin classifier, a gradient-boosted classifier that outputs a probability for each of 13 throughput bins. The selector passes x to the expert of the most likely bin, k̂ = argmaxk gk(x), a gradient-boosted regressor trained under the pinball loss, which predicts log throughput. Exponentiating gives the prediction (Equation 4). Experts are ordered from the lowest to the highest throughput range.

Figure 7 Hardware type ranked first by LEAP, as a share of launches, for ten model types over one week. Each launch makes one routing call; only calls that returned a non-empty ranking are counted. A row with a single color would indicate that one hardware type is always preferred for that model type.

Figure 8 w20 of 30 consecutive nightly retrains. Each model is trained on the previous month and scored on the following day’s partition. The median is 77.0%, and individual nights range from 73.5% to 80.6%.

papers.abstract: In speculative decoding, parallel drafters such as DFlash make drafting cheap, so target verification dominates each round. A central choice is the verification length, the number of tokens that the target processes in each round. Verifying more draft tokens can accept more of them, but work after the first rejection is wasted. For hybrid target models that combine Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers, verification time grows much faster with this length than for dense models. In a single-request profile of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with DFlash, it grew by 71% from length 4 to 16, almost entirely in GDN and MoE layers, compared with 4%-6% for a dense Qwen3-4B target. Each GDN layer must update a recurrent state at every token and recover it at the end of the accepted prefix. The MoE cost depends on the experts that the tokens activate, which are known only once verification runs. We present HybridSpec, which selects the verification length on the GPU from draft-side acceptance estimates and measured target latency. Verification then runs this length plus one extra token up to the first MoE router, before any expert runs. There, a lightweight routing correction uses the observed expert assignments to decide whether to keep that token. The rest of verification runs only on the selected tokens. Block-parallel GDN kernels avoid storing a state after every token and reconstruct the accepted state of every GDN layer in one launch. In isolated benchmarks at verification lengths 4 to 16 with every draft token accepted, these kernels, including accepted-state reconstruction, are $1.54\times$-$4.04\times$ faster than the default kernels. With three GDN-MoE target models in single-request greedy decoding, HybridSpec is $1.75\times$-$1.88\times$ faster than autoregressive decoding and $1.30\times$-$1.33\times$ faster than DFlash.
authors: Haiyu Wang, Sai Qian Zhang, Zechun Liu, Steven Li
bullets: Verification cost rises sharply with length in hybrid GDN-MoE targets because GDN state updates and MoE expert execution dominate.
The GPU selects verification length using draft acceptance estimates and measured target latency.
A routing correction uses early MoE expert assignments to determine whether to retain the first uncertain token.
Block-parallel GDN kernels reconstruct accepted recurrent states efficiently without storing every intermediate state.
Across three models, HybridSpec achieves 1.75×–1.88× speedup over autoregressive decoding and 1.30×–1.33× over DFlash in single-request greedy decoding.

papers.abstract: Effective world modeling requires compressing salient history information that facilitates future prediction. However, most existing approaches inherit tokenization and conditioning mechanisms from video generation, where objectives are centered around perceptual realism rather than predictive utility. This discrepancy limits the world model's effectiveness, especially in environments dominated by visual nuisances or task-irrelevant background details. To this end, we introduce Compression Forcing (CF), a general framework that aligns history compression with the predictive objective of world modeling. Compression Forcing features Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT), a novel tokenization method that compresses history observations into a sequence ordered by decreasing dynamics saliency. Built on a diffusion backbone, this structure enables Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H), allowing selective amplification of dynamics-salient information during inference. Extensive experiments across various environments demonstrate improved prediction fidelity, physical realism, and downstream decision-making performance, establishing Compression Forcing as a highly flexible and effective approach for world modeling.
authors: Siqiao Huang, Partha Kaushik, Michael Chen, Hengkai Pan, Kaiwen Geng, Omar Chehab, Fernando Moreno-Pino, Max Simchowitz
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between video-generation tokenization and world-modeling objectives, particularly under visual nuisances.
Introduces Dynamics-Aware Tokenization, which orders compressed history tokens by decreasing dynamics saliency.
Uses Hierarchical History Guidance with a diffusion backbone to selectively amplify salient information during inference.
Experiments across varied environments report better prediction fidelity, physical realism, and downstream decision-making.
Scope: designed for environments where task-irrelevant visual details can hinder predictive modeling.

papers.abstract: Long-context inference is bound by the KV cache, which 2-bit codes could shrink about sixfold if their error stays in check. The usual remedy rotates keys before quantizing, assuming rotation always helps. However, we observe that it does not: rotation flattens a spiky piece of a key but can give a flat one a new peak, and both coexist within one key. We therefore propose FlagRot, which stores each 32-channel piece rotated or as is, whichever has the smaller calibrated attention error, and rotates the query instead when reading. We further show that how often to decide follows the quantization axis: per-channel caches such as KIVI need one decision per head, at no write cost, while per-token caches decide per key, with the choice stored in existing sign bits. At 2.5 bits per value, FlagRot lowers the twelve-model KL divergence of KIVI from 18.7 to 12.4 x 10^-3, below RotateKV on 9 of 12 models. Served as a vLLM plugin, it raises RULER at 128k tokens by +2.9 points and the LongBench v1 mean by +0.4 to +1.9 points on the three of four models where 2-bit KIVI loses accuracy. It also lowers the error of 4-bit integer and FP4 caches.
authors: Kunming Shao, Xijie Huang, Jierun Chen, Jiaqi Shao, Yanli Wang, Jiangnan Yu, Qiwei Li, Wei Zhang, Kwang-Ting Cheng, Chi Ying Tsui
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory bottlenecks by making 2-bit quantization more reliable.
For each 32-channel key piece, chooses between rotation and no rotation using calibrated attention error.
Rotates queries at read time to match each stored key representation.
Decision frequency follows the cache axis: per head for per-channel caches and per key for per-token caches, using existing sign bits for storage.
At 2.5 bits per value, reduces KIVI’s twelve-model KL divergence from 18.7 to 12.4 × 10⁻³ and improves long-context benchmark scores in affected models.

papers.abstract: Fast Dominance Estimation Clustering (FastDEC) is an efficient variant of Density Peak Clustering (DPC) that achieves high clustering quality through dominance-based density estimation, but remains constrained by the computational cost of exact k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) construction and dominance component (DC) processing. We present SymWarp-FastDEC, a GPU-accelerated implementation of FastDEC. At its core is SymTrikNN, an exact self-k-NN kernel that exploits search symmetry using upper-triangular traversal and warp-cooperative top-k selection. We also introduce WP-DC, a warp-parallel DC reduction algorithm designed for modern GPUs. Combined with memory-adaptive execution planning and stream scheduling, WP-DC eliminates DC reduction as a runtime bottleneck. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that SymWarp-FastDEC produces clustering outputs identical to the original FastDEC on all evaluated equivalence benchmarks. Compared with a FastDEC variant using FAISS GpuIndexFlatL2 for exact k-NN search, our approach achieves approximately 1.7x to 4.9x higher end-to-end performance, with the advantage generally increasing with dimensionality. Compared with the original single-threaded Python FastDEC implementation, speedups reach approximately 2.5 x 10^4 in a very high-dimensional case where its k-d-tree-based search degrades; this extreme result is not representative of typical acceleration.
authors: Mi Li, Eibe Frank, Bernhard Pfahringer
bullets: Targets the computational costs of exact k-nearest-neighbor construction and dominance-component processing in FastDEC.
Uses SymTrikNN, an exact self-k-NN GPU kernel based on search symmetry, upper-triangular traversal, and warp-cooperative top-k selection.
Introduces WP-DC, a warp-parallel reduction method that removes dominance-component processing as a runtime bottleneck.
Achieves about 1.7–4.9× higher performance than a FAISS GPU exact-k-NN variant, with gains generally increasing in higher dimensions.
Reports up to about 2.5 × 10^4 speedup over the original single-threaded Python implementation in a very high-dimensional case; this extreme result is not typical.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: The grid of point blocks used by the exact self-k-NN kernel. (a) Because the reference set and query set are identical, only the upper-triangular and diagonal tiles (j ≥ i) are computed. Each computed tile is reused, through a second (reverse) selection pass, for its transposed position rather than recomputed, reducing the number of GEMM calls by approximately one half. Diagonal tiles (i = j) require updates only once. (b)Detail of a computed tile. A single GEMM computes the−2QR⊤ term for the entire tile, which is combined with precomputed squared norms to form the distance tile. The resulting distances are then processed by two independent warp-cooperative kernels that update the top-k heaps of both the query block and the reference block from the same computation.

papers.title: Accelerating FastDEC Clustering Algorithm with GPUs
papers.tldr: SymWarp-FastDEC accelerates FastDEC clustering on GPUs while preserving identical outputs and delivering substantial end-to-end speedups.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adapters (LoRA) let one base model serve many fine-tuned variants: multi-tenant engines keep a single copy of the base and batch the requests of many tenants, each with its own adapter. As base models move to 8-bit (FP8) and 4-bit formats, their general matrix multiplications (GEMMs) become cheaper, but the adapters do not: engines run them as separate small GPU kernels beside the GEMM, whose latency takes a growing share of every decoding step. An adapter projects its input down to a low rank and back up, and our key observation is that the GEMM needs the down-projection only in its epilogue, the final stage in which it writes its output. EpiLoRA, a plugin for the vLLM engine, therefore launches the down-projection first and the low-precision GEMM as a dependent kernel that streams its weights meanwhile and adds every tenant's up-projection in its epilogue. On NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, EpiLoRA decodes for a single adapter with up to 24% lower time per token than vLLM's fastest configuration, and faster than SGLang and TensorRT-LLM; with many tenants, its adapter kernels deliver more throughput than vLLM's on most GPU-model pairs we tested. The same low-precision base also trains: a LoRA reinforcement-learning trainer that computes on the engine's FP8 weights needs no 16-bit copy, so a 27B model trains on one 48 GB GPU, and an engine that then keeps activations in 16 bits removes most of the remaining mismatch between the model generating training data and the one trained.
bullets: Targets the growing latency cost of running LoRA adapters as separate kernels alongside FP8 or 4-bit base-model GEMMs.
Launches each adapter’s down-projection first, then fuses the up-projection into the dependent GEMM’s epilogue.
Implemented as a vLLM plugin for serving multiple tenants and adapters.
On NVIDIA Hopper, reduces single-adapter decoding time per token by up to 24% versus vLLM’s fastest configuration and outperforms SGLang and TensorRT-LLM in the reported comparison.
An FP8-based LoRA RL trainer avoids a 16-bit model copy, allowing a 27B model to train on one 48 GB GPU; results are reported primarily for tested GPU-model pairs.

papers.title: EpiLoRA: Fusing Many LoRA Adapters into Low-Precision GEMMs for Serving and RL

papers.abstract: Reasoning substantially improves language models' ability to solve difficult problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved. We investigate whether open-weight models can generate less verbose reasoning by changing the form of their own earlier thoughts, without retraining. Our intervention rewrites prior reasoning into compact state records before pending tool results are revealed, then compares continuations from original and compact histories. Across the tested models, accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning; a coding case study also shows less repeated verification after a shared candidate solution. In software-agent deployments, compaction can reduce total spending, although task quality and rewrite-inclusive time depend on the target and compressor. These findings identify reasoning history as one way to reduce future reasoning-token use and motivate model-specific compaction policies evaluated for both efficiency and retained capability.
bullets: Long reasoning traces improve problem-solving but can be expensive due to repetition and low-value text.
The study compacts earlier reasoning before pending tool results are revealed, then compares generation from original versus rewritten histories without retraining.
Across tested models, accepted compact histories generally shortened subsequent reasoning; a coding case showed less repeated verification.
Software-agent deployments achieved lower total spending, but task quality and rewrite-inclusive time varied by target and compressor.
The results motivate model-specific compaction policies that balance efficiency with retained capability.

papers.title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost

papers.abstract: Simulation benchmarks are the standard way to compare robot policies, but each benchmark brings its own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention, and evaluation is slow: 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes with one simulator and one model on one GPU take 359.7 minutes. Profiling the official StarVLA evaluator shows that simulation occupies CPU cores while the GPU averages 14.3% utilization. RoboScope Kit wraps each model once in a Python class called a Policy, and each benchmark once in an adapter around the benchmark's own evaluator, so the benchmark's rules and scoring stay unchanged. Scheduling runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, sizes both from measured probes, and shards work deterministically across GPU instances; runtime optimization renders only the observations an action-chunk Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. On LIBERO-Long with a StarVLA checkpoint on one 48 GiB RTX 4090, the concurrency search selects twelve simulator workers sharing three Policy replicas, which evaluate 500 episodes 4.45$\times$ faster than the official StarVLA evaluation with equivalent success rates, 2.78$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 1.52$\times$ faster than vla-eval at its tuned configuration. With CUDA MPS, which lets the replicas run their kernels concurrently, the search selects sixteen workers sharing four replicas, 6.16$\times$ faster than StarVLA, 3.85$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 2.10$\times$ faster than vla-eval. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation complete the 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04$\times$ faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps.
authors: Deng-Ke Wu, Yifan Jin, Yida Yang, Lei Qian, Zhaoye Zhou, Hongru Zhang, Kai Ye, Shuyuan Hu, Yiran Mao, Zewei Ye, Bo Zhao
bullets: Addresses fragmented benchmark interfaces and low GPU utilization in slow simulation-based evaluation.
Wraps models as reusable Policy classes and benchmarks as adapters while preserving their original rules and scoring.
Separates simulator workers from Policy replicas, sizes them using probes, and deterministically shards work across GPUs.
Supports six benchmark families and renders only observations required at action-chunk boundaries when applicable.
Achieves up to 6.16× speedup on LIBERO-Long with CUDA MPS and 25.04× on RoboTwin Easy across four GPUs, with unchanged reported outcomes.

papers.title: RoboScope Kit: Unified Interfaces for Fast and Scalable Embodied-AI Evaluation
papers.tldr: RoboScope Kit standardizes embodied-AI evaluation and accelerates simulator-heavy benchmarks through unified adapters, parallel scheduling, and selective observation rendering.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.
authors: Serdarcan Dilbaz, Arjun Krishna, Kiran Kamble, Daniel M. Bikel
bullets: DSA’s full-cache indexer scan dominates decode time at long contexts, while adjacent layers choose nearly identical tokens.
MLI lets each layer attend to the preceding layer’s selection, allowing indexer computation to overlap with attention.
It requires no retraining or new weights; the default implementation runs in SGLang without kernel changes, with an optional fused kernel.
Combined with IndexCache, MLI improves decoding speed by up to 14.5% on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at equal retention.
Long-context accuracy on LongBench, RULER, and LongBench v2 remains within a few percentage points of IndexCache.

papers.selection_reason: Optimizes sparse attention and long-context LLM decode, directly fitting efficient attention and long-context model developments.
papers.title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) hides DeepSeek Sparse Attention’s expensive indexer scans by reusing the previous layer’s token selection, delivering faster long-context decoding without retraining.

papers.abstract: Language models are typically trained with a single choice of architecture on diverse domains and data sources. Modern transformers have been extensively refined for such general-purpose learning, but are they equally effective across different subsets of the pretraining data? We investigate this question by training small language models from scratch on representative subsets of pretraining data such as web text, code, and mathematics. We introduce variants of transformers in which standard activation functions are replaced with learned splines tuned on specific datasets, providing a simple way to modify their inductive biases. Using a mix-and-match of architectures and datasets, we evaluate cross-domain transfer, i.e. how well does an architecture tuned for one domain perform on data from another? We find that the tuned transformer variants improve training efficiency or generalization on all seven of our tested datasets, but the gains are often domain-specific. For example, architectures tuned on a natural language dataset such as FineWeb perform well on TinyStories, whereas those tuned on mathematics perform poorly on natural language. We identify several mechanisms underlying these improvements, including wider loss basins and more abundant "lottery tickets". Our results show that different subsets of pretraining data can benefit from different learning mechanisms, highlighting a limitation of the prevailing trend towards a small set of general-purpose architectures and optimizers. This points to an opportunity to improve data efficiency by developing domain-specific learning strategies that retain the ability to train general-purpose models.
authors: Damien Teney, Liangze Jiang, Zachary Shinnick, Hemanth Saratchandran, Simon Lucey
bullets: The study tests small language models trained from scratch on web text, code, and mathematics.
It replaces standard transformer activations with learned splines tuned to specific datasets.
Cross-domain evaluations show that architectures tuned for natural language transfer better within language domains, while math-tuned variants perform poorly on natural language.
Improvements appear across all seven tested datasets, with mechanisms linked to wider loss basins and more abundant lottery tickets.
The findings suggest domain-specific learning strategies could improve data efficiency while supporting general-purpose models.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Validation performance of models trained on three datasets representative of natural language, code, and mathematics. Dots represent models trained with different seeds or nonlinearities (see legend on the left). Coloured outlines represent approximate distributions. With some exceptions, most panels show a good correlation, indicating a compatibility between language and code datasets. See the discussion in Section 4.1.

Figure 6: Generalist vs. specialist models on MATH (i.e. trained on all vs. individual question types). We observe larger improvements from learned nonlinearities in specialist models. This means that each type of math question can benefit from question-specific inductive biases. Note that we adjust the amount of training tokens such that the overall accuracy is similar between generalist and specialist baselines. See Figure 10 for a detailed view including the full set of labels on the Y axis.

This likely requires different inductive biases than standard subword tokenization because of longerrange interactions, different typical entropy in the predictions, etc. As a result, the architectures optimized for this dataset (SHAKESPEARE-CHAR, vertical axis) work badly on others (FINEWEB, ENWIK8) and vice versa.

We specialize a transformer variant for a source domain D1 (left) by replacing nonlinearities with parameterized splines, pre-trained in a warm-up phase. We then reuse these frozen components to train a model on a target dataset D2 (right). Only very few parameters are transferred.

Figure 2: Typical training curves during the warmup phase (on CSN-PYTHON here), where we optimize both the weights of transformers and their nonlinearities, initialized as constant functions (left). papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that domain-specific inductive biases (e.g., learned splines) improve LLM training efficiency and generalization, relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Language Models Can Benefit from Domain-Specific Inductive Biases
papers.tldr: Domain-specific transformer inductive biases can improve language-model training efficiency or generalization, but their benefits often do not transfer across domains.

papers.abstract: Deploying deep learning on microcontrollers (MCUs) requires fitting both the model weights and runtime activations within tens to hundreds of kilobytes of SRAM and Flash. Existing approaches either use an interpreter with a pre-written kernel library or combine a Python code generator with hand-written C kernels. This incurs dispatch overhead and requires framework dependencies. None produces self-contained, dependency-free C code specialized to a given model. In this paper, we present te-comp, the first complete MLIR-based compiler that takes a standard model in .tflite or .safetensors format and emits all C source files needed for deployment: the inference engine (kernels, weight arrays, memory layout) and the RTOS integration layer with zero runtime dependencies. On 10 MCUNet CNN benchmarks, te-comp outperforms MCUNet TinyEngine by using 38% less SRAM (up to 5.9$\times$) and 15% less Flash, while generating complete C code rather than linking a pre-written kernel library. To demonstrate, we use te-comp to compile an 8.3M-parameter GPT-Neo transformer (TinyStories-v2) and deploy it on a single-core Cortex-M7 at 160MHz. The full firmware uses 249KB of 512KB SRAM and 3.62MB of 4MB Flash and achieves approximately 1 token/s interactive text generation via Q4_0 weight quantization, a stateful int4 KV cache, and vocabulary pruning -- a capability no existing MCU inference framework supports.
bullets: Targets the tight SRAM and Flash limits of microcontrollers while avoiding interpreter dispatch and framework dependencies.
Compiles .tflite or .safetensors models into complete C sources, including kernels, weights, memory layout, and RTOS integration.
Uses MLIR-based specialization to generate model-specific inference code without linking a pre-written kernel library.
On 10 MCUNet CNN benchmarks, it uses 38% less SRAM and 15% less Flash than MCUNet TinyEngine.
Demonstrates 1-token/s interactive GPT-Neo generation on a Cortex-M7 using quantization, an int4 KV cache, and vocabulary pruning.

papers.abstract: Two-tier LLM serving escalates selected requests from a small model to a large one, but prompt-based routers cannot see whether retrieved evidence supports an answer, and they treat the GPU cost of an escalation as constant. We study TRIAGE, which conditions escalation on a post-generation reliability state and on a load-dependent GPU price, and we report both what held and what did not on one A40 serving Qwen2.5-7B and 32B (AWQ) under VLLM. Escalation cost rose 21.9x from 1 to 10 requests/s but showed no monotone dependence on KV-cache headroom, and a pre-registered claim that the reliability state detects corrupted evidence (AUROC>=0.70) was falsified at 0.571, although any prompt-only router scores exactly 0.500 by construction. Post hoc, a semantic evidence judge raised detection to 0.846 (0.926 on never-served items) and predicted wrong small-model answers at AUROC 0.90-0.96 on RGB and three RouterBench model pairs; the resulting cascade stayed within about 3 pp of GPT-4 at 79.5% lower API cost for GPT-3.5->GPT-4, yet fell below random routing for open-model pairs with 2-3x price ratios. End to end, the 7B->32B pair showed only a +2.88 pp held-out gap, so the allocator rightly declined to escalate and the headline is a null that a small pre-launch gate failed to expose.
authors: Basavaraj R M, Aryan Bharat Kumar
bullets: Two-tier routers need to assess whether retrieved evidence supports an answer and account for load-dependent escalation cost.
TRIAGE conditions escalation on post-generation reliability and GPU price; a semantic evidence judge is evaluated as a post hoc enhancement.
On one A40 serving Qwen2.5-7B/32B, escalation cost increased 21.9× from 1 to 10 requests/s, without monotonic dependence on KV-cache headroom.
The pre-registered corrupted-evidence detector failed its AUROC≥0.70 target, reaching 0.571; the semantic judge later reached 0.846, or 0.926 on never-served items.

The GPT-3.5→GPT-4 cascade stayed about 3 percentage points from GPT-4 at 79.5% lower API cost, while open-model pairs could underperform random routing; the 7B→32B end-to-end gain was only 2.88 points.

papers.title: TRIAGE: Reliability- and Load-Conditioned Escalation for Two-Tier LLM Serving with a Semantic Evidence Judge
papers.tldr: TRIAGE shows that reliability- and load-aware escalation can reduce API cost, but a failed pre-launch reliability gate and weak open-model results limit its end-to-end benefit.

papers.abstract: We introduce ShamAN-Q, a sub-1-bit post-training quantization method that extends NanoQuant by replacing each its diagonal reconstruction geometry with a tractable dense curvature metric, using a general paradigm popularized by the Shampoo optimizer. For each linear weight, ShamAN-Q fits a Kronecker product to the empirical Fisher information matrix of a small calibration set by Kullback--Leibler minimization, forming a Mahalanobis reconstruction loss from the result. The continuous ADMM updates from NanoQuant become solutions to Sylvester equations, while its discrete projection and deployment format remain unchanged. Because the curvature is local to a given set of weights, ShamAN-Q re-measures the input curvature statistic for each layer immediately before layer factorization, periodically refreshing all statistics on the partially quantized model. ShamAN-Q also redistributes the uniform rank from NanoQuant across layers at the same total number of bits. On Qwen3-Base, ShamAN-Q lowers WikiText-2 perplexity at $\approx$1 bpw from 27.56 to 22.96 (0.6B), 19.21 to 16.72 (1.7B), and 14.29 to 13.80 (4B) while matching or improving zero-shot accuracy on the Eleuther LM Evaluation Harness. On 0.6B, ShamAN-Q at $\approx$0.8 bpw matches the published perplexity of NanoQuant at $\approx$1.0 bpw.
bullets: Extends NanoQuant with a Shampoo-inspired Kronecker-factored approximation of empirical Fisher curvature.
Uses KL-fitted curvature to define a Mahalanobis reconstruction loss; continuous ADMM updates solve Sylvester equations.
Refreshes layer-local input curvature during quantization and reallocates rank across layers without increasing total bits.
On Qwen3-Base near 1 bpw, reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 27.56 to 22.96 (0.6B), 19.21 to 16.72 (1.7B), and 14.29 to 13.80 (4B).
At about 0.8 bpw on the 0.6B model, matches NanoQuant’s published perplexity at about 1.0 bpw while matching or improving zero-shot accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 3: ShamAN-Q pipeline for one layer. Calibration fits and shrinks the curvature statistics, yielding the transported metric (A,G) and diagonal maps (D̃in, D̃out). Preconditioning maps W to W̃. Kron–LB–ADMM returns the continuous weight factors (U ,V) and scale vectors (s1, s2). The transported statistics alter only the continuous U/V optimization component; Euclidean consensus leaves SVID, dual updates, scale extraction, and sign extraction unchanged from NanoQuant.

Figure 2: ShamAN-Q end to end. Phase 1 runs the calibration set through the frozen teacher, fits and shrinks the curvature statistics (Aγ ,Gγ) of every linear layer, and allocates ranks at bit parity. Phase 2 processes decoder blocks in order. The factorized prefix and the untouched full-precision suffix are frozen while block b is tuned (TUNEFP), factorized layer by layer by Kron–LB–ADMM under the transported statistics (A,G) (Figure 3), and refined by latent STE. The statistics of the unfactorized layers are refreshed on the partially quantized model after every ∆ blocks. Phase 3 distills only the scale vectors against the teacher, with the sign matrices frozen. Flames mark trained parameters, snowflakes frozen ones, and blue blocks denote differences between ShamAN-Q and NanoQuant.

papers.selection_reason: Sub-1-bit post-training quantization of LLM weights reduces model memory footprint, fitting memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: ShamAN-Q: Shampoo Augmented NanoQuant for Sub-1-bit LLM Weights
papers.tldr: ShamAN-Q improves sub-1-bit post-training quantization by using locally fitted dense curvature to guide weight reconstruction, substantially reducing perplexity at similar bit rates.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) perform strongly in face recognition (FR), yet their fixed-depth inference limits deployment in resource-constrained settings. We propose SD-ViT, a training framework that gives a usable exit at every block depth by making every depth produce discriminative embeddings, for budget-selected fixed-depth exits. Standard ViTs supervise intermediate layers only through backpropagation, so their intermediate representations are not directly optimized to form usable identity embeddings. SD-ViT adds a stochastic auxiliary signal: at each iteration a randomly selected intermediate block is passed through the same embedding head as the final layer and trained with a weighted margin-penalty softmax loss. The objective is thus stochastically sampled deep supervision through a shared classifier. Because both loss terms share that head and classifier, intermediate tokens are trained to map into the same embedding space as final-layer tokens. This matters for FR, where matching is by similarity: a probe processed at an early exit can be compared directly against full-depth gallery embeddings, with no gallery recomputation or adaptation layers. On established benchmarks, SD-ViT stays within 0.4 IJB-C points of the same backbone trained conventionally at full depth, while its early-exit probes recover over 96% of their own full-depth performance at 50% of the computational cost without modifying the reference gallery. A single verification threshold calibrated at full depth remains usable from quarter depth onward.
bullets: Fixed-depth ViTs are inefficient for resource-constrained face-recognition deployment because intermediate layers lack directly optimized identity embeddings.
At each iteration, a randomly selected intermediate block is trained through the final embedding head and shared classifier with a weighted margin-penalty softmax loss.
Shared supervision aligns early-exit and final-layer embeddings, allowing early probes to match unchanged full-depth gallery embeddings without adaptation layers or gallery recomputation.

On established benchmarks, the method remains within 0.4 IJB-C points of conventional full-depth training; at half the computational cost, early exits retain over 96% of their own full-depth performance.
A single threshold calibrated at full depth remains usable from quarter depth onward.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of SD-ViT. A face image is tokenized and processed by L blocks. The full-depth tokens z(L) form the primary exit. At each iteration a secondary exit is read out at a uniformly sampled block z(k), k ∼ U{1, . . . , L−1}. Both are decoded by the same head H and scored against the same prototypes W under a margin-penalty loss, combined with weight ω (Eq. 4). Sharing H and W across depths places all embeddings in one space, so at inference a probe may exit at any depth k (Eq. 5) and match a gallery enrolled once at full depth.

Figure 2. Per-exit accuracy under both protocols. Top (a-c): self-evaluation, with probe and gallery embedded at the same exit, for three configurations. Color denotes the configuration and line style the method (see the legend panel). Baseline early exits collapse while SD-ViT degrades far less, on every backbone and both training sets. Bottom (e-g): the gallery-fixed protocol of Sec. 4.4, an exit-k probe against a gallery enrolled once at the final block, for ViT-S/12. Here the Baseline is near zero on the harder benchmarks below half depth, and Feature-MSE lies between it and SD-ViT. (b) Loss: comparable early-exit accuracy under AdaFace and ArcFace. (c) Depth: the gains hold at L=15. (d) Where to supervise: sampling degrades smoothly toward exit 1, while fixed exits collapse below the chosen depths. (e) Auxiliary objective: teacher KD and feature-MSE raise early exits above the baseline yet collapse at shallow depths, while SD-ViT stays far above them at early exits.

One threshold, calibrated once at full depth, held fixed across exits (ViT-S/12, WF4M, gallery-fixed protocol). τ is chosen on a development half of the pairs so that the full-depth FAR equals the target. All rows then apply that same τ on the held-out half, so the full-depth FAR deviates from the target only through the split. per-exit τ re-calibrates τ on each exit’s own development scores and is an upper bound that a deployed system cannot use.

Blocks (i) and (ii) are strict controls: one run from scratch with the backbone, data, schedule and seed of SD-ViT, changing only the marked component. Block (iii) needs a full-depth model trained beforehand, and its GPU-h count only the second stage. shared: the final exit’s. separate: one extra set shared by all intermediate exits. per-exit: one per depth. frozen: fixed at the prior full-depth solution. none: the auxiliary exit is trained by feature-MSE onto the model’s own final embedding and sees no prototypes. #s: intermediate exits supervised per step. self : each exit against itself. gf : gallery-fixed (Sec. 4.4).

Reading its intermediate blocks through the shared head is the training-free ViT-FREE [12] protocol. ViT-FREEFT trains one projection and one prototype set per exit on that frozen Baseline. Truncated are ViTs of 3 and 6 blocks trained from scratch, i.e. dedicated single-budget networks, so each of their rows is that network’s only exit. ViTFREEFT was not designed for this protocol (Sec. 2).

papers.title: Stochastic Deep Supervision for Gallery-Consistent Early-Exit Face Recognition
papers.tldr: SD-ViT enables ViTs to perform gallery-consistent early-exit face recognition by stochastically supervising intermediate depths in a shared embedding space.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models produce large KV caches during multi-round video generation. Keeping all these KV chunks would consume substantial memory, while rebuilding discarded caches would significantly delay video chunk generation. This paper presents ReelCache, a KV cache compression system for efficient multi-round, long video generation. ReelCache combines an intra-chunk compressor with an inter-chunk cache manager. The compressor applies low-rank decomposition across channels and video coding to the resulting coefficients, predicting the decomposition rank per transformer layer online to meet retained-energy targets. The cache manager shares basis directions across consecutive chunks and organizes chunk states in a tree, allowing generation branches to share historical state while supporting restoration for resume, rewind, and fork. Experiments across five video generation models show that ReelCache reduces KV storage by 14.46-21.13x relative to baselines and accelerates next-chunk generation by 1.25-3.36x, with less than 1% drop in six representative VBench metrics. GitHub: https://github.com/Tianyu9748/ReelCache
bullets: Addresses the large memory cost and regeneration delay of KV caches in autoregressive video diffusion.
Combines online low-rank, video-coded intra-chunk compression with inter-chunk basis sharing and tree-based cache management.
Supports efficient cache restoration for resume, rewind, and fork generation branches.
Across five video generation models, reduces KV storage by 14.46–21.13× and accelerates next-chunk generation by 1.25–3.36×.
Reports less than a 1% drop in six representative VBench metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 9. Overview of ReelCache.
Figure 15. P50 and P90 next-chunk latency of ReelCache compared to baselines across models and workloads.

Figure 12. Chunk state tree in ReelCache. (a) Three operations for basis sharing in consecutive chunks: reuse, augment, and refit. (b) Session pointer and user operations: resume, rewind, and fork. shown in Figure 12(b). The multi-round video generation then becomes tree operations: resume continues from this node; rewind selects an ancestor; and fork starts a new branch whose first chunk is a child of any existing node and leaves the parent’s branch untouched. Existing nodes remain unchanged, allowing branches to share their common history without copying it. The detailed algorithm for determining if a node can share the basis of its parent node is in §H.

Bottom: the KV of the most recent chunks is kept in a rolling cache window (three chunks shown). Chunk i attends to the cached KV. papers.title: ReelCache: An Efficient KV Cache Compression and Management System for Multi-Round Video Generation
papers.tldr: ReelCache compresses and organizes KV caches to reduce memory use and speed up multi-round, long video generation with minimal quality loss.

papers.abstract: Most parameters of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model belong to its experts, and standard training keeps every expert gradient in GPU memory until the optimizer step. This memory grows with the number and size of the experts, so it rises as MoE models scale. We introduce Sonar-MoE, which updates each expert tensor during the backward pass and frees its gradient right away. It brings optimizer-in-backward from dense models to batched MoE expert tensors, so the GPU never holds more than one layer of expert gradients. When we fine-tune OLMoE-1B-7B and Granite-3.1-3B-A800M in bf16 with two expert-kernel backends, Sonar-MoE lowers peak memory by 19% to 22%. Its updates are bitwise identical to standard training without expert gradient clipping, and held-out loss stays within 0.003 of all baselines. Each step also takes 17% to 23% less time than standard training with global-norm clipping. Updating whole batched tensors rather than individual experts is what keeps Sonar-MoE fast, as it avoids a 20% to 72% slowdown while using the same memory. Sonar-MoE matches optimizer-in-backward over all parameters in memory and speed while still clipping the dense parameters.
bullets: Addresses GPU memory growth caused by retaining gradients for all MoE experts until the optimizer step.
Updates batched expert tensors in backward, limiting retained expert gradients to one layer at a time.
Reduces peak memory by 19–22% and step time by 17–23% in the reported bf16 fine-tuning experiments.
Preserves bitwise-identical updates without expert gradient clipping, while held-out loss remains within 0.003 of baselines.
Whole-batched-tensor updates avoid the slowdown associated with updating experts individually; dense parameters can still use gradient clipping.

papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient MoE training method directly relevant to LLM architectures and efficient AI.
papers.title: Sonar-MoE: In-Backward Expert Updates for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Training

papers.abstract: Timely and accurate crop health diagnosis is essential for sustainable agricultural production, yet accurate diagnosis often requires expert knowledge that is not readily available. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, and natural-language interaction, creating new opportunities for intelligent crop health assessment. However, deploying VLMs on resource-constrained devices remains challenging due to their substantial computational and memory requirements. This paper presents PlantVLM-Edge, a quantized vision-language framework for conversational crop health diagnosis that can run entirely on resource-constrained edge devices. PlantVLM-Edge combines agricultural domain adaptation, post-training quantization, and on-device serving with an offline chat interface, allowing growers to ask open-ended questions and receive diagnoses, symptom explanations, and management guidance without cloud connectivity. The framework is backbone-agnostic: we validate it with two different VLM types with varying scale and architecture (Qwen3-VL-2B and LLaVA-1.5-7B), four quantization schemes, and two diagnostic domains (plant diseases and insect pests), and we deploy all variants on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Eight-bit quantization affects answer quality minimally relative to the full-precision model, and 4-bit activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) retains 98.6% of full-precision answer quality on both domains while reducing the weight memory of the 2B backbone by 49%. In its most compact form, PlantVLM-Edge requires 2.01 GiB of weight memory, returns its first token in about 0.12 s, and completes a 64-token diagnostic response in 0.78 s. These results demonstrate that timely and accurate crop health diagnosis is practical on edge devices, providing a foundation for next-generation crop monitoring and decision support systems.
bullets: Addresses the need for expert-quality plant disease and insect pest diagnosis without cloud connectivity.
Combines agricultural domain adaptation, post-training quantization, and offline on-device serving with chat-based interaction.
Evaluated two VLM backbones, four quantization schemes, and two diagnostic domains on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin.
Eight-bit quantization has minimal impact on answer quality; 4-bit AWQ retains 98.6% of full-precision quality while reducing 2B model weight memory by 49%.
The compact configuration uses 2.01 GiB of weight memory, produces its first token in about 0.12 seconds, and completes 64-token responses in 0.78 seconds.

papers.abstract: Computer programmers chain together the same reusable computational primitives, for example, conditional statements or loops, but in different orders to implement different algorithms. In contrast, existing language model architectures always execute their layers in the same order. We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically orders its layers during inference to solve the problem at hand. LoL has a single hyperparameter, the size of its global library of transformer blocks, that allows it to transition seamlessly between parameter reuse and sparsity, generalizing the parameter-efficiency and FLOPs-efficiency tradeoffs of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts architectures in one unified family. We show that LoL achieves competitive performance with all three above baselines when pretrained on text data. On synthetic sudoku and maze data, we observe that the model employs distinct layer orderings to implement different solution strategies, and we can intervene on routing to force a model to apply a specific solution strategy to a problem instance. In a multilingual natural language setting, we find that LoL chooses different layer order patterns based on language and script. Similarly, we train LoL on safety data and fit probes to its router outputs, finding that these probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC. LoL provides a path toward a future in which models dynamically compose their own computational graph, enabling more efficient and controllable reasoning.
bullets: Addresses the fixed layer ordering used by standard language models.
Uses a global library of transformer blocks whose runtime routing determines layer order.
A single library-size hyperparameter spans parameter reuse and sparsity, unifying efficiency tradeoffs across dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture-of-experts models.
Matches the performance of these baselines on text pretraining and exhibits distinct routing patterns for sudoku, mazes, languages, and scripts.
Routing can be intervened on to force solution strategies, while router probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC.

Figure 2: Library of Layers uses strided window attention and a top-1 router to allow for efficient training. LoL is made up of a prelude, a routed core, and a coda. The layers in the prelude and coda can attend over the whole sequence. In the core, the sequence is split into windows of W tokens, and at every routed depth a router selects one layer from the shared library per window (topleft). Attention is restricted to each window, but the window boundaries shift by S tokens between successive routed depths, allowing information to flow across windows (Strided Window Attention, top-right). Window 0 has no history, so its router uses the first token and a learned vector e(ℓ) for routed depth ℓ (bottom-left). For window i > 0, the router averages the mean hidden states of earlier windows 0, . . . , i − 1 and selects one layer (bottom-right). With W = 4 and S = 2, Layers 1 and 3 share the same boundaries while Layer 2 is offset, so information can pass between neighboring windows. Token 5 is highlighted in red to show this: in Layer 1 it is the first token in a new window, while in Layer 2 its window includes tokens 3 and 4.

papers.abstract: LLM agents for GPU kernel optimization sit at two ends of a structure-freedom tradeoff. Scripted agents fix what the model does at each step, via a learned policy, an optimization menu, or fixed roles, and are sample-efficient where the recipe applies and stall where it does not. Open-ended agents let a self-directed model mutate a population of kernels and pay for the freedom in trials: thousands of evaluations, repeated edits, and wrong candidates. Both respond to hard targets by equipping the agent with more: parsed profiler output, disassembly analysis, retrieval over documentation and libraries, and stores of lessons. We argue that both lack direction, a hypothesis about where the remaining gap is, and that a short question asked at the right moment supplies it without narrowing what the agent may do next. We present KernelSeek, a question-driven agent that makes an existing CUDA kernel faster with no operator-specific knowledge and no faster implementation to imitate: a general-purpose coding agent, a minimal harness that enforces a verifiable goal, and questions at decision points, first from a human, then from a bank the agent applies to itself. On the same task, evaluator, hardware, and week, a tool-rich autonomous agent built in the prevailing style plateaued at 0.50x FlashAttention-3 after 133 model-driven steps; KernelSeek reached 1.13x. It then produced dependency-free FlashAttention forward kernels for Hopper and Blackwell, single CUDA files with no CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, or cuDNN, correct on all 182 scenarios per architecture and 1.16x FlashAttention-3 and 1.46x FlashAttention-4 (geometric mean). Across 162 human messages and 11.5K agent tool calls, every large gain followed a question that moved the agent to a different layer of the system or rejected a claimed limit, never one that supplied information. We release the kernels, harness, question bank, and all traces.
bullets: Open-ended kernel-optimization agents can waste many evaluations, while scripted agents may stall outside their prescribed recipes.
KernelSeek combines a general-purpose coding agent with a minimal verifiable harness and questions from humans or a self-applied question bank.
On the reported task, a prevailing tool-rich agent plateaued at 0.50× FlashAttention-3, whereas KernelSeek reached 1.13×.
It produced dependency-free CUDA FlashAttention forward kernels for Hopper and Blackwell, correct across all reported scenarios.
The study reports that every large gain followed a question prompting a new system layer or challenging an assumed limitation, rather than providing information.

papers.abstract: Matrix multiplication dominates both PHY signal processing and Deep Neural Network (DNN) inference, yet these domains place opposing demands on the matrix engine. Signal processing requires low-latency execution of relatively small matrix operations, whereas DNN inference, particularly at large batch sizes, prioritizes high throughput and energy efficiency for large matrix multiplications. While offering efficient memory access profile, a Systolic Array (SA) adds fill and drain delays per matrix. Those can be amortized for large matrices but not for small matrices. Conversely, a tensor unit completes the kernel in few cycles but would require repeated reads of same operand tiles over large matrices. This makes SA too slow for signal processing and tensor too inefficient for AI. We show that this need not be a choice between systolic and tensor structuring of Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) units. We propose a single engine that operates primarily as a SA and, through low-cost reconfiguration, transforms into a tensor-style engine on a per-operation basis. MUXes create both the spatial reduction adder tree and temporal reduction accumulators from the existing MACs and registers within the systolic array. The proposed reconfigurable SA simulated using modified SCALESim simulator, verified on an Zynq 702 FPGA and synthesized using ASAP 7nm FinFET library. SCALE-Sim simulations shows up to 7.5x lower latency for small complex value PHY kernels. Even on DNN workloads, it achieves up to 1.65x speedups over vanilla SA execution with trivial increase of memory accesses, retaining the systolic array's memory access advantage. Synthesis results estimate reconfigurable fabric costs only 8% power and 13.6% area overheads.
bullets: Signal processing favors low latency for small matrices, while DNN inference favors throughput and energy efficiency for large matrices.
The design reconfigures a systolic array into a tensor-style engine on a per-operation basis using MUXes, existing MACs, and registers.
Simulations report up to 7.5× lower latency for small complex-valued PHY kernels and up to 1.65× speedup on DNN workloads versus a vanilla systolic array.
The design preserves the systolic array’s memory-access advantages with only an estimated 8% power and 13.6% area overhead.
The engine was evaluated through simulation, FPGA verification on Zynq 702, and synthesis using a 7nm FinFET library.

papers.abstract: Attention remains a substantial computational cost in Transformer training, particularly at long context lengths. NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs provide high-throughput low-precision matrix multiplication, but exploiting it in attention requires addressing quantization overhead, causal information leakage through shared scales, and numerical inconsistencies between the forward and backward passes. We present FLAMIA, a family of attention kernels for Blackwell with MXFP8 and mixed NVFP4/FP8 training paths. Our design combines token-block scaling that reuses quantized operands across matrix orientations, targeted safeguards against scale-induced leakage, and consistent forward and backward computations. Fused quantization and architecture-specific kernel optimizations reduce overhead, while document-local scaling and workload-aware scheduling support variable-length documents directly in packed layouts without repacking. Across various causal packed-document workloads, the MXFP8 path accelerates the combined forward and backward attention call, including quantization, by factors of $1.10$--$1.40\times$ on B200 and $1.06$--$1.42\times$ on B300 relative to the fastest evaluated baseline for each workload. We validate training stability and quality preservation on pretraining Llama-style models. These results show how jointly designing quantization, training numerics, and document scheduling translates low-bit hardware throughput into practical attention acceleration.
bullets: Targets attention’s high computational cost at long context lengths on Blackwell GPUs.
Introduces MXFP8 and mixed NVFP4/FP8 attention kernels with reusable token-block scaling and leakage safeguards.
Maintains consistent forward and backward computations while fusing quantization and applying architecture-specific optimizations.
Supports variable-length causal documents in packed layouts through document-local scaling and workload-aware scheduling.
Achieves 1.10–1.40× speedups on B200 and 1.06–1.42× on B300 for the MXFP8 path, while preserving training stability and quality in Llama-style pretraining.

papers.abstract: Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs without per-LLM fitting, and no law names the factors that set it. From closed-form expressions of LLM inference's computational and memory-access complexity, we derive the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache and next-token computation cost. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from several families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1-3.5x below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration. SIMPLE explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and higher GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy linearly relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; accuracy rises but energy rises faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x range. Moving to agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0x, as both prefill and KV-cache terms grow with input length; prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%), but not KV-cache cost, so even a cached agentic request costs 4.8x more.
bullets: Derives energy scaling from inference computation and memory-access complexity, separating prefill from decode costs.
Evaluated on 13 dense LLMs across NVIDIA H100 traces, achieving R² = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE without per-LLM fitting.
Shows prefill energy grows quadratically with hidden dimension, while higher GQA grouping linearly lowers per-token energy versus MHA.
Longer reasoning budgets can exceed the energy-minimizing output length: accuracy improves, but energy rises faster and Intelligence per Joule declines.
Agentic serving greatly increases request energy; prefix caching removes most prefill cost but leaves substantial KV-cache cost.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient large language model (LLM) fine-tuning, and recent methods incorporate curvature-aware strategies. However, in the high-dimensional parameter space of LLMs, these methods inherently suffer from exploding gradient variance and prohibitive costs. Conversely, confining updates to a low-dimensional subspace reduces variance but discards critical high-dimensional information, degrading performance. This creates a fundamental dilemma: full-space optimization is informative but has high variance, while subspace optimization has low variance but loses information. To break this trade-off, we propose ENGINE (Endogenous Variational MultiScale). Inspired by computational mechanics, we adapt static Variational MultiScale (VMS) theory to dynamic optimization, treating low- and high-dimensional spaces as resolved coarse and unresolved fine scales. Through a multigrid-style V-cycle, ENGINE alternates between spaces, dynamically probing fine-grained information in the high-dimensional space and injecting it to correct the efficient low-dimensional sampling process. Under appropriate assumptions, statistical analysis characterizes variance reduction and correction of curvature-induced bias, and convergence analysis establishes a stationarity bound for the corrected coarse updates. Evaluations on standard LLM benchmarks show that ENGINE achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence than existing ZO methods, achieving up to a $2.61\times$ speed-up in forward passes with zero additional peak memory overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/ENGINE.
bullets: ZO fine-tuning is memory-efficient but faces high gradient variance in full parameter spaces and information loss in low-dimensional subspaces.
ENGINE applies dynamic Variational MultiScale optimization, treating low- and high-dimensional updates as coarse and fine scales.
A multigrid-style V-cycle alternates between spaces to inject fine-scale information into efficient coarse-space sampling.
Theoretical analysis addresses variance reduction, curvature-induced bias correction, and convergence to stationarity.
On standard LLM benchmarks, ENGINE improves accuracy and convergence, with up to 2.61× fewer forward passes and no additional peak memory overhead.
