papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient zeroth-order LLM fine-tuning with multiscale variance reduction and faster convergence.
papers.title: ENGINE: Endogenous Variational MultiScale Optimization for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: ENGINE combines low- and high-dimensional zeroth-order updates to reduce variance and improve the efficiency of LLM fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising approach for memory-efficient large language model (LLM) post-training, yet its reliability in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) under the mismatched-data regime produces a $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification that sets an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale $μ$ decreases, whereas Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT) under the matched-data regime eliminates this amplification via noise cancellation. We further derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants that cleanly separate the two regimes. These results motivate the ZO-BOLT algorithm, which builds on BOLT's matched-data advantage for reliable ZO optimization of an RLVR-aligned objective. Controlled perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched end-to-end comparisons validate the predicted effect of data matching. Experiments across three models and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks further show that ZO-BOLT consistently improves over the pretrained baseline while retaining a near-inference memory footprint. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianmin-chen/the_cost_of_mismatch.
bullets: Studies why zeroth-order gradient estimation is unreliable in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.
Shows that mismatched data causes $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification and an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale decreases.
Finds that matched-data evaluations, as in BOLT, cancel this amplification and yield cleaner convergence guarantees.
Introduces ZO-BOLT, which applies this matched-data principle to a ZO RLVR-aligned objective.
Experiments across three models and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks support the predicted effect and show gains over pretrained baselines with near-inference memory use.

papers.title: The Cost of Mismatch: Noise Amplification in Zeroth-Order Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Matching data across zeroth-order finite-difference evaluations avoids the noise amplification that limits on-policy RL, enabling more reliable and memory-efficient RLVR optimization.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) typically process large numbers of multimodal tokens from audio-visual inputs, incurring substantial computational costs and a large memory footprint for the key-value (KV) cache. Aggressive token pruning can alleviate this problem while maintaining competitive performance on multiple-choice tasks, which require only a single option as output. However, we observe substantial quality degradation when generating long-form, open-ended responses. We attribute this gap to query-guided selection, which can retain sufficient evidence for answer selection while discarding details needed for comprehensive generation. This motivates reducing overlapping information across tokens, termed structural redundancy, while preserving diverse content. However, the retained representations may still contain precision redundancy due to unnecessarily high numerical precision in their cached values. To address these two levels of redundancy in token representations, we introduce a training-free framework named R$^2$-Omni. First, Structure-Aware Token Consolidation (STC) consolidates redundant representations using spatiotemporal similarity in video and local continuity in audio. Then, Semantic-Sensitivity Guided Precision Allocation (SSPA) allocates value precision to the retained representations according to the estimated reduction in attention-output error under quantized keys, with query attention and audio-visual alignment providing a semantic prior. Extensive experiments on long-form generation benchmarks demonstrate an average 5.0$\times$ reduction in the memory footprint while preserving 97.98% of baseline generation quality and achieving a 1.48$\times$ end-to-end speedup, highlighting the benefits of jointly reducing structural and precision redundancy.
bullets: Targets quality degradation from aggressive token pruning in long-form, open-ended generation.
Uses Structure-Aware Token Consolidation to merge structurally redundant video and audio representations.
Uses Semantic-Sensitivity Guided Precision Allocation to assign lower or higher value precision based on estimated attention-output sensitivity.
Achieves a 5.0× average memory-footprint reduction, 97.98% of baseline generation quality, and a 1.48× end-to-end speedup.
The framework is training-free and evaluated on long-form generation benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Reduces structural and precision redundancy in omni-LLMs via token consolidation and KV-cache precision allocation.
papers.title: R$^2$-Omni: Reducing Structural and Precision Redundancy in Omni-LLMs for Long-Form Generation
papers.tldr: R²-Omni reduces redundant multimodal tokens and their numerical precision to make long-form Omni-LLM generation substantially more memory- and time-efficient while retaining most baseline quality.

papers.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is costly because attention repeatedly reads a growing key-value (KV) history. We introduce Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention (CISA), which retrofits pretrained dense attention models without gradient updates. CISA selects fixed-size KV chunks using compact summaries of existing keys, avoiding token-level indexing and a separate full-length index cache. It uses one indexing query per KV group and shares selected chunks across queries in that group. During prefill, QShare reuses selections across adjacent queries to reduce indexing cost and improve KV reuse and GPU utilization. We evaluate CISA on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano and Ultra, and Inkling-Small. In one-layer BF16 benchmarks at batch size 32 using Ultra's per-device attention dimensions, core attention is 11.7x faster for prefill queries near the end of a 1M-token prompt and 13.0x faster during decode. Including chunk scoring, selection, and all other measured GPU work, speedups are 8.6x and 3.0x. On Ultra NVFP4 with a 4,096-chunk budget, aggregate scores stay within 1.5 percentage points of dense attention on MRCR, LongBench v2, and GraphWalks. RULER sweeps on Nano and Ultra BF16 up to one million tokens show scores within 2.05 percentage points of dense attention with 8-16x fewer KV reads. Serving million-token prompts with 32 concurrent requests and 4K output tokens per request, CISA achieves 2.29x the end-to-end throughput of dense attention using Nemotron 3 Ultra NVFP4 on four NVIDIA B300 GPUs. Selecting fewer chunks increases throughput to 2.61x; in separate GraphWalks evaluations, the smaller budget widens the aggregate score gap from 1.49 to 3.59 percentage points. These results expose a practical quality-speed tradeoff without sparse training.
bullets: Targets the high cost of repeatedly reading growing KV histories during long-context inference.
Indexes fixed-size KV chunks using compact key summaries, with one query per KV group and shared selections across group queries.
QShare reuses chunk selections across adjacent prefill queries to reduce indexing overhead and improve KV reuse.
Reports up to 8–16× fewer KV reads, 2.29× end-to-end throughput, and quality within roughly 1.5–2.05 percentage points of dense attention in evaluated settings.
Using fewer chunks raises throughput to 2.61× but widens the GraphWalks quality gap to 3.59 percentage points.

papers.selection_reason: Chunk-indexed sparse attention retrofits dense models, reducing KV reads for long-context inference.
papers.title: CISA: Retrofitting Dense Attention Models with Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: CISA retrofits pretrained dense-attention LLMs with chunk-level sparse attention, achieving substantially faster million-token inference while keeping quality close to dense attention without retraining.

papers.abstract: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity. Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3. These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/DepthGraft.
bullets: Addresses information dilution in deep Pre-LN language models without adding substantial cross-layer computation or memory access.
Uses stride-aligned shallow–middle source pairs to reconstruct deep-layer keys and values.
KV-sharing edges provide non-local gradient paths that sharpen key retrieval directions and enrich value representations.
Evaluated on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters under GQA and MLA, with consistent downstream gains.
On a 16B MoE model, reports improvements of 7.0% on MMLU-Pro, 6.6% on CMMLU, and 6.4% on C3.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a hierarchical KV-sharing LLM architecture that reduces KV cache by a third while improving downstream performance, fitting both efficiency and LLM architecture interests.
papers.title: DepthGraft: Structural Regularization through Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction
papers.tldr: DepthGraft hierarchically reuses KV projections across layers to regularize deep representations, reduce KV-cache memory by roughly one third, and improve language-model performance.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential in robotic surgery for question answering, scene understanding, and grounded assistance, but their high computational cost limits real clinical deployment. Knowledge distillation provides a practical way to build compact surgical MLLMs, yet direct distillation is not well suited to surgical data because surgical samples vary greatly in difficulty, visual ambiguity, and required clinical context, making uniform teacher-student transfer unstable. In addition, the role of supervision changes during training: early stages require stronger teacher guidance for multimodal alignment, while later stages rely more on task supervision for effective optimization. To address these challenges, we propose SurgPace, a complexity-aware continuous curriculum framework for progressive distillation of surgical vision-language models. SurgPace estimates sample complexity using predictive confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency, and uses the fused score to guide a continuous easy-to-hard training process. We further introduce hierarchical representation alignment, which aligns the student with the teacher at the feature, logit, and probability levels, while gradually shifting the training focus from teacher imitation to task supervision. This design separates sample-level curriculum from objective-level scheduling, leading to more stable and effective distillation. We evaluate SurgPace on Surg-396K, a benchmark built from four public surgical datasets and covering five dialogue paradigms. SurgPace consistently outperforms strong MLLM distillation baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness for building compact, memory-efficient surgical MLLMs with faster decoding under controlled benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/hezhicheng2002/SurgPace.
bullets: Addresses unstable uniform distillation caused by varying surgical sample difficulty, ambiguity, and clinical context.
Uses predictive confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency to create a continuous easy-to-hard curriculum.
Aligns teacher and student at feature, logit, and probability levels while shifting from teacher imitation to task supervision.
Evaluated on Surg-396K across five dialogue paradigms, where it consistently outperforms strong distillation baselines.
Produces memory-efficient models with faster decoding under controlled benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed complexity-aware curriculum framework for progressive distillation. Teacher confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency are fused into a permissive complexity score, which guides continuous curriculum pacing from easy-first sampling to balanced training. This pacing is coupled with progressive objective interpolation and hierarchical representation alignment, jointly establishing a more structured optimization process that enables stable and efficient compression of surgical vision-language models.

Figure 1: Overview of the proposed SurgPace framework. Given surgical multimodal data, a teacher model first estimates sample complexity offline using complementary confidence and geometric consistency signals, which are permissively fused so that lower scores indicate easier samples. The resulting complexity estimates are then used to guide online curriculum training, where easier samples are emphasized earlier and harder samples are gradually incorporated as training progresses. During this process, the student model learns from the teacher through hierarchical representation alignment at the probability, logit, and feature levels, while a progressive objective schedule adjusts the balance of supervision over time. Together, these components enable stable and efficient compression of surgical MLLMs into a lightweight student model with reduced computational demands.

Figure 3: Qualitative visualization of a representative same-image case across five dialogue paradigms. For the same surgical scene, the figure compares ground truth, teacher, and student outputs for single-phrase QA, visual QA, region-based QA, grounding QA, and detailed description. The example shows that the student preserves the main clinical semantics and spatial relationships while remaining compact.

papers.abstract: Block-scaled lookup-table (LUT) formats, which represent weights as indices into a small value set (the grid), have become standard for low-bit LLM quantization, ranging from NF4 and BOF4 to the 3-bit LUT instruction in NVIDIA Rubin. While these formats leave the grid definition flexible, existing implementations rely on fixed grids derived either from numerical data types (INT, FP) or assumed weight distributions (NF, BOF). We demonstrate that no single fixed grid is universally optimal; the best fixed grid varies with bit-width: BOFS at 2 bits, NF at 4 and 5 bits, and INT at 6 bits. We introduce SHq, a closed-form family of grids parameterized by two critical degrees of freedom: a companding strength α that interpolates level spacing from uniform to floating-point-like, and an offset c that introduces asymmetry. This offset allows the sign bit of the FP8 block scale, otherwise unused, to select between the grid and its mirror image, up to doubling the number of distinct values available per block. SHq modifies only the lookup table contents and serves as a drop-in replacement for the grid in any such format. Across five models ranging from 3B to 35B parameters, including a mixture-of-experts architecture, evaluated at 2-6 bits using RTN and GPTQ, SHq achieves the lowest KL divergence in every setting at 3 and 4 bits and in most settings at 2, 5 and 6 bits. It outperforms the best fixed grid by up to 34% and remains superior under mixed-precision configurations. At 4.5 bits per weight, the SHq format reduces the KL divergence of NVFP4 by 41-67% while improving downstream accuracy. Grid families incorporating both spacing and offset parameters perform comparably, whereas those lacking an offset exhibit clearly higher error, confirming that these two degrees of freedom drive the observed gains. We therefore propose SHq as the standard grid for block-scaled lookup-table formats.
bullets: Fixed grids are not universally optimal: the best choice varies with bit-width.
SHq uses companding strength α and offset c to control spacing and asymmetry; the offset can exploit the FP8 scale sign to select mirrored grids.
It is a drop-in replacement for lookup-table grids in block-scaled formats and supports 2–6-bit quantization with RTN or GPTQ.
Across five 3B–35B models, SHq achieves the lowest KL divergence in all tested 3- and 4-bit settings and most other settings.
SHq improves KL divergence by up to 34% over the best fixed grid and reduces NVFP4 divergence by 41–67% at 4.5 bits while improving downstream accuracy.

papers.abstract: Fusing independently normalized attention heads can increase the number of explicit key-value entries, or atoms, needed to preserve their output. We prove a sharp separation for $W_d(q)=\sum_{j=1}^dσ(q_j)$: its $d$ two-atom heads use $2d$ head-atom terms, whereas its minimum single-head representation has exactly $2^d$ atoms, even with arbitrary fixed replacement keys, scalar values, and positive masses. The same lower bound holds for every fixed uniform error below $1/2$ on $\mathbb R^d$, and the threshold is sharp. The proof uses exposed-key normal cones; exact equality on any nonempty open query domain inherits the bound. The resulting atom bound for a fixed head count is tight when that count divides $d$. A normalized family retains its exponential exact minimum while approaching a constant on fixed-radius query balls. For pretrained-model caches, a classical affine-rank bound and a certified instance exclude exact vector preservation at a specified atom count. Learned-cache comparisons on two disjoint banks of 64 contexts show budget-dependent reversals and calibration effects.
bullets: A function formed by d two-atom heads uses 2d head-atom terms but needs exactly 2^d atoms in any equivalent single-head representation.
The 2^d lower bound holds for every fixed uniform error below 1/2 on all of R^d and for exact equality on any nonempty open query domain.
The proof uses exposed-key normal cones; the bound is tight for fixed head counts when the count divides d.
A normalized construction preserves the exponential exact minimum while approaching a constant on fixed-radius query balls.

Cache experiments on two disjoint 64-context banks show budget-dependent reversals and calibration effects; a classical affine-rank bound and certified instance rule out exact preservation at a specified atom count.

papers.abstract: Representation alignment (REPA) is widely used to accelerate the training of latent-space diffusion transformers (DiTs). However, applying it to pixel-space models such as Just Image Transformers (JiT) is challenging. Our analysis reveals a pronounced representation conflict between discriminative alignment and pixel-space generation. Compared with its latent counterpart, JiT learns representations that are substantially less aligned with DINOv2. Applying REPA to JiT consistently reduces the reconstructability of its intermediate representations, whereas this effect is not observed in Latent JiT. We attribute this conflict to JiT directly reconstructing pixels, which requires its representations to hierarchically encode discriminative semantics and reconstruction-relevant visual information across network depths. To address these challenges, we propose Routed Representation Alignment (RouteREPA), which uses lightweight, representation-dependent routers to adaptively route task-oriented representations for alignment and generation. We further apply routing across multiple network depths to accommodate their depth-dependent representation requirements. Extensive experiments on ImageNet-1K at 256x256 resolution show that RouteREPA consistently improves JiT across model scales and training budgets, outperforming standard REPA. On JiT-H/16, RouteREPA further surpasses PixelREPA using only one-third of its training epochs without classifier-free guidance.
bullets: REPA is difficult to apply to pixel-space JiT because discriminative alignment can harm intermediate representation reconstructability.
JiT representations must encode both hierarchical semantics and pixel-reconstruction information, unlike latent JiT representations.
RouteREPA uses lightweight, representation-dependent routers to direct task-specific features for alignment or generation.
Multi-depth routing accounts for different representation requirements across network layers.
On ImageNet-1K at 256×256, RouteREPA consistently improves JiT over standard REPA and surpasses PixelREPA on JiT-H/16 with one-third the training epochs, without classifier-free guidance.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by reducing the sequential cost of token-by-token generation. Advanced SD methods reduce proposal cost with parallel drafters that predict entire blocks in one forward pass, but overall speedup still depends on acceptance length. On-policy distillation (OPD) can push well-trained drafters beyond acceptance-length plateaus, yet conventional pipelines collect supervision through sequential draft-and-verify rollouts. Our key insight is that on-policy supervision need not inherit these dependencies: a draft block can be supervised using only its reference prefix and draft-sampled history. We propose SpecOPD, a branch-parallel OPD framework that parallelizes draft sampling and target supervision across independent branches drawn from the evolving drafter policy at reference anchors. We pack these branches into proposal trees to share target-prefix computation, using tree masks for full attention, branch-consistent indexer groups for sparse attention, and indexed state replay for linear attention to preserve each branch's history. We train the drafter with an E2E-TV surrogate that directly targets acceptance length. Our study spans 8B full-attention (GQA), 27B full-linear (GQA--GDN), and 125B sparse-linear (QSA--GDN) targets, three parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark, and DFlash V2), and four task domains (dialogue, coding, mathematics, and agentic). SpecOPD achieves up to 41.45% higher mean acceptance length, $16.09\times$ supervised-token throughput over sequential-rollout OPD under native configurations, and up to $3.56\times$ generation speedup over autoregressive decoding.
bullets: Addresses the sequential rollout bottleneck in conventional on-policy distillation for speculative decoding.
Samples independent draft branches from reference anchors and supervises them in parallel using draft-sampled histories.
Packs branches into proposal trees to share target-prefix computation while preserving branch-specific histories across attention types.
Uses an E2E-TV surrogate that directly optimizes acceptance length.

Across multiple target architectures, draft models, and domains, achieves up to 41.45% higher mean acceptance length, 16.09× higher supervised-token throughput, and 3.56× generation speedup over autoregressive decoding.

papers.abstract: Prompt compression is aimed at reducing input prompt lengths to enable cheaper, faster, and potentially higher-quality LLM predictions. However, existing prompt compression methods are often limited by modest compression gains, a risk of hallucination, and/or high compression latency. We propose EffComp, an Efficient prompt Compression framework for RAG-based question answering (QA). EffComp employs BERT-style document reranker and sentence selector models to allow fast extractive prompt compression at the sentence level. Its extractive nature prevents hallucinations in the compressed prompts. Additionally, the training process using a hybrid reinforcement and supervised learning approach is designed to optimize the compression ratio while preserving LLM accuracy. Experiments on various QA datasets demonstrate that EffComp outperforms state-of-the-art prompt compression methods achieving the best trade-off between compression ratio and accuracy with minimal latency. This makes it practical for real-world applications.
bullets: Targets costly, slow, and potentially unreliable prompt compression for RAG-based QA.
Uses BERT-style document reranking and sentence selection for efficient extractive compression.
Combines reinforcement and supervised learning to optimize compression while maintaining LLM accuracy.
Experiments across QA datasets show the best reported trade-off between compression ratio and accuracy with minimal latency.
Extractive compression limits hallucination risk and supports practical deployment.

papers.abstract: On-device multimodal agents are limited by two deployment mismatches: pretrained attention structures may not divide evenly across the compute cores of an edge accelerator, causing irregular partitions; and standard prefix caching keeps historical visual tokens in the persistent KV cache, whose capacity grows with the number of rounds. We present PARC, which combines parallelism-aligned structured pruning with lifetime-aware KV-cache reorganization. At the model level, it uses first-order Taylor importance and grouped-query-attention-aware selection to make attention dimensions divisible by the target core count while preserving the query-to-key/value ratio and head dimension. At runtime, it separates the system prompt, persistent text history, and transient visual observations by lifetime, updating text history during tool execution so that historical images leave the persistent cache and more interaction rounds fit a fixed budget. On 2,062 GUI actions, the incremental interface shows no accuracy regression, and task-aware recovery training restores 98.7% of the action-type accuracy gap and the coordinate hit rate to the original level. Under seven-core deployment, hardware-aligned pruning reduces vision-encoder latency by 11.4%, improves decoding throughput by 23.8%, and lowers per-heap high-water memory by 12.7%; a parameter-matched control confirms that the speedup stems mainly from core alignment rather than parameter reduction.
bullets: Addresses uneven attention partitioning across edge-accelerator cores and cache growth from multi-round visual interactions.
Uses Taylor-based, grouped-query-attention-aware structured pruning while preserving key attention dimensions and target-core divisibility.
Reorganizes KV-cache contents by lifetime, updating text history during tool execution so past images do not remain persistent.
On 2,062 GUI actions, the incremental interface shows no accuracy regression; recovery training restores 98.7% of the action-type accuracy gap and coordinate hit rate to the original level.
With seven cores, pruning reduces vision-encoder latency by 11.4%, raises decoding throughput by 23.8%, and lowers per-heap memory high-water usage by 12.7%.

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is increasingly constrained by the cost of maintaining an ever-growing KV-cache. Low-rank K/V projections provide a promising way to compress the KV-cache with minimal quality loss, but prior work has largely optimized KV-cache compression in isolation, leaving distributed inference, especially with tensor parallelism where attention computation is partitioned across multiple GPUs, largely underexplored. We make two observations: (i) tensor-parallel communication is an important cost when deploying low-rank KV-cache compression in distributed inference; and (ii) Value compression can be associated with the output projection, allowing the same low-rank Value representation to reduce both Value-cache width and tensor-parallel communication. Based on these observations, we propose BasisKV, a low-rank KV-cache compression method for communication-intensive, long-context LLM inference. BasisKV jointly optimizes the low-rank factors across per-GPU attention partitions against the complete attention output, rather than fitting each partition in isolation. The compressed Value cache is further reused to help identify which Key pages should be accessed: it predicts part of the Key information needed for routing, while a Key-specific residual stores what cannot be recovered from Value. The original Keys are then retrieved only for the selected pages to compute exact QK scores. Across multiple LLM families and system settings, BasisKV achieves a better quality--efficiency tradeoff than existing low-rank baselines, reaching up to 1.42x end-to-end speedup under 8-GPU tensor-parallel inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/alexz949/BasisKV
bullets: Targets KV-cache growth and communication overhead in distributed, tensor-parallel inference.
Jointly optimizes low-rank factors across GPU attention partitions against the complete attention output.
Uses compressed Values to predict routing-relevant Key information, with a Key residual for unrecoverable details.
Retrieves original Keys only for selected pages to compute exact query–key scores.
Reports a better quality–efficiency tradeoff than low-rank baselines, with up to 1.42× end-to-end speedup in 8-GPU tensor-parallel inference.

papers.abstract: Learned sparse attention, used in production models such as DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5, lets each query attend to only k keys chosen by a lightweight indexer, but the indexer still scores every key in the prefix. At one million tokens, this selection takes more than half of prefill time. Two-stage selection over contiguous blocks, as in HiSA, reduces this cost, but its recall declines as context grows at a fixed candidate budget. We present AttentionIndex, which routes each query over an inverted-file index that groups indexer keys by similarity and refines the candidates with the native indexer score. AttentionIndex builds the index during prefill, making new keys searchable immediately, reusing previous clustering to keep maintenance cheap, and exposing each query only to clusters built from its own prefix. On GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at one million tokens, AttentionIndex delivers 1.3-1.8 times the prefill throughput of exhaustive selection, and at throughput within 5% of HiSA, it recovers 17.0 and 10.0 percentage points more of the exhaustive top-k, respectively. AttentionIndex also improves accuracy on long-context benchmarks by up to 18.4 percentage points over HiSA at the same candidate budget.
bullets: Exhaustively scoring every prefix key makes sparse-attention selection a major prefill bottleneck at long contexts.
It routes queries through a causal inverted-file index, then reranks retrieved candidates with the native indexer score.
The index is built online during prefill, immediately includes new keys, reuses prior clustering, and restricts queries to prefix-derived clusters.
On GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at one million tokens, it achieves 1.3–1.8× exhaustive-selection prefill throughput.
At similar throughput to HiSA, it recovers 17.0 and 10.0 more percentage points of exhaustive top-k recall and improves long-context accuracy by up to 18.4 points.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of AttentionIndex for one indexed layer. Update path: new keys enter an open window and are searchable at once; every W keys the window is sealed into local clusters, and every R tokens a refit regroups the prefix. A new index version is visible only to queries whose prefix contains all of its keys.

papers.abstract: Geometry-aware neural operators face substantial computational and memory demands when learning across complex physical domains. We introduce Architecture-Aware Mixed Precision (AA-MP), a replica-exchange training strategy that allocates numerical precision according to replica roles and architecture-specific operations. By retaining FP32 for refinement while selectively employing BF16 for exploration, AA-MP preserves predictive accuracy while improving training efficiency. Across fluid dynamics and three-dimensional structural mechanics benchmarks, AA-MP achieves comparable accuracy to full-precision training over an ensemble of runs, while reducing hot-replica peak GPU memory by 46.9% and training time by up to 25.8%. It also outperforms naive Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) in memory efficiency and computational cost, with increasing memory advantages at larger model and geometry scales. Ablation studies show that retaining FP32 in the cold-replica is important for predictive accuracy, while additional FP32 operations in the exploratory replica provide limited benefits relative to their computational cost. Finally, conformal prediction for uncertainty calibration shows that AA-MP achieves near-nominal coverage with narrower prediction intervals than the alternatives. These results advance the scalability of geometry-aware scientific machine learning by reducing computational costs without compromising predictive accuracy or uncertainty quantification.
bullets: Targets the computational and memory demands of neural operators on complex physical domains.
Assigns precision by replica role and architecture operation, using FP32 for refinement and selective BF16 for exploration.
Maintains accuracy comparable to full-precision training across fluid dynamics and 3D structural mechanics benchmarks.
Reduces hot-replica peak GPU memory by 46.9% and training time by up to 25.8%, outperforming naive AMP in efficiency.
Conformal prediction achieves near-nominal coverage with narrower prediction intervals; scope is evaluated on the reported benchmark domains.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed AA-MP ArGEnT–DeepONet training framework. The exploratory hot replica uses a manually controlled BF16 live model, while the latent reduction, prediction-error and energy reductions, master parameters, and optimizer states are maintained in FP32. The cold replica executes the same network entirely in FP32. (b) Two replicas are evolved using preconditioned reSGLD at Tc < Th. The higher-temperature hot replica promotes broader exploration, whereas the FP32 cold replica performs low-temperature refinement and model evaluation. Replica-exchange proposals periodically exchange the parameter and associated optimizer states between the two replica slots.

papers.abstract: Looped language models can stop iterating early, and recent work shows that post-hoc readouts of the loop trajectory often rival the learned exit gate of the looped model Ouro. Such comparisons reduce each method to one operating point chosen by a selection rule. We ask whether that rule decides the outcome. On a frozen Ouro-1.4B with four loops, we compared a trained stability probe ($π_1$-x) with Ouro's native gate, adapted to a per-question stopping decision, in pre-registered studies; the confirmatory study was designed after an exploratory finding on development data and evaluated once on a sealed test set of 8,517 questions. In the pre-registered confirmatory comparison, which selected operating points with a bootstrap-screened 1 pp accuracy-loss rule, the probe saved more of the four-loop budget than the native gate (+0.053 gross macro saving over three benchmarks, 95% CI [+0.049, +0.057]), mostly from CommonsenseQA, where the probe's test upper bound on accuracy loss exceeded 1 pp. Under a point-only rule, a pre-specified secondary analysis on the same test set reversed the preference (-0.022 [-0.026, -0.018]), with operating points that exceeded the budget. In pre-specified secondary comparisons, the probe showed no demonstrated advantage over an untrained KL divergence between successive loops (+0.00125 [-0.0041, +0.0065]); we emphasise this result post hoc and claim no equivalence. The probe also broke its budget on one of two out-of-distribution benchmarks (3.26 pp loss on Social IQa). Savings are estimated from stored full-depth traces, not measured inference time, and our screen carries no formal risk-control guarantee. We conclude that halting methods should be compared as signals together with selection procedures, with strong untrained baselines and out-of-distribution checks.
bullets: On frozen Ouro-1.4B with four loops, a trained stability probe was compared with Ouro’s native gate for per-question stopping.
Under a bootstrap-screened 1 percentage-point accuracy-loss rule, the probe saved more loop budget than the native gate across three benchmarks.
Under a point-only rule, the preference reversed, with operating points exceeding the budget.
The probe showed no demonstrated advantage over an untrained KL-divergence baseline and exceeded its budget on one out-of-distribution benchmark.
Savings came from stored full-depth traces rather than measured inference time, and the selection screen has no formal risk-control guarantee.

papers.title: When Does Adaptive Halting Win? Selection Rules Matter in Looped Language Models
papers.tldr: Selection rules can reverse which adaptive halting signal appears better, so looped-language-model halting should be evaluated jointly with its operating-point selection procedure.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM serving by drafting tokens that the target model verifies in one pass, and its gain grows with the drafts the target accepts. Structured outputs should be an ideal case, because much of a record follows from relations among its fields: an itinerary's days follow from its cities' stays and flights. Serving engines, however, draft such text by proposing it from the prompt or a learned head, and their grammar masks enforce only syntax, so the model must satisfy the relations, which it violates: on NATURAL PLAN's trip problems, Qwen3-8B writes a valid itinerary for 10%, and retries that name the violated relation raise this to 14%. We present FactorSpec, which serves exact relational constraints as speculative drafts. FactorSpec compiles a JSON Schema and its relations into a factor graph with an exact feasibility check, drafts every token the constraint determines as certain, verifies each request at a width chosen for it, and computes the masks in worker processes outside the scheduler while the GPU runs. In SGLang, its drafts yield up to 10.5 tokens per verify step, up to 1.9x those of the fastest n-gram drafter, and it decodes up to 1.43x faster than speculators tuned per load, at a grammar mask's cost; it also leads in vLLM. Because every record is also valid, it serves up to 13.9x the valid records per GPU-second of syntax-only baselines.
bullets: Targets relational violations in structured generation, which grammar masks alone cannot prevent.
Compiles JSON Schema and field relations into a factor graph with exact feasibility checking.
Drafts constraint-determined tokens, adapts verification width per request, and computes masks off the scheduler path.
In SGLang, reaches up to 10.5 tokens per verify step and 1.43× faster decoding than load-tuned speculators; it also leads in vLLM.
Produces only valid records, reaching up to 13.9× more valid records per GPU-second than syntax-only baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Speculative decoding for LLM serving reduces latency, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: FactorSpec: Serving Exact Relational Constraints as Speculative Drafts
papers.tldr: FactorSpec accelerates structured-output serving by drafting tokens that are guaranteed by exact relational constraints, achieving faster decoding and far more valid records than syntax-only approaches.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models process hundreds of visual tokens, making visual representations a major computational bottleneck. We argue that visual token pruning should be formulated not as identifying individually important tokens, but as preserving the dominant low-rank spectral structure of the visual representation. Based on this formulation, we introduce SVD-Prune, a training-free framework that leverages Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and statistical leverage scores for globally informed token selection. SVD-Prune is architecture-agnostic and can be applied at different stages of the multimodal pipeline, including encoder-side, decoder-side, and hybrid configurations Extensive experiments across VLM and VLA benchmarks demonstrate strong robustness under extreme compression. SVD-Prune reduces the visual token. SVD-Prune cuts the visual token budget by up to 99.3%, while, at a 16-token budget, encoder-side pruning lowers inference FLOPs by 82.4% and achieves a 4.18x end-to-end speedup, including pruning overhead.
bullets: Targets the computational bottleneck caused by hundreds of visual tokens in VLMs and VLAs.
Formulates pruning as preserving dominant low-rank spectral structure rather than ranking tokens independently.
Uses training-free SVD and statistical leverage scores for globally informed, architecture-agnostic selection.
Supports encoder-side, decoder-side, and hybrid multimodal pipeline configurations.
At 16 tokens, encoder-side pruning reduces inference FLOPs by 82.4% and achieves a 4.18× end-to-end speedup, including pruning overhead.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a token pruning method for VLMs/VLAs using SVD, directly fitting token pruning and eviction.
papers.title: SVD-Prune: Spectral Vision Token Pruning under Extreme Compression
papers.tldr: SVD-Prune uses SVD-based global token selection to preserve visual representations under extreme compression, reducing visual tokens by up to 99.3%.

papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention scores, and each layer scores its own cache. To our knowledge, no eviction method asks which layer should score. We find, across twenty-one models, that the depth of the scoring layer governs eviction quality. On the eighteen models with per-layer caches, spanning 0.5B to 109B, long-context retrieval accuracy collapses at shallow layers, peaks between 0.4 and 0.75 of depth, and degrades at the last layer. The curve arises because a layer judges tokens well only once it has used the question to find the answer, which takes several layers. Modeling eviction as a top-$k$ cut, we compute answer survival probability from prefill attention and reproduce the measured curves. This approach selects the scoring layer using calibration prompts with known answers, and the selected layer is the best layer measured on most models and never significantly below it. It improves on the own-layer default on sixteen of the eighteen models, with significant gains on seven, all at 14B or below, while on larger models the default is already close to the best mid-depth layer. Scoring every cache from the selected layer while keeping one set of tokens for all heads also beats per-head SnapKV by 18 to 43 points on five models up to 14B under tight budgets. This gain carries over to financial filings at 32K context, all at the same memory budget, with no extra forward pass. The same curve explains a penalty in shared-cache models, where several layers read one cache and the layer that writes it scores by default. On Gemma-4-E2B the writer is shallow and loses 28 points to a mid-depth reader at a 10% budget. We also find that in open-book question answering (LongBench) no mid-depth layer beats the own-layer default.
bullets: Eviction quality depends strongly on scoring-layer depth: it is poor near the input, peaks around 40–75% depth, and declines at the final layer.
The pattern reflects when layers have incorporated the question enough to identify answer-relevant tokens; a top-k survival model reproduces the observed curve.
Calibration prompts with known answers select an effective scoring layer, improving on the default in 16 of 18 per-layer-cache models and significantly in 7.
Using the selected layer to score all heads beats per-head SnapKV by 18–43 points on five models up to 14B, including financial filings at 32K context, without extra forward passes.

The benefit is model- and task-dependent: larger models often have near-optimal defaults, shared-cache writers can be substantially worse, and no mid-depth advantage appears on LongBench open-book QA.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates which layer should score KV-cache eviction, directly improving cache efficiency.
papers.title: Who Should Score the Cache? Mid-Depth Layers Are the Best Judges of KV-Cache Eviction
papers.tldr: Mid-depth transformer layers are generally the best judges for KV-cache token eviction, improving long-context retrieval when a single selected layer scores caches.

papers.abstract: Diffusion driving vision-language-action models repeatedly execute the backbone at every denoising stage, incurring substantial inference cost, while it remains unclear whether all scenes require the same decoding computation. To distinguish when a trajectory becomes readable from how much further refinement it requires, we analyze trajectory readout across network depth and decoding progress. We identify a depth-decoding dissociation in which late-layer representations already support useful trajectory readout after the first forward sweep, whereas early-layer representations benefit more from continued decoding. We further find that both the preferred readout layer and decoding depth vary across scenes. Based on these observations, we propose a scene-adaptive readout and decoding framework. A scene-conditioned readout MoE adaptively weights and combines trajectory predictions from layer-specific late-layer representations after a single backbone sweep, while an adaptive decoding policy applies additional native refinement only when required by the scene. We evaluate our framework on two diffusion driving VLAs across the Waymo E2E and nuScenes benchmarks. Our method improves validation RFS by up to 0.56 while also improving test performance, and achieves an end-to-end speedup of up to $6.0\times$ on Waymo E2E, while consistently reducing trajectory error on nuScenes. These results demonstrate that scene-level readout and decoding allocation improves planning quality while avoiding unnecessary decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjyu001/SARD
bullets: Diffusion driving VLAs repeatedly run the backbone during denoising, but scenes differ in the decoding needed for reliable trajectories.
Late-layer features can support useful readout after one backbone sweep, while early-layer features benefit more from continued refinement.
A scene-conditioned readout MoE combines layer-specific predictions, and an adaptive policy adds native decoding only when needed.
Across two VLAs on Waymo E2E and nuScenes, the method improves planning quality, reduces trajectory error, and achieves up to 6.0× end-to-end speedup on Waymo E2E.
papers.selection_reason: Scene-adaptive readout and decoding for diffusion driving VLAs, improving planning quality while cutting inference cost; fits VLA and efficiency.
papers.title: Scene-Adaptive Readout and Decoding in Diffusion Driving VLAs
papers.tldr: A scene-adaptive framework reduces diffusion driving VLA inference cost by selecting where to read trajectories and how much to decode per scene.

papers.abstract: Studies of neural network generalization and robustness often summarize smoothness with a single number, such as a Lipschitz constant or a Hessian curvature statistic. However, Lipschitz constants summarize global worst-case sensitivity and Hessian statistics summarize local curvature; neither captures how model responses vary with the size, direction, and location of perturbations encountered in real-world deployment. To measure smoothness under these perturbations, we introduce a finite-difference roughness spectrum that profiles model responses across these conditions. Our roughness spectrum generalizes scalar smoothness measures, bringing Lipschitz sensitivity and directional Hessian curvature into a common framework across perturbation scales. We connect this spectrum to classical Besov theory, which describes how a function's variation changes with scale. Our theoretical analysis also proves that a larger output shift can cause less task damage than a smaller one, and that local curvature alone can miss the blocks most vulnerable to finite perturbations. In image classification, Roughness Source Control (RSC) suppresses margin roughness along noise directions and improves noise robustness in a comparison of 80 checkpoints across four model--dataset combinations. In post-training quantization, we identify blocks that need higher precision by measuring task-loss increases from perturbations matched to the size and direction of each block's quantization error. Our mixed-precision allocation achieves lower perplexity than the Hessian-based HAWQ-V2 baseline under the same GPTQ weights and bit budgets in all 14 settings across seven held-out large language models.
bullets: Scalar Lipschitz and Hessian measures miss how responses vary with perturbation size, direction, and location.
A finite-difference roughness spectrum unifies global sensitivity and directional curvature across scales, grounded in Besov theory.
The analysis shows that larger output shifts can sometimes cause less task damage than smaller shifts, and local curvature can overlook vulnerable blocks.
Roughness Source Control improves noise robustness across 80 image-classification checkpoints spanning four model–dataset combinations.
For post-training quantization, spectrum-guided mixed precision achieves lower perplexity than HAWQ-V2 in all 14 tested settings across seven held-out language models.

papers.title: Scalar Smoothness Is One Point on a Besov Spectrum
papers.tldr: The paper replaces single-number smoothness metrics with a perturbation-scale roughness spectrum that better identifies task-relevant vulnerabilities and improves robustness and quantization decisions.

papers.abstract: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. Reasoning models that fit edge memory budgets can produce long reasoning traces, increasing sequential decoding, end-to-end latency, energy consumption, and KV-cache memory pressure. We present MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models designed for edge deployment, targeting this accuracy-generation-efficiency trade-off. Our recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine, and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused LLM teacher; a four-stage post-training curriculum comprising two SFT stages followed by two RL stages with hard-sample mining; and an edge deployment evaluation spanning multiple GGUF quantization variants and real-device inference on laptop and smartphone hardware. On seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B while being 6.75x smaller; MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points despite being less than half its size. On HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses it by 11.66 points despite being ~16x smaller. Beyond accuracy, MedPsy reduces average response length by 1.7x (1.7B) and 3.2x (4B) versus its Qwen3 backbones, while Q4_K_M quantization preserves the aggregate score within 1 point of BF16 with ~69% lower disk footprint. In real-device inference, MedPsy-4B's shorter generations translate into 75% lower median end-to-end latency and estimated energy per answer than its Qwen3 backbone at matched quantization, while peak RAM remains below 5 GB across our tested laptop and smartphone configurations.
bullets: Targets the gap between capable but oversized medical LLMs and compact models that struggle on knowledge-intensive healthcare tasks.
Uses synthetic medical data, teacher-generated chain-of-thought targets, two SFT stages, and two RL stages with hard-sample mining.
Across seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B and matches MedGemma-27B; MedPsy-1.7B also exceeds MedGemma-1.5-4B.
MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B on HealthBench-Hard while using far fewer parameters.
Shorter outputs, quantization, and edge testing yield lower latency, energy use, and storage needs, with peak RAM below 5 GB in tested configurations.

papers.abstract: Delta-rule linear attention underlies language models such as Kimi Linear and Qwen3-Next. Chunkwise implementations expose matrix parallelism, but their backward passes compute unnecessary auxiliary adjoints. We present ReWY, an algebraic reformulation that reduces this work before optimizing accelerator execution. Differentiating the chunk correction as one triangular residual system eliminates the inverse adjoint and reduces seven local WY matrix products to three. Two complementary transformations expose further reuse: centered matrix contractions replace pairwise vector-gate processing, and scalar-gate reductions reuse key-gradient products instead of forming a key Gram matrix. These identities simplify backward computation for DeltaNet, GDN, KDA, and GDN2 while preserving the recurrence and gradients in exact arithmetic, without changing the architecture or training objective. We implement the reduced graph on GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Under matched recomputation and full-saving policies, precision-qualified six-shape comparisons with frozen FLA references yield 1.15-1.81$\times$ geometric-mean complete low-level backward speedups on NVIDIA GPUs. All four operators achieve 1.18-1.70$\times$ on H100 and H200 while retaining original FP32 working matrices. A separate public-autograd evaluation on Ascend 950DT, including gradient conversions, yields 1.09-2.89$\times$ under available matched policies. Paired ablations establish further ReWY gains after optimizing the complementary contractions. Complete-gradient checks validate the recorded operator cases; supplementary full-model backward measurements assess integration into community FLA models and a GDN2 layer port. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/flashserve/ReWY.
bullets: Targets redundant auxiliary adjoints in chunkwise Delta-rule linear-attention backward passes.
Uses a triangular residual-system formulation plus centered contractions and scalar-gate reductions to expose reuse.
Applies across DeltaNet, GDN, KDA, and GDN2 without changing the architecture or training objective.
Reports 1.15–1.81× geometric-mean low-level backward speedups on NVIDIA GPUs and 1.09–2.89× on Ascend 950DT under matched policies.
Validation includes precision-qualified operator checks, ablations, complete-gradient checks, and selected full-model integration measurements.

papers.selection_reason: Presents an algebraic reformulation that reduces backward-pass matrix multiplications for delta-rule linear attention, directly improving attention efficiency.
papers.title: ReWY: Faster Backpropagation for Delta-Rule Attention - From 7 to 3 Matrix Multiplications
papers.tldr: ReWY reformulates Delta-rule attention backpropagation to reduce seven local WY matrix multiplications to three, delivering faster GPU and NPU backward execution while preserving exact gradients.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agentic systems are increasingly combined with CoT reasoning to solve tasks that require accurate reasoning, external knowledge, and multi-step deliberation. Yet, explicit CoT incurs substantial generation overhead, while implicit CoT, which replaces textual rationales with compact continuous tokens, does not naturally support the explicit communication interface required for agentic tool-use. We propose TAC-CoT, a tool-empowered adaptive implicit CoT framework that replaces explicit reasoning traces with compact latent reasoning segments while retaining textual tokens only for tool calls, observations, and final answers. This interleaved design enables agentic tool-use without verbalizing every intermediate reasoning step. Experiments on agentic math and QA benchmarks show that TAC-CoT improves accuracy by up to 8.8 points while reducing model forward passes by up to 6.8x. Furthermore, analyses show that TAC-CoT improves tool-use quality in both single- and multi-tool settings.
bullets: Addresses the generation overhead of explicit chain-of-thought and the limited tool-use interface of implicit reasoning.
Uses compact latent reasoning segments, while retaining textual tokens for tool calls, observations, and final answers.
Evaluated on agentic math and question-answering benchmarks.
Reports accuracy gains of up to 8.8 points and up to 6.8× fewer model forward passes.
Analysis indicates improved tool-use quality in both single- and multi-tool settings.

papers.abstract: Linear recurrences are becoming an increasingly common building block in large language models, replacing the growing KV cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state that enables efficient decoding. However, the quantization stack has largely been developed around softmax Transformers, whose numerical properties and inference state differ from those of recurrent models. Our goal is to understand these differences and study the design space of quantization methods for recurrent models. In our analysis, we differentiate between two targets. First, extra-state quantization concerns weights and activations outside the recurrent state, whose distributions are shaped indirectly by the sequence mixer during training. In controlled 1.3B parameter models, we find that decayed recurrences develop weaker residual outlier channels than softmax attention and are therefore easier to quantize without incoherence processing. Second, intra-state quantization concerns the recurrent state itself during decode, where repeated updates create a different numerical problem from KV cache quantization. We instantiate our findings as LoReS, a state quantization pipeline combining value-axis scale grouping to match output channel magnitude, decay-based mixed-precision to protect slowly decaying heads or channels, and stochastic rounding to limit error accumulation under repeated requantization. Across Qwen-3.5 9B, Nemotron-H 8B, and Kimi-Linear 48B-A3B, LoReS supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower effective precision on shorter decode horizons. We implement LoReS in vLLM and demonstrate end-to-end decode speedups.
bullets: Recurrent models require separate treatment of extra-state weights/activations and the recurrent state itself.
Decayed recurrences develop fewer residual outlier channels than softmax attention, reducing the need for incoherence processing.
LoReS combines value-axis scale grouping, decay-aware mixed precision, and stochastic rounding to control recurrent-state quantization error.
It supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower precision for shorter decode horizons across several large models.
A vLLM implementation demonstrates end-to-end decoding speedups.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generation has achieved impressive results on short clips, yet generating long videos remains challenging due to error accumulation over extended horizons, where each predicted frame depends on potentially imperfect previous frames. Existing approaches typically rely on static context management strategies, such as sliding-window caches that discard early frames or fixed sink frames that permanently preserve initial content. These designs either lose critical long-range context or anchor generation to outdated information, which can lead to degraded fidelity, motion stagnation, and reduced diversity. In this paper, we propose Learning to Memorize (L2M), a learned context memory management framework that dynamically retains, evicts, and evolves historical frames according to predicted importance. The framework consists of an importance prediction router that estimates the relevance of each historical frame, degradation-aware training that improves robustness to noisy or corrupted context, and a dynamic memory initialization and evolution mechanism that updates long-term memory using exponential moving average (EMA) importance scores. This allows high-quality frames to replace stale anchors and enables memory to adapt naturally to scene evolution. Trained with a teacher-student distillation objective and sparsity regularization, L2M makes efficient use of a fixed KV-cache budget while preserving the most informative contextual information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that L2M improves long-horizon video generation quality and temporal consistency over existing baselines, providing a learned strategy for context memory management in long autoregressive video generation.
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and degraded quality in long video generation caused by static context strategies.
Uses an importance-prediction router to retain, evict, and update historical frames based on relevance.
Combines degradation-aware training, EMA-based memory evolution, teacher–student distillation, and sparsity regularization.
Experiments report improved long-horizon video quality and temporal consistency over existing baselines.
Scope: focuses on learned context management within a fixed KV-cache budget.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of L2M. (a) Training phase: Given the current chunk feature f̄b and historical latent frame features {f̄i}i<(b−1)Bf+1, the importance-aware frame router predicts importance scores for each historical latent frame. Binary frame selection masks mi ∈ {0, 1} are obtained via GumbelSoftmax discretization. The pruned context is fed to the student network, which is supervised by the teacher operating on the full context. Degradation-aware training augments a subset of historical frames with degradations, encouraging the router to assign them lower retention probabilities. (b) Inference phase: The router predicts frame importance scores, and low-scoring latent frames are evicted to meet the cache budget. High-scoring frames are dynamically selected as long-term memory and periodically updated using maintained EMA scores, continuously promoting informative historical frames.

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers have become the most powerful models for visual generation, but still suffer from massive computation costs. To solve this problem, feature caching has been proposed to cache the features of diffusion models in the previous computation steps and then reuse them in the following caching steps, which brings significant acceleration but also degradation in generation quality. To address this problem, this paper proposes Z-cache as a feature caching method that can maintain high-quality generation through self-reflection. Concretely, we observe that the error from feature caching tends to be sharply reduced after each full computation. Based on this observation, Z-Cache is designed to first predict the features in the future caching steps and then perform a full computation. After that, Z-Cache returns to the caching steps and re-predicts them based on the previous and the current computation steps, which brings correction in features. Experiments demonstrate that with Z-Cache, diffusion transformers achieve comparable generation quality to the original model but with faster inference speed, for instance, 6.22X acceleration on FLUX-dev for text-to-image generation. Our code is released on GitHub.
bullets: Feature caching reduces diffusion-transformer computation but can degrade image quality.
Z-Cache predicts features for future caching steps, periodically performs full computation, and uses it to correct subsequent predictions.
Experiments report comparable generation quality with faster inference, including 6.22× acceleration on FLUX-dev for text-to-image generation.
The method targets inference acceleration for diffusion-transformer-based visual generation.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Visualization of videos generated by Hunyuan Video with different feature caching methods. The annotated speedups denote FLOPs reductions relative to 50-step sampling.

Figure 3: Pipeline of Z-Cache. The figure uses the reverse-diffusion notation t, t − 1, . . . for visualization, while the text uses a sampling-order index that increases along denoising. Traditional feature caching forecasts an active window from a past full-computation anchor and directly moves to the next window. In contrast, Z-Cache treats the window as provisional: after obtaining the next scheduled full-computation anchor, it revisits the same window, constructs dual-anchor hidden estimates, re-samples the window trajectory, and commits the reflected window-end latent. Z-Cache therefore performs in-loop trajectory correction without adding extra full-computation steps.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex speech models execute dense model inference for every audio frame throughout a live interaction. This uniform framewise schedule creates sustained GPU load across dialogue states whose computation has strong, reusable temporal structure. ReFrame formulates full-duplex inference as a silence-aware computation problem. Mutual Silence Speculation (MSS) operates when both participants are silent: it evaluates multi-frame Temporal continuations, verifies text and hidden-state stability, and applies batched Mimi audio-token correction. Listening Frame Folding (LFF) operates while the user speaks and the agent listens: it processes already-arrived user frames through parallel Temporal execution and frame-batched audio-token generation while accepting only the verified prefix. Frame-Budget Reinvestment (FBR) assigns the released frame intervals to resumable external retrieval and language-model workers, then injects timely references through Moshi's conditioning interface. We instantiate ReFrame on five full-duplex models spanning Moshi-family, phase-structured, and flattened autoregressive generation. Across the complete 1,225-conversation FDBench, ReFrame reduces measured GPU execution time by 18.80-31.01% and retains 96.92-100% non-PAD text agreement on five different models. On HaluEval tests, FBR increases the number of correct generated spoken answers from 86 to 205 under the same auxiliary-service budget. ReFrame turns recurring dialogue structure into lower inference cost and higher end-to-end service capability.
bullets: Targets the sustained GPU cost of dense frame-by-frame inference during silence and listening phases.
Uses Mutual Silence Speculation, Listening Frame Folding, and verified-prefix processing to reuse and batch temporal computation.
Reinvests freed compute intervals in resumable retrieval and language-model workers via the model’s conditioning interface.
Evaluated on five full-duplex models across 1,225 FDBench conversations, reducing measured GPU execution time by 18.80–31.01%.
Maintains 96.92–100% non-PAD text agreement; retrieval reinvestment increased correct spoken answers from 86 to 205 under the same auxiliary-service budget.

papers.abstract: Position-independent caching reuses chunk KV caches across positions and requests. Independent encoding, however, omits cross-chunk interactions and can degrade accuracy. In our study, neither PIC training nor rule-based recomputation, alone or combined, consistently recovers full-prefill accuracy. Oracle-guided recomputation on PIC-trained models improves accuracy at the same budget, motivating better selection. We present CacheWeave, which adapts the full backbone to PIC, then freezes it and trains a model-native block selector on the adapted model's oracles. The selector uses compact cached chunk features and question hidden states without extracting backbone attention scores. It selects contiguous token blocks aligned with KV blocks to support efficient recomputation and limit copy-on-write amplification. Its runtime, CacheWeave-Serve, supports private and shared KV caches, keeps selection and recomputation on the GPU, and stages sliding-window KV for hybrid attention models. Across three models and four tasks, CacheWeave outperforms CacheBlend and ProphetKV by 7.2 and 3.5 percentage points on average at a 5% recomputation budget, with a mean relative accuracy loss of 1.6% to full prefill. With 32-token blocks, CacheWeave-Serve cuts single-request TTFT by up to 16.1x over full prefill and 1.7x over ProphetKV, and raises SLO goodput under load by up to 7.8x.
bullets: Position-independent KV caching is efficient but loses cross-chunk interactions, hurting accuracy.
CacheWeave adapts the backbone to position-independent caching, then trains a model-native selector using oracle-guided recomputation.
The selector uses compact cached features and question hidden states, avoids backbone attention extraction, and chooses contiguous KV-aligned blocks.
Across three models and four tasks, it improves over CacheBlend and ProphetKV by 7.2 and 3.5 percentage points at a 5% recomputation budget, with 1.6% mean relative accuracy loss versus full prefill.
CacheWeave-Serve supports private/shared caches and hybrid attention; with 32-token blocks, it cuts single-request TTFT by up to 16.1× and improves loaded-system SLO goodput by up to 7.8×.

papers.tldr: CacheWeave learns which cached token blocks to recompute, recovering near-full-prefill accuracy while greatly reducing time-to-first-token.

papers.abstract: Query-conditioned sparse KV selection reduces long-context inference cost by attending to a subset of historical KV entries at each decoding step. Existing selectors must wait for the target-layer query before scoring candidates and generating indices, placing routing on the immediate pre-attention path. We introduce EarlySelectKV, a training-free transformation that uses proxy queries from earlier hidden states to precompute selected KV indices while retaining the real target-layer query for final attention. Tests with RocketKV, Quest, and Loki show no consistent pattern of quality degradation across the evaluated settings. In the primary RocketKV evaluation, ES-RocketKV differs by +0.018 points on LongBench, approximately -0.01 points on RULER, and +0.25 percentage points on representative NIAH/Passkey settings. In a TensorRT-LLM deployment with CPU-offloaded routing, ES-RocketKV improves end-to-end output throughput by up to 12.4% and reduces GPU-resident memory by 11.1% of the combined KV/K-summary pool. This makes routing timing an explicit optimization target alongside KV subset selection in sparse long-context decoding. Code is available at https://github.com/sea-with-sakura/EarlySelectKV.
bullets: Addresses routing latency caused by waiting for each target-layer query before selecting historical KV entries.
Uses a training-free transformation to anticipate selected KV indices from proxy queries in earlier hidden states.
Evaluated with RocketKV, Quest, and Loki, with no consistent quality degradation reported across tested settings.
In TensorRT-LLM with CPU-offloaded routing, improves output throughput by up to 12.4% and reduces combined KV/K-summary GPU memory by 11.1%.
Frames routing timing—not only KV subset selection—as an optimization target for sparse long-context inference.

papers.abstract: Analog In-Memory Computing (IMC) is a promising paradigm for accelerating GEMM-based AI workloads by executing computations directly within the memory array in the analog domain. While IMC delivers substantial energy and throughput improvements, it can suffer from significant task accuracy degradation due to analog-to-digital converter (ADC) quantization noise, which occurs at the GEMM output and is thus different from weight/activation quantization, which occurs at the GEMM input. Mixed ADC resolution allows IMC modules to choose between high- and low-resolution ADC modes with different energy costs, offering a compelling accuracy-energy trade-off. However, selecting ADC resolutions across IMC units while respecting hardware granularity constraints remains challenging. In this paper, we propose SMART-AIMC, a Sensitivity-aware Mixed ADC Resolution framework with fine-grained Tunability for Analog In-Memory Computing. SMART-AIMC correlates the algorithmic task loss to hardware ADC quantization noise in the form of an ADC Channel Sensitivity (ACS) metric. Using this metric, SMART-AIMC systematically, and in a disciplined manner, allocates ADC resources to critical computations. Furthermore, we introduce a sensitivity-based channel reordering scheme that overcomes the hardware granularity constraints with no runtime overhead and approaches the optimal ADC quantization possible for the model. Evaluated across diverse workloads, SMART-AIMC unlocks a superior accuracy-energy Pareto frontier, providing (1) higher task accuracy at matched energy budgets and (2) fine-grained tuning across efficiency targets, from aggressive energy savings to near-digital inference accuracy. At the latter operating point, SMART-AIMC achieves $6.99\times$ higher modeled system-level energy efficiency for linear projections than the INT8 digital baseline with negligible accuracy degradation.
bullets: ADC quantization noise at GEMM outputs can significantly degrade IMC task accuracy, creating a distinct challenge from input quantization.
The framework uses an ADC Channel Sensitivity metric to relate algorithmic loss to ADC noise and prioritize critical computations.
Sensitivity-based channel reordering bypasses hardware granularity constraints without runtime overhead.
Across diverse workloads, SMART-AIMC offers higher accuracy at matched energy and fine-grained tuning from aggressive savings to near-digital accuracy.
Near the digital-accuracy operating point, it reports 6.99× higher modeled system-level energy efficiency than an INT8 digital baseline for linear projections, with negligible accuracy degradation.

papers.abstract: The sparse path, comprising sparse operations and collective communication, is a critical component of large-scale recommendation models. However, these operations are often represented as opaque nodes in the training computation graph, hindering whole-graph optimization. We present SparseLift, a low-overhead compiler for the sparse path of large-scale recommendation training. It exposes sparse computation and communication to whole-graph analysis to expand the optimization space and improve training efficiency. By analyzing model structure and runtime information, SparseLift reconstructs opaque nodes as analyzable subgraphs, recovering the resource semantics of sparse computation and communication within the graph. Building on the recovered semantics, we design incremental cost models and a constraint-aware planner to automatically select and organize subgraph optimizations into an execution plan that is reused during subsequent steady-state training. We evaluate SparseLift on an industrial video-platform recommendation task with 100B sparse parameters and the public DLRM benchmark. SparseLift improves steady-state throughput for ordinary industrial training steps by 16.5\% over the native baseline. On DLRM, it achieves $1.60\times$ and $1.26\times$ model-execution speedups over DLRM-Baseline and TorchRec, respectively.
bullets: Targets opaque sparse operations and collective communication that limit whole-graph optimization in large-scale recommendation training.
Reconstructs opaque nodes into analyzable subgraphs using model structure and runtime information, recovering resource semantics.
Uses incremental cost models and a constraint-aware planner to generate reusable optimization plans for steady-state training.
Improves industrial training throughput by 16.5% and achieves 1.60× over DLRM-Baseline and 1.26× over TorchRec on DLRM.

papers.abstract: GPTQ is Babai's nearest-plane algorithm on the lattice of the Cholesky factor of the layer's input second moment $Σ$. In the high-rate, entropy-coded regime it needs $\tfrac12\log_2(\AM/\GM)$ of its Cholesky pivots more bits than WaterSIC, which is within $0.255$ bit of the rate-distortion limit for every $Σ$; random rotations close most of this gap in practice, and Ordentlich and Polyanskiy asked for the worst-case gap between rotated GPTQ and WaterSIC. We show that after a Haar rotation the $k$-th pivot converges almost surely, uniformly in $k\geδn$ and over spectra $ν$ of bounded condition number, to $1/S_ν(-k/n)$, a classical formula from the theory of Lyapunov exponents, and use it to answer the question. Over spectra with condition number $κ$ the worst rotated gap is $\tfrac12\log_2κ-\log_2\lnκ+\tfrac12-\tfrac1{\ln2}+o(1)$ bits, attained only by two-point spectra, just $\tfrac12\log_2\lnκ+O(1)$ bits below the worst case without rotation, so rotation cannot replace waterfilling in general. It nearly can on real layers: rotation cuts the cost of an $η$-fraction of outlier eigenvalues of size $μ$ from about $ημ$ to $η^2μ/2$ to leading order, but cannot remove spectral spread on a logarithmic scale; for non-Gaussian weights it also adds a weight-side rate cost, which we characterize exactly under a standard high-rate assumption. On $96$ Hessians of Qwen3 and Llama-3.1 the rotated gap has median $0.04$ bit and maximum $0.36$ bit, against $2$--$5$ bits in the worst case for the same condition numbers, and the limit matches it to within $0.009$ bit.
bullets: After Haar rotation, GPTQ’s Cholesky pivots converge to a classical Lyapunov-exponent formula, enabling sharp worst-case analysis.
For condition number κ, the worst rotated gap is ½log₂κ − log₂lnκ + ½ − 1/ln2 + o(1) bits, attained only by two-point spectra.
Rotation improves the penalty from rare large eigenvalues from about ημ to η²μ/2, but cannot eliminate logarithmic spectral-spread costs.
For non-Gaussian weights, rotation introduces an additional weight-side rate cost that is characterized under a standard high-rate assumption.
Across 96 Qwen3 and Llama-3.1 Hessians, the rotated gap had median 0.04 bit and maximum 0.36 bit, with theory accurate within 0.009 bit.

Right: WikiText-2 perplexity at equal entropy-coded rate (lines; blue Qwen3-1.7B, orange Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; seed 0) and of fixed-rate INT-b g128 with and without Hadamard (crosses; rates include scales).
