papers.abstract: A causal video generator writes every segment it produces into a key--value (KV) cache, and later segments know the past only through it. Self-rollout training stops the gradient at this cache, and Self Gradient Forcing (SGF) restores it, but applies it to the same weights that generate the current segment. We find that writing and generating are different roles: in a pretrained generator the written KV already differs from the KV used for denoising, and on shared weights the gradient from future reads is negatively aligned with the gradient of generation. We propose dKV Forcing (dKV denotes differentiable KV), which gives the write its own parameters, a low-rank residual used only when a segment enters the cache, and trains them with the gradient of the later segments that read what they wrote. Opening this gradient through the cache in common use exhausts GPU memory. We trace this to checkpoint replay re-writing the cache, not to the gradient path, which removes the need for the second reconstruction pass of SGF. dKV Forcing keeps the cache as persistent differentiable pages and computes the exact gradient in one temporal traversal, with an $11\%$ lower memory peak and $28\%$ less resident memory. With pages that store hidden states, it trains 15\,s clips on which the two-pass reconstruction runs out of memory. Trained on 5\,s clips, dKV Forcing reaches the highest VBench-Long quality score at 60\,s and 240\,s and outperforms SGF by $3.6$ and $6.1$ points of aesthetic quality, with a higher dynamic degree.
bullets: Shared generation and cache-writing weights receive conflicting gradients, motivating separate write parameters.
A low-rank residual writes segment representations into a persistent, differentiable KV cache.
The method computes exact gradients in one temporal traversal, avoiding SGF’s second reconstruction pass.
It reduces peak memory by 11% and resident memory by 28%; hidden-state pages enable training 15-second clips where two-pass reconstruction runs out of memory.
When trained on 5-second clips, it achieves the highest reported VBench-Long quality at 60 and 240 seconds and improves aesthetic quality over SGF by 3.6 and 6.1 points.

figures.caption: Figure 2. A separate writer learns what to store from the segments that read it, in one temporal traversal. For each segment the shared generator Gθ (gray) predicts x̃ts i , which enters the video loss, and the memory writer Kθ,ϕ (orange, with the writer LoRA ϕ) turns the detached prediction into the KV of that segment. The KV is committed once to a write-once slot of the page table, and later segments read it through handles. In backward (purple, dashed) the gradient of every later prediction returns through the handles to the page it read and to the writer that produced it, while replay only reads the pages.

Figure 3. Only pages and handles carry the memory gradient through replay. (a) Self Forcing detaches the cache: each replay is released, and the writes receive no gradient. (b) With the gradient passing through the in-place cache, every replay writes the cache again and its activations stay attached until backward runs out of memory. (c) dKV Forcing stores the values in a page table, written once outside replay, and a zero-valued handle h carries the gradient to the write, so replay only reads and is released.

The two-pass reconstruction keeps no graph in the rollout but retains the whole second-pass forward (violet) and replays it layer by layer in backward (cyan), with the cache resident between steps (red). dKV Forcing allocates the page table once (green), keeps only group entry states during the rollout, and in backward adds one contiguous gradient per page (light green) and the local replay of five-block groups.

Each forward reads a snapshot of the visible pages (orange dashed arrows), while backward returns an independent, contiguous gradient buffer (purple rectangles) to each page’s writer (purple dashed arrows).

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language model (VLM) inference without altering the output distribution, yet two factors limit its gains. Existing drafters either lack the image evidence required for visually grounded tokens or pay to condition on every visual token, although a short draft block typically depends on only a few image regions. Moreover, the value of verifying additional candidates varies with GPU load, so no fixed verification structure is efficient across serving conditions. We present Uni-LaSpec, a block-parallel speculative decoding framework that addresses both factors. To improve draft quality, Uni-LaSpec reuses the verifier's own attention: the query retained from the preceding verification ranks the cached, int8-quantized visual keys, and a cross-layer vote selects a few visual tokens that the drafter fuses through gated cross-attention. Acceptance-aware training further weights each draft position by its contribution to the accepted prefix. To allocate verification, a marginal-cost criterion selects the structure per request and per round: draft trees exploit idle verifier capacity under light load, whereas a dynamic head truncates linear drafts under heavy load. Across six VLMs from three model families and 17 text and multimodal benchmarks, selecting eight visual tokens retains at least 98.6% of the acceptance obtained from the full image at sub-millisecond selection cost. With greedy decoding at concurrency one, Uni-LaSpec achieves up to 5.11x text and 3.24x multimodal throughput over autoregressive decoding. Across six load levels and three GPU types, it outperforms autoregressive decoding in every setting and matches or exceeds the best fixed verification strategy in 123 of 144 settings; under bursty arrivals, it reduces mean end-to-end latency by 47.6% relative to linear verification.
bullets: Reuses verifier attention to rank cached visual keys and select a small set of image tokens for drafting.
Uses gated cross-attention and acceptance-aware training to improve visually grounded draft quality.
Dynamically chooses tree or truncated-linear verification based on marginal cost and current load.
Selecting eight visual tokens preserves at least 98.6% of full-image acceptance at sub-millisecond cost.
Achieves up to 5.11× text and 3.24× multimodal throughput gains, and reduces bursty-arrival latency by 47.6% versus linear verification.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of Uni-LaSpec. Left: the frozen verifier caches the auxiliary hidden states Haux and quantized visual keys. Its last retained query, at position j−1 for the current root xj , scores the visual tokens in every selector layer, and a cross-layer vote selects the positions Sj . Right: the drafter fuses the projected Haux with the selected visual embeddings through gated cross-attention and decodes a masked block in one pass. The LM head emits draft tokens, and the dynamic head emits survival probabilities. Bottom: the candidates (a dynamically truncated linear draft or a draft tree) are verified in one verifier pass, and the accepted tokens start the next round.

Fig. 6. Parallel verification and scheduling of draft trees. (a) Attention mask for a single request. The root is the previous round’s bonus token; each node attends to the cached prefix x1:j−1, its ancestors, and itself. (b) Best-first tree construction with nodes indexed in topological order. Rotary positions follow tree depth, pos(u) = j+ |u|, independently of the packed KV-cache indices. (c) Batched execution of two draft trees and a prefill chunk. The logical attention mask is block diagonal across requests, preserving each tree’s ancestor dependencies and the prefill chunk’s causal order. (d) Scheduling under a shared token budget. The numbered events illustrate deferral of a tree that exceeds the remaining budget (1), allocation of residual capacity to prefill (2), verification of the root alone near the context limit (3), discarding drafts during continued prefill (4), preemption under KV-cache pressure (5), and suspension of new admissions (6). The logical attention mask isolates requests: tree queries attend to their own cached history, ancestors, and themselves, while linear queries follow causal order within their request. (c) Acceptance and state retention are resolved independently for each request. The accepted tree path or linear prefix is retained with its corresponding KV cache and recurrent state. Accepted tokens are committed with a bonus token. Structure selection is repeated in the next round as load changes.

papers.abstract: Sparse mixtures of experts combine multiple prediction models while evaluating only a small subset for each input. Although this architecture reduces computation, how expert separation and routing sparsity jointly govern expert recovery remains an open problem. In this paper, we address this question for location Gaussian mixtures of experts with a fixed number of experts by establishing how expert separation and spatial arrangement determine recovery rates. For dense models, our results reveal that when experts form well-separated clusters, the separation geometry is governed by the size of the largest cluster; without a prescribed cluster structure, this geometry is instead driven by the total number of experts. For sparse models, the separation geometry on retained routing regions is determined by the number of active experts, while the contribution of omitted regions is controlled by their total probability. Consequently, activating fewer experts reduces the separation complexity in these bounds. Furthermore, Top-1 routing yields a particularly striking result: experts can be recovered at a rate independent of the separation quantity. Our technical approach combines polynomial interpolation and Gaussian reproducing-kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) test functions with quantitative restriction inequalities that extend pointwise comparisons to expert functions.
bullets: Studies location Gaussian mixtures of experts with a fixed number of experts.
For dense models, recovery depends on cluster geometry or, without structure, the total number of experts.
For sparse models, retained regions depend on the number of active experts, while omitted regions are weighted by their probability mass.
Top-1 routing enables recovery at a rate independent of expert separation.
Uses polynomial interpolation, Gaussian RKHS test functions, and quantitative restriction inequalities.

papers.title: When Does Sparse Routing Help? The Geometry of Expert Separation in Mixture of Experts
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes when sparse MoE routing improves expert recovery, showing that fewer active experts can reduce separation complexity and that Top-1 routing can remove separation dependence from recovery rates.

papers.abstract: Cryptographically secure inference faces two practical challenges: making secure programming accessible to AI developers and data scientists, and achieving efficient execution across deployment environments. Developers must compose cryptographic primitives correctly, while performance depends on hardware, networks, and evolving ciphertext states. We present CipherFlow, a compiler framework that takes a high-level AI computation graph, available cryptographic primitives, and a target hardware and network configuration to generate an executable, latency-optimized secure inference program. CipherFlow automates cryptographic execution decisions through three techniques: MicroBench profiles deployment-specific primitive costs; state-expanded planning jointly optimizes homomorphic encryption (HE) and secure multi-party computation (MPC) placement, conversions, and ciphertext maintenance under cryptographic-state constraints; and BlockFold summarizes branched regions to scale planning to Transformer graphs. Evaluation using measured HE/MPC backend costs across CPU/GPU and network settings shows up to 16.5$\times$ speedup on BERT-base and over 22$\times$ on ViT compared with static hybrid placement baselines. CipherFlow separates model programming from cryptographic execution decisions, enabling developers to express AI computations while the compiler constructs efficient secure programs.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of programming secure inference and optimizing it across hardware, networks, and evolving ciphertext states.
MicroBench profiles deployment-specific costs for available homomorphic encryption and secure multi-party computation primitives.
State-expanded planning jointly optimizes HE/MPC placement, conversions, and ciphertext maintenance under cryptographic-state constraints.
BlockFold summarizes branched regions to make planning scalable for Transformer graphs.
Measured evaluations report up to 16.5× speedup on BERT-base and over 22× on ViT versus static hybrid-placement baselines.

papers.abstract: Processing every video frame through Vision-Language Models (VLMs) adds significant inference cost and limits their ability to comprehend real-time video. Existing approaches either sub-sample frames uniformly, ignoring content and missing important events, or prune visual tokens inside the VLM to cut per-call cost while still invoking the model on every sampled frame. We introduce FOCUS, a training-free three-layer framework that reduces the number of invocations and steers each one towards what matters. Temporal gating measures inter-frame dissimilarity in the patch-embedding space of a smaller VLM from the same family, triggering burst captures only when the scene changes in a semantically meaningful way. Patch-level dissimilarity is then accumulated across the burst and fused with a top-down attention prior into a spatial focus map that encodes where motion and semantic relevance coincide. That map calibrates the VLM's value cache during generation, progressively amplifying vision tokens in task-relevant regions and attenuating off-target ones, without removing any token from the context. The loop closes after each response: text-to-vision cross-attention is extracted from the decoder and fed back as the prior for the next burst, letting the system converge on semantically important regions over successive observations. We evaluate FOCUS on the 500-video EgoSchema subset in streaming mode, with a single Qwen3-VL-8B backbone shared by every method. It reaches 74.8% accuracy using 25.4 VLM calls per clip, against 74.6% with 55 calls for uniform sampling and 74.2% with 55 calls for BOLT. On egocentric video captioning across four domains, it matches the best baseline's quality while issuing 57% fewer VLM invocations than uniform sampling.
bullets: Detects meaningful scene changes with patch-embedding dissimilarity and triggers burst captures selectively.
Combines motion-based patch changes with top-down attention to focus on task-relevant regions.
Reweights, rather than removes, visual tokens during generation using a calibrated value cache.
Feeds decoder text-to-vision attention back into the next observation cycle for iterative refinement.
On a 500-video EgoSchema subset, achieves 74.8% accuracy with 25.4 calls per clip; captioning matches the best baseline with 57% fewer calls than uniform sampling.

papers.abstract: Attention kernels on Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) often underutilize their matrix units (MXUs) because of repeated matrix operand loads, vector-intensive computation, and dependencies that leave MXUs idle. We present FlyWheel, a set of fast TPU kernels for both softmax and linear attention. FlyWheel reformulates softmax and triangular inversion to reduce vector work, while coordinating data layouts to improve matrix operand reuse. It then overlaps independent computation to hide execution latency. We apply these techniques to both softmax attention and Gated DeltaNet on TPU v6e and v7x. FlyWheel speeds up softmax attention by up to $4.14\times$ over the state-of-the-art RPA kernel and $1.80\times$ over Splash Attention, reaching 81% of peak BF16 throughput on v6e. It also speeds up Gated DeltaNet prefill by up to $3.61\times$. Integrated into vLLM serving Qwen3.8-27B, FlyWheel improves prefill throughput by up to $1.56\times$ while maintaining comparable accuracy.
bullets: Targets TPU attention kernels whose MXUs are underutilized due to repeated loads, vector-heavy work, and execution dependencies.
Reformulates softmax and triangular inversion, coordinates data layouts for operand reuse, and overlaps independent operations.
Supports both softmax attention and Gated DeltaNet on TPU v6e and v7x.
Achieves up to 4.14× speedup for softmax attention, 3.61× for Gated DeltaNet prefill, and 1.56× higher vLLM prefill throughput while maintaining comparable accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Optimizes attention kernels for TPUs to improve matrix operand reuse and reduce latency, contributing to efficient attention mechanisms.
papers.title: FlyWheel: Attention Kernels Built for the TPU

papers.abstract: Agentic robots combine a vision-language brain, a tool-using harness, and a vision-language-action (VLA) policy. Serving a fleet of these agents introduces two coupled resource constraints: the brain repeatedly revisits long, growing key-value (KV) cache states, while the VLA executes action chunks under tight control deadlines. We characterize 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes generated by GPT-6-Astra, RPent, and pi0.5 (1,862 brain turns and 1,582 VLA inference chunks), profile both layers on H800 graphics processing units (GPUs), and replay the resulting agent programs on a vLLM serving engine. Brain contexts reach 215k tokens; the median Astra request takes 7.78 s, while the intervening environment-step gap is only 1.0 s. Under a 0.25 s action-chunk deadline, one VLA GPU meets the 1% starvation target for one robot; under a 1.0 s deadline, its measured capacity reaches at least 32. In sustained brain replay, increasing concurrency from 20 to 32 robots reduces throughput from about 2.4 to 0.6 requests/s as repetitive prefill displaces generation. A static active-episode cap restores 2.24-2.25 requests/s and raises completed trace-program throughput from 1.30 to 5.00-5.55 episodes/min. Our measurements expose the workload-dependent shift between action deadlines and brain KV residency, and establish practical principles for capacity planning and admission in sustained agentic robot fleets.
bullets: Characterizes 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes spanning 1,862 brain turns and 1,582 VLA inference chunks on H800 GPUs.
Brain contexts grow to 215k tokens; repeated long-context prefills can displace generation as robot concurrency increases.
A single VLA GPU supports one robot under a 0.25-second action deadline and at least 32 robots under a 1.0-second deadline.
Increasing sustained brain concurrency from 20 to 32 robots cuts throughput from about 2.4 to 0.6 requests/second.
A static active-episode cap restores roughly 2.24–2.25 requests/second and increases completed episodes to 5.00–5.55 per minute.

papers.selection_reason: Characterizes the resource constraints (KV-cache thrashing) of serving fleets of agentic robots, providing insights into system-level efficiency for embodied AI agents.
papers.title: Serving Agentic Robot Fleets: Workload Characterization, KV-Cache Thrashing, and Admission Control
papers.tldr: Agentic robot fleets face competing VLA action deadlines and brain KV-cache demands, but workload-aware admission control can prevent KV thrashing and sustain much higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate tokens in parallel via iterative denoising, but their bidirectional attention prevents the KV caching used by autoregressive models and recomputes the full attention map at every step, incurring quadratic per-step cost. Existing sparse attention methods for dLLMs construct a sparse mask after an initial full-attention warm-up and reuse it for the remaining steps, while allocating the sparsity budget uniformly across heads. We argue both choices ignore key structural properties of attention in dLLMs: empirically, attention patterns are only locally consistent across steps and shift abruptly at certain transitions, and different heads concentrate their attention mass to very different extents. To this end, we design Step-dLLM, which periodically refreshes a block-sparse mask at anchor steps along the denoising trajectory and reuses it within each locally consistent interval, while employing a head-adaptive global budget that more aggressively compresses heads with concentrated attention. Backed by a fused IO-aware Triton kernel for block-sparse attention, Step-dLLM applies to pre-trained LLaDA-1.5 and Dream-7B-Instruct without retraining, achieving a 2.78x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context with 256 denoising steps and 90% sparsity, while improving the accuracy-latency trade-off over prior sparse-attention methods.
bullets: Diffusion LLMs repeatedly recompute bidirectional attention, causing quadratic cost at every denoising step.
Attention patterns are only locally stable across steps and vary substantially in concentration between heads.
The method refreshes sparse masks at anchor steps and reuses them within locally consistent intervals.
A head-adaptive sparsity budget compresses concentrated heads more aggressively than uniform allocation.
With a fused Triton kernel, it achieves 2.78× end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context, 256 steps, and 90% sparsity.

The next ∆−1 steps reuse only these masks, recomputing Q,K, V and the attention weights from the current hidden states (Stage 3). A single query block per head is illustrated.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Step-dLLM, an adaptive step-aware sparse attention mechanism for efficient Diffusion LLM inference, directly relevant to efficient attention.
papers.title: Step-dLLM: Adaptive Step-aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Diffusion LLM Inference
papers.tldr: Step-dLLM accelerates diffusion LLM inference by adapting block-sparse attention masks to denoising-step changes and attention differences across heads.

papers.abstract: Streaming video question answering (QA) requires real-time reasoning over continuous video streams under strict latency and active-context budgets. Current streaming vision-language models (VLMs) often give confident yet ungrounded answers when queries are ambiguous or have false premises, or when relevant visual evidence is no longer in the active context. Proactive clarification can help, but must satisfy the same latency and memory constraints. We present StreamClarify, a training-free framework for grounded streaming QA that combines a pre-answer uncertainty check with hierarchical memory. The check uses the entropy of a binary pre-answer judgment as a lightweight uncertainty score to decide whether to answer directly or request clarification. To support re-answering, a temporal-pyramid KV cache maintains a bounded active visual context, while a CPU-side semantic retrieval archive provides access to historical frames. We further construct StreamClarify-QA, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,837 QA pairs from StreamBench and OVO-Bench, spanning standard, referential ambiguity, and unanswerable scenarios. Across three VLM backbones, StreamClarify improves Macro accuracy by up to 8.2 points over backbone-matched baselines. At comparable trigger rates, entropy-based selection achieves more than 18 points higher precision than random selection in identifying initially incorrect answers. Under oracle user guidance, clarification improves Macro accuracy by up to 3.5 points. We also report a controlled, oracle-assisted Qwen3-VL simulation on Ambiguous QA with generated questions and referent-only user replies, where the entropy-gated condition improves accuracy by 8.3 points.
bullets: Targets confident but ungrounded answers caused by ambiguous queries, false premises, or missing active-context evidence.
Uses a training-free entropy-based pre-answer uncertainty check to decide between answering and asking for clarification.
Maintains bounded visual memory with a temporal-pyramid KV cache plus CPU-side semantic retrieval of historical frames.
Introduces StreamClarify-QA, a 1,837-pair diagnostic benchmark covering standard, ambiguous, and unanswerable scenarios.
Across three VLM backbones, improves Macro accuracy by up to 8.2 points; oracle clarification adds up to 3.5 points, while entropy selection substantially outperforms random triggering.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of StreamClarify. The framework augments a frozen streaming VLM with a pre-answer uncertainty check in a twostage generation loop and hierarchical memory. (a) When pre-answer entropy does not exceed the trigger threshold, the system answers directly using the active temporal-pyramid KV (TP-KV) cache. (b) TP-KV keeps recent frames at full resolution and compresses older observed frames within a fixed active budget. (c) When entropy exceeds the threshold, the system requests clarification and converts the resulting user guidance into a retrieval query. (d) Semantic search retrieves relevant past clips from the archive and combines them with the active TP-KV context for answering after clarification.

papers.tldr: StreamClarify enables grounded, low-latency streaming video QA by detecting uncertain answers, requesting clarification, and retrieving relevant historical visual context.

papers.abstract: Multi-LoRA serving allows many task-specific adapters to share a common base model, but scaling to large adapter fleets introduces substantial storage, loading, and execution overheads. Post-hoc compression can reduce the memory footprint of trained LoRA adapters, yet smaller ranks do not automatically translate into faster serving. For instance, padding, factor access, and generic kernels can obscure the retained low-rank structure, while independently recompressing thousands of modules also incurs significant preparation overhead. We present LoRAForge, a system connecting batched factor construction to rank-specialized execution through an explicit retained-rank representation. It supports two allocation policies: uniform retention ratios (LoRAForge-U) and spectral-energy budget allocation (LoRAForge-S). Both share FlashTSQR factor construction and the same serving backend. FlashTSQR exploits parallelism across modules and row tiles, accelerating factor construction by up to $2.28\times$ over matched library QR. In a fixed-work Qwen control, the shared runtime adds $1.17$--$1.22\times$ throughput across both compressed policies, with negligible gains on original adapters. Across 85 trained open-weighted Qwen and Llama adapters, the spectral policy's floored quality configuration retains about 7.7% of adapter parameters with fleet-average score drops of at most 1.2 points on a 0--100 scale. The same rank-floored $1/12$ spectral exports achieve substantial token-throughput gains on both AMD and NVIDIA GPUs.
bullets: Addresses storage, loading, and execution overheads when serving large fleets of task-specific LoRA adapters.
Uses an explicit retained-rank representation linking batched factor construction to rank-specialized execution.
Provides uniform-ratio and spectral-energy allocation policies, sharing FlashTSQR construction and a common serving backend.
FlashTSQR accelerates factor construction by up to 2.28× over matched library QR; the runtime adds 1.17–1.22× throughput in fixed-work Qwen tests.

A floored spectral configuration retains about 7.7% of adapter parameters with fleet-average score drops of at most 1.2 points across 85 Qwen and Llama adapters, while improving token throughput on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs.

papers.abstract: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content-position or bias-position terms. Unlike RoPE, which encodes position via per-token rotations directly on the queries and keys, relative-position terms generally require pairwise offset-dependent computation or lookups, complicating their integration into fused attention kernels and introducing severe memory, bandwidth, and compute overheads as sequences scale. To address this bottleneck, we propose an exact attention algorithm that incorporates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled computation. Our method (1) uses offset-aware tiling to avoid redundant indexing and memory accesses, (2) computes only the necessary key/query-relation products and reuses them across token pairs in both forward and backward passes, and (3) uses offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation, eliminating atomic contention. We provide a unified, efficient Triton implementation across diverse relative-position attention mechanisms and evaluate it against naive and specialized implementations. For 8K-token sequences, our method speeds up the forward (backward) pass by 1.8-6.4$\times$ (2.0-21$\times$) and reduces peak memory up to 2.9-128$\times$ (1.4-54$\times$) over the strongest baseline for each mechanism, enabling long-context end-to-end transcription that is 1.8$\times$ faster and uses 2.4$\times$ less memory. Our method thus provides a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.
bullets: Addresses the pairwise offset computation and memory overhead that hinder efficient relative-position attention.
Introduces offset-aware tiled computation, reusable query/key relation products, and offset-based gradient aggregation without atomic contention.
Provides a unified Triton implementation supporting diverse relative-position attention mechanisms.
At 8K tokens, reports 1.8–6.4× faster forward passes, 2.0–21× faster backward passes, and up to 2.9–128× lower peak memory than the strongest mechanism-specific baselines.
Enables end-to-end long-context transcription that is 1.8× faster and uses 2.4× less memory.

papers.abstract: Existing serving systems for large language models batch requests for many different LoRA adapters on one GPU. However, these systems reject adapters from other parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as DoRA, (IA), VeRA and OFT. One solution to this is to convert these adapters to LoRA, but this induces a significant memory and accuracy cost. Instead, we show that, under some modifications, a batched LoRA kernel can serve all of these methods exactly and efficiently. We achieve this by writing each method in one normal form, a LoRA computation with six slots for an adapter's own vectors and matrices. Some slots can merge into an adapter's weights at load time; the others remain live and induce a cost. We give ways to efficiently pay this cost and predict it from a zero-parameter byte model. We package this system, Scute, and build it on top of vLLM. Scute serves all five methods, coming as checkpoints from the Hugging Face PEFT library, in one batch, and it matches that library with a mean error of at most 1.5% of each adapter's effect. Under a burst of requests on an RTX A6000, a mix of these methods takes 5-17% more decode time than the same number of LoRA adapters. Furthermore, using Scute, the same GPU can serve 64 to 1024 (IA) and VeRA adapters at 1.5x to at least 2.5x the request rate of their LoRA conversions.
bullets: Existing systems typically reject DoRA, (IA), VeRA, and OFT adapters or incur memory and accuracy costs by converting them to LoRA.
Scute expresses five PEFT methods in a common six-slot LoRA normal form, merging some components at load time and efficiently handling the rest during serving.
A zero-parameter byte model predicts the runtime cost of the remaining live components.
Built on vLLM, Scute serves Hugging Face PEFT checkpoints in one batch with at most 1.5% mean error relative to the PEFT library.
On an RTX A6000, mixed-method bursts take 5–17% more decode time than equivalent LoRA batches, while (IA) and VeRA can achieve 1.5× to at least 2.5× the request rate of LoRA conversions.

papers.abstract: Persistent homology (PH) is a mathematically principled multi-scale topological descriptor of shape and connectivity in data. It is widely applied in image classification, segmentation, and shape analysis across medical and aerial imaging, providing structural information that pixel-wise deep learning may overlook. Standard cubical PH decomposes an image into cubical cells (vertices, edges, and squares) and reduces them sequentially in filtration order. This sequential reduction has $Θ(n)$ parallel depth for an $n$-pixel image, limiting within-image GPU parallelism and constraining its use in topology-aware deep learning. We introduce CuPH, a GPU-based parallel algorithm for computing cubical PH on 2D images that operates directly on pixels rather than cubical cells. CuPH buckets pixels by filtration values, activates them with a level-synchronous sweep, and tracks connected components with a lock-free union-find method. We prove that CuPH produces persistence diagrams identical to standard cubical PH on integer inputs, with a stability bound for floating-point inputs. CuPH reduces parallel depth from $Θ(n)$ to $O(L\log n)$ for an image with $L$ intensity levels. We implement the level sweep as a single CUDA kernel, eliminating cross-level kernel-launch overhead. Empirically, CuPH is $18.6$--$99.6\times$ faster than the existing GPU baseline (CMP). As a drop-in PH backend, CuPH accelerates topology-aware classification ($4.2$--$16.7\times$) and segmentation ($8.3$--$44\times$) while preserving accuracy. It also enables computing full-image PH losses on high-resolution images, improving segmentation Dice by $2.2$--$4.6$ points over patch-local PH baselines and accelerating training by $25$--$31\times$.
bullets: Addresses the limited within-image GPU parallelism of standard, sequential cubical persistent homology.
Buckets pixels by filtration value, sweeps levels synchronously, and uses a lock-free union-find to track connected components in one CUDA kernel.
Proves equivalence to standard cubical PH for integer-valued inputs and provides a stability bound for floating-point inputs.
Reduces parallel depth from Θ(n) to O(L log n), where n is image size and L is the number of intensity levels.
Reports substantial speedups for PH, topology-aware classification and segmentation, while enabling full-image PH losses that improve segmentation over patch-local baselines.

papers.abstract: Semantic caching lowers the cost of serving large language models (LLMs) by reusing stored responses for similar requests. In multi-turn conversations, whether a cached response is acceptable depends on both conversations' histories, which embedding similarity of requests and histories predicts poorly (AUC 0.62--0.74 on five workloads). We therefore learn the \emph{reuse risk}, the probability that a cached response is unacceptable, from judge feedback, and choose a budgeted set of conversation states to cache by weighing the generation cost a reuse avoids against a price for unacceptable reuse. We propose CUCB-SC-MT, which learns a cache from logged conversations with a suboptimality guarantee, and CLCB-LS-MT, which learns online and has $\tilde O(\sqrt N)$ regret over $N$ requests when conversation states recur. On math-tutoring (SocraTeach) and movie-ticketing (Taskmaster-3) conversations, both achieve lower loss than prior semantic caching approaches: ContextCache, multi-turn variants of ElastiCache and vCache, and single-turn semantic caching at every cache budget. With 1,000 cache entries, CLCB-LS-MT avoids 35--41\% of the generation cost through acceptable reuses, against at most 22--25\% for the baselines, and lowers estimated serving latency by 19--35\%.
bullets: Request and history embedding similarity poorly predicts whether a cached response is acceptable, with AUC 0.62–0.74 across five workloads.
The approach learns reuse risk—the probability that a cached response is unacceptable—and balances avoided generation cost against reuse risk under a cache budget.
CUCB-SC-MT learns from logged conversations with a suboptimality guarantee, while CLCB-LS-MT learns online with ~O(√N) regret when conversation states recur.
On math-tutoring and movie-ticketing conversations, both methods outperform prior semantic-caching approaches at every evaluated cache budget.
With 1,000 cache entries, CLCB-LS-MT avoids 35–41% of generation cost through acceptable reuse and reduces estimated latency by 19–35%.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon reasoning and agentic workloads strain KV-cache capacity and decode attention throughput. We present Jet-QSparse, a training-free method that combines compact NVFP4 cache storage with native FP4 query-key computation on Blackwell tensor cores. A dense scan scores the full key history and selects 128-token blocks for sparse FP16 value aggregation with FP32 accumulation, preserving higher precision in the output-forming step while enabling contiguous tile loads. Calibrated key centering and at most two BF16 pages per sequence and layer address quantization error; FP8 prefill uses a temporary arena while the persistent cache is packed directly from BF16 activations. Across four hybrid LLMs, a budget of 128 blocks per KV head shows no detected accuracy loss on the evaluated mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks, although some smaller budgets incur losses. With 64 blocks, Qwen3.8-27B achieves a $1.94\times$ end-to-end decode speedup over dense BF16 at 128K context and batch size 16 on one GB300, and the measured Qwen KV pools provide $2.58$-$2.76\times$ BF16's token capacity.
bullets: Targets KV-cache capacity limits and decode-attention throughput in long-horizon reasoning and agentic workloads.
Uses training-free NVFP4 cache storage, native FP4 query-key computation, dense history scoring, and sparse FP16 value aggregation.
At 128 selected blocks per KV head, no accuracy loss was detected across evaluated mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks.
At 64 blocks, Qwen3.8-27B achieved a 1.94× end-to-end decode speedup at 128K context and batch size 16 on one GB300.
Measured Qwen KV pools stored 2.58–2.76× as many tokens as BF16; smaller budgets could reduce accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Presents Jet-QSparse, a training-free method for accelerating LLM inference using 4-bit sparse attention and quantized KV cache, directly relevant to efficient attention and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Jet-QSparse: Accelerating Agentic LLM Inference with 4-Bit Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: Jet-QSparse accelerates long-context agentic LLM decoding by combining 4-bit KV-cache storage with sparse attention while preserving evaluated accuracy at a sufficient sparsity budget.

papers.abstract: Pretrained text embeddings encode semantic structure in high-dimensional continuous spaces whose coordinates are difficult to interpret. We introduce Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding (ISBC), which learns a small set of binary dimensions from frozen embeddings without taxonomy labels or downstream outcomes. A trainable encoder and affine decoder combine reconstruction with controls on activity, factor utilization, dependence, and activation uncertainty. Individual bits and their conjunctions select overlapping document groups; complete activation profiles provide finer contexts for conditional comparisons. We evaluate these representations across corpora, backbones, and code configurations through reconstruction, geometry, predictive probes, and document inspection. Empirical cases identify both distinctions within existing categories and shared content across their boundaries. In a mixed-domain corpus, the most frequent profiles predominantly identify source collections, while selected within-source comparisons reveal sentiment and migration contrasts. Selected associations persist in additional documents encoded without refitting. In an engagement application, bits alone improve prediction of log-transformed outcomes over a constant reference, while their combinations identify within-event content contrasts associated with engagement. The results support using binary coordinates and their combinations for empirical interpretation, with complete profiles providing a fine, partly initialization-dependent description rather than a unique discrete taxonomy.
bullets: Learns binary dimensions without taxonomy labels or downstream outcomes.
Combines reconstruction with controls for sparsity, factor use, dependence, and activation uncertainty.
Uses bits, conjunctions, and complete activation profiles for document grouping and conditional comparisons.
Evaluations across corpora and embedding backbones find source, sentiment, migration, and engagement-related contrasts.
Complete profiles offer fine-grained but partly initialization-dependent descriptions, not a unique taxonomy.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding (ISBC) for text embeddings, offering a sparse, interpretable representation that aligns with token pruning and LLM representation learning.
papers.title: ISBC: Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding of Pretrained Text Embeddings
papers.tldr: ISBC converts frozen text embeddings into interpretable sparse binary codes whose individual bits and combinations reveal document groups and contextual distinctions.

papers.abstract: Early-exit language models decide for each token how much computation to spend, usually by stopping once the prediction is confident. Yet a token is not a fixed unit: tokenizers cut words into different numbers of pieces in different languages. We ask where inside a word such a policy spends its budget. In Qwen3, along two adaptive axes (the timesteps of a spiking conversion and the layers of the original Transformer), confidence stopping gives the continuation pieces of a word less computation than its first piece in English, German, and Turkish, but more in Bangla. Segmentation drives this. Re-segmenting the same parallel passages with BPE-dropout shifts the gap by up to eight exits on both axes, small models trained under two tokenizers shift Bangla's gap by six exits, and BLOOM and mGPT, which split Bangla less finely, give it the English pattern. Characters per token do not predict the gap across languages; within-word surprisal explains 75% of its variance. A learned stopping head beats confidence stopping by 7 to 8 points, but gains less than one point over the best mix of fixed exits at equal cost, and sometimes loses. All results come from offline analysis, not measured speedups.
bullets: In Qwen3, continuation pieces generally receive less computation than first pieces in English, German, and Turkish, but more in Bangla.
Changing tokenization with BPE-dropout shifts within-word computation gaps by up to eight exits; tokenizer choice also reverses Bangla’s pattern across models.
Characters per token do not explain the gaps across languages, while within-word surprisal explains 75% of their variance.
A learned stopping head improves over confidence stopping by 7–8 points, but offers less than one point over the best fixed-exit mixture at equal cost and can sometimes underperform.
The study is based on offline analysis, so it does not measure actual speedups.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes adaptive computation and early-exit behavior in LLMs as a function of tokenization, relevant to efficient inference and LLM architecture.
papers.title: A Token Is Not a Unit of Difficulty: Segmentation Controls Where Adaptive Computation Goes Inside a Word
papers.tldr: Adaptive computation is allocated differently across word pieces largely because tokenizer segmentation shapes where models perceive difficulty.

papers.abstract: Image denoising is a fundamental problem in mobile photography. Despite a large number of solutions proposed for this task, the majority of them are trained on synthetically produced noisy images, and are additionally too computationally heavy for processing full-resolution images on mobile devices. This creates a need for efficient deep learning-based models that are not only performant but can also be deployed on constrained mobile hardware. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose the participants to design fast solutions that can denoise Full HD resolution photos while running on popular smartphone GPUs from Qualcomm and Arm. For this, the participants were provided with a large-scale dataset consisting of noisy-clean image pairs captured in the wild. The runtime of all models was evaluated on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 chipsets with the Adreno and Mali GPUs, respectively. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to perform high-quality image denoising under 100 milliseconds on both platforms while reaching a PSNR score of over 37 dB. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.
bullets: Targets the computational and realism limitations of existing denoising methods trained on synthetic noise.
Participants developed fast models for full-HD image denoising on constrained smartphone hardware.
Models were trained or evaluated using large-scale noisy–clean image pairs captured in real-world conditions.
Runtime was measured on Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 devices using Adreno and Mali GPUs.
Top solutions achieved over 37 dB PSNR with sub-100 ms processing on both platforms.

papers.abstract: Image super-resolution is widely used on mobile devices for upscaling various types of image data. This creates a need for efficient deep learning-based models that are not only performant but can also be deployed on neural processing units (NPUs) present in the majority of mobile and IoT chipsets. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose the participants to design fast solutions that can upsample images from Full HD to 4K resolution while running on popular mobile NPUs from Qualcomm and MediaTek. For this, the participants were provided with the DIV2K dataset and trained models to do an efficient 3X image upscaling. The competition had two tracks: in the first track, the models had to be fully quantized (INT8), and the runtime of all models was evaluated on the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 NPU. In the second track, the participants were developing floating-point solutions that were evaluated on the MediaTek Dimensity 9500 NPU. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to reconstruct 4K images under 5 milliseconds while reaching a PSNR score of 30 dB. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.
bullets: Motivation: enable efficient deep-learning super-resolution on widely used mobile and IoT NPUs.
Task: upscale Full HD images to 4K resolution using models trained with DIV2K.
Track 1 required fully quantized INT8 models evaluated on the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 NPU.
Track 2 evaluated floating-point models on the MediaTek Dimensity 9500 NPU.
Top solutions achieved sub-5-ms reconstruction with 30 dB PSNR; the paper surveys the challenge models.

papers.abstract: Replacing the matrix in an iteration with random low-rank matrices can reduce the cost of matrix-vector multiplication. However, even if the sampled matrices equal the original matrix in expectation, the expected squared norm of the random iterates may grow while the original iteration converges. Under a fixed rank bound, we study how to choose the distribution of these random matrices to minimize this growth when sampling independently at each step. We derive an exact formula for the optimal asymptotic growth factor and use it to determine when the expected squared norm can converge to zero. We then characterize precisely when a fixed sampling distribution achieves this optimal factor and construct finite-support optimal distributions in every attainable case. These results determine the minimum rank required for stability and provide optimal sampling designs under the prescribed rank constraint.
bullets: Unbiased random matrix approximations can still make expected squared iterates grow, even when the original iteration converges.
For independently sampled approximations with a fixed rank limit, the study derives the exact optimal asymptotic growth factor.
It establishes when the expected squared norm converges to zero and determines the minimum rank needed for stability.
The work characterizes all sampling distributions attaining the optimum and constructs finite-support optimal designs whenever attainable.

papers.abstract: Calling a tool through generated text adds decoding steps, even when the computation itself is short. We study an alternative: a small neural module that runs inside a language model's forward pass. A learned writer turns hidden states into a symbolic tape, a short sequence of discrete symbols that encodes the computation. The module, trained separately and then frozen, reduces the tape to a result, and a learned reader returns that result to the model. We evaluate arithmetic and object tracking in gemma-3-1b-it. With a writer trained on labelled tapes, the layer answers all 750 items of BIG-Bench Hard's tracking shuffled objects correctly. At seven people it needs about 1/10 of the GPU kernel time of a text-tool baseline that uses the same host model and exact code, with accuracy 1.00 against 0.99. The writer can also be learned from answers alone, guided by a hand-written copying prior, but less reliably: 5 of 6 runs succeed in the 1B host and 2 of 4 in the 4B host. Two independently trained layers keep their task accuracy when attached to one model, and a learned gate keeps them silent on the tested general-text and look-alike prompts. The results support a narrow use case: a bounded computation that returns one symbol can avoid the decoding cost of a textual tool call. Extracting the right input reliably, and deciding when to act, remain the main open problems.
bullets: Targets arithmetic and object-tracking tasks in Gemma-3-1B-IT.
A learned writer encodes hidden states into a short discrete symbolic tape; a frozen module computes on it, and a reader returns the result.
With labelled tapes, the layer correctly answers all 750 BIG-Bench Hard shuffled-object tracking items.
At seven people, it uses about one-tenth the GPU kernel time of a text-tool baseline, with accuracy 1.00 versus 0.99.
Answer-only tape learning is less reliable; extracting inputs and deciding when to invoke the module remain open problems.

papers.abstract: Streaming 3D reconstruction models keep past video frames in a recurrent state, fast weights from test-time training, or a key-value (KV) cache. Each written frame shifts the coordinate frame of later cameras or occupies GPU memory. Training-free rules decide what to write from a signal of the current frame. How much they write accounts for their mean accuracy: spending the update budget of a gate at uniformly spaced frames, with no signal, matches nine published gates, and the budget bounds the drift of the state wherever the writes fall. We propose SceneBound, a training-free rule that writes a frame only when its predicted camera pose lies at least a fixed radius from every stored keyframe. Its keyframe count stays within a constant factor of the covering number of the visited poses, the fewest views that keep a keyframe near every camera, so the count grows with the places visited and stays flat when the camera returns. In large scenes, SceneBound closes a submap once decoding its first frame again reveals drift. SceneBound uses one radius across four released models and three memory types. In the recurrent state of CUT3R and the KV cache of StreamVGGT, it achieves the lowest mean trajectory error among the published training-free rules we evaluate, in one pass and over nine passes of a scene, where its keyframes grow by 3% to 6%.
bullets: Uniformly spacing updates can match published signal-based gates, suggesting update budget largely determines mean accuracy and bounds state drift.
SceneBound stores a frame only when its predicted camera pose is outside a fixed-radius neighborhood of existing keyframes.
Its keyframe count tracks the covering number of visited poses: it grows with exploration but remains stable when the camera revisits locations.
For large scenes, it closes submaps when decoding the first frame reveals renewed drift.
Across four models and three memory types, it achieved the lowest mean trajectory error among evaluated training-free rules for CUT3R and StreamVGGT, with only 3%–6% keyframe growth over nine passes.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free keyframe-selection rule controlling memory (recurrent state, KV cache) in streaming 3D reconstruction; relevant to 3D perception and memory efficiency.
papers.title: SceneBound: How Much Should a Streaming 3D Reconstruction Model Remember?
papers.tldr: SceneBound is a training-free memory-writing rule that limits streaming 3D reconstruction drift while keeping memory tied to the camera poses actually visited.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) show promise for clinical image understanding, but their computational and memory requirements hinder deployment on resource-constrained clinical hardware. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers a practical compression strategy without retraining, yet its effectiveness depends strongly on the calibration data. We propose CoreCalib, a training-free and quantizer-agnostic framework for constructing compact calibration sets that preserve the target medical VQA distribution. CoreCalib stratifies data by clinical question class, identifies representative visual modes using frozen DINOv2 features with UMAP and HDBSCAN, and expands selected images into class-balanced question-answer pairs. On Kvasir-VQA-x1, we evaluate CoreCalib with MASQuant, GPTQ, and QIG using a fixed 128-pair budget. CoreCalib achieves the best METEOR with all three quantizers and the best ROUGE-L with MASQuant and GPTQ. With W4A8 MASQuant, it improves METEOR from 0.5672 with COCO calibration to 0.6234, recovering approximately 41% of the degradation relative to BF16. These results support CoreCalib as a data-centric component for resource-efficient medical VLM deployment. Project page: https://magnusdtd.github.io/CoreCalib/ .
bullets: Addresses the challenge of deploying medical VLMs on hardware with limited compute and memory.
Constructs calibration sets by balancing clinical question classes and selecting representative visual modes with frozen DINOv2 features, UMAP, and HDBSCAN.
Is training-free and quantizer-agnostic, evaluated with MASQuant, GPTQ, and QIG using 128 question-answer pairs on Kvasir-VQA-x1.
Achieves the best METEOR for all three quantizers and the best ROUGE-L for MASQuant and GPTQ.
With W4A8 MASQuant, raises METEOR from 0.5672 using COCO calibration to 0.6234, recovering about 41% of the degradation relative to BF16.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of CoreCalib and its role in resource-efficient medical VLM deployment. (B) CoreCalib constructs a compact calibration workload by (1) stratifying the medical VQA data by clinical question class, (2) selecting densityaware representative images using frozen DINOv2 features with UMAP and HDBSCAN, (3) expanding representative images into multiple QA pairs and balancing them across question classes, and (4) forming a small calibration set, such as 128 QA pairs from 23 images. (C) The calibration set can be used with different PTQ methods, including MASQuant, GPTQ, and QIG, to produce a quantized medical VLM with improved capability retention.

papers.abstract: Subliminal learning allows AI models to inherit hidden preferences from seemingly unrelated training data, such as number sequences. Safety audits may evaluate models at standard 16-bit precision, while deployments may use compressed, quantized weights. We ask whether quantization changes the expression of a subliminal preference and what drives any resulting change. To investigate, we implant a "favourite animal: panda" preference into Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. We define its net strength as the difference in mean panda-answer probability between subliminal models and neutrally trained controls under the same quantization setting. Applying this metric across different compression levels reveals a stark contrast. While behaviour remains stable at 8 bits, 4-bit quantization triggers severe, opposing shifts depending on the quantizer. Half-Quadratic Quantization (HQQ) amplifies the preference, raising the subliminally trained model's panda probability from roughly 55% at 16 bits to 64% at 4 bits, while the controls stay near 17%. This raises the trait's net strength ~1.3 times its 16-bit value. In contrast, NormalFloat (NF4) at 4-bit suppresses it, shrinking the net strength to just ~0.3 times its 16-bit value, despite producing rounding errors of the same size to within 4%. We examine the structure of the rounding errors and find that their arrangement drives the divergence. Randomly shuffling HQQ's errors within each quantization group, without changing their magnitude, shifts the trait's net strength between 0.2 and 1.6 times its 16-bit value. Despite these opposing shifts, the underlying fine-tuning signal remains largely intact. Because a model's internal state and outward behaviour diverge so unpredictably under compression, a 16-bit audit cannot reliably bound real-world risks. Safety evaluations must test the exact quantized weights intended for deployment.
bullets: The study implants a hidden “panda” preference into Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and measures its net behavioral strength against neutral controls.
Behavior is stable at 8-bit precision but diverges sharply at 4 bits depending on the quantizer.
HQQ amplifies the preference, while NF4 suppresses it, despite producing similarly sized rounding errors.
Shuffling error arrangements changes preference strength substantially, indicating that error structure—not just magnitude—drives the effect.
The underlying fine-tuning signal remains largely intact, but compressed internal states and outputs become difficult to predict from 16-bit behavior.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview. Left: A 16-bit audit of a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct student, fine-tuned on a panda-loving teacher’s number sequences that never mention pandas, finds a “favourite animal: panda” preference at 55% against 17% for a neutrally trained control; this gap, normalized, defines the baseline net strength R = 1. Middle: Deploying these exact same weights at 4 bits using two quantizers with identical targeted layers, group sizes, and error magnitudes moves the preference in opposite directions: R ≈ 1.3 under HQQ and R ≈ 0.3 under NF4. In contrast, an explicitly trained student of matched strength remains stable at R ≈ 1. Right: Both quantizers preserve more than 99% of the fine-tuning delta. The quantized weights are nearly identical, yet the resulting behaviours are a factor of four apart; the 16-bit measurement bounds neither.

Fig. 2. Experimental pipeline. (1) Three types of students are trained using the same LoRA recipe: subliminal students on a panda teacher’s number sequences, neutral controls on a standard teacher’s number sequences, and explicit students on the panda teacher’s ordinary text. (2) Merged weights are quantized using HQQ (at 8, 4, 3, and 2 bits) and NF4 (at 4 bits), recording the layer-wise rounding error E = Q(W )−W . (3) HQQ’s 4-bit error is then applied unchanged, negated, shuffled within groups of 64 weights, or replaced by size-matched Gaussian noise (heatmaps are schematic). (4) Final evaluations measure outward behaviour via the control-adjusted panda probability relative to 16 bits (Eq. (1)), and internal stability by tracking how much of the fine-tuning delta and installed activation direction survive.

papers.abstract: We introduce GateTrim, an adaptive-rank post-training quantization method for large language models that learns matrix-specific ranks through gate optimization and threshold-based rank selection. GateTrim standardizes the low-rank factors of a quantized low-rank--residual representation, learns a separate gate vector for each target weight matrix, and uses a shared threshold to automatically determine its retained rank. The resulting ranks can differ across matrices, and the compact quantized representations are subsequently reconstructed. We evaluate GateTrim under W4A8 on Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Across all five models, we observe a counterintuitive finding: increasing the threshold from $τ=0.3$ to $τ=0.7$ reduces the mean retained rank by 46.60%--67.89% while simultaneously lowering WikiText-2 perplexity by 0.59%--5.17%. Threshold 0.7 achieves the lowest mean retained rank and final perplexity among the three tested thresholds, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7, and reduces measured target-export size by 1.50%--4.25% relative to 0.3. GateTrim uses an $8\times512$-token fitting pool and a separate development pool of the same size. Its Qwen3-4B/8B/14B perplexities at $τ=0.7$ are numerically below TwinQuant's published W4A8 values, reported with a $128\times2048$-token calibration pool, in a cross-study comparison. On Qwen3-8B, the threshold-0.7 configuration already has the lowest perplexity before reconstruction under both tested initialization seeds; reconstruction improves it further without increasing retained rank or export size.
bullets: Learns matrix-specific ranks using gate vectors and a shared threshold in a quantized low-rank–residual representation.
Evaluated on five Qwen3 and Llama models under W4A8, using separate fitting and development pools.
Raising the threshold from 0.3 to 0.7 cuts mean retained rank by 46.60%–67.89% and lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 0.59%–5.17%.
At threshold 0.7, measured target-export size is reduced by 1.50%–4.25% versus threshold 0.3.
Reconstruction further improves Qwen3-8B perplexity without increasing retained rank or export size; cross-study comparisons to TwinQuant are not directly controlled.

papers.abstract: Serving and fine-tuning a large language model on the same GPUs can turn the idle capacity between inference bursts into training progress, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) makes this co-location cheap because both workloads read a single frozen copy of the base weights. The difficulty lies in the fine-tuning backward pass, which has no counterpart in inference. Current co-serving systems schedule backward work per serving iteration: each iteration carries a fixed backward budget, and requests that arrive in the meantime wait for it to finish, so fine-tuning dictates inference latency whenever load spikes. We observe that the backward pass of a LoRA microbatch decomposes into per-layer tasks over the same weights that the inference forward pass visits, which allows backward work to be scheduled at layer rather than iteration granularity. Building on this observation, LayerLoom attaches same-layer backward tasks to the inference forward pass and, at each layer, runs only as many of them as the latency slack of in-flight requests permits. To keep a ready task at every layer, LayerLoom maintains a wavefront of fine-tuning microbatches staggered across layers, and it bounds the wavefront's activation memory by offloading microbatch state to host memory and prefetching it ahead of the layer where the scheduler plans to use it. A fused kernel serves the paired forward and backward GEMMs from a single read of each base weight. Because all backward work of an iteration finishes within its forward pass, new requests join the next iteration as in continuous batching. On an RTX 4090 GPU running Llama-3.1-8B under a bursty production trace, LayerLoom raises joint SLO attainment by 13.5-21.8 points over prior works with fine-tuning throughput that is comparable or up to 12% higher, and it reaches the same training losses.
bullets: Problem: Iteration-level backward scheduling makes fine-tuning delay inference during request bursts.
Method: Attach per-layer LoRA backward tasks to inference forward passes and execute only work allowed by each layer’s latency slack.
System design: A staggered microbatch wavefront, host-memory offloading/prefetching, and fused forward-backward GEMMs maintain readiness while limiting activation memory and base-weight reads.

Results: On an RTX 4090 serving Llama-3.1-8B under a bursty production trace, joint SLO attainment improves by 13.5–21.8 points over prior work, with comparable or up to 12% higher fine-tuning throughput.
Scope: The abstract reports results for LoRA co-serving on one GPU/model and trace; broader generality is not established.

papers.abstract: Activation recomputation saves accelerator memory by replaying forward segments during the backward pass, but replay is only correct if it sees the state the original forward pass saw. Mutable buffers, aliased bytes and random-generator state can change in between, so re-executing unchanged code can differentiate a different computation. We make this state explicit. A versioned replay contract specifies what replay must restore, and a joint planner chooses, per segment, between activation retention, whole-buffer snapshots and selective-region preservation, charging each option its measured memory and recovery cost. Independent derivative and byte-level checks validate the contract, and a Torch/JAX cohort retains all 5,900 execution records, including matches, rejections and divergences. On frozen sparse-write H100 workloads, each measured over fifty fresh processes, joint planning reduces paired step time by 18.16% against a correctly costed eager/whole planner at a 44 GiB budget (approximate 97.5% ratio interval $[.8172,.8195]$). At 32 GiB, where the eager/whole planner has no feasible static policy, joint planning is 4.98% faster than fixed regions at 29.94 rather than 26.20 GiB. A complete CIFAR-100 dense-queue application runs seven methods for 100 encoder and 25 probe epochs at six training seeds, with byte-identical test scores within each seed. There, joint planning uses 22.41% more allocated memory than whole snapshots, with a process-time geometric-mean ratio of 1.0080 (seed range $[.9845,1.0191]$). Together, the results map where selective preservation pays off: sparse writes with large activations benefit, while in the dense-queue workload whole snapshots use less allocated memory.
bullets: Replay can diverge when mutable buffers, aliased bytes, or RNG state change between forward and backward passes.
Versioned replay contracts specify required state restoration and support derivative and byte-level correctness checks.
A joint planner chooses activation retention, whole-buffer snapshots, or selective-region preservation using measured memory and recovery costs.
On frozen sparse-write H100 workloads, it reduced paired step time by 18.16% at 44 GiB and enabled a feasible policy at 32 GiB.
In a dense-queue CIFAR-100 workload, whole snapshots used less allocated memory, while process time was similar.],

papers.abstract: Adam keeps two FP32 moments per parameter, twice the bytes of the FP32 weights, yet compressing them is risky: the update divides by the square root of the second moment, so small reconstruction errors can change the restored computation substantially. We study guarded moment compression, in which a coordinate's decoded moments are accepted only if they reproduce the native FP32 Adam update to within a tolerance $τ$, in units of the learning rate, for every gradient in a clipped domain; all other coordinates are stored exactly. The natural certificate, which ranges each update separately over gradient intervals, fails: on one million trained OPT-125M coordinates it escapes 98.9% of coordinates and the payload grows to 126.6% of raw FP32. Our key observation is that both updates consume the same gradient and parameter. Bounding their difference directly, with FP32 rounding-error allowances and a fixed mixed linear-logarithmic gradient partition, cuts escapes to 0.53% and the payload to 28.3% at $τ=0.01$. Across 120 complete-checkpoint restores of OPT-125M and ResNet-18, with four trained seeds and three training fractions per model, guarded 8-bit log codes shrink moment payloads by 69.5% and 71.9% relative to FP32, 40.8% and 45.4% relative to equally guarded BF16, and 29.3% and 37.6% relative to equally guarded blockwise 8-bit, and every restored first update stays within tolerance. Encoding and restoration together take 2.3-2.6$\times$ as long as guarded BF16 but less time than guarded blockwise 8-bit. Searching both moment codes jointly saves under 0.001% more bytes at 6% more codec time, so per-moment rounding suffices. The guarantee covers the first restored update under a pinned Torch operation model; we measure subsequent training empirically.
bullets: Naive per-update interval certificates are too loose, causing 98.9% coordinate escapes and payload growth to 126.6% of FP32.
The method directly bounds the difference between native and decoded Adam updates over a shared clipped-gradient domain, including FP32 rounding errors.
With tolerance τ=0.01, escapes fall to 0.53% and the payload reaches 28.3% of raw FP32.
Across OPT-125M and ResNet-18 restores, guarded 8-bit log codes reduce moment payloads by 69.5% and 71.9% versus FP32.
The guarantee applies to the first restored update under a pinned Torch operation model; later training behavior is evaluated empirically.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference with a drafter whose proposed tokens are verified by the target model in parallel. Under lossless speculative sampling, a draft token is accepted with probability one minus the total variation (TV) distance between the target and draft distributions, yet drafters are often trained with cross-entropy (CE) or KL. We first show that under matched and well-tuned training, TV matches or surpasses several published draft-training objectives when fine-tuning, and a fixed TV and KL mixture does the same when training from scratch. We identify two remaining problems, TV's vanishing gradients on undercovered tokens and the prefix products that starve later positions in acceptance-length objectives. To address both, we derive TVP, a loss family based on expected acceptance length, whose power parameter interpolates between coverage and acceptance oriented objectives. Annealing the power from zero to one gives the highest or tied-highest acceptance length across three drafter architectures and three target models, including longer drafts and block verification. TVP improves acceptance length over CE by 9.8% when fine-tuning, and over the public DFlash2 training recipes by 6.2 to 12.9%.
bullets: Speculative decoding accepts draft tokens according to their total variation distance from the target distribution.
TV can match or outperform existing CE/KL-based objectives, but suffers from vanishing gradients and prefix-product effects.
TVP addresses these issues with a power-parameterized expected-acceptance-length loss.
Annealing the power from zero to one performs best or ties for best across three drafter architectures and three target models.
TVP raises acceptance length by 9.8% over CE and 6.2–12.9% over public DFlash2 recipes.

papers.abstract: Structured channel pruning for convolutional neural networks (CNNs) plays an important role in pattern recognition and deep learning. Nevertheless, existing methods usually calculate channel importance scores based on the magnitudes of individual filters, making it difficult to distinguish shared redundancy from individual channel contributions. To tackle this limitation, we propose a novel structured channel pruning method termed bi-sparse matrix factorization (BSMF). Specifically, BSMF characterizes the convolutional weight matrix as output-channel coefficients over a shared basis with row-wise $\ell_{2,p}$-norm and column-wise $\ell_{2,q}$-norm regularization terms, respectively. Note that $p,q\in[0,1)$, which, to our best knowledge, has not been explored in the literature. To solve the resulting non-convex optimization problem, we develop an efficient update scheme built upon the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), in which all subproblems admit closed-form solutions. After that, a compact CNN is obtained by reconstructing the convolutional filters from the learned factors and discarding the redundant channels. Extensive experiments on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K datasets demonstrate that our proposed BSMF achieves significant network compression while maintaining high reconstruction accuracy. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/xianchaoxiu/BSMF
bullets: Addresses the limits of filter-magnitude importance scores, which may confuse shared redundancy with individual channel contributions.
Uses bi-sparse matrix factorization with row-wise and column-wise ℓ₂,p/ℓ₂,q regularization, where p,q∈[0,1).
Solves the resulting non-convex optimization with an ADMM-based update scheme whose subproblems have closed-form solutions.
Reconstructs filters from the learned factors and removes redundant channels to produce compact CNNs.
Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K report significant compression while maintaining high reconstruction accuracy.

papers.title: Structured Channel Network Pruning with Bi-Sparse Matrix Factorization
papers.tldr: BSMF prunes redundant CNN channels by factorizing convolutional weights into a shared basis and sparse channel coefficients, enabling compact models with high reconstruction accuracy.

papers.abstract: The rapid scaling of large language models (LLMs) has unlocked remarkable capabilities across various domains. However, deploying LLMs on mobile devices remains challenging because of their high computational and memory requirements. Low-bit quantization (e.g., 4-bit weights, 8-bit activations) can reduce model size while preserving accuracy, but its practical efficacy on mobile GPUs has been limited so far. In this paper, we identify that the performance gap stems primarily from frequent data type conversions between quantized and floating-point values, and dynamic and inefficient memory access patterns caused by the growing Key-Value (KV) cache during autoregressive decoding. We introduce BitLLM, a mobile inference engine that addresses type conversion overhead and suboptimal memory accesses in quantized LLMs. Our approach features an adaptive layout and packing strategy for the KV cache that ensures efficient memory access throughout LLM decoding. This is coupled with an integer-native execution pipeline that defers and overlaps type conversion outside the compute hot path, keeping the critical MatMul stages in the integer domain. Implemented on off-the-shelf mobile GPUs, BitLLM outperforms leading engines, i.e., LLAMA.CPP, MNN-LLM, LiteRT-LM, and MLC-LLM, achieving average speedups of 1.78$\times$, 1.73$\times$, 1.58$\times$, and 1.47$\times$, respectively, across various models and quantization levels. Under long-context generation, BitLLM reduces average energy consumption (per token) by up to 88.9%.
bullets: Mobile deployment is constrained by LLM computation and memory demands, while low-bit inference is hindered by conversion overhead and inefficient KV-cache access.
An adaptive KV-cache layout and packing strategy maintains efficient memory access during autoregressive decoding.
An integer-native execution pipeline moves and overlaps type conversions outside the critical MatMul path.
On off-the-shelf mobile GPUs, BitLLM achieves average speedups of 1.78×–1.47× over four leading inference engines across models and quantization levels.
For long-context generation, it reduces average energy consumption per token by up to 88.9%.

papers.abstract: Parallel speculative drafters use a lightweight serial head to recover token dependencies within a block generated in parallel. Each head step updates only a small state, yet projects that state through the same vocabulary-sized matrix. Step-wise execution repeatedly transfers this large, immutable projection, making the head a meaningful source of latency despite its low arithmetic cost. We present Weights That Stay, an execution design that keeps projection shards on chip for the entire serial draft walk. A persistent megakernel couples weight residency with GPU-side token selection and state advancement, reusing resident weights while exchanging only compact state between steps. The design supports full or partial residency and accommodates both Markov and recurrent heads on H100 and B200. Integrated into SGLang, Weights That Stay improves throughput for Markov drafting on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, with gains of up to 12.3%. At the head level, the DSpark walk is up to 11.6$\times$ faster than the fastest measured SGLang reference path. These results show that aligning weight residency with the full draft walk translates cross-step reuse into end-to-end serving gains.
bullets: Serial heads repeatedly transfer the same large projection matrix despite updating only a small state, creating latency overhead.
A persistent GPU megakernel combines resident projection shards with token selection and state advancement, exchanging only compact state between steps.
The design supports full or partial on-chip residency and both Markov and recurrent heads on H100 and B200 GPUs.
Integrated with SGLang, it improves Markov-drafting throughput by up to 12.3% on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B.
The DSpark walk is up to 11.6× faster than the fastest measured SGLang reference path at the head level.
