papers.abstract: On hardware whose fastest matrix datapath is INT8$\times$INT8, such as the Neural Accelerators of Apple's M5 GPUs, 4-bit weights must become INT8 operands. Existing MXFP4 kernels already map FP4 (E2M1) values to integers by doubling them, but apply every 32-element block scale inside the reduction. We show when no per-block work is needed: a row of MXFP4 weights is exactly one INT8 vector times one power-of-two scale if its block exponents span at most three, so a linear layer becomes a single INT8 GEMM with one rescale per output. Enforcing the condition adds at most 1/16 of a row's largest rounding error to the blocks it changes, and real weights already satisfy it: 97.9-99.97% of rows across seven models, including 99.93% of the 95M rows of a 125B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. The resulting spread-constrained MXFP4 files stay standard MXFP4. With integer instead of power-of-two block multipliers, an integer-exact format (16-wide blocks, multipliers 1..10, 4.26 bits) runs as one exact INT8 GEMM and is more accurate than NVFP4 (4.5 bits) with its standard scale rule on five small models, within 0.06 perplexity of NVFP4 with scale search. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's routed experts with INT8 activations it is as close to the FP8 model as NVFP4 with scale search (KL divergence 0.0557 vs. 0.0553) and closer than MLX's MXFP4 and affine INT4; with every matrix quantized it solves 94.8% of GSM8K vs. 91.0% for MLX's MXFP4. Quantizing only the 74k routed expert matrices (96% of the parameters) to either of our formats with INT8 activations costs at most 0.2% perplexity. A complete W4A8 system on the M5 produces outputs bit-identical to the quantized reference; prefill is 1.34-1.74x faster than MLX on a dense model, 1.10-1.57x on two MoE models up to 35B parameters and 1.22-1.29x on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, where shared non-GEMM work bounds the gain.
bullets: MXFP4 rows can be converted to a single INT8 vector and one power-of-two scale when block exponents span at most three, eliminating per-block work inside the reduction.
Enforcing this condition changes rounding error by at most 1/16 of a row’s largest block error, while already covering 97.9–99.97% of rows across seven models.

An integer-exact 16-wide format with multipliers 1–10 uses 4.26 bits and achieves accuracy better than standard NVFP4 on five small models, and nearly matches scale-searched NVFP4 on a large MoE model.
On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, the proposed formats outperform MLX MXFP4 and affine INT4 on routed-expert KL divergence; full quantization reaches 94.8% GSM8K versus 91.0% for MLX MXFP4.

A complete W4A8 implementation is bit-identical to its quantized reference and accelerates prefill by 1.10–1.74× on tested dense and MoE models, with gains limited by non-GEMM work in the largest MoE.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a quantization scheme for running MXFP4 LLMs on INT8 matrix units, directly reducing inference compute.
papers.title: Integer-Exact Microscaling: Running MXFP4 Language Models on INT8 Matrix Units
papers.tldr: A spread-constrained MXFP4 representation enables exact, efficient INT8 GEMMs for 4-bit language-model weights, delivering near-NVFP4 accuracy and substantial M5 speedups.

papers.abstract: Deploying small language models on resource-constrained hardware requires compression, yet practitioners lack systematic guidance on how quantization, pruning, and post-compression recovery interact when combined. We present a factorial ablation study evaluating 72 compression configurations across four SLM architectures (2.7B-7B parameters), extended with a 48-configuration ordering analysis, benchmark accuracy validation on 30 compressed models, and robustness checks including multi-seed validation and full-corpus perplexity evaluation. INT8 quantization is effectively lossless (<0.5% accuracy degradation), while NF4 quantization combined with L1 magnitude pruning causes model collapse in all 16 tested combinations. LoRA-based fine-tuning reduces degraded perplexity by up to 97% after aggressive pruning; an ablation against standard fine-tuning without a teacher model shows the recovery is driven by LoRA adaptation itself rather than the distillation signal. Compression ordering shows no significant effect among viable configurations (ANOVA p = 0.96) but determines viability for NF4+pruning combinations. INT8 quantization alone provides 40-45% memory reduction with no quality loss. On-device CPU deployment via llama.cpp confirms these findings transfer off the GPU: 4-bit quantization runs 46-54% faster than 8-bit for a perplexity difference under 0.5 points, while un-structured pruning yields no CPU latency or memory benefit, consistent with its dense storage format.
bullets: Evaluates 72 compression configurations across four 2.7B–7B-parameter SLM architectures, plus ordering and robustness analyses.
INT8 quantization causes under 0.5% accuracy degradation and reduces memory use by 40–45%.
NF4 quantization with L1 magnitude pruning causes collapse in all 16 tested combinations.
LoRA fine-tuning reduces degraded perplexity by up to 97% after aggressive pruning; recovery is attributed to LoRA adaptation rather than distillation.
Compression order has no significant effect for viable configurations, while unstructured pruning provides no CPU latency or memory benefit in llama.cpp.

papers.title: Compression Technique Interactions in Small Language Models: A Factorial Ablation Study
papers.tldr: A factorial study finds INT8 quantization is nearly lossless and reliably useful for small language models, while NF4 combined with unstructured pruning can cause collapse; LoRA recovery helps, but pruning alone does not improve CPU efficiency.

papers.abstract: High-resolution video diffusion relies on attention over long token sequences, making attention efficiency critical to generation latency. Our analysis identifies repeated maximum reductions and accumulator rescaling in online softmax as a bottleneck in long-context TPU attention. We propose CLiS (Certified Loop-invariant Stabilization), a training-free, plug-and-play optimization for video diffusion inference. CLiS fixes per-row stabilizers before the KV loop and certifies numerical safety per head, falling back to online softmax when certification fails. It integrates into existing fused-attention kernels without changing model weights or architecture. On Wan 2.2 and LTX-2 across TPU v6e and TPU7x, CLiS reduces diffusion transformer (DiT) step latency by up to 19.6% relative to tuned online softmax without measurable quality loss. Controlled TPU adaptations of prior GPU stabilization methods show performance or numerical-safety limitations. Preliminary causal LLM experiments also show up to 13.5% higher training throughput in continued pretraining and 7.7% in supervised fine-tuning.
bullets: Targets repeated maximum reductions and accumulator rescaling that bottleneck online softmax in long-token TPU attention.
Uses a training-free, plug-and-play optimization that fixes per-row stabilizers before the KV loop and certifies safety per head.
Falls back to online softmax when certification fails, preserving numerical safety while integrating with existing fused-attention kernels.
Evaluated on Wan 2.2 and LTX-2 across TPU v6e and TPU7x; preliminary causal LLM tests also report throughput gains.
Scope includes TPU inference and preliminary training results; benefits depend on successful stabilization certification.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models expand model capacity by activating only a subset of experts for each token. On accelerators with static execution plans, expert capacities and placement are fixed before routing reveals each expert's load. Uniform worst-case capacities waste work on padding; smaller capacities tied to expert identities can overflow. We present RankLane, which ranks each device's experts by current load and assigns them to fixed-capacity lanes. Runtime indices select experts and token rows while tier populations, shapes and device placement remain fixed. An aggregation graph preserves device ownership and reduces each token's local contributions on one core. Routing calibration and measured execution costs guide tier selection; overflowing chunks rerun at full capacity. We evaluate full-model prefill of Qwen3-30B-A3B and Gemma 4 26B-A4B with MXFP6 weights on four Cloud AI 100 Ultra SoCs, using 128-2048-token chunks and including overflow detection and in-program recovery support. Against a dense baseline, RankLane achieves end-to-end prefill speedups of 1.27-4.18x on Qwen3 and 1.93-3.46x on Gemma.
bullets: Static uniform capacities waste computation through padding, while identity-based small capacities risk expert overflow.
Experts are ranked by current load at runtime, with fixed lane populations, tensor shapes, and device placement preserved.
Runtime indices select expert and token rows; overflowing chunks are rerun at full capacity for recovery.
An aggregation graph preserves device ownership while consolidating each token’s local contributions on one core.
On four Cloud AI 100 Ultra SoCs, RankLane delivers 1.27–4.18× speedups for Qwen3-30B-A3B and 1.93–3.46× for Gemma 4 26B-A4B versus a dense baseline.

papers.abstract: Smartphone applications increasingly require large language models to process long contexts, whereas high prefill latency and memory demands constrain local inference. Block-sparse attention reduces computation and memory traffic, but its irregular selections conflict with mobile NPUs' preference for large, regular tiles. Efficient execution must exploit cross-query reuse while avoiding redundant computation and preserving selections needed for accuracy. In this paper, we present TileWeave, which partitions sparse attention by this cross-query reuse: highly shared key blocks run in coarse NPU tiles, while low-reuse blocks run on the GPU only for the query blocks that selected them. In addition, we design an NPU-native pooled-key selector that keeps selection inexpensive, and a runtime that publishes GPU partials in the order the NPU consumes them and merges them in its existing output store. On RULER, HeteroSparse matches XAttention's accuracy with Qwen3-1.7B and improves it with Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; its mean LongBench scores match XAttention as well. On Snapdragon SM8750 and SM8850 phones, it achieves 1.35--3.23$\times$ faster full-model prefill than XAttention over 1k--16k tokens and up to 1.58$\times$ faster than dense attention.
bullets: Targets long-context mobile inference bottlenecks: high prefill latency and memory demands.
Uses coarse NPU tiles for highly reused key blocks and GPU execution for low-reuse blocks selected by specific query blocks.
Adds an NPU-native pooled-key selector and runtime coordination for ordered GPU partials and NPU-side merging.
Matches XAttention accuracy on Qwen3-1.7B and mean LongBench scores, while improving accuracy on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct.
On Snapdragon SM8750/SM8850, delivers 1.35–3.23× faster full-model prefill than XAttention and up to 1.58× faster than dense attention across 1k–16k tokens.

papers.abstract: Memory capacity and bandwidth are major bottlenecks in LLM inference, motivating weight compression beyond conventional 4-bit quantization. Vector quantization (VQ) enables approximately 2-bit weight storage but often relies on codebooks incompatible with native FP4 computation. We introduce MXCode (MX-Native Codebook Quantization), a framework bridging ultra-low-bit VQ compression with MicroXcaling (MX)-native FP4 computation. MXCode proposes three strategies: PostScale, which quantizes learned codebooks to MXFP4; PreScale, which extracts MX scales before codebook learning; and PreScale+, which further compresses these scales using VQ. These strategies explore tradeoffs among quantization quality, scale overhead, and codebook granularity. All reconstruct MX-native W4A4 operands without materializing intermediate high-precision weights. We evaluate MXCode on Qwen3 (235B), DeepSeek-R1 (671B), and GLM-5.2 (753B) using the Microsoft MX Emulation Library. MXCode achieves approximately 2 bits per weight with competitive, workload-dependent model quality. On GB300 hardware, experiments with Qwen3 (235B) show approximately 50% lower model-load memory than Native FP4 while maintaining near-Native-FP4 serving throughput. Under memory-constrained prefix reuse, P90 TTFT improves by up to 94.5%. These results demonstrate software-based reconstruction on existing FP4 hardware and inform the development of future MX-native inference systems.
bullets: Targets memory-capacity and bandwidth limits that constrain large-model inference beyond conventional 4-bit quantization.
Introduces PostScale, PreScale, and PreScale+ strategies to balance quantization quality, scale overhead, and codebook granularity.
Avoids materializing intermediate high-precision weights during MX-native operand reconstruction.
Evaluated on Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, and GLM-5.2 with the Microsoft MX Emulation Library; quality is competitive but workload-dependent.
On GB300 with Qwen3, reports about 50% lower model-load memory than Native FP4, near-Native-FP4 serving throughput, and up to 94.5% better P90 TTFT under memory-constrained prefix reuse.

papers.selection_reason: Ultra-low-bit vector quantization for MX-native LLM inference directly reduces model memory footprint, fitting efficient AI memory-efficiency goals.
papers.title: MXCode: Vector Quantization for MX-Native Inference at Scale

papers.abstract: Speech language models encode audio at a much higher rate than text, causing the KV cache to dominate the memory, bandwidth, and decoding cost of long-form generation. KV retrieval can reduce per-step access by attending to only a query-dependent subset of the cache, but existing methods are designed primarily for text and do not account for the structure of audio attention. We first show that retrieval errors may compound autoregressively into generation drift. We then analyze full audio attention during long-form generation and identify three properties relevant to retrieval: unequal attention concentration across query heads, non-contiguous audio support, and temporal continuity across decoding steps. Guided by these observations, we propose $C^3$(Cluster-Compete-Compete), which organizes audio KVs in a hierarchical key-space index, lets query heads sharing a KV head compete for a common retrieval budget, and adaptively reallocates retrieval resolution through paired split-merge updates. Across long-form speech recognition, translation, and summarization on four SpeechLLMs, $C^3$ achieves the strongest overall performance among retrieval methods under comparable final-KV access budgets, with particularly large gains in the tight-budget regime, while improving long-context decoding efficiency and accelerator-memory scaling.
bullets: Audio is encoded much more densely than text, making the KV cache a major memory, bandwidth, and decoding bottleneck.
Retrieval errors can accumulate autoregressively, causing generation drift; audio attention also has unequal head concentration, non-contiguous support, and temporal continuity.
C3 uses a hierarchical key-space index, shared retrieval-budget competition among query heads, and adaptive split-merge updates to adjust retrieval resolution.
Across long-form speech recognition, translation, and summarization on four SpeechLLMs, C3 performs best among comparable retrieval methods, especially under tight KV-access budgets.
The method improves long-context decoding efficiency and accelerator-memory scaling.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses memory efficiency in long-context speech LLMs by proposing a hierarchical KV retrieval method (C3) tailored to the structure of audio attention.
papers.title: C3: Speech-Guided KV Retrieval for Long-Context SpeechLLM Inference
papers.tldr: C3 enables efficient long-context SpeechLLM inference by retrieving only the most relevant audio KV cache entries while preserving generation quality.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory burden of large model deployment by casting the high precision trained weights to fewer bits. While this promotes memory-efficient inference, it also incurs quantization error that impairs model performance. To compensate for quantization error, the present contribution decomposes the original trained weights into a quantized matrix, a low-rank component, and a sparse matrix that accounts for outlier rows in the weights. Due to analytical intractability and the discrete structure of the decomposition, a simulated annealing search is employed to explore candidate decompositions while avoiding poor local minima. Numerical tests demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach across a broad suite of large language models, including Llama 3.2 1B, Llama 3.2 3B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen2.5 7B, evaluated on natural language generation benchmarks using 4-bit NF4 and FP4 quantizers. The novel method can markedly outperform direct quantization while incurring minimal memory overhead.
bullets: Addresses performance loss from quantization error in memory-efficient large-model deployment.
Decomposes weights into a quantized matrix, a low-rank component, and a sparse matrix for outlier rows.
Uses simulated annealing to search the discrete, analytically difficult decomposition space.
Evaluated on several Llama and Qwen models with 4-bit NF4 and FP4 quantizers on natural language generation benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks deployed on smart glasses must adapt to changes in the distribution of incoming data while adhering to strict privacy and device constraints. We present No Frames, Just Frequencies, a bandwidth-efficient source-assisted adaptation framework that characterizes distribution shifts using compact frequency descriptors computed on-device. Rather than transmitting camera frames, the glasses compute and send frequency descriptors to a host device that contains a replica of the model. The host device maps the received frequency descriptor to a distribution shift operator that synthesizes out-of-distribution data and adapts a model replica using a pre-defined adaptation protocol. We evaluate the framework on mixtures of ImageNet-C corruptions using convolution-based (ConvNeXtV2-Femto), self-attention-based (DeiT-Tiny), and hybrid (TinyViT-5M) vision models, on person classification (Visual Wake Words), and on object detection (MS-COCO). Our results reveal that adaptation driven solely by the transmitted descriptors recovers $93-95\%$ of the supervised oracle adaptation gain on all three architectures, $82\%$ on Visual Wake Words and $94$--$98\%$ on MS-COCO. Notably, adaptation quality degrades gracefully as the descriptor resolution decreases from $224 $ to $28$ pixels, consistently across architectures, enabling bandwidth reductions from $213\times$ to $784\times$ across the frequency descriptors.
bullets: Addresses distribution shifts in on-device vision under strict privacy and bandwidth constraints.
The glasses compute frequency descriptors; a host maps them to shift operators, synthesizes out-of-distribution data, and adapts a model replica.
Evaluated across ImageNet-C, Visual Wake Words, and MS-COCO with convolutional, attention-based, and hybrid vision models.
Descriptor-only adaptation recovers 93–95% of supervised oracle gains across architectures, 82% on Visual Wake Words, and 94–98% on MS-COCO.
Reducing descriptor resolution from 224 to 28 pixels degrades performance gracefully while enabling 213×–784× bandwidth reductions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: System overview of the proposed bandwidth-efficient TTA framework. An edge device (i.e., Smart Glasses) computes compact frequency descriptors (RAPSD, DCT, or DWT statistics) from incoming camera frames on-device. Only these descriptors are transmitted to the host device, keeping the per-frame uplink within a low-bandwidth budget instead of streaming raw frames. The host device maps the received descriptor to a synthetic corruption distribution through a sequential pipeline of training corruptions. The host device generates synthetic corrupted data batches from locally stored in-distribution images, and adapts a model replica using a pre-defined adaptation protocol [19, 44]. Finally, the updated parameter subset is transmitted back to the edge device.

Figure 5: Descriptors ablation at 224 input resolution: the NFJF adaptation loop re-run with the frequency descriptor replaced by the model-based alternatives. ActStats denotes the first layer and block activation statistics and FeatFinal the pooled pre-logits embedding. Same layout as Fig. 2. ActStats attains the highest adaptation accuracy, improving on DCT by 0.67pp on average and approaching Oracle - CE within 0.71pp. This adaptation gain costs on average 2.3× the DCT payload (a fixed 708B versus architecture-dependent 768–3072B). Computing ActStats requires executing the deployed model’s first layer and block, ≈ 100× the number of DCT FLOPs (∼ 150-180 versus 1.6MFLOPs), whereas the frequency descriptors need no model execution.

Figure 2: Per-architecture accuracy across four input resolutions (28, 56, 112, 224), reported for each frequency descriptor (RAPSD, DCT and DWT). NFJF is compared against three resolution-independent references: No Adapt and Oracle - E baselines and the Oracle - CE empirical upper bound. Bars report the mean over the 63 test DAGs of ImageNet-C; error bars indicate ±𝜎 . Oracle - E accuracy markedly improves on NoAdapt only for ConvNeXtV2-Femto and destabilizes on DeiT-Tiny and TinyViT-5M, confirming the fragility of unsupervised entropy-based adaptation under distribution shift. NFJF accuracy improves on No Adapt across all three architectures for resolutions > 28 and it surpasses Oracle - E at all resolutions on DeiT-Tiny and TinyViT5M. For ConvNeXtV2-Femto, NFJF mostly surpasses Oracle - E at 112 and 224 input resolutions.

Figure 3: Descriptor visualizations under a sample DAG (brightness→ shot noise→ contrast, each at severity 2; Section 5.1), normalized with clean-data statistics. Brightness amplifies the DC component across all descriptors and resolutions; shot noise amplifies high frequencies, an effect that diminishes at lower resolutions since the reduced-scale JPEG decode acts as a low-pass filter. Contrast reduces the midfrequency bands left free by the other two corruptions.

Table 2: Framework generality across person classification and object detection. The No Adapt row reports the absolute performance under shift, the common reference of every adaptation gain. The best per-column adaptation gain is reported in bold. The trends observed in Fig. 2 persist: every adaptation gain is positive and approaches the supervised Oracle as the resolution increases, whereas Oracle - E (VWW) collapses below No Adapt.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) serving systems must balance latency and throughput while efficiently utilizing distributed GPU resources. This challenge arises because inference consists of two fundamentally different phases: prefill, which determines time-to-first-token (TTFT), and decode, which determines inter-token latency (ITL). The use of tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and hybrid configurations exposes different trade-offs between these latency dimensions, making the optimal parallelism configuration highly dependent on workload characteristics, latency requirements, and context length. Moreover, despite the widespread adoption of distributed inference, there is still limited understanding of how parallelism configurations should be selected under varying workload conditions and service-level objectives (SLO). In this paper, we develop a systematic framework for characterizing LLM inference parallelism via throughput-latency trade-offs, SLO-aware serving, and long-context scalability. We introduce the notion of parallelism operating regions by constructing TTFT-ITL feasible sets and Pareto frontiers across different workload compositions, thereby revealing a systematic transition from TP-dominant to PP-dominant configurations as workloads become increasingly prefill-heavy. We further formulate SLO-aware parallelism selection using goodput, showing that stringent TTFT requirements favor PP-dominated configurations, whereas relaxed latency constraints progressively shift the optimality toward TP-dominated configurations with higher serving capacity. Finally, we demonstrate that increasing context length fundamentally changes the relative advantages of parallelism configurations, with PP-dominant configurations exhibiting more favorable scalability and SLO attainment in the long-context regime.
bullets: LLM inference has distinct prefill and decode phases, governed by time-to-first-token (TTFT) and inter-token latency (ITL).
It characterizes configurations using TTFT–ITL feasible sets and Pareto frontiers, defining parallelism operating regions.
As workloads become more prefill-heavy, the preferred configuration shifts from tensor-parallelism-dominant to pipeline-parallelism-dominant designs.

SLO-aware selection via goodput favors pipeline-dominated configurations under stringent TTFT requirements, while relaxed latency constraints favor tensor-dominated configurations with greater capacity.
For long-context workloads, pipeline-dominated configurations provide more favorable scalability and SLO attainment.

figures.caption: Figure 1: TTFT-ITL feasible region and Pareto frontier for different parallelism configurations. TP-dominant configurations achieve lower ITL but higher TTFT, while PP-dominant configurations achieve lower TTFT at the expense of higher ITL. As workloads transition from decode-heavy to prefill-heavy, the Pareto-optimal operating point shifts systematically from TP-dominant configurations, through hybrid configurations, toward PP-dominant configurations.

Figure 3: Left Plot: TTFT distribution (Prefill), Right plot: ITL distribution (decode). PP-dominant configurations achieve lower TTFT, while TP-dominant configurations achieve lower ITL, thereby highlighting the latency trade-off between prefill and decoding across different parallelisms.

Figure 2: TTFT vs. ITL for various OSL. The effect of OSL is not uniform across parallelism configurations. Longer OSL mainly improves ITL through better amortization of decode overheads, with the largest benefit observed for TPdominant configurations.

Figure 4: Latency compliance and serving capacity trade-off for fixed workload w = (1200, 2800, 256) with Lseq = 4000. Filled marker in each Ts, indicates the parallelism configuration that yields the maximum goodput for the corresponding Ts.

Figure 5: Goodput vs. TTFT SLO for fixed workload w = (1200, 2800, 256) where Lseq = 4000. As TTFT SLO is relaxed, the optimal parallelism shifts from PP-dominant configurations to TP-dominant configurations.

Figure 6: Goodput vs. Sequence Length for workload w = (Lin, 1000, 128) where Lin varies to construct values of x-axis. Left plot: Ts = 5(s). Right Plot: Ts = 2(s). Increasing sequence length progressively favors PP-dominant parallelism over TP-dominant parallelism, highlighting PP’s stronger scalability for long context workloads.

Figure 7: CDF vs. Sequence Length for workload w = (Lin, 1000, 128) where Lin varies to construct values of x-axis. Left plot: Ts = 5(s). Right plot: Ts = 2(s). PP-dominant configurations maintain higher SLO attainment as sequence length increases, especially under tight TTFT SLOs.

papers.abstract: Non-injective mappings in neural networks map distinct inputs to the same representation, thereby implicitly inducing equivalence relations in the input space. However, the input differences eliminated by these mappings may still be required by downstream tasks, creating a mismatch between operator-induced indistinguishability and task-required distinctions. For non-injective linear operators realized in the current forward pass, their null spaces exactly characterize these invisible input variations. We propose Task-Relevant Null-Space Residuals (NSR), a general residual framework for non-injective linear mappings. NSR combines null-space component extraction from pre-mapping representations, member-level encoding and gating, and application-specific integration to exploit potentially task-relevant information under downstream supervision while preserving the original aggregation or merging rules. We evaluate NSR in two structurally different settings: token merging and graph aggregation. In token merging, NSR achieves higher semantic segmentation performance than the corresponding compressed baselines in 34 out of 36 evaluated configurations, with a maximum observed gain of 31.51 mIoU points under strong compression. In graph aggregation, NSR achieves 100% training accuracy on Tree-NeighborsMatch at depths d=2--6 across three backbones, alongside gains on heterophilic node classification and molecular graph regression. Together, these results support null-space residuals as a practical complement to non-injective linear mappings, enabling downstream models to learn from input distinctions invisible in the original operator's output.
bullets: Non-injective mappings collapse distinct inputs, potentially removing distinctions needed by downstream tasks.
NSR extracts null-space components before mapping, encodes and gates them at the member level, and integrates them under downstream supervision.
The framework preserves the original aggregation or merging rules while exposing otherwise invisible information.
For token merging, NSR outperforms compressed baselines in 34 of 36 configurations, with a maximum gain of 31.51 mIoU points.
For graph aggregation, it reaches 100% training accuracy on Tree-NeighborsMatch at depths 2–6 across three backbones and improves other graph tasks.

papers.abstract: Agentic workflows are increasingly shifting towards long-horizon tasks, such as open-ended scientific work, where models benefit from long context windows. However, at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens), full attention is prohibitively expensive. A promising approach is sparse attention, in which a dedicated indexer selects a subset of keys for the attention. Yet current methods of indexing either still have quadratic cost in context size or lose accuracy at ultra-long context scale. We address this with Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), an efficient attention method that maintains accuracy at ultra-long context. In LSA, keys are hierarchically clustered in a learned latent space, and queries score the hierarchy of clusters instead of scoring every key, making prefill, decode and training faster at long context. We propose two variants, Distilled-LSA (D-LSA), which can be applied to pre-trained models via distillation, and Native-LSA (N-LSA), which is trained natively on the next-token loss alone. On GLM-5.3-FLASH (QWEN-3.8-27B) at 10M tokens, D-LSA speeds up one attention layer by 22.7x (72.4x) in prefill and 4.6x (42.5x) in decode over its original sparse attention (full attention), while keeping similar accuracy across a variety of tasks. N-LSA matches the accuracy of full attention with a training speedup of 1.6x per layer at 128k tokens. LSA offers practical and efficient attention for models to benefit from ultra-long context.
authors: Ales Kubicek, Andrea Caciolai, Liangzu Peng, Sukrit Sumant, Benjamin Hoover, Fraser Greenlee, Ruairidh M. Battleday, Radim Urban, Torsten Hoefler, James C. R. Whittington
bullets: Targets the prohibitive cost and accuracy degradation of existing sparse attention beyond 1M tokens.
Organizes keys into a learned latent hierarchy, allowing queries to score clusters rather than all keys.
Introduces Distilled-LSA for adapting pretrained models and Native-LSA for native next-token-loss training.
At 10M tokens, D-LSA substantially accelerates prefill and decode while maintaining similar accuracy across evaluated tasks.

papers.abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) trains a few-step student using the difference between a teacher's score and an online critic's estimate of the student distribution's score. We investigate what the critic needs, in capacity and in information, to provide a reliable training signal. On the capacity side, controlled experiments across seven SiT model sizes on ImageNet show that increasing teacher size while keeping a small critic fixed can degrade student quality and cause training collapse. Scaling the critic alongside the teacher, a strategy we call joint scaling, prevents collapse in our experiments and allows the student to benefit from larger teachers. On the information side, rather than forcing the critic to model a step-agnostic mixture of student outputs, we introduce a step-aware critic (STAC) that conditions on the student's generation step to estimate step-specific scores. Together, joint scaling and STAC consistently improve few-step distillation across class-conditional ImageNet generation, text-to-image generation with SDXL and FLUX.2, and text-to-video generation with Wan2.1.
authors: Zongze Wu (Adobe), Xianbang Wang (MIT), Zhengyang Geng (Adobe), Mingdeng Cao (Adobe), Zhoutong Zhang (Adobe), Richard Zhang (Adobe), Eli Shechtman (Adobe), Ruiming Cao (Adobe)
bullets: Larger teachers can hurt student quality and trigger training collapse when the critic remains small.
Joint scaling—growing the critic alongside the teacher—prevents collapse in controlled ImageNet experiments.
STAC conditions the critic on the student’s generation step instead of modeling a step-agnostic output mixture.
Joint scaling and STAC improve few-step distillation for class-conditional images, text-to-image, and text-to-video generation.

papers.selection_reason: Improves few-step distillation for diffusion models, reducing inference steps; evaluated on text-to-video generation.
papers.title: A Better Critic Matters for Distribution Matching Distillation
papers.tldr: Reliable critics are essential for DMD: scaling them with the teacher and conditioning them on generation step improves few-step distillation across image and video generation tasks.

papers.abstract: In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT's KV conversion achieves a 6.5-21.2 times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget.
authors: Yuzhe Liu, Haolin Tian, Tonghan Wang
bullets: Addresses the cost of recomputing shared context when dynamically switching among heterogeneous LLMs.
Uses three components: Cartographer selects relevant tokens, Allocator distributes a shared KV budget, and Compiler converts source KV into target-compatible sparse KV.
Evaluated on five general-capability benchmarks and six context-dependent tasks.
Matches or exceeds original target-model performance with 75% less KV cache.
At roughly 19K-token contexts, KV conversion is 6.5–21.2× faster than target context prefill.

papers.abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage over a few billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.
authors: Leon Lufkin, Cutter Dawes, Alexander Speicher, Kamesh Krishnamurthy, Tom\'as Figliolia, Beren Millidge
bullets: Addresses quadratic attention cost, which limits long-context scaling.
Builds a hierarchical tree of compressed key summaries that queries traverse to select sparse keys.
Joint routing and attention cost grows subquadratically—sublinear in sequence length for the relevant computation, but still superlinear overall.
Can be added to pretrained models using a short KL-distillation stage and maintains long-context retrieval, reasoning, math, and coding performance.
The authors report strong scaling beyond 1 million tokens and potential context windows of hundreds of millions to billions of tokens; performance depends on the method’s tree-based indexing scope.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the ZHA architecture: (a) tree construction and (b) sparse routing. During tree construction, for each chunk of contiguous key nodes, we construct a compressed key node at the higher level by an attention-weighted sum of the keys, where the attention is computed with respect to the learned reference queries. In practice, we use multiple reference queries and store the key nodes for each in parallel. This process continues recursively with higher level key nodes being constructed from the summaries of lower levels. During routing, we start at the top of the tree and compute dot-product similarity scores between our query and the key nodes of that level. We select the set of nodes to expand using top-p, and then recursively descend the tree until we reach the leaf nodes corresponding to raw KV cache entries. The union of all the leaves we reach defines the sparse KV cache subset that we dispatch to the main attention.

Figure 8: For a fixed top-p, and hence sparsity level, ZHA (here, R = 1, C = 8, p = 0.75) scales subquadratically according to our decode roofline model, eventually dramatically outperforming both dense attention and the MSA sparse attention variant. Importantly, we have not empirically validated the scaling at these ultra-long context lengths due to the lack of existing LLMs which can operate at these contexts. Because of this, while we can obtain subquadratic latency, it is unclear to what extent reasoning and retrieval performance degrades at the level of depths required for these ultra-long contexts. Latencies are modeled per-token decode times for the attention subsystem of one layer at batch size 1.

papers.abstract: Looping re-applies a block of layers so that each token passes through the block more than once. Adding a loop to a trained model is attractive because it leaves the parameter count, and hence the disk size, the memory footprint and the training cost unchanged. Unfortunately, every generated token pays for the loop. Re-applying m of N layers makes each token about (N+m)/N times as expensive. Loops that a model learns during large-scale pretraining justify this price, but whether loops added after pretraining justify this cost remains unclear. We compare a looped model with two simple baselines. We first compare it with the same model trained identically without the loop (equal parameters). Secondly, we compare it with the best unlooped use of the same inference floating-point operations (equal FLOPs). Across Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models from 0.8B to 9B parameters, only the looped 0.8B model beats both baselines. At 4B and 9B, the looped model does not beat the first baseline, i.e. the same model trained without the loop. This is not because the benchmarks are too easy, since on the same benchmarks the unlooped 9B model still scores up to 13 points higher than the 4B model, showing that there is ample room for improvement. Introducing loops in an already pretrained model therefore only pays for small models with a fixed parameter budget.
bullets: Looping re-applies layers, preserving parameter count, storage, memory, and training cost but increasing per-token compute.
The study compares looped models against an identically trained unlooped model and the best unlooped model at equal inference FLOPs.
Experiments use Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models ranging from 0.8B to 9B parameters.
At 4B and 9B, looping did not outperform the same model trained without a loop.
The results suggest post-training loops pay off only for small models under a fixed parameter budget.

papers.title: There Is No Free Loop: When Does Looping a Trained Model Pay for Its Inference Compute?
papers.tldr: Post-training loops rarely justify their extra per-token inference cost: across 0.8B–9B models, only the 0.8B looped model outperformed both equal-parameter and equal-FLOP baselines.

papers.abstract: Linear attention scales linearly with sequence length, but its finite-state memory can limit long-context retrieval. In gated linear recurrences, memory retention depends on state decay, which is shaped jointly by gate parameters A_log and dt_bias and by input activations. In controlled Gated DeltaNet (GDN) experiments, both parameters remain highly correlated with their initial values after training, highlighting the importance of initialization. Therefore, we introduce Dual-Axis Memory Initialization (DAMI), which jointly configures these parameters before training. DAMI assigns geometric timescales across heads for varied retrieval distances and a low-high-low input-sensitivity profile across layers. A small activation sample calibrates the GDN-family implementation to match both behavioral targets without adding trainable parameters. Across GDN, KDA, GDN2, Mamba-2, and RWKV-7, DAMI improves average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29 to 16.71 percentage points over the corresponding random-initialization baselines. Performance on language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval remains broadly comparable to those baselines. Our code is available at https://speedai.com/research/dami.
authors: Zhangchi Feng, Harry Jiang, Yangyifei Luo, Ray Zhang, Richong Zhang
bullets: Finite-state memory and initialization can limit long-context retrieval in linear attention.

A small activation sample calibrates the implementation to these targets without adding trainable parameters.
Across five gated linear-attention families, DAMI raises average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29–16.71 percentage points over random initialization.
Language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval performance remains broadly comparable to baseline initialization.

papers.abstract: Modern visual tokenizers aim to preserve fine-grained visual details while learning high-level semantic representations for downstream generation and understanding. Query-based 1D visual tokenizers encode images into flexible latent sequences, yet how individual learnable queries gather and encode image information remains poorly understood. We reveal that these queries spontaneously develop complementary roles under semantic supervision: a small set of Content queries captures high-level semantic information, while a larger set of Detail queries preserves fine-grained visual details for reconstruction. To adapt token processing to these heterogeneous roles, we introduce MoETok, a 1D visual tokenizer that routes tokens through sparsely activated experts. Jointly optimized with reconstruction and semantic objectives, the router learns role-specialized processing paths adapted to each token's representation. Across model scales and token budgets, MoETok consistently improves reconstruction, semantic representation, and autoregressive generation over dense tokenizers under matched supervision and active computation. On ImageNet, it combines strong reconstruction and semantic representation with state-of-the-art class-conditional generation within the 1D tokenizer family. We further validate MoETok at scale in a unified autoregressive model jointly trained for understanding and generation with a next-token cross-entropy objective. The resulting model combines competitive visual understanding with state-of-the-art generation among unified discrete models, matching or surpassing diffusion-based models such as BAGEL and Qwen-Image on benchmarks including DPG-Bench (87.61), GenEval2 (40.04 GM), and WISE (0.49).
authors: Jiahao Guo, Bao Tang, Haoxiang Cao, Jingfeng Yao, Bo Li, Wenyu Liu, Kun Gai, Changqian Yu, Xinggang Wang
bullets: Query tokens naturally separate into Content queries for high-level semantics and Detail queries for fine-grained reconstruction.
MoETok routes tokens through sparsely activated, role-specialized experts.
It consistently outperforms dense tokenizers across model scales and token budgets under matched supervision and active computation.
On ImageNet, it achieves strong reconstruction and semantic representation plus state-of-the-art class-conditional generation within 1D tokenizer methods.
At scale, its unified autoregressive model reaches competitive understanding and state-of-the-art generation among unified discrete models, with DPG-Bench 87.61, GenEval2 40.04 GM, and WISE 0.49.

papers.abstract: Weight pruning can reduce the storage and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), but preserving quality at high sparsity levels remains challenging. Existing methods face a quality-cost trade-off in this regime. One-shot pruning is cheap but degrades sharply as sparsity increases, even when followed by post-pruning recovery. A growing line of work instead optimizes the mask directly from the dense model under the end-to-end objective; among these methods, [Lee et al.,2026], the recent state of the art at extreme sparsity, reaches high quality but at the cost of model-sized optimizer state and auxiliary variables. To address this gap, we propose ETAPS, which prunes gradually and adapts sparsely: it tightens a global sparsity constraint in progressive stages while training a sparse delta with a small, fixed budget. Our key observation is that gradual weight removal keeps each pruning step small enough for sparse adaptation to compensate, allowing the adapted model to provide end-to-end gradients that guide the next pruning decision without model-sized optimizer state. Across six models from 125M to 13B parameters, ETAPS achieves lower perplexity than ELSA at every evaluated sparsity from 50% to 90%, with perplexity reductions of up to 42%. ETAPS is also far cheaper: at 90% sparsity, it prunes LLaMA2-7B on a single H200, where ELSA uses four, with $5.0\times$ smaller total persistent state and 49% fewer GPU-hours. Together, our findings point to a promising direction for achieving high quality in demanding regimes such as extreme sparsity at substantially lower cost.
authors: Jean Lucien Randrianantenaina, Hung Nguyen, Nasib Ullah, Jinbin Zhang, Nilesh Gupta, Inderjit S. Dhillon, Rohit Babbar
bullets: Targets the quality–cost trade-off of pruning LLMs at high sparsity, where one-shot pruning degrades sharply and end-to-end methods require large auxiliary state.

papers.selection_reason: Gradual pruning of LLMs at extreme sparsity reduces model memory and inference cost; directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Prune Gradually, Adapt Sparsely: Efficient Pruning of Large Language Models at Extreme Sparsity
papers.tldr: ETAPS gradually prunes LLM weights while using a small sparse adaptation to preserve quality at extreme sparsity with much lower resource costs.

papers.abstract: Biological neural systems achieve impressive computational capabilities under tight metabolic constraints, relying on sparse cortical representations that minimise total neural activity. This combination of efficiency and representational power has motivated growing interest in sparse coding as a computational strategy for artificial systems. Artificial models designed to produce binary sparse codes span three broad paradigms, theoretical methods grounded in efficient coding, deep learning methods trained via backpropagation, and biologically plausible methods that learn through local Hebbian rules, each yielding codes whose quality depends not only on achieving low activation density but also on preserving the informational structure of the input. The latter property, however, lacks an agreed-upon quantitative definition, leaving the field without a principled basis for comparing methods. We propose a set of metrics that formalise information preservation as similarity preservation, measuring how faithfully a binary sparse code reproduces the relational geometry of the input space, and apply this framework to compare four representative methods under matched conditions. The results reveal a consistent trade-off in which models that achieve high information preservation do so at the cost of sparsity, while models approaching the uniformity of an optimal random sparse code tend to sacrifice it. Competitive Sparse Codes, a biologically plausible approach, is the only architecture to occupy a region of near-maximal sparsity while retaining meaningful information preservation. These findings frame the simultaneous satisfaction of both factors as an open challenge for the field and provide a reusable evaluation framework for measuring progress toward it.
authors: Jose Miguel Ramos, Luis SaCouto, Andreas Wichert
bullets: Binary sparse representations aim to combine biological energy efficiency with useful information retention.
Existing approaches span efficient-coding theory, backpropagation-trained deep models, and local Hebbian methods.
The proposed metrics treat information preservation as similarity preservation: how well codes retain the input data’s relational geometry.
Across four methods under matched conditions, greater information preservation generally comes with reduced sparsity.
Competitive Sparse Codes uniquely achieve near-maximal sparsity while retaining meaningful information, though balancing both goals remains unresolved.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Conceptual framework for the results that follow, sparsity and information preservation define two axes along which each method’s codes can be positioned. The high-sparsity, high-information quadrant (top right) is the desired outcome the central hypothesis holds is difficult to reach; the low-sparsity, low-information quadrant (bottom left) is trivial and uninteresting. The two off-diagonal quadrants represent the trade-off itself, sparsity gained at the cost of information, or information retained at the cost of sparsity.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates energy-efficient binary sparse representations and information preservation, relevant to the broad efficient-AI interest in reducing energy and computational cost.
papers.title: Binary Sparse Codes: Where are we on Energy Efficient Representations?
papers.tldr: The paper introduces metrics for evaluating binary sparse codes by jointly measuring sparsity and preservation of input-space relationships, revealing a persistent trade-off between the two.

papers.abstract: Multiple local updates are widely used in decentralized optimization to enhance communication efficiency, often in conjunction with stochastic gradients when exact gradient computation is costly. However, such algorithms generally converge only to a neighborhood of the optimum, whose size depends on the stepsize and the variance of gradient noise. Variance reduction has been incorporated into ADMM-based methods to achieve exact convergence in expectation, but their stepsizes typically scale inversely with both the square root of the network size and the cube of the number of local updates, leading to slow convergence as the network size or the number of local updates increases. In this paper, we propose a novel primal-dual-based decentralized optimization algorithm that integrates variance reduction with multiple local updates, with a stepsize independent of the network size and inversely proportional to the number of local updates (rather than its cube), thereby enabling significantly larger stepsizes and faster convergence. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, we establish the first linear convergence guarantee in expectation for decentralized optimization with multiple local updates under stochastic gradients in the strongly convex setting. Beyond the theoretical guarantee, the proposed method exchanges only one variable per round, halving the communication cost compared with gradient-tracking-based methods. Numerical experiments further demonstrate its advantages in convergence speed and accuracy.
authors: Jie Liu, Nicola Bastianello, Wenying Xu, Daniel W. C. Ho
bullets: Addresses neighborhood convergence caused by stochastic-gradient noise in decentralized optimization with local updates.
Uses variance reduction in a primal-dual framework with stepsizes independent of network size and inversely proportional to the number of local updates.
Provides the first expected linear-convergence guarantee for strongly convex decentralized optimization with multiple stochastic-gradient updates, according to the authors.
Communicates only one variable per round, halving communication relative to gradient-tracking methods.
Experiments show faster convergence and higher accuracy, though the stated guarantee is for the strongly convex setting.

papers.selection_reason: Communication-efficient decentralized optimization with variance reduction and local updates is transferable to efficient training of large AI models.
papers.title: Variance Reduction for Decentralized Stochastic Optimization with Multiple Local Updates
papers.tldr: A primal-dual decentralized method combines variance reduction with multiple local updates to achieve linear convergence using larger stepsizes and lower communication.

papers.abstract: Transformers retain an explicit history of the sequence, allowing attention to directly retrieve past representations. However, the size of the KV-Cache and the cost of a new token increase with the context length. State Space Models compress the past into a fixed-size recurrent state, at the cost of reduced addressability. We present the Dynamical Memory Transformer (DMT), a hybrid architecture that separates sequence encoding from information reading. The encoder uses several memory units, each implemented by a dynamical system with a complex diagonal recurrent matrix. An input-dependent leak rate controls their updates. The decoder then uses attention to read and combine their outputs, without going through the token history. The formulation of the recurrence allows an associative scan with O(T ) total work and O(log T ) parallel depth, with fixed dimensions. During autoregressive inference, the recurrent states and the convolution cache remain fixed in size. We compare DMT with Mamba and Transformer on cognitive and language modeling tasks, and show its strengths and limitations: DMT achieves the best results on several cognitive tasks and language modeling performance close to that of Transformer, but remains behind Mamba in language modeling. On selective copy, DMT also shows stronger length extrapolation than Mamba and Transformer. These results demonstrate that parallel dynamical memory units are a promising mechanism for retaining and using information over sequences.
bullets: Addresses Transformer KV-cache growth and the limited addressability of fixed-state State Space Models.
Uses multiple complex-diagonal dynamical memory units with input-dependent leak rates to encode sequences.
A decoder attends to memory outputs rather than the full token history; recurrence supports O(T) work and O(log T) parallel depth.
Matches Transformer closely in language modeling, outperforms both baselines on several cognitive tasks, and remains behind Mamba on language modeling.
Shows stronger selective-copy length extrapolation than Mamba and Transformer; performance has task-dependent limitations.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Dynamical Memory Transformer (DMT), a hybrid architecture combining dynamical systems with attention to achieve constant cost attention and efficient memory retention.
papers.title: Dynamical Memory Transformer: Selective Recurrent Memories with Constant Cost Attention
papers.tldr: Dynamical Memory Transformer combines selective recurrent memories with attention-based reading to provide fixed-size inference state and efficient long-context processing.

papers.abstract: Vector Quantization (VQ) is a rapidly evolving technique for compressing Large Language Model (LLM) weights, reducing memory usage, and speeding up inference. However, extreme compression deteriorates model performance, which is challenging to recover due to the discrete nature of VQ parameters. Existing methods employ training-free approaches that are limited to layer-wise reconstruction loss minimization. To address this limitation, we propose TVQ, a novel method that leverages straight-through estimation to enable gradient descent-based optimization of vector-quantized LLMs. By reformulating VQ LLM optimization with trainable latent weights, TVQ enables arbitrary objective minimization. We constitute our approach by applying TVQ in a block-wise knowledge distillation paradigm, which balances quality and training efficiency, and propose several practical solutions to accelerate training. In experiments on modern LLMs, we demonstrate that TVQ is compatible with modern VQ schemes. As a result, TVQ achieves state-of-the-art quality in low-bit post-training quantization settings with a modest training budget and straightforward PyTorch implementation. For instance, TVQ achieves near-lossless 2-bit quantization for LLaMA2-70B with only 1% accuracy drop on popular Question-Answering benchmarks.
authors: Anastasiia Prutianova, Alina Bogdanova, Mikhail Shutov, Dmitrii Poimanov, Anatoly Gorkov, Ilia Zharikov
bullets: Addresses performance degradation from aggressive VQ compression and the limits of training-free, layer-wise reconstruction.
Uses straight-through estimation with trainable latent weights to support gradient-based optimization under discrete quantization.
Applies block-wise knowledge distillation to balance quantization quality and training efficiency, with practical training accelerations.
Is compatible with modern VQ schemes and achieves strong low-bit post-training quantization quality with a modest budget.
Reports near-lossless 2-bit quantization of LLaMA2-70B, with a 1% accuracy drop on popular question-answering benchmarks.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. This figure illustrates the proposed TVQ method, applied to a single linear layer with the weight matrix W . During optimization, these matrices are updated: the indices matrix I, the weight matrix W , and (optionally) the codebook C. TVQ involves three main operations: I is calculated according to (3); The dequantized weight matrix W q is gathered from C and I according to (2) and used to calculate the loss function; The gradients of the loss are propagated from W q to W and C, W (and optionally C) is updated with gradient descent. After training, only the compressed representation consisting of C and I is stored and used for inference instead of the original weight matrix.

papers.selection_reason: Trainable vector quantization compresses LLM weights, reducing memory and speeding inference, directly fitting memory-efficient inference.

papers.tldr: TVQ makes vector-quantized LLM weights trainable, enabling objective-driven optimization that substantially improves extreme low-bit quantization quality.

papers.abstract: Tabular transformer models such as TabPFN achieve strong predictive performance but incur substantial inference costs, making them difficult to deploy in resource-constrained settings. While looped transformers reduce parameter count through weight sharing, they can lose significant predictive power when stopped early. To address this challenge, we introduce the Elastically Looped Tabular Transformer (ElTab), a single model trained to operate across different computational budgets through supervision at randomly sampled early exits. Across 30 OpenML classification datasets, a single ElTab model matches six depth-specific looped models while cutting training cost by more than half, and matches a 12-layer TabPFN-style baseline with 25% fewer inference FLOPs. These results show that elastic-depth training yields a single model that adapts to the deployment budget at hand, offering a favorable trade-off among predictive performance, storage, and computational cost.
authors: Mieszko Komisarczyk, Saurabh Mathur, Maurice Kraus, Sriraam Natarajan, Kristian Kersting
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of tabular transformers in resource-constrained deployments.
Uses shared weights with supervision at randomly sampled early exits to support multiple computational depths.
Across 30 OpenML classification datasets, matches six depth-specific looped models while cutting training cost by more than half.
Matches a 12-layer TabPFN-style baseline with 25% fewer inference FLOPs.
Provides a deployment-flexible trade-off among predictive performance, storage, and computation.

papers.selection_reason: Elastic-depth tabular transformer reduces inference FLOPs and storage, fitting the broad efficient-AI interest in reducing computation and memory.
papers.title: ElTab: Elastically Looped Tabular Transformers
papers.tldr: ElTab is a single tabular transformer trained for flexible early exiting, achieving comparable accuracy across budgets while reducing training and inference costs.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks for time series classification (TSC) are trained almost exclusively by error backpropagation, which imposes update locking and the weight-transport problem. Backpropagation-free learning rules such as Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA), Direct Random Target Projection (DRTP), and the diffusion-inspired NoProp relax these constraints but have been evaluated almost exclusively on 2D image benchmarks. We adapt these three learners to univariate TSC with 1D convolutional architectures and present the first systematic study of them across 112 datasets from the UCR time series archive, with one hyperparameter-optimized configuration per method. The optimized learners reach mean F1 scores of 0.76 to 0.79, below ROCKET (0.83) and InceptionTime (0.84). We propose an analysis framework that relates the per-dataset gap to InceptionTime to dataset properties and tests convolutional feature learning by replacing the flatten readout with global average pooling, measured as a difference-in-differences (DD) against a backpropagation control on the identical architecture. Intra-class temporal variability is the dataset property most consistently associated with the gap for all three learners (partial Spearman $\rho$ from $0.28$ to $0.40$). Pooling harms DFA and DRTP more than backpropagation (DD $-0.025$ and $-0.055$), consistent with near-random convolutional features, whereas NoProp tolerates pooling as backpropagation does (DD $+0.013$). Relative to backpropagation on the same architectures, DRTP reduces training floating-point operations (FLOPs) by 33% and trains faster only on series longer than about 700 time steps, DFA yields no computational reduction, and NoProp reduces peak memory by 38% at the cost of 48% longer training.
authors: Miha Kap\v{s}, Bla\v{z} Bertalani\v{c}, Carolina Fortuna
bullets: DFA, DRTP, and NoProp were adapted to 1D convolutional architectures and systematically evaluated across 112 UCR datasets.
Their mean F1 scores were 0.76–0.79, below ROCKET (0.83) and InceptionTime (0.84).
Intra-class temporal variability was the property most consistently linked to the performance gap versus InceptionTime.
Pooling results suggest near-random convolutional features for DFA and DRTP, while NoProp preserved feature learning more effectively.
DRTP cut training FLOPs by 33% and helped mainly on series longer than about 700 steps; NoProp cut peak memory by 38% but took 48% longer to train.

papers.abstract: Looped language models can strengthen reasoning through repeated computation with shared weights, increasing execution depth without adding independent parameters. However, each additional pass increases training floating-point operations (FLOPs), making these gains more expensive to obtain. To address this cost, we propose UpLoop, a pretraining schedule that uses upcycling to train looped Transformers while exactly matching a standard dense baseline in final parameter count, total training tokens, and training FLOPs. Specifically, UpLoop begins with a shallow Transformer, progressively grows its depth by copying learned layers, and uses the computation saved early to support repeated execution of a shared middle block later in training. Experiments across model scales show improvements in language modeling and downstream performance, with the average score across 22 downstream tasks increasing from 22.99 to 27.52 at 1.3B parameters. These gains also extend to mathematical reasoning after supervised fine-tuning.
authors: Cheng Liang, Tengfei Zhang, Ya Zhang, Yanfeng Wang, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Looped models can improve reasoning through shared-weight repeated computation, but normally require more training FLOPs.
UpLoop starts with a shallow Transformer, copies learned layers to grow depth, and later repeats a shared middle block.
It exactly matches a standard dense baseline in final parameter count, training tokens, and total training FLOPs.
Across model scales, it improves language modeling and downstream performance; at 1.3B parameters, the 22-task average rises from 22.99 to 27.52.
Benefits also extend to mathematical reasoning after supervised fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Residual connections underpin Transformers, but they implicitly tie the residual width carried through depth to the compute width used inside each layer. We introduce Hierarchical Residuals (HiRes), a minimalist architectural change that decouples these dimensions, widening the residual state while keeping per-layer compute width fixed. HiRes groups layers into blocks: standard d-dimensional PreNorm layers operate inside each block, while a wider D-dimensional PostNorm outer residual connects blocks. Learned read/write projections bridge the two spaces at block boundaries, leaving individual Transformer layers unchanged. Across different model sizes and depths, HiRes consistently outperforms vanilla residual addition, with fitted scaling laws indicating a 1.30-fold improvement in FLOPs efficiency. On OLMoE-1B-7B pretraining for 500B tokens, HiRes achieves 0.0208 lower training loss and 1.14-point higher downstream accuracy. HiRes is also competitive with other residual expansion methods such as VWN, mHC and AttnRes with less activation memory and I/O costs. Built from only dense projections and normalizations, it requires neither specialized kernels nor infrastructure-level optimizations. HiRes thus exposes residual width as a practical scaling variable using only standard operators.
authors: Ziteng Wang, Jianqiao Lu, Xinyu Ma, Jintao Zhang, Jun Zhu, Yiyuan Ma, Jianfei Chen
bullets: Problem: Standard residuals force the state width carried through depth to match each layer’s compute width.
Method: Group layers into blocks with d-dimensional PreNorm layers and a wider D-dimensional PostNorm outer residual, linked by learned projections.
Contribution: Makes residual width an independent scaling variable using only dense projections and normalizations.
Results: Reports 1.30× better FLOPs efficiency, 0.0208 lower training loss, and 1.14-point higher downstream accuracy in the stated experiments.
Scope: Designed to reduce activation memory and I/O relative to other residual-expansion methods without specialized kernels or infrastructure changes.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks for image recognition are typically trained using mini-batches, with a forward pass to compute predictions and losses followed by a more computationally expensive backward pass to update model parameters. However, not all training samples contribute equally to learning, suggesting that computation can be reduced by performing backward passes only on informative samples. The challenge is that sample informativeness changes throughout training: difficult samples may be valuable early on, improving samples become important later, and class diversity becomes increasingly relevant toward the end. Existing methods often rely on fixed selection rules or computationally expensive per-sample gradient calculations. We propose OT-CAL, an adaptive data selection method that automatically adjusts its sampling preferences during training. OT-CAL represents each sample using five informativeness features, including difficulty, learnability, and uncertainty. A curriculum vector describes the currently preferred sample characteristics, and optimal-transport-based matching assigns selection weights according to how closely samples match this target. The curriculum vector is then updated using the selected samples, forming a feedback loop that adapts without a manually defined schedule. Experiments on three standard visual learning benchmarks show that, when selecting 50% of each mini-batch, OT-CAL improves performance by 1.3--2.1 points over AdaSelection while achieving 1.18--1.24 times faster training than full-data training.
bullets: Targets the unequal informativeness of samples during mini-batch training to reduce costly backward passes.
Represents samples with five features, including difficulty, learnability, and uncertainty.
Uses an optimal-transport curriculum to match samples to evolving training preferences.
Updates the curriculum from selected samples, enabling feedback-driven adaptation without a manual schedule.
Selecting 50% of each mini-batch improves performance by 1.3–2.1 points over AdaSelection and trains 1.18–1.24× faster than full-data training on three benchmarks.

papers.abstract: We introduce Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. Local neighbor graphs constrain communication across polymer chains and their surrounding environments, while explicit all-pair attention incurs quadratic cost. RKA maps atomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout enable global feature exchange at linear cost in atom count for fixed feature dimensions. We insert the invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and obtain conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its radial coordinate dependence. We evaluate energy and force prediction for finite polymer-derived clusters in OPoly26. Our models are trained on the official training split for 12 epochs and evaluated directly after training on the complete official validation split. A matched 5M comparison shows that RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. The 20M RKA model is compared with UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation structures. The 20M model attains a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/angstrom; its per-atom energy MAE is 0.1182 meV/atom. RKA provides a compact global communication pathway that improves energy and force prediction on the evaluated polymer-derived clusters.
authors: Wenbo Fu, Chenghui Mao, Chengwen Hu, Haifeng Lv, Zhou Lv
bullets: Addresses the tension between local neighbor graphs that miss long-range interactions and quadratic-cost all-pair attention.
Maps centroid-relative atomic distances to learned radial features and combines them with content-dependent queries and keys.
Uses factorized aggregation and readout for linear scaling with atom count at fixed feature dimensions.
Inserted between EquiformerV3 local blocks, with conservative forces obtained by differentiating the energy.
On OPoly26 polymer-derived clusters, matched 5M models reduce per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%; the 20M model achieves 15.81 meV total-energy MAE and 2.619 meV/angstrom force MAE.

figures.caption: Figure 2: RKA in an equivariant atomic potential. Each local block updates the geometric representation. RKA reads its scalar channels and positions, and writes a scalar residual before the next block. The final scalar readout gives atomic energies. Shared elemental references and screened repulsion complete the total energy, whose coordinate derivative defines the forces. Charge/spin conditioning and repulsion are present in both 5M models.

Figure 1: Radial Kernel Attention. A finite structure defines a centroid and node radii. Learned radial features organize content-dependent key–value statistics over the entire structure. Each node reads the shared statistics through its radial features and query, and receives a scalar residual update. The basis curves are schematic, rather than fitted checkpoint values.

papers.title: Radial Kernel Attention for Long-Range Modeling in Polymer Machine Learning Force Fields
papers.tldr: Radial Kernel Attention adds a linear-cost global communication pathway that substantially improves energy and force prediction for polymer machine-learning force fields.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has become a standard reasoning strategy in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), showing strong performance in complex vision-language tasks such as reasoning segmentation. However, our analysis reveals that indiscriminate CoT usage can lead to degraded performance by inducing unnecessary reasoning, a phenomenon we term overthinking. In reasoning segmentation, overthinking often leads to misalignment between the query's intent and visual grounding. To address this, we propose Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT), a training-free adaptive framework that selectively triggers CoT based on the input's intrinsic difficulty. We find that the entropy of the model's attention maps reliably reflects task difficulty: low entropy indicates confident, localized grounding, while high entropy suggests uncertainty and potential benefit from CoT. DA-CoT uses this entropy signal to determine whether to apply CoT prompting. Additionally, we introduce a Bidirectional Rethinking mechanism that enables the model to automatically flip its reasoning decision when the initial output fails, enhancing robustness by recovering from failures induced by overthinking and underthinking. DA-CoT demonstrates its effectiveness by achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Reasoning Segmentation benchmarks while significantly improving inference efficiency.
authors: Chanseul Cho, Jaesung Jun, Dongheon Lee, Youngmin Ro
bullets: Problem: Always-on CoT can cause overthinking, misaligning visual grounding with the query.
Method: Estimate input difficulty from attention-map entropy; high entropy triggers CoT, while low entropy skips it.
Robustness: Bidirectional Rethinking reverses the initial reasoning choice when the output fails.
Results: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on reasoning segmentation benchmarks and improves inference efficiency.
Scope: Training-free adaptive inference for multimodal reasoning segmentation.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of the proposed DA-CoT framework during inference. If Hagg ≥ τ , the model follows the Difficulty-Aware Prompting Path with CoT for structured reasoning; otherwise, it takes the direct path without CoT for efficient inference. When the initial reasoning path fails to produce a valid output, a discrete flipping signal activates the Bidirectional Rethinking Path, enabling re-evaluation and recovery from overthinking or underthinking. The final bounding boxes or point prompts are then passed to the segmentation head to produce the reasoningaware segmentation result.

The visualized attention entropy (bottom right of each map) provides an intrinsic signal that distinguishes when CoT is helpful or harmful.
