papers.abstract: Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. Without architecture-specific tuning, BYOD induces diffusion generation in Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B; to our knowledge, this is the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of a Mistral model. The adapters comprise 4.1-5.8% of final parameters while every base-model parameter remains frozen; each 25,000-iteration conversion needs at most 102.4M tokens, processed in 3.1-4.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. All four models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context in a controlled attention test, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge. BYOD-Gemma is the strongest BYOD conversion on our nine-task evaluation, reaching 50.6% average accuracy compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. Open-generation quality at low network function evaluation (NFE) budgets remains the principal limitation: BYOD perplexity is 8.3-11.1 versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2-3.0 for the AR parents when generating 128 tokens in 64 steps. To enable further experimentation and inspection, we provide a standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four conversions. BYOD thus provides a practical route for extending diffusion generation to other existing model families while identifying the gap that efficient conversion must next close.
authors: Ruurd J. A. Kuiper, Robert A. Bagheri
bullets: Addresses the high pretraining and full-fine-tuning costs of building diffusion language models.
Uses an architecture-agnostic, LoRA-only conversion recipe with all base-model parameters frozen.
Demonstrated on Gemma 2, Llama 3.1, Qwen2.5, and Ministral; the latter is reported as the first Mistral AR-to-DLM conversion.
Converted models support fully masked generation, bidirectional context, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge.

papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient LoRA-only conversion of autoregressive LLMs to diffusion language models is directly relevant to LLM architecture advances and training-efficiency methods.
papers.title: BYOD: Build Your Own DLM - Efficient Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Language Model Conversion
papers.tldr: BYOD converts pretrained autoregressive language models into diffusion language models using only lightweight LoRA adapters, enabling efficient experimentation without modifying base-model weights.

papers.abstract: Long-context diffusion repeatedly pays for both token interaction and feed-forward computation. We formulate these costs as two separate budgets: the edges available to an attention graph and the experts activated for each token. This view connects local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming that sparsity alone preserves document-level information. We specify normalized masked attention, distinguish denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derive graph and compute bounds. A reported sparse-expert configuration, denoted DualBudget, is analyzed across scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. All supplied table measurements are retained. The length study shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K, together with measurable degradation as length increases. Ablations reveal mixed changes across the three reported scores, while the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. The analysis separates these observations from unmeasured claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence, and deployment memory.
authors: Alexandros Christoforos, Chadbourne Davis, Paul Raj
bullets: Models long-context diffusion costs using two budgets: attention-graph edges and activated feed-forward experts.
Unifies local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming sparsity preserves document-level information.
Defines normalized masked attention, distinguishes denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derives graph and compute bounds.
Evaluates the DualBudget configuration on scientific summarization, multi-hop QA, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction.
Results show gains over listed baselines through 16K, mixed ablation effects, and measurable degradation as sequence length grows.

papers.selection_reason: Sparse long-context text diffusion under attention and expert budgets is relevant to efficient attention and long-context generation.
papers.title: Sparse Text Diffusion under Dual Budgets: Context Connectivity and Expert Activation
papers.tldr: A dual-budget framework analyzes sparse diffusion models by separately constraining attention connectivity and expert activation, with reported gains through 16K tokens but degradation at longer lengths and a 20% cost reduction under an unspecified timing convention.

papers.abstract: Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, yet long-context prefill remains costly due to dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage. We introduce SparseGDN, a hardware-aware framework that combines structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent recurrent-event selection while producing outputs for every token. A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, while a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions, reducing computation and memory traffic. We evaluate SparseGDN on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B across RULER tasks and context lengths from 4K to 128K. Retaining approximately 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.
authors: Jiedong Zhuang, Peng Zhao, Jialin Tang, Haoji Hu
bullets: Targets the high cost of dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate storage in long-context GDN prefill.
Uses a block-adjacent solver for approximate local Delta computation and an input-dependent selector for recurrent-event allocation across head pairs.
Materializes only selected updates and reconstructs token outputs from compact state snapshots and group-local interactions.
On Qwen3.5-4B/9B across RULER and 4K–128K contexts, retaining about 29% of recurrent events yields 1.50–1.94× GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including selection overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 3 End-to-end SparseGDN execution pipeline. The block-adjacent intra-chunk kernel computes transformed values U, compact update coefficients, and selector scores. The dynamic selector converts these scores into a structured event mask. Only selected events trigger deferred W materialization and recurrent-state updates, producing compact event states. During output reconstruction, the mapped output kernel retrieves the appropriate preceding event state from HBM and applies the accumulated gap decay, while computing group-local interactions and producing outputs for every token.

papers.abstract: Neighbourhood-based detectors such as KNN, LOF and LUNAR remain among the most accurate methods for tabular anomaly detection, but they compare every query with the stored training set, so their inference cost and memory grow with the data and the data must be kept at deployment. We ask whether the neighbourhood geometry these detectors exploit can be compiled into a small network that scores a query with a single forward pass. We propose the Cauchy Displacement Network (CDN), which regresses each normal point onto the mean of its $k$ nearest training neighbours with a single-hidden-layer network of Cauchy activations and scores a query by the length of its predicted displacement. This displacement is an empirical mean-shift vector, whose fixed-radius population counterpart locally approximates a scaled gradient of the log density. We show that Cauchy units exactly represent the score fields of a structured family of Student-$t$ expert densities, and establish a constructive approximation bound for the corresponding population neighbourhood-mean map using a single-hidden-layer Cauchy network. We further show that the bounded network output guarantees asymptotically linear residual-score growth along every fixed direction. On 46 benchmark datasets against 28 baselines, CDN obtains the best mean rank under both AUC-ROC and AUC-PR, while scoring $10^4$ queries in a few milliseconds on a single CPU thread, up to three orders of magnitude faster than neighbourhood-based detectors, with a model whose size does not depend on the training set.
bullets: Addresses the inference-time and memory costs of retaining the full training set for KNN-, LOF-, and LUNAR-style detectors.
Uses a single-hidden-layer network with Cauchy activations to predict each point’s mean $k$-nearest-neighbour displacement; anomaly score is the residual length.
Connects the displacement to empirical mean shift and, locally, to the gradient of log density.
Provides theoretical results on Student-$t$ score-field representation, approximation of the population neighbourhood-mean map, and asymptotic residual growth.
On 46 datasets and 28 baselines, achieves the best mean rank for both AUC-ROC and AUC-PR; scores $10^4$ queries in a few milliseconds on one CPU thread.

papers.title: Anomalies as Residuals: Cauchy Displacement Networks

papers.abstract: Training-free expert pruning makes two decisions: which experts to remove, and what the layer computes when its router still selects a removed expert. Published methods change both at once. Holding the mask fixed, we compare replacement operators from three families on OLMoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight, with Granite as a fourth router, using paired, multiplicity-corrected tests. The largest effect is a choice usually left implicit: the survivors' gate scale. On routers trained without top-k renormalization, renormalizing the survivors' gates, a common implementation choice, costs 0.8-8.5 points and reverses whether rerouting beats MoNE's mean-output replacement; on two routers trained with renormalization, the trained scale wins at 50% pruning. We introduce the tilted novice, a closed-form low-rank map of the pruned expert's input whose rank-0 case is MoNE's constant. At 50% pruning it adds 1.2-1.8% parameters and gains 3.45 and 1.37 points over the constant on OLMoE and Moonlight, stable across calibration draws and largely unchanged by 4- and 3-bit quantization. No operator dominates: trained-scale rerouting is best on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and a partial copy of each pruned expert is statistically indistinguishable from the tilted novice on two models. Evaluation can change conclusions: at 25% pruning MoNE's constant keeps 92-97% of dense multiple-choice accuracy but only 5-65% of GSM8K and 0-17% of code scores, and the calibration domain moves the mask 4-9 times more than resampling. We propose a five-item reporting checklist.
authors: Ezza Ali, Sehrish Bibi, Momina Moetesum, Faisal Shafait
bullets: The study isolates replacement operators while keeping the pruning mask fixed across several MoE models and routers.
Survivor gate renormalization can reduce accuracy by 0.8–8.5 points on routers not trained with top-k renormalization and can reverse method rankings.
The proposed tilted novice improves over MoNE’s constant replacement by 3.45 points on OLMoE and 1.37 points on Moonlight at 50% pruning, with small parameter overhead.
Operator performance is model-dependent: trained-scale rerouting leads on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, while partial expert copies match the tilted novice on two models.

Evaluation task and calibration domain matter substantially; multiple-choice retention can overstate performance on math and code tasks, while calibration shifts the pruning mask more than resampling.

papers.title: What We Keep of What We Forget: Replacement Operators and Routing Semantics in Training-Free MoE Expert Pruning
papers.tldr: Replacement semantics—especially survivor gate scaling—strongly affect training-free MoE pruning results, and no single replacement operator is best across models or tasks.

papers.abstract: Length-aware scheduling reduces request latency in LLM serving by prioritizing shorter requests. However, despite their large model sizes, length predictors can suffer degraded ranking performance under domain and task shifts, and adapting them can require costly retraining. Their prediction overhead can further offset the benefits of scheduling. To improve the generalization and efficiency of length-aware scheduling, we propose \textbf{LEAP}, a length prediction system with fast online adaptation and asynchronous CPU execution. LEAP reuses the serving model's prefill hidden states, which contain information about the output length, and extracts this signal through a linear readout. To adapt to substantial domain and task shifts, it updates the readout at test time through recursive least squares, using completed requests as supervision without gradient computation or historical-data replay. Prediction and updates run asynchronously on CPU, while prediction and initial batch ordering overlap the remaining GPU prefill. Across the evaluated cross-domain transfers, LEAP retains strong ranking performance, and online adaptation improves Spearman correlation by 64.7\% under a larger domain shift. Serving experiments show that LEAP reduces average per-token latency by 15.9--40.8\% compared with the evaluated length predictors, while achieving 1.9\% higher throughput with $30{,}569\times$ fewer predictor parameters than the strongest evaluated baseline.
authors: Kwan Yan, Jialun Zhong, Yanzeng Li
bullets: Addresses degraded length-prediction ranking under domain/task shifts and the cost of predictor inference or retraining.
Uses a linear readout over serving-model prefill hidden states, adapted online via recursive least squares from completed requests.
Runs prediction and updates asynchronously on the CPU while overlapping prediction and initial scheduling with GPU prefill.
Improves Spearman correlation by 64.7% under a larger domain shift and reduces average per-token latency by 15.9–40.8% in serving experiments.
Achieves 1.9% higher throughput than the strongest evaluated baseline with 30,569× fewer predictor parameters.

papers.abstract: Sparse MoE mechanism significantly improves the trade-off between model capacity and inference efficiency. However, practical deployment still requires storing all experts, resulting in substantial memory overhead. We show that expert outputs in MoE layers exhibit structured redundancy. Across different models and task categories, the stable rank and entropy effective rank of expert outputs are consistently far below the nominal number of experts, while expert output distributions also exhibit fewer effective modes. Motivated by these observations, we reformulate expert pruning as a structure-preserving expert subset selection problem and efficiently optimize it via a greedy strategy, rather than only independently scoring and ranking individual experts or exhaustively searching over expert combinations. We propose two expert pruning methods under the unified structure-preserving framework: Projection Energy Expert Pruning (PEEP), which preserves the functional subspace by maximizing weighted projection energy, and Distributional Coverage Expert Pruning (DCEP), which preserves the distributional geometry by minimizing weighted coverage error. Both methods incorporate router-derived weights as priors, enabling them to jointly preserve the global structural relationships among experts while accounting for the local importance of individual experts. Experiments on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate that, at the expert retention ratios of 75% and 50%, our methods outperform the state-of-the-art baselines on the majority of benchmarks and consistently achieve the best average performance across both general tasks and mathematical reasoning tasks.
authors: Tian Wang, Yongding Tao, Yihong Dong, Xiaoming Wu, Ying Guo, Ge Li
bullets: MoE expert outputs contain substantial, structured redundancy, with fewer effective modes than the nominal expert count.
Expert pruning is formulated as structure-preserving subset selection rather than independent expert ranking or exhaustive combination search.
PEEP preserves the experts’ functional subspace, while DCEP preserves their distributional geometry; both use router-derived importance weights.
On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, both methods perform best on average across general and mathematical reasoning benchmarks at 75% and 50% expert retention.

papers.title: Experts Exhibit Structured Redundancy: Structure-Preserving Expert Pruning for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models
papers.tldr: The paper prunes MoE experts by preserving their output structure, reducing memory while retaining model performance better than prior pruning approaches.

papers.abstract: Disaggregated LLM inference separates the prefill and decode phases across GPU pools, generating massive KV-cache transfers. Because these transfers last hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, they behave as mega elephant flows that dominate link bandwidth utilization. In this regime, stateless ECMP can perform poorly: hash collisions may overload one spine link while leaving others idle, stretching transfer times by seconds. Yet this same persistence makes coordination practical. Since these flows are long-lived, even lightweight one-to-all coordination can be amortized over their lifetime. We present ARK, a distributed elephant-flow path reservation mechanism. ARK coordinates senders to choose source ports whose hashes map concurrent flows onto distinct spines, without requiring switch changes or receiver-side packet reordering. Packet-level RDMA simulations show that ARK reduces mean and P95 FCT by up to 27.3% and 34.0% under moderate load, and further reduces mean TTFT by up to 12.9%.
authors: Hung-Chun Lin, Ting-Wei Hsu, Chung-En Ho, Ahmed Saeed
bullets: Disaggregated prefill/decode inference creates long-lived, bandwidth-heavy KV-cache transfers.
Stateless ECMP can hash concurrent transfers onto the same spine link, causing congestion and delays.
ARK reserves paths by coordinating senders to select source ports that map flows across distinct spines.
The mechanism requires no switch changes or receiver-side packet reordering.
RDMA simulations report up to 27.3% lower mean FCT, 34.0% lower P95 FCT, and 12.9% lower mean TTFT under moderate load.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the efficiency of KV cache transfers in disaggregated LLM inference by introducing ARK, a distributed path reservation mechanism to avoid routing collisions and reduce latency.
papers.title: ARK: Avoiding Routing Collisions for KV Cache Transfer in Disaggregated LLM Inference
papers.tldr: ARK coordinates KV-cache transfer paths to avoid ECMP collisions, reducing flow completion time and time to first token in disaggregated LLM inference.

papers.abstract: Quantization of Large Language Models (LLMs) has be- coming increasingly important for reducing the computa- tional costs and resource requirements for practical deploy- ment.Growinginterestinthisareahasmotivatedthecommu- nity to move beyond 8-bit quantization towards 4-bit preci- sion, leading to the development of customized 4-bit formats such as MXFP4 and NVFP4. Recently, HiFloat4 (HiF4) has emerged as a competitive alternative which adopts a Block Floating-Point(BFP)formatwithathree-levelscalinghierar- chy, thereby achieving a significantly larger dynamic range. While quantization can substantially reduce memory usage and accelerate inference, it frequently introduces accuracy degradation. Calibration is therefore essential for narrowing theperformancegapbetweenlow-precisionquantizedmodels and their full-precision counterparts. Nevertheless, existing calibration methods are mainly designed and validated us- ing integer-precision formats, such as INT4, lacking support for HiF4 due to its hierarchical BFP structure. In this paper, weinvestigatethreecalibrationapproaches,namelyHiGPTQ, HiAutoRound, and HiFlatQuant, to further enhance model quantizationbasedontheHiF4format.Extensiveexperiments demonstratethatallthreeproposedapproachesimproveinfer- ence accuracy compared with direct HiF4 conversion, reduc- ing the gap between HiF4 and BF16 to less than 1% and out- performing the state-of-the-art NVFP4 format across various models and downstream tasks.
authors: Jing Huang, Yu Cheng, Ziwei Yu, Lan Zhao, Sitan Li, Guangxiu Yao, Xin Wang, Yuanyong Luo, Hengyi Liang, Ting Li, Bo Liu, Hu Liu, Michael Bi Mi, Heng Liao
bullets: HiFloat4 uses a three-level hierarchical block floating-point structure to provide greater dynamic range than other 4-bit formats.
Existing calibration methods largely target integer formats and do not directly support HiF4’s hierarchical structure.
The paper introduces HiGPTQ, HiAutoRound, and HiFlatQuant for calibrating HiF4-quantized models.
Experiments show all three methods improve over direct HiF4 conversion.
The methods reduce the HiF4–BF16 accuracy gap to below 1% and outperform NVFP4 in the reported evaluations.

papers.tldr: Three HiF4-specific calibration methods substantially improve 4-bit LLM quantization, narrowing the accuracy gap to BF16 to under 1% and outperforming NVFP4 across evaluated models and tasks.

papers.abstract: Self-distillation methods for large language models with an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher already retain a history of student updates. Muon nevertheless stores a separate momentum buffer, increasing persistent training memory. We propose Muon with Reused Teacher (Muon-RT), which reuses the teacher-student displacement to eliminate momentum buffers for hidden weight matrices. We show that this displacement encodes an exponentially weighted history of applied updates and smooths temporally uncorrelated noise under a local model. Muon-RT removes its radial component, normalizes it spectrally, and mixes it with the current gradient after Newton-Schulz (NS) orthogonalization. Under explicit regularity and alignment assumptions, we establish linear contraction of an expected objective-gap bound toward a residual error level. With Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Muon-RT improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.6 points with 42% less persistent memory, and over momentum Muon by 5.4 points with 27% less persistent memory. With Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) on Olmo-3-7B-Instruct, it improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.0 points.
authors: Aryan Das, Vinay Kumar Verma, Aakansha Mishra
bullets: Targets the extra persistent memory required by Muon’s momentum buffer in EMA-teacher self-distillation.
Reuses, radial-adjusts, and spectrally normalizes the teacher–student displacement, then combines it with the NS-orthogonalized gradient.
Theoretical analysis gives linear contraction toward a residual error level under regularity and alignment assumptions.
On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with SDFT, it improves average accuracy by 2.6 points over AdamW and 5.4 points over momentum Muon, using 42% and 27% less persistent memory, respectively.
On Olmo-3-7B-Instruct with SDPO, it improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.0 points.

(b) Newton–Schulz approximately orthogonalizes the gradient G into O. The radial component of the teacher–student displacement WT −WS is removed to obtain H, which is spectrally normalized into P. The update combines both directions as U = (1− α)O+ αP. (c) The EMA-teacher tracks the student’s parameter trajectory with a temporal lag.

papers.abstract: Estimating whether a problem is too complex for a large language model (LLM) before the model attempts it can guide model routing, how to allocate test-time compute, and suggest the need for new tools to aid the agent. While existing estimators rely on the problem text, LLM-annotated task difficulty labels, or signals obtained after a model attempts to solve the problem, such as its hidden states, none explicitly leverage the constraint structure inherent in the problem: the variables to assign and how the constraints over them interact. We introduce CIRCE, which extracts a problem's structure by using a cheap LLM to construct a Constraint Intermediate Representation that deterministically compiles into the constraint graph. Across seven reasoning benchmarks (including SAT, logic, and math) and four LLMs, even a randomly initialized GNN encoder improves predictions of LLM response correctness, reducing negative log-likelihood from 0.465 to 0.423 and increasing AUROC from 0.691 to 0.727 relative to the strongest baseline for each metric.
authors: Chenhao Hong, Jiakai Xu, Kaushiki Singh, Yusen Zhang, Eugene Wu
bullets: Targets pre-attempt difficulty estimation for model routing, test-time compute allocation, and tool selection.
Uses a cheap LLM to convert problems into a Constraint Intermediate Representation, which deterministically compiles into a constraint graph.
A graph neural network encodes the constraint structure to predict LLM response correctness.
Evaluated across seven SAT, logic, and math reasoning benchmarks and four LLMs.
Improves prediction over the strongest baselines, lowering NLL from 0.465 to 0.423 and raising AUROC from 0.691 to 0.727.

papers.abstract: Security operations centers (SOCs) need to turn terabytes of alerts, logs and flows into trusted, affordable decisions to unveil hidden threats. We present LanG 2.0, an agentic system that detects threats, correlates evidence and writes rules, investigating whether small local models can replace frontier models affordably and safely when structural safeguards, not model accuracy, provide the guarantees. It incorporates entity-anchored correlation, human approval of rule changes and a tamper-evident ledger. Tests span eight flow datasets from five networks, real XDR alerts and multistage campaigns. Against its predecessor, campaign correlation precision rises from 18.75% to 51.81%, and rule acceptance from at most 60.00% to 98.33%. Against Claude Opus 5.5, scoring flows against each network's normal traffic detects attacks on unseen networks at 73.42% F1 without false positives, versus 58.10% with 49.00% false positives, for at least 650 times less energy. Finetuned models statistically match it on alert classification and rule writing for 5.6 to 59 times less energy. The work demonstrates LanG's practical scalability, processing 3.33 million records in 6.4 minutes, over 30 million hourly, and its safeguards resisted prompt injection, label poisoning and ledger tampering, so small local models can carry most SOC detection affordably and safely.
authors: Anes Abdennebi, Nadjia Kara, Laaziz Lahlou, Hakima Ould-Slimane
bullets: Correlates entities and evidence, detects campaigns, and proposes detection rules for semi-automated security operations.
Uses human approval for rule changes and a tamper-evident ledger to improve safety and accountability.
Improves campaign-correlation precision from 18.75% to 51.81% and rule acceptance from at most 60.00% to 98.33% over its predecessor.
Achieves 73.42% F1 on attacks from unseen networks without false positives, using at least 650× less energy than Claude Opus 5.5.
Scales to 3.33 million records in 6.4 minutes and resists prompt injection, label poisoning, and ledger tampering.

papers.abstract: Large language models have been shown to memorise and reproduce verbatim sequences from their training data, raising concerns about privacy leakage, intellectual property exposure, and the limits of generalisation. Recent theoretical work suggests that attention heads may contribute to this behaviour by functioning as associative memory mechanisms, with memorisation capacity scaling with the number of heads. At the same time, empirical work has shown that many attention heads are redundant and can be pruned with limited impact on downstream performance. Despite these parallel findings, the effect of pruning redundant heads on memorised-sequence reproduction remains unexplored. In this work, we demonstrate that zeroing out a substantial fraction of attention heads prior to inference can significantly suppress verbatim memorisation while preserving, or even improving, language modelling performance on the benchmark used to identify redundant heads. Evaluating GPT-2-XL(1.5B) on known memorised sequences, we find that pruning 729 task-redundant heads reduces the memorisation count by 91.5%, while improving WikiText-103 perplexity by 0.92. These findings suggest that attention-head redundancy can be exploited to mitigate memorisation at inference time, without retraining or modifying the training data.
bullets: Addresses privacy and intellectual-property risks from large language models reproducing training sequences.
Zeros out task-redundant attention heads before inference, without retraining or changing training data.
On GPT-2-XL, pruning 729 heads reduced memorisation count by 91.5%.
WikiText-103 perplexity improved by 0.92 after pruning.
The result suggests attention-head redundancy can be used for inference-time memorisation mitigation.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in deep learning has substantially advanced automated grading of ophthalmologic pathologies, supported by large annotated datasets and improved representation learning. However, a significant gap remains between state-of-the-art performance and clinical scalability. In particular, foundation models have reshaped image-based medical screening and diagnosis. These large-scale architectures trained on extensive datasets learn rich, generalizable feature representations that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks. In ophthalmology, RETFound, one of the most relevant foundation models for retinal images, performs strongly across classification, segmentation, and risk prediction tasks. Despite their effectiveness, foundation models are often computationally prohibitive, hindering their deployment in real-world clinical environments where hardware constraints and latency are critical. To bridge this gap, we introduce CAMEL (Cross-Architecture Masked Embedding Learning), a novel cross-architecture distillation framework that uses an asymmetric masking strategy during embedding learning to effectively transfer knowledge from massive teacher foundation models to compact, lightweight student models. Our experimental evaluation across four datasets shows that CAMEL preserves accuracy while drastically reducing computational complexity, enabling lightweight yet highly accurate models suitable for resource-limited clinical settings.
authors: Andre Guarnier De Mitri, Giovani Decico Lucafo, Miller Matheus Lima Anacleto Rocha, Diego Furtado Silva
bullets: Addresses the deployment barriers of large retinal foundation models, including hardware requirements and latency.
Uses cross-architecture knowledge distillation with asymmetric masking during embedding learning.
Transfers representations from massive teacher models to lightweight student architectures.
Evaluated across four datasets, with reported accuracy preservation and greatly reduced computational complexity.
Targets resource-limited clinical screening and diagnosis settings.

papers.abstract: The bottleneck of attention mechanisms, which are the fundamental building block of modern language models, is their quadratic complexity in terms of context size. There has thus been an increasing interest in the compression of the context, also called KV-cache compression. In this article, we consider the problem of compressing the context of attention mechanisms by first formulating it in the Hilbert space associated with its kernel. In this formalism, attention can be represented as the ratio of two linear maps whose interpolant is also the ratio of interpolants, this allows us to consider the interpolation of the linear maps directly. We thus introduce two novel KV-cache compression methods which we call GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on the Generalized Empirical Interpolation Method (GEIM) and the Q-Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (Q-DEIM), respectively. As the cost of these methods is quadratic in terms of context length, we propose surrogate models based on the Taylor series, the Performer and the Random Fourier Features method which allow the compression to be done in linear time. Finally, we extend this result to the streaming attention setting, providing new methods which allow one to penalize the selection of interpolation nodes based on the previously interpolated context and to update the previous interpolation based on new information. We then provide numerical results on the convergence of the residuals and the output error in future queries and preliminary results on the LongBench-E benchmark showing performance comparable to the state-of-the-art methods. These experiments suggest that the range revealed by our Q-DAIM method could help identify where information is concentrated in the KV cache, thus enabling an efficient compression.
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of attention with increasing context length by compressing the KV cache.
Formulates attention in a kernel-associated Hilbert space, representing it as a ratio of linear maps whose interpolants can be compressed directly.
Proposes GAIM and Q-DAIM methods based on GEIM and Q-DEIM interpolation techniques.
Uses Taylor-series, Performer, and Random Fourier Features surrogates to reduce compression cost from quadratic to linear time, and extends the approach to streaming attention.

Numerical experiments evaluate residual and future-query output errors; preliminary LongBench-E results show performance comparable to existing methods, while suggesting Q-DAIM can reveal where KV-cache information is concentrated.

papers.abstract: High-dimensional tensors are ubiquitous in real-world applications but lead to massive storage overhead. Functional tensor decomposition addresses this by employing neural networks to map element coordinates to tensor cores, significantly reducing the parameters for data compression. However, existing functional methods typically flatten high-order tensors into 1D sequences. This folding operation causes highly overlapping local coordinate sequences and struggles to capture complex cross-mode spatial dependencies, severely limiting their expressiveness on diverse datasets. To tackle these challenges, we propose TensorSSM, a novel Implicit Neural Representation (INR) for functional decomposition method that memorizes spatial positions within a dynamic State Space Model (SSM). Specifically, TensorSSM first decomposes mode-wise coordinates into sequences spit by K-ary rule, encoding spatial tokens from coarse to fine, which effectively captures spatial variations. Furthermore, we extend the SSM's state space to explicitly map cross-mode spatial dependencies, allowing inter-mode interactions to enhance the updates of each mode. By integrating cross-mode information from previous hidden states into the current state transitions, TensorSSM effectively expands tensor representation along two dimensions: the sequence dimension for coarse-to-fine spatial tokens, and the state dimension for cross-mode memorization. This design effectively integrates spatial information into the state space and the tensor core, substantially advancing the state adaptability and enhancing the expressiveness of the data compression. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TensorSSM achieves significantly high reconstruction accuracy and storage efficiency, exhibiting robust expressiveness across diverse tensor datasets without relying on strict spatial assumptions.
authors: Sheng Zhang, Xinyi Wang, Maolin Wang, Xiangyu Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limitations of flattening high-order tensors into 1D coordinate sequences, which can lose complex spatial relationships.
Decomposes mode-wise coordinates using a K-ary rule to encode spatial tokens from coarse to fine.
Extends the SSM state space to memorize cross-mode spatial dependencies and interactions.
Reports high reconstruction accuracy and storage efficiency across diverse tensor datasets without strict spatial assumptions.

papers.abstract: Mobile GUI agents are typically fine-tuned 7B-scale vision-language models (VLMs) that generate each action as text. However, these VLMs decode every action token by token, and even agents that score candidate actions keep a large language model or VLM in the loop, making them slow and memory-hungry. To address these issues, we propose GUI-JEPA, to our knowledge the first decoder-free GUI agent policy built on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), which selects actions in the latent space of a JEPA encoder pretrained on unlabelled GUI screenshots. Its action- and region-conditioned latent predictor turns the screen latent into one latent per candidate action, letting lightweight heads score all candidates against the instruction in a single batched pass, without decoding a token. We further show that the scorer relies on this latent pathway and that the predictor is trained for the decision itself: a randomly initialised predictor does just as well as one pretrained on screen dynamics. On AndroidControl, GUI-JEPA is 2.8-4.0x faster on the same GPU than a Qwen2.5-VL-7B agent we fine-tune with the same inputs, while reaching 86-92% of its in-distribution accuracy with 6% of its parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/bcwang-sjtu/GUI-JEPA
bullets: Targets the latency and memory costs of token-by-token VLM action generation for mobile GUI agents.
Uses a JEPA encoder pretrained on unlabeled screenshots and an action- and region-conditioned predictor to produce one latent per candidate action.
Lightweight heads score all candidates against the instruction in a single batched pass without language decoding.
On AndroidControl, it is 2.8–4.0× faster than a comparable fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B agent and reaches 86–92% of its in-distribution accuracy with 6% of its parameters.
The predictor’s decision-focused training is supported by similar performance from a randomly initialized predictor and one pretrained on screen dynamics.

papers.selection_reason: Decoder-free JEPA policy for GUI agents that scores candidate actions in latent space; substantial speed and parameter-efficiency contribution.
papers.title: GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents
papers.tldr: GUI-JEPA is a decoder-free mobile GUI agent that scores candidate actions in JEPA latent space, achieving substantially faster inference with far fewer parameters than a fine-tuned 7B VLM.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models can benefit from test-time scaling, but continued reasoning may become ineffective or harmful, a phenomenon termed overthinking. Evaluations against full thinking compare accuracy and token usage but lack references for overthinking severity and strategies' theoretical mitigation potential. To characterize overthinking at the model-task level, we first introduce Step-wise Truncation Probing (STP), repeatedly generating answers from multiple retained prefixes along each fixed sampled reasoning trajectory. Using each trajectory's earliest measured position attaining maximum empirical accuracy as a reference, we define Overthinking Ratio and Accuracy Degradation as the fraction of thinking tokens generated afterward and the accuracy decrease from this reference to full thinking, respectively. Secondly, we then formulate dynamic routing, fixed budgets, and dynamic early exit within a unified framework to quantify the theoretical mitigation potential of different termination strategies. Based on this unified framework, we use the complete STP measurements to construct a token-accuracy Pareto frontier for each strategy under a common normalized thinking-token budget. We further develop OTBench, a reusable benchmark built from the STP process, which produced 70.5B reasoning tokens and the corresponding probing measurements across six models and four benchmark groups.
bullets: Overthinking occurs when continued test-time reasoning stops helping or harms accuracy, but existing evaluations lack severity references and theoretical comparisons.
Step-wise Truncation Probing (STP) evaluates answers from multiple prefixes of fixed reasoning trajectories.
It defines Overthinking Ratio and Accuracy Degradation relative to each trajectory’s earliest prefix achieving maximum measured accuracy.
A unified framework compares dynamic routing, fixed budgets, and dynamic early exit by constructing token–accuracy Pareto frontiers under a normalized budget.
OTBench provides STP-based measurements across six models and four benchmark groups, totaling 70.5B reasoning tokens.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses token-accuracy tradeoffs and early termination for reasoning models, directly relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: Constructing Pareto Frontiers of Optimal Reasoning Termination Methods for Overthinking in Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: The paper introduces a framework and benchmark for measuring overthinking and comparing reasoning-termination strategies through token–accuracy Pareto frontiers.

papers.abstract: Due to limited support for intra-tensor heterogeneous precision in conventional accelerators, neural network quantization remains largely restricted to per-tensor precision assignment. We present ShatterQuant, a hardware-software co-designed framework enabling mixed-precision quantization within each tensor by assigning independent bit-widths to blocks of a weight projection. ShatterQuant couples precision granularity with PE configuration, such that each precision determines an effective block height. We introduce (1) a hardware-aware post-training method that assigns intra-tensor precision based on block-level standard deviation and weight sensitivity; (2) the ShatterQuant Transformer Accelerator supporting 1/2/4/8-bit weight precision, precision-dependent PE configuration, block rescaling, and integrated softmax and piecewise-linear nonlinearities; and (3) an evaluation of model-hardware tradeoffs using an implementation in the TSMC 16nm PDK operating at 1 GHz, achieving 1.5 TOPS, 760 GOPS/$mm^2$ area efficiency, and 2.8 TOPS/W energy efficiency. On DeiT and ImageNet-1K, ShatterQuant achieves accuracy within $3.3\%$ of state-of-the-art mixed-precision techniques while using a 2 bit lower effective bitwidth, while for PixelDiT demonstrates comparable generation quality. ShatterQuant demonstrates how fine-grained intra-tensor mixed-precision can be realized through hardware-software co-design.
bullets: Assigns independent 1/2/4/8-bit precisions to weight blocks based on block variability and sensitivity.
Links precision granularity to processing-element configuration and effective block height.
Introduces a systolic Transformer accelerator with block rescaling, integrated softmax, and piecewise-linear nonlinearities.
A 16nm, 1GHz implementation achieves 1.5 TOPS, 760 GOPS/mm², and 2.8 TOPS/W.
On DeiT/ImageNet-1K and PixelDiT, it maintains comparable accuracy or generation quality with lower effective bitwidth than referenced mixed-precision approaches.

papers.abstract: We present FloodDiffusion 2 (FD2), an efficient and controllable framework that builds upon FloodDiffusion (FD1), a state-of-the-art streaming motion generation model. While FD1 produces plausible motion, it suffers from low efficiency and limited controllability, as its attention design requires repeated computation over the entire history, and it lacks precise trajectory control for real-world applications. To address these limitations and improve generation quality, FD2 introduces three advances. First, Partial Attention makes finalized history representations independent of the active window, enabling KV-cached inference and shared-history packing for efficient training. Second, we establish a necessary-and-sufficient Bregman criterion for regression losses to preserve diffusion's conditional-mean velocity field. This criterion guides an FK-induced quadratic loss that incorporates motion geometry without online FK evaluation. Third, FD2 introduces precise path conditioning to control the character's root trajectory while preserving natural body motion. Experiments show that FD2 reduces training computation by 4.6$\times$ and accelerates denoising by 11.29$\times$, reaching 2.303 ms per update on long sequences. Alongside these efficiency gains, FD2 improves motion quality over FD1 and achieves state-of-the-art FID scores among streaming methods, with 0.048 on SEED and 0.053 on HumanML3D.
bullets: Targets FD1’s repeated-history computation and limited trajectory control.
Uses Partial Attention for KV-cached inference and shared-history packing during training.
Introduces a Bregman-based criterion and FK-induced quadratic loss to incorporate motion geometry without online forward-kinematics evaluation.
Adds precise root-path conditioning while preserving natural full-body motion.
Reports 4.6× lower training computation, 11.29× faster denoising, and improved FID over FD1, including 0.048 on SEED and 0.053 on HumanML3D.

figures.caption: Figure 1: FloodDiffusion 2 generates continuous human motion from time-varying text prompts while following a specified path. papers.abstract: Modern LLMs strain device memory through large model weights and attention states, particularly in resource-constrained scenarios. Existing systems separately provision memory for model weights and attention states, imposing fixed fixed boundaries that cannot adapt to the changing memory demands of workloads. Under heavy workloads, insufficient state capacity limits request concurrency and reduces throughput; under light workloads, idle memory in one region cannot be reallocated to another, wasting device memory. Meanwhile, modern LLM architectures introduce heterogeneous tensors with diverse layouts and lifetimes, further complicating memory management. These problems motivate unified memory management for heterogeneous tensors. However, a shared pool alone does not make memory directly reusable across tensors with different allocation granularities and execution layouts. This paper presents Rimuru, a modern LLM serving system that unifies memory management through elastic expert offloading. Rimuru establishes a shared page pool to enables elastic memory sharing across heterogeneous tensors. To accommodate different allocation granularities, Rimuru introduces memory views that allow each tensor type to interpret the shared memory space using its own page size and page table. Furthermore, Rimuru combines huge-page alignment with a multi-level page allocator that splits and merges pages, enabling cross-type capacity reuse. A page-table-aware fused MoE kernel directly accesses non-contiguous expert weights, avoiding copy overhead. Building on these mechanisms, Rimuru employs a workload-aware adjuster that dynamically reallocates pages across tensor types according to runtime demands. Implemented on top of vLLM, Rimuru remains compatible with modern LLMs. Evaluations show that Rimuru achieves up to 19.03x baseline throughput and reduces TTFT by 98.1% on average.
bullets: Fixed partitions for model weights and attention states waste memory and limit concurrency under changing workloads.
Rimuru uses a shared page pool with tensor-specific memory views and page tables to support different layouts and allocation granularities.
A multi-level allocator enables page splitting, merging, and cross-tensor capacity reuse, while a fused MoE kernel accesses non-contiguous expert weights without copying.
A workload-aware adjuster reallocates pages at runtime based on demand and is implemented in vLLM.
The system reports up to 19.03× baseline throughput and an average 98.1% reduction in time to first token (TTFT).

papers.abstract: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.
authors: Jiongfan Yang, Weichen Fan, Haiwen Diao, Zhongang Cai, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Global attention captures low-frequency structure, while high-frequency detail is modeled locally.
Each spatial anchor expands into DCT-band-specific slots; only the lowest-frequency slots use global attention.
A spatial head adds local corrections while generation, targets, and loss remain in pixel space.
On ImageNet-512, SpecSlot improves FID by 2.84 with 3.9% fewer FLOPs than a matched JiT control.
It also approaches JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost and surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench at 40.6% lower forward cost.

papers.abstract: Predicting how many tokens a large language model (LLM) will decode, using only prefill-phase hidden states, is a key primitive for inference scheduling. We show that current benchmarks conflate predictor quality with task hardness: when the target model, dataset, or sampling configuration changes, reported accuracy collapses even though the predictor is unchanged. We trace this instability to an overlooked error source---the inherent stochasticity of autoregressive decoding---and derive bounds that every prefill-side method must obey. Our analysis treats decoding as a stopped stochastic process. The per-step stopping probability of a response is not constant but ramps up over hundreds of steps, so the decode length inherits a central limit theorem from the many local decisions that determine where a response ends; this yields per-prompt normality with an explicit error term, together with an affine variance law $\sigma=\alpha\mu+b$ whose slope is the coefficient of variation of the number of response segments. Empirically, the normal law reproduces the per-prompt MAE and the central mass of the decode-length distribution to within a few percent, and the residual departures from normality (mild right skew, slight excess kurtosis) are the ones predicted by the sampling-noise correction. Under fixed model, data, and sampling conditions, a broad design space of predictors (MLP, EGTP, FiLM, soft-label, and Mixture-of-Experts variants) converges to similar performance close to the bound, confirming that \emph{system error dominates model error}. We argue for a benchmarking protocol that fixes the model, data, and sampling parameters and that reports relative-error metrics alongside absolute ones. Code and analysis tools are available at https://github.com/ShwStone/DecodingPredict.
authors: Haowen Shi, Xuzhe Yan, Fahao Chen, Peng Li
bullets: Existing benchmarks mix predictor quality with task difficulty: changing the model, dataset, or sampling setup can sharply change accuracy.
A stopped-stochastic-process analysis shows decode lengths are approximately normal per prompt, with an affine standard-deviation–mean relationship.
Sampling noise creates an irreducible error floor for all prefill-only predictors.
Experiments find the predicted distribution matches empirical MAE and central mass within a few percent, with expected mild skew and kurtosis.
Under fixed conditions, diverse predictors perform similarly near the bound, indicating system error dominates model error; relative-error metrics are recommended alongside absolute ones.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes fundamental limits of prefill-based decode-length prediction for LLM inference scheduling; relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: On the Fundamental Limits of Prefill-Based Decoding Length Prediction
papers.tldr: Prefill-based decode-length prediction is fundamentally limited by autoregressive sampling noise, so benchmark results should control evaluation conditions and compare against stochasticity-derived bounds.

papers.abstract: The rapid growth in the size of state-of-the-art machine-learning (ML) models has led to increasing compute demands, spurring the development of energy-efficient hardware accelerators. Physical systems trained to perform ML inference, known as physical neural networks, have been proposed as accelerators in part because of their potential to be highly energy efficient. However, the ML inference accuracies reported in most investigations of physical neural networks have been substantially below the state of the art for conventional digital neural networks. In this work, we show in simulation studies that by applying modern ML training practices, including model compression, various candidate physical neural networks based on nonlinear dynamical systems can achieve accuracies as high as 99.2% on MNIST handwritten-digit recognition. We also show for one dynamical system that using it as the core building block of a parameter-efficient ML architecture inspired by MLP-Mixers enables accuracies of up to 86.4% on CIFAR-10 image classification (92.2% with pretraining and knowledge distillation), compared with 64% for the same system without the mixer architecture. The mixer approach achieved its accuracy while using $>5\times$ fewer trainable parameters than the baseline. Finally, we present back-of-the-envelope estimates for inference energy efficiency and speed when using an example physical dynamical system, suggesting that orders of magnitude improvements may be possible over digital-electronic neural networks.
authors: Tyler King, Magnus Saebo, Jeremie Laydevant, Haoting Zhen, Maxwell G. Anderson, Tatsuhiro Onodera, Peter L. McMahon
bullets: Physical neural networks are explored as energy-efficient accelerators, addressing the computational cost of increasingly large ML models.
Simulated nonlinear dynamical systems achieve up to 99.2% accuracy on MNIST when combined with modern training practices and model compression.
An MLP-Mixer-inspired architecture raises CIFAR-10 accuracy to 86.4%, or 92.2% with pretraining and knowledge distillation, versus 64% without the mixer.
The mixer architecture uses more than five times fewer trainable parameters than the baseline.
Back-of-the-envelope estimates suggest possible orders-of-magnitude gains in inference energy efficiency and speed, though results are simulation-based and partly prospective.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Overview of machine learning based on the controllable evolution in time of nonlinear dynamical networks (DynNets). (A) depicts the pipeline for classifying a sample MNIST input. The input image is padded with zeros and encoded in the initial conditions of a dynamical system. The output is taken as the state of the dynamical system at some time T . The process of optimizing the controllable parameters θ of the physical system adjusts the dynamics such that the input is mapped to a useful feature vector by the evolution of the system ϕ. We show that a variety of controllable dynamical systems can perform competitively for this optimization task, including (B) an inductively coupled network of Chua Circuits—chaotic electronic circuits; (C) Kuramoto coupled oscillators—a canonical dynamical system for modeling synchronization; (D) the coherent Ising machine—a coupled network of optical oscillators (shown as ring resonators here); and (E) a crossbar oscillator architecture with a feedback loop—a network representing sigmoidal oscillator dynamics.

FIG. 2: Dynamics and test accuracy of KuraNN architecture during MNIST training. (A)-(C) Mean KuraNN oscillator dynamics and class histograms for MNIST at epochs 2, 20, and 150. (D) Log-linear plot of test accuracy during training, achieving a maximum test accuracy of 98.88%. (E) End-of-training log-scale confusion matrix on the MNIST test set. (F) Oscillators associated with classes 3 and 6, exhibiting class separation between the two groups over the time horizon.

FIG. 3: Visualization of the coupling connectivity of the KuraNN as it trains with pruning. (A) MNIST image of a “3” with all couplings connected to the oscillator at index (7, 6). (B) Density of couplings from all oscillators to the oscillator at (7, 6) for epochs 100, 250, and 400. (C) Test accuracy during training on MNIST; final accuracy of 98.96%. (D) Connection density per epoch; we geometrically decay the connection density until we reach a desired density level (in this case, 10%). (E) Magnitudes of coupling coefficients between all 196 image oscillators.

The first section details our results, the second section details results from other physically plausible architectures, the third details other continuous-time architectures, and the last one details three convolutional frameworks that obtain ≈90%, ≈95%, ≈99% on CIFAR-10. Pru. indicates pruning, Dist. indicates knowledge distillation, and Pre. indicates ImageNet pretraining.

TABLE I: Test accuracy averages and standard deviations over 5 runs with and without pruning on MNIST along with trainable parameter counts. Bolded results are the best-performing architecture for the pruned and unpruned settings. Note that our models involve downsampling inputs while most other architectures leverage the full MNIST image. Additional comparisons from both simulated physical systems and continuous-time neural network architectures are also included.

V and are fully calculated in Appendix F. Pruned KuraNN models retain 10% of couplings via locality-aware magnitude pruning. Each inference spans 15.9 oscillator periods.

papers.selection_reason: Physical nonlinear dynamical systems as neural-network accelerators for energy-efficient inference; directly relevant to efficient AI hardware.
papers.title: Nonlinear Dynamical Systems as Scalable and Efficient Physical Neural Networks
papers.tldr: Modern training and compression techniques can make nonlinear dynamical physical neural networks substantially more accurate and potentially far more energy-efficient than conventional digital implementations.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation commonly serves separate models for reranking and answering, duplicating model residency and passage processing. We introduce Glance, which equips the generator with a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to score candidate passages from a shared prefill. Short relevance probes branch from the cached context, producing one score per passage without separately prefilling each query-passage pair. A single resident 9B backbone supports generation, general decisions and reranking, with approximately 0.1 GiB of additional memory per decision skill. After 39 minutes of MS MARCO fine-tuning, Glance achieves nDCG@10 of 0.741 on SciFact and 0.345 on NFCorpus, compared with 0.721 and 0.326 for bge-reranker-v2-m3. On 300 HotpotQA questions, its selected context improves answer F1 by 0.045 over cross-encoder-selected context under the same base generator (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.014, 0.076]). In a scaling study, reranking quality keeps rising up to 200 candidates (43k tokens) scored from one shared prefill, where it exceeds the cross-encoder by 0.058 nDCG@10, and a probe-only activated adapter lets generation continue from the original passage cache. These initial results demonstrate generator-based reranking with one resident backbone; evaluation currently covers two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset and one backbone family.
bullets: Uses a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to score passages from one shared prefilling of the cached context.
A single resident 9B backbone supports generation, decision-making, and reranking with about 0.1 GiB extra memory per decision skill.
After brief MS MARCO fine-tuning, it reports higher nDCG@10 than bge-reranker-v2-m3 on SciFact and NFCorpus.
On 300 HotpotQA questions, Glance-selected context improves answer F1 over cross-encoder-selected context under the same generator.
Reranking quality continues improving to 200 candidates, but evaluation is limited to two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset, and one backbone family.

papers.selection_reason: Generator-as-reranker with shared prefill and lightweight adapters is a memory-efficient inference contribution.
papers.title: Glance: The Generator Is Its Own Reranker
papers.tldr: Glance turns a single generator into both an answerer and passage reranker, improving retrieval and QA context selection while reducing duplicated model residency and processing.

papers.abstract: Agents powered by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress in solving complex reasoning tasks. However, LLM agents often falter on long-horizon tasks due to cognitive overload, as their working memory becomes cluttered with expanding and irrelevant information, which dilutes their attention and hinders effective planning and reasoning. To mitigate this challenge, we introduce Cognitive Resource Self-Allocation (CORAL), a novel reasoning paradigm that empowers agents to proactively optimize their context. Implemented as an agent-callable working memory management toolset, CORAL allows an agent to checkpoint its task progress and verified facts, and adaptively initiate a new problem-solving episode by resetting cluttered context while preserving only the checkpointed information, enabling it to resume reasoning from a clean state. We further enhance the agent's checkpointing capabilities using a Multi-episode Agentic Reinforced Policy Optimization algorithm. On the GAIA benchmark, CORAL with an 8B model achieves 42.8% average accuracy, with particularly strong gains on the most challenging long-horizon tasks (Level 2 and Level 3). Crucially, these gains come at a substantially lower inference cost: CORAL consumes 6-7$\times$ fewer input tokens than a ReAct agent. It also generalizes to multi-hop Knowledge QA benchmarks and to the considerably harder BrowseComp, where it improves a strong proprietary agent by 8.0 points.
authors: Zheng Zhu, Xiaozhuan Liang, Xi Chen, Bei Yu, Jiaya Jia
bullets: Long-horizon agents can suffer from cognitive overload as irrelevant context accumulates and disrupts planning.
CORAL provides an agent-callable working-memory toolkit for checkpointing progress and verified facts, then starting fresh reasoning episodes with only that information retained.
A Multi-episode Agentic Reinforced Policy Optimization algorithm improves the agent’s checkpointing decisions.
On GAIA, an 8B model with CORAL reaches 42.8% average accuracy, with especially strong gains on difficult Level 2 and Level 3 tasks.
CORAL uses 6–7× fewer input tokens than ReAct and also improves performance on multi-hop Knowledge QA and BrowseComp.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison of the ReAct and CORAL frameworks; both rows read left to right as the context grows. Top (ReAct). One context accumulates N ReAct blocks (thought, action, observation) above the system prompt and user task, and nothing is ever removed. Bottom (CORAL). The same blocks are interleaved with two agent-callable tools. Memory Management (MM) writes into the persistent MEMORY panel below the trace, holding task progress (the plan, each sub-goal pending or completed) and verified facts, so that panel evolves while the raw trace only grows. Context Optimization (CO), the vertical bar, ends the current episode: everything to its left is discarded and the next episode restarts from only the system prompt, the user task, and the current panel. A trajectory is thus a sequence of episodes (here 0–3).

Figure 2: Multi-episode ARPO. The reward is computed from a trajectory’s final episode (which contains the answer) and propagated to all preceding ones; episodes from all sampled trajectories are then pooled for group-based advantage estimation, enabling credit assignment across episode boundaries.

Table 1: Main results on GAIA (Pass@1, Avg@8). Marking convention: rows are compared within parameter-size brackets and across all three paradigms, not within paradigm blocks. The 7–8B bracket holds the four 7–8B agentic systems and the Qwen3-8B CORAL rows; the other holds everything ≥32B or of undisclosed proprietary size, including all DIRECT INFERENCE rows and the Claude Sonnet 4 CORAL rows. Per bracket and column we boldface the best and underline the second best, so each column carries two bold entries and the best need not lie in the CORAL block.

papers.selection_reason: LLM agent working-memory management with context checkpointing/reset directly targets agent memory and inference efficiency.
papers.title: Don't Lose the Thread: Empowering Long-Horizon LLM Agents with Cognitive Resource Self-Allocation
papers.tldr: CORAL helps LLM agents solve long-horizon tasks by selectively checkpointing useful information and resetting cluttered context, improving accuracy while reducing token use.

papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization enables efficient deployment of large language models by reducing memory footprint and computational cost. Achieving high accuracy at low precision requires selecting quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding decisions. Existing approaches typically optimize these components independently using local reconstruction objectives, which fail to account for the varying impact of quantization errors on downstream predictions. Direct optimization of task-level metrics would provide a more faithful objective, but is challenging due to the discontinuous nature of quantization operations and the high computational cost of evaluating their downstream effects. In this work, we derive a Hessian-guided approximation of the output change induced by joint weight and activation quantization. Based on a tractable Fisher approximation, we formulate a unified post-training quantization framework that enables the joint optimization of quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under a common output-sensitivity objective. The resulting method remains practical for modern large language models and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transformation and rounding methods across both channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.
authors: Mads Toftrup, Marco Federici, Boris van Breugel, Paul Whatmough, Markus Nagel
bullets: Targets the limitations of independently optimized, local reconstruction objectives that overlook downstream prediction sensitivity.
Approximates output changes from joint weight and activation quantization using a Hessian and tractable Fisher approximation.
Jointly optimizes quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under one output-sensitivity objective.
Designed to remain practical for modern large language models.
Consistently outperforms existing transformation and rounding methods across channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Relationship between the KL divergence between the original and quantized model outputs and several layer-local error proxies across linear layers of Llama 3.2 1B Instruct under W4A4 quantization. Conventional reconstruction metrics, such as the output Frobenius norm, exhibit weak correlation with downstream output degradation. Fisher-weighted weight error fails to capture the effect of activation quantization. Output Fisher-weighted error correlates more strongly with the KL divergence, and our proposed Kronecker factorization of the Output Fisher retains this correlation.

Weighting the quantization error using the proposed Fisher estimate consistently exceeds the best reconstruction objective without requiring hyperparameter tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Post-training quantization for LLMs directly reduces model memory and inference cost, fitting memory-efficient inference under Efficient AI.
papers.title: A Unified Hessian-Guided Framework for Post-Training Quantization
papers.tldr: A Hessian-guided framework jointly optimizes key quantization decisions to improve low-bit LLM post-training quantization.

papers.abstract: Looping in transformer models reuses weights by repeatedly applying the same transformer, or parts of it, making the model deeper without increasing its parameter count. Whether looping is useful depends on which constraint dominates: model size, training compute, or autoregressive inference efficiency. We study these trade-offs jointly in dense decoder-only transformers trained from scratch, varying which parts of the model are looped, how many loops are applied, and how information is passed between loops. Our experiments span models with up to 1B parameters, trained on up to 155B tokens with up to $1.07\times10^{21}$ FLOPs and 32 loops. We find that looping the full transformer generally gives the strongest quality at a fixed parameter budget, whereas looping a middle block of layers gives a better return when training FLOPs are constrained. Adding loops is not uniformly beneficial: gains eventually saturate, reverse, or become unstable. This motivates asking whether forcing every loop to use the same weights limits the benefit of deeper looping. We address this by adding small loop-specific low-rank adapters that improve quality, with larger gains as more loops are added. Looped transformers also suffer a decoding slowdown proportional to the number of loops. Parallel Loop Transformers address this by passing hidden states between loops across adjacent token positions, allowing loop stages to run concurrently. However, in our experiments the original formulation does not consistently retain the quality gains of ordinary looping. We find that preserving the current-token embedding and separately normalizing it and the previous-token hidden state before combining them recovers strong performance across model scales and training budgets. Together, these results show that effective looping requires matching the design to the resource constraint and inference setting.
authors: Chanakya Ekbote, Artidoro Pagnoni, Devendra Singh Sachan, Shruti Bhosale, Mike Lewis, Maryam Fazel-Zarandi, Shashank Rajput, Sujan Kumar Gonugondla
bullets: Full-model looping generally gives the best quality at a fixed parameter budget, while looping a middle layer block is more compute-efficient during training.
Increasing the number of loops eventually yields diminishing, reversed, or unstable gains.
Small loop-specific low-rank adapters improve quality, with larger benefits as more loops are added.

Looping slows autoregressive decoding; Parallel Loop Transformers enable concurrent loop execution but need separate normalization and preservation of the current-token embedding to recover strong performance.
The study evaluates dense decoder-only transformers across model sizes, training budgets, and up to 32 loops.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Looping can improve data and compute efficiency (in over-trained regimes) while retaining downstream quality. We compare Vanilla (no looping), Standard Looping (repeatedly applying the same Transformer sequentially), and our modified versions Parallel Loop Transformer (PLT) (Wu et al., 2025) and Looped Transformers. Left: for 1B models trained across TPP 10–160, all looping methods achieve a given DCLM (Li et al., 2024) bits-per-byte (BPB) value with fewer training tokens than the fitted Vanilla baseline, with the modified PLT variants providing the largest relative data-efficiency gains. Center: across model sizes from 100M to 1B, we compare Vanilla models trained at TPP = 160 with two-loop models trained at TPP = 80. All looping methods achieve a given DCLM BPB with fewer training FLOPs than the fitted Vanilla baseline, and the modified PLT and Looped variants are more efficient than Standard Looping. Right: for 1B models across TPP 10–160, looping retains or improves mean NLL-ranked accuracy across eight reasoning and question-answering tasks; the modified PLT variants match or exceed Standard Looping. See Appendix D for the efficiency calculation and task-level results.

Figure 2 Looping designs: what is repeated, where, and in what order. Top: the looped component can be the complete transformer block, attention alone, the MLP alone, or attention and the MLP separately. Bottom: full-stack looping traverses the complete transformer for L loops, whereas per-layer looping completes L loops of each block before advancing to the next. Middle-stack and middle-layer looping restrict the corresponding schedule to the central blocks. For a model containing B blocks, the first and last ⌊B/3⌋ blocks are run once.

Figure 3 Full-Stack Looping is favored under fixed parameter-count and training-data budgets, whereasMiddle-Stack Looping is favored under FLOP constraints. DCLM validation BPB versus the number of loops or total training FLOPs for 100M and 500M models. Each panel holds the model size and training-data budget constant, so the differences reflect how each strategy uses the additional computation introduced by looping. The advantage of full-stack looping becomes clearer at larger model scales and training budgets. Middle-Stack Looping with fewer loops achieves lower BPB when compute is limited, whereas Full-Stack Looping can attain lower BPB when more compute is available. Increasing the number of loops does not improve quality indefinitely: the 100M results exhibit saturation, regression, and instability when more loops are used. Lower BPB is better; red triangles indicate unstable or clipped runs.

papers.selection_reason: Studies looping in decoder-only transformer architectures, a novel LLM architecture with explicit parameter, compute, and inference efficiency trade-offs.
papers.title: How to Loop Your Transformer: Loop Scaling, Specialization, and Parallel Inference
papers.tldr: Looped transformers can improve quality without adding parameters, but their benefits depend on the resource constraint and require specialized designs for efficient inference.

papers.abstract: Large language model serving is limited by facility power. Energy per token determines how many tokens a datacenter can serve, while a latency target bounds how quickly each user receives them. During decode, every weight is read from memory for every generated token. Batching amortizes this read across users but makes no individual user faster. Speculative decoding does: a drafter proposes several future tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass that reuses the same weight read. Because every drafted token must be verified whether or not it is accepted, the energy speculation saves depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted. This saving is hard to pin down. It varies across target models from different attention families and across drafting schemes, and it depends on the text being served. Every drafter we evaluate accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on Romansh, a low-resource language, than on English. We measure speculative decoding under production serving conditions (SGLang, CUDA graphs enabled) on H100 and H200 GPUs, at batch sizes up to 64 across 5 corpora. On dense models, verification, not drafting, dominates the energy cost. The saving shrinks as the batch grows, because batching has already shared the weight read that speculation would divide among the accepted tokens. At large batch sizes, block drafters push verification past the balance point between arithmetic and memory traffic into the compute-bound regime, where the saving becomes a loss, and a drafter with low acceptance raises energy per token. Meeting a tighter latency target with speculation then costs additional energy. Larger batches lower energy per token without speculation. Speculation adds to that saving only when acceptance is high, and on the model we tested it leaves little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS.
authors: Bole Ma, Ayesha Afzal, Jan Eitzinger, Harald Koestler, Gerhard Wellein
bullets: Energy savings depend on accepted drafted tokens because every proposal still requires verification.
Acceptance varies by model, drafting scheme, and text: it is lower for conversation than code and for Romansh than English.
Measurements on H100/H200 GPUs with SGLang show verification dominates energy for dense models.
Larger batches already amortize weight reads, shrinking speculation’s benefit; aggressive drafting can make verification compute-bound and energy-inefficient.
Speculation provides little room for latency-preserving DVFS on the evaluated model.
