papers.title: Only Accepted Tokens Count: An Energy Accounting of Speculative Decoding Under Latency Targets
papers.tldr: Speculative decoding saves energy under tight latency targets only when token acceptance is high and batching is limited; at large batches or low acceptance, it can increase energy use.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) increasingly rely on axial attention mechanisms, but despite their empirical success, the theoretical properties of axial attention remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we extend the Single Location Regression framework introduced in Marion et al. [2025] to 2D structured data, in order to study sparse information settings where a target depends on a small number of tokens. We formulate an analytically tractable axial attention-type predictor and rigorously analyze its statistical properties and training dynamics. We prove that under a specific asymptotic regime and with knowledge of the underlying oracle parameters, our predictor achieves Bayes optimality, whereas a class of semi-linear simplifications strictly fails to do so, underlining the role of the inner non-linearity. We prove that for a specific temperature scaling, Projected Gradient Descent converges globally to the optimal oracle parameters. Extensive numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings and highlight the critical role of inverse temperature scheduling in empirical convergence.
bullets: Extends Single Location Regression to 2D structured data for analyzing sparse-information settings.
Introduces an analytically tractable axial-attention predictor and studies its statistical properties and training dynamics.
Proves Bayes optimality in a specific asymptotic regime when oracle parameters are known.
Shows semi-linear simplifications fail strictly, emphasizing the importance of the inner non-linearity.
Proves global convergence of Projected Gradient Descent under a specific temperature scaling; experiments support the theory and the role of inverse-temperature scheduling.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretically analyzes axial attention, an efficient attention mechanism; results on optimality and training dynamics are transferable to efficient attention design.
papers.title: Understanding axial attention in TSFMs through single location regression
papers.tldr: This work theoretically explains when axial attention can be Bayes-optimal for sparse 2D time-series prediction and how to train it successfully.

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers (DiTs) have become the dominant architecture for high-fidelity image synthesis, yet they suffer from slow training convergence and high computational cost. Two recent lines of work address this from complementary angles: Representation Alignment (REPA) accelerates DiT training by aligning intermediate features with a pretrained external representation model (e.g., DINOv2), while Representation Auto-Encoders (RAE) replace the pixel-space VAE with a compact representation-space tokenizer learned from self-supervised features. However, these approaches are developed and applied in isolation: REPA still relies on a pixel-space VAE for latent diffusion, and RAE does not exploit the alignment signal that accelerates the diffusion backbone. We present \textbf{UniRA}, a unified framework that couples representation alignment and representation auto-encoding into a single objective. UniRA learns a representation-space tokenizer whose output serves simultaneously as the diffusion target and the alignment anchor, so the tokenizer, the diffusion backbone, and the external representation model are co-optimized. We give a theoretical result showing that this joint optimization preserves the representation quality of the external model while accelerating diffusion convergence, and we derive a principled weighting that balances the reconstruction, alignment, and generation objectives. On ImageNet class-conditional generation at 256*256 and 512*512, UniRA matches or surpasses state-of-the-art DiTs (SD3, REPA, RAE) in FID while reducing training steps by up to 5*. We further show that the unified representation space supports improved zero-shot classification and linear probing, confirming that generation and understanding benefit from a shared, aligned latent space.
authors: An Lanji, Dawei Liu, Jin Li, Haoran Xu, Mei Chen, Yu Tian
bullets: Addresses slow convergence and high computational cost in diffusion transformers, which existing alignment and auto-encoding approaches tackle separately.
Jointly learns a representation-space tokenizer used as both the diffusion target and alignment anchor, co-optimizing it with the diffusion backbone and external representation model.
Provides a theoretical guarantee for preserving external representation quality and derives weighting across reconstruction, alignment, and generation objectives.
On ImageNet class-conditional generation at 256×256 and 512×512, matches or surpasses reported DiT baselines in FID while reducing training steps by up to 5×.

The shared latent space also improves zero-shot classification and linear probing, though the abstract reports results only for ImageNet class-conditional generation and related representation evaluation.

Figure 8. Additional analysis. Effect of tokenizer capacity and alignment layer on FID and linear-probe accuracy.

papers.title: UniRA: Unified Representation Alignment and Auto-Encoding for Efficient Diffusion Generation
papers.tldr: UniRA unifies representation alignment and auto-encoding to accelerate diffusion-transformer training while preserving high-quality generation and improving representation usefulness.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in gigapixel-level imaging have brought High-Resolution Wide shots to the forefront of research. However, these images present significant challenges: extreme sparsity of foreground, gigapixel-level resolutions and diverse target counts. This makes traditional close-up detectors inaccurate and slow as they are overwhelmed by the background. Although previous research has explored sparse backbones, their fixed sparsity patterns lack the adaptability required to handle diverse target numbers. To address this, we introduce ElasticFormer, a sparse backbone that dynamically allocates computational resources based on foreground proportion. After scoring windows based on variance, proposed ElasticSelector module will predict the foreground proportion for top-k selection. The mechanism guides the model to select target-containing windows, scaling resources in areas where objects are clustered. We introduce a novel loss function combined with the 3-phase training strategy for ElasticSelector, allowing it to function properly when bounding box annotations are missing. A WSOD study is carried on PASCAL VOC 2007 to evaluate its extensibility. Further, ElasticNet is created to verify its backbone-agnostic nature. In experiments on the PANDA gigapixel benchmark, ElasticFormer reduces backbone FLOPs by 80% while achieving a significant improvement in AP50 when compared to fixed-ratio sparse methods.
authors: Wenxi Li, Jingchen Huang, Chenyang Lyu, Moran Liu, Haozhe Lin, Guiguang Ding, Yuchen Guo
bullets: Targets sparse, extremely high-resolution images with few objects and variable target counts, where conventional detectors are slow and inaccurate.
Scores image windows by variance, then uses ElasticSelector to estimate foreground proportions and choose top-k regions adaptively.
Introduces a specialized loss and three-phase training strategy so the selector can operate without bounding-box annotations.
On PANDA, reduces backbone FLOPs by 80% and significantly improves AP50 over fixed-ratio sparse methods.
Evaluates extensibility on PASCAL VOC 2007 WSOD and develops ElasticNet to demonstrate backbone compatibility.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in gigapixel-level imaging have brought High-Resolution Wide shots to the forefront of research. However, these images present significant challenges: extreme sparsity of foreground, gigapixel-level resolutions and interleaving of foreground and background. This causes traditional detectors and attention mechanisms to be hindered by background, resulting in inefficiency and inaccuracy. To tackle this problem, we propose BiHashFormer, a dual sparsified branch transformer built on hashing. RoI Selector will predict the foreground proportion for top-k selecting target-containing windows. The compression branch processes windows selected and refines attention into HashAttention by discarding half of the key-value pairs, reducing cost and improving efficiency. The compensation branch uses HashMiner to perform low-cost hash searches in the remaining regions, recovering features of missed objects. Experiments confirm that the selection relationship in HashAttention is one-way and reveal the preference of different queries for keys. In experiments on the gigapixel benchmark PANDA, BiHashFormer reduces 37.5% backbone FLOPs while improving AP50 to 81.0%. Moreover, this parallel dual-branch structure allows the model to avoid inference delays caused by inter-branch dependencies, while achieving much greater stability than single-branch models, specially with low rates of RoI selection.
authors: Jingchen Huang, Wenxi Li, Chenyang Lyu, Moran Liu, Haozhe Lin, Yuchen Guo
bullets: Targets sparse foreground by selecting the top-k windows most likely to contain objects.
A compression branch applies HashAttention, discarding half of key-value pairs to reduce computation.
A compensation branch uses low-cost HashMiner searches in unselected regions to recover missed objects.
On PANDA, it reduces backbone FLOPs by 37.5% and reaches 81.0% AP50.
Parallel branches avoid inter-branch inference delays and remain more stable at low RoI-selection rates.

papers.title: BiHashFormer: Hash-Driven Dual-Branch Transformer for Efficient Object Detection in HRW Shots

papers.abstract: Linear attention stores historical information in a recurrent state of fixed size, providing a compact memory representation for long-context inference. Reducing state precision further lowers per-request storage requirements, but quantized writeback errors enter subsequent recurrences, degrade prediction quality on long-reasoning tasks, and can be accompanied by repetitive generation and excessively long outputs. We propose Global Gradient-aware Allocation (GGA) and the Pure-Write Sliding Window (PW) to address precision allocation and recent-information maintenance. GGA combines candidate quantization residuals with gradient sensitivity to future prediction loss to allocate head bit widths under a model-wide mixed-precision budget. PW independently maintains recent pure writes as FP8 vector pairs, propagates them through the full GDN state transition, and merges them into the low-bit historical state only after they leave the window. Across seven evaluations on Qwen3.5-4B/9B, GGA allocation alone improves over STEPQuant@4 by 19.48/29.84 percentage points. Adding PW-S8 yields seven-task macro-averages of 69.83%/78.63%, improving over STEPQuant@4 by 38.39/41.21 percentage points, respectively. Both precision reallocation and window maintenance improve task scores while mitigating excessively long outputs: at @6, GGA reduces mean generation length, averaged equally across tasks, by 10.45%/14.65% relative to STEPQuant; adding PW-S8 to GGA@4 further reduces mean generation length by 32.32%/36.77%. Comparisons at similar storage budgets further show that using additional capacity to maintain recent writes yields higher task scores and shorter mean outputs than solely increasing the bit width of the accumulated state.
authors: Qinghang Huang, Xuchu Huang, Xunzhao Yin
bullets: Low-precision writeback errors accumulate in linear-attention recurrent states, harming long-context reasoning and causing repetitive or excessively long outputs.
Global Gradient-aware Allocation (GGA) assigns mixed-precision head bit widths using quantization residuals and sensitivity to future prediction loss.
Pure-Write Sliding Window (PW) keeps recent writes as FP8 vector pairs, then merges them into the low-bit historical state after they leave the window.
Across seven evaluations on Qwen3.5-4B/9B, GGA and PW improve task scores over STEPQuant@4 and substantially shorten mean generation length.
At comparable storage budgets, reserving capacity for recent writes outperforms using it only to increase accumulated-state bit width.

papers.selection_reason: Quantization of recurrent state for linear-attention LLMs reduces memory and improves long-context inference; directly fits memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Low-Bit GDN Recurrent-State Quantization: Global Gradient-aware Allocation and Pure-Write Sliding Windows
papers.tldr: GGA and PW improve low-bit recurrent-state quantization by allocating precision where gradients matter and preserving recent writes, boosting task performance while reducing overly long generation.

papers.abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) distills multi-step diffusion models into few-step generators by minimizing reverse KL divergence. Despite its strong performance, DMD guides samples by local density alone, which introduces two limitations: teacher scores can be unreliable in regions of low teacher density, and the mode-seeking behavior of reverse KL can collapse the student onto a subset of the teacher modes. We first connect DMD to Wasserstein gradient flow, showing that its gradient follows from a fixed-point formulation with integral KL (IKL) as the energy functional. This perspective motivates augmenting IKL with an optimal transport term that addresses these limitations by guiding outlier samples toward the target and promoting mode coverage. We realize this term using Sinkhorn divergence estimated from finite batches. In practice, however, errors in the estimated Sinkhorn velocity can perturb in-domain samples for which IKL guidance is already accurate. To this end, we introduce sDMD, which adaptively activates the Sinkhorn correction based on discriminator outputs, focusing on outlier samples where IKL may be unreliable. With 2--4 sampling steps on FLUX.1-dev, Qwen-Image-20B, and Wan2.1-14B, sDMD outperforms distillation baselines on GenEval, DPG, WISE, and VBench while improving sample diversity over DMD2.
authors: Jaihoon Kim, Lingxiao Li, Soshi Shimada, Roshni Cooper, Minhyuk Sung, Yiwei Zhao
bullets: DMD can suffer from unreliable teacher scores in low-density regions and reverse-KL mode collapse.
The method interprets DMD through Wasserstein gradient flow with integral KL as its energy.
It adds a finite-batch Sinkhorn divergence term to guide outliers toward the target distribution and improve mode coverage.
An adaptive discriminator-based gate limits Sinkhorn corrections on in-domain samples where standard IKL guidance is reliable.
With 2–4 sampling steps, sDMD outperforms distillation baselines across reported quality benchmarks and improves diversity over DMD2.

papers.abstract: We study post-training for dynamically routed mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, focusing on integrating independently optimized specialists while keeping consolidation efficient. Our approach combines calibrated multi-teacher on-policy distillation (C-MOPD), which matches each selected teacher on a local Top-$K$ support with teacher-wise loss normalization and clipping, with an execution path that uses post-capacity bounded-width dispatch, final-route replay, and asynchronous rollout--training overlap. On Turing-20B-A2B, the selected model achieves a four-domain normalized integration score of 0.9988 and retains at least 90.16\% of the measured specialist gain in every domain. At matched $K=32$, the full calibration objective scores 0.9962, compared with 0.9724 without calibration and 0.9834 without clipping. At a matched 8K response cap, the model exceeds both shared SFT and Qwen3-8B on all four reasoning-enabled mathematics and code benchmarks (unweighted mean: 85.92, versus 80.33 for Qwen3-8B and 74.21 for SFT), and improves over SFT on ten of twelve broader evaluation metrics. In a PPU-based profile, the combined execution configuration reduces consolidation step time from 398.7 to 139.3 seconds, an observed 2.86$\times$ speedup over serial execution. These results demonstrate strong specialist integration alongside more efficient consolidation, while reflecting the complete training and execution framework rather than any single component.

Uses local Top-K teacher matching with teacher-wise normalization and clipping, plus bounded dispatch, route replay, and asynchronous rollout–training overlap.
On Turing-20B-A2B, achieves a 0.9988 four-domain integration score while retaining at least 90.16% of specialist gains in each domain.
At matched settings, calibration and clipping improve the objective score; the model also outperforms shared SFT and Qwen3-8B on four reasoning-enabled math and code benchmarks.
The combined execution configuration reduces consolidation step time from 398.7 to 139.3 seconds, a measured 2.86× speedup over serial execution.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on Multi-Head Attention (MHA) for sequence modeling, but scaling to long contexts is constrained by the quadratic cost of attention, motivating sub-quadratic recurrent alternatives. This paper formalizes a Dynamic Wave recurrent layer, based on input-dependent exponential damping and cosine phase modulation, and evaluates three 10.94M-parameter configurations (Pure Transformer, Pure Wave, and Hybrid Wave-Attention) on TinyStories under perplexity, latency, throughput and peak VRAM profiling up to 4096 tokens. The Hybrid configuration reaches the best perplexity, 5.95 on the full held-out split against 6.93 for the Transformer and 7.26 for Pure Wave. The efficiency picture, however, is governed by implementation rather than by architecture. Against an unfused attention baseline, Pure Wave uses 78.7% less peak VRAM at a 4096-token context (1404.3 MB vs. 6601.6 MB); against a fused scaled-dot-product attention kernel the same comparison yields no advantage at all (1404.3 MB vs. 1403.6 MB), and in training mode Pure Wave is 8.3% more expensive than the Transformer. Likewise, hoisting elementwise terms out of the recurrence loop speeds the layer up 2.53-fold with no custom kernel, reducing its latency gap to attention from 2.48-fold to 1.12-fold. A hybrid stack is found to inherit the cost of its more expensive mixer rather than the advantage of its cheaper one, its peak VRAM matching the Pure Transformer to within 0.1%. A closed-form memory model reproduces these measurements and predicts the context length beyond which attention overtakes the vocabulary projection. The findings indicate that reported efficiency gains for recurrent attention replacements must be stated relative to a named attention backend and a named implementation, and that hybridization is best justified on quality grounds.
bullets: The paper targets attention’s quadratic long-context cost with an input-dependent recurrent layer using exponential damping and cosine phase modulation.
On TinyStories, the Hybrid Wave-Attention model achieves the best held-out perplexity (5.95), versus 6.93 for Pure Transformer and 7.26 for Pure Wave.
Pure Wave substantially reduces VRAM versus unfused attention at 4096 tokens, but offers no VRAM advantage over fused attention and is more costly during training.
Optimizing recurrence implementation improves Wave latency 2.53×, narrowing its gap with attention; hybrid stacks inherit the cost of the more expensive mixer.
Efficiency claims should specify the attention backend and implementation; hybridization is primarily justified by quality gains.

papers.abstract: KV cache quantization is well studied for autoregressive language models, where cached prefix states are exact under causal attention and quantization is mainly a cache reconstruction problem. Diffusion language models (dLLMs) break this assumption. Fast dLLM inference reuses KV states across denoising steps, but bidirectional token representations can change as masked tokens are revealed, so the reused cache may already differ from full recomputation before quantization is applied. We study KV cache quantization under this cache-reuse error. We adapt KIVI and KVQuant to Fast-dLLM-style prefix and dual cache reuse, and introduce TRACE and dLLM-KVQ. TRACE reconstructs feasible dLLM reveal trajectories from prompt-answer pairs, providing calibration states that match iterative masked decoding. dLLM-KVQ uses these trajectories to choose per-layer K-cache entries that remain in high precision according to output- and attention-level behavior metrics, while applying standard low-bit value quantization. Across LLaDA and Dream evaluations on GSM8K, HumanEval, MATH, and MBPP, dLLM-KVQ achieves the highest average score among quantized methods across the reported 4-bit and 2-bit prefix/dual cache settings.
authors: Yan Tai, Yunan Ding, Guangzhao Li, Siqi Luo, Chaoyang Zhang, Guangtao Zhai, Guodong Guo, Xiaohong Liu
bullets: Diffusion language models reuse KV states across denoising steps, but bidirectional representations can change as masked tokens are revealed.
The study adapts KIVI and KVQuant to Fast-dLLM-style prefix and dual cache reuse.
TRACE reconstructs reveal trajectories from prompt–answer pairs to produce calibration states that better match iterative decoding.
dLLM-KVQ selectively keeps important K-cache entries in high precision while quantizing values to low bitwidth.
Across LLaDA and Dream on GSM8K, HumanEval, MATH, and MBPP, it achieves the highest average score among evaluated quantized methods at 4-bit and 2-bit cache settings.

papers.abstract: Unlike autoregressive large language models (AR-LLMs), diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising many tokens in parallel, offering a promising path to efficient inference. Existing serving frameworks, however, schedule dLLM requests with policies designed for AR models, namely first-come-first-served (FCFS) admission and prefill priority. We find that both policies are ill-suited to dLLMs, wasting much of their speed. FCFS ignores that a dLLM request's decoding cost is highly heterogeneous and unknown at arrival, causing severe head-of-line blocking. Prefill priority, widely used in AR-LLM serving to keep time-to-first-token low, sharply cuts dLLM efficiency, as rounds that run only prompts leave most of the batch idle. We present DWISE, a Denoising Workload-Informed Scheduling Engine for efficient dLLM serving. DWISE schedules requests by their remaining work, measured in a block-level unit shared by prefill and denoising, so both phases share a round. To predict the unknown denoising workload, DWISE combines a lightweight prompt-based predictor at admission with a single refinement from the first denoising round's hidden states, which capture model-specific information absent from the prompt and require no additional model execution. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on five models from three dLLM families under bursty workloads, DWISE reduces mean end-to-end latency over SGLang by 5.4$\times$ on average and up to 14.9$\times$ while preserving task accuracy. The code will be released publicly.
authors: Lie Li, Wen Li, Junxiao Shen, Jindong Gu, Guosheng Hu
bullets: Existing FCFS and prefill-priority scheduling causes head-of-line blocking and underutilized batches in diffusion LLMs.
DWISE uses a shared block-level measure of remaining work so prefill and denoising can run in the same round.
It predicts denoising workload with a lightweight prompt-based estimate refined once using first-round hidden states, without extra model execution.
Implemented in SGLang and evaluated across five models from three diffusion LLM families under bursty workloads.
The abstract reports 5.4× average and up to 14.9× lower mean end-to-end latency while preserving task accuracy.

papers.abstract: The tension between the established technologies of connectionist AI and their neuromorphic challengers is attracting growing attention, above all because of the enormous energy demand of the former and the low power consumption of the latter. Developing and running large AI models consumes gigawatt- to terawatt-hours of energy, while the human brain operates on a continuous 20 watts. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) counter this energy demand with a frugal approach and bring elements of self-organization into the methodological repertoire of AI: local learning instead of global error backpropagation, event-driven computing, and time as a carrier of information. They do not replace today's AI but extend it; in hybrid systems each approach can be deployed where its strengths lie. This monograph explains the field in a generally accessible yet mathematically rigorous way. Using the text-generation module of ChatGPT as an example, the principle, elegance, and computational cost of transformer-based AI are presented and compared with the coding, learning, and network-design methods of SNNs. Throughout, relevant mechanisms of the human nervous system serve as model and reference point. Topics include spike-timing-dependent plasticity, population and temporal coding, the Neural Engineering Framework, neuromorphic hardware from Loihi 2 to commercial edge processors, and the prospects for classical and neuromorphic AI to complement and extend each other.
bullets: Motivated by the high energy demands of large, connectionist AI models and the brain’s much lower power consumption.
Explains transformer-based AI through ChatGPT’s text-generation module, including its principles and computational costs.
Introduces SNN mechanisms such as event-driven computing, local learning, temporal coding, and self-organization.
Relates SNNs to human nervous-system mechanisms and surveys neuromorphic hardware, from Loihi 2 to commercial edge processors.
Presents neuromorphic AI as an extension rather than a replacement for classical AI, with hybrid deployment as a key prospect.

papers.abstract: Adaptive inference systems balance accuracy and inference cost by routing inputs to models with varying capabilities. Although jointly training models and routers is empirically more sample-efficient than training them separately, principled losses for joint training remain underexplored. We address this gap in a classification setting by proposing cost-sensitive hinge losses for jointly training classifiers with single-stage or cascade routers. Single-stage routers directly select a model per input, whereas cascade routers sequentially decide at each stage whether to predict with the current model or defer to the next stage, which uses a more accurate but more costly model. For both settings, we prove linear calibration bounds establishing Bayes consistency: minimizing the hinge risk recovers the Bayes-optimal risk under the target cost-sensitive zero-one loss. Moreover, since routers can require more labeled data to train than classifiers, we propose a novel post-training prediction-powered inference (PPI) procedure that uses unlabeled data to refine a trained single-stage router. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that the proposed hinge losses are effective for joint training and that PPI can correct routing errors when labeled data is scarce.
authors: Shirley Xiaoqi Liu, Florence Regol, Antonios Valkanas, Patrick Rebeschini, Mark Coates
bullets: Targets adaptive inference, where inputs are routed among models with different accuracy–cost trade-offs.
Introduces hinge losses for both single-stage model selection and sequential cascade routing.
Proves linear calibration bounds showing that minimizing the proposed surrogate risk recovers the Bayes-optimal cost-sensitive classification risk.
Proposes post-training prediction-powered inference (PPI) to refine single-stage routers using unlabeled data.
Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show effective joint training and improved routing when labeled data is scarce.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos, but the quadratic cost of 3D full attention dominates their inference. Dynamic block-sparse attention reduces this cost by computing exact attention only on key/value blocks selected from current activations. However, its fidelity degrades under aggressive sparsity: blocks are scored from coarse summaries or formed by costly global clustering, pruned blocks vanish from the softmax, and whole tiles are kept or dropped even when only a few of their keys matter. To address these limitations, we propose Accurate Block Attention (AB-Attention), a training-free method that accurately approximates dense attention at high sparsity. Its Intra-Block Clustering Selector (IBCS) estimates block importance faithfully yet cheaply by clustering queries only within each query block, without permuting tokens. Sampling with Inclusion-Probability Weighting (SIP) then samples blocks in proportion to these estimates and reweights them by inverse inclusion probability, so that one pass estimates dense attention rather than truncating it. Finally, its kernel gathers key/value blocks much smaller than a tile into full tensor-core tiles, refining selection at no extra tensor-core cost. On Wan2.1 and HunyuanVideo, AB-Attention skips 89--92\% of attention, whereas the baselines compute 1.8--3.6$\times$ as much, yet it still improves PSNR by up to 4.4~dB over the strongest baseline and achieves up to 2.23$\times$ end-to-end speedup. Our code is available at https://github.com/InfRec-Cardinal/AB-Attention.
authors: Bin Xu, Mo Zhang, Zhengfeiyang Zhang, Xinfeng Yang, Yixing Ma, Wei Wang, HeXin Wang, Pengfei Zhou, Wangbo Zhao

Gathers smaller key/value blocks into tensor-core tiles for finer-grained selection without extra tensor-core cost.
On Wan2.1 and HunyuanVideo, skips 89–92% of attention, improves PSNR by up to 4.4 dB over the strongest baseline, and reaches up to 2.23× end-to-end speedup.

papers.abstract: One-step and few-step text-to-image generation must accurately render the details specified in the prompt despite limited opportunities for refinement. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) uses score differences to bring the generated distribution closer to a reference distribution. Following prior work, we estimate this difference with internal velocity branches, avoiding a separate fake-score network. We ask whether an explicit moment constraint improves this learned score supervision. A decomposition of the reverse-KL field into a Gaussian moment component and a non-Gaussian residual identifies statistics that can be constrained explicitly. We introduce Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM), which retains the full DMD correction and matches feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations using the generator's exponential-moving-average (EMA) copy, requiring no external feature encoder. Experiments use full-parameter and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) tuning on Z-Image-Turbo 6B and Qwen-Image 20B. At two network evaluations, IDM reaches 94.25% and 90.20% on Chinese and English LongText-Bench, the highest scores among the compared methods at this budget. Controlled ablations show gains from the added moment loss, while generator EMA features perform competitively with an external DINOv2 encoder across the five reported metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/IDM.

papers.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into agentic architectures has substantially increased token consumption, raising concerns about their energy footprint. Yet, estimating the energy consumption of proprietary API-based models remains challenging, and existing approaches focus primarily on generated output tokens while overlooking the impact of the large input contexts characteristic of agentic workflows. To address this gap, we systematically profile compute time and energy consumption across a wide range of prefill (input) and decode (output) token lengths. Using generalized linear models, we show that decode compute time and energy scale linearly with output length, whereas prefill compute time and energy exhibit both linear and quadratic scaling with input length. These findings demonstrate that input context becomes a relevant factor for large-context workloads. Furthermore, we show that compute time serves as a reliable proxy for energy consumption when direct energy measurements are unavailable. Our mapping framework enables precise energy estimation and supports more sustainable deployment decisions for agentic AI.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn conversations with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reuse input context, but long multimodal inputs increase time to first token (TTFT). Query-aware hard pruning reduces prefill tokens but permanently excludes information that later questions may require. We propose Raincheck, a framework for deferred multimodal prefill that decouples initial token selection from later information availability. An existing pruning method selects tokens for initial prefill; Raincheck preserves and progressively prefills unselected tokens in source order using unused compute capacity during decode. Unfinished prefill continues after answer return during available scheduling gaps. Attention visibility control and affine state mapping enable context updates after generation begins in full-attention and hybrid recurrent models. Prefill-decode fusion reduces repeated weight reads. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B with 30% initial multimodal-token retention. Across both models and four pruning methods, Raincheck recovers on average 77.7% and 60.4% of the quality lost to matched hard pruning on MultiVerse and ConvBench, respectively. On MultiVerse, the SGLang implementation reduces mean first-turn TTFT by up to 24.1% relative to full prefill, with less than 0.5% increase in mean time per output token (TPOT).

Supports full-attention and hybrid recurrent models through attention visibility control and affine state mapping.
Prefill-decode fusion reduces repeated weight reads.
With 30% initial token retention, recovers 77.7% and 60.4% of hard-pruning quality loss on MultiVerse and ConvBench; TTFT falls by up to 24.1% on MultiVerse with under 0.5% TPOT increase.

papers.abstract: One-step distillation turns pretrained diffusion models into fast generators, but strong results often require substantial training machinery and compute. Pure adversarial distillation offers a simpler route, yet has struggled at modern text-to-image scale. To address this limitation, we propose ROAD (Representation-grounded One-step Adversarial Distillation), a one-stage framework that distills text-to-image models with one adversarial objective and a lightweight representation-space critic. First, we replace the classical convolutional head with a Lipschitz-controlled Transformer head with token-level text conditioning, which matches the semantic tokens of modern visual encoders. Second, we observed a fixed random feature mixing leads to long-horizon degradation. We attribute it to generator-critic co-adaptation around one realization-specific view, and periodically re-draw the mixing to keep the randomization effective. Third, for our dense and vector-valued logits, we introduce Jacobian R1 which penalizes the full input-logit Jacobian, overcoming pooled R1's limitation of neglecting most of logit sensitivities. A single adversarial objective then suffices: in one step, ROAD reaches 11.03 FID on SDXL and 13.73 on SD3.5-M on COCO-10K, surpassing the multi-step teachers at a fraction of distribution matching's training compute.
authors: Xiaoou Li, Shan You, Tao Huang

Introduces Jacobian R1 regularization to capture sensitivities across dense, vector-valued logits.
Reports 11.03 FID on SDXL and 13.73 on SD3.5-M on COCO-10K, with a fraction of distribution-matching training compute.

papers.abstract: Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes. We study \textit{conditional interaction}, a predict--gate--execute--update loop: System-1 estimates each candidate's utility, System-2 executes those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and the outcomes update System-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application. Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching $1/\rho_u$, where $\rho_u$ is the density of utility-relevant interactions (cost-weighted when costs differ); prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the saving. We bound selection regret by predictor error and the utility margin. These results motivate our central hypothesis: $\rho_u$ is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency and makes informative compute a better description of scaling than total compute.
authors: Qi Wang, Yun Qu, Lizhou Cai, Heming Zou, Haoang Chi, Yiqin Lv, Xiang Li, Haiyan Feng, Mengyu Ge, Yize Geng, Yuhang Jiang, Yixiu Mao, Xiangyang Ji
bullets: Introduces conditional interaction: predict utility, gate candidates, execute selected actions, and update the predictor.
Applies the framework to training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decisions, and agentic tool use.
Under ideal screening, execution compute can decrease roughly with the inverse density of utility-relevant interactions.
Prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift limit compute savings.
Proposes utility-relevant interaction density as a scaling-efficiency measure beyond total compute.

figures.caption: Figure 7 The generative model, and where System 1 cuts in. The cost is paid in full on generating the sequence 𝑦, while the information lies in the verdict 𝑜 = V(𝑦), often a single bit. System 1 forecasts the belief change that verdict will cause before 𝑦 exists, and the gate generates only if the forecast clears 𝜅𝑡 ; suppressed candidates cost only 𝑐pred. Realized verdicts refit System 1. With information gain as the utility the forecast is the expected Bayesian surprise; for any other declared utility the pipeline forecasts that utility instead.

Figure 1 An Illustrative Roadmap to AGI and its Beyond. As AI development progresses, broad capability resembles a summit that systems approach but may hit diminishing returns due to constraints in data, compute, and parameters. In Era 1 (2012–2020) progress came mainly from scaling model capacity, and in Era 2 (2020–2025) from scaling data and computation. For Era 3 (2026+), this work emphasizes a next-scaling lens: co-designing a cost-effective System-1 that prioritizes interactions by expected utility and a resource-intensive System-2 for complicated tasks. This emphasis becomes increasingly consequential for foundation models and embodied agents as they depend on generation, computation, tool use, and environmental interaction, and thus on the cost of each.

Figure 5 The predict-then-gate mechanism. System 1 scores every candidate at cost 𝑐pred, and the threshold 𝜅𝑡 admits to System 2 only those predicted to be informative. Suppressed candidates cost only 𝑐pred; executed outcomes, together with a small audit sample of suppressed candidates, are logged and refit System 1 (Theorem 14).

Figure 4 Static cascades versus adaptive co-design. (a) A standalone fast model routes each request once and is never updated by the outcomes. (b) In co-design, System 1 schedules System 2’s compute and storage, System 2’s outcomes recalibrate System 1, and the two are optimized jointly, so System 1’s judgements track an executive that keeps changing. Figure 2 The Super Parrot Hypothesis. As AI increasingly produces the data and feedback it learns from (AI for AI), deciding which self-generated interactions are worth executing becomes a central efficiency problem.

The co-designed pair would spend both only where they change the answer, so its frontier (green) is hypothesized to dominate: the same success more cheaply (red), or more of it at the same budget (blue). This expresses the co-design objective.

papers.abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) enable powerful multi-image synthesis but incur substantial computation from long visual contexts. While token pruning offers a direct route to accelerating inference, existing methods are primarily adapted from understanding tasks, suffering from insufficient reference image exploration, confused conditional guidance, and pooling-induced ambiguity that degrades generation quality. To address these issues, we propose CATP, the first training-free context-compression method tailored to UMM generation, which \textbf{C}alibrates the discrepancies of general \textbf{A}ttention-based \textbf{T}oken \textbf{P}runing for better quality-efficiency trade-off. Concretely, building on independent layer-wise pruning during denoising, we introduce Guidance-Consistent Pruning (GCP) to synchronize pruning decisions across conditioning branches, and a Taylor-Calibrated Attention Metric (TCAM) that derives a theoretically grounded second-order correction for pooling-induced bias. In addition, a Fast Scoring Operator (FSO) fuses the calibration into tiled online Softmax to reduce pruning cost. Extensive experiments across representative UMMs and benchmarks demonstrate that CATP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art token-reduction methods, achieving up to 2.09$\times$ attention-core speedup.

bullets: Targets the high computation cost of long visual contexts in UMM generation.
Introduces Guidance-Consistent Pruning to align pruning decisions across conditioning branches.

Adds a Fast Scoring Operator that integrates calibration into tiled online Softmax for lower pruning overhead.
Experiments across UMMs and benchmarks report up to 2.09× attention-core speedup and consistent gains over prior token-reduction methods.

papers.abstract: Linear recurrences are emerging as practical alternatives to softmax attention in large language models, appearing in both standalone and hybrid architectures. However, despite their rapid emergence, low-precision inference remains much less developed for these models than for softmax attention. During prefill, chunkwise-parallel algorithms cast much of the recurrence as dense matrix multiplications, suggesting a natural path to low-precision execution. Simply quantizing these operations in their native form, however, can be fragile. In this work, we identify functional invariances that preserve the full-precision computation while making the operands more amenable to quantization. Building on this observation, we introduce LinQuant, a framework for low-precision recurrent prefill based on seven such invariances, including rotations, diagonal rescalings, and alternative placements of recurrent decay and write factors. We derive when these transformations remain valid across common recurrence families spanning linear, gated, and delta-rule updates, and show that they provide complementary degrees of freedom for improving low-precision accuracy. Finally, we translate this framework to production by augmenting SSDi8, an existing low-precision prefill pipeline for Mamba-2, with the applicable invariances. LinQuant improves perplexity at matched latency on Mamba-2 1.3B, 2.7B, and 8B and Nemotron-H 8B, demonstrating the practical utility of invariance-based quantization for recurrent models.
authors: Neehal Tumma, Philipp Nazari, Rohan Cherukuri, Daniela Rus, T. Konstantin Rusch

Improves perplexity at matched latency across Mamba-2 1.3B, 2.7B, 8B and Nemotron-H 8B models.

papers.abstract: Training language models whose parameters and optimizer state exceed a single node's memory requires sharding these tensors across devices. Under tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon introduce communication to perform global matrix operations across shards. We propose Dobb (Distributed Optimizer with Block-diagonal Eigenbases), a matrix-aware optimizer designed to compute updates locally within parameter shards. Dobb approximates the input-activation second moment with diagonal blocks and tracks a complete basis within each block. It projects momentum into these bases, applies sign normalization to the coefficients, and reconstructs the update. When each block lies within one shard under TP or FSDP, Dobb applies its matrix update locally, requiring no communication beyond data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. We benchmark Dobb against Dion, a distributed matrix-aware optimizer designed to retain the benefits of orthonormalized updates while reducing communication. On GPT-2 XL (1.56B parameters), Dobb with 16 blocks reaches a validation loss of 2.476, compared with 2.511 for Dion at rank fraction 1/16. Under FSDP on 32 H100 GPUs, Dobb reduces the amortized optimizer-call time from 124.1 ms for Dion to 9.2 ms.
authors: Shi-Yuk Fong, Shuhua Yu, Jiawei Zhang
bullets: Targets matrix-aware optimization for models whose parameters and optimizer states are sharded across devices.

Requires no communication for matrix updates when blocks fit within shards; only activation-second-moment synchronization remains.
On GPT-2 XL, Dobb with 16 blocks achieves 2.476 validation loss versus Dion’s 2.511 at rank fraction 1/16.
Under FSDP on 32 H100 GPUs, optimizer-call time decreases from 124.1 ms with Dion to 9.2 ms with Dobb.

papers.selection_reason: Distributed optimizer with shard-local preconditioning; reduces communication and memory in LLM training.
papers.title: Dobb: Shard-Local Preconditioning in Block-Diagonal Eigenbases

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) can condition robot actions on generated visual futures, but this additional context is neither cost-free nor uniformly beneficial. We examine what a predicted future actually changes: the action delta $\Delta a$ between the future-conditioned and future-free execution paths of the same model. Under a shared WAM checkpoint, this delta barely shifts average benchmark success ($+0.8$ points on LIBERO, $-0.8$ on RoboTwin~2.0), while generating visual futures increases inference latency by 1.7--1.9$\times$. These aggregate metrics conceal a concentrated failure mode that we term \emph{future-induced negative transfer}: while predictive deltas benefit long-horizon tasks ($+2.4$ points on LIBERO-Long) and remain negligible on most routine manipulations, they induce severe degradation on precision tasks---with \emph{Press Stapler} and \emph{Place Can Basket} losing 54.0 and 34.0 points, recurring as top failure modes across independently trained WAM variants. We introduce \textbf{Utility-WAM} for in-place correction of future-conditioned control. Its primary learning component is a residual adapter that repairs future-induced velocity deltas under a frozen shared WAM by aligning them with ground-truth dynamic guidance and penalizing excess error beyond the future-free baseline. The adapter selectively eliminates the majority of severe task drops (reducing losses to 6.0 and 14.0 points) while preserving long-horizon foresight. To eliminate superfluous video computation, a lightweight pre-generation gate reuses counterfactual action outcomes to selectively bypass video generation on 75.5\% of RoboTwin queries, cutting latency by 38\% while improving average success to 93.3\% on RoboTwin~2.0 and 98.9\% on LIBERO. On physical bimanual manipulation across three real-world tasks, Utility-WAM succeeds in 53 of 60 trials, compared to 43 for FAST-WAM.
authors: Feihong Zhang, Xi Lin, Yulong Shi, Zuxing Lu, Yanghong Mei, Zhaopeng Gu, Tingyu Yuan, Zihao Liang, Yinuo Wang, Zhaowen Li
bullets: Future-induced action changes provide little average benefit and can severely hurt precision tasks, despite helping long-horizon tasks.
A residual adapter repairs future-conditioned velocity changes against dynamic guidance while preserving the shared WAM and its foresight.
A lightweight gate bypasses video generation for 75.5% of RoboTwin queries, reducing latency by 38%.
Utility-WAM reduces major task losses, reaches 93.3% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.9% on LIBERO, and succeeds in 53/60 real-world trials versus 43/60 for FAST-WAM.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Utility-WAM repairs future-induced action changes before allocating future-generation compute. Stage 1 trains a shared WAM with matched future-free and future-visible action paths. Stage 2 freezes the WAM and trains a residual adapter on self-generated future features, using beneficial ground-truthfuture velocity deltas and the future-free path as supervision. These two stages establish the core correction method. Stage 3 reuses the adapter’s paired final-action outcomes to train a gate. At inference, the gate runs before video generation: it either executes the future-free path and skips that compute, or invokes future generation and the corrected future-conditioned path. papers.abstract: This letter proposes MulClip, a lightweight activation function for reservoir computing (RC) on microcontrollers (MCUs). In a ring reservoir, a representative sparse RC topology, multiply-accumulate operations are few, and evaluating tanh accounted for 75% of the state-update time on a Cortex-M4. MulClip introduces curvature into the response using only comparison, absolute value, multiplication, and subtraction, and places its clipping threshold not at the extremum but at the point where the response returns to zero after passing the extremum. As a result, a single function has both a monotonic regime and a nonmonotonic folding regime that increases the expressiveness of a single unit. Which regime is used is determined by the usual hyperparameter search, e.g., over the input scale, so no task-specific threshold tuning is required. The state-update time measured on hardware was 0.34 times that of tanh and shorter than that of any of the 11 evaluated tanh approximations. In PC-based evaluation, third-order MulClip achieved a 22% lower NMSE than tanh on NARMA-20, where the pre-activations remained in the monotonic regime, and on 8-bit parity it raised the accuracy from 0.76-0.78 for the monotonic-clip variant without folding to 0.97-0.98. For these two tasks, on-device inference yielded nearly the same values as on the PC.
authors: Guren Matsumura, Masato Takemoto, Shinzo Koyama
bullets: Targets the high cost of tanh evaluation in microcontroller reservoir computing.
Uses comparisons, absolute value, multiplication, and subtraction, avoiding lookup tables.
Provides monotonic and nonmonotonic folding regimes within one activation; input scaling selects the regime.
Hardware state updates took 0.34× the time of tanh and were faster than 11 evaluated tanh approximations.
Third-order MulClip reduced NARMA-20 NMSE by 22% and improved 8-bit parity accuracy to 0.97–0.98; PC and device results were nearly identical.

papers.selection_reason: Lightweight activation for reservoir computing on microcontrollers; reduces compute and latency.
papers.title: MulClip: A table-free activation function with monotonic and folding regimes for reservoir computing on microcontrollers
papers.tldr: MulClip is a lightweight, table-free activation that speeds reservoir-computing updates on microcontrollers while improving task performance through monotonic or folding behavior.

papers.abstract: Unlimited OCR ushers the era of long-horizon parsing, substantially mitigating the growth of working memory as document lengthens. However, as document length scales to hundreds of pages, the visual context grows substantially, sharply increasing the computational cost of each decoding step and limiting the scalability of ultra-long document parsing. Inspired by human book transcription via localized focus without re-scanning preceding pages, we introduce Unlimited OCR 2, a document parsing model that looks only at what it transcribes. Building on Unlimited OCR, we upgrade all the decoder attention modules to Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention (SR-SWA), bounding active reference tokens to a fixed capacity and thus sustaining constant computational costs across arbitrarily long documents. By combining SR-SWA with Unlimited-Horizon Decoding Paradigm, Unlimited OCR 2 enables document parsing over virtually unlimited lengths without prohibitive memory overhead. At the hundred-page scale, Unlimited OCR 2 achieves 7.0$\times$ and 5.6$\times$ per-step speedups over Full Attention and R-SWA, respectively. Furthermore, it delivers state-of-the-art end-to-end performance on both MPDocBench and MarathonDocBench, our newly proposed benchmark targeting hundred-page document parsing. Ultimately, the capacity for uninterrupted, one-shot document parsing signifies a fundamental paradigm shift into the OCR 3.0 era.
authors: Shu Wei, Jingjing Wu, Qunyi Xie, Lingshu Zhang, Xiangcheng Du, Yannian Fu, Mengjie Wang, Zuyi Wang, Zhichao Liu, Yangliu Xu, YY, Yi Yang
bullets: Addresses the rising per-step computation and memory costs of parsing documents hundreds of pages long.
Introduces Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention (SR-SWA), which bounds active reference tokens to a fixed capacity.
Combines SR-SWA with Unlimited-Horizon Decoding for constant-cost decoding across document lengths.
At the hundred-page scale, reports 7.0× and 5.6× per-step speedups over Full Attention and R-SWA.
Achieves state-of-the-art end-to-end results on MPDocBench and the proposed MarathonDocBench.

figures.caption: Figure 5 | Performance comparison on multi-page benchmarks. Unlimited OCR 2 (Ours) consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluation categories.

Figure 3 | Inspired by the process of humans copying books, we propose Unlimited OCR 2. SRSWA combines Page Gate and Token Sieve to construct a fixed-length set of working reference visual tokens, substantially reducing computational and memory overhead while keeping both independent of document length throughout generation.

Figure 4 | Comparison of (a) standard decoding and (b) our Unlimited-Horizon Decoding paradigm. Standard decoding retains visual KV caches for all pages, causing GPU memory usage to grow linearly with document length and eventually overflow. Our paradigm divides long documents into manageable chunks and processes them sequentially, reusing the KV cache of shared boundary pages and releasing inactive caches to keep GPU memory usage bounded while preserving cross-chunk continuity.
Figure 2 | MarathonDocBench versus MPDocBench. MarathonDocBench extends document length from tens to hundreds of pages (a), with substantially richer cross-page structures as shown in (b) and (c).

Figure 6 | Performance and efficiency comparison across varying document lengths. UnlimitedOCR 2 demonstrates (a) robust parsing accuracy and (b) near-constant decoding latency (ms/step) as document length scaling.

Figure 1 | R-SWA vs SR-SWA. R-SWA computes attention over all visual tokens across pages, inducing extreme visual redundancy; SR-SWA sparsely attends to relevant visual regions, aligning machine decoding with human reading intuition.

papers.title: Unlimited OCR Works 2
papers.tldr: Unlimited OCR 2 enables virtually unlimited-length document parsing by restricting each decoding step to a fixed-size, localized visual context.

papers.abstract: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) typically uses uniform coverage across Transformer layers despite heterogeneous positional requirements. Phase-off interventions reveal non-uniform, model-specific rotary-phase dependence, while coverage interventions relate it to coverage-upgrade benefits. We propose profiling-guided layer-wise RoPE allocation, assigning high/low coverage under a fixed budget using early coverage-benefit profiles. The framework supports fixed-width query/key representations and physical rotary-dimension allocation in Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). Normalized-depth mapping transfers profiles within model families, enabling small-model measurements to guide larger-model allocations before pretraining. A brief analysis relates selection and transfer to score calibration and inter-layer interactions. From-scratch experiments demonstrate validation-loss improvements over available budget-matched baselines, while analytical resource accounting identifies favorable quality--storage--compute trade-offs for physical MLA. These results connect positional demand to transferable, efficient architecture design.
authors: Zhiwei Liu, Boao Kong, Bing Liu
bullets: RoPE dependence varies across layers and models, motivating non-uniform allocation.
Early coverage-benefit profiles identify layers for high or low rotary coverage.
Normalized-depth mapping transfers allocation profiles from smaller to larger models before pretraining.
The framework supports fixed-width query/key representations and physical rotary-dimension allocation in MLA.
From-scratch experiments improve validation loss over budget-matched baselines, with favorable quality–storage–compute trade-offs for physical MLA.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates autoregressive inference by leveraging the memory bound nature of decoding, verifying multiple draft tokens in a single forward pass. For mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, prior work predicts a concave speedup-batch size relationship, with gains peaking at intermediate batch sizes due to expert saturation. We evaluate this across 10 sparse MoE models (30B--1T parameters, 8--512 experts) and find recent fine-grained models break this trend, showing higher speedup at low batch size. We find verification cost is governed not only by activated-expert bytes, but also by temporal overlap across draft tokens and GPU execution dynamics. At low batch size, MoE layers in fine-grained models account for a much smaller share of runtime than of weights; on H100, kernel profiling attributes this mainly to higher bandwidth utilization of MoE kernels relative to attention, with L2 absorbing repeated reads of co-routed experts. Across draft tokens, routing overlap further reduces the unique experts activated during verification relative to independence assumptions. We model this effect using a maximum-entropy Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) framework that predicts unique expert counts from routing-overlap statistics with less than 4\% error, and substantially narrows the gap to real-model curves and captures the qualitative low-batch trend from synthetic routing.
authors: Ekagra Ranjan, Komal K. Teru, Bharat Venkitesh, Acyr Locatelli
bullets: Across 10 sparse MoE models spanning 30B–1T parameters and 8–512 experts, fine-grained models show greater speedup at low batch sizes rather than the expected intermediate-batch peak.
Verification cost depends on temporal overlap across draft tokens and GPU execution dynamics, not just activated-expert bytes.
At low batch sizes, MoE layers consume less runtime than their weight share; on H100, higher MoE-kernel bandwidth utilization and L2 reuse of co-routed experts help explain this.
Routing overlap across draft tokens reduces the number of unique experts activated during verification compared with independence assumptions.
An entropy-maximizing IPF model predicts unique expert counts with under 4% error and captures the qualitative low-batch trend in synthetic routing.

papers.title: Why Speculative Decoding Works Better Than Predicted on Sparse MoE Models
papers.tldr: Speculative decoding can outperform predictions on fine-grained sparse MoE models because GPU execution, caching, and routing overlap make verification cheaper than expert-count estimates suggest.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) serving only while the GPU has spare compute, so the best draft length, the number of tokens a small drafter guesses per step, shrinks as the batch grows. vLLM lets operators set the draft length for each batch size with a hand-written table, but nothing measures or corrects that table. We present TableTune. Its tuner times the decoding step for every batch size and draft length on vLLM's own serving path and computes, in minutes, the table that maximizes throughput. Its controller, a vLLM plugin, tracks how many guesses are accepted in live traffic and rebuilds the table while serving. We measure TableTune only against other ways to speculate. On an H100, the tuned table delivers at least 94% of the throughput of the best fixed draft length at every load in four of five drafter settings (88% in the fifth) without the operator having to know which length that is. Against reimplementations of TurboSpec- and Nightjar-style control on the same engine, its worst-case loss is never higher than theirs, and with the EAGLE-3 drafter it is 3% against 9% and 12%. On a mixture-of-experts model, vLLM's documented table loses up to 18% and the tuned table at most 3%. Starting from mistuned tables, the controller raises throughput by up to 58% (up to 45% on vLLM's default runner), and after a workload switch with the DFlash drafter it recovers 96% of a stale table's loss. In llm-d's optimized-baseline deployment as shipped, two Qwen3-32B replicas on four GPUs, the tuned table is up to 32% faster than a fixed draft length of 3 and up to 25% faster than vLLM's documented table at high load, and the controller raises the documented table's throughput by up to 29%.
authors: Abhishek Malvankar, Paul Castro, Nick Mitchell, Lionel Villard
bullets: Problem: Hand-written draft-length tables in vLLM can become inefficient as load, models, or workloads change.
Method: Benchmark decoding time across batch sizes and draft lengths, then build a throughput-maximizing table; a serving plugin refreshes it using live token-acceptance data.
Contribution: An automated tuner and self-correcting controller integrated with vLLM.

Results: The tuned table reaches at least 94% of the best fixed-length throughput in four of five drafter settings and improves throughput by up to 32% over fixed or documented tables in deployment tests.
Scope: Evaluated on H100 and mixture-of-experts settings, including vLLM and llm-d deployments; performance depends on the drafter and serving workload.

papers.selection_reason: Dynamic speculative decoding draft-length tuning directly targets inference latency and throughput, fitting Efficient AI.
papers.title: TableTune: Measured, Self-Correcting Draft-Length Tables for Dynamic Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: TableTune automatically measures and continuously updates speculative-decoding draft lengths, maintaining near-best throughput across changing batch sizes and workloads.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase computational capacity through the repeated application of shared blocks, but their recurrent depth makes conventional full-depth decoding expensive. While existing speculative pipelines accelerate generation by processing consecutive token positions at varying depths, they are typically limited by sequential decoding overheads. We introduce CopyLoop, a training-free decoding algorithm that combines low-cost context-copy proposals with shallow screening and continuous recurrent scheduling. Rather than step-by-step generation, CopyLoop proposes multi-token suffixes from repeated context. It then evaluates them early at a shallow recurrent depth to efficiently filter out incorrect branches, processing newer blocks concurrently while earlier blocks are still progressing toward full-depth verification. We evaluate CopyLoop across six model checkpoints from the Ouro, Raven, and Huginn families, covering code generation and multi-step mathematical reasoning. CopyLoop achieves decoding speedups of 2.98x--10.70x over full-depth autoregressive decoding on Base models and 2.74x--3.52x on Thinking models, consistently outperforming or closely matching all competing baselines across evaluation tasks. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm a strong synergy between shallow screening and continuous scheduling, while our analyses show that CopyLoop requires only lightweight model calibration and yields greater speedups on longer generations with reusable contexts.
bullets: Targets the sequential overhead of conventional full-depth decoding in recurrent, looped Transformers.
Uses training-free multi-token context-copy proposals, shallow recurrent screening, and concurrent continuous scheduling.
Evaluated on six Ouro, Raven, and Huginn checkpoints for code generation and multi-step mathematical reasoning.
Reports 2.98×–10.70× speedups on Base models and 2.74×–3.52× on Thinking models, generally matching or outperforming baselines.
Ablations find shallow screening and continuous scheduling work synergistically; benefits increase for longer generations with reusable contexts.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free decoding acceleration for looped Transformers via context copying and shallow screening; reduces inference latency.
papers.title: CopyLoop: Fast Looped Transformer Decoding via Context Copying and Shallow Screening
papers.tldr: CopyLoop accelerates looped Transformer decoding by proposing context-copied token sequences, screening them shallowly, and continuously scheduling deeper verification.

papers.abstract: Agentic AI drives significant productivity gains across diverse domains, but concurrent long-context prefills from multiple agents can saturate GPU compute resources. Although CPUs offer a viable alternative, existing CPU attention kernels fall short in adapting to multi-tier cache hierarchies and lack effective thread scheduling. To address this, we introduce CACPU, a high-performance attention kernel featuring tiered cache blocking and an in-kernel task dispatching mechanism designed for causal full-sequence prefilling. CACPU achieves up to a 2.01x speedup over PyTorch SDPA, FlexAttention, and SGLang attention kernels. Integrated into SGLang, it reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) of Llama-3.1-8B by up to 1.74x while preserving model accuracy.
authors: Kwun Fung Lau, Frost Mitchell, Kanya Mo, Emani Ashok
bullets: Targets CPU attention bottlenecks caused by multi-tier cache hierarchies and inefficient thread scheduling.
Uses tiered cache blocking with in-kernel task dispatch for causal full-sequence prefilling.
Reports up to 2.01× speedup over PyTorch SDPA, FlexAttention, and SGLang attention kernels.
Integrated with SGLang, it reduces Llama-3.1-8B TTFT by up to 1.74× while preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: We run Kroko, a 65.7M-parameter streaming Zipformer2 transducer for English, on the ESP32-P4, a microcontroller with two 400 MHz RISC-V cores, a 128-bit SIMD extension (PIE) and 32 MB of PSRAM, but no neural accelerator. Without any training, the encoder's 290 matrices are stored with 2 or 4 bits per weight in Hadamard-rotated groups: the width of each matrix comes from its measured sensitivity, and each matrix is first corrected toward the original model's output, then rounded with GPTQ and a search over the group norms. The released 71 MB of int8 weights become a 26.65 MB file. Activations are int16 between the matrix products and int8 into them. A C engine with hand-written PIE kernels processes each 1.28 s chunk of audio in 0.90 s on both cores, beam search included, and its PC build computes the same bits as the chip, so accuracy is measured on whole test sets. LibriSpeech WER is 4.34% on test-clean and 10.26% on test-other, against 3.94% and 9.17% for the released model; on FLEURS and Common Voice the gap grows to 2.3 and 1.1 points. A GPU simulator shows that the integer arithmetic costs nothing and that the whole gap comes from the weights, and an ablation on all of test-clean shows that GPTQ does most of the work. We also report the port's speed history, from 51.3 s to 0.62 s of encoder time per chunk, each design step measured again in one build, an attempt to reach 16 MB that stopped at 19.63 MB, and what did not work. We did not measure energy. The inference engine, the firmware and the 2/4-bit weights are available at https://github.com/BoumedineBillal/esp32-pie-asr.
bullets: Kroko is deployed on a dual-core 400 MHz RISC-V microcontroller with 32 MB PSRAM and no neural accelerator.
Sensitivity-based 2/4-bit weight quantization uses Hadamard rotation, GPTQ correction, and group-norm search, reducing weights from 71 MB to 26.65 MB.
A hand-optimized C engine with PIE SIMD kernels supports real-time-enough streaming inference, including beam search.
LibriSpeech WER rises from 3.94% to 4.34% on test-clean and from 9.17% to 10.26% on test-other; degradation is larger on FLEURS and Common Voice.
The study finds GPTQ is the main contributor to quantization quality; a 16 MB target was not reached, and energy was not measured.

papers.title: Streaming Speech Recognition on a Microcontroller: a 65.7M-Parameter Transducer in 2 and 4 Bits on the ESP32-P4

papers.abstract: Packing a 3D volume into a token sequence is not merely long-sequence modeling. Once the volume is packed, sequence order no longer encodes the geometry of the sample---so a positional mechanism indexed by sequence position can learn the memory layout rather than the object. This is a general failure mode for attention over packed geometric data. We introduce PACK3D, a local-global attention operator that separates memory layout from attention geometry. PACK3D keeps local neighborhood attention exact, compresses only distant context into contiguous 3D block summaries, and indexes every query-key interaction with axial RoPE on true token-grid coordinates rather than packed positions. Because the rotation is applied before a block is summarized, the query-to-summary logit remains a weighted sum of query-relative 3D displacements; compressed global context therefore stays spatially interpretable after packing, instead of collapsing to anonymous pooled content. We measure the failure mode directly. On a controlled synthetic task---train on one packing, change only the memory order of the tokens, hold the physical labeling rule fixed---learned positional embeddings and packed-sequence RoPE solve the training layout perfectly yet collapse under Morton, block-contiguous, and random repacking, while axial grid-coordinate RoPE stays exact throughout. The same coordinate system carries to real data: on Allen WTC-11 hiPSC microscopy, PACK3D improves over a parameter-matched 3D U-Net on the 15-structure joint task and over a matched learned-position local-global baseline, with controls isolating the coordinate system, not encoder capacity, as the source of the gain. A fused Triton implementation matches windowed-attention latency at 65k tokens while supplying the long-range context windowing cannot---so the operator is not only correct but trainable at scale.
authors: Amil Khan, Anantajit Subrahmanya, B. S. Manjunath
bullets: Packed sequence positions can encode memory layout rather than physical object geometry.
PACK3D combines exact local attention with compressed summaries of distant 3D blocks.
Axial RoPE uses true token-grid coordinates, keeping query-to-summary relationships spatially interpretable.
On a controlled repacking task, packed-position methods fail after reordering, while grid-coordinate RoPE remains exact.
On hiPSC microscopy, PACK3D improves over matched 3D U-Net and learned-position baselines; a fused implementation scales to 65k tokens with windowed-attention latency.

papers.selection_reason: Packed 3D attention with axial coordinate RoPE; core technical contribution is efficient local-global attention over geometrically structured 3D volumes.
papers.title: Geometry Matters in Packed 3D Attention
papers.tldr: PACK3D preserves 3D geometry in attention over packed volumes by using true grid coordinates for local and compressed global interactions, remaining robust to token repacking.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory footprint of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but lowering bit widths while maintaining task performance remains challenging. Existing work has used sensitivity estimates from calibration data to assign bit widths to different model components. However, using task success directly to guide mixed-precision allocation is underexplored because closed-loop evaluations are costly and the effect of quantizing one component depends on the precision of other components. To this end, we propose \textbf{QbD-VLA}, a task-guided mixed-precision quantization method that uses task success from short closed-loop evaluations to assign weight and activation bit widths while accounting for interactions between model components. Experiments covering four VLA models and all four LIBERO suites show strong task performance at average precisions of approximately 4 bits for weights and fewer than 6 bits for activations. On SIMPLER, the gain over uniform quantization is small. On a Franka Research 3 robot arm, simulation-selected allocations show no detected success-rate loss on X-VLA but fail on $\pi_{0.5}$. These findings support using task success to guide mixed-precision VLA quantization, while highlighting the need for real-world evaluation before deployment. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/jiuyixu25/QbD-VLA}{\texttt{github.com/jiuyixu25/QbD-VLA}}.
authors: Jiuyi Xu, Xiao Hu, Meida Chen, Song Wang, Yang Ye, Yangming Shi
bullets: PTQ can reduce VLA memory use, but selecting low bit widths without harming task success is difficult.
QbD-VLA guides per-component weight and activation precision using task success and accounts for interactions between components.
Across four VLA models and all four LIBERO suites, it maintains strong performance at approximately 4-bit weights and fewer than 6-bit activations on average.
On SIMPLER, it provides only a small gain over uniform quantization.
Simulation-selected precisions showed no detected loss for X-VLA on a Franka Research 3 arm but failed on π₀.₅, motivating real-world validation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The overview of QbD-VLA. A VLA policy (X-VLA) with one weight / activation bit-width per group and the allocation shown has an effective W4.16 / A5.90 and is deployed unchanged on the FR3 arm. A group is lowered by one level, the policy is rolled out in simulation, and the move is kept only if its success estimate stays above the floor. The search repeats until no move passes.
Figure 3: Some example trials on the FR3 arm.

Figure 2: π0.5 rollouts of the LIBERO-Goal task put the wine bottle on the rack from the same initial state. Rows, top to bottom: full precision, uniform W4A4, uniform W4A6, and the QbD-VLA allocation. papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) based on Transformer architectures have achieved remarkable performance across artificial intelligence tasks, but their computational cost remains a major bottleneck. Structured sparsification provides a promising approach to reducing this cost. In particular, $\ell_{1,\infty}$ projections can induce column-wise sparsity in model matrices, but existing proximal methods (Prox) typically require $\mathcal{O}(nm\log(nm))$ operations for matrices in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$, limiting their computational and energy efficiency. In this paper, we introduce Two-Stage Clipping (TSC), an efficient structured sparsification operator inspired by bilevel optimization. Rather than solving a bilevel optimization problem in the strict sense, TSC decomposes the computation into two successive stages. First, group-level quantities are projected to allocate the global sparsity budget and identify active groups. Second, the resulting values are used as group-wise clipping thresholds for the matrix coefficients. For square attention matrices ($n \times n$), the complexity of our TSC method is $O(n^2)$, which is linear in the number of matrix coefficients. We establish a theoretical bound on the discrepancy between TSC and the exact proximal projection and show on synthetic data that the additional Euclidean approximation cost remains small in practice. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate substantial runtime improvements over proximal baselines and validate the theoretical norm identities underlying the proposed construction.
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of exact ℓ₁,∞ proximal projections, which typically require O(nm log(nm)) operations.
Uses two stages: project group-level quantities to allocate sparsity and identify active groups, then clip matrix coefficients using group-wise thresholds.
Runs in O(n²) for square attention matrices, linear in the number of coefficients.
Theoretical analysis bounds its discrepancy from the exact proximal projection, while synthetic experiments find small additional Euclidean cost.
Benchmarks report substantial runtime gains over proximal baselines and support the proposed norm identities.

papers.abstract: Linear attention and state space models (SSMs) offer efficient alternatives to softmax attention by maintaining a fixed-size recurrent state, but this design requires careful management to preserve useful historical associations and limit interference. The delta rule helps reduce interference through correction of the value associated with each key, but it does not explicitly account for how related value features are distributed across the state. We observe that a state $\boldsymbol{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_k\times d_v}$ can be viewed as a bank of $d_k$ addresses storing $d_v$-dimensional values. While a key-side read $\boldsymbol{S}^\top\boldsymbol{k}$ retrieves the value associated with $\boldsymbol{k}$, a value-side read $\boldsymbol{S}\boldsymbol{e}$ aggregates addresses whose stored value features match the selector $\boldsymbol{e}$. Based on this observation, we propose Dual DeltaNet (DDN), which extends Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) with a two-sided delta rule. The key-side delta rule reads with the current key to correct its associated value, while the complementary value-side delta rule reads with selected features of the current value to reorganize the addresses it occupies. We derive a chunkwise parallel training algorithm and a rank-2 recurrence that increases arithmetic intensity during inference. Compared with KDA, GDN-2, and Mamba-3, DDN achieves the strongest overall performance across language modeling, zero-shot downstream tasks, and retrieval, while incurring modest training and inference overhead relative to KDA. Code: https://github.com/ReichtumQian/DualDeltaNet
authors: Yixiao Qian, Yaxin Zhang, Song Chen, Jiaxu Liu, Shengze Cai, Chao Xu
bullets: Targets interference and poor organization in fixed-size recurrent states used by linear attention and SSMs.
Extends Kimi Delta Attention with complementary key-side and value-side delta rules.
Introduces chunkwise parallel training and a rank-2 recurrence for higher inference arithmetic intensity.
Reports strongest overall performance among DDN, KDA, GDN-2, and Mamba-3 across language modeling, zero-shot tasks, and retrieval.
Adds modest training and inference overhead compared with KDA.
