papers.abstract: Frontier large language models write correct CUDA kernels for most single-operator benchmark tasks, yet their accuracy collapses on accelerators whose architecture and programming language they have rarely seen. We present a case study of an LLM agent loop built for such accelerators. Our example is the FuriosaAI RNGD NPU, programmed in a recent, sparsely documented Rust DSL, where the loop optimized three Gemma-4-12B decode kernels over 12 days on a shared, scarce device. The loop builds its own target knowledge: it writes and checks a summary of the DSL documentation, measures the chip with microbenchmarks, records compiler-derived legality rules, and revisits this knowledge when the toolchain changes, rechecking rules and measurements where it can. A role-based search over per-kernel Design Trees explores whole-kernel designs and accumulates small accepted changes in the best version of each kernel. Because device time is scarce and readings are noisy, cheap checks screen new designs before any device run, and late in the run a change was accepted only after repeated comparisons with the best kernel on the device. The final kernels reach a 9.293x geomean speedup over the official baseline, each within 1.25x of the cycles needed just to move its weights. Our prompts, profiler and acceptance test are available at https://github.com/bgchun-fs/multi-agent-kernel-gen-loop.
bullets: Targets the challenge of LLM-generated kernels failing on unfamiliar accelerator architectures and languages.
Builds and updates target knowledge from documentation summaries, microbenchmarks, compiler legality rules, and toolchain checks.
Uses role-based search over per-kernel Design Trees, with cheap screening before scarce, noisy device evaluations.
Applies repeated on-device comparisons late in the process to validate accepted changes.
The final kernels are each within 1.25× of the cycles required to move their weights; prompts, profiler, and acceptance test are released publicly.

papers.selection_reason: LLM agent loop optimizing kernels for an AI accelerator is directly relevant to efficient AI compute.
papers.title: A Case Study of a Multi-Agent Kernel-Optimization Loop That Learns a New AI Accelerator
papers.tldr: A multi-agent LLM loop learned an unfamiliar Rust-based NPU programming environment and optimized three Gemma-4-12B decode kernels to a 9.293× geometric-mean speedup over the official baseline.

papers.abstract: Perception tasks for navigation in robotics, including aerial platforms such as drones and autonomous driving systems, are inherently structured. Drone-mounted cameras typically capture sky above, terrain below, and obstacles or man-made structures in between, while driving data often contains organized road layouts, lane markings, and surrounding agents. Motivated by these axis-aligned structural priors, we note that such information is typically more structured than in generic image tasks. We hypothesize that processing information in a quadtree-esque manner can not only model features effectively in a hierarchical manner, but also offers an efficient linear-time alternative to vanilla attention mechanisms, which run in quadratic time. In this paper, we propose Sibling-Selective Quadtree Attention (SSQA), which models image tokens hierarchically as a structured, full quadtree. We show analytical complexity analysis that guarantees linear-time feature modeling, in addition to empirical experiments comparing inference speeds with other popular modeling approaches, such as Mamba 2 and Quadtree Attention. Our results, benchmarked across several tasks, show that we achieve results at least as good, if not notably better, as others at a fraction of the computational costs.
authors: Yufan Chen, Arnav Bali, Angela Liu, Laura Zheng, Ming C. Lin
bullets: Targets structured navigation perception in robotics, including drones and autonomous driving.
Organizes image tokens as a structured full quadtree based on axis-aligned scene priors.
Introduces sibling-selective attention to support hierarchical feature modeling.
Provides analytical guarantees of linear-time complexity instead of quadratic vanilla attention.
Experiments across several tasks report competitive or better results at a fraction of the computational cost, including comparisons with Mamba 2 and Quadtree Attention.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Mean Epoch Wall Times (s) across 50 epochs on IllusionAnimals classification (2242 inputs) on A100 GPU. Despite other methods also modeling attention in linear time, a practical caveat is the lack of compute optimization in practice. As a result, some methods are even slower than vanilla ViT [6] out-of-the-box from official implementations. SSQA is both easy to integrate and requires no additional practical optimizations, our results show that SSQA maintains or even improves performance over other hierarchical modeling baselines.

Fig. 2: Top-Down vs. Bottom-Up Gating; Squares indicate leaf nodes. Our work has a key difference from previous work in hierarchical quadtree-based attention approaches: bottom-up gating. Previous works (a) avoid subdivisions into tokens with smaller granularity if possible by selecting top-k tokens with highest saliency during training. As a result, tokens on the same level outside of top-k saliency neglect hierarchical reasoning, even if there agents present in those patches. For example, in a driving scene, one patch may have a higher density of pedestrians, but it shouldn’t imply less attention on the single agent falling outside of the same patch. In our approach, we model features from bottom-up, ensuring that features are modeled hierarchically across the entire image. Doing so not only improves performance on various benchmarked tasks, but also maintains linear complexity with respect to number of tokens (shown in §III-G).
Fig. 4: Model Efficiency. SSQA is substantially lighter by reducing the number of parameters by nearly 3x and more compute-efficient by up to a factor of 8x for classification test.
Fig. 3: Training Dynamics. SSQA (a) converges faster and (b) reaches target accuracy earlier than the ViT baseline.

papers.title: SSQA: Sibling-Selective Quadtree Attention for Hierarchical Modeling in Perception Tasks
papers.tldr: SSQA uses sibling-selective quadtree attention to hierarchically model structured perception features with linear-time complexity and lower computational cost than standard attention.

papers.abstract: AI compute is becoming large and fast-changing electrical loads. Its impacts on data center infrastructure and power grids depend not only on total energy consumption, but also on how their power draw moves over sub-second to minute timescales, including peaks, ramps, and synchronized fluctuations across accelerators. Existing energy benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) report aggregate quantities such as joules per token and rarely release the underlying time-series measurements, leaving these power dynamics poorly characterized and difficult to model. We introduce LLM-PowerTrace, an open dataset of time-resolved, per-GPU power traces for LLM fine-tuning and inference, sampled every 100\,ms on varying NVIDIA platforms paired with complete workload and system metadata. For fine-tuning, LLM-PowerTrace profiles open model families spanning a wide range of model sizes and fine-tuning methods, together with controlled sweeps over batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, and checkpointing. For inference, it covers variations in concurrency, GPU frequency, KV-cache and weight quantization, prompt and output lengths, and request-arrival patterns. LLM-PowerTrace profiles a set of open model families across a wide range of model sizes, and controlled sweeps over batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, and checkpointing for fine-tuning, and it sweeps concurrency, GPU frequency, KV cache and weight quantization, prompt and output lengths, and request arrival patterns for inference. Built upon power traces, we define power-grid-facing metrics as well as AI-compute power\&energy scaling law for extrapolating beyond the measured settings. Together, LLM-PowerTrace provides a dataset foundation for modeling, forecasting, and managing the fast-changing electrical behavior of AI compute.
authors: Jiansheng Wang, Jaskeerat Singh, Haochen Xu, Xinyi Li, Mingyuan Yan, Shaohui Liu, Yuzhuo Li, Yize Chen, Wenqi Cui
bullets: Addresses the gap between aggregate energy benchmarks and missing sub-second-to-minute power dynamics such as peaks, ramps, and synchronized fluctuations.
Provides per-GPU power traces sampled every 100 ms across NVIDIA platforms, with complete workload and system metadata.
Covers broad controlled variations in model size, batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, checkpointing, concurrency, frequency, quantization, and request patterns.
Introduces power-grid-facing metrics and an AI-compute power and energy scaling law for extrapolation beyond measured settings.
Supports modeling, forecasting, and management of rapidly changing AI-compute electrical loads.

Energy per token follows the same order, from 0.14 J for Qwen3-8B to 0.52 J for Qwen3-32B (Fig. 27c). Mean and 95th-percentile power rise only modestly with size, from 493 to 516 W on average (Fig. 27d). The ramping rate falls from 78 to 48 W/s between Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B, with the MoE model (76 W/s) close to Qwen3-8B, while spectral entropy is highest for the MoE model (0.74 against 0.58–0.60) (Figs. 27e, 27f).

Figure 34: [Inference] Complete quantitative comparison across different KV-cache precisions. The panels report request latency, energy per request, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It compares BF16 and FP8 (E4M3) KV caches across the six metrics (five models on A100, H100, and H200, BF16 weights). Request latency changes by less than 1%, and energy per request and per token fall by about 2% on average (a median 2.7% and at most 5% across the 13 same-host pairs) (Figs. 34a, 34b, 34c). Mean power falls slightly, from 574 to 559 W (Fig. 34d). The ramping rate rises from 80 to 89 W/s, less than its run-to-run spread, and spectral entropy falls from 0.60 to 0.58 (Figs. 34e, 34f).

Figure 15: [Fine-tuning] Model size. Complete quantitative comparison across different model sizes for fine-tuning tasks. The panels report iteration duration, energy per iteration, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes how the six fine-tuning metrics vary with active parameter count. Mean iteration duration and energy per iteration increase with model size, with a particularly pronounced increase for the largest models (Figs. 15a, 15b). Energy per token exhibits a similar upward trend at larger model sizes, while remaining non-monotonic across intermediate configurations (Fig. 15c). Mean and upper-tail power increase initially before approaching a broad plateau, whereas lower-tail power varies more modestly (Fig. 15d). Ramping rate increases toward medium–large models but remains non-monotonic across configurations, while spectral entropy exhibits no consistent relationship with model size (Figs. 15e, 15f).

Figure 26: [Inference] Numerical-precision examples for Qwen3-14B on one H100: (a) BF16, (b) FP8 weights, (c) GPTQ-INT4 weights, and (d) FP8 KV cache with BF16 weights, over 60 s taken 120 s into the measurement window. Runs (a)–(c) ran on a host with the GPU power limit lowered to 575 W.

Figure 24: [Inference] Workload sweeps: (a) maximum concurrency from 1 to 256 for Qwen3-32B on one A100; (b) input/output length from 128/128 to 2048/2048 tokens for Qwen3-14B on one H200 with 32 requests in flight. Each setting is a separate run; 30 s of each run are shown side by side, separated by grey lines, so the segments are not contiguous in time.

Figure 31: [Inference] Complete quantitative comparison across different Poisson arrival rates. The panels report request latency, energy per request, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes the effects of the arrival rate on the six inference metrics (Qwen3-8B, 14B, and 32B on H200, free-length generation; Qwen3-32B at TP 2). Request latency rises only slightly with rate, from 3.1 to 4.1 s, while energy per request falls from 1.9 kJ to 109 J (Figs. 31a, 31b). Energy per token falls from 4.9 to 0.28 J as idle time is amortized over more requests (Fig. 31c). The 5th-percentile power stays near idle up to 0.5 requests/s (117–128 W on one GPU and 261–270 W for the two-GPU Qwen3-32B node) and rises to 577–638 W on one GPU (1.28 kW for Qwen3-32B) at 8 requests/s, as the GPUs stop draining between requests (Fig. 31d). The ramping rate stays at 410–490 W/s up to 1 request/s and drops to 42–48 W/s from 4 requests/s, while spectral entropy peaks at 1 request/s (Figs. 31e, 31f).

Figure 36: [Inference] Complete quantitative comparison across different SM clock frequencies. The panels report request latency, energy per request, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes the effects of the locked SM clock on the six inference metrics (Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Llama-3.1-8B on one H100, closed loop; the 1980 MHz setting throttles to a median of 1830 MHz). Request latency falls from 14.4 s at 345 MHz to 5.8 and 5.7 s at 1605 and 1980 MHz, while energy per request and per token are lowest at 1200 MHz (66 J and 0.13 J) and rise again at higher clocks (Figs. 36a, 36b, 36c). Mean power rises from 184 to 535 W, with a narrow band at every clock (Fig. 36d). The ramping rate grows at every clock step, from 8 to 68 W/s, while spectral entropy falls from 0.48 to 0.43–0.45 (Figs. 36e, 36f).

Figure 32: [Inference] Complete quantitative comparison across different input/output lengths. The panels report request latency, energy per request, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes the effects of the forced input/output length on the six inference metrics (Qwen3-8B, 14B, and 32B on one H200 with 32 requests in flight). Request latency and energy per request grow mainly with the output length, from 1.7 s and 33 J at 128/128 to 35 s and 753 J at 2048/2048 (Figs. 32a, 32b). Energy per output token is highest for long prompts with short outputs (0.89 J at 2048/128) and 0.26–0.37 J otherwise (Fig. 32c). The 2048-token prompts hold power within a few percent of the 700 W limit, with the 5th percentile at 681 W (Fig. 32d). The same workloads have the smallest ramps (20 W/s against 39–56 W/s) and the highest spectral entropy (Figs. 32e, 32f).

Figure 20: [Fine-tuning] Sequence length. Quantitative comparison across different sequence lengths. The panels report iteration duration, energy per iteration, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes the effects of sequence length on the six fine-tuning metrics. Iteration duration and energy per iteration increase sharply beyond 256 tokens (Figs. 20a, 20b), while energy per token decreases from 16 to 256 tokens before approaching a plateau (Fig. 20c). Mean, 5th-percentile, and 95th-percentile power increase with sequence length, although upper-tail power begins to saturate at the longest sequences (Fig. 20d). Ramping rate shows no clear monotonic trend, while spectral entropy decreases toward 256 tokens before increasing again at longer sequences (Figs. 20e, 20f).

Figure 16: [Fine-tuning] Batch size. Complete quantitative comparison across different batch sizes. The panels report iteration duration, energy per iteration, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It summarizes the effects of batch size on the six fine-tuning metrics. Iteration duration and energy per iteration increase with batch size as more samples are processed per optimizer step (Figs. 16a, 16b). In contrast, energy per token generally decreases, indicating that larger batches amortize fixed computational and synchronization overheads over more tokens (Fig. 16c). Mean and 95th-percentile power increase only moderately, while 5th-percentile power rises sharply at small batch sizes before leveling off (Fig. 16d). Ramping rate also increases with batch size, whereas spectral entropy varies non-monotonically and peaks at intermediate batch sizes (Figs. 16e, 16f).

Figure 19: [Fine-tuning] GPU platform. Complete quantitative comparison across different GPU platforms. The panels report iteration duration, energy per iteration, energy per token, power distribution, ramping rate, and spectral entropy. It compares A100, H100, H200, and L40S GPUs across the six metrics. L40S has the longest mean iteration duration, followed by A100, while H100 and H200 complete iterations substantially faster (Fig. 19a). Energy per iteration and per token follow the same broad ordering, with H100 and H200 consuming less energy than A100 and L40S (Figs. 19b, 19c). In contrast, H200 and H100 operate at higher mean and upper-tail power, with H200 showing the highest values (Fig. 19d). H200 also has the highest ramping rate, whereas L40S has the lowest (Fig. 19e). Spectral entropy is lower on H100 and H200 than on A100 and L40S (Fig. 19f), indicating more regular power traces.

Figure 21: [Inference] Tensor-parallel degree: Qwen3-14B on (a) one, (b) two, and (c) four H100 GPUs. Each row shows per-GPU power (left) and their sum (right) over 60 s taken 120 s into the measurement window. The TP 1 run ran on a host with the GPU power limit lowered to 575 W; TP 2 and TP 4 ran at 700 W.

Figure 22: [Inference] GPU platform: Qwen3-14B at TP 4 on (a) A100, (b) H100, and (c) H200. Each row shows per-GPU power (left) and their sum (right) over 60 s taken 120 s into the measurement window.

papers.selection_reason: Time-resolved GPU power traces and scaling laws for AI compute energy are relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: LLM-PowerTrace: A Dataset of Time-Resolved GPU Power Traces for AI Compute
papers.tldr: LLM-PowerTrace is an open, high-resolution dataset for analyzing and modeling the time-varying GPU power demands of LLM fine-tuning and inference.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) represent images and videos as long visual-token sequences, substantially increasing inference costs. These costs motivate visual-token pruning, whose effectiveness depends on both what signal is used for selection and when that signal becomes available. Our analysis reveals complementary limitations: visual-side [CLS] attention produces scattered, background-biased selections under aggressive compression, while stronger query-conditioned signals become available after substantial computation within the large language model (LLM). This raises a natural question: can structurally coherent, query-aware token selection be performed before consulting the LLM? We therefore propose ST-Pruner (Spectral-Textual Pruner), a training-free framework for pre-LLM visual-token selection. It combines attention-independent spectral saliency with inverted patch-text similarity through parameter-free multiplicative fusion. Across diverse LVLMs, ST-Pruner retains over 95% of full-token performance using at most 11.1% of visual tokens and achieves a 3.2x end-to-end speedup on LLaVA-NeXT. Code is available at https://github.com/sejong-rcv/ST-Pruner.
authors: Intaek Shin, Geuntaek Lim, Sungjune Park, Yukyung Choi
bullets: LVLMs face high inference costs from long visual-token sequences.
Visual [CLS] attention can select scattered, background-biased tokens, while query-aware signals typically require costly LLM computation.
ST-Pruner is training-free and operates before LLM processing.
It fuses attention-independent spectral saliency with inverted patch-text similarity using parameter-free multiplication.
Across diverse LVLMs, it achieves a 3.2× end-to-end speedup on LLaVA-NeXT while retaining over 95% of full-token performance.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of ST-Pruner. Given pre-LLM visual features Z, the spectral branch derives its saliency score from a randomized low-rank SVD, while the semantic branch computes inverted patch–text relevance using a query embedding from the corresponding frozen text encoder of the paired vision–language model. Their parameter-free multiplicative fusion determines the top-K visual tokens, which are retained in their original sequence order before LLM inference. The textual query is independently tokenized for the standard languagemodel input.

Figure 2. Why Not Ask the LLM? (a) Pre-LLM inverted patch–text similarity (−sim) and in-LLM query-to-patch attention at representative decoder layers, visualized by their top-K token selections. (b–c) Evaluations on GQA (n = 12,578). (b) Re-inference accuracy when retaining only the top-K tokens selected by each LLM layer, with the full-token model and pre-LLM −sim as references. (c) Layer-wise overlap between the pre-LLM −sim and in-LLM top-K token sets, normalized by the expected overlap of two random K-token subsets, such that 1× denotes random overlap.
Figure 1. Structural Saliency Comparison. (a) Selection of K = 64 tokens using [CLS] attention and our spectral criterion. (b) F1 score on POPE across token budgets using each structural signal.

Table 7. Inference efficiency on LLaVA-NeXT-7B. Results are measured over the full POPE evaluation set of 8,910 samples on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU under FP16. The cross-method comparison uses a 320-token target budget. Prefill and total latency include methodspecific pruning and scoring overhead. Total denotes end-to-end generation latency with a maximum generation length of 16 tokens. Values in parentheses denote speedup or FLOPs reduction factors relative to the unpruned model.
Table 4. Cross-architecture comparison on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. ST-Pruner (Spectral) denotes the proposed spectral criterion without the semantic branch.

Table 6. Robustness to fusion strategy and spectral rank. Values denote mean performance retention over GQA, POPE, TextVQA, MMEP, and MMB, normalized by the matched fulltoken reproduction used for these ablations. For entropy-weighted fusion, we report the strongest setting (τ = 0.5) from the full temperature sweep. Complete per-benchmark results are provided in the supplementary material.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes ST-Pruner, a training-free framework for visual token pruning in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), using spectral saliency and patch-text similarity to reduce inference costs.
papers.title: Don't Ask the LLM: Visual Token Pruning with Spectral Structure and Semantic Relevance
papers.tldr: ST-Pruner enables efficient pre-LLM visual-token pruning by combining spectral structure with patch-text relevance, preserving over 95% of full-token performance while using at most 11.1% of tokens.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) achieve strong image recognition performance, but their self-attention increases quadratically with the number of input tokens and makes them computationally expensive. The standard implementation of ViT models treats all patch tokens with equal importance across every layer of the model. This uniform treatment introduces redundant computation and may reduce the model's focus on the most discriminative object regions. In this paper, we propose ConvRoute-ViT, a convolutional token routing mechanism for efficient vision transformers that performs token reduction through convolutional routing. Our model preserves the most relevant patch tokens according to class-token attention at selected layers, while the remaining tokens are spatially reorganized and compressed into a compact set of convolutional summary tokens. This design reduces the sequence length without completely removing the contextual information of the less informative tokens. By applying the routing process hierarchically, the proposed framework constructs compact and discriminative representations for deeper layers. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet show that ConvRoute-ViT improves computational efficiency while maintaining classification accuracy compared with the base ViT.
authors: Manish Das, Shiv Ram Dubey, Satish Kumar Singh
bullets: Addresses redundant computation from treating all ViT patch tokens equally and the quadratic cost of self-attention.
Uses class-token attention to preserve relevant tokens at selected layers.
Spatially reorganizes and convolves remaining tokens into compact summary tokens rather than discarding them.
Applies routing hierarchically to build compact, discriminative representations in deeper layers.
Experiments on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet report improved computational efficiency with maintained classification accuracy versus base ViT.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed ConvRoute-ViT architecture. The input image is converted into patch tokens with positional encoding and a CLS token, creating an input size of B×N ×D. After initial transformer processing up to kth transformer layers, the ConvRoute Token Routing Module computes the token importance score and retains the top-R important tokens. The remaining tokens are passed through the ConvRoute Compressor where they are spatially reshaped to generate compact ConvSummary tokens, resulting in B ×M ×D and are processed by transformer layers from k+1→ l. A second ConvRoute Token Routing Module is applied at layer l to further reduce the sequence and is then passed through the subsequent transformer blocks for final classification.

Fig. 2. Attention heatmaps for representative CIFAR-100 samples [24]. Each example consists of three panels arranged from left to right: the input image, the base ViT attention map, and the ConvRoute-ViT attention map.
TABLE III COMPARISON WITH REPRESENTATIVE CNN AND TRANSFORMER BASELINES ON CIFAR-100 AND TINYIMAGENET. RESULTS ARE TAKEN FROM [26], AND MODELS MARKED WITH † ARE IMPLEMENTED FROM SCRATCH.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes ConvRoute-ViT, a convolutional token routing mechanism for Vision Transformers that reduces computational cost by selectively retaining and compressing patch tokens.
papers.title: ConvRoute-ViT: Convolutional Token Routing for Efficient Vision Transformers
papers.tldr: ConvRoute-ViT efficiently reduces ViT token sequences by retaining important patches and compressing the rest into convolutional summary tokens while preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Loss spikes in language model pretraining can waste substantial compute and derail otherwise healthy training runs. A primary driver of these instabilities is the growth and divergence of output logits in the final language modeling (LM) head. In this work, we study a particularly costly form of this instability associated with output logit growth: delayed, terminal divergences that emerge only after prolonged training, which we call time-bomb spikes. We find that these instabilities are preceded by rapidly growing quantization error in the LM head, which eventually culminates in a loss spike. Crucially, reducing numerical precision accelerates time-bomb spikes, while increasing precision improves stability. We then propose a simple yet effective mitigation that replaces AdamW on the LM head with SGD with momentum, suppressing logit growth and improving stability over long training horizons. Finally, we find that existing mitigation techniques from the literature (along with our own) all reduce quantization error, suggesting a shared numerical mechanism behind their effectiveness. Together, our results identify finite precision error as a hidden driver of time-bomb spikes and show that suppressing this error is key to stable long-horizon pretraining.
authors: Zaiqian Chen, Aditya Somasundaram, Sophie Li, Sean McLeish, John Kirchenbauer, Tom Goldstein, Micah Goldblum
bullets: Studies delayed terminal divergences in language-model pretraining, termed “time-bomb spikes.”
Finds that rapidly increasing LM-head quantization error precedes these loss spikes.
Lower numerical precision accelerates instability; higher precision improves stability.
Replacing AdamW with momentum SGD on the LM head suppresses logit growth and improves stability.
Existing mitigations appear to work partly by reducing quantization error, indicating a shared numerical mechanism.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Increasing LM head β1 is more effective than tuning its learning rate alone. Left: Final evaluation loss across trunk learning rates. Head learning rate tuning yields modest gains, while β1 = 0.99 closes much of the gap to LM head SGD-M. Adding µ-centering or z-loss improves some settings, but all AdamW variants diverge or time-bomb at the largest trunk learning rate, whereas SGD-M remains stable. Dashed lines denote tuned head learning rates. Right: output logit norm trajectories, showing how each method constrains LM head growth.

Figure 7: Methods that prevent time-bomb failure suppress quantization error. For 28Mparameter models trained in BF16 mixed at peak LR 0.1, the unmitigated baseline develops timebomb spikes (left) together with orders-of-magnitude growth in logit quantization error (middle) and predictive distribution quantization error (right). All mitigation methods prevent the time bomb and keep both numerical-error metrics bounded across five seeds. Solid lines show medians and faint lines show individual runs. The same effect is more pronounced under BF16 true training; the unmitigated baseline fails catastrophically after significant growth in numerical error (Figure 20).

Figure 1: Reduced precision accelerates time-bomb spikes, while LM head SGD-M prevents them. Lowering LM head precision brings the failure earlier, with BF16 true diverging first, BF16 mixed later, and FP32 remaining stable throughout training (left). Output logit norm grows under every AdamW baseline, including FP32 (middle), but it destabilizes training only in reduced precision, where LM head quantization error grows by orders of magnitude before each failure (right). Quantization error is measured as the RMS difference between native BF16 logits and FP32 logits computed from the same hidden states. Replacing AdamW with SGD-M on the LM head keeps both logit norm and quantization error nearly flat, preventing the time bomb even in BF16 mixed precision. Results are for 28M parameter models trained at peak learning rate 0.1 for ∼28× the Chinchilla optimal token horizon, using AdamW throughout (baselines) or SGD with momentum on the LM head (SGD-M).

Figure 9: Skipping a small fraction of high-loss tokens eliminates loss spikes but hurts convergence. A 162M model trained at the Chinchilla-optimal token budget with peak learning rate 0.15. One run is the baseline; the other skips high-loss tokens identified via a rolling window threshold.

Figure 3: Long horizon training can result in time-bomb instability. Two 404M parameter models train similarly for most of pretraining, but the higher LR run exhibits delayed, unrecoverable loss increases accompanied by accelerating output logit growth.

Figure 14: LM head SGD-M is the only intervention stable across the spike-prone learning rate regime at both model sizes. Final evaluation loss versus peak learning rate for 162M and 404M models. µ-centering and z-loss diverge at some η ∈ [10−1, 3×10−1] at both sizes, and row-centering, while stable at 162M, diverges inconsistently at 404M and is omitted there. LM head SGD-M remains stable throughout and achieves the lowest loss at the high end.

Figure 15: LM head SGD-M also stabilizes training at 1.4B scale and pairs well with Muon. Training loss curves for 1.4B models at peak learning rate η = 0.07 (single seed). Replacing AdamW with SGD-M (β = 0.99) on the LM head reaches a lower final training loss than AdamW, µ-centering, and z-loss, and combining a Muon backbone with LM head SGD-M reaches the lowest loss of any configuration shown.

Figure 16: Time-bomb instability emerges across the long-horizon learning rate sweep alongside accelerating output logit growth. Evaluation loss (left), output logit norm (middle), and output logit mean (right) for 404M-parameter models trained for 96B tokens across peak learning rates from 3× 10−4 to 3× 10−1. Runs train similarly for much of pretraining, while higher-learning rate settings exhibit substantially greater late stage logit norm growth and, in several cases, deterioration in evaluation loss.

Figure 17: Longer training horizons are associated with increasingly severe late stage LM head growth. Evaluation loss (left), output logit norm (middle), and output logit mean (right) for 28M parameter models with parameterized RMSNorm, and peak LR of 0.1 trained with horizons of 4B, 8B, 12B, and 16B tokens. Extending training exposes progressively larger output logit norm growth and late stage loss deterioration, consistent with time-bomb instability becoming more prominent during prolonged training.

Figure 2: Learnable gain parameters in normalization layers stabilize training and can prevent fast loss spikes. Comparing a 162M spiking run with the same seed and configuration only differing in the inclusion of learnable RMSNorm parameters, the parameterized norm configuration exhibits no fast spikes, output logit swings, or large logit norm growth.

Figure 6: Reduced precision in the LM head accelerates time-bomb instability and increases quantization error as logits grow. For 28M parameter models trained at peak LR 0.1, BF16 true runs fail earliest, BF16 mixed runs deteriorate later, and FP32 remains stable across five seeds (left). The same ordering appears in the quantization error between BF16 native and FP32 reference logits (middle) and in the KL divergence between the corresponding predictive distributions (right), indicating that loss spikes coincide with increasingly large finite precision error. Solid lines show the median across seeds and faint lines show individual runs.

Figure 10: A single-token context swap collapses the logit distribution at a spike. Full-vocabulary logits (V = 50,260) at the Rank-1 spike event before (blue) and after (orange) replacing the final context token Command with a comma, with the target token ery held fixed. The standard deviation contracts 17×, from 121.87 to 6.87, recovering the range typical of non-spiking steps.

Figure 13: Parameterized RMSNorms effectively mitigate fast loss spikes. The five parameterized runs are highly consistent and overlap closely, indicating low seed-to-seed variability relative to the parameter-less runs.

Figure 12: Skipping high-loss batches defers rather than eliminates fast spike instability. Following Karpathy (2024), we skip any batch whose loss exceeds 7 standard deviations from a rolling 1000-step window and revert the optimizer state. Reverting to either the previous or second-toprevious optimizer state does not prevent subsequent fluctuations in output logit mean characteristic of spike events.

Figure 20: Methods that prevent time-bomb spikes also suppress quantization error. For 28Mparameter models trained in BF16 true at peak learning rate 0.1, the unmitigated baseline develops severe unrecoverable loss spikes (left) together with orders-of-magnitude growth in logit quantization error (middle) and predictive distribution quantization error (right). µ-centering, z-loss, and LM head SGD-M prevent the time bomb and keep both numerical-error metrics bounded across five seeds. Solid lines show medians and faint lines show individual runs.

Figure 18: Normalized logit error grows as the logit mean becomes large relative to variation across logits. Across BF16 true and BF16 mixed baseline runs, the normalized RMS error between native BF16 logits and FP32 reference logits, RMS(zbf16 − zfp32)/std(zfp32), increases with the relative logit mean, |mean(z)|/std(z). Colors indicate precision, markers indicate peak learning rate, and lines trace individual training trajectories.

Figure 4: SGD-M is competitive in both optimization quality and control of LM head growth. Across trunk learning rates, µ-centering, z-loss, and LM head SGD-M improve stability relative to the AdamW baseline, while differing in both final evaluation loss (left) and the degree of LM head growth suppression (right). Across high learning rates, µ-centering and LM head SGD-M strongly suppress output logit norm growth, whereas the baseline develops the largest late growth and corresponding time-bomb spikes (right). Faint curves show individual learning rates; solid curves and shaded regions show the median and interquartile range across learning rates.
Figure 11: Fast loss spikes coincide with sharp swings in the output logit mean. A spiking 162M run compared with a non-spiking run using the same configuration and differing only in random seed.

Figure 19: Lower precision triggers time-bomb spikes at smaller learning rates. Fraction of seeds exhibiting a time-bomb instability across peak learning rates and numerical precision settings. As precision decreases from FP32 to BF16 mixed to BF16 true, instability emerges at progressively smaller learning rates. A time-bomb is defined as three consecutive post-midpoint evaluations at least 0.01 above the running-best evaluation loss.

Table 2: Learning rate sweep across the spike-prone regime (η ∈ [10−1, 3×10−1]) for 162M and 404M models. Final evaluation loss (↓ lower is better) is reported. † marks runs whose loss spiked during training and did not recover.

Table 1: A single-token context swap collapses the spike. Top-5 predicted tokens at the Rank-1 spike event before and after replacing the final context token Command with a comma. Before the swap, the model assigns extreme logits to unrelated subword tokens; after the swap, the top predictions are ordinary function words with logits in a normal range, and the loss falls from 610.00 to 12.73. denotes a leading space.

Table 3: Tuned SGD-M on the LM head suppresses spikes and remains competitive on evaluation loss. Final evaluation loss and training-loss spike score (defined in Section A.6) at peak learning rate η = 0.15 for 162M and 404M models. Values are mean ± standard error across 5 seeds; bold marks the lowest evaluation loss for each model scale.

papers.selection_reason: Studies quantization error and numerical precision in LM-head training, relevant to efficient low-precision LLM training.
papers.title: The Role of Quantization in Loss Spikes
papers.tldr: Finite-precision quantization error in the LM head can trigger delayed loss spikes, while higher precision or momentum SGD improves long-horizon training stability.

papers.abstract: Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP2) maintains parameters and gradients as per-parameter tensors, whereas its collective path operates on flat, rank-major buffers. Converting between these layouts copies all-gather outputs into parameter storage and packs gradients into full-group fp32 buffers. Layout conversion alone accounts for 6.4% of step time in Llama-3.1 70B training at 8K tokens per GPU. Communication kernels impose a second cost: a default NCCL reduce-scatter can slow a concurrent GEMM that would otherwise complete in a single wave by 69%. We present TIDE, a set of zero-copy collectives built on public NCCL 2.31+ APIs. TIDE preserves FSDP2's per-parameter storage and compute kernels while folding layout placement into collective addressing. TIDE-AG delivers shards directly to parameter storage using NVSwitch multicast and paced recursive-doubling RDMA, with no SMs used for transport or placement. TIDE-RS consumes per-parameter bf16 gradients directly and reduces them into fp32 shards (a mixed-precision mode that NCCL does not provide) using copy engines and short-lived thread blocks (CTAs) for node-local accumulation and NVSwitch for cross-node reduction. A two-phase pipeline separates gradient reads from network progress; Slot-Reuse optionally stages gradients in vacated all-gather slots. On 64 GPUs, TIDE reduces step time by up to 27.1% relative to Stock FSDP2 and 6.0% relative to FSDP2+SymmMem across Llama-3.1 70B, Wan2.2, and Qwen3-30B-A3B. It reduces reduce-scatter SM time by factors of 12.5-14.5 and cuts interference with concurrent compute by up to an order of magnitude. Its reduce-scatter buffer remains nearly constant from 16 to 64 GPUs at a fixed per-GPU output size, and its peak memory is up to 4.7 GiB below FSDP2+SymmMem's and, with Slot-Reuse on Wan2.2, below Stock FSDP2's.

It reduces reduce-scatter SM time by 12.5–14.5× and lowers memory usage, with scope focused on public NCCL 2.31+ APIs and the evaluated GPU configurations.

papers.abstract: Weight-only, lossy quantization substantially reduces the storage and memory requirements for serving large language models (LLMs), but the growing key-value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for long-context inference on personal devices. We present Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (GAAC), a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits exponent redundancy to reduce storage and accelerate attention without introducing KV approximation. GAAC encodes BF16 exponents using calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges. GAAC adapts code widths across small groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit. A fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots support incremental cache updates and paged serving. Across five tested models, GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407$\times$ lossless BF16 KV compression. We also study compression performance on low-precision tensors FP8 E4M3 caches ( 1.09-1.14$\times$) and E5M2 caches (1.25-1.30$\times$). On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC accelerates decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19-1.27$\times$ and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04-1.15$\times$. In serving, it reduces resident KV memory by approximately 26% and increases aggregate throughput by 13-29% under comparable KV-memory budgets. On Apple M4, GAAC achieves 1.02-1.25$\times$ attention speedups, demonstrating portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.
authors: Yipin Guo, Arun M George, Siddharth Joshi
bullets: Addresses KV-cache growth as a bottleneck for long-context LLM serving on memory- and bandwidth-constrained devices.
Uses adaptive base-plus-offset coding for BF16 exponent groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit.
Fused attention reconstructs compressed KV tiles on demand, supporting incremental updates and paged serving without full-cache decompression.
Across five models, achieves 1.405–1.407× BF16 KV compression, about 26% lower resident KV memory, and 13–29% higher serving throughput under comparable memory budgets.
Reports attention speedups on NVIDIA DGX Spark and Apple M4, including 1.19–1.27× at 64K-token context on DGX Spark and 1.02–1.25× on M4.

Each code is an offset from a calibrated per-channel base, ci = ei − bw,i. In the illustrated example, one exponent outside the 3-bit window causes the entire group g+1 to use 4-bit mode. papers.abstract: Serverless platforms increasingly host machine learning (ML) inference workflows, modeled as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of interdependent functions. Beyond container startup, each ML node must load libraries, model weights, and CUDA kernels before it can run. These costs accumulate along dependent DAG paths and place initialization on the end-to-end critical path. Existing systems optimize one half of this problem. DAG-agnostic pre-loading prepares nodes the request may never reach, wasting host and GPU memory. DAG-aware serving routes and scales whole functions, leaving the loading stages inside a node untouched. This paper presents GearUp, a serverless DAG inference serving system that removes ML-node loading from the end-to-end critical path at low resource cost. GearUp profiles the loading stages of each node and schedules them inside the slack time the DAG exposes, hiding initialization behind upstream execution. It reuses initialized instances within and across requests to avoid redundant cold starts. A probabilistic, traffic-adaptive keep-alive policy sets how long idle instances are retained, balancing memory cost against cold-start risk under bursty load. On the AMBER Alert and FINRA-ML workflows with NVIDIA L40S GPUs, GearUp reduces median end-to-end latency by 64.5% and 75.9% against SMIless, for median speedups of 3.1x and 10.0x over cold execution. Integrated GPU and host memory allocation fall by up to 83.9% and 94.6% against eager pre-loading in InstaInfer. GearUp achieves 4.2x strong scaling on four workers.
authors: Qi Qi, Yifan Sui, Hanfei Yu, Hong Zhang, Hao Wang
bullets: Targets initialization delays from libraries, model weights, and CUDA kernels on DAG critical paths.
Profiles each node and schedules loading in exposed slack time, hiding it behind upstream execution.
Reuses initialized instances across and within requests to reduce redundant cold starts.
Uses traffic-adaptive probabilistic keep-alive to balance retained-memory cost against cold-start risk.
On two GPU workflows, reduces median end-to-end latency by 64.5% and 75.9% versus SMIless, while cutting memory use by up to 83.9% (GPU) and 94.6% (host) versus eager pre-loading.

papers.abstract: A recurring design choice in building AI systems is whether, when a task is too hard for a model, to expand the model (make it larger, better-prompted, fine-tuned), or to decompose the task (extract the parts that admit a deterministic solution to a host, leaving the model only the irreducibly fuzzy residue). We make three claims. First, that many tasks commonly delegated whole to a model are in fact deterministic tasks with a small generative core. Second, and our central empirical result, that decomposing such a task yields a measurable and desirable property we call parity by construction: on the extracted sub-tasks the model-size performance curve becomes flat, because no model performs them at all. We measure this across nine models spanning a 494M-parameter local checkpoint to a frontier Opus-class model, a thirty-fold parameter range on the local family alone: once the host resolves the context, operation selection scores identically for all nine models and selector resolution for eight of nine, while the one task that does not decompose, labelling, remains sloped across the same range. Because the task leaves the model, a stock checkpoint suffices: no task-specific training and no fine-tuning. Third, that this is a general design discipline, not a domain trick: we show the same move recurring across physics setup, motion retargeting, and object-model editing, and in a Web-CLI tool family (same author, so not an independent replication). We give a method for locating the cut, the construction that makes a cut exist (a deterministic surface and a closed grammar over it), and a way to make the residue safe (resolve the deterministic context; verify the generative output), position the work against neuro-symbolic AI, tool-augmented language models, and generate-and-verify approaches, and are explicit about what is measured (one domain) versus illustrative (the rest).
bullets: Many apparently generative tasks contain deterministic sub-tasks that can be extracted and delegated to a host system.
The proposed “parity by construction” makes model performance flat on extracted sub-tasks because the model no longer performs them.
Across nine models, operation selection became identical after deterministic context resolution, and selector resolution matched for eight of nine; labelling remained model-dependent.
The approach uses a deterministic surface, a closed grammar, resolved context, and verification of generative outputs—without task-specific training or fine-tuning.
Examples span physics setup, motion retargeting, object-model editing, and a Web-CLI tool family; only one domain is empirically measured, with others illustrative.

The three drivers (top) enter through the same DSL; they share one model of the scene and one history/undo, which runs beneath the surface.

papers.abstract: Physical-layer fingerprinting (PLF) has emerged as a promising authentication approach for Internet of Things devices. However, most PLF systems acquire and process a fixed-length waveform for every authentication query, burdening resource-constrained edge nodes. To address this issue, we propose a progressive-observation PLF method that adapts the waveform length to each query. Specifically, a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) first rejects clearly unknown devices from a short observation. Spectral matching then accepts clearly registered devices from a slightly longer observation. Only ambiguous queries proceed to the same matching on the full-length waveform, reducing both data acquisition and computation. Because fingerprints drift across days, we also design an adaptive calibration algorithm to avoid retraining the CNN. The algorithm realigns the features and decision thresholds using a few current-day references from registered devices. We evaluate the method with 100BASE-TX Ethernet devices of two controller types on held-out days. Compared with fixed-length processing, it keeps the false rejection and false acceptance rates equal or lower for both controller types on both days. It also reduces the waveform data per query by 75.1% and the CPU processing time on a Raspberry Pi 5 by 73.7% on average. With the same monitoring bandwidth, an edge node can therefore serve about four times as many authentication queries.
authors: Chenming Zhang, Jiaxiang Geng, Aiqun Hu, Azzedine Boukerche, Peng Sun
bullets: Targets the fixed-length waveform and resource burden of physical-layer fingerprinting on edge nodes.
Uses a lightweight CNN on short observations, spectral matching on longer ones, and full-length processing only for ambiguous queries.
Introduces adaptive calibration to realign features and thresholds using a few current-day registered-device references, avoiding CNN retraining.
Evaluated on 100BASE-TX devices across held-out days, it achieved equal or lower false rejection and false acceptance rates than fixed-length processing.
Reduced waveform data by 75.1% and Raspberry Pi 5 CPU time by 73.7% on average, enabling about four times as many queries at the same bandwidth.

papers.abstract: Neural representation has emerged as a powerful tool to mitigate the demand for increasingly higher-resolution images. However, a fundamental trade-off remains between structured (e.g., feature grids, which offer spatial consistency) and unstructured (e.g., 2D Gaussians, which adaptively capture local variances) representations. This choice significantly affects how well an algorithm represents an image. Here, we present Gaussian-Grid, a hybrid neural representation that adaptively integrates structured and unstructured primitives. By dynamically partitioning computation between 2D Gaussian distributions and their attached multi-resolution feature grids based on the local frequency content, Gaussian-Grid automatically optimizes its architecture to match the underlying complexity of the target signal. We evaluate our approach using high-resolution natural images and demonstrate its applications as GPU-native dataset storage, showing $1.24$-$2.14\times$ decoding speed improvement and PCIe data traffic reduction of $23\times$-$176\times$ over JPEG + ZIP data archiving. The results show that Gaussian-Grid maintains small memory footprints while achieving high reconstruction fidelity across a variety of datasets.
authors: Anatolii Evdokimov, Stavros Diolatzis, Bingxuan Li, Akshay Jindal, Patsorn Sangkloy, Qi Sun
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between spatially consistent structured grids and locally adaptive unstructured Gaussian representations.
Dynamically partitions computation between Gaussian primitives and attached feature grids based on local signal complexity.
Evaluated on high-resolution natural images, including GPU-native dataset storage.
Reports 1.24–2.14× faster decoding and 23×–176× lower PCIe traffic than JPEG + ZIP archiving.
Maintains small memory footprints while providing high-fidelity reconstruction across varied datasets.

papers.abstract: LLM-based generative recommendation reads long, text-rich interaction histories but generates only short semantic identifiers (SIDs). This asymmetry makes supervised fine-tuning inefficient: encoding the history is expensive, yet each history usually provides supervision for only one target. We present Merge and Branch (M&B) to reduce input cost and learn more from each encoded history. Merge compresses each historical item's SID and text into a small number of learned tokens. Branch uses the compressed history to predict multiple target SIDs. To share history computation while keeping these targets independent, M&B organizes each example as a shallow, wide tree. We develop tree FlashAttention to execute this layout efficiently, processing the shared history once and propagating gradients from every branch for end-to-end training. A tree-structured key/value cache extends history sharing to constrained decoding. Experiments on public benchmarks show that M&B outperforms strong recommendation baselines while substantially improving training and decoding efficiency.
bullets: Addresses the costly encoding of long, text-rich histories when each history typically supervises only one short semantic identifier.
Merge compresses each historical item’s SID and text into a few learned tokens; Branch predicts multiple target SIDs from the shared representation.
Uses a shallow, wide tree with tree FlashAttention to share history computation while keeping target branches independent.
A tree-structured key/value cache extends computation sharing to constrained decoding.
On public benchmarks, it outperforms strong baselines while improving training and decoding efficiency.

papers.abstract: A widely held assumption in knowledge distillation is that teacher and student representations must occupy a compatible or explicitly aligned feature space. We propose RPKD (Random Prototype Knowledge Distillation), which discards this assumption by comparing both networks against a shared bank of randomly initialized, frozen prototype vectors. Alignment is therefore carried out in an external reference space rather than in the teacher's native feature coordinates: the teacher side is projected by fixed random maps that carry no trainable parameters, and only the student adapts. Two branches handle the transfer: a logit branch aligning global prototype similarity distributions and a feature branch matching spatially-resolved prototype activation maps. Both operate within the same fixed prototype space, which can be interpreted as a random feature embedding that approximately preserves inter-sample similarity structure, so the prototype bank and the distillation objective stay unchanged across teacher-student pairs while only the input projections are instantiated per architecture. In low-category settings, decoupling the prototype vocabulary from the task label space yields richer supervision than the label space alone, an advantage absent from logit-based methods, whose supervisory signal collapses as class count shrinks. This advantage is especially relevant in real-world scenarios where the label space is typically constrained. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RPKD, achieving a maximum gain of +7.98% over OFA on CIFAR-100, +12.44% on ImageNet-100, and +1.28% on ImageNet-1K. Source code is available at https://github.com/HamzaEtcibasi/RPKD

The prototype vocabulary is independent of task labels, providing richer supervision in low-category settings.
Reports gains over OFA of up to 7.98% on CIFAR-100, 12.44% on ImageNet-100, and 1.28% on ImageNet-1K.

papers.abstract: Latent multi-agent systems reduce inference cost by keeping intermediate reasoning and inter-agent communication in continuous representations.\ Reusable skills, however, are commonly supplied as text or stored as layer-wise Key-Value states or skill-specific model parameters, introducing repeated processing or substantial per-skill storage.\ We introduce \textbf{SkillMem}, which represents each reusable skill as a small external latent memory and makes it directly available during latent multi-agent reasoning.\ A role-conditioned cross-attention reader allows the same memory to guide different agents according to their roles and current hidden states.\ We train the skill memories and shared reader through behavioral distillation, matching the change in token predictions induced by a textual skill while keeping the backbone frozen.\ For our experiments, we obtain textual skills from paired successful and failed multi-agent trajectories, although existing skills can also be compiled directly.\ Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models ranging from 4B to 14B parameters, SkillMem provides strong gains for smaller backbones while preserving efficient latent multi-agent inference across model scales.\ We use the same $8\times256$ memory configuration across all evaluated model scales, requiring 9.6\,KB of skill-specific storage per skill, including its retrieval embedding.\ For a library of 100 skills, SkillMem reduces total storage by more than $38\times$ compared with alternative skill representations and achieves up to a $4.23\times$ end-to-end inference speedup.\ These results show that compact procedural memories can be reused without sacrificing the efficiency of latent multi-agent reasoning.
authors: Yuxuan Zhu, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Pin-Yu Chen, Keerthiram Murugesan
bullets: Addresses the repeated processing and high per-skill storage costs of text, Key-Value, and parameter-based skill representations.
Stores each skill in a small external latent memory accessed through role-conditioned cross-attention.

Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models from 4B to 14B parameters, it provides especially strong gains for smaller models.
Uses 9.6 KB per skill; for 100 skills, it cuts storage by over 38× and delivers up to 4.23× end-to-end speedup.

papers.abstract: Pre-training foundational models is computationally expensive as models scale. In this work, we introduce Bi-Phase Training (BPT), a parameter-efficient pre-training method that preserves the high-rank learning dynamics observed in full-parameter optimization with substantially reduced trainable parameters. BPT parameterizes each weight update as a composition of constrained high-rank left/right transformations via trainable diagonal matrices and low-rank adapters whose updates are periodically merged into the frozen base weights, resulting in a compounding expansion of accessible directions during training. Across language-model pre-training from scratch (Qwen2.5 models from 100M to 1.5B parameters and OLMo-2-1B) on FineWeb-Edu (10B and 100B tokens), BPT achieves validation perplexity close to full-parameter baselines while using far fewer trainable parameters; e.g., at the 1.5B scale, BPT uses 66% fewer trainable parameters with only a small validation-perplexity gap. Additionally, a comprehensive evaluation across diverse downstream tasks shows that BPT preserves much of the full-parameterized model's downstream performance.

Evaluated on Qwen2.5 models from 100M to 1.5B parameters and OLMo-2-1B using FineWeb-Edu.

papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) caching is a core mechanism in large language models, where intermediate key and value representations are stored to accelerate autoregressive decoding. As generation length increases, KV cache memory and computation grow linearly, making compression critical for efficient long-output reasoning. Dictionary-based sparse KV compression is appealing because it represents each token's KV states as a sparse combination of learned basis elements (atoms) in a dictionary, preserving token-level structure without enforcing a global low-rank constraint. However, existing dictionary-based methods face two practical limitations during decoding: iterative sparse coding methods such as Orthogonal Matching Pursuit add decoding-time overhead, and static dictionaries may mismatch evolving KV distributions under test-time generation. While adaptive dictionary updates can reduce this mismatch, naive append-only strategies lead to dictionary growth during generation. We propose FAD-KV, a \textbf{F}ast \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{D}ictionary KV caching framework for efficient reasoning decoding. FAD-KV integrates (i) a screening-based sparse coding scheme, where a one-shot Top-\(n\) selection identifies a small candidate pool followed by lightweight coefficient refinement, and (ii) a fixed-size dictionary adaptation mechanism that reuses inactive atoms instead of expanding the dictionary. By controlling both sparse coding cost and adaptive dictionary growth, FAD-KV provides a memory-bounded and computation-efficient KV compression framework for long reasoning workloads. Experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks show that FAD-KV achieves a strong quality-efficiency trade-off while avoiding unbounded dictionary growth during decoding.
authors: Yuxuan Zhu, David H. Yang, Parisa Shiravani, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Tejaswini Pedapati, Subhajit Chaudhury, Keerthiram Murugesan, Pin-Yu Chen
bullets: KV cache memory and decoding cost grow linearly with generation length, motivating compression for long reasoning outputs.

The dictionary adapts during decoding by reusing inactive atoms rather than expanding indefinitely.
Experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks show a strong quality–efficiency trade-off while maintaining bounded dictionary size.

papers.abstract: Spiking reservoir computing combines the training efficiency of fixed recurrent reservoirs with the energy efficiency of event-driven inference, where computation is triggered by sparse spikes rather than executed densely at every timestep. However, existing spiking reservoirs almost exclusively rely on Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons, whose low-pass dynamics limit their ability to distinguish information encoded at different temporal frequencies. We introduce HRF-Res, a liquid state machine in which LIF neurons are replaced by a heterogeneous population of Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire (HRF) neurons. These neurons exhibit intrinsic oscillatory dynamics and selectively respond to input frequencies, enabling the reservoir to capture frequency-specific temporal patterns. The result is more discriminative representations and higher classification accuracy than LIF-based reservoirs, achieved without sacrificing the energy efficiency of spiking computation, with up to 19x lower energy consumption than an equivalent non-spiking oscillatory reservoir. Evaluated on ten benchmarks spanning time series, sequential images, audio spike trains, and neuromorphic vision, HRF-Res achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among spiking reservoir methods. These results demonstrate that introducing frequency-selective dynamics into spiking reservoirs improves representational quality and classification performance while preserving their inherent energy efficiency.
authors: Aurora Micheli, Claudio Gallicchio, Nergis Tomen
bullets: LIF neurons’ low-pass dynamics limit discrimination of frequency-specific temporal patterns.
Replaces LIF neurons with heterogeneous Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire neurons featuring intrinsic oscillations.

papers.abstract: Modern automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems have achieved remarkable accuracy by scaling model depth and capacity, but at the cost of increased memory, energy, and computational demands. On edge devices where ASR is often most needed, such as watches and glasses, deploying such large models is infeasible due to extremely constrained resources. This raises a fundamental question: can we achieve high representational power in deep ASR models without scaling up parameterization? In this work, we revisit the role of depth and identify layer wise representational dynamics, in which most layers learn functionally similar transformations. Motivated by this insight, we propose a block-recurrent ASR architecture that replaces parameterized depth with a small set of recurrent blocks, each consisting of weight-shared layers, thereby preserving effective depth while drastically reducing model size. Through representation-guided grouping and knowledge distillation, block-recurrent models retain the accuracy of large reference models while using an order of magnitude fewer parameters. Across Open ASR Leaderboard benchmarks, a model with only two shared blocks recovers 97.4% of the accuracy of large models on average. The compact backbone further enables efficient on-device personalization through lightweight MoE-LoRA adaptation, allowing user-specific models to match or surpass the accuracy of general-purpose ASR systems with significantly lower inference cost. By reusing weights across recurrent steps, the proposed architecture reduces memory-access overhead and inference energy consumption. Together, these results show that high quality ASR can be achieved without large parameterization, and that structured recurrence provides a principled path towards ultra-compressed, energy-efficient, and personalized speech recognition on the edge.

papers.abstract: Efficient communication remains a major bottleneck in large language model multiagent systems. Latent communication reduces repeated natural-language exchange by transferring internal model states between agents, but these transfers remain costly and are typically designed around conventional KV-cache representations. We address this problem from two complementary perspectives. We introduce SelectKV, a boundary-aware method that selectively communicates KV states while protecting inherited context, and HyLaMAS, which extends latent collaboration to hybrid linear-attention models by communicating both KV caches and recurrent states through a shared workspace. Across six benchmarks, SelectKV reduces communicated KV positions and logical KV payload by 9.7-9.9%, with accuracy unchanged on two benchmarks, within one percentage point on three, and six points lower on HumanEval+. Across Qwen3.5 model scales, HyLaMAS reduces decoded output tokens by 53-80% and achieves 1.16-2.78x speedups relative to text-based multi-agent communication. Together, these independently evaluated methods represent two complementary approaches to efficient latent-state communication across conventional Transformer and hybrid model architectures.
authors: Miles Liao, Aaron Smieszek, Yuhao Ge
bullets: Efficient communication is a bottleneck in large language model multi-agent systems.
SelectKV selectively communicates KV-cache states while protecting inherited context, reducing communicated KV positions and payload by 9.7–9.9%.
HyLaMAS enables hybrid linear-attention agents to share both KV caches and recurrent states through a common workspace.
Across six benchmarks, SelectKV largely preserves accuracy, though it performs six points lower on HumanEval+.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is used to reduce the inference cost of language models. One-step diffusion drafters propose a block of multiple tokens in parallel, reducing the sequential cost of speculative decoding. On-policy distillation trains these drafters using verifier feedback on their own proposals. However, parallel drafting makes this feedback difficult to use: the drafter predicts each token without observing the preceding tokens sampled within the same block, while the verifier conditions its prediction on those tokens. Different sampled prefixes therefore give different verifier targets for the same drafter prediction. We show that distilling against these targets separately can suppress tokens that are plausible after some prefixes but unlikely after others, harming draft acceptance. We explain the effects of this mismatch and introduce Multi-Draft On-Policy Distillation (MDraft), a new parallel drafter distillation method which samples several draft blocks from the same context and aggregates the verifier's full-vocabulary conditionals across their prefixes. We use all the drafts to collect information from the verifier, allowing support from alternative prefixes to influence the training target. The resulting algorithm improves the acceptance length of a parallel drafter beyond the level of pre-training, and alleviates the effects of the distributional mismatch. MDraft changes only training, retaining the drafter's architecture and inference procedure, allowing the resulting drafter to be used as-is in place of the pretrained checkpoint. Experiments on a suite of mathematical, coding, and conversational tasks show longer accepted drafts than prior distillation methods.
authors: Petr Molodyk, Yuchen Zhu, Jaemoo Choi, Molei Tao, Yongxin Chen
bullets: Parallel drafters make on-policy distillation difficult because verifier targets depend on sampled within-block prefixes that the drafter does not observe.
Training separately on these inconsistent targets can suppress tokens that are plausible under alternative prefixes, reducing draft acceptance.
MDraft samples multiple draft blocks from the same context and aggregates the verifier’s full-vocabulary conditionals across their prefixes.
The method improves accepted draft length beyond pre-training and outperforms prior distillation methods across mathematical, coding, and conversational tasks.
It changes only training, preserving the drafter architecture and inference procedure.

papers.abstract: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8359 test decisions this way with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%). For the rest, stopping each thought as soon as its answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy, against 82.7% for always thinking, with 72% of the thought tokens. Choosing when to think from System 1's confidence alone saves less, because the decisions System 1 is least sure of are often not the ones thinking fixes. On the public items of JevBench, an independent benchmark of typed-decision services, Qwen3.5-27B thinks on 29.4% and is not distinguishable in accuracy from the two thinking APIs listed (exploratory). Code and data generators are available at https://github.com/ding-xiaolu/ThinkJev.
authors: Xiaolu Ding, Kai Yang, Dongdong Liu
bullets: Targets typed decisions where direct one-pass probabilities can fail on multi-step tasks.
Builds fast and slow systems from one hybrid-thinking model, using the same option probabilities before or after reasoning.
A single sampled thought supports answers at every thinking-token budget, enabling adaptive stopping without repeated work.
On 8,359 test decisions, Qwen3.5-27B safely answered 24.5% directly at a 5% error target; adaptive reasoning reached 81.6% accuracy versus 82.7% for always thinking using 72% of thought tokens.
Performance depends on labeled development data for error control; confidence alone is a weaker escalation signal, and the JevBench comparison is exploratory.

papers.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer scalable capacity for Web applications, but uneven routing creates computation and communication bottlenecks. Existing placement and replication methods redistribute this workload, yet additional expert copies compete with token-related buffers for limited GPU memory. We present LRMoE, a memory-aware MoE training system that jointly recalibrates backward demand and balances the retained workload. During forward execution, it plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints while preserving all routed computations. During backpropagation, a load recalibration metric estimates each token-expert pair's contribution to the expert update and selects pairs within these quotas. A capacity-aware routing algorithm distributes retained pairs among eligible instances of their original experts. Physical compaction then forms smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs, reducing backward traffic, computation, and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B show that LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2-44.8% relative to SYMI.
authors: Jiaming Hu, Zhida Jiang, Zhaolong Xing, Yu Li, Zhen Chen, Ke Zhang
bullets: Targets routing-induced computation and communication imbalance under limited GPU memory.
Plans retention quotas and expert placement during the forward pass without dropping routed computations.
Uses backward-demand recalibration to select token–expert pairs and capacity-aware routing to distribute them across expert instances.
Compacts retained pairs into smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B, reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2–44.8% versus SYMI.

papers.abstract: Spectral compression reduces the storage and scoring costs of dense retrieval by projecting embeddings onto a smaller principal subspace. However, its corpus-derived weighting rules tie all retained directions to a shared spectral trend, without directly accounting for their individual contributions to relevance. To address this, we propose Relevance-Guided Residual Calibration (RRC), a closed-form method for refining spectral weights using relevance judgments. RRC estimates margin-based weights from the means and variances of positive--negative score contributions along each retained direction. It retains directions with positive estimated weights, decomposes their log weights into a fitted power-law trend and a residual, and adds the residual to the compressor's log weights on this support. This allows relevance judgments to adjust individual directions while preserving the compressor's overall spectral trend. RRC applies to PCA, Whitening, and SpecTemp, and incorporates the corrections into the existing transformation shared by documents and queries, without iterative model training or an additional inference stage. Experiments with three encoders on nine datasets covering conventional and reasoning-intensive retrieval show that SpecTemp + RRC achieves the highest mean effectiveness among tested compressors on the BEIR group and BRIGHT at every target dimension. On the five evaluated BRIGHT datasets, it improves over SpecTemp by an average of 2.34 nDCG@10 points at 768 dimensions. The gains also persist under scalar and product quantization, improving the trade-off between per-document storage and retrieval effectiveness. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rrc-spectral-compression-B5CE/
authors: Yongkang Li, Panagiotis Eustratiadis, Evangelos Kanoulas
bullets: Addresses the limitation that corpus-derived spectral weighting does not directly reflect each retained direction’s relevance contribution.
Uses a closed-form, margin-based calibration from positive–negative score means and variances, without iterative training or extra inference.
Applies to PCA, Whitening, and SpecTemp through the existing shared document/query transformation.
Across three encoders and nine datasets, SpecTemp + RRC had the highest mean effectiveness among tested compressors at every target dimension on BEIR and BRIGHT.
On five BRIGHT datasets at 768 dimensions, RRC improved over SpecTemp by an average of 2.34 nDCG@10 points, with gains persisting under scalar and product quantization.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex speech models listen and speak at the same time, which makes them promising for natural, open-ended conversation. But can they sustain a coherent conversation for tens of minutes? Because they generate a token every frame, even while listening, they exhaust their context windows within minutes. Yet existing benchmarks evaluate only single turns or a few conversational rounds, too short to expose the long-horizon problem. We introduce the Full-Duplex Long-Horizon Benchmark (FD-LHB), which tests five recent full-duplex models on long replayed conversations and in live conversation with an LLM partner. Every evaluated model eventually either degrades or exhausts its context. Models that keep the full history often degrade before their context runs out, while sliding-window models still fall into repetition, silence, and gibberish. For sliding-window models, we identify two contributing mechanisms. Gibberish and silence are linked to Initialization-Anchor Eviction, where the sliding window discards the first KV entry. Repetition is also reinforced by the model's own recent outputs. Guided by this diagnosis, we apply two simple fixes: Initialization-Anchor Pinning (IAP) keeps that first entry, and Duplex Repetition Penalty (DRP) discourages echoing while guarding against prolonged silence. Together, they support the diagnosis and, without retraining, substantially reduce conversational collapse in replays of up to an hour while running in real time.
bullets: Existing short-turn benchmarks miss failures that emerge over tens of minutes.
FD-LHB evaluates five full-duplex models on long replayed conversations and live conversations with an LLM partner.
All tested models eventually degrade or exhaust context; failures include repetition, silence, and gibberish.
Sliding-window failures are linked to evicting the initial KV entry and reinforcing the model’s own recent outputs.
Initialization-Anchor Pinning and Duplex Repetition Penalty reduce collapse without retraining, while preserving real-time operation.
