papers.abstract: Streaming data analytics helps businesses identify opportunities and spot risks in a timely fashion. As large language model (LLM) usage grows, people are exploring incorporating agents or LLMs in streaming data pipelines to help find patterns in datasets without supervision or interpret natural languages for content moderation. However, most streaming systems are currently optimized for data movement and perform poorly on GPU intensive workloads such as performing inference with LLMs. We introduce a system on Google Cloud Dataflow designed to tackle hybrid streaming machine learning workloads with co-designed autoscaling on heterogeneous worker pools and prefix-aware batching. This increases throughput 1.5x to 2x for streaming pipelines using LLMs while maintaining similar latency with up to 75% peak resource savings and 84% lower peak tail latency compared with existing streaming data processing systems.
authors: RuiLong Jiang, Dustin Rhodes, Danny McCormick, Yuta Labur, Reza Rokni
bullets: Targets the poor GPU-workload performance of conventional streaming systems as LLMs enter analytics and moderation pipelines.
Co-designs autoscaling across heterogeneous worker pools with prefix-aware batching for hybrid streaming machine-learning workloads.
Reports 1.5–2× higher throughput while maintaining similar latency.
Achieves up to 75% peak resource savings and 84% lower peak tail latency versus existing streaming data-processing systems.

papers.abstract: Model merging offers a promising solution for combining multiple fine-tuned checkpoints into a single model through parameter arithmetic. However, finding optimal merging coefficients requires an extensive search that becomes prohibitively expensive as models scale in both size and number, due to high memory requirements and combinatorial growth in the search space. We show that, within the same model family, models exhibit highly congruent performance distributions over merging coefficients across different model sizes. This distributional similarity enables a practical paradigm we call \textit{$α$Transfer}: searching for optimal coefficients on a small proxy model, then directly transfer them to larger target models. We verify $α$Transfer across multiple merging methods, model families, and tasks. Experimental results demonstrate a 6$\times$ speedup and 70\% memory reduction on vision transformers, and a 20$\times$ speedup and 85\% memory reduction on large language models, while maintaining comparable performance. Our findings establish $α$Transfer as an efficient and generalizable approach to scaling model merging.
bullets: Optimal coefficient search becomes costly as model size and the number of merged checkpoints grow.
Models in the same family show similar performance distributions across merging coefficients at different sizes.
The approach searches coefficients on a small proxy model, then applies them directly to larger target models.
Validated across multiple merging methods, model families, and tasks.
Reports up to 6× speedup and 70% memory reduction for vision transformers, and 20× speedup and 85% memory reduction for large language models, with comparable performance.

papers.abstract: Deep ensembles improve robustness in mobile sensing, but repeatedly executing many models over continuous sensor streams is costly. Selecting only a few members reduces this cost, yet adaptive selection often requires additional model execution to obtain reliable evidence about inactive candidates. We present MetaSE, an active ensemble framework that exploits short-term persistence in per-model reliability. MetaSE maintains a small active set across windows, uses post-execution evidence to reject unreliable members, and invokes lightweight routing only when replacement is needed. This stateful design accesses the diversity of a larger pool without repeated full-pool evaluation. Across four HAR datasets and four model architectures, MetaSE consistently improves over a fixed three-model ensemble and achieves accuracy comparable to substantially more expensive adaptive and full-ensemble inference. On a Raspberry Pi 4B, MetaSE is 2.7x faster and uses 69% less memory than full ten-model inference.
bullets: Targets the cost of repeatedly running many models on continuous sensor streams.
Maintains a small active ensemble across time windows, exploiting persistence in model reliability.
Uses post-execution evidence to discard unreliable members and lightweight routing only when replacements are needed.
Across four HAR datasets and four architectures, it improves over a fixed three-model ensemble and matches more expensive adaptive or full-ensemble inference.
On a Raspberry Pi 4B, it is 2.7× faster and uses 69% less memory than full ten-model inference.

papers.abstract: Different visual token pruning strategies retain different subsets while maintaining similar task performance. This motivates a combinatorial question: how many visual subsets can preserve model behavior, and how does their abundance depend on the query? We introduce visual sufficiency landscapes to characterize this abundance. At a fixed layer and budget, visual sufficiency probability is the fraction of uniformly sampled subsets that jointly preserve the dense model's answer, reference-answer likelihood, and output distribution. Independent sampling replicates separate input variation from estimation noise. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2-8B, and LLaVA-v1.5-7B, differences between inputs on GQA and TextVQA exceed replication error, and different questions about the same GQA image produce distinct landscapes. Sufficiency probability also improves failure prediction for full pruning methods. On LLaVA, adding this probability increases AUC by 0.1151 for FastV, 0.0683 for VisionZip, and 0.1401 for SparseVLM, while reducing log loss and Brier score. Several architecture-adapted configurations on the other two models reproduce these gains. Under controlled selection rules, predictors trained on the original images reduce log loss on new images by 9.0%, 13.0%, and 14.1%, respectively. These results establish successful-subset abundance as a measurable dimension of local prunability and connect it to the identification of high-risk pruning conditions.
bullets: The study asks how the abundance of behavior-preserving visual subsets varies with the query.
It defines sufficiency probability as the fraction of sampled subsets preserving the dense model’s answer, reference-answer likelihood, and output distribution.
Across three vision-language models, landscapes differ by input and by question for the same image beyond sampling error.
Sufficiency probability improves failure prediction for FastV, VisionZip, and SparseVLM, with reported AUC gains and lower log loss and Brier scores.
The work frames successful-subset abundance as a measurable dimension of local prunability and a signal for high-risk pruning conditions.

papers.abstract: Running prompt tokens through fewer routed experts during prefill makes mixture-of-experts (MoE) serving cheaper, but what it damages has not been measured. We locate the damage with token-, layer- and attention-path interventions in four MoE families on short-answer question answering. At half the experts the F1 loss is mostly answer form: the model still finds the answer but no longer answers briefly. The loss is made at a few tokens: the two chat-template tokens before the answer in Qwen3-30B-A3B, and the first 8-32 tokens, where the instruction sits, in DeepSeek-V2-Lite. Keeping them at full experts removes most of the F1 loss and about half and a fifth of the increase in answer NLL. These tokens are not the familiar suspects: reduction leaves the first-token sink within 4%, and restoring super experts or massive activations recovers at most a quarter of the loss. On real prompts the localisation becomes a placement rule: with about 4% of tokens at full experts, putting them on the task interface keeps F1 within one point of the unmodified model, while the same budget scattered in the documents is about 3 points worse in both prespecified primary tests of this comparison. Time to first token falls about 14% on 11K-token prompts.
bullets: At half the experts, models usually identify the answer but lose F1 because responses become less concise.
Damage concentrates on two chat-template tokens in Qwen3-30B-A3B and the first 8–32 instruction tokens in DeepSeek-V2-Lite.
Keeping these tokens at full experts removes most F1 loss and reduces roughly half to one-fifth of the answer-NLL increase.
Allocating full experts to about 4% of task-interface tokens keeps F1 within one point of the unmodified model; scattering the budget in documents is about three points worse.
This placement rule reduces time to first token by about 14% on 11K-token prompts.

Qwen1.5’s loss is measured by containment (whether the gold answer appears), since its F1 rises.
Table 8: Joint batch, cycle 1 (all 760 prompts): median TTFT ratio, median end-to-end ratio and throughput ratio at concurrency four, each against the unmodified model in the same cycle.

Table 6: Negative-control batch (Qwen3-30B-A3B, vLLM 0.31, one H100, 2,098 marked prompts, 8 → 4, quality only). F1 differences on seven QA datasets, equally weighted; code is edit similarity. Table 11: Interface batch (vLLM 0.31, one H100, quality only, F1 points). Unadjusted 95% bootstrap intervals; p is Holm-adjusted within each model over the listed secondary comparisons. Both primaries are undecided under their prespecified rules (Appendix I). Header only: the eight-token assistant header full and the rest of Interface-Full’s budget at random in the documents. papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the impact of expert reduction in MoE models during prefill, identifying specific critical tokens (instruction, chat template) that cause performance loss and proposing a placement rule for efficient serving.
papers.title: Where Prefill Expert Reduction Hurts MoE Models: A Few Prompt Tokens Carry Most of the Short-Answer F1 Loss
papers.tldr: Reducing routed experts during MoE prefill mainly hurts short-answer F1 through a small set of task-interface tokens, and protecting those tokens preserves quality while retaining latency gains.

papers.abstract: Self-attention plays a key role in long-sequence modeling, but its quadratic time complexity fundamentally limits the scaling of Large Language Models. Recently, Multi-State Linear Attention (MSLA) mechanisms have been proposed to make sequence modeling more efficient by splitting the context into segments and compressing each in its own memory state. MSLA aggregates the information extracted from each memory state using only the mean alignment between a query and each segment's keys, ignoring how the alignment is distributed within the segment. In order to model the relevance of a segment to a query more comprehensively and incorporate the variance of the alignment in the aggregation, we propose MERLIN (MomEnt Routing for multi-state LINear attention), a method that tracks the first and second moments of each segment's keys. Using the moments of keys, a query can recover both the mean and the variance of its alignment with each segment to perform a more content-aware aggregation of per-state readouts. Experiments on multi-state variants of Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and Mamba-2-780M show that MERLIN consistently outperforms existing aggregation methods on various long-context tasks. In particular, MERLIN outperforms baselines on RULER needle-in-a-haystack and long-context QA (+8.3% for Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and +7.0% for Mamba-2-780M) and diverse subtasks in LongBench (+13.5% and +12.0%). It even outperforms baselines that consume 4x more memory. MERLIN provides a simple and general routing mechanism for improving long-context capabilities of MSLA models.
authors: Hee Seung Hwang, Sanghyuk Chun, Xindi Wu, Olga Russakovsky, Zhiwei Deng
bullets: MSLA reduces the cost of long-sequence modeling by compressing context segments into separate memory states, but standard routing uses only mean query–key alignment.
MERLIN tracks each segment’s first and second key moments to estimate both mean and variance of query alignment.
This enables more comprehensive, content-aware aggregation of per-state readouts.
On RULER, long-context QA, and LongBench, MERLIN consistently outperforms existing routing methods, including baselines using 4× more memory.
Reported gains include up to 8.3% on RULER/QA and 13.5% on LongBench for the evaluated models.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes moment-based routing for multi-state linear attention, improving efficient attention and long-context modeling.
papers.title: Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing
papers.tldr: MERLIN improves long-context multi-state linear attention by using first- and second-order key statistics for more content-aware routing across memory states.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models offer a promising path to efficient agents through parallel token generation. However, efficient interaction requires adapting both where computation is spent and how much text is generated. We introduce a metacognitive controller that guides diffusion generation according to the needs of the current response and the agent's interaction with the environment. It learns when to finalize tokens and how far generation should extend, reducing overall computation within responses. Our controller, a lightweight plug-in for the diffusion backbone, is trained on agent trajectories to balance correctness and generation cost. This approach connects the agent's generation process to the interaction the agent serves. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that our approach reduces inference FLOPs by 20.6% on average compared with the most efficient baseline, while maintaining competitive task accuracy. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of our approach.
authors: Mingyu Zhao, Shuhang Lin, Ligong Han, Xiaojing Yu, Zhenting Wang, Yifei Pang, Yang Zhou, Dimitris N. Metaxas
bullets: Targets the challenge of reducing computation while preserving agent response quality.
Learns when to finalize tokens and how far generation should continue.
Trained on agent trajectories to balance correctness with generation cost.
Reduces inference FLOPs by 20.6% on average across five benchmarks versus the most efficient baseline, while maintaining competitive task accuracy.
Ablation studies support the controller’s effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive token finalization and generation-length control reduce inference FLOPs for diffusion language agents, fitting efficient token-level computation.
papers.title: Metacognitive Decoding: Efficient Inference for Diffusion Language Agents
papers.tldr: A lightweight metacognitive controller makes diffusion language agents more efficient by adapting token finalization and response length to interaction needs.

papers.abstract: As executable environments for language agents scale, generating and verifying their rollouts becomes increasingly expensive. Under finite rollout budgets, this raises an important question: can data management at the environment level make agentic reinforcement learning (RL) more efficient by organizing, evaluating, and scheduling task instances together with the environments that determine their tools, states, transitions, and verification? To address this question, we introduce EnvSched (Environment-aware Scheduling), an online scheduler that learns from rollout history. EnvSched assigns scheduling value through two complementary modeling choices: exploitation prioritizes tasks likely to provide informative reward differences, while coverage spreads each batch across underobserved environments and interaction patterns. EnvSched organizes environment--task pairs as nodes in a dual-relation graph, with within-environment edges capturing task semantics and shared tool, state, and verifier structure, and cross-environment edges capturing abstract execution and reward topology. By propagating historical rollout statistics along both edge types, it predicts within-task reward variance. These predictions guide a scheduler that allocates each batch to tasks with high predicted reward variance and underobserved environments and tasks. Environment quotas and a similarity penalty further limit concentration and redundancy, yielding informative and diverse batches without additional pilot rollouts. In RL on Qwen3-8B, EnvSched achieves an average score of 48.81 across BFCL-v3, tau-Bench, and ACEBench-Agent after 40 training steps, exceeding the highest score attained by random task selection after 120 steps. It also improves downstream performance across model sizes at the same training budget.
authors: Sihan Yang, Weichen Bai, Ruichuan An, Yiming Cheng, Zhiyuan Feng, Tianyi Jiang, Renye Yan, Ning Ding, Yifan Zhang, Renrui Zhang, Yehui Tang, Wentao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high cost of generating and verifying agent rollouts under finite budgets.
Uses exploitation of tasks with predicted high reward variance and coverage of underobserved environments and interaction patterns.
Models environment–task pairs as a dual-relation graph linking semantic, tool/state/verifier, execution, and reward structure.
Applies environment quotas and similarity penalties to reduce concentration and redundant batches without pilot rollouts.

On Qwen3-8B, reaches an average score of 48.81 across BFCL-v3, tau-Bench, and ACEBench-Agent after 40 steps, outperforming random selection’s best score after 120 steps; gains extend across model sizes.
papers.selection_reason: Environment-level scheduling to reduce rollout costs in agentic RL directly targets computation/data efficiency and is transferable to broader efficient-training pipelines.
papers.title: EnvSched: Environment-Aware Scheduling for Rollout-Efficient Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: EnvSched improves rollout efficiency in agent RL by scheduling diverse, informative environment–task pairs using rollout-history-based reward-variance predictions.

papers.abstract: Developing on-device image models requires considering practical user needs, task types and device resource constraints. However, existing benchmarks provide limited guidance on identifying capability gaps between on-device models and server-side models. We introduce MoI-Bench, a benchmark grounded in mobile user needs, comprising 64 subtasks and 1150 samples. It defines 16 operations, such as removal and replacement, and eight visual target categories covering content such as portraits and text. These form two orthogonal axes whose applicable combinations define specific tasks, such as removing facial makeup. To better guide model improvement, we further propose MoI-Eval, which introduces task-specific criteria covering instruction following, visual quality and detail preservation. We further construct sample-level evaluation questions and aggregate their scores into overall quality and capability profiles along the operation, target and criteria axes. We evaluate representative on-device and server-side models and measure mobile deployment costs. Results show that this decoupled Operation x Target design provides finer-grained guidance for improving compact models. For example, it highlights the need to prioritize specific capability gaps (e.g., text-replacement) over broad application-level goals (e.g., improving text editing). Unlike conventional benchmarks that rank models using a single score, we introduce a two-dimensional Quality-Deployability capability map to assess models for practical mobile use. The map shows that current on-device models can achieve efficient generation or editing but expanding their task coverage deserves greater attention than further improving deployment efficiency. Further progress requires improving editing quality, particularly identity preservation and text rendering, while broadening task coverage.
authors: Kailai Feng, Haoxiang Rao, Yuxiang Wei, Bo Chen, Junsong Li, Yang Pan, Chengkun Cai, Jagmohan Chauhan
bullets: Covers 64 subtasks and 1,150 samples across 16 operations and eight visual target categories.
MoI-Eval assesses instruction following, visual quality, and detail preservation using task-specific criteria.
Its Operation × Target design exposes specific capability gaps, such as text replacement, rather than broad application-level weaknesses.
A Quality–Deployability map evaluates practical mobile suitability beyond single-score model rankings.
Findings emphasize expanding task coverage and improving editing quality, especially identity preservation and text rendering.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and evaluation protocol for on-device image generation and editing that explicitly measures deployment efficiency, relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: MoI-Bench: A Benchmark for Image Generation and Editing on Mobile Devices
papers.tldr: MoI-Bench evaluates mobile image generation and editing models with fine-grained task and deployability analysis grounded in practical user needs.

papers.abstract: Self-attention mechanisms have established the Transformer as the dominant backbone across natural language processing, source code intelligence, and automated theorem proving. However, all-to-all pairwise token comparison enforces a quadratic $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ compute and memory barrier alongside severe softmax attention dilution as sequence length $N$ scales beyond the training horizon. Inspired by recent advances in algebraic graph learning (\textbf{WPNet}), this work introduces \textbf{GTFormer}, a syntax-free hierarchical Graph Neural Network (GNN) that replaces flat self-attention for general long-context sequence modeling. GTFormer organizes raw token streams into a bounded-degree hierarchy combining a balanced binary reduction tree ($\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ depth), horizontal boundary-bridging shift edges, random expander shortcuts, multi-channel convex highway gating, and a top-down broadcast pass. Across eight long-context code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks trained exclusively on sequences of length $N \le 512$, GTFormer extrapolates zero-shot to $N = 4{,}194{,}304$ ($8192\times$) on a single commodity GPU in linear $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, maintaining near-perfect accuracy where standard and RoPE Transformers suffer from out-of-distribution attention collapse and out-of-memory exhaustion.
bullets: Targets quadratic compute and memory costs, plus attention dilution, in very long sequences.
Uses a bounded-degree hierarchy with binary reduction, boundary-bridging edges, expander shortcuts, convex highway gates, and top-down broadcasting.
Trained only on sequences of length ≤512 and evaluated zero-shot at lengths up to 4,194,304 tokens.
Across eight code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks, it reportedly maintains near-perfect accuracy on a commodity GPU.
The abstract reports scope limited to the benchmarked long-context tasks and extrapolation setting.
papers.selection_reason: Linear-time graph-network sequence model achieves extreme long-context extrapolation.
papers.title: GTFormer: A Syntax-Free Graph Network Alternative to Transformers for 8192$\times$ Length Extrapolation in Linear Time
papers.tldr: GTFormer replaces quadratic self-attention with a syntax-free hierarchical graph network that extrapolates from length 512 to 4,194,304 tokens in linear memory.

papers.abstract: Integrated sensing and communication allows wireless networks to recognize human activity from the channel estimates that the receiver computes anyway. The inference, however, runs on the general-purpose processors of the base station, access point or handset, which are the first components a device switches off to save energy. Always-on sensing therefore requires a classifier that is small enough to remain powered while the rest of the system sleeps. We investigate whether Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) can provide such a classifier. To this end, we generate SNN accelerators for micro-Doppler activity recognition on the public DISC dataset (IEEE 802.11ay at 60 GHz) with the open-source Spiker+ framework, and implement them together with a spike encoder on a ZCU208 RFSoC, so that the complete chain from micro-Doppler frame to activity label runs in programmable logic. A fully connected SNN with 132 neurons achieves 94.7 % accuracy (90.7 % macro-F1) on unseen subjects and performs an inference in 206 microseconds. Compared to conventional networks of the same topology on the same device, it requires an eighth of the logic and 3.4X less dynamic energy per decision than a network fed the same binary spikes, at comparable accuracy, and 7.6X less than a network fed the 16-bit spectrogram, at 1.2 points lower accuracy. Quantization-aware training reduces its weights to 3 bits within half a percentage point of the 6-bit network at the same encoder threshold
authors: Anthony S\'anchez, Rafael Ruiz, Jos\'e A. Belloch, Jes\'us O. Lacruz, Joerg Widmer
bullets: Targets always-on sensing when conventional base-station, access-point, or handset processors are powered down.
Implements a complete micro-Doppler-to-label pipeline using an SNN, spike encoder, and ZCU208 RFSoC programmable logic.
A 132-neuron fully connected SNN reaches 94.7% accuracy and 90.7% macro-F1 on unseen subjects, with 206 μs inference latency.
Uses one-eighth the logic and 3.4× less dynamic energy than a comparable network processing the same binary spikes; energy is 7.6× lower than with 16-bit spectrogram input.
Quantization-aware training reduces weights to 3 bits with less than a 0.5-point accuracy drop versus the 6-bit network.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a spiking neural network accelerator for low-energy always-on inference, directly relevant to Efficient AI.
papers.title: Keeping Inference in the Radio: Design and Measurement of a Spiking Accelerator for mmWave ISAC Activity Recognition
papers.tldr: A compact spiking accelerator enables always-on mmWave activity recognition in programmable logic with high accuracy, low latency, and substantially reduced hardware energy use.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference on memory-constrained edge platforms is often dominated by expert-weight movement rather than computation. Although each token activates only a small subset of experts, routing is input-dependent, so all experts must remain accessible and memory movement dominates latency. Existing approaches such as uniform pruning and expert dropping overlook two properties of MoE execution: expert combinations are highly skewed in frequency, and experts contribute asymmetrically within each combination. We present CRISP, a combination-aware framework that co-designs pruning and runtime scheduling for efficient MoE serving on memory-constrained edge platforms. CRISP reorders neurons by importance so one stored expert can support multiple execution widths, assigns differentiated execution to hot, warm, and cold combinations based on frequency and expert role, and exploits heterogeneous widths to overlap expert loading with computation. Across Mixtral-8x7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B, CRISP improves throughput by up to $2.1\times$ at the same memory budget while limiting accuracy loss to 3.6\% relative to full-width inference. Our results highlight that efficient edge MoE serving requires jointly optimizing which expert capacity is preserved and how expert execution is scheduled.
authors: Congwei Zhang, Youming Tao, Yifei Zou, Yu Yang, Ruirui Zhang, Xiaoyu Zhang, Falko Dressler, Xiuzhen Cheng, Dongxiao Yu
bullets: Targets memory-constrained edge servers where expert-weight movement dominates MoE inference latency.
Uses combination-aware pruning that accounts for skewed expert-combination frequency and asymmetric expert importance.
Reorders neurons to support multiple stored expert widths and assigns differentiated execution to hot, warm, and cold combinations.
Overlaps expert loading with computation through heterogeneous execution widths.
Evaluated on Mixtral-8x7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B, achieving up to 2.1× higher throughput at the same memory budget with 3.6% relative accuracy loss versus full-width inference.
papers.selection_reason: Co-designs expert pruning and scheduling for efficient MoE inference on edge servers.
papers.title: CRISP: Co-designing Pruning and Scheduling for Efficient MoE Inference on Edge Servers
papers.tldr: CRISP jointly co-designs MoE pruning and runtime scheduling to reduce expert-weight movement and improve edge inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory during interactive decoding at small batch sizes. Because most intermediate channels in a routed expert contribute little to any single token, channel selectors predict which channels matter and read only their weights, typically keeping channels above a threshold calibrated on offline data. We show that channel selection needs no calibration data. First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads, because the number of channels passing it varies across inputs; Prox with thresholds calibrated for an 18% read budget actually reads only 12.9% on average across our benchmarks. Second, top-k keeps each token's k highest-scoring channels and needs no calibration data. At the calibrated budget, a selector's top-k version matches or beats its threshold version on the same score in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets, including all 23 on generation tasks. The top-k versions also avoid the repetition-loop collapse that calibrated thresholds cause on Gemma 4. Calibrating a threshold thus provides neither of the two things selectors use it for: a known read budget and a consistent accuracy gain at that budget. We furthermore introduce a reader built entirely from the model's weights, which screens channels with a ternary sketch and recovers the skipped ones with a low-rank map. Across three post-trained MoE models, our reader retains 98.1% of full-model accuracy at 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with Triton kernels running MoE blocks 1.60 to 1.90x faster than optimized vLLM at batch one and up to 2.69x at larger batches on the same three models.
bullets: Threshold calibration does not guarantee a fixed read budget: an intended 18% budget averaged only 12.9% reads in benchmarks.
Replacing thresholds with per-token top-k selection requires no calibration data and matched or outperformed threshold selection in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets.
Top-k selection avoided the repetition-loop collapse observed with calibrated thresholds on Gemma 4.
A weight-only reader uses a ternary sketch to screen channels and a low-rank map to recover skipped ones.
Across three post-trained MoE models, the reader retained 98.1% of full-model accuracy using 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with reported speedups up to 2.69×.
papers.selection_reason: Channel selection reduces routed-expert memory reads during MoE decoding, improving memory efficiency of inference.
papers.title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data
papers.tldr: Calibration-free top-k channel selection provides predictable MoE read budgets and preserves accuracy, while a weight-only reader achieves substantial decoding speedups with sparse expert reads.

papers.abstract: We present EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model which natively represents text, images, audio, video, and combinations thereof in a unified space. Our approach introduces improvements such as simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage curriculum with modality and objective progression which ensure strong quality across unimodal, cross-modal, and mixed-modal evaluations. Notably, in comprehensive embedding benchmarks across all modalities, EmbeddingGemma 2 establishes a new Pareto frontier, outperforming both specialist models and models two to twelve times larger. Furthermore, our design offers flexibility for resource-constrained environments, supporting selective modality encoder loading, adjustable vision token budgets, truncatable embedding dimensions, and quantized weights. We present ablations analyzing key decisions and release EmbeddingGemma 2 to promote further research.
authors: Henrique Schechter Vera, Sahil Dua, Jovan Andonov, Sara Smoot, Sebastian Russo, Ivan Llanos, Max Matveev, Jae Hyeon Yoo, Kat Black, Shih-Cheng Huang, Josiah Aklilu, Maarten Grootendorst, Omar Sanseviero, Chandramouli Amarnath, Ian Ballantyne, Zhe Li, Daniel Salz, Ibrahim Alabdulmohsin, Ilya Philippov, Kristen Quan, Glenn Cameron, Edouard Yvinec, Luciano Martins, Doug Reid, Sindhu Raghuram Panyam, Weiyi Wang, Hengxuan Ying, Madhuri Shanbhogue, Tanmaya Dabral, Shanfeng Zhang, Juyeong Ji, Renjie Wu, Joe Zou, Xu Chen, Yunan Zhang, Yu-Hui Chen, Matthew Soulanille, Vinod Mamillapalli, Yi-Chun Kuo, Wai Hon Law, Matt Kreileder, Alice Zheng, Suril Shah, Mogan Shieh, Pooja Consul, Alberto Montes, Andreas Hess, Andres Sevilla, Babak Samari, Brendan McCloskey, Brian Potetz, Daniel Cer, Georgios Kathareios, Gustavo Hern\'andez \'Abrego, Hesen Zhang, Ji Ma, Jiaxing Wu, Keegan Mosley, Paul Suganthan, Rui Meng, Shen Gao, Shengcao Cao, Yi-Ting Chen, Yichang Chen, Zhongli Ding, Kendra Byrne, Cormac Brick, Olivier Lacombe, Qin Yin, Tris Warkentin, Armand Joulin, Tom Duerig, Mojtaba Seyedhosseini
bullets: Represents individual modalities and multimodal combinations in a shared embedding space.
Uses simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage curriculum that progressively varies modalities and objectives.
Reports a new Pareto frontier on comprehensive multimodal embedding benchmarks, outperforming specialist models and models 2–12× larger.
Supports resource-constrained deployment through selective encoder loading, adjustable vision token budgets, truncatable embeddings, and quantized weights.
Includes ablations and is released to enable further research.
papers.selection_reason: Unified multimodal embedding model spanning text, image, audio, and video directly fits multimodal foundation models, with efficiency-oriented design choices relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations
papers.tldr: EmbeddingGemma 2 is an open, efficient multimodal embedding model that unifies text, image, audio, and video representations while achieving strong quality across diverse evaluations.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require substantial memory, motivating low-bit weight quantization for efficient deployment. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods often improve accuracy by increasing the effective coding dimension, which can complicate independent lookup and local codeword updates. We propose CoS-VQ (Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization), which preserves low-dimensional codewords while jointly optimizing hard indices and their shared scale across positions. The key challenge is scale-induced coupling: the optimal scale depends on the entire codeword combination and, in turn, changes candidate rankings across positions, so pointwise updates can stall even after scale re-optimization. CoS-VQ collects candidates at multiple probe scales and constructs a tangent separable upper bound for the residual-aware quadratic objective. By reducing candidate comparisons to lower envelopes of lines over positive scales, it identifies finitely many representative intervals for joint index--scale updates without exhaustively enumerating codeword combinations. On Qwen3.8-27B, CoS-VQ outperforms QTIP and LLVQ on the evaluated language modeling, coding, and reasoning benchmarks. Ablations from the same initialization further show larger gains from joint updates than from scale-only refinement, highlighting joint selection as an alternative to increasing codeword dimensionality. The code is available at https://github.com/xzktx003/Cos_VQ.
authors: Zukang Xu, Zhixiong Zhao, Xing Hu, Zhe Jiang, Xin Si, Dawei Yang
bullets: Targets memory-efficient LLM deployment through low-bit weight quantization.
Uses multi-scale candidate probing and a tangent separable upper bound to enable joint index–scale updates efficiently.
Reduces candidate selection to lower envelopes of lines, avoiding exhaustive codeword-combination enumeration.
Outperforms QTIP and LLVQ on evaluated language modeling, coding, and reasoning benchmarks for Qwen3.8-27B.
Ablations indicate joint updates provide greater gains than scale-only refinement.
papers.selection_reason: Low-bit vector quantization for LLM weight memory reduction, directly relevant to memory-efficient model deployment.
papers.title: CoS-VQ: Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: CoS-VQ improves low-bit LLM quantization by jointly optimizing codeword indices and shared scales without increasing codeword dimensionality.

papers.abstract: In this work, we propose Subspace Clifford Networks, a reformulation that replaces global cyclic rolling with grouped subspace interactions. Instead of sampling sparse cyclic diagonals across the entire $D$-dimensional channel space, we project the features into an aligned space $\R^{\tilde{D}} = \bigoplus_{g=1}^{G} V_g$ partitioned into $G$ low-dimensional groups $V_g \cong \R^k$ with $k \in \{2, 3, 4\}$. Within each $k$-dimensional group, we compute all $\binom{k}{2}$ wedge coordinates and concatenate them with $\operatorname{SiLU}$-activated coordinate-wise products, while sandwiching the grouped interaction between learnable $1\times 1$ linear projections to enable cross-group channel mixing. This design reduces intermediate feature expansion from $2|\mathcal{S}|D$ (typically $10D$ for 5 shifts) down to $1.5\tilde{D}$ ($k=2$), $2.0\tilde{D}$ ($k=3$), or $2.5\tilde{D}$ ($k=4$). Furthermore, exploiting the small, fixed group size $k \in \{2, 3, 4\}$, we implement a fused CUDA kernel that evaluates the forward interaction and a recomputation-based analytical backward pass using thread-local variables without allocating global-memory buffers for elementwise intermediates. Finally, we extend the backbone from an isotropic columnar layout to a multi-resolution Hierarchical Clifford Network with configurable per-stage subspace dimensions. Experiments on CIFAR-100 show that the proposed models substantially reduce parameter count and training time across both regimes, while the hierarchical variants also improve classification accuracy over the evaluated shift-based hierarchical baselines.
bullets: Groups channels into low-dimensional subspaces of size 2–4 and computes wedge coordinates plus SiLU-activated products.
Uses learnable 1×1 projections before and after grouped interactions to enable cross-group channel mixing.
Reduces intermediate feature expansion compared with shift-based designs, depending on group size.
Introduces a fused CUDA kernel with recomputation-based analytical backpropagation to avoid global-memory intermediate buffers.
On CIFAR-100, models reduce parameter count and training time; hierarchical variants improve accuracy over evaluated shift-based hierarchical baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient grouped subspace interactions and a fused CUDA kernel reduce parameters and training time, relevant to efficient AI even though not token/attention/KV specific.
papers.title: Subspace Clifford Networks
papers.tldr: Subspace Clifford Networks replace global cyclic shifts with efficient grouped subspace interactions, reducing expansion and training cost while retaining or improving classification performance.

papers.abstract: Current 3D scene understanding pipelines typically concatenate vast numbers of 3D object tokens with text tokens and feed the resulting sequence to a Large Language Model (LLM). However, existing 3D-LLMs for scene understanding encounter two major limitations: (i) excessive inclusion of task-irrelevant object data, introducing noise that reduces reasoning accuracy and increases hallucinations; and (ii) reliance solely on point cloud data, which inherently lacks the rich semantic information available in complementary 2D modalities, such as color, material properties, texture, and high-level contextual relationships. To address these challenges, we introduce 3D-SceneQ, a 3D LLM that unifies adaptive token pruning with multimodal semantic enrichment, markedly advancing scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding. Specifically, we propose a Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) module that adaptively selects task-relevant objects based on the intended meaning of user instructions, leveraging a learnable latent query to retain critical information while effectively suppressing irrelevant noise. In addition, we introduce a Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) module, which integrates 2D feature embeddings from pre-trained models into 3D representation to enrich object-level semantic information. Evaluations show that 3D-SceneQ outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks (e.g., +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D), demonstrating its remarkable capabilities in various 3D language reasoning tasks.
authors: Yongqi Shan, Lu Zhang, Jiazuo Yu, Yunzhi Zhuge, Huchuan Lu
bullets: Addresses noise from feeding large numbers of task-irrelevant 3D object tokens to LLMs.
Uses Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) to retain objects relevant to the user instruction.
Uses Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) to integrate pretrained 2D features into 3D representations.
Outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks, including +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D.
Targets 3D scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding tasks.
papers.selection_reason: 3D LLM with query-guided adaptive token pruning and multimodal feature enhancement for 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: 3D-SceneQ: Empowering 3D LLM With Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning and Multi-Modal Feature Enhancement
papers.tldr: 3D-SceneQ improves 3D-language reasoning by pruning irrelevant objects according to the query and enriching 3D features with 2D multimodal information.

papers.abstract: Pruned language models are judged almost entirely by accuracy and perplexity, which assumes that preserved output behaviour implies preserved internal computation. We test this assumption with a factorial pruning study on GPT-2, crossing two importance criteria (magnitude, random), two component types (attention heads, MLP neurons) and three sparsity levels (3%, 50%, 70%). Using the fully characterised indirect object identification (IOI) circuit as ground truth, we measure circuit integrity with activation patching, path patching and direct logit attribution. We find two qualitatively distinct failure modes. Magnitude head pruning >= zeroes the circuit: output-facing heads are removed, and the model falls to near-chance. Magnitude neuron pruning at 30% inverts it: all 26 circuit heads remain intact, but Name Mover contributions flip sign, and the model systematically prefers the wrong name (17.7% accuracy). Perplexity ranks it as less damaged than random head pruning (74.6 vs 140.1). A replication of the Greater-Than circuit shows that the critical component type depends on the circuit's architecture. These results show that output metrics and structural checks can both miss mechanistic damage, motivating circuit-level causal analysis as a complementary evaluation of compressed language models.
bullets: The study tests magnitude and random pruning of GPT-2 attention heads and MLP neurons across multiple sparsity levels.
Circuit integrity is evaluated using activation patching, path patching, and direct logit attribution, with IOI as the primary ground truth.
Magnitude head pruning can remove output-facing circuit heads and reduce performance to near chance.
Magnitude neuron pruning can leave all circuit heads intact while reversing Name Mover contributions, yielding systematically wrong predictions.
A Greater-Than circuit replication shows that pruning sensitivity depends on circuit architecture; circuit-level causal analysis is therefore needed alongside perplexity and structural checks.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates mechanistic failure modes of weight pruning in Transformers using mechanistic interpretability. This provides a deeper understanding of how pruning affects internal computation, relevant to LLMs and model efficiency.
papers.title: Mechanistic Failure Modes of Weight Pruning in Transformer Language Models
papers.tldr: Weight pruning can preserve or obscure output-level performance while severely damaging the internal circuits that produce model behavior.

papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has been widely adopted for aligning language models with human preferences. Recent empirical work has revealed that DPO induces remarkably sparse parameter updates, yet no theoretical explanation for this phenomenon has been offered. We analyze DPO's optimization dynamics under a neural tangent kernel linearization and show that the logistic structure of the DPO loss gives rise to an implicit maximum-margin bias. Building on this observation, we introduce the concept of dual sparsity: the DPO update direction is a sparse linear combination (data-level sparsity, driven by support vectors) of sparse gradient feature vectors (parameter-level sparsity, arising from gradient cancellation between preferred and dispreferred responses). We formalize this structure in our main theorem, bound the number of support pairs by a margin-dependent spectral quantity, and present a framework relating dual sparsity to weight disentanglement---a condition favorable for model merging. Experiments on GPT-2 Small and Medium and on 7--9B instruction-tuned models (Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B) with the Anthropic HH-RLHF and UltraFeedback datasets confirm both sources of sparsity, and experiments on GPT-2 show that DPO reduces cross-task interference by up to $35{\times}$ compared to supervised fine-tuning.
bullets: DPO’s logistic loss creates an implicit maximum-margin optimization bias.
Its update is sparse at two levels: support-vector-like data sparsity and gradient-cancellation-driven parameter sparsity.
A theorem bounds the number of support pairs using a margin-dependent spectral quantity.
The framework connects dual sparsity with weight disentanglement, a property useful for model merging.
Experiments across GPT-2 and several 7–9B instruction-tuned models confirm both sparsity mechanisms; on GPT-2, DPO reduces cross-task interference by up to 35× versus supervised fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the sparsity of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) updates, providing a theoretical explanation for weight disentanglement. This connects alignment (LLMs) with efficiency (sparsity) and model merging.
papers.title: On the Sparsity of Direct Preference Optimization: Weight Disentanglement in the NTK Regime
papers.tldr: DPO’s sparse parameter updates are theoretically explained by dual sparsity in the NTK regime, which also promotes weight disentanglement and reduces cross-task interference.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods adapt large models by introducing a small number of trainable parameters. However, we find that these parameters still contain redundancy and can be further compressed while maintaining strong task performance. To this end, we propose a novel hierarchical low-rank reparameterization method. Its core idea is to reorganize the trainable parameters of PEFT methods into an approximately square matrix and then express it via a low-rank decomposition, which can be applied recursively. This forms a multi-level structure with factors compressed level by level, drastically reducing the number of trainable parameters. In our experiments, we combine this reparameterization with LoRA, DoRA, MoSA, and RaSA. We evaluate commonsense reasoning on LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, with additional GSM8K math reasoning experiments on LLaMA-3.1-8B. Under comparable trainable-parameter budgets, our method combined with LoRA or DoRA achieves better performance. Furthermore,when the parameter count of the original methods is compressed by approximately an order of magnitude, our method can still maintain competitive task performance and even surpass the corresponding baselines in average accuracy across the eight commonsense reasoning benchmarks.
authors: Rong Huang, Yi Xiong, Yuan-Yuan Cheng, Xiao-Ming Fu
bullets: Targets redundancy in the trainable parameters of existing PEFT methods.
Reorganizes parameters into an approximately square matrix and applies recursive low-rank decomposition to create a multi-level compressed structure.
Combines with LoRA, DoRA, MoSA, and RaSA, evaluated on commonsense and GSM8K reasoning tasks.

With comparable parameter budgets, LoRA- and DoRA-based variants perform better; roughly tenfold compression can retain competitive performance and sometimes exceed baselines on average commonsense accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical low-rank reparameterization compresses PEFT parameters, reducing training memory and compute within the scope of efficient AI.
papers.title: Hierarchical Low-Rank Reparameterization for Parameter-Efficient
papers.tldr: Hierarchical low-rank reparameterization recursively compresses PEFT parameters, reducing trainable-parameter requirements while preserving or improving task performance.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised vision transformers are increasingly used as reusable encoders for Earth observation, but their inference cost on the hardware available in the field is rarely characterized. We deploy a pretrained SAR-optical masked-autoencoder encoder on three commodity x86 nodes, from a low-power CPU without AVX2 to an AVX2+VNNI reference, at FP32, FP16 and INT8 on the CPU and, where present, the integrated GPU, and report latency, energy (RAPL and wall plug) and linear-probe accuracy. Quantization is accuracy-neutral: INT8 changes micro-mAP by only +0.0006, within the seed spread, so precision becomes a pure cost decision. INT8 lowers CPU latency on every node, by 1.45x even on the CPU without AVX2, and CPU energy wherever it is measured, and the VNNI reference (1.53x) suggests a further gain beyond AVX2. The Pareto-optimal device shifts from the integrated GPU, which is 4.38x faster than the CPU on the weakest node, to the CPU as the CPU class improves.
bullets: Evaluates a pretrained self-supervised SAR-optical masked-autoencoder encoder across three commodity x86 nodes.
Compares FP32, FP16, and INT8 inference on CPUs and, where available, integrated GPUs using latency, energy, and linear-probe accuracy.
INT8 is accuracy-neutral, changing micro-mAP by only +0.0006 within seed variation.
INT8 reduces CPU latency on every node, including 1.45× on a CPU without AVX2; VNNI hardware suggests further gains.
The Pareto-optimal device shifts from the integrated GPU on weaker hardware to the CPU on more capable systems.
papers.selection_reason: Quantization and edge-inference efficiency study for a self-supervised encoder, directly fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Quantized Edge Inference of a Self-Supervised SAR-Optical Encoder on Commodity x86 Hardware
papers.tldr: INT8 quantization preserves SAR-optical encoder accuracy while reducing CPU inference latency and energy on commodity x86 hardware, making the best device choice hardware-dependent.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) by retrieving external evidence and conditioning generation on the retrieved context. Although dense retrieval is effective for local semantic matching, independently ranked retrieval can return redundant passages, miss cross-chunk dependencies, and provide incomplete evidence for multi-hop reasoning. We propose SpectRAG, a spectral graph-augmented retrieval framework that combines hybrid candidate seeding, weighted chunk graph construction, graph-based expansion, spectral relevance propagation, and token-budgeted context selection. Document chunks are represented by dense semantic embeddings and graph-spectral coordinates derived from a weighted chunk graph whose edges encode semantic similarity, document adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citation links, and similarity between LLM-generated utility questions. At query time, SpectRAG builds a high-recall seed set using exact inner-product search and hybrid relevance signals, expands it over the chunk graph, re-scores candidates using graph proximity and spectral information, and assembles the final context under a fixed token budget. The goal is not merely to retrieve individually similar chunks, but to construct a context that is relevant, diverse, structurally connected, and sufficient for grounded reasoning. Experiments on MultiHopRAG, UltraDomain, and long-document question-answering settings show that SpectRAG improves broad evidence recovery and achieves competitive generation quality against dense, hybrid, HyDE, LightRAG, and NaiveRAG baselines. The results further indicate that graph-spectral structure is particularly useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, while highlighting trade-offs in early precision, computational cost, and domain-dependent performance.
authors: Zafer Sahinoglu, Abdulazeez Mohammed, Buse Yaren Kazangirler, Cahit Berkay Kazangirler
bullets: Addresses redundant retrieval, missed cross-chunk dependencies, and incomplete evidence from independently ranked dense retrieval.
Combines hybrid seed retrieval, graph expansion, spectral re-scoring, and token-budgeted context assembly.
Constructs chunk graphs using semantic similarity, document structure, shared entities, citations, and utility-question similarity.
Improves broad evidence recovery and delivers competitive generation quality across multi-hop and long-document settings.
Graph structure is especially useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, but involves precision, compute, and domain-dependent trade-offs.
papers.selection_reason: Token-budgeted context selection for RAG using graph-spectral retrieval, relevant to efficient inference and external retrieval/memory for LLMs.
papers.title: SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.tldr: SpectRAG uses weighted chunk graphs and spectral relevance propagation to select diverse, connected, token-budgeted evidence for multi-hop RAG.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable multimodal capabilities but suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to the massive number of visual tokens. While token pruning is a promising solution, existing methods still suffer from two major drawbacks: 1) unreliable pruning criteria that fail to accurately localize task-specific regions due to inherent attention biases or query-agnostic designs, and 2) suboptimal pruning strategies that employ rigid, non-adaptive schedules, overlooking the dynamic evolution of token redundancy across different model depths. To address these challenges, we propose LearnPrunerV2, which extends the previous two-stage heuristic framework (LearnPruner) into a fully learnable architecture. Specifically, we integrate lightweight learnable modules into every layer of the VLM backbone, which estimate token importance by fusing intrinsic visual saliency with extrinsic query relevance captured via a shadow token. By uncovering a consistent staircase redundancy pattern across VLM layers, we further introduce Budget-Deterministic Pruning (BDP) to establish a hardware-friendly schedule with fixed per-layer budgets. Extensive experimental results across various benchmarks and VLMs demonstrate that LearnPrunerV2 consistently outperform previous state-of-the-art methods. Notably, LearnPrunerV2 preserves 99.8% of the original performance when pruning 77.8% of visual tokens on LLaVA-v1.5, achieving a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
authors: Rinyoichi Takezoe, Yaqian Li, Weiren Wang, Zihao Bo, Huihong Shi, Anzhou Hou, Mo Guang, Jiale Yan, Kaiwen Long
bullets: Targets excessive computation from the large number of visual tokens in VLMs.
Uses lightweight per-layer modules to estimate token importance from visual saliency and query relevance via a shadow token.
Introduces Budget-Deterministic Pruning, a fixed per-layer schedule guided by the observed staircase pattern of token redundancy.
Across benchmarks and VLMs, it reportedly outperforms prior state-of-the-art pruning methods.
On LLaVA-v1.5, it retains 99.8% of original performance while pruning 77.8% of visual tokens.
papers.selection_reason: Learnable token pruning for vision-language models.
papers.title: LearnPrunerV2: Learnable Progressive Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: LearnPrunerV2 makes visual-token pruning in vision-language models fully learnable and progressively adaptive, retaining nearly all performance while removing most visual tokens.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models keep a key-value (KV) cache only in their few full-attention layers, but this cache is still the part of a prompt's state that grows with the prompt and that must be stored or moved to reuse it. We present DCKV, a differentiable codec for the KV cache and the first KV-cache codec that is trained end to end. Its transform, its quantizer and its entropy models, which are conditioned on the prompt tokens and on already decoded neighbouring positions, are optimized together against the frozen language model, both for the code length that the entropy models assign and for the change of the model's output. On Qwen3.5-2B, DCKV stores a compressed token in more than 55 times fewer bytes than bf16 at a loss of at most 1.8 points on three long-context benchmarks, and in more than 100 times fewer bytes at a loss of at most 3.6 points.
authors: Egor Maximov, Aleksei Merkelov, Vasiliy Alekseev, Ivan Krivorotov, Valentin Beliaev, Nikita Arsenin, Dmitry Bocharov, Aleksei Goncharov
bullets: Targets the growing, transferable KV cache used by full-attention layers in hybrid language models.
Jointly learns a transform, quantizer, and token-conditioned entropy models.
Optimizes both estimated code length and the frozen model’s output preservation.
On Qwen3.5-2B, achieves over 55× compression with at most a 1.8-point loss on three long-context benchmarks.
Exceeds 100× compression with at most a 3.6-point loss.
papers.selection_reason: Learned KV cache compression for efficient inference in hybrid LLMs.
papers.title: DCKV: Learned Transform Coding of the Prompt KV Cache in Hybrid Language Models
papers.tldr: DCKV is an end-to-end learned codec that compresses hybrid language-model prompt KV caches by over 55× with limited benchmark degradation.

papers.abstract: Camouflaged object detection (COD) depends on weak texture and boundary cues that can be destroyed by aggressive post-training quantization (PTQ). Existing PTQ methods mainly optimize quantizers or reconstruct network blocks, while using a single precision-allocation domain throughout hierarchical backbones. Instead, we introduce AxisQ, a depth-adaptive bit-allocation framework motivated by the observation that the useful allocation axis changes with feature depth. Under a fixed per-layer average activation-bit budget, AxisQ allocates precision in the channel domain for shallow features and in the local-frequency domain for deep features, using COD-aware sensitivity to better preserve subtle foreground regions and ambiguous boundaries. We also formulate a boundary-aware Hessian approximation for reconstruction by incorporating boundary-weighted gradient and error statistics. Experiments across multiple COD models and diverse benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy over the strongest baselines at low bit widths, with relative weighted F-measure gains of 12.7% for CFRN and 33.3% for CamoFormer-P on CAMO under W2A2 quantization. These results support adapting the allocation domain to feature depth as a transferable quantization strategy for hierarchical COD models.
authors: Chi Ruan, Tianqi Li, Xin He, Xue Geng, Ming-Ming Cheng, Yun Liu
bullets: Addresses the risk that aggressive PTQ destroys weak texture and boundary cues in COD.
Allocates activation bits in the channel domain for shallow features and local-frequency domain for deep features under a fixed average bit budget.
Uses COD-aware sensitivity to preserve subtle foreground regions and ambiguous boundaries.
Introduces boundary-aware Hessian-based reconstruction using boundary-weighted gradient and error statistics.
Reports relative weighted F-measure gains of 12.7% for CFRN and 33.3% for CamoFormer-P on CAMO with W2A2 quantization.
papers.selection_reason: Post-training quantization approach for efficient deployment; depth-adaptive bit allocation is a transferable efficiency strategy for vision models.
papers.title: AxisQ: Depth-Adaptive Channel--Frequency Quantization for Camouflaged Object Detection
papers.tldr: AxisQ improves low-bit post-training quantization for camouflaged object detection by adapting precision allocation from channels to local frequencies as feature depth increases.

papers.abstract: Remote sensing (RS) image-text retrieval plays a critical role in understanding massive RS imagery. However, the dense multi-object distribution and complex backgrounds in RS imagery make it difficult to simultaneously achieve fine-grained cross-modal alignment and efficient retrieval. Existing methods either rely on complex cross-modal interactions that lead to low retrieval efficiency, or depend on large-scale vision-language adaptation, which requires massive data and computational resources. To address these issues, we develop a fast-then-fine (FTF) retrieval framework centered on interaction-free multi-granular recall and parameter-free text-guided cross-modal reranking with the Balanced Text-guided Interaction Block (BTIB). Specifically, interaction-free multi-granular recall pre-computes gallery embeddings and matches them with the corresponding query embedding without full-gallery token-level text-image interaction, while text-guided cross-modal reranking with BTIB refines local semantic correspondence within the top-K candidate set. Furthermore, an inter- and intra-modal loss is designed to jointly optimize cross-modal alignment across multi-granular representations. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate that the FTF achieves competitive retrieval accuracy while significantly improving retrieval efficiency compared with existing methods.
authors: Xi Chen, Xu Chen, Xiamgyang Jia, Wei Wang, Xu Zhang, Zhenyuan Shun
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between fine-grained cross-modal alignment and efficient retrieval in complex remote-sensing imagery.
Uses precomputed gallery embeddings for fast, interaction-free multi-granular candidate recall.
Applies the parameter-free BTIB module to refine local image–text correspondence within the top-K candidates.
Jointly optimizes alignment across multi-granular representations with an inter- and intra-modal loss.
Experiments on public benchmarks show competitive accuracy with significantly improved retrieval efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient image-text retrieval via interaction-free recall and reranking; relevant to efficient multimodal inference.
papers.title: Efficient Remote Sensing Image-Text Retrieval via Interaction-Free Recall and Text-Guided Reranking
papers.tldr: The FTF framework enables efficient remote-sensing image–text retrieval by combining interaction-free multi-granular recall with text-guided reranking of top candidates.

papers.abstract: Reasoning language models answer math problems by writing long chains of thought, and sampling many chains per problem and taking a majority vote raises accuracy at a large cost in generated text. A popular way to cut that cost scores each chain by the model's confidence in each token it writes, where a token is a word or part of a word. The method averages this confidence over a sliding window of 2048 tokens and keeps or stops chains based on the lowest average. We treat the confidence, recorded token by token, as a signal in the sense of audio or radio, and examine the method with standard signal-processing tools such as spectral analysis and statistical tests for detecting a sudden change. We sampled 16 chains for each of 500 problems from two math benchmarks with a small open reasoning model. The windowed-minimum score turns out to measure mostly how long a chain is. Ranking chains by length alone does as well as or better than the confidence score, and once length is accounted for the score carries no information about correctness. Signal processing explains why: the minimum of a longer stretch of a slowly drifting signal is lower by chance alone, and the confidence signal drifts slowly enough that this effect dominates. The spectrum does hold a small signal that length does not explain, since incorrect chains carry more rapid token-to-token fluctuation, but it is too weak to improve the vote. For stopping chains early, neither the sliding average nor a classical change detector beats the simpler choice of sampling fewer chains.
bullets: The study audits token confidence as a signal using spectral analysis and change-point tests.
Across 16 chains for each of 500 problems from two math benchmarks, chain length matched or outperformed the windowed-minimum confidence score.
After accounting for length, the confidence score contained no useful correctness information.
Incorrect chains showed more rapid token-level fluctuations, but this weak signal did not improve majority voting.
Neither confidence-based stopping method outperformed simply sampling fewer chains.
papers.selection_reason: Audits token-confidence stopping rules for reasoning LLMs, with direct implications for reducing inference cost.
papers.title: Is Token Confidence Just Chain Length? A Signal-Processing Audit of Reasoning Traces
papers.tldr: Token-confidence scoring mainly measures reasoning-chain length, not correctness, so simpler length-based selection or sampling fewer chains is at least as effective.

papers.abstract: Diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) process their entire input at every denoising step. Since visual tokens make up 89-97% of this input on the benchmarks we study, most of the decoding computation is spent repeatedly processing the same image. Visual token pruning methods partially relieve this burden by removing part of the visual tokens, but they lose the removed information and still process the remaining image at every step. To measure how often the image is actually needed, we compare LLaDA-V's predictions with and without the image at every decoding step and find that removing the image changes a token being unmasked at only 22.8% of steps on average and at as few as 7.9%. We therefore propose LOWN, a decoding method that decides at every step whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask. LOWN predicts the masked tokens without the image and processes the image only when this prediction disagrees with the last image-conditioned prediction. Agreement certifies the earlier prediction for reuse, and the number of certified tokens sets how many are unmasked in that step. We further observe that the need for the image differs across benchmarks, so LOWN's adaptive decision is needed rather than a fixed schedule. Without training or a tuned threshold, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score on ten benchmarks at 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average. LOWN also generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, composes orthogonally with visual token pruning, and runs under key-value caching for further efficiency gains. Code and project page are available at https://hyeon9698.github.io/LOWN/
authors: Donghyeon Cho, Joowon Kim, Seungho Shin, Eunho Yang
bullets: DVLMs repeatedly process mostly redundant visual tokens at every denoising step.
The method compares image-free and image-conditioned predictions to certify when prior predictions can be reused.
It adaptively decides both whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask, without training or a tuned threshold.
Across ten benchmarks, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V’s score while using 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average.
It generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, combines with visual token pruning, and supports key-value caching.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive visual routing reduces decoding FLOPs for diffusion VLMs.
papers.title: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs
papers.tldr: LOWN makes diffusion VLMs process image tokens only when needed, preserving nearly all performance while substantially reducing decoding computation.

papers.abstract: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune state coordinates, scoring each channel independently in the native basis. We examine trained Mamba-2 states and find that energy is almost rank-one, but the output does not read the energetic directions: energy concentrates in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while the content the output reads lives in a low-dimensional subspace that is not aligned with the state's coordinates. Even output-aware scores are computed coordinate by coordinate, so they miss the directions that determine the input--output map. Compression should therefore target the write--read subspace rather than individual coordinates. We propose \method{}, a post-training transform that instantiates balanced truncation with full controllability and observability Gramians and applies the rotation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Because the useful rank varies widely across layers, we further introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving both perplexity and retrieval over uniform budgets. Calibration takes a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than GHOST's released protocol, with lower peak memory. With HARP, \method{} halves the state dimension at an average WikiText-2 perplexity increase of $0.3$ points ($1.8\%$) across 130M--2.7B, versus $1.6$ ($9.3\%$) for GHOST, and the gap widens at 25\% retention.
bullets: Mamba-2 state energy is nearly rank-one, but the useful output-read content lies in a different low-dimensional, non-coordinate-aligned subspace.
The proposed post-training method applies balanced truncation using full controllability and observability Gramians, with an exact rotation enabled by Mamba-2’s scalar-identity transition.
HARP allocates layer-specific ranks from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers instead of using uniform budgets.
Using one-pass calibration, the method halves state dimension with a 0.3-point average WikiText-2 perplexity increase across 130M–2.7B models, compared with 1.6 points for GHOST.
The approach is evaluated for perplexity and retrieval; performance degradation increases at 25% retention.
papers.selection_reason: Mamba-2 state compression reduces memory; fits memory efficiency.
papers.title: Balanced State Subspaces for Mamba-2 State Compression
papers.tldr: Balanced state-subspace compression preserves Mamba-2’s input–output behavior better than coordinate-wise compression by targeting controllable and observable directions.

papers.abstract: Low-precision training often relies on stochastic rounding (SR) to keep quantized gradients unbiased and prevent small updates from rounding to zero. Standard SR draws an independent random threshold for every gradient element. However, accelerators generate random numbers on vector units whose throughput lags far behind their matrix units. Drawing one threshold per element saturates the vector unit and can make INT8 training with SR slower than BF16 training. Sharing random thresholds across tensor elements removes this cost but forces those elements to round in the same direction and shifts their rounding errors by a common offset. We find that this offset degrades training primarily through the activation gradient, which propagates the error backward into earlier layers. Because earlier layers cannot cancel an incoming offset using their own local rounding errors, the offset must be removed at the layer where it originates. We propose Structured Subspace Stochastic Rounding (S3R), which quantizes each upstream gradient once for both the activation and weight gradient matrix multiplications and shares a single threshold per token across the hidden dimension. Its error correction, S3R-EC, subtracts the structured mean rounding error from the activation and weight gradients while leaving the optimizer unchanged. In LLM pre-training experiments, uncorrected threshold sharing degrades convergence, whereas S3R-EC eliminates this degradation and matches the validation loss of independent SR. Furthermore, S3R-EC accelerates full INT8 training steps of dense LLMs on TPU v5p by 1.24x to 1.32x over BF16 and by 1.11x over independent SR.
authors: Zeyu Wang, Yiheng Duan, Tao Chen, Donghyun Koo, Sihan Liu, Wenbo Zhang, Chuan He, Liang Liu
bullets: Independent stochastic rounding is costly because generating one random threshold per gradient element bottlenecks accelerator vector units.
Naively sharing thresholds reduces randomness overhead but introduces a common rounding offset that harms convergence through activation gradients.
S3R quantizes each upstream gradient once for both activation and weight computations, sharing one threshold per token across hidden dimensions.
S3R-EC removes the resulting structured mean rounding error without changing the optimizer.
In LLM pre-training on TPU v5p, S3R-EC matches independent-SR validation loss and achieves 1.24–1.32× speedup over BF16 and 1.11× over independent SR.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces structured subspace stochastic rounding to accelerate low-precision training, fitting the efficient-AI scope.
papers.title: Efficient Quantization Training with Stochastic Rounding via Structured Subspace Randomness
papers.tldr: S3R-EC makes stochastic rounding practical for fast full-INT8 LLM training by sharing token-level randomness while correcting its structured rounding bias.

papers.abstract: Handwritten civil-status registers across Sub-Saharan Africa are being photographed, but rarely transcribed, which leaves their content unsearchable. Local administrations that hold these records typically lack GPUs, reliable connectivity, and the budget for external digitization services. We study whether a frugal pipeline, with consumer-grade capture and CPU-only inference, can make such registers machine-readable. We introduce a corpus of 1,568 smartphone images of handwritten birth, marriage, and death records from a municipal registry in Chad, with line-level transcriptions for 185 records. Our pipeline combines a fully classical preprocessing stage, running at about 2.6 images per second on a laptop CPU, with a Kraken recognizer fine-tuned from a pretrained model in about four hours on a free-tier GPU. On manually corrected line segmentation and a single-registry test set whose writers also appear in training, fine-tuning reduces the character error rate from 14.53% to 0.50% and the word error rate from 56.93% to 3.37%. On a six-core laptop CPU, the recognizer weighs 61 MiB, peaks below 2.6 GiB of RAM, and processes an image in under 6 s on average, excluding line segmentation. Finally, a downstream information-extraction task shows that residual recognition errors cost about 9 F1 points on role resolution, compared with a 36.7-point gap between the fine-tuned and pretrained recognizers. These results are evidence of feasibility within one registry, not of performance on unseen writers or sites; we discuss these limitations in detail.
authors: Ousmane Hamadou, Jean Louis Kedieng Ebongue Fendji
bullets: Targets digitization barriers in Sub-Saharan administrations lacking GPUs, reliable connectivity, and external-service budgets.
Introduces 1,568 smartphone images from 185 handwritten birth, marriage, and death records in a Chadian municipal registry, with line transcriptions.
Combines classical preprocessing with a Kraken recognizer fine-tuned on a pretrained model; inference runs on a laptop CPU without a GPU.
On manually corrected segmentation and a same-writer test setting, fine-tuning reduces character error rate from 14.53% to 0.50% and word error rate from 56.93% to 3.37%.
Residual recognition errors reduce downstream role-resolution F1 by about 9 points; results demonstrate feasibility only within the studied registry.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a frugal pipeline for handwritten text recognition that optimizes for CPU-only inference and memory usage, relevant to memory efficiency.
papers.title: Frugal Handwritten Text Recognition for Sub-Saharan Civil-Status Registers: A Smartphone-to-Records Pipeline with CPU-Only Inference
papers.tldr: A frugal smartphone-to-CPU pipeline can make handwritten civil-status records searchable within a single registry, but its strong accuracy has not been validated on unseen writers or sites.

papers.abstract: Attention Matching (AM) compacts a KV cache by keeping some keys per head, refitting their values and adding a bias to each kept key's logit. FlashAttention and vLLM's paged caches have no input for it. We fold the bias into the keys along one closed-form direction per head, fitted on context queries, giving a plain cache with AM's size and head dimension and the model's own query path; the output error is bounded by how far each query's projection on that direction is from 1. With equal per-head budgets, unmodified vLLM serves folded caches through a KV connector, matching Hugging Face's answers on all 51 Qwen3-4B questions and its greedy output on 180 of 200 Qwen3-14B LongBench samples. With equal budgets on QuALITY (Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, 8B, Llama-3.1-8B) and LongHealth (three Qwen3 models), the fold is within noise of AM's accuracy in 13 of 14 settings, with lower KL to the full cache than dropping the bias in all 12 where both ran. Under the published per-head budgets, on Qwen3-4B, its Instruct-2507 variant and Llama-3.1-8B, it is within noise of AM in 9 of 10, no longer beats dropping the bias in KL, and the two each win once in accuracy.
bullets: AM compresses KV caches by retaining selected keys, refitting values, and adding per-key logit biases—but standard kernels cannot consume those biases.
The proposed closed-form, per-head key adjustment absorbs each bias along one fitted direction, preserving the model’s normal query path and cache dimensions.
Unmodified vLLM serves the folded caches through a KV connector; outputs closely match Hugging Face and retain most greedy generations in the reported tests.
Across equal-budget evaluations, folding matches AM within noise in 13 of 14 settings and generally produces lower KL divergence than omitting the bias.
Under published per-head budgets, folding remains comparable to AM in 9 of 10 settings, though its KL advantage disappears.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses KV cache compaction and memory-efficient inference by folding attention biases into keys.
papers.title: Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels
papers.tldr: Folding Attention Matching’s key biases into the keys enables compact KV caches to run on standard FlashAttention/vLLM kernels with nearly unchanged accuracy.
