papers.abstract: Compact electroencephalography (EEG) decoders enable embedded brain--computer interfaces (BCIs), but compression can alter adversarial robustness without proportional hardware savings. We present ORBITAL, a robustness-constrained framework combining hardware-realizable structured compression, recovery-aware operating-point selection, multi-attack evaluation, and native edge validation. Across nine subjects and three seeds on BCI Competition IV-2a, S25-TRADES achieves the highest observed mean true-union robustness among compressed EEGNet models (23.06% vs 21.27% for standard Full), with 26.27% fewer parameters and 25.10% fewer MACs. Matched controls identify TRADES as the main source of robustness recovery, improving S25 union accuracy by 6.74 percentage points over clean recovery (p=0.0039), while per-example analysis reveals boundary redistribution rather than uniform margin expansion. On Jetson Orin Nano, FP16 compression reduces board energy by up to 16.20% and latency by 8.00%. Despite 99.3% prediction agreement, native INT8 Q/DQ incurs about twice the FP16 latency and energy, demonstrating the need for joint robustness and hardware-aware optimization.
bullets: Structured compression can change adversarial robustness without matching hardware gains.
S25-TRADES achieved the highest observed mean true-union robustness among compressed EEGNet models, while reducing parameters and MACs versus Full.
TRADES was the main driver of robustness recovery, improving S25 union accuracy over clean recovery in matched controls.
On Jetson Orin Nano, FP16 compression reduced energy by up to 16.20% and latency by 8.00%.
Native INT8 Q/DQ showed roughly twice the FP16 latency and energy despite 99.3% prediction agreement, highlighting hardware-dependent trade-offs.
papers.selection_reason: Robustness-constrained low-precision compression for edge inference, reducing memory, energy, and latency; relevant to efficient AI via memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: ORBITAL: Optimization of Robust Brain--Computer Inference Through Architecture-Aware Low-Precision Compression
papers.tldr: ORBITAL jointly optimizes compressed EEG decoders for adversarial robustness and real edge-hardware efficiency, with FP16 compression offering the strongest practical trade-off.

papers.abstract: Modeling multi-scale dynamics in urban road networks is essential for intelligent transportation systems but is often hindered by the computational cost of long-range historical context and the challenge of fusing heterogeneous modalities. Existing spatio-temporal frameworks face a trade-off between sequence length and memory overhead, while frequently neglecting the transient effects of exogenous factors such as road incidents and weather. To address these limitations, we propose SpecLST, a frequency-enhanced long-short-term spatio-temporal multimodal framework. SpecLST leverages a fast Fourier transform-based frequency-domain representation module to efficiently encode multi-week historical dependencies, bypassing the memory bottlenecks of standard attention mechanisms over raw long sequences. Heterogeneous context is integrated through attention-based fusion, followed by a sparse Mixture-of-Experts backbone with graph augmentation for spatio-temporal representation learning. Additionally, a frequency-enhanced residual head isolates high-frequency transients, improving sensitivity to abrupt traffic anomalies. At the 60-minute horizon, SpecLST achieves mean relative error reductions of 14.10% in MAE, 10.35% in RMSE, and 15.78% in MAPE across eight neural forecasting baselines and four datasets, with the dataset- and metric-specific average reductions ranging from 5.63% to 22.21%.
authors: Kenan Kang, Matthew M. Y. Kuo, Weihua Li
bullets: Addresses the memory cost of long historical sequences and weak handling of heterogeneous, time-varying factors such as incidents and weather.
Uses FFT-based frequency representations to encode multi-week dependencies more efficiently than attention over raw long sequences.
Fuses heterogeneous context with attention, then applies a sparse Mixture-of-Experts backbone with graph augmentation.
Adds a frequency-enhanced residual head to capture high-frequency, abrupt traffic anomalies.
At a 60-minute horizon, reports average error reductions of 14.10% in MAE, 10.35% in RMSE, and 15.78% in MAPE across four datasets and eight baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Frequency-domain long-sequence encoding reduces memory overhead of attention; transferable to efficient AI.
papers.title: SpecLST: Spectral-Enhanced Long-Short Term Spatio-Temporal Multimodal Modeling for Traffic Forecasting
papers.tldr: SpecLST combines frequency-domain long-term modeling, multimodal fusion, graph-enhanced sparse experts, and transient detection to improve multi-scale traffic forecasting.

papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a key mechanism for efficiently specializing foundation models into many task- and user-specific variants. Serving many LoRA adapters under a shared resource budget turns post-hoc compression into a two-level allocation problem: rank must be distributed across layers within each adapter and across adapters within the fleet. Although trained LoRAs contain substantial spectral redundancy, spectral reconstruction alone does not determine how much compression an adapter can functionally tolerate. We formulate fleet compression through a functional rank-distortion frontier for each adapter, followed by fleet-level minimax allocation under a shared rank budget. Given exact frontiers, this decomposition is equivalent to joint optimization over all layer ranks. We introduce Functional Rank Allocation (FRA), an unlabeled method for constructing practical frontiers. FRA measures isolated module truncations end to end, uses these measurements as an additive search surrogate solved by dynamic programming, remeasures every complete candidate, and takes the lower-risk envelope with a complementary spectral proposal before exact minimax allocation over the constructed frontiers. Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, FRA improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget regimes. Fixed-budget probes show that isolated costs rank candidates well, but their calibration shifts across proposal shapes; end-to-end verification and the spectral proposal therefore limit functional-search error.
bullets: LoRA fleet compression must allocate rank both across layers within adapters and across adapters under a shared budget.
The method builds per-adapter functional rank-distortion frontiers from isolated module truncation measurements and dynamic programming.
Complete candidates are re-evaluated end to end and combined with a spectral proposal before exact fleet-level minimax allocation.
Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, FRA improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget settings.
Isolated measurements rank candidates effectively, but calibration varies with proposal shape, making end-to-end verification important.
papers.selection_reason: Post-hoc LoRA adapter compression reduces memory/compute for serving many adapters, fitting the Efficient AI topic even without a specific subtopic.
papers.title: LoRA on a Budget: Function-Aware Post-Hoc Compression for Adapter Fleets
papers.tldr: FRA compresses fleets of LoRA adapters by allocating rank according to measured end-to-end functional degradation rather than spectral redundancy alone.

papers.abstract: For efficiency, industrial large language model (LLM) labelers often pack many candidate labels into one prompt and generate a YES/NO answer for each, even when each decision depends only on the entity and one candidate. Generating these independent decisions as one answer list couples them, spends decoding on the list, and relies on the list being well-formed. In this paper, we present an end-to-end recipe that reformulates the labeler as semantic scoring, fine-tuning it on single-candidate prompts to return each decision as one answer-token score from a prefill-only pass. We also adapt Multiple-Item Scoring (MIS) to score hundreds of candidates in one sequence with attention masked between them. Deployed for profile qualification labeling at LinkedIn, semantic scoring changes at most 0.01% of decisions when candidates are reordered and matches the agreement with reference labels that packed generation reaches only with about 4.7x as many training pairs. The MIS-based stack raises throughput over the deployed stack by 1.24x offline and 1.9x in model serving under a one-second p99 latency target. For offline batch inference, we implement MIS-based scoring as a reusable, model-agnostic Ray Data API proposed for upstream adoption. Model serving uses MIS support contributed to SGLang.
authors: Jian Sheng, Sriram Vasudevan, Sundara Raman Ramachandran, Yang Hu, Junyu Zhou, Xiaojing Ma, Haolan Qin, Tiffany Zhou, Vedant Vipul Jhaveri, Ashwini Bhingare, Chinmay Kini, Qing Lan, Xiaoqing Wang, Suleyman Cetintas, Fedor Borisyuk
bullets: Packed generation couples independent candidate decisions, wastes decoding, and can fail when the output list is malformed.
The proposed method fine-tunes single-candidate prompts to produce one answer-token score and uses attention-masked Multiple-Item Scoring to evaluate hundreds of candidates together.
Semantic scoring changes at most 0.01% of decisions when candidate order changes and reaches reference-label agreement with roughly 4.7× fewer training pairs than packed generation.
The MIS-based system improves throughput by 1.24× offline and 1.9× in serving under a one-second p99 latency target.
The work includes a reusable Ray Data API for offline inference and MIS support contributed to SGLang.
papers.selection_reason: Reformulates LLM labeling as prefill-only scoring and improves serving throughput; relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: From Generation to Scoring: Scaling LLM-Based Semantic Labeling at LinkedIn
papers.tldr: LinkedIn replaces coupled YES/NO list generation with independent prefill-only semantic scoring, improving robustness and serving throughput for large-scale label classification.

papers.abstract: Prefix caching enables a Large Language Model (LLM) servers to reuse the Key-Value (KV) states and accelerate prefill computation stage for requests that share a prefix with earlier prompts, thus reducing latency and serving cost. With limited memory resource, the KV cache eviction policy becomes a decisive factor in determining the overall benefits of prefix caching. Production traffic may have single-turn, multi-turn, agentic, or a mixture of any combination of these request types. Our findings indicate that agentic steps return within seconds and favor recency, while popular prompts and long conversations return after many other requests and favor frequency. Across 20 mixes, no single policy is always best: vLLM's default strategy LRU provides 12% higher cache hits as compared to the frequency-oriented S3FIFO on agentic-heavy mixes but trails it by up to 22% elsewhere, and even a single workload parameter can flip the winner even for any particular mix. We present WAKMan, a workload-aware KV cache manager that picks its eviction policy from live traffic without knowing request types or reading prompts. It improves hit rate over LRU by 5 percentage points on average, with the lowest mean and worst-case optimality gap of all policies.
authors: Suhas Kumar Morisetty, Vaibhavi Lokegaonkar, Sachin Mathew Varghese, Wesley Harris
bullets: Prefix caching benefits depend heavily on how KV-cache entries are evicted under limited memory.
Agentic requests favor recency, while popular prompts and long conversations favor frequency.
No single eviction policy is consistently best across diverse workload mixes.
WAKMan selects an eviction policy from traffic behavior without identifying request types or reading prompts.
It improves hit rate over LRU by 5 percentage points on average and has the smallest mean and worst-case optimality gaps among evaluated policies.
papers.selection_reason: Workload-aware KV cache eviction policy for LLM serving, directly contributing to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: WAKMan: Workload Aware KVCache Manager
papers.tldr: WAKMan adapts KV-cache eviction to live workload patterns, improving prefix-cache hit rates over fixed policies.

papers.abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) improves model efficiency by sharing representations across related vision tasks, but it often suffers from negative transfer when task updates interfere with one another. Existing conflict-mitigation methods typically operate in gradient space, requiring explicit task-gradient manipulation and additional optimization steps. We propose Conflict-Resolution through Low-Rank Matrices for Multi-Task Learning (CRLoMTL), a parameter-efficient framework that mitigates task interference in the low-rank parameter-update space. CRLoMTL learns task-specific LoRA updates through task-specific passes, where each task updates its own low-rank matrices, and integrates these updates through global shared-subspace fusion. Specifically, we introduce a shared-subspace resolver based on singular value decomposition (SVD), referred to as the SVD resolver, which extracts a common low-dimensional orthonormal basis across task adapters and projects task updates into this shared space before merging them into a single deployment-time update. The resulting update can be folded into the backbone, preserving the inference structure of the original model without additional runtime branches. Experiments with Swin Transformer backbones on PASCAL-Context, NYUD-v2, and CelebA show that CRLoMTL achieves a favorable accuracy-parameter trade-off, improving over single-task baselines by up to 2.77% on PASCAL-Context, 5.03% on NYUD-v2, and 3.50% on CelebA, while training only a small fraction of the parameters used by single-task models.
authors: Ahmed Agiza, Tasneem Shaffee, Rahil Badkul, Sherief Reda
bullets: Addresses interference between task updates while avoiding explicit gradient manipulation and extra optimization steps.
Learns task-specific LoRA updates and merges them through a shared subspace extracted with SVD.
Fuses the resolved updates into the backbone, preserving the original model’s inference structure.
With Swin Transformer backbones, reports gains of up to 2.77% on PASCAL-Context, 5.03% on NYUD-v2, and 3.50% on CelebA over single-task baselines.
Uses only a small fraction of the parameters required by single-task models, targeting a favorable accuracy–parameter trade-off.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient multi-task learning via low-rank LoRA updates and shared-subspace fusion; reduces training parameters and task interference in vision backbones.
papers.title: CRLoMTL: Conflict-Resolution through Low-rank matrices for Multi-Task Learning
papers.tldr: CRLoMTL reduces negative transfer in multi-task learning by resolving task conflicts in a shared low-rank update space with no added inference branches.

papers.abstract: Video Large Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in video understanding and reasoning, but processing long visual sequences incurs substantial computational, latency, and memory overhead. This survey examines training-free inference acceleration, focusing on reducing inference costs while preserving task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence. We organize existing methods by their intervention stages in the inference pipeline, covering input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is discussed separately as a cross-stage extension with varying calibration requirements. We analyze how intervention position affects evidence preservation and computational savings, and why local efficiency improvements may not translate into end-to-end acceleration. We complement this analysis with quantitative evidence from prior studies and our own experiments under a shared evaluation setting to assess accuracy-latency trade-offs.
authors: Yuqi Li, Chuanyue Yan, Neil Rodrigues, Xianglong Wang, Xiaoqin Feng, Junming Liu, Xi Xiao, Zhongwei Cheng, Wei Li, Lin Chen, Yingli Tian
bullets: Video VLMs face high computation, latency, and memory costs on long visual sequences.
Methods are categorized by intervention stage: input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding.
Post-training quantization is treated as a cross-stage approach with different calibration requirements.
The survey examines how intervention location affects preservation of task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence.
Prior results and shared-setting experiments assess accuracy–latency trade-offs and highlight that local gains may not yield end-to-end speedups.
papers.selection_reason: Survey of training-free inference acceleration for video LLMs, organizing token pruning and memory-efficient techniques for long-video understanding.
papers.title: Training-Free Inference Acceleration for Video Large Language Models: Methods, Trade-offs, and Evaluation
papers.tldr: This survey organizes training-free methods for accelerating video VLM inference, analyzing their efficiency–evidence-preservation trade-offs across the pipeline.

papers.abstract: Large-scale linear programs with millions of variables and constraints strain time and memory budgets. First-order methods such as the primal-dual hybrid gradient scale to this regime because they avoid matrix factorizations, but they require many iterations. Learned accelerators can reduce these iterations, yet fewer iterations do not guarantee a shorter solve. Learning inference also takes time, and running the accelerator longer trades solver time for inference time. Existing unrolled accelerators handle this trade-off poorly: each layer processes every variable and constraint, the predicted iterates still need solver refinement, and every instance runs the same layers. We therefore ask: What neural accelerator design achieves end-to-end speedups on large-scale linear programs across sizes and target accuracies? We introduce AHEAD, an accelerator that predicts step sizes for first-order linear programming solvers while keeping their update rules. Its weight-shared predictor reads compact solver statistics and rescales the primal and dual step sizes, so each warm-start iteration stays inexpensive and a short warm-start phase hands the solver a warm start. A learned handoff policy sets the number of warm-start iterations for each instance and target accuracy, after which the solver finishes under its own termination criterion. On packing linear programs with up to $10^7$ variables, AHEAD achieves $6.5$--$11.6\times$ end-to-end speedups over Gurobi's first-order solver from a cold start, including on instances of unseen sizes and distributions. The gains extend to PageRank linear programs and hold across difficulty levels and target accuracies.
authors: Sihao Liu, Zhichao Hou, Huayue Gu, Raiyan Rahman, Liang Wu, Ruozhou Yu, Xiaorui Liu
bullets: Targets the high iteration counts and inference–solver trade-off in learned acceleration for massive linear programs.
Uses a weight-shared predictor over compact solver statistics to rescale primal and dual step sizes while preserving the solver’s update rules.
A learned handoff policy selects the warm-start duration based on each instance and target accuracy.
Evaluated on packing LPs with up to 10^7 variables, including unseen sizes and distributions, and on PageRank LPs.
Reported gains hold across difficulty levels and target accuracies.
papers.selection_reason: Learned accelerator reduces end-to-end solve time for large-scale linear programs; relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: AHEAD: Adaptive Neural Acceleration for Large-Scale Linear Programming
papers.tldr: AHEAD accelerates large-scale linear programming by learning solver step sizes and when to hand control back, achieving reported 6.5–11.6× end-to-end speedups over Gurobi’s first-order solver.

papers.abstract: Navigation vision-language-action (VLA) policies repeatedly invoke costly semantic reasoning even when the next command remains unchanged. Command reuse can reduce computation but risks missing instruction-dependent turns or stops. We introduce ASPEN, an event-triggered scheduler based on command persistence prediction: estimating whether the frozen base policy would reissue its previous command. A lightweight multimodal predictor combines temporal observations, language instructions, execution history, and cached VLA confidence. At eligible command boundaries, sufficient predicted persistence permits command reuse. Otherwise, ASPEN triggers fresh semantic reasoning from the VLA. Evaluated with frozen NaVILA on cross-dataset RxR-CE val-unseen, ASPEN reduces VLA calls by 9.5% and estimated inference time by 8.1%, including scheduling overhead. It maintains comparable navigation performance and preserves identical baseline action sequences on 92.1% of episodes.
bullets: Targets redundant semantic reasoning in navigation VLAs when the next command is likely unchanged.
Uses a lightweight multimodal predictor over observations, instructions, execution history, and cached VLA confidence.
Reuses commands when predicted persistence is sufficient; otherwise triggers fresh VLA reasoning.
With frozen NaVILA on RxR-CE val-unseen, reduces VLA calls by 9.5% and estimated inference time by 8.1%.
Maintains comparable navigation performance, with identical baseline action sequences in 92.1% of episodes.
papers.selection_reason: Improves efficiency of navigation VLAs via command persistence prediction, relevant to Embodied AI navigation and Efficient AI.
papers.title: ASPEN: Adaptive Semantic Reasoning via Command Persistence Prediction for Efficient Navigation VLAs
papers.tldr: ASPEN reduces costly VLA reasoning by predicting when the previous navigation command can safely be reused, cutting VLA calls and inference time while preserving navigation behavior.

papers.abstract: The information bottleneck (IB) trades compression of an input $X$ against prediction of a target $Y$ through a multiplier $\beta=1/\lambda$, yet each operating point is usually served by training, or fully conditioning, a new encoder. For jointly Gaussian data, we show that the IB solution factorizes as $A(\beta)=D(\beta)W$: the information-bearing directions $W$ do not depend on $\beta$, and $\beta$ acts only through scalar gains. We ask whether this separation of \emph{representation} from \emph{rate control} survives beyond Gaussian models, treating the budget as a given operating parameter rather than a quantity to be optimized. For a budget-free representation \(F(X)\), the \emph{separation gap} is controlled by the \emph{sufficiency deficit} $\epsilon_F=I(X;Y\mid F(X))$: We show there is at least $\epsilon_F$ in the worst case for finite inputs, and it is bounded uniformly in $\lambda$ by a function of $\epsilon_F$ for finite label alphabets. The same certificate extends to a new target distribution and to pooled multi-domain data, where a conditional-alignment term appears. On MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10 and STL-10 (10 seeds, eight prespecified budgets), a frozen CNN representation with one compressor--decoder pair per budget reduces estimated training multiply--accumulate operations (MACs) by $7.7\times$ and wall-clock time by about $2\times$ relative to end-to-end VIBs, and attains higher budget-averaged accuracy ($65.6\%$ versus $57.3\%$ per domain; $67.1\%$ versus $57.1\%$ pooled), with the advantage concentrated at strong compression, where the VIBs collapse. At weak compression ($\lambda\le0.036$), VIB has higher cross-entropy and ECE; its surrogate Lagrangian is higher per domain, indistinguishable from the pooled VIB in the macro average, and lower on the pooled test set.
bullets: For Gaussian data, the IB encoder’s informative directions are independent of the compression parameter, which only changes scalar gains.
Beyond Gaussian models, the separation gap is controlled by the representation’s sufficiency deficit, with extensions to new targets and pooled multi-domain data.
Experiments on MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, and STL-10 show 7.7× fewer training MACs and roughly 2× lower wall-clock time than end-to-end VIB training.
The frozen-representation approach achieves higher budget-averaged accuracy, especially under strong compression where VIBs collapse.
At weak compression, VIB has better cross-entropy and calibration, so the proposed approach does not dominate on every metric or operating regime.
papers.selection_reason: Separates representation learning from rate control and demonstrates large compute savings via frozen representations; relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: What Should an Information Bottleneck Encoder Learn? Separating Representation Learning from Rate Control
papers.tldr: A learned representation can be separated from information-bottleneck rate control, enabling one frozen encoder to support many compression budgets with theoretical guarantees and lower training cost.

papers.abstract: Learning velocity fields directly in pixel space is difficult and slow. We show that coarse second-order image statistics can ease this task: frozen Wiener estimates improve velocity learning, with gains extending beyond the linear predictions they explicitly provide. Moreover, we observe similar but complementary gains from frozen bases and pixel decoding. These observations motivate Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD), which uses statistical knowledge both for direct prediction and to organize decoder computation without modifying native blocks. WiD combines a trainable Wiener prediction path with coefficient interfaces that inject features into the native decoder and return its predicted coefficient corrections, with these components initialized with data statistics. All introduced parameters, including the spectrum and coordinate transforms, are trained jointly under the original pixel-space velocity objective. Across model scales and decoder architectures, WiD accelerates training and improves generation quality with modest parameter overhead. It also yields smoother gradient trajectories and remains effective with representation alignment. WiD improves class-conditional and text-to-image generation across different resolutions. On ImageNet 256 x 256, PixelDiT-XL with WiD reaches FID 1.53 after 500 epochs, achieving comparable quality to PixelDiT with 37.5% fewer training epochs. Statistical denoisers contribute beyond the estimate: their computational structure can also ease pixel-space training.
bullets: Frozen Wiener estimates improve velocity-field learning beyond their direct predictions.
WiD combines a trainable Wiener path with coefficient interfaces that augment native decoder computation without changing its blocks.
Statistical initialization, smoother gradients, and compatibility with representation alignment support training across model scales and decoder architectures.
On ImageNet 256×256, PixelDiT-XL with WiD reaches FID 1.53 after 500 epochs, matching PixelDiT quality with 37.5% fewer epochs.
The approach improves class-conditional and text-to-image generation across resolutions, with modest parameter overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Training-efficiency technique for pixel-space flow models is transferable to efficient generative model training.
papers.title: Beyond the Estimate: Wiener-Informed Decoding for Easier Training of Pixel-Space Flow Models
papers.tldr: Wiener-informed Decoding uses image statistics to make pixel-space flow models train faster and generate higher-quality images with little extra overhead.

papers.abstract: Sparse expert execution does not remove the stored states needed to adapt a mixture-of-experts language model. We present DuplexTune, a framework for replaying coupled hidden states through pretrained attention and expert modules. Trainable width bridges connect two residual streams to the backbone. Bridge warm-up precedes backbone adaptation, with router weights kept frozen. We analyze the implicit state-recovery equation and identify the convergence and replay conditions needed for reconstruction. On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, the single-H800 evaluation reports 38.8 GB peak memory, versus 64.8 GB for supervised fine-tuning with checkpointing, and throughput of 25.1 versus 19.9 samples/s. DuplexTune achieves 67.2% MMLU, 75.6% GSM8K, and 7.69 MT-Bench, with a weaker multilingual score than the checkpointed baseline. The results characterize a configuration-dependent tradeoff among state storage, throughput, and adaptation quality.
authors: Paul Raj, Simon Caldwell, Daniel Whitmore, Mutlu Mete
bullets: Addresses the memory cost of storing states during sparse MoE adaptation.
Uses trainable width bridges between two residual streams, with bridge warm-up before backbone adaptation and frozen router weights.
Analyzes convergence and replay conditions for reconstructing hidden states.
On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, reports 38.8 GB peak memory and 25.1 samples/s, versus 64.8 GB and 19.9 samples/s for checkpointed supervised fine-tuning.
Reports 67.2% MMLU, 75.6% GSM8K, and 7.69 MT-Bench, while multilingual performance is weaker than the checkpointed baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient MoE LLM adaptation by replaying coupled hidden states, substantially reducing peak memory with moderate quality tradeoffs.
papers.title: DuplexTune: Coupled-State Replay for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Adaptation
papers.tldr: DuplexTune reduces memory use for MoE adaptation by replaying coupled hidden states through frozen-routing pretrained modules, with higher throughput but some quality tradeoffs.

papers.abstract: Variable-length training creates conflicting parallelism requirements across the layers of a hybrid-attention model. The longest samples require wide sequence-parallel (SP) groups of 16 or 32 ranks for full attention, whose cost grows quadratically with sequence length. Sparse-attention layers, dominated by near-linear MoE work, can instead balance most evaluated workloads within node-local SP8 groups. Reusing the wide groups for these layers pushes their all-to-all communication across nodes, where the observed effective rate is 7.0x lower. Yet switching to smaller groups changes which ranks own each sample; a separate redistribution at every full-sparse boundary would introduce another data transfer. Layerwise Repacking keeps each SP16/32 parent for full attention and repacks its samples into node-local sparse children at SP{1, 2, 4, 8}, where hidden states persist between full layers. The layout change rides on the two existing full-layer Ulysses sites: at each, one variable-size all-to-all performs both the head exchange and the sample repacking, so no redistribution pass is added. Because the balance the children can reach depends on which samples share a parent, an auxiliary parent solver rebalances parent membership before the children are formed. On all 22 steps with SP16/32 parents among the first 200 training steps of a 1F3S hybrid-attention model (one full-attention layer per three sparse-attention layers), repacking alone reduces the mean end-to-end time by 5.95% and raises model FLOPs utilization (MFU) by 3.75 percentage points over the baseline with repacking disabled; with the improved solver, end-to-end time falls by 7.61% and MFU rises by 4.83 percentage points.
authors: Jiahao Zhang, Junwei Feng, Dongliang Huang, Xiaoling Zhou, Yiqiao Liao, Chengru Song
bullets: Full-attention layers benefit from wide SP16/32 groups, while sparse-attention layers are better balanced with node-local SP1–8 groups.
The method repacks samples from each wide parent group into smaller sparse-attention child groups at existing Ulysses all-to-all sites.
An auxiliary solver rebalances parent membership to improve the load balance achievable by the sparse children.
Across 22 evaluated steps, repacking alone reduces mean end-to-end time by 5.95% and increases MFU by 3.75 percentage points.
With the improved solver, time decreases by 7.61% and MFU increases by 4.83 percentage points versus no repacking.
papers.selection_reason: Communication-efficient sample repacking across sequence-parallel groups improves hybrid-attention training efficiency and MFU.
papers.title: Layerwise Repacking: Variable-Length Hybrid-Attention Training without an Extra Redistribution Pass
papers.tldr: Layerwise Repacking improves variable-length hybrid-attention training by combining sample redistribution with existing communication, avoiding an extra pass and reducing training time.

papers.abstract: Conditional memory layers, such as DeepSeek's Engram, attach large hashed n-gram tables to a language model, and removing them from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash costs 36.8 PopQA points. Low-bit quantization loses long-tail facts first, and the standard remedy, giving more bits to frequently accessed rows, backfires: refining lookups by access frequency is worse than refining them at random. We trace this to the gate that scales each retrieved row. A lookup's quantization error is weighted by its gate, which is small for frequent n-grams, large for the rare n-grams of long-tail entities, and computable from a 1-bit code. GateRQ therefore stores each row as a ladder of 1-bit residual codes, keeps level 1 in GPU memory to compute the gate, and reads deeper levels only for the lookups the gate ranks highest. Without retraining, GateRQ cuts GPU table memory by 7.8x on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, which raises vLLM throughput by 11%-31% over FP8 tables, while losing about 1 PopQA point at 1.50 bits read per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models.
authors: Tianqi Chen, Xunchao Li, Linchuan Xie, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu, Peisong Wang, Jian Cheng
bullets: Frequency-based precision allocation can hurt because frequent lookups often have small gates, while rare long-tail entity lookups have larger gates and greater quantization impact.
GateRQ stores each row as progressively refined 1-bit residual codes and uses an always-resident first level to estimate gates.
Deeper residual levels are fetched only for lookups ranked as most important by their gate values.
Without retraining, it reduces GPU table memory by 7.8× and improves vLLM throughput by 11%–31% over FP8 tables.
It loses about 1 PopQA point at 1.50 bits per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models.
papers.selection_reason: Gate-aware quantization of conditional LLM memory drastically cuts table memory and improves throughput while preserving long-tail fact recall.
papers.title: Let the Gate Decide: Per-Lookup Precision for Quantized Conditional Memory in LLMs
papers.tldr: GateRQ improves quantized conditional memory by allocating extra precision per lookup based on the row’s gate value, preserving long-tail facts while reducing memory and improving throughput.

papers.abstract: Solving long-horizon agentic tasks requires language agents to interact with their environments over multiple steps, and reliable performance often comes from the expensive capable models available through cloud providers. Meanwhile, alternative efficient models with inferior performance but a much lower cost are emerging, including lower-tier cloud models and smaller open-weights models deployable on local hardware. This raises a natural question that remains less explored than traditional query-level routing: can capable and efficient models collaborate within a single long-horizon agentic task to substantially reduce cost while preserving task accuracy? In this paper, we systematically investigate key design choices for such collaboration through model handoffs, where one model takes over from another, focusing on handoff direction and context transfer. We find that efficient-to-capable handoffs generally underperform capable-only execution with limited or even no cost reduction, whereas capable-to-efficient handoffs at suitable stages of task progress largely preserve or even improve accuracy while substantially reducing cost. These findings suggest that a one-time, simple, well-timed handoff strategy is good enough for cost-effective agent collaboration, motivating AgentBaton, a lightweight detector that learns when to hand off from recurring patterns in task progress. Across 11 model pairs and two representative benchmarks, AgentBaton reduces API costs by 65.9% on average while largely preserving task accuracy, with accuracy gains of up to 8.8 percentage points over capable-only execution. Experiments across various reasoning-effort settings further show that AgentBaton extends the empirical accuracy-cost Pareto frontier.
authors: Junlong Li, Jindong Jiang, Yonggan Fu, Jiarui Yao, Hanrong Ye, Wonmin Byeon, Peter Belcak, Hao Zhang, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Studies collaboration between capable and efficient models through model handoffs within a single agentic task.
Finds that capable-to-efficient handoffs are generally more effective than efficient-to-capable handoffs.
Introduces a lightweight detector that learns recurring task-progress patterns to trigger a one-time handoff.
Across 11 model pairs and two benchmarks, reduces API costs by 65.9% on average while largely preserving accuracy.
Reports accuracy improvements of up to 8.8 percentage points and extends the empirical accuracy-cost Pareto frontier across reasoning-effort settings.
papers.selection_reason: Capable-to-efficient model handoffs in long-horizon agentic tasks; relevant to cost-efficient LLM inference and deployment.
papers.title: AgentBaton: Efficient Model Collaboration in Agentic Tasks
papers.tldr: AgentBaton lowers the cost of long-horizon agent tasks by handing control from capable to efficient models at well-timed progress points while largely preserving or improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Distributed speculative decoding has emerged as a promising approach for device--server collaborative large language model (LLM) inference, but its decoding speedup is often limited by the vocabulary-scale communication overhead. In existing distributed speculative decoding methods, exact rejection sampling requires transmitting full token distributions over the LLM vocabulary between the device and the server, which becomes costly in bandwidth-constrained environments. To address this issue, we propose DISCO, a communication-efficient framework for distributed speculative decoding, that eliminates vocabulary-scale distribution transfer while preserving the exact target distribution. DISCO achieves this by introducing a server-side replica of the draft small language model (SLM), which enables the server to locally obtain the draft-side distribution required for rejection sampling. As a result, DISCO exchanges only drafted token indices and scalar probability values between the device and the server. Experimental results on multiple datasets show that DISCO consistently achieves higher decoding speedup than existing distributed speculative decoding methods, particularly under stringent bandwidth constraints.
authors: Joohyun Shin, Byeonghyeon Park, Keumseo Ryum, Joonhyuk Kang
bullets: Targets bandwidth overhead in distributed speculative decoding caused by transmitting full vocabulary distributions.
Uses a server-side replica of the draft small language model to locally reconstruct the draft distribution for exact rejection sampling.
Communicates only drafted token indices and scalar probability values between device and server.
Experiments across multiple datasets show higher decoding speedups than existing methods, especially under stringent bandwidth constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Communication-efficient distributed speculative decoding for LLM inference directly targets inference latency and bandwidth reduction under efficient AI.
papers.title: Distributed LLM Inference via Communication-Efficient Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: DISCO accelerates device–server LLM inference by preserving exact speculative decoding while replacing vocabulary-scale communication with compact token and probability exchanges.

papers.abstract: Low-bit weight--activation quantization reduces the memory and computation needed to deploy large language models, but activation rounding can still degrade accuracy after calibration. Reconstruction from rounded inputs cannot distinguish activations within the same quantization bin. We propose ResCom, a low-rank correction that uses the activation rounding residual to compensate for the resulting layer-output error. An output-aware calibration procedure selects residual directions by their contribution to output reconstruction and computes the correction in closed form, without gradient training or updates to the calibrated weights. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weights and activations, rank-32 attention corrections reduce WikiText-2 perplexity from 7.708 to 7.147, improve MMLU by 2.89 percentage points, and raise five-shot GSM8K accuracy from 23.96 to 36.16 percent. Evaluations on models from 1B to 70B parameters and on held-out C4 test the method beyond this setting. The evaluated FP32 implementation adds 2.25 percent to 4K prefill time; a separate compact-storage implementation retains a 27.7 percent peak-memory reduction relative to FP16.
authors: Ning Yang, Bohan Cui, Zhuowen Liu, Yuting Wang
bullets: Targets accuracy loss caused by activation rounding in weight–activation quantization.
Selects output-relevant residual directions during calibration and computes corrections in closed form without gradient training or changing calibrated weights.
On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weights and activations, rank-32 attention corrections improve WikiText-2 perplexity, MMLU, and five-shot GSM8K accuracy.
Evaluations span 1B–70B models and include held-out C4 testing.
The evaluated FP32 version adds 2.25% to 4K prefill time; compact storage preserves a 27.7% peak-memory reduction versus FP16.
papers.selection_reason: Activation residual compensation for low-bit LLM quantization; reduces memory and computation for LLM deployment.
papers.title: ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization
papers.tldr: ResCom improves low-bit LLM quantization by using activation-rounding residuals to correct layer-output errors with a lightweight, training-free low-rank adjustment.

papers.abstract: AI applications often invoke a model before they determine whether inference is necessary. That default is useful for ambiguous generative tasks, but it is poorly matched to work that is structured, deterministic, policy-bound, lookup-oriented, or directly verifiable. KORA introduces deterministic-first execution control: a pre-inference control layer that represents requests as task paths, attempts deterministic or structured routes first, validates route outcomes, records telemetry, and escalates to a model-candidate path only when deterministic handling is insufficient. This paper presents KORA as a deterministic-first execution-control architecture and reports bounded evidence from reproducible benchmark and validation workloads. In a reproducible 100-task deterministic-heavy benchmark, KORA-controlled execution avoided 80 of 100 simulated model invocations versus a naive direct baseline, with zero mismatches in the deterministic subset. The workload is intentionally deterministic-heavy: it includes categories such as FAQ lookup, policy/rule checking, schema or format validation, deterministic transformation, and a smaller set of model-needed ambiguous or generative tasks. A separate synthetic customer-support local/no-network validation workload demonstrates route measurement and avoided model-call accounting in an application-shaped setting. These results support bounded model-invocation reduction and validation visibility in documented workloads. They do not establish production behavior, real-provider outcomes, energy outcomes, API-cost reduction, or broad superiority.
bullets: Targets structured, policy-bound, lookup-oriented, and verifiable workloads that do not always need inference.
Uses a pre-inference control layer with task paths, deterministic/structured routing, validation, telemetry, and model escalation.
Avoided 80 of 100 simulated model invocations with zero deterministic-subset mismatches in a deterministic-heavy benchmark.
A synthetic local customer-support workload demonstrated route measurement and avoided-call accounting.
Evidence is bounded to documented workloads; production, cost, energy, and broad-superiority claims remain unestablished.
papers.selection_reason: Pre-inference deterministic-first execution control reduces unnecessary model invocations, directly supporting efficient AI goals of reducing compute and latency.
papers.title: KORA: Deterministic-First Execution Control for AI Workloads
papers.tldr: KORA reduces unnecessary AI model calls by trying validated deterministic routes before escalating ambiguous tasks to a model.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) enable flexible generation through iterative masked denoising, but incur substantial inference cost because token representations are repeatedly recomputed across denoising steps. Existing cache-based methods reduce this cost by reusing intermediate results across denoising steps and recomputing only a subset of positions at each step, chosen either on a fixed schedule or by heuristic signals of change. Our trajectory experiments instead point to decoding trajectory as the more relevant quantity. Cached generation remains accurate when it stays close to the full-denoising trajectory, with errors concentrated around unmask-order deviations and reduced as longer reference prefixes are recovered. This suggests a more direct principle: limiting representation error helps, but keeping generation on the full-denoising trajectory is a more direct route to accurate decoding. We therefore formulate efficient dLLM inference as trajectory-guided querying. Rather than broadly repairing representation error, we use full-denoising trajectories to supervise which unresolved positions should receive limited fresh computation. Based on this formulation, we introduce TRACEQUERY, a lightweight sparse decoding framework that predicts a small set of near-future trajectory-relevant positions, queries only those candidates, and lets the backbone select which one to commit from their fresh predictions. TRACEQUERY delivers the strongest quality-computation trade-off among cache-based approaches, sustaining high accuracy with substantially fewer fresh token computations, and generalizes across tasks, model variants, and families. Code: https://github.com/fish1928/tracequery.git
bullets: dLLMs are expensive because token representations are repeatedly recomputed during iterative denoising.
The authors find that decoding accuracy depends more directly on staying close to the full-denoising trajectory than merely limiting representation error.
TRACEQUERY predicts a small set of future trajectory-relevant positions, computes fresh predictions only for them, and lets the backbone choose which position to commit.
It achieves the strongest quality–computation trade-off among cache-based methods and generalizes across tasks, model variants, and model families.
The approach relies on full-denoising trajectories as supervision for efficient sparse querying.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces TraceQuery, a trajectory-guided sparse decoding framework for diffusion LLMs to reduce recomputation costs during inference.
papers.title: TraceQuery: learning what to recompute from full-denoising trajectory in diffusion language models
papers.tldr: TRACEQUERY accelerates diffusion language model decoding by using full-denoising trajectories to predict which masked positions need fresh computation, preserving accuracy with fewer token updates.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) impose substantial computation and memory costs as context sizes increase, motivating methods that compress a context into a shorter representation before inference. Existing soft-prompt compression methods typically use the same Transformer backbone as used in the target model, where producing the compressed representation leads to significant latency overheads. This restricts them to the offline setting where context is compressed once and then reused across many queries. We propose the Boa Compressor, a plug-and-play online context compressor built on a Mamba state-space model (SSM) that encodes arbitrary-length context in a single linear-time pass, producing a representation on which we condition a frozen target LLM. The SSM is trained by distillation, matching the next-token logit distribution from the LLM ingesting the full context (as teacher) to the same LLM ingesting the compressed representation (as the student). At equal compression ratios, Boa matches or surpasses the performance of existing state-of-the-art offline compression baselines, while being an order of magnitude faster than Transformer-based implementations, thereby reducing end-to-end latency rather than adding compression time overhead. We demonstrate that Boa also scales well to longer contexts and to compression ratios as aggressive as 16x. By enabling effective compression that is cheap enough to run on every query at inference time, Boa becomes a practical and general tool for efficient long-context inference.
bullets: Addresses the latency and memory costs of long contexts and the overhead of Transformer-based compression.
Distills a state-space encoder to match the target LLM’s next-token distributions from full versus compressed context.
Matches or surpasses state-of-the-art offline compression at equal compression ratios.
Runs an order of magnitude faster than Transformer-based compressors, reducing end-to-end latency.
Scales to longer contexts and compression ratios up to 16×, supporting per-query compression.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Boa Compressor, a linear-time context compression method using Mamba SSMs, directly addressing memory and latency in LLM inference.
papers.title: Linear-Time Context Compression with State-Space Encoding
papers.tldr: Boa Compressor uses a Mamba state-space model to compress arbitrary-length contexts in one linear-time pass, enabling fast online long-context inference with a frozen LLM.

papers.abstract: KV caching reduces the serving cost of large language models (LLMs), but the growing KV cache footprint is increasingly exceeds GPU and host-memory capacity. Therefore, people use SSD to expand the KV cache storage capacity with high I/O bandwidth. However, in production LLM workload, such as multi-round conversation and LLM agents, the total amount of KV cache writes significantly exceeds SSD capacity, shortening SSD lifetime from years to months. To improve SSD lifetime, a natural solution is to reduce the KV cache writes by gating the KV cache writes via historical access patterns. However, that significantly lowers the KV cache hit rate (and increase the LLM serving cost) since KV caches from different attention types might have identical historical access pattern but different future access patterns. Our insight is that, to reduce KV cache writes without hurting KV cache hit rate, one need to not only consider the access pattern, but also application-level information such as the attention type of KV cache. Leveraging this observation, we propose Gandalf , the first SSD KV cache offloading system with SSD life time awareness. Gandalf prioritize the admission of full-attention KV cache into SSD over the cache generated by other types of attention, which significantly increases SSD lifetime without sacrificing cache hit rate. Our evaluation shows that Gandalf extends the SSD lifetime by 7.3X on average, while having negligible impact on cache hit rate across multiple workload traces and wide range of hardware capacity. Gandalf design can be extended to other flash-based storage, such as High Bandwidth Flash (HBF).
bullets: LLM KV-cache writes can overwhelm SSD capacity in workloads such as multi-round conversations and LLM agents, reducing device lifetime from years to months.
Write gating based only on historical access patterns can lower cache hit rates because different attention types may share similar histories but have different future reuse.
Gandalf combines access patterns with application-level attention-type information to guide SSD cache admission.
It prioritizes full-attention KV caches over caches from other attention types, reducing writes while preserving cache effectiveness.
Across multiple workload traces and hardware capacities, Gandalf extends SSD lifetime by 7.3× on average with negligible cache-hit-rate impact; the design may also apply to high-bandwidth flash.
papers.selection_reason: SSD-aware KV cache offloading directly targets KV cache and memory efficiency in LLM serving.
papers.title: Gandalf: Flash Shall Not Die! Increasing Flash Storage Lifetime for KV Cache Offloading in LLM Serving
papers.tldr: Gandalf extends SSD lifetime for LLM KV-cache offloading by prioritizing full-attention caches without meaningfully reducing cache hit rates.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become a key technology for serving large-scale personalized large language models and diffusion models in the cloud. However, the co-occurrence patterns, resource contention relationships, and evolutionary regularities of adapters under production inference workloads have not been systematically or quantitatively studied. Based on GenTD26, Alibaba's production diffusion model inference dataset, this paper adopts a graph-theoretic framework to construct an adapter co-occurrence network and conducts a characterization from both static structure and dynamic evolution. Our main findings are as follows. (1) The co-occurrence network is extremely sparse, and adapter usage frequency follows a significant heavy-tailed distribution. (2) Introducing the first adapter incurs a 66.1% execution-latency overhead, with diminishing marginal costs afterwards. (3) Co-occurrence relationships are driven by base models: in 90.6% of multi-adapter requests, all adapters share the same dominant base model; 66.2% of significant co-occurrence edges connect same-model adapter pairs; and in 85.8% of multi-adapter requests, all adapter pairs form significant co-occurrence edges. (4) The adapter ecosystem exhibits a core-periphery bipolar structure, with a weekly Jaccard similarity of 0.696 at the model level and a churn rate of 54.5% for the top-10 hottest models within a 12-hour window. Based on these findings, we propose a preloading strategy built on top-k co-occurrence statistics; offline experiments show that it covers 81.0% of test-set co-occurrence pairs at k=3, and sensitivity analyses across frequency thresholds and time windows verify the robustness of the conclusions. These results provide a data-driven basis for cache preloading, adaptive scheduling, and GPU memory management in LoRA inference services.
bullets: Adapter usage is highly heavy-tailed, while the co-occurrence network is extremely sparse.
Adding the first adapter causes substantial latency overhead, with diminishing marginal costs for additional adapters.
Co-occurrence is strongly organized by base models: most multi-adapter requests use adapters from the same dominant model.
The adapter ecosystem has a core-periphery structure with both persistent model-level patterns and rapid turnover among the hottest models.
A top-k co-occurrence preloading strategy covers 81.0% of test co-occurrence pairs at k=3 in offline evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes data-driven preloading strategy for LoRA adapters to improve inference efficiency, relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Co-occurrence Patterns of LoRA Adapters in Production Diffusion Model Inference Services
papers.tldr: A graph-based analysis of production LoRA usage reveals sparse, base-model-driven co-occurrence patterns and supports top-k preloading for more efficient diffusion inference services.

papers.abstract: Attention over tens of thousands of visual tokens dominates the inference of video diffusion transformers (DiTs). Existing methods reduce this cost through sparsity, low precision, or both, but use a single precision for all kept tiles. We observe that the output error introduced by approximation varies widely across tiles. Many tiles can be skipped with little error, others must be computed but gain little beyond low precision, and a few retain substantial error even at low precision. We present Triage, a training-free attention method that assigns each tile one of three approximation tiers: skipping it by replacing it with its block means, skimming it in NVFP4, or refining it with NVFP4 residual correction. A lightweight router predicts each tile's error under each tier from block statistics and moves a tile to a more accurate tier only when the predicted error reduction justifies the extra compute, with a single price setting this trade-off. A fused kernel executes all three tiers in a single pass on the FP4 tensor cores of RTX Blackwell GPUs. Across Wan2.2, HunyuanVideo, and LTX-2.5, Triage accelerates end-to-end generation by up to 2.32x over dense FlashAttention, and in each of five settings it runs faster than every baseline while reaching 0.3-3.0 dB higher PSNR than the highest-PSNR baseline.
authors: Yeonjae Kim, Omin Kwon, Seong Hoon Seo, Jae W. Lee
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of attention over tens of thousands of video tokens.
Assigns each tile to skip, NVFP4 skim, or NVFP4 residual refinement.
A lightweight router uses block statistics and one price parameter to balance error against compute.
A fused kernel executes all tiers in one pass on RTX Blackwell FP4 tensor cores.
Across three video diffusion models and five settings, it achieves up to 2.32× end-to-end speedup and 0.3–3.0 dB higher PSNR than the strongest baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Tiered attention-tile skipping and low-precision refinement for video diffusion transformers, directly relevant to efficient attention and token/tile pruning.
papers.title: Triage: Skip, Skim, or Refine Attention Tiles in Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: Triage speeds up video diffusion attention by adaptively skipping, low-precision computing, or refining each tile based on its predicted error.

papers.abstract: Uniform frame sampling can miss brief evidence in sparse-event videos when the VLM sees only K frames. We propose EARS (Evidence-Aware Retrieval via Sound and motion), a training-free, query-free front-end that ranks frames using optical-flow motion and audio energy, then applies temporal non-maximum suppression for diversity. The evidence score alone has frame-level AP 0.39; used only to select frames for the VLM, EARS with temporal diversity reaches localization AP 0.94, compared with 0.88 under Uniform sampling. In the updated matched study, at K = 1 EARS reaches XD-subset F1 0.660 versus 0.614 for centered Uniform (the paired interval includes zero); earlier backbone studies use separate protocols. On mostly-silent UCF-Crime, however, EARS slightly trails Uniform. A single configuration is used across both benchmarks; the new controls do not repeat the original held-out search. EARS therefore targets low-budget videos whose salient evidence aligns with motion or audio; on dense narratives or stealthy events, uniform or semantic selection remains preferable, and cheap modality statistics cannot reliably route between them. Code: https://github.com/mikeslin-ir/EARS
bullets: Targets sparse-event videos where uniform sampling may miss brief evidence under a frame budget.
Training-free, query-free retrieval ranks frames by optical-flow motion and audio energy, then applies temporal non-maximum suppression for diversity.
With temporal diversity, EARS achieves localization AP 0.94 versus 0.88 for uniform sampling; at K=1, XD-subset F1 is 0.660 versus 0.614, with an interval including zero.
Performance slightly trails uniform sampling on mostly-silent UCF-Crime videos.
Scope is limited: uniform or semantic selection may be better for dense narratives or stealthy events, and modality statistics cannot reliably choose the strategy.
papers.selection_reason: Evidence-aware frame retrieval for budgeted video reasoning; fits video understanding and efficiency.
papers.title: EARS: Evidence-Aware Retrieval via Sound and Motion for Budgeted Video Reasoning
papers.tldr: EARS improves low-budget video reasoning by selecting diverse frames using motion and audio cues, outperforming uniform sampling when salient events align with these signals.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models keep the KV of past chunks as retrieval memory so that revisited places stay consistent. On a single consumer machine (one RTX 4090, 32 GiB of host memory, one NVMe SSD), long sessions with such memory hit two walls. The first is capacity: the KV of Matrix-Game 2.0 exhausts host memory after 45 seconds of video in bf16 and after 2.8 minutes in int4. The second is the model's positional horizon of 4.3 minutes. We show that this memory is capacity-bound rather than bandwidth-bound and that its access set is known before compute, because the camera pose is an input. An analytical model built on these observations predicts spill points to within one chunk and classifies zero versus non-zero stalls correctly on held-out configurations. Guided by it, WorldPager stores int4 KV in a GPU/DRAM/NVMe hierarchy instead of recomputing it, prefetches each chunk's memory from the extrapolated pose, never waits on a miss, and writes back in the background; to our knowledge, it is the first to place the KV memory of an interactive world model on an NVMe tier with zero-stall prefetching. With training-free position handling, it generates 37.5 minutes of video continuously with zero stalls and constant host memory, at about 9.5 frames per second. On a sealed test set, int4 storage shows no measurable quality loss; on long-gap revisits it lowers image quality by about one MUSIQ point.
bullets: Addresses host-memory exhaustion and the model’s limited positional horizon during long interactive sessions.
Uses an analytical access model based on known camera poses to predict spill points and classify potential stalls.
Stores KV memory in a GPU/DRAM/NVMe hierarchy, prefetches before computation, avoids waiting on misses, and writes back asynchronously.
Generates 37.5 minutes of continuous video at about 9.5 FPS with zero stalls and constant host memory on a single RTX 4090 system.
Reports no measurable quality loss with int4 storage on a sealed test set, but about a one-point MUSIQ drop for long-gap revisits.
papers.selection_reason: Presents tiered memory and zero-stall prefetching for interactive world model KV caches, relevant to efficient inference and world model deployment.
papers.title: WorldPager: Zero-Stall Tiered Memory for Long-Horizon World Models on a Single Consumer GPU
papers.tldr: WorldPager enables continuous, zero-stall long-horizon world-model video by paging int4 KV memory across GPU, DRAM, and NVMe with pose-guided prefetching.

papers.abstract: Deploying large vision-language models (LVLMs) on resource-constrained embodied agents for 3D visual question answering necessitates cloud-edge collaboration. However, offloading massive visual data to the cloud over bandwidth-limited and noisy channels introduces severe latency and transmission distortion. To address this, we propose TP-JSCC, an efficient token pruning and joint source-channel coding method for LVLMs-based 3D-VQA in Cloud-Edge Collaboration. First, we develop a Local and Global Semantics-based Hybrid Token Pruning (LGS-HTP) module to significantly reduce the visual token count. By decoupling foreground-background tokens and jointly selecting local and global semantics, LGS-HTP effectively reduces redundancy while preserving reasoning-critical tokens. Second, we introduce a lightweight Token Joint Source-Channel Coding (T-JSCC) module to further compress the pruned tokens and ensure their robust transmission over error-prone channels. By employing lightweight cascaded linear layers and Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)-adaptive mechanism, this module adapts to fluctuating channel conditions while maintaining minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments on ScanQA and SQA3D datasets indicate the exceptional efficiency and robustness of our approach. Specifically, on ScanQA validation set, the LGS-HTP module could achieve 90% pruning ratio while incurring less than a 1% CIDEr loss. Building on this, the T-JSCC further compresses the tokens by 18 times, resulting in an overall 180 times data volume reduction for robust transmission, while saving 90% in computational complexity for LVLM deployment. Our code is available at https://github.com/yuanhui0325/TP-JSCC.
authors: Zhengxin Li, Chongzhen Tian, Hui Yuan, Hao Liu, Sam Kwong
bullets: Targets latency and distortion caused by offloading large 3D visual inputs from resource-constrained agents.
LGS-HTP jointly selects local and global semantic tokens while separating foreground and background information.
T-JSCC applies lightweight compression with SNR adaptation to handle changing channel conditions.
On ScanQA validation, it prunes 90% of tokens with less than 1% CIDEr loss and achieves 18× further compression.
The combined approach reduces transmitted data volume by 180× and deployment computational complexity by 90%, as reported on ScanQA and SQA3D.
papers.selection_reason: Token pruning and joint source-channel coding for LVLMs in 3D-VQA; directly fits efficient AI.
papers.title: TP-JSCC: Efficient Token Pruning and Joint Source-Channel Coding for LVLMs-based 3D-VQA in Cloud-Edge Collaboration
papers.tldr: TP-JSCC enables efficient and robust cloud-edge 3D-VQA by pruning redundant visual tokens and compressing the remainder for noisy-channel transmission.

papers.abstract: In the past few years, Vision Transformer (ViT) has achieved excellent performance in the field of computer vision. However, there still some problems remain. For instance, ViTs heavily rely on large-scale training data since they simply contain a large number of trainable parameters, which slows down their learning efficiency and limits their applicability in resource-constrained scenarios. In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning model, namely All-Convolutional Self-Attention Network (ACSAN), which applies convolution operations to replace fully-connected matrices multiplications in the ViT framework. To implement ACSAN, we firstly design Dynamic Convolutional Self-Attention (DCSA) as the basic module, which employs multi-scale dilated convolutions to generate Query, Key, and Value. We defined spatial self-attention and channel self-attention to generate attention features respectively. The two attention features are finally merged as the output of the DCSA module. Based on DCSA, we then construct the basic ACSAN block. Comparing with ViT, we use DCSA to replace the regular self-attention operations, and use convolution layers to replace MLPs. To evaluate the performance of the proposed method, we train ACSAN on three widely-used image classification databases, i.e. CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1k, from scratch. Experimental results show that ACSAN achieves excellent classification accuracy comparing with standard ViT with comparable or fewer parameters, as well as other state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies verify that each component contributes positively to the final performance.
authors: Zimian Wei, Tianqi Zhang, Hengyue Pan
bullets: Targets ViT’s reliance on large training datasets and many trainable parameters, which limits resource-constrained use.
Introduces Dynamic Convolutional Self-Attention (DCSA), using multi-scale dilated convolutions to generate queries, keys, and values.
Combines spatial and channel self-attention features within each DCSA module.
Builds ACSAN by replacing standard self-attention with DCSA and MLPs with convolutional layers.
Trained from scratch on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1k; reports accuracy comparable to or better than standard ViT and other state-of-the-art methods with comparable or fewer parameters.
papers.selection_reason: All-convolutional self-attention network reduces ViT parameter and computation overhead; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: ACSAN: All-Convolutional Self-Attention Network Integrating Convolutional Operations with Vision Transformer
papers.tldr: ACSAN replaces ViT’s fully connected operations with convolution-based self-attention to improve data and parameter efficiency while maintaining strong image-classification performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models incur substantial training and inference costs in personalized search and recommendation, as growing interaction histories lengthen request inputs and repeatedly expose the same item text to the model. We propose \textbf{C}omposable and \textbf{R}eusable \textbf{I}tem \textbf{M}emory (CRIM), a framework that separates item-level semantic encoding from request-level history modeling. A small set of learnable summary tokens compresses each item into compact continuous memories, while segment-level readout tokens (REC tokens) introduce predictive supervision within the interaction history. These memories are independent of users and queries and can therefore be reused across requests. At inference time, CRIM composes cached memories in interaction order and incorporates an optional query to produce a personalized retrieval representation, reducing repeated item-text encoding while retaining request-dependent contextual modeling. We further introduce a joint training mechanism that combines cached memories with sampled live re-encoding. Re-encoding only a few history items per request allows the retrieval objective to jointly optimize the item and request encoders at limited computational cost, while periodic cache refreshes maintain consistency. Extensive evaluation and cost analysis on MovieLens-1M, Qilin, and our new LazSeq dataset show that CRIM achieves state-of-the-art retrieval performance with substantially lower inference costs at the same backbone scale, while limiting item re-encoding during joint training. We will publicly release our code and dataset.
authors: Haolin Li, Haipeng Zhang, Mang Li, Zhaohui Xia, Xun Zhu, Miao Li, Yu Zhang, Ji Wu
bullets: Addresses rising training and inference costs caused by long interaction histories and repeated item-text encoding.
Separates item semantic encoding from request-level modeling using learnable summary tokens and predictive REC tokens.
Composes cached, user- and query-independent item memories in interaction order, with an optional query for personalization.
Jointly trains cached memories with limited live re-encoding and periodic cache refreshes to maintain consistency.
Evaluations on MovieLens-1M, Qilin, and LazSeq report state-of-the-art retrieval with substantially lower inference costs at the same backbone scale.
papers.selection_reason: Cached item memories reduce repeated item-text encoding and inference cost in LLM-based retrieval, matching memory-efficient inference and LLM external-memory interests.
papers.title: CRIM: Composable and Reusable Item Memory for Efficient Personalized Retrieval
papers.tldr: CRIM makes personalized retrieval more efficient by caching compact, reusable item memories while preserving request-specific history modeling.

papers.abstract: Adaptive robot perception systems must balance detector accuracy, inference latency, and energy consumption, particularly when high ambient temperatures cause processors to thermally throttle. We propose Thermal-Headroom Routing (THR), a lightweight model-selection policy that forecasts processor temperature using a closed-form RC thermal model and excludes detector configurations predicted to cross a throttling threshold. We evaluate THR with four YOLO11 configurations across seven real-world perception traces, eight ambient temperatures, and 20 randomized seeds, comparing it with latency-aware routing, fixed-threshold thermostats, duty caps, and a matched-compute-budget control. At ambient temperatures of 45-55 degrees C and a tight inference deadline, THR eliminates throttling in simulation, reduces deadline misses by 3.9-7.5 percentage points, and reduces energy per on-time frame by approximately 12-13% relative to a latency-belief router. A separate experiment using deadline-paced, nonoverlapping frame execution yields miss-rate reductions of 6.2-9.5 percentage points. A tuned thermostat or duty cap can match THR at a fixed operating point; predictive routing is most useful when ambient conditions or calibrated thermal parameters differ from those used to tune static policies. Measurements on an Apple M5 support the single-node heating approximation but do not validate hardware throttling. The results characterize the conditions under which thermal forecasting improves the efficiency and timeliness of resource-constrained robot perception.
authors: Sparsh Roy, Kevin Zhou, Arhaan Shah, Shreyan Garg, Vihaan Joshi-Apte, Maxim Kudryashov, Nanda Cheruvanthala
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between detection accuracy, latency, and energy when high temperatures cause processor throttling.
Uses a closed-form RC thermal model to predict temperature and avoids detector configurations likely to exceed a throttling threshold.
Evaluated four YOLO11 configurations across seven perception traces, eight ambient temperatures, and 20 randomized seeds against static and latency-aware baselines.
At 45–55°C with tight deadlines, it eliminates simulated throttling, lowers deadline misses, and cuts energy per on-time frame relative to a latency-belief router.
Predictive routing is most beneficial when operating conditions or thermal parameters differ from those used to tune static policies; hardware throttling itself was not validated.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Thermal-Headroom Routing (THR), a lightweight model-selection policy for robot perception that forecasts processor temperature to avoid thermal throttling. This addresses efficiency and timeliness in resource-constrained AI systems.
papers.title: Thermal-Headroom Routing for Efficient Robot Perception in Extreme Heat
papers.tldr: Thermal-Headroom Routing uses thermal forecasting to select robot perception models, reducing throttling, deadline misses, and energy use in extreme heat.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative video models have improved visual realism, making detection increasingly dependent on subtle temporal inconsistencies. However, these signals are weak and spatially localized, while most of the video content is redundant. This creates a fundamental mismatch: existing detectors rely on heavy backbones to model full videos, which leads to high computational cost and limited scalability. In this work, we rethink AI-generated video detection from a representation perspective. Instead of modeling entire videos, we restructure them into compact temporal slice representations that isolate informative temporal evolution. We introduce a lightweight framework using frequency-aware temporal slice consistency learning, where informative spatial rows and columns are aggregated over time to form slice-domain inputs. This reparameterization suppresses redundant appearance while preserving discriminative temporal dynamics, enabling efficient and targeted detection. By constructing slices from both high- and low-frequency regions, our method exposes complementary temporal artifacts, including unstable details and abnormal motion smoothness. We instantiate this idea in a Temporal Slice Consistency Network, which integrates task-driven slice localization, hierarchical positional encoding, and a lightweight Transformer to model cross-slice and cross-frequency dependencies. We further introduce AI-Artist, a new benchmark with artist-curated videos from recent high-fidelity generators, including Seedance and Kling. Experiments on GenVideo and AI-Artist show that our method achieves strong performance while requiring over 400$\times$ fewer model-forward FLOPs and 3.6$\times$ faster model inference than the strong video-based baseline ReStraV (2.9$\times$ faster end to end, including preprocessing), enabling scalable and practical deployment.
authors: Wei Shang, Zhiyuan Li, Shengfeng He
bullets: Targets the redundancy and high computational cost of full-video detectors, where generation artifacts are weak and spatially localized.
Aggregates informative spatial rows and columns over time into compact slices, suppressing appearance redundancy while preserving temporal dynamics.
Uses high- and low-frequency slices to capture complementary artifacts such as unstable details and abnormal motion smoothness.
Implements Temporal Slice Consistency Network with task-driven slice localization, hierarchical positional encoding, and a lightweight Transformer.
Evaluated on GenVideo and the new AI-Artist benchmark; reports strong performance, 3.6× faster model inference, and 2.9× faster end-to-end processing than ReStraV.
papers.selection_reason: Temporal-slice representation learning for AI-generated video detection fits video understanding and drastically reduces compute.
papers.title: Temporal Slice Learning for AI-Generated Video Detection with 400$\times$ Fewer FLOPs
papers.tldr: A lightweight temporal-slice representation detects AI-generated videos by focusing on subtle temporal artifacts, reducing model-forward computation by over 400× while accelerating inference.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) ground a referring expression in one of two ways. They decode the box as coordinate tokens, which is precise but takes one sequential step per token, or they regress it from a hidden state with a small head, which takes one step but loses accuracy at high IoU. The two fail differently: a head usually finds the right object but places its edges loosely, while coordinate tokens place edges precisely. We therefore use the regression head as a speculative drafter for the model's own coordinate tokens. Locus writes the head's box as coordinate tokens and checks them with the same backbone by Jacobi iteration over a shared image prefix. The fixed point is the model's greedy coordinate-token answer, reached in about 5.60 sequential passes on average instead of 18.46 decoding steps; head and verifier are one set of weights, trained jointly. On the 8 RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg splits, verification raises Locus-2B's Acc@0.9 from 54.87 for its own head to 59.13, and the one-pass head is ahead at Acc@0.5 of every published model with at most 3B parameters except Florence-2-L. Against Jag, the strongest open regression-head model, at its own size and training budget, Locus ties at Acc@0.5 and, with typical acceptance, gains +4.52 points at Acc@0.9, with paired significance tests. Exact answers come 1.5x faster than vLLM greedy-decoding the same coordinate tokens with the same weights; a pure regression head remains faster still.
bullets: Uses the regression head to draft a box, then verifies and refines its coordinate tokens via Jacobi iteration with the same backbone.
Reaches the model’s greedy coordinate-token answer in about 5.60 sequential passes on average, versus 18.46 decoding steps.
On RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg splits, verification improves Locus-2B Acc@0.9 from 54.87 to 59.13.
The one-pass head achieves strong Acc@0.5 performance, while verified outputs provide more precise box edges.
Exact answers are obtained 1.5× faster than vLLM greedy decoding with the same weights, though pure regression remains faster.
