papers.selection_reason: Draft-and-verify visual grounding improves VLM coordinate-token decoding; relevant to multimodal LLMs, spatial grounding, and inference efficiency.
papers.title: LOCUS: Locate Once, Check Until Settled. Draft-and-Verify Visual Grounding with a Box Head and Coordinate-Token Verification
papers.tldr: LOCUS combines a fast box-regression head with coordinate-token verification to improve high-IoU visual grounding while reducing sequential decoding passes.

papers.abstract: End-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue models enable natural, real-time spoken interactions with interruptions, backchannels, and overlapping speech. Prior evaluations have assessed diverse interaction capabilities and identified some degradation patterns across conversational turns. However, how model behavior evolves over extended sessions remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we address this gap by systematically characterizing long-session degradation and developing efficient methods to mitigate it. We introduce a closed-loop evaluation framework for long-session stability and apply it to several publicly available full-duplex speech models, revealing degradation over time in responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency. To mitigate this degradation, we propose a self-distillation-based training framework for lightweight LoRA adaptation that improves long-session stability with a small amount of additional training. We further introduce a two-resolution context (TRC) architecture that preserves recent interactions in full detail while compressing older interaction history into key-value representations. We evaluate our methods on three models with distinct architectures, assessing long-session stability, information retention, and computational efficiency. Across all three models, we show that LoRA adaptation mitigates performance degradation over ten-minute sessions, while adding TRC extends these gains beyond the training session length and reduces KV-cache growth by more than 90%.
authors: Junho Kim, CheHyun Lee, Donghun Kang, Youngho Cho, Dongwook Lee, Heeseung Kim, Sungroh Yoon
bullets: Long sessions cause declines in responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency.
A closed-loop evaluation framework measures stability, information retention, and efficiency over extended interactions.
Self-distillation with lightweight LoRA adaptation mitigates degradation across three architecturally distinct models.
Two-resolution context preserves recent exchanges in detail while compressing older history into key-value representations.
LoRA improves stability over ten-minute sessions, while TRC extends gains beyond training-session lengths and reduces KV-cache growth by more than 90%.
papers.selection_reason: Two-resolution context compression reduces KV-cache growth by over 90% for long-session models.
papers.title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Long-Session Degradation in Full-Duplex Speech Models
papers.tldr: The study diagnoses degradation in full-duplex speech models during extended conversations and improves stability using LoRA self-distillation plus compressed long-term context.

papers.abstract: Pretrained transformers spend a large share of their inference compute inside self-attention, yet the per-head query-key interaction is structurally low-rank by construction. We ask a diagnostic question: across layers and architectures, which heads actually use the full rank budget on real data, and which do not? We propose SVD-Attention, a post-hoc method that decomposes the per-head interaction matrix $M_h$ and scores every singular mode by both its spectral magnitude and its activation variance across tokens on a small calibration set. The score keeps the modes the head can amplify and that real data actually activates, and discards the rest; the resulting factorization is exact for the retained modes and needs no finetuning. Across seven pretrained models and five task types, the diagnostic finds a task-dependent pattern: redundancy sits in the early to middle layers for sentiment and image classification and for generation, and in the late layers for dense prediction and extractive question answering. It is also predictive: truncating the layers it flags costs at most $1.75$ F1, while truncating the same number of layers elsewhere in the same model costs up to $50$ F1. SVD-Attention is an analysis tool rather than a compression method: acting on it reduces inference FLOPs by $0.8$-$1.5\%$ on its own and by $8$-$11\%$ when composed with weight pruning, with $0$-$4\%$ change in task quality.
authors: Debopam Sanyal, Hongjie Chen, Riya Elizabeth Kuriyan, Arth Tak, Divya Kothandaraman, Akshay Mehra, Joshua Kimball, Alexey Tumanov
bullets: Motivation: Transformer self-attention is costly, but many heads may not use their full rank capacity.
Method: Decomposes each head’s interaction matrix and scores singular modes using spectral magnitude and token-level activation variance from a small calibration set.
Finding: Redundancy appears in early-to-middle layers for sentiment, image classification, and generation, but in late layers for dense prediction and extractive question answering.
Validation: Flagged-layer truncation costs at most 1.75 F1, versus up to 50 F1 when truncating the same number of other layers.
Scope: The method is primarily diagnostic; it yields 0.8–1.5% standalone FLOP reduction and 8–11% with weight pruning, with 0–4% task-quality change.
papers.selection_reason: SVD-based attention redundancy analysis enables layer truncation and inference FLOP reduction.
papers.title: SVD-Attention: Efficiently Analyzing Attention Blocks in Transformers
papers.tldr: SVD-Attention identifies which attention singular modes are both important and activated by real data, revealing task-dependent redundancy with minimal quality loss.

papers.abstract: GUI agents built on vision-language models interact with continuously evolving interfaces, yet conventional inference repeatedly recomputes representations of largely overlapping observations and histories. This mismatch makes multi-step interaction costly, while changes in context, interface content, and action arguments prevent straightforward cache reuse. We introduce GUIFlow, a framework for full-pipeline incremental inference in multi-image GUI interaction. Our central insight is that advancing a decision need not require rebuilding all supporting representations: each interaction step can instead selectively update computational states maintained across the trajectory. To support new decisions as the context evolves, GUIFlow adapts how past computation is reused: historical KV states are position-aligned and injected into the current context; change signals guide selective updates of current-observation states in the vision encoder and language model; and earlier action responses serve as speculative drafts verified by the target model. Together, these mechanisms enable cross-step reuse throughout visual encoding, prefill, and decoding without additional training, a separate draft model, or changes to the model-visible inputs and action interface. Experiments demonstrate up to 3.39x geometric-mean speedup across offline multi-image benchmarks and up to 3.49x in online, closed-loop interaction on OSWorld, while maintaining task performance broadly comparable to the dense baseline.
authors: Ye Li, Haoran Ding, Huanan Liu, Yuan Meng, Yutian Shen, Yuansong Wang, Kangye Ji, Hanyun Cui, Hongbo Duan, Chen Tang, Jiawei Li, Shu-Tao Xia, Zhi Wang
bullets: Addresses the high cost of repeatedly recomputing overlapping observations and histories during GUI interaction.
Reuses position-aligned historical KV states and uses change signals to selectively update vision-encoder and language-model states.
Speculatively reuses prior action responses and verifies them with the target model.
Provides full-pipeline reuse across visual encoding, prefill, and decoding without a separate draft model or additional training.
Reports up to 3.39× offline and 3.49× online speedups, with task performance broadly comparable to dense inference.
papers.selection_reason: Incremental KV reuse and selective state updates for efficient vision-language model inference.
papers.title: GUIFlow: Temporal Redundancy-Aware Incremental Inference for GUI Agents
papers.tldr: GUIFlow accelerates multi-step GUI agents by selectively reusing and updating computations across changing visual and interaction contexts, achieving substantial speedups without retraining or changing the agent interface.

papers.abstract: Reasoning language models generate thousands of tokens per answer, and generation speed is limited by memory bandwidth, so storing weights in two bits instead of bfloat16 can potentially make inference 8$\times$ cheaper. Two-bit methods are usually judged by perplexity and multiple-choice question-answering accuracy, both of which say little about whether a model can still reason through more difficult problems. We present ThinkBit, a strictly scalar two-bit framework built to preserve reasoning, in which every weight is an integer codeword times a bfloat16 scale shared by a group of weights. We first use a sensitivity metric to assign each layer a ternary, 2-bit, or 3-bit tier to allocate bitwidths optimally among layers. This is followed by a layerwise Gumbel-softmax-based scalar quantization algorithm that searches for optimal codewords block by block. Since a layerwise scheme does not capture how quantized layers interact with each other, we recalibrate scales, with the codewords frozen, using a knowledge-distillation-based loss against the teacher model. We then perform a short quantization-aware training (QAT) stage that lets the model mimic the base model's distribution by reassigning codewords. Finally, a paired reasoning test on training problems selects the final checkpoint between the recalibration stage and the QAT stage. On Qwen3-1.7B at matched size, our recalibrated checkpoint scores 46.7 on MATH-500 against 30.0 for EfficientQAT trained on the same data, and 73.0 after QAT on reasoning traces; at 0.52 GB it is smaller than every published 2-bit GGUF of the model yet more accurate on MATH-500. We show that this framework scales and up to 14B, a 3.74 GB model scores 94.8 on MATH-500, against 97.5 for the 29.5 GB bfloat16 model.
bullets: Targets the memory-bandwidth bottleneck of long-form reasoning by compressing model weights to roughly 2 bits.
Assigns ternary, 2-bit, or 3-bit precision per layer using sensitivity, then searches quantization codewords block by block with Gumbel-softmax.
Recalibrates shared scales using knowledge distillation and applies short quantization-aware training to better match the base model’s output distribution.
Uses paired reasoning tests to select between recalibration and QAT checkpoints rather than relying only on perplexity or multiple-choice accuracy.
On Qwen3-1.7B, reports 46.7 MATH-500 after recalibration and 73.0 after QAT; a 3.74 GB model reaches 94.8 versus 97.5 for the 29.5 GB bfloat16 model.
papers.selection_reason: Two-bit weight quantization with bitwidth allocation and scale recalibration reduces LLM memory footprint while preserving reasoning.
papers.title: ThinkBit: Search Codewords, Recalibrate Scales, Select by Reasoning
papers.tldr: ThinkBit is a scalar 2-bit quantization framework that preserves challenging mathematical reasoning through sensitivity-based bit allocation, codeword search, scale recalibration, and reasoning-guided checkpoint selection.

papers.abstract: Document layout analysis (DLA) faces a long-standing dilemma: existing methods either capture rich local details at prohibitive computational cost (e.g., Transformer-based approaches with quadratic complexity) or achieve efficient global modeling but sacrifice fine-grained structural awareness (e.g., state-space models). This trade-off hinders deployment in resource-constrained scenarios. We present LayoutMamba, a hybrid framework that synergistically combines sparse-attention Transformers for localized feature extraction (O(n) complexity) and the recurrent state-space mechanism of Mamba for dilution-free long-range dependency modeling across the 2D document canvas. Our two-stage paradigm first uses a lightweight Transformer encoder to hierarchically distill salient local semantics; second, Mamba propagates global contextual dependencies without attention dilution, enabling precise, efficient, and scalable layout understanding. We further identify a critical yet overlooked issue in existing DLA benchmarks: the inherent low-overlap distribution bias of layout objects, which we mitigate through a novel Geometric Overlap Penalty Loss (GOPLoss), a dual-optimization objective that minimizes redundant bounding box overlaps and encourages geometrically consistent predictions. Extensive experiments on PubLayNet and D4LA show that LayoutMamba surpasses state-of-the-art AP on PubLayNet with 8x fewer parameters and maintains leading performance on D4LA, ranking top-3 among published methods, achieving an unprecedented balance between accuracy, efficiency, and scalability. Our work pioneers a cognition-inspired paradigm for document analysis, advancing practical deployment in edge computing and resource-limited environments.
bullets: Targets the trade-off between Transformer-based detail and state-space-model efficiency in resource-constrained DLA.
Uses a two-stage design: a lightweight Transformer extracts local semantics, then Mamba models long-range 2D document dependencies.
Introduces Geometric Overlap Penalty Loss to reduce redundant bounding-box overlaps and improve geometric consistency.
Outperforms prior methods on PubLayNet with 8× fewer parameters and ranks among the top three published methods on D4LA.
Designed for scalable deployment, including edge and resource-limited environments.
papers.selection_reason: Hybrid Mamba-Transformer for efficient document layout analysis; fits efficient AI via reduced complexity.
papers.title: LayoutMamba: Efficient Document Layout Analysis with Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Networks
papers.tldr: LayoutMamba combines sparse-attention Transformers, Mamba, and geometric overlap regularization for efficient and accurate document layout analysis.

papers.abstract: Rubric-based evaluation asks which level of a rubric a response meets. It is usually done by prompting a large language model (LLM) as a judge, which needs a generative call per judgment and reads every level description, so its cost grows with the rubric. We present RubriX, a rubric judge whose architecture is inspired by contrastive language models (CLM): a LoRA-adapted encoder embeds the input and each level description, and a softmax over scaled cosine similarities gives a probability for every level without text generation. Trained on public rubric data and proprietary synthetic data, RubriX reaches 75.4% exact accuracy on held-out rubrics, against 57.1% for TypeSafe's Jev and 49.8% for a Qwen3-8B judge. On eight human-labelled benchmark sets it is within 6 percentage points of Jev's accuracy on most of them, while Jev keeps a larger lead on two and ranks responses best on average; against the results reported in the G-Eval paper, RubriX outperforms G-Eval with GPT-3.5 on every SummEval dimension and both QAGS subsets. With level embeddings cached, RubriX's latency stays at about 28 ms per judgment as level descriptions grow from 10 to 3,000 tokens, while Jev's (approximate network time subtracted) rises from 44 ms to 211 ms and the Qwen3-8B judge's from 32 ms to 516 ms, making RubriX 7.7x faster than Jev and 18.8x faster than the Qwen3-8B judge at 3,000 tokens per level.
bullets: Addresses the cost and latency of LLM-based rubric judging, which requires generation and processes all level descriptions.
Uses a LoRA-adapted encoder to embed responses and rubric levels, then predicts levels with a softmax over scaled cosine similarities.
Achieves 75.4% exact accuracy on held-out rubrics, exceeding the reported baselines in the abstract.
Remains about 28 ms per judgment as level descriptions grow to 3,000 tokens, substantially faster than Jev and a Qwen3-8B judge.
On human-labelled benchmarks, it is close to Jev on most sets, though Jev leads on two and ranks responses best on average.
papers.selection_reason: Non-autoregressive judge with substantially lower latency fits efficient-AI interests.
papers.title: RubriX: A Fast, Fine-Tunable Non-Autoregressive Rubric Judge
papers.tldr: RubriX is a fast, non-autoregressive rubric judge that classifies responses by matching them to rubric levels without generating text.

papers.abstract: Much of the information needed for data analysis is buried in text columns: an analyst may infer customer frustration from complaint text and use it to explain resolution time. We call workloads in which processing text columns is central to subsequent data analysis TADA (\emph{Text Analysis in Data Analytics}). In an agentic setting, the user's query dynamically specifies this processing, and answering it interleaves LLM-based semantic steps with exact SQL or Python operations. This mixed execution raises two design questions: which work should be neural and which symbolic, and which semantic outputs later steps can reuse. We address them for agent-planned TADA workflows with two complementary, query-driven semantic atoms. Each atom takes a sequence of text items and a natural-language query specifying the semantic task: \textbf{Tagging} returns one string per input item, while \textbf{Categorization} returns $M$ category objects over $N$ input items. Tagging results are materialized as a row-aligned column and Categorization results as a category table; SQL or Python then performs exact computation over this exposed state. We realize this interface in TADA-Agent, whose atoms run inside generated Python programs and internally handle inputs beyond a reliable context window. We evaluate TADA-Agent on TABench, a benchmark of 40 complete analysis requests over spreadsheet tables spanning workflow composition, input--output structure, and literature-grounded analytical scenarios. Against a semantic-operator baseline and relative to a held-out TADA reference run, TADA-Agent delivers comparable row-level semantic quality, has higher complete-artifact preservation estimates, and uses over an order of magnitude fewer semantic-model requests under the evaluated native execution paths.
authors: Jinxiang Xie, Zihao Li, Rui Ding, Bartuer Zhou, Shi Han, Dongmei Zhang
bullets: Targets text-analysis-in-data-analytics (TADA), where insights from text columns support downstream structured analysis.
Introduces Tagging for row-aligned labels and Categorization for category tables, both driven by natural-language queries.
Embeds these atoms in generated Python programs and handles inputs larger than a reliable context window.

On the 40-request TABench benchmark, it achieves comparable row-level semantic quality, higher estimated complete-artifact preservation, and over an order of magnitude fewer semantic-model requests than the evaluated baselines/reference paths.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces semantic-model requests via reusable semantic atoms, fitting efficient-AI interests.
papers.title: Semantic Atoms for Scalable Text Analysis in Data Analytics in the Era of LLM-Based Agents
papers.tldr: TADA-Agent uses two reusable LLM-driven semantic atoms to integrate text understanding with exact SQL/Python analysis for scalable, agent-planned data workflows.

papers.abstract: Recent generic reference-based image generation models natively support multiple conditions by concatenating all reference image and text tokens into a joint sequence processed by a single Diffusion Transformer (DiT). However, this versatile paradigm comes at an efficiency cost: accommodating multiple references leads to a token explosion, incurring massive $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ computational complexity. Most acceleration methods operate inside the DiT, showing limited capability in reducing spatial redundancy and failing to alleviate peak VRAM. While some pre-model token reduction alternatives exist, they inevitably introduce external models. This raises a question: Is it possible to achieve acceleration and memory savings while preserving compatibility with in-model techniques and requiring no additional parameters? In this work, we realize this goal by proposing the early Token reduction via Downsampled self-Probing (ToDoPro). By executing a few denoising steps on spatially $2\times$ downsampled reference images, this cheap probing stage utilizes the DiT model itself to effectively and efficiently extract reference token importance. Using the probed importance, we apply a hierarchical reduction before the main denoising stage: we completely discard low-importance tokens, substitute mid-importance tokens with their downsampled counterparts to cheaply preserve global context, and keep high-importance tokens. Experiments across three base models and two benchmarks demonstrate that our early reduction accelerates inference significantly and mitigates peak GPU memory. Furthermore, we can improve generation quality by safely filtering out noisy, uninformative reference tokens, enabling the model to concentrate its limited attention capacity on genuinely useful tokens. The code will be released at https://github.com/scy639/ToDoPro
authors: Caiyi Sun, Yujing Sun, Siu-Ming Yiu
bullets: Addresses token explosion and quadratic compute from combining multiple image and text references.
Runs a few denoising steps on 2× downsampled references to estimate token importance without adding external models or parameters.
Hierarchically discards low-importance tokens, downsamples mid-importance tokens, and preserves high-importance tokens before full denoising.
Experiments on three base models and two benchmarks show significant inference acceleration and reduced peak GPU memory.
Filtering noisy, uninformative tokens can improve quality by focusing attention on useful references.
papers.selection_reason: Early token reduction for diffusion transformers directly matches token pruning and eviction for efficient inference and memory savings.
papers.title: ToDoPro: Faster and Better Reference-Based Generation: Early Token Reduction via Downsampled Self-Probing
papers.tldr: ToDoPro uses the DiT itself to identify and reduce redundant reference tokens early, accelerating reference-based image generation while lowering peak memory and potentially improving quality.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal video fusion aims to generate temporally coherent videos with salient targets and rich structural details by integrating complementary information from heterogeneous sensors. However, existing video fusion methods commonly rely on optical flow estimation and feature warping for inter-frame alignment and cross-frame information aggregation to maintain temporal consistency, thereby introducing considerable computational overhead and making the fusion performance vulnerable to flow estimation errors. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an efficient multi-modal video fusion network with dynamic region-guided temporal interaction. Specifically, the proposed spatio-temporal interaction module leverages the Test-Time Training paradigm to model temporal dependencies with linear complexity. Building on this design, the module restricts temporal modeling to key dynamic regions in the video sequence, as static background regions provide limited temporal cues. By excluding low-variation tokens from unnecessary temporal interaction, this selective strategy contributes to improved fusion quality and temporal consistency. In addition, leveraging the strong ability of pretrained MAE features to capture global structural dependencies, we introduce a feature-level temporal consistency constraint to suppress local flickering by aligning the inter-frame variation directions of the fused and source videos. We further propose a new MAE-based temporal metric that quantifies directional distance between their temporal variations within dynamic regions. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared with existing state-of-the-art methods, our method achieves superior fusion quality and temporal consistency on multiple benchmark datasets, while exhibiting high computational efficiency under edge-device deployment settings.
authors: Jingxue Huang, Xiaosong Li, Yi Lin
bullets: Addresses the computational cost and error sensitivity of optical-flow-based frame alignment.
Uses test-time training for linear-complexity spatio-temporal interaction.
Focuses temporal modeling on dynamic regions while skipping low-variation background tokens.
Applies a pretrained-MAE-based consistency constraint to reduce local flickering.
Reports superior fusion quality and temporal consistency with high efficiency on edge-device settings across multiple benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient video fusion with dynamic region-guided token selection and linear-complexity temporal interaction directly fits efficient AI token pruning and efficient attention.
papers.title: Efficient Multi-modal Video Fusion Network with Dynamic Region-Guided Temporal Interaction
papers.tldr: An efficient multi-modal video fusion network improves temporal consistency by modeling only dynamic regions and enforcing feature-level temporal alignment without optical-flow warping.

papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as the dominant paradigm for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models. Standard all-layer LoRA applies adaptation throughout the transformer, despite heterogeneous contributions from its components. In this work, we conduct a systematic mechanistic interpretability analysis to understand how LoRA affects model internals. We observe that LoRA's adaptation effect is highly non-uniform, with significant component-wise and layer-wise sparsity. Most critically, we find that important layers are highly task-dependent, with limited overlap across tasks. Motivated by these insights, we propose Adaptive-LoRA, a calibration-driven method that automatically identifies task-specific layers via frozen-base zero-ablation, enabling efficient layer selection without exhaustive search. Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-1.5B across 11 diverse reasoning tasks demonstrate that Adaptive-LoRA outperforms full-layer LoRA while using only 30% of layers, achieving a $3.5\times$ reduction in adapter parameters. This work bridges mechanistic interpretability and practical efficiency, providing both fundamental insights and a principled approach for adaptive fine-tuning.
authors: Fei Zuo, Yizhou Huang, Kezhi Wang
bullets: LoRA’s effects are highly non-uniform across transformer components and layers.
Important layers vary substantially by task, with limited cross-task overlap.
Adaptive-LoRA uses frozen-base zero-ablation calibration to select task-specific layers without exhaustive search.
On Qwen2.5-1.5B across 11 reasoning tasks, it outperforms full-layer LoRA while using 30% of the layers.
This reduces adapter parameters by 3.5×, though the evaluation scope is limited to the reported model and tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Presents layer-sparse adaptive LoRA for parameter-efficient LLM fine-tuning; fits efficiency-oriented AI methods.
papers.title: Mechanistic Insights into LoRA: Layer Sparsity for Adaptive Fine-Tuning via Path Patching
papers.tldr: Adaptive-LoRA identifies task-relevant layers for fine-tuning, matching or exceeding full-layer LoRA with substantially fewer adapter parameters.

papers.abstract: Vision--language--action (VLA) models increasingly run on edge devices aboard robots, where inference latency constrains closed-loop robot control. However, it remains unclear how to design VLA models, their inference software and edge hardware so that robots can run VLA inference in real time. Most VLA models report only task success, while prior studies cover limited action-generation strategies, divide inference into at most three stages, and lack comparisons of inference optimizations on the same models.benchmarking 18 open VLA models across released and alternative backends on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395, with a seven-stage inference breakdown. Our study reveals three insights. First, action-generation strategy matters more than model size. It dominates 14 of 19 Jetson configurations, latency varies by $82\times$ on Jetson and $157\times$ on AMD, and parameter count explains at most 15% of latency variance. Models that generate long action chunks in a few flow-matching steps keep up with control, whereas token-by-token decoding does not. Second, kernel fusion with 4-bit weights helps most, running $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7 2.6--2.9$\times$ faster than PyTorch with \texttt{torch.compile}, but it exists for only these two models and only on the Jetson. Optimization also moves the time to the stages it shortens least, as CPU preprocessing grows from 12\% to 39\% of the GR00T N1.7 call. Third, after optimization, memory bandwidth limits only the stages that process few tokens on the Jetson, such as the denoising steps, whereas software limits all other stages, from unfused kernels to serial preprocessing on the host CPU. Overall, low-latency edge VLAs should use few action-generation iterations, inference software should extend kernel fusion and low-bit weights to more models and platforms, and edge hardware needs high memory bandwidth and a fast host CPU.
authors: Borui Xu, Hongshi Tan, Wenqi Jiang, Bingsheng He, Ming Wu, Jason Zeng, Michael Heinrich
bullets: Benchmarks 18 open VLA models across multiple backends on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395, using a seven-stage latency breakdown.
Action-generation strategy dominates latency in most Jetson configurations; long action chunks with few flow-matching steps are more control-friendly than token-by-token decoding.
Kernel fusion with 4-bit weights substantially accelerates the two supported models on Jetson, while optimization shifts bottlenecks toward CPU preprocessing.
After optimization, memory bandwidth limits selected Jetson stages, whereas software inefficiencies constrain other stages across the pipeline.
The study recommends few-step action generation, broader low-bit kernel fusion, high-memory-bandwidth hardware, and faster host CPUs.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark of VLA inference latency on edge hardware; relevant to VLA and efficient AI.
papers.title: VLA-HWBench: Where the Time Goes When VLA Models Run on Edge Hardware
papers.tldr: VLA-HWBench shows that action-generation strategy and inference software—not model size alone—largely determine whether VLA models can run in real time on edge hardware.

papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language models such as CLIP typically rely on independently parameterized transformer blocks across depth. We investigate the extent to which these blocks can instead be reused recurrently while preserving the transferable capabilities of CLIP. We study recursive transformer backbones in which a small set of $N$ transformer blocks is applied $M$ times per forward pass. By holding $N \cdot M$ fixed to the depth of a standard ViT-B, our models preserve computational depth while progressively increasing parameter sharing. We consider two recursive CLIP model families: rCLIP, where only the vision encoder is recursive, and r$^2$CLIP, where recurrence is also introduced in the text encoder. We study these models under both direct contrastive training and through knowledge distillation from a strong ViT-B/16 teacher pretrained on DFN-2B, using the substantially smaller CC3M and CC12M datasets. We evaluate the resulting models on zero-shot classification and cross-modal retrieval, and further study their adaptability through few-shot learning, visual grounding, and concept unlearning. Our results show that CLIP can tolerate substantial recurrent block reuse, although its effect depends on the encoder and downstream task. Recurrence also provides parameter efficiency by construction, since fewer distinct transformer blocks need to be stored and adapted. Our results establish recurrent block reuse as a practical design space for vision-language models and highlight its implications for knowledge transfer, downstream adaptation, and parameter efficiency.
authors: Szymon Mazurek, Alberto Presta, Micha{\l} Byra
bullets: Replaces independently parameterized transformer layers with a small set of blocks reused recurrently across depth while preserving total computational depth.
Introduces rCLIP with recursive vision encoding and r²CLIP with recurrence in both vision and text encoders.
Studies direct contrastive training and distillation from a strong ViT-B/16 teacher using smaller CC3M and CC12M datasets.
Evaluates zero-shot classification, cross-modal retrieval, few-shot learning, visual grounding, and concept unlearning.
Finds recurrence is a practical parameter-efficiency design space, but its benefits and costs depend on the encoder and downstream task.
papers.selection_reason: Recursive CLIP with recurrent block reuse; relevant to multimodal foundation models and parameter efficiency.
papers.title: Recursive CLIP: Vision-Language Distillation with Looped Transformer Blocks
papers.tldr: Recursive transformer blocks can substantially reduce distinct parameters in CLIP while retaining useful vision-language capabilities, though performance effects vary by encoder and task.

papers.abstract: Visual-token compression is usually evaluated by clean accuracy and efficiency, but these averages do not reveal failures that compression introduces under an image shift where the uncompressed model stays correct. We introduce VTC-AUDIT, which estimates this incremental risk only on pairs where the full model is correct on both images and the compressed model is correct on the clean image. The four arms then cross two binary choices: which image selects the retained token positions, and which image supplies the visual features. We audit three open 8-9B vision-language models on four tasks and eight pre-specified shifts. We evaluate two training-free compressors---hard-pruning DivPrune and prune-and-merge ApET---at a matched 25% retained-position budget, producing 708,000 inference records. Reselecting positions on the shifted image, rather than reusing the clean-image positions, raises the failure rate in all six model-compressor settings. The increase is 3.04-9.60 percentage points for DivPrune and 2.05-4.20 percentage points for ApET, with every 95% interval above zero. Repeating the audit on a separately resampled second manifest reproduces all six increases. In a pooled monitor audit across the four benchmarks, support Jaccard instability fails the practical AUROC criterion of 0.65 in all six settings, whereas clean compressed-model uncertainty clears it. Thus, support turnover is a weak ranking signal under the audited benchmark mixture, while clean compressed-model uncertainty is substantially more informative. These results suggest that future visual-token compression evaluations should report conditional reliability alongside clean accuracy and efficiency.
bullets: Measures incremental risk only when the full model remains correct under both clean and shifted images and the compressed model is correct on the clean image.
Crosses whether retained token positions and visual features come from the clean or shifted image, auditing hard-pruning and prune-and-merge compressors at a matched 25% budget.
Across three vision-language models, four tasks, and eight shifts, selecting positions from the shifted image increases failure rates in all six model–compressor settings.
The increases are reproduced on an independently resampled manifest, supporting the robustness of the finding.
Support Jaccard instability is a weak ranking signal, while clean compressed-model uncertainty is more informative in the pooled audit.
papers.selection_reason: Audits visual-token compression reliability under image shifts; directly relevant to token pruning/eviction.
papers.title: VTC-AUDIT: An Interventional Reliability Audit for Visual-Token Compression under Paired Image Shifts
papers.tldr: VTC-AUDIT shows that visual-token compression can add substantial shift-related failures, and recommends conditional reliability audits alongside clean accuracy and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are increasingly used for robot manipulation because they map camera images and a language instruction directly to actions. Robots that cannot be tethered to a workstation, such as mobile manipulators and humanoids, must run them on onboard embedded boards, where the prefill latency of the language backbone grows with the hundreds of visual tokens processed at every control step. To meet real-time limits, training-free accelerators recompute only a subset of the visual tokens and skip the rest, either by pruning them or by reusing their cached key-value (KV) states. The two options save nearly the same computation, yet existing methods apply only one of them to every skipped token. Through a token-level diagnostic, we show that which option keeps the action closer to full recomputation depends on the token's drift, the change in its shallow-layer value since its cache was computed. On both backbones tested, reusing tokens below a drift threshold was no worse than pruning them, whereas beyond it, reuse yields up to 4.4x the action error of pruning; the same diagnostic calibrates this threshold per backbone. Building on this finding, we propose TRIAGE, which deems a cache valid when its drift is below this threshold and it is not too old. TRIAGE recomputes a fixed budget of tokens, prioritizing important tokens with invalid caches, reuses every other token with a valid cache, and prunes the rest; prune-only and reuse-only methods are the two extremes of this partition. Because the budget fixes the number of recomputed tokens, it directly sets the prefill latency. On LIBERO and SimplerEnv, TRIAGE stays within 3 pp of full recomputation in average success rate while cutting prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin by up to 48%, and with only 7% of visual tokens recomputed, it beats the strongest baseline by 24.4 pp on LIBERO-Object.
authors: Sooyoung Kwon, Carlee Joe-Wong, Kyunghan Lee
bullets: Targets onboard VLA inference, where processing hundreds of visual tokens causes high prefill latency.
Finds that reuse is effective for low-drift tokens, while pruning is preferable for high-drift tokens.
Uses a calibrated drift threshold and cache age to classify tokens as reusable, invalid-and-recompute, or prune.
A fixed recomputation budget directly controls latency.

On LIBERO and SimplerEnv, remains within 3 percentage points of full recomputation while reducing Jetson AGX Orin prefill latency by up to 48%; with 7% of tokens recomputed, it exceeds the strongest LIBERO-Object baseline by 24.4 points.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free VLA inference acceleration via joint token reuse and pruning with drift-based cache validity fits VLA and token/KV efficiency.
papers.title: TRIAGE: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Inference Needs Both Reuse and Pruning
papers.tldr: TRIAGE combines token reuse and pruning based on cache drift to reduce VLA prefill latency while preserving near-full-recomputation robot performance.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models are costly to serve because they are large and because they generate long chains of thought (CoT). Weight pruning and CoT compression address these two costs separately, but they interfere in that pruning adds redundant reasoning on problems the model still solves and incomplete reasoning on those it no longer solves, and on harder problems makes the model less compressible by subsequent length-preference optimization. We trace this to a blind spot on each side: pruning criteria do not distinguish necessary from redundant reasoning, and preference-based CoT compression receives no training signal on problems a pruned model always or never solves. We propose Contrastive Set-Difference (CSD), which identifies neurons enriched in redundant reasoning by contrasting their activations on long and short correct solutions of the same problem and prunes them preferentially, and we extend preference pairs to the problems a pruned model always or never solves. Pruning 20\% of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the combination uses 8--22\% fewer thinking tokens on four math benchmarks than pruning with reasoning-aware calibration (RAC) followed by the same compression, with accuracy within 0.5 points.
authors: Tao Jing, Chen Kang, Feifei Zhai, Pengyuan Liu, Dong Yu
bullets: Pruning and chain-of-thought compression can interfere: pruning may induce redundant or incomplete reasoning and reduce later compressibility.
The method, Contrastive Set-Difference (CSD), contrasts neuron activations between long and short correct solutions to identify neurons associated with redundant reasoning.
It also adds preference-training pairs from problems a pruned model always solves or always fails to solve.
With 20% pruning of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the combined approach used 8–22% fewer thinking tokens across four math benchmarks than RAC followed by the same compression.
Accuracy remained within 0.5 percentage points of the comparison pipeline.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Contrastive Set-Difference (CSD) to prune redundant reasoning neurons in pruned models, improving the compressibility of Chain-of-Thought outputs.
papers.title: Improving the Chain-of-Thought Compressibility of Pruned Reasoning Models via Long--Short Contrastive Pruning
papers.tldr: Long–Short Contrastive Pruning makes pruned reasoning models more compressible, reducing thinking tokens while largely preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Conveyor belts are vital arteries in continuous bulk material handling, particularly in heavy process industries such as cement manufacturing. Undetected structural anomalies (longitudinal tears, holes, degraded patch repairs, and impact punctures) cause catastrophic belt snapping, costly downtime, and severe safety hazards. While deep learning offers high accuracy, existing models rely on power-hungry workstation GPUs, hindering practical deployment at remote industrial edge points. In this paper, we propose, implement, and validate an end-to-end, low-power edge AI vision system for real-time conveyor belt defect detection deployed on a Raspberry Pi 5 accelerated by a Google Coral Edge TPU coprocessor. The system leverages an optimized YOLOv11 nano (YOLOv11n) architecture trained on a multi-source industrial corpus exceeding 3,000 augmented samples from an operational cement plant in West Java, open-source datasets, and automated captures. The model undergoes post-training full integer quantization (INT8) compiled for systolic tensor execution. Experimental results demonstrate robust detection capability, achieving precision of 0.742, recall of 0.730, and mAP@0.5 of 0.764 across four defect classes. Deployed on-site in an IP-rated enclosure interfaced with an RTSP PoE industrial camera, the system achieves stable throughput of 30-40 FPS at 320x320 resolution with an end-to-end latency of 70-90 ms. Operational profiling under harsh clinker dust confirms thermal equilibrium at 55 +/- 5 deg C on the host CPU and ~65 deg C on the Edge TPU with zero frame loss. This demonstrates that edge AI bridges the gap between high-accuracy computer vision and cost-effective predictive maintenance in continuous manufacturing.
authors: Muhammad Nur Bijak Bestari, Mulki Indana Zulfa
bullets: Targets tears, holes, degraded patch repairs, and impact punctures that can cause belt failures, downtime, and safety risks.
Uses an INT8-quantized YOLOv11n model trained on over 3,000 augmented samples from industrial and open-source sources.
Achieves precision 0.742, recall 0.730, and mAP@0.5 0.764 across the four defect classes.
Runs at 30–40 FPS with 70–90 ms end-to-end latency at 320×320 resolution on an enclosed, on-site deployment.
Maintained zero frame loss during clinker-dust profiling, with host CPU temperature near 55 ± 5 °C and Edge TPU temperature around 65 °C.
papers.selection_reason: Edge AI vision system with INT8 quantization and Edge TPU acceleration; relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: Real-Time Conveyor Belt Defect Detection via Edge TPU-Accelerated YOLOv11 on Raspberry Pi 5
papers.tldr: A quantized YOLOv11n system running on a Raspberry Pi 5 with Coral Edge TPU detects four conveyor-belt defect types in real time under industrial conditions.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a promising approach for fast, high-quality novel-view rendering. However, its large parameter size remains a bottleneck for storage and transmission. We propose RacerGS, a compact 3DGS compression framework that achieves scene reconstruction at significantly reduced storage sizes with preserved fidelity. To obtain compact and spatially coherent features, we design a hash projection model that projects the anchor hash encodings into compact context features. Additionally, we introduce a FiLM-modulated autoregressive GRU context model that utilizes causal dependencies among anchor feature groups and uses recurrent hidden states to refine entropy-model parameters, improving bitrate efficiency. Furthermore, we adaptively entropy-code quantized anchor-attribute residuals relative to their context-predicted means, leveraging spatial consistency to reduce symbol entropy. Overall, RacerGS achieves more than 150x compression over vanilla 3DGS and 28x over Scaffold-GS, while providing comparable rendering quality. Extensive experiments across five datasets demonstrate that RacerGS outperforms prior 3DGS compression methods in both storage reduction and rate-distortion performance.
authors: Wenqing Wang, Huimin Zeng, Yun Fu
bullets: Addresses the large storage and transmission cost of 3DGS.
Projects anchor hash encodings into compact, spatially coherent context features.
Uses a FiLM-modulated autoregressive GRU to model causal dependencies and refine entropy parameters.
Entropy-codes quantized anchor-attribute residuals relative to context-predicted means.
Reports over 150× compression versus vanilla 3DGS and 28× versus Scaffold-GS, with comparable quality across five datasets.
papers.selection_reason: 3D Gaussian Splatting compression via autoregressive context and entropy coding; relevant to 3D vision and storage efficiency.
papers.title: RacerGS: Residual-Autoregressive Context for 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression
papers.tldr: RacerGS compresses 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes using spatial context and residual entropy coding, achieving substantial storage reduction while preserving rendering quality.

papers.abstract: Scalable 3D Gaussian Splatting allows one scene representation to serve different Gaussian-count budgets, yet its quality-budget curve may lag behind models optimized separately for each budget. Reducing the number of Gaussians changes both the selected members and the reconstruction tasks carried by the survivors; parameters inherited from a high-budget model may fit a low-budget representation poorly. We propose ParetoGS, which describes member changes and parameter evolution with a small set of adapted budget anchors and decodes intermediate budgets without separate optimization at every requested count. ParetoGS alternates pruning and fixed-member adaptation to build nested anchors with persistent identities, and encodes their parameter changes relative to the full model in a compact residual atlas. At decoding, it interpolates the states of shared members and gradually introduces the rendering contributions of new members, connecting sparse anchors into a continuous-budget representation. Across 13 scenes, ParetoGS attains better average PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS with fewer Gaussians than the compared prefix methods at 10% of each method's own full model. From a shared full model, it also outperforms FlexGS-imp at its trained 1%, 5%, and 10% budgets and NanoGS-imp at the 1% and 0.1% budgets. On Garden, its non-anchor quality approaches an empirical reference from independently optimized GNS models at higher retention ratios and exceeds it at some lower-budget points. Across 13 scenes, encoding reduces mean additional state from 390.0 to 85.7 MB with an average PSNR change of 0.01 dB. Project page: https://xiaobin2001.github.io/ParetoGS-Web/
authors: Xiaobin Deng, Changyu Diao, Min Li, Duanqing Xu
bullets: Addresses quality degradation when pruning a high-budget Gaussian model for lower budgets, where surviving parameters may no longer fit well.
Builds nested, persistent-identity anchors through alternating pruning and fixed-member adaptation.
Stores parameter changes in a compact residual atlas and decodes intermediate budgets by interpolating shared members and gradually adding new members.
Across 13 scenes, improves average PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS over prefix methods at 10% retention and outperforms several budget-trained baselines at selected budgets.
Reduces mean additional encoding state from 390.0 MB to 85.7 MB with only a 0.01 dB average PSNR change.
papers.selection_reason: Continuous-budget 3D Gaussian Splatting with pruning and compact residual encoding; relevant to 3D representation and efficiency.
papers.title: ParetoGS: High-Quality Continuous-Budget 3D Gaussian Splatting with Sparse Adapted Anchors
papers.tldr: ParetoGS enables high-quality, continuously adjustable 3D Gaussian Splatting budgets using sparse adapted anchors and interpolation instead of optimizing every Gaussian count separately.

papers.abstract: High-resolution 3D Gaussian Splatting training increases pixel and Gaussian-tile intersection counts, expanding rasterization caches that coexist with projection and gradient state at peak memory. A complete-view update aggregates gradients across the view; each region's forward and backward caches can be released after its contribution is collected. BoundedGS separates rasterization and projection backward passes and bounds the active local rasterization working set according to its measured load. Candidate-indexed projection and compact gradient storage address the view-level peaks exposed by this change, while CPU-assisted structure rebuilding and bounded image supply manage resources outside rendering. In a resolution sweep at a fixed count of about 6M Gaussians, the measured rendering working set stays within 1.073-1.077 GiB from 1K to 16K; at 11K, a warm pass takes 19.79 seconds versus 21.76 for full-frame execution. Across five native 5K outdoor scenes, full training reduces the mean rendering working set from 9.97 to 1.76 GiB (82.3%), retains similar reconstruction quality, and shortens training time from 36.7 to 33.9 minutes. Project page: https://xiaobin2001.github.io/BoundedGS-Web/
authors: Xiaobin Deng, Changyu Diao, Min Li, Duanqing Xu
bullets: High-resolution 3DGS exceeds memory limits because rasterization caches grow alongside projection and gradient state.
It separates rasterization from projection backpropagation and limits the active rasterization working set using measured load.
Candidate-indexed projection, compact gradients, CPU-assisted rebuilding, and bounded image supply control additional memory use.
At roughly 6M Gaussians, rendering memory remains nearly constant at 1.073–1.077 GiB from 1K to 16K resolution.
Across five native 5K outdoor scenes, rendering memory drops 82.3% while quality remains similar and training becomes faster.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient high-resolution 3D Gaussian Splatting training; reduces memory footprint and fits efficient AI and 3D vision.
papers.title: BoundedGS: Memory-Efficient High-Resolution Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: BoundedGS enables memory-efficient high-resolution 3D Gaussian Splatting by bounding rasterization memory while preserving reconstruction quality and improving training time.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) enables flow-matching models to acquire complementary capabilities from specialized teachers through supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, different evaluation dimensions, such as aesthetics and OCR accuracy, and different tasks, such as image generation and editing, emphasize different aspects of the denoising process, suggesting that their effective supervision may occur at different stages. Existing methods typically select supervision states from predefined timestep distributions, which may overlook these phase-dependent differences and incur unnecessary computational overhead. This motivates two critical timing decisions: when to adaptively query teachers for effective supervision based on the evolving generative process, and when to skip the remaining rollout to avoid redundant computation. In this paper, we introduce PhaseOPD, a phase-aware query-and-skip framework that identifies generative phases online from revisions of predicted-clean latents, using existing student velocity predictions without additional model evaluations. For each task-assigned teacher, PhaseOPD selects a supervision state based on its phase preference and skips the unused rollout suffix once all query decisions are finalized, preserving the single-query velocity-distillation objective. On SD3.5-M, PhaseOPD executes only 5.56 of 16 rollout positions per local batch, reducing training time by 41.3% relative to DanceOPD while improving Aesthetic, GenEval, and OCR scores.
authors: Renye Yan, Junyi Zhan, Jikang Cheng, Wei Peng
bullets: Different tasks and evaluation goals may need teacher supervision at different denoising stages.
The framework identifies phases online from changes in predicted-clean latents, reusing student velocity predictions without extra model evaluations.
Task-specific teachers are queried at preferred phases, while unnecessary rollout suffixes are skipped after query decisions are complete.
On SD3.5-M, it uses 5.56 of 16 rollout positions per local batch and reduces training time by 41.3% versus DanceOPD.
It also improves Aesthetic, GenEval, and OCR scores in the reported setting.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive query-and-skip in flow-matching distillation reduces training computation, fitting the efficient-AI scope of reducing compute.
papers.title: Timing Matters Twice: When to Query and When to Skip in Flow-Matching On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: PhaseOPD makes on-policy distillation more efficient by adaptively choosing when to query teachers and when to stop rollouts based on the evolving generation phase.

papers.abstract: Instruction-based image editors built on diffusion transformers run tens of denoising steps. Training-free acceleration either reuses features across steps (step caching) or stops computing the regions an edit leaves untouched (region freezing), and the two have been combined before. We ask how a high speed-up target should be split between them. On Qwen-Image-2.1, freezing does more than remove tokens: it lowers the cost of every step, so the step cache can reach the same overall speed-up with a conservative threshold that keeps its error small. A per-step cost model fitted on development runs predicts held-out latency with a median error of 4.0% and reproduces the speed ceilings of the region methods we re-implemented (2.73$\times$ predicted vs. 2.70$\times$ measured for RegionE). Driving frozen tokens to the model's one-step $x_0$ estimate beats returning them to the reference image on every development sample, and in 90% of measured cases the composed error stays below the sum of the two individual errors. The resulting method, FreezePlan, keeps five full steps and gives the rest of the budget to TaylorSeer. On a pre-registered test split it runs 5.05$\times$ faster end to end at 29.8 dB PSNR to the original output, with no significant drop in a VLM judge score; TaylorSeer at 5.02$\times$ reaches 23.5 dB. The curve extends to 5.99$\times$ at 28.0 dB. Swapping in the region selectors of prior methods under our schedule lowers median PSNR by only 0.5--0.6 dB, which places the gain in the schedule and budget split rather than in the selector.
bullets: Region freezing reduces the cost of every denoising step, allowing step caching to operate in a lower-error regime.
A fitted per-step cost model predicts held-out latency with 4.0% median error and accurately estimates method speed ceilings.
Using the model’s one-step x₀ estimate for frozen tokens outperforms restoring the reference image across development samples.
FreezePlan keeps five full steps and allocates the remaining computation budget to TaylorSeer.
On a preregistered test split, it achieves 5.05× end-to-end speedup at 29.8 dB PSNR with no significant VLM-judge score drop; it reaches 5.99× at 28.0 dB.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free acceleration for diffusion image editing via region freezing and step caching; directly reduces compute by pruning spatial tokens and reusing features.
papers.title: Freeze What Is Settled, Cache What Is Smooth: Spatial Freezing Keeps Step Caching in Its Low-Error Regime
papers.tldr: FreezePlan combines spatial region freezing with conservative step caching to achieve 5.05× faster diffusion image editing while preserving output quality.

papers.abstract: Indoor IoT cameras can support assisted living and activity-aware spaces, but exporting raw RGB frames raises privacy concerns by exposing facial, clothing, and household details that body-motion tasks often do not require. We present StickFigure, a pose-only IoT camera system that, during real-time monitoring, keeps raw frames local and ephemeral while exporting only compact skeleton streams sufficient for downstream human activity recognition (HAR). While pose estimation has matured on GPUs, extracting accurate pose streams on resource-constrained IoT cameras remains difficult. To overcome these challenges and enable on-device pose streams on (almost) any IoT camera, we present two core designs in StickFigure: an activation-aware pose backbone that allocates channel capacity after spatial downsampling and a lightweight hierarchical MLP refiner that selectively corrects elbow and wrist coordinates using intermediate visual features and kinematic context. We fully implement StickFigure and evaluate it on public benchmarks and real-world deployment. Compared with state-of-the-art MCU pose models, StickFigure achieves the highest pose accuracy and downstream HAR utility on both NTU RGB+D and Penn Action, while using 96.5% fewer parameters and 99.3% fewer MACs per frame than RTMPose-S-based baselines, achieving 0.107 s p95 latency on a representative STM32H753 MCU. We believe StickFigure establishes a new operating point for privacy-aware edge vision on massive IoT cameras.
bullets: Keeps raw RGB frames local and ephemeral, reducing exposure of facial, clothing, and household details.
Uses an activation-aware pose backbone and a lightweight hierarchical MLP refiner for accurate on-device pose estimation.
Improves elbow and wrist coordinates using visual features and kinematic context.
Achieves strong pose accuracy and downstream HAR utility on NTU RGB+D and Penn Action benchmarks.
Runs with 96.5% fewer parameters, 99.3% fewer MACs, and 0.107 s p95 latency on an STM32H753 MCU versus RTMPose-S-based baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Pose-only edge vision system with drastically reduced parameters and MACs, fitting efficient AI broadly.
papers.title: StickFigure: Enabling Pose-Only IoT Cameras for Privacy-Preserving Edge Vision
papers.tldr: StickFigure enables privacy-preserving human activity recognition by processing pose locally on IoT cameras and exporting only compact skeleton streams.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding significantly accelerates autoregressive text generation in Large Language Models (LLMs), but its efficacy depends largely on two key factors: the distributional alignment between the draft and the target model, and the draft model's latency during inference. However, existing approaches typically utilize independently pretrained small draft models or seek to prune the target model to a manually chosen architecture, thereby failing to explicitly balance the trade-off between draft model alignment and token generation efficiency. To address this gap, we formulate draft model design as an optimization problem and propose T2D, a framework that constructs draft models directly from the target model using latency-aware structured pruning and knowledge distillation. In this manner, T2D obtains draft models that are jointly optimized for both measured inference latency and cross-entropy loss on the target model's responses, resulting in superlative speculative decoding performance. Through extensive experiments on multi-domain speculative decoding benchmarks and across several target model families of differing scale, we demonstrate how T2D prunes up to 92\% of the target model to obtain highly performant draft models compared to competitive baselines. Moreover, draft models obtained via T2D can also be utilized by other speculative decoding token-alignment and knowledge distillation methods in a plug-and-play fashion, leading to further gains. Our findings underscore the importance of jointly navigating the draft model architecture-alignment frontier to unlock the full potential of speculative decoding for LLMs.
authors: Shahriar Kabir Nahin, Xiao Ye, Muhao Chen, Ben Zhou, Anshuman Chhabra
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between draft-model inference latency and distributional alignment with the target model.
Uses latency-aware structured pruning plus knowledge distillation to formulate draft-model design as an optimization problem.
Prunes up to 92% of the target model while maintaining strong speculative decoding performance across multiple domains and target-model scales.
The resulting draft models can plug into other token-alignment and distillation methods for additional gains.
Scope: effectiveness depends on measured latency and cross-entropy alignment with the target model’s responses.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes T2D, a framework for pruning and adapting draft models to optimize speculative decoding efficiency and alignment simultaneously.
papers.title: T2D: Target-to-Draft Model Pruning & Adaptation for Efficient Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: T2D builds latency-efficient draft models directly from a target LLM by jointly optimizing structural pruning and target-model alignment for speculative decoding.

papers.abstract: Deep learning facilitates rapid single shot three dimensional (3D) reconstruction using fringe projection profilometry (FPP), but recovering accurate surface height from a single high frequency fringe image remains challenging because both long-range spatial consistency and fine geometric details must be preserved. Convolutional networks are limited in modeling long range dependencies, whereas window-based Transformers establish global interactions only progressively with increasing depth. To address these limitations, a hybrid Mamba Transformer network is proposed for fringe to height regression. The network adopts a Swin based U shaped architecture and introduces visual state space modeling at the intermediate resolution encoder stage. An axial and dilated vision state space (ADVSS) block is further developed to enhance prescan feature encoding through local, dilated, and axial depthwise convolutions while retaining four directional selective scanning. This design combines linear complexity long range modeling with direction aware preservation of local fringe structures. Experiments on a publicly available FPP dataset show that the proposed method outperforms hNet, SwinConvUNet, UHRNet, and HiDNet in mean absolute error(MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), absolute relative error, and structural similarity index measure (SSIM). Using only one deformed fringe image, the proposed method achieves an RMSE of 0.548 mm and an SSIM of 0.9985, reducing RMSE by 65.2% and 59.6% relative to UHRNet and HiDNet, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining selective state space modeling with hierarchical window based attention for accurate single-shot FPP reconstruction.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of preserving both global spatial consistency and fine geometric details in single-shot fringe projection profilometry.
Uses a Swin-based U-shaped encoder–decoder with visual state space modeling at an intermediate resolution.
Introduces an axial and dilated vision state space block with local, dilated, and axial convolutions plus four-directional selective scanning.
On a public FPP dataset, outperforms hNet, SwinConvUNet, UHRNet, and HiDNet across MAE, RMSE, absolute relative error, and SSIM.
Achieves 0.548 mm RMSE and 0.9985 SSIM from a single deformed fringe image; evaluation is limited to the reported public dataset and metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a hybrid Mamba-Transformer network for single-shot 3D reconstruction, combining efficient long-range modeling with local detail preservation.
papers.title: Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Network for Single-Shot 3D Reconstruction from Fringe Patterns
papers.tldr: A hybrid Swin Transformer–Mamba network enables accurate single-shot 3D reconstruction from one high-frequency fringe image by combining long-range modeling with fine-detail preservation.

papers.abstract: Automated classification of gastrointestinal (GI) findings in endoscopic images could support early diagnosis, but architectures are often chosen on accuracy alone. We present a controlled, reproducible benchmark of ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 for eight-class GI classification on the public Kvasir dataset (4,000 images), using a stratified split (400 test images) and stratified group 5-fold cross-validation over all images. In cross-validation, ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 reached 92.12% and 91.70% accuracy, and a two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure showed equivalence within a +/-3 percentage-point margin (difference +0.43 points, 90% CI -0.33 to +1.18; p < 0.001). The architectures differed mainly in cost: ResNet50 had 3.6 times fewer parameters and 4.3 times fewer operations, 2.5-fold lower single-image CPU latency (69 vs. 177 ms) and 3.8-fold higher GPU throughput. Cross-validated calibration was similar (expected calibration error 0.021 vs. 0.023). An edge-oriented transformer, MobileViT-S, was most accurate on the test split (95.5%) but lost 9.4 points when an acquisition artefact present in some classes (the ScopeGuide inset) was occluded, whereas ResNet50 was not significantly affected. On 500 unseen polyp images with expert masks, both models' Grad-CAM maps focused on the lesion (3.6 times chance). On a de-duplicated external subset of GastroVision (1,998 images), accuracy fell to 78-80% for all three models and differences between them remained small. Accuracy differences between architectures were thus small relative to the effects of shortcut learning and domain shift, whereas efficiency differences were large. An efficient CNN is a defensible default for resource-constrained screening, but no model is deployment-ready without local validation.
bullets: On Kvasir’s eight-class task, ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 were statistically equivalent within a 3-point accuracy margin.
ResNet50 used fewer parameters and operations, with lower CPU latency and higher GPU throughput than ViT-B/16.
MobileViT-S achieved the highest test-split accuracy but was vulnerable to the ScopeGuide artefact, indicating shortcut learning.
Both ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 showed similar calibration and lesion-focused Grad-CAM explanations.
Accuracy dropped substantially on the external GastroVision subset, highlighting domain-shift risks and the need for local validation.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a benchmark comparing the efficiency (latency, throughput) of ResNet50 and Vision Transformers, highlighting architectural trade-offs for resource-constrained deployment.
papers.title: Accuracy Is Not Enough: An Efficiency- and Statistics-Aware Benchmark of ResNet50 and Vision Transformer for Explainable Multi-Class Gastrointestinal Diseases Classification
papers.tldr: ResNet50 matches ViT-B/16 accuracy for GI disease classification while being substantially more efficient, but shortcut learning and domain shift limit deployment readiness.

papers.abstract: We introduce TrackTok, an efficient video tokenization framework that produces object-centric tokens, i.e., tokens that consistently encode the same semantic objects across time, even as it moves, deforms, or undergoes partial occlusion. Conventional patch-based or existing holistic tokenizers produce token identities often tied to fixed image locations. In contrast, our approach learns temporally persistent object-centric representations that bind visual features across frames into stable semantic units. This enables substantially more compact, continuous latent video representations, reducing the number of tokens required for downstream generative modeling with state-of-the-art flow models, while preserving the semantic structure needed for high-quality synthesis. Our tokenizer offers a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. TrackTok achieves comparable class-conditional generative FVD on UCF-101 dataset at 8 times fewer latent tokens and better latency, and outperforms existing 1D tokenization baselines on frame prediction task on Kinetics-600 across low token budgets. These results suggest that object-aligned and temporally persistent tokenization is a promising direction for scalable video generation, where reducing latent token counts is critical for efficient modeling. Our code for this work is available at https://github.com/phamleyennhi/tracktok.
authors: Nhi Pham, Christopher Wewer, Bernt Schiele, Jonas Fischer, Jan Eric Lenssen
bullets: Addresses the instability of patch-based and holistic tokens whose identities are tied to fixed image locations.
Learns tokens that track the same objects across motion, deformation, and partial occlusion.
Produces compact continuous latent representations for downstream flow-based video generation.
Matches class-conditional FVD on UCF-101 with 8× fewer latent tokens and lower latency.
Outperforms 1D tokenization baselines on Kinetics-600 frame prediction at low token budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces object-centric video tokenization that reduces token count for efficient video generation and understanding, directly addressing token efficiency and video representation.
papers.title: TrackTok: Object-Centric Video Tokenization with Semantically Persistent Tokens
papers.tldr: TrackTok tokenizes videos into semantically persistent object-centric tokens, enabling efficient generation with far fewer latent tokens while maintaining video quality.

papers.abstract: Typed decision-making tasks in agents, such as UI element selection, product recommendation, and chart matching, require models to choose from a set of discrete candidates. While prior work demonstrates that text-only System One models achieve four key properties including candidate-order invariance, scalability, and cache reuse via separate request-candidate encoding, extending them to multimodal settings where candidates are visual remains underexplored. We introduce Iris, a framework that accommodates image, text, or hybrid candidates while preserving the core decision module. We prove that order invariance and exact cache reuse hold for any per-candidate encoder under Iris, and derive the closed-form latency reduction. We construct a visual-candidate benchmark from Multimodal-Mind2Web (K=16, deduplicated, order-shuffled, three generalization splits). Independent encoding (Iris) achieves 78.4 / 72.1 / 74.8 percent accuracy with zero-flip rate under candidate reordering. Joint encoding reaches 90.6 / 89.5 / 91.6 percent but suffers an 8 to 10 percent answer-flip rate when shuffled. To bridge this gap, we propose a design that encodes each candidate conditioned on the request state without inter-candidate cross-attention; it preserves strict order invariance, enables forked cache sharing, and attains 91.7 / 86.5 / 90.0 percent accuracy at one-third of OneJev latency with calibrated null probabilities (AUROC 0.93 to 0.97). Reusing image candidates across requests cuts latency by 37x at K=256 and 191x at K=2048. On MetaEncoder benchmarks, Iris-4B achieves 100 percent on JevBench original and easy, outperforming 30B MetaEncoder and 27B OpenJev. Finally, we resolve a systems bottleneck on Ampere GPUs: reformulating Qwen3.5 patch-embedding Conv3d into its exact matrix-product form accelerates processing by 350x. Code, data, and checkpoints: https://github.com/lllfx/Iris.
bullets: Targets typed-choice tasks such as UI selection, recommendation, and chart matching with visual candidates.
Uses per-candidate encoding, including request-conditioned encoding without inter-candidate cross-attention, to preserve strict order invariance and reusable caches.
The proposed design reaches 91.7/86.5/90.0% accuracy across three splits, with one-third of OneJev’s latency and AUROC 0.93–0.97 for calibrated null probabilities.
Reusing image candidates reduces latency by 37× at K=256 and 191× at K=2048.
An exact Conv3d-to-matrix-product reformulation accelerates Qwen3.5 patch embedding by 350× on Ampere GPUs.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal decision framework with order-invariant candidate encoding and reusable inference cache; relevant to memory-efficient inference and latency reduction.
papers.title: Seeing the Options: Typed Decisions over Visual Candidates with Reusable Option Memory
papers.tldr: Iris enables order-invariant, cacheable decisions over visual, textual, or hybrid candidates while achieving strong accuracy and major latency savings.

papers.abstract: Unrolled variational networks achieve state-of-the-art performance for accelerated MRI reconstruction, but standard end-to-end training becomes prohibitively memory intensive as the number and width of cascades increase. We propose a memory-efficient training framework that updates a randomly sampled cascade while retaining supervision from the final reconstruction loss. The error signal is propagated from the end of the chain to the sampled cascade using an activation-light backward pass that avoids storing full chain activations, thereby decoupling training memory from chain length. A time-conditioned network shared across cascades further keeps the parameter count independent of chain length. The backward pass is approximate only through frozen normalization statistics, and a trained exact gradient control shows the approximation leaves reconstruction quality unchanged. The framework remains trainable at chain lengths and cascade widths where standard end-to-end backpropagation exhausts GPU memory. On fastMRI single-coil knee and multi-coil brain reconstruction, our method consistently outperforms other local training approaches. On high-SNR knee slices, our method surpasses E2E-VarNet at $8\times$ and matches it at $4\times$, while on the complete brain validation set it surpasses E2E-VarNet at $8\times$ and achieves comparable performance at $4\times$, with fewer parameters, lower peak memory, and faster per-iteration training. Code is available at https://github.com/emehillaj/scalable-unrolled-mri.
bullets: Randomly samples a cascade for updating while retaining supervision from the final reconstruction loss.
Uses an activation-light backward pass to propagate error without memory scaling with chain length.
Shares a time-conditioned network across cascades, keeping parameter count independent of chain length.
Maintains reconstruction quality despite approximate gradients caused by frozen normalization statistics.
Outperforms other local-training methods and matches or exceeds E2E-VarNet in the reported fastMRI knee and brain settings, with fewer parameters, lower peak memory, and faster iteration training.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a memory-efficient training framework for unrolled variational networks in MRI reconstruction, fitting 3D Vision and Efficient AI.
papers.title: Scalable Unrolled Chains for MRI Reconstruction
papers.tldr: A memory-efficient training framework makes very deep and wide unrolled MRI reconstruction networks trainable without storing activations from the full cascade chain.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning substantially reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing methods are mostly training-free and plug-and-play. They treat the resulting performance drop as an inevitable cost of compression and pursue increasingly complex pruning rules. We rethink this view through two questions: how much of the loss can post-training rescue, and, building on this recovery, how can joint compression push pruning to its limit? We curate a 282K-sample post-training mixture covering general VQA, reasoning, OCR, and grounding, and post-train 36 configurations that drop or merge tokens under a unified protocol. Post-training rescues most of the loss, even for OCR and grounding, and its adaptation gain in closing the gap between the pruned and the dense model grows as the budget tightens. For joint compression, we find that the vision encoder, not the LLM, dominates prefill time in native-resolution MLLMs, so where tokens are removed matters more than how many: keeping 40% of tokens at the encoder runs faster than keeping 10% at the projector. Our best configuration prunes the encoder lightly and the projector aggressively, leaves the LLM intact, and keeps general understanding and reasoning at the dense level. It accelerates the LLM stage by 3.49x but the end-to-end time-to-first-token by only 1.54x, showing that LLM-stage speedups overstate end-to-end gains. We hope these findings offer insights for future research on joint visual token compression. Our data, protocol, and code will be released.
authors: Peiran Yin, Hao Wu, Zihao Yang, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Post-training largely restores pruning-induced performance loss, including on OCR and grounding tasks.
A 282K-sample mixture spanning VQA, reasoning, OCR, and grounding supports a unified evaluation of 36 compression configurations.
In native-resolution MLLMs, the vision encoder dominates prefill time, making encoder-side pruning more impactful than projector-side pruning.
The best setup lightly prunes the encoder, aggressively prunes the projector, and keeps the LLM unchanged while preserving general understanding and reasoning at dense-model levels.
A 3.49× LLM-stage speedup translates to only a 1.54× end-to-end time-to-first-token improvement.
papers.selection_reason: Rethinks visual token pruning in MLLMs, introducing post-training recovery and joint compression strategies, fitting Efficient AI and Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: Rescuing Your Pruning: Rethinking Visual Token Pruning and Post-Training Recovery in MLLMs
papers.tldr: Post-training can recover most of the accuracy lost to visual token pruning, while pruning location—not just token count—is critical for end-to-end MLLM speed.

papers.abstract: Pavement crack segmentation under low light is degraded by reduced contrast, shadows, headlight glare, joints, stains, and wet seams. Existing crack segmentation methods mostly assume good illumination. Low-light enhancement methods improve visual quality, but they do not explicitly preserve crack topology.
