papers.abstract: Trajectory transfer from rollout to training affects both learning quality and system efficiency in large language model reinforcement learning (RL). Enforcing batch-wide training requirements can delay the admission of completed trajectories, resulting in higher architectural staleness: the additional parameter-version gap from disaggregated pipelining relative to colocated execution. Beyond admission, misalignment between data access and training consumption causes redundant movement and unnecessary waiting when transferring large trajectory payloads. We present KnitTrans, a system that coordinates the rollout-to-training path through three designs. First, constraint-preserving mini-batch admission allows flexibility in early mini-batch composition, while checking that enough capacity remains to satisfy the remaining quotas. Second, on-demand trajectory data access matches storage units to consumer assignments and overlaps micro-batch data preparation with computation. Third, multimodal encoding deduplication supports reuse across a mini-batch while preserving gradient contributions from all backbone micro-batches. Experiments show up to 93% lower architectural staleness than with train-batch admission, narrowing the learning-quality gap between disaggregated execution and colocated execution. On multimodal workloads, KnitTrans reduces transfer latency by two orders of magnitude and achieves a speedup of up to 5.8 times in transfer plus training over the baseline.
authors: Bangjun Xiao, Chiheng Lou, Xiaodong Ji, Xiangwei Deng, Yikai Zhao, Gang Huang, Hailin Zhang
bullets: Reduces architectural staleness by up to 93% versus train-batch admission, narrowing the quality gap with colocated execution.
Uses constraint-preserving mini-batch admission to accept trajectories earlier while meeting remaining training quotas.
Matches trajectory storage access to consumer assignments and overlaps data preparation with computation.
Deduplicates multimodal encoding across a mini-batch while retaining gradient contributions from all backbone micro-batches.
Cuts multimodal transfer latency by two orders of magnitude and delivers up to 5.8× faster transfer plus training than the baseline.
papers.selection_reason: System-level efficiency for LLM reinforcement-learning trajectory transfer; fits efficient AI by reducing latency, staleness, and data movement.
papers.title: KnitTrans: Coordinated Trajectory Transfer for Effective and Efficient LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: KnitTrans improves LLM RL efficiency and learning quality by coordinating trajectory admission, data access, and multimodal encoding across rollout and training.

papers.abstract: Cognitive workload estimation from physiological signals is increasingly relevant in high-risk environments, where continuous and unobtrusive monitoring can inform adaptive systems and safety interventions. This paper presents FOCUS (Frequency-band Optimized Cognitive-load Ultralight SSM), a compact Mamba-2-based model for EEG-based binary workload classification under constrained data conditions. Rather than learning frequency sensitivity from data, FOCUS encodes preprocessed multi-channel EEG using a fixed FFT decomposition that covers the five canonical EEG bands. The proposed model combines depthwise-separable convolution and a weight-shared encoder-bottleneck Mamba-2 pair, with 0.04 million parameters and 0.11 GFLOPs. Evaluated in a pilot study with 11 participants under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation across three cognitively distinct tasks, FOCUS achieves 74.75% accuracy on the full dataset at 0.08 ms GPU model-forward latency. In the weight-sharing ablation, the shared configuration achieves 4.55 percentage points higher accuracy on the full dataset than the non-shared variant while reducing the SSM parameter budget; however, this difference does not reach statistical significance under a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test ($p=0.083$). Overall, the selected FOCUS configuration provides a favorable trade-off between classification performance and computational cost within this controlled pilot setting.
authors: Ioannis Kyprakis, Stefanos Gkikas, Chariklia Chatzaki, Zongyi Jiang, Randy Gomez, Raul Fernandez Rojas
bullets: Targets binary cognitive-workload classification from multichannel EEG under constrained data conditions.
Uses fixed FFT decomposition across five canonical EEG bands, depthwise-separable convolution, and a weight-shared Mamba-2 encoder-bottleneck.
Has 0.04 million parameters and 0.11 GFLOPs, with reported 0.08 ms GPU model-forward latency.
In a pilot study of 11 participants with leave-one-subject-out validation across three tasks, it achieved 74.75% accuracy.
Weight sharing improved full-dataset accuracy by 4.55 percentage points over the non-shared variant, but the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.083).
papers.selection_reason: Ultralight Mamba-2 EEG classifier; fits Efficient AI's compute and latency reduction focus.
papers.title: FOCUS: A Lightweight Mamba-2 Model for EEG-Based Cognitive Workload Classification
papers.tldr: FOCUS is a compact Mamba-2 EEG model that uses fixed frequency-band features to classify cognitive workload efficiently in a small-data pilot setting.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require a robot to remember what it has done and what it has seen. Frontier vision-language models can plan such tasks without task-specific training, but how such a planner should remember an episode is an open question. We argue that its memory must keep track of what the planner has done and learned, and must let the planner choose what to look at, since every frame costs tokens; a note rewritten at every step meets both poorly. We propose LogLook, whose execution-grounded memory lets the system keep the record, an execution log and the model's earlier notes, while the model decides where to look: frames are returned only where it expects a change, and demonstrations are skimmed before it inspects the parts it chooses. Measured with the benchmark's motion planner, LogLook matches the success of a note-only memory with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, and fails far fewer episodes through what it remembered or saw. With direct control, LogLook solves 93.5% of the RoboMME test set.
authors: Tianyi Jiang, Tianyao Tong, Zhenshan Bing
bullets: Addresses how frontier vision-language robot planners should remember actions and observations during manipulation tasks.
Maintains an execution log alongside the model’s notes instead of rewriting a note at every step.
Uses model-directed visual access: it requests frames where changes are expected and selectively inspects demonstrations.
Matches note-only memory success with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, while causing fewer memory- or perception-related failures.
Achieves 93.5% success on the RoboMME test set with direct control.
papers.selection_reason: Execution-grounded memory for VLM-based robot planners that selectively retrieves frames, relevant to embodied memory, VLA, and token efficiency.
papers.title: LogLook: Execution-Grounded Memory for Frontier-Model Robot Planners
papers.tldr: LogLook improves robot-planning memory by grounding it in execution logs and letting the model selectively inspect frames and demonstrations, reducing visual context while maintaining or improving task success.

papers.abstract: Looped language models run each token through the same layers several times, and each run is one iteration. To save compute, an extra layer, the halting head, gives after each iteration the probability that the token stops there, so that easy tokens can stop early. Pretraining models from scratch, up to 1.3B parameters, we find two problems. First, heads trained on a mix of all iterations predict that tokens need under half the iterations, yet under the standard stopping rule tokens run almost every iteration, because this training never scores the single iteration where a token stops. Scoring every iteration instead fixes this, but in our runs it works only with a strong penalty favoring early stops. Second, savings are commonly reported as an average number of iterations per token, but when sequences are generated in batches that run until their slowest token stops, a model without a head is almost as good at that cost. The reported average can therefore overstate the saving. We recommend reporting the iterations tokens actually run, with the stopping threshold and batch size, and give a test, run before training a head, that bounds its gain.
authors: Tsung-Han Wu, Minsuk Heo, Kenny Tan
bullets: Mixed-iteration training can predict early stopping but fail under the standard stopping rule because the actual stopping iteration is not scored.
Scoring every iteration improves halting, but the reported runs required a strong penalty favoring early stops.
Batch generation runs until the slowest token finishes, so average iterations per token can overstate practical savings.
The authors recommend reporting actual iterations run, stopping threshold, and batch size.
They also propose a pretraining test to bound the potential benefit of a halting head.
papers.selection_reason: Reevaluates compute savings of halting heads in looped LLMs; relevant to efficient inference and LLM architecture.
papers.title: Do Halting Heads Really Save Compute in Looped Language Models?
papers.tldr: Halting heads may provide far less real compute savings than average iteration counts suggest, especially in batched generation.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) to FP4 has emerged as a key technique for reducing large language model inference cost, especially on Blackwell GPUs, which offer native FP4 tensor core support. Direct PTQ to FP4, however, still leaves a noticeable accuracy gap. Recent work on SVDQuant mitigates the errors introduced through FP4 quantization for diffusion models by adding high-precision low-rank corrections obtained via SVD. However, this high-precision low-rank correction requires many bits per rank, and it runs on the same tensor cores as the main FP4 GEMM. We introduce BiLoCo, a low-rank correction method whose left and right factors are stored as binary ${\{\pm 1\}}$ sign vectors rather than as BF16 numbers. The signed format uses $16{\times}$ less storage per rank-one component, and since the correction now consists of additions/subtractions, this can be run on CUDA cores concurrently with the FP4 tensor-core GEMM. On 4B--72B LLMs, BiLoCo matches or improves memory-matched SVDQuant for PTQ. We implement BiLoCo on B300 as a fused single kernel, where the FP4 GEMM runs on tensor cores, the bit-packed correction on the CUDA cores of the same launch, and the two are combined in the GEMM epilogue. With batch size $1$, the fused kernel is at most $11\%$ slower than the FP4-only GEMM for every rank up to $512$. At rank $128$, it is at most $20\%$ slower up to batch size $8$.
authors: David Jin, Beshr IslamBouli, Tarushii Goel, Han Guo, Yoon Kim
bullets: Addresses the accuracy gap caused by direct FP4 post-training quantization.
Stores low-rank factors as binary ±1 sign vectors, reducing storage per rank-one component by 16× versus high-precision corrections.
Runs the correction through additions/subtractions on CUDA cores concurrently with the FP4 tensor-core GEMM.
On 4B–72B LLMs, matches or improves memory-matched SVDQuant for PTQ.
A fused B300 kernel is at most 11% slower than FP4-only GEMM at batch size 1 for ranks up to 512, and at most 20% slower at rank 128 through batch size 8.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces binary low-rank corrections (BiLoCo) for post-training quantization to reduce memory usage and latency in LLM inference, running efficiently on tensor cores.
papers.title: BiLoCo: Binary Low-Rank Corrections for Post-Training Quantization
papers.tldr: BiLoCo uses binary low-rank corrections to recover FP4-quantized LLM accuracy with far less storage and limited inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Fixed-window Vision Transformer (ViT) decoders run at deployment resolution as overlapping tiles: every token in an overlap band is processed by several full decoder instances. In the 2.4B-parameter MiniMax-H3 video decoder, about half of all per-token computation is duplicated. Removing the tiles fails because attention, global tokens and coordinates are bound to them. TileShare keeps each released tile's attention and computes every other operation once per token. The released computation changes at one kind of step only: an overlap token's per-tile results are blended into one shared state with the released weights. Interventions show that this blend costs quality where attention reads the shared states, mainly in the first few layers, which TileShare therefore keeps per tile. Without training, keeping six layers per tile decodes 1.38-1.51x faster than batched and compiled tiling on two GPU types (up to 1.96x with FP8) and is equivalent to the released decoder in PSNR, LPIPS and DISTS on DAVIS videos. On unseen UVG videos with the setting frozen beforehand, it matches PSNR and DISTS and improves LPIPS. TileShare carries over to two further decoders and is again confirmed on unseen data. It is equivalent in PSNR and DISTS on MAGI-1. On the ViTok-v2 image autoencoder at 2K-4K, it matches overlapping tiling in PSNR, improves LPIPS and DISTS and decodes 1.5-1.8x faster. How many layers stay per tile is measured once per model (for decoders, without labels); we report it for 14 decoders and encoders. Optionally, two GPU-hours of self-distillation let MiniMax-H3 share every layer without a loss in PSNR, and a coordinate field trained while the network stays frozen brings fully shared CLIP-based open-vocabulary segmentation to parity with sliding windows on seven benchmarks.
authors: Xiangzhong Ye, Zhongshen Li, Shen You, Ziyang Meng, Liang Xu, Junkai Ji, Qiuzhen Lin, Xiangtao Li, Ka-Chun Wong
bullets: Overlapping tiles duplicate roughly half of per-token computation, but naively removing tiling disrupts attention, global tokens, and coordinates.
TileShare preserves tile-specific attention and blends overlap-token states, while keeping early layers per tile to protect quality.
Training-free decoding is 1.38–1.51× faster, up to 1.96× with FP8, while matching or improving reported perceptual metrics across tested video and image decoders.
The approach transfers to additional decoders and encoders, with validation on unseen video data and high-resolution image autoencoding.
Optional self-distillation enables sharing every layer; a separately trained coordinate field supports shared open-vocabulary segmentation.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free acceleration of overlapping tiled ViT decoding by sharing duplicate computation; a clear efficiency contribution.
papers.title: TileShare: Training-Free Acceleration of Overlapping Tiled ViT Decoding
papers.tldr: TileShare accelerates overlapping tiled ViT decoding without retraining by sharing most per-token computation while preserving quality.

papers.abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) in sub-8-bit arithmetic promises substantial gains in memory bandwidth and compute throughput, yet FP4 formats introduce quantization error severe enough to destabilize optimization if left unaddressed. We present ALTO, an open-source training recipe for GPT-OSS-20B, a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, on the MLPerf Small MoE Training benchmark under the MXFP4 microscaling format. The recipe combines established techniques from Abecassis, Felix et al. [arXiv:2509.25149] (hybrid 1D/2D block quantization, randomized Hadamard transforms, and stochastic rounding) with a simplified weight de-oscillation scheme adapted from TetraJet-v2 [arXiv:2510.27527]. On C4 validation at global batch size 16, MXFP4 + RHT + SR + de-oscillation reaches a validation loss of 3.3350 at 16,128 steps, only 0.007 above the BF16 baseline (3.3283), closing roughly 50% of the gap left by MXFP4 without de-oscillation (3.3418). Measured by steps to reach the MLPerf quality target (validation loss 3.34), de-oscillation cuts the FP4 convergence overhead relative to BF16 from +20.0% to +5.0%. We also report negative end-to-end results from differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping, and macro-block scaling, despite each showing operator-level SNR gains. All experiments use simulated MXFP4 kernels on AMD MI300 hardware and wall-clock speed has not been optimized.
authors: Han Wang, Zhitao Wang, Natalia Frumkin, Xuanwu Yin, Alireza Khodamoradi, Dong Li, Emad Barsoum
bullets: MXFP4 training is challenging because FP4 quantization error can destabilize optimization.
ALTO combines hybrid block quantization, randomized Hadamard transforms, stochastic rounding, and simplified weight de-oscillation.
On C4 validation, the recipe reaches loss 3.3350 versus 3.3283 for BF16, recovering about half the gap from MXFP4 without de-oscillation.
De-oscillation reduces convergence overhead relative to BF16 from +20.0% to +5.0% at the MLPerf quality target.
Differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping, and macro-block scaling did not improve end-to-end results despite operator-level SNR gains.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a training recipe for an MoE LLM in MXFP4, relevant to large-language-model training and compute/memory efficiency.
papers.title: Training an MoE LLM in MXFP4: How We Closed the Gap to BF16
papers.tldr: ALTO combines quantization and stabilization techniques to train an MoE LLM in MXFP4, reducing the convergence gap to BF16 to near parity in validation loss and overhead.

papers.abstract: Large language models often acquire specialized capabilities through successive pretraining stages, but these gains can come at the cost of forgetting earlier knowledge. In this work, we investigate whether such trade-offs can be improved by changing how strongly each domain contributes to learning while keeping its data exposure fixed. We find that, in controlled knowledge--mathematics experiments, loss reweighting produces a single checkpoint that surpasses the best knowledge and reasoning scores attained along either stage trajectory. This reveals an independent control that data-mixture ratios alone do not capture. Building on this finding, we propose LARE (Loss-Adaptive Reweighting under fixed Exposure), which automatically adjusts domain weights from running loss statistics. Motivated by a theoretical analysis of gradient noise, its normalized inverse-square-root rule balances relative loss scales without changing the sampled mixture or requiring additional runs to search for weights. Across knowledge, mathematics, and code, \Method{} improves all five evaluated benchmarks for a 1.5B model trained on 240B tokens, averaging +7.84 pp over a matched direct mixture, including gains of +17.06 pp on GSM8K and +9.00 pp on MATH. These findings demonstrate that adjusting domain loss scales can improve joint capabilities without additional domain exposure.
authors: Jiazheng Li, Huaqing Zhang, Jing Xu, Tianle Cai, Jingzhao Zhang
bullets: Motivation: Sequential pretraining can improve specialized abilities but may cause forgetting of previously learned knowledge.
Core method: LARE automatically adjusts domain loss weights using running loss statistics, following a normalized inverse-square-root rule motivated by gradient-noise analysis.
Key finding: Loss reweighting provides an independent control beyond data-mixture ratios and can outperform both stages of sequential pretraining in controlled knowledge–mathematics experiments.

Results: On a 1.5B-parameter model trained on 240B tokens, LARE improved all five evaluated benchmarks across knowledge, mathematics, and code, averaging 7.84 percentage points over a matched direct mixture.
Scope: The approach improves capabilities without changing sampled data exposure or requiring additional weight-search runs.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes loss reweighting for fast LLM pretraining, a methodological contribution to efficient training of large models.
papers.title: Beyond Data Schedule: Fast LLM Pretraining on Data Mixtures by Loss-Reweighting
papers.tldr: LARE improves joint LLM capabilities by reweighting domain losses while keeping the data mixture and domain exposure fixed.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is a key technique for efficiently deploying large language models, as it compresses weights into low-bit representations without retraining. Existing PTQ solvers, including GPTQ, LDLQ, and block coordinate descent, commit each weight block to a single codeword before its neighbors are considered, leaving near-optimal alternatives unexplored. In this work, we cast row-wise PTQ as posterior inference over discrete codebooks, in which existing solvers correspond to a zero-temperature, hard-decision limit retaining only the top codeword per block. We propose Message-Passing Quantization (MPQ), which preserves soft posterior information across blocks during inference and commits to hard codewords only at the output stage. MPQ first uses vector approximate message passing to compute approximate blockwise posteriors, then refines a hard-decision initialization by exact block coordinate descent. Across 2-bit lattice and 3- and 4-bit scalar quantization on dense language models from Llama, Qwen, and Mistral families, MPQ improves perplexity and zero-shot accuracy over strong hard-decision baselines, and composes favorably with preprocessing techniques such as activation-aware scaling and incoherence processing. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/MPQ.
authors: Yanshuo Chen, Chenxi Liu, Reza Shirkavand, Heng Huang
bullets: Reframes row-wise PTQ as posterior inference over discrete codebooks.
Identifies GPTQ, LDLQ, and block coordinate descent as hard, zero-temperature decisions that discard alternative codewords.
Uses vector approximate message passing for soft blockwise posteriors, followed by exact block coordinate descent for refinement.
Evaluated on 2-bit lattice and 3-/4-bit scalar quantization across Llama, Qwen, and Mistral models.
Reports improved perplexity and zero-shot accuracy over hard-decision baselines, with compatibility with activation-aware scaling and incoherence processing.
papers.selection_reason: Post-training quantization of LLMs directly reduces model memory requirements for efficient inference.
papers.title: MPQ: A Message-Passing View of Post-Training Quantization
papers.tldr: MPQ improves post-training quantization by passing soft information between weight blocks before making final low-bit decisions.

papers.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a powerful paradigm for scaling Neural Machine Translation (NMT) and managing language heterogeneity. However, practical limitations hinder its deployment on resource-constrained devices: the entire expert pool must remain in memory, and the per-token compute budget is statically fixed during training by rigid top-k routing. We introduce EDWARD-NMT (Elastic Dimensions With Adaptive Routing and Dual-consistency for NMT), a novel MoE encoder-decoder architecture designed for a train once, deploy anywhere paradigm that exposes a family of deployable sub-networks at inference time. EDWARD-NMT integrates three key innovations: (i) Matryoshka-style elastic dimensions to flexibly reduce the memory footprint; (ii) an adaptive sigmoid router with a learned, task-conditioned threshold, allowing each token to dynamically determine its active expert count; and (iii) a dual-consistency objective to maximize the performance of the extracted sub-networks. Extensive experiments on PhoMT (En-Vi), WMT-14 (En-De), multilingual OPUS-16, and a multi-domain De-En benchmark validate our approach. The full-capacity architecture matches or exceeds strong MoE baselines with improved parameter efficiency. Furthermore, the sub-networks seamlessly extracted from a single checkpoint consistently outperform comparably sized dense Transformers without any retraining.
authors: Edward Nguyen, Thai Tran, Kiet Anh Hoang, Duy Hoang, Duy Vo, Khanh Le, Vu Le
bullets: Addresses MoE deployment constraints: large expert memory requirements and fixed per-token top-k computation.
Uses elastic Matryoshka-style dimensions to reduce memory footprint at inference.
Employs an adaptive sigmoid router with a learned task-conditioned threshold for token-dependent expert selection.
Adds dual-consistency training to preserve the quality of extracted sub-networks.
Experiments across multiple translation and multilingual benchmarks show strong full models and sub-networks outperforming comparably sized dense Transformers without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse MoE architecture with elastic dimensions and adaptive routing reduces inference memory/compute; transferable to efficient AI.
papers.title: EDWARD-NMT: Elastic Dimensions With Adaptive Routing and Dual-consistency for Neural Machine Translation
papers.tldr: EDWARD-NMT enables one MoE NMT model to produce memory- and compute-flexible sub-networks that remain effective without retraining.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce computation through sparse activation, but storing their expert parameters remains a major memory bottleneck. We introduce GS-MoE, a training-free compression framework that addresses redundancy across and within experts through two compression axes: shared-subspace rank and expert intermediate width. Groupwise low-rank representations capture shared structure across experts while retaining expert-specific projections, and Nystr\"om-based neuron compression reduces intermediate width within each expert. For fixed shared subspaces, we derive per-expert reconstruction-error reductions from the reconstruction objective and use them to guide expert grouping. Budgets are allocated hierarchically using a gradient-free layer-importance score to guide the allocation of rank and width budgets across layers, which eigenvalues and leverage then distribute as non-uniform ranks across groups and intermediate widths across experts. Experiments demonstrate the complementary benefits of compression along both axes, particularly at high compression rates on fine-grained MoE models. On DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base, at a 60% reduction in total model parameters, GS-MoE retains approximately 90% of the uncompressed model's average reasoning performance, compared with 73% for D$^2$-MoE, while achieving 20% lower out-of-domain perplexity. We provide a code implementation at: https://github.com/cbacary/GS-MoE
authors: Carson Cary, Yukai Jin, Yihao Huang, Zhankai Ye, Fangyi Li, Ting Hua, Xin Liu, Shangqian Gao
bullets: Targets the memory bottleneck caused by storing parameters for many MoE experts.
Combines groupwise low-rank subspace sharing with Nyström-based neuron compression within experts.
Uses reconstruction error to group experts and gradient-free importance scores to allocate layer, rank, and width budgets.
On DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base, retaining about 90% of average reasoning performance at 60% parameter reduction, versus 73% for D²-MoE.
Also achieves 20% lower out-of-domain perplexity at that compression level; results emphasize fine-grained MoE models and high compression rates.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free MoE compression via groupwise subspace sharing and pruning; fits Efficient AI.
papers.title: GS-MoE: Training-Free MoE Compression via Groupwise Subspace Sharing and Pruning
papers.tldr: GS-MoE is a training-free method that compresses MoE models by sharing expert subspaces and pruning expert widths while preserving performance under high compression.

papers.abstract: We introduce TWIG (Tree-structured Weights with Inherited Gates), a representation in which every weight of a neural network is the end of a path of small discrete decisions: a sign, a shift by a power of two, a zero gate, an index into a shared table. Weights that belong together share the upper part of their paths, and each decision is inherited by every weight below it, so it is stored once and applied once. This simple change has three consequences. Any trained network can be written as a TWIG, and when the decisions are powers of two its weight layers become circuits made almost entirely of wires and adders, suited to chips whose weights are fixed at fabrication. Pruning, quantization, low-rank factorization, codebooks and weight sharing become edits of one object, so a single optimizer can choose among all of them for a whole network. And choosing the decisions is the ground-state problem of a higher-order Boltzmann machine whose interactions follow the paths of the tree, the problem class that annealers and quantum optimizers are built to solve. Today these questions are handled apart: each compression method brings its own format and solver, a circuit with fixed weights needs a dedicated constant multiplier for every weight, and discrete solvers reach only narrow subproblems such as rounding. Weight formats have long been moving toward shared decisions, through group scales, shared exponents, microexponents and sparse weights; TWIG takes this trend to its end, and every common format is a shallow TWIG at no extra cost. On five weight matrices of a large language model, a flat tree whose signed power-of-two terms are chosen per weight for circuit cost, with no group scales, needs 9--15\% fewer additions than GPTQ at equal layer error at 3- and 4-bit accuracy on typical matrices, and 20--55\% fewer on matrices with strong outliers.
bullets: Each weight is formed by inherited choices such as sign, power-of-two shift, zero gates, or shared-table indices.
Shared path prefixes store and apply decisions once, making pruning, quantization, low-rank factorization, codebooks, and weight sharing edits of one representation.
Power-of-two TWIG layers can be implemented largely with wires and adders, avoiding a dedicated constant multiplier per weight.
Selecting decisions corresponds to a higher-order Boltzmann-machine ground-state problem suitable for annealing and quantum optimization.
On five large-language-model weight matrices, TWIG used 9–15% fewer additions than GPTQ at equal layer error for typical matrices, and 20–55% fewer for matrices with strong outliers.
papers.selection_reason: Unified weight compression and quantization representation via shared discrete decisions; fits Efficient AI.
papers.title: Every Weight Is a Path of Shared Discrete Decisions
papers.tldr: TWIG represents neural-network weights as paths of shared discrete decisions, unifying compression and enabling efficient fixed-weight circuits and discrete optimization.

papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) in neural networks is a promising learning approach for updating the knowledge of deployed systems based on new data encountered at run time, that have not been learned during the offline training phase. To enable their power/energy-efficient CL processing, neuromorphic continual learning (NCL) concept with sparse event-based operations have recently been introduced. However, state-of-the-art NCL methods typically employ the memory-hungry data/experience replay, coupled with costly global learning rule (i.e., backpropagation-based surrogate gradient). To address these limitations, we propose ENCL, a novel methodology that enables efficient NCL by employing a lightweight local learning rule and sub-network freezing strategy. ENCL leverages the temporally- and spatially-local learning rule to perform efficient credit assignment for training new tasks, alleviating the expensive cost of global learning rule. ENCL also employs a sub-network freezing strategy based on the given tasks to avoid the needs for network architecture expansion, hence further improving the efficiency and scalability of the NCL training process. To efficiently support this, we train each task with a small number of epochs as well as adjusted learning rate and timestep. Experiment results on task-incremental learning (TIL) scenario show that, our ENCL consistently achieves strong performance across different datasets as compared to state-of-the-art works. Specifically, ENCL achieves competitive accuracy comparable to that of the state-of-the-art data/experience replay, while reducing memory cost by up to 88%, NCL training time by up to 51%, average power consumption by up to 40%, and energy consumption by up to 65% across different benchmarking datasets (i.e., Split MNIST, Split Fashion MNIST, Split CIFAR-10, and Split CIFAR-100).
authors: Rachmad Vidya Wicaksana Putra, Shuochen Zhou, Hassan Raza, Muhammad Shafique
bullets: Targets the memory and computational costs of experience replay and global backpropagation-based learning in neuromorphic continual learning.
Uses temporally and spatially local learning for efficient credit assignment when learning new tasks.
Freezes task-associated sub-networks to avoid network expansion and improve scalability.
In task-incremental experiments across Split MNIST, Split Fashion MNIST, Split CIFAR-10, and Split CIFAR-100, it achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art replay methods.
Reports reductions of up to 88% in memory, 51% in training time, 40% in average power, and 65% in energy consumption.
papers.selection_reason: Neuromorphic continual learning with local learning rules and network freezing; fits continual learning and efficiency topics.
papers.title: ENCL: Enabling Efficient Neuromorphic Continual Learning with Local Learning Rule and Sub-Network Freezing Strategy
papers.tldr: ENCL enables more efficient neuromorphic continual learning by combining a local learning rule with task-based sub-network freezing, reducing memory, time, power, and energy costs while maintaining competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large neural networks are increasingly deployed with 1-4 bit weights and 16- or 32-bit activations, yet their dot products still use one multiplier per element. We show that a length-n dot product with k-bit weight codes can be computed with n+2^k additions and at most 2^k decodes and 2^k multiplications. Each weight code is used directly as an address offset that selects one of 2^k accumulators; each activation is added into the selected accumulator; and the accumulated sums are decoded and multiplied only once, at the end, in a fused decode-and-multiply step. The decoded weight vector is never formed. The refactoring is exact for integer arithmetic, works with integer or floating-point operands and with arbitrary, including nonlinear, decoders, and extends to group-wise scales and to matrix and tensor products. The multiplier count falls by n/2^k, while total arithmetic energy improves by a smaller, bounded factor that we quantify with a cost model. We describe a scatter-accumulate processing element (SA-PE) that replaces the MAC unit in a weight-stationary systolic array, with a load/stream/reduce/drain schedule in which a small, time-shareable multiplier runs only 2^k times per tile. Because decoded weights are not stored, local weight memory shrinks by up to w_d/k for w_d-bit decoded weights. An RTL implementation synthesized for FPGA and compared with a matched MAC array shows that an unshared SA-PE is larger than a MAC PE, and that the saving appears when the reduction multiplier is shared across PEs. Software models confirm exact integer equivalence and floating-point error no worse than the conventional pipeline. We do not claim the underlying identity is new, and we discuss related work on weight sharing and lookup-based kernels.
bullets: Uses each k-bit weight code to route activations into one of 2^k accumulators, avoiding explicit weight decoding.
Requires n+2^k additions and at most 2^k decodes and multiplications for a length-n dot product.
Extends to nonlinear decoders, group-wise scales, and matrix or tensor products without storing decoded weights.
Reduces multiplier count by n/2^k and can shrink local weight memory by up to w_d/k, though energy gains are smaller and bounded.
FPGA results show benefits when the reduction multiplier is shared across processing elements; exact integer equivalence and no worse floating-point error are reported.
papers.selection_reason: Hardware-efficient dot-product refactoring for quantized weights reduces multipliers and energy; fits Efficient AI.
papers.title: Decode Late, Multiply Once: Rethinking the Dot Product for Quantized Weights
papers.tldr: A scatter-accumulate reformulation computes dot products with quantized weights exactly while replacing per-element multiplications with late, shared decode-and-multiply operations.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) process increasingly long sequences, attention becomes a major computational bottleneck. Sparse attention mostly targets inference, yet many methods still train densely or cannot support sparse training, and their added complexity makes sparsity hard to turn into wall-clock speedups, leaving dense attention widely used in practice. This paper introduces LazyFlash, a forward-dense, backward-sparse attention method built on the observation that attention training is dominated by the backward pass. LazyFlash keeps the forward pass exactly dense, so the trained model remains a standard dense model that existing systems such as vLLM can serve without any change. For the backward pass, LazyFlash proposes a gradient-aware block sparsification design that ranks query blocks by their attention-output gradient norms and skips those contributing negligibly to parameter updates, turning the dense backward into a block-sparse one. A gradient-mass budget adapts the amount of skipped computation to each head and training step, while importance sampling preserves the dense gradient in expectation. These designs are implemented inside the tiled FlashAttention backward kernel, where skipped blocks are never loaded or computed, translating gradient sparsity into real wall-clock acceleration. Experiments on long-context text and speech LLMs show that LazyFlash maintains downstream performance while achieving up to 5.7x attention-backward speedup over FlashAttention and 1.7x end-to-end training speedup.
authors: Keqi Deng, Ruchao Fan, Jinyu Li
bullets: Addresses the training-time bottleneck of dense attention, which limits practical speedups from sparse methods.
Uses gradient-aware block sparsification to rank query blocks by attention-output gradient norms and skip negligible updates.
Adapts sparsity with a per-head, per-step gradient-mass budget while importance sampling preserves dense gradients in expectation.
Integrates skipping into the tiled FlashAttention backward kernel, avoiding loads and computation for skipped blocks.
Maintains downstream performance while delivering up to 5.7× attention-backward and 1.7× end-to-end training speedups.
papers.selection_reason: Backward-sparse attention accelerates long-context LLM fine-tuning, directly fitting efficient attention and long-context methods.
papers.title: LazyFlash: Forward-Dense, Backward-Sparse Attention for Accelerated Long-Context Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: LazyFlash accelerates long-context fine-tuning by keeping attention dense in the forward pass while skipping low-impact blocks during the backward pass.

papers.abstract: Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. Local deployment requires models to fit within limited memory and execute efficiently with the available computational resources. Recent work has shown that learning sparse-plus-low-rank representations enables elastic compression of a single checkpoint to multiple memory budgets. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into faster inference. Indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparse components can offset computational savings. To address this critical deployment barrier, we introduce S-SALAAD, a unified framework that jointly learns the model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components during training. The framework supports a family of hardware-compatible structured sparsity patterns. It couples this structure learning with budget-aware compression and dedicated CPU and GPU kernels that exploit the learned structure for acceleration, enabling efficient inference from a single checkpoint across memory budgets. Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S-SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.
authors: Tianxiang Xia, Kai Lion, Niao He, Michael Muehlebach, Melanie Zeilinger, Hao Ma
bullets: Motivated by the need to run large models locally despite limited memory, compute, unreliable connectivity, and privacy constraints.
Addresses the gap between parameter compression and real inference speed caused by indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparsity.
Jointly learns model weights, low-rank representations, and hardware-compatible structured sparse patterns during training.
Combines budget-aware compression with dedicated CPU and GPU kernels to accelerate inference across multiple memory budgets.
Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 across pretraining and distillation report improved perplexity–memory–latency trade-offs over evaluated baselines on multiple platforms.
papers.selection_reason: Structured sparsity and low-rank learning for efficient large-model inference; directly fits Efficient AI.
papers.title: Learning Structured Sparsity for Large Models: Bridging Model Compressibility and Efficient Inference
papers.tldr: S-SALAAD jointly learns structured sparsity and low-rank components so one checkpoint can support memory-efficient, faster large-model inference on edge devices.

papers.abstract: Synthetic rewrites, where a language model rewrites a natural document e.g. into a target style, are now a standard ingredient of pretraining corpora. However, critical aspects of their use remain poorly understood, such as how much compute should be spent rewriting training data and whether a model trained on rewrites can outperform the rewriter. We study these two questions by proposing a rewriting scaling law that predicts loss from model size, training tokens, the fraction of training tokens that are rewrites, and the number of epochs over the natural data, charging the compute spent generating rewrites. We fit this scaling law in two settings. In the compute-limited setting, natural data is plentiful and rewrites come from a third-party rewriter trained with more compute than our largest run. We find that the estimated optimal rewrite fraction increases with compute, from under $10\%$ at $3\times10^{18}$ FLOPs to $32\%$ at $10^{22}$ FLOPs. Our scaling forecast extrapolates $33\times$ in FLOPs to train a 22B-parameter model, whose final loss is within $1.1\%$ of our prediction. This model achieves a better BPB than its rewriter on several web domains at one-tenth the rewriter's training compute. In the data-limited setting, we assume we only have a fixed seed set of natural data and that our rewriter is a model of the same size as the target, pretrained on that seed set. Again, we find the optimal rewrite fraction increases with the compute budget. We also demonstrate that a model trained on rewrites of its own pretraining data, generated by a rewriter of the same size, beats the best run on natural data alone at every model size up to 3B. Our results show that synthetic rewriting can be studied through the scaling law lens: that optimal methodological choices are predictable and scaling does not necessarily break down beyond the rewriter's capabilities.
authors: Nicholas Roberts, Ahmed Ahmed, Suhas Kotha, Percy Liang, Yu Wang, Alex Renda, Nitya Mani
bullets: Studies the tradeoff between rewrite-generation compute, model size, training tokens, rewrite fraction, and data epochs.
Fits the law in compute-limited and data-limited settings, accounting for the cost of generating rewrites.
In the compute-limited setting, the optimal rewrite fraction rises from under 10% at 3×10¹⁸ FLOPs to 32% at 10²² FLOPs.
A 22B-parameter model’s loss was within 1.1% of the scaling forecast after a 33× FLOPs extrapolation.
Models trained on synthetic rewrites can outperform their rewriters and natural-data-only baselines, including across sizes up to 3B parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Derives scaling laws for synthetic data generation under compute constraints, offering a transferable technical insight into data efficiency and pretraining optimization.
papers.title: Rewriting Scaling Laws for Synthetic Data with Compute and Data Constraints
papers.tldr: A proposed scaling law predicts how much synthetic rewriting to use under compute and data constraints, finding that the optimal rewrite fraction grows with available compute and can let models outperform their rewriters.

papers.abstract: Tool-calling agents are mostly optimized for accuracy; in deployment, however, their growing cost is latency: every tool call is decoded autoregressively. Speculative decoding accelerates this without changing the output, and retrieved past calls make strong drafts under real use, where each user's behavior tends to repeat. Yet existing systems keep no cross-session memory, or build the draft store once and never update it. We propose SpecMem, a tool-call memory kept alive and managed throughout deployment: verified calls are written back online into bounded per-user stores with LRU eviction, and a side-effect gate defers irreversible calls until verification confirms. On multi-session, multi-user query streams served by three open-weight models, a frozen store steadily loses acceptance while SpecMem holds it: a 27% gap in mean accepted tokens (+11% to +34% across benchmarks, tracking how much novel work arrives after the store is built) and up to 1.74x wall-clock speedup. Ablations attribute the gain almost entirely to keeping the store live; local per-user scoping adds no acceptance but closes a measured cross-user leakage channel, and gating on declared side effects, rather than on retrieval confidence, is what eliminates irreversible mistakes.
authors: Zihe Song, Wenting Zhao, Ye Liu, Yuanjie Zhu, Ke Xu, Shanghao Li, Philip S. Yu
bullets: Addresses latency from autoregressive decoding of repeated tool calls, beyond accuracy optimization.
Maintains bounded, per-user call stores online with verified write-back and LRU eviction.
Uses a side-effect gate to defer irreversible calls until speculative drafts are verified.
Across three open-weight models, it improves mean accepted tokens by 27% over frozen stores and reaches up to 1.74× wall-clock speedup.
Live memory drives nearly all gains; per-user scoping prevents measured cross-user leakage without improving acceptance.
papers.selection_reason: Live tool-call memory with online updates, LRU eviction, and side-effect gating directly targets LLM agent inference latency and persistent memory.
papers.title: SPECMEM: Accelerating Agentic Tool Calling via Live Memory Management
papers.tldr: SpecMem accelerates agentic tool calling by continuously updating per-user memories for speculative decoding while gating irreversible actions until verification.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is a technique that accelerates the inference speed of autoregressive large language models (LLMs) by sampling from a faster, lower quality draft model. Traditionally, a fundamental characteristic of speculative decoding is that it is lossless with respect to the verifier distribution, guaranteeing speed without sacrificing quality. This differs from recently developed diffusion LLMs (dLLMs), which are notably able to achieve substantial speedups by degrading the quality of their outputs with less diffusion effort. Because diffusion models are able to sample faster than autoregressive models by generating tokens in parallel, they are considered strong candidates for draft models in speculative diffusion. While it is widely understood that diffusion models can sacrifice quality for speed, speculative decoding itself can also be generalized to generate lossy samples faster using more lenient acceptance criteria with respect to the verifier distribution. Presented with the two parameters of diffusion effort and speculative decoding leniency, this paper explores the full achievable Pareto frontier via joint variations of these parameters. Our experiments show that jointly varying diffusion effort and acceptance leniency can extend the speed-quality Pareto frontier over single step diffusion drafting.
authors: Aaron Zorel, Guy Van den Broeck, Aditya Grover, Daniel Israel
bullets: Diffusion language models can serve as fast, parallel-generating draft models for speculative decoding.
Unlike traditional lossless speculative decoding, both diffusion effort and acceptance leniency can deliberately trade quality for speed.
The paper maps the achievable speed–quality Pareto frontier by jointly varying these two parameters.
Experiments show joint tuning extends the frontier beyond using single-step diffusion drafting alone.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the tradeoffs between speculative decoding and diffusion models for inference acceleration, providing insights into efficient generation techniques for LLMs.
papers.title: Speculative Diffusion is a Tale of Two Tradeoffs
papers.tldr: Speculative diffusion accelerates LLM inference by jointly tuning diffusion effort and verification leniency to improve the speed–quality tradeoff.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) transformers, the standard backbone for modern large-scale deep learning, employ conditional computation: only a sparse subset of model weights is used in each forward pass. In MoE transformers, this sparsity arises in the MoE operator, which generalizes the multi-layer perceptron in the classical transformer. In this work, we explore an alternative mechanism for conditional computation that analogously generalizes the attention operator. The sparsity induced by this mechanism naturally nests (i.e., hierarchically composes) with the sparsity induced by the MoE operator. We show that a transformer employing this nested sparsity mechanism, which we call Nestor, performs better than a conventional MoE transformer at equal compute and equal sparsity in language model pretraining. We also show that Nestor is well-suited for continual pretraining: it can be adapted to longer contexts more effectively than conventional MoEs, as well as adapt more efficiently to new domains while forgetting less on old domains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these benefits persist as model size, dataset size, and context length grow. Our results demonstrate the potential of alternative conditional computation mechanisms for deep neural network architectures. Code and checkpoints are available on GitHub at https://github.com/Ma-Lab-Berkeley/Nestor .
authors: Tianzhe Chu, Druv Pai, Yi Ma
bullets: Introduces an alternative conditional-computation mechanism that generalizes attention and naturally nests with MoE sparsity.
Outperforms conventional MoE transformers at equal compute and sparsity during language-model pretraining.
Adapts more effectively to longer contexts and new domains during continual pretraining.
Forgets less about previously learned domains while adapting to new ones.
Benefits persist as model size, dataset size, and context length increase.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces 'Nestor', a transformer architecture with nested sparsity for scalable pretraining and continual learning, offering a transferable technical contribution to efficient model architectures.
papers.title: Nested Sparsity for Scalable Pretraining and Continual Learning
papers.tldr: Nestor adds hierarchical sparsity to the attention mechanism alongside MoE sparsity, improving scalable pretraining and continual learning.

papers.abstract: A bug report describes what went wrong, but rarely where the code should change. Existing repository-level localization methods often let language models iteratively decide what code to inspect next, requiring repeated model calls and substantial token usage. We investigate whether these inspection decisions can instead be planned before source retrieval. In this research, we introduce CuraLoc, which first selects candidate files and represents their symbols using compact behavioral and structural descriptions. In a single planning decision, the model jointly selects starting symbols, chooses code relationships to inspect from each, and forms hypotheses about likely edits. Deterministic retrieval collects the requested source for a final ranking informed by those hypotheses, concentrating model reasoning on choosing and comparing code rather than directing each retrieval step. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach on the SWE-Bench Lite and Verified datasets. On SWE Bench Verified with GPT-5.2, CuraLoc raises Func@1 from LocAgent's 53.8% to 59.3% while using 90.3% fewer recorded tokens, and also outperforms RepoSearcher (56.2%) and Agentless (39.6%) on Func@1. On SWE-bench Lite, CuraLoc achieves a high 83.8% Func@5 accuracy improving on Agentless by more than 15% in relative accuracy. Additionally, CuraLoc supports different model backbones, with strong localization accuracy demonstrated using both GPT-5.2 and GPT-6 Astra. These results provide evidence that repository-level code inspection can be planned effectively without iterative model-controlled navigation.
authors: Sangeeta Warrier, Anush Sankaran, Ryen White
bullets: Targets the high cost and repeated model calls of language-model-driven repository navigation.
Selects candidate files, summarizes symbols behaviorally and structurally, and makes one joint plan for symbols, code relationships, and likely edits.
Uses deterministic retrieval to gather requested source, then ranks locations using the planned hypotheses.
On SWE-bench Verified with GPT-5.2, improves Func@1 from LocAgent’s 53.8% to 59.3% while reducing recorded tokens by 90.3%.
Achieves 83.8% Func@5 on SWE-bench Lite and supports multiple model backbones, including GPT-5.2 and GPT-6 Astra.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for planning code inspection to reduce token usage in LLMs, a transferable technical idea for improving efficiency in LLM-based agents.
papers.title: CuraLoc: Repository-Level Fault Localization via Planned Code Inspection
papers.tldr: CuraLoc plans repository code inspection upfront, achieving stronger fault localization with far fewer recorded tokens than iterative approaches.

papers.abstract: Federated unlearning (FU) aims to remove a designated target client's influence from a trained model without the prohibitive cost of retraining from scratch. Existing methods largely treat unlearning as a post-hoc, stateless operation, overlooking that client influence is path-dependent: contributions made during training, particularly during critical learning periods (CLPs), can have disproportionate and persistent effects. Moreover, knowledge overlap and intermittent client availability make relying on all retained clients inefficient and impractical. We introduce PDF, a path-dependent client-selection framework based on the insight that retained clients are not equally valuable for unlearning. During training, PDF maintains lightweight, target-agnostic, CLP-weighted histories summarizing each client's accumulated update direction and global-model alignment. Upon an unlearning request, these histories identify and rank retained clients that are globally informative yet weakly coupled to the target, enabling retraining-based unlearning with only the top-$k$ clients over a small number of rounds. Experiments on FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 under IID and non-IID settings show that PDF achieves effective forgetting and strong retained utility with substantially fewer retained clients. In particular, PDF achieves $0\%$ forgetting accuracy with retraining-like MIA AUC on non-IID CIFAR-10, improves retained accuracy by up to $6.91$ percentage points over the strongest competing FU baseline on CIFAR-100, and reduces communication by approximately $69\%$ and computation by $57$--$61\%$ relative to Retrain.
bullets: Client influence is path-dependent, especially during critical learning periods, so retained clients are not equally valuable for unlearning.
PDF tracks lightweight, target-agnostic, CLP-weighted histories of each client’s update direction and alignment with the global model.
When unlearning is requested, it ranks clients that are globally informative but weakly coupled to the target and retrains using only the top-k clients.
Across FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 in IID and non-IID settings, PDF preserves retained utility while using substantially fewer clients.
On non-IID CIFAR-10 it reaches 0% forgetting accuracy with retraining-like MIA AUC; relative to Retrain, it cuts communication by about 69% and computation by 57–61%.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a path-dependent client selection framework for federated unlearning, which is a transferable technical idea regarding memory management and adaptation in distributed learning systems.
papers.title: Not All Retained Clients Are Equal: Client Selection for Federated Unlearning
papers.tldr: PDF selects the most useful retained clients for federated unlearning, enabling effective forgetting with much lower communication and computation than full retraining.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) can jointly process a broad range of modalities, such as text, audio, and video, enabling stronger multimodal understanding and reasoning capabilities, but often at substantial inference cost. We observe that the benefit of additional modalities varies across queries, indicating that a fixed modality configuration can be inefficient. Motivated by this, we study query-wise modality selection, which keeps the underlying Omni-LLM fixed while adaptively selecting which modalities to provide for each query. We formulate the problem as an accuracy-cost optimization problem and develop a cost-sensitive learning approach for modality selection. We evaluate our approach on WorldSense using Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni under three inference-cost measures: input tokens, latency, and monetary cost. Across both models, query-wise modality selection consistently improves the accuracy-cost trade-off and can even outperform the standard setting in which all available modalities are provided to the Omni-LLM. For Qwen2.5-Omni, our cost-sensitive approach matches or exceeds this full-modality accuracy while requiring only approximately 41% of the input tokens, 39% of the latency, and 61% of the monetary cost.
authors: Shuqi Liu, Yuzhou Cao, Luke Ong
bullets: Additional modalities are not equally useful for every query, making fixed all-modality inference inefficient.
The method adaptively selects query-specific modalities while keeping the underlying Omni-LLM unchanged.
It formulates selection as an accuracy–cost optimization problem and uses cost-sensitive learning.
Evaluated with Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni on WorldSense across token, latency, and monetary costs.
For Qwen2.5-Omni, it matches or exceeds full-modality accuracy at about 41% of input tokens, 39% of latency, and 61% of monetary cost.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses efficiency in multimodal foundation models by proposing query-wise modality selection to optimize the accuracy-cost trade-off, which is a transferable technique for reducing inference costs in embodied agents.
papers.title: Efficient Omni-modal Large Language Model Inference via Per-Query Modality Selection
papers.tldr: Per-query modality selection makes Omni-LLM inference substantially cheaper while preserving or improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) aims to predict human sentiments by integrating signals from different modalities such as text, video, and audio. However, raw multimodal sequences often suffer from semantic inconsistency--exhibiting redundancy or conflicts within and across modalities--which hinders robust understanding and increases computational cost. To this end, we introduce ConsMSA, which explicitly formalizes semantic distribution consistency across both $\textit{intra}$- and $\textit{inter}$-modality, providing a consistency-aware mechanism for robust and efficient multimodal sentiment prediction. Specifically, ConsMSA projects multimodal token features into a shared sentiment space to compute an Intra- and Inter-modality Consistency Score ($I^2CS$). By coupling this score with predictive relevance, we formulate consistency-aware importance signals that are utilized: (i) as a consistency regularizer to align latent distributions during training, (ii) to derive semantic-aware weights for adaptive multimodal token reweighting, and (iii) as a practical criterion to prune redundant or conflicting tokens. Extensive experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS demonstrate that ConsMSA achieves state-of-the-art performance while remaining robust under aggressive token compression--retaining only 10% of tokens yields comparable accuracy. These results establish semantic distribution consistency as a promising foundation for synergizing predictive robustness with computational efficiency.
authors: Pan Wang, Lipeng Ke, Huajun Ying, Pritish Mohapatra, Rohan Sarkar, Suresh Lakhani, Sankar Venkataraman, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Addresses semantic inconsistency, redundancy, and conflicts in text, video, and audio sequences.
Projects multimodal tokens into a shared sentiment space to calculate intra- and inter-modality consistency scores.
Uses consistency-aware signals for distribution regularization, adaptive token weighting, and token pruning.
Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS report state-of-the-art performance and comparable accuracy when retaining 10% of tokens.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces ConsMSA for multimodal sentiment analysis that leverages semantic distribution consistency for robust token pruning, combining multimodal reasoning with efficiency techniques.
papers.title: ConsMSA: Semantic Distribution Consistency Learning for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
papers.tldr: ConsMSA improves multimodal sentiment analysis by aligning semantic distributions across modalities while reweighting and pruning redundant or conflicting tokens.

papers.abstract: We present a surrogate-accelerated Bayesian history-matching framework, demonstrated on a realistic synthetic model ($N=100{,}188$ cells). The forward map $\mathcal{G}$ is replaced by a Fourier neural operator $\mathcal{G}_\theta$ trained in a closed loop, $\hat{x}_{n+1}=\mathcal{G}_\theta(u,\hat{x}_n)$, with the discrete black-oil residual $R(x_{n+1},x_n)$ as a physics-informed neural operator (PINO) penalty, truncated backpropagation and noise injection. We assimilate production data and 4-D seismic using adaptive regularised ensemble Kalman inversion (aREKI), and synthesise $\Delta V_p$ inside the rollout via a closed-form Gassmann transform of the surrogate, under a two-stage schedule (aREKI on production, then an ensemble smoother with multiple data assimilation, ES-MDA, on both). To temper the ill-posedness, we invert $(\log K,\phi)$ not in $\mathbb{R}^{2N}$, where $N_e\ll 2N$ leaves a rank-deficient covariance and a null space the data never inform, but on a chart $u=\Psi(\tilde m)$, $\tilde m\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, $d\ll 2N$, given by a Parseval-exact truncated cosine transform or a variational auto-encoder decoder. The ensemble then spans its own search space; the directions the data cannot constrain are cut to those the chart can express, and every member decodes to a geologically plausible field. For the rollout we prove an exposure bound $W_1\le\sum_j L^{\,n-1-j}\mathbb{E}e_j$, a physics-penalty contraction $\|D_x\mathcal{G}_\theta\|\le\alpha 0.999$ on pressure and saturation and rolls out in $0.579$ s, a $\sim2500\times$ speed-up, bringing an $N_e=190$-member, $N_a=10$-iteration joint inversion within one GPU-hour.
authors: Clement Etienam, David Blom, Hari Pattathil, Tsubasa Onishi, Harpreet Sethi, Lalson Vincent, Suraj Pawar, Kishan Ramesh Kumar, Pandu Devarakota, Faruk O. Alpak
bullets: Replaces the reservoir forward simulator with an autoregressive Fourier neural operator trained using black-oil residual penalties, truncated backpropagation, and noise injection.
Assimilates production and 4-D seismic data through a two-stage aREKI and ES-MDA workflow, with seismic changes synthesized using a Gassmann transform.
Restricts inversion of permeability and porosity to low-dimensional cosine-transform or variational-autoencoder charts to reduce unidentifiable directions and promote plausible fields.
Provides an exposure-bound analysis and reports stable rollouts, a roughly 2500× speed-up, and completion of the stated ensemble inversion within one GPU-hour on the synthetic model.
Demonstration is limited to a realistic synthetic model with 100,188 cells.
papers.selection_reason: Uses autoregressive Physics-Informed Neural Operators as surrogates for reservoir dynamics, acting as a fast predictor of environment states (world model) and improving computational efficiency.
papers.title: Autoregressive Physics-Informed Neural Operator Surrogates and Joint 4-D Seismic-Production Bayesian History Matching
papers.tldr: A physics-informed Fourier neural operator surrogate enables fast joint production–4-D seismic Bayesian history matching in a low-dimensional geological parameter space.

papers.abstract: We consider the problem of model order reduction (MOR) in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs). We prove generalizations of well-known necessary interpolatory conditions for norm-optimal reduced-order models, originally stated for rational functions in $H_2$ Hardy-Hilbert spaces. We construct an alternative to the iterative rational Krylov (IRKA) algorithm for RKHSs with differentiable kernels to obtain norm-optimal reduced-order models. Then, we introduce generalized Malmquist-Takenaka (GMT) functions that can be used to define orthonormal bases in an arbitrary RKHS. Using GMT functions, we propose unitary transformations between separable RKHSs. This allows us to extend our optimality conditions and subsequent algorithms to MOR problems posed in RKHSs with non-differentiable kernels. The potential and versatility of the proposed MOR framework is demonstrated in several numerical experiments. We perform norm-optimal MOR on various machine learning models such as support vector machines and deep ReLU networks. In addition, we show how the proposed MOR framework can be used to solve seemingly unrelated problems. In particular, we provide an example for fitting high degree polynomials to data and also obtain a FEM-like method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with an optimal kernel basis.
authors: Tam\'as D\'ozsa, Andrea Angino, Rolf Krause, Matthias Voigt
bullets: Generalizes necessary interpolatory optimality conditions for reduced-order models in RKHSs.
Develops an IRKA alternative for differentiable kernels and uses generalized Malmquist–Takenaka functions for arbitrary RKHSs.
Constructs unitary transformations between separable RKHSs, extending the framework to non-differentiable kernels.
Demonstrates applications to support vector machines, deep ReLU networks, polynomial fitting, and PDE solution methods.
Numerical experiments illustrate the framework’s potential across these diverse problems.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces generalized Malmquist-Takenaka functions for norm-optimal model order reduction in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, contributing to model efficiency and compression.
papers.title: Norm-optimal model order reduction in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces
papers.tldr: A general RKHS framework extends norm-optimal model order reduction beyond rational Hardy-space models to differentiable and non-differentiable kernels.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents compact their context for the question at hand, but the compacted context must also serve questions that come later. We evaluate compaction on these later questions, using four corpora that annotate the evidence of several questions per text and recorded agent trajectories, and compare every method with random deletion at the same budget. On MultiRC, keeping the sentences that gpt-6-luna (through the OpenAI Decisions API) judges necessary for the current question raises its accuracy on that question by 11.4 points at 25% of the tokens. On the later questions, however, no method that selects sentences for the current question does detectably better than deleting sentences at random. Deleting words instead of sentences does better: LLMLingua-2, which ignores the question, beats random sentence deletion at the same token count by 12.5 points on the later MultiRC questions. It keeps about twice random deletion's share of the evidence's content words, and at equal content-word retention its gain shrinks to 7.3 points (exploratory). On FEVER, label accuracy can overstate what the kept text supports: the gain of sentence selection is no longer detected when answers are scored against the kept evidence, and the 21.0-point gain of LLMLingua-2 is not shown to rest on the kept text. The ranking also depends on the setting: on Evidence Inference sentence selection beats LLMLingua-2 at a nominal 25% budget, and on $τ$-bench trajectories, whose later tool calls need exact identifiers, it beats random deletion while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain. Scores on the question a compaction was made for do not reliably show how it serves later ones.
bullets: The study evaluates context compaction on later questions using four evidence-annotated corpora and recorded agent trajectories, with random deletion as a matched-budget baseline.
Selecting sentences for the current question improves current-question accuracy but generally performs no better than random deletion on later questions.
Question-agnostic word deletion with LLMLingua-2 improves later MultiRC performance over random sentence deletion, partly by retaining more evidence content words.
Results vary by setting: sentence selection helps on Evidence Inference and τ-bench, while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain on τ-bench.
Label accuracy can overstate whether the retained text supports an answer, especially on FEVER; evaluating only the original question is therefore insufficient.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates context compaction and token/sentence deletion methods for LLM agents, directly relevant to token pruning and eviction.
papers.title: Evaluating Context Compaction on the Questions That Come Later
papers.tldr: Context compaction optimized for the current question does not reliably preserve evidence for later questions, and performance depends strongly on the compression method and evaluation setting.

papers.abstract: Long chain-of-thought decoding is memory-bound: the KV cache of the generated tokens grows linearly with the test-time compute being spent. Evicting cache entries does not fix this, because a model never trained on a cache with entries removed generates longer, often up to the length limit. We instead train the model to compress its own output. AbridgeKV compresses each completed block of generated text into the KV entries of a few learned pause tokens. These are extra input tokens with trained embeddings that produce no output. Once the pause tokens have encoded the block, AbridgeKV frees the block's original cache; subsequent tokens attend to the pause tokens' KV entries in its place. Three novel choices make this work: the pause tokens' KV entries take positions inside the block they replace, the cache budget is allocated across layers according to the measured value of each layer's entries, and compression operates on relatively large blocks. On 446 competition problems from AIME, HMMT, AMC, BRUMO, CMIMC and SMT with 32K-token generations, keeping a quarter of the generated cache matches an identically trained full-KV model in accuracy and output length; the strongest published evictor at a matched budget writes far longer, and the closest trained compressor, retrained on the same data, loses 10 points. Served in vLLM, the cache is 3.5x smaller per sequence and a saturated H100 finishes a problem 3.2x faster than with full KV.
bullets: Addresses the linear KV-cache growth caused by long chain-of-thought decoding.
Compresses completed text blocks into a few learned pause tokens, then frees the blocks’ original cache entries.
Uses in-block pause-token positions, layer-wise cache allocation based on entry value, and relatively large compression blocks.
On 446 competition problems with 32K-token generations, one-quarter of the generated cache matched an identically trained full-KV model in accuracy and output length.
In vLLM, it reduced cache size 3.5× per sequence and improved saturated-H100 problem completion speed 3.2× versus full KV.
papers.selection_reason: Training learned pause tokens to compress long reasoning into a much smaller KV cache is a direct contribution to memory-efficient LLM inference and persistent memory.
papers.title: AbridgeKV: Compressing Long Reasoning into the KV Cache of Learned Pause Tokens
papers.tldr: AbridgeKV compresses long reasoning into learned pause-token KV entries, reducing cache use while preserving performance and speeding inference.

papers.abstract: Looped LMs are parameter efficient and promise dynamic computation (saving memory and FLOPs on easy tokens). However, state-of-the-art open Looped LMs trained with this dynamic computation capability (Ouro models) do not realize it in practice as each loop iteration (depth) requires its own level of KV-cache, necessitating all loop computations. Moreover, Ouro's early-exit prior is enforced on each token equally, which results in static lower-depth like processing of all tokens regardless of difficulty. In this work, we propose a simple "best-available" KV caching strategy that works out-of-the-box, creating a new frontier in the performance vs depth space. Our approach enables up to 30% reduction in FLOPs and KV memory while retaining full-depth performance, showing the true flexibility of Looped LMs. Furthermore, training looped LMs with awareness about this KV caching strategy improves performance and efficiency. Finally, we apply a small but effective fix to the early-exit prior enforcement objective that makes tokens exit at truly heterogeneous depths based on effort. Our findings are validated on Ouro models as well as smaller looped LMs pre-trained from scratch.
bullets: Existing Ouro Looped LMs require KV-cache storage for every loop depth, forcing all loop computations despite supporting dynamic computation.
The proposed “best-available” KV caching strategy enables up to 30% lower FLOPs and KV memory without losing full-depth performance.
Training with awareness of this caching strategy further improves efficiency and performance.
A revised early-exit objective produces heterogeneous token depths based on token difficulty rather than uniform shallow processing.
Results are validated on Ouro models and smaller looped LMs pretrained from scratch.
papers.selection_reason: KV-cache strategy for looped language models enables dynamic computation with reduced memory and FLOPs, fitting efficient inference and LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Enabling Dynamic Computation in Looped LMs
papers.tldr: A practical KV-cache strategy and improved early-exit training make Looped LMs dynamically allocate computation, reducing costs while preserving full-depth performance.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by drafting multiple tokens in parallel, with tree-based methods further improving efficiency through hierarchical structures. Dynamic-tree methods such as EAGLE-3 perform well under greedy decoding via deterministic top-K expansion and global pruning. However, in stochastic decoding (T>0), this mechanism collapses the draft distribution into one-hot probabilities, causing a severe drop in acceptance rate. This creates a dilemma: dynamic-tree methods sacrifice stochastic sampling to preserve context-aware topology, while static-tree methods preserve stochastic sampling with context-agnostic structures. The issue arises because the same probability distribution is used for two conflicting tasks: constructing the tree and verifying tokens. This coupling makes direct injection of randomness challenging due to the resulting stochastic process. We resolve this by decoupling these roles: RheoSampling assigns a token sampled from the draft distribution a proxy probability for tree expansion and pruning alongside its true sampling probability for verification. Specifically, we inject a sampled token among the deterministic top-K slots and treat it with different probabilities during construction and verification, making RheoSampling the first dynamic-tree method with both context-aware top-K construction and stochastic sampling while maintaining losslessness. We establish the lossless guarantee through an equivalence-class analysis that compresses the stochastic tree space into tractable classes. An OT-based verification strategy and a sparse draft mechanism ensure that theoretical gains translate into practical efficiency. Experiments across LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate improvements in acceptance rate and speedup over state-of-the-art dynamic tree methods. This framework may provide a template for analyzing stochastic tree structures.
bullets: Dynamic-tree methods can collapse to one-hot draft distributions under stochastic decoding, sharply reducing acceptance rates.
RheoSampling injects a sampled token into deterministic top-K expansion and assigns separate proxy and true probabilities for construction and verification.
An equivalence-class analysis establishes losslessness despite the resulting stochastic tree process.
Optimal-transport verification and sparse drafting improve practical efficiency.
Experiments across LLMs and benchmarks report higher acceptance rates and speedups than prior dynamic-tree methods.
papers.selection_reason: Speculative decoding method that accelerates LLM inference while preserving stochastic sampling; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: RheoSampling: Resolving the One-Hot Dilemma in Stochastic Dynamic-Tree Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: RheoSampling decouples tree construction from token verification to enable lossless stochastic sampling in dynamic-tree speculative decoding.

papers.abstract: Quantization offers a practical path to deploying diffusion models with reduced memory and computation, but aggressive compression can cause quantized outputs to deviate substantially from their full-precision counterparts. Sampling-stage correction methods seek to compensate for such deviations during sampling, but existing approaches rely primarily on local information and underexploit trajectory history, limiting their ability to correct errors that propagate across timesteps.
