In this work, we formulate sampling with a quantized denoiser as an online estimation problem, using the history of quantized denoiser outputs to recover the underlying full-precision outputs required by the sampler. We propose QuAKE, a Quantization-Aware Kalman Estimator that combines a smooth trajectory prior with a conditional Gaussian observation model. At each sampling step, QuAKE recursively updates the posterior over the output window in closed form and feeds its posterior mean to the sampler. QuAKE is a lightweight plug-and-play corrector that requires no modification to the quantized network and naturally supports arbitrary high-order multistep ODE samplers. Experiments across W4A4-quantized text-to-image diffusion models show that QuAKE consistently outperforms existing methods in reducing the distributional discrepancy from full-precision sampling.
bullets: Addresses errors from aggressive diffusion-model quantization that accumulate across sampling timesteps.
Models sampling as online estimation of full-precision denoiser outputs from quantized outputs and trajectory history.
Combines a smooth trajectory prior with a conditional Gaussian observation model for closed-form recursive updates.
Is a lightweight, plug-and-play correction method compatible with arbitrary high-order multistep ODE samplers.
Across W4A4-quantized text-to-image models, it consistently reduces distributional discrepancy from full-precision sampling more than existing methods.
papers.selection_reason: Quantization-aware diffusion sampling correction reduces memory/compute, fitting Efficient AI.
papers.title: Quantization-Aware Kalman Estimation for Diffusion Sampling
papers.tldr: QuAKE uses a Kalman-style estimator to exploit denoiser-output history and correct quantization errors during diffusion sampling.

papers.abstract: Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models, and yet prevailing approaches based on pooling or learned projections remain underperforming. We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression: input tokens define a regression problem whose fitted coefficients form the compressed representation. Importantly, the regression problem is learned end-to-end via backpropagation, while its coefficients are computed efficiently in closed form during the forward pass. This leads to TTR-Compressor, a general alternative to conventional pooling and projection-based compression. We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for multimodal large language models. On block-wise sparse attention, TTR-Compressor improves RULER performance over attention-based compressors by a large margin. For visual token merging, it consistently outperforms the standard MLP merger and matches its performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. These results establish test-time regression as an effective primitive for sequence compression in efficient language and multimodal models.
bullets: Addresses the information bottleneck and limited performance of pooling- and projection-based sequence compression.
Computes regression coefficients in closed form during inference while learning the regression setup end-to-end with backpropagation.
Evaluated for block-wise sparse attention and visual token merging in multimodal large language models.
Achieves a large RULER improvement over attention-based compressors and matches an MLP merger using 55.6% fewer visual tokens.
Demonstrates test-time regression as a general compression primitive for efficient language and multimodal models.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time-regression sequence compression for sparse attention and visual token merging is an efficiency contribution.
papers.title: Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression
papers.tldr: TTR-Compressor uses differentiable test-time regression to turn input-token relationships into compact representations, improving sequence compression for language and multimodal models.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based models have become the backbone of a wide range of tasks, but their intensive computation and data movement incur substantial energy overhead. Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) offers an energy-efficient alternative, yet its inherent hardware non-idealities perturb stored weights and can significantly degrade model performance. Although existing noise-aware training (NAT) methods improve robustness by injecting noise during training, they largely overlook the critical role of attention mechanisms in Transformer inference.To bridge this gap, we analyze how CIM-induced noise reshapes attention in Transformers and identify two key observations: (1) the divergence between clean and noisy attention maps increases substantially in deeper layers, and (2) conventional NAT can remain overconfident even when its attention routes deviate markedly from the clean reference. Motivated by these findings, we propose ABNAT, an attention-based noise-aware training framework that teaches the noisy student to preserve the clean teacher's headwise attention routes rather than merely reproduce answers, without hardware changes or inference overhead; selective variants further reduce training cost.Extensive experiments across vision, language, and multimodal Transformers show that ABNAT consistently improves robustness over corresponding NAT baselines, improving noise-degraded accuracy by up to 11.28% and reducing attention deviation by up to 85.77%.
bullets: Analog CIM hardware noise perturbs weights and can significantly degrade Transformer performance.
Noise causes increasing divergence between clean and noisy attention maps in deeper layers.
ABNAT uses clean-teacher, noisy-student training to align headwise attention routes, not just final predictions.
The framework requires no hardware changes or inference overhead; selective variants reduce training cost.
Across vision, language, and multimodal Transformers, ABNAT improves noise-degraded accuracy by up to 11.28% and reduces attention deviation by up to 85.77%.
papers.selection_reason: Attention-aware noise-aware training improves robustness of Transformers on energy-efficient analog compute-in-memory hardware.
papers.title: ABNAT: Attention-Based Noise-Aware Training for Robust Transformers on Analog Compute-in-Memory Systems
papers.tldr: ABNAT improves Transformer robustness to analog compute-in-memory noise by training noisy models to preserve clean attention routes.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks in coding, mathematical logic, and iterative reasoning, especially by coordinating effectively within multi-agent systems (MAS). However, language agents traditionally communicate via text exchange, which introduces a bottleneck in information transfer and adds prefill latency for downstream agents. Recent work proposes that directly sharing the key-value (KV) cache between language models can enable efficient latent collaboration, entirely bypassing standard text-based communication. To enable latent communication between heterogeneous models of different sizes, prior work introduces trained fusion adapters for each model pair, which limits practical deployment. We introduce CacheFuse, a training-free method which demonstrates that augmenting a downstream model with an upstream model's KV cache using linear interpolation consistently enables superior performance than the standalone downstream model can achieve. We systematically analyze CacheFuse across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks and demonstrate up to 8.6 percentage points higher accuracy compared to single-model baselines and up to 12.2x TTFT speedup compared to text-based communication in multi-model inference.
bullets: Addresses text-based communication bottlenecks and downstream prefill latency in multi-agent systems.
Combines an upstream model’s KV cache with a downstream model through linear interpolation, without fusion-adapter training.
Evaluated across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks.
Reports up to 8.6 percentage-point accuracy gains over single-model baselines.
Achieves up to 12.2× faster time to first token than text-based multi-model communication.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free KV-cache sharing between language models reduces latency and enables efficient latent LLM communication.
papers.title: Think Before You Speak: Enabling Training-Free Latent Communication Between Language Models
papers.tldr: CacheFuse enables training-free latent communication between heterogeneous language models by linearly interpolating their KV caches, improving accuracy while reducing communication latency.

papers.abstract: Processing long videos with Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is bottlenecked by the quadratic cost of visual tokens, making long-form inference prohibitively expensive. While single-axis compression methods mitigate this, they hit a hard efficiency floor because they treat spatial and temporal redundancy independently. We present VETO (Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision-Language Models), a training-optional plug-in that eliminates this bottleneck through dual-axis compression: (i) an intra-frame compressor that merges semantically similar tokens within each frame via optimal-transport inspired matching, and (ii) an inter-frame compressor that identifies and merges temporally redundant frames. The key design insight is hierarchical ordering: by first compressing spatial dimensions, VETO drastically reduces the cost of subsequent global temporal matching, bypassing the efficiency wall of single-axis approaches, with an advantage that grows with modern fully-fused attention infrastructure. Empirically, VETO achieves up to 45% faster inference (e.g., on LLaVA-OneVision-7B) while preserving or improving accuracy. Under extreme token starvation (10% budget), VETO outperforms VFlowOpt (54.9%), VisionZip (52.6%), and FastV (47.9%) with 55.7% accuracy. We demonstrate universal applicability across LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL-2.5, and LongVA, with zero-shot accuracy preserved or improved in all cases.
bullets: Targets the quadratic visual-token cost that makes long-form video inference expensive.
Uses a training-optional dual-axis plug-in: optimal-transport-inspired intra-frame token merging followed by inter-frame redundant-frame merging.
Hierarchical ordering makes global temporal matching cheaper by first reducing spatial tokens.
Achieves up to 45% faster inference and maintains or improves zero-shot accuracy across LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL-2.5, and LongVA.
At a 10% token budget, reaches 55.7% accuracy, exceeding the cited VFlowOpt, VisionZip, and FastV results.
papers.selection_reason: Dual-axis spatial and temporal token compression directly targets efficient long-video VLM inference.
papers.title: VETO: Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision Language Models
papers.tldr: VETO accelerates long-video VLM inference by hierarchically compressing redundant spatial and temporal visual tokens while preserving or improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Physical control tasks in the natural world, such as driving or object manipulation, frequently exhibit dramatic variations in sensory and compute complexity over time. Correspondingly, a natural resource-efficient choice for robot control is to dynamically switch between control modes with varying resource allocations. However, such "mode-switching controllers" (MSCs) have historically required laborious, expert-driven design and synthesis for each new task. Driven by these design difficulties, modern robotic control architectures often fall back to a wasteful "monolithic" one-size-fits-all structure, where resource allocation is permanently anchored to the hardest, most resource-intensive task phases. To facilitate the design of performant yet efficient MSCs, we propose LLM-Guided synthesis of Efficient Mode-Switching Control Architectures (LEMCA). LEMCA represents MSC designs as interpretable programs to be iteratively refined in an evolutionary loop. To evaluate design fitness, we propose MSC-compatible extensions of automated controller synthesis approaches, such as reinforcement learning in simulation. LEMCA then leverages the semantic priors, reasoning, and coding capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively edit controller modes, their corresponding sensory-compute resource allocations, and mode transitions. Our experiments across diverse control benchmarks show that LEMCA consistently discovers strategies that surpass the Pareto frontier of monolithic designs by reclaiming wasted resources during "easy" task phases. LEMCA thus presents an automated, low-effort path to synthesize resource-efficient MSC designs.
bullets: Addresses the expert effort required to design mode-switching controllers (MSCs) for tasks with varying sensory and compute demands.
Represents MSCs as interpretable programs and iteratively refines their modes, resource allocations, and transitions.
Evaluates candidate designs with MSC-compatible controller synthesis, including reinforcement learning in simulation.
Experiments across diverse control benchmarks show LEMCA surpasses monolithic designs’ Pareto frontier by reclaiming resources during easier phases.
Provides an automated, low-effort approach for synthesizing efficient MSC architectures.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-guided evolutionary synthesis of mode-switching robot controllers that reduce resource use; relevant to robot control and efficient AI.
papers.title: LEMCA: LLM-Guided Synthesis of Efficient Mode-Switching Control Architectures
papers.tldr: LEMCA uses LLM-guided evolutionary program synthesis to automatically design resource-efficient robot controllers that switch modes as task difficulty changes.

papers.abstract: The symbiotic scaling of artificial intelligence models and high-performance computing systems continually creates algorithmic challenges in their convergence. Foundation models (FMs) are a crucial example, requiring months-long training on thousands of cutting-edge GPUs. Sharded data parallelism (DP) is the dominant strategy to accelerate such computations by splitting data and models across multiple GPUs. However, it incurs prohibitive communication overhead when deployed at scale, particularly on multi-tier interconnects with heterogeneous performance. Inspired by the efficient communication principles of federated learning (FL), this work introduces two hybrid algorithms - FL+FSDP and FL+HSDP - interleaving sharded DP with FedAvg-style aggregations. Such approaches decouple large DP deployments into smaller, loosely-coupled federation groups, requiring minimal inter-group traffic while keeping the global batch size bounded by the groups' size. Formal analysis of communication costs and experimental validation prove their scalability and flexibility. A Llama3.1 8B pre-training on 512 A100 GPUs shows that, under identical hyperparameters, FL+FSDP and FL+HSDP achieve up to 8.04 faster data processing and 4.48 lower evaluation perplexity than their counterparts, demonstrating superior computational efficiency and improved model quality. These properties stem from reduced communication overhead and the bounded growth of the global batch size relative to the federation group size.
bullets: Addresses prohibitive communication overhead in sharded data parallelism across heterogeneous, multi-tier GPU interconnects.
Introduces FL+FSDP and FL+HSDP, which combine sharded data parallelism with FedAvg-style aggregation across loosely coupled federation groups.
Keeps global batch-size growth bounded by federation-group size while minimizing inter-group traffic.
On Llama3.1 8B pre-training with 512 A100 GPUs, the methods achieved up to 8.04× faster data processing and 4.48× lower evaluation perplexity under identical hyperparameters.
Validated through communication-cost analysis and experiments, with scope focused on large-scale foundation-model training.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces communication overhead and accelerates large-scale model training, fitting the Efficient AI scope.
papers.title: Accelerating Sharded Data Parallelism at Scale with Federated Learning
papers.tldr: FL-inspired hybrid sharded data-parallel algorithms reduce cross-group communication while improving training throughput and model quality at scale.

papers.abstract: Local learning reduces cross-layer training dependencies, but an efficient accelerator must still retain operands, accumulate gradients, and select quantization scales. We present an FPGA system that trains a CNN and its regional auxiliary classifiers using a shared integer matrix engine. Compact errors are expanded on chip, gradients are folded tile by tile, and historical scales permit direct output conversion. At 200 MHz, the KV260 prototype achieves 76.57% accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 91.85% on SVHN at approximately 4.20 W mean module power. Effective matrix throughput is 31.22 and 31.57 GMAC/s, respectively. Against the same integer method on Jetson Orin Nano, measured training energy is 40.4% and 42.1% lower, with $1.86\times$ and $1.82\times$ longer runtime; measurements use the respective platform power domains. Selected state checks and matching complete-run prediction counts support functional agreement with the software reference.
bullets: Targets the storage, gradient accumulation, and quantization-scale challenges of efficient local learning accelerators.
Uses a shared integer matrix engine; errors are expanded on chip, gradients are folded tile by tile, and historical scales support direct output conversion.
A 200 MHz KV260 prototype reaches 76.57% accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 91.85% on SVHN at about 4.20 W mean module power.
Achieves 31.22 and 31.57 GMAC/s effective matrix throughput on CIFAR-10 and SVHN, respectively.
Uses 40.4–42.1% less measured training energy than the same integer method on Jetson Orin Nano, but runs 1.82–1.86× longer; comparisons use platform-specific power domains.
papers.selection_reason: Energy-efficient integer-only local CNN training on edge FPGAs directly targets reduced computation and energy in AI systems.
papers.title: LocalTrain: Integer-Only Local Learning for Energy-Efficient CNN Training on Edge FPGAs
papers.tldr: LocalTrain enables integer-only CNN training with local auxiliary classifiers on edge FPGAs, achieving efficient CIFAR-10 and SVHN training at low power.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling has emerged as a key inference strategy for reasoning models, where a model generates a large number of candidate solutions in the hope of finding at least one correct solution. Running all candidate solutions to completion can be computationally demanding, so recent work prunes the candidate pool after generating only a short prefix, committing further computation only to the surviving candidates. Existing pruning strategies divide broadly into two categories: Quality-based methods assign a score to each partial solution and discard those predicted to ultimately lead to an incorrect final solution, while diversity-based methods select partial solutions that follow different reasoning trajectories and are therefore likely to cover different final solutions. The tension between these two objectives is an instance of exploration versus exploitation, yet little to no prior work on pruning exposes this trade-off directly, let alone optimizes it. In this paper, we introduce a pruning procedure that addresses this trade-off directly by optimizing pass@$k$ over the selected solution pool. In particular, it chooses the pool to maximize the probability that at least one of its partial solutions, when continued to completion, yields a correct answer. Because this objective simultaneously rewards high-quality partial solutions and penalizes redundancy among them, quality and diversity are naturally balanced by the criterion itself rather than through separate ad-hoc design choices. On eight open-weight reasoning models, our method outperforms existing quality-based and diversity-based pruning strategies. The gains are particularly pronounced when the pruning procedure keeps a moderate number of partial solutions for continued generation, highlighting the value of directly balancing quality and diversity during pruning.
authors: Mahdi Salmani, Adel Javanmard, Devansh Gupta, Meisam Razaviyayn
bullets: Test-time reasoning generates many candidates, but completing all of them is computationally expensive.
Existing pruning methods favor either predicted correctness (quality) or distinct reasoning paths (diversity), leaving their trade-off implicit.
The proposed method selects partial solutions to maximize the chance that at least one continuation is correct.
This objective rewards strong candidates while penalizing redundant ones, balancing quality and diversity without separate heuristics.
Across eight open-weight reasoning models, it outperforms both quality- and diversity-based pruning, especially at moderate pool sizes.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces test-time reasoning computation by directly optimizing candidate selection under a pass@k objective; relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: Direct Pass@$k$ Optimization for Thought Pruning: Balancing Quality and Diversity in Test-Time Reasoning
papers.tldr: A pruning method directly optimizes pass@$k$ to balance reasoning-path quality and diversity, improving test-time reasoning efficiency.

papers.abstract: Constructing accurate and computationally tractable approximation spaces is a fundamental task in scientific computing. Partially trainable neural networks bridge fixed random features and fully adaptive representations. This paper quantifies a phase transition pattern in approximation bounds and observes analogous behavior in training errors: a rapid but smooth initial improvement followed by diminishing returns, with a sharper transition under greater initialization mismatch. Under polynomial spectral decay with exponent $\alpha>1$ and leverage compatibility, we establish a squared $L_2$ approximation rate $\mathcal{O}((\kappa_P\log(m/\delta)/m)^\alpha)$ for two-layer networks of width $m$ and trainable proportion $P$, where $\kappa_P=(P/\kappa_1^*+(1-P)/\kappa_0^*)^{-1}$. The bound holds uniformly over the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) with probability at least $1-\delta$. The constants $\kappa_0^*$ and $\kappa_1^*$ quantify the fixed and trainable groups' sampling mismatches relative to the target RKHS. For spherical biased-ReLU features in dimension $d$, we verify these assumptions with $\alpha=(d+2)/(d-1)$ and $\kappa_0^*=4\sqrt{2}\tau(d+1)/d$ for initialization scale $\tau\ge1$, and $\kappa_1^*=1$ under ridge leverage sampling. For $d=5$ and $\tau=10$, a trainable proportion of approximately $4.1\%$ captures $90\%$ of the reduction in the approximation bound from $P=0$ to $P=1$. A structured three-layer example illustrates how a few trainable first-layer neurons exploit fixed downstream blocks through nonlinear composition. Numerical experiments across diverse settings, including networks with up to 15 layers, exhibit similar phase transitions in training errors.
authors: Xin He, Huan Lao, Xiliang Lu, Shijun Zhang
bullets: The paper studies the transition from fixed random features to fully adaptive two-layer networks within an RKHS approximation framework.
It derives a high-probability squared-$L_2$ approximation bound under polynomial spectral decay and leverage compatibility, parameterized by the trainable proportion and sampling mismatches.
For spherical biased-ReLU features, the theory gives explicit mismatch constants; in one example, training about 4.1% of neurons achieves 90% of the bound reduction obtained by full training.
A structured three-layer construction shows how a small number of trainable first-layer neurons can leverage fixed downstream blocks through nonlinear composition.
Experiments, including networks up to 15 layers, show similar rapid-improvement-then-diminishing-returns behavior in training errors.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes trainable-versus-frozen parameter trade-offs in partially trainable networks with phase transitions; informative for efficient model design and training.
papers.title: Phase Transition from Random Features to Fully Trainable Networks
papers.tldr: Partially training a neural network can rapidly capture most of the approximation gains of fully trainable networks, with diminishing returns as more parameters become trainable.

papers.abstract: Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers. During inference, each recurrence generates independent KV-caches, causing memory to grow linearly. To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth), finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences without quality loss, a property we denote as KV-shareability. However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it. In this paper, we study how KV-shareability can be enabled in looped models. We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use stochastic depth during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence's KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model's quality. As a result, BeNice! enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning's unshared validation perplexity. Using BeNice!, we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g., fp8, mxfp8, nvfp4). Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.
authors: Hayden Prairie, Jacob M. Ryan, Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick, Daniel Y. Fu
bullets: Looped architectures otherwise require separate KV-caches for each recurrence, causing memory usage to grow linearly with depth.
The method combines stochastic-depth pretraining with post-training that broadcasts the final recurrence’s KV-cache to earlier recurrences.
BeNice! achieves KV-shareability while matching standard fine-tuning’s unshared validation perplexity.
KV-sharing composes with sequence mixers and low-precision KV-cache quantization.
In simulated low-memory, long-context inference, it improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, throughput by up to 23.6%, and p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes KV-sharing to reduce inference memory in looped architectures, directly targeting KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: BeNice! Closing Looping's Inference-Memory Gap via KV-Sharing
papers.tldr: BeNice! enables looped models to share KV-caches across recurrences, reducing inference memory and latency without sacrificing validation quality.

papers.abstract: Generating 360-degree panoramas requires both local perspective fidelity and global spherical continuity. Existing representations face a trade-off: equirectangular projection (ERP) enables seamless panorama modeling but suffers from severe distortion and a domain gap to pre-trained image generators, whereas cubemaps preserve perspective geometry but often produce inconsistent faces and visible seams. We present Squaring-the-Sphere, a panoramic image generation framework built on a novel representation CubeAtlas, which unfolds all cubemap faces into a single compact canvas. By arranging orientation-aligned, rotated polar regions alongside the equatorial faces, this representation preserves the perspective geometry of cubemaps while organizing the cross-face relationships required for seamless panorama assembly. It further enables a pretrained diffusion transformer to model the complete panorama jointly in a single pass, without altering the backbone architecture or positional encoding. While CubeAtlas has a token count comparable to ERP, its structured layout makes many dense attention interactions unnecessary. We therefore introduce a layout-aware sparse attention mask that preserves the interactions required for panorama continuity while removing geometrically irrelevant token pairs. As a result, CubeAtlas achieves better quality than ERP modeling with lower attention computation. Furthermore, we introduce a training-free super-resolution technique and a fusion scheme that enhance fine details in distortion-free perspective space before achieving the final ERP panorama. Experiments on various benchmarks demonstrate that our method improves geometric fidelity, cross-view consistency, and high-resolution visual quality over previous methods.
authors: Xuhui Zuo, Chenjie Cao, Tengfei Wang, Junta Wu, Yisu Zhang, Chunchao Guo
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between ERP’s distortion and cubemaps’ cross-face seams.
Unfolds rotated cubemap regions into one compact, orientation-aligned canvas for joint panorama modeling.
Uses layout-aware sparse attention to preserve continuity while reducing unnecessary attention computation.
Adds training-free super-resolution and fusion in perspective space to improve fine details.
Experiments report better geometric fidelity, cross-view consistency, and high-resolution quality than prior methods.
papers.selection_reason: Layout-aware sparse attention for diffusion transformers reduces attention computation; transferable efficiency technique.
papers.title: Squaring-the-Sphere: Distortion-Free and Seamless Panorama Generation via CubeAtlas
papers.tldr: CubeAtlas enables distortion-free, seamless 360° panorama generation by jointly modeling cubemap faces with efficient sparse attention and perspective-space refinement.

papers.abstract: We propose a new regression method named Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona) that directly uses samples to estimate the state and its derivatives at a query point, along with their admissible bounds, without long global training. By casting the values and derivatives at the query and neighbouring samples as latent variables in a constrained optimisation problem, the burden of long training loops becomes one of on-demand local solves. We establish Diona's theoretical properties including finite-sample coverage and, in the noiseless case, convergence to the true state and derivatives under dense sampling. In a nonlinear regression benchmark on six functions of three to eight dimensions, Diona was more accurate than a Gaussian process (GP) on noiseless data especially with denser data sets. Furthermore, as with GP, it produced uncertainty bounds that contained the true value at more than 95% of query points in four functions. Diona's time to a first prediction after a data set update was three to four orders of magnitude shorter than that of the GP, and two to three orders shorter than that of a neural network, which was more accurate but offers no uncertainty quantification. This low latency is paid for by on-demand predictions, so this latency advantage applies when relatively few predictions are needed between data updates.
bullets: Directly estimates a query point’s state, derivatives, and admissible bounds from nearby samples.
Formulates these quantities as latent variables in a constrained local optimisation problem, replacing long global training.
Theoretically provides finite-sample coverage and converges to the true state and derivatives under dense, noiseless sampling.
On six nonlinear benchmark functions, it outperformed Gaussian processes on noiseless data, especially with denser samples.
Prediction after data updates was substantially faster than GP and neural networks, but the advantage applies mainly when few predictions are needed between updates.
papers.selection_reason: On-demand local regression that avoids global training and gives fast first predictions after data updates; relevant to test-time optimization and efficient inference.
papers.title: Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona)
papers.tldr: Diona performs local, training-free regression with uncertainty bounds, offering fast updates and strong accuracy under dense sampling.

papers.abstract: Apple Silicon is among the most widely used platforms for local LLM inference, yet nearly all inference optimizations are designed and validated on server-class NVIDIA GPUs under batched serving workloads. Which optimizations retain their benefits when moved to Apple Silicon, and what determines their applicability? We evaluate four optimization families: KV-cache pruning, speculative decoding, ported GPU kernels, and post-training quantization. Experiments span four Apple machines under a common single-request decode workload, with matched RTX 4090 comparisons where possible. KV-cache pruning can reach up to 1.75 times end-to-end throughput on Apple but can reduce throughput on desktop NVIDIA GPUs. Under the common benchmark, all evaluated speculative decoding methods reduce throughput on Apple, despite reported 2-6 times gains on server GPUs. CUDA kernel designs transfer only partially: public Metal lacks asynchronous copy, and batch-one decode makes several serving-oriented mechanisms inapplicable, although transferable components yield up to 1.20 times decode throughput. Quantization gains vary by machine. Across four families, a reported speedup is not a portable property of a technique alone but a joint function of technique, runtime, hardware contract, and workload regime.
authors: Kyrylo Yemets, Andrii Yaroshevych, Victor Muryn, Ostap Khomenko, Pavlo Kryven, Maksym Kmet, Maksym Shamrai, Mariya Hirna
bullets: Evaluates KV-cache pruning, speculative decoding, ported GPU kernels, and post-training quantization on four Apple machines under single-request decoding.
KV-cache pruning reaches up to 1.75× end-to-end throughput on Apple but can reduce throughput on desktop NVIDIA GPUs.
All tested speculative decoding methods lower Apple throughput, contrasting with reported gains on server GPUs.
GPU-kernel portability is partial because Metal lacks asynchronous copy and batch-one decoding limits serving-oriented mechanisms; transferable components reach up to 1.20× decode throughput.
Quantization benefits vary across Apple machines, showing that optimization speedups are not portable properties of techniques alone.
papers.selection_reason: Systematic evaluation of LLM inference optimizations including KV-cache pruning and quantization on Apple Silicon; relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Evaluating the Applicability of LLM Inference Optimizations on Apple Silicon
papers.tldr: Inference optimizations developed for server GPUs do not transfer uniformly to Apple Silicon; their effectiveness depends on the technique, runtime, hardware, and workload.

papers.abstract: Point cloud transformers aim to capture detailed local geometry and relationships across a scene at a manageable computational cost. Two common approaches are window attention and global attention. They differ in how they enable scene-wide interaction, which refers to information exchange among tokens across a scene. Window attention reduces computational cost by restricting self-attention to groups of tokens called windows; in serialized designs, each window contains a fixed number of consecutive tokens from a spatially ordered sequence. Because each block only directly connects tokens within the same window, information exchange across windows relies on changes in window membership across blocks and hierarchical pooling. Global attention, in contrast, directly connects all tokens within a scene, but computing attention over all token pairs can be costly when the number of tokens is large. To balance computational cost and scene-wide interaction, we introduce MixPT, a point transformer that uses a mix of window and global attention blocks in an interleaved schedule, while retaining a single fixed serialization pattern for its window blocks. For scenes with a large number of tokens, MixPT applies global attention to spatially pooled tokens and returns residual updates to the original-resolution stream. Across indoor and outdoor benchmarks, MixPT achieves competitive accuracy with lower latency than representative window and global attention baselines. We further demonstrate the feasibility of scaling the attention stage in depth by repeating the interleaved pattern of window and global attention blocks.
authors: Minkyun Seo, Hyungtae Lim, Jaesik Park
bullets: Window attention lowers cost but limits direct communication across windows; global attention enables scene-wide interaction but is expensive for large token sets.
MixPT interleaves window and global attention blocks while keeping one fixed serialization pattern for window processing.
For large scenes, global attention operates on spatially pooled tokens and sends residual updates back to the original-resolution stream.
Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show competitive accuracy with lower latency than representative window- and global-attention baselines.
The interleaved attention pattern can be repeated to scale the attention stage in depth.
papers.selection_reason: Point transformer with interleaved window and global attention, contributing to efficient attention and 3D point cloud processing.
papers.title: MixPT: Point Transformer with Interleaved Window and Global Attention
papers.tldr: MixPT balances local detail, global scene interaction, and efficiency by interleaving window and pooled-token global attention in a point transformer.

papers.abstract: KV cache compression for multimodal LLMs usually selects the visual tokens to keep once, at prefill, and reuses that selection for the whole generation. We show that this one-shot selection is severely limited on long-form generation: on detailed image description, even an oracle that selects with the attention of the uncompressed answer reaches only 0.44-0.52 ROUGE-L agreement with the uncompressed output, because the evidence the model reads moves as the description unfolds. Re-selecting whenever attention drifts out of the kept set is the natural remedy, but we find that a fixed drift threshold fails systematically: drift magnitudes are not comparable across samples, so low-drift samples are almost never refreshed although they benefit the most. We propose Rate-Controlled Refresh (RCR), which lets drift decide when and where to re-select while a per-sample controller regulates how often, combined with a low-rank drift detector, candidate-restricted re-selection, and a decision that stays on the GPU. With one setting for all models and tasks, RCR outperforms the per-step retrieval method InfiniGen by 1.6-3.8 ROUGE-L points on five of six model-task settings with no significant difference on the sixth, while staying within 1.7 points of exact per-step re-selection, with comparable estimated data movement per step and a 4x smaller GPU-resident detector. On DetailCaps, drift-chosen timing beats random timing at the same refresh rate and periodic timing even at a higher rate, by 2.0-5.0 points. On pre-registered video description, where drift is homogeneous across samples, RCR is on par with InfiniGen on Qwen2-VL and exceeds it on Qwen3-VL but no longer beats a fixed threshold at the nearest tested rates, consistent with the diagnosis; object-level evaluation shows that RCR achieves higher object F1 against the uncompressed output than InfiniGen on two of three models.
bullets: One-shot prefill-time token selection degrades on long descriptions because the model’s visual evidence shifts during generation.
Fixed drift thresholds refresh inconsistently: low-drift samples may rarely refresh despite benefiting most.
RCR combines drift-based timing and location selection with per-sample refresh-rate control, low-rank detection, candidate restriction, and GPU-resident decisions.
Across six model-task settings, RCR beats InfiniGen by 1.6–3.8 ROUGE-L points in five, matches it in one, and remains close to exact per-step re-selection with a smaller detector.
On image description, drift-based timing outperforms random or periodic refresh; on video description, performance aligns with the method’s assumption that drift varies across samples.
papers.selection_reason: Rate-controlled KV re-selection for long-form multimodal generation; a strong contribution to KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: Drift Says When, Budget Says How Much: Rate-Controlled KV Re-selection for Long-Form Multimodal Generation
papers.tldr: Rate-Controlled Refresh dynamically re-selects visual KV tokens when attention drifts, improving long-form multimodal generation under a controlled refresh budget.

papers.abstract: Vector quantization (VQ), in particular lattice-based methods, offer strong rate-distortion trade-offs for low-bit large language models (LLMs), yet their behavior under quantization-aware training (VQ-QAT) remains poorly understood. We scale lattice VQ-QAT to billion-parameter LLMs and multi-billion-token training regimes, and introduce SQuAT, a shape-gain VQ-QAT approach trained with a separate straight-through estimator (STE) for the shape and gain. SQuAT decomposes weights into direction and magnitude: normalized directions are quantized using an $E_8$-derived spherical codebook, while gains are quantized independently with low-bit scalar quantizers. We show that, unlike a standard STE applied to the full quantizer, which ignores the shape-gain structure, these separate STEs induce tangent-space updates for directions, yielding an implicit form of spherical (Riemannian) optimization. To enable scalability, we develop a distributed exact nearest-neighbor assignment scheme, in which workers quantize disjoint weight blocks and communicate only discrete indices, reducing VQ-QAT training time by 12.8$\times$ and allowing us to scale it to 10B tokens. Across instruction-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen3-4B, and base Qwen3-1.7B, SQuAT consistently outperforms standard VQ-QAT STE under identical quantizers and initialization, and achieves SOTA VQ-QAT accuracy.
authors: Sebastian Loeschcke, Ivan Koryakovskiy, Tycho F. A. van der Ouderaa, Riccardo Del Chiaro, Mart van Baalen, Paul N. Whatmough, Markus Nagel
bullets: Addresses the limited understanding and scalability of VQ-QAT for billion-parameter LLMs.
Decomposes weights into normalized directions and gains, quantizing them with spherical-codebook and scalar quantizers.
Uses separate straight-through estimators that produce tangent-space updates, approximating spherical/Riemannian optimization.
Introduces distributed exact nearest-neighbor assignment, reducing VQ-QAT training time by 12.8× and scaling training to 10B tokens.
Outperforms standard VQ-QAT STE across several LLaMA and Qwen models and achieves state-of-the-art VQ-QAT accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Spherical lattice vector quantization-aware training for low-bit LLM weights; directly relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: SQuAT: Spherical Lattice Vector Quantization-Aware Training
papers.tldr: SQuAT makes lattice-based vector quantization-aware training scalable and more accurate for low-bit LLMs by separately optimizing weight direction and magnitude.

papers.abstract: Tree-based speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by verifying multiple candidate branches in parallel. However, in practical serving scenarios, similar requests repeatedly induce overlapping candidate branches. While retrieval-based methods mitigate this by reusing historical drafts, the resulting candidate trees often contain many low-quality branches as the candidate tree grows, which reduces verification efficiency and wastes target-side computation. To address this, we propose ValuSpec, a plug-and-play candidate valuation mechanism that filters low-quality branches from a supplied candidate tree before expensive target-side verification. ValuSpec introduces transfer-based supervision to align filtering with the target model's behavior. A filtering threshold is estimated from the target model's greedy trajectories on a calibration split, without any parameter training. The target model then verifies the filtered tree under the output-identical greedy rule, so accepted tokens are guaranteed to match standard autoregressive decoding exactly. Experimental results on HumanEval, GSM8K, Dolly, and SpecBench show that, in our main evaluation, ValuSpec achieves up to 2.38x end-to-end speedup in retrieval-based tree settings. Furthermore, integrating ValuSpec into the EAGLE-3 dynamic tree framework yields up to 2.78x end-to-end speedup without modifying its tree construction strategy, demonstrating that ValuSpec serves as a generally applicable and plug-and-play candidate valuation module.
authors: Liang He, SiYuan Ma, Qishi Zhan, Yongqi Fan, Mingyu Cao, Qizhen Lan, Zhaolu Kang, Xilu Wang
bullets: Addresses redundant, low-quality branches in retrieval-based tree speculation that waste target-side verification computation.
Uses transfer-based supervision and a calibration-derived threshold from target-model greedy trajectories, requiring no parameter training.
Prunes a supplied candidate tree before verification and is compatible with existing tree-construction methods.
Reports up to 2.38× end-to-end speedup in retrieval-based settings and up to 2.78× when integrated with EAGLE-3 across the evaluated benchmarks.
Scope: evaluated on HumanEval, GSM8K, Dolly, and SpecBench; results are reported for greedy decoding.
papers.selection_reason: Improves inference efficiency by filtering low-quality candidate branches before target-side verification in speculative decoding.
papers.title: ValuSpec: Plug-and-Play Candidate Valuation before Target Verification for Tree-Based Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: ValuSpec filters low-quality speculative-decoding branches before target-model verification, accelerating inference while preserving greedy-decoding outputs exactly.

papers.abstract: Scaling embedding capacity alongside Transformer computation is an emerging trend in language models. This trend makes high compression rates increasingly useful. Hence, we study extreme compression of Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which follow this trend and account for 35.2% of the parameters of Gemma 4 E4B. At such rates, conventional quantizers give each token-layer vector its own code of only a few bytes. We instead develop OPTIC (Output-Path-fitted, Token-shared Indexed Codes), which stores one quantized code tuple per token and decodes it at every layer with a layer-specific affine decoder. Codes and decoders are fitted to the PLE output path rather than to the stored vectors. At about $100\times$ PLE compression of bfloat16 (BF16) E4B, OPTIC retains an aggregate 97.8% of the uncompressed model's performance across seven benchmarks, whereas product quantization, the strongest of six conventional baselines, retains 66.3%. At $594\times$ and $1,002\times$ PLE compression of BF16 E4B, OPTIC retains 90.5% and 84.1%. On the official E4B release with 4-bit linear weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16), OPTIC retains 96.9% at about $100\times$ PLE compression. During inference at about $100\times$ PLE compression, BF16 E4B uses 29.7% less GPU memory than with uncompressed PLE at the same key-value cache size, while running at most 0.40% slower.
authors: Jiacheng Liu, Yaxin Luo, Xiaohan Zhao, Peng Sun, Xinyi Shang, Jiacheng Cui, Yonina C. Eldar, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Per-layer embeddings account for 35.2% of Gemma 4 E4B’s parameters, motivating extreme compression.
OPTIC stores one quantized code tuple per token and decodes it at each layer using layer-specific affine decoders.
It fits codes and decoders to the model’s output path rather than directly to stored embedding vectors.
At about 100× BF16 PLE compression, OPTIC retains 97.8% aggregate performance across seven benchmarks, versus 66.3% for the strongest conventional baseline.
At the same compression level, inference uses 29.7% less GPU memory and runs at most 0.40% slower; performance remains 84.1% at 1,002× compression.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces cross-layer latent vector quantization for extreme per-layer embedding compression, directly reducing LLM memory footprint.
papers.title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization
papers.tldr: OPTIC enables roughly 100× compression of per-layer embeddings while preserving most of the model’s benchmark performance and reducing inference memory with minimal slowdown.

papers.abstract: Search is a central component of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems and has been deeply investigated for classical ASR modeling based on Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). However, in work on current sequence-to-sequence ASR architectures it is often simplified to a small fixed-size beam search without external Language Model (LM). In this work, we present a comparative analysis of search space complexity and efficiency for Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) and neural transducer models under different pruning strategies and LM configurations. We show that these end-to-end (E2E) models work with a small search space most of the time but exhibit large temporary peaks in hypothesis count during periods of uncertainty. Score-based pruning dynamically adapts the search to model uncertainty, leading to a significantly lower Real-Time Factor (RTF). Our results highlight the limitations of search with low fixed-size beam pruning and provide practical guidelines for efficient search in E2E ASR.
authors: Simon Berger, Larissa Kleppel, Ralf Schl\"uter
bullets: Analyzes search-space complexity and efficiency in CTC and neural-transducer ASR models.
Evaluates different pruning strategies and external language-model configurations.
Finds that hypothesis counts are usually small but can temporarily grow substantially during uncertain speech segments.
Shows that score-based pruning adapts to uncertainty and substantially reduces real-time factor.
Provides practical guidance and identifies limitations of fixed-size beam search.
papers.selection_reason: ASR search-space pruning and efficiency analysis fits efficient AI's latency-reduction scope.
papers.title: A Systematic Comparison of Search Space Complexity and Efficiency for Time-Synchronous End-to-End ASR Models
papers.tldr: A comparative study shows that adaptive score-based pruning makes CTC and neural-transducer ASR search more efficient than low fixed-size beams, especially during uncertainty spikes.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based models have shown strong performance across diverse tasks, but their reliance on self-attention mechanisms often leads to high computational costs. Token sparsification, which reduces the number of tokens processed in transformer layers, offers a promising solution to maintain performance while improving efficiency. However, although widely studied in the vision and language domains, token sparsification remains underexplored in audio, with existing work often limited to a single method, model size, or dataset. This work presents a comprehensive evaluation of token sparsification techniques for audio transformers. We assess a range of token pruning and merging strategies across multiple datasets and model sizes, under both post-training and fine-tuning settings. Furthermore, we introduce a novel sparsification approach that combines attention scores with spectral cues derived from the frequency content of token embeddings. Our experiments show that frequency-aware approaches, particularly those based on spectral flatness and low-frequency energy, consistently outperform attention-only methods. We also find that sparsification based on spectrogram patch intensity is especially effective for longer audio inputs. These results highlight the value of incorporating frequency-domain and input-specific information into sparsification strategies to enhance performance in audio tasks.
authors: Shreya Sajid, Fabrizio Julian Piva, Hiram Rayo Torres Rodriguez, Elif Ceren Gok Yildirim, Murat Onur Yildirim, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Audio token sparsification is less explored than in vision and language, motivating a broader evaluation.
The study compares token pruning and merging across multiple datasets, model sizes, and post-training or fine-tuning settings.
It introduces a method combining attention scores with spectral cues from token-embedding frequency content.
Spectral-flatness and low-frequency-energy methods consistently outperform attention-only sparsification.
Spectrogram patch intensity is especially effective for longer audio inputs.
papers.selection_reason: Systematic study of token pruning and merging for audio transformers, directly matching token sparsification and efficiency interests.
papers.title: Muting Tokens: Exploring Token Sparsification for Efficient Audio Transformers
papers.tldr: A comprehensive study shows that frequency- and input-aware token sparsification can make audio transformers more efficient while preserving stronger performance than attention-only methods.

papers.abstract: Real-time polyp segmentation in computer-assisted colonoscopy is hampered by the difficulty of deploying high-accuracy models under strict latency budgets. Frame skipping, which performs inference every K frames and reuses or interpolates the rest, improves throughput but introduces motion blur and lesion misalignment that degrade temporal consistency. To close this gap, we propose the Lightweight Frame Compensator (LFC), a 77K-parameter plug-and-play module inserted before a frozen segmentation backbone. Operating on a three-frame window, LFC fuses consecutive frames via spatio-temporal attention into a single compensated frame, and is trained only on pseudo-labels generated by a differently seeded model, without any expert annotation. Experiments on three polyp video benchmarks show that LFC recovers most of the accuracy degraded by direct frame skipping and, in several settings, reaches the accuracy of frame-by-frame inference, while retaining a 2.05X--2.55X throughput gain. We further evaluate the temporal stability of three backbones spanning CNN, pyramid Transformer, and global-attention Transformer architectures, revealing a spectrum of sensitivity to frame skipping that arises from how locally or globally each architecture aggregates misaligned input. The compensation gain of LFC follows this spectrum: it is largest for high-capacity Transformer backbones, which achieve the best static accuracy but suffer the most under skip-frame inference. LFC thus offers a lightweight, pluggable, and deployment-friendly route to real-time polyp segmentation.
bullets: Addresses motion blur and lesion misalignment caused by skipping frames during real-time colonoscopy segmentation.
Uses a 77K-parameter, plug-and-play module before a frozen backbone to fuse a three-frame window with spatio-temporal attention.
Trains solely on pseudo-labels from a differently seeded model, requiring no expert annotations.
Across three polyp-video benchmarks, often matches frame-by-frame accuracy and recovers most skipping-related degradation.
Benefits high-capacity Transformer backbones most, as they are more sensitive to misaligned skipped-frame inputs.
papers.selection_reason: Lightweight temporal frame compensator enabling accurate real-time polyp segmentation under frame skipping.
papers.title: Lightweight Frame Compensation for Real-Time Polyp Segmentation under Frame Skipping
papers.tldr: LFC is a lightweight, annotation-free frame-compensation module that largely restores polyp-segmentation accuracy lost from frame skipping while preserving a 2.05×–2.55× throughput gain.

papers.abstract: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) aims to recover well-exposed and perceptually faithful images from severely degraded observations. Recent diffusion-based generative methods achieve strong perceptual quality by leveraging powerful image priors, but their iterative sampling incurs substantial computational cost, limiting practical deployment. Despite recent efficiency gains in generative LLIE, high-quality enhancement with a single function evaluation and low overall computation remains challenging, particularly under diverse real-world low-light conditions. We introduce GLOW-FM, a one-step latent flow-matching framework for efficient generative LLIE. GLOW-FM performs conditional transport in the latent space of a frozen Tiny-VAE and leverages Terminal Velocity Matching (TVM) to enable enhancement with a single function evaluation. Matched comparisons with alternative one-step objectives support TVM as an effective design choice, and, to the best of our knowledge, this is its first adaptation to image restoration and specifically to LLIE. Extensive experiments on challenging real-world benchmarks demonstrate that GLOW-FM achieves competitive image quality and state-of-the-art cross-dataset generalization while requiring only a single function evaluation and 34 GFLOPs for the small variant. These findings highlight the potential of GLOW-FM to bring generative LLIE closer to practical deployment through single-step inference and compact latent modeling. Code will be made publicly available upon publication.
authors: Ariel Lapid, Yuval Haitman, Reuven Peretz, Arnon Netzer, Idit Diamant
bullets: Targets the high cost of iterative diffusion-based enhancement under diverse real-world low-light conditions.
Performs conditional transport in the latent space of a frozen Tiny-VAE.
Uses Terminal Velocity Matching (TVM) to support one-step inference.
Experiments on challenging real-world benchmarks show competitive quality and state-of-the-art cross-dataset generalization.
The small variant requires 34 GFLOPs and one function evaluation; code is planned for public release.
papers.selection_reason: One-step latent flow matching for highly efficient low-light image enhancement.
papers.title: GLOW-FM: Efficient Generative Low-Light Image Enhancement with One-Step Latent Flow Matching
papers.tldr: GLOW-FM enables high-quality generative low-light image enhancement in a single function evaluation using latent flow matching, reducing computation for practical deployment.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) introduce unique quantization challenges due to their iterative denoising process. In this work, we reveal that quantization sensitivity is both taskand time-dependent, with different downstream tasks exhibiting distinct precision requirements across denoising steps. We further show that these patterns can be predicted without groundtruth labels or task-specific evaluation metrics. Building on these findings, we introduce T 2Quant, a task and time-aware mixedprecision quantization framework that uses a label-free sensitivity signal to optimally allocate activation precision across denoising steps under a fixed bit-width budget. Extensive experiments across three DLMs and six benchmarks demonstrate that T 2Quant consistently improves the average accuracy of existing quantization methods, achieving gains of up to 6.7 percentage points under the same budget.
authors: Ofek Avivi, Eliron Rahimi, Avi Mendelson, Chaim Baskin
bullets: Quantization sensitivity varies by both downstream task and denoising timestep.
These sensitivity patterns can be predicted without ground-truth labels or task-specific evaluation metrics.
T²Quant allocates activation precision across timesteps under a fixed bit-width budget.
Experiments across three DLMs and six benchmarks improve existing quantization methods by up to 6.7 percentage points in average accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Task- and time-aware mixed-precision quantization for diffusion language models improves efficiency under bit-width budgets, relevant to efficient AI and language foundation models.
papers.title: Different Tasks, Different Timesteps: Temporal Task-Aware Quantization for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: T²Quant improves diffusion language model quantization by assigning task-specific activation precision across denoising steps using label-free sensitivity signals.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models generate multiple token positions in parallel, but few-step decoding makes parallel commitment difficult: tokens that appear reliable individually may be jointly inconsistent, while premature commitments can prevent later context-dependent refinement. In this paper, we introduce SetCommit, a training-free method for coordinated parallel token commitment. Instead of selecting tokens independently by confidence, SetCommit selects a commitment set that balances token reliability against local joint commitment risk, preserving conditioning opportunities for subsequent denoising steps. It further performs budget-neutral local exchanges, replacing vulnerable earlier commitments when newly revealed context supports more reliable alternatives. SetCommit requires no retraining or architectural modification and is compatible with existing diffusion decoding strategies. Experiments with LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B on GSM8K, MATH-500, MBPP, and HumanEval show accuracy/pass@1 gains of up to 7.4 percentage points over native decoding at 32 model evaluations. At common quality targets, geometric-mean incremental speedups range from $1.44$ to $1.74\times$. Code is available at https://github.com/Kissmetothemoon/SetCommit.
authors: Yuannuo Feng, Yubing Ye, Wenshuai Yao, Yizhe Chen, Ngai Wong, Wenyong Zhou, Wang Kang
bullets: Addresses inconsistent parallel commitments and lost opportunities for later context-dependent refinement.
Selects token sets using both individual reliability and local joint commitment risk.
Uses budget-neutral local exchanges to replace vulnerable commitments when new context reveals better alternatives.
Training-free, requires no architectural changes, and works with existing diffusion decoding strategies.
Across LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B benchmarks, it achieves up to 7.4-point accuracy/pass@1 gains and 1.44–1.74× incremental speedups at common quality targets.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free coordinated token commitment improves diffusion LM decoding accuracy and speed, directly relevant to efficient inference and language foundation models.
papers.title: SetCommit: Coordinated Token Commitments for Few-Step Diffusion Language Model Decoding
papers.tldr: SetCommit improves few-step diffusion language model decoding by coordinating which tokens to commit, boosting quality and speed without retraining.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is a popular decode acceleration method. As such, it is particularly relevant to long-output generation, which requires an increasingly large KV cache. KV cache compression offers a way to constrain costs in long-context drafting. However, compression methods that focus on prefill information can lose relevance as the output length grows. We term this phenomenon decode staleness and show that it degrades draft model accuracy under selection-based KV cache compression. We introduce RIFT, a family of selection-based KV cache compression strategies that balance prefill information and recent generated tokens. We show that refreshing the KV cache selection during token generation significantly improves the drafter's quality at the cost of additional decode latency. To alleviate the refresh costs, we propose an adaptive KV refresh strategy that reduces the number of score calculations while retaining the drafter's quality. We further demonstrate how a compressibility-driven drafter training phase, based on sparse attention masks, can improve the drafter's quality under a compressed KV cache. Combined with compressibility training, RIFT enables Qwen3.5-4B, drafting for Qwen3.5-122B, to retain over 98% of its full-cache acceptance length on 32K-token inputs, 4K-token outputs, and an 8K-token KV cache budget.
authors: Dor Tsur, Maor Ashkenazi, Maximilian Golub, Peter Hicks, Yaniv Galron, Talor Abramovich, Yoav Miron, Tiyasa Mitra, Bita Darvish Rouhani, Ran Zilberstein
bullets: Identifies decode staleness: prompt-focused KV selection becomes less relevant during long generation and harms draft accuracy.
Balances prefill information with recently generated tokens through selection-based KV cache compression.
Uses adaptive KV refreshes to reduce score calculations and associated decode latency while preserving quality.
Adds sparse-attention, compressibility-driven drafter training to improve performance under compressed caches.
With training, Qwen3.5-4B drafting for Qwen3.5-122B retains over 98% of full-cache acceptance length under the stated 32K-input, 4K-output, and 8K-cache-budget setting.
papers.selection_reason: KV cache compression for draft models in speculative decoding fits memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: RIFT: KV Cache Compression for Draft Models with Complementary Compressibility Training
papers.tldr: RIFT improves speculative decoding with compressed KV caches by balancing prompt and recent-token information, adaptively refreshing selections, and training drafters for compressibility.

papers.abstract: Efficient custom operators are essential for modern deep learning workloads, yet developing high-performance kernels for Ascend NPUs remains slow, expert-intensive, and difficult to automate. Although AI agents now approach expert performance on GPU kernel benchmarks, current models remain less capable of generating AscendC kernels for NPUs, potentially reflecting the relative scarcity of relevant training data. We thus present CAKE, a CANN-native system for deployable custom operators that combines adaptive multi-DSL routing, separate Generation and Evolution modes, and reviewed knowledge reuse through CAKE Book and a Self-Evolving Agent. On 53 CANN-Bench v1.1 operators on Ascend 950PR, CAKE's aggregated results achieve $100\%$ case pass rate on the standard set (1,060/1,060) and $98.28\%$ on the hidden set (4,167/4,240), with an overall mean score of 78.63 out of 100 and an average performance speedup of $1.334\times$ over the baseline. Evolution then pushes correct operators further: EngramGateFusion cuts aggregate device time by $46.6\%$ over 20 rounds and roughly halves the mean roofline gap. These results offer a practical path toward closing Ascend's AI-for-kernel capability gap.
authors: Deng Pan, Xue-Jian Gao, Junyi Fan, Bin Du, Jiasheng Li, Xinxian Chen, Nok Yan Chang, Xinlin Li, Lingchao Zheng, Jun Li, Yuwei Fan
bullets: Targets the slow, expert-intensive process of creating high-performance AscendC kernels for Ascend NPUs.
Uses adaptive multi-DSL routing, separate Generation and Evolution modes, CAKE Book knowledge reuse, and a Self-Evolving Agent.
On 53 CANN-Bench v1.1 operators on Ascend 950PR, it passes 100% of standard cases and 98.28% of hidden cases.
Achieves a mean score of 78.63/100 and 1.334× average speedup over the baseline.
Evolution further reduces EngramGateFusion device time by 46.6% over 20 rounds and approximately halves its mean roofline gap.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic kernel generation and evolution for NPUs reduces operator latency and compute, fitting the broad efficient-AI topic.
papers.title: CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU
papers.tldr: CAKE is a CANN-native multi-agent system that automates Ascend NPU custom-kernel development and achieves high correctness with meaningful performance gains.

papers.abstract: Many language-model pipelines end in a closed-set decision, such as selecting a tool. Prompting a large language model for it is slow and order-sensitive. We ask how small an encoder for such decisions can be and whether it should read the options jointly or separately. In a three-seed study at 32 million parameters, per-option scoring beats joint scoring on a held-out sample of a 37-benchmark decision suite by 5.8 points of chance-corrected skill at matched optimizer steps and by 2.8 at approximately matched training compute; two external benchmarks agree, though not significantly on their unseen tasks. Crossing reader with initialisation shows that the advantage requires a reranker initialisation, whose query-candidate pair input matches per-option reading; from the raw encoder the two readers are indistinguishable. Per-option scoring needs 5 to 13 times more encoder passes: at most twice the median latency, but more than four times the mean. Of six released joint encoders (17 million to 1 billion parameters), the 68- and 150-million-parameter models exceed a 435-million-parameter DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot classifier by 4.9 and 5.9 accuracy points on 209 overlap-audited System1-Arena tasks and are at least on par with it on the 145 tasks unseen in training. The smallest answers a median request in 14 milliseconds on 16 processor threads, against 728 for the classifier. Reordering options changes 12 to 23% of the joint models' answers (per-option scoring: none). Up to 68 million parameters, they lead their size range on a public leaderboard's private, mainly in-distribution tests.
bullets: At 32M parameters, per-option scoring outperforms joint scoring by 5.8 chance-corrected skill points at matched optimizer steps and 2.8 at roughly matched compute.
The per-option advantage appears only with reranker initialization; raw encoders show no meaningful difference between readers.
Per-option scoring requires 5–13× more encoder passes, reaching up to 2× median and over 4× mean latency, while remaining invariant to option reordering.
Among joint encoders, 68M and 150M models outperform a 435M DeBERTa-v3 classifier by 4.9 and 5.9 accuracy points on 209 overlap-audited tasks.
The smallest joint model answers requests in 14 ms on 16 processor threads versus 728 ms for the classifier; joint models remain sensitive to option order on 12–23% of answers.
papers.selection_reason: Compact encoders replace slow LLM prompting for closed-set decisions, directly addressing latency and computational efficiency.
papers.title: Joint or Per-Option? Compact Encoders for Closed-Set Decisions from 17 Million to 1 Billion Parameters
papers.tldr: Compact encoders can make closed-set decisions far faster and more order-robustly, with per-option scoring generally more accurate but substantially more expensive than joint scoring.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention reads only a small subset of the key-value cache, and how to treat the unread tail remains a key challenge. Discarding the tail biases the output, and sampling it as previous approaches do fails at reads of 5% and below, where the tail likely holds heavy hitters the selector missed. Our key observation is that the simplest possible proxy, one token that folds the entire tail into its count-aware mean, already yields lower output error than a sample at every read behind a practical selector. We further show in closed form that at low reads sampling nearly doubles the weight error of discarding while a single proxy stays below it. Building on these findings, we explore approximating the dense attention distribution with a few proxies that target the tail. We propose OpenAttention, a pipeline of clustering, ErrorGate and top-k selection followed by a count-aware mean proxy. To implement clustering and selection both efficiently and effectively, we design training-free Query-Geometry Clustering (QGC) and a Query-Geometry Selector (QGS), which compress the keys while respecting the query directions. Additionally, unlike prior methods that rank clusters by centroid alone, ErrorGate allocates the exact read by the estimated weight error of each cluster. On RULER-32K HARD with Llama-3.1-8B, OpenAttention retains 99% of dense accuracy at a 1% read. It also achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across models, context lengths and datasets. Our customized attention kernel, OpenAttention.flash, runs the decode attention stage 10$\times$ faster than dense attention at a 1% read.
authors: Hyunwoo Yu, Jongbeom Lee, Hyunbin Kim, Sungjun Park, Jaemin Choi, Jincheol Yang, Seunghun Moon, Bongjoon Hyun, Kyomin Sohn, Kyeongbo Kong, Suk-Ju Kang
bullets: Sparse attention can be biased when unread tail tokens are discarded, while sampling performs poorly at very low read rates.
A single count-aware mean proxy for the entire tail reduces output and weight error more effectively than sampling.
The pipeline combines Query-Geometry Clustering, Query-Geometry Selection, ErrorGate, top-k selection, and tail proxies.
On RULER-32K HARD with Llama-3.1-8B, it retains 99% of dense accuracy at a 1% read.
OpenAttention.flash reports 10× faster decode attention than dense attention at a 1% read.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse attention with tail proxies and query-geometry clustering directly targets efficient KV-cache reading and attention acceleration.
papers.title: OpenAttention: One Percent Is Enough with Tail Proxies
papers.tldr: OpenAttention uses query-aware clustering, error-guided selection, and a count-aware tail proxy to preserve 99% of dense-attention accuracy while reading only 1% of the key-value cache.

papers.abstract: Random projections (RP) offer an effective method for reducing computational and storage overhead while preserving the geometric structure of data. However, existing studies have primarily focused on the optimal generalization performance of specific kernel-regularized algorithms with RP in the well-specified setting and under restrictive conditions. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive and improved analysis of the generalization performance of RP-based spectral algorithms under general conditions \change{without sacrificing statistical efficiency}. By leveraging the embedding property of the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) and a refined analysis of the operator similarity, we establish optimal learning rates in Sobolev norms that match the minimax lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. For two common implementations of RP, randomized sketches and Nystr\"{o}m sub-sampling (uniform or leverage-based), we show that the projection dimension required for optimality is proportional to the average or maximal effective dimension, yielding a significant reduction in computational cost while maintaining the statistical efficiency. Our results do not rely on the uniform boundedness assumption on the regression function and are valid across a wide range of source conditions, i.e., $s> \alpha_0-1/\beta$, where $s,\beta$, and $\alpha_0$ denote the smoothness index, capacity index, and the embedding index, respectively. In the benign case when $\alpha_0=1/\beta$, the optimality holds for all $s\in (0,2\tau]$ with $\tau$ and $\gamma$ denoting the qualification index and norm index. Experimental results demonstrate both the theoretical validity and the practical effectiveness of the proposed method.
bullets: Analyzes random-projection-based spectral algorithms under broad conditions, beyond restrictive well-specified settings.
Uses RKHS embedding properties and refined operator-similarity analysis to establish optimal Sobolev-norm rates.
Covers randomized sketches and Nyström subsampling, with projection dimensions tied to average or maximal effective dimension.
Results hold across broad source conditions without assuming the regression function is uniformly bounded.
Experiments support the theoretical guarantees and practical effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Random projections and sketching reduce computational and storage cost while preserving statistical efficiency, fitting the broad Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: Random Projections for Spectral Algorithms: Optimal Rates in Sobolev Norms
papers.tldr: Random projections can accelerate spectral algorithms while preserving statistically optimal learning rates in Sobolev norms, up to logarithmic factors.

papers.abstract: Space data centers (SpaceDCs) are emerging as platforms for large language models (LLMs), supported by continuous solar-energy harvesting and high-speed interconnections. The mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture supports distributed LLM inference by deploying experts across satellites. However, skewed expert activation creates uneven computation power demands despite uniform solar-power supply at the dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit (SSO). Consequently, active experts remain power-constrained while harvested power at idle experts is underused. These reduce inference efficiency and increase latency. To address this supply-demand mismatch, we propose the SpaceWPT framework, which uses inter-satellite laser-based wireless power transfer (WPT) to redistribute harvested power. The key design challenge is to balance the computation demands of power-donating and power-receiving satellites under WPT losses: transferring more power accelerates computation at the receiver but leaves less power for the donor. After deriving design principles that simplify WPT control, we characterize the resulting latency tradeoff through a tractable surrogate of average inference latency. Minimizing the surrogate yields a novel two-sided water-filling strategy that determines whether each active expert donates, retains, or receives power according to the water level and its WPT link efficiency. Simulations with Mixtral-8x7B and Phi-3.5-MoE show up to 29.25% lower inference latency than without WPT, with larger gains under more compact formations and higher transfer efficiencies.
authors: Haotian Zheng, Zhanwei Wang, Kaibin Huang
bullets: MoE expert activation skews create power-demand imbalances: active experts are constrained while idle satellites waste harvested power.
SpaceWPT transfers power between satellites, balancing computation needs while accounting for wireless-transfer losses and donor costs.
A tractable latency surrogate leads to a two-sided water-filling strategy that classifies experts as donors, retainers, or receivers.
Simulations using Mixtral-8x7B and Phi-3.5-MoE report up to 29.25% lower latency than inference without WPT.
Benefits increase in more compact satellite formations and with higher power-transfer efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: MoE inference latency reduction via wireless power transfer in space data centers.
papers.title: Low-Latency MoE Inference in Space Data Centers: A Wireless-Power-Transfer Perspective
papers.tldr: SpaceWPT reduces MoE inference latency in space data centers by redistributing solar power between satellites via laser-based wireless power transfer.

papers.abstract: An AI system can produce more economically valuable work while delivering less value for the energy it consumes. We therefore ask: How much economic value does an AI system create per unit of energy consumed? We formalize economic value in two ways: (1) net dollar value, the output's dollar value minus AI-system execution cost, and (2) time saving, the expert's completion time minus the AI system's completion time. Dividing each by measured end-to-end energy yields Net Value per Joule (NVJ) and Time Saving per Joule (TSJ), reported in USD/MJ and hours/MJ. We study 220 public GDPval tasks across 44 occupations, serving five open-weight models locally and evaluating four accelerator types. First, the occupation groups where AI systems succeed most often, deliver the greatest dollar value, or save the most time do not necessarily provide the greatest economic return per joule.
