For example, among the tested tasks, engineering work delivers about 10% more net dollar value per task than software development. Yet software development delivers about 27% more net value per joule. Second, GLM 5.2 delivers the highest average net dollar value, at $72.27 per task using 0.430 MJ, equivalent in energy to about four hours of active laptop use. By contrast, Gemma 4 31B delivers 56% of that net dollar value using just 23% of the energy, achieving approximately 2.5 times the NVJ and 2.8 times the TSJ. Third, across four single-accelerator deployments, Qwen3.6-27B's NVJ varies by a factor of 4.32 and TSJ by 9.27, with B200 leading both. Additionally, one and eight H100s deliver similar net dollar value, but eight reduce completion time by 22% at 3.24 times the energy. Our framework makes output value and expert time saving under an energy budget explicit objectives for improving models, accelerators, and software, while offering a new basis for assessing AI's potential economic effect on occupational work.
authors: Amirreza Zeinali, Jon Saad-Falcon, Avanika Narayan, Mersad Abbasi, Jonathan S. Hartley, John Hennessy, Christopher Re, Azalia Mirhoseini
bullets: Defines Net Value per Joule (NVJ) as net dollar value per energy consumed and Time Saving per Joule (TSJ) as expert time saved per energy consumed.
Evaluates 220 GDPval tasks across 44 occupations using five open-weight models and four accelerator types.
Economic value, task success, and time savings do not consistently identify the most energy-efficient occupations or systems.
Gemma 4 31B achieves about 2.5× higher NVJ and 2.8× higher TSJ than GLM 5.2, despite producing lower net value per task and using less energy.
For Qwen3.6-27B, NVJ varies 4.32× and TSJ 9.27× across accelerator deployments, highlighting the importance of hardware configuration.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses energy efficiency and economic value of AI systems across models and accelerators.
papers.title: Joules-to-GDP: How Much Economic Value Do AI Systems Produce per Unit of Energy?
papers.tldr: The paper introduces value-per-energy metrics showing that AI systems and deployments with higher output value are not necessarily the most economically efficient per joule.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based audio-visual generation methods typically perform joint denoising of audio and video latents throughout the entire sampling trajectory, repeatedly executing modality-specific denoising branches and cross-modal attention at every timestep. However, we observe that such uniform joint computation is not always necessary. The key is a modality-asymmetric recoverability: audio-side drift introduced by mid-stage caching can be substantially reduced by only a few terminal joint denoising steps, whereas video-side degradation caused by caching leads to persistent loss of motion and temporal details. This asymmetry suggests that inference acceleration should selectively cache recoverable audio-side computation while preserving full video refinement. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{Convergence-Adaptive Audio-Visual Cache (CAVC)}, a training-free modality-asymmetric caching framework. CAVC adopts a sandwich-structured computation allocation: after detecting that audio denoiser outputs enter a cache-tolerant regime, it caches and reuses the audio denoiser output to bypass audio denoising and cross-modal attention in the middle stage, while the video branch continues independent spatio-temporal refinement; a few joint steps are then restored at the end to reduce accumulated cross-modal drift and improve synchronization. Experiments across multiple public benchmarks demonstrate that CAVC achieves 1.10--1.35x wall-clock acceleration, improves several visual dynamics and temporal statistics, and maintains competitive audio fidelity and audio-visual alignment.
authors: Lifan Jiang, Yibo Zhao, Senlin cheng, Bolei Xu, Xiaobo Li, Can Ye, Dehai Zhao, Deng Cai, Boxi Wu
bullets: Addresses unnecessary joint audio-video denoising and cross-modal attention at every sampling step.
Uses a training-free, convergence-adaptive cache with sandwich-structured computation allocation.
Caches audio denoiser outputs in a cache-tolerant middle regime while video undergoes full spatio-temporal refinement.
Restores a few terminal joint denoising steps to reduce cross-modal drift and improve synchronization.

Across public benchmarks, achieves 1.10–1.35× wall-clock acceleration while maintaining competitive audio fidelity and audio-visual alignment and improving several visual dynamics and temporal statistics.
papers.selection_reason: Accelerates audio-visual diffusion generation via modality-asymmetric caching, relevant to video diffusion and inference efficiency.
papers.title: CAVC: Convergence-Adaptive Audio-Visual Cache for Modality-Asymmetric Diffusion Generation
papers.tldr: CAVC accelerates audio-visual diffusion generation by caching recoverable audio computation mid-sampling while preserving video refinement and restoring joint denoising at the end.

papers.abstract: Real-image editing commonly relies on inversion and iterative sampling, while efficient one-step editors often stabilize a large update by estimating and averaging editing fields at multiple noise levels. We ask a stricter question: is a single temporal field evaluation sufficient for reliable inversion-free editing? Our answer rests on a previously underused duality in a variance-preserving (VP) one-step model: one source-target query at a shared noisy state simultaneously determines a local angular semantic tangent and a clean endpoint displacement. We integrate the tangent over the analytically known remaining VP angle to obtain a nominal one-step transport, and use the endpoint displacement to correct its long-horizon extrapolation through a constrained projection. This transport-first, correction-second construction yields Endpoint-Calibrated Transport (ECT), a closed-form, training-free editor requiring only one noise level, two text conditions packed into one denoiser batch, and one latent update. ECT requires no image inversion, trajectory integration, second temporal observation, or iterative optimization, and can be directly applied to pretrained epsilon-prediction VP one-step generators. Across the reported benchmark settings, ECT delivers stable gains in editing quality within an extremely short editing time.
authors: Lifan Jiang, Taiyang Chen, Senlin cheng, Bolei Xu, Xiaobo Li, Can Ye, Dehai Zhao, Deng Cai, Boxi Wu
bullets: Addresses the cost and instability of inversion-based or multi-evaluation image editing.
Uses a VP-model duality to derive both a local semantic tangent and clean endpoint displacement from one source-target query.
Integrates the tangent over the remaining VP angle, then corrects long-horizon extrapolation via constrained projection.
Training-free and closed-form: requires one noise level, one denoiser batch with two text conditions, and one latent update.
Reported benchmarks show stable editing-quality gains with extremely short editing time.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free one-step image editing reduces inference cost, fitting Efficient AI.
papers.title: One Evaluation Is Enough: Inversion-Free Image Editing with Trajectory Correction
papers.tldr: ECT enables stable, inversion-free one-step image editing using a single shared-noise field evaluation and endpoint correction.

papers.abstract: Predicting relative trained performance from architectural specifications can guide design when training costs limit experimentation. Neural Spectral Capacity (NSC) provides such a heuristic, but scores projections independently and assigns identical scores to compatible reorderings of the same layer configurations. We introduce Residual-Aware Neural Spectral Capacity (ResNSC) for Transformers, using a specification-derived statistical reference for accumulated residual updates to determine the input and residual-state statistics in each projection's capacity calculation, while retaining additive evaluation without data or instantiated weights. When residual widths vary, earlier choices affect later scores, so we augment NSC's allocator (NSC-DP) with residual history beyond its layer-and-budget state. ResNSC-DP jointly allocates residual and feed-forward widths under a resource budget, with certified bounds on the best numerically evaluated ResNSC score within a specified finite candidate set. At the 121M and 374M pretraining scales, selected architectures achieve lower mean perplexity than uniform, variable-width, and tapered allocations on FineWeb-Edu, WikiText-2, and LAMBADA at comparable parameter budgets. In inherited-weight LLaMA-7B pruning using the LoNAS supernet, ResNSC-DP improves eight-task average accuracy over NSC by 3.28--5.46 percentage points across eight matched parameter budgets. Paired reversals preserve the projection shapes and NSC scores yet worsen performance in both settings, exposing performance differences hidden by position-independent scoring. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/Optima-CityU/neural-spectral-capacity.
authors: Chenyu Zhu, Ruoyu Zhao, Zhichao Lu
bullets: Addresses NSC’s inability to distinguish compatible layer reorderings and its position-independent projection scoring.
Uses specification-derived statistics of accumulated residual updates, without data or instantiated weights, to score projections contextually.
ResNSC-DP jointly allocates residual and feed-forward widths while tracking residual history and provides certified bounds over a finite candidate set.
Selected architectures outperform uniform, variable-width, and tapered allocations in reported pretraining experiments, while improving eight-task LLaMA-7B pruning accuracy over NSC.
Paired reversals reveal performance differences hidden by conventional NSC scores; results are evaluated at specific model scales, budgets, and task settings.
papers.selection_reason: Architecture allocation and pruning under resource budgets fits Efficient AI.
papers.title: Neural Spectral Capacity with Residual Context for Heterogeneous Resource Allocation within Transformers
papers.tldr: ResNSC extends Neural Spectral Capacity with residual-context awareness to allocate Transformer widths more effectively under fixed resource budgets.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models reduce computation through sparse activation but still incur substantial storage costs. Mixed-precision post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces these costs by quantizing different model components at different bit widths, but existing methods often struggle to preserve generation quality under tight bit budgets. We identify two key challenges: (1) nonlinear quantization errors at extremely low precision are underestimated when cross-layer propagation is ignored; (2) direct router fine-tuning may cause routing drift, and calibration gains may not generalize to downstream tasks. To address these issues, we propose ProQuant, a weight-only PTQ framework for MoE models. Prune-or-Prioritize Mixed-Precision Allocation (PoP) jointly optimizes expert pruning and bit-width assignment. It allows higher-precision experts to substitute for severely degraded ones while improving bit-budget utilization. Routing-Consistent RMSNorm Finetune (RoCo) adapts expert input representations through mathematically equivalent transformations. It compensates for quantization errors to reduce routing drift. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ProQuant outperforms existing methods across diverse generative tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/ThrowBug/ProQuant.git.
authors: Jiaqi Chen, Xianglong Yan, Chengzhu Bao, Xie Chen, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Targets storage overhead and quality loss in mixed-precision PTQ for sparsely activated MoE models.
PoP jointly optimizes expert pruning and bit-width allocation, letting higher-precision experts replace severely degraded ones.
RoCo finetunes RMSNorm-equivalent transformations to compensate for quantization errors while preserving routing behavior.
Experiments across diverse generative tasks show ProQuant outperforms existing methods.
The approach is scoped to weight-only post-training quantization and relies on calibration-aware adaptation.
papers.selection_reason: Weight-only mixed-precision quantization for MoE LLMs directly targets storage and memory efficiency.
papers.title: ProQuant: Preserving Expert Quality over Quantity in Ultra-Low-Bit Quantization of Mixture-of-Experts Models
papers.tldr: ProQuant preserves MoE generation quality under ultra-low-bit weight-only quantization by jointly allocating precision, pruning experts, and stabilizing routing.

papers.abstract: This paper presents AgentDP, which aims to deploy pre-trained AI models on heterogeneous embedded devices by fully automating model optimization and adaptation (O&A) with Large Language Model (LLM) agents. AgentDP not only significantly reduces human effort via automation but also enhances model inference efficacy by integrating LLMs with device-specific domain knowledge. To deliver a robust automation framework, AgentDP develops novel solutions to address three key technical challenges: 1) To help users elicit clear requirements, we propose a user requirement standardization module; 2) To mitigate the execution environment mismatch between AI models and heterogeneous embedded devices, we design an operator-aware model partition paradigm that enables different parts of the model to be efficiently executed on distinct inference engines. 3) To avoid re-searching optimization hyperparameters for new tasks, we propose a configuration reuse module that heuristically retrieves previous hyperparameter configurations for efficient reuse. Extensive experiments demonstrate that by fully automating the entire O&A process, AgentDP reduces entire model adaptation time by up to 80% compared with manual O&A while achieving higher task accuracy (more than 13% on average) than the baselines. Additionally, a comprehensive user study also exhibits the robust generalizability of AgentDP in adapting to different user requirements for heterogeneous embedded devices.
authors: Leming Shen, Qiang Yang, Xinyu Huang, Zijing Ma, Yuanqing Zheng
bullets: Targets the high human effort and environment mismatch involved in deploying models across diverse embedded hardware.
Standardizes user requirements to make deployment goals clearer for automated optimization and adaptation.
Uses operator-aware model partitioning to execute model components across different inference engines.
Reuses previously effective hyperparameter configurations to avoid repeated optimization searches.
Experiments report up to 80% lower adaptation time and over 13% higher average task accuracy than baselines, with a user study indicating broad adaptability.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-agent-driven model optimization and operator-aware partitioning for embedded deployment, plausibly transferable to efficient AI.
papers.title: AgentDP: Towards Automated Model Deployment for Heterogeneous Embedded AI Applications
papers.tldr: AgentDP uses LLM agents to automate adapting pre-trained AI models to heterogeneous embedded devices, reducing adaptation time while improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Flow matching is now the dominant approach for vision-language action (VLA) robot policies, thanks to its expressiveness and simple training objective. However, inference for standard flow matching requires iteratively solving an ODE, limiting the control frequency at deployment. While several works have proposed novel methods to allow for single-shot action generation, we ask whether such additional objectives are actually necessary. We find that across six flow matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale: multi-step integration confers little to no consistent advantage at inference. We empirically find that this holds as long as models are sufficiently trained and have enough capacity. Practically, the implication is that for large VLAs, the single-step policy comes essentially for free from the multi-step model, enabling low-latency deployment without retraining, distillation, or auxiliary objectives.
authors: Shivakanth Sujit, Luca Nunziante, Rousslan Fernand Julien Dossa, Kai Arulkumaran
bullets: Flow-matching VLA policies typically require iterative ODE integration, which limits deployment control frequency.
Across six flow-matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale.
Multi-step integration provides little or no consistent inference advantage in the studied setting.
The finding depends on models having sufficient training and capacity.
Large VLAs can use single-step inference directly, without distillation, retraining, or auxiliary objectives.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study showing one-step Euler integration suffices for large flow-matching VLA policies, improving deployment latency.
papers.title: When One Step Is Enough: An Empirical Study of Euler Integration in Flow-Matching Policies
papers.tldr: For sufficiently trained, high-capacity flow-matching VLA policies, one-step Euler inference performs about as well as multi-step sampling while enabling much lower-latency control without retraining.

papers.abstract: Training-free few-step samplers are often described as nearly quality-lossless under conventional FID/CLIP-style evaluation. It remains unclear whether that conclusion transfers to more realistic and complex generation-quality benchmarks. We first systematize the quality metrics used to evaluate training-free sampling acceleration for diffusion and flow-matching models. We find that representative training-free step-shortening methods often remain nearly lossless under FID/CLIP-class metrics, yet can suffer substantial quality degradation when evaluated with semantic-composition, dense-instruction, and long-text-rendering benchmarks such as GenEval, DPG-Bench, and LongTextBench. Parallel sampling is a notable exception: by retaining the full-step discretization and removing only the solver's temporal dependency, it can preserve near-lossless quality while accelerating sampling. Building on this observation, we propose \textit{ParaLin++}, a step-parity parallel sampler that preserves the full-step discretization while accelerating the solver iterations. Experiments across Stable Diffusion-v2, LSUN Church, FLUX.1-dev, and Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 show that ParaLin++ preserves the full-step Euler quality profile at $2.6\times$--$4.8\times$, $1.68\times$ on FLUX, and $1.21\times$ on Ming. Project page: https://paralinplus.github.io/.
authors: Jianrong Lu, Zhiyu Zhu, Hui Liu, Junhui Hou
bullets: Conventional FID/CLIP metrics can miss substantial degradation from training-free few-step samplers on complex generation tasks.
Semantic-composition, dense-instruction, and long-text-rendering benchmarks provide a more demanding evaluation of sampling quality.
Parallel sampling avoids quality loss by retaining full-step discretization and removing only the solver’s temporal dependency.
ParaLin++ is a step-parity parallel sampler that accelerates solver iterations without shortening the discretization schedule.
It achieves reported speedups of 2.6×–4.8× on Stable Diffusion-v2 and LSUN Church, 1.68× on FLUX.1-dev, and 1.21× on Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 while preserving full-step Euler quality.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free parallel diffusion integrator reduces sampling latency and fits efficient AI.
papers.title: ParaLin++: Accelerating Parallel Diffusion Integrator via Intrinsic Partially Linear Structure
papers.tldr: ParaLin++ accelerates diffusion and flow-matching sampling while preserving the quality of full-step Euler discretization, especially on demanding semantic and text-generation benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly act as controllers in structured decision pipelines, yet their decisions are still executed by autoregressive text decoding. Hierarchical RAG is one such setting: at each frontier of a document tree, an LLM commits to $b$ of $k$ sections under an input-dependent action grammar, executed as either failure-prone free-form JSON or reliable but strictly serial grammar-constrained generation. We show that this serialization is unnecessary for bounded-horizon control: the reachable future forms a shallow action-prefix tree, which we compile --- one root prefill plus one tree-causal probe evaluate every prefix-conditioned action distribution with serial decoding's tokens, positions, and causal ancestry. A prefix-state lemma makes compiled control policy-exact in exact arithmetic: the same policy with a two-forward critical path and zero output tokens. One further probe pass certifies the exact order-marginalized MAP set. Across four document-disjoint splits and two scales on the primary MetaX device, compiled control matches the serial policy on $84$--$89\%$ of questions --- every instrumented divergence a floating-point near-tie --- and cuts control latency by $35$--$47\%$ versus token-wise serial decoding and $6$--$7\%$ versus an idealized chunked engine; an H800 repetition preserves the ordering.
authors: Zehao Lin, Qianfeng Shen, Xixuan Hao, Shaobo Cui, Chunyu Li, Kai Chen, Bo Tang, Zhenjun Wang, Jin Yan, Zhiyu Li, Feiyu Xiong
bullets: Hierarchical RAG controllers normally decode action choices serially, despite operating over a shallow, bounded action-prefix tree.
The method uses one root prefill and one tree-causal probe to evaluate every prefix-conditioned action distribution without generating output tokens.
A prefix-state lemma establishes policy equivalence to serial grammar-constrained decoding in exact arithmetic, with a two-forward-pass critical path.
Across four document-disjoint splits and two scales, compiled control matches the serial policy on 84–89% of questions; reported divergences are floating-point near-ties.
Control latency decreases by 35–47% versus token-wise serial decoding and 6–7% versus an idealized chunked engine, with the ordering preserved on an H800.
papers.selection_reason: Compiles serial LLM control into parallel tree-causal probes and reduces control latency, a transferable efficiency contribution for LLM pipelines.
papers.title: Compiling Autoregressive LLM Control into Policy-Exact Parallel Inference for Hierarchical RAG
papers.tldr: A tree-causal compilation method executes bounded-horizon LLM control for hierarchical RAG in parallel while preserving the serial policy in exact arithmetic and substantially reducing latency.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in foundation-model agents have enabled increasingly capable embodied systems for long-horizon planning and interaction. However, embodied agents require fast, closed-loop decisions as they continuously perceive and act on a changing environment. Deploying strong cloud agents leaves the platform idle for seconds between consecutive actions, while lightweight local models respond quickly but are more vulnerable to errors. Existing hierarchical architectures typically assign models fixed roles, whereas conventional model routers make stateless per-request decisions. We present CARE, a critic-guided adaptive execution framework that dynamically determines when to escalate control from a local executor to a stronger cloud model. A lightweight critic model monitors execution reliability and triggers escalation when local execution becomes unreliable; once escalated, control persists until the agent recovers, avoiding step-wise switching. To support such control transfer, a shared handoff memory maintains execution context and task-level progress across executors, enabling the model to intervene without restarting from scratch. Across diverse embodied benchmarks, CARE improves task success by 6.3-18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline. CARE further approaches or exceeds Cloud-only success while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8-82.6%.
authors: Wei Zhang, Lirong Xiang, Charles Fleming
bullets: Targets the latency of cloud-only agents and the error vulnerability of lightweight local agents in long-horizon embodied tasks.
Uses a lightweight critic to monitor local execution and trigger persistent escalation rather than making stateless per-step routing decisions.
Maintains shared handoff memory so cloud control preserves execution context and task progress without restarting.
Across diverse embodied benchmarks, improves task success by 6.3–18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline.
Approaches or exceeds Cloud-only success while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8–82.6%.
papers.selection_reason: Critic-guided cloud/local escalation with shared handoff memory for embodied agents; improves latency while maintaining task success.
papers.title: Know When to Escalate: Critic-Guided Adaptive Execution for Cloud-Local Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: CARE adaptively escalates embodied-agent control from a fast local model to a stronger cloud model when a critic detects unreliability, improving success while reducing action latency.

papers.abstract: Weight-only quantization keeps LLM activations in floating point and stores weights as low-bit integers, turning the dominant workload into floating-point-integer (FP-INT) general matrix multiplication. Recent quantizers reach a 2-3-bit average with mixed precision, but hardware has not kept pace: GPUs dequantize weights to FP16 before the tensor-core multiply-accumulate, and bit-parallel FP-INT accelerators run at a single weight precision, so fewer bits save memory but not computation. In this paper, we present FIGFLEX, an algorithm-hardware co-designed mixed-precision accelerator whose bit-parallel datapath scales throughput as precision falls. FIGFLEX contributes (1) a shift-add, radix-4 reformulation of FP-INT multiplication that fuses the multiply-accumulate into a unified, precision-flexible partial-product reduction and roughly halves the partial products, together with a novel INT3 optimization that reclaims the idle datapath radix-4 leaves at that precision; and (2) a mixed-precision quantizer that assigns each channel group its bit-width according to the error GPTQ cannot compensate, with a per-input-channel column scaling whose power-of-two normalization keeps the scaled activations out of the FP16 subnormal range, so that the quantized model maps directly onto FIGFLEX's datapath with the same accuracy as on a GPU. On LLaMA-2-7B, FIGFLEX attains 5.85 and 8.77 WikiText-2 perplexity at 3- and 2-bit average precision, lower than GPTQ, AWQ, SliM-LLM, AMQ, and QuIP# (without fine-tuning), while delivering 1.56x and 1.42x higher whole-chip throughput per area on the linear GEMMs of a 3-bit mixed-precision model than AxCore and FIGLUT, respectively.
authors: Faraz Tahmasebi, Haocheng Xu, Andrew Trauger, Yomal Perera, Zhenyu Tang, Nael Chowdhury, Sitao Huang
bullets: Targets weight-only quantized LLMs, whose main computation is floating-point–integer GEMM.
Uses a shift-add, radix-4 FP-INT formulation that unifies accumulation, reduces partial products, and optimizes INT3 execution.
Introduces channel-group bit allocation based on quantization error and power-of-two column scaling for direct hardware mapping.
On LLaMA-2-7B, reports 5.85 and 8.77 WikiText-2 perplexity at 3- and 2-bit average precision without fine-tuning.
Achieves 1.56× and 1.42× higher whole-chip throughput per area than AxCore and FIGLUT, respectively, on 3-bit mixed-precision GEMMs.
papers.selection_reason: Mixed-precision FP-INT accelerator design and low-bit LLM quantization directly target inference efficiency.
papers.title: FIGFLEX: A Mixed-Precision FP-INT GEMM Accelerator Co-Designed with Low-Bit LLM Quantization
papers.tldr: FIGFLEX co-designs mixed-precision low-bit LLM quantization with a precision-scalable FP-INT GEMM accelerator to improve efficiency while preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Kernelized attention provides a useful perspective for understanding self-attention as a similarity-based aggregation mechanism, but existing approaches often rely on fixed or stationary kernels, limiting their ability to adapt the similarity structure to complex token interactions. In this paper, we propose flow-based spectral kernel attention (FSKA), a framework for learning expressive nonstationary attention kernels. FSKA formulates kernelized attention through spectral density learning and parameterizes the resulting bivariate spectral density with normalizing flows. This design enables flexible and regularizable kernel learning while remaining compatible with scalable linear-attention computation. We further show that expressive kernel learning enables a simplified attention design with removed query--key projections and fixed orthogonal value projections, resulting in a more parameter-efficient architecture. Controlled experiments on classification, ablation, and scalability profiling show that FSKA achieves competitive or improved performance over existing attention mechanisms, while reducing projection-related trainable parameters by approximately $40\%$--$47\%$ compared with most baselines and maintaining favorable linear-attention memory scaling. Code Available: https://github.com/ziyang18/FSKA.
authors: Zi Yang, Ying Li, Alejandro Lancho, Dar\'{i}o C. Larese, Pablo M. Olmos, Michael Minyi Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited adaptability of fixed or stationary kernels in kernelized self-attention.
Learns a bivariate spectral density using normalizing flows for expressive, regularizable kernel modeling.
Removes query–key projections and fixes orthogonal value projections to simplify the attention architecture.
Reports competitive or improved results in classification, ablation, and scalability experiments.
Reduces projection-related trainable parameters by approximately 40%–47% versus most baselines while retaining favorable linear-attention memory scaling.
papers.selection_reason: Learnable nonstationary attention kernels with linear-attention memory scaling fit efficient-attention research.
papers.title: Flow-based Spectral Kernel Learning for Nonstationary Attention
papers.tldr: FSKA learns flexible nonstationary attention kernels with normalizing flows, enabling parameter-efficient linear attention with competitive performance.

papers.abstract: In recent years, Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have gained massive attention as an energy-efficient neural computing paradigm due to their event-driven and sparse computing capability. However, maintaining accuracy under low-precision constraints, necessary for practical deployment, has been largely unexplored for SNN models. In addition, existing Hessian-based approaches for quantization, such as HAWQ-V2, incur significant memory and computational overhead due to temporal unrolling across multiple SNN timesteps. We propose a spike-aware gradient-based mixed-precision quantization framework for SNNs that adaptively assigns bit-widths using first-order gradient information, avoiding costly second-order Hessian computations. We evaluate our method across various SNN-based architectures, including VGG, ResNet, and Vision Transformer models obtained from both ANN-to-SNN conversion and direct training frameworks, on CIFAR10/100, ImageNet, and DVS-CIFAR-10 datasets. Notably, on ResNet-34 evaluated on ImageNet, our method achieves 73.30% accuracy at 4.78$\times$ compression, which is comparable to that provided by HAWQ-V2, while reducing memory consumption by 2.31$\times$ and bit-allocation runtime by 100$\times$. We also present an energy analysis for mixed-precision SNNs showing that the proposed quantization strategy enables energy-efficient deployment without compromising performance.
authors: Rajshekhar Rakshit, Devgokul B. V, Rakshitha Kalkura, Gopalakrishnan Srinivasan
bullets: Targets accuracy degradation under the low-precision constraints needed for practical SNN deployment.
Uses first-order, spike-aware gradient information to adaptively assign layer bit-widths without costly Hessian computations.
Evaluated on VGG, ResNet, and Vision Transformer SNNs from both ANN-to-SNN conversion and direct training across CIFAR10/100, ImageNet, and DVS-CIFAR-10.
On ImageNet ResNet-34, achieves 73.30% accuracy at 4.78× compression, comparable to HAWQ-V2, with 2.31× lower memory use and 100× faster bit allocation.
Includes an energy analysis indicating efficient mixed-precision SNN deployment without compromising performance.
papers.selection_reason: Mixed-precision quantization reduces memory and compute for SNN deployment; relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Spike-Aware Gradient-Based Mixed-Precision Quantization of Spiking Neural Networks for Vision Applications
papers.tldr: A spike-aware, gradient-based mixed-precision method compresses SNNs efficiently while preserving accuracy and avoiding the overhead of Hessian-based quantization.

papers.abstract: Coding agents spend substantial computation generating actions and processing long interaction histories. Poor action choices can steer agents into low-value states, wasting computation and increasing API costs. Sampling and verifying alternative actions can improve the agent's decisions, but applying this procedure at every step adds substantial overhead. We introduce SWE-Verifier, a lightweight generative model that selectively triggers candidate sampling and verification. It scores the coding agent's proposed action to determine when additional candidate sampling is needed, then ranks the resulting actions before execution. We train SWE-Verifier from Qwen3.5-4B using preference data that groups contrasting actions with their resulting environment observations and rubric-guided teacher scores. Using the mini-swe-agent harness, SWE-Verifier improves resolution from 75.47% to 77.20% on MiniMax-M2.7 at 1.09 times cost and generalizes to DeepSeek-V4-Flash without training on its actions, improving resolution from 72.60% to 74.27% at 1.13 times cost. Across both models, SWE-Verifier verifies fewer than 4% of steps and achieves comparable or higher resolution than the trajectory and all-step baselines at substantially lower cost. These results demonstrate that selective candidate sampling and lightweight verification provide complementary gains in coding-agent performance and inference efficiency. Our model, code, and data are available at https://github.com/zkjzou/SWE-Verifier.
authors: Kaijian Zou, Vaibhav Chennareddy, Yunxiang Zhang, Naihao Deng, Longju Bai, Jiaxin Pei, Rada Mihalcea, Lu Wang
bullets: Targets wasted computation and API costs caused by poor action choices and long interaction histories.
Uses a lightweight generative verifier to decide when to sample alternatives, then ranks candidate actions before execution.
Trained from Qwen3.5-4B with preference data pairing contrasting actions, environment observations, and rubric-guided scores.
On two coding agents, resolution improves while verification is used on fewer than 4% of steps, at 1.09–1.13× cost.
Generalizes to an agent whose actions were not used during training; code, model, and data are publicly available.
papers.selection_reason: Selective verification reduces computation and API cost for coding agents, matching the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: SWE-VERIFIER: Selective Verification for Cost-Efficient Coding Agents
papers.tldr: SWE-Verifier selectively verifies coding-agent actions to improve task resolution while adding minimal inference cost.

papers.abstract: To enable Industry 5.0, where autonomous systems are widely adopted and integrated with people to promote sustainable development in industries, it is imperative to adapt complex deep learning models to operate efficiently on resource-constrained hardware for edge inference. However, adapting these models remains challenging due to the hardware heterogeneity of edge computing in industrial settings, performance degradation caused by model compression, and the lack of clear guidance on which compression techniques are practical and effective for applications such as predictive maintenance. To address these challenges, this paper presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of four state-of-the-art model compression techniques applied to a high-performance convolutional neural network for predictive maintenance using a real-world dataset of rotating machinery, equipment typically used in industry. The compressed models were evaluated across a heterogeneous set of nine computing platforms, ranging from highly constrained edge computing devices to general purpose and high-performance processors, reflecting the diversity and fragmentation typical of industrial edge environments. By jointly prioritizing classification performance, inference speed, and compression ratio, we found that compression using knowledge distillation emerged as the most effective approach. The model had more than 90% speedup across all devices while maintaining a 91.22% balanced F-score, with a very small drop in predictive performance relative to the uncompressed model, along with a 98.9% size reduction. Through successful deployment across multiple edge platforms and a systematic comparison of compression strategies, we demonstrated a clear path to achieving Industry 5.0 targets, drastically cutting computational costs and, consequently, energy consumption without sacrificing predictive performance.
authors: Matheus Calheira Guimar\~aes de Oliveira, Marco Aur\'elio da Silva Cruz, Regis Cardoso, Lucas Cambuim, Rafael Macieira, Arthur Paim, Helaine Neves, Alex Santos, Lilian Guarieiro, Jean Schmith, Prashant Kumar, Erick G. Sperandio Nascimento
bullets: Addresses the challenge of deploying deep learning on heterogeneous, resource-constrained industrial edge platforms.
Compares four model-compression techniques for rotating-machinery predictive maintenance across nine computing platforms.
Evaluates classification performance, inference speed, and compression ratio jointly.
Knowledge distillation achieved over 90% speedup on all devices, a 91.22% balanced F-score, and 98.9% model-size reduction.
Demonstrates practical multi-platform deployment with substantially lower computational and energy requirements; scope is limited to the studied model, use case, and platforms.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks model compression for edge inference; fits efficient AI despite no specific subtopic.
papers.title: Benchmarking Model Compression Techniques Across Heterogeneous Edge Platforms: A Predictive Maintenance Use Case for Rotating Machinery
papers.tldr: A comparative study finds knowledge distillation is an effective way to compress predictive-maintenance CNNs for diverse edge hardware while preserving performance and greatly improving efficiency.

papers.abstract: Global warming and climate change are major catalysts for plant diseases, significantly affecting food production worldwide. Addressing this issue requires continuous monitoring and early detection of plant diseases. While recent advancements in deep learning offer potential solutions, most models demand high processing power and struggle to perform efficiently on low-end electronic hardware. Furthermore, many existing works focus on specific crop diseases, limiting their broader applicability. This paper presents a lightweight Group Equivariance Attention Network (GANet) designed for the prediction and monitoring of 38 types of plant diseases. GANet introduces a novel Group Attention block and Group-Wise Feature Fusion block, making it both sparse and efficient. With only 0.001M parameters, the model achieves an impressive 99.99% accuracy on the PlantVillage dataset. Additionally, GANet is optimized for deployment on edge devices such as the Raspberry Pi 4b and Jetson Nano, where it reaches 5 FPS and 11 FPS, respectively, demonstrating its potential for real-time plant disease monitoring on low-power devices.
authors: Anubhab Tripathi, Bibek Das, Asfak Ali, Sheli Shinha Chaudhuri
bullets: Targets efficient, broad plant-disease monitoring where conventional deep-learning models are too resource-intensive.
Introduces Group Attention and Group-Wise Feature Fusion blocks to produce a sparse, lightweight architecture.
Contains 0.001M parameters and achieves 99.99% accuracy on the PlantVillage dataset.
Runs at 5 FPS on Raspberry Pi 4b and 11 FPS on Jetson Nano, supporting edge deployment.
Scope is demonstrated on PlantVillage and the specified embedded platforms.
papers.selection_reason: Lightweight group attention network for edge deployment; directly relevant to efficient attention and low-resource inference.
papers.title: GANet: A Lightweight Group Attention Network for Plant Disease Identification on Embedded Systems
papers.tldr: GANet is a highly compact attention-based network for recognizing 38 plant diseases on low-power edge devices in near-real-time.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models scale model capacity efficiently by activating a small subset of parameters per token. However, in long-context inference, memory remains a major bottleneck because the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length. Existing KV cache compression methods reduce this cost for dense transformers, but overlook a problem specific to MoE: KV eviction can change which experts are selected during answer generation, degrading the generation quality. We propose MoEZip, a routing-aware KV cache compression for sparse MoE language models. To estimate the sensitivity of expert routing to perturbation, we propose a novel metric based on the Fisher information matrix of routing distributions. MoEZip combines this metric with attention weights for routing-aware scoring of contexts. Finally, we compose a complementary scoring system that combines eviction methods for dense and sparse-MoE architectures. Experiments show that MoEZip achieves robust performance under aggressive cache compression on various benchmarks. At a KV retention ratio of 10\%, MoEZip improves over the SoTA baseline by +24 and +20 points on average on LongBench and RULER, corresponding to 2.3$\times$ and 4.9$\times$ higher scores, respectively.
bullets: Addresses KV-cache memory growth in long-context MoE inference, where eviction can alter expert selection and harm quality.
Scores context tokens using both attention weights and a Fisher-information-based measure of routing sensitivity.
Combines routing-aware eviction with complementary dense-model KV compression methods.
At 10% KV retention, improves over the prior state of the art by 24 points on LongBench and 20 points on RULER on average.
Demonstrates robust performance under aggressive compression across multiple benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces routing-aware KV cache compression for MoE LLMs, directly targeting memory-efficiency in inference.
papers.title: MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.tldr: MoEZip compresses KV caches in sparse MoE LLMs while preserving expert-routing decisions, enabling strong long-context performance with only 10% KV retention.

papers.abstract: AI agents require interfaces to interact with external systems such as files, APIs, databases, and cloud services. Two competing paradigms have emerged: CLI (Command Line Interface), where agents execute shell commands directly, and MCP (Model Context Protocol), a structured JSON-RPC protocol providing governed, typed tool access. This paper presents a comparative analysis across 14 evaluation dimensions, supported by worked examples, security assessment against established compliance frameworks, and economic modeling. Our analysis indicates that CLI provides superior efficiency for single-user, local-only workflows, while MCP addresses requirements that CLI fundamentally cannot satisfy, including fine-grained access control, credential isolation, structured audit, and multi-tenant governance. We further examine how progressive disclosure techniques eliminate MCP's historical weakness (context window overhead), yielding token efficiency comparable to CLI while preserving its architectural benefits. A hybrid architecture is recommended for production systems. This analysis draws upon academic, government, and industry sources including NSA formal guidance (CSI U/OO/6030316-26), OWASP security standards, and economic modeling from BCG and Gartner.
authors: Arun Malik, Nitish Talasu, Bradley Klemick, Vineet Tushar Trivedi, Prachi Shah, Sanay Devi, Junjie Zhang, Kunal Sonawane
bullets: Compares CLI and MCP across 14 dimensions, including usability, security, governance, and economics.
CLI suits single-user, local-only tasks with direct shell access.
MCP provides typed, governed tool access with fine-grained permissions, credential isolation, structured auditing, and multi-tenant support.
Progressive disclosure can reduce MCP’s context-window overhead to near-CLI token efficiency.
The analysis recommends combining CLI and MCP in production architectures.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the token efficiency and architectural trade-offs between CLI and MCP (Model Context Protocol) for tool integration, focusing on context window overhead and governance.
papers.title: MCP vs CLI for AI Agents: A Comparative Analysis of Tool Integration Strategies for Autonomous Systems
papers.tldr: CLI is efficient for simple local workflows, while MCP offers stronger governance and security for production AI agents; a hybrid approach is recommended.

papers.abstract: Every interaction between AI agents begins with a handshake: the initiating agent must locate its counterpart, learn what it can do, and establish a session before the first useful message can be sent. Surveys of agent communication protocols name handshake overhead as an efficiency criterion, yet none report measurements. This paper presents the first empirical, phase-decomposed benchmark of the handshake in three major agent protocols: MCP (in both its 2025 initialize and 2026 discover eras), A2A, and ACP. Using each protocol's official SDK, we instrument every request for round trips, per-phase latency, wire bytes, and token cost across cold-start, warm-repeat, capability-mismatch, and degraded-metadata scenarios (N=50 per cell, on loopback and under an emulated 50 ms RTT). Round-trip count dominates handshake cost. A legacy MCP handshake takes three round trips and 230 ms at 50 ms RTT; A2A needs one round trip and 61.0 ms. Round trips are not the whole bill: when an LLM reads the counterpart's metadata, handshake cost scales with the counterpart's capability inventory at 24-107 tokens per capability, so a 200-capability counterpart spends 11% of a 200k-token context window before the agent reads its own task. MCP's own 2026 revision cuts its handshake from three round trips to two and, with era pinning, to zero on warm reconnects, protocol evolution that corroborates the cost we measure. We release the full harness, raw data, and analysis at https://github.com/pvarshh/handshake-benchmark.
bullets: The study benchmarks handshake phases in MCP, A2A, and ACP across cold, warm, mismatch, and degraded-metadata scenarios.
Round-trip count is the primary cost driver: legacy MCP uses three round trips and takes 230 ms at 50 ms RTT, while A2A uses one and takes 61.0 ms.
LLM-readable metadata adds 24–107 tokens per advertised capability; a 200-capability counterpart can consume 11% of a 200k-token context window.
MCP’s 2026 revision reduces the handshake from three to two round trips, and era pinning enables zero-round-trip warm reconnects.
The authors release the benchmark harness, raw data, and analysis.
papers.selection_reason: Empirically measures handshake overhead (latency, bytes, token cost) in agent communication protocols, directly addressing efficiency and token usage in AI systems.
papers.title: The Cost of Saying Hello: An Empirical Study of Handshake Overhead in AI Agent Communication Protocols
papers.tldr: Handshake overhead in AI agent protocols is dominated by round trips and can become substantial when agents inspect large capability inventories.

papers.abstract: Lossless tensor compression could reduce memory usage during training, but training requires tensors to be repeatedly re-encoded. We introduce Losslessly Compressed Tensors (LCT), a GPU execution framework designed for this repeated encode-decode regime. LCT exploits the natural redundancy in floating point data to reduce storage for weights, activations and optimizer states. Highly optimized GPU kernels implement Huffman coding with precomputed codebooks for low compression and decompression overhead, essential for training. Our analysis characterizes LCT's storage costs and adaptation to magnitude shifts. LCT achieves a compression ratio of up to $1.455\times$, and is demonstrated in training and finetuning settings. On a 162M-parameter NanoGPT, LCT reduces memory usage by $24.6\%$ for a $7.2\%$ step-time increase. In Qwen3-4B fine-tuning, LCT saves up to $23.8\%$ of peak memory, enabling a $3.5\times$ larger context length in training on the same GPU.
bullets: Targets repeated compression and decompression of weights, activations, and optimizer states during training.
Uses GPU-optimized Huffman coding with precomputed codebooks to keep encoding overhead low.
Achieves compression ratios of up to 1.455× and adapts to shifts in tensor magnitudes.
Reduces NanoGPT memory usage by 24.6% with a 7.2% step-time increase.
During Qwen3-4B fine-tuning, saves up to 23.8% peak memory and enables 3.5× longer context on the same GPU.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a GPU-friendly framework for losslessly compressed tensors during training, reducing memory usage by 24.6% while maintaining acceptable step-time overhead, a significant contribution to memory efficiency.
papers.title: LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training
papers.tldr: LCT reduces training memory by losslessly compressing tensors with GPU-efficient encode/decode, trading modest runtime overhead for substantially larger context capacity.

papers.abstract: We introduce FORGE (Fast On-chip Rotor Generation for Experts), a procedural weight generation system for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference. Rather than storing and loading every expert weight tensor from HBM, we show how a compact accelerator inside each Streaming Multiprocessor can regenerate them on-the-fly from $O(\log^2 d)$ rotor parameters per projection. Per replaced layer, gigabytes of stored expert weights are approximated with under a megabyte of seeds. This addresses the dual memory bottleneck of autoregressive Sparse MoE decode, where per-expert FFN operations are HBM-bandwidth-bound at small routed-token counts and the aggregate expert footprint forces multi-node Expert Parallelism (EP) with all-to-all traffic. We realize the approach as the Rotor Generation Unit (RGU), a fixed-function datapath that generates FFN weight tiles without competing with Tensor Core execution. With 30% of the MoE FFN layers replaced across five Sparse MoE models, we estimate 1.3-2.8x higher system throughput at matched GPU count and 1.10-1.15x lower per-user decode latency at short context. In exchange, downstream accuracy on three model families falls below that of the same model fine-tuned without rotor replacement, and the replacement ratio controls this tradeoff. FORGE also expands KV cache capacity by 1.2-2.6x. It is agnostic to the bit width at which weights are stored, so it can compose with quantization. The RGU is fully implemented/verified in SystemVerilog at ~0.9% SM area overhead (0.032 mm^2/SM, 7nm).
bullets: Targets HBM bandwidth bottlenecks and large expert-storage footprints during autoregressive Sparse MoE decode.
Uses a Rotor Generation Unit to generate FFN weight tiles from compact rotor parameters instead of storing full expert tensors.
Replacing 30% of MoE FFN layers is estimated to improve system throughput by 1.3–2.8× and short-context per-user latency by 1.10–1.15×.
Expands KV-cache capacity by 1.2–2.6× and can compose with weight quantization.
The accuracy–efficiency tradeoff depends on the replacement ratio; accuracy decreases relative to fine-tuned models without rotor replacement.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a procedural weight generation system (FORGE) for Sparse MoE inference that reduces memory footprint and expands KV cache capacity, addressing key efficiency bottlenecks in large model deployment.
papers.title: FORGE: Procedural Weight Generation for Sparse MoE Inference
papers.tldr: FORGE accelerates Sparse MoE decoding by regenerating approximate expert weights on-chip, reducing memory and communication demands at the cost of some accuracy.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) reduces the cost of adapting foundation models by focusing training on a small parameter subset. Complementary to this idea, we introduce RoSA (Rotational Sparse Adaptation), which narrows adaptation to a subset of layers at a time. RoSA freezes lower layers close to the input throughout training and rotates a trainable block over later layers, progressively increasing the number of frozen layers close to the input. This design reduces optimizer-state memory, shortens backpropagation, and even forward propagation if activations at the last frozen layer are cached. Because RoSA is orthogonal to the choice of trainable parameterization, it can be combined with PEFT methods or sparse optimizers within each active block. Experiments across multiple LLM architectures and tasks show that RoSA reduces peak memory while maintaining strong fine-tuning performance.
bullets: Targets the memory and computational costs of adapting foundation models.
Freezes lower, input-near layers and shifts the trainable block across later layers during training.
Can reduce optimizer-state memory, backpropagation cost, and—when activations are cached—forward-propagation cost.
Works alongside PEFT methods and sparse optimizers within each active block.
Experiments across multiple LLM architectures and tasks report lower peak memory with strong fine-tuning performance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a memory-efficient fine-tuning method (RoSA) that reduces optimizer-state memory and computation by freezing layers and rotating trainable blocks, directly addressing memory bottlenecks in LLM training.
papers.title: RoSA: Rotational Sparse Adaptation for Memory-Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: RoSA reduces fine-tuning memory and computation by rotating a trainable layer block through later layers while progressively freezing earlier ones.

papers.abstract: Existing sequential recommenders usually allocate a fixed computational budget to every item in a user's interaction history, regardless of the item's contribution to the final prediction. We challenge this de facto design with two diagnostic findings. (1) Non-uniform computational need: items within the same sequence vary drastically in how much computation they require. Most converge after shallow processing while a critical minority only stabilizes at full depth. (2) Suboptimality of fixed allocation: given oracle access to the target item, a non-uniform depth assignment consistently outranks the fixed one, indicating that existing uniform computation both wastes capacity on already-converged items and sacrifices overall recommendation quality. These observations motivate a shift from fixed-depth computation to item-level adaptive reasoning. To this end, we propose LoopRec. LoopRec recursively applies a single weight-shared block and introduces a lightweight gate at each recursion boundary that makes a binary exit-or-continue decision for every item independently. Items whose representations have sufficiently matured exit early, while those requiring deeper reasoning continue to subsequent recursions. This design converts the fixed global depth into a learned, per-item property without auxiliary depth labels, and is readily adaptable to diverse backbone architectures. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks with four backbone families demonstrate that LoopRec consistently outperforms matched fixed-depth counterparts. Further analysis reveals that LoopRec's learned allocation exhibits interpretable patterns aligned with our post-hoc oracle analysis: lower-frequency items and more recent interactions naturally receive deeper computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/Elpmis117/LoopRec.
authors: Zhanshuo Cao, Jiakai Tang, Yuqi Zhou, Sunhao Dai, Jun Xu
bullets: Items in an interaction history have highly variable computational needs, making uniform processing inefficient.
LoopRec uses a weight-shared recursive block with a lightweight per-item gate that decides whether each item exits or continues.
The method learns per-item computation depth without auxiliary depth labels and can adapt to different backbone architectures.
Experiments across four backbone families and public benchmarks show consistent gains over matched fixed-depth models.
The learned allocation gives deeper processing to patterns such as lower-frequency items and more recent interactions.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive per-item recursion reduces computation in sequential recommenders, transferable to efficient inference.
papers.title: Think Harder Where It Matters: Item-Level Adaptive Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
papers.tldr: LoopRec improves sequential recommendation by adaptively allocating more recursive computation to items that need deeper reasoning and exiting easy items early.

papers.abstract: Vietnamese pre-trained encoders have improved rapidly, but the strongest ones are large, multilingual-vocabulary models or depend on external word segmentation, which makes them costly to deploy. We present GoiBERT, a family of two compact Vietnamese encoders with 26M and 49M parameters that operate directly on raw text. GoiBERT learns from two complementary teachers. A same-tokenizer Vietnamese encoder first teaches general-purpose representations. A much larger teacher then provides task-level guidance through soft labels that are generated without ever labeling its own training data. Across eight benchmarks covering text classification, aspect-based sentiment analysis, natural language inference, and named entity recognition, GoiBERT-large achieves the highest average score among non-teacher models. It does so with fewer than half the parameters of the strongest compact baseline and twice its throughput. GoiBERT-base retains 99% of that baseline's performance at a quarter of its size. Our analysis shows that compression is nearly lossless for sentiment and classification tasks but remains costly for inference and entity recognition, which points to clear directions for future work. Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/Nhantran65/GoiBERT.git
authors: Quang Anh Kiet Tran, Nam Anh Tran, Manh Hung Trinh, Thanh Danh Le, Khang Nhat Hoang Vo, Huynh Dai Nhan Tran
bullets: Addresses the deployment cost of large Vietnamese models and systems requiring external word segmentation.
Introduces 26M- and 49M-parameter encoders trained from a same-tokenizer Vietnamese teacher and a larger teacher providing task-level soft-label guidance.
Across eight benchmarks, GoiBERT-large achieves the highest average score among non-teacher models, with less than half the parameters and twice the throughput of the strongest compact baseline.
GoiBERT-base retains 99% of the compact baseline’s performance at one-quarter its size.
Compression is nearly lossless for sentiment and classification, but more costly for inference and named entity recognition.
papers.selection_reason: Compact Vietnamese language models via two-stage knowledge distillation; contributes to reducing model size and inference cost.
papers.title: GoiBERT: Compact Vietnamese Language Models via Two-Stage Knowledge Distillation
papers.tldr: GoiBERT uses two-stage knowledge distillation to build compact Vietnamese encoders that work on raw text while retaining strong benchmark performance.

papers.abstract: Uniform diffusion language models (UDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising sequences of ordinary vocabulary tokens, any of which may be corrupted and subsequently revised. During training, UDLMs must denoise from a context that may itself be unreliable, whereas masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) always condition on a clean context. This challenging training objective makes UDLMs more FLOP-intensive to train than MDLMs, but it yields stronger downstream reasoning performance. Recently, selective looping, which recursively applies a few early Transformer layers within each denoising step, has been shown to improve training efficiency in MDLMs under an iso-FLOP budget. We investigate looping in UDLMs while keeping the training objective and sampler unchanged. We find that looping significantly improves training efficiency: looped UDLMs reach the validation NLL of a non-looped UDLM trained on about 0.5 trillion tokens with up to 2.8x fewer training FLOPs on OpenWebText and 3.3x fewer on FineWeb-Edu. We also find that, at a matched NFE budget, looped UDLMs reach up to 9.8% lower generation perplexity than the non-looped UDLM, with most gains achieved at moderate loop counts. Finally, we study different loop-count distributions and find that sampling smaller loop counts more frequently during training improves inference efficiency: on downstream tasks, this strategy uses 12% fewer loops than uniform loop-count sampling without degrading accuracy.
authors: Saiteja Utpala, Chieh-Hsin Lai, Yuki Mitsufuji, Praneeth Vepakomma
bullets: UDLMs are costly to train because they must denoise while conditioning on potentially corrupted context.
The method recursively reuses early Transformer layers within each denoising step, while keeping the training objective and sampler unchanged.
Looped UDLMs match the validation NLL of a model trained on roughly 0.5 trillion tokens with up to 2.8× fewer FLOPs on OpenWebText and 3.3× fewer on FineWeb-Edu.
At matched function-evaluation budgets, looping improves generation perplexity by up to 9.8%.
Sampling smaller loop counts more often reduces downstream inference loops by 12% without hurting accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Looping in diffusion language models improves training and inference efficiency for language foundation models.
papers.title: Looped Uniform Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Selective looping makes uniform diffusion language models substantially more training- and inference-efficient without changing their objective or sampler.

papers.abstract: Increasing the attention context length significantly improves streaming video generation quality, while incurring prohibitive memory and computational costs as the context grows. Existing methods attempt to capture this contextual information through attention selection or compression, but remain limited by bounded representations and lack explicit attention-level supervision to retain historical contributions to current queries. To address this, we introduce Attn-Forcing, a novel framework that preserves full-context attention contributions for streaming video generation under bounded memory and computation. We achieve this by introducing attention proxies that continuously approximate the attention responses induced by the historical context. Specifically, we implement the proxies as learnable visual latents and employ a Proxy Update Module to incorporate visual context from historical latents. Moreover, we propose an Attention Matching Loss to explicitly constrain the attention behavior of the learned proxies using full-context attention supervision. Extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate that Attn-Forcing consistently improves streaming video generation quality and achieves state-of-the-art performance over existing baseline methods.
authors: Junyao Gao, Sibo Liu, Jiaxing Li, Yanan Sun, Hanxin Zhu, Weidong Zhang, Jun Zhang, Cairong Zhao
bullets: Longer attention contexts improve quality but create prohibitive memory and computational costs.
The method uses learnable visual latents as attention proxies for historical context.
A Proxy Update Module continuously incorporates context from historical latents.
An Attention Matching Loss provides explicit supervision from full-context attention behavior.
Experiments report consistent quality improvements and state-of-the-art performance over existing baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Learns full-context attention proxies for streaming video generation under bounded memory/compute; relevant to efficient attention and video generation.
papers.title: Attn-Forcing: Learning Full-Context Attention Proxies for Streaming Video Generation
papers.tldr: Attn-Forcing enables higher-quality streaming video generation by approximating full-history attention with learned visual proxies under bounded memory and computation.

papers.abstract: Language 3D Gaussian Splatting enables open-vocabulary scene understanding by associating Gaussian primitives with language features. These semantic attributes increase model storage, while most existing 3DGS compression methods are designed mainly to preserve RGB rendering quality. One straightforward approach is to apply sparsification and quantization sequentially. However, pruning based only on rendering quality can remove Gaussians that have small RGB contributions but are important for semantic prediction. Once removed, their semantic information cannot be recovered by later quantization. We propose ClunoGS, a compact framework for Language 3DGS that combines semantics-aware Gaussian sparsification and vector quantization in a unified constrained objective. Semantic supervision is used during sparsification, and the objective jointly considers rendering quality, semantic accuracy, and compactness. We optimize the unified objective with alternating primal, sparsification, quantization, and dual updates. We evaluate ClunoGS on open-vocabulary localization and segmentation using the LERF and ScanNet-10 benchmarks. Under aggressive compression, our unified, semantics-aware formulation substantially alleviates the degradation of semantic representations caused by sequential compression and semantics-agnostic Gaussian sparsification. Ablations further show that jointly coordinating sparsification and quantization better preserves semantic accuracy than applying them independently.
authors: Jian Xu, Yi Li, Ying Huang, Siyi Wu, Bingzhe Li, Yuede Ji, Miao Yin
bullets: Addresses the loss of important semantic information when RGB-focused Gaussian pruning is followed by quantization.
Combines semantics-aware Gaussian sparsification and vector quantization in one constrained objective.
Balances rendering quality, semantic accuracy, and compactness using alternating primal, sparsification, quantization, and dual updates.
Evaluated on open-vocabulary localization and segmentation with LERF and ScanNet-10.
Under aggressive compression, better preserves semantic representations than sequential or independently applied compression.
papers.selection_reason: Semantics-aware compression of language 3D Gaussian splatting; fits 3D vision and efficiency.
papers.title: ClunoGS: Compact Language 3D Gaussian Splatting via Unified Optimization
papers.tldr: ClunoGS compresses Language 3D Gaussian Splatting while preserving both visual rendering and semantic understanding through unified, semantics-aware optimization.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based models achieve strong performance on blind compressed image restoration (CIR) under unknown compression settings, but their densely stacked projection operators make deployment costly. We study training-free acceleration for such models through an empirical, operator-level analysis. Specifically, we profile where computation is concentrated, characterize channel-wise activation distributions under compressed inputs, and examine the singular-value decay of representative projection weights. These measurements identify the recurring projections in the attention, feed-forward, convolutional, and prompt-conditioning pathways as effective low-rank replacement targets that preserve the original inference graph. They further establish truncated SVD (TSVD) as a principled training-free baseline for blind CIR and reveal why a uniform low-rank objective is mismatched to the channel-imbalanced feature distributions of compressed images. Accordingly, we formulate Activation-Calibrated Singular Value Decomposition (ASVD) for this restoration setting, deriving low-rank factors entirely offline from pretrained weights and lightweight activation statistics gathered from only a few compressed calibration images. By weighting the decomposition with channel-wise activation magnitudes, our ASVD assigns larger penalties to errors on more active channels, requiring neither retraining nor online calibration and leaving the restoration pipeline intact. When instantiated on PromptCIR at rank 64, ASVD consistently improves PSNR-B over TSVD across four standard benchmarks under identical parameter and MAC budgets. At this operating point, the factorized model cuts parameters by 59% (34.75M to 14.34M) and computation by 16.1% (258.79 to 217.16 GMACs for a 256 x 256 input), enabling acceleration without retraining.
authors: Suhang Yao, Xin Li, Xijun Wang, Yufei Wang, Yeying Jin, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Targets costly attention, feed-forward, convolutional, and prompt-conditioning projections in transformer-based CIR models.
Uses truncated SVD as a training-free baseline, but accounts for channel-imbalanced activations caused by compressed images.
Derives low-rank factors offline from pretrained weights and lightweight statistics from a few compressed calibration images.
On PromptCIR at rank 64, ASVD improves PSNR-B over TSVD across four benchmarks under equal parameter and MAC budgets.
Reduces parameters by 59% and computation by 16.1% for 256×256 inputs, without retraining or changing the inference pipeline.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free low-rank acceleration for transformer image restoration; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: Training-free Acceleration for Blind Compressed Image Restoration via Activation-Calibrated Singular Value Decomposition
papers.tldr: ASVD accelerates blind compressed image restoration without retraining by using activation-aware low-rank factorization of pretrained projection layers.

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers are widely used in image-editing services. To preserve both efficiency and privacy, existing systems commonly rely on cloud-device collaboration. Keeping request-specific inference on the device avoids sending personal images and prompts to the cloud. These workloads often use common templates, such as in face swapping and virtual try-on, enabling KV state to be precomputed and reused across requests. However, this reusable state is large and scales with the number of templates, making it impractical to store all of them on mobile devices. Storing them in the cloud addresses this capacity issue, but cache transfer is placed onto the inference path and can even be slower than on-device computation, especially under fluctuating mobile networks. We introduce SAKURA, a cloud-edge architecture that delivers reusable attention state to mobile devices under a bandwidth budget. It first uses a fine-grained token-importance-aware compression method to preserve image quality under limited transfer budgets. At runtime, SAKURA adaptively selects the cache representation for each upcoming shard based on network bandwidth. To enable efficient execution, we develop a pipelined runtime that overlaps cache transfer and reconstruction with on-device execution. We evaluate SAKURA using three editing tasks and two diffusion models, using a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone. SAKURA reduces latency by 1.82x and 3.27x over CacheGen adapted to DiT and on-device generation, respectively. It also reduces cache storage by 3.06x over uncompressed cache, while preserving image quality.
authors: Shuncheng Jie, Desen Sun, Ri Hong, Yuyang Tian, Hong Zhang, Sihang Liu
bullets: Targets cloud-device image editing where request-specific inference stays on the phone for privacy, but reusable KV caches are too large to store locally.
Uses token-importance-aware cache compression to preserve image quality within a bandwidth budget.
Selects cache representations according to current network bandwidth and overlaps transfer, reconstruction, and on-device execution through pipelining.
Evaluated on three editing tasks and two diffusion models using a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone.
Reports 1.82× and 3.27× lower latency than CacheGen adapted to DiT and on-device generation, respectively, with 3.06× lower cache storage than uncompressed caches while preserving image quality.
papers.selection_reason: Compresses and transfers attention KV cache under bandwidth constraints, fitting memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: SAKURA: Serving Attention Key-Value State Under Rate Adaptation for Private Image Editing on Phones
papers.tldr: SAKURA accelerates private, template-based diffusion image editing on phones by compressing and adaptively streaming reusable attention KV states under changing network bandwidth.

papers.abstract: Generative image compression (GIC) delivers strong perceptual quality at low bitrates. However, GIC methods with strong perceptual quality often rely on pretrained diffusion models with high latency, while recent lightweight GIC methods reduce latency but deliver lower perceptual quality. We observe that, for lightweight GIC methods at low bitrates, coarse deterministic quantization can collapse nearby encoder latents corresponding to different fine details to the same point, making these details difficult to recover. Motivated by this, we propose GR-GIC, an efficient GIC that delivers competitive reconstruction performance with fast inference. For better performance, we introduce Guided Refinement (GR), which combines latent refinement guided by entropy context with adaptive perturbations for training regularization, jointly improving reconstruction at low bitrates. For fast inference, we introduce reorganized projected residual vector quantization (P-RVQ), which equivalently reorganizes residual updates into low-dimensional lookups to expose greater parallelism and reduce sequential computation. Experiments on Kodak show that for performance, compared with OneDC, GR-GIC achieves BD-rate savings of 23.19%, 37.71%, 22.30%, and 22.14% for LPIPS, DISTS, PSNR, and FID, respectively. For fast inference, the highly optimized implementation of GR-GIC encodes and decodes in 4.60 and 5.98 ms on an NVIDIA A100. Specifically, the reorganized P-RVQ implementation achieves a $3.14\times$ average speedup over the original implementation under the same FP32 setting. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, GR-GIC achieves latency comparable to lightweight GIC methods.
authors: Hao Cao, Yinhuan Huang, Wenqi Guo, Zhijin Qin, Jungong Han
bullets: Addresses detail loss caused when coarse quantization maps distinct encoder latents to the same point.
Introduces Guided Refinement, combining entropy-context guidance with adaptive perturbations for training regularization.
Uses reorganized projected residual vector quantization to expose parallelism and reduce sequential computation.
On Kodak, reports BD-rate savings over OneDC across LPIPS, DISTS, PSNR, and FID.
Runs at 4.60 ms encoding and 5.98 ms decoding on an NVIDIA A100; latency is comparable to lightweight GIC methods on Jetson Orin NX.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces latency and computation in generative image compression, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Efficient Generative Image Compression with Quantized Latents Refinement
papers.tldr: GR-GIC improves low-bitrate generative image compression by refining quantized latents while enabling fast, highly parallel inference.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures scale model capacity efficiently, yet their substantial memory footprint poses a major barrier to deployment. Expert pruning reduces this footprint, but most methods focus on which experts to remove and prune every layer equally. We propose SPARE (Sparsity Allocation via Routing Entropy), a training-free, selector-agnostic method that decides how many experts to remove from each layer using routing entropy, the entropy of tokens' normalized Top-K gate weights on calibration data. When a token's gate weight is spread evenly, removing one active expert discards little of it, so SPARE prunes layers with more diffuse routing more aggressively. A perturbation bound under random pruning formalizes this intuition, and controlled interventions with a fixed selector link concentrated routing to larger output changes. With the same selector and budget, SPARE improves average accuracy over uniform allocation on Mixtral, Qwen3, and DeepSeek models, especially at high pruning ratios. At 50% expert pruning, it raises the eight-task average of Qwen3-30B-A3B from 57.2% to 63.8%, and the math, code, and science average of DeepSeek-R1 from 80.1 to 82.8.
authors: Yifan Yang, Hanling Yi, Dongquan Yang, Feng Lin, Rong Xiao, Aijun Li, Xiaotian Yu
bullets: Targets the memory cost of MoE deployment by choosing how many experts to remove per layer.
Uses token gate-weight entropy on calibration data: layers with more diffuse routing are pruned more aggressively.
Training-free and selector-agnostic; supported by a perturbation bound and controlled interventions.
Outperforms uniform allocation on Mixtral, Qwen3, and DeepSeek models, particularly at high pruning ratios.
At 50% pruning, Qwen3-30B-A3B improves from 57.2% to 63.8%, while DeepSeek-R1 improves from 80.1 to 82.8% on the reported task averages.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a training-free method for expert pruning in Mixture-of-Experts to reduce memory footprint, fitting 'Token Pruning and Eviction'.
papers.title: SPARE: Sparsity Allocation via Routing Entropy for Efficient MoEs
papers.tldr: SPARE uses routing entropy to allocate expert pruning across MoE layers, improving accuracy over uniform pruning at the same sparsity budget.

papers.abstract: Edge medical segmentation must reconcile small model size, high accuracy, and fast inference. TernScope addresses this tradeoff through model--hardware co-design, learning a compact segmentation network whose low-bit operators also simplify hardware execution. Split-channel large-kernel blocks preserve spatial context with limited computation, while branch fusion removes redundant inference paths. Ternary Progressive Quantization-aware Training (TPQ) then adapts the fused network from deep to shallow layers, through the decoder, and finally to the input and prediction layers. All 25 convolutions use ternary weights and 8-bit activations, enabling packed storage and multiplier-free computation. The resulting model uses 0.2483 M parameters and 0.0949 GMACs while retaining competitive segmentation accuracy on in-domain and external datasets. Under the same 45 nm technology, TernScope reduces compute-array area by 88.46% compared with the original Gemmini, a systolic-array accelerator with 8-bit $\times$ 8-bit multipliers. These results demonstrate a path from accurate lightweight medical segmentation to compact low-bit hardware.
authors: Zhuoyu Wu, Wenhui Ou, Qiawei Zheng, Xuhong Qiu, Wenqi Fang, Rapha\"{e}l C. -W. Phan
bullets: Targets the tradeoff among model size, segmentation accuracy, and inference speed in edge medical imaging.
