Uses split-channel large-kernel blocks and branch fusion to preserve spatial context while reducing computation.
Applies Ternary Progressive Quantization-aware Training across the network, with ternary weights and 8-bit activations for packed, multiplier-free execution.
The model has 0.2483 M parameters and 0.0949 GMACs while maintaining competitive accuracy on in-domain and external datasets.
At 45 nm, its compute-array area is reduced by 88.46% versus the original Gemmini accelerator.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient low-bit model-hardware co-design for medical segmentation reduces compute and memory, matching Efficient AI.
papers.title: TernScope: Model-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient Ternary Endoscopic Segmentation
papers.tldr: TernScope co-designs a compact ternary segmentation model and low-bit hardware to enable efficient endoscopic segmentation at the edge.

papers.abstract: Linear-attention language models keep their context in a recurrent state of fixed size, where an inference system stores one copy of this state for every sequence it decodes at the same time. Storing the state at lower precision therefore lets more sequences share an accelerator. Existing state quantizers round the state after every generated token and report that four bits lose accuracy unless the bit width is raised or the model is fine-tuned.\par We introduce PACE, a post-hoc four-bit state quantizer. PACE rounds the state only once every few generated tokens, as chunked kernels already do once per chunk during prefill, and keeps the tokens generated in between in a small buffer. Rounding less often reduces the error that accumulates in the state. Additionally, we find that the large entries of the gated-delta state gather in columns, because some channels of the update written at each token remain large across many tokens. PACE therefore shares each quantization scale within one column. It also keeps the heads that retain rounding error longest at eight bits. On four hybrid models from 4B to 35B parameters, PACE with mixed four- and eight-bit heads is competitive with eight-bit DAMP on the three larger models at about two thirds of its memory, PACE with four-bit heads throughout scores higher than Q-Mamba at equal memory, and rounding every few tokens preserves the decoding speedup of the buffer.
authors: Patrick Haller, Filipe Laitenberger, Alan Akbik
bullets: Targets memory overhead in linear-attention language models, where each concurrent sequence stores a recurrent state.
Buffers several generated tokens and rounds the state once per chunk instead of after every token, reducing accumulated quantization error.
Shares quantization scales within state columns, exploiting channels whose update magnitudes remain large over time.
Keeps heads with persistent rounding error at eight bits while quantizing others at four bits.
Across four hybrid models, PACE matches eight-bit DAMP on larger models at roughly two-thirds the memory and outperforms Q-Mamba at equal memory; buffered rounding preserves decoding speedups.
papers.selection_reason: Post-hoc quantization of recurrent states in linear-attention LLMs to reduce memory footprint during inference.
papers.title: PACE: Periodic and Channel-Aligned Encoding of Four-Bit Recurrent States
papers.tldr: PACE is a post-hoc recurrent-state quantizer that improves four-bit inference by rounding less often, aligning scales by channel, and selectively using eight-bit heads.

papers.abstract: Direct preference optimization (DPO) incurs training costs in output scoring, sequence execution, and backpropagation, so reducing supervision alone does not necessarily save computation. We introduce a unified framework for stochastic pruning of the DPO computation graph that independently samples response positions for scoring, response prefixes for execution, and preference branches for backpropagation. By making these selections before the corresponding operations, the framework omits computation at each stage of a training step. Our analysis characterizes the objective changes induced by position and sequence pruning and uses inverse-probability weighting to obtain a conditionally unbiased single-branch gradient estimator for the sampled objective. Controlled measurements show that position and sequence pruning primarily reduce peak memory, with most output-memory savings attributable to an implementation that retains full response supervision. Branch pruning yields a $1.426\times$ step-time speedup over a concatenated DPO baseline and reduces training time by about 30\% relative to stock DPO across two model families, with slightly lower mean accuracy and benchmark-dependent changes in open-ended scores. These findings relate the resource benefits of stochastic graph pruning to the computation omitted and the resulting changes in the training objective.
authors: Yubing Wu, Wei Chen, Junmei Yang, Delu Zeng, Tiewen Pan
bullets: Targets DPO’s output scoring, sequence execution, and preference-branch backpropagation costs.
Samples response positions, response prefixes, and preference branches before their corresponding computations.
Uses inverse-probability weighting to produce a conditionally unbiased gradient estimator for the sampled objective.
Branch pruning provides the main speedup; position and sequence pruning primarily reduce peak memory.
Quality changes are modest but include slightly lower mean accuracy and benchmark-dependent open-ended scores.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces DPO training compute and memory through stochastic pruning of response positions and branches; fits efficient-AI methods.
papers.title: Stochastic Pruning of the DPO Computation Graph: 1.4x Faster Training and Lower Peak Memory
papers.tldr: Stochastically pruning DPO’s scoring, execution, and backpropagation graph cuts training cost—achieving a 1.426× step-time speedup and about 30% lower training time, with modest quality trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by employing a compact draft model to propose candidate tokens that are verified in parallel by a target model. Conventional training relies on soft-label distillation, which forces the draft model to mimic the target's full output distribution, including high-entropy regions that degrade acceptance rates and increase early rejection risk. We propose RCSD (Reinforcement and Continual Learning for Speculative Decoding), a training framework that aligns draft model optimization with the system-level objective of maximizing acceptance length. RCSD leverages naturally occurring accepted and rejected sequences during speculative inference to construct implicit preference pairs, with masked loss to avoid penalizing target-aligned tokens. Evaluated across multiple benchmarks, RCSD improves average acceptance length by 35% over HASS and achieves 1.35x faster end-to-end inference than HASS on practical workloads, without compromising generation quality.
authors: Mingkang Liu, Weiming Meng, Peipei Jiao, Jiawei Zhang, Tianyuan Liu, Junyan Li, Lichen Pang
bullets: Conventional soft-label distillation can make draft models imitate uncertain target outputs, increasing rejection risk.
RCSD uses reinforcement and continual learning with accepted/rejected inference sequences as implicit preference pairs.
A masked loss avoids penalizing tokens that already align with the target model.
Across multiple benchmarks, RCSD improves average acceptance length by 35% over HASS.
It achieves 1.35× faster end-to-end inference than HASS on practical workloads without compromising generation quality.
papers.selection_reason: Speculative decoding training framework that accelerates LLM inference, fitting the efficient-AI scope.
papers.title: RCSD: Reinforcement and Continual Learning for Domain-Specific Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: RCSD trains speculative-decoding draft models to maximize accepted token sequences, improving acceptance length and end-to-end inference speed without reducing generation quality.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward visual geometry models, exemplified by VGGT, have demonstrated strong multi-view reconstruction capabilities through dense global attention. However, the resulting all-to-all cross-view computation scales quadratically with the number of input views, making long-sequence inference particularly expensive due to substantial frame-level redundancy among highly overlapping observations. We uncover a topology-first, geometry-later evolution in VGGT camera tokens: shallow-layer tokens reliably capture local view neighborhoods, whereas deeper-layer tokens progressively encode globally organized inter-view geometry. Motivated by this observation, we introduce BlazeVGGT, a training-free framework for structure-aware frame-level key--value sparsification. At each global-attention block, BlazeVGGT constructs a view-level similarity kernel from camera-token relations and employs greedy determinantal point process inference to select a compact set of mutually complementary views. The selected views constitute the key--value context, while all input frames are retained as queries. This asymmetric attention design preserves dense per-frame predictions while eliminating redundant cross-view computation, allowing our method to be directly integrated into pretrained VGGT as a plug-and-play module without parameter updates. Its advantages become increasingly pronounced with sequence length: at 2,000 frames, BlazeVGGT achieves approximately 13$\times$ faster inference than VGGT while reducing the Chamfer Distance from 0.41 to 0.32. Extensive experiments demonstrate a favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-off in point-cloud reconstruction and camera-pose estimation, compatibility with existing VGGT accelerators such as FastVGGT and LiteVGGT, and transferability to VGGT-based models including StreamVGGT and PAGE-4D. Codes are publicly available at https://github.com/MagiciannnY/BlazeVGGT.git.
authors: Shujun Yao, Junhui Lin, Congying Han, Tiande Guo, Ziwen Liu, Bonan Li
bullets: VGGT’s all-to-all attention becomes costly for long, highly overlapping image sequences.
The method uses camera-token similarities to identify local-to-global view structure across network layers.
Greedy determinantal point process selection chooses complementary frames as sparse key–value context, while retaining all frames as queries.
At 2,000 frames, inference is approximately 13× faster and Chamfer Distance decreases from 0.41 to 0.32.
The plug-and-play approach transfers to VGGT variants and supports point-cloud reconstruction and camera-pose estimation.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces BlazeVGGT, a training-free framework for sparsifying camera tokens in multi-view geometry models, fitting 3D Vision and Efficient AI.
papers.title: BlazeVGGT: 13x Faster VGGT at 2,000 Frames via Camera Token without Training
papers.tldr: BlazeVGGT makes VGGT about 13× faster on 2,000-frame sequences by sparsifying redundant cross-view attention without retraining, while improving reported reconstruction accuracy.

papers.abstract: Full 3D attention is costly in video Diffusion Transformers. Block-sparse attention reduces this cost by computing only selected attention blocks. However, existing methods either overlook the potential to optimize sparsity allocation or rely on heuristic rules or local metrics to guide it. In this work, we observe that sparsifying attention in different layers and at different denoising steps affects final-video fidelity to substantially different degrees. Yet the identities of the most sensitive layer-step pairs remain nearly unchanged across inputs. Building on these findings, we propose Allocating Layer-step Latency by Output Tests (ALLOT), a training-free sparsity allocation method. Treating each layer-step pair as a cell, ALLOT estimates each cell's contribution to final-video error through (i) cell probing and (ii) trajectory calibration, then jointly optimizes cell densities under a measured-latency budget. It preserves existing selection strategies and kernels, replacing only the allocation component. At equal or shorter wall-clock time, ALLOT outperforms every compared allocation strategy with XAttention, with an 11.8 dB PSNR gain on HunyuanVideo. Extensive experiments across four additional published pipelines on Wan2.1, Wan2.2, and HunyuanVideo show that ALLOT outperforms or ties the default in all nine settings.
authors: Tianze Xia, Xiaoling Zhou, Ruya Lan, Yiqiao Liao, Chengru Song, Shiming Xiang
bullets: Full 3D attention is expensive, and different layer–step pairs have unequal effects on final-video fidelity.
ALLOT estimates each pair’s error contribution using cell probing and trajectory calibration.
It jointly optimizes sparsity densities under a measured-latency budget while retaining existing block-selection strategies and kernels.

Across five video diffusion pipelines and nine settings, ALLOT outperforms or matches the default allocation; with XAttention, it achieves an 11.8 dB PSNR gain on HunyuanVideo at equal or lower runtime.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes ALLOT, a training-free method to optimize block-sparse attention allocation in Video Diffusion Transformers, directly addressing efficiency and video generation.
papers.title: Sparsity Should Be ALLOTted by Output: Training-Free Allocation of Block-Sparse Attention for Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: ALLOT is a training-free method that allocates block-sparse attention across layer–denoising-step pairs to improve video diffusion quality under a latency budget.

papers.abstract: Jet tagging is one of the most important applications of machine learning at the Large Hadron Collider. Recent models build in more physics knowledge or rely on large-scale pretraining, but the experiments place strict limits on their inference cost. Knowledge distillation can transfer their performance to small students that are cheap to run. We ask which properties of a teacher help the student, how small a student can get and how close it can come to the state of the art. On a jet tagging benchmark, we distil six teachers that differ in architecture, symmetry and pretraining, including two foundation models, into five small students. Every teacher improves every student, and the gain depends mainly on the strength of the teacher. We then shrink our two strongest distilled students, Transformer and L-GATr-slim, in width and in depth. With 20 thousand parameters, a distilled L-GATr-slim outperforms every published jet tagger trained from scratch at a fraction of the inference cost of every teacher. Even with two thousand parameters, it matches ParT, a model with a thousand times as many parameters. We also study what the students learn from their teachers. Our benchmark of inference cost shows that students of the same size can differ by almost an order of magnitude in speed. We release the code and the weights of all trained models.
authors: Jay Agarwal, Siddharth Khare, Dhruv Kumar
bullets: Distils six teachers across architectures, symmetries, and pretraining setups into five compact students.
Every teacher improves every student, with gains driven mainly by teacher strength.
A 20,000-parameter distilled L-GATr-slim outperforms published from-scratch taggers at lower inference cost than the teachers.
A 2,000-parameter student matches ParT despite having roughly 1,000 times fewer parameters.
Students with the same parameter count can differ by nearly an order of magnitude in speed; code and weights are released.
papers.selection_reason: Knowledge distillation to dramatically reduce inference cost for jet taggers directly fits the Efficient AI scope.
papers.title: How Far Can Foundation Models Be Distilled for Efficient Jet Tagging?
papers.tldr: Knowledge distillation transfers strong jet-tagging performance from diverse and foundation-model teachers to extremely small, fast student models.

papers.abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) aims to recover reasoning capabilities in low-bit large language models (LLMs). Existing recipes typically supervise the quantized student with the original full-precision model on fixed response sequences. However, the resulting low-bit quantized models still struggle on long-horizon reasoning tasks and often fail to terminate within a token budget that suffices for the full-precision model. We identify two challenges in closing this gap. First, fixed-response supervision leaves a mismatch between training prefixes and those encountered during student generation, and this trajectory divergence grows as responses lengthen. Second, on its own prefixes, the student underpredicts some next-token candidates and overpredicts others, and this distributional misalignment becomes more frequent at high-entropy prefixes. We present OnQ, a low-bit recovery pipeline that combines on-policy distillation and candidate-wise Dynamic KL. Starting from block-wise calibration, the quantized student generates responses and receives full-precision teacher supervision on its own prefixes. Dynamic KL weights forward and reverse KL by each candidate's teacher-student probability ratio to balance correction of under- and overprediction. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, OnQ achieves the highest nine-benchmark average, with the largest gains on long-horizon reasoning benchmarks. At 2 bits, it outperforms every baseline on every benchmark at every model size, improving the Qwen3-8B average by 10.26 points over the strongest baseline. It also produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitive errors.
authors: Boyuan Zheng, Jing Xiong, Chenwei Wu, Hui Shen, Zesen Zhao, Hei Ting Una Chan, Xueshen Liu, Zhen Zhang, Liyue Shen, Zechun Liu, Z. Morley Mao
bullets: Fixed-response QAT creates a training–generation trajectory mismatch that worsens for longer reasoning sequences.
The quantized student also miscalibrates next-token probabilities, especially at high-entropy prefixes.
OnQ combines block-wise calibration, on-policy distillation, and candidate-wise Dynamic KL to correct under- and overprediction.
Across Qwen3 1.7B–8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, it achieves the best nine-benchmark average, with particularly large long-horizon reasoning gains.
At 2 bits, it beats all baselines on every benchmark and produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitions.
papers.selection_reason: Recovers reasoning in low-bit quantized LLMs via on-policy distillation and dynamic KL, improving efficiency of deployed language models.
papers.title: Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories
papers.tldr: OnQ recovers long-horizon reasoning in low-bit LLMs by distilling teacher behavior on the quantized student’s own trajectories with adaptive KL correction.

papers.abstract: Recent electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models increasingly emphasize model scale, potentially limiting their deployment on resource-constrained devices and in everyday environments. We argue that transferable EEG features can instead be learned with a compact architecture and introduce BrainCodes, a lightweight foundation model pretrained through self-supervised learning on more than 800 hours of recordings from over 1,000 participants. Our architecture combines a quantization-based neural tokenizer with a spatiotemporal encoder that supports arbitrary electrode configurations. The pretraining objective explicitly encourages representations that capture spatial connectivity through channel positional encoding, and sensitivity to narrowband neural oscillations through an auxiliary training objective. Our model matches or surpasses the state of the art across diverse neurophysiological monitoring tasks, including sleep staging, attention assessment, and cognitive load estimation. BrainCodes transfers effectively to low-resource wearable devices while using up to 97% fewer trainable parameters than comparable architectures. Beyond predictive accuracy, our evaluation framework characterizes the geometry and invariances of learned EEG representations across measurable spatial, temporal, and spectral signal properties.
authors: Kleanthis Avramidis, Ivan Tashev, Dimitra Emmanouilidou
bullets: Targets the resource and deployment limitations of increasingly large EEG foundation models.
Pretrained self-supervised on more than 800 hours of recordings from over 1,000 participants.
Combines a quantization-based neural tokenizer with a spatiotemporal encoder for arbitrary electrode configurations.
Encourages spatial-connectivity and narrowband-oscillation sensitivity through positional encoding and an auxiliary objective.
Matches or surpasses state of the art across sleep staging, attention assessment, and cognitive-load estimation, using up to 97% fewer trainable parameters than comparable architectures.
papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces a compact EEG foundation model with 97% fewer trainable parameters, fitting the efficiency-focused topic.
papers.title: BrainCodes: A Lightweight EEG Foundation Model over Discrete Neural Codes
papers.tldr: BrainCodes is a compact EEG foundation model that learns transferable representations from discrete neural codes while supporting varied electrode layouts and efficient wearable deployment.

papers.abstract: Language models are being explored as the interface through which space robots interpret operator commands and select among verified skills. Running them onboard calls for low-bit compression, and flight use adds requirements that generic post-training quantization leaves implicit: a fixed memory budget and storage format, a static artifact under configuration control, and behavior close to the full-precision model validated on the ground. We treat compression as a ground-segment step and study QSelect, which composes one static low-bit model from compatible AWQ, GPTQ, and AutoRound checkpoints by assigning each linear module to one quantizer family and scoring every substitution at the final next-token distribution. The default fidelity mode needs no labels or tuned thresholds and accepts a substitution only when the forward KL divergence from the BF16 reference decreases; an optional target-adapted mode adds answer likelihood on a small labeled set. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-3.2-3B at 3 and 4 bits, composed models reach lower mean held-out perplexity than every single-family model in all six settings, and the fidelity mode lowers perplexity and KL further. In a matched scaffold, final-output scoring gives lower held-out KL than representation-similarity scoring in all 12 paired runs. With labels from training or development splits of the evaluated task families, the target-adapted mode raises 3-bit pooled accuracy on the two Llama models by 4.3 and 4.5 points over the best single-family model. At 3 bits, unquantized embedding and output layers make up 43-46% of the packed artifact. All evaluations use general-domain benchmarks on a ground GPU; space-domain tasks and flight hardware are left to future work.
authors: Jia Deng, Zizhe Wang, Xin Lu, Yi Huang, Zehao Jia
bullets: Evaluates compression for space robots requiring a controlled, static artifact and behavioral fidelity to a BF16 reference.
Assigns each linear module among AWQ, GPTQ, and AutoRound variants using final next-token distribution scores.
A label-free fidelity mode accepts substitutions that reduce forward KL; an optional target-adapted mode uses labeled data.
Across three language models and 3-/4-bit settings, composed models achieve lower held-out perplexity than every single-family baseline.
Target adaptation improves pooled 3-bit accuracy on the two Llama models by 4.3 and 4.5 points; evaluations remain limited to general-domain benchmarks on ground GPUs.
papers.selection_reason: Composes low-bit quantized LLM checkpoints under a fidelity constraint for onboard deployment, directly targeting model memory efficiency.
papers.title: Compressing Onboard Language Models for Space Robots under a Behavioral-Fidelity Requirement
papers.tldr: QSelect composes compatible low-bit checkpoints into static onboard models that better preserve full-precision behavior under fixed storage constraints.

papers.abstract: Finding K most similar elements for a query in a large gallery of neural network (NN) embeddings is essential in various areas of computer science and industrial applications of artificial intelligence. This paper proposes search algorithms for structured latent spaces (LS) of NNs which allow to speed up top K item retrieval owing to O(1) complexity small candidate gallery subset search. ArcFace-pretrained IResNet50 models are finetuned using Latent Space Configuration (LSC) methodology to obtain new distribution of embeddings with desired geometric properties. Applying the proposed algorithms to embeddings obtained from finetuned models leads to several times speed-up over baseline exhaustive search. Specifically, we report up to 3 times speed-up on GPU and 40% speed-up on CPU compared to the baseline method GPU speed. These results are obtained for the original and reduced numbers of LS dimensions. The results show that LS dimensionality reduction allows to further accelerate the search and even improve rank-N metrics.
bullets: Targets efficient retrieval of the K most similar items from large embedding galleries.
Fine-tunes ArcFace-pretrained IResNet50 models to impose structured geometric properties on the latent space.
Uses structured latent-space search with an O(1)-complexity candidate subset instead of exhaustive comparison.
Reports up to 3× GPU speed-up and 40% CPU speed-up relative to the stated baseline.
Dimensionality reduction further accelerates retrieval and can improve rank-N metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Latent space configuration and dimensionality-reduction methods for fast top-K embedding retrieval; relevant to efficient AI serving.
papers.title: Latent space configuration for neural network finetuning, fast ranking, and embedding dimensionality reduction
papers.tldr: Latent Space Configuration reshapes neural-network embeddings to enable faster top-K similarity search, while dimensionality reduction can further improve speed and ranking quality.

papers.abstract: Visual question answering from low-altitude UAV imagery must deliver timely and accurate judgments to support disaster response under limited edge computing resources. Routine questions may be answered through direct decisions, whereas more challenging questions may benefit from step-by-step reasoning. However, existing research primarily focuses on improving models' visual understanding and generative reasoning capabilities, with limited exploration of efficient direct decision-making and its adaptive coordination with generative reasoning. We develop Disaster-S1 based on a vision-language model adapted to the disaster domain. Trained for option discrimination, it outputs a probability distribution over answer options in a single multimodal forward pass for fast decision-making. We further propose DisasterRoute, a dual-system routing framework that combines prediction confidence with disaster evidence to decide whether to accept the initial answer or invoke the disaster reasoning model DisasterVL for review. By allocating inference computation on demand, the framework retains the efficiency of direct decision-making and improves overall question-answering accuracy through selective review. Experiments on DisasterBench show that Disaster-S1 achieves superior accuracy with low latency, while DisasterRoute further improves accuracy through selective review at substantially lower latency than full reasoning.
authors: Tan Zhang, Xing Deng, Lu Zhang, Xiaofeng Zhu, Ping Hu
bullets: Targets timely UAV-based disaster QA under limited edge-computing resources.
Disaster-S1 performs fast option discrimination in a single multimodal forward pass.
Routes answers using both prediction confidence and disaster evidence.
Invokes DisasterVL selectively for review instead of applying full reasoning to every question.
On DisasterBench, selective review improves accuracy while maintaining substantially lower latency than full reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Dual-system routing between fast direct VQA decisions and generative reasoning; relevant to multimodal LLM deployment and selective computation allocation.
papers.title: DisasterRoute: Evidence-Guided Dual-System Routing for Visual Disaster Question Answering
papers.tldr: DisasterRoute efficiently improves visual disaster question answering by routing only uncertain or insufficiently supported answers to a slower reasoning model.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires video-LLMs to process incoming video continuously while answering user queries with low latency. Recent methods reduce query-time cost by prefilling frames into KV caches during idle time and reusing the cached KVs at query time. To bound per-frame computation over unbounded video streams, these methods restrict the context available during prefill. This creates a fundamental context mismatch: the restricted context may omit information needed to properly contextualize video tokens, yet, still contain information irrelevant to the eventual query, which is unknown during prefill. We propose FrameBlend, a simple yet effective plug-and-play method to address this mismatch through selective KV recomputation, without requiring any additional training. At query time, FrameBlend re-prefills selected video tokens using query-relevant context and replaces their cached KVs with recomputed ones. Crucially, this recomputation enables shorter attention windows during idle-time prefill, substantially reducing prefill cost while improving accuracy. Experiments across three SVU frameworks and five streaming and offline benchmarks demonstrate accuracy gains of up to 3.9 pp. On RVS-Ego, FrameBlend reduces per-frame prefill FLOPs by over 20% and total processing time by 14-59% for retrieval-based frameworks, including the cost of query-time recomputation. These results demonstrate that a simple change in how contextualization is distributed between idle time and query time can improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off for SVU.
authors: Junhyeok Lee, Sangyoon Lee, Jaeho Lee
bullets: Problem: Idle-time KV prefill must use restricted context, causing a mismatch because relevant query information is unavailable and irrelevant context may be included.
Method: At query time, re-prefill selected video tokens with query-relevant context and replace their cached KVs; no additional training is required.
Contribution: Enables shorter idle-time attention windows, lowering prefill computation while preserving or improving contextualization.
Results: Across three SVU frameworks and five benchmarks, accuracy improves by up to 3.9 percentage points.
Efficiency: On RVS-Ego, per-frame prefill FLOPs decrease by over 20%, while total processing time drops by 14–59% for retrieval-based frameworks.
papers.selection_reason: Selective KV recomputation for streaming video LLMs; directly combines video understanding with cache-efficiency and memory reduction.
papers.title: Cache Locally, Recompute Selectively for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: FrameBlend improves streaming video understanding by selectively recomputing cached video-token representations with query-relevant context, reducing preprocessing cost while increasing accuracy.

papers.abstract: Autonomous industrial inspection requires strictly deterministic real-time inference under tight memory and computational constraints. However, existing Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) models suffer from prohibitive scaling: dense temporal memory grows with spatial resolution and sequence length, while fixed-capacity decoders fail to exploit the inherent sparsity of industrial scenes, creating a practical memory wall on resource-constrained edge platforms. We present DetM-Tracker, a streamlined VIS framework for autonomous industrial inspection, where target objects often exhibit highly similar appearance under constrained "micro" fields of view. DetM-Tracker eliminates architectural redundancy through three synergistic components: (1) Compact Scalar Memory, which condenses high-dimensional instance features into four-scalar descriptors, reducing temporal memory complexity from $O(T \cdot N \cdot R)$ to $O(T \cdot \hat{N})$. This mechanism effectively compresses frame-level representations into a bank of active instances, where $R$ denotes resolution, $N$ and $\hat{N}$ represent global and window-specific instance counts, respectively and $T$ the temporal window size; and (2) Dynamic Instance Channels, which adaptively allocate query capacity according to the actual number of visible objects; and (3) Entropy-Gated Skip Connection, which concentrates computational budget on high-uncertainty spatial regions to refine object boundaries in a single forward pass without auxiliary refinement heads. Our approach effectively bridges the gap between modern VIS models and the practical demands of industrial edge deployment, reducing inference latency by approximately 20$\times$ and VRAM consumption by 6$\times$ compared to state-of-the-art dense-feature baselines.
authors: You-Rui Lin, Jen-Chieh Wu, Tzu-Ti Wei, Jen-Jee Chen, Yu-Chee Tseng
bullets: Targets the memory and compute limits of edge platforms running autonomous industrial inspection.
Uses Compact Scalar Memory to reduce temporal memory complexity from O(T·N·R) to O(T·N̂) with four-scalar instance descriptors.
Dynamically allocates instance channels based on the number of visible objects.
Uses entropy-gated skip connections to refine uncertain object boundaries in a single forward pass.
Reports approximately 20× lower inference latency and 6× lower VRAM use than dense-feature baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient deterministic video instance segmentation for edge deployment; fits temporal visual understanding and inference efficiency.
papers.title: DetM-Tracker: Deterministic and Memory-Efficient VIS for Autonomous Industrial Inspection
papers.tldr: DetM-Tracker enables deterministic, memory-efficient real-time video instance segmentation for industrial inspection by exploiting sparse scenes and compressing temporal instance memory.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding uses a target model to verify a tree of draft tokens in parallel. We study whether the resulting next-token distributions can help select the next tree. For unrestricted target models, we show that guaranteed exact reuse requires a distribution computed at the next round's complete context. We characterize when retaining this distribution requires sacrificing accepted tokens and establish conditions under which this loss persists across decoding rounds. Across six targets, we find that reranking first-token branches with a separately computed distribution at the current context improves expected acceptance over draft ranking, especially with small tree budgets. Drawing the first token from this distribution before allocating the tree further improves expected acceptance over pruning a preselected tree, even at equal mean tree size. In our experiments, both selection rules also decode faster than draft ranking when the separate target pass overlaps standalone drafting. Our findings show that making target probabilities available before tree allocation can improve the efficiency of speculative decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/TargetRows.
authors: Jungseob Lee, Giyoon Jang, Chailin Nam, Jiwoo Kum, Sihyeon Lee, Kyojun Choo, Jihun Song, Eunseo Song, Chanjun Park
bullets: Exact reuse of target distributions generally requires computing them on the next round’s full context.
Retaining reusable distributions may require sacrificing accepted tokens, with this loss sometimes persisting across rounds.
Reranking first-token branches using a separately computed current-context target distribution outperforms draft-based ranking in expected acceptance across six targets.
Sampling the first token before tree allocation improves acceptance over pruning a preselected tree, even at equal mean tree size.
Both target-informed selection methods can decode faster when the separate target pass overlaps standalone drafting.
papers.selection_reason: Studies target probability reuse in speculative decoding to improve LLM inference efficiency.
papers.title: Understanding Target Probability Reuse in Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: Making target-model probabilities available before speculative-tree allocation can improve token acceptance and decoding efficiency, especially with small tree budgets.

papers.abstract: Executing vision-language models (VLMs) aboard low-Earth orbit satellites enables flexible processing of observation data without first downlinking it to the ground. On commercial off-the-shelf payloads, however, a request may span multiple execution windows: power and thermal constraints, fault-triggered reboots, and competing payload demands can interrupt inference before it completes. Each shutdown discards volatile activations and KV caches, forcing an unprotected request to repeat work after restart. We present OrbitWeaver, a framework that preserves VLM inference progress across onboard interruptions through coordinated checkpointing and recovery. Its phase-aware checkpointing selects recovery boundaries according to the state lifetimes and computational characteristics of vision encoding, language-model prefill, and decoding, balancing storage traffic against recomputation. Its dependency-aware dynamic recovery schedules restoration from partially completed states across the layer and token-chunk dimensions. By overlapping checkpoint and weight reads with recomputation, it reduces restart latency; the recovery planner computes an optimal execution order under its scheduling model within 100 ms. Experiments on satellite payload hardware using on-orbit telemetry traces show up to a 4.07-fold end-to-end speedup and a 3.56-fold reduction in SSD write volume over the evaluated baselines. A 72-hour deployment on two low-Earth orbit satellites demonstrates that OrbitWeaver retains inference progress and resumes execution across repeated bus-enforced shutdowns.
authors: Xiaolong Huang, Yinyuan Zhang, Daliang Xu, Yun Ma, Qing Li, Mengwei Xu, Shangguang Wang, Gang Huang, Xuanzhe Liu
bullets: Addresses interruptions caused by power, thermal, faults, and competing payload demands that otherwise discard activations and KV caches.
Uses phase-aware checkpointing across vision encoding, language-model prefill, and decoding to balance storage overhead with recomputation.
Employs dependency-aware recovery across layers and token chunks, overlapping checkpoint and weight reads with recomputation.
The recovery planner finds an execution order within 100 ms under its scheduling model.
On satellite hardware and telemetry traces, it achieved up to 4.07× end-to-end speedup and 3.56× lower SSD write volume; a 72-hour deployment resumed inference across repeated shutdowns.
papers.selection_reason: Checkpointing and recovery framework for VLM inference that reduces restart latency and storage writes; relevant to efficient inference systems.
papers.title: Resuming Vision-Language Inference across Onboard Interruptions
papers.tldr: OrbitWeaver enables vision-language inference on satellites to resume efficiently after shutdowns by checkpointing and intelligently recovering partial progress.

papers.abstract: We study how to improve training efficiency on Ascend NPUs. In the NPU training programs we study, framework-level compilation optimizations such as operator fusion are only partially applied, leaving fragmented computation and avoidable execution overheads. Profiling-guided tuning can address these inefficiencies, but it often requires costly trial and error. To make training on NPUs more efficient, we propose TrainBridge, an agentic approach for transferring GPU optimization guidance to NPU training. TrainBridge uses the highly optimized execution produced by mature GPU compilation stacks as a task-specific reference for NPU tuning. It extracts optimization intents from the GPU training execution to guide NPU program rewrites and further refines the rewritten program through iterative profiling. Our GPU-to-NPU migration experiments show that TrainBridge achieves an average 1.7x speedup across four workloads covering LLM pretraining, image classification, and vision-language training, and an average speedup of nearly 2.0x across 27 Modded-NanoGPT speedrun records with highly optimized GPU implementations.
authors: Yupeng Chen, Kunxiang Zhao, Xingjian Wang, Yue Zhao, Yijing Wu, Ye Liu, Kai Li, Congliang Chen, Ruoyu Sun
bullets: Targets fragmented NPU computation and overhead caused by partially applied framework-level optimizations such as operator fusion.
Extracts task-specific optimization intents from mature GPU execution and transfers them to NPU program rewrites.
Iteratively refines rewrites using profiling to reduce costly trial-and-error tuning.
Reports an average 1.7× speedup across four workloads and nearly 2.0× across 27 Modded-NanoGPT speedrun records.
Evaluated workloads span LLM pretraining, image classification, and vision-language training.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic GPU-guided optimization for NPU training improves training efficiency, matching the Efficient AI parent topic.
papers.title: TrainBridge: Agentic NPU Training Optimization Guided by GPU Compilation Evidence
papers.tldr: TrainBridge uses optimized GPU compilation behavior to guide agentic NPU rewrites, achieving substantial training speedups on Ascend NPUs.

papers.abstract: Synthesizing high-fidelity 7T MRI from routinely acquired 3T scans offers a practical pathway to enhanced neuroimaging without the prohibitive cost of ultra-high-field scanners. While existing deep learning approaches have achieved promising results, state-of-the-art methods typically rely on either large-scale architectures exceeding 45 million parameters or computationally intensive ensemble strategies, limiting their practicality in resource-constrained clinical environments. In this work, we propose a compact multi-domain attention framework, termed DGCM-SSFA, that achieves competitive synthesis quality with only 11M parameters. The proposed architecture integrates two complementary modules into a U-Net Transformer backbone. First, a Dual-Granularity Cross-Modulated Feature Modulator (DGCM) is embedded at multiple hierarchical levels to enhance local edge and texture details through Sobel-guided spatial attention and depthwise frequency-aware channel attention with cross-branch gating. Second, a Sparse Strip Frequency Attention (SSFA) module at the bottleneck captures global spatial context via strip-pooled attention with near-linear complexity, while simultaneously performing FFT-based spectral modulation in the frequency domain. These two modules operate synergistically with the backbone's native channel attention, forming a triple-granularity feature refinement pipeline. Extensive experiments on the UNC and BNU 3T-to-7T MRI datasets across T1w and T2w modalities demonstrate that DGCM-SSFA achieves strong structural fidelity, attaining an SSIM of 0.8431 on BNU T2w---approaching the best benchmark value of 0.8624---and 0.8100 on BNU T1w, while using substantially fewer parameters than Transformer-based alternatives such as ResViT (123.4M) and FS-RWKV (45.4M).
authors: Zhichun Fan, Zhiqiang Chen, Lanling Liu, Lingjun Liu, Zhonghua Xie
bullets: Addresses the high cost of 7T MRI and the impractical computational demands of existing synthesis models.
Combines dual-granularity cross-modulated feature refinement with sparse strip spatial and frequency-domain attention in a U-Net Transformer.
Uses Sobel-guided spatial attention, frequency-aware channel gating, strip-pooled global context, and FFT-based spectral modulation.
Evaluated on UNC and BNU datasets for T1w and T2w MRI; it achieves SSIM values of 0.8431 on BNU T2w and 0.8100 on BNU T1w.
Offers substantially fewer parameters than cited Transformer alternatives, including ResViT (123.4M) and FS-RWKV (45.4M).
papers.selection_reason: Compact MRI synthesis architecture with sparse strip frequency attention near-linear complexity provides transferable efficient attention ideas.
papers.title: DGCM-SSFA: Dual-Granularity Cross-Modulation and Sparse Strip Frequency Attention for Efficient 3T-to-7T MRI Synthesis
papers.tldr: DGCM-SSFA enables efficient 3T-to-7T MRI synthesis with competitive structural fidelity using only 11M parameters.

papers.abstract: Full fine-tuning has achieved remarkable success on reasoning-intensive tasks, but it often requires substantial GPU resource consumption. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) provides a promising alternative for reducing this cost, yet we observe a substantial performance gap on reasoning-intensive tasks. In this paper, we present three key observations showing that this gap is closely associated with norm-related under-adaptation, where PEFT produces markedly smaller weight-update norms than full fine-tuning. Based on these observations, we propose Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (NormTune), a simple yet effective strategy that adaptively strengthens insufficiently updated layers according to their weight-update norms. Extensive experiments show that NormTune consistently enhances multiple PEFT methods across challenging reasoning benchmarks. Specifically, when trained on S1K-1.1, integrating NormTune into rank-8 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA yields substantial average accuracy improvements of 24.24\%, 11.33\%, and 16.21\% , respectively, across AIME 2024, MATH 500, GPQA, and AIME 2025. Moreover, NormTune-enhanced rank-256 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA achieve performance comparable to S1 full fine-tuning, with respective average gains of 2.17\%, 0.93\%, and 3.00\% over this baseline.
authors: Zhangming Li, Qinghao Hu, Weifan Guan, Yifan Zhang, Peisong Wang, Jian Cheng
bullets: PEFT can underperform full fine-tuning on reasoning-intensive tasks because it under-adapts certain layers.
The method identifies insufficient adaptation using weight-update norms and adaptively strengthens those layers.
NormTune improves rank-8 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA across AIME 2024, MATH 500, GPQA, and AIME 2025.
With S1K-1.1 training, average accuracy gains are 24.24% for LoRA, 11.33% for Bone, and 16.21% for MoRA.
At rank 256, NormTune-enhanced methods reach performance comparable to S1 full fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that reduces training cost; fits Efficient AI broadly, though no specific subtopic applies.
papers.title: NormTune: Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Reasoning-Intensive Tasks
papers.tldr: NormTune improves parameter-efficient fine-tuning for reasoning tasks by strengthening layers whose weight updates are unusually small.

papers.abstract: Blind all-in-one image restoration must adapt a shared model to heterogeneous and sometimes mixed degradations without a task label at test time. We introduce WaFIR, a decoder module that decomposes features into Haar subbands, summarizes each subband with a compact Fourier descriptor, and routes it to prompt-conditioned spectral modulation experts. Unlike image-level frequency conditioning, WaFIR makes routing decisions at the subband level, enabling frequency-specific processing while retaining the task context learned by the backbone. Under a unified training and evaluation protocol for denoising, deraining, and dehazing, WaFIR improves average PSNR over the three tasks by 0.48 dB over the PromptIR baseline and by 0.38 dB over the recent Up-Restorer. Matched-capacity and routing controls show that the gain is not explained by additional parameters alone. On unseen noise intensities, descriptor-based routing is more robust than a discrete label-conditioned alternative and remains on par under compound degradations, while routing analyses show stable subband-dependent expert use across degradation types. These results support subband frequency structure as an interpretable complement to prompt-based conditioning for blind image restoration. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/WaFIR/README.md
authors: Trong Nhan Nguyen, Vu Hoang Minh Doan, Thanh Dat Le, Truong Tien Vo, Thi Thu Ha Vu, Tan Hung Vo, Jaeyeop Choi, Junghwan Oh, Truong-Son Hy
bullets: Targets denoising, deraining, and dehazing without degradation labels at test time.
Decomposes features into Haar subbands and makes frequency-specific, subband-level routing decisions.
Combines subband Fourier descriptors with prompt-conditioned spectral modulation experts.
Improves average PSNR by 0.48 dB over PromptIR and 0.38 dB over Up-Restorer under a unified protocol.
Routing remains robust to unseen noise intensities and compound degradations, with stable subband-dependent expert usage.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces subband-adaptive routing with Fourier descriptors and sparse spectral modulation, offering a transferable efficient attention design.
papers.title: WaFIR: Wavelet-Fourier Mixture-of-Experts with Subband-Adaptive Routing for Blind All-in-One Image Restoration
papers.tldr: WaFIR improves blind all-in-one image restoration by routing Haar subbands to prompt-conditioned spectral experts using compact Fourier descriptors.

papers.abstract: A typed decision maps evidence, a question and a fixed set of options to a probability for every option, computed in one forward pass, by reading a language model's logits or a small head over its hidden states, instead of generating and parsing text. The commercial system Jev popularised this System~1 interface, and open reproductions have followed. We report two uses of the pattern. \emph{Part I} describes an in-house System~1 judge that triages about 148K agentic coding session records for a training corpus. It replaces a frontier LLM judge that cost on the order of \$1,000 per pass and whose stored labels matched a fresh two-judge consensus on only 26.9\% of the sessions where the two judges agreed; a self-hosted frozen backbone with a rank-16 LoRA adapter and a pointer head answers three typed questions in one forward pass, judges 1,000 sessions in about three minutes of one GPU, about \$0.06 at a reference rate and roughly 1\% of the frontier judge's cost, and keeps every session inside the organisation. \emph{Part II} asks whether a readout that adds no parameters can be competitive and whether training one helps. Applying the public Eikos recipe and corpus of about 25K decisions to three further backbones (1B, 2B and 35B), we read the frozen output layer of a LoRA-adapted decoder. On the 111 public hard items of JevBench our single-seed 35B, developed with those items in view, scores 79.3\%, not significantly different from the commercial reference (73.0\%, unadjusted $p=0.12$) and ahead of five open systems after Holm--Bonferroni correction; our 2B is ahead of all four kev checkpoints on the leaderboard. A single-seed ablation finds no detectable benefit from training the 26 letter rows of the output layer, and a retrain on a later corpus release moves the 2B's hard-tier accuracy by 11.7 points, which shows how little small evaluations resolve.
authors: Yuchuan Weng, Chi Liu, Xin Chen, Srinivasan Manoharan
bullets: An in-house judge triages about 148K coding-session records using a frozen backbone, rank-16 LoRA adapter, and pointer head for three typed questions.
It evaluates 1,000 sessions in about three minutes on one GPU at roughly $0.06—about 1% of the frontier judge’s cost—while keeping data in-house.
A parameter-free output-layer readout reaches 79.3% on JevBench’s 111 hard items with a 35B model, not significantly different from the commercial reference.
Training the output-layer rows showed no detectable benefit, and a later corpus release shifted 2B hard-tier accuracy by 11.7 points.
Results are limited by single-seed evaluation and development with public benchmark items in view.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient one-forward-pass LLM judge with LoRA and pointer head; substantially reduces inference cost and latency, relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Our Own Jev: Typed Decisions in One Forward Pass, from an In-House Judge to Open LoRA Models
papers.tldr: Typed one-pass decisions can provide a fast, private, and low-cost alternative to text-generating judges, while small evaluations remain unstable.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning (RL) requires both efficient rollout generation and training on long sequences. However, the memory requirements and model-specific operators of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next make this difficult with existing open-source implementations. To resolve these limitations, we introduce FlashNext-RL, a model-specific RL training optimization framework based on prime-rl, with vLLM for software engineering (SWE) rollout generation. Our main focus is BF16 training of the full 48-layer model on a single 8xB200 node, with the first two layers, the n-gram table, the sparse-attention indexer and the multi-token prediction head frozen. We optimize host offload, gradient accumulation and the kernels for mixture-of-experts, sparse attention and the gated residual stream. In the full-model development study, non-padding training throughput increases from approximately 395 tokens/s/GPU in the initial 32K-token configuration to 4,438 tokens/s/GPU in the optimized 131K-token configuration, with hardware matmul throughput (aka without considering the cost of attention components) increasing from approximately 20 to 213 TFLOPs/GPU. A controlled cumulative study on an 8-layer model further quantifies the contributions of individual optimizations. Together with three inference nodes, the system supports a live SWE RL run with a target batch of 1,024 trainable rollouts and a 131,072-token context limit. Over steps 5-15, an iteration takes 22.4 minutes on average, with bounded entropy and trainer-sampler mismatch KL. These results highlight the importance of tailoring RL training to the model's architecture, memory layout and kernel requirements, rather than relying only on general-purpose RL infrastructure.
bullets: Targets the memory and custom-operator challenges of full-model, long-sequence agentic RL.
Builds on prime-rl and vLLM, using host offload, gradient accumulation, and optimized MoE, sparse-attention, and gated-residual kernels.
In a full-model study, training throughput rose from about 395 to 4,438 non-padding tokens/s/GPU across the reported configurations.
Supports a live SWE RL run with 1,024 trainable rollouts and a 131,072-token context limit; iterations averaged 22.4 minutes over steps 5–15.
The study emphasizes architecture-specific optimization over reliance on general-purpose RL infrastructure.
papers.selection_reason: System optimization for long-horizon agentic RL training of an LLM; reduces memory and increases throughput.
papers.title: FlashNext-RL: A System Optimization Study for Long-Horizon Agentic RL of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
papers.tldr: FlashNext-RL makes long-horizon RL for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next substantially more practical by optimizing memory use, training, and model-specific kernels for large-context SWE rollouts.

papers.abstract: Transformers are deployed as a special model class. Neural processing units (NPU) add dedicated operators for attention and normalization, and quantization relies on Transformer-specific algorithms. We show the computation does not force this. Every Transformer block, with attention, LayerNorm and a GELU MLP, compiles exactly into a generic deep neural network built from fixed affine maps, routing and the square, sigmoid and inverse square root, plus GELU or its sigmoid approximation. Without activation-activation products, every transform-wise compilation adds at least $N^2$ scalar nonlinear evaluations per head for dense scores. Keeping that one operation type removes this cost; its elementwise form, present on every surveyed NPU, suffices with the sigmoid and inverse square root. For top-$k$ attention with exchangeable tail scores, we prove that exact or conditional-mean tail mass gives an unbiased, minimum-mean-square-error estimate of the attention distribution, while tail drop is conditionally biased. When queries or agents cluster, centroids choose the keys first, reducing the number of computed scores from $N^2$ to $Nk$ per head. On DeiT-Tiny, MambaIRv2-Light and Pythia-70M the compiled models match their references with all keys, standard post-training quantization applies, and the exact tail-mass estimate beats tail dropping with half as many keys on DeiT-Tiny and, for $k\le8$, on Pythia-70M.
authors: Sergey Salishev, Zeev Volkovich, Oleg Granichin
bullets: Every Transformer block—including attention, LayerNorm, and GELU MLPs—can be represented using fixed affine maps, routing, square, sigmoid, inverse square root, and GELU-related operations.
Removing activation-activation products incurs at least N² additional scalar nonlinear evaluations per head for dense attention scores; retaining elementwise products avoids this cost.
For top-k attention with exchangeable tail scores, exact or conditional-mean tail-mass estimates are unbiased and minimum-MSE, unlike conditionally biased tail dropping.
Clustering queries or agents selects keys through centroids, reducing per-head score computation from N² to Nk.
Compiled models match reference models with all keys, support standard post-training quantization, and show improved approximation from tail-mass estimation on the reported models.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces attention score computation via clustering and tail-mass estimation; fits efficient attention.
papers.title: Transformers as Generic Deep Neural Networks: Exact Compilation, the Cost of Removing Activation-Activation Products, and Multi-Agent Attention Clustering
papers.tldr: Transformers can be compiled exactly into generic neural-network operations, while clustered top-k attention reduces computation and principled tail-mass estimation improves approximation over tail dropping.

papers.abstract: Safe robotic task planning requires planners that can reliably achieve task goals while satisfying safety constraints. Classical planners search over explicit symbolic task representations and can provide formal guarantees with respect to encoded safety constraints, but require rigid input formats. Their computational cost also increases rapidly with the search space. In contrast, large language models (LLMs) offer flexible task interfaces and strong generalization capabilities, but they are large, power-hungry, and pre-trained with little robot-specific safety data and knowledge. Thus, they can be difficult to deploy locally on robotic systems with limited resources. To address these limitations, we present SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic compression and fine-tuning framework for training foundation-model-based robotic task planners with Small size, Low power demand, and Safety awareness. The framework first constructs a safety-aware dataset using classical planners, an advanced teacher LLM, and formal verifiers, followed by two training stages: supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning guided by a verification-based reward machine to enforce safety alignment. We evaluate SLoSa across four Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) domains, two household simulation environments, local edge platforms, and a desktop robotic arm. Across the PDDL tasks, verifier-guided post-training raises the success rate of compact 4B-14B planners to 70.5-76.0%, while INT4 deployment on a Jetson Orin requires 17.85-26.41 W of average power. Results in household simulators and on the physical robot further demonstrate the applicability of SLoSa across diverse robotic task settings.
authors: Weizhe Xu, Jialiang Fan, Essien Taylor, Zijun Wang, Russell Joseph, Fanxin Kong
bullets: Addresses the deployment and safety limitations of large language models and the rigidity and computational cost of classical planners.
Builds a safety-aware dataset from classical planners, a teacher LLM, and formal verifiers.
Uses supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning guided by a verification-based reward machine.
Evaluated across PDDL domains, household simulators, edge platforms, and a desktop robotic arm.
Compact 4B–14B planners achieve 70.5–76.0% success on PDDL tasks; INT4 deployment on Jetson Orin uses 17.85–26.41 W average power.
papers.selection_reason: Safety-aligned compact LLM planners for robotic task planning with edge deployment, relevant to embodied AI and efficient AI.
papers.title: SLoSa: Small, Low-Power, and Safe Foundation Models for Robotic Task Planning
papers.tldr: SLoSa trains compact, low-power robotic task planners that combine language-model flexibility with symbolic safety verification for local deployment.

papers.abstract: NVIDIA tensor cores have supported 2:4 semi-structured sparsity since Ampere, and the pattern composes with quantization. When the two are combined, the practical question is which step to take next: from a given precision, add 2:4 sparsity or drop to the next lower precision? We compare the two at equal bits, with sparsity metadata counted, and at equal nominal tensor-core tiers, over all six GEMM operands of a transformer layer, with kernels measured on three GPU generations and online pruning and quantization included. Our results show that as long as a lower precision is available, adding 2:4 is the worse step, both less accurate and slower, because the energy that 2:4 discards from each group of four along the hardware-forced axis does not shrink with bits, while quantization error does. Once quantization reaches the lowest precision the hardware supports, 2:4 still speeds up linear layers by 1.3--1.7\x{}, and on an H100 a retrained 2:4 model served in FP8 by vLLM reaches 27\% higher prefill throughput than the dense FP8 model, with GSM8K accuracy on par. Its quality has to be won back by retraining, however, which restores perplexity long before reasoning; on Blackwell, whose sparse FP4 uses a pairwise 4:8 pattern, the loss is larger and our retraining budget did not recover it.
bullets: The study compares 2:4 sparsity and lower-bit quantization at equal bits and nominal tensor-core tiers, counting sparsity metadata.
It evaluates all six GEMM operands in transformer layers across three GPU generations, including online pruning and quantization overheads.
Adding 2:4 sparsity is both less accurate and slower than lowering precision when another precision level is available.
At minimum supported precision, 2:4 sparsity speeds up linear layers by 1.3–1.7×; on H100, retrained sparse FP8 reaches 27% higher prefill throughput with GSM8K accuracy on par with dense FP8.
Retraining recovers perplexity before reasoning quality; the loss is larger for Blackwell’s pairwise 4:8 sparse FP4 and was not recovered within the reported retraining budget.
papers.selection_reason: Compares 2:4 sparsity and quantization for efficient LLM inference; fits Efficient AI.
papers.title: Is 2:4 Sparsity Still Worth It? Semi-Structured Sparsity versus Quantization in LLM Inference
papers.tldr: When lower precision is available, quantization is generally preferable to adding 2:4 sparsity; sparsity becomes useful mainly at the hardware’s minimum precision.

papers.abstract: Selecting intermediate features from a frozen diffusion model for discriminative tasks is non-trivial because the useful signal is distributed across the denoising trajectory, network depth, and channels. In practice, this requires choosing a timestep, a block, and a channel subset. Existing methods either fix these choices by hand or optimize only a few extraction hyperparameters, most often the timestep, then reuse the same rule across inputs and budgets. We introduce Policy-Mask, a budget-conditioned policy trained on the downstream objective that jointly selects all three under a prescribed channel budget. Without normalization, the channel-score contribution grows with the number of selected channels and dominates the timestep and block updates. We normalize it by subset cardinality, keeping the three policy heads on comparable scales and stabilizing joint training. At matched budgets, Policy-Mask improves over fixed extraction and feature-filter baselines across segmentation, classification, and semantic correspondence, reaching 38.9 mIoU on ADE20K, 75.4% top-1 on CIFAR-100 at 128 dimensions, and 76.3 PCK@0.1 on SPair-71k. Component-wise ablations show that block selection materially affects downstream accuracy, and the highest recorded channel-budget score occurs at 256 retained channels, identifying a practical operating point for compact diffusion representations. We further adapt Policy-Mask to diffusion transformers, including PixArt-$\Sigma$ and SD3.5 MMDiT, by replacing U-Net channels with image-token hidden dimensions.
authors: Ivan Listopadov, Maksim Nakhodnov, Aibek Alanov
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of extracting task-relevant features distributed across diffusion trajectories, depths, and channels.
Trains three coordinated policy heads under a prescribed channel budget, with channel-score normalization to stabilize joint optimization.
Improves over fixed-extraction and feature-filter baselines across segmentation, classification, and semantic correspondence.
Reports 38.9 mIoU on ADE20K, 75.4% top-1 on CIFAR-100 at 128 dimensions, and 76.3 PCK@0.1 on SPair-71k.
Finds block selection materially affects accuracy; 256 retained channels is the highest-scoring recorded budget, and the approach extends to diffusion transformers.
papers.selection_reason: Budget-aware selection of diffusion features for discriminative tasks; fits efficient feature/token selection under resource constraints.
papers.title: Policy-Mask: Budget-Aware Adaptation of Diffusion Features to Discriminative Tasks
papers.tldr: Policy-Mask learns a budget-aware policy to jointly select diffusion timesteps, network blocks, and channels for compact discriminative representations.

papers.abstract: The weights of a trained network do not have uniform sensitivity to model accuracy: the 1% most sensitive weights carry about a fifth of the damage a bit flip can do. This distribution decides the bit-flip tolerance of a model, the fraction of weights a code must cover and the bits each weight needs; existing schemes work with the distribution training leaves. We show that we can systematically modulate or alter the weight sensitivity distribution of a trained model, thereby shifting weights from one sensitivity bin to another. The sensitivity of a stored weight is the product of its gradient and the step a flip takes in the storage format, and LEAN adds a composite regularizer on both factors, a range term that bounds the flip step and a tail term that lowers the gradient of the most sensitive weights, with one coefficient {\lambda} setting how far the distribution moves. Ten epochs with the term, as a fine-tune or as the last epochs of training, shrink the sensitive tail 5 to 13 times on nine vision models (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, VGG-16 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet) within 0.5 points of accuracy; real flips confirm that the reshaped weights do less damage, a plain gradient-norm penalty does not reproduce the effect, and a preliminary extension to three small language models shows the same tail shaping. With a BCH code over 1% of the weights the model then survives 300 progressive bit-search flips in every training seed and 500 in two of three, where three of four published defenses with the same code fail by 300 and WCAT falls to 75% at 500. The reshaped distribution also cuts the parity for a fixed guarantee 3.7 times and makes a sensitivity-ordered 8/6/4/3-bit format affordable, which stores ImageNet ResNet-50 at a 3.29-bit weight payload, 2.4 times smaller than INT8, above the accuracy of LSQ at 3 bits.
bullets: Targets the uneven sensitivity of stored weights, where a small fraction can cause disproportionate bit-flip damage.
Adds a composite regularizer that limits storage-format flip steps and reduces gradients among the most sensitive weights; a single coefficient controls the reshaping strength.
Across nine vision models, ten epochs reduced the sensitive tail by 5–13× while staying within 0.5 accuracy points; real bit flips confirmed lower damage.
With BCH protection over 1% of weights, models survived hundreds of progressive bit-search flips, and the reshaped distribution reduced parity requirements by 3.7×.
Supports sensitivity-ordered mixed-precision storage, achieving a 3.29-bit weight payload for ImageNet ResNet-50 and preliminary tail shaping in three small language models.
papers.selection_reason: Reshapes weight sensitivity for error tolerance and reduced bit-width storage, reducing model memory and enabling efficient deployment.
papers.title: LEAN: Loss-Engineered Modulation of the Model Weight-Sensitivity Distribution for Efficient, Error-Tolerant Neural Networks
papers.tldr: LEAN reshapes neural-network weight sensitivities during training, substantially improving bit-flip tolerance and enabling lower-overhead error protection and storage.

papers.abstract: Progress on foundation model pretraining is gated by who can afford a trial, and relational pretraining is no exception. Recipes are developed inside individual labs, reported under private protocols, and do not accumulate. Speedrun leaderboards remove that barrier by decentralizing the search rather than the training run. The problem is fixed, the stack is open, entries are ranked by wall-clock time to a quality target, and one GPU is enough to hold the record. We introduce modded-nanoRT, the first such leaderboard for Relational Transformers. Which database to hold out decides whether the benchmark can resolve improvements at all, so we fix it by calibration, ranking six candidates by how sharply a 45-minute learning curve separates improvement from seed noise. We open the leaderboard with typed trilinear attention, a relational operator that conditions attention scores and values on the foreign key traversed, together with Muon and SIGReg. The recipe reaches the target in 305.63 seconds on one NVIDIA H200, 8.11x faster than the reference implementation, and wins 13 of 15 pairs outside the development database. We will release the benchmark, its frozen artifacts, and the record runs. Our code is available at https://github.com/kunumi/nanoRT.
authors: Gabriel Wedson Mendon\c{c}a de Souza Veloso, Luan Borges Teodoro Reis Sena, Denis Oliveira Correa, Francisco Galuppo Azevedo
bullets: Addresses the lack of shared, affordable protocols for comparing relational pretraining recipes.
Calibrates and fixes the held-out database by ranking six candidates for sensitivity to improvement versus seed noise.
Uses typed trilinear attention with Muon and SIGReg in the opening recipe.
Wins 13 of 15 pairwise comparisons outside the development database.
Releases the benchmark, frozen artifacts, and record runs; code is publicly available.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a speedrunning leaderboard for relational foundation model pretraining to improve training efficiency and speed.
papers.title: Speedrunning Relational Foundation Model Pretraining
papers.tldr: modded-nanoRT introduces an open, one-GPU speedrun leaderboard for relational foundation-model pretraining and reaches its target in 305.63 seconds, 8.11× faster than the reference.

papers.abstract: Automated judges of clinical artificial intelligence (AI) outputs are necessary, but large language model (LLM) judges are costly and slow at scale. We compared Jev, a decision language model that returns structured judgments, with frontier and open-weight LLM judges in four use cases. On 118 pediatric answers, Jev's agreement with physicians' ordinal quality ratings (Gwet's AC2 0.50; expected score 0.53) matched or exceeded that of seven of 12 LLM judges, including frontier models, Claude Opus 5.5 (0.49) and GPT-6 (0.38). On physician-graded binary HealthBench criteria, Jev matched or exceeded four of six LLM judges. On MedHELM's open-ended tasks, Jev's agreement with a three-LLM jury approached or exceeded the jurors' internal agreement. On HealthBench Professional, Jev matched the benchmark's reference judge, GPT-5.4, on 91% of criteria (other judges, 91-93%). Frontier judges cost 73-294 times more than Jev and took 7-57 times longer. Jev may enable efficient clinical AI evaluation at scale.
authors: Rotem Gershon, Seffi Cohen, Dean Ariel, Havatzelet Bilavsky-Yarden, Amiel Sberro, Shai Yitzhaki, Osnat Tausky, Naama Golan, Maayan Rabinovitch, Ariel Avraham Hasidim, Itay Arianu, Maya Dagan, Ran Balicer, Noa Dagan
bullets: Addresses the high cost and latency of LLM-based clinical AI evaluation.
Compared Jev with frontier and open-weight LLM judges across four clinical evaluation settings.
Jev matched or exceeded several LLM judges on physician-aligned ordinal and binary assessments.
Its agreement with a multi-LLM jury on open-ended tasks was comparable to the jury’s internal agreement.
Frontier judges cost 73–294× more and took 7–57× longer than Jev; findings support scalable evaluation, with scope limited to the tested use cases.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a decision language model (Jev) as an affordable and rapid alternative to LLM judges, focusing on cost efficiency.
papers.title: Decision language models as affordable and rapid alternatives to LLM judges of clinical generative AI
papers.tldr: Jev, a structured decision language model, can evaluate clinical AI outputs with agreement comparable to many LLM judges while being substantially cheaper and faster.

papers.abstract: Aggressive low-state weight quantization can substantially reduce neural-network representational flexibility, making predictive performance difficult to preserve when only a few discrete weight states are available. We investigate this regime for Transformer-based electricity-load forecasting using 3-, 5-, 7-, and 16-state weight quantization across feed-forward-only and attention-plus-feed-forward quantization. Two tasks predict either the next hour or the next 24 hours from the preceding 48 hours across two co-primary electricity-consumption datasets. Direct post-training quantization (PTQ) increased mean normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) relative to full precision by 6.25 and 7.04 percentage points in Datasets A and B, whereas quantization-aware fine-tuning (QAT-FT) recovered approximately 90.2% and 94.5% of these penalties. Quantization-aware training from random initialization (Scratch-QAT) also produced competitive low-state solutions, with particularly favorable behavior at three states. We further introduce accumulated-update thresholding, which accumulates optimizer-proposed weight changes before commitment. Relative to paired Scratch-QAT controls, this reduced committed shadow-weight updates by approximately 99.7% and discrete state transitions by approximately 77--80%, while mean NRMSE changed by only +0.042 and +0.197 percentage points. These results show that useful Transformer forecasting can be retained under highly discrete weight representations while strongly suppressing target-state activity, supporting a prospective route toward compact, low-activity edge forecasting using multilevel synaptic devices.
authors: Muhammad Sabbir Alam, Harindra Sandun Mavikumbure, Victor Cobilean, Milos Manic, Jayasimha Atulasimha
bullets: Studies 3-, 5-, 7-, and 16-state weight quantization for next-hour and next-24-hour forecasting from the previous 48 hours.
Direct post-training quantization worsened mean NRMSE, while quantization-aware fine-tuning recovered about 90.2%–94.5% of the added error.
Quantization-aware training from scratch produced competitive low-state models, with particularly favorable behavior at three states.
Accumulated-update thresholding reduced shadow-weight updates by about 99.7% and discrete state transitions by about 77–80%, with minimal NRMSE change.
Results support compact, low-activity edge forecasting with highly discrete or multilevel synaptic devices.
papers.selection_reason: Extreme low-state weight quantization for Transformers targets memory-efficient edge inference; relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Extreme Low-State Quantized Transformer for Electricity-Load Forecasting
papers.tldr: Transformer electricity-load forecasting remains effective with extremely low-state weights, especially when quantization-aware training and accumulated-update thresholding are used.

papers.abstract: Non-uniform allocation can improve post-training pruning of large language models, yet quality can still degrade sharply at high sparsity. To control degradation as sparsity increases, we introduce LADDER (Layer-Wise Allocation via Damage-Driven Evaluation and Refinement), which allocates sparsity incrementally. At each step, it evaluates pruning an additional fraction of weights from each eligible layer and commits the layer update that causes the least end-to-end degradation per removed parameter. This process produces non-uniform sparsity profiles and exactly nested masks across multiple budgets. We evaluate LADDER on five OPT, Llama, and Qwen models across 10-90% sparsity, using SparseGPT as its candidate-generation backend and comparing against uniform and adaptive allocation baselines. Results reveal a clear operating-regime trade-off: LADDER is comparable or slightly weaker at benign sparsity but becomes substantially more robust from 70% onward. This high-sparsity advantage largely persists after posterior distillation across four of five models and translates into improved retention of aggregate zero-shot accuracy.
authors: Nicol\'as Mauricio Cuadrado \'Avila, Ivo Gollini Navarrete, Martin Tak\'a\v{c}, Samuel Horv\'ath
bullets: Targets sharp quality degradation in large language models under aggressive post-training pruning.
Evaluates candidate pruning steps per layer and selects the update with the smallest end-to-end degradation per removed parameter.
Produces non-uniform sparsity profiles and exactly nested masks across multiple sparsity budgets.
Across OPT, Llama, and Qwen models, its main advantage emerges at 70% sparsity and above.
The high-sparsity benefit generally persists after posterior distillation, though performance is comparable or slightly weaker at benign sparsity.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces incremental sparsity allocation for LLM post-training pruning, directly reducing model compute and memory footprint.
papers.title: Building a Nested LADDER for LLM Unstructured Post-Training Pruning
papers.tldr: LADDER incrementally allocates layer-wise sparsity to create nested pruning masks, improving robustness and zero-shot accuracy retention at high sparsity.

papers.abstract: LLM-driven evolutionary search is a promising paradigm for scientific discovery, but existing methods remain costly and slow, often applying expensive reasoning uniformly while underusing evidence from failed, redundant, and saturated trials. We introduce Speculative Evolution (SpecEvo), a multi-LLM framework that coordinates lightweight and frontier models through continual consolidation of search evidence. Lightweight models power both parallel Speculators, which generate and refine candidate programs, and an Advisor, which distills accumulated successes, failures, and saturated directions into persistent guidance for subsequent exploration.
