At sparse checkpoints, a frontier-model Navigator inspects the evolving population and intervenes through synthesis, surgical refinement, or reframing according to search stagnation. This speculate-then-consolidate workflow delegates routine exploration and evidence consolidation to inexpensive models while reserving frontier reasoning for strategic interventions whose benefits extend across many subsequent low-cost evaluations. Across 176 tasks spanning four scientific and algorithmic discovery domains, SpecEvo matches or outperforms frontier-model baselines while reducing API cost by up to 80%, achieves up to 1.5x greater evaluation efficiency than cost-efficient baselines on equation discovery, and improves over the strongest CO-Bench baseline by 3.8%. These results support trajectory-conditioned model coordination as an effective approach to cost-efficient scientific discovery.
authors: Ha Minh Hieu, Tongyao Zhu, Do Xuan Long, Min-Yen Kan
bullets: Targets the high cost and slow speed of existing LLM-based evolutionary search, which often treats all reasoning as equally expensive.
Uses lightweight Speculators to generate and refine candidate programs and an Advisor to consolidate successes, failures, and saturated directions into persistent guidance.
Deploys a frontier-model Navigator only at sparse checkpoints for synthesis, surgical refinement, or reframing when search stagnates.
Across 176 tasks in four scientific and algorithmic domains, matches or outperforms frontier-model baselines while reducing API cost by up to 80%.
Reports up to 1.5× higher evaluation efficiency than cost-efficient baselines on equation discovery and a 3.8% improvement over the strongest CO-Bench baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a cost-efficient multi-LLM framework (SpecEvo) for scientific discovery, focusing on reducing API costs and improving evaluation efficiency.
papers.title: SpecEvo: Speculative Evolution with Large Language Models for Cost-Efficient Scientific Discovery
papers.tldr: SpecEvo makes LLM-driven scientific discovery more cost-efficient by combining lightweight models for routine evolutionary search with occasional frontier-model guidance.

papers.abstract: Disaggregated \textsc{LLM} serving separates prefill and decode across node pools, placing a network fabric between \textsc{KV}-cache computation and consumption. This breaks a key assumption of classical cache policies: a miss no longer incurs only local recomputation, but also network transfer to the decode node. Likewise, admitting a block to the global cache requires an additional transfer, so poor retention decisions waste both memory and bandwidth. We present \textbf{KVLearn}, a learning-based framework for cost-aware \textsc{KV}-cache retention in disaggregated serving. KVLearn includes: (i) a lightweight Prefix Reuse Predictor (\textsc{PRP}) that estimates reuse probability from structural and temporal prefix features without modifying model weights; (ii) a Cost-Aware Retention Score (\textsc{CARS}) that converts reuse probability into keep/admit decisions using recomputation, transfer, and storage costs; and (iii) an Adaptive Threshold Controller (\textsc{ATC}) that adjusts admission thresholds online from observed hit rates and memory pressure. We integrate KVLearn into a globally disaggregated serving topology and evaluate it on text and multimodal workloads, including large image/video-derived \textsc{KV} blocks with heterogeneous reuse patterns. KVLearn reduces end-to-end time-to-first-token by up to 56% versus No-Cache, 38% versus LRU-Pool, and 33% versus Mooncake-style baselines, while cutting inter-node \textsc{KV} transfer volume by up to 53% versus LRU-Pool. On MM-Session, throughput remains within ${\sim}5%$ of oracle. Code is available at https://github.com/FastLM/KVLearn.
authors: Dong Liu, Yanxuan Yu, Eric Jiang, Shu Wang, Ying Nian Wu
bullets: Disaggregation makes cache misses costly because they require both recomputation and network transfer; cache admission also consumes bandwidth.
A lightweight Prefix Reuse Predictor estimates reuse from structural and temporal prefix features without changing model weights.
The Cost-Aware Retention Score balances reuse probability against recomputation, transfer, and storage costs.
An Adaptive Threshold Controller updates admission thresholds online using hit rates and memory pressure.
KVLearn reduces time-to-first-token by up to 56% versus No-Cache and cuts inter-node KV transfer by up to 53% versus LRU-Pool; throughput stays within ~5% of an oracle on MM-Session.
papers.selection_reason: Cost-aware KV-cache retention for LLM serving directly targets KV-cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: To Keep or Not to Keep: Learning KV Cache Retention in Disaggregated LLM Serving Systems
papers.tldr: KVLearn learns cost-aware KV-cache retention decisions for disaggregated LLM serving, reducing latency and inter-node KV traffic across text and multimodal workloads.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve strong robotic manipulation performance but incur high computational costs from processing long token sequences at every control step, limiting real-time deployment. Visual token pruning offers a direct solution, as visual patches dominate the input sequence and contain considerable redundancy. Existing approaches, however, either rely on indirect training-free heuristics, such as attention scores and motion thresholds, or require costly fine-tuning of the base VLA model. We introduce VLA-ACL (Action Consistency Learning), which learns a lightweight visual token pruning policy through action-level supervision while keeping the base VLA model entirely frozen. The training objective encourages actions produced from pruned visual contexts to remain consistent with the full-context teacher, with ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision. This directly ties token selection to its effect on the downstream control output. Experiments on LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks show that VLA-ACL prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens while retaining competitive performance, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5x inference speedup. These results establish a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods and demonstrate the value of action-level supervision for visual token selection. Code is available at https://github.com/du-owen/VLA-ACL.
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of processing redundant visual tokens during robotic control.
Trains a lightweight pruning policy with action-level consistency supervision, using full-context predictions as a teacher and ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision.
Keeps the base VLA model completely frozen, avoiding costly end-to-end fine-tuning.
On LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks, prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5× inference speedup.
Demonstrates a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces VLA-ACL, a method for efficient visual token pruning in VLA models using action-level supervision without fine-tuning the base model.
papers.title: VLA-ACL: Action-Consistent Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: VLA-ACL efficiently prunes visual tokens in frozen vision-language-action models by learning which tokens preserve the model’s control actions.

papers.abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) can accelerate language-model decoding by drafting several tokens and verifying them in a single target-model pass. However, the best speculation horizon changes with context: longer drafts offer greater amortization when reliable, but can waste compute on suffixes discarded after a rejection. Unlike autoregressive drafting, where a stopping rule can decide token by token, MTP must fix the horizon before drafting, as all heads fire in the same forward pass. We therefore formulate horizon selection as an online control problem, using verification feedback to learn how far the draft can be trusted in each context, and introduce Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction (AMTP): a lightweight controller that requires no retraining and leaves the exact verifier unchanged. To guide horizon selection, we characterize the expected number of tokens committed at each horizon via acceptance survival, the probability that a draft prefix is fully accepted. Before each round, AMTP predicts how far the draft is likely to survive and picks the horizon with the highest expected tokens per second, learning freely from every verification pass. Theoretically, we show that any online learner's prediction error translates into throughput regret against the best horizon for each context, and in turn into a bound on wall-clock completion time. With online gradient descent, this regret is sublinear. Across five draft-target pairings built on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with Medusa heads, Meta's MTP models, and Qwen3-4B-Inst-2507-MTP, evaluated on AIME 2025 and GSM8K, AMTP decodes up to 4.1x faster than standard decoding and matches or outperforms the fixed window in 8 of 10 settings, with throughput gains of up to 10%.
authors: Emile Anand, Mohammed Rehan Parwani, Xinyuan Cao
bullets: MTP faces a context-dependent trade-off: longer drafts can improve amortization but waste compute when rejected.
AMTP treats horizon selection as online control and predicts draft-prefix survival before each decoding round.
It chooses the horizon with the highest expected tokens per second using feedback from every verification pass.
Theoretical analysis links horizon-prediction error to throughput regret and wall-clock completion time; online gradient descent gives sublinear regret.
Across 10 draft-target settings on AIME 2025 and GSM8K, AMTP reaches up to 4.1× faster decoding and matches or exceeds fixed-window MTP in 8 settings, with up to 10% throughput gains.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive horizon selection for multi-token speculative decoding directly reduces LLM inference latency and improves throughput, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction: How far should we go?
papers.tldr: AMTP adaptively selects the multi-token speculation horizon from verification feedback, accelerating decoding without retraining or changing the verifier.

papers.abstract: Despite the success of video world models, extending them to multiple agents is difficult because it requires generating several agent-specific video streams that are consistent in time and between agents. To address this gap, we introduce OverSeer, a multi-agent world model that augments egocentric agent views with auxiliary camera views. We suggest that, by fixing the auxiliary views in space, they act as a proxy for a world-centric representation: Unlike the agents' views, which can change entirely due to a simple change in agent position, changes in the auxiliary views directly map to localized changes in the world state. We show that these fixed views substantially help the model to maintain consistency. We also show that, due to their redundant and semi-static nature, the auxiliary views can be efficiently compressed with a delta-VAE that encodes only the changes relative to a static reference image, reducing the number of tokens required to process them. Experiments in Minecraft and Doom demonstrate improved world and agent consistency, with qualitative results on real-world multi-camera captures indicating that the approach is not tied to game engines. Our compression analysis further shows that delta-VAE substantially reduces the computational overhead of auxiliary-view generation. We conclude that these fixed views provide a simple and efficient way to improve multi-agent world models.
authors: Runjia Li, Kam Woh Ng, Minghao Chen, Junlin Han, Jianyuan Wang, Zhaochong An, Juan-Manuel Perez-Rua, Andrea Vedaldi, Shikun Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of generating multiple temporally and cross-agent-consistent video streams.
Augments egocentric agent views with spatially fixed auxiliary cameras as a proxy for world-centric state.
Uses a delta-VAE to encode only changes from static reference images, reducing auxiliary-view token and computation costs.
Experiments in Minecraft and Doom show improved world and agent consistency; qualitative real-world multi-camera results suggest broader applicability.
Scope: demonstrated primarily in game environments, with real-world evidence limited to qualitative results.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-agent video world model with fixed auxiliary views and delta-VAE compression; fits video world models and efficient auxiliary-view processing.
papers.title: OverSeer: Multi-Agent World Models Beyond What Agents See
papers.tldr: OverSeer improves multi-agent world models by adding compressed fixed-camera views that help maintain consistency across agents and time.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses the weights of a trained model with limited compute and data. Down to 4 bits it is near-lossless, but at 2 bits scalar PTQ configurations fall to chance-level accuracy. We study three choices usually treated as implementation details that matter little at 4 bits but decide 2-bit quality: the quantization representation, the calibration data, and the recovery fine-tuning data, across six dense and mixture-of experts models (ranging from $3.8$ to $32$B parameters). Representation is the largest factor and vector codebooks restore usable models where scalar PTQ pipelines collapse. Most of the remaining loss in accuracy is on \emph{generative} tasks, and the amount of performance drop is model-dependent. Furthermore, at a short recovery budget, calibration and recovery data are coupled. The best recovery data depends on the calibration data, so the two must be chosen jointly. The resulting recipe involves a vector codebook representation, a small task-aligned calibration mixture, and an inexpensive codebook-only recovery stage. Including codebooks, it uses about $2.3$ effective bits per weight and retains $89$ to $97\%$ of full-precision question-answering (QA) accuracy where scalar PTQ is at chance, and, including recovery, uses $1.4$ to $30\times$ less compute than the strongest quantization-aware-training (QAT) baseline.
authors: Rhea Sanjay Sukthanker, Riccardo Grazzi, James Hensman, Pashmina Cameron
bullets: At 2 bits, scalar PTQ can collapse to chance-level accuracy, making representation, calibration data, and recovery data critical.
Vector codebook representations are the most important factor for restoring usable low-bit models.
Calibration and recovery data interact under limited recovery budgets and should be selected jointly, with task alignment.
Across six 3.8B–32B dense and mixture-of-experts models, the method retains 89–97% of full-precision QA accuracy using about 2.3 effective bits per weight.
Including recovery, it requires 1.4–30× less compute than the strongest QAT baseline; generative-task degradation remains model-dependent.
papers.selection_reason: Post-training quantization reduces model memory footprint, directly fitting memory-efficient inference under Efficient AI.
papers.title: Beyond 4 bits: Data-Centric Post-training Quantization and Recovery
papers.tldr: A data-centric 2-bit PTQ recipe using vector codebooks and jointly chosen calibration/recovery data preserves most QA accuracy at far lower compute than QAT.

papers.abstract: Smart glasses can help users understand their activities and surroundings, but small vision-language models must preserve useful evidence within limited computation. This is difficult because redundant frames consume the visual budget, while aggressive spatial compression can discard relevant details. Although gaze identifies the wearer's focus, the question may require evidence from the surrounding scene. To address these constraints, we propose GazeLens, which combines frame selection with gaze- and question-guided token reduction. First, HOG transitions and image sharpness select frames before visual encoding. For each selected frame, Gaussian pooling then forms gaze-focused and complementary summaries. Because their relevance depends on the question, a lightweight gate blends them into a primary token. Together with a global scene token, this retains both focused and contextual summaries within two tokens per frame. On StreamGaze, GazeLens achieves higher macro and micro accuracy than the evaluated full-grid and token-reduction baselines, with lower input-forward FLOPs than the shared-backbone token-reduction baselines.
authors: Trong-Thang Pham, Anh Nguyen, Hien Van Nguyen, Ngan Le
bullets: Addresses limited computation in smart-glasses VQA while preserving both gaze-focused evidence and surrounding context.
Selects frames using HOG transitions and image sharpness before visual encoding.
Uses Gaussian pooling to create gaze-focused and complementary summaries, then applies a lightweight question-guided gate.
Represents each selected frame with a blended primary token plus a global scene token.
On StreamGaze, outperforms evaluated full-grid and token-reduction baselines in macro and micro accuracy while using fewer input-forward FLOPs than shared-backbone token-reduction baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Gaze-driven adaptive token reduction for egocentric video QA; directly fits token pruning/eviction and video-language understanding.
papers.title: GazeLens for Efficient Egocentric Video Question Answering with Simple Gaze-Driven Adaptive Token Reduction
papers.tldr: GazeLens improves egocentric video question answering efficiency by selecting informative frames and compressing each into two question- and gaze-aware visual tokens.

papers.abstract: For efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs), methods of ultra-low-bit backbones reduce weight storage, memory traffic, and linear-layer execution cost, while multi-token prediction (MTP) methods reduce sequential decoding steps by predicting multiple future tokens in parallel. Although complementary, the direct combination of these methods cannot accelerate decoding at comparable quality: masked drafting lacks intermediate token input supplied in next-token training, while wider computation and causal key-value (KV) updates can offset the savings from fewer steps. To address these challenges, we propose BitMTP, an algorithm-system co-design framework for efficient MTP on ultra-low-bit LLM backbones. A joint next-token prediction and MTP objective equips a single model with both autoregressive (AR) generation and block-causal drafting. Confidence-only decoding, speculative-only decoding, and hybrid decoding provide different quality-throughput operating points without using separate draft and verifier models. Accepted-prefix alignment keeps the committed prefix, materialized causal KV boundary, and CUDA Graph replay state consistent for continued generation. BitMTP uses this contract to select width-specialized low-bit execution and reuse captured graphs over shared KV storage. On NVIDIA H20, BitMTP with hybrid decoding achieves five-task mean speedups of 2.2x on BitNet b1.58-2B and 2.1-2.4x on 1.7B-4B Bonsai models at comparable task quality. On RTX 3090 and Jetson Orin, it further achieves up to 2.0x in five-task mean throughput and 3.3x on MBPP+, respectively. These results demonstrate that BitMTP accelerates ultra-low-bit LLM generation across backbones, model sizes, and GPU types. The source code is released at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/BitMTP
authors: Ning Zhang, Shihao Wang, Jinrui Zhang, Chaodong Xiao, Lei Zhang
bullets: Combines joint autoregressive and block-causal training so one model supports both regular generation and multi-token drafting.
Offers confidence-only, speculative-only, and hybrid decoding without separate draft and verifier models.
Uses accepted-prefix alignment, shared KV storage, and width-specialized CUDA Graph execution to reduce decoding overhead.
Reports 2.1–2.4× speedups on selected Bonsai models and up to 3.3× throughput on Jetson Orin across evaluated tasks and hardware.
papers.selection_reason: Co-design for multi-token prediction on low-bit LLMs, reducing decoding steps and KV/memory overhead in LLM inference.
papers.title: BitMTP: When Multi-Token Prediction Meets Low-Bit Large Language Models
papers.tldr: BitMTP co-designs multi-token prediction with ultra-low-bit LLM execution to accelerate generation while maintaining comparable task quality.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model inference over long contexts is increasingly bottlenecked by the cost of attending to a growing Key-Value (KV) cache. Sparse attention reduces this cost by accessing only a fraction of the cache, but existing methods face a trade-off between deterministic retrieval, which captures high-scoring tokens but discards residual attention mass, and sampling, which improves coverage at the cost of higher variance. Hybrid methods combine top-$k$ retrieval with uniform sampling, yet still exhibit a substantial gap from dense attention at aggressive sparsity. We introduce \emph{Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA)}, a unified framework combining deterministic retrieval with score-guided sampling. SSA deterministically attends to high-scoring tokens while sampling the residual using proxy attention scores and correcting for their inclusion probabilities, thereby recovering attention mass beyond the retrieval set. SSA encompasses top-$k$, top-$p$, and hybrid top-$k$+sampling as special cases. Across RULER, LongBench, LOFT, and AIME, and five models ranging from 3B to 27B parameters, SSA consistently improves over the baselines at matched sparsity. On RULER-HARD with Ministral-3-8B, SSA improves accuracy over the strongest practical baseline from 81.8\% to 84.2\% at 32K and from 63.8\% to 69.3\% at 128K under $50\times$ attention sparsity, recovering 94\% and 85\% of dense-attention performance, respectively. With optimized CUDA kernels, SSA achieves up to $2.96\times$ decode speedup over FlashInfer at 1M context, demonstrating that its accuracy gains translate into practical long-context inference acceleration. We open-source our code at https://github.com/skylight-org/SSA-Paper-Code.
authors: Sahil Joshi, Prithvi Dixit, Aryan Katiyar, Agniva Chowdhury, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Anshumali Shrivastava, Aditya Desai, Kumar Krishna Agrawal
bullets: Targets KV-cache attention costs for long-context LLM inference, where sparse methods lose attention mass or suffer sampling variance.
Combines deterministic selection of high-scoring tokens with score-guided sampling of residual tokens and inclusion-probability correction.
Generalizes top-k, top-p, and hybrid top-k-plus-sampling methods.
Improves matched-sparsity performance across four benchmarks and five models, including stronger RULER-HARD accuracy at 50× sparsity.
With optimized CUDA kernels, reaches up to 2.96× decode speedup over FlashInfer at 1M-token context.
papers.selection_reason: Stratified sparse attention improves long-context efficiency by combining retrieval and sampling, directly relevant to efficient attention and KV cache.
papers.title: Stratified Sparse Attention: Reducing the Sparse-to-Dense Gap at Extreme Sparsity
papers.tldr: Stratified Sparse Attention narrows the accuracy gap between sparse and dense attention at extreme sparsity while enabling faster long-context inference.

papers.abstract: Head-dimension compression can reduce the memory required by the key-value (KV) cache, but existing methods often reconstruct full-dimensional representations during inference, adding significant decoding FLOPs overhead. We formalize the design considerations for converting pretrained attention into a natively reduced-dimensional form that reduces both KV-cache storage and attention computation using a calibration set. Specifically, we consider reductions that (1) apply a shared projection to queries and keys so that they remain in a common reduced feature space, (2) derive this projection jointly from query and key activations to better preserve their interaction, and (3) are compatible with the pretrained RoPE transformation. To obtain a reconstruction-free realization of this reduction, we restrict it to coordinate selection and theoretically show that RoPE compatibility then holds if and only if complete rotary pairs are retained. Building on this characterization, we introduce RACE, a post-training method that selects rotary pairs using their joint query-key activation energy. We theoretically show that this criterion minimizes a separable, calibration-dependent upper bound on post-RoPE query-key product approximation error. The resulting reductions are folded into the model weights and require neither runtime reconstruction nor specialized kernels. Across three model families and different compression levels, RACE outperforms structured pruning and remains competitive with reconstruction-based methods on language-modeling, zero-shot, and long-context tasks. At 50% KV-cache retention and 256K context, RACE reduces total inference FLOPs by 47.8%, yielding 1.79x higher throughput, 43.2% lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and 28.1% lower allocated GPU memory in comparison to an uncompressed model.
authors: Irene Tenison, Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem, Daniel Karl I. Weidele, Nima Dehmamy, Dan Gutfreund
bullets: Targets head-dimension reduction while avoiding the decoding FLOPs overhead of reconstructing full-dimensional keys and values.
Uses a shared query-key projection derived from calibration activations and retains complete rotary pairs to preserve RoPE compatibility.
Selects rotary pairs by joint query-key activation energy, minimizing a separable upper bound on post-RoPE query-key approximation error.
The folded, post-training method requires no runtime reconstruction or specialized kernels and outperforms structured pruning across evaluated tasks.
At 50% KV-cache retention and 256K context, it reports 47.8% lower inference FLOPs, 1.79× higher throughput, 43.2% lower TTFT, and 28.1% lower allocated GPU memory versus an uncompressed model.
papers.selection_reason: RoPE-compatible KV-cache compression reduces memory and inference FLOPs, fitting efficient attention and cache efficiency.
papers.title: RACE: RoPE-Aligned Attention Compression Based on Query-Key Activation Energies
papers.tldr: RACE compresses attention heads by selecting RoPE-compatible rotary pairs using joint query-key activation energy, reducing KV-cache memory and inference computation without runtime reconstruction.

papers.abstract: A growing body of work proposes dynamic expert-skipping methods for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that adjust the number of experts activated per token during inference, aiming to preserve model quality while further reducing the number of active parameters. These methods have added calibrated importance scores, inter-expert similarity metrics, or learned per-token allocators in order to identify experts to skip. However, different calibration regimes, different reductions in the effective number of experts, and evaluation suites make comparisons difficult. We classify four representative prior methods into a unified taxonomy and benchmark them against a natural, simple baseline: statically reducing the number of experts $k$ (i.e., same reduced $k$ across all layers and tokens). We provide a fair comparison of these methods at matched expert-compute budget, on two modern MoEs (Gemma4-26B-A4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B) in a text-only setting and a contemporary vision-language model (Qwen3-VL) in a multimodal setting. Surprisingly, we find that the simple baseline is hard to outperform consistently across models, modalities, benchmarks, and calibration settings. The methods we benchmark often underperform the baseline and achieved gains, when present, are minor. We further find that the effective $k$ achieved (or optimized for) in calibration can diverge from the effective $k$ in testing, resulting in over- or under-estimating the compute at inference time. Based on these findings, we recommend a calibration-free per-modality static $k$ reduction and validate this on a held-out model and modality. We further argue that a static control at matched measured compute is the baseline any dynamic skipping method must beat.
authors: Jakob Steimle, Thomas Elsken, Daniel Ehrhardt, Lukas Rinder, Daniel Cremers, Xi Wang
bullets: Unifies four dynamic expert-skipping methods and compares them with using the same reduced expert count across layers and tokens.
Evaluates methods at matched measured expert-compute budgets across two text MoEs and one vision-language model.
The static baseline is difficult to consistently outperform across models, modalities, benchmarks, and calibration settings; observed gains are usually minor.
Calibration can produce an effective expert count that differs from testing, causing inference compute to be over- or underestimated.
Recommends calibration-free, per-modality static expert reduction and validates it on a held-out model and modality.
papers.selection_reason: Controlled comparison of dynamic expert skipping in modern MoE LLMs; relevant to efficient inference and LLM architecture.
papers.title: Don't Skip the Baseline: A Controlled Comparison of Dynamic Expert Skipping in MoEs
papers.tldr: A controlled study finds that simple static expert reduction is often as effective as dynamic MoE expert-skipping methods and should be the baseline for fair comparisons.

papers.abstract: Adapting Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) to medical imaging via LoRA has become standard practice, yet model selection is guided almost entirely by downstream task metrics, treating backbones with similar performance as interchangeable. We investigate whether equal performance implies equal internal representational shift. We analyse four ViT-B/16 backbones, DINOv3, SigLIP2, MerMED-FM, and BiomedCLIP, pre-trained with different objectives (self-distillation vs. contrastive vision-language) and on different data domains (natural vs. medical images). We adapt each to brain tumour segmentation and evaluate on six datasets covering both segmentation and Alzheimer's disease classification. Using attention divergence, weight-change analysis, and activation patching, we find that the four models converge to similar segmentation performance (mean Dice 78-81%) through markedly different internal dynamics, yet diverge in cross-task transfer: segmentation adaptation improves Alzheimer's disease classification for DINOv3 but degrades it for the other three backbones. We reveal a dissociation between modification magnitude and causal importance: the most heavily modified layers are not the causally relevant ones, with early-to-mid layers identified as sufficient for segmentation recovery. Restricting LoRA to these layers matches or approaches full-layer segmentation while reducing classification degradation in the three affected backbones, providing a mechanistically grounded strategy that is more parameter-efficient and more robust than standard full-layer adaptation.
authors: Cecilia Diana-Albelda, Fiona Kekwick, Raghav Mehta, Aleksandra Kulbaka, Paul M. Matthews, Jesus Bescos, \'Alvaro Garc\'ia-Mart\'in, Wenjia Bai, Bernhard Kainz
bullets: Four ViT-B/16 backbones reached comparable segmentation performance despite distinct representational shifts.
Segmentation adaptation improved Alzheimer’s classification for DINOv3 but harmed it for the other three models.
Layer modification magnitude did not indicate causal importance; early-to-mid layers were sufficient for segmentation recovery.
Restricting LoRA to these layers matched or nearly matched full-layer segmentation while reducing cross-task degradation.
The findings support mechanism-aware model and layer selection rather than choosing backbones solely by task metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes layer-restricted LoRA adaptation that is more parameter-efficient, relevant to efficient adaptation of foundation models.
papers.title: Convergent Performance, Divergent Mechanisms in LoRA-Adapted Vision Foundation Models for Brain MRI
papers.tldr: LoRA-adapted vision backbones can achieve similar brain MRI segmentation performance through different internal changes, so targeting causally important early-to-mid layers improves transfer robustness and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Large language models can solve complex problems across a variety of subjects, such as mathematics and coding. For such complex analytical tasks, models with a long context perform better. Serving models with long context is currently mostly done on powerful systems with multiple GPUs, which are too expensive for most users. An alternative is local inference, or serving a model on a user's own machine, which removes per-token costs and rate limits, besides keeping sensitive data private and giving users full control over the models they run. The common understanding, however, is that local LLMs need compression (e.g., quantization) to run on a single GPU. In this paper, we set out to study the limitations that prevent serving long-context models for single users, besides the capacity issue. Rather than characterizing a single model on one GPU, we analyze how different models behave across several GPU generations. This lets us uncover not just individual bottlenecks but broader trends in where inefficiencies arise. Our analysis confirms that, as expected, self-attention dominates the runtime for long-context inference. More unexpectedly, our evaluation reveals that the current structure of self-attention leaves key GPU resources significantly underutilized, and the newest GPU is often the least well served. Many of these findings are fundamentally data management problems, from paging the KV cache to improving cache utilization and synchronization in the GPU, which is why we bring this study to the Data Systems community. To engage this community, we present our findings as a series of experimental observations and formulate recommendations for future work.
bullets: Local inference can reduce serving costs and rate limits while improving privacy and user control.
The study analyzes multiple models across several GPU generations rather than focusing on one model-device pair.
Self-attention dominates runtime for long-context inference.
Self-attention underutilizes important GPU resources, with newer GPUs often receiving less effective utilization.
Key challenges include KV-cache paging, cache utilization, and GPU synchronization; the paper offers observations and recommendations for future work.
papers.selection_reason: Analysis of long-context LLM inference bottlenecks with focus on self-attention and KV-cache data management.
papers.title: Local Inference of LLMs on Long Contexts: A Data Systems Perspective
papers.tldr: Long-context LLM inference on a single local GPU is constrained not only by memory capacity but also by substantial self-attention and data-management inefficiencies.

papers.abstract: Token merging is an effective approach to reducing KV-cache memory consumption in autoregressive video generation by clustering temporally redundant tokens and retaining only a small set of representatives. Existing methods, however, typically apply a uniform merging ratio across all attention layers and heads. We observe that different layers and heads exhibit substantially different yet jointly correlated sensitivities to token merging, and that these sensitivity patterns remain consistent across prompts. Based on this observation, we introduce CALM, a Calibrated Allocation for Layer-Head Merging that uses offline calibration to improve online cache compression. Exhaustively evaluating all possible layer-head allocations is prohibitively expensive. To enable efficient calibration, we show that attention-output error strongly correlates with end-to-end video quality and can therefore serve as a lightweight proxy for allocation risk assessment. We evaluate different allocation strategies using this proxy and construct a fixed layer-head risk map offline. Given a cache budget at inference time, CALM uses dynamic programming to determine the best allocation of merging ratios. Experiments across three different autoregressive video models demonstrate that CALM consistently outperforms uniform token merging under the same memory budget, by reducing the LPIPS to original videos by around 21% with higher video-quality scores.
authors: Zhen Wang, Ning Lai, Qingtao Yu
bullets: Uniform token-merging ratios overlook substantial, prompt-consistent sensitivity differences across attention layers and heads.
CALM uses attention-output error as a lightweight proxy for end-to-end video-quality risk during offline calibration.
It builds a fixed layer-head risk map, then selects merging ratios dynamically for a given cache budget.
Across three autoregressive video models, CALM outperforms uniform merging, reducing LPIPS to original videos by around 21% while achieving higher video-quality scores.
papers.selection_reason: Offline-calibrated layer-head token merging for KV-cache compression in autoregressive video generation.
papers.title: Offline Makes Online Better: Calibrated Cache Compression for Video Generation
papers.tldr: CALM uses offline layer-head sensitivity calibration and dynamic programming to allocate token merging, improving autoregressive video-generation quality at the same KV-cache budget.

papers.abstract: Telecom language models must combine broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband services, access technologies, and operational diagnostics while remaining practical to deploy as a single model. We present an end-to-end framework that builds source-grounded synthetic training data from structured networking taxonomies and expert graphs, materializes 212,559 routed training records across fourteen networking routes, trains six frozen specialist LoRA teachers over one shared continued-pretrained backbone, and consolidates their behavior into one deployable student adapter using Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation (RSOD). In RSOD, the committed student generates each trajectory, the route-assigned specialist teacher-forces the exact native token sequence, compact teacher hidden states are reconstructed through the shared frozen output head, and only the student LoRA is updated. A controlled reconstruction validation shows mean absolute logit error of 7.26 x 10^-6 with 100% top-1 agreement between native and reconstructed teacher logits. On four RTX 6000 Ada GPUs, the completed 2,000-step run produced 16,000 trajectories with zero observed student-version or token- ID mismatches. Under the primary route-conditioned evaluation over 2,850 held-out questions, the raw Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model scores 12.8661/25 micro (13.0172/25 macro), the combined routed six-teacher system scores 21.7641/25 micro, and the consolidated RSOD student, released as Llama-CalixCLM v1, reaches 21.7112/25 micro (21.8006/25 macro) on the same five dimension LLM-judge rubric. Under a separate neutral deployment-like prompt, the same student reaches 20.0028/25 micro (20.0778/25 macro). The consolidated student remains within 0.0529 micro-score points of the combined routed-teacher system while retaining a numerically validated and auditable train-serve execution path.
authors: Anil Srirangapatna Nagesh, Nitin Gupta, Anuj Taneja, Vivek Singh, Shane Eleniak, Theo Zhao, Moulidharan N, Shashank Keshetty
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband, access technologies, and diagnostics in a single practical model.
Builds source-grounded synthetic data from networking taxonomies and expert graphs, yielding 212,559 routed records across 14 networking routes.
Uses Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation: the student generates trajectories, route-specific teachers provide token-level supervision, and only the student LoRA is updated.
Teacher-logit reconstruction achieved 7.26 × 10^-6 mean absolute error and 100% top-1 agreement; the completed run reported zero student-version or token-ID mismatches.
On 2,850 held-out questions, Llama-CalixCLM v1 scored 21.7112/25 micro versus 21.7641/25 for the combined routed teachers and 12.8661/25 for the base model.
papers.selection_reason: End-to-end framework for domain-specialist post-training and distillation of deployable telecom LLMs.
papers.title: Building Telecom Language Models with RSOD: Domain Data, Specialist Post-Training, Memory-Conscious Distillation, and Networking Evaluation
papers.tldr: RSOD consolidates six telecom-specialist LoRA teachers into one deployable student while preserving nearly all of the routed system’s evaluated performance.

papers.abstract: The Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3) has achieved significant progress in Promptable Concept Segmentation (PCS) by processing short noun phrases to generate segmentation masks with unique instance identifiers. While SAM3 excels at single-concept segmentation, it falls short in complex, real-world environments where multiple concepts must be segmented simultaneously. In particular, SAM3 typically fails to simultaneously process concepts with semantic overlap, leading to semantic misclassifications and redundant mask predictions. Moreover, as the number of concepts increases, the independent inference paradigm introduces prohibitive inference latency. To address these limitations, we propose the Dense Competitive Representations SAM (DCR-SAM) framework. By decoupling cross-modal interactions, the proposed method alleviates the inference latency. To resolve semantic misclassifications, DCR-SAM dynamically aligns textual concepts with visual representations and incorporates a dense competition head to enforce explicit inter-class competition. Furthermore, a learnable background token is applied to absorb non-target objects dynamically. These mechanisms effectively suppress overlapping predictions and generate high-fidelity masks. Extensive experimental evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed framework: (1) achieves a 2.3% $\sim$ 10.7% performance improvement over state-of-the-art methods, (2) delivers a 33$\times$ inference speedup compared to the native SAM3, and (3) exhibits strong robustness across diverse scenarios.
authors: Wenbin Liao, Hao Zhu, Yike Ma, Hao Jiang, Feng Dai
bullets: Addresses SAM3’s semantic confusion, redundant masks, and high latency when segmenting multiple concepts simultaneously.
Decouples cross-modal interactions to reduce inference cost.
Dynamically aligns text concepts with visual features and uses a dense competition head for explicit inter-class competition.
Introduces a learnable background token to absorb non-target objects and suppress overlapping predictions.
Reports 2.3%–10.7% improvements over state-of-the-art methods and a 33× speedup over native SAM3 across multiple benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient SAM3 adaptation for multi-class segmentation with large inference speedup; fits Efficient AI latency reduction.
papers.title: Efficient SAM3 Adaptation for Multi-Class Semantic Segmentation via Dense Competitive Representations
papers.tldr: DCR-SAM adapts SAM3 for faster, more accurate simultaneous multi-class segmentation by enforcing competition among overlapping concepts.

papers.abstract: Model compression makes large language models deployable, but today's evaluation tells an incomplete story. Standard practice measures retained task performance and stops there. This misses a critical fact: compression perturbs the distributed knowledge embedded across billions of weights, and task scores alone cannot reveal which underlying abilities survive and which quietly collapse. To solve this question, we introduce ACE-Compression, an ability-centric evaluation framework. Instead of asking only "does the compressed model still answer correctly?", we ask "which of its core abilities remain intact?" Our framework probes four deployment-facing dimensions: procedural reasoning and constraint execution, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social cognition and affective understanding, and persona fidelity and stylistic consistency. Across more than 35 compressed checkpoints from six open-weight LLMs-covering quantization and pruning-we find that compression redistributes ability profiles. Coarse, local, and surface-level signals often persist, while fine-grained, long-tail, and context-dependent abilities become fragile. Quantization consistently outperforms pruning in retention, but the practical meaning of that gap depends entirely on which ability an application requires. Based on our findings, deployers can choose compression methods by the ability profile their application needs, not just by a leaderboard average. And algorithm designers gain diagnostic signals to build compression methods that preserve what matters. We believe that ACE-Compression turns compression from a black-box accuracy drop into an interpretable intervention-one we can measure, understand, and ultimately improve.
authors: Jiahui Ning, Liang Chen, Yuchen Liang, Yi Zhang, Fenglei Fan
bullets: Introduces an ability-centric framework covering procedural reasoning, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social cognition, and persona/style consistency.
Evaluates over 35 compressed checkpoints from six open-weight LLMs using quantization and pruning.
Finds that compression redistributes ability profiles: coarse and surface-level abilities often persist, while long-tail and context-dependent abilities are more fragile.
Quantization generally retains abilities better than pruning, but the practical choice depends on an application’s required capabilities.
Supports capability-aware deployment decisions and provides diagnostics for designing more ability-preserving compression methods.
papers.selection_reason: Ability-centric evaluation of compressed LLMs, directly relevant to LLM efficiency and understanding how compression affects language model capabilities.
papers.title: ACE-Compression: An Ability-Centric Evaluation of Compressed Large Language Models
papers.tldr: ACE-Compression evaluates compressed LLMs by which underlying abilities they preserve—not just by aggregate task accuracy—revealing that compression selectively weakens fine-grained and context-dependent capabilities.

papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models have recently achieved remarkable progress in Real-world Image Super-Resolution (Real-SR). However, existing methods consistently exhibit a persistent seesaw effect: enhancing perceptual realism compromises structural fidelity. This effect, we argue, is not intrinsic to diffusion models, but largely stems from the architectural constraints of prevailing two-stage frameworks. To address this challenge, we propose PixelSR, a novel single-stage Pixel Diffusion Transformer for Real-SR that operates directly in pixel space. Specifically, PixelSR consists of two core designs: Pixel-space Conditional Diffusion and Orthogonal Flow Decoupling. The former establishes an effective pixel-space restoration framework by integrating spatially aligned LR conditioning, visual semantic guidance, and lightweight texture refinement, thereby bypassing VAE compression and enabling end-to-end optimization directly in RGB space. Complementarily, the latter decomposes the asymmetric flow target into a low-rank semantic component and a noise-free orthogonal texture component. By routing these components to specialized branches, it achieves decoupled optimization with reduced mutual interference. Benefiting from these designs, our PixelSR restores perceptually realistic details while faithfully preserving structural content. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that PixelSR not only achieves competitive performance, but also effectively mitigates the fidelity--realism seesaw effect.
authors: Xiang Lv, Kai Zhao, Qiang Wang, Qiao Mo, Chao Zhou, Mingwen Shao
bullets: Targets the realism–fidelity trade-off attributed to architectural limitations in two-stage diffusion frameworks.
Uses pixel-space conditional diffusion with aligned low-resolution conditioning, semantic guidance, and lightweight texture refinement.
Introduces Orthogonal Flow Decoupling to separate low-rank semantic and orthogonal texture components into specialized branches.
Avoids VAE compression and enables end-to-end optimization directly in RGB space.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks show competitive performance and mitigation of the fidelity–realism seesaw effect.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a pixel-space diffusion transformer and orthogonal flow decoupling for super-resolution, offering a novel approach to diffusion efficiency and architecture.
papers.title: PixelSR: Pixel-Space Orthogonal Flow Decoupling for Real-World Image Super-Resolution
papers.tldr: PixelSR is a single-stage pixel-space diffusion transformer designed to improve Real-SR perceptual detail without sacrificing structural fidelity.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) reconstructs 3D scenes from images in a single forward pass, making it well-suited to applications that must operate within limited resource budgets. To further improve its practicality, recent budget-controllable FF3DGS methods allow the number of Gaussians to be adjusted at inference, so that the output meets a given storage limit or rendering-latency constraint. However, these methods overlook the cost of inference itself: to produce a representation with the target number of Gaussians, they first predict a dense set of Gaussians and then prune or select from it, requiring nearly constant latency and peak memory regardless of the budget. We therefore propose RLSplat, a resource-linear budget-controllable FF3DGS framework whose representation size, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the Gaussian budget is reduced. Instead of pruning or selection, RLSplat learns a Gaussian allocation policy that distributes the budget across local scene regions, so that exactly the requested number of Gaussians is generated. These Gaussians are then refined through resource-linear Gaussian decoding, in which each Gaussian attends only to nearby Gaussians found via an efficient hierarchical neighbor search, so that the decoding cost decreases linearly with fewer Gaussians. In zero-shot evaluation, RLSplat outperforms prior budget-controllable methods at every budget, surpassing the strongest baseline even with 4$\times$ fewer Gaussians, while running up to 4.1$\times$ faster with 9.6$\times$ less peak memory at low budgets.
authors: Injae Kim, Minseok Joo, Jihwan Park, Sehyung Kim, Minseong Bae, Hyunwoo J. Kim
bullets: Existing methods generate a dense Gaussian set before pruning, so inference cost remains nearly fixed regardless of the final budget.
RLSplat learns how to allocate exactly the requested number of Gaussians across local scene regions.
A resource-linear decoder refines Gaussians using efficient hierarchical neighbor search and local attention.
In zero-shot evaluation, it outperforms prior budget-controllable methods at every budget, including a stronger baseline with 4× fewer Gaussians.
At low budgets, RLSplat runs up to 4.1× faster and uses 9.6× less peak memory.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes RLSplat, a resource-linear budget control method for 3D Gaussian Splatting. This addresses efficiency in 3D foundation models and falls under token/pruning strategies for resource management.
papers.title: RLSplat: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: RLSplat makes feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting truly budget-controllable by reducing representation size, inference latency, and peak memory linearly with the requested Gaussian budget.

papers.abstract: LiDAR-based 3D object detection is a core perception service for autonomous driving, but deployment requires robustness to point-cloud corruption while meeting latency and memory requirements. Existing approaches address robustness and resource efficiency separately, resulting in compact detectors that are fragile under corruption or robust detectors that remain costly to deploy. We therefore formulate LiDAR perception provisioning as constructing a detector that remains accurate under point-cloud corruptions while meeting constraints on inference latency and peak GPU memory. To achieve robustness, we first craft corrupted samples that mimic extreme weather conditions. Then we train candidate detectors offline by ordering clean and corrupted samples by perturbation sensitivity, through which detectors learn more from hard corrupted samples. We estimate perturbation sensitivity using an ensemble of seven heterogeneous 3D detectors by tracking changes in confidence, BEV overlap, and unmatched detections. To improve efficiency, we narrow the network and use offline neighborhood-density measurements to determine how many points and neighbors each sampling stage processes. We evaluate our method using AP (Average Precision) under clean and corrupted conditions, inference latency, and peak allocated GPU memory. On KITTI for Car detection with PointRCNN, our method improves Moderate AP under corruption by 3.32 points over the original detector while reducing mean latency by 19.8% and peak allocated GPU memory by 53.9%. Across two datasets, two detector architectures, and three object classes, our method improves AP under corruption by 4.03 points on average over the corresponding original detectors, while reducing mean inference latency and peak allocated GPU memory by 14.4% and 38.0%, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/drunklibai/robust-efficient-lidar-perception.
authors: Tingxu Han, Zijie Shen, An Guo, Lyuke Wang, Chunrong Fang, Zhenyu Chen, Wei Song
bullets: Targets the deployment trade-off between point-cloud corruption robustness and resource efficiency.
Generates extreme-weather-like corruptions and prioritizes hard samples using perturbation sensitivity.
Estimates sensitivity with an ensemble of seven heterogeneous 3D detectors using confidence, BEV overlap, and unmatched detections.
Narrows the network and uses offline neighborhood-density measurements to reduce processed points and neighbors.
Across two datasets, two architectures, and three classes, corruption AP rises 4.03 points on average, while latency and peak GPU memory fall 14.4% and 38.0%.
papers.selection_reason: Robust and efficient LiDAR 3D detection; directly fits 3D perception and efficiency optimization.
papers.title: Provisioning Robust and Efficient LiDAR Perception for Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: A LiDAR detector provisioning approach improves corruption robustness while reducing inference latency and GPU memory use.

papers.abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) aims to understand user-generated videos by integrating multiple modalities. Existing methods often treat modalities as symmetric, overlooking the fact that language provides a dominant semantic prior while nonverbal signals are complementary and noise-prone. To address this, we propose a Text-Anchored Modality Experts with Uncertainty-Guided Routing, termed TAME, that reformulates MSA as an uncertainty-guided refinement paradigm, where the language prior is calibrated and enhanced by selectively trusted nonverbal evidence. Specifically, TAME adopts an asymmetric Mixture-of-Modality-Experts framework, in which textual features act as a fixed and always-activated shared expert, while audio-textual and video-textual cross-modal branches serve as dynamically routed auxiliary experts. Furthermore, we introduce lightweight Prophet Heads to quantify the sample-level predictive uncertainty of each individual modality, and this uncertainty metric is further incorporated into the modality router to realize reliability-aware expert aggregation and fusion. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS datasets demonstrate that TAME achieves state-of-the-art performance on the majority of metrics while reducing parameter count by up to 78.7% and FLOPs by up to 41.2% over the mixture-of-expert baseline. %These results confirm that asymmetric expert construction with uncertainty-guided routing is an effective paradigm for MSA.
authors: Xiaohua Huang, Bingrui Lei, Xiuyan hao, Ling Zhou, Yuan Zong, Wenming Zheng, Guoying Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limitation of treating text, audio, and video as equally reliable, despite language providing a stronger semantic prior.
Uses an asymmetric mixture-of-modality-experts design with an always-active text expert and dynamically routed audio-textual and video-textual experts.
Introduces lightweight Prophet Heads to estimate modality-specific, sample-level uncertainty for reliability-aware expert routing and fusion.
Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS report state-of-the-art performance on most metrics.
Compared with a mixture-of-experts baseline, reduces parameter count by up to 78.7% and FLOPs by up to 41.2%.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal sentiment analysis with uncertainty-guided MoE routing; transferable to video-language understanding and efficient expert routing.
papers.title: Text-Anchored Modality Experts with Uncertainty-Guided Routing for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
papers.tldr: TAME improves multimodal sentiment analysis by anchoring fusion on language and routing complementary audio/video evidence according to predictive uncertainty.

papers.abstract: Memory-based temporal graph neural networks (TGN) rely on recurrent node memories to capture evolving interaction histories. However, temporal mini-batching introduces a trade-off between computational efficiency and temporal fidelity: when a node appears multiple times within the same batch, later interactions are evaluated using stale pre-batch memory because the intermediate memory updates have not yet been committed. This problem becomes more severe as temporal batch size increases. To overcome this challenge, we propose AnchorRM, an anchor-based residual memory mechanism that reconstructs event-specific intra-batch node states without executing sequential recurrent updates. AnchorRM treats the last committed node memory at the beginning of each batch as a pre-batch fixed anchor and uses causally preceding same-batch interactions to infer the missing state evolution relative to that anchor. The learned residual then calibrates the anchor to reconstruct an event-specific node memory for each interaction. Because each event-specific residual is predicted directly from the fixed anchor and its causal history, reconstructed states do not depend on previously reconstructed states and can therefore be computed in parallel within the batch while preserving temporal causality. Experiments across four temporal graph datasets and three memory-based backbones demonstrate that AnchorRM achieves an average 6.16x training speedup (up to 10.05x) and 28.67x batch scaling (up to 40x). These results demonstrate that AnchorRM substantially improves the scalability and training efficiency of memory-based temporal graph learning while maintaining competitive predictive performance.
authors: Haroon Gharwi, Kai Shu, Yue Dai
bullets: Addresses stale pre-batch memory when nodes appear multiple times within a temporal mini-batch.
Uses the last committed memory as a fixed anchor and predicts residual updates from causally preceding same-batch interactions.
Reconstructs each event-specific state independently, allowing parallel computation without sequential recurrent updates.
Across four temporal graph datasets and three memory-based backbones, reports 6.16× average training speedup and 28.67× batch scaling on average.
Maintains competitive predictive performance while improving scalability and efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Parallel intra-batch state reconstruction substantially accelerates memory-based temporal graph training; efficiency-focused contribution.
papers.title: AnchorRM: Parallel Intra-Batch State Reconstruction with Anchor-Based Residual Memory for Temporal Graph Neural Networks
papers.tldr: AnchorRM enables parallel, causally consistent reconstruction of intra-batch node memories, substantially accelerating memory-based temporal graph neural network training.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) attaches small low-rank matrices to a frozen backbone, and public repositories host many LoRAs per backbone, each for a different concept or task. Combining several LoRAs in one generation forces a trade-off. Merging their weights into one update needs a single forward pass, but LoRAs trained for different concepts interfere and quality drops. Running each LoRA in its own forward pass (composite) preserves quality, but inference time grows linearly with the number of active LoRAs. We study a property of LoRA pools overlooked by prior multi-LoRA work. In real LoRA pools, the stacked low-rank factors need far fewer directions than their summed ranks. Using singular value decomposition, we find the minimal subspace that keeps 99% of the factor energy. On three diffusion pools, only 46% to 57% of the summed LoRA ranks is needed, and the subspace grows sub-linearly with pool size. A 48-LoRA sub-pool of LoRA-Hub on FLAN-T5 tasks shows comparable overlap (62%), while the diversity-curated LoRA-Retriever benchmark sits near the no-overlap baseline (96%), so pool composition rather than modality predicts where compression is large. We build on this overlap with LoRASpace, a training-free method that computes the subspace once per pool and reuses it in two inference modes, a static mode at merge cost and a dynamic mode for input-dependent routing. On the diffusion pools, static LoRASpace matches composite quality at merge cost, and dynamic LoRASpace is more than 6x faster than composite with six active LoRAs on a 17-LoRA pool, mainly because it runs one backbone pass instead of six. In an ablation, static variants at the same rank match LoRASpace, so the quality gain does not depend on the pool-wide basis. On the near-orthogonal LoRA-Retriever benchmark, compression is small and gains come from coupling with external retrieval.
authors: Thamirawaran Sathiyalogeswaran, Navindu De Silva, Chamikara Siriwardane, W. K. Alwis, Jason Mars, Udaya Sampath K. Perera Miriya Thanthrige, Ranga Rodrigo
bullets: LoRA pools often occupy a subspace much smaller than their summed ranks, but compression depends on pool composition.
It computes one shared subspace per pool and supports static merging or dynamic, input-dependent routing without training.
Static LoRASpace matches composite quality at merge cost; dynamic inference is over 6× faster than six separate LoRA passes in one reported setting.
Compression is substantial for overlapping pools but limited for near-orthogonal, diversity-curated pools.
Ablations indicate the quality gain comes from the method’s coupling, not specifically from using the pool-wide basis.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free multi-LoRA composition substrate reduces inference cost; fits efficient AI interests.
papers.title: LoRASpace: A Pool-Wide Shared Substrate for Static and Dynamic Multi-LoRA Composition
papers.tldr: LoRASpace exploits shared directions among LoRAs to preserve composite quality while reducing multi-LoRA inference cost.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention limits the keys used by each query, but finding those keys can still require a full-prefix scan at every layer. We introduce \textbf{MLIPS (Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing)}, a training-free method that shares candidate search while retaining each consumer's own scoring and selection. A producer publishes a top-$M$ pool larger than the attention budget $K$; subsequent layers select their own top-$K$ from that pool. Measurements across three sparse-attention model families show substantially higher coverage from broad pools than overlap between final selections. We implement layerwise sharing, persistent decode reuse, and a coarse producer in vLLM for DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Across four long-context suites, three consumer layers per producer give $1.14$--$1.40\times$ speedups and $14.8$--$27.4\%$ lower GPU energy, with observed accuracy changes of $-1.49$ to $+0.29$ percentage points in single runs. More extensive sharing exposes task-dependent quality losses. Sampled prefill traces also reveal recurring selected KV positions across query groups and layers. We characterize this shared working-set structure and use it to motivate Top-$G$, an exploratory bounded pool construction for prefill. Its deployment, task accuracy, and serving benefits remain open.
authors: Samkit Jain, Sai Kishan Pampana, Shlok Agarwal
bullets: Sparse attention still incurs costly full-prefix key searches at every layer.
A producer publishes a top-M candidate pool; each consumer independently selects its own top-K keys.
Implemented in vLLM for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, sharing three consumer layers per producer improved serving efficiency across four long-context suites.
Single-run accuracy changes ranged from −1.49 to +0.29 percentage points; more aggressive sharing can reduce quality.
Recurring KV-position reuse motivates Top-G, an exploratory prefill method whose deployment and benefits remain open.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free sharing of sparse-attention candidate search improves long-context LLM serving efficiency and GPU energy.
papers.title: MLIPS: Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing
papers.tldr: MLIPS accelerates sparse attention by sharing broad candidate-key pools across layers, achieving 1.14–1.40× speedups with 14.8–27.4% lower GPU energy but task-dependent quality trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Learned post-training quantization (PTQ) calibration fits quantizer parameters on a small calibration set, and for a text embedder the natural supervision is retrieval relevance. We ask two questions that are usually conflated: how far to calibrate, and whether to calibrate at all. Across three embedders (e5-base-v2, BGE-M3, EmbeddingGemma-300m) at 4-bit weight quantization, 161 calibration runs, the outcome of a fixed procedure ranges from a gain to catastrophic degradation, and the driver is the dose of the update, measured as the functional displacement D_func of the quantized model from its uncalibrated start. On EmbeddingGemma the same learning-rate grid gives +1.47 to -71.53 points of in-domain NDCG@10 change; a label-free cosine objective collapses at the same dose (-69.52 vs -71.63), so the collapse is a property of learnable calibration rather than of retrieval supervision. Objective sensitivity is heterogeneous: on e5, ranking calibration is substantially more robust than cosine at matched displacement (+14.16 +/- 4.34 pp, 95% t-CI [+3.37, +24.96], three paired slates), whereas on BGE-M3 the ordering is directionally opposite but unresolved ([-5.18, +2.38]). Dose is the main axis but not a sufficient statistic: equal D_func reached along different paths differs by up to 1.61 pp. We therefore treat calibration as an optional intervention. A pre-registered rule that accepts a checkpoint only when a per-query paired confidence interval on a 25% calibration-validation split clears the uncalibrated baseline was run on 6 independent slates and five arms. It never selected a checkpoint below its slate's baseline (0 harmful selections in 30 decisions), retained 8 of 11 beneficial updates, and paid a mean oracle regret of 1.52 pp with one abstention that forfeited 11.13 pp, a safety-opportunity trade-off, not a free improvement. We report what remains open, including label efficiency.
authors: Hyojung Han, Ryangkyung Kang, Youngeun Kim, Seung-Hun Jeon
bullets: Across three embedders and 161 4-bit calibration runs, outcomes ranged from gains to severe degradation, largely tracking functional displacement from the uncalibrated model.
On EmbeddingGemma, the same learning-rate grid produced changes from +1.47 to −71.53 NDCG@10 points; a label-free cosine objective showed a similar collapse at the same dose.
Objective robustness varied by embedder: ranking calibration was more robust than cosine on e5, while BGE-M3 showed an unresolved opposite trend.
Functional displacement was the main risk axis but not sufficient: equal displacement reached through different paths differed by up to 1.61 points.
A validation rule made 0 harmful selections in 30 decisions, retained 8 of 11 beneficial updates, and incurred mean oracle regret of 1.52 points, including one missed 11.13-point gain.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes post-training quantization calibration for text embedders, directly relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: When PTQ Calibration Helps or Hurts: Dose-Driven Collapse and Validation-Gated Abstention in Quantized Text Embedders
papers.tldr: PTQ calibration can greatly improve or catastrophically damage quantized text embedders, so validation-gated abstention offers a safer—but opportunity-costly—way to deploy it.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have advanced rapidly in multimodal reasoning, yet they remain limited on tasks requiring fine-grained understanding of small or easily overlooked image regions. Recent thinking with images approaches mitigate this limitation by allowing models to inspect images through operations such as zooming, cropping, or code execution. While effective, their multi-turn interactions with VLMs introduce redundant token computation and slow inference, and separate region inspection from the reasoning step that depends on it. To address these issues, we propose Look Before You Reason (LoRe), an implicit visual thinking framework for efficient visual reasoning within a single-turn VLM interaction. Given an image and a question, LoRe predicts the most relevant image region, aligns it with the corresponding image patch features, and strengthens the associated key-value (KV) cache entries, enabling subsequent decoding to directly exploit the selected visual cues without additional visual inputs or explicit tool calls. We further employ reinforcement learning to guide the VLM toward identifying informative image regions and leveraging them during reasoning. To support fine-grained evaluation of multimodal reasoning, we introduce COCO-ObjQA, a large-scale benchmark for object-centric multimodal reasoning. Experiments on three challenging multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that LoRe consistently improves VLM reasoning performance with low additional inference overhead.
authors: Zerui Chen, Changrui Chen, Fei Ni, Jiankang Deng
bullets: Addresses overlooked small image regions and the inefficiency of zooming, cropping, or code-based visual inspection.
Predicts a relevant region, aligns it with image-patch features, and strengthens corresponding KV-cache entries in a single interaction.
Uses reinforcement learning to encourage selection and use of informative visual regions during reasoning.
Introduces COCO-ObjQA for fine-grained, object-centric multimodal reasoning evaluation.
Improves reasoning across three challenging benchmarks with low additional inference overhead.],
papers.selection_reason: Improves VLM reasoning efficiency via implicit visual thinking and KV cache strengthening; fits multimodal LLM and efficient inference interests.
papers.title: Look Before You Reason: Implicit Visual Thinking for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: LoRe enables VLMs to identify and amplify relevant image regions internally, improving fine-grained multimodal reasoning without costly multi-turn visual tool use.

papers.abstract: Few-step trajectory distillation aims to learn accurate global updates from dense local supervision along a teacher's sampling trajectory. Existing approaches construct within-step dynamics using specific trajectory parameterizations or discrete interval predictions, tying the learned update to a prescribed temporal structure. We propose \method, which directly learns a continuous trajectory primitive representing cumulative displacement along the teacher trajectory. By supervising finite differences of the primitive with local teacher velocities, \method learns the accumulated motion directly, while obtaining global updates through endpoint differences. This formulation avoids prescribing a temporal basis or fixed query grid and instead learns the temporal evolution of cumulative displacement from local supervision. We further establish a local-to-global error bound to characterize how local regression errors affect full-interval displacement accuracy, and introduce endpoint absorption to eliminate the auxiliary primitive branch while preserving one-network-evaluation inference. Experiments on large-scale text-to-image generation show that \method achieves a T-FID of 20.92 and an HPSv2 score of 28.35 at one NFE, improving both metrics over a trajectory-distillation baseline. After endpoint absorption, it retains comparable performance, achieving a T-FID of 20.86 and an HPSv2 score of 28.33.
bullets: Targets few-step trajectory distillation, where global updates must be learned from dense local supervision.
Learns cumulative displacement directly and obtains global motion from endpoint differences, avoiding a prescribed temporal basis or query grid.
Provides a local-to-global error bound linking local regression errors to full-interval displacement accuracy.
Endpoint absorption removes the auxiliary primitive branch while retaining one-network-evaluation inference.
On large-scale text-to-image generation, reaches T-FID 20.92 and HPSv2 28.35 at one NFE; endpoint absorption remains comparable at 20.86 and 28.33.
papers.selection_reason: Trajectory primitives for few-step distillation improve generation efficiency and dynamics modeling, relevant to video generation and efficient AI.
papers.title: PRIMFLOW: Learning Trajectory Primitives for Few-Step Distillation
papers.tldr: PRIMFLOW learns continuous cumulative trajectory primitives from local teacher velocities to enable accurate one-step diffusion distillation without a fixed temporal parameterization.

papers.abstract: Learned image compression (LIC) has achieved promising rate-distortion performance, but most methods lack scalability for diverse platforms with varying computational and storage constraints. Existing slimmable LIC methods achieve flexible complexity via consecutive-channel activation but suffer from two limitations: forced consecutive-channel selection degrades narrow-model performance at low bitrates, and the lack of stable variable-rate control limits adaptability to varying bandwidth. We propose a channel-level mask-guided slimmable image compression method. A learnable channel-wise mask with sparsity-promoting regularization enables non-contiguous top-w channel selection, letting narrow models use the most informative channels. After training, mask merging and channel reordering convert the model into a standard slimmable network via Mask-to-Slimmable (M2S) conversion, enabling efficient inference without architectural changes. For variable-rate control, we combine lambda- and width-conditioned modulation with quantization-step scaling and a progressive training pipeline stabilized by a freeze-then-fine-tune strategy. Experiments on Kodak across E2E, Hyperprior, and Checkerboard backbones show superior rate-distortion performance across widths and bitrates, with large gains for narrow models at low bitrates. At w=48, it achieves up to 19.22%, 24.11%, and 22.76% BD-rate savings over the same-width Slimmable baseline on E2E, Hyperprior, and CKBD, respectively. A single VBR model replaces 40 independent models, reducing storage by 14.8x to 15.9x. Code: https://github.com/sjtu-tcloud/MGSIC.
authors: Chen Chen, Chenggang Wu, Yongbiao Chen, Weidong Qiu, Zhengwei Qi, Haibing Guan
bullets: Addresses poor low-bitrate performance from forced consecutive-channel selection and unstable variable-rate control.
Learns sparse channel masks to select informative non-contiguous channels for narrow models.
Uses Mask-to-Slimmable conversion, channel reordering, and modulation with quantization-step scaling for efficient variable-rate inference.
Progressive freeze-then-fine-tune training stabilizes the combined width- and rate-conditioned model.
On Kodak across three backbones, reports stronger rate-distortion performance; one VBR model replaces 40 models with 14.8×–15.9× lower storage.
papers.selection_reason: Slimmable learned image compression with channel-level masking directly targets computational/storage efficiency in AI inference.
papers.title: Channel-Level Mask Guidance for Slimmable Image Compression
papers.tldr: A mask-guided slimmable image compression method improves narrow-width and variable-rate performance while consolidating many bitrate models into one.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) have become a mainstream way to scale Large Language Models (LLMs), because each token activates only a small subset of experts, reducing inference cost. However, MoE decode remains highly memory-bound and exhibits strongly skewed, time-varying expert loads. 3D-stacked DRAM near-memory processing (NMP) provides the bandwidth that decode demands, yet its tiled organization makes load balancing expensive: expert parallelism (EP) preserves locality but suffers from hotspot-induced imbalance, while more distributed strategies weaken locality and increase NoC traffic. To address this locality-balance conflict, we observe that domain-specialized token routing creates offsetting expert-load fluctuations across decode steps, a property we call expert complementarity. Using this insight, we propose 3D-MoE, a hardware--software co-designed system for MoE decode on 3D-stacked NMP. 3D-MoE uses offline, one-time complementarity-guided grouping and locality-aware mapping to establish coarse-grained inter-group balance, handles residual intra-group hotspots through a lightweight Collaborative Memory-Network (CMN) that streams each hot expert's weight tiles once from its host DRAM channel to helper cores over a reconfigured local broadcast path, and uses cost-aware online remapping to remain robust to workload drift. Across MoE models, 3D-MoE achieves an average 4.63$\times$ MoE-layer speedup over EP and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.58$\times$--1.86$\times$ over the strongest NMP baselines, with 2.11\% additional logic-die area.
authors: Yudong Pan, Lian Liu, Shixin Zhao, Yintao He, Kaiyan Chang, Tianhua Han, Chenyang Ai, Haonan Zhu, Mengdi Wang, Yinhe Han, Ying Wang
bullets: MoE decode is memory-bound, with skewed and time-varying expert loads that make tiled NMP load balancing difficult.
The approach exploits complementary expert-load fluctuations across decode steps for offline inter-group balancing.
A Collaborative Memory-Network streams hot experts’ weight tiles once to helper cores, mitigating residual intra-group hotspots.
Cost-aware online remapping adapts the system to workload drift.
Across MoE models, it reports 4.63× average MoE-layer speedup over expert parallelism and 1.58×–1.86× end-to-end throughput gains over NMP baselines, with 2.11% additional logic-die area.
papers.selection_reason: Hardware-software co-design for memory-bound MoE inference, directly reducing memory traffic and latency; fits Efficient AI.
papers.title: 3D-MoE: Complementarity-Guided Hardware-Software Co-Design for MoE Decode on 3D-Stacked NMP
papers.tldr: 3D-MoE co-designs expert grouping, locality-aware mapping, and lightweight broadcast-based hotspot handling to balance MoE decode on 3D-stacked NMP.

papers.abstract: Online action detection (OAD) identifies ongoing actions in streaming videos.
