Many existing OAD systems combine RGB appearance with optical flow, but dense-flow extraction remains a major computational bottleneck. Codec motion vectors (MVs) are available during decoding, avoiding a separate optical-flow computation. On THUMOS'14, optical flow exceeds MVs by 11.2 mAP points with motion-only inputs, whereas the gap narrows to 3.7 points after RGB fusion, with the largest reduction in action-category discrimination. We propose CodecMotion-OAD, which replaces optical flow with decoder-provided MVs while retaining existing temporal detector architectures. Its two-stage training first aligns MV features with a pretrained flow-feature interface without action labels and then trains RGB+MV detectors using ground-truth labels and soft predictions from a frozen RGB+Flow teacher. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of codec MVs to frame-level OAD. On THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD, CodecMotion-OAD achieves 68.3 mAP versus 70.9 mAP for matched-distillation RGB+Flow, while reducing decoder-to-prediction processing time by 11.48-fold on CPU and 2.04-fold on GPU.
authors: Zepeng Sun, Naichuan Zheng, Hailun Xia, Junjie Wu
bullets: Optical-flow extraction is a major OAD bottleneck; codec motion vectors are available directly during video decoding.
The method retains existing temporal detector architectures and uses two-stage feature alignment and teacher-guided RGB+MV training.
On THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD, it reaches 68.3 mAP versus 70.9 mAP for matched-distillation RGB+Flow.
Decoder-to-prediction processing is 11.48× faster on CPU and 2.04× faster on GPU.
Scope: evaluated on THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD; performance remains below the optical-flow counterpart.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient online action detection using codec motion vectors instead of optical flow.
papers.title: CodecMotion-OAD: Efficient Online Action Detection with Compressed-Domain Motion
papers.tldr: CodecMotion-OAD replaces costly optical flow with decoder-provided motion vectors for efficient online action detection, achieving near-flow accuracy with substantially faster processing.

papers.abstract: Sparse routing reduces per-token computation but leaves the full expert bank resident in memory. We study expert pruning for speech-centric omni-modal models, where pooling calibration statistics can obscure the different expert demands of acoustic-input processing and text-answer generation. We propose PW-Pruning, a phase-aware extension of DO-ACP that constructs separate importance-weighted kernels for acoustic-prefill and teacher-forced answer tokens, then combines phase-weighted log-determinant marginal gains to select one static expert bank. On Qwen3-Omni, retaining 32 of 128 experts per layer improves MMAU-mini and MMSU accuracy over matched pooled selection by 3.20 and 4.38 percentage points, respectively, after supervised fine-tuning, averaged over three runs. Single-phase and shuffled-label controls on this public backbone suggest that semantic phase information contributes to these gains. Experiments on a non-public Qwen3.5-Omni backbone and English-only zero-shot evaluation of Nemotron provide complementary evidence. Across the tested Qwen budgets, AU gains are larger under stronger pruning, without inference-time mask switching.
authors: Junjie Cao, Fengping Tian, Wenjie Zhou, Xuanfan Ni, Chenyang Lyu, Siyou Liu, Longyue Wang, Weihua Luo
bullets: Pooling calibration statistics can miss the distinct expert needs of acoustic-prefill and answer-generation tokens.
The method builds phase-specific importance-weighted kernels and combines log-determinant marginal gains to choose one static expert bank.
On Qwen3-Omni, retaining 32 of 128 experts per layer improves MMAU-mini and MMSU accuracy by 3.20 and 4.38 percentage points over pooled selection after fine-tuning.
Controls indicate that semantic phase information contributes to the gains, which increase under stronger pruning across tested Qwen budgets.
The approach avoids inference-time mask switching; additional evidence comes from non-public Qwen3.5-Omni and English-only zero-shot Nemotron evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Phase-aware expert pruning reduces inference cost for speech-centric omni-modal models, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: PW-Pruning: Phase-Aware Expert Selection for Speech-Centric Omni-Modal Models
papers.tldr: PW-Pruning improves static expert pruning for speech-centric omni-modal models by selecting experts separately for acoustic input and text generation phases.

papers.abstract: Systems that combine several large language models (LLMs) often use one context for many questions. When the context is passed between models as text, the receiving model processes all of its tokens again for every question. Avoiding this cost requires a context representation that is compact, reusable across questions, and readable by a different LLM. Existing compression and latent communication methods each provide only some of these properties. We introduce LatComm, a Latent Communication interface that provides all three by separating encoding from reading: the context is encoded once without the question, and the receiver selects what to read for each question. A frozen context encoder LLM compresses the context into a fixed-size packet and sends it to a different frozen receiver LLM, which reads the packet through cross-attention, with gates computed from its prompt. On 12 multiple-choice question-answering datasets, LatComm improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points. On QuALITY, it reduces the receiver's input by 57x and answers the questions of an article 3x faster.
authors: Huawei Lin, Jinting Liu, Tan Yu, Weijie Zhao
bullets: Addresses the repeated token-processing cost of passing shared context between LLMs.
Uses a frozen encoder to create a fixed-size latent packet and a different frozen receiver that reads it via prompt-conditioned cross-attention.
Combines compactness, cross-model readability, and reuse across multiple questions.
Improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points across 12 multiple-choice QA datasets.
On QuALITY, reduces receiver input by 57× and answers article questions 3× faster.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LatComm, a reusable context compression method for LLMs, which reduces memory requirements and processing time by compressing context into a fixed-size packet.
papers.title: LatComm: Reusable Context Compression for Latent Communication between Large Language Models
papers.tldr: LatComm enables reusable, compact communication between LLMs by encoding context once and letting the receiver selectively read it per question.

papers.abstract: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (https://github.com/NX-AI/KronLSTM) and models (https://huggingface.co/collections/NX-AI/kronlstm) are open-source.
authors: Anamaria-Roberta Hartl, Levente Z\'olyomi, Michael List, G\"unter Klambauer, Sebastian B\"ock, Sepp Hochreiter
bullets: Extends the xLSTM family with memory revision that corrects targeted associations along a single matrix-space direction.
Reduces interference with stored information compared with standard delta-rule updates.
Its memory dynamics form a convergent Markov chain with uniformly bounded expected memory norm, without extra stabilization or normalization.
Experiments find performance competitive with or often better than linear attention baselines, especially on long-context benchmarks.
Code and pretrained models are publicly available.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, offering stable memory dynamics and improved efficiency for long-context language modeling.
papers.title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
papers.tldr: KronLSTM introduces a minimally invasive Kronecker Delta Rule for stable, high-performing long-context linear attention.

papers.abstract: Expert human readers process large inputs (e.g., code repositories and long documents) by skimming to closely read only what matters. On the other hand, language models process all input tokens through each model layer, resulting in significant processing costs for long-context inputs. We introduce TokenGate, a small, drop-in component that extends existing trained models to enable end-to-end learnable token pruning over long-context inputs for fast and memory-efficient prefill. To enable end-to-end learning despite the non-differentiable top-K operator for token pruning, we introduce token-gated attention, a mechanism inspired by Mixture-of-Experts that re-weights attention logits using token importance scores. Across diverse tasks, TokenGate achieves $1.4$-$11.3\times$ faster time-to-first token (TTFT) and $1.5$-$3.4\times$ lower peak memory at no accuracy degradation for prefill in transformers. Compared to the best-performing prior methods for token-pruning, TokenGate gives up to $6.4\times$ faster prefill and $2\times$ lower peak memory. TokenGate natively extends both standard transformers (e.g., Qwen3) and hybrid-attention models (e.g., Qwen3.5) with simple lightweight adaptation comparable to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We make our code available at: https://github.com/tokengate-models/TokenGate.
authors: Liana Patel, Rishabh Ranjan, Ion Stoica, Matei Zaharia, Carlos Guestrin
bullets: Addresses the high cost of processing every token across all layers during long-context prefill.
Uses a small drop-in component that learns token importance and prunes less relevant tokens.
Introduces token-gated attention to enable end-to-end training despite non-differentiable top-K pruning.
Reports 1.4–11.3× faster time-to-first-token and 1.5–3.4× lower peak memory with no accuracy degradation.
Supports standard and hybrid-attention transformers through lightweight adaptation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes TokenGate, a learnable token pruning mechanism for LLMs, to achieve fast and memory-efficient prefill, directly addressing token pruning and memory efficiency.
papers.title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning
papers.tldr: TokenGate adds lightweight learned token pruning to existing LLMs, substantially reducing long-context prefill time and memory without degrading accuracy.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical abstraction is a fundamental principle across many data modalities, enabling complex sequences to be represented compositionally at multiple levels. Learning such hierarchies directly from data, without explicit structural supervision, remains a central challenge in representation learning. We investigate whether meaningful hierarchical structure can emerge from compression alone. While autoencoders learn compressed representations through reconstruction, this objective does not necessarily favour meaningful compositional structure. We study this challenge through unsupervised grammar induction, where the underlying hierarchy can be evaluated explicitly. We introduce a hierarchical token-merging autoencoder that recursively combines adjacent tokens into increasingly abstract representations, compressing entire sequences through a variational information bottleneck. The model jointly learns representations and hierarchical structure by marginalising over possible binary trees using dynamic programming. To address training instability, we combine independently trained models through unsupervised consensus and distillation. Experiments on a synthetic, ambiguous grammar demonstrate the emergence of meaningful hierarchical structure without structural supervision. The resulting model achieves 93% grammatical parse-validity and 93% exact reconstruction on held-out sequences, compared with 42% parse-validity for the strongest trivial baseline. These findings establish a proof of concept for hierarchical token merging as a mechanism for unsupervised structure discovery and abstraction learning.
bullets: Addresses unsupervised discovery of meaningful compositional hierarchies without structural supervision.
Recursively merges adjacent tokens into abstract representations through a variational information bottleneck.
Marginalises over possible binary trees with dynamic programming to jointly learn representations and structure.
Uses unsupervised consensus and distillation across independently trained models to improve training stability.
On held-out synthetic sequences, reaches 93% parse validity and exact reconstruction, versus 42% parse validity for the strongest trivial baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a hierarchical token-merging autoencoder for unsupervised grammar induction, which is a form of token-level compression and structure discovery relevant to token pruning and efficiency.
papers.title: Hierarchical Token Merging with Recursive Autoencoders for Unsupervised Grammar Induction
papers.tldr: A recursive autoencoder learns hierarchical grammatical structure from compression alone, achieving 93% parse validity and exact reconstruction on a synthetic ambiguous grammar.

papers.abstract: Hybrid architectures offer a promising approach to efficient language modeling by combining a small number of full-attention layers with a larger number of efficient sequence layers, such as sparse attention and recurrent layers. While full-attention layers maintain a KV cache that grows linearly with sequence length, efficient layers typically rely on separate, fixed-size states rather than accessing this richer existing memory. Recent work has begun exploring ways to allow efficient layers access to the KV cache, but the theoretical benefits of such access, and the extent to which existing approaches can realize them remain poorly understood. We investigate these questions by analyzing the expressive power of individual hybrid blocks on function composition, a well-studied task in sequence-model expressivity associated with multi-hop reasoning. We first establish that both conventional hybrid blocks and those with top-$\kappa$ KV-cache access require $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ capacity to compute even two-function composition over a domain of size $n$. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the \emph{Multi-hop Retrieval Attention} (MuRA) hybrid block, a simple architecture that enables multi-hop retrieval from a shared KV cache while preserving asymptotic computational and memory efficiency. We prove that a single fixed size $m$-hop MuRA block can compute $m$-function composition, whereas computing $(m+1)$-function composition with the same retrieval depth requires polynomial model size, establishing a strict expressivity hierarchy in retrieval depth. Synthetic experiments support this hierarchy, showing that increasing retrieval depth enables learning progressively deeper compositions, substantially outperforming existing hybrid architectures. Together, our results identify multi-hop retrieval as a promising mechanism for improving the expressive power of efficient hybrid architectures.
authors: Yam Eitan, Gilad Yehudai, Haggai Maron
bullets: Hybrid models combine a few full-attention layers with more efficient sparse-attention or recurrent layers, but efficient layers typically cannot exploit the full KV cache.
Conventional hybrid blocks and top-κ KV-cache access require Ω(√n) capacity even for two-function composition over a domain of size n.
The proposed Multi-hop Retrieval Attention (MuRA) block supports multi-hop access to a shared KV cache while preserving asymptotic computational and memory efficiency.
A fixed-size m-hop MuRA block can compute m-function composition, while computing (m+1)-function composition at the same depth requires polynomial model size.
Synthetic experiments support a retrieval-depth hierarchy, with deeper retrieval enabling progressively deeper compositions and outperforming existing hybrid architectures.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a multi-hop retrieval attention block for efficient hybrid language architectures, improving expressivity while preserving asymptotic efficiency.
papers.title: Improving the Expressive Power of Hybrid Sequence Models via Multi-Hop Retrieval
papers.tldr: Multi-hop retrieval substantially increases the expressive power of efficient hybrid sequence models, enabling deeper compositional reasoning with fixed-size retrieval depth.

papers.abstract: Standard self-attention compares tokens by similarity but does not account for how much of a past state survives to the present. We introduce Dynamical Kernel Attention (DKA), which derives attention from robust estimation of a latent state evolving under stochastic dynamics. As a past state decays toward equilibrium under the dynamics, the information it carries about the present vanishes, bounding the total evidence a head can draw. Unlike recency biases, DKA can abstain when relevant evidence is weak and guarantees a bounded error when old tokens are discarded. DKA preserves the parallel structure and computational cost of standard attention. We present the model and its theory; empirical evaluation is deferred to a subsequent version.
bullets: Standard self-attention measures similarity but ignores how much information from past states remains relevant to the present.
DKA derives attention by robustly estimating a latent state evolving under stochastic dynamics.
Information from past states decays toward equilibrium, limiting the total evidence an attention head can use.
Unlike simple recency biases, DKA can abstain when relevant evidence is weak and provides error guarantees when old tokens are discarded.
The abstract presents theory and the model; empirical evaluation is deferred to future work.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an attention mechanism with bounded-error token discarding, directly relevant to efficient attention and token eviction.
papers.title: Dynamical Kernel Attention: Estimating the Present from a Record of the Past
papers.tldr: Dynamical Kernel Attention incorporates stochastic state dynamics into attention, enabling principled decay, abstention under weak evidence, and bounded error from discarding old tokens without added computational cost.

papers.abstract: Consumer phones and wearables increasingly collect physiological time-series data, yet most mobile systems treat these streams as summaries or text rather than as temporal evidence. This representation is poorly matched to personal health systems that need to retrieve, route, or summarize sensor evidence while preserving temporal structure. Cloud-hosted time-series language models avoid smartphone limits, but they repeatedly move sensitive physiology off the device and add latency and per-query compute cost. Mobile model alternatives that aggregate time-series data into statistical features or serialize raw samples as text either compress temporal structure or exhaust the context and memory budgets of small on-device models. We present PocketTSLM, a mobile-native deployment of OpenTSLM SoftPrompt, the soft-prompt variant of the OpenTSLM time-series language model. PocketTSLM runs fully on a consumer smartphone by injecting encoded time-series windows as embeddings instead of tokenizing time series as text. A numerical parity protocol verifies identical greedy-decoded token sequences between the Swift port and a Python reference using Apple's MLX machine-learning framework. Answers also match the PyTorch reference, although rationale wording can differ. An on-device context-economics benchmark compares the soft-prompt path with a text-serialized baseline on the same backbone. In our benchmark format, soft-prompting uses approximately 12 times fewer time-series tokens and reduces prompt-prefill cost. PocketTSLM processes 30-second Sleep-EDF electroencephalography clips for sleep staging and a 1,000-sample (10 s) 12-lead electrocardiogram clip from ECG-QA. In comparison, text-serialized baselines exceed the phone's context or memory budget at longer time-series windows. All inference runs entirely on the device, with no health data transmitted during inference.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between text-based mobile models and temporally structured physiological data, while avoiding cloud privacy, latency, and compute costs.
Injects encoded time-series windows as embeddings rather than serializing samples as text, preserving temporal input within mobile context limits.
Implements the OpenTSLM SoftPrompt model in Swift using Apple’s MLX framework and verifies numerical parity with a Python reference.
Processes Sleep-EDF EEG clips for sleep staging and 1,000-sample, 12-lead ECG clips from ECG-QA on a consumer smartphone.
Soft-prompting uses approximately 12× fewer time-series tokens than the text-serialized baseline and avoids context or memory overflow at longer windows.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a soft-prompting approach for on-device time-series language models that significantly reduces the number of tokens required compared to text serialization, improving memory and context efficiency.
papers.title: PocketTSLM: Deploying an On-Device Soft-Prompt Time-Series Language Model for Privacy-Preserving Smartphone Reasoning
papers.tldr: PocketTSLM brings soft-prompt time-series language modeling to smartphones, enabling private on-device reasoning over physiological signals without transmitting health data.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) achieve high-fidelity image and video generation, but they suffer from substantial inference costs due to repeated transformer evaluations across many denoising steps. Feature caching reduces this cost by reusing features across denoising steps. Recent forecasting methods extend this idea by extrapolating features to skipped steps instead of reusing them. However, existing forecasting methods extrapolate the features they predict uniformly, even though the spatial-frequency components of these features change most at different stages of denoising. They also overlook that denoising progresses nonuniformly, so equal step intervals can correspond to very different amounts of change. These mismatches amplify forecast errors as more steps are skipped, limiting the achievable acceleration. We propose SpecKCast, a training-free method that forecasts the model output in the frequency domain. SpecKCast applies a 2D discrete cosine transform (DCT) to the output and tracks each coefficient with a lightweight Kalman filter along a band-specific time coordinate derived from the noise schedule. The filter tracks each coefficient's value and rate of change, and the transformer is evaluated only when the filter's forecast uncertainty exceeds a threshold. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev, Qwen-Image, Wan2.1-14B, and HunyuanVideo show that SpecKCast achieves a better trade-off between acceleration and fidelity than existing caching and forecasting methods, reaching up to 6x speedup with less than 0.05 GiB of additional memory.
authors: Javad Rajabi, Hakki Can Karaimer, David B. Lindell, Babak Taati, Michael S. Brown
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of repeated DiT evaluations during denoising.
Uses a 2D DCT to decompose outputs and tracks each frequency coefficient with a lightweight Kalman filter.
Accounts for nonuniform denoising via band-specific time coordinates derived from the noise schedule.
Triggers transformer evaluations only when forecast uncertainty exceeds a threshold.
Demonstrates a better acceleration–fidelity trade-off across four image and video generation models, with under 0.05 GiB extra memory.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free diffusion acceleration via spectral Kalman forecasting, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: SpecKCast: Spectral Kalman Forecasting for Diffusion Acceleration
papers.tldr: SpecKCast accelerates diffusion Transformers by forecasting frequency-domain outputs with band-specific Kalman filters, achieving up to 6× speedup while preserving fidelity.

papers.abstract: Context compression improves long-context efficiency but may introduce faithfulness issues through an information bottleneck. Existing evaluations rely on QA metrics, but a reader can still answer correctly from an unfaithful compression, so these metrics underestimate such loss. To bridge this gap, we introduce KEEP-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that directly assesses compression faithfulness with 4,102 cases across three challenging settings that require keeping evidence for plausible reference resolutions, explicit qualifiers, and minority perspectives. Experiments show that even with tailored prompting, the strongest models remain unreliable: despite context windows exceeding 100K tokens and inputs averaging only 3.1K tokens, the best open-weight model (31B) preserves all required evidence in only 66.8% of cases, and the best proprietary model in only 61.6%. Performance also varies sharply across evidence structures, so conclusions from limited structures may be biased. We further introduce a metric, Evidence Preservation Return (EPR), to relate evidence recall to inference FLOPs, and find that it peaks at moderate scales (4B-8B), where recall remains low. Additional output budget mainly benefits already strong models and widens capability gaps, yet the stronger preservation of these models comes at a steep computational cost. These findings highlight the importance for future work to investigate compressors with strong information preservation under a small computation budget, rather than relying on a large output budget or model scaling.
authors: Ziqing Man, Di Wu, Jia-Chen Gu, Junyi Zhang, Kai-Wei Chang, Nanyun Peng
bullets: Introduces a 4,102-case diagnostic benchmark covering reference resolution, explicit qualifiers, and minority perspectives.
Directly evaluates evidence faithfulness, addressing the gap between answer correctness and faithful compression.
Even the strongest evaluated models preserve all required evidence in only 66.8% and 61.6% of cases for the best open-weight and proprietary systems, respectively.
Evidence-preservation performance varies substantially by evidence structure, making narrow evaluations potentially misleading.

Proposes Evidence Preservation Return (EPR), finding that preservation efficiency peaks at moderate model scales but remains low; extra output budget mainly helps stronger models at high computational cost.
papers.selection_reason: Context-compression faithfulness benchmark is directly relevant to long-context and efficient inference.
papers.title: KEEP-Bench: Evaluating Evidence Preservation in Context Compression
papers.tldr: KEEP-Bench shows that context compressors often lose crucial evidence despite strong QA performance, motivating efficient methods that preserve information reliably.

papers.abstract: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) is designed to support flexible representation sizes by jointly optimizing nested prefixes. While effective, this design lacks an explicit constraint to ensure that the leading portion provides a suitable compact encoding. To address this, we propose SpecMRL, which reorganizes the feature space to enable more effective prefix readout. Specifically, we extend MRL with a parameter-derived spectral basis organized with feature importance. SpecMRL otherwise follows standard MRL, with prefix readout performed in the learned spectral space. Experiments on MTEB show that SpecMRL outperforms MRL at all evaluated reduced dimensions, with larger gains under more aggressive compression. These results suggest that the learned spectral basis better prioritizes informative directions, enabling more effective representation compression. Notably, SpecMRL extends the performance frontier of MRL, surpassing full-dimensional MRL with only half the embedding dimensions.
authors: Zhongxin Chen, Songhao Wu, Heng Cui, Cong Li, Xiao Zhou, Rui Yan
bullets: MRL supports flexible representation sizes but does not explicitly ensure that leading dimensions form a strong compact encoding.
SpecMRL derives a spectral basis from model parameters and orders features by importance.
It retains standard MRL training while performing prefix readout in the learned spectral space.
On MTEB, SpecMRL outperforms MRL across evaluated reduced dimensions, with larger gains under stronger compression.
The method reportedly exceeds full-dimensional MRL performance using half the embedding dimensions.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces embedding representation size and memory cost, fitting the efficient-AI scope.
papers.title: SpecMRL: Redesign Matryoshka Representation Learning within Parametric Spectrum
papers.tldr: SpecMRL improves compact embedding quality by reorganizing MRL features into a learned, importance-ordered spectral basis for more effective prefix readout.

papers.abstract: Brain encoding models aim to predict neural responses to stimuli. The most widely used approach fits readouts from frozen pretrained backbones. Using neural data to train large models from scratch or fully fine-tune them after task-pretraining has proven difficult because neural data is costly and limited. We show that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables us to effectively adapt very large pretrained backbones for brain encoding with a small number of trainable parameters. To make it computationally practical, we exploit the backbone's causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in a single pass instead of using sliding windows, significantly reducing feature-extraction cost. This enables efficient fine-tuning of multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters, the largest model adapted for brain encoding to our knowledge. Trained with a low-rank adapter (LoRA) and a lightweight readout, our approach consistently improves brain encoding performance across nine diverse multimodal backbones. On the same Qwen3-Omni backbone as the prior state-of-the-art (SoTA), our method BrainLoRA achieves the best published performance on the Algonauts 2025 Challenge. We also show the adapted multimodal backbones remain interpretable: modality attribution recovers the canonical sensory topography that prior work often obtains by construction from separate unimodal encoders, and neural adaptation increases the contribution of audio inputs and cross-modal mixing within the backbone. To scale out the number of adapted models, we develop a multi-LoRA kernel that accelerates joint training of multiple LoRAs on a shared backbone. This enables an ensemble of 200+ adapted models that ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard at the time of writing. Together, our results highlight PEFT as an efficient and powerful paradigm for brain encoding.
authors: Zhuofan Josh Ying, Guanglong Sun, Nolan Ho, Kieran Liu, Rui Yang, Andrew Chen, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte, Pony Ma, Hossein Adeli
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of training or fully fine-tuning large models with scarce, costly neural data.
Uses LoRA adapters plus a lightweight readout, while exploiting causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in one pass.
Scales adaptation to multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters and improves encoding performance across nine backbones.
BrainLoRA achieves the best published performance on the Algonauts 2025 Challenge using the Qwen3-Omni backbone.
A multi-LoRA kernel supports efficient joint training of 200+ adapted models; adapted models remain interpretable and show increased audio and cross-modal contributions.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning for brain encoding; reduces compute and memory for large multimodal backbones, fitting the efficient-AI theme.
papers.title: Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding
papers.tldr: BrainLoRA uses parameter-efficient adaptation and causal multi-timepoint processing to efficiently scale brain encoding to very large multimodal backbones, achieving state-of-the-art challenge performance and interpretable neural adaptation.

papers.abstract: Benchmark compression reduces evaluation cost by selecting a small set of samples. Existing methods typically guide selection using a single metric, although benchmarks often assess models along multiple dimensions. We find that model rankings are often weakly correlated across metrics, indicating that different metrics capture distinct aspects of model performance. Samples selected for one metric do not reliably preserve scores and rankings on others when used for compressed evaluation. At 80\% compression, each of the five single-metric baselines yields higher reconstruction error than equal-size random sampling in over 70\% of cross-metric comparisons. To address this challenge, we present HoloCosm, which jointly minimizes normalized score-reconstruction error across source models and metrics while constraining ranking distortion. We evaluate HoloCosm across multiple compression rates on 15 language, multimodal, VLA, and agent benchmark configurations with 85 component metrics. With 80\% compression, HoloCosm outperforms Random, the strongest baseline overall: average NMAE drops by 35.3\% to 0.236, worst-component NMAE drops by 39.5\% to 0.330, and average Spearman correlation rises from 0.884 to 0.915. In addition, HoloCosm remains competitive with existing baselines in single-metric evaluation. We will release our code and experimental results.
authors: Yupei Lin, Zhongzhan Huang, Junxin Li, Guoming Ling, Shanshan Zhong, Hefeng Wu, Yukai Shi, Liang Lin
bullets: Single-metric selection often fails to preserve performance across other metrics, with higher cross-metric reconstruction error than random sampling in most comparisons at 80% compression.
HoloCosm jointly minimizes normalized score-reconstruction error across models and metrics while constraining ranking distortion.
Evaluated across 15 language, multimodal, VLA, and agent benchmark configurations covering 85 component metrics.
At 80% compression, HoloCosm improves average and worst-component NMAE over random sampling and raises average Spearman correlation from 0.884 to 0.915.
It remains competitive with existing baselines for single-metric evaluation.],
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark compression reduces evaluation cost across multiple metrics, fitting the efficient-AI scope.
papers.title: HoloCosm: Beyond Single-Metric Benchmark Compression Across Multiple Metrics
papers.tldr: HoloCosm compresses multi-metric benchmarks while better preserving model scores and rankings than single-metric or random sampling.

papers.abstract: Smartphone GUI agents complete tasks in mobile apps by repeatedly reading the screen and asking a model for the next action. Mobile neural processing units (NPUs) enable local execution, keeping screen contents on the phone, but model latency accumulates with every action. Hybrid linear attention models reduce memory requirements, yet reusing their recurrent state requires checkpoints at the appropriate input positions. Agent requests retain instructions but rewrite recent history, so checkpoint policies designed for chat continuation can miss reusable prefixes. Retaining rollback states for speculative decoding can also move prompt processing off the NPU's matrix unit, adding overhead that outweighs decoding savings on short action outputs. A loaded model can further hold the NPU awake between tasks. We present Tandem, a runtime for hybrid GUI agents on mobile NPUs. Tandem saves recurrent state where consecutive prompts diverge, allowing later requests to reuse previously processed context. It keeps most prefill on the matrix unit and produces rollback states through a short per-token tail. Its verification kernel reads each weight block once for all proposed tokens. Between request bursts, Tandem releases NPU power votes without unloading the model. We implement Tandem in llama.cpp and evaluate it on recorded agent interactions across two Snapdragon generations. On a Snapdragon 8 Elite, Tandem reduces per-step latency by 30% for text-based screen descriptions and 16% for screenshots relative to llama.cpp's fastest NPU configuration, reduces energy per text step by 33%, and lowers standby power with the model loaded from 0.76 to 0.22 W.
authors: Zhuomin Chen, Jingchao Ni, Xu Zheng, Yong Chen, Mo Sha, Wei Cheng, Dongsheng Luo
bullets: Targets latency and energy overhead from repeatedly processing evolving GUI-agent prompts on smartphones.
Saves recurrent states at prompt-divergence points so later requests can reuse shared context.
Keeps most prompt processing on the NPU matrix unit and generates rollback states with a short per-token tail.
Uses a verification kernel that reads each weight block once for all proposed tokens, and releases NPU power votes between request bursts.
On Snapdragon 8 Elite, reduces per-step latency by 30% for text descriptions and 16% for screenshots, cuts text-step energy by 33%, and lowers loaded-model standby power from 0.76 to 0.22 W.
papers.selection_reason: Runtime for hybrid linear-attention GUI agents on mobile NPUs; reduces latency and energy via recurrent-state checkpoint reuse and efficient verification.
papers.title: Tandem: Serving Hybrid Linear-Attention GUI Agents on Mobile NPUs
papers.tldr: Tandem is a mobile-NPU runtime that accelerates hybrid linear-attention GUI agents by reusing prompt state efficiently while reducing energy and standby power.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) relies on retaining and using relevant observations. Yet growing histories introduce redundancy, and retained information may remain underused. We introduce ReInsBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines history utilization through controlled continuation trials. Its results show that history-review reinstruction can recover navigation failures using the existing task context. Motivated by this finding, we propose ReInsVLN, a training-free framework supporting memory construction and utilization in frozen navigators. Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression constructs compact visual context through temporal redundancy reduction, coverage-aware protection, and instruction-guided token selection. Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders guide navigators to revisit retained observations according to a predefined schedule, without additional model calls. On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN improves success rates by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points over the native StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1, reaching 64.27% and 64.44%, respectively. Visual compression largely preserves navigation performance while reducing prefill latency and KV cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%, respectively, on matched observation workloads. Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the applicability of ReInsVLN to sequential instruction following and ordinal navigation.
authors: Siwei Cheng, Hao Wu, Zitong Qi, Xinming Zhang, Haoyu Xi, Peiran Yin, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Xiaoyu Shen, Wei Zhang
bullets: ReInsBench diagnoses how effectively vision-and-language navigators use historical observations through controlled continuation trials.
Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression removes temporal redundancy while preserving instruction-relevant visual context.
Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders prompt frozen navigators to revisit retained observations on a predefined schedule without extra model calls.
On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN reaches 64.27% and 64.44% success, improving over StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1 by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points.
Visual compression reduces prefill latency and KV-cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%; robot trials support broader sequential instruction-following use.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free VLN with history compression and reminders, improving navigation while reducing KV cache; fits VLN, embodied memory, and token/cache efficiency.
papers.title: ReInsVLN: Revisiting Historical Evidence for Training-Free Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: ReInsVLN is a training-free memory framework that compresses and periodically reactivates navigation history, improving VLN performance while reducing inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Block diffusion drafters accelerate speculative decoding by generating multiple draft tokens in a single forward pass. However, each pass produces only a fixed-length block from a single target-generated anchor, limiting how far the draft can extend. Meanwhile, target verification computes hidden states even at positions beyond the first rejection, but these states are typically discarded rather than reused. We propose ReAnchor, a training-free method that reanchors a pretrained drafter at shifted positions using discarded verifier states to generate parallel draft blocks. These blocks improve predictions within the original block and extend coverage beyond its endpoint. At sampling temperature of T=0, ReAnchor achieves its largest average gains on Gemma 4-12B, improving acceptance length by 19.4% and decoding speed by 17.9% across eight benchmarks. Averaged equally over four target models and eight benchmarks, it improves acceptance length by 15.2% and decoding speed by 13.4% with pretrained DFlash drafters.
authors: Sanghyun Lee, Wonjin Nam, Seungho Jang, Jaeho Lee, Jiho Park, Jaewoon Lee, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses fixed-length drafting and wasted verifier states beyond the first rejected token.
Reanchors pretrained drafters at shifted positions using verifier states to improve within-block predictions and extend draft coverage.
Training-free and compatible with pretrained DFlash drafters.
At T=0, reports average gains of up to 19.4% in acceptance length and 17.9% in decoding speed on Gemma 4-12B across eight benchmarks.
Across four target models and eight benchmarks, improves acceptance length by 15.2% and decoding speed by 13.4%.
papers.selection_reason: Reuses discarded verifier states to reanchor diffusion drafters, improving speculative decoding speed and memory efficiency.
papers.title: ReAnchor: Reusing Rejected Verifier States for Diffusion Drafting
papers.tldr: ReAnchor reuses discarded verifier hidden states to shift diffusion-drafter anchors, generating parallel blocks that improve speculative decoding acceptance and speed without training.

papers.abstract: In this work, we address real-time fine-grained human activity recognition (HAR) in industrial assembly and introduce PDNet, a new framework that jointly exploits structured pruning and knowledge distillation for 3D convolutional networks. We start by training a 3D-CNN backbone in a supervised manner. Then, PDNet applies channel-wise structured pruning to obtain a more compact network. In the third step, our method is optimized using knowledge distillation from the large unpruned teacher to recover accuracy lost due to pruning. On the challenging MECCANO dataset with an X3D-M backbone, the pruned model without distillation reaches a Top-1 accuracy of 25.54 %, while PDNet raises this to 39.46 %, with only 6.90 MB model size and 3.78 GFLOPs. These results show that distillation within PDNet is highly effective in restoring pruned model performance and highlight its high potential for resource-constrained HAR in industrial assembly.
authors: Malek Baba, Thinesh Thiyakesan Ponbagavathi, Alina Roitberg
bullets: Targets real-time, fine-grained human activity recognition in industrial assembly.
Uses channel-wise structured pruning to reduce the 3D-CNN model, followed by distillation from the unpruned teacher.
On the MECCANO dataset with X3D-M, distillation improves Top-1 accuracy from 25.54% to 39.46% after pruning.
The resulting model is 6.90 MB with 3.78 GFLOPs, supporting resource-constrained deployment.
Scope is demonstrated on one dataset and backbone; broader generalization is not established in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces PDNet, a framework that jointly exploits structured pruning and knowledge distillation for 3D CNNs in human activity recognition. This directly addresses efficiency in model size and computation.
papers.title: PDNet: Exploring Pruning and Distillation for Real-Time Worker Activity Recognition in Industrial Assembly
papers.tldr: PDNet combines structured pruning with knowledge distillation to make 3D-CNN-based industrial activity recognition more compact while recovering accuracy lost through pruning.

papers.abstract: The limited onboard computing resources of robots make the inference demands of vision-language-action (VLA) models costly to accommodate. Reducing these demands through aggressive compression, however, can degrade manipulation performance beyond what supervised fine-tuning alone recovers. We present SPAR (Structural Pruning and Action Recovery), which simultaneously prunes the hidden and feed-forward intermediate dimensions of the large language model (LLM) backbone through pruning-aware tuning, then applies reinforcement learning (RL) to recover policy performance. Applied to $\pi_{0.5}$, SPAR reduces the language backbone from 2.34B to 0.09B parameters and the full model from 3.37B to 1.12B, removing approximately 96% and 67% of their parameters, respectively. At this compression level, RL raises average success across the four LIBERO suites from 84.55% to 93.45%, an 8.90-percentage-point gain. The compressed policy achieves a $1.98\times$ full-policy inference speedup over the unpruned model. These results identify substantial intermediate-dimension redundancy and show that post-pruning RL can recover manipulation performance in compact policies.
authors: Shenli Zheng, Zhou Fang, Yuan Du, Yijiang Liu, Li Du
bullets: Targets costly VLA inference on resource-constrained robots, where aggressive compression can harm manipulation performance.
Prunes the LLM backbone’s hidden and feed-forward intermediate dimensions through pruning-aware tuning.
Uses post-pruning reinforcement learning for action-policy recovery.
On π₀.₅, reduces the language backbone by about 96% and the full model by about 67%.
Across four LIBERO suites, RL improves average success from 84.55% to 93.45%, with a 1.98× inference speedup.
papers.selection_reason: Structural pruning and RL-based recovery for vision-language-action models; directly relevant to VLA and robot manipulation, with an efficiency contribution.
papers.title: SPAR: Structural Pruning and Action Recovery for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: SPAR aggressively compresses a vision-language-action model and uses reinforcement learning to recover—and improve—robot manipulation performance while substantially accelerating inference.

papers.abstract: Expand-and-sparsify ($\texttt{EaS}$) representations lift an input to a much higher dimension through a linear map and keep only the $k$ largest coordinates. Existing theory builds that map at random and needs the expanded dimension to grow exponentially in the input dimension, which puts the construction out of practical reach. We ask what is gained by learning the map by gradient descent instead, and how that gain depends on how wide the expansion is. We sweep $73$ OpenML classification tasks and $48$ regression tasks under a protocol that holds the datasets, expanded dimensions, sparsity levels and splits fixed across every method, and we summarise each comparison by a median over datasets and a Wilcoxon signed rank test. We report four findings. First, learning the expansion helps most when the expansion is narrowest, and its advantage over a random map decays to nothing by the widest expansions we run, so a learned $\texttt{EaS}$ layer can be made small. Second, with the map learned, a top-$k$ representation that keeps at most a tenth of its coordinates is indistinguishable from a dense $\texttt{ReLU}$ layer of the same expanded dimension at every expansion factor we test, while GELU and SiLU are not. Third, when the representation is forced to be binary the sparse code is the better of the two, and the reason is that binarization costs it nothing while it costs the dense layer accuracy. Fourth, how sparse the representation can be is governed by how wide it is: the sparsity level that is free rises as the expansion grows, so there is no fixed limit on how sparse it can be. The regression tasks reproduce the first finding and qualify the second and third.
authors: Alireza Asghari, Parikshit Ram, Kaushik Sinha
bullets: Learned expansion maps outperform random ones most at narrow widths; the advantage disappears at the widest tested expansions.
Keeping at most 10% of coordinates can match a same-width dense ReLU layer, unlike GELU or SiLU, across tested expansion factors.
Under binary representations, sparse codes outperform dense ones because binarization does not reduce sparse-code accuracy.
The sparsity level that remains effectively free increases with expansion width, rather than being capped by a fixed limit.
Findings are based on 73 classification and 48 regression tasks; regression reproduces the learning benefit but qualifies some comparisons.
papers.selection_reason: Learned expand-and-sparsify representations with top-k sparsity are relevant to reducing computation in AI systems.
papers.title: On Learning Expand-and-Sparsify Representations
papers.tldr: Learning the expansion map makes sparse expand-and-sparsify representations practical, with narrower expansions benefiting most and allowable sparsity increasing with expansion width.

papers.abstract: An inference budget is useful only when the system delivers an answer within it. We study a fixed-budget policy combining first-valid-box stopping with a charged finalization cue. On 100 fresh, independently audited GSM8K test questions per model, it improves delivered endpoint accuracy over first-box stopping by 8.0 percentage points for Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and 7.0 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. A prelocked repeat on the same questions gives 7.0 and 10.0 points; neither seed shows a gross harm relative to first-box stopping. The point estimates of incremental physical-slot savings are below one percent. A finalization-only ablation separates cue recovery from stopping, and a fixed scalar reader tests extraction as an alternative explanation. The cue is prior art; the contribution is a component and readout analysis with charged injections and verified paths. Results cover two checkpoints, one task, one prompt family, and two fixed seed conditions.
authors: Yupeng Chang, Linyuan Gao, Zhiyuan Li, Yuan Wu, Yi Chang
bullets: Evaluated on 100 independently audited GSM8K test questions per model using Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B.
Improved endpoint accuracy over first-box stopping by 8.0 and 7.0 percentage points, respectively; a prelocked repeat yielded 7.0 and 10.0 points.
Finalization-only ablations and a fixed scalar reader distinguish cue recovery, stopping, and extraction effects.
Incremental physical-slot savings were below 1%, and no seed showed gross harm relative to first-box stopping.
Scope is limited to two checkpoints, one task, one prompt family, and two fixed seed conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Fixed-budget stopping and finalization policy for LLM answer delivery under shared token budgets.
papers.title: Answer Delivery Under a Shared Token Budget: An Audited Study of Stopping and Finalization
papers.tldr: A charged finalization cue combined with first-valid-box stopping improves delivered GSM8K endpoint accuracy under a shared token budget, though physical-slot savings are negligible.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling can improve LLM reasoning, but existing approaches typically adapt generation or apply answer selection after a predetermined generation schedule. We study within-instance allocation: under a hard per-instance prompt-plus-completion token cap, when should inference stop, generate another candidate, or spend residual tokens adjudicating candidates already observed? BOSS is a training-free policy for this three-way decision, with worst-case budget checks before every generation and judge call. Its key contribution is online generation-adjudication allocation under one shared token ledger. Across two Llama-3.1 models and four reasoning benchmarks, BOSS attains the highest accuracy in 22 of 24 model-task-budget cells under the common hard cap. At Llama-3.1-8B and B=4k, it reaches 60.5 macro-average accuracy versus 58.6 for Adaptive-Consistency, 59.1 for TALE-EP, and 58.9 for fixed-schedule League. On identical Stage-I candidate pools, randomized A/B judging with repeated voting improves plurality from 58.4 to 60.3, with the full BOSS selector reaching 60.5. Approximately matched-cost controls further characterize how the benefit of adjudication changes with available inference budget. Together, these results establish generation-adjudication allocation as a distinct design axis for reasoning under strict per-instance caps.
authors: Yupeng Chang, Yahan Li, Chenlu Guo, Diana Inkpen, Yuan Wu, Yi Chang
bullets: Addresses within-instance inference allocation rather than relying on fixed generation schedules or post-hoc selection.
Uses a training-free policy with worst-case token checks before every generation and judge call.
Maintains one shared token ledger for online generation and adjudication decisions.
Achieves the highest accuracy in 22 of 24 model-task-budget settings across two Llama-3.1 models and four reasoning benchmarks.
At Llama-3.1-8B with a 4k-token cap, BOSS reaches 60.5 macro-average accuracy; its scope is reasoning under hard per-instance token caps.
papers.selection_reason: Token-budgeted online sampling and adjudication for LLM reasoning under hard per-instance caps.
papers.title: BOSS: Token-Budgeted Online Sampling and Selection for LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: BOSS adaptively decides whether to stop, generate another reasoning candidate, or adjudicate existing candidates under a strict per-instance token budget.

papers.abstract: Irregular multivariate time series forecasting (IMTSF) requires capturing temporal dynamics and cross-variable dependencies from sparse, asynchronous observations. Existing methods often rely on learned temporal encoders, coupling historical representation construction with model optimisation and repeatedly processing the same observations. We propose CTLite, a lightweight forecasting framework that decouples historical summarisation from learned prediction. Specifically, a parameter-free continuous-time moment encoder summarises local levels and trends at multiple temporal scales while suppressing poorly supported slope estimates. A compact readout combines damped local extrapolation with a low-rank cross-variable correction that accounts for observation freshness, target availability, and forecast horizon. Since the historical summaries are independent of trainable parameters and forecast queries, they can be reused across optimisation steps and repeated predictions for an unchanged history without altering predictions or parameter gradients. Experiments on four real-world benchmarks show that CTLite achieves the best or second-best mean MSE and MAE among the evaluated methods with only 88-2,537 trainable parameters. Under matched GPU workloads at batch size 32, CTLite reduces inference latency by 18.6-87.3% compared with the latest models, including the cost of historical encoding. Reusing summaries further reduces total runtime by approximately 52% over 16 forecast calls on the same history compared with recomputing the encoder for every call, including the initial encoding cost. The code is at: https://github.com/SSMa913/NICLab-CTLite.
authors: Shusen Ma, Xudong Zuo, Yangchun Xie, Yun-Bo Zhao
bullets: Targets irregular multivariate time series with sparse, asynchronous observations and cross-variable dependencies.
Uses a parameter-free, multi-scale continuous-time moment encoder to summarize local levels and trends while suppressing unreliable slopes.
Combines damped local extrapolation with a compact low-rank correction for cross-variable effects, observation freshness, target availability, and forecast horizon.
Achieves the best or second-best mean MSE and MAE on four real-world benchmarks using only 88–2,537 trainable parameters.
Reduces inference latency by 18.6–87.3% and cuts runtime by about 52% across 16 repeated forecasts when summaries are reused.
papers.selection_reason: Lightweight forecasting framework with reusable summaries and large inference-latency reductions fits the efficient-AI interest.
papers.title: CTLite: Lightweight Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting with Reusable Continuous-Time Summaries
papers.tldr: CTLite enables lightweight, efficient forecasting of sparse asynchronous multivariate time series by reusing parameter-free continuous-time historical summaries.

papers.abstract: Work on efficient large-language-model inference has concentrated almost entirely on reducing the cost of decoding once a request is complete. The quantity a user experiences, however, is the interval between submitting a request and receiving a usable response, and that interval can be shortened without making decoding itself faster. While a request is being composed it is already partially specified, yet conventional deployments begin no computation until submission. We propose and study streaming generation, a decoding regime in which the model begins producing a response from an incomplete request and revises it as the remaining input arrives, so that only a small residue of the answer remains to be computed once the request is submitted. We evaluate the regime on autoregressive and diffusion language models, characterise the conditions under which it reduces user-visible latency, and analyse the mechanism responsible.
authors: Nikita Dragunov, Matvey Mikhalchuk, Anton Razzhigaev
bullets: Targets user-perceived latency rather than decoding cost alone.
Generates from incomplete requests and updates the response as more input arrives.
Evaluated with both autoregressive and diffusion language models.
Characterizes when the approach reduces latency and analyzes why it works.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes streaming generation to reduce user-visible LLM latency, directly fitting efficient-inference interests.
papers.title: Answering While You Type: Optimizing Time-to-Answer with Streaming Generation
papers.tldr: Streaming generation computes an answer while the user is still typing, then revises it as input arrives to reduce time-to-answer after submission.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Diffusion Transformers have emerged as a powerful paradigm for long video generation. However, they are often constrained by prohibitive computational overhead and substantial memory footprints. This inefficiency arises from dense computation mechanisms that allocate uniform processing resources across all spatiotemporal regions, failing to leverage the inherent temporal redundancy of video where motion is typically confined to sparse areas. In this paper, we propose Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention (DASA), a unified framework that shifts from dense computation to sparse, motion-driven generation to eliminate both storage and computational redundancies. Inspired by video codec principles, our approach explicitly decouples video content into dynamic and static regions. To mitigate memory bottlenecks, we selectively compress the historical KV cache by retaining only dynamic features within the generated chunk. Furthermore, to reduce computational overhead, we employ a region-level computation allocation strategy based on localized dynamics. Additionally, a dynamics-guided distillation method is introduced to enhance performance via a lightweight distillation training process. Experiments on VBench demonstrate that our approach accelerates autoregressive video generation by 2.16x, while preserving high visual fidelity.
authors: Yuanyu He, Zhuokun Chen, Yefei He, Zhiwei Tang, Jiasheng Tang, Yinghao Yu, Jianfei Cai, Bohan Zhuang
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and memory usage of dense autoregressive video diffusion.
Separates dynamic and static regions to exploit temporal redundancy in videos.
Compresses historical KV caches by retaining dynamic features and allocates computation according to localized motion.
Uses dynamics-guided distillation to improve performance with lightweight training.
On VBench, achieves 2.16× faster generation while maintaining high visual fidelity.
papers.selection_reason: Directly targets efficient autoregressive video diffusion with sparse attention and KV cache compression, fitting efficient AI and video generation interests.
papers.title: Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Autoregressive Video Diffusion
papers.tldr: DASA makes autoregressive video diffusion more efficient by focusing computation and memory on regions with motion while preserving visual quality.

papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) reason over speech, environmental sounds, music, and other acoustic information. However, their audio encoders produce dense token sequences that make long-form audio costly to process. Existing audio pruning methods reduce this cost using heuristics such as attention, representation similarity, or temporal sampling, but do not explicitly learn which tokens are most useful for a given question. We propose AudioScorer, a lightweight model that scores audio tokens according to the user question. It is trained by distilling the ranking of audio tokens under the frozen LALM's answer-gradient saliency, together with downstream answer supervision. Compared with other pruning methods, AudioScorer achieves the best or tied-best result at 10% token retention on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks, including speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification.
bullets: Targets the high cost of processing dense, long-form audio token sequences in Large Audio Language Models.
Scores tokens conditioned on the user’s question rather than relying on attention, similarity, or temporal-sampling heuristics.
Distills token rankings from a frozen LALM’s answer-gradient saliency and uses downstream answer supervision.
At 10% token retention, achieves the best or tied-best performance on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks.
Evaluated across speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification, among other tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Question-aware audio token pruning for large audio language models; directly fits token pruning/eviction and multimodal LLM efficiency.
papers.title: AudioScorer: Learning Question-Aware Token Relevance for Large Audio Language Models
papers.tldr: AudioScorer learns question-aware audio-token relevance to reduce LALM processing costs while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos but remain computationally expensive. Sparse attention and temporal caching reduce computation within and across denoising steps, respectively, offering a natural composition. However, predictions produced with sparse attention become sources for temporal reuse, coupling their errors along the sampling trajectory. We observe that improving the accuracy of these sources recovers fidelity without changing the reuse schedule, and that sparsification errors remain directionally aligned across nearby steps, suggesting that correction information can be shared rather than recomputed. These observations motivate RECAP, a training-free method that couples sparse attention with hierarchical caching through reciprocal correction, adaptively coordinated by online error feedback. Cached dense refinement corrects omitted interactions in current sparse estimates, while fresh sparse statistics track input changes and regulate the aging correction. The resulting predictions then renew the sources for whole-step prediction reuse, allowing prediction history to advance between dense refreshes. We evaluate RECAP on multiple video diffusion models against sparse-attention methods, caching methods, and their direct compositions. On HunyuanVideo at 720p 5-second generation, RECAP achieves a 3.05x speedup and outperforms all tested direct compositions in both fidelity and inference speed.
authors: Tiange Xu, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of diffusion transformers for high-quality video generation.
Uses training-free reciprocal correction: cached dense refinement fixes sparse-attention omissions, while fresh sparse statistics monitor input changes.
Employs online error feedback to coordinate sparse attention, hierarchical caching, and correction aging without changing the reuse schedule.
Evaluated across multiple video diffusion models against sparse-attention, caching, and direct-composition baselines.
On HunyuanVideo at 720p for 5-second videos, reports a 3.05× speedup and better fidelity and speed than tested direct compositions.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses efficient video diffusion via sparse attention and hierarchical caching, fitting both efficient AI and video diffusion interests.
papers.title: RECAP: Reciprocal Sparse Attention and Hierarchical Caching for Efficient Video Diffusion
papers.tldr: RECAP accelerates video diffusion by combining sparse attention and hierarchical caching with reciprocal error correction, achieving faster and higher-fidelity generation than direct combinations of existing methods.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion has emerged as a leading paradigm for efficient video generation, yet its practical deployment remains bottlenecked by the trade-off between generation quality and inference efficiency. We attribute this bottleneck to three error sources in AR rollouts: the base model error, the train-inference distribution mismatch, and the upstream error propagation. Building on this decomposition, we derive closed-form upper bounds on the per-step and cumulative errors, providing a principled basis for jointly optimizing generation quality and inference efficiency. Guided by this analysis, we propose TriTD, a Tri-Partite Trajectory-Distribution co-optimized distillation framework with three complementary modules. First, for ODE initialization, we adopt a Next-Node Trajectory Distillation (NTD) objective, which shortens the supervision horizon and admits a lower regression-error floor. Second, we introduce Chunk-Graded Noising (CGN), a monotonically non-decreasing per-chunk noising schedule that helps narrow the expected train-inference noise mismatch and removes redundant KV-cache updates, yielding substantial speedups at no quality cost. Third, we propose Orthogonal-Parallel DMD (OP-DMD), a distribution-matching loss that retains the original DMD supervision while introducing an additional regression constraint in the orthogonal subspace to suppress off-axis drift, improving both training stability and final generation quality. Extensive experiments show that TriTD consistently surpasses existing baselines in visual quality while reaching a real-time throughput of 26.8 FPS on a single H100 GPU, delivering a balanced quality-efficiency solution for interactive streaming video generation.
authors: Jia Li, Xurui Peng, Haowei Zhu, Tianyu Zhao, Jiexi Wang, Youwei Zheng, Yuxi Ren, Xinglong Wu, Xing Wang, Hayden Kwok-Hay So
bullets: Targets three AR rollout issues: base-model error, train–inference distribution mismatch, and upstream error propagation.
Derives closed-form bounds for per-step and cumulative errors to guide quality–efficiency optimization.
Combines Next-Node Trajectory Distillation, Chunk-Graded Noising, and Orthogonal-Parallel DMD.
Chunk-Graded Noising reduces redundant KV-cache updates without sacrificing quality, while OP-DMD improves stability and generation quality.
Experiments report consistent visual-quality gains over existing baselines and real-time throughput for interactive streaming video generation.
papers.selection_reason: Autoregressive video generation distillation with KV-cache efficiency improvements.
papers.title: TriTD: Tri-Partite Trajectory-Distribution Distillation for Real-Time Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.tldr: TriTD improves autoregressive video diffusion by jointly reducing rollout errors, enabling higher visual quality and real-time generation at 26.8 FPS on a single H100 GPU.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models enable parallel token generation, offering a promising alternative to sequential autoregressive decoding. Existing acceleration methods use predictive confidence to enable parallel token commitment while preserving generation quality. However, confidence-based selection prioritizes reliable token predictions without explicitly considering how token positions shape the remaining decoding schedule. Moreover, such ordering does not always reflect inter-token dependencies, suggesting that confidence need not be the sole criterion for token selection. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Balance-Aware Pivot Decoding (BPD), which favors central pivots within contiguous masked intervals and decodes the selected positions in parallel. Balanced pivots yield logarithmic decoding depth in the interval length. Our practical method accounts for model uncertainty by combining confidence-based prefilling with confidence-thresholded center selection. We evaluate the resulting quality-efficiency tradeoff on LLaDA and Dream across five mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks. Our implementation is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DLM_random_pivot-EE62/
authors: Yejin Lee, Hyundong Jin, Yo-Sub Han
bullets: Confidence-only decoding overlooks the structure of remaining masked intervals and token dependencies.
BPD selects central pivots within contiguous masked spans, decoding selected positions in parallel.
Balanced pivoting provides logarithmic decoding depth with respect to interval length.
The practical strategy combines confidence-based prefilling with confidence-thresholded center selection.
Evaluated on LLaDA and Dream across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Balance-aware pivot selection for parallel diffusion LLM decoding, improving efficiency via token selection.
papers.title: Balance-Aware Pivot Selection for Parallel Diffusion LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: Balance-Aware Pivot Decoding accelerates diffusion LLM generation by combining confidence with center-focused parallel token selection to reduce decoding depth.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters. They are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT). To save training compute, BPTT is often truncated to the last few loops, although this may weaken the benefit of looping. To study this tradeoff systematically, we jointly vary model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loop counts across nearly 600 training runs and fit a unified scaling law that captures the effects of looping and truncation through effective parameters. Despite the training-compute savings of truncation, our fitted law favors full BPTT when forward and backward loop counts are jointly optimized. In matched-compute runs, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently outperforms truncated settings of the same compute. The law further shows that at fixed model size, the compute-optimal loop count and training-token budget both grow with compute. When model size is also free, the law identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. Experimentally, this setting achieves lower loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.
authors: Xuyuan Xiong, Siyu Chen, Zihan Shao, Yue Su, Weiyang Jin, Ping Luo, Zhuoran Yang, Xihui Liu
bullets: Looped transformers reuse a shared layer block to add depth without adding trainable parameters.
The study varies model size, training tokens, and forward/backward loop counts across nearly 600 runs.
A unified scaling law models looping and truncation using effective parameters.
When compute is matched, full BPTT with fewer loops consistently beats truncated BPTT.
With model size optimized, two fully trained loops achieve lower loss than a compute-optimal non-looped model using about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and 8% more training compute.
papers.selection_reason: Scaling study of looped transformers with truncated backpropagation; relevant to LLM architecture advances and training-efficiency tradeoffs.
papers.title: Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation
papers.tldr: A large scaling study finds that full backpropagation through looped transformers is generally better than truncated training, with two fully trained loops offering an efficient tradeoff.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong potential for time series reasoning, while models that reason over time series are usually with long chains of thought. However, this process often consumes thousands of tokens, directly leading to substantial latency during inference. In contrast, System 1 models such as Jev make decisions instantly and can naturally be an alternative, but raw time series are not compatible with the embedding space of these models, thus hindering the reasoning performance, especially when input series contain thousands of numeric points. In this paper, we make a very early attempt to propose a time series System 1 model, namely TimesJev. Specifically, we first formalize System 1 sufficiency in time series reasoning, which motivates a compressed representation for time series with key frequency patterns preserved. To construct this representation, we derive a dimension reduction objective that combines (i) a sufficiency divergence that measures the core information lost during compression, and (ii) a realizability divergence that quantifies the incompatibility of the System 1 model to the optimal prediction given this representation. We optimize this objective by learning time series compression with a gating mechanism for sufficiency, and then aligning the selected representation with the embedding space for realizability. Finally, experiments on 13 datasets demonstrate that TimesJev outperforms reasoning models by over 62% with 62.9% less inference time than their fine-tuned versions on average.
authors: Chenghao Liu, Wei Fan, Jindong Han, Dongjie Wang, Aniket Mahanti, Pengyang Wang, Hao Liu
bullets: Targets the high latency of long chain-of-thought reasoning over lengthy time series.
Defines System 1 sufficiency and compresses series while retaining important frequency patterns.
Combines sufficiency and realizability divergences to guide compression and embedding alignment.
Uses a gating mechanism to select sufficient information and align it with the System 1 model’s embedding space.
Across 13 datasets, it reportedly outperforms reasoning models by over 62% while reducing inference time by 62.9% versus fine-tuned versions.
papers.selection_reason: System 1 time-series reasoning model reduces inference latency versus long chain-of-thought.
papers.title: TimesJev: Thinking Fast on Time Series with System 1 Sufficiency
papers.tldr: TimesJev enables fast time-series reasoning by compressing signals into System 1-compatible representations while preserving key information.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reasoning models rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) for complex tasks, yet often overthink easy inputs, increasing token cost and latency, and sometimes degrading accuracy. Existing methods optimize reasoning length during training or impose external control at inference, but leave the underlying reasoning mechanism a black box. We find that fast and slow thinking exhibit distinct expert-routing patterns: holding the input fixed and varying only the prompted reasoning tempo produces stable routing shifts. Suppressing slow-thinking experts shortens the reasoning chain, whereas suppressing fast-thinking experts lengthens it, providing causal evidence that these experts influence reasoning depth. Based on this finding, we propose TempoMoE, a training-free, two-stage framework. It identifies fast- and slow-thinking experts via tempo-contrastive routing analysis and redistributes routing weights within the original top-k set according to sample difficulty. It amplifies fast-thinking experts and suppresses slow-thinking experts on easy inputs and reverses this adjustment on hard ones, enabling difficulty-adaptive control over reasoning depth. We evaluate TempoMoE on Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL, and ERNIE-4.5-VL across six benchmarks. Compared with Vanilla, TempoMoE consistently improves accuracy while reducing output tokens, with accuracy gains of up to 2.6 points and token reductions of up to 35.4%.
authors: Xiyue Zhang, Keru Zhou, Ziyi Wang, Bing Hu, Li Wang
bullets: Identifies distinct expert-routing patterns associated with fast versus slow reasoning and shows they causally affect chain-of-thought depth.
Uses a training-free, two-stage tempo-contrastive analysis to identify these experts.
Redistributes routing weights within the original top-k experts based on input difficulty: favoring fast experts for easy inputs and slow experts for hard ones.
Evaluated on Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL, and ERNIE-4.5-VL across six benchmarks, improving accuracy by up to 2.6 points and reducing output tokens by up to 35.4%.
Scope: controls reasoning depth through expert routing without changing model training.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free expert routing steering for efficient multimodal reasoning; reduces token cost and latency in MLLMs.
papers.title: TempoMoE: Identifying and Steering Fast-Slow Thinking Experts for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: TempoMoE adaptively steers fast- and slow-thinking experts to reduce unnecessary multimodal reasoning while improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) enables constant-bit-size transformers to perform general-purpose computation through generated tokens (Li and Wang, 2025a), whereas looped transformers carry out the same computation by recurrence in hidden states (latent thought). We construct a family of constant-bit-size looped transformers that interpolates between CoT and latent thought.
