For a prescribed loop count $L=L(n)$ and a fixed integer $k\ge1$ satisfying $s(n)^{1/k}=\Omega(L)$, our transformer simulates a time-$t(n)$, space-$s(n)$ Turing machine using a context window of $O(s(n)/L)$ and $O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}/L)$ generated tokens, reducing both resources by a factor of $L$ relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation. The construction also holds with softmax attention at constant bit-size, under the finite-precision kernel specified in this paper.
bullets: Bridges explicit CoT, which uses generated tokens, and latent thought, which uses recurrence in hidden states.
For loop count L=L(n) and fixed k≥1 with s(n)^(1/k)=Ω(L), the model simulates a time-t(n), space-s(n) Turing machine.
Uses context window O(s(n)/L) and O(t(n)s(n)^(1/k)/L) generated tokens.
These resources are each reduced by a factor of L relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation.
The construction also works with constant-bit-size softmax attention under the paper’s finite-precision kernel.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical construction of looped transformers that internalize chain-of-thought, reducing context and generated tokens; relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Internalizing Chain-of-thought into Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: A constant-bit-size looped transformer can internalize chain-of-thought into recurrent hidden-state computation while reducing context and generated-token requirements by a factor of the loop count.

papers.abstract: Tool-use agents pay per decision: at each hop a language model re-reads the state and thinks for seconds, though its actions are finite and decisions recur. We present NIOCIS, a routing layer that folds execution logs into a loop-collapsed action graph (forward transitions plus recovery back-edges) answering one typed question: which declared option at a state, plus stop, does the fleet take next? A small model reads a calibrated distribution over them in one pass, emitting no text. On 1,615 production security-operations episodes we measure what the layer replaces, returns and is bounded by. Replaces: the typed encoder matches the logged next hop on 32.2% of the 3,875 held-out decisions (34.9% within the declared options) in 10 ms of encoder time (19.5 ms for the typed-choice form), against 2.2 s per LLM hop; two feature readouts reach 32.8% and 32.3%, an ordering the paired test does not resolve, so the typed layer is chosen for cost, not a separated lead. Tuning: jpt-4b reaches 9.9% zero-shot and 31.9% fine-tuned, a gap an exact paired test does not resolve (p=0.68), at 244 ms. Returns little: the realised hop falls outside the declared options for 7.9% of decisions and outside the model's top twenty for 9.3%; the most confident 15% holds 91.9% accuracy. Bounded: a cross-trace leave-one-out test puts the released state's ceiling at 25.6--44.9% as the state key grows more specific, i.e. repeated states disagree more often than they agree; the option-space ablation attributes the gain to per-node candidate restriction (+3.5 points over a flat catalog) rather than graph traversal (zero within its interval); a gated self-evolution loop lifts every arm above its anchor yet ends below full supervision; a confidence-gated cascade loses agreement when the escalation arm is the zero-shot stand-in; and agreement past a third of the fleet needs a state carrying the plan and the observation.
authors: Jin Han, Mingfeng Xin, Feng Liang, Jingtao Yu
bullets: Builds a loop-collapsed action graph with forward transitions and recovery back-edges, then predicts the next declared option or stop in one pass without generating text.
On 3,875 held-out decisions, the typed encoder matched logged next hops on 32.2% overall and 34.9% within declared options, versus roughly 2.2 seconds per LLM hop.
Node-conditioned candidate restriction contributed a +3.5-point gain over a flat catalog; graph traversal showed no measurable additional gain within the reported interval.
Behavior is difficult to reproduce: 7.9% of realized hops were outside declared options, and repeated states often disagreed, limiting the state-conditioned ceiling to 25.6–44.9%.
The most confident 15% of predictions reached 91.9% accuracy, while broader agreement above one-third of the fleet required state information containing both the plan and observation.
papers.selection_reason: Routing layer replacing expensive LLM hops with small-model decisions; reduces latency and token cost, fits efficient AI.
papers.title: NIOCIS: Typed-Decision Next-Hop Routing with Node-Conditioned Option Spaces for Tool-Use Agents
papers.tldr: NIOCIS accelerates tool-use routing by predicting a typed next action from a node-specific option set, replacing costly LLM decisions with millisecond-scale inference but achieving only partial agreement with logged behavior.

papers.abstract: Multi-hop question answering (QA) requires models to chain intermediate conclusions while remaining cost-aware. Existing training-free self-reflective protocols (generate -> critique -> revise) improve accuracy but operate on a flat token stream: revisions cannot identify which prior step is unreliable, and early stopping cannot exploit structural convergence. We introduce GraphEvoResearcher, a training-free protocol that lifts EvoResearcher's self-reflective meta-reward onto an explicit reasoning graph - nodes are intermediate conclusions/evidence and edges encode support, contradict, and depends_on. A graph-aware meta-reward combines correctness, efficiency, reflection, diversity, and four structural signals (connectivity, acyclicity, branch coverage, path convergence) to decide whether to revise, backtrack, or stop. A graph-convergence early-stop terminates when evidence branches converge on a single conclusion. On a real LLM (DeepSeek), over GSM8K, MATH, and BBH (n=50 each), GraphEvoResearcher reaches 98%, 92%, and 82% respectively, the highest of all baselines, with the largest gains on the hardest set (MATH: +24 pp over single-shot, +12 pp over flat reflection), while keeping construction cost bounded at ~2 steps / 4.5-5 nodes. Our results indicate the structural signal of a reasoning graph is most valuable exactly where single-step reasoning is unreliable.
bullets: Addresses flat generate–critique–revise protocols, which cannot localize unreliable reasoning steps or exploit structural convergence.
Represents intermediate conclusions and evidence as graph nodes with support, contradiction, and dependency edges.
Uses graph-aware rewards covering correctness, efficiency, reflection, diversity, connectivity, acyclicity, branch coverage, and path convergence.
On DeepSeek across GSM8K, MATH, and BBH (50 examples each), achieves 98%, 92%, and 82%, respectively; MATH gains are +24 percentage points over single-shot and +12 over flat reflection.
Keeps construction cost bounded at approximately 2 steps and 4.5–5 nodes; evaluation is limited to the reported model and benchmark samples.
papers.selection_reason: Graph-aware self-reflective reasoning with structural early stopping reduces reasoning cost.
papers.title: GraphEvoResearcher: Graph-Aware Training-Free Self-Reflective Reasoning for Cost-Bounded Multi-Hop Question Answering
papers.tldr: GraphEvoResearcher improves cost-bounded multi-hop QA by using a self-reflective reasoning graph to target revisions and stop when evidence converges.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can improve problem solving, but models often keep generating after the correct answer is already reachable; the extra steps raise serving costs and may replace a correct intermediate result with an incorrect one. We propose GLOBE (Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit), an online, training-free algorithm that terminates the model's CoT process early. GLOBE embeds each completed reasoning segment as a point on a unit sphere and reads the shape of the resulting semantic trajectory. GLOBE first applies a trial phase that generates short trial answers in a separate branch, stopping the main stream on an accepted trial after checking confidence against a threshold. If generation continues, a trajectory phase stops the stream once this path repeatedly reverses direction with little net progress. On five benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, tool calling, and agent memory, GLOBE cuts output tokens by 49.7% and active end-to-end wall time (E2E) by 51.0% across two models, and achieves a five-task average of 80.58%, comparable to Full CoT.
authors: Xinyue Peng, Zhenlin Liang, Meng Cai, Hua Wang
bullets: Addresses unnecessary CoT generation, which increases serving cost and can turn correct intermediate reasoning into incorrect final answers.
Embeds completed reasoning segments on a unit sphere and analyzes their semantic trajectory online.
Uses a trial phase with short branch answers and confidence thresholds, followed by a trajectory phase that detects repeated reversals with little progress.
Across five tasks and two models, reduces output tokens by 49.7% and active end-to-end wall time by 51.0%.
Achieves an 80.58% five-task average, comparable to Full CoT.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free early exit for chain-of-thought reduces output tokens and latency, fitting efficient inference.
papers.title: GLOBE: Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit via Unit-Sphere Trajectories
papers.tldr: GLOBE is a training-free early-exit method that uses confidence checks and geometric trajectory patterns to stop chain-of-thought reasoning earlier, reducing computation while preserving Full-CoT-level performance.

papers.abstract: Most existing approaches to LLM swarm optimization are utility-driven, focusing on final task utility while leaving the processing, integration, and reliance of information within individual interactions largely implicit. To address this, we study LLM swarm interactions from an information-flow-based view and introduce behavioral probes to quantify information flow patterns. Specifically, we repurpose External Context Score (ECS) and Parametric Knowledge Score (PKS)---originally designed for hallucination analysis---to measure a node's external-context dependence and parametric-knowledge dependence, respectively. Across controlled and realistic swarm settings, we observe consistent patterns: ECS increases with input relevance and distinguishes useful multi-source contributions, while PKS decreases as informative context accumulates. Building on this heuristic interpretation, we demonstrate how these probes can complement utility-driven structure optimization in two controlled applications. Probe-guided node pruning reduces redundant communication and token consumption, and probe-guided reasoning-path search accelerates convergence compared to utility-only baselines. Our empirical results suggest that behavioral probes can make the internal information flow of LLM swarms observable and serve as effective auxiliary signals for structure optimization.
authors: Junhui Chen, Yu Zhang, Lantian Li, Dong Wang
bullets: Reframes swarm analysis from final utility to how agents process, integrate, and rely on information.
Uses ECS to measure external-context dependence and PKS to measure parametric-knowledge dependence.
ECS rises with input relevance and captures useful multi-source contributions, while PKS falls as informative context accumulates.
Probe-guided pruning reduces redundant communication and token use; probe-guided path search accelerates convergence versus utility-only baselines.
Demonstrates probes as auxiliary signals for swarm structure optimization across controlled and realistic settings.
papers.selection_reason: Probe-guided pruning reduces token consumption and communication in LLM swarms; transferable to efficient AI.
papers.title: Behavioral Probes for Information Flow in LLM Swarms
papers.tldr: Behavioral probes based on ECS and PKS make information flow in LLM swarms measurable and support more efficient communication and reasoning-path optimization.

papers.abstract: Offline compaction of the key--value cache (KV-cache) reduces the cost of repeatedly querying a fixed context by constructing a smaller cache once and reusing it subsequently. The central challenge of compaction is deciding which cache entries to delete and which to retain. Existing methods score each candidate for deletion on its own, with the rest of the cache being held fixed. However, softmax renormalization of the attention operation couples these decisions in a nonlinear manner: removing one entry changes the attention weights of every remaining one. In this work, we introduce KV-Surgeon, which uses calibration data to take interactions into account in a tractable way. We derive a quadratic surrogate that admits closed-form expressions for jointly making the optimal greedy removal decision as well as compensation within the remaining entries. On QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena, and at every evaluated compaction ratio, KV-Surgeon substantially advances the cost--accuracy Pareto frontier of dense and mixture-of-experts models from 4B to 30B parameters. At $50\times$ compaction, KV-Surgeon improves question-answering accuracy by up to four points over attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026), the state of the art, at comparable cost. Lastly, we introduce an even faster variant, which also exceeds the state of the art while requiring only two fifths of its cost.
authors: Moritz Wagner, Christophe Roux, Max Zimmer, Sebastian Pokutta
bullets: Existing methods evaluate cache entries independently, overlooking how deleting one entry changes attention over all others.
KV-Surgeon uses calibration data and a quadratic surrogate to jointly choose greedy deletions and compensate remaining entries.
It improves the cost–accuracy Pareto frontier across QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena for dense and mixture-of-experts models.
At 50× compaction, it improves question-answering accuracy by up to four points over attention matching at comparable cost.
A faster variant also surpasses the prior state of the art at two-fifths of its cost.
papers.selection_reason: Directly targets KV-cache compaction and memory-efficient LLM inference with compensation-aware offline pruning.
papers.title: The KV-Surgeon: Compensation-Aware Offline KV-Cache Compaction
papers.tldr: KV-Surgeon improves offline KV-cache compaction by modeling interactions caused by softmax renormalization, achieving better accuracy–cost tradeoffs than prior methods.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models primarily rely on general-purpose ODE-based numerical methods for training-free accelerated sampling, but performance degrades with coarse time discretization. In this paper, we propose optimal linear leaps (LEAP), a specialized method grounded in theoretical and empirical investigations of sampling trajectory geometry. Built upon low-dimensionality and cross-trajectory consistency, LEAP formulates a supervised least-squares optimization problem within the local trajectory subspace, achieving a precise approximation of future states without model evaluations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LEAP outperforms previous methods across diverse modalities, including text-to-image (Stable Diffusion 3.5, FLUX.1-dev) and image-to-3D (TRELLIS.2) generation. Furthermore, LEAP can be seamlessly integrated into existing solver-based methods, offering a plug-and-play enhancement for modern diffusion models. Code is available at https://github.com/zju-pi/LEAP.
authors: Haowei Zheng, Zhenyu Zhou, Jiawei Chen, Can Wang, Defang Chen
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by coarse time discretization in accelerated diffusion sampling.
Uses low-dimensionality and cross-trajectory consistency to formulate a supervised least-squares optimization problem.
Approximates future sampling states without additional model evaluations.
Works across text-to-image and image-to-3D generation, including Stable Diffusion 3.5, FLUX.1-dev, and TRELLIS.2.
Can be integrated as a plug-and-play enhancement with existing solver-based methods.
papers.selection_reason: Accelerates ODE-based diffusion sampling with optimal linear leaps (LEAP). This improves inference efficiency for diffusion models, relevant to efficient AI and video diffusion.
papers.title: LEAP: Accelerating ODE-based Diffusion Sampling with Optimal Linear Leaps
papers.tldr: LEAP accelerates ODE-based diffusion sampling by predicting future states through optimal linear extrapolation in a local trajectory subspace, reducing the need for model evaluations.

papers.abstract: Automated Gleason grading of prostate whole slide images (WSIs) enables faster and more consistent cancer risk stratification. However, it remains a challenging task due to the subtle morphological differences between grades, the severe class imbalance arising from rare patterns, and the diagnostic features that span multiple spatial scales. Pathology foundation models (FMs) extract strong patch representations but often operate at a single-scale, which limits spatial context and disproportionately affects classes that depend on broader context. The challenge of fusing multiple scales and complementary models, with minimal data and computational resources, remains unresolved. We propose a multi-scale classifier built on state-space models. Our method combines two complementary feature sources: a frozen foundation model, and a lightweight FastVim, pre-trained on ImageNet and distilled from the foundation model, that reads the raw image crops. At each scale, a Mamba model encodes the features from both sources with linear-time spatial context, and a jointly trained head fuses the encoded representations into one prediction. On the PANDA dataset, our method reaches macro F1 of 0.894 and Gleason 5 F1 of 0.802 under 5-fold cross-validation, a 12% and 21% relative improvement over the best single-scale model. A controlled study over 5 foundation models, 5 base classifiers and 3 scales confirms that the gain holds across encoders, with larger improvements observed at smaller scales.
authors: Zihe Zhang, Weimiao Yu, Piumi Don Simonge
bullets: Addresses subtle morphology, class imbalance, and multi-scale context challenges in prostate WSI grading.
Uses frozen foundation-model features alongside ImageNet-pretrained, foundation-model-distilled FastVim features from raw crops.
Mamba encoders provide linear-time spatial context at each scale, followed by joint feature fusion for prediction.
On PANDA with 5-fold cross-validation, achieves 0.894 macro F1 and 0.802 Gleason 5 F1.
Improvements are consistent across tested foundation models and classifiers, with larger gains at smaller scales.
papers.selection_reason: Fuses foundation model features with Fast Vision Mamba for pathology grading. The use of Mamba (state space models) and foundation models is relevant to multimodal foundation models and efficient AI architectures.
papers.title: Multi-scale Fusion of Fast Vision Mamba and Foundation Model Features for Patch-Level Gleason Grading in Computational Pathology
papers.tldr: A multi-scale Mamba-based model fusing pathology foundation-model and FastVim features improves patch-level Gleason grading, especially for rare Gleason 5 patterns.

papers.abstract: Large self-supervised speech models provide powerful representations for speaker verification, but full fine-tuning is expensive. Most conventional adapters insert small trainable modules to modify the output of each layer, while keeping the original residual connections unchanged. Building on our preliminary study of manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections in speaker encoders, we explore parameter-efficient adaptation of both residual paths and feature selection across layers. We first propose a Manifold-Constrained Residual Adapter (MCRA), which splits the hidden dimensions of each Transformer residual state into N groups and uses a small Sinkhorn-normalized matrix to exchange information among them. A learnable gate controls the balance between the original and mixed residual paths. The gate adds only one scalar parameter at each residual connection and initially favors the original path, allowing gradual adaptation. We further propose Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation (FALA), an attention-based aggregation method that uses a single learned query shared across all utterances to compute layer weights separately for each speech frame. Because the layer representations depend on the input, the resulting weights vary across both utterances and frames, unlike the fixed weights of a conventional layer-weighted sum. Compared with a frozen WavLM baseline using a fixed layer-weighted sum, our method achieves relative EER reductions of 22.4% on VoxCeleb1-O and 2.9% on CN-Celeb, with trainable adaptation parameters equivalent to only 0.0009% and 0.0016% of the WavLM-Large parameters, respectively.
authors: Zezhong Jin, Xiaoyu Wang, Zhe Li, Chong-Xin Gan, Siqing Qin, Man-Wai Mak, Kong Aik Lee
bullets: MCRA splits residual states into groups, exchanges information using a Sinkhorn-normalized matrix, and learns a gate balancing original and adapted paths.
FALA uses a shared learned query to assign input-dependent layer weights separately for every speech frame.
The method targets efficient adaptation without full fine-tuning of large self-supervised speech models.
Relative EER reductions are 22.4% on VoxCeleb1-O and 2.9% on CN-Celeb versus a frozen WavLM baseline.
Adaptation uses only 0.0009%–0.0016% of WavLM-Large’s parameters, depending on the evaluation set.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient residual adaptation and layer aggregation reduce trainable parameters, transferable to efficient fine-tuning of large models.
papers.title: Manifold-Constrained Residual Adaptation with Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation for Speaker Verification
papers.tldr: A highly parameter-efficient speaker-verification adaptation method jointly modifies residual paths and selects Transformer layers dynamically for each speech frame, substantially reducing EER over a frozen WavLM baseline.

papers.abstract: Unlike on-policy distillation (OPD), which depends on a separate teacher model, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) leverages a single language model acting simultaneously as the student and the teacher, with the teacher conditioned on privileged information. Despite this architectural simplicity, synchronous rollout generation dominates overall training time, creating a severe systems bottleneck when scaling OPSD. To address this, we introduce Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation (AsyncOPSD), a framework that decouples rollout generation from learner updates to improve training throughput. Since the teacher and student share parameters, AsyncOPSD eliminates the multi-model coordination overhead inherent to OPD architectures in asynchronous training. As the student policy evolves, buffered trajectories generated by older policies become stale, potentially degrading performance. To mitigate this, we introduce a distillation objective based on staleness-aware policy control and token-level entropy weighting. Across three model sizes and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, AsyncOPSD improves the training throughput by $1.96$--$2.25\times$ over synchronous OPSD while increasing average benchmark accuracy.
authors: Xidong Wu, Qi Qi, Yuqiong Ji, Shangqian Gao
bullets: Synchronous rollout generation is a major throughput bottleneck in on-policy self-distillation.
AsyncOPSD decouples rollout generation and learner updates, avoiding multi-model coordination overhead because teacher and student share parameters.
It addresses stale buffered trajectories with staleness-aware policy control and token-level entropy weighting.
Across three model sizes and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, it achieves 1.96–2.25× higher training throughput than synchronous OPSD and improves average accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Asynchronous on-policy self-distillation improves LLM training throughput by ~2x; reduces training compute/time.
papers.title: Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: AsyncOPSD accelerates on-policy self-distillation by asynchronously separating rollout generation from learner updates while maintaining or improving reasoning accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models often produce lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) traces mixing useful intermediate steps with unnecessary ones. Recent methods explore step-level signals such as attention mass and step entropy to identify and suppress unnecessary steps. Despite their effectiveness, such signals reflect the model's behavior at a step rather than that step's contribution to the answer. To address this, we propose the interventional step credit (ISC), which takes a causal-intervention view and assesses step importance to the reasoning through targeted parameter-level interventions. Building on ISC, we further propose IGPO, which uses ISC to guide fine-grained advantage rescaling in reinforcement learning, reducing redundant steps while preserving the important ones. Experiments across two model scales and nine benchmarks show that IGPO achieves up to 62% average token reduction and better overall performance among compared methods.
authors: Guanda Li, Xuefeng Bai, Yulong Chen, Zhiyong Wang, Kehai Chen, Min Zhang
bullets: Long reasoning traces often mix useful and redundant intermediate steps.
Existing step signals describe model behavior but not each step’s causal contribution to the answer.
Interventional Step Credit (ISC) estimates step importance through targeted parameter-level interventions.
IGPO uses ISC to rescale reinforcement-learning advantages at fine granularity.
Across two model scales and nine benchmarks, IGPO reduces average tokens by up to 62% while improving overall performance versus compared methods.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces redundant chain-of-thought steps in large reasoning models via interventional step credit, directly relevant to efficient LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Learning to Reason Efficiently with Interventional Step Credit
papers.tldr: IGPO uses causal, intervention-based step credit to shorten chain-of-thought reasoning while preserving important steps and improving performance.

papers.abstract: Allocating limited trainable capacity across convolutional layers is a central challenge in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of pretrained three-dimensional (3D) networks. We propose Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation, which jointly selects input- and output-channel ranks under a fixed adapter-parameter budget while preserving the spatial kernel modes. To guide rank selection, we learn task-specific proxy updates from downstream training data and approximate them using candidate Tucker rank pairs. A perturbation analysis bounds the output discrepancy between the fixed proxy network and its Tucker approximation in terms of layerwise reconstruction residuals, motivating residual-based allocation. We normalize each squared residual by the corresponding proxy-update energy to compare relative approximation errors across layers. Dynamic programming minimizes their sum under a global budget constraint that accounts for both channel factors and the Tucker core. This yields a globally optimal allocation over the specified candidate rank pairs. We evaluate the method on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort for predicting conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease within 36 months, using hippocampal segmentation pretraining. Across five random seeds, the proposed method achieves a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.7706, compared with 0.7239 for fixed-ratio Tucker adaptation and 0.7430 for full fine-tuning. The total number of trainable parameters is limited to approximately 0.618 million, accounting for only 1.45% of the full model. Adaptive Tucker rank allocation thus provides an effective approach to parameter-efficient transfer learning in 3D medical imaging.
authors: Guanghua He, Hancan Zhu, Gaohang Yu, An Zhang
bullets: Targets parameter-efficient fine-tuning of pretrained 3D networks for 36-month MCI conversion prediction.
Learns task-specific proxy updates and approximates them with candidate input/output Tucker rank pairs while preserving spatial kernel modes.
Uses normalized layerwise reconstruction residuals and dynamic programming to find a globally optimal rank allocation under a fixed adapter budget.
On ADNI, achieves mean AUC 0.7706 across five seeds, versus 0.7239 for fixed-ratio Tucker adaptation and 0.7430 for full fine-tuning.
Uses approximately 0.618 million trainable parameters, or 1.45% of the full model; evaluation is scoped to ADNI with hippocampal-segmentation pretraining.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning via adaptive Tucker rank allocation under a fixed parameter budget; directly targets training efficiency.
papers.title: Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient MCI Conversion Prediction
papers.tldr: A residual-guided dynamic-programming method allocates Tucker ranks across 3D convolutional layers under a strict parameter budget, improving MCI-to-Alzheimer’s conversion prediction over the compared baselines.

papers.abstract: Rollout decoding affects both which trajectories are used for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and how many completion tokens are spent collecting them. We study whether candidate-token support should remain fixed or widen during training in the context of rollout sampling efficiency. Our main schedule moves from top-K=10 to K=20 and then to full support as the attempted-token budget increases. In a 4B code-RLVR setting, the schedule has a higher interpolated 150M-token validation value than its matched fixed-K=10 continuation in all three runs, with a mean gain of $1.80{\pm}0.42$ points. The schedule also performs comparably to a separately trained fixed-K=20 baseline, the strongest fixed-support setting in our sweep. Follow-up experiments suggest that late widening to full support is the most promising variant, although the evidence remains noisy, and mixed-reward-group diagnostics do not clearly explain the gain. An exploratory single-run test replay yields identical point estimates for the schedule and fixed $K=10$. Overall, our results show that rollout support is an important control for sampling efficiency in RLVR and motivate further study of adaptive support schedules.
authors: Zhaonan Li, Zelei Cheng, Amritansh Mishra, Chia-Hsuan Lee, Mann Patel, Sambit Sahu, Ben Zhou, William M. Campbell
bullets: Fixed versus widening candidate-token support is studied for efficient RLVR rollout sampling.
The main schedule increases support from top-K=10 to 20, then to full support as the token budget grows.
In a 4B code-RLVR setting, it outperformed matched fixed-K=10 training across three runs, with a mean gain of 1.80 ± 0.42 validation points at 150M tokens.
Performance was comparable to separately trained fixed-K=20, the strongest fixed-support baseline tested.
Late widening to full support appeared most promising, but diagnostics and a single-run replay did not provide a clear explanation or consistently reproduce the gain.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive rollout decoding reduces token cost in reinforcement learning, offering a transferable efficiency-oriented training technique.
papers.title: Adaptive Decoding Methods for Token-Efficient Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Adaptive widening of rollout token support can improve token-efficient RLVR training, though the evidence is noisy and needs further study.

papers.abstract: Training high-quality diffusion models is computationally expensive, and inference-time guidance often adds further sampling cost. In this work, we introduce Swift, a simple yet effective self-guided training method that uses a frozen weak denoiser to improve a stronger model without adding inference overhead. For each noisy input, Swift extrapolates the clean regression target away from the weak denoiser's prediction, amplifying components that remain underfit. The weak guide can be an early training checkpoint, requires no backpropagation during main-model training, and is discarded afterward. The resulting model retains the original sampler and supports both conditional and unconditional generation without label dropout or an unconditional branch. We explain this mechanism through a spectral analysis of finite-time population gradient flow in an RKHS. With an early-stopped weak guide, we prove that a nonempty range of extrapolation strengths yields strictly lower posterior-mean error than matched standard training, despite shifting the regression target away from the posterior mean. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 demonstrate improvements across model scales and representations. In one ImageNet-256 configuration, Swift surpasses the baseline's best FID using roughly half the total training compute, including guide preparation and training overhead. On RAEv2, it achieves FID 1.15 without inference-time guidance and 0.99 with guidance. These results establish target extrapolation as an effective approach to weak-to-strong diffusion training with efficient single-model inference.
authors: Yanjin He, Cuifeng Shen, Wanzhou Lei, Maohua Li, Tao Lan, Kan Liu, Hanlin Tang, Qing Qu
bullets: Addresses the high training cost of diffusion models and the sampling cost of inference-time guidance.
Uses an early checkpoint or other frozen weak denoiser to identify underfit components and shift clean regression targets away from its predictions.

The guide requires no backpropagation during main training and is discarded afterward; the final model retains the original sampler and supports conditional and unconditional generation without label dropout.
An RKHS spectral analysis explains the method and proves that some extrapolation strengths can reduce posterior-mean error versus matched standard training.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 show improvements across scales and representations; one ImageNet-256 setup reaches the baseline’s best FID with roughly half the total training compute, while RAEv2 achieves FID 1.15 without and 0.99 with inference guidance.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes self-guided diffusion training that reduces training compute without inference overhead, transferable to efficient generative model training.
papers.title: SWIFT: Self-guided Weak-to-strong dIFfusion models via Target extrapolation
papers.tldr: SWIFT trains stronger diffusion models using a frozen weak denoiser to extrapolate targets, improving quality without adding inference-time overhead.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) supervises student-generated trajectories with a reference-conditioned version of the same base model. We ask whether every trajectory supplies distinct supervision that warrants its distillation cost. Gradient measurements on Qwen3-1.7B at initialization reveal that correct and incorrect responses have similar individual gradient magnitudes, but incorrect responses have approximately three times the coherent gradient share. Their estimated population-mean directions also largely overlap. A signal--noise model fitted at a small group size tracks alignment at larger group sizes without refitting. Motivated by these measurements, we introduce correctness-filtered OPSD (C-OPSD), which generates one response per problem and distills only a subset of incorrect responses. Removing unselected rows before both distillation forwards avoids their teacher/student forward and student backward work. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, C-OPSD achieves on-par performance with full OPSD. In a measured micro-batch-size-four implementation, executed rows decrease by approximately 68%, and with retained rows packed into full micro-batches, training takes about 40% less time while rollout generation remains unchanged. Together, the measurements and training results connect outcome-conditioned supervision redundancy to more compute-efficient distillation.
authors: Harrison Zhao, Lei Huang, Fei Liu, Wen Shi, Zijian Jin
bullets: Incorrect responses provide more coherent gradient signal than correct responses despite similar individual gradient magnitudes, suggesting supervision redundancy.
C-OPSD generates one response per problem and distills only a selected subset of incorrect responses.
Filtering rows before teacher/student forwards and student backpropagation reduces executed rows by approximately 68%.
Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, C-OPSD performs on par with full OPSD.
With packed retained rows, training takes about 40% less time; rollout generation is unchanged.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a method to filter incorrect training trajectories during self-distillation, effectively pruning tokens/rows to reduce computational cost. Directly addresses efficiency in training.
papers.title: Not Every Rollout Needs Distillation: Correctness-Filtered On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: Correctness-filtered on-policy self-distillation removes most incorrect trajectories from distillation while preserving full-OPSD performance and reducing training compute.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models can write several tokens in one forward pass, and they decide during generation how many passes to spend. Two outputs of the same token length can therefore vary a lot in cost. To understand the underlying factors of this cost variation, we analyze two diffusion models across 10 tasks. We find that the number of forward passes per token depends heavily on the task. Text copied or lightly edited from the input is cheap, while open-ended writing is costly. In DiffusionGemma, generating a token for story writing requires more than three times as many forward passes as for grammar correction. Two output properties explain much of this gap: how much of it is new relative to the input, and how rare its words are within the task. The same holds within a single response when thinking is involved. The final answer is cheap when it repeats the model's reasoning trace and costly when it adds something new. In multilingual generation, we find that highly tokenized languages also require more passes per token, adding to the cost they already pay with more tokens. Finally, cost tracks correctness: on the same math problem, wrong answers take more passes per token than correct ones, and weighting candidate answers by decoding speed beats majority voting by up to 4.2 points at no extra cost. Taken together, our results show that diffusion's computational advantage depends on how much of the output is already determined, while its decoding effort offers a practical signal for making inference more efficient and reliable.
authors: Mohsen Fayyaz, Ali Modarressi, Daniel Israel, Lucas Bandarkar, Nanyun Peng
bullets: Across 10 tasks, copied or lightly edited text is cheaper to generate than open-ended writing.
In DiffusionGemma, story writing needs over three times as many forward passes per token as grammar correction.
Generation cost is largely explained by output novelty relative to the input and word rarity; this also applies to reasoning traces and final answers.
Highly tokenized languages require more passes per token, compounding their cost from producing more tokens.
Wrong math answers take more passes per token than correct ones; speed-weighted answer selection improves over majority voting by up to 4.2 points without extra cost.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and exploits decoding-cost variation in diffusion language models, offering a practical signal for more efficient inference.
papers.title: Diffusion Language Models Change Speed Across Tasks and Languages
papers.tldr: Diffusion language models spend more decoding effort on novel, rare, highly tokenized, and incorrect outputs, making generation cost strongly task- and language-dependent.

papers.abstract: Micro-expert pruning reduces the capacity of mixture-of-experts (MoE) models by removing coupled channels within routed experts. However, finer pruning granularity alone does not guarantee the preservation of downstream capabilities, as similar language-modeling perplexity can accompany substantially different task performance. We revisit micro-expert mask construction as two distinct decisions: allocating retained capacity across experts and selecting channels within that capacity. We propose UC-RAMP, a two-stage post-training pruning framework that explicitly separates these decisions. CAPE uses cross-domain calibration evidence to redistribute expert widths under an exact layer-wise budget, while RAMP refines channel composition at fixed widths through one-out, one-in exchanges guided by a channel-interaction surrogate. Across three MoE models at 25% and 50% routed-expert channel pruning, UC-RAMP achieves the highest ten-task mean accuracy among evaluated pruning methods in five of six settings. At 50% pruning, it outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline by 8.19, 3.96, and 6.14 percentage points across the three models, respectively. In a single-A100 deployment at 25% pruning, UC-RAMP reduces measured time to first token by 19.7--23.9% and time per output token by 20.2--22.3% relative to the unpruned model. The code is available at https://github.com/xzktx003/UC_RAMP.
authors: Zukang Xu, Xinpei Gao, Xing Hu, Zhe Jiang, Dawei Yang
bullets: Micro-expert pruning can maintain language-modeling perplexity yet degrade downstream tasks, motivating better mask construction.
CAPE redistributes retained expert widths using cross-domain calibration under exact layer-wise budgets.
RAMP refines channel selection at fixed widths via one-out, one-in exchanges guided by channel interactions.
Across three MoE models and two pruning levels, UC-RAMP achieved the best mean accuracy in five of six settings.
At 25% pruning, it reduced single-A100 time to first token by 19.7–23.9% and time per output token by 20.2–22.3% versus the unpruned model.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes UC-RAMP, a two-stage pruning framework for Mixture-of-Experts models that separates expert width allocation from channel selection to improve efficiency and accuracy.
papers.title: Fine-Grained Units, Flat Decisions: Hierarchical Micro-Expert Pruning for Mixture-of-Experts Models
papers.tldr: UC-RAMP improves MoE pruning by separately reallocating capacity across experts and selecting channels within each expert, preserving task performance while reducing inference latency.

papers.abstract: Layer-level pruning is attractive for large language model (LLM) deployment as it reduces the model size while preserving a dense architecture that can be efficiently executed on standard hardware. Current methods typically follow a one-shot paradigm, which first removes selected layers to reach a target model size and then performs additional training to recover model capabilities. However, pruning directly to the target size can substantially degrade reasoning capabilities, making subsequent recovery more difficult under a limited training budget. Moreover, this paradigm separates layer selection from recovery, limiting the use of recovery information to guide selection and potentially hindering the recovery of reasoning capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose LOOP, a Layer-level Recovery-Oriented On-Policy Pruning framework that interleaves pruning and recovery across multiple shots. In each shot, LOOP removes a single layer and performs short on-policy distillation, mitigating the abrupt degradation in reasoning capabilities associated with one-shot pruning. To guide layer selection in subsequent shots, LOOP reuses on-policy trajectories and optimization signals from recovery to jointly assess each remaining layer's reasoning contribution and recovery sensitivity, thereby making layer selection recovery-aware. Evaluations on several benchmarks show that LOOP consistently outperforms one-shot baselines in average accuracy across different model scales and pruning ratios.
authors: Liang Xu, Shufan Shen, Zhongni Hou, Yufei Zhang, Wei Lin, Guojun Yin, Shuhui Wang
bullets: One-shot pruning can sharply damage reasoning, making capability recovery difficult under limited training budgets.
LOOP removes one layer at a time across multiple shots, applying short on-policy distillation after each removal.
Recovery trajectories and optimization signals help estimate each remaining layer’s reasoning contribution and recovery sensitivity.
Across several benchmarks, LOOP consistently achieves higher average accuracy than one-shot baselines across model scales and pruning ratios.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes iterative layer pruning with on-policy distillation to reduce LLM size, fitting efficient AI objectives.
papers.title: LOOP: Recovery-Aligned Iterative Layer Pruning via On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: LOOP improves LLM layer pruning by interleaving gradual layer removal with on-policy recovery and using recovery signals to guide later pruning decisions.

papers.abstract: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) enables efficient deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet activation outliers remain a key challenge for low-bit quantization. Existing global transformation methods overlook heterogeneous channel sensitivity to quantization noise, leading to suboptimal accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. To address this, we propose \textbf{Locally Isolated Rotation Quantization (LIRQuant)}, a sensitivity-aware framework that selectively applies transformations. LIRQuant identifies sensitive channels using a noise-weighted sensitivity metric, applying expressive learnable rotations only to these channels and lightweight fixed rotations to the remaining ones. This decoupled design reduces optimization complexity without sacrificing outlier smoothing capability. Extensive experiments across the LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, Qwen3, and Mixtral families demonstrate that LIRQuant achieves state-of-the-art accuracy under the challenging W4A4KV4 setting. Meanwhile, LIRQuant calibrates LLaMA-3-8B in only 25 minutes with 20.3 GB peak GPU memory, achieving the fastest calibration and the lowest memory footprint among recent learnable-rotation methods, and its fused inference kernels deliver up to $2.3\times$ prefill speedup and $3.5\times$ memory saving over FP16.
authors: Desheng Xu, Hanglin Li, Tianchen Song, Zhiyong Zhao, Kun Zhan
bullets: Addresses activation outliers and heterogeneous channel sensitivity in post-training quantization.
Uses a noise-weighted metric to identify sensitive channels.
Applies learnable rotations to sensitive channels and lightweight fixed rotations elsewhere.
Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across several LLM families under W4A4KV4.
For LLaMA-3-8B, calibration takes 25 minutes with 20.3 GB peak GPU memory; fused kernels provide up to 2.3× prefill speedup and 3.5× memory savings over FP16.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes LIRQuant, a sensitivity-aware quantization method for LLMs that reduces memory footprint and improves inference speed through selective learnable rotations and fused kernels.
papers.title: LIRQuant: An Efficient Locally Isolated Rotation Quantization Method for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: LIRQuant improves low-bit LLM quantization by applying stronger rotations only to sensitive channels, enabling accurate and efficient W4A4KV4 deployment.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching models achieve impressive visual generation quality but remain computationally expensive due to iterative sampling. Caching-based acceleration provides a practical training-free solution by reusing or predicting intermediate features. However, existing methods largely enforce a forward-only information flow: approximations produced for skipped model evaluations are immediately committed to the sampling trajectory and cannot benefit from feedback generated by later full-computation steps. We propose \textbf{PoSTCache} (\emph{Postdictive Smoothing Trajectory Cache}), a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates diffusion caching as revisable trajectory inference. PoSTCache first uses an existing caching strategy to construct forward proposals for skipped steps. At a later full-computation step, the discrepancy between the refreshed prediction and its forward proposal yields a correction signal, which PoSTCache propagates backward to refine and reintegrate the preceding predictions. Viewing full-computation steps as sources of corrective feedback also changes how they should be selected. We therefore introduce the Posterior Variance Reduction (PVR) strategy, which estimates cross-timestep dependencies from offline denoising trajectories and selects anchors according to their expected reduction in surrogate trajectory uncertainty rather than local approximation error alone. Experiments on representative image and video generation models show that PoSTCache consistently improves the quality--efficiency trade-off over representative caching methods.
authors: Liwei Lan, Hui Chen, Jungong Han, Guiguang Ding
bullets: Existing caching methods commit forward-only approximations that cannot incorporate later feedback.
PoSTCache uses an existing cache for forward proposals, then propagates discrepancy-based corrections backward from later full-computation steps.
Its PVR strategy selects full-computation anchors by estimated reduction in trajectory uncertainty using offline denoising trajectories.
Experiments on image and video generation models show consistent improvements over representative caching methods.
The framework is training-free and plug-and-play, with results scoped to the evaluated models and tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a revisable trajectory cache for diffusion models that uses postdictive smoothing to correct previous steps, improving the efficiency-quality trade-off of inference.
papers.title: PoSTCache: From Forecasting to Postdictive Smoothing for Revisable Diffusion Caching
papers.tldr: PoSTCache makes diffusion caching revisable by using later full computations to correct earlier skipped-step predictions, improving the quality–efficiency trade-off.

papers.abstract: Looped (weight-tied) transformers enable adaptive computation by allocating more iterations to harder inputs. Fixed-Point Reasoners (FPRM) achieve this with a damped fixed-point solver, but operate in an unbounded Euclidean residual space with coupled rescaling and relative-norm halting. We introduce Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners (SFPRM), which perform the same computation on the unit hypersphere of normalized transformers (nGPT). Input injection, damping, and halting become geodesic operations, yielding boundedness by construction and eliminating coefficient coupling. We prove fixed-point existence, local convergence under an explicit step-size condition, and global convergence under strong injection. On Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, and Mini-ARC, SFPRM achieves 96.6%, 87.9%, and 59.1% test accuracy, respectively, outperforming FPRM and other baselines while allocating test-time compute more effectively. Its converged geometry is also interpretable: token-input angles capture puzzle structure and predict correctness.
authors: Arber Zela, Artavazd Maranjyan, Pol Puigdemont, David Berghaus, Valentyn Boreiko, Volkan Cevher
bullets: Recasts Fixed-Point Reasoners in normalized-transformer geometry, replacing Euclidean residual updates with geodesic operations.
Hyperspherical updates provide boundedness by construction and remove coupled rescaling in input injection, damping, and halting.
Establishes fixed-point existence, local convergence under an explicit step-size condition, and global convergence under strong injection.
Reports 96.6% on Sudoku-Extreme, 87.9% on Maze-Hard, and 59.1% on Mini-ARC, outperforming FPRM and other baselines.
Converged token-input angles are interpretable, encoding puzzle structure and predicting correctness.
papers.selection_reason: Spherical fixed-point looped transformers with adaptive halting improve compute allocation and reasoning; relevant to transformer architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners: Adaptive Loop Halting on the Hypersphere
papers.tldr: SFPRM adapts looped-transformer computation on the unit hypersphere, offering theoretically grounded halting and strong puzzle-solving performance.

papers.abstract: State space models (SSMs) combine fast inference and fixed state size with competitive language-modeling performance. Recently, state souping has been proposed as a procedure whereby an SSM independently encodes chunks of tokens like documents, tool definitions, or memory records. The resulting state encodings may be cached and recombined to cheaply construct a context for downstream queries. However, both state souping and vanilla SSMs deteriorate on long, crowded contexts, limiting their utility for long-horizon domains. To address this issue, we propose weighted state souping, a simple method that learns query-dependent weights for composing cached states. The resulting models improve long-context performance substantially across both single- and multi-hop document question answering, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use. Our method can be further adapted into an efficient sparse variant, yielding near-constant encoding cost with respect to context length while preserving (and sometimes improving) performance. We also present simple theoretical arguments that illustrate why souping works and when it may fail, and discuss informally the advantages of weighted souping. Weighted state souping thus combines reusable context representations with selective retrieval, offering an efficient approach to language modeling over large collections of documents, tools, and other forms of structured context that increasingly dominate modern agentic workloads.
authors: William L. Tong, Aryo Lotfi, Emmanuel Abbe, Josh Susskind, Cengiz Pehlevan, Eran Malach
bullets: Addresses performance degradation of vanilla SSMs and standard state souping on crowded, long contexts.
Learns query-dependent weights to compose independently encoded and cached context chunks.
Improves performance across document QA, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use.
A sparse variant offers near-constant encoding cost as context length grows while maintaining or sometimes improving performance.
Includes theoretical arguments describing why state souping works and when it may fail.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes weighted state souping for efficient long-context retrieval, directly relevant to long-context language models and efficiency.
papers.title: Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval
papers.tldr: Weighted state souping improves long-context retrieval in state-space models by selectively combining cached document or memory states based on the query.

papers.abstract: Identifying which visual interventions interact in a vision-language model requires comparing their joint and separate effects. The resulting four-output difference can be small enough for rounding error to obscure it. We introduce the Finite Interaction Lens (FIL), a mixed-precision method for evaluating finite intervention families. At each selected linear projection, FIL decomposes each candidate's input into a native state, two single-intervention components, and a full-dimensional mixed residual. It projects the single-intervention components at higher precision and reuses the same numerical contributions in the joint candidates, while retaining every mixed residual and nonlinear trajectory. We derive a local cancellation identity and a conditional bound on error propagation through a smooth nonlinearity. In one MLP of Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, FIL reduces final interaction MSE by 94.4% on 16 synthetic families and by 99.85% and 99.35% in two separate four-image COCO studies, relative to a control that has the same nominal BF16-product budget and higher-precision single interventions but projects each joint candidate independently. One image accounts for most of the absolute gain in each COCO study. Higher-accuracy multi-product BF16 arithmetic on all candidates gives lower aggregate error at similar total query times. Single-product BF16 already recovers the reference choices in both candidate-selection tasks we tested. On these development inputs, FIL improves interaction fidelity at a fixed nominal precision budget. Its practical value depends on a task that needs the extra fidelity.
bullets: Targets small four-output interaction differences that can be obscured by rounding error.
Decomposes inputs into native, two single-intervention, and full-dimensional mixed-residual components at selected linear projections.
Reuses higher-precision single-intervention contributions across joint candidates and derives a local cancellation identity plus a conditional nonlinear error bound.
In reported Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct studies, it reduced interaction MSE by 94.4% on synthetic families and 99.35–99.85% in two four-image COCO studies versus a matched control.
Scope is limited to development inputs and tasks requiring extra interaction fidelity; higher-accuracy multi-product BF16 arithmetic achieved lower aggregate error at similar query times.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a mixed-precision method (FIL) for evaluating visual interventions in VLMs, contributing to both Multimodal Foundation Models and Efficient AI.
papers.title: Finite Interaction Lens: Structured Precision Sharing for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: FIL improves the numerical fidelity of finite intervention interaction estimates by sharing high-precision single-intervention computations across joint candidates while preserving mixed residuals.

papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are becoming a powerful alternative to conventional tabular learning, adapting to new datasets in context without task-specific training. Current architectures, however, face a trade-off: models that preserve cell-level representations are expensive because they repeatedly attend across rows and columns, while faster models collapse each row into a fixed embedding and lose this fine-grained state. We introduce Factorized Tabular Foundation Models (FTFM), which preserve cell representations while factorizing their computation through one contextual latent per row and one per column. Cells no longer attend to one another directly; instead, each cell is updated through the interaction of its row and column latents, reducing repeated attention while retaining feature-specific information. FTFM achieves competitive predictive performance in tabular classification on major benchmarks such as TabArena and BeyondArena.
bullets: Existing TFMs either incur high costs from repeated row- and column-wise attention or lose detail by compressing each row into one embedding.
FTFM assigns one contextual latent to each row and each column.
Cells interact indirectly through their corresponding row and column latents rather than attending to one another directly.
The approach retains feature-specific cell representations while reducing repeated attention computation.
FTFM achieves competitive tabular-classification performance on benchmarks including TabArena and BeyondArena.
papers.selection_reason: Factorized computation via row/column latents reduces repeated attention; efficiency idea transferable to efficient attention mechanisms.
papers.title: FTFM: Factorized Tabular Foundation Models
papers.tldr: FTFM preserves fine-grained cell information in tabular foundation models while reducing computation through factorized row and column latents.

papers.abstract: Real-time streaming video question answering with vision-language models must answer queries that arrive at any time with low latency while sustaining the video-processing rate required by the application. Existing systems construct key-value (KV) caches for the entire video as it arrives, although a query typically uses only a few of the preceding frames as evidence. This highlights a fundamental trade-off: performing more computation as video arrives reduces query-time computation but can increase processing lag, whereas deferring computation can increase the video-processing rate but requires additional query-time computation for retrieved content. We present StreamAhead, an algorithm-system co-design that exploits this trade-off through adaptive precomputation: dynamically controlling how much computation to complete for each video segment before a query arrives. StreamAhead encodes video segments independently and lets each remain at a different representation level, from inexpensive visual features to costly KV caches, completing KV caches only for the retrieved segments when a query arrives. StreamAhead profiles offline the cost of advancing a segment to each representation level. Its runtime uses these profiles to schedule segment computation concurrently with query execution, pipelining it across heterogeneous CPU and GPU resources while maintaining the required video-processing rate. StreamAhead achieves accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art methods with up to 10.4x lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and up to 5.9x lower TTFT than state-of-the-art streaming systems. It sustains 30 FPS with P95 TTFT under 0.5 s, and up to 57 FPS with P95 TTFT under 2 s. To our knowledge, StreamAhead is the first real-time streaming video QA system with competitive accuracy, setting a new Pareto frontier between video-processing rate and TTFT.
authors: Haoyang Fan, Dhruv Parikh, Rajgopal Kannan, Viktor Prasanna
bullets: Targets streaming video QA, where queries can arrive at any time and only a few preceding frames are typically relevant.
Encodes segments independently at varying representation levels, from inexpensive visual features to full KV caches.
Dynamically completes retrieved segments and pipelines computation across CPU and GPU resources using offline cost profiles.
Reports competitive accuracy with up to 10.4× lower time-to-first-token than prior methods and up to 5.9× lower than streaming systems.
Sustains 30 FPS with P95 TTFT below 0.5 s, or up to 57 FPS with P95 TTFT below 2 s.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces StreamAhead for real-time streaming video QA, addressing video understanding and optimizing KV cache computation for efficiency.
papers.title: StreamAhead: Real-Time Streaming Video Question Answering via Adaptive Precomputation
papers.tldr: StreamAhead adaptively precomputes video representations to balance continuous processing with low-latency question answering.

papers.abstract: Coding agents keep working on runs that will fail verification, and asking a frontier model to watch for this is expensive in its own right. We introduce StopLoss, a small external monitor that learns failure recognition from completed trajectories and their verifier outcomes. The name is inspired by the stop-loss order in finance: StopLoss ends a run early when the run is likely to fail, which saves resources. Final outcomes label earlier local windows, so a fine-tuned language model can score the most recent tool steps in a single forward pass, and a threshold calibrated on successful runs turns that score into an abort decision without changing the executor. Trained on GPT-family SWE-rebench trajectories and evaluated on SWE-bench Verified and a SWE-bench Pro subset with GPT and Claude executors, StopLoss is compared against six general-purpose judges reading identical windows. Outcome supervision lifts failure prediction from near chance to a useful signal at the first check, at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost per check than any tested judge. This translates into savings: relative to completing every task, StopLoss lowers cost per retained solve by 4.5\% on Verified while preserving 99\% of successful runs, and by up to 31\% on the costlier Pro subset, reaching 48\% with a Qwen3-8B backbone, and in all four settings its cost per retained solve is below that of every judge policy. Outcome-trained small monitors can make failure recognition cheap enough for early stopping to pay for itself.
authors: Jiarong Liang, Xueguang Ma, Dongfu Jiang, Yuxuan Zhang, Ping Nie, Wenhu Chen
bullets: Uses completed trajectories and verifier outcomes to supervise failure prediction on earlier local tool-step windows.
Scores the latest steps in one forward pass and applies a threshold calibrated on successful runs, without modifying the executor.
Evaluated with GPT and Claude executors on SWE-bench Verified and a SWE-bench Pro subset, against six general-purpose judges.
Reports 4.5% lower cost per retained solve on Verified while preserving 99% of successful runs, and up to 31% savings on Pro (48% with Qwen3-8B).
The monitor’s per-check cost is one to two orders of magnitude below tested judges, with lower cost per retained solve in all evaluated settings.
papers.selection_reason: Early stopping of failing coding agents reduces computation, fitting the broad Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: StopLoss: Teaching Agents to Predict Failure and Stop Early
papers.tldr: StopLoss is a small, externally trained monitor that detects likely-failing coding-agent runs and stops them early to reduce costs while preserving most successful runs.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.
bullets: Fixed sampling budgets overlook both query difficulty and GPU contention, which can raise energy use by up to 4.1× for the same query.
ATEST-Online incrementally samples, estimates answer stability, monitors GPU conditions, and learns sampling cost online without offline calibration.
ATEST-Calibrated chooses per-query budgets from offline accuracy and cost models, making it better suited to stable workloads.
Across four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online stayed within energy budgets while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increased.

Online adaptation improves robustness but can increase tail latency and reduce throughput on short tasks; offline calibration used 42× less GPU time and 48× less energy in the evaluated workload when profiling was included.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes resource-aware test-time scaling to reduce energy and compute for LLM inference, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference
papers.tldr: ATEST adaptively scales LLM test-time sampling based on query uncertainty and live GPU energy costs, maintaining accuracy within energy budgets under changing load.

papers.abstract: We introduce ReDT, a feed-forward visual geometry transformer designed to scale multi-view reconstruction to high-definition (HD) inputs. Existing visual geometry transformers are typically trained at fixed, standard definition (SD) resolutions and exhibit degraded reconstruction quality and poor computational scaling to high input resolutions. While recent efficient architectures reduce the complexity of inter-frame attention, expensive intra-frame and encoder attention remain largely unaddressed, making HD reconstruction impractical with existing architectures. ReDT addresses both limitations with a resolution-aware architecture designed to scale to high-resolution inputs. The key idea of ReDT is to first map each view to a fixed-size set of basis tokens, compute correspondences in this compact constant-size basis space, and then project the outputs back to the original resolution for dense prediction. By decoupling the internal representation from input resolution during attention, ReDT substantially reduces the computational cost of high-resolution 3D reconstruction and improves model performance at all resolutions. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets spanning SD to FHD (2K) show that ReDT outperforms state-of-the-art visual geometry transformers in both reconstruction quality and computational efficiency. For instance, on the ETH3D (2K) dataset, ReDT achieves a $16\times$ speedup, a $34\%$ reduction in peak GPU memory usage, and a $33\%$ reduction in chamfer distance over VGGT-$\Omega$. \href{https://redt.github.io}{Project Website.}
authors: Abteen Arab, Guile Wu, Dongfeng Bai
bullets: Existing visual geometry transformers scale poorly to HD inputs because intra-frame and encoder attention remain expensive.
ReDT maps each view to a fixed-size set of basis tokens, computes correspondences in this compact space, and projects results back for dense prediction.
Experiments across SD to FHD (2K) datasets show improved reconstruction quality and computational efficiency at all tested resolutions.
On ETH3D at 2K, ReDT reports 16× faster inference, 34% lower peak GPU memory, and 33% lower Chamfer distance than VGGT-Ω.
papers.selection_reason: Resolution-decoupled visual geometry transformer for efficient HD multi-view reconstruction; fits 3D foundation models and efficient attention.
papers.title: ReDT: Resolution-Decoupled Visual Geometry Transformer
papers.tldr: ReDT enables efficient high-resolution multi-view 3D reconstruction by decoupling attention computation from input resolution.

papers.abstract: Agents that work for many turns outgrow the context window of the model that serves them, and on small language models (SLMs) and constrained inference systems that window is small. Context compaction replaces older turns with a summary so a session can continue, but it is lossy, costs a model call, and can help or hurt depending on when it runs. We describe Bud ContextCompact 2.0, the compaction built into the Bud agent runtime, and evaluate it in two settings. On recall questions over recorded agent sessions, compaction to a 16K budget raised a 1.2B-parameter model's accuracy to 0.335, from 0.247 with truncation and 0.176 with its full 32K history (p < 0.001), and raised a 9B model from 0.515 (truncation) to 0.577 (p = 0.04). On 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks run end to end by a 27B reasoning model on a 49K-token window (556 graded sessions), compaction raised the resolve rate on long sessions from 41% to 53% (+12.3 points, 95% CI +1.6 to +23.0, McNemar p = 0.043), left short sessions unchanged, and used 13% fewer tokens per solved task at equal total cost. The main failure without compaction was not the history overflowing but a reasoning turn exhausting the room the history left. The gain has limits: it vanished under a 45-minute session budget, because each summary took a median of 161 s, and in a threshold study it appeared only when compaction triggered early enough to leave room. An 8B model submitted after about ten turns at 5-8K tokens and never needed compaction. We argue that the accuracy results transfer across hardware, including CPU inference, for an equivalent model and window, while the time cost scales with the hardware and must be budgeted for.
bullets: Compaction replaces older agent turns with summaries to prevent long sessions from exhausting usable context.
On recall tasks, compaction improved accuracy for both 1.2B and 9B models versus truncation.
In 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks, long-session resolution rose from 41% to 53%, with 13% fewer tokens per solved task at equal total cost.
Benefits appeared when compaction triggered early enough to preserve room for reasoning; short sessions did not benefit.
The gain disappeared under a 45-minute session budget because summaries took a median of 161 seconds; an 8B model often avoided compaction entirely.
papers.selection_reason: Context compaction for constrained windows addresses long-context processing and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Bud ContextCompact 2.0: Context Compaction for Agent Success and Accuracy with Small Language Models and Constrained Context Windows
papers.tldr: Early context compaction improves long-session agent accuracy on constrained context windows, but its latency cost can erase the benefit under tight time budgets.

papers.abstract: To determine where computation is needed in volumetric segmentation networks, we analyze block-level redundancy and stage-wise token-mixer contribution. Centered Kernel Alignment reveals high input-output representational similarity within blocks of representative convolutional, hybrid, and Transformer-style segmentation networks. Similarity-guided pruning reduces their parameter counts by 39-75% while decreasing mean Dice by less than 0.4 percentage points. To examine token mixers within blocks, we introduce Anatomical Relation Distortion, which quantifies how bypassing a mixer distorts feature relations between labeled anatomical positions. Applied to an unpruned candidate architecture, Centered Kernel Alignment indicates high representational redundancy in intermediate encoder mixers, whereas Anatomical Relation Distortion shows that they contribute little and the bottleneck mixer most. These findings motivate SlimFormer++, which uses Selective Mixing blocks with windowed Mamba mixing in the first encoder stage and only residual channel MLPs in deeper stages. At the bottleneck, Augmented Mixing injects similarity-weighted sparse long-range context into the axial taps of a depthwise convolution at cost linear in voxel count. Evaluated against 12 baselines across eight public CT, MRI, and ultrasound datasets (1,809 cases), SlimFormer++ achieves the highest mean Dice (87.84%) and lowest mean HD95 (6.50 mm) with the fewest parameters (5.98 million). These results support stage-aware token mixing as a design strategy for improving the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in volumetric segmentation. The source code is available at https://github.com/WHHHHHY822/SlimFormerPlusPlus
authors: Yang Hong, Lei Zhang, Zhihong Liu, Jianqing Mo, Xujiong Ye
bullets: Block-level redundancy analysis shows 39–75% parameter pruning can reduce mean Dice by less than 0.4 percentage points.
Anatomical Relation Distortion indicates early and intermediate encoder mixers contribute little, while bottleneck mixing is most important.
The model uses windowed Mamba mixing early, residual channel MLPs in deeper stages, and augmented sparse long-range mixing at the bottleneck.
Across eight public CT, MRI, and ultrasound datasets, it reports 87.84% mean Dice and 6.50 mm mean HD95 with 5.98M parameters.
The findings support stage-aware token mixing as a strategy for efficient volumetric segmentation.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient volumetric segmentation via block pruning and selective token mixing; fits efficient attention and 3D perception.
papers.title: SlimFormer++: Token Mixing Where It Matters for Efficient 3D Medical Image Segmentation
papers.tldr: SlimFormer++ improves the accuracy–efficiency trade-off in 3D medical image segmentation by concentrating token mixing where it matters most.

papers.abstract: Post-training compression of pretrained medical segmentation models commonly uses quantization, pruning, or distillation to reduce model size and computational cost. Existing medical segmentation quantization studies mainly evaluate Dice, model size, memory, and latency, but this is incomplete for safety-critical use because compressed models should also preserve uncertainty signals that indicate unreliable predictions. We study this problem in compressed MRI/CT segmentation and formalize why Dice can remain stable while uncertainty changes. Motivated by this failure mode, we propose score-guided aggregate-validated mixed precision (SGAV-MP), a post-training compression framework that selects layer precisions under reliability constraints. SGAV-MP ranks quantization actions with a compact benefit-risk score and accepts them only after full-model reliability validation on a calibration set. Across five 2D backbones and three 3D benchmarks, SGAV-MP preserves FP32-level Dice and high uncertainty-map agreement, achieving $3.59\times$--$7.8\times$ compression in 2D and $4.73\times$--$7.82\times$ in 3D. We also report backend-supported TensorRT deployment measurements separately to distinguish runtime execution from reliability-preserving storage compression.
authors: Sagar Kumar, Shailja Sharma, Tirthajit Baruah, Punit Rathore
bullets: Problem: Dice alone may remain stable after compression even when uncertainty estimates change, which is risky in safety-critical MRI/CT segmentation.
Method: A post-training mixed-precision framework ranks quantization actions by benefit–risk score and validates each accepted change using full-model reliability checks on calibration data.
Contribution: Introduces reliability-constrained compression that explicitly preserves uncertainty-map agreement alongside segmentation quality.
Results: Across five 2D backbones and three 3D benchmarks, it preserves FP32-level Dice and achieves 3.59×–7.8× compression in 2D and 4.73×–7.82× in 3D.
Scope: TensorRT runtime measurements are reported separately from reliability-preserving storage compression.
papers.selection_reason: Post-training compression framework for medical segmentation that reduces model size and compute while preserving reliability, fitting the efficient-AI scope.
papers.title: Reliability-Preserving Compression for Deployable Medical Image Segmentation
papers.tldr: SGAV-MP compresses medical image segmentation models while preserving both segmentation accuracy and uncertainty signals needed for reliable deployment.

papers.abstract: Decision models return probabilities over supplied options, but a deployed agent may also need to reply in words. The present study introduces System X, a large language model (LLM) decision model that adds a text-reply option to the LLM-as-Jev readout. When this option wins, or confidence is low, the same model continues from the decision's key-value (KV) cache, avoiding a repeated prompt prefill. Qwen3-0.6B has been fine-tuned with LoRA on Reason-9k and Bitext reply rows. JevBench accuracy shows no statistically significant change (55.4% to 54.5%, p=0.87), while expected calibration error falls from 0.292 to 0.169. Held-out Bitext routing accuracy reaches 98.3%.
