Cache reuse saves 15-37% of latency on an Apple M4 Pro, with token-identical replies in the FP32 demonstration cases. Scoring options on copies of the prompt cache matches full-sequence scoring to within 1.4e-6 in probability. Adding dialogue, industry and complaint data (System X+) improves support-task results but lowers IFEval accuracy from 55.5% to 45.0%. System X v4 uses Qwen3-1.7B, rebalanced data and teacher-rewritten reply targets. Against its base LLM, JevBench accuracy rises from 55.0% to 61.0% (p=0.04), with no statistically significant IFEval change (p=0.71). A matched latency test on unadapted Qwen3-1.7B saves 17-39%. One LLM judge prefers v4 replies to an unadapted 1.7B second call (31 to 11 pairs, p=0.003); the other's preference is not significant. These reply comparisons also differ in prompts and generation limits. State conflicts and unsupported reply details remain failure modes. Further studies with several seeds, human raters and real support data are recommended.
authors: Syed Usama Khalid Bukhari, Syed Safwan Khalid, Muhammad Aamir
bullets: Adds a text-reply option to the LLM-as-Jev decision readout and continues generation from the existing KV cache when selected or when confidence is low.
On Qwen3-0.6B, JevBench accuracy was statistically unchanged, while expected calibration error decreased from 0.292 to 0.169 and Bitext routing accuracy reached 98.3%.
KV-cache reuse reduced latency by 15–37% on an Apple M4 Pro; copied-cache option scoring matched full-sequence scoring within 1.4e-6 probability.
System X v4 with Qwen3-1.7B increased JevBench accuracy from 55.0% to 61.0% versus its base model, without a significant IFEval change.
Failure modes include state conflicts and unsupported reply details; broader validation with multiple seeds, human raters, and real support data is needed.
papers.selection_reason: Reuses KV cache to avoid prompt prefill, reducing latency for LLM decision models.
papers.title: System X: An LLM Decision Model That Replies from Its Own KV Cache
papers.tldr: System X lets an LLM decision model generate replies directly from its decision KV cache, improving calibration and reducing latency while preserving roughly similar decision accuracy, though unsupported details remain a limitation.

papers.abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache is the main memory bottleneck of long-context LLM inference. Token eviction methods such as SnapKV, H2O, AdaKV and L2Norm shrink it, but they give every transformer layer the same budget, although layers differ in which tokens they need. We present MOSAIC, a multi-objective neural architecture search that learns per-layer KV-cache budgets for any eviction method. One search maps the trade-off between average budget and task score; its best allocation transfers to every target budget without further search, and an optional budget-constrained search refines it. Across four eviction methods on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, MOSAIC beats uniform allocation in 146 of 154 (task, method, budget) settings, by up to +48 points on RULER and +11.9 on LongBench (LCC). On both models, it reaches the score of uniform allocation with up to 4x less KV cache (75% smaller). Against EvolKV, MOSAIC explores a ~10^40 x larger search space with 4x fewer evaluations and 18% fewer GPU-hours per budget, and scores higher in 5 of 6 settings. The learned allocations consistently favour a small set of middle layers.
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of assigning every transformer layer the same KV-cache budget despite differing token needs.
Uses multi-objective neural architecture search to find per-layer allocations compatible with existing eviction methods.
A single search captures the budget–task-score trade-off and transfers across target budgets; an optional constrained search further refines allocations.
Across four eviction methods and two LLMs, it outperforms uniform allocation in 146 of 154 evaluated settings and can match uniform performance with up to 75% less cache.
Allocations consistently concentrate cache on a small set of middle layers; compared with EvolKV, MOSAIC searches a much larger space with fewer evaluations and GPU-hours.
papers.selection_reason: Learns per-layer KV-cache budgets for token eviction methods, directly targeting efficient LLM inference and cache memory reduction.
papers.title: MOSAIC: Multi-Objective Search for Allocating Inference Cache Across LLM Decoder Layers
papers.tldr: MOSAIC learns layer-specific KV-cache budgets that substantially reduce LLM inference memory while preserving or improving task performance.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face significant scalability challenges in long-video understanding due to quadratic attention complexity and context window constraints. Existing retrieval-based approaches typically rely on supervised learning from static keyframe annotations. However, these label priors often fail to align with the actual information required by downstream MLLMs for complex reasoning, creating a misalignment between the training target and inference needs. To bridge this gap, we propose a probabilistic framework that reformulates frame selection as latent-variable inference. We first initialize a lightweight policy using supervised learning to capture general visual saliency. Then, we treat a frozen MLLM as a task environment and use its answer likelihood as dense task evidence to refine the policy via Bayesian Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Within this formulation, the negative log-likelihood (NLL) over ground-truth answer tokens provides a principled dense reward, while a prior-matching KL term preserves semantic consistency with the elicited label prior. This process transitions the selection principle from static label priors to task evidence. Extensive experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate that our selector achieves competitive accuracy with MLLM-based scorers while retaining the inference efficiency of lightweight methods. The selector is trained once with a frozen MLLM environment and transfers directly to multiple downstream MLLMs without retraining. Code is available at \url{github.com/Miraclecsc/Frame_Selection_GRPO}.
authors: Shuochen Chang, Bingjie Gao, Qingyang Liu, Qianli Ma, Yibo Miao, Haonan Zhao, Zhaohe Liao, Xiaofeng Zhang, Jiangtong Li, Li Niu
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between static keyframe-label supervision and the evidence needed for complex downstream reasoning.
Initializes a lightweight saliency policy with supervised learning, then refines it against a frozen MLLM environment.
Uses answer-token negative log-likelihood as a dense reward and a KL term to preserve consistency with the learned prior.
Achieves competitive accuracy with MLLM-based frame scorers while retaining lightweight inference efficiency on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench.
The selector is trained once and transfers across multiple downstream MLLMs without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient long-video frame selection for MLLMs; fits video understanding and token selection efficiency.
papers.title: From Label Priors to Task Evidence: Efficient Long-Video Frame Selection via Bayesian GRPO
papers.tldr: A Bayesian GRPO frame selector uses downstream MLLM answer likelihoods as task evidence to efficiently select informative frames from long videos.

papers.abstract: Given the high cost of expert annotation and limited fine-tuning resources, effective data selection from large unlabeled pools under strict budgets has become a crucial step in adapting LLMs to specialized domains. Existing label-dependent methods risk distorted selection when using pseudo-labels, while traditional active learning methods do not explicitly characterize instruction-tuning dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose Hidden Cartographer (HC), a two-stage framework that uses hidden states to guide annotation and exact training dynamics to select the final training subset. The first stage is Progressive Candidate Expansion, which utilizes the proxy to iteratively select top unlabeled candidates for expert annotation, merging them to recompute training dynamics and update the proxy until the annotation budget is exhausted; the second stage is Exact Cartography Pruning, which ranks these annotated candidates by their exact dynamics scores to isolate a compact subset under the final training budget. Experiments across the medical, legal, and financial domains demonstrate that HC achieves the highest average accuracy among all budgeted baselines, requiring annotation for only 20--30% of the original pool and fine-tuning on just 10--15%.
authors: Zixuan Qin, Qi Qin, Erbo Li, Ting Wei, Yifan Sun, Zhaoxin Fan
bullets: Targets costly expert annotation and limited fine-tuning resources for domain adaptation.
Progressive Candidate Expansion iteratively selects unlabeled examples for annotation using a hidden-state proxy.
Exact Cartography Pruning ranks annotated candidates by exact training-dynamics scores to form the final subset.
Across medical, legal, and financial domains, it reports the highest average accuracy among budgeted baselines.
Uses annotation for 20–30% of the original pool and fine-tuning on 10–15%.
papers.selection_reason: Hidden-state-guided data selection reduces annotation and fine-tuning budgets for LLM instruction tuning.
papers.title: Hidden Cartographer: Hidden State Guided Data Selection for Dual Budgeted Instruction Tuning
papers.tldr: Hidden Cartographer uses hidden-state-guided annotation followed by training-dynamics-based pruning to select effective instruction-tuning data under separate annotation and fine-tuning budgets.

papers.abstract: Traffic forecasting models based on spectral graph convolution offer an interpretable account of how information is mixed between sensors, but they rely on an eigendecomposition of the graph Laplacian. It costs cubic time, is fixed by the road network, and provides a symmetric operator that cannot represent the directed propagation of traffic congestion. Attention-based spatio-temporal transformers remove these limitations but generate a dense sensor-by-sensor attention map at each layer and time step, so memory, rather than accuracy, becomes the binding constraint on large networks. We introduce the spectral adaptive graph transformer, whose spatial operator is learned rather than derived from the Laplacian, directed rather than symmetric, and conditioned on the current traffic state rather than a static state, at a cost linear in the number of sensors. A sparse road graph diffusion branch provides the strictly local propagation that a low-rank operator cannot express, and a zero-initialized gate learns the balance between the two. Before spatial mixing, a unit-mean-gain frequency-bin attention module reweights each sensor's short-term periodicities according to its identity and current context. Across six public benchmarks spanning 170 to 1843 sensors, evaluated over three random seeds, the proposed model attains the lowest error of any single end-to-end model on one benchmark and remains competitive with the strongest current attention models on the others, while using about a quarter of their memory and training about twice as fast.
authors: Amirhossein Ghaffari, Susanna Pirttikangas, Ekaterina Gilman
bullets: Addresses cubic eigendecomposition costs, static symmetric propagation, and dense attention memory demands.
Learns a directed, traffic-state-conditioned spatial operator with linear scaling in the number of sensors.
Combines low-rank global propagation with sparse road-graph diffusion through a zero-initialized balancing gate.
Reweights each sensor’s short-term periodicities using context- and identity-dependent frequency-bin attention.

Across six benchmarks, achieves the best single-model error on one benchmark, competitive results elsewhere, about one-quarter the memory use, and roughly twice the training speed of strong attention models.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a learned low-rank spatial operator plus sparse diffusion to replace dense attention, reducing memory and compute for spatio-temporal forecasting.
papers.title: Spectral Adaptive Graph Transformer for Efficient and Scalable Traffic Forecasting
papers.tldr: A scalable traffic forecasting transformer replaces costly spectral decomposition and dense attention with state-adaptive directed low-rank mixing plus sparse local diffusion, reducing resource use while maintaining competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Understanding when during a video a model makes its critical observations is essential for interpreting video-understanding systems. However, existing attribution methods often spread evidence diffusely across near-duplicate frames. We introduce Sufficient Frame Subsets: compact sets of frames in which all other frames are masked, yet each subset independently preserves the model's prediction. We evaluate our method on two complementary benchmarks, UCF101 and Something-Something v2, using both CNN- and transformer-based architectures. Our results show that the proposed algorithm identifies highly compact and effective frame subsets for explaining model decisions. We also find that models capable of relying on a greater number of sufficient frame subsets tend to perform better, possibly because they are more robust, consistent with prior research. Finally, the extracted frame subsets help us analyze model failure cases, reveal which aspects of a video the model has learned to emphasize, and identify opportunities for improving future training procedures.
bullets: Addresses diffuse attribution across near-duplicate frames in video understanding.
Masks all frames outside each candidate subset and tests whether the prediction is preserved.
Evaluated on UCF101 and Something-Something v2 with CNN- and transformer-based models.
Finds highly compact, effective subsets and links reliance on more sufficient subsets with better model performance.
Supports failure analysis, inspection of learned visual emphasis, and future training improvements.
papers.selection_reason: Identifies compact sufficient frame subsets for video model decisions; relevant to video understanding and frame/token selection.
papers.title: Sufficient Frame Subsets for Video Understanding
papers.tldr: Sufficient Frame Subsets identifies compact groups of video frames that independently preserve a model’s prediction, enabling more focused explanations of video decisions.

papers.abstract: We show that a video can be represented with just a few keyframes without sacrificing a given model's belief about the video. Our method is the first of its kind that extracts these keyframes conditioned on the model's prediction, which is massively helpful for building explainable video models. We then fairly distribute the importance of the video to the model among the keyframes with game theoretically fair Shapley values. Through qualitative and quantitative experiments, we show that keyframe attribution is superior to the traditional frame attribution. Further, we conduct preliminary exploration on highlighting the important changes among the frames by looking at the differences between adjacent keyframes.
bullets: Extracts keyframes conditioned on the model’s prediction.
Represents videos with few keyframes without changing the model’s belief.
Uses game-theoretic Shapley values to distribute importance fairly across keyframes.
Experiments show keyframe attribution outperforms traditional frame attribution.
Also explores highlighting important changes between adjacent keyframes.
papers.selection_reason: Keyframe extraction for video model explanation; relevant to video understanding and frame/token selection.
papers.title: MoCKEFA: Model-Conditioned Keyframe Extraction and Fair Attribution for Video Model Explanation
papers.tldr: MoCKEFA explains video models by selecting a few prediction-preserving keyframes and fairly attributing the model’s decision among them.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning language models on consumer GPUs is constrained by computation and memory. Although LoRA reduces trainable parameters and optimizer state, frozen projections remain expensive, and activations retained for backward can dominate memory usage. We present PACT, a LoRA fine-tuning system that accelerates frozen projections with native NVFP4 GEMMs while reducing quantization and dequantization overhead and limiting quantization error. To reduce activation memory, PACT reuses quantized RMSNorm outputs and saves gate/up activations in NVFP4 for backward. To limit numerical error, it preserves BF16 inputs for forward nonlinear operations and calibrates frozen weights offline using GPTQ adapted to NVFP4 scales and quantized activations. Fused nonlinear kernels and cached forward and backward weight layouts reduce quantization and dequantization overhead. Evaluations across multiple models and tasks on a 16\,GB RTX~5080 show lower memory usage and faster LoRA fine-tuning with competitive accuracy, enabling model adaptation on resource-constrained consumer hardware.
authors: Lei Gao, Hossein Entezari Zarch, Chaoyi Jiang, Murali Annavaram
bullets: Addresses the computation and activation-memory costs that remain in LoRA fine-tuning, especially for frozen projections.
Uses native NVFP4 GEMMs, quantized activation storage, and reuse of quantized RMSNorm outputs to reduce memory and overhead.
Preserves BF16 inputs for nonlinear operations and applies GPTQ-style offline calibration to limit quantization error.
Fuses nonlinear kernels and caches weight layouts to reduce quantization/dequantization costs.
Evaluations across multiple models and tasks on an RTX 5080 report lower memory use and faster fine-tuning with competitive accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: NVFP4 data-flow LoRA fine-tuning reduces memory and accelerates training on consumer GPUs, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: PACT: NVFP4 Data-Flow LoRA Fine-Tuning on Consumer GPUs
papers.tldr: PACT enables faster, lower-memory LoRA fine-tuning on 16 GB consumer GPUs by using NVFP4 data-flow optimizations while maintaining competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: As LLM adoption surges, scaling model serving requires unlocking stranded GPU capacity alongside deploying more GPUs. Speculative decoding brings two models into the serving process: a small draft model proposes tokens that a larger target model verifies. Yet compiling these models individually leaves their shared execution outside the compiler's optimization boundary. We introduce CONJUGATE COMPILATION, which reframes speculative decoding as a cross-model compilation problem and jointly optimizes the draft and target models within their shared execution rather than treating each in isolation. Our key insight is that cross-model compilation should be informed by the measured performance of the co-located shared execution it produces: an optimization that improves a kernel in isolation need not improve the models when they execute together. To expand cross-model opportunities, we devise operand layouts that interleave blocks from both models within common tiles, co-locating GEMM and non-GEMM work while preserving their mathematics. We realize CONJUGATE COMPILATION through a self-improving agentic search system in which an LLM edits cross-model optimization plans using the compiler and GPU execution as its environment. Each proposed plan is compiled and evaluated through its co-located shared execution, whose measured score, together with kernel-level verdicts and compiler feedback, informs subsequent proposals, while Monte Carlo tree search accumulates rewards to guide exploration. Across six single-GPU speculative-decoding configurations on NVIDIA B300 and RTX 5090 GPUs, CONJUGATE COMPILATION achieves a geometric-mean per-round speedup of 1.37x over conventional execution. Interleaved kernels raise this speedup to 1.45x, reaching 1.59x in the best case. CONJUGATE COMPILATION also improves GPU utilization on average by 1.46x on RTX 5090 and 1.50x on B300.
authors: Annabelle Sujun Tang, Rohan Mahapatra, Christopher Priebe, Hanyang Xu, Manya Ghobadi, Christopher Rossbach, Hadi Esmaeilzadeh
bullets: Targets the lost optimization opportunities when draft and target models are compiled independently despite sharing execution.
Uses an LLM-driven search loop that edits optimization plans, compiles and measures co-located execution, and applies Monte Carlo tree search to guide exploration.
Introduces interleaved operand layouts that place blocks from both models in common tiles while preserving mathematical correctness.
Across six single-GPU configurations, achieves 1.37× geometric-mean per-round speedup, rising to 1.45× with interleaved kernels and 1.59× in the best case.
Improves average GPU utilization by 1.46× on RTX 5090 and 1.50× on NVIDIA B300.
papers.selection_reason: Joint compiler optimization for speculative decoding improves GPU utilization and latency, fitting efficient AI broadly.
papers.title: Conjugate Compilation: Self-Improving Agentic Co-Compilation for Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: Conjugate Compilation jointly optimizes speculative-decoding draft and target models through measured co-execution, using an agentic compiler search to improve GPU efficiency and speed.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) promises instant scene reconstruction with high-quality novel-view synthesis. Yet, fine-grained geometry and appearance remain difficult to recover, motivating us to revisit how feed-forward models represent, aggregate, and refine detailed visual information. We introduce FineSplat, a feed-forward 3DGS framework built around fine-grained image patches. Since global multi-view attention becomes prohibitively expensive at such high token resolutions, we develop a dual-grouping strategy that combines two complementary forms of locality: view-wise grouping enables efficient interaction among neighboring views, while 3D spatial grouping reconnects geometrically related tokens that may never have interacted under view-wise grouping by lifting them into the 3D scene space. We further leverage reconstruction error as direct feedback, providing an explicit rendering-based signal to recover fine-grained structures and appearance, thereby overcoming the limitations of one-pass feed-forward prediction. Finally, a compact Gaussian generation scheme preserves the benefits of fine-grained features without unnecessarily increasing the number of primitives. Together, these designs enable FineSplat to recover richer geometry and appearance while remaining efficient and compact, achieving state-of-the-art results by a substantial margin, under the same or smaller Gaussian budgets than existing methods.
authors: Hyebin Kim, Hwasik Jeong, Joonhyuk Park, Gyeongjin Kang, Jungwoo Kim, Younghyun Kim, Eunbyung Park
bullets: Targets the difficulty of recovering fine-grained geometry and appearance in feed-forward 3DGS.
Uses view-wise grouping for efficient neighboring-view interaction and 3D spatial grouping to reconnect geometrically related tokens.
Uses rendering reconstruction error as explicit feedback to refine structures and appearance beyond one-pass prediction.
Generates a compact set of Gaussians to retain fine-detail benefits without unnecessarily increasing primitive counts.
Reports state-of-the-art performance by a substantial margin under the same or smaller Gaussian budgets, according to the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Feed-forward 3DGS with dual-grouping attention and compact Gaussian generation; relevant to 3D reconstruction and efficient attention.
papers.title: FineSplat: Fine Patches, Local Groups, Detailed Splats
papers.tldr: FineSplat improves feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting by combining fine image patches, local view/3D grouping, reconstruction-error feedback, and compact Gaussian generation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) encode images into dense visual token sequences, creating substantial attention and KV-cache overhead. Existing visual token compression methods reduce this cost by pruning low-saliency tokens in shallow layers, but this practice couples temporary computational deactivation with irreversible information deletion. We show that this coupling breaks an intrinsic inference pattern in MLLMs. Through layer-wise attention analysis, we identify \textbf{Visual Backtracking}: visual pivots remain spatially stable, yet in middle layers they actively retrieve context from tokens that appeared unimportant earlier. Thus, early low-saliency tokens can be inactive for computation while still being useful for later reasoning. Motivated by this finding, we propose \textbf{ReTrace}, a backtracking-aware compression framework that introduces a dormant token state. ReTrace caches non-pivot tokens outside expensive layer-wise computation, restores them during the backtracking window, and prunes only after their information has been absorbed. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3 demonstrate nearly 90\% reductions in FLOPs and KV cache, a 2.83$\times$ prefilling speedup, and strong performance retention across complex vision-language benchmarks.
authors: Guangzong Si, Dong Wang, Yifan Yu, Miao Liu, Panwang Pan, Wentao Zhu
bullets: Visual token compression can harm reasoning by permanently deleting tokens that appear unimportant in early layers.
Layer-wise analysis reveals visual backtracking: stable visual pivots later retrieve context from previously low-saliency tokens.
ReTrace adds a dormant token state, caching non-pivot tokens outside expensive computation and restoring them during a backtracking window.
Tokens are pruned only after their information has been absorbed, preserving more visual context for reasoning.
Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3 report nearly 90% lower FLOPs and KV-cache usage, a 2.83× prefilling speedup, and strong benchmark performance retention.
papers.selection_reason: Backtracking-aware visual token compression reduces FLOPs and KV cache in MLLMs.
papers.title: ReTrace: Visual Backtracking for Efficient Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: ReTrace accelerates MLLM inference by temporarily sidelining visual tokens while restoring them when later layers need their information.

papers.abstract: Weather transformers process dense reanalysis fields whose reliability varies across variables, locations, and weather regimes. Token merging can reduce computation, but feature similarity alone does not account for this heterogeneous input uncertainty. We introduce UtoMe, an observation-uncertainty-guided token merging framework that combines dynamics saliency with ensemble data assimilation spread as a relative input-reliability proxy. The resulting importance score protects selected tokens as anchors and calibrates bipartite matching between the remaining tokens. Three variants use external uncertainty at both training and inference, during training only, or neither stage. In ERA5 72-hour forecasting at two spatial resolutions, UtoMe improves Overall error over train-time ToMe at matched token budgets. At $1.40625^\circ$ and 50% token reduction, UtoMe-E lowers Overall error from 67.32 to 53.00 at the same 0.55x encoder FLOPs. Small reductions remain close to the full-token baseline; larger reductions incur measurable accuracy losses. Component ablations and spatial uncertainty controls support combining dynamics with aligned uncertainty when allocating a weather transformer's token budget.
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Janet Wang, Xi Xiao, Jihun Hamm, Xiao Wang
bullets: Weather inputs have heterogeneous reliability, which similarity-only token merging does not capture.
UtoMe combines dynamics saliency with ensemble data-assimilation spread to score token importance and protect anchor tokens.
It supports uncertainty use during both training and inference, training only, or neither.
In ERA5 72-hour forecasting, UtoMe-E reduced Overall error from 67.32 to 53.00 at 50% token reduction and 0.55× encoder FLOPs.
Accuracy remains near the full-token baseline for small reductions but declines at larger compression levels.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-guided token merging for weather transformers directly targets efficient token reduction.
papers.title: UtoMe: Observation-Uncertainty-Guided Token Merging for Weather Foundation Models
papers.tldr: UtoMe uses observation uncertainty and weather dynamics to merge less informative tokens while preserving forecasting accuracy under reduced computation.

papers.abstract: The throughput gains of speculative decoding depend on the trade-off between acceptance length and execution latency. We ask when additional acceptance is worth the cost of obtaining it. We establish a comparison protocol spanning training, inference, and evaluation, remeasuring released checkpoints and retraining six drafter recipes on shared target-generated data across ten benchmarks and two target models. Alignment changes the picture: gaps that appear large in published comparisons shrink substantially under shared training and inference conditions. This narrowing motivates two deeper questions: how is acceptance improved at different costs, and when do these gains improve throughput? We find that acceptance can be improved through nearly free objective and context changes or more expensive token-to-token conditioning. DCore illustrates the former route as a strong baseline with little additional measured drafting overhead. The payoff is conditional: task uncertainty and serving conditions affect acceptance returns, execution costs, and the preferred drafter and budget. These findings inform future drafter design and deployment choices.
authors: Yongchao Long, Chunrui Zheng, Yuxuan Zhou, Guangkun Nie, Tian-Chi Ma, Chao Pang, Shuohuan Wang, Yuchen Ding, Xianbin Wen, Dianhai Yu, Junyuan Shang, Yuxi Zhou, Shenda Hong
bullets: A controlled comparison across six drafter recipes, ten benchmarks, and two target models finds that published performance gaps shrink under shared training and inference conditions.
Acceptance can improve through nearly free objective/context changes or more expensive token-to-token conditioning.
DCore is presented as a strong baseline with little additional measured drafting overhead.
The throughput payoff depends on task uncertainty, serving conditions, drafter choice, and computation budget.
papers.selection_reason: Controlled study of speculative decoding trade-offs; relevant to efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: When Does Better Acceptance Pay? A Controlled Study of Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: Speculative decoding’s acceptance gains improve throughput only when their extra drafting cost is justified by the task and serving conditions.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention speeds up long-context decoding by reading few keys of the KV cache, but existing methods do not control the error of a query, and on real KV caches their errors have heavy tails. We show that perturbing the score of every key with an independent Exp(1) variable turns threshold retrieval into sampling keys with probability proportional to their attention weights. Lowering the threshold along a geometric grid gives nested samples, a Horvitz--Thompson estimate of the output at every level, and confidence bounds that hold simultaneously over all levels, so each head stops at the first level whose certificate meets the target error $\varepsilon$. With fresh perturbations at every decoding step, each certificate fails with probability at most $\delta$ during generation. At a suitable threshold, the estimator reads $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))$ values regardless of the context length, and no adaptive method reads fewer, up to constants. A 4-bit scan with deterministic bounds, shared across a grouped-query-attention group, generates the candidates exactly but reads every key. On three LLMs and ten settings at 16K--128K tokens, no certificate is violated, and at equal keys read our 90th-percentile error is 4.6--7.9$\times$ lower than that of the best of 15 baseline families. At equal bytes, the best baselines have 0.6--1.6 times our 90th-percentile error and at least 4.9 times our largest. End to end, our method stays within one point of dense attention on tasks and within 0.1\% in PG-19 perplexity, and the strongest baselines at equal bytes score as well. On CPU, decoding steps at 32K--128K tokens run 1.1--1.4$\times$ faster than dense attention on the same 16-bit cache.
bullets: Perturbing key scores with independent Exp(1) noise converts threshold retrieval into sampling proportional to attention weights.
Nested samples across thresholds enable Horvitz–Thompson output estimates and simultaneous confidence certificates.
Each head stops when its estimated error is below ε; with fresh perturbations, certificate failure is bounded by δ during generation.
The estimator needs O(ε⁻² log(1/δ)) reads, independent of context length, and this read complexity is optimal up to constants.
Across 16K–128K contexts, certificates were never violated; decoding was 1.1–1.4× faster than dense attention on CPU while maintaining near-dense task quality.
papers.selection_reason: Certified sparse attention with perturbed retrieval reduces KV-cache reads for long-context decoding, fitting efficient attention and long-context model interests.
papers.title: Certified Sparse Attention via Perturbed Retrieval
papers.tldr: Certified Sparse Attention uses perturbed retrieval and adaptive sampling to provide high-probability error guarantees while reading far fewer KV-cache values during long-context decoding.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents face a fundamental allocation problem as interaction histories grow: which information to retain, how much context to devote to it, and at what granularity. Existing memory mechanisms largely focus on relevance, retrieval, or compression, leaving this allocation trade-off implicit. We introduce MemPrice, which treats active context as a shared resource and dynamically allocates it across memories and representation levels. MemPrice turns accumulated memory pressure into an adaptive price on context, encouraging detail only when its estimated retention value justifies the additional footprint. This pressure persists across memory refreshes, allowing the contents of memory to evolve while preserving long-run control over context usage. We show that irreversible compression can force linear worst-case regret against hindsight following its own memory trajectory, and introduce a same-state benchmark to evaluate allocation on MemPrice's realized memory states. MemPrice enforces the hard context budget at every round and regulates long-run occupancy through adaptive pricing, without prior knowledge of the interaction horizon. Under priced-frontier regularity, its average allocation-regret bound against this benchmark vanishes when accumulated estimation error is sublinear. We evaluate the framework under matched memory budgets on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, AppWorld, and WebShop across three foundation models, spanning both query-blind memory construction and goal-directed agent context management.
authors: Yiming Zong, Shiyuan Piao, Jiashuo Jiang, Fugee Tsung
bullets: Addresses the growing-context trade-off between retaining information, representation granularity, and context usage.
Converts accumulated memory pressure into a price that favors additional detail only when its estimated retention value warrants the cost.
Maintains pressure across memory refreshes, enabling evolving memories while enforcing a hard context budget each round.
Introduces a same-state benchmark and shows vanishing average allocation regret under priced-frontier regularity and sublinear cumulative estimation error.
Evaluates matched-budget performance on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, AppWorld, and WebShop with three foundation models.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive pricing for memory allocation in long-horizon LLM agents; fits LLM memory and efficient context management.
papers.title: MemPrice: Online Memory Allocation via Adaptive Pricing for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.tldr: MemPrice dynamically allocates an agent’s limited context among memories and detail levels using adaptive pricing, providing long-run budget control without knowing the interaction horizon.

papers.abstract: Poisson equations frequently appear in various fields, such as mathematics, physics and informatics. Solving Poisson equation, however, is challenging. Traditional methods are not data-specific, although have high certainty. They require a large number of iterations due to the CFL numerical stability. In contrast, deep learning methods are data-driven and more efficient, but require accurate training data and suffer from heavy computation. To tackle these issues, we propose a wavelet-inspired Poisson solver with 24 trainable scalars. The proposed network has several advantages. First, it is compact. It has four independent $5\times5$ kernels, each represented by six parameters, leading to 24 scalars in total. Such compact format can be deployed on most devices. Second, thanks to the loop design, it achieves higher accuracy than previous methods. A residual loop reuses the wavelet block without increasing its parameters. Numerical experiments confirm that such loop indeed improves the solving accuracy. On 10000 images, one, two, and three loops of the wavelet block lead to PSNRs of $47.27$, $74.14$, and $100.74$ dB, respectively. Third, the proposed method is computationally fast. Thanks to the wavelet transform, the proposed method has linear computation complexity, leading to high computation performance. In short, we propose a novel looped wavelet neural network with compactness, accuracy and efficiency for solving Poisson equations. Our method can be applied in various fields, such as computational fluid dynamics, image reconstruction, biomedical engineering, electromagnetic field simulation.
bullets: Addresses the high iteration cost of traditional Poisson solvers and the data and computation demands of deep-learning methods.
Uses four independent 5×5 wavelet-inspired kernels, each encoded by six learnable parameters.
A residual loop reuses the wavelet block without adding parameters, improving solution accuracy as loop count increases.
On 10,000 images, one, two, and three loops achieved PSNRs of 47.27, 74.14, and 100.74 dB, respectively.
Wavelet-based computation has linear complexity, supporting fast deployment across devices and application areas.
papers.selection_reason: Compact looped wavelet network with 24 parameters and linear complexity; efficiency-oriented design fits efficient AI.
papers.title: LowNet: Looped Wavelet Neural Networks with 24 Learnable Parameters for Solving Poisson Equations
papers.tldr: LowNet is a compact, looped wavelet neural network with only 24 trainable scalars that efficiently solves Poisson equations while improving accuracy through residual reuse.

papers.abstract: Temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) have shown strong performance on dynamic graph learning tasks by continuously updating node memories from evolving interactions (i.e., events) and leveraging these memories for downstream predictions. As graphs grow rapidly in modern applications, training requires processing an increasing number of events; meanwhile, each event can update node memories used by later events, creating dependencies that constrain parallel execution and limit the benefits of additional computing resources. These costs motivate an upstream question: Are all events, and the dependencies they introduce, necessary for learning? We investigate this question through two roles of temporal events: prediction targets and historical events sampled as inputs. We observe that targets involving stable node memories tend to exhibit lower prediction loss, while filtering historical events associated with stable memories can retain similar training-loss trajectories in several evaluated settings. Together, these observations suggest an opportunity to identify input redundancy through changes in node memories. Building on this opportunity, we propose RAFT, a redundancy-aware input-filtering framework for TGNN training. RAFT tracks memory changes during training and uses them to guide two filters: a root-event filter removes selected prediction targets before training, and a support-event filter excludes selected historical context during sampling. Filtering inputs before their downstream preparation and processing reduces the work they trigger. Across three TGNN models and five datasets, RAFT reduces training inputs by 35.23% on average and up to 97.11%, while reducing recorded training time by up to 52.56\% with negligible changes to model precisions.
authors: Yue Dai, Sarah Zhou, Youtao Zhang
bullets: TGNN training becomes costly because rapidly growing event streams create sequential memory dependencies that limit parallelism.
RAFT identifies redundancy through the stability of node memories associated with prediction targets and historical inputs.
A root-event filter removes selected prediction targets, while a support-event filter excludes redundant historical context during sampling.
Across three TGNN models and five datasets, RAFT reduces training inputs by 35.23% on average and up to 97.11%.
Recorded training time falls by up to 52.56% with negligible changes to model precision.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a redundancy-aware input filtering framework for training Temporal Graph Neural Networks. This falls under Efficient AI (Token Pruning and Eviction) and offers a method to reduce computational load in dynamic graph learning, which is transferable to other sequential data processing tasks.
papers.title: RAFT: Redundancy-Aware Input Filtering for Temporal Graph Neural Network Training
papers.tldr: RAFT accelerates temporal graph neural network training by filtering redundant target and historical events based on node-memory changes, substantially reducing processing with negligible precision loss.

papers.abstract: A general observation in agentic workflows, especially bounded ones, is that the decision space of the LLM, when we separate a decision from generation, starts approaching saturation: the agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones. LLMs generally don't treat these decisions as an optimization problem and instead re-derive them from their context/prompt on every turn. We show that treating decision making within reasonable bounds as an optimization problem, solving it once, and reusing the solved decisions can often make an agent faster, cheaper and more reliable. Our approach, which we call Discretize, Then Decide, starts from data such as the workflow's own logs or, when none exists, runs of the LLM agent itself. It reads each conversation into discrete states and estimates the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move, until no new states appear and the probabilities stop changing. It then solves the resulting Markov decision process. The solution runs as a controller around the model, sending moves whose content is fixed in the state, such as a tool call or a templated reply, and any state it hasn't seen is sent back to the LLM. We call an LLM run this way a Bellman language model (BLM), after Richard Bellman's equation for the best move in each state. On $\tau^2$-bench telecom, the controller with no model solves 79% of tasks. As a BLM, Qwen3.8-27B, an open model, goes from 29% to 96% with 93% fewer model calls. For Claude Opus 5.5, which solves 96% of tasks on its own, running it as a BLM cuts model calls and cost per task by about 98% and lets it solve 2 more tasks. On InventoryBench, the solved policy with no model beats every published method. Where the hard part is writing content rather than choosing moves, such as resolving SymPy issues, few decisions can be solved in advance, and a BLM helps little.
bullets: LLM agents repeatedly encounter the same states but typically re-derive decisions from context each turn.
“Discretize, Then Decide” extracts states, outcomes, costs, and transitions from workflow or agent logs, then solves the resulting MDP.
A controller reuses fixed actions for known states and delegates unseen states to the LLM.
On τ²-bench telecom, Qwen3.8-27B improved from 29% to 96% task success with 93% fewer model calls; Claude Opus 5.5 reduced calls and cost by about 98%.
The approach helps less on tasks dominated by generating novel content, such as resolving SymPy issues.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces LLM agent compute and cost by solving recurring decisions as an MDP; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: Bellman Language Models: Solving the Recurring Decisions of LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Bellman Language Models pre-solve recurring agent decisions as a Markov policy, making bounded workflows faster, cheaper, and often more reliable.

papers.abstract: Generative AI workflows execute user tasks by composing sequences of LLM calls, where each call performs a sub-task (e.g., summarization or translation), forming a workflow. Executing such workflows requires decisions over workflow structure, model assignments, and deployment configurations, which jointly determine latency, cost, and accuracy under dynamic workloads and resource constraints. Existing systems optimize these decisions in isolation or fix them early, leading to suboptimal cost and goodput. We make two key observations. First, efficient serving requires jointly exploring all combinations of workflows, model choices, and deployment configurations under dynamic cluster state. Second, reuse of deployed LLMs is critical for reducing cost, but must be performed on-the-fly, as reuse depends on current load and resource availability. Together, these make selecting a workflow-variant-a combination of workflow, models, and deployment configuration-a time-critical problem. We present FlowMaker, which exposes a task-level interface and selects workflow-variants on behalf of users. To realize this, we design a constraint-guided load-aware pruning algorithm for fast, on-the-fly decisions. FlowMaker improves goodput by up to 10.14$\times$ and reduces cost by up to 2.77$\times$ compared to state-of-the-art baselines, including Murakkab.
authors: Dimitrios Liakopoulos, Prasoon Sinha, Neeraja J. Yadwadkar
bullets: Generative AI workflows must jointly optimize structure, model assignment, and deployment configuration because these choices affect latency, cost, and accuracy.
Existing systems often optimize these decisions separately or commit to them early, resulting in poorer cost and goodput.
FlowMaker provides a task-level interface and selects workflow variants—workflow, model, and deployment combinations—on demand.
Its constraint-guided, load-aware pruning algorithm enables fast decisions while reusing deployed LLMs when current load and resource availability permit.
Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, FlowMaker improves goodput by up to 10.14× and reduces cost by up to 2.77×.
papers.selection_reason: Cost-efficient deployment and load-aware pruning for generative AI workflows directly reduce serving cost and latency.
papers.title: FlowMaker: From Tasks to Cost-Efficient Generative AI Workflow Deployments
papers.tldr: FlowMaker dynamically selects cost-efficient combinations of workflows, LLMs, and deployment configurations to improve generative AI serving under changing workloads and resources.

papers.abstract: Small Language Models with quantisation and parameter-efficient adaptation are widely offered as the route to multilingual AI under compute constraints, and their efficiency is almost always reported as a single memory figure. We show that this figure is measured in English and does not transfer. Across a 131k-sentence corpus spanning eleven Indic scripts, TinyLlama-1.1B's tokeniser emits 1.34 subword tokens per Latin-script word and 22.60 per Kannada word. This is not inefficiency; it is absence. Its vocabulary contains 0% of Odia's codepoints, 1% of Telugu's and 2% of Kannada's, and for five of eleven scripts the measured fertility sits at the UTF-8 byte-fallback ceiling, on Odia at 99.6% of it, with 93.6% of emitted tokens being raw bytes. Because SentencePiece byte fallback never raises an unknown-token marker, this failure is entirely silent: TinyLlama's UNK rate is 0.0% on every script, including the one it reads as bytes. We further show that low fertility can indicate the opposite of efficiency: mBERT posts its best score anywhere (1.10 tokens/word, on Odia) while discarding 87.9% of the text as UNK. MuRIL, an Indic-vocabulary encoder with a fifth of TinyLlama's parameters, reads every script at 1.23-2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and zero byte fallback. The binding constraint is the vocabulary, not the parameter count. The consequence is concrete: on a 2048-token context window, the same model gives an English user 1,528 words of usable context and a Kannada user 91.
bullets: Across 11 Indic scripts, TinyLlama’s tokenization ranges from 1.34 tokens per Latin-script word to 22.60 per Kannada word.
Its vocabulary covers 0% of Odia, 1% of Telugu, and 2% of Kannada codepoints; five scripts reach the byte-fallback ceiling.
The failure is silent: TinyLlama reports 0% UNK even when 93.6% of emitted tokens are raw bytes.
Low fertility can be misleading: mBERT’s 1.10 tokens/word on Odia accompanies 87.9% discarded text as UNK.
MuRIL handles all tested scripts at 1.23–2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and byte fallback, despite having one-fifth as many parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Shows tokenizer vocabulary coverage bounds effective context and efficiency for Indic scripts, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Efficiency Measured in English: Tokeniser Coverage Bounds Small Language Models on Indic Scripts
papers.tldr: For Indic scripts, small-model efficiency depends more on tokenizer vocabulary coverage than parameter count, and English-based metrics can hide severe byte-level fallback.

papers.abstract: On-device fine-tuning lets a large language model (LLM) learn from its user's private data without uploading it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces the trainable parameters, but each first-order training step still multiplies by the frozen base-model weights during the forward pass, activation recomputation, and input-gradient computation. A phone's neural processing unit (NPU) already holds these weights for inference; using it for training also requires computing input gradients, which its inference interface does not support. We present a system that runs all three frozen-weight products on the NPU while keeping the training graph, adapters, and optimizer on the CPU. Its input-gradient kernels reuse the resident weight tiles and the forward dequantizer, avoiding a transposed weight copy and ensuring forward and backward use the same effective weights. To preserve usable gradients, the system selects precision by gradient sensitivity and applies a per-row range guard for half-precision (FP16) outputs. Its runtime fuses the remaining CPU operators and overlaps NPU execution with adapter computation, while resumable execution and thermal pacing let training proceed as a background job. We evaluate it on two Qualcomm Snapdragon platforms using four LLMs from the Qwen and Llama families. Our workloads cover nightly personalization with labels supplied on the phone and the public LaMP-2 benchmark; comparisons include an optimized CPU trainer, a phone-GPU trainer, forward-only training, and GPU-trained references.
authors: Xu Zheng, Wei Cheng, Zhuomin Chen, Dongkuan Xu, Mo Sha, Jingchao Ni, Dongsheng Luo
bullets: Targets private, on-device LLM personalization without uploading user data.
Runs forward, activation-recomputation, and input-gradient products with resident NPU weights, avoiding transposed weight copies.
Uses gradient-sensitive precision selection and FP16 per-row range guarding to preserve gradient quality.
Fuses CPU work, overlaps NPU and adapter computation, and supports resumable, thermally paced background training.
Evaluated on two Snapdragon platforms with four Qwen and Llama models across personalization and LaMP-2 workloads.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient on-device LoRA training system reducing memory and compute on phone NPUs.
papers.title: First-Order LoRA Training with Phone NPUs
papers.tldr: A phone-NPU system enables practical first-order LoRA fine-tuning by offloading frozen-weight operations to the NPU while retaining training control on the CPU.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning aims to reduce inference cost while preserving the capabilities of the original VLM. Yet existing evaluations rely on aggregate task accuracy and retained token count as proxies for pruning quality and actual efficiency. We reveal two limitations: 1) Aggregate accuracy can obscure whether a pruning method truly identifies critical visual tokens; many examples remain solvable under arbitrary token removal and models can exploit textual shortcuts when visual evidence is degraded. 2) Retained token count is an unreliable proxy for efficiency, as identical token budgets can incur different end-to-end costs depending on where and how pruning is performed. Consequently, comparisons based on aggregate accuracy and retained token counts fail to recover the global performance-efficiency Pareto frontier across methods. We introduce PAA-Bench, a plug-and-play evaluation framework for existing benchmarks, to evaluate whether pruning succeeds through meaningful token selection and whether this success translates into real speedup. To determine when token choice actually matters, we propose Random-Pass@k to measure how often an example remains correct under random pruning, enabling comprehensive evaluation across different levels of selection difficulty. To compare efficiency fairly, we introduce Preservation-Constrained Speedup (PCS) to report the maximum end-to-end speedup each method achieves under a shared preservation target. Experiments across 8 methods, 3 VLM backbones, and 9 benchmarks show that stronger token compression does not necessarily yield greater speedup, method differences widen on examples where token selection matters, and efficiency rankings change with the preservation target.
authors: Geng Li, Guohao Chen, Shilin Shan, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Aggregate accuracy can hide arbitrary token removal and reliance on textual shortcuts.
Equal retained-token budgets can produce different real inference costs depending on pruning location and procedure.
Random-Pass@k measures how often examples remain correct under random pruning, revealing when token selection matters.
Preservation-Constrained Speedup (PCS) compares maximum end-to-end speedup at a shared preservation target.
Across 8 methods, 3 VLM backbones, and 9 benchmarks, compression strength, speedup, and method rankings do not consistently align.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes evaluation framework for VLM token pruning, directly relevant to token pruning and efficiency.
papers.title: Are We Evaluating VLM Token Pruning Right? Looking Beyond Accuracy and Token Count
papers.tldr: PAA-Bench shows that VLM token pruning should be evaluated by meaningful token selection and measured end-to-end speedup, not aggregate accuracy and token counts alone.

papers.abstract: Adam is widely used for training large language models (LLMs) owing to its strong optimization performance and training stability, but its element-wise estimation for the first and second moments incur substantial memory overhead. Although numerous memory-efficient optimizers have been proposed, many incur additional computational overhead or require additional tuning of hyperparameters. Consequently, Adam remains a dominant and reliable choice for LLM pre-training. We propose AdamPM (Adam with Pooled Moments), a simple and memory-efficient variant of Adam that groups adjacent moment entries along the row or column dimension and represents each group by a single shared mean. AdamPM can well inherit Adam's hyperparameter settings and is readily integrated into existing Adam optimizer implementations, with less memory overhead. We systematically investigate pooling of both first and second moment estimates and identify second moment pooling as the effective design. With a group size of $s$, AdamPM reduces second moment memory to $1/s$ of the original requirement. Extensive experiments on language model pretraining, fine-tuning and multimodal learning demonstrate that AdamPM maintains model performance and training speed while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/jixiaowei95/AdamPM}.
authors: Xiaowei Ji, Lishan Xu, Jianing An, Jie Luo, Wenjun Wu, Lei Huang
bullets: Addresses Adam’s substantial memory overhead from element-wise first- and second-moment estimates in LLM training.
Groups adjacent moment entries and represents each group with a shared mean, requiring no additional hyperparameter tuning beyond Adam’s settings.
Finds that pooling the second-moment estimates is the effective design.
With group size s, reduces second-moment memory to 1/s of Adam’s requirement.
Experiments across language-model pretraining, fine-tuning, and multimodal learning show maintained performance and training speed.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient optimizer for LLM training, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: AdamPM: Memory-Efficient LLM Optimization via Moment Pooling
papers.tldr: AdamPM reduces Adam’s optimizer-state memory by pooling moment estimates while preserving training performance and speed.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for autonomous driving. However, the massive parameter scale of VLAs strains onboard computational resources during real-time inference. This directly increases energy consumption and limits vehicle battery range, making it critical to minimize computational overhead without compromising driving capability and explainability. Current research on efficient VLA-based driving focuses on sequential adaptation (\textit{e.g.}, Chain-of-Thought and token adjustment), leaving structural adaptation underexplored despite parameter redundancy across dynamic driving scenes. To address this gap, we propose Scene-Adaptive VLA, an efficient framework leveraging dynamic layer routing to adjust active parameters based on real-time scenes. Inspired by the temporal continuity of scenes and model predictive uncertainty, our approach characterizes model-perceived scene complexity via frame-level temporal scene variations and decision deviations. To uncover latent scene-to-parameter correspondences, we encode this characterization into scene-aware tokens, alongside two specialized queries. A budget-conditioned layer routing mechanism evaluates these refined queries to allocate a budget that determines the active parameter ratio and subsequently selects appropriate layer combinations. The entire framework is optimized end-to-end. Extensive evaluations on the Bench2Drive benchmark show that when adapted to a state-of-the-art VLA model, our approach significantly reduces inference-time computational overhead by 53.5\% with negligible degradation in driving and language capabilities. Code is available at https:github.com/yang-luvu/Scene-Adaptive-VLA.
authors: Yujia Yang, Quan Yuan, Jiawei Fan, Yang Li, Tiange Fu, Xiaoyuan Fu, Guiyang Luo, Jinglin Li
bullets: Addresses the high computational and energy costs of large VLA models for real-time autonomous driving.
Uses temporal scene variations and decision deviations to estimate scene complexity and model uncertainty.
Encodes this information into scene-aware tokens and specialized queries for budget-conditioned layer routing.
Dynamically selects layer combinations and active parameter ratios through end-to-end optimization.
On Bench2Drive, reduces inference-time computational overhead by 53.5% with negligible capability degradation.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-Language-Action driving model with dynamic layer routing for efficient inference, fitting embodied VLA and efficient AI.
papers.title: Scene-Adaptive VLA: Efficient Autonomous Driving via Dynamic Layer Routing
papers.tldr: Scene-Adaptive VLA dynamically activates model layers according to driving-scene complexity, reducing inference computation while largely preserving driving and language performance.

papers.abstract: Instance-dependent early stopping (IES) reduces training computation by skipping backpropagation for examples whose losses have stabilized, but the second-order loss-difference criterion used by IES lacks a theoretical justification. We develop Theory-Guided Instance-Dependent Early Stopping (TG-IES), which analyzes this criterion under explicit assumptions and derives a noise-calibrated mastery threshold and a conditional stability bound for instance exclusion. We show that second-order differencing has a favorable bias-variance trade-off over first- and third-order differences in a specific signal-to-noise regime, and that its signal contains both gradient-drift and curvature terms. TG-IES derives its stopping threshold and patience from training-run statistics rather than using the manually selected threshold of IES. Across CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, TG-IES saves 53-58% of backpropagation instances in its main convolutional settings while keeping accuracy within 0.1-0.9 percentage points of full training; in the primary ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 setting, this corresponds to 35.7% FLOP-normalized savings. The method also transfers to ViT-Tiny, where it achieves smaller savings and incurs a modest accuracy cost. These results provide a theoretical basis for second-order instance-dependent early stopping and show that theory-guided calibration can substantially reduce training computation under the assumptions and experimental settings studied.
authors: Ahad Bin Islam Shoeb, Jamal Uddin Tanvin, Kamrul Hasan, Alve Reduan, Imtiaz Ahmed
bullets: Analyzes the bias-variance trade-off of second-order loss differences and identifies contributions from gradient drift and curvature.
Derives a noise-calibrated mastery threshold and conditional stability bound for excluding stabilized instances.
Sets stopping thresholds and patience from training-run statistics instead of manual tuning.
Saves 53–58% of backpropagation instances in reported convolutional settings, with accuracy within 0.1–0.9 percentage points of full training.
Transfers to ViT-Tiny with smaller savings and a modest accuracy cost, indicating scope-dependent effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a theory-guided method for instance-dependent early stopping to reduce training computation, fitting the Efficient AI category.
papers.title: Theory-Guided Instance-Dependent Early Stopping via Second-Order Loss Dynamics
papers.tldr: TG-IES theoretically calibrates second-order instance-dependent early stopping to reduce backpropagation computation while largely preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is important for modern intelligent applications but remains constrained by peak memory during prompt prefill. Existing KV cache compression reduces decoding memory but typically requires full-prompt prefill to preserve global context, retaining a high construction peak. Online chunk-level eviction lowers memory earlier but selects before each layer has observed the complete prompt, potentially degrading cache construction and decoding. We present TideKV, an on-GPU cache-construction architecture using layer-major delayed eviction. TideKV processes all prompt chunks within each Transformer layer, retains full-prompt KV only for the active layer, and evicts at layer end. This schedule preserves full-prompt-aware selection while reducing activation and temporary memory. Experiments across multiple computing platforms show that TideKV preserves the inference quality and final cache size of the evaluated compression methods. At 64K on A100, it reduces the construction-time transient footprint by 83.89%. On RTX 4090, it increases time to first token by only 1.06% at 64K and enables 128K prefill. TideKV also completes 128K on Jetson, whereas matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory on both resource-constrained platforms. These results show that delayed layer-end eviction substantially expands feasible context lengths without sacrificing cache utility.
authors: Yu Wang, Zhu Wang, Ning Hu, Yifan Guo, Xiu Ma, Bin Guo, Zhiwen Yu
bullets: Targets high transient memory from full-prompt KV-cache construction, which limits long-context inference.
Processes prompt chunks layer by layer, retaining full-prompt KV only for the active layer before evicting it.
Preserves full-prompt-aware cache selection while reducing activation and temporary memory.
At 64K context, cuts construction-time transient memory by 83.89% on A100; on RTX 4090, TTFT increases only 1.06%.
Enables 128K prefill on RTX 4090 and Jetson, where matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory.
papers.selection_reason: Layer-wise delayed KV eviction reduces long-context LLM prefill memory; fits KV cache/memory efficiency and long-context inference.
papers.title: TideKV: Delayed KV Eviction via Layer-Wise Chunked Prefill for Memory-Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference
papers.tldr: TideKV reduces peak memory during long-context LLM prefill by delaying KV-cache eviction until each Transformer layer finishes processing the full prompt.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised speech models commonly consist of a set of convolutional neural network (CNN) layers used as a local feature extractor, followed by transformer layers. The CNN layers are computationally demanding, and are also similar across models and resemble the much simpler mel spectral features. We hypothesize that the CNN layers can be replaced by a simple, universal model. To test this hypothesis, we learn a two-layer feature extractor via distillation from one or more teacher models (HuBERT, data2vec, and WavLM). Experiments on SUPERB(-SG) benchmark tasks show that our model largely retains the performance of the teacher models and can also be used in an unseen model (wav2vec 2.0). Our feature extractor requires only 3% of the MACs of the CNNs, resulting in a $>$20% overall inference runtime reduction.
authors: Jessica Yang, Marcelo Beramendi Caballero, Ju-Chieh Chou, Karen Livescu
bullets: Self-supervised speech models use computationally expensive CNN local feature extractors that resemble simpler mel features.
The proposed universal extractor is learned by distillation from HuBERT, data2vec, and WavLM teachers.
On SUPERB(-SG), it largely retains teacher performance and transfers to the unseen wav2vec 2.0 model.
It uses only 3% of the CNNs’ MACs and reduces overall inference runtime by more than 20%.
Scope: evaluation focuses on SUPERB(-SG) benchmark tasks and the tested teacher/model families.
papers.selection_reason: Distills speech front-end into a universal lightweight feature extractor, reducing MACs and inference runtime.
papers.title: Toward a Universal Local Speech Feature Extractor Through Distillation
papers.tldr: A distilled two-layer speech feature extractor replaces costly CNN front ends while largely preserving downstream performance and reducing inference cost.

papers.abstract: Improving every agent in an LLM-based multi-agent system can be prohibitively costly, making it important to identify which agent should be prioritized to achieve the greatest system-level gain with limited resources. Failure attribution can inform this decision, but an agent's responsibility for failures does not directly reveal the system-level gains achievable by improving it. We therefore introduce IF-MAP, an influence-function-inspired method for identifying agents with high potential for system-level improvement. For each agent, IF-MAP measures end-to-end loss changes under controlled semantic prompt perturbations, fits a regularized local response model in a low-dimensional prompt-embedding subspace, and uses the estimated response norm as a priority score. This black-box procedure requires no access to model parameters or gradients and produces agent priorities that can guide subsequent improvement effort. We evaluate IF-MAP across six multi-agent workflows spanning code generation, question answering, and mathematical reasoning, using the same priorities for prompt optimization and model upgrades. Optimizing the selected agents' prompts achieves a macro-average gain of 3.81 percentage points, compared with 1.85 for uniform agent selection. Across five target models, upgrading the selected agents yields macro-average gains of 7.62-16.42 percentage points, compared with 3.81-8.62 for uniform agent selection. Despite its probing overhead, IF-MAP reduces Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V3.2 token use by 74.2% and 35.2%, respectively, relative to optimizing every agent, and reduces target-model tokens by 63.6-64.9% relative to upgrading every agent. These results support the use of IF-MAP to identify promising agents and direct improvement effort toward greater end-to-end performance gains.
authors: Jie Mao, Pingchen Lu, Zikun Qu, Jiahang Sun, Xiangyi Wang, Zhiwei Shang, Zhiyong Wang, Guojun Xiong, Zhongxiang Dai
bullets: Targets the gap between failure attribution and the improvement potential of individual agents.
Measures end-to-end loss responses to controlled semantic perturbations and fits a regularized local model in a low-dimensional prompt-embedding space.
Uses the estimated response norm as an agent-priority score without requiring model parameters or gradients.
Across six workflows, selected-agent prompt optimization and model upgrades outperform uniform selection in macro-average gains.
Reduces token use substantially versus optimizing or upgrading every agent, despite probing overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Influence-function-based agent prioritization reduces token and compute cost in multi-agent LLM systems, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: IF-MAP: Influence-Function-Inspired Agent Prioritization in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.tldr: IF-MAP prioritizes which agents to improve by estimating their system-level influence through black-box semantic prompt perturbations, achieving larger gains while reducing optimization cost.

papers.abstract: Activation steering provides a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for controlling large language model behavior. Existing methods, however, often face a trade-off between efficiency and expressiveness: fixed steering vectors incur negligible inference overhead but cannot adapt to the current model input, whereas input-dependent nonlinear interventions provide greater flexibility at additional runtime cost. We introduce \textbf{WAQS} (\textbf{W}eight \textbf{A}bsorption for \textbf{Q}uadratic probing and affine \textbf{S}teering), a framework that obtains state-dependent steering, without additional inference-time computation. WAQS models a concept with a quadratic probe, whose gradient yields an affine, activation-dependent steering direction. We show that this affine intervention can be folded exactly into adjacent linear transformations through an offline weight update. Moreover, we prove that quadratic functions form the maximal class of smooth concept scores whose gradient-based interventions are affine and therefore exactly absorbable into linear layers. Under a Gaussian representation model, our formulation admits an interpretation as the difference of class-conditional Mahalanobis pulls and naturally generalizes linear discriminant and difference-in-means steering. To scale to high-dimensional representations, we introduce a low-rank parameterization of the quadratic term. Across truthfulness, refusal, and sycophancy steering tasks, quadratic steering matches or improves upon constant linear steering while preserving model utility, with the absorbed implementation introducing no additional inference-time operations. Our results suggest that quadratic probes provide a practical middle ground between static linear steering and computationally expensive dynamic nonlinear interventions.
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–expressiveness trade-off between fixed steering vectors and costly dynamic interventions.
Uses a quadratic concept probe whose gradient produces an activation-dependent affine steering direction.
Exactly folds this affine intervention into adjacent linear layers through an offline weight update.
Proves quadratic scores are the maximal smooth class yielding affine, exactly absorbable gradient interventions.
Across truthfulness, refusal, and sycophancy tasks, it matches or improves linear steering while preserving utility; a low-rank form supports high-dimensional representations.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces weight absorption to make state-dependent LLM steering inference-time-free, an efficiency contribution.
papers.title: WAQS: Weight Absorption for Quadratic Probing and Affine Steering
papers.tldr: WAQS enables input-dependent quadratic activation steering with no added inference-time computation by absorbing the resulting affine intervention into model weights.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose a block of tokens that the target model verifies in one parallel pass. Autoregressive drafters generate this block one token at a time, whereas block diffusion drafters such as DFlash generate it in one pass, making drafting faster. However, these diffusion drafters predict each token independently, ignoring dependencies between tokens in the block. We introduce FlashMap, a continuous flow drafter that conditions a flow map language model on the target model's hidden states and generates the whole block in one forward pass while capturing inter-token dependencies. On Qwen3-8B, FlashMap is faster than a matched DFlash baseline on every benchmark, with 7% higher average speedup and up to 6.1x lossless acceleration.
authors: Jeff Shen, Zhejian Zhou, Ryan Lee, Jonathan May, Shirley Ho
bullets: Speculative decoding uses a lightweight drafter to propose tokens that the target LLM verifies in parallel.
Existing block-diffusion drafters generate blocks quickly but predict tokens independently.
FlashMap conditions a continuous-flow language model on the target model’s hidden states to capture inter-token dependencies.
It generates the entire token block in one forward pass.
On Qwen3-8B, FlashMap outperforms matched DFlash across all benchmarks, with 7% higher average speedup.
papers.selection_reason: Flow-map speculative decoding drafter for lossless LLM inference acceleration; directly relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: FlashMap: Flow Map Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: FlashMap accelerates speculative decoding by generating dependent token blocks in one flow-based pass, achieving up to 6.1× lossless acceleration on Qwen3-8B.

papers.abstract: Deploying a large language model (LLM) requires choosing the right accelerator, parallelization strategy, engine configuration, and replica count amongst ~140 other variables across clouds, regions, and markets. These decisions are intertwined, and the best cluster-wide plan continually changes as jobs contend for shared capacity on shifting workloads. We present Koi, a self-calibrating cluster planner for heterogeneous, multi-cloud fleets. Koi uses a Recursive Language Model (RLM) hierarchy to propose hypotheses and reason over deployment while deterministic components predict serving behavior, score candidates, and control placement. It represents inference behavior as a fixed causal graph linking decisions (e.g., accelerator, parallelism), runtime mediators (e.g., KV-cache pressure, communication overhead), and outcomes (e.g., latency, throughput). Each deployment strengthens or weakens scoped causal relationships, building a comprehensive playbook for inference that the planner employs to guide future decisions. Job-wise configurations are composed into cluster-wide plans and evaluated against serving objectives, resource constraints, SLO risks, and cost. Across benchmarks, Koi achieves 1.18x greater goodput than the strongest baseline while reducing $/token by 20% in a real heterogeneous cluster. Ablations isolate the contribution of Koi's architecture: a pure language model attains a composite score of 35.3, the same model equipped with Koi's deterministic tools reaches 51.6, and the full Koi planner reaches 70.8.
authors: Mankeerat Sidhu, Gangmuk Lim, Hetarth Chopra, Maximillian Eisenberg, Quan Hao Ng, Aryan Gosaliya, Shu Liu, Luka Govedi\v{c}, Jiaxin Shan, Hongkuan Zhou, Vikram Sharma Mailthody, P. Brighten Godfrey, Ion Stoica
bullets: Addresses the changing, interdependent choices involved in selecting accelerators, parallelism, engine settings, replicas, placement, and cost across multi-cloud fleets.
Uses a Recursive Language Model hierarchy to generate deployment hypotheses, while deterministic tools predict serving behavior, score candidates, and control placement.
Builds a fixed causal graph linking deployment decisions, runtime factors such as KV-cache pressure and communication overhead, and outcomes including latency and throughput.
Updates scoped causal relationships after deployments to create a reusable inference playbook and composes job-level configurations into cluster-wide plans.

Reports 1.18× higher goodput than the strongest baseline and 20% lower cost per token in a real heterogeneous cluster; ablations show the full planner outperforming tool-augmented and pure language-model variants.
papers.selection_reason: Self-calibrating planner for heterogeneous LLM inference fleets that improves goodput and reduces serving cost; relevant to efficient AI deployment.
papers.title: Koi: Evidence-Guided, Self-Calibrating Planning for Multi-Cloud, Heterogeneous LLM Inference Fleets
papers.tldr: Koi combines language-model reasoning with deterministic prediction and self-calibrating causal evidence to optimize heterogeneous, multi-cloud LLM inference deployments.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA), video-action (VA), and world action models (WAMs) form the backbone of modern physical AI systems, yet their real-time single-batch inference remains a defining bottleneck. Latency is dominated not by individual kernel computation, but by system-level overhead: thousands of short kernel launches, intermediate data movement across operator boundaries, and redundant recomputation across consecutive decisions. General-purpose graph compilers cannot address these costs, as they optimize individual calls in isolation and lack visibility into cross-call state semantics and global pipeline structure. We present FLASHRT-PAI, a low-latency inference engine built around model-hardware pipeline co-design rather than isolated kernel optimization. FLASHRT-PAI combines three core mechanisms: deep kernel fusion with launch overlap eliminates inter-operator boundaries and launch gaps; an execution contract formalizes the pipeline's stage DAG, update rates, and named buffers to enable cross-decision state reuse and selective refresh; and execution-state capsules enable fast snapshot, restore, and fork of persistent pipeline state. The system also supports drop-in acceleration of unmodified PyTorch models via parity- and latency-gated kernel replacement. Evaluation covers six policies on RTX 5090 and four on Jetson AGX Thor. At matched 16-bit precision, FLASHRT-PAI is 1.3-3.7x faster than official compiled paths. Combining pipeline co-design with reduced precision delivers 3.38-12.66x speedup over official eager implementations.
