In LIBERO-10, four-bit pi0.5 achieves 94.04% success on Thor and 93.32% on RTX 5090, compared with 92.4% for the measured official FP16 reference. FLASHRT-PAI is open source, distributed via Hugging Face Kernel Hub, and its opt-in pi0.5 kernels have been adopted into the LeRobot framework.
authors: Liang Su, David Chen, Jason Li, Kevin Guo, Teresa Lv
bullets: Targets real-time single-batch inference bottlenecks from kernel-launch overhead, data movement, and redundant recomputation across decisions.
Uses deep kernel fusion with launch overlap, an execution contract for cross-decision state reuse, and execution-state capsules for fast snapshot, restore, and fork operations.
Supports drop-in acceleration of unmodified PyTorch models through parity- and latency-gated kernel replacement.
Across evaluated policies and hardware, achieves 1.3–3.7× speedup at matched 16-bit precision and 3.38–12.66× over official eager implementations with reduced precision.
In LIBERO-10, four-bit pi0.5 reaches 94.04% success on Jetson AGX Thor and 93.32% on RTX 5090, near or above the reported FP16 reference.
papers.selection_reason: Low-latency inference engine for VLA and world action models, directly relevant to embodied AI and efficient AI.
papers.title: FlashRT-PAI: Fast Kernels Are Not Fast Pipelines for Physical AI Inference
papers.tldr: FLASHRT-PAI accelerates physical-AI inference by optimizing the entire execution pipeline—not just individual kernels—achieving substantial speedups while preserving task performance.

papers.abstract: A low-precision agent can call its full-precision (BF16) model at selected decisions as a fallback. A learned precision router chooses where to call it from the disagreement between the two models and is judged by end-to-end success. An inserted BF16 action, however, can rescue a failing task or damage a succeeding one. We argue that a fallback's value is the number of tasks it saves minus the number it spoils, measured for the intervention that will actually run. From restored states, we run paired branches that cross which model supplies the current action with which model continues, separating replacement of one action, takeover of later execution, and both. On Qwen3 agents with simulated 4-bit weights in tau2-bench, replacing the first action where the two models differed in tool use changed many task outcomes, but rescues and damages nearly cancelled, and on held-out telecom tasks the action-only estimate was negative. Replacing both the action and the continuation had a positive net gain in two of five exploratory lower-bit stress settings. Two references changed outcomes at fixed bit width: replacing an action with that of a second 4-bit checkpoint changed about as many outcomes as replacing it with the BF16 action, and reordering tool-argument keys changed outcomes while the executed tool call stayed identical. At common states, the additional value of the BF16 action over that checkpoint remained unresolved. A frozen uncertainty trigger found more outcome changes than random selection, while its net benefit stayed within the range of random selection. We recommend evaluating each fallback by its signed task benefit under the intended continuation, against same-precision references, before attributing gains to more bits.
authors: Sicheng Lyu, Xinyu Wang, Yu Gu, Lei Ding, Ziyang Song, Xiao-Wen Chang
bullets: A disagreement-based router selects when a low-precision agent should invoke its BF16 model, with evaluation based on end-to-end task success.
Paired branch interventions separate the effects of replacing one action, taking over later execution, or replacing both action and continuation.
In Qwen3 agents on tau2-bench, first-action BF16 replacement changed many outcomes, but rescues and damages nearly cancelled; the held-out telecom estimate was negative.
Replacing both action and continuation produced a positive net gain in only two of five exploratory lower-bit settings.
Same-precision references and even tool-argument ordering also changed outcomes, while an uncertainty trigger found more changes than random selection without clear net benefit.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the value of precision upgrades in closed-loop agents, directly addressing efficiency in AI systems.
papers.title: Measuring the Task Value of Precision Upgrades in Closed-Loop Agents
papers.tldr: Precision fallbacks should be judged by their net task benefit under the exact intervention and continuation that will run, because they can rescue and spoil tasks in nearly equal measure.

papers.abstract: Training large language models directly in 4-bit floating-point (FP) formats promises substantial improvements in throughput and energy efficiency. While some recipe design choices have been validated at scale, many promising approaches remain untested beyond small models and short token horizons, leaving open the question of which trends will hold. We present a systematic comparison of recent NVFP4 recipes at medium model scale, evaluating dense 8B and 30B-A3B MoE models trained for up to 1T tokens, with a focus on which ingredients are necessary for accuracy recovery. We propose a final recipe grounded in the principles behind established stable NVFP4 training at scale, incorporating state-of-the-art techniques such as unbiased gradient estimation with lower quantization error than stochastic rounding. To the best of our knowledge, this is the strongest FP4 training result demonstrated at this scale to date in loss gap to BF16. Through ablation studies, we find that: (i) each technique in the optimized recipe measurably improves loss trajectory, (ii) selective high-precision layers are necessary for recovering accuracy at scale, (iii) not all tensors in the backward pass benefit equally from de-biasing, leaving room to apply complementary error-reduction techniques to the remaining tensors.
authors: Anjulie Agrusa, Andrei Panferov, Elizabeth Wei, Keith Wyss, Paul Gibbons, Erik Schultheis, Jinhang Choi, Frank Sun, Tijmen Blankevoort, Dan Alistarh
bullets: Evaluates NVFP4 training recipes on dense 8B and 30B-A3B MoE models for up to 1T tokens.
Proposes an optimized recipe combining established stable-training principles with unbiased gradient estimation that reduces quantization error.
Finds that every component of the optimized recipe improves the loss trajectory.
Shows selective high-precision layers are necessary for accuracy recovery at scale.
Finds de-biasing benefits vary across backward-pass tensors, motivating complementary error-reduction methods.
papers.selection_reason: Comparative study of low-precision FP4 pretraining recipes for LLMs; directly addresses training efficiency and energy reduction in AI systems.
papers.title: What Matters for NVFP4 Training? A Comparative Study of Low-Precision Pretraining Recipes
papers.tldr: A systematic study identifies which techniques enable effective NVFP4 pretraining at medium scale, showing that selective high-precision layers and carefully targeted de-biasing are key to narrowing the loss gap to BF16.

papers.abstract: BERT-based models require thousands of labeled samples to train. Larger models like GPT-X require only 1-5 examples per class. However, performance, cost and time tradeoffs of such models remain under-explored. In this work, we classify survey text data into 16 classes. We focus on experimental approaches and results on performance, cost, and time taken for this problem. We compare these parameters of a trained RoBERTa-based model, and an (off-the-shelf) GPT-3.5 model for text classification. Baseline experiments show that the time taken by GPT-3.5 for generating predictions on 10,000 records is 6 hours, whereas a RoBERTa-based model takes only 12 mins on a T4 GPU. To identify the best prompting approach for GPT-3.5, we explore batch prompting. We experiment with (1) batch-size, and (2) few-shot sampling. We find the best batch size is 20 with human few-shot curation. Experiments show the F1 score of a trained RoBERTa-based model (96%) is much higher than a GPT-3.5 model (83%). In case of GPT-3.5, batch prompting is beneficial in lowering inference costs by ~70%, without hindering task performance. We find the best approach is an ensemble of a RoBERTa-based and GPT-3.5 model (F1: 97.5%) incurring only 4.4% of inference cost compared to a standalone GPT-3.5.
authors: Shivam Mathur, Sri Harish Popuri, Priya Krishnan Sundararajan, Kevin Horecka, Michael Mugo
bullets: Compares a trained RoBERTa model with off-the-shelf GPT-3.5 for 16-class survey-text classification.
RoBERTa processes 10,000 records in 12 minutes on a T4 GPU, versus 6 hours for GPT-3.5.
RoBERTa achieves 96% F1, compared with 83% for GPT-3.5.
Batch prompting with batch size 20 and human-curated few-shot examples reduces GPT-3.5 inference cost by about 70% without hurting performance.
An RoBERTa–GPT-3.5 ensemble reaches 97.5% F1 at 4.4% of standalone GPT-3.5 inference cost.
papers.selection_reason: Cost-performance study of small models vs LLMs with batch prompting and ensemble to reduce inference cost.
papers.title: Best of Both Worlds: Fine-Tuned Small Models Complement LLMs for Cost and Performance Benefits
papers.tldr: A fine-tuned RoBERTa model delivers faster, stronger classification, while combining it with GPT-3.5 achieves the best reported F1 score at a fraction of GPT-3.5’s inference cost.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a prominent paradigm for training reasoning models, but its computational cost makes efficient data selection increasingly important. Since training examples contribute unequally to learning, selecting a small, informative subset can offer a more efficient alternative to using the entire data pool. The training-free selection method estimates prompt value with hidden states from complete greedy rollouts. However, in our datasets, $26$--$32\%$ of these rollouts fail to terminate within the generation budget. We introduce LIFT, a training-free data selector that identifies impactful prompts using only partial reasoning rollouts. At its core, LIFT uses Partial Rollout Context Lift (PRCL), a score inspired by pointwise $\mathcal{V}$-information that accumulates token-level log-likelihood ratios between a question-conditioned context and a null context with the question removed. This enables prompt scoring from a short rollout prefix rather than a complete trajectory. Across Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B, prefixes retaining at least 90\% and 95\% of the full-rollout PRCL score, respectively, require only 26\% and 4.7\% of the tokens generated by full rollouts. Compared with SHIFT, LIFT reduces selection cost by 3.7--9.1$\times$ while achieving competitive downstream RLVR performance, with the highest six-benchmark average in three of six settings.
authors: Lei Jiang, Honghui Bao, Yue Zhou, Zhengyao Gu, Langzhou He, Natalie Parde
bullets: Complete greedy rollouts used for prompt scoring can fail to terminate within the generation budget 26–32% of the time.
LIFT scores prompts with Partial Rollout Context Lift (PRCL), based on token-level log-likelihood ratios between question-conditioned and null contexts.
Short prefixes can retain at least 90–95% of full-rollout PRCL scores while using only 26% or 4.7% of full-rollout tokens across the evaluated models.
Compared with SHIFT, LIFT reduces selection cost by 3.7–9.1× and achieves competitive RLVR results, attaining the highest six-benchmark average in three of six settings.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free prompt selection with partial rollouts reduces RLVR computation, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Training-Free Prompt Selection for Efficient Reinforcement Learning With Partial Rollouts
papers.tldr: LIFT enables training-free RLVR prompt selection from short partial rollouts, substantially reducing selection cost while maintaining competitive downstream performance.

papers.abstract: Context-to-LoRA methods encode documents as low-rank parameter updates, allowing language models to answer without retaining the source text in their decoding context. How reliably do these updates preserve facts and support their use under different instructions? Controlled diagnosis of existing context-to-LoRA methods separates fact discrimination, target retention, and response adaptation. Competing sources influence answers, while target-only construction and memory-state optimization improve recovery at fixed update size. Recovering facts also does not ensure that answers follow response instructions. We introduce Cache2LoRA, which uses each query to aggregate evidence from a reusable frozen document cache before generating LoRA updates. Trainable encoding operates only on the query and memory-token suffix, and multi-style supervision teaches both evidence preservation and answer expression. Across 17 tasks, Cache2LoRA improves on existing context-to-LoRA methods and achieves macro F1 of 0.663, approaching full-context in-context learning at 0.671. For 32K documents and 256-token outputs at batch size 16, its decoding throughput is 5.9$\times$ that of full-context ICL. At matched memory size, generated LoRA preserves answer accuracy more reliably than the learned-KV variant under long, diverse intervening text and combines more effectively with retained document KV, yielding higher hybrid F1 and EM.
authors: Yi Fang, Gaurav Srivastava, Zhenyu Bi, Sirui Ding, Xuan Wang
bullets: Diagnoses context internalization through fact discrimination, target retention, and response adaptation.
Aggregates query-relevant evidence from a frozen document cache, then encodes only the query and memory-token suffix into LoRA updates.
Uses multi-style supervision to preserve evidence and better follow answer-format instructions.
Across 17 tasks, reaches 0.663 macro F1 versus 0.671 for full-context in-context learning, with 5.9× higher decoding throughput in the reported setting.
Generated LoRA is more robust than learned-KV under long intervening text and combines effectively with retained document KV.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Cache2LoRA to improve context internalization in LoRA methods, enhancing throughput and accuracy through memory-efficient techniques.
papers.title: Cache2LoRA: Understanding and Improving Context Internalization
papers.tldr: Cache2LoRA improves context-to-LoRA by querying a reusable document cache before generating updates, nearing full-context accuracy while substantially increasing decoding throughput.

papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) trains a shared model across data-owning clients without centralizing raw data, but client data difficulty and compute budgets can differ. We study local early-exit Vision Transformer (ViT) inference, where an intermediate classifier may return a prediction before the final Transformer stage. The proposed method replaces one global acceptance threshold with a client-specific base threshold from label entropy and shallow-exit confidence, then adjusts each input using predictive entropy, confidence, top-two class margin, and exit depth. Aggregation uses only clients that updated a parameter. Security-aware routing reaches 88.70% CIFAR-10 accuracy with 32.0% depth saving and 73.7% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 30\% saving. On matched six-client non-IID CIFAR-100, full-depth accuracy is 72.28% versus 68.20--71.80% for four heterogeneous-FL baselines; robustness-aware routing reaches 70.01% with 32.55% saving.
authors: Sahar Refaei Ghalibafan, Samira Nazari, Christian Herglotz, Maksim Jenihhin, Mahdi Taheri
bullets: Addresses differing client data difficulty and compute budgets in federated early-exit ViT inference.
Uses client-specific thresholds based on label entropy and shallow-exit confidence, with input-level adjustments from entropy, confidence, class margin, and exit depth.
Aggregates updates only from clients that modified a parameter.
Reports 32.0% CIFAR-10 depth savings at 88.70% accuracy and 30% ImageNet-1K savings at 73.7% top-1 accuracy.
On matched non-IID CIFAR-100, full-depth accuracy reaches 72.28%, while robustness-aware routing achieves 70.01% accuracy with 32.55% savings.
papers.selection_reason: Early-exit ViT inference reduces computation and latency, fitting the broad Efficient AI topic even without a specific listed subtopic.
papers.title: Client-Aware Security Adaptive Early Exit Vision Transformers for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
papers.tldr: A client-aware, security-adaptive early-exit ViT improves efficiency in heterogeneous federated learning while maintaining strong accuracy across datasets.

papers.abstract: Native multimodal large language models (native MLLMs) jointly encode visual and linguistic sequences within a unified autoregressive Transformer, emerging as a promising paradigm for multimodal understanding. Unlike conventional ViT-based MLLMs relying on external vision encoders, ViT-free native MLLMs tokenize pixel patches directly, potentially suffering severe visual token redundancy. A pilot study confirms this: unlike ViT-based models that degrade under compression, ViT-free MLLMs tolerate aggressive compression with near-lossless or even improved performance. Yet existing compression methods target ViT-based settings, leaving native MLLMs, which stand to gain the most, unexplored. To close this gap, we introduce an analysis pipeline centered on token discriminability and cross-dimensional heterogeneous redundancy, revealing that (i) redundancy is distributed independently and heterogeneously along height and width axes, and (ii) early-layer visual tokens are indiscriminable and uniformly redundant. Guided by these findings, we propose PACE (Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs), the first visual token compression framework tailored for native MLLMs with Multimodal-RoPE. Leveraging dimensional decoupling of positional encoding, PACE decomposes attention into two orthogonal spatial saliency estimates along height and width, gated by a positional attention signal, yielding direction-aware importance with negligible overhead. It further casts token budget allocation as Pareto optimization over performance preservation, inference efficiency, and spatial coverage, jointly identifying optimal compression depths and retention ratios. Experiments show PACE maintains near-lossless performance at only 25%-50% visual token retention, even improving several benchmarks, while delivering over 2x FLOPs reduction.
authors: Lei Tian, Chunzheng Zhu, Kai Wu, Yifan Zhang, Haihua Yang
bullets: Native MLLMs tokenize image patches directly, creating substantial visual-token redundancy that existing ViT-oriented compression methods do not address.
Analysis finds redundancy is heterogeneous and independently distributed across height and width, while early-layer tokens are broadly indiscriminable.
PACE estimates direction-aware spatial importance by decoupling Multimodal-RoPE attention along height and width with negligible overhead.
It allocates token budgets through Pareto optimization across performance, inference efficiency, and spatial coverage.
Experiments report near-lossless performance at 25–50% visual-token retention, with improvements on several benchmarks and over 2× FLOPs reduction.
papers.selection_reason: Visual token compression framework for native MLLMs, directly relevant to token pruning/eviction and multimodal LLM efficiency.
papers.title: PACE: Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs
papers.tldr: PACE efficiently compresses visual tokens in native MLLMs, retaining 25–50% of tokens with near-lossless or improved performance and over 2× lower FLOPs.

papers.abstract: Long video understanding requires VideoLLMs to answer queries about videos spanning tens of minutes to hours, but such long videos produce far more visual tokens than current VideoLLMs can process. To address this issue, keyframe selectors are proposed to select the most query-relevant frames by computing the similarity between frame and query embeddings. Existing selectors either encode frames independently without temporal context or process chunks in isolation with ranking objectives that are difficult to optimize. To alleviate those limitations, we propose FrameScout with two core designs: (i) a streaming selector architecture that leverages a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to produce temporally-contextualized frame embeddings; (ii) a frame-query contrastive objective that aligns frame and query embeddings in a shared space, directly training the selector to distinguish relevant frames from irrelevant ones. Extensive experiments on three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs demonstrate that FrameScout consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Hubert-1102/FrameScout.
authors: Haonan Hu, Shuhao Chen, Weisen Jiang, Lizhao Gao, James Kwok, Yu Zhang
bullets: Targets the excessive visual-token cost of videos lasting tens of minutes to hours.
Uses a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to encode frames with temporal context.
Trains frame and query embeddings with a contrastive objective to distinguish relevant from irrelevant frames.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance across three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs.
Scope: focuses on query-guided frame selection for long-video question answering.
papers.selection_reason: Query-relevant frame selection for long-video VideoLLMs with streaming KV cache; fits video understanding and token/frame efficiency.
papers.title: FrameScout: Scouting Query-Relevant Frames for Long Video Understanding
papers.tldr: FrameScout selects query-relevant frames from long videos using temporally contextualized streaming representations and contrastive frame-query alignment, improving VideoLLM long-video understanding.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning is increasingly used to reduce the memory and inference costs of vision-language models. Existing work has largely focused on designing method-specific selectors and demonstrating incremental improvements over prior methods at selected token budgets. It remains unclear whether the resulting performance reflects an inherent limit of visual token pruning or the limitations of current token-selection algorithms. We take a complementary perspective and ask: \emph{how well can visual token pruning perform when offline search cost is not the primary constraint?} We formulate pruning for general image understanding as selecting, under a fixed budget, one shared visual-token subset that supports a broad distribution of questions about an image. We approximate this utility with a finite auxiliary QA set generated by a frontier VLM and optimize a teacher-forced answer-probability objective with the evaluated model frozen. Motivated by the conceptual monotonicity and diminishing returns of adding visual evidence, we construct nested subsets greedily and introduce \emph{QA mini-batch greedy} (QA-MBG), which estimates token marginal gains from randomly sampled QA components at each step. Empirically, QA-MBG is both cheaper and more effective than full greedy. With one frontier-VLM call and approximately $0.5$ H100 GPU-hours per image, it produces a nested subset trajectory covering keep ratios up to $0.3$. Across Qwen3-VL-4B and Gemma~4 E4B on $900$ images from nine benchmarks, we find significant headroom over evaluated pruning baselines on held-out QA and image-grounded long-form generation, while the searched subsets substantially narrow the gap to full-token inference.
authors: Janghoon Cho, Shubhankar Borse, Reza Pourreza, Juntae Lee, Jihwan Bang, Munawar Hayat, Fatih Porikli
bullets: Frames pruning as selecting one shared, fixed-budget visual-token subset per image for diverse downstream questions.
Uses auxiliary QA generated by a frontier VLM and a teacher-forced answer-probability objective with the evaluated model frozen.
Introduces QA mini-batch greedy, which builds nested subsets by estimating token gains from sampled QA components.
On Qwen3-VL-4B and Gemma 4 E4B across 900 images from nine benchmarks, searched subsets outperform evaluated pruning baselines on held-out QA and image-grounded long-form generation.
Scope: optimization requires substantial offline computation—one frontier-VLM call and about 0.5 H100 GPU-hours per image—and covers keep ratios up to 0.3.
papers.selection_reason: Visual token pruning limits and selection for VLMs; fits token pruning and eviction.
papers.title: How Much Can We Prune? Exploring the Performance Limits of Visual Token Pruning
papers.tldr: QA-MBG shows that visual token pruning has substantial untapped potential when token subsets are optimized offline for broad image-question utility.

papers.abstract: Line-parallel language models advance multiple lines concurrently for substantial speedups. However, frameworks like the Line-Coupled Language Model (LCLM) enforce a fixed commitment schedule across lines. Because dependencies vary within text, a fixed schedule cannot hold back a line whose prerequisites remain uncomputed, forcing premature commitments and cascading reasoning errors. To address this limitation, we introduce the Lattice Language Model (LatLM), making commitment schedules an adaptive decoding-time choice. Text occupies a 2D lattice where eligible frontier tokens are scored each round; a policy commits confident candidates while deferring unready ones for extended context. One forward pass supervises entire sampled trajectories via 2D causal masking, while an append-only cache retains exact states. At 482M parameters, we establish two findings. (1) LatLM matches a data- and capacity-matched autoregressive model on held-out text when decoded sequentially, while its adaptive parallel decoder achieves near-autoregressive accuracy on independent-line tasks using 25--41% as many decoding rounds. (2) When cross-line dependencies cause LCLM's fixed schedule to fail, deferred commitment substantially improves accuracy while retaining parallelism where dependencies permit. On mixed dependency chains, LatLM achieves 96.5% accuracy versus LCLM's 78.5%, using fewer than half the decoding rounds of the autoregressive baseline.
authors: Shaorong Zhang, Shiyuan Li, Longxuan Yu, Greg Ver Steeg
bullets: Addresses fixed line-commitment schedules that can force premature decisions and cascading errors.
Represents text on a 2D lattice and scores eligible frontier tokens at each decoding round.
Uses trajectory-wide supervision with 2D causal masking and an append-only cache for exact states.
Matches a matched autoregressive model under sequential decoding and uses 25–41% as many rounds on independent-line tasks.
On mixed dependency chains, reaches 96.5% accuracy versus LCLM’s 78.5%, with fewer than half as many rounds as the autoregressive baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive parallel decoding for language models with deferred commitment; relevant to LLM architecture and inference efficiency.
papers.title: LatLM: Line-Parallel Language Models with Deferred Commitment
papers.tldr: LatLM adaptively defers uncertain token commitments, preserving accuracy while decoding dependent text in parallel with far fewer rounds.

papers.abstract: Automatically generating high-performance kernels with LLM-based agents promises substantial gains in development efficiency, but two obstacles remain. First, while increasing multi-turn interaction with execution environments is crucial for refining generation quality, continuous context accumulation rapidly exceeds the model's effective context window. Second, training long-horizon tasks via GRPO inherently incurs sparse rewards due to its reliance on terminal outcome evaluation, severely hindering step-level credit assignment; To address these obstacles, we propose ATRL (Ascend Triton Reinforcement Learning), a post-training method that refines GRPO into a compaction-aware, segment-level objective for long-horizon kernel generation. We also design a lightweight agent harness providing cascaded compilation, correctness, and profiling feedback, alongside an Ascend-specific knowledge base injected during agentic RL training and evaluation to compensate for the base model's missing platform expertise. Evaluations on NPUKernelBench and KernelBench, both executed on Ascend hardware, show that ATRL consistently surpasses all baselines, including GRPO, in both correctness and speedup.
authors: Chuansai Zhou, Yanlin Liu, Bingning Huang, Shidi Xi, Chao Huang, Boxing Chen, Mingming Zhu, Guanghuan Fang, Ben Feng, Zongzuo Wang
bullets: Addresses context-window overflow from multi-turn kernel refinement and sparse terminal rewards in GRPO.
Uses a compaction-aware, segment-level objective to improve step-level credit assignment.
Provides cascaded compilation, correctness, and profiling feedback through a lightweight agent harness.
Injects Ascend-specific knowledge during agentic RL training and evaluation.
On Ascend hardware, outperforms reported baselines, including GRPO, in correctness and speedup on NPUKernelBench and KernelBench.
papers.selection_reason: RL-based generation of high-performance kernels with compaction-aware long-horizon training; relevant to efficient computation and LLM-agent context management.
papers.title: Compaction-Aware Reinforcement Learning For Ascend Triton Kernel Generation
papers.tldr: ATRL improves long-horizon LLM-based Ascend Triton kernel generation by combining context compaction, segment-level reinforcement learning, and platform-specific feedback.

papers.abstract: Collaborative inference serves as a critical methodology in edge intelligence. Existing collaborative inference methods operate by splitting the deep neural network (DNN) model between edge devices and cloud servers. However, these methods need to load different models for multiple split points when the communication or device changes, thus resulting in long switching times and substantial storage overhead on the edge side. To address this issue, we propose a Dynamic Split Network (DS-Net), which not only enables efficient split point switching but also enhances the collaborative speed and accuracy across various scenarios. Specifically, we design a dynamic switching framework that enables flexible selection among multiple split points within a single model, thereby reducing storage, memory, and switching overhead. To mitigate the feature distribution shifts and task-relevant information loss caused by dynamic splitting and high-ratio compression, we further propose a hierarchical compensation mechanism. Local alignment calibrates the decoded feature distribution at each split point, while task-specific global compensation restores task-relevant information at the global level. In addition, we incorporate sample-adaptive global compensation selection into split-point selection based on sample complexity and runtime resource conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that DS-Net reduces memory overhead by 74.6% and achieves millisecond-level switching latency. Moreover, under a 10 Mbps bandwidth constraint on the Nano platform, DS-Net outperforms state-of-the-art collaborative methods by achieving 1.2% higher accuracy on the COCO dataset, reducing latency by 42.5%, and improving throughput by a factor of 1.8$\times$.
authors: Xinyun Zhang, Li Wang, Lei Jin, Lianming Xu, Zhu Han
bullets: Addresses storage and switching delays caused by maintaining separate models for different split points and changing communication or device conditions.
Uses a single dynamic model with flexible split-point selection, reducing edge memory overhead and enabling millisecond-level switching.
Applies local feature-distribution alignment and task-specific global compensation to recover information lost through dynamic splitting and compression.
Selects global compensation adaptively based on sample complexity and runtime resources.
On Nano under 10 Mbps bandwidth, reports 74.6% lower memory overhead, 42.5% lower latency, 1.8× higher throughput, and 1.2% higher COCO accuracy than prior collaborative methods.
papers.selection_reason: Dynamic split network for edge-cloud inference reduces memory and latency; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: DS-Net: A Dynamic Split Network for Edge-Cloud Collaborative Inference
papers.tldr: DS-Net enables fast, low-overhead switching among edge-cloud split points within one model while preserving accuracy through hierarchical feature compensation.

papers.abstract: Pretraining scaling laws treat training data as a one-dimensional quantity: a token count. Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) inherits this scalar abstraction, but modern synthesis pipelines now generate \textit{tasks}, \textit{environments}, and \textit{trajectories} independently and at very different costs, turning data into a structured design space. This raises a question pretraining never had to answer: given a synthesis budget, \textit{which axis} should be scaled? We address this question end-to-end with three tightly coupled contributions. First, we decompose agentic data into three cardinality axes (task, environment, trajectory), plus a reward-density control variable, and fit per-axis scaling relations on different large language models (LLMs) across math+code, SWE, web, and UI/tool application domains. Across all model sizes, model families, domains, and RL algorithms (PPO and GRPO) we measured, the scaling exponents order as environment $>$ task $>$ trajectory. When environment diversity is decomposed into world and environment-structure diversity, its advantage is mainly driven by the former, while the latter is just comparable to the task diversity. Second, we use the fitted laws as a common ruler to price synthesis methods, capturing each method's efficiency as a per-axis discount factor and identifying critical synthetic-to-real ratios at which collapse begins; these ratios differ by an order of magnitude across axes. Third, we cast budget allocation as a constrained optimization under our laws and discounts, deriving a Chinchilla-style compute-optimal recipe and validating it at held-out scale. The empirical results demonstrate that following the recipe yields up to $1.7\times$ compute efficiency over the dominant ``scale-the-trajectories'' practice.
authors: Bowei He, Yankai Chen, Xiaokun Zhang, Changjiang Han, Ye Yuan, Chong Li, Xue Liu
bullets: The study models agentic data using task, environment, and trajectory cardinalities, plus reward density, under a synthesis budget.
Across tested LLMs, domains, and PPO/GRPO, scaling exponents rank environment > task > trajectory; world diversity chiefly drives the environment advantage.
Fitted scaling laws price synthesis strategies through per-axis discounts and identify axis-specific synthetic-to-real collapse thresholds.
A constrained, Chinchilla-style budget allocation recipe is derived and validated at held-out scale.
Following the recipe achieves up to 1.7× compute efficiency compared with primarily scaling trajectories.
papers.selection_reason: Data-axis scaling laws and compute-optimal budget allocation for agentic RL; directly contributes to efficient AI training.
papers.title: How Data Scales in Agentic Reinforcement Learning: Laws and Synthesis Strategies
papers.tldr: Agentic RL data should be scaled across task, environment, and trajectory axes—not just by trajectory count—with environment diversity providing the strongest scaling benefit.

papers.abstract: The size of the KV cache grows linearly with context length, making it a major memory bottleneck in LLM serving. Motivated by recent progress in identifying the functional roles of attention heads, a growing body of work compresses the KV cache non-uniformly across heads. Existing methods either fix the important heads via offline profiling or select them using attention signals from the prefill stage. In both cases, however, accuracy fluctuates substantially across workloads. While investigating the cause of this instability, we find that the active heads shift between the prefill and decode stages even within a single input. Along the decode path, by contrast, the activehead composition remains stable across content tokens once format tokens are filtered out. Based on this observation, we propose PeekKV. PeekKV observes a single content token immediately after prefill - a one-token peek - to jointly obtain head-group scores and token-importance scores. Guided by these scores, PeekKV allocates KV cache budgets to head groups in proportion to their group scores and retains only the top-scoring tokens within each budget. PeekKV requires no offline profiling or training and thus applies directly to unseen workloads and new models. Across four public benchmarks, PeekKV achieves the highest accuracy in more than half of the per-model comparisons against state-of-the-art methods, and stays closest to the full-cache accuracy on RULER and LongBench. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, PeekKV retains 95.7% of the full-cache accuracy at a 10% memory budget on RULER with 16K contexts and 95.9% at a 1.5% budget on LongBench.
bullets: KV-cache memory grows with context length, while existing non-uniform head compression methods can be unstable across workloads.
The method finds that active-head composition shifts between prefill and decode but remains stable across later content tokens after filtering format tokens.
PeekKV performs a one-token peek to jointly score head groups and token importance, then allocates cache budgets and retains the highest-scoring tokens.
It applies directly to unseen workloads and models because it requires neither offline profiling nor additional training.
Across four benchmarks, it is closest to full-cache accuracy on RULER and LongBench; reported retention reaches 95.7% and 95.9% of full-cache accuracy at low memory budgets on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
papers.selection_reason: KV cache budget allocation via one-token peek and token retention directly targets memory-efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: PeekKV: The First Content Token Already Knows Which Heads Matter
papers.tldr: PeekKV uses the first content token after prefill to dynamically identify important attention heads and KV tokens, enabling accurate KV-cache compression without profiling or training.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference through parallel verification of tokens proposed by a drafter. Diffusion drafters further parallelize proposal generation, but greater proposal capacity or higher mean accepted tokens (MAT) need not yield higher throughput. Because verification accepts only a consecutive prefix, early rejections can render later correct predictions ineffective, limiting MAT gains, while even higher MAT may not improve throughput if per-round latency increases. We introduce DScout, which uses two complementary factorizations to guide diffusion drafter training and inference for higher throughput. For training, DScout factorizes position-wise loss into inclusion, weighting, and prediction loss. This guides the design and combination of mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss to align supervision with prefix acceptance and improve MAT. For inference, DScout factorizes throughput as the ratio of MAT to per-round latency, guiding target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and inference block size selection to identify a high-throughput configuration for each workload. Across six benchmarks, DScout achieves $3.84\times$ and $4.14\times$ mean speedups over autoregressive decoding on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, respectively, improving mean speedup over the state-of-the-art baseline by 9.1% and 7.1%. Across models and concurrency settings, our inference configuration policy provides up to 9.75% additional mean speedup over DScout's fixed configuration.
authors: Jiakun Fan, Min Xiao, Qiang Wang, Neiwen Ling, Zhichao Liu, Zhihao Jia, Dimitrios S. Nikolopoulos, Zijun Wei
bullets: Diffusion drafters can achieve higher mean accepted tokens without improving throughput because early prefix rejections invalidate later predictions and larger proposals may increase latency.
Training factorizes position-wise loss into inclusion, weighting, and prediction components to combine mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss.
Inference factorizes throughput into mean accepted tokens divided by per-round latency, guiding target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and block-size selection.
Across six benchmarks, DScout reaches mean speedups of 3.84× on Qwen3-4B and 4.14× on Qwen3-8B over autoregressive decoding.
Its workload-specific configuration policy adds up to 9.75% mean speedup over DScout’s fixed configuration.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-drafted speculative decoding factorizes training and inference to improve LLM throughput, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Factorization-Guided Training and Inference for Diffusion-Drafted Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: DScout improves diffusion-drafted speculative decoding by jointly optimizing prefix acceptance during training and the MAT–latency tradeoff during inference, delivering higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Vector quantization is widely used for large-scale data compression and approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS). Multi-codebook quantization (MCQ) is a practical paradigm that represents database vectors with compact codes and supports efficient retrieval through asymmetric distance computation (ADC). However, existing shallow MCQs encode vectors independently within each inverted file (IVF) cluster, without exploiting local references. Therefore, we propose Spatio-Topological Linkage Quantization (STLQ), a topological shallow MCQ method that organizes each IVF cluster as a directed-forest with compact codes and scaling coefficients. Its basic encoding phase first quantizes vectors independently, while the linked encoding phase re-encodes relative residuals with respect to selected reconstructed parents, reusing local reconstruction information to obtain finer representations. The corresponding linked-ADC preserves linear scanning complexity. STLQ further compresses the scaling coefficients and directed-forest structure to control the additional topology overhead. Extensive experiments show that STLQ achieves higher recall than the evaluated shallow MCQs at comparable bit budgets, although at a higher offline construction cost. Meanwhile, it has a competitive recall-QPS tradeoff against deep MCQs. The code is available at https://github.com/ighxiy/STLQ.
authors: Kuizhi Liu, Junying Zhang, Xindi Ma, Xiangyu Wang, Qi Jiang, Sheng Gao, Chen Gong, Jianfeng Ma
bullets: Targets shallow multi-codebook quantization methods that encode vectors independently and miss local references.
Organizes each IVF cluster as a directed forest using compact codes and scaling coefficients.
Re-encodes residuals relative to reconstructed parent vectors, reusing local information for finer representations.
Compresses the forest structure and scaling coefficients to limit topology overhead; linked-ADC retains linear scanning complexity.
Reports higher recall than evaluated shallow MCQs at comparable bit budgets, with higher offline construction cost, and a competitive recall–QPS tradeoff against deep MCQs.
papers.selection_reason: Vector quantization for approximate nearest neighbor search reduces memory and retrieval cost.
papers.title: STLQ: Spatio-Topological Linkage Quantization for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.tldr: STLQ improves approximate nearest neighbor search by exploiting local topological links within IVF clusters while preserving efficient linear-scan distance computation.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models(VLMs)have advanced Visual Document Retrieval (VDR) by enabling OCR-free, multi-vector representations. However, these models generate excessive tokens to preserve dense visual details, which severely limits retrieval scalability. Existing compression methods mitigate this overhead but rely on isolated heuristics that fail to balance token importance, semantic redundancy, and coverage capacity. We propose a visual token compression framework formulated as an Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) problem. Our approach unifies these three objectives into a single alternating optimization process. Furthermore, we theoretically show that minimizing the transport cost upper-bounds the MaxSim retrieval error, ensuring ranking stability. Extensive experiments on the ViDoRe V1 and V3 benchmarks demonstrate that our method preserves fine-grained document semantics and improves the efficiency-effectiveness trade-off over state-of-the-art base-lines. Code is available at https://github.com/shhhhhyy/Unbalanced-Optimal-Transport-for-EVDR.
authors: Hoyeon Shin, Jeongyeon Kim, Yeong Jun Koh, Yeoneung Kim, Hanul Kim
bullets: Addresses the scalability problem caused by excessive tokens in OCR-free, multi-vector VLM-based visual document retrieval.
Formulates token compression as an Unbalanced Optimal Transport problem balancing token importance, semantic redundancy, and coverage.
Uses alternating optimization to jointly optimize these compression objectives.
Provides a theoretical guarantee that lower transport cost bounds MaxSim retrieval error, supporting ranking stability.
Experiments on ViDoRe V1 and V3 show a better efficiency–effectiveness trade-off than existing baselines while retaining fine-grained semantics.
papers.selection_reason: Visual token compression for retrieval directly targets token-level efficiency in multimodal systems.
papers.title: Unbalanced Optimal Transport for Efficient Visual Document Retrieval
papers.tldr: An Unbalanced Optimal Transport framework compresses visual document tokens while preserving retrieval quality and improving efficiency.

papers.abstract: Native NVFP4 promises to accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs), but achieving stable learning across separate training and sampling engines remains challenging. We show that matching model weights and numerical formats is insufficient to ensure consistent policy evaluation, highlighting the importance of cross-engine numerical execution. We introduce miniTE, a lightweight framework that combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and efficient native W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) GEMM computation for LLM RL. It improves numerical execution consistency without modifying the RL objective, while reducing implementation overhead to realize the benefits of native low-bit computation. Long-horizon RL experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate stable training and benchmark performance close to BF16, outperforming naive Transformer Engine (TE) NVFP4 in evaluation quality. On single NVIDIA B300 GPU node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s, yielding 1.39x and 1.47x the throughput of BF16 and TE NVFP4, respectively, for complete learner updates. We released the framework, kernels, diagnostics, and training configurations to make native low-bit RL easier.
authors: Zhen Li, Mingfa Feng, Yiming Zhang, Yang Yu, Changhai Zhou, Pengxiang Li, Dongkuan Wu, Congkai Xie, Hongxia Yang
bullets: Matching weights and numerical formats alone does not guarantee consistent policy evaluation across engines.
The framework combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and native W4A4 GEMM kernels without changing the RL objective.
Long-horizon experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B achieve stable training and benchmark quality close to BF16, outperforming naive TE NVFP4 in evaluation quality.
On a single NVIDIA B300 node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s—1.39× BF16 and 1.47× TE NVFP4 throughput for complete learner updates.
The framework, kernels, diagnostics, and configurations are released; results focus on the reported model and hardware setup.
papers.selection_reason: Native low-bit NVFP4 RL execution alignment and W4A4 GEMM improve LLM training throughput, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: miniTE: Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: miniTE makes native NVFP4 reinforcement learning more stable and efficient by aligning numerical execution across training and sampling engines.

papers.abstract: Layer pruning reduces the size and inference cost of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but selecting a deployable configuration requires deciding both which layers to remove and how to recover task performance. These decisions depend on the model and task, and a failed trial can reflect either the deletion set or insufficient recovery. We present AutoPruner, an agent-driven framework that jointly searches pruning structures and recovery recipes through closed-loop experimentation. Offline layer interventions measure changes in action output to provide functional evidence. An LLM agent combines this evidence with evaluation history and retained diagnoses to propose deletion sets and recovery recipes within a search budget. Each proposal is executed and evaluated on the target tasks, and the resulting feedback guides the next experiment. Across OpenVLA-OFT, StarVLA, and FastWAM on four LIBERO suites, AutoPruner removes 16.7--87.5% of backbone layers while maintaining task success above 90%, with measured inference speedups of up to 2.50$\times$. Further analysis shows that functional probes identify action-sensitive layers despite high representation similarity, and that recovery can make previously failing structures viable.
authors: Tao Lin, Yikeng Chen, Qiwei Liang, Zinan Xie, Zhengtu Liang, Renjing Xu
bullets: Targets the joint problem of selecting layers to remove and choosing recovery procedures after pruning.
Uses offline action-output interventions, evaluation history, and retained diagnoses to guide an LLM agent’s next pruning and recovery proposal.
Evaluates each proposed configuration on target tasks within a fixed search budget.
Across three VLA models and four LIBERO suites, removes 16.7–87.5% of backbone layers while maintaining over 90% task success.
Reports inference speedups up to 2.50×; functional probes reveal action-sensitive layers that representation similarity may miss.],
papers.selection_reason: Agent-driven depth pruning of vision-language-action models to reduce inference cost, relevant to embodied AI and efficient AI.
papers.title: AutoPruner: Agentic Depth Pruning for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: AutoPruner uses an agentic closed-loop search to prune VLA model layers and recover performance, achieving substantial compression while preserving high task success and improving inference speed.

papers.abstract: Adaptive VLM ensembles save computation by stopping early on easy images and escalating harder ones. Although a single conformal threshold can make the final predictor marginally valid, it can still fail severely along individual computational routes. We characterize this failure precisely: if a route has prevalence pi, marginal 1-alpha coverage allows its conditional coverage to fall to max{0, 1-alpha/pi}. To address this mismatch, we learn the router on development data, freeze all routing choices, and calibrate the returned score separately for early exits and escalated inputs. We call this pipeline SAGE-CP. Its calibration step applies Mondrian split conformal prediction to the operational groups created by the router. Under exchangeability, the resulting prediction sets achieve finite-sample coverage within each route. Across 10 benchmarks, 4 frozen VLMs, and 5 aligned splits, both global calibration and SAGE-CP achieve 0.900 marginal coverage at a 0.90 target, but their route behavior differs substantially. SAGE-CP raises mean worst-route coverage from 0.623 to 0.887 and reduces the mean route-coverage gap from 0.324 to 0.025, using the same routed scores and 1.177 source calls per image. The stronger guarantee increases the mean prediction-set size from 1.893 to 2.212; nevertheless, the sets remain smaller than those of the full ensemble (2.486) while requiring 70.6 percent fewer source calls. The route-level reliability persists across 6 fixed query fractions, while finer exit-depth groups demonstrate the need for additional calibration data on rare routes. Across 5 datasets, SAGE-CP also reduces measured batch-one latency by 58.8 to 63.4 percent and gross GPU energy by 55.7 to 57.5 percent relative to full inference. Thus, routing provides computational savings, while route-stratified calibration attaches coverage guarantees to the operational paths created by the router.
bullets: Problem: Marginal conformal coverage can conceal severe failures for rare early-exit or escalation routes.
Method: Freeze the learned router and apply Mondrian split conformal calibration separately to operational route groups.
Guarantee: Under exchangeability, prediction sets achieve finite-sample coverage within each route.
Results: At 0.90 target coverage, SAGE-CP raises mean worst-route coverage from 0.623 to 0.887 and shrinks the route-coverage gap from 0.324 to 0.025.
Trade-off and scope: Sets are larger than with global calibration but remain smaller than full-ensemble sets, with 70.6% fewer source calls; rare, finer-grained routes require more calibration data.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive VLM routing with route-stratified conformal calibration reduces compute, latency, and energy; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: SAGE-CP: When Marginal Coverage Hides Route-Conditional Failures in Adaptive VLM Ensembles
papers.tldr: SAGE-CP makes adaptive VLM ensembles conformally reliable not only overall, but across each computational route, while retaining substantial efficiency gains.

papers.abstract: Adaptive speculative decoding changes the active batch size B and draft length d from one decode step to the next, whereas a CUDA Graph replays a fixed launch configuration. The resulting verification width M = B d forces serving systems to pre-capture many shapes, capture new ones on the serving path, or pad every step to the largest draft. We present PolyGraph, a plan-buffer mechanism for custom Triton kernels that avoids this choice. PolyGraph captures one maximum-grid graph and writes the active shape to GPU memory before each replay. Kernels skip tiles beyond that shape, while graph topology, allocations, layouts, pointers, and launch grids remain fixed; the update transfers only 28 bytes. On one NVIDIA H800, a trace-driven prototype with Qwen2.5-3B dimensions replaces 64 shape-specific graphs with one, matches the warmed baseline in observed step latency (17.7 vs. 17.8 ms P50), and reduces measured pre-serving graph-build time from 3,915 to 93 ms. Fixed-draft controls show that the benefit comes from avoiding padded payload: the P99 difference from MaxPad is negligible at zero padding waste but reaches an 18.7% reduction at 100% waste. Our evidence establishes a bounded work-shape mechanism for custom kernels, not a production serving system, and is limited to synthetic traces on one GPU.
bullets: Addresses changing batch size and draft length, which otherwise require many graphs, runtime captures, or padding to the largest shape.
Uses a maximum-grid graph whose kernels skip inactive tiles based on a 28-byte shape update before replay.
Replaces 64 shape-specific graphs with one while matching warmed step latency: 17.7 vs. 17.8 ms P50.
Reduces measured pre-serving graph-build time from 3,915 to 93 ms.
Compared with MaxPad, reduces P99 latency by up to 18.7% at 100% padding waste; evaluation is limited to synthetic traces on one NVIDIA H800.
papers.selection_reason: Plan-buffer CUDA graphs reduce overhead in adaptive speculative decoding; fits efficient AI inference.
papers.title: PolyGraph: Plan-Buffered CUDA Graphs for Adaptive Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: PolyGraph enables adaptive speculative decoding with one reusable CUDA Graph by buffering the active shape in GPU memory, avoiding per-shape captures and padding.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has become a mainstream technique for accelerating large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to generate candidate tokens that are subsequently verified by the target model. However, agentic workloads introduce long and continuously evolving contexts and frequent multi-turn interactions. Under such workloads, we observe that existing draft models suffer from up to an 80% degradation in acceptance length, while maintaining their historical KV cache introduces substantial system overhead. In this paper, we identify the growing historical context as a common source of both problems and introduce DLite, a history-free speculative decoding framework for agentic AI. DLite directly reuses contextual hidden states from the target model and performs local speculative prediction without explicitly maintaining the historical context, transforming an increasingly complex modeling problem into local simple prediction problem. A lightweight sequential head further restores intra-block causal dependencies with low overhead. To effectively train this heterogeneous history-free architecture, we introduce a tailored two-stage training strategy. Experiments on general-purpose, long-context and agentic workloads show that DLite achieves 2-6 acceptance length and outperforms the state-of-the-art speculative decoding method, DSpark, up to 70%.
authors: Jiaming Xu, Hanzhen Wang, Tianlang Zhao, Jiewen Xiao, Chengze Yuan, Jiayi Pan, Yongkang Zhou, Jiancai Ye, Yu Wang, Guohao Dai
bullets: Agentic workloads’ long, evolving histories reduce draft-model acceptance length and make historical KV-cache maintenance costly.
DLite reuses target-model hidden states for history-free, local speculative prediction.
A lightweight sequential head restores dependencies within each speculative block.
A two-stage training strategy supports the heterogeneous history-free architecture.
Across general-purpose, long-context, and agentic workloads, DLite achieves 2–6 acceptance length and up to 70% improvement over DSpark.
papers.selection_reason: History-free speculative decoding reduces KV cache and memory overhead; directly relevant to efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI
papers.tldr: DLite accelerates speculative decoding for agentic AI by avoiding historical context while preserving effective local prediction.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based protein structure prediction models produce all-atom structures in about 200 denoising steps, and that cost has driven a number of few-step samplers. We present Blitz, a few-step distillation framework that uses a geometric noise schedule to distribute steps more evenly across noise scales, then learns those updates through multistep consistency training. Physical steering and target-free candidate selection help reduce the remaining geometric defects at inference. We apply Blitz to AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2, reducing denoising from 200 steps to eight. Because published few-step results use different benchmarks and scoring procedures, we compare both distilled models with their teachers and other few-step methods under a common evaluation protocol covering structural accuracy, interface quality, ligand placement, and stereochemical validity. Blitz retains teacher-level structural accuracy, with AF3-Blitz outperforming all evaluated few-step baselines and exceeding its teacher on several accuracy metrics.
authors: Vinay Saji Mathew, Soundar Kumara, Gretta Kellogg, William K. M. Lai
bullets: Addresses the high inference cost of diffusion-based all-atom protein structure prediction.
Uses a geometric noise schedule and multistep consistency training for few-step distillation.
Adds physical steering and target-free candidate selection to reduce geometric defects.
Evaluates AF3-Blitz and Boltz-2-Blitz under a common protocol covering structure, interfaces, ligand placement, and stereochemistry.
AF3-Blitz outperforms evaluated few-step baselines and exceeds its teacher on several accuracy metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Few-step distillation reduces diffusion inference cost, directly relevant to Efficient AI.
papers.title: Blitz: Accelerating the Diffusion Modules of AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2
papers.tldr: Blitz distills AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2 diffusion samplers from 200 denoising steps to eight while preserving teacher-level structural accuracy.

papers.abstract: Dense assistance methods such as speculative decoding repeatedly verify draft tokens with a target model, keeping target computation coupled to generation. We study sparse collaborative decoding, where a draft model generates most tokens and a target model is invoked only for short corrective segments. The key problem is deciding when to call the target. We show that local uncertainty is a weak trigger: entropy, negative log-likelihood, logit margin, top-$k$ mass, and velocity features give near-chance failure prediction, with AUC 0.50-0.53. In contrast, aggregate trajectory-shape features over the draft confidence path reach AUC 0.86 using a lightweight logistic predictor trained only from draft correctness labels. This induces a trigger-timing tradeoff: early calls have more leverage but weaker evidence, while later calls have stronger evidence but less ability to redirect the trajectory. Used online, learned sparse collaborative decoding improves over the best open-loop schedule by +5.3 to +20.0 accuracy points across five GSM8K draft-target pairs. On MATH-500, it gains 7.0-13.5 points when early prediction and target competence align, but loses when either is weak. On StrategyQA, it improves over open-loop by 5.0-8.3 points, showing transfer beyond arithmetics.
authors: Amit Ranjan Trivedi, Sruthikesh Surineni, Kyong Ho Lee, Mohit Mittal, Steven Li, Rex Hill
bullets: Sparse decoding uses a draft model for most tokens and invokes the target only for short corrective segments.
Local uncertainty features are weak failure predictors (AUC 0.50–0.53), while aggregate confidence-trajectory features reach AUC 0.86.
A lightweight logistic predictor, trained only on draft correctness labels, learns when to trigger target-model intervention.
Online triggering improves over the best open-loop schedule by 5.3–20.0 accuracy points on five GSM8K pairs and transfers to MATH-500 and StrategyQA.
Performance depends on timing and alignment between early prediction quality and target-model competence; gains can disappear when either is weak.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse collaborative decoding reduces target-model computation via trajectory-triggered invocation, fitting efficient inference.
papers.title: Trajectory-Triggered Sparse Collaborative Decoding
papers.tldr: A trajectory-based trigger lets sparse collaborative decoding call the target model more effectively than fixed schedules, improving accuracy across several reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. For linear factorization models, we show that Muon admits minimum-cost exact representations with redundant hidden width, whereas under the BMuon oracle geometry and a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost representation is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a minorization-maximization surrogate for the exact allocation problem. On ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16, BMuon improves over Muon under gradual structured MLP pruning, and its learned allocations provide a more effective pruning criterion than weight magnitude. On a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves over Muon under post-training MLP channel pruning.
authors: Rida Assalouh, Tom Jacobs, Rebekka Burkholz, Yani Ioannou, Umut \c{S}im\c{s}ekli
bullets: Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when MLP hidden channels are pruned after training.
BMuon makes channels across blocks compete for a global, interpretable allocation budget instead of using a sparsity penalty coefficient.
Its oracle is normalized steepest descent under norms interpolating between Muon’s geometry and structured sparse geometries.
For linear factorization, scarce BMuon budgets force minimum-cost representations to use minimal width, unlike Muon.
BMuon outperforms Muon under structured MLP pruning on ViT-S/16 ImageNet-1K and a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb; learned allocations beat weight magnitude for pruning decisions.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces 'Budget Muon' to modify the optimizer's geometry, improving the efficiency and compressibility of Transformers during training and pruning.
papers.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
papers.tldr: BMuon adapts Muon’s spectral geometry with a shared channel budget, improving the structured compressibility of trained Transformers under MLP pruning.

papers.abstract: LLMs and LVLMs are increasingly deployed across heterogeneous hardware, ranging from data-center GPUs to resource-constrained edge devices. Their fixed-size architectures limit the ability to reuse a single model across deployment settings with different compute, latency, and model-size targets. We introduce HydraLLM, an elastic MQA-based architecture. Its number of active attention heads determines the effective widths of the embeddings, attention projections, feed-forward layers, and the output head, forming a nested family of subnetworks within a single parameter set. We introduce a static-to-elastic conversion pipeline that, starting from a pre-trained model checkpoint, includes importance-driven weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with knowledge distillation. We extend this principle to multimodal inference through an elastic projection module whose output width follows the active text width. HydraLLM covers a wider range of active parameter configurations than FFN-only elastic architectures. With 75% of heads active, HydraLLM achieves 2.2 percentage points higher TriviaQA accuracy than a state-of-the-art nested baseline configuration which has 17.25% more parameters. With 50% of heads active, our multimodal model achieves a CLIPScore comparable to that of the 7$\times$ larger Gemma 3 4B model. With only 25% of heads active, HydraLLM increases token-generation throughput by 75.3% over the full-width configuration.
authors: Oscar Kemme, Janek Haberer, Ali Hojjat, Olaf Landsiedel
bullets: Uses the number of active attention heads to jointly control embedding, attention, feed-forward, and output widths.
Converts pretrained checkpoints into elastic models through importance-based weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with knowledge distillation.
Adds an elastic multimodal projection whose width matches the active text-model width.
Reports higher TriviaQA accuracy than a larger-parameter nested baseline at 75% active heads, comparable CLIPScore to a much larger Gemma 3 4B model at 50%, and 75.3% higher token throughput at 25%.
papers.selection_reason: Elastic width slicing for efficient LLM/LVLM inference, fitting efficient AI and foundation-model topics.
papers.title: HydraLLM: Adaptive Width Slicing for Elastic Text and Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: HydraLLM turns one text or vision-language model into a flexible family of width-adjustable subnetworks for different hardware and efficiency targets.

papers.abstract: Evaluating candidate changes (hypotheses) to recommendation models requires full-scale training runs consuming thousands of GPU-hours, severely limiting the hypothesis space engineers can feasibly explore. We introduce Predictable Scaling (PS), a systematic framework that exploits empirically verified regularity conditions to predict full-scale model performance from small-scale proxies. PS constructs scaled-down variants via composable scaling functions along distinct resource axes, and projects metrics to the target scale via curve fitting with calibrated uncertainty estimates. We compare three prediction strategies of increasing expressiveness: even the simplest (raw proxy) achieves prediction error within the empirical noise floor of repeated-run variance; the most expressive (Gaussian Process) provides an indicative 15% relative MAE improvement and calibrated uncertainty. Evaluation on two ranking models of increasing complexity---a task-specific model and a foundation model---demonstrates that PS correctly ranks actionable hypotheses across diverse hypothesis types at 79-88% compute reductions.
authors: Aishwarya Wesanekar, Sheng-Tao Yang, Jiawei Zhang, Flavio Sales Truzzi, Chen Chen, Nader Beigiparast, Shengyuan Huang, Roshanak Zilouchian Moghaddam, Vitor Cid, Colin Clement, Vinayak Thapliyal, Sebastian Ament, Jihao Andreas Lin, Vincent Huang, Kai Han, Boyi Jiang, Wenlin Chen, Chaorong Chen, Ashwin Kumar, Maximilian Balandat, David Eriksson, Yifei Zhang, Pan Zhong
bullets: Addresses the cost of evaluating recommendation-model changes, which can require thousands of GPU-hours per full-scale run.
Builds smaller model variants through composable scaling functions across distinct resource axes.
Projects performance to the target scale using curve fitting with calibrated uncertainty estimates.
Tests prediction strategies from raw proxy metrics to Gaussian Processes; the latter improves relative MAE by 15%.
Across a task-specific ranking model and a foundation model, correctly ranks actionable hypotheses while reducing compute by 79–88%.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a framework to predict full-scale model performance from small-scale proxies, reducing compute costs for model exploration, directly addressing Efficient AI.
papers.title: Predictable Scaling: Efficient Model Exploration via Scaling-Law Prediction
papers.tldr: Predictable Scaling forecasts full-scale recommendation-model performance from small-scale runs, enabling reliable hypothesis ranking with 79–88% less compute.

papers.abstract: Resampling is the standard remedy for weight degeneracy in particle filters, but in high dimensions it distorts the spectrum of the ensemble covariance in a way that is computable from the importance weights. This paper studies the inverse problem: recovering the pre-resampling spectrum from the observed weights and the empirical spectrum alone, and using it without biasing the filter. We first show that the forward spectral law extends to random importance weights once one conditions on the weights together with the realized offspring counts, rather than on the weights alone. We then construct a regularized free-deconvolution estimator, prove its consistency with an explicit error budget at a fixed resolution scale, and certify model mismatch through a computable forward residual. The repaired spectrum enters the filter only as the preconditioner of a Metropolis-adjusted rejuvenation move, so that spectral error affects mixing efficiency but not the invariant target. For the full filtering cycle, we derive a geometrically summable error recursion under stable scalar dynamics and an explicit law for the cost of abstaining from repair. Pre-registered simulations show that the inversion reduces the spectral error by an order of magnitude, that the corrected preconditioner recovers about 90% of the oracle's sampling efficiency in an anisotropic regime, and that the cost of abstention depends on when abstentions occur rather than on how many. The repair recovers eigenvalue laws, not eigenvectors, and is certified only within an explicitly stated exogenous-weight regime.
authors: Deming Song, Chi-Kin Lam, Kefeng Li, Hui Yu, Xilin Li, Huagang Lin
bullets: Resampling distorts ensemble-covariance eigenvalue distributions, motivating recovery of the pre-resampling spectrum from weights and observed spectra.
The method conditions on importance weights and realized offspring counts, then applies regularized free deconvolution with consistency guarantees and a computable model-mismatch residual.
The repaired spectrum is used only to precondition a Metropolis-adjusted rejuvenation step, so spectral errors affect mixing efficiency but not target invariance.
Simulations report an order-of-magnitude reduction in spectral error and roughly 90% of oracle sampling efficiency in an anisotropic setting.
The approach recovers eigenvalue laws rather than eigenvectors and is certified only for an explicitly stated exogenous-weight regime.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses spectral distortion in high-dimensional particle filters using a regularized deconvolution estimator to improve mixing efficiency, fitting the Efficient AI category.
papers.title: Regularized free deconvolution for spectral repair of resampling distortion in high-dimensional particle filters
papers.tldr: A regularized free-deconvolution method repairs resampling-induced covariance spectra in high-dimensional particle filters while preserving the filter’s invariant target.

papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of complex models across large-scale networks of edge devices while keeping data localized. However, data heterogeneity and high communication overhead remain fundamental bottlenecks. Recently, the spectral optimizer Muon has demonstrated remarkable advantages over Adam-like methods in centralized training. While recent efforts have attempted to transition Muon to FL, naive integrations into traditional architectures fail short. Crucially, existing approaches do not support the the communication compression and local steps --- the two foundational techniques of efficient FL. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel spectral FL method that utilizes both local updates and compression. We establish rigorous convergence guarantees under mild assumptions, notably eliminating the restrictive bounded heterogeneity condition. Empirical evaluation on standard image classification benchmarks validates the efficiency and robustness of our approach.
authors: Dmitriy Bystrov, George Chirkov, Daniil Medyakov, Dmitry Bylinkin, Aleksandr Beznosikov
bullets: Targets data heterogeneity and communication overhead in federated learning.
Addresses the incompatibility of prior Muon-based FL methods with local steps and compressed communication.
Introduces a spectral FL approach supporting both efficient communication and local updates.
Proves convergence under mild assumptions while removing the restrictive bounded heterogeneity condition.
Experiments on standard image-classification benchmarks demonstrate efficiency and robustness.
papers.selection_reason: Communication compression and local steps in federated learning reduce communication overhead, an efficiency-oriented contribution.
papers.title: Bridging Compressed Communication and Local Steps via Spectral Method in Federated Learning
papers.tldr: A spectral federated learning method combines Muon-style optimization with local updates and communication compression, offering convergence guarantees without bounded heterogeneity assumptions.

papers.abstract: The recurrent neural network transducer (RNN-T) remains a practical choice for streaming speech recognition, but training requires large intermediate tensors. We present Flash RNN-T, a joint and loss implementation combining specialized kernels with optional tiled recomputation over the full alignment space and vocabulary. Tiled and untiled Flash form the entire measured throughput-memory frontier on medium and long workloads. On H100, untiled Flash achieves 24-39% higher throughput with 26-56% less memory than the fastest baseline on these workloads wherever it fits. Tiling reduces memory further through recomputation. On medium, tiled Flash uses ninefold less memory than that baseline at 16% lower throughput when both use one backward call per batch. On long, it fits where all tested alternatives with that backward schedule run out of memory with 80 GB. These comparisons use each implementation's lowest-memory configuration reaching at least 95% of its peak throughput.
bullets: Addresses the large intermediate tensors required to train streaming RNN-T models.
Uses specialized joint-network and transducer-loss kernels across the full alignment space and vocabulary.
Untiled Flash delivers 24–39% higher throughput with 26–56% less memory than the fastest baseline on supported H100 workloads.
Tiled Flash further reduces memory through recomputation, using ninefold less memory on medium workloads at a 16% throughput cost.
On long workloads, tiled Flash fits in 80 GB where tested alternatives run out of memory under the same backward schedule.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient RNN-T joint and loss computation reduces training memory and increases throughput, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Flash RNN-T: Memory-Efficient Joint Network and Transducer Loss Computation
papers.tldr: Flash RNN-T reduces training memory and often improves throughput by combining specialized kernels with optional tiled recomputation.

papers.abstract: Modern deep learning systems increasingly rely on high-dimensional vector operations, in which large input and parameter vectors are repeatedly stored, transferred, and processed. Although substantial research has focused on reducing neural-network model size through pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation, and efficient architectures, the storage, memory-traffic, and communication costs associated with repeatedly presented high-dimensional input vectors remain important practical considerations, particularly in distributed and edge-computing environments. This paper proposes the SETAREH (Sorting-assisted Energy-concentrating Transform for Approximate Representation using Haar wavelets) transform, a Haar-wavelet-based sparsification approach for approximating the inner product between a fixed high-dimensional coefficient vector and successive input vectors. By applying the same sequence of permutations and Haar transforms to both vectors, SETAREH preserves the exact inner product before truncation. It then retains only a subset of the transformed coefficient-input pairs, reducing their representation cost while introducing a controllable approximation error. To evaluate SETAREH, we consider two complementary experimental settings: a synthetic Gaussian-vector baseline and a real apparent-age estimation task using a convolutional neural network on the APPA-REAL dataset. The results show that SETAREH can approximate the evaluated inner products using substantially fewer transformed coefficient-input pairs than the original vector dimension. The findings support its use as a potential structured data-representation method for repeated inner products with fixed weights, while the practical benefit depends on approximation accuracy and the cost of storing or transmitting permutation metadata.
bullets: Targets storage, memory-traffic, and communication overhead for repeatedly presented high-dimensional inputs with fixed weights.
