Applies identical permutations and Haar transforms to the coefficient and input vectors, preserving their exact inner product before truncation.
Keeps only selected transformed coefficient–input pairs to reduce representation size while introducing approximation error.
Evaluated on synthetic Gaussian vectors and an apparent-age estimation task using a CNN on APPA-REAL.
Practical gains depend on the accuracy required and the cost of storing or transmitting permutation metadata.
papers.selection_reason: Wavelet-based sparsification reduces representation cost of high-dimensional vectors for approximate inner products, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: SETAREH Transform: A Sorting-Assisted Haar-Wavelet Sparsification Method for Approximate Inner-Product Computation
papers.tldr: SETAREH uses shared sorting and Haar-wavelet transforms to sparsify repeated high-dimensional inner products, reducing the number of stored or transmitted coefficient–input pairs at a controllable approximation cost.

papers.abstract: Real-time inference on small devices needs low activation memory without extra latency, which makes operator order the most valuable memory lever: it is free in time. We show that the usual way of deploying a better order, handing it back to the compiler and regenerating code, is unreliable. In PyTorch Inductor the regenerated program misses its predicted peak in 22 of 54 CPU configurations. It is worse than the stock program in 9 of them and in 19 of 50 on a GPU, and on the GPU it also changes numerical results. We instead profile the generated program, model its memory exactly from its own statements and their read/write effects, and permute those statements. We prove that this realizes the modeled peak whenever allocation does not depend on history. It does so to the byte, with bitwise-identical results, in all our CPU runs. On the GPU we characterize why the caching allocator breaks the condition. To know when to stop, we give forward and reverse "trap" lower bounds, each computable with $O(n^2)$ minimum cuts. They certify the found order optimal for 94% of held-out wrapper graphs and all 16 microcontroller-class models we study, in under a second. So most inference graphs are already scheduled optimally. Branching networks are the exception, where reordering is free and pays, e.g. 10.0% on DeepLabV3. In compiled training we save up to 7.6%. Beyond the certified optimum we study selective recomputation with per-operator caps. It is strongly NP-hard for every fixed cap even at treewidth two, encodes knapsack exactly on series-parallel graphs, and is solvable exactly on bounded treewidth. It is useless on public tiny models whose peak is a single layer, but on architectures that hold a cheap value for a late reuse it pays: on the public ReDimNet speaker networks, whose order is already optimal, it lowers the peak by 5.2-6.1% at under 0.4% extra MACs, with bitwise-identical outputs.
authors: Ivan Fomin, Ivan Koryabkin, Boris Sheludko
bullets: Compiler regeneration often fails to realize predicted memory savings and can worsen memory use or alter GPU results.
Profiling generated code and reordering its statements exactly matches modeled peak memory and preserves bitwise-identical outputs on CPU.
Forward and reverse minimum-cut bounds certify optimal schedules for most tested graphs, including all studied microcontroller-class models.
Branching networks benefit most from reordering; compiled training saves up to 7.6%, while DeepLabV3 improves by 10.0%.
Selective recomputation is strongly NP-hard under fixed caps, but reduces peak memory by 5.2–6.1% on ReDimNet with under 0.4% extra MACs.
papers.selection_reason: Exact peak-memory scheduling and recomputation limits for inference directly target memory-efficient AI.
papers.title: Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust: Exact Realization, Certified Optimality, and the Limits of Recomputation for Inference
papers.tldr: The paper presents a reliable, certifiably optimal operator-ordering approach for reducing inference peak memory, while showing when recomputation is useful or computationally hard.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) repeatedly process hundreds of visual tokens across decoder layers, incurring substantial computation and memory costs. Existing inference-time visual token pruning methods often irreversibly remove low-ranked tokens, although the set of visual tokens receiving high query-conditioned attention can change across decoder depth. Recoverable routing preserves skipped tokens for later reconsideration, but re-admits them with stale representations after bypassing intermediate transformations. We further find that replacing stale re-admitted states with their current-depth oracle states from a full-token reference trajectory substantially improves grounding performance. We therefore propose CatchUp, a training-free framework for depth-aware visual-token re-admission. CatchUp repeatedly re-evaluates query-conditioned visual relevance, processes only selected visual tokens through each decoder interval, and preserves deferred tokens for later re-admission. Upon re-admission, CatchUp approximates missed representation evolution using reference-to-current transition signals from semantically and spatially related visual tokens. Across three referring-expression grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the highest average relative retention in both benchmark groups at 64-, 128-, and 192-token budgets. At a 64-token budget with 88.9% fewer active visual tokens, CatchUp retains 92.17% of the full model's performance on average across six multimodal benchmarks while reducing end-to-end latency by 8.0%. Code is available at https://github.com/pej0918/CatchUp
bullets: Problem: Irreversible visual-token pruning can discard tokens that become relevant later, while recoverable routing may re-admit them with stale representations.
Method: Re-evaluates query-conditioned token relevance at each decoder interval, processes only selected tokens, and preserves deferred tokens for later re-admission.
Key idea: Uses transition signals from semantically and spatially related tokens to approximate the representation evolution missed by skipped tokens.
Results: Across three grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the highest average relative retention at 64-, 128-, and 192-token budgets.
At 64 tokens, it uses 88.9% fewer active visual tokens, retains 92.17% of full-model performance on average, and reduces end-to-end latency by 8.0%.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free depth-aware visual token re-admission for efficient LVLMs; directly targets token pruning/eviction and MLLM efficiency.
papers.title: CatchUp: Depth-Aware Re-Admission of Visual Tokens for Efficient Large Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: CatchUp is a training-free method that efficiently prunes and later re-admits visual tokens across decoder depth while approximating their updated representations, preserving LVLM performance with lower latency.

papers.abstract: A common way to make language models and agents more accurate is to spend more compute at inference time: generate many candidate solutions and submit the one a verifier prefers. Success then requires that some candidate is correct and that the verifier picks it. The first grows predictably with the number of samples; the second does not, because real verifiers (unit tests, majority votes, LLM judges, reward models) accept wrong answers, reject right ones, and make correlated mistakes. With a fixed budget, a practitioner must decide how many samples to draw, which models to draw them from, and how much to spend on verification, and today these choices are made by rules of thumb. We introduce SPLIT, which makes them from a small labelled pilot. It rests on an exact formula for the probability of submitting a correct answer under accept/reject and top-score selection that accounts for varying task difficulty, blind spots shared across models, and correlated repeated verifier calls. SPLIT fits the formula by empirical Bayes and uses it to plan budgets on unseen tasks. Across seven benchmarks spanning math, science QA, code and software-engineering agents, 26 models, 175 agent systems and six kinds of real verifiers, all from public releases, SPLIT lands within 0.02-0.8 percentage points of the best allocation in hindsight, while every fixed rule we test loses at least 2.5 points in some setting. Regret depends only on how well SPLIT ranks configurations, and it stays near-optimal under compute, price and latency costs and online. The formula also explains when asking more LLM judges lowers precision. As a forecaster far beyond the pilot, SPLIT beats power-law fitting when the verifier caps success, and we report where it loses.
bullets: Test-time accuracy depends on both generating a correct candidate and having the verifier select it; real verifiers can make correlated false accepts and rejects.
SPLIT fits an exact success-probability formula with empirical Bayes, modeling task difficulty, shared model blind spots, and repeated-verifier correlations.
It plans sample counts, model mixtures, and verification effort for unseen tasks under compute, price, latency, and online constraints.
Across seven benchmarks, SPLIT came within 0.02–0.8 percentage points of the hindsight-best allocation; fixed rules lost at least 2.5 points in some settings.
The analysis identifies when additional LLM judging reduces precision and when SPLIT loses as a long-range forecaster.
papers.selection_reason: Optimal allocation of test-time compute under imperfect verifiers is a meaningful efficiency contribution for LLM inference.
papers.title: Sample, Mix, or Verify? Allocating Test-Time Compute under Imperfect Verifiers
papers.tldr: SPLIT uses a small labelled pilot to allocate test-time sampling and verification compute effectively despite imperfect, correlated verifiers.

papers.abstract: Small-to-large language model routing can reduce inference cost by escalating difficult inputs while retaining easier ones on a smaller model. Its success, however, depends on identifying examples that benefit from escalation, and the reliability of confidence across multilingual tasks remains unclear. We present a systematic evaluation of confidence-based routing across three model families, four languages, and three task types, covering 72 model, dataset, language, and scale configurations and 42,288 predictions. We compare global confidence routing with random routing, equal-quota confidence routing, and an oracle upper bound. Confidence identifies beneficial escalations on the Belebele reading comprehension and SIB-200 topic classification datasets, with mean correction-detection AUCs of 0.612 and 0.705. At 50% escalation, it improves over random routing by 1.40--4.67 percentage points on Belebele and 2.54--5.63 points on SIB-200. In contrast, the mean AUC on the MMLU-ProX-Lite knowledge and reasoning dataset is only 0.510, and routing provides no consistent improvement over random selection because small models often remain highly confident while incorrect. Global confidence routing also creates language escalation gaps up to 30.33 percentage points, whereas equal-quota routing removes this disparity with little aggregate accuracy cost. These results show that confidence routing is task-dependent and can allocate computation unevenly across languages. Code is available at https://github.com/sabbir5622r/multilingual-llm-routing
authors: Md Sabbir Hossen, Anichur Rahman, Pabon Shaha, Airin Afroj Aishi, Andrew H. Sung, Md Shohel Rana
bullets: Evaluates routing across three model families, four languages, and three task types, covering 72 configurations and 42,288 predictions.
Confidence successfully identifies inputs benefiting from escalation on Belebele and SIB-200, outperforming random routing at 50% escalation.
Routing is ineffective on MMLU-ProX-Lite because small models can be confidently wrong.
Global confidence routing produces language escalation gaps of up to 30.33 percentage points.
Equal-quota routing removes language disparities with little aggregate accuracy cost.
papers.selection_reason: Confidence-based small-to-large LLM routing directly targets inference cost reduction and analyzes efficiency trade-offs across languages/tasks.
papers.title: Who Pays for Efficient Inference? Confidence-Based Small-to-Large LLM Routing Across Tasks and Languages
papers.tldr: Confidence-based small-to-large LLM routing can reduce inference cost, but its effectiveness and fairness depend strongly on the task and language.

papers.abstract: Detecting faithfulness hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for their safe deployment in high-stakes domains. Recent approaches address this by contrasting contextual against parametric knowledge utilization, yet measuring context reliance typically demands noticeable overhead, such as materializing attention maps, running additional forward passes, or training auxiliary probes. In this work, we show that context reliance can be estimated by projecting hidden states onto the dark space - directions that compose weakly with the unembedding matrix. Beyond its recognized function as an initial-token attention sink, we show that this subspace actively mediates context processing, and that its share of hidden-state norm - termed the Dark Matter Ratio (DMR) - provides a direct score of context utilization. Pairing DMR with a parametric knowledge score yields DarkLens, a lightweight faithfulness detector operating strictly within a single forward pass. Evaluated across three QA and summarization benchmarks on six open-weight LLMs (4B-13B parameters), DarkLens matches or outperforms a wide range of baselines without requiring extra forward passes or probe training.
authors: Alexandra Kuleshova, Andrey Volodichev, Daria Kotova, Alexey Zaytsev
bullets: Context reliance is estimated from the hidden-state norm in weakly unembedded directions, called the Dark Matter Ratio (DMR).
The dark space is shown to mediate context processing, beyond its known role as an initial-token attention sink.
Combining DMR with a parametric knowledge score yields the lightweight DarkLens detector.
Across three QA and summarization benchmarks and six open-weight LLMs, DarkLens matches or outperforms many baselines without extra passes or probe training.
papers.selection_reason: LLM internal-state faithfulness detection with single-forward-pass efficiency, relevant to LLM understanding and efficient inference.
papers.title: What LLMs Do in the Shadows: Reading Context Reliance from the Unembedding Dark Space
papers.tldr: DarkLens detects LLM faithfulness hallucinations in a single forward pass by measuring hidden-state reliance on the unembedding matrix’s “dark space.”

papers.abstract: Recent speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) increasingly rely on large models and complex multi-stage pipelines for neural decoding. However, in speech BCI, where training data are scarce, noisy, and expensive to collect, the benefits of model scaling remain unclear. This work revisits a fundamental question: are large models truly necessary for accurate neural decoding? We propose BEST (Brain-Encoding-Speech-Text), a two-stage framework for efficient neural-to-text decoding. Instead of relying on large generative models or phoneme-centric pipelines, BEST introduces hierarchical intermediate representations and a compact speech-oriented decoder that directly maps neural activity to text. This design preserves essential structure while significantly reducing computational cost, enabling robust generalization in low-resource settings and practical deployment under constrained resources. On the Brain-to-Text '24 and '25 benchmarks, BEST achieves word error rates (WERs) of 6.19% and 1.62%, respectively, using only 3.85% of the parameters required by comparable methods. Beyond these results, we provide three key insights: (1) decoder scaling yields non-monotonic gains; (2) cross-modal alignment is more critical than model size; and (3) overfitting degards sequence-level performance. Representation analysis further reveals a consistent neural-audio-text alignment pathway.
authors: Zehui Feng, Weichuan Wang, Xiaohan Chen, Cuntai Guan, Ting Han
bullets: Speech BCI data are scarce, noisy, and costly, making the value of model scaling uncertain.
BEST uses two stages with hierarchical intermediate representations and a compact speech-oriented decoder that maps neural activity to text.
It reports 6.19% and 1.62% WER on the Brain-to-Text ’24 and ’25 benchmarks, respectively, using 3.85% of the parameters of comparable methods.
The study finds that decoder scaling has non-monotonic benefits, cross-modal alignment matters more than model size, and overfitting harms sequence-level performance.
Representation analysis indicates a consistent neural–audio–text alignment pathway, supporting efficient deployment in low-resource settings.
papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces BEST, a framework for efficient neural-to-text decoding that drastically reduces parameters (3.85%) while maintaining performance, directly addressing the Efficient AI subtopic of Token Pruning and Eviction through compact decoder design.
papers.title: Do Speech BCIs Need Larger Models? Rethinking Neural Decoding beyond Scaling
papers.tldr: BEST shows that compact, hierarchically structured decoders can achieve strong speech BCI neural-to-text performance without relying on large models.

papers.abstract: On AWS Trainium2, every component of a diffusion model runs as a program compiled ahead of time for fixed shapes, while pipelines differ across models, prompt lengths across requests, and caching decisions across denoising steps. We present Difflet, a serving engine in which five model pipelines share one compilation backend, joint attention is split across cores by attention head, and a host controller decides at each denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse its earlier output. A small probe program computes the caching signal on the device and returns one number per step, and a resident model process keeps every program loaded across requests. Across five image and video model families, fused attention accelerates denoiser steps by 1.2-4.3x over the same framework using PyTorch/XLA attention, and at 32.8k visual tokens it is the only attention that compiles. On four of the five models, resident serving is 1.5-3.4x faster than standalone runs that reload weights from a warm file cache for each generation.
authors: Bin Ma, Min Yu, Vijay Kodamalla, Jialin Liu, Dong Li
bullets: Addresses fixed-shape compilation constraints across varying pipelines, prompt lengths, and denoising-time caching decisions.
Uses one compilation backend for five pipelines, splits joint attention across cores by head, and fuses attention computation.
A host controller selectively reuses denoiser outputs, guided by a device-side probe that produces one caching signal per step.
Fused attention is 1.2–4.3× faster than PyTorch/XLA attention and is the only attention variant compiling at 32.8k visual tokens.
Resident serving is 1.5–3.4× faster than reloading weights for each generation on four of five models.
papers.selection_reason: Presents Difflet, a fast inference engine for diffusion transformer models on AWS Trainium, optimizing attention computation and caching to improve serving efficiency.
papers.title: DIFFLET: A Fast Inference Engine for Diffusion Transformer Models on AWS Trainium
papers.tldr: Difflet speeds diffusion-transformer inference on AWS Trainium2 through shared compilation, fused attention, adaptive caching, and resident model serving.

papers.abstract: On neuromorphic chips, spiking neural networks (SNNs) consume far less energy than artificial neural networks (ANNs), but the limited memory of these chips requires low-bit synaptic weights and membrane potentials. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods provide them without retraining and, like those for ANNs, minimize numerical errors such as the mean squared error (MSE). In an SNN, however, a quantization error reaches later layers only through the spikes it flips. We find that errors of equal MSE can cause very different accuracy losses, whereas errors that flip the same fraction of spikes cause the same loss. We therefore propose SpikeQ, a spike-guided PTQ framework. For weights, we select the level of each weight by simulating the downstream neurons and minimizing their spike errors. For membrane potentials, most existing methods quantize the state after the reset, whereas neuromorphic chips compare the threshold with the membrane potential stored at a fixed bit width. We target this pre-fire quantization and build a reset-aware grid that places the threshold on a rounding boundary, so rounding never flips the spike at the current time step. We evaluate SpikeQ on seven benchmarks of image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection. With 2-bit pre-fire membrane potentials, every existing grid collapses, whereas SpikeQ retains most of the full-precision accuracy. With both at 4 bits, the models stay within 2.59 points of full precision, shrink their memory footprint 7.8--7.9 times, and use 6.4--6.9 times less energy.
authors: Kai Sun, Peibo Duan, Zhanglu Yan, Guowei Zhang, Yongsheng Huang, Levin Kuhlmann
bullets: SNN quantization errors matter primarily when they flip downstream spikes, not when they increase MSE.
For weights, SpikeQ simulates downstream neurons and selects quantization levels that minimize spike errors.
For membrane potentials, it quantizes the pre-fire state with a reset-aware grid that prevents current-step spike flips.
Across seven image classification, segmentation, and detection benchmarks, SpikeQ retains most full-precision accuracy with 2-bit membrane potentials.
At 4-bit weights and membrane potentials, models remain within 2.59 percentage points of full precision while reducing memory 7.8–7.9× and energy use 6.4–6.9×.
papers.selection_reason: Spike-guided post-training quantization for SNNs reduces memory and energy use, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: SpikeQ: Spike-Guided Post-Training Quantization for Spiking Neural Networks
papers.tldr: SpikeQ improves post-training quantization for SNNs by minimizing spike flips rather than numerical error, preserving accuracy at very low precision while reducing memory and energy use.

papers.abstract: Mainstream point cloud completion methods are unanimously based on deep learning architectures. On one hand, these methods tend to repetitively stacking attention modules to enhance network performance, which drifts away from the neat design of unified and interpret-able networks; on the other hand, nearly all existing architectures rely solely on feed-forward connections to propagate information, neglecting feedback from deeper layers. The recurrent neural architecture, formed by feedforward-feedback loops, have shown its ability to generate Illusory Contours (ICs) in the V1 brain region of mammals; and ICs are essentially a completion mechanism of the brain for visual information. Motivated by this, we design a Brain-inspired Recurrent Illusory Contour Encoder (BRICE) to "imagine" what is missing in the incomplete 3D point clouds. Building upon the foundation model of Predictive Coding (PC), the plug-and-play nature enables BRICE to be seamlessly integrated into mainstream point cloud completion baselines. Experimental results show that BRICE can enhance various completion baselines on different 3D datasets such as MVP2K, PCN, and PlantPCom. Our code: Https://github.com/wangyunlei-wyl/BRICE.
authors: Yunlei Wang, Dawei Li, Xue-song Tang
bullets: Addresses the reliance on stacked attention and purely feed-forward information propagation in existing completion networks.
Models illusory-contour formation in the visual cortex through feedforward-feedback recurrent connections.
Provides a plug-and-play encoder that can be integrated with mainstream point-cloud completion baselines.
Enhances multiple baselines across the MVP2K, PCN, and PlantPCom datasets.
The abstract does not report specific quantitative gains or limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Point cloud completion with a recurrent brain-inspired encoder; relevant to 3D vision and efficient plug-and-play enhancement of existing baselines.
papers.title: BRICE: Brain-inspired Recurrent Illusory Contour Encoder for Point Cloud Completion
papers.tldr: BRICE improves point-cloud completion by adding a brain-inspired recurrent encoder that uses predictive-coding feedback to infer missing geometry.

papers.abstract: Minimizing the wall-clock time required to reach a target accuracy is crucial in federated learning (FL), where many applications require frequent model updates as data distributions evolve over time. Nevertheless, in heterogeneous environments, slow clients with limited computational and communication capabilities can delay global synchronization, forcing faster clients to wait and increasing the overall training time. To mitigate this straggler effect, recent studies have introduced per-round time constraints and adapted client workloads within the available time. However, these approaches primarily focus on local computation, whereas communication can become a major bottleneck in communication-limited environments, motivating the joint optimization of training workload and communication compression. Although previous studies have explored such joint optimization, determining an effective training--communication balance under a fixed per-round time budget remains challenging, as the resulting model performance depends on both training progress and compression-induced degradation. We therefore propose TALLOP, which jointly optimizes the local training workload and communication compression under per-round time constraints. TALLOP predicts the training loss achievable under different computation budgets from the early-stage mini-batch loss trajectory (LENS), and estimates the degradation caused by communication compression using a compression-error model (CLEN). TALLOP combines these predictions to select the training-communication allocation that minimizes the post-compression loss under the given round time constraint. Experiments in heterogeneous FL environments show that TALLOP generally achieves competitive or improved time-to-accuracy compared with approaches that optimize only local training or neither, although the benefit over training-only adaptation depends on the setting.
authors: Honoka Anada, Yafei Ou, Shinya Takamaeda-Yamazaki
bullets: Addresses stragglers and communication bottlenecks in heterogeneous federated learning.
Uses LENS to predict training loss for different computation budgets from early mini-batch loss trajectories.
Uses CLEN to estimate loss degradation caused by communication compression.
Selects the computation–compression balance minimizing predicted post-compression loss within each round’s time budget.
Generally matches or improves time-to-accuracy over training-only or non-adaptive approaches, though gains depend on the setting.
papers.selection_reason: Jointly optimizes local training and communication compression to reduce wall-clock time in federated learning, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: TALLOP: Joint Optimization of Local Training and Communication Compression for Time-Constrained Federated Learning
papers.tldr: TALLOP jointly allocates local computation and communication compression under per-round time limits to reduce federated learning time-to-accuracy.

papers.abstract: Long-context decoding in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly bottlenecked by the memory and computation required to attend over an ever-growing Key-Value (KV) cache at each autoregressive step. Although token-level sparse attention reduces this burden by restricting computation to a small subset of relevant past tokens, its practical gains are often offset by repeatedly recomputing layer-wise sparse indices as the context grows. A common remedy is to share sparse indices across layers by computing them only at designated anchor layers, but such static reuse ignores the layer-wise evolution of attention patterns, causing the reused indices to progressively deviate from the layer-specific optima and incur substantial attention loss. By revisiting cross-layer sparsity from the perspective of attention dynamics, we find that inter-layer salient token shift is highly localized: although the exact top-$\kappa$ indices differ across layers, the core high-attention tokens remain stable, with changes concentrated near the expanded boundary of previously selected regions. Motivated by this, we propose Prism Attention, a proposal-refined sparse attention framework. It replaces rigid cross-layer index reuse with a coarse-to-fine strategy, preserving layer-wise adaptability while retaining the efficiency benefits of cross-layer sharing. Extensive experiments show that Prism Attention achieves state-of-the-art performance among mainstream sparse attention methods on both reasoning and long-context benchmarks, while attaining a $3.4\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup over FlashAttention at 128K context length.
authors: Zhenxu Tian, Kebin Liu, Zhengwu Yang, Yi Su, Qingqing Dang, Yanlin Sha, Kaipeng Deng, Dianhai Yu, Yanjun Ma, Juntao Li, Min Zhang
bullets: Long-context decoding is bottlenecked by repeated attention over the growing KV cache.
Static cross-layer index sharing is efficient but can lose accuracy as attention patterns evolve across layers.
The method observes that salient-token changes are localized near the boundaries of previously selected regions.
Its coarse-to-fine proposal-refinement strategy preserves layer adaptability while reducing index recomputation.
It reports state-of-the-art performance among mainstream sparse-attention methods and a 3.4× decoding speedup over FlashAttention at 128K context.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse attention with cross-layer index sharing reduces KV-cache memory and decoding compute.
papers.title: Prism Attention: Proposal-Refined Index Sharing Mechanism for Efficient LLMs Inference
papers.tldr: Prism Attention accelerates long-context LLM decoding by refining shared sparse-attention indices across layers instead of rigidly reusing them.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have become a common backbone for high-quality text-to-image and text-to-video generation, but repeated dense self-attention remains a major inference bottleneck as token sequences grow and the same operator is invoked across many denoising steps. Our study suggests that dense attention in pretrained DiTs contains reusable layer/head-specific high-mass structure that can be identified from a small offline calibration set and reused across future generations. This leads to Sink-Sparse Hybrid Attention, a train-free attention replacement that reuses static sink masks and supplements them with a lightweight pooled-KV branch, while leaving model weights and sampling schedules unchanged. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, the method attains 1.54$\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining generation quality. On Z-Image-Turbo, it attains 1.57$\times$ end-to-end speedup with competitive GenEval2 performance. These results indicate that reusable importance-aware sparse support can provide an effective train-free acceleration path for both T2V and T2I DiTs.
authors: Bingxin Xing, Yu Zhang, Jiatong Ding, Lei Lu, Ping Wang
bullets: Targets the inference cost of repeated dense self-attention in DiTs with long token sequences and many denoising steps.
Uses small offline calibration to identify reusable, layer/head-specific high-mass attention structure.
Combines static sink masks with a lightweight pooled-KV branch as a train-free attention replacement.
Achieves 1.54× end-to-end speedup on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B while maintaining generation quality.
Achieves 1.57× end-to-end speedup on Z-Image-Turbo with competitive GenEval2 performance; scope covers T2V and T2I DiTs.
papers.selection_reason: Train-free sparse attention replacement for efficient T2I/T2V diffusion transformers.
papers.title: Sink-Sparse Hybrid Attention for Efficient Inference in T2I/T2V Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: Sink-Sparse Hybrid Attention accelerates pretrained text-to-image and text-to-video diffusion Transformers by reusing calibrated sparse attention structure without retraining or changing sampling schedules.

papers.abstract: Visual information worth extracting from an image and the token budget it warrants depend on the text query. Yet modern vision and vision-language models largely encode images independently of the query and allocate a fixed visual token budget to every input. We introduce the Query-Adaptive Recurrent Tokenizer (QART), a backbone-agnostic module that makes visual representations both query-steerable and budget-adaptive. QART steers the visual representation toward query-relevant evidence while adapting its token budget to the amount of information required. Its key principle is simple. Additional tokens are allocated until the visual features relevant to the query are represented with sufficient fidelity. Starting from frozen encoder features, QART recurrently constructs a compact representation and uses reconstruction quality over the query-relevant visual support to control token allocation. On Visual7W and VQAv2, QART achieves 81.96% and 76.37% accuracy using only about 29 visual tokens, reducing token counts by 20-25x relative to dense VLM inputs. It further reaches 92.0% P@1 on CORE and 36.3% PR-AUC on PODS, outperforming SteerViT on PODS by 8.4%. Together, these results show that visual representations need not be fixed in either content or capacity and can instead adapt to what each query requires.
authors: Bavesh Balaji, Pranav Gopinath, Pouya Sadeghi, Sirisha Rambhatla
bullets: Addresses fixed, query-independent visual representations and token budgets in vision-language models.
Uses frozen encoder features and recurrently builds a compact representation steered toward query-relevant evidence.
Controls token allocation through reconstruction quality over the query-relevant visual support.
Achieves 81.96% on Visual7W and 76.37% on VQAv2 with 20–25× fewer tokens than dense inputs.
Also reaches 92.0% P@1 on CORE and 36.3% PR-AUC on PODS, outperforming SteerViT on PODS by 8.4%.
papers.selection_reason: Query-adaptive recurrent token allocation for efficient VLM inference.
papers.title: Query-adaptive Recurrent Tokenization
papers.tldr: QART makes visual tokenization query-aware and dynamically allocates only as many tokens as each query requires, achieving strong performance with about 29 tokens.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise for generalist robotic manipulation, but their inference cost remains a major bottleneck for real-time control. This limitation is especially pronounced in flow-matching VLAs such as $\pi_{0.5}$, where the action expert is evaluated repeatedly during iterative denoising. We introduce MambaAct, an efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual-language prefix encoder of $\pi_{0.5}$, while replacing its transformer-based action expert with a compact Mamba-based action expert. Within this expert, Mamba serves as the action mixer that models dependencies across the noisy continuous-action sequence. To preserve visual-language conditioning without repeated token-level cross-attention, MambaAct uses a lightweight Context Compressor to map Vision-language model (VLM) prefix tokens into a compact conditioning signal that gates and modulates each Mamba action block. MambaAct uses a $10\times$ smaller action expert and reduces flow-matching denoising latency by $64.8\%$ on LIBERO and $58.8\%$ in real-world deployment, while improving mean LIBERO success by $1.08$ percentage points across three independent fine-tuning seeds and maintaining gains on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks. Our code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/giakhuyendihoc/MambaAct.
authors: Khuyen Pham, Tran Nguyen Le, Edoardo Fazzari, Cesare Stefanini
bullets: Targets the repeated action-expert evaluations that make flow-matching VLAs costly for real-time robotic control.
Retains π₀.₅’s pretrained vision-language encoder and uses Mamba to model dependencies across noisy continuous-action sequences.
Compresses vision-language prefix tokens into a conditioning signal that gates and modulates Mamba blocks without repeated token-level cross-attention.
Uses a 10× smaller action expert and reduces denoising latency by 64.8% on LIBERO and 58.8% in real-world deployment.
Improves mean LIBERO success by 1.08 percentage points across three seeds, with gains also reported on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies; directly relevant to embodied VLA and robot manipulation with latency reduction.
papers.title: MambaAct: Efficient Mamba Action Experts for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: MambaAct replaces the transformer action expert in flow-matching VLA models with a compact Mamba-based expert, substantially reducing inference latency while preserving or improving manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: The Levenberg-Marquardt (LMA) algorithm is a widely used nonlinear least-squares solver known for its rapid convergence. For small-scale neural networks, LMA provides better convergence and architectural robustness than first-order optimizers like Adam. However, LMA imposes prohibitive memory and computational costs. These costs are primarily from the Jacobian matrix, whose dimensions scale with both the number of samples and parameters. This bottleneck prevents its use in large-scale neural networks. Recent efforts scale LMA using preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) solvers to avoid materializing the Jacobian. However, PCG only approximates the solution, requiring many network propagations and a task-specific preconditioner. Other studies optimize LMA to reduce costs, but they restrict their methods to specific tasks or network architectures. As a result, LMA remains impractical for training general large-scale neural networks. In this paper, we propose LeMA, a distributed LMA algorithm for large-scale neural network training on multi-GPU platforms. Our contributions are twofold: First, an exact dual formulation of LMA removes the memory dependence on the parameter dimension. Second, a Jacobian sharding strategy computes Jacobian shards on the fly and in parallel to avoid materializing the full Jacobian. For large-scale neural networks, LeMA reduces the memory footprint of LMA from quadratic in the number of parameters to quadratic in the batch size. This makes exact LMA steps feasible for billion-parameter models without approximate PCG solves. Furthermore, for a convolutional neural network with 1,000,022,632 parameters on an 8-GPU node, LeMA achieves a 7.97x speedup over a single GPU, corresponding to a 99.7% strong scaling efficiency.
authors: Xianghao Wang, Johan Barth\'elemy, John Taylor
bullets: LMA can converge rapidly but is normally impractical at scale because storing and processing its Jacobian is prohibitively expensive.
LeMA uses an exact dual formulation to eliminate memory dependence on the number of parameters.
It computes Jacobian shards on the fly and in parallel, avoiding materialization of the full Jacobian and approximate PCG solves.
The resulting memory footprint scales quadratically with batch size rather than parameter count.
On an 8-GPU node, LeMA achieves 7.97× speedup and 99.7% strong-scaling efficiency for a 1-billion-parameter CNN.
papers.selection_reason: Distributed exact Levenberg-Marquardt training framework that drastically reduces memory and compute for large networks, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Scalable Levenberg-Marquardt Training Framework for Deep Learning
papers.tldr: LeMA makes exact Levenberg–Marquardt training feasible for billion-parameter neural networks by distributing Jacobian computation across multiple GPUs.

papers.abstract: Token merging improves the efficiency of Vision Transformers by combining redundant tokens, but existing methods largely rely on feature similarity to determine which tokens to merge. This criterion is effective for semantic segmentation, yet can fail in instance segmentation, where adjacent objects of the same class often have highly similar features. We identify this failure mode as cross-instance token fusion. We introduce MaskMerge, an instance-aware token merging method that uses coarse intermediate mask predictions to constrain feature-based merging and preserve instance boundaries. We evaluate MaskMerge on two diverse instance segmentation domains characterized by high inter-instance visual similarity: PanNuke and iSAID. Against the SOTA token merging method ALGM, MaskMerge improves mAP from 30.1 to 32.1 on PanNuke while reducing computation from 229 to 153 GFLOPs and running 1.18x faster, and from 33.1 to 36.2 on iSAID while reducing computation from 198 to 182 GFLOPs and running 1.23x faster. Additionally, we also test it on Cityscapes and match ALGM's performance while using fewer FLOPs. The gains also transfer to an MAE pretrained backbone, demonstrating that instance-aware merging enables more aggressive compression when appearance similarity alone cannot reliably preserve object identity.
authors: Bavesh Balaji, Letian Jiang, Alexander Wong, David Clausi, Sirisha Rambhatla
bullets: Feature-similarity merging can blur boundaries between adjacent same-class instances, causing cross-instance token fusion.
MaskMerge constrains feature-based token merging with intermediate mask predictions to preserve instance identities.
On PanNuke and iSAID, it improves mAP while reducing computation and increasing speed relative to ALGM.
On Cityscapes, it matches ALGM’s performance with fewer FLOPs.
The approach also transfers to an MAE-pretrained backbone, supporting more aggressive compression when appearance similarity is ambiguous.
papers.selection_reason: Token merging method for efficient instance segmentation using mask constraints.
papers.title: MaskMerge: Structure-aware Token Merging for Efficient Instance Segmentation
papers.tldr: MaskMerge makes token merging more efficient for instance segmentation by using coarse masks to prevent tokens from different objects being fused.

papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a powerful machine learning framework that allows building a global model from the contributions of multiple, distributed clients, while ensuring the privacy of their local data. However, its heavy computational and communication overheads challenge its use for contemporary AI workloads such as natural language processing (NLP) and multimodal analysis. For this reason, this paper presents a novel small language model that leverages byte-level text and multimodal data processing, enhanced by a linear attention mechanism, to enable manageable Federated Learning of NLP and multimodal analysis tasks. The proposed model, nicknamed FederatedBytes, manages to process text and any other data types, including images, by treating its input as a mere sequence of bytes, while its lean linear attention mechanism allows abating the overall memory and computational footprint. To prove the effectiveness of the proposed model we have carried out an extensive performance evaluation on sentiment analysis tasks in multilingual and multimodal settings over the Multilingual Amazon Reviews and ScienceQA datasets. The experimental results show that FederatedBytes has been able to outperform comparable models such as ByT5 and LSTM, achieving higher accuracy while significantly reducing memory and communication overheads.
authors: Ali Sarabadani, Massimo Piccardi, Mehran Abolhasan, Farzad Tofigh, Ian Zhou, Justin Lipman
bullets: Targets the computational and communication costs that hinder federated NLP and multimodal learning.
Processes text, images, and other modalities uniformly as byte sequences, without tokenization.
Uses lean linear attention to reduce memory and computational requirements.
Evaluated on multilingual and multimodal sentiment analysis using Multilingual Amazon Reviews and ScienceQA.
The abstract reports higher accuracy than ByT5 and LSTM, alongside substantially lower memory and communication overheads.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a tokenizer-free, byte-level small language model for efficient federated learning, utilizing linear attention to reduce memory and computational footprint.
papers.title: FederatedBytes: Tokenizer-Free, Byte-Level Small Language Models for Efficient Multimodal Federated Learning
papers.tldr: FederatedBytes is a tokenizer-free, byte-level small language model using linear attention to make multimodal federated learning more efficient while maintaining strong sentiment-analysis performance.

papers.abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has emerged as a prevalent strategy for adapting large pre-trained models. Among PEFT techniques, reparameterization-based methods, particularly those that employ low-rank or sparsity structures, have attracted significant attention. However, these approaches often underperform full fine-tuning. Specifically, low-rank methods constrain the update rank, which is misaligned with the inherently high-rank nature of full fine-tuning. In contrast, sparsity-based techniques limit the flexibility of the parameter space and compromise connectivity across weights. To overcome these limitations, we explore the use of Toeplitz matrices, whose entries are constant along each diagonal, therefore providing a compact parameterization without imposing explicit rank or sparsity constraints. A straightforward approach is to update weights via a product of Toeplitz matrices. However, similar to RNNs, long multiplicative chains often lead to gradient instability. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{ToPA}, a more refined version of this idea that replaces standard Toeplitz matrices with block-wise Toeplitz, greatly increasing each factor's capacity and shortening the chain, thereby stabilizing training and improving expressiveness. We theoretically show that products of block-wise Toeplitz matrices can approximate arbitrary matrices under shorter chain length, justifying the structural design of ToPA. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ToPA offers greater expressivity than existing low-rank and sparse parameterizations. Empirical evaluations across 21 NLP and CV datasets, spanning 5 model architectures, consistently validate the effectiveness of ToPA.
authors: Sicong Li, Qianqian Xu, Zhiyong Yang, Zitai Wang, Longtao Huang, Xiaochun Cao, Qingming Huang
bullets: Low-rank PEFT restricts update rank, while sparse methods limit connectivity and flexibility.
ToPA replaces long products of standard Toeplitz matrices with shorter products of higher-capacity block-wise Toeplitz factors.
Theoretical analysis shows these products can approximate arbitrary matrices with shorter chains.
Experiments across 21 NLP and computer-vision datasets and 5 model architectures consistently support ToPA’s effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Block-wise Toeplitz parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces adaptation cost while improving expressivity; relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: ToPA: Block-wise Toeplitz Adaptation for Expressive and Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: ToPA uses block-wise Toeplitz parameterizations to make parameter-efficient fine-tuning more expressive and stable than conventional low-rank or sparse updates.

papers.abstract: Tree search enhances multi-step reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet prevailing methods expand every step with a fixed budget, irrespective of the marginal utility of expansion. We first show, across existing search algorithms, that continuations sampled from a shared intermediate state are largely duplicates and collapse to a few distinct answers. Critically, we find that the semantic dispersion of sibling actions predicts the redundancy of their downstream continuations, permitting a subtree's budget to be fixed before expansion. An information-theoretic analysis motivates this: treating the per-step budget as the Monte Carlo sample size for estimating a step's residual answer entropy, we derive a sufficient budget that shrinks with sibling dispersion. We accordingly propose $\textbf{Uncertainty-Aware Allocation}$ (UAA), a training-free framework that decouples value from uncertainty: values determine which candidates are promising, while uncertainty, estimated from sibling dispersion at no additional model cost, determines how many merit expansion, via uncertainty-aware pruning and uncertainty-aware budgeting. Across mathematical reasoning, logical reasoning, and planning benchmarks, UAA reduces token usage by up to $90\%$ and latency by up to $9\times$ at comparable accuracy, generalizing across four tree search algorithms and both open- and closed-source LLMs.
authors: Jianguo Huang, Zhiyi Lyu, Fuxiang Zhang, Yanchen Deng, Deheng Ye, Bo An
bullets: Sibling continuations from the same intermediate state are often redundant and collapse to a few distinct answers.
Semantic dispersion among sibling actions predicts downstream redundancy and can estimate uncertainty before subtree expansion.
UAA is training-free and separates candidate value from uncertainty: value selects promising candidates, while uncertainty controls pruning and expansion budgets.
Across reasoning and planning benchmarks, UAA reduces token use by up to 90% and latency by up to 9× at comparable accuracy.
The framework generalizes across four tree-search algorithms and both open- and closed-source LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-aware budget allocation reduces token usage and latency in LLM tree search; fits efficient AI and LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Budget Allocation for Efficient LLM Tree Search
papers.tldr: UAA makes LLM tree search more efficient by allocating expansion budgets according to sibling-action uncertainty rather than using a fixed budget at every step.

papers.abstract: Speed-limit sign recognition on an automotive camera system-on-chip (SoC) must fit a detector and a classifier (the reader) into the memory, arithmetic, and energy budgets of the device. In our two-stage recognizer, the detector, a YOLO-family network with ReLU and hard-sigmoid operators, is compressed by channel replay: an iterative pruning cascade identifies the channels to remove, the recorded deletions are replayed on the original task-trained network, the parent, and one continuous knowledge-distillation recovery follows. On a YOLOv5n, replay removes 60.3% of the parameters at the accuracy of the parent and, in validation mAP50-95 over five matched seeds, outperforms iterative pruning and training from scratch, and its per-step variant (per-step replay) is the most accurate pruning method. On a YOLOv8n, replay and per-step replay outperform every other method and the unpruned parent. The reader, a five-layer CNN with 18k parameters, and the post-processing of the YOLOv5n and YOLOv8n heads use integer arithmetic only. With 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations (W4A8), the reader matches FP32 accuracy in 12.1 KB of on-chip memory, and an executable streaming model reproduces the INT8 class predictions of its runtime on all 9,850 test crops. On a Jetson AGX Orin, INT8 is faster than FP16 only in the implicit formulation of TensorRT, and the replay detector runs fastest on the deep-learning accelerator (DLA). Trained on public data only, the combined system of 0.72 M parameters recognizes 95.2% of the signs of a held-out automotive camera at 90% precision and 94 frames per second.
authors: Se Un Park, Kyungkeon Chung, Huigeol Kim, Junyoung Park
bullets: Channel replay removes 60.3% of YOLOv5n parameters while maintaining parent accuracy; replay variants outperform competing pruning methods on YOLOv5n and YOLOv8n.
A five-layer, 18k-parameter reader achieves FP32-equivalent accuracy with 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations in 12.1 KB of on-chip memory.
Integer-only post-processing and reader inference support executable streaming deployment, reproducing runtime INT8 predictions on all 9,850 test crops.
The combined 0.72M-parameter system reaches 95.2% sign recognition at 90% precision and 94 frames per second on a held-out automotive camera.
On Jetson AGX Orin, INT8 is faster than FP16 only for TensorRT’s implicit formulation; replay detection runs fastest on the DLA.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes replay pruning and few-bit integer inference for hardware-efficient speed-sign recognition, relevant to Efficient AI.
papers.title: Replay Pruning and Few-Bit Integer Inference for Hardware-Efficient Speed-Sign Recognition
papers.tldr: A replay-pruned detector and few-bit integer reader enable accurate, real-time speed-sign recognition within automotive SoC memory and compute constraints.

papers.abstract: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming $k$-PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3\% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132.
authors: Xinyu Luo, Jincheng Zhou, Mengbo Wang, Zilin Shen, Nadia Atallah Lanman, Petros Drineas, Bruno Ribeiro, Brian Bullins
bullets: Targets the stale-subspace problem in gradient-projecting low-rank optimizers such as GaLore.
Uses an Oja++-inspired streaming $k$-PCA algorithm for frequent, on-the-fly tracking of principal gradient directions.
Reduces the performance gap to full-rank optimization by up to 69.3% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task.
Achieves the best performance in 10 of 16 RoBERTa-Base fine-tuning scenarios.
Designed for stringent low-rank constraints with low per-step tracking cost.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming low-rank gradient subspace tracking reduces LLM training memory.
papers.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
papers.tldr: Ori tracks slowly drifting gradient subspaces online with streaming $k$-PCA, improving very low-rank LLM training toward full-rank accuracy.

papers.abstract: Standard autoregressive decoding advances one token at a time, even when several upcoming tokens can be predicted together. We propose CADENCE (Context-Adaptive DEcoding), a generation method that learns both what to draft and how far to draft. Gaussian prediction heads represent future spans as continuous latent vectors, and a shared decoder converts the selected vector into token predictions in parallel. A learned router selects the prediction length from the model's own hidden states and predicted Gaussian parameters, adapting generation granularity to the current context with single-token generation as a fallback. The backbone verifies each proposed continuation and retains the prefix that matches its greedy predictions. Experiments with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on Alpaca, GSM8K, and HumanEval show that router-selected positions yield higher draft acceptance than applying the corresponding prediction length everywhere. CADENCE achieves up to 1.3x higher generation throughput than standard greedy decoding.
authors: Sai Sreenivas Chintha, Chidera Biringa, Rishab Sharma, Anusha Agrawal, Prachi Badarayani, Gemma Zhang, Nigel Boachie Kumankumah, Marco Ayala, Sulaiman Vesal
bullets: Standard decoding generates one token at a time despite predictable multi-token continuations.
Gaussian prediction heads encode future spans as continuous latent vectors, which a shared decoder converts into parallel token predictions.
A learned router selects the draft length from hidden states and Gaussian parameters, with single-token decoding as a fallback.
The backbone verifies drafts and keeps the prefix matching its greedy predictions.
On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across Alpaca, GSM8K, and HumanEval, CADENCE achieves up to 1.3× higher throughput than greedy decoding; adaptive routing also improves draft acceptance over fixed lengths.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive decoding length improves LLM generation throughput.
papers.title: Next Token or Vector? Learning How Far to Decode
papers.tldr: CADENCE accelerates autoregressive generation by adaptively choosing how many future tokens to draft and verify at each step.

papers.abstract: Scale calibration learns an update for one model representation. We study how much of that update can be reused by another representation of the same pretrained model. Our transfer procedure extracts positive group-wise gains and installs them in the recipient's weights or native quantization scales without recipient-side optimization. On a quantized recipient, it preserves integer codes, zero points and storage layout. For a Qwen3-1.7B floating-point/GPTQ INT3 pair, bidirectional transfer retains 76.9-90.5% of the text-loss improvement from recipient-specific calibration on fresh WikiText and C4 cohorts excluded from project development. Shuffling the same gain values within each projection worsens both recipients, showing that their learned group assignment matters after transfer. A Llama-3.2-3B control keeps the initial native tensors at all four calibrated projections identical and changes nine projections elsewhere. Cross-installation retains 98.6-99.3% of the text-calibration benefit, alongside a small, resolved preference for each recipient's own gain. These results quantify both the adaptation carried by a reusable calibration update and the remaining benefit of recipient-specific training.
bullets: Problem: Determine whether calibration updates learned for one model representation can be reused by another representation.
Method: Extract positive group-wise gains and install them into recipient weights or native quantization scales while preserving quantized codes, zero points, and storage layout.
Main result: For a Qwen3-1.7B floating-point/GPTQ INT3 pair, transfer retained 76.9–90.5% of recipient-specific text-loss improvement on held-out WikiText and C4 cohorts.
Shuffling gain values within projections degraded both recipients, indicating that learned group assignments are important.
A Llama-3.2-3B control retained 98.6–99.3% of text-calibration benefit after cross-installation, with a small remaining preference for recipient-specific gains.
papers.selection_reason: Quantization calibration transfer improves memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Reusing Calibration Gains across Model Representations
papers.tldr: Calibration gains learned for one representation can be transferred to another representation of the same pretrained model, preserving most of recipient-specific calibration benefits without recipient-side optimization.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) for visual question answering (VQA) often pass long visual-token sequences to the language model, making visual-token pruning attractive but risky for medical images, where answers may depend on localized boundary and texture evidence. We study training free pre-decoding pruning and treat pruning as a subspace stable evidence preservation problem. The retained tokens should remain close to the dominant visual evidence subspace induced by the full token set. To this end, we propose \emph{Subspace-Transition Token Pruning} (\method{}), which estimates each token's spectral support from principal component space and constructs a compact representation subspace. To better reflect medical image structure, \method{} further uses a bounded token-grid transition prior to promote boundary and texture sensitive tokens. We evaluate \method{} on the closed-ended SLAKE and OmniMedVQA benchmarks and on RadImageNet-VQA, which provides both closed-ended and open-ended evaluations, using Lingshu-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B backbones. \method{} delivers consistently strong performance on both the closed-ended and open-ended RadImageNet-VQA evaluations. These results show that \method{} is an effective training free pruning framework for medical domain VQA.
authors: Mengchen Fan, Qizhen Lan, Xi Xiao, Lin Zhao, Liang He, Tianyang Wang, Xiaoqian Jiang, Pulin Che, Baocheng Geng
bullets: Medical VQA often uses long visual-token sequences, but pruning can remove localized evidence needed for accurate answers.
MedSTP estimates tokens’ support in principal-component space to preserve the dominant visual evidence subspace.
A bounded token-grid transition prior promotes tokens capturing medical-image boundaries and textures.
Evaluated on SLAKE, OmniMedVQA, and RadImageNet-VQA with Lingshu-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B.
It shows consistently strong performance on both closed- and open-ended RadImageNet-VQA evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses token pruning in medical VLMs using subspace stability, directly relevant to Multimodal Foundation Models and Efficient AI.
papers.title: MedSTP: Preserving Subspace and Transition Evidence for Medical VQA Token Pruning
papers.tldr: MedSTP is a training-free medical VQA token-pruning method that preserves dominant visual evidence while retaining boundary- and texture-sensitive tokens.

papers.abstract: Advances in frontier coding agents have sharply increased the token costs of AI-assisted software engineering. Their token efficiency is typically evaluated on isolated tasks, whereas real-world developers use them to continuously build, update, and maintain large-scale projects. This mismatch motivates us to evaluate agents over sequences of realistic coding tasks, where we find that agents exhibit recurring environment-dependent token costs that existing methods struggle to reduce. To minimize these costs, we introduce TokenEconomizer, an external controller that cuts environment-specific token costs over a sequence of tasks. These cuts come from determining (i) which operational micro-skills to inject, (ii) which persistently irrelevant tools to prune, and (iii) when to intervene in unproductive failure loops. Across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI paired with frontier models, TokenEconomizer reduces the average token cost by 18.4-30.9% with comparable task success. Savings hold in every repository under every tested agent-model setting and generalize to diverse domains such as sequential web development and security auditing, where costs fall by 6.4-21.2% depending on task structure. Our work establishes adaptive black-box cost control as a promising direction for reducing token costs of coding agents in realistic settings.
authors: Aaron J. Li, Weijia Xu, Chandan Singh, Zixiao Chen, Jeevana Priya Inala, Charlotte Siska, Acar Tamersoy, Bin Yu, Ion Stoica, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao
bullets: Evaluates agents on continuous, multi-task development and maintenance workflows rather than isolated tasks.
Uses an external black-box controller to inject useful operational micro-skills, prune persistently irrelevant tools, and interrupt unproductive failure loops.
Reduces average token costs by 18.4–30.9% across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI with frontier models, with savings reported for every tested repository and agent-model setting.
Generalizes to sequential web development and security auditing, yielding cost reductions of 6.4–21.2% depending on task structure.
The approach targets environment-dependent recurring costs and is evaluated within the tested agents, repositories, and domains.
papers.selection_reason: Black-box token cost control for coding agents, reducing compute cost under Efficient AI.
papers.title: TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents
papers.tldr: TokenEconomizer adaptively reduces coding-agent token costs across sequences of realistic software-engineering tasks while maintaining comparable success.

papers.abstract: Augmenting softmax attention with forget gates typically relies on summing decay contributions along the key--query path. Because such accumulation is monotonic, these mechanisms cannot selectively erase intermediate context while preserving older, structurally relevant tokens. We propose First Passage Attention (FPA), which shifts from path summation to path extrema by lowering a key's logit proportionally to the deepest dip of a learned scalar field below that key's level over the intervening span. FPA encompasses the Forgetting Transformer (FoX) as a special case, and when the field and levels follow a shared learned walk, the alive keys with unpenalised logits naturally form a stack. We show that a constant-dimension FPA head realises any subset of keys left alive by subsequent dips, whereas softmax heads with positional biases or token-level forget gates require a head dimension linear in the number of keys. In synthetic experiments, one-layer FPA heads converge to these target sets while comparable softmax and FoX baselines fail on every seed. Scaling to a 110M-parameter language model, FPA matches FoX in perplexity and uniquely achieves perfect passkey retrieval at $8\times$ the training length, even with its key--value cache compressed to about $25\%$.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of monotonic decay mechanisms that cannot erase intermediate tokens selectively.
Uses path extrema: logits are penalized according to the deepest dip of a learned scalar field across the key–query span.
Includes the Forgetting Transformer as a special case; under a shared learned walk, unpenalized keys form a stack.
A constant-dimensional FPA head can realize arbitrary subsets of surviving keys, unlike comparable softmax-based mechanisms requiring dimension linear in key count.
In experiments, FPA converges to target key sets, matches FoX perplexity, and achieves perfect passkey retrieval at 8× training length with a cache compressed to about 25%.
papers.selection_reason: Novel attention mechanism with forget gates and KV cache compression, directly relevant to efficient attention and memory.
papers.title: First Passage Attention
papers.tldr: First Passage Attention enables selective forgetting of intermediate context while preserving older relevant tokens, outperforming comparable mechanisms on synthetic memory tasks and long-context passkey retrieval.

papers.abstract: Existing video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) organize observations primarily in time, but embodied spatial reasoning requires organizing them in space. Consequently, their visual representations can remain locally consistent across nearby frames while lacking a persistent spatial context that is stable across viewpoints and time. We exploit depth and camera pose, which are naturally available to embodied agents, to explicitly establish this spatial correspondence. We introduce Cambrian-BEV, which extends Cambrian-S with a parameter-free geometric tokenization scheme that back-projects visual patch features from each frame into a shared bird's-eye-view (BEV) coordinate frame and averages features that fall within the same spatial cell. Thus, observations of the same physical location, regardless of viewpoint or time step, are aggregated into a common spatial token. In addition to providing a persistent scene representation, this formulation acts as an efficient compression mechanism: 128 frames containing approximately 100K DINOv3 patch features are consolidated into a fixed 27$\times$27 grid of only 729 BEV tokens, cutting LLM prefill time by $2.9\times$ and peak memory by $3.6\times$. Cambrian-BEV requires no architectural modification beyond BEV tokenization and uses a frozen DINOv3 vision encoder with a trainable multimodal projector and LLM. On VSI-Bench, our model reaches 63.48, $+8.5$ points over an identically fine-tuned frame-token control with $12.6\times$ fewer visual tokens, with particularly large gains on room size ($+24.5$) and relative direction ($+34.1$). On ReVSI, it reaches 44.68, $+4.5$ over the corresponding control.
authors: Faizan Siddiqui, Nirav Savaliya, Sahith Reddy Chada, Enna Sachdeva
bullets: Addresses the lack of stable spatial context in video MLLMs that primarily organize observations over time.
Back-projects visual patch features using depth and camera pose into shared BEV coordinates, averaging features within spatial cells.
Compresses 128 frames and roughly 100K patch features into 729 BEV tokens without architectural changes beyond tokenization.
Reduces LLM prefill time by 2.9× and peak memory by 3.6×.
Outperforms the matched frame-token control on VSI-Bench and ReVSI, with especially strong VSI-Bench gains in room-size and relative-direction reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: BEV tokenization compresses video MLLM visual tokens while improving embodied spatial reasoning, combining spatial intelligence, token merging, and video understanding.
papers.title: Thinking from Above: Efficient Spatial Reasoning with Bird's-Eye-View Visual Tokens
papers.tldr: Cambrian-BEV improves embodied spatial reasoning by aggregating multi-view video features into a compact, persistent bird’s-eye-view representation.

papers.abstract: We study personalized LLM routing, where a router selects among heterogeneous models with different costs and capabilities. The router must minimize cumulative inference cost while ensuring reliable realized response quality, even though user preferences are unknown and must be learned from feedback during deployment. We formulate this problem as a constrained contextual bandit and develop an algorithm that learns preferences while balancing cost and quality. Under a logistic preference model and a strict-feasibility condition, we establish sublinear expected cost regret relative to an optimal stationary randomized contextual oracle and a high-probability guarantee on realized cumulative satisfaction. The framework extends beyond LLM routing to broader online model-selection problems with reliability requirements.
authors: Ameya Anjarlekar, Rasoul Etesami, R Srikant
bullets: Addresses personalized routing across heterogeneous LLMs with different costs and capabilities.
Models routing as a constrained contextual bandit with unknown preferences learned from deployment feedback.
Uses chance constraints to control realized cumulative user satisfaction, not just expected quality.
Under a logistic preference model and strict feasibility, proves sublinear expected cost regret and high-probability satisfaction guarantees.
Applies more broadly to online model selection with reliability requirements.
papers.selection_reason: Cost-aware LLM routing with reliability constraints reduces inference cost.
papers.title: Chance-Constrained Personalized LLM Routing with Online Preference Learning
papers.tldr: An online contextual-bandit router learns user preferences to minimize LLM inference costs while maintaining reliable response quality.

papers.abstract: The training loss of binary and ternary neural networks, expanded as a multilinear polynomial over the discrete weights, is structurally equivalent to the energy of a hierarchical high-order Ising model. We exploit this equivalence to apply Ising solvers to discrete-weight network training, while accounting for a fundamental difference in objectives: an Ising solver seeks the ground state of a fixed energy function, whereas training seeks solutions that generalize to unseen data. Our key contribution is $\Sigma\Delta$-Sampler, an optimizer that reconciles these objectives by embedding a stochastic sampling-and-annealing step as a noisy quantizer inside a first-order $\Sigma\Delta$ noise-shaping loop. The loop pushes noise from weight quantization, high-order frustration, and mini-batch sampling out of the low-frequency adaptation band, so that discrete weight updates follow the smooth descent trajectories embedded in the rugged loss landscape. We validate the framework on a planted quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) benchmark with a known minimizer; on CIFAR-10, where a $13$M-parameter ternary model comes within $1\%$ of full-precision accuracy; on ImageNet-1k, where a ternary ResNet-18 comes within $0.4\%$ Top-5 accuracy of a ternary baseline; on class-incremental continual learning, where prior-task accuracy is preserved; and on MatMul-free language models up to $2.7$B parameters, where it outperforms a straight-through-estimator baseline under matched continued pre-training. Compared with standard quantization-aware training, $\Sigma\Delta$-Sampler reduces the training memory footprint by over $50\%$, delivers an order-of-magnitude speed-up, and reduces weight-update memory traffic by four orders of magnitude, making it attractive for on-device training and fine-tuning of large binary and ternary models.
authors: Zihao Chen, Zhili Xiao, Rui-Jie Zhu, Yipeng Wang, Jason Eshraghian, Shantanu Chakrabartty
bullets: Recasts discrete-weight training as hierarchical high-order Ising optimization while accounting for the need to generalize beyond a fixed ground state.
Uses a noisy stochastic quantizer within a first-order ΣΔ loop to suppress quantization, frustration, and mini-batch noise from the adaptation band.
Validated on QUBO, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1k, continual learning, and MatMul-free language models up to 2.7B parameters.
Reports competitive accuracy, including near-full-precision CIFAR-10 performance and close ImageNet-1k ternary-baseline performance.
Compared with standard quantization-aware training, reduces training memory by over 50%, speeds training by 10×, and cuts weight-update traffic by 10,000×.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient on-device training of binary/ternary models with large memory and speed reductions.
papers.title: Noise-shaped Sampling and Annealing for Scalable On-the-edge Training of Binary and Ternary AI Models
papers.tldr: ΣΔ-Sampler enables scalable on-device training of binary and ternary neural networks by combining stochastic annealing with ΣΔ noise shaping to make discrete updates follow smooth optimization trajectories.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) promise parallel text generation, but in practice face an unresolved speed-quality trade-off. Exact decoding fills in only one masked position per model pass, while faster multi-token decoding schemes are lossy. Speculative decoding is the standard lossless acceleration for autoregressive models. However, it does not transfer directly to DLMs, which must choose both what to generate and where. We show that this order is the missing piece: the model's own predictions from the previous pass already give the right token at 92-100% of positions, but not which position comes next. Based on this observation, we introduce Speculating Positions Order Trajectory (SPOT), which learns to predict this order. A 0.62M-parameter model reads only the target's output distributions and proposes a tree of candidate continuations, and the target verifies all of them in a single pass by checking whether each equals its own next state. On the verification side, our analysis shows that prior block-diffusion verification approaches either assume $T=0$ or a sequential proposal interface. To support tree-based speculation at any temperature, we propose using coupled-noise match verification for diffusion blocks, following shared-Gumbel-noise coupling approaches. Our comprehensive experiments show that SPOT cuts target passes by up to 6.8x and reaches up to 3.2x the throughput of standard decoding, beating the calibrated and training-free drafting baselines in every task and budget at $T=0$ and $T=1$. In addition, we show that the learned drafter transfers across models, demonstrating successful transfer across six different DLMs. Project page: https://eliezer318.github.io/SPOT-dLLM/
authors: Eliezer Shlomi, Eliron Rahimi, Avi Mendelson, Chaim Baskin
bullets: DLMs must decide both what token to generate and which position to commit, limiting direct transfer of autoregressive speculative decoding.
SPOT uses a 0.62M-parameter drafter that reads target output distributions and predicts candidate commit-order trajectories.
A single target pass verifies the proposed tree using coupled-noise matching, supporting diffusion blocks at arbitrary temperatures.
Experiments report up to 6.8× fewer target passes and up to 3.2× higher throughput than standard decoding.
The learned drafter transfers across six different diffusion language models and outperforms calibrated and training-free baselines across tested tasks and budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Speculative decoding for diffusion language models via commit-order prediction, reducing target passes and improving throughput; fits efficient inference.
papers.title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
papers.tldr: SPOT accelerates diffusion language model decoding by predicting the order in which positions should be committed, enabling lossless tree-based speculation and up to 3.2× higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Distributed Transformer inference across co-located edge devices is fundamentally communication-bound, as exchanging activations between sequence-parallel partitions dominates inference latency under commodity edge bandwidths. Existing compression schemes reduce this cost but retain a structural bottleneck: the received data must still undergo key/value projection before attention can proceed, serializing computation behind communication. This paper presents Transformer Residual Activation Codebook Encoding (Trace), a framework that addresses these limitations. Trace places a Vector Quantizer (VQ) at the post-attention residual of every Transformer layer and precomputes codebook-indexed key/value representations. During inference, exchanged activations are encoded into compact codebook indices, allowing receivers to directly recover keys and values through table lookup instead of executing the downstream computations required to derive them. By eliminating the received data downstream computation, Trace enables communication--computation overlap and reduces a key latency bottleneck in distributed Transformer inference. A hierarchical clustering further structures the learned codebook into a multi-resolution hierarchy, enabling runtime adaptation of the communication bitrate without retraining. The framework supports two operating variants: one prioritizing accuracy and the other balancing accuracy and efficiency through buffer-compatible quantization.
