Experiments on ViT-Base (ImageNet-1K and CIFAR-100) and ViViT-B (UCF-101) show that Trace achieves up to 1.89% higher accuracy and up to 1.27x end-to-end inference speedup compared with the state-of-the-art VQ-based distributed inference framework. Compared with uncompressed sequence-parallel inference, Trace reduces communication overhead by up to 22,624x.
authors: Muhammad Azlan Qazi, Alexandros Iosifidis, Qi Zhang
bullets: Targets communication-bound inference across sequence-parallel edge devices, where activation exchange dominates latency.
Places a vector quantizer after attention and precomputes codebook-indexed key/value representations for direct receiver-side lookup.
Enables communication–computation overlap and runtime bitrate adaptation through a hierarchical multi-resolution codebook.
Offers accuracy-focused and buffer-compatible accuracy–efficiency variants without retraining for bitrate changes.
Experiments report up to 1.27× end-to-end speedup, 1.89% higher accuracy than a VQ-based baseline, and 22,624× lower communication overhead than uncompressed inference.
papers.selection_reason: Codebook-based activation compression and communication-computation overlap for distributed transformer inference, reducing latency and communication overhead in efficient AI.
papers.title: TRACE: Transformer Residual Activation Codebook Encoding for Communication-efficient Distributed Edge Inference
papers.tldr: TRACE accelerates distributed Transformer inference by encoding residual activations into codebook indices that directly reconstruct attention keys/values, reducing communication and avoiding downstream computation bottlenecks.

papers.abstract: In a small language model the vocabulary is the single largest part. In Gemma 3 270M the embedding table holds 168M of 268M parameters, and because quantisation methods leave the embedding in 16-bit, it is also most of the file once the rest of the model is compressed. We ask what that table actually buys. We replace it with one frozen table of 512-bit codes, 16 MB, with no trainable parameters, derived once from a pretrained embedding by principal-component projection and sign binarisation, and we train the same Gemma-shaped body from scratch on the same 2.05B tokens with and without it. The learned table buys 0.20 nats of validation loss for 2.6 times the trainable parameters, but on LAMBADA, HellaSwag and PIQA the frozen-table model is better or tied; only ARC-Easy favours the learned table. With a ternary BitNet b1.58 body the whole model is a 46 MB file, still ties the float model on LAMBADA and PIQA, and on a laptop CPU generates 615 to 740 tokens per second in 62 MB of memory, five to six times the speed of the float model's 8-bit GGUF in llama.cpp at a seventh of the memory. The frozen table wins by 1.7 to 2.3 nats on rare words, accepts 10,000 new words after training with a 3% cost where the learned table collapses by 43%, and all of it is released with the weights, the data and every evaluation answer.
bullets: Learned embeddings improve validation loss by 0.20 nats but require 2.6× more trainable parameters.
The frozen-table model is better or tied on LAMBADA, HellaSwag, and PIQA; ARC-Easy favors learned embeddings.
Combined with a ternary BitNet b1.58 body, the model is 46 MB and generates 615–740 tokens/s on a laptop CPU.
The frozen table performs 1.7–2.3 nats better on rare words and supports 10,000 new words with only a 3% cost.
Scope: results target small Gemma-shaped and ternary models, with the table derived from a pretrained embedding via PCA and sign binarization.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces language model memory via frozen embedding table, relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Embeddings Are Overpriced? A Frozen 16 MB Vocabulary for Small and Ternary Language Models
papers.tldr: A frozen 16 MB binary vocabulary can replace a large learned embedding table in small and ternary language models with competitive evaluation performance and much lower memory use.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems communicate in text, which is lossy and wasteful: the sender throws away the reading it already did. A growing literature instead transmits the KV cache, the natural carrier of that reading. We study the most appealing form of the idea: both models stay frozen and the sender's cache is substituted for the reader's with nothing trained. It does not work, and the obstruction belongs to the reader. A frozen transformer reads only caches close to the one it would have written itself, a region we call its tolerable set. We show that geometric similarity to that cache does not predict whether the reader can use it, and the failure is not gradual, so a more faithful substitute is not the remedy it appears to be. We explain this phenomenon with competitive attention. Experimentally, we test eight diverse substitution methods against two measured anchors: an uninformative cache baseline and the reader's own accuracy from having read the passage. All sit at the baseline. That turns a long tail of separate negative results into one outcome with a stated condition for overturning it. A different design does work: if the reader keeps its own cache and attends over the sender's as extra context, adapting only its queries, it beats its own baseline, and also clears the baseline with eight senders pooled where undirected attention over the same union falls below it. We offer this as a characterization on one probe, not a leaderboard claim. Our central contribution is a redirection: pursuing faithful substitute caches is the wrong target; adding a cache to what the reader already has is the promising one.
bullets: The study examines training-free KV-cache substitution between frozen LLMs as a less lossy alternative to text communication.
Readers only tolerate caches near those they would have produced themselves, but geometric similarity does not predict usability and failure is abrupt rather than gradual.
Competitive attention is offered as an explanation for why more faithful cache substitutes do not solve the problem.
Eight substitution methods perform at the uninformative-cache baseline, while a query-adaptation design that preserves the reader’s cache exceeds its own baseline in the reported probe.
The authors characterize this as a redirection from replacing reader caches to augmenting them with sender caches, not as a broad leaderboard claim.
papers.selection_reason: Studies KV cache substitution and cache-augmented inference in LLM systems, directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Close Enough is Nowhere Near: Fidelity-Consumability Decoupling in KV Caches
papers.tldr: Frozen readers cannot reliably use substituted sender KV caches, even when those caches are geometrically similar; retaining the reader’s cache and adding the sender’s as context is more promising.

papers.abstract: Reducing radiation exposure in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is important for patient safety; however, ultra-low-dose imaging suffers from severe noise, which may affect diagnostic interpretation without appropriate image enhancement. While current 3D deep generative models, particularly diffusion models, have shown strong reconstruction fidelity, their practical use can be limited by long inference times. In contrast, faster 2D-based alternatives may have difficulty maintaining volumetric consistency, an important consideration for whole-body PET imaging analysis. To bridge this gap, we propose a one-pass conditional 3D rectified flow (3D Flow) framework for whole-body PET image denoising that incorporates a novel optimized non-uniform sampling strategy. The model is trained with a one-pass linear-interpolant velocity-matching objective. This approach reconstructs a full 3D volume in approximately 30 seconds in our implementation, compared with multi-hour inference for the evaluated 3D DDPM baseline. Evaluations including zero-shot transfer to an independent clinical dataset show that our model achieves favorable global image quality and lesion conspicuity compared with the evaluated 3D DDPM and DDIM baselines, including on challenging short-acquisition data. Furthermore, the proposed method shows promising zero-shot transfer performance across the evaluated datasets and unseen dose levels (down to 1/100 of the standard dose), with artifact-focused visual comparisons supporting the need for further lesion-level validation. By balancing reconstruction fidelity and computational efficiency, this work presents a candidate approach for ultra-low-dose whole-body PET image denoising.
bullets: Targets severe noise from ultra-low-dose PET to support safer imaging.
Uses conditional 3D rectified flow with a one-pass velocity-matching objective and optimized non-uniform sampling.
Reconstructs a full 3D volume in approximately 30 seconds in the reported implementation, versus multi-hour inference for the evaluated 3D DDPM.
Shows favorable global quality and lesion conspicuity against evaluated 3D DDPM and DDIM baselines, including short-acquisition data.
Demonstrates promising zero-shot transfer across evaluated datasets and unseen dose levels down to 1/100 of standard dose; lesion-level validation remains needed.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces an efficient 3D rectified flow model for PET image denoising, addressing both 3D reconstruction and computational efficiency.
papers.title: Efficient 3D Whole-Body PET Image Denoising via Conditional Rectified Flow With Optimized Sampling Strategy
papers.tldr: A one-pass conditional 3D rectified-flow model enables efficient whole-body PET denoising while preserving volumetric image quality and lesion conspicuity at ultra-low doses.

papers.abstract: Token merging has emerged as an effective training-free strategy for accelerating diffusion models by reducing redundant token computation while minimizing generation degradation. A key challenge is determining which tokens can be safely merged and which should be preserved for subsequent computation. Existing method addresses this by preserving prompt-aligned foreground regions, thereby protecting semantically relevant structures. However, this text-relevance criterion overlooks background objects, local details that are not explicitly mentioned in the prompt, leading to degraded structural coherence. In this work, we propose Dynamics-aware Token Merging (DaTMe), a training-free framework that grounds token merging in the underlying diffusion dynamics. Our key insight is that token importance should reflect whether a token remains unresolved during denoising and whether it carries structural information. To this end, DaTMe constructs a dynamics- aware importance map from the Tweedie denoised estimate. The map combines a temporal signal, measuring inter-step changes in the predicted clean image, with a structural signal, capturing local high-frequency content such as boundaries and fine details. Using this map, DaTMe adaptively assigns tokens into merging roles under a given compression ratio: important tokens are preserved as anchors, while tokens that are both temporally stabilized and structurally homogeneous are selected as safe merge candidates. Experiments on PixArt-a and FLUX demonstrate that DaTMe maintains visual fidelity across the entire image, highlighting diffusion dynamics as an effective token-level merging decision in efficient generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/SeungJuCha/DaTMe.
authors: SeungJu Cha, Ye-Chan Kim, HyunGee Kim, Sungho Koh, Dong-Jin Kim
bullets: Existing token-merging methods prioritize prompt-aligned foregrounds but may lose unmentioned background objects and local details.
DaTMe is a training-free framework that builds token-importance maps from Tweedie denoised estimates.
Its map combines temporal changes across denoising steps with local high-frequency structure such as boundaries and fine details.
Important or unresolved tokens are preserved as anchors, while temporally stable and structurally homogeneous tokens are merged.
Experiments on PixArt-a and FLUX show maintained visual fidelity under compression.
papers.selection_reason: Dynamics-aware token merging for diffusion generation; fits token pruning/merging efficiency.
papers.title: Which Tokens to Merge? Diffusion Dynamics for Efficient Image Generation
papers.tldr: DaTMe accelerates diffusion image generation by merging tokens according to denoising dynamics and structural importance, preserving visual fidelity across the image.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow models generate a sample over iterative steps, each a full pass through a large network, and that pass dominates generation cost. Training-free caching accelerates them by reusing activations from recent evaluations instead of recomputing them. Dynamic caching methods decide when to refresh by accumulating a cheap probe of the network input into a staleness signal and spending a fresh evaluation once it crosses a threshold. They perform hard caching: the signal is a binary switch between refresh and reuse, and every step, fresh or cached, advances by the prescribed step size. We observe that the signal carries much more than this switch. How far it sits below the threshold, its headroom, predicts the error induced by reuse. We propose SoftCache, which performs soft caching: instead of a binary switch, the headroom sets how far each cached step goes. Where the headroom is large, the sampler jumps past several scheduled nodes, and as a refresh nears, its steps shrink back toward the original step. These adaptive jumps may land between the scheduled nodes, taking the sampler off its fixed grid. SoftCache requires no training and adds no per-backbone settings: on FLUX for images and on HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 for video, at speedups from $3.5\times$ to $6.9\times$, it is ahead of every baseline on all four fidelity metrics.
authors: Shimon Malnick, Nadav Orenstein, Ohad Fried, Shai Avidan
bullets: Dynamic caching traditionally makes a binary refresh-versus-reuse decision at fixed step sizes.
SoftCache converts the staleness signal’s headroom into adaptive step sizes: larger headroom enables longer jumps, while refreshes restore smaller steps.
Adaptive jumps can move the sampler between the original scheduled nodes rather than remaining on a fixed grid.
Evaluated on FLUX, HunyuanVideo, and Wan2.1, SoftCache achieves 3.5×–6.9× speedups and leads baselines on all four reported fidelity metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive step-size caching for diffusion transformers; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: SoftCache: Adaptive Step Size Caching for Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: SoftCache accelerates diffusion and flow-model sampling by using cache staleness headroom to adaptively skip and shrink steps without training or backbone-specific tuning.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video generators enable streaming generation, yet they run every token through the final denoising step, regardless of how much refinement it needs. We find this uniform computation is often unnecessary: many tokens already closely match their eventual full-step outputs in the initial steps, while others require refinement until the end. We introduce Speculative Forcing, a framework that treats intermediate clean estimates as drafts and predicts when individual tokens can be safely accepted early. Once accepted, a token is frozen as its final output and undergoes no further denoising, while its cached keys and values remain available as context for the remaining tokens. We explore two alternative verifier designs: a training-free one based on similarity to clean content and stability across steps, and a learned one that reads the frozen generator's intermediate features to estimate each token's remaining gap to its full-step output. Across short-video, long-video, and world generation, Speculative Forcing preserves the quality of full-step sampling while substantially reducing computation. On LongLive, it matches the four-step generator with ~1.7 denoising steps per token, running over 1.5x faster at 41.7 and 37.8 fps. On Lingbot-World 2.0, where camera motion continually changes the visible content, it maintains quality with ~2.5 denoising steps per token and runs 1.35x faster at 24.5 fps.
authors: Hyunwook Choi, Seungryong Kim, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun
bullets: Uniformly denoising every token to the final step wastes computation because some tokens stabilize early.
The method treats intermediate clean estimates as drafts and uses verifiers to decide when tokens can be accepted and frozen.
Frozen tokens stop denoising while their cached keys and values remain available as context for later tokens.
Two verifiers are explored: a training-free similarity-and-stability test and a learned feature-based predictor of remaining error.
It preserves full-step quality while reducing computation, achieving over 1.5× speedup on LongLive and 1.35× on Lingbot-World 2.0.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient early token acceptance for autoregressive video generation; fits efficient AI and autoregressive video models.
papers.title: Speculative Forcing for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.tldr: Speculative Forcing accelerates autoregressive video generation by safely freezing tokens once their intermediate predictions are sufficiently accurate.

papers.abstract: Computer-use agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks, where running a frontier model at every step is expensive and a small open-weight model alone often fails. Weak-to-strong escalation offers a middle ground where a weak agent acts by default and hands control to a strong one only when needed. The core challenge is deciding when to escalate, which requires an uncertainty signal cheap enough to check at every step. However, even after handoff, the strong agent can still get lost, but a black-box API that the strong agent is usually served exposes no internals to monitor. To this end, we propose LEASH, a training-free framework that unleashes the strong agent only when the weak agent's latent uncertainty signals it is needed, and keeps it on a leash afterward. LEASH has three layers: (1) initial task uncertainty for early routing, (2) step-level uncertainty for runtime escalation, and, after handoff, (3) a shadow observer for continued oversight of the strong black-box agent. Here, we use latent uncertainty as a fuel for all three layers. Specifically, we compare the weak model's hidden states with those from its past successful and failed trajectories, and a state that looks more like the failures signals higher uncertainty. During weak-agent execution, our uncertainty estimator reuses activations already produced during action generation, so it needs no extra forward pass or dedicated monitor training. Experiments on OSWorld across four contemporary model backbones show that LEASH consistently improves over standalone weak agents and outperforms random escalation by 6.55--11.94 points at matched escalation rates. With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, LEASH achieves 73.66% task success at $0.4117 per task, matching always-on Claude Opus 5 (72.90%) while reducing inference cost by 19.2%.
authors: Qingni Wang, Changdae Oh, Yuzhe Yang, Sharon Li, Jiachen Yang, Ang Li, Xin Eric Wang
bullets: Targets long-horizon computer-use tasks where weak agents fail and always-on strong agents are expensive.
Uses three stages: task-level routing, step-level escalation, and shadow oversight after handoff.
Estimates uncertainty by comparing weak-agent hidden states with successful and failed trajectory states, without extra forward passes or monitor training.
On OSWorld, it outperforms random escalation by 6.55–11.94 points at matched escalation rates.
With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, it reaches 73.66% success at $0.4117 per task, matching the reported always-on Claude Opus 5 success while cutting inference cost by 19.2%.
papers.selection_reason: Cost-efficient escalation for computer-use agents via uncertainty; reduces inference cost.
papers.title: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents
papers.tldr: LEASH cheaply routes computer-use tasks from weak to strong agents using latent uncertainty, then monitors the strong agent to improve success while reducing cost.

papers.abstract: Small language models are increasingly deployed on edge devices and robotic systems to meet cost and latency constraints, yet their limited capabilities can make reliable deployment challenging. Stronger models can provide assistance when needed, but deciding when to route a weak-model response to a stronger model often relies on signals of response correctness. In open-ended and agentic tasks, however, obtaining such signals can require costly ground-truth supervision that is difficult to obtain at scale. We revisit the foundations of weak-to-strong routing and ask whether routing decisions can instead be guided by signals that do not require ground-truth supervision. We first characterize the optimal weak-to-strong routing policy, while allowing for multiple weak-model responses generated through local inference. Building on this characterization, we derive a principled approximation to the optimal routing based on model-to-model comparison. In particular, we introduce a notion of model disagreement that can be measured directly from model-generated responses, without ground-truth supervision. Importantly, the approximation becomes increasingly accurate as the strong model becomes a better proxy for the ground-truth distribution. Across agentic and single-turn tasks, our approach effectively navigates the trade-off between routing cost and response accuracy without ground-truth supervision. Moreover, even when ground-truth correctness signals are available for training, disagreement-based routing can outperform methods trained directly to predict correctness
authors: Sima Noorani, Shayan Kiyani, George Pappas, Hamed Hassani
bullets: Targets reliable deployment of small models on edge and robotic systems where stronger-model calls are costly.
Characterizes the optimal weak-to-strong routing policy, including multiple locally generated weak responses.
Approximates this policy using model-to-model disagreement measured directly from generated responses.
Works without ground-truth supervision and improves as the strong model better approximates the ground-truth distribution.
Effective on agentic and single-turn tasks; can outperform correctness-prediction methods even when correctness labels are available.
papers.selection_reason: Weak-to-strong routing reduces inference cost; disagreement-based routing is a transferable efficiency technique.
papers.title: Disagreement-Guided Weak-to-Strong Routing
papers.tldr: A ground-truth-free routing method uses disagreement between weak and strong model responses to decide when escalation is worthwhile, balancing cost and accuracy across tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models present a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, but closed-loop deployment is often limited by inference efficiency: at each timestep, high-resolution, often multi-view images are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens that dominate transformer computation and latency. Token compression via attention is a natural solution but is challenging for VLA control because (1) decision-critical tokens are determined by the task, not generic visual saliency, and (2) the token budget varies substantially across steps, so static metrics and budgets waste computation or discard control-critical tokens. We introduce FastVLA, a training-free, task-aware, and temporally adaptive visual token compression framework. At each step, FastVLA scores token importance via task-to-vision attention and adaptively sets the compression rate from the importance-distribution uniformity, measured by an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration. We evaluate FastVLA on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT across LIBERO and SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot. In simulation, it reduces LLM-backbone FLOPs by 35-59\% and action latency by 9-32\% (a 1.09$\times$-1.46$\times$ speedup) while maintaining task success, achieving a comparable or better efficiency-performance trade-off than existing plug-and-play token compression/pruning/reuse baselines. On the real robot, it cuts end-to-end latency by 20\% (1.25$\times$ speedup) at comparable success. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/FastVLA.
authors: Jiuyi Xu, Chengyuan Qian, Zhengzhong Tu, Yang Sui, Yangming Shi
bullets: Targets VLA inference bottlenecks caused by hundreds of visual tokens from high-resolution, multi-view observations.
Ranks tokens using task-to-vision attention rather than generic visual saliency.
Adapts compression rates from attention-distribution uniformity using an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration.
Evaluated across OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT in LIBERO, SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot.
Reduces simulation backbone FLOPs by 35–59% and action latency by 9–32% while maintaining success; real-robot end-to-end latency drops 20% at comparable success.
papers.selection_reason: Task-aware and temporally adaptive visual token compression for efficient VLA inference, directly relevant to VLA and token pruning.
papers.title: FastVLA: Task-Conditioned and Temporally Adaptive Visual Token Compression for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: FastVLA accelerates vision-language-action robot control by selecting task-relevant visual tokens and adapting their budget over time without retraining.

papers.abstract: A perception system that must brake for a pedestrian does not need a low average latency. It must deliver an answer before the deadline on every frame, the worst case included. Commodity edge accelerators optimize the mean through dynamic scheduling, OS jitter, thermal throttling, and contention, so their per-frame latency can be measured but not bounded. We build FALCON, a camera-based 3D occupancy front-end on the AMD Kria KR260, an embedded FPGA drawing 4.3 W idle and up to 6.6 W under inference, and make the latency guarantee layered and explicit: programmable-logic (PL) compute is cycle-bounded analytically; inference is a measured envelope over 100k-frame traces; and a watchdog enforces output delivery, publishing the previous output flagged stale when a frame is late. The deadline runs use a fixed-work proxy of six ResNet-50 DPU inferences per frame, not the full occupancy network: across three 100k-frame enforced runs, all 300k proxy frames delivered an output within the 100 ms deadline plus at most 10.2 ms, the worst of the three runs. The full six-camera FlashOcc pipeline composes to about 1.3 s per frame on the board and is not yet a 10 Hz system. The two operations the DPU cannot run, a view-transform gather and a bilinear resize, become fixed-trip-count PL IPs numerically matched to their software references. On the full Occ3D-nuScenes validation set the board reaches mIoU 29.88, 92.8% of an FP32 baseline the DPU cannot run. On a ResNet-50 probe over 100k frames the KR260 tail stays within 1.5 times its median (2.0 times for the six-inference proxy), where Jetson Orin reaches 4.4 times and the worst datacenter GPU run (NVIDIA L4) 23.6 times. The deployment recipe, HLS sources, and raw timing traces are released.
authors: Haohua Que, Mingkai Liu, Handong Yao
bullets: Targets worst-case deadline compliance rather than average latency for autonomous-driving perception.
Implements unsupported view-transform gather and bilinear resize operations as numerically matched FPGA logic.
On three 100k-frame proxy runs, all 300,000 frames produced an output within the 100 ms deadline plus at most 10.2 ms.
Achieves 29.88 mIoU on the full Occ3D-nuScenes validation set, or 92.8% of the FP32 baseline.
The full six-camera FlashOcc pipeline takes about 1.3 s per frame and is not yet a 10 Hz system; deployment artifacts and timing traces are released.
papers.selection_reason: FPGA-accelerated occupancy network with worst-case latency guarantees and low-power edge inference; directly fits efficient AI and 3D perception.
papers.title: FALCON: FPGA-Accelerated Latency-Certifiable Occupancy Networks for Camera-Based Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: FALCON uses fixed-trip-count FPGA kernels, measured latency envelopes, and a watchdog to provide certifiable camera-based occupancy inference timing, though the full pipeline remains far from 10 Hz.

papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) cache management has become a critical bottleneck for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to long-context scenarios due to linear memory growth. While recent eviction methods have moved beyond simple attention-score heuristics to incorporate value representations, they typically face a fundamental trade-off: the underlying optimization for minimizing output perturbation is an NP-hard combinatorial problem, leading to mathematically suboptimal heuristics or implementations that are difficult to kernelize. In this work, we propose DropKV, a simple principled eviction framework based on Decoupled Residual-Output Perturbation. By decoupling the joint eviction decision into independent per-token scoring, DropKV circumvents combinatorial intractability and admits a provable constant-factor approximation guarantee under a cone condition that we empirically verify on three long-context LLMs. To ensure practical viability, we provide a high-performance implementation using fused Triton kernels that avoid materializing the full attention matrix, delivering a 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup that translates to up to a 9.9% matched-batch end-to-end prefill speedup. Extensive evaluations on the RULER and LongBench benchmarks demonstrate that DropKV consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines at equivalent cache budgets, achieving the lowest inference latency among eviction methods while also remaining faster than the dynamic cache baseline.
authors: Aozhong Zhang, Selcuk Gurses, Yanxia Deng, Naigang Wang, Chi-Chun Liu, Davis Wertheimer, Derrick Liu, Xin Li, Zi Yang, Felix X. -F. Ye, Penghang Yin
bullets: Targets the linear KV-cache memory growth that limits long-context LLM scaling.
Decouples residual-output perturbation into per-token scores, avoiding the underlying NP-hard combinatorial optimization.
Provides a provable constant-factor approximation under a cone condition empirically verified on three long-context LLMs.
Uses fused Triton kernels without materializing the full attention matrix, yielding a reported 19.8× scoring-kernel speedup and up to 9.9% end-to-end prefill speedup.
On RULER and LongBench, outperforms evaluated baselines at equal cache budgets and achieves the lowest reported inference latency among eviction methods.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a principled KV-cache eviction method with approximation guarantees and efficient kernels.
papers.title: DropKV: Decoupling Residual-Output Perturbation for Near-Optimal KV-Cache Eviction
papers.tldr: DropKV enables fast, near-optimal KV-cache eviction for long-context LLMs by replacing an intractable joint optimization with independently scored token decisions.

papers.abstract: Splatting-based radiance-field representations have recently gained popularity in robotic perception, enabling high-quality novel-view synthesis (NVS) through explicit scene primitives. However, existing splatting methods typically rely on iterative nonlinear optimization that jointly optimizes millions of coupled primitive parameters, resulting in substantial computation time, peak GPU memory consumption, and susceptibility to local minima. In this paper, we propose CF-Splat, a novel closed-form triangle-splatting framework for efficient scene appearance estimation over a known mesh either pre-existing or provided by upstream mapping or reconstruction pipelines. Our key insight is that, by properly formulating the problem over the given mesh geometry and calibrated cameras, the rendered pixel colors can be expressed linearly with respect to the per-vertex spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients, allowing multi-view scene appearance estimation to be formulated as a global linear least-squares (LLS) problem without the need of iterative nonlinear optimization. To guarantee a well-posed solution under uneven multi-view observation coverage, we introduce adaptive SH regularization that constrains insufficiently supported high-order SH coefficients and yields a unique global minimizer. To ensure the scalability to large-scale scenes, we develop a triangle-structured matrix-free preconditioned conjugate-gradient solver that avoids explicitly constructing the large sparse normal system while producing the same LLS solution. Experiments on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate that CF-Splat achieves competitive or superior NVS quality compared with state-of-the-art splatting methods. While, CF-Splat requires approximately 27.5-378.0 times less computation time and 1.8 times lower peak GPU memory on average than 3DGS across scenes of different scales on a consumer-grade laptop.
bullets: Targets the high computation, memory use, and local-minima susceptibility of nonlinear splatting optimization.
Represents rendered colors linearly using per-vertex spherical-harmonics coefficients over calibrated cameras and mesh geometry.
Uses adaptive SH regularization to produce a unique solution despite uneven multi-view coverage.
Employs a matrix-free, preconditioned conjugate-gradient solver for large-scale scenes without forming the normal system.
Reports competitive or better NVS quality than state-of-the-art splatting, with substantially lower computation time and lower peak GPU memory than 3DGS.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-form triangle splatting for efficient novel-view synthesis over meshes, relevant to 3D vision and computational efficiency.
papers.title: CF-Splat: Closed-Form Triangle Splatting with Mesh Priors
papers.tldr: CF-Splat replaces iterative splatting optimization with a scalable closed-form linear solve for estimating scene appearance on known meshes.

papers.abstract: Byte-level language models such as the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) run their large global model once per patch and start a patch where a small model's next-byte entropy is high. This rule rarely starts a patch at in-line computed results, such as the number after "=" in a worked solution, and accuracy on them collapses under tight patch budgets. We propose novelty patching, motivated by LZ77-style compression: start a patch where the upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the recent context. The rule is a lookup table over the previous two bytes, fitted in seconds on raw text with no labels, reference model or losses. In BLT-style models trained from scratch on a 1.9 GB math corpus at a matched ~11% patch rate (3 seeds each), it has no clear effect at 1M parameters, raises final-answer accuracy from 47% to 72% at 12M, and at 50M raises computed-result accuracy from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy from 60% to 90%; a table fitted on the raw pretraining corpus keeps the gain. Outside math the advantage shrinks: novelty lowers bits per byte on prose and ties entropy on source code and on synthetic execution traces. An analysis of where boundaries fall explains the pattern. Computed results have ordinary surprisal for the patcher's model, so surprisal-seeking rules pass over them: entropy concentrates patch starts on high-surprisal bytes most strongly of all rules (boundary enrichment 1.61) and is the worst on computed results, while the best rules sit near chance enrichment. Novelty works where new content begins at segment starts close to the computation, as in written math; a learned chunker (H-Net) finds such structure on its own, in math and in code. We also report what did not work: typed uncertainty as a training rule, switching rules after training, and a context-aware novelty predictor.
bullets: Entropy-based patching often misses inline computed results because they have ordinary surprisal for the patching model.
Novelty patching starts patches where upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the recent two-byte context, using a label-free lookup table fitted on raw text.
At 50M parameters, computed-result accuracy rises from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy from 60% to 90% at a matched ~11% patch rate.
The benefit is strongest in written math, shrinks on prose, and ties entropy on source code and synthetic execution traces.
Typed uncertainty, post-training rule switching, and a context-aware novelty predictor did not work; learned chunking finds related structure in math and code.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes compute-efficient patch selection for byte-level language models, relevant to token-level efficiency and LM architecture.
papers.title: Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute
papers.tldr: Novelty-based byte patching directs compute toward new content near mathematical computations, substantially improving computed-result and final-answer accuracy under fixed patch budgets.

papers.abstract: Recent work shows that depth recurrence can be retrofitted into pretrained language models. In this work, we adapt this paradigm for visual understanding, using depth recurrence to reduce the parameter footprint of a pretrained vision-language model (VLM). To this end, we prune layers from the language backbone of the VLM and loop over a subset of the remaining layers. At each step of the loop, a linear adapter merges the block's output with the token representations from the preceding layers and projects the fused representation back into the block. As the pruning impacts the original model performance, we propose a three-stage recovery training: first, we leverage a language-only pretraining to recover the performance of the language backbone, followed by an alignment of the vision-language projector, and a full fine-tuning of the model via visual instruction tuning. In the first and the last stage, we distill the outputs of the pretrained non-recurrent model into the recurrent model, which further improves the recovery. We evaluate the proposed approach on the TinyLLaVA-1.4B backbone without introducing any new vision-language data during retrofitting. Our experiments demonstrate that the retrofitted recurrent model outperforms the unpruned baseline trained with the same recovery data while storing 23.3% fewer language parameters. We further show that the proposed retrofitting recurrence outperforms the setup of converting a recurrent LM into a VLM on the same data. Additionally, our ablations show how design choices, such as the adapter between recurrences and a larger recurrent block, lead to the improved performance of our approach. Finally, we find that our proposed model gains on reasoning-oriented benchmarks, whereas its performance on basic visual understanding benchmarks remains on par with the baseline.
authors: Madhav Iyengar, Andreas Geiger, Hilde K\"uhne
bullets: Prunes the language backbone and repeatedly applies a subset of its layers, using linear adapters to merge representations across recurrences.
Uses three-stage recovery: language-backbone training, vision-language projector alignment, and visual instruction tuning.
Distills outputs from the original non-recurrent model during the first and final recovery stages.
On TinyLLaVA-1.4B, the retrofitted model outperforms an equally recovered unpruned baseline without adding vision-language data.
Improvements are strongest on reasoning benchmarks; basic visual understanding remains comparable to the baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces VLM parameters via recurrence, fitting both multimodal foundation models and efficiency.
papers.title: Retrofitting Recurrent Vision-Language Models from Pretrained Backbones
papers.tldr: A pretrained vision-language model can be made recurrent and 23.3% smaller in language parameters while matching or improving performance through structured recovery training and distillation.

papers.abstract: Current heterogeneity-aware training systems for large models balance workloads by assigning unequal numbers of layers across pipeline stages, a strategy aimed at equalizing execution time through a unique pipeline configuration. However, this approach fails to address critical memory constraints and suffers from inherently coarse balancing granularity. In this paper, we propose Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism (HPP), a novel approach enabling efficient and fine-grained data balance across heterogeneous pipelines. To address HPP's key challenges, prohibitive search overhead for optimal configurations and high communication overhead from asymmetric All-Reduce, we design the ETH training system. ETH employs a hierarchical workload balance framework that jointly optimizes balance across heterogeneous pipelines and within individual pipeline stages. To mitigate asymmetric communication costs, ETH implements block-wise gradient aggregation. Furthermore, it integrates specialized optimizations that dramatically reduce HPP configuration search overhead. Evaluations demonstrate ETH achieves up to 2x training speedup while reducing configuration generation overhead by up to 56x compared to state-of-the-art systems. The code is available at https://github.com/YuMJie/ETH.
authors: Mianjie Yu, Zhongmin Zhao, Zizhao Mo, Jianxiong Liao, Wenxuan Li, Yulin Qiao, Huanle Xu, Wenquan Yang, Yongqiang Yang, Zeren Li, Ruifeng Tang, Chengzhong Xu
bullets: Existing heterogeneous pipeline methods use coarse layer-count balancing and may not satisfy memory constraints.
ETH introduces Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism for data balance across and within heterogeneous pipelines.
A hierarchical balancing framework jointly optimizes inter-pipeline and intra-stage workloads.
Block-wise gradient aggregation reduces communication costs from asymmetric All-Reduce.
Evaluations report up to 2× training speedup and 56× lower configuration-generation overhead versus prior systems.
papers.selection_reason: Heterogeneous pipeline parallelism for large-model training reduces training time and configuration overhead, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: ETH: Data-Balanced Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism for Training Large Models
papers.tldr: ETH enables fine-grained workload balancing across heterogeneous pipeline configurations, achieving up to 2× faster large-model training with up to 56× lower configuration-generation overhead.

papers.abstract: Context: Organizations increasingly delegate code review to multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines billed per token. Low code quality raises human maintenance effort, but its effect on agent review cost has not been measured. Objective: We test whether baseline CodeHealth predicts the token cost of agentic review and fix beyond pull request (PR) footprint. Method: In a pre-registered observational study, we sampled 465 agent-authored PRs from 246 repositories in AIDev, jointly stratified by CodeHealth and footprint under repository caps. A frozen five-agent review-and-fix pipeline processed every PR with three different LLMs. Per LLM, we fitted a mixed model of log tokens on CodeHealth and log PR footprint, with a repository random intercept. Results: For all three LLMs the CodeHealth coefficient was negative, with 95% CI excluding zero; each CodeHealth point was associated with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost. CodeHealth was unrelated to PR footprint, so PR size does not explain the association. Two of three registered smells predicted fix cost; batch fixing left median CodeHealth unchanged. Exploratory analyses located the association in the review stage, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without writing more comments. Adjusting for the size of the scored files absorbed the association, which we interpret as mediation by file size. Conclusions: A quality metric calibrated against human maintainability also predicts the inference cost of multi-agent review and fix. The effect is modest per point and not carried by PR size, so the refactoring case extends to agent-reviewed code when it changes structure and file size, not only the score. Data Availability: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22127920
authors: Lo Gullstrand Heander, Markus Borg, Emma S\"oderberg, Christofer Rydenf\"alt
bullets: CodeHealth negatively predicted agentic review-and-fix token cost across all three tested LLMs, independent of PR footprint.
Each additional CodeHealth point corresponded to 3.5%–6.1% lower token cost.
The association appeared during review, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without producing more comments.
Adjusting for scored-file size removed the association, suggesting file size mediates the relationship.
Two registered code smells predicted fix cost, while batch fixing did not change median CodeHealth.
papers.selection_reason: Studies the token cost of agentic code review, providing empirical insights into the efficiency of LLM inference pipelines.
papers.title: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests
papers.tldr: In a pre-registered study of 465 agent-authored PRs, healthier code consistently required modestly fewer tokens for multi-agent review and fixing, largely because it involved smaller scored files.

papers.abstract: Grid foundation models (GridFMs) are graph transformers pretrained on a masked power-flow objective, and evaluate power flow orders of magnitude faster than an iterative solver. Their size, however, targets data-centre inference, whereas low-inertia operation increasingly asks for inference at the edge, next to the measurement, at batch size one and within a single synchrophasor (PMU) reporting frame. We distil a 20.1M-parameter, 12-layer GridFM teacher into a 0.62M-parameter, 6-layer student, a $32.5\times$ parameter reduction at half the message-passing depth, using an objective that combines the masked power-flow loss with output, physics-residual, latent-state and attention transfer. The physics-residual term, which matches the teacher's power-residual profile, has not previously been applied to typed power-grid graphs. We evaluate on a renewable variant of the IEEE 118-bus benchmark grid in which 26 of the conventional (synchronous) generators are replaced by inverter-based renewables with battery flexibility and standardised reactive-power limits (IEEE 1547), giving $97\,529$ physically valid (AC-OPF-feasible) operating scenarios, and we ablate all eight combinations of the transfer terms, reporting accuracy against ground truth and fidelity to the teacher separately. Distillation lowers student error on all four predicted quantities, by up to $48\%$ on active-power dispatch, and every distilled student is more accurate than its teacher on reactive-power dispatch. The gain is largely carried by the output matching term. The physics-residual term, in the layer-aggregated form used here, is consistently harmful, which we attribute to the spatial averaging it applies to a bus-level residual field. The resulting student is $32.5\times$ smaller in parameter count and has half the message-passing depth, making it a candidate for subsequent edge-device benchmarking.
authors: Vlad Alexandru S\u{a}nduleac, Shahariya Rasheed Rayamarakkarveettil Puthanpurayil, Noman Khan, Remus Teodorescu
bullets: Targets real-time, batch-size-one grid inference at the edge within a single PMU reporting frame.
Distils a 20.1M-parameter, 12-layer teacher into a 0.62M-parameter, 6-layer student using output, latent, attention, masked power-flow, and physics-residual transfer losses.
Evaluated on a renewable IEEE 118-bus variant with 97,529 AC-OPF-feasible operating scenarios and separate accuracy and teacher-fidelity analyses.
Student error decreases for all four predicted quantities, with up to 48% lower active-power dispatch error; all distilled students outperform the teacher on reactive-power dispatch.
Output matching provides most of the benefit, while layer-aggregated physics-residual matching is consistently harmful, likely due to spatial averaging of bus-level residuals.
papers.selection_reason: Distillation of a grid foundation model for real-time edge inference directly targets computation and latency reduction.
papers.title: Physics-Aware Distillation of a Grid Foundation Model for Real-Time Edge Inference
papers.tldr: Physics-aware distillation compresses a large GridFM into a 32.5× smaller student that improves power-flow prediction accuracy, though the tested physics-residual transfer term hurts performance.

papers.abstract: Aggressive quantization of neural networks can expose activation functions as bottlenecks for efficient hardware acceleration. Implementing quantized activations as multi-threshold operations has been shown to be a promising optimization, allowing for efficient hardware implementation of few-bit activations. However, current implementations are limited to monotonically increasing functions, quantization schemes with one-dimensional (per-channel) granularity and a small set of predefined activation-quantizer combinations. We formalize the multi-threshold representation to extend it to non-monotonic functions and fine-granular parameters, i.e., multi-dimensional thresholds. For automated conversion of quantized function compositions into threshold representation, we propose a systematic approach via algebraic rules integrated into the ONNX-based compiler infrastructure. We experimentally validate our solution on a selection of monotonic and non-monotonic functions by extending the binary search based multi-threshold operator that is integrated into the FINN framework for end-to-end synthesis of custom-tailored FPGA accelerators. The cost of hardware support for non-monotonicity and fine-granularity is characterized in comparison to an alternative approach utilizing existing operators via graph-level decomposition. We compare our method to prior work as well as the approach taken by the hls4ml framework. As an outlook, we demonstrate the prospects of using the multi-threshold representation during the training of a neural network as a form of quantization aware training.
authors: Christoph Berganski, Felix Jentzsch, Marco Platzner
bullets: Addresses hardware bottlenecks caused by aggressively quantized activation functions.
Formalizes multi-threshold representations for non-monotonic functions and multidimensional thresholds.
Introduces algebraic compiler rules in an ONNX-based infrastructure to automatically convert quantized function compositions.
Validates the approach on monotonic and non-monotonic functions using FINN’s binary-search multi-threshold operator and end-to-end FPGA synthesis.
Characterizes hardware costs against graph-level decomposition, prior work, and hls4ml; also explores multi-threshold representations for quantization-aware training.
papers.selection_reason: Compiling quantized activations into multi-threshold operators for custom DNN accelerators directly targets efficient AI inference on hardware.
papers.title: Compiling Multi-Threshold Operators for Quantized Non-Monotonic and Fine-Granular Activations in Custom-Tailored DNN Accelerators
papers.tldr: The paper extends multi-threshold activation compilation to support non-monotonic functions and fine-grained, multidimensional quantization for custom FPGA-based DNN accelerators.

papers.abstract: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity through selective lookup, but the full embedding table must remain available for every possible input. We introduce Conditional Program (CP), a compressed representation that reconstructs only the rows an input requests. CP represents each row by a short code and a local scale, with a reconstruction program shared across the table. We instantiate this representation with a Gaussian trellis, norm restoration and independently decodable row records. CP's two-bit code lowers output KL by 41--63\% relative to 2-bit round-to-nearest. Analysis across three trained n-gram memory families shows that Gaussian-like coordinate statistics coexist with learned relationships among rows; at matched storage budgets, the shared trellis outperforms the fitted codebooks and low-rank residual variants we test. For DeepSeek, it reduces table storage from 203GB to 51GB, leaving room for larger workloads when the table is kept on GPU.
authors: Donghoon Han, Minseop Jung, Dong Woo Kwak, SeungJae Lee, Junhoo Lee
bullets: Targets conditional memories whose full embedding table must remain available for lookup.
Encodes each row with a short code and local scale, using a shared Gaussian-trellis reconstruction program.
Adds norm restoration and independently decodable row records for practical access.
Reduces output KL by 41–63% versus 2-bit round-to-nearest quantization.
Cuts DeepSeek table storage from 203GB to 51GB, enabling larger GPU-resident workloads.
papers.selection_reason: Quantizes large LLM n-gram lookup tables with compressed reconstructable codes, drastically reducing model memory footprint while preserving output quality.
papers.title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Conditional Program compresses language-model lookup tables to two bits per value while reconstructing requested rows on demand, substantially reducing storage and quantization error.

papers.abstract: Weight quantization below four bits shrinks memory and bandwidth at a perplexity that looks acceptable, but often at the cost of factual knowledge and task accuracy. Ternary weights have mostly been obtained by training from scratch or long fine-tuning. We introduce RoleQ, a quantization framework that places scales by the functional roles of Transformer units rather than by the layout of the weight matrix, as conventional formats do. Vectors that read from the residual stream take one scale per output unit; those that write to it, one per input unit. The rule is structural, needs no search, calibration or stored state, and holds on integer and ternary grids. In a rotated basis it matches a per-layer axis search at half the solver work, and at ternary it cuts perplexity by up to half against layout-based placement in two families at every size from 0.6B to 14B, where per-row scales leave MMLU at chance. Our lightweight post-training pipeline converts an existing checkpoint to 1.59 bits per weight in a few GPU-hours, a fraction of the cost of learned ternarization, and leads every post-training ternary method at matched or lower memory-resident bits on perplexity, zero-shot accuracy and MMLU, most widely on knowledge. A sparse second ternary plane placed by a per-unit Fisher saliency keeps the matmul multiplication-free and recovers what ternary loses first: at 8B, a fraction of a bit returns about half the MMLU that conversion costs, well ahead of random or Hessian-based placement at equal bits.
authors: Johannes Knittel, Alec Helbling, Hanspeter Pfister
bullets: Targets sub-four-bit quantization, where memory savings often degrade factual knowledge and task accuracy.
Assigns scales by Transformer unit function: residual-stream readers use per-output-unit scales, while writers use per-input-unit scales.
Requires no search, calibration, or stored state, and converts existing checkpoints to 1.59 bits per weight in a few GPU-hours.
In two model families from 0.6B to 14B parameters, ternary RoleQ reduces perplexity by up to half versus layout-based scaling; per-row scaling leaves MMLU near chance.
A sparse second ternary plane selected by Fisher saliency recovers about half of the lost 8B MMLU performance with a fraction of a bit.
papers.selection_reason: Ternary quantization of LLMs reduces model memory, fitting efficient AI memory-efficiency.
papers.title: RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary
papers.tldr: RoleQ converts pretrained language models to ternary weights using role-aligned scaling, preserving knowledge and accuracy better than layout-based quantization at low memory cost.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal semantic segmentation benefits from complementary sensors, but this benefit is fragile when some modalities are degraded or missing at test time. Many existing methods rely on dedicated fusion modules or multi-branch cross-modal encoders, and the fusion often becomes unreliable when modalities are absent, leading to substantial performance drops. We propose \textbf{FuseAdapt}, a parameter-efficient framework that performs fusion within the adaptation space of a frozen vision foundation model (VFM), exploring whether VFM priors can serve as an effective shared backbone for multi-modal segmentation. Instead of attaching a standalone fusion network, FuseAdapt assigns each modality a lightweight adaptation branch and performs \emph{adaptation-space fusion} by keeping Q/V low-rank adaptation private to each modality and routing only FFN low-rank residual activations across modalities inside the frozen backbone. The pretrained VFM remains fixed while modality-specific corrections and explicit cross-modal interaction are learned through the adaptation paths. To handle missing modalities, we further introduce \textbf{Predictive Modality Modeling (PMM)}, a direct representation-level objective for cross-modal redundancy. During training, PMM masks a target modality and predicts its embedding from the visible ones, supervised by a teacher target computed under full-modality input. PMM is used only during training and adds no inference-time overhead. Across three multi-modal segmentation benchmarks (MCubeS, DELIVER, MUSES), FuseAdapt consistently improves both modality-complete and modality-incomplete segmentation with a small trainable budget, yielding up to +3.01 mIoU under full modalities and +12.56 mIoU under missing modalities over prior state-of-the-art. Project page: https://devinxzhang.github.io/FuseAdapt-Page/.
bullets: Addresses performance degradation when modalities are absent or corrupted at test time.
Uses modality-specific low-rank adaptation branches inside a frozen vision foundation model.
Fuses modalities by routing only FFN adaptation residuals across modalities while keeping Q/V adaptations private.
Introduces Predictive Modality Modeling to reconstruct masked modality embeddings during training without inference overhead.
Improves complete- and incomplete-modality segmentation across three benchmarks, with gains of up to 3.01 and 12.56 mIoU, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient multimodal fusion in a frozen vision foundation model; relevant to efficient adaptation and spatial segmentation.
papers.title: FuseAdapt: Parameter-Efficient Multimodal Fusion for Semantic Segmentation with Missing Modalities
papers.tldr: FuseAdapt enables robust multimodal semantic segmentation with missing sensors by learning lightweight cross-modal adaptations within a frozen vision foundation model.

papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a compelling pathway toward energy-efficient artificial intelligence, fundamentally anchored in presynaptic input-driven sparsity. However, a substantial yet chronically overlooked source of computational overhead persists: the continuous subthreshold dynamics of postsynaptic neurons. Quantitative analysis reveals that up to 44% of neurons in an ImageNet-trained ResNet-18 model reside in a deeply inhibited state, imposing a persistent computational burden despite having a negligible probability of firing. To address this inefficiency, the Dormant Spiking Neuron (DSN) model is introduced. By incorporating a state-driven dynamic gate, the DSN allows a neuron to enter a dormant state when its membrane potential falls below a predefined negative threshold, dynamically pruning redundant computations at the instance level. Crucially, this dormancy mechanism is directly integrated into the neuronal dynamics and trained end-to-end via backpropagation through time using surrogate gradients, enabling the network to actively learn a robust dormancy policy that adaptively preserves critical information flow. Extensive experiments across static and neuromorphic datasets demonstrate that the DSN framework consistently reduces computational energy by 40% to over 70%. Notably, on the large-scale ImageNet dataset, the DSN outperforms state-of-the-art static pruning techniques at comparable reported cost reductions and simultaneously improves the corresponding baseline SNN accuracy by 1.34%. By establishing a trainable, state-driven sparsity paradigm orthogonal to conventional input-driven methods, the DSN unlocks synergistic efficiency gains, presenting an effective approach for advancing neuromorphic computing.
authors: Ruichen Ma, Yicai Chen, Pujun Zhou, Yue Zuo, Chongyang Li, Shuang Liu, Shaogang Hu, Guanchao Qiao
bullets: SNNs incur substantial overhead from continuously updating postsynaptic neurons unlikely to fire; up to 44% are deeply inhibited in an ImageNet-trained ResNet-18.
DSN adds a state-driven gate that places neurons below a negative membrane-potential threshold into a dormant state.
The mechanism is integrated into neuron dynamics and trained end-to-end with backpropagation through time and surrogate gradients.
Experiments on static and neuromorphic datasets report 40%–over 70% lower computational energy.
On ImageNet, DSN exceeds static-pruning performance at comparable reported cost reductions and improves baseline SNN accuracy by 1.34%.
papers.selection_reason: State-driven dormant neuron gating reduces computational energy in SNNs, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: The Dormant Spiking Neuron: A State-Driven Mechanism for Efficient Spiking Neural Networks
papers.tldr: Dormant Spiking Neurons reduce SNN computation by dynamically skipping deeply inhibited neurons while preserving—and sometimes improving—accuracy.

papers.abstract: Echo State Networks (ESNs), as lightweight implementations of reservoir computing, provide efficient solutions for temporal data processing in resource-constrained environments. While standard ESNs offer computational efficiency, their dense readout layers inflate the stored model and the per-sample inference cost. This paper introduces a Smooth-L1 regularized ESN (SL1ESN) that promotes sparsity in the readout layer while preserving differentiability for gradient-based optimization. The method employs a twice-differentiable Smooth-L1 approximation compatible with Newton's method, which we exploit both for centralized training and for a second-order (Newton-step) federated aggregation scheme. Under a single fixed shrinkage threshold shared by every dataset and both settings, experiments on seven time-series classification benchmarks show that SL1ESN learns readouts that are $77$--$95\%$ sparse in the centralized setting and $75$--$95\%$ sparse in the federated one, while staying within $0.7$ accuracy points of the strongest dense baseline on five of the seven benchmarks in the centralized setting and within $1.6$ points on the same five in the federated one, and the second-order federated update converges in only a few rounds. The resulting sparsity compresses the stored model, the per-sample inference cost, and the server-to-client broadcast by a comparable factor. These results demonstrate the practical value of sparse readouts for edge computing and IoT deployments.
authors: Gengcheng Lyu, Manuel R\"oder, Frank-Michael Schleif
bullets: Targets the storage, inference, and communication costs of dense ESN readout layers in resource-constrained edge and IoT settings.
Uses a twice-differentiable Smooth-L1 regularizer to promote sparsity while enabling Newton-based centralized training and federated aggregation.
With one fixed shrinkage threshold across datasets and settings, readouts reach 77–95% sparsity centrally and 75–95% federated.
On seven benchmarks, accuracy remains within 0.7 points of the strongest dense baseline centrally and 1.6 points federated on five benchmarks.
The sparse readouts provide comparable reductions in model storage, per-sample inference cost, and server-to-client broadcasts; federated training converges in a few rounds.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse readouts in Echo State Networks compress model and reduce inference and federated broadcast costs; relevant to efficient edge AI.
papers.title: Sparse Federated Echo State Networks for Time-Series Classification via Smooth-L1 Regularization
papers.tldr: A Smooth-L1-regularized Echo State Network produces highly sparse readouts for efficient centralized and federated time-series classification with limited accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Fixed-function CNN accelerators make edge inference fast and energy-efficient, but they execute only networks that obey a precise numerical contract. On the MAX7800x family, this contract requires power-of-two, per-tensor, symmetric scales, 8-bit activations and biases, integer-only arithmetic, and one statically configured shift per layer. We present ShiftQAT, the quantization-aware training (QAT) flow we developed for this family, which produces networks satisfying the contract by construction. It is the default training path of ai8x-training, the family's open-source training toolchain. ShiftQAT resolves residual, concatenation, and weight-sharing dependencies so that activation scales propagate statically and each layer's requantization reduces to one offline-configured shift. It also trains weights and biases on a joint power-of-two grid that fits the 8-bit bias budget. Among the compared methods, only ShiftQAT satisfies all of the contract's scaling constraints, including signed 8-bit activation storage. Even so, on ImageNet it matches the W8A8 accuracy drop of less constrained QAT methods and stays within 2.9 percentage points of FP32 at W4A8. On MAX78002 silicon, ShiftQAT-trained MobileNetV2 and ResNet-18 classify ImageNet images in 14.6 and 8.4 ms at 5.1 and 2.8 mJ per inference.
authors: Oguzhan Buyuksolak, Osman Erman Okman, Mehmet Gorkem Ulkar
bullets: Targets fixed-function MAX7800x accelerators requiring per-tensor symmetric power-of-two scales, signed 8-bit activations and biases, integer arithmetic, and one shift per layer.
Statically propagates activation scales through residuals, concatenations, and weight sharing, reducing requantization to offline-configured shifts.
Trains weights and biases on a joint power-of-two grid within the 8-bit bias budget.

It is the only compared method satisfying all stated scaling constraints, while matching the accuracy drop of less constrained W8A8 QAT and remaining within 2.9 percentage points of FP32 at W4A8 on ImageNet.
On MAX78002 silicon, MobileNetV2 and ResNet-18 classify ImageNet images in 14.6 ms/5.1 mJ and 8.4 ms/2.8 mJ per inference, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Quantization-aware training enforcing a fixed-function edge CNN accelerator numerical contract, directly targeting efficient inference.
papers.title: ShiftQAT: Quantization-Aware Training for the Numerical Contract of a Fixed-Function Edge CNN Accelerator
papers.tldr: ShiftQAT trains CNNs to meet the MAX7800x accelerator’s strict integer-only, power-of-two quantization contract while preserving strong accuracy and efficient edge inference.

papers.abstract: Biomedical research articles are mainly written for experts and often contain terms that are difficult for the general public to understand. Automated lay summarization has become a solution to make biomedical knowledge easier for patients and the public to understand. However, generating lay summaries from full-text articles requires more computing power because the articles are long and costly to process. Fine-tuning large language models for this task also requires substantial resources. This study asks two questions: (1) whether abstracts contain enough information to produce lay summaries as good as those based on full-text articles, and (2) whether few-shot learning performs as well as task-specific fine-tuning. The study used two public biomedical lay summarization datasets and two recent models, evaluated for readability, factual consistency, semantic similarity, and runtime efficiency. Results show that abstract-based summarization performs better overall. Across both datasets and models, abstract fine-tuning is 4.70 times faster, while abstract zero- and few-shot prompting is 5.31 times faster than full-text methods. These results show that abstract-based prompting reduces runtime cost while maintaining lay summary quality.
authors: Egecan \c{C}elik Evgin, \.{I}lknur Karadeniz, Olcay Taner Y{\i}ld{\i}z
bullets: Compares abstract- versus full-text input for biomedical lay summarization.
Evaluates zero-/few-shot prompting and task-specific fine-tuning using two models and two public datasets.
Assesses readability, factual consistency, semantic similarity, and runtime efficiency.
Abstract-based summarization performs better overall across datasets and models.
Abstract fine-tuning is 4.70× faster, while abstract zero-/few-shot prompting is 5.31× faster than full-text approaches.
papers.selection_reason: Shows that abstract-based input reduces runtime cost while maintaining summarization quality, a practical efficiency contribution for LLM inference.
papers.title: Abstracts or full text? Evaluating input scope and computational efficiency in biomedical lay summarization
papers.tldr: Biomedical abstracts can produce lay summaries as effectively as full articles while substantially reducing computational cost.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformer architectures have showcased impressive performance on semantic segmentation, yet their quadratic attention complexity hinders practical applications. Recent works have focused on merging tokens to reduce sequence length and thus improve transformer efficiency. However, existing token merging methods primarily rely on feature similarity to identify similar tokens, overlooking spatial consistency, which may introduce segmentation errors in semantic segmentation. In this work, we propose SCMerge, a training-free token merging method that jointly considers feature similarity and spatial consistency in pairing similar tokens. The pairwise tokens are then merged within the encoder, and the resulting token sequences are reconstructed onto the original patch grid after decoding. The proposed method is flexible and can be plugged into existing vision Transformer-based semantic segmentation pipelines. Extensive experiments on the benchmark datasets ADE20K, Pascal Context, and Cityscapes show that SCMerge consistently achieves a better trade-off between segmentation accuracy and efficiency than baseline methods.
authors: Junfeng Ren (Southern University of Science and Technology), Yi Gong (Southern University of Science and Technology), Yuan Zeng (Shenzhen Technology University)
bullets: Addresses the quadratic attention cost of Vision Transformers in semantic segmentation.
Pairs tokens using both feature similarity and spatial consistency to reduce segmentation errors from spatially inconsistent merges.
Merges tokens in the encoder and reconstructs the decoded sequences onto the original patch grid.
Plug-and-play with existing Vision Transformer semantic segmentation pipelines.
Experiments on ADE20K, Pascal Context, and Cityscapes show a better accuracy–efficiency trade-off than baseline methods.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free token merging with spatial consistency for efficient semantic segmentation directly fits token pruning/merging.
papers.title: SCMerge: Spatial-Consistency-Aware Token Pair Merging for Efficient Semantic Segmentation
papers.tldr: SCMerge is a training-free token-merging method that improves Vision Transformer segmentation efficiency by combining feature similarity with spatial consistency.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has been a critical paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) reasoning and agentic capabilities, but its efficiency remains a major bottleneck. Existing RL systems commonly rely on asynchronous execution to overlap rollout generation with policy optimization for enhanced efficiency. However, this approach faces inherent limitations: mild policy staleness offers only limited training efficiency gains, whereas aggressive asynchrony can degrade model quality and yields diminishing efficiency gains. The dynamic nature of LLM RL and multi-turn agentic workloads further challenges RL system design, as resource demands shift over time, making static resource allocation and generation strategy inefficient. This paper presents ReFlow, a system-algorithm co-designed RL framework for efficient LLM post-training. Its key insight is that, unlike existing RL frameworks which consume each trajectory only once, experience replay of recent trajectories enables effective sample reuse, thereby amortizing the high cost of rollout generation without incurring excessive policy staleness. To fully exploit this opportunity, ReFlow adopts a decoupled and adaptive architecture with three key designs: a dual replay data cycle supports efficient experience reuse while balancing training throughput and optimization stability; an elastic resource pool enables dynamic resource placement to accommodate evolving RL workloads; an adaptive scheduler coordinates generation strategies and resource allocation to improve resource utilization and boost generation throughput. Experiments across representative single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic RL tasks show that ReFlow improves training throughput by up to $2.06\times$ over state-of-the-art synchronous and asynchronous RL systems, while maintaining comparable or better model performance.
authors: Yukun Tian, Junwei Su, Haofeng Xu, Lansong Diao, Zhengping Qian, Weibo Zhao, Wenchao Zhou, Ruiting Zhou, Chuan Wu
bullets: Addresses rollout-generation overhead, policy staleness, and inefficient static resource allocation in LLM RL.
Uses experience replay to reuse recent trajectories and amortize rollout costs.
Introduces a dual replay data cycle, elastic resource pool, and adaptive scheduler in a decoupled architecture.
Evaluations on single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic tasks report up to 2.06× higher training throughput with comparable or better performance.
papers.selection_reason: System-algorithm co-design for efficient LLM RL post-training via experience replay and elastic resource allocation; fits efficient AI broadly, though not a specific configured subtopic.
papers.title: ReFlow: Replay-Driven Decoupling for Efficient RL Post-Training
papers.tldr: ReFlow improves LLM RL post-training efficiency by replaying recent trajectories and dynamically coordinating resources and generation without sacrificing model quality.

papers.abstract: Recent feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods have enabled effective multi-view 3D reconstruction by predicting Gaussian primitives in a single forward pass. However, existing approaches predominantly adopt a pixel-aligned paradigm that predicts one Gaussian per input pixel, coupling the Gaussian count to the input resolution and number of views. This also leads to redundant primitives in textureless regions and insufficient coverage in geometrically complex areas. We present Anchor3DGS, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework that replaces pixel-aligned prediction with a compact anchor-based representation. Guided by information entropy, our method places a set of 3D anchors in the scene, concentrating them in regions of higher visual complexity while maintaining broad spatial coverage. Each anchor performs occlusion-aware aggregation of multi-view image features, exchanges information with other anchors, and is decoded into a set of local Gaussians. A lightweight feature enhancement module further refines the coarse RGB output from Gaussian splatting and improves rendering fidelity. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that our Anchor3DGS achieves state-of-the-art novel view synthesis quality while only using an order of magnitude fewer Gaussian primitives.
authors: Sheng Ye, Jiangke Lin, Fudong Wang, Yi Yuan, Zhen-Hui Dong, Yong-Jin Liu
bullets: Addresses redundant Gaussians in textureless regions and insufficient coverage in geometrically complex areas.
Uses entropy-guided 3D anchors to concentrate representation where visual complexity is higher while preserving scene coverage.
Anchors aggregate multi-view features with occlusion awareness, exchange information, and decode into local Gaussian sets.
A lightweight enhancement module refines Gaussian-splatting RGB outputs for improved rendering fidelity.
Experiments on diverse benchmarks report state-of-the-art novel-view synthesis quality with an order of magnitude fewer Gaussian primitives.
papers.selection_reason: Feed-forward 3DGS with compact anchor-based representation for efficient multi-view reconstruction, fitting 3D vision and efficiency interests.
papers.title: Anchor3DGS: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Compact Anchor-Based Representation
papers.tldr: Anchor3DGS enables pose-free, feed-forward 3D reconstruction with far fewer Gaussians by using entropy-guided scene anchors instead of one Gaussian per input pixel.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. However, generating each token still involves sequential computation and repeated access to model weights, leading to high decoding latency. Recent pipelined self-speculative decoding methods reduce this delay by drafting tokens from early-loop predictions and asynchronously advancing tokens at different recurrent depths in the same batch, but they do not fully exploit early-loop features for longer lookahead and still spend computation verifying incorrect speculative branches. We introduce \method, a speculative decoding framework for looped transformers that enables earlier drafting of future tokens and assigns complementary roles to different recurrent depths. A lightweight lookahead drafter (LAD) predicts multiple future tokens with early-loop states, and deeper-loop feedback helps decide which draft branches to continue and which to pause, while the full-depth model makes the final token decisions. LoopAhead achieves up to 7.82x decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding while preserving the target model's output distribution.
authors: Zixuan Liu, Nan Xue, Rui Bao, Yuhang Xu, Xiaofeng Cao, Jiangchao Yao, Zhiyong Chen
bullets: Addresses decoding latency from sequential token generation and repeated weight access in looped language models.
Uses a lightweight lookahead drafter to predict several future tokens from early-loop features.
Employs deeper-loop feedback to continue promising draft branches and pause likely incorrect ones.
The full-depth model retains final control, preserving the target model’s output distribution.
Reports up to 7.82× decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a speculative decoding framework that reduces inference latency for looped language models, fitting the efficient AI scope.
papers.title: LoopAhead: Speculating Ahead for Faster Decoding in Looped Language Models
papers.tldr: LoopAhead accelerates decoding in looped Transformers by using early-loop states to draft multiple future tokens while deeper loops selectively verify them.

papers.abstract: Real-world video denoising for communication systems must handle mixed degradations such as sensor noise, compression artifacts, and motion-induced inconsistency while remaining deployable under tight latency budgets.
