Purely deep models often achieve high accuracy but come with significant computational cost, whereas classical filters are robust and efficient but insufficiently adaptive. We present FilterFusion, a prior-guided multi-frame denoising framework that combines temporally-aware learned features with an interpretable bank of denoising branches. The model predicts a low-cost guidance signal and uses it to adaptively mix a compact set of denoising responses at the original resolution. The lightweight design uses only 109K parameters and explicitly injects temporal variance and spatial variance cues into the low-resolution controller. On CRVD (real sensor noise), it reaches 34.72 dB PSNR and 0.9330 SSIM with only 0.18 GFLOPs (network-only). Because the filter-bank operations are simple and regular (Gaussian blur, median, weighted sum), a straightforward compiled C implementation of the synthesis path achieves 17.9ms per frame (55.9 FPS) on a single CPU thread at 1080p---exceeding real-time and 122--252 times faster than lightweight CNN baselines that require over 2 seconds per frame. The results demonstrate a strong quality-efficiency-speed trade-off and a practical route to real-time denoising through low-resolution control and explicit filter-based synthesis.
authors: Wenlong Yang, Weihang Yuan, Canran Jin, Jiahao Li, Henrik Turbell, Lifeng Sun
bullets: Targets mixed real-world degradations, including sensor noise, compression artifacts, and motion inconsistency, under tight latency constraints.
Combines temporally aware learned features with an interpretable bank of denoising branches at the original resolution.
Injects temporal and spatial variance cues into a low-resolution controller that predicts adaptive filter mixing.
Uses 109K parameters and 0.18 GFLOPs; on CRVD, achieves 34.72 dB PSNR and 0.9330 SSIM.
A compiled CPU synthesis path processes 1080p frames at 17.9 ms per frame (55.9 FPS), supporting real-time deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient video denoising via low-resolution control and filter-bank synthesis, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: FilterFusion: Prior-Guided Adaptive Filter Fusion for Efficient Video Denoising
papers.tldr: FilterFusion enables real-time video denoising by using low-cost, prior-guided control to adaptively combine simple filter responses.

papers.abstract: Reusing the attention KV cache across requests is a standard way to cut prefill cost in long-context LLM serving, and production systems increasingly back the per-engine cache with a remote tier shared by every engine. We study such a tier in a disaggregated deployment of GLM-5.3, an FP8 mixture-of-experts model with multi-head latent attention (MLA), on 8xB300 nodes running prefill context parallelism (PCP8). Enabling the remote tier (LMCache with a Valkey store) left median time-to-first-token unchanged but raised the 16k-token p99 from 3.96 s to 17.3 s. Replaying a production request stream on an isolated engine, we find that a remote hit took 0.88 s against 0.31 s to recompute the prompt, and that synchronous loading turned a hit-heavy stream into an unstable queue: p99 83.32 s with the GPUs 7% busy. A two-term cost model explains both: a hit pays off only if the tier delivers more than B* = sR (2.53 GB/s for this model and GPU), and a fixed per-hit engine cost (T0 ~ 0.33 s) means that hits on prompts shorter than about 17k tokens cannot beat recompute at any bandwidth. Guided by the model, we (i) shard the MLA KV store across PCP ranks, with a proof that the existing minimum-over-ranks lookup returns the longest cached prefix and a load protocol that can never desynchronize collectives; (ii) partition the remote tier by rank, one server instance per rank with no coordination, which raises GET bandwidth 6.3x to 10.76 GB/s; (iii) add asynchronous loading to the sharded store; and (iv) fix three client bugs that caused unbounded stalls. On the hit-heavy stream, with 98.5% of prompt tokens served from the remote tier, p99 falls from 83.32 s to 0.67 s. The sharded store raises prefill throughput by 14%, and by 34% together with an upstream kernel fix. All changes are submitted upstream to LMCache.
bullets: A remote LMCache/Valkey tier increased 16k-token p99 latency from 3.96 s to 17.3 s, despite unchanged median time-to-first-token.
Remote hits initially took 0.88 s versus 0.31 s for prompt recomputation; synchronous loading caused severe queueing and 83.32 s p99 latency.
A cost model shows caching helps only above 2.53 GB/s and for prompts longer than roughly 17k tokens.
The proposed design shards MLA KV state and the remote tier across PCP ranks, adds asynchronous loading, and fixes three stalling client bugs.
The optimized system reduced hit-heavy p99 latency to 0.67 s, increased prefill throughput by 14%, and by 34% with an upstream kernel fix.
papers.selection_reason: Scales remote KV cache tiers for context-parallel prefill; directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill
papers.tldr: Remote KV caching can be slower than recomputing prompts, but sharding, bandwidth scaling, asynchronous loading, and client fixes make it effective for long-context PCP serving.

papers.abstract: Large language models can produce fluent answers that the supplied context does not support. A compact frozen proxy model can detect such answers by reading the context and another model's response, even from a proprietary generator. Attention-based detectors use summary statistics of the proxy's attention weights, but standard pipelines materialize the attention matrix, whose memory grows quadratically with sequence length. We compute these statistics without materializing attention, by accumulation in the FlashAttention pass, sparse lookups after it, or a second tiled pass over the scores, and classify them by this path into nearly free and costlier ones. On an H100, the statistics of five published detectors add 16% to the latency of a Qwen3-8B forward at 2K tokens, falling to 1.4% at 35K, and store 22.5 KiB per response token. On three benchmarks, probes trained on frozen Qwen3 proxies of 0.6B to 8B parameters prove strong detectors: a 4B proxy outperforms the strongest of nine zero-shot 4-9B LLM judges in F1 on two of the three, the proxies match or outperform specialized grounding checkers of up to 7B parameters, probing each proxy beats prompting it as a judge, and adding attention features significantly improves F1 in half of the 12 benchmark-proxy pairs, never significantly lowering it.
authors: Andrei Volodichev, Maksim Savichev, Nikita Sviridov, Artem Yuliy, Dmitry Simakov, Alexey Zaytsev
bullets: Targets unsupported but fluent LLM answers, including responses from proprietary generators.
Computes attention statistics during FlashAttention, via sparse lookups, or with a second tiled score pass, avoiding quadratic memory materialization.
On an H100, five detectors add 16% latency at 2K tokens and 1.4% at 35K, using 22.5 KiB per response token.
Across three benchmarks, frozen Qwen3 probes are strong detectors; a 4B proxy beats nine zero-shot LLM judges on two benchmarks and matches or exceeds specialized checkers.
Attention features significantly improve F1 in 6 of 12 benchmark–proxy pairs and never significantly reduce it.
papers.selection_reason: Computes attention statistics without materializing the attention matrix, reducing memory and latency for attention-based detectors.
papers.title: FlashAttention with Statistics: Low-Overhead Attention Features for Compact Hallucination Detectors
papers.tldr: FlashAttention-based computation makes attention features practical for compact, frozen-model hallucination detectors without storing the full attention matrix.

papers.abstract: Device-cloud speculative decoding reduces server computation, but growing a deep draft tree with a small language model (SLM) requires repeated passes on a mobile neural processing unit (NPU). We present HyCo, which assigns depth to the server model's native multi-token prediction (MTP) head, executed on the device, and alternative branches to one SLM pass. The server returns the hidden state, input embedding, and key-value entries needed by the head instead of executing its sequential steps. Quantization, a restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window fit both drafters to the NPU. An {\epsilon}-threshold rule additionally relaxes exact preservation of the verifier's sampling distribution. In single-client runs with a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, HyCo reduces server GPU time per output token relative to server-side MTP self-speculation by 38.6% on Spec-Bench and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization. With the same acceptance rule, three Spec-Bench runs per system show 9.0 percentage points more saving and 1.9x delivery speed than an SLM-only drafter. HyCo differs from Cloud+MTP by +0.2 judge-score points (paired 95% CI: -0.9 to +1.3); exploratory translation favors SpecEdge-{\epsilon}. Without relaxation, HyCo exact saves 27.7% and 11.9% on the two datasets.
authors: Hanbin Bae, Heejin Choi, Joohyung Lee, Byoung Jin Choi, Sangjun Park, Hoon-Young Cho
bullets: Targets the repeated mobile-NPU passes required to grow deep draft trees in device-cloud speculative decoding.
Assigns draft-tree depth to the model’s native MTP head and alternative branches to one SLM pass, with required server states sent to the device.
Uses quantization, restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window to fit both drafters on a mobile NPU; an ε-threshold can relax exact sampling preservation.
On a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, reduces server GPU time per output token by 38.6% on Spec-Bench and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization versus server-side MTP self-speculation.
With the same acceptance rule, saves 9.0 percentage points more and delivers 1.9× higher speed than an SLM-only drafter; exact mode still saves 27.7% and 11.9%.
papers.selection_reason: Hybrid mobile-cloud speculative decoding that reduces server GPU time; fits efficient inference.
papers.title: HyCo: Hybrid Drafting for Cost-Efficient Mobile-Cloud Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: HyCo combines a server model’s multi-token prediction head with a single mobile SLM pass to reduce cloud computation and speed up speculative decoding.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models achieve high-quality image generation but remain computationally expensive due to iterative denoising across many timesteps. Existing acceleration methods mainly reduce per-sample latency, but gains along this axis are becoming saturated. We instead explore an orthogonal throughput-oriented direction by processing multiple samples within a single denoising evaluation. To this end, we propose ManiFusion, a backbone-agnostic framework for multi-sample generation through fused-space computation. ManiFusion jointly processes multiple samples by fusing them before the denoising backbone and separating them afterward through unfusion. We provide a geometric perspective on how multiple samples can share a fused representation while retaining the information needed to guide their individual generation trajectories. To better align fusion allocation with denoising stages, ManiFusion uses Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which dynamically adjusts fusion factors throughout sampling. ManiFusion generalizes across diffusion families, including both U-Net and transformer backbones in pixel and latent spaces. We further show that ManiFusion composes with existing acceleration methods and reaches throughput regimes unattainable by prior approaches with minimal quality degradation.
authors: Minkyu Kim, Baekseung Kim, Junhoo Lee, Jangho Kim, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Targets throughput rather than only reducing latency for individual samples.
Fuses multiple samples before the denoising backbone and separates them afterward.
Uses Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling to adapt fusion factors across denoising stages.
Works across U-Net and transformer diffusion models in pixel and latent spaces.
Composes with existing acceleration methods and enables higher-throughput regimes.
papers.selection_reason: Throughput-oriented diffusion acceleration via fused multi-sample computation; efficiency technique.
papers.title: ManiFusion: Unlocking the High-Throughput Generation via Superposition in Manifold Space
papers.tldr: ManiFusion boosts diffusion image-generation throughput by jointly denoising multiple samples in a shared manifold-space representation, with only minimal quality degradation.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now fix software, operate computers and serve customers, but their harnesses, the programs that run them, call a large LLM at every step, which makes long tasks slow and costly. Most of these calls end in a multiple-choice decision, such as which tool to call next. Decision models such as Jev answer these questions directly, at a fraction of an LLM call's time and price. We ask how a harness can delegate these decisions to a decision model with little loss of success. To evaluate decision models in agentic tasks, we build AgentDecisionBench, which tests them from isolated questions up to control of a running agent, on public benchmarks and our DecisionGym environment. The decision model most accurate on isolated questions solved only 69.5% of agent tasks, and without a fitted confidence threshold, delegating tool choices lowered success by 19.0 points. Building on these findings, we then design JevAgentHarness, which fits this threshold for each choice on the agent's own trajectories and lets the LLM decide below it. Because existing decision models never see the states an agent reaches after its own mistakes, we train AgentDecision-4B, an open 4B model, on such states with Jev's answers as labels. On tasks unlike its training data, the agent solved 91.5% of them with AgentDecision-4B and 82.0% with Jev. On tasks like their training data, 4B models trained this way made agents 81.1-89.0% cheaper and up to 2.5 times faster, without losing 3 or more points of task success. The models, data, and harness will be released at https://github.com/JevAgentHarness/JevAgentHarness.
authors: Kunlun Zhu, Tao Feng, Xu Han, Heng Wang, Ling Yang, Xiangru Tang, Jiaxuan You, Heng Ji
bullets: AgentDecisionBench evaluates decision models from isolated choices to controlling running agents across public benchmarks and DecisionGym.
Accuracy on isolated decisions did not reliably predict agent-level performance: the best model solved 69.5% of agent tasks, and uncalibrated delegation reduced success by 19.0 points.
JevAgentHarness fits per-choice confidence thresholds on the agent’s own trajectories, allowing the LLM to handle uncertain decisions.
AgentDecision-4B is trained on states reached after agent mistakes, using Jev’s decisions as labels.

On reported tasks, AgentDecision-4B achieved 91.5% success on tasks unlike its training data; on similar tasks, trained 4B models reduced cost by 81.1–89.0% and reached up to 2.5× speedup without losing 3 or more points of success.
papers.selection_reason: Delegating agent decisions to small models reduces cost and latency while preserving task success; relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: JevAgentHarness: Benchmarking, Deploying and Training Decision Models That Share Control with LLMs
papers.tldr: JevAgentHarness enables agents to delegate many tool-choice decisions from LLMs to faster, cheaper decision models while preserving task success through confidence calibration and trajectory-based training.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems rely on generative models for expert execution, workflow planning, and artifact review. Yet many coordination operations require only bounded decisions, such as selecting the next expert or judging artifact quality. Profiling three representative MAS frameworks, we find that routing and review account for 31.7-43.5% of generative-LLM tokens. However, replacing these operations with low-cost decision models introduces two interface gaps: generative planners produce execution plans and handoff instructions (planning gap), while reviewers provide actionable feedback for repairing flawed artifacts (review gap), which bounded decisions alone cannot provide. We introduce Jev-LiteMAS, a multi-agent framework that bridges both gaps by combining a lightweight decision model (Jev) with generative execution and feedback. To address the planning gap, Jev selects experts dynamically from the task and prior expert outputs, using accumulated context to ground subsequent execution without a pre-generated trajectory. To address the review gap, Jev screens intermediate artifacts against task criteria: passing artifacts proceed directly, whereas flagged ones undergo LLM re-review for acceptance or corrective feedback. Across four benchmarks and two backbones, Jev-LiteMAS reduces generative-LLM tokens by 12.7-54.6% over LAS, maintaining accuracy within 1.34 percentage points and lowering latency in seven of eight settings. Grounding routing in substantive expert outputs prevents up to 18.0 points in accuracy loss.
authors: Kaixiang Wang, Zhaijiacheng Zhou, Jiong Lou, Jie Li
bullets: Routing and review consume 31.7–43.5% of generative-LLM tokens in profiled multi-agent systems.
The framework combines Jev for bounded decisions with generative models for execution and feedback.
Jev dynamically selects experts from task context and prior outputs, avoiding pre-generated workflows.
Jev screens artifacts; only flagged results receive full LLM re-review and corrective feedback.
Across four benchmarks and two backbones, it cuts generative-LLM tokens by 12.7–54.6%, keeps accuracy within 1.34 points, and lowers latency in seven of eight settings.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces generative-LLM token usage and latency in multi-agent workflows via lightweight decision models; fits efficiency interests.
papers.title: Jev-LiteMAS: Separating Decisions from Generation in Multi-Agent Workflows
papers.tldr: Jev-LiteMAS reduces generative-LLM use in multi-agent workflows by replacing routine routing and review decisions with a lightweight decision model while preserving task performance.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly deployed at the edge to support complex tasks that require collaboration and information exchange among multiple agents. However, when task contexts are passed across agents, shared context that has already been processed by upstream agents often needs to be prefilled again, resulting in substantial redundant computation. Reusing an already prefilled key--value (KV) cache can avoid this recomputation, but requires the reusable KV state to be transferred across the network before the receiving agent can begin generation. Under strict time-to-first-token (TTFT) deadlines and unreliable edge links, delivering the complete KV cache may be infeasible, making it necessary to prioritize and protect the most valuable KV information within a limited transmission budget. This paper proposes PriorityFEC, a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that jointly exploits model-side KV importance and transport-side reliability. PriorityFEC first constructs a utility-aware source stream by placing high-utility KV blocks at earlier transmission positions. It then protects the ordered stream using a feedback-adaptive Streaming Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) mechanism, which schedules repair packets according to receiver feedback before the TTFT deadline. We implement PriorityFEC on a distributed edge LLM serving prototype and evaluate it with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple datasets. Results show that PriorityFEC achieves superior task quality over the compared transport schemes, with its advantages becoming particularly pronounced under stringent deadline constraints. These results demonstrate the importance of jointly optimizing KV-cache utility and deadline-aware transport reliability when reusable LLM state must be handed off across unreliable edge networks.
authors: Han Shen, Qifu Tyler Sun, Fanyang Meng, Ye Wang, Yongsheng Liang
bullets: Addresses redundant prefill computation when shared context moves between agents.
Orders KV blocks by model-side utility so the most valuable information is transmitted first.
Uses feedback-adaptive streaming FEC to schedule repairs before the receiver’s TTFT deadline.
Evaluations on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple datasets show better task quality than compared transport schemes, especially under tight deadlines.
Scope: effectiveness depends on KV-utility estimation, link reliability, and available transmission time.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on deadline-aware KV-cache handoff and transport for edge multi-agent LLM systems, relevant to KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware Streaming FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent Systems
papers.tldr: PriorityFEC improves KV-cache handoff for edge multi-agent LLMs by prioritizing valuable cache blocks and adaptively protecting them under TTFT deadlines and unreliable links.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly place a multi-billion-parameter model inside the feedback loop, repeatedly recomputing task context whenever they predict a new action chunk. Yet task understanding changes far more slowly than the robot state. We introduce Fast-VLA, which invokes a frozen 4B VLM once per episode to contextualize the instruction and initial views as fixed, multi-layer key-value task memory. During execution, a lightweight online actor fuses learned time- and arm-indexed queries with current visual and proprioceptive feedback to form action queries. These queries retrieve task context from the fixed memory and predict action chunks without re-running the foundation model. Fast-VLA achieves 92.46% and 92.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean and Randomized, and 95.95% and 79.11% on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus evaluation. Against three continually conditioned baselines on the same hardware, it reduces RoboTwin amortized policy inference time by 10.9-17.1x and requires 1.22 GiB of post-prefill online resident memory. Task-memory swaps further show that the actor relies on episode-matched task memory. These results show that task context can be established once while closed-loop control remains responsive throughout execution. Project page: https://garfield-kh.github.io/FastVLA
authors: Kehong Gong, Guanli Hou, Xiaoxu Zheng, Qi Wang, Mingxi Xu, Anbang Zhai, Xiaoyu He, Mingyuan Zhang, Michael Bi Mi
bullets: Addresses the high inference cost of repeatedly recomputing task context in VLA policies.
Stores instruction and initial-view context as fixed, multi-layer key-value task memory.
A lightweight actor combines current visual/proprioceptive feedback with learned time- and arm-indexed queries to predict action chunks.
Reports strong success across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, with 10.9–17.1× lower amortized RoboTwin inference time than continually conditioned baselines.
Task-memory swaps indicate that performance depends on episode-matched task context.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language-action policy with fixed KV task memory for efficient closed-loop manipulation; strongly relevant to VLA and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Fast-VLA: You Only Think Once for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: Fast-VLA runs a 4B vision-language model once per episode, then enables efficient closed-loop robot control with a lightweight actor.

papers.abstract: Block Influence (BI) ranks Transformer blocks for depth pruning from their input-output cosine change, but the ranking depends on the calibration distribution. We study whether English calibration transfers to Indian languages in Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-1B, and Gemma-2-2B. English, Hindi, Marathi, and Tamil use disjoint Wikipedia articles for calibration and evaluation; every selector receives the same 150-chunk budget, and Tamil is excluded from multilingual aggregation to test cross-script transfer. Across all three models, late-block BI is 20.7-55.5% higher for the three Indian languages than for English, and every predeclared late-minus-middle contrast has a 95% bootstrap interval above zero. This mismatch changes the low-BI blocks selected for removal despite high global rank correlations. Averaging BI over equal English, Hindi, and Marathi budgets mitigates the resulting perplexity damage for Qwen at six removed blocks and for Gemma at all tested depths, including held-out Tamil. The mitigation is not universal: on Llama, balancing improves Hindi and Marathi at two removed blocks but severely harms Tamil, while larger pruning budgets select the same blocks and collapse perplexity regardless of calibration. Rank-mean and minimax-rank aggregators do not dominate the raw mean. These results support a diagnostic claim rather than a universal pruning rule: English-only BI systematically misses late-layer activity for Indian-language text, but multilingual calibration must still be validated per architecture and pruning budget.
bullets: BI rankings depend strongly on calibration language, despite high overall rank correlations.
Across Qwen2.5, Llama-3.2, and Gemma-2, Indian-language calibration produces higher late-block influence than English.
This shifts which low-influence blocks are selected for removal.
Equal-budget English–Hindi–Marathi averaging mitigates perplexity damage for Qwen and Gemma, including held-out Tamil in some settings.
The benefit is not universal: effects vary by architecture and pruning depth, and larger budgets can cause perplexity collapse.
papers.selection_reason: Studies calibration effects on block-influence pruning in multilingual LMs, directly relevant to efficient model compression.
papers.title: Calibration Language Shapes Block-Influence Pruning in Multilingual Language Models
papers.tldr: English-only calibration systematically underestimates late-block influence for Indian languages, while multilingual calibration can reduce pruning damage but is architecture- and budget-dependent.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce computation by routing each token to a small set of experts, but each selected expert is still used at a fixed precision. We present DPA-MoE, a runtime precision control framework that makes routed experts any-precision. DPA-MoE encodes expert feed-forward weights as prefix-decodable chunks using SharedScale AnyBCQ, profiles per-expert reconstruction residuals offline, and allocates chunks at inference time using live router gate scores. This post-routing allocation lets a single encoded MoE checkpoint operate at multiple effective weight budgets without retraining or re-encoding. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeekMoE-16B show that DPA-MoE improves KL divergence and downstream accuracy over uniform chunk allocation at matched budgets, with modest steady-state throughput overhead in our prototype.
authors: Jaeyun Kim, Hoonki Lee, Susie Shin, Hyunmin Kim, Dahyun Lee, Sangyeob Kim
bullets: Addresses the fixed-precision limitation of routed MoE experts.
Encodes expert FFN weights into prefix-decodable SharedScale AnyBCQ chunks and profiles reconstruction residuals offline.
Allocates precision at inference time using live router gate scores and per-expert residual profiles.
Outperforms uniform chunk allocation on KL divergence and downstream accuracy at matched weight budgets.
Evaluated on Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeekMoE-16B, with modest steady-state throughput overhead in the prototype.
papers.selection_reason: Runtime precision allocation for MoE expert weights reduces inference memory; fits memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: DPA-MoE: A Runtime Precision Control Framework for MoE Inference
papers.tldr: DPA-MoE enables runtime, token-aware precision allocation for MoE experts from a single encoded checkpoint without retraining or re-encoding.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) mitigates the performance degradation of source-pretrained models on unlabeled test data under distribution shifts. Recent backpropagation-free token-purging methods address 3D point cloud distribution shifts by filtering unreliable tokens. However, their reliance on predefined purge-size candidates requires multiple forward passes per sample and increases inference cost. We propose SATOR (Sample-Adaptive TOken Routing), a source-free and backpropagation-free 3D TTA framework that eliminates this search by deriving both the partitioning threshold and routing decision directly from each sample. SATOR computes token abnormality scores from complementary attention and geometric relation graphs. It then derives a sample-specific partition into retained and pruned tokens via Otsu-based separability, without evaluating candidate sizes. Keep-ratio-calibrated routing then selects the pruned prediction only when its entropy, penalized by the keep ratio, is lower than that of the original prediction. Experiments on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C demonstrate that SATOR achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on three 3D corruption benchmarks.
authors: Inseok Kong, Geunyoung Jung, Jiyoung Jung
bullets: Addresses distribution shifts in 3D point clouds without source data or backpropagation.
Computes token abnormality from attention and geometric relation graphs.
Uses Otsu-based separability to derive each sample’s retained/pruned token partition.
Routes to the pruned prediction only when keep-ratio-penalized entropy favors it.
Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C.
papers.selection_reason: Source-free 3D test-time adaptation with sample-adaptive token routing; fits test-time learning and token pruning.
papers.title: SATOR: Backpropagation-Free 3D Test-Time Adaptation via Sample-Adaptive Token Routing
papers.tldr: SATOR enables efficient backpropagation-free 3D test-time adaptation by routing tokens using sample-specific decisions instead of costly purge-size searches.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) effectively transfers capabilities from a teacher to a student through feedback on student-generated rollouts. However, generating complete student rollouts and computing teacher feedback for every token make OPD computationally expensive. We introduce Stochastic Truncated On-Policy Distillation (STOPD), which accelerates OPD by randomly truncating student rollouts and correcting the resulting sampling bias with blockwise inverse-probability weighting (IPW). At each training step, we sample a stopping position for each rollout before generation and let the student generate until that position or natural termination. We obtain teacher feedback on every generated token and use blockwise IPW to compensate for the lower probability of retaining later tokens while controlling the weights. We prove that this weighting preserves Vanilla OPD's gradient sum in expectation and derive one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon. We evaluate STOPD across multiple teacher-student model pairs, task domains, and optimizers. STOPD reduces generated tokens by 25-48% while maintaining accuracy comparable to Vanilla OPD, achieving 1.3-2.2x training speedups.
authors: Zhengxin Zhang, Maosen Tang, Ning Wang, Changhao Li, Jingren Zhou, Bo Dai, Sainyam Galhotra, Alex Townsend, Claire Cardie
bullets: OPD is costly because it completes student rollouts and obtains teacher feedback for every token.
STOPD samples a stopping position before generation and truncates each rollout at that point or at natural termination.
Blockwise inverse-probability weighting compensates for the reduced chance of retaining later tokens while controlling weight magnitude.
The method preserves Vanilla OPD’s gradient sum in expectation, with update-error bounds derived for SGD, Adam, and Muon.
Across multiple model pairs, domains, and optimizers, STOPD achieves 1.3–2.2× training speedups.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes stochastic truncated on-policy distillation with IPW to reduce training computation, relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Does On-Policy Distillation Need to Complete Every Rollout?
papers.tldr: STOPD speeds up on-policy distillation by randomly truncating student rollouts and correcting sampling bias, cutting generation by 25–48% while preserving comparable accuracy.

papers.abstract: Exact $k$-nearest-neighbor (kNN) search over image descriptors and embeddings underlies visual retrieval, near-duplicate detection, the evaluation of learned representations, and increasingly the memory of LLM agents. However, exhaustive search computes every distance at full precision, whereas approximate indexes return recall below one. We observe that exact search only needs a proof that each excluded vector cannot be a neighbor. Because such a proof only has to be conservative, it can be checked in low precision, much as the retina examines the whole scene at low resolution. We call this principle certified exclusion and realize it in an exact kNN method for GPUs, which we call \certex. Specifically, \certex\ stores a lower-bounding projection of each vector in half precision and folds a rounding certificate into the same tensor-core dot product, so that only the few vectors that the test keeps need exact distances. We prove that \certex\ returns the exact kNN of every query. On sixteen datasets with up to 100M vectors, \certex\ is exact for every query at 7.1$\times$ to 18.0$\times$ the throughput of the fastest cuVS search on one H100 and outperforms quantized and graph indexes whenever every query must be exact.
bullets: Targets exact visual retrieval, where exhaustive search is costly and approximate indexes may miss neighbors.
Stores conservative lower-bounding projections in half precision and incorporates rounding certificates into tensor-core dot products.
Computes exact distances only for vectors that pass the exclusion test.
Proves that every returned result is the exact kNN set.
Across 16 datasets with up to 100M vectors, reaches 7.1×–18.0× the throughput of the fastest cuVS search on one H100 when exactness is required.
papers.selection_reason: Exact kNN acceleration via certified low-precision exclusion; efficiency technique transferable to retrieval and memory systems.
papers.title: CertEx: Exact Visual Retrieval at Scale by Certified Exclusion
papers.tldr: CertEx achieves exact GPU kNN retrieval at scale by cheaply certifying which vectors can be excluded before computing exact distances.

papers.abstract: Although Graph Neural Networks are widely used in various domains, they remained mostly unexplored in computer vision. Convolutional Neural Networks and Vision Transformers were leading the field, until the quite recent introduction of Vision Graphs (ViG) that treat images as a set of nodes and apply graph convolution on their k-NN graphs. ViGs show impressive accuracy on image classification but their computational cost remains relatively high. Inspired by optimization methods for GNNs, we present CoViG, a novel approach combining graph coarsening and ViGs. Our method introduces an additional MinCUT pooling step within the Grapher component of intermediate ViG blocks. By simplifying the intermediate graphs and thus decreasing the number of nodes of specific blocks, our approach considerably reduces the computational cost of ViG during inference. We evaluated our approach on ImageNet with several ViG architectures, and we obtained accuracies equivalent to the original ViG models with only about 51\% of FLOPs.
authors: Martial Guidez, Stefan Duffner, Christophe Garcia
bullets: Vision Graphs model images as nodes connected through k-NN graphs, but their computational cost is relatively high.
CoViG adds a MinCUT pooling step within the Grapher component of intermediate ViG blocks.
Graph coarsening reduces the number of nodes processed in selected blocks.
On ImageNet across several ViG architectures, CoViG achieves comparable accuracy using about 51% of the original FLOPs.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces graph coarsening to reduce the computational cost of Vision Graphs (ViGs). This technique of reducing node count is analogous to token pruning and offers a method for improving inference efficiency in vision models.
papers.title: CoViG: Coarsened Vision GNN for Image Classification
papers.tldr: CoViG reduces Vision Graph Network inference cost by coarsening intermediate graphs while maintaining accuracy comparable to standard ViGs.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demand efficient inference, where the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations in linear projections dominate compute and energy cost. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost by mapping weights and activations to low-bit integers. Power-of-Two (PoT) weight quantization promises efficient multiplier-free LLM inference via shift-add logic, but suffers significant accuracy degradation at low bitwidths due to its coarse base-2 quantization grid. We introduce Fractional PoT (FPoT), a base-$\sqrt{2}$ (half-octave) fractional PoT grid that achieves practical 4-bit weight quantization while preserving a fully integer shift-add datapath. The method combines (i) the base-$\sqrt{2}$ weight grid with uniform integer activations, (ii) a calibration-time grid-alignment refinement absorbed into the static per-channel scale, and (iii) a lightweight 1-adder $\sqrt{2}$ approximation whose error is absorbed during weight calibration via approximate-grid quantization, yielding a processing element (PE) with significantly fewer gates than a 4-bit integer multiplier. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weight and activation quantization, FPoT improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning performance by 8.72% relative to the PoT baseline, while maintaining performance close to the uniform integer baseline, with only a negligible 0.4%p degradation. These results hold across various configurations spanning seven models and three bit-widths. Furthermore, FPoT can be integrated with state-of-the-art LLM PTQ methods, demonstrating framework-agnostic applicability.
authors: Sunghyun Wee, Geunjae Choi, Hyeonjin Kim, Suyoung Kim, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses the coarse base-2 grid of Power-of-Two quantization, which causes severe low-bit accuracy degradation.
Uses a base-√2 weight grid, uniform integer activations, calibration-based grid alignment, and approximate-grid quantization.
Implements √2 with a lightweight one-adder approximation, producing a processing element with fewer gates than a 4-bit multiplier.
On Llama-3-8B, improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning by 8.72% relative to PoT and remains within 0.4 percentage points of the uniform integer baseline.
Generalizes across seven models, three bit-widths, and existing LLM post-training quantization frameworks.
papers.selection_reason: Multiplier-free LLM quantization directly targets efficient inference.
papers.title: Fractional Power-of-Two Quantization for Efficient and Effective Multiplier-Free LLM Inference
papers.tldr: FPoT enables practical 4-bit multiplier-free LLM inference by using a fractional base-√2 quantization grid with integer shift-add hardware while substantially reducing PoT accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Point-cloud streams are central to autonomous driving and robotics, yet existing segmentation networks process every frame from scratch, although consecutive frames largely overlap. We observe that the intermediate features of point-cloud transformers remain semantically consistent across frames for the same spatial region, especially in deep stages. Building on this, we present SpaceCache, a training-free feature cache that reuses these features across frames. Tokens of previously observed regions skip a sequence of transformer blocks and take their cached features, only the remaining tokens are computed, and the full token layout is restored for dense prediction. Lightweight cache management keeps reused features reliable by limiting each entry's age and evicting low-confidence entries. Unlike token merging, SpaceCache selects tokens at negligible cost and runs its cache operations once per encoder stage. On both outdoor and indoor benchmarks, such as nuScenes, Waymo, and ScanNet, with two transformer backbones of Utonia and LitePT-B, SpaceCache achieves up to 1.65x speedup with less than 1-point mIoU drop and consistently outperforms token-merging methods.
authors: Dongheon Yang, Beomseok Kang, Jae-Joon Kim
bullets: Addresses redundant frame-by-frame processing caused by substantial overlap in consecutive point-cloud streams.
Uses a training-free cache to let previously observed tokens skip transformer blocks while computing only new or changed tokens.
Maintains reliability by limiting cache-entry age and evicting low-confidence features; cache operations run once per encoder stage.
Evaluated on nuScenes, Waymo, and ScanNet with Utonia and LitePT-B backbones.
Achieves up to 1.65× speedup with less than a 1-point mIoU drop and consistently outperforms token-merging methods.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free feature cache for point-cloud transformer segmentation with token reuse and eviction; relevant to efficient AI and 3D perception.
papers.title: SpaceCache: Intermediate Feature Reuse for Efficient Semantic Segmentation on Point Cloud Streams
papers.tldr: SpaceCache accelerates point-cloud stream segmentation by reusing reliable intermediate transformer features from previously observed spatial regions.

papers.abstract: Synchronous data-parallel training usually assigns every rank the same number of records, even when record costs vary by orders of magnitude. For variable-length models, this converts input variation into idle time because each step waits for its most expensive rank-local batch. We present Batch Cost Lookahead (BCL), a coordination-free data-loading policy that buffers a bounded rank-local window and repartitions it into fixed-cardinality packs with balanced estimated cost. BCL preserves the trainer's record-count contract and requires neither cross-rank metadata exchange nor runtime modification. In simulation over public workload distributions, enabling BCL reduces per-rank estimated batch-cost variability by up to 82.8%. Across 13 NeMo-RL SFT corpora on eight H200 GPUs, rank-local BCL runs 1.050 to 1.167 times faster than pooled MFFD. Compiled H200 measurements on an internal sequence workload show speedups of 1.197 to 1.343 times over packed execution from one to four nodes. We also identify a memory-feasibility boundary: a p99 cap for high-variance or OOM-prone data bounds outliers before BCL balances the rest. These results show that substantial variable-cost imbalance can be removed at the data-loader boundary, while clarifying when data preparation or broader coordination is still necessary.
authors: Tao Huang, Chen Zhu, Antonio Alonso, Daming Li, Adarsh Goura, Jaideep Ray, Yitong Zhou
bullets: Variable-length records can leave ranks idle because each step waits for the most expensive local batch.
BCL buffers a bounded local window and repartitions it into fixed-size packs with balanced estimated cost.
It preserves record-count requirements and operates entirely at the data-loader boundary.
Simulations reduce estimated per-rank batch-cost variability by up to 82.8%; experiments report faster execution across public and internal workloads.
A p99 memory cap is needed for extreme or OOM-prone outliers, and some cases still require data preparation or broader coordination.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces training latency and idle time via workload-balanced data loading, fitting the broad efficient-AI interest in reducing computation and latency.
papers.title: Coordination-Free Workload Regularization for Variable-Cost Distributed Training
papers.tldr: Batch Cost Lookahead reduces variable-cost workload imbalance in synchronous distributed training without cross-rank coordination or trainer changes.

papers.abstract: Dual-system vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a high-frequency fast policy with a slow, expensive module, and published trigger mechanisms for invoking it lack a shared objective, measured costs, and any standard separating schedule quality from module quality. We provide the missing account: invocation is formalized as a calibrated decision problem whose fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated schedules are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value of Intervention (VoI); a renewal baseline proves the optimal schedule periodic under state-independent collapse, with adaptive gains governed by the cost ratio $\rho$ and the dispersion of collapse. Measured systems span three orders of magnitude in $\rho$ (FiS-VLA $0.95$; RoboICL about $10^3$), and a direct test confirms the low-$\rho$ prediction: calibrated gains vanish under homogeneous collapse and grow with heterogeneity. Fourteen closed-loop arms on LIBERO test the contested middle of the continuum ($\rho=1.53$): the adaptive trigger allocates its queries exactly as the threshold rule predicts, yet the language-rewrite channel cannot convert them into success on either suite, and a revert actuator that undoes a failed rewrite is the only intervention with zero net downside on both LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal, where the rewrite deficit deepens from thirteen to forty-two points. A four-measure leak-free protocol cuts apparent early-warning AUC from $0.93$ to $0.62$ on $929$ deployment traces, a detection-limited frontier theorem converts detection quality into a schedulability statement, and a compilation loop turns measured value functions into per-task refresh periods within $2.4\%$ of the closed-loop oracle. Together these results turn slow-module invocation from a design opinion into a measured decision.
authors: Shilin Zhang (North China University of Technology)
bullets: Unifies fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated triggers as special cases of Value of Intervention; periodic scheduling is optimal when collapse is state-independent.
Adaptive scheduling benefits depend on intervention cost relative to fast-policy operation and on heterogeneity in policy collapse.
At intermediate cost (ρ=1.53), the adaptive trigger follows its predicted threshold, but language rewrites fail to improve either LIBERO suite; only reverting failed rewrites avoids net downside.
A leak-free evaluation protocol reduces apparent early-warning AUC from 0.93 to 0.62 across 929 deployment traces.
A detection-limited theorem and compilation loop connect measured intervention value to schedulability and produce refresh periods within 2.4% of a closed-loop oracle.
papers.selection_reason: Formalizes slow-module invocation in dual-system VLA models; relevant to VLA and efficient scheduling of expensive modules.
papers.title: When to Ask for Help: A Decision-Theoretic Account and Measurement Standard for Slow-Module Scheduling in Dual-System Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: Frames slow-module invocation in dual-system VLA models as a calibrated Value-of-Intervention decision problem and introduces a leak-free standard for measuring schedule and intervention quality.

papers.abstract: Spoken Dialogue Models (SDMs) typically share a speech-token space for generation and synthesis, leading to long autoregressive sequences and costly inference. Lower-rate speech tokenizers shorten sequences but may introduce compression-quality trade-offs and costly replacement without breaking this coupling. To address this limitation, we propose CoSTA, a compatibility-preserving post-hoc framework that decouples generation and synthesis token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder. CoSTA extends the generation token space with compressed representations via mean-initialized vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, followed by deterministic expansion back to the original speech-token space before synthesis. On bilingual speech-dialogue benchmarks, CoSTA achieves approximately $1.7\times$ expanded speech-token generation speed, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput while preserving response quality. Analyses show more sustained interaction under limited budgets and a practical trade-off among compression, decoding efficiency, and quality. Further experiments demonstrate cross-architecture transfer and complementarity to low-rate tokenization.
authors: Yingzhuo Deng, Chong Li, Bingxin Liu, Yi Shu, Tianyu Peng, Can Xie, Siyao Song, Shuo Ren, Jiajun Zhang
bullets: Addresses long autoregressive sequences and costly inference caused by tightly coupled generation and synthesis token spaces.
Decouples the token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder.
Uses vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, then deterministically expands compressed tokens before synthesis.
Reports approximately 1.7× faster expanded speech-token generation, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput on bilingual benchmarks.
Supports sustained interaction under limited budgets, transfers across architectures, and complements low-rate tokenization.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient speech-token compression for spoken dialogue models; relevant to efficient inference and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: CoSTA: Compressed Speech Token Adaptation for Efficient Spoken Dialogue Models
papers.tldr: CoSTA makes spoken dialogue generation more efficient by using compressed speech tokens while preserving the original synthesis pipeline and response quality.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) dominate video generation but suffer from high inference cost due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Sparse attention mitigates this by skipping unnecessary computation in the attention matrix, but existing methods apply a fixed sparsity ratio throughout denoising and struggle to accurately determine which computations to skip. To address these limitations, we analyze attention dynamics through attention entropy and mean attention distance, and find that attention becomes increasingly concentrated across denoising steps. We further observe that blocks selected early continue to capture a large fraction of the total attention weight at later steps. These findings suggest two acceleration opportunities: the sparsity ratio should grow as denoising progresses, and earlier search results can be reused to reduce the search space. Based on these findings, we propose Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search (GSRS), a training-free framework that retains more computation early and progressively reduces it later, while restricting subsequent searches to an early candidate set to reduce search overhead. GSRS adopts Top-p selection for adaptive sparsity control, supported by a precise evaluation scheme that computes exact attention weights within the FlashAttention computation at negligible overhead. Experiments on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1 validate that GSRS achieves 1.55$\times$--2.21$\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality comparable to full attention.
authors: Yun Dai, Yuyun Chen, Jiarui Wen, Huiping Zhuang, Cen Chen, Ziqian Zeng
bullets: Video DiTs are slowed by quadratic self-attention, while fixed-sparsity methods poorly reflect changing attention patterns during denoising.
Attention becomes increasingly concentrated over denoising steps, and early-selected blocks retain much of the later attention weight.
GSRS is training-free: it keeps more computation early, reduces it progressively, and restricts later searches to an early candidate set.
Top-p selection provides adaptive sparsity, with exact attention-weight evaluation integrated into FlashAttention at negligible overhead.
Validated on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1, GSRS delivers 1.55×–2.21× speedup while maintaining quality comparable to full attention.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free sparse attention acceleration for video diffusion with growing sparsity and reduced search; relevant to efficient video generation.
papers.title: Sparse Attention for Video Generation Acceleration via Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search
papers.tldr: GSRS accelerates video diffusion Transformers by progressively increasing attention sparsity and reusing early search results, achieving 1.55×–2.21× speedups with comparable quality to full attention.

papers.abstract: Sparse KV compression reduces long-context inference costs by retaining selected historical states, yet these states typically keep their coordinates from the full history. Under Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), gaps left by evicted tokens continue to affect query-key matching, potentially limiting the use of retained evidence. We study post-selection positional geometry on a fixed selector-produced cache, examining how positional organization affects the use of retained information and which coordinate and continuation rules improve answer quality. To reorganize this geometry, we propose RoPERelay, which assigns compact, order-preserving RoPE coordinates, relocates cached key phases through inverse rotation and re-rotation, and synchronizes the current query and subsequent generation. It reuses existing K/V without renewed selection, historical re-prefill, or additional cache budget. Across 36 comparisons spanning two models, six sparse selectors, and three long-term memory tasks, RoPERelay improves answer quality in 32 cases. For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with BM25 on LongMemEval-S, accuracy increases from 23.6% to 35.4%. Measured complete-request time overhead is approximately 1%-3% in the evaluated configurations. These findings establish positional organization as a distinct optimization dimension for sparse KV caches after content selection.
bullets: Sparse KV caches retain selected states, but gaps from evicted tokens can distort RoPE query–key matching.
The method assigns compact, order-preserving coordinates and relocates cached key phases while synchronizing queries and generation.
It operates on a fixed selector-produced cache without renewed selection or historical re-prefill.
Across 36 comparisons, answer quality improved in 32 cases; one reported result rose from 23.6% to 35.4%.
Measured complete-request overhead was approximately 1%–3% in the evaluated configurations.
papers.selection_reason: Directly targets sparse KV cache compression and improves retained-state use through positional reorganization, fitting KV-cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches
papers.tldr: RoPERelay improves sparse KV-cache use by reorganizing RoPE positions after token selection, boosting answer quality without selecting more tokens or increasing cache size.

papers.abstract: Peer review is under strain from the growth of submissions, and review comments written by humans or AI can misstate what a paper says. We introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels such factual errors in review comments under one definition across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences, and that measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. A frontier LLM checks comments well but must read the whole paper for each check, while cheap decision models, which score whether a statement holds in a text, fall far short on whole comments that mix several implicit assertions. PremiseCheck is a framework that combines the two. An LLM rewrites each comment as explicit premises without reading the paper, and a decision model checks each premise against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, PremiseCheck reaches accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across all three fields at about half its cost, and on NLP reviews at a quarter of its cost and less than half its latency.
authors: Dingjie Song, Zhiling Yan, Ziqian Zhang, Yuxuan Zhang, Lichao Sun
bullets: ReviewFact benchmarks factual errors in peer-review comments across NLP, machine learning, and natural sciences, while measuring accuracy, cost, and latency.
Whole-comment checking by cheap decision models performs poorly because comments may contain multiple implicit assertions.
PremiseCheck uses an LLM to extract explicit premises without reading the paper, then applies a decision model to verify each premise against the paper.
It achieves accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across three fields at roughly half the cost; for NLP reviews, it uses about one-quarter the cost and less than half the latency.
The framework is evaluated on comments checked independently; its scope beyond this setting is not established by the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Cost- and latency-aware fact-checking framework that combines an LLM with cheap decision models; relevant to efficient AI inference pipelines.
papers.title: PremiseCheck: Efficient Fact-Checking of Human and AI Peer Reviews
papers.tldr: PremiseCheck efficiently fact-checks human and AI peer-review comments by decomposing them into explicit premises and verifying each against the paper.

papers.abstract: Reasoning-conditioned embeddings can improve retrieval by progressively refining semantic constraints. However, additional reasoning may introduce over-generalized or semantically noisy abstractions that weaken retrieval specificity. Existing methods largely supervise reasoning through final retrieval outcomes, providing limited guidance over the refinement process itself. We propose AURA, a framework that directly supervises intermediate reasoning states according to how well they separate relevant documents from hard distractors. AURA further trains a lightweight utility estimator over prefix-conditioned embeddings to adapt reasoning depth at inference time. On the reasoning-intensive BRIGHT benchmark, AURA-4B achieves 34.7 average nDCG@10 while using 2.8 reasoning steps and 96 generated tokens per query. Under matched deployment conditions, adaptive stopping reduces latency from 4.6 to 0.76 seconds relative to full-trajectory reasoning. Results on MS MARCO further suggest that this specialization need not substantially degrade conventional in-domain retrieval.
authors: Yingtao Luo, Kangyi Zhao, Shiyi Du, Yubo Li
bullets: Reasoning-conditioned embeddings can sharpen retrieval but may become noisy or overly general with additional steps.
AURA supervises intermediate reasoning states by their ability to distinguish relevant documents from hard distractors.
A lightweight utility estimator selects reasoning depth at inference time using prefix-conditioned embeddings.
On BRIGHT, AURA-4B reaches 34.7 average nDCG@10 with 2.8 reasoning steps and 96 generated tokens per query.
Adaptive stopping reduces latency from 4.6 to 0.76 seconds versus full-trajectory reasoning; MS MARCO results suggest limited impact on conventional retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive reasoning-depth control with a utility estimator reduces retrieval latency; fits efficient inference interests.
papers.title: Learning When to Think: Utility-Guided Adaptive Reasoning for Efficient Text Retrieval
papers.tldr: AURA adaptively stops retrieval reasoning when further refinement is no longer useful, improving efficiency while preserving retrieval quality.

papers.abstract: Data selection reallocates training support across visual concepts, including objects, attributes, color, texture, and backgrounds. Different allocation strategies may produce varied downstream model behavior, especially for tail concepts supported by only a few samples. Discarding them can hurt test-time robustness, while overemphasizing samples lying on category boundaries may introduce unstable training signals. This work explicitly investigates this relationship across fine-grained, spurious-correlation, and general image classification, as well as multimodal pretraining. Specifically, we use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract concept activations from individual images. During selection, we accumulate the dataset-level concept support for each added sample. Applying diminishing returns to this distribution down-weights well-represented concepts and shifts the focus to the distribution tail. We then incorporate local support to find samples that reliably strengthen under-supported concepts. Empirical results show consistent improvements over strong data selection baselines across all benchmarks. We also reveal the connection between concepts our method enhances and the induced behavioral changes, including improved robustness against out-of-distribution and spurious contexts. This work establishes concept support, beyond individual sample importance, as a useful principle for data-efficient and robust learning.
authors: Ziheng Zhang, Neha Hulkund, Colin Lee, Zheda Mai, Hui Shen, Ying Ding, Tanya Berger-Wolf, Sara Beery, Wei-Lun Chao, Jianyang Gu
bullets: Data selection can neglect tail concepts or overemphasize category-boundary samples, harming robustness and training stability.
Sparse autoencoders extract visual concept activations from individual images.
A diminishing-returns objective down-weights well-supported concepts and shifts selection toward the concept-support tail.
Local support helps identify samples that reliably strengthen under-supported concepts.
The method consistently outperforms strong selection baselines across classification and multimodal pretraining benchmarks, with improved robustness to out-of-distribution and spurious contexts.
papers.selection_reason: Concept-aware data selection using sparse autoencoders; relevant to efficient training and data-efficient learning.
papers.title: Mind the Tail: Data Selection Through Sparse Concepts
papers.tldr: Select training data by prioritizing samples that support underrepresented visual concepts, improving data efficiency and robustness.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models are notoriously expensive to train, requiring large-scale datasets to learn how to gradually reverse the noise from images over multiple small denoising steps. Current approaches focus on distilling the number of diffusion steps, neglecting potential redundancies of the training data. In this paper, we explore the potential of harnessing eigensamples to train diffusion models on significantly smaller datasets, while preserving model performance. To mitigate the sensitivity to affine transformations of eigenimages, we harness the latent space of a pre-trained CLIP model. We next compute latent eigenvectors by performing principal component analysis (PCA) in CLIP space. Further, we employ eigenvectors as reference points to guide the selection of a representative training set comprising comprising both exemplars (images whose embeddings are closest to eigenvectors) and diverse images. Our comprehensive experiments with different diffusion models applied on multiple datasets indicate that our approach (EigDiff) can reduce training data by up to 14x and accelerate subset selection by up to 1607x, with marginal performance differences.
authors: Andrei Jarca, Vlad Hondru, Florinel-Alin Croitoru, Radu Tudor Ionescu
bullets: Targets redundancy in diffusion-model training data, complementing methods that reduce denoising steps.
Computes PCA eigenvectors in the latent space of a pretrained CLIP model to identify representative samples.
Builds subsets from exemplars closest to eigenvectors plus additional diverse images.
Experiments across multiple diffusion models and datasets reduce training data by up to 14× and accelerate subset selection by up to 1607×.
Reports only marginal performance differences, though results are scoped to the evaluated models and datasets.
papers.selection_reason: Data-efficient diffusion training via CLIP-space eigensample subset selection; directly targets reducing training cost and subset-selection overhead.
papers.title: EigDiff: Eigensample Diffusion - or how to significantly reduce training dataset size with marginal performance variation?
papers.tldr: EigDiff selects a much smaller, representative diffusion-model training set using PCA-derived eigensamples in CLIP space, retaining comparable performance while greatly speeding subset selection.

papers.abstract: Compiler transformations interact, making GPU kernel optimization a search for combinations that preserve the computation while improving performance. We introduce HOW TO TRAIN YOUR LITTLE DRAGON, a training method that teaches a small language model both to construct complete optimization scripts and to improve existing ones. Instead of ranking candidates or generating kernel code, our model generates optimization scripts. We devise a compact, lossless representation whose deterministic decoding reconstructs the exact compiler trace, preserving its transformation parameters and dependencies. We use a compiler framework TVM MetaSchedule to build training data on 54,116 distinct workloads, and construct 108,594 examples in two training sets: 60,236 teach the model to generate an optimized script from an unoptimized kernel, while 48,358 teach it to produce a better script given the kernel and a somewhat optimized script. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to construct and improve optimization scripts from these search-derived examples. We then add reinforcement learning with a shaped reward that combines correctness with measured performance, awarding a latency-based bonus only to numerically correct kernels. We apply this training method to a model with 8 billion parameters. After supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, the model achieves per-attempt correctness of 91.27% for construction and 92.01% for refinement, while reinforcement learning produces faster kernels than supervised training on 88 of 102 construction tasks and 145 of 170 refinement prompts. With only 8B parameters, our LITTLE DRAGON achieves higher per-attempt correctness and better kernel performance than six frontier LLMs: GPT-6 Astra, Opus 5, Kimi-K3, and GLM-5.3 among them, each with hundreds of billions to trillions of parameters, for which task-specific training is unavailable or expensive.
authors: Annabelle Sujun Tang, Wei Tang, Songyao Jiang, Tianhui Li, Shengzhe Xu, Jiin Woo, Kaan Ozkara, Youngsuk Park, Zhen Jia, Hadi Esmaeilzadeh
bullets: Targets compiler-transformation search by generating optimization scripts rather than kernel code or candidate rankings.
Uses a compact lossless representation that deterministically reconstructs exact compiler traces, including parameters and dependencies.
Trains on 108,594 search-derived examples from 54,116 workloads using TVM MetaSchedule.
Combines supervised fine-tuning with correctness-aware, latency-based reinforcement learning.

Reinforcement learning improves kernel speed over supervised training on most evaluated construction and refinement tasks; the 8B model outperforms six much larger frontier LLMs in reported correctness and kernel performance.
papers.selection_reason: Uses a small language model to construct and refine GPU optimization scripts, reducing latency of ML workloads within efficient AI.
papers.title: How to Train Your Little Dragon: Teaching a Small Language Model to Construct and Refine GPU Optimization Scripts
papers.tldr: Little Dragon trains an 8B-parameter language model to construct and refine GPU optimization scripts, achieving high correctness and faster kernels through supervised learning plus reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Occupancy predictors rely on large persistent banks of Gaussians or learned queries whose size is fixed by hand. Common pruning proxies, such as opacity, activation frequency, or parameter magnitude, do not measure whether removing a row changes the model's voxel decisions. We introduce Decision-FLIP, a budget-free compilation framework whose scoring and structure selection need only unlabeled calibration inputs. Exact Mean-FLIP scores each persistent row by the number of voxel argmax decisions that change when the row is removed from the readout; a guarded Otsu split of the log-score distribution selects the survivor count without a target and abstains when the split is unsupported; and the survivors are physically compiled into a smaller checkpoint, so camera sampling, attention, and aggregation shrink with the bank. For streaming banks, scores are integrated over each row's lifecycle through warp, death, and refill. Across four Gaussian-bank model-dataset settings and one persistent-query transfer, the automatically selected cuts remove 12-79% of eligible rows and cut bank/query-dependent latency by 7-45% across settings with component profiles, with whole-model savings of up to 8.0% on the primary endpoints bounded by fixed-cost image, voxel, and sensor modules and peak-memory savings of up to 16.6%. Under matched one-epoch recovery controls, semantic mIoU changes by at most 0.18 point. Same-$K$ controls show that the ranking, not only the bank size, matters: random removal collapses GaussianFormer-1 and OccFormer, while label-free Mean-FLIP matches or outperforms supervised Taylor ranking on all five settings where that control was run. The method applies when removable primitives keep a stable checkpoint-row identity; it is budget-free in survivor count, not parameter-free.
authors: Jingxing Li, Anurag Paul, Subhasis Das, Cindy Xu
bullets: Scores each persistent row by how many voxel argmax decisions change when it is removed, rather than using opacity, activation, or parameter magnitude.
A guarded Otsu split selects survivors automatically and abstains when the score distribution does not support a reliable split.
Across five model–dataset settings, it removes 12–79% of eligible rows, reducing bank/query-dependent latency by 7–45% and peak memory by up to 16.6%.
With matched one-epoch recovery, semantic mIoU changes by at most 0.18 point; ranking quality matters, as random removal can collapse models.
Applies to removable primitives with stable checkpoint-row identities; it is budget-free in survivor count, not parameter-free.
papers.selection_reason: Label-free structured pruning for Gaussian occupancy models; directly relevant to efficient AI through latency and memory reduction.
papers.title: Decision-FLIP: Budget-Free Structured Pruning for Gaussian Occupancy Models
papers.tldr: Decision-FLIP uses unlabeled calibration inputs to identify and physically remove Gaussian or query rows that do not affect voxel decisions, automatically shrinking occupancy models without a preset pruning budget.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding pairs a cheap drafter with parallel verification against the target. At ultra-long context it stops paying, because a drafter that attends over the full prefix inherits the target's context-dependent cost, so the speedup it was meant to provide first erodes and then reverses. The standard response is to build a long-context drafter, by training or fine-tuning one, or by using a multi-token-prediction head shipped inside the target checkpoint. We argue this is unnecessary, because the drafters in use are target-conditioned, reading hidden states the target computed over the entire prefix, so distant context already reaches them without their own attention, and verification corrects what they miss. We therefore freeze released short-context drafters and run them far past their training length under two inference-time mechanisms, one bounding the attention cache they see, which fixes their cost, and one re-basing their rotary position indices into the trained range. No weight is touched and the only tunable saturates early, so one vLLM-side configuration spans 4k to two million tokens, costing at most 0.16x of speedup at short length. We prove when a common index shift leaves the drafter's computation exactly unchanged, and decompose acceptance into two measurable gaps with sharp bounds. Whatever speedup a frozen drafter delivers at short context, it retains out to two million tokens, across three target-drafter pairs and five corpora. The claim concerns the flatness rather than the multiple, and removing either mechanism eliminates it. The gain is conditional on the speculative cost per emitted token staying below the matched target-only cost.
authors: Aref Jafari, Vansh Bhatia, Matt Qin, Subhajit Dutta Chowdhury, Ben Lee, Vikram Appia, Ali Ghodsi, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh
bullets: Long-context drafting becomes uneconomical when the drafter attends over the full prefix.
The approach freezes existing drafters and uses bounded attention-cache visibility plus rotary-position re-basing, with no weight updates.
A single vLLM-side configuration covers 4k–2M-token contexts; tuning saturates early and costs at most 0.16× short-context speedup.
Across three target–drafter pairs and five corpora, the drafter retains its short-context speedup up to two million tokens.
The result concerns stable speedup rather than its absolute magnitude and depends on speculative decoding remaining cheaper per emitted token than target-only decoding.
papers.selection_reason: Long-context speculative decoding with frozen short-context drafters.
papers.title: Long-Context Drafting Does Not Require Long-Context Drafters
papers.tldr: Frozen short-context drafters can support speculative decoding at up to two-million-token contexts when inference-time cache and position handling prevent their cost from growing with context length.

papers.abstract: We investigate whether per-layer, per-task-phase (prompt/reasoning/response) expert-routing statistics in a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model can guide layer-wise mixed-precision quantization of routed-expert FFN tensors (down/gate and up). To attain layerwise routing statistics, we build a routing-capture and profiling pipeline for Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B in ik_llama.cpp, derive a composite sensitivity score from routing entropy/decisiveness, coefficient of variation (CV), Jaccard/phase-fragility, and top-1 expert strength, and use coordinate descent to tune a layer allocation that respects a fixed average bits-per-weight budget. Notably, the profiling pipeline is applicable to standard top-k MoE architectures. Across independent experimental conditions (about 4.0 bpw flat, about 2.7 bpw steep, and about 2.7 bpw random allocation as a control), reallocation fails to outperform the uniform baseline within each quality tier. In the flat regime, reallocation is statistically neutral (z about 0.9). For the steep tier, the random reallocation performs within 1 SE of the routing-guided reallocation at the same tier, indicating a structural loss at this quality rung caused by mandatory downgrades and Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KLD) tail injection. This aggressive-budget condition shows a decisive loss (z greater than 4 SE) replicated across three independent weight vectors. We argue that the deeper issue is that routing-behavior statistics are an unvalidated proxy for true per-layer quantization cost.
bullets: The study tests whether routing entropy, decisiveness, variability, phase fragility, and top-1 expert strength can guide layer-wise bit allocation.
A routing-capture pipeline profiles Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B in ik_llama.cpp and uses coordinate descent under fixed average bit budgets.
Routing-guided reallocation does not outperform uniform allocation in the tested quality tiers; at the flatter budget it is statistically neutral.
At the aggressive budget, mandatory downgrades and KLD-tail injection cause a replicated quality loss, while random reallocation performs similarly to routing-guided allocation.
The results suggest routing behavior is an unvalidated proxy for true per-layer quantization cost.
papers.selection_reason: Quantization sensitivity analysis for efficient MoE LLM inference.
papers.title: Task-Phase-Conditioned Expert Routing Is Not a Reliable Proxy for Quantization Sensitivity in MoE FFN Tensors
papers.tldr: Routing statistics by task phase do not reliably identify which MoE expert FFN layers are most sensitive to mixed-precision quantization.

papers.abstract: Automating organizational work means answering many small typed questions about one piece of state (does this email need a reply, how urgent is it, who owns it) with probabilities good enough to act on without a human. The open typed-decision model we compare against, like a standard cross-encoder, answers each question with a separate pass over the input. We present Verdict-MQ, an open encoder that reads a case once and answers all of its questions: given identical retained state tokens after truncation (verified on every reported case), a structured attention mask makes the state encoding independent of the questions, keeps questions from influencing each other, and makes option order irrelevant by construction. On the typed-decisions benchmark, a 395M Verdict-MQ matches the soft gold labels significantly better than the released 421M Laya specialist on all five fresh seeds (KL 0.080 vs 0.117, Brier 0.045 vs 0.061), an advantage that survives per-system temperature scaling; its higher accuracy (0.801 vs 0.767) lies past the benchmark's own saturation point, so we read that margin as closer agreement with the benchmark's labelling teacher. On RACE, BoolQ and MultiRC, against a matched fine-tuned baseline it wins on MultiRC and loses on RACE and on BoolQ, where its training is unstable; we measure zero-shot references ourselves, including a closed general system (Jev) that beats every fine-tuned encoder. A controlled comparison measures what the shared state costs: giving each question its own question-aware copy of the state gains 0.9-3.5 points on RACE and MultiRC at 1.4-2.5x the per-case latency, and nothing measurable on typed decisions, with the invariance guarantees unchanged.
bullets: Structured attention makes state encoding independent of questions, prevents question interaction, and makes option order irrelevant.
On the typed-decisions benchmark, the 395M model beats the released 421M specialist on soft-label agreement and accuracy across five seeds.
Against a matched fine-tuned baseline, it wins on MultiRC but loses on RACE and BoolQ, where training is unstable.
Question-specific state copies improve RACE and MultiRC by 0.9–3.5 points at 1.4–2.5× latency, but show no measurable benefit on typed decisions.
The study also reports zero-shot references, including a closed general system that outperforms all fine-tuned encoders.
papers.selection_reason: Structured attention mask enables shared state encoding across many questions, reducing per-case latency.
papers.title: Verdict: Encode Once, Decide Many
papers.tldr: Verdict-MQ encodes each case once to answer many typed questions, improving typed-decision calibration and accuracy while trading some performance for lower repeated-processing cost on standard QA tasks.

papers.abstract: Calibrating a conformal prediction set at each early exit does not preserve coverage once a data-dependent exit is selected. We construct one terminal path score from prefix maxima, calibrate a single split-conformal quantile, and return nested prefix sets that all contain the valid terminal set. The guarantee is selection-safe without an alpha/L correction and holds simultaneously for every post-calibration label-free stopping policy that preserves terminal-set containment. We also bound the efficiency cost of the path maximum by the empirical tail of the early-over-terminal score excess. Across eight encoder task-backbone cells, pathwise selection attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814 for naive layerwise selection, with average set size 1.41 and latency fraction 0.71. On CIFAR-100 with a 24-exit ViT-L/16 (n_cal=500), first-eligible stopping at budget b=4 attains coverage 0.902, set size 2.76, and latency fraction 0.57, and the same calibration supports deployment-time budget changes without refitting.
