In a joint exit-count/calibration-size sweep at n=100, pathwise set size moves only from 3.02 to 3.11 as exits increase from 4 to 24, while Bonferroni degenerates to the full label space for 12 or more exits. Paired comparison against MinSE valid selection at (n,L)=(100,24) gives a set-size difference of 0.80 [0.47, 1.13]. Full-vocabulary decoder experiments remain a negative boundary, with sets of 7,162-9,620 tokens. Pathwise calibration is most useful when candidate exits are many relative to calibration size, when budgets change after calibration, and when shallow heads return actionable sets.
authors: Adria Binte Habib, Ibne Farabi Shihab
bullets: Naive layerwise calibration loses coverage after data-dependent exit selection; pathwise calibration attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814.
One split-conformal quantile yields nested prefix sets that contain the valid terminal set, supporting any post-calibration label-free stopping policy preserving containment.
Across eight task-backbone cells, average set size was 1.41 with latency fraction 0.71; on CIFAR-100, budget-4 stopping achieved coverage 0.902, set size 2.76, and latency fraction 0.57.
Pathwise calibration remained stable as exits increased from 4 to 24, while Bonferroni became degenerate at 12 or more exits; deployment budgets can change without refitting.
The approach is less effective for full-vocabulary decoding, producing sets of 7,162–9,620 tokens, and is most useful with many exits, limited calibration data, or actionable shallow-head sets.
papers.selection_reason: Conformal early-exit calibration for latency-efficient inference.
papers.title: Selection-Safe Conformal Early Exit: Distribution-Free Coverage under Adaptive Depth
papers.tldr: A prefix-max pathwise conformal score preserves distribution-free coverage under adaptive early-exit selection without alpha/L correction, while keeping prediction sets efficient across changing budgets.

papers.abstract: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
authors: Shiyu Ji, Peng Ling, Chen Lin, Shupeng Li, Yixuan Wang, Qingfu Zhu, Wanxiang Che
bullets: Targets errors in 2-bit MLA KV caches that affect both attention matching and value reconstruction.
Uses offline calibration with a learned shared rotation and coupled quantization thresholds and reconstruction gains.
Supervises calibration through prediction matching and attention-output matching while keeping model weights frozen.
Achieves the highest average accuracy among compared 2-bit methods across three MLA models and six benchmarks.
On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, delivers 3.96× BF16 KV capacity and 2.51× decode throughput at 256K-token inputs in SGLang.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces rotation and range calibration for 2-bit KV cache quantization in MLA, directly targeting memory-efficient long-context inference.
papers.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention
papers.tldr: RoLaQ improves 2-bit KV-cache quantization for multi-head latent attention by jointly calibrating rotations and quantization ranges, enabling higher accuracy and greater long-context capacity.

papers.abstract: We expand the exponential kernel of attention into a truncated Taylor series of $n$ terms and factorize each term into a tensor-power inner product, which collapses the causal history into exactly $n$ recurrent states, each updated by one rank-one outer product per token and independent of context length $N$. The recursion is lossless with respect to the truncated kernel ($2.2 \times 10^{-16}$ in float64), and the states are additive across chunks ($5.7 \times 10^{-14}$), so prefill admits a parallel scan. Measured exponents are $t \propto N^{2.28}$ for softmax against $N^{0.91}$ for states, with a crossover at $N \approx 728$ and $20.8\times$ at $N = 8192$; per-token decoding latency is constant at $7.3\,\mu$s against $N^{1.04}$ for softmax, giving $76.0\times$ at $N = 65536$. Accuracy improves exponentially in $n$ while cost grows combinatorially, since the $m$-th state is $\binom{d+m-1}{m}$ wide---a bound confirmed by SVD---so the optimum is second order, $n = 3$, at $6.5 \times 10^{-4}$ error and $9{,}945$ elements per head. Query and key normalization is a prerequisite: without it the argument exceeds the convergence radius and adding terms stops helping.
bullets: Approximates the exponential attention kernel with n Taylor terms and tensor-power factorization.
Maintains exactly n recurrent states using one rank-one outer-product update per token, independent of context length.
States combine additively across chunks, enabling parallel-scan prefill and constant per-token decoding latency.
The method scales more favorably than softmax attention for long contexts, with reported speedups up to 20.8× in prefill and 76.0× in decoding.
State width grows combinatorially with order; second order (n = 3) is identified as optimal, while query/key normalization is required for convergence.
papers.selection_reason: Linear-time attention via Taylor expansion with fixed recurrent states.
papers.title: Expanding Attention: A Taylor-Series Route to Linear-Time Transformers with a Fixed Number of Recurrent States
papers.tldr: A truncated Taylor expansion replaces softmax attention with a fixed number of recurrent states, enabling linear-time sequence processing while exposing a cost–accuracy trade-off.

papers.abstract: Sampling from continuous flow-based generators such as flow matching models requires numerical ODE or SDE integration, making inference cost depend on the number of function evaluations (NFEs). In practice, the sampling budget is inherited from prior work or selected through expensive FID-versus-NFE sweeps, using FID to assess image-generation quality, requiring sample generation and evaluation at multiple budgets. This makes sampling-budget selection dependent on repeated empirical evaluation. We therefore ask a complementary question to solver design and timestep allocation: for a fixed pretrained model and solver, what numerical resolution is sufficient? We introduce FLOWBUDGET, a training-free estimator of solver-relative sampling complexity. Using simulation-free interpolation probes of the learned dynamics, FLOWBUDGET normalizes the leading one-step discretization error by the motion, estimates its coefficient from interpolation probes, and maps a numerical tolerance to a step budget using the solver order. We derive estimators for numerical solvers in flow~matching sampling, namely Euler and Heun for ODE sampling and additive-noise Euler--Maruyama for SDE sampling, and connect the ODE coefficients to terminal integration error. Experiments on SiT, FlowDCN and Rectified Flow models, spanning flow-model architectures and formulations, test whether FLOWBUDGET can estimate the NFE budget without generating samples at multiple budgets or performing an FID-versus-NFE sweep. The code is available at https://github.com/Yasaman-dt/FlowBudget
authors: Zahra Dehghani, Pablo Piantanida, Mohammadhadi Shateri
bullets: Addresses the costly, empirical selection of numerical resolution for pretrained flow-based generators.
Uses training-free, simulation-free interpolation probes of learned dynamics to estimate normalized one-step discretization error.
Derives budget estimators for Euler and Heun ODE solvers and additive-noise Euler–Maruyama SDE sampling.
Maps a target numerical tolerance to an NFE budget using solver order and relates ODE estimates to terminal integration error.
Evaluated across SiT, FlowDCN, and Rectified Flow models and formulations.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses efficiency in generative models by estimating sampling budgets for flow matching, a technique relevant to both video generation and efficient inference.
papers.title: FlowBudget: Training-Free Sampling-Budget Estimation for Flow Matching Models
papers.tldr: FLOWBUDGET estimates the sampling NFE budget needed by flow-matching models without repeated sample generation or FID-versus-NFE sweeps.

papers.abstract: Injecting skills into a frozen language model currently costs a million parameters and a reinforcement-learning pipeline. We introduce DecSteer, a System-1 decision operator trained by behavior cloning that lowers this cost by roughly two orders of magnitude. The default operator uses 330K parameters to match a 1.33M-parameter operator trained with reinforcement learning, exceeds or achieve comparable performance, while collapsing 3,685-token deliberation into a 6-token decision with no loss in accuracy. A rank-4 variant with 23K parameters, 1/58 of the strongest published skill operator, suffices for SearchQA and near-suffices for LiveMath, where higher rank still helps; the same recipe transfers across five tasks and three backbones, with out-of-distribution gains persisting on LiveMath problems released months after training. The gap to prior work is trainability, and it is set jointly by initialization and architecture. The initialization of prior operators zeroes the gradient of both large factor matrices at the first optimization step, whereas our zero-initialized output projection inside a shared low-rank backbone receives a gradient immediately, which a gradient-flow probe confirms directly. The gain isn't chain-of-thought compression. 23 of 57 LiveMath points beat the base model's best-of-8 sampling, and a logit-lens probe shows the operator amplifies the answer along the model's existing late-layer pathway, not writing it earlier. Gains track the base model's headroom across 13 base-task pairs, and skills compose as approximately linear operators that can be added, interpolated, and hot-swapped at inference time.
bullets: Reduces operator size from roughly 1.33M to 330K parameters while matching or exceeding the reinforcement-learned baseline; a 23K rank-4 version often suffices.
Compresses deliberation from 3,685 tokens to 6 decision tokens without accuracy loss.
Transfers across five tasks and three backbones, with out-of-distribution gains reported on later-released LiveMath problems.
Improved trainability comes from architecture and initialization: the shared low-rank backbone receives useful gradients immediately.
Operators can be added, interpolated, and hot-swapped, with skill composition behaving approximately linearly.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient low-rank activation steering reduces LLM decision cost by orders of magnitude.
papers.title: Learning to Decide, Not to Reason: Parameter-Efficient Decision Operators via Low-Rank Activation Steering
papers.tldr: DecSteer is a behavior-cloned, low-rank decision operator that equips frozen language models with transferable skills using far fewer parameters and much shorter inference than prior operators.

papers.abstract: Long-context decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, because every output token reads the KV cache of every layer. Sparse decoding reduces this cost by reading only part of the KV cache. We observe that the number of pages a query needs varies widely across KV heads, layers and steps. Fixed budgets are simple, but they are sized for demanding cases and tuned per workload; adaptive budgets follow this variation more flexibly, but existing designs pay for it with extra selection cost or training. At the kernel level, FlashAttention-3 (FA3) and FlashInfer are designed for rows of similar length: with page lists whose length differs per KV head, they either pad the lists (forfeiting much of the sparse saving), leave thread blocks unbalanced, or rely on a host-side plan that runs outside the CUDA graph. We propose MOIRA, a training-free sparse decode path in vLLM whose budget adapts per KV head and per layer. For every request, layer, KV head and step, a coverage rule keeps the smallest set of pages whose estimated attention mass reaches a fraction $γ$. A new kernel, self-planning attention, lets each thread block derive its own share of the work from the list lengths, so the whole decode step stays inside the CUDA graph. On an H200, at RULER's 128k context, MOIRA with $γ=0.99$ matches dense accuracy while reading about 30% of the pages and reduces the time per output token (TPOT) by 2.2-2.5$\times$ relative to dense FA3; with $γ=0.98$ it reduces TPOT by 2.7$\times$ and stays within the noise of dense. Under high serving load it raises throughput by up to 51%. These results suggest that a budget adapted per head and layer, paired with a kernel that keeps such budgets inside the CUDA graph, makes sparse decoding both flexible and fast.
bullets: Long-context decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound because each token accesses every layer’s KV cache.
MOIRA selects the smallest set of pages reaching a target attention-mass coverage per request, layer, KV head, and decoding step.
Its self-planning attention kernel handles variable page-list lengths without padding, imbalance, or host-side CUDA-graph breaks.
On an H200 with 128k-token contexts, it reads about 30% of pages at γ=0.99 and achieves 2.2–2.5× lower TPOT than dense FA3 while matching dense accuracy.
At γ=0.98, TPOT improves by 2.7× and serving throughput increases by up to 51%, according to the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse adaptive-budget KV-cache decoding for long-context LLMs; strong efficiency contribution.
papers.title: MOIRA: Mass-Oriented Indexing with Ragged Attention for Long-Context Decoding
papers.tldr: MOIRA enables fast, training-free long-context decoding by adaptively reading only the KV-cache pages needed by each layer and KV head while preserving dense-model accuracy.

papers.abstract: Existing geometry-aware Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly rely on external 3D encoders to provide structural priors, but executing these additional encoder paths at inference introduces substantial latency and computational overhead. We propose GeoThinker-$F$, an efficient framework that internalizes spatiotemporal perception by transforming causal MLLM hidden states into predictive latent world representations. Our key insight is that intermediate semantic representations contain sufficient information to predict useful representations of current geometry and future semantics, without requiring an exact reproduction of features from a dedicated 3D encoder. To realize this idea, GeoThinker-$F$ adopts a decoupled two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, the MLLM backbone is frozen while lightweight Latent Frame Prediction (LFP) heads learn from an offline 3D geometry expert and next-frame semantic targets. In the second stage, the external expert is removed, and the model is jointly optimized to generate and selectively integrate its self-predicted priors through a specialized Spatial-Grounded Temporal (SGT) Fusion module. Extensive evaluations show that GeoThinker-$F$ eliminates runtime dependence on external 3D geometry encoders while maintaining competitive performance across diverse spatial intelligence benchmarks. It achieves up to a $3.6\times$ inference speedup, reducing latency from $1.45\,\mathrm{s}$ to $0.40\,\mathrm{s}$ while retaining strong spatial reasoning performance.
authors: Haoyuan Li, Qihang Cao, Huanyuan Zhou, Xin Hu, Sijia Chen, Zihan Guo, Kun Xiang, Yunshuang Nie, Tao Tang, Xinlong Zheng, Jia-Wang Bian, Xianming Liu, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Addresses the latency and computational overhead caused by external 3D geometry encoders in geometry-aware MLLMs.
Transforms intermediate MLLM hidden states into predictive representations of current geometry and future semantics.
Uses two-stage training: lightweight latent frame prediction heads first learn from geometry and next-frame semantic targets, then the external expert is removed during joint optimization.
Introduces Spatial-Grounded Temporal Fusion to selectively integrate self-predicted spatial-temporal priors.
Reports latency reduction from 1.45 s to 0.40 s while retaining competitive performance across diverse spatial intelligence benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-aware MLLM with predictive world representations and faster spatial intelligence inference.
papers.title: GeoThinker-$F$: Endogenous Predictive World Representations for Fast Spatial Intelligence
papers.tldr: GeoThinker-F internalizes spatial and temporal world representations in an MLLM, removing external 3D encoders and achieving up to 3.6× faster inference while maintaining strong spatial reasoning.

papers.abstract: Scaling up transformers has produced models with broad capabilities, deployed across heterogeneous hardware and fluctuating workloads. Yet, model families offer only a few fixed sizes (e.g., S, B, L), forcing users to commit to a model based on hardware and latency constraints. This rigidity is often suboptimal under varying query loads. We introduce a retraining-free method that elastifies pre-trained transformers into a single model that adapts on-the-fly across a continuum of computational budgets. Our key contribution is a differentiable relaxation of the functional unit-ranking problem: unlike prior work, which optimizes a single importance weight per MLP block or attention head, we rank every individual MLP neuron and attention head jointly, on a common scale, by minimizing the model's loss under soft pruning across many sparsity targets, all at once. Across 27 vision and text transformer encoders ranging from 22M to 8B parameters, our method yields smooth degradation up to 60% sparsity and outperforms one-shot baselines under deep pruning. For example, pruning DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 to 50% sparsity removes 427M parameters while reducing ImageNet-1k linear-probing accuracy by only 0.8%, without the need for weight correction or retraining. At 60% sparsity, a pruned AugReg ViT-B/16 model achieves up to $1.80\times$ higher throughput and $1.26\times$ lower single-query latency on an A100 GPU. Elastic models are produced in minutes, with construction time scaling sub-linearly with parameter count.
authors: Walter Simoncini, Dheeraj Varghese, Gertjan J. Burghouts, Cees G. M. Snoek
bullets: Addresses the rigidity of offering transformers in only a few fixed sizes under changing hardware and workload constraints.
Jointly ranks individual MLP neurons and attention heads on a shared importance scale using differentiable soft pruning across multiple sparsity targets.
Evaluated on 27 vision and text transformer encoders spanning 22M–8B parameters, with smooth degradation up to 60% sparsity.
Pruning DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 to 50% sparsity removes 427M parameters with only a 0.8% ImageNet-1k linear-probing accuracy drop.
At 60% sparsity, AugReg ViT-B/16 reaches up to 1.80× higher throughput and 1.26× lower single-query latency on an A100; models are built in minutes without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Retraining-free elastic pruning of transformer neurons/heads enables adaptive compute; fits Efficient AI.
papers.title: Your Transformer Is Secretly Elastic
papers.tldr: A retraining-free method turns fixed-size transformers into smoothly adjustable models that trade accuracy for compute across a continuum of sparsity levels.

papers.abstract: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction
authors: Yingfa Chen, Xingyu Shen, Chaojun Xiao, Xu Han
bullets: Targets the memory and attention costs of large KV caches during generation.
Initializes compact caches using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity.
Distills attention outputs and log-normalizers from the full cache, then jointly optimizes the cache while freezing model weights.
Uses only generic document prompts, without downstream questions or answers.
Achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32× compression on a RULER task versus 40.0% for KVZip+, with gains across RULER, LongBench, Phonebook Lookup, Qwen3, and MiniCPM5.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time training compresses KV caches for long contexts; directly fits KV-cache efficiency and test-time learning.
papers.title: Latent Compaction with Test-Time Training
papers.tldr: Latent Compaction uses document-specific test-time training to compress KV caches while preserving long-context retrieval accuracy.

papers.abstract: We introduce an approach for self-supervised representation learning designed to be used as a tokenizer for generative modeling. Our objective supervises a representation loss by factorizing the pointwise mutual information of the data, which we estimate by taking information differences between conditional predictions from a learned generative model. We justify our algorithm theoretically and empirically, demonstrating that our generative approach to representation learning avoids dimensional collapse and feature suppression in cases where commonly used methods like DINO and LeJEPA fail. Moreover, we show our representation learning technique is scalable; expending more compute leads to predictably better latent tokenization. For the first time, we perform a careful analysis of the combined flop efficiency of tokenizer and generative model and demonstrate that our approach is a compute-optimal improvement over direct diffusion for pixel-space generation, obtaining an FID-50K of 2.18 with JiT-L. Applied to ImageNet and the text-to-image dataset GPIC, we show tokenizer encoder scaling laws for diffusability, where extrapolating our approach achieves representations in 7x fewer FLOPs than DINOv2 on ImageNet and 8x fewer FLOPs than WebSSL on GPIC.
authors: Alan Baade, Kyle Sargent, Vincent Sitzmann, Eric Ryan Chan, Justin Johnson, Li Fei-Fei, Gordon Wetzstein
bullets: Factorizes pointwise mutual information using information differences between conditional predictions from a learned generative model.
Theoretically and empirically avoids dimensional collapse and feature suppression observed with DINO and LeJEPA in tested settings.
Scaling compute yields predictably better latent tokenization and favorable tokenizer–generator compute trade-offs.
Achieves FID-50K 2.18 with JiT-L and reports projected 7× and 8× lower FLOPs than DINOv2 and WebSSL for studied datasets.
Scope includes ImageNet, GPIC, and pixel-space diffusion comparisons; some efficiency claims rely on extrapolation.
papers.selection_reason: Latent tokenization with compute-optimal efficiency analysis; transferable to efficient generative modeling.
papers.title: Generative Representation Learning for Scalable Latent Tokenization
papers.tldr: A generative self-supervised objective produces scalable latent tokenizers that avoid representation collapse and improve compute efficiency for image generation.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting multiple tokens per step, yet feature-based drafters rely on target hidden features whose contextual emphasis may not align with the needs of subsequent draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models maintain compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, offering an efficient source of complementary context for speculative drafting. We introduce ReaDy, the first speculative decoding method, to the best of our knowledge, to leverage HLA recurrent states for position-specific context retrieval during drafting. ReaDy equips each draft position with a learned query to retrieve supplementary context directly from the target's committed recurrent states. A lightweight state reader integrates this context into draft representations through residual updates, while low-rank state reads and fused operators keep additional computation and I/O overhead low. Building on DSpark's parallel backbone and sequential prediction head, ReaDy employs a lightweight two-stage adaptation strategy, with reader capacity, state sources, and residual placement examined through ablation studies. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and dialogue, ReaDy achieves an average $3.16\times$ decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3.8-27B on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. It outperforms DSpark on every benchmark, improving throughput by 7.97% and acceptance length by 8.50% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/StartLuxLabs/ReaDy.
authors: Bohan Sun, Zunhai Su, Xialie Zhuang, Jianjin Li, Ngai Wong, Chuan-Wei Kuo
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between target hidden features and the contextual needs of later draft positions.
Uses learned per-position queries and a lightweight state reader to retrieve and fuse supplementary context via residual updates.
Reduces overhead with low-rank state reads and fused operators, building on DSpark’s parallel backbone and sequential prediction head.
Across seven math, code, and dialogue benchmarks, reports a 3.16× average speedup over autoregressive decoding on Qwen3.8-27B.
Outperforms DSpark on all benchmarks, with average throughput and acceptance-length gains of 7.97% and 8.50%, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Speculative decoding using recurrent states in hybrid linear attention LLMs; directly relevant to efficient attention, memory-efficient inference, and LLM architecture.
papers.title: ReaDy: Recurrent States as Dynamic Context for Speculative Drafting in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models
papers.tldr: ReaDy accelerates speculative decoding in hybrid linear-attention LLMs by retrieving position-specific context from the target model’s recurrent states.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM generation through lightweight drafting and parallel verification. It is particularly promising for long inputs, where KV-cache access costs can be amortized over multiple accepted tokens. Yet most drafters are trained on short sequences and degrade on long inputs, while long-context training is costly. Existing training-free approaches restrict the context window, rescale positions, or augment recent context with retrieved distant entries. Drafters, however, read target hidden states that already encode contextual and positional information, and their lightweight architecture makes full-history attention affordable. We propose FOLD, a training-free method that preserves exact local positions and treats all distant entries as far memory at a shared position. To counter attention dilution as the memory grows, we sharpen attention within it to emphasize relevant entries while separately controlling its total weight relative to the local window. Across six target-drafter pairs and diverse benchmarks of up to 256K tokens, FOLD predominantly delivers the highest speedup, with the best case more than doubling the speedup over autoregressive decoding, from 2.08$\times$ to 4.22$\times$.
authors: Shuxuan Li, Jialiang Kang, Yanghao Zhou, Ziye Zhu, Xiao Yang
bullets: Addresses drafter degradation on long inputs without costly long-context training.
Preserves exact positions for recent tokens while assigning distant entries a shared far-memory position.
Sharpens attention over distant memory and controls its total influence to reduce attention dilution.
Evaluated across six target–drafter pairs and benchmarks up to 256K tokens.
Predominantly achieved the highest speedups; the best case improved from 2.08× to 4.22× over autoregressive decoding.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free long-context speculative decoding with position-free far memory; fits KV-cache efficiency and long-context language modeling.
papers.title: FOLD: Position-Free Far Memory with Local Order for Long-Context Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: FOLD is a training-free long-context speculative-decoding method that improves drafting by combining exact local positions with sharpened, weight-controlled far-memory attention.

papers.abstract: With the rapid development of vision-language models (VLMs), Web-GUI agents have achieved promising performance in interacting with real-world interfaces through screenshot-based grounding. However, high-resolution screenshots and multi-turn histories introduce excessive visual tokens, causing substantial inference overhead. Existing token pruning methods, mainly designed for natural images, often select tokens independently based on importance scores, which can fragment the local visual structures required for recognizing small GUI elements such as buttons, icons, and hyperlinks. In this work, we propose STP-GUI (Spatially-aware Token Pruning for GUI agents), a query-guided token pruning framework that preserves fine-grained instruction-conditioned token scoring while performing spatially coherent window-level selection under aggressive token reduction. A lightweight selector is optimized through policy learning while the VLM backbone remains frozen. Experiments on Online-Mind2Web show that \papername achieves a favorable efficiency-performance tradeoff under low token budgets. At 21% token retention, it preserves 77.7% of full-token performance while reducing inference latency by 31% and FLOPs by 57%. Results on Android in the Wild further suggest that the method transfers to mobile GUI environments.
authors: Shuo Wang, Sifan Zhou, Xiaobo Wang, Tianyu Fu, Chenxu Zhao, Anyang Su, Hanning Wang, Ping Jiang, Minghui Wu
bullets: Addresses inference overhead from high-resolution screenshots and multi-turn visual histories.
Uses query-guided token scoring with spatial window-level selection to avoid fragmenting small GUI elements.
Trains a lightweight selector with policy learning while keeping the VLM backbone frozen.
On Online-Mind2Web, retaining 21% of tokens preserves 77.7% of full-token performance, reducing latency by 31% and FLOPs by 57%.
Results on Android in the Wild suggest transfer to mobile GUI environments.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Spatially-Aware Token Pruning (STP-GUI) for VLMs, preserving fine-grained visual structures required for GUI agents while significantly reducing inference overhead.
papers.title: STP-GUI: Spatially-Aware Token Pruning for Efficient Web-GUI Agents
papers.tldr: STP-GUI makes Web-GUI agents more efficient by pruning screenshot tokens in spatially coherent, instruction-guided windows while preserving important interface structures.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models activate only a few experts per token, yet all expert weights must be stored. Mixed-precision quantization reduces this storage cost by assigning higher bit-widths to sensitive experts and lower bit-widths to resilient ones, but expert rankings alone do not determine how strongly to weight their errors. To address this gap, we propose NatScale, a contrast-calibrated allocation framework for mixed-precision MoE quantization. It uses a model-specific power transformation to calibrate gradient-based expert weights to an information-theoretic contrast target while preserving rankings. We jointly evaluate each expert's gate, up and down configurations to estimate its output error. We then combine these errors and calibrated weights with an existing prior based on weight spectra, variance and precision decay to select configurations under a storage budget. Across three models, NatScale achieves the lowest native-to-quantized KL divergence and the highest top-token agreement in all nine settings against five allocation baselines. It also yields the lowest perplexity in seven settings. These findings highlight the importance of objective-aware precision allocation.
authors: Renjie Xie, Juncheng Yang, Aoting Hu, Yan Liang, Mingxi Zhang, Zheheng Hong, Wei Xu, Yanzhi Chen
bullets: MoE models require storing all expert weights, making quantization important despite sparse activation.
Expert sensitivity rankings do not indicate how strongly each expert’s errors should affect precision allocation.
NatScale applies a model-specific power transformation to calibrate gradient-based weights while preserving rankings.
It jointly evaluates experts’ gate, up, and down configurations, combining output errors with calibrated weights and prior statistics.
Across three models and nine settings, it achieved the lowest KL divergence and highest top-token agreement in every setting, plus the lowest perplexity in seven.
papers.selection_reason: Mixed-precision quantization for MoE LLMs reduces model memory, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Beyond Expert Rankings: Contrast Calibration for Mixed-Precision MoE Quantization
papers.tldr: NatScale improves mixed-precision MoE quantization by calibrating expert importance weights to better allocate precision under a storage budget.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference. This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training. Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training. Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at $256 \times 256$ resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of $1.19$ among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming.
authors: Woobin Park, Jaeyeon Kim, Yilun Du, Sitan Chen, Bohyung Han
bullets: One-step generators avoid costly multi-step inference but are difficult to train directly with distributional objectives.
The method uses two stages: fixed-noise reconstruction training, followed by feature-space distributional post-training.
The reconstruction stage alone removes the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, according to the authors.
Experiments span class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, improving the training-compute/quality trade-off.
On ImageNet 256×256, the model reports a one-step FID of 1.19 using about one-tenth the training compute of comparable prior methods.
papers.selection_reason: One-step generator training reduces inference compute and improves the training-compute/quality Pareto frontier, relevant to efficient generative modeling and world modeling applications.
papers.title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?
papers.tldr: Priming Models make one-step generation simpler and more compute-efficient by pretraining with reconstruction before feature-space distributional training.

papers.abstract: Orthogonal transforms have emerged as an effective tool for low-bit quantization of large language models (LLMs), as they reshape activation distributions without changing the underlying model function. Existing approaches typically rely either on fixed data-agnostic transforms, such as Hadamard rotations, or on calibration-time optimization of learned rotations. We study rotation selection from first principles and show that maximizing covariance leads to spectral alignment and provides a principled criterion for constructing quantization-friendly orthogonal transforms. Based on this insight, we propose SpectrumQuant, a closed-form rotation method that estimates activation covariance from calibration data and uses it to construct a covariance-aware orthogonal transform for post-training quantization. Our formulation characterizes quantization-friendly rotations as compositions of alignment and mixing components, while recovering Hadamard matrices as a special case. Interestingly, a class of butterfly matrices belongs to this category. In the realm of LLM quantization, SpectrumQuant bridges the gap between data-agnostic structured rotations and learned rotations, providing an effective and efficient data-aware alternative for post-training quantization. Experiments on Llama and Mistral models show that SpectrumQuant is competitive with state-of-the-art rotation strategies while requiring less than one-third of the GPU memory and significantly less time than learned rotations approaches like SpinQuant and DartQuant.
authors: Dwaipayan Haldar, Indranil Patra, Azhar Yousuf, Chandra Sekhar Seelamantula
bullets: Identifies covariance maximization and spectral alignment as principles for selecting effective orthogonal transforms.
Builds a covariance-aware rotation from calibration activations without calibration-time optimization of learned rotations.
Unifies alignment and mixing components, recovering Hadamard matrices as a special case and including some butterfly matrices.
On Llama and Mistral, is competitive with state-of-the-art rotation methods while using less than one-third the GPU memory and substantially less time than SpinQuant and DartQuant.
Targets efficient, data-aware post-training quantization rather than fully data-agnostic or learned rotation strategies.
papers.selection_reason: Covariance-aware orthogonal rotations for low-bit LLM quantization reduce memory and time, fitting the efficient AI research interest.
papers.title: SpectrumQuant: Spectrum Alignment for LLM Quantization
papers.tldr: SpectrumQuant uses calibration-data covariance to construct closed-form, quantization-friendly rotations for efficient low-bit LLM post-training quantization.

papers.abstract: Parallel drafters such as DFlash and DSpark reduce proposal latency, but early mismatches limit how much of each block can be accepted. Retaining alternatives introduces parent states and candidate choices that reference-conditioned training does not directly supervise. We introduce TreeSpark, a unified training and inference framework extending the semi-autoregressive DSpark architecture. It constructs parent-conditioned candidate trees from one backbone pass and replays their expansion, pruning, and budgeted packing during training. Survival negative log-likelihood weights retained edges by reference-derived path mass, while a capped coverage hinge promotes target-important alternatives near local selection boundaries. Both objectives reuse reference-chain target distributions without additional target forward passes. We evaluate greedy decoding with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on nine general benchmarks and six writing domains. Across targets and suites, TreeSpark improves mean acceptance length over DSpark by 23.4% to 31.6% and mean single-request throughput by 15.1% to 25.0%. Batched Qwen3-4B throughput improves by 12.6% to 17.2%. At fixed attention capacity and inference policy, the proposed supervision further improves mean acceptance length by approximately 6.4% and mean system throughput by 4.2% to 5.0% on Qwen3-4B.
authors: Jihao Zhao, Qianyu Jiang, Shuaishuai Zu, Pengfei Li, Guanghuan Fang, Ben Feng, Biao Qin, Zhibin Wang, Baochuan Yang
bullets: Addresses early proposal mismatches and the lack of direct supervision for parent states and alternative candidates.
Extends semi-autoregressive DSpark by constructing parent-conditioned trees from one backbone pass and replaying their expansion, pruning, and packing during training.
Uses survival negative log-likelihood weighted by reference-derived path mass plus a capped coverage hinge for target-important alternatives, without extra target forward passes.
Across Qwen3-4B/8B, nine general benchmarks, and six writing domains, improves mean acceptance length by 23.4–31.6% and single-request throughput by 15.1–25.0% over DSpark.
Also improves batched Qwen3-4B throughput by 12.6–17.2%; under fixed attention capacity and policy, gains are about 6.4% in acceptance length and 4.2–5.0% in system throughput.
papers.selection_reason: TreeSpark improves speculative decoding via parent-conditioned candidate trees and new training objectives; relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: TreeSpark: Learning to Draft the Trees You Verify for Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: TreeSpark trains speculative decoders to draft and prioritize alternative candidate trees, substantially improving acceptance length and throughput over DSpark.

papers.abstract: Current video object removal methods suffer from prohibitive latency (minutes per video) and non-causal processing that prevents real-time interaction. We present StreamErase, enabling sub-second latency with up to 26 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU. Our approach first augments a text-to-video model with mask input to generate high-quality videos that erase target objects and synthesize coherent backgrounds, but does not perform inference on the fly. As such, we progressively transfer the erasing capability from a powerful bidirectional foundation model to an efficient unidirectional streaming eraser, enabling long-horizon erasing without sacrificing visual fidelity. Several key challenges arise when generating videos over long, potentially infinite horizons: (1) bridging the domain gap from training on finite length and extrapolating to long horizons, (2) sustaining high quality by preventing error accumulation, and (3) maintaining fast inference, without increasing computational cost as the context grows. To address these challenges, we carefully designed sliding-window causal attention with attention sinks. By incorporating self-rollout with attention sinks and KV cache rolling during training, we simulate inference-time extrapolations with a fixed context window, enabling constant-speed generation of arbitrarily long videos. Finally, we establish a dedicated benchmark, LongErase, for streaming long-video object removal. Our model achieves strong performance compared to existing video object erasing models and generalizes well to real-world video scenarios, uniquely enabling infinite-length streaming. With StreamErase, users can input a mask and see the erasing results unfold in real-time, delivering a truly interactive experience.
authors: Zhuobai Dong, Xiaobing Tu, Xiantao Zhang, Jinkui Ren, Yinggui Wang, Yue Ma, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high latency and non-causal processing of existing video object removal methods.
Transfers erasing capability from a text-to-video foundation model to an efficient unidirectional streaming eraser.
Uses sliding-window causal attention, attention sinks, self-rollout, and KV-cache rolling to maintain fixed-context, constant-speed generation.
Reports sub-second latency and up to 26 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU.
Introduces the LongErase benchmark and supports interactive, infinite-length video erasing with strong real-world generalization.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming video object removal with causal attention, attention sinks, and KV cache rolling directly targets video generation and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: StreamErase: Towards Ultra-Fast Streaming Video Erasing
papers.tldr: StreamErase enables real-time, arbitrarily long video object removal by distilling bidirectional erasing quality into a causal streaming model.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are moving onto edge devices, but little is known about how much energy they draw on single-board computers with NPU or GPU accelerators, or where that energy goes. We measure total-system energy, latency, and thermal behavior of Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and its text-only sibling on a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Hailo-10H NPU and on a Jetson Orin Nano Super, on both CPU and accelerator, and separate the fixed energy of each request from the energy that grows with output length. Because the accelerators use different quantization and serving software, we compare deployment stacks rather than silicon. Three findings stand out. First, NPU offloading makes the Pi a much more efficient VLM platform: it cuts energy per generated token by about two-thirds, leaves the host CPU largely free, and avoids the thermal throttling that the CPU backend reaches in sustained use. Second, an image adds both fixed and per-token energy, but at typical response lengths generating the answer costs far more than processing the image. Third, the Jetson GPU favors short responses through its lower fixed cost per request, whereas the Pi NPU favors longer ones through its lower cost per output token; their energy curves cross near 40 output tokens.
authors: Junlin Liao, Harshit Kondle, Di Liu, Zonghua Gu
bullets: Measures system energy, latency, and thermal behavior across Raspberry Pi 5 CPU/NPU and Jetson Orin Nano Super CPU/GPU deployments.
Separates fixed per-request energy from energy that scales with generated output length, while comparing deployment stacks rather than hardware alone.
Pi NPU offloading reduces energy per generated token by about two-thirds and prevents the thermal throttling seen with sustained CPU inference.
Image inputs increase both fixed and per-token energy, but answer generation typically dominates total energy at common response lengths.
Jetson GPU has lower fixed request cost; Pi NPU has lower per-token cost, with energy curves crossing near 40 output tokens.
papers.selection_reason: Characterizes the energy efficiency, latency, and thermal behavior of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on edge hardware, directly addressing efficiency and multimodal deployment.
papers.title: Seeing at the Edge: Energy Characterization of Vision-Language Model Inference on Edge Platforms
papers.tldr: NPU acceleration makes Raspberry Pi 5 inference for a 2B vision-language model substantially more energy-efficient and thermally stable, while Jetson GPU is better for short responses.

papers.abstract: We present several advances on neural operators by viewing the action of operator layers as the minimizers of Bregman regularized optimization problems over Banach function spaces. The proposed framework allows interpreting the activation operators as Bregman proximity operators from dual to primal space. This novel viewpoint is general enough to recover classical neural operators as well as a new variant, coined Bregman neural operators, which includes the inverse activation operator and features the same expressivity of standard neural operators. Numerical experiments support the added benefits of the Bregman variant of Fourier neural operators for training deeper and more accurate models.
authors: Abdel-Rahim Mezidi, Jordan Patracone, Saverio Salzo, Amaury Habrard, Massimiliano Pontil, Remi Emonet, Marc Sebban
bullets: Recasts neural-operator layers as minimizers of Bregman-regularized problems on Banach function spaces.
Interprets activation operators as Bregman proximity operators mapping dual spaces to primal spaces.
Recovers classical neural operators and defines a new Bregman neural operator with an inverse activation operator.
The Bregman variant retains the expressivity of standard neural operators.
Experiments indicate improved training of deeper and more accurate Fourier neural operator models.
papers.selection_reason: Characterizes the energy efficiency, latency, and thermal behavior of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on edge hardware, directly addressing efficiency and multimodal deployment.
papers.title: A Bregman Proximal Viewpoint on Neural Operators
papers.tldr: A Bregman-optimization perspective generalizes neural operators and introduces a Bregman variant that supports deeper, more accurate Fourier neural operator models.

papers.abstract: Accurate nuclei segmentation underpins quantitative computational pathology, yet remains challenging due to morphological variability, weak boundaries, nuclear crowding, and pronounced domain shifts arising from differences in tissue preparation, staining, and acquisition. While deep learning and recent foundation models have improved segmentation performance under matched distributions with the original training data, their generalization across heterogeneous histopathology domains remains limited. We introduce GDBA-Net, a parameter-efficient nuclei segmentation framework built around the proposed Gated Dual-Branch Adapter (GDBA). GDBA-Net adapts a frozen SAM2 encoder by integrating pretrained semantic representations with explicit frequency-derived structural priors. The complementary representations are independently transformed through Grid MLP branches and dynamically integrated using sample-adaptive channel-wise gating, selectively emphasizing structural cues relevant to nuclear delineation. Despite using only 4.3 million trainable parameters, GDBA-Net achieves state-of-the-art in-dataset performance and consistently superior cross-dataset generalization across six diverse nuclei segmentation benchmarks under fully supervised, cross-dataset, and five-shot adaptation protocols, outperforming competing CNN-, transformer-, and foundation model based methods. Comprehensive ablations confirm that these gains arise from the coordinated design of semantic-frequency complementarity and adaptive gating rather than increased model capacity. By uniting transferable semantic representations with explicit structural priors, GDBA-Net provides a robust, annotation-efficient solution to domain variability in nuclei segmentation. https://github.com/biplabpoudel25/GDBA_Net
authors: Biplab Poudel, Betserai Albert Magarire, Anish Kumar Shah, Jiacheng Xie, Dong Xu
bullets: Addresses domain shifts caused by tissue preparation, staining, acquisition, and challenging nuclear morphology.
Uses a parameter-efficient Gated Dual-Branch Adapter to combine pretrained semantic representations with frequency-derived structural priors.
Grid MLP branches independently transform the complementary features, while sample-adaptive channel gating selects relevant cues for delineation.
Reports state-of-the-art in-dataset performance and stronger cross-dataset generalization across six benchmarks under supervised, cross-dataset, and five-shot adaptation settings.
Ablations attribute the gains to semantic–frequency complementarity and adaptive gating rather than increased model capacity.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient gated adapter for SAM2 segmentation, transferable to efficient adaptation of vision foundation models.
papers.title: GDBA-Net: A Gated Dual-Branch Adaptation of SAM2 for Robust Cross-Domain Nuclei Segmentation
papers.tldr: GDBA-Net improves nuclei segmentation across diverse histopathology domains by efficiently adapting a frozen SAM2 encoder with gated semantic and frequency-based structural features.

papers.abstract: Transformers can perform in-context reinforcement learning without parameter updates. However, existing theoretical constructions often require context sizes that grow with the number of sampled transitions, leading to increasing memory costs in large-scale problems. This raises a fundamental scalability question: how much context is intrinsically necessary to carry out such learning? We answer this question for fixed-policy TD evaluation. We show that, with a shared linear decoder, the minimum context dimension required to exactly reproduce the first $L$ TD iterates is the Krylov dimension induced by the sampled transitions. When the available context dimension $m$ falls below this threshold, exact reproduction is no longer possible. In this regime, we characterize the optimal approximation error and show that it decays as $\Theta(\gamma^m\max\{1,1/(m(1-\gamma))\})$ where $\gamma$ is the discounting factor. Moving from representation complexity to actual memory cost, we characterize the optimal retained memory for exact continuous representations as $\Theta(nk_L)$ and show experimentally that on a sampled task whose exact rank is full but whose numerical rank is small, a context accurate to $10^{-2}$ is $88.7\%$ smaller than the sparse sufficient statistics of TD. Finally, we establish the learnability of the shared executor through pretraining by proving global convergence of an auxiliary objective over effective attention parameters under suitable task diversity. Experiments across diverse TD evaluation problems validate parameter recovery and the predicted context--accuracy tradeoff.
authors: Yajie Zhao, Yingjun Mo, Zhiyong Wang, Bo Tang, Chao Xu, Fang Kong
bullets: For fixed-policy TD evaluation with a shared linear decoder, exact reproduction of the first L TD iterates requires context dimension equal to the transitions’ induced Krylov dimension.
Below this threshold, exact reproduction is impossible; the optimal approximation error decays as Θ(γ^m max{1, 1/[m(1−γ)]}).
The optimal retained memory for exact continuous representations scales as Θ(nk_L).
On a sampled task with full exact rank but low numerical rank, context accurate to 10⁻² used 88.7% less memory than TD’s sparse sufficient statistics.
The paper also proves global convergence for pretraining the shared executor under suitable task diversity, with experiments validating parameter recovery and the context–accuracy tradeoff.
papers.selection_reason: Provable transformer context compression and memory-accuracy tradeoffs directly relate to efficient token/context handling.
papers.title: Provable Transformer Context Compression for In-Context Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes the minimum context and memory needed for transformers to reproduce or approximate TD-learning iterates in-context, and shows substantial compression is possible when sampled transitions have low numerical rank.

papers.abstract: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine parameter reuse with sparse computation to improve performance under matched budgets. Prior work demonstrates that different loop visits can play different roles even when they share parameters. To probe the contributions of different loop visits, we learn separate residual coefficients in a model that applies a shared block twice, observing a smaller scale in the first visit. Fixed coefficient experiments show that reducing the first visit's scale preserves or improves performance, whereas the same reductions to the second hurt it. This asymmetry motivates us to explore asymmetric compute allocation. We propose \textbf{LatentLoop}, which compresses the first visit's sequence, retains full resolution in the second, and reallocates saved computation to increase the hidden size. We further learn how strongly the first visit updates the full sequence, and share MoE weights across visits while using separate attention parameters to accommodate their different sequence resolutions. Across 15 configurations spanning 1.3B--7B parameters, with the largest budget exceeding $10^{21}$ FLOPs, LatentLoop consistently lowers validation NLL. At a fitted NLL of 1.988, predicted compute savings are 19.0\% and 7.9\% relative to vanilla MoE and the looped baseline. It also improves average scores on nine benchmarks at all sizes in 0-shot and 5-shot settings. These results suggest asymmetric compute allocation is a promising direction for looped MoE models.
authors: Zefeng He, Yunkai Chai, Xiaoyang Chen, Tong Zhu, Zongliang Wu, Yun Luo, Yafu Li, Yu Cheng
bullets: Different loop visits contribute asymmetrically: reducing computation in the first visit is less harmful than reducing it in the second.
The method compresses the first visit’s sequence, keeps the second at full resolution, and increases hidden size with the saved compute.
It learns the first visit’s update strength, shares MoE weights across visits, and uses separate attention parameters for differing resolutions.
Across 15 configurations from 1.3B to 7B parameters, it consistently lowers validation NLL and improves average scores on nine benchmarks in 0-shot and 5-shot settings.
At fitted NLL 1.988, it predicts 19.0% and 7.9% compute savings versus vanilla MoE and the looped baseline, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Looped MoE language model architecture with asymmetric compute allocation and sequence compression for efficiency.
papers.title: LatentLoop: Scaling Looped MoE Models with Asymmetric Compute Allocation
papers.tldr: LatentLoop improves looped MoE efficiency by compressing the first loop visit and reallocating its saved computation to model capacity.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly predict future visual states and robot actions, but processing dense future-frame tokens incurs substantial inference latency. We propose CF-Prune, a training-free framework for pruning future-frame tokens in pretrained WAMs. Our key insight is that future visual predictions support action generation and therefore need not preserve every visual detail required for high-fidelity video synthesis. CF-Prune combines instruction and action attention to identify task-relevant tokens during the initial denoising forward pass, even when future-frame and action representations remain highly noisy. An entropy-based phase identification mechanism further retains dense computation during precision phases to mitigate pruning-induced performance degradation. Experiments on RoboLab, RoboCasa, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent inference speedups. At a 35% pruning ratio, CF-Prune achieves average speedups of 1.19-1.27x while improving task success rates. At a 50% pruning ratio, it achieves 1.29-1.33x average speedups on both simulation benchmarks, with overall success rates within 1.0 percentage point of the baseline.
authors: Baekseung Kim, Junhoo Lee, Sohyeon Hong, Suhyun Jeon, Minkyu Kim, Seungyeon Kim, Donghoon Han, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses high inference latency from dense future-frame token processing in world action models.
Uses instruction and action attention to identify task-relevant tokens during early denoising, without training.
An entropy-based phase mechanism keeps dense computation during precision-sensitive phases.
At 35% pruning, it delivers 1.19–1.27× speedups while improving task success rates.
At 50% pruning, it reaches 1.29–1.33× speedups on simulation benchmarks with success within 1.0 percentage point of baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free future-frame token pruning for world action models, improving inference efficiency on manipulation tasks.
papers.title: Complementary Future Token Pruning for World Action Models
papers.tldr: CF-Prune accelerates pretrained world action models by pruning less task-relevant future-visual tokens while preserving robot-action performance.

papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to scale, their energy consumption during inference has become a critical concern. While Autoregressive (AR) models are the industry standard, Diffusion Language Models (DLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative capable of parallel token generation. In this paper, we perform a comparative energy benchmark of diffusion models (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B) against AR counterparts (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B). We analyze the trade-offs between model architecture, KV-cache optimization, and Joules-per-token efficiency. Our results show that at longer sequences (200--600 tokens), diffusion models achieve 2.5--2.7 J/token, approximately 2$\times$ more efficient than AR models with KV-cache (5.3--5.7 J/token). KV-cache provides substantial benefits for AR models at longer sequences (50--70\% energy reduction).
bullets: Compares energy use during inference for diffusion models LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B with AR models Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B.
Analyzes architecture, KV-cache optimization, and joules-per-token efficiency.
For 200–600-token sequences, diffusion models use 2.5–2.7 J/token versus 5.3–5.7 J/token for AR models with KV-cache.
KV-cache reduces AR energy consumption by 50–70% at longer sequence lengths.
Scope is limited to the evaluated models and sequence lengths.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks energy consumption and KV-cache efficiency of diffusion versus autoregressive language models, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Energy Consumption Analysis of Discrete Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models
papers.tldr: Diffusion language models can use roughly half the inference energy per token of autoregressive models on longer sequences, while KV-cache substantially improves AR efficiency.

papers.abstract: Memory-efficient subspace optimization has emerged as a practical approach to reducing the memory cost of LLM training while preserving optimization performance. Previous algorithms typically rely on the leading singular subspace of stochastic gradients, yet the gradient noise may dominate the subspace in later training stages and can prevent convergence. To overcome this limitation, we adopt a residual correction framework, which maintains the optimizer states in the subspace and adds the orthogonal residual gradient to the parameter update. We first integrate this scheme into momentum SGD to develop SMRC, which attains an $O(T^{-1/4})$ convergence rate for a fixed orthonormal basis, matching that of full-space momentum SGD. Our analysis introduces a subspace virtual iterate to resolve the coupling between the momentum and the residual correction. Furthermore, we extend SMRC to a multi-stage variant which periodically recomputes bases to track the evolving dominant subspace and retains the same rate. Since each basis refresh breaks the consistency of the virtual iterates, we devise a boundary correction approach that aligns them across stages. Beyond momentum SGD, we incorporate our framework into Muon and propose PMRC, which applies the matrix sign to the projected momentum. Through a weighted momentum tracking analysis that accounts for the residual gradient, we establish an $O(T^{-1/4})$ convergence rate for PMRC, which matches the rate of full-space Muon. We also design a multi-stage PMRC with periodically refreshed bases, which maintains a convergence rate of the same order. Extensive experimental results confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithms.
authors: Sifan Yang, Hongyi Tao, Dingzhi Yu, Haomin Bai, Wei Jiang, Silin Gao, Pi Bu, Lijun Zhang
bullets: Addresses convergence degradation when gradient noise overwhelms the leading singular subspace late in training.
Introduces SMRC, which keeps optimizer states in the subspace and adds the orthogonal residual gradient to updates.
Extends SMRC to multi-stage basis refreshes using boundary correction to maintain consistency across stages.
Introduces PMRC for Muon by applying the matrix sign to projected momentum, with weighted momentum tracking analysis.
Theory gives O(T^{-1/4}) convergence for both SMRC and PMRC, matching their full-space counterparts; experiments support effectiveness and efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes memory-efficient subspace optimization for LLM training, directly relevant to reducing memory requirements in AI systems.
papers.title: Memory-Efficient Subspace Optimization with Residual Correction: From Momentum SGD to Muon
papers.tldr: Residual correction makes subspace-based momentum SGD and Muon memory-efficient while preserving full-space convergence rates under fixed or refreshed subspaces.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are evolving from a single model calling tools to planners that orchestrate multiple expert models whose capabilities live in distinct weights. This shift breaks a hidden assumption of today's serving systems: that the working set of models fits in GPU memory. On the memory-constrained GPUs typical of private and edge deployments, naive whole-model swapping serializes weight transfer with computation and, without host-backed KV restoration, discards session state at a switch. We present JointServe, a serving system that treats weight shards and KV blocks as residency objects competing for one unified memory budget. JointServe exploits three structural properties of agent workloads (directed calls, gapped execution, and dual-state residency) to prepare models before they are called: an intent signal parsed from the caller's own output stream triggers prefetch during generation, partial k* residency reduces switching to incremental layers, and a preemptive transfer scheduler protects live-session KV with a guaranteed bandwidth share. A carve-out control step adjusts the weight/KV allocation as workload demands change. Evaluations show that JointServe reduces session completion time by 21.7% over the strongest whole-model swap baseline and stays usable in a crash regime where every whole-model swap baseline fails to finish (a 46-fold gap). On replayed SWE-bench, tau-bench, and OSWorld traces, it cuts session completion time by up to 49% and lifts SLO attainment from 2.8-24.5% to 76.8-100%.
bullets: Targets agent workloads whose multiple expert models cannot simultaneously fit in GPU memory.
Uses caller-output intent signals to prefetch models, partial k* residency for incremental switching, and bandwidth-aware transfer scheduling to protect live-session KV state.
Dynamically reallocates the unified memory budget between weights and KV blocks as workload demands change.
Reduces session completion time by 21.7% versus the strongest whole-model-swapping baseline and remains usable in crash scenarios where those baselines fail.
On SWE-bench, tau-bench, and OSWorld traces, improves completion time by up to 49% and raises SLO attainment to 76.8–100%.
papers.selection_reason: Serving system optimizing weight/KV memory on constrained GPUs; directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: JointServe: Serving Multi-Model Agents on Memory-Constrained GPUs
papers.tldr: JointServe accelerates multi-model LLM-agent serving on memory-constrained GPUs by jointly managing model weights and KV cache residency.

papers.abstract: An agent that drives an LLM sends the model the same conversation again and again, and each turn adds only a little text at the end. Inference engines reuse the KV cache of the shared prefix, so only the new tokens pass through the model. However, tokenization has no such shortcut. The CPU front end of the serving engine converts every request back into token IDs from its first character, which lengthens the time to first token (TTFT) and consumes CPU on every turn. We present Delta Tokenizer, a CPU tokenization front end that tokenizes only the delta between a request and the previous request of the same session. It retains the earlier token sequence, encodes again only the appended text and the short tail whose tokens the append could affect, and joins the two only at a position the tokenizer's splitting rules themselves cannot move, which keeps the result exact. For long requests with no state to reuse, it cuts the text where practical tokenizers already keep neighboring pieces independent, encodes the pieces on several cores at once, and concatenates the outputs into the reference encoding, exactly. A shared CPU pool schedules these chunks together with the short incremental updates, so an update runs between two chunks rather than behind an entire long job. The incremental path shortens the tokenization of a session turn by roughly 40x relative to the Hugging Face reference tokenizer, and on 16 cores the chunk-parallel path encodes a four-million-character request 8.2x faster than a serial encode and 1.6-2.1x faster than LoPT. Inside SGLang, Delta Tokenizer reduces the median TTFT through the chat interface by 59% at 100K tokens and brings the P99 TTFT of agent sessions down 9.5x under load and 23x when long requests tie up the front end. Every output we checked matches the reference, among them 41.8 billion documents encoded by its fast encoder.
bullets: Targets agent sessions where each request repeats a long prefix and appends only a small delta, avoiding full re-tokenization.
Re-tokenizes only the appended text plus a short affected tail, then joins it at a tokenizer-safe boundary for exactness.
Splits stateless long requests into independently encodable segments and processes them in parallel across CPU cores.
A shared scheduler interleaves incremental updates with long-request chunks to reduce queueing delays.
Reports roughly 40× faster incremental tokenization, up to 8.2× faster long-request encoding on 16 cores, and lower TTFT in SGLang.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient incremental and parallel tokenization for long prompts; directly reduces LLM serving latency.
papers.title: Delta Tokenizer: Reference-Identical Tokenization of Session Deltas and Segment-Parallelism for Long Prompts on Multicore CPUs
papers.tldr: Delta Tokenizer accelerates repeated and long-prompt tokenization on multicore CPUs while preserving exact reference-tokenizer outputs.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding's effectiveness is governed by two quantities: the acceptance rate of drafted tokens and the cost of producing them. We show the two objectives can be co-optimized with algorithm-system co-design, and present JetSpec++, which retains a strong learned draft model while hiding its cost almost entirely. JetSpec++ combines three components: intra-block self refinement, which trains the draft model to iteratively correct its own parallel predictions within a block of tokens; inter-block foresight drafting, which begins the next block before the current one is verified; and pipelined drafting and verification, which overlaps the two stages so drafting's marginal wall-clock cost approaches zero. In comparison with state-of-the-art speculative decoding methods, JetSpec++ attains a wall-clock speedup of up to $7.45\times$ over autoregressive (AR) decoding and $1.54\times$ over DSpark, with up to 1,361 tokens per second for a single request on GB200, and an average acceptance length of 8.94 across seven benchmarks, while preserving the target model's output distribution. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/JetSpec.
authors: Zhaoxiang Feng (UC San Diego), Lanxiang Hu (UC San Diego), Haoran Yuan (UIUC), Yu-Yang Qian (Nanjing University), Jihui Yang (Meta), Peng Zhao (Nanjing University), Yibo Zhu (StepFun), Tajana Rosing (UC San Diego), Hao Zhang (UC San Diego)
bullets: Uses intra-block self-refinement to iteratively correct parallel draft predictions.
Starts drafting the next token block before verifying the current one via inter-block foresight.
Pipelines drafting and verification to nearly hide drafting’s wall-clock cost.
Reports up to 7.45× speedup over autoregressive decoding and 1.54× over DSpark, while preserving the target model’s output distribution.
Achieves an average acceptance length of 8.94 across seven benchmarks and up to 1,361 tokens/s for a single request on GB200.
papers.selection_reason: Speculative decoding with pipelined drafting and verification; directly reduces LLM inference latency.
papers.title: JetSpec++: Foresight Parallel Drafting with Self Refinements
papers.tldr: JetSpec++ accelerates speculative decoding by co-optimizing token acceptance and drafting cost through self-refinement, foresight, and pipelined execution.

papers.abstract: Large protein language models provide a powerful framework for learning sequence-function relationships and guiding experimental design. However, architectural improvements are underexplored, especially in low-compute regimes of relevance for resource-constrained research laboratories. We show that the training cost for encoder-only transformer architectures can be reduced by leveraging modern architectural refinements, offering an encouraging performance / compute-efficiency trade-off. We introduce ProtModernBERT, a modernized BERT-style model pre-trained on amino acid sequences, and compare it with ProtBert, Amplify, and ESM2 across a set of supervised structural tasks -encompassing secondary structure prediction, disorder prediction, and subcellular localization- and ProteinGym's zero-shot functional benchmark. We find that ProtModernBERT matches or closely tracks the performance of Amplify-120M and ProtBert with up to 80-90\% reduction in pre-training FLOPs, and narrows the gap to ESM2 when controlling for pre-training. Our analysis using a cluster-based validation protocol for hyperparameter selection and randomly initialized models disentangles the contributions of architecture and data, showing that modern components provide stronger inductive biases that are more consequential than parameter count in low-compute regimes.
authors: Alberto Mart\'inez, Natalia Flechas Manrique, Lloren\c{c} Espinosa-Portal\'es, Luc Andrea
bullets: Targets compute-efficient protein language modeling for resource-constrained research.
Introduces ProtModernBERT, an encoder-only model with modern architectural refinements, and evaluates it on structural, localization, and zero-shot functional tasks.
Matches or closely tracks Amplify-120M and ProtBert while reducing pre-training FLOPs by up to 80–90%.
Narrows the performance gap to ESM2 under controlled pre-training budgets.
Finds that modern architectural inductive biases matter more than parameter count in low-compute regimes.
papers.selection_reason: Compute-efficient protein language modeling with architectural refinements; fits efficiency-focused AI methods.
papers.title: ProtModernBERT: Compute-Efficient Protein Language Modeling
papers.tldr: ProtModernBERT modernizes BERT-style protein language modeling to achieve comparable task performance with substantially lower pre-training compute.

papers.abstract: Action-chunking vision-language-action (VLA) models predict sequences of future robot actions. Under fixed-horizon execution, the robot executes a fixedlength prefix of each predicted chunk before invoking the policy again, leaving the remaining predictions unused. For a given number of executed actions, short execution horizons require more policy calls. Extending the execution horizon amortizes policy inference cost over more actions. However, uniformly applying long horizons across episodes can limit opportunities for precise corrections. To address this limitation, we propose PICES (Perturbation-Informed Chunk and Execution Horizon Selection), a training-free method that jointly selects an action chunk and the number of actions executed before the next policy call. Within a single policy call, the action expert generates a batch of action chunks from multiple initial noise samples and their locally perturbed counterparts, using the same conditioning features across all samples. PICES exploits differences between corresponding actions in each nominal chunk and its counterpart to determine candidate-specific execution horizons and select a nominal chunk for execution. Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that PICES achieves speedup by up to 2.3x in wall-clock policy inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor relative to fixed horizon baselines while improving the success rate.
authors: Jehun Lee, Hajun Lee, Jimin Ryu, Youhan Lee, Beomseok Kang, Jonghyun Choi, Jae-Joon Kim
bullets: Fixed-horizon execution can waste predicted actions and incur excessive policy calls at short horizons.
PICES is training-free and jointly selects an action chunk and how many actions to execute before replanning.
It compares nominal action chunks with versions generated from locally perturbed noise samples under shared conditioning features.
Experiments in simulation and real-world manipulation show up to 2.3× faster wall-clock inference on Jetson Orin and Thor, with improved success rate.
The method targets adaptive execution: longer horizons for stable predictions and shorter horizons for precise corrections.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free action chunk and execution horizon selection that accelerates VLA inference while improving manipulation success.
papers.title: Accelerating VLA Inference with Perturbation Informed Execution
papers.tldr: PICES accelerates VLA robot control by adapting both the selected action chunk and execution horizon using perturbation-based uncertainty cues, improving speed and success.

papers.abstract: Long-output inference in large language models suffers from severe KV cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks. While KV cache quantization alleviates this issue, low-bit quantization (e.g., 2-bit) severely degrades model accuracy. Recent mixed-precision key-cache quantization methods mitigate this degradation by allocating higher precision to important key channels, but estimate channel saliency using only key statistics. Through attention logit perturbation analysis at the RoPE channel-pair level, we show that quantization errors in channel pairs with large query--key pair-norm products contribute significantly to logit variation. Based on this insight, we propose PN-Mix, a mixed-precision key-cache quantization method for RoPE-based decoder-only LLMs, which allocates higher precision to salient channel pairs identified once during the prefill stage and reused throughout decoding. Across standard reasoning, code-generation, and AIME benchmarks, PN-Mix with 2.26-bit average precision achieves comparable or better average accuracy than prior mixed-precision methods using 2.32--2.39 bits. Furthermore, in our Pareto sweep, PN-Mix degrades gracefully down to 1.5 bits, whereas the compared baselines exhibit sharper performance drops below 2.25 bits.
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks in long-output LLM inference.
Uses RoPE channel-pair attention-logit perturbation analysis to identify salient pairs via query–key pair-norm products.
