Closed-form memory and traffic models locate the memory limits of each layout. On the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to 9B pair, the disaggregated layout matches the LM loss of the colocated run with the same loss and is faster than that run; our fused loss also lets a colocated run train on as few nodes at faster speed, while the split is memory efficient when the student spans several nodes. On the larger pairs, colocated runs with a fused loss still run OOM where the split trains, because teacher weights and student states fill the budget.
bullets: Teacher replicas stream hidden states to student nodes, avoiding colocated teacher-memory limits.
A row-window and vocabulary-shard KD loss matches the full-vocabulary loss in exact arithmetic without materializing full logits.
A prefetch ring coordinates teacher production and student training, while memory and traffic models identify layout limits.
On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to 9B, the split matches colocated LM loss and runs faster; larger pairs fit in split layouts when colocated runs OOM.
The fused loss also reduces node requirements and increases speed for colocated training.
papers.selection_reason: Disaggregated knowledge distillation reduces per-GPU memory and enables training larger teacher-student pairs.
papers.title: DisaggKD: Efficient Knowledge Distillation through Teacher-Student Disaggregation and a Fused Loss
papers.tldr: DisaggKD separates teacher and student across nodes and uses a fused, memory-efficient distillation loss to enable larger KD workloads without changing the loss.

papers.abstract: Since scaling laws were introduced for modern LLMs (Kaplan et al., 2020), several works have extended them to account for quantization, tracking the emerging low-precision data types supported on AI accelerators. We develop a more accurate scaling law for quantized pretraining with mixed precision across the forward and backward passes, grounded in optimization theory and validated empirically. Our formulation separates the effects of quantization on model capacity and on optimization efficiency, and explicitly models the persistent optimization error from forward and backward quantization identified through convergence analysis. To select the regimes for fitting and evaluating our law, we first decompose existing 4-bit training recipes into their forward and backward components, isolating those that most affect loss. Our Qwen3 experiments under selected 4-bit regimes, together with published Llama-style experiments, show that our law predicts loss with up to $11\times$ lower MSE than existing laws as model size and token count scale. Finally, we extend our law to layer-wise mixed precision and identify the optimal quantized-pretraining recipe, i.e., model size, training tokens, and per-layer forward/backward precision, under a hardware-aware compute budget. Unlike prior precision scaling laws, our law predicts that the optimal precision increases with the compute budget.
authors: Jinuk Kim, Rajarshi Saha, Muhammed Fatih Balin, Youngsuk Park
bullets: Separates quantization effects on model capacity from optimization efficiency.
Models persistent optimization error from forward and backward quantization using convergence analysis.
Decomposes 4-bit training recipes to identify forward/backward regimes most affecting loss.
Validated on Qwen3 and published Llama-style experiments, achieving up to 11× lower MSE than prior laws.
Extends to layer-wise mixed precision and predicts that optimal precision increases with compute budget.
papers.selection_reason: Scaling laws for mixed-precision quantized pretraining directly target compute and memory efficiency of LLM training.
papers.title: Mixed Precision Scaling Laws for Quantized Pretraining
papers.tldr: A mixed-precision scaling law more accurately predicts quantized pretraining loss and identifies hardware-aware optimal precision, model size, and token allocations.

papers.abstract: Complex and long-horizon agent tasks often rely on frontier models deployed in the cloud to achieve strong performance. However, using these models for every step of a long-horizon trajectory incurs substantial inference cost, even though not all steps may require the same level of model capability. In this paper, we find that allocating the LLM to only a small subset of key steps can achieve performance comparable to full LLM execution while significantly reducing inference cost. Motivated by this observation, we propose EdgeWise, an edge-cloud collaboration framework that deploys an SLM on the local device as the primary solver and selectively delegates critical steps to a cloud LLM when stronger model capacity is needed. To enable autonomous delegation without additional models at inference time, we introduce a step-level RL method that jointly optimizes task solving and delegation, with fine-grained credit assignment for individual delegation decisions. We also introduce an external judge-based delegation strategy and use it to systematically investigate key design choices in edge-cloud collaboration, including when to delegate, how delegation decisions should be made, what context should be shared, and how frequently the cloud LLM should be invoked. Experiments show that EdgeWise matches or outperforms pure-LLM execution while reducing inference cost up to 62% on SWE-Rebench and 34% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. We further deploy EdgeWise on a local workstation, demonstrating comparable cost savings in a practical edge-cloud setting.
authors: Zeru Shi, Jindong Jiang, Ryo Hachiuma, Yonggan Fu, Byung-Kwan Lee, Peter Belcak, Saurav Muralidharan, Ayush Agarwal, Ruixiang Tang, Ambrish Dantrey, Pavlo Molchanov, Anjul Patney, Subhashree Radhakrishnan
bullets: Targets the high cost of using frontier cloud models at every step of complex agent trajectories.
Uses an edge SLM as the primary solver and delegates only critical steps requiring greater capability.
Introduces step-level reinforcement learning with fine-grained credit assignment for autonomous delegation.
Also evaluates an external-judge delegation strategy and design choices around timing, context, and invocation frequency.
Reports cost reductions of up to 62% on SWE-Rebench and 34% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, with comparable or better performance than pure-LLM execution.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces inference cost via selective cloud delegation for long-horizon agent tasks, fitting efficiency-focused AI research.
papers.title: EdgeWise: Bringing Long-Horizon Agents to the Edge via Selective Cloud Delegation
papers.tldr: EdgeWise lets a local small language model solve long-horizon tasks while selectively delegating difficult steps to a cloud LLM, preserving performance and cutting inference costs.

papers.abstract: Recent video super-resolution (VSR) models achieve efficient one-step generation through diffusion distillation. However, high-resolution inference remains costly, and distilled models are difficult to align with human preferences. These challenges call for improvements in both model architecture and training strategy. We present \textbf{FlashVSR+} to address both limitations. On the architecture side, we introduce hybrid attention based on the strong locality observed in pretrained VSR models, while retaining sparse global interaction for long-range consistency. It achieves up to $2\times$ DiT speedup and 45\% lower peak memory, enabling spatially untiled 4K VSR on a single 24GB RTX 4090. On the training side, we propose Reward-Yield Distribution Matching Distillation (Ry-DMD) for preference-aligned one-step generation. Ry-DMD uses reward-weighted teacher rollouts to incorporate black-box rewards into distribution matching, without backpropagating through the reward model. We further show that Ry-DMD generalizes beyond VSR to T2I generation. Together, FlashVSR+ delivers stronger restoration quality and substantially improves high-resolution efficiency, with consistent gains in user preference. We release our code, models, and training data at \href{https://www.flashvsr.tech}{\textcolor{FlashBlue}{\textbf{www.flashvsr.tech}}}.
authors: Ruchang Yao, Shi Guo, Junhao Zhuang, Mingde Yao, Xin Cai, Jiahao Zhan, Bin Fu, Xinyuan Chen, Yu Qiao, Tianfan Xue
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of high-resolution VSR and the difficulty of aligning distilled models with human preferences.
Uses hybrid attention that emphasizes local interactions while preserving sparse global context for long-range consistency.
Introduces Reward-Yield Distribution Matching Distillation (Ry-DMD), which uses reward-weighted teacher rollouts without backpropagating through the reward model.
Reports up to 2× DiT speedup and 45% lower peak memory, enabling untiled 4K VSR on a single 24GB RTX 4090.
Achieves stronger restoration quality and consistent user-preference gains; Ry-DMD also generalizes to text-to-image generation.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient video super-resolution via diffusion distillation and hybrid attention, relevant to video diffusion and efficient attention.
papers.title: FlashVSR+: Efficient Video Super-Resolution via Hybrid Attention and Reward-Yield Distribution Matching
papers.tldr: FlashVSR+ makes one-step video super-resolution faster and more preference-aligned through hybrid attention and reward-weighted distillation.

papers.abstract: While it is known that quantization of large language models (LLMs) reduces memory usage via lower-bit weights, studies quantifying the resulting impact on energy usage and carbon intensity are scarce. We present the first unified evaluation of weight-only quantization strategies for LLM inference across varying input/output lengths and GPUs, highlighting differences in energy efficiency in addition to accuracy degradation and runtime. We study quantized inference on Llama 2 7B, Phi 3.5 Mini Instruct, OLMo 1B, Qwen 2.5 7B, and Qwen 2.5 14B across GLUE MNLI, MMLU, HumanEval, and GSM8K datasets, evaluating 10 post-training quantization (PTQ) strategies on NVIDIA H100, A6000, A100, and L4 GPUs. We identify a novel trend showing that quantization techniques tend to exhibit peak energy efficiency relative to full-precision baselines when inputs are sufficiently long and outputs are short. Furthermore, we show that quantization strategies become marginally more energy-efficient relative to full-precision models as batch sizes increase, though gains are modest. Notably, fused-kernel implementations such as EETQ int8 and Bitsandbytes int8 offer the highest energy savings, up to 4x compared to FP32 on short text generation, with negligible accuracy loss. Finally, we observe that energy usage closely tracks runtime on our evaluated benchmarks, indicating that, in practice, latency optimization can serve as a reliable proxy for reducing the environmental footprint of LLM services. We conclude with suggested directions for strategically selecting low-carbon quantization strategies based on specific inference requirements.
bullets: Quantization is assessed for energy use, carbon intensity, runtime, and accuracy across five LLMs, four GPUs, four benchmarks, and 10 PTQ strategies.
Energy efficiency relative to full precision is strongest when inputs are long and outputs are short; batch-size increases provide modest additional gains.
Fused-kernel methods, particularly EETQ int8 and Bitsandbytes int8, achieve up to 4× energy savings versus FP32 on short-text generation with negligible accuracy loss.
Energy consumption closely follows runtime, making latency optimization a practical proxy for reducing inference environmental impact.
The findings support selecting quantization methods according to workload and low-carbon inference requirements.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates energy efficiency of quantized LLM inference across GPUs; directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Towards Green AI: Evaluating Energy Efficiency for Quantized LLM Inference
papers.tldr: A broad evaluation shows that weight-only quantization can reduce LLM inference energy—especially with long inputs, short outputs, larger batches, and fused int8 kernels—while often preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: We propose a unified spatial-density signal to score token importance for both inference phases: bipartite merge for prefill and KV eviction for decode, yielding measurable gains in each stage. To isolate the two phases, we split benchmarks by scoring logic. Prefill probes (MMBench, POPE, ScienceQA) evaluate only the first decoded token; their accuracy reflects prefill logits argmax before any decode KV eviction. Full-pipeline probes (TextVQA, DocVQA, MM-Vet) assess the complete generated sequence and capture both phases. We identify a critical evaluation pitfall: decode pruning claims validated solely on prefill probes measure prefill quality, not decode performance. Experiments show discarding all visual KV during decode barely affects prefill-probe accuracy but degrades TextVQA and MM-Vet drastically; this insensitivity stems from the scoring rule, not compression intensity.Evaluated on seven model variants (InternVL-3.5, Qwen3-VL, LLaVA-1.5) and three full-pipeline benchmarks, our method achieves a three-way Pareto frontier across compute, memory and accuracy. Density-based prefill compression maintains strong accuracy, scales linearly with visual token count, and delivers 100x faster token selection at high resolution. For decode, density top-k KV eviction consistently outperforms strong baselines H2O, SnapKV and StreamingLLM on TextVQA and MM-Vet across three retention ratios. At 0.125 keep ratio on TextVQA, it surpasses H2O by 9.6 points; InternVL-3.5 models (2B to 38B) maintain a 7 to 10 point advantage. Compression scales favorably with model size: every measured 8B to 38B model transition reduces accuracy loss instead of worsening it. We suggest MM-Vet or DocVQA as mandatory full-pipeline validation for any decode-phase claims. Our code is available at https://github.com/Kai-Liu001/TwinPrune
authors: Kai Liu, Anqi Li, Junxian Li, Zhixin Wang, Zhikai Chen, Renjing Pei, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Motivation: Prefill-only probes can hide severe decode-phase quality degradation, so pruning claims require full-pipeline evaluation.
Method: Apply density-based scoring for bipartite visual-token merging during prefill and top-k visual KV eviction during decode.
Contribution: Establishes separate benchmarks and evaluation guidance, recommending MM-Vet or DocVQA for decode-pruning validation.
Results: Prefill selection is up to 100× faster at high resolution; decode pruning outperforms H2O, SnapKV, and StreamingLLM across tested retention ratios.
Scope: Evaluated across seven model variants and multiple vision-language benchmarks; performance gains are reported for both stages.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes density-aware token pruning and KV eviction for vision-language models, directly addressing efficiency in both prefill and decode phases.
papers.title: TwinPrune: Density-Aware Two-Phase Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: TwinPrune uses spatial-density-aware token pruning separately for prefill merging and decode KV eviction, improving the compute–memory–accuracy trade-off while exposing pitfalls in phase-specific evaluation.

papers.abstract: Training recipes are tuned by hand for one model, cluster and workload, and every new model, accelerator, framework version or dataset means tuning again. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, yet a configuration can run to completion while it silently changes training. ATTUNE is a single coding agent that tunes any working recipe for the workload and stack at hand, unattended, within a GPU-hour budget the user sets. It diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time, guided by a catalog of lessons from past campaigns, and ships a recipe only if it passes a correctness gate: a configuration check against objective-changing settings and known stack defects, and a convergence check of its loss curve against the baseline's. On four held-out models at 64-128 GPUs, ATTUNE raises mean throughput over the strongest public recipe run on our stack by 6.7% on Llama-3.1-405B (best campaign 11.9%) and 33.9% on GLM-4.5 (54.7%), whose public recipe was written for H100. It keeps Mixtral-8x22B's recipe, where nothing it finds clears the noise band. Under a common GPU-hour budget it beats OptiCo, Bayesian optimization and random search on GLM-4.5 and MiniMax-M2; on GLM-4.5 its mean gain is more than four times the best alternative's at less than half the GPU-hours, and on both models its tuning pays for itself within a day of training. The gate rejects no legitimate run and catches 16 of 24 faulty runs, missing only ones that barely move the 20-step loss. Ablations tie its best campaigns to one of its search rules: retrying an out-of-memory layout with recomputation. We release ATTUNE's code and TrainingThroughputBench, a leaderboard of the fastest known recipes for MoE models up to 744B parameters on up to 256 GPUs, each with its throughput, cost per million tokens and a passed correctness check, at https://github.com/amazon-science/attune.
authors: Leo Fan, Hongyang Wang, Wenbo Chen, Jingguo Liu, Xian Li, Xuan Wang, Ruochen Wen, Yiming Yan, Hao Wu, Zheshen Wang, Benoit Dumoulin
bullets: Addresses the need to retune recipes across models, hardware, software stacks, and datasets, while avoiding silent objective-changing configurations.
Uses a coding agent that diagnoses runs, changes one lever at a time, and reuses lessons from prior tuning campaigns within a user-defined GPU-hour budget.
Accepts a recipe only after configuration checks and a loss-curve convergence check against the baseline.
Improves mean throughput by 6.7% on Llama-3.1-405B and 33.9% on GLM-4.5; it leaves Mixtral-8x22B unchanged when gains remain within noise.
Outperforms competing search methods on GLM-4.5 and MiniMax-M2 under a common budget; the correctness gate catches 16 of 24 faulty runs.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic throughput tuning for LLM training reduces GPU-hours; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
papers.tldr: ATTUNE is an agentic tuner that improves LLM training throughput while verifying that optimized recipes preserve training behavior.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices can act as agents that call external software tools to complete complex tasks, but the major challenge of supporting on-device mobile agentic AI with LLMs is the long latency of LLM tool calling on mobile devices. In particular, the decode phase is the main contributor of such long latency, but is hard to speed up on mobile processors as it is bound by memory bandwidth rather than compute power. To address this limitation, in this paper we present SchemaWeaver, a new on-device mobile agentic AI technique that enforces schema-guided parallel decoding in the decode phase of LLM tool calling, to reduce its latency by producing multiple tokens in each decode pass. SchemaWeaver can be generically applied to the LLM inference engine on mobile devices without involving any training efforts or changes on LLMs, and our experiment results on major mobile SoCs and LLM families show that SchemaWeaver can reduce the LLM tool calling latency by up to 3.9 times, compared to the competitive baselines.
bullets: Targets the decode-phase latency bottleneck in mobile LLM tool calling, which is constrained by memory bandwidth.
Enforces schema-guided parallel decoding to generate multiple valid tokens in each decode pass.
Integrates generically with mobile LLM inference engines without training changes or LLM modifications.
Evaluations across major mobile SoCs and LLM families report up to 3.9× lower tool-calling latency than competitive baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces LLM tool-calling latency via schema-guided parallel decoding, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: SchemaWeaver: Accelerating On-Device Mobile Agentic AI via Schema-Guided Parallel LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: SchemaWeaver accelerates on-device mobile AI agents by using tool-call schemas to decode multiple LLM tokens per pass, reducing tool-calling latency without retraining or modifying the LLM.

papers.abstract: Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch-Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch-Muon improves over Monarch-AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch-Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.
authors: Alexander Miasnikov, Ruslan Kabirov, Gleb Molodtsov, Dmitrii Vlashchuk, Vladimir Aletov, Nail Bashirov, Daniil Tikhonov, Maxim Krutikov, Aleksandr Shestakov, Aleksandr Beznosikov
bullets: Targets the compute and memory costs of dense Muon updates for large language models.
Parameterizes weights with Monarch factors, reducing weights, gradients, and optimizer state.
Replaces dense orthogonalization with independent blockwise update problems, formalized via a trust-region view.
Improves over Monarch-AdamW in reported dense and MoE quality runs, and matches dense AdamW with fewer parameters in a two-block MoE.
For 6.89B-parameter systems, reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient structured optimizer for LLM pretraining, relevant to both efficient AI and language foundation models.
papers.title: Monarch-Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining
papers.tldr: Monarch-Muon makes Muon-style pretraining more memory- and time-efficient by exploiting structured Monarch factorization while maintaining or improving model quality.

papers.abstract: Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) periodically prunes and regrows connections, inducing a discrete dynamical mechanism over network topologies. At extreme sparsity ($\ge 99\%$), this dynamic tends to destroy input-output information pathways, and performance with standard magnitude/random updates degrades sharply. We formalize forward, backward, and functional reachability on layered sparse graphs, derive closed-form expectations for reachable neurons and edges, and show that Monte Carlo realizations match the theory. Guided by this reachability-based structure, we bias pruning toward non-functional edges and regrowth toward functionally consistent candidates. We introduce this reachability-driven modification of topology evolution as Reachability-guided in DST, referred to as guided DST. On CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet, guided DST recovers large accuracy gaps versus unguided DST (up to $+14.4$ points at $99.9\%$ sparsity on CIFAR-100), and on MLP-Mixer guided DST remains trainable at $99.99\%$ sparsity while unguided random regrowth degrades sharply. These results cast extreme-sparse training as a connectivity-preserving dynamical process. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/mzjaworski/ea_dst.
authors: Mohammad Pasande, Mateusz Jaworski, Jeroen Rook, Elena Mocanu
bullets: Extreme Dynamic Sparse Training can destroy input–output pathways, causing sharp performance degradation at sparsity levels of 99% or higher.
The paper formalizes forward, backward, and functional reachability in layered sparse graphs and derives expected reachable neurons and edges.
Reachability-guided DST prunes non-functional edges preferentially and regrows connections that maintain functional consistency.
Theory agrees with Monte Carlo realizations of sparse topologies.
On CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet, guided DST recovers substantial accuracy gaps; it remains trainable at 99.99% sparsity for MLP-Mixer, where unguided regrowth degrades sharply.
papers.selection_reason: Dynamic sparse training at extreme sparsity reduces compute and memory, fitting the efficient AI theme.
papers.title: When Sparsity Breaks Connectivity: Functional Reachability and Guided Topology Dynamics in Extreme Sparse Training
papers.tldr: At extreme sparsity, preserving functional connectivity during dynamic pruning and regrowth substantially improves sparse-training viability.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers incur high computational costs when processing long visual token sequences. Existing reduction methods typically rank tokens independently and discard those deemed unimportant or redundant. We propose a reconstruction-guided framework for visual token condensation (ReConV), which summarizes the complete visual sequence with a compact Summary Bank (SMB) and retains tokens whose information is not adequately captured by the SMB, as indicated by their reconstruction residuals. At each compression layer, a lightweight position-conditioned decoder reconstructs the current tokens, leaving shared information compressed in the SMB while explicitly preserving poorly reconstructed details. Experiments on image classification and multimodal understanding demonstrate favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs: ReConV surpasses the uncompressed baseline with 48\% fewer GMACs on ImageNet and enables reusable image-level representations for efficient multi-turn inference. Code is available at TokenDrop.
authors: Xiaoya Tang, Shilong Liu, Daniel Smolyak, Xiwen Li, Quynh Nguyen, Tolga Tasdizen
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of Vision Transformers on long visual token sequences.
Uses a position-conditioned decoder to reconstruct tokens from a Summary Bank at each compression layer.
Retains tokens with large reconstruction residuals, rather than ranking tokens independently.
Achieves favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs in image classification and multimodal understanding.
On ImageNet, surpasses the uncompressed baseline with 48% fewer GMACs and supports reusable image-level representations for efficient multi-turn inference.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes reconstruction-guided visual token condensation, directly fitting token pruning/eviction for efficient vision and multimodal inference.
papers.title: Bottlenecked semantic compression by representation reconstruction
papers.tldr: ReConV compresses long visual token sequences by reconstructing shared information in a compact summary bank and retaining tokens with unrecovered details, improving efficiency while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models accelerate generation by decoding multiple masked positions per forward pass. However, accuracy is known to drop when parallel decoding trajectories deviate from their sequential counterparts, which are slow and expensive "oracles" that adhere to the joint distribution of language. In this paper, we propose Parallel Inconsistency Guidance (PIG), a new paradigm that uses a trained auxiliary model to directly estimate the inconsistency between parallel and sequential generation from a single model forward pass. During inference, masked positions are traversed by decreasing confidence, and tokens are added to the parallel decode set one-at-a-time until the total estimated inconsistency between the parallel and sequential generation exceeds a threshold. Surprisingly, it suffices to train a lightweight ~2M parameter auxiliary model on a small mixture drawn from OpenCoder, GSM8K-train, MATH-train, and MBPP-train. For LLaDA-8B Instruct and NemotronDiffusion-3B Instruct, PIG extends the accuracy-TPF frontier on GSM8K, MATH500, MBPP, HumanEval, and MMLU, when compared to the industry standard Fast-dLLM and measures favorably on LLaDA-8B Instruct against DAPD, KLASS, EB-sampler, and other learned unmasking policies.
authors: Quentin Fruytier, Anton Xue, Sanjay Shakkottai, Sujay Sanghavi
bullets: Diffusion language models decode multiple masked positions in parallel, but accuracy can suffer when their trajectories diverge from slower sequential decoding.
PIG uses a lightweight auxiliary model to estimate parallel–sequential inconsistency from a single forward pass.
Tokens are considered in decreasing confidence order and added one at a time until estimated inconsistency exceeds a threshold.
A roughly 2M-parameter auxiliary model is trained on a small mixture of coding, math, and reasoning data.
On LLaDA-8B Instruct and NemotronDiffusion-3B Instruct, PIG extends the accuracy–throughput frontier across several reasoning, coding, and language benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method to accelerate diffusion language model decoding, directly targeting inference efficiency.
papers.title: PIG: Parallel Inconsistency Guidance for Accelerating Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: PIG accelerates diffusion language model decoding while preserving accuracy by estimating and controlling the inconsistency of parallel generation with sequential decoding.

papers.abstract: Video language models represent a video as a long sequence of visual embeddings in a decoder's input. Every visual embedding is processed by every decoder layer during prefill, stored in the key value cache, and attended by every generated token, so a long video raises prefill, memory, and generation cost at once. We present WIRE (Weight Space Implicit Representation Encoding), which reduces this recurring cost by moving part of the video conditioned computation of a frozen video language model from its input activations into a temporary low rank update of its weights. WIRE keeps a short explicit visual context, so the update acts as a correction rather than a replacement of the video. WIRE first compresses the full resolution embeddings of each frame into a small set of carrier tokens using a question conditioned bidirectional selective scan, and physically contracts the decoder input so every decoder layer, cache entry, and decoding step operates on the shorter sequence. Hypernetworks at selected decoder layers read the compressed forward pass together with a readout of the full resolution features removed by contraction and generate LoRA updates to the attention and feedforward projections. The updates are merged after prefill, so autoregressive decoding runs the unmodified frozen backbone. On Qwen3-VL-8B, WIRE with 16 carrier tokens per frame contracts the visual stream by $3.5\times$, reduces decoder prefill time by $3.35\times$ at 256 frames and $4.14\times$ at 1024 frames, shrinks the key value cache proportionally, and keeps per token decoding latency approximately constant. Across nine benchmark settings at 256 frames, it obtains the highest average accuracy among efficient video language models we evaluate under a common 256 frame budget.
authors: Ameen Ali, Tamim Zoabi, Lior Wolf, Chaim Baskin
bullets: Addresses the rising prefill, KV-cache, and attention costs caused by long video embedding sequences.
Compresses each frame into carrier tokens using a question-conditioned bidirectional selective scan, then contracts the decoder input.
Uses hypernetworks to generate LoRA updates from compressed features and removed full-resolution information at selected decoder layers.
Merges updates after prefill, allowing autoregressive decoding to use the unmodified frozen backbone.

On Qwen3-VL-8B with 16 carrier tokens per frame, achieves 3.5× visual-stream contraction, 3.35–4.14× faster prefill, proportional KV-cache reduction, and top average accuracy across nine benchmark settings at 256 frames.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a method to compress visual tokens and reduce KV cache/prefill cost in frozen video LLMs, directly targeting efficiency in multimodal inference.
papers.title: WIRE: Weight Space Implicit Representation Encoding of Frozen Video LLMs
papers.tldr: WIRE makes frozen video LLMs more efficient by replacing most long visual inputs with a short context plus temporary low-rank weight updates that preserve video information.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents revise their working context as information becomes obsolete, but deleting text does not erase its influence on cached computation. Later key-value (KV) states remain conditioned on the deleted content, while recomputing the entire retained suffix can be costly. We introduce budgeted KV-cache repair: recovering task performance by recomputing a user-chosen fraction of the retained suffix. Comparing repair allocations under identical relevance scores and token budgets, we find that refreshing coherent regions can substantially outperform refreshing isolated tokens. This finding motivates Semantic-Unit Refresh (SUR), which allocates the budget to query-relevant text regions using inexpensive embedding scores, without training or an auxiliary transformer forward. To execute these repairs efficiently, a layer-packed executor processes selected states together at each layer while preserving full causal cache access. Across five models, SUR achieves strong recovery in controlled deletion tasks while recomputing only 2-5% of the suffix. On four natural multi-hop QA datasets, it achieves near-full-recompute exact match at a 5% budget with lower post-edit latency. The executor accelerates fragmented refresh by up to 16.1x over interval-wise execution.
authors: Han Yu, Wenhui Zhu, Jincheng Cao, Rui Cai, Yuanda Xu, Zhengze Zhou, Xiwen Chen, Hao Wang, Xuanzhao Dong, Han Shi, Menglin Zhou, Shayan Mohajer Hamidi, Lin Su, Mina Razghandi, Sayan Ghosh, Qing Lan, Rohit Jain, Alborz Geramifard
bullets: Deleting context leaves later KV states influenced by obsolete text, but fully recomputing the retained suffix is costly.
Budgeted KV-cache repair studies how to recover performance by recomputing only a chosen fraction of the suffix.
Semantic-Unit Refresh (SUR) uses inexpensive embedding relevance scores to refresh coherent regions without training or an auxiliary transformer pass.
A layer-packed executor efficiently processes selected cache states while preserving causal access, accelerating fragmented refresh by up to 16.1× over interval-wise execution.
Across five models and four natural multi-hop QA datasets, SUR uses 2–5% recomputation and reaches near-full-recompute exact match at a 5% budget.
papers.selection_reason: KV-cache repair for evolving contexts directly targets cache memory efficiency and inference cost.
papers.title: Budgeted KV-Cache Repair for Evolving Contexts
papers.tldr: SUR repairs stale KV caches after context edits by refreshing only query-relevant text regions, achieving near-full-recompute quality with about 5% recomputation and lower latency.

papers.abstract: As demand for LLM inference grows and consumer GPUs grow more capable, edge deployment is becoming increasingly attractive. WebGPU is compelling in this setting because it offers cross-platform portability and browser accessibility. However, these same strengths also make high performance difficult to achieve, as an implementation that performs well in one context may not perform well in another. To address this, we present GPU Goldmines, a framework for specifying, executing, and tuning WebGPU kernels. We instantiate GPU Goldmines with kernels for key LLM building blocks: matrix multiplication, matrix-vector multiplication, and flash attention. We characterize performance across diverse devices, shapes, and browsers, and use the resulting database to accelerate subsequent autotuning and configuration selection. On shapes drawn from Llama and Qwen models, our matrix multiplication kernels outperform ONNX Runtime and llama.cpp WebGPU kernels by 7.0x and 1.41x geometric mean, respectively, and deliver end-to-end improvements of 1.48x in the prefill stage of llama.cpp for chat workloads.
authors: Rithik Sharma, Reese Levine, Zheyuan Chen, Ananthajit Srikanth, Yanwen Xu, Tyler Sorensen
bullets: Targets the challenge of achieving consistent high performance with portable, browser-accessible WebGPU implementations.
Supports key LLM operations: matrix multiplication, matrix-vector multiplication, and flash attention.
Characterizes performance across diverse devices, tensor shapes, and browsers, building a database for autotuning and configuration selection.
On Llama- and Qwen-derived shapes, matrix multiplication kernels achieve 7.0× over ONNX Runtime and 1.41× over llama.cpp WebGPU kernels in geometric mean.
Improves llama.cpp chat prefill performance by 1.48× end to end.
papers.selection_reason: Autotuned WebGPU kernels for efficient edge LLM inference, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: GPU Goldmines: Tunable WebGPU Kernels for Edge LLM Inference
papers.tldr: GPU Goldmines provides tunable WebGPU kernels and performance-guided configuration selection to accelerate edge LLM inference across devices, browsers, and workloads.

papers.abstract: Generating images beyond the training resolution of Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) remains challenging, as the number of tokens grows rapidly with resolution, full attention becomes expensive, and outputs often suffer from structural distortions and degraded detail. We identify uniform full attention as the common source of both problems. Attending to all tokens at every step causes quadratic cost and exposes the model to more tokens and relative distances beyond the training range, pushing the model out of distribution. We observe that attention's effective receptive field narrows during denoising, from global in early steps that form structure to local in later steps that refine details. We propose AReA, a training-free attention mechanism whose receptive field evolves from coarse to fine, following the denoising progression. In early steps, AReA applies cross-scale coarse attention over downsampled keys and values, capturing global context, while in later steps it applies local attention within progressively shrinking windows. Without additional parameters or training, experiments show that AReA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art training-free baselines across target resolutions and different models, while also being faster and more efficient.
authors: Javad Rajabi, Koorosh Roohi, David B. Lindell, Babak Taati
bullets: Addresses quadratic full-attention costs and structural/detail degradation when DiTs generate beyond training resolution.
Uses coarse cross-scale attention in early denoising steps to capture global structure.
Progressively switches to shrinking-window local attention in later steps for detail refinement.
Training-free and adds no parameters, while reported experiments show consistent gains over training-free baselines with improved speed and efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces AReA, a training-free attention mechanism that adapts receptive fields from coarse to fine, directly improving efficiency in high-resolution Diffusion Transformers.
papers.title: AReA: Adaptive Receptive-Field Attention for Efficient High-Resolution Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: AReA enables more efficient high-resolution Diffusion Transformers by adapting attention from global to local as denoising progresses.

papers.abstract: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) compresses the KV cache into a latent representation, reducing inference memory and bandwidth. Existing MHA2MLA/TransMLA methods do not support QKNorm and require costly recovery on modern LLMs, especially MoE. We present MLAfication, a QKNorm-compatible, parameter-efficient extension of MHA2MLA. It combines calibrated KNorm, parameter-efficient distillation, contribution-aware Partial-RoPE, and activation-aware joint KV initialization. Across MHA and GQA models, including QKNorm- and MoE-equipped variants, MLAfication preserves performance under substantial KV-cache compression, surpasses the current SOTA on commonsense and long-context benchmarks, and extends MLA conversion to modern architectures. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, MLAfication delivers up to $5.35\times$ the serving throughput of BF16 GQA and, combined with 4-bit KV quantization, reduces the KV-cache footprint by $94.73\%$. Our code is available at https://github.com/JT-Ushio/MLAfication.
authors: Zile Wang, Zhide Xie, Tao Ji
bullets: Addresses the limited compatibility and costly recovery of existing MHA-to-MLA methods, especially for QKNorm and MoE models.
Introduces calibrated KNorm, parameter-efficient distillation, contribution-aware Partial-RoPE, and activation-aware joint KV initialization.
Preserves model performance across MHA and GQA models under substantial KV-cache compression.
Surpasses prior state of the art on commonsense and long-context benchmarks.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B, achieves up to 5.35× BF16 GQA serving throughput and reduces KV-cache footprint by 94.73% with 4-bit KV quantization.
papers.selection_reason: Converts modern LLMs to MLA with large KV-cache compression and throughput gains, directly relevant to efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: MLAfication: Efficiently Enabling High-Fidelity MLA for Modern LLMs
papers.tldr: MLAfication efficiently converts modern LLMs to high-fidelity MLA, supporting QKNorm and MoE architectures while sharply reducing KV-cache costs.

papers.abstract: Linear-time sequence models typically store long-context information in a recurrent state. A fixed-size state limits how much information can be stored, while hybrid architectures that add full attention for better recall incur quadratic sequence cost. Alternatively, sparse attention with continued pretraining (CPT) can extend the effective context length. Generalization beyond the trained length remains challenging, however, and CPT can be costly. We introduce FreeSolo, a native sparse attention mechanism with a short-range sliding window branch and a long-range branch that selects keypoint cells for direct token attention. Its linear-time variant, FS-L, learns to prune the prefix before query-dependent selection through short CPT. FS-B searches balanced trees with $O(N\log^2 N)$ algorithmic cost including radix-sort construction. FreeSolo demonstrates better zero-shot length extrapolation than the baselines without long-context fine-tuning.
authors: Zekun Shi, Alastair James Arthur Price
bullets: Addresses the limited memory of fixed-size recurrent states and the quadratic cost of full attention.
Combines a short-range sliding-window branch with a long-range branch that selects keypoint cells for direct token attention.
FS-L prunes the prefix before query-dependent selection, while FS-B searches balanced trees with O(N log² N) cost.
The method shows better zero-shot length extrapolation than baselines without long-context fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Linear-time sparse attention with zero-shot length extrapolation, relevant to efficient attention and long-context processing.
papers.title: FreeSolo: Linear-time Sparse Attention with Zero-Shot Length Extrapolation
papers.tldr: FreeSolo is a sparse-attention mechanism that enables linear-time long-context modeling and stronger zero-shot length extrapolation without long-context fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Decision models such as Jev score candidate answers or actions. A small decision head trained label-free can recover about 99% of a frozen language model's multiple-choice accuracy while using only two-thirds of its transformer layers. It learns the full model's answer probabilities with KL divergence, without correct-answer labels for training. One backbone pass reads the question and all options together; the head returns probabilities for every option. We call this model FunDM (Fun Decision Model). Using 24 of Qwen3-8B's 36 layers and skipping the LM head, its +1T variant reaches 75.0% mean accuracy over eight benchmarks, versus 75.7% for the full model. On MMLU-Pro, both heads achieve 1.56 to 1.57 times batched vLLM throughput with about one-third lower peak GPU allocator memory. Both heads score higher than released Contrastive Language Models (CLM), fine-tuned CLM, and CLM-shaped heads trained from scratch on the eight multiple-choice benchmarks and coding-agent selection. Separately trained agent heads learn judge probabilities without pass/fail labels and select passing runs for 74.4 to 74.6 of 100 held-out tasks on average, versus 74 for the full-model judge and 52.0 for a CLM-shaped action-trained head. Code is available at: https://github.com/Ujjawal-K-Panchal/FunDM
bullets: Recovers about 99% of the frozen model’s multiple-choice accuracy using only two-thirds of its transformer layers.
Learns option probabilities via KL divergence, without correct-answer labels; one pass processes the question and all options together.
With 24 of Qwen3-8B’s 36 layers, FunDM reaches 75.0% mean accuracy across eight benchmarks versus 75.7% for the full model.
On MMLU-Pro, it provides 1.56–1.57× batched throughput and about one-third lower peak GPU allocator memory.
Label-free agent heads select passing runs on 74.4–74.6 of 100 held-out tasks, outperforming a CLM-shaped action-trained head.
papers.selection_reason: Frozen-LLM decision heads reduce compute and memory while preserving accuracy, fitting efficient inference interests.
papers.title: FunDM: Cheap & Label-Free Decision Models from Frozen Language Models
papers.tldr: FunDM distills a frozen language model into a cheap, label-free decision head that nearly preserves accuracy while reducing inference cost.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving requires rich spatiotemporal representations to support scene understanding and trajectory planning under strict latency constraints. However, most systems initialize their visual encoders from generic image pretraining and densely process all patch tokens for each camera view and input frame, limiting both representation quality and inference efficiency. To address these challenges, we present ConDenseDrive, a knowledge-dense and token-sparse visual encoder for end-to-end autonomous driving. Our three-stage framework first makes the encoder knowledge-dense by distilling complementary visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from three vision foundation models. It then adapts the distilled encoder to multi-frame end-to-end driving and integrates spatiotemporal context into register tokens for planning. Finally, it makes the encoder token-sparse by applying register-guided token compression, reducing redundant patch computation and yielding a 2.0$\times$ speedup while improving planning performance. ConDenseDrive achieves 94.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and reaches 37.4 HD-Score in zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM. Extensive experiments and qualitative analyses demonstrate that visual encoder design provides an effective route to reliable and efficient end-to-end driving.
authors: Shengzhen Li, Yongkang Li, Hao Gao, Chenxi Wu, Yajing Sun, Lu Hou, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang
bullets: Addresses the limited representation quality and high latency caused by generic visual pretraining and dense patch processing.
Distills complementary visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from three vision foundation models.
Adapts the encoder to multi-frame driving and stores spatiotemporal context in register tokens for planning.
Uses register-guided token compression to reduce redundant patch computation while improving planning performance.
Reports 94.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 90.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and 37.4 HD-Score in zero-shot HUGSIM evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Builds a knowledge-dense, token-sparse visual encoder for end-to-end autonomous driving, improving planning and achieving 2x speedup via register-guided token compression.
papers.title: ConDenseDrive: Knowledge-Dense, Token-Sparse Visual Encoder for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: ConDenseDrive distills diverse visual knowledge into a token-sparse encoder that improves planning while delivering 2.0× faster inference for end-to-end autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training with generative reward models (GenRM) has become a central recipe for improving large language models (LLMs), and it is also increasingly resource-intensive: policy rollout, GenRM-based reward evaluation, and policy training all compete for GPU resources. However, existing colocated and disaggregated systems rely on static resource allocation for these roles. Such allocation cannot adapt as each role's workload changes during RL and therefore leaves a role's resources underutilized. We present PivotRL, an RL post-training system that dynamically shifts resources among different roles according to their runtime demands. PivotRL introduces a resource-shiftable runtime built on a Global Parameter Storage, together with a unified mechanism that efficiently shifts role-specific context. A shift-aware scheduler enables sequence migration upon a shift, while a planner considers the aggregate throughput benefit and the shift overhead to determine when and how to shift. We evaluate PivotRL on a 128-GPU cluster using four model groups spanning dense and mixture-of-experts models. PivotRL enables resource shifting within seconds and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.81-2.05 times over colocated deployment and 1.50-1.95 times over disaggregated deployment, while preserving RL convergence.
authors: Yanfeng Zhao, Haoyang Li, Sheng Lin, Yuming Zhou, Jiawei Jiang, Bin Cui, Fangcheng Fu
bullets: Addresses underutilized resources caused by static allocation across RL post-training roles.
Uses global parameter storage and unified context transfer to support rapid resource shifting.
A shift-aware scheduler migrates sequences, while a planner balances throughput gains against shift overhead.
Evaluated on 128 GPUs across four dense and mixture-of-experts model groups.
Shifts resources within seconds and improves throughput by 1.81–2.05× over colocated and 1.50–1.95× over disaggregated deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a resource-shiftable runtime for RL post-training that dynamically reallocates GPU resources to improve throughput, fitting the broad Efficient AI interest in reducing AI-system resource waste.
papers.title: Efficient Resource-Shiftable RL Post-training with Generative Rewards
papers.tldr: PivotRL dynamically reallocates GPUs among RL rollout, generative reward evaluation, and policy training to improve post-training throughput while preserving convergence.

papers.abstract:
This paper presents GpFlash, a Gaussian process library that is focused on fast training and posterior evaluations, minimal memory usage, and scalability to high-dimensional problems. GpFlash was compared to the popular GP libraries scikit-learn, GPy, GPflow, GPyTorch, and SMT on a MacBook Pro and the supercomputer Trillium. GpFlash was found to use less memory and to be faster for training and posterior evaluations relative to the other GP libraries for all cases considered. For example, when using $
x = 10^4$ training points in a 10-dimensional space GpFlash required 9.6 to 35 times less memory and was 2.6 to 54 times faster than the other GP libraries for the evaluation of the marginal log likelihood and its gradient. The memory reduction was achieved by only using one matrix of size $
x 	imes 
x$ to store different symmetric matrices in its lower and upper triangular entries. The computational speedup was the result of designing algorithms to access memory efficiently, using BLAS and LAPACK methods extensively, and factoring kernel equations so that expensive exponential calculations could be reused. GpFlash was more than 440 times faster than all of the other GP libraries considered when evaluating the posterior mean together with its gradient for the case with $10^4$ training points and 10 dimensions. GpFlash is available at https://github.com/marchildon/gpflash.
bullets: Targets fast training, posterior evaluation, low memory use, and scalability in high-dimensional settings.
Uses one n×n matrix to store multiple symmetric matrices in separate triangular regions, reducing memory requirements.
Improves speed through memory-efficient algorithms, extensive BLAS/LAPACK use, and reuse of expensive kernel calculations.
Outperformed scikit-learn, GPy, GPflow, GPyTorch, and SMT in all reported comparisons on a MacBook Pro and Trillium.
For 10⁴ points in 10 dimensions, it used 9.6–35× less memory and achieved up to 54× faster likelihood-gradient evaluation; posterior mean plus gradient evaluation was over 440× faster.
papers.selection_reason: Gaussian process library focused on faster training and lower memory usage, fitting the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: GpFlash: Maximizing Speed and Minimizing Memory for Gaussian Process Training and Prediction
papers.tldr: GpFlash is a memory-efficient Gaussian process library that substantially accelerates training and posterior evaluation, including for high-dimensional problems.

papers.abstract: Progressive depth growth builds large networks by starting with shallow models and inserting layers during training. Recent advances in large language models have renewed interest in this longstanding approach, demonstrating benefits for training efficiency and reasoning alongside changes in internal computations. However, how growing affects representation quality and computational patterns in self-supervised vision transformers remains unclear. In this work, we systematically investigate progressive depth growth in two popular self-supervised families, namely masked autoencoders (MAE) and DINOv3, and analyze how growing affects downstream performance, intermediate representations, and internal computations. Across global and dense tasks, we show that growing improves downstream performance while reducing training FLOPs by 13.9--24.8%, with ImageNet linear-probe accuracy gains of up to 3.36 percentage points. Growing also improves downstream performance at intermediate layers and reshapes internal computational patterns, introducing recurring alternations between global and localized attention in MAE and earlier local-to-global attention progression in self-distilled DINOv3. Together, these findings establish progressive depth growth as an effective and efficient pretraining strategy for improving downstream performance across global and dense visual tasks with less computation, and advance our understanding of how growing shapes visual computation.
authors: Amir Mohammad Karimi Mamaghan, Ferdinand Kapl, Andrea Dittadi, Karl Henrik Johansson, Kaitlin Maile, Johannes von Oswald, Stefan Bauer
bullets: Studies progressive depth growth in masked autoencoders (MAE) and self-distilled DINOv3.
Reports 13.9–24.8% lower training FLOPs and up to 3.36 percentage-point higher ImageNet linear-probe accuracy.
Improves performance across global and dense vision tasks, including at intermediate layers.
Finds that growth reshapes computation: MAE develops alternating global/local attention, while DINOv3 reaches global attention earlier.
Scope: focuses on progressive depth growth’s effects on self-supervised vision-transformer representations and internal computation.
papers.selection_reason: Progressive depth growth reduces training FLOPs for self-supervised ViTs, an efficiency-oriented pretraining method.
papers.title: Growing to See: Efficient Pretraining of Self-Supervised Vision Transformers
papers.tldr: Progressive depth growth makes self-supervised vision-transformer pretraining more compute-efficient while improving representations and downstream performance.

papers.abstract: Vision foundation models (VFMs) provide transferable visual representations, but their inference cost limits deployment in many settings. Fine-tuning specializes a VFM without shrinking it; distillation shrinks it, but through expensive teacher-guided training. Structured pruning offers a more direct route by extracting a compact subnetwork from the VFM. However, as compression gets aggressive, existing methods fail because they treat subnetwork selection and recovery as separate axes. Across layers, capacity must follow task sensitivity rather than spread uniformly. Within a layer, a removal cannot be judged by importance alone; its impact also depends on how well the lost contribution can be recovered from what remains. Selection and recovery must therefore be decided jointly. We introduce Carve VFM, which resolves this interdependence. Given a VFM, a calibration set, and a parameter budget, it (i) searches for task-specific capacity allocations across layers; (ii) guides the search via an adaptive recovery-aware fitness criterion; and (iii) reconstructs removed behavior through iterative closed-form low-rank corrections merged into the surviving weights. The result is a dense encoder produced in minutes on a single GPU without backbone retraining. Across twelve benchmarks and four models from DINOv3 and MetaCLIP-2, Carve VFM achieves the highest reported mean accuracy in seven of eight backbone-budget configurations among the evaluated dense structured-pruning methods. Further fine-tuning surpasses the strongest evaluated edge model (88.1% vs. 85.8%), and carved models cut compute and memory while delivering 1.3-2.0x higher GPU throughput than the uncompressed one. These results show that the compact model you need is inside the VFM; it only has to be carved out.
authors: Lotfi Abdelkrim Mecharbat, Abdelrahman Elsayed, Ibrahim Almakky, Martin Tak\'a\v{c}, Mohammad Yaqub
bullets: Addresses the high inference cost of VFMs while avoiding expensive teacher-guided distillation.
Jointly optimizes layer-wise capacity allocation and within-layer pruning based on task sensitivity and recoverability.
Uses iterative closed-form low-rank corrections to reconstruct removed behavior in the surviving weights.
Produces dense encoders in minutes on a single GPU and reduces compute and memory use.
Across 12 benchmarks and 4 models, it reports the best mean accuracy in 7 of 8 evaluated backbone-budget settings; throughput improves 1.3–2.0× over uncompressed models.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a structured-pruning framework that jointly selects and recovers task-specific subnetworks from vision foundation models, directly reducing compute and memory.
papers.title: Carve VFM: Carving Specialists out of Generalists, Automatic Task-Specific Compression of Vision Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Carve VFM automatically extracts task-specific, compact subnetworks from vision foundation models using recovery-aware structured pruning, without backbone retraining.

papers.abstract: Adaptive optimization methods have received considerable attention in recent years due to their strong empirical performance. However, they generally require maintaining a preconditioning matrix, which incurs prohibitive computational overhead in large-scale applications. To address these limitations, we investigate the acceleration of preconditioned optimization methods through frequent directions (FD), a widely used matrix sketching technique. We first propose FTSL by integrating FD with adaptive subgradient methods under the primal-dual framework and adding back the cumulative information discarded by FD. FTSL obtains a tighter regret bound than existing state-of-the-art results. We then apply a doubling trick that further reduces the time complexity of FTSL, while maintaining the same regret guarantee. We also consider optimization over matrix-valued decision variables and exploit their structural properties to construct sketched preconditioners. We develop FTSL-Shampoo by adapting FD to Shampoo and give a novel analysis under the primal-dual framework. To further mitigate its computational complexity, we design one-sided variants of FTSL-Shampoo under both mirror descent and primal-dual frameworks. Our algorithms not only reduce the computational cost of FTSL-Shampoo, but also achieve tighter regret bounds. We extend our methods to offline stochastic convex optimization and exploit smoothness to achieve faster convergence rates. Finally, we introduce practical variants of our algorithms and empirically demonstrate their efficiency and effectiveness across a broad range of tasks.
authors: Sifan Yang, Yuanyu Wan, Yibo Wang, Lijun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of maintaining full preconditioning matrices in adaptive optimization.
Introduces FTSL, which combines Frequent Directions with adaptive subgradient methods and restores information discarded by sketching.
A doubling trick reduces FTSL’s time complexity without changing its regret guarantee.
Extends the approach to matrix-valued optimization through FTSL-Shampoo and more efficient one-sided variants.
Also develops stochastic convex-optimization extensions and reports empirical efficiency across diverse tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Matrix sketching for preconditioned optimization reduces computational and memory overhead in large-scale ML, fitting Efficient AI.
papers.title: Efficient Preconditioned Optimization Methods with Frequent Directions
papers.tldr: Frequent Directions sketching makes adaptive preconditioned optimization more scalable while preserving or improving theoretical regret guarantees.

papers.abstract: Visual token compression has emerged as a critical technique for reducing the inference cost of Vision-Language Models. Existing methods select tokens based on text relevance, visual diversity, or a fixed combination of both---treating the relevance-diversity balance as a universal constant independent of the input. We conduct a systematic analysis to challenge this assumption. At the dataset level, grid-searching the optimal relevance-diversity weight per benchmark reveals substantial cross-task variation. More critically, we further maximize per-sample answer likelihood to recover sample-level oracle weights, finding that their distributions not only differ markedly across benchmarks but also exhibit high within-benchmark variance. Based on these observations, we propose SAVER, a framework for Sample-Aware relevance-diversity balanced Visual tokEn Reduction. We first derive a Geometric Intent Prior (GIP) from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens to infer a sample-specific relevance-diversity weight, and then apply this weight to jointly select tokens via a Weighted Text Centroid (WTC) for relevance scoring and a Visual Marginal Coverage Gain (VMCG) for diversity. SAVER requires no additional training and achieves sample-aware balancing entirely at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAVER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, retaining 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B with only 11.1% of the original visual tokens, and further generalizing to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.
authors: Yihang Huang, Peisong Wen, Chenhao Zhou, Difu Feng, Qianqian Xu
bullets: Fixed relevance–diversity weights vary substantially across tasks and even among samples within the same benchmark.
SAVER infers a sample-specific weight from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens using a Geometric Intent Prior.
It combines Weighted Text Centroid relevance scoring with Visual Marginal Coverage Gain diversity selection.
The training-free method retains 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B while using 11.1% of the original visual tokens.
It also generalizes to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.
papers.selection_reason: Sample-aware visual token reduction for VLMs balancing relevance and diversity at inference time.
papers.title: When 1+1 Backfires: Rethinking Relevance-Diversity Balancing for Sample-Aware Visual Token Reduction
papers.tldr: SAVER improves visual token compression by adapting the relevance–diversity trade-off to each input sample at inference time.

papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly used to enhance the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in solving complex multi-turn tasks. During rollout, agentic RL exhibits a workload pattern distinct from that of traditional RL: multi-turn interactions repeatedly introduce prefill requests, causing prefill and decode workloads to coexist throughout rollout. This workload makes prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation, a design widely used for online LLM serving, promising for speeding up agentic RL rollout. This paper shows that PD disaggregation can improve rollout efficiency by (a) mitigating interference among data-parallel attention modules, (b) enabling stage-specific parallelism, and (c) reducing end-to-end trajectory completion time. However, a fixed prefill-decode allocation may fail to sustain these benefits as workload composition varies across tasks and over time. We therefore present Prorsa, an agentic RL framework for prediction-guided prefill-decode resource allocation. Prorsa observes the lifecycle of every trajectory to forecast short-horizon prefill and decode demand. These forecasts then guide worker allocation decisions and trigger role switching of rollout engines, aligning prefill and decode capacity with anticipated workload demand. Across synchronous and asynchronous agentic RL settings, Prorsa achieves end-to-end rollout speedups of 1.11x-4.05x over prefill-decode colocation.
authors: Chiheng Lou, Xiangwei Deng, Bangjun Xiao, Xiaodong Ji, Yikai Zhao, Xin Jin, Hailin Zhang
bullets: Agentic RL’s multi-turn rollouts repeatedly mix prefill and decode requests, creating interference and changing workload demands.
Prefill-decode disaggregation improves efficiency through reduced attention-module interference, stage-specific parallelism, and shorter trajectory completion times.
Prorsa forecasts near-term prefill and decode demand from each trajectory’s lifecycle.
It reallocates workers and switches rollout-engine roles to match anticipated workload composition.
Across synchronous and asynchronous settings, Prorsa achieves 1.11×–4.05× rollout speedups over colocated prefill and decode.
papers.selection_reason: Improves LLM serving and agentic RL rollout efficiency via prediction-guided prefill-decode disaggregation, fitting the Efficient AI scope.
papers.title: Prorsa: Unleashing the Potential of Prefill-Decode Disaggregation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Prorsa speeds up agentic RL rollouts by dynamically allocating resources between prefill and decode workloads based on predicted demand.

papers.abstract: Relevance prediction between user queries and items is a fundamental component of e-commerce search systems. Traditionally, high-quality relevance labels are obtained through human judgment, which is reliable but expensive, slow, and difficult to scale. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) enable automated relevance judgment at scale, achieving performance comparable to human annotators. However, such systems often rely on large commercial LLMs with complex prompts, resulting in high inference costs and limited throughput. In this work, we propose a framework that bridges this gap by distilling a high-performing LLM-based relevance judgment system into efficient multimodal student models. We first curate a small, high-quality human-annotated dataset to serve as ground truth. Using this dataset, we develop a reliable LLM-as-a-judge pipeline through careful prompt engineering and iterative refinement. This pipeline is then used to generate large-scale relevance labels, which serve as training data for compact multimodal models. Our distilled models achieve performance close to the teacher system while significantly improving latency, cost, and scalability. This approach enables practical deployment of high-quality relevance prediction systems in production environments.
authors: Tomasz Gniazdowski, Mohammadreza Momenifar, Nadia Vase, Shahram Khadivi, Wiktor Walentynowicz, Nicola Ueffing, Jan Pawlowski, Piotr Szymanski, Abraham Bagherjeiran
bullets: Addresses the cost, latency, and scalability limits of LLM-based relevance labeling.
Builds a reliable teacher pipeline from a small, high-quality human-annotated dataset and iterative prompt refinement.
Uses the teacher to generate large-scale relevance labels for training compact multimodal student models.
Students perform close to the teacher while improving inference efficiency and deployment practicality.
The abstract does not report specific datasets, metrics, or numerical gains.
papers.selection_reason: Distills a large LLM teacher into compact multimodal students to reduce latency and cost, fitting the Efficient AI scope.
papers.title: From a Large-Scale Teacher to Efficient Multimodal Students for Search Relevance Prediction
papers.tldr: A distillation framework turns an expensive LLM-based relevance judge into efficient multimodal students for scalable e-commerce search.

papers.abstract: Feature caching has become a mainstream training-free strategy for accelerating video diffusion models by reusing intermediate outputs across denoising steps. However, existing adaptive methods rely on heuristic difference measures misaligned with actual generation quality, employ a single global threshold that ignores heterogeneous phase dynamics, and never validate their budget estimates against true approximation error, allowing systematic bias to propagate uncorrected. We propose \textbf{AlignCache}, a closed-loop caching framework that directly aligns scheduling decisions with their true influence on the final generated video through three tightly coupled components: (1) phase-adaptive budget routing that partitions the denoising trajectory into structurally distinct phases, each governed by an independent threshold and a staleness-aware guard; (2) closed-loop threshold calibration that exploits counterfactual error measurement at the classifier-free guided output level to adjust decision boundaries online via an EMA feedback loop; and (3) momentum-augmented draft synthesis combining direction-magnitude gated residual extrapolation with anchor-guided unconditional correction. By transforming scheduling from a static risk accumulator into a feedback-driven, self-correcting controller, AlignCache consistently achieves superior acceleration-quality trade-offs across state-of-the-art video generation models. Our code is available at https://github.com/jiangjyjy/AlignCache.
authors: Jiyue Jiang, Zhiyu Huo, Yuhan Chen, Yanruisheng Shao, Gong Zhang, Lei Deng
bullets: Targets heuristic caching decisions, global thresholds, and uncorrected approximation error in existing methods.
Routes caching budgets across denoising phases with independent thresholds and staleness-aware safeguards.
Calibrates thresholds online using counterfactual classifier-free-guided error measurements and EMA feedback.
Uses momentum-based draft synthesis with gated residual extrapolation and unconditional correction.
Reports consistently better acceleration–quality trade-offs across state-of-the-art video generation models; specific gains are not given.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free feature caching for video diffusion acceleration; directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Heuristics are Not Enough: Calibrated and Corrected Caching for Video Diffusion Acceleration
papers.tldr: AlignCache improves training-free video diffusion acceleration by using phase-aware, calibrated, and self-correcting feature caching.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity efficiently by activating only a small subset of experts for each input, while still requiring all parameters to be stored in memory, resulting in substantial memory overhead. Expert merging techniques have recently emerged as a promising compression paradigm that reduces this overhead by consolidating multiple experts into a smaller set. However, existing approaches have two key limitations: (i) direct convex interpolation in parameter space is not generally guaranteed to yield meaningful interpolation of expert functions; and (ii) estimating expert similarity or merging coefficients often relies on calibration data, introducing dependence on the calibration distribution. To address these limitations, we propose Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging (SLEM), a calibration-free expert merging framework that occurs in a structured latent representation of expert weights using a VAE. SLEM groups experts within and across layers based on latent similarities and derives merging coefficients from expert weight spectra. It then performs geometry-aware latent interpolation and decodes the resulting representations into merged expert weights. Compared with existing expert merging methods, SLEM achieves comparable or better performance on general knowledge benchmarks and higher average performance on generation benchmarks involving mathematical reasoning and code generation.
authors: Dohyeon Kim, Bedionita Soro, Bruno Andreis, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: MoE models reduce computation but retain all expert parameters, creating substantial memory overhead.
Existing merging methods may produce poor function interpolation and depend on calibration data.
SLEM uses a VAE-based latent representation, grouping experts by latent similarity within and across layers.
It derives merge coefficients from expert weight spectra and applies geometry-aware latent interpolation.
The method achieves comparable or better general-knowledge performance and higher average performance on math-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses memory efficiency in Mixture-of-Experts models through expert merging in a latent space, relevant to efficient AI and LLMs.
papers.title: SLEM: Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging
papers.tldr: SLEM compresses Mixture-of-Experts models without calibration data by merging experts in a spectrum-aware latent space.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models at scale is increasingly limited by the memory cost of backpropagation. Zeroth-Order (ZO) optimizers reduce this burden by relying only on forward function evaluations, but they still exhibit a substantial performance gap to first-order (FO) optimizers such as Adam. We argue that this gap does not arise solely from the absence of explicit gradients: FO fine-tuning also benefits from informative low-rank optimization geometry, large-scale signal aggregation, and well-conditioned update directions. Motivated by this, we introduce StructZO, a structured Zeroth-Order optimization framework for memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning. StructZO performs large-query ZO estimation within an activation-induced informative subspace and applies spectral control to the resulting reduced-space update before mapping it back to the original parameters. This lets ZO aggregate useful directional signals in a compact, geometry-aware space while avoiding the activation and optimizer-state memory costs of backpropagation. We show theoretically that, when the induced subspace captures concentrated optimization-relevant directions, StructZO reduces the effective ZO estimation dimension from $mn$ to $mr$, with the remaining projection error governed by the spectral tail of the activation Gram matrix. Empirically, across OPT-series and Llama3.1-8B on diverse downstreamtasks, StructZO improves over the strongest existing ZO baselines by up to $8.7%$ relative on average and up to $26.9%$ relative on individual tasks, while remaining within $1.5%$ of FO-Adam on average. These results suggest that structured and spectrally controlled ZO updates can substantially narrow the gap between ZO and FO optimization.
authors: Xuanlin Yang, Jia Li, Zhouchen Lin
bullets: Targets the high memory cost of backpropagation and optimizer states in large-language-model fine-tuning.
Uses large-query zeroth-order estimation within an activation-induced informative subspace, then spectrally controls and maps updates back to the full parameter space.

Theoretical analysis reduces the effective estimation dimension from $mn$ to $mr$ when optimization-relevant directions are concentrated; projection error depends on the activation Gram matrix’s spectral tail.
Across OPT-series and Llama3.1-8B downstream tasks, it improves over existing ZO baselines by up to 8.7% on average and 26.9% on individual tasks, while staying within 1.5% of FO-Adam on average.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a memory-efficient fine-tuning method using structured zeroth-order optimization, directly addressing memory efficiency in LLMs.
papers.title: StructZO: Structured Zeroth-Order Optimization for Memory-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: StructZO narrows the gap between memory-efficient zeroth-order and Adam fine-tuning by estimating updates in a compact, activation-informed subspace with spectral control.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models, particularly Diffusion Transformers, achieve strong image and video generation quality but remain expensive at inference time due to repeated denoiser evaluations. Feature caching offers a deployment-friendly acceleration strategy by reusing or predicting intermediate representations without retraining the generator or modifying the sampler. However, existing cache-then-forecast methods often rely on Taylor-style finite-difference extrapolation, which can become unstable over longer cache intervals, and typically predict local module outputs whose errors may accumulate through subsequent denoiser blocks. We propose \textbf{BeziCast}, a training-free diffusion acceleration framework that forecasts output-proximal denoising representations using low-order B'ezier trajectories. BeziCast estimates B'ezier control points via Tikhonov-stabilized fitting, providing a smooth, capacity-controlled temporal parameterization that avoids explicit high-order derivative estimation and decouples trajectory capacity from cache-query density. To moderate aggressive extrapolation, we further derive equivalent forecasting weights and introduce a convex-hull-inspired guardrail that detects high-risk predictions and softly pulls them toward a conservative simplex-projected estimate. Extensive evaluations across advanced image and video diffusion models demonstrate the effectiveness of BeziCast. In particular, BeziCast accelerates FLUX.1 by up to (4.79\times) and HunyuanVideo by up to (4.11\times), while preserving substantially better generation quality than competing acceleration baselines.
authors: Lei Zhu, Mujie Lin, Ruochong Zheng, Guangyi Wang, Hao Li, Peng Jin, Chang Liu, Jie Chen
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of repeated denoiser evaluations in image and video diffusion models.
Uses low-order Bézier trajectories with Tikhonov-stabilized fitting to avoid unstable high-order derivative extrapolation.
Forecasts output-proximal representations, reducing error accumulation across subsequent denoiser blocks.
Applies a convex-hull-inspired guardrail that softly shifts risky forecasts toward conservative simplex-projected estimates.
Reported speedups reach 4.79× for FLUX.1 and 4.11× for HunyuanVideo, with better quality preservation than competing baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free diffusion acceleration via feature forecasting directly targets inference efficiency.
papers.title: Tikhonov-Stabilized Bezier Representation Forecasting for Training-free Diffusion Acceleration
papers.tldr: BeziCast accelerates diffusion inference without retraining by forecasting denoising representations along stabilized Bézier trajectories with a safety guardrail.
