papers.abstract: Industrial recommendation rankers keep scaling in width and depth to billions of parameters, but this increasingly incurs costs in parameter growth, distributed communication overhead, and training inefficiency. We introduce \underline{C}hain \underline{D}imension \underline{S}caling (CDS), a scaling strategy orthogonal to width and depth. CDS repeatedly applies a single feature-interaction block with parameters shared across iterations, so the number of iterations (the chain length) becomes a new scaling dimension that adds no parameters. A lightweight intra-chain residual connection stabilizes optimization and improves quality. CDS enables two regimes. In the \emph{compression regime}, shallow blocks with a longer chain match deeper baselines with fewer parameters and faster training; in the \emph{quality-scaling regime}, increasing chain length under a fixed parameter budget yields consistent offline and online gains, suggesting the chain dimension adds modeling capacity beyond parameter reuse. We evaluate CDS in a large-scale multi-task short-video ranking system in production. In the compression regime, CDS stays within $0.03\%$ of baseline offline quality while reducing trainable parameters by 26.6\% and improving training throughput by 6.4\%, with neutral-to-positive online participation. In the quality-scaling regime, quality improves monotonically with chain length. Wall-clock analysis shows the efficiency gain comes mainly not from reduced FLOPs but from lower cross-device synchronization overhead and reduced optimizer update cost. These results position parameter-shared iterative computation as a practical, communication-efficient scaling axis for industrial ranking systems.
authors: Zhimeng Jiang, Yuening Li, Ruixiao Sun, Yuanzhen Lin, Kun Jin, Chuan He, Liang Liu
bullets: Addresses the parameter growth, distributed synchronization, and training inefficiency of width/depth scaling.
Shares block parameters across a configurable chain length, with an intra-chain residual connection for stable optimization.
Compression regime: matches baseline offline quality within 0.03% while reducing trainable parameters by 26.6% and increasing training throughput by 6.4%.
Quality-scaling regime: longer chains under a fixed parameter budget produce monotonic offline and online quality gains.
Efficiency gains primarily come from reduced cross-device synchronization and optimizer-update costs rather than lower FLOPs.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-shared iterative scaling reduces communication overhead and training cost, marginally relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Chain Dimension Scaling: Communication-Efficient Loop-Style Scaling for Industrial Short-Video Ranking
papers.tldr: Chain Dimension Scaling reuses one feature-interaction block across iterative steps to scale industrial short-video rankers with fewer parameters and lower communication overhead.

papers.abstract: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) improve parameter efficiency by recursively reusing shared Transformer modules, yet their repeated computation over evolving recurrent states poses new challenges for low-bit deployment. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods, largely designed for feed-forward Transformers, fail to account for cross-loop activation dynamics, heterogeneous loop sensitivity, and recursive error propagation, leading to substantial performance degradation at low precision. To address these challenges, we propose LoopQuant, a loop-aware PTQ framework for accurate and efficient low-bit quantization of LoopLMs. LoopQuant is built on three core components: 1) Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization (CLDC) learns a shared quantization-friendly representation across recurrent states while preserving parameter sharing; 2) Interaction-Aware Loop-wise Precision Allocation (ILPA) allocates activation precision under a fixed bit budget by modeling task-level loop sensitivity and cross-loop interactions; and 3) Loop-Conditioned Task Calibration (LCTC) further aligns quantized inference with the low-bit recursive trajectory through lightweight task-space calibration. Extensive experiments across LoopLM architectures demonstrate that LoopQuant consistently outperforms existing low-bit PTQ methods. On Ouro-2.6B, LoopQuant under W4A4 surpasses all W4A8 baselines in performance, while reducing model memory by 65.3% with only 3.4% additional storage overhead over naive INT4 and achieving a 1.7 times decoding speedup over BF16. These results demonstrate a strong balance among accuracy, compression, and inference efficiency, providing a practical and deployment-friendly solution for low-bit LoopLM inference. The code is available at [https://github.com/Kishon-zzx/LoopQuant].
authors: Zhixiong Zhao, Zukang Xu, Xing Hu, Lifeng Liu, Guangyu Sun, Dawei Yang
bullets: Addresses activation shifts, heterogeneous loop sensitivity, and recursive error propagation that undermine standard PTQ methods.
Uses Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization to learn a shared quantization-friendly representation while preserving parameter sharing.
Allocates activation precision through interaction-aware, loop-wise sensitivity modeling under a fixed bit budget.
Applies lightweight loop-conditioned task calibration to align quantized inference with low-bit recursive trajectories.
On Ouro-2.6B, W4A4 surpasses W4A8 baselines, cuts memory by 65.3%, and achieves 1.7× BF16 decoding speed with 3.4% storage overhead over naive INT4.
papers.selection_reason: Loop-aware quantization for efficient LLM inference; fits efficient AI and language models.
papers.title: LoopQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: LoopQuant enables accurate, efficient low-bit post-training quantization for recursively computed LoopLMs by modeling cross-loop dynamics and sensitivity.

papers.abstract: Self-attention assigns two functions to one mechanism-where to read and how to mix-at the price of O(L^2) training, an O(T) decode state, and position signals bound to the training length. Existing attention-free alternatives all optimize the single function of generation. We propose FON (Fusion-Organ Network), which differentiates one weight stack into a drafting organ (multi-tap learnable delays + content-adaptive recursion; causal, O(S) training, O(1) decode state, no sequence-level quadratic attention) and a revision organ that re-processes the written prefix through multi-scale ripple kernels injected via weak gates, never generating. At 30M parameters, iso-parameter and iso-token budget, FON reaches perplexity 131.03 on WikiText-103, beating Transformer (197.73) and Mamba2 (152.53); the advantage persists under all depth-aligned baselines and at the 70M tier (-20.8%). At 8x length extrapolation FON degrades by ~8-9% without positional-encoding engineering, between ALiBi and RoPE. The revision channel provides a structural pathway for in-domain infilling that causal architectures lack in principle (+19% over on-demand coupling), at a perplexity cost indistinguishable within measurement precision. We report all costs and boundaries: impaired long-range retrieval, synthetic-task disadvantages, weaker out-of-domain code infilling than a same-recipe Transformer, and a 6.5-12.3x wall-clock gap.
authors: Helong Hu (Zhanjiang Campus, Guangdong Ocean University, Zhanjiang, Guangdong, China), Hongdan Pan (Maoming Administrative Service Center, Maoming, Guangdong, China), Shuiqing Hu (China Pacific Insurance)
bullets: Drafting uses learnable delays and content-adaptive recursion with O(S) training and O(1) decode state; revision reprocesses prefixes via gated multi-scale ripple kernels.
At 30M parameters, FON achieves 131.03 perplexity on WikiText-103 versus 197.73 for Transformer and 152.53 for Mamba2; gains persist at 70M parameters.
At 8× length extrapolation, perplexity degrades by about 8–9% without positional-encoding engineering.
Revision enables in-domain infilling, improving performance by 19% over on-demand coupling at no measurable perplexity cost.
Limitations include impaired long-range retrieval, weaker synthetic-task and out-of-domain code-infilling performance, and a 6.5–12.3× wall-clock gap.
papers.selection_reason: Attention-free LLM architecture with efficient training/decode; fits language foundation models and efficient AI.
papers.title: FON: A Draft-Revise Dual-Organ Language Model without Sequence-Level Quadratic Attention
papers.tldr: FON combines causal drafting with non-generative prefix revision to avoid sequence-level quadratic attention while improving language-modeling perplexity under matched budgets.

papers.abstract: Training neural networks in reduced precision can yield significant efficiency gains, yet all existing methods that scale to standard computer vision benchmarks retain floating-point in at least one stage, typically the weight update or optimizer state. We present a training algorithm that scales to modern deep neural networks, in which every tensor (weights, gradients, and activations) is stored as INT8, and every operation (forward pass, backward pass, weight update, optimizer update) is performed in integer arithmetic. Specifically, tensors are stored as signed integer mantissas paired with explicit power-of-two exponents, on which integer-only operations are performed using five custom composable building blocks (products, sums, divide-by-constant, nonlinear functions, and weight updates). This allows complete implementation of trainable integer layers, including convolutions, batch and layer normalization, softmax, and GELU. A per-group velocity mechanism with independent exponent tracking preserves gradient precision across neurons and channels with diverse magnitudes. As every tensor fits in INT8, training memory is roughly 4x smaller than the FP32 baseline. We validate our training algorithm on CNNs (ResNet-18/34/50/101, MobileNetV2) and Vision Transformers (ViT-Ti / B), demonstrating for the first time that training neural networks with INT8 tensors and integer arithmetic can achieve competitive accuracy on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet at a reduced memory budget.
authors: Hazem Hesham Yousef Shalby, Fabrizio Pittorino, Manuel Roveri
bullets: Addresses the floating-point weight updates or optimizer states retained by prior reduced-precision training methods.
Represents INT8 mantissas with explicit power-of-two exponents and uses five composable integer building blocks for core training operations.
Supports integer implementations of convolutions, normalization, softmax, GELU, and optimizer updates.
Uses per-group velocity and independent exponent tracking to preserve gradient precision across differently scaled channels and neurons.
Evaluated on CNNs and Vision Transformers across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, achieving competitive accuracy with roughly 4× lower training memory than FP32.
papers.selection_reason: Integer-only training reduces memory; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: Memory-Efficient Integer-Only Training of Deep Neural Networks
papers.tldr: An integer-only training method stores all tensors in INT8 and performs every training operation with integer arithmetic, reducing memory use while maintaining competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Quantization has emerged as one of the primary techniques for reducing the memory footprint of large language models during inference. A prominent example is Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss (QJL), which compresses KV caches using 1-bit asymmetric quantization while approximately preserving the inner products required by the attention mechanism. Recent theoretical and practical work aims at replacing the dense Gaussian projections used by the aforementioned transforms with more structured embeddings $-$ such as compositions of randomized Hadamard transforms $-$ while retaining the same embedding dimension. In this paper, we introduce two constructions based on a composition of randomized Hadamard transforms, albeit with a Gaussian rather than Rademacher diagonal in the second stage. The first adds Gaussian dithering to smooth the quantizer, while the second inserts a random permutation to regularize the covariance structure of the resulting Gaussian measurements. We prove embedding-dimension and running-time guarantees analogous to those of Fast JL in the non-quantized setting. The first construction achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(d/\delta))$, while the second achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(d/\delta))$ under a restriction on $m$. Both constructions can be applied in $O(d\log d)$ time.
bullets: Targets efficient KV-cache compression for attention via approximate inner-product preservation.
Replaces dense Gaussian projections with compositions of randomized Hadamard transforms and Gaussian diagonals.
Gaussian dithering smooths quantization in the first construction; a random permutation regularizes measurement covariance in the second.
Both methods run in O(d log d) time.
Embedding dimensions are O(ε⁻² log²(d/δ)) for the first and O(ε⁻² log(d/δ)) for the second, with a restriction on m for the latter.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces structured quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss transforms for KV cache compression, fitting memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Fast Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss Transforms
papers.tldr: Two fast structured constructions make 1-bit Quantized Johnson–Lindenstrauss transforms computable in near-linear time while preserving theoretical embedding guarantees.

papers.abstract: Mamba-based super-resolution models are efficient alternatives to Transformer-based restoration backbones, but their low-bit post-training quantization remains challenging because selective scan, Mamba's input-dependent state-space operator, induces different activation ranges across spatial tokens. Thus, a single layer-wise clipping range poorly matches all tokens. We propose Token-Group Quantization, a hardware-friendly activation PTQ framework that statically approximates a hardware-unfriendly post-scan grouping oracle, where tokens with similar preferred clipping ranges are assigned to the same group. To avoid runtime post-scan grouping in static low-bit inference, a lightweight predictor infers the groups from pre-scan features available before the quantized scan path. During calibration, we form pseudo-labels by clustering post-scan activation descriptors that capture similar rounding--clipping behavior. At inference, the frozen predictor maps pre-scan features to groups and selects entries from offline-calibrated group-wise clipping-bound tables, without runtime statistics collection, dynamic clipping updates, or post-scan group assignment. To address low-bit restoration degradation, we further introduce a Frequency-Preserving Refinement (FPR) objective for clipping-bound calibration. FPR aligns Fourier amplitude and phase between full-precision teacher and quantized student outputs to preserve high-frequency structures. Across PTQ protocols, bit-widths, backbones, and tasks, our method consistently outperforms prior Mamba and SR PTQ baselines, transfers to Transformer SR and Vision Mamba classification, composes with rotation-based quantization, and achieves 2.23x speedup on Jetson Orin Nano over FP16. Code is available here.
bullets: Mamba’s selective scan creates token-dependent activation ranges, making one layer-wise clipping range ineffective.
A lightweight pre-scan predictor assigns tokens to groups using offline-calibrated, group-wise clipping bounds—without runtime statistics or post-scan grouping.
Pseudo-labels come from clustering post-scan activation descriptors with similar clipping and rounding behavior.
Frequency-Preserving Refinement aligns teacher and quantized outputs in Fourier amplitude and phase to retain high-frequency details.
The method reportedly improves over prior PTQ baselines across settings, transfers beyond Mamba SR, and reaches 2.23× FP16 speed on Jetson Orin Nano.
papers.selection_reason: Hardware-friendly activation quantization for efficient low-bit inference; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: Hardware-Friendly Token-Group Activation Quantization for Low-Bit Mamba Super-Resolution
papers.tldr: Token-Group Quantization enables hardware-friendly low-bit post-training quantization for Mamba super-resolution by predicting token-specific clipping groups before scanning and preserving image frequencies during calibration.

papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics jointly captures molecular state, tissue morphology, and spatial organization, yet spatial-domain methods are typically compared only at late training checkpoints, obscuring differences in convergence efficiency. We introduce MP-MNCA, a morphology-prior masked neighbor cross-attention framework that preserves the full 3,000 dimensional highly-variable-gene representation while selectively routing molecular information across spatial neighbors, with histological similarity incorporated as a continuous attention prior under a self-supervised masked neighbor-contrastive objective. Across 12 heterogeneous human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) sections, MP-MNCA is evaluated against established spatial-domain baselines using both convergence trajectories and epoch-wise spatial-domain visualizations. Our results show that MP-MNCA (i) reaches coherent spatial-domain structure in substantially fewer training epochs, as reflected quantitatively by convergence curves and qualitatively by progressive spatial grids, and (ii) maintains strong clustering quality, achieving a mean peak refined ARI of 0.546 versus 0.549 for the strongest baseline (STAIG), while attaining the highest mean refined NMI of 0.657 versus 0.640. Moreover, MP-MNCA outperforms STAIG on 7 of 12 sections in ARI and 11 of 12 in NMI, demonstrating faster convergence without sacrificing spatial-domain quality.
bullets: Addresses the limited comparison of spatial-domain methods during training by evaluating convergence trajectories and epoch-wise spatial visualizations.
Preserves the full 3,000-dimensional highly variable gene representation and selectively routes molecular information across spatial neighbors.
Uses histological similarity as a continuous attention prior within a self-supervised masked neighbor-contrastive objective.
Across 12 human DLPFC sections, it reaches coherent spatial structure in fewer epochs than established baselines.
Its mean peak refined ARI is 0.546 versus 0.549 for STAIG, while mean refined NMI is higher at 0.657 versus 0.640; it outperforms STAIG on 7/12 sections in ARI and 11/12 in NMI.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a novel attention mechanism (Masked Neighbor Cross-Attention) designed for efficiency in spatial domain identification. The technical contribution of an efficient attention mechanism is transferable to the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: MP-MNCA: Morphology-Prior Masked Neighbor Cross-Attention for Efficient Spatial Domain Identification
papers.tldr: MP-MNCA accelerates spatial-domain identification in spatial transcriptomics by combining morphology-guided neighbor attention with masked contrastive learning, while preserving competitive clustering quality.

papers.abstract: Dynamic sparse training (DST) aims to reduce training costs while maintaining accuracy. Existing DST methods mask out parameters but keep matrix dimensions unchanged. Training speedups therefore depend on specialized support, such as sparse kernels. We introduce BARTER, a structured DST framework that reduces training cost using standard dense kernels by keeping training tensors physically compact while dynamically reallocating capacity across layers. Unlike existing works that require computing gradients for all parameters, BARTER instead uses statistics collected only from active units during ordinary backpropagation to prune and clone attention heads and feed-forward channels under separate fixed global budgets. At each topology update, it resizes the affected parameter tensors and remaps their optimizer states, so subsequent training steps operate directly on the compact model. Training and fine-tuning experiments with Transformer-based vision models on two image classification benchmarks at densities from $0.1$ to $0.7$ show competitive Top-1 accuracy relative to full-tensor DST baselines. On an NVIDIA L40, BARTER achieves speedups of up to $6.29\times$ in measured training segments and reduces peak allocated GPU memory by up to $81.3\%$ relative to these implementations. An iPhone 13 Pro Max training benchmark additionally shows a $2.78\times$ speedup over the full-tensor DST baseline.
authors: Yueyuan Sui, Payal Mohapatra, Qi Zhu, Stephen Xia
bullets: Targets the overhead of conventional DST methods that mask parameters but retain full matrix dimensions.
Uses active-unit statistics from ordinary backpropagation to prune and clone attention heads and feed-forward channels under separate global budgets.
Resizes affected tensors and remaps optimizer states after topology updates, so later steps run on the compact model.
Across Transformer vision models and image-classification benchmarks, it maintains competitive Top-1 accuracy at densities of 0.1–0.7.
Reports up to 6.29× training speedup and 81.3% lower peak allocated GPU memory on an NVIDIA L40; an iPhone benchmark reaches 2.78× speedup.
papers.selection_reason: Structured dynamic sparse training that physically compacts model tensors to reduce training compute and memory, relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: BARTER: Compact Dynamic Sparse Training with Standard Dense Kernels
papers.tldr: BARTER makes dynamic sparse training faster and more memory-efficient by physically compacting Transformer tensors while dynamically reallocating sparse capacity using standard dense kernels.

papers.abstract: Serving stacks for large language models manage context through four recurring mechanisms: incremental edits to a growing context, branching and snapshotting for tree search, identification of reusable prefixes for KV-cache reuse, and encoding of repeated segments. Each mechanism is served today by a different specialist structure. We show that all four reduce to a single persistent weight-balanced rope whose every node carries a polynomial hash of its subtree over a Mersenne prime, so that the structure supports logarithmic edits and logarithmic verified content-identity queries at the same time. We validate each mechanism with pre-registered, replicated experiments, then compare against a deployed specialist per mechanism: the Ropey editing library, a faithful PagedAttention copy-on-write block table, and the vendored SGLang radix matcher. On workloads that interleave edits with identity queries, Hashrope is net-superior to Ropey by a factor that grows without bound (369.7x at one million characters). Against the radix matcher on a live vLLM stack serving Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M on four A100 GPUs, Hashrope identifies a one-million-token shared prefix exactly and 1.20x faster, at a context length the dense engine cannot even prefill.
authors: Muntaser Syed (Florida Institute of Technology), Ameerah Alsulami (Florida Institute of Technology), Marius Silaghi (Florida Institute of Technology)
bullets: Targets incremental editing, branching/snapshotting, KV-cache prefix reuse, and repeated-segment encoding.
Stores a polynomial subtree hash over a Mersenne prime in every rope node to support content-identity checks.
Uses persistent structure sharing for logarithmic updates and queries across evolving contexts.
Validated through pre-registered, replicated experiments against Ropey, a PagedAttention copy-on-write table, and SGLang’s radix matcher.
Reported 369.7× advantage over Ropey at one million characters and 1.20× faster exact detection of a one-million-token shared prefix than the radix matcher in a live vLLM setup.
papers.selection_reason: Persistent data structure for LLM context and KV-cache management; directly relevant to efficient serving and long-context handling.
papers.title: Hashrope: A Persistent Data Structure for Mechanisms of LLM Context Management
papers.tldr: Hashrope unifies four LLM context-management mechanisms in one persistent, hash-augmented weight-balanced rope with logarithmic edits and verified identity queries.

papers.abstract: Hour-long videos, streaming feeds, and movie-length content are pushing vision-language models (VLMs) past their breaking point -- the standard recipe of encoding each frame into visual tokens yields sequences that grow linearly with video length, causing prohibitive memory consumption and inference latency. Existing approaches, such as token reduction and keyframe selection, shorten the token sequence but leave the O(n) scaling intact, failing to resolve the fundamental bottleneck. We propose FramePack-U, a strikingly simple, training-free frame packing framework that compresses arbitrarily long videos into a fixed size visual representation at constant memory cost. FramePack-U requires no fine-tuning or architectural modification -- it plugs directly into off-the-shelf VLMs at inference time. Inspired by FramePack from the generation literature, we propose a content-aware compression strategy for visual understanding under a fixed token budget. Specifically, FramePack-U (1) scores each frame by its semantic similarity to the text prompt and ranks frames in a diversity-driven manner, and (2) packs the selected frames at varying resolutions into a fixed-length context window. This concentrates the memory budget on frames that are both instruction-relevant and visually diverse. While FramePack-U can in theory pack arbitrarily many frames into the fixed budget, we identify an empirical instantiation that generalizes robustly across settings. Extensive experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME show that FramePack-U consistently outperforms full-resolution baselines and prior token reduction and keyframe selection methods across diverse model families, parameter scales, and frame budgets. Notably, on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, FramePack-U yields gains of +12.9\%, +10.6\%, and +9.7\% over the official model on the three benchmarks, respectively.
authors: Shuo Gao, Chenhao Zheng, Zhongzheng Ren
bullets: Addresses the linear memory and latency growth caused by encoding every video frame as visual tokens.
Uses a training-free, inference-only strategy that ranks frames by prompt relevance and diversity, then packs them at varying resolutions.
Works with off-the-shelf VLMs without fine-tuning or architectural changes.
Experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME report consistent improvements over full-resolution, token-reduction, and keyframe-selection baselines.
On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, gains are 12.9%, 10.6%, and 9.7% on the three benchmarks, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Constant-memory frame packing for long-video understanding; efficient token/frame selection.
papers.title: Elephant in the Fridge: Constant-Memory Frame Packing for Long Video Understanding
papers.tldr: FramePack-U enables VLMs to understand arbitrarily long videos with constant memory by packing prompt-relevant, diverse frames into a fixed-size visual representation.

papers.abstract: Neuromorphic sensing and computing promise low latency and high energy efficiency for robotics, yet most event-based visual place recognition (VPR) pipelines reintroduce dense, frame-like computation downstream of an inherently sparse sensor, forfeiting the sensor's latency advantage. In this paper, we address the problem of resolving an event-based VPR query in tens of microseconds on a commodity CPU. We train a two-layer spiking neural network (SNN) with additive spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), which drives the learned weight matrix towards a strongly bimodal distribution, amenable to aggressive magnitude pruning. At inference, our pipeline exploits this sparsity by reading only the pruned weights corresponding to the query's active pixels. As surviving weights share a near-uniform magnitude, each neuron's score reduces to an integer count of matching synapses instead of a weighted sum, lowering per-query latency. This computation is small enough to remain resident in a CPU's fast on-chip cache. On three event-based VPR benchmarks, our sparse SNN exceeds the recall of LENS, an existing event-based SNN, while reducing per-query latency by 5.5-6.2x to tens of microseconds. It matches the recall of a dense variant of our network and of the sum-of-absolute-differences (SAD) baseline, while reading 10x fewer weights than the dense variant. We further characterise how recall and latency scale with the number of active pixels and reference places. These results suggest that the sparsity of both event-based input and learned weights can already be exploited for low-latency inference on conventional processors.
authors: Somayeh Hussaini, Tobias Fischer, Michael Milford
bullets: Targets the compute bottleneck caused by dense, frame-like processing in event-based VPR pipelines.
Uses additive STDP to produce bimodal weights that support aggressive magnitude pruning.
Exploits sparse active pixels and near-uniform surviving weights, replacing weighted sums with integer synapse-match counts.
Across three event-based VPR benchmarks, achieves 5.5–6.2× lower query latency than LENS while improving recall.
Reads 10× fewer weights than the dense variant and studies scaling with active pixels and reference places.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse SNN inference for event-based visual place recognition reduces latency; efficiency contribution.
papers.title: Removing the Compute Bottleneck for Event-based Visual Place Recognition with Spiking Neural Networks
papers.tldr: A pruned two-layer spiking neural network enables event-based visual place recognition in tens of microseconds on a commodity CPU by reducing inference to sparse integer matching.

papers.abstract: For context-based question answering, using one large model for both evidence extraction and answer reasoning requires substantial memory and computation. Existing approaches trade accuracy for efficiency within a single model only. We propose a multi-model approach for efficient inference: our method, PAIR, employs two differently sized models for evidence extraction and answer reasoning, respectively. A smaller Reader model processes and retains the full context, while a larger Reasoner model sees only the question and generated sequence without directly attending to the context. These capabilities are fused at the logit level: at each token, both Reader and Reasoner produce a prediction, and their logits are combined into one, behaving as a single next-token-prediction model. Fine-tuning further boosts their performance. On HotpotQA, PAIR with a 32B Reasoner retains 96% of that same 32B model's full-context accuracy while using roughly one quarter of its KV memory. At 45.7K-token contexts, PAIR achieves up to 3.2$\times$ higher end-to-end throughput than the full-context 32B model on the same GPU. PAIR also improves the accuracy-memory and accuracy-throughput trade-offs over evaluated token-reduction baselines. Its accuracy-preserving behavior generalizes across Qwen2.5, OLMo-3, and Gemma-3 model families.
authors: Sejun Park, Haocheng Xia, Yongjoo Park
bullets: Addresses the memory and computation costs of using one large model for both evidence extraction and answer reasoning.
The Reader processes the full context, while the Reasoner receives only the question and generated sequence.
Combines Reader and Reasoner logits at each token to form a single next-token prediction; fine-tuning improves performance.
On HotpotQA, a 32B Reasoner retains 96% of full-context accuracy while using about one quarter of the KV memory.
At 45.7K-token contexts, throughput improves by up to 3.2×, with gains generalizing across three model families.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a memory-efficient inference method for LLM QA by fusing reader and reasoner logits, directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: PAIR: Memory-Efficient and Fast Inference with Reading--Reasoning Fusion
papers.tldr: PAIR combines a small full-context Reader with a larger context-free Reasoner to deliver near-full-context QA accuracy with substantially lower memory use and higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Spiking Transformers achieve energy efficiency by discarding softmax normalization in favor of thresholded, binary attention. However, this removal breaks the thermodynamic framework used to analyze attention networks, as the normalized measure and partition function cease to exist. We restore this theoretical foundation by proving that softmax-free spiking attention operates exactly as the zero-temperature limit of a product of independent two-level systems. This correspondence places spiking attention strictly in the frozen ordered phase of the thermodynamic phase diagram for all inputs. Consequently, the entropic cost of organizing attention collapses, replaced by a Landauer-type physical floor governed by action-potential generation. Furthermore, this ordered-phase pinning mathematically explains the optimization difficulty caused by vanishing surrogate gradients. We validate this theory with forward-relaxation experiments, placing both standard and neuromorphic attention mechanisms on a unified thermodynamic axis.
authors: Roberto C. Sotero, Pouya Taghipour, Jose M. Sanchez-Bornot
bullets: Reintroduces a thermodynamic framework for binary, thresholded attention without softmax normalization.
Proves that spiking attention remains in the frozen ordered phase for every input.
Shows that attention’s entropic organization cost collapses, leaving a Landauer-type floor tied to action-potential generation.
Connects ordered-phase pinning to vanishing surrogate gradients and difficult optimization.
Forward-relaxation experiments place standard and neuromorphic attention mechanisms on a unified thermodynamic axis.
papers.selection_reason: Provides theoretical grounding for softmax-free spiking attention, an efficient attention mechanism.
papers.title: Softmax-Free Attention in Spiking Transformers as the Zero-Temperature Limit of Two-Level Systems
papers.tldr: Softmax-free spiking attention is shown to be the zero-temperature, fully ordered limit of independent two-level systems, explaining both its energy efficiency and optimization challenges.

papers.abstract: Predictive coding networks (PCNs) promise properties not offered by backpropagation-trained networks: learning from purely local information, a single network that both discriminates and generates, and flexible inference by energy minimization. However, their iterative inference is expensive, making hardware acceleration desirable, and a useful, efficient accelerator needs both depth and aggressive quantization. Canonical state-based PC delivers neither: its inference signal decays exponentially with depth, so deep models fail to train, and low precision makes it worse. We show that pairing two recent methods carries the full PCN property set into the deep, 4-bit regime: bidirectional PC (bPC), which unifies discrimination and generation, and the error-based reparameterization (ePC), which optimizes prediction errors rather than states during inference. Error optimization delivers the output signal to every layer in a single backward pass, removing the signal decay; one additional element, global-norm clipping of the error gradients, stabilizes the error dynamics at depth. The resulting ePC+bPC model trains stably up to at least eight layers and retains its full-precision accuracy and clean class-conditional generation under W4A4E4 quantization-aware training, across FP4 and three posit formats. On six-layer networks, where state-based bPC collapses to chance, ePC+bPC classifies more than 50 accuracy points above it after one epoch of training, with class-conditional generations 5-9x better in RMSE. 4-bit quantization is nearly free: full-precision and 4-bit accuracies differ by at most ~5 points, and by under two in the best-performing formats. We characterize the two failure modes the method overcomes, bounded signal decay in state-based PC and error divergence in unregularized error optimization, and discuss implications for a 4-bit-native PCN accelerator.
bullets: Canonical state-based predictive coding suffers from signal decay with depth, worsened by low-precision quantization.
The method combines bidirectional predictive coding with error-based inference and global-norm clipping of error gradients.
It trains stably to at least eight layers and supports W4A4E4 quantization across FP4 and three posit formats.
On six-layer networks, it substantially outperforms state-based bPC after one epoch and produces better class-conditional generations.
Quantization causes little accuracy loss, though the study focuses on the tested architectures and formats.
papers.selection_reason: Enables deep 4-bit predictive coding networks, directly reducing memory/compute for neural inference.
papers.title: Error-Based Bidirectional Predictive Coding Enables Deep, 4-Bit Predictive Coding Networks
papers.tldr: Error-based bidirectional predictive coding enables stable deep PCNs with 4-bit inference while preserving classification and generation capabilities.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video generation enables long-horizon synthesis but requires repeated forward passes through large diffusion transformers. Training-free caching reduces this cost by reusing intermediate computation, yet existing controllers often couple two decisions: when to synchronize the cache exactly and how much computation to repair between synchronizations. We introduce Frequency-Step Cache (FSC), which separates these roles. FSC schedules exact full-computation anchors on a dense-to-sparse trajectory, while a lightweight latent-space risk based on frequency-resolved drift and token age controls inter-anchor repair through whole-step replay, selective token recomputation, or full repair. On SkyReels-V2, whole-step reuse provides most of the acceleration, while selective token computation is most effective as fidelity repair. A controlled ablation shows that using one reactive signal for both synchronization and repair reduces fidelity at matched latency, with the same separation advantage observed on FramePack and Matrix-Game. Across multiple autoregressive video backbones, FSC improves speed-quality trade-offs. On SkyReels-V2, FSC-Speed reaches 2.36x speedup versus MotionCache's 2.275x while improving SSIM by 0.019 and PSNR by 0.5 dB. At MotionCache-matched speed, FSC-Quality improves SSIM by 0.031 and PSNR by 1.0 dB and lowers LPIPS by 0.024. Without retuning, FSC-Quality transfers to SkyReels-V2 14B at 2.12x speedup versus 1.79x for MotionCache.
authors: Kerry Xu, Param Misra, Zachary Stenglein, Athri Karunamurthy, Fanjiang Ye, Yuke Wang
bullets: Targets the high cost of repeated diffusion-transformer passes in long-horizon autoregressive video generation.
Uses dense-to-sparse exact-computation anchors for synchronization and frequency-resolved drift plus token age to select repair intensity.
Supports whole-step reuse, selective token recomputation, or full repair; whole-step reuse drives most speedup, while selective computation mainly restores fidelity.
On SkyReels-V2, FSC-Speed achieves 2.36× speedup with +0.019 SSIM and +0.5 dB PSNR over MotionCache; FSC-Quality improves matched-speed quality, including +0.031 SSIM and +1.0 dB PSNR.
Transfers without retuning to SkyReels-V2 14B and shows benefits on FramePack and Matrix-Game.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient caching for autoregressive video diffusion; fits video generation and efficient AI.
papers.title: Frequency-Step Cache: Separating Synchronization and Repair for Efficient Autoregressive Video Diffusion
papers.tldr: Frequency-Step Cache accelerates autoregressive video diffusion by independently scheduling exact cache synchronization and adaptive latent-space repair, improving speed–quality trade-offs across multiple backbones.

papers.abstract: Large language model serving is increasingly limited not only by model size and GPU speed, but also by scheduling during autoregressive decoding, where continuous batching interleaves requests at token granularity as sequences arrive and finish. We study whether lightweight scheduling policies can improve latency-throughput tradeoffs without changing model architectures, kernels, or deploying learned schedulers. We implement a Python/PyTorch continuous-batching testbench with real Hugging Face execution and evaluate eight policies across 1,152 GPU-model-scheduler-workload runs using ShareGPT-derived traffic, six Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral models, and Modal L40S, A100, and H100 GPUs. Scheduler choice changes throughput, TTFT, completion latency, and tail behavior under fixed model, GPU, workload, batch size, and prefill budget. Aging shortest-prompt-first is the strongest practical baseline in many L40S and mixed-workload settings, while oracle remaining-length scheduling shows that job-size knowledge alone is insufficient because batching and hardware effects also shape performance. The custom dataset has been uploaded to Hugging Face.
authors: Ashman Mehra, Akshan Agarwal, Aryeh Carmi
bullets: Scheduling during autoregressive decoding affects throughput, time to first token, completion latency, and tail behavior.
The study evaluates eight policies across 1,152 GPU–model–scheduler–workload configurations using real Hugging Face execution.
Experiments span six Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral models, ShareGPT-derived traffic, and L40S, A100, and H100 GPUs.
Aging shortest-prompt-first performs well in many L40S and mixed-workload settings.
Oracle knowledge of remaining sequence length is insufficient by itself; batching and hardware effects also influence performance.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of lightweight scheduling policies for continuous-batching LLM serving, directly targeting latency-throughput efficiency.
papers.title: Lightweight Scheduling Policies for Continuously Batched LLLM Serving Across GPU Architectures
papers.tldr: Lightweight scheduling policies can substantially shape continuous-batching LLM serving performance, with aging shortest-prompt-first often providing a strong practical tradeoff across hardware and workloads.

papers.abstract: Training-free pruning removes weights from pretrained large language models to reduce their deployment cost. However, existing approaches typically consider only the total number of retained weights. Consequently, their pruning decisions do not account for how target hardware stores and processes those weights. These methods select a sparsity structure in advance and apply it uniformly to all projections, rather than accounting for how each structure trades pruning error against latency and memory across sublayers. We propose Heterogeneous Structured Pruning (HSP), a hardware-aware pruning framework that combines two components: (i) a heterogeneous search space of dense, unstructured, 2:4, block-sparse, and head / channel (H/C) pruning options and (ii) structure-regularising constraints based on latency and memory models. Our contribution generalises existing importance-based methods: a global solver selects one option per sublayer to minimise proxy pruning loss under a resource budget, thereby assigning each projection a structure and density. We evaluate HSP on OPT and LLaMA models for an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super edge device, where it improves the quality-resource frontiers over training-free baselines. A project page and updated links for the related code is maintained at: cameronbarker.me/publications/hsp.
authors: Cameron Barker, Andreas Paraskeva, Jan N. van Rijn, Elliot J. Crowley, Henry Gouk
bullets: Existing pruning methods often optimize retained weight count without accounting for hardware-specific storage and processing costs.
HSP searches over dense, unstructured, 2:4, block-sparse, and head/channel pruning options.
A global solver selects one structure per projection by minimizing proxy pruning loss under a resource budget.
Evaluations on OPT and LLaMA models using an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super show improved quality–resource frontiers over training-free baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Hardware-aware heterogeneous structured pruning reduces LLM memory and latency, fitting the efficient-AI theme of memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Heterogeneous Structured Pruning Under Resource Constraints for Hardware-Efficient Large Language Models
papers.tldr: HSP enables hardware-aware, training-free pruning by assigning different sparsity structures and densities to each sublayer under latency and memory constraints.

papers.abstract: Cross-model KV cache sharing reduces prefill computation by allowing a receiver model to reuse prefix KV states generated by a related sender model. Existing methods optimize such reuse for latency and generation quality, but its safety implications remain unclear. In this work, we systematically evaluate this issue across diverse sender-receiver pairs and reuse configurations. We refer to deviations from the receiver's native safety behavior as safety incompatibility. Our study shows that both the direction and magnitude of safety incompatibility depend on the model pair and reuse configuration, with value reuse causing substantially larger deviations than key reuse across all evaluated pairs. Furthermore, we propose VReparo, a technique that learns per-layer and per-KV-head affine maps offline to align reused sender value tensors with their receiver-native counterparts before decoding. Across two model pairs under full KV reuse and the state-of-the-art selective reuse setting, VReparo reduces the average HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) from 57.28% to 39.21% and the average StrongREJECT score from 0.4215 to 0.2163 upon our benchmarks, while retaining an average Time to First Token (TTFT) reduction of 85.62%.
authors: Zhiwei Lin, Jiahao Liu, Yan Liu, Chengpeng Wang
bullets: Safety incompatibility varies with the sender–receiver model pair and cache-reuse configuration.
Reusing value tensors causes larger safety deviations than reusing key tensors.
VReparo learns offline per-layer, per-KV-head affine maps to align sender values with receiver-native values.
Across evaluated settings, VReparo lowers average HarmBench ASR from 57.28% to 39.21% and StrongREJECT from 0.4215 to 0.2163.
It retains an average 85.62% reduction in time to first token.
papers.selection_reason: Studies cross-model KV cache reuse and proposes a mitigation for safety incompatibility, relevant to KV-cache-based efficient inference.
papers.title: To Cache or Not to Cache: Understanding and Mitigating Safety Incompatibility in Cross-Model KV Cache Reuse
papers.tldr: Cross-model KV-cache reuse can substantially alter safety behavior, but VReparo mitigates these deviations while preserving most of the latency benefit.

papers.abstract: Linear attention promises the efficiency needed for long-context language modelling, yet its fixed-size recurrent state must simultaneously support ongoing computation and preserve information from an ever-growing history. This coupling has reinforced a prevailing view that the state's memory capacity defines the model's long-context capability. We challenge this presumed ceiling: \emph{recurrent computation need not bear the full burden of long-term storage}. We introduce NoteBank, a sparse episodic memory that archives selected text before future queries are known, uses the backbone's native features for writing and addressing, and reads retrieved evidence through its native forward computation via replay. This \emph{training-free, plug-and-play} interface requires no external embedding model, separately trained retriever, or separate neural reader. At one million tokens, it raises Gated DeltaNet's mean accuracy across six RULER retrieval tasks from 1.7% to 70.3%, with no observed significant retrieval degradation from 4K to 1M tokens. This recovery adds $\leqslant$0.025% to analytical FLOPs, with persistent context storage approximately 1/2,600 that of a Transformer's full MHA KV cache at matched width, depth, and precision. Experiments extend from three 1.3B recurrent backbones to Mamba-2-8B and post-trained Qwen3.5-9B, demonstrating gains on LongBench v1/v2 and MemoryAgentBench. Together, these results show that sparse evidence storage and native replay can substantially expand the long-context capability of pretrained linear attention models while retaining the efficiency of recurrent computation.
authors: Li Nanbo, Firas Laakom, Yilan Zhang, Piotr Pi\k{e}kos, Yimeng Chen, Liangyu Wang, Yifan Xu, Mateusz Ostaszewski, Dandan Guo, Wenyi Wang, Yanning Dai, Yuhui Wang, J\"{u}rgen Schmidhuber
bullets: Linear attention’s fixed recurrent state must handle both computation and long-term storage, limiting context retention.
NoteBank archives selected text before queries are known, addresses it using native backbone features, and replays retrieved evidence through the model’s forward computation.
The training-free, plug-and-play method requires no external embedder, separately trained retriever, or separate neural reader.
On one-million-token RULER retrieval tasks, Gated DeltaNet’s mean accuracy improves from 1.7% to 70.3%, with no significant retrieval degradation from 4K to 1M tokens.
The approach adds at most 0.025% analytical FLOPs and uses far less persistent storage than a Transformer KV cache; evaluations cover multiple recurrent backbones and long-context benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse episodic memory and native replay expand long-context capability of linear attention, directly relevant to memory efficiency and LLM memory.
papers.title: History Replays Itself: Unleashing Long-Context Capability in Linear Attention
papers.tldr: NoteBank substantially extends linear-attention models’ long-context memory by sparsely storing and natively replaying past evidence without retraining or external retrieval components.

papers.abstract: Linear attention and recurrent models compress past tokens into a fixed-size state that is updated at every step. However, storing these states in high precision incurs substantial memory and bandwidth costs at large batch sizes, motivating low-bit state quantization. Unlike weights and key--value caches, a recurrent state is requantized after every update, so its quantization errors accumulate across steps. Our analysis shows that these errors are highly coherent across steps, so reducing per-step errors alone is insufficient. This coherence arises mainly from small updates that are lost in rounding. To preserve these updates, we intervene both before and at rounding. Before rounding, we propose Low-Rank Bypass (LRB), which accumulates small updates in a compact low-rank buffer and periodically merges its sufficiently large elements into the state. At rounding, we observe that a state element can even move opposite to its update, and such reversals prove particularly harmful. Therefore, we propose Bounded Directional Rounding (BDR), which rounds reversed elements toward their updates without additional storage. Although BDR enlarges the rounding error, it improves the model, suggesting that the direction of an update matters more than its rounding error at a single step. Across Gated DeltaNet, GLA, Mamba2, and RetNet, our training-free method substantially outperforms INT4, while reducing state memory by up to 5.3$\times$ and speeding up decoding by up to 1.9$\times$ relative to FP32 states.
authors: Haotian Li, Liran Dong, Kaicheng Xiao, Guoliang Xing
bullets: Recurrent states are requantized after every update, causing coherent errors that accumulate over time.
Low-Rank Bypass (LRB) stores small updates in a compact low-rank buffer and periodically merges them into the state.
Bounded Directional Rounding (BDR) rounds reversed state updates toward their intended direction without extra storage.
Evaluated across Gated DeltaNet, GLA, Mamba2, and RetNet, the method outperforms INT4, cuts state memory by up to 5.3×, and speeds decoding by up to 1.9× versus FP32 states.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes low-bit recurrent state quantization with update-preserving techniques, directly targeting memory and decoding efficiency for recurrent/linear-attention models.
papers.title: Preserving Updates in Low-Bit Recurrent State Quantization
papers.tldr: A training-free low-bit recurrent-state quantization method preserves small update directions, substantially improving INT4 state performance while reducing memory and accelerating decoding.

papers.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) used as on-device agents must balance accuracy and latency as their context grows. Mixed precision helps manage this tradeoff by assigning different precisions to weight tensors according to their size and sensitivity. However, these choices depend on the operating conditions, so a configuration selected for a short context may no longer provide the best tradeoff at a longer one. We calibrate a timing model from measurements at different precisions and context lengths, and combine it with tensor sensitivities to choose configurations under a latency or accuracy budget. We argue that fewer bits do not always mean faster execution, so our predictor estimates latency from calibrated execution costs rather than weight bytes alone. Under a latency budget, reading the larger key-value (KV) cache leaves less time for weight operations, leading the allocator to select lower precisions. This gives a schedule of tensor changes that can be prepared before execution. Our runtime follows the schedule while retaining the session's KV cache. We evaluate executed schedules on a laptop GPU, including a longer-context schedule with three weight formats and a tool-use benchmark measuring full response time and correctness. Under an accuracy budget, measured error from a quantized KV cache determines the budget left for weights. The allocator can raise or lower weight precision as this estimate changes. These experiments show where context-aware precision helps and where accuracy recovery remains limited.
authors: Mukund Athmaram, Manoj Rao, Liang Ma
bullets: Targets on-device SLM agents whose accuracy–latency tradeoff changes as context grows.
Calibrates execution-time costs across precisions and context lengths, then combines them with tensor sensitivities to allocate precision under latency or accuracy budgets.
Accounts for the fact that lower-bit weights are not always faster by predicting latency from measured execution costs rather than weight size alone.
Adjusts weight precision as the KV cache grows or becomes quantized, with schedules prepared before execution and followed while preserving the session cache.
Laptop-GPU and tool-use experiments identify cases where context-aware scheduling helps, while showing that accuracy recovery remains limited.
papers.selection_reason: Context-aware mixed-precision scheduling for on-device SLMs, directly targeting KV-cache and inference memory/latency efficiency.
papers.title: Context-Aware Precision Scheduling for Small Language Models
papers.tldr: A context-aware mixed-precision scheduler adapts SLM weight precision to changing context lengths, balancing latency and accuracy while retaining the KV cache.

papers.abstract: Choosing a mixed-precision configuration for large language model (LLM) serving trades speed against accuracy. Allocators that use average bit-width or a memory budget as a speed proxy can miss changes in the resource that limits execution. We argue that served speed can be limited by compute, weight loading, or key-value (KV) cache access, depending on the phase, batch size, and context length. A byte-based proxy does not capture all of these costs, so fewer bits do not always mean faster serving. To address this gap, we build a cost model that accounts for the binding resource and use it in two ways. First, as a predictor: given a configuration and operating point, it estimates serving latency using constants calibrated for the model, GPU, and serving stack. We evaluate its accuracy across three hardware classes. Second, as an allocator: we combine modeled time costs with measured per-tensor accuracy costs and use a dynamic program to select a configuration under a latency or accuracy budget. We compare its configurations against byte-aware and sensitivity-only allocation.
authors: Mukund Athmaram, Manoj Rao, Liang Ma
bullets: Serving speed depends on phase, batch size, context length, and the resource that becomes limiting.
The model predicts latency from a configuration and operating point using hardware- and stack-specific calibrated constants.
A dynamic-programming allocator combines modeled latency costs with measured per-tensor accuracy costs.
The approach is evaluated across three hardware classes and compared with byte-aware and sensitivity-only allocation.
Scope: performance depends on calibration for the target model, GPU, and serving stack.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses mixed-precision LLM serving efficiency, including KV-cache access and memory/latency trade-offs.
papers.title: The Price of Precision: A Calibrated Cost Model for Mixed-Precision LLM Serving
papers.tldr: A calibrated cost model improves mixed-precision LLM serving by accounting for compute, weight loading, and KV-cache bottlenecks instead of relying on bit-width or memory alone.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) unify visual world modeling and action generation, yet their real-world deployment is heavily bottlenecked by iterative action denoising and the sequential execution of visual prefilling and action prediction. We demonstrate that the action-denoising trajectories in WAMs are approximately straight, rendering the first-step velocity a strong estimate of the final action direction. Building on this observation, we introduce 1Step-WAM, a framework that transforms multi-step action denoising into one single forward. Specifically, we employ a lightweight calibrator to directly correct the first step velocity, and use bandwidth-constrained action decoding to further reduce errors in the calibrated one-step actions. Compressing action generation into a single step enables it to execute in parallel with visual prefilling, completely breaking the sequential bottleneck of the traditional imagination-then-action paradigm. Evaluations on RoboTwin and LIBERO show that 1Step-WAM largely preserves multi-step task success with only about 13.4M trainable parameters, while achieving inference speedups of $7.44\times$, $5.98\times$, and $24.84\times$ for FastWAM, ImageWAM and Kairos, respectively. Furthermore, real-world robotic deployments using the FastWAM backbone confirm a consistent 7.44$\times$ speedup while maintaining close success rate to the multi-step baseline. Code is avaliable at https://github.com/changdong1687/1Step-WAM.
authors: Rundong Su, Pengtao Chen, Haohan Geng, Sha Zhang, Zhihang Yuan, Yicheng Rong, Chong Yu, Hao Huang, Tao Chen
bullets: WAM deployment is slowed by iterative action denoising and sequential visual prefilling followed by action prediction.
The method observes that WAM denoising trajectories are approximately straight, using first-step velocity to estimate final action direction.
A lightweight calibrator corrects the one-step velocity, while bandwidth-constrained decoding reduces residual action errors.
One-step generation can run in parallel with visual prefilling, removing the traditional sequential bottleneck.
Experiments on RoboTwin, LIBERO, and real robots report speedups up to 24.84×, with success rates close to multi-step baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Speeds up World Action Models for robotic action generation via one-step denoising; relevant to robot learning and inference efficiency.
papers.title: 1Step-WAM: Your World Action Model but Faster using 1-Step Action Generation
papers.tldr: 1Step-WAM converts multi-step WAM action denoising into a single calibrated forward pass, substantially accelerating inference while largely preserving task success.

papers.abstract: Post-training expert pruning is a promising deployment technique for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. The calibration set is an integral part of the pruning process, however, its correlation with evaluation performance is largely misunderstood and unintuitive. In this work, we present an empirical study of the robustness of calibration perturbations, specifically in MoE models. Showing how calibration size, language, and data distribution affect layer-wise expert pruning for gpt-oss-20b. Our findings reveal that (1) domain-general pruning quality receives minimal benefit from scaling calibration data beyond small sample sizes, (2) cross-lingual calibration transfers effectively, with English-only calibration maintaining strong performance across seven languages of varying typologies and scripts, and (3) a diverse calibration data resembling the pretraining distribution can yield comparable or superior performance to test-distribution data. Ultimately, we provide practical insights as a recipe for better understanding calibration for more effective domain-general expert pruning.
authors: Luis Frentzen Salim, Chia-Chun Wu, Tran Van Nhiem, Lun-Wei Ku, Yung-Hui Li
bullets: Examines how calibration-set size, language, and data distribution affect layer-wise expert pruning in gpt-oss-20b.
Increasing calibration data beyond small sample sizes provides minimal benefit for domain-general pruning quality.
English-only calibration transfers effectively across seven languages with varied typologies and scripts.
Calibration data resembling the pretraining distribution can match or outperform test-distribution data.
Provides practical guidance for constructing robust calibration sets for MoE pruning.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses efficient deployment of MoE models via calibration-aware expert pruning.
papers.title: Towards Robust Calibration Dataset for Domain-General Mixture of Experts Pruning
papers.tldr: An empirical study finds that small, diverse, and often English-only calibration sets can robustly guide domain-general MoE expert pruning across languages.

papers.abstract: Structural pruning followed by a recovery stage is the standard recipe for compressing large language models (LLMs), yet the two stages are typically designed and tuned in isolation. In this work, we study how their interaction shapes the compressed model, sweeping ordering, the data that drives each stage, and the alignment of their training objectives. We find that instruction-following is the first capability to collapse under pruning, well before knowledge, reasoning, or core language modeling, and that much of the pruning in-domain loss is likely not knowledge loss but a domain-agnostic failure to respond coherently to the prompt. We find in our setting that in-domain data is the strongest pruning signal, whereas instruction-style data recovers the most. Stage order matters little, but only marginally. We further analyze how the importance ranking drifts before and after pruning. Together these results give practitioners a concrete recipe for composing pruning and recovery.
authors: Luis Frentzen Salim, Komang Rinartha, Chia-Chun Wu, Tran Van Nhiem, Lun-Wei Ku, Yung-Hui Li
bullets: Instruction-following collapses before knowledge, reasoning, or core language modeling during pruning.
Much of the in-domain loss appears to reflect incoherent prompt responses rather than knowledge loss.
In-domain data provides the strongest pruning signal in the studied setting.
Instruction-style data delivers the strongest recovery.
Pruning and recovery alter parameter-importance rankings, while reversing their stage order has only a marginal effect.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes interaction of structural pruning and recovery in LLMs, yielding a practical recipe for efficient compression.
papers.title: The Fragility and Dynamics of LLM Pruning-Recovery Steps
papers.tldr: LLM pruning primarily disrupts instruction-following, while instruction-style recovery data most effectively restores behavior, making pruning–recovery design choices important even when stage order has limited impact.

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models represent an emerging paradigm for language modeling. They generate text in parallel by iteratively refining continuous representations and mapping them back to tokens through a decoder. However, realizing the efficiency advantage of parallel generation requires maintaining generation quality with only a few denoising steps. Even when the number of steps is fixed, their placement along the denoising trajectory remains flexible. In this paper, we demonstrate that changing timestep placement alone can substantially alter the final latent representations and thereby affect the decoded token distributions. Building on these findings, we introduce StepTune, an algorithm that searches for timestep placements that improve generation quality. The search is conducted on a small calibration set and guided by a language-aware objective, with the model and sampling budget fixed. Once calibrated, the timestep placement is fixed and reused across inputs. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in unconditional generation perplexity and conditional task metrics across all evaluated sampling budgets. In particular, StepTune enables 16-step sampling with a frozen model to outperform its native 64-step baseline on both XSum summarization and WMT14 translation and reduces end-to-end latency by approximately $3.8\times$. These results establish timestep placement as a practical means of improving the quality-efficiency trade-off in continuous diffusion language models.
authors: Shutian Zheng, Zhihong Yu, Linye Wei, Zeyang Zhang, Meng Li
bullets: Timestep placement alone can substantially change latent representations and decoded token distributions.
StepTune searches for effective timestep schedules using a small calibration set and a language-aware objective.
The optimized schedule is fixed after calibration and reused across inputs, with the model unchanged.
It consistently improves unconditional perplexity and conditional task metrics across evaluated sampling budgets.
With 16 steps, StepTune surpasses the native 64-step baseline on XSum and WMT14 while reducing latency by approximately 3.8×.
papers.selection_reason: Optimizes timestep placement in continuous diffusion language models to improve quality-efficiency trade-off and reduce latency.
papers.title: A Step in the Right Place: Understanding and Optimizing Timestep Placement in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: StepTune improves continuous diffusion language model generation by optimizing where denoising steps occur, enabling faster sampling without changing the model or sampling budget.

papers.abstract: Adaptive image tokenizers compress an image into a variable number of tokens matched to its complexity, and recent work makes this allocation controllable: conditioned on a target reconstruction error, the tokenizer itself decides how many tokens an image needs. However, the fidelity measure guiding this allocation shapes which aspects of the image are preserved under compression. The pixel-wise error used in prior work is blind to the spatial structure that carries an image's meaning, and under heavy compression such tokenizers are prone to abruptly discarding tokens that encode essential content. We introduce GIST (Guided Image Semantic Tokenizer), an adaptive tokenizer that can be steered toward a requested semantic fidelity. Its token allocation is jointly controlled by pixel-level and semantic target errors, with semantic error measured in the feature space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder. This joint control enables semantic protection: with the semantic target fixed at zero, the reconstruction target can be relaxed to discard pixel detail while preserving what the image depicts. In a controlled comparison on ImageNet-100, GIST outperforms its pixel-controlled counterpart KARL at every token count, with up to $30\%$ lower LPIPS and $37\%$ lower DreamSim. On average, lowering its semantic target reduces LPIPS $2\times$ faster per token than lowering the reconstruction target, and up to $5\times$ in the low-token regime. Semantic fidelity is thus an effective control signal for adaptive tokenization: it lets a tokenizer see, and so preserve, what an image depicts.
authors: Danilo de Goede, Mohammad Mahdi Derakhshani, Yuki M. Asano, Cees G. M. Snoek
bullets: Pixel-wise error can discard semantically important content when token budgets are tight.
GIST uses a frozen DINOv3 feature space to measure semantic error alongside reconstruction error.
Fixing the semantic target while relaxing pixel fidelity enables detail removal without losing what the image depicts.
On ImageNet-100, GIST improves over KARL at every token count, with up to 30% lower LPIPS and 37% lower DreamSim.
Semantic targets reduce perceptual error faster per token, especially in low-token settings.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive image tokenization with semantic-fidelity-controlled token allocation; directly relevant to token pruning and efficiency.
papers.title: Semantically Steerable Image Tokenization
papers.tldr: GIST adaptively allocates image tokens using both pixel and semantic fidelity, preserving image content better under compression than pixel-only control.

papers.abstract: Large language models make decisions through parallel prefill and sequential decoding. Although effective, this approach incurs decoding costs and does not explicitly expose decision probabilities. Existing task-specific classifiers require per-task training and offer limited generalization to unseen decision schemas. We propose Large Decision Models (LDMs), repurposing language models to return explicit probabilities over labels specified at run time using one prefill forward pass. We first adapt models to this interface through Diverse Decision Supervision (DDS), covering varied domains, rules and labels. To further narrow the performance gap to a reasoning model, Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation (SPRD) adds tasks generated by a frozen teacher, filters them for answer consistency, and trains on label distributions obtained from repeated teacher reasoning. We evaluate on DecisionVista, pairing new-schema tests with held-out human-labelled sources. Across three base models, the recipe improves accuracy over a step-matched baseline by 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving a 182-fold speedup in latency over reasoning rollout on Gemma-4-31B. Reasoning remains stronger on the new-schema test, motivating a confidence router for uncertain decisions. On development sets, routing recovers a median 92% of reasoning's accuracy advantage while generating 27-58% of its tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/LDM.
authors: Ziyi Chen, Yan Zhang, Jianhui Wei, Jianing Yin, Daoan Zhang
bullets: LDMs support run-time-specified labels, improving generalization beyond task-specific classifiers.
Diverse Decision Supervision trains the model across varied domains, rules, and decision schemas.
Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation uses teacher-generated, consistency-filtered tasks and label distributions to narrow the reasoning gap.
Across three base models, LDMs improve accuracy over a step-matched baseline by 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points, with up to a 182× latency speedup over reasoning rollout on Gemma-4-31B.
A confidence router recovers a median 92% of reasoning’s accuracy advantage on development sets while using 27–58% as many tokens; reasoning remains stronger on new schemas.
papers.selection_reason: Repurposes LLMs as single-pass decision makers with large latency gains, relevant to LLM methods and efficient inference.
papers.title: Large Decision Models: Repurposing Large Language Models as Single-Pass Decision Makers
papers.tldr: Large Decision Models turn language models into fast, single-pass classifiers that output explicit label probabilities while retaining much of the accuracy of slower reasoning models.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models activate only a few experts per token, but when their expert weights are offloaded to host memory, host-to-device (H2D) expert transfers enter the critical path of decoding. Speculative decoding verifies several draft tokens in one forward pass, yet in an MoE model each verified token activates its own experts, so a larger draft tree transfers more experts. Because of this H2D cost, speculative decoding commits several tokens per verification cycle yet is sometimes even slower than autoregressive decoding. Based on this observation, we propose SpecFit, which chooses the verified draft subtree to maximize predicted throughput rather than acceptance length. SpecFit estimates the expected number of committed tokens from draft path probabilities and predicts cycle time from the node count and the per-layer union of the experts the subtree activates; this union is a monotone submodular coverage function, so each node pays only for the experts it adds. An exact search over ancestor-closed subtrees returns the subtree with the highest predicted throughput; run after each draft level, the same search also decides when to stop drafting, and the unmodified target verifies the result. On CNN/DailyMail summarization and a GSM8K subset with Qwen3-30B-A3B, SpecFit decodes 21.6% and 7.0% faster than EAGLE-3 with the same expert cache and 1.97x and 1.72x as fast as vanilla EAGLE-3. Code is available at https://github.com/Chlience/SpecFit.
authors: Hongliang Cao, Xiuyu Li, Siqi Wang, Ziming Wang, Jingmin Zhu, Hailong Yang
bullets: Offloaded MoE inference makes host-to-device expert transfers a decoding bottleneck, so longer drafts are not always faster.
SpecFit predicts committed tokens from draft-path probabilities and cycle time from subtree size and the experts activated across layers.
It searches ancestor-closed draft subtrees using a monotone submodular expert-coverage cost and also determines when to stop drafting.
With Qwen3-30B-A3B, it decodes 21.6% faster on CNN/DailyMail and 7.0% faster on a GSM8K subset than EAGLE-3, using the same expert cache.
Scope: results are reported for the stated summarization and math benchmarks with an offloaded MoE model.
papers.selection_reason: Improves MoE inference efficiency via speculative decoding and expert offloading, directly relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: SpecFit: Not All Draft Tokens Cost the Same in Offloaded MoE Inference
papers.tldr: SpecFit speeds up speculative decoding for offloaded MoE models by selecting draft subtrees that maximize throughput while accounting for expert-transfer costs.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong generalization across a broad range of reasoning and generation tasks, but their large parameter counts impose substantial memory and computation costs, hindering deployment in practical resource-constrained settings. One-shot low-rank compression is a promising solution since it reduces model size and inference cost effectively. However, existing SVD-based methods primarily target multiple-choice benchmarks and often fail to preserve performance on generation tasks. Moreover, their rank allocation strategies are typically heuristic. We propose GA-SVD, a generation-aware low-rank compression framework for LLMs. First, we introduce Generation-Aware Weight Whitening (GAWW), which leverages gradients from on-policy knowledge distillation to construct whitening transformations aligned with generative behavior. Second, we develop an evolutionary global rank allocation method that searches for effective layer-wise rank allocation under a given global compression ratio. Across extensive experiments on Mistral-7B, Qwen3 series, and Llama-3.3 models, evaluated on both multiple-choice and generative benchmarks, GA-SVD consistently outperforms existing SVD-based baselines and achieves state-of-the-art (SoTA) results. We further demonstrate scalability by applying our method to models with up to 70B parameters.
authors: Shengkun Tang, Cong Zeng, Zongfang Liu, Dan Alistarh, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Targets the difficulty of preserving generative performance under low-rank LLM compression.
Uses Generation-Aware Weight Whitening based on gradients from on-policy knowledge distillation.
Employs evolutionary search to optimize layer-wise rank allocation for a target global compression ratio.
Evaluated on Mistral-7B, Qwen3, and Llama-3.3 across multiple-choice and generative benchmarks.
Reports consistent gains over existing SVD-based baselines and scalability to models up to 70B parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Low-rank LLM compression reduces model memory and inference cost.
papers.title: GA-SVD: Generation-aware Singular Value Decomposition for LLM Compression
papers.tldr: GA-SVD improves one-shot SVD-based LLM compression by allocating ranks and whitening weights with generation quality in mind.

papers.abstract: Structured pruning is typically formulated as identifying which model dimensions to remove, often within the model's original representation. However, the effect of coordinate deletion fundamentally depends on the basis in which pruning is performed. This raises a more fundamental question: how should the basis be chosen specifically for coordinate deletion? We introduce WUSPruner, a transform-based framework for structured pruning of large language models. We formulate basis selection as a local linear reconstruction problem that directly minimizes the reconstruction loss induced by pruning. Inspired by the second-moment transformation in WUSH, we consider a WUS transform constructed jointly from activation and weight statistics. We show that under positive-definite second moments, WUS transform minimizes the local reconstruction loss over all invertible changes of basis. In the resulting basis, the activation and weight second moments are simultaneously diagonalized and balanced, causing the deletion error to decompose into independent spectral contributions and yielding a principled criterion for coordinate selection. Guided by this result, we develop a scalable pruning method based on blockwise WUS transformations and compact input projections. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models from 8B to 72B parameters show consistent improvements over structured pruning baselines across language modeling, knowledge, commonsense reasoning, mathematics, and code generation benchmarks, while also delivering practical reductions in inference latency and memory usage.
authors: Shengkun Tang, Dan Alistarh, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Structured pruning performance depends on the coordinate basis used for deletion.
The method selects a basis by minimizing local linear reconstruction loss caused by pruning.
Under positive-definite second moments, WUS jointly diagonalizes and balances activation and weight statistics, making deletion error spectrally separable.
A scalable implementation uses blockwise WUS transforms and compact input projections.
Experiments on 8B–72B Llama and Qwen models report consistent gains over pruning baselines across diverse benchmarks, with reduced latency and memory usage.
papers.selection_reason: Structured pruning of LLMs directly targets memory and inference efficiency.
papers.title: WUSPruner: Second-Moment-Optimal Transforms for Structured Pruning
papers.tldr: WUSPruner chooses an optimal pruning basis using activation and weight second moments, enabling principled structured pruning with improved quality and lower inference cost.
