papers.abstract: Compressing the key-value (KV) cache is essential for serving long-context large language models (LLMs) under memory constraints. While current scalar quantization methods achieve significant compression, they typically face a quality-fidelity trade-off, either suffering from performance instability at 2-bit precision or necessitating 3-bit keys to maintain model quality. In this work, we demonstrate that a uniform low-bit k2v2 configuration (2-bit keys and 2-bit values) can preserve near-baseline quality by using vector quantization (VQ) based on the $E_8$ lattice for KV keys. We show that structured VQ exploits correlations across adjacent dimensions to achieve signal-to-quantization-noise ratios (SQNR) higher than those of independent scalar quantization at the same key payload rate. To ensure practical utility, we adapt a table-based asymmetric scoring algorithm that avoids explicit codebook dequantization during attention computation and preserves decode-throughput parity with scalar baselines. Across five LLM families, our $E_8$ k2v2 approach yields \textasciitilde$6\times$ KV compression, roughly 20\% smaller than scalar k3v2 (3-bit keys and 2-bit values), while retaining near-baseline long-context perplexity. In our full-suite perplexity evaluation, $E_8$ improves over scalar k3v2 in 80\% of model--dataset--context settings. These results indicate that $E_8$ lattice VQ improves quality per byte while keeping throughput at parity, suggesting that structured key quantization is a useful primitive for KV-compression stacks. Overall, our work provides a low-overhead primitive for expanding the quality-memory frontier in long-context LLM inference.
authors: Sasho Nedelkoski, Alexander Acker, Soeren Becker, Dominik Scheinert, Odej Kao
bullets: Addresses the quality instability of 2-bit KV-cache quantization and the memory cost of using 3-bit keys.
Uses E8-lattice vector quantization for keys to exploit correlations across adjacent dimensions and improve quantization efficiency.
Applies table-based asymmetric attention scoring to avoid explicit codebook dequantization.
Across five LLM families, E8 k2v2 is about 20% smaller than scalar k3v2 and improves perplexity in 80% of evaluated settings.
Provides a structured, low-overhead primitive for improving the quality–memory trade-off in long-context inference.
papers.selection_reason: E8 lattice vector quantization for low-bit KV-cache compression in long-context LLM inference.
papers.title: E8 Lattice Key Quantization for Low-Bit KV-Cache Compression
papers.tldr: E8-lattice vector quantization enables 2-bit keys and values to compress LLM KV caches by about 6× while retaining near-baseline long-context quality and scalar-baseline decode throughput.

papers.abstract: Large language models are generally more capable than smaller ones, but their memory requirements can make local deployment difficult. We ask whether part of this capability gap can instead be recovered by running a smaller or more compressed model multiple times and selecting among its outputs using public or model-generated tests. Single-user local inference can leave hardware underutilized, allowing parallel candidate generation to trade additional test-time computation for accuracy at modest latency cost. Across four code-generation benchmarks, verified retry recovers substantial accuracy lost to model size or compression. A 7B Qwen model with eight parallel attempts essentially matches a 32B model on MBPP+ and exceeds it on the other three benchmarks, while using about $4\times$ less model memory, running up to $6\times$ faster, and using less energy, as measured on Nvidia GPU. We observe similar tradeoff across model sizes, compression levels and hardware choices, although exact benefit depends on the hardware profile and problem setting. These results show that model capacity can be traded for verified test-time computation when correct solutions remain reachable within a modest retry budget.
authors: Tomer Galanti, Josh Susskind, Eran Malach
bullets: Runs multiple candidate solutions in parallel and selects them using public or model-generated tests.
Across four code-generation benchmarks, retries recover substantial accuracy lost from smaller or compressed models.
A 7B Qwen model with eight attempts nearly matches a 32B model on MBPP+ and surpasses it on the other benchmarks.
The approach can reduce model memory by about 4×, run up to 6× faster, and use less energy in the reported Nvidia GPU setting.
Benefits vary with hardware and problem setting, and depend on correct solutions being reachable within a modest retry budget.
papers.selection_reason: Studies verified retry to recover capability under memory constraints, trading test-time compute for accuracy and energy; relevant to efficient LLM deployment.
papers.title: Fewer Bits, More Tries: Recovering Capability Under Memory Constraints
papers.tldr: Verified parallel retries let smaller or compressed language models recover much of the code-generation capability of larger models under tight memory limits.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models enable streaming generation of long videos but suffer from significant memory overhead due to the rapidly growing KV cache. Existing KV cache quantization methods are primarily designed for LLMs and transfer poorly to video models, where activations exhibit different statistics and strong spatiotemporal redundancy. We observe that the video KV cache is largely predictable over time, with a clear asymmetry. Keys are highly predictable from their temporal history, while values depend primarily on the current key and need a short history of preceding values. Based on these observations, we propose \textbf{\method}, a training-free predictive KV cache quantization framework for AR video generation. \method predicts keys and values according to their distinct dependencies and stores only the residuals at low precision. Both predictors are lightweight, calibrated once offline by linear regression on a small set of BF16 samples, and remain fixed across prompts and generation runs. Experiments on Self-Forcing, Causal Forcing, and LongCat-Video-13B show that \method consistently achieves higher generation quality than existing KV cache quantization methods at comparable or higher compression ratios, reaching up to $6.71\times$ KV cache compression with the best overall quality--efficiency tradeoff. Our code will be released on GitHub.
authors: Jiahui Hu, Weile Mo, Peiliang Cai, Jiacheng Liu, Jinkui Ren, Xiantao Zhang, Xiaobing Tu, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: AR video diffusion models face rapidly growing KV-cache memory overhead during long-video streaming generation.
Existing LLM-oriented KV quantization methods transfer poorly because video activations have distinct statistics and strong spatiotemporal redundancy.
TempoKV predicts keys from temporal history and values from the current key plus a short value history, then stores residuals at low precision.
Predictors are calibrated once offline with linear regression on a small BF16 sample set and remain fixed across prompts and runs.
Across Self-Forcing, Causal Forcing, and LongCat-Video-13B, it reports better quality than existing methods at comparable or higher compression, with up to 6.71× compression.
papers.selection_reason: Predictive KV cache quantization for autoregressive video generation directly targets memory efficiency in inference.
papers.title: TempoKV: Predictive KV Cache Quantization for Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.tldr: TempoKV uses lightweight, training-free predictors to compress autoregressive video-generation KV caches by quantizing only prediction residuals, achieving up to 6.71× compression while preserving generation quality.

papers.abstract: Efficient neural architecture search (NAS) requires accurate performance estimation under limited evaluation budgets. Existing zero-cost proxies (ZCPs) provide fast training-free signals, but each proxy usually captures only a partial property of an architecture, leading to unstable rankings across datasets and search spaces. In contrast, GNN-based predictors can improve accuracy, but often depend on labeled architectures, graph encoders, and costly representation learning, which makes them less suitable for extreme few-shot settings. We propose FENAS, a topology-agnostic few-shot prediction framework that turns complementary initialization priors into robust ranking signals. Its core component, CAST, is a feature pipeline that combines copula alignment and synergy transformation. CAST maps heterogeneous ZCPs into a compact feature manifold, enabling lightweight meta-learners to produce reliable rankings from scarce supervision. On NAS-Bench-201, with only 0.5% labeled samples, FENAS achieves a Kendall's Tau ($\tau$) of 0.70, outperforming representative topology-based few-shot predictors in this low-label regime. In closed-domain search, FENAS evaluates the NAS-Bench-201 space in approximately 1138 seconds and achieves competitive test accuracy. By providing a fast, reliable, and structurally simple evaluation mechanism, FENAS supports the design of automated neural architectures under limited evaluation budgets.
authors: Yifeng Mao, Yuze Feng, Yutong Shen, Liyang Gao, Zhixiang He
bullets: Targets unstable architecture rankings from individual zero-cost proxies and the high labeling cost of GNN-based predictors.
CAST uses copula alignment and synergy transformation to map heterogeneous proxies into a compact, unified feature space.
A topology-agnostic meta-ensemble produces rankings from very limited labeled architectures.
With 0.5% labeled samples on NAS-Bench-201, FENAS reaches Kendall’s τ of 0.70 and evaluates the search space in approximately 1138 seconds.
The reported scope includes closed-domain NAS on NAS-Bench-201; broader generalization is not established by the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Few-shot NAS with zero-cost proxies reduces architecture evaluation cost.
papers.title: FENAS: A Few-Shot Meta-Ensembling Framework for Efficient Neural Architecture Search with Synergized Zero-Cost Proxies
papers.tldr: FENAS combines complementary zero-cost proxies with lightweight meta-learning to rank neural architectures accurately under extreme few-shot NAS budgets.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a new approach to wearable-sensor-based human activity recognition. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) further introduces similar motion examples and discriminative sensor knowledge, enabling decisions grounded in observations relevant to the current query. More evidence, however, does not necessarily mean better-organized evidence. When online prompts and LLM agents primarily orchestrate inference, decisions about which activities to compare and when to invoke discriminative knowledge remain concentrated at inference time. As the activity vocabulary grows, the model must repeatedly process more candidates and associated knowledge, whereas pruning candidates too early risks excluding the true activity. We propose confusion-hierarchy evidence-aware reasoning (CHEAR), which moves part of this knowledge organization offline. CHEAR constructs and validates an activity hierarchy from recurrent cross-subject retrieval errors and builds corresponding activity-pair knowledge. At inference time, the hierarchy orders candidate comparisons; the LLM retains candidates progressively, and local discriminative knowledge is accessed only for the remaining activities. Across eight datasets, CHEAR achieves 86.79\% mean cross-subject accuracy, a 75.91\% candidate reduction rate, and 96.44\% true-activity retention. Per-sample token use is 85.15\% lower on average than in a variant without the hierarchical structure. Mean accuracy across eight cross-dataset transfer directions is 88.81\%. These results show that organizing candidates and discriminative knowledge around observed activity confusions reduces online LLM input while maintaining recognition performance.
authors: Xiangqing Lu, Tao Zhu, Mingxing Nie, Liming Chen
bullets: Builds and validates an activity hierarchy from recurring cross-subject retrieval errors.
Uses the hierarchy to order candidate comparisons and retrieve local pairwise knowledge only for surviving activities.
Across eight datasets, reports 86.79% mean cross-subject accuracy, 75.91% candidate reduction, and 96.44% true-activity retention.
Reduces average per-sample token use by 85.15% versus a non-hierarchical variant.
Reports 88.81% mean accuracy across eight cross-dataset transfer directions.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces LLM inference cost through offline hierarchical candidate organization, substantially lowering per-sample token use while preserving accuracy.
papers.title: CHEAR: Confusion-Hierarchy Evidence-Aware Reasoning for Cost-Efficient Human Activity Recognition
papers.tldr: CHEAR organizes activity candidates and discriminative evidence using an offline confusion hierarchy, reducing LLM inference cost while maintaining strong wearable-sensor activity recognition.

papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the cost of serving reasoning models but can substantially degrade long chains of thought. Each step reads cached keys and values spanning thousands of tokens, allowing quantization errors to accumulate along the trajectory. Standard calibration operates on short segments that omit the earlier context needed by later reasoning steps. Even when this context is retained, cache reconstruction error alone does not capture how quantization errors affect subsequent attention. We present RECAP, a post-training quantization method that calibrates reasoning models on the history they read. Dynamic-prefix calibration separates long historical context from short-block reconstruction. It regenerates prefix keys and values with the current quantizer and rotates the active block to supervise every position along the trajectory. Prefix read geometry further supervises historical cache errors according to their effects on attention outputs, weighting key and value errors asymmetrically. With both components applied only during calibration, RECAP outperforms the baseline across multiple reasoning models and quantization settings. Under W4A4KV4, RECAP improves accuracy over the baseline by 13.3 percentage points on MATH500 with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 15.8 points on AIME-120 with Qwen3-4B. These results highlight the importance of preserving historical dependencies during calibration for low-bit reasoning.
authors: Chi Ruan, Yujie Chen, Zixiang Zhao, Jingcai Guo, Haotong Qin
bullets: Low-bit quantization can degrade long-chain reasoning as cache errors accumulate across thousands of historical tokens.
RECAP uses dynamic-prefix calibration to reconstruct long prefixes and supervise each position along the reasoning trajectory.
Prefix read geometry weights historical key and value errors by their effects on attention outputs.
Applied only during calibration, RECAP outperforms the baseline across multiple models and quantization settings.
Under W4A4KV4, it improves accuracy by 13.3 points on MATH500 and 15.8 points on AIME-120 in the reported settings.
papers.selection_reason: Low-bit quantization method for reasoning models that calibrates on cached historical context, directly targeting KV cache error accumulation and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: RECAP: Calibrating Low-Bit Reasoning Models on the History They Read
papers.tldr: RECAP improves low-bit quantization of reasoning models by calibrating on the long histories their attention actually reads.

papers.abstract: Tool-using agents alternate between model generation and tool execution, waiting for each tool call to complete before starting the next generation. This sequential execution is costly during agentic reinforcement learning (RL), which requires large batches of multi-turn rollouts. We introduce ObsSpec, an observation speculation pipeline for agentic RL that uses a small world model to predict tool outputs while the environment executes, allowing the policy to begin its next generation early. ObsSpec retains speculative work only when the predicted and actual observations match exactly, making rollout collection lossless, while co-training keeps the world model up to date as the policy learns. On terminal-use tasks, predictions from a 0.6B world model exactly match actual observations in 66.4% of attempts and arrive roughly 16 times faster. Using these predictions, ObsSpec reduces agent latency by 9.3% and 14.2% for 8B and 32B policies. Across controlled experiments, we characterize the regimes in which ObsSpec reduces agent latency under shared policy resources. Finally, because ObsSpec overlaps policy generation with tool execution, it is architecturally compatible with existing techniques for accelerating RL. Code is available at https://github.com/kylemontgomery1/verl-recipe/tree/obsspec/obsspec.
authors: Kyle Montgomery, Wang Zhang, Chenguang Wang
bullets: Targets the latency caused by sequential policy generation and tool execution in multi-turn agentic RL.
Uses a small co-trained world model to predict tool outputs, letting the policy start generating before execution finishes.
Keeps speculative generations only when predictions exactly match actual observations, avoiding rollout changes.
A 0.6B world model matches terminal-use observations in 66.4% of attempts and predicts them about 16× faster.
Reduces agent latency by 9.3% for 8B policies and 14.2% for 32B policies in reported experiments.
papers.selection_reason: Uses a co-trained world model to speculate tool observations and accelerate agentic RL rollouts.
papers.title: ObsSpec: Accelerating Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Observation Speculation
papers.tldr: ObsSpec speeds up agentic RL rollouts by speculating tool observations in parallel with tool execution while preserving lossless training.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). However, ZO optimization suffers from high variance in high-dimensional parameter spaces. While recent methods restrict perturbations to random low-rank subspaces, these subspaces often misalign with task-specific descent directions. We propose AdaSub-ZO, a novel forward-only fine-tuning framework in learnable low-rank subspaces. Instead of relying on fixed random matrices, AdaSub-ZO iteratively learns layer-wise projection matrices directly from finite-difference feedback to track task-aware descent directions. Furthermore, AdaSub-ZO incorporates a subspace momentum acceleration mechanism to smooth noisy gradient estimates across evolving subspace bases. Extensive experiments on natural language understanding tasks demonstrate that AdaSub-ZO outperforms existing ZO baselines, substantially reducing gradient estimation variance and accelerating convergence.
bullets: ZO fine-tuning avoids storing backpropagation gradients but suffers from high-variance estimates in high-dimensional parameter spaces.
AdaSub-ZO learns layer-wise projection matrices from finite-difference feedback instead of using fixed random subspaces.
A subspace momentum mechanism smooths gradient estimates as the learned subspaces evolve.
Experiments on natural language understanding tasks show lower estimation variance and faster convergence than existing ZO baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient forward-only fine-tuning of LLMs in learnable low-rank subspaces.
papers.title: Zeroth-Order Fine-Tuning of LLMs in Learnable Low-Rank Subspaces
papers.tldr: AdaSub-ZO improves memory-efficient zeroth-order LLM fine-tuning by learning task-aligned low-rank subspaces and using momentum to reduce noisy updates.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking
bullets: Investigates how generating outputs from intermediate layers affects LLM jailbreak vulnerability.
Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreaks than deeper exits.
Deeper exits allow adversarial suffixes to be optimized more effectively, achieving lower attack loss.
Adversarial suffixes degrade utility similarly across different exit depths.
Findings can inform more jailbreak-robust dynamic inference designs.
papers.selection_reason: Studies robustness of depth-based dynamic inference, an efficiency-oriented inference method, relevant to efficient AI design.
papers.title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: A study finds that earlier exits in depth-based dynamic LLM inference are generally more resistant to jailbreak attacks than deeper exits, revealing a robustness–depth trade-off.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reuses the same documents across many requests, making non-prefix KV-cache reuse attractive. Yet a cached document state is not reusable text: it is a context-conditioned causal state whose keys and values depend on the prefix, position, and preceding documents under which it was computed. We formulate non-prefix KV reuse as a behavior-preservation problem with full prefill on the exact prompt as the reference, and introduce SAFE-KV, which repairs a composed cache by re-encoding the causal suffix from a selected start document. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, prefix-conditioned composition preserves only 47.2% of HotpotQA-500 and 37.8% of 2Wiki-500 full-prefill answers; SAFE-KV with risk-guided K2 selection restores 99.8%/98.4% (donor-copy protocol) and 100.0%/98.4% with actual suffix forwarding. Document-only and fixed-window repairs recover far less, because the document states after the repaired region keep histories that omit it. Reuse without repair is exact up to four documents and degrades at sixteen, where suffix repair recovers 98-100%. Faithful repair re-encodes most of the context, so in a single-request L40S study SAFE-KV's operating rule serves every workload by full prefill. SAFE-KV thus establishes the causal-state contract for non-prefix reuse and a validated repair mechanism that meets it.
bullets: Non-prefix KV reuse is difficult because cached states depend on the prompt prefix, positions, and preceding documents.
SAFE-KV selects a repair start document using risk-guided K2 selection and re-encodes the causal suffix.
On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, recovery reached 99.8%/98.4% on HotpotQA-500/2Wiki-500 with donor-copy repair and 100.0%/98.4% with actual suffix forwarding.
Unrepaired composition degraded from exact behavior at four documents to substantially worse behavior at sixteen; document-only and fixed-window repairs were less effective.
Faithful repair re-encodes most of the context, and in the reported single-request L40S study full prefill remained the operating choice.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses KV cache reuse and memory-efficient inference in RAG, fitting the KV cache and memory efficiency subtopic.
papers.title: SAFE-KV: Causal Suffix Repair for Behavior-Preserving Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in RAG
papers.tldr: SAFE-KV repairs non-prefix KV-cache compositions by re-encoding a causal suffix, restoring behavior close to exact full-prefill generation.

papers.abstract: Existing depth-compression methods for large language models (LLMs) score layers individually or group only adjacent or contiguous layers, implicitly assuming that functional redundancy is local. We test this assumption by computing full pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity matrices for thirteen LLMs from six architecture families (1.6B-14B parameters). Non-adjacent layers have 3.6-15.9x more high-similarity pairs than adjacent ones, a structure that prior similarity-based layer merging has not systematically exploited. We propose Fusion via Community Mining (FCM), which builds the full L x L similarity graph, uses spectral community detection to find clusters of functionally equivalent layers, keeps the highest-Block-Influence layer in each cluster, and applies LoRA recovery; a pre-specified rule computed only on calibration data chooses between cosine and CKA similarity. At 2x compression, FCM lowers mean perplexity below ShortGPT on twelve of thirteen models, significantly on ten (Welch's t-test with Holm-Bonferroni correction; up to 50% on Qwen3-4B), with Mistral-7B the only loss (+13.4%). Against FlattenGPT, SWM, and DeltaLLM under matched calibration and recovery, FCM gives the best perplexity on ten of thirteen models (mean rank 1.15), and it also outperforms MKA on three anchor models. FCM matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning cells and also improves MMLU, LAMBADA, HumanEval pass@1, and free-form generation quality. The 2x-compressed Qwen2.5-7B has 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on a single A100. Spectral grouping outperforms Fisher contiguous segmentation by 41% and uniform partitioning by 51%, and FCM's advantage grows beyond a 2x crossover up to 3x and persists at the 14B scale. Code: https://github.com/Usama1002/fcm-layer-fusion
bullets: Full pairwise CKA analysis across 13 LLMs finds substantially more high-similarity non-adjacent than adjacent layer pairs, challenging local-redundancy assumptions.
FCM constructs a layer-similarity graph, detects functional communities spectrally, retains the highest-Block-Influence layer per cluster, and applies LoRA recovery.
At 2× compression, FCM beats ShortGPT in mean perplexity on 12 of 13 models and is best among several baselines on 10 of 13.
It matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning evaluations and improves several downstream generation and language benchmarks.
For compressed Qwen2.5-7B, FCM reports 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on one A100; Mistral-7B is the main exception, with a perplexity loss.
papers.selection_reason: Graph-guided layer fusion compresses LLMs, reducing memory and improving inference throughput.
papers.title: Beyond Adjacent Layers: Graph-Guided Layer Fusion for Compressing Large Language Models
papers.tldr: FCM compresses LLM depth by grouping functionally similar non-adjacent layers, achieving strong perplexity and efficiency improvements at up to 3× compression.

papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. We present the first Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP scaling study of a spiking language model, sweeping SpikeGPT-family models (RWKV backbone) from width 384 to 1536 across compute budgets from $3\times10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ FLOPs on FineWeb-EDU. We report two findings. First, the compute-optimal frontier is $N_{opt} \propto C^{0.56}$, close to the 0.50 that Hoffmann et al. report for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters and data should be traded off under a compute budget. Second, against non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines trained the same way, the loss gap splits into a backbone cost of about 0.16 nats that does not change with compute and a spiking cost that falls from 0.34 to about 0.23 nats and then levels off. These results give the first compute-optimal recipe for spiking language models and quantify the accuracy cost of their sparsity.
authors: Dan Saunders, Benjamin Ren, Catherine He
bullets: Studies SpikeGPT-family models with an RWKV backbone across widths 384–1536 and compute budgets of 3×10^17–10^19 FLOPs.
Finds the compute-optimal parameter scaling exponent is 0.56, close to the 0.50 reported for dense Transformers.
Decomposes the loss gap versus non-spiking baselines into a roughly compute-invariant backbone cost of 0.16 nats and a spiking cost that decreases before leveling off near 0.23 nats.
Provides a compute-optimal scaling recipe and quantifies the accuracy cost associated with spiking activations.
papers.selection_reason: Compute-optimal scaling laws for spiking language models inform efficient language model design and scaling.
papers.title: Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language Models
papers.tldr: A large-scale scaling study finds that spiking language models follow dense-model compute-optimal parameter–data tradeoffs while incurring a persistent accuracy penalty from sparsity.

papers.abstract: Linear-attention and state-space LLMs carry long context in a fixed-size recurrent state, and quantizing that state is the natural way to cut its cost during long decode. Unlike a weight tensor, the state is rewritten at every step, so a quantizer applied at each step sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound. INT4 that leaves synthetic recall perfectly intact at the start destroys it a thousand steps later. The mechanism is a feedback between the quantizer scale and the state it is derived from. Yoking that scale to a full-precision reference removes the resulting norm explosion entirely, yet recovers only 1.8 of the 5.4 nats lost, so numerical instability and functional degradation are separable failures. The remainder is a resolution problem that locating outliers does not solve, since every outlier-aware scheme here loses to plain persistent scaling. Allocating bits across layers does help, but under article-disjoint splits a learned allocation collapses onto the trivial rule of protecting the first few layers. Run out to 32K, group-wise INT4 is worth no more than discarding the state. Contain the scale rather than locate outliers, and report the decode horizon at which a bit-width was certified.
bullets: Quantization errors compound because the recurrent state is rewritten at every decoding step.
Tying the quantizer scale to a full-precision reference eliminates norm explosion but recovers only part of the lost performance, separating instability from resolution limits.
Outlier-aware quantization does not resolve the remaining degradation; persistent scaling performs better in the reported comparisons.
Learned bit allocation helps mainly by protecting the first few layers, and group-wise INT4 provides little value at 32K context.
Quantization claims should report the decode horizon over which a bit-width is validated.
papers.selection_reason: Recurrent-state quantization for linear-attention and SSM LLMs directly targets memory-efficient long-decode inference.
papers.title: When Dynamic Scaling Fails: A Scale-State Feedback Governs Recurrent-State Quantization in Linear-Attention and SSM LLMs
papers.tldr: Recurrent-state INT4 quantization in linear-attention and SSM LLMs fails over long decoding because scale feedback causes instability, while preventing scale explosion does not fully restore functionality.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity closed-loop simulation for autonomous driving increasingly relies on dense multi-view 3D reconstruction. While recent feed-forward geometric foundation models have revolutionized per-scene optimization, applying them to continuous, long-horizon driving sequences is computationally intractable due to GPU memory limits and the quadratic complexity of global attention. Existing scaling strategies are fundamentally limited, as causal streaming suffers from compounding scale drift and trajectory deviation, while rigid "chunk-then-align" heuristics fragment global context and produce trajectory discontinuities. To address these limitations, we introduce Drive3R, a block-wise streaming geometric foundation model. Its block-wise causal attention resolves the scalability bottleneck of fully bidirectional attention while avoiding the loss of local future context in purely causal streaming. Its confidence-aware re-anchoring further mitigates long-range drift by detecting unreliable streaming states, re-initializing the KV cache, and stitching refreshed segments through SE(3) alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Drive3R establishes a new state-of-the-art on nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo. Specifically, on nuScenes, it improves over the recent DVGT-2 baseline from 0.1806 to 0.1081 in AbsRel, from 0.6750 to 0.5344 in point-cloud Accuracy, and from 1.5812 to 0.9092 in ATE.
authors: Tianyi Yang, Haojun Yang, Jipeng Xiao, Xuesong Chen, Shaoshuai Shi, Li Jiang, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses GPU-memory and quadratic-attention limits in continuous multi-view 3D reconstruction.
Uses block-wise causal attention to retain local future context while scaling beyond full bidirectional attention.
Detects unreliable streaming states, re-initializes the KV cache, and stitches refreshed segments with SE(3) alignment to reduce drift and trajectory discontinuities.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo; on nuScenes, it improves AbsRel, point-cloud Accuracy, and ATE over DVGT-2.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming geometric foundation model for multi-view 3D reconstruction, with block-wise attention and KV cache re-anchoring for long-horizon driving.
papers.title: Drive3R: Block-wise Streaming Geometric Foundation Models for Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: Drive3R enables scalable, drift-resistant 3D reconstruction for long-horizon autonomous-driving sequences through block-wise streaming attention and confidence-aware re-anchoring.

papers.abstract: LLM multi-agent systems split work across agents that communicate through text. An agent summarizes its findings, another agent receives the text. This constrains communication to discrete tokens and costs redundant compute, limiting bandwidth and capabilities of multi-agent systems. Recent works demonstrate KV-cache transfer between LLMs but they either require the LLMs to be within the same family or cannot function across context, thus requiring the receiver to prefill text. We present SwaT (Swarm Telepathy), the first cross-family KV-cache transfer method that allows prefill-free communication in multi-family multi-agent systems. In an agent-to-agent communication setting, combining SwaT with recent advances in KV-cache compaction beats text-to-text communication in both accuracy and speed, with a mean of $40\%$ higher accuracy and a mean of $4\times$ faster wall-clock time. Experiments show SwaT achieves high performance on 17 benchmarks across 12 LLMs and 6 families. Additionally, given a sender Vision-Language Model (VLM), SwaT is able to transfer the vision capabilities to a text-only receiver LLM exceeding text-to-text communication despite SwaT being trained on text-only data. SwaT keeps both sender and receiver models frozen without fine-tuning and only requires $<50M$ tokens and $<1$ GPU-day to train.
authors: Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem, Irene Tenison, Yang Zhang, Yada Zhu, Boris Katz, Dan Gutfreund
bullets: Addresses the bandwidth, redundant-compute, and context limitations of text-only communication between agents.
Transfers KV caches across model families without requiring the receiver to prefill the communicated text.
Combined with KV-cache compaction, it reports 40% higher mean accuracy and 4× faster mean wall-clock time than text-to-text communication.
Evaluated across 17 benchmarks, 12 LLMs, and 6 model families.
Can transfer a sender VLM’s vision capabilities to a text-only receiver, while keeping both models frozen.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-family KV-cache transfer for prefill-free multi-agent LLM communication; directly targets KV-cache efficiency and LLM systems.
papers.title: Swarm Telepathy: Prefill-Free KV-Cache Transfer Across Families
papers.tldr: SwaT enables fast, prefill-free KV-cache communication between different LLM families, outperforming text-based agent communication in accuracy and speed.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents operate in iterative loops: they modify code, run tools, inspect the results, and decide what to do next. We call the design of this process loop engineering, which includes context management, model selection, compaction, and termination. Existing efficiency work mainly compresses tool observations or routes selected turns to cheaper models, but the practical opportunity for these optimizations remains unclear. We analyze 600 publicly released coding-agent trajectories spanning two agent scaffolds and two language models. Median observations contain only 118-286 tokens, while the large build logs commonly used to motivate compression occur near the ninety-ninth percentile. Moreover, 98.6% of input tokens are served from a prefix cache, so flat input pricing overestimates loop cost by roughly 7x on average under near-ideal caching. We derive and empirically validate a closed-form break-even condition for model delegation. Delegation increases cost in half of the evaluated settings, near the predicted boundary. More broadly, turn count explains 84% of the variance in log trajectory cost, compared with 4% for mean observation size; the most expensive trajectories have the most turns despite having the smallest observations. These associations suggest that observation-focused methods target a secondary cost factor, and identify unnecessary turns as the larger and largely unexamined opportunity, though we do not establish that turns can be removed while holding task success fixed. We release TurnCost, a tool for re-scoring trajectory corpora under alternative caching, pricing, compression, and routing policies.
bullets: Analyzes 600 coding-agent trajectories across two scaffolds and two language models.
Median observations are small (118–286 tokens); large build logs are uncommon, appearing near the 99th percentile.
Prefix caching serves 98.6% of input tokens, making flat input pricing overestimate loop cost by about 7× on average.
Turn count explains 84% of variance in log trajectory cost, versus 4% for mean observation size.
Delegation raises cost in half of evaluated settings, and the study does not show that reducing turns preserves task success.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes coding agents and focuses on cache efficiency (prefix cache) and loop engineering, directly addressing memory efficiency in LLM agents.
papers.title: TurnCost: Turns, Not Observations: Cache-Aware Loop Engineering for Coding Agents
papers.tldr: Coding-agent cost is driven far more by the number of turns than by typical observation size, especially when prefix caching is accounted for.

papers.abstract: Quantization plays a crucial role in efficiently deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained devices. Post-training quantization does not require access to the original dataset or retraining the full model. Current methods that achieve high performance close to baseline results typically require INT8 fixed-point integers. However, achieving higher model compression with lower bit-widths often leads to significant performance degradation. In this paper, we propose VLCQ, a post-training quantization method that relaxes the fixed-point encoding constraint, enabling more flexible exploration of quantization techniques through variable-length encoding. This approach achieves competitive or improved performance while reducing bit-widths, without requiring access to training data or model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments on image classification, segmentation, and object detection demonstrate that VLCQ improves model compression and accuracy compared with state-of-the-art post-training quantization approaches. For per-channel quantization, VLCQ surpasses FP32 accuracy and Piece-Wise Linear Quantization (PWLQ) on most evaluated models, achieving up to 6x compression compared with FP32 and up to 1.7x compared with PWLQ. When prioritizing compression with limited accuracy loss, VLCQ achieves up to 12.25x compression compared with FP32 with less than 4% performance degradation. For per-tensor quantization, VLCQ is competitive with Data-Free Quantization (DFQ), while providing greater flexibility to achieve lower bit rates across different tasks and models.
authors: Reem Abdel-Salam, Ahmed H. Abdel-Gawad, Amr G. Wassal
bullets: Avoids access to training data and model fine-tuning.
Relaxes fixed-point encoding constraints through variable-length coding.
Evaluated on image classification, segmentation, and object detection.
Per-channel quantization reaches up to 6× FP32 compression and up to 1.7× PWLQ compression, with accuracy sometimes exceeding FP32.
Can reach up to 12.25× FP32 compression with less than 4% performance degradation; per-tensor results are competitive with DFQ.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces variable length coding for post-training quantization, a technique that manipulates tokens/weights to improve efficiency, fitting the token pruning and eviction subtopic.
papers.title: VLCQ: Post-training quantization for deep neural networks using variable length coding
papers.tldr: VLCQ enables data-free, post-training quantization with variable-length encoding to achieve stronger compression at low bit-widths while preserving or improving model accuracy.

papers.abstract: Transformer architectures have achieved strong results in natural language processing and computer vision, but their deployment is limited by high computational, memory and storage costs, motivating research into model compression techniques, such as pruning, while preserving performance. Prior work has shown substantial redundancy in large language models (LLMs), and redundancy in vision transformers has also been investigated, but it remains less systematically analyzed than in LLMs. In this work, we extend similarity-based redundancy analysis to vision models by measuring cosine similarity between layer inputs and outputs to identify transformations with minimal impact. We study redundancy patterns across several transformer architectures and find that deep vision transformers such as DINOv2 and SwinV2, like language models, exhibit significant redundancy. We then evaluate how this redundancy can be exploited to improve efficiency, analyzing the trade-off between inference speed and performance degradation under different pruning strategies. Our results show that moderate pruning can yield substantial acceleration with limited impact on accuracy, and that 20% of the DINOv2 blocks can be removed without any retraining, for a 1.24x throughput gain and a 20% lower energy per image at a relative accuracy loss below 1% on ImageNet-1K. We further propose a model selection pipeline that automatically identifies the best pruned configuration for a given dataset, reducing FLOPs by 13% to 27% on average across architectures with an average accuracy change between -0.3 and +1.0 points.
bullets: Analyzes redundancy by measuring cosine similarity between layer inputs and outputs across multiple Vision Transformer architectures.
Finds substantial redundancy in deep models, including DINOv2 and SwinV2.

Moderate pruning provides favorable speed–accuracy trade-offs; 20% of DINOv2 blocks can be removed without retraining for 1.24× throughput and 20% lower energy per image, with under 1% relative accuracy loss on ImageNet-1K.
A model-selection pipeline automatically chooses pruned configurations, reducing FLOPs by 13–27% on average with accuracy changes from −0.3 to +1.0 points.
papers.selection_reason: Layer pruning of vision transformers to reduce compute and memory fits efficient AI.
papers.title: Retraining-Free Depth Pruning of Vision Transformers: A Cross Domain Study of Layer Redundancy
papers.tldr: Vision Transformers contain exploitable layer redundancy: pruning blocks without retraining can improve efficiency while largely preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models adapt to new datasets through in-context learning (ICL), and, like most transformers, they tie computational depth to the number of independently parameterized layers. We ask whether the ICL stage of such a model needs a distinct set of parameters for every layer, or only depth. We introduce Tab-Loop, which replaces the 12 untied ICL blocks of TabICLv2 with 4 tied blocks applied $k$ times and changes nothing else: the encoders, decoder, synthetic prior and training recipe are shared with an untied baseline trained for the same compute. At matched pretraining compute (18.2 EFLOP) and matched inference compute (12 block applications), Tab-Loop matches the baseline with 62\% fewer parameters (10.4M vs.\ 27.6M): held-out log loss is 0.4583 vs.\ 0.4588, mean accuracy on 200 TALENT datasets is 84.10\% vs.\ 83.92\%, and Elo on 38 TabArena datasets is 1409 vs.\ 1396. A 4-block untied control with Tab-Loop's parameter count, which sees 32\% more training tables for the same compute, trails both (83.46\%; Elo 1343). Because weights are shared, depth becomes a choice made at inference. Accuracy rises with the number of loops through the trained range and holds beyond it, and continued training with deeper loops extends the useful range, reaching the baseline's stage-2 scores at 4--5$\times$ its inference compute. At this scale, the ICL stage of a tabular foundation model needs depth more than it needs distinct parameters.
authors: Tejas Vaidhya, Gaurav Sahu, Irina Rish
bullets: Replaces 12 untied ICL blocks with 4 tied blocks repeated multiple times, leaving other components and training matched to the baseline.
At matched compute, uses 10.4M versus 27.6M parameters while achieving comparable or slightly better log loss, TALENT accuracy, and TabArena Elo.
A parameter-matched 4-block untied model performs worse, suggesting recurrence—not merely parameter reduction—drives the gains.
Inference-time loop count controls effective depth; accuracy improves across the trained range and remains robust beyond it.
With further training using deeper loops, the model reaches baseline stage-2 scores at 4–5× the baseline inference compute.
papers.selection_reason: Recurrent weight-tied in-context learning blocks reduce parameters by 62% at matched compute; relevant to efficient foundation model design.
papers.title: Recurrent In-Context Learning for Tabular Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Tab-Loop shows that recurrently reusing a small set of blocks can preserve or improve TabICLv2’s tabular in-context learning performance while reducing parameters by 62%.

papers.abstract: Pipeline parallelism has become a critical technique for training large language models. To address the throughput limitation of existing sequence-level methods that schedule subsequences unidirectionally, we propose bidirectional sequence-level interleaved pipeline parallelism (BSIPipe), which co-schedules two opposing V-shaped interleaved pipelines at the subsequence level. To bound the activation accumulation from subsequence scaling, BSIPipe introduces a basic-unit concatenation mechanism that keeps activation memory invariant to the subsequence count. To eliminate communication deadlock risk from bidirectional scheduling, BSIPipe employs a communication optimization strategy that combines topology-aware device mapping with communication-computation overlap. In addition, BSIPipe composes with tensor parallelism to overcome the memory limitation of single-dimensional parallelism, neutralizing its bidirectional memory overhead while maintaining throughput. Experiments on GPT and LLaMA3 demonstrate that BSIPipe achieves average speedups of 1.11$\times$ to 1.13$\times$ in long-sequence training over SOTA sequence-level baselines.
bullets: Addresses throughput limits of unidirectional sequence-level pipeline parallelism.
Co-schedules two opposing V-shaped pipelines at the subsequence level.
Uses basic-unit concatenation to keep activation memory invariant to subsequence count.
Combines topology-aware device mapping and communication-computation overlap to avoid deadlocks and reduce communication costs.
Experiments on GPT and LLaMA3 report 1.11×–1.13× average speedups over state-of-the-art sequence-level baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Pipeline parallelism for long-sequence LLM training improves training throughput and fits efficient AI.
papers.title: BSIPipe: Bidirectional Sequence-Level Interleaved Pipeline Parallelism for Long-Sequence Large Language Model Training
papers.tldr: BSIPipe accelerates long-sequence LLM training by co-scheduling bidirectional interleaved pipelines while controlling activation memory and communication overhead.

papers.abstract: Ultra-low-bit scalar quantization offers a regular arithmetic structure for efficient deployment of large language models, but preserving predictive behavior at extreme precision remains challenging: with only a few reconstruction levels, accurate weight representation must translate into consistent predictions from a small calibration set. We propose FidelityQ, a scalar quantization framework that preserves predictive fidelity at weight precisions down to 2 bits. For accurate quantization, we introduce Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC), which shapes each weight row toward a centered symmetric source via randomized Hadamard mixing and fits a mirrored four-level minimum-distortion quantizer to its empirical weights. Every level set in this family decomposes exactly into two sign-valued bases with associated scales, combining source-adaptive reconstruction with lookup-free decoding compatible with scaled integer arithmetic. Our analysis further shows that residual predictive discrepancies are heavy-tailed and concentrate on tokens the teacher predicts confidently, motivating Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC) for consistent quantization. KIC ranks sequences by the tail of token-wise teacher-student divergence, allocates a limited calibration budget to the highest-scoring samples, and restores predictive agreement by updating only quantization levels and scales under teacher supervision, keeping pretrained weights frozen. Experiments on the LLaMA and Qwen families demonstrate the effectiveness of FidelityQ in weight-only and joint quantization settings. On LLaMA-2-7B, FidelityQ achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 6.62 at W2A16 and improves the prior state-of-the-art W2A4KV4 result from 8.31 to 6.96, while reducing linear-layer weight memory by 8.0x relative to FP16.
authors: Yujie Chen, Weiyan Zheng, Yiwu Yao, Tianchi Hu, Bo Wang, Jiyu Guo, Wenzhan Li, Jingcai Guo, Michele Magno, Haotong Qin
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of maintaining predictive behavior when weights use only a few quantization levels.
Introduces Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC): randomized Hadamard mixing and a symmetric four-level quantizer with lookup-free sign-basis decoding.
Introduces Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC), which selects high-divergence calibration sequences and updates only quantization levels and scales while freezing pretrained weights.

Experiments on LLaMA and Qwen show effectiveness for weight-only and joint quantization; on LLaMA-2-7B, it reports 6.62 WikiText2 perplexity at W2A16 and improves W2A4KV4 perplexity from 8.31 to 6.96.
Reduces linear-layer weight memory by 8× versus FP16.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces FidelityQ, a quantization framework that preserves predictive fidelity while reducing model memory requirements, directly addressing memory efficiency.
papers.title: FidelityQ: Preserving Predictive Fidelity in Ultra-Low-Bit Language Model Quantization
papers.tldr: FidelityQ enables accurate 2-bit language-model quantization by combining source-adaptive weight coding with targeted calibration that preserves teacher-like predictions.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models interleave Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, whose recurrent memory has a fixed size, with full-attention layers, whose key-value (KV) cache grows with the context and dominates serving memory. In this paper, we ask whether the recurrent memory already knows what the attention memory will need. We first show that which GDN heads of Qwen3.8-27B keep long memories is fixed by the weights rather than by the document. Next, we define the future utility of a KV entry by how much removing it changes the attention output over the model's own continuations, and find that the write gate, decay and write magnitude that GDN layers emit during prefill anticipate this utility before any query is seen. Because the relation is spread across many GDN heads and layers, and a linear map recovers its trend but less of its high-utility tail than a nonlinear one, we propose GateSight, which learns it with lightweight per-head multilayer perceptrons that read these signals and no attention score. Their predicted utility decides which entries each attention layer keeps, and how much each layer keeps is set by the model's native attention output gate, whose mean differs by more than an order of magnitude across layers. Finally, at serving time, GateSight scores the cache once after prefill and physically releases discarded KV entries. Experimental results on SCBench and RULER-4096 with Qwen3.8-27B and, with the same recipe, the sparse-attention model Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, up to the 262K-token limit of the models, show that with a tenth of the attention KV cache, GateSight is the most accurate of five query-agnostic methods on three of the four model-benchmark pairs and leads KVzip on all four, by 9.5 to 47.2 points. Notably, it scores a full-length context with negligible overhead relative to prefill.
authors: Junjie Li, Jiong Lou, Jie Li
bullets: GDN prefill signals—write gate, decay, and write magnitude—anticipate future KV-entry utility before attention queries are available.
Lightweight per-head nonlinear predictors estimate utility without using attention scores.
The model’s native attention output gate determines the retention budget separately for each attention layer.
After one post-prefill scoring pass, discarded KV entries are physically released for serving.

At one-tenth of the KV cache, GateSight leads KVzip across all four model-benchmark pairs and is the most accurate of five query-agnostic methods on three; scope covers Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next up to 262K tokens.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes query-agnostic KV eviction for hybrid LLMs to reduce attention cache memory, directly targeting inference memory efficiency.
papers.title: GateSight: Recurrent Memory Anticipates Attention Memory for Query-Agnostic KV Eviction in Hybrid LLMs
papers.tldr: GateSight uses recurrent Gated DeltaNet signals to predict which attention KV-cache entries will matter, enabling query-agnostic cache eviction with substantially lower memory and little scoring overhead.

papers.abstract: Extreme low-bit weight-only quantization is an effective approach to reducing the deployment costs of large language models. Below 3 bits, scalar quantization often suffers severe accuracy loss, while vector quantization (VQ) better preserves accuracy through more expressive joint encoding. However, existing VQ methods still exhibit substantial degradation on real-world tasks, and two design challenges remain underexplored: (1) protecting sensitive weight channels within jointly encoded vectors; and (2) allocating a fixed bit budget among representation components, such as direction and radius, to suit different weight matrices. To address these challenges, we propose SAGE: Split Adaptation and Grouping by Energy for weight-only vector quantization. First, Energy-Stratified Grouping (ESG) couples channel grouping with activation-weighted fitting, grouping channels from different energy tiers within each subvector to prioritize sensitive channels. Second, Adaptive Bit Split (ABS) balances direction-codebook capacity and radius precision per matrix, selecting the split with the lowest activation-weighted reconstruction error under a fixed budget. Across benchmarks covering knowledge, mathematics, code generation, instruction following, and tool use, SAGE achieves state-of-the-art performance in the 2-bit quantization setting. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it retains 95.3% of the BF16 model's average benchmark score. With our custom-designed CUDA kernel, SAGE delivers up to a 2.55-fold non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16. The code is available at https://github.com/Zincwolf/sage.
authors: Xianglong Yan, Zenan Wu, Kewei Zhang, Kaicheng Yang, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Targets severe accuracy degradation in sub-3-bit weight-only quantization, especially on real-world tasks.
Energy-Stratified Grouping mixes channels across energy tiers and uses activation-weighted fitting to protect sensitive channels.
Adaptive Bit Split assigns the fixed bit budget between direction and radius for each weight matrix based on reconstruction error.
Achieves state-of-the-art 2-bit quantization performance across knowledge, math, code, instruction-following, and tool-use benchmarks.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B, retains 95.3% of BF16 average benchmark score and reaches up to 2.55× non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16 with a custom CUDA kernel.
papers.selection_reason: Extreme low-bit weight quantization reduces LLM memory and deployment cost, fitting efficient AI and memory efficiency.
papers.title: SAGE: Pushing 2-Bit Vector-Quantized LLMs toward Real-World Usability
papers.tldr: SAGE improves the accuracy and deployment efficiency of 2-bit vector-quantized LLMs through energy-aware channel grouping and adaptive bit allocation.

papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models enable high-quality video generation, but video VAE encoding and decoding remain computationally expensive. Existing methods use stage-specific lightweight operators, yet either constrain spatial and temporal computation jointly or remove temporal computation altogether, without distinguishing their compression sensitivities in pretrained Conv3D. To address these limitations, we present LightVAE, a compression framework that exploits redundancy in temporal modeling and network depth. LightVAE exactly reparameterizes eligible causal Conv3D layers into an aggregate spatial response and a difference-driven temporal correction. Based on their distinct compression sensitivities, temporal low-rank compression (TLR) keeps the aggregate spatial kernel dense and applies layer-specific low-rank approximation only to the temporal correction. An algebraically equivalent folded implementation converts the arithmetic savings into practical acceleration. LightVAE further uses width-preserving block pruning to reduce depth and probe-guided feature alignment, guided by feedback from a frozen teacher suffix, to recover quality after compression. The framework also extends to video encoders. Across three video VAE backbones and two GPU platforms, LightVAE consistently accelerates decoding. For the Wan VAE family, it achieves up to $2.24\times$ and $1.11\times$ the decoding throughput of state-of-the-art efficient VAE decoders on NVIDIA H100 and RTX~5090, respectively, with higher DAVIS PSNR and lower LPIPS. On MiniMax-H3, it achieves up to $2.97\times$ the original decoding throughput while retaining 99.51\% of the original model's overall VBench-2.0 score. Our code is available at https://github.com/ModelTC/LightVAE.
authors: Shiqiao Gu, Yang Yong, Fengjun Zhong, Ruihao Gong, Chengtao Lv, Xiangyu Fan, Lei Yang, Xianglong Liu
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of video VAE encoding and decoding in latent diffusion pipelines.
Reparameterizes causal Conv3D layers into dense spatial responses plus temporal corrections, then applies layer-specific temporal low-rank compression.
Uses width-preserving block pruning and teacher-guided feature alignment to recover quality after compression.
Provides a folded implementation for practical acceleration and extends the framework to video encoders.

Across three VAE backbones and two GPUs, reports up to 2.97× original decoding throughput while retaining 99.51% of MiniMax-H3’s VBench-2.0 score; Wan VAEs also show improved DAVIS PSNR and lower LPIPS.
papers.selection_reason: Compresses video autoencoders via low-rank temporal approximation and block pruning, directly reducing compute and memory.
papers.title: LightVAE: Towards Compact and Efficient Video Autoencoders
papers.tldr: LightVAE compresses video VAEs by separately reducing temporal computation and network depth, delivering faster decoding while largely preserving video quality.

papers.abstract: On-device inference imposes constraints on model storage and operand traffic and thus benefits from compressed operand representations, which mandate the use of encoding and decoding operators. However, na\"{\i}ve placement of codec operators can cancel the operand traffic gains sought from compression. In this work, I present an algorithm to place codec operators into a source computational graph to make it compatible with target hardware. The edges of the graph are colored so that each induced subgraph is weakly connected and has a maximal node that both postdominates all subgraph inputs and dominates all subgraph outputs; this unique node - dubbed the $\textit{absolute dominator}$ - is the natural location to observe the traffic flowing through the subgraph and learn parametric codec operators. The algorithm's time complexity is linear in the source graph's size. With respect to na\"{\i}ve local codec placement, the algorithm reduces modeled operand traffic by $24\%$-$44\%$ across four models, including $24\%$ on SigLIP and $34\%$ on SmolLM2.
bullets: Addresses the problem that naive local codec placement can negate compression benefits by increasing operand traffic.
Colors computational-graph edges into weakly connected subgraphs with a unique absolute dominator for codec placement.
The algorithm runs in linear time with respect to the source graph size.
Modeled operand traffic is reduced by 24%–44% across four models versus naive local placement, including 24% on SigLIP and 34% on SmolLM2.
Scope: results are based on modeled operand traffic and target hardware compatibility, as described in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a linear-time algorithm for codec operator placement to reduce operand traffic, fitting the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: Linear-Time Non-Local Codec Placement for Machine Learning Model Compression
papers.tldr: A linear-time graph algorithm places compression codecs at absolute dominators to preserve operand-traffic savings for on-device inference.

papers.abstract: LLM-augmented data workflows often involve multiple heterogeneous models operating over substantial shared context, such as schemas, tool specifications, interaction history, and intermediate results. Although prefix caching can reduce prefilling overhead, existing approaches are largely limited to reuse within the same model because KV states are tightly coupled to model-specific architectures. We present MapFlow, a system for efficient heterogeneous LLM serving via cross-model attention map reuse. Instead of reusing KV states, MapFlow reuses attention maps, which capture token dependency patterns and are more transferable across models. To enable efficient and accurate reuse, we combine partial recomputation with lightweight linear translation across layers and heads. To make attention reuse practical for long contexts, we further introduce block-level sparse compression and a fused retrieval kernel. Experiments show that MapFlow reduces prefilling latency and improves end-to-end serving efficiency while preserving generation quality across heterogeneous model pairs and multi-turn routing workloads. These results suggest that attention maps provide an effective reusable state for heterogeneous LLM serving, especially in prefix-heavy data workflows. Our code is available: https://github.com/PKU-DAIR/MapFlow.
authors: Zhan Jin, Yuze Luo, Bin Cui, Xupeng Miao
bullets: Targets prefix-heavy workflows where multiple models share long contexts such as schemas, tools, histories, and intermediate results.
Combines partial recomputation with lightweight linear translation across layers and heads to enable accurate cross-model reuse.
Uses block-level sparse compression and a fused retrieval kernel to make attention-map reuse practical for long contexts.
Experiments report lower prefilling latency and better end-to-end serving efficiency while preserving generation quality across heterogeneous models and multi-turn workloads.
papers.selection_reason: Presents cross-model attention map reuse for efficient heterogeneous LLM serving, directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Accelerating Cross-Model LLM Inference via Attention Map Reuse
papers.tldr: MapFlow accelerates heterogeneous LLM serving by reusing transferable attention maps instead of model-specific KV states.

papers.abstract: Training-free sparse attention is a practical route to efficient video diffusion transformer inference, yet existing methods typically fix the competition domain at each query row for every attention head. Prior work primarily addresses how to estimate token-level importance within this fixed domain; whether the domain itself should adapt to head heterogeneity remains under-specified. We introduce EG-Sparse, a training-free framework that routes low-entropy heads to a grouped cross-head pool while retaining per-row local selection for high-entropy heads, using only scores already materialized by the sparse pipeline. A controlled diagnostic fixes the ranking score and varies only the competition rule: grouped cross-head selection reduces low-entropy-head reconstruction error by 9.8%, whereas forcing high-entropy heads into an all-head global pool increases it by 7.9%. Across four configurations, EG-Sparse achieves higher video quality while reducing attention density and GPU denoising latency compared with strong training-free sparse-attention baselines. Mechanism ablations further show that selective domain adaptation outperforms uniform, random, and fixed domain-assignment policies. These results support competition-domain adaptation as a distinct design axis within centroid-guided training-free sparse attention.
authors: Tiantian Liu, Meng Wan, Zhiqiang Liang, Jue Wang, Ningming Nie, Yangang Wang
bullets: Existing methods use a fixed competition domain for every attention head, despite head heterogeneity.
EG-Sparse routes low-entropy heads to grouped cross-head selection while keeping high-entropy heads on per-row local selection.
A controlled diagnostic found grouped selection reduced low-entropy-head reconstruction error by 9.8%, while global pooling increased high-entropy-head error by 7.9%.
Across four configurations, the method improved video quality while lowering attention density and GPU denoising latency versus strong training-free baselines.
Ablations favored selective domain adaptation over uniform, random, and fixed assignment policies.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free sparse attention for video diffusion transformers; fits efficient attention and video diffusion.
papers.title: Competition Domains Matter: Selective Head Globalization for Training-Free Sparse Attention in Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: EG-Sparse improves training-free sparse attention for video diffusion by adapting the token-selection competition domain to each head’s entropy.

papers.abstract: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) has emerged as a powerful dynamic scene representation, supporting real-time high quality rendering but suffers from prohibitive storage overhead. Existing methods typically attempt to solve this by treating compression as a per-scene optimization problem, limiting generalizability and applicability where low-latency compression is required. In this work, we leverage existing image and video codecs and propose a generalized post-training compression framework for 4DGS to address these issues. Specifically, we apply importance-based adaptive quantization to Gaussians according to their importance levels, effectively refining bitrate allocation while remaining fully compatible with existing codecs. To further improve compression efficiency, we utilize the statistical properties of 4DGS and propose motion- and importance-aware packing to reorganize attributes into codec-friendly 2D maps. Our approach can achieve over 40x compression rate in seconds while maintaining high quality, facilitating the practical deployment of 4DGS.
authors: Chengzhen Wu, Kelei Liu, Sicheng Li, Lu Yu, Yiyi Liao
bullets: Addresses 4DGS storage overhead and the slow, scene-specific nature of prior compression methods.
Uses importance-based adaptive quantization to allocate bitrate according to Gaussian importance.
Introduces motion- and importance-aware packing that reorganizes attributes into codec-friendly 2D maps.
Leverages existing image and video codecs for post-training compression without per-scene optimization.
Compresses 4DGS in seconds while maintaining high quality, supporting practical deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Post-training compression of 4D Gaussian splatting; relevant to 3D scene representation and efficient storage.
papers.title: TETRIS-4DGS: Efficient Post-Training Compression of 4D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: TETRIS-4DGS enables fast, generalized compression of 4D Gaussian Splatting with over 40× storage reduction while preserving high rendering quality.

papers.abstract: Can autoregressive video diffusion be accelerated further when only four denoising steps remain? Existing feature caching approaches struggle in this regime, as large feature changes between denoising timesteps undermine both direct reuse and lightweight predictors. We observe that features across video chunks remain strongly correlated at matching denoising timesteps, offering a complementary source of guidance. Building on this insight, we introduce TGuide, a framework that accelerates autoregressive video diffusion through a lightweight Anchor-Transport-Correct (ATC) predictor guided by historical sampling trajectories. Our ATC combines two complementary references: the current chunk's preceding-step features preserve its spatial structure, while the previous chunk's same-timestep features provide information at the target denoising stage. By integrating these references through spatial retrieval and adaptive correction, ATC improves velocity prediction accuracy despite the large gaps between denoising steps. To mitigate error accumulation across both denoising steps and video chunks, we train the predictor on its own autoregressive rollouts, allowing it to adapt to states shaped by its own earlier predictions. An optional confidence-aware scheduler further adjusts the quality-efficiency trade-off. Experiments on Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, and HY-WorldPlay show that TGuide preserves generation quality while achieving denoising speedups of up to $1.89\times$ over the original 4-step generators. On Self Forcing, TGuide generalizes from 81-frame training videos to 333-frame generation, approximately four times the training length, while exceeding the original model's VBench score.
authors: Zhuo Chen, Bin Zou, Fanyue Wei, Lixin Duan, Angela Yao, Wen Li
bullets: Addresses feature-caching failures caused by large changes between the few remaining denoising steps.
Uses an Anchor-Transport-Correct predictor combining the current chunk’s preceding-step features with the previous chunk’s same-timestep features.
Applies spatial retrieval and adaptive correction to improve velocity prediction across large denoising gaps.
Trains on its own autoregressive rollouts to reduce error accumulation across denoising steps and video chunks.
Evaluated on Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, and HY-WorldPlay; on Self Forcing, it generates 333-frame videos from 81-frame training videos while exceeding the original model’s VBench score.
papers.selection_reason: Accelerates autoregressive video diffusion via historical trajectory guidance; fits video diffusion, autoregressive video, and efficiency.
papers.title: TGuide: Faster Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Historical Trajectory Guidance
papers.tldr: TGuide accelerates 4-step autoregressive video diffusion by guiding feature prediction with historical trajectories, achieving up to 1.89× denoising speedups while preserving or improving quality.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive robot video world models based on discrete visual tokens remain unreliable over long rollout horizons. Retaining the entire generated history does not necessarily improve prediction quality. We investigate a possible memory-role conflict in Full Context decoding: persistent scene information, recent visual-action states, and stale generated history compete for attention despite their different predictive roles. This perspective motivates ReCAP (Receding Context with Anchor Preservation), a training-free context-scheduling method for long-horizon robot video world models. ReCAP keeps the pretrained tokenizer, world model, and visual decoder frozen. It preserves the initial scene anchor and a contiguous window of recent complete visual-action blocks while evicting older generated history. The schedule preserves within-block structure and temporal order, requires no additional modules or parameter updates, and bounds active-context growth independently of rollout length. We evaluate ReCAP on RT-1, BridgeV2, LIBERO-90, and CALVIN using frozen autoregressive world models. Across evaluated environments and horizons, ReCAP improves visual fidelity, action-conditioned consistency, and robot structure preservation relative to Full Context. On BridgeV2, it reduces LPIPS by 63.3%. In the system benchmark at H=64, it reduces the logical KV footprint by 73.3% and p50 latency by 6.51%. Attention analyses show increased attention to retained recent states, while history interventions associate larger amounts of stale context with higher prediction error. These observations are consistent with the memory-role-conflict hypothesis, although they do not isolate it from context-length and position-handling effects. Our results support inference-time context scheduling as a practical approach to improving long-horizon robot video prediction and computational efficiency without retraining.
authors: Hao Wu, Tianyu Shao, Shengju Qian, Yizhou Zhao, Fan Zhang, Penghao Zhao, Weiyan Wang, Yufei Huang, Fan Xu, Kun Wang, Xin Wang, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Yuxuan Liang
bullets: Full-context decoding can make persistent scene information, recent states, and stale generated history compete for attention.
ReCAP is a training-free context schedule that freezes the tokenizer, world model, and decoder.
It preserves temporal order and complete recent visual-action blocks while bounding active context growth independently of rollout length.
Across RT-1, BridgeV2, LIBERO-90, and CALVIN, it improves visual fidelity, action consistency, and robot-structure preservation over Full Context.
On BridgeV2, LPIPS falls 63.3%; at H=64, logical KV footprint falls 73.3% and p50 latency falls 6.51%. The memory-conflict explanation remains confounded by context-length and positional effects.
papers.selection_reason: Context scheduling for long-horizon robot video world models; fits video world models and inference memory efficiency.
papers.title: Remembering What Matters for Long-Horizon Robotic World Models
papers.tldr: ReCAP improves long-horizon robot video prediction by retaining the initial scene and recent visual-action context while evicting stale history, without retraining.

papers.abstract: As frontier LLMs gain more capabilities, the cost to run them also goes up. At the same time, small language models (SLMs) also gain more capabilities but have largely been able to keep their cost stable, offering 5-40 times cheaper inference for the narrow, repetitive subtasks that agents decompose work into. However, the standing limiting factor is getting the correct behavior out of a small model in a fast, efficient, and economical way. Unfortunately, in most cases, zero-shot small models fail narrow production tasks. Furthermore, retraining one every time the behavior changes is too slow to iterate on. We propose doing both in sequence. First, develop the desired behavior in prompt space, on a frontier model, with immediate feedback from live traffic. Then, once the behavior converges, distill the recorded production behavior (not synthetic imitations of it) into an SLM through supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We show a proper use case of this method through a scheduling agent for home-care agencies that fans out a single yes/no safety decision per caregiver-shift pair on GPT-5.4-nano. A LoRA-tuned Qwen3-8B trained on 11.6k recorded production decisions reaches 0.913 agreement, while the teacher (GPT-5.4-nano), re-run on its own recorded prompts, agrees with itself only 72.7% of the time, pointing to the fact that the SLM may also be more consistent. Furthermore, when the two disagreed, a blinded professional scheduler sided with the student 48-29. Finally, we find that the SLM has approximately 2.5 times lower median latency and is a fraction of the cost. We believe this lifecycle of quick building, live feedback, and cheap inference is a blueprint for others building similar systems.
bullets: Frontier LLMs enable rapid prompt-based iteration, while SLMs offer substantially cheaper inference for narrow, repetitive agent subtasks.
The proposed lifecycle records converged production behavior and uses it—not synthetic examples—for supervised fine-tuning of an SLM.
In a home-care scheduling safety task, a LoRA-tuned Qwen3-8B achieved 0.913 agreement with recorded GPT-5.4-nano decisions.
The SLM was more consistent than the teacher on replayed prompts, and a blinded professional scheduler preferred it in disagreements.
The SLM also had approximately 2.5× lower median latency and a fraction of the cost.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-to-SLM distillation for low-cost, low-latency production agents; relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Iterate on an LLM, Serve on an SLM
papers.tldr: Develop behavior quickly with a frontier LLM, then distill real production decisions into a cheaper, faster SLM for deployment.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) inference is driving a growing share of datacenter carbon emissions. Although carbon-aware scheduling can reduce these emissions in geo-distributed datacenters by exploiting the spatiotemporal variations in grid carbon intensity, the latency-sensitive nature of LLM serving constrains this design space. While prior studies investigate the carbon savings achievable through spatial scheduling, they oversimplify the dynamics of modern inference engines, such as queueing and continuous batching, which strongly shape inference latency.
