We address this issue by designing and evaluating a latency-centric, geo-distributed inference simulator, calibrated with hardware-grounded latency and power measurements, that reproduces these dynamics and enables the study of carbon savings under strict service-level objectives (SLOs). We then formulate a series of SLO- and carbon-aware schedulers of increasing sophistication, from per-request heuristics to batch-level optimization: (i) a greedy heuristic, (ii) an integer linear programming (ILP)-based scheduler jointly assigning batches of requests, (iii) an iterative ILP-based solution projecting its own assignments back into the load estimates to capture load coupling, and (iv) a facility mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) scheduler pricing the energy of batched requests collectively rather than in isolation. Across three LLMs under MLPerf SLOs and varying system loads, the MILP-based option offers the best carbon-SLO balance, reducing carbon emissions by up to 60% relative to the round-robin policy, with an average SLO violation of 3%. Our characterization further shows that savings grow with the spread of carbon intensity across datacenters and shrink as system load increases, while SLO attainment depends on how frequently schedulers receive datacenters' load updates.
authors: Burak Topcu, Musa Cim, Zuhal Ozturk, Mahmut Taylan Kandemir
bullets: Modern inference dynamics—including queueing and continuous batching—create a key tension between carbon reduction and latency guarantees.
The study builds a hardware-calibrated simulator that models latency, power, queueing, and continuous batching across datacenters.
It evaluates schedulers ranging from per-request heuristics to batch-level ILP and facility-level MILP optimization.
The MILP scheduler reduces carbon emissions by up to 60% versus round-robin, with an average SLO violation of 3%.
Carbon savings increase with cross-datacenter carbon-intensity differences and decrease at higher system loads; SLOs also depend on load-update frequency.
papers.selection_reason: Carbon-aware scheduling for geo-distributed LLM serving directly targets energy/carbon efficiency of AI systems, fitting the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: Dissecting the Carbon-SLO Tension in Geo-Distributed LLM Serving
papers.tldr: A latency-aware geo-distributed simulator and carbon-conscious schedulers show that batched MILP scheduling can substantially reduce LLM serving emissions while largely respecting strict latency SLOs.

papers.abstract: In autoregressive video generation, retaining all historical key-value (KV) states increases memory usage and per-step attention costs as videos grow longer. A fixed cache budget bounds these costs but raises the challenge of preserving historical content that supports consistent, high-quality generation. Existing methods control cache size through history selection or consolidation, yet deciding what to retain and how to limit the loss of useful content remains a shared challenge. Our analysis shows that spatial queries depend on different historical content and that higher current attention coverage does not necessarily yield better long-video quality. We introduce FrameFold, a training-free KV cache consolidation method that compares the content retrieved by the same recent historical queries before and after merging to guide both representative construction and merge selection. Exploiting temporal redundancy between adjacent historical entries, FrameFold merges their KV states into shared representatives while retaining complete spatial grids. It fits value-merging coefficients in closed form by matching conditional attention responses, then selects the merge with the lowest remaining response distortion. Under matched KV cache budgets, experiments on Self Forcing and Causal Forcing at 30 and 60 seconds and on LongLive at 120 seconds demonstrate improved consistency and visual quality. Continuous eight-minute Self Forcing rollouts further show less quality degradation than the baselines.
authors: Muyu Liu, Mingming Liu, Hong Gu, Yuyao Zhang, Qin Lu
bullets: Fixed-size KV caches reduce memory and attention costs but risk discarding content needed for temporal consistency.
FrameFold uses recent historical queries to compare attention responses before and after candidate merges.
It merges temporally redundant adjacent KV entries into shared representatives while preserving complete spatial grids.
Value-merging coefficients are solved in closed form, and merges are selected to minimize response distortion.
Experiments across 30-second to eight-minute rollouts show better consistency, visual quality, and slower degradation than baselines under matched cache budgets.
papers.selection_reason: KV cache consolidation for autoregressive video generation.
papers.title: FrameFold: Response-Guided KV Cache Consolidation for Autoregressive Long Video Generation
papers.tldr: FrameFold is a training-free method that consolidates historical KV caches for long video generation while preserving attention responses and improving long-horizon quality under fixed memory budgets.

papers.abstract: Deploying language models (LMs) on the edge presents unique memory, latency, and power challenges absent in high-performance computing. KV-cache compression emerges as a promising approach to address these challenges. However, the effectiveness of current KV-cache compression methods has not been thoroughly examined on edge devices. Moreover, we show that existing evaluation methods do not always involve the KV-cache under test. We propose EdgeLLM-Nano, a measurement study of KV-cache compression using a nano-scale decoder-only LM (transformer) testbed that has 8.39M parameters, i.e., 33.6 MB, to enable end-to-end examination of each backend, seed, and power sample. Our results give a negative verdict for a polar-guided key-cache quantizer (round-to-nearest (RTN) control causes an order of magnitude less damage), as well as a consistency-anchored progressive weight pruner (one-shot magnitude-based pruning performs as well as, if not better). We also introduce Long-Context Decode Fidelity (LCDF) evaluation, a token-by-token examination of teacher-forced log-losses using the KV-cache under test. Unlike perplexity that gives the same 5.461 score to all methods, LCDF distinguishes different KV-cache compression backends thanks to its paired statistics across seeds and effect sizes. Our companion Raspberry Pi 5 measurement shows all compression backends we tested to be less energy-efficient per token compared to uncompressed FP16 inference. Except for KIVI that is close to lossless in terms of LCDF, our findings indicate KV-cache compression can be improved. LCDF offers a simple and effective way of shedding light on KV-cache compression methods, whose negative impacts have been overlooked by perplexity.
authors: S M Mahbub Murshed, Hayden Bright, Rezaul Karim, Ali Shiri Sichani
bullets: Audits KV-cache compression on an 8.39M-parameter, 33.6 MB decoder-only LM with end-to-end edge measurements.
Finds polar-guided key-cache quantization performs poorly; RTN causes roughly an order of magnitude less damage.
Finds consistency-anchored progressive pruning is no better than one-shot magnitude pruning.
Introduces Long-Context Decode Fidelity (LCDF), which uses teacher-forced, token-level log-losses and distinguishes compression backends missed by perplexity.
On a Raspberry Pi 5, tested compression backends use more energy per token than uncompressed FP16; KIVI is close to lossless by LCDF.
papers.selection_reason: Audits KV-cache compression methods for edge deployment, introducing a new evaluation metric (LCDF) to assess fidelity.
papers.title: EdgeLLM-Nano: Auditing Polar-Guided Key-Cache Compression and Consistency-Anchored Pruning on a 33.6 MB On-Device Language Model
papers.tldr: EdgeLLM-Nano finds that several KV-cache compression methods underperform on-device, while LCDF reveals quality losses that perplexity misses.

papers.abstract: Asynchronous rollout improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by reducing under-utilization during long-tail generation. Sustained concurrency also concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps, increasing the KV workload per step. We characterize this \emph{KV concentration} and find that KV cache quantization delivers substantially greater acceleration than weight-only and weight-activation quantization in our matched-workload comparisons. However, INT4 KV rollout can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). We propose \emph{KV4-RL}, which combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context. Protecting a bounded number of positions reduces sampler mismatch while retaining most of the speedup from INT4. Across 400 iterations of Qwen3-8B-Base GRPO training, KV4-RL achieves $1.80\times$ cumulative rollout speedup and $1.27\times$ cumulative full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout, reaching $1.97\times$ rollout speedup over the final 50 iterations. Under a common BF16 evaluator, its final six-benchmark mean accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.
authors: Sihwan Park, Sung-Yub Kim, Doohyuk Jang, Eunho Yang
bullets: Asynchronous rollouts increase KV-cache workload per decode step, making KV quantization especially impactful.
KV4-RL uses calibration-free INT4 KV quantization and protects attention sinks plus recent context in INT8.
The selective protection reduces sampler mismatch and mitigates learning degradation from fully INT4 rollouts.
Across 400 GRPO iterations, it achieves 1.80× cumulative rollout speedup and 1.27× full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout.
Final accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training on six benchmarks for Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.
papers.selection_reason: INT4 KV cache quantization for faster asynchronous RLVR rollouts, directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization
papers.tldr: KV4-RL accelerates asynchronous RLVR rollouts with INT4 KV-cache quantization while preserving nearly BF16-level training accuracy through selective INT8 protection.

papers.abstract: Computational coarse-graining aims to replace a sequence of updates with a cheaper module while preserving task performance. We present a continuation-relative evaluation framework that assesses replacements through the computation that follows them, using downstream task quality and total execution cost as joint criteria. The framework distinguishes boundary representations, summaries of skipped computation, executed operations, and downstream loss. It makes interfaces and permitted deployment information explicit, combines fine-path references with directly trained controls using the same shortened architecture, and accounts for selection overhead. An exact loss decomposition separates replacement effects at a fixed downstream action from effects of changing that action. A finite construction shows how retained information can reduce the stipulated cost of zero-error prediction under fixed information and controller restrictions. Experiments in two frozen pretrained language models show that representation fidelity and task loss can favor different fitting objectives. In a prespecified comparison on a 1.7-billion-parameter model, next-token-loss training lowers in-distribution negative log-likelihood by 0.1901 nats per scored token compared with reconstructing the skipped blocks' output, using the same optimizer and update count. This ranking reverses in all nine paired comparisons under distribution shift. In a recursive expert prototype, the jointly adapted candidate lowers task error relative to frozen-bank and router-only baselines, but trails directly trained controls, and the tested input-only selectors fail the joint quality-cost criteria. Together, the protocol and studies provide explicit criteria and diagnostics for distinguishing useful computational replacement from local approximation gains within specified interfaces and evaluation settings.
authors: Shihua Yu, Yanzhi Wang, Tianchi Chen
bullets: Defines explicit interfaces, skipped-computation summaries, downstream actions, losses, and selection overhead for coarse-graining evaluation.
Separates replacement effects from effects caused by changing the downstream action through an exact loss decomposition.

In two frozen language models, next-token-loss training improved in-distribution NLL over skipped-block-output reconstruction by 0.1901 nats per scored token, but reversed in all nine distribution-shift comparisons.

In a recursive expert prototype, jointly adapted candidates beat frozen-bank and router-only baselines but trailed directly trained controls; input-only selectors failed the joint quality-cost criteria.
Provides diagnostics for distinguishing useful computational replacement from local approximation gains within specified interfaces and deployment settings.
papers.selection_reason: Computational coarse-graining to replace expensive updates with cheaper modules, relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Coarse-Graining Recursive Expert Computation: Continuation-Relative Interfaces and Failure Modes
papers.tldr: A continuation-relative framework evaluates computational replacements by downstream task quality and total cost, revealing that local representation fidelity may not predict useful end-to-end performance.

papers.abstract: Generating an image with a diffusion or flow-matching model typically involves integrating a velocity field for hundreds of sequential steps. That computation suits a GPU poorly and an analog neuromorphic substrate well, where one fast, low-power physical relaxation could replace the whole sequence. Two things are needed: a generative algorithm whose computation is a relaxation, and a way to train it without backpropagation, whose global gradient transport is hard to realise in analog. Energy Matching supplies the first, sampling by gradient-descent relaxation on a time-independent potential - but obtaining the gradient that descent follows is itself a backward pass, once per integration step. We prove that a predictive coding network with a single linear injection term added to its energy relaxes to a state whose visible layer carries that gradient inherently, with an error that vanishes for small injection strengths. An Energy Matching model trained by backpropagation can therefore be loaded into this network unchanged and sampled by relaxation alone, matching the original model's FID to within 0.04 at CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 scale. The network can also be trained without backpropagation: Equilibrium Propagation reproduces backpropagation's parameter updates to a cosine similarity of 0.9998, and training end to end with those updates reaches an FID of 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 against 3.54 for backpropagation. To our knowledge this is the first CIFAR-10 generative model trained with Equilibrium Propagation, and the first at competitive quality by any backpropagation-free rule. This quality does not require group normalisation or attention: an architecture of only convolutions and pointwise nonlinearities, both native to an analog crossbar, reaches an FID of 3.51 when trained by backpropagation.
bullets: Targets the cost of hundreds of sequential diffusion or flow-matching steps and the difficulty of implementing global gradient transport on analog hardware.
Uses Energy Matching with a predictive-coding network whose injected energy term makes the visible state approximate the required gradient during relaxation.
A backpropagation-trained model can be sampled by relaxation alone, matching the original model’s FID within 0.04 on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32.
Equilibrium Propagation closely reproduces backpropagation updates (cosine similarity 0.9998) and achieves FID 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 versus 3.54 for backpropagation.
The convolutional, pointwise architecture avoids group normalization and attention, supporting implementation on analog crossbars.
papers.selection_reason: Backprop-free training via equilibrium propagation motivated by low-power analog neuromorphic computation, relevant to energy-efficient AI.
papers.title: PotentialEP: Backprop-Free Training of CIFAR-Scale Generative Models via Equilibrium Propagation
papers.tldr: PotentialEP enables CIFAR-scale generative modeling through physical relaxation and trains the model without backpropagation using Equilibrium Propagation, while retaining near-backpropagation quality.

papers.abstract: Benchmark scores tell us what an LLM can do, but not how much energy is required to deliver that capability. We directly measure this trade-off for 86 open-weight model checkpoints, evaluated on seven benchmarks and six hardware platforms ranging from a consumer GPU to an eight-GPU server. We find large differences in energy efficiency even among models with similar capability. Most configurations lie away from the score--energy Pareto frontier: they use a median of 2.6--4.8$\times$ more energy than another configuration that scores at least as well, with differences reaching 27$\times$. Reasoning can improve capability, but enabling thinking increases energy by about 3.7$\times$ on average, and the benefit depends strongly on the model family and output budget. Generated-token count is also an imperfect proxy for energy, misordering 18--24\% of model pairs. In contrast, FP8 reduces energy by roughly a quarter with little change in score, while changing hardware largely rescales energy without changing the relative ranking of models. These results show that capability alone gives an incomplete picture of efficiency. We argue that benchmark scores should be reported together with measured energy consumption under a specified serving regime and output budget.
bullets: Measured 86 open-weight checkpoints across seven benchmarks, six hardware platforms, and different reasoning modes.
Models with similar scores can differ substantially in energy use; many configurations consume 2.6–4.8× more energy than an equally capable alternative, with gaps up to 27×.
Enabling reasoning improves capability in some cases but raises energy use by about 3.7× on average, depending on model family and output budget.
Generated-token count is an imperfect energy proxy, while FP8 cuts energy by roughly a quarter with little score change.
Hardware mostly rescales energy and preserves model rankings, motivating joint reporting of scores and measured energy.
papers.selection_reason: Directly measures and analyzes inference energy efficiency of LLMs across models and hardware.
papers.title: Measuring the Inference Energy Efficiency of Open-Weight LLMs across Benchmarks, Reasoning Modes, and Hardware
papers.tldr: Inference energy varies dramatically across open-weight LLMs, so benchmark capability should be reported alongside measured energy under clearly specified serving conditions.

papers.abstract: Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization (DTR) trains neural networks under a memory budget by evicting tensors and recomputing them on demand. A natural expectation is that a budget large enough to complete training stays sufficient when it is increased. Using DTR's reference simulator, simrd, to replay the public DTR training traces, we show that this expectation fails. We call the exceptions feasibility holes: memory budgets at which an eviction policy runs out of memory although both a smaller and a larger budget complete, a form of non-monotone feasibility. Under a written sweep protocol with dated amendments, a 0.01-step budget grid shows no such hole for DTR on any of six confirmatory traces, although unresolved timeouts prevent it from establishing monotonicity. Finer sampling finds holes on InceptionV4 (three regions) and U-Net (two regions), in addition to one on the ResNet-32 development trace. Every hole is reproduced by three repeats and by unmodified simrd. For one InceptionV4 pair (0.2343 versus 0.235 of peak memory) we trace the failure to individual allocations. The larger budget avoids one eviction at an operator where the smaller budget was 173,479 bytes short. The extra data it carries forward forces a later eviction of a tensor needed three operators afterwards, and rebuilding that tensor triggers a recomputation cascade that cannot fit. Keeping that one tensor resident under the same budget prevents the failure. The two simple score changes we tested do not remove holes across traces; both add failing budgets on some traces. All results are from simulation, with no allocator model; behaviour on GPU hardware is untested.
bullets: DTR can exhibit non-monotone feasibility: a budget may fail even when both smaller and larger budgets succeed.
Fine-grained sweeps found feasibility holes on InceptionV4, U-Net, and a ResNet-32 development trace; each hole was reproduced repeatedly and with unmodified simrd.
One InceptionV4 failure arose when extra memory prevented an eviction, causing a later eviction of a tensor needed shortly afterward and an unfittable recomputation cascade.
Two tested score changes did not eliminate holes across traces and introduced failures on some traces.
Results are simulation-only; GPU allocator behavior was not evaluated, and timeouts prevented establishing monotonicity on all confirmatory traces.
papers.selection_reason: Studies memory-efficient training via dynamic tensor rematerialization, fitting the Efficient AI focus on reducing memory use.
papers.title: When More Memory Fails: Hidden Feasibility Holes in Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization
papers.tldr: More memory can paradoxically make Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization fail because eviction choices trigger later recomputation cascades.

papers.abstract: Accurate sampling from continuous-time generative models can require many model evaluations. Low-step sampling reduces cost, but coarse updates introduce endpoint errors that can accumulate and degrade generation quality. We introduce TraceSampler, a post-training method that corrects these errors without modifying the pretrained model. Rather than optimising low-step updates directly, TraceSampler models endpoint error as a sample-specific prediction problem. A higher-step reference integration over the same interval provides the supervised target, while a compact representation makes high-dimensional error predictable from the sampling trace. This representation combines shared residual structure, trace-derived directions, and a low-rank remainder, so shallow per-step MLP heads predict sample-dependent coefficients. These coefficients drive a two-stage learned residual correction: the first stage predicts the full endpoint residual, while an intermediate backbone evaluation provides new trace information to predict the remaining residual; this evaluation is reused by the following step. TraceSampler is evaluated with Rectified Flow on CIFAR-10, SiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256, and SD3.5 Medium for text-to-image generation. At 10 steps, it reduces trajectory MSE relative to matched-step Euler by 90.5% on CIFAR-10 and 85.6% on ImageNet-256, while achieving FID scores of 2.692 and 2.189, close to 120-step Heun references of 2.601 and 2.056 with 24$\times$ fewer backbone evaluations. On SD3.5 Medium, TraceSampler improves image quality and prompt following; at 10 steps, ImageReward rises from 0.752 to 0.906 while trajectory MSE falls by 70.7%. These gains preserve Euler's backbone-evaluation budget, add less than 0.4% inference FLOPs, and incur negligible wall-clock overhead, showing that coarse-step sampling error can be made predictable from the sampling trace and efficiently corrected.
authors: George Matthew (University of Exeter, United Kingdom), Guoqiang Zhang (University of Exeter, United Kingdom), Kenta Niwa (NTT Communication Science Laboratories, Japan)
bullets: Targets accuracy degradation caused by coarse, low-step updates in continuous-time generative models.
Uses a higher-step reference trajectory to supervise a compact trace-based error representation with shared residuals, trace-derived directions, and a low-rank remainder.
Applies a two-stage learned residual correction, reusing an intermediate backbone evaluation for the next step.
At 10 steps, reduces trajectory MSE by 90.5% on CIFAR-10, 85.6% on ImageNet-256, and 70.7% for SD3.5 Medium.
Matches 120-step Heun quality closely on the reported image benchmarks with 24× fewer backbone evaluations, under 0.4% extra inference FLOPs, and negligible wall-clock overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Post-training correction of sampling errors in generative models reduces sampling steps and compute.
papers.title: TraceSampler: Making Sampling Errors Predictable and Correctable for Accelerated Generative Sampling
papers.tldr: TraceSampler predicts and corrects sample-specific endpoint errors in low-step generative sampling, substantially improving quality with negligible extra computation and no pretrained-model changes.

papers.abstract: Foundation models like V-JEPA are increasingly deployed across a heterogeneous edge-cloud continuum spanning smart glasses, phones, robots, and servers. Yet, they are typically trained as rigid, fixed-capacity networks bound to one device, supporting neither reconfigurable compute budgets nor collaborative execution. Existing approaches address only one axis at a time: slimmable and NAS-based methods provide width elasticity but assume single-device inference, whereas split-computing methods enable cross-device collaboration only for fixed partitions and static capacities. We introduce Elastic V-JEPA (EV-JEPA), a single model trained once and deployable everywhere along the continuum. Its width is reconfigurable, and it is natively partitionable across heterogeneous devices. At its core is Transition-Aware Triplet Training (T3). At each step we pick a narrow and a wide width, and train three paths: each width alone, plus a hybrid path that runs the early layers narrow and the rest wide. The hybrid switch point is where one device hands off to another, so the same weights learn both single-device and cross-device execution. Across various benchmarks, EV-JEPA falls within 1 accuracy point of independently trained baselines while improving over previous elastic training approaches by up to 11 accuracy points. Narrow-to-wide cross-device hybrid execution recovers to within 1.1 points of the highest-capacity standalone model and supports many-to-one, any-to-any, and variable-split configurations. Finally, we show that the elastic principle extends beyond the backbone to an elastic token compression mechanism that exposes controllable trade-offs among on-device computation, latency, and accuracy.
authors: Anxhelo Diko, Jieyu Lin, Stefano Ambrogio, Ziyun Li, Mahmoud Assran, Th\'eo Moutakanni, Barbara De Salvo, Chiao Liu
bullets: Supports reconfigurable model widths for different device compute budgets.
Enables native cross-device execution with flexible split points and many-to-one or any-to-any configurations.
Uses Transition-Aware Triplet Training to jointly train narrow, wide, and hybrid narrow-to-wide execution paths.
Matches independently trained baselines within 1 accuracy point and improves prior elastic methods by up to 11 points.
Extends elasticity to token compression, trading on-device computation and latency against accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Elastic V-JEPA enables reconfigurable width and cross-device inference with elastic token compression, reducing compute.
papers.title: EV-JEPA: Elastic V-JEPA for Any Device and Cross-Device Inference
papers.tldr: EV-JEPA is a single V-JEPA model that flexibly adapts its width and splits computation across heterogeneous devices with near-baseline accuracy.

papers.abstract: Speech large language models (LLMs) are often built using pretrained acoustic encoders as an audio interface to an LLM decoder. However, LLMs scale poorly with input sequence length, while acoustic encoders tend to produce substantially longer sequences than typical textual inputs. This motivates learning to compress encoder outputs while preserving task-oriented information. To this end, we introduce ASSET, a reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework that learns to adaptively compress encoder outputs by first partitioning them into variable-duration segments and then pooling each segment into a continuous audio token. We use group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) to train a segmenter with task performance feedback and a token-rate penalty. In automatic speech recognition (ASR) experiments, ASSET achieves performance comparable to a transcript-assisted character-boundary oracle with approximately 25% fewer audio tokens on English LibriSpeech, while improving on a phone-boundary oracle at a similar token rate on Mandarin AISHELL. Exploratory experiments on non-ASR tasks further illustrate how learned segmentation changes when the framework is adapted to tasks beyond transcription.
authors: Cihan Xiao, Yuan Tseng, Matthew Wiesner, Desh Raj, Leibny Paola Garcia Perera, Sanjeev Khudanpur, David Harwath
bullets: Addresses the sequence-length mismatch between long acoustic-encoder outputs and speech LLM inputs.
Learns variable-duration segments and pools each into a continuous audio token.
Trains the segmenter with GRPO using task-performance feedback and a token-rate penalty.
Matches a transcript-assisted character-boundary oracle with about 25% fewer tokens on English LibriSpeech.
Outperforms a phone-boundary oracle at a similar token rate on Mandarin AISHELL; non-ASR behavior is explored but not fully characterized.
papers.selection_reason: RL-based adaptive compression of speech encoder outputs into fewer audio tokens for speech LLMs; relevant to token efficiency and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: ASSET: Adaptive Speech Segmentation via Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: ASSET uses reinforcement learning to adaptively segment and compress speech encoder outputs into fewer task-relevant audio tokens while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Tensor parallelism ends every layer with an all-reduce that sits between two dependent matrix multiplications, so its cost cannot be hidden and grows as compute outpaces interconnect bandwidth. Sending 4-bit instead of 16-bit values would cut this cost by nearly 4x, but the all-reduce must add the values it carries, and rounding the sum injects an error at every call. Model quality depends on how these errors accumulate over layers, yet existing methods treat each call on its own. We present Echo, a 4-bit all-reduce for training and inference that controls the accumulated error. Echo moves data in 4 bits and sums in high precision, so each value is quantized at most twice per call for any number of GPUs. The summation reveals each injected error, and Echo feeds it back into later calls, so old errors cancel instead of accumulating. We prove that the accumulated error stays bounded independently of depth. On A100 GPUs, Echo is 2.09x faster than the 16-bit NCCL all-reduce on 1 GB messages. It speeds up the time to first token by up to 1.16x and the training step by up to 1.09x on an idle interconnect, and by up to 1.44x and 1.38x as background traffic grows. It keeps the average accuracy over seven benchmarks within 0.4 points of 16-bit inference on Qwen3-8B. In 10B-token pretraining, its final loss is less than 0.9% above that of 16-bit training. Echo needs no FP8 or FP4 hardware.
authors: Xingyu Xie, Xiaoyong Xie, Zhouchen Lin, Kim-Chuan Toh
bullets: Problem: 16-bit all-reduce communication limits tensor-parallel LLM training and inference, while naïve 4-bit quantization introduces repeated rounding errors.
Method: Data moves in 4 bits, sums in high precision, and each value is quantized at most twice per call; revealed errors are fed back into later calls.
Guarantee: The accumulated communication error is proven to remain bounded independently of network depth.
Results: Echo is 2.09× faster than 16-bit NCCL all-reduce on 1 GB A100 messages, with up to 1.44× faster time to first token and 1.38× faster training under background traffic.
Quality and scope: Accuracy stays within 0.4 points of 16-bit inference across seven benchmarks, and final pretraining loss is under 0.9% higher; no FP8 or FP4 hardware is required.
papers.selection_reason: 4-bit tensor-parallel all-reduce with error compensation directly targets communication and inference/training efficiency.
papers.title: Echo: Error-Compensated 4-Bit Tensor-Parallel Communication for LLM Training and Inference
papers.tldr: Echo enables accurate 4-bit tensor-parallel communication by feeding quantization errors forward so they cancel rather than accumulate.

papers.abstract: Softmax attention in Transformers suffers from quadratic complexity in sequence length, making it impractical for long-context applications. Linear attention alleviates this issue by replacing the exponential kernel with alternative functions that enable linear-time computation. Among existing linear attention approaches, recent studies have shown that polynomial kernels are particularly effective, as they exhibit sparse and spiky behavior similar to softmax attention, which emphasizes large dot products while suppressing irrelevant interactions. However, the exact computation of high-degree polynomial kernels is infeasible for high-dimensional representations. As a result, prior work relies on approximate polynomial kernels. This introduces a non-negligible approximation error. In this paper, we show that, from the perspective of polynomial kernel approximation, existing linear attention methods are still suboptimal. We propose \textbf{L}earnable \textbf{Lo}w-Rank \textbf{P}olynomial \textbf{S}ketch (LLoPS), a principled and flexible framework for approximating polynomial kernels with linear attention. Our method learns a low-rank polynomial sketch that provably achieves a strictly smaller approximation error than existing approaches. Experiment results show that LLoPS achieves the highest performance across extensive benchmarks, comparing with various linear attention baselines.
authors: Zongyue Qin, Haoran Deng, Jason Cong, Yizhou Sun
bullets: Softmax attention has quadratic sequence-length complexity, limiting long-context use.
Polynomial kernels can mimic softmax’s sparse, spiky attention patterns but are costly to compute exactly in high dimensions.
LLoPS learns a low-rank polynomial sketch to reduce approximation error in linear attention.
The framework is theoretically shown to outperform existing polynomial-kernel approximation methods in error.
Across extensive benchmarks, LLoPS achieves the best performance among the compared linear-attention baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Learnable low-rank polynomial sketch for linear attention, directly targets efficient attention.
papers.title: Learnable Low-Rank Polynomial Sketch for Effective Linear Attention
papers.tldr: LLoPS improves linear attention by learning a low-rank sketch that more accurately approximates high-degree polynomial kernels while retaining linear-time computation.

papers.abstract: Studying model training requires checkpoint trajectories, whose storage cost limits temporal resolution. Although adjacent checkpoints are numerically close, existing lossless codecs either operate on XOR bit patterns or ignore trajectory-specific conditional structure. We show that a reference weight's exponent predicts the bit length of its displacement in ordered floating-point space without side information. We introduce \textbf{ULPack}, a lossless codec which exploits this dependence by conditioning entropy models of ordered-integer residuals on the reference exponent. Across bfloat16, float16, and float32 trajectories, ULPack reduces storage by up to 27\% against ZipNN, 21\% against zstd-19, and 11.5\% against FM-Delta. Across two dense trajectories, compression improves as updates shrink and reference conditioning strengthens, while near uniform low-order bits set the remaining compression floor and earlier checkpoints add little information.
bullets: Checkpoint trajectories are storage-intensive despite adjacent checkpoints being numerically close.
The method encodes ordered-integer residuals using entropy models conditioned on the reference weight’s exponent, without side information.
Evaluated on bfloat16, float16, and float32 trajectories, ULPack improves compression over ZipNN, zstd-19, and FM-Delta.
Compression strengthens as training updates shrink and reference conditioning becomes more predictive.
Near-uniform low-order bits limit further compression, while earlier checkpoints contribute little additional information.
papers.selection_reason: Lossless checkpoint-trajectory compression via reference-conditioned entropy coding; reduces storage overhead in AI training.
papers.title: ULPack: Reference-Conditioned Lossless Compression of Checkpoint Trajectories
papers.tldr: ULPack losslessly compresses neural-network checkpoint trajectories by conditioning residual entropy models on reference-weight exponents, reducing storage by up to 27%.

papers.abstract: Smart glasses are a promising platform for vision-language assistants, but private split inference remains expensive: protecting visual representations before transmission does not remove the cost of on-device vision encoding, wide protected tokens, or hardware-unaware execution. We present SAGE (Smart-glasses-Aware Guarded Encoding), a hardware-aware framework for efficient protected VLM inference on smart glasses. SAGE keeps raw images and unprotected visual tokens on the trusted device, reduces visual input cost, executes shape-specialized INT8 graphs, and compresses protected representations into compact 256-dimensional INT8 packets before transmission. Unlike efficiency methods optimized only for nominal model size, SAGE selects its operating point using downstream answer quality together with measured latency, memory, and thermal behavior on real Mentra Live glasses. On a matched Qwen workload, SAGE reduces glasses inference latency by 39.18%, device-sensor temperature rise by 21.91%, and protected packet size by 96.56%, while retaining 85.62% of the protected reference's relaxed utility and comparable prompted containment. Direct glasses-to-phone tests deliver all 192 packets and reduce median packet-plus-acknowledgment time from 71.3 to 10.0 ms. The compact protected interface also transfers across four additional VLM families. These results show that private wearable VLM inference must be optimized jointly across representation protection, communication, and real-device execution rather than through model compression alone.
authors: Zhimin Li, Pan Wang, Jingxian Chen, Yuantao Tang, Qian Lou, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Keeps raw images and unprotected visual tokens on the trusted glasses device while reducing visual input cost.
Uses shape-specialized INT8 execution and compresses protected representations into compact 256-dimensional INT8 packets.
On Mentra Live glasses, reduces inference latency, temperature rise, and protected packet size while retaining substantial protected-reference utility.
Direct glasses-to-phone tests reduce median packet-plus-acknowledgment time from 71.3 ms to 10.0 ms with all packets delivered.
The compact protected interface transfers across four additional VLM families.
papers.selection_reason: Hardware-aware efficient protected VLM inference on smart glasses, reducing latency, memory, and communication.
papers.title: SAGE: Efficient Protected Vision-Language Inference on Smart Glasses
papers.tldr: SAGE enables more efficient private vision-language inference on smart glasses by jointly optimizing protected representations, communication, and hardware-aware execution.

papers.abstract: Large language models typically support different inference budgets through separate model sizes or fixed compute configurations. In multi-turn interactions, however, compute demand can vary substantially across turns. Using a high-compute model for every turn wastes computation, while routing among independent models may require rebuilding model-specific history states after switches. We therefore ask whether a single shared model can support multiple compute budgets that can be flexibly assigned across turns. We introduce Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE, which jointly supports token-to-concept compression ratios of 2, 4, and 8 (CR2/CR4/CR8) within a shared backbone. Lightweight full-token modules reduce compression-independent cost, ratio-specific boundary routers support distinct compression levels, and cross-ratio training enables mixed-ratio processing within the same context. Across PTBench and SFTBench, the three fixed modes outperform their compute-matched MoE baselines in all 6 comparisons while remaining competitive with independently trained fixed-ratio specialists. On CodeChat and CoSQL, mixed-ratio inference improves the accuracy--compute trade-off, outperforming the Large MoE by 5.87 and 2.68 percentage points while reducing FLOPs by 41.1% and 12.3%, respectively. Under the same turn-wise budget schedule, Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE further reduces FLOPs by 78.4% and 46.9% relative to routing among independent models. These results demonstrate that a single shared model can provide multiple compute budgets for flexible compute allocation across turns.
authors: Yiyang Fu, Zihao Huang, Dongchen Han, Shukai Gong, Zhen Dong, Qiyang Min, Daquan Zhou
bullets: Addresses variable per-turn compute needs without using separate models or rebuilding history states when switching.
Uses lightweight full-token modules, ratio-specific boundary routers, and cross-ratio training in a shared backbone.
Fixed-ratio modes outperform compute-matched MoE baselines in all six reported comparisons and remain competitive with specialists.
Mixed-ratio inference improves the accuracy–compute trade-off on CodeChat and CoSQL, with lower FLOPs than the Large MoE.
Under matched turn-wise budgets, it reduces FLOPs versus routing among independent models, demonstrating flexible shared-model inference.
papers.selection_reason: Single shared MoE model supporting multiple compute budgets via token-to-concept compression, fitting efficient AI and LLM architecture topics.
papers.title: One Model, Multiple Compute Budgets: Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE for Flexible Compute Across Turns
papers.tldr: Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE enables one shared model to flexibly use 2×, 4×, or 8× token-to-concept compression across conversation turns, improving accuracy–compute trade-offs while avoiding model-switching overhead.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention visits few keys, yet finding them can still require scoring every key with every indexer head. We introduce DoSA (Dots Sparse Attention), a lossless method for making this computation conditional while preserving exact token selection. Its central observation is that Top-K selection requires sufficient evidence to reject a candidate, not necessarily its full score. A seed set supplies a lower bound on the winning threshold. Nonnegative head projections and joint residual bounds upper-bound positive contributions, while activation-informed aggregation bounds the magnitude subtracted by negative heads. The certificate directs full scoring toward candidates that remain eligible; exact-score filtering further reduces writeback and selection work. We establish the certificate and its exact-selection conditions, and analyze how geometry and selection margins govern its effectiveness. Our GPU implementation accelerates the complete Indexer by up to 2.74 times over SGLang and 1.69 times over LiteTopK across English, Chinese, and code workloads. End-to-end evaluation on GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2 achieves up to 1.94 times and 1.50 times time-to-first-token speedups over the two baselines, respectively.
bullets: Sparse attention can remain expensive because every candidate may still be scored by each indexer head.
A seed set establishes a lower bound on the Top-K threshold, while bounds identify candidates that cannot be eliminated without full scoring.
The method uses nonnegative projections, residual bounds, and activation-informed bounds for negative contributions, followed by exact-score filtering.
GPU experiments report up to 2.74× faster indexing than SGLang and 1.69× faster than LiteTopK across English, Chinese, and code workloads.
End-to-end time-to-first-token improves by up to 1.94× on GLM-5.2 and 1.50× on DeepSeek-V3.2 versus the baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Lossless conditional sparse attention with exact Top-K key selection; directly targets efficient attention and token selection for LLM inference.
papers.title: DoSA: Dots Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: DoSA accelerates sparse-attention index selection by conditionally avoiding unnecessary key scoring while preserving exact Top-K results.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have emerged as an effective paradigm for scaling large language models, yet their massive parameter footprint poses severe memory challenges for deployment. Existing compression methods typically treat expert pruning and merging as disjoint operations and rely on greedy heuristics, often leading to irreversible information loss or representational pollution. In this paper, we propose PRIME, a unified optimization framework for MoE compression via adaptive PRunIng and MErging. PRIME casts the discrete prune-merge assignment step as a global Integer Linear Programming over a frequency-weighted surrogate objective, jointly selecting pruning and merging decisions while accounting for expert usage. We motivate the frequency-aware objective through an error-bound analysis under fixed representative assignments, and show that the formulation favors high-frequency experts as centroids, promoting routing stability. Extensive experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B demonstrate that PRIME achieves strong accuracy retention across knowledge, coding, math, and long-context tasks, while serving benchmarks of merged models quantify the memory and throughput benefits of expert compression in vLLM.
authors: Shanfeng Huang, Rongqian Zhang, Zhou Fang, Song Xiao, Hai Du
bullets: Addresses memory challenges from the large parameter footprint of MoE models.
Jointly optimizes prune-and-merge assignments with global Integer Linear Programming rather than separate greedy decisions.
Uses expert-usage frequency in a surrogate objective to favor frequently used experts as merge representatives and improve routing stability.
Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B show strong accuracy retention across knowledge, coding, math, and long-context tasks.
Serving benchmarks with vLLM quantify memory and throughput benefits after compression.
papers.selection_reason: MoE LLM compression via expert pruning and merging for memory and throughput, relevant to efficient AI and large language models.
papers.title: PRIME: Frequency-Aware Unified Pruning and Merging for MoE Compression
papers.tldr: PRIME unifies frequency-aware expert pruning and merging for MoE compression, preserving accuracy while reducing deployment costs.

papers.abstract: Distributed inference depends on GPU collective communication that must keep pace with evolving hardware and specialized workloads. However, existing works often couple the semantics, orchestration (where and when data moves), and datapath (how data moves) of collective communication. This coupling makes it costly to adopt new hardware mechanisms and customize communication for applications. We present Purlin, a scale-up communication framework that separates these concerns. At the top of Purlin, we specify collectives as a naming of an input and output layout and a copy or reduction operation. In the middle, we introduce a shared orchestration protocol, Stage, Notify, And Consume (SNAC), which derives coordination from these specifications. Below SNAC sits a hardware-specific datapath we call Atom, which implements two key data movement primitives for collectives: copy and reduce. This separation lets us customize collectives and adopt new hardware mechanisms while reusing orchestration via SNAC. We evaluate Purlin on A100, H200, and B200 GPUs. Across seven collectives, Purlin achieves latency speedups of up to 5.14x and bandwidth improvements of up to 4.50x over baselines. Integrated into SGLang, Purlin improves offline LLM serving throughput and interactivity by 1.13x on average and up to 1.37x over baselines. For online LLM inference, Purlin improves interactivity by 1.26x on average and up to 2.85x, with the largest gain occurring under overload. For diffusion image generation, Purlin reduces end-to-end latency by up to 1.13x.
bullets: Existing collective systems tightly couple what data moves, when and where it moves, and how movement is implemented, limiting customization and hardware adoption.
Purlin specifies collectives through input/output layouts and copy or reduction operations.
Its SNAC protocol provides reusable orchestration, while the Atom layer implements hardware-specific copy and reduce primitives.
Evaluated on A100, H200, and B200 GPUs across seven collectives, Purlin achieves up to 5.14× lower latency and 4.50× higher bandwidth than baselines.
Integrated into SGLang, it improves LLM serving throughput and interactivity and reduces diffusion-generation latency, with gains varying by workload and load.
papers.selection_reason: Optimizes GPU collective communication for distributed LLM inference by separating orchestration from the datapath, significantly reducing latency and improving throughput.
papers.title: Purlin: Separating Orchestration from the Datapath of Collectives
papers.tldr: Purlin improves GPU collective communication by separating collective semantics, orchestration, and hardware-specific data movement, delivering substantial gains across GPUs and inference workloads.

papers.abstract: Host-resident layer streaming enables full-parameter LLM fine-tuning beyond GPU memory, but data-parallel ranks compete for shared host resources. Replicated transfers amplify traffic, while strong scaling can expose host work as computation windows shrink. We present SlideDP, a synchronous data-parallel runtime for shared-host multi-GPU systems. It maintains one authoritative host state, decouples communication routes from state layout, and pipelines parameter delivery, gradient aggregation, and CPU updates across ranks and chunks. An analytical step-time model characterizes resource bottlenecks and pipeline exposure; runtime measurements guide communication, chunking, and activation policies under a GPU memory budget. In matched-batch sweeps, SlideDP achieves geometric-mean throughput ratios of 1.46-2.64$\times$ over SlideFormer, MegaTrain, and ZeRO-Offload. On four H100s, SlideDP approaches GPU-resident FSDP2 throughput for Qwen3-14B at a smaller batch size. With a larger batch, it processes over 1M tokens per step and exceeds FSDP2's measured peak throughput by 11.2%. Separately, it supports 256K-token sequences for the same model and fine-tunes Qwen2.5-72B on four RTX 4090 GPUs. Project page: https://github.com/RegiaYoung/SlideDP.
authors: Ruijia Yang, Shiyuan Lin, Yulong Ao, Zhiyu Li, Yingli Zhao, Xianduo Li, Yonghua Lin, Zeyi Wen
bullets: Addresses shared-host contention and redundant transfers in data-parallel host-resident LLM fine-tuning.
Uses one authoritative host state, flexible communication routes, and pipelined parameter delivery, gradient aggregation, and CPU updates.
Combines an analytical step-time model with runtime measurements to tune communication, chunking, and activation policies under GPU memory limits.
Reports 1.46–2.64× geometric-mean throughput over SlideFormer, MegaTrain, and ZeRO-Offload in matched-batch sweeps.
Supports Qwen3-14B on four H100s, including over 1M tokens per step and 256K-token sequences, and fine-tunes Qwen2.5-72B on four RTX 4090s.
papers.selection_reason: Data-parallel runtime for host-resident LLM fine-tuning that reduces memory traffic and improves throughput; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: SlideDP: Scaling Host-Resident LLM Fine-Tuning Across Multiple GPUs
papers.tldr: SlideDP enables efficient multi-GPU fine-tuning of models larger than GPU memory by coordinating host-resident state, communication, and pipelined updates.

papers.abstract: How many dimensions does a language model's computation actually use? The question is ill-posed until one names a functional. Task-weighted charts make it well-posed: low-dimensional coordinate systems fit against a chosen functional of the representation, under the functional's own metric, turning distillation into plain least squares. Across six models from three families, spanning 70m to 7B parameters, next-token prediction needs 70--90% of the residual stream's width to stay within 5% of intact perplexity, a width consumed by the rare tail of language, and the variance profile predicts none of it: two directions carry 90% of GPT-2's activation variance and almost none of its function. Dimension is per-functional: the model's own uncertainty reads from six coordinates where the full predictive distribution needs hundreds; and it grows with depth. The dissociation is exploitable: when only a few dimensions can be kept, charts trained under the functional's metric preserve the model's predictions better than variance-based or optimal linear compression.
bullets: Next-token prediction requires 70–90% of residual-stream width to remain within 5% of intact perplexity across six models.
The needed dimensions are driven by the rare tail of language, not dominant activation-variance directions.
Two directions explain 90% of GPT-2’s activation variance but capture almost none of its predictive function.
Dimensionality depends on the functional: model uncertainty uses six coordinates, while the full predictive distribution needs hundreds, and dimensionality grows with depth.
Functional-metric charts preserve predictions better than variance-based or optimal linear compression when dimensions are limited.
papers.selection_reason: Task-weighted low-dimensional charts compress LM representations while preserving function, relevant to efficient AI and LLM analysis.
papers.title: Function Lives Where Variance Doesn't: Task-Weighted Charts of a Language Model's Computation
papers.tldr: Task-weighted charts reveal that a language model’s functional computation is often high-dimensional and poorly predicted by activation variance.

papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability identifies sparse subsets of heads and MLP blocks that carry specific behaviors. We ask whether such causal signals can guide where to place a small PEFT budget more effectively than the cheap heuristics practitioners already use. \method{} scores attention heads and MLP blocks by normalized activation-patching recovery on clean/corrupted probes and trains LoRA/QLoRA only on the selected sites; \methodc{} adds bounded credit for small within-layer joint subsets. We compare against random, magnitude, activation-norm, and gradient/Fisher on Ministral-8B/NF4 in three cells: Swahili span-JSON information extraction (IE) at $b{=}0.25\%$ and $1.0\%$, and English$\to$Swahili machine translation (MT) at $b{=}1.0\%$. The causal selectors never win the primary metric. On the headline IE cell (3 seeds, paired-bootstrap CIs over $600$ predictions), \methodc{} beats random by $+0.079$ span+type F1 and gradient/Fisher by $+0.174$, but trails activation-norm by $0.028$, with the smallest cross-seed std ($\pm 0.003$). On MT all four selectors lie within $0.30$ BLEU and every paired CI includes zero. A schema-versus-span decomposition explains the IE gap: activation-norm captures the rigid JSON routine, while causal scores track content-sensitive sites. We distill a preliminary diagnostic -- prefer activation-norm when output structure dominates, treat causal selectors as a hypothesis for content-dominated tasks -- and release masks, scores, predictions, and evaluation files for direct replay.
bullets: Evaluates causal head/MLP selectors for LoRA/QLoRA against random, magnitude, activation-norm, and gradient/Fisher baselines.
Tests Swahili span-JSON information extraction and English→Swahili machine translation on Ministral-8B/NF4 under small PEFT budgets.
Causal selectors do not win the primary metric; the joint causal selector beats random and gradient/Fisher on the headline IE cell but trails activation-norm.
In MT, selector differences are small, with all paired confidence intervals including zero.
IE analysis suggests activation-norm favors rigid schema behavior, while causal scores identify content-sensitive sites; released artifacts enable replay.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse PEFT site selection via causal scoring is an efficiency-oriented LLM adaptation method, transferable to efficient AI.
papers.title: MechSparse: Mechanism-Guided Sparse PEFT Selection Is Task-Shaped
papers.tldr: Mechanistic signals can guide sparse PEFT site selection, but cheap activation-norm heuristics perform best when output structure dominates.

papers.abstract: Compact acoustic models face a challenging quality-capacity trade-off. We investigate two factors in this regime: encoder context and Mel-spectrogram supervision. A receptive-field-scaling study shows that expanding self-attention beyond 15 phonemes provides no consistent gains in pitch, energy, or duration prediction. Guided by this finding, we introduce a fixed-receptive-field convolutional encoder that reduces the respective prediction errors by 36.0%, 17.3%, and 3.4%. We further show that directly transferring image-domain gradient-variance supervision restores fine-scale variation but degrades predicted quality, motivating a Mel-specific formulation with axis-specific gradients, overlapping local statistics, and log-domain variance matching. GrainSpeech contains only 264.8K parameters and achieves 17.9x real-time Mel generation on a microcontroller (MCU), while attaining UTMOS scores comparable to substantially larger models with less than 1.5% of their parameters. Source code and demos are available at https://github.com/lab-emi/GrainSpeech.
bullets: Expanding encoder attention beyond 15 phonemes yields no consistent gains in pitch, energy, or duration prediction.
A fixed-receptive-field convolutional encoder reduces prediction errors by 36.0% for pitch, 17.3% for energy, and 3.4% for duration.
Image-domain gradient-variance supervision restores detail but harms quality; GrainSpeech instead uses axis-specific gradients, overlapping local statistics, and log-domain variance matching.
The 264.8K-parameter model generates Mels at 17.9× real time on an MCU and reaches UTMOS scores comparable to much larger models.
Scope: the approach targets compact, resource-constrained acoustic modeling, with results focused on Mel generation and predicted speech quality.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a compact speech synthesis model that reduces context length (receptive field) to improve efficiency, relevant to token-level efficiency methods.
papers.title: GrainSpeech: Less Context, More Detail for Compact Speech Synthesis
papers.tldr: GrainSpeech shows that compact speech synthesizers can retain fine acoustic detail with limited context, using a fixed-field encoder and Mel-specific gradient-variance supervision.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a least squares approach for the training of quadratic neural networks with regularization. The proposed methodology yields a lower bound on the solution of the training optimization problem for the case where the regularization coefficient is positive. Moreover, it yields closed-form expressions for the approximate solution and its sensitivity The lower bound is tight and the approximate solution is the optimal solution when the regularization coefficient is zero. Having a closed-form expression for the weights reduces considerably the computational time when compared with iterative numerical methods such as backpropagation that can get stuck in local minima. The proposed approach has three main contributions, namely, (i) it yields an analytical expression for the weights, (ii) an analytical expression for the sensitivity of the weights to errors in the data is also provided, (iii) it establishes a connection between the optimization to compute a lower bound and nuclear norm minimization. The proposed least squares training is successfully applied to a nonlinear system identification example where the proposed lower bound is compared with the optimal value.
bullets: Derives a lower bound for the training objective when the regularization coefficient is positive; the bound is tight.
Provides closed-form expressions for approximate network weights and their sensitivity to data errors.
The approximation becomes optimal when the regularization coefficient is zero.
Links the lower-bound optimization problem to nuclear norm minimization.
Demonstrates the method on a nonlinear system identification example by comparing the lower bound with the optimal value.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-form least-squares training reduces computational cost versus iterative backpropagation, a meaningful efficiency contribution.
papers.title: Regularized Least Squares Training of Quadratic Neural Networks with Applications to System Identification
papers.tldr: A regularized least-squares method provides near-closed-form training and sensitivity analysis for quadratic neural networks, with an application to nonlinear system identification.

papers.abstract: Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) doubles the cost of every training step, yet its benefit concentrates where training ends. We study where an expensive training mode should be spent and propose Temperon: a plain-SGD explorer for the first 43% of the epoch budget, then one scheduled hand-off that gives the entire final cosine anneal to a SAM-wrapped Muon refiner. On CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet (five seeds, times reported as epochs-to-target times an idle-GPU-calibrated epoch cost), Temperon matches the best full-time-SAM recipe on accuracy everywhere while reaching the hardest common target 35%, 34% and 32% sooner on three of the four, and sits a tier above the published SAM+SGD recipe at level cost. Ablations make the attribution exact: the Muon refiner is worth +0.85pp with everything else fixed; the explorer's shape and its restarts are worth nothing, and we withdraw them as contributions. Re-running the closest rival, late-phase SAM, at matched budget shows the frontier: it is fastest to every mid-level target, but the tier the Muon refiner buys (0.83 on CIFAR-100, 0.97 on CIFAR-10) is reached by no SGD-refined method in any seed, and on Tiny ImageNet, where Muon buys no tier, the rival simply wins -- the measured boundary of the method. The allocation law transfers to GPT-2 pretraining (full-SAM quality at -29% wall-clock) and GLUE fine-tuning (never worse than full-time SAM at a third of its SAM cost). Two constants organize the economics: skipping SAM early buys a fixed credit, and a Muon epoch costs 1.50x a SAM+SGD epoch on all four datasets. Finally, the hand-off cannot be timed from the trajectory: under cosine schedules the accuracy curve is plateau-then-surge, so the information lives in the schedule, making the scheduled switch principled rather than convenient. Code and a pip-installable implementation are released.
bullets: Uses plain SGD for the first 43% of training, followed by one scheduled hand-off to a SAM-wrapped Muon refiner for the final anneal.
On CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, and Tiny ImageNet, it matches the best full-time-SAM accuracy; it reaches the hardest common target faster on three of four datasets.
The Muon refiner provides the measurable gain (+0.85 percentage points), while the explorer’s shape and restarts contribute nothing in ablations.
Late-phase SAM remains faster for mid-level targets; Temperon’s advantage is limited to quality tiers enabled by Muon, and it loses this benefit on Tiny ImageNet.
The allocation strategy also transfers to GPT-2 pretraining and GLUE fine-tuning, with reported savings versus full-time SAM.
papers.selection_reason: Training-time efficiency via scheduled SAM/Muon optimization, reducing wall-clock cost while preserving quality; fits Efficient AI.
papers.title: Temperon: Full-Time SAM Quality at a Third Less Wall-Clock
papers.tldr: Temperon skips costly SAM early, then applies SAM-wrapped Muon during the final cosine-annealing phase to match full-time SAM quality with substantially less wall-clock time.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex voice agents make many small, closed decisions, which current systems answer by slow autoregressive decoding. We propose DuplexJev, which feeds ASR-encoder hidden states through a small connector into a frozen LLM and reads each question as a single-token distribution over its options. Nothing is decoded, and an 8-GPU node answers 80 decisions about eight utterances in about 0.1 s. With a last-layer connector, spoken QA stays close to reading the transcript (90% vs. 91%). DuplexJev also hears the speaker: gender and emotion accuracy both reach 90% (from 55% and 28%) with a cross-attention connector, whose spoken QA drops by only 1 point (83% to 82%). We train decisions with cross-entropy on the read-out answer token, instead of the usual transcript distillation, whose teacher never hears the voice, and keep distillation for content. Encoders and LLMs are interchangeable; we release weights, training recipe, a batched-inference pipeline for full-duplex serving and a bilingual spoken-QA set.
bullets: Maps ASR-encoder representations into a frozen LLM and reads each question as a single-token option distribution.
Uses answer-token cross-entropy for decision supervision while retaining distillation for speech content.
Handles spoken QA, speaker gender, and emotion, with cross-attention improving paralinguistic recognition while slightly reducing QA accuracy.
Batches 80 decisions over eight utterances in about 0.1 seconds on an 8-GPU node.
Provides interchangeable encoder/LLM components, released weights and recipe, a full-duplex inference pipeline, and a bilingual spoken-QA set.
papers.selection_reason: Extends a frozen LLM with speech encoder features for batched single-token decisions; fits multimodal LLMs and efficient inference.
papers.title: Batched Speech Decisions Without Decoding: Single-Token Supervision Lets a Frozen LLM Hear Beyond the Transcript
papers.tldr: DuplexJev enables a frozen LLM to answer many speech-based decisions in parallel from ASR hidden states without autoregressive decoding.

papers.abstract: Muon improves large-scale training by applying a spectral-norm steepest-descent update to matrix parameters, but practical models also contain parameter blocks that do not fit dense-matrix geometry. One important case is the tied vocabulary table, which appears in language models and other token generators and can receive multiple structurally different gradient sources, from sparse input lookups to dense output-classifier updates. In the reference recipe these blocks are handed to an auxiliary AdamW optimizer, which restores second-moment state and updates the aliased table as a generic tensor. We propose AF-Muon, an AdamW-free extension of Muon that keeps the Muon matrix update for hidden weight matrices while using a support-aware finite-cap linear minimization oracle for tied vocabulary tables and an RMS-normalized update for one-dimensional auxiliary parameters. AF-Muon therefore trains every parameter class with a single first-moment buffer and no second-moment state, saving around 20% optimizer-state memory relative to Hybrid Muon in our benchmark. Across nine tied-token settings - decoder-only language models from 124M to 1B parameters, a fully shared T5-style encoder-decoder, and ImageGPT-style image-token, protein, and sparse-MoE variants, spanning text, image, and protein-sequence data - AF-Muon improves mean validation loss and perplexity over both Hybrid Muon and a SCION-style Sign endpoint. Long-horizon runs and hyperparameter sensitivity studies confirm the gain is robust, and identical-momentum diagnostics attribute it to the finite cap, which preserves more within-row magnitude than Sign while bounding the coordinate concentration of row-RMS. These results identify tied vocabulary tables as a distinct optimizer geometry and yield a robust AdamW-free Muon variant across models, modalities, and architectures, with about 1% step-time overhead in matched training.
bullets: Addresses tied vocabulary tables that receive both sparse input-lookup and dense output-classifier gradients.
Keeps Muon updates for matrix weights, uses a support-aware finite-cap oracle for tied tables, and RMS-normalized updates for 1D parameters.
Uses only first-moment state, saving around 20% optimizer-state memory versus Hybrid Muon.
Improves mean validation loss and perplexity across nine tied-token settings, including language, image, protein, encoder-decoder, and sparse-MoE models.
Reported overhead is about 1% of matched training step time; diagnostics attribute gains to the finite cap preserving within-row magnitude while limiting coordinate concentration.
papers.selection_reason: Presents an optimizer that reduces memory and compute overhead for tied-embedding models; fits efficient AI via reduced training memory and step-time cost.
papers.title: AF-Muon: An AdamW-Free Muon Optimizer for Tied-Embedding Models
papers.tldr: AF-Muon extends Muon to tied-embedding models without AdamW, reducing optimizer-state memory while improving validation performance across diverse modalities and architectures.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models maintain fixed-size recurrent states, but existing quantizers typically use eight bits or more. Quantization errors persist according to channel decay rates. We derive distortion weights from the observability Gramian and combine them with normalized state ranges for mixed-precision bit allocation, without calibration data, rotation, or training. We also quantize decay rates logarithmically. With per-token state quantization, a four-bit mean payload reduces excess negative log-likelihood by factors of 3.3--27.9 relative to the best of seven baselines across three hybrid models; metadata costs vary. At six bits, negative log-likelihood differs from the FP32-state baseline by less than 0.005 nats. Ablations separate gains from variable bit widths, decay weighting, and range normalization. With less frequent write-backs, gains diminish and depend on the model and budget.
bullets: Existing recurrent-state quantizers generally use at least eight bits, while persistent errors depend on channel decay rates.
The method allocates bits using observability-Gramian distortion weights and normalized state ranges, and logarithmically quantizes decay rates.
It requires no calibration data, rotations, or retraining, and supports per-token state quantization.
Across three hybrid models, four-bit mean payloads reduce excess negative log-likelihood by 3.3–27.9× versus seven baselines; metadata costs vary.
At six bits, negative log-likelihood is within 0.005 nats of the FP32-state baseline; benefits diminish with less frequent write-backs and depend on model and budget.
papers.selection_reason: Low-bit quantization of recurrent states in hybrid language models reduces memory footprint; directly relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Low-Bit Recurrent States in Hybrid Language Models
papers.tldr: A calibration-free mixed-precision quantizer enables accurate low-bit recurrent states in hybrid language models, with four-bit states substantially reducing quantization error and six-bit states nearly matching FP32 performance.

papers.abstract: We propose a linearized Physics-Informed Neural Network (lPINN), a reduced-order neural basis method for forward and inverse differential equations. In an offline stage, lPINN learns operator-compatible continuous neural basis functions from an ensemble of numerical solutions. The basis functions are differentiable through automatic differentiation and are pretrained using solution data together with either derivative information or physics residuals. For each new problem instance, the basis functions are frozen and the solution is obtained by minimizing the governing-equation residual together with applicable initial, boundary, regularization, and observational terms. Unlike surrogate and operator-learning methods, the training data define the trial space offline, while the instance-specific solution is computed online by enforcing the governing physics. Relative to vanilla PINNs, lPINN pretrains the nonlinear hidden-layer representation offline and performs online inference only in the final linear layer. We evaluate lPINN on forward and inverse problems for the advection-diffusion equation, Burgers' equation, and the nonlinear pendulum equation. Compared with vanilla PINNs, lPINN achieves lower solution and parameter errors while reducing online inference times by approximately one to more than three orders of magnitude, with the largest gains generally observed for limited residual or measurement data. Cross-resolution experiments show that the learned continuous representation can be evaluated on finer meshes without retraining and with nearly unchanged accuracy.
bullets: Targets faster and more data-efficient solution of forward and inverse differential equations than vanilla PINNs.
Learns differentiable, operator-compatible basis functions from ensembles of numerical solutions, derivative data, or physics residuals.
Freezes the nonlinear representation for each new instance; online optimization enforces governing equations and relevant initial, boundary, observational, and regularization terms.
Evaluated on advection-diffusion, Burgers’, and nonlinear pendulum equations.

Compared with vanilla PINNs, reports lower solution and parameter errors and online speedups of roughly one to over three orders of magnitude, especially with limited residual or measurement data; supports finer meshes without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Instance-specific online residual minimization over frozen pretrained layers is a test-time optimization method with substantial inference-speed gains.
papers.title: Linearized PINN with pretrained nonlinear layers
papers.tldr: lPINN pretrains physics-compatible neural basis functions offline, then solves new forward or inverse differential-equation problems online using only a linear output layer and physics constraints.

papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) maintain a fixed-size recurrent state, but reading and writing it at every decoding step can bottleneck hybrid models. This eager state management causes large state I/O with low arithmetic intensity, leaves speculative decoding no cheap rollback, and feeds state quantization error into subsequent recurrent updates. We introduce ReplaySSM, which unrolls the recurrence to represent the state as a checkpoint and a buffer of recent SSM inputs. This separates output computation from checkpoint updates. By updating the checkpoint periodically, ReplaySSM avoids state writes on most steps and roughly halves the dominant state memory traffic. Keeping recent inputs also makes speculative rollback a buffer-pointer operation and enables output-only verification without materializing intermediate states. The same separation allows a low-precision checkpoint to serve output computation on most steps while a higher-precision checkpoint serves recurrent updates, so rounding error in the low-precision copy never enters later updates. We implement ReplaySSM in vLLM for Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet. At serving batch size 256, it accelerates standard decoding by $1.20$--$1.47\times$ over a tuned vLLM baseline across four hybrid models, and delivers about $1.8\times$ the throughput of vLLM's speculative decoding on the two 120B-class models. Separate state precisions also reduce output KL divergence and downstream accuracy losses compared with a shared low-precision checkpoint.
authors: Ze-Wei Liou, Harris Nover, Amey Naik, Andrii Skliar, Igor Shovkun, Ido Shahaf, Tri Dao
bullets: SSM state I/O can bottleneck decoding because each step reads and writes a fixed-size recurrent state.
ReplaySSM represents state with a periodic checkpoint plus a buffer of recent inputs, avoiding most state writes and roughly halving dominant state-memory traffic.
Input buffering makes speculative rollback a pointer operation and supports output-only verification without materializing intermediate states.
Separate low-precision output and high-precision update checkpoints prevent rounding errors from propagating through recurrent updates.
In vLLM implementations for Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet, standard decoding reaches 1.20–1.47× speedup, while speculative decoding reaches about 1.8× throughput on two 120B-class models.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces state memory traffic and improves inference throughput for SSM-based hybrid models, directly targeting memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State
papers.tldr: ReplaySSM accelerates hybrid SSM decoding by caching recent inputs instead of updating recurrent state every step, while enabling cheap speculative rollback and safer state quantization.

papers.abstract: Low-bit inference on accelerators with native 4-bit support requires quantizing both weights and activations to realize the full throughput gains these formats provide. While post-training weight quantization has been extensively studied, activation quantization remains considerably more challenging and typically requires calibration data. In this work, we introduce DUALQUANT, a dual-scale, calibration-free post-training quantization framework that directly minimizes the weight-reconstruction Mean Squared Error (MSE) and, as an immediate by-product, yields per-channel activation rescalings prior to activation quantization. Our key observation is that the scaling factors obtained by minimizing weight-reconstruction error provide effective activation rescalings, enabling competitive activation quantization without calibration data. We formulate DUALQUANT as a non-differentiable weight-reconstruction problem and develop an efficient solver based on variable splitting and block coordinate descent, where each subproblem admits a closed-form update. DUALQUANT provides a unified algorithm supporting a wide range of formats, including the full MX family and NVFP4. To our knowledge, DUALQUANT is the first dual-scaling method to formally support MX and NV block formats. Across Llama and Qwen models evaluated on WikiText-2, C4, and zero-shot downstream tasks, DUALQUANT matches or exceeds the accuracy of calibration-based SmoothQuant across most models and formats, and substantially outperforms calibration-free baselines, with large gains for MX and NV block formats. We validate these gains with a real packed W4A4 inference path for Llama-3.1-8B on an RTX 4090. The resulting implementation closely matches the accuracy of fake quantization while delivering up to 2.61x memory reduction and up to 2.46x throughput speedup over BF16.
authors: Mahsa Salmani, Sayeh Sharify, Hesham Mostafa
bullets: Targets the challenge of activation quantization, which typically requires calibration data to preserve LLM accuracy.
Derives per-channel activation rescalings from weight-reconstruction MSE minimization, avoiding calibration data.
Uses variable splitting and block coordinate descent with closed-form subproblem updates.
