Supports diverse formats, including the full MX family and NVFP4, with reported gains especially for MX and NV block formats.
On Llama-3.1-8B with packed W4A4 inference, achieves up to 2.61× memory reduction and 2.46× throughput speedup versus BF16.
papers.selection_reason: Calibration-free weight-and-activation quantization for LLMs that reduces memory and accelerates inference, fitting the Efficient AI scope.
papers.title: DualQuant: Dual-scale Calibration-free Weight-and-Activation Quantization for LLMs
papers.tldr: DUALQUANT enables calibration-free 4-bit weight-and-activation quantization for LLMs using dual-scale rescaling, achieving competitive accuracy and practical memory and throughput gains.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot's actions together with the observations those actions will produce. However, the strongest models rely on video diffusion transformers that are far too computationally expensive for resource-constrained edge devices. We present SmolWAM, a latent WAM that we derive from the 2B-parameter Cosmos Policy by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding its inference interface: single-frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk's attention sinks, 12 of 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in one rectified-flow step. Trained in 3.6 GPU-hours, SmolWAM succeeds in 95.5% of 400 LIBERO episodes at 57 ms and 2.3 TFLOP per 16-action chunk with 2.4 GiB of GPU memory, 11x faster than its teacher with 18.5x fewer FLOPs and 3.2x less memory, and its world head still forecasts scene motion.
authors: Timi Owolabi, Hikmah Olawore, Frances Adelakun, Ayotomiwa Oyewumi
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of video-diffusion world-action models on resource-constrained edge devices.
Rebuilds a pretrained 2B-parameter model’s inference interface using visual latents, cached text features, 12 transformer blocks, and a single rectified-flow step.
Achieves 95.5% success across 400 LIBERO episodes with 57 ms inference latency and 2.4 GiB of GPU memory.
Runs 11× faster than its teacher while using 18.5× fewer FLOPs and 3.2× less memory.
Its world head retains the ability to forecast scene motion.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient latent world-action model for robotic manipulation; fits VLA, manipulation, interactive world modeling, and edge-device efficiency.
papers.title: SmolWAM: A Latent World-Action Model for Robotic Manipulation on Edge Devices
papers.tldr: SmolWAM compresses a large world-action model into an edge-friendly latent model that rapidly predicts robot actions and future scene observations.

papers.abstract: Efficient attention mechanisms, such as linear and sliding window attention, aim to reduce the computational complexity of Transformers from quadratic to linear. However, their degraded in-context recall often necessitates interleaving full attention layers, leaving the quadratic bottleneck unresolved in long-context processing. To address this, we introduce Orthros attention, which shifts the efficiency paradigm from structural allocation to phase-aware decoupling. As a unified module, it dynamically switches its computation pattern across different phases of sequence processing, enabling linear complexity prefilling and full attention decoding. Our design grants Orthros attention a lower asymptotic complexity compared to vanilla Transformers in prevalent long-context scenarios characterized by heavy prefilling and light decoding. Beyond theoretical formulation and complexity analysis, extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate Orthros's superiority across multiple dimensions. First, we validate its fundamental language modeling capabilities, demonstrating scalability across varying model sizes and strong competitiveness in comprehensive architectural comparisons. Second, Orthros exhibits exceptional conversion feasibility via a data-efficient Transformer-to-Orthros conversion, yielding performance that even surpasses the original Transformer. Finally, Orthros achieves a $21.9\times$ prefilling speedup over Transformers with end-to-end inference gains, while preserving long-context capabilities, as demonstrated by near-perfect 128K needle-in-a-haystack results and Transformer-level performance on real-world in-context recall tasks. Overall, these advantages in high performance, flexibility, and efficiency position Orthros as a promising candidate to succeed the Transformer in industrial applications.
authors: Yuhong Chou, Zehao Liu, Yuqi Pan, Qian Liu, Xianwei Chen, Zhongzhu Zhou, Jibin Wu
bullets: Addresses degraded in-context recall in efficient attention methods that still require costly full-attention layers.
Dynamically switches computation patterns by sequence-processing phase rather than statically mixing attention structures.
Achieves lower asymptotic complexity in long-context workloads dominated by prefilling.
Reports up to 21.9× prefilling speedup with end-to-end inference gains.
Preserves long-context performance, including near-perfect 128K needle-in-a-haystack results and Transformer-level real-world recall.
papers.selection_reason: Phase-aware heterogeneous attention provides linear-complexity prefilling and full-attention decoding, a direct efficient-attention contribution.
papers.title: Orthros: Phase-Aware Heterogeneous Attention for Efficient Transformers
papers.tldr: Orthros is a phase-aware attention mechanism that uses linear-complexity prefilling and full-attention decoding to accelerate long-context Transformers while preserving recall.

papers.abstract: Long-context serving runs out of KV memory before the hardware reaches its useful throughput. HiSparse stores history in host memory and fetches only the selected entries, but it uses one cache budget at every load and does not handle draft-model speculative decoding such as DSpark and DFlash2. We present Adaptive DHiSparse, which supports speculative decoding over hierarchical sparse KV and adapts residency to load. It protects the required working set, retains additional history while GPU memory is spare, and recovers the rest through exact fused retrieval. DSpark and DFlash2 keep their proposal and acceptance rules: queries share missing-row retrieval, draft KV uses a window-bounded ring, and verification staging is reused across layer groups. At 100K context and concurrency 128, GLM-5.3 with DFlash2 delivers 793 output tokens/s per decode GPU, 1.45$\times$ HiSparse and 1.27$\times$ non-speculative adaptive serving. Held to the same latency bounds as HiSparse, it sustains up to 4$\times$ the concurrency and 2.3 to 3.7$\times$ the output, depending on the per-token bound. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 500K context and concurrency 512, Adaptive DHiSparse with DSpark delivers 1.85$\times$ the output of resident serving with DSpark. In a load step, optional residency reduces host fetches from 14.2% to 1.4% of selected rows at low load and releases memory under pressure.
bullets: Addresses KV-memory exhaustion and fixed cache budgets in long-context serving, including compatibility with DSpark and DFlash2.
Protects the required working set, uses spare GPU memory for extra history, and exactly retrieves missing entries from host memory under pressure.
Reuses speculative-decoding mechanisms such as shared missing-row retrieval, window-bounded draft-KV caching, and verification staging across layers.

At 100K context and concurrency 128, achieves 793 output tokens/s per GPU with GLM-5.3 and DFlash2; the abstract reports higher throughput and concurrency than HiSparse and non-speculative adaptive serving.
At low load, optional residency reduces host fetches from 14.2% to 1.4% of selected rows, while memory is released as load increases.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes load-adaptive hierarchical KV cache management with speculative decoding for long-context LLM serving, directly fitting efficiency and long-context topics.
papers.title: Adaptive DHiSparse: Speculative Decoding over a Load-Adaptive KV Hierarchy
papers.tldr: Adaptive DHiSparse combines load-adaptive hierarchical sparse KV caching with speculative decoding to improve long-context serving throughput while preserving latency bounds.

papers.abstract: Linearizing softmax attention offers a route to efficient Transformer inference, but preserving pretrained attention remains challenging. We identify an important source of approximation error overlooked by standard linearization methods: a small number of outlier dimensions contribute disproportionately to query-key dot products and account for a large fraction of the approximation error. Motivated by this heterogeneity, we propose Outlier-Aware Attention Linearization (OAL), a dimension-aware method for constructing quadratic attention approximations. Starting from a second-order Taylor approximation, we introduce a Hadamard-product formulation that makes individual query-key contributions explicit. This formulation relaxes globally shared coefficients to support dimension-specific linear terms and cross-dimensional quadratic interactions while preserving separable evaluation. To retain this flexibility with fewer parameters, OAL groups dimensions with similar contribution scales to share coefficients, while allowing distinct treatment of the few outliers. The resulting positive quadratic kernel is calibrated against pretrained attention outputs and admits linear-time evaluation with respect to sequence length for fixed head dimensions. On Qwen2.5-0.5B, OAL reduces frozen-attention output relative MSE by approximately 8.9% compared with DiJiang. Replacing middle-layer attention modules and jointly fine-tuning the kernel coefficients with LoRA further lowers WikiText-103 perplexity from 31.71 to 27.50 compared with a learned global quadratic, while improving accuracy on PIQA, HellaSwag, and ARC-E. These results demonstrate the value of outlier-aware dimension grouping for both attention approximation and pretrained-model conversion. The code is available at https://github.com/wuqianyue09/OAL
authors: Weiqi Sun, Qianyue Wu, Wenjia Wang, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Standard attention linearization can incur large errors because outlier dimensions disproportionately affect query–key dot products.
OAL uses a second-order, Hadamard-product formulation with dimension-specific linear and cross-dimensional quadratic terms.
Dimensions with similar contribution scales share coefficients, while outlier dimensions receive distinct treatment, preserving separable and sequence-length-linear evaluation.
On Qwen2.5-0.5B, OAL reduces frozen-attention output relative MSE by approximately 8.9% versus DiJiang.
With LoRA fine-tuning, OAL lowers WikiText-103 perplexity from 31.71 to 27.50 versus a learned global quadratic and improves PIQA, HellaSwag, and ARC-E accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Outlier-aware attention linearization with grouped quadratic kernels directly targets efficient attention for Transformer inference.
papers.title: Not All Dimensions Are Equal: Outlier-Aware Attention Linearization with Grouped Quadratic Kernels
papers.tldr: OAL improves linearized softmax attention by treating a few influential dimensions separately and grouping the rest by contribution scale.

papers.abstract: Dynamic vocabularies built on-the-fly via Lempel-Ziv-Welch (LZW) compression let a language model represent the same text in fewer tokens, but prior work shows that this efficiency comes at a cost to reasoning and perplexity. We show that this quality gap is not a fundamental price of compression but can be substantially closed through targeted improvements to the compression layer and LZW codec, without modifying the underlying pretrained language model. Our analysis reveals four key issues: (1) LZW's compression algorithm creates an implicit conflict between the input embedding and the output embedding, a tension that a single shared embedding cannot resolve; (2) naively applying RoPE to LZW-compressed sequences ignores that merged tokens can span multiple tokens; (3) merging certain tokens (notably digits) disproportionately hurts downstream accuracy; and (4) dynamic vocabularies introduce an inherent segmentation ambiguity that confounds standard evaluation. We address these through decoupled input/output dynamic embedding layer, size-aware RoPE positioning, and a modified LZW codec supporting selective merges and multi-view segmentations. Across four models, our recipe improves perplexity on every corpus we evaluated as well as mathematical reasoning accuracy, closing roughly half the quality gap between zip2zip and the uncompressed baseline at a similar compression ratio on general text. This represents a significant step toward lossless adaptive-vocabulary compression for language models.
authors: Saibo Geng, Andrea Gentilini, Xinxian Ma, Nathan Ranchin, Yunzhen Yao, Robert West
bullets: Identifies four issues: shared input/output embeddings, RoPE misalignment for merged tokens, harmful digit merging, and segmentation ambiguity.
Uses decoupled input/output dynamic embeddings, size-aware RoPE, selective token merges, and multi-view segmentations.
Improves perplexity across all evaluated corpora and improves mathematical reasoning accuracy across four models.
Closes roughly half the quality gap between compressed zip2zip and the uncompressed baseline at a similar general-text compression ratio.
Targets adaptive-vocabulary compression while preserving the underlying model.
papers.selection_reason: Inference-time token compression via dynamic LZW vocabularies and token merging directly targets token-level efficiency.
papers.title: zip2zip++: Towards Inference-Time Token Compression with Minimal Quality Loss
papers.tldr: zip2zip++ reduces the quality loss of inference-time LZW token compression through targeted embedding, positional, codec, and evaluation improvements—without changing the pretrained language model.

papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) achieve strong performance on speech-text tasks, but standard audio encoders produce hundreds of tokens for even short audio clips. Because self-attention scales quadratically in sequence length, this inflates inference-time compute substantially. Current training-free token compression methods prune or merge tokens based solely on coarse attention or feature similarity. However, treating audio tokens as generic, isotropic features smooths over spectral transitions, destroying fine-grained phonetic transitions essential for decoding speech. In contrast, speech signals exhibit highly structured temporal patterns where information density peaks at acoustic transitions. We propose AudioTETRIS, a training-free, two-stage framework that uses the audio encoder's representation geometry as an acoustic prior for token importance before applying attention-based compression. Instead of discarding encoder structure after the encoding stage, AudioTETRIS propagates this prior directly into the LLM decoder to compute a per-token fused score. This score drives progressive top-$k$ token selection across decoder layers without requiring additional training or auxiliary models. Evaluated on Qwen2-Audio-7B, Phi-4-Multimodal, and Audio Flamingo 3, AudioTETRIS retains near-uncompressed performance on several speech tasks using only 25% of audio tokens, matches or surpasses full-token accuracy at moderate compression rates, and consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines.
authors: Shreya Sajid, Anna Vettoruzzo, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Targets the high inference cost caused by hundreds of audio tokens and quadratic self-attention.
Uses encoder representation geometry to identify transition-rich, information-dense tokens.
Fuses acoustic-prior and decoder attention signals into per-token importance scores.
Progressively selects top-k tokens across decoder layers without training or auxiliary models.
Evaluated on three audio LLMs, it retains near-uncompressed speech-task performance and outperforms training-free baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free token elimination for audio LLMs using acoustic transition priors; fits token pruning and multimodal LLM efficiency.
papers.title: AudioTETRIS: Token Elimination via Transitional Importance Signals for Efficient Audio LLMs
papers.tldr: AudioTETRIS efficiently compresses audio tokens by preserving acoustically important transitions, maintaining near-full performance with only 25% of tokens.

papers.abstract: We present Rationally Linearized Multilayer Perceptrons(RaLiMPs), a new approach to efficiently linearizing MLPs using low-degree rational approximations of standard activation functions. Inspired by polynomial-based MLP linearization, we show that rational approximations can provide accurate representations at substantially lower degree. RaLiMPs exploit these approximations to construct kernel representations with narrow bottlenecks, enabling efficient composition across MLP layers. We provide theoretical guarantees for the resulting approximation and evaluate RaLiMPs across applications ranging from implicit 3D models to large language models. Our experiments demonstrate favorable accuracy--efficiency tradeoffs, with RaLiMPs achieving competitive or improved accuracy while substantially reducing inference cost.
authors: Arijit Sehanobish, Byeongchan Kim, Avinava Dubey, Min-hwan Oh, Krzysztof Choromanski
bullets: Uses rational approximations of standard activations instead of higher-degree polynomial approximations.
Constructs narrow-bottleneck kernel representations for efficient composition across MLP layers.
Provides theoretical guarantees for the resulting approximation.
Evaluates applications including implicit 3D models and large language models.
Reports favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs, including competitive or improved accuracy with substantially lower inference cost.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient MLP linearization via rational approximations reduces inference cost, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Rationally Linearized MLPs
papers.tldr: RaLiMPs efficiently linearize MLPs using low-degree rational activation approximations, reducing inference cost while maintaining competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Speech recognition on low-cost microcontrollers is, in practice, limited to keyword spotting or a fixed list of commands. We present O\'ido, an inference engine that runs open-vocabulary English speech recognition entirely on an ESP32-S3 (240 MHz dual-core Xtensa LX7, 512 KB of SRAM, 8 MB of PSRAM, 16 MB of flash, no neural accelerator). O\'ido executes a 13M-parameter Conformer-CTC model with int8 weights, per-frame dynamic int8 activations and int8 attention on the chip's SIMD instructions, with a schedule designed around flash and PSRAM bandwidth. On LibriSpeech test-clean/test-other the on-device arithmetic reaches 3.70%/8.23% word error rate (WER), within 0.12 points of full precision, and 3.33%/7.15% with an on-chip 1.3M-parameter language model; a transducer head gives 2.99%/6.67% and an int4 variant fits in 8.3 MB. This is 2.3-2.8x fewer errors than the vendor's recognizer on the same chip, and fewer than Whisper tiny.en and Moonshine tiny in full precision on a laptop, including in real noise and reverberation. Measured on a physical board, the firmware runs at 1.97x the duration of the audio on one core, with transcripts identical to an instruction-exact emulator: accurate, but not yet real time (a 4 s command is transcribed about 8.7 s after it ends). The two-core schedule gives wrong results on silicon and is disabled. A streaming variant shows partial text while the speaker talks and delivers the final text 4.1-11.1 s after clips of 3.6-10.6 s (7.2-22.4 s in utterance mode) at 4.86%/11.03% WER; a Spanish model makes 34-60% fewer errors than multilingual Whisper tiny. Code and models are released.
authors: Daniel Varela S\'anchez, Guillermo Mart\'in-Coello Ju\'arez
bullets: Addresses the limitations of low-cost microcontrollers, which typically support only keyword spotting or fixed commands.
Runs a 13M-parameter Conformer-CTC model using int8 quantization, SIMD-optimized attention, and flash/PSRAM-aware scheduling.
Achieves 3.70%/8.23% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean/test-other, with improved results from language-model and transducer variants.
On a physical board, runs at 1.97× audio duration on one core; streaming provides partial transcripts but still has multi-second latency.
Code and models are released; the two-core schedule is disabled because it produces incorrect results on silicon.
papers.selection_reason: On-device ASR with int8/int4 memory-efficient inference; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: O\'ido: Open-Vocabulary Speech Recognition on a $5 Microcontroller without a Neural Accelerator
papers.tldr: O’ido brings open-vocabulary English speech recognition to a $5 ESP32-S3 microcontroller without a neural accelerator, achieving strong accuracy but not yet real-time performance.

papers.abstract: Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) is a theoretically sound algorithm for nonparametric learning, which is also often used to investigate properties of deep learning. However, the exact KRR formulation incurs time and memory costs preventing applicability to large datasets, motivating the development of approximate solvers. These algorithms rely on (i) iterative methods, to avoid the computational burden of direct solutions; (ii) sketching or batching, to reduce the problem size; and (iii) preconditioning, to accelerate convergence. While crucial for fast convergence, preconditioning incurs memory costs that can be managed by lowering the number of free parameters of the model, potentially at the expense of expressivity and hence accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose BLOKS, a Conjugate Gradient-based solver for Nystr\"om-sketched KRR built around a novel preconditioner that combines a block Jacobi approximation with sketching. The BLOKS preconditioner has memory cost independent of both the dataset size and the number of parameters, allowing scaling to large models. We provide a memory-efficient, GPU-accelerated implementation and show that BLOKS achieves excellent accuracy while retaining favorable time/memory complexity. Indeed, on standard large-scale datasets used to benchmark kernel solvers, BLOKS achieves comparable or better performances than state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Giordano Vitale, Giacomo Meanti, Marco Rando, Blanca Ayuso de Dios, Lorenzo Rosasco
bullets: Targets the time and memory barriers of exact kernel ridge regression on large datasets.
Uses a Conjugate Gradient solver for Nyström-sketched KRR with a block-Jacobi preconditioner augmented by sketching.
The preconditioner’s memory cost is independent of both dataset size and model parameter count.
Provides a memory-efficient, GPU-accelerated implementation.
Reports excellent accuracy and comparable or better performance than state-of-the-art kernel solvers on standard large-scale benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes BLOKS, a memory-efficient GPU-accelerated solver for Kernel Ridge Regression using sketched block preconditioning, addressing computational efficiency in nonparametric learning.
papers.title: BLOKS: Scaling Kernel Solvers with Sketched Block Preconditioning
papers.tldr: BLOKS scales Nyström-sketched kernel ridge regression by combining conjugate gradients with a memory-efficient sketched block-Jacobi preconditioner.

papers.abstract: Mamba-3 introduces input-dependent rotations into recurrent state updates, but their contribution beyond state retention remains unclear. We interpret these ro- tations as underdamped second-order dynamics, providing a framework for in- vestigating the role of oscillation in sequence modeling. Controlled comparisons show that underdamped dynamics outperform non-oscillatory damping regimes on state-tracking tasks, while language-model pretraining demonstrates benefits for long-context prediction and length generalization. Interventions in pretrained models further establish the importance of learned phase, and state analysis sug- gests that rotation regulates how retained information combines with incoming up- dates. Taken together, these findings identify underdamped dynamics as a useful mechanism for recurrent computation and suggest that oscillation supports long- context processing by regulating how information accumulates.
bullets: Reframes Mamba-3 rotations as second-order underdamped dynamics rather than simple state retention.
Controlled comparisons find underdamped dynamics outperform non-oscillatory damping on state-tracking tasks.
Language-model pretraining shows benefits for long-context prediction and length generalization.
Interventions indicate that learned phase is important, while state analysis suggests rotation regulates how retained and incoming information combine.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes Mamba-3, a state-space model architecture for LLMs, focusing on its oscillatory dynamics and efficiency compared to standard recurrent models.
papers.title: Understanding Mamba-3 Through Oscillatory Dynamics
papers.tldr: Mamba-3’s input-dependent rotations act as underdamped oscillations that improve state tracking and support long-context sequence modeling.

papers.abstract: Serving a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model pays for expert precision twice: the resident footprint pays for every expert the router can reach, while each batch-one decode step pays only for the experts it selects. These are two different rate functionals over the same per-expert widths, yet published per-expert MoE allocators constrain only the first. We call the difference the store-read gap; in the released BitsMoE checkpoint, 2.54 bits per weight (bpw) of storage become 7.50 bpw of decode traffic. We propose DuoRate, which stores once and reads per workload. Offline, it stores one uniform tier of a prefix-readable weight stream and bakes a distortion tensor. Online, it profiles a workload's own prefill without labels and solves a Lagrangian rate-distortion allocation under the decode functional; routing frequency provably cancels from every per-expert decision, and the solve costs one dot product per expert and a bisection. A deployment therefore keeps a single artifact that prefill reads at the stored rate and decode reads at the workload's own rate. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, DuoRate reading 2.3 bpw exceeds every 2-bit-class baseline by 6.3 to 47.0 points of average accuracy, and at 2.9 bpw it matches 4-bit formats that read 1.4-1.6 bpw more. The advantage is largest under long decoding: on GSM8K, DuoRate at 2.9 bpw matches or exceeds every 4-bit format and trails BF16 by only 0.25 points, and at 2.6 bpw it still matches or exceeds the 4.5-bit NF4 and FP4. Against controls in its own format, the allocation alone is worth 0.07-0.11 bpw of read rate. Code will be released upon publication.
authors: Mengqi Guo, Zhe Wei, Yuan Yuan, Jiunn Bin Lim, Boyi Pan, Michael Bi Mi
bullets: MoE serving has separate storage and decode-rate costs, but prior allocators optimize only storage.
DuoRate stores one uniform, prefix-readable artifact and uses workload-specific, label-free profiling to allocate decode precision online.
Its optimization reduces to one dot product per expert plus bisection; routing frequency cancels from individual expert decisions.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it outperforms 2-bit-class baselines at 2.3 bpw and approaches 4-bit-format accuracy at 2.9 bpw.
Benefits are strongest for long decoding; on GSM8K, 2.9 bpw trails BF16 by only 0.25 points and remains competitive at 2.6 bpw.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes DuoRate, a two-rate precision allocation strategy for Mixture-of-Experts serving, optimizing memory and compute efficiency for large language models.
papers.title: DuoRate: Two-Rate Per-Expert Precision Allocation for Mixture-of-Experts Serving
papers.tldr: DuoRate allocates per-expert precision for both storage and workload-specific decode traffic, substantially improving MoE accuracy at low read rates.

papers.abstract: Agentic workloads resend long contexts that barely change between calls. Prefix caching now skips most of their prefill, yet every request must still be tokenized in full before the cache can even be consulted. Tokenization, a CPU stage long treated as negligible, becomes the largest part of time-to-first-token (TTFT), and a frontend that tokenizes for a whole GPU fleet limits how many GPUs it can feed. We present GraphTok, a GPU tokenizer that runs the entire encoding pipeline, from pre-tokenization through byte-pair encoding (BPE) merging to token-ID assembly, as one replayable CUDA graph. GraphTok reproduces the reference token IDs bit-for-bit on GPT-2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, DeepSeek-V3, and Gemma 3, hands short inputs to a CPU engine where the GPU cannot win, and plugs into unmodified vLLM and NVIDIA Dynamo. GraphTok encodes one million GPT-2 tokens in 1.7-3.2 ms including data transfers, and on Llama 3 it is 4.7-6.0x faster than gigatoken, the strongest CPU tokenizer. On TokTier's own single-request benchmark, it is 2.6-3.9x faster than gigatoken and up to 18.1x faster than TokTier. In vLLM with a cached prefix, it lowers mean TTFT by 2.1-2.4x. The largest gain is capacity. Within a 2 s P99 target, one Dynamo frontend with GraphTok sustains 518 requests/s of 121k-token traffic, the busiest-hour load of 56 GPUs, against 296 with gigatoken and 18.5 with the default tokenizer. Across 121k to one million tokens, this is 1.75-2.5x the load gigatoken sustains, with a P99 up to 64x lower where gigatoken's tail breaks.
authors: Mohammad Siavashi, Pascal Schwinte, Ali Banaei, Gerald Q. Maguire Jr., Marco Chiesa, Dejan Kosti\'c
bullets: Agentic requests resend mostly unchanged long contexts, but full CPU tokenization occurs before prefix-cache lookup and becomes a major TTFT bottleneck.
GraphTok performs pre-tokenization, BPE merging, and token-ID assembly on GPUs, while routing short inputs to CPU when more efficient.
It reproduces reference token IDs bit-for-bit across GPT-2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, DeepSeek-V3, and Gemma 3, and integrates with unmodified vLLM and NVIDIA Dynamo.
It reduces cached-prefix mean TTFT by 2.1–2.4× in vLLM and sustains substantially higher frontend load under a 2-second P99 target.
The approach targets long-input, high-throughput serving; short inputs may remain on the CPU path.
papers.selection_reason: GPU tokenizer reduces TTFT and increases LLM serving capacity, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Taking Tokenization off the Host for Agentic LLM Serving
papers.tldr: GraphTok moves full tokenization from CPU to a replayable CUDA graph, substantially reducing TTFT and increasing the request capacity of agentic LLM serving.

papers.abstract: Partial differential equation (PDE) surrogate modeling often relies on either dense observations or access to governing equations/physics constraints. In practice, observations can be sparse and partial, and the underlying physics may be partially specified or unavailable. We introduce SBNO, an equation-free paired-data diffusion bridge matching framework that learns conditional operators for both forward and inverse PDE problems under partial observations. SBNO uses diffusion Schr\"odinger bridge matching to learn a pair of time-dependent drifts from a mask-aware endpoint coupling that preserves empirical input-solution pairing during training and supports both PDE-task directions within a single framework. At inference time, SBNO produces a deterministic point reconstruction by integrating the probability-flow ODE constructed from the learned drift pair, without inference-time observation or PDE guidance-weight tuning. On five PDE benchmarks with 5% observations, SBNO achieves superior or comparable accuracy to baselines while demonstrating lower test-instance error dispersion. Furthermore, SBNO is at least $9.7 \times$ faster and reduces GPU memory by at least $4.3 \times$ compared to guided-diffusion baselines.
authors: Jaehyeon Park, Inhyeok Jeong, Noseong Park
bullets: Addresses PDE modeling when observations are sparse and governing equations are partially specified or unavailable.
Learns conditional forward and inverse operators using mask-aware diffusion Schrödinger bridge matching and paired input–solution data.
Generates deterministic reconstructions by integrating a probability-flow ODE from the learned drift pair.
Across five PDE benchmarks, achieves comparable or better accuracy than baselines with lower test-instance error dispersion.
Compared with guided-diffusion baselines, is at least 9.7× faster and uses at least 4.3× less GPU memory.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a Schrödinger Bridge Neural Operator for PDE forward/inverse problems, which models environment dynamics and offers significant speed/memory efficiency improvements.
papers.title: SBNO : Schr\"odinger Bridge Neural Operator for the Forward and Inverse Problems under Missing Information
papers.tldr: SBNO is an equation-free Schrödinger bridge neural operator that solves forward and inverse PDE surrogate tasks from only 5% observations without inference-time physics or guidance tuning.

papers.abstract: The escalating environmental footprint of the Information and Communication Technol- ogy (ICT) sectorwith global Data Center electric- ity usage potentially reaching 3% by 2030 and the imperative for real-time responsiveness in smart buildings demand a foundational shift towards Edge Computing. This article proposes a holis- tic architectural and algorithmic approach for cre- ating autonomous, resilient, and privacy-preserving learning systems within smart buildings, advancing the core concept of the building itself as the data center. Our contributions, demonstrating originality compared to conventional centralized systems, are structured around three main pillars: 1) Validation of resilient data acquisition chains using the af- fordable Arduino ecosystem (Uno R4 WiFi/BME280) and secure persistence solutions including centralized archiving (Node-RED/MySQL) and secure remote transfer (Python/rsync/SSH). 2). The proposal of a lightweight, KOptim orchestration framework, inter- operable with the FIWARE standard, for the dynamic management of Service Level Agreements (SLA). 3) The adaptation and experimental valida- tion of the Generalized Hebbian Algorithm (GHA) for Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on low- power microcontrollers,We introduce and compare an iterative learning strategy using data buffers, featuring sorting and explicit preservation of extreme samples to maintain diversity. Experimental results on the high-dimensional Tour Perret sensor data confirm that this novel method, despite introducing a necessary temporal complexity of O(W log W ) due to sorting, achieves convergence and final result quality that is visually equivalent to processing the entire dataset in full memory, reliably identifying two distinct operational states.
bullets: Addresses ICT energy use and the need for real-time smart-building responsiveness by treating the building as a local data center.
Uses Arduino-based sensing with centralized and secure remote data persistence.
Introduces KOptim, a lightweight FIWARE-interoperable framework for dynamic SLA management.
Adapts Generalized Hebbian Algorithm PCA to low-power microcontrollers using buffered, sorted data while preserving extreme samples.
On Tour Perret sensor data, the method identifies two operational states with quality visually equivalent to full-memory processing, at added O(W log W) temporal complexity.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses algorithmic adaptation and memory constraints in edge computing systems for smart buildings, relevant to efficient AI and adaptation strategies.
papers.title: Sustainable Cloud-Fog-Edge Systems for Smart Buildings: Algorithmic Adaptation under Memory Constraints and Dynamic Orchestration Strategies
papers.tldr: A smart-building cloud–fog–edge architecture combines resilient sensing, dynamic SLA orchestration, and memory-efficient PCA learning for autonomous and privacy-preserving operation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit complementary capabilities, yet selecting the most suitable expert for a given image-question query remains challenging due to heterogeneous multimodal inputs and varying expert strengths. Existing routing approaches rely on text-based cues or static model profiles, failing to capture fine-grained visual evidence and expert-specific failure patterns. To address this, we propose MHR-Router, a multimodal heterogeneous retrieval-enhanced adaptive routing framework for VLM inference. It accurately dispatches each multimodal query to the most suitable VLM expert via local retrieval evidence. MHR-Router consists of two stages: (1) Multimodal Routing Representation, which fuses frozen multimodal features into a comprehensive query representation; and (2) Heterogeneous Retrieval-Enhanced Adaptive Routing, which retrieves expert-specific success and failure memories as local evidence and employs a shared scorer to adaptively select the optimal expert. Experiments show that MHR-Router effectively achieves heterogeneous modality routing and consistently improves accuracy over traditional baselines.
authors: Wenjuan Zhu, Zheming Yang, Yunqing Hu, Qi Guo
bullets: Addresses the challenge of selecting among VLM experts with complementary strengths and heterogeneous failure patterns.
Fuses frozen multimodal features into a comprehensive representation of each query.
Retrieves expert-specific success and failure memories as local routing evidence.
Uses a shared scorer to select the expert best suited to the query.
Experiments report consistent accuracy improvements over traditional routing baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Retrieval-enhanced adaptive routing for VLM inference improves efficiency and multimodal expert selection.
papers.title: MHR-Router: Multimodal Heterogeneous Retrieval-Enhanced Adaptive Routing for VLM Inference
papers.tldr: MHR-Router adaptively routes each image-question query to the most suitable VLM expert using multimodal representations and expert-specific success/failure memories.

papers.abstract: Set-based language model routing aims to increase the coverage of the event where at least one model answers a query correctly while controlling the number of inference calls made. Existing risk-controlled routing policies bound the all-miss risk (the probability that every model in the selected set fails) by calibrating a single conformal threshold and applying it to a nested family of model sets. Because each model is scored in isolation, these policies ignore the dependence structure of model failures. Models that share training data or architecture tend to fail on the same queries, so two individually strong models can be jointly redundant while a weaker but complementary model covers the queries that the others miss. To account for this dependence, which existing risk-controlled policies ignore, we propose CopRoute, which orders models by how many new queries each one answers correctly beyond those already selected, decides per query how far down that order to go, and then picks the smallest cutoff that still meets the target risk. We show that CopRoute's ordering attains, on the design data, the best guarantee any efficient fixed-ordering algorithm can give for the average number of calls to the first correct model, and that a separate calibration step certifies the all-miss risk of the deployed sets. On RouterBench and RouterEval, CopRoute attains the fewest certified calls on nine of ten datasets at a target risk of 0.05 and on eight of ten at 0.10, making up to 79 percent fewer calls (median 24 percent) than the state-of-the-art risk-controlled policy at the same certified all-miss risk.
authors: Siva Rajesh Kasa, Santhosh Kumar Kasa, Karan Gupta
bullets: Existing routing methods score models independently and overlook correlated failures, causing redundant model selections.
CopRoute orders models by their incremental correctness on design data, then selects the smallest per-query prefix meeting the target all-miss risk.
A separate conformal calibration step certifies the probability that all selected models fail.
On RouterBench and RouterEval, it achieves the fewest certified calls on 9/10 datasets at risk 0.05 and 8/10 at risk 0.10.
It reduces calls by up to 79%—24% at the median—relative to the compared risk-controlled policy at the same certified risk.
papers.selection_reason: Dependence-aware conformal routing reduces LLM inference calls while controlling risk; an efficiency method.
papers.title: CopRoute: Dependence-Aware Conformal Routing for Language Models
papers.tldr: CopRoute improves risk-controlled language-model routing by exploiting complementary failure patterns to reduce inference calls while preserving certified coverage.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose Data-Adaptive Mahalanobis Cross-Head Attention (DAMCHA), a simple and effective attention mechanism that generalizes Multi-Head Attention (MHA) through the lens of metric learning. Standard MHA implicitly learns a static, head-wise Euclidean similarity corresponding to the diagonal blocks of a unified cross-head metric matrix, discarding all off-diagonal interactions across heads. DAMCHA addresses this limitation via two key innovations. First, it learns the full cross-head metric matrix, inducing a Mahalanobis-like similarity that explicitly captures inter-head interactions beyond the restricted block-diagonal structure of MHA. Second, it parameterizes the metric matrix as an input-dependent function, enabling the attention geometry to dynamically adapt to the intrinsic manifold structure of the data rather than remaining fixed after training. We further introduce principled regularization strategies, most notably stack-wise parameter sharing, to ensure computational efficiency and stable optimization. DAMCHA serves as a drop-in replacement for MHA and its variants in various Transformer architectures, delivering superior expressive power and learning performance with comparable or reduced computational overhead. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DAMCHA-based Transformers consistently outperform competing baselines across a range of benchmark tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/erwinmsmith/DAMCHA.
authors: Zhenke Duan, Xin Li, Jiqun Pan, Dong Xiaofei, Hanwen Ning, Xinyuan Song
bullets: Generalizes multi-head attention by learning a full cross-head metric instead of a block-diagonal, head-wise Euclidean metric.
Makes the metric input-dependent so attention geometry can adapt to the data’s intrinsic structure.
Uses regularization, including stack-wise parameter sharing, to support stable optimization and computational efficiency.
Acts as a drop-in replacement for MHA and its variants across Transformer architectures.
Experiments report consistent improvements over competing baselines on benchmark tasks with comparable or lower computational overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Data-adaptive attention mechanism with reduced overhead and parameter sharing; relevant to efficient attention.
papers.title: Data-Adaptive Mahalanobis Metric Learning for Cross-Head Attention in Transformers
papers.tldr: DAMCHA extends Transformer attention with an input-adaptive Mahalanobis metric that models interactions across attention heads for more expressive and efficient representations.

papers.abstract: In-context-learning Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) are uniquely suited to scenarios with limited resources or privacy constraints, as they solve new tasks without additional training. However, their architecture consists of multiple transformer blocks, resulting in high computational and memory footprints. Meanwhile, traditional alternatives like Gradient-Boosted Decision Trees (GBDTs) remain highly competitive and run efficiently on CPUs, suggesting that tabular tasks may not inherently require deep architectures. This contrast raises a fundamental question: can TFMs be simplified by removing architectural redundancies without sacrificing performance? To answer this, we introduce a closed-form, label-free affine translator that replaces a contiguous window of up to 96% of the blocks, leaving the rest unchanged. Evaluating eight frontier TFMs on 171 classification datasets, we reveal that tabular transformers are vastly overparameterized: replacing half of a model's blocks costs at most $0.002$ median AUROC across all architectures, with the half-depth TabFM still outperforming every other full-depth TFMs and tuned GBDTs. Furthermore, different model families are overparameterized in different ways: TabPFN-3 relies on its encoders, maintaining performance regardless of which single block is retained. Other single-axis models spread computation thinly, needing only their first block, while dual-axis models concentrate it in one critical block. Ultimately, removing depth saves up to 1.5B parameters, speeds up GPU inference by up to $6\times$ at a median cost of $0.03$ AUROC, while a single-block TabPFN-3 serves cached queries $2.4\times$ faster using $6\times$ less memory at negligible cost.
bullets: The work addresses the high resource demands of deep in-context-learning tabular transformers.
A label-free, closed-form affine translator replaces up to 96% of contiguous transformer blocks without retraining.
Across eight TFMs and 171 classification datasets, removing half the blocks costs at most 0.002 median AUROC.
Shallower models can save up to 1.5B parameters and provide up to 6× faster GPU inference, with a median 0.03 AUROC cost.
Different model families concentrate useful computation differently, so the best retained blocks vary by architecture.
papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that tabular foundation models are overparameterized and can be made substantially more efficient by removing blocks, directly fitting Efficient AI.
papers.title: Tabular Foundation Models Are Effectively Shallow
papers.tldr: Tabular foundation models can be made dramatically shallower with little performance loss, reducing their computational and memory costs.

papers.abstract: Time-series foundation models use the same network depth for every input, although forecasting windows differ in structure and difficulty. We test whether whole Transformer blocks can be removed at inference time in two pretrained models: Chronos-Bolt and TimesFM 2.5. Our bypasses avoid the original block computation and preserve the dense model exactly when all blocks are enabled. Masks are selected only on calibration windows and evaluated on 1,088 held-out windows from ETTh1, Traffic, Weather, and Exchange. At moderate sparsity, Chronos-Bolt with 7/11 candidate blocks and TimesFM with 16/20 blocks show little change in mean relative forecasting quality across datasets while reducing median A100 batch-1 latency by 11.2% and 13.4%. More aggressive TimesFM skipping accelerates inference further but substantially harms Traffic and Weather. Across both models, different equal-budget masks win on different windows, and a retrospective oracle significantly improves over the best static mask on every dataset. However, dataset-specific masks transfer inconsistently, and Chronos representations do not support reliable unseen-domain routing. These results establish cross-architecture structured redundancy and input-dependent opportunity, but not a deployable dynamic inference method.
bullets: Evaluates structured whole-block skipping in Chronos-Bolt and TimesFM 2.5 using calibration-selected masks and 1,088 held-out windows across four datasets.
Moderate sparsity reduces median A100 batch-1 latency by 11.2% for Chronos-Bolt and 13.4% for TimesFM with little change in mean relative forecasting quality.
More aggressive skipping can accelerate TimesFM further but substantially degrades performance on Traffic and Weather.
Different masks are best for different windows; a retrospective oracle outperforms the best static mask on every dataset.
Dataset-specific masks transfer inconsistently, and Chronos representations do not enable reliable unseen-domain routing.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates structured block skipping in time-series foundation models to reduce inference latency. A technical contribution to Efficient AI methods.
papers.title: How Much Computation Does Every Forecast Need? Structured Block Skipping in Two Time-Series Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Pretrained time-series foundation models can skip some Transformer blocks to reduce latency with little average quality loss, but reliable input-adaptive routing remains unsolved.

papers.abstract: Fast rollout generation for long-context reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) requires reducing KV-cache traffic without changing the response groups used for policy optimization. In our profiled RLVR workloads, attention accounts for 72--76\% of autoregressive decoding kernel time. Sparse attention reduces these reads, but sampling directly from a sparse policy changes the response groups used for learning. For group-relative optimization, we show that even exact response-wise reweighting does not generally recover the expected dense-policy update because the advantage of each response depends on the rewards of other group members. We propose Self-Sparse Speculative Rollouts (S$^3$R). It uses sparse attention to propose tokens, then generates responses through full-attention verification and exact speculative sampling. Drafting and verification share the same policy parameter, eliminating the need to train or update a separate drafter. The resulting response groups follow the dense-policy distribution. Under S$^3$R, we characterize speedup conditions and the costs of drafting and verification. We found that dense verification still requires the complete historical KV cache. A KV-aware scheduler therefore limits KV-cache repeated offloading and restoration while maintaining rollout parallelism. % OR thrashing In a matched ablation with an aggressive sparse drafting budget, S$^3$R maintains stable training while direct sparse sampling with training-side correction becomes unstable. On long-context mathematical reasoning, S$^3$R achieves $1.39\times~1.35\times$ the end-to-end training throughput of autoregressive rollouts on Qwen3 model, with comparable task performance.
authors: Yuhang He, Hongyu Ge, Zihan Lin, Siyi Liu, Yongqi Zhang
bullets: Direct sparse sampling can bias group-relative policy updates because each response’s advantage depends on other group members’ rewards.
S$^3$R uses the same policy for sparse drafting and full-attention verification, avoiding a separately trained drafter.
A KV-aware scheduler reduces repeated KV-cache offloading and restoration while preserving rollout parallelism.
Aggressive sparse drafting remained stable in training, unlike direct sparse sampling with training-side correction.
On long-context mathematical reasoning, it reports 1.35–1.39× end-to-end training throughput with comparable task performance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Self-Sparse Speculative Rollouts (S$^3$R) to reduce KV-cache traffic in RL rollouts using sparse attention and verification. A strong technical contribution to Efficient AI.
papers.title: S$^3$R: Fast and Faithful RL Rollouts via Self-Sparse Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: S$^3$R accelerates long-context RLVR rollouts by using sparse attention for proposals and exact full-attention speculative verification, preserving dense-policy response distributions and training quality.

papers.abstract: Power sampling improves large language model (LLM) reasoning at test time by sampling from a sharpened version of the base model's distribution. Its sampler, PowerMH, is slow because its Metropolis--Hastings (MH) updates are sequential: each accept/reject decision sets the state from which the next proposal is generated. Prior work reduces this cost by changing the sampler or the model (e.g., sequential Monte Carlo, approximate lookahead, distillation). We propose Predictive SubTree Prefetching (PreSTO), which accelerates PowerMH by prefetching future proposals and provably leaves its MH transition kernel unchanged. PreSTO views future MH outcomes as a tree of accept/reject decisions: in each model call, it generates the proposals of a \textit{prefetched subtree} of this tree in one batch, then follows the realized path with the original MH acceptance rule. We also observe that MH reaches only a sparse, nearly unary part of each prefetched subtree, we further design a \textit{predictive traversal rule} that chooses the subtree to maximize the predicted number of completed transitions. Across seven datasets and five base LLMs, PreSTO achieves median speedups of $1.71\times$, $1.91\times$, and $2.33\times$ on PowerMH and its follow-ups EntropyCut and MultiTryMH, respectively; on the first two, it makes a median of $3.9\times$ fewer model calls, each only $2.1\times$ longer. On LCB V6 with Qwen3.5-9B, the predictive traversal rule is a further $1.25\times$--$1.37\times$ faster than the default breadth-first traversal.
authors: Nan Jiang, Panagiotis Theodoropoulos, Wei Deng
bullets: PowerMH is slow because sequential Metropolis–Hastings decisions require each proposal to depend on the previous outcome.
PreSTO organizes possible future accept/reject outcomes as a tree and prefetched subtrees of proposals in parallel model calls.
A predictive traversal rule selects subtrees expected to complete more MH transitions, exploiting the sampler’s sparse, nearly unary paths.
Across seven datasets and five base LLMs, it reports median speedups of 1.71× for PowerMH, 1.91× for EntropyCut, and 2.33× for MultiTryMH.
For LCB V6 with Qwen3.5-9B, predictive traversal is 1.25×–1.37× faster than breadth-first traversal.
papers.selection_reason: Accelerates LLM power sampling via predictive subtree prefetching, reducing latency and model calls, fitting efficient AI interests.
papers.title: PreSTO: Predictive Subtree Prefetching for Fast LLM Power Sampling
papers.tldr: PreSTO speeds up PowerMH-based LLM power sampling by batching predicted future MH proposals while preserving the original transition kernel.

papers.abstract: AI agents depend on repeated decisions to accomplish tasks, with large language models (LLMs) commonly serving as their core decision makers. The recent emergence of Jev offers an opportunity to make these decisions faster and at lower cost. However, it remains unclear whether such local savings can be translated into efficient and reliable task completion. In this paper, we investigate this efficiency transfer across five agents in two representative application settings, embodied tasks in ALFWorld and mobile app use in AndroidWorld. Across 4,500 task executions, we jointly evaluate task effectiveness, decision-level and task-level resource use, and execution behavior. Experimental results show that Jev integration substantially reduces decision cost and latency across all five agents, with task-level gains varying by workflow. Task success remains close to baseline levels on ALFWorld and declines more substantially in two mobile agents. Auxiliary reasoning and additional interactions absorb decision savings, while failed recovery and premature completion limit successful delivery. Mean cost per successful outcome increases in one agent even as spending per attempt falls. These findings highlight the importance of preserving progress, supporting recovery, and verifying completion when integrating efficient decision models into agent workflows. Their practical value should be assessed through successful task delivery, recovery behavior, and resources per delivered outcome.
authors: Yuchen Ling, Shengcheng Yu, Zhenyu Chen, Chunrong Fang
bullets: Evaluates Jev across five agents and 4,500 executions in ALFWorld and AndroidWorld.
Jev substantially reduces decision-level cost and latency across all agents.
Task-level benefits depend on the workflow: success stays near baseline in ALFWorld but declines more in two mobile agents.
Auxiliary reasoning, extra interactions, failed recovery, and premature completion can absorb savings or reduce delivery success.
Efficiency should be measured by successful outcomes, recovery behavior, and resources per delivered task—not per-attempt spending.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of efficient decision models in LLM agent workflows, relevant to efficiency and agent reliability.
papers.title: When Faster Decisions Do Not Make Better Agents: An Empirical Study of Jev in Agent Workflows
papers.tldr: Jev makes agent decisions faster and cheaper, but workflow overhead and weaker recovery can prevent those savings from improving successful task completion.

papers.abstract: Recent work on large audio-language models (LALMs) explores adaptive reasoning to balance accuracy and efficiency. However, existing approaches often rely on coarse-grained difficulty estimation, overlooking the diverse factors that determine reasoning effort. We address this limitation by deriving five-dimensional difficulty scores and compressed reasoning traces from complementary offline assessments. Based on this characterization, we propose SWEAR, a difficulty-aware reasoning framework that learns difficulty signals during supervised fine-tuning and uses reinforcement learning to adapt reasoning allocation across reasoning stages. Experiments on MMAU-test-mini and MMAR show that SWEAR improves accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens, shortening reasoning for easy instances without sacrificing performance on difficult ones.
authors: Yixuan Li, Minghao Lv, Xuenan Xu, Zihao Zheng, Mengyue Wu
bullets: Addresses coarse difficulty estimation in adaptive reasoning for large audio-language models.
Derives five-dimensional difficulty scores and compressed reasoning traces from complementary offline assessments.
Learns difficulty signals during supervised fine-tuning and uses reinforcement learning to adapt reasoning across stages.
On MMAU-test-mini and MMAR, it improves accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens.
Shortens reasoning for easy instances while preserving performance on difficult ones.
papers.selection_reason: Difficulty-aware adaptive reasoning for audio-language models, relevant to multimodal LLMs and inference efficiency.
papers.title: SWEAR: Section-Wise Efficient Audio Reasoning via Self-Rated Difficulty
papers.tldr: SWEAR improves audio-language reasoning efficiency by allocating effort according to fine-grained, stage-specific difficulty.

papers.abstract: KV-cache reuse in large language model serving is commonly limited to exact prompt prefixes, preventing reuse when the same retrieved document appears after different system prompts, conversation histories, or dynamic metadata. We present KV-Repurpose, an open-source, vLLM-based system for developing and evaluating segment-wise KV-cache reuse beyond exact prefixes. The system combines cache-aware segment scheduling, prompt construction, capacity management, workload generation, and runtime monitoring. Experiments on long-context benchmarks show that naive segment reuse largely preserves output quality for single-document question answering and summarization, while exposing clear limitations in cross-document reasoning. Under a Zipfian RAG-style workload in which 20% of requests share a fixed prefix, KV-Repurpose achieves a substantially higher token-level cache hit rate than prefix caching at the same 30 GB cache capacity, 63.9% versus 3.3%, resulting in lower TTFT. Even with 1 TB of cache capacity, prefix caching reaches only a 17.9% hit rate in this workload. Source code is available under the Apache-2.0 license at https://github.com/taiga333/eval-kv-repurpose.
authors: Taiga Ikeda, Daisuke Miyashita, Jun Deguchi
bullets: Addresses the inability of exact-prefix caching to reuse repeated documents across varying prompts and metadata.
Provides an open-source, vLLM-based testbed with segment scheduling, prompt construction, cache management, workload generation, and monitoring.
Naive segment reuse largely preserves output quality for single-document QA and summarization.
At 30 GB cache capacity, token-level hit rate reaches 63.9% versus 3.3% for prefix caching under a Zipfian RAG workload, with lower TTFT.
Cross-document reasoning remains a clear limitation; source code is Apache-2.0 licensed.
papers.selection_reason: Non-prefix KV-cache reuse for efficient serving.
papers.title: KV-Repurpose: A Testbed for Evaluating Non-Prefix KV-Cache Reuse
papers.tldr: KV-Repurpose evaluates segment-wise KV-cache reuse beyond exact prompt prefixes, substantially improving cache hits and reducing time to first token in RAG-style workloads while revealing cross-document reasoning limitations.

papers.abstract: Recurrent-depth language models improve inference-time reasoning by repeatedly applying a shared network to refine internal representations, but the additional recurrent computation also increases inference cost. This overhead is particularly pronounced during long-context prefill, where the full input sequence is repeatedly processed across recurrent depth. Weight-and-activation quantization offers a natural way to accelerate this computation through lower-precision arithmetic, yet repeatedly applying quantized computation introduces numerical perturbations that accumulate along the recurrent trajectory. We systematically analyze how such errors propagate across recurrent depth and show that quantization errors introduced earlier are attenuated by more subsequent recurrent steps and therefore have a smaller effect on the final representation. Matched-budget experiments strongly support this prediction, showing that placing quantized computation earlier in recurrent depth consistently yields the best fidelity. Based on this insight, we introduce RAMP (Recurrent Adaptive Mixed Precision), which performs early recurrent refinement using low-precision weight-and-activation computation and restores high precision for terminal refinement. Across context lengths up to 4K, RAMP preserves near-full-precision prefill quality while achieving up to 1.16x end-to-end first-prefill speedup on an NVIDIA H100, corresponding to a 13.9% latency reduction.
bullets: Quantization errors introduced earlier in recurrent depth are attenuated by later refinement steps.
Matched-budget experiments find that assigning low precision to early recurrent steps gives the best fidelity.
RAMP applies low-precision weight-and-activation computation early, then restores high precision for terminal refinement.
Across contexts up to 4K, RAMP achieves up to 1.16× end-to-end first-prefill speedup on an NVIDIA H100.
The reported evaluation focuses on prefill efficiency and quality preservation at context lengths up to 4K.
papers.selection_reason: Mixed precision for efficient prefill in recurrent-depth LMs, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: RAMP: Recurrent Adaptive Mixed Precision for Efficient Prefill in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
papers.tldr: RAMP speeds up long-context prefill in recurrent-depth language models by using low precision early and high precision late, preserving near-full-precision quality with up to 13.9% lower latency.

papers.abstract: Evaluating deep learning optimizer is challenging because confounding factors such as hyperparameter tuning and optimizer-model co-design often obscure true algorithmic performance. We present results of the updated AlgoPerf V1 benchmark, in which we evaluate a new set of training algorithms on wall-clock time-to-target across nine workloads on fixed hardware. This report focuses on the results of the benchmark's self-tuning ruleset, which requires submissions to use a single configuration across all workloads. Out of the 13 submissions in PyTorch and JAX, Schedule-Free AdamW ranked first. In addition to the wall-clock scores, we also analyze the trade-offs between step efficiency and wall-clock execution, revealing that matrix-preconditioned and two-loop methods achieve good sample efficiency but require more aggressive computational optimizations to be competitive in runtime. Finally, our hyperparameter saliency and retention analyses show that the learning rate and momentum are highly sensitive across domains and algorithms, highlighting the need for methods that are more robust against hyperparameter tuning and can generalize well to new tasks.
authors: Priya Kasimbeg (Alice), Ahmed Khaled (Alice), Aahlad Chandrabhatta (Alice), Yifan Wang (Alice), Andy Liu (Alice), Niccol\`o Ajroldi (Alice), David Tweedle (Alice), Xingyu (Alice), Yang, Isaac Patole, Frank Schneider, George E. Dahl
bullets: The benchmark evaluates training algorithms by wall-clock time-to-target across nine workloads on fixed hardware.
Its self-tuning ruleset requires one configuration to be used across all workloads, reducing workload-specific tuning advantages.
Schedule-Free AdamW ranked first among 13 PyTorch and JAX submissions.
Matrix-preconditioned and two-loop methods showed good sample efficiency but needed stronger computational optimization for competitive runtime.
Learning rate and momentum were highly sensitive across domains, motivating more robust, transferable optimizers.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates training algorithms (optimizers) for efficiency on a new benchmark, highlighting the trade-offs between step efficiency and wall-clock execution. This contributes to the understanding of computational efficiency in deep learning.
papers.title: Towards Easier-to-Tune Training Algorithms: New Results from AlgoPerf
papers.tldr: AlgoPerf V1 finds that Schedule-Free AdamW performs best under a single self-tuning configuration, while hyperparameter robustness remains a key challenge.

papers.abstract: Multi-view representations enable pretrained image and video vision-language models to understand 3D scenes, but their long visual token sequences make inference costly. Redundancy arises both from repeated observations of the same scene regions across views and from processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer, regardless of their relevance to the current computation. We propose GeoGR, a two-stage framework that jointly compresses scene representations and visual computation. At the projector level, GeoSemZip consolidates cross-view observations into 3D voxel tokens and combines semantic saliency with spatial coverage to construct a compact scene representation. Unselected voxel features are aggregated into contextual anchors to retain scene information that would otherwise be discarded. At the LLM level, we identify an effective visual computation window and observe that query-conditioned token relevance remains locally stable but changes over longer layer intervals. Guided by these findings, GroupRoute combines late entry and early exit with recoverable group-wise skipping. Low-relevance tokens bypass complete LLM layers while retaining their hidden states and can rejoin the active group at subsequent anchor layers selected under a computation budget. For compression-aware post-training, we construct a compact dataset of 67K samples by retaining 30% of the original training pool. With this protocol, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of the dense post-trained models' performance on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Video-3D LLM-7B, respectively, while accelerating LLM prefill by $6.8\times$ and $6.1\times$. These results demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of GeoGR across 3D VLMs with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding, highlighting a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/GeoGR.
authors: Yongxin Zheng, Hao Wu, Fang Li, Hu Fu, Peiran Yin, Xudong Wang, Haozhe Hu, Xinghao Chen, Yunpu Ma, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Addresses high inference cost from repeated cross-view observations and processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer.
GeoSemZip builds compact 3D voxel-token representations using semantic saliency and spatial coverage, while retaining discarded information in contextual anchors.
GroupRoute uses late entry, early exit, and recoverable group-wise skipping to adapt visual computation to token relevance.
Using a 67K-sample compression-aware post-training set, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of dense-model performance on two 7B 3D VLMs.
It accelerates LLM prefill by 6.8× and 6.1×, demonstrating applicability to models with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding.
papers.selection_reason: Compresses 3D visual tokens and skips LLM layers for efficient 3D VLMs, directly relevant to token pruning and multimodal efficiency.
papers.title: GeoGR: Spatial-Semantic Token Compression and Group Routing for Efficient 3D VLMs
papers.tldr: GeoGR makes multi-view 3D vision-language models substantially faster by compressing redundant scene tokens and selectively routing visual tokens through LLM layers while preserving most performance.

papers.abstract: Decoder hidden states from different layers of large language models (LLMs) often encode complementary information. However, existing speculative decoding methods typically rely on a small set of target-model layers chosen using fixed, position-based heuristics. Selecting an optimal subset of layers is inherently a combinatorial problem, making exhaustive evaluation infeasible even for moderately deep models. In this work, we present a principled framework for multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding based on two complementary criteria: informativeness, measured through matrix-entropy analysis, and diversity, quantified using centered kernel alignment (CKA). We investigate layer-wise Shannon entropy, aggregate entropy under hidden-state concatenation, and pairwise CKA dynamics across depth, revealing distinct geometric and informational compartments within decoder representations. Motivated by these findings, we propose entropy and CKA-based layer selection algorithms that favor hidden-state sets that are both highly informative and minimally redundant. As part of this framework, we introduce token-entropy filtering, which removes hidden states associated with low predictive-entropy tokens, thereby improving the quality of layer-selection statistics. In EAGLE3-style speculative decoding, our selected sets outperform fixed baseline choices, including the default $[2, N//2, N-3]$ rule, while providing a clearer explanation of why some defaults can remain competitive. Our results provide a practical recipe for multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding, insights into the geometry and information in LLM decoder states, and a foundation for extending similar analysis to related applications.
authors: Raghavv Goel, Sudhanshu Agrawal, Mukul Gagrani, Risheek Garrepalli, Mingu Lee
bullets: Existing methods often use fixed, position-based layer subsets, while optimal selection is combinatorial and costly to evaluate exhaustively.
The framework measures layer informativeness with matrix entropy and representation diversity with centered kernel alignment (CKA).
Analysis reveals distinct informational and geometric compartments across decoder depth, including layer-wise entropy, concatenated-state entropy, and pairwise CKA patterns.
Token-entropy filtering removes low-predictive-entropy tokens to improve the reliability of layer-selection statistics.
Selected layer sets outperform fixed baselines such as [2, N//2, N-3], while explaining why some heuristic choices remain competitive.
papers.selection_reason: Principled hidden-state selection for speculative decoding improves LLM inference efficiency.
papers.title: Surfing the Activation Wave: Analyzing the Information and Geometry of LLM Hidden States for Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: A principled entropy- and CKA-based framework selects informative, nonredundant LLM layers for speculative decoding, outperforming fixed layer-selection heuristics in EAGLE3-style settings.

papers.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable advances in complex reasoning. However, scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora can substantially increase training cost without proportional performance gains. In this study, we therefore ask: how far can reasoning supervision be compressed without sacrificing capability? To this end, we propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework that concentrates supervision and optimization on the reasoning trajectories most valuable for learning. Specifically, rather than treating a teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) as a single realized path, we construct uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision by building Monte Carlo reasoning trees around intermediate reasoning states to expose process-level uncertainty. This uncertainty first contracts the original corpus into a compact teacher-informed pool. A second, learner-aware contraction then performs online routing during SFT, concentrating optimization according to the student's evolving learning state. Together, the two stages progressively contract both supervision and optimization, substantially reducing the student training budget. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLM families show that our method uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data SFT, over 450x less training exposure, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Notably, our framework generalizes well across heterogeneous student families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer. This indicates that it is not only a way to accelerate training but can also enhance reasoning capability.
authors: Suorong Yang, Jiaxin Wang, Jiaming Su, Chentao Yue, Furao Shen, Peng Ye, Soujanya Poria
bullets: Targets the high cost and diminishing returns of scaling reasoning post-training data.
Builds Monte Carlo reasoning trees to estimate process-level uncertainty around teacher-generated chains of thought.
Progressively contracts training in two stages: teacher-informed data selection, then learner-aware online routing during SFT.
Uses as little as 0.22% of the full-data SFT optimization budget—over 450× less training exposure—while maintaining or improving performance.
Works across diverse benchmarks, LLM families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-guided contraction drastically reduces LLM reasoning post-training budget.
papers.title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training
papers.tldr: Uncertainty-guided progressive contraction compresses reasoning supervision and training exposure while preserving or improving LLM reasoning performance.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, but still require multiple sampling steps to produce high-quality text. In this paper, we investigate whether a model can learn to generate an entire sequence in a single forward pass. We propose Seq-Drifting, a framework that applies drifting to sequences of continuous token representations and directly learns a map from Gaussian noise to text. Unlike existing DLMs that derive the supervision at each position directly from the observed token in a training sequence, Seq-Drifting builds a drift field whose position-wise targets adapt to the current generated context. At each position, attraction guides each output toward a set of contextually plausible token representations, while repulsion discourages collapse across samples and repetition within sequences. The generator learns from this drift field during training and produces all tokens jointly in one pass at inference. Empirically, Seq-Drifting achieves a generative perplexity of 36.01 on LM1B in one step and performs competitively in both unconditional and conditional generation. Experiments on translation, summarization, and reasoning further demonstrate the applicability of the framework beyond open-ended generation. These results suggest that drifting over token sequences offers a promising path toward effective one-step text generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/jyliu-ai/Seq-Drifting.
authors: Jiayu Liu, Ruizhi Zhao, Tianyun Ji, Yee Whye Teh, Zhenya Huang, Ning Miao
bullets: Targets the challenge of reducing diffusion language generation from multiple sampling steps to a single forward pass.
Operates on continuous token representations and jointly generates all sequence positions.
Uses contextually adaptive attraction to plausible tokens, plus repulsion to reduce sample collapse and within-sequence repetition.
Reports a generative perplexity of 36.01 on LM1B in one step and competitive unconditional and conditional generation.
Demonstrates applicability to translation, summarization, and reasoning tasks.
papers.selection_reason: One-step text generation via drifting reduces sampling steps; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: One-Step Text Generation by Seq-Drifting
papers.tldr: Seq-Drifting enables one-step text generation by learning to map Gaussian noise directly to coherent token sequences through context-adaptive drifting.

papers.abstract: Fewer latent tokens promise cheaper diffusion. Yet aggressive latent compression creates a reconstruction-generation dilemma: adding channels improves reconstruction but makes generation harder. We introduce APEX, short for Asynchronous Prefix denoising for EXtreme compression, which pairs a hierarchical latent space with asynchronous denoising over channel groups. Our autoencoder orders channel prefixes from structure to detail, while one shared denoiser generates them at staggered local times without adding tokens. On ImageNet-512, APEX outperforms existing methods at every evaluated channel count under 64x and 128x compression. At matched training and guided sampling compute, it also outperforms a 256-token model at every evaluated budget, with larger gains at lower compute. Code is available at https://daviddinkevich.github.io/APEX.
authors: David Dinkevich, Nisan Chiprut, Yoav HaCohen, Dani Lischinski
bullets: Addresses the reconstruction–generation trade-off in aggressively compressed latent spaces.
Uses an autoencoder with channel prefixes ordered from global structure to fine detail.
A shared denoiser generates channel groups at staggered local times without adding tokens.
On ImageNet-512, it outperforms prior methods across evaluated channel counts at 64× and 128× compression.
It also surpasses a 256-token model at matched compute, with larger gains at lower budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a compression method for diffusion models using asynchronous denoising, improving efficiency in video generation and addressing token management.
papers.title: APEX: Asynchronous Prefix Denoising for Extreme Compression
papers.tldr: APEX enables extreme latent compression by asynchronously denoising hierarchical channel groups, improving image generation quality without increasing token count.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation aims to train a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher model for resource-constrained environments. However, the process of distillation is typically data-intensive and computationally expensive, particularly for generative tasks. Few-shot distillation offers an alternative by transferring teacher knowledge using limited training samples. However, we observe that few-shot distillation performance is heavily dependent on the choice of these training samples. In fact, we demonstrate that using more uncertain samples near the teacher's decision boundary can significantly deteriorate distillation performance.
