Motivated by this observation, we propose Counterfactual-guided Few-shot Distillation in Open-book Question Answering (COFFEQA), a novel strategy that aptly uses counterfactuals to provide additional supervision around challenging factual samples. In the generative QA setting, we define a counterfactual as a minimally modified context that induces the teacher to change its response to an alternative answer. We provide geometric insights on how factual-counterfactual pairs can constrain the deviation between the teacher's and student's decision boundaries. We further introduce a new metric, Context Following Difficulty (CFD) that further validates counterfactuals prior to distillation based on agreement with the intended alternative answer and dependence on the modified context. COFFEQA uses CFD-validated factual-counterfactual pairs for few-shot distillation. Experiments across five in-domain and three out-of-domain QA benchmarks using T5 and Qwen2.5 families show that COFFEQA outperforms factual-only distillation baselines under the same few-shot budget. For instance, on TriviaQA, COFFEQA improves over the factual-only baseline by 8.77 average EM points and 9.98 average F1 points under the T5 setting with 32 few-shot pairs.
bullets: Few-shot distillation is highly sensitive to training-sample selection; uncertain samples near the teacher’s decision boundary can harm performance.
The method creates minimally modified contexts that cause the teacher to switch to an alternative answer, forming factual–counterfactual pairs.
A Context Following Difficulty (CFD) metric validates pairs based on teacher agreement and reliance on the modified context.
Across five in-domain and three out-of-domain benchmarks with T5 and Qwen2.5, COFFEQA outperforms factual-only distillation under the same few-shot budget.
On TriviaQA with T5 and 32 few-shot pairs, it improves average EM by 8.77 points and average F1 by 9.98 points.
papers.selection_reason: Few-shot distillation with counterfactual supervision reduces the cost of deploying smaller QA models, aligning with efficient AI goals.
papers.title: COFFEQA: Counterfactual-Guided Few-Shot Distillation for LLM Question Answering
papers.tldr: COFFEQA improves few-shot distillation for open-book QA by selecting CFD-validated factual–counterfactual pairs that better supervise challenging examples.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual speech enhancement (AVSE) improves speech intelligibility in noisy environments but often relies on computationally expensive models unsuitable for resource-constrained edge devices. This paper introduces a reinforcement learning-driven neural architecture search (RL-NAS) framework to discover compact, efficient AVSE architectures. The search space preserves temporal alignment between audio and visual streams, while a novel reward function jointly optimises speech enhancement performance, measured by SI-SNR improvement, and model compactness. Using proximal policy optimisation with constraint-aware action masking, the framework evaluates only 35 candidate architectures and identifies a model with 2.9 million parameters, compared with 22 million in the baseline. The proposed architecture achieves a 14.5 dB SI-SNR improvement, only 0.7 dB below the baseline, while reducing model size by approximately nine-fold. Evaluation on commercial mobile CPUs demonstrates a 4.3-fold reduction in real-time factor, supporting practical on-device deployment. Compared with random search, RL-NAS achieves 92% higher search efficiency. Architectural analysis reveals that shallower but wider temporal convolutional blocks and aggressive visual pathway pruning can maintain enhancement performance while substantially reducing computational requirements. These findings demonstrate the potential of reinforcement learning-guided architecture search for developing lightweight, efficient and deployable multimodal speech enhancement systems.
authors: Khubaib Ahmed, Ahsan Adeel, Nasir Saleem, Kia Dashtipour, Ahsan Ulhaq, Amir Hussain
bullets: Targets computationally expensive audio-visual speech enhancement models for resource-constrained edge devices.
Uses PPO with constraint-aware action masking and a reward balancing SI-SNR improvement with model compactness.
Searches 35 temporally aligned candidate architectures and selects a 2.9M-parameter model versus a 22M-parameter baseline.
The model achieves 14.5 dB SI-SNR improvement, within 0.7 dB of the baseline, with roughly nine-fold lower model size and 4.3× lower real-time factor on mobile CPUs.
Shallower, wider temporal convolutions and aggressive visual-pathway pruning support efficiency; RL-NAS is reported as 92% more search-efficient than random search.
papers.selection_reason: RL-based neural architecture search for compact audio-visual speech enhancement directly targets on-device efficiency and latency reduction.
papers.title: Efficient Audio-Visual Speech Enhancement via Reinforcement Learning-Based Neural Architecture Search
papers.tldr: An RL-driven neural architecture search finds a compact AVSE model that nearly matches baseline enhancement quality while substantially reducing size and mobile inference cost.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct scenes from unposed images, but the quadratic cost of global attention limits their scalability to large view sets. We present Zebra3D, a layerwise sparse-linear hybrid attention framework that improves the efficiency of pretrained 3D foundation models without training from scratch. Across VGGT, HunyuanWorld-Mirror, and $\pi^3$, we observe a broadly consistent depth-wise pattern: early stages are relatively tolerant to linear replacement, while sensitive middle-to-late stages tend to exhibit more concentrated attention. Zebra3D exploits this structure by assigning linear-centered attention to tolerant stages and tile-sparse attention to sensitive stages, using landmark summaries to preserve unselected context. Closed-form affine fitting enables training-free conversion, while optional post-conversion training combines task supervision with output and relational feature distillation. Across all three backbones, Zebra3D achieves strong reconstruction and camera-pose accuracy at high attention sparsity, with training-free variants remaining close to their dense counterparts. End-to-end speedups increase with input view count, reaching up to $7.1\times$ at 1,024 views. After post-conversion training, Zebra3D-VGGT reaches 80.5\% RealEstate10K AUC@30 at 94\% mean attention sparsity, within 1.1 percentage points of dense VGGT fine-tuned on the same data and schedule.
authors: Utkarsh Saxena, Ruijing Yang, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh, Akash Haridas, Vikram Appia, Emad Barsoum
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of global attention in feed-forward 3D foundation models for unposed-image reconstruction.
Assigns linear-centered attention to tolerant early stages and tile-sparse attention with landmark summaries to sensitive middle-to-late stages.
Converts models without training from scratch using closed-form affine fitting; optional distillation-based post-conversion training further improves performance.
Across VGGT, HunyuanWorld-Mirror, and π³, maintains strong reconstruction and camera-pose accuracy at high attention sparsity.
Zebra3D-VGGT reaches 80.5% RealEstate10K AUC@30 at 94% mean sparsity, within 1.1 percentage points of dense fine-tuned VGGT; speedup reaches 7.1× at 1,024 views.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a layerwise sparse-linear hybrid attention framework to improve the scalability of 3D foundation models, directly addressing efficiency in 3D reconstruction.
papers.title: Zebra3D: Efficient Hybrid Foundation Models For Scalable 3D Reconstruction
papers.tldr: Zebra3D makes pretrained 3D reconstruction models scalable to many views by replacing dense attention with layerwise hybrid sparse-linear attention, achieving up to 7.1× speedup with limited accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Efficient autoregressive generation is increasingly limited by the memory footprint of the key-value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length, batch size, and model depth. Existing approaches such as Multi-Query Attention (MQA), Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), and Tensor Product Attention (TPA) reduce this cost through different trade-offs, but often sacrifice expressivity, require additional positional-encoding machinery, or impose restrictive low-rank structure. We propose Kronecker Product Attention (KPA), which represents key and value activations as sums of Kronecker products of compact, token-dependent matrix factors. KPA strictly generalizes TPA: rank-one vector-outer-product factorization arises as a degenerate Kronecker split, while non-degenerate matrix factors can represent richer block-structured patterns. We further show that a structured rotary embedding operator matched to the Kronecker representation preserves the relative-position property of RoPE while rotating only the compact factors, removing the need for a decoupled RoPE branch as in MLA. Empirically, KPA matches or exceeds TPA, MHA, MQA, GQA, and MLA across four model scales and nine downstream benchmarks under identical training conditions, while achieving up to 10x KV cache compression. The Kronecker head split is a tuneable hyperparameter that allows practitioners to navigate the compression-accuracy trade-off at design time without architectural changes.
authors: Bahareh Nikpour, Hossein Rajabzadeh, Maryam Dialameh, Vahid Partovi Nia, Parsa Omidi
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory growth with sequence length, batch size, and model depth.
Represents key/value activations as sums of Kronecker products, strictly generalizing Tensor Product Attention.
Introduces a matched structured rotary embedding that preserves RoPE’s relative-position property without a separate positional branch.
Matches or exceeds several attention baselines across four model scales and nine benchmarks, with up to 10× KV-cache compression.
A tunable Kronecker head split controls the compression–accuracy trade-off without architectural changes.
papers.selection_reason: KV cache compression via structured Kronecker factorization, directly relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: Kronecker Product Attention: Memory-Efficient KV Compression via Structured Factorization
papers.tldr: Kronecker Product Attention compresses autoregressive KV caches by factorizing keys and values into compact, token-dependent Kronecker factors while preserving positional information and attention expressivity.

papers.abstract: Sparse computation can scale the parametric capacity of LLMs without proportionally increasing active computation, but pretraining sparse architectures remains expensive and data-hungry. Existing sparse upcycling methods mainly target Mixture-of-Experts models, where expert homogeneity, sample inefficiency, and system overheads can limit practical scalability. Static sparse memory offers predictable access and token-specific updates that can help address these challenges, but naively integrating it into pretrained computation yields poor returns. In this work, we introduce STAPLE, a recipe built upon STEM for integrating static sparse memory into pretrained models. Whereas STEM replaces FFN up-projections with token-indexed embeddings, STAPLE retains them and adds the embeddings as a residual pathway, preserving pretrained computation while learning complementary token-specific information in a scalable manner. On OLMo-2 1B, STAPLE improves over continued dense training by 4.27 points on HumanEval, 2.80 on MBPP, 2.27 on GSM8K, and 1.65 on DROP. Average performance increases with static capacity, and improvements persist on the larger OLMo-2 7B backbone. STAPLE also outperforms static sparse baselines such as STEM and an Engram-style model, and achieves a higher average score than an MoE upcycling baseline while decoding 2x faster with less than half its GPU model memory and measured GPU energy per token in our throughput-oriented decoding evaluation. Importantly, despite introducing billions of parameters late in training, our host-offloaded implementation keeps generation throughput within 1.5% and training throughput within 3% of the dense baseline, while caching only the ~5% most frequent embeddings on GPU. These results show that static sparse memory can provide a sample-efficient, scalable, and sustainable path for expanding pretrained models without sparse pretraining from scratch.
authors: Ranajoy Sadhukhan, Euijin Hong, Sheng Cao, Zechun Liu, Shuowei Jin, Sha Li, Changlong Yu, Xin Liu, Qin Lu, Zhenyu Shi, Priyanka Nigam, Beidi Chen
bullets: Addresses the cost and data demands of pretraining sparse architectures, especially limitations of MoE upcycling.
Retains pretrained FFN up-projections and adds STEM-based token-indexed embeddings as complementary residual information.
Performance improves with static memory capacity and transfers to both 1B and 7B OLMo-2 backbones.
Outperforms dense continued training and static sparse baselines across coding, math, and question-answering benchmarks.
Compared with an MoE upcycling baseline, achieves higher average performance while decoding 2× faster and using less GPU memory; throughput stays close to dense training and generation baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Static sparse memory upcycling improves LLM capacity and inference efficiency.
papers.title: STAPLE: Static Sparse Upcycling of Pretrained Checkpoints via Embedding Modules
papers.tldr: STAPLE efficiently expands pretrained LLMs by adding token-indexed static sparse embeddings as a residual pathway, improving task performance with minimal training and decoding overhead.

papers.abstract: A latent recurrent language model applies a shared block of layers repeatedly, so one checkpoint can trade inference compute for accuracy by changing the loop count. At one loop, however, such models typically fall well short of a non-recurrent model of the same size, a one-loop tax that makes a separate non-recurrent model the better choice whenever latency matters. We present Elastic Latent Recurrence (ELR), a recipe for training looped language models without this tax. At one loop, an ELR model costs the same to serve as a non-recurrent model of the same size and, trained on the same data, reaches similar accuracy. Each additional loop then buys more accuracy for more inference compute. Three choices make this work: a gated state update with a learned step size, loop counts mixed within each optimizer update, and conditioning each pass on its loop index and budget. The first two preserve one-loop accuracy, and the third lowers loss at every additional loop. Mixed depths can be introduced late in pretraining to limit the added training cost, and with zero-initialized conditioning added at the switch, this late schedule reaches lower loss than mixed-depth training from scratch. In MoE models, reusing first-loop expert routes on later loops cuts mixed-depth update time by 11.7% with no measurable change in accuracy. At inference, keeping only the last loop's attention KV cache holds attention KV memory at its one-loop level while retaining most of the gain from additional loops. On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE hybrid models, ELR at one loop is 0.52 points below and 1.04 points above its matched baseline on a ten-task average, and four loops add 7.25 and 4.75 points. Carried through post-training, the recipe yields Koi-4B, a single checkpoint that scores an estimated 18 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at one loop, matching Qwen3.5-4B, and 29 at four loops.
authors: Faisal Ladhak, Shantanu Acharya, Santiago Akle Serano, Simeng Sun, Boris Ginsburg, Krishna C Puvvada
bullets: Addresses the one-loop accuracy tax that often makes recurrent models unattractive under latency constraints.
Uses gated state updates with learned step sizes, mixed loop counts during training, and loop-index/budget conditioning.
Late mixed-depth training can reduce added training cost; reusing MoE expert routes cuts update time by 11.7% without measurable accuracy loss.
Retaining only the final loop’s attention KV cache keeps KV memory at the one-loop level while preserving most multi-loop gains.

On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE models, four loops improve ten-task averages by 7.25 and 4.75 points, respectively; the post-trained Koi-4B reaches estimated Intelligence Index scores of 18 at one loop and 29 at four.
papers.selection_reason: Elastic latent recurrence for looped LLMs with one-loop tax removal and KV-cache memory savings; strong architectural and efficiency contribution.
papers.title: One Model to Loop Them All: Elastic Latent Recurrence for Language Models
papers.tldr: Elastic Latent Recurrence trains one language-model checkpoint to match non-recurrent accuracy at one loop while gaining accuracy as additional loops increase inference compute.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose multiple tokens that are subsequently verified in parallel by the target model. Recent diffusion-based drafters make this paradigm particularly attractive: deep attention-based neural backbones provide strong predictions, while drafting multiple future positions in parallel avoids the sequential cost of autoregressive generation. This parallelism, however, comes at a cost. Tokens within a draft block are predicted without access to the realized identities of preceding draft tokens, removing intra-block dependencies that would naturally be available under autoregressive generation. We introduce DCOCO (DFlash Contextual Corrector), a lightweight mechanism that restores these dependencies while preserving parallel drafting. Rather than committing to each position's top prediction, DCOCO retains multiple candidate tokens and evaluates their contextual compatibility across adjacent draft positions in parallel, enabling contextually informed token selection at low additional cost. Across four verifier backbones and ten benchmarks, DCOCO achieves the highest average throughput in every evaluated configuration, spanning greedy and stochastic decoding with and without extended reasoning, with speedups of up to 6.6x over vanilla decoding. Its advantage persists under concurrent serving: DCOCO outperforms the strongest competing method by 6-23% across 4-32 concurrent requests, while other sequential correctors fall below uncorrected DFlash at these loads. These results demonstrate that recovering intra-block dependencies through parallel contextual scoring delivers consistent acceleration across decoding regimes and serving loads.
authors: Roy Eisenstadt, Harel Lidar, Tal Gonen, Omer Luxembourg, Itamar Zimerman, Lior Wolf, Eli David, Ilan Naiman
bullets: Parallel diffusion-based drafters lose access to preceding draft-token identities, weakening intra-block consistency.
DCOCO retains multiple candidates per position and scores their compatibility across adjacent positions in parallel.
Evaluated across four verifier backbones and ten benchmarks, it achieves the highest average throughput in every tested configuration.
Speedups reach up to 6.6× over vanilla decoding and remain 6–23% better than the strongest competitor under 4–32 concurrent requests.
papers.selection_reason: Parallel contextual correction for speculative decoding; a meaningful LLM inference-acceleration contribution under Efficient AI.
papers.title: Contextual Correction of Parallel Draftsfor Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: DCOCO restores dependencies between parallel draft tokens through contextual candidate scoring, accelerating speculative decoding while preserving parallelism.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models maintain a growing attention key-value (KV) cache, making memory a key bottleneck for long video generation. Recently, clustering-based quantization has emerged as an effective method to compress video KV caches by grouping similar key and value vectors then quantizing residual errors. However, when later frames attend to the compressed history, small reconstruction errors can compound as the video grows. Beyond the within-layer similarity exploited by clustering, we find strong dependencies across cache layers in video models. This motivates Coral-KV - Calibrated Offline, Residual-coded, and Adapted Locally - a KV-cache compression framework that uses cache states in each layer to predict keys and values in subsequent layers, then quantizes the remaining prediction residuals. We construct compact block-diagonal-plus-low-rank (block-DPLR) predictors: block-diagonal components model channel relationships within each attention head, while a global low-rank term models dependencies between heads. Coral-KV exposes a flexible fidelity-memory trade-off: it can reuse its predictors across videos or refit lightweight block-diagonal predictors to the current video for higher fidelity. Across extensive evaluations on both HY-WorldPlay and MAGI-1, our reusable configuration improves PSNR over QVG-4 by 0.32 dB and 4.95 dB, respectively, while using 48% and 37% less cache memory. Against QVG-Pro, our video-adapted configuration improves MAGI-1 PSNR by 3.77 dB while using 33.7% less cache memory. Coral-KV also maintains higher reconstruction fidelity over extended generation and reduces temporal discontinuities while retaining comparable generation latency.
authors: Albert Ge, Akash Haridas, Utkarsh Saxena, Ruijing Yang, Ian Colbert, Frederic Sala, Vikram Appia, Emad Barsoum
bullets: Addresses growing KV-cache memory and error accumulation in long video diffusion generation.
Uses block-diagonal-plus-low-rank predictors to capture within-head channel and across-head dependencies.
Supports reusable predictors for efficiency or lightweight video-specific refitting for higher fidelity.
Improves PSNR while reducing cache memory versus QVG-4 and QVG-Pro across HY-WorldPlay and MAGI-1.
Maintains fidelity over extended generation and reduces temporal discontinuities with comparable latency.
papers.selection_reason: KV-cache compression for autoregressive video diffusion models; directly relevant to memory-efficient inference and video generation.
papers.title: CORAL-KV: Compact Cross-Layer Prediction and Residual Coding for Autoregressive Video KV Caches
papers.tldr: Coral-KV compresses autoregressive video KV caches by predicting later-layer states from earlier layers and quantizing only the residuals, reducing memory while preserving video quality.

papers.abstract: Sensing-aided beam prediction can reduce the beam-training overhead of millimeter-wave (mmWave) systems by leveraging environmental information from complementary modalities such as vision and position. However, the resulting sensing and inference pipeline can be energy-intensive, motivating the use of energy-efficient spiking neural networks (SNNs) as an alternative to conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs). In this work, we develop SNN architectures for beam prediction and systematically compare them with ANNs using position-only, vision-only, and multimodal inputs. Our results show that compact ANNs consistently outperform SNNs for position-only sensing. In contrast, for vision and multimodal sensing, SNNs achieve higher accuracy than ANNs at similar energy costs and require up to an order of magnitude less energy at a comparable accuracy. For example, the multimodal SNN achieves 58.08% top-1 accuracy, outperforming the closest-energy ANN by 18.11 percentage points. We further show that SNN accuracy is limited by the binary communication between layers rather than by model size. These results demonstrate the potential of SNNs for energy-efficient sensing-aided beam prediction while highlighting their accuracy limitation.
authors: Nhan Thanh Nguyen, Phuong Nam Tran, Mengyuan Ma, Huy T. Nguyen, Ahmed Alkhateeb, Markku Juntti
bullets: Sensing-aided beam prediction reduces mmWave beam-training overhead by using position and/or vision information.
The study compares SNNs and ANNs with position-only, vision-only, and multimodal inputs.
Compact ANNs outperform SNNs for position-only sensing.
For vision and multimodal inputs, SNNs provide higher accuracy at similar energy or use up to an order of magnitude less energy at comparable accuracy.
The multimodal SNN reaches 58.08% top-1 accuracy, 18.11 percentage points above the closest-energy ANN.
papers.selection_reason: Energy-efficient SNNs for sensing-aided beam prediction; fits efficient AI energy reduction focus.
papers.title: Energy-Efficient Spiking Neural Networks for Sensing-Aided Beam Prediction
papers.tldr: Spiking neural networks can make vision- and multimodal sensing-aided mmWave beam prediction substantially more energy-efficient, though their accuracy is limited by binary inter-layer communication.

papers.abstract: Small language models trained on a single local machine leave little room for architectural trial and error. Kairos combines bidirectional gated-DeltaNet linear attention and sliding-window attention over shared projections (LiZAttention2), block-wise Attention-Residual aggregation, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) feed-forward layer and a multi-scale byte-level codec, trained with a uniform-noise denoising objective over one byte space shared by text, image, audio, video, lidar and control streams; this report asks whether the combination optimizes at all before asking whether it is useful. We give code-derived algorithms for each component, including a cross-session recurrent-state memory gate, then run convergence sanity checks: overfittinga single 440-byte sentence at 1--15M parameters, text only, with three seeds for codec and attention choices and single-run sweeps for seven further factors. The two attention variants tested at 3\,000 steps (LiZAttention2 and window attention alone) reach a minimum loss near $10^{-3}$. After 600 steps, the mean minimum loss ranges from 0.018 (patch codec) to 0.354 (depthwise convolutional codec) with an identical ranking on three seeds. An apparent advantage of shared over separate attention projections closes with more steps or more diverse data and reverses when the projections are frozen: it is a convergence-speed effect, not a capacity effect. These checks suggest that the implementation optimizes; they say nothing about generalization, multimodal training or comparison with existing models, which a planned pretraining run is meant to address. The Discussion sizes a 200M-total/25M-active target analytically; none of its throughput figures is measured. Code is available at https://github.com/fabienfrfr/Kairos . Python package at https://pypi.org/project/kairos-fm/ .
bullets: Combines bidirectional gated-DeltaNet and sliding-window attention, shared projections, block-wise attention-residual aggregation, sparse MoE layers, and a multi-scale byte codec.
Uses uniform-noise denoising across a shared byte space intended for text, images, audio, video, lidar, and control streams.
Convergence checks overfit one 440-byte sentence at 1–15M parameters; both tested attention variants reach minimum loss near 10⁻³ at 3,000 steps.
Codec choices produce different early optimization behavior, while the apparent shared-projection benefit is attributed to convergence speed rather than capacity.
Results do not establish generalization, multimodal training, model superiority, or the proposed throughput; larger pretraining is planned.
papers.selection_reason: Byte-level multimodal foundation model with linear attention and MoE; fits multimodal LLM and efficient attention interests.
papers.title: Kairos: Toward a Byte-Level Foundation Model for Every Modality
papers.tldr: Kairos proposes a byte-level multimodal foundation-model design and finds that its components can optimize on a tiny text-only memorization task, without yet demonstrating generalization or multimodal usefulness.

papers.abstract: In this article, we propose algebraic integer number formats (AINF) as a framework for highly configurable and accurate compressed computation. A key property of AINF is its straightforward reduction to purely integer arithmetic, enabling error-free multiply-accumulate operations. We develop a matrix multiplication engine that exploits this property, obtaining performance within a predictable factor of the most efficient numerical counterparts on modern hardware accelerators. Another key advantage of AIQ is the freedom to select algebraic integers tailored to the numerical characteristics of a given use case, offering optimization opportunities that are fundamentally unavailable in floating-point or fixed-point formats. Motivated by these properties, we introduce algebraic integer quantization (AIQ), a lossy compression format for large language model (LLM) inference, and provide results demonstrating that AIQ achieves competitive accuracy compared to the industry-standard MX format across a diverse set of models and benchmarks at equivalent bit-per-parameter budgets. The experiments presented in this article employ algebraic integers of degree two (quadratic integers); generalizations to higher-order and, in particular, multidimensional algebraic integers promise even greater computational advantages and remain a promising direction for future work.
authors: Anthony Kostal-Vazquez, Vassil Dimitrov, Branden Butler
bullets: Algebraic integer number formats reduce computation to integer arithmetic, enabling error-free multiply-accumulate operations.
The proposed matrix multiplication engine delivers performance within a predictable factor of efficient numerical alternatives on modern accelerators.
Algebraic integers can be selected to match the numerical properties of specific applications, offering flexibility beyond floating-point and fixed-point formats.
AIQ achieves competitive accuracy with the industry-standard MX format across diverse models and benchmarks at equivalent bits per parameter.
Experiments use quadratic integers; higher-order and multidimensional extensions are left for future work.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel number format (Algebraic Integer Quantization) for LLM inference, directly addressing computational efficiency and compression.
papers.title: Algebraic Integer Quantization for Machine Learning Applications
papers.tldr: Algebraic integer quantization enables configurable, integer-only compressed computation for LLM inference with accuracy competitive with MX at matched bit budgets.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) can clone a voice from seconds of audio. Yet the quality comes from billion-parameter diffusion transformers whose size and multi-step sampling put them out of reach of the on-device, assistive, and real-time applications that need them most. Post-training quantization (PTQ) shrinks such models without retraining, but it has been built for language and vision, not speech. At 4 bits, a strong quantizer leaves intelligibility close to full precision but consistently erodes speaker timbre, so error rates stay low while the voice drifts from the target speaker. We ask why quantization hurts speech, where the damage lives, and whether it can be repaired without retraining. To find out, we run the first 4-bit weight-and-activation (W4A4) PTQ study of a TTS diffusion transformer at 1B and 3.5B. The timbre cost comes from both the weight and the activation quantization, but only the activation part has the timestep structure a precision schedule can exploit. We therefore introduce TTS-Q, which selects hard-to-quantize items from task-matched calibration candidates and applies a budget-balanced mixed-precision schedule that assigns higher precision to late-step feed-forward activations. TTS-Q recovers timbre best at both scales, at no cost to intelligibility. Separately, the deployed calibrated-W4A4 reference reduces peak memory on GPU, providing a practical reference for resource-constrained TTS deployment.
authors: Xiaoqin Feng, Yuqi Li, Weilun Feng, Yi-Cheng Lin, Kai Li, Xianglong Wang, Kuo Yang, Chuanguang Yang, Yingli Tian, Wei Li, Zhongwei Cheng, Lin Chen
bullets: Targets the memory and latency barriers of billion-parameter, multi-step zero-shot TTS models for on-device and real-time use.
A W4A4 study at 1B and 3.5B shows that quantization damages timbre through both weights and activations, while intelligibility remains relatively robust.
Only activation quantization has timestep-dependent structure that can be addressed with a precision schedule.
TTS-Q uses task-matched calibration candidates and budget-balanced mixed precision, assigning higher precision to late-step feed-forward activations.
It achieves the best timbre recovery at both model scales without reducing intelligibility; the calibrated-W4A4 reference also lowers peak GPU memory.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses efficient AI by proposing a post-training quantization method for large diffusion transformers, reducing model memory requirements and compute.
papers.title: TTS-Q: Perception-Guided Post-Training Quantization of Text-to-Speech Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: TTS-Q improves 4-bit post-training quantization of TTS diffusion transformers by preserving speaker timbre without sacrificing intelligibility.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) achieve remarkable performance in video synthesis, but their iterative denoising process suffers from high inference latency. To address this, caching has emerged as an effective acceleration strategy by capitalizing on inter-step redundancy during denoising. Existing dynamic caching methods typically estimate the error that cache reuse would introduce at each denoising step (step error) to guide cache decisions, whereas our concern is how much quality loss cache reuse would cause in the final generated video (terminal error). We show that step error does not directly correspond to terminal error and that latent information helps capture their relationship, thereby informing cache decisions. Moreover, existing threshold-based methods cannot provide precise speedup control, making it difficult to meet practical requirements for user-specified acceleration targets. To address these limitations, we introduce MORCA, a cache scheduling framework trained through offline-to-online reinforcement learning to make latent-aware reuse/recompute decisions under user-specified acceleration targets. Extensive experiments on different video generation models across multiple target acceleration ratios demonstrate that MORCA achieves better generation fidelity than state-of-the-art caching methods under comparable computational budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/x10ngyx/MORCA.
bullets: Existing caching methods optimize per-step error, which does not reliably reflect final video quality loss.
MORCA learns the relationship between latent information, cache decisions, and terminal generation error.
Its policy makes reuse-versus-recompute decisions under explicit acceleration targets, offering finer speedup control than threshold-based methods.
Experiments across multiple video generation models and acceleration ratios show better fidelity than prior caching methods at comparable computational budgets.
papers.selection_reason: RL-based cache reuse to accelerate video diffusion; fits efficient inference and video diffusion.
papers.title: MORCA: Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Cache Reuse in Video Diffusion Acceleration
papers.tldr: MORCA uses latent-aware offline-to-online reinforcement learning to adaptively schedule cache reuse in video diffusion, improving fidelity while meeting user-specified acceleration targets.

papers.abstract: Mid-prefill pruning can reduce the sequence processed by deeper transformer layers, but attention concentration alone does not certify that discarded context is dispensable. We formulate EntroPrefill as a Renyi-guided proposal mechanism coupled to explicit constraints on discarded attention mass. Sink-isolated, regularized head pooling respects grouped-query attention while exposing a quantitative trade-off between specialization and worst-head coverage. We derive a mixture-to-head deletion envelope, a computable upper bound on feasible token removal, and a finite-sample observer guarantee that remains valid when the pruning layer is selected adaptively. We then establish a conditional transformer perturbation bound with explicit sufficient Lipschitz constants and a first-token decision-margin corollary. A counterexample shows why shallow observations alone cannot imply an unconditional future-output guarantee. The systems analysis distinguishes query-head unions, physical page allocation, and KV-transfer payload, and gives an arithmetic break-even condition for pruning. This manuscript is theoretical in scope: it defines the procedure, its assumptions, and its formal limits, but does not report measured acceleration or task-accuracy preservation. Experiments are reserved for subsequent validation of the assumptions, approximation tightness, and end-to-end resource trade-offs.
bullets: Addresses the lack of formal guarantees that low-attention context tokens are safely dispensable.
Uses Rényi-guided proposals, sink-isolated regularized head pooling, and constraints on discarded attention mass.
Derives deletion bounds, adaptive finite-sample observer guarantees, and conditional transformer perturbation and decision-margin bounds.
Separates attention-head unions, physical page allocation, and KV-transfer payloads, yielding an arithmetic break-even condition for pruning.
Theoretical only: no measured speedup or task-accuracy results are reported, and guarantees depend on stated assumptions.
papers.selection_reason: Context pruning with guarantees for RAG; directly fits token pruning and KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: EntroPrefill: Renyi-Guided Context Pruning with Conditional Stability Guarantees for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.tldr: EntroPrefill provides a theoretically bounded method for pruning RAG context during prefill while clarifying when output stability and systems-level savings can—and cannot—be guaranteed.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive language models through bidirectional diffusion-based token generation. However, their growing model sizes and high inference costs make efficient deployment challenging: full-sequence denoising repeatedly invokes compute-intensive forward passes, while block-diffusion models additionally introduce a memory-intensive KV-cache. Low-bit weight-activation quantization is therefore attractive, yet existing dLLM post-training quantization methods rely on calibration data despite activation distributions shifting across masking states and denoising steps. We present SoloQ, a calibration-free quantization framework that maps weights and activations into a normalized rotated basis with a predictable marginal distribution, enabling data-independent quantization. SoloQ combines a structured K-RPBH rotation with a lightweight rescaling correction for calibration-free quantization. Its predictable post-rotation distribution supports both distribution-matched codebooks and hardware-native NVFP4. For block-diffusion models, SoloQ further applies commit-time KV-cache quantization to compress persistent states without perturbing the actively denoised block. Across full-sequence dLLMs (LLaDA and Dream) and block-diffusion dLLMs(Fast-dLLM v2 and Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion), SoloQ retains accuracy under 4-bit quantization and outperforms calibration-based baselines on knowledge- and reasoning-intensive benchmarks. With NVFP4, SoloQ reduces peak memory by up to 2.61X and accelerates end-to-end inference by up to 2.24X.
bullets: Addresses the high compute and memory costs of repeated denoising and KV-caches in diffusion language models.
Normalizes a rotated weight-activation basis using structured K-RPBH rotation and lightweight rescaling, avoiding calibration data.
Supports distribution-matched codebooks and hardware-native NVFP4 quantization.
Adds commit-time KV-cache quantization for block-diffusion models without perturbing the actively denoised block.
Across four dLLM families, retains accuracy under 4-bit quantization and achieves up to 2.61× lower peak memory and 2.24× faster inference with NVFP4.
papers.selection_reason: Calibration-free quantization for diffusion LLMs with KV-cache compression and inference memory/latency reduction, fitting efficient AI and KV-cache memory efficiency.
papers.title: SoloQ: Calibration-Free Quantization for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: SoloQ enables calibration-free 4-bit quantization for diffusion language models, preserving accuracy while substantially reducing memory use and inference time.

papers.abstract: Large language models rely on KV caching to reduce repeated prefill computation in long context and interactive applications. As lightweight adapters evolve, cached states reflect earlier versions, so stale reuse distorts current model outputs, while complete affected suffix recomputation restores fidelity at substantial cost. We seek minimal recomputation that recovers current adapter behavior. Existing systems track token, context, or stable adapter identity, but neither represent caches from earlier adapter versions nor distinguish update propagation from the recomputation required for behavioral recovery. To address these gaps, we introduce CacheReforge, which represents stale KV caches as layerwise mixed-version objects. It combines per-layer adapter anchors, calibrated sensitivity, accumulated drift, and executable restart boundaries to select direct reuse, bounded recomputation, or complete affected-suffix recovery. We distinguish dependency depth from the functional recomputation horizon and use cumulative tail influence to characterize when bounded recovery preserves current-model behavior. We evaluate CacheReforge on Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B with continual LoRA updates, including 16K HotpotQA and 2WikiMQA workloads. CacheReforge reduces mean KL divergence by 92.4% relative to stale reuse, while recomputing only 5.44% of layers and reducing cache-maintenance time by 93.2% relative to fresh full prefill. These results show that version-aware recovery preserves model fidelity and most KV caching gains.
bullets: Represents stale caches as layerwise mixed-version objects rather than assuming a single stable adapter version.
Uses adapter anchors, calibrated sensitivity, accumulated drift, and restart boundaries to choose reuse, bounded recomputation, or full suffix recovery.
Separates dependency depth from the functional recomputation horizon and uses cumulative tail influence to assess recovery fidelity.
On Qwen2.5 models with continual LoRA updates, it reduces mean KL divergence by 92.4% versus stale reuse while recomputing 5.44% of layers.
Reduces cache-maintenance time by 93.2% versus fresh full prefill, preserving most KV-caching benefits.
papers.selection_reason: Bounded recovery of stale KV caches under evolving adapters for efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: CacheReforge: Bounded Recovery for Stale KV Caches under Evolving Adapters
papers.tldr: CacheReforge restores current-model behavior from stale KV caches under evolving LoRA adapters while recomputing only a small portion of affected layers.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) process long contexts, including long documents and lengthy conversations, but face token-level memory usage that increases proportionally to input length. Although model optimization and lossy prompt compression are widely used, these methods still fail to solve the long-context recall problem beyond pretrained and size-constrained context windows. This paper proposes a long-context recall method that maintains near-constant GPU memory usage as context length increases, without additional training. The main idea is to reconstruct facts using parameter activations in the LLM's feed-forward layers, which store residual vectors representing facts from the source document. Utilizing residual vectors allows the LLM to deterministically reconstruct query relevant facts without referencing the original document, preserving high fidelity and reducing memory usage without fine-tuning weights. Experimental results show that the proposed method enables answering single-fact questions in two-million-token story contexts where previous methods fail.
bullets: Targets long-context recall while avoiding memory growth proportional to input length.
Stores source-document facts in residual vectors from the LLM’s feed-forward layers.
Reconstructs query-relevant facts deterministically without rereading the original context or fine-tuning weights.
Answers single-fact questions in two-million-token story contexts, where prior methods fail.
Scope: demonstrated for single-fact question answering in long story contexts.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free long-context recall via residual vectors with near-constant memory; fits long-context and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Residual Vector-based Reconstruction as Long-Context Recall Regardless of Context Window Size
papers.tldr: A training-free method uses feed-forward residual vectors to recall facts from contexts far beyond standard context-window limits with near-constant GPU memory.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a low-cost draft model to propose tokens that the full-size target model verifies in parallel. Parallel and semi-autoregressive (semi- AR) drafters improve drafting efficiency by proposing an entire block in a single forward pass, but training them raises a new difficulty: the draft distribution for a given position depends on where the decoding round starts, and where rounds start depends on how many tokens earlier rounds accepted. Existing training objectives typically rely on block-local surrogates that ignore this cross-round coupling, and therefore do not directly optimize the global decoding efficiency. In this work, we develop a theoretical framework for training and evaluating these drafters by representing speculative decoding as a Markov reward process. This formulation yields the Expected Decoding Rounds (EDR) objective, which weights local rejection costs by state occupancies and exactly equals the expected number of decoding rounds. Unlike prior surrogate objectives, EDR introduces no auxiliary hyperparameters. We then derive an exact temporal-difference gradient that supports unbiased stochastic optimization from target-model rollouts. The same framework also yields an exact offline evaluator for round counts, enabling paired drafter comparisons on shared target rollouts without running speculative decoding. Finetuning two state-of-the- art drafters, DSpark and DFly, with EDR consistently improves mean accepted length and outperforms existing training objectives across nine benchmarks spanning math reasoning, code generation, and chat.
bullets: Frames speculative decoding as a Markov reward process to capture cross-round dependencies.
Introduces Expected Decoding Rounds (EDR), an exact, hyperparameter-free objective for global decoding efficiency.
Derives an exact temporal-difference gradient for unbiased training from target-model rollouts.
Provides an exact offline evaluator for comparing drafters using shared target-model rollouts.
EDR fine-tuning improves mean accepted length and outperforms prior objectives for DSpark and DFly across nine math, code, and chat benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a theoretical framework and objective (EDR) for training speculative draft models to minimize decoding rounds, directly addressing inference efficiency.
papers.title: Training Parallel Speculative Draft Models by Directly Minimizing Expected Decoding Rounds
papers.tldr: EDR directly trains parallel speculative draft models to minimize expected decoding rounds, improving token acceptance and performance across diverse tasks.

papers.abstract: Instruction-tuning datasets for large language models (LLMs) are often large, redundant, and imbalanced, limiting efficient adaptation. Naive large-batch fine-tuning repeatedly includes overrepresented sample groups while weakly covering underrepresented but informative ones, especially under data parallelism (DP) across multiple GPUs. We propose CluSTER, a Cluster-aware balanced Sampling framework for Training Efficient data Reduction in DP instruction tuning. CluSTER curates a representative reduced dataset through gradient-space clustering and DP-aware balanced allocation, ensuring dual-level coverage across clusters and workers, while preserving the original data distribution by weighted update. As a result, CluSTER reduces redundant computation and improves training stability without compromising model quality. Across multiple instruction-tuning datasets, CluSTER reduces training time by up to 69.6% with almost no accuracy loss compared to prior sampling and data reduction methods. Code is available at https://github.com/kaist-dmlab/CluSTER.
bullets: Targets redundancy and imbalance in large instruction-tuning datasets under data parallelism.
Uses gradient-space clustering and DP-aware allocation to balance coverage across clusters and workers.
Preserves the original data distribution through weighted updates.
Reduces training time by up to 69.6% with almost no accuracy loss across multiple datasets.
Scope: focuses on efficient data reduction for data-parallel instruction tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses data parallelism and sampling efficiency in LLM fine-tuning, reducing redundant computation and improving training stability.
papers.title: Clustering-Based Balanced Sampling and Allocation with Data Parallelism for High-Performance Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: CluSTER accelerates distributed LLM instruction tuning by selecting representative, balanced data while preserving model quality.

papers.abstract: Natively training joint video-audio generation models at higher resolutions empowers them to learn richer visual details and sharper motion dynamics. However, full attention incurs quadratic cost and, as resolution increases, spreads attention over increasingly redundant tokens, diluting learning signals for informative content and disrupting pretrained priors. Existing sparse attention methods either target training-free acceleration or overlook the unique structure of joint video-audio data, where cross-modal interactions are inherently concentrated around sound-producing regions. To address this, we propose Prism, a dynamic sparse attention framework for natively training joint video-audio generation models at 2K. In particular, Prism organizes the token sequence into spatiotemporal macro-zones, enabling the attention structure to adapt to local content. For each zone, it estimates local information structure via video feature variance along the channel and feature norms from the audio-to-video cross-attention, jointly capturing how visual content varies directionally and how strongly audio influences each visual region. Based on these signals, Prism dynamically assigns a tailored block shape to each zone, applying finer partitioning along axes of rapid visual content variation and strong audio-visual coupling. This encourages tokens within each block to remain semantically coherent, allowing block-level features to capture both visual content and joint video-audio interaction patterns. Prism further adopts a hybrid block selection strategy to dynamically determine per-query sparsity. Experiments show that Prism achieves 2.5$\times$ training speedup compared to full attention, while surpassing it in generation quality.
bullets: Targets the quadratic cost and diluted learning signals of full attention at high-resolution joint video-audio generation.
Organizes tokens into spatiotemporal macro-zones and adapts attention blocks to local visual variation and audio-visual coupling.
Uses video feature variance and audio-to-video cross-attention norms to choose zone-specific block shapes.
Employs hybrid block selection for dynamically varying sparsity across queries.
Reports 2.5× training speedup over full attention while surpassing it in generation quality.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces dynamic sparse attention for efficient joint video-audio generation training, fitting efficient attention methods.
papers.title: Prism: Dynamic Sparse Attention for Native 2K Joint Video-Audio Generation Model Training
papers.tldr: Prism enables native 2K joint video-audio model training with dynamic, content- and audio-aware sparse attention, achieving faster training and higher generation quality than full attention.

papers.abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) evaluates candidate networks, but fully training enough architectures to rank an entire space is expensive. Zero-cost proxies score architectures at initialization, yet their ranking quality varies across search spaces. Learned predictors reduce evaluation cost but typically require fully trained labels or partial-training features for individual candidates. We introduce $\textbf{RiPPLE}$, $\underline{\textbf{R}}$anking v$\underline{\textbf{i}}$a $\underline{\textbf{P}}$refix-$\underline{\textbf{P}}$ropagated $\underline{\textbf{L}}$abel $\underline{\textbf{E}}$xtrapolation, which treats partial training as a source of labels for a small coverage set of anchors. RiPPLE trains these anchors to an early prefix, extrapolates their learning curves to surrogate labels, and propagates the labels over label-free architecture features. The early-training signal remains a label on the anchors rather than a per-candidate feature. Feature, readout, and encoding rules are selected without held-out accuracy and reused across search spaces. We evaluate the method on twelve benchmark cells from four search-space families and on the larger DARTS space. The results examine ranking quality, label efficiency, architecture selection, and the roles of readout, coverage, and propagation. RiPPLE provides a whole-space ranking from a fractional anchor-training budget, with comparisons interpreted under their respective evaluation and cost protocols.
bullets: Addresses the high cost of fully training many candidate architectures in neural architecture search.
Trains a small coverage set of anchors to an early prefix, extrapolates their learning curves, and uses the resulting surrogate labels.
Propagates labels over label-free architecture features; early-training signals are used only for anchors, not as per-candidate features.
Selects feature, readout, and encoding rules without held-out accuracy and reuses them across search spaces.
Evaluated across twelve benchmark cells from four search-space families and the larger DARTS space, examining ranking, label efficiency, selection, coverage, and propagation.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a method for cross-space performance prediction in Neural Architecture Search (NAS) using early training labels. This contributes to efficient model design and training, fitting the 'Efficient AI' taxonomy.
papers.title: RiPPLE: Cross-Space Performance Prediction from Early Training for Neural Architecture Search
papers.tldr: RiPPLE predicts rankings across an entire NAS search space by extrapolating early training results from a small set of anchor architectures and propagating them through architecture features.

papers.abstract: In this work, we show that a single Transformer block, applied recurrently, can match the accuracy of a full-depth vision encoder at comparable inference FLOPs without intermediate feature distillation. reViT restores depth-specific transformations by representing the FFN at each recurrent depth as a convex combination of a small shared expert bank. A continuous normalized-depth coordinate programs this mixture, defining a resampleable trajectory through FFN parameter space. We evaluate this design in two regimes: supervised ImageNet-1k training and distillation from a DINOv2 teacher. Across both regimes, controlled adaptations identify weight-space merging as the strongest tested MoE family at a matching one-FFN budget, ahead of the token-dispatch and output-mixture alternatives. Trained from scratch, reViT-B/16 attains DeiT III accuracy with about 70\% fewer stored parameters. An 8-experts model distilled using only the teacher's output features retains nearly all of its DINOv2 teacher's linear-probe accuracy and transfers across classification, segmentation, and depth prediction. Elastic-depth training allows one checkpoint (trained model) to operate at multiple tested depths by resampling the same normalized coordinate interval. For fixed-depth deployment, the recurrent block can be materialized as a conventional dense graph, removing online routing and merging without changing the one-FFN-per-depth compute but expanding deployment storage.
authors: Adrian Bulat, Yassine Ouali, Georgios Tzimiropoulos
bullets: Represents each recurrent-depth FFN as a convex combination of shared experts, guided by a normalized continuous-depth coordinate.
Weight-space merging is the strongest tested one-FFN-budget MoE design, outperforming token-dispatch and output-mixture alternatives in the reported comparisons.
From-scratch reViT-B/16 reaches DeiT III accuracy with about 70% fewer stored parameters.
An 8-expert model distilled from DINOv2 preserves nearly all teacher linear-probe accuracy and transfers to classification, segmentation, and depth prediction.
Elastic-depth training enables one checkpoint to run at multiple tested depths; fixed-depth materialization removes online routing but increases storage.
papers.selection_reason: Recurrent vision transformer with shared expert bank reduces stored parameters; fits efficient AI architecture research.
papers.title: One Block, Multiple Depths: Recurrent Vision Transformers with Depth-Programmed Experts
papers.tldr: reViT reuses one recurrent Transformer block while depth-programmed expert mixtures recover depth-specific behavior, matching full-depth vision encoders with far fewer stored parameters.

papers.abstract: Quantizing AdamW's optimizer states reduces persistent storage, but quantization errors propagate through the moment recurrences and perturb subsequent adaptive updates. We redesign 4-bit optimizer-state quantization for AdamW from the perspective of \emph{rounding space}: the coordinate in which a quantizer chooses between adjacent reconstruction levels. For the second moment, a local analysis of the quantization cell adjacent to zero shows that small mean state error need not imply small mean preconditioner error at the next step. A one-dimensional quadratic construction further shows qualitatively different optimization dynamics under state-space and preconditioner-space rounding. These results motivate Zero-Inclusive Preconditioner-space Stochastic Rounding (\textbf{ZIP-SR}), which retains zero in the second-moment codebook and computes stochastic-rounding probabilities in preconditioner space. As a complementary route, Zero-Excluding EDEN calibration (\textbf{ZE-EDEN}) uses a zero-excluding second-moment codebook and rescales the quantized second-moment block to mitigate the preconditioner distortion caused by the positive quantization floor. Both configurations use 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) for the first moment, with targeted stochastic rounding of the LM-head first moment during the final 10\% of training. Across GPT- and Llama-style pretraining experiments ranging from \textbf{130M} to \textbf{2.7B} parameters, both methods reduce TorchAO 4-bit AdamW's mean validation-loss gap to 32-bit AdamW at every evaluated model size, with the largest reported gap reduction reaching \textbf{70\%}. In full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, both recipes achieve lower validation loss than TorchAO while remaining close to 32-bit AdamW on downstream tasks.
authors: Hanyang Li, Shao Tang, Daniel Thomas Braithwaite, Gregory Dexter, Leonardo Neves, Aman Gupta, Hiroto Udagawa, Abhishek Shivanna, Daniel Silva, Rohan Ramanath
bullets: Optimizer-state quantization errors propagate through AdamW’s moment recurrences and can distort adaptive preconditioners even when state error appears small.
The paper analyzes this mismatch and shows qualitatively different optimization dynamics for state-space versus preconditioner-space rounding.
ZIP-SR keeps zero in the second-moment codebook and computes stochastic-rounding probabilities in preconditioner space.
ZE-EDEN instead uses a zero-excluding second-moment codebook with block rescaling to reduce distortion from its positive quantization floor.
Across 130M–2.7B-parameter GPT- and Llama-style models, both methods reduce the validation-loss gap to 32-bit AdamW relative to TorchAO 4-bit AdamW; the largest reported reduction is 70%.
papers.selection_reason: Redesigns 4-bit optimizer-state quantization to reduce memory; fits memory-efficiency goals of Efficient AI.
papers.title: Rounding in Preconditioner Space: Redesigning 4-bit AdamW Optimizer-State Quantization
papers.tldr: ZIP-SR and ZE-EDEN redesign 4-bit AdamW state quantization around preconditioner-space rounding, reducing validation-loss degradation versus standard 4-bit AdamW across pretraining and fine-tuning experiments.

papers.abstract: While caching key-value (KV) states accelerates Large Language Model (LLM) decoding, this cache can dominate memory usage at long context lengths. One solution is to compress this memory by exploiting inter-layer cache similarities. However, most existing techniques necessitate architectural changes to LLMs and incur substantial overhead. In this work, we propose a symmetry-aware value cache merging strategy that reduces cache memory while avoiding both harmful performance degradation and architectural overhead during decoding. Furthermore, we show that this approach can be exploited alongside existing cache compression techniques, composing with high-ratio quantization or key cache pruning to reach compression ratios that neither method reaches alone, with minimal additional cost. Ultimately, our findings reveal a major source of underutilized capacity in the value cache, offering a simple yet highly effective direction for scaling context windows under memory constraints.
authors: Neha Verma, Sungwon Kim, Kenton Murray, Kevin Duh
bullets: Addresses KV-cache memory growth at long context lengths, especially underused capacity in value caches.
Uses a symmetry-aware cross-layer value-cache merging strategy during decoding.
Designed to avoid harmful performance degradation and substantial architectural modifications.
Composes with high-ratio quantization and key-cache pruning for additional compression.
Supports scaling context windows under memory constraints with minimal extra cost.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes symmetry-aware cross-layer value cache compression to reduce memory usage in LLMs, directly targeting KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: VFold: Symmetry-Aware Cross-Layer Value Cache Compression
papers.tldr: VFold compresses LLM value caches by merging symmetry-aware representations across layers, reducing memory use without architectural changes or major decoding overhead.

papers.abstract: The memory-bound nature of the decoding stage of large language model (LLM) inference incurs significant latency. Layer-wise training-free network pruning approaches guided by the Hessian have been a prominent solution to this problem, as pruning reduces the number of nonzero parameters read from memory during decoding. Nevertheless, typical methods in this line compute the Hessian using pre-collected natural sequences, whereas the model is fed self-generated tokens during decoding, creating a distribution shift between the two sequences. The Hessian calculated on the natural sequence is different from that calculated on the generated sequence. We observe that this discrepancy causes the activation distribution during generation to deviate from that used for pruning, further hurting the pruned model performance. Moreover, most existing LLM pruning methods that bring actual speedup primarily target the sparse matrix-matrix (SpMM) multiplication, providing limited support for the sparse matrix-vector (SpMV) operations, which dominate decoding. To solve these problems, we introduce SparseDecoding, a principled decoding-aware pruning framework tailored for accurate and efficient LLM decoding. Specifically, at the algorithmic axis, SparseDecoding constructs calibration matrices from layer-wise activations collected during the dense-model autoregressive generation, excluding prefill, thereby aligning the pruning objective with the decoding activations. At the system axis, we develop an optimized N:M sparse matrix-vector kernel with bitmask indexing and fixed-step traversal. Substantial empirical results on representative LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-14B / 32B) demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms standard fixed-text calibration on the long-form generation benchmarks while achieving up to 1.48x end-to-end wall-clock decoding speedup on A100 GPUs.
authors: Qitong Wang, Xinwei Niu, Mingluo Su, Shanwei Zhao, Shiai Zhu, Huan Wang
bullets: Addresses distribution shift between natural-text calibration and autoregressive decoding, which can degrade pruned-model quality.
Collects layer-wise activations during dense-model generation, excluding the prefill stage, to make pruning decoding-aware.
Introduces an optimized N:M sparse matrix-vector kernel using bitmask indexing and fixed-step traversal.
Outperforms standard fixed-text calibration on long-form generation benchmarks across several representative LLMs.
Achieves up to 1.48× end-to-end decoding speedup on A100 GPUs.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces decoding-aware pruning for LLM inference to improve efficiency and accuracy.
papers.title: SparseDecoding: Decoding-Aware Pruning for Accurate and Efficient LLM Inference
papers.tldr: SparseDecoding improves LLM decoding accuracy and efficiency by calibrating pruning on generated-token activations and accelerating sparse matrix-vector operations.

papers.abstract: Most image generation models rely on uniform tokenization, allocating the exact same computational budget to equally-sized image patches. This static paradigm cannot adapt to different resource constraints at inference time, and yields suboptimal quality-cost tradeoff by devoting the same effort to both plain backgrounds and intricate details. We propose BudgetPix, an adaptive tokenization framework that dynamically allocates compute based on visual complexity and spatial layout, enabling flexible computational budgeting at inference time. BudgetPix comprises three key components: (1) an adaptive encoder that maps a fixed-size image to a variable-length token sequence using an entropy-guided quadtree alongside a multi-scale patch embedder; (2) a scale-aware decoder reconstructs fixed-resolution images from multi-scale token sets; and (3) a flexible training and sampling schedule that enables pixel-space denoisers to operate across variable token counts. BudgetPix seamlessly integrates with existing pixel-space diffusion architectures, enabling a single checkpoint to be operated at a wide range of compute budgets. Evaluated on text-to-image generation, BudgetPix matches the fidelity of MiniT2I-L at $512^2$ and PixelDiT at $1024^2$ using just 25% of the original compute budget. In class-conditional generation using a MeanFlow backbone, BudgetPix requires merely 60% of the full compute budget to produce images with near-zero quality degradation, observing a marginal 0.8-point increase in FID. Comprehensive assessments by human and VLM judges confirm that BudgetPix establishes a significantly improved quality-efficiency tradeoff over prior budget-adaptive baselines. More details are available at our project page: https://karaozgur.com/BudgetPix
authors: Ozgur Kara, Yujia Chen, Daniel Watson, David Forsyth, James Matthew Rehg, Wen-Sheng Chu, Du Tran
bullets: Uniform patch tokenization wastes compute on simple regions and cannot adapt to inference-time resource constraints.
An entropy-guided quadtree and multi-scale patch embedder produce variable-length token sequences based on visual complexity.
A scale-aware decoder and flexible training/sampling schedule support variable token counts in existing pixel-space diffusion models.
It matches reported baselines at 512² and 1024² using 25% of their compute budget, and achieves near-unchanged class-conditional quality at 60% compute, with a 0.8-point FID increase.
Human and VLM evaluations report better quality–efficiency tradeoffs than prior budget-adaptive methods.
papers.selection_reason: Compute-adaptive tokenization for pixel-space diffusion, dynamically selecting tokens by complexity, fitting token-level efficiency methods.
papers.title: BudgetPix: Compute-Adaptive Tokenization for Pixel-Space Image Diffusion
papers.tldr: BudgetPix adaptively allocates pixel-space diffusion compute according to image complexity, allowing one model to operate across flexible inference budgets with improved quality–efficiency tradeoffs.

papers.abstract: Understanding large language model (LLM) reasoning requires looking beyond behavioral performance to examine how reasoning ability is reflected in internal organization. Inspired by neuroscience findings linking higher intelligence to stronger small-world organization in functional brain networks, we investigate small-world connectivity as a structural signature of LLM reasoning. We construct functional graphs from attention-head activation similarities and find that a higher small-world index (SWI), capturing local clustering and short global paths, consistently correlates with better fluid reasoning performance across models and training checkpoints. Since local clustering is central to small-world organization, we further examine how heads important for model performance connect within and across communities. We find that these heads tend to have a larger share of connection weight within their own communities (high core scores) and a more concentrated weight distribution across communities (low bridge scores). These observations motivate the hypothesis that high core and low bridge scores serve as structural indicators of head importance for reasoning capability. We validate this hypothesis through pruning, introducing Small-World Allocation (SWA), a hierarchical sparsity allocation method guided by these scores. Across six LLMs, SWA better preserves small-world organization and model performance than competing allocation strategies, reducing WikiText perplexity by up to 20%. Together, these findings identify small-world functional connectivity as a measurable signature of LLM reasoning performance, offering a structural perspective that complements behavioral evaluation.
authors: Zheng Huang, Sansheng Cao, Enpei Zhang, Weikang Qiu, Elynn Chen, Xiang Zhang, Yaoqing Yang, Rex Ying, Dawei Zhou, Yujun Yan
bullets: Functional graphs built from attention-head activation similarities show that higher small-world index correlates with stronger fluid reasoning across models and checkpoints.
Reasoning-important heads tend to connect strongly within their own communities, yielding high core scores and low bridge scores.
These structural signals motivate Small-World Allocation (SWA), a hierarchical sparsity-allocation method for pruning.
Across six LLMs, SWA better preserves small-world structure and model performance than competing allocation strategies, reducing WikiText perplexity by up to 20%.
The work offers a structural complement to behavioral evaluation of reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Links LLM small-world connectivity to reasoning and uses it for structured pruning, relevant to both LLM analysis and efficient AI.
papers.title: Looking Inside LLMs: Small-World Connectivity as a Signature of Reasoning Performance
papers.tldr: Small-world organization in attention-head connectivity consistently tracks LLM reasoning ability and can guide pruning to preserve performance.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have made remarkable progress in bridging vision and language, facilitating various perception tasks essential for human-machine interaction, robotics, and autonomous driving. However, existing MLLM-based perception methods predominantly rely on text-based coordinate representation, which suffers from excessive token overhead, or fixed-range quantization, which suffers from range and precision constraints, especially for 3D domains with unbounded spatial range and high localization accuracy requirements. To address these challenges, we propose a dynamic vector decoding method named DVD, which unifies the representation of 2D and 3D perception tasks. Specifically, we first transform diverse perceptual representation (i.e., 2D bounding boxes, 2D masks, and 3D bounding boxes) into 1D vector sequences, which are then mapped to compact discrete tokens in the high-dimensional space. Then, a lightweight de-tokenizer enables seamless integration with MLLMs by decoding output tokens back to original 2D and 3D perceptual representations. Extensive experiments on 2D and 3D perception benchmarks including RefCOCO series, SUN-RGBD, KITTI, Hypersim, nuScenes demonstrate that DVD achieves superior performance in 2D and 3D tasks and reduces significantly the token overhead and inference latency. DVD provides an efficient and general framework for integrating perception capabilities into MLLMs, overcoming the inherent limitations of existing methods.
authors: Jinghua Hou, Zhe Liu, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of text-based coordinates and the range/precision limits of fixed quantization, particularly for unbounded 3D scenes.
Converts 2D boxes, 2D masks, and 3D boxes into 1D vector sequences mapped to compact discrete tokens.
Uses a lightweight de-tokenizer to reconstruct the original 2D or 3D representations from MLLM outputs.
Evaluated on RefCOCO, SUN-RGBD, KITTI, Hypersim, and nuScenes, with reported strong performance across 2D and 3D perception tasks.
The abstract reports reduced token overhead and inference latency, while the method unifies representation across perception tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses efficiency in MLLMs for perception tasks using dynamic vector decoding to reduce token overhead, relevant to both Multimodal Foundation Models and Efficient AI.
papers.title: DVD: Dynamic Vector Decoding for Efficient MLLM-based Perception
papers.tldr: DVD efficiently represents 2D and 3D perceptual outputs as compact dynamic vector tokens, reducing token overhead and inference latency in MLLM-based perception.

papers.abstract: Topological Deep Learning extends graph-based learning to higher-order domains, such as hypergraphs, cellular, and simplicial complexes. These domains are typically constructed from patterns in an input graph through a process of graph lifting. Full-domain training constructs and stores the complete lifted representation before model execution. On large and dense datasets like Reddit (233k nodes and 57.3M edges), this global materialization becomes a severe computational bottleneck, often rendering training infeasible. To address this limitation, we introduce Cluster-TNN, a domain-agnostic framework that avoids this bottleneck by lifting locally instead. After partitioning the input graph during preprocessing, at runtime Cluster-TNN dynamically samples groups of node clusters, reconstructs their induced subgraphs to form mini-batches, and applies the chosen lifting within each mini-batch. Retaining all edges among sampled nodes preserves the connectivity needed to construct higher-order structures across clusters, producing topological mini-batches that existing Topological Neural Networks can process directly. Across 21 matched comparisons with full-graph execution, Cluster-TNN reduces peak GPU memory in every configuration, by 83.2% on average while maintaining competitive predictive performance. Notably, such a reduction enables, to our knowledge, the first training of multiple different higher-order Topological Neural Networks on large datasets such as Reddit and OGBN Products. These results establish Cluster-TNN as a general strategy for scaling Topological Deep Learning beyond the limitations of global domain construction.
authors: David Leko, Luka Beni\'c, Guillermo Bern\'ardez, Nina Miolane, Olga Fink, Lev Telyatnikov
bullets: Global lifting of graphs into hypergraphs, cellular complexes, or simplicial complexes can make training prohibitively expensive on large, dense datasets.
The method partitions the input graph, samples groups of node clusters, reconstructs their induced subgraphs, and applies lifting separately within each mini-batch.
Keeping all edges among sampled nodes preserves connectivity needed to build higher-order structures across clusters.
Across 21 matched comparisons, Cluster-TNN reduced peak GPU memory in every configuration by 83.2% on average while retaining competitive predictive performance.
The approach enabled training multiple higher-order Topological Neural Networks on large datasets including Reddit and OGBN Products.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses scalability in topological deep learning via local lifting, fitting Efficient AI.
papers.title: Batch Before You Lift: Scalable Topological Deep Learning on Large Graphs
papers.tldr: Cluster-TNN makes higher-order topological learning on large graphs feasible by constructing lifted domains locally in sampled cluster mini-batches instead of materializing the full domain.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) routing distributes inference work across different models, advancing the cost-quality Pareto frontier of LLM serving. While coarse-grained routing at the session or query level has been widely adopted in production systems, recent algorithmic work shows that fine-grained token-level routing can yield substantial efficiency and quality gains. However, efficiently serving token-level routed inference poses significant challenges to existing systems. Built on single-LLM assumptions, current systems suffer from severe step desynchronization and frequent batch admission delays under token-level routing, and they also impose high implementation complexity on developers. To address these challenges, we design TokenRouter, an efficient and developer-friendly serving system for token-level routed LLM inference. TokenRouter follows the principle of request-centric programming, model-centric execution: developers describe routing logic from the perspective of a single request, while the runtime launches a subserver for each LLM and dispatches requests asynchronously. Each subserver employs a delayed-batching scheduler, whose optimal hyperparameters are derived from a mathematical throughput model of the system. Across diverse routing algorithms, workloads, and model pairs, TokenRouter achieves 2.01-64.15x higher decoding throughput than existing systems, substantially advancing the serving efficiency of token-level LLM routing. Our code is available at https://github.com/thu-nics/TokenRouter.
authors: Tianyu Fu, Tengxuan Liu, Ruoxi Wang, Yixin Dong, Yi Ge, Yichen You, Yu Wang
bullets: Token-level routing can improve the cost-quality tradeoff but causes desynchronization and batch-admission delays in existing single-LLM serving systems.
Developers specify routing logic per request, while TokenRouter runs a separate subserver for each model and dispatches requests asynchronously.
