papers.tldr: PAGE makes KV-cache eviction safer by deciding per input whether compression is appropriate, sharply reducing catastrophic accuracy failures without retraining the evictor.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models faces the problem of unstable verification cost caused by input-dependent expert loading. To study the physics of this process, we formulate speculation-budget selection as an offline Stochastic Shortest Path (SSP) problem over reference sequences and build a diagnostic Oracle that uses counterfactual simulation to account for MoE verification cost. A detailed analysis of the Oracle's decisions on the Qwen3-Coder and EAGLE-3 pairing, in the space of marginal deltas (Delta Space), shows that rejected candidates form a strict linear boundary. This result demonstrates that a complex global optimization is locally governed by a necessary condition balancing marginal cost against expected progress ($\frac{\Delta \mathbb{E}[Cost]}{\Delta \mathbb{E}[a]}$), providing a rigorous mathematical reference point for designing future adaptive online heuristics.
bullets: MoE speculative decoding has unstable verification costs because expert loading depends on the input.
The authors formulate speculation-budget selection as an offline Stochastic Shortest Path problem over reference sequences.
A counterfactual Oracle simulates verification costs to diagnose optimal budget decisions.
For the Qwen3-Coder/EAGLE-3 pairing, rejected candidates follow a strict linear boundary in marginal-delta space.
The analysis provides a mathematical reference for future adaptive online heuristics; its scope is tied to the studied pairing and offline Oracle setting.
papers.selection_reason: Formal analysis of speculative decoding budgets in MoE, a latency-reducing inference technique transferable to efficient AI.
papers.title: The Limits of Speculation: Bounding Speculative Decoding in Mixture-of-Experts
papers.tldr: Speculative decoding in MoE models can be bounded by a local marginal cost–progress condition despite input-dependent expert-loading costs.

papers.abstract: Structured pruning is a promising approach for reducing the substantial inference costs of Large Language Models (LLMs) while maintaining hardware efficiency. Many existing methods assess the importance of prunable units (e.g., channels or heads) in isolation, implicitly assuming that pruning errors are additive. This independence assumption is often invalidated by the non-orthogonality of model weights and strong correlations between unit activations, potentially leading to performance degradation. To address this, we propose a Correlation-Aware Structured Pruning method. We formulate the pruning objective as a cardinality-constrained binary quadratic program that explicitly models cross-unit dependencies in the reconstruction error. Since this binary quadratic program is NP-hard and difficult to solve exactly, we develop a greedy interaction algorithm based on dependency-aware marginal costs to optimize unit selection. Furthermore, we incorporate a gradient-based strategy to achieve adaptive layer-wise sparsity allocation across the entire model. Extensive experiments on mainstream LLMs demonstrate that incorporating correlation information yields competitive accuracy-efficiency trade-offs compared to representative structured pruning baselines.
authors: Sicheng Xu, Hao Shi, Wei Zhang, Haoran Pang, Zhenyu Ming, Hao Wu, Zhongyi Huang, Xin Yao, Gong Zhang
bullets: Existing pruning methods often evaluate channels or heads independently, overlooking correlated activations and non-orthogonal weights.
The method formulates pruning as a cardinality-constrained binary quadratic program that captures cross-unit reconstruction-error dependencies.
A greedy interaction algorithm approximates the NP-hard optimization using dependency-aware marginal costs.
Gradient-based adaptive layer-wise sparsity allocation distributes pruning across the model.
Experiments on mainstream LLMs show competitive accuracy–efficiency trade-offs against structured-pruning baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Presents correlation-aware structured pruning for LLM inference efficiency, matching the efficient-AI research area.
papers.title: Correlation-Aware Structured Pruning for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: A correlation-aware structured pruning method models interactions between LLM units to improve accuracy–efficiency trade-offs while reducing inference cost.

papers.abstract: Accuracy of Low-bit quantization of linear layers is often dominated by a small number of outliers. Although existing methods, such as smoothing, rotation, or residual-based approaches, may mitigate this problem, they often introduce new accuracy bottlenecks to weights. Besides, most of these techniques are implemented as online approaches, which can result in heavy execution overheads. To address the afore-mentioned issues, We propose PRQuant (Permutation Residual Quantization), a training-free and low-overhead framework that combines channel reorganization with static weight-side residual compensation. After AWQ-style scaling, PRQuant identifies the input channels that contribute most to weight quantization error, permutes them into contiguous tail blocks, and constructs their residual weight sub-tensors offline. During inference, this contiguous structure enables the activation side to use tail blocks seamlessly without the expensive online gathering operation, and turns scattered residual compensation into a regular tail-augmented GEMM, substantially reducing latency. Experiments demonstrate that PRQuant effectively reduces down-projection reconstruction error. Ablation studies confirm that smoothing and residual compensation are the primary drivers of numerical improvement, while permutation provides a consistent marginal numerical benefit and, more importantly, enables a hardware-friendly contiguous layout that eliminates dynamic gathering overhead. Overall, PRQuant outperforms default MXFP4 and the evaluated PTQ baselines in average accuracy across five downstream benchmarks, improving over MXFP4 by 1.24 and 0.55 on Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, respectively.
authors: Peiran Wang, Anqi Wang, Jiaying Zhao, Huiwen Yang, Zhenyu Ming, Rongqian Wang, Yiwu Yao, Kun Tian, Xin Yao, Gong Zhang, Fan Yang, Zhongyi Huang
bullets: Targets quantization errors caused by outlier-sensitive channels in linear layers.
Applies AWQ-style scaling, identifies high-error input channels, and permutes them into contiguous tail blocks.
Builds residual weight sub-tensors offline, enabling regular tail-augmented GEMM instead of costly online gathering.
Ablations find smoothing and residual compensation drive numerical gains, while permutation mainly improves hardware efficiency.
Outperforms default MXFP4 and evaluated PTQ baselines across five downstream benchmarks; gains over MXFP4 are reported on two Qwen3 models.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free permutation residual quantization for low-overhead LLM inference.
papers.title: PRQuant: Permutation Residual Quantization for Low-Overhead Inference
papers.tldr: PRQuant is a training-free quantization framework that uses channel permutation and offline residual compensation to improve low-bit accuracy while reducing inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by letting a cheap drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Recent block drafters make drafting nearly free: a single backbone pass emits an entire block of draft tokens. Draft trees promise a further gain -- several alternative continuations verified in one target forward -- but existing constructions rank candidates by per-position marginals that ignore which parent a candidate extends, so on semi-autoregressive drafters wider trees mostly add mis-ranked nodes; and a tree of fixed size ignores how much speculation each decoding round, and each serving load, can support. We introduce TreeSpark, which reads a parent-conditioned distribution from the drafter's existing Markov head at negligible cost, calibrates it into an edge-acceptance estimate, and lets path survival govern everything else: best-first expansion, per-round stopping, and a load-adaptive serving policy. Sampling siblings without replacement, with matching residuals in recursive rejection, keeps decoding lossless at any temperature. Adaptive trees improve on matched fixed budgets at every temperature; against a tuned chain on the same drafter, TreeSpark accepts 15-25% more draft tokens per round and decodes 8-14% faster in single-request wall-clock, and under rising load it gracefully shrinks the tree back to the chain. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/PopSoda2002/TreeSpark
authors: Huapeng Zhou, Huayu Wang, Xinyu Wang
bullets: Addresses mis-ranked tree nodes caused by per-position marginals and fixed-size trees that ignore round capacity and serving load.
Uses the drafter’s existing Markov head to estimate edge acceptance at negligible cost.
Builds trees via best-first, path-survival-guided expansion and stops each round adaptively.
Samples siblings without replacement with recursive residual matching, preserving losslessness at any temperature.
Accepts 15–25% more draft tokens per round and decodes 8–14% faster than a tuned chain; shrinks toward a chain as load rises.
papers.selection_reason: Load-adaptive draft trees reduce LLM inference latency, a meaningful efficiency contribution though not matching the listed subtopics.
papers.title: TreeSpark: Calibrated, Load-Adaptive Draft Trees for Semi-Autoregressive Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: TreeSpark uses calibrated parent-aware draft trees with load-adaptive sizing to accelerate lossless speculative decoding.

papers.abstract: AI is beginning to make substantive contributions to LLM inference optimization. Existing AI optimizations are predominantly profiling-based. Profiling-bound feedback confines the search to the capabilities and performance of an existing software stack, preventing a fundamentally better architecture of LLM inference systems from being identified. To enable the AI-driven LLM inference system architecting loop, we argue that a general workload representation, a verifiable mutation space, and an implementation-independent evaluator are required. We present the RoofLang domain-specific language (DSL) that provides these features. In our evaluation, RoofLang reveals that DeepSeek V4-series models could achieve 3.5-39.5$\times$ higher peak decode throughput than other representative models. This gap is disproportionate to their total parameter counts and arises largely from compact KV-cache designs that support larger batches and reduce memory traffic. A persistent optimizer agent further discovered several new architectures that improved both throughput and interactivity of DeepSeek V4 Pro on NVIDIA B300 by 6.23-50.1%.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of profiling-based AI optimization, which cannot search beyond existing inference architectures.
Introduces a DSL with general workload representation, verifiable mutations, and an implementation-independent evaluator.
Finds that DeepSeek V4-series models could achieve 3.5–39.5× higher peak decode throughput than representative models, largely through compact KV-cache designs.
A persistent optimizer agent discovered architectures improving DeepSeek V4 Pro throughput and interactivity on NVIDIA B300 by 6.23–50.1%.
Scope: results are reported for the evaluated DeepSeek models and NVIDIA B300 platform.
papers.selection_reason: Domain-specific language and optimizer for LLM inference architecture, emphasizing KV-cache design and memory-traffic efficiency.
papers.title: RoofLang: Enabling AI-Driven Architecting of LLM Inference Systems
papers.tldr: RoofLang enables AI to explore and evaluate new LLM inference architectures beyond profiling existing software stacks, uncovering substantial throughput gains and novel optimizations.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc sparse attention accelerates long-context prefill by routing each query to a small set of token-level interactions. Hard selection, however, assigns zero probability to every omitted chunk: a routing miss cannot be recovered, and a fixed expansion budget spends the same work on easy and ambiguous queries. We introduce Coarse-to-fine Error-aware Dynamic Attention Routing (CEDAR), a coarse-to-fine method that keeps the language model frozen while preserving global coverage. Each semantic chunk contributes a cheap key--value summary to a residual attention path; chunks with high estimated approximation error are then expanded to exact token attention. Exact and summarized contributions are combined in a single softmax normalization, so refinement replaces, rather than duplicates, coarse evidence. We derive an output-error bound governed by within-chunk key/value dispersion and use it to allocate a variable refinement budget. A controlled clustered-attention study shows that residual summaries reduce reconstruction error by more than 98% relative to hard dropping at equal exact-chunk budgets. Experiments on long-context benchmarks demonstrate that CEDAR recovers most of the quality lost by hard sparse routing while maintaining approximately $3\times$ kernel speedup at 128K context.
bullets: Targets routing misses and wasteful fixed budgets in post-hoc sparse attention.
Keeps the language model frozen and summarizes every semantic chunk for global coverage.
Uses an error bound based on within-chunk key/value dispersion to dynamically refine ambiguous chunks.
Combines exact and summarized evidence under one softmax, so refinement replaces rather than duplicates coarse attention.
In controlled and benchmark studies, reduces reconstruction error by over 98% versus hard dropping and recovers most lost quality.
papers.selection_reason: Error-bounded sparse attention routing with residual summaries for efficient long-context prefill; fits efficient attention and long-context methods.
papers.title: CEDAR: Error-Bounded Residual Routing for Efficient Long-Context Attention
papers.tldr: CEDAR improves efficient long-context attention by replacing hard token dropping with error-aware coarse summaries and adaptive exact refinement, recovering most lost quality while retaining about 3× speedup at 128K context.
